column36: Effectiveness of a consumer-targeted pharmacist-led educational intervention to reduce inappropriate prescriptions
column37: As Canadians age, the probability of suffering from different medical conditions and having to take many medications increases. As the number of medications increases, so too does the risk of side effects. Some medications pose greater risks than others. For example, some medications can cause a person to fall, have trouble with their memory, or lead to hospital emergency room visits for low blood sugar. When medications are prescribed for which safer alternatives exist, it is called "inappropriate prescribing". National specialist consensus panels regularly publish lists of inappropriate drugs that pose an elevated risk of adverse effects, yet unfortunately inappropriate prescribing persists. As many as 1 in 4 Canadian seniors on public drug programs consume one or more inappropriate medications. Our project proposes a novel intervention whereby pharmacists provide educational materials to both seniors and their primary care providers on the risks of taking inappropriate prescriptions. Recommendations to change inappropriate prescriptions to safer alternatives are provided. Forty-six community pharmacies in Quebec will help us recruit 400 of clients to this project. We hope to show that empowered patients can play a role in helping health professionals reduce inappropriate prescriptions and increase medication safety in the elderly.

column36: Muscle-bone interactions in Canadians: a national, population-based study
column37: Osteoporosis is a common bone disorder that can affect people of any age, even children. The role of muscle as a determinant of bone health is increasingly recognized, but factors influencing muscle-bone interactions across the lifespan have not been investigated in detail. Overall Objective: In this study we will elucidate determinants of muscle-bone interactions in Canadians from 6 to 79 years of age. Study Design: The Canadian Health Measures Survey (CHMS) is a fully operational program for determining health indicators the Canadian population that is led by Statistics Canada. Statistics Canada has agreed to our proposal to collect data on musculoskeletal health in a population-based sample of 10,000 Canadians from 6 to 79 years of age. Participants will undergo peripheral quantitative computed tomography to assess muscle and bone characteristics at the lower leg, muscle function tests, as well as biomarkers of bone metabolism. The aims are (1) to develop reference data for key musculoskeletal parameters; (2) to assess the muscle-bone relationship in healthy subjects and (3) to assess the effect of common obesity on the muscle-bone relationship. Statistics Canada has agreed to contribute $5,700,000 to this project. Clinical Importance: These studies will improve tools to study muscle-bone interactions and identify factors that can be targeted for interventions. As CHMS makes raw data of all studies available to the Canadian scientific community, the present project establishes a research platform that can be accessed by multiple investigators in Canada.

column36: Multiple Sclerosis Research
column37: The Blood-Brain Barrier (BBB) restricts the passage of noxious molecules and cells from the blood to the brain. In diseases like Multiple Sclerosis (MS), the BBB fails to prevent entry of aggressive white blood cells (leukocytes) into the brain. These leukocytes are thought to induce damage of brain cells. Dr Prat's work focuses on both the intact and damaged BBB and its role on the development of inflammatory diseases directed to the brain. Dr Prat's research goals are to understand the molecular mechanisms involved in the formation of a tight and impermeable BBB and to study the dysregulation of these mechanisms in MS. As MS is the most prevalent neurological disorder of young adults in Canada and the first cause of permanent handicap, Dr Prat's research can have a significant impact on the health status of thousands of young Canadians.

column36: HIV/AIDS and Urban Population Health
column37: Inner city populations, particularly injection drug users, are at extremely high risk of many harms including HIV, hepatitis C and overdose death. Martin Schechter is studying these vulnerabilities, with a particular focus on young Aboriginal drug users, in order to help design prevention programs. He is also studying young people in the aftermath of the twenty-year conflict in Northern Uganda to help stop the spread of HIV there. To improve the treatment of addiction, he is conducting innovative clinical trials that involve medically-prescribed heroin and hydromorphone in order to benefit people with the most severe cases of heroin addiction.

column36: Molecular Microbiology
column37: The overall goal of Dr. Chris Whitfields Tier 1 CRC research program is to understand the processes involved in the assembly of complex polymers on the surfaces of bacterial cells. column36: The Hippo pathway as a regulator of ovarian follicle development
column37: Oocytes develop and mature in the ovary within structures called follicles. Follicles are recruited from a reserve and grow under the influence of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) produced by the pituitary gland. Once terminally developed, the follicle ruptures to release the (now mature) oocyte at the moment of ovulation. Ovulation itself is triggered by a second pituitary hormone, luteinizing hormone (LH), which also causes the reorganization of the ovulated follicle into a new glandular tissue termed the corpus luteum, which secretes the large amounts of progesterone necessary for the establishment and maintenance of pregnancy. Whereas we have long known FSH and LH to be major players in ovarian follicle development, how exactly they exert their effects remains incompletely understood. Ourselves and others have recently found that a signaling pathway called Hippo is inactivated during FSH-mediated follicle growth, but is rapidly activated during LH-mediate ovulation/luteinization, suggesting that FSH and LH exert their effects, at least in part, via Hippo signaling. This proposal will seek to confirm these preliminary results, in part by studying mice that lack the Hippo pathway genes Yap, Taz, Lats1 and Lats2, in which we expect defects in FSH- and LH-mediated ovarian processes. We will also study the mechanisms whereby Hippo transmits biological signals, and identify the genes that it regulates. Together, our studies will uncover new information regarding how FSH and LH act, and about the biological roles of Hippo signaling in the ovary. This research should also provide new insight into fertility disorders such as ovulatory failure and luteal insufficiency.

column36: Inherited susceptibility to cancer: from gene discovery to mechanisms to clinical applications
column37: Cancer is a common disease which is typically the result of genetic changes that lead to aberrant growth and behaviour of affected cells, which then produce tumours which can spread throughout the body. Some individuals are at higher risk for cancer because of a family history of the disease. In these families, critical genetic alterations are inherited from one generation to the next in cancer predisposition genes. A better understanding of these predisposing genetic changes is not only useful to help the individuals who are mutation carriers, but it also improves our general understanding of how cancers develop in everyone else in the population by better understanding which genes are involved and how. The work performed in our laboratory for the past 20 years has focused on the study of inherited cancers in high risk families. This work led us to identify a number of new cancer susceptibility genes where genetic alterations can cause disease. In addition, we have also identified very specific changes, referred to as founder mutations, which are observed at higher frequency in our local Quebec populations. There are several reasons to continue this important work. 1) The discovery of novel cancer susceptibility genes / mutations provides at risk patients with surveillance and prevention options for their cancers. This can improve the odds for patients to survive their cancer and can also improve their psychological well-being by giving them a measure of control over their disease. 2) The establishment of population-specific screening panels provides cost effective avenues for genetic screening tailored to local populations, making screening more financially accessible to the health care system providing this service locally. 3) Identification of mutations can allow physicians to choose more effective treatment options for some cancers by using targeted treatments based on the molecular profile of the patients and the tumours they harbour.

column36: Enteric neural and glial control of gastrointestinal function in health and inflammatory disease.
column37: The function of your digestive system is key to good health. During digestion food moves from the stomach to the small intestine, where absorption of nutrients occurs, and finally to the colon for elimination. Movement of food through the intestines requires precise control. Not only does the gut move and digest food, but while doing so it must protect the rest of the body from ingested pathogens and from the microbes that live in its lumen. These microbes are essential for health, but must remain in the intestine or they can cause harm. Thus the gut has a dual role: digestion and defense. Digestion and defense are sufficiently complex that a "brain" is required to regulate and control them. This brain in the gut is called the enteric nervous system (ENS). The ENS is composed of nerves and specialized cells called enteric glial cells. Enteric glial cells were originally thought to be passive support cells, but through my research we know that nerves and glial cells actively communicate with each other by releasing chemical messengers. This bi-directional nerve-glial communication is important for the ENS to control the movement of food through the gut and for defense. Alterations in chemical communication in the ENS appears to be responsible for many of the symptoms of gastrointestinal disease. The vision of my research program is to discover new ways to alleviate the symptoms of gut disorders through studies of enteric nerve-glial communication. I will study the movements of the gut in the normal state and establish how nerves and glial cells communicate to regulate them. I will build on this information to find new ways to correct the abnormal gut movements that occur in disease. I will also focus on how microbes in the gut influence the neural and glial regulation of gut functions in health and disease. My ultimate goal is to develop better treatments for debilitating conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease and irritable bowel syndrome.

column37: The current proposal is founded on the discovery of a new approach for the treatment of autoimmune disease (occurring when the white blood cells of our immune system mistakenly recognize and attack natural components of our own tissues). Traditionally, vaccines have been used to expand white blood cells affording protection against viruses, bacteria or cancer, or to delete white blood cells causing autoimmune diseases like type 1 diabetes (T1D) and multiple sclerosis (MS). We have developed a new type of 'vaccine' based on nanotechnology (using particles thousands of times smaller than the size of normal white blood cell) that can stop anti-self immune responses by selectively expanding what we call 'autoregulatory' white blood cells. These 'autoregulatory' white blood cells put the brakes on the disease-causing autoimmune attack, by inhibiting the activation of all the disease-causing white blood cells, resulting in their complete suppression. As a result, these nanomedicines can blunt highly complex autoimmune responses in mice, including T1D, MS, primary biliary cirrhosis and arthritis, without causing generalized suppression of the immune system. Importantly, we have established that human disease-relevant nanomedicines can effectively trigger the expansion of human autoregulatory white blood cells in 'humanized' mice (mice carrying white blood cells from patients), indicating that this approach is applicable to humans. Here, we will dissect the cellular origin of the disease-suppressor cell type triggered by our nanomedicines, as well as the mechanisms and the downstream cellular targets through which it suppresses disease. Furthermore, we will use mice 'humanized' with white blood cells from T1D patients to select the corresponding drug candidates for clinical development. We anticipate that these studies will open new lines of inquiry in immunity and autoimmunity and will propel a promising new therapeutic avenue for autoimmunity to the clinic.

In humans, lower PC7 levels are also associated with a more efficient iron metabolism, higher levels of the good cholesterol high density lipoprotein (HDL) and lower levels of the bad triglycerides. column37: Changes in normal cognition are a characteristic feature of schizophrenia. Although our current drugs are quite successful in treating hallucinations and delusions, they largely fail in treating these cognitive deficits. Told to look away from a flash of light, they are unable to resist the automatic urge to glance at the stimulus. Subjects without the disorder can override the impulse. My goal is to understand the role of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in cognition from the level of single brain cells to the communication in the entire brain. By understanding how brain areas interact and how certain drugs can improve cognitive processes, we hope to identify drugs that will improve the cognitive deficits in schizophrenia.

column37: Circulating in the blood is a myriad of cells with different functions that are critical for our health, including red blood cells that carry oxygen, platelets that help to stop bleeding and immune cells that fight off infections and cancers. In this complex process, banks of genes are turned on and off in precursor cells to "steer" their differentiation toward one specialized cell type or another. This occurs primarily through the action of proteins called transcription factors, which reside in the cell nucleus and can regulate the activity of thousands of genes simultaneously. Not surprisingly, mistakes sometimes occur in this complex process and can lead to a number of very serious diseases. Over 20 years ago, I co-discovered two transcription factors (Gfi1 and Gfi1b) and was the first to determine the role of Gfi1 in blood diseases including leukemia. column36: Thymus biology and the molecular definition of the immune self
column37: Self/nonself discrimination by T lymphocytes is a fundamental requirement of life in vertebrates and is implicated in most fatal diseases in humans. Indeed, i) nonself recognition is essential for elimination of microbes and cancer cells, while ii) immune responses against self antigens cause classic autoimmune diseases (e.g., type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis) and are instrumental in chronic inflammatory diseases, hypertension and atherosclerosis. T lymphocytes learn how to distinguish self from nonself in the thymus. Importantly, the thymus ages more rapidly than all other organs, and by the age of 45 y, 75% of the thymus is lost in humans. Thymus senescence decreases the ability to recognize new antigens and responsiveness to vaccines, and increases the risk of infection, cancer and autoimmune diseases in ageing people. Hence, it is a sobering thought that our understanding of the molecular composition of the immune self is very rudimentary and that we do not understand the mechanisms of thymic involution. Accordingly, the two main themes of my research program are thymus biology and the molecular definition of the immune self. My specific objectives are i) to discover the molecular composition of the immune self, ii) to uncover how the immune self is perturbed in cancer cells, iii) to understand the rules governing T lymphocyte education in the thymus, and iv) to find a strategy to rejuvenate the thymus. Answers to these questions will be instrumental in i) treating thymus atrophy, the most common cause of immune deficiency in humans, ii) understanding the molecular bases of self-tolerance and enabling molecular evidence-based treatment of autoimmune and inflammatory conditions, and iii) discovering cancer-specific antigens that can be used as personalized vaccines for cancer treatment.

column36: Defining critical pathways for neuronal loss and dysfunction in Parkinsons disease and stroke
column37: Stroke and Parkinson's disease are devastating neurological disorders with devastating personal, social, and economic consequences. Stroke affects 15 million people a year worldwide and is the third leading cause of death. Parkinson's disease, a movement disorder, affects 10 million people worldwide and is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder. We now realize that there are incredibly sophisticated processes that govern the death of brain cells in these conditions. Our work is focused on understanding these complex processes and blocking the signals that lead to death thereby eliminating or reducing the brain injury in these conditions. While seemingly simple in concept, this strategy is incredibly difficult. For example, multiple signals likely control the death process, some of which work in parallel to control the long-term survival of brain cells. Also, how/whether manipulation of these signals ultimately lead to a proper functioning brain circuit is unclear. Finally, because it is difficult to actually work in humans to manipulate these signals, the development and use of appropriate animal models of study are critical. Our research program takes all these complex issues into consideration to systematically work through the issues that are impeding effective therapeutic strategies to treat stroke and PD. We have exciting and novel insights into the complex network of events that occur in a brain damaged by stroke or in PD. We will critically test whether these signals effectively lead to improved brain circuitry and animal behavior in these diseases. Together with a team of researchers and clinicians, we are working to define the appropriate strategies to treat these devastating neurological conditions. Our work is central to this important effort.

column36: Dietary Flaxseed as a Nutritional Intervention for Cardiovascular Disease
column37: High blood pressure (hypertension) is an important silent killer that can cause heart attacks and stroke. Not only is hypertension a deadly disease, it also cost $76 B last year in the US alone. Current drugs used to control hypertension are costly, can induce unwanted side-effects and they are not always effective in controlling blood pressure (BP) in all hypertensive patients. Having a food that will control BP represents a less expensive intervention than drugs. We have recently completed a major tightly controlled trial in which patients with peripheral arterial disease were supplemented daily for one year with flaxseed in their diet. Patients who entered the trial with high BP were the most affected by dietary flaxseed and systolic BP decreased by 15 mm Hg, an effect comparable to most hypertensive drugs available today. This decline in BP would lower the incidence of heart attacks and strokes by more than 50%. In the Foundation grant, we will continue our research with an on-going CIHR clinical trial to determine if flaxseed will lower BP in patients with high BP but without secondary disease. We will also study if flaxseed can delay or reduce the need for anti-hypertensive drugs. In a separate line of study in animal models, we will also examine the potential for dietary flaxseed to reduce damage to the heart after a heart attack has occurred. The mechanisms responsible for the anti-hypertensive action of flaxseed as well as its effects on heart protection from heart attacks will be studied. Providing low cost alternatives to drug therapy that can be used alone or in conjunction with medication has enormous appeal for the Canadian health care system. Even more importantly, this low cost alternative to expensive medication for high BP represents an appealing choice for third world countries and poor communities everywhere that cannot afford the drugs they need to lower BP and protect themselves from heart attacks and strokes.

column36: Quantitative Magnetic Resonance Imaging of the Human Brain: Technical Innovation and Application to Neurological Disorders
column37: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides unparalleled insight into human disease. Through continued technical innovation, we will further its utility by advancing image acquisition, quantitative analysis, and physics knowledge. Our novel brain MRI methods will be applied to stroke patients, where current MRI protocols are insufficient for accurate diagnosis in some patient subgroups (e.g. transient ischemic attack, wake up strokes). These MRI methods will also provide insight into typical brain development with age, a process important for 'normal' cognitive and behavioural maturation that may also provide clues about vulnerability to neurological or psychiatric disorders. column36: Ultra-high field Magnetic Resonance Imaging of Brain Structure and Function in Multiple Sclerosis
column37: Canada's multiple sclerosis (MS) prevalence rate is amongst the highest in the world at 240 per 100,000 population, for reasons we don't understand. Fortunately, there are drugs that can reduce the symptoms and slow the progression of the disease, but these drugs are very expensive. The lifetime cost of these drugs for a single MS patient is about $1 million. If we could come up with a way to decide when, and what dose of drug to deliver to each patient, we could save the health care system billions of dollars. The goal of our research program is to develop and use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) methods to inform such decisions, by measuring biomarkers of the disease. MRI has been used for many years as part of the diagnosis of MS. However normal MRI findings have not correlated well with clinical symptoms and have not demonstrated significant ability to predict the course of the disease. This may be related to the fact that conventional MRI visualizes only some of the lesions and damage seen by pathologists in brain slices. Ultra-high magnetic field MRI systems have the potential to be more sensitive to the microscopic changes in tissue properties that occur as MS begins and progresses. MRI machines at such magnetic field strengths are undergoing approvals for clinical diagnostic use. Using a 7 Tesla (140,000 times the earth's magnetic field) human MRI system, we will develop MRI techniques that can characterize MS in patients on a microscopic scale. This could lead to earlier diagnosis of MS, and therefore the ability to intervene sooner with drug treatments. Earlier intervention results in better patient outcomes and lower treatment costs

We will also use our animal models to gain a better understanding of how cardiac birth defects make the heart more vulnerable to other cardiovascular problems. Such knowledge will help design therapies for prevention and treatment that are presently unavailable. The results of our research will continue to impact diagnosis and care of individuals with heart disease or with a family history of the disease.

column36: Tuberculosis: From Genomics to Control
column37: As a doctor and a scientist, I ask why many people are exposed to the bacterium, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, but only a minority develop the disease tuberculosis (TB). To understand these variable outcomes, I have established CIHR-funded programs of research that study the spread of this bacterium (epidemiology) and the fundamental biology of the disease (looking from both the perspective of the bacterium and that of the human host). The present application brings together three themes of TB research that share conceptual and methodologic synergies. In molecular epidemiology work (theme 1), our group makes a DNA 'fingerprint' of bacteria to track chains of transmission. This information, integrated with Public Health data, will define better ways to intervene with antibiotics in settings with drug sensitive and multidrug resistant settings. In bacteria-based studies (theme 2), our group compares the bacteria that causes TB with related bacteria that live in the environment and do not cause a contagious disease. These studies will uncover bacterial targets to neutralize in a new vaccine. In host-based studies (theme 3), our group studies how a part of the immune system, called innate immunity, recognizes Mycobacterium tuberculosis and how this translates into effective control of the infection. These studies will define host responses to be enhanced by a new vaccine. Together, these studies, carried out at the level of human populations and within a laboratory setting, will identify critical bacterial- and human-determinants of disease. I am one of very few TB researchers in the world who has the necessary training and a track record of success to lead this combination of studies. The information gained will drive the best application of existing antibiotics, to better control TB, and inform the development of a new vaccine, to eliminate TB.

column36: Insomnia: Research Innovations to Optimize Treatment Outcome in Primary Care
column37: Sleep problems are among the most common health complaints, with insomnia affecting 20% of adults at least occasionally and 10% on a chronic basis. Insomnia is characterized by difficulties initiating or maintaining sleep associated with distress and impairments of daytime functioning. Chronic insomnia produces significant psychological (increased risks of depression), physical (increased risk of hypertension), and economic burdens (reduced productivity and increased absenteeism). Despite some recent progress in insomnia research, there are still some major gaps in understanding and treating this sleep disorder. First, little is known about its risk factors and long-term consequences. Secondly, although chronic sleep disturbances are often associated with co-existing medical and psychiatric conditions, the specific role of psychological and biological factors in insomnia is still poorly understood. Thirdly, despite its high prevalence, insomnia often remains untreated and when treatment is initiated, it is usually limited to prescribed or over-the-counter drugs. Long-term use of sleep medications is often problematic due to their adverse effects and risks of tolerance and dependency. Behavioural therapies for insomnia are effective and well accepted by patients, yet they are not readily available and are infrequently used in practice. The main objectives of this research proposal are to: a) document the natural history, risk factors, and long-term health consequences of insomnia; b) develop more efficient and cost-effective therapies; and c) examine how we can make these interventions more accessible to those who need it (i.e., patients and health care practitioners). This research program is likely to have practical implications by producing new knowledge that will improve our understanding of insomnia and how best to treat it in clinical practice, hence reducing the individual and societal burden of this important public health problem.

The program will also offer a unique opportunity to implement a personalized, patient-centered approach to treatment for CSA children and youth in Canada. My program includes: 1) Implementing the Ottawa SAH Rule to identify headache patients at risk for subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH); 2) Developing the Canadian TIA Score to identify transient ischemic attack (TIA) patients at risk for subsequent stroke; 3) Conducting trials for recent-onset atrial fibrillation (RAF); and 4) Optimizing and measuring knowledge translation (KT) for each condition. SAH is a life-threatening hemorrhagic stroke, which is worse with a delayed diagnosis. We developed the Ottawa SAH Rule to determine which headache patients need investigations to rule-out SAH. We have proven the Ottawa SAH Rule to be safe, but further study is needed to 1) assess its impact and 2) optimize physician use. TIAs precede up to 20% of strokes. We developed the Canadian TIA Score, to determine the impending stroke risk. This study will test the Canadian TIA Score in 5,000 new TIA patients to confirm it is accurate to identify patients' risk of stroke within 7 days. The Canadian TIA Score will improve patient outcomes through the efficient use of existing resources. RAF results in a rapid heart rate, requiring urgent treatment to restore normal heart rhythm. RAF is the most common rhythm disorder managed in the ED. No studies have been conducted comparing an electrical shock (Shock Only) or drugs followed by shock (Drug-Shock). Our trial compares these two strategies for conversion to normal rhythm. Given a consistent failure to translate new and existing research into clinical and public health practice, this research program will measure the KT implementation of The Ottawa SAH Rule, The Canadian TIA Score and clinical practice guidelines for RAF and acute headache (including all causes of headache). This research will build the science of KT in acute settings and optimize uptake of new evidence from our research program.

column36: Promoting Reflexive Family Physical Activity: A test of Habit and Identity Formation
column37: Regular physical activity (PA) has enormous health benefits. Among children and adolescents, PA protects against metabolic syndrome, low bone density, depression, and obesity, and forms the behavioral patterns necessary to foster health benefits across the life course. Unfortunately, very few Canadians engage in enough PA to reap its health benefits. There is a clear need to promote PA within the family unit yet interventions focused on the family have been scarce and have had negligible impact. My research career has focused on the theoretical underpinnings of family-level PA and the application of these factors to PA promotion. Much of the past research on family-based PA has focused on increasing the knowledge base of PA's benefits in an attempt to raise intentions to act. My research has shown that most parents already agree that regular PA is important for them and their children but have difficulty following through on supportive PA intentions. My team's ongoing and recently completed research trials have examined how to promote the factors that bind good intentions to behaviour. The primary objectives of this foundation grant will be to expand upon these prior results by promoting two potentially important factors that have not received enough research attention. One of these factors is parental support habits (trial 1) and the other is parental support identity (subsequent trial 2). The key outcome in these trials will be child PA (measured objectively through a monitoring device). My team will compare whether a habit/identity promotion program focused on parental support of PA can improve child PA beyond basic education and goal-setting over six months. Participants will be families with at least one child between 6 and 12 years old who is not active. All of this research has the potential to be directly applied to national promotion campaigns and physical activity programs for families and contribute to long-term economic health outcomes of Canadians.

column36: The pancreatic islet in human health and diabetes
column37: I am a world-leading expert on the insulin producing pancreatic islets of Langerhans. My work focuses on understanding the cellular mechanisms that control insulin secretion, and how these process is impaired in type 2 diabetes (T2D). The insulin-producing pancreatic islets of Langerhans are central to nearly all forms of diabetes, since these are destroyed through autoimmunity in type 1 diabetes (T1D; ~10% of cases) and are dysfunctional in T2D (~80% of cases). The result is an impaired regulation of metabolism that leads to an increased risk of stroke, heart disease, kidney failure, blindness, and amputation. Diabetes affects nearly 3 million Canadians and costs our healthcare system $17 billion annually. My group is ideally positioned address key questions about insulin secretion in clinically relevant tissue samples from patients with and without diabetes. To achieve this I have established a human pancreas tissue program, allowing us to study clinically relevant tissue from organ donors with and without diabetes. My group combines this with molecular, imaging, and cell physiological approaches to study: biochemical connections linking cellular metabolism with insulin secretion; the organization of insulin release at the cell membrane; and processes that underlie insulin secretory dysfunction in human T2D islets and animal models of diabetes. My lab is making important inroads in these areas, leading to a better understanding of insulin secretory function in health and diabetes. This work is informing drug development and testing through partnerships with industry, and providing new insights into how secretory dysfunction in T2D may be reversed.

column36: Immune Regulation during Chronic Disease
column37: Persistent viral infections are a global health concern, with over 500 million people infected with HIV and hepatitis B and C viruses. A major cause of morbidity and mortality during these persistent infections is the co-infections and cancers they foster. Strategies to enhance immune activity to clear these persistent viral infections or prevent co-infection/cancer have so far been unsuccessful largely because they cannot adequately rehabilitate the dysfunctional host immune response. The proposed experiments will define critical immune dysfunctions during persistent infection and develop immune redirecting therapies to eliminate persistent viruses and the co-diseases that arise during them. Further, many of the same pathways that suppress immunity during persistent viral infections, are also being identified to inhibit the immune response from eliminating many cancers. We will translate the mechanisms of immunosuppression we uncover in the persistent virus infection into cancer to identify conserved mechanisms of immunosuppression and targets for therapeutic intervention. Ultimately, we propose a unifying principle of immunosuppression in chronic diseases and that by understanding the underlying roots of immunosuppression it will be possible to target these pathways at their core to cure multiple chronic diseases. The mechanisms and paradigms we reveal will have the potential to lead to new strategies to treat disease.

column36: Genetic analysis of susceptibility to infections and to inflammation
column37: Infections caused by new emerging bacterial and viral pathogens, or by common microbes that have become drug resistant, and that we are exposed to in the nosocomial or community settings or during travel abroad, remain a serious threat to the health of Canadians. column36: New biomarkers and interventions for life-threatening infections: malaria as a model
column37: Rationale and Goals: Life-threatening infections (LTIs) remain leading causes of global illness and death especially for children and pregnant women in low-resource settings. The goals of our translational research program are: (1) to characterize the mechanisms underlying LTIs; and (2) to develop new triage tools and treatments to prevent death and brain injury in survivors. While malaria is the primary model used, the findings have broad implications for other LTIs and causes of adverse birth outcomes. Given Canada's leadership role in global maternal-child health, these goals are directly relevant to both Canadian and global health priorities. Specific Research Aims and Impact: i. Next generation diagnostics: Our research is contributing to the next generation of rapid triage and diagnostic tests that will not only diagnose infection but will also determine how severe the infection is and help predict outcome. This approach could enable personalized medicine rapidly, inexpensively and at point-of-care. ii. Novel therapies to prevent death and brain injury: Despite potent antimicrobials and supportive care, fatality rates for LTIs remain high and survivors often have brain injury. Our research has identified new interventions that are in human trials to improve survival and prevent brain injury in severe malaria. These studies have broad implications for many LTIs. iii. Improving pregnancy outcomes: Preventing poor birth outcomes is a global health priority; but we know relatively little about how and why they happen. Our studies have addressed important knowledge gaps and have identified new potential interventions to improve pregnancy outcomes and to prevent brain injury in offspring. Outcomes: Our research will help to identify new tools and treatments for LTIs that are appropriate for use in low resource settings. These advances have the potential to change global policy and practice for LTIs in maternal-child health.

column36: Informing health care policy makers on health care financing and sustainability
column37: The Canadian population is aging and chronic diseases are becoming more common, leading to increasing health care costs and demand for system-wide change to improve sustainability. In a recent international study of 11 peer countries, Canada's health care system ranked 10th. The major reasons for this poor performance include: (1) Canada's health care system funds hospitals and physicians, and hence is not optimally constructed to care for people with chronic diseases whose care accounts for more than two-thirds of current Canadian health care expenditures; (2) Canada's physician fee-for-service model rewards high-volume care by a single physician, which is not the ideal model for care for people with chronic diseases where multidisciplinary team-based care has a central role; and (3) Many Canadians with drug insurance continue to experience financial barriers to drug access due to the structure of cost-sharing between the patient and the health care system. The proposed research will lead to the development of new evidence-based health policies regarding optimal physician payment models and drug formulary cost-sharing structures. Research deliverables will empower government decision-making to improve health system sustainability, quality of care, equitable access and efficiency. My work has already led directly to changes in health policy in Canada.

column36: Chromosome instability and synthetic lethality in yeast and cancer
column37: Effective cancer therapy exploits specific biological differences between cancer cells and normal cells. Cancer cells often have defects that reduce the efficiency of chromosome transmission. Indeed, mutations in cancer cells that cause chromosome instability (CIN) are now widely recognized to be an important driver in cancer initiation and progression. These CIN mutations also represent tumour specific genetic vulnerabilities that could be exploited in developing new cancer treatments. Because the same building blocks are used to construct organisms as diverse as yeast, worms, and humans, "model organisms" provide powerful experimental tools for investigating the mechanistic basis of disease and for developing potential therapeutic interventions. The goals of our work are to understand the mechanisms of chromosome transmission at the levels of genes, pathways, and networks using yeast and the nematode worm as models, and to directly relate our studies to cancer and the development of new cancer therapies. Using yeast genetic techniques, in particular, global synthetic lethality analysis, we will identify yeast genes, and the corresponding human gene counterparts, that define potential therapeutic targets for selective killing of cancer cells relative to normal cells. We will use yeast to rapidly test millions of possible combinations of tumour-associated defects, drug targets, and chemotherapeutic agents to identify effective combinations, and will prioritize them for further testing in tumour cell cultures. The results of our proposed research will provide a basic understanding of the mechanisms of normal chromosome transmission, and of the corresponding defects associated with cancer pathology. Our results will also lead to the identification of new drug targets and will enable the identification of new small molecule inhibitors and combination therapies that could be used for the selective killing of cancer cells in patients.

column36: Molecular regulation of muscle stem cell function in regenerative myogenesis
column37: I am interested in understanding the mechanisms that control stem cell function and applying this knowledge to improve health. Our studies are focused on muscle stem cells and how they function in the growth and repair of skeletal muscle. The research is critical for developing novel treatments for many muscle-wasting diseases, for example Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD). Our studies have already transformed our understanding of the mechanisms that control muscle stem cell function and have led to the development of a protein called Wnt7a as a novel therapy. First, we will investigate the mechanism by which Wnt7a stimulates muscle regeneration and test therapeutic strategies to treat muscle-wasting disease. The experiments will direct the development of Wnt7a as a drug and clinical trials will be conducted with Wnt7a in the near future. Second, we will define the mechanisms that regulate the division of muscle stem cells as this is a central control point that governs regeneration efficiency. We will investigate these control mechanisms with the longer-term goal of identifying targets and hence drugs that could be used to stimulate muscle stem cell function. Third, we will map the regulatory networks of proteins called transcription factors that control the expression of genes in muscle stem cells from healthy versus diseased tissue. This information is key to understanding how these stem cells function. Finally, we will identify new drugs capable of stimulating muscle stems cells to enhance muscle regeneration. In parallel, we will validate our findings on human muscle stem cells to transition our therapeutic strategies into the clinic. In conclusion, the research will advance our knowledge of stem cell function and lead to novel treatments for diseases involving wasting of skeletal muscle. Importantly, this work will improve the health of patients, and also benefit the families and care givers that are affected by these devastating diseases.

column37: This research proposal is aimed at developing new understanding of autoimmune disease pathogenesis that will drive the development of novel markers and treatments to improve diagnosis, management and health outcomes. We will also study the effects of these gene variants on disease progression and treatment responses in our patient populations. The second thrust of this proposal builds on our derivation of mice carrying specific genetic changes associated with development of autoimmune disease. Because we know the altered gene/protein that causes disease in these animals, we can explore and thereby characterize the molecular pathways whereby these gene/protein changes induce disease. Such studies provide unique opportunity to identify new targets for drug therapy and to explore the potential for such therapies to ameliorate disease. Via these strategies, this research will identify the gene variants that cause and influence outcome of two prototypical autoimmune diseases and elucidate the mechanistic pathways that link such variants to disease. This new knowledge will illuminate novel biomarkers and more effective therapies that will alleviate the enormous medical and socioeconomic burden imposed by autoimmune diseases.

column36: Towards new therapeutics through manipulation of glyco-enzymes
column37: The surfaces of every cell in the human body are coated with specific sugars. These play several roles, principally providing a way for the cell to interact with other cells and their components. Invading bacteria and viruses also use these sugars as an entry point, thus an understanding of these interactions and of how the specific sugars are built and degraded, can lead to new therapeutics. An example is the influenza virus drug Tamiflu, which blocks the critical viral enzyme that cuts a sugar off our cell surfaces and allows the virus to spread. Our recent research has shown that some of the enzymes used by disease-causing bacteria and parasites in order to infect human cells are unlike any enzymes present in human cells. This allows us to design and synthesize new classes of drug to either specifically block these enzymes, as with Tamiflu, or to liberate toxins specifically within the invader. Using such approaches, in collaboration with microbiologists, we shall develop new strategies for treatment of antibiotic-resistant bacteria, as well as the parasites that cause Chagas disease in South America. In a second part of our work we shall use enzymes to modify these cell surface sugars for a variety of applications. In one case we use enzymes to cut specific sugars off the surface of red blood cells, thereby changing their blood type from A or B (or AB) to the "universal donor" Type O. Using an approach that mimics the process of natural evolution, but accelerates it, we shall engineer these enzymes to speed them up for clinical use. This work should greatly improve our supply of blood for transfusions. In a second case we shall use enzymes to improve the performance of increasingly important protein-based drugs such as antibodies and growth factors. Most such proteins have sugars on their surface that play important roles. We shall engineer enzymes to add sugars in a highly controlled manner, yielding drugs of improved performance.

column36: Beyond Structured Administrative Data (BEST DATA)
column37: To monitor how our health care system functions, researchers use data routinely collected through public services, such as bills from physician visits, hospital discharge information, and social data from non-health services. Using the extensive person-level data available at MCHP, we will follow patient exposure to antibiotics over time while considering travel history and other contributing factors. Thus, the inclusion of free text analysis adds an additional dimension to our understanding of antibiotic resistance and will help to curb this growing problem. column36: Neurovascular and neuroimmune interplay in retinal vasculopathies
column37: Loss of eyesight is the most feared ailment in North America after cancer. The part of the eye that senses visuals scenes and transmits them to the brain is a structure rich in nerve cells and blood vessels called the retina. This structure is biochemically part of the brain. In debilitating diseases of the retina such as the sight-threatening diabetic retinopathy, retinopathy of prematurity and age-related macular degeneration, the degeneration of blood vessels precipitates loss of nerve cell function. These retinopathies are the leading causes blindness in the industrial world and account for over 25 million cases of compromised vision in North America. The degeneration of blood vessels in the retina prevents nutrient and oxygen delivery and leads to a constellation of biochemical changes that deregulate cellular function. While the body attempts to repair and restore blood vessels, there are a number of yet unknown factors that hinder reparative vessel growth and consequently aggravate the loss of nerve cell function. Current treatment paradigms are largely inefficient and focus on destroying diseased blood vessels instead of repairing those that provide oxygen and essential nutrients. An attractive alternative approach would be to regenerate functional vessels into zones of the retina where vessels were damaged. In this proposal we outline a therapeutic strategy that would restore healthy blood vessels to the retina in retinopathies. This approach will help design new medications and be achieved by molecularly altering the response of retinal nerve cells to vascular injury.

column36: Targeting the dynamics and genomics of clonal evolution in cancer patients
column37: Cancers evolve over time and the gene mutations driving them can change. A major bottleneck in the treatment of epithelial cancers is a lack of diverse therapeutic / treatment options. This is especially relevant in cancer, as tumours are able to evolve/adapt to "escape" from single-agent treatment (similar to what occurs in antibiotic-resistant bacteria, where a combination of drugs is required to treat the infection); breast cancers often develop drug resistance so that their tumors recur, and mutational evolution likely underlies this event. It is critical to identify new options/approaches to target tumours that have become drug-resistant, as a result of mutational evolution. We know that clonal complexity - the so called "cellular superbug" phenomenon, is associated with instability in the tumour's genetic sequence (driven by the inability of DNA to repair itself). We hypothesize that specific sections of the genome, with unique DNA structures may be targetable through directed approaches, and plan to explore novel approaches that target structural vulnerabilities within the human genome. By combining chemical genomics of DNA targeting with genetic technologies to uncover conditional genetic interactions and methods for measuring clonal structure, we expect to derive a completely new mechanistic approach to targeting genomically unstable epithelial cancers. Our studies have the potential to answer specific questions about how breast cancer arises, progresses, and becomes resistant to treatment. These findings will have a global impact within the cancer research community, allowing the design of improved and more effective therapies. In short, the practical application of cancer cell genetics will become a reality in the clinic -- representing a significant step forward in direct translational benefits for patients.

column37: Many hormones and transmitters have their biological effects by modulating the activity of receptors located at the surface of cells. Among these, G protein-coupled receptors (GPCR) represent the largest family of protein involved in transferring information from the outside to the inside of the cells. With more than 800 members, GPCR control many distinct physiological functions such as neurotransmission, cardiac contraction, vascular tone, endocrine secretion, metabolism, etc.... As a consequence, they represent privileged targets for the development of drugs for many distinct clinical indications. It is estimated that more than 30% of the current prescription drugs act through GPCR. Yet, only a limited fraction of the therapeutic potential of GPCR has been exploited to date. Many receptors with important roles have not yet been targeted and new developments in molecular pharmacology and structural biology offer new opportunities for the development of drugs with greater therapeutic efficacies and less undesirable effects. In particular, new tools allowing to unravel their structures and to monitor their signaling activities with unprecedented sensitivity and spatiotemporal resolution open the perspective of developing new drugs based on an intimate understanding of their mode of action at the molecular level. Therefore, the present proposal aims at further understanding the molecular mechanisms controlling GPCR activity, with the intention of identifying novel processes that could be pharmacologically targeted for therapeutic purposes. column36: Living Kidney Donation: Improving Safety, Access, and Outcomes
column37: Kidney Failure: Kidney failure is a serious health condition that affects more than 40,000 Canadians. The best treatment for kidney failure is a new kidney by transplantation. Unfortunately, patients with kidney failure often wait years to receive a new kidney. Many patients die while they are waiting. Living Kidney Donation: It is safe for a living person who is healthy to donate one of their kidneys. Family and friends of patients who need a kidney often volunteer to donate one of their kidneys. With advances in transplantation, the donor and recipient do not have to be related or be of the same gender, race, or age. Canada and other countries are looking for ways to safely increase living kidney donation. Barriers to Living Kidney Donation: Unfortunately, many patients who would benefit from a kidney transplant do not receive one. There are many reasons for this. Doctors do not always talk to their patients about transplantation. Patients are often uncomfortable discussing living kidney donation with family and friends. Many people do not realize that it is safe to donate a kidney; some are told they are too old to donate despite new research showing it is safe if they are healthy. As well, donor evaluation often takes a year to complete (when it should only take 3 months). A long evaluation process has negative consequences for both donors and recipients. Safely Increasing Living Kidney Donation: My research team is working with living kidney donors and transplant programs to develop and test solutions to overcome barriers to living kidney donation. As well, we are studying a large group of living kidney donors over many decades to confirm long-term safety. Information from our studies will enable more patients with kidney failure to safely receive transplants, and will help candidates make informed decisions about becoming living kidney donors.

column37: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most serious intestinal disease among newborn babies, mostly those who are born prematurely. These procedures help babies survive, but are not a cure. Taking care of these children is hard for their families and very expensive for the health care system. As an expert internationally recognized for my work on NEC and a surgeon caring for these babies, I know first-hand that NEC remains a challenge. We do not completely understand what causes NEC, or why it becomes more serious in some newborns. To improve the outlook for babies with NEC, help their families, and reduce costs to the health care system, we need to find out why and how babies develop NEC, and test new ways to treat it. I have dedicated my scientific and clinical career to advancing pediatric surgery, focusing on caring for babies with NEC - and have developed promising new ways to treat it. My leadership in the surgical and NEC fields led to my active recruitment to Canada. My research here will improve the health of babies with NEC. I will establish and lead a program that will produce exciting new basic science discoveries, and will test new approaches to heal babies with NEC in the clinic. This research will deliver new and improved treatments for NEC, helping babies survive and thrive, and easing the burden of NEC on families and the health care system.

column36: New Resources for Chemical Genomics and Metabolomics in Biomedicine
column37: Small molecule compounds such as drugs, nutrients and pollutants affect our health in many ways. Nutrients are needed to sustain life, drugs are needed to cure us of illnesses, while pollutants can kill us. Millions of these compounds exist. The complete collection of these compounds is called the "metabolome" -- derived from the word metabolite (a substance produced by metabolism). The study of how the metabolome affects us is called metabolomics. While metabolomics is a relatively new field, scientists have been collecting detailed information about metabolites for ~100 years. Unfortunately, most of this data is scattered in millions of textbooks and journal articles. The lack of centralized databases or electronic resources for metabolomics means that we still know very little about the chemical universe around us. We don't know how many metabolites there are, we struggle to identify or measure them, we don't know where they come from, we can't tell if they are good or bad and we rarely know how they act on our cells or modify our genes. My long-term research goal is to develop the resources needed to address these problems. Using advanced methods in information technology and analytical chemistry, my lab has created a number of databases and software tools that are helping to answer some of these questions. Our plan is to greatly improve these resources by using the latest techniques in artificial intelligence. By using computers to automatically identify and harvest vast amounts of data from the literature and learn from that data, it should be possible to develop far better resources that will allow us to better characterize, predict and exploit the chemical universe around us. This work will not only revolutionize metabolomics, it will greatly accelerate the discovery of new drugs, identify the underlying chemical causes of diseases, enable improved diagnostics and help predict those at risk of developing diseases such as cancer, heart disease and diabetes.

column37: Approximately 1 in 10 adults have chronic kidney disease (CKD), a condition that is associated with poor health outcomes and poor quality of life. Patients with earlier stages of CKD are cared for by family doctors, while those with more severe disease are cared for by nephrologists in special clinics. Not all of these patients, however, receive appropriate treatment. This is known as a risk-treatment paradox; a mismatch between a patient's risk profile, and the treatment they actually receive. There is also a focus on care that reflects provider, rather than patient, goals. The potential risk-treatment paradox and lack of patient engagement suggests our current approach to CKD care is not optimal. I am a physician with expertise in clinical research in CKD. I hold a Research Chair, have 351 publications, and have received over $16 million in funding as lead investigator. My research has influenced international practice guidelines for CKD, thereby shaping clinical practice, and has led to changes in health policy in Alberta. My research program has been directly informed by patients, and I have integrated patients into all aspects of my work. The goal for my research program is to improve CKD care using a personalized and patient-centered approach. Over the next 7 years I will: 1) test use of a risk prediction tool in primary and nephrology care to identify a patient's risk to guide care and referral; and 2) develop, implement and test tools that are tailored for patients and their families, to help them manage their kidney disease and be active partners in the decision making related to their care. My program of research will address key priorities for improving care identified by CKD patients , care providers and decision makers. I aim to reinvent CKD care to make it personalized and patient-centered, to ultimately improve outcomes, enhance the patient experience and provide economic benefits through cost savings for the health system.

column36: Discovery and characterization of alternative splicing regulatory networks with critical roles in development and disease
column37: We have shown that almost all human genes encode multiple protein products through a process known as alternative splicing. Each gene is transcribed into an RNA copy that contains coding and non-coding segments. RNA splicing joins the coding segments into a contiguous messenger RNA that can be translated into a functional protein product. Alternative splicing occurs when the coding segments are spliced in different combinations such that a single gene can produce multiple RNA and protein products. This process greatly diversifies the regulatory and functional capacity of genes, resulting in biological complexity. Alternative splicing is frequently disrupted by mutations that cause or contribute to human diseases and disorders. Moreover, some disease mutations can affect entire programs of alternative splicing by targeting the factors that regulate this process. However, we currently know nothing about the specific functions of most individual protein variants generated by alternative splicing, nor how these variants, when mis-regulated, contribute to human diseases. These questions represent key challenges for future biomedical research and form the main goals of this proposal. We will draw on our world-leading expertise in the areas of alternative splicing, functional genomics, and proteomics, to provide the first large-scale map of splice variant function in the context of both normal physiology and human disease. We will systematically dissect the regulatory pathways that control functionally important and disease-associated splicing events. Finally, we will use information generated by our project to develop new therapeutic strategies for correcting altered splicing programs that underlie human diseases and disorders, focusing on autism. Our research will yield unprecedented new insight into the multitasking functions of our genes, and it will further facilitate the development of a new generation of splicing-directed therapeutics.

column36: Fundamental and Translational Studies of Diabetic Dyslipidemia in Insulin Resistant States
column37: I have been a senior scientist in both basic scientific and clinical research for over 25 years. Due to numerous achievements and publications, my laboratory is now recognized as a leader in both fields with major national and global impact. The main focus of my research program has been to develop an understanding of how lipid (fat) metabolism is regulated in diabetic states. Obesity and diabetes are major risk factors for heart disease, and have been increasing at an alarming rate in both children and adults. These conditions are associated with intestinal dysfunction and an overproduction of harmful fat particles (called "chylomicrons"), greatly increasing the risk of heart disease. The critical importance of the intestine in diabetes is now widely recognized as intestinal bypass surgery can rapidly cure type 2 diabetes and normalize blood sugar in diabetic patients. My research program has been investigating how dietary fat absorption and generation of fat particles by the intestine is regulated and altered in diabetic states. We have identified important hormones in the gut and brain that can regulate dietary fat uptake, and have shown that the balance of these hormones is disrupted in diabetic states. Understanding the factors that control dietary fat uptake by the gut may lead to direct benefits in management of lipid disorders in obesity and diabetes. Most of our research in this area has been performed using a hamster model of pre-diabetes, but our findings have recently been confirmed in adult human studies. Now, due to the growing number of children and adolescents with obesity and type 2 diabetes, we plan to investigate the levels of intestinal lipids and gut hormones in the pediatric population. First, we will determine the normal levels of these factors in healthy children of different ages and sexes. Then we will investigate how these levels change in children attending pediatric obesity and diabetes clinics at the Hospital for Sick Children.

column36: Neuron-Glia interactions in brain disease
column37: The goal of my research is to prevent neuronal death and brain impairment that occurs following stroke and during neurodegeneration. My work in the past has shown that the preservation of a healthy brain requires communication between the nerve cells and the surrounding cells termed glia, such as astrocytes and microglia. My research will show how glia respond to brain diseases and traumatic damage and how they aid in recovery. The major cause of patient mortality after stroke or brain injury is brain swelling called brain edema. We have found a new pathway allowing chloride to enter nerve cells that leads to increased water entry into neurons. We will determine how to block chloride entry and brain swelling in nerve cells and we will investigate the contributions of glia to the control of chloride entry into neurons and brain swelling. The goal is to discover the triggers that cause brain swelling and how therapeutic compounds could block brain edema to reduce brain damage and patient mortality. One type of glia, called microglia are the immune cells of the brain and respond to infections and to damage by repairing surrounding tissue and removing debris. Sometimes however microglia can themselves cause damage and brain impairment. We will determine the factors that cause microglia to switch from protecting the brain to releasing factors to cause damage or impair brain function. This will guide us in developing drugs to prevent microglia-induced damage. The brain is the most metabolically active region of the body and requires a constant supply of oxygen and glucose (sugar) via the blood via processes regulated by astrocytes, another glial cell. Experiments will be undertaken to carefully determine the conditions under which astrocytes regulate neuronal activity and cerebral blood flow in normal brains and in conditions of neurodegeneration such as Alzheimer's. This work will guide the development of new therapies to maintain brain health.

column36: FROM PROTEOLYTIC NETWORKS TO HUMAN BIOLOGY AND DISEASE: Protease regulation of signal transduction in chronic inflammatory diseases
column37: Chronic inflammatory diseases like periodontitis, arthritis and lupus affect 82% of Canadians and for the 1/2000 Canadians with immunodeficiencies, untreatable infections are imminent threats as drug resistance rises. These diseases commonly involve loss of disease-fighting defense proteins. I discovered that defense proteins are lost after they are cut by white blood cell immune proteases. In immunodeficiencies, inherited genetic defects reduce defense proteins in white blood cells. These crucial discoveries were possible by my innovative and highly advanced techniques known as degradomics. Degradomics is a method of uniquely identifying the cut ends of proteins by selectively purifying them from the rest of the protein. As cuts are formed only during active disease, these segments are highly valuable as disease markers to develop new clinical tests. By detecting and treating earlier, inflammatory diseases are easier to manage before disease worsens, and thus reduce long-term disability. Also, as part of the international Human Proteome Project consortium, I am using degradomics to identify the natural ends of all human proteins. This will allow us to characterize the functions of normal vs. diseased proteins and hence reveal new disease mechanisms. I will now use degradomics to generate clinically relevant knowledge on how proteases damage disease-fighting defense systems in human inflammatory and immunodeficiency diseases. I will obtain human tissues discarded in treatment, e.g. inflamed gum from wisdom teeth extractions, and study white blood cells from patients. As defense proteins are alike in many diseases, my results will be broadly applicable. This knowledge will translate to develop new drugs to combat inflammatory and autoimmune diseases. From identifying cut protein ends in these diseases, I will reveal the damaging proteases that can be targeted with new drugs to improve health of Canadians and thereby ensuring sustainable health care costs.

column36: Using artificial pancreas closed-loop systems for the treatment of type 1 diabetes
column37: In healthy individuals, blood sugar levels are tightly controlled by 2 hormones: insulin and glucagon. Secretion of insulin, a vital hormone to reduce blood sugar, is lost in type 1 diabetes (T1D). Thus, patients with T1D are treated by insulin therapy using multiple daily injections or insulin pump. Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) is frequent in T1D individuals and can lead to malaise, convulsions and death. In case of hypoglycemia, patients might need glucagon, a key hormone to raise blood glucose. Our team has developed a wearable artificial pancreas (WAP) that regulates sugar levels for patients with T1D. The WAP is composed of three components: continuous glucose sensor (to measure blood sugar changes), infusion pumps (to provide insulin with or without glucagon) and an intelligent dosing method that links the sensor with the pump to implement dose changes with the pump based on the blood sugar fluctuations. Two configurations of the WAP have been developed: one that infuses insulin and another that infuses insulin and glucagon. Completed trials demonstrate that, compared to conventional pump therapy, both WAP versions increase the time that sugar levels remain within recommended targets and reduce hypoglycemic risk. The objectives of this application are: 1) to improve daytime sugar control after meal & during exercise, two remaining challenging situations; 2) to conduct clinical trials in 2 key populations: patients with a reduced perception of hypoglycemia and children with T1D; 3) to perform a 6-month trial with the WAP targeting A1c improvement (marker of diabetes control & risk of complication) and severe hypoglycemia. The WAP has a great potential to improve patients' quality of life, reduce the risk of complication (e.g. blindness, kidney failure), prevent hypoglycemia (malaise), provide confidence for physical activities and meals as well as alleviate the burden of diabetes for families and healthcare providers.

column36: Mitochondrial targeting as a novel therapeutic approach to human disease: a translational program
column37: One of the major ways that normal cells can get sick is when their fuel's supply to demand balance is disrupted. The "power plants" that regulate the handling of fuel (oxygen, sugars, lipids) in the cell are organelles called mitochondria. We now know that there is mitochondrial dysfunction in many common diseases (like diabetes or cancer for example) but also in more rare but deadly diseases like pulmonary hypertension, where the blood vessels of the lungs are gradually destroyed leading to shortness of breath and premature death. There are no effective treatments that prolong the life of patients with pulmonary hypertension, similar to cancer. Here we propose to perform studies in order to understand better how the mitochondria dysfunction leads to pulmonary hypertension. We have drugs that can normalize mitochondrial function and we will test to see whether they may become therapies for pulmonary hypertension. We will use animal models and human organs that we receive at the time of transplant surgery. We also plan to test some of these drugs to actual patients in order to answer the critical questions that exist before testing them in large groups of patients to prove that they help without harm. The breadth and depth of our work provides a superb training environment in which to train future doctors and scientists to discover novel therapies for deadly human diseases. Our previous success in this field of research and the strong support from our institution and our collaborators make us confident that we will succeed to actually improve the lives of patients in addition to advancing our scientific knowledge.

column36: Increasing safe mobility of older Canadian pedestrians and drivers
column37: I will develop solutions to enable seniors to walk with less chance of falling and to drive safely. The ability to continue walking and driving safely is key to staying independent. Falls and accidents not only cause pain and cost but the resulting need for assistance with mobility creates a burden on family at home and may result in earlier admission to an institution. One component of my research will focus on opportunities to prevent falls by reducing environmental causes. We have provided evidence supporting changes to the Building Code of Canada to make stairs safer. That work will be extended to include standards for handrails on stairs, pathways and ramps as well as grab bars in bathrooms. In addition, many seniors are injured because of falls on ice. Fear of walking outside in winter causes many people to reduce their outings and their exercise. We will continue developing tests to guide consumers in the selection of safer footwear that will dramatically increase safety when walking on slippery surfaces. In parallel with walking research, I will focus on safer driving. One of the most devastating moments is being told that you can no longer drive safely and your keys are being taken away. As we grow older we need our cars more than ever because our walking is more limited, particularly in winter. Yet, our driving abilities may be challenged by vision or cognitive problems. It is neither safe nor practical to subject older people with, for example, dementia to challenging highway driving tests across all weather conditions. This research will focus on the ability to create realistic and valid driver testing using an advanced driving simulator. One of the main questions to be answered is whether such tests could be used to support a program of customized driving licenses. Such a program could limit driving for an individual, for example, to local streets in daylight where that person can be demonstrated to be safe rather than banning driving outright.

column36: Using the eye movement system to study brain function and dysfunction
column37: One of the most pressing challenges in neuroscience is to understand how human perception, memory, and action, become dysfunctional with neurological and psychiatric disease. We use eye movements, and pupil dilation systems to study intact and impaired sensory, motor, and cognitive processes, employing behavioural testing, neuroimaging, neurophysiology and computational modeling. Our approach has the potential to revolutionize not only our understanding of the brain, but also the diagnosis and rehabilitation of patients with brain disorders and development of animal models for therapeutic drug testing. We study non-human primates (NHPs) and compare recordings from single neurons in crucial regions of the cerebral cortex and brainstem to determine how active vision is both coordinated and controlled. NHPs have similar sensory, motor, and cognitive systems as humans, thus the knowledge gained from detailed neurophysiological and behavioural experiments can be used to search for behavioural biomarkers in neurological and psychiatric patient groups. Knowledge gained from patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) is now guiding a reverse translational effort: we are using our knowledge of patient pathology to generate and study a form of AD in NHPs. Because there has been great difficulty translating therapies that work in rodents to the specific human disease condition, shifting to NHPs with a brain similar to humans is crucial. In AD there is a build-up of toxic molecules in the brain called amyloid-beta oligomers (ABOs). We have shown that injection of these ABOs into the NHP brain leads to similar brain pathology as found in AD patients. We are now examining if there are changes in behaviour and cognition, and if so, how therapeutics can prevent or reverse those changes. The expected outcome of the proposed studies is the identification of a strategy that could slow AD progression and/or interrupt the onset of AD.

column36: Discrete dynamic complexes and phase-separated states of disordered proteins in neurobiology
column37: Proteins are the molecular machines that perform most biological functions. Some proteins have stable structure but others, called intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), are highly flexible. Disorder is very abundant in brain proteins, particularly those associated with neurological diseases, as flexibility is advantageous for protein interactions, which are essential for regulating key biological processes. We have pioneered studies of disordered proteins and their interactions, leading the development of methodology to study them and defining a new paradigm for protein binding that relies on dynamic interactions. Our studies of disordered proteins have been published in major journals (including Nature, Molecular Cell, PNAS, EMBO) and have led to 164 invitations to speak at conferences and universities, as well as 32 invitations to write review articles. Our work has changed the way proteins interactions are viewed, including those between two, multiple or even huge numbers of protein molecules, which can come together in a process called phase-separation to form liquid droplets involved in organizing the cell. Brain function is poorly understood and there are no effective drugs for major neurological disorders, such as autism, Parkinson's and Alzheimer's. The previously dominant static view of protein binding has hindered progress and we propose that our perspective focusing on the role of dynamic interactions of disordered proteins will fundamentally change the understanding of brain function. We will apply our considerable expertise and powerful methods to key disordered proteins involved in brain function and their interactions. We hypothesize that loss of regulation and rigidification of dynamic complexes of these disordered proteins leads to pathology in the brain. We will test this hypothesis and glean information to enable novel therapeutics for a variety of neurological diseases.

column36: Investigating mRNA translational control in the quest to cure human disease.
column37: Cancer is promoted by increased amounts of eIF4E, a protein that I discovered in 1978. The main role of eIF4E is to promote protein synthesis, which is a process that controls how much proteins are made, and is critical for cells to proliferate. It is now well established that eIF4E is present at high levels in many types of human cancer and may serve as a prognostic tumor marker. Moreover, eIF4E-binding proteins (4E-BPs) antagonize eIF4E activity, and act as tumor inhibitors. I, together with my research team, have not only discovered these proteins but have determined how they function and have defined their importance in many physiological and pathological conditions. Learning and memory is dependent on many of these proteins and mutant mice in which initiation of protein synthesis is enhanced demonstrate improvement in memory as compared to control mice. More recently, we discovered that eIF4E and 4E-BPs play important roles in causing an autism-like disease, and showed that by manipulating eIF4E activity we can reverse many abnormalities in mouse models of autism. We also demonstrated that eIF4E and 4E-BPs regulate circadian rhythms or an organism's "internal biological clock". The overarching research theme of my laboratory is the study of the mechanisms by which gene expression is controlled at the level of protein synthesis in health and disease. We will strive to discover drugs, in collaboration with pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies, to treat diseases that are caused by dysregulated protein synthesis including cancer, autism, Fragile X syndrome, and metabolic disorders.
