column36: Decoding gene regulation
column37: The goal of this research is to understand how human genes are regulated. The human genome consists of 3 billion bases, only 1% of which encodes protein-this is the proportion to which the "genetic code" applies. A much larger fraction - up to 10% by some estimates - functions to regulate the protein-coding genes. The details of how regulatory DNA works are still opaque, and how it is read by DNA binding proteins has been called the "second genetic code" - the next frontier in human genetics. We aim to crack this second code by studying the proteins that bind DNA, how they work together, and what they do to turn genes on and off, on a global level. The results of our research will enable us to make sense of how genes work normally, how they are impacted by common genetic variants, and how disease-causing mutations influence genetic regulatory programs.

column36: Contextual modulation of signalling pathways in human disease.
column37: All cells have the ability to receive outside messages and to communicate with neighboring cells. Genes encode proteins that undergo a series of molecular events, that allows a cell to translate the information and modify their behaviour to ensure that the cell functions properly in its environment. Many complex diseases such as cancer are the result of a disruptions in this information transfer referred to as cell signaling and cell-cell communication. In my laboratory, we study three signalling pathways: Wnt, TGFbeta (Transforming Growth Factor-beta) and Hippo pathways. Although molecularly distinct, these core pathways interact extensively and this crosstalk plays a key role in ensuring normal cell function under varying conditions. Failure in an individual pathway or in the way the pathways crosstalk, can lead to serious diseases such as cancer. My overall objective is to uncover the fundamental biology behind cell signalling and communication and to apply advanced, multidimensional screening approaches to identify novel protein targets and candidate drugs. The goal is to translate our findings so that they can be further developed as potential therapeutics to restore normal communication in diseased cells.

column36: Lipid nanomedicines for health and disease
column37: Current drugs suffer from two major limitations. First, they go everywhere in the body and only a small proportion arrives at a disease site such as a cancerous tumour. This results in toxic "side effects" due the effects of the drug on healthy tissue, as well as limited potency. Second, most drugs used today are "small molecules" that are small enough to penetrate into cells in the body to affect disease. The ability to use larger "genetic" drugs based on RNA and DNA to enable genetic therapies would have revolutionary consequences. Such drugs use natural regulatory processes in the body to treat disease leading to new potential treatments for most human diseases. The goal of this project is to develop "smart" nanomedicines that target small molecule drugs more accurately to disease sites and that enable genetic drugs to be used as therapeutics. These smart nanomedicines consist of the drug encapsulated into a nanoparticle that is administered by intravenous injection. These nanoparticles have dimensions of 100 nm or less, approximately 100 times smaller than a cell in the body. They are therefore able to permeate through most tissues and can be readily accumulated by most cells in the body. Specific goals of the project are to: 1) Development of triggered release lipid nanoparticle (LNP) systems to release therapeutic concentrations of small molecule drugs at sites of disease; 2) Development of LNP systems to extend applications of genetic drugs to extra-hepatic tissues; 3) Development of LNP systems containing genetic drugs that are not immunogenic; 4) Demonstrate efficacy of LNP systems in animal models of osteoporosis, diabetes, inflammation, neurological disorders, prostate cancer and leukemia. This research program builds on a strong record in drug development, as well as a well-established interdisciplinary network of collaborators in academia and industry.

column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a leading cause of cancer death and will increase with Canada's aging population. For the proposed program of research, my objectives are to 1) identify the best direct correspondence strategy to improve CRC screening program participation and 2) compare the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of two screening tests, Fecal Immunochemical Testing (FIT) and Flexible Sigmoidoscopy (FS). We have assembled a diverse team with expertise in epidemiology, clinical trials, population-health, and economic evaluation to ensure this research program produces high-quality rigorous research, and because our team of experts includes leaders of the CCC program, and other Canadian screening programs, our results will be translated into changes in screening programs across Canada. The support of Cancer Care Ontario through the CCC program, makes this proposal feasible; this is an important opportunity to leverage existing resources. This innovative program of research will produce effective strategies to improve participation in CRC screening through correspondence, and will evaluate the role of 2 important screening methods - our findings will be implemented in Ontario and disseminated nationally and to programs worldwide. With my leadership position at CCO and integration with policy makers, I am confident that this research will impact CRC screening policy and service delivery in Canada.

column36: Evaluating and Understanding the Impact of Tobacco Control Policies of the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control in a Rapidly Changing Global Tobacco Market: The International Tobacco Control Policy Evaluation Project
column37: This century, 1 billion people will die from tobacco use. The 2003 WHO treaty, the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC) obligates 180 countries (90% of the world's population) to implement policies to reduce global tobacco use. If fully implemented, the FCTC would be the greatest disease prevention initiative in history. But FCTC implementation has been slow, weakened by tobacco industry influence. The International Tobacco Control Policy Evaluation (ITC) Project is a global research program addressing the urgent need for strong evidence about FCTC policy impact by (1) evaluating FCTC policies, (2) understanding determinants of tobacco use vs. quitting, (3) identifying differences in global FCTC policy impact. The ITC research team of >100 tobacco control experts has conducted cutting edge evaluation studies of FCTC policies in 22 countries, home to >70% of the world's tobacco users. ITC has consistently reported evidence used globally to strengthen tobacco policies that improve population health (www.itcproject.org). Since its start 13 years ago, ITC data have been used to strengthen tobacco control policies in many countries, including Canada. We propose to continue this global project by: 1) continuing our rigorous evaluation of FCTC policies, focusing on regions where the tobacco industry is increasing its attention (e.g., Asia, Africa, Middle East); 2) expand ITC to evaluate new leading-edge policies (e.g., plain packaging, additive bans), 3) conduct the first-ever international cohort study of e-cigarettes to answer critical questions about their impact on tobacco use; and 4) strengthen dissemination efforts to bring our evidence to governments to support stronger tobacco control globally. ITC has advanced science, improved population health initiatives, and built strong collaborations with governments and health communities globally. We will strengthen our efforts to use science to combat the world's leading preventable cause of death and disease.

column36: Targeted radiopharmaceuticals to improve cancer diagnosis and treatment
column37: The purpose of this research is to develop novel imaging and therapeutic agents, which have radioactive tags ("radioisotopes") that bind to markers found specifically at the surface of cancer cells. This allows for them to be delivered to specific cancer sites, while avoiding healthy tissues. We then observe these markers using a sensitive imaging method known as positron emission tomography that can be combined with other imaging methods such as CT or MRI scans. We developed several compounds that home in on cancer cells, with very high accumulation relative to healthy surrounding tissues. As part of this research, we will continue to develop and improve new compounds to deliver a radioactive payload to cancer cells, for diagnosis or treatment. We will focus on introducing these radiopharmaceuticals in early phase clinical trials, to set the stage to evaluate them across centres in Canada. Some radioisotopes can be used for treatment, to deliver radiation that localizes to cancer from an intravenous injection. We will use potent radioisotopes called alpha emitters, to kill cancer cells while minimizing damage to normal organs. Imaging probes that have exceptional signal in tumours, with minimal accumulation in normal tissue, are very promising for this purpose. The anticipated outcomes of this research program will be the introduction of novel imaging agents in the clinic, to benefit patients suffering from breast, prostate and other cancers. Our radiotracers will be shared with facilities across Canada, with the goal of multi-centre clinical trials, and eventual introduction into clinical use. Canadians will benefit by gaining early access to new imaging technologies, as well as proper cancer staging with the goal of improving survival / reducing mortality for cancer patients. Ultimately, with the appropriate radioisotope, some of these compounds will also be suitable to treat patients with advanced cancers that do not respond to conventional approaches.

column36: Neural circuits underlying aberrant motivated behaviour
column37: The rising rate of obesity poses the biggest challenge to our health care system, such that obesity is complicated with many other comorbidities. Prevention of obesity and its comorbities is likely the best strategy to reduce health care costs and improve health. This is difficult in a society where easily accessible, inexpensive, highly palatable and caloric foods are abundant; we are forced to temper our 'heightened motivation' and engage our 'willpower' to prevent us from eating beyond satiety. The ventral tegmental area, and its inputs and outputs, engages individuals in motivated behaviour whereas the orbitofrontal cortex functions to assess the current value of rewards and updates our actions based on these values and underlies 'willpower'. We propose that once obesity sets in, the neural circuits that underlie 'heightened motivation' and 'willpower' are altered by obesity so that is harder to resist overeating palatable food. We will test how peripheral signals modulate these circuits in a lean and obese state. Thus a research strategy of understanding how these circuits are impacted with obesity provides a unique opportunity to really understand why we overeat. I have the unique expertise to address this problem as we employ techniques that can address changes at the synaptic, circuitry and behavioral level in lean and obese animals.

column36: Dynamic Imaging of the Musculoskeletal System: From Cells to Humans
column37: The focus of this program is the development and application of quantitative 3D imaging systems for applications related to musculoskeletal disease. Bone and joint conditions (including arthritis, osteoporosis, and trauma) cause morbidity, disability and huge economic impact, affecting over 11 million Canadians and costing the Canadian economy over $30B annually. This integrated program involves quantitative imaging at all scales - from microscopy to clinical imaging - with an emphasis on dynamic imaging of cells, animals, and human subjects under physiological loads. The goal is to improve our understanding of the way that skeletal tissues respond to mechanical loading and the conditions that lead to joint failure and degradation. Biomedical imaging is an important tool in this research, and we now have the opportunity to develop new systems, using state-of-the-art technologies, to obtain entirely new information about the skeletal system. The objectives of this program include the development of: new ways to image animals and tissue specimens during pre-clinical research; novel dynamic microscopy techniques; and new ways to look at moving and loaded joints in human subjects, during clinical trials and - ultimately - during routine health care delivery. This program will lead to new techniques, devices and tools that will improve our understanding of the initiation and progression of bone and joint conditions. Research findings from this program will have an impact on the development of novel therapies for musculoskeletal disease, mobilized through collaborations with clinical Program Experts. Our studies will help to answer important questions, such as: Why do some tissues (like cartilage) degrade in damaged joints? How does the mechanical micro-environment within skeletal tissues influence remodeling? Which conditions will respond to exercise, rehabilitative therapy, or joint-preserving surgery, and which will require joint replacement surgery?

column36: Imaging neural circuit dynamics in the awake developing brain: Identifying origins of neurodevelopmental disorders
column37: The primary goal of my research is to understand how brain circuits form during early development and how mutations and errors give rise to dysfunctional circuits that underlie common neurodevelopmental disorders such as Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD) and Epilepsy. The distinctive feature of our research approach is the development of multi-disciplinary and highly innovative imaging tools that combine electrophysiology, genetics and technology development in microscope design to see brain neural network activity and growth. In addition to the development of these tools, I also developed a leading model of vertebrate brain circuit formation by taking advantage of the unique development features of the albino Xenopus tadpole. Specifically, the external development and transparency of the embryos allows us to directly image brain circuit formation in live animals. Another example of our novel approach involves labeling individual brain neurons using single-cell electroporation, a technique I invented to tag neurons and control their gene expression so that we can image 3D growth in real time using ultrafast microscopes constructed in my lab. Our research has demonstrated that neural activity in response to external stimuli guides neuronal growth and connectivity in a manner that allows for self-organization and optimization in processing the input encountered during development. Our findings on brain circuit formation have provided important insight into the origins of ASD where a large proportion of associated gene mutations disrupt the function of synaptic proteins. We also created single-cell models of ASD to express mutant genes in order to test alterations in growth, synapse formation and encoding. In parallel, we study Epilepsy to test whether seizures hijack activity-driven growth events. Once we understand how normal and dysfunctional brain circuits are formed, we will develop and evaluate new interventions for preventative and corrective treatments.

column36: Molecular And Cellular Mechanisms Leading To Pancreatic Cancer Heterogeneity
column37: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is the fourth leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Canada. This cancer has been called a "silent killer" because it often does not cause symptoms until very late stages of the disease. At this point, treatment options are limited because the tumor is very resistant to chemotherapy and surgery is often not an option. There are, however, documented cases of patients responding exceptionally well to therapy. This variable therapeutic response emphasizes that there are differences between tumors, which is also known as heterogeneity. Pancreatic cancer heterogeneity has also been observed through differential expression of genes between tumors, but it is unclear what molecular or cellular mechanisms underlie the development of this variability. To improve disease outcomes, we need to better understand what causes this heterogeneity so that we can identify diagnostic tools to robustly identify tumor subtypes. If we can identify tumor subtypes, we can then develop effective treatments against those subsets. To begin to understand heterogeneity, we will use animal models to manipulate characteristics underlying tumor initiation and examine their impact on tumor heterogeneity. Briefly, we will examine whether combinations of different initiating cell types or gene mutations result in differences in tumor appearance, gene expression, or the type of additional mutations present in the tumor. We will then determine whether key differences identified in our models identify subsets of human tumors with distinct clinical outcomes. These studies will expand our understanding of factors underlying the development of tumor heterogeneity and also provide preclinical models to test novel therapeutic strategies potentially revealed by our studies. The knowledge generated by this research will aid identification of molecular markers that can reproducibly identify human PDAC subtypes with distinct therapeutic responses and clinical outcomes.

column36: Testing existing and new therapeutic interventions in a novel animal model of acute Spot Positive intracranial hemorrhage
column37: There is no effective treatment for bleeding into the brain or ICH. While we cannot do anything about the initial ICH, expansion of a bleed is the most important cause of bad outcome in ICH. We first described the Spot Sign which, when seen in ICH, strongly predicts expansion. We developed clinical trials (that are ongoing) selecting patients for treatment with drugs that stop bleeding based on the presence or absence of the Spot sign. There is evidence now however to suggest that this approach is flawed as the Spot sign represents varying rates of ICH expansion rather than an all-or-none situation. In other words, some Spot positive bleeding may be so quick that no medical treatment will be effective while others so slow that no treatment is needed because no meaningful expansion will occur. The problem is that current studies will not tell us what rates of bleeding are responsive to existing medicines and will likely fail because we did not consider the rate of bleeding. We have therefore developed a unique animal model that most closely mimics the Spot positive bleeding that occurs in humans. By aiming ultrasound beams from outside the head to specific brain regions we are able to damage the walls of small vessels causing them to rupture. By controlling the power of the ultrasound delivered we can adjust the rate of bleeding by targeting different vessel sizes. We propose using this model to test existing (medicines) and new (new medicines, using ultrasound to stop bleeding and surgical) ways to minimize expansion of bleeds based on the rate of bleeding associated with Spot positive bleeds. Once the ranges of bleeding rates responsive to our proposed medicines and novel treatments are established we can test these in humans using existing imaging sequences that measure rates of bleeding. By selecting patients based on these measures we can tailor treatment to the particular rate of bleeding ensuring better outcomes, less dependency and lower cost to society

Canada, though one of the driving forces behind the CRC, has consistently fallen short of the desired level of compliance with and reporting on CRC. While reporting difficulties might be explained by Canada's federal structure, it is also possible that inadequate reports reflect inadequate compliance. A comprehensive monitoring tool can facilitate the compliance and reporting. This project is intended to help to align Canadian internal processes with our international obligations and commitments to the CRC, by creating a monitoring and accountability tool. We propose creation of the GlobalChild (GC), a comprehensive child rights monitoring platform based on a framework of indicators designed to correlate government policy, implementation structures and processes with children's health and developmental outcomes. In addition to providing a fully contextualised database available to different levels of government and researchers, GC would address consistent weaknesses in Canadian CRC reporting. Ultimately it will provide credible evidence to evaluate existing government service delivery against international standards and to guide the development of more effective policies and procedures. Based on our decade of work with the UN Committee, we have developed and tested the "Early Childhood Rights Indicators" (ECRI), which is a CRC monitoring tool for children 0-8 years old. We have demonstrated the usefulness of the concept and created international interest in both the ECRI and the possibility of a tool like GC. We intend to build on this to create GC, a fully digitized, bilingual tool for all children in Canada, paying particular attention to our Indigenous children.

column36: The impact of political conflict on the dynamics of sex work and the HIV/STI and HCV epidemic in Ukraine
column37: Female sex workers (FSW) often bear a high burden of HIV and in order for HIV, sexually transmitted (STI) and Hepatitis C (HCV) prevention programs to effectively control these epidemics, they need to understand how sex work operates so they can design and deliver interventions that match the needs of those most at risk. Sex work is not static; it is constantly adapting to the local context. At times of conflict, the organization, pattern and practice of sex work may change; and as a result, the HIV/STI/HCV risks faced by FSW and their clients may also change. The goal of this project is to examine the impact of the conflict in Ukraine on sex work and the spread of HIV/HCV in the FSW/client populations. This project will be conducted in Dnipropetrovsk (DNK), 200km from the conflict zone in the eastern region of Ukraine. DNK is a strategic location as frontline Ukrainian forces regularly pass through this city. DNK has also recently become a destination for many internally-displaced people. Moreover, having the highest HIV rates in Europe, a further rise in HIV cases in Ukraine will have important implications beyond its borders. There is very limited data about how conflict affects FSW and their HIV/STI/HCV risks. Building on our previous work which examined early HIV risk among young women and FSW in DNK (a project that was ongoing when conflict first erupted), our team is uniquely positioned to carry out this 5-year study. We will use complementary methods to characterize how conflict shapes FSW's daily lives and influences sex work and HIV/STI/HCV risks, and to estimate the extent to which conflict alters the spread of HIV and HCV among FSW and clients. Our study will generate important information for our Ukrainian partners who design and implement HIV prevention programs in DNK as well as address an important knowledge gap globally.

column36: The physiological role of the axo-myelinic synapse
column37: Multiple sclerosis, stroke and spinal cord injury are common and devastating human disorders. The central nervous system is composed of two different types of tissue: gray matter, which comprises the nerve cell bodies, and white matter, which represents the nerve fibers connecting nerve cells to each other. Nerve fibers in the brains of mammals are highly specialized, being very thin (to pack millions of fibers into a small volume) and wrapped by an insulating fatty material called myelin to prevent short circuits. How this all-important myelin is damaged in human neurological disorders, and how the nerve fiber tells the myelin to start wrapping and insulating it, remain mysteries. This ongoing project has focused on chemical communication between axons (nerve fibers) and their myelin sheaths. We discovered that axons signal their myelin sheaths using chemical transmitters in a way that is very similar to how nerve cells communicate: through a chemical "synapse". This new axon-myelin synapse causes damage to myelin when excessively activated, and may be the first step in myelin loss in MS for instance. This project will explore the purpose of this axon-myelin synapse: why do axons need to talk to their myelin sheaths? What might myelin do for its axon when it senses a lot of electrical traffic traveling down the axon? We propose that myelin supports its axon by physically transferring material essential for the axon's long term survival. A breakdown of this communication and transfer may underlie diverse diseases such as MS, cerebral palsy and even psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia and autism.

column36: Restoring binocular vision in amblyopia by through engagement of stimulus-specific adaptive compensatory mechanisms
column37: Amblyopia is characterized by the loss or attenuation of vision in one eye despite the eye being normal and healthy. Currently, most approaches to understanding amblyopia treat this disorder as one where all vision in the amblyopic eye is suppressed. This idea holds insofar as it describes the main symptoms of amblyopia, but it does not explain the many ways in which vision in the amblyopic eye is integrated with that of the dominant eye. For example, peripheral vision is largely unaffected in amblyopia, as is vision for more blurred patterns or moving patterns. We propose a different paradigm for understanding amblyopia--we propose that amblyopia involves the selective integration of information from the two eyes, a process we call adaptive compensation. The process is adaptive because it requires suppression to be modulated by the specific stimuli present in a given scene, and compensatory because it seeks to make up for vision lost in the amblyopic eye. The adaptive compensatory model explains many features of amblyopia and makes important predictions as to how vision in amblyopia can be improved through training.

column36: A Randomized Trial of Regional Radiotherapy in Luminal A Breast Cancer
column37: Studies have shown that radiotherapy to the chest wall and regional nodes following mastectomy and radiotherapy to regional nodes after breast conserving surgery reduces the risk of recurrence and breast cancer mortality in women with node positive breast cancer. While these benefits are important, it is recognized that there is a large group of patients with node positive breast cancer who are unlikely to recur or benefit from radiotherapy. Biomarkers are increasingly used to identify breast cancers that are likely to recur or respond to treatment. The luminal A breast cancer subtype has a low risk of recurrence and is less likely to respond to chemotherapy. Recent evidence from MA.20 a randomized trial of radiotherapy to the regional nodes supports that such cancers were less likely to respond to radiotherapy. This suggests that regional radiotherapy may not be necessary in patients with node positive luminal A breast cancer. The objective of this study is to determine if radiotherapy to the chest wall and regional lymph nodes following mastectomy or radiotherapy to the regional nodes following breast conserving surgery can be safely omitted in women with 1-3 positive axillary lymph nodes and luminal A cancer. An international multicentre randomized trial will be performed. Patients treated by mastectomy will be randomized to radiotherapy to the chest wall and regional nodes or not. Patients treated by breast conserving surgery will be randomized to radiotherapy to regional nodes or not. Radiation following surgery is associated with significant short-term and long-term side effects. The luminal A subtype of breast cancer accounts for up to 40% of patients with node positive breast cancer. If regional radiotherapy could be avoided in this group of patients it would have substantial benefits not only for women with breast cancer and their families, but the health care system at large.

column36: Resolution of inter- and intra-tumoral heterogeneity in DLBCL using mass cytometry
column37: Recent work has shown that patients with cancer often have tumors that are composed of several different types of cancer cells, each with a slightly different set of genetic mutations. This variability, or "heterogeneity", means that successful therapy must target not just one, but perhaps several different cancers at the same time. As well, there is renewed appreciation for the importance of the patient's own immune system in defeating cancer, and some therapies are even focused at reawakening the patient's immune cells to attack the cancer. Thus, cancer can no longer be regarded simply as an overgrowth of one particular type of cell, but may better be considered as a complex ecosystem with multiple interconnected and constantly evolving parts. In order to diagnose cancer more accurately and to treat it more effectively, it is important that we understand the full complexity of the tumor ecosystem. We propose here to use a cutting-edge technology called mass cytometry , or "CyTOF", to examine patients' tumors one cell at a time in order to get an ultra high definition, widescreen picture of the problem at hand. We will also use the most up-to-date genomics tools to understand which genes are mutated in which cells and how those cells are functioning abnormally. We will use this information to develop a new, cost-effective, same-day test that can be provided to each and every patient and will help doctors to better understand what sort of tumor is present, if and how well the patient's immune system is responding, and what the best treatment options may be.

column37: Forty percent of patients that require dialysis for kidney failure die within three years mostly due to heart disease. In patients without kidney disease, spironlactone reduces heart scarring which reduces heart related deaths and hospitalizations. Kidney failure appears to trigger progressive changes in the heart that lead to heart scarring and ultimately heart related deaths. It therefore makes sense that spironolactone will help patients with kidney failure. Although spironolactone is promising, there are no large studies to tell us if it helps patients live longer or better lives. In addition, current dialysis does not effectively clear all toxins from the blood the way natural kidneys do. Some of the molecules that are not cleared build up and can affect the blood vessels and the heart. A new type of dialysis filter, the Theranova, effectively clears many of these potential toxins. However, it is not clear if removing these toxins will improve patient's lives or if there are potential negative consequences. We will perform a large study in several countries that will give physicians and patients the information they need to determine if spironolactone or the Theranova reduces heart related deaths and hospitalizations and/or reduce the symptoms of dialysis. We call this study the Aldosterone antagonism and enhanced Clearance for Health Improvement EValuation in End-stage renal disease (ACHIEVE).

column36: Development and evaluation of a decision support tool to guide theory-informed knowledge translation practice in health care
column37: Efforts to change behaviour, practice or policy in health care can be challenging. One approach known to improve the likelihood for success is to apply appropriate theories when designing and evaluating knowledge translation (KT) interventions. Compared to models and frameworks, theories uniquely attempt to explain how and why certain results are achieved and identify 'active ingredients' influencing implementation success. Despite this, evidence suggests that theories are used infrequently in KT practice and support tools are needed to help address this challenge. The objectives of this research are to systematically identify all existing KT theories, and use the findings to develop and test an online tool to guide researchers and front-line implementers (i.e. individuals working on or supporting KT activities in health care organisations) through the process of selecting and applying appropriate theory to inform their KT activities. Phase 1 will include a systematic scoping review to identify all existing KT theories. Phase 2 will involve focus groups and interviews with end-users of the tool to determine their specific needs. We will use the needs of the end-users (Phase 2 results) and the volume and content of Phase 1 results to determine the focus for the tool; specifically, it could focus on theories addressing the entire implementation process or on theories for one or more sub-processes such as scalability and sustainability of interventions. Phase 3 will evaluate the usability of the tool and Phase 4 will consist of a pilot randomized trial to further test the acceptability of the tool. This research is unique because it will be the first comprehensive review of all KT theories, and will result in the creating and testing of a tool to support the use of KT science to inform KT practice. The tool has the potential to benefit the health care system by helping users develop better strategies and achieve more success when implementing evidence into practice.

column37: Gliomas affect approximately 2800 Canadians yearly, the majority being aggressive, high-grade glioblastomas with dismal prognosis. Although there has been progress in the treatment of GBM as a result of a treatment regimen that combines maximum surgical resection with radiotherapy and concurrent and adjuvant chemotherapy, five-year survival rates are only a mere 10%. Thus the current therapies can be considered palliative at best. This need is further emphasized based on a recent study from the United States demonstrating that brain and CNS tumors represent the number one cancer for years of potential life lost of adults, highlighting the major societal impact of this disease. This proposal focuses on the brain environment and how it impacts brain tumor progression. For several decades, therapeutic approaches have focused almost entirely on the cancer cells. While this strategy has led to a better understanding of the disease, advances in the clinic for patients with brain tumours remains disappointing despite the development of molecularly targeted drugs and survival is still measured in months. While there are a large number of potential contributing factors for clinical failure including tumor heterogeneity, and lack of effective drug delivery across the blood-brain-barrier, we propose that the unique microenvironment for which the glioma cells reside within the brain is a major contributor to the complexity and challenges of treating this disease. The tumor microenvironment consists of cells, soluble factors, signaling molecules and extracellular matrix that can be co-opted by the cancer cells to fuel tumor growth as well as contribute to therapeutic resistance. This proposal is in line with the emerging shift in therapeutic emphasis from the glioma cells that contain numerous genetic mutations to one of modulating and/or targeting the normal cellular environment to suppress tumor growth and prolong overall survival of glioma patients.

column37: One could compare our genome to a large library that contains numerous shelves, each with an extraordinary large number of books. The combined information contained in all the books represents our genetic information and is required to make us who we are. In this paraphrase, the bookshelves represent our chromosomes. Due to the heavy use of the books and because the whole library, including the shelves, need to be duplicated each time a cell divides, there is continued wear and tear on the terminal bookends on the shelves. Without continued upkeep and repair, the bookends will eventually become dysfunctional, causing books to fall off the shelves and get lost. The telomeres and the telomerase enzyme that we study are, respectively, the bookends and the maintenance operator for the bookends. In real life, it is essential to ensure the integrity of the ends of our chromosomes. The telomerase enzyme is composed of several subunits; two of which, one protein and one RNA molecule are required for the enzyme to work in a minimalistic test-tube system. Inadequate supply of any of the components, causing instability of the chromosomes, is associated with aging and human disease, foremost cancer, but also dyskeratosis congenita (DKC) and other congenital disorders now called telomeropathies. Using a simple but powerful model system, we propose to investigate the biology of telomeres and the telomerase enzyme. In particular, we plan to identify all the components, learn more about how they interact, are regulated and localized. Most importantly, we will determine when and how telomerase operates at its most important location, namely on telomeres. Given that telomere and telomerase function and regulation are highly conserved across many species, from yeast to humans, our studies will provide critical clues and input into how telomere biology could be exploited for the benefit of human health.

column36: Molecular and cellular biology of T regulatory cells
column37: The goal of my research is to understand how our immune system regulates itself and to use this information to develop new ways to treat patients with immune-related diseases, such as autoimmunity or transplant rejection. A healthy immune system must strike a balance between attacking infectious or dangerous substances while not reacting to our own cells and tissues. This delicate balancing act is called immune tolerance. Both autoimmune diseases and transplant complications are caused by disrupted immune tolerance. At present, immunosuppressive drugs are our only treatment for these conditions. Yet these drugs suppress all immune responses, putting patients at risk of infection and cancer, often without controlling their disease. We need to find better ways to prevent harmful immune responses. I am an expert is the study of a type of white blood cell called T regulatory cells, or Tregs, which coordinate immune responses and maintain immune tolerance. My work has defined how Tregs develop and function, and led to clinical trials to test use of Tregs as a cell therapy in transplantation and autoimmunity. I developed methods to monitor the presence of Tregs in blood and tissues, allowing more precise measurement of immune tolerance. If used as a treatment, Tregs could control pathological immune responses without altering healthy immune balance. Towards this aim, the next stage of my research has 3 goals, to: 1) create "designer" Tregs that are engineered to be active only in the presence of a transplant and test their ability to prevent transplant rejection and preserve normal immunity; 2) design new ways to alter Tregs so their function is tailored to specific disease contexts; and 3) identify biological pathways that regulate Tregs, so that they can be targeted for new treatment options. My research will enable new Treg-based therapies to prevent and treat the many chronic diseases that are caused by a failure of immune tolerance.

column36: Functional Protein Dynamics in Health and Disease
column37: Protein molecules play critical roles in cellular function and they catalyze many of the biochemical reactions that are necessary for life. The three-dimensional shapes of these molecules are necessary for guiding proper function and they can change with time due to interactions with other molecules, during the process of carrying out specific functions, or simply the result of random fluctuations. Thus, static pictures of proteins that have been generated to date often do not completely explain results from functional biological assays, nor do they necessarily illuminate the path for engineering new functions or for rational drug design. The goal of this research is to develop new Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) Spectroscopy based techniques for studying motional processes in proteins and for relating these to function and to apply the methodology to important protein systems that are implicated in cancer, neurodegeneration and amyloidosis. They will inform how function can be manipulated by changing how parts of proteins move in relation to each other and provide clues about how to design, in a rational manner, new classes of drug molecules. Advances that are made in the laboratory will be translated into potential drugs through collaborations with leading medicinal chemists and clinician scientists.

column36: Regulation of postsynaptic expression and function of ionotropic neurotransmitter receptors
column37: Normal function of the brain depends on tightly regulated communication between neurons. The neurons communicate with one another through junction sites called synapses via "synaptic transmission". During this process, neurotransmitter molecules are released from presynaptic neurons and bind to receptors on the postsynaptic neurons. Deregulated synaptic transmission is believed to be at the root of many brain diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, schizophrenia, anxiety disorders, epilepsy, and stroke. I believe that by better understanding the mechanisms controlling the efficacy of the synaptic transmission among neurons there is the potential to identify targets and thereby to create better therapeutics for these brain disorders. Theoretically, the strength of synaptic transmission can be regulated by altering either the presynaptic neurotransmitter release or the responsiveness of postsynaptic neurotransmitter receptor. Research in our laboratory has focused on the regulatory mechanisms which determine the responsiveness of postsynaptic ionotropic receptors. Strong evidence accumulated from our work and other labs suggest that both function and number of these receptors may be rapidly altered. These rapid changes may be responsible for the pathogenesis of many brain disorders. Currently, we are proposing experiments to investigate how rapid changes in the function and number of postsynaptic receptors, therefore synaptic transmission strength, is regulated. The main objective of our research is to identify molecular processes underlying the regulation of the efficacy of synaptic transmission. Through these fundamental investigations we aim to identify new therapeutic targets and develop new drugs to treat brain disease. Since inter-neuronal communication is a pivotal component of brain function and the alteration of this process underlies many disorders, our proposed studies can be expected to lead to better treatment for these diseases

column36: Alternatives to antibiotics: New strategies for treating multi-drug resistant infections
column37: Antibiotics are the most successful medical intervention in human history. They are critical for preventing and treating life-threatening infections. A lack of effective antibiotics would lead to difficulties with major surgeries, chemotherapy, transplantations, and early-term births; even minor injuries could become infected and deadly. Thus the relentless and concerning increase in multi-drug resistance to antibiotics in the face of a inadequate pipeline for new antibiotics has caused great concern for public health officials and the general public. Indeed, in Sept 2016, all 193 member countries of the United Nations declared antimicrobial resistance "the biggest threat to modern medicine". Here we will investigate the mechanisms of adaptive, multiple-antibiotic resistance in the important pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa, one of the most difficult to treat bacterial "Superbugs" in our society. Adaptive resistance is a feature of specific bacterial "lifestyles" that are triggered during growth in patients; we will investigate the mechanisms of such resistance in the context of growth circumstances that occur during infections. To tackle adaptive and acquired resistance and provide new therapies that address the poor success of modern antibiotic discovery, we will then develop three alternatives to antibiotics: 1) Novel anti-biofilm peptides to treat adaptive multiple-antibiotic resistance due to the growth of bacteria on body surfaces as multicellular colonies termed biofilms (representing two thirds of all hospital infections); 2) Peptides that enhance the anti-infection properties of the immune system; and 3) Compounds that will reverse the inability of the immune system to respond to pathogens in patients with sepsis (causes 8% of all deaths worldwide). A feature of these strategies is that they will assist in making available antibiotics work better. Our research will move our discoveries to clinical testing during the funding period.

column36: Leveraging Essential Genes and Genetic Networks to Cripple Human Fungal Pathogens
column37: The impact of fungal pathogens on human health is devastating. They infect billions of people around the globe, and kill more than 1.5 million each year. The most vulnerable are people with reduced immune function, such as those with HIV or those undergoing immune suppressing treatments for cancer or organ transplants. One of the leading fungal pathogens of humans is Candida albicans. It kills ~40% of people suffering from bloodstream infections. Treating these infections is extremely difficult, as fungi are closely related to humans and there are very few drugs that kill the fungus but not the host. With the emergence of drug resistance, it is now critical to develop new therapeutic strategies. To address this important clinical need, it is critical to uncover the genes and genetic networks that are required for the pathogen to survive and cause disease. We are one of the first academic labs to obtain a powerful resource that will allow us to test the function of almost every gene in the C. albicans genome. Through collaboration with a pharmaceutical company, we now have access to the largest library of C. albicans mutants, which enables genetic depletion of ~40% of genes in the genome. We will use sophisticated computational approaches to predict essential genes, and will expand this resource to cover them all. This resource provides an unprecedented opportunity to identify which genes are essential for the pathogen, and to determine their molecular function and interactions. We will use this platform to characterize the impact of reducing the dosage of each gene on growth, cellular physiology, and traits associated with the capacity to cause disease. We will perform state-of-the-art screens to identify new molecules that target essential genes, and will evaluate their therapeutic potential. This research will reveal new approaches to cripple the pathogen, and enable development of novel therapeutic strategies to improve clinical outcome for millions of people.

column36: Optogenetic visualization and manipulation of neural activity
column37: Life on the earth's surface is bathed in the white light of the Sun. This light provides energy to support life through photosynthesis, but life on earth has evolved to harness light in a myriad of other critical ways. For example, receptors in our eyes respond to certain wavelengths of light, such as those reflected from the corals of a tropical reef. The receptors send electrical signals to our brain that we perceive as colour. We are harnessing light as a research tool to understand how our nervous systems work. Light-based tools will advance our understanding of many nervous system disorders, such as neurodegenerative diseases, brain damage from stroke, and chronic pain. Biologists can now borrow natural systems that interact with light and transplant them in mice and other organisms that serve as models of human disease. These transplanted systems are called "optogenetic tools," and they have revolutionized our ability to visualize and manipulate biology in live animals. They have a particularly big impact in neuroscience. Optogenetic tools now help neuroscientists to watch the electrical signals from thousands of individual neurons in a model animal's brain. They also let researchers effectively write a memory into a mouse brain using light - a capability that was in the realm of science fiction until just a few years ago. Knowledge that we gain from these studies in animals with optogenetic tools can be applied to treating nervous system disorders in humans. My research program develops new optogenetic tools for neuroscience research. My speciality is borrowing the proteins that give coral their colour and altering them to create innovative research tools. One theme of my research is equipping neuroscientists to visualize the chemical communication between neurons of the brain that increases or decreases neuron activity. Another theme is creating more subtle and specific methods to activate key biochemical processes in neurons with light.

column36: Microbial Biofilms: Molecular mechanisms to therapeutics
column37: Bacteria typically live as collections of cells attached to a moist surface surrounded by a slimy coating. This mode of growth is called a biofilm and is beneficial to bacteria because the self-produced slimy coating protects them from antibiotics and our immune system, and provides a perfect environment for them to evolve and acquire antibiotic resistance. This protection and the bacteria's ability to grow on a large range of different types of moist surfaces, including human cells, make biofilms a major medical problem. Biofilms are responsible for ~80% of all infections in the body. This includes infections of the inner ear, urinary tract and pulmonary system, and those associated with contaminated medical devices such as catheters, heart valves and prosthetic joints. The failure of current antibiotics to clear biofilm infections results in serious health complications for patients and highlights the urgent need for effective new therapies to treat these often-fatal infections. A critical component of the protective biofilm coating are long chains of sugars units. Biofilms cannot form if the bacteria are unable to produce these sugar chains or when the chemical composition of the sugars is altered. Our goal is to understand how the bacteria make these sugar chains and to use this knowledge to develop novel anti-biofilm therapeutics. Our goal is to develop two types of therapeutics: the first would be used to prevent biofilm formation and hence eliminate the life-threatening complications that frequently occur; while the second would be used to treat and clear biofilms, thus improving health outcomes for individuals suffering from chronic infections.

Moreover, this evidence must be integrated and communicated in a manner that is accessible to the general population to affect change not only through regulatory decision making but also through individual-level behavioural changes. Our research program will address these issues in a number of important ways. The first theme will focus on developing new exposure models for airborne pollutants in metropolitan areas. One example includes combustion-related nanoparticles that have been shown to reach the brain and may contribute to neurological illnesses. The second theme will apply these new models to population-based cohorts to evaluate population health risks. The third theme will focus on panel studies of local environmental health issues that can inform policy interventions. One example includes evaluating the impact of air pollution from residential wood burning on children's health. The fourth component will integrate knowledge across program areas to provide direct dissemination of results to government stakeholders and the public. Our vision is to identify and evaluate new environmental risk factors for chronic diseases to decrease the burden of illness associated with environmental contaminants originating from human activities and climate change.

column37: Most mutations in human DNA that cause disease are not in sequences that code for protein but rather in regulatory sequences that determine whether particular proteins, or parts of proteins, are made. column36: Sustaining evidence-based chronic disease management
column37: Canada is a nation of pilot projects, with a lot of resources spent on implementation but failure to address sustainability. column36: Regenerative biomaterials in vascularized tissue engineering
column37: Our goal is to create new medical devices to address unmet needs in medicine. The materials that are used to build current devices provoke a scar which prevents their integration with the host. This is a fundamental challenge to tissue engineering in which tissue constructs are created to act as "spare body parts" to replace diseased tissues and organs. Such constructs require blood vessels in order to supply the tissue with oxygen and enable tissue survival and integration. We have pioneered two approaches to forming the needed blood vessels. In one method ("modular tissue engineering") collagen gel pieces are coated with endothelial cells, the cells that line blood vessels. However, vessel formation is slow and the resulting vessels are imperfect. Here we address the barriers (low oxygen, inflammation) to successful vessel formation in order to accelerate this process. We are using this approach to enable under the skin delivery of pancreatic islets to resolve the issues with this promising treatment for the 1% of Canadians who live with insulin dependent (type 1) diabetes. We have also discovered that materials that incorporate methacrylic acid cause blood vessels to grow once the material is implanted. This vascular regenerating effect is unique among biomaterials. Unfortunately we don't understand why we are getting blood vessels (instead of the conventional "scar" response), although we have some clues as to the origins of this seemingly "magical" effect. We propose to deepen our understanding of the magic by using a method that analyses the critical means by which cells respond to changes in their environment (here our unique biomaterial). We expect these results will help us design better materials and better devices for use in diabetes (e.g., better glucose sensors) and in other situations which are as yet precluded by the limitations of existing materials.

column36: Optimizing cardiac energy metabolism to treat heart disease
column37: The very high energy demands of the heart are met by continous metabolism of sugars, fatty acids, ketones and amino acids. Normally, there is a balance between the use of these fuels. However, in clinical conditions such as heart failure, myocardial ischemia (i.e. such as following a heart attack), obesity or diabetes, energy production in the heart switches towards an excessive use of fatty acids. This excessive use of fatty acids causes the heart to be less efficient at using energy, which can compromise heart function. Our research has shown that a major contributor to this excessive use of fatty acids is due to changes in the levels of a molecule called malonyl CoA within the heart muscle, and due to an increase in a process caused post-translational acetylation. The studies proposed in this grant application will determine the cellular mechanisms responsible for how malonyl CoA levels and acetylation are regulated in the heart, and how alterations in these processes alters fatty acid use by the heart. We will also determine if preventing the switch from sugar to fatty acid metabolism, can be used as a therapeutic strategy to protect the heart in heart failure or following myocardial ischemia. We will also examine the molecular mechanisms responsible for the maturation of cardiac fatty acid oxidation following birth, and what impact congenital heart defects (that are seen in approximately 2% of infants) has on this maturation of energy metabolism. These experimental studies will be translated into clinical studies in which energy metabolism is optimized to improve heart function in patients with heart failure. Understanding how energy metabolism is regulated in heart should lead to the development of therapies that optimize energy use by the heart and decrease the severity of heart disease.

column37: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) remains a global health challenge. Despite the significant advances made over the past decades with respect to our understanding of how HIV causes AIDS, the hope for a definitive cure has been frustrated by the seemingly endless propensity of HIV to subvert host defenses and to persist in long-lived viral reservoirs (VR) that cannot be eliminated by current antiretroviral therapies (ART). HIV eludes host immune defenses and establishes VRs in part because it encodes a set of small accessory proteins, whose function is to overcome various types of antiviral immune response. My Team discovered and characterized two of the six accessory proteins encoded by HIV and we are world leaders in understanding the role of these virulence factors in HIV transmission, pathogenesis and persistence. Given their crucial roles in overcoming host defense mechanisms, these accessory proteins are attractive targets for the design of HIV cure strategies aimed at eradicating persistent HIV infection. Our research program will focus primarily on two of the accessory proteins encoded by HIV-1, namely Viral protein U (Vpu) and Viral Protein R (Vpr), to unravel the full spectrum of their activities and better define their functions in HIV persistence, to elucidate how they operate at the molecular and cellular levels and to identify new areas of their biology that are applicable to therapeutic intervention. This work will uncover viral and host targets for HIV persistence reversal and provide new insights that will inform and guide HIV cure strategies. While conducting these studies, our dynamic and forward-looking training and mentoring program will provide trainees with a conceptually and technically deep experience and skills that are sought by employers in academia, government and the private sector

column36: Innate immunity and its disruption by microbial and genetic factors
column37: Approximately 1/150 Canadians have Inflammatory Bowel Diseases (IBD) like Crohn's Disease and Ulcerative Colitis. These diseases devastate affected individuals and their families, and significantly burden our health care system. IBD are caused by a combination of genetic and environmental factors, including how our bodies interact with bacteria. Genetic studies link IBD to innate immunity. Innate immunity encompasses the tissue and cellular defenses that protect us from infection. Innate immunity allows us to co-exist with the many 'good' bacteria in our guts, and to kill the 'bad' bacteria that we encounter. The factors that regulate innate immunity and its alterations in IBD are not clear. Our research will examine innate immunity in three ways. First, we will study a critical component of innate immunity that is linked to IBD, called autophagy. Autophagy is a process that delivers cellular contents to specialized compartments called lysosomes, where they are broken down. This process protects our cells during stressful conditions like bacterial infections. We will build 'maps' of how the autophagy machinery interacts with other cellular components under normal conditions, and how it changes in IBD. Second, we will study how two bad bacteria, Salmonella and Listeria, hide inside our cells during infection. These bacteria use toxins that disrupt our innate immune defenses, and can teach us how innate immunity is regulated. Third, we will study genes linked to IBD, and ask how they change autophagy and other innate immune defenses. Our studies will advance scientific understanding of how innate immunity controls our interactions with bacteria, and will provide knowledge that can be used to develop new ways to treat IBD.

column36: Neighbourhood Design and Physical Activity: Generating Evidence to Inform Healthy Public Policies
column37: Creating health supportive environments has the potential to improve population-level health, including increasing physical activity participation in Canadian adults. column36: Targeting sleep to optimize brain recovery and slow neurodegeneration
column37: Breakthrough discoveries in rodents have revealed that sleep is crucial for generating neurons, strengthening synapses, and clearing brain waste products. In the next 5 years, I will identify patients with sleep apnea at risk of neurodegeneration. I will produce new evidence regarding the neurodegenerative profile of treated vs. untreated patients. My research program has the potential to transform and improve clinical care protocols by including sleep management among treatment priorities.

column36: The intertwined biology, pathobiology and translational implications of factor VIII and von Willebrand factor.
column37: The two most common inherited bleeding disorders, von Willebrand disease (VWD) and hemophilia A (HA), are the result of deficiencies and/or dysfunction of two critical proteins in the human blood clotting system - von Willebrand factor (VWF) and factor VIII (FVIII). column36: Novel Approaches Directed to Prevention and Treatment of Huntington Disease
column37: Huntington disease (HD) is an inherited brain disease that affects approximately 1 in 7300 people in the Western world. HD is caused by a mutation in one copy of the HTT gene, which produces a toxic mutant huntingtin (mHTT) protein. This mutant protein disrupts many vital cellular functions and is ultimately responsible for the brain cell death associated with HD. There is no treatment for this disease. We propose targeting different steps of the disease process, including suppression of the mutant HTT gene, increasing clearance of the mutant protein, and inhibiting its toxic effects to advance complementary therapies for treating HD. One therapeutic strategy to prevent production of mHTT is to silence (or turn off) the mutant HTT gene using antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeted to genetic variations found in mutant HTT. Our goal is to develop multiple ASO drugs targeting the most common genetic variations in HD patients, maximizing the number that could be treated through gene silencing of mutant HTT. ASOs are unable to enter the brain when delivered in the blood and must be injected directly into the fluid that bathes the brain. This procedure is invasive, and ASOs delivered this way do not reach all susceptible areas of the brain. Therefore, we are developing new non-invasive ways to enhance delivery of ASOs to the brain. Another strategy is to reduce levels of mHTT protein by increasing its degradation in the cell through a process called autophagy. Autophagy is abnormally reduced in HD which may be due to altered protein modifications of mHTT. We will target specific mechanisms that could increase clearance of mHTT from the cell and reduce its toxicity. Our final therapeutic strategy is to target pathways that are disrupted by the presence of toxic mHTT. We are investigating the effect of modifying molecular components of these pathways using small molecules to promote protection and survival of brain cells, and in the long run improve patient outcomes.

column36: Beyond the Exome: Decoding the Next Frontier of the Rare Disease Genome
column37: Around 7000 rare genetic diseases (RDs) affect more than 1 million Canadians, most of them children. When considered together, RDs are a common cause of disability, early mortality, and healthcare costs. Over the past several years my research program has efficiently examined the protein-coding portion of the genome (~1%) to understand the cause of many RDs; however, as many as 60% of patients remain undiagnosed after this analysis. These patients often undergo a diagnostic journey involving multiple specialist consultations, imaging studies, invasive investigations, and other laboratory and genetic tests; a slow (5 to 30 years for 25%) process referred to as the diagnostic odyssey. These families are faced with significant uncertainty surrounding treatment, prognosis and the chances of future children or other family members also being affected. The goal of my research is to understand the genetic cause of unsolved RDs to end the diagnostic journey for as many Canadians with RD as possible. Given the rarity of all of the diseases we study, my program will help design and employ international RD patient data-sharing so that we, and indeed all RD scientists, can readily identify families with the same disease and changes in the same gene to prove causality. To look more broadly, my program will use the latest and most comprehensive technologies to examine a person's entire genome to identify the genetic cause of unsolved RDs. Finally, my program will develop new tests to determine whether a given genetic change has an impact on protein function. The outputs of my RD research program will lead to new insights into human biology in health and disease, develop novel diagnostic tools and tailor management to improve the care for Canadians with RDs, while enhancing global synergy, thereby ensuring continuing Canadian leadership in this realm.

column37: It was always believed that the adult brains cannot regenerate damaged brain tissue and that brain cells (neurons) must last throughout life. Recently, it was found that the adult brain contains active stem cells and progenitor cells, which have the capacity to regenerate new neurons. A major challenge is that most neural stem cells lie dormant in the adult brain and their numbers decline with age. It is therefore essential to identify new strategies to activate and expand the adult stem cell population. Defects in mitochondria, the energy producing powerhouse of the cells, is associated with neurodegenerative diseases. Our preliminary data shows that adult stem and progenitor cells are highly sensitive to changes in mitochondrial dynamics and loss of mitochondrial function causes a severe impairment in the development of new neurons in the adult brain. In these studies we will manipulate mitochondrial dynamics in an effort to prevent the decline of adult neurogenesis in the aging brain or in neurodegeneration. The overall goal is develop new treatment strategies by which to regenerate damaged brain tissue.

column36: Targeting GABA-A receptors to mitigate postanesthetic cognitive deficits
column37: General anesthetics are an essential component of modern medical care. Each year, millions of patients undergo anesthesia worldwide. Despite their widespread use, general anesthetics are inherently unsafe and their molecular mechanisms are poorly understood. Such lack of knowledge has stalled the discovery of safer anesthetics and the development of treatments for their adverse effects. Our research program addresses three questions that have perplexed scientists for over a century: How do anesthetics depress brain function? What are their adverse effects? How can such adverse effects be treated? We discovered a mechanism and potential treatments for a major adverse effect: persistent postanesthetic cognitive deficits. The results are important because many patients experience long-term cognitive deficits and delirium after anesthesia and surgery. Such cognitive deficits are associated with poor long-term outcomes, increased mortality, and higher healthcare costs. The causes are unknown, and no effective treatments are available. We showed that anesthetics target both astrocytes (the most abundant support cells in the brain) and neurons. Activation of anesthetic-sensitive sensors in astrocytes may cause both the desired, acute memory-blocking effects of anesthetics and the undesired, persistent cognitive deficits. Anesthetics stimulate astrocytes to release soluble factors. These factors modify the function of neurons, which causes persistent cognitive deficits that last long after the anesthetics have been eliminated. We will determine how astrocyte-neuron crosstalk causes both the desired and undesired effects of anesthetics. We will also develop new treatments based on our patented drugs and other newly discovered compounds. Overall, this research program will advance our understanding of anesthetic mechanisms and will allow the development of new treatments to ensure that patients don't simply survive anesthesia but thrive in the postoperative period.

column36: Promoting Brain Health to Prevent Dementia: Roles of Covert Vascular Brain Injury and Cognitive Reserve in Age-Related Cognitive Decline
column37: Dementia is Canada's largest, and growing, public health problem, affecting more than 500,000 Canadians and costing more than either cardiovascular disease or cancer. There is encouraging evidence that, for persons of a given age, the risk for dementia has decreased somewhat. Other scientists have proposed that this is because people's brains are healthier (that is, that they have more cognitive reserve) or that they are less like to get silent strokes (small strokes seen on brain scans in people at risk for cognitive decline), but without proof. Meanwhile, the risk for Alzheimer's disease has probably not changed, and it remains incurable. My Foundation program is designed to identify the factors that promote healthier brain aging and lower risk of silent strokes, and to explore new ways of diagnosing and monitoring symptomatic patients. My background in neurology, epidemiology, and neuroimaging has prepared me well for this work. At the University of Calgary I have established one of the world's largest brain MRI analysis centres. Leading a national team of Program Experts, I will examine risk for stroke and cognitive decline in persons recruited from the community in two studies (with 9,700 and 1,500 participants) all of whom have had a brain MRI. We will repeat the brain MRI in six years in 1,500 to see who has had new silent strokes or excessive brain tissue loss (i.e., atrophy). We will look at many potential protective factors including education, occupation, income, diet, physical activity, social activities, and stress levels. In another study I will examine markers of disease-related brain changes in persons with Alzheimer's disease and a related blood vessel condition called cerebral amyloid angiopathy. These studies will point to effective strategies to promote brain health and to diagnose and monitor symptomatic patients.

column36: Targeting the Mammalian Mitochondrial Interactome to Dissect Macromolecular Assemblies and Pathways in Health and Disease
column37: Mitochondria (mt) generate the majority of a cell's energy supply, which is consumed by neurons in the brain to execute diverse cellular functions. Beyond its essential role, defects in mitochondrial protein (MP) function can cause or contribute to neurodegenerative disorders (NDs), for which no effective long-term cure currently exists. This is likely owing to the central involvement of MPs in a myriad of interconnected essential functions in neurons, including the quality control (QC) systems that support cellular homeostasis by maintaining healthy mt for proper neuronal function and integrity. However, impairment in QC during energy demands causes accumulation of damaged and dysfunctional mitochondria, resulting in neuronal death. Despite detailed mechanistic investigations of individual MPs, our understanding of the relationship between how all human MPs globally function and interact together at the level of complexes and cellular pathways still remains incomplete. Emerging evidence suggests that QC systems play a key role in the development of Parkinson's disease (PD), and potentially influences mt homeostasis and neuronal death. While this presents an avenue for therapeutic development, the intricate network of interacting MPs in complexes/pathways is not yet fully understood, hindering progress. My proposal aims at addressing the aforesaid gaps by drawing on our recent advances in proteomic and genetic platforms to provide the first high-resolution view on the molecular organization and mechanistic operation of human MP assemblies, and to uncover the pathway-level relationships for genes encoding the components of QC machineries linked to PD. This work will yield molecular models for new binding partners in mt processes, provide valuable data resources for the community, facilitate discovery of potential new therapeutic targets for NDs, and inspire further research into novel treatments for sustainable health care.

column36: Porphyrin Nanomedicine for Cancer Imaging and Therapy
column37: Despite decades of research, applying cancer nanomedicine for patient care still faces many challenges including inefficient nanoparticle delivery to tumours, safety concerns associated with inorganic nanomaterials, the diverse architecture of tumours, and over-complexity in nanoparticle design. In 2011, we discovered first-in-class organic nanoparticles, termed porphysomes, with the ability to address these limitations. They are non-toxic, being made from lipid (i.e., fat) and natural pigment porphyrins (i.e., chlorophyll in plants and heme in blood). Furthermore, they are simple in design, yet can exhibit multifunctional imaging and therapeutic properties, stemming from a single porphyrin-lipid building block. These diverse properties include the ability to bind metals, and transform locally delivered light energy into heat, sound waves or chemicals toxic to cancer cells. In this Foundation Project, we will build upon porphysomes' inherent multifunctionality to expand knowledge and address key issues in cancer nanomedicine, phototherapy, and drug delivery through the creation of a new generation of porphyrin biomaterials: 1) porphyrin microbubbles and biomimetic porphyrin nanoparticles able to effectively target brain tumour therapy beyond the blood-brain barrier; 2) porphyrin nanoparticles that harness the immune system to enhance lung cancer therapy; 3) stimuli-responsive porphyrin nanoparticles that improves phototherapy efficacy and safety; 4) nanoparticles made of expanded porphyrin molecules with the ability to bind metals for nuclear and radiation medicine. The clinical translation of these materials will be facilitated via our fifth Program pillar, which establishes clinical safety and efficacy of prototypical porphysome. Ultimately, the outcome of this program will be the development of clinically relevant materials that realize the potential of cancer nanomedicine in improving current cancer therapy regimens.

column37: Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, Two Spirit and queer (LGBTQ) adolescents face persistent health gaps compared to their straight and cisgender peers in Canada and globally. Is it getting better? Our Stigma and Resilience Among Vulnerable Youth Centre at UBC has developed leading evidence to answer this question: some health gaps are narrowing, but only for some LGBTQ youth (mostly gay boys) and these trends are not yet documented for rural or ethnoculturally diverse LGBTQ youth. Likewise, families are important sources of support for adolescents, but trends show parental support for LGBTQ youth is not improving. Interventions are needed to help all families better support their LGBTQ youth, and to reach youth and families in rural areas. Our Vision: to reduce stigma, foster resilience, and improve health equity for LGBTQ youth in Canada and throughout the world. Our 7-year program of research has 4 primary aims: 1) to track trends in health and health disparities for LGBTQ youth from diverse ethnocultural groups in Canada, Europe, and New Zealand; 2) to identify how families reject or support LGBTQ youth in different cultural groups in these same regions, and examine the link between family support and LGBTQ youth health; 3) develop and test new culturally-relevant on-line and smartphone-based interventions to build parental support and lower family rejection of LGBTQ youth; and 4) develop & test similar technology-based health promotion interventions for diverse and rural LGBTQ youth. Our participatory mixed-methods approaches will use population-based surveys, on-line focus groups, longitudinal research methods, and pilot tests of on-line and text message interventions. With our team of experts from Canada, the USA, New Zealand, and Europe, we will identify culturally-specific knowledge to improve clinical care of LGBTQ youth and families, and create new, culturally relevant family and youth interventions, to narrow the health gaps for LGBTQ youth.

column37: Over half of Canadians are overweight or obese. Obesity leads to higher levels of blood insulin and glucose. These are features of prediabetes, which leads to type 2 diabetes. Diabetes has serious consequences to our health and economy. Even prediabetes contributes to over 2 million annual deaths worldwide. Existing treatments help control blood sugar usually by increasing insulin. However, existing treatments focus on glucose, but do not address the root cause of prediabetes progression during obesity. Higher insulin can accelerate obesity and promote "insulin resistance". The discovery of insulin has saved many lives by controlling blood sugar. Now we need to stop the progression of prediabetes. After every meal or snack containing sugars, insulin is secreted and then cleared from the blood. Obesity slows clearance of insulin, exposing the body to more insulin. This can add up over time to further worsen obesity and prediabetes. Drugs that change insulin clearance all the time (not just after a meal) have failed and we still do not have good weight loss drugs that change eating behaviour or the body's ability to burn more energy. It is very important to discover ways to reduce the repeated exposure of the body to prolonged insulin after each meal. A key problem was that we did not understand enough about what changes insulin levels after eating. My lab discovered that bacteria in the gut produce factors that can lower insulin. The trillions of bacteria in our gut are an untapped source of new drugs. My lab has already found one part of bacteria that makes insulin work better. The next step is finding out how bacteria are sensed by the immune system to alter insulin. This research will combine unique resources across Canada to find out which parts of bacteria can be used to stop or slow prediabetes. This research may lead to new ways to target insulin and the development of prediabetes, which are different from the current drugs that focus on blood glucose.
