column36: Origins, Consequences and Outcomes of Neuroprogression in First Episode Schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia is an illness that causes a high degree of personal disability, caregiver burden, and societal impact. Despite the advances in medical, psychological and social aspects of care in the last 60 years, less than 1 in 7 people with schizophrenia achieve paid employment. Existing treatments have a good effect on reducing 'positive' symptoms of schizophrenia (hearing voices, having false beliefs), but currently, there are no treatments to reduce the 'negative' (reduced motivation, interests, and activity) and 'cognitive' symptoms that are central to the persistent disability seen in many patients. We lack understanding of what brain processes, when affected, produce these resistant symptoms. One promising area is to look at the process of continuous loss of brain tissue that occurs in this illness. Patients who have poor outcomes have a higher rate of brain tissue loss; abnormalities in brain's innate defense mechanisms against infection may contribute to continued tissue loss. We now have very sophisticated brain-imaging facilities that allow us to study this over the course of illness using the magnetic field. As these brain scans are non-invasive and do not involve harmful radiation, we can repeat them multiple times. We propose to study patients experiencing the first episode of schizophrenia and follow them up over 1 year to assess the course of change in brain tissue and symptoms. The objective of this study is to develop an insight on the triggers of tissue loss and how it eventually leads to a poor outcome, enabling us to discover treatments to reverse this process. There are several protective treatments that can prevent brain tissue damage, but we must first identify the right patients to treat. Treating intractable cognitive, negative and persistent positive symptoms could potentially result in a reversal of functional deterioration to an appreciable extent and promote patients' journey towards recovery from this debilitating illness.

column37: The medial temporal lobe (MTL) is a brain network that plays an important role in memory, spatial navigation, and social cognition. This research program is centered on assessing whether these problems can be understood through a comprehensive evaluation of the anatomy and wiring of the different elements in the MTL. By studying epileptic patients before and after surgery, we can evaluate consequences of temporal lobe resection on brain networks mediating these cognitive and affective skills. The program builds on my expertise in studying the MTL and my experience in assessing how neuroimaging markers relate to cognitive outcomes in healthy and epileptic populations. It will provide a foundational account of how impairments following surgery can be understood and prevented. In particular, integrated investigations of the functional and psychological aspects of MTL anatomy will advance theoretical perspectives concerning the role of this brain network in memory and emotional processing. Our framework may help to predict surgical outcomes in epileptic patients, and identify candidates suitable for targeted rehabilitative therapies.

column37: La scoliose est une deformation de la colonne vertebrale affectant 2-4% des adolescents. Le traitement par corset est le seul traitement conservateur efficace pour limiter la progression de la deformation. C'est un traitement difficile pour les jeunes (inconfort, atteinte de l'image de soi, limitation des activites) qui doivent porter cette orthese rigide 20 a 23 hres/jr durant toute la croissance. L'efficacite du traitement est reliee au temps de port du corset. Toutefois, il existe un probleme inquietant de participation au traitement car en moyenne, le corset n'est porte que 12 hres/jr. Cette non-participation du patient a porter son corset mene assurement a l'echec du traitement. Les objectifs de ce projet sont de mieux cibler les sujets a traiter; offrir un corset plus efficace pour corriger la deformation; developper un questionnaire de mesure de qualite de vie et de confort du corset et mettre en place une equipe d'intervenants pour encourager une meilleure adhesion au traitement. Notre equipe travaillera a changer radicalement le traitement par corset en selectionnant mieux les candidats a traiter en evaluant le risque de progression de leur scoliose afin d'eviter de porter un corset inutilement, et en offrant un corset plus efficace pour les patients qui sont a risque de progression. Nous analyserons aussi les resultats du questionnaire pour verifier sa capacite a informer le personnel sur les raisons du refus au traitement et nous interviendrons aupres du patient non-adherent selon ses besoins. Cette nouvelle approche ameliorera la correction apportee par le corset afin d'amener un meilleur taux de succes au traitement qu'obtenu precedemment. Notre nouveau corset devrait etre plus confortable, mieux tolere et donc apprecie des patients. Finalement, l'equipe transmettra les outils developpes dans ce programme afin que les technologies et les interventions demontrees efficaces soient disponibles pour tous les patients dans les centres specialises.

column36: Cortical and basal ganglia mechanisms in movement disorders
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is one of the commonest neurodegenerative diseases. It is due to dysfunction of parts the brain known as the basal ganglia and the cortex, and different parts of the brain are abnormally connected to each other. Theme 1 of the research program will use several state of the art techniques such as functional magnetic resonance imaging, magnetoencephalography and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to determine how the connections in the brain are altered in PD. We will develop novel treatment to normalize these connections. Theme 2 will define the inhibitory functions of the basal ganglia that are particularly relevant to impulse control disorder and gait disturbance in PD. Electrical activities of the basal ganglia will be directly recorded from deep brain stimulation (DBS) electrodes implanted in the basal ganglia and with stimulation applied at selected times during inhibition tasks to define the role of the basal ganglia in inhibitory functions. Theme 3 will promote changes in the brain by combining a surface magnetic brain stimulation technique (TMS) with DBS, and will test this approach as a novel treatment for PD. Theme 4 will determine how electrical activities in deep brain structures are related to different clinical states of PD patients. We will use this information to develop new DBS systems that will automatically adjust stimulation parameters depending on the clinical status to produce the optimal stimulation effects. This will lead to new and improved DBS treatment for PD. The program will be conducted by the Program Leader with a group of Program Experts who are established investigators with diverse expertise. It provides an excellent training environment for future researchers. The findings will advance our knowledge of PD, and lead to improved treatment for PD patients.

column36: Improving Transition of Care and Outcomes of Cardiovascular Disease Using an Innovative Big Data Approach
column37: Heart disease continues to pose a significant burden on healthcare systems in Canada and around the world. Each year, more than 600,000 patients present to the emergency department for chest pain assessment, more than 80,000 patients are hospitalized with a heart attack, and more than 60,000 patients undergo coronary angioplasty to treat heart blockages in Canada. Although there have been significant advancements in the prevention and management of heart disease, patients continue to be at risk for serious events. For example, heart attack patients have a ~10% chance of dying and ~40% chance of being readmitted to the hospital in the first year after their initial events. Emerging data suggest many adverse events occur because the care during transitions of patients from hospital to home, or from the emergency department, is suboptimal. This proposal consists of a series of innovative, large-scale projects that will close the gap in the quality of care received by heart disease patients during care transitions. We will examine how to measure care properly, assess the current level of care, and understand what the drivers of these deficiencies are. Next, we will create tools to help patients and clinicians in order to improve the quality of care. Lastly, we will create a Learning Health System so that we can align the priorities of patients, clinicians and policy makers. The ultimate goal of this research program is to build capacity and sustainability to continue to improve the care and outcomes patients with heart disease.

column36: Identification and Characterization of Human Hematopoietic and Leukemia Stem Cells and Elucidation of their Role in Regenerative Medicine and Disease
column37: Blood is the most regenerative human tissue with a trillion cells produced daily. The dozen mature cell types that compose adult blood originate from rare hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). Only HSCs have the capacity to give rise to other HSCs while regenerating the entire blood system. When the mechanisms controlling normal blood development go awry, it can lead to leukemia, a form of blood cancer. Our lab was the first to show that acute leukemias possess a hierarchical structure similar to that of normal blood development. We discovered that cancer stem cells (CSCs) are at the apex of this hierarchy and possess the ability to self-renew and produce all of the cells of the tumour. CSCs are responsible not only for initiating and maintaining acute leukemias, but also for therapy resistance and recurrence of disease after treatment. Through CIHR's Foundation Program, we will identify and study the molecular mechanisms underpinning the unique properties of HSCs and CSCs, especially those that enable CSCs to resist treatment and cause relapse. Our research findings will lay the foundation for the development of new methods to enhance HSCs from cord blood, making them more amenable for transplantation. HSC transplantation is an effective treatment for many diseases; however, two thirds of patients who require a transplant cannot receive it because they lack a matched donor. Findings from our Foundation program will also lead to the development of new prognostic and predictive biomarkers for leukemia and identify new therapeutic targets to eliminate leukemia CSCs while sparing normal HSCs. Although most adults with acute leukemia (B-ALL and AML) respond initially to conventional therapy, 50-75% of patients experience a relapse and >60% of adult patients succumb to their disease. We will work with our clinical and industry partners to ensure that our research findings are translated to improve the health of Canadians.

column36: Oncohistones in Cancer
column37: Histones package our genetic information (DNA) and regulate all processes needed for a cell to grow or differentiate. There are several changes in the histone tail that act in concert with other factors (epi-genome) to govern gene activity states and the overall function of our genetic identity. Indeed, the epigenome is like the symphony of our cells, the partition that makes sense of the musical notes (DNA). Therefore, aberrant histone and chromatin modifications disrupt these normal cellular processes leading to the development of cancer. Our ground-breaking discovery of mutations in these histone genes (oncohistones as we named them with mutations at three specific residues in the histone 3 tails) in deadly brain cancers in children has linked human normal development and what we now know are epigenetic-driven cancers. We also recently uncovered oncohistones in other bone or muscle cancers, leukemia and head an neck cancers. We aim in this program to understand how this new mechanism of cancer promotes aberrant growth, identify targets amenable to therapy, provide relevant models to test the effects of these therapies prior to rapidly translating them by using our collaborative network to clinical trials at the bedside. Ultimately, if successful, our program will positively change the bleak outcome of oncohistone-associated cancers.

column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is the 3rd leading cause of death worldwide and affects 1 in 4 adults. Asthma affects about 1 in 3 and is the most common chronic disease of children. Previous studies have shown that women, people of some ethnic backgrounds, people with some comorbidities, immigrants, indigenous people and other groups are vulnerable to asthma and COPD and/or their poor health outcomes. COPD and asthma practice guidelines and health policy, however, are based on evidence obtained from studies that enrolled mostly white participants in controlled settings with little consideration of these factors. This is not sufficient for Canada's diverse, multicultural population where studies in diverse real world populations are needed to customize approaches for those most vulnerable to disease burden. The main objective of my program is to determine the best COPD and asthma care for affected Canadians of different sexes, ages and other backgrounds. My program will use big data from millions of Canadians containing information on age, sex, ethnic background, immigrant status and other patient characteristics as well as health behaviours (eg. smoking), medical information (eg, medications), lung function, air pollution and other factors to answer the question: What is the best way to prevent acute exacerbations of asthma and COPD in people of diverse backgrounds? Our will be translated into an online risk calculator whereby patients entering their characteristics can determine their own risk of asthma or COPD exacerbation, as well as receive customized, detailed education on how to reduce this risk. This tool will be expanded and adapted to provide clinicians, educators, program leaders and government aggregate information on the diverse populations they provide care or set policy for. Once we have perfected these methods for asthma and COPD, we plan to expand them to other respiratory diseases.

column36: Genetic and epigenetic mechanisms of pituitary development, function and disease
column37: The gene expression program of a cell defines its identity, i.e. it tells us, and the cell itself, who it is, what is its role and how to play it in complex organisms like ours. We study mechanisms for the control of gene expression and their misregulation in disease. The blueprint for this control is in our DNA and changes in this blueprint result in mutations. In addition to studying this genetic level of gene regulation, we also investigate epigenetic mechanisms, ie mechanisms that govern the wrapping of genetic material (DNA) into chromosomes. Both genetic and epigenetic mechanisms orchestrate the complex development of a functional human and their deregulation cause diseases. We use a hormone-coding gene of the pituitary gland as our model system and throughout the years we have discovered new regulators and new mechanisms that account for normal processes but also disease states. We have thus predicted a form of hormone deficiency that is lethal to neonates, explained it and provided a treatment that fully recovers the lethal outcome of this condition. The new frontier in the field is the epigenetic level of regulation and we are exploring this with state-of-the-art high-throughput massive DNA sequencing technologies. We also identified mechanisms involved in development of the pituitary tumors that cause Cushing disease. This disease is particularly deleterious because of excessive uncontrolled hormone production leading to hypertension, diabetes, osteoporosis, and metabolic disruption. We have partly explained the resistance to hormone feedback that characterises these tumors and we now seek to determine how cell growth is deregulated in order to develop novel treatment approaches.

column36: Cellular and molecular mechanisms regulating the progression of atherosclerosis: exploiting macrophage reverse transendothelial migration as a therapeutic strategy
column37: Atherosclerosis is a chronic inflammatory disease of arteries and remains the principal cause of death in our society despite effective cholesterol-lowering therapies. Atherosclerosis develops silently for decades before causing heart attacks and strokes. My research focuses on cells and genes that participate in atherosclerosis. Currently, there are no therapies targeting cells in the artery wall to inhibit the formation and progression of atherosclerosis. These therapies would benefit patients with risk factors, such as high blood cholesterol. Dendritic cells (DCs) are white blood cells and important components of the immune system. DCs are found in the inner artery wall of healthy humans and animals, in areas where atherosclerosis develops. DCs in mice with high cholesterol engulf lipid and become "foam cells". This is the first step in the formation of atherosclerosis, and is followed by other white blood cells entering the artery and becoming foam cells. Recently, we discovered a novel protective mechanism by which up to half of DCs in the normal artery exit into the bloodstream in response to inflammatory stimulus or exposure to bacteria. However, engulfed lipid blocks DC exit. Our goal is to elucidate the mechanisms underlying DC exit from the normal arteries so that we can determine the changes that shut off this process in foam cells. This is an important endeavor since we believe that in the future we can overcome these inhibitory mechanisms so that accumulated lipid can be removed from the artery wall by exiting lipid-loaded foam cells. This could become a unique approach to reduce both the lipid burden and foam cells. In atherosclerotic lesions, the number of foam cells increases with time in part due to cell division. Moreover, after DC exit their numbers recover within a day because remaining cells divide. Thus, therapeutic strategies that promote foam cell exit from aorta must also target molecules that promote cell division.

column36: Engineering stem cell fate and function
column37: Regenerative medicine (RM) offers an opportunity to address the root causes of chronic diseases, which typically result from the breakdown of tissues maintained by stem cells (SC). In Canada, chronic disease consumes 67% of direct health care costs, with approximately $68 billion attributable to treatment costs. Canada is a leader in SC-based RM and my group has contributed to discovery and innovation in this sector. Early RM technologies focused on the transplantation of cells from the same individual. RM is now at a stage where cell products, such as blood SC, are manufactured for clinical testing. My proposed program is building the next generation of RM therapeutics - living cells and tissues designed to treat specific indications. My vision is to understand, at a fundamental level, the mechanisms by which complex tissues develop from SC, and to use this understanding to advance new cell therapies and regenerative medicines. Our approach is based on three complementary thrusts. First, we are developing computer simulations of normal and diseased human tissue development. These simulations allow us to connect the genetic coding inside SC to the environment that influences SC growth. These simulations will one day dramatically shorten the time it takes to develop new therapies for degenerative diseases. Second, we are rewiring the genetic code in, and the environment around, SC to understand the key requirements of SC-based tissue development and to increase the quantity and quality of SC-derived cells produced. Third, with our partners, we are moving promising discoveries towards the clinic using advanced models of disease, with a focus on testing specialized blood cells as blood cancer and autoimmune disease therapeutics. Our work will reveal new rules that govern tissue development, generate new technologies for RM applications, and yield new SC-based therapies. Our work contributes to the CIHR mission to improve the health and welfare of Canadians.

column36: Structural Biology of Calcium-Dependent Cellular Processes in Health and Disease
column37: As the most abundant mineral in the body, calcium has long been recognized as vital to the formation and maintenance of living systems. Bones, where calcium is stored in the solid state, continuously release ions or salts of this mineral (i.e., Ca2+) into the body, and this soluble form of calcium plays a central role as a messenger within cells. We call this the biological calcium signal. However, too much Ca2+ (or too much calcium signal) is detrimental to cells, and uncontrolled calcium levels in our body are life-threatening. In cancer, the calcium signal is largely deregulated for the advantage of cancer cell growth. In order to understand how normal and cancer cells produce and respond to calcium signals, we will investigate the molecular details of the calcium-dependent cellular processes that we think are most relevant to cancer. In this proposal, we attempt to answer key questions: (i) how is the calcium signal generated and how does it become deregulated in cancer?; (ii) how does the calcium signal influence other signaling circuits that drive the growth and proliferation of cancer cells?; and (iii) how does the calcium signal affect the proper cell adhesion of normal cells, and contribute to metastatic properties of cancer cells? Part of this program is also relevant to immunodeficiency, as genetic defects (mutations) in the calcium signal generators we study (called STIM/ORAI) cause severe combined immune disease or SCID. The proposed program will contribute to a better understanding of how cancer cells use the calcium signal circuits to promote their survival and growth, as well as how immune cells battle infectious agents in the human body. Deeper understanding of the calcium signal transduction system will provide new clues for novel therapeutic strategies to treat patients with immunodeficiency and cancer.

column36: Addressing gender-based health inequities among immigrants to Canada
column37: Despite progress towards gender equity in the last decades, age-old patriarchal structures and attitudes that promote male dominance are still the norm in many countries. Canada increasingly receives large numbers of immigrants and refugees from countries where the status of women is lower than that of men. Gender inequities manifest in various health disadvantages for girls and women over the life span across the world. These include female-selective abortions, excess child mortality for girls, poorer quantity and quality of healthcare, dating and intimate partner violence, and fewer opportunities to achieve their full potential compared to males. However, little is known about whether such patterns persist among immigrants settling in Canada and how their health, development and wellbeing are affected. To fill these critical knowledge gaps we will use state-of-the-art methods to analyze rich information obtained by linking multisectoral databases encompassing all immigrants arrived to Manitoba and Ontario in the last three decades and their offspring born in Canada. This research program will generate valuable information to assist with a healthier integration of immigrants to the Canadian society and help advance gender equity initiatives in Canada and beyond. This research program brings together a multidisciplinary and interprofessional team of researchers, government and immigrant community partners who will collaborate to ensure that the research findings translate into improved programs, policies and services for the benefit of children, women and families in the affected minorities and in the population at large.

column36: Heterogeneity through space and time drive the clinical behaviour of childhood medulloblastoma
column37: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. Medulloblastoma is really made up of four diseases, of which two types, Group 3 and Group 4, account for the majority of cases, as well as the majority of children who are dying of their disease. The main tumor 'lump' in the cerebellum is called the 'primary tumor'. The primary tumor can spread (metastasize) to cover other regions of the surface of the brain and spinal cord. The most damaging therapies for children with Group 3 and Group 4 medulloblastoma (radiation) are necessary to treat the metastases. The dream of curing cancer through precision medicine has entailed sequencing cancer genomes to identify tumor specific mutations, which could in turn be targeted by pathway specific drugs that are lethal to the tumor but harmless to a child's normal cells. While this model is showing early success for some adult cancers, it holds limited promise for treatment of medulloblastoma; recent results from our lab have shown that most medulloblastomas harbor few of these tumor specific mutations and that the tumours differ greatly both across a given 'lump' and between the primary tumor and the metastases. Instead, medulloblastomas appear to be driven by large deletions or insertions of genes. We now also know that some of these differences are seen regularly in medulloblastomas and the metastases and this makes them an excellent choice for the development of targeted therapy. We have begun developing new tools, and aim to use these tools to study these differences which occur in the tumours and between the primary tumor and the metastases-we strongly believe this is the best, and perhaps the only way to improve survival for children with medulloblastoma.

These findings have inspired us to extend application of identified mechanisms to choroidal thinning which seems to precede other degenerative retinal changes in AMD. column37: Breast cancer is the most common female cancer. Despite advances in its detection and treatment, women die from breast cancer due to poor treatment options for aggressive versions of the disease and spreading to distant organs such as bone. Bone cancer is relatively rare but it afflicts adolescents, and current treatments to fight this disease are very limited. My goal has been to enhance the biological understanding of these two cancers with a purpose of developing more effective therapies. My research focuses on two central themes: one aims to understand the intricacies of the tissue environment that surrounds cancer-prone cells, and the other aims to find genes that drive cancer cell growth. My previous work in these areas has yielded new insights on the importance of enzyme inhibitors that maintain tissue structure integrity, and growth signals that expand breast cancer precursor cells. I also used computational methods and innovative experimental systems to find new genes that are instrumental for aggressive bone cancers. These findings have led to the positioning of clinical trials with new therapies aimed at preventing breast cancer formation and bone cancer recurrence. Using my unique mouse models and valuable cancer gene discovery systems, I will decipher the role of specialized enzyme inhibitors and their molecular targets which create a tissue environment conducive to cancer formation, finding new means to control their detrimental effects. I will also investigate the function and importance of carefully selected candidate genes to determine their ability to promote bone cancer. I will identify new genes responsible for cancer spread from breast to bone to conceptualize new therapies. Collectively, my recognized expertise in these research areas together with an outstanding group of program experts and cutting-edge technologies will enable my research program to continue to make key discoveries that benefit therapeutic outcomes in bone and breast cancer

column36: Exploring the evolutionary battle between phages and bacteria: from CRISPR-Cas systems to phage-derived antibacterial weapons
column37: My work focuses on viruses that infect bacteria, called phages. Bacteria have developed "immune" systems to protect themselves from attack by phages. One of these systems is known as CRISPR-Cas and it is able to cleave phage genomes at specific spots, guided by an RNA sequence. In recent years, certain CRISPR-Cas systems, called Cas9, have been developed into technology that can be used to efficiently alter the human and other genomes. The advent of this technology has opened the possibility of curing human disease. My laboratory has discovered naturally occurring proteins that can potently inhibit CRISPR-Cas9 systems. These proteins will be used to improve CRISPR-Cas9 methods to make them safer for human therapeutic purposes. We will also investigate mechanisms and other uses for CRISPR systems. My laboratory also investigates structures that form parts of the phage particle itself. In particular, we work on phage tails, which bind to bacterial cell surfaces and inject the phage DNA into cells. Naturally occurring bacterial machineries, called tailocins, are closely related to phage tails and can be used to kill bacteria in a highly specific manner. We are developing methods to engineer these tailocins to kill any desired bacterial strain. These engineered tailocins will be used to manipulate the human microbiome to alleviate disease conditions, such as Crohn's Disease. Tailocins also have the potential to treat antibiotic-resistant bacterial infections.

column37: Focused ultrasound is a non-invasive means to deliver energy into targeted tissue within the body. At high power levels, focused ultrasound, when combined with quantitative MR imaging for on-line guidance, can be used to produce well-defined regions of thermal coagulation. The first generation of clinical focused ultrasound devices showed major benefits for the health care system through (1) reduced recovery times and hospital stays, (2) lower rates of complications such as infection, and (3) only light sedation or local anaesthesia needed for outpatient treatment. Our vision for the next decade of focused ultrasound development centres on the discoveries that focused ultrasound can be used for many more clinical indications if other non-thermal effects of ultrasound are used. If this research is even partially successful, it will have a huge impact on patient care by addressing the knowledge gap between the mechanisms involved with the non-thermal bio-effects and by translating these treatments to wide clinical use. It would provide new treatments that are non-invasive and more effective as well as that have lower complication rates and shorter recovery times. These treatments could be used for many brain and body disorders, including brain tumours, Alzheimer's Disease, embolic stroke and deep vein thrombosis.

column36: Pinpointing pathways for pathogenesis and therapeutic intervention by identifying disease modifiers
column37: Genetic modifiers are factors that improve or worsen the presentation of a disease. Knowledge of modifiers reveals pathways for disease pathogenesis, predicts disease outcome and provides an ideal starting point for treatment. However, gene modifiers are hard to find in humans. Identifying genetic modifiers in a model organism allows for their validation and translation to humans. I carried out a modifier screen in a mouse model for Rett syndrome, a neurological disorder, which uncovered missing pathway members, revealed new genetic interactions, and pinpointed new drug targets. The modifiers revealed unexpected facets of Rett syndrome, which has changed the health management of Rett patients and suggested therapies. Using unparalleled resources in Canada for mouse work and human genome sequencing, we will collaborate with a multi-disciplinary team of outstanding researchers in the areas of neuroscience, epigenetics, imaging, genome editing and sequencing to 1) understand additional modifiers that provide surprising disease insight; 2) make sure our findings are relevant to humans and other neurological conditions, 3) determine how the modifiers alter the phenotype of people carrying Rett mutations, and 4) inform treatment strategies. Greatly improved health in Rett mice that carry modifiers from two pathways suggests that combination therapy will confer amazing improvement. Outcome-predicting biomarkers, identified through our studies, will be employed as we inform strategies for clinical trials with our company ArRETT. Our approach is paradigm-shifting, because it illustrates the power of unbiased modifier screens to discover therapeutic targets, providing proof-of-principle for a modifier approach to be considered for other rare disorders, which currently have no treatment options. The knowledge will impact the health of Canadians by broadly informing clinical outcome of neurological disorders, reducing the financial burden on the health care system.

column36: Synaptic alterations underlying major brain disorders.
column37: BROAD GOALS The overarching theme of this research is to establish the molecular mechanisms by which synaptic transmission is modulated in the CNS and how errors in this process contribute to major brain disorders. We will focus on the process known as long-term depression (LTD), which we will study at synapses within the rodent hippocampus. BACKGROUND Information is stored in the brain via a process known as synaptic plasticity. The two most extensively studied forms of synaptic plasticity are long-term potentiation (LTP) and LTD. Increasing evidence suggests that errors in these processes may cause or contribute to many of the most severe neurological and psychiatric disorders. Our working hypothesis is that the cognitive deficits that are associated with these disorders are due, at least in part, to an exaggerated LTD process. It is now believed that LTD is a normal physiological process that is necessary for synaptic development and for learning and memory throughout the life-span. LTD involves the weakening of synaptic transmission and can lead to physiological synaptic elimination (pruning). We believe that LTD is normally tightly regulated but that in numerous brain disorders this regulation breaks down, due to environmental and or genetic causes. Aggressive LTD may explain the initial cognitive deficits and synapse loss. RESEARCH AIMS 1. Discover the key missing components in the process of hippocampal synaptic plasticity, with a focus on LTD. 2. Determine how hippocampal synaptic plasticity, in particular LTD, becomes altered in rodent models of neurodegenerative, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders. 3. Identify new drug targets and develop new compounds with novel actions on synaptic plasticity, as part of the process to develop better treatments for major brain disorders.

column36: Low Cost and Distributed Health Care Applications Based on Cell-free Systems
column37: We have recently developed two exciting new technologies for applications in healthcare. The first was a portable and low cost system for detecting the Zika virus (< $1 per test) and the second was the manufacture of protein therapeutics outside of the laboratory in a system that, much like instant noodles, just requires water to be added. Together these disease-specific applications will extend our proof-of-concept work and technology development to meet real world needs at home and abroad. These applications were chosen to serve unmet needs and thus will develop new research capacity in Canada and ultimately have the potential to improve care. It is with great anticipation that our lab begins to translate these technologies here in Canada, where we can help shape and contribute to the health research community, its trainees and research translation.

column36: Investigating Mechanisms for Synapse and Circuit Dynamics using the C. elegans Model
column37: A human brain consists of numerous neurons that communicate with each other. Abnormal communications, caused by inabilities to form structural connections, send or receive signals, or control signal intensity, lead to neurological disorders. Using a small animal model called C. elegans, whose nervous system contains only a few hundred neurons, we have discovered new genes that are critical for either the structural development, or activity tuning of neuronal communication. Through collaboration with other biologists, human geneticists, and neurologists, we have demonstrated that not only do these genes function similarly in other animals, human mutations that cause their functional anomalies lead to neurological disorders. Here we continue to use the C. elegans model to uncover genes and pathways that are critical for brain development and function. A specific question that we aim to address is how development impacts function. Like all animals, we continue to grow after birth. The ability for animals, humans included, to sense signals from the environment, and select and execute meaning motor responses is essential for the viability of both individuals and the specie. This ability, called sensorimotor function, is governed by a nervous system that changes structure and property after birth. How does a nervous system coordinate growth and functionality? We will address this question through comparing the structure and function of neural circuits during development. Applying already acquired insights, we have established C. elegans models for several human neurological disorders, whose cognitive and functional defects have fundamental developmental origins. By applying similar interrogations to these models, our studies will not only shed light on fundamental mechanisms that define the dynamic changes of the nervous systems, but also address the physiological and developmental origins of neurological disorders.

column36: Innovative biomechanical and molecular strategies to fight fibrosis
column37: Different precursor cells are activated to rapidly repair injured tissues. Examples for injury are skin trauma or burn wounds, infarct or chronic overload of the heart, lung epithelium damage, liver infection or alcohol abuse, and kidney damage because of high blood pressure. The activated cells are called myofibroblasts (MFs) because they secrete fibrous collagen matrix ("fibro") that is contracted ("myo") into mechanically stabilizing scar tissue. Although MFs are essential to restoring mechanical integrity of damaged tissue, they never truly regenerate organs and scar formation comes at the cost of reduced organ function. Worse, MF deregulation leads to excessive tissue and organ scarring - a condition called fibrosis. Fibrosis contributes to ~45% of deaths in industrialized nations by causing malfunction and failure of vital organs, such as heart, liver, kidney, lung, and vasculature. Fibrosis promotes tumor progression in the stroma reaction, leads to implant failure in foreign body responses, jeopardizes mesenchymal stem cell therapies by turning stem cells into scar cells and disfigures skin. MFs are key pharmaceutical targets but anti-MF therapies have not yet been translated to clinical treatments of fibrosis. Identifying the joint mechanical and biochemical regulators of MFs, which are incompletely understood, will be essential to promote healing with intervention therapies. Our unrivalled, state-of-the-art research will provide new insights into understanding disease progression, establish novel markers for wound healing therapies, enable the production of innovative technology for use in mechanobiology cell studies, and develop industry-standard drug screening devices. New drug targets, screening tools, biomarker and treatment strategies have tremendous commercial potential/value and will improve the quality of life of fibrosis patients in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Explaining activation changes during the early stages of Alzheimer's disease and promoting processes of compensation and brain plasticity
column37: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) starts with a long "silent" phase during which the disease is present in the brain, but symptoms are minimal. This may explain why up to 200 medications to treat the disease have failed in the last 30 years, as all of them have been introduced "late", missing this early silent phase. Understanding what is happening in the brain during this phase of the disease, and predicting which mildly impaired individuals will progress to AD is crucial to our development of cures. This early period may represent a critical time for pharmacological or non-pharmacological interventions intended to halt the progression of the disease or to mitigate symptoms. Many older adults with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or with a subjective complaint decline (SCD) stand in this early stage of the disease. Thus, studying these individuals might provide the precursor markers of AD. This program proposes to identify their brain and clinical symptoms using advanced neuroimaging and cognitive techniques. We have previously found hyperactivation during that stage, i.e., greater brain activation than healthy older adults. We want to better understand this phenomenon, as it may provide insight into how the brain attempts to counteract the effects of neurodegeneration. We will test the hypothesis that hyperactivation is due to intense compensatory neuroplastic processes. We will also follow subjects longitudinally to see if a combination of functional imaging and other measures can accurately predict who will progress to dementia. Finally, we will assess if cognitive training programs can increase neuroplastic compensatory processes during that early phase of AD and identify the optimal program and dose and the type of training that is most adapted to different individuals. If successful, this program will allow for an earlier diagnosis of AD and develop novel approaches to non-pharmacological prevention strategies for older Canadians who are at risk of cognitive decline.

column36: Improving Clinical Decision Making for Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects 1 in 10 Canadian adults, and can lead to kidney failure requiring dialysis. In most cases, CKD remains stable, and can be safely managed by a family doctor. However, for some patients, it can progress quickly and needs specialist care. In 2011, we developed an equation that accurately identifies patients at the highest risk of progression. We are now proposing national studies that will test how our equation can be integrated in patient care. First, we want family doctors to use the equation to talk to their patients about their risk of kidney failure and how to reduce it. Doctors will use the equation to determine whether a patient needs to see a kidney specialist or not. Second, we want kidney specialists to use the equation to plan for dialysis or transplantation, but only for patients at the highest risk of kidney failure. These studies will help ensure patients are involved in making health care decisions with their doctor and will help provide clinical care specific to each patient. In the next 5 years, these studies will transform care for CKD in Canada and beyond our borders.

column36: Immune Regulation of Placental Development and Function During Normal and Pathological Pregnancy.
column37: Preeclampsia is a serious and prevalent disease of pregnancy. It is clinically diagnosed by severe, sudden-onset high blood pressure and blood vessel damage that can lead to organ dysfunction and death in pregnant women. Preeclampsia is a major cause of maternal and infant illness and death in Canada and worldwide, with up to 76,000 maternal and 500,000 infant deaths attributed to the disease globally, and there is no known cure. The major cause of preeclampsia is defective development of the placenta, which is the organ that embeds itself into the mother's uterus and is responsible for nourishing the baby throughout pregnancy. We know little about why the placenta does not develop properly in these pregnancies. Without this knowledge, devising better management strategies and interventions is not possible. Therefore, the objective of this research is to determine underlying factors that cause placental maldevelopment during early pregnancy. Based on our preliminary data, we hypothesize that abnormal behaviour of a unique subset of highly abundant uterine immune cells has a causative role in disrupting placental development. In this project, we will determine how aberrant activity of these uterine immune cells leads to placental dysfunction and affects fetal health. We will also examine whether the absence of these immune cells can improve placental and fetal health. Collectively, this project will test the applicability of targeting uterine immune cells to improve placental development, and will form a foundation by which we can decrease or prevent the incidence of preeclampsia.

column36: What is the cause of chromosome segregation error in the mammalian preimplantation embryo?
column37: The health of the newly fertilised embryo is an important determinant of fertility. One problem commonly experienced by women undergoing fertility treatments is that the early embryo has cells with the wrong number of chromosomes - termed 'aneuploid' cells. Embryos with aneuploid cells are considered unlikely to give rise to a healthy baby. Indeed, many clinics use the presence of aneuploid cells to discard bad-quality embryos rather than transfer them back to the patient. The presence of aneuploid cells in the early embryo indicates that errors have taken place during chromosome segregation - the process of sharing the chromosomes between the daughter cells at the time of cell division. However, despite the clear importance in human fertility, the cause of these chromosome segregation errors in early embryos is unknown. Our laboratory specialises in the use of state-of-the-art imaging approaches to observe and investigate the process of chromosome segregation, and we have developed an assortment of techniques for observing these processes in embryos. Here we will perform some of the first examinations of how chromosome segregation works in the early mammalian embryo, and try to understand why this process goes wrong so often. Most of our experiments will use mouse embryos, with some experiments using human embryos that can no longer be used for treatments. This work will shed light upon the causes of chromosome mis-segregation in the embryo, helping to explain the problems experienced by many fertility patients, and we hope that our experiments will directly lead to improved methods for selecting embryos for transfer to patients in the clinic.

column36: Optimizing the Curative Treatment for High Risk Prostate Cancer: Combining Advanced Imaging, Trans-perineal Mapping Biopsies, and Dual Air Kerma Strength LDR Brachytherapy Implants to Minimize Radiation Dose to Normal Tissues
column37: Radiotherapy plus hormonal treatment is the recommended form of treatment for men with high risk prostate cancer. An increase in the delivered treatment dose has been shown to improve treatment success rates in these patients. The downside, however, is increased treatment side-effects. The ASCENDE-RT trial, a recent multi-center randomized trial at the BC Cancer Agency, shows that men treated with external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) followed by low-dose-rate prostate brachytherapy (LDR-PB) boost had better treatment results compared to conventional dose-escalated EBRT (DE-EBRT). Though, worse side-effects, mostly in the form of urethral strictures, were also observed. LDR-PB is particularly well suited to target tumors of the prostate. However, since determining the tumor location cannot be reliably done (and, therefore, is usually not done) the extra-dose is given to a majority of the prostate gland. By identifying tumor locations and focusing higher treatment doses to these areas and a lower dose to healthy tissue (i.e. 'focal LDR-PB boost') we expect less treatment side-effects in men with high-risk prostate cancer. We propose to develop and evaluate a new alternative for treatment of high-risk prostate cancer which involves: 1- Template-guided, trans-perineal mapping biopsy (TTMB) for accurate tumor localization. 2- Multi-modal, multi-parametric imaging (MRI, ultrasound, and PET/CT) for patient selection and follow-up. 3- Novel dual-source based focal LDR-PB for improved targeting of the tumor. Cancer maps created from multi-modal, multi-parametric imaging will ultimately be used to guide or replace TTMB for patient selection, treatment planning and follow-up. We expect the proposed approach to provide a treatment alternative with fewer adverse effects for approximately 15-20% of men with high-risk PCa.

column36: Mechanisms and Markers of Reduced Penetrance in LRRK2 Mutation Carriers using Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells
column37: Parkinson disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disorder affecting movement and cognition. The greatest burden is to patients and families, affecting over 100,000 Canadians with >2.5 billion dollars. The main drug treatment is L-dopa which helps the motoric symptoms but fails to halt the progression of disease. Development of treatment to halt disease progression has been limited. The most common pathogenic mutation that causes sporadic and familial PD is LRRK2 (Leucine-rich repeat kinase 2) p.G2019S. LRRK2 mutations accounts for up to 40% of sporadic PD in Tunisia. However, the penetrance of LRRK2 p.G2019S is highly variable. Given the relatively high rate of occurrence of LRRK2 mutations, finding markers for and elucidating mechanisms of reduced penetrance has a high imperative. I have previously identified DNM3 (Dynamin 3) as a potential genetic modifier of disease penetrance in LRRK2 p.G2019S carriers. I now hypothesize that biological mechanisms including dynamin-related proteins can modulate the phenoconversion of LRRK2 p.G2019S and the identification of these mechanisms will provide insight for developing treatments for patients. We propose that there are large genetic and biological influences that explain the differences in age-at-onset in families with LRRK2 p.G2019S. We will select skin cells from specific individuals to make induced pluripotent stem cells (IPSCs) to differentiate into human neurons. Molecular, cellular and physiological studies of LRRK2 p.G2019S human will be characterized at a high-throughput 'omics' level.

column36: Timing of referral to nephrology care and impact on kidney failure, hospitalization and mortality in people with chronic kidney disease
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects about one in 10 Canadians and is associated with increased risks of cardiovascular disease and kidney failure. In an attempt to lower these risks, guidelines recommend early referral to kidney specialist services for people with CKD. However, the studies supporting this recommendation are of low quality and may have led to biased conclusions. Specifically, existing studies include only people who eventually started dialysis, as opposed to the vast majority of CKD population not yet treated with dialysis and whose family doctors must decide whether to refer to a kidney specialist, and when. In addition, the observation in existing studies that longer pre-dialysis nephrology care leads to better patient outcomes following dialysis start could be explained by the fact that people who have rapidly progressive kidney disease tend to require dialysis sooner making the length of pre-dialysis care is shorter. These people tend to be sicker and are therefore more likely to have poor health outcomes. In contrast, people who are healthy and have kidney disease that progresses more slowly tend to be followed for a longer time in pre-dialysis clinics. It is unclear if longer pre-dialysis care is a marker for a healthier patient, or if the care provided in pre-dialysis clinics leads to improved patient outcomes. The proposed research will take these factors into account and leverage detailed Alberta provincial data sources to assess the impact of timing of referral to kidney specialist services on kidney failure, hospitalization and death in people with CKD. Given the large patient population, the widespread practice of early referral and limited health care resources, this unique work is expected to provide high-quality evidence to inform referral guidelines and health policy, identify areas of clinical focus to improve outcomes, and stimulate future research.

column37: The "Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD)" hypothesis suggests that a healthy growth and development in pregnancy and early childhood is critical for optimal health and lifetime wellbeing. Yet, Canada's children are falling behind. Nearly 1 in 3 Canadian children are overweight or obese, 1 in 4 is not developmentally ready for school, and 1 in 5 has a mental health problem. Early interventions can improve child health and development. Our study will evaluate the effectiveness of an intervention on child obesity and broader indicators of child development. Our trial, TROPHIC (TRajectories Of healthy life using Public Health and primary care Interventions in Canada), will take a 'cumulative-impact' approach, designed to improve health behaviours and reduce modifiable risk factors across the entire early child developmental period. TROPHIC will randomise pregnancy-planning women to evaluate a 4-phase intervention, from preconceptually all the way through early childhood. Its innovative design will enable the collection of family-level data, by including fathers/partners preconceptionally, and following more than one child within the family. TROPHIC comprises of a pan-Canadian team of 48 established investigators, from 21 institutions, across 6 provinces with proven expertise to successfully undertake this Healthy Life Trajectories initiative (HeLTI) project. The proposed project is aligned with the international HeLTI studies. column36: Disease-modifying Drug Safety and Effectiveness in Multiple Sclerosis [DRUMS]
column37: The goal of our research is to determine how safe and effective the drugs used to treat multiple sclerosis (MS) are when used in the real world. Canada has some of the world's highest rates of MS. This chronic disease of the brain and spinal cord often affects young adults and there is no known cure. In the last two decades, over 10 different drugs have been approved to treat people with MS. These drugs are very expensive and can require regular injections as well as frequent blood tests to monitor safety (side effects). We know how well these drugs work in the short-term, but only against certain aspects of MS. In the real world, people with MS may take these drugs for many years but we do not yet understand all their possible benefits and side effects. There have been few studies as large as ours investigating such a range of possible side effects, including cancer, stroke and infections. We will also look at whether the MS drugs have benefits which are often hard to measure, such as MS disability and fewer hospital or doctors' visits. Our research brings together medical data collected for over 2 decades within multiple large health databases in several Canada provinces. No study as large or as comprehensive as ours has ever been done. Our team approach enables findings to be directly relevant to Canadians, including people in poorer communities or those with co-existing medical conditions, who are often excluded from studies. Our research will be independent from the pharmaceutical industry, the manufacturers of MS drugs. This important research will help develop a framework in which to evaluate the benefits and side effects of both the current and future new drugs for MS across Canada. Our study findings will provide much needed information to help treatment-related decision making for both patients and doctors. Ultimately our study findings will directly benefit the outcomes related to treatment and health-related quality of life of people living with MS.

column36: Host microbe interactions in health and disease
column37: Humans have evolved with microbes. Although a subset of microbes have long been known to cause infectious diseases, there is growing appreciation of the critical role they play in health and chronic diseases. This new development also opens up powerful opportunities to find new ways of treating diseases and improving health outcomes. To this end, my lab has been studying how Salmonella and pathogenic E. coli cause diarrhea and related diseases, using new techniques to gain a much more comprehensive understanding of these diseases. Moreover, we have found that normal microbial inhabitants of the gut - the microbiome - can be used to inhibit these pathogens, thus we are pursuing these as potential therapeutics. We have also shown that certain early life microbes can affect the risk of asthma, and these are being explored as potential asthma preventatives. This work is being expanded to related food allergies, especially in the context of very early life gut microbes. A novel mouse model has been developed for malnutrition and an associated intestinal disease (environmental enteropathy). This model will allow us to gain a better understanding of these worldwide problems, as well as to test new products that can then be used to prevent these diseases. Recently, we have begun to explore the gut-brain axis in the context of microbes affecting brain function in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's/dementia. Exciting preliminary data indicate that the microbiomes in these patients are different, and we have new experiments planned to mechanistically probe this initial finding. Important next steps include the development of clinical tools that can be used to decrease these brain diseases. I am proposing a compelling and ambitious program to study these host-microbe interactions. Collectively, this research has significant potential to impact on many major Canadian health issues, including intestinal infections, asthma and allergies, malnutrition and degenerative brain diseases.

column36: Transcriptional control of cancer metabolism
column37: Cancer cells need specific nutrients and to transform these nutrients using specific biochemical pathways to generate enough energy and building blocks to sustain their growth and rapid division. My research program is centered on understanding how cancer cells adapt their metabolism to favor their proliferation and resistance to therapeutic intervention. More precisely, our team is investigating changes in the expression of specialized genes that modify the metabolic program of cancer cells. These changes in gene expression often result from the aberrant activity of proteins known as transcription factors. The normal function of transcription factors is to respond to cellular needs by modulating gene expression so that the cells have the necessary tools to perform their normal activities during the development and lifespan of the organism. However, cancer cells highjack transcription factors to promote tumour growth and their metastasis to distant organs. The abnormal action of transcription factors in cancer is best-exemplified by a class of proteins known as nuclear receptors, which include the estrogen and androgen receptors that promote the growth of breast and prostate cancer, respectively. In recent years, my research program has been focused on studying the roles played by nuclear receptors and other transcription factors in regulating energy metabolism, notably how cancer cells differentially process nutrients such as amino acids, sugars and lipids to fuel their growth. Our goals are to find differences between the action of transcription factors in normal and cancer cells and to exploit these differences to induce metabolic vulnerabilities in tumours, thus making them more responsive to anti-cancer drugs. The ultimate outcome of this program should be improvement in the treatment and quality of life of cancer patients.

column37: The type 1 cannabinoid receptor (CB1R) is present at high levels throughout the brain and other parts of the body. CB1R is activated by the body's own cannabinoids (anandamide and 2-arachidonoylglycerol), synthetic cannabinoids, and cannabinoids from marijuana (e.g. THC and cannabidiol). CB1R is considered a potential target for the regulation of appetite and the treatment of addiction, pain, spasticity in multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, epilepsy, post-traumatic stress disorder, and anxiety. Despite its potential as a therapeutic target, we are still learning how the many naturally occurring and synthetic cannabinoids that exist affect CB1R and how CB1R in turn produces distinct effects in the body. To this end, new compounds known as allosteric modulators are being developed that can increase or decrease CB1R's response to the body's cannabinoids, but lack intrinsic activity and will not, therefore, produce the intoxicating effects associated with other cannabinoids. The goals of my research are: (1) to develop allosteric modulators of CB1R that alter the body's response to its own cannabinoids, (2) test those modulators in animal models, and (3) to apply the knowledge gained from goals 1 and 2 to specific disease states where cannabinoids might be therapeutically beneficial. This research project will provide insight into the mechanisms of CB1R activity, important considerations for the use of cannabinoids as a medicine, and lead to the development of new drug compounds.

column36: A foundation grant for bridging the mutation and interactome landscapes of the eukaryotic cell
column37: Every two individuals are genetically different due to mutations inherited from their parents or new mutations that have accumulated during their lifetime. Most of these mutations have no noticeable consequences. Yet, a small number have strong effects and lead to inherited diseases and somatic ones, such as cancers. Some healthy individuals can tolerate the complete loss of genes, while others develop diseases in response to these mutations. The difference between benign and harmful mutations comes from the organization of the cellular machinery and the interaction between this organization and the thousands of mutations that make everyone unique. For instance, the human genome contains hundreds of genes with multiple copies and having these backup copies could be a strong determinant of the resilience of the cell to otherwise harmful mutations. Here we propose an innovative research program that will elucidate these mechanisms of resilience and sensitivity to mutations of the eukaryotic cell. Our approach will involve cutting edge technologies in genome sequencing, high-throughput screening, genome editing and bioinformatics to determine what are the effects of disease and non-disease mutations directly on the inner organization of the cell. Our discoveries will shed light on the mechanisms of resilience and fragility to mutations in addition to providing mechanistic details on how human disease mutations alter the inner cell machinery. This will lead to more powerful approaches for the prediction of disease susceptibility and outcome from genome sequences, as well as to the development of knowledge-guided drug development.

column36: Physical Activity and Cancer Outcomes: Generating Practice-Changing Evidence
column37: My research program focuses on physical activity (PA) in cancer patients. Specifically, I am interested in how PA may help cancer patients prepare for treatments, cope with treatments, recover after treatments, and improve long-term survival. The long term goal of my research program is to reduce the negative impact of cancer by ensuring that all cancer patients have access to high quality exercise programs. Research has shown that PA improves fitness and quality of life in cancer survivors but clinical practice has not really changed. I have argued that the chances of PA being offered in clinical oncology practice would be greatly increased if PA was shown to improve survival. The overall aim of my proposed research program is to find out if PA can actually improve survival in cancer patients. I am proposing to study this question with 5 projects including: (a) the Alberta Moving Beyond Breast Cancer (AMBER) Study, which is the first study examining the associations between objective PA, fitness, and breast cancer survival in 1,500 newly diagnosed breast cancer patients, (b) the Colon Health and Life-Long Exercise Change (CHALLENGE) Trial, which is the first experimental study examining the effects of a 3 year exercise program on survival in 962 colon cancer patients, (c) the Intense Exercise for Survival (INTERVAL) Trial, which is the first experimental study examining the effects of a 2 year exercise program on survival in 866 patients with advanced prostate cancer, and (d) 2 smaller studies in rectal cancer patients receiving combined chemoradiation therapy and prostate cancer patients receiving no treatments. PA is a low cost, low risk intervention that improves fitness and quality of life in cancer survivors but it has not been put into practice to help cancer patients. If PA can be shown to improve cancer survival, it would likely be offered to all cancer patients in Canada and around the world as part of their standard care.

column36: Replication stress and pulmonary hypertension: Role for checkpoint kinase 1
column37: Patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension have a dysfunction of the cells constituting the wall of their arteries in the lungs. Like cancer cells, PAH cells are characterized by exaggerated capacity to multiplicate and resistance to death resulting in a progressive narrowing or obstruction of the vessels. Indeed, if the blood vessels tighten up, making the space for the passage of blood narrower, it takes greater pressure to get the same amount of blood through to its destination. The heart has to work harder to pump blood through those arteries. The heart progressively fails causing shortness of breath and poor exercise capacity, which rapidly culminate in death. In spite of recent progress in our understanding of the mechanisms involved in this disease, no substantial modification of the rapid progression and fatal course of this disease has been achieved, leaving lung transplantation as the only treatment in end-stage PAH. Therefore, the identification of new therapeutic targets is a pressing need. Although exposed to stressful conditions that jeopardize their survival, PAH cells continue to multiplicate indicating that these cells have developed adaptive protective response allowing them to survive. Nevertheless, the factors implicated in this pathological protective response remains largely unknown. In the present proposal, we hypothesize that a factor called CHK1 known to confer resistance to harmful stress conditions is overexpressed in PAH cells leading to the development of PAH. To test the validity of our hypothesis, we will 1) determine whether CHK1 is increased in PAH cells and contributes to PAH cells' anomalies; 2) decorticate the mechanisms by which CHK1 acts; and 3) assess whether inhibition of CHK1 improve PAH in animal models.

column36: Harnessing Neuron-Astrocyte Communication for Promoting Brain Health
column37: A common feature in nearly all brain disorders and diseases is a breakdown in brain homeostasis. Key to brain homeostasis are highly specialized cells called astrocytes. Astrocytes play fundamental roles in brain function including controlling extracellular ion and neurotransmitter levels, brain energetics, and cerebrovasculature. Astrocytes perform diverse functions through their complex molecular, functional, structural properties. However, the mechanisms that create and sustain differences among astrocytes that allow them to fulfill unique physiological roles in the brain remain poorly understood. We discovered a completely new mechanism involving neurons for making different types of astrocytes in the brain. Communication between neurons and astrocytes enables astrocytes to produce key molecules including neurotransmitter transporters and receptors, adhesion molecules, potassium channels, and water channels. Thus, neurons in the mature brain control astrocytes to ensure that astrocytes acquire and maintain specialized properties that are precisely tuned to associated brain circuits. In this grant, we will determine how different astrocytes are created and maintained in the brain to support neuronal health and circuit function and identify how the properties of astrocytes can be harnessed to mitigate brain disorders and diseases.

column37: Many researchers are developing drugs for the treatment of cancer. These drugs are administered in to the body and they kill cancer cells as well as healthy cells because the drug can go all over the body. This leads to excruciating side effects. Nanotechnology involves the use and design of structures, particles, or materials that have at least one dimensions smaller than 100 nm. Many researchers and companies are developing strategies to package drugs into a nanotechnology that can be further engineered to target and release the drug at the cancer cells in the body. The successful achievement of this would lead to increased therapeutic outcome and reduce side effects. The Chan group's research showed that 7 out of 1000 administered nanotechnology can target the solid tumour, 3 out of 100,000 can reach the cancer cells, and only 2 out of 100 cancer cells will be targeted by the nanotechnology. Thus, the delivery efficiency to each of the cancer components is low because the body is a hostile environment with biological traps such as the liver that removes the nanotechnology and prevents them from targeting cancer cells. With the funding from the CIHR Foundation grant, the Chan lab is aiming to solve the problem of delivery for nanotechnology. This will be achieved by studying how the nanotechnology interacts with each of the biological traps. These studies will allow us to develop a blueprint to build a nanotechnology that can escape them and identify strategies to increase the delivery efficiency to greater than 10% in the solid tumour. We will finally correlate the delivery efficiency with therapeutic outcome and side effects. Beyond seven-years, we will examine the optimized strategy derived from this study in human patients. column37: The control of gene expression is key to all cellular processes. One universal player in this regulation is the Mediator complex. Because it is an enzyme, the activity of CKM is in principle "drug-able" but before this can be achieved, a better understanding of how it works is required. column37: A large segment of the adult population suffers from periodontal diseases (PDs) that can result in loss of teeth, a financial burden, and potentially contribute to many systemic conditions. The pathogenesis of PDs is a complex process in which intricate subgingival bacterial biofilm induces inflammation that leads to tissue degradation and bone loss. In health, junctional epithelium (JE) links the gingiva to the tooth enamel, creating a seal and preventing bacteria from entering the gingival tissue. In PD, bone loss develops around the teeth with periodontal pockets and the JE transforms into pocket epithelium (PE). However, it is not clear how JE/PE participates in the regulation of periodontal inflammation. In the inflammatory infiltrate, the outcome of the cytokine response is regulated by the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines that are countered by anti-inflammatory cytokines. These cytokines need to be activated for biological function. An integrin known as alpha-v-beta-6 can activate them. Mutations in this integrin cause PD in mice and humans. We have shown that JE constitutively expresses this integrin and these anti-inflammatory cytokines. In PD, the expression of this integrin in PE is strongly downregulated, resulting in "acquired integrin deficiency." This integrin-mediated cytokine activation in JE appears to be crucial for the maintenance of periodontal health and preventing systemic inflammation. The factors leading to the downregulation of this integrin expression in PE cells are not known. In the present proposal, we will determine the mechanisms through which this integrin expression is downregulated in JE/PE in periodontal disease and how this integrin "deficiency" regulates cytokine expression in epithelial cells. The long-term goal is to determine the molecular mechanism of periodontal inflammation and use this information for preventive therapies.

column37: Most minor strokes are due to lack of blood getting to a part of the brain. When this occurs, patients get sudden loss of function in that region of the brain. If less lucky, the disability persists due to a minor stroke. Minor stroke and TIA account for about 50% of all strokes in Canada. This subgroup of patients can benefit from aggressive therapy with clot-busting drugs. The usual clot-busting drug usually used in Stroke is called tPA. A newer drug used in patients with heart attack called TNK works faster and is safer than tPA. In the TEMPO-2 clinical trial, we will determine if TNK, given as a single dose, is better than usual care for patients with minor stroke with a proven blocked artery. Patients will have a 50:50 chance (i.e. like the toss of a coin) of getting either treatment or usual care. Patients will be assessed 3 months after the event for evidence of disability. If this study shows that the clot busting medicine should be used in minor stroke and TIA with blocked blood vessels then this will change care of patients throughout the world.

column37: Background: The VANISH2 trial is designed to determine the best treatment for people who have life-threatening abnormalities of heart rhythm. Heart attacks leave scars in the heart muscle. The scars can interfere with the normal signaling within the heart that controls the heart beat. In some cases, the interference can cause a very dangerous abnormal heart rhythm known as ventricular tachycardia (VT). This rhythm is the most common cause of sudden death in Canada. When patients are at high risk for recurrences of VT, a defibrillator (ICD) can be implanted which can shock the heart back to normal rhythm from a cardiac arrest. These devices are life-saving but do not prevent the abnormal rhythm, they just provide a rescue when it occurs. In order to prevent dangerous arrhythmias, doctors use strong rhythm control drugs or a procedure called catheter ablation. An ablation is performed by advancing wires through the blood vessels into the heart, using X-rays and other imaging to see where they are and the short circuits within the scar can then be identified and interrupted (ablated). Neither the drugs nor the ablation procedure work perfectly and both carry risk. This trial is designed to determine which treatment is the best. Study design: Patients who have had heart attacks and develop VT will be randomly allocated (50:50) to be treated either with rhythm control drugs or catheter ablation. All patients will receive an implanted defibrillator. We will enroll a total of 366 patients and follow them for at least 2 years to see which group does the best with respect to recurrent abnormal heart rhythms and survival. Expected Outcomes: This trial will determine whether the best treatment for VT is heart rhythm drugs or catheter ablation. This evidence will permit more optimal treatment for many thousands of patients worldwide.

column36: Adequate intake of choline in pregnancy may be critical for MTHFD1 synthetase deficiency, a common genetic variant in folate metabolism
column37: Folate and choline are important nutrients required to support healthy pregnancies. Inadequate intake of these nutrients before and during pregnancy can increase the risk of birth defects and other pregnancy complications. Folate is a critical vitamin that provides the building blocks for DNA (e.g. purines) and methyl groups for a host of biosynthetic reactions. Choline is required to produce important components of cell membranes, and the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. Choline becomes even more important when folate metabolism is disturbed, because it replaces folate for certain functions. Although most Canadian women are aware of the importance of folate and reach the recommended intakes due to folate fortification programs and use of folate supplements, 85-90% do not have adequate choline intakes. Gene variants in folate metabolism, such as MTHFD1 R653Q, may also increase risk for neural tube defects, heart defects and other pregnancy complications. About 20% of Canadians have the QQ genotype, which we have shown to impair MTHFD1 function and decrease purine synthesis. Some studies have suggested that QQ women are more sensitive to low choline intake. Our goal is to determine whether inadequate choline contributes to the reproductive complications associated with the 653QQ genotype, and whether supplementation with choline or choline metabolites can overcome the effect of the genetic defect. We will examine human placentas from women with the 653RR and QQ genotypes with high and low folate intakes to assess the effects of diet and genotype on choline metabolism. We will use our mouse model for the variant to determine if low choline diets impair embryonic development and see if different types of choline supplements improve pregnancy outcomes. Our research will highlight a neglected aspect of nutrition during pregnancy and lay the groundwork for personalized dietary recommendations based on R653Q genotype to prevent reproductive complications.
