column36: Improving responsiveness across the continuum of kidney health care in rural and remote Manitoba First Nation communities (I-KHealth)
column37: Manitoba First Nations (MFNs) have the highest documented prevalence and the second highest incidence of end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) in Canada. Those living in rural/remote locations and requiring care experience significant barriers. Although preventable, nephrologists heard FN patients, especially from "renal families" (where other members have chronic kidney disease, CKD/ESKD), report that ESKD is inevitable. These statements likely reflect limited opportunities for maintaining health in the face of barriers including racism, perpetuating risk factors and undermining prevention efforts. This partnership-based program of research brings together community-based researchers from the Nanaandawewigamig Diabetes Integration Program (hereafter DIP, a part of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs), FN patients with lived experience of renal disease, University of Manitoba (UM) university-based researchers and members of the MRP (nephrologists, nurses, dietitian, social worker). We propose a 5 year program of research with 2 broad objectives: 1. To improve access to effective PC-based care for patients identified at being at low and medium risk of CKD; and 2. To expand the number of dialysis modalities available to FNs through the development of a FN-centric assisted PD model (APD), developed in partnership with FN communities. ESKD/CKD continues to fundamentally impact the lives of Indigenous patients, their families and communities. Despite repeated reviews and the implementation of a range of renal service plans, access to dialysis (in varied forms) in Manitoba rural and remote communities, including MFN communities, remains poor and still results in family dislocation. The critical questions outlined in this application remain unanswered, and stand to make a significant impact on primary care, treatment options and outcomes.

column36: Targeting Key Autophagy Proteins/Pathways for Treatment of Human Leukemia
column37: Blood cancer (leukemia) is common, with ~55,000 cases expected in the United States and Canada in 2017. The National Cancer Institute (US) calculated an overall 5-year survival rate of 56% for various blood cancers. This is because drug resistance and relapse pose significant challenges. Life-long treatment is required, with potential side-effects and a high cost. Blood cancer cells generally respond to drug therapy at the onset, but the drugs lose their effectiveness after 6-12 months. We and others have discovered that this is mainly due to the inability of current therapies to eradicate blood cancer stem cells, which maintain the potential for relapse. There is thus an urgent need to develop new therapies that specifically target blood cancer stem cells so that these cells can be eliminated, leading to a cure. We have found that ATG4B, a novel drug target and key driver in autophagy, displays abnormal activity in blood cancer stem cells, particularly in drug-resistant patients. However, there is currently no drug that blocks autophagy in a specific and potent way, nor any related drugs for autophagy inhibition that are approved as therapeutics. We have identified several promising new drugs that specifically target ATG4B in blood cancer stem cells. Combining these with current anti-cancer drugs more effectively inhibits blood cancer stem cell growth in culture than single drug treatment; this treatment strategy also doesn't have side-effects on normal blood stem cells. This study will thus investigate if this combination therapy will more effectively eradicate blood cancer stem cells obtained from drug-resistant patients, using our established animal cancer models. This will provide ultimate proof-of-concept for the development of more effective therapies with fewer side effects than currently used therapies. More immediate economic benefits are also expected from the commercialization and drug development that will be fuelled by this research.

column36: Cell cycle regulation of human pancreatic endocrine cell development.
column37: Diabetes occurs when the insulin-producing pancreatic B-cells die or stop functioning resulting in uncontrolled blood sugar levels. Current treatments for diabetes include replacing the function of these cells either through insulin injection or the use of oral drugs that help control blood sugar levels. However, often these therapies fail, resulting in extended periods of high blood sugar levels that can be damaging to nerves, eyes, and organs. Alternatives to injectable and oral therapies, including improving the function of insulin-producing cells or transplanting replacement insulin-producing cells, have been shown to reduce the damage caused by high glucose. Unfortunately, not enough is known about how normal B-cells work and not enough transplantable donor tissue is available to treat the increasing number of people with diabetes. Currently, we are able to form cells that resemble B-cells from stem cells but in order to improve the efficiency of this process we will need to better understand human pancreas development. In addition, we are unsure whether these stem cell-derived B-cells will function normally after transplantation into those with diabetes or if they will return to being stem cells. In this project we aim to study how the cell cycle, the process where a cell grows and divides to produce copies of itself, controls human B-cell formation. This study will be the first to investigate the role of the cell cycle during human pancreas development and will improve our understanding of how human B-cells are formed and are maintained. This knowledge could lead to new approaches to generate treatments for the over 10 million Canadians that are living with diabetes or prediabetes.

column36: Targeting platelet-specific molecules in periodontal disease
column37: Periodontitis, or gum disease, is a very common infection of the mouth that causes inflammation of the gum tissues and also destroys the connective tissues and bone that support the teeth. Unfortunately, periodontitis is detected only after the gums and teeth have already been affected (and often irreversibly) by disease. The tools currently available to dentists do not allow them to predict those patients (or teeth) who may be at high risk for future gum disease. In addition, the treatments for gum disease often involve costly and invasive gum surgical procedures that do not target specific molecules responsible for the disease process. During periodontal infection, white blood cells release signaling molecules known as cytokines, some of which can aggravate periodontal disease. In addition, platelets control blood coagulation (clotting) but also release cytokines that can promote inflammation. The goal of this grant application is to study platelet-specific cytokines and to determine whether shutting down the function of these molecules might help to prevent tissue damage caused by gum disease. This is a unique approach to studying this very common disease and may, over the long term, lead to improved, less invasive treatments that would benefit dental patients in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Ubiquitin-mediated regulation of membrane proteins
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada, with 1 in 2 Canadian developing cancer in their life time and 1 in 4 dying from it. Breast cancer is the most prevalent cancer in women. Over the past decade, major efforts have been devoted to tailor drug treatment to each cancer patient (personalized medicine). This is enabled by routine sequencing of tumor DNA to identify the mutations that cause or enhance tumor growth, and tailor drugs to the abnormal protein discovered; most often this involves targeting abnormal modification of the protein by a phosphate, a process called phosphorylation. Equally important is ubiquitination, a process where a small protein called ubiquitin is attached to a target protein to mark it for destruction. This process is abnormal in many cancers, yet so far, with the exception of one drug used to treat one type of blood cancer, there are no drugs that interfere with ubiquitination. My lab is working towards closing this huge gap, focusing here on investigating the role of the ubiquitin system in cancer and develop drugs to target its components. My lab has made seminal contributions to our understanding of the ubiquitin system over the past 20 years, focusing on a family of enzymes (proteins) of the ubiquitin system called the Nedd4 family. Using both cells and animal models, we have learned that this family is important for regulating both normal animal development and growth of cancer cells and tumors. We plan to now investigate how the Nedd4 family enzymes work, what regulates them, and how they regulate tumor growth (focusing on breast cancer). Moreover, we plan to perform drug screens to find drugs that can alter the function of Nedd4 proteins, with the ultimate goal of using these drugs for cancer therapy.

column37: Autoimmune diseases are chronic inflammatory diseases whereby the immune system attacks tissues of the body. However, these therapies are not a cure and they come with risks such as susceptibility to infection. Moreover, they don't always work in all patients. For example, 30% of patients who have inflammatory bowel disease and receive anti-TNF (Tumour Necrosis Factor) do not respond to the drug. Thus, we need to design better therapies that are less risky and more effective. Genetics are very important in determining ones possible risk of developing an Autoimmune Disease, and mutations in genes of the TNF superfamily (TNFSF) have been implicated in several autoimmune diseases. However, genetics are not the only determinant accounting for Autoimmune Disease - we know that environmental risk factors such as diet, smoking, microbial exposure, drugs/antibiotics etc also play an important role in increasing ones risk of getting an autoimmune disease. However, we know far less about environmental risks of disease compared to genetics. Our team is interested in the "black box" of environmental risk in the context of autoimmune disease. In particular, we would like to know how the TNFSF cooperates with a particular dietary factor - Vitamin A, as well as the microbiome (the microbes that co-exist with us in/on our bodies), to mediate effects on the immune system. As we define how specific environmental risk factors that cooperate with TNFSF, we can then re-visit the design of TNFSF-directed therapies to include potential co-therapies. This will likely improve existing therapies, making them more effective in larger groups of patients. It will also provide invaluable insights into how autoimmune diseases develop in humans.

column36: RAS-MAPK signal transduction in normal and cancer cells
column37: RAS proteins are key regulators of cell division. Significantly, over a third of human cancers are associated with activating mutations in RAS genes, which makes them the most frequently mutated oncogenes. Yet, despite considerable efforts, there are still no approved drugs that suppress directly hyperactive RAS. Important advances have nonetheless been made in recent years by targeting RAS effector proteins. My lab has a long-standing interest in a group of proteins (RAF, MEK, and MAPK) that transmit RAS signals in normal and cancer cells. Markedly, inhibition of these proteins by pharmacological means curtails tumor growth. While this path has yielded some clinical successes, severe limitations emerged, including drug resistance and toxicity. We recently brought to light a central mechanism underlying RAF activation by RAS, which contributes in part to resistance to RAF inhibitors. We propose to extend our understanding of this mechanism and, based on learned principles, develop new classes of RAF inhibitors to evade drug resistance. Innovative strategies to directly inhibit RAS function will be also explored. Using the fruit fly model organism, we also found unexpected mechanisms that selectively control MAPK protein levels. We will study these mechanisms to identify novel means to manipulate RAS-MAPK activity. Given the high degree of evolutionary conservation of the pathway, these mechanisms will also be studied in human cells as they will provide alternative entry points for therapeutic intervention. Cancer research is a long and intricate process and it is only through multi-pronged approaches that valuable therapies will emerge. We have generated knowledge, tools, and partnerships with other groups that place us in a unique position to make major contributions to the cancer field. Given the high incidence of RAS-MAPK dependent cancers, we expect that efficacious compounds targeting this critical pathway will bring enormous benefits to human health.

column36: macroH2A shapes self-renewal properties in glioblastoma
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common malignant brain tumor in adults. It is incurable, with average patient survival of about 14 months even with an aggressive therapeutic regimen consisting of maximal tumor resection, and concomitant chemotherapy and radiotherapy. One of the reasons for therapeutic failure is the complex functional heterogeneity in this brain tumor. In fact, not all cells are functionally identical in GBM, but a small population has properties reminiscent of normal stem cells, whereby they are uniquely responsible for tumor growth and recurrence. We call these specialized cells "cancer stem cells," or tumor-initiating cells. Whereas current treatments are relatively successful at targeting the other cells in this tumor, cancer stem cells have ways of evading current therapeutic intervention. We have recently shown that one feature that distinguishes cancer stem cells from the other cells in GBM is the way DNA is packaged. Cancer stem cells have regions of highly compacted DNA, which is caused by low levels of a protein that binds the DNA and relaxes its architecture. This protein is called H3.3. We have now identified macroH2A as another protein that may play a role in DNA packaging in cancer stem cells. We will characterize macroH2A, its function in orchestrating DNA packaging in cancer stem cells, and the way it affects the dynamics of tumor growth. These data will be used to rationally deploy a new generation of drugs that can affect DNA packaging. By changing the architecture of the DNA in cancer stem cells, we may be able to kill them or reprogram them into less lethal cell types that can be targeted by standard therapies. Eliminating cancer stem cells with novel techniques will be key to obliterating the ability of a tumor to grow and recur.

column36: Structural studies of neurodegenerative diseases
column37: The brain is the most fragile organ both physically and biochemically. Brain cells do not regenerate so they have to last a lifetime in face of wide range of stresses: physical, chemical, and biological. To deal with these, neurons have evolved protective mechanisms. The goal of our research is to understand these defences and develop new therapies to treat or prevent the progression of neurodegenerative diseases, which are an increasingly serious public health problem. We are focusing on Parkinson's disease, which afflicts some 60,000 Canadians, and a genetic disease, ARSACS, first identified in Quebec. Both diseases involve perturbations in the ubiquitin-proteasome system, part of the cellular recycling machinery that is used to identify and remove damaged proteins and organelles. The approach we are using is to visualize protein complexes in the ubiquitin-proteasome system using the tools of structural biology. Seeing how the proteins work will allow us to design therapies. Parkinson's disease can be caused by mutations in a quality control system for mitochondria. In healthy neurons, a protein kinase PINK1 detects damaged mitochondria and then signals Parkin, a component in the ubiquitin-proteasome system, to start the degradation process. Defects in either step cause a genetic, early onset form of Parkinson's disease. The second disease, ARSACS, is caused by loss of Sacsin, a protein chaperone that helps mitochondria split apart (mitochondrial fission). Through mechanisms not yet understood, this leads to a slow progressive loss of Purkinje cells, which control movement. Understanding and developing treatments for these diseases will also help in the treatment of other dementias. There is evidence for impaired mitochondrial function in Alzheimer's, Huntington's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The proposed studies of the ubiquitin-proteasome system will set the stage for the development of new drugs for neurodegenerative diseases.

column36: Role of Prohibitins and SUMOylation in Osteoarthritis Pathogenesis
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of joint disease and the major cause of chronic disability in adults. It is commonly assumed that multiple factors, including genetic and developmental, metabolic and traumatic factors can trigger OA. Although OA affects more than 300 million people worldwide, a clear understanding of its causes is still lacking. Moreover, the early stages of OA progression are not well understood mainly due to the difficulties in assessing these events in aging humans. We have discovered that cartilage forming cells from OA patients cannot produce a protein, termed PITX1. PITX1 proteins are essential during the development for the formation of cartilage joints and hind limb bones but its disappearance during adult life could cause knee or hip joint OA. The team led by Dr. Alain Moreau has discovered that loss of PITX1 in cartilage and bone is caused by an aberrant accumulation of a protein termed Prohibitin (PHB1) and depletion of a related family members (PHB2) in nuclei of bone and cartilage forming cells of patients suffering of knee or hip OA. This research project will investigate the causes by which nuclear accumulation of PHB1 and depletion of PHB2 occur in OA. Notably, we will examine the contribution of SUMO (small ubiquitin-like modifier) proteins given that when they attach to other proteins (a process called SUMOylation), they contribute to trap PHB1 in the nuclei of bone and cartilage forming cells in OA through their physical interactions with a SUMO-binding module presents in PHB1 protein. Our preliminary data showed an elevation of SUMOylation activity in primary OA. Elucidation of these mechanisms could be important for the development of effective treatments for OA and may lead to the development of better molecular tools to assess the risk of developing OA and monitor disease progression.

We recently discovered one of these mechanisms, namely an inhibitory network that suppresses a population of immune cells called Natural Killer cells. As implied by their name, Natural Killer cells effectively kill tumor cells. To develop, tumors need to inactivate Natural Killer cells, but it is not clear how they do so. We found that tumors cause Natural Killer cells to produce inhibitory molecules. When Natural Killer cells express these inhibitory molecules, called checkpoint receptors, they no longer effectively fight cancer. We are requesting support to i) determine how checkpoint receptors suppress Natural Killer cells, ii) understand how checkpoint receptors are induced on Natural Killer cells in the tumor environment and iii) design and test novel immunotherapies to rescue the anti-tumor activity of Natural Killer cells. Our studies will involve both mouse models of cancer and experimentation with samples from cancer patients. Our goal is to understand the inhibitory circuits that suppress the immune system in cancer in order to develop new strategies to activate our own immune cells against tumors.

column36: Do Land-Centered Mitigation Strategies Positively Impact Indigenous Health and Wellbeing in subarctic Canada?
column37: Indigenous Knowledge is a body of knowledge and beliefs transmitted orally, being both cumulative and dynamic. During the 1970s, Indigenous knowledge gained credibility on the international stage. When there is more than one way of knowing, all ways should be used to contribute to a more complete understanding of complex environment-and-health issues, such as, development on Indigenous traditional homelands. The proposed project will use Indigenous knowledge and mainstream science as complementary ways of knowing and doing, in order to evaluate land-centered mitigation strategies related to development projects on Indigenous homelands. It is well recognized worldwide that Indigenous groups have significantly lower standards of health compared to their non-Indigenous counterparts, and although many closing-the-gap programs have been initiated, this gap remains. Recently, there has been a movement away from this deficit model with more attention being paid by governments and researchers to the importance of time on the land as related to health and wellbeing. The proposed project will evaluate two existing land-centred mitigation programs. To evaluate the programs, we will use both quantitative and qualitative methods. We are trying to identify the key elements of these land-centered mitigation programs that promote health and wellbeing in Indigenous homelands, in the context of development. We want to develop a best practices framework that can be used to help inform future negotiated agreements between governments (or other proponents of development) and Indigenous groups, and also inform other government-administered programs. The proposed study will provide Indigenous communities, health care professionals, development proponents, and policy makers with new information on health and wellbeing, with respect to land-centered mitigation strategies.

column36: Evaluating innovations in transition to adult care: Transition Navigator Trial
column37: Transition to adult care is a challenging and complex time for adolescents and young adults with chronic health conditions. Many patients and families struggle to adapt to adult health care settings, and report difficulties accessing needed services to manage their health conditions into adulthood. Similarly, adult care providers feel unprepared to care for transferred pediatric patients with chronic health conditions, and lack necessary resources and time to manage the complexity and diversity of their psychosocial and medical needs. As a result, transferred patients experience difficulties navigating an unfamiliar adult health care system, and some experience significant and irreversible health deterioration. These gaps in transitional care undermine the long-term benefit of significant investments made in child health. Limited studies to date evaluate the effectiveness of interventions to improve transitional care across multiple health care settings. We propose to evaluate the impact of a patient navigator service to coordinate transition to adult care of adolescents and young adults living with a chronic health condition in Alberta. Our primary outcome of interest is emergency room/urgent care visits. We will also conduct interviews and focus groups to develop an in-depth understanding of participants' and their families' perceptions about the patient navigator role to reduce modifiable barriers to care. We will also create a comprehensive cost model to determine the net health care cost impact attributable to the patient navigator intervention. This study will provide urgently needed data to guide pediatric and adult health care providers and policy makers regarding optimal transitional care delivery and will benefit the growing population of young adults living with chronic health conditions.

column36: Novel Live TB Vaccines to Replace BCG
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the top 10 causes of death worldwide. In 2015, there were an estimated 1.4 million TB deaths, and an additional 0.4 million deaths resulting from TB disease among people living with HIV, 480,000 new cases of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) were reported, and cases of extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB) were detected in 105 countries. Because of these situations, effective vaccines are urgently needed. BCG, an attenuated live bacterium, is the only available vaccine against TB. Over 90% of children worldwide are vaccinated with BCG and >120 million doses of BCG are administered annually, making it the world's most widely used vaccine. However, BCG is not an ideal vaccine and has a limited effect against pulmonary TB in adolescents and adults. We have recently identified several molecular factors that affect the vaccine properties (safety and effectiveness) of BCG. Based on these findings, I have developed two strategies to construct new TB vaccines to replace BCG. Firstly, we have constructed a novel recombinant BCG by genetically manipulating regulatory proteins PhoP-PhoR to enhance the immunogenicity and protective efficacy of BCG. Secondly, we have constructed an attenuated live vaccine strain of M. tb (lsr2 deletion mutant), which has the ability to induce macrophage apoptosis and promote antigen presentation. We have made substantial and promising progress on each of this strategy. I describe in this proposal a number of experiments to complete the studies of our promising lead candidates. The outcome of our study will provide more effective TB vaccines to replace BCG, which will help to end the TB epidemic.

column37: Despite a decline in the number of breast-cancer related deaths in recent years, the overall incidence is increasing. Breast cancer progresses through different stages, and modern techniques can identify pre-cancerous lesions. In this project we have four aims to test this hypothesis. 1) We will examine a large number of samples from breast cancer biopsies and determine if changes in Par6 correlate with patient outcomes; 2) We will identify whether different Par6 expression patterns correlate with different signaling pathways that could contribute to cancer progression; 3) Determine the consequence of different Par6 expression patterns on breast cancer progression using novel mouse models.

column36: Mechanisms driving prefrontal cortex development in adolescence
column37: Adolescents are more likely to experience mental health disorders than individuals in any other age group. In Canada 50% of mental illnesses begin during the teenage years and about 1 out of 4 youth meets criteria for a psychiatric disorder. Several strategies are being launched to identify high-risk groups and to improve treatment and prevention programs for the youth. Yet, research on the biological causes of the heightened risk for psychopathology in adolescence is still very much needed to guide these initiatives. My research is concerned with the neurobiology of the developing adolescent brain and its susceptibility to psychopathology. I investigate whether and how environmental factors known to increase or to protect against psychiatric disorders alter adolescent brain development. My ultimate goal is to identify therapeutic targets for early intervention. My work focuses on the prefrontal cortex (PFC), a region that develops until early adulthood and undergoes dramatic changes during adolescence. The PFC mediates higher cognitive processing, including decision-making, planning, and motivation. Interestingly, its function is compromised in psychiatric conditions with an adolescent onset, including depression, substance abuse, and schizophrenia. Through studies in rodents and humans, my team identified a set of genes that controls PFC development specifically in adolescence and that are tightly associated with these disorders. My research project seeks to determine (1) how these genes control PFC development, (2) whether they are modulated by adverse experiences, and (3) whether they could serve as biomarkers of vulnerability. My research will have significant implications for the development of early prevention/intervention strategies.

column36: Mechanistic studies of the SMX tri-nuclease with direct links to genome stability
column37: The preservation of genetic material is essential for survival. However, cells are continuously exposed to a plethora of DNA-damaging agents (e.g. sunlight, chemicals). If not repaired, damaged DNA can lead to deleterious consequences, ranging from mutations and chromosomal aberrations to cell death. Cells contain sophisticated DNA repair pathways to preserve genome integrity. Our understanding of the mechanisms that underpin these networks is incomplete. This knowledge is of utmost importance since defects in DNA repair lead to various diseases, including neurological defects, immunodeficiency, and cancer. In order to determine how and why errors in DNA repair lead to these pathologies, we first need to understand the fundamental mechanisms of DNA repair and genome stability. Most DNA repair pathways require nucleases, which are molecular scissors that cut damaged and abnormal DNA structures. This is a critical activity because the failure to remove such structures compromises genome stability. In humans, a protein called SLX4 orchestrates the assembly of a large multi-nuclease complex called SMX. I have recently shown that SMX removes DNA structures that would compromise normal cell function. My work highlights an essential role for SMX in DNA repair and genome stability. However, key questions about SMX structure, assembly, and nuclease activity remain to be addressed. The overarching goal of our research is to understand how the SMX complex operates in human cells. Complementary biochemical and cellular approaches will be used to elucidate the molecular interactions that promote SMX assembly and nuclease activity. These studies will provide a solid framework for understanding how the SMX tri-nuclease functions in DNA repair and genome stability. Likewise, this research will significantly advance our understanding of the essential cellular pathways that go awry in a spectrum of human diseases, including cancer.

column36: Increasing the effectiveness of weight loss programs for emotional eaters: Training emotional eaters to use acceptance-based techniques for weight loss and maintenance
column37: Currently, over 15 million Canadian adults are overweight or obese. Standard behavioral treatment programs are right now the most effective way to achieve lasting weight loss. Emotional eaters lose less weight in such programs and easily gain it back. Emotional eating is defined as overeating in response to negative emotions. The current proposal aims to find ways to make weight loss programs more effective for emotional eaters. We propose to do this by using Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) techniques. ACT techniques are increasingly recognized as tools to avoid emotional overeating and help emotional eaters lose weight. Rather than trying to control negative emotions through change or problem solving (which has been shown not to work for emotional eaters), ACT techniques teach individuals to accept their negative emotions and to react to them in other ways than by eating. We propose to further strengthen the effectiveness of the weight loss program by training the emotional eaters to habitually apply ACT techniques when they have the urge to eat in response to emotions. We will assign overweight or obese emotional eaters randomly to either a standard behavioral treatment weight loss program or our ACT program. In the ACT program, participants will use concrete action plans (if-then plans) to apply ACT techniques to deal with negative emotions that would normally make them eat. In the standard program, participants will use if-then plans to apply cognitive behavioral techniques. We expect that the ACT program will lead to (1) greater and more sustained weight loss than the standard behavioral treatment program and (2) a greater reduction of weight-related risk factors for diabetes and cardiovascular diseases than the standard program. Further, we expect that (3) the greater weight loss is due to higher distress tolerance, better emotion coping habits, and less emotional eating.

column36: The crosstalk of myeloid cells and innate lymphocytes at mucosal surfaces
column37: The gastrointestinal tract is the body's largest mucosal surface. The number of microorganisms seeding this environment vastly outnumber the body's own cell numbers. The intestinal epithelium, a single layer of tightly connected cells, is the first physical barrier to these microbes, while the inner and outer mucus layer serve as chemical barriers and contain antibodies and anti-microbial peptides. Breaching of these barriers by microbes results in inflammation, tissue damage, organ failure and death. It is thus an obvious task to maintain the intestinal barrier function whilst avoiding overriding immune activation. This task demands about 60% of the body's total immune cell mass and further emphasizes the importance of maintaining the homeostasis of the intestinal tract. Macrophages (MP) and Dendritic cells (DC), also termed mononuclear phagocytes (MNP) are the body's major sentinel cells. Their key function is the phagocytosis of foreign antigens, its processing and presentation to T cells as an MHC-peptide complex. This process requires contextual interpretation of the local microenvironment to initiate an inflammatory response against pathogens, or immunologic tolerance towards commensals and food. The molecular cues required to interpret the intestinal microbial composition are poorly defined. It is further completely enigmatic how immunologic tolerance to this vastly great number of bacterial antigens is achieved. The quest for the molecules and mechanisms initiating this process are of great importance, as a growing number of autoimmune pathologies are associated with alterations in the intestinal microbial community. This proposal aims to understand the fundamental signals and mechanisms that are required to initiate the crosstalk of innate immune cells of the intestine, to ultimately control immunity to luminal antigens.

column36: FER as a novel therapeutic target in breast cancer
column37: Cancer is a complex continuum of diseases caused by dysregulated expression of the genes controlling cell proliferation and survival. Unfortunately, many genes can be involved, which explains why cancers are so diverse in clinical behaviour and response to treatment. More effective treatments require more knowledge of the defective regulatory pathways in individual cancers and new therapies to regulate these pathways. In practical terms this means that more effective cancer treatments will involve combinations of therapeutic agents and greater understanding of how their targets regulate normal and cancer cell behaviour. In our previous work we have studied the function of an enzyme called FER in the hope that it might represent a potential novel therapeutic target in breast cancer. To test this, we genetically engineered mice to no longer produce functional FER and found that they are overtly healthy, suggesting that humans might also tolerate inhibition of FER without serious toxicity; an important consideration for any therapeutic target. When these FER-deficient mice were bred to a strain of transgenic mice which develop breast cancer, we observed a significant attenuation in tumor development. We also learned that FER-deficient tumor cells have greatly reduced potential to spread from the site of tumor origin to other organs. These exciting result suggests that FER might represent a novel therapeutic target in breast cancer, and potentially other cancers as well. We have learned a great deal about how FER contributes to cancer cell behaviour, including metastasis and sensitivity to specific therapeutic drugs currently used to treat breast and other cancers. We now propose to validate FER as a therapeutic target in breast cancer, begin developing inhibitors of FER suitable for clinical use, and determine which drugs to combine with FER inhibitors to achieve maximum therapeutic effects.

column36: Examining the consequences of child abuse on cerebral myelination
column37: Child abuse, defined as childhood sexual, physical or emotional abuse or neglect by a parent or caregiver, causes lasting pain and hardship for millions of Canadians. The aim of this research is to understand the nature of the white matter alterations that have been described in people with a history of child abuse. White matter in the brain consists of myelinated axons, which are analogous to insulated electrical wires allowing brain regions to communicate with each other. Neuroimaging studies have found alterations in the organization of white matter in people with a history of child abuse. Unfortunately, the resolution offered by such brain scans in not sufficient to understand the cellular and molecular nature of these alterations. Postmortem human brain samples make it possible to scrutinize the fine neuroanatomy and molecular composition of white matter. Having both the expertise and a direct access to well-characterized postmortem brain samples from the Douglas-Bell Canada Brain Bank, we propose to conduct this research by comparing brain tissues from individuals having suffered from severe child abuse to matched controls. In two major white matter tracts involved in the regulation of mood and emotion, we will isolate myelin-producing cells and determine their molecular and epigenetic profiles. We will also characterize the fine morphology of myelinated axons in these tracts. This research will provide novel insights regarding the cellular and molecular nature of altered brain connectivity associated with child abuse. This may in turn help identify novel therapeutic targets, and better inform public policies aimed at preventing child abuse or minimizing its impact on mental health.

column36: Endothelial Progenitor Cell Exosomes and MicroRNA Transfer as Therapy for Acute Kidney Injury
column37: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a serious condition in which kidney function falls rapidly (often over minutes to hours), commonly because of loss of blood flow. AKI is frequent, affecting about one out of every twenty people in hospital. In severe cases treatment includes dialysis, but kidney function recovers in only about one half of patients, and mortality is high. Unfortunately, there are no treatments to improve kidney repair after AKI. Use of stem cells may help kidneys recover from AKI. Recently, we isolated "progenitor" cells from human umbilical cord blood and infused them into mice with AKI caused by temporary blockage of blood flow to the kidneys. While the cells reduced kidney damage, they did not incorporate into the kidneys, but rather appeared to release factors that stimulated recovery. In fact, the cells shed tiny membrane particles ("exosomes") that contain a substance called "miR-486-5p". Injection of mice with the exosomes strongly protects them from kidney injury, and the benefits may relate to transfer of miR-486-5p. Use of exosomes may be preferable to cell treatments, since exosomes have a low risk of immune "rejection", and are not likely to cause abnormal cell growth. However, several questions must be answered before exosomes can be given to humans with AKI. Do infused exosomes target specific kidney cells to promote repair, and does miR-486-5p transfer to these cells? How does transfer of miR-486-5p from exosomes reduce kidney injury, and what other effects may occur in the kidney with this treatment? Do exosomes protect against other causes of AKI, such as due to kidney toxins? In this grant, we will conduct animal studies to address these key questions. Detailed animal studies will also be performed to determine the effects of exosome dose, timing of administration, and differences in response according to sex. Our proposal represents the critical next step in developing exosome treatments that could help humans with AKI.

column36: Understanding the assembly, trafficking and signalling of G protein-coupled receptor dimers.
column37: Most of the drugs currently used to treat heart failure and related diseases (including beta-blockers) are directed against the largest family of cell surface receptors (which transduce signals outside of the cell into activity inside the cell), the so-called G protein-coupled receptors or GPCRs. These drugs target ligand-binding sites, i.e. the site where endogenous compounds interact with the receptor. Drugs thus act as either agonists, mimicking the effects of the natural ligand or as antagonists, which block the effects of the natural ligand. The problem is that all of these drugs produce significant side effects. This, in part is due to the fact that targeting the ligand binding site may not be specific or selective enough to elicit or block only the desired effect. This is likely due to the nature of the receptor and how it's downstream signalling pathways are organized. These receptors do not as previously believed interact with their signalling partners in a random fashion as a result of agonist stimulation. Recent data has shown that 1) each single receptor can be coupled to multiple signalling pathways in the same cell ; 2) receptors are physically and stably associated with their signalling pathways even before they are activated and 3) these complexes form during biosynthesis, i.e. before the receptor gets to it's final destination in the cell membrane. How then, can we make drugs that are more specific and have less side effects? This project is aimed at characterizing individual receptor signalling complexes, their organization and specificity and how they are assembled. Once we know 1) what is in any given signalling complex in specific cell types and 2) how it is assembled and localized in the cell we can in principle, we can thus reduce the number of side effects seen with current therapeutic approaches to diseases such as cardiovascular disease.

column36: Optimizing outcomes in survivors of childhood, adolescent and young adult cancer
column37: With modern cancer therapies, most children and teenagers diagnosed with cancer will become long-term survivors. Unfortunately, the treatments that lead to their cure also cause significant long-term health problems in many of these individuals. All cancer survivors require life-long medical care that is focused on preventing, or detecting and treating, these long-term side effects of therapy in order to maximize both the length and quality of their lives. My clinical research program is focused on defining Precision Survivor Care: how to ensure that survivors of childhood and teenage cancer receive the most appropriate health care based on their specific long-term risks by considering different clinical settings and health care providers, and how to deliver these services in a way that is most cost-effective for Canada's health care system. To achieve our research goals, we will take advantage of several large North American databases that contain detailed information on over 40,000 survivors of childhood and teenage cancer treated over the last 40 years. We will 1) explore which clinical settings and health care providers lead to the best health outcomes for survivors; 2) develop tools that help us to predict which survivors are at greatest risk for serious health problems, such as heart disease and new cancers, so that we can appropriately screen these individuals; and 3) conduct a study to find out how we can ensure that the greatest number of survivors follow guidelines for screening. The findings from this research will have direct impact on the health and quality of lives of cancer survivors across the country and will inform provincial cancer systems about how best to care for this growing population of young Canadians. This program will also create many opportunities to train the next generation of researchers and health care providers who will focus on ensuring the best possible outcomes for children and teenagers diagnosed with cancer.

column36: T-cell signaling and cancer immunotherapy
column37: T-cells of the immune system recognize and eliminate foreign pathogens. Over the past decade, it has become clear that the same cells can recognize and kill tumor cells responsible for cancer. T-cells express stimulatory and inhibitory receptors that determine how they will respond to tumors. Positive receptors include the T-cell receptor (TCR) and a co-receptor called CD28, while inhibitory co-receptors CTLA-4 and PD-1 reduce T-cell responses. Blockade of these inhibitory co-receptors with antibodies in 'immune checkpoint blockade" (ICB) and the generation of chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) in immunotherapy has now revolutionized the treatment of cancer patients with unprecedented response rates against certain tumors. Despite this success, most patients are not cured, and some cancers are unresponsive. New modalities will depend on an understanding of the make-up of signaling pathways in T-cells engaged by receptors on their cell surface. This grant proposes to discover new pathways that regulate specific T-cells, to uncover how they operate mechanistically and to apply this knowledge to the development of new immunotherapies against cancer. We propose to take a multipronged approach by uncovering the signaling mechanism used by T-cell co-receptors to promote anti-tumor immunity, to 'stop or arrest' T-cells in tumors so that they accumulate to kill the tumor and to block the expression of inhibitory PD-1 and CTLA-4 with small molecules that have therapeutic advantages over present therapies.

column36: Role of Hey2 in heart progenitors and cardiac regeneration
column37: Heart disease remains the major cause of death in North American adults. Lost heart muscle is not replaced following events such as heart attacks. The heart compensates for this to maintain sufficient pump function in a way that ultimately leads to heart failure. Further, congenital heart defects occur in close to 1% of live births, and can have a severe impact on the health and mortality of children. Despite many years of research, little is known about the stem cells that go on to form the different types of cells found in the heart. These cells are called cardiac progenitors. As they are the "building blocks" of the heart, cardiac progenitors are an ideal vehicle to fix the damaged heart. We study this in zebrafish embryos, which allow live and direct visualization of all stages of heart development. Further, the adult zebrafish heart can fully regenerate, a process we seek to understand in order to allow human cardiac repair. In this project, we aim to uncover how a gene called Hey2 regulates the way in which cardiac progenitors make the components of the heart. We have found that Hey2 acts as a master "brake" on stem cells, with cardiac progenitors dividing more and adding more cells to the heart in the absence of Hey2 function. Further, during adult heart regeneration, Hey2 expression is turned off immediately after injury, suggesting that again it is a master brake that must be relieved to allow regeneration. Learning how Hey2 regulates embryonic development and adult heart regeneration are critical first steps towards finding means to drive repair of the human heart. This knowledge will be used to devise therapies based on activating regenerative pathways to heal the damaged heart, and using zebrafish embryos to screen for potential drugs to alleviate the burden of congenital heart defects. Discovering how zebrafish cardiac progenitors are made and develop will therefore drive future efforts to repair what is at present irreparable heart disease.

column36: Mechanisms of tricellular junction formation and regulation
column37: Cells such as those found in the intesting, kidney or skin are used to form barriers between your body the environment to ensure pathogens like bacteria and virsuses do not move into or through the body and to ensure that your blood or other body fluids are contained. Cell do this by creating junctions or barriers made of proteins between neighbouring cells and when three cells meet at the corners cells also make a tricellular junction. It is clear how the permeability barrier forms at the boundary between two cells but less is known about how the corners of cells create the permeability barrier. To understand how this important junction forms and is regulated, we will identify and study those proteins that are uniquely located at this tricellular junction using the model system Drosophila (fruit fly). In fruit flies we can easily discover new proteins and test their functions.. If we understand how this tricellular junction is controlled we can then understand how it functions. We know this complex is highly conserved in humans but the function of these proteins the tricellular junction has never been studied. Therefore we can take advantage of the ease of the genetics and cell biology capable in Drosophila to understand the function of this family of proteins in epithelial cells in all animals.

column36: Translating human development to new therapies with pluripotent stem cells
column37: The goal of my Foundation application is to develop new stem cell-based therapies to treat blood, heart and liver diseases that affect millions of Canadians. Despite large investments by the pharmaceutical industry to bring new drugs to the market, heart disease remains the number one killer world-wide and the incidence of liver disease is increasing rapidly in the industrialized world. Given these statistics, new therapies are desperately needed. The studies proposed in this Foundation program seek to develop novel cell-replacement therapies to regenerate blood cells or specific cell types in the heart or liver damaged by disease or age. The cells for these therapies will be generated from a unique type of stem cell known as a pluripotent stem cell. These stem cells have the potential to produce virtually any cell type in the human body when directed to do so in the Petri dish. For our proposed studies, we will take advantage of our success over the past two decades in identifying the key regulatory factors that allow us to make different cell types from these stem cells. With these advances, we are now able to produce all the different blood cells in the body as well as most of the cells found in the human heart and liver in the Petri dish. My proposed Foundation program will focus on testing specific blood cell progenitors, heart cells and liver cells in pre-clinical animal models of human disease to determine if they can repair and regenerate damage tissue and restore normal organ function. These studies represent the next major step in the path to translating our findings from stem cell biology to new therapies. Cell-based therapies will represent a fundamental change in our approach to treating blood, heart and liver disease and will dramatically improve the quality of life of Canadians who suffer from them. Such changes will have a significant impact on health outcomes as well as on the cost to the Canadian health care system.

column36: Regulation of opioid analgesia by the TRPV1 channel
column37: Thousands of Canadians (1/5) live with chronic pain in their daily lives, pain that can start with an injury, infection or autoimmune disease but persists long after the initial inflammation subsides. This unresolved form of pain is caused by maladaptive processes (sensitization) that take place at the periphery and in the brain. Clinical pain management relies mainly on opioid drugs, however the recent "opioid epidemic", generated by the limited analgesic effect and the addictive properties of narcotics demonstrates that our understanding of the regulatory mechanisms of opioid receptor function in pathological pain is far from complete. Our project will delineate the mechanisms by which sensitization modulates opioid analgesia. We have identified the Transient Receptor Potential channel Vanilloid member 1 (TRPV1) channel, as a central regulator of opioid receptor function during inflammation. TRPV1, also known as capsaicin receptor, is an important sensor of inflammatory mediators and thus contributes to the transmission and modulation of pain signals. Using genetic, pharmacological and molecular approaches, we will set out to define the mechanisms of TRPV1 - opioid receptor interaction and determine the role of TRPV1 in opioid analgesia. Our findings could validate the use of available TRPV1 ligands, such as capsaicin cream, as combination therapy that improves opioids efficacy, mitigate the development of tolerance and thus relieve the suffering of millions of people worldwide.

column36: Examining how memories are formed, stored and used in mice
column37: Disorders of the brain, ranging from autism to Alzheimer's disease and from depression to post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), cost Canada in excess of $50 billion a year (roughly 2.8% of 2011 GDP). In addition to the heavy financial cost in terms of healthcare and lost earnings, these disorders exact an enormous social and personal burden. To develop novel approaches for the prevention and treatment of these devastating disorders that derive from brain dysfunction, it is imperative to understand normal brain function. The goal of my lab is to understand how we learn and remember, and how these processes might be altered in disease. Our studies are conducted in mice, where we manipulate and image neurons/circuits to understand behavior. Memories are stored by ensembles of neurons, referred to as engrams. Computational theories predict that memories are sparsely encoded. My lab was one of the first to identify how this sparse coding may be regulated and how individual neurons are assigned or allocated to an engram. Here we propose to build on this exciting foundation and determine the mechanisms underlying allocation as well as its overall function. We will combine multiple types of state-of-the-art tools to approach this question from several angels. Insights into the basic mechanisms of allocation in mice and humans may provide a platform for developing the next generation of treatments for human conditions associated with a breakdown in the optimal structuring of information.

column36: Overcoming immune resistance in Gram-negative bacteria
column37: Just like antibiotic resistance genes render bacteria unresponsive to traditional antibiotic therapy, there are bacterial gene products that have evolved to weaken our natural host defenses. These anti-immunity genes carried by bacteria confer intrinsic susceptibility to individuals during infection because of their neutralizing effects on our normally robust systems of immunity. This Project Scheme application builds on 10 years of research towards a comprehensive understanding of how enteric pathogens overcome host immunity by integrating a spectrum of virulence and fitness genes during host infection. Born out of our pioneering work on regulatory evolution as a mechanism of pathogen emergence, we have identified bacterial virulence proteins that inhibit natural host defense systems. Importantly, we have shown that these immune antagonists can be blocked to restore natural host immunity, even against drug-resistant organisms. Therefore, we believe there are strategies to re-sensitize pathogens to our innate immune system and create novel opportunities in anti-infective medicine. Using new technologies in genomics and microbial chemical biology, we are creating an unprecedented opportunity for insight into the interface of human and microbial biology that is informing novel strategies to combat infections and drug resistance. This knowledge base creates opportunities for innovative drug target discovery with tangible impact into public health.

column36: Novel therapies for thrombosis
column37: Thrombosis, blood clots in arteries or veins, is responsible for 1 in 4 deaths in Canada and worldwide. Thrombosis causes heart attacks, strokes and deep-vein thrombosis (DVT), clots in the deep leg veins. Vein clots can dislodge and travel to the lungs producing fatal pulmonary embolism (PE). Clots forming on medical devices such as heart valves can break off and cause PE or stroke. We aim to reduce death and disability from thrombosis by developing safer anticoagulants (blood thinners), manufacturing coatings to prevent clotting on medical devices, and raising awareness about thrombosis. Anticoagulants are a cornerstone of thrombosis treatment. The goal of such therapy is to prevent clotting without causing bleeding. Currently available anticoagulants do not meet this goal and cause bleeding, which can be fatal. Therefore, we need safer anticoagulants. We identified factor (F) XI as a target for safer anticoagulants by showing that an agent that lowers FXI levels is effective and safe for DVT prevention after knee replacement surgery. However, this agent takes several weeks to work. Therefore, we have developed faster acting FXI inhibitors that we will test at the bench, in animals, and in surgical patients. Clotting on medical devices leads to device failure or to PE or stroke. Devices trigger clotting by activating FXI. We have coatings that block this process and we will test them at the bench and in animals before moving to humans. Global awareness about thrombosis lags behind that of disorders such as cancer and AIDS. To overcome this, we launched a year-long educational program culminating in World Thrombosis Day to enhance awareness so that patients can advocate for thrombosis prevention and treatment. We have 1000 partners and a global reach of 2.7 billion and plan to further increase our reach. Therefore, by raising thrombosis awareness and developing novel strategies to prevent and treat it, we will reduce death and disability from thrombosis.

column36: Understanding Schwann cell heterogeneity for improved nerve repair
column37: Traumatic injuries to nerve and other disorders affecting nerve (called neuropathies) are common conditions, resulting in severe paralysis, sensory loss and pain in many Canadians. Techniques to repair nerve injuries to date allow some recovery of function, but most patients continue to have significant neurological dysfunction and debilitating pain. We propose a cell-based therapy to improve outcomes. The adult skin, which can be obtained from patients with minimal side-effects, contains unique stem cells (skin-derived precursors, or SKPs) that can be differentiated into a repair type of cell that normally provides support to nerve cells. This cell, called a Schwann cell, supports nerve cell axons, along with providing insulating myelin and growth factors, which helps axons regenerate following injury. We have already developed techniques to rapidly generate skin Schwann cells (SCs) from human skin, and have preliminary data on their ability to repair nerve and to produce some myelin. In this proposal, we aim to optimize SCs for repair potential and then validate their effect after delivery in a rodent nerve injury model. The optimization of SCs will include approaches to genetically re-program cells and the use of advanced cell identification and sorting techniques to isolate and then expand cells that are most potent for repair. We will deliver the optimized SCs via an approved for human use nerve guidance conduit, leveraging state-of-the-art innovation from a partner company, to examine the functionality of these cells in nerve injury and repair in rodents. We have put together a dynamic team with expertise in nerve surgery and repair (Midha), stem cell biology (Biernaskie) and neural development and genetic reprogramming (Schuurmans) and have some promising preliminary results. This research has the potential to improve the way in how nerve injury is managed, thereby positively impacting the health and well-being of many Canadians.

column36: Control of epidermal growth factor receptor signaling by clathrin signalosomes
column37: Tumours are made up of cells that can be recognized by doctors and scientists by several changes they exhibit compared to normal cells. Some of these changes involve alteration in the abundance and function of proteins found on the outer surface of the tumour cells. These changes in the function of cell surface proteins are required for tumours to grow and spread throughout in the body (metastasis). Hence, obtaining a better understanding of how cells control the function of proteins found on their outer surface has the potential to provide new ways to treat cancer. One of the types of cell surface proteins altered in cancer cells is hormone receptors, in particular one named Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR). EGFR signals to cells to grow and migrate and when uncontrolled, these traits can lead to cancer and metastasis. The cell surface is like that of a soccer-ball in that it is made up of "patches". As the hexagonal patches on a soccer ball are of different colours, the "patches" on the outer surface of a cell, termed microdomains, also have unique properties. We have discovered that a particular type of microdomain on the cell surface, called a clathrin signalosome, determines how a cell responds to certain hormones. The hormone receptor EGFR is found within the clathrin signalosomes on the surface of a cell, yet how clathrin signalosomes control hormone receptors such as EGFR remains a mystery. To uncover how clathrin signalosomes control the function of EGFR and thus cancer progression, we will use several different approaches including advanced microscopy of cells engineered to contain fluorescent versions of specific key proteins, allowing us to "see" EGFR within microdomains. This research will reveal how clathrin signalosomes work within healthy and cancerous cells to control EGFR function. Since alterations in the normal function of EGFR cause cancer cells to grow and metastasize, this work may reveal new ways to treat various types of cancer

column36: Investigating LKB1-mediated inflammation as a mediator of tumour progression
column37: It is now appreciated that the immune system plays an important role in controlling cancer progression. Recent work in understanding how T cells respond to the tumour microenvironment has led to transformative therapies - so called "immune checkpoint blockade" therapies - used to treat cancer by unleashing anti-tumour immune responses. However, inflammation is a double-edged sword. Tumour-associated inflammation has been shown to be an important contributing factor to cancer progression. Understanding how inflammation is regulated in the tumour microenvironment may help us to design rational therapies that circumvent the tumour-promoting effects of inflammation while maintaining or enhancing anti-tumour immune responses. Current models propose that immune cell interaction with the tumour microenvironment promotes cancer-associated inflammation. Our results indicate that the tumour suppressor LKB1, mutated in multiple cancers including lung, breast, and pancreatic cancer, can regulate tumour-intrinsic and tumour-extrinsic effects on cancer-associated inflammation. This proposal investigates the role that inflammation controlled by LKB1 has on cancer development and progression, and whether we can use existing drugs to block inflammation and reduce cancer incidence.

column36: Histone variant H2A.Z as a novel therapeutic target for Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a devastating form of dementia characterized by memory loss and accumulation of amyloid beta plaques and tau tangles. Developing effective therapies relies on uncovering common mechanisms that underlie memory loss and AD pathology. Here, we will test the role of a newly identified memory suppressor, histone H2A.Z, as a key contributor to memory loss and AD pathology in several mouse models of AD. We recently discovered that H2A.Z impairs memory in normal mice and that levels of H2A.Z are increased in a mouse model of AD, suggesting that therapies aimed at inhibiting H2A.Z may reverse memory deficits. We will test this hypothesis using four approaches. First, we will use genome-wide sequencing to characterize AD-related changes in H2A.Z levels and distribution across the genome, allowing us to identify key genes and gene regions affected in AD. Next, we will determine if learning-induced changes in H2A.Z binding are impaired in mouse models of AD by quantifying 2 distinct histone pools that regulate stimulus-induced changes in H2A.Z. Third, we will test the efficacy of H2A.Z and the proteins that regulate its binding for treating memory loss and pathology in mouse models of AD. We will use virally-mediated approaches to deplete genes encoding H2A.Z, or the H2A.Z-regulating proteins Anp32E and Scrap. Finally, we will validate H2A.Z as a target in human AD brains, and use human cell lines to directly test the ability of H2A.Z to reverse AD pathology. The use of multiple H2A.Z regulators allows us to test several promising new targets as potential AD therapies, with the potential to simultaneously reverse memory deficits and the underlying plaques and tangles through a novel category of histone proteins.

column36: Cellular and molecular mechanisms of neurogenesis in the retina: towards improved cell therapies for retinal dystrophies
column37: In retinal degenerative diseases, the progressive loss of the light-sensing photoreceptor cells eventually leads to blindness. Cell-based therapies are generating excitement for the treatment of retinal degeneration, as they offer the potential to restore vision. But this approach still faces major challenges. Photoreceptor cells are highly specialized neurons and generating them from stem cells remains inefficient. While some improvement was made in recent years to increase rod photoreceptor production from various populations of stem cells, the generation of a large number of cone photoreceptors, essential for daylight vision, remains a challenge. Our hypothesis to explain this limited success is that current protocols do not take into consideration the intrinsic identity of stem cell-derived progenitors. As in normal retinal development, we believe that stem cell-derived retinal progenitors have an intrinsic temporal identity that restricts their competence to generate specific populations of cell types produced during a given time window. Cone photoreceptors, for example, are produced at early stages during retinal development, whereas rod photoreceptors are produced late. Understanding how progenitors change over time to switch from cone-producing phase to a rod-producing phase is essential towards improving cell replacement protocols. We posit that manipulating the temporal identity of stem cell-derived retinal progenitors will increase cone production, which could be used for grafting or disease modelling. We will test this idea using human embryonic stem cell-derived retinal progenitors and provide mechanistic insights on how temporal identity is regulated in retinal progenitors during retinal development using mouse models. We will also test whether temporal factors can be used to reprogram retinal glial cells into photoreceptors, which would bypass the need for costly stem cell culture and grafting by stimulating endogenous regeneration.

column37: Pain is a major public health issue and societal problem that affects millions of Canadians (more than those with heart disease, cancer, and diabetes combined), costs >$43B annually and is difficult to treat when chronic because it is not well understood. Brain stimulation has been used to treat chronic pain but is effective for only a minority of patients. What distinguishes responders from non-responders is not known. We recently discovered that healthy people differ in how an area of the brain called the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) communicates with the brain's pain modulation circuitry, and this difference can contribute to how they modulate pain. In this project, I will characterize neural activity within the sgACC and its communication with the brain's pain control system, and determine whether it is abnormal in patients with different types of chronic pain. I also measure the functioning of the sgACC system in patients before and after they have undergone nerve decompression surgery to alleviate chronic pain associated with carpel tunnel syndrome. This project will provide fundamental knowledge about the individuality of the pain modulation system in the brain. The project will also identify particular characteristics of the sgACC system that are present in patients prior to ineffective or effective surgery. This information could then be used to predict which patients will benefit from carpel tunnel surgery. More broadly, the information could be used to select patients most likely to benefit from other procedures that stimulate that brain that could be developed to modify how effectively the brain's pain modulation system works.

column37: Injuries are not accidents; they are predictable and preventable. Injuries are the leading cause of ill health and mortality in Canadian youth. The foundation of my program will include comprehensive injury surveillance that I have developed and validated in youth sport. My research program has influenced best practice and policy through sustainable solutions that have had significant public health impact by reducing the burden of youth S&R injury. My research program will engage youth, parents, coaches, clinicians, sport organizations, educators, and policy makers across health care, education, and public health. The program will target a 25% improvement in decreasing the number of youth S&R injuries and enabling more youth to return safely to health and daily activities by reducing injury consequences and economic burden

column36: Commensal fungal metabolism in lymphoid organ development and maintenance
column37: In our intestine, there is a large cohort of microbes, including bacteria and fungi. Their presence is important for our immune system development. In germ-free mice (no microbes in the gut), lymph nodes in the host are small and incapable of mounting efficient responses against invading pathogens. For many years, we know this dependence of our immune system on those "microbial guests", but no molecular understanding was available. The presence of these fungi in our gut microbiota drives a group of retinoic acid-producing dendritic cells (a type of immune cells) to leave the gut and come the growing lymph nodes, where they stimulate the structural development. They do so by inducing a particular set of molecules, PNAd, at the entry portal of lymph nodes. Interestingly, in the early weeks, lymphocytes entering those sites are educated to return to the gut to build the defense there first. This makes sense as the microbial burden is the heaviest in the gastrointestinal tract after birth. To follow up on those findings, we plan to study what types of fungal productions are driving these cells to leave the gut, and how these dendritic cells change the chemotaxis molecule expression in the peripheral lymph nodes. We also wish to study whether the homing of lymphocytes from the peripheral lymph nodes is critical to the initial gut immune homeostasis in the neonates. These questions are critical for us to comprehensively understand the interplays between our microbiota and the health of our immune system.

column36: ROS metabolism and mitochondrial function in the aging process and in age-dependent diseases.
column37: Most diseases that threaten Canadians, including cancer, heart disease, metabolic diseases, and neurodegenerative disease (such as Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease) are associated with age: they are much more likely in older individuals. Our goal is to understand the role that free radicals (also called reactive oxygen species (ROS)) play in the overall process of aging and in age-dependent diseases. Free radicals are chemically reactive molecules, which means that they can potentially damage cellular constituents. However, we have discovered that, rather than causing aging, the important role of free radicals as regulators of cell function contributes to longevity by helping cells and organisms to react to, and combat, various stresses. On the other hand, in aging individuals, the production and removal of these free radicals becomes much less well-balanced. It is in this situation that free radicals can be produced in excess, thus leading to damage to cells and promoting the development of disease. We are studying the role of free radicals in both situations, beneficial in young individuals and potentially deleterious old individuals, in order to learn both to harness their beneficial properties and protect from their deleterious effects.

column36: Minimizing Lung Injury during Mechanical Ventilation
column37: Over 90,000 Canadians each year become critically ill and need a life-support device called a mechanical ventilator; this forces oxygen into the lungs through a breathing tube, and helps the patient to breathe. While mechanical ventilation saves lives there is also a serious price: forcing air into the lungs causes additional lung damage that can lead to disability or death. The current grant application builds on two novel findings in my laboratory. First, our laboratory reported that an old-fashioned 'Iron Lung' could be applied to the outside of the abdomen (not the chest) in conjunction with conventional mechanical ventilation; the effect was to selectively open up the lower parts of the lung without over-stretching (and injuring) the upper lung regions. We will understand how this works, and then by knowing which patients might benefit, will rapidly move to test the approach in volunteers and then in patients. If successful, this would represent a fundamental advance in mechanical ventilation. Second, briefly disconnecting a ventilator, a common occurrence to carry out routine patient care, can result in rapid deflation of the lung. This was traditionally thought to be without consequence. However, using laboratory models we have discovered that this may cause significant harm, and have preliminary data explaining how and where in the lung this harm occurs. We will determine the exact mechanisms and then determine if this occurs in patients, and devise approaches to its prevention. These two complementary lines of research will make mechanical ventilation safer (and more effective) and if successful, will save the lives of many critically ill patients.

column36: Characterizing RecQ helicase Sgs1 in maintaining genomic stability during aging
column37: Cancer and aging are seemingly distinct events. However, similar changes in the ability of our cells to respond to environmental challenges are observed in both aging and cancer. For example, damage to DNA, our hereditary material, accumulates in both cancer cells and older cells. Normally, when DNA becomes damaged, pathways become activated to repair the damage. These repair pathways are known to become disrupted in cancer and now some pathway components are proving to be effective targets in particular types of cancer therapy. In older cells, DNA damage accumulates, however the underlying reason for this is not known. To date, most work in cancer research has been performed in young cells, young model organisms or in human cancer cell lines. Since most cancers occur in older individuals, we believe that it will be much more relevant to study DNA repair during aging, especially since there is very little known about how these processes might change or contribute to cancer development. Confounding issues certainly arise with age, but at the cellular level, where cancer and aging biologically converge, pathways that protect our DNA from mutations clearly need to be studied in cells that have aged. My lab uses the model organism budding yeast. Over the past 60 years, work in yeast has provided a foundation of knowledge critical for understanding the molecular events leading to cancer in humans. Since yeast cells are well characterized regarding DNA repair and they also age, they represent a powerful model for rapidly asking how age is related to DNA repair. Thus, characterizing DNA repair in old yeast cells will provide important clues for why DNA repair efficiency decreases and cancer increases exponentially with age in our population.

column37: Depression is a debilitating mental disorder affecting over 350 million people globally and is associated with high personal and socioeconomic burden. Efficacy of classical antidepressant medications, including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressants is compromised by extended delays to achieve therapeutic efficacy. Sadly, 50% of patients with treatment-resistant depression (TRD) do not obtain remission with traditional antidepressants. One of the most exciting discoveries in neuropharmacology in two decades is that a single intravenous infusion of ketamine has robust, rapid and sustained antidepressant effects in individuals with TRD lasting up to 1-2 weeks. Not surprisingly, this discovery has inspired great interest in identifying the underlying molecular mechanisms. Ketamine blocks the NMDA class of glutamate receptors, consistent with dysfunctions within the glutamatergic system and dysregulation of synaptic plasticity in the pathophysiology of depression. Systematic investigations of ketamine's effects on in vivo synaptic plasticity in animal models of depression, as well as direct contribution of synaptic plasticity changes to ketamine's antidepressant effects, are key to understanding the mechanisms by which ketamine and other candidate drugs achieve their unique effects. Proposed experiments will utilize a genetic model of depression (Wistar-Kyoto WKY rat). In preliminary experiments we observed weakness in synaptic plasticity that was rescued by ketamine. Therefore, we hypothesize that impaired synaptic plasticity in WKY rats causes depression-like deficits in motivation, cognition, and social interaction. Furthermore, we propose that restitution of synaptic plasticity is a crucial mediator of the antidepressant response to ketamine. Novel candidate compounds will be screened using the WKY model of TRD.
