column36: Predictors of poor health and functional recovery following road trauma: An emergency department inception cohort study.
column37: BACKGROUND: Each year in Canada, road trauma causes over 2,000 deaths and 10,000 serious injuries. Disability after an injury is a major public health concern, but the long term health outcome after road trauma is poorly investigated and based mostly on outdated research that does not reflect modern vehicle safety features or modern medical treatment, and largely ignored cyclists and pedestrians. In addition, there is almost no research that helps healthcare providers know which patients are most likely to have a bad outcome following a crash - making it difficult to provide them with the care they require. It is important for policy makers to know the healthcare costs and lost productivity that results from road trauma, but this information has not been well studied. Our study will provide this missing information. METHODS: We will interview patients who visit an emergency department after a car crash. The interview will ask about their general health before the crash, the injuries they had from the crash, and other details of the crash. We will interview them again at 2, 4, 6, and 12 months after the crash to find out about problems they had since the crash. The follow-up interview will ask about pain, ability to go about their usual activities, whether they have returned to work, and about the medical care they required after the crash. STUDY FINDINGS and IMPORTANCE: Our study will help doctors and nurses know how quickly people recover from their injuries and which patients are likely to have long term health problems after a car crash. We will also describe how much medical treatment these patients require and how much work they miss. This information will also help policy makers make informed decisions on how much money and resources to devote to crash prevention or to treatment programs for crash victims.

column36: Mutational mechanisms of pancreatic cancer development
column37: A diagnosis of pancreatic cancer is often fatal. This deadly tumour is highly aggressive, metastasizes rapidly in patients, and is resistant to nearly all forms of cancer therapy. This disease is expected to be the second leading cause of cancer-related death in the coming decade. Improving clinical outcomes has proven to be stubbornly difficult in pancreatic cancer and highlight an urgent need for scientific advances. This deadly disease often strikes "out of nowhere," and the cancer is usually inoperable by the time the patient experiences symptoms. The cause of pancreatic cancer's frequent appearance at an advanced stage has long been a medical mystery. Using whole genome sequencing, our group reconstructed the history of pancreatic cancer development in 150 independent tumours. Unexpectedly, we found that many of the important genetic events that cause this cancer actually occur 'all at once', similar to the idea of the 'big-bang". These results provide fresh insights into how these tumours develop and help to explain why this disease is so aggressive. These 'big-bang' type events, which are so frequent in pancreatic cancer, are rare in cancers that are not as aggressive. This leads us to believe that they play an important role in the biology of pancreatic cancer. Our goal is to evaluate the impact of these 'big-bang' events on pancreatic cancer development. Overall, we plan to determine if these events are the actual cause this cancer, how they influence metastasis, and therapy resistance. By better understanding the biology of this lethal tumour, we hope to eventually design more effective therapies to improve patient outcomes.

column36: Role of cerebrovascular abnormalities in the pathophysiology of autism spectrum disorders.
column37: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) alter the child's development, affecting motor skills and social interactions. Genetic anomalies (mutations) have been identified as possible origins for ASD, leading for instance to delays in the maturation of neurons. About 1% to 2% of children worldwide have been diagnosed with ASD, but the causes of ASD remain enigmatic. Brain maturation heavily depends on a steady supply of oxygen and nutrients from the blood stream. As such, key vascular features ensure proper brain maturation: the growth of blood vessels, the maintenance of blood vessel permeability, and the regulation of blood flow. Early life impairments in these vascular features will alter the normal course of brain development. Very few studies have investigated the possible contribution of vascular deficits to this group of disorders. Several studies suggested a link between ASD and altered cerebral blood flow, and a recent postmortem study using brains of young ASD patients suggested a possible impairment in the formation of brain blood vessels. But these observations have not been thoroughly verified, nor tested in a robust animal model of the disease. As a result, involvement of the brain vasculature to the onset and/or progression of ASD remains to be elucidated. We propose to address this gap of knowledge by thoroughly investigating 1) the health of the brain vasculature in a genetically-engineered animal model of ASD, and 2) the consequences on neuronal development when only brain blood vessels (not neurons) are affected by a known, ASD-associated mutation. Our goal is to test novel questions: How do blood vessels develop in the ASD brain? What role(s) do vascular deficits play in the progression of ASD? Our research program proposes a new angle to ASD research, providing novel insight into the involvement of brain blood vessels in ASD. Identification of new players in ASD pathogenesis is essential to the develop new therapeutic strategies.

column37: As part of our everyday lives we are exposed to a wide variety of chemicals derived from consumer products, such as foam, electronic equipment and plastics. Most of these chemicals are present at very low concentrations. However, exposure to even low doses of substances that disrupt hormones can exert important biological effects. In particular, exposures to endocrine disrupting chemicals are suspected of contributing to the declines in human fertility reported from the developed world. In the past decade governments across the world have regulated the production, uses and importation of specific environmental chemicals that have been shown to disrupt hormone actions. As a consequence, alternative chemicals have entered the market to fill the "gaps". However, there is often little information on the extent to which we are exposed to these replacements or on their health impacts. Our research will focus on a major group of such chemicals, the organophosphate esters (OPEs), that is in rapidly increasing use. We will test the hypothesis that exposure to these compounds is associated with adverse effects on the male and/or female reproductive systems. Cells with key endocrine functions will be used to identify genes and pathways that are disrupted by OPEs and may serve as biomarkers of their effects on fertility. Using an animal model we will elucidate the effects of exposure to the mixture of OPEs found in Canadian house dust on male and female fertility. Finally, we will assess the association of human OPE body burden with female and male infertility. These studies will enhance our understanding of the health consequences of exposure to a family of widely used chemicals for which we currently have very limited data. In addition, we expect that they will contribute to the development of policies to ensure the identification of alternative chemicals that are safer and have a reduced environmental impact prior to their use as replacements.

column37: Cardiovascular disease, which includes coronary heart disease and stroke, affects more than 1 million Canadians and 300 million persons worldwide, and results in 18 million death each year. One of the most effective and widely used approaches to prevent cardiovascular disease is antithrombotic treatment (e.g., aspirin, clopidogrel, warfarin, newer direct acting oral anticoagulants) that prevent potentially harmful blood clots from forming at the site of atherosclerotic plaques. The most important side-effect of these treatments is bleeding. The importance of bleeding has been vastly under-rated. We paid little attention to bleeding, thinking that for the most part this was easily treatable, and much less important than heart attack and stroke. We now know that bleeding is not only common, affecting thousands of Canadians with cardiovascular disease each year, but is also a powerful risk factor for heart attack and stroke, the very events that these treatments aim to prevent. My research program focuses on determining why persons with cardiovascular disease develop bleeding, and why those who bleed are at such high risk of attack and stroke after bleeding. Having identified the risk factors and mechanisms, my subsequent studies will evaluate whether targeted interventions can prevent cardiovascular events and mortality related to bleeding.

column36: Molecular and physiological understanding of the protein tyrosine phosphatome towards clinical applications.
column37: For the past 25 years, my laboratory focused on elucidating the function of a family of genes named "protein tyrosine phosphatases" (PTPs). The PTP family contains 107 different genes in humans that control a plethora of normal cell functions. PTPs have one common property: to remove a phosphate molecule added to specific tyrosine residues present in many cellular proteins, which confer, or deny, various properties to proteins. Our main purpose is to understand PTP function and to transfer this knowledge into common scientific knowledge and towards clinical applications. Herein we propose three experimental sections. Section 1 is a continuation of our recent work on PTPN1(also known as PTP1B) and PTPN2 (also known as TC-PTP) in characterizing their roles in the immune system. We plan to examine their function in a type of immune cells named "T-cell ". These comprise several subsets of T-cell with different function that kill tumor cells and maintain surveillance against cancer cells. Our proposal is to use small molecule inhibitor of PTPs to reactivate patients T- cells or improve the novel cancer immunotherapeutic approaches of CAR-T cells. Section 2 is pursuing a new system of proteins (the PRL-CNNM proteins) that we first reported in 2014. Involved in the supplies of magnesium to all higher organisms, PRL PTPs are upregulated in almost all cancers to sustain growth and invasion. By understanding their roles and preventing their binding to CNNMs, we intend to develop a novel class of anti- cancer drugs. Finally, section 3 has for objective to explore further this large and relatively still unknown gene family. Our previous data showed that most PTPs are involved in the immune system. We plan to assess the function of each one of the entire gene family towards inhibiting or activating the immune system response against cancer. We are confident that this program will contribute original and important scientific advances and novel clinical applications.

column37: Cancer is the leading cause of mortality in Canada representing 30% of all deaths. One in 2.3 individual will get cancer and 1 in ~3.8 will die from it, incurring $1.16 trillion in direct cost worldwide in 2010. Genomic instability is a common feature of tumor cells and is thought to represent a basic mechanism to acquire the several genetic alterations required during the neoplastic process. Double-strand breaks (DSBs), the most lethal kind of DNA lesions, can be repaired by two pathways; homologous recombination (HR) or non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ). The choice between NHEJ and HR involves an intricate network of resection enzymes whose interplay and hierarchy remain largely unexplored. It is becoming increasing clear that not only failure, but also misuse, of these pathways can trigger genomic instability leading to cancer, the biggest killer in Canada. Paradoxically, defects in the DSB pathways provide weaknesses that can be exploited to design new targeted cancer therapies. The DSB repair machinery can thus be seen as a double-edged sword in cancer protection and treatment, making the understanding of its regulatory mechanisms of crucial importance in the cancer research field. This proposal aims to obtain a comprehensive view of the functions of HR enzymes. By funding this Foundation Program, it will ensure that the mechanisms of these enzymes are defined. Furthermore, using novel inhibitors discovered by our group, we will inhibit the functions of these enzymes to target the vulnerabilities of cancer cells to improve patient care.

column36: Needles without tears: Inoculating children against pain and fear
column37: Not just a poke, needle pain and related fear are in fact major health concerns. All Canadian children undergo painful needle procedures; hospitalized children undergo multiple procedures daily. Pain causes unnecessary suffering, fear, procedure complications (e.g., fainting, failed procedures), and avoidance behaviours. An alarming 20% of unvaccinated 6- 18-year-old children (herein called youth) refuse vaccination due to fear of needle-related pain. This leaves them at risk of acquiring and spreading disease. My vision is to make children all over the world healthier by improving their experiences during needle procedures which will increase needle procedure acceptance. In previous work, I led the creation of a Clinical Practice Guideline (CPG) to address pain and fear and documented gaps for youth. The current project has been developed with key user groups to address these gaps using real-world solutions. Over 7 years, I will build on my successes with my CIHR-funded Help ELiminate Pain in Kids & Adults (HELPinKids&Adults) team to address key unanswered questions. Specifically, to help close the pain care gap for youth, I will: 1) identify best practices for injection techniques, 2) implement and evaluate a novel tool/game developed by youth teaching youth how to reduce pain, fear and fainting, and 3) create both an updated CPG that incorporates this new evidence and a national plan to facilitate integration into healthcare systems. I expect improvements in patient-prioritized outcomes (pain, fear, fainting and needle procedure acceptance); I estimate a 5% absolute increase in school-based vaccine uptake alone. Long-term, I expect improved health outcomes and health cost savings due to improved compliance and efficiency. Importantly, this research program engages youth and other stakeholders to address youth's most pressing concern about healthcare - the needle - and fulfills our ethical obligation to first, do no harm.

column36: Mechanochemical signalling in embryonic wound repair
column37: An outstanding question in biology is how cells coordinate their behaviours. Cells coordinate their movements to sculpt, repair, or invade tissues. A common feature of collective cell movements in development, repair, and disease is the reorganization of the cytoskeleton, the network or proteins that cells use to generate mechanical forces. However, the mechanisms that promote cytoskeletal redistribution during collective cell migration are not understood. We found that highly reactive, oxygen-containing molecules (reactive oxygen species) are critical for cytoskeletal rearrangements during collective cell movement. In addition, we and others showed that cytoskeletal proteins can be regulated by the mechanical forces sustained by cells in living animals. We will use the process of epidermal wound repair in fruit fly embryos to model collective cell movements and establish the basic molecular and physical mechanisms of cytoskeletal reorganization during collective cell migration. Fruit fly embryos are transparent, allowing visualization of coordinated cell movements with high spatial and temporal detail; they are easy to manipulate genetically, and also with drugs and lasers; and over 75% of the genes involved in human disease exist in fruit flies. We will apply advanced microscopy and image analysis to track the distribution of molecules in living embryos; mathematical modelling to develop hypotheses about how changes in chemical or mechanical signals may affect cytoskeletal protein dynamics and cell behaviour; and pharmacological, genetic and biophysical manipulations to test modelling predictions and determine the molecular pathways by which reactive oxygen species and mechanical forces affect cytoskeletal dynamics. Our results will reveal the mechanochemical signals that coordinate cell movements, and will enable subsequent efforts to manipulate cell migration for tissue engineering or cancer research applications.

column37: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), such as hydrocephaly, lissencephaly, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and intellectual disability affect up to 1 in 8 children born and represent a significant challenge to the health care system and resources available to Canadian families. In Ontario alone, an estimated 300,000 children are diagnosed with developmental disorders of the brain, while ASD alone occurs at a high frequency of 1/88, and is associated with a lifetime cost per individual of $5.5 million. NDDs are thought to arise from abnormal brain formation in the fetus. Yet the underlying genetic and cellular mechanisms remain largely unknown and treatment options are extremely limited. One of the key brain regions involved in NDDs is the neocortex. Its formation relies on the production of a diverse set of neuronal populations and their organization into specific networks important for cognition. Understanding what controls the differentiation and migration of neurons is crucial as alterations in brain anatomy are seen in patients with a range of psychiatric illnesses. We have identified a novel regulator of neocortical organization that when mutated in the mouse gives rise to several hallmarks of developmental disorders of the human brain, including the abnormal formation of neural circuits, enlarged ventricular spaces, reduced axonal growth, and an abnormal accumulation of cells near the ventricles. We propose to study use this mouse model to advance our knowledge of the cellular and molecular processes that contribute to the formation of the neocortex and its connections to regions of the brain important for emotion and cognition. In so doing we will identify diagnostic events and therapeutic strategies for addressing developmental disorders of the brain.

column36: Scaling up shared decision making for patient-centred care
column37: Most Canadians wish to stay at home in their old age, but to still have access to healthcare. With new medical technologies (such as alarm bracelets), more and more seniors can stay at home for longer and receive care from home care teams. But seniors living at home often face difficult decisions, such as "Who will look after me when I can't look after myself any more, or if I have dementia?" or "Should I move to a nursing home, or stay here?" For the caregiver, the decision may be "Can I continue to care for my loved one at home?" When more than one option is possible, home care teams can help seniors and their families who are making these hard decisions by giving them the information they need and asking about their values and preferences. This way, seniors and their caregivers can know more about their choices and choose options that reflect what is important to them. We call this 'shared decision making', and it has been shown to improve patient experiences (less disappointment, anxiety or regret) and better use of healthcare dollars. More and more, seniors will be making such decisions in consultation with their home care teams. Over the years we have developed tools and training programs to help home care teams support seniors and their caregivers in making the decision about whether a senior who is no longer independent should stay at home with more help, or move to a nursing home. However, most of our research has been at the regional level. Too many pilot projects that could benefit far more people stay hidden at the local level. So we plan to scale up the tools, programs and systems that seem to work well for one decision and one region. We will adapt and apply them to home care in other places across Canada and to other difficult decisions, so that more seniors and their caregivers benefit from shared decision making and can make decisions together that are better for their health, their pocket, and their quality of life.

column36: Molecular Targeting of Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia and Bone Marrow Regeneration
column37: Cancer has become a major healthcare issue for Canada, and is now the leading cause of death in our country. 1 in 2 Canadians may be afflicted with cancer, and 1 in 4 Canadians are expected to die from it. Although progress in therapy has been made in many cancers, such as breast and prostate, treatment options for other cancers remain stagnant. This is exemplified by acute myeloid leukemia (AML), a type of blood cancer where dysfunctional leukemic cells take over the blood system. Disease burden can initially be reduced by lowering the leukemic cell numbers (called remission) with chemotherapy, but the disease usually comes back within 2 years (called relapse). When AML relapses, the option is to re-treat the cancer with the same chemotherapy but at a higher dose, and for longer. Unfortunately, the disease usually becomes resistant to treatment and can no longer be controlled. However, the exact reason for AML relapse and resistance to chemotherapy remains unclear. Our program group in Hamilton, Ottawa and London has now identified rare leukemic cells that: a) survive chemotherapy and b) regrow to give rise to relapsed disease. Detailed tests on these unique cells revealed that before they regenerate AML disease, they begin to express leukemia-specific proteins that give them a growth advantage in the bone marrow space where they live. Furthermore, we have revealed that the bone marrow space itself changes to support leukemia, and is directly affected by chemotherapy. Available drugs can inhibit some changes in the bone, and our early findings indicate these drugs can reduce relapse when combined with chemotherapy. Our team of physicians, biochemists and stem cell biologists will define and test a series of new drugs that target proteins that inhibit surviving leukemic cells and change the bone marrow environment that will prevent relapse before it occurs, and activate normal blood stem cells to combat leukemia in patients in the next 7 years of support.

column36: Systematically mapping functional human sequence variation and context-dependent protein interactions
column37: There are few cases where we fully understand how DNA sequence variants impact gene function, and how these changes propagate through networks of molecular and cellular interactions to yield human disease. My team is developing genomic technology to address two distinct goals to improve our understanding of genetic disease: 1) Mapping sequence-function relationships to identify human DNA sequence variants affecting their gene product; and 2) Mapping the downstream network of macromolecular interactions, including their dynamics and context-dependence, to better understand how the connection from genotype to phenotype is mediated. Towards the first goal, we developed a hybrid experimental/computational platform for deep mutational scanning (DMS), in which the functional effects of missense variants are exhaustively mapped in specific target human disease genes. These maps have already been validated for two human disease genes: calmodulin and cystathionine beta-synthase, with the former map already in clinical use. We will continue improving the DMS technology: extending it to human cell models and experimentally detecting the impact of both intronic and exonic variation on splicing and gene function, and applying it to ~100 human disease genes over the next 7 years (approximately 2% of the ~4000 annotated human disease genes). Towards the second goal, we developed a 'barcode-fusion genetics' (BFG) strategy, enabling two reagent libraries to be coupled so that all reagent pairs are tracked via combined ('fused') barcodes. This allows efficient mapping of protein interactions under different environments and genetic backgrounds. We recently developed a prototype method, 'messenger BFG', in which fused barcodes are transcribed, sensing interaction dynamics on the time scale of minutes. We will continue developing this approach, adapting it to human cell-based protein interaction assays, and applying it at proteome scale to both human and yeast proteomes.

column36: Cachexia, the last illness: Translational research on mechanisms, diagnostic criteria and clinical management
column37: Patients with cancer often experience noticeable weight loss, which can start prior to diagnosis and which rapidly increases when the disease reaches an advanced stage. Over the course of the disease, affected people become thin sometimes to the point of becoming "skin and bones". This wasting, known as cachexia, is causes patients to become weak, frail and increasingly dependent on others for daily tasks and self care. Wasting also has important medical implications. Patients with wasting show very poor ability to tolerate cancer treatments and are sometimes forced to stop chemotherapy early due to severe side effects. There are no approved treatments for cancer-associated wasting. While all of the reasons for this are unclear, we may simply know too little about how body weight is controlled in people with cancer to be able to succeed. My vision is to discover new ways to alleviate cancer associated wasting. I developed a highly successful and internationally acclaimed research team in this area, which is unrivalled in its capacity to make key strides forward so that we can alleviate the suffering associated with this condition. 1. I will develop standardized criteria for diagnosis and early detection, so that every patient with risk of developing wasting can be identified as early as possible. 2. I will work to reveal the diverse factors which lead to wasting, so that we can provide a personalized and specific treatment approach to each patient. 3. I will also develop personalized chemotherapy dosing to limit toxicity in patients with wasting, allowing them to complete and benefit from their treatment plan. 4. I will continue to catalyze research partnerships to rapidly advance basic and clinical research and multiply the productivity of this unique Canadian-led effort.

column36: Modeling antibody diversification processes through Cas9-mediated mutagenesis
column37: The immune system plays a major role in protecting humans from bacteria, viruses, and toxins (known as antigens). One of the ways that the immune system accomplishes this is by producing antibodies that bind to and neutralize these antigens. Antibodies are small molecules made by B cells. Each B cell makes only one type of antibody which will bind to only one antigen. By changing the antibody stalk, the properties of the antibody are changed. For example, IgM antibodies can be changed to IgG antibodies which can be used by macrophages to engulf bacteria that are coated by these antibodies, or to IgA antibodies that can be secreted into mucosal tissue and neutralize pathogens in the lung or the gut. Changing the antibody class is accomplished by the class switch recombination process, and the key enzyme that initiates this process is called AID. However, much needs to be learned about this process. In this grant proposal, we plan determine the types of mutations and the enzymes that are required by AID to induce class switch recombination. In addition, since AID has been shown to induce chromosomal translocations that are central to the development of lymphomas, this proposal will also examine the types of mutations and enzymes involved in the development of these cancer-causing events. Hence, the proposed work will allow us to determine how an effective antibody response is generated against pathogens, and will also characterize molecular pathways that play important roles in cancer development. This new information will in turn influence vaccine development or the generation of therapeutic agents that target lymphomas.

column36: Host cell protein substrates of enterovirus proteases
column37: Enterovirus infections are associated with several acute and chronic diseases worldwide and in Canada. Most enterovirus infections are cleared by the immune system, however, infection by certain enteroviral species and strains can be more severe. Poliovirus is the most well-known member which causes paralytic poliomyelitis. The non-poliovirus members are more common such as rhinovirus, which causes the common cold, and coxsackievirus and EV71, which are associated with more debilitating diseases such as viral myocarditis, Type I diabetes, and hand-foot-and-mouth disease, and in rare cases, meningitits. Although enteroviruses have been studied for several decades, the molecular basis of infection and the pathogenic mechanisms leading to disease are still poorly understood. One of the signature properties of enteroviruses is that the virus expresses a protein, called a protease, which cleaves host proteins in the cell to facilitate virus infection. Currently, the extent of host proteins targeted by the viral protease is not known. In this study, we will utilize a novel unbiased proteomics approach to comprehensively identify all of the targets of the proteases from coxsackievirus. Unlike other methods, this new approach is sensitive and can identify the location of the cleavage site on the target protein. The identification of novel targets will provide a catalog of the host processes that viruses affect. Importantly, the knowledge gained will allow us to identify new targets for antiviral therapy. The development of this strategy can be exploited to identify the repertoire of host targets of proteases from other viruses.

column36: Identifying Autosomal Recessive Genes for Intellectual Disability
column37: The program goals are to identify new genes for intellectual disability (ID), focusing mainly on autosomal recessive (AR) causes, to deduce their functions, to direct findings back to the clinic, and to identify therapeutic opportunities. The vast majority with ID currently receive no molecular diagnosis-a shortcoming that significantly impacts health and lifespan. Knowing the causative gene benefits through diagnosis, care and treatment, overall health and lifespan, and counselling and planning for families. AR forms of ID are believed to account for a large proportion of affected individuals, and are the main genetic cause of ID in countries where within-family marriage (consanguinity) is common. However, attempts to map the genes responsible have been poorly explored. Mapping genes for autosomal recessive disorders can be performed with great efficiency in consanguineous families with multiple affected individuals (MPX) using microarray genotyping combined with next generation DNA sequencing approaches. We have completed studies of 192 MPX consanguineous non-syndromic ID families and identified 38 new genes. We aim to continue with >300 additional MPX, and >100 single affected (SPX) families (or proband/mother/father trios) from countries where consanguinity is common. We aim to identify causative genes/mutations in these families, using a combination of genotyping and next generation sequencing. Genes identified in consanguineous families are also relevant to outbred populations, thus we plan to survey the genes identified in >2500 ID patients from Canada. Our studies to date have already had an impact on diagnosis, and the proposed work will add significantly to this legacy. The results will also help illuminate the pathophysiology, facilitating the development of treatments. Understanding the genetics of these diseases will improve diagnosis and treatment in the long term.

column36: Thrombosis and Thrombocytopenia: Novel mechanisms and treatments
column37: Platelets are small blood cells that aggregate and are responsible for bleeding arrest (hemostasis) at sites of injury. They are also key targets in many diseases. High platelet activity may result in heart attack and stroke (thrombosis), which are leading causes of death worldwide, while low platelet number may cause severe bleeding and miscarriages (thrombocytopenia). Our goal is to elucidate underlying mechanisms of these diseases and develop novel therapeutics. Platelet surface integrin alphaIIb beta3, is traditionally thought to exclusively bind fibrinogen (Fg)/VWF and mediate cross-linking of platelets (aggregation) during hemostasis/thrombosis. My discovery of Fg/VWF-independent thrombosis, proved that unidentified proteins ("X" ligands) bind beta3 integrin to support platelet aggregation. However, these ligands and their role in thrombosis still need to be delineated. We will use chemically engineered beads coupled with alphaIIb beta3 to pull down with high purity unidentified plasma and platelet proteins that bind alphaIIb beta3 (GPIIbIIIa). Specific alphaIIb beta3-protein interactions will be measured and the roles of new ligands in platelet biology, thrombosis and hemostasis will be studied using platelet function assays. We expect these ligands may affect both facets of platelets (activation and inhibition) and may be targeted to control many diseases. Immune-mediated thrombocytopenias involve targeting of self- or non-self (e.g. fetal)-platelet antigens by antibodies leading to platelet destruction known as autoimmune (ITP) and fetal/neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (FNAIT), respectively. We have shown antibodies targeting different platelet surface receptors (i.e. GPIIbIIIa vs. GPIbalpha) can lead to very different disease outcomes and response to treatment. We will continue to explore these differences between the anti-GPIIbIIIa and GPIbalpha immune response in ITP and FNAIT to enhance treatment efficacy.

column36: The Development and Genetics of the Face
column37: We study structural birth defects of the face. Upwards of 3% of children are born with either structural birth defects of the face such as cleft lip or holoprosencephaly or a genetic disease that affects the face. Both types of conditions cause suffering for affected children and their families. Individualized treatment of diseases such as birth defects is a key goal of precision medicine. Variation among individuals produces differences in responses to treatments. To understand birth defects one has to understand the causes of this variation. We aim to understand how genetic influences act through development to produce variation of the face. Ultimately, the goal is use the knowledge gained to alleviate suffering by either preventing birth defects or, when they occur, to offer the most appropriate treatment for each patient. We propose to modulate central pathways of craniofacial development to determine how they and their interactions determine variation in morphology, cellular dynamics and the expression of downstream genes. We employ novel imaging, genetic and analysis methods to integrate multiple datasets for individual embryos in order to study the mechanisms that drive variation. The PIs have a track record of productive collaboration (3 NIH R01 grants, 30 publications, 13 co-supervised trainees) that has been transformative by integrating morphometrics with developmental biology to study the mechanisms for quantitative variation in morphology.

column36: Unraveling sensory coding dysfunctions that underlie chronic pain
column37: Intractable pain continues to be the single most common cause of disability that impairs quality of life. Unfortunately, current pain treatments rarely achieve complete pain control, and are often associated with disabling side effects. This is concerning, since persistent untreated pain is associated with several brain disorders, including cognitive deficits, anxiety, depression and addiction. New approaches are needed to address this public health issue. To address this medical problem, the objective of my research program is to elucidate how the nervous system processes pain signals and how this is disrupted in chronic pain syndromes. For example, what makes a normal touch be misinterpreted by the brain as signalling pain? To gain these new insights, we design and use advanced light-based technologies to view and control both healthy and diseased brain circuits; develop new tools to analyse data from physiological, cellular and molecular studies, and develop computer-based approaches to model brain functioning to address issues that are not easy to tackle experimentally. This combination of novel approaches has allowed us to identify new therapeutic targets and develop new drugs that have potential to reverse abnormal pain. We will continue to refine our drug discovery strategies so that we can ultimately help bring relief to those suffering from chronic pain.

column36: Synaptic Plasticity and Dysfunction in the Brain
column37: The development of the brain is an enormously complex task that requires the formation and refinement of trillions of connections between billions of brain cells (neurons). These connections, known as synapses, are critical for all brain functions. They control our movement and senses; they regulate our emotions and decisions. They make us who we are. Dysfunctions in the development or function of synapses are thought to be central to many brain disorders including intellectual disability, schizophrenia, autism, Alzheimer's disease and addiction. If we are to develop targeted therapeutic and behavioral interventions for brain disorders, then studying the fundamental mechanisms of how synapses form and function is crucial. The overarching goal of my lab is to elucidate specific cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying synapse formation and function, and then use this information to probe synaptic dysfunctions that contribute to diseases of the brain. In order to develop a comprehensive understanding of synapses and to modify synapse function at the molecular level, we use rodent models. Mice and rats share similar genes with humans, have related brain structures (including synapses), and can learn and remember simple tasks. My work will identify and manipulate specific molecular targets that are essential for proper synapse development and brain function. This will result in a better understanding of which disruptions in synaptic function lead to brain disorders, and set the stage for refined approaches that can be leveraged to develop new therapeutics for restoring brain function and cognition. Collectively, my work will address: the molecular and cellular mechanisms of how we learn and remember; how disrupting proper synaptic communication in the brain can lead to brain disorders; and whether improving synaptic function later in life might be a therapeutic target for restoring cognitive and functional abilities.

column36: Correlative Studies to Improve Blood and Marrow Transplantation and Leukemia Immunotherapy in Children
column37: My objective is to improve the efficacy and safety of blood and marrow transplantation (BMT), and, ultimately, to expand its clinical applications. BMT is a life-saving procedure and the only immune therapy for leukemia with established long-term curative outcomes. BMT comes with a high cost of long-term complications. The complication that really limits the ability of BMT to help cure people a disease called chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGvHD). cGvHD is caused by the donor's transplanted immune system (graft) attacking the recipient's tissues (host) that received the new transplanted graft. cGvHD can be fatal but more commonly causes long term disabilities such as inability to walk, write, or take care of one's self with more than twice as many medications and doctor visits as a person who had a BMT and did not develop cGvHD. cGvHD can also be life long affecting a person's ability to work or attend school. Children and adolescents due to their long expected life are particularly vulnerable to the long-term problems of cGvHD. Our ability to get rid of cGvHD is limited by our inability to predict when it will of will not happen and which medical approaches will work best to treat it. One way to decrease cGvHD is to have better blood tests or biomarkers that cane be used to assist in guiding medical care. Our group at BC Children's Hospital is the only one worldwide to work on cGvHD biomarkers for children and we are close to have tests that will help to minimize this serious disease in the next few years. With our work we hope to use cGvHD biomarkers to personalize therapy, develop new therapies, and expand its use of BMT.

column37: Dementia is a syndrome that affects your memory, thinking, and behavior, resulting in significant burden to your family, friends, and overall, the Canadian health-care system. In addition to Alzheimer's disease, there are many causes of dementia, which are often overlapping, complex, and multi-faceted. In contrast to many research studies that only look at a single disease, the Sunnybrook Dementia Study was created to study the real-world of patients that come to our clinic with a variety of complicated, difficult to diagnose, comorbid dementias such as vascular cognitive impairment, Parkinson's Lewy Body disease, and frontotemporal dementia, to name a few. Recognizing that each patient is different from the next, our personalized approach to the urgent challenge of dementia treatment embeds our research into clinical care. Continuing with the clinical, neuropsychological, MRI, and genetic assessments, our future research will use the knowledge we have acquired to expand our research to a larger scale, and will include more assessment tools such as PET imaging, blood-based biomarkers, and autopsy info. Leaving no stone unturned, our personalized approach will also examine new avenues for dementia treatment, such as the re-purposing of blood pressuring lowering drugs for delaying dementia and cognitive decline, the role of sleep problems in clearing brain waste products such as amyloid, and the potential use of focused ultrasound to deliver novel drug therapies to the brain. Under the direction of Dr. Sandra E. Black, a world leader in dementia research, we hope that our patient-centered research will translate into disease-modifying therapies that target dementia, the greatest looming public healthcare challenge facing society.

column36: The Regulation of Alternative Splicing in Dopaminergic and Serotonergic Neurons
column37: Information from our genes flows from DNA to messenger RNA, an intermediate that will ultimately carry instructions to produce proteins, the principal building blocks for our cellular machinery. In multi-cellular animals, a phenomenon known as alternative messenger RNA splicing provides the capacity to encode multiple proteins from single genes, diversifying our repertoire of protein building blocks. Differential usage of alternative splicing has served as a mechanism contributing to customizing the functions of individual brain cells. However, the rules by which different cells of the nervous system utilize alternative splicing to contribute to their unique functions is unclear. This proposal will aim to better understand the rules used to create these differences in two important types of brain cells that secrete dopamine and serotonin, chemicals that can alter brain states. Dysfunction of these cells can lead to neurological disorders such as Parkinson's disease and depression. Thus, in addition to providing fundamental insights into the inner workings of specific brain cells in animals, our work has the potential to shed light on how these mechanisms can go awry in diseases of the nervous system.

column36: Molecular mechanisms underlying the clinical efficacy of inhaled corticosteroid/long-acting beta2-adrenoceptor agonist combination therapies in asthma
column37: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease, characterised by intermittent airways constriction and occurs in up to 10% of individuals. Regular inhaled glucocorticoids are clinically referred to as inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) and dampen lung inflammation to control mild to moderate asthma. However, more severe disease and asthma exacerbations are poorly controlled by ICS and clinical guidelines recommend the addition of a long-acting beta2-adrenoceptor agonist (LABA). These drugs enhance the effectiveness of the ICS to a level that is not achieved by increasing the glucocorticoid dose. The glucocorticoid receptor (GR), the protein target by which glucocorticoids act, is responsible for modulating gene expression to mediate beneficial effects in asthma. In the context of LABA, combinatorial effects between glucocorticoid and LABA-activated pathways result in enhanced clinical effectiveness of ICS/LABA therapies. However, the mechanistic basis, and the genes modulated, are not established and therefore cannot be selectively targeted. The current proposal will elucidate mechanisms underlying this clinically important effect. In this context, it is salient that the pharmaceutical sector is currently testing novel drugs that activate GR in ways that are different to conventional glucocorticoids. These compounds enhance some aspects of GR function relative to other activities. While, the objective is to improve the clinical efficacy of GR-based therapies, it is important to stress that we do not know which aspects of GR function are most important for synergy with LABA. There is therefore a risk of failing to identify novel GR ligands that most effectively synergise with LABAs. This will preclude maximising benefit from future combination therapies. The current project addresses this key knowledge gap by identifying mechanisms of GR action that are important for synergy with LABA. Such data will help guide the discovery of improved combination treatments for asthma.

column36: Modulation of Innate Immune Responses as a Therapy for Muscular Dystrophy
column37: Muscular Dystrophy is a collection of genetic disease that lead to progressive skeletal muscle degeneration and eventual death. Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is cause by a mutation in the dystrophin gene (mdx) that normally helps anchor muscle cells to the muscle sheath. This leads to chronic muscle damage and a gradual replacement of health muscle tissue with fat and scar tissue as the body makes a failed attempt at tissue repair. Intriguingly, we find that perturbing these cells in mice carrying the mdx gene can dramatically alter the disease progression. Accordingly, we propose to use a variety of novel techniques we have developed to skew the behaviour of these cells as a potential therapy for slowing the progression DMD. Because DMD is relatively frequently leads and to death in late adolescence, the ability to slow the progression of muscle degeneration and fibrosis could have a profound effect on the quality of life for huge number of Canadians.

column36: Progression to Type 2 Diabetes in the 1st Decade after Glucose Intolerance in Pregnancy: Pathophysiology and Clinical Implications
column37: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is defined as high blood sugar that is first recognized during pregnancy. It is a common condition affecting up to 14% of pregnant women. Importantly, women who have had GDM are at increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes (T2DM), particularly within the first 10 years after their pregnancy. Indeed, we have previously shown that women with recent GDM have subtle abnormalities shortly after their pregnancy including a reduced ability of the pancreas to secrete insulin. It is not known, however, if further decline in this ability to secrete insulin ultimately leads to T2DM in affected women or if this process can be tracked by following certain factors in the blood (called biomarkers). The aim of our research is to determine whether deterioration of insulin secretion is the key factor that leads to the development of T2DM in young women following GDM. Towards this goal, we have recruited a cohort of women with and without GDM who are undergoing evaluation in pregnancy and at regular intervals for the first 9 years thereafter. At each study visit, we are assessing their ability to secrete insulin, the levels of certain biomarkers in the blood, and whether or not they have T2DM. This study will help to shed light on the early changes in the body that lead to the development of diabetes in young women of childbearing age (who represent the segment of the Canadian population that has had the largest increase in diabetes in recent years). This research may lead to improved ways to treat these early changes and thus possibly prevent the development of T2DM in women.

column36: Inducing Mismatch Repair Deficiency in Cancer Cells for Therapeutic Benefit
column37: Cancer immunotherapy has been approved for treatment of multiple cancers including lung cancer and melanoma. Unlike chemotherapy and radiation, cancer immunotherapy enhances the power of the patient's own immune system. Immunotherapy drugs today only work in a subset of patients and not everyone. Interestingly, a small group of patients with a specific mutation in their tumors respond very well to these drugs. This is mainly because the mutation in their tumors attracts immune cell to enter the tumor and make it sensitive to immunotherapy. In this study, we aim to transform 3 different cancers with different genetic and tissue backgrounds-lung cancer, breast cancer, and neuroblastoma (a form of childhood cancer) sensitive to immunotherapy by inducing the same mutations that naturally-occur in cancers that show the best response to these drugs. We will use a novel technology (CRISPR) to edit the genome of cancer cells and mutate genes that are involved in mismatch repair (MMR) DNA pathway, namely MLH1 and MSH2. We will conduct genetic and immunological studies to learn whether induction of this genetic defects in these cancers makes them better targets for immunotherapy. Our proposed studies, for the first time, will allow us to learn from nature and what makes a small group of patients responders to immunotherapy and translate that to a much larger group of cancers with the goal of developing a new treatment strategy for most cancer patients, independent of their type and genetic background of cancer.

column36: Effect of aberrant inflammation during pregnancy on subsequent risk of cardiovascular disease in mothers and their offspring
column37: Conditions during pregnancy can have long-term effects on the health of mothers and babies. Pregnant women who have high blood pressure and their urine contains protein are said to suffer from pre-eclampsia. Women and babies afflicted by pre-eclampsia have a higher chance of getting heart disease later in life. Babies with low birth weight (LBW) also have increased risk of heart disease later in life. Interestingly, excessive inflammation in pregnancy is linked to pre-eclampsia and LBW. We want to determine if and how abnormal inflammation in pregnancy increases the risk of subsequent heart disease in mothers and their children. To accomplish these goals, we developed a rat model of pre-eclampsia and LBW. In this model, inflammation in pregnant rats is induced by administration of a bacterial substance called lipopolysaccharide (LPS). Rats injected with LPS develop a condition similar to pre-eclampsia and their pups have LBW. We plan to monitor these rats and their pups after delivery to look for signs of increased risk of cardiovascular disease. We previously found that certain anti-inflammatory agents and exercise prevent inflammation and LBW induced by LPS. Therefore we will conduct studies to determine if exercise or treatment with anti-inflammatory agents mitigates risk of disease. Higher risk of disease in women and children who suffer from pre-eclampsia and LBW is linked to modifications in the DNA structure or in DNA-associated proteins. These modifications are called 'epigenetic alterations'. We plan to determine if inflammation in pregnancy leads to epigenetic alterations that could predict disease later in life. For this, we plan to use our rat model as well as blood samples from women and babies collected at the time of delivery. Our proposed studies are important because, if exercise and anti-inflammatories reduce the risk of disease in pregnant women and their children, this could lay the groundwork for to new treatments to prevent heart disease.

column36: The genetics of erythrocyte volume homeostasis
column37: One cell out of four in the human body is a red blood cell (RBC), also known as erythrocyte. These RBCs play a critical role by carrying oxygen from the lungs to the organs, and carbon dioxide from the organs back to the lungs. Given their importance, it is not surprising that that defects in the production or function of RBCs can lead to severe, often life-threatening, diseases. In this project, we propose to study the genes that control RBC volume, an important determinant of many human blood disorders. By combining human genetic approaches (e.g. genome-wide association studies, next-generation DNA sequencing) and functional characterization methods (e.g. genome editing), we will identify the genes and biological pathways that control RBC volume. Our results could impact the prediction, prevention, and treatment of diseases like sickle cell disease and malaria, which affect millions of patients worldwide.

column36: Interactions between serotonin signalling and autophagy in the context of gut inflammation
column37: Serotonin also known as 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) is an important molecule in the human body that controls many normal and disease processes. Serotonin action is changed in experimental colitis and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Recently we showed that serotonin has a critical role in activating immune cells and in generating colitis, in our laboratory experiments with cells and mice. Another normal process that may be disrupted in diseases such as IBD is autophagy, which is the body's process to clear out old and damaged cells. A powerful new research method called Genome Wide Association Studies has identified genes that put people at higher risk for IBD. Identifying those genes also links IBD to autophagy. Both autophagy and changes in serotonin action are connected to IBD. However, we still don't know if serotonin signalling affects autophagy action in IBD. Our research will explore if defective autophagy and changes in serotonin action are pivotal players in IBD. We hypothesize that more serotonin action increases the severity of gut inflammation by reducing autophagy in the key cells involved in the generation and/or perpetuation of inflammation. We plan to pin down three key points: 1) How do serotonin and autophagy interact in gut inflammation? 2) How do serotonin and autophagy interact in affecting production of pro- inflammatory cytokines in key cells involved in gut inflammation? 3) How does serotonin change signals inside cells to affect autophagy in our immune system and gut inflammation? This research will help us understand the roles of serotonin and autophagy in gut inflammation, and how they interact. Our results will point to new targets for treating various health disorders, including IBD, that exhibit dysregulated autophagy.

column36: Role of PI3Kinase alpha in Cardiovascular Disease and Cardiotoxicity
column37: Cardiovascular diseases and cancer are the two leading causes of mortality and morbidity worldwide. PI3Kalpha(a) is an interesting molecule as it is involved in both, heart physiology and cancer development, but it plays opposing roles in these two scenarios. In the heart, PI3Ka is required for healthy function, whereas in cancer, its inhibition has become the most effective treatment in anti-cancer therapies. As such, several drugs have been developed that directly/indirectly target PI3Ka. As a result, cancer patients who receive these drugs show promising improvements in tumor growth regression and recovery from cancer, but a significant fraction of them end up with heart failure. While the adverse effects of the anti-cancer drugs on the heart and the vasculature are now well established, the molecular mechanism underlying these unfortunate side-effects have not been yet determined. Our research to date has identified PI3Ka, an enzyme that mediates various cellular responses (growth, death, proliferation) as the key player. We have generated genetic mouse models that lack PI3Ka in specific cells (cardiomyocytes in heart; endothelial cells in vessels). We have also obtained the pharmacological inhibitor of PI3Ka, BYL719, currently in clinical trial for anti-cancer therapies. We will use our genetic models, and the pharmacological inhibitor of PI3Ka, in combination with models of heart disease, and other conventional anti-cancer drugs to reveal the central role of PI3Ka in the cardiovascular toxicities associated with anti-cancer treatments. We will take a comprehensive approach which will include animal disease models, functional assessment of heart and arteries, electrical activity of the heart, and detailed molecular/cellular analyses. We will also use the cancer patient registry in Alberta to determine the connection between the type of anti-cancer treatment/drugs that patients receive and the severity of cardiac and vascular complication

column36: Role of lysosomal enzymes cathepsins B and D in neuronal vulnerability: potential implications in Alzheimer's disease pathology
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a brain disease characterized by a gradual loss of memory, followed by deterioration of higher cognitive functions such as language, calculation and judgement. The pathological features associated with AD brain include the loss of nerve cells in selected regions along with abnormal deposits of certain molecules such as amyloid beta (Ab) peptide and tau protein in structures called plaques and tangles, respectively. The brain regions which are severely affected in AD are hippocampus and cortex, whereas certain other regions such as cerebellum and striatum are relatively spared. It is believed that accumulation of Ab peptide can trigger the loss of nerve cells, but why only selected cells die in AD brains remain unclear. There is evidence that leakage of lysosomal enzymes called cathepsins B and D from their storage sites is markedly increased in nerve cells before they die in AD brains, but the role of these enzymes in the death of these cells is not fully understood. In a series of experiments, we will first establish the significance of the leakage of cathepsins in Ab-induced death of nerve cells grown in Petri dishes and the underlying cause of leakage of these enzymes from their storage sites. In parallel, we will measure the levels and activity of these enzymes in affected as well as unaffected regions of genetically modified animal models of AD and in post-mortem human AD brain samples. Subsequently, we will determine whether nanoparticles that have been shown to restore leakage of cathepsins can protect nerve cells against Ab-mediated toxicity in Petri dishes and in animal models of AD. This study will establish the role of cathepsins in the selective loss of nerve cells in AD brains. Additionally, these results could lead to identification of new molecular targets for the early diagnosis and/or development of new therapeutic opportunities such as nanoparticles in preventing the loss of nerve cells in AD brains

column36: Follicle-stimulating hormone regulation of bone physiology and pathophysiology
column37: Osteoporosis is a common and debilitating disorder of bone fragility in aging populations, which is associated with increased fracture rates. In women, the incidence of osteoporosis increases markedly following menopause. As estrogen promotes bone health, it is the postmenopausal loss of estrogen that is usually linked to osteoporosis. Indeed, many therapies target the estrogen receptor to prevent or treat postmenopausal osteoporosis. Recent observations over the past decade challenge this current dogma, attributing bone loss to the actions of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) from the pituitary gland. Estrogen and FSH levels in the bloodstream are tightly linked as FSH stimulates the ovaries to make estrogen. When estrogen levels fall at menopause, FSH levels rise, ostensibly to stimulate more estrogen production. However, the ovaries lack the ability to produce estrogen at this stage of life. Therefore, postmenopausal women have both low estrogen and high FSH, and some researchers have recently argued that it is the elevated FSH that is driving bone loss. In support of their view, they identified receptors for FSH on osteoclast cells in the bone. The normal function of osteoclasts is to degrade bone and FSH has been argued to increase osteoclast activity, and therefore bone loss. As a result of these observations, efforts are being made to develop inhibitors of FSH to treat bone loss in postmenopausal women. This new approach is highly controversial as many investigators question whether previous studies on FSH in bone physiology were correctly interpreted. Here, we propose to resolve this controversy using mouse models unique to our research team. The results of our work will definitely establish whether or not FSH regulates bone.

column36: Cortical contributions to visually-guided locomotion in the cat
column37: This project is designed to determine the contribution of one part of the cerebral cortex, known to be involved in the planning of voluntary movements (the premotor cortex) to the planning of visually-guided gait modifications. While locomotion is sometimes thought of as a relatively automatic behavior in which the major function is to produce rhythmical, alternating movements of the limbs, it is actually a highly complex activity requiring cognitive and voluntary control under natural circumstances. On uneven terrain, for example, decisions have to be made about where to make the next step and frequently one plans a sequence of steps to avoid an obstacle. Walking in the street, one must decide how to walk around objects and people and how and when to step on and off a curb. Even indoors, one must navigate the furniture and objects on the floor. These behaviours require processing of visual information about the environment and a means to integrate this information with the immediate and long-term locomotor goals of the subject and the state of the limbs at the time of making the decision (e.g. which limb is in stance and which in swing and how do I adjust gait to most efficiently. or quickly, step over that obstacle). In the current project, I intend to test the hypothesis that the premotor cortex contributes to several essential aspects of goal-directed locomotion, including: decision processes that determine which limb will step over an obstacle; determining the parameters of the gait modification (trajectory and/or muscle activation patterns); and in more complex circumstances determining the sequence of steps required to clear a series of obstacles (e.g. a boulder field on a walking trail).

column36: Functional Roles and Therapeutic Potentials of Invariant NKT Cells in Sepsis
column37: Sepsis is a life-threatening illness caused by a disproportionate host response to microbes. It is characterized by early, severe inflammation followed by impaired immunity to opportunistic infections. Successful treatment of sepsis may thus require a two-step approach, namely to prevent excessive inflammation in the early phase and to boost antimicrobial immunity in the later phase. Natural killer T (NKT) cells are a tiny but powerful subset of lymphocytes with a unique ability to recognize glycolipids (molecules composed of sugar and fat). Promptly after activation, NKT cells secrete large quantities of soluble molecules called cytokines that mediate cell-to-cell communications in the immune system. Importantly, NKT cells can be manipulated to produce cytokines that either promote or suppress inflammation. The proposed research will follow 4 Specific Objectives. Objective 1 will test how NKT cell depletion in mouse models of sepsis may affect host responses, morbidity and mortality. In Objective 2, we will use glycolipid stimuli of NKT cells in a "two-hit" experimental model that simulates early and late phases of sepsis. Mice will be treated sequentially with anti- and pro-inflammatory glycolipids in the above phases, respectively, and will be evaluated for their ability to clear secondary infections. In Objective 3, we will generate mice that harbor either the entire human immune system or human NKT cells. "Humanized" mice will be rendered septic and treated with glycolipid stimuli of NKT cells. In Objective 4, we will obtain blood samples from septic patients shortly after presentation and shortly after resolution of their symptoms. Immune cells will be isolated, exposed to NKT cell stimuli and subjected to functional analyses. Collectively, the proposed studies will reveal the role of mouse and human NKT cells in sepsis, and also importantly hold the promise of introducing new and effective treatments for this dangerous and potentially fatal illness.

column36: Pharmacogenetics of Methadone Maintenance Treatment Response
column37: Opioids are commonly used medications for pain but have very high liability for misuse and addiction. There are also street opioids such heroin and the deadly fentanyl and carfentanil. Toward this end, the proposed study will leverage innovations in genomic approaches to systematically examine individual variation in MMT response in a large sample of opioid addiction MMT patients. Our hypothesis is that MMT outcomes are significantly determined by genes that can inform future treatment decisions and the study's fundamental goal is to rigorously test this hypothesis using multiple cutting edge methodologies.

column37: Bacterial resistance to antibiotics has become a global medical concern as shown by recent reports on the rise of highly drug resistant bacterial strains. Although this resistance was predictable, research to identify new antibiotics or cellular drug target has dropped drastically. Furthermore, many of the most commonly used and often last resort antibiotics have debilitating side effects. In stark contrast, we now appreciate that microbes in human microbiomes play crucial roles in maintaining good health. It is now clear that commensal bacteria in the intestine of mammals accomplish many beneficial functions. Although symbiotic bacteria and mammals have co-evolved and adapted to each other, the ecological niche offered by the host is plagued with environmental insults, to which the bacteria need to adapt rapidly and continuously. In response to stressful environment, bacteria express small regulatory RNAs to coordinate gene expression and adapt to various stress. Our recent work with small regulatory RNAs strongly suggest there is a large amount of unknown yet significant RNA-RNA interactions within bacterial cells. These interactions might regulate virulence and pathogenicity as well as antibiotic resistance. We will map the global RNA-RNA interactions quantitatively within the model bacterium E. coli as well as the major human pathogen Salmonella. Concurrently with this long-term goal, we will investigate the most promising RNA-RNA interactions to establish novel mechanisms of gene expression. We already have established the extended interactome of a few specific sRNAs in E. coli using a novel approach that we developed in the lab. Deciphering the most critical RNA-based regulations (including sRNA-mRNA, mRNA-mRNA, tRNA-mRNA), in bacterial cells. New RNA-RNA interactions are creating specific targets to test novel RNA-based therapies for medical doctors, pharmaceutical companies and drug developers.

column36: Unconventional NMDA Receptor Signalling in Neocortical Plasticity
column37: Few would probably dispute that one of the most important functions of the brain is learning and memory. If you open up any modern neuroscience textbook, you will learn that NMDA receptors are critical for memory formation in the brain. It is therefore perhaps not so surprising that these receptors have been implicated in devastating neurological diseases such as Alzheimer's, epilepsy, and schizophrenia. In recent years, however, its become clear that our understanding of NMDA receptors is incomplete. For example, they are sometimes located on transmitting instead of receiving side of neuronal connections, where they cannot function according to the standard textbook view on how learning in the brain operates. Furthermore, they sometimes signal metabotropically, i.e. in the absence of depolarising neuronal activation, which completely changes how neuroscientists think about their function. This proposal will explore tow unorthodox modes of NMDA receptor signalling: on the transmitting side, and metabotropically. This is a virtual blank on the map, and must be understood to treat major neurological pathologies such as Alzheimer's and epilepsy.

column36: Targeting vulnerabilities in SMARCA4-deficient lung cancers
column37: Cancer is a heterogeneous disease. Distinct subtypes of cancers from the same primary site of origin can be defined by their unique molecular pathological features. Consequently, cancer therapy is shifting towards strategies aimed at genes specific to each patient, where mutated cancer-causing genes in tumors are targeted by highly selective inhibitors. These drugs are often very effective and have minimal side effects as normal tissues do not harbor the cancer-causing mutations, which are being targeted. Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most common type of lung cancer and is the leading cause of cancer death worldwide and in Canada. NSCLC consists of different subtypes characterized by distinct cancer-causing mutations. For subtypes with mutations activating genes such as EGFR (10-35%) or ALK (3-7%), there are potent drugs that target these activated gene products and have significantly improved patient survival. In contrast, 10-37 % of NSCLCs are deficient in SMARCA4, a known tumor suppressor gene lost in many cancer types and which to this date remains undruggable. Therefore, effective treatment of these patients remains an unmet clinical challenge. In this proposal, we will first exploit a molecular weakness of SMARCA4-deficiceny in NSCLCs. We have previously uncovered a vulnerability of SMARCA4 loss in an ovarian cancer subtype, which can be targeted using an FDA-approved drug originally developed for treating breast cancers. To extend our findings to NSCLCs, we will use a variety of model systems, including cell culture, mouse preclinical cancer models, and tumor samples from lung cancer patients. Independently, we will use powerful genetic tools to identify novel vulnerabilities of SMARCA4-deficiceny in NSCLCs that can be exploited therapeutically. Our goal is to provide potential treatment strategies to treat SMARCA4-deficient NSCLCs and provide a clinical benefit for cancer patients.

column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a devastating neuromuscular disorder with no cure available. The results of this project will provide data that can be directly translated into large animal models of DMD and subsequently into clinical trials in patients with deletions in the DMD gene. Furthermore, these pre-clinical proof of concept studies will pave the way for development of therapeutic approaches for other inherited conditions caused by large genomic rearrangements.

column37: Human chromosome ends are protected from damage by a stretch of repetitive DNA sequence known as telomeres. In healthy mortal cells, telomere DNA is gradually shortened during successive rounds of replication as a cell ages, and ultimately instructs cells to naturally terminate. In cancerous cells the enzyme telomerase ensures maintenance of a stable telomere length and therefore enables the indefinite growth and uncontrolled division characteristic of tumor formation. Active telomerase is diagnostic of cancer progression, as has been identified in the vast majority of malignant cancers. In this proposal, we seek to understand the regulation of telomerase by enzymes known as helicases that exert their effects through prevention of proper telomerase assembly. Our work aims to provide a template for the rational design of therapeutics to attenuate telomerase activity.

Treatments have been selected for ease of translation (9 of 11 treatments are already used in patients for other medical conditions or are in clinical trials), so that promising results can be moved quickly to childhood cancer survivors. Ultimately, our goal is to ensure that cancer survivors have the same opportunities and quality of life as their cancer-free peers.

column36: Age-associated inflammation alters myeloid cell development and function
column37: Our immune system changes as we age. As an example, we begin to produce more of some kinds of white blood cells (monocytes and neutrophils) and less of others (B and T cells). Since monocytes and neutrophils are required to protect us from infection, you might think that this would protect older adults from infections, but what actually happens is that these cells don't mature properly and enter into the bloodstream prematurely. These immature monocytes don't help fight infection but actually make some infections worse. Furthermore, these immature monocytes produce a lot of inflammation which also has a negative impact on our health as we age. The purpose of this proposal is to determine why we start to produce more monocytes as we get older, to determine why these monocytes do not mature properly and to identify ways in which we might be able to restore this process. To do this we will collect blood from young and older adults and assess how maturity decreases with age and determine whether this immaturity correlates with levels of inflammation. Specifically we believe that a molecule called TNF might be involved because when we aged mice that did not have TNF, they did not have any changes in the development or function of their monocytes with age. To determine if this is the case in humans, we have collected samples from humans who are undergoing anti-TNF therapy. We predict that when their TNF is high, their monocytes will be less mature and when their TNF goes down due to their therapy, their monocytes will become normal. We will use our unique colony of old mice (18-22 mo), including old mice that don't make TNF (called TNF knockout mice) to determine which cells make this TNF. The long-term goal of this project is to find novel ways to keep us healthier as we get older. Because monocytes protect us from infections but can also contribute to diseases that increase with age (e.g. cardiovascular disease), we hope these findings will have broad applications.

column36: Inference-Based Cognitive Therapy versus Exposure and Response Prevention for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: A 16-Session Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a highly disabling psychiatric illness, characterized by obsessional thoughts that cause patients to perform time-consuming and distressing compulsive rituals. Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP) is a first-line psychological treatment of choice, which requires patients to face their fears by being exposed to feared stimuli. ERP has been shown to reduce symptoms among those who comply with treatment. However, there is still a significant portion of patients that do not improve, especially those who firmly believe their obsessions are realistic and reasonable (i.e. OCD with Overvalued Ideation). Also, a large proportion of patients refuse the treatment or drop out during treatment due to the distress provoked by ERP. That leaves at most 3-4 out of 10 people with OCD who benefit from ERP, and even then, residual symptoms often remain, or symptoms eventually reappear after treatment. One evidence-based approach to the treatment of OCD, termed inference-based cognitive therapy (IBCT) has been shown to be as effective as ERP with the potential to overcome the limitations of ERP. Since IBCT is a cognitive approach, the treatment does not require exposure to feared stimuli and likely more tolerable for patients with OCD. Also, there is evidence that IBCT is more effective than ERP for those with overvalued ideation, since it directly targets the distorted reasoning that is responsible for the intensity and persistence of the obsession. The current study aims to directly compare ERP with this promising evidence-based cognitive therapy, which is expected to be significantly more effective for those with overvalued ideation, as well as significantly more tolerable with lower rates of treatment refusal, drop-out and higher treatment satisfaction. The project is designed to maximize potential beneficial health outcomes and offer a new evidence-based treatment option for the large proportion of patients unable to benefit from ERP.

column37: Phosphate and vitamin D are critical for many physiological functions including skeletal development, mineral balance, energy metabolism, and proper nerve and muscle function. The kidney is a major player in the maintenance of the body's phosphate and vitamin D balance, by virtue of its ability to regulate: (i) the amounts of phosphorus it reclaims before it gets lost in the urine based on the body's needs, and (ii) the production and thereby the levels of vitamin D in blood, important for the absorption of phosphorus from the intestine. These processes at the level of the kidney are very tightly regulated mainly by two hormones: parathyroid hormone (PTH), and the more recently-identified fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23). Genetic diseases of phosphate and vitamin D metabolism with have high FGF23 and low vitamin D levels in the blood have been described. For the most common form, XLH, it is estimated as high as 1 in 10,000 newborns are affected. Children with XLH have rickets (bone deformities including short stature and bow or knock-leggedness) that progress to poor skeletal mineralization with soft, brittle bones, and calcification of tendons and ligaments in adulthood. Studies proposed in this application, a continuation of our previous work funded by the KFOC and published recently in a prestigious clinical research journal, aims to use transgenic mice and molecular biology techniques to understand the mechanism by which high levels of FGF23 affects bone development by altering the concentration of vitamin D locally in bone. We aim to show that, whether by genetics or by pharmacotherapy, this process can be altered to allow better bone formation to take place. Findings arising from this work will help uncover previously unrecognized targets and strategies for the treatment of patients with these genetic disorders.
