column37: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a major health problem that is caused by extra fat building up in a person's liver cells. Worldwide, this disease affects about 30% of the adult population and over 70% of people with obesity. The health risk for people with NAFLD is that this disease can progress to more serious problems: -inflammation and swelling of their liver, called non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) -normal liver tissue being replaced by non-living scar tissue, called cirrhosis -end-stage liver disease and liver failure, the most common reason for needing a liver transplant Having NAFLD or NASH also places people at much greater risk for type 2 diabetes, heart disease and end-stage kidney disease. Today, we have no effective treatments for NASH. My research team has discovered that a protein called TGH affects distribution and storage of fat. Our experiments show that TGH has profound effects on circulating fat in the blood and on development of NAFLD. We showed that reducing the amount TGH in mice protects the liver from developing NAFLD and NASH and improves insulin signaling. Because TGH regulates how fat is stored in the liver, this protein could be a good target for drugs to prevent or treat NAFLD and NASH. My research aims to find out how TGH regulates the amounts of fat that people store in the liver and in the blood. Understanding the mechanisms that this protein uses to regulate fat storage may lead to new treatments for NAFLD/NASH and diseases triggered by NAFLD/NASH.

column36: Novel therapies to augment neurological benefits of cellular therapies for traumatic spinal cord injury
column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a leading cause of permanent neurological disabilities affecting over 2.5 million individuals worldwide. In Canada, there are over 86,000 patients who are afflicted with lifelong consequences of SCI with approximately 4,200 new cases each year. The lifetime medical cost of each SCI patient is estimated at 1.6 to 3 million dollars. Thus, SCI has a profound impact on patients, their caregivers, and the healthcare system. Currently, there is no effective treatment for SCI and new therapies are needed to allow neurological improvement in patients. Extensive research by our group and others show that transplantation of neural stem cells offers tremendous possibility for SCI repair. Indeed, based on these experimental discoveries, neural stem cell transplantation has moved to clinical trials in recent years. Initial outcomes of these trials indicate that while neural stem cells are safe and promising for treatment of SCI, their benefit for neurological recovery of patients is only modest. We have made the same observation in our experimental evaluations, establishing a need for combinatorial therapies to augment the functional outcomes of current cellular therapies. To this end, we have discovered new therapeutic targets with the potential to harness the regenerative capacity of neural stem cells for repairing the injured spinal cord. We have identified that formation of a glia scar around the lesion and increased production of inhibitory molecules in the scar limit the benefits of neural stem cell transplantation. We show that inhibiting these factors facilitates the longterm survival of stem cells and their abilities for tissue regeneration. We are currently investigating several aspects of these strategies and importantly their potential in improving functional recovery in an animal model that clinically reflects human SCI. Our goal is to develop effective regenerative medicine strategies for improving the quality of life in SCI patients.

Collectively this research proposal will further clarify the role of the uPAR system in tumor growth and its spread to the skeleton. Results from these studies will play a key role in the optimization and clinical development of novel uPAR targeted therapeutic approaches alone and in combination setting against breast and prostate cancer growth and bone metastasis.

column36: Structural Basis of Cyclic Nucleotide Signal Translation and Inhibition
column37: Pancreatic, endocrine and cardiac tumours as well as intellectual disabilities and abnormal bone growth in children are caused by defective reading of the signal transmitted within cells by a messenger molecule called cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). Furthermore, a closely related molecule, cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP), plays a critical role in the replication of the malaria parasite, Plasmodium falciparum. The goals of this project are to study two proteins that bind to cAMP and cGMP, i.e. the cAMP-dependent protein kinase A in mammals (PKA) and cGMP-dependent protein kinase G in P. falciparum (pfPKG), and to: (a) elucidate the structural and dynamical changes caused by inherited mutations that lead to incorrect translation of the cAMP signal and diseases such as cancer and developmental defects; (b) to understand how to suppress the signals carried by the cAMP and cGMP cyclic nucleotides to improve current cancer and malaria treatments. We will use nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy to investigate how modified molecules that resemble cAMP and cGMP, and which may serve as future cancer and malaria drugs, interact with PKA and pfPKG, respectively. Their effects on these proteins are currently poorly understood at the structural and dynamical level, and NMR has only recently been used to investigate these interactions at atomic resolution. NMR will reveal the structural and dynamical changes in PKA and pfPKG caused by cAMP and cGMP analogs, respectively, as needed to fully understand how to modulate these proteins' activities. NMR is also ideally suited to unveil how disease-causing inherited mutations alter the physiological interactions of PKA with cAMP. Elucidating the structural and dynamical changes caused by disease-related mutations and modified cyclic nucleotides will help understand the molecular origins of multiple tumours and pediatric disorders, and will also facilitate the design of improved cancer and malaria drugs.

column36: Bayis Il Tus - A Strong Breath: Community-Based Research to Identify the Prevalence of and Contributors to Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease in Remote and Rural First Nations Communities in British Columbia
column37: First Nations peoples in Canada have more challenges with their lung health compared to non-First Nations people. They are often exposed to more air pollution and cigarette smoke and have a high prevalence of cough, wheeze and shortness of breath. Although there is a high use of health care services for chronic lung diseases like chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), this disease is not "on the radar" in many First Nations communities. This may be because we do not know how many First Nations people have COPD, especially those living in remote and rural areas. We know that cigarette smoking causes COPD, but there is much less known about the effects of household, historical/community/cultural, and work-related factors on the burden of COPD in First Nations people. This project is a new partnership between UBC, Carrier Sekani Family Services and eleven partner Nations. This study is unique in being able to address the individual, community, and historical risks of COPD in remote and rural First Nations communities. The goal of this study is to better understand the burden of COPD in remote and rural First Nations communities. Aim 1: Estimate how many people have COPD and how many people have not been diagnosed. Aim 2: Find out if there is a link between inhaled pollutants (from household, work-related, and historical/community/cultural sources) and: 1) symptoms; 2) blocked airflow; and 3) health care use. In order to do this, we will recruit adults from randomly-selected households in eleven First Nations communities in northern BC. We will collect detailed measures of lung function, symptoms, self-reported current & past exposure to lung irritants, and health care use. We will also collect indoor air quality measures from homes and community buildings. With the study results, communities will be able to better plan for health services, and create prevention strategies to reduce the chance of First Nations people developing COPD in the future.

column37: First Nations peoples in Canada face more challenges with their lung health compared to non-First Nations. Aim 1: Understand current physical activity practices, by doing in depth interviews, using photography tools, and measuring physical activity using monitors, to understand values and practices of physical activity. Aim 2: Develop relevant patient and family education materials that is informed by both Indigenous and Western knowledge and perspectives, which can be accessed in culturally-appropriate ways. Aim 3: Test the feasibility of a novel pulmonary rehabilitation program delivered by established tele-health systems in remote and rural First Nations communities. This study is unique in being able to address the culturally-relevant treatment and education of COPD in remote and rural First Nations communities. We hope that in the long term, this study will increase lung-related health services to remote northern BC First Nations communities and support similar efforts in other communities.

column37: Canadian youth 16-25 are the vital future of society and their health and wellness are the concern of all Canadians. Deserving serious attention, however, is the evidence that the health of Indigenous youth living in Canada is disproportionately worse than the general Canadian population. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission's Calls to Action outlined the historical processes of colonization as the most critical social determinant of Indigenous youth health, which perpetuates realities of poverty, racism, and discrimination that hinder their healthy development, particularly within urban contexts where Indigenous youth are on the 'front-lines' of experiencing the stereotypes and prejudices of non-Indigenous Canadians. While observing variations across sties, it is anticipated that Indigenous youth who participate in action research of this kind will show significant increases on various health and resilience measures. The health related knowledge from this project will also: 1) inform effective Indigenous youth engagement strategies; 2) improve social determinants of health impacting Indigenous youth in urban contexts; and 3) guide effective program and policy interventions promoting greater health equity for Indigenous youth across Canada.

column36: RESTORE: Robot Enhanced Stroke Therapy Optimizes Rehabilitation
column37: Treatment after stroke often involves rehabilitation. Rehabilitation involves learning to move and feel again through intensive practice. It may require tens of thousands of repetitions of a particular movement to relearn it after stroke. Robots can help increase intensity as many therapists cannot help someone do thousands of repetitions of a movement in today's healthcare system. We are specifically interested in when is the best time to start rehabilitation and how much do we need to best retrain someone to use their arm after stroke? Our first objective is to determine whether one hour per day or two hours per day of robotic rehabilitation is better. Our second objective is to determine if we should start having stroke survivors work on rehabilitating their arms a few days after their stroke or wait a few weeks to begin. We think that starting early and working harder will lead to the best possible outcomes. Our third objective involves using information from brain scans and electrical measures of brain function to determine who responds best to early rehabilitation. Stroke survivors will play robotic rehabilitation games to improve their strength, sensation, range of motion and overall function in the arm. We will randomize stroke survivors to one of five groups. The first will begin working with the robot 8 days after their stroke for 1 hour per day. The second will begin working with the robot 8 days after their stroke for 2 hours per day. The third will begin working with the robot 21 days after their stroke for 1 hour per day. The fourth will begin working with the robot 21 days after their stroke for 2 hours per day. A fifth will receive standard of care treatment. At different times during the study we will measure arm function with various scales as well as brain MRI's to determine which treatment is best. The study will also help us to decide when to begin rehabilitation and the amount of rehabilitation needed to get the best result.

column36: Biological and translational implications of replication repair deficiency and hypermutation in human cancer
column37: The human cell needs to duplicate each DNA molecule to enable it to divide into 2 daughter cells. This important process is called DNA replication and is not mistake free. The human replication repair genes responsible for fixing these mistakes are therefore extremely important to avoid accumulation of such mutations. We found that mutations in the replication repair genes which result in replication repair deficiency or RRD, can be inherited or as a part of tumor formation and cause an important group of cancers characterized by thousands of mutations hence termed hypermutant cancers. These hypermutant cancers are common, can occur in all tissues and are resistant to common therapies but sensitive to novel treatments such as immunotherapy. In this project, we will extend our recent discoveries to study RRD cancers using newly developed zebrafish, mouse and human stem cell models. We will screen for compounds that can be developed into novel therapies for patients with hypermutant cancers and will test thses therapies in these models. Finally, winning combinations will be tested on our international clinical trial for which we will pefrom the clinical and molecular analysis. Completion of this project will open a new window for the understanding, our ability to diagnose and treat human hypermutant cancers.

column37: Autoimmune diseases result from a dysfunction of the immune system in which immune cells attack the body's own organs, tissues and cells. Guillain Barre Syndrome (GBS) is an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the peripheral nerves. Two thirds of cases are preceded by virus or bacterial infection. column36: Impact of low testosterone on cardiac structure/function in aging
column37: Heart disease increases with age in men and women as sex hormone levels fall. Since a women's risk of heart disease goes up after menopause, there has been a lot of interest in the idea that estrogen influences heart disease. However, it is now clear that testosterone decreases with age not only during "manopause" in men, but in women too. Marketing campaigns focused on the benefits of testosterone have led to an increase in the use of testosterone supplements in older people. This is important, because low testosterone increases the risk of diseases like heart failure, where the heart cannot pump blood very well, but high testosterone can be harmful too. We discovered that age decreases the ability of male hearts to contract by changing the ability of heart cells to regulate internal calcium. To mimic low testosterone in aging, we removed the testes from male mice. We found that low testosterone upsets the ability of heart cells to contract and regulate calcium, just like the effects of age. Some calcium is needed for the heart to contract, but the balance needs to be right. When calcium is disrupted it can lead to diseases like heart failure. There is still a great deal more to know about how testosterone affects the heart. We plan to look at how long term exposure to low testosterone changes contraction in whole hearts and affects contractions and calcium levels in individual heart cells in males and females. We will start to look at effects in middle age (1 year old mice) and follow them until they reach 2 years of age, which is about 85 human years. We will also treat male and female mice with testosterone to find out if testosterone therapy is beneficial or harmful and if this depends on the dose used. This research project will help us understand the links between testosterone, aging and heart disease. It will help us recognize whether testosterone supplementation is good or bad in vulnerable older people with heart diseases.

column36: The role of circ-Itga9 in cardiac remodeling
column37: Cardiac diseases are the leading cause of death in developed countries. Over time, as hearts age or become senescent, adverse remodelling that is initially beneficial, progressively leads to reduced cardiac functioning. Our research aims to understand the molecular mechanisms that underlie this remodeling and repair. Circular RNAs are closed continuous loops of RNA that were recently detected in eukaryotic cells, and may affect cell physiology through a variety of mechanisms. Our work revealed that the circular RNA circ-Itga9 is tightly associated with heart diseases. We hypothesize that circular RNAs may regulate cell senescence and tissue repair by binding to protein regulators of cardiac senescence. To test this, we will modify cardiomyocytes and cardiac fibroblasts so that they express more of the circular RNAs in question. We can also use the reverse approach to silence circular RNA expression, and observe the changes in function. Using these approaches, in conjunction with standard experimental models, we can better understand the function of circular RNAs in cardiac diseases. There are two unique aspects to our proposed study. Firstly, we are among the first to produce a stable expression construct allowing long-term studies of circular RNAs. The second unique approach is our inhibitor system that is designed to block the function of individual circular RNAs in cell and animal models. These allow us to specifically study individual circular RNAs, and better understand any causal relationships. Our proposed experiments will help us explore the regulatory roles of circular RNAs in both cardiac aging and other cellular repair contexts. The agents developed may be used as tools in understanding the role of circular RNAs in heart development, aging, disease-associated injury and tissue regeneration. With these approaches, we hope to design therapies to intervene against the adverse remodeling associated with age-related heart disease.

column36: Epigenetic regulation of repeat expression by RB and EZH2 in cancer
column37: Cancer cells possess a number of features that distinguish them from the normal cells in our bodies. This grant application is focused on studying the remnants of ancient infections that leave behind foreign DNA sequences called repeats. Their expression can be uniquely misregulated in cancer, creating a feature that distinguishes cancer cells from surrounding normal cells. In most cases these repeat sequences are sufficiently altered that they no longer generate viruses or cause new diseases. However, some pieces of these DNA sequences can be expressed and this leads to two major outcomes for host cells. The first is that expressing these sequences creates the opportunity for repeat sequences to move to a new location in the cell nucleus. This is called transposition and it is potentially damaging to the cell as it can alter the expression and function of the cell's normal genes at its new location. From a cancer perspective this can be the source of changes in DNA sequence (mutations) that cause the disease. While this is bad, the second consequence of expressing repeat sequences is that it can lead the host cell to appear as though it has been infected. This can trigger an immune response in which our natural defence system will kill the 'infected' cell. Thus these repeat sequences are an attractive means to recruit our natural defences to help fight cancer. This grant proposal will study repetitive sequences with the aim of using this information to design more effective ways to kill cancer cells.

column36: Interactions and Assemblies of Protein Disordered States: Principles and Diseases
column37: The biological function and disease-causing malfunction of proteins are underpinned by their structures and interactions with themselves and other biomolecules. Despite tremendous progress in past decades, the basic driving forces of protein conformational changes are not well understood, limiting the application of biophysical knowledge of disease-related proteins in therapeutics development. The need for a deeper physical understanding is especially acute for intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) that lack a stable structure. Comprising ~30% of the proteome, IDPs are prominently involved in cellular regulation, a role facilitated by IDPs' ability to perform dynamic, multi-site recognition of other biomolecules. Malfunctioning of IDPs causes numerous diseases, notably various forms of cancer and neurological degeneration. A remarkable recent discovery is that liquid-liquid phase-separated IDPs -- like oil droplets in water -- are a major component of functional compartments in the cell. However, the biophysical basis of individual and collective IDP properties remains mostly undeciphered. The proposed research builds on the fundamental advances we have recently made, particularly in understanding how IDP phase separation depends on their amino acid sequences. Harnessing the unique interdisciplinary expertise of our own research group as well as those of our collaborators, we endeavour to expand significantly our fundamental physico-chemical knowledge of biomolecular organization and recognition for the novel multi-site interactions and liquid-liquid phase behaviours of IDPs. Results of our investigation will enable advances in understanding disease processes and ultimately to developing new therapies.

column36: Alberta Moving Beyond Breast Cancer (AMBER) Cohort Study
column37: With improvements in early detection and treatment, survival rates for breast cancer have improved. Unfortunately, breast cancer treatments can cause both short and long term physical and psychological side effects. More specifically, breast cancer survivors are at a higher risk for breast cancer recurrence, second cancers, heart disease, weight gain, bone loss, fatigue, anxiety and depression. Previous research has shown that regular physical activity can improve the physical and psychological function of breast cancer survivors, help manage some short term side effects of treatment and reduce the risk of having a recurrence. However, this research has not been adopted into regular oncology practice because specific exercise advice cannot be provided regarding the type and volume of exercise necessary for improving quality of life and survival of breast cancer survivors. We initiated the Alberta Moving Beyond Breast Cancer cohort study in 2011 with a CIHR Team Grant. The aim is to determine if physical activity can help breast cancer survivors manage the side effects of treatments, enhance quality of life, reduce their risk of disease recurrence and improve survival. Study participants are asked to complete questionnaires, undergo tests for physical fitness tests and lymphedema (swelling in the arms), have their body composition measured (body fat, lean mass, bone density), give a fasting blood sample and wear devices that objectively measure their physical activity and sedentary behavior (time spent sitting) at breast cancer diagnosis and again at 1, 3, and 5 years. They are then followed for breast cancer outcomes. To date, we have recruited 75% of our cohort of 1500 and are now seeking funding to complete the recruitment and follow-up of all participants. A better understanding of precisely how physical activity and physical fitness affect breast cancer recurrence and survival will lead to improvements in exercise recommendations for breast cancer survivors.

column36: Role of CLEC12B+ macrophages in the pathogenesis of vitiligo and melanoma
column37: For the past 17 years, my laboratory has been studying skin diseases caused by abnormalities of melanocytes, the cells that produce melanin pigment that protects our skin from the harmful effects of ultraviolet light in the sun. More than 50 million people worldwide develop a severe disfiguring disease called vitiligo, which is caused by patchy loss of normal skin color due to death of melanocytes. In addition, more than 300 thousand of people develop melanoma each year in the world, which is caused by the opposite change in the melanocytes, i.e. uncontrolled multiplication of cancerous melanocytes. The exact mechanisms leading to the opposite fates of melanocytes in these two diseases are unclear. There is an urgent need to develop better therapies for vitiligo and melanoma. My laboratory recently found a new type of innate immune cells in the surroundings of the melanocytes in the skin, the CLEC12B+ macrophages. These cells are important participants of the immune response to pathogens attacking our skin, such as bacteria, allergens and viruses. They are also required for stopping the immune responses when the pathogens are eliminated, so that the immunologic balance is restored, tissue injuries are repaired, and damaged cells are replenished. My lab found that in vitiligo, there is a shortage of these cells, where as in melanoma, there is an excess. In culture dishes, these macrophages secrete growth factors that can enhance melanocyte survival, but suppress professional killer cells, such as the natural killer cells and killer lymphocytes. Therefore, I speculate that deficiency of these macrophages is the reason for vitiligo development, and that over population of these cells have the opposite effect, that is, unchecked growth of the melanoma cells. In this project, I will test these hypotheses using cultured cells in petri dishes and in animal models. The results generated will help develop more effective therapies for vitiligo and melanoma.

This study will tell us if olanzapine reduces vomiting in children receiving chemotherapy for bone marrow transplant and the side effects that these children experience. column36: Targeting perinodal adipose tissue for lymphedema therapy
column37: Lymphedema is a condition of uncontrolled fluid accumulation and tissue swelling that affects ~140 million people worldwide. Lymphedema can cause discomfort, immobility and organ dysfunction. Edematous tissue in lymphedema presents a high risk of infection. The major cause of lymphedema in the world is lymphatic filariasis. In Canada, the major cause of lymphedema is the damage to the lymphatic vessels and LNs associated with cancer and cancer therapies, which impacts almost all of the cancer types that involve cancer spread via the lymphatic vessels. Infection and obesity are the major risk factors of lymphedema in cancer survivors: 38-89% of breast cancer patients will eventually develop lymphedema. Currently, there is no cure for lymphedema, mainly due to the lack of mechanistic understanding of its development. Some lymphedema patients exhibit significant body disfigurement and need life long intervention with compression garments, which cause a huge psycho-social and economic impact on these patients. The lack of knowledge regarding the regulation of lymph flow has been the barrier for the disease prevention or treatment. Lymphatic vessels maintain fluid balance and transport tissue waste, pathogens and cells to lymph nodes for protection by the immune system. In the lymph node, lymph flow direction determines the time, the location and the cell types that antigens will encounter after immune stimulation. Lymph nodes are typically surrounded by fat tissue and I have found that this perinodal fat may partially compensate for the immune protection function when lymph flow via lymphatic vessels is compromised. In this study, I will determine how fat tissue around the LN participates in fluid balance and combating bacterial infection when lymphatic vessel function is compromised. Our work aims to target perinodal adipose tissue in order to develop potential therapeutic methods to reduce edema and improve host immune protection.

column37: Inherited diseases arise from mutations in our genes, and similarly genetic mutations underlie the development of a variety of cancers. These mutations arise from DNA damage that is repaired incorrectly in our cells, and ironically radiation or drugs that damage DNA are the most common form of cancer therapy. Thus, if you can manipulate DNA repair you can also enhance DNA damage in cancer cells as a means of therapy. In 2013, scientists discovered that you could efficiently edit DNA in human cells using a system from bacteria called CRISPR (clustered regularly-interspaced short palindromic repeats). CRISPR represents a primitive immune system found in many species of bacteria, which provides them with the ability to "fight" viruses by cutting the viral DNA into pieces. CRISPR/Cas9 can be applied to genome editing by using the DNA cutting activity to repair damaged genes, or to insert new genes; and for this advance, CRISPR/Cas9 was named "Breakthrough of the Year" by Science Magazine in 2015. Using a novel assay based on CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing we have identified a new small molecule inhibitor of DNA repair called HRK1, which we will characterize as a potential new cancer therapy. In addition, we have partnered with the Centre for Drug Research and Development (Vancouver B.C.) to screen for both enhancers and inhibitors of CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing. Enhancers of CRISPR/Cas9 can be used to improve the efficiency of gene editing; whereas inhibitors will likely block DNA repair, and thus can be used to sensitize cancers to radiation and chemotherapy. Ultimately, the compounds we identify and characterize will provide new therapeutics for cancer and agents to enhance the efficiency of gene therapy.

column36: Marijuana legalization policy: Impact on prevalence and risk behaviours among youth and young adults in Canada.
column37: In 2018, Canada will become only the second country to legalize recreational cannabis use. The current study will examine the impact of cannabis legalization on Canadian youth and young adults. The study will examine the extent to which legalization is associated with changes in five primary outcomes: 1) the prevalence and patterns of cannabis use, including use among 'minors'; 2) risk behaviours, including driving after cannabis use; and 3) the commercial retail environment, including the price and the type of products used; 4) perceptions of risk and social norms; and 5) the effectiveness of specific regulatory policies, including advertising restrictions, product labelling and warnings, public education campaigns, and the use of cannabis in public spaces and workplaces. The proposed study consists of a quasi-experimental design with prospective cohort surveys conducted in Canada, as well as in two 'control' jurisdictions: US states where recreational cannabis use remains illegal ('US Illegal' states), and US states where recreational cannabis use has been legalized ('US Legal' states). A cohort of youth and young adults (aged 16 to 30) will be recruited at 'baseline'- prior to the implementation of legalization in Canada- and at 12-, 24-, and 36-month 'post-implementation'. Representative samples will be recruited from each of three study conditions: Canada (n=10,000; 1,000 in each province), 'US Illegal' states (n=10,000), and 'US Legal' states (n=10,000). Analyses will examine national-level changes in Canada over time compared to 'US Legal' and 'US Illegal' states, as well as between provinces to examine differences in policy implementation. Overall, the proposed research will provide a rigorous design for evaluating the impact of national-level cannabis legislation in Canada using 'within-country' and 'between-country' controls over time. This time-sensitive research is urgently needed to inform future policy in Canada and internationally.

column36: The impact of lesion location on contralesional plasticity and its role in motor recovery after ischemic brain injury
column37: Stroke can damage different regions of the brain. After the injury, patients often suffer the loss of functions of the hand. Time and rehabilitation can provide some recovery of function but it is usually incomplete. Better treatments are necessary, but to achieve this we need to understand the mechanisms involved in recovery. Some imaging studies report that after a stroke, the unaffected regions of the brain change their activity during recovery. This suggests that these spared areas could be involved in recovery. However, the way they can do so remains unclear. This is particularly a problem for the areas in the hemisphere opposite to the lesion, the contralesional hemisphere. Some studies suggest that this hemisphere helps the recovery while others show it hinders recovery, and this appears to be influenced by the location of the lesion. The broad goal of our project is to understand how lesion location affects changes in contralesional areas and, as a result, the role these areas undertake in recovery. To address these questions, we use monkeys because their motor areas are similar to the ones in humans. In different groups of animals, we will provoke lesions similar in sizes but destroying progressively more brain regions involved in the control of hand movements. During the recovery, we will record the activity of the neurons in the contralesional hemisphere and study how it changes. After the animal has completed its spontaneous recovery (without any treatment), we will use drugs to inactivate each contralesional area. This will reveal the new role the contralesional areas undertook for recovery of the paretic hand after different types of lesion. Finally, we will inject anatomical tracers and study the rewiring of connections of the contralesional areas. Our experiments will greatly increase our understanding of the mechanisms that allow contralesional areas to take a good or bad role in recovery and how the location of lesion affects these processes

column36: Investigating the contribution of Shank3 in Alzheimer's disease
column37: More than 740,000 Canadians are living with Alzheimer disease (AD) or related dementia, a number expected to double by 2031. Compared to other prevalent diseases, the absence of effective treatments for AD is shocking. It is of prime importance for AD patients, their loved ones and the society as a whole, that we rapidly develop new therapeutic strategies. To achieve that aim, the identification of new relevant drug targets is the key. My laboratory has always been trying to understand why neurons fail to communicate in AD and whether it is caused by loss of proteins located in "synapses", where neurons interconnect with each other. My specific interest in one of those synapse proteins, Shank3, started when I learned 5 years ago that the child of one of my close friend had mental retardation due to a lack of this protein. I could witness with my own eyes the consequence of a loss of 50% of this protein on a child's capacity to learn and memorize. If lacking Shank3 has such an effect on a child, could it do the same in AD? We then found that there is almost 50% less Shank3 in the brain of AD patients. Since we know that children born missing 50% of the gene coding for Shank3 display extensive cognitive impairments, it seems likely that a comparable loss of Shank3 protein in AD may contribute to symptoms. To test that hypothesis, we thus propose to determine whether the consequences of shutting down half of Shank3 in animal models leads to signs and symptoms similar to AD. In summary, the proposed experiments in animal models will establish whether (i) Shank3 deactivation causes or aggravates behavioral, functional and biochemical markers of AD, (ii) it is possible with 3 selected treatments to reverse the deleterious effects of a Shank3 loss. The ultimate goal is to find out whether Shank3 could be a suitable target to develop new treatments for AD.

column37: Psoriasis is a common skin disease responsible for the formation of psoriatic plaques with a penalizing aesthetic aspect and various secondary effects such as arthritis. Our hypothesis is that the formation of psoriatic plaques is induced by a nervous stress, and cutaneous sensory nerves trigger locally an initial neuroinflammation leading to the formation of the psoriatic plaque. Developing a new therapy aiming to inhibit this neurogenic inflammation could be very innovative and effective in the treatment of this disease.

column36: Wide-field polarimetric imaging for targeted and rapid high-sensitivity analysis of breast cancer margins and heterogeneity with mass spectrometry
column37: Accurate detection and diagnosis of breast cancer remains a major problem in today's society. Even when something suspicious is diagnosed and breast surgery is decided upon, the success of surgery depends on the doctor's ability to accurately identify (and remove!) all cancer regions within the surrounding healthy breast tissue. Unfortunately, some tumor is often left behind (as it does not look very different from healthy tissue), and surgery must be repeated at a later time. A promising new method to definitively address this issue uses a technique called mass spectrometry (MS). It is very sensitive and accurate at distinguishing tumors, but also slow. This makes it impractical for use in the operating room. If, however, MS could be directed to only examine suspicious cancer regions, the examination time could be cut down dramatically and made practical for the clinic. Here we propose to use polarized light imaging ("polarimetry") to get a rapid overview of the exposed breast tissue, identifying potential cancer regions that will benefit from targeted MS diagnosis. Polarimetry is indeed well suited for this task -- it is fast, robust, able to image large tissue regions, and yields useful information for directing MS. The unique combined polarimetry-guided MS instrument will draw upon the strengths of the two technologies and should prove useful as a rapid, accurate and practical method to improve the success of breast cancer surgery.

column36: Pathophysiology of Narcolepsy and Idiopathic Hypersomnia: a Multimodal Neuroimaging Study
column37: Narcolepsy is a disorder characterized by excessive sleepiness: patients fall asleep during the day without being able to resist the urge to sleep. Narcolepsy is often accompanied by sudden episodes of muscle weakness triggered by emotions and termed cataplexy. Research in the past decade demonstrated that daytime sleepiness in narcoleptic patients who present cataplexy is related to a lack of a substance in the brain called hypocretin. However, some patients with narcolepsy never experience episodes of cataplexy. Furthermore, other patients presenting daytime sleepiness and no cataplexy closely resemble narcoleptic patients, but they tend to sleep for longer durations during the night and during daytime naps, without feeling refreshed after naps. This disorder is called idiopathic hypersomnia. No consistent lack of hypocretin has been observed in narcolepsy without cataplexy and idiopathic hypersomnia, and the brain abnormalities responsible for sleepiness in these disorders are poorly understood. This lack of knowledge considerably limits the possibility of developing optimal treatments. In the absence of more effective interventions, many patients with idiopathic hypersomnia or narcolepsy are dramatically affected by severe daytime sleepiness, which causes threatening risks of accidents, and impairs productivity and quality of life. Our objective is to analyze complementary modalities of brain imaging in patients with narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia. This will allow us to identify brain regions and networks that are affected by these disorders, and will thus help us clarify the distinct brain mechanisms of daytime sleepiness in these different conditions. Understanding the brain regions and networks responsible for the disruption of daytime functioning in narcolepsy and idiopathic hypersomnia will be critical for developing new treatments, which will target the brain mechanisms specifically involved in each of these disabling disorders.

column36: Novel interactive roles of cAMP/cGMP in synaptic plasticity, learning and memory
column37: Understanding the molecular mechanisms of learning and memory is essential for designing effective therapies for brain disorders such as Alzheimer's disease. The proposal aims to study the role of critical neuronal signals mediated by cyclic AMP and cyclic GMP (cAMP/cGMP). We will utilize our newly established techniques that allow for their rapid and independent manipulation by light. Brain synapses undergo long-lasting changes in the strength of communication known as synaptic plasticity, which is the accepted cellular mechanism for learning and memory. Signalling via cAMP and cGMP are deemed important for the process, yet, the detailed nature of their regulation at (e.g. time course, response size and interactions) remains obscure owing to a lack of precise methods and tools. To decipher the roles of cAMP/cGMP, I will apply our newly established technologies to light-dependently control their levels in a location-specific manner by the use of advanced microscopy and engineered light-sensitive proteins. Utilizing these technologies, we will reveal how cAMP and cGMP interact to control synaptic function, plasticity and cognitive performance. The proposed research and light-sensitive technologies will advance our knowledge of brain function and provide an in-depth understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying brain function in health and disease. The work is directly relevant to understanding and treating brain disorders that affect cognitive function, including Alzheimer's disease. The expected outcomes include the development of novel optical technologies and valuable tools to elucidate the role of signalling cascades in broad research fields. cAMP, cGMP and other signals to be studied are used by all cells in the body and hence the work has applications to a wide range of medical conditions. The new knowledge will form the basis for development of novel strategies for patients afflicted with devastating brain disorders.

column36: Regulation of T cell central tolerance by non-apoptotic mechanisms
column37: Protection against pathogen infections and cancers is provided by the immune system. However, the immune system is responsible for the development of autoimmunity in genetically susceptible individuals. A white blood cell type critical for both immune protection and induction of autoimmunity is the T cell. During their development, T cells undergo rigorous selection processes in the thymus in an attempt to enrich the body with protective T cells and limit the presence of potentially harmful T cells. Much attention has been focused on the physical removal of T cells that recognize one's own healthy cells during development through a cell death mechanism. However, it is becoming clear that the ability of T cells to recognize one's own cells results in the generation of T cell populations that can protect against damage. Furthermore, we have evidence that, as opposed to the physical elimination of potentially harmful T cells, functional inactivation of these T cells is a more potent way to prevent autoimmunity. We propose to investigate the important events that regulate the development of protective T cell populations and to determine the relative importance of, and key molecules involved in, the functional inactivation of potentially harmful T cells during their development. Information generated from our experiments will provide valuable information into how the body normally avoids autoimmunity and will also generate insight into treatment options and therapeutics for cancer immunotherapy, chronic infections and organ transplantation.

column36: Macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF), a novel factor regulates hyperphagia and obesity associated with atypical antipsychotics
column37: Severe mental disorders such as schizophrenia or bipolar disorder affect more than 2% of the Canadian population, especially youth. Atypical antipsychotics (AAPs) are the first-line medications for treating these diseases, while they are often associated with severe metabolic side-effects (insulin resistance and diabetes) and heart disease. Increasing evidence is accumulating that metabolic abnormalities play a crucial role in the development of heart disease. Thus, studying the molecular mechanisms through which AAPs induce metabolic dysfunction and their effects on heart metabolism are essential to understanding the development of heart disease following AAP treatment. Macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) is a pro-inflammatory factor, well known to be involved in inflammation and also to play a role in regulating metabolism. Our preliminary data indicate that schizophrenic patients following treatments of AAPs for 2 months have increased plasma MIF. MIF plays a crucial role in the development of metabolic dysfunction induced by a classical AAP, olanzapine. Thus, we will use olanzapine as a representative atypical drug to explore the possible mechanisms of MIF in AAP induced metabolic dysfunction. Our research will include multiple techniques related to basic medicine and molecular biology. I hope to develop a novel strategy to inhibit metabolic side effects and heart disease during atypical antipsychotic treatment. We believe that MIF inhibitors will improve the clinical psychiatric treatment with atypical antipsychotics. Based on the results of these experiments, in our future studies, we are planning to extend the use of MIF inhibitors to clinical practice by collaborating with Dr. Donghong Cui in Shanghai Mental Health Center, China. We would then explore the pharmaceutical possibility of making a combined MIF inhibitor and AAP therapy.

column37: The protection of the airway lining is extremely important since it is a single cell layer thick and its integrity allows for oxygen exchange. Immune responses to infectious microbes and to innocuous environmental agents like pollen have to be balanced to clear serious challenges yet not over react to harmless ones. This balance in immune responses depends on several immune mediators called "cytokines". Several cell types can make cytokines but one relatively new immune cell type called innate lymphoid cells (ILCs) have been found to play important roles in recovering from infections by initiating repair but are also capable of triggering allergic reactions that can lead to asthma. We work on a cytokine receptor molecule, CD127 or IL-7Ralpha that is a known surface protein on ILCs. We know it has diverse roles in other immune cells that display it but its unknown what its exact role in ILCs is. We will determine that using selective gene targeted mouse models, gene profiling and large immune profiling approaches in 2 models of airway diseases: asthma and influenza. We expect that this study will shed light on how CD127 signals direct ILC development and function and how this is changed in the diseases above. This will allow identification of better targets to treat such diseases.

column36: Discovery and development of VISTA antagonists that restore antitumor immunity
column37: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) represent a new class of typically antibody-based agents that restores the body's natural immune response directed at cancer cells. They do so by blocking signals, often sent by cancer cells to immune cells to dampen immune responses directed at them. ICIs thus allow for the release of tumor-directed immune responses. These blocking agents, namely anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1 and anti-CTLA-4 monoclonal antibodies, have led to impressive clinical results in patients with advanced melanoma and lung cancer, particularly when combined together or with other established cancer therapies. However, these treatments only prolong patient survival in certain types of cancers. One key reason is that our immune system has evolved many checkpoints to control its responses directed at infections or to dampen them to avoid self-immunity. One key checkpoint pathway that works in parallel with PD-1 and PD-L1 involves a molecule called VISTA. We propose to develop VISTA inhibitors since the expression of this molecule has recently been shown to increase on both immune and cancer cells of prostate cancer patients that do not respond to anti-CTLA-4 therapy. This finding indicates that tumor cells are evading recognition from immune responses by de-activating immune cells such as T cells through their VISTA pathway. We propose to develop and test several classes of VISTA inhibitors that will work with approved ICIs to restore immunity towards tumors.

column36: What will it take to decrease the burden of the HIV and STI epidemics among MSM in British Columbia, Canada? A sexual network modeling analysis, combining syndemic theory, to evaluate the impact of behavioural and biomedical interventions for HIV and STI prevention
column37: Gay, bisexual, two-spirited and other men who have sex with men (MSM) are disproportionally affected by the HIV epidemic in high-resource countries. Since 2004, in British Columbia (BC), the proportion of new diagnoses among MSM have plateaued, while those of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), especially syphilis, have been rapidly increasing, consistent with a substantial level of condomless anal intercourse. Today, there are three powerful strategies available to prevent HIV infection among MSM, including: the use of condoms, treatment as prevention (TasP), and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). In this 5-year study, our key contribution will be to develop a new methodology to forecast the consequences and benefits of emerging programs and policies for HIV and STI prevention among MSM prior to their implementation. This methodology will provide a deep understanding of the heterogeneity in sexual practices within MSM networks over time, enabling a more accurate assessment of the impact of different interventions targeting these networks. The proposed analyses accounts for the role of key factors affecting HIV and STI transmission among MSM, including demographic (e.g., age, income level), psychosocial (e.g., substance abuse, history of partner violence, childhood sexual abuse), and health-related factors (e.g., health status). Our ability to confidentially link administrative databases of all people diagnosed with HIV and at risk of acquiring HIV in BC, and assess surveillance testing data, makes this one of the first interdisciplinary research studies of how co-occurring STIs and risk behaviour are fuelling the HIV epidemic within MSM sexual networks. Importantly, this study will provide highly relevant new information for decision makers to inform resource prioritization and policies as they address the future impact of HIV, STIs and utilization of healthcare resources by HIV infected MSM in BC, Canada and internationally.

column36: Role of HSP90-alpha in preserving immunoprivilege of allogenic mesenchymal stem cells in the ischemic heart
column37: Heart disease is one of the leading causes of death in Canada. Unfortunately, there are no effective therapies available that can provide permanent solution to the problem. Identifying, new research approaches that can offer permanent therapies for this disease are needed. Patients with heart disease require constant long-term treatment and care. Therefore, it imposes a significant economic burden on Canadian healthcare system. The strategy of transplanting stem cells into damaged heart has emerged as a novel therapy for the treatment of heart disease as stem cells have the ability to transform into heart cells and replace dead cardiac cells. Bone marrow derived allogeneic (unrelated donor) mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) from young healthy donors have emerged as ideal candidates for cardiac repair, because these cells have the ability to suppress the host immune system and survive in the heart after transplantation. Moreover, there are no ethical issues involved with these cells. However, recent reviews of animal studies and initial clinical trials reported that allogeneic MSCs were rejected by host immune system that impaired the benefits of allogeneic MSCs mediated therapy. Therefore, understanding the cell signaling pathways that regulate transplanted stem cell survival/rejection in the heart will help in developing new therapeutic agents that could prevent stem cell rejection and enhance the benefits of stem cell therapy. column36: HEARTBiT: A novel multi-marker blood test for management of acute cardiac allograft rejection
column37: Heart transplantation is a life saving therapy for people with end stage heart failure. Acute rejection, a process where the immune system recognizes the transplanted heart as foreign and mounts a response against it, remains a clinical problem despite improvements in immunosuppressive drugs. Acute rejection occurs in 20-30% of patients within the first 3 months post-transplant, and is currently detected by highly invasive heart tissue biopsies that happen 12-15 times in the first year post-transplant. Replacing the biopsy with a simple blood test is of utmost value to patients and will reduce healthcare costs. The goal of our project is to develop a new blood test to monitor heart transplant rejection. Advances in biotechnology have enabled simultaneous measurement of many molecules (e.g., proteins, nucleic acids) in blood, driving the development of new diagnostics. Our team is a leader in using computational tools to combine information from numerous biological molecules and clinical data to generate "biomarker panels" that are more powerful than existing diagnostic tests. Our sophisticated analytic methods has recently derived HEARTBiT, a promising test of acute rejection comprising 9 RNA biomarkers, from the measurement of 30,000 blood molecules in 150 Canadian heart transplant patients. Our objective is to study a custom-built HEARTBiT test in a setting and on a technology that enable clinical adoption. We will evaluate the new test on 400 new patients from 5 North American transplant centres. We will also track patients' HEARTBiT scores over time to help predict future rejection, and explore use of proteins and micoRNAs to improve HEARTBiT. Our work will provide the basis for a future clinical trial. The significance of this work rests in that it will provide a tool to identify acute cardiac rejection in a fast, accurate, cost-effective and minimally invasive manner, allowing for facile long-term monitoring and therapy tailoring for heart transplant patients.

column36: Viral determinants of natural human cytomegalovirus transmission
column37: Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection causes birth defects in >2 per 1,000 births worldwide. As such, a vaccine to prevent CMV infection is needed. Most people in the world acquire CMV during early childhood from CMV in breast milk, saliva or urine. Children are often infected with CMV by their mothers, but mothers are frequently also infected by children, and interrupting the cycle of transmission between mothers and children is the key to reducing the enormous global health burden from CMV. Our study will guide the development of a CMV vaccine by characterizing the specific viral variants and modes of transmission between mothers and children. We have shown that only one or very few individual viruses that are able to successfully establish infection, which we call transmitted/founder (T/F) viruses. We are able to capture CMV transmission events between mothers and children, and determine the precise time of infection. Because CMV is highly genetically variable, we can use next-generation sequencing (NGS) to distinguish viruses from different individuals, as well as between compartments (e.g., breast milk, saliva, or urine) in the same individual. Thus, we are able to determine the exact source of a CMV infection. We can also measure the number of viruses present, and sequence of the entire genome of T/F viruses that initiate CMV infection. We will enroll a prospective cohort of 100 pregnant Kenyan women and their children, and collect samples of breast milk, saliva, urine, and blood to measure CMV viral loads and sequence the T/F viruses that infect infants and mothers. Our project will be conducted in Nairobi, Kenya, where our team has worked for >20 years on maternal-child viral infections, and brings together experts in epidemiology, virology, genomics, and mathematical modeling. This work will be invaluable for defining optimal CMV vaccine targets and evaluating vaccine strategies to prevent the transmission and morbidity of CMV.

column36: Enhancing ovarian cancer immunogenicity by increasing antitumoral responses using engineered oncolytic vaccines
column37: Cancer immunotherapy is a revolutionary approach based on methods that stimulate the immune responses in our body to kill the cancer cells. Immune cells called cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) specifically recognize cancer cells to eliminate them. However, when a tumor is established, cancer cells use several mechanisms that dampen the immune system. Growing tumors establish an immunosuppressive microenvironment that renders CTLs dysfunctional. Tumors also escape from immune recognition by their ability to decrease the expression of proteins in their cell surface called major histocompatibility complex I (MHC-I). In this project, we propose to combine different approaches in cancer immunotherapy to efficiently target and eliminate tumor cells. First, oncolytic virus (OV) are able to specifically replicate and kill tumor cells directly but also by stimulating CTL responses. Second, OV can be modified to make them express proteins that will empower immune cells sitting in the tumor niche. Using OV modified to express the proteins IL-15 and IL-21, tumor cells will produce a more supportive environment for CTLs to execute their killing capacities and generate a long-lasting protection against tumor cells. Third, MHC-I proteins can be increased on tumor cells by delivering NLRC5, a master protein that promotes the expression of MHC-I and other related proteins to increase tumor cell visibility towards CTLs. We have developed an infected cell vaccine (ICV) platform using tumor cells infected with the OV Maraba MG1 modified to express IL-15 and IL-21. The ICV-IL15+IL21 expressing NLRC5 will be used as a vaccine to stimulate the activation of antitumoral CTLs. Focusing on ovarian cancer, a cancer that is in dire need of more effective treatments, the combination of these three approaches should result in a treatment that generates robust CTL responses and stimulates the formation of memory that will confer long-lasting protection against relapse.

column36: Modulating peri-ischemic neuronal hyperexcitability
column37: In the healthy brain, neuronal functioning depends on continual tuning of blood flow in proportion to the level of local neuronal activity. A blockage of a major artery during stroke results in a sharp decline in blood flow, killing the neurons and inducing sudden paralysis, impaired speech, and/or loss of vision. Despite the availability of treatments for clot dissolution in the acute and rehabilitation regimens in the chronic stage, most patients suffer significant long-term disabilities and up to a third are institutionalized. Development of more effective therapies is hindered by the uncertainty surrounding the cellular changes required for complete recovery. Recent evidence suggests that the activity of the neurons in the peri-infarct zone, the damaged but potentially salvageable brain region surrounding the site of stroke, greatly influences recovery. Using advanced imaging techniques in rats, we will monitor the function of peri-infarct neurons in the hours following stroke induction. We will inject the brains of these rats with viruses that carry specific membrane channels to allow us to modulate the activity of peri-infarct neurons non-invasively, by illuminating them with light of specific wavelength. These finely controlled experiments will allow us to determine activity levels of these neurons that minimize short- and long-term functional deficits. We will then attempt to achieve comparable activity profiles by tuning the dose of locally delivered novel anti-convulsant medication. These experiments will establish the ways by which brain functioning can be affected early post stroke so as to improve neuronal function. The insights gained will guide the development of next generation, non-invasive treatments that can be readily combined with current therapies to enhance recovery from ischemic stroke.

column36: Pharmacological chaperones that bind F508del-CFTR and their mechanisms of action
column37: Proteins are string-like molecules that play many vital roles in the human body. They are made up of about 20 different building blocks called amino acids, which are in a particular sequence that enables the string to fold up into its correct 3 dimensional structure. When the sequence is changed due to a genetic mutation, the protein may not fold up correctly and cause disease. Misfolded proteins are often mislocalized and degraded, but if they can reach their normal cellular location they are still functional. This is what happens in cystic fibrosis, in which the misfolded protein is called CFTR. Drugs that correct the localization and function of CFTR have been developed, but they provide only a small benefit for most patients and better drugs are needed. We have identified new compounds that bind directly to CFTR and correct it's trafficking, but to improve them we need to answer questions such as "Where do they bind? Do different drugs bind at different sites? How do they work to trigger correction? Which combination of these correctors gives the most therapeutic benefit? These questions will be addressed in this grant proposal with a view to developing better therapies for protein trafficking diseases.

column36: The influence of microglia on the developing hypothalamus
column37: The human hypothalamus is only about the size of an almond and yet, it is very important to our survival. Indeed, the hypothalamus is essential for regulating key physiologies such as when to eat, sleep, drink, reproduce, shiver, and even love. To control these physiologies, the hypothalamus acts as a thermostat, first by sensing cues and then eliciting a response via its many neurons. Interestingly, even during embryonic development, the hypothalamus is still responsive to its environment. Microglia are another type of sensing cell in the brain but instead of responding to external cues, microglia respond to internal ones. For example, microglia are tasked with detecting injury and trying to repair it, as well as identifying unnecessary debris (e.g., dying cells) and clearing them away. Recent studies are starting to show that microglia also influence fetal brain development. Our own work has demonstrated a unique role for microglia in the developing hypothalamus. We have discovered that microglia in the embryonic hypothalamus are particularly activated, clustering around a discrete niche of the dorsal third ventricle. We showed that hypothalamic microglia interact with progenitors and can influence normal developmental programs. Consistent with these findings, elimination of microglia during gestation caused newborn pups to be born obese, strongly supporting a role for microglia in hypothalamic development. From these data and others, we hypothesize that microglia communicate with hypothalamic RGCs to influence development, particularly tanycytes. In this proposal, we will test the intriguing notion that cells whose primary purpose is to sense insults (e.g., microglia) are used to establish the key brain region essential to sensing homeostatic cues throughout life.

column36: Of Worm and Man: Using C. elegans to uncover genetic modifiers for rare human disorders
column37: High-throughput sequencing has accelerated the pace at which gene-disease associations are established. However, we need to start addressing the next challenge: why two individuals with the same rare disease-causing variant may have different clinical presentation of the disease? Genetic modifiers are factors that can either alleviate or exacerbate the severity of the disease-causing variants. Identification of such modifiers provides important information about the biological functions of human disease genes and mechanistic role they play in the development of the disease. This in turn allows for better disease outcome prediction, planned prevention protocols and development of targeted treatments. Complexity of human biology makes it difficult to address this challenge effectively; however, fundamental aspects of human disease had been in past and will be in future efficiently addressed through analysis of orthologous genes using experimentally tractable model organisms. The goal of my research is to combine powers of unbiased mutagen-induced modifier screens using Caenorhabditis elegans model and whole genome sequencing (WGS) in order to accelerate discovery of new disease-associated genes, modifiers of known disease-associated genes and potential Orphan drug targets. This research is of high importance as it will establish C. elegans as a model organism for systematic high-throughput heritable genetic modifier screens with high potential for direct impact on diagnosis, prognosis and treatment of rare diseases, in particular the ones with no treatment options (currently >95% of rare diseases).

column36: Regulation and impact of productive AID targeting during antibody responses.
column37: Antibodies are a major component of the human immune system. A large repertoire of specialized cells named B-lymphocytes, each producing a different antibody, are constantly renewed to be able to detect any of innumerable and constantly evolving pathogens. The initial recognition of a pathogen, by the antibody on the surface of a B-lymphocyte, signals the onset of changes in the genes encoding the antibody, which will allow improving its affinity and effectivity to eliminate the infection. Most vaccination strategies rely on stimulating the B-lymphocytes that produce antibodies against known pathogens so that they expand and undergo the AID-mediated antibody improvements before any exposure to the actual pathogen. The genetic mechanisms that shape the antibodies and mediate immunity are initiated by an enzyme named AID. As a side effect of changing the antibody genes, AID can also cause collateral genetic damage. This can predispose to cancer or negatively affect the B-lymphocyte's ability to multiply, which is critical for the process of generating a protective response. We study the mechanisms that balance these beneficial and detrimental effects of AID. We investigate how AID reaches the genome and how much it works once there, which have a direct impact on the antibody response. On one side, these mechanisms need to allow sufficient AID activity to produce useful antibodies. On the other hand, they need to protect the genome from excessive damage. Our results would allow explaining the cause of immunodeficiency when the mechanisms we study do not work and enable manipulations for therapeutic applications. Salient examples would be to treat autoimmune diseases mediated by antibodies, boosting the efficacy of immunization in aged people, or enhancing vaccination to increase the chances of generating infrequent antibodies, such as those that neutralize rapidly evolving viruses.

column36: Molecular Basis of Quebec Platelet Disorder
column37: Platelets are small blood cells that help control bleeding. Our team is studying an inherited disorder called Quebec platelet disorder (QPD) that alters platelets and causes serious bleeding. Our team has made important discoveries about QPD including its genetic cause. In Canada, about 1:200,000 Quebecers has QPD and each person with QPD has a 50:50 chance of passing on QPD each of their children. QPD causes bleeding because it increases a clot busting enzyme called urokinase plasminogen activator (uPA). Persons with QPD have very high levels of uPA in platelets but not in other cells - we are trying to find out why. QPD is caused by a "duplication mutation" which means that a person with QPD an extra copy of the uPA gene and nearby DNA. In QPD cells that make platelets, uPA production is >100 times normal, which is far more than expected for having one extra uPA gene. Additionally, the overproduction of uPA occurs only in QPD cells that make platelets. We explored why and found that QPD duplicates a gene enhancer ("turn on switch") for vinculin (the next gene) - this switch is active only in cells that make platelets. QPD puts the extra copy of this switch right front of the uPA gene. We suspect this is why the gene for uPA becomes turned on too much in QPD cells that make platelets. We will use special methods, including "chromatic conformation capture methods" to test this "swtich" and if it is the reason that the uPA gene in is switched on in QPD cells that make platelets. We will also use special methods to alter genes to test if we can correct the problem in QPD cells that make platelets. Our team has made important discoveries about QPD. We have exciting new information and the technical skills that are needed to study what causes QPD. The study will give us important new information on how genes are controlled when the body makes platelets and how this is changed by QPD. The study will give us new insights on what causes platelet disorders

column36: Hockey Fans in Training (Hockey FIT): A pragmatic cluster randomized controlled trial of a gender-sensitized weight loss and healthy lifestyle program for men who are overweight or obese
column37: About 40% of Canadian men are overweight and another 20% are obese. Approximately 70% of men's staggering health care costs (estimated at $36.9 billion annually) could be prevented if men improved their lifestyles (i.e., got active, ate better, and lost weight); however, few men engage in lifestyle change. The apparent reluctance of men to engage in healthy lifestyle programs may reflect the fact that men with excess weight tend to be less aware or concerned than women about their overweight status. Research has shown that programs situated in a sporting context, where men have a strong sense of affiliation as a fan, are effective and lead to high satisfaction among men. Hockey Fans in Training (Hockey FIT) is adapted from Football Fans in Training and our own HealtheSteps lifestyle prescription program. Hockey FIT is a 12-month (3-month active phase and 9-month maintenance phase) weight loss and healthy lifestyle program for middle-aged, overweight/obese male hockey fans, delivered by trained coaches in collaboration with teams in the Canadian Hockey League (CHL). Across the CHL, there are 52 teams spanning small to large urban centres, located throughout Canada. In the proposed study, 32 sites (affiliated with major junior hockey teams and local YMCA facilities) will be randomly assigned to either the intervention (Hockey FIT program) or comparator (wait-list control). At each site, 40 male hockey fans at-risk for chronic diseases will be recruited to take part in the study. Sites assigned to the comparator will offer the Hockey FIT program to their enrolled male hockey fans after 12 months. Through the Hockey FIT program, our study aims to promote weight loss, increase physical activity levels, and improve other health measures through a cost-effective solution that is acceptable and appealing to men who are overweight or obese. Indeed, findings from our pilot study indicate that Hockey FIT has the potential to achieve these goals.

column36: Understanding molecular control of lipid metabolism in brain aging
column37: While perturbed lipid metabolism has been implicated as a risk factor for aging-related neurological degeneration, it remains unknown how the perturbed lipid metabolism arises during the aging process. Importantly, bioactive lipids have been shown as controllers to regulate neural stem cell function that plays an essential role in learning and memory by producing adult-born neurons. To this end, we are interested in understanding molecular mechanisms that control lipid metabolism to regulate neural stem cell function in the context of aging brain with the long term goal of identifying the molecular target for drug discovery to treat aging-associated cognitive decline. Recently, we discovered a signaling-induced molecular pathway that is required to maintain homeostatic neurogenesis and new memory formation during normal aging. This molecular pathway involves the direct phosphorylation of CBP, a histone acetyltransferase, by atypical protein kinase C (aPKC). We recently identified that monoacylglycerol lipase (Mgll), an enzyme that converts endocannabinoid (2-AG) into arachidonic acid, is a downstream target of the aPKC-CBP pathway. Importantly, we observe that the attenuation of the aPKC-CBP pathway causes upregulation of Mgll expression occurring in both normal and Alzheimer's Disease aging brain of animal models. Thus, we hypothesize that deregulation of the aPKC-CBP pathway in brain aging impairs lipid composition and adult neurogenesis that culminate in the cognitive decline, a phenotype associated with brain aging. Together, our experiments will provide important new information regarding regulation of lipid metabolism and provide fundamental knowledge towards the development of therapeutic strategies fighting against the aging process.

column36: Effects of GPR55 on synapse formation and remodeling during development.
column37: Functional connections between nerve cells (called synapses) are essential to establish the architecture of the nervous system. The modification of synapses is thought to be one of the mechanisms by which learning and memory occur. It has been known for decades that cannabis consumption has a profound influence on learning and memory and that maternal marijuana smoking during perinatal period causes cognitive and social deficits that last in the adulthood of the offspring. For the moment, we do not know if these effects are mediated by the classic CB1 and CB2 cannabinoid receptors or by other receptors such as the GPR55. Altogether, these observations led us to investigate a novel function for cannabinoids (like cannabidiol (CBD)) or other GPR55 ligands in regulating the formation and the maintenance of synapses. We have shown that GPR55 stimulation increases the synapse number and blockade of this receptor decreases it. Therefore, the main objective of this project is to identify the contribution and the mechanisms by which GPR55, and its ligands modulate the synapse number. The identification of a fundamental molecular mechanism regulating the connections between nerve cells will provide important insight into normal brain function and learning process. Furthermore, it will probably permit the discovery of new pharmacological targets and the development of innovative therapeutic strategies aiming at treating congenital or neurodegenerative diseases. This project is timely because Canadians are among the highest consumers of cannabis in the World and its consumption might be on the rise when it will be legalized in 2018. Moreover, the GPR55 system is the target of several compounds in the pipelines of pharmaceutical companies (Sativex(THC+CBD), Epidiolex, and GWP42003(CBD)). Thus, the results obtained from the proposed experiments will potentially explain some of the side effects produced by these drugs.

Very little is known about how the mammalian brain regulates this fundamental process of decision making that can potentially go awry in psychological disorders such as addiction, in which the 'approach' tendency takes predominant control, and others such anxiety, which involve heightened 'avoidance' tendencies. Furthering our understanding of the neural basis of approach avoidance conflict resolution, and the identification of differential neural pathways for the control of approach/avoidance behaviour has the potential to create new therapeutic avenues for psychological disorders in which 'approach' or 'avoidance' tendencies are aberrantly dominant.

column36: Development of Viral Sensitizing Antibody Drug Conjugate and Oncolytic virus Combination Regimens for the Treatment of Breast Cancer
column37: Oncolytic viruses are safe viruses engineered to specifically infect and kill cancer cells, and can also stimulate the immune system to recognize tumors. Although they have the potential to treat a broad range of malignancies, the inconsistency of treatment response remains a major challenge and poor infection of tumors is a recognized issue. We have pioneered the development of small molecules that we termed "viral sensitizers" that are able to sensitize tumors to viral infection and potentiate the activity of oncolytic viruses. However, for these molecules to act at maximum efficacy, they currently need to be injected directly into the tumor, which is often not possible. To overcome this issue, we propose to exploit a technology that allows for targeting chemotherapeutics to tumors by piggy-backing on tumor-targeting antibodies. This strategy has notably led to Kadcyla(R), an approved chemotherapy-conjugated version of Trastuzumab(R) (Herceptin(R)) that targets the tumor protein HER2 expressed in a subset of breast cancers. Coincidentally, we have discovered that the type of chemotherapeutic conjugated to Kadcyla has viral sensitizing properties and we have gathered data in cell lines and in immune-deficient mice carrying human breast tumors that combining an oncolytic virus with Kadcyla leads to improved cancer control. This particular approach could be rapidly tested in humans, but before this, we must gather more data in mice with HER2-expressing breast cancer that have immunological characteristics that more closely resemble what we would observe in a human. Furthermore, we will attempt to modify this strategy to deliver our most promising viral sensitizing molecules, and to bypass the need for tumors to express HER2 in order to be effective. To maximize the likelihood of success and eventual impact on cancer outcomes, we have partnered with antibody-drug conjugation experts at the Centre for Drug Research and Development.
