column36: Mechanisms of cell death in inherited retinal degeneration caused by rhodopsin mutations
column37: Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a devastating genetic disorder of the retina in which patients slowly lose their vision, resulting in blindness. The gene most commonly involved in RP is rhodopsin, which produces a protein that detects light. There are large quantities of rhodopsin protein in the light-sensitive rod photoreceptor cells of the retina. Mutations in the rhodopsin gene result in death of rods. However, it is unclear how rhodopsin mutations kill rods. It is proposed that because rods make so much rhodopsin, even subtle rhodopsin defects can result in drastic consequences. We pioneered the use of genetically modified Xenopus laevis frog tadpoles to study this problem. It is easy to make numerous types of genetic changes (e.g., different disease-causing mutations) in this animal to reproduce and compare different forms of the disease. We demonstrated that there are different types of rhodopsin mutations that kill rods in various ways. Two of these ways kill rods faster if the animals are exposed to light. Although the two light-exacerbated mechanisms are caused by mutations in the same gene, and although to an ophthalmologist, patients with these mutations appear to have the same disease, we find that these are actually two very distinct forms of RP that respond differently to treatment. In fact, certain treatments that benefit one form of RP actually worsen the other form. This has important implications for patient treatment: genetic testing will be necessary to test treatments and establish which treatments to use. We propose experiments that will help us understand how these mutations kill rod cells and key ways these mechanisms differ. Our new knowledge of the underlying cell death mechanisms, the unique genetic aspects of the system, and technical advances in manipulating the X. laevis genome will be of value to the scientific community and patients who suffer from RP.

column37: Retinal degenerative diseases are genetic disorders of the retina in which patients slowly lose their vision, resulting in blindness. Retinitis pigmentosa is a disorder causing death of rod photoreceptors, while other retinal degenerations affect both rods and cones, or primarily cones. Rods and cones are the light sensitive cells of the retina. They are named for the shapes of their light sensitive outer segment organelles, which are modified non-motile cilia. The outer segments contain a highly organized stack of non-contiguous (rods) or contiguous (cones) disk-shaped membranes that contain very high concentrations of the G-protein coupled receptor rhodopsin. The exact mechanism by which these disks form is unclear. However, it is clear that defects in biosynthesis of both the disks themselves, and disk components such as rhodopsin, are responsible for inherited human retinal disease. Disk biosynthesis is proposed to involve the proteins prcad-21 and prominin-1 which form a complex that may be involved in a step such as disk evagination or sealing. We propose to examine the roles of prcad-21 and prominin-1 in disk formation using X. laevis and D. Rerio (frog and fish) knockout animal models, in combination with our newly developed assays for disk membrane synthesis. We will also use transgenic and knockout X. laevis and novel transgene tools to examine the biosynthesis and quality control of the disk component rhodopsin, including the role rhodopsin codon usage in biosynthesis, the roles of different degradation pathways in rhodopsin quality control, and roles of glycosylation and chromophore binding on regulating pathway use.

column36: Function of Flaviviridae viral RNAs in the host cell nucleus
column37: Pathogenic RNA viruses of the Flaviviridae family include Zika (ZIKV), West Nile (WNV), Dengue (DV), and Hepatitis C (HCV). ZIKV outbreaks are occurring in more than 80 countries and in 2016 the World Health Organization (WHO) declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. DV is endemic in at least 100 countries and WHO estimates that nearly 400 million infections occur yearly, while HCV causes serious liver damage with more than 170 million individuals infected worldwide. A central tenant of Flaviviridae virus biology, and one that guides therapeutic strategies, is that the virus production cycle occurs within the cytoplasm of host cells. However, we recently discovered that the RNA genomes of ZIKV and HCV shuttle in and out of the host cell nucleus. The movement of ZIKV and HCV RNA genomes through the host nucleus has not been explored in the literature, and the functional importance of nuclear viral RNAs remains completely unknown. Critically, altering the transport of ZIKV and HCV RNAs through the nucleus negatively impacts virus production, pointing to a crucial, yet uncharacterized, role for the nucleus in Flaviviridae biology. We hypothesize that the vRNA genomes of ZIKV and HCV enter the host nucleus to (1) engage nuclear pathways that aid in virus production and (2) to regulate host cell gene expression including activition of cell defence mechanisms. We expect that our research will produce new knowledge, technologies, and methodologies that will establish an area of research with pan-Flaviviridae therapeutic opportunities.

column37: Cilia, the antenna-shaped structures found on most human cells, have recently emerged as major hotspots for genetic diseases called ciliopathies. Over 30 different ciliopathies, caused by mutations in nearly 200 genes, are currently known. Defects in the functions of cilia, which play critical roles in physiology and development, result in many clinical ailments. These include blindness, polycystic kidney disease, morbid obesity, skeletal anomalies and brain defects. Since 2003, my group has made seminal contributions to the understanding of cilia and ciliopathies. In particular, we were the first to link a multi-organ genetic disorder, Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS), to defective cilia function. We discovered that several components (proteins) implicated in BBS specifically function in a process termed intraflagellar transport (IFT), which is responsible for the formation and functions of cilia. We also identified and uncovered the functions of novel IFT-associated proteins, all of which are now associated with ciliopathies. The central goal of our research proposal is to establish an experimental system in which we can decipher or 'model' the mechanisms by which different patient ciliopathy mutations cause IFT and ciliary defects. To further enhance our ability to understand how patient mutations affect IFT, we will conduct genetic, cell biology and biochemistry experiments to shed new insights into the functions and regulation of the IFT system. We will accomplish these goals by taking advantage of innovative resources and experimental tools that are either not available for, or not easily applicable to, other researchers using mammalian (e.g., human cells) or vertebrate (e.g., zebrafish) model systems. Collectively, our findings will help unravel fundamental mechanisms of cilia formation and function, and importantly, provide molecular diagnostic tools necessary to understand how IFT mutations can lead to an important and growing class of human disorders.

column36: Reducing HIV target cells in the female genital tract: Determining the mechanism of inducing immune quiescence.
column37: The two basic elements of successful Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) transmission are a viable virus and a susceptible target host cell. Activated immune cells are more susceptible to HIV infection than resting cells and, once infected, they produce up to 1000 times more virus. It is known that inflammation brings activated HIV target cells to the site of irritation. Most of biomedical prevention approaches focus on either keeping HIV away (condom use) or neutralizing it once it is present in the genital tract (antiviral drugs, microbicides, vaccines). However, what has not been a focus of HIV prevention efforts, is trying to limit the availability of susceptible HIV-target cells at the genital tract. We conducted a pilot study to determine if a common anti-inflammatory drug acetylsalicylic acid (ASA or Aspirin) could decrease inflammation among low-risk Kenya women. The results showed ASA reduced the number of HIV target cells in the female genital tract by 35%. In this current study, we build on those finding using detailed molecular studies to determine the molecular mechanism(s) involved in ASA's effect on the recruitment of HIV target cells in the genital tract. We will also determine if daily administration of ASA will reduce HIV target cells numbers at the genital tract Kenyan female sex workers who are at high risk of acquiring HIV. We will also determine which dose of ASA is most effective, the duration of the effect and whether there are any side-effects on the vaginal microbiome. The long-term goal of this study is to provide a novel HIV-prevention approach that is both readily available and non-stigmatizing. If we can demonstrate that ASA is able to reduce HIV target cells among women at high risk of acquiring HIV, then we will be one step closer to a much needed novel HIV prevention.

column36: Glycine Transporter Blockade and Neuroprotection
column37: Stroke is the 3rd leading cause of death and is a leading cause of long-term disability in Canada, with the risk of stroke doubling every 10 years after the age of 55. The Canadian Stroke Network's Burden of Ischemic Stroke (BURST) study has calculated that 50,000 new strokes occur each year. This leads to health-care costs in excess of $2.5 billion. For the most part there is not much we can do to treat or prevent strokes at this time other than encourage patients to develop good lifestyle habits that promote cardiovascular health. The clot-busting drug tPA is used to treat patients who have a large stroke and results in very favorable outcomes. However, the vast majority of strokes are "covert" strokes with no obvious clinical presentation. The cumulative impact of these strokes leads to substantial, irreversible neuronal damage. Our research aims to characterize a new mechanism by which we can protect the brain against these stroke events. In this proposal, we set out a series of experiments to characterize a potential new avenue for stroke therapy. Our preliminary results show that administration of drug that increases brain glycine, called NFPS, leads to a dramatic decrease in stroke size. In our proposed experiments, we will elucidate the molecular mechanism that underlies this phenomenon and also determine the therapeutic window of NFPS as a stroke treatment. NFPS is well tolerated in the clinic and our discovery will open up new avenues for treatment using a drug that is readily available. This will greatly improve the health of Canadians and lessen the economic costs associated with stroke recovery.

column36: Ectosteric inhibitors of cathepsin K: their mechanism and in vivo efficacy
column37: Worldwide, 1 in 3 women and 1 in 5 men over 50 years of age will experience osteoporotic fractures. Current osteoporosis treatments have various shortcomings such as poor bone quality and several skeletal and non-skeletal side effects. Therefore major investments have been made into the development of more effective drugs that are less prone to side effects. Due to efforts of ourselves and many others it has been discovered that bone-degrading cathepsin K (CatK) is a highly suitable drug target whose inhibition led to increased bone quality and reduced fracture rates in clinical osteoporosis trials. Although there is little doubt about the validity of CatK as a drug target, none of the CatK inhibitors have been approved because of various safety concerns. Based on our research, this might be due to the multifunctional character of the enzyme, where total inhibition leads to the observed side effects. However, the osteoporosis relevant activity of this enzyme is limited to its potent collagenase activity, which should be selectively blocked. Based on our previous studies on the mechanism of collagen degradation by CatK, we have developed a strategy to specifically block the collagen-degrading activity without affecting other biologically important actions of this protease. We termed this novel and innovative type of drugs "ectosteric inhibitors" and our proposed project is aimed at characterizing these substrate-specific drugs at their molecular, cellular and in vivo levels of action and efficacy as anti-resorptives. We have identified compounds that have a similar bone-preserving potency in cell assays and in an osteoporosis mouse model similar to the most advanced clinically evaluated CatK inhibitor without affecting non-bone-related pathways. This proposal introduces the novel concept of substrate-selective inhibitors that are superior to all previously developed protease drugs and aims to develop potent, efficacious, and side effect free osteoporosis drugs.

column37: In recent years, it has become clear that the beneficial non-pathogenic bacteria in our intestines, that together form our microbiota, have a strong influence on the immune system and therefore also have an effect on both health and disease. These immune cells are found in high numbers in the intestine and are important in preventing inflammation in response to the normal microbiota. It is known that the function of these immune cells is shaped by the bacterial composition of the microbiota. However, it is known whether these immune cells recognize these beneficial bacteria in the same classical way like they recognize for example a virus following infection. The proposed project uses newly developed experimental tools to study this. Furthermore, this project will also study how, in return, different activated immune cells that recognize specific bacteria change the functional properties of these bacteria. Last but not least, we will also investigate how the microbiota modulates the production of antibodies that are specific for the bacteria within the microbiota. The main aim of the project is to better understand how the microbiota can modulate these immune responses. This is important to know for the development of novel approaches to treat chronic inflammatory disorders that make use of the capacity of the microbiota to modulate immune responses.

column36: Functional Dissection of Germline Small RNA Pathways
column37: Patterns of gene expression distinguish different cell types (i.e. brain, hair, and muscle cells express different sets of genes to make them different from each other). Misregulated gene expression can lead to developmental disorders, infertility, cancer, and other diseases, thus there are many cellular safety mechanisms that regulate the process. One key mechanism for controlling gene expression involves sRNA pathways that can act in different cellular compartments and at several steps in the process of turning a gene on or off. Small RNA pathways play key gene regulatory roles in a variety of organisms, and rely on conserved Argonaute effector proteins, which utilize sRNAs to provide sequence-specific identification of target genes. Our research focuses on understanding how sRNA pathways regulate gene expression in the nuclei of cells known as germ cells (sperm and egg). The nucleus is where the process of gene expression initiates, and sRNA activities in the nucleus are currently poorly understood, especially in animals. Our studies focus on understanding the molecular mechanisms by which sRNA pathways impact chromatin (how chromosomes are packaged), using the nematode, C. elegans, as a powerful model system, and applying integrated genetic, genomic, molecular and cell biology approaches. Uncovering the molecular mechanisms of sRNA-mediated gene regulation in germ cell nuclei reveals a deeper understanding of basic cellular functions that contribute to development, differentiation, fertility and disease, and provides a more precise means to manipulate gene expression, leading to more effective sRNA-based therapeutics and laboratory techniques.

column36: Role of alternative polyadenylation in Ras-driven cancers
column37: Cancer is a disease of genes, which are blueprints for proteins that carry out the work of cells. Genes make proteins through an intermediate template called messenger RNA (mRNA). Proto-oncogenes can be thought of as gas pedals that drive cell proliferation. Mutations that convert proto-oncogenes into oncogenes push the "pedal to the metal", causing cells to over proliferate and form tumours. Oncogenes drive cell proliferation in simple organisms like worms by same mechanisms as they function in humans. Despite sequencing thousands of cancer genomes we still lack an understanding of how oncogenes drive tumour growth. Taking advantage of the powerful gene manipulation techniques of the tiny worm C. elegans we found that an oncogene called Ras cooperates with insulin signalling to promote tumour growth, which is also conserved in human tumour cells. We show that Ras requires an intact insulin pathway to sustain its oncogenic activity, and that this is achieved by dictating where messenger RNA tails are placed. These tails have sections where specific molecules can bind and put the brakes on to prevent its translation into protein. Cancer cells produce too much protein, which is required to fuel their rapid growth. We hypothesize that inhibiting insulin signalling promotes the formation mRNAs with longer tails containing sites to apply the brakes on activated oncogenes, and suppress tumour formation. To understand how this works we will combine the powerful gene manipulation technologies available in C. elegans, human cells, and mice. By exploiting these models we hope to identify new drug targets that can prevent abnormal tumour cell growth in humans.

column36: A New Entity of Cardiac Arrhythmia Associated with Loss of Cardiac Ryanodine Receptor Function
column37: In the heart, muscle contraction is triggered by the release of calcium from the internal calcium stores through the calcium release channel, called the ryanodine receptor type 2 (RyR2). It has been well established that enhanced RyR2 activity as a result of gain-of-function (GOF) RyR2 mutations can lead to irregular heart rhythm and sudden death. An increasing body of evidence indicates that suppressed RyR2 activity due to loss of function (LOF) RyR2 mutations can also cause sudden cardiac death. However, the molecular mechanism underlying sudden death caused by LOF RyR2 mutations is largely undefined. Despite their fundamental differences, unfortunately, patients with LOF RyR2 mutations are currently being diagnosed and treated the same way as those with GOF RyR2 mutations. As a result, patients with LOF RyR2 mutations are often misdiagnosed and mismanaged, which may lead to sudden death. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop effective diagnostic tests and treatments for these patients. The objective of this research proposal is to explore the mechanism, diagnosis, and treatment of heart dysfunction associated with LOF RyR2 mutations. To achieve this goal, we propose to identify and characterize LOF RyR2 mutations and their associated heart defects, to understand the molecular and cellular mechanisms of their actions, and to develop novel diagnostic tests and therapeutic strategies for RyR2 LOF mutation associated diseases. These proposed studies will gain new insights into the mechanism of RyR2 LOF-associated heart dysfunction, and may lead to the development of novel diagnostic tests and treatments for this new entity of heart disease.

column36: Stem cell related genesis and maintenance of glioblastoma
column37: Brain cancers, particularly glioblastomas (GBM), are amongst the worst human cancers. The 5-year survival is <10%, effectively rendering patients with this diagnosis to a death sentence. Patients are desperate for better treatments. A major barrier to finding better treatments has been a poor understanding of the mechanisms of brain tumor initiation and growth. My research group found that GBM growth was dependent on a few cells in the tumour that have stem cell properties, these cells lie at the root of GBM growth and are also resistant to conventional therapies. We have found that human GBM stem cells depend on the Sox2 gene, which is a master gene of stem cells. These findings suggest that the Sox2+ normal stem cells in the brain may be the cells that give rise to glioblastoma, but how, when, and why they do is not known. In this proposal, we will study the role of the brain's normal Sox2 expressing cells in the genesis and growth of glioblastoma, using experimental approaches that cannot be performed with human cells, by creating tumours in the brains of mice. We will test whether normal Sox2+ neural stem cells in the mouse give rise to experimental glioblastomas and how activation or suppression of the growth activity of these cells affects the emergence of glioblastoma. We will also determine if the growth of these tumors, and their therapeutic resistance depends on subpopulations of Sox2+ cells. These studies will complement and extend knowledge derived in research of human cells by allowing us to study all stages of glioblastoma, from the earliest tumors to full-blown cancers both pre- and post-treatment. We cannot easily get access to the first steps of the disease, nor some of its worst forms, so this work in mice will fulfill areas of unmet need in the research of this cancer. We will then use these models to test preventative measures and to develop more effective therapies.

column36: Synaptic, cellular and molecular mechanisms of depression susceptibility
column37: Depression is the leading cause of disability worldwide and existing antidepressant therapies have limited efficacy. It is well known that chronic stress can lead to depression, yet not all those who encounter stress will become depressed. Understanding what makes some people especially vulnerable to depression is essential for developing proper treatment and for possibly even preventing the disorder. Stress experienced in early life is one factor known to increase risk for depression but key questions remain unanswered. What are the enduring changes in brain function that are induced by early life stress to mediate life-long susceptibility to depression? Can neural signatures of aberrant brain function be detected before depression is observed? To answer these questions, we will employ a multi-disciplinary approach integrating advanced neuroscience techniques with robust mouse models to probe the enduring effects of early life experience on neuronal activity and the underlying changes in gene expression in a key brain circuit implicated in depression, the ventral hippocampus projection to the nucleus accumbens. We will use ex vivo measurements of neuronal connectivity, in vivo imaging of neuronal activity and post-mortem assays of genome-wide gene expression to examine how maternal separation in mice, a form of early life stress, shapes neuronal function and gene networks in the ventral-hippocampus to nucleus accumbens circuit to increase susceptibility to chronic stress in adulthood. Elucidating both the alterations in brain circuit function and the underlying gene networks that render an individual susceptible to depression will provide the knowledge necessary to develop treatments to treat and even prevent depression. This research will open the door to new interventions to regulate brain activity to mitigate susceptibility before depression emerges, reducing the enormous societal costs and improving the lives of millions of Canadians struggling with depression

column36: Assessing the role of adolescent hormonal contraceptive use on risk for depression
column37: Young women in Canada often use hormonal contraception (HC), and its popularity is increasing. The use of HC is highly effective in preventing teenage pregnancies and has a number of positive societal and economic consequences. However, HC was originally developed as a medication for adults, and much remains unknown about the potential side effects for teenagers of using HC. For example, because adolescence is a life stage during which major brain development is still ongoing, use of HC during this period could have effects on brain development with long-lasting consequences on young women's mental health. Our proposed research builds upon the growing evidence that relationships may exist between the synthetic hormones that are contained in HC, patterns of brain development, and mental functioning. We will conduct a three-year study of young women aged 13-18, documenting their use of HC during this period along with their stress reactivity, social competence, and depression symptoms. Thus, our study is designed to examine not only whether young women who use HC are at increased risk for developing depression, but also why such a relationship might exist, and which women may be particularly sensitive to such side effects of using HC. Women are approximately twice as likely as men to develop depression in their lives. Depression is a leading cause of years lived with disability and reduced quality of life, unemployment and lost wages, and risk for suicide. We expect that our research will advance scientific understanding about why women might be at particular risk for developing these disorders. We also hope that our research will contribute new data relevant to an important ongoing conversation in the medical community and in the public about the prescription of HC to adolescent women, ultimately promoting more informed dialogue and decision-making.

column36: Deciphering the role of DCIR in HIV-1 pathogenesis
column37: Several studies have shown that early or pre-exposure treatments help prevent HIV-1 infection and the consequent destruction of the immune system which is then able to regain some control over the infection. In link with these observations, identification of new targets for HIV-1 involved in the first stages of infection remains the best option to eradicate HIV-1 infection. Dendritic cells (DCs) are the first immune cells which recognize HIV-1 in mucosal tissue. The initial interaction between HIV-1 and DCs occurs through attachment factors and we have identified the dendritic cell immunoreceptor (DCIR) as a key receptor. The binding of HIV-1 to DCIR allows the virus to be internalized, to escape the mounting of an immune response and to be transported to the lymphoid organs, where it gains entry into CD4 expressing T cells (CD4TL) by cell-to-cell transmission from DCs. Subsequent virus replication causes severe and irreversible depletion of CD4TL, bereaving the infected person of an efficient immune response against HIV-1. We are now interested in a possible role of DCIR in the early step of infection that appear to interfere with and ultimately compromise the immune response to HIV-1. We propose to test this hypothesis in vitro and in vivo using well-characterized cell models and humanized mouse models. We hope this novel approach will constitute a springboard for the development of new innovative therapeutic strategies against HIV-1 by blocking HIV-1 binding to DCs via DCIR without affecting the specific immune responses.

column36: Roles of Alkali Cation/Proton Exchangers in Organellar Function and Neurodevelopmental Disorders
column37: The human brain has one of the highest rates of consumption of biochemical fuel (i.e., glucose) needed to sustain neuronal electrical activity. This in turn produces significant levels of metabolic ionic byproducts, such as protons (acid), bicarbonate and phosphates (bases) that must be effectively buffered, recycled for other purposes, or removed in order to maintain a suitable acid-base (pH) milieu for optimal brain function. Abnormal disturbances in brain pH balance are associated with the progression of various pathophysiological conditions, including newborn asphyxia, stroke, epilepsy, intellectual disability, and neuropsychiatric disorders - debilitating conditions that have an enormous human and economic impact on society. However, the molecular and cellular mechanisms that control brain pH levels are not fully understood. This project examines the roles of one major class of pH-regulating ion transport proteins called alkali cation/proton exchangers (i.e., SLC9A gene family), with a specific focus on the SLC9A6 transporter that is located in mobile membrane-bound vesicles located inside most brain cell types. Recent studies have identified mutations in SLC9A6 that cause an increasing diagnosed form of severe intellectual disability, epilepsy and autistic behaviour called Christianson Syndrome. We have isolated the SLC9A6 gene and are currently studying the effects the mutations have on neuronal function. We hypothesize that these defects impair the proper pH and functioning of vesicles that carry neurotransmitter receptors and other proteins to synapses of neurons, which in turn affects brain electrical activity and function. This assumption will be tested using a range of molecular, cellular, genetic and electrophysiological techniques in cultured cells and mouse animal models; thereby shedding new insights into the contributions of SLC9A6 to human health and disease, and identification of efficacious strategies for disease treatment.

column36: The neural basis of cognitive reserve, the brain's principal defense against Alzheimer's dementia and normal age-related cognitive decline
column37: Cognitive reserve (CR) is the principal source of resilience against dementia and normal age-related cognitive decline. Behavioral evidence indicates that CR is related to the degree of knowledge acquisition over the lifespan, but its neurobiological basis is unknown. We will use advanced optical neural activity imaging methods in both normal mice and in an animal model of dementia, to establish the neurophysiological basis of CR and to show that these CR biomarkers are associated with protection from dementia in the Alzheimer's mouse model. These measures will be correlated with behavioral & cognitive measures of CR, biological age, and AB load . We expect new and unanticipated insights into how the brain creates CR and will help establish a basis for comparison with abnormal brain dynamics that may underlie or be consequences of several neurological and cognitive disorders, in particular, normal aging and age-related dementia

column36: MR-Guided Management of Occlusive Peripheral Arterial Disease
column37: Occlusive peripheral arterial disease occurs when blockages in blood vessels limit the blood supply to the leg. This disease is widespread and represents a major societal burden. Approximately 20% of those over the age of 59 years suffer from this disease, which results in over 160,000 limb amputations being performed per year in the US alone. Our goal over the next 5 years is to extend the role of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to increase the success rates in patients who can have this disease treated using minimally invasive percutaneous techniques using catheters and wires advanced through blood vessels. X-ray fluoroscopy, the imaging modality that is currently used to guide percutaneous procedures, has relatively poor soft tissue contrast. This makes it difficult to visualize blockages and to ensure that a revascularization device stays within the vessel during the procedure. This limits success rates and restricts minimally invasive treatment to short blockages in large arteries (which occur much less frequently than long occlusions further down the leg). Other treatment options include bypass surgery, which has substantial associated risk, and medical therapy, which has been shown to have limited effectiveness. MRI, unlike x-ray, has excellent soft-tissue contrast and with MRI it is possible to develop a detailed picture of blocked vessels and downstream tissue that can greatly aid in guiding revascularization procedures. Through a program of technical developments we plan to advance methods which will improve revascularization of blocked blood vessels. We anticipate this will facilitate less invasive treatment in a significant population that would ordinarily be subjected to more invasive surgery or to less effective treatments.

column37: Heart Failure (HF) remains the leading cause of mortality worldwide, representing a major economic burden on the healthcare system. The ER is the largest membrane-bound organelle that participates in a wide array of cellular processes in eukaryotic cells. Instabilities in its structure and function can lead to activation of ER-dependent cellular pathways ultimately resulting in cardiac dysfunction. Defects in ER formation and function have been shown to result in numerous related diseases including neurological hereditary spastic paraplegia, cardiac dysfunction and eventual heart failure. Therefore, proper ER formation and maintenance of ER homeostasis are critical factors for understanding the pathophysiology of ER-related diseases. While the formation of the ER is not fully understood, an important group of proteins that mediate the formation and maintenance of the ER are receptor expression enhancing proteins (REEPs). Here, we propose to investigate the role of Reep5 in muscle pathologies, including cellular ER stress and heart failure. We aim to examine the physiological role of Reep5 utilizing Reep5 conditional knockout (KO) mice. Ultimately, understanding the role of Reep5 will provide greater insights into ER-related cardiac disease.

column36: Do community-based food security interventions influence use of community services, food security, social integration and health among new users?
column37: In Canada, hunger jeopardizes the health and well-being of one out of eight households. Donations of food banks are a well-known attempt to resolve the problem, but not everyone agrees on their benefit. Some think they are part of the problem, because they undermine the movement to adopt policies to fight against poverty. Others see them rather as a bridge to other community services that help people pull through. Who is right? For now, there is insufficient scientific data available to settle the matter. In a previous study we demonstrated the positive effects of food donation on food safety and on the physical and mental health of those using these community organizations. The results must be confirmed, however, and several questions remain. What is the trajectory of the people who call on these organizations? Do they find the guidance they need to overcome the hardships at the root of their request for food? In what way? On what conditions? Is the situation different in Montreal, in the periphery, or in rural areas? It is in an attempt to answer these questions that our team proposes to meet, three times over two years, 1,800 new users of 180 community organizations offering food donations in four regions of Quebec (Montreal, Estrie, Lanaudiere, and Mauricie-Centre-du-Quebec). Interviews with organization heads and with users with different pathways will help complete the picture. Our team brings together veteran and new researchers, and also 16 organizations intimately familiar with the environments to be studied. Together, they will communicate their results to practitioners, managers, and decision-makers to improve public and community network planning and intervention practices and to guide public policies on food security.

column36: Identifying Therapeutic Vulnerabilities of Brain Arteriovenous Malformations
column37: Brain arteriovenous malformations (BAVMs) are a tangle of large, abnormal blood vessels within the brain. The resulting high blood flow can cause these blood vessel malformations to rupture and bleed, which may lead to severe illness or even death. BAVMs are a leading cause of bleeding in the brains of children and young adults. The main reason to treat a BAVM is to prevent a rupture. Treatment of BAVMs with surgery or radiation carries significant risk, and is both invasive as well as costly. There are currently no drugs available to treat this disorder and the cause of BAVMs is not known. We have identified spontaneous, non-inherited genetic mutations in a gene called KRAS in the majority of BAVM patients. These mutations occur in the cells that line blood vessels within BAVMs, but do not occur elsewhere in the patient. The KRAS gene codes for a protein that serves as an ON-OFF switch in blood vessel cells. When the KRAS gene is mutated, blood vessel cells are stuck in the 'ON' state and think that they are receiving cell growth and migration signals, even when they are not. In this proposal, we first aim to identify the defective genes in BAVMs that do not have mutations in KRAS, and second to understand how KRAS mutations influence the formation of BAVMs. To do this, we will introduce mutations in KRAS in blood vessel cells of mice and zebrafish; both common animal models to study blood vessel development and disease. In addition to testing whether these animals develop BAVMs, we will also use drugs to block cellular signalling pathways downstream of the 'ON' switch to determine whether we can treat BAVMs in these animal models. This may help us to discover drugs that could be used to treat this disorder in humans.

column36: Signaling and chromatin mechanisms of Paneth cell differentiation in intestinal development and disease
column37: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is one of the most common and deadly gastrointestinal diseases in human infants. With 30% mortality, it is characterized by inflammation and death of intestinal cells. Currently, how NEC initiates is unknown. As newborns become exposed to gut microbiota after birth, intestinal cells begin to differentiate into Paneth cells, a critical cell type controlling immune response. Therefore, we hypothesize that proper gut microbiota exposure is essential for intestinal cell differentiation into Paneth cells, thereby preventing NEC initiation. Indeed, our preliminary work demonstrates that gut microbiota exposure is critical for intestinal cell differentiation into Paneth cells, and its proper differentiation is critical to the prevention of NEC in early postnatal development. Interestingly, antibiotic treatment significantly reduced the number of immune cells. We will investigate further how gut microbiota promotes Paneth cell differentiation through immune cells. During cell differentiation, the chromatin structure, a massive protein complex that organizes and protects DNA, must open to make the DNA accessible to processes that will bring about major changes in gene expression. However, the chromatin mechanisms underlying Paneth cell differentiation are unknown. By analyzing chromatin and gene patterns of Paneth cells and intestinal progenitors isolated from pups treated with antibiotics, we will define the role of gut microbiota in Paneth cell-specific regulation of chromatin. By modifying chromatin, we also aim to restore Paneth cell differentiation, thereby rescuing NEC-like symptoms. Our work will provide important insight into the chromatin mechanisms of Paneth cell differentiation, identifying novel Paneth cell regulators and effective biomarkers for NEC. Additionally, this work will help advance the development of novel therapies.

column36: Contributions of the Ventral Auditory Cortical Pathway to Auditory Cognition
column37: Auditory categorization enables listeners to efficiently identify and respond to auditory stimuli. It is a computational process in which auditory stimuli are classified and grouped into sound categories based on their acoustic features, perceptual representations, or other types of information. For example, when we hear the word "fundable" from different speakers, we can categorize the sex of each speaker based on the pitch of the speaker's voice. On the other hand, to analyze the linguistic content transmitted by speech stimuli, we ignore the unique pitch, timbre etc. of each speaker's voice and categorize it into the distinct word category "fundable". Despite an important literature on the neuronal mechanisms of auditory categorization, many issues remain unknown or have yet to be fully elucidated. First, no studies have identified the sites in the brain that contain the information needed to create categorical representations. Second, and relatedly, there is not a clear understanding of distinct contributions of different brain regions to different types of auditory categorization. Finally, although our world is inherently multisensory, it is not known the degree to which the ventral auditory pathway contributes to multisensory categorization. The accomplish these goals, we combine high-density recordings within and across brain regions, rigorous and quantitative behavioral studies, and causal manipulations in rhesus monkeys to address these issues and identify the mechanisms underlying auditory categorization. These studies will provide important insights into hearing dysfunction and hearing perception. This understanding is crucial for guiding the development of more effective clinical approaches to alleviating hearing difficulties in complex acoustic environments- difficulties which are common in the elderly, the hearing impaired, and in individuals with cochlear implants or certain developmental disorders.

column36: Type IV pilins - multifunctional subunits of bacterial virulence factors
column37: Many bacterial pathogens use hair-like filaments called type IV pili (T4P) as mini grappling hooks to stick to their hosts and rapidly spread. T4P are thus potential targets for new antimicrobial therapies such as vaccines. Each filament is made of thousands of small lollipop-shaped proteins called pilins. The "stick" of the lollipop is very conserved and has a number of important functions. It stores pilins in the cytoplasmic membrane; forms the inner core of the pilus; and acts as a recognition domain for sensor proteins that monitor pilin inventories, so more are made only if needed. We will investigate how these monitoring systems recognize pilins, so we can fool them into shutting down even if there aren't enough pilins available. In contrast, the "lollipop" part of a pilin is diverse, making it harder to design a vaccine that will cover all possible "flavours". We are trying to understand the causes and consequences of pilin diversity, to inform the design of new treatments. We study Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa), a pathogen designated by the World Health Organization as a critical priority for new therapies due to its high level of resistance to antibiotics. We searched thousands of Pa DNA sequences to find all of its pilin flavours, and constructed a panel of different pilins in a common genetic background. This unique and expandable resource will allow us to ask how the immune system "sees" different pilins - when is recognition lost? We think that diversity arises from attempts to escape from viruses that stick to the pili. Changing a pilin's sequence or hiding it with sugars blocks attachment. Remarkably, some viruses can bind to very different pilins, suggesting they see a non-obvious common feature. We will characterize how those viruses interact with diverse pilins. They are of interest as therapeutics, as they can kill multidrug resistant bacteria. Together, this work will give us an unprecedented understanding of how pilus diversity is shaped.

column36: Base Excision Repair in Cancer- New Mechanisms, Dependencies and Vulnerabilities
column37: Cancer develops following increased alterations within DNA, which are usually repaired by complex groups of proteins involved in DNA repair. Defects in one or more DNA repair mechanisms cause the accumulation of changes in DNA, called mutations, that increase the possibility that certain cells become tumorigenic. Paradoxically, once cancer cells emerge they are acutely dependent on certain DNA repair mechanisms, even more so than normal cells, because they proliferate rapidly and their metabolism generates highly reactive DNA-damaging molecules. Hence, to survive cancer cells must adapt by increasing their capacity to repair specific types of DNA damage. As a by-product of this adaptation, cancer cells become more resistant to therapies that cause DNA damage, such as chemotherapy and radiation. We have discovered one strategy that cancer cells use to augment their DNA repair capability. They can increase the expression of proteins that stimulate the activity of DNA repair enzymes. In contrast to DNA repair enzymes, these accessory proteins are not essential to normal cells under physiological conditions, but are required by cancer cells. This provides a therapeutic window to develop new drugs targeting accessory proteins to which cancer cells have become addicted to. Our characterization of the CUT domain family of proteins has established a paradigm in this field. We now have identified a novel accessory factor that stimulates a different DNA repair enzyme. In the current project, we will characterize the activity of this accessory protein, determine which cancers are dependent on it and demonstrate why cancer cells die without it whereas normal cells can survive. We will develop biochemical tests that are amenable to high-throughput screening in order to identify small molecules that inhibit the accessory protein. These studies are expected to target multiple cancers and eventually to provide new mechanisms to treat cancer.

column37: Fragile X Syndrome is the greatest inherited cause of intellectual disabilities and autism spectrum disorder worldwide and yet has no cure. Despite their promise, the lack of understanding of the mechanics that control these specialized cell types has prevented their widespread use, depriving many patients of a potentially curative therapy for their disease. Our work aims to uncover proteins that are required for blood stem cells to carry out regeneration and to perform experiments that will shed light on how they operate. While in the past, much research has focused on defining the molecular players that work on the DNA of these blood stem cells to make their RNA intermediate, we have new evidence that how this RNA intermediate is changed to impact the final step of protein production is of major importance to the regenerative capacity of blood stem cells. Our study will focus on systematically identifying and understanding the players that act on RNA in these rare and clinically valuable cell types in the hopes that we can capitalize on them and on this previously underappreciated layer of control to promote blood stem cell-based regeneration.

column36: Mechanism of Microtubule assembly by CKAP2
column37: When cells divide, the DNA in form of chromosomes is pulled into the two new daughter cells. The machinery, that exerts the force necessary for separating the chromosomes and is made out of tiny flexible tubes that we call microtubules. Microtubules have to form and grow very quickly and precisely during cell division. They have to be very stable and very dynamic at the same time and constantly be replenished. To make these microtubules, help them grow, stabilize them and ultimately break them apart again, cells use an army of proteins, called MAPs (microtubule-associated proteins). While we know some MAPs, the large majority of these proteins is still not well characterized or completely unknown. We are investigating a MAP that makes new microtubules and helps them grow extremely fast. The same MAP is involved in causing several types of cancer as well as making these cancers more aggressive. We will attempt to solve how this protein makes microtubules grow, how it is involved in building the machinery that divides chromosomes, why cell division is not working well when the protein is misregulated, and how that can cause cancer. In addition, we will solve the structure of that protein bound to microtubules, which might help developing new anti-cancer drugs.

column36: Mechanisms of action of antiestrogens: towards improved treatment of relapse in ER+ breast cancer
column37: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer and second leading cause of cancer death among Canadian women. Estrogens contribute to breast tumorigenesis by acting via a specific effector, estrogen receptor alpha (ER), present in 2/3 breast tumors. Inhibition of estrogenic action is achieved for therapeutic purpose via different drugs that have distinct mechanisms of action, collectively known as hormonal therapies. However, resistance occurs in 30-50% of breast cancer patients treated with hormonal therapies. The mechanisms of action of antiestrogens, a class of drugs frequently used for both first and second line hormonal treatment of ER+ breast cancer, are still not fully understood, preventing their optimal use in patients relapsing after hormonal therapies. The Mader lab has uncovered novel mechanisms of action for antiestrogens that explain the spectrum of clinical profiles displayed by this class of molecules, and has characterized the impact of different antiestrogens in models of resistance to hormonal treatments due to different genetic changes in the estrogen receptor. The current application will further characterize aspects of the mechanisms of action of antiestrogens that remain poorly understood, such as the proteins that cooperate with the estrogen receptor to lead to resistance to these agents. The team will also investigate novel therapeutic combinations that would increase response in progressing patients by suppressing estrogen signalling more efficiently.

column37: The cells of all organisms need to adapt to changes in their environment. One mechanism enabling adaptation to environmental changes, including variation in nutrient availability and cellular stressors such as heat, is the ability of cells to tune their levels of specific proteins. This process, known as proteostasis, is of great interest to researchers because it is now well recognized that disruptions in proteostasis contribute to various diseases including various neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson and Alzheimer disease. Further, proteostasis appears to become slowly impaired in processes such as aging. One mechanism that has emerged as a regulator of proteostasis is the modification of a set of proteins, found on the inside of cells, with specialized sugar units. We have recently uncovered that this sugar modification regulates the stability of proteins right at the moment of their creation and extending on to when they are found in large protein complexes that fulfill essential roles in the cell. Because this sugar modification is abundant within cells and depends on the amount of available nutrients, we aim to understand the scope of this modification and its impact on the broad set of sugar modified proteins. We further aim to evaluate the locations of sugar modification and to then determine which of these are physiological important for cell function. These data will help guide more targeted strategies to manipulate this promising but poorly understood pathway that has already delivered compounds into clinical trials.

column36: The Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database: Expanded tools for molecular surveillance of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in the environment, agriculture, and clinic
column37: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is among the most pressing public health crises of the 21st Century as bacteria are evolving drug resistance faster than we can discover new drugs. Once treatable infectious diseases now include nearly untreatable strains. In addition, many of the 'miracles' of modern medicine, such as chemotherapy or routine surgery, are under threat due to a degraded ability to control secondary infection. Discovery of new antimicrobials is furthermore at an all-time low, making stewardship of our current antimicrobial arsenal critical. Yet, we have recently seen emergence of very serious threats to our last two 'drugs of last resort' - carbapenem effectiveness has been undermined by emergence of NDM-1 in 2006 and colistin effectiveness by emergence of MCR-1, first reported in November 2015. As such, while there is an urgent need to re-boot the drug discovery process for antimicrobials, we have an increasing need for better data for clinical practice, antimicrobial stewardship, and public health policy. In both a Canadian and global perspective, we need to know which resistance genes are prevalent, which genes are moving around, and which pose a threat. This Project Scheme proposal is focused on the accurate detection of resistome (the complement of resistance genes and mutations) and subsequent accurate prediction of antibiogram (the range of antimicrobial resistance and susceptibility) from raw DNA sequencing data. Building upon our successful Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database, we propose development and application of AMR gene detection models, high resolution prediction of resistance phenotype, and powerful prediction of molecular epidemiological context to push AMR genomic surveillance beyond its current state. Our key scientific objective is to supersede the current paradigm of basic sequence similarity detection tools with intelligent systems for DNA sequencing based molecular epidemiology of infectious pathogens.

column36: Nuclear Receptor Signaling in High-Fat Diet and Glucocorticoid-Induced Metabolic Disease
column37: Metabolic diseases, including diabetes and obesity, are reaching epidemic levels in the Western world. Chronic activation of the glucocorticoid receptor signaling pathway by stress hormones can contribute to diabetes and metabolic dysfunction. Diabetes is characterized by elevated blood glucose levels (hyperglycemia) caused by the body's inability to properly secrete insulin and/or respond to increasing insulin levels. A high-fat diet and long-term therapeutic use of glucocorticoid drugs can cause obesity and type 2 diabetes. These negative effects are due in part to the glucose production pathway being strongly induced by glucocorticoid drugs in the liver and by the increased delivery of glucose precursors from other tissues, such as fat. We have a strong interest in understanding the molecular connections between high-fat diet, stress hormones (glucocorticoids) and the ultimate response obtained in tissues such as the liver and adipose tissue. We will use new proteomic and sequencing technologies to uncover the different signaling mechanisms involved, and in the process, identify new determinants of glucocorticoid specificity. This project has high public relevance because it will allow us to identify new drug targets to benefit patients with metabolic disease and potentially identify pathways that can be targeted to allow safer glucocorticoid drug use for the future.

column36: White matter plasticity in brain synchronisation and memory
column37: Our brain connections are insulated with a fatty white substance called myelin. Across the entire brain this insulation is called white matter. White matter helps in sending messages in the brain and the growth of new white matter - or white matter plasticity - is thought to be very important in brain communication. Disrupted white matter plasticity occurs in many brain disorders and can cause difficulties in thinking. Despite this problem, it is not yet known how white matter plasticity has an impact on the brain communication that produces learning and memory. It is important to know this because understanding these links can help us in creating and testing new treatments for brain disorders. In this proposal we will ask whether white matter plasticity helps in remembering through fine-tuning brain communication. To answer this question we will study: (a) children and adolescents who have memory impairment and disrupted white matter growth because of their treatment for a brain tumour, (b) mice whose genes have been edited to disturb white matter plasticity, and (c) computer simulations of brain function. Using neuroimaging we will measure the growth of white matter and brain activation during a memory task in children and adolescents who were treated with cranial radiation for brain tumours and healthy children. In mice we will measure the impact of genetically disrupting white matter plasticity on the growth of new myelin, brain communication, and memory. Using computer simulations we will model the impact of disturbing white matter plasticity on brain activation. By studying children with white matter injury, mice where we can genetically modify white matter plasticity, and computer models - all at the same time - we can decode the role of white matter plasticity in brain communication and remembering. Through this work we can identify people with brain disorders who are at-risk for long-term learning problems and develop treatments to help them.

column36: The HeLiX Trial: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Tranexamic Acid Versus Placebo to Reduce Perioperative Blood Transfusion in Patients Undergoing Liver Resection

column36: The role of episodic, declarative, and spatial memory systems in the planning and control of real-world action tasks
column37: The ability to skillfully interact with objects is critical in most daily tasks and, therefore, impairments to this ability, which often occur following stroke or neurological disease, are particularly devastating. To date research on object manipulation has focused on simple object lifting movements. However, real-world action tasks, such as making a cup of tea or preparing a meal, involve interacting with multiple objects as they are lifted, moved about in space, and lifted again. Skilled performance of such tasks requires keeping track of the weights of the objects based on their appearance and, especially when handling similar looking objects, their location. Thus, not only do manipulation tasks require declarative and spatial memory resources, involved in encoding the properties (e.g., weight) and locations of objects, they engage an 'episodic-like' memory that, as the task unfolds, links object weights to particular locations at particular points in time. This raises the provocative idea that medial temporal lobe (MTL) structures, which have been implicated in episodic, declarative and spatial memory, are engaged in object manipulation tasks. The broad objective of this research project is to investigate, using advanced neuroimaging methods, the role of MTL structures in the planning and control of object manipulation tasks. Motivated by extremely promising initial results, the proposed experiments will test a series of highly novel hypotheses about how MTL structures encode and combine information about object weights and locations during manipulation tasks.

We plan to study how this novel cilium might cause lung disease. This research is highly innovative because it applies basic new imaging technologies, capable of visualizing molecules in cells more clearly than ever before, to better understand an important clinical problem. Our findings may lead to a change in the way scientists currently think about sensory and motile cilia, and will likely improve our understanding of many other conditions related to cilia function.

column36: Implementation Research to Improve Scale-Up of Depression Services in Vietnam (IRIS-DSV)

We are currently testing the effectiveness of a supported-self management (SSM) intervention for depression in Vietnam. When effectiveness research studies are over, however, services are often not expanded to benefit the people who need them. More research is needed about how to ensure that services are "scaled-up" to reach people in need. This area of study has been recognized as a gap in global health research. Our study has three goals: 1) To understand what features of SSM might prevent or promote its effective delivery; 2) To understand how factors in the social and political context of Vietnam might help or hinder the scale-up of SSM, and 3) To work with government officials to ensure that the results of the study inform policy and planning for SSM delivery. We will also communicate with government partners regularly so that they can use the study results to inform planning and program decisions related to the SSM intervention. The results of this study will lead to improved availability of depression treatment for people in Vietnam. This study will also generate findings that are important for other countries undertaking similar initiatives, helping them to understand the drivers and barriers to scaling-up mental health services.

column36: Role of Pexophagy in Peroxisome Biogenesis Disorders
column37: Peroxisome Biogenesis Disorder (PBD) is a group of rare genetic diseases affecting children. Presently there is no cure for this devastating disease. Using advanced cell imaging and genetic approaches, we will determine the mechanisms that control peroxisome turnover. column37: Identifying new therapies to treat common age-related diseases such as Alzheimer's, diabetes, and cancer is one of the biggest challenges the current century. In Canada, over $68 billion is spent annually to treat chronic diseases, many of which are age related. Moreover, this cost is expected to surge over the next 30 years as the population of those over the age of 65 doubles. Therefore, for both economic as well as medical reasons, new treatments for age-related disease are imminently needed. Remarkably, molecular biology research has recently identified a key set of pathways that influence aging and many common age-related diseases. For example, this proposal relates to a pathway that has been shown to increase lifespan and protect against multiple age-related illnesses including various cancers, neurodegeneration, and heart disease in mice. In this project we will be characterizing how this pathway works at the molecular level and also investigating strategies for how to "activate" it pharmacologically for therapeutic purposes. We anticipate that this project will contribute to both the economy and patient health by advancing the development of single drugs capable of treating multiple age-related diseases simultaneously.

column36: Role of VPS33B-VPS16B in platelet granule formation
column37: Each drop of blood contains over a million platelets. These tiny cells patrol the bloodstream, and when they encounter cuts they initiate clotting to stop bleeding. Disease processes can also trigger the platelet clotting response, such as inflammation and rupture or atherosclerotic plaques. This can produce clots (thrombi) that cause heart attacks, strokes and other internal damage. Platelets also contribute to wound healing and immunity, and to plaque development and the spread and growth of cancers. The wide-ranging impacts of platelets on health and disease are linked to their ability release an assortment of proteins that are packed in structures called a-granules. These granules originate in megakaryocytes, large cells found in the bone marrow that can each shed thousands of platelets into the bloodstream. My group has identified several proteins required for a-granule development, including VPS33B and VPS16B. This research project will determine how these proteins and the complex they form, VPS33B-16B, control the early stages of a-granule development. We will employ approaches and techniques where my research group has gained internationally-recognized expertise, such as microscopy imaging and the development of animal and cell model systems. We will also work with local experts in advanced techniques such as molecular structure determination. The results of this project will advance understanding of platelet biology, which will assist efforts to control the negative impacts of platelets on health and enhance their positive roles. We will also open up new avenues of research, and since the proteins we are studying influence other processes besides a-granule development, our findings will be relevant to many aspects of cell biology, health and disease.

column36: Heptose-containing metabolites in Neisseria gonorrhoeae immune evasion and immunopathogenesis
column37: Neisseria gonorrhoeae has re-emerged as a global public health concern as it now causes nearly 100 million new infections each year and isolates have emerged that are resistant to all clinically-relevant antibiotics, prompting the US Center for Disease Control to name it as one of three 'urgent' microbial threats. The success of this organism is attributable in part to its capacity to colonize the female genital tract without obvious clinical manifestation, allowing it to persist undetected as it is spread to sexual partners. Consistent with this, N. gonorrhoeae does not express factors with overt virulent potential, but instead exhibits a lifestyle intent on avoiding and actively subverting immune detection. In this context, disease arises when the innate immune system eventually recognizes and responds to the infection with an overzealous neutrophil-based inflammatory response that damages the mucosal tissues. However, inexplicable in this context, this innate response does not lead to an adaptive immune response, so infected individuals remain susceptible to re-infection by even closely-related strains. This research project aims to understand the fine balance between immunity and immunopathogenesis in the context of N. gonorrhoeae infection, with a specific focus on the contribution of a bacterial-derived metabolite that we have recently discovered to have both immune modulatory and immune stimulatory properties.

column36: Enhancing immunotherapy with ultrasound stimulated bubbles
column37: Immunotherapies in cancer are used to help kick-start the body's natural defences to attack tumours. They are showing highly promising results in many cancer patients, while in others the effect is unfortunately limited, temporary or nonexistent. It is becoming increasingly clear that to broaden the impact of immunotherapies they will generally have to be combined with other therapies. In the case of a major class of immunotherapies- checkpoint inhibitors- a primary approach is to combine with therapies that can make tumour more 'hot' from an immune perspective. In recent work we have shown for the first time that when FUS is combined with microbubbles it can improve the tumour killing effects of a major checkpoint inhibitor. This project has the overall goal of investigating the mechanism of how this happens and how best to harness and control this effect. The work will be carried out in tumours that are located in the liver, as these affect a large number of patients and can benefit from locally applied treatments. The project is divided into three parts. In the first part we will use a cutting edge custom microscope to look directly at the effects of our FUS exposures on blood vessels in a specialized tumour model. This will tell us how vessels are affected, how to hone in on the appropriate settings, and what types of signals to 'listen' to from the bubbles when this is happening. Using this information, we will then use a custom MRI guided FUS system to create a control method for exposing realistic tumour models located in mouse livers. This will involve using the bubble signals as feedback to control the exposures. Finally we will investigate the therapeutic effects of using this method coupled with an immunotherapy in a realistic liver tumour model. The end result with be a validated new method to potentiate immunotherapy, which has the potential to impact the treatment of a large patient population.

column36: Priming Notch-activated basal like breast cancer for immune checkpoint blockade
column37: Genes that control normal breast growth can also be involved in the development of breast cancer. For example, genes called "Notch" control breast development but when active at the wrong time and place, can lead to breast cancer. Our group has previously shown that patients, whose breast cancers have abnormal Notch, have very aggressive disease and poor survival rates. We have recently discovered that Notch helps breast cancer grow by causing the release of special proteins called "cytokines" from tumor cells. Cytokines act as beacons to attract immune cells to the tumor. Against expectations, some of these immune cells actually help the tumor grow and spread. Scientists have known for decades that cytokines encourage the onset of diseases like arthritis and kidney disease. For this reason effective drugs that destroy cytokines (anti-cytokine drugs) have been developed. Based on our work, these drugs may be useful to fight breast cancers that depend on Notch. We predict that cancers with abnormal Notch, high levels of certain cytokines, and large numbers of specific immune cells will be the best candidates for anti-cytokine treatment, but the details need to be learned. In this project anti-cytokine drugs will be tested in mice that develop breast cancer. This project will provide evidence that breast cancer patients can be effectively treated with anti-cytokines. Repurposing these drugs for cancer could rapidly bring them into the cancer clinic, reducing time and cost and saving the lives of patients who previously had few options.

column36: The Canadian ADNI BraIn Donation and Neuropathology Network (CABIN) - Optimizing Canadian Participation in the Neuropathology Program of ADNI
column37: Canadian sites have been active in the Alzheimer Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) since its inception. ADNI is a major study to track the progression of Alzheimer Disease (AD), devise tests to use as outcomes for potential interventions, and to develop accurate means of risk assessment for AD. Currently, there are Canadian ADNI centres in Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, and London Ontario. ADNI has a neuropathology component to obtain brain autopsies in any of the >1000 participants who succumb to their illness. Unfortunately, Canadian sites have provided few brain autopsies in ADNI. Our relatively poor performance here reflects the lack of a national program and infrastructure for research brain donation and tissue banking at the Canadian sites. In contrast, brain donation programs and academic neuropathology cores are present in all U.S. centres. In this grant we are proposing to establish the infrastructure necessary to maximize the brain autopsies for the ADNI program in Canada; referred to here as the Canadian ADNI BraIn bank Network (i.e. CABIN). The coordinating centre for CABIN will be under direction of Dr. Ian Mackenzie (University of British Colombia), an internationally recognized neuropathology expert in dementia. He will work with a team of dementia neuropathologists and clinicians, at the respective Canadian ADNI centres. Not only will CABIN provide brain samples for ADNI, but it will establish the organization, planning, oversight, personnel and physical infrastructure needed to promote brain donations for other ongoing and future dementia research programs in Canada. The creation of this infrastructure will be transformative to the ability to study the causes of these diseases in Canada.

column36: The Frequency of Screening and SBT Technique Trial: The FAST Trial (North American Weaning Collaborative)
column37: Background: The sickest patients who are admitted to an intensive care unit (ICU) often require assistance with their breathing. When patients start to get better, they gradually do more of the breathing and the machine does less-this is called weaning. Although ventilator use saves lives, the longer it is used, the more complications can occur. Clinicians aim to wean patients from ventilators in a timely and safe manner. In most ICUs, patients are screened (looked at) once per day to see if they are ready to undergo a weaning test (using a variety of techniques) to see if the breathing tube can be removed. Screening more than once per day may allow more weaning tests to be conducted. Knowing the best way to do a weaning test is important because some methods may better determine who can have the breathing tube removed safely. At present, we don't know the best way to wean patients from ventilators. Patients: Adults in North American ICUs who are on ventilators for at least 24 hours and who can take breaths on their own. Interventions: Patients in our study will receive one type of screening and one type of weaning test at random. In the 'once daily' screening groups, clinicians will screen patients each morning. In the 'two or more times daily screening' groups, patients will be screened in the morning, afternoon, and whenever else clinicians wish to screen. When screening criteria are met, patients will undergo one of two weaning tests with low ventilator support or no support. Outcomes: The main outcome of this study will be the time for patients to be successfully removed from the ventilator - an outcome important to patients, families, and clinicians. Relevance: For patients, this study will clarify the best way to remove them from ventilators in a timely and safe manner. For clinicians and our health care systems, this study holds promise to improve patient outcomes and change how care is delivered in North American ICUs.

column36: Giving Voice to Mothers; Measuring access to high quality, respectful maternity care in Canada
column37: Person-centred care values the preferences and cultures of patients, supports informed decision-making, and is linked to improved outcomes and reduced healthcare costs. By contrast, lack of involvement in decision-making and mistreatment during the course of pregnancy and birth can lead to several adverse outcomes, including impacts on mental health and parenting success. In Canada very little is known about whether childbearing women are encouraged to lead decisions about their care, if they feel pressured or coerced into accepting interventions or tests, or if they feel their preferences for care are respected by care providers. Patients who experience mental illness, poverty, lifestyle, immigrant status, or other vulnerabilities during pregnancy may face barriers to access to their preferred modes of care. Our team includes consumers, researchers, clinician leaders and community partners. We will use a community-led process to design a study that focuses on the World Health Organization standards for high quality, respectful maternity care: "safe, effective, equitable and person-centred care". Using a patient-designed survey instrument we will examine experience and outcomes of maternity care across diverse communities in Canada. Our previous studies, Changing Childbirth in BC and Giving Voice to Mothers: US, used best practices for patient-oriented research. We will recruit a broad sample of people who had care during a pregnancy in the last 5 years, using community networks, social media, and Survey Cafes at locations where members from targeted communities access services, with peer assistance for data-entry. We will support communities to interpret results and tell the story to clinicians, hospitals, and government. Our study will raise awareness about options and rights in maternity care, improve health professional education, and lead to data-driven policies to improve health outcomes and to lower costs associated with the quality of maternity care.

column36: Adapting and scaling-up "Peer Navigators" to targeted populations of street-involved youth in Canada and Kenya to increase linkage to HIV prevention, testing, and treatment
column37: Today, the people most at risk of HIV are those who are vulnerable, marginalized, and living in difficult situations. One such group is homeless youth. We already know that homeless youth are driven to the streets by poverty, family dysfunction, and child abuse and neglect. The circumstances of their lives once on the street involve many challenges including poverty, substance abuse and addiction, mental health issues, and vulnerability to sexual violence and trafficking; all of which raise their risk of acquiring and dying from HIV since they are also hard to engage in HIV care and treatment. We also know that homeless youth in Canada's cities are more likely to come from marginalized communities, including lesbian, gay, bisexual, trans, queer, Two-Spirited and other Indigenous youth. Almost no research exists to guide HIV and other health service providers in successfully engaging with and caring for these extremely vulnerable populations. We are proposing a Peer Navigator (PN) program to engage homeless youth in Canada and western Kenya in HIV prevention, testing, and treatment. The PN model is based on the idea that peers-people who have themselves experienced youth homelessness and live with or are at-risk of HIV-intimately understand the challenges facing other homeless youth in a way that no researcher or healthcare worker can. As a result, peers are uniquely able to guide, connect, refer, and educate, and accompany homeless youth through the process of HIV prevention, testing and treatment.This project has three objectives:1) Adapt the Peer Navigator Model to three Canadian and two Kenyan sites: Toronto, London, Montreal, Kitale, and Huruma. 2) Describe and evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and ethics of the PN program among homeless youth, community, and stakeholders. 3) Evaluate the equitability (reach, uptake) and sustainability (cost, impact, uptake) of the PN program across the implementation sites.
