column36: Scaling up PrEP for HIV Prevention: Optimizing strategies for targeting and delivering PrEP to MSM in British Columbia and Ontario
column37: Gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (MSM) account for over half of new HIV infections in Canada each year. Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is an effective, safe and acceptable HIV prevention option among MSM, and holds great promise for reversing the course of the epidemic. However, for PrEP to achieve its full public health potential, two challenges must be overcome. First, PrEP must be targeted to those at highest HIV risk. Evidence suggests that having certain bacterial sexually transmitted infections or scoring highly on a validated risk index are particularly strong predictors of subsequent HIV. Since public health units routinely generate these data through daily activities, personnel could readily build such PrEP targeting strategies onto existing healthcare encounters. Second, more providers are needed within the healthcare system to deliver PrEP at scale. Engaging primary care providers, sexual health clinics nurses and PrEP-specific clinics in PrEP delivery may relieve the bottleneck of having too few specialists. Our experienced, multidisciplinary team in British Columbia and Ontario will implement and study the scale-up of these targeting and delivery strategies. Public health units and PrEP delivery sites in 5 cities will routinize a cascade of steps including identifying MSM with these criteria, offering PrEP services, linking patients to care, and ultimately initiating and retaining them on PrEP over time. Our research team will document how well the cascade is operationalized, tabulate healthcare costs, analyze qualitative and quantitative data on barriers and facilitators, and provide ongoing feedback to program implementers to inform how they modify programs. By synthesizing findings in mathematical models of HIV transmission we will determine the optimal strategies for targeting and delivering PrEP to MSM that maximize infections averted for the least additional cost, across a range of social, health systems and epidemic contexts.

column36: DRUM 2: First Nation and Metis Communities Working in Partnership to Develop Integrated Shared Care Models for HIV and other STBBI
column37: What is DRUM? With funding from CIHR, we are building upon ten years of work with the Aboriginal Community Resilience to HIV/AIDS (ACRA) project through continued partnership with three Northern Alberta First Nation communities. DRUM is culturally grounded, community-led and based on identified strengths. We are working together to develop, test and evaluate shared-care models (SCM) for HIV, Hep C and other STBBI prevention and care services on-reserve. Our team includes members from each community (including community research associates (CRAs)), Elders, people with lived experience, policy makers, clinicians/health care providers, FNIHB regional representation, and researchers from BC, Alberta, Saskatchewan and the Canadian Aboriginal AIDS Network. There is a strong two-way capacity-strengthening component built into the project. Through our work together on DRUM, we have learned there is promise in our approach. What is DRUM 2? DRUM 2 will build on the work of DRUM. Our team will continue our work with communities of different Indigenous cultures and in different regions of Alberta, supporting each other as we improve HIV, Hep C and other STBBI prevention and care services within a SCM development process for First Nation and Metis communities. With guidance from an Elders Council, we will study how programs are developed, adapted, implemented, and whether they meet their implementation goals. The CRAs from DRUM 1 will act as mentors/resources for the DRUM 2 new communities who participate in the DRUM process to develop and implement their own SCM. Importantly, DRUM 2 also provides the opportunity to learn by comparing different community approaches for shared care, including communities who use the DRUM process, and other communities in other regions of Canada who have developed their own shared care models. We will develop online resources for First Nation and Metis communities to share what we learn about developing and assessing STBBI SCMs.

column36: Addressing sexual- and drug-related HIV risk among young gay, bisexual and other MSM
column37: In BC and many other contexts, there are increasing concerns that HIV and other sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections (STBBIs) diagnoses (e.g., chlamydia, gonorrhea, syphilis) are accumulating among young gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM) at higher rates than previous generations. Epidemiological evidence links high-risk sexual behaviour with substance use, including the use of stimulants (e.g., crystal methamphetamine) and sedatives (e.g., GHB). While the need for innovative interventions to address sexual- and drug-related HIV risk among young gbMSM is high, the information available to inform more effective interventions in this area remains limited. Over the next five years, our team will develop new harmonized data systems, launch new training and mentoring opportunities, build multi-sectoral capacity and identify actionable strategies to inform the scale up of two key interventions in this area: (a) Mpowerment, a community-initiated intervention that aims to enhance the health and well-being of young gbMSM; and (b) Health Initiative for Men (HIM), a non-governmental organization that provides gbMSM-centered sexual health services at five community clinics across Metro Vancouver and the Fraser Valley. Our team reflects a novel multi-disciplinary mix of new and senior investigators, trainees, youth co-researchers and key knowledge users. Our team's level of interaction and integration will be high, and we have designed our research approach, governance structure and scale up activities to facilitate this approach to collaboration. The results of the conceptually linked research activities will build capacity in relation to intervening through a multi-faceted, 'systems-level' approach and, in so doing, will also be making innovative methodological, empirical and ethical contributions to the scholarship and application of HIV implementation science.

column36: Understanding contextual factors to effectively and equitably scale up GetCheckedOnline to diverse populations and geographic settings
column37: Digital health services are thought to be cost-effective and improve access particularly in rural areas, despite limited evidence and challenges to their implementation. We need to examine the "rhetoric and reality" of these services, and understand what external factors influence their success or failure. GetCheckedOnline (GCO) is an effective program developed by the BC Centre for Disease Control to reduce barriers in accessing testing for sexually transmitted infections and blood borne infections (STBBI). Research from the Vancouver pilot phase of GCO has found the service to be acceptable and effective in reaching people with barriers to accessing testing. Our initial analysis of GCO's scale-up to other urban, suburban and rural communities in two regional health authorities (RHA) in BC has found differences from Vancouver and between expansion sites (e.g., in the proportions of first-time testers). Further scale-up in BC is planned to other RHA, and eventually to other parts of Canada. However, further adaptation of GCO may be needed to reach other populations facing barriers to STBBI testing. Our team's overall goal is produce research which leads to the best implementation and maximum effectiveness of GCO for multiple populations affected by STBBI, and that informs further scale-up in BC and potentially in other parts of Canada. We do this in order to reduce barriers to accessing testing, leading to earlier diagnosis and linkage to care for STBBI in Canada. Our research approach uses an implementation science framework to: (1) understand what works, for whom, during scale-up; (2) adapt the intervention for better impact in minority language communities, men sex workers, and people who inject drugs; (3) assess the feasibility of implementation in a different health care system (Toronto); and (4) describe external factors influencing GCO implementation and whether access is improved equitably across populations who use it.

column37: Canada is experiencing a public health emergency related to medical (prescription) opioids and, in some regions, illicitly produced opioids (e.g., fentanyl, heroin). Services are being expanded in many jurisdictions, but progress is slow and only patchworks of public health interventions and treatment services are currently in place across the country. Without scaling up evidence-based programs in different regions and among different populations, the individual and population burden of opioid use will continue to be high. This proposal was written in response to CIHR's Request for Applications to the Canadian Research Initiative on Substance Misuse (CRISM) network for a directed grant addressing the opioid emergency (https://tinyurl.com/y9sgx64x). CRISM is a unique CIHR funded national research network of researchers, system managers, people with lived experience, and decision-makers. Its purpose is to conduct research and support knowledge translation to enhance delivery of evidence-based interventions for substance misuse.CRISM will develop and execute a program in four thematic areas that have high potential for reducing the individual and population burden of opioid use: (1) scaling up public health interventions (i.e., safer consumption services and naloxone delivery); (2) optimizing opioid use disorder treatments (i.e., oral and injectable opioid pharmacotherapy); (3) improving the evidence base for withdrawal management, psychosocial and recovery-based treatment options; and (4) collaboratively developing new intervention approaches to meet the needs of high-risk target populations. The proposed implementation science program will be developed purposively, capitalizing on service innovations that are rapidly being deployed at the regional level; strategically, by developing effective longer-term working relationships with groups disproportionately affected by the opioid emergency; and collaboratively, through a structured process to engage CRISM member expertise and people with lived experience of opioid problems. The overall aim is to inform and support the implementation of an improved national intervention continuum to address this complex health challenge.

column36: CRISM Implementation Science Program on Opioid Interventions and Services - Prairies
column37: Canada is experiencing a public health emergency related to medical (prescription) opioids and, in some regions, illicitly produced opioids (e.g., fentanyl, heroin). Services are being expanded in many jurisdictions, but progress is slow and only patchworks of public health interventions and treatment services are currently in place across the country. Without scaling up evidence-based programs in different regions and among different populations, the individual and population burden of opioid use will continue to be high. This proposal was written in response to CIHR's Request for Applications to the Canadian Research Initiative on Substance Misuse (CRISM) network for a directed grant addressing the opioid emergency (https://tinyurl.com/y9sgx64x). CRISM is a unique CIHR funded national research network of researchers, system managers, people with lived experience, and decision-makers. Its purpose is to conduct research and support knowledge translation to enhance delivery of evidence-based interventions for substance misuse. CRISM will develop and execute a program in four thematic areas that have high potential for reducing the individual and population burden of opioid use: (1) scaling up public health interventions (i.e., safer consumption services and naloxone delivery); (2) optimizing opioid use disorder treatments (i.e., oral and injectable opioid pharmacotherapy); (3) improving the evidence base for withdrawal management, psychosocial and recovery-based treatment options; and (4) collaboratively developing new intervention approaches to meet the needs of high-risk target populations. The proposed implementation science program will be developed purposively, capitalizing on service innovations that are rapidly being deployed at the regional level; strategically, by developing effective longer-term working relationships with groups disproportionately affected by the opioid emergency; and collaboratively, through a structured process to engage CRISM member expertise and people with lived experience of opioid problems. The overall aim is to inform and support the implementation of an improved national intervention continuum to address this complex health challenge.

column37: The brain is often conceived of as modules that process particular bits of information. Like all computers, brain modules also have to communicate with each other. column37: An essential component of every living organism is DNA, which provides the blueprint for life. Paradoxically, DNA is highly susceptible to damage. A major goal of my research is to understand how cells become cancerous. By focusing on nucleases, which are scissors that eliminate damaged DNA, we will elucidate how healthy cells maintain genome stability. This information will help us to understand what goes wrong in cancer cells and facilitate the development of highly effective treatments.

column36: YOUTH WELLBEING IN CHINA AND CENTRAL AMERICA:IMPLEMENTATION OF AN INTEGRATED PREVENTION AND INTERVENTION PROGRAM
column37: High rates of mental illness and addiction (often associated with self-harm) have been reported in China and Central America. Stigma, poor mental health knowledge, and limited awareness and/or accessibility to health services lead to low help-seeking, further compounding the problem. Thus, there is an urgent need for strategies to promote mental health knowledge to enable early identification and treatment and to improve help-seeking behaviour. The aim of this 5-year project is to implement and evaluate a multi-level, integrated mental health education, screening, and intervention program to improve functioning and well-being in youth in China, Honduras and El Salvador. About 5000 students in China, 2000 students in Honduras and 2000 students in El Salvador will be recruited. Participants will receive a 12-week mental wellness and leadership program (MWL) online (at universities) or in class (at vocational/technical schools). Curriculum topics will include mental health education (illness and stigma, help-seeking, stress management), social responsibility (prejudice, violence, gender-based violence), and leadership (values, skills). Students will be assessed on psychosocial function (e.g.distress, coping, stress, academic performance) and physiological measures of stress (saliva and hair cortisol) before and after MWL completion. An open-access phone app will be created to screen for emotional difficulties and addictive behaviours and will be available to MWL and non-MWL students. Those students who screen positive for significant emotional difficulties, as well as those with depression, anxiety and/or addictive behaviours who are referred by health professionals, will receive one of two forms of an 8-week internetbased cognitive-behavioural therapy (iCBT) program. The iCBT emotional well-being program will target mood and anxiety symptoms, and the iCBT addictions program will target substance abuse (including alcohol and tobacco) and problematic internet use. Students will be assessed on symptom and functional improvement as well as on physiological measures of stress before and after program completion. This project offers the opportunity to implement and evaluate the broad benefits of a novel integrated prevention and psychological intervention program for youth in culturally differing regions. The program will be adapted and incorporated into existing postsecondary institutions in the three countries with measurement of cross-cultural acceptability, efficacy, fidelity of implementation, and sustainability. It is proposed that the project will improve the mental wellness of transitional youth with good sustainability in two distinct global regions, and furthermore, it offers an opportunity to objectively evaluate to cost and benefit of this implementation.

column36: Implementation research: community intervention to prevent repeated suicide attempts in Ningxia China and Nunavut Canada
column37: BACKGROUND: Suicide is the most serious outcome of a variety of mental illnesses, including depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, eating disorders and substance abuse. Reducing suicide mortality is an important objective of the World Health Organization's 2013-2020 Global Mental Health Action Plan and the United Nation's 2015-2030 Sustainable Development Goals. A prior suicide attempt is the most important risk factor for death by suicide, but regular brief community follow-up after an attempt can prevent repeated suicidal behavior. AIMS: This 5-year implementation science project will develop methods for adapting the WH0 SUPRE-MISS intervention for suicide attempters in parallel projects in Ningxia, China, and among Inuit in Nunavut, Canada. These methods for adapting SUPRE-MISS will then be promulgated in Inuit and other indigenous populations, other parts of China, other low- and middle-income countries, and other low-resourced settings in high-income countries. METHODS: PHASE 1. Conduct focus groups with local stakeholders to identify local factors that need to be considered when developing a location-specific version of SUPRE-MISS that provides a brief educational intervention about suicide prevention to individuals who have recently made a suicide attempt and periodic social support and access to emergency services to these highrisk individuals. PHASE 2. Pilot-test the adapted intervention in a small number of settings for one year. PHASE 3. Revise and then scale-up the intervention to more settings for 30 months and continuously collect outcome measures, process measures, and resource utilization measures (for cost-effectiveness assessment). PHASE 4. Conduct post-intervention focus groups with stakeholders to identify the strengths and weaknesses of the intervention. Integrate these qualitative results with the quantitative results (e.g., rates of repeated suicidal behavior) to prepare a report on the process of implementing the SUPRE-MISS intervention in low-resource settings. Work with administrators and policy makers in China, Nunavut, and other locations to develop policies that will widely promulgate the use of this approach to suicide prevention. FEASIBILITY: A strong multidisciplinary team with extensive experience in suicide prevention in the target communities has been assembled and the active support of local administrators and policy makers who can provide practical support for the project and develop policies to promote its results has been obtained. EXPECTED OUTCOMES: This project will develop methods that can be widely disseminated to help achieve the United Nation's ambitious goal of reducing suicide mortality by 1/3 by 2030. Combining findings from parallel projects in a low-middle-income country with those from a low-resource setting in a high-income country will provide a unique case example of how implementation science can be used to address complex mental health problems in different low-resource settings.

column36: Enhanced Measurement-Based Care Effectiveness for Depression (EMBED): A Canada-China Implementation Project
column37: Depression affects 300+ million people globally and is now the leading cause of disability and burden of disease worldwide. In China, the National Mental Health Work Plan 2015-20 specifies improving the ability of healthcare facilities to identify depression and increase the treatment rate by 50%. Measurement-based care (MBC) - the routine use of validated outcomes such as the PHQ-9 depression questionnaire to guide clinical decision-making - is a simple evidence-based practice (EBP) that may help meet these objectives. However, there is still a significant care gap in the implementation of MBC in China and elsewhere. In Canada, we have adopted the concept of enhanced MBC (eMBC), in which technology can engage both patients & physicians in using MBC; eMBC enhancements include web and mobile app tools for patients to track their own progress with the PHQ-9, and an evidence-based, lowcost, low-intensity psychological treatment (guided self-management with telephone coaches) that has embedded patient measurement and feedback to physicians. EMBED: a Canada-China implementation project, proposes to develop a novel EBP implementation strategy by adapting, implementing and evaluating eMBC in diverse community mental health clinics in Shanghai, modeled on programs implemented in Canada. EMBED addresses 4 broad aims: 1) identify contextual enablers & barriers to MBC implementation; 2) explore physicianand patient-level factors as mediators for an EBP implementation; 3) provide clinical & health economic outcomes to establish effectiveness of eMBC; and 4) build knowledge & capacity for scale up of eMBC in China and beyond. Our hypothesis is that physician & patient factors that are barriers for implementation of standard MBC will be enablers for implementation of eMBC. To achieve these aims, we will first conduct a Situation Analysis to determine the key barriers & enablers for MBC implementation in Shanghai. We will adapt a Canadian eMBC program for the Chinese context, then will use a hybrid implementation-effectiveness design (an adaptive cluster randomized evaluation) to compare eMBC with standard MBC implementation in 12 community clinics, 240 physicians, and 1200 patients. We hypothesize that eMBC implementation will lead to superior implementation, patient and costeffectiveness outcomes, compared to standard MBC. EMBED will advance the international literature on MBC broadly by focusing on the understudied role of patients in implementation of MBC. EMBED will also further implementation science by creating new knowledge on contextual factors, including mediating effects of physician- and patient-level factors, together, on EBP implementation outcomes. Moreover, the unique partnership of the EMBED team with the APEC Digital Hub for Mental Health will ensure a pathway for integrated knowledge & policy translation so that findings will have significant scale-up and spread potential in other regions in China, the Asia-Pacific and worldwide.

column36: Linking Hearts: Advancing Mental Health Care of University Students Through Interdisciplinary Collaboration (in Jinan)
column37: Young people are vulnerable to the onset of mental illness. Research shows that delayed treatment of mental illness leads to negative outcomes. In China, prevalence of depression among university students is as high as 20 to 30%. However, 9 out of 10 people diagnosed with a mental disorder never sought mental health care. Stigma and low mental health literacy are among the most important help-seeking barriers. Further, mental health services, largely at specialized hospitals only, are overstretched, while community and informal levels of care are underdeveloped. To address this, the study will examine the implementation of an evidence-based intervention, Acceptance and Commitment to Empowerment - Linking Youth and 'Xin' (hearts) (ACE-LYNX), to: (1) decrease stigma (attitude), (2) increase mental health literacy (knowledge), and (3) promote individual well-being (outcomes) and the collective capacity to collaborate (action) to promote mental health and form an integrative network of care for students. ACE-LYNX consists of two components: Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), a mindfulness-based cognitive-behavioral intervention, and Group Empowerment Psychoeducation (GEP), psychoeducation integrated with principles of equity, empowerment, and social justice. The study will take place in three regions of Jinan, Shandong, China. We will engage one hospital and two universities in each region. We will begin with an assessment of contexts, consisting of a university student survey (n= 600), student focus groups (n=144), and stakeholder and professional focus groups (n=144). The data will inform intervention adaptation. Using a train-the-trainer model, we will train 90 interdisciplinary professionals to become ACE-LYNX-Pro Champions. They will in turn train the "2nd generation" ACELYNX- Pro Champions (n=270) and students to become ACE-LYNX Student Champions(n=360) with a lay version of the intervention. All champions will form a collaborative integrated mental health care network supported by a community of practice through a Learning Management System and Weixin (WeChat). The champions will be followed over 6 months for their outreach and health promotional activities, including using Weixin to form a Student Mental Health Virtual Network. The RE-AIM framework will be used to examine Reach, Effectiveness, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance/Sustainability of ACE-LYNX and the integrated network. Psychometric measures will track the intervention's impact on attitude (CAMI), knowledge (MAKS), empowerment (Bulls-Eye, monthly activity logs), and mental health outcomes (DASS-21, AAQ-II), while service volumes and Social Network Analysis will be used to examine the functioning of the real and virtual networks. We will apply an Integrated Knowledge Translation framework to engage key stakeholders throughout the study to ensure maximal impact and dissemination with the aim of system transformation at the micro, meso, and macro levels.

column36: Shared Care for ADHD in Children and Youth: Merging the Canadian and Chinese Experiences
column37: In the context of modern China, children experience a tremendous pressure to perform at high levels. This stressful environment is associated with depressive symptoms, suicidal ideation and attempts in adolescence. Children with a diagnosis of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) are highly inattentive, restless, impulsive, and therefore at high risk, despite a normal intellectual potential. ADHD is easy to diagnose and treat, but difficult to diagnose and treat well. The treatment effects are dependent on the quality of care and on the coordination of different interventions, planned according to individual needs. The first main barrier to treatment is the shortage of qualified clinicians. In response, our main strategy will be to implement a shared care between general practitioners (GPs) and specialists. The second barrier is the lack of training in GPs. We will implement a focused ADHD training targeted to the needs of GPs. A third barrier is the lack referral process. We will implement stepped care in which the patient is treated at the most appropriate level of care, depending on complexity or outcome. We will adapt the Canadian shared care model for ADHD to the Chinese context. To test its flexibility, it will be implemented within the pediatric care system in two districts of Shanghai and within the mental health care system in one district of Beijing. We will first assess how ADHD guidelines are used, and the existing collaboration between GPs and specialists. After a Consensus Conference, we will implement a shared care pathway and we will produce actionable findings in a formative evaluation to improve implementation. At the end of the setup phase, we will assess the use of guidelines, the deviation from the intended protocol, how its members evaluate the care process, examine the effectiveness with regard to ADHD outcome, and functioning of the pathway, in terms of patient flow and timing. Once the shared care model is functionally implemented, we will scale up the care system horizontally by linking it progressively with schools selected randomly in the target districts. Using already established collaborations with the educational psychologists, we will first survey the knowledge and perceived needs of teacher, then implement a screening strategy for ADHD problems in the schools, as well as web-based effective strategies to educate parents and teachers about ADHD and mitigate its impact. We will assess the effectiveness of the intervention, and how it changes the perception of ADHD and the help-seeking process, as well as the rate of referrals into the shared care system. These two steps will allow defining the scalable unit that could be used in further implementation of the model. A costeffectiveness analysis is integrated in the project in order to support its scalability. Beyond ADHD, this shared care model will be able to respond to various mental health treatment challenges, both in children and adults.

column36: Screening and management of perinatal depression within primary care
column37: Depression during pregnancy and after an infant's birth is more common in China than in high-income countries and can harm the mother, infant, and family. Chinese women's mental health needs are unmet given lack of investment in mental health, unequal distribution of mental health services, and few specialized healthcare providers to support mental health issues. Our goal is to create an effective perinatal depression screening and management (PDSM) program that will be sustainable within the maternal and child healthcare system in China. Our implementation strategy is guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research and RE-AIM (Reach x Efficacy, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance) and includes 2 Phases: (1) Pilot in Ma'anshan City, Anhui Province during which we will, through stakeholder engagement, adapt current evidence and test the feasibility and acceptability of the adapted screening guidelines and psychosocial intervention (internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy; iCBT) by healthcare providers and women. We will use mixed-methods to (a) identify and evaluate various implementation strategies (e.g., individual, organizational) to promote uptake of the screening guidelines and iCBT; (b) evaluate acceptability (i.e., knowledge, attitudes, and behavior) before and after implementation of guidelines and iCBT; (c) evaluate reach by determining the degree to which the population that is eligible to benefit from the program actually received it; (d) evaluate treatment fidelity by determining the extent to which the screening guidelines and iCBT was implemented as designed by monitoring adherence, dosage of delivery (i.e., the number of weeks completed), and program quality. (2) Scale-up to Hefei (capital and largest city), Bengbu (mid-sized urban city), and Fuyang (urban city) adapting the screening guidelines and iCBT based on Phase 1, and using steps (a)-(d) to promote uptake. Our monitoring and evaluation plan includes evaluating impact, effectiveness, and quality (i.e., public health impact) in both the Pilot and Scale-up phases. Our project is jointly supported by Chinese and Canadian researcher, focuses on implementation research related to depression, an affective disorder that will become the second leading cause of disease by 2010. It also, addresses women's mental health during pregnancy and following birth when vulnerability to depression is intensified, and promotes uptake screening which promotes use of mental health service and iCBT a psychosocial self-administered intervention with support from a trained mental health care provider that promotes reduction in depressive symptoms. Our study will enable integration of PDSM into the maternal and child healthcare system with flexible guidelines that considers context, ensures mental healthcare is personalized and responsive to Chinese women's needs, and promotes implementation outcomes of acceptability, reach, and fidelity.

column36: Standardizing the treatment, prevention, and management of depression in China: a multi-disciplinary approach
column37: Depression is a common mental disorder affecting approximately 350 million people worldwide and representing the third leading contributor to the global disease burden (World Health Organization [WHO], 2012). However, much of the literature on the depression derives from studies conducted in Western Europe and North America. Consequently, there is a need for novel depression research in low- and middle-income countries, including China. In China, depression is highly prevalent but is not treated in existing community mental health programs, limiting many residents' access to mental health care and contributing to the large treatment gap. Currently, mental health care for depression exists at urban mental health centres; additionally, there is a lack of integration between primary and mental health care and the absence of mental health training for primary care physicians. Collectively, these factors hinder access to mental health care in rural and urban areas, and across communities of various socioeconomic backgrounds, languages and dialects. Thus, the development of community mental health prevention and treatment programs for depression would increase access to mental health care for residents of China in both rural and urban areas. Additional barriers that contribute to the treatment gap include culturally ingrained negativistic attitudes towards mental disorders that contribute to social- and self-stigma, and lack of education about mental disorders and their treatment. Consequently, our research endeavors, involving coordination between Canada and China, are as follows: (1) to help develop community-based mental health services for the early identification of individuals with depressive symptoms and prevention of clinical depression, (2) to improve access to mental health care and the management of patients with depression in community- and hospital-based settings, and (3) to establish international psychosocial networks or systems to monitor the quality of care. In addition, we aim to implement prevention and intervention strategies that address the aforementioned barriers to improve the quality of depression management and increase willingness to seek mental health care. Studies have reported that screening individuals with depressive symptoms and the subsequent provision of psychological therapy to prevent the onset of clinical depression is a cost-effective intervention, compared to treatment after depression onset. If depression prevention strategies become a standard part of mental health services, unnecessary suffering due to depression will be greatly reduced.

column36: Developing resilience to obesogenic food environments through food literacy
column37: More Canadians now die from diseases caused by poor diet than from smoking-related illnesses, and diets low in fruit and vegetable intake cost Canadians 3.3 billion dollars a year. The food environment profoundly influences diet and is associated with diseases such as obesity and diabetes. This environment has evolved so that children and adolescents are constantly fed cues to consume unhealthy foods. Nutrition "knowledge" may come from social media or advertisements and slick marketing may shape food preferences. All of these factors affect current and future dietary practices. Food literacy is the foundation of healthy dietary practices and provides youth with an opportunity to build resilience to unhealthy food environments. Yet, we know very little about how food literacy is acquired and the level of literacy needed to make healthy dietary decisions. The proposed research will address these knowledge gaps. The purpose of this study is to examine the connections between food literacy, food environments and health indicators among youth. To address the knowledge gaps, we will conduct 1) an environmental scan of food literacy learning opportunities for children and adolescents (consisting of a scoping review, interviews with practitioners followed by a survey) and 2) a cross-sectional survey on food literacy, food environments and health indicators among youth. Results will be translated to practitioners and policy makers through guidelines for enhancing food literacy to promote optimal health. Food literacy will equip youth with the abilities, knowledge and self-efficacy to make healthy food choices, which will reduce risk for diseases and decrease healthcare costs. This research will strengthen Health Canada's healthy eating strategy to improve healthy eating and protect vulnerable populations by understanding how to improve food literacy and make healthy dietary choices in unhealthy food environments.

column36: Repenser l'ergotherapie au soutien a domicile pour favoriser la participation sociale des aines (REPAIRS): vers le deploiement et l'implantation d'un continuum d'interventions innovantes
column37: Les personnes qui ont une vie sociale active sont en meilleure sante et vivent plus longtemps. Or, en vieillissant, une personne sur deux est a risque de vivre de l'isolement social et de la solitude. Heureusement, il est possible d'agir efficacement pour reduire l'isolement social des aines et les aider a s'integrer plus facilement dans la communaute. En effet, les cliniciens, dont les ergotherapeutes, peuvent offrir un eventail d'interventions demontrees economiquement rentables pour ameliorer la vie sociale des aines. Par exemple, les ergotherapeutes peuvent batir des liens avec des ressources de loisirs de la communaute ou offrir aux aines des interventions en groupe, en plus de suivis personnalises pour les aider a avoir une vie sociale pleine de sens pour eux. Cependant, ces interventions sont actuellement peu offertes dans les services d'ergotherapie a domicile aupres des aines, notamment en raison d'un manque de soutien pour les implanter. Ce projet de recherche permettra a des chercheurs, des decideurs, des membres de la communaute et des ergotherapeutes de documenter l'implantation d'interventions qui favorisent la participation sociale des aines. Les chercheurs inviteront d'abord un groupe d'ergotherapeutes a choisir, parmi un eventail de possibilites, les interventions qu'ils desirent implanter. Les chercheurs consulteront egalement les ecrits scientifiques afin d'identifier les strategies a privilegier pour faciliter l'implantation de ces interventions. Grace a ces connaissances, les ergotherapeutes integreront ensuite les interventions a leur pratique reelle. Les participants decriront finalement les conditions qui expliquent l'implantation reussie ou non des interventions choisies et les defis associes. Ces recommandations seront utiles pour guider les cliniciens, les decideurs et les membres de la communaute dans l'implantation de services a domicile qui ameliorent durablement la sante et le bien-etre de la population vieillissante canadienne.

column36: Dene First Nations Youth-Led Health Messaging Program in a Community Context
column37: In Canada, First Nations are fighting devastating health issues using Indigenous healing knowledge. Health problems are most concerning for First Nations youth, who face the remnants of colonialism, cultural genocide, intergenerational trauma from residential schools, and poverty. Although many national groups have called for Indigenous youth as leaders in decision making, little action has been taken to explore Indigenous youth leadership initiatives in Canada. Researchers in the field of health risk communication, which is broadly concerned with how people communicate about the risks associated with health issues such as obesity and disease, have recently conducted some successful projects with Indigenous youth. Youth have contributed to better understandings of health problems and solutions, enhanced their strengths and health, and created positive rippling effects in their communities. A promising health intervention appears to be participatory risk communication, an approach that lets First Nations youth take the lead to create and present messages about health. At the same time, they learn Indigenous traditional knowledge skills and how to be co-researchers. This approach aims to improve youth's health, health communications, and community health outcomes, but requires further validation across various First Nations, Inuit, and Metis communities. I will conduct one case study with the Yellowknives Dene First Nations (YKDFN) in Ndilo and Dettah, NT. I will use an Indigenous community-based participatory research approach to highlight community strengths and Indigenous knowledge while identifying my connections to the community as a YKDFN member. During multiple participatory stages of health message development, based on Indigenous traditional knowledge and culture, YKDFN youth will exercise leadership, develop on-the-land skills that promote health, strategize to reduce health risk behaviors, and co-research outcomes of the intervention.

column36: Trends in the use of oral anticoagulation therapies and outcomes in patients with atrial fibrillation
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common and important cardiac arrhythmia in the world, characterized by an irregular heartbeat from quivering of the upper chambers of the heart (atria). AF is emerging as the next epidemic in cardiovascular medicine. It is estimated that 5 million patients are being diagnosed with AF each year worldwide and its prevalence is expected to double in the next 20 years. AF independently increases the risk of stroke, death, cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular events. One-fifth of all strokes are attributable to AF with significant morbidity and mortality. Substantial advances have been made in stroke prophylaxis for AF patients in the last few years including the development of new oral anticoagulants (NOAC). However, it is unclear whether these new therapies have been widely adopted in clinical practice and if this has translated into an improvement in patient outcomes. In Canada and around the world, there is great interest in improving the performance of the healthcare system. Our study will explore if there are gaps in current practice and if patients are receiving optimal care. Analysis of this real-world data will create targets for future Quality Improvements efforts in our healthcare system, which will ultimately ensure that patients are receiving the best possible care. The study results will have important implications for patients with heart disease, hospitals and policy-makers.

column36: Dynamic phenotyping of pathologic mood instability across affective disorders
column37: Mood instability, defined as an emotional dysregulation, mood swings, or emotional impulsiveness, is a common feature of mood and anxiety disorders. Mood instability is associated with elevated risk of suicide and reduced treatment responsiveness in individuals with a psychiatric diagnosis. Considering its dynamic nature, traditional surveys that assess mood variability once a week or once a month may not be the best way to capture the complex picture of mood instability. Fortunately, with recent technological advances and mobile applications, it is now easy to collect, at random occasions in the day, all sorts of information from research participants such as symptoms or mood states in their everyday life. It is likely that mood instability reflects a dysfunction in the neural circuits of the brain, however, little is known regarding its associated brain mechanisms. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain allows us to capture both static information, such as the structure of brain regions, and dynamic information, such as the connectivity between regions. In this research project, I propose to investigate whether abnormalities in the structure and connectivity of brain networks are related to mood fluctuations within the day, in order to disentangle the trait (static) and state (dynamic) signatures of mood instability.

column37: La deficience intellectuelle (DI) est un handicap mental caracterise par des limitations importantes du fonctionnement intellectuel et du comportement adaptatif qui se manifestent avant l'age de 18 ans. Les groupes de defense des droits des personnes presentant une DI militent depuis plusieurs annees pour l'inclusion sociale de cette population longtemps tenue a l'ecart. Au Quebec, des changements importants survenus dans l'offre de services specialises ont permis a la majorite de ces personnes d'acceder a des milieux residentiels plus << normalisants >>, au sein de la communaute, plutot que d'etre hebergees en milieu institutionnel. Si l'acces a des ressources residentielles hors institution a represente un progres indeniable vers l'inclusion des personnes presentant une DI dans la societe, cette population demeure peu presente dans l'espace public. En effet, les personnes presentant une DI peinent a acceder a des roles sociaux valorises (locataire, travailleur, parent, etc.), ce qui se traduit par leur exclusion des principaux lieux de socialisation. De plus, tres peu de connaissances sont disponibles sur leurs perceptions et usages des espaces publics. Cette etude vise a mieux comprendre l'experience que font des personnes presentant une DI de leur environnement residentiel. Pour ce faire, des parcours commentes seront realises avec les personnes elles-memes. Ces trajets a pied dans le quartier de residence des participants permettront de connaitre leur point de vue sur leur milieu de vie. En devoilant la realite de cette population la plupart du temps invisible, cette etude vise a contribuer a l'amelioration des conditions de vie offertes a ces personnes. column36: The rise of transnational city networks and the formation of global urban authority: Strong Cities and the C40 Climate Group
column37: My research investigates recent political efforts by cities to confront global challenges. It examines the rise of "city-networks" as a response to a range of transnational issues from natural disasters and health pandemics to nuclear proliferation and terrorism. Specifically, it examines the efforts of two city-networks, the C40 City Climate Leadership Group and the Strong Cities Network, which address climate change and violent extremism respectively. It examines why and how these city-networks emerged and the strategies they employ when attempting to influence global politics. It further asks about the conditions under which these networks are successful in achieving their policy objectives. In addition to improving our understanding of how cities are meeting the challenges of climate change and violent extremism, this examination provides insight into the changing nature of the global political order. Are cities in these networks becoming more influential, in the sense that they are writing new rules and commanding legitimacy in these issue areas? And if cities are making rules and influencing global politics beyond the state, what does this mean for our traditional system of international authority? By analyzing how contemporary global politics is functioning, we can better understand which political strategies are effective and which are not, and with that knowledge, learn more about how to overcome political gridlock on pressing global issues.

column36: Etude des modulations de l'expression des genes et de l'epissage des ARNm cellulaires dans le cadre d'une infection par differents Flavivirus: le virus du Nil occidental, le virus de la fievre jaune et le virus Zika
column37: Les Flavivirus, tel que le virus Zika, le virus du Nil occidental, et le virus de la fievre jaune, sont des virus transmis par les moustiques auxquels plusieurs milliards de personnes sont exposees au niveau mondial. Ces virus sont etroitement apparentes, mais ils causent des maladies distinctes. De facon generale, tous les Flavivirus peuvent infecter le systeme nerveux et causer des inflammations du cerveau. Par contre, seulement certains Flavivirus, dont le virus de la fievre jaune, peuvent causer des fievres hemorragiques. De plus, le virus Zika est le seul Flavivirus associe au developpement de microcephalie, soit une croissance anormalement faible du cerveau chez le foetus, lorsque la mere est infectee durant la grossesse. Il est connu que les virus deregulent un grand nombre de processus cellulaires de l'hote dans le but de favoriser l'infection. Par contre, les mecanismes par lesquels les virus causent ces changements restent a etre elucides. Dans cette etude, nous investiguons l'infection de cellules avec trois differents Flavivirus, soit le virus du Nil occidental, le virus de la fievre jaune, et le virus Zika, dans le but de comprendre comment ces virus interagissent avec l'hote. En effectuant les infections dans les memes conditions, il est egalement possible de comparer les differents virus et leurs effets sur les cellules, en plus de determiner des deregulations communes aux trois virus ainsi que des deregulations uniques a chaque virus. Ces resultats permettront de mieux comprendre comment ces virus affectent l'hote et pourquoi ils causent des maladies differentes.

column36: Enhancing and Expanding the "Know Your Status" Initiative in on-reserve Indigenous Communities in Saskatchewan: A Community-engaged Intervention to Increase Diagnosis, Linkage to Care and Prevention of HIV, HCV and STBBIs
column37: First Nations people living on-reserve in Saskatchewan have the highest rates of HIV infection in Canada, with an incidence approximately 7.3-times higher than the national average. They also have the least access to care and to life saving antiretroviral therapy. To address this need, a comprehensive on-reserve HIV testing and treatment initiative called "Know Your Status" (KYS) was launched in 2011. KYS is a community-designed and community-managed program based on partnerships and collaborations between First Nations communities and care providers. Key components of KYS include: community involvement and leadership, education, prevention, specialized nursing support, support for mental health and addictions, lab testing and accessible and culturally-safe clinical management that meets clients where they are located. Culturally supportive services, such as mentorship from Elders and traditional teachings, are also integrated within the program. Thus far, KYS has been primarily implemented to care for HIV and sexually transmitted infections on a few on-reserve communities. However, there is a need to expand the program to include hepatitis C testing, linkage and treatment, as a result of similarly high on-reserve rates. The research team, in close partnership with First Nation communities, intends to refine, adapt, and expand the KYS intervention to communities with the greatest need. Traditional experimental designs to evaluate the KYS initiative cannot be used for various reasons. Instead, the team will use practical, though rigorous, methods to evaluate the effectiveness, acceptability and sustainability of the expanded KYS program, while ensuring that community needs are met. First Nations leaders and communities, policy makers and other physicians will be engaged throughout the project to build community and provincial capacity to treat on-reserve HIV and hepatitis C, and to ensure program sustainability for years to come.

column36: Regulation of gonadotropin action by Slit/Robo signaling in the mammalian ovary
column37: Oocytes develop and mature in the ovary within structures called follicles. Follicles are recruited from a reserve and grow under the influence of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) produced by the pituitary gland. Once terminally developed, the follicle ruptures to release the (now mature) oocyte at the moment of ovulation. Ovulation itself is triggered by a second pituitary hormone, luteinizing hormone (LH), which also causes the reorganization of the ovulated follicle into a new glandular tissue termed the corpus luteum, which secretes the large amounts of progesterone necessary for the establishment and maintenance of pregnancy. Whereas we have long known FSH and LH to be major players in ovarian follicle development, how exactly they exert their effects remains incompletely understood. Ourselves and others have shown that a class of secreted signaling molecules called SLITs, along with their receptors called ROBOs, are expressed in the ovary in a pattern suggesting their involvement in follicle development. Our preliminary data indicate that, when follicle cells are treated in vitro with SLIT ligand, gonadotropin signaling and action is suppressed. This proposal will seek to confirm these preliminary results, in part by studying mice that lack Slit1, Slit2, Robo1 and Robo2, which we expect to be hyperfertile due to augmented FSH- and LH-mediated signaling processes. We will also study the molecular mechanisms whereby Slit/Robo and gonadotropin signaling interact. Together, our studies will uncover new information regarding how FSH and LH act, and about the biological roles of Slit/Robo signaling in the ovary. Importantly, this research may also identify new and valuable pharmacologic targets that could be exploited in the clinical context, in fields of application as wide-ranging as the treatment of fertility disorders, contraception, and recovery of fertility following chemotherapy.

On a per capita basis, this translates to a Canadian equivalent of almost $18-billion annually. Although we hear with our brains little is known about what occurs to the brain as a consequence of deafness. In this proposal we will be studying what happens inside the brain following the onset of deafness shortly after birth or in adulthood. Specifically, we will be studying the regions of the brain that normally process sounds in hearing individuals. To do this we will examine deafness in an animal model. This approach will permit us to examine the activity of individual neurons, to examine changes in brain circuitry and activity, and to examine how changes in the brain affect perception and behavior. If the part of the brain that normally processes hearing is not receiving sound, then what is it doing? Is it processing visual information? Is it processing information concerning touch? If it is processing sight, then it may very well help explain the increased visual abilities of deaf humans. Changes in the brain such as this are known as "plastic" changes, or simply "plasticity". These changes are also called "compensatory" because they help the subject enhance their ability to use their remaining senses. Therefore, the goal of this study is to examine the natural plasticity of the brain. Knowing how the brain responds to changes in its inputs in this way will help us develop appropriate therapeutic strategies to help increase brain plasticity and help patients to overcome conditions such as deafness and blindness.

column36: Correlates of Healthy Aging in Geriatric HIV: CHANGE HIV STUDY
column37: The population of persons living with HIV (PLWH) is aging due to effective HIV therapy and new infections occurring in older individuals. Much needs to be learned about what it means to age with HIV. Although organ diseases (like heart and brain) are increased in PLWH, aging is more complex and health evaluations must consider the impact of these conditions on a person's ability to function well. We propose to bring together this new interdisciplinary team and the CHANGE HIV (Correlates of Healthy aging in Geriatric HIV) STUDY. We will invite men and women living with HIV >65 years of age from primary care and hospital HIV clinics in Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver to join. At regular clinic visits we will add tests of physical, cognitive, mental, social function and quality of life and collect data on external factors like housing, behaviors and stigma that might influence health. We will analyze the way the factors interact to identify the ones that contribute most to healthy aging well if these differ by sex or gender. From the data, we will calculate a healthy aging score that can inform care and research by assessing a person's overall health status and track changes with time or therapy. The knowledge gained will inform interventions and strategies to improve healthy aging and help us know which ones are the most important, feasible and acceptable to those aging with HIV. Our data can be used to advocate for changes to health and social policies and appropriate allocation of resources for services for aging PLWH. A program strength is to train and stimulate new academic and community investigators building future research capacity in HIV and aging. Community members will be meaningfully involved in all stages ensures our research is feasible, ethical and relevant and supports the development of knowledge that is useful to key. Our learning's will advance understanding of aging in PLWH and ultimately lead to improved clinical and community practice and policy.

column36: Healthy Living for HIV-exposed Uninfected Children - cognitive, behavioural, neuroimaging and animal studies to assess the impact of in utero exposure to HIV and antiretrovirals.
column37: The use of HIV medications in pregnancy has enabled a radical reduction in the rate of vertical HIV transmission. As a consequence, there is now a large and growing number of HIV-exposed uninfected children (HEU)-children born to women living with HIV that are not HIV infected. While most HEU children are in good health, some studies suggest that these children may experience developmental delays compared to their peers, including learning difficulties, issues with their memory, and behavioural problems. We know that the environment the child is exposed to during pregnancy (the in utero environment) can influence their long-term health. However, we don't know how HIV and HIV medications change the in utero environment and whether these changes affect the long-term health of HEU children. Our team will investigate how exposure to HIV and various HIV medications during pregnancy affects brain development and mental health in HEU children. We will perform cognitive and behavioural tests and brain imaging studies in a cohort of HEU and HIV unexposed children of similar age and background. We will examine correlations between their brain anatomy and behavioural and cognitive performance. We will measure various factors in the cord blood of these children (collected at the time of birth) to better understand how HIV and HIV medications change the in utero environment. We will perform similar tests in a mouse model where we can directly compare different HIV medications, examine how they affect brain development and behaviour of the pups, and design and test therapies that will improve outcomes. Our duty to HEU children does not stop with the prevention of HIV infection. We must understand how HIV and HIV medications alter the in utero environment and influence long-term health, so we can optimize HIV treatment in pregnancy and ensure the best health outcomes for HEU children.

column36: Canadian HIV-Ageing Multidisciplinary Programmatic Strategy (CHAMPS) in NeuroHIV
column37: Scientists have made extraordinary advances in understanding and treating HIV infection over the past 20 years. Even with antiretroviral therapy, HIV-1 is still able to infect and damage the nervous system. This continues to be a major problem for people who are living with HIV/AIDS. The main problems when HIV-1 infects a person's nervous system are difficulties in thinking and persistent pain from damaged nerves. These problems are part of a condition called NeuroHIV. They diminish a person's quality of life, impair their sleep, reduce their ability to hold a job, affect their mood and isolate them socially. Over the past 5 years, our team has defined how often these problems occur and their severity. We have also discovered new disease processes and used that knowledge to develop and test new approaches to diagnose and treat NeuroHIV. For example, we uncovered new biological markers for people who have cognitive problems and pain from NeuroHIV. We found new possible treatments for these cognitive problems and pain, and we are testing those treatments in clinical trials. We have also identified specific sex and gender factors that make some people with NeuroHIV more vulnerable to thinking problems and pain from damaged nerves. NeuroHIV causes other problems that need research. These problems are linked to sex and gender diversity, and to how aging affects people with NeuroHIV. Our team of researchers from different areas of science and health will map basic pathways in the biology of NeuroHIV. Discovering these pathways can help us to analyze symptoms and risk factors for NeuroHIV. Understanding the pathways will also lead to new ways to diagnose and treat NeuroHIV. Part of our work will be to build broader community knowledge of NeuroHIV and its related problems.

column36: Action for Positive Brain Health Now
column37: Older people living with HIV worry about their memory, and with good reason. A third or more have problems with thinking or concentration, despite good control of their HIV infection. Rates of depression, anxiety and poor motivation are also high. Separately or together, these brain health problems affect function and quality of life. The causes of brain health symptoms in HIV are not fully understood, and we don't know whether brain health inevitably worsens over time. Our team has developed new ways to assess these problems in the clinic, identified the factors that relate to poor brain health in a large on-going cohort study, and provided preliminary information about whether these symptoms can be treated. Here, we build on this foundation to meet three broad aims: (1) Understand the factors that lead to poor brain health, focusing on viral, cerebrovascular, and social contributors; (2) Empower people living with HIV and the clinicians who care for them with practical tools to assess brain health and personalize treatment; (3) Act to help people living with HIV improve brain health through lifestyle changes. We will extend the existing cohort study to provide crucial information about whether brain health worsens over longer follow-up. We will add a second wave of participants, including more women, to help us provide personalized brain health recommendations suited to a wide range of people. We will implement the assessment tools that we have developed in our current study as easy-to-use apps. We will work closely with the HIV clinicians and community partners on our team to ensure these are user-friendly and clinic-ready. We will test an innovative, two-phase intervention to help people with brain health challenges pursue health goals tailored to their own priorities and risks, to improve their memory, mood and quality of life. This study will provide the knowledge and tools that people living with HIV need to take charge of their brain health now.

column36: SEARCH (active Surveillance and Evaluation of Adverse Reactions in Canadian Healthcare) & PREVENT (Pharmacogenomics of Adverse Reaction EVEnts National Team)
column37: The debilitating and lethal consequences of severe adverse drug reactions (ADRs) are a striking failure of modern medicine. The consequences for patients who experience severe ADRs are catastrophic. In Canada, there are an estimated 200,000 severe ADRs, claiming 10,000-22,000 lives, and costing $14-18 billion each year. To tackle this complex problem requires a multi-faceted collaborative linking of scientists, clinicians and regulators sharing complementary expertise in an environment that promotes teamwork. The Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network (DSEN) Active Surveillance and Evaluation of Adverse Reactions in Canadian Healthcare (SEARCH) initiative was first funded in 2011, with the overarching goal of conducting active surveillance to identify important drug risks, reduce the occurrence of severe ADRs and improve drug safety in Canadians. In close collaboration with the Drug Safety and Effectiveness (DSEN) Pharmacogenomics of Adverse Reaction EVEnts National Team (PREVENT) the work of SEARCH is strengthened through the discovery of pharmacogenomics biomarkers - that is understanding the genetic variation between patients that affects their individual drug response. This inter-individual variation acts as key predictors of ADRs for many drugs in clinical use today. Our team will build on its broad experience in active surveillance methods, pharmacogenomics expertise and its established network of ADR surveillance clinicians in Canadian health centres. These surveillance clinicians are located at 13 pediatric academic health centers and 13 adult academic health centers and their role is to identify and report ADRs, and collect DNA and the detailed clinical information that is needed to evaluate potential drug risks. This will allow SEARCH & PREVENT to continue active surveillance in areas of importance to the CIHR Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network, Health Canada and other pertinent stakeholders.

column36: Mechanisms of cell clearance during tissue homeostasis and regeneration using freshwater planarians

column37: Persistent viral infections such as those caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV), the hepatitis C virus (HCV) or the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) are a major global health problem. It is estimated that more than 500 million people in the world are infected with at least one of these viruses. Currently, only HBV infection can be prevented through vaccination while the development of vaccines against HCV or HIV is still a long-term goal. Although a number of highly effective antiviral drugs were recently developed against all three viruses, these are not able to cure HIV infection or have variable success rates against HBV and HCV infections. In Canada, HCV infection constitutes the most frequent indication for liver transplantation and together with HBV, these pathologies account for 1000 deaths annually while the number of people living with HIV continues to rise. There is therefore a great need for further research aimed at better understanding the fundamental mechanisms employed by these chronic viruses to escape the host immune response and establish persistence. One common feature between these three infections is the appearance of dysfunctions in the B cell response with important pathological consequences. The main objectives of this research program are therefore to better understand the mechanisms that contribute to these dysfunctions and to develop clinical interventions to restore normal B cell responses during chronic viral infections. This knowledge will prove very useful for the rational design of vaccines or improved antiviral drugs.

column36: Rhinovirus induced modulation of epithelial phenotype in asthma
column37: Asthma is a chronic airway disease that affects 300 million people worldwide. Although all children get multiple infections with human rhinovirus (HRV - the "common cold virus") in early life, only a subset get HRV-induced wheezing illnesses, and are far more likely to develop asthma by age 6. It is not clear why only some children get HRV-induced wheezing illnesses, but the interaction of HRV and development of allergies may play a role. Human airway epithelial cells (HAE) are the main site of HRV infection and it is thought that HRV affects asthma by changing HAE biology. The characteristic features (phenotype) of HAE are altered in asthma, and these altered HAE interact with nearby structural and immune cells to help cause asthma. Despite the central role of HAE in regulating airway diseases, the effects of HRV infection on HAE phenotype have not been well characterized. We have found that HRV infection of HAE from normal people causes transient changes in cell biology. In this proposal, we will fully characterize the effects of HRV on epithelial phenotype and will define the mechanisms by which HRV causes these changes. We will determine if repeated infections with HRV cause greater effects in HAE than a single infection. In addition, we will test the idea that HRV infections (single or repeated) in the setting of an "allergic" environment produce more profound alterations in HAE that mimic the phenotype seen in asthma. We will compare HAE from asthmatic children to those from normal children to see if they have greater responses to HRV. Finally, we will experimentally infect normal and asthmatic volunteers with HRV to test the idea that HAE in asthmatic patients show greater response to HRV in vivo. By understanding how HRV infections alter epithelial responses, alone and in an allergic setting, we may be able to develop ways to prevent or reduce the effects of HRV in asthma in order to improve the well-being of patients with asthma.

column36: The functions of mammalian TRAPP complexes and their role in disease
column37: The Transport Protein Particle (TRAPP) complexes were first discovered in yeast. Subsequent work identified related, conserved complexes in humans. These complexes function in moving proteins between various intracellular compartments within a cell. Although they share a core of common proteins, there are unique proteins that are associated with the core to form the various complexes (three complexes in yeast, two in higher eukaryotes). While the functions of the complexes in yeast are better understood, the functions of the mammalian complexes are less clear. In addition, several of the subunits that associate with the complex in humans have been shown to have functions independent of the complex. Furthermore, recent work has led to the identification of individuals that have mutations in TRAPP proteins. Curiously, these individuals all have different phenotypes depending on which TRAPP protein is mutated. Thus, understanding the functions of the mammalian TRAPP proteins and their role in disease is a necessary next step in our understanding of these complexes. This present application seeks to understand the functions of two specific subunits called C11 and C2L. In order to facilitate this work, we are developing a simplified in vitro assay that reconstitutes transport in the secretory pathway. We will use wild type TRAPP complexes as well as complexes harboring mutations in the aforementioned proteins to assess their ability to reconstitute membrane traffic in this pathway. The results of these studies will provide insight into specific human disorders that are linked to TRAPP mutations and will allow clinicians to more quickly assess new disorders that may be linked to these complexes.

column36: Impact of obesity-associated inflammation on breast cancer progression
column37: There is a strong association between chronic inflammation, and the risk of developing cancer. column36: A randomized controlled trial of symptom screening by children with cancer and feedback to providers
column37: Most children with cancer survive because they are given intensive treatments. Unfortunately, these treatments are associated with distressing symptoms. Poor symptom control occurs because children do not have a way to report and track their symptoms, healthcare providers are not aware of these symptoms, and guidelines for symptom management are not easy to access. To address these gaps, we developed the Symptom Screening in Pediatrics Tool (SSPedi) specifically for children receiving cancer treatments. We also created evidence-based guidelines to help providers know how to manage symptoms. To bring identification and management of symptoms together, we created a web-based application called Supportive care Prioritization, Assessment and Recommendations for Kids (SPARK). SPARK consists of two components: (1) Symptom screening component centered on SSPedi and (2) Supportive care guideline component. The next step is to establish that these tools improve the lives of children with cancer. We will conduct a randomized controlled trial which evaluates the effectiveness of daily symptom screening by children seen in hospital daily for 5 days and feedback of symptom reports to healthcare providers with links to guidelines for symptom management. Participants in the control arm will receive the standard of care in which symptom screening with feedback is not performed. We will include English-speaking children and adolescents 8-18 years of age expected to be in hospital daily for 5 days. The primary endpoint will be the day 5 total SSPedi score which ranges from 0 to 60 (higher means more bothersome symptoms). We plan to enroll 345 children across 7 Canadian institutions over 4 years. This research will enable children to report symptoms and will help providers know how to manage symptoms using the best available evidence. Ultimately, SPARK implementation will lead to better symptom control and quality of life for children receiving cancer treatments.

column36: Characterization of quality control pathways that target cytosolic misfolded proteins with missense mutations for proteasome degradation
column37: Gene mutations that cause diseases often do so by causing misfolding and degradation of the mutant proteins. Protein misfolding occurs when a protein does not attain its so-called native structure, which is reached when the protein is properly folded to perform its function in the cell. Our goal is to better understand how mutant proteins that misfold are recognized by elements of the ubiquitin proteasome system. The ubiquitin proteasome system consists of groups of enzymes that first mark proteins targeted for degradation by attaching to them a small protein tag called ubiquitin. These ubiquitin-tagged proteins are then recognized by the proteasome, which eliminates them from the cell. Our main hypothesis is there are several degradation paths for different groups of proteins that misfold due to mutations. To test this idea, we will analyze using different cell-based assays a large panel of mutations that have been associated to genetic disorders or diseases. More specifically, we will focus on missense mutations that induce the change of single amino acids. First, we will identify which mutated cytosolic proteins are degraded by the ubiquitin proteasome system from a large panel of known disease-associated mutations. We will then determine which known elements of the ubiquitin proteasome system target these misfolded mutant proteins. A major question is how E3 enzymes that attach ubiquitin recognize misfolded proteins. To address this question, we will employ the identified mutant proteins as model substrates to better identify which regions or domains on E3 enzymes recognize the misfolded proteins. Finally, we will set up a screen to identify novel genes involved in targeting misfolded proteins for degradation. By better understanding how misfolded proteins are triaged within the cell, we will gain fundamental knowledge of disease mechanisms, leading to potential novel therapeutic approaches.

column36: Stress, Brain and Neurodevelopment in Children Born Preterm

column36: Multi-centre Temporal Ultrasound Image Analysis for Prostate Cancer Diagnosis
column37: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most common cancer diagnosed in Canadian men, with about 25,000 new cases per year. The gold standard for PCa diagnosis and prognosis is ultrasound (US)-guided needle biopsy with pathologic grading. The biopsy procedure is not patient specific; rather, it involves taking "blind" biopsy cores, leading to frequent re-biopsy or over diagnosis of insignificant cancer. There is an acute need for patient-specific targeting techniques that have higher chance of detecting early aggressive PCa. Aggressive PCa must be diagnosed early and accurately to appropriately treat patients at higher risk of morbidity and mortality. Meanwhile, it is critical to balance against over-treatment of indolent PCa, of which is more appropriately managed using an active surveillance approach. The best biopsy technique today is to localize PCa with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and use its fusion with US to improve the detection rate of aggressive PCa. However, this method alone is not able to accurately differentiate indolent PCa and cannot reliably detect small lesions of aggressive PCa. In this project, we propose a turnkey technology, where subtle variations of backscattered US signals from a tissue location over a short time span, i.e., temporal enhanced US, are used to detect physical properties of the underlying tissue using a machine-learning framework. Our objective is to establish the efficacy of this technology in identifying clinically significant PCa in real-time US, so that accurate biopsy targeting is achieved. In a series of clinical studies, we will develop and deploy this technology across multiple institutions. This technology is expected to positively and rapidly benefit the lives of all patients suffering from PCa. Collaboration with leading investigators in Canada and USA will create an effective environment for leading international development of next generation cancer diagnosis imaging tools.

column36: Establishing the importance of diet and insulin resistance in modulating immune function in obesity
column37: Obesity is associated with several risk factors (for example, high blood sugar, poor insulin response and inflammation) that increase the risk of developing cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes (T2DM). Obesity is also associated with abnormalities in the immune system and an increased risk of infection. Specific components of the diet such as high dietary intake of fat and sugar influence not only the development of obesity but also the immune system. Therefore, it is still unclear if the immune dysfunction associated with obesity in human are attributable to 1- the excess of body fat per se and/or 2- the metabolic complications also often associated with obesity such as elevated blood glucose and/or 3- the overall poor diet quality of an individual. We are proposing a study where we will characterize, in controlled feeding conditions, the functionality of the immune system by investigating a panel of makers of the immune system (inflammation in the blood and the response of immune cells). At the end of a 4-week feeding period where participants will all consume the same standardized diet, we will compare the immune system of three groups of adults with obesity: a. obesity with normal blood glucose concentrations; b. obesity with marginally elevated blood glucose concentrations; and c. obesity with T2DM. All groups will be matched for age, sex and body mass index, and compared to a group of healthy normal weight subjects. By comparing these four groups, we will be able to gain an understanding of the immune complications associated with obesity alone (e.g. excess of body fat per se) and the association of blood sugar and diet in modulating these immune complications. This is essential to subsequently identify dietary interventions to counteract the immune dysfunctions associated with obesity.
