column36: Mechanisms of REM sleep behaviour disorder
column37: REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) affects 2-6% of the elderly population and is characterized by excessive movement during REM sleep. These movements are typically so violent that they result in patient injuries, which often require medical attention. However, the most alarming aspect of RBD is that 80-90% of patients eventually develop a brain disease like Parkinson's disease or dementia after being diagnosed with RBD. During healthy REM sleep, most of the body's muscles are paralyzed. However, in RBD muscle paralysis is lost, which causes RBD patients to actively move during REM sleep. Because RBD is tightly associated with brain degeneration and this degeneration begins in brain regions that cause REM sleep paralysis, it is hypothesized that RBD is caused by degeneration of the brain regions that control REM sleep paralysis. However, it still remains unclear which cells in the brainstem control REM sleep paralysis and if damage to these cell circuits underlies RBD. This medical research will be of importance to Canadians because it identifies the brain mechanisms that cause healthy REM sleep and it determines if degeneration of these regions causes RBD.

column37: Protein degradation constitutes a major cellular function that is responsible for maintenance of the normal cellular physiology by breaking down proteins. The ubiquitin-proteasome system is one of the major mechanism responsible for protein degradation within cells. The regulation of protein stability by this pathway is critical in the molecular basis of carcinogenesis, as it is involved in the regulation of cell growth and preventing abnormal accumulation of proteins. Additionally, ubiquitin modification of target proteins signals many cellular processes other than proteolysis that are also important for the development of cancer. Deregulation of ubiquitin ligases, which are proteins involved in many biological processes including protein degradation, results in uncontrolled proliferation, genomic instability and cancer. Attempts to develop general protein degradation inhibitors for cancer therapy have been questioned because it is highly toxic, and could results in long-term effects from the accumulation of misfolded proteins that is the hallmark of neurodegenerative diseases. Thus, there is great interests in identifying specific proteins involved in this process that could be targeted instead. We identified UBBP4, a gene encoding novel ubiquitins that could be involved in such specific ubiquitination of proteins. The main goal of studying ubiquitin and ubiquitin ligases is to develop drugs that specifically target these enzymes. Thus, it is crucial to identify the substrates of these ubiquitin ligases and understand their cellular functions. column36: Integrated phylogenetic, molecular and functional analyses of the within-host latent HIV reservoir
column37: Thanks to the advent of combination antiretroviral therapies, HIV infection is now considered a chronically manageable condition. These drugs however do not completely eliminate HIV from the body; as such, an HIV cure is actively being pursued. HIV is able to persist in the body because the virus establishes "latent HIV reservoirs", long-lived cells that harbor a dormant copy of the HIV genome within them. HIV can persist for decades within these cells, but the virus may reactivate at any time to produce infectious particles. It is for this reason that HIV therapy needs to be maintained for life. Establishment of latent HIV reservoirs is a continuous process that begins shortly after infection. Moreover, HIV is continually evolving within a given host. Thus, by the time an individual reaches chronic infection, their latent HIV reservoir is expected to comprise a genetically diverse pool of viral sequences that constitute a "fossil record" of HIV evolution in that individual. Importantly, latently-infected cells are likely to differ in key respects including their ability to reactivate to produce infectious HIV particles and their susceptibility to recognition by the immune system. Methods to study HIV reservoir diversity and to identify key characteristics that associate with reservoir reactivation would greatly aid efforts towards an HIV cure. Our interdisciplinary team, comprising molecular biology, bioinformatics, and clinical experts, has developed an innovative genetics-based method for determining when a given HIV sequence "went dormant" within a host. We now seek to apply our method to address foundational gaps in our understanding of HIV persistence. We believe that our integrated approach will provide a versatile and potentially transformative addition to the growing armamentarium of tools in HIV cure research, towards the ultimate goal of developing strategies for HIV reservoir elimination.

column36: Unravelling the contribution to the hypoxic ventilatory response of purinergic and glial signalling in the preBotzinger Complex
column37: The mammalian brain depends on a constant supply of oxygen to meet its energy needs. If this supply fails for even a few minutes permanent brain damage or death can result. A host of adaptive responses have evolved to protect brain oxygen. Prominent among these is the biphasic hypoxic ventilatory response (HVR) in which a fall in blood oxygen (hypoxia) supplying the brain triggers an initial increase in breathing. If this increase does not restore oxygen levels, breathing falls in what is called the secondary hypoxic respiratory depression. Release of the excitatory neurochemical ATP in breathing centers of the brain helps maintain the increased breathing. However, this ATP is degraded to adenosine; brain hypoxia also causes widespread release of adenosine. Adenosine causes widespread depression of neuronal activity. This depression is highly adaptive in most brain regions because it reduces metabolic demand and hypoxic brain injury. However, depression of breathing is highly maladaptive because it is only through increases in breathing that oxygen levels can be restored. The net result is that the initial hypoxia-induced increase in breathing is followed by a secondary depression that is potentially fatal in premature infants who suffer from apnea of prematurity; it is also problematic in adults with sleep-disordered breathing where repeated, cyclic falls in oxygen exacerbate cardiovascular disease. Thus, there is great clinical interest in understanding the mechanisms underlying the HVR. The interaction between ATP excitation and adenosine inhibition of breathing is emerging as key in determining the magnitude of the hypoxic depression. The aim of this proposal is to use rodent models to determine the factors that control the balance between the excitatory actions of ATP and inhibitory actions of adenosine during hypoxia and develop strategies to shift the balance in favor of excitation to counteract the life-threatening hypoxic respiratory depression.

column37: Cancers are caused by mutations and genetic alterations. Conventional origins of mutations from chemicals in the environment or inherited mutations are known, but we have just begun to understand that some mutations that contribute to cancer originate from within our own cells. There are enzymes that exist in our cells that can alter the DNA sequence. Usually these enzymes act for our benefit and use their activity to alter the DNA sequence of viruses to make the viral DNA nonfunctional. However, sometimes when the levels of these enzymes are not kept in check, they can become too high and they can alter the DNA sequence of the human cell. If these mutations occur in genes that contribute to cellular replication, they can induce the formation or propagate maintenance of a cancer cell. This research is focused on the internal origins of these mutations caused by a specific family of enzymes, called the APOBEC3 enzymes. If we can identify how their activity becomes unregulated we can design inhibitors to limit their function to slow cancer progression or use their unregulated activity as an early risk factor for cancer development.

column36: Genetic instability of the haploid male germ cells
column37: Genetic diversity is provided by de novo transmittable mutations and it is now known that most new mutations are male- driven. During the formation of spermatozoa, the final steps involves a major change in the way DNA is packaged and we demonstrated that this is accompanied by the formation of transient DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) in spermatids of both human and mouse pointing to an evolutionary-conserved mechanism. These DSBs arise in haploid cells where there is a single set of chromosome. The repair process cannot therefore proceed using the homologous chromosome as template as in normal somatic cells and must rather rely on a end-joining process. These end-joining repair processes are less reliable and known to induce DNA deletions and insertions. Our hypothesis is that mutations can therefore be induced when the DSBs are repaired in the subsequent steps of the spermatid's differentiation process. Our goal is therefore to confirm whether this process is indeed genetically unstable and if specific regions are involved in the ethiology of genetic diseases since our first screen suggest that neurodevelopmental genes are targeted with high significance. DSBs are also observed during yeast gamete formation emphasizing the conserved nature of this transition and providing a powerful genetic tool to decipher the DSBs mechanism. These investigations may confirm the discovery of a novel mechanism contributing to genetic diversity, evolution and possibly to neurodevelopment disorders such as autism.

column37: Sepsis (ie. blood poisoning) is triggered by harmful microorganisms or their toxins in the blood or tissues. These harmful agents can cause a vicious cycle of blood clot formation and inflammation, which may lead to multiple organ failure and death even after the microorganisms have been cleared with antibiotics. In Canada, there are approximately 90,000 patients with sepsis each year. Of these, 30% to 50% of these patients will die. Many anti-sepsis drugs have been tested in humans, but all of these clinical studies have failed. This suggests that some fundamental knowledge is lacking in our current understanding of why sepsis kills patients. In recent years, neutrophils (a type of white blood cells) have been shown to release web-like structures (called NETs) to capture and kill microorganisms. NETs consist of DNA, histones, and neutrophils enzymes. However, NETs can also cause collateral damage to the body. We have previously shown that the DNA and histone components of NETs can trigger blood clotting and prevent blood breakdown. We have also shown that high levels of DNA in the blood of septic patients is a strong predictor of death. In a mouse model of sepsis, injection of DNAse (an enzyme that breaks down DNA) results in improved organ function and improved survival rates. In the current proposal, we plan to further study how DNA and histones triggers blood clots and inflammation in sepsis. We will perform studies of blood cells and blood molecules in test tubes. By comparing blood samples from septic and non-septic ICU patients, we can identify the precise biological pathways that lead to high levels of DNA in septic patients. We will also perform studies in a mouse model of sepsis to see if removal of DNA and/or histones from the blood can improve survival in septic mice. Our research thus has the potential to identify new anti-sepsis strategies that will improve the lives of septic patients.

column37: Streptococcus pneumonia (the pneumococcus) is a bacterium that often lives in the nose and throats of humans. This relationship is most often benign but this microorganism is also an accomplished disease-causing germ that can cause mild ailments, such as earaches, to lethal illnesses like pneumonia, blood poisoning, and infections of the brain and central nervous system. There are effective vaccines and medicines (antibiotics) to treat infections caused by the pneumococcus; however, this germ is constantly adapting to avoid both of these medical interventions. The importance of S. pneumoniae as a disease-causing germ dictates intense research efforts be directed to understand how it causes infections with the aim of using this knowledge to guide new treatment strategies. The human body has large amounts of carbohydrates with complex structures, termed glycans, displayed on the surface of cells and coating the surfaces of tissues (e.g. mucous). Remarkably, the pneumococcus relies on its ability to attack these glycans to colonize humans and ultimately cause disease. Our research is aimed at determining how this happens. What glycans does the germ attack? What pneumococcal factors do this? What is the outcome of destroying a host sugar? Armed with the fundamental insight from examining these questions we plan to develop and study molecules that can be used to prevent S. pneumoniae from attacking host glycans; such molecules are proving useful as research tools but may also provide a platform for developing new treatments to combat S. pneumoniae infections.

column36: Replication of guanine-rich DNA
column37: The broad goal of the research proposed here is to improve our understanding of how DNA, the hereditary information that determines the development and functioning of all living organisms, is maintained over a human lifetime. Specifically, I propose to focus on the replication of DNA that is enriched for guanine, one of the four DNA bases, in normal development and genome instability. The proposed research is a logical extension of earlier, published work from my laboratory. Following studies on the purification and self-renewal of blood forming stem cells, we focused on the role of telomeres, the normal ends of chromosomes, in normal and malignant cell proliferation. This work led us to studies of the pathways that ensure proper replication of the guanine (G)-rich DNA. In the course of this work, we discovered several genes including DOG-1 (FANCJ) and RTEL that are required for replication of G-rich DNA. Interestingly, both these genes encode for proteins with helicase activity: that is they are capable of unwinding secondary DNA structures of G-rich DNA, called guanine quadruplex (G4) structures. Recently we found that the Bloom helicase protein, deficient in patients with the cancer-prone Bloom syndrome, is required to suppress recombination at G-rich DNA. Here we propose further studies on the pathways required to resolve G4 structures and faithfully replicate Grich DNA at telomeres and at genes. The goal of these studies is to better understand the nature of the lesions that cause problems during replication of G-rich DNA and the pathways that different cells have available to solve such problems. Our studies will generate new knowledge about DNA replication and DNA repair and pathways that prevent genome instability. A better understanding of these pathways has broad potential for our understanding of normal development and aging as well specific disorders linked to DNA repair defects including specific types of cancer.

column36: Mechanisms of long-term change to neuronal activity and secretion
column37: My research focuses on nerve cells from the brain. I am interested in how the bio-electrical properties of nerve cells are controlled. These properties are governed by minute holes in nerve cells called channel proteins, which pass ions (like calcium, sodium or potassium) in and out of the cell. Because ions are charged, their movement through channels results in the flow of electrical current. Nerve cells harness currents to receive sensations, code information, and signal other nerve cells, muscles, or glands. Signalling involves the release of either small chemicals or specialized proteins, termed neuro-peptides, from a nerve cell. My objective is to examine how nerve cells use channels in a coordinated fashion to release neuro-peptides and initiate behaviour. Taking a reductionist approach, I employ the brain of a sea snail, called Aplysia, which has large and identifiable nerve cells. In particular, I study the bag cells, which are motivational cells that evoke reproduction, a behaviour essential to all animals. My work concerns how, after only a very short stimulus, the action of certain channels allows these nerves cells to respond with a prolonged episode of neuro-peptide release to trigger reproduction. I will investigate the mechanisms that allow channels to remain open for lengthy time periods. This includes interactions with structures inside the bag cells, known as mitochondria, which normally act as an energy source, but in this case regulate channel function. Long-term responses are found in nerve cells from many animals, and are essential for handling sensory information, learning, movement, and controlling drinking, eating, ovulation, birth, or breast feeding. Thus, my findings will apply to processes such as perception, memory, and fundamental behaviours. Furthermore, because the channels permit a nerve cell to be active on its own, there may be implications for epilepsy, where bio-electrical properties are inappropriately adjusted.

column36: Ecological Momentary Assessment of Simultaneous Cannabis and Alcohol Use
column37: Cannabis and alcohol are widely used among young adults in Canada and both substances are often used at the same time. Rates of simultaneous use of alcohol and cannabis may increase as a result of legalization and increased access to cannabis in Canada. Combining cannabis with alcohol can increase risk for harms such as psychological and physical symptoms, social problems, and risk for substance use disorders. This study will use real-time mobile data collection to examine patterns of simultaneous cannabis and alcohol use in individuals' daily lives. Young adults who regularly use cannabis and alcohol will be asked to track their use of both substances using a smartphone app for three, 21-day periods spaced 6 months apart. On mornings following alcohol and/or cannabis use, participants will complete measures of substance use consequences. Data will be used to examine patterns of simultaneous use, including the frequency of co-use, the overall quantity of each substance used, and the temporal ordering of each substance (e.g., cannabis before alcohol or vice versa). Contextual influences on simultaneous use and the subjective effects of combining cannabis with alcohol will also be investigated. Further, the unique risks of combining cannabis and alcohol (e.g., risky behaviours, hangovers) will be examined relative to the use of either substance alone. Finally, changes in patterns of simultaneous use will be examined over a one-year period in relation to health outcomes such as symptoms of substance use disorders. The findings will improve our understanding of the unique health risks of cannabis and alcohol co-use, which will have direct implications for public health policies as cannabis becomes legal in Canada.

column36: Quantifying Brown Adipose Tissue Thermogenesis in Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes
column37: Brown fat is the only organ able to burn energy to directly produce heat. This tissue allows small animals to live in cold environments without having to rely on muscle shivering. Brown fat is present in adults and can be seen using 'positron emission tomography' imaging (or 'PET imaging') with injection of a radioactive sugar label (or 'sugar tracer') that is taken up by brown fat when it is activated upon cold exposure. PET imaging with a sugar tracer is currently the standard method to measure brown fat. We have found that brown fat in adults burns energy mostly by utilizing its own fat content. We have demonstrated that PET imaging with a sugar tracer underestimates the total contribution of brown fat to energy expenditure, especially in people with type 2 diabetes. The contribution of brown fat to energy balance cannot be precisely determined using the current methods we have. As brown fat is currently viewed as a promising target for the treatment of obesity and type 2 diabetes, it is essential to quantify its role in energy expenditure in people without and with obesity and/or type 2 diabetes. We propose here to develop and validate new methods to quantify brown fat energy expenditure by measuring its own fat utilization with a combination of PET imaging with a novel fat tracer and magnetic resonance imaging techniques. We will apply these novel techniques during cold exposure and stimulation with a drug known to activate brown fat in people. Our laboratory has made outstanding contributions to the field of brown fat research through the imaging innovations we made and our integrated approach to the study of energy metabolism directly in people. This project will lead to new standard methods to measure brown fat energy expenditure and will provide essential knowledge on brown fat as a target to prevent and treat obesity and type 2 diabetes.

column36: Systematic Analysis of Post-transcriptional Regulatory Mechanisms and Functions in Drosophila
column37: DNA is copied into messenger RNAs (mRNAs), which in turn encode proteins. For most of the second half of the 20th Century it was thought that the regulation of which proteins are made in any particular cell of the body or stage of development is at the level of transcription (production of mRNA from DNA). However, it has become clear in the last decade that a great deal of this regulation occurs post-transcriptionally via control of mRNA stability, localization within the cell and/or in the translation of the mRNA into protein. These processes are regulated by RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), which together with their bound mRNAs and other associated proteins, regulate these processes. In order to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the molecular mechanisms of post-transcriptional control and how the compendium of proteins in each cell type is assembled, we will use the powerful model organism, the fruit fly Drosophila, to systematically identify the mRNAs bound to each of 68 RBPs in the early embryo together with other associated RNAs and proteins. We will use experimental and computational methods to identify the binding sites for each of these 68 RBPs. Finally, we will assess the molecular functions of these binding sites in control of the post-transcriptional processes listed above. Together these studies will provide the first insights into how the 'post-transcriptional code' is read out as the compendium of proteins present in a cell. Given that RBPs and their binding sites tend to be highly evolutionarily conserved and that 90% of the closely related human RBPs have been associated with a variety of diseases, our results will lead directly to insights into the components and functions of post-transcriptional processes in other organisms, including humans.

column36: Precision medicine in smoking cessation: nicotine metabolism genetics in nine clinical trials
column37: Cigarette smoking is the leading cause of preventable illness and death in Canada; using precision medicine genomics approaches we plan to personalize smoking cessation treatment choices. In this proposal, we seek to identify genetic factors that influence the nicotine metabolite ratio (NMR), a measure of nicotine inactivation that predicts treatment outcomes in multiple smoking cessation clinical trials. NMR is also associated with the amount smoked, dependence, reactivity to smoking cues, risk for lung cancer, and many other smoking-related behaviours; in general, faster nicotine metabolizers (higher NMR) smoke more, are more dependent, have lower quit rates, and a higher risk for lung cancer, compared to slower metabolizers. Up to 80% of NMR variability between smokers is due to genetics, however only a small fraction of this genetic variation is known. While NMR itself could be used clinically to personalize smoking cessation, this is not yet possible because measuring NMR requires sophisticated techniques; there are no commercially available NMR kits and NMR is not routinely measured. In contrast, DNA, from which genetic information can be determined, is more easily collected. Thus, using genetics to better understand NMR, and how NMR is related to smoking and illness, we will enhance quitting and reduce tobacco-related illness and death. Our goal is to sequence (i.e. read) the major nicotine inactivation gene in ~1,000 smokers to identify specific variants affecting NMR. We also have data from 9 smoking cessation clinical trials, where >5,000 smokers with NMR will be examined for the variants identified in our sequencing analyses. We will then study how these variants functionally influence NMR, smoking behaviours, and cessation outcomes using this unparalleled clinical resource. Through these analyses, we will improve our ability to genetically tailor treatment, which will ultimately improve smoking cessation rates and the mortality associated with smoking.

column36: Regulation of Salmonella pathogenesis by transposon-encoded small regulatory RNAs
column37: Gastrointestinal infections by Salmonella and related enteropathogenic bacteria can lead to severe diarrheal disease and accordingly present a serious human health problem. Infection requires passage of Salmonella from the GI tract into epithelial cells lining the lower intestine. This cell invasion process requires the expression of a large set of genes encoded on a 40 kb chromosomal DNA segment called Salmonella pathogenicity island 1 (SPI-1). The control of SPI-1 gene expression is complex involving a positive feed-forward cascade that includes several different transcription factors. We recently discovered that the insertion sequence IS200 encodes small regulatory RNAs (tad-sRNA for short) that contribute to SPI-1 gene expression. Part of the current proposal is focused on defining what genes in SPI-1 tad-sRNAs regulate and how this regulation occurs. Further investigation into the scope of tad-sRNA gene regulation in Salmonella led to the discovery that tad-sRNAs also regulate the expression of genes required for cysteine biosynthesis. As cysteine biosynthesis plays an important role in oxidative stress response and Salmonella needs to mount an aggressive oxidative stress response to propagate in certain cell types, we will test the possibility that tad-sRNA regulation of cysteine biosynthesis contributes to Salmonella pathogenicity. Finally, we will determine if host gene regulation by tad-sRNAs is a widespread phenomenon in bacteria. Overall, we expect results from this proposal to provide valuable new information in three important biomedical areas including: (1) how bacterial pathogenicity is controlled; (2) how the expression of a component of central metabolism (cysteine biosynthesis) is regulated and (3) why insertion sequences are stably maintained in bacterial genomes - notably insertion sequences can make major contributions to the development of antibiotic resistance in bacteria.

column36: Role of beta-PIX and CdGAP in the pathogenesis of proteinuria
column37: Leakage of proteins into urine (proteinuria) is a hallmark of many kidney diseases. When you have a lot of proteinuria, you are more likely to progress to kidney failure. This is why it is important to find effective treatments to stop proteinuria. Current treatments are non-specific with a lot of undesired side effects and not always effective. What is blocking the discovery of specific and effective treatments is the fact that we do not know how proteinuria develops. Normal kidneys have a barrier function that allows the passage of water and waste products into the urine while retaining proteins that are essential for body function. In the kidney, cells called podocytes are maintaining this barrier function. When podocytes are injured, this causes proteinuria. The proposed research will define what is happening in podocytes when they are injured. Our recent research identified that in proteinuric kidney diseases, the molecule called Rac1 is activated in podocytes and this makes podocytes to malfunction. When the Rac1 activation is persistent, eventually podocytes are lost in the urine and that leads to kidney failure. Thus, blocking Rac1 is a promising treatment strategy for proteinuria. However, Rac1 is expressed in all the cells in the body and blocking Rac1 itself will likely harm the body. Instead, we have identified two proteins, called beta-PIX and CdGAP that regulate Rac1 in podocytes. We will study how these proteins work in podocytes and establish if they could be good therapeutic targets. The results of the research will make us understand how proteinuria occurs and allow the development of a better therapeutic approach.

column36: Iron and inflammatory regulation of hepcidin: implications for anemias and infectious diseases
column37: Iron is an essential nutrient but also a potential biohazard; therefore, its metabolism is tightly controlled. Most of body iron is utilized within red blood cells for oxygen transport to tissues. Aged red blood cells are cleared by tissue macrophages, which liberate iron and recycle it to the bloodstream for new erythropoiesis. Iron efflux from macrophages and other cells is inhibited by hepcidin, a liver-derived hormone. The expression of hepcidin is primarily regulated by iron, inflammatory and erythropoietic cues. Genetic defects in hepcidin pathways cause hemochromatosis, a disease of iron overload. Pathological suppression of hepcidin also occurs in anemias with ineffective erythropoiesis, such as beta thalassemia, and contributes to iron overload. During infection, inflammatory induction of hepcidin triggers iron sequestration from the bloodstream to macrophages. This is considered a protective response by reducing iron availability to invading bacteria but may favor growth of intracellular pathogens. Prolonged inflammatory induction of hepcidin reduces iron availability for erythropoiesis and contributes to the anemia of inflammation, the most common cause of anemia among hospitalized patients. Two situations that are highly relevant to real life will be examined. The first experiment will examine whether giving prebiotics (inulin and oligofructose) to pregnant rats at the same time that they receive antibiotics will reduce the risk of obesity in their offspring. Fecal transplant studies will help us determine the direct role of intestinal bacteria in providing protection with prebiotics. column37: The pandemic increase in obesity is leading to serious obesity-related complications including diabetes, stroke, heart disease, infectious disease and many cancers. Two types of fat (adipose tissue) exist: white fat and brown fat. White fat store excess energy, while brown fat burns energy (thermogenesis). Impaired brown fat activity causes obesity in preclinical models and is associated with obesity in humans. Therefore, understanding the molecular determinants that control brown fat activation holds great promise in the fight against obesity. This proposal seeks to understand the underlying molecules that control a newly identified metabolic pathway in brown fat. Furthermore, the the health benefits of this pathway will be examined at the whole body level by using genetically engineered mouse models and by exploring the association of this pathway to human obesity. We have previously shown that creatine metabolism supports energy expenditure and is necessary to combat diet-induced obesity. However, the underlying mechanism that controls the anti-obesogenic action of creatine metabolism is not fully understood. This work will identify the molecular determinants that control creatine-dependent energy expenditure and will examine the role of these new molecules in regulating thermogenesis and providing protection from obesity. The proposed research has tremendous potential to discover new molecules that can be exploited therapeutically to combat obesity. Importantly, thermogenic brown fat has been found in humans, and so understanding how to activate this tissue has direct implications toward human health and well-being. The findings that come out of this proposal hold promise for improving the health of individuals and the population.

column36: Role of enteroviral infection in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
column37: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), commonly known as Lou Gehrig's disease, is a devastating disease marked by the deterioration of nerve cells that control muscles, leading to paralysis and ultimately death. ALS afflicts approximately 30,000 people in North America; however, there is currently no cure for this disease. ALS can be genetically inherited or can occur sporadically in people without any apparent history of the disorder in their family. The cause(s) of sporadic ALS remain(s) unknown. Infection with enteroviruses, a family of RNA viruses that include poliovirus, coxsackievirus, enterovirus-A71, and enterovirus-D68, has been proposed as a possible factor because they can target muscle-controlling nerve cells and polio survivors have been reported to experience new weakening in muscles that were previously affected by viral infection. However, definitive evidence of the role of enteroviruses in sporadic ALS is lacking. We recently made an exciting discovery that enteroviral infection results in the hallmark molecular and pathological features of ALS. In the present project, we will examine whether enteroviral infection induces ALS-like symptoms in normal mice and/or accelerates disease onset and progression in mice that are genetically susceptible. We will also test whether application of anti-enterovirus drugs can lessen the development of ALS. Moreover, we will investigate the possible mechanisms involved, with an emphasis on the RNA metabolic pathway, the host disposal system for damaged proteins and organelles, and the spreading mechanisms of ALS. We expect that the results of this project will not only uncover a potentially powerful new factor that contributes to the development of ALS, but also will allow for the development of novel forms of treatments for ALS.

column36: Molecular, Cellular, and Subunit-dependent Regulation of Voltage-Gated Calcium Channels
column37: The human heart continuously beat over a person's lifetime at a regular pace (more than 2 billion heartbeats in a 70-year lifespan). For the heart to function properly, its upper (atria) and lower (ventricle) chambers must fill with and pump blood in an organized manner. This is achieved through an intricate network of electrical signals. Electrical signals are propagated through specialized proteins called ion channels. Each ion channel must fulfill a very specific function to ensure that the electrical impulse is transmitted normally. By bringing in the cell the calcium ions necessary for the heart contraction (beating), the L-type calcium channel is one of most important proteins for the heart function. Change in the function of the channel will affect the amount of calcium ions coming in the cell. Excess calcium ions in the cell trigger a series of maladaptive reactions that could ultimately result in fatal heart failure. It is therefore paramount to understand how calcium ions transit through the ion channel. L-type calcium channels are made from multiple proteins or subunits that ensure the controlled passage of calcium ions from the circulation to the cardiac cell. This project investigates the role of the "Cavalpha2delta1" subunit in bringing in calcium in the cell. Too many calcium ions will kill the cell and not enough calcium ions will make beating impossible. We are identifying the hotspots of the "Cavalpha2delta1" protein that are critical for incoming calcium ions under normal physiological conditions. We are further investigating the variations in the expression of "Cavalpha2delta1" in pathological settings, using rat models of heart failure. We use molecular tools that label regions of "Cavalpha2delta1" and we track their role by measuring the electrical activity of the protein. This knowledge will provide valuable insight into future gene and pharmacological therapies to target the active sites and design improved calcium channel blockers.

column37: Research shows that poor diet is linked to diseases such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and cancer. Adolescence is a critical time to promote healthy diets because lifelong eating habits begin in childhood and diet quality tends to decline sharply around age 14. Smartphone 'apps' may provide a major opportunity for resolving this public health issue because they are increasingly popular and they have the capacity to deliver individually targeted information and activities. Our team is proposing to undertake a research project to make use of an existing smartphone app called SmartAPPetite to provide high school youth (13-18 years) with healthy food information, including nutrition tips, recipes, and directions to nearby healthy food retailers. Our Primary Objective is to assess whether this app is effective at changing knowledge of healthy food and healthy eating behaviours among youth in a full range of urban, suburban and rural settings across Southwestern Ontario. We will monitor progress in three ways. First, participation with the app will be tracked using web analytics software. Second, surveys including dietary recall and food behaviour questionnaires will be administered online to all participants before and after they use the app for a 12-week period. Third, we will conduct focus groups with participants to gain insight into their experiences using the app to enhance the product for future versions. We will also be considering how low-income youth and youth at risk for health issues (e.g. diabetes or obesity) benefit from using the app. This will provide a model on how to use smartphone technology for promoting healthier diets and behaviours.

column36: ICOS signaling in T cell tolerance and gut homeostasis
column37: Our immune system works under two major rules: i) recognize and destroy pathogens ii) do not harm body's own cells. Failure of the first rule causes immunodeficiency whereas breach of the second rule leads to autoimmune diseases. White blood cells termed "T cells" play important roles in enforcing these rules. To perform this duty, T cells are guided by a group of cell surface sensors including "ICOS (inducible costimulator)". Highlighting the importance of ICOS in promoting immunity, humans lacking ICOS suffer from severe immunodeficiency repeatedly coming down to infections. However, some patients are affected by both immunodeficiency and autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis. It has been puzzling how the lack of ICOS increases the chance of autoimmune attack in patients whose ability to fight pathogens is weakened. Using genetically modified mouse models, Dr. Suh's research team began to understand why: on one hand, ICOS supports "helper T cells" that facilitate immune responses against pathogens; on the other hand, it promotes a particular subset of "regulatory T cells" whose role is to stop autoimmune T cells from erroneously attacking body's own cells. Building up on these observations, Dr. Suh's team will elucidate what biochemical events ICOS evokes inside T cells and how those change T cells' behavior ultimately leading to immune disorders. This study will not only advance basic T cell biology but also help devise new ways to treat immunodeficiency and autoimmune diseases.

column37: Hundreds of millions of people world-wide are exposed to the natural element arsenic in their drinking water. This has resulted in a global public health crisis because arsenic causes cancer in humans. In Canada, arsenic "hot-spots" naturally exist with levels in well water potentially exceeding acceptable levels. As a waste product of industry (especially mining), arsenic is also a serious Canadian concern. While reducing human exposure to arsenic should be a major priority, evidence suggests that humans are susceptible to arsenic-induced disease for decades following cessation of chronic exposure. Furthermore, in many regions, removing exposure is not economically feasible. Thus, strategies for the treatment and prevention of As-induced disease, in addition to exposure reduction, are necessary. Selenium is an essential trace element which is toxic in excess. Selenium reduces the toxic effects of arsenic in laboratory animals by increasing its elimination from the body. Low blood selenium levels in humans chronically exposed to arsenic have been associated with increased risk for arsenic-induced disease. Clinical trials for testing the ability of selenium tablets or selenium-enriched diets to prevent arsenic-induced disease have been initiated in arsenic-endemic regions. The study of how selenium modifies the toxicity of arsenic in human tissues has been largely ignored. Furthermore, selenium comes in many different chemical forms and the best form for supplementation and prevention of arsenic-induced disease is not known. The overall goal of this research is to understand the influence of different forms of selenium on arsenic metabolism and transport in human liver and red blood cells. Ultimately, this information is critical for optimizing human selenium supplementation and for the prevention and treatment of arsenic-induced disease.

column36: Influence of visual and proprioceptive feedback during voluntary motor actions
column37: A basketball player must make split second decisions on how to avoid her opponent as she drives for the net. Even if the opponent bumps into her, skilled players rapidly make adjustments to score the basket. This ability to move and interact in a complex world is a key aspect of voluntary control. The present proposal will apply mechanical disturbances (small bumps to the arm) and/or visual disturbances (shift a cursor representing hand position) and observe how monkeys generate motor corrections under a range of behavioural contexts. Critically, we will also record in primary motor cortex (M1), a key region involved in voluntary control, to understand how it supports rapid motor corrections. The first project will modify specific features of the environment (target shape or presence of obstacles) to observe how neural activity in M1 of monkeys and corresponding motor corrections change based on these features of the environment. Preliminary observations highlight how M1 responses to a visual disturbance increase when the monkey must generate a more vigorous correction to attain a small target as compared to a large target. Our second project addresses the fact that we can use different types of feedback (visual or proprioceptive feedback of the limb) to make motor corrections. The question is how do you combine these different types of feedback. We use mathematical models that consider features of sensory feedback (noise and transmission times) to predict how each sensory signal should contribute to online control. Preliminary data highlight how feedback from the limb has a much more powerful influence on motor corrections than vision. Examination of the pattern in M1 of activity associated with different types of sensory feedback highlight that these sources of sensory feedback are broadly distributed across this motor region. The results will provide important properties on brain circuits control that support our ability to move and interact in the world.

column37: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, Systemic Sclerosis, and Sjogren's Disease, are all Systemic Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases (SARD). These conditions share many clinical, immune, and genetic features, including high blood levels of antibodies that react against the nucleus of the patient's own cells, called anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA). These antibodies can be seen in SARD patients many years before development of symptoms. Although this finding suggests that it may be possible to identify people that are going to develop SARD prior to the onset of symptoms, high levels of autoantibodies can also be seen in healthy people who will never develop SARD. Because the SARD conditions at disease onset can already be associated with extensive inflammation and damage of various organs, the ability to identify people at high risk of developing SARD prior to the onset of organ damage would improve the prognosis of these conditions. However, to do this we need to have blood tests that accurately identify those individuals who will develop clinical disease and a better knowledge of what immune pathways would be best to target with drug treatment. In previous work, we identified several immune changes that are seen in individuals with ANAs who have no SARD symptoms or insufficient symptoms to make a diagnosis, and compared them with patients with new onset SARD. This has led us to propose a model for the critical immune events that lead to SARD development. In this study we seek to further develop this model and to determine whether it accurately predicts the individuals with a positive ANA test who will progress to clinical SARD. This will allow us to develop a biomarker panel that more accurately predicts individuals who are at high risk of developing SARD and to determine the best treatment to prevent and/or delay disease onset.

column36: Impact of temporary lesions of frontoparietal cortex on feedback processing during voluntary motor actions
column37: We take for granted our ability to perform simple daily activities such as reaching for a cup of coffee. Impressively, if we are accidentally bumped while reaching we automatically make swift and agile corrections to reach and grasp the cup. These motor corrections require the brain to quickly process sensory information about the body and the world around us, and convert this information into patterns of muscle activity to attain the goal. While cerebral cortex has been known to be involved in planning voluntary motor actions, recent studies suggest cerebral cortex may play a more prominent role in processing sensory feedback from the limb during voluntary movements. In Project 1, we will directly test this idea by transiently reducing neural activity (by cooling the cortical surface) in one of two key cortical regions in monkeys and quantifying how motor corrections to unexpected disturbances of the contralateral arm are altered during voluntary motor actions. Our preliminary data demonstrate that inhibiting neural activity in one of two brain regions, dorsal premotor cortex (PMd) or parietal area 5 (A5), alters the ability of the animal to generate motor corrections, demonstrating their causal role in feedback control of the arm. We develop mathematical models that highlight the patterns of errors associated with each cortical region are similar to that expected if PMd is involved in generating motor commands, and A5 is involved in sensory processing for online control. In Project 2, we will explore whether these cortical areas also influence feedback corrections with the ipsilateral arm by observing how cooling of PMd and A5 bilaterally or unilaterally impact motor corrections to unexpected limb disturbances. This work provides important new knowledge on the role of cerebral cortex in voluntary control that will guide our ongoing clinical studies quantifying motor impairments associated with various brain injuries and diseases.

column36: Understanding and managing the limits of physiological tolerance in heat vulnerable individuals during rest and physical activity
column37: Canada is entering unchartered territory as it experiences record high temperatures. However, our understanding of the effects of heat exposure on vulnerable Canadians remains incomplete, limiting our ability to make evidence-based decisions on the best strategies to implement to protect the most vulnerable. Recently, we showed that the body's response to heat is impaired in healthy adults as young as 40 years. This impairment is worse in older adults and in those with even well-controlled diabetes. In these individuals, heat tolerance is reduced as the body is unable to cool itself via the evaporation of sweat, placing them at increased risk of heat-induced illnesses or death. Further, we showed that commonly recommended exposure limits such as the American Conference of Governmental Industrial Hygienists Threshold Limit Values (TLV(R)) to manage the health and safety of individuals during exercise in the heat do not protect middle-aged and older adults from potentially dangerous increases in body heat storage and therefore core temperature. Our project will build on this work by using our air calorimeter (a device to accurately measure the heat dissipated and stored by the body) to assess how the presence of hypertension in older adults, with and without type 2 diabetes, may affect the body's ability to lose heat. Using this gold-standard method we will define the heat thresholds where age- and disease-related impairments in the body's capacity to dissipate can lead to dangerous increases in the amount of heat stored in the body (and therefore core temperature) during simulated exposures to hot weather conditions at rest and during exercise. Our project findings will enable 1) the identification of age- and disease-specific 'high risk' weather and exercise conditions, and 2) the development of short-term (heat advisories, work/exercise exposure limits, etc.) and long-term (heat adaptation strategies) heat protection measures to safeguard health during hot weather.

column37: Ankylosing spondylitis (AS), also referred to as Axial Spondyloarthritis, imposes immense burdens on Canadians with this disease in terms of function and quality of life. The chronic pain, stiffness, and fatigue of this condition leads not only to a symptomatic burden but left unchecked the chronic inflammation can lead to total fusion of the spine and marked disability as a result. Despite advances in symptomatic treatments there is no cure at present and no treatment which reliably prevents spinal fusion over time. Recent insights into the genetic and immune basis of AS have revealed that the inflammation in the joints is accompanied by chronic inflammation in the gastrointestinal tract. Our research focusses on identifying factors which lead to activation of these white blood cells in the gut and their subsequent migration to the joints. We will analyze both the unique pattern of white blood cells migrating between gut and joint in order to define what distinctive aspects of the immune response account for the inflammatory attack on tissues. We will also define the genetic signature of the white blood cells which are activated in AS and which maintain the inflammation in the joints. The outcome of our research can have significant impact on the treatment and diagnosis of patients with AS. First, identifying the molecules which direct white blood cells from the gut to the joint sets the stage for novel treatments to block such cell traffic. Secondly, identifying receptors on the critical white blood cells opens the possibility of identifying what activates these cells and what innovative approaches could interrupt the activation of these inflammatory cells. Finally, the addition of genetic profiling of T cells to currently known risk factors could contribute to earlier diagnosis of AS.

column36: Trans PULSE Canada: A National Study of Transgender Health
column37: Transgender (trans) persons are those whose gender identity differs from the sex they were assigned at birth. This project builds on our success in Trans PULSE Ontario (2005-2014), a trans health study that documented major inequalities and changed social and health care policies. Trans PULSE Canada aims to describe and compare health outcomes and access to care for trans people across provinces/territories and within four priority population subgroups: those who are Indigenous, sex workers, immigrants, and/or those who identify as gender non-binary. In addition, we will make comparisons to Ontario's 2009-2010 trans population, as well as to the general population from Statistics Canada data. Grounded in community-based research (CBR) processes, we will conduct a development process that will both shape the priority population sections of the survey and launch a companion Indigenous gender diversity grant. We will conduct a national survey of 3000 trans people. We will then undertake an intensive knowledge translation phase. All Canadian residents 16 and older whose gender identity does not match their sex assigned at birth will be eligible to complete a 'long form' survey or, if unwilling or unable, to choose a 'short form'. Both will span all content areas, with the short form prioritizing key items. The survey (in English or French) will be accessed online or on paper, and can be completed by phone with an interpreter in another language if needed. In ten cities, peer workers will also visit community organizations with electronic tablets, collecting data from trans people who are homeless, street-involved, and/or sex workers. column36: Uncovering the structural basis for the mechanical properties of elastin
column37: The proper function of many human tissues, such as major arteries, lungs, and skin, depends on their capacity for elastic extension and recoil. The protein called elastin is responsible for these vital properties, and defects in the elastic matrix formed by elastin lead to various cardiovascular and pulmonary diseases. In addition, biological techniques have made it possible to generate artificial materials with mechanical properties resembling those of human elastin, with important potential applications as biomaterials for tissue repair and drug delivery. However, to understand the role of elastin in health and disease and to design useful materials with tuneable mechanical properties, we must first understand how elasticity is controlled at the molecular level. In this project, we will use a combination of computer simulations, NMR spectroscopy, and other biophysical approaches to uncover the molecular basis for the mechanical properties of elastin. We have developed simplified model systems that encapsulate the key properties of the entire protein and enable us for the first time to obtain detailed information about how this protein imparts critical mechanical properties to elastic tissues. In particular, we will investigate how the molecular structure of elastin controls extensibility and elastic recoil (how spring-like these materials are), resilience (how much heat is dissipated in every stretching and recoil cycle), and stress relaxation (how much energy it takes to keep them extended). This work will provide critical insight into the factors underlying susceptibility to highly-prevalent vascular diseases such as hypertension, atherosclerosis, and aneurysms. Ultimately, this insight will also guide the rational design of biomimetic materials of high significance to the health and well-being of Canadians, with potential for use in artificial skin for burn victims, vascular grafts for heart patients, or in scaffolds for growth of artificial tissues and organs.

column36: Neurocognitive effects of osteocalcin in type 2 diabetes
column37: As they age, people with type 2 diabetes (T2DM) suffer a faster decline in memory and thinking abilities, allowing dementia to set in on average 2 years earlier than in people without T2DM. As people live longer with T2DM, strategies to protect the brain from the debilitating and costly cognitive complications of T2DM are urgently needed. Current medications for T2DM improve blood sugar control, but they do not fully correct the hormone changes seen in T2DM. New evidence suggests that lower levels of a particular hormone released from bone during exercise, osteocalcin, is associated with brain changes and thinking abilities in older people. This hormone is 35% lower in people with T2DM, but it remains to be seen whether it can explain the deficits in memory that commonly occur in T2DM. We aim to show that lower levels of osteocalcin in the blood predict poorer memory and thinking abilities in people with T2DM. We also aim to show that the benefits of a 6 month exercise program are limited in T2DM by low osteocalcin levels. We will follow people with T2DM as they undertake either 6 months of exercise or an education intervention, to see if exercise increases osteocalcin levels. We will also compare the exercising T2DM group to a control group without T2DM of similar age, gender and body weight undertaking the same exercise intervention to see if people with T2DM can attain the same increases in osteocalcin and cognition when they exercise as people without T2DM. Overall, this study will determine if the body uses osteocalcin to protect against cognitive decline, and if T2DM blocks these benefits. The study will determine whether the osteocalcin system could be targeted with new drugs to prevent cognitive decline in people with T2DM.

column36: Premature carotid atherosclerosis evolution and plaque vulnerability assessed by quantitative ultrasound biomarkers in HIV-infected individuals
column37: Atherosclerosis development is multifactorial and involves the accumulation of lipids within the artery wall. At the early development stages of the disease, the cross-sectional area of the artery is not modified as only an inward vessel wall thickening is observed. With more advanced progression of the disease, partial and total artery blockage may occur thus impacting the flow of oxygen and nutrients to downstream organs. An occluding artery is known in the medical field as a stenosis, whereas the thickening of the artery wall at the origin of this flow obstruction or stenosis is labeled a plaque or an atherosclerotic plaque. Carotid arteries are particularly prone to atherosclerosis and the rupture of a plaque by mechanical stresses (due to the blood pressure and cyclic pulsation of the artery) can lead to the formation of a blood clot, its migration within the arterial system of the brain, leading to a subsequent stroke. Although knowledge on characteristics defining carotid plaques at risk has advanced, predicting rupture is very challenging. A few imaging methods have been developed for this objective, namely magnetic resonance imaging, X-ray computed tomography, positron emission tomography and ultrasound imaging. These technologies provide imaging biomarkers of risk but none of them aim imaging biomechanical stresses at the origin of plaque rupture. We developed a method that can directly image the deformation of the artery wall likely contributing to the initiation of plaque rupture. We are also developing quantitative ultrasound imaging methods to study plaque structural characteristics. The objective of our proposal is to further develop these methods to provide a computer platform to process ultrasound images and extract these new mechanical and tissue biomarkers for clinical evaluation of HIV patients at higher risk of atherosclerosis evolution and stroke.

column36: Cryobiology of Cardiomyocytes and Engineered Living Cardiac Tissue
column37: Heart failure occurs when damaged heart muscle cells cannot pump enough blood and is the cause of over 30% of deaths worldwide. Heart muscle cells, called cardiomyocytes, have almost no ability to replace themselves. Promising treatments involve replacing dead cardiomyocytes with live cardiomyocytes, either as cells or as engineered (lab-grown) tissues. Co-Investigator Radisic's group has developed a new type of tissue from cardiomyocytes, called "Biowires". These can be used as a substitute for heart muscle tissue in research, for example, to test how well new heart drugs work or to test whether other drugs are toxic to heart tissues, a major reason for drug recall. A critical obstacle to the use of cardiomyocytes and Biowires is the inability to store them and keep them alive until needed. Cryopreservation uses temperatures as low as that of liquid nitrogen (-196 C) to preserve biological materials and is the only way to store mammalian (including human) cells and tissues long term. Cryopreservation is used routinely in medicine; cryopreserved stem cells are used to treat blood disorders and cryopreserved heart valves to replace faulty valves (heart valves are not made of cardiomyocytes). Despite the need for cardiomyocytes, there has been no comprehensive research on cryopreserving them. This study will develop procedures to cryopreserve heart muscle cells and engineered heart tissues in such a way that live and functioning cells are recovered when thawed. Principal Investigators Elliott and McGann will use their cryobiology and cryopreservation expertise to carry out the first comprehensive cryobiological study of cardiomyocytes with the outcome of making cardiac cells and tissues available on demand. This collaboration between Canada's leading cryobiology centre at the University of Alberta and Canada's leading tissue-engineering centre at the University of Toronto will advance Canada's international reputation in regenerative medicine and biotechnology.

column36: Pre-dementia at-risk states: a longitudinal study of cognition and neuroimaging biomarkers in Mild Behavioural Impairment (PARADIGM)
column37: Early detection of dementia is essential to implement preventative interventions and optimize treatment. The current approach to detection is to identify overt impairment in memory and thinking as a marker of dementia. However, the vast majority of treatments at this stage have not been successful, with the explanation that disease course is too advanced by the time cognitive impairment is recognized. A new approach to detecting dementia risk earlier involves assessing the emergence of changes in behaviour or personality in later life as potential indicators of brain dysfunction leading to dementia. A neurobehavioural syndrome called Mild Behavioural Impairment (MBI) has been described by an Alzheimer's Association consensus group, which identifies later-life onset of neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS- eg. changes in behaviour or personality, onset of apathy or social disinhibition) as a high-risk group for developing dementia. For some, NPS may be the earliest manifestation of dementia, first noticed by family members and caregivers. Often, these changes in behaviour and personality are attributed to a psychiatric illness, and the connection to dementia is not appreciated. Further, the neuroanatomy of these symptoms is poorly understood. We will recruit people with MBI and perform brain scans and cognitive testing, at baseline and at 2 year follow up. We will compare brain scans in these patients to those collected in other studies funded by Brain Canada and the Canadian Institutes of Health Research to determine the neural signatures of MBI. We will also compare the rates of cognitive decline in MBI to those without MBI, and progression to dementia. This study will help identify symptoms for early diagnosis of dementia and potential targets for early treatment. It will also help us understand the importance of monitoring for emerging changes in personality and behaviour in older adults, as a cost-effective method for identifying people with a high risk of dementia.

column36: Intracrine endothelin signalling in heart cells
column37: Enlargement and stiffening of the heart occurs when the heart is continuously exposed to conditions such as elevated blood pressure and/or increases in the amount of certain molecules, such as hormones, in the blood. Certain factors, including endothelin, also stimulate the heart to enlarge, or hypertrophy, by acting on cardiomyocytes - the muscle cells of the heart. In addition, fibroblasts, another type cell in the heart, become activated, increase in number, and make the walls of the heart stiffer and less able to relax. Relaxation of the heart with each heartbeat is essential for the heart to fill with blood for the next contraction. We are investigating how endothelin, a naturally occurring regulatory protein, is involved in fibroblast activation and cardiomyocyte enlargement. If the underlying cause for these processes (e.g., increased endothelin release, high blood pressure) continue to be present, a point is reached where the heart can no longer function properly. In this proposal, the means by which endothelin stimulates the cells (cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts) of the heart are being studied. There are many steps in the chain of events initiated by endothelin acting upon heart cells. The first step is the interaction of endothelin with specialized proteins, dedicated to binding endothelin, called receptors. The final results include changes in the growth and function of the heart. The cells of the heart contain two types of endothelin receptor. These receptors activate a network of signalling systems, similar to a telephone network, within the cell. In this project, the function of endothelin receptors that are located on the cell nucleus will be studied to determine their role in regulating the growth and function of muscle cells in the heart. The goal of this research it to identify novel targets for the development of drugs to be used to prevent or treat heart diseases.

column36: Characterizing cerebral thrombus composition with Phase-based MRI
column37: In Canada, over 50,000 people suffer a stroke every year. Of those, 85% are ischemic - i.e. caused by a clot that blocks an artery in the brain. Not all clots are the same, and studies have shown that knowing the composition of the clot can help doctors plan the best therapy. For example, some clots can be removed to restart blood-flow and thereby improve patient outcome. Clot composition can also help to infer the source of the clot (i.e. did it come from the heart or break off from a large artery); this is important to determine the best post-stroke treatment to prevent a second stroke. Unfortunately, there are no current methods that can be used to determine clot composition in stroke patients. We have developed a fast new MRI method that that - for the first time - can create different types of images, which are sensitive to the different components of stroke-causing clot (i.e. red blood cells, platelets, fibrin, lipid, calcifications). We plan to determine the relationship of the different MRI parameters and clot composition by first imaging clot samples that have been removed from patients with a stroke (as part of treatment) and correlating these images against histological measures of composition. We will then image patients who have suffered a stroke and still have the thrombus in their brain vessels. Using a combination of MRI parameters we will be able for the first time to distinguish between strokes caused by clots that have come from the heart versus clots that have broken off from a large artery. Knowledge of the source will enable doctors to more appropriately treat patients who have a clot from a cardiac source (usually related to irregular heart rhythm) earlier by giving blood thinners, that results in preventing repeat strokes. Ultimately, our new method can also be used in the emergency department, to determine the best treatment option for each patient's stroke.

column36: Precision diagnostics in childhood diabetes; therapeutic implications
column37: Our research aims to address the problem of certain uncommon forms of diabetes that are often incorrectly diagnosed and, as a consequence, prescribed a treatment that is not the best for the specific patient. There are different causes of diabetes but, in children, the most common form is type 1 diabetes (T1D) that results from autoimmune destruction of the beta cells in the pancreas that produce insulin. Insulin by injections or by pump is the only treatment. Type 2 diabetes, due to obesity and sedentary life, can rarely be seen in teenagers but in a non-obese individual under the age of 18, a high blood sugar is automatically diagnosed as T1D and treated with insulin injections. This is correct in most cases but about 1% of children diagnosed as T1D have uncommon genetic forms of diabetes. These patients have the same symptoms as T1D and are clinically indistinguishable from T1D but they have intact beta cells that only need some "help" and can be treated with pills. We propose that the percentage of these cases is higher than 1%, because we have evidence that not all genes whose mutations cause these uncommon forms have been discovered. In our cross-country collaboration, we will test 5,000 Canadian children and we will select about 1,000 who are the best candidates for a whole exome sequencing, a state-of-the-art technology that allows a thorough examination of all 18,000 known human genes. With the new genes that we will discover, we expect that the total number of such cases will be considerably more than 1%. The number of cases is small, but across Canada there are as many as 3,000 or more patients that can benefit from this life-changing diagnosis. More important than pills vs. injections is that the pills allow much better control of the blood sugar that helps prevent the long-term complications of diabetes (blindness, kidney failure, amputations)

column36: Alberta oil sands development: impact on reproductive health
column37: The oil sands in Northern Alberta have undergone intense development over the past decade. There are widely opposing views of the industry with oil sands supporters highlighting the significant economic benefits for Canadians, and critics raising concerns regarding environmental and human health impacts of oil sands development. The people who are most affected by the oil sands industry are the First Nations communities living in the Peace-Athabasca Delta. Elders and community members are concerned that chemicals produced from oil sands activity are contaminating the water supply and harming the health of wildlife and humans. One of the major areas of concern is related to reproductive health. Oil and gas contaminants have the potential to impact fertility of Indigenous men, women and children as well as the unborn generations. In addition, reduced reproductive success in wildlife means population declines which impact the cultural, economic and social well-being of Indigenous communities through the erosion of the trust they have in their natural environment, and as a consequence, impacts on their ability to harvest and consume traditional foods. column36: Neural and Molecular Basis of Opioid-Induced Respiratory Depression
column37: Opioid medications are widely used in pain management, but present the side-effect of respiratory depression that can be lethal with overdose. Opioid drugs induce sedation, i.e. loss of consciousness, and considerably reduce breathing. When overdosed, opioids can shut down the nervous system, completely stop breathing, induce severe hypoxemia and patients may eventually die. The current epidemic of opioid overdoses is resulting in over 2,500 in Canada according to the Public Health Agency of Canada. Opioid drugs are responsible for thousands of emergency visits every year, causing a severe health and financial burden. Nevertheless, opioids remain the pharmacological cornerstone of modern pain therapy and there are currently no treatments to prevent respiratory depression by opioids without reducing their analgesic properties. The current opioid antagonist naloxone is very effective at blocking mu -opioid receptors, i.e. the receptors that mediate respiratory depression by opioid drugs, but it also blocks opioid analgesia so it cannot be used as a preventive treatment. The development of new therapies has been hindered by a lack of knowledge about how opioid medications alter brain activity and what mechanisms underlie respiratory depression by opioids. This research program proposes to identify the mechanisms underlying respiratory depression by opioids and to find new therapeutic solutions to prevent it. Without a preventive treatment to reduce the severity of respiratory depression, opioid medications will continue to present severe health issues and the death toll associated with opioid drugs will continue to rise.

column36: Stress Hydrocortisone in Pediatric Septic Shock (The SHIPSS trial)
column37: Septic shock accounts for up to 8% of pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) admissions worldwide, carries significant morbidity and has a mortality rate between 5% and 40% depending on the geographic region in which it occurs. Mainstays of treatment involve antibiotics, fluids and medications to improve blood pressure. However, the high morbidity and mortality of pediatric septic shock have led physicians to consider corticosteroids for unstable patients since corticosteroids are inexpensive and widely available. However, although the use of corticosteroids for septic shock has been widely debated for over 40 years, there is no clear evidence for or against this practice. Some pediatric studies have reported an improvement in blood pressure and organ function with corticosteroids while other studies have suggested an increase in blood sugar and the inability to fight infection. We therefore plan to conduct a randomized controlled trial to determine if hydrocortisone (a corticosteroid) compared to placebo improves outcomes (as measured by mortality and quality of life) in children with septic shock. This study will enroll 1032 patients in 30 centres across Canada and the US. Eligible children will include those from age 1 month to 17 years, with a severe infection and need for medications to support their blood pressure. We will exclude patients that have a known reason for receiving corticosteroids, who have malaria or a fungal infection and those who do not wish to participate. We will also assess organ function, potential side effects and healthcare costs in the hydrocortisone and placebo groups. Our study will be the first pediatric septic shock trial that is large enough to assess the potential benefits of corticosteroids and the first trial to assess the effect of a treatment for septic shock on quality of life. The results of this study will provide evidence on which to base recommendations for corticosteroid administration in pediatric septic shock.

column36: The physiology of adult neural stem cells
column37: Since the beginning of the 19th century, the adult brain was considered as an organ deprived of any regenerating capacity. This dogma was, however, shaken by the discovery of neural stem cells in certain regions of the adult human brain and their ability to produce new neurons. This discovery raised an exciting possibility of using endogenous brain regenerative capacity to cure brain damage and neurodegenerative diseases. Yet, although promising, the use of neural stem cells to heal these devastating diseases is far from reach. The main reason for this is that endogenous neural stem cells in the human brain are found in their quiescent "dormant" state and in order to induce brain regenerative capacity we need to understand what are the signals and mechanisms that control the transition of stem cells from their quiescent to proliferative states. In this project using mouse models, advanced imaging and genetic tools, in vivo monitoring of stem cells activity, and pharmacological interventions we will study intrinsic mechanisms underlying maintenance of quiescent state and their entry into the proliferative phase. Our study will allow better understanding of the mechanisms that maintain stem cells quiescence and control their proliferation. This, in turn, will provide new strategies to increase neurogenesis and "turn on" brain regenerative capacity to heal devastating neurodegenerative diseases and brain trauma.

column36: Targeting RIPK3 as a key regulator in the development of SLE
column37: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease that affects approximately one in every 1000 Canadians, and can result in life-long suffering and premature death. Individuals with SLE develop an immune response against their own cells, but it is not known how or why this abnormal immune response arises. Treatment of SLE often involves broad suppression of the immune response, with consequences for the patient's resistance to infection. A better understanding of how SLE arises will lead to more selective drugs that target the specific biological processes that cause SLE. The aim of the proposed research is to investigate how SLE originates. Using an animal model of SLE developed by us, we identified an important protein called "RIPK3". RIPK3 regulates cell death and inflammation, and is essential for the development of SLE in our animal model. In this study, we will determine whether RIPK3-dependent effects on cell death or inflammation, or both, are responsible for murine SLE. Moreover, we will ask whether RIPK3-dependent cell death is increased in cells from SLE patients, and, if so, how the patient's immune system responds to dying cells. For our murine model, we will use mice that are deficient in either cell death or inflammation processes regulated by RIPK3 to identify which of these processes is required for initiating SLE. We will then use drugs (pharmacologic agents) to specifically block these RIPK3-dependent processes. Our research in animal models will provide proof that targeting RIPK3-dependent mechanisms may lead to the prevention or improvement of SLE. Our findings with human cells will indicate whether RIPK3-dependent cell death is important in human SLE. In summary, our proposed research has the potential to generate a novel innovation that can impact both knowledge about SLE and patient care. An improved understanding of SLE will ultimately result in better treatment and prevention of this chronic and debilitating disease.
