column36: The Hsp70 chaperone system and protein quality control
column37: Age-related diseases are a growing medical challenge for an aging population. These include neurodegenerative diseases which have no known cure, such as Parkinson disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), and which are characterized by the accumulation of insoluble protein aggregates. Normally folded proteins can become damaged by mutation or stress, leading to misfolding and aggregation. The chaperone proteins are critical cellular defenses against aggregation. They bind misfolded proteins to promote folding, or help remove permanently damaged proteins by degradation. Nevertheless, damaged proteins build up during aging and are thought to overwhelm the chaperones. Hsp70 is one of the most important chaperones, as it has key roles in protein folding and prevention of aggregation. The different functions of Hsp70 are determined by its regulatory co-chaperone proteins. Recently, another role of Hsp70 was found, in the solubilization of proteins out of aggregates. We propose that disaggregation of proteins is an important pathway for their degradation by proteasomes, which may have an advantage over the slower degradation of aggregates by autophagy. We will examine Hsp70-mediated disaggregation using purified proteins and in live cells, to determine its biochemical mechanisms. A focus will be the co-chaperones and chaperones required for disaggregation. Next, we will address the importance of disaggregation and proteasomal degradation in models of ALS, caused by mutations in the SOD1 protein leading to its aggregation. We will then address other cellular proteins that are at risk of aggregation when the Hsp70 system is impaired. Post-translational modifications on Hsp70 that regulate its function under different stress conditions will be identified. Our project will explore how Hsp70 acts and fails in protein aggregation diseases, and the possibility of enhancing its function towards future therapies.

column36: Pol II and its R-loops in the control of rDNA and genome stability
column37: The human body is composed of trillions of cells, the longevity of which is dependent on the balance between forces that promote or stall growth. On one hand, early cell stalling is known as senescence and it can lead to premature cellular aging if kept unchecked. On the other hand, uncontrolled cell growth can lead to cancer. Critical to the cell's ability to strike the right balance between growth and senescence are highly repetitive DNA regions known as ribosomal DNA (rDNA) repeats. These rDNA repeats harbour genes from which molecules known as ribosomal RNA (rRNA) are produced. rRNA production is critical to general protein production and cell growth. In contrast, DNA damage at rDNA repeats can lead to premature senescence. How cells strike the right balance between the impact of rDNA repeats on growth and senescence remains unclear. Here, we pursue new findings suggesting that a new protein complex localizes to poorly understood spacers located between rDNA units in order to optimize protein production and growth while limiting DNA damage and cell senescence. We have two main objectives. First, we wish to decipher the rDNA-regulatory role of this complex at rDNA in order to reveal new mechanisms that are critical to the regulation of growth and senescence in human cells. Second, we will exploit the new knowledge of this mechanism to preferentially induce early senescence and limit tumorigenic potential in breast cancer cells. Overall, this work will uncover key health-related knowledge pertaining to the balance between cell growth and senescence while revealing how it can be exploited to combat deadly human diseases.

The other two groups are patients who had bypass surgery after the recommended time and those who had stenting. The proposed study will help strengthen health care in Canada. Our research will add new data from a large number of patients treated at various times after treatment decision. The data will help doctors to compare delayed surgery and immediate stenting. column36: Oriented cell division in prostate stem cell homeostasis and cancer
column37: Prostate cancer is one of the most common and most deadly cancers in males. Over the years, research has mostly focused on the identification of treatments against advanced forms of prostate cancer. In this grant proposal, we rather aim to understand the cellular environment that promote cancer initiation, to eventually devise preventative treatments aimed at maintaining a healthy prostate tissue organization. Such approach is not currently available for prostate cancer. Our recent results in mouse models show that when the cells of the prostate divide in the plane of the tissue (horizontal), they maintain a proper tissue architecture made of one layer of basal cells and one layer of luminal cells. However, when the cells divide vertically, they create an aberrant layer of cells that lose their polarity, proliferate more and harbor stem/progenitor cell characteristics. We believe that this cellular environment promotes the birth and growth of tumor initiating cells. Here, we will study how cells defective in the orientation of cell divisions generate this abnormal cell population and will identify new regulators that promote vertical divisions. We will also generate cancer initiating cells (single cells missing the tumor suppressor Pten) and identify the detailed characteristics in the cellular environments that promote their growth. We expect the normal prostate epithelium to suppress cancer initiation but the aberrant depolarized cell populations to promote it. We will corroborate our results in premalignant human tissues obtained from our clinical collaborators and link these results to disease outcome. Together these results will greatly advance our understanding of oriented cell division and the maintenance of tissue architecture. More importantly, it will identify the characteristics of premalignant lesions that are associated with cancer initiation and progression. These results will be critical to develop interventions aimed at preventing prostate cancer.

column36: Neuroimaging Prodromal Neurodegeneration in Synucleinopathy
column37: Neurodegenerative diseases like Parkinson's disease (PD) and Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) have a long prodromal interval, meaning that symptoms have started but the disease is not yet fully developed. Studying prodromal PD and DLB was limited until the discovery that >80% of people with idiopathic REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD), a disorder in which people act out their dreams at night, actually have prodromal PD/DLB. This means that studying people with iRBD gives a rare opportunity to directly observe the earliest stages of disease. Although routine clinical scans in PD/DLB are normal, there have been major recent developments. PET and SPECT scanning can find loss of the dopamine system which underlies motor parkinsonism. We have developed a new PET scan of the cholinergic system, to help understand cognitive loss. Also, there are new MRI scan techniques with exciting potential to identify early PD/DLB. We will recruit 40 iRBD patients and 20 controls. They will have a comprehensive clinical prodromal marker assessment as part of our ongoing cohort study (our center has the largest cohort of iRBD patients in the world). We will follow patients each year, to see the scans predict development of disease over time. column37: Brain arteries control how much blood is delivered to nerve cells. To ensure the right amount of blood is delivered, cells in the artery alter their electrical activity using "ion channels". As their name suggests, ion channels allow sodium, chloride, potassium and calcium to move across a membrane and there are many different types. One, called the inward rectifying K+ (KIR) channel is unique as it breaks away from expectations, leading us to raise key questions. Is KIR a simple channel or is it regulated in a way we haven't defined? What is the function of this unique channel and what impact does disease have on it? We propose that KIR channels in brain blood vessels are regulated by plasma membrane lipids. Specific lipids allow KIR channels to sense blood pressure and flow and when cholesterol rises, this channel is compromised. Goal, Aims: We will examine KIR channels in brain blood vessels and determine the chemical agents and stimuli which control them. There are three aims and they include: 1)Defining whether membrane lipids regulate KIR. 2)Defining whether blood pressure/flow regulate KIR. 3)Defining whether high cholesterol impairs KIR. Methods, Expertise: We will test ideas in cells and brain blood vessels from rats, genetically altered mice and humans. We will use computer models, measure the electrical activity of isolated cells, see how vessel size changes and quantify brain perfusion. Our work is supported by a network of collaborators. Impact: This grant challenges the idea that KIR is a boring background channel. We argue that KIR is uniquely regulated by membrane lipids, enabling them to sense blood pressure/flow, the dominant factors setting vessel size and tissue perfusion. We incorporate Knowledge Translation by working with neurosurgeons who provide brain arteries so that we can validate our ideas in humans. We also use animal models of high cholesterol to see whether this lipid impairs KIR and consequently blood vessel size.

column37: Optimal self-regulation, the ability to set limits and manage one's own emotions, attention, and behaviour is vital to health and success in life. Since the building blocks of self-regulation begin to develop at conception, maternal health problems, dietary imbalances, and physical inactivity during pregnancy can lead to self-regulation difficulties in offspring. Many Canadian women consume an unhealthy diet and/or fail to get enough exercise during pregnancy. It is not surprising then that up to 40% of women enter pregnancy overweight and that even more (up to 75%) gain too much weight during pregnancy. Despite these facts, no studies in humans have examined if interventions that optimize maternal diet and exercise during pregnancy can improve the emotional and/or behavioural functioning of their children. To address this knowledge gap, we propose a study that will follow the offspring of the 250 women that will be enrolled in an ongoing study of a nutrition+exercise intervention in pregnant women. The nutrition component of this intervention consists of an individualized nutrition plan that is tailored to women's needs, as well as educational sessions with a dietitian. column36: Molecular characterization of VHL-HIF axis in cancer
column37: Oxygen homeostasis or balance is a vital organizing principle for human development and physiology. A universal response to compromised oxygen availability involves a protein called hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF), which accumulates during low oxygen levels or hypoxia to trigger the expression of numerous genes including those that promote new blood vessel formation (angiogenesis), anaerobic metabolism, and the production of oxygen-carrying red blood cells to facilitate adaptation and survival in hypoxia. We and others have shown that von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) tumour suppressor protein targets HIF for oxygen-dependent degradation. Mutations in VHL cause VHL disease, characterized by the development of tumours in multiple organs including the kidney, as well as a chronic condition called polycythemia where patients produce too many red blood cells. Notably, kidney cancer remains to be the leading cause of both morbidity and mortality for VHL patients. More recently, mutations in HIF have been reported to cause certain types of cancers also observed in VHL patients as well as polycythemia, revealing a new class of HIF-driven disease. However, it remains unclear what drives the metastatic process of kidney cancer and why certain HIF mutations cause cancer while other HIF mutations cause polycythemia. This proposal, based on our promising preliminary data, aims to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying these mysteries with important clinical implications.

column37: Chronically insufficient sleep is common in our society and is increasingly recognized as a cause of health and safety problems with significant economic costs. Insights gained from the proposed research could have significant health and economic impacts since sleep is so important, yet so often sacrificed for other activities. Ultimately, the proposed research will help us develop innovative strategies for coping with the negative impacts of reduced sleep and help reduce the adverse impacts of chronic sleep loss on the health of both men and women.

column37: In recent years, we have shown that proteins called LAR-family phosphatases are necessary for the normal maturation of the connection between the ureter and the bladder. Using this DNA we found that some of these patients seem to carry mutations in the programmed cell death pathway we identified. We will characterize further these mutations and validate them in mouse models. column37: One in five Canadians suffers from chronic pain, a debilitating condition that requires prompt access to care for effective treatment. Individuals with chronic pain report the lowest health-related quality of life among all patients with chronic conditions. We will begin by looking at the unique needs of patients in each province and adjusting the service to best address them. Next, we will launch the service in select regions within each province and identify any challenges we face. Lastly, we will expand the services provincially, measure their outcomes on patients' care, and create a series of communication tools that can be used by others looking to launch eConsult in their own regions. Our team includes experts in eConsult and chronic pain care, as well as patient partners who will review the entire process and have a say in how the project is run. column36: Organization of the Cerebellum
column37: The majority of neurons (up to 85%) in the brain are found in the cerebellum. The cerebellum integrates information from various sensory systems and is involved in numerous processes including motor control, learning and cognition. How the cerebellum organizes information from the various senses is still poorly understood. The cerebellum has a unique organization: some neurochemicals are expressed as "stripes" throughout the cerebellum. The most thoroughly studied of these neurochemicals is the enzyme aldolase C, also known as zebrin. Although the exact role of zebrin is not clear, it is expressed in the same way in all vertebrate species studied, indicating that it is essential for cerebellar function. The organization is such that there are stripes of neurons that express zebrin alternating with stripes of cells that do not express zebrin. The goal of the proposed research is to understand how these stripes relate to function and processing of information in the cerebellum. We use a part of the cerebellum known as the vestibulocerebellum as a model. This is an area where visual, vestibular and spinal information is integrated in order to control eye movements, posture, locomotion, and balance. To understand how information is organized with respect to the zebrin stripes, we will determine how the visual, vestibular, and spinal connections are associated with particular zebrin stripes in the vestibulocerebellum. Moreover, we will record from neurons in particular zebrin stripes to determine the nature of sensory processing within each stripe. These studies will provide basic information about the principles of fundamental sensory organization in the cerebellum. This is critical for understanding diseases of the vestibulocerebellum that cause disturbances of visuo-motor behaviour (e.g., oscillopsia, oculomotor abnormalities, vertigo), and diseases that affect the cerebellum in general such as Wernicke's encephalopathy, Alzheimer's disease and autism.

column37: The brain has two main cell types - neurons and glia - and interactions between them are crucial for many processes involved in brain development and information processing. For example, their two-way communication regulates the number and types of cells that are produced, and influences how neurons communicate chemically with one another at their sites of contact called synapses. We are particularly interested in how glia use Excitatory Amino Acid Transporters EAATs) to take up important chemical transmitters like glutamate from synapses, and to act as channels for the passage of chloride ions in and out of cells. Defects of EAATs are a common feature of a variety of disorders such as ataxia, stroke, epilepsy and neurodegenerative diseases. Historically there has been a dearth of tools to study and manipulate glial subtypes in the laboratory. We have spent several years generating and collecting such tools, and we have launched new approaches to study neuron-glial interactions. In particular we are using a genetically tractable model organism, the fruit fly, because it has a simple yet sophisticated brain and central nervous system (CNS) in which neurons and glia perform many of the same functions they do in humans. It is also easy to study how the CNS controls behaviors like movement and sleep. The fruit fly has two EAATs that predominate in two distinct subtypes of glia. In this proposal we are specifically addressing the following questions: What is the role of the EAAT1 chloride channel? How do mutations of the EAAT1 cause episodic ataxia? column37: Brain tumors are the most common cause of death and long term disability in children, and adolescent/young adults (AYA). Low grade gliomas (LGG) are the most common brain cancer in this age group. Childhood and adult LGG have very different biology and patient outcomes. Most children with LGG have excellent survival rates but have suffered from long term sequelae of over-aggressive therapy. In contrast, adult LGG typically transform to high grade glioma resulting in very poor outcome even with aggressive therapy. Importantly, some AYA LGG behave like childhood LGG and unfortunately get unnecessary toxic treatments. Similarly, some childhood LGG behave as adult LGG and die from their tumor. We will then the right new therapy to fit the right mutation. Finally, we will treat these children and AYA with targeted therapies which will replace the current toxic surgery and chemo-radiation approaches. Completion of this project will transform our way of treating these children and young adults to improve survival rates for these patients. This study can serve as a model for other cancers in this vulnerable age group.

column36: The influence of heme on the gut microbiota and colon carcinogenesis
column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the 2nd most commonly diagnosed cancer in Canada, with an average of 72 Canadians being diagnosed with CRC every day. A link between red meat consumption and the development of CRC has been documented by many studies, and has been partially attributed to the presence of heme in the red meat. Heme, an essential part of the protein hemoglobin, is an iron-containing molecule that serves to bind oxygen. An important role in the development of CRC has also been attributed to the gut microbiota, the complex community of microorganisms, mainly bacteria, that live in the digestive tract. Because bacteria compete for iron, an essential metal indispensable for their growth, and not all bacteria are equipped with the necessary tools to capture and utilize heme iron, we think that heme may change the gut microbiota composition by promoting the growth of certain bacteria over others and cause a bacterial imbalance (dysbiosis). We have generated preliminary results suggesting that dietary heme induces dysbiosis, aggravates inflammation of the colon (colitis, as seen in Inflammatory Bowel Disease), and promotes CRC development in rodents. The overall goal of our research is to determine the role and the mechanisms by which dietary heme modulates the gut microbial composition. In addition, we will test different strategies based on natural and engineered probiotics to reverse the non-beneficial effects of heme-induced microbiota shifts. The high incidence of CRC in Canada compared to other countries has increased the need for preventive measurements, for which it is critical to understand contributing mechanisms. This project will further our understanding of the link between heme, microbiota, and CRC, and how to reverse gut microbiota imbalances (dysbiosis), opening novel avenues for CRC prevention. This project builds on our team's unique expertise in iron metabolism, microbiology, and bioengineering as well as specialist platforms in the institute.

column36: Cancer Therapy exploiting Conditional Synthetic Lethality based on Genotoxic Stress levels
column37: Because cancer cells have lost checkpoints that healthy cells have, they have increased levels of DNA damage. This DNA damage causes particular problems during replication, when cells make a copy of their DNA. (When a cell divides, both cells should have a complete set of the DNA.) Cancer cells therefore have higher stress levels than healthy cells and they rely on certain remaining pathways to survive this stress. An important signaling pathway after replication stress is initiated by a protein called ATR. Another important signaling protein is Wee1. Our unpublished studies indicate that cancer cells strongly rely on these two proteins to survive, and inhibiting the function of Wee1 or ATR by selective drugs is harmful to the cancer cells. But if both, ATR and Wee1, are inhibited, the cancer cell killing is stronger than one would expect from just an additive effect of each drug alone. We call this "Synergy". This promises to get a much better therapy response with a novel treatment combining the two drugs. Furthermore we see the synergistic killing in cancer cells at doses well tolerated by healthy cells. This is important to avoid side effects which are due to killing of healthy cells. In our preclinical studies, using human cancers grown in mice, we will test the combination treatment targeting ATR and Wee1 for the ability to inhibit tumour growth and prevent metastasis. In addition we hope to understand which tumours are most likely to respond to the combined inhibition of Wee1 and ATR inhibition. Because the Wee1 and ATR inhibitors we are using for our studies are drugs already being tested in the clinic (on their own, not in combination), our knowledge could soon find application in actual patient treatment. Because our lab focuses on breast cancer, we first will study that type of cancer. Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women in Canada and worldwide.

column37: Schizophrenia is associated with long-lasting health, social and financial burden for patients, families, caregivers and society. According to the World Health Organization, this burdensome illness is one of the top 10 causes of disability in developed countries. The costs associated with hospitalization, lifelong treatment and loss of productivity lead to a great economic burden. In Canada, the total annual costs associated with schizophrenia are over $10 billion. The main reason for this heavy burden is that 25-30% of schizophrenia patients respond very poorly to antipsychotic medication. Moreover, psychotherapeutic treatment alternatives are very limited for this suffering population. This unmet clinical need requires innovation and action. Psychotherapeutic treatment alternatives such as Cognitive Behavior Therapy (CBT) are very limited and provide at best moderate results. Virtual reality (VR) opens new exciting avenues to treat this illness. With immersive VR, we recently tested a novel psychotherapeutic intervention, Avatar Therapy (AT), where the therapist engages in a dialogue with the patient through a virtual representation of their distressing voice. This relational and experiential approach offers a unique opportunity to help patients gain control over their voice. The preliminary results of our randomized-controlled trial (RCT) pilot showed a large effect on auditory verbal hallucination for AT and a moderate effect for CBT. The main goal of the currently proposed RCT study will be to show that AT is superior to CBT for the treatment of chronic auditory hallucinations in schizophrenia. As evidence-based therapeutic options are limited for this burdensome illness and provide only modest symptomatic relief, the current trial will contribute to the validation of a novel approach answering a fundamental clinical need. The demonstration of the superior efficacy of AT would be a great breakthrough and will open new avenues to clinical treatment.

column36: Molecular mechanisms controlling the phase behavior and biosynthetic activity of the nucleolus
column37: Living cells are divided into specialized compartments called organelles. Typically, membranes form a selective barrier between organelles and the cytoplasm, such that each compartment can maintain a distinct biochemical composition that is tailored to its function. By concentrating substrates and isolating reactions, membrane-bound organelles increase the rate and efficiency of cellular metabolism. However, cells also contain organelles that are not enclosed by membranes. With no physical barrier, molecules can freely exchange between these compartments and the surrounding cytoplasm or nucleoplasm. Recent progress has focused on the composition and assembly of membraneless organelles, but their function remains poorly understood. The proposed research aims to establish how the unusual structure of membraneless organelles impacts their function. To answer this question, we will use quantitative imaging to visualize the nucleolus in the model organism C. elegans. The nucleolus is a membraneless organelle that produces ribosomes, molecular machines that a cell needs to grow. Indeed, cancer cells, which experience uncontrolled growth, have enlarged and hyperactive nucleoli. Moreover, there is increasing evidence that links neurodegenerative disorders, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Huntington's disease, to changes in the fluidity and activity of stress granules and other membraneless organelles. Thus, understanding the relationship between the fluidity and activity of the nucleolus in the worm has the potential to advance the diagnosis, treatment and prevention of human disease.

column37: Most cells that give rise to cancer in the skin, breast, lung, colon or many other organs have a common feature: they are epithelial cells. Epithelial cells have to lose their characteristic cell shape either partially or completely to initiate tumor formation or invade other organs to form metastases. This process is called epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and is a key step in cancer progression. We will study EMT in a novel unique model to gain insight into cancer formation that will ultimately help to diagnose and combat cancer. Epithelial cells are held together by a molecular glue called adherens junctions. These structures prevent epithelial cells from excess proliferation to form tumors or from migration to other organs to form metastases. It has been established that the loss of adherens junctions occurs during EMTs and is a key early step in promoting cancer. We have established a model in which the loss of adherens junctions during EMTs can be investigated with unprecedented clarity, and is analyzed with computational tools that reveal details of the process that have not been seen before. The application of state-of-the-art live imaging approaches has greatly advanced our understanding of how cell change shape and molecules control cell behavior in recent years. EMTs occur in cancer but also in normal development, and the underlying mechanisms are believed to be essentially the same. Cells in the fruit fly embryo that give rise to the nervous system undergoes an EMT-like process in a context that is uniquely accessible to advanced live imaging methods. Fruit flies are a proven model in cancer research; combining the powerful genetic and molecular tools available in the fly with our state-of-the-art imaging capabilities, and the ongoing development of computational tools for image analysis will give us novel insights into a core process in cancer progression.

Our hypothesis is that Foxp3+ Bregs develop in lymph nodes, then migrate to the nervous system and restrain inflammation (e.g. via anti-inflammatory molecules); however, neutrophils counteract these Bregs by inhibiting their development via proinflammatory mediators, thereby promoting EAE. To test this, we will use state-of-the-art techniques to: 1) clarify the nature and fate of Foxp3+ Bregs in two forms of EAE; 2) validate that neutrophils suppress the development of Foxp3+ Bregs and elucidate the underlying mechanism; and 3) determine the ability of Foxp3+ Bregs to attenuate EAE when altered by genetic manipulations or when transplanted into EAE mice. Results will be confirmed in human. This project will unveil the existence of a neutrophil-Breg connection of great clinical relevance. For example, this connection offers a mechanism by which neutrophils may contribute to MS without entering the brain. This project will also help to identify new biomarkers and therapeutic strategies (e.g. anti-inflammatory drugs, autologous transplantation of Bregs) for MS and other immune conditions.

column36: Contribution of Dioxin-Like Chemicals to Beta Cell Death and Dysfunction in Diabetes
column37: Diabetes prevalence is rising at an alarming rate, yet the factors that trigger disease onset and drive disease progression are still poorly understood. Generally, diabetes is caused by a deficiency in insulin-secreting beta cells, which are located throughout the pancreas in endocrine clusters called 'islets'. There is mounting evidence that exposure to environmental chemicals is linked to increased diabetes risk, but the effects of pollutants on beta cells are only beginning to emerge. Our project will investigate the contribution of environmental pollutants to beta cell death and dysfunction during diabetes. We will first examine the impact of a specific pollutant called 'TCDD' in mouse models of diabetes to determine: a) whether mice with long-term TCDD exposure are more susceptible to an environment that promotes diabetes than non-exposed mice (controls), and b) whether pre-diabetic mice are more sensitive to TCDD exposure than healthy mice. Since TCDD is the most potent member of the 'dioxin' family, it serves as a useful model for the ~400 'dioxin-like' chemicals in the environment. Therefore, we will also examine how a variety of related dioxin-like chemicals impact human beta cell function and survival. Finally, we will measure the concentration of environmental pollutants in human islets from organ donors, and determine if pollutant exposure is linked to beta cell health or diabetes incidence. If we identify environmental chemicals that are associated with pancreatic beta cell death or dysfunction in human tissues, then subsequent studies will explore the role of chronic exposure to these predicted beta cell toxins in diabetic mouse models. Overall, this important work will inform the clinical community and policy makers about priority chemicals of concern for diabetes risk.

column36: Investigating mechanisms of in vivo variability in spindle assembly checkpoint strength
column37: Uncontrolled cell division forms the basis for all cancers. Consequently, most anti-cancer drugs block the cell cycle, with many specifically targeting mitosis (e.g. Taxol). Variable drug efficiency is a major obstacle in the development of robust cancer therapies. It is not known why cancer cell responses vary, but underlying differences in core mitotic processes may contribute. Proper cell division is also vital to maintain the function of many adult tissues, allowing adult stem cells to sustain normal tissue turnover and to promote tissue regeneration following damage. A decline in stem cell function has been linked to a range of age-related pathologies, including organ failure and the development of cancer. A significant gap in our understanding of mitosis derives from the lack of model systems to study cells dividing within their native environment. Consequently, we know very little about how mitosis occurs within specific cell types, within the complex physiological environment of a living organism. Importantly, mitosis in both adult stem cells and tumor cells will be influenced by these in vivo factors. The goal of this proposal is to investigate how mitosis occurs in vivo and to uncover how key aspects of mitotic regulation are affected by cell fate and broader physiological factors. We use a small nematode worm (C. elegans) as a model system, which permits live-imaging studies of mitosis within intact living animals that are challenging in mammalian models and not possible in human subjects. As many C. elegans genes perform conserved functions in humans and several major mitotic proteins were discovered in C. elegans, it is highly likely that the mechanisms uncovered in my lab will be important for mitosis in human cells. Understanding how mitosis occurs in vivo will fill a major gap in our understanding of the cell biology of mitosis and inform the development of new, more effective drugs designed to improve adult stem cell function or to treat cancer.

column36: Predicting Seizure Responsiveness to Neuromodulation Using Connectomic Profiling
column37: Epilepsy is the most common serious neurological condition that affects children. Active epilepsy interferes with normal childhood development, leading to disability and diminished quality-of-life. One-third of children will continue to have seizures despite the best available medications and therefore surgical treatments are increasingly utilized to reduce seizure frequency and mitigate the burden of the illness. For the most severely affected children, vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) offers hope of seizure control. An electrical nerve stimulator is attached to the vagus nerve at the neck and an implanted battery delivers continuous electrical stimulation that ascends to the brain, rendering the brain less susceptible to seizures. At present, however, only a minority of children implanted with VNS achieve meaningful reduction in seizures. There are no pre-operative means to identify those who will and will not respond to treatment. This lack of knowledge unnecessarily subjects some children to the risks of surgery and also deprives others, who would be better candidates from potential benefit. Because of the high cost of VNS, this also imposes a significant burden on the Canadian healthcare system. Using multiple, complementary advanced neuroimaging techniques, we will study how the connectivity of the brain circuits that mediate the effects of VNS differ between those who do and do not respond to treatment and compare them to typically-developing children. Findings from these multiple modalities will be used to train a machine learning algorithm to prospectively predict whether or not a child is likely to respond to VNS. For children and their families, these findings will mean less uncertainty about surgical outcomes. For healthcare providers, this will provide the means to deliver the correct treatment to the right child. For the Canadian healthcare system, this will translate into better allocation of limited healthcare resources.

column37: Background: Obesity and the linked cardiovascular risk factors are common in youth, and are associated with health problems later in life. Changing health behaviours is effective in reducing risk factors, but hard to implement. The Living Green and Healthy for Teens app has been rigorously developed as an evidence-based, user-friendly, stakeholder-reviewed tool to facilitate healthy behaviour change. Goals: This research will determine whether the gamified LiGHT app for youth and parents will improve healthy eating and activity habits among 10-15 year-olds over 2 years. It will also determine the effects on body fat, weight, fitness, quality of life, as well as parents' eating and activity habits. Methods and expertise: 500 youth from the Hamilton community who have at least one smartphone in the family will be randomly assigned to receive either the interactive gamified LiGHT app which has both youth and parent interfaces, or a simple list of online resources (control). Visits at 6 months, 1 and 2 years will evaluate questionnaires on food intake, screen and sleep time, as well as 1 week of movement sensor (accelerometry) data to quantify physical activity and sedentary time. The research team has expertise in recruitment and retention among cohorts of youth, as well as successful completion of large randomized trials, and development and community-based implementation of behavioural interventions for obesity treatment and prevention. Expected outcomes: Many health apps are either not developed based on evidence or are not engaging for users, and very few are studied systematically for their effectiveness in improving health, especially among youth. This trial will evaluate the fairly long-term use of an app that has been developed in Canada based on these principles. If effective, wide dissemination on a population scale through simple electronic channels will facilitate improved cardiovascular risk profiles for any family with access to a smartphone.

column36: Overcoming chemotherapy-resistance in triple-negative breast cancer
column37: Over 20,000 Canadian women are diagnosed and more than 5,000 die each year from Breast cancer (BCa). BCa is subdivided into at least five different subtypes. Some BCa patients benefit from targeted therapies. However, those with Triple-Negative BCa (TNBC) can only be treated with chemotherapy, which fails to cure most patients with metastatic disease due to the development of chemotherapy-resistant tumours within a few years of treatment. Hence, there is an urgent need to understand how resistance develops to find better therapies against TNBC. We and others showed that resistance to drug treatment across different cancer types relies on "cosmetic" changes to the DNA, known as "epigenetics". In parallel, we recently developed over 40 new drugs preventing cosmetic changes. Finally, we created preclinical models of chemotherapy resistance in TNBC derived from patients' tumours. Hence, we now have the means to identify and to drug the cosmetic changes to the DNA arising in chemotherapy-resistant TNBC using the most relevant preclinical models to work towards finding a cure against this deadly disease. From this project, we expect to identify the epigenetic basis for chemotherapy resistance, to uncover new means to treat chemotherapy-resistant TNBC and to demonstrate their efficacy in preclinical trial settings using patient tumour derived models. Together, this should identify new effective strategies to eradicate TNBC. This application builds upon the complementary expertise of Dr. Lupien, Senior Scientist and expert in epigenetics and drug resistance in breast cancer; Dr. Arrowsmith, Senior Scientist leading the epigenetic drugs design; Dr. Cescon, a Breast Medical Oncologist expert facilitating the incorporation of research discoveries to the clinic and improve breast cancer treatment. Together, these investigators have made impactful discoveries in breast cancer and now propose a research program poised to significantly improve the care of TNBC patients.

column36: Genomics of Aortic Stenosis - an International Collaboration
column37: Aortic valve disease is the most common form of heart valve disease in the developed world and a major burden to society. With the ageing of the Canadian population, aortic valve disease is expected to become increasingly common. Currently, over 2.5 million individuals in North America have aortic stenosis, which is a narrowing of the aortic valve, the main valve of the heart, and leads to symptoms of heart failure and sometimes death. Despite the major importance of this disease worldwide, there are currently no medical treatments to prevent the development of aortic stenosis. The lack of preventative treatments stems in large part to a poor understanding of the causes of this disease. Using cutting-edge genetic technologies, we plan to build on our recent genetic discovery linking an unusual type of cholesterol to this disease. In this proposed project, we will scan the entire genome of several thousand individuals with and without aortic stenosis to try to pinpoint regions in the DNA that may predispose to the development of this disease. This may provide clues for why certain people develop this disease. We hope to use these clues to identify currently available drugs that could be useful to treat this disease. Using this strategy, we have already identified one potential new therapy that we will be tested soon to evaluate whether this can stop the disease process. If successful, our program would be notable in several ways. First, it will represent the largest study of this type worldwide. Second, we expect to glean major insights into the biology of aortic stenosis that may help us identify a treatment. Ultimately, a new treatment for aortic stenosis would significantly impact the cardiovascular health of many individuals in Canada and throughout the world.

column36: Quantity of Opioids for Acute Pain and Limit Unused Medication (OPUM study)
column37: Opioids (morphine and morphine-like substances) are often prescribed to patients to manage pain after an emergency department visit. In the past 20 years, opioid prescriptions have risen sharply, accompanied by a significant rise in opioid misuse (e.g., recreational or non-medical use, potentially leading to addiction or overdose). One explanation for this crisis is the availability and easy access of leftover opioid pills in Canadian homes, allowing family members (including children) and friends to take them for reasons other than pain relief. Canada has no recommendations for the dosage, duration, or quantity of opioids that physicians should prescribe to manage acute pain at home. Physicians are therefore left guessing as to how much to prescribe when a patient with a condition like a fracture or renal colic is discharged from the emergency department. Our preliminary study showed that two-thirds of the pills from the initial opioid prescription to treat acute pain actually remained unused and were therefore available for potential misuse. We propose to determine how many opioid pills are consumed by patients who suffer from acute pain as they recover at home. We will ask 2,560 patients (from 6 Canadian hospitals) to record their pain medication consumption in a 14-day diary. We will also determine, their pain intensity level, whether or not they had new opioid prescriptions, and health services revisits. In case of missing information, patients will be contacted by phone at 2 weeks. The overall aim is to help emergency department physicians prescribe the right number of pills in order to manage patients' pain and at the same time reduce substantially leftovers available for potential misuse.

column36: The role of muscle pyruvate kinase 2 (Pkm2) in cardiomyocyte proliferation and cardiac repair.
column37: Heart failure occurs when the heart is unable to pump enough blood to meet the demands of the body. In the adult, the heart is not able to repair itself to any significant degree. As such, after a heart attack, the damage to the heart is permanent with a loss of heart muscle cells. While the heart attempts to repair itself, it is unable to replace the lost heart muscle cells. The medications that we use can only slow this chain of events and over time the function of the heart becomes worse and patients die. We wish to find ways to help the heart heal itself by allowing it to renew and replace the lost heart muscle cells. This type of research is not only of scientific importance but can have an impact on a large number of Canadians who have heart attacks and develop a failing heart. The heart muscle cells need a lot of energy to function properly and allow the heart to act as a pump. When the heart fails, there are major changes that occur in the source and amount of energy that is generated in the heart muscle cells. This is controlled by a family of molecules called muscle pyruvate kinase (Pkm). In the cancer field, specific Pkm's have been shown to also control how cancer cells multiply and produce more of themselves. How this happens has still not been clearly defined. Interestingly, the observations that have been made in the cancer field can also be seen in the heart. More specifically, if we change the amount of the Pkm protein produced, the heart is protected from the damage that occurs during a heart attack and the heart actually repairs itself by replacing heart muscle cells through a process called proliferation. Therefore, we wish to work in this exciting area of research to define the mechanisms that are responsible for repair in the heart after it is injured. This work will allow us to develop new drugs and provide the foundation to do clinical trials in the future.

column37: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a life-threatening lung disease. It is a major cause of suffering and death in Canada and places a large burden on our healthcare system. The objective of our research is to investigate whether cigarette smoking impairs the ability to fight bacterial infections because of a weakened immune system. To do this, we will investigate immune function in smokers and patients with COPD, as well as experimental models of cigarette smoke exposure. The goal of our research is to understand how smoking damages the immune system and how to rebuild protective immunity against harmful bacteria. To accomplish this goal, we have assembled a team of world experts in clinical research, immunology, microbiology, and virology to tackle this challenging health problem. By pursuing this research, we will gain a better understanding of the harmful effects of cigarette smoke on the immune system. Our goal is to develop novel drugs to restore immune function in patients with COPD. Our experimental approach is innovative, as we aim to prevent infections rather than deal with the often irreversible damage caused by infections.

column37: On a daily basis, our DNA, the genetic material that determines who we are and how we function, is under constant insult by chemicals and radiation found in the food we eat and in the environment we live. Fortunately cells in our body have evolved a number of mechanisms to ensure that damaged DNA is repaired promptly and properly so that the integrity of our DNA is maintained. One of these repair mechanisms is specifically evolved to repair DNA in which breaks occur in both strands (double strand breaks). DNA double strand breaks are extremely deleterious and if not repaired properly, they can lead to loss or deregulation of genes that help prevent cancer. As we age or in some genetic conditions, this break repair mechanism is altered or weakened, favoring the development of cancer. In addition, cancer can also arise from a disruption in the maintenance of telomeres, specialized structures found at the ends of our chromosomes. Understanding how DNA double strand breaks are repaired and how telomeres are maintained will be crucial to finding solutions to eradicate cancer or to slow down cancer progression. The proposed research aims to elucidate the role of CSB, a protein recently uncovered to play a role in DSB repair and telomere maintenance, in cancer cells. The knowledge gained from this proposed research will not only deepen our understanding of these two processes but also lay the foundation for future exploration of CSB as a target in cancer therapeutics.

column36: Effectiveness of Interventions in Early Daycare to Prevent Disruptive Behaviours in Children of Low-Income Neighbourhoods (I-CARE): A 2x2 Factorial Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial.
column37: Disruptive behaviour problems (DBPs) violate social norms and generate high costs to society. Adults with DBPs have problems ranging from mental health issues to substance abuse, spousal abuse, depression, and suicide. Disruptive behaviours begin in early childhood. Toddlers do not know how to express and meet their needs, so they may kick, hit, scream, and fight. As they grow older, they learn more acceptable ways to obtain what they want and disruptive behaviours fade away. Studies in the USA in the 1960s-80s show that child care-based interventions with parental support have long-term positive impacts in low-income neighbourhoods. In Canada today, where healthcare is universally available and daycare use is common, the same conditions do not necessarily apply. We need information on which interventions work best for low-income families in real-life situations and which are the most cost-effective. For example, parenting skills interventions are 3 times more expensive than daycare-based programs. Daycares are essentially preschools where parents send their children during working hours. We will conduct a trial comparing 3 different programs to reduce disruptive behaviour in 2-4-year-olds in daycare. We will enrol 80 daycares, i.e. about 1280 toddlers. Daycares will be randomly selected to receive one of the following: 1) training of educators to improve social skills in daycare; 2) at-home training for parents of the most disruptive children; 3) daycare and home-based training; and 4) a control group with daycare services as usual. Daycares will be chosen from low-income areas in Greater Montreal and Sherbrooke (Quebec). The program will last 2 years and then be evaluated. A biobank of saliva and hair samples will also be kept and analysed to test markers of disruptive behaviour and to measure improvement. Results will help decision-makers set up evidence-based best practice programs that are both useful and cost-effective and can be applied on a larger scale

column36: Sex-specific investigations of Parkinson's disease mouse models: application for gonadal drugs repurposing.
column37: Both the prevalence and the incidence of Parkinson's disease (PD) are well documented to be higher in men than in women and these sex differences could be due to effects of the circulating sex hormones. Most PD patients experience gastrointestinal dysfunctions often preceding motor dysfunctions. PD might originate in the peripheral nervous system spreading later to the brain. Drugs for PD only improve motor symptoms: no drug is yet available to limit disease progression. It is thus important to identify pharmacological agents that would interfere with peripheral dysfunctions before spreading to the brain. This project will investigate two drugs to target the gut-brain axis for PD therapy: 1) dutasteride that inhibits the enzyme 5alpha-reductase already approved to treat prostate hyperplasia and 2) raloxifene that selectively modulates estrogen receptors already approved to treat post-menopausal osteoporosis. We have shown that these drugs possess anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties in a male toxin-induced mouse model of PD. We hypothesize that these drugs will have an effect as well in male than female mice but to a different extent. We will also start investigating the sex difference in an alpha-synuclein mouse model of PD with the hypothesis that alpha-synuclein accumulation is less in females due to estrogen neuroprotection. Our objectives are to evaluate A) the pharmacological properties of dutasteride and raloxifene in an early peripheral model of neurotoxin-induced PD with male and female mice to determine the contribution to the disease of male and female hormones, B) investigate the sex differences in alpha-synuclein accumulation in alpha-synuclein genetically modified intact and gonadectomised mice and C) investigate mechanisms implicated in cells. This project will validate novel indications for two drugs already approved for human administration to accelerate their use by PD patients. This project has high translational potential.

column36: The role of state-dependent neural correlations in population coding and behavior
column37: As you are reading this text, neurons in your brain coordinate their activities, thereby enabling you to correctly perceive and interpret the visual input forming on your retina. Our senses play a primordial role in enabling us to interact with our environment on our day to day lives. This is however not the case for a significant portion of the population suffering from sensory disorders. In fact, Autism spectrum disorders are associated with symptoms indicating impaired sensory processing. Growing evidence shows that perception of the sensory environment relies on the coordinated firing of large groups of neurons within our brain: this is known as population coding. What complicates our understanding of population coding is that the neural activities are not independent of one another but are rather related (i.e., "correlated"). Neural correlations have been observed across multiple brain areas but how they impact coding remains largely controversial. This is in part due to the fact that they change depending on sensory input as well as the brain's internal state (e.g., attention). The primary goal of this research project is to understand the functional role of neural correlations in sensory coding. Our preliminary data shows that correlations can vary dynamically as a function of behaviorally relevant stimulus attributes, thereby providing information. Our project aims at understanding the nature of the underlying mechanisms. This research will provide key knowledge into how neural populations can encode sensory input, which in turn will lead to better understanding of how changes in brain architecture can lead to pathologies and better treatment options for patients.

column36: Targeting Kcnn4 in polycystic kidney disease : a preclinical mechanistic proof of concept study
column37: Human autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most frequent hereditary disorder, afflicting 1 in 500 individuals. ADPKD is a severe condition with major impact on health and accounts for ~10% of all cases of end stage renal disease in Canada and worldwide. It is characterized by development of multiple renal cysts that can be detected in childhood, and grow in number and size over time, completely destroying the kidneys. Other organs are also frequently affected like liver, brain, and heart. Presently, progression of ADPKD is unstoppable: kidneys become non-functional and patients die if they have no access to hemodialysis or kidney transplant. A therapeutic strategy for ADPKD that could prevent or even delay renal destruction by a factor of 2- to 3-fold, would minimize cystic disease, improve quality of life and prolong very significantly lifespan. This research project aims at understanding the cellular and molecular mechanism(s) that lead to ADPKD. The PKD1 gene is responsible for ~85% of ADPKD cases. We study the molecular pathology associated with defective PKD1 gene in the mouse, the best experimental system. Our laboratory developed novel genetically modified Pkd1 mouse models that reproduce typical kidney symptoms of ADPKD. We will investigate the mechanism(s) of cyst formation and expansion with Pkd1 models. Cyst expansion is governed by proliferation and fluid secretion under the control of ion-fluid channels as KCNN4. We will test whether KCNN4 is the major channel responsible for cyst expansion by complementary genetic and pharmacologic approaches. We will also dissect the cellular and molecular mechanisms of KCNN4 in ADPKD pathology. Significantly, a KCNN4 specific inhibitor has been developed and tested in sickle cell disease clinical trials. We hope to repurpose this drug for ADPKD and delay renal destruction as prevention if not cure, and even be valuable to target at large, other renal cystic diseases.

column36: Rapid correction of vitamin D deficiency in pediatric critical illness: A phase III multicentre randomized controlled trial
column37: Vitamin D plays an important role in calcium balance, heart and lung health, inflammation, infection prevention, and muscle strength. Due to these roles, it has been suggested that critically ill patients with low levels might have higher rates of death and worse long term health. We believe that identifying critically ill children with vitamin D deficiency and then restoring vitamin D levels quickly could represent a safe, easy and inexpensive means of reducing patient illness, preventing death and improving quality of life. This application seeks funding for a clinical trial that will determine whether rapid normalization of vitamin D deficiency improves survival and health-related quality of life following critical illness. The project is designed as a multicentre trial in ten Canadian Pediatric Intensive Care Units. Critically ill children who agree to participate (consent given by caregivers) will have their blood vitamin D level measured, and those who are deficient will be randomized to receive a single dose of either high dose vitamin D3 or placebo (no drug). Study participants assigned to the high dose vitamin D arm will receive 10000 IU/kg of enteral cholecalciferol (up to a maximum of 400000 IU). We have tested this dose in a pilot trial, and no patient experienced serious adverse events related to vitamin D administration. Patients will be followed for 90 days to determine whether they survived and had a significant change in their health and quality of life. Vitamin D deficiency is a common problem not only among critically ill Canadian children, but in PICUs worldwide. In addition to being applicable in Canada, our study protocol has been designed to be generalizable and meaningful to critically ill children worldwide.

column36: Investigating the RNA-binding protein HuD and CARM1 as novel therapeutic targets for Spinal Muscular Atrophy
column37: Loss of a protein named SMN (for 'Survival of Motor Neurons') is responsible for spinal muscular atrophy, a disease that affects 1 in every 10000 newborns and is the leading genetic cause of infant mortality. It is characterized by a degeneration of the motor neurons in the spinal cord, resulting ultimately in muscle weakness, paralysis and death during early childhood. SMN has recently been dubbed 'the master assembler', because it acts as a molecular scaffold to promote the assembly of large macromolecular complexes involved in various cellular processes, related to the biology of RNA. However, this function of SMN should be equally important for all cells and it remains unclear why only spinal cord motor neurons are affected by loss of SMN. It is thought that the many protein-protein interactions in which SMN is involved might be regulated by a protein modification, namely arginine methylation. This has led to the identification of novel functions for SMN and helped us rationalize how deficiencies in functions essential to all cells can cause specific degeneration of the motor neurons of the spinal cord. We are proposing in the current proposal to test the potential of a new strategy for therapeutic intervention, which is based on all the basic science work we have done in the past 10 years.

column36: Novel determinants of CMG DNA helicase activity and their impact on Primordial Dwarfism
column37: Human genes are encoded on long DNA molecules that act as instruction manuals. Each 'manual' is organized as a helix made of two matching DNA strands, on which information is inscribed. Every time a cell divides, this script needs to be faithfully duplicated. This requires the two DNA strands to be separated and copied to generate a new set of instruction manuals, one for each of the two new cells. We study how a specialized "molecular motor" separates the two DNA strands when cells divide. This motor is called the 'CMG helicase', and gets its name from the ability to unwind the two strands of the DNA double helix. DNA cannot be copied unless the two DNA strands are first separated. The CMG helicase is therefore required for human life, and its functions allow multicellular organisms to grow as cells multiply. Our group recently identified rare defects in the CMG helicase that cause dwarfism. Our preliminary results suggest that these defects have a profound effect on the cell's ability to multiply. We therefore hypothesize that defects in the CMG helicase cause dwarfism by preventing cells from copying DNA in a timely manner, thereby diminishing their ability to multiply which leads to short stature. We have assembled a team with specialized expertise that will determine how and why defects in the CMG helicase cause short stature. Our team is the first to reconstruct DNA unwinding by the human CMG helicase in the context of these defects. Our cellular, biophysical, and biochemical studies will provide conclusive results explaining why defects in the CMG helicase have such profound effects on growth. It may also lead to the design of new therapies and diagnostic tests for children born with CMG helicase defects and dwarfism.

column36: Wnt activation as a therapeutic strategy for treatment-refractory childhood medulloblastoma
column37: Brain tumors represent the leading cause of childhood cancer mortality, due to their highly aggressive and often incurable nature. Medulloblastoma (MB), the most common malignant pediatric brain tumor, is defined by four molecular subgroups (Wnt, Shh, Group 3, Group 4) based on gene expression profiles. Clinically, Wnt MB patients who have high activity of a developmental signaling pathway called Wnt, have the most favorable prognosis with a >95% 5-year survivorship. By contrast, non-Wnt MB patients are characterized by metastatic disease, increased rates of recurrence, and intermediate-poor overall survivorship. Given that Wnt MBs represent the only subgroup in which metastasis is not indicative of a poor prognosis, it has been suggested that Wnt signaling may contribute to their remarkable response to therapy. Given the excellent clinical outcome in Wnt-driven MB, we aim to convert treatment-resistant Group 3 and 4 MBs into ostensibly benign tumors by activation of Wnt signaling. Our preliminary results show that the non-Wnt MB cells have reduced growth when they are treated with Wnt activators. By using animal models, we found that Wnt-activated cells have decreased tumorigenicity. In the current work we aim to understand the mechanism by which the Wnt pathway can be modulated for therapy of poor prognosis MBs. We also aim to identify novel Wnt activators through genetic screens using CRISPR technology. Ultimately, this work will lead to increasing our molecular understanding of treatment-refractory MB, and identify new therapeutic targets for MB patients who still die from relapse.

column36: Aging in Autism Spectrum Disorders: Changes in Brain Structure and Function
column37: We know very little about how aging changes the brain in Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), a neurodevelopmental disorder that affects more than half a million Canadians. People with ASD have difficulties in social interactions and communication and show restricted and repetitive behaviours. Poor outcomes have been reported for a large percent of adults with ASD. With long life expectancy as well as increasing prevalence of ASD, we need to understand the impact of the ASD diagnosis on the brain later in life. Age related changes of brain structure and function in healthy adults are well known, but there are no studies regarding such changes in those with ASD. Individuals with other developmental disabilities (such as Down syndrome) have accelerated age-related cognitive losses. As brain development is atypical in childhood in ASD, it is likely that these early brain differences will influence age-related decline in ASD. The overarching goal of our research is to characterize the changes with aging in brain structure and function in people with ASD and link these with their symptoms and longer-term outcomes. We will invite 64 participants ages 30-40 and matched controls who already have longitudinal imaging to enroll in this project. We will then recruit 120 high functioning adults with ASD (40- 75years old), and 120 age- and sex-matched healthy adult controls. Brain imaging will be used to allow us to assess the impact of aging on structure, function, functional connectivity in the autistic brain in relation to symptoms and behaviour with aging. Participants will be followed in 4 years from first scan. Our combined team has extensive experience in diagnosing ASD, managing adults with ASD, imaging ASD and imaging aging. This study is fundamental in understanding structural and functional brain changes with age in ASD to be better equipped to help these individuals as they age.

column36: Estimating the effect size of rare genomic variants on cognitive and behavioral traits underlying neurodevelopmental disorders
column37: Neurodevelopmental disorders (NDs) include intellectual disabilities, severe learning disabilities, autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are frequent with a prevalence of 1%, 6%, and 1,4% respectively. They represent a significant health burden with handicaps present throughout life. The genetic contribution to NDs is as high as 80%. With the routine implementation of genetic testing in the neurodevelopmental clinic, rare mutations that contribute significantly to neurodevelopmental symptoms are identified in 10 to 20 % of children with NDs. However, for most "pathogenic" mutations reported back to patients, we have little or no data to estimate their quantitative impact on neurodevelopment. It is therefore difficult for clinicians to estimate the extent to which a genetic variant may contribute to the neurodevelopmental symptoms in a patient. This is due to 2 major issue: 1) Over 75% of "pathogenic" mutations are very rare and observed only once or a few times in patients. It is therefore impossible to conduct individual association studies and 2) Most studies have focussed on associating mutations with complex categorical diagnoses such as ASD or intellectual disabilities. The cognitive mechanisms underlying these associations remain unknown. To address this issue of undocumented mutations, we propose a novel strategy to understand the effects of CNVs genome-wide, on cognitive and brain measures involved in neurodevelopmental disorders. The deliverables are algorithms estimating the effect size of any CNV or SNV on cognitive and behavioral traits assessed along a continuum. This will, allow clinicians to estimate the level of contribution of one or several rare mutations to the neurodevelopmental symptoms in a given patient. It will also provide insight into the mechanisms by which mutations may lead to neurodevelopmental disorders.

column36: Examining the mechanistic impact of the HNF-1aG319S polymorphism on beta cell function and its contribution to early-onset type 2 diabetes
column37: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is increasing at an alarming rate in Canada. Disproportionally affected are Canada's Indigenous Peoples. The Oji-Cree linguistic group that lives in Central Canada experiences up to 5X higher rates and much earlier onset of T2D compared to the general Canadian population. Almost 20 years ago, it was discovered that a considerable number of Oji-Cree people carry a genetic variant in the hepatocyte nuclear factor-1 alpha (HNF-1a) gene. The gene variation is called HNF-1aG319S or just G319S. This gene variant not only strongly associates with T2D in the Oji-Cree sub-population, but also strongly associates with a younger age-of-onset of T2D. Despite being discovered almost 2 decades ago, we currently do not understand how this gene variant affects the insulin-secreting beta cells leading to increased risk for T2D development. In this study, we will use newly developed, state-of-the-art mouse models (cells and whole animal) to examine how the G319S variant affects insulin secretion from the beta cell as well as how the G319S variant influences the susceptibility of the beta cell to relevant environmental stresses associated with T2D in the Oji-Cree. Finally, we will study the impact of the G319S variant on human beta-like cells derived directly from people who carry the G319S variant. This study will be the first to examine the mechanistic impact of the G319S variant on both mouse and human beta cells and will provide much needed understanding of the basic pathophysiology of a gene variant that strongly influences the health of a considerable number of Indigenous Canadians. The new knowledge gained from this study will not only inform potential modifications to current treatment regimens for G319S carriers living with T2D, but also identify novel drugable targets for the development of new, more effective treatment approaches for carriers of HNF-1a mutations.

column36: Engineering therapeutics for the treatment of anemia in oncology patients
column37: Anemia (a low number of red blood cells or low amount of hemoglobin in blood) affects many cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy, leading to fatigue, weakness, shortness of breath and other symptoms, which severely reduce the patients' quality of life. Cancer-related anemia is also associated with shorter survival times. While treating anemia with the hormone erythropoietin (EPO) has been highly successful, the use of EPO in cancer-related anemia is sometimes considered unsafe since it also encourages tumor growth. Previous research has shown that the desired response to EPO (red blood cell production) likely occurs via a different mechanism than the undesired tumor-promoting effects. That is, the stimulation of red blood cell production depends on a cell surface receptor called EPOR, while tumor-stimulating effects depend on other cell surface receptors unrelated to EPOR. These observations suggest that the development of molecules capable of stimulating only the desirable EPOR-dependent responses may provide novel avenues for a more effective treatment of cancer-related anemia. We have developed a rapid and efficient method to engineer protein variants of EPO and antibodies that attach to EPOR. This involves searching through large collections of EPO-like variants or antibodies for molecules that attach to EPOR and stimulate its activity. The effect of these novel molecules on EPOR activation is assessed in cultured cells and screened in cultured tumor cells to identify molecules that do not stimulate tumor growth. The proposed project builds on current knowledge from available anemia treatments by creating novel, improved molecules that will stimulate production of red blood cells via an EPO-dependent mechanism, but unlike natural EPO, they will not stimulate other pathways that lead to undesired side effects. Therefore, this project has the potential to greatly improve the quality of life and survival for cancer patients.

column36: Characterization of the Relationship Between Innate Immune Activation and Intestinal Stem Cell Homeostasis.
column37: Our gastrointestinal tract establishes a physical barrier that allows essential nutrients to enter circulation, and keeps harmful microbes at bay. This barrier is maintained throughout our lives by a population of stem cells that grow and replace dead or dying cells at the gut surface. If stem cells fail to divide at an adequate rate, gut barriers break down, and noxious molecules breach the animal interior. In contrast, excess stem cell growth often disturbs gut architecture. In many cases, prolonged overgrowth of stem cells enables the development of intestinal tumors. For example, in inflammatory bowel disease, persistent activation of immune responses to gut bacteria drives excess growth of stem cells. The subsequent disruptions to intestinal function negatively impact quality of life, and elevate the risk of colorectal cancer in patients by approximately twenty-fold. Researchers in my group generated a transgenic fly that allows us to experimentally mimic the immune-dependent growth of stem cells. We showed that persistent immune responses to gut bacteria caused a rapid expansion of stem cells and a harmful loss of gut organization. In follow-up work, we identified the bacteria responsible for immune-dependent overgrowth of stem cells. We showed that immune responses to the bacterial cell wall interrupts conventional growth programs, and fuels the disorganized expansion of stem cells. In this project, we will determine the exact effects of immune activity on gut stem cell growth and determine how bacteria modify these responses. Flies are excellent models for this work, as the biological blueprint for gut formation and function was established very early in animal evolution. Thus, work in flies provides important insights into critical aspects of human gut biology.

column37: Ependymoma is a major cause of childhood cancer related morbidity and mortality. Current therapies are limited to aggressive surgeries and external beam irradiation, which is effective in only 50% of cases, while resulting in significant lifelong neurocognitive sequelae in survivors. column36: Finding the molecular drivers of calcific aortic valve stenosis
column37: The human heart consists of four chambers that contract in a repeated, rhythmic and synchronized manner to pump blood in the body. The heart also has four valves that ensure that blood flow goes only in one direction. One of these valves is called the aortic valve. The aortic valve lies between the main heart chamber (left ventricle) and the aorta, which is the largest artery that distributes blood to all parts of the body. Calcification of the aortic valve, or more specifically aortic stenosis, is the most frequent heart valve disease and the third leading cause of heart disease in adults. The incidence increases with age, and with the current shift toward an older population, it is becoming a major societal and economic burden. There is currently no medical treatment available other than surgery to replace the diseased native valve by a prosthetic heart valve. It is thus urgent to understand the causes of the disease at the most fundamental levels in order to elucidate new therapeutic options. Many factors are predicted to cause the disease and an important genetic predisposition was demonstrated. However, only a small number of studies have tried to identify the susceptibility genes. In this research program, we plan to expand this work using a series of complementary genomic approaches. This program will take advantage of the large volume of clinical and biological materials that we have collected during the last few years to study patients with aortic stenosis. The most modern genomics and bioinformatics approaches will be used to find new therapeutic targets to treat this condition. Data collected in this proposal will serve for many years and strengthen our research program which ultimately, aims at finding a cure for aortic stenosis. Overall, this proposal will increase our understanding of the disease processes, which will lead to innovative therapeutic strategies to treat this life-threatening and frequent disease.

column36: Mitochondrial quality control during hemorrhagic shock: positive impact of remote ischemic conditioning.
column37: Traumatic injury is a major cause of death and disability among the civilian population. One of the major causes for these outcomes is loss of blood related to the injury. Patients either die due to massive blood loss or they survive but suffer from the morbid effects of the injury. Blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock, contributes to these effects by injuring cells, leading to poor function of entire organs. One important way that shock exerts this effect is by causing dysfunction of mitochondria, the main source of energy in cells. Our group has recently demonstrated that a simple intervention, performed by applying a tourniquet to an extremity, and cycling it on and off, so called "Remote Ischemic Conditioning (RIC)" can protect against cellular and organ damage. Our preliminary studies indicate that RIC might exert these effects by improving mitochondrial quality. The purpose of our studies is to examine the effect of shock on mitochondrial quality and understand how RIC might lessen the detrimental effect of hemorrhagic shock on their function. Together, these studies will elucidate potentially novel therapeutic targets aimed at improving outcomes in people sustaining traumatic injury.

column36: Delineating the Mechanisms Underlying Nitric Oxide Induced Muscle Wasting During Cachexia
column37: Cachexia is a debilitating syndrome characterized by uncontrollable body weight loss that arises in patients with pro-inflammatory conditions, such as cancer. Numerous pathophysiological events have been associated with cachexia, including anorexia, liver dysfunction, fat tissue depletion, and, notably, loss of skeletal muscle mass. Loss of muscle mass during cachexia leads to weakness, lower quality of life, and is associated with reduce response to disease treatment. While our understanding of how cachexia is initiated is still incomplete, it is well established that chronically elevated proinflammatory hormones, also known as cytokines, are a primary driver of the condition. However, therapies against these cytokines have proven ineffective, indicating that no one inflammatory hormone is the primary driver of this syndrome. This highlights the need to identify common downstream pathways that are induced in affected tissues for targeted therapeutics. Recently, impairment of mitochondrial function and metabolic aberrations in muscle have been associated with the cachectic phenotype. However, the intra-cellular mechanisms leading to this dysfunction remain elusive. We have acquired preliminary data suggesting that elevated nitric oxide (NO) levels produced from inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) during cytokine exposure is a primary cause of mitochondrial impairment in skeletal muscle. In past studies, we also showed that iNOS/NO is a key mediator of the cachectic phenotype by affecting the expression of factors, such as MyoD, which are required for muscle formation. Thus, we propose to study in this grant how NO production from iNOS alters metabolic function and the expression of factors such as MyoD in muscles exposed to cachectic stimuli, as well as the impact of these changes on muscle function. In doing so, we hope to increase our understanding of how cytokines induce atrophy and dysfunction in muscle and identify novel targets for therapeutic development.
