column37: Our project begins with a question "Qanuikkat Siqinirmiut?" or "How are the people in the south?" The number of Inuit living in southern cities is increasing rapidly, with just over 27% (17,695) now living outside the traditional territories of Inuit Nunangat. In contrast to those in the north, very little is known about the health of Inuit in the south. It is clear that Inuit in the north and the south experience significant health disparities when compared to the majority population. In southern Quebec the development of services for health promotion, prevention, and the treatment of illness is limited by a near complete absence of data on the health of the population. This project is intended to build a knowledge base on the health and wellbeing of Inuit in the south through the development and implementation of a population health survey. The project is uses a culturally-adapted Community-Based Participatory Research research strategy to , A collaboration between the Southern Quebec Inuit Association and a group of university-based researchers, the team includes researchers, community members, service providers, students, and political and social organizations who are poised to act on the findings of the research. Qualitative interviews, ethnographic and participatory visual research techniques will bring context and depth to the understanding of Inuit health and wellbeing. The survey tools used in from other studies of Inuit health will be adapted and expanded with the results of the qualitative methods in order to reflect the realities of those in the south. Additional Scientific outcomes include a better understanding of urban Inuit health and its relationship to northern health issues. Our goals are to develop an understanding of community health and wellbeing that is based in Inuit experience order to build capacity to address health disparities and community need.

column37: Since April 2016, British Columbia (BC) has been in a state of public health emergency due to opioid-related overdoses and deaths, in which Indigenous people have been disproportionately affected. The First Nations Health Authority (FNHA) assumed the responsibilities of Health Canada's First Nations Inuit Health Branch-Pacific Region in 2013 and is governed by First Nations individuals and communities across BC. Responding to the opioid crisis has been a top priority for the FNHA since the start of BC's opioid crisis. Harm reduction is an effective way to reduce stigma and harms associated with opioid use and other licit and illicit drugs. An Indigenous approach to health research and health care service delivery is critically needed to develop effective practices for Indigenous Peoples in Canada. However, an Indigenous approach to harm reduction for opioid use has not been studied extensively, and there is limited literature on community-based harm reduction practices for First Nations in Canada. The main objectives of this project are to: 1) synthesize current Indigenous approaches to harm reduction for opioid use using a Western scoping review that includes Indigenous storytelling methods, 2) refine and/or implement and measure Indigenous harm reduction interventions in all five health regions in BC, and 3) develop an Indigenized harm reduction model for opioid use. First Nation communities will lead the research with the support and guidance of project team members as needed. A multidisciplinary research team with experience exploring substance use, mental health and wellness, and harm reduction will work together to implement this five-year project. Results will be used to improve harm reduction initiatives and better support Indigenous people who use opioids, ultimately informing the FNHA's health programs and services and other harm reduction initiatives across Canada.

column37: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is a prevalent and serious mental illness. Symptoms of BPD include intense and rapid mood swings, unstable relationships, and engagement in self-harm or suicidal behaviors. Effective psychotherapeutic treatments for BPD have been developed, such as dialectical behavior therapy (DBT). There is still, however, much room for improvement when it comes to alleviating key interpersonal problems in BPD. Therapeutic interventions that increase self-compassion (reacting to one's own suffering with kindness and understanding) may improve the treatment of these interpersonal difficulties. This study will evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of adding self-compassion training to DBT skills groups and will explore whether the added self-compassion training impacts interpersonal functioning. Participants diagnosed with BPD will be randomized to complete either thirteen weeks of group DBT skills training, or thirteen weeks of group DBT skills training modified to include self-compassion training. Feasibility and acceptability of the programs will be assessed post-treatment and compared between the two groups. Outcome variables, including interpersonal functioning, will be measured pre-treatment, immediately post-treatment, and at follow-up thirteen weeks later. It is anticipated that there will not be differences in acceptability and feasibility between groups, and participants that receive self-compassion training will show greater improvement in interpersonal functioning. This research will determine whether self-compassion training is a potentially useful addition to evidence-based care for BPD. Furthermore, this research has the potential to reduce the significant personal suffering and healthcare toll of BPD by informing improvements in treatment.

column36: A National Research Network on Lyme Disease
column37: Lyme Disease (LD) is an emerging microbial threat and new approaches are required to help contain this risk to human health. LD is caused by the bacterial pathogen, B. burgdorferi that is transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected tick. LD is of increasingly urgent concern in Canada; between 2009-2016 there was a 700% increase in the number of reported cases. Additionally, areas of Canada that were once considered to be at low-risk are transitioning to high risk as tick populations become further established due to climate change. Further research is necessary to address the many critical knowledge gaps that exist in Canada. We will establish the Canadian Lyme Disease Research Network (CLyDRN) which is composed of researchers, clinicians, patients, community members and other stakeholders with the ultimate vision of reducing the impact of LD on the health of Canadians. We will accomplish this vision by creating foundational resources and spearheading new research initiatives. This includes the creation of Canada's first repository for tissue samples from LD patients and an associated clinical database that will include detailed patient information. We will also develop national research capacity and support training of new LD researchers. These resources will support research initiatives in four areas: 1)Develop and evaluate new diagnostic tools and methods, 2)Identify preventive measures, interventions, and population health approaches to decrease risk of occurrence of LD, 3)Determine the burden and natural history of disease, clinical management and risk factors and 4)Attend to the contextual complexity through patient and community engagement, training and integrated KT research. Our Network will mobilize and build LD-specific capacity and training opportunities, improve clinical science and practice, provide best evidence in testing and patient care, improve patient outcomes and inform policy.

column37: To stay healthy, we need to have an immune system that works properly: it needs to attack foreign cells, but leave our own cells alone. If our immune system attacks our cells, it causes an illness called an autoimmune disease. There are many types of autoimmune disease, including type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, celiac disease, and rheumatoid arthritis. Two million Canadians of all ages live with an autoimmune disease. Researchers and healthcare professionals are working hard to find new and better ways to treat these lifelong diseases. But we face the challenge that there is not a consistent set of established 'recipes' (called standard operating procedures, or SOPs) for the ways that researchers collect, process, and analyze samples to make discoveries or test new treatments. Here, we have brought together a Canada-wide group of experts to create the Canadian Autoimmunity Standardization Core (CAN-ASC), which will develop SOPs for the most important tests and methods that are needed by the researchers who study autoimmune diseases. We will work together and with our colleagues to produce and test the SOPs. Then we will make the SOPs available via the web and train researchers and students to use them. In this way, we will ensure that Canadian researchers have ideal methods to study what causes autoimmunity in humans and to develop new treatments that can restore normal immune system function.

column37: Infertility affects 15% of couples world-wide, and male factors contribute to half of cases. The most severe form of male infertility, termed non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA) occurs where no sperm are produced due to defective spermatogenesis. An overwhelming 70% of these cases have no known cause. Treatment options are limited and involve a surgical procedure termed microTESE where a surgical microscope is used to identify dilated seminiferous tubules in the testis that are most likely to contain a degree of preserved sperm production, compared to the vast majority of collapsed tubules lacking sperm production. This technique is the last option for fertility and is only successful in approximately half of cases; thus, research is desperately needed to understand the mechanisms underlying these severely infertile men with NOA to progress care This study will investigate the mechanisms that distinguish active and defective spermatogenesis with the aim to identify novel therapeutic targets. To do this, we will compare testis tissue from men with NOA and control men with normal sperm production. We will use state-of-the-art single cell sequencing which allows us to study the precise genetic expression within each individual cell from each testis biopsy. Using advanced analysis techniques, we will identify differences in cell-type-specific gene isoforms and expression between normal controls and men with NOA including comparisons between dilated tubules (with spermatogenesis) and collapsed tubules (defect spermatogenesis). Using specialized 3-D organoid cultures, we will investigate the regulatory differences in germ cell and somatic cell interactions among the experimental groups. Results from this study will contribute to our understanding of the mechanisms and identification of novel therapeutic targets among severely infertile men with no presently available treatment.

column37: One of health care's largest outstanding issues is that many patients do not respond to treatment or are harmed by a treatment. Approximately 90% of drugs are effective for less than 50% of patients, resulting in significant individual, social, and economic impacts. Variable treatment response also contributes to the rising cost of drug development, currently estimated at around $2.6 billion per drug. A fundamental driver of these inefficiencies is the variability that exists in the human genome of patients. To better understand this variability, and develop more effective drugs and customized treatment approaches, we need to better integrate the variable human genome datasets being studied globally. This proposal addresses key fundamental, internationally important, challenges to enable effective global genomic data sharing and harmonization. The project builds on existing databases and infrastructural resources, including Europe's largest controlled access database - EGA - and a worldwide collection of human genome datasets, including major cohort studies in Canada. Specifically this Canada-EU joint project addresses: federated data discovery, secure authentication and authorization to access data, and standardization of the data (in particular other contextual data associated with the genomic data which is currently poorly organized). The project will demonstrate the effectiveness of this data harmonization, enabling joint cohort analysis with targeted clinical applications. This project will also incorporate important outreach and training initiatives, and address particular ethical, legal and social issues associated with this federated data analysis. This work will address key gaps in the development of the personalised medicine vision described in the ICPerMed Action Plan and by CIHR. The analyses enabled by this project will advance scientific knowledge in ways not previously possible.

column37: Rapid progress in information and biotechnologies offers the promise of better, personalized health strategies using rich phenotypic, environmental and molecular (omics) profiles of every individual. To capitalize on this great promise, the key challenge is to relate these profiles to health and disease while accounting for high diversity in individuals, populations and environments. Both Europe and Canada have long-term investments in population-based prospective cohort studies providing essential longitudinal data. These data must be analyzed in unison to reach statistical power, however, presently cohort data repositories are scattered, hard to search and integrate, and data protection and governance rules discourage central pooling. EUCAN-Connect will enable large-scale integrated cohort data analysis for personalized and preventive healthcare across EU and Canada. This will be based on an open, scalable data platform for cohorts, researchers and networks, incorporating FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) for optimal reuse of existing data, and building on maturing federated technologies, with sensitive data kept locally and only results being shared and integrated, in line with key data governance guidelines. Widespread uptake will be promoted via beyond state-of-the-art research in close collaboration with leading cohort networks, focused on early-life origins of cardio-metabolic, developmental, musculoskeletal and respiratory health and disease impacting human life course. To address challenges of sustainability and curation, we will deliver innovative solutions for distributed, low-cost data harvesting and preservation, community curation/harmonization, privacy protection, open source bioinformatics toolbox development, and international governance. EUCAN-Connect platform and collaborations will be coordinated through BBMRI-ERIC (EU) and Maelstrom Research (Canada) to sustain long-term benefits to science and citizens worldwide.

column37: Personalised medicine approaches are highly needed in the domain of cardiology, as cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the major contributors to mortality and morbidity worldwide. To date, cardiovascular research has been conducted by interrogating biomedical data in single cohorts, but these are often limited to specific populations, geographical areas, or data type. In Canada, CVD research has been at the forefront of multi-cohort approaches through the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) (MUHC, McGill, McMaster, ICES). The CAHHM exploited Canadian know-how in legal data (McGill) and in harmonisation and integration (MUHC) to create a centralised longitudinal super-cohort from 8 Canadian cohorts for enhanced data sharing in cardiovascular research. However, infrastructures and models to facilitate integrated sharing of information and data between Canadian and European cohorts are missing. The euCanSHare project proposes to leverage, extend and integrate two complimentary initiatives in Canada (CAHHM) and Europe (BiomarCaRE) to develop a robust ecosystem for enhanced data sharing, integration and exploitation in CVD research. In this way, existing Canadian and European tools will be put on a Common IT platform developed within euCanSHare, and will offer extensive services and functionalities. Comparative analysis of legal frameworks in Canada and Europe will be led by experts from Canada (McGill) to inform the shared automation of such services. The integrated cloud-based collection of technologies, policies and standardised procedures will reduce the cost of research, allowing efficient data management at scale across international projects.

column36: Canadian "Rare Diseases: Models and Mechanisms" (RDMM) Network
column37: Thousands of rare genetic diseases (RDs) affect one million Canadians, mostly children, and cause significant disability, lead to early death, and almost all have no treatment. Genomic sequencing (decoding a person's DNA) has transformed our ability to identify gene mutations that cause RDs, but we understand very little about the impact of those genes and mutations on biology and health. As a result, we don't know how to treat most of these devastating diseases. Studying gene mutations in model organisms (such as yeast, worm, fly, fish, and mouse) provides important information about how mutations cause disease and can identify potential therapies. However, geneticists discovering genes that cause RD do not usually conduct research in model organisms, and model organism scientists are not usually aware of genes being discovered by geneticists. Thus, in 2014 we established the Canadian 'Rare Diseases: Models and Mechanisms' Network ('The RDMM Network') to a) connect geneticists discovering RD genes with model organism scientists able to study that gene and b) provide small grants to support collaborative research. The RDMM Network has engaged these communities, made connections for 72 RD genes, and funded 79 projects. Our research has already led to original scientific publications, successful large-scale grants, and identified two life-changing therapies. These results are very promising, and we want to expand the impact and reach of the RDMM Network. To do so we will: - Further engage the clinical and model organism communities - Enable connections when model organism expertise is not available in the country where the gene was discovered, by linking similar networks around the world - Support more projects by partnering with Canadian organizations interested in co-funding research. Building on our experience running the RDMM Network, we will support more than 50 collaborative projects to generate new knowledge that will improve the care of Canadians with RD.

column36: Neuroimmune guidance cues, MicroRNAs & Inflammatory responses: Sex differences in cardiovascular diseases (MISs-CVD)
column37: Atherosclerotic vascular disease continues to be a leader of morbidity and mortality. Although sex hormones are known to play a role in this lipid- and inflammatory-driven disease, the underlying mechanisms are largely unclear. Neuroimmune guidance cues (NGCs) are key regulators of cell movement and positioning, and have emerged as significant players in inflammation. We have previously reported a role for Netrin-1 on macrophage emigration from plaques as well as key regulation of lipid metabolism by microRNA (miRNA)-33. Recently, we have uncovered sex-biased miRNAs targeting NGCs and hypothesize that these miRNAs provide missing mechanistic links in the endothelial-monocyte interactions and macrophage retention in the vascular wall during atherosclerosis in women vs men. We now seek to fully characterize the clinically relevant sex-biased miRNAs and NGCs in monocytes, plasma and aorta specimens from healthy subject and patients with atherosclerosis. We will also use primary endothelial cells and assess direct interactions between the sex-biased miRNAs and NGCs and unravel the functional impact of promising miRNAs on endothelial permeability, monocyte and macrophage trafficking and atherosclerosis using an innovative 3D vessel-on-a-chip platform and in vivo mouse models. This ambitious interdisciplinary project requires combined expertise of molecular cell biology, bioinformatics and physiology to provide crucial understanding of the gender differences in atherosclerosis and may provide novel gender specific therapeutic avenues to combat atherogenesis in both men and women.

column36: Unravelling proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) mechanisms in calcific aortic valve disease: from aortic valve sclerosis to stenosis
column37: Calcific aortic valve stenosis (CAVS) is a fatal pathology that affects 2-3% of the population. Yet, drug therapies are ineffective, leaving the urgency to fully characterize the aetiology of aortic valve calcification (AVC) to develop innovative therapies. Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) binds to and targets the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR). It was recently shown that individuals with loss-of-function genetic variant at the PCSK9 gene have low levels of atherogenic lipoprotein concentrations (LDL and Lipoprotein(a)) and reduced risk of coronary heart disease and CAVS. However, the mechanisms through which altered PCSK9 activity could protect against or cause CAVS is lacking. Our preliminary data suggest that PCSK9 plays an active role in CAVS. We will, therefore, determine whether PCSK9 is a causal risk factor for CAVS using genetic epidemiology. Further, we will shed light on the molecular underpinnings through which PCSK9 causes CAVS in humans using state-of-the-art in vivo as well as in vitro models in combination with next-generation sequencing. As a complementary and potential pre-clinical model, we will determine the role of PCSK9 in the development of aortic valve calcification in mice. The overarching aim of this research program is to provide the required biological evidence using a highly translational approach to support PCSK9 as a therapeutic target for the prevention and treatment of patients with CAVS.

column37: Cardiovascular diseases are by far the most prevalent cause of death in developed countries. These diseases, including heart attacks and strokes, often result from atherosclerosis. Atherosclerosis is a fatty deposit of cholesterol, blood cells and fibres in the wall of arteries. Atherosclerotic plaques develop slowly over time. They gradually encroach onto the interior of blood vessels, and only become symptomatic when a blood vessel is obstructed by 70% or more. A more serious situation arises when the atherosclerotic plaque ruptures suddenly. This happens because the contents of the plaque include fatty deposits that provide poor resistance to daily wear and tear. If a large fatty deposit is accompanied by a thin cap (the cap forms a protective fibrous layer between the atherosclerotic plaque and the interior of the blood vessel), the risk of rupture is enhanced. When a rupture occurs, the contents of the atherosclerotic plaque are exposed to the blood flowing in the vessel, leading to the formation of a blood clot within the vessel. This may completely and suddenly block the vessel, causing heart attack or stroke. Our proposed research will investigate a new treatment option that would reinforce the plaque cap, rendering plaques less susceptible to rupture, based on molecules that influence protein synthesis within cells.

This is an important step towards the development of better treatments for disorders in which this process is aberrant, such as in MS.

column36: Role, function, and regulation of the delta opioid receptor and its implications for the treatment of pain
column37: Despite the existence of a multitude of drugs with analgesic properties, the treatment of pain often remains problematic. Notwithstanding significant side effects (constipation, nausea, sedation), alkaloid compounds remain the most effective drugs to relieve chronic pain. The best known of all alkaloids undoubtedly remains morphine, belonging to the family of opiates. Morphine and its derivatives bind and activate at least three subtypes of G protein-coupled receptors, the mu (MOP), delta (DOP) and kappa (KOP) opioid receptors. Although these three receptor subtypes possess analgesic properties, the actions of the majority of opioids used clinically target MOP. In contrast to the latter, activation of DOP leads to few unwanted effects. Under normal conditions (i.e. in healthy animals), the analgesic potency of delta selective agonists is lower than that of morphine. In recent years, however, it has been shown that under certain conditions, the activation of DOP can counter the painful sensations with an efficacy close to morphine. In my laboratory we are interested in studying the mechanisms regulating the trafficking of DOP toward the plasma membrane of nociceptive neurons under conditions of chronic pain. A better understanding of these mechanisms could help develop strategies to increase the effectiveness of pain therapies and thus improve the quality of life of patients.

column37: The Cardiovascular Health Awareness Program (CHAP) is a community-based, volunteer-led cardiovascular risk assessment and blood pressure monitoring program with health education/promotion sessions for older adults living in the communities. We will conduct several meetings to present CHAP-P; discuss the needs to prepare for its implementation including preparing materials and equipments, personnel training, and cost-sharing; and set-up ways to monitor and evaluate CHAP-P so that the community residents can benefit from the program more. column36: Targeting potassium channel to disrupt the cellular hierarchy and suppress malignant growth of pediatric brain tumor
column37: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. The conventional treatment, which combines surgery, irradiation and chemotherapy, is toxic to normal brain cells and produces life-long side effects such as lowered intelligence, early aging, and increased chance to develop other cancer. Therefore, identifying the molecules that fuel aggressive MB growth but are dispensable for normal cells is key to develop cancer-specific therapy. Ions, such as potassium and chloride, are essential constituents of human cell. Ion channel proteins form tiny pores to control ion to move in or out of cell. The movement of ions can change the electrical and physical properties of the cells, which control biological processes including tumor growth. We recently found that potassium channel Eag2 is required for MB growth, discovered a drug as a novel Eag2 blocker, and showed that the drug had marked anti-MB efficacy in mice and a MB patient. Therefore, we pioneer in identifying ion channels as novel regulators for MB and developing ion channel-targeting therapy. Brain tumor-initiating cells (BTICs) are rare cells that generate multiple tumor cell types to fuel the malignant brain tumor growth. Since BTICs are insensitive to irradiation and conventional chemotherapy, they are the roots for tumor initiation and recurrence. While Eag2 regulates the growth of non-BTICs, our unpublished study identified that potassium channel Kcnb2 is present in MB BTICs. We discovered that genetic deletion of Kcnb2 reduced the number of BTICs and suppressed MB growth, but it did not overtly alter the normal development of mice. We propose to define the mechanism by which Kcnb2 regulates BTICs and MB growth, and determine the therapeutic efficacy of combining Kcnb2 inhibition and conventional therapy. By completing our studies, we will uncover the unrealized potential of targeting ion channels to treat brain cancer by attacking the root of brain tumor growth and recurrence.

column36: Unitization: a strategy to circumvent memory deficits in aging and amnesia.
column37: Memory is the repository of our personal histories and stored knowledge, and it is essential to planning our futures and maintaining a sense of self. By 2036, almost a quarter of Canadians will be aged 65 and older, and many will experience memory decline. As memory declines, other cognitive functions are affected, as are daily activities. To support our aging population we must develop simple, cost-effective cognitive strategies to alleviate age-related memory declines. We recently discovered that a cognitive strategy, unitization, supports memory function in older adults and even in cases of amnesia who have severe impairments in memory. Through unitization, information about multiple items is represented as a single unit through an interaction between new and existing knowledge. In order to ultimately use unitization more widely to improve cognition in memory-impaired individuals, we must first understand what level of cognitive and neural function is needed for the strategy to be successfully used. We will use neuropsychological and neuroimaging studies to examine the cognitive functions and brain regions that correlate with the successful use of unitization. This will allow us to predict which people would be most likely to benefit from unitization. Additionally, we will examine if unitization can support inference, a cognitive function that relies on memory. The ability to infer information beyond what is directly observed is essential to daily living, as it plays a role in problem solving and in guiding behavior in social interactions. Successful use of unitization to alleviate impairments in inference will show how unitization has broad potential to support declining cognition, allowing older adults to maintain their independence and quality of life for longer.

column36: Structural analysis of mycobacterial oxidative phosphorylation and targeting it to treat tuberculosis
column37: Cells use oxygen to convert chemical energy from diverse sources into the universal energy currency ATP before use. This process, called oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos), is performed by a series of large molecular machines that reside in cell membranes. In OxPhos, electrons stripped from fuel molecules ("oxidation") are passed between several of the molecular machines (Complexes I, II, III, and IV) with oxygen serving as the final electron acceptor, reducing it to water. During electron transfer Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons from one side of the membrane to the other, establishing a chemical and electrical proton gradient. A final machine, known as ATP synthase, allows protons back across the membrane, using the energy released to make ATP. While example atomic-resolution structures have now been determined for all OxPhos complexes it is still not clear how electron transfer is coupled to the proton pumping that powers aerobic life. Understanding OxPhos has important biomedical implications. Tuberculosis (TB), caused by the organism Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is a leading causes of death worldwide and an important health issue in Canada's indigenous populations. The breakthrough TB drug bedaquiline inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase. Mycobacterial Complexes III and IV form an unusual supercomplex (CIII2CIV2) with a dramatically different structure than the human Complexes III and IV. This structure is both unique and essential, making it an attractive target for developing TB drugs. We will determine structures for CIII2CIV2 and ATP synthase from mycobacteria. The unique CIII2CIV2, which carries out two thirds of the electron transfer pathway in a self contained stable assembly, provides a valuable tool for understanding universal principles of electron transfer. Structures of CIII2CIV2 and mycobacterial ATP synthase in complex with approved and candidate antimycobacterial drugs will provide key insights into how these drugs work and can be improved.

column36: Exploring the role of phosphoinositides in the trafficking of proteins to the apical complex in the malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum.
column37: Malaria is one of the world's most common infectious diseases, with approximately 274 million cases each year and 400 000 deaths, and thus represents one of the most devastating global public health problems. The lack of an effective vaccine, the emergence of resistance to first-line drugs like artemisinines, combined with the small number of suitable new drugs against the malaria parasite demonstrate the urgent need for the development and implementation of novel intervention strategies in the form of drugs, vector control measures and an effective vaccine. Indeed, it is expected that if the trend in malaria prevalence stays on its current upwards course, the death rate could double in the next twenty years. Invasion of a red blood cell by Plasmodium falciparum parasites is an essential step in the malaria lifecycle and host response to parasite antigens are an important component of human malarial immunity. Consequently, the molecular players involved in erythrocyte invasion are key targets for both therapeutic and vaccine-based strategies to block parasite development. Several of these invasion proteins are stored in the apical complex of the parasite, a structure containing secretory organelles called dense granules, micronemes and rhoptries, and are released at different times during invasion. Because of its essential role, interfering with the generation of the apical complex represents a very attractive target for the design of a new kind of antimalarial. Our studies will focus on trying to understand how the parasite directs proteins to the different structures of the apical complex. Understanding this complex process will likely provide a wealth of new targets for the development of strategies to block apical complex generation and preventing malaria pathogenesis.

column36: The discovery of new antibiotics derived from inhibitors of sporulation
column37: Antibiotics are used to treat bacterial infections such as pneumonia, tuberculosis, sepsis and various kinds of infection that result from surgery or in patients whose immune system is compromised by chemotherapy. They are therefore at the front line of virtually all aspects of modern medicine. The efficacy of these incredible drugs, mostly discovered during the period from 1940-60, is being rapidly eroded through the antibiotic resistance. As a result, new antibiotics are desperately needed if we are to sustain our current standard of care. But the classical approaches to antibiotics discovery are not working all that well. The reason for this is that all of the available molecules in the world have been tested for the inhibition of growth of pathogens. New approaches are therefore desperately needed. We have discovered that the filamentous bacteria of the genus Streptomyces provide a fascinating alternative approach. Because these bacteria are filamentous in structure, they use many elements of the core molecular machinery (cell wall biosynthesis, cell division, chromosome segregation etc) differently than rod shaped or coccoid bacteria - which include almost all of the pathogens. Many processes which are essential for viability in pathogenic bacteria are employed primarily for sporulation in the streptomycetes. Our hypothesis therefore, is that screening for inhibitors of sporulation in Streptomyces has the potential to reveal novel inhibitors of these core processes and that these inhibitors might be developed as antibiotics against "conventional" bacteria. We have tested this hypothesis and thereby discovered three novel antibiotics: EN-7, Min-1 and Fil-1. In this project we will further develop these compounds in the hopes that we can provide valuable leads for fighting infectious disease.

column36: Molecular control of neural stem cell fate decisions
column37: The neocortex is the region of the brain where higher cognitive functioning occurs, allowing us to perceive stimuli in the environment and have conscious thought. The original dogma was that new neurons could not be generated after embryonic development since there were no stem cells to replace lost neurons. However, more recent studies have identified a pool of neural stem cells that reside in the adult brain. Moreover, it has been found that these stem cells are first born in the embryonic period, persisting in an inactive state until adulthood. We have been studying how neural stem cells decide to be inactive, or divide and differentiate into neurons in the embryonic brain. These studies have focused on proneural genes, which we found mark a pool of slow-dividing neural stem cells in the embryo and adult. We now try to understand how the proneural genes control whether neural stem cells remain inactive, divide or differentiate. We have three aims in this study. In the first aim we examine how slow-dividing stem cells that express these proneural genes respond to a brain injury, and trace their embryonic progeny. In the second aim, we ask how these proneural genes can be manipulated to induce neural stem cells to produce new neurons in development and after brain injury. In the third aim, we begin to model the roles of these proneural genes in a primate system, using monkey tissue and generating brain organoids from human cells as a surrogate model system. These studies are important because re-invigoration of these dormant stem cells by manipulating the proneural genes may aid brain repair.

After an extensive co-creation process and pilot phase, ongoing funding is needed to extend recruitment and reach the scope of a full-scale trial. The study will randomly assign 450 youth to receive either hospital-based care or ICCT services to compare the effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of the two service pathways for youth with MHA challenges. As provincial, national, and international efforts to implement ICCT-type models of care advance under significant public and private investment, it is critical that robust data be collected to examine their effectiveness. column36: Repairing the brain of sick newborns: From bench to bedside
column37: At birth, some babies experienced a condition called asphyxia, which means that their brain and other organs did not receive enough blood and/or oxygen. This life-threatening condition accounts for 23% of all babies' deaths around the world, and often leads to cerebral palsy and trouble with learning and functioning in everyday life. At this time, no treatment is available to repair the brain damage in these babies. Sildenafil (Viagra(R)) already is given safely to babies suffering from increased blood pressure in their lungs for other reasons than asphyxia at birth. Our recent studies in an animal model of asphyxia at birth suggested that sildenafil may improve the damage to the brain. Also, our recent pilot study with human babies showed that it is feasible to give sildenafil to babies who suffer from asphyxia at birth. We hypothesize that (1) sildenafil can repair the damage to a baby's brain by stimulating the growth of new nerve cells and decreasing brain swelling; and that (2) sildenafil can be safely increased up to 6 mg/kg/day in these babies and may improve how their brain and heart/lungs work. We will use a rat model of asphyxia at birth to study the mechanisms involved in repairing the brain after it is damaged. We also will determine the optimal dose of sildenafil that can be given to human babies who suffered from asphyxia at birth to improve their brain, heart, and lungs. This project will enable us to understand the repair mechanisms involved in the damaged baby's brain after asphyxia at birth and to determine whether sildenafil is a promising treatment for repairing this damage. This project may provide new solutions for these babies to reduce the consequences of asphyxia at birth and improve their future life. Thus, it may help many families around the world who are dealing with this devastating condition.

column37: Our immune system has the incredible ability to launch immune responses which target specific molecular signatures within pathogens. However, this highly specific targeting requires careful control over which molecules are targeted, as the accidental targeting of a self-molecule can lead to debilitating diseases in which a patient's immune system destroys their own body. Our immune systems have multiple levels of control, each intended to ensure that responses against pathogens are strongly activated, while those against harmless agents - e.g. the billions of cells that our bodies turn-over daily - are suppressed. In this grant we will further explore this pathway, to determine how it functions and its role in mediating the activation of the immune system.

column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the most common form of inherited skeletal muscle disorders. column36: Hearts in Rhythm Organization (HiRO): Improving detection and treatment of inherited heart rhythm disorders to prevent sudden death
column37: Inherited heart rhythm disorders include Long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, and catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. These conditions affect 150,000 Canadians and are the major cause of sudden cardiac death in the young. Early diagnosis of these disorders can provide the most effective care, including personalized exercise restriction, personalized medications and more appropriate use of implantable cardioverter defibrillators (ICDs) to regulate heart rhythms. These conditions pose a high risk for cardiac arrest and sudden death, and new methods for identifying those at risk are urgently needed. The primary goal of this research is to develop more effective methods for predicting who are at greatest risk of a serious cardiac event. To do this, we will use healthcare data collected from participants in the Hearts in Rhythm Organization (HiRO) research database. This includes inherited heart rhythm disorder patients from 19 specialized adult and pediatric clinics across Canada. Our additional goal is to create a patient-oriented research program that addresses the current and future needs of these patients, their families and their communities. In the long-term, we expect this research to result in improved screening practices to better identify at-risk patients and individualize their treatment to prevent and decrease the tragedy of sudden cardiac death. Involving patients in the research process will ensure that we are addressing issues that are most pertinent to their well-being. We envision that this will improve communication between the healthcare provider and patients, so that patients are well informed about their condition and ensuring that they can take an active role in managing their health and improve their quality of life.

column36: Risky decision making as a cause, consequence and treatment target for addiction.
column37: Whether someone is dependent on a chemical substance like cocaine, or has developed a behavioural addiction such as gambling disorder, the maladaptive choice to pursue the addiction at the expense of other goals lies at the heart of the problem. Indeed, individuals with an addiction disorder, or who later develop problems with addiction, score poorly on laboratory-based decision-making tests such as the Iowa Gambling Task (IGT) that involve the weighing of costs and benefits. One hypothesis is that decision-making impairments may be compounded as the addiction develops because of the way in which addictive drugs, and also engagement in addictive behaviours, affect brain function, biasing the decision-making process in favour of the addiction. Choosing to abstain from the addictive substance or behaviour then becomes really hard. We have successfully developed an animal model of cost/benefit decision making based on the IGT: the rat Gambling Task (rGT). On both human and animal tests, subjects must choose between four different options, each of which is associated with different amounts of potential reward and loss. By avoiding high-risk, high-reward options, subjects can maximise gains. Most rats develop this optimal strategy, although some animals instead favour the risky options. These risk-preferring rats are uniquely and adversely affected by taking cocaine: their decision making gets worse and they show increased drug-seeking in withdrawal indicative of greater relapse risk. Adding sound and light cues when the rats win on this gambling task significantly increases the proportion of rats biased towards the risky options. We now want to use this model to understand why the addition of these "bells and whistles" potentiates risky choice and addiction vulnerability, and harness that knowledge to pilot potential therapies for addiction.

column36: Engineering of a probiotic bacterium for precise microbiome editing
column37: We propose to develop a safe-to-use, efficient and programmable conjugative probiotic (COP) as a highly innovative tool to precisely edit the microbiome and fight multidrug resistant pathogens. The E. coli Nissle 1917 probiotic strain, which has previously been shown to be clinically safe, is used as the COP chassis for our experiments. COP bacteria also include potent bacterial conjugation machineries for high-efficiency delivery of CRISPR-Cas9 systems into the microbiota. The CRISPR-Cas9 system can easily be programmed to cleave DNA simply by providing custom guide RNA (gRNA) spacer sequences that match the desired target sites. Targeting DNA sequences located in a bacterial chromosome leads to cell death by compromising genome integrity. The CRISPR-Cas9 system can also cure cells from plasmids carrying antibiotic resistance or virulence genes, thereby "disarming" potentially dangerous bacteria by restoring susceptibility to antibiotics. Unlike broad-spectrum antibiotics, the COP system is designed to be highly specific, with selectivity conferred by carefully chosen CRISPR-Cas9 target sequences and tuning of the host range through the selection of appropriate COP conjugative machineries. This new technology would also constitute a powerful microbiome manipulation tool for fundamental research, and to progressively advance towards clinical applications. Once established, this innovative method could have a significant impact on medicine by eventually offering a new tool to treat dysbiosis or as an alternative to antimicrobials for the prevention or treatment of many infectious diseases.

column36: Functional Genomics of Neurodegenerative Diseases: Defining Molecular Pathogenesis and Targets for Biomarkers and Personalised Therapies
column37: Neurodegenerative dementias are the fourth leading cause of death worldwide, affecting >24 million people at a cost of >US$172 billion annually. Despite a lot of effort, apart from a handful of mildly effective symptomatic treatments there are no proven ways of stopping these diseases. This proposal addresses takes an innovative approach to develop therapies that address this unmet need. The program is built upon our recent success in identifying genes that carry DNA variants that increase risk of dementia. We have noticed that these genes cluster into functional groups ("cellular pathways"). Two of the largest clusters are of particular interest. One cluster regulates the function of brain inflammatory cells (microglia), which search the brain for damaged cells and aggregated proteins. Another function of these cells is to prune unwanted nerve connections (synapses). The other cluster contains proteins that can change their conformation in order to facilitate key cellular functions (such as making proteins in synapses that are crucial for memory, or regulating the function of microglial cells). Because these clusters contain multiple different genes with DNA sequence changes that increase risk of dementia, it is clear that these clusters govern pathways that are very important in causing synaptic damage leading to dementia. A vital clue is that some of the genes in these pathways also contain variants that actually protect the patient from developing clinical disease. This clearly suggests that mimicking the effect of these protective genetic variants could be a way of preventing/slowing the progression of these diseases. The current program will therefore develop a better understanding of the components in these disease causing pathways, understand how they are regulated, and identify specific components that could be used as molecular targets for treatments that would make the pathway function normally.

column36: Testing a conceptual model of adjustment and compliance in couples seeking fertility treatment
column37: Infertility is a growing public health issue, affecting 12-16% of Canadian couples. Although advances in assisted reproductive technologies now allow more couples to become parents, treatment is strenuous, has limited success rates, and can disrupt both partners' psychological, relationship, and sexual adjustment. Hence, despite a favourable prognosis, 20-30% of couples choose to end treatment before achieving birth. Yet, fundamental knowledge about compliance with fertility treatment is still lacking. The most common reasons for dropout are physical and psychological burden of treatment and relationship strain. Research in this area, however, suffers from important flaws, including the use of retrospective designs and the use of general descriptors to identify causes of discontinuation. Evidence about the predictors of non-compliance is also scare. This 2-year prospective study will examine predictors of treatment non-compliance in both partners of 350 couples seeking fertility treatment. Patient, treatment, and clinic factors, as well as psychological, relational and sexual strain are expected to predict treatment discontinuation. This study will 1) provide novel prospective data about factors associated with treatment burden and discontinuation in couples seeking fertility treatment, 2) help identify barriers to treatment compliance, 3) help inform the development of interventions to guide couples through their decisional process, and 4) highlight clinical factors that could be modified to promote better patient care, prevent undue treatment termination, and improve cumulative pregnancy rates.

column37: Platelets are circulating blood particles normally responsible for stopping bleeding by forming blood clots (platelet aggregates). By the end of our studies we expect to have established that the two platelet subtypes differ in their response to antiplatelet drugs and that heart attack patients with an elevated ratio of non-NO-producing to NO-producing platelets may not fully respond to current anti-platelet therapy. Lastly, these studies have the potential to inform personal anti-platelet therapy, and to potentially inform the future development of more effective anti-platelet drugs.

column36: Novel Mechanisms of Leishmania Pathogenesis
column37: Leishmaniases are a group of infectious diseases caused by parasites that infect 12 million people worldwide with 1.3 million new cases every year. Like many neglected diseases, leishmaniasis is primarily endemic to developing nations and thus presents additional socioeconomic burdens to already impoverished people. Leishmania donovani-the focus of this project-causes visceral leishmaniasis with severe morbidity and mortality. There are no effective vaccines and current treatments have limited efficacy and significant toxicities. The mechanisms that enable intracellular pathogens such as leishmania to chronically infect macrophages -pivotal cells of the innate immune system- are a focus of intense interest. Research is proposed here to investigate two novel mechanisms of leishmania pathogenesis. The first mechanism relates to investigate the roles of small, non-coding RNAs (snRNAs) in immunity to intracellular infection. These snRNAs are found in both animals and plants and some viruses and are well conserved and recognized as a vital component of genetic regulation. snRNAs have been implicated in stress, cancer, infection and innate immunity. Our hypothesis is that leishmania uses small RNA-based effector mechanisms to establish chronic infection. Research relevant to the second novel mechanism of pathogenesis relates to exploitation of host cell signaling pathway-PI3K-Akt in particular- by leishmania to create an environment which is permissive to survive inside the host. Our hypothesis is that PI3K functions as a master regulator of innate immunity to leishmania and promotes chronic infection. We will study the molecular mechanism of PI3K-Akt regulation by leishmania. This research will greatly improve the current understanding of leishmania biology and pathogenesis, and has the potential to aid in the discovery and development of novel therapeutics and vaccines to both treat and prevent leishmania infection and disease.

column37: Cancer is a deadly disease. Despite decades of research, cancer remains the leading cause of death worldwide. As early detection and treatment can greatly improve patient outcomes, better diagnostic and therapeutic agents are urgently needed. One method physicians used to diagnose cancers is by giving patients an imaging scan called positron emission tomography. Patients receive a small dose of a radioactive agent, which selectively targets tumours and sends a signal to a detector to pinpoint their location. These imaging agents can be easily modified to carry a more potent radioactive element to kill cancer cells for therapeutic applications. While radioactive imaging/therapeutic agents designed for various cancers have been developed, these existing agents are encumbered by severe limitations. The most common problem is their high accumulation in kidneys. The high accumulation leads to very bright signal coming from kidneys, overshadows nearby small tumours, and makes it harder to detect tumours adjacent to kidneys. Similarly, the high accumulation of the radioactive agents can result in severe damage to kidneys. The goal of this proposed research is to develop a general strategy to minimize accumulation of radioactive imaging and therapeutic agents in kidneys. Most importantly, this strategy is expected to have very broad applicability, and can be used to reduce the high kidney accumulation of most of the previously reported radioactive imaging and therapeutic agents, and facilitate their clinical translation. The success of this research will generate more sensitive imaging agents for cancer detection and more efficacious therapeutic agents with minimized toxicity to kidneys. Overall, the success of this proposed research will significantly improve the diagnosis and prognosis of cancer patients in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Deciphering the role of the newly uncovered dopaminergic pathways to brainstem locomotor circuits in mammals: from cell to behaviour.
column37: Brainstem cells generate the walking command sent to the spinal cord to activate the leg muscles. In Parkinson's disease, dopamine cells die in the brain, resulting in walking deficits. Classically, the connection between dopamine and brainstem cells is considered as solely indirect and to involve intermediary brain regions. However, direct connections between dopaminergic and brainstem cells were recently uncovered. These direct connections promote locomotion in basal vertebrates. In mammals, such connections could play a key role in locomotor control as well. In Parkinson's disease, the loss of such direct connections could be involved in the walking deficits. However, we still do not know the functional role of such direct connections in mammals. Our goal is to identify in mice the locomotor role of the direct connections between dopaminergic cells and brainstem cells. The brainstem cells targeted by the dopaminergic cells will be identified using high-resolution examination of brain anatomy, where the different cells will appear in different colors. Using in vivo optogenetics, we will determine whether turning on these direct dopaminergic connections is sufficient to initiate or speed up locomotion. Using in vivo chemogenetics, we will determine whether turning off these dopaminergic connections impairs gait or stop locomotion. Finally, the cellular mechanisms through which dopamine controls brainstem cells will be identified using patch-clamp electrodes able to detect the electric currents underlying brain cell activities. The proposed project will provide important new knowledge on the mechanisms through which the walking commands are controlled by dopamine in the brain. This knowledge is essential to understand why the walking commands are impaired by the loss of dopaminergic cells in Parkinson's disease. This will allow us to propose new strategies to improve locomotor function in Parkinson's disease and other locomotor disorders.

column36: Harnessing the power of Monocytes/Macrophages in Intestinal Immunity to Candidiasis
column37: Invasive fungal infections affect more than 2 million people worldwide annually, and result in death for more than half of these patients. In a healthy immune system, a hormone called GM-CSF activates antifungal defenses to protect against fungal infection. One molecule that controls GM-CSF, called CARD9, appears to be highly important, because humans that have mutations that interfere with the function of CARD9 spontaneously develop life-threatening invasive fungal infections, including of the brain. Although the roles of GM-CSF and of CARD9 in protecting against fungal infections are therefore clear, HOW they protect specific organs is not understood. We believe that these molecules do so by preventing fungus in the gut from escaping into the body. When GM-CSF or CARD9 are malfunctioning, we hypothesize that macrophages in the gut are defective, which allows the fungi normally residing in the gut to escape from the gut tissue and then into specific circulating cells (called monocytes), that then carry the hidden fungus to specific organs, like the brain, leading to life threatening disease. My research aims to understand how GM-CSF and CARD9 enable monocytes and macrophages to combat fungal infections at the level of the gut, blood and brain. I will use innovative cutting-edge techniques to investigate these processes, in whole mice and in cells. This exciting research will provide important and new insights into organ- and cell-specific immunity to fungal infections, opening the door to developing new ways to treat these devastating infections.

column36: Understanding the contribution of the peripheral nervous system to central neuropathic pain
column37: Chronic pain can develop in patients with the disease Multiple Sclerosis (MS). Because the central nervous system (spinal cord and brain) is affected in disease like MS-this type of chronic pain is referred to as 'central neuropathic pain' (CNP). CNP affects nearly half of the people with MS and is incredibly distressing. Currently there is no effective treatment for CNP. Finding a treatment that can target the spinal cord or brain directly can be very challenging and comes with the risk of unwanted side effects. On the other hand, the 'peripheral nervous system' (the nerves and cells that reside outside of the spinal cord and brain but communicate with them) is much easier to target, is often more amenable to treatment and is the focus of our proposed research. Our research to date has revealed that sensory neurons which reside in a structure of the peripheral nervous system known as the 'dorsal root ganglion' become stressed when disease affects the spinal cord and brain. Stressed sensory neurons can begin to send inappropriate signals into the central nervous system and we hypothesize that this is a major factor that establishes CNP in diseases like MS. Our studies will examine this at a variety of levels. First, we aim to understand the specific changes that arise in a stressed sensory neuron that can cause it to function inappropriately. We will then examine several novel therapeutic strategies aimed at relieving the stress on the neurons and determine if this will restore normal function and relieve CNP.

column37: In 2014, the World Health Organization labeled antibiotic resistance a "global threat" that requires urgent action. This message has been reinforced by many reports including a UK report, which predicts that if no steps are made to curtail antibiotic resistance, an extra 10 million people a year worldwide will die by 2050. The media has captured the essence of this report with the sound bite "Superbugs to kill 'more than cancer' by 2050". The present situation is indeed alarming in that there are no antibiotics to which bacteria have not developed resistance and many bacteria have multiple resistance mechanisms, making infections caused by superbugs nearly impossible to cure. Aggravating the situation is the fact that for economic reasons, the pharmaceutical industry has largely abandoned new antibiotic drug development. To address this pressing healthcare threat, a multi-pronged approach is required. Most importantly, in addition to curtailing the indiscriminate and unnecessary usage of antibiotics, one crucial aspect to pursue is to study the mechanisms by which bacteria resist the effects of antibiotics and exploit this information for the development of new antibiotic therapies that are less impacted by such resistance mechanisms. Therefore, we will examine in atomic detail how superbugs are resistant to two different classes of antibiotics. We know that these bacteria have dedicated enzymes that detoxify many antibiotics, and the research will reveal how this is exactly achieved. We will than take these insights and explore how we can slightly alter the antibiotics by chemical means so that they can no longer be detoxified, while still retaining their antibiotic properties. Complementary, we will also examine if we can prevent the bacterial enzymes from detoxifying the antibiotics in the first place, using a blocking strategy. Either avenue should provide us with new and much needed solutions for treating infections caused by superbugs.

column37: Les maladies cardiovasculaires (MCV) sont la cause la plus frequente de deces dans le monde occidental et representent un defit pour la recherche et la medecine moderne. Les MCV sont les manifestations cliniques de l'atherosclerose qui correspond au depot de cholesterol, sous forme de plaque, dans les parois des arteres pouvant causer leur obstruction. La rupture de la plaque atherosclerotique est impliquee dans approximativement 70% d'infarctus fatal du myocarde et/ou de mort subite. Meme si les techniques actuelles de diagnostic de MCV permettent d'evaluer l'etendue de la plaque atherosclerotique et le niveau de stenose arteriel, elles ne permettent pas d'evaluer avec precision la stabilite de la plaque. La stabilite de la plaque atherosclerotique depend fortement du niveau d'inflammation a l'interieur de la plaque. Les resultats de plusieurs travaux suggerent que l'huile d'olive, en reduisant l'inflammation systemique, permet d'augmenter la stabilite de la plaque atherosclerotique. Cependant, il n'existe pas de donnees concernant l'effet de l'huile d'olive sur l'inflammation arterielle qui reste le meilleur marqueur de la fragilite de la plaque. L'imagerie par tomographie d'emission par positrons (TEP) est une technique utilisee en clinique pour, a la fois quantifier l'inflammation au sein de la plaque atherosclerotique mais aussi pour suivre l'effet d'interventions ciblant de ce type d'inflammation. Cependant, le probleme d'accessibilite a ce type d'imagerie et les couts eleves qui lui sont associes limitent son utilisation.

column36: Ultrasound-Mediated Drug Delivery to the Spinal Cord
column37: The brain and spinal cord have protective barriers that regulate their environment. While these barriers are beneficial in healthy individuals, in patients with brain or spinal cord disorders, these barriers prevent drugs from reaching their target. This work will investigate the use of ultrasound to temporarily open the barrier between the blood vessels and spinal cord in order to deliver drugs more efficiently. Medical ultrasound (US) has many potential therapeutic applications, one of which is facilitating drug delivery in the brain by temporarily opening the barrier between the blood and the brain. This is accomplished when the US interacts with micro-sized gas spheres that are injected in the blood stream and causes them to vibrate, stimulating the blood vessels walls. By focusing the US energy to a small volume, this effect can be directed to specific sites without impacting the surrounding tissue. In the brain, a number of anti-cancer agents have been delivered in preclinical studies using this method and have shown improved effects in combating tumors. In preliminary studies, this technique has also been used to open the barrier to the spinal cord, and recently a positive therapeutic effect was seen in an animal model. We hypothesize that US-based drug delivery can safely increase the therapeutic efficacy of drugs delivered to the spinal cord. In rats, we will examine the effects of ultrasound on the spinal cord, develop methods to safely control the treatment exposures, and test this method as a treatment for spinal cord tumors.Using benchtop measurements and experiments in a large animal model we will also investigate how the human spinal geometry will impact treatment monitoring and control techniques. If this study is successful it could lead to a noninvasive treatment option for patients with spinal cord disease and encourage the investigation of new drug interventions for these conditions.

column36: Advancing the methodological frontiers of adaptive treatment strategies
column37: While our current understanding of how well biomedical treatments work is based on population averages, the average effect of a treatment across a population may not be a good indicator of whether or not to recommend a particular treatment for an individual patient. This is because individual patients may respond differently to the same treatment due to their unique combinations of factors such as pre-existing health conditions, genetics, environmental factors, and lifestyle choices. Moreover, a patient may respond differently to the same treatment over time, e.g. as he/she ages. These two types of variability (between individuals and within a single individual over time) motivate the need for targeted treatment plans in which patient care is improved by using information on an individual's changing health status to adapt treatment recommendations accordingly. Examples include the management of chronic conditions, treatments that require frequent adjustments, or clinical decisions based on events such as remissions or intolerable side effects of a drug therapy. This approach, known as precision medicine, relies on "adaptive treatment strategies" where treatment plans account for between and within individual differences over time. The goal is to help physicians deliver the best treatment for each patient each time a treatment decision is made. These strategies provide answers to questions like "If a patient has not responded to an antidepressant, should the dose of that drug be increased, or should a new drug be prescribed?" While the concept of adaptive treatment strategies has existed for more than 2 decades, new statistical methods and tools are needed to gain maximum insight from contemporary "big data" datasets and to accommodate new treatments that have been developed . My research goals for the next 7 years are to advance statistical theory and develop the needed methods and tools for answering clinically relevant questions related to HIV and mental health.

column36: Frailty and the Kidney Transplant Wait List
column37: Many people with advanced kidney disease will benefit from a kidney transplant. Some people are not eligible because they are have health conditions that put them at a high risk of dying before receiving a transplant or high risk of deteriorating health after a transplant. Deciding who is able to receive a transplant involves a detailed evaluation of a person's health and a review by transplant specialists. Some people with kidney disease who are being considered for a kidney transplant have difficulties in their health, mobility or function that put them at a risk for a shortened lifespan. This is often referred to as frailty. Currently, we do not know how being frail might affect the health of those who are waiting for a kidney transplant. Knowing this information could be helpful in a number of ways. It would provide transplant specialists with information to allow them to make an informed, objective decision about whether patients should be put on the wait list and not rely solely on their clinical impression. It would also provide a more complete picture of a person's overall health in addition to the tests that are currently used to better inform patients who are deciding about being put on the wait list. In this study, we aim to examine what happens to people who are frail and wait listed for a kidney transplant compared with those who are not frail. We will use several different tools to assess frailty. We will follow patients to see if they die or are removed from the wait list before they can receive a transplant in addition to a number of other important outcomes such as being admitted to hospital or changes in their quality of life. We hope that the results of this study may lead to better allocation of kidney transplant organs and a more objective method of evaluating eligibility for the wait list.

column36: Studying telomeres maintenance by telomerase using live cell imaging
column37: In order to properly grow and divide, normal cells must maintain the integrity of their genome. Telomeres cap the ends of chromosomes and are essential to maintain their stability. Telomere shortening leads to genomic instability and favors the rise of cancers. In most eukaryotes, telomerase is a specialized enzyme used to elongate telomeres. Most of our knowledge on telomerase relies on the detection of its activity in large populations of cells. However, little is known about the behavior of telomerase in single cells, as it acts on a single telomere. For this purpose, we developed an assay to image both telomerase molecules and telomere in single living cells, using the budding yeast as a model organism. Using this approach, the events leading to the recruitment of telomerase at a single short telomere will be studied in real time, in single cells. We will particularly focus on the role of sister telomeres cohesion during telomerase recruitment at short telomeres. We will explore how telomerase is regulated in a telomere-specific manner by focusing especially on its interaction with telomeric repeat-containing noncoding RNA (TERRA). Finally, we will use live cell imaging to study the dynamics of telomerase molecules and their recruitment at telomeres in living human cancer cells. Identifying the pathways involved in the regulation of telomerase and telomeres will help understand how tumors arise and develop into cancer, and also reveal new potential targets for cancer therapy.

column36: Ski is a negative regulator of cardiac fibrosis
column37: Patients surviving a heart attack or those with hypertension develop chronic heart disease. These patients make too much collagen in their heart muscle, wherein non-muscle cells called myofibroblasts secrete excessive collagens, which stiffens the heart. Most of the "glue" (extracellular matrix) between muscle cells in healthy hearts is made of tough collagen proteins. Too much collagen leads to cardiac fibrosis which results in weak muscle contraction and relaxation. Despite this, there is currently no treatment for cardiac fibrosis, nor are there any specific cardiac drugs approved to fix cardiac fibrosis. In recent years, we have found a new protein called Ski. Ski turns off this over-deposition of matrix, in diseased heart cells. Further, we have made progress of how Ski actually achieves this positive change. We are now poised to extend our understanding of how Ski corrects cardiac fibrosis. We discovered that Ski is able to deactivate cells that cause fibrosis, and this is associated with normal control of the extracellular matrix; but our also work shows that Ski somehow is redirected and lost in heart failure. So, we hypothesize that loss of Ski's function in sick hearts may contribute to cardiac fibrosis and speed up the onset of heart disease - our experiments will test this hypothesis directly in mice wherein we specifically turn off Ski in cells making extracellular matrix. Finally we hypothesize that Ski turns off the function of special proteins that normally promote fibrosis in sick hearts. Experiments designed to answer this will show the mechanism of Ski's beneficial effects. column36: Harnessing neuroinflammation to develop new treatments for multiple sclerosis and glioblastoma
column37: In response to insults, the body launches an immune response to eradicate the threat and instigate tissue repair. Unfortunately, chronic excessive inflammation leads to tissue damage while dampened immune responses may favor the development of tumors. My research programs are centered on inflammation within the brain and spinal cord, termed neuroinflammation. I focus my research activities on multiple sclerosis (MS) and glioblastoma (the most malignant and deadly form of brain tumor), where MS exhibits chronic neuroinflammation that destroys cells within the brain and spinal cord, and glioblastoma has suppressed immunity that allows brain tumor cells to escape detection and being killed. Indeed, brain tumor cells change the nature of immune cells and exploit them for cancer growth. My research programs thus seek to: 1) stop immune cells from going into the brain and spinal cord to inflict injury in MS, and neutralize the injury that immune cells can produce within the brain/spinal cord; 2) understand and harness the beneficial aspects of the immune system to facilitate the repair of myelin, particularly in aging subjects where the newly formed myelin can protect nerve fibers and thus slow the progression of disability in MS; and 3) rejuvenate the compromised immune system in glioblastoma in order that immune cells can perform their evolutionary function of fighting threats and eliminate the brain tumor. Thus, rather than considering MS and glioblastoma as distinct entities that should not be researched together, I have taken the unique approach of removing the silos from these diseases to study them together. By understanding why they lie on opposite ends of a spectrum, the lessons and drugs acquired in MS can be used to inform and treat glioblastoma, and vice versa. Thus, the overall research seeks to acquire new knowledge and enable recovery from devastating MS and glioblastoma.

column36: Cytoneme-mediated growth signalling in Drosophila
column37: The growth of embryonic tissues is controlled by "growth factors" that are produced by discrete populations of cells, move through the tissues, and stimulate cells at a distance to grow and divide. We expect that our finding in flies will provide much-needed insights into the role these proteins are likely to play in cell-cell signaling in humans, both during normal physiology and in disease.

column37: According to the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one the largest threats to public health and economic growth. Recently, the WHO for the first time divided pathogens into three categories according to the urgency of need for new antibiotics: critical, high and medium priority. The most critical group of all includes multidrug resistant bacteria that pose a particular threat in hospitals, nursing homes, and among patients whose care requires devices such as ventilators and blood catheters. They include Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas and various Enterobacteriaceae that cause severe and often deadly infections such as bloodstream infections and pneumonia. Despite significant investments by industry and academia into antibiotic discovery and development over the past decades, no new antibiotic class with novel mode(s) of action to fight these pathogens has been approved in half a century. The reasons for this failure have been identified and are caused by the inability of current compounds to penetrate into bacteria (low permeability) and their likelihood of being pumped out (efflux). To overcome this bottleneck in antibacterial drug discovery, we plan to develop helper molecules (adjuvants) designed to enhance membrane permeability, reduce efflux of antibiotics and prevent or delay resistance development against these pathogens. The overall goal of this proposal is to identify optimized helper molecules capable of rescuing antibiotics from resistance in animal models of infection against multidrug-resistant priority pathogens and to understand their mode of actions.

column36: Regulation of cerebral blood flow in obstructive sleep apnea
column37: In healthy humans, brain blood flow is influenced by changes in the levels of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the circulating blood. However, the brain's important ability to regulate its blood flow is impaired in disease processes such as obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). People who have OSA stop breathing intermittently throughout the night, resulting in repeated episodes of low oxygen and high carbon dioxide in the blood. Because of these repeated episodes, the ability of the brain vessels to regulate blood flow becomes impaired. This impairment can lead to hypertension and stroke. The mechanisms that regulate brain blood flow in health, and how these mechanisms become impaired with disease, is poorly understood. It is thought that nitric oxide (NO) plays a major role in regulating blood flow in several vascular beds, including the brain. In a first study, we will determine, in an experimental human model of intermittent hypoxia during sleep, the effects of intermittent hypoxia on the regulation of brain blood flow and the role of changes in brain blood flow on the stability of breathing. In a second study, we will determine the extent to which the brain blood flow response to low oxygen is altered in a broad range of patients with moderate to severe OSA. Finally, our research will determine if the brain blood flow impairments observed in untreated OSA patients can be corrected after treatment with night-time continuous positive airway pressure. This work may help us better understand conditions such as hypertension, OSA, stroke and aging, in which endothelium-dependent relaxation (i.e., relaxation of cells that line brain blood vessels) by NO is impaired. Our research will provide useful information about how well treatment for OSA reverses brain blood flow impairments that may lead to stroke. Ultimately, this will translate into improved health and disease prevention for Canadians.
