column36: BRD4 Inhibition in Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension: a Phase 2 Clinical Trial
column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive condition characterized by the chronic elevation of pulmonary artery (PA) pressure leading to failure of the heart. In spite of recent advances in approved therapies, PAH remains a serious disease with significant mortality. In contrast to the earlier belief that contraction of pulmonary vessels played a key role in PAH, it is now established that excessive proliferation of the cells within the pulmonary artery wall is a pivotal component of pulmonary vascular obliteration, a currently irreversible feature of PAH for which available pharmacotherapies have no/limited efficacy. In recent years, it has become increasingly appreciated that, in addition to rare mutations in genes, changes in their expression in the absence of changes in their structure (i.e. epigenetics) largely contributes to this phenomenon in PAH. Changes in gene expression influence numerous functions of the cells. We recently documented that by regulating genes known to be deregulated in PAH, Bromodomain-containing Protein-4 (BRD4) largely contributes to excessive cell proliferation and pulmonary vascular obliteration in PAH. More importantly, we observed that the pharmacological inhibition of BRD4, reverses PAH in human cells and animal models of PAH. Very recently, apabetalone, an orally available BRD4inhibitor, was shown to be safe, well tolerated and effective in treating cancers vascular cell proliferation leading to other types of vascular obliteration such as coronary artery disease. The time is thus right to translate our findings in human PAH. This proposal addresses a very novel and promising therapeutic avenue to treat and is one of the first steps of personalized medicine in PAH. We propose an early phase clinical trial to determine whether: BRD4 inhibition with apabetalone is safe and effective and; patients' characteristics can predict response to therapy in adult patients with symptomatic PAH.

column37: About 5 to 10% of Canadians live with chronic pain in their mouth, jaws and face (called orofacial pain) caused by temporomandibular disorder (or TMD, meaning issues with your jaw or the muscles that control it). TMD's cause is unknown and there are no specific molecular markers for TMD to help diagnose, predict or treat it. While TMD has some inherited genetic components that are passed on through families, how are genes work can be modulated by environmental factors such as exposure to stress, inflammation, diet, and medication. One way that environmental factors alter how our genes work is by adding 'marks' to the DNA through a process called methylation. We will study blood and tissue samples provided by healthy people and people with TMD, as well as people with other chronic pain conditions. All samples will be examined for genome-wide methylation patterns. These studies will allow us to identify how methylation patterns affect TMD, who will get TMD and who will not, and whose TMD will persist over time. In addition, by comparing to samples from other types of chronic pain, we will identify methylation patterns in people that are common to TMD and other chronic pain conditions. Ultimately this will help us understand more about how the environment affects a person's genetics in terms of their risk of TMD and how better to predict, diagnose, and ultimately treat or prevent painful TMD.

column36: Targeting the epigenetic state of refractory and relapsing acute myeloid leukemia
column37: In 2013, according to the Canadian Cancer Society, 1315 patients in Canada were diagnosed with the blood cancer acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and 1047 died of the disease. AML is the most common adult blood cancer and one of the most deadly forms of cancer. Unfortunately, these numbers have not changed much in the last 30 plus years. This is due primarily because only minor changes to therapy have occurred over this time period. About 40 year ago, an innovative chemotherapy known as induction therapy was introduced as the frontline treatment for AML patients. While some modest improvements have been made to induction therapy, new innovative therapeutic approaches are necessary to make substantive improvements to the survival of AML patients. In contrast to the "one size fits all" induction therapy, we propose to implement a "precision medicine" strategy to treat AML patients. To implement precision medicine in AML, we need to identify different sub-classes of AML, identify which patients fit a particular subclass, develop targeted therapies for these sub-classes of AML and treat the patients accordingly. In this proposal, we will focus on the "epigenetic state" of AML because these states can be reversed. Recently, we demonstrated in mice that we can reverse the epigenetic state of a group of AML patients who are resistant to induction therapy. This group of patients are known as "refractory" AML patients. In this proposal, we aim to determine how different drugs reverse the epigenetic state of this group of refractory AML patients and perform additional experiments to enable us to file for a precision medicine clinical trial in this group of AML patients. We will also develop the tools to treat other groups of refractory and relapse AML patients. These tools include methods to identify these patients at diagnosis and novel drugs to treat these normally drug resistant AML cells.

column36: MGMT promoter methylated breast cancer: An opportunity for a targeted treatment with alkylating agent temozolomide in combination with existing breast cancer therapeutics.
column37: Breast cancer (BC) is responsible for 25% of all female cancer diagnoses annually, affects 1 in 8 women, and is the 2nd leading cause of cancer death among Canadian women. Temozolomide (TMZ) is a well-tolerated oral chemotherapy used to treat brain cancers and its efficacy is linked to down regulation of a protein named MGMT. MGMT is involved in the the repair of DNA damage and is expressed in normal human cells; however, in cancer cells the modification (methylation) of the MGMT gene promoter leads to down regulation of the MGMT protein. MGMT when present, repairs the damage caused by TMZ promoting cancer survival and when absent allows cellular death. Down regulation of MGMT has been consistently noted in certain subtypes of BC, and we hypothesize that TMZ may be a novel, targeted, therapeutic option that can be combined with other DNA targeting therapies such as PARP inhibition in patients whose tumors apriori fail to express MGMT.

column37: Since 1990, the CIHR Canadian HIV Trials Network (CTN) has supported a thriving community of researchers and stakeholders who collaborate to produce impactful clinical research in HIV. Despite advancements in HIV treatment and practice, the need for reliable, outcome-oriented research to stem the epidemic is paramount. The CTN will address this need while engaging key populations affected by HIV, Hepatitis C and/or other sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections (STBBIs) as well as other related health conditions, while focusing on prevention and treatment. Backed by the CTN National Centre (which houses central administrative, methodological, and management services) and the CTN Research Core structure (which drives the HIV research agenda in Canada), the CTN has catalyzed collective action to test hypotheses and build the capacity of young researchers and community members living with and affected by HIV and related conditions. It does so by centralizing and sharing resources and expertise among researchers, clinical sites and leading health and research institutions and by engaging knowledge-brokers and members of the HIV community in both official languages. Seen through the lens of the World Health Organization's 'cascade of care', the CTN recognizes that HIV prevention, testing, ART initiation, adherence and treatment success are all influenced by several factors such as social stigma, discrimination and other barriers. These priorities are underpinned by the prospect for a cure and the quest to understand and eliminate viral reservoirs. The CTN proposes a renewed scientific vision for 2019-2024 through a National and Strategic Research Agenda for HIV research in Canada. This will be actualized by teams of researchers working within the CTN's four Research Cores (Prevention; Co-infections & Related Conditions; Clinical Care & Management; and Vaccines & Immunotherapies) and through the CTN's proposed Cross-Core Community Collaboration Teams.

column36: IMPACTT: A Microbiome Research Core based on Integrated Microbiome Platforms for Advancing Causation Testing and Translation
column37: Our body surfaces, including the gut, mouth, skin, and lung are colonized by trillions of microbes. This colonization is a dynamic process that begins primarily at birth and is heavily influenced by environmental factors, including mode of birth, diet, antibiotic use, hygiene and health status. Alterations in microbial communities are associated with a number of diseases, such as allergy, autoimmunity, autism, and obesity. However, association is not the same as causation. Changes in the microbiome could lead to disease, occur as a result of disease, or both. Therefore, researchers must now clearly define microbial function and identify the molecular mechanisms by which the microbiome interacts with the human host to influence health. Such functional studies will facilitate the design of new approaches for disease treatment and prevention. We will establish a Microbiome Research Core based on Integrated Microbiome Platforms for Advancing Causation Testing and Translation (IMPACTT). IMPACTT is a multi-centre collaboration to provide expertise and sharing of resources to foster and standardize microbiome research across Canada. The new gnotobiotic facility at the University of Calgary will form the basis for the study of complex functional interactions between the microbiome and the host. It will allow for precise control of all colonizing microbes to identify mechanistic links between the microbiome and the host. IMPACTT will also facilitate microbiome studies in human cohorts by providing expertise for study design, sample collection, and computational analysis. IMPACTT will establish and maintain a large repository of microbes, with genetic and metabolic information, available to microbiome researchers across Canada to enable functional microbiome studies. Finally, we will also develop a platform to discover links between microbial genes, proteins, and metabolism with microbial function, and then further link this to human health and disease.

column37: Hypertensive heart disease (HTN-HD) develops secondary to left ventricle (LV) pressure overload and neurohormonal hyperactivation induced by hypertension (HTN). column37: Les maladies cardiometaboliques (MCM), qui regroupent les maladies cardiovasculaires, l'hypertension, le diabete de type 2 et les accidents vasculaires cerebraux, sont l'une des principales causes de deces et d'incapacite chez les adultes ages de 50 ans et plus. Des recherches recentes suggerent que le bien-etre psychologique, c'est-a-dire le fait d'avoir des sentiments positifs envers la vie, joue un role protecteur dans le developpement et la progression des MCM. Cependant, les etudes existantes se sont principalement concentrees sur le bien-etre psychologique mesure a un seul moment dans le temps: les relations entre l'evolution longitudinale du bien-etre psychologique et le developpement des MCM n'ont pas ete etudiees pour l'instant. Ce projet investiguera les relations entre les trajectoires d'evolution du bien-etre psychologique et le risque d'incidence de MCM chez des adultes ages de 50 ans et plus. Premierement, cette recherche examinera les differentes trajectoires d'evolution du bien-etre psychologique chez 11,391 hommes et femmes sur une periode de 14 ans. Deuxiemement, cette etude verifiera si les trajectoires d'evolution du bien-etre psychologique predisent la survenue de MCM. Par exemple, un bien-etre continuellement eleve pourrait etre associe a un risque reduit de MCM comparativement a un bien-etre continuellement faible ou qui decline dans le temps. Troisiemement, cette recherche examinera le role mediateur de marqueurs biologiques, a savoir si la relation entre le bien-etre psychologique et le risque de MCM s'explique par des alterations de marqueurs biologiques associes a la fois a la sante mentale et aux MCM comme la proteine C-reactive, le cholesterol HDL et la composition du microbiome intestinal. Une meilleure comprehension du role du bien-etre psychologique dans le developpement des MCM permettra de developper de nouvelles interventions psychosociales visant a augmenter et a soutenir le bien-etre pour proteger la sante cardiometabolique.

column36: Developing and enhancing novel cancer immunotherapies by harnessing the anti-cancer abilities of patients' own Natural Killer immune cells
column37: Ovarian and lung cancer are among the most deadly cancers; the majority of patients with these diseases do not survive 5 years. For such poor prognosis cancers, there is a critical need for new effective treatments. The body's immune system is its primary protection mechanism against cancer: immune cells constantly survey the body and eliminate cancerous cells. However, cancer develops when malignant cells overwhelm this system. Therefore, reinforcing the body's natural immune defenses against cancer in the form of immunotherapy is emerging as a promising treatment modality for cancers that are resistant to current therapies. Natural Killer (NK) cells are immune cells that play a critical role in the body's defense against cancer due to their capacity to kill cancer cells without harming healthy cells. Given this ability, they have attracted attention as a promising cancer immunotherapy and have proven effective in treating blood cancers. Despite the therapeutic potential, immune therapies including NK cells have had limited success against solid tumours, such as ovarian and lung cancer, due to the hostile environment produced by tumours which impairs immune cell function. This impairment also limits efficacy of current therapies, such as antibody therapies which function largely through NK cells. Thus, understanding how the tumour environment alters NK cells is paramount to developing strategies to block inhibition and extend their therapeutic ability to solid tumours. The current project will uncover key changes in NK cells that impair their function after exposure to the tumour environment. Once identified, we will assess if blocking these changes can overcome NK cell inhibition and improve their therapeutic ability to reduce tumour burden. This project will uncover feasible targets to enhance NK cell function against ovarian and lung cancer in order to provide new effective therapies and improve outcomes of current therapies for cancers with poor prognosis.

column36: Role of FGFRs in modulating fibrogenicity of perivascular cells in cerebrovascular diseases
column37: Improper blood flow within the brain impairs neural activity, physical movement and cognitive ability, and these negative effects can occur at any age. Important cellular events within the wall of brain arteries control blood flow throughout the brain by changing the diameter of these vessels. When this control is impaired, the long-term consequence may be insufficient blood flow and ischemia, or the rupture of small vessels and bleeding within the brain. Recently, we have identified a novel genetic defect in a protein, the type 1 IP3 receptor (IP3R1), that disrupts this control, similar to what is observed in patients. I believe that this dysfunction is a direct result of the important role played by IP3R1 in regulating Ca2+ movement within small arteries of the brain. I hypothesize that genetically modified IP3R1s negatively affect Ca2+ movement in cells of the vessel wall, the control of vessel diameter and blood flow throughout the brain. Thus, my research will utilize microscopic imaging techniques to investigate how this type of protein defect observed in patients impairs Ca2+ movement in small arteries within the brain, and identify new strategies that minimize its negative impact on cerebral blood flow. To do so, we have created genetically modified mice that exhibit defects in this key protein similar to those found in patients, allowing us to study its impact on Ca2+ movement in arterial smooth muscle and endothelial cells. These studies will thus provide new information on blood vessel function and possibly how to manipulate these vessels in patients to maintain normal blood flow and brain activity.

column36: Long-term trends in acute stroke care and outcomes: A population-based study using administrative data from 2003-2018
column37: Stroke is a common and potentially devastating condition caused by lack of blood flow or bleeding in the brain. Invasive measures are often taken to prevent death in the days to weeks following a stroke. However, people who survive stroke can commonly be left with severe disabilities in motor, speech, and cognitive domains, which may significantly reduce their quality of life. Many interventions for stroke, such as feeding tubes, can prolong life successfully, but people surviving often have full dependence on others and require long-term care. Although stroke mortality is decreasing over time, studies have been limited to short time periods after stroke. In addition, we do not know whether disability is also decreasing, or if more people are surviving with higher levels of dependence. We plan to use Alberta and Ontario administrative data to study how mortality, disability, home-time and chronic care after stroke have changed over a 15-year period between 2003-2018. Our findings will demonstrate whether the there have been reductions in long-term mortality over time. Furthermore, our results will add insight to our use of aggressive and life-sustaining care after stroke, and how this affects specific groups of people based on age, sex, and stroke type. Lastly, the findings will identify important trends in post-stroke dependence and help plan for providing services to people with disability after stroke in Canada, including rehabilitation, home care, and chronic care facilities.

column37: Heart disease and stroke are the second and third most common cause of death in Canadians. Currently, doctors use a tool based on a patient's medical history and cholesterol levels to predict if they will have a heart attack or stroke in the next 5-10 years. Patients in whom heart attack or stroke are likely, can be offered medications to prevent this from happening. Unfortunately, these tools are difficult to use in every-day clinical practice. The purpose of this project will be to develop a new tool that will use a patient's age, gender and routine bloodwork to predict who is likely and unlikely to develop a heart attack or stroke. This tool can be automated into laboratory reports so that a prediction for future heart attack or stroke is reported to the physician alongside bloodwork results. This tool has the potential to streamline physician's workflow during patient encounters and ensure high quality care is delivered efficiently without lost opportunities to offer live-saving treatments.

column37: Smoking is the leading cause of preventable illness and death in North America. Unfortunately, treating tobacco addiction is difficult. A majority of smokers who attempt to quit relapse, even when using smoking cessation aids. A better understanding of the factors that impact responses to smoking cessation aids may help with the development of more effective cessation strategies, which could help more people to quit. This could reduce the harms (eg. stroke, heart disease, cancer, death) of long-term smoking. The goal of this research is to examine how individual genetic and psychological differences influence laboratory measures of smoking relapse (ability to delay cigarette smoking and number of cigarettes smoked) following the use of two types of smoking cessation aids: nicotine replacement therapy and very low nicotine content cigarettes. Genetic differences will be measured with the nicotine metabolite ratio (NMR), which is an indicator of how quickly the body breaks down nicotine. Breaking down nicotine more quickly (higher NMR) is associated with heavier smoking and greater difficulty quitting. Psychological differences will be measured by giving participants different instructions about the nicotine content of smoking cessation aids. Previous research shows that being told that a product contains nicotine is effective in reducing cigarette craving, regardless of whether or not the product actually contains nicotine. This will be the first study to examine the combined impact of genetic and psychological differences on responses to smoking cessation aids. Results of this research could help show how biological and psychological factors impact the effectiveness of smoking cessation aids. This knowledge could help with development of new smoking cessation strategies that are more effective in helping people to quit.

column36: Vaccine effectiveness against persistent human papillomavirus infection in gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men in Vancouver, Toronto and Montreal
column37: Gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (MSM) are recommended to get the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine. Most Canadian provinces have introduced publicly funded HPV vaccination programs for boys and high-risk males such as MSM, but we do not know how well the HPV vaccine works in these populations outside of a clinical setting. MSM have higher rates of HPV-associated diseases like anal cancer compared to the general population. In part, this is because they have higher rates of HIV. Based on clinical studies, we know that the HPV vaccine protects against infection about 75-78% of the time in healthy MSM who have had relatively few lifetime sex partners. However, less information is known about how this translates to vaccine protection in a real-life setting or in higher risk groups, such as those who have multiple sex partners or prior HPV infection or in those living with HIV. My PhD will study how well the HPV vaccine protects against ongoing HPV infection in MSM over a one-year period. I will estimate the percent of MSM infected with HPV at the beginning of the study and 12 months after enrollment; identify patient characteristics, such as sexual behaviours or HIV status, associated with infection; and measure the amount of protection from HPV vaccine. I will use data from a community-based study of MSM aged 16-30 years in Vancouver, Toronto, and Montreal known as Engage-HPV. At each study visit, men answered questions about their sexual health, including self-reported HPV vaccination status. They were also asked to self-collect oral and anal specimens for HPV testing. This research will fill an important knowledge gap about ongoing HPV infection in this population and will provide a real-world measure of HPV vaccine effectiveness. My findings will help evaluate targeted HPV vaccination programs recently implemented in three Canadian cities with large populations of MSM and contribute to the design of optimal HPV prevention strategies.

column36: Conceptualizing Learning Health Systems from an Indigenous Perspective: A Multiple Case Study in Northwest Territories
column37: This research involves Indigenous Peoples. If you go to the doctor with a problem and the doctor tells you there is nothing wrong, you might feel rejected and misunderstood. Maybe in your community there is no other doctor to go to, so next time you are ill you decide not to go to the doctor at all, making things worse. Unfortunately, this situation is common in many parts of Canada. Our health care system assumes disease is the cause of illness. However, there is more than one way to understand health. This study will help to build a health care system that learns from our different understandings, and constantly improves to provide better care. Many Indigenous peoples do not see health as an absence of disease, but as the result of good relationships with their family, community, environment, and spirit. The differences between these beliefs and the beliefs of our health care system mean that Indigenous patients often receive unhelpful, and even harmful, care. One idea is to build "learning health systems" that continuously improve care by learning from a variety of information sources, including patients. To improve care for Indigenous patients, learning health systems must know what to learn, how, and from whom. This research will take place from 2019 to 2022 in Northwest Territories, where 51% of the population is Indigenous. We will use sharing circles and interviews with Indigenous Elders and communities to find answers to two questions. First, in the eyes of Indigenous community members, what is a learning health system? Second, in what ways can a health system learn from the Indigenous communities it serves? These questions have not been studied before. Our results will indicate how the Northwest Territories health system can improve care for Indigenous patients, but will also benefit places across Canada and the world that have many cultural groups with different beliefs about health.

column36: Targeting mRNA translation to effectively treat metastatic breast cancer
column37: Current treatments for metastatic breast cancer are ineffective for disease that has spread (metastasized) to other organs. Moreover, while new immunotherapies are promising for other cancer types, their effect in breast cancer is limited. Therefore, when laboratory scientists uncover promising new leads, it is imperative to determine how they can be applied to benefit patients. Our findings and preclinical results have shown that the final stage of protein production is dysregulated in all metastatic breast cancer cells. We and others have shown that new drugs blocking this do not affect the production of all proteins equally, but selectively inhibit proteins needed for the aggressive behavior of breast cancer cells. We have also shown that these drugs can unleash immune responses suppressed by tumor cells, potentially stimulating the immune system to attack metastatic breast cancer. In this project, we will test these drugs in sophisticated models of metastatic breast cancer and bring them to the clinic for phase I trials in breast cancer patients. Our team unites world-leading Canadian fundamental and translational scientists with breast cancer clinical trials experts. We will carry out a pan-Canadian clinical trial testing our new therapeutic strategy and use unique resources, including extensive banks of tumour tissue and specialized animal models, to determine how these drugs work and how future treatments can be improved. We will identify all proteins whose production is altered by these drugs, identify responsive breast cancer subtypes and therapeutic combinations that allow us to maximize their effects, and determine whether their immunity-enhancing actions can be harnessed to further increase their effectiveness. We will function as a closely-knit multidisciplinary team, sharing data, methods, materials and information on an ongoing basis with advice from dedicated, passionate patient advocates to ensure progress in this innovative project.

column36: Survival of the fittest: cell competition in cancer progression
column37: Despite decades of research and development of diagnostic technology, cancer is still often diagnosed based on relatively large abnormalities in the tissue - growths, lumps, or bumps visible to the naked eye. The size of the smallest detectable tumor is still approximately a billion cells. Furthermore, it is often only possible to detect cancer cells that have spread from the initial tumor site to distant organs at late stages, when the cancer has progressed past the point of being curable. Thus, being able to identify cancer cells at very early stages and low numbers could enable identification of molecules to mark cancerous and pre-cancerous cells, and lead to development of therapies to kill cancer cells before the cancer spreads. One potential way to identify cancer cells at early stages is by discovering novel mechanisms cancer cells use to promote their own growth and survival. Cell competition is a process by which faster growing ("winner") cells kill the slower growing ("loser") cells around them, in order to enable their own growth. Although cell competition is known to be important for animal development and for maintaining tissue health, it has not been extensively studied in cancer in animals. I will use a zebrafish model of melanoma to investigate if cancer cells use cell competition to promote their own growth by killing the cells around them. I will transplant melanoma cells into transparent fish and use cutting-edge live, whole-animal microscopy to investigate if tumors cause the death of the surrounding normal cells. In parallel, I will induce cell competition in tumors by upregulating the cancer-promoting gene Myc, and perform a drug screen to identify molecules that inhibit competition and tumor growth, to provide insight into signaling pathways that could be driving cell competition in cancer. These studies will detail molecules that promote cancer progression, and describe potential targets for development of drugs to block cancer spreading.

column36: The roles of microRNAs in the regulation of heart development and human congenital heart disease
column37: Congenital heart diseases (CHD) are caused by structural abnormalities of the heart that are present at birth. CHD occurs in 1% of all births worldwide and are the leading cause of death from birth defects. 257,000 Canadians have CHD, most of them adults who require multiple surgeries and interventions. Surprisingly, the cause of the majority of CHD cases is unknown due to the large number of genes that can be affected or mutated in this disease. This is why I propose to study the genes involved in CHD, and more specifically, the regulation of the intermediary messenger RNA produced by these genes. The regulation of these messenger RNAs (mRNAs) by other small non-protein coding RNAs (miRNAs) is essential for the production of heart structures, such as the valves, which are often found to be abnormal in CHD. I will use powerful next-generation sequencing techniques and generate mutants of candidate genes to study their role in heart development and ultimately use these candidates in human genetic analyses to further the study of congenital heart disease.

column36: Sleep problems of autistic children with intellectual disabilities or language disorder.
column37: Autism Spectrum Disorders affect hundreds of thousands of individuals, their families and community. More than 80% of parents and caregivers of children with ASD complain about sleep problems, which lead to parental stress and decrease in family well-being. Up to now the majority of sleep research has focused on autistic individuals without intellectual disabilities. However, between 38% and 55% of individuals with autism has intellectual disabilities and/or language disorder. Studies have found that sleep difficulties in children with autism were associated with greater severity of symptoms, including social communication difficulties, and challenging behaviours such as tantrums. Moreover, poor sleep negatively impacts learning and memory. Hence, improving sleep in autistic children with intellectual, could improve their functioning. This research aims to characterize the nature and causes of poor sleep in autistic children with intellectual disabilities or language disorder, and measure the impact it has on daytime learning and memory functioning. Participants will complete sleep questionnaires, physiological sleep measures will be recorded at the laboratory, and they will perform two cognitive tasks measuring learning and memory. This protocol will allow us to establish a sleep profile, verify the presence of physiological causes associated with poor sleep, and determine whether sleep has an impact on cognitive functioning (learning and memory). The results will help developing specific interventions, according to their clinical status, to improve sleep in these children, therefore increase their quality of life, the well-being of families and reduce the pressure on health and social systems.

column36: Evaluating gender-sensitive interventions for people who use drugs in the context of British Columbia's opioid overdose crisis
column37: Overdose death rates have increased dramatically in Canada in recent years, largely driven by contamination of the drug supply with illicitly manufactured synthetic opioids such as fentanyl. The overdose crisis has been hardest felt in British Columbia (BC), which declared a public health emergency in 2016. Strategies to address the overdose crisis have therefore become an urgent public health priority. Previous research and evidence have shown that gender plays a key role in shaping contexts of drug use (e.g., within sex work or intimate partnerships) and access to treatment and harm reduction services. Women access treatment with more severe substance-related profiles relative to men (e.g., physical/sexual violence and trauma), yet few services are women-specific. New Vancouver Coastal Health guidelines highlight grave gaps in supports and prevention for marginalized women, and several new models of care are being rolled out (e.g., women-only supervised consumption rooms). Clinical interventions to address the overdose crisis and expand access to evidence-based treatments in BC include randomized clinical trials (RCTs) on the efficacy of opioid agonist therapies (OAT), slow-release oral morphine (SROM), and psychedelic-assisted therapy. However, the gender-related impacts of these interventions remain poorly understood and under investigated. The proposed research will evaluate the impacts of 'naturally occurring' and clinical interventions (i.e., through prospective methods and RCTs) to address the overdose crisis using a gendered lens, to identify gender differences in treatment outcomes and barriers to accessing services. This project also aims to widely disseminate findings to support scale-up of gender-sensitive substance use programs and policies, and inform directions for future research. It is hoped that this research will make important contributions to optimizing gender-specific treatment and care for people who use drugs in Canada and internationally.

column36: Les facteurs influencant le pronostic medical lors de grossesses avec malformations congenitales ou a risque d'accouchement premature.
column37: Ce projet etudie les facteurs qui font que les medecins font des predictions erronees sur le devenir du nouveau-ne chez les femmes avec grossesse a risque. En effet, certaines grossesses peuvent etre compliquees par des decouvertes de malformations congenitales chez le foetus ou un risque d'accouchement premature. Les parents dans de telles situations font face a des choix difficiles tels que poursuivre ou non la grossesse ou quels soins apporter a la naissance de leur nouveau-ne. Ils doivent faire ces choix en considerant le bien-etre futur du nouveau-ne et de leur famille. Les medecins accompagnent les parents dans ces decisions critiques de vie et de mort en leur faisant part de leurs predictions quant aux chances de survie, handicap et de qualite de vie future pour leur enfant. Or, ces predictions futures, appelees pronostics, peuvent etre tres variables d'un medecin a l'autre, et sont souvent plus pessimistes que la realite. Cette variation peut s'expliquer par la presence de nombreux facteurs agissant comme des biais. Il est important de comprendre l'influence de ces facteurs sur le pronostic du medecin, car ils peuvent mener a des choix irreversibles par les parents. Ce projet s'interesse particulierement aux facteurs relies au medecin, soit sa personnalite, son attitude face au handicap et s'il fait le suivi a long terme des patients nes de grossesse a risque. Aussi, ce projet de recherche propose la creation de strategies pour reduire l'impact de ces facteurs sur leurs predictions pour l'enfant a venir. Ce projet permettra de donner l'heure juste aux parents quant a la prediction du bien-etre futur possible de l'enfant. Il pourra etre integre dans l'education des futurs medecins. De plus, cette recherche unique et pionniere pourrait s'etendre a d'autres situations ou les medecins se prononcent sur le futur de leur patient pouvant parfois mener a des decisions de soins importantes.

column36: Suicidalite chez les jeunes atteints d'un premier episode psychotique : trajectoires d'evolution et facteurs associes.
column37: Le suicide est un grave probleme de sante publique representant une cause importante de mortalite. Plus de 5 % des individus atteints d'un trouble psychotique meurent par suicide (Melle & Barrett, 2014). Au cours des premiers stades de la psychose, le risque suicidaire est 60 % plus eleve qu'au cours des stades subsequents (Bornheimer, 2018). La psychose est caracterisee par une alteration du contact avec la realite, des hallucinations et des idees delirantes (Abdel-Baki, Lalonde, & Gingras, 2016). Peu d'etudes ont evalue de facon approfondie les facteurs de risque de la suicidalite. De plus, aucune etude quebecoise ou canadienne n'a etudie ce phenomene chez les jeunes atteints d'un premier episode psychotique (PEP). Objectifs : Les objectifs sont de decrire la frequence des differents types de suicidalite (idees suicidaires, tentatives de suicide et suicide complete), d'identifier les facteurs de risque de la suicidalite, de determiner les trajectoires d'augmentation, de maintien ou de diminution de la suicidalite sur une periode de cinq ans chez les jeunes atteints d'un PEP et d'explorer les predicteurs de ces trajectoires. Methode : Cette etude a lieu dans deux services d'intervention precoce en psychose en milieu urbain a Montreal (Quebec). L'echantillon est compose de 567 Jeunes souffrants d'un PEP ayant ete suivis par ces services pendant une periode de cinq ans. Les donnees sociodemographiques, les symptomes, la suicidalite, le fonctionnement global, la consommation d'alcool et de drogues, les traumatismes vecus pendant l'enfance et le diagnostic des participants sont consideres pour mieux comprendre les facteurs associes aux trajectoires de la suicidalite. Retombees : Le projet permettra de mieux soutenir les jeunes atteints d'un PEP qui sont a risque de passage a l'acte suicidaire en developpant de meilleurs outils pour predire le suicide et en mettant en place des strategies preventives specifiques a cette population.

column36: In silico elucidation and functional characterization of human intestinal microbiota enzymes targeting host-derived carbohydrates
column37: Within the human intestinal tract reside an enormous consortium of bacterial species. Although a full picture of human-bacteria interactions is still emerging, it is clear that these microbes play important roles in human health, as patients suffering from gastrointestinal diseases typically posses fewer species than healthy individuals. One critical responsibility of intestinal bacteria is digestion of the elaborate array of complex carbohydrates from dietary sources, which largely remain untouched by human enzymes. Bacterial carbohydrate digestion ultimately yields short-chain fatty acid end products which collectively benefit their human host. Short-chain fatty acids serve as a main energy source for epithelial cells in the colon, have anti-tumorigenic and anti-inflammatory properties and reduce the incidence of type II diabetes and obesity. In addition to dietary polysaccharides, some bacteria digest polysaccharides produced by human cells. These processes are important for in how bacteria colonize the gut and regulate the immune system throughout life. Recent advancements have allowed us to grow the complete human intestinal microbiome within mixed communities in the lab. This has resulted in increased bacterial DNA yields and richer DNA sequence datasets. The goal of this research is to use computational approaches to search through DNA sequences and identify novel genes involved in degradation of human-derived polysaccharides. From there, we will identify which organism it is derived from, and purify the enzyme it encodes. Biochemical experiments on these enzymes will elucidate their precise substrates. Insights from this research may be important for the development of therapeutic strategies and preventative measures favouring the proliferation of beneficial bacterial species important for intestinal wellbeing.

column36: Elucidating the microstructural and genetic risk architecture of major adolescent-onset psychiatric disorders in early life
column37: One in five Canadians are affected by mental illness, with a high proportion of these individuals experiencing their first symptoms in adolescence. This dynamic and critical time period in the lifespan of an individual holds key milestones in the development of white matter "highways" in the brain, and offers a unique and informative target to study alongside genetic information. Genome-wide association studies have rapidly increased our knowledge of the genetic risk architecture that underlies individual psychiatric disorders, but there is a need to look beyond current symptom-based definitions, which do not map onto biological findings. This project will harness the rich genotypic, imaging and phenotypic data from nearly 12,000 children recruited for the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study and findings from multiple genome-wide association studies to build a multivariate model of polygenic risk for schizophrenia, bipolar, major depressive, anxiety, and eating disorders. I aim to capture the unique and shared contributions of psychiatric polygenic risk in one score using cutting-edge genomic data science methods. This score will then be related to measures of white matter in the brain that can be assessed non-invasively with magnetic resonance imaging. I will then integrate findings of microstructural features most related to polygenic risk for psychiatric disorders to maladaptive behaviours in childhood that could be predictive of the onset of future psychiatric symptoms. This project will provide an important neurobiological framework to assess psychiatric risk in early life that represents a significant departure from the classical definitions of psychiatric disorders, with the hope of re-routing current treatment plans to better meet the needs of patients and their families.

column36: Understanding the preconception health of women with disabilities in Ontario: Service user and provider perspectives
column37: Being healthy before pregnancy is vital, as preconception health (PCH) impacts maternal and infant outcomes. However, half of pregnancies are unplanned and improving health at the first prenatal visit is too late to prevent poor outcomes. Women with disabilities (WWD) represent about 10% of women of reproductive age and are becoming pregnant at similar rates to women without disabilities; yet, there is little research on the PCH of WWD in Canada. Attending to the PCH of WWD is important, as WWD experience physical and psychological health disparities that put them at increased risk for poor PCH. Further, compared to women without disability, WWD have lower rates of contraception use and experience higher rates of unplanned pregnancy, short spacing between pregnancies, and sexual violence. Using qualitative methods, this study aims to (1) understand the PCH of WWD in Ontario, (2) explore how social, health, and health care factors may impact the PCH of WWD, and (3) identify how knowledge of barriers to care and risks for poor PCH outcomes can be used to improve care for WWD. Women from three disability subgroups (physical, sensory, intellectual and developmental) and health care providers will be interviewed. Analysis will explore similarities and differences across disability subgroups, as well as compare WWD and health care providers' responses, to identify key PCH health needs of WWD, what might be contributing to PCH disparities among WWD, and which interventions may be most effective. This study will be one of the first to explore similarities and differences across disability groups from the perspective of both WWD and care providers. This study will have important implications for reducing health disparities among WWD; it will inform the development of interventions to improve the PCH of WWD, which may in turn contribute to better outcomes for WWD and their infants.

column36: Brain connectivity and cognitive control in children with Tourette syndrome: the impact of comorbid attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
column37: Tourette syndrome (TS) is a neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by multiple motor tics and at least one phonic tic. TS patients often faces various comorbid disorders, such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). For a child with TS, having comorbid ADHD comes with a lot of complications, such as more inhibitory deficits and increased impulsivity. Our project aims to assess the brain function of children with TS and/or ADHD. We want to identify markers that would facilitate an earlier diagnosis of these conditions. An earlier diagnosis would enable treatment strategies to be put in place more quickly. For instance, earlier treatment of ADHD symptoms could prevent the development of several behavioral problems in adulthood. To evaluate the brain function of these children, we will use electroencephalography, which records the electrical activity of the brain. We will evaluate the connections between some regions of the brain during different conditions. We will first use a cognitive control task. Cognitive control is very important in TS patients because it allows them to control their tics in certain situations and for short periods. In addition, we will evaluate brain function directly while children with TS are voluntarily attempting to suppress their tics. We expect that having both TS and ADHD will have a negative impact on cognitive control. This should also be reflected in brain function, which should differ between children with TS, those with ADHD, and those with both TS and ADHD.

column36: Maternal prenatal depression and past trauma: Intergenerational effects on fetal neurobehavior and early childhood mental health
column37: There is ample evidence that when a mother is distressed during pregnancy (e.g., depression, anxiety, stressful life events), this can lead to greater risk that her child will develop mental health problems such as depression, anxiety, ADHD, and conduct problems. What remains unclear are the mechanisms or pathways through which maternal distress can transcend to the fetus to influence child development; a potential pathway is through the methylation of genes in the placenta. What also remains unclear is whether past maternal trauma can also influence child mental health outcomes, beyond exposure to maternal prenatal distress. The group that I will study are women and their children followed throughout pregnancy and childhood who are part of the Environmental Influences on Child Health Outcomes (ECHO) consortium, a multi-site study of 62 cohorts across the United States under the auspices of the National Institutes of Health (NIH). My research will be part of the Boricua Youth Study, which includes a high-adversity sample of Puerto Rican women - these women have been followed from childhood to adulthood to the second generation of children, allowing for the study of how the mother's exposure to Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs, a well known measure of trauma) may affect the next generation. During my Fellowship under the supervision of Dr. Monk at Columbia University Medical Center in New York, my aim is to expand my training in perinatal development to include skills such as: the assessment of fetal neurobehavior in utero, the extraction DNA from biospecimens, procedural knowledge to conduct observational studies, the development of treatment interventions, and proficiency in translational research. Overall, I aim to gain new knowledge to underscore the need for preventative healthcare and to inform specific, time-sensitive interventions to improve the mental health of women and their children in the first years of life.

column36: Development of a framework for assistive technology policy development (TemplAT) and evaluative tool (EvaluAT) to enhance global capacity for assistive technology provision
column37: Only one in ten people with disabilities who need assistive technologies to complete day to day tasks currently have access to those technologies. Assistive technologies are devices, services, and systems which allow people with disabilities to maintain or enhance their independence. To reach the anticipated needs of 2 billion individuals by the year 2050, a global coordinated effort is needed. Most importantly, national governments have the responsibility to address the needs of their citizens by providing these devices at an affordable cost with the right services in place to ensure safe and effective use. Currently, very few governments have policies which support timely, effective, and affordable distribution of assistive technologies. Over the next two years, we will develop and test a framework that can be used by national governments to assess their current policies, or craft new ones which meet the specific needs of their citizens, in their countries. Critically, this framework will provide guidance on the criteria necessary to craft effective policy, while maintaining flexibility necessary to accommodate local customs and cultures. We will do this in partnership with the World Health Organization's Global Cooperation on Assistive Technology, by incorporating current research, and the opinions of experts from around the world. Ultimately, this project will provide a structure for countries to provide safe and effective access to assistive technologies and promote independence and inclusion for all individuals with disabilities.

column36: Sustained engagement in HIV care: Novel approaches to identify and evaluate the impact of socioeconomic disparities
column37: HIV remains a global public health threat, with 37 million people living with HIV (PLWH). Advancements in HIV therapy have transformed the clinical landscape increasing life expectancies and reducing new HIV infections. But benefits rest on the lifetime commitment of PLWH to adhere to treatments. Over the last 20 years, the proportion of patients virally suppressed- and therefore those with controlled infections- has risen from 25% to over 80% in the United States (US). Although encouraging, progress is uneven and falls short of global targets. Race continues to play a differentiating role in the inequality of HIV infections. African Americans make up more than half of new cases while only representing 14% of the US population. Moreover, even in cities with universal health care coverage such as San Francisco, where overall ~85% of PLWH are virally suppressed, that number plummets to 30% among those marginally housed and homeless. Worldwide, people who fare poorly in HIV care have little or no access to care, face stigma and encounter socio-structural barriers. Socioeconomic status and race have been shown to predict health outcomes. But research on this topic has not optimally captured the multi-dimensional ways in which disparities interact and how this leads to adverse health outcomes for PLWH. For example, low income is often the consequence of mental illness, substance abuse, limited education. Even though each of these factors has been shown to be associated with poor health outcomes, the extent to which these factors intersect to create underlying expressions of socioeconomic deprivation remains to be explored. Identifying and understanding the consequences of disparities is the first step in addressing inequalities through targeted interventions and health policies. Results from this research will characterize and evaluate the role of socioeconomic drivers of HIV care engagement, which will ultimately play a critical role in ending the HIV epidemic.

column36: TSMS Optimization of Developmental Trajectories in Preschoolers with Stroke (TOTS): Parent-directed, home-based, non-invasive neurostimulation for infants and toddlers with perinatal stroke and hemiparetic cerebral palsy
column37: Stroke in the newborn affects 10,000 Canadian children and is the primary cause of lifelong weakness on one side, a form of cerebral palsy. Evidence-based physical interventions for children with newborn stroke are limited and are often initiated after two years of age. This time period falls beyond the most critical window of opportunity to capitalize on the remarkable ability of the developing brain to change. Early therapies targeting activity of the affected arm have the potential to drive brain development toward better lifelong function. Home therapy may be ideal, but methods to effectively engage and empower families and optimize outcomes are yet to be established. Non-invasive brain stimulation technologies have been shown to augment therapy in older children affected by newborn stroke. While existing technologies are not feasible for small children in the home, a new simple, portable and inexpensive static stimulation has effects that may enhance motor therapy. We propose a clinical trial to establish the safety, feasibility and possible efficacy of combining transcranial static magnetic stimulation with home-based movement therapy to improve motor function in infants and toddlers with newborn stroke. We will enrol 24 children aged 6 to 48 months. Families will complete a six-month home-based goal directed program, with random assignment to either active or placebo stimulation during therapy. Changes in activity levels, motor skill performance, individualized goal achievement, and family well-being will be assessed before, following, and 6-months after the intervention. For the first time, this study brings together non-invasive brain stimulation and early intervention in young children with newborn stroke. Caregivers are directly engaged and empowered to improve their child's motor function. This early, personalized, family-centred, patient-oriented approach has the potential to benefit many of the millions of children globally affected by cerebral palsy.

column36: Measuring and Valuing Health Benefits for Economic Evaluations in Breast Cancer: Development and Validation of a Scoring Algorithm for the BREAST-Q Utility Scale (BREAST-QU)
column37: Explicit rationing attempts to battle fiscal debt and increasing demand for healthcare were the focus of 2018 Ontario provincial elections. While rationing is one of the options to curb health care costs, it slowly disinherits us from the core principles of the Canada Health Act. An alternative solution is to base budget allocation decisions on "value" of healthcare interventions (cost vs. outcome). Quality-adjusted life-years (QALY) is the preferred metric for valuing health outcomes in terms of quality of life (QOL). Once cost per QALY is determined, service with the lowest cost per QALY is chosen. Traditionally, generic preference-based measures (PBM) have been used to calculate QALYs. However, they do not include concerns unique to breast cancer patients (body image, appearance, sexual) and hence lack sensitivity. The BREAST-Q is a widely used and validated breast cancer-specific QOL instrument, but it cannot be used to calculate QALYs. Hence, a descriptive classification system, the BREAST-Q Utility (BREAST-QU), was developed from BREAST-Q using patient interviews and input from an international team of experts. My postdoctoral research will advance this work by generating a scoring algorithm (i.e., preference weights for health states defined by BREAST-QU). A representative sample of the general population and women with breast cancer will be asked to participate in choice-based tasks (discrete choice experiment and best-worst scaling) to identify their preferences for various breast cancer health states. The responses will be analyzed using advanced statistical techniques, resulting in scoring algorithm for the BREAST-QU. The reliability, validity, and responsiveness of BREAST-QU will be assessed. The use of BREAST-QU in clinical practice, economic evaluation and policy-making will be promoted through publications, presentations, and professional networks; ultimately resulting in "biggest bang for the buck" in breast cancer and improved population health.

column36: Modeling the long-term contribution of incarceration and of prison-based prevention strategies to drug-related harms among people who inject drugs
column37: Drug use is criminalized at various degrees globally. Incarceration and the period post-release can increase risk for HIV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections and overdose among people who inject drugs (PWID). Thus, over time, incarceration is likely to be "responsible" for a significant proportion of the total new cases of these health-harms among PWID. Yet, no study has attempted to estimate its potential contribution over time. In addition, access to prison-based strategies such as opioid agonist treatment, needle and syringe provision and naloxone kits, with continuation upon release, can prevent the occurrence of these health harms but no study has yet estimated their potential long-term prevention benefit. This study seeks to address these gaps using mathematical modeling. This technique enables the forecasting of the future burden of an epidemic and of the potential impact of introducing an intervention on its course. Such modelling outputs are widely used by policy-makers to inform their decisions regarding the control of diseases. Given that different global settings have distinct incarceration levels and distinct realistic scenarios of future scale-up of prevention strategies within prisons, these simulations must be tailored to specific settings. In this study, we will carry out the simulations in two distinct settings, Montreal, Canada and Nairobi and Mombasa, Kenya. For each setting, the model parameters will be informed by data collected through two studies (HEPCO, Montreal and TLC-IDU, Nairobi and Mombasa, Kenya). Altogether, this study has the potential to provide estimates on the extent to which incarceration may be fueling HIV and HCV transmission and overdose among PWID, and the necessary scale-up levels of prison-based prevention interventions to achieve meaningful reductions in these health harms over time. In the long-run, findings could inform appropriate public health and policy changes to reduce the burden of HIV, HCV and overdose.

column36: Growth trajectories of children with autism spectrum disorder: Latent class growth model analysis using two sources of primary care data
column37: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) may be at high risk of obesity because of restricted diet with a preference for processed foods, low levels of physical activity participation, excessive screen time, and use of medications that may contribute to weight gain. Previous scientific work has suggested that obesity risk in children with ASD might be seen early, with unhealthy weight gain between 2 to 5 years of age. However, we do not truly understand how patterns of weight gain over time (weight trajectories) are different in ASD than in typically-developing children. As ASD now affects about 1 in 68 individuals, results will be important to a large group of Canadian children. I will explore weight trajectories in ASD, using two sources of data: (1) the Applied Research Group for Kids (TARGet Kids!), which collects rich early childhood data from paediatricians' and family doctors' offices, and (2) the Electronic Medical Record Administrative data Linked Database (EMRALD(R)), which contains electronic medical record data from family doctors in Ontario. Using statistical methods, I will see how weight trajectories in children with ASD compare to weight trajectories in children without ASD. If the ASD group shows unhealthy weight trajectories (for example, early development of obesity), the time when growth becomes abnormal will be explored. In addition, I will identify what nutritional, behavioural and medical factors are linked with abnormal weight trajectories in ASD. We know that addressing obesity is important, because unhealthy weight is associated with negative impacts on health, quality of life, and use of health services. We also know that children with ASD likely need different types of intervention for obesity than typically developing children. Results of my work will help in preventing and treating obesity specifically in children with ASD, thereby making an important contribution to improving the health of Canadian children.

column36: Dissecting tissue-resident memory T cell heterogeneity in human tissues
column37: Despite the extraordinary advances in medicine over the last few decades, infectious disease remains among the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Our understanding of how protective immune responses can be generated and augmented by vaccines or immunotherapies are therefore of prime importance for improving human health. Recent studies have identified a heterogeneous population of non-circulating memory T cells, known as tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM), that are distributed in mucosal/barrier sites and are essential in mediating protective immunity during infection and after vaccination. However, due to the difficulty of studying immune cells directly in human tissues, basic questions of how TRM function and how they differ across multiple tissues within the same individual remain unanswered. My research will utilize a unique human tissue resource in which multiple mucosal and lymphoid organs are obtained from research-consented organ donors in order to dissect the similarities and differences between TRM subsets across tissue sites. I will use a combination of cutting-edge techniques including high-dimensional immune profiling, multi-parameter imaging, and single cell transcriptomic approaches to generate a "human atlas" of TRM phenotype and function throughout the human body. With this investigation, my objective is to define and characterize TRM identity and function using a one-of-a-kind tissue resource that allows unprecedented access to study human tissue immunity. Understanding how TRM function in humans is central to the design of new vaccines and immunotherapies aimed at boosting tissue immunity, with the ultimate goal reducing deaths from infectious disease.

column36: Spatial molecular profiling at single-cell level during hPSCs to HSCs differentiation in both in vitro and teratoma models using tFISSEQ
column37: Haematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) are specialized stem cells (SCs) that give rise to the blood and immune cells. First HSCs emerge during the embryogenesis. These new HSCs have a higher ability for proliferation and differentiation into different cell types than the adult HSCs, suggesting that their environment influences their fate. Previous studies showed that SCs reside in small niche environment. Such environments provide a special setting for cell-cell communication, extracellular matrix construction, and control of signalling between the cells. Yet, genes/pathways and expression profile of individual cells within the human embryonic HSCs niches remain poorly understood. Our current inability to generate bona fide human HSCs from pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) suggests that these HSCs derived in vitro may have different gene expression profile than the ones developed in embryos due to different stem cell niche environments. Studying these niche environments was difficult until the recent development of the Fluorescent In Situ Sequencing (FISSEQ) by the Church lab. FISSEQ enables single-cell transcriptome sequencing of fixed, intact tissue samples. Subsequent development of a modified version of FISSEQ called targeted FISSEQ (tFISSEQ) allows detection of small RNAs and even proteins by FISSEQ. These technologies, for the very first time, enable us to evaluate the gene expression landscape of SCs and all other cells in the SCs niche, in the context of their native spatial environment. Human PSCs-derived teratoma engrafted in immunodeficient mice, develops HSCs that possess good repopulation ability in secondary recipient mice. This could be a faithful model that represents at least in part the heamogenic emergence process in the embryo. Using tFISSEQ to obtain spatial expression landscape of proteins and miRNAs in the teratoma and PSC-to-HSCs in vitro models will finally shed light on the key effectors and pathways in heamogenic development in human embryos.

column36: Key stakeholder engagement to define the core components and presentation for a collaborative Longitudinal Care Plan e-Tool prototype
column37: Health professionals often work in silos. If any health information is communicated, the most common formats are paper or fax. This fragmentation has been shown to compromise patient safety by leading to inefficient, low-quality and low-value care. The ideal would be to use a longitudinal care plan, which is intended to be a single, reconciled source of health information shared between health professionals and patients to address a unified set of treatment and care goals. It should be patient-centered, dynamic and integrated with local electronic health records to facilitate real-time updates and bi-directional communication. The purpose of this research project is to inform the design and development of a collaborative Longitudinal Care Plan e-Tool (eLCP). Objectives: 1) To describe the current state of information exchange during care transitions for patients managed by multiple health professionals and services 2) To define key information needs, core components and desired presentation to inform the design of an eLCP prototype Methods: In-depth, unstructured interviews with patients and family members, workflow observations of health professionals, and medical document review will be used to develop comprehensive patient journey maps to understand the current state of care coordination and information exchange during care transitions to identify gaps for improvement. Focus groups will be conducted using semi-structured interview guides with patients, family members, and various health professionals to identify key information needs, core components and desired presentation of an eLCP. Separate Delphi processes will be conducted to refine the lists of information needs and components, and to prioritize by value added to the eLCP for 'patient and family' and 'health professional' views. Final rank-ordered lists will be created to inform the design and development of an eLCP prototype.

column36: Identifying the neuronal activity of adult born neurons in the dentate gyrus that support behavioural pattern separation.
column37: Until as recently as the 1990s it was assumed that in the adult brain cells die, but are never born. This was shown to be incorrect: in some regions of the brain - and of interest to us, the dentate gyrus (DG) of the hippocampus - new cells are born. Evidence increasingly suggests that these adult born neurons (ABNs) are essential for hippocampal function; specifically, in the formation of distinct representations of similar inputs, a mechanism known as pattern separation (PS). Abnormalities in adult neurogenesis, and consequent PS impairments, were then linked to several neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric diseases, such as Parkinsons, Alzheimer's, Huntingtons disease and schizophrenia. Although we know about ABNs involvement in PS, we know almost nothing about how ABNs operate at the network level to support it. This is in part because determining the answer to this question is difficult: it requires recording from multiple, sparsely-organized neurons along with precise and well-controlled assessment of a subtle aspect of cognition. To do so, we proposed to use Miniscopes, that allow us to visualize the activity of large populations of neurons during behavior, in combination with genetically targeted expression of a calcium indicator to ABNs in the DG. By combining cutting-edge technology in calcium imaging with precise assessment of behavioral PS we are confident that we can determine how ABNs supports PS hippocampal processing at the network and behavioral levels. Because of the paucity of information on the role of ABNs in cognition, using precise molecular and behavioural tools to discover clear evidence of this relationship along with underlying mechanism will be high-impact and transformative; understanding the basis of this process will help us to develop new tools for an early diagnosis of different disorders, such as Alzheimer's disease or dementias, and will unveil new targets for intervention in neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric diseases.

column36: Reducing patient boarding practices and impact on patient mortality by using optimization and machine learning methodologies that account for the heterogeneity of individual patients
column37: Critically ill patients, requiring timely and specialized treatment, are subject to substantial delays before admission into intensive care units (ICUs) due to patient overcrowding and the lack of staffed ICU beds. Patient "boarding" has become a common strategy for hospitals to provide care for patients despite bed allocation problems in the ICU and involves caring for patients in alternative locations, such as emergency departments, until an ICU bed is available. However, these alternative locations are generally neither trained for, nor designed to treat critically ill patients, compromising the quality of care provided. As such, patient boarding and delays in ICU admission significantly increases increase patient mortality The development of optimization and simulation tools have been promising towards reducing the number of boarded patients and delays to admission but rarely account for differences between each individual patient. By assessing patients at an individual level, hospitals may more accurately measure the impact of delays to ICU admission on patient survival. The goal of my proposed research is to develop a novel optimization model, integrated with machine learning algorithms, that accounts for the heterogeneity of individual patients to reduce boarding practices and patient mortality. To do this, I will estimate the difference in survival between boarded and nonboarded patients based on individual patient demographics and disease characteristics, and operating information from hospitals. I will then develop an optimization model to optimize decisions regarding patient boarding, bed capacity, and staffing to maximize the predicted survival of each patient. The novel combination of predictive and optimization methodologies will allow hospitals to minimize the effects of patient boarding, reduce and eliminate boarding practices, and ultimately increase patient survival.

column36: Generation of Human Pluripotent Stem Cell-Derived Left Ventricular Cardiomyocytes for the Treatment of Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome
column37: The normal human heart has two pumping chambers: the right ventricle and left ventricle. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs (low-pressure system), whereas the left ventricle pumps blood to the rest of the body (high-pressure system). Some children are born without a left ventricle, a malformation called hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS). To survive, these children must undergo surgery to connect the right ventricle to the rest of the body. However, the right ventricle, which is designed to pump blood into a low-pressure system, is often unable to sustain the high pressure of the rest of the body, and gradually starts failing, leading to heart failure and death. Unfortunately, we currently have no drugs to treat this type of heart failure. The goal of our project is to develop a novel therapy for HLHS using human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs). These cells are unique in that they can give rise to all the cell types in the body. Our lab has previously designed a protocol to generate heart muscle cells - called cardiomyocytes - from hPSCs. However, all cardiomyocytes are not identical, and there are significant differences between cardiomyocytes in the right versus left ventricle. We hypothesize that cardiomyocytes from the left ventricle are better suited to sustain high pressure and that transplanting left ventricular cardiomyocytes into a pressure-overloaded right ventricle could prevent heart failure. The aims of our proposal are to 1) understand the molecular differences between right and left ventricle cardiomyocytes; 2) elaborate a protocol to make left ventricle cardiomyocytes from hPSCs; 3) transplant left ventricle cardiomyocytes into pigs with a pressure-overloaded right ventricle to see if these cells can prevent failure. If successful, this project could transform the care of children with HLHS. This would have a profound impact on our healthcare system, as HLHS has become the largest driver of cost in pediatric cardiovascular care.

column36: Study of the mechanisms underlying seizures and epilepsy after traumatic brain injury in a zebrafish model.
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) occurs in 160,000 Canadians yearly, more than the combined number of patients with breast cancer, HIV/AIDS, spinal cord injury, and multiple sclerosis. One of the effects of TBI is seizures or epilepsy, and TBI is the most common cause of symptomatic epilepsy in people ages 15 to 24. There is no treatment to prevent epilepsy after TBI. Animal studies in rodents are expensive and time-consuming. Most of the conducted studies had a small sample size and there is a need to move toward larger and more randomized animal studies. Studies in zebrafish would allow for more rapid screening of potential targets before moving to rodent studies. Zebrafish are widely used in other disease studies because their genomes are 70% similar to humans, they spawn hundreds of eggs per week, they are cheap to breed, and are readily genetically modifiable. The overall aim of this project is to establish a zebrafish model of severe TBI to understand how this leads to seizures or epilepsy. We will confirm that the spontaneous seizures we have seen in this model are due to abnormal electrical activity in the brain and will also determine whether inflammation and abnormal proteins are involved in the development of epilepsy by using genetic studies. This project will apply modern engineering techniques in neuroscience to enhance our understanding of why some TBI patients develop seizures while others do not. Findings from this project are expected to help in developing treatment options to prevent post-traumatic epilepsy.

column36: Identification of novel vulnerabilities and therapeutic strategies for breast cancers with acquired resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors
column37: Improvements in the early detection and drug treatments for breast cancer have led to increased rates of survival and cure. However, metastatic breast cancer that has spread to other parts of the body remain incurable and represent a major challenge. The recent development of a new targeted treatments called CDK4/6 inhibitors (CDK4/6i) have substantially improved the ability to control disease in the most common form of metastatic breast cancer. Unfortunately, this therapy does not provide a cure. Despite the initial response to the treatment, resistance to CDK4/6i eventually develops and tumors continue to grow. Since the tumors evolve during this process, finding new strategies for breast cancers that acquire resistance to CDK4/6i is an imperative for improving survival rates. To address this health challenge, I will use cutting edge laboratory tools identify the factors which the drug-resistant breast tumors rely on to survive and grow. Then, blocking the function of these genes by using specific targeted drugs will allow us to tackle the tumor cell vulnerabilities, and develop new approaches to improve the survival of these patients. My discoveries could be tested through clinical trials, and linked to specific markers to permit "personalized" treatment in this setting. The findings from this project have the potential to be rapidly integrated into the clinical management of patients and to ultimately improve breast cancer survival.

column36: Prognostic Value of a Prospective, Longitudinal Evaluation of Body Composition in Patients with Cirrhosis Evaluated for Liver Transplantation
column37: Two main body compartments, skeletal muscle and adipose tissue (fat), exhibit independent functions. Patients with liver cirrhosis frequently experience body composition abnormalities including loss of muscle and subcutaneous fat but not visceral fat (around internal organs). Liver cirrhosis, characterized by liver failure and replacement of normal tissue by scarring is the main indication for liver transplantation. These body composition abnormalities are associated with higher risk of complications such as infections, longer recovery after surgeries, and higher probability of death. The aim of this study is to evaluate muscle and subcutaneous fat abnormalities in relation to adverse outcomes both before and after liver transplantation. Muscle and fat amount and condition will be assessed using high resolution image-based techniques (computed tomography) at 6-month intervals in cirrhotic patients being evaluated for liver transplantation. During liver transplantation surgery, a small biopsy of muscle and fat will be obtained for analysis of cell types and signals. This information will establish the real burden of body composition abnormalities and their behavior in patients with cirrhosis over time to improve the prediction of outcomes, identify potential targets for treatment, and facilitate development of clinical trials for these conditions.

column36: Can Blending Together Traditional and Western Knowledge Improve Diabetes and Obesity Health Outcomes in Urban Indigenous Communities?
column37: Indigenous peoples in Canada suffer from significantly higher rates of diabetes and obesity, resulting in reduced quality of life. Health, government and community organizations often lack Traditional Knowledge and community ownership, required to decrease healthcare gaps and burden of disease. The limited impact of Western health services on improving health in Indigenous peoples needs to be addressed.
