column36: An examination of individual and community-level social factors and health outcomes associated with experiences in the child welfare system among Indigenous peoples in Canada
column37: The health and wellness of Indigenous peoples today continue to be impacted by the harmful colonization practices enforced by the Government of Canada. While we have shown the long-term impacts of the Residential School system in relation to health and wellness, there remains a large gap in understanding the health impacts of other collective traumas such as the Sixties Scoop and the continued inequities within the child welfare system. During the Sixties Scoop, large numbers of children and youth were removed from their families and the practice of taking Indigenous children and youth from their families and communities continues today. As a result, family units and connections to Indigenous culture have and continue to be impacted, however, the empirical evidence on health and wellness are largely unavailable. The current proposal addresses this gap by taking a mixed methods approach to understand the risk factors of child welfare involvement within communities and the effects of the Sixties Scoop and child welfare system on Indigenous health and wellness. In the current project we will work with large national survey data to examine the individual-level and community-level factors associated with child welfare system involvement and the impacts on health. We will also work together with the 60's Scoop Legacy of Canada, a non-profit organization focused on healing and wellness for Sixties Scoop Survivors to conduct a quantitative survey across Manitoba. Broadly we will examine experiences within the child welfare system, and the direct and intergenerational impacts of the loss of culture and community on Indigenous health and wellness. It is expected that this work will help promote an understanding of the long-term outcomes and healing opportunities required for Indigenous peoples who have been affected by the child welfare system. This work will also help provide evidence informed policy changes related to child welfare practices for Indigenous children.

column36: Sustainable Healthy Cities: The Interplay between Urban Interventions, Gentrification, and Population Health
column37: The way our cities are designed influences population-level physical activity, social participation, well-being and health inequalities. Although massive investments are made in urban infrastructure, even well-intentioned change may adversely affect vulnerable populations through gentrification processes. The goal of this research is to analyse how urban interventions, gentrification, and population health and health inequalities relate. Specifically, we aim to: 1) document if urban interventions (e.g., new bike lanes) aiming to improve quality of life tend to be located primarily in more deprived areas. 2) assess whether urban interventions lead to gentrification or vice versa, or if both processes are at play 3) measure the impact of urban interventions, neighbourhood gentrification, and experienced residential gentrification on physical activity, social participation and well-being, and 4) analyse differences in health outcome trajectories between low SES individuals who were displaced from gentrified neighbourhoods and those who could stay, and lastly 5) build a pilot simulation tool to help decision makers choose the best urban intervention scenario for health and equity. This study will build on an existing CIHR-funded team (INTERACT, 2016-2021), adding study participants to an existing cohort to specifically analyse effects of urban change on health and health inequalities while accounting for gentrification processes in Montreal. GIS and spatial analysis tools will be used to analyse retrospective and prospective dynamics of urban change, gentrification, and health. A battery of tools including online questionnaires, smartphone apps and dedicated sensors will provide detailed data about daily mobility, physical activity, and well-being. Results will provide insights on how urban form changes impact population health outcomes and health inequalities, and support local and regional decision makers in designing and creating healthier communities.

column36: Lung cancer early detection and classification using methylome analysis of plasma cell free DNA
column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related death in Canada. Early diagnosis can have a dramatic influence on lung cancer survival, but the tests that are currently available for early detection of lung cancer presents many challenges that lessen their impact. Therefore, new kinds of tests will be needed to fully realize the potential of early detection of lung cancer on reducing cancer-related deaths in Canada. We have developed a new kind of test that uses cell-free DNA from a simple blood draw. This 'liquid biopsy' approach has generated intense interest from researchers but so far has failed to perform well enough for early detection of lung cancer. Our recent breakthrough discovery now opens the door to new diagnostic tests for many cancer types including for the early diagnosis of lung cancer. This project will develop our promising new liquid biopsy technology into a bona fide lung cancer early detection diagnostic test. Since lung cancer consists of several distinct subtypes, we will first need to attain a significantly deeper understanding of the biology of different subtypes of lung cancer. Each of these subtypes will require different features to be included in a lung cancer early detection liquid biopsy test. To identify these important new features, we will undertake comprehensive and complementary approaches to profiling blood and tumour samples from hundreds of lung cancer patients and controls. By the completion of this project, we expect to turn our current lung cancer liquid biopsy test into a robust diagnostic tool for early detection of lung cancer. In the future, this new liquid biopsy test could be validated in lung cancer screening studies in order to prove how useful it can be for preventing lung cancer deaths. This project will also produce a valuable body of new knowledge regarding the biology of lung cancer subtypes that could someday lead to new therapies for the prevention or treatment of lung cancer.

column36: Causes of muscle spindle afferents excitability changes associated to chronic myalgia
column37: We have all experienced muscle pain in our life, whether after strenuous or eccentric exercise or just repetition of unaccustomed movements. The pain following these movements is caused by minor damage or inflammation to the muscle and is usually not felt at rest. The soreness or tenderness perceived upon palpation of the exercised muscle or an attempt to move is usually considered as a subclinical situation since it is short lasting and recess by itself without need for treatment. However, in some people it leads to a debilitating chronic condition where the pain eventually spreads to several muscles rendering movements very difficult and sometimes even just contact with objects like a chair or a bed become painful. Normally, painful stimuli activate the nerve endings of specialized sensory neurons that inform the brain of their presence. Every type of sensory neuron is specialized for the type of stimuli it is designed to detect. Sensory neurons in the eye detect light but not sound, for instance. In a previous study, we made small injections (2 injections, 2 days apart) of an acidic solution into muscles to mimic, in an animal model, the changes that occur in muscles that are slightly damaged or inflamed, and found that a type of sensory neuron, which is not normally associated to pain perception, becomes abnormally hyperactive. These sensory neurons should detect muscle stretch and not painful stimuli, but because the period of their hyperactivity lasted for as long as the muscle pain lasted in the animals, we asked if the two are related. The aim of this project is to understand the sequence of cellular events that leads to this abnormal activity and to understand how abnormal activity in these cells ends up causing the brain to feel pain instead of muscle stretch.

column36: Unravelling the complex roles of TDP-43 and FUS ALS variants in the vertebrate nervous system
column37: Amid the great diversity of neurodegenerative disorders, there is a growing body of evidence suggesting that synapses are preferentially altered early in the disease process. Though there is compelling evidence that de-innervation of neuromuscular junctions (NMJ) occurs early and throughout the clinical progression of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), the cellular mechanisms that result in loss of NMJ connectivity remain poorly understood. To investigate these defects, my laboratory uses zebrafish ALS models. This animal is uniquely suited for investigations pertaining to the fundamental nature of NMJ defects in ALS as it permits investigations of in vivo physiological function resulting from the expression of mutant ALS-causing genes. We study two ALS genes: TARDBP and FUS, these encode the RNA-binding proteins TDP-43 and FUS respectively, and in ALS mutations in these two genes are believed to interfere with the normal processing of transcripts involved with synaptic function. We have developed genetic animal models of ALS in which analogous disease-causing mutations have been CRISPR-edited into tardbp (encoding zebrafish tdp-43) and fus (encoding zebrafish fus). These models develop an ALS-like motor phenotype and die prematurely. We propose to investigate the synaptic transcripts processed by tdp-43 and fus specifically in the spinal cords and motor neuron cell population and examine how these transcripts are processed differently in our ALS models. In parallel, we will use an array of physiological approaches to explore physiological defects that arise in synaptic function at the NMJ. We propose that furthering our understanding of synaptic defects arising in ALS will provide the necessary foundation for a more complete understanding of the disease, which we believe is needed for therapeutic development.

column36: Ciliary Pathways in Neurogenetic Disease
column37: Cilia function a bit like a satellite antenna, protruding from most cells and relaying information from the surroundings back to the cell. Specific aims study the mechanistic basis of hydrocephalus, examine the Hedgehog signaling pathway which depends on the primary cilium for function, and investigate the contribution of vesicular shedding to this area of cell biology. column36: Desmocollin 1 (DSC1) and atherosclerosis
column37: Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) causes 28% of deaths across Canada and represents the #1 cause of mortality worldwide. Preventive and therapeutic efforts (exercise, smoking cessation, diet, reduction of LDL-C, control of diabetes and treatment of hypertension) have had a major beneficial impact on the health of Canadians. Yet, the burden of disease remains considerable. Attempts to harness the properties of high density lipoproteins (HDL- the "good" cholesterol) to reduce the risk of ASCVD have failed in large clinical trials. HDL removes cholesterol from the arterial wall but this pathway remains untapped. We have found a protein, desmocollin 1 (DSC1) that prevents the removal of cholesterol from cells and is found in large quantities in human atherosclerosis lesions. Our laboratory work indicates that blocking this pathway is feasible and may provide benefit to prevent fatty buildup in arteries. We have found an inhibitor of DSC1 by virtual screening of over 10 million pharmacological compounds. Our top candidate, Docetaxel is an FDA approved drug for cancer treatment. We found that Docetaxel inhibits DSC1 in minute quantities (0.7 nonomolar), a concentration much lower that used in cancer treatment. We will first study Docetaxel in the laboratory using cholesterol-laden cells (similar to the ones found in the atherosclerotic plaque) and determine optimal conditions. Then, we will study the effects of Docetaxel in preventing atherosclerosis in an early-stage mouse model, but also to treat atherosclerosis in a late-stage model of atherosclerosis. In a separate objective, we will measure DSC1 levels in the blood of patients with heart attacks and healthy individuals to determine whether DSC1 levels can be a biomarker of atherosclerosis. These studies will pave the way for first-in-man trials of very low dose Docetaxel to prevent and treat atherosclerosis.

column36: The influence of Cytomegalovirus infection on cystic fibrosis disease progression
column37: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common lethal genetic disease of Canadians. In CF, a vicious cycle of infection and inflammation leads to lung destruction. Understanding how this process contributes to disease progression is key for those with CF to live longer, healthier lives. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) causes a chronic viral infection in humans. The immune system acts to control CMV but it is never cleared from the body. Its prevalence increases over time and >50% of adults have evidence of CMV infection. CMV reactivation and invasion in to various organ systems causes tremendous disease specifically in immune-suppressed individuals. However, an increasing body of literature has demonstrated that CMV may have negative consequences even in general populations. CMV positive individuals have increased rates of chronic inflammatory diseases including cancers, dementia and heart disease. Indeed, CMV positive individuals live shorter lives. How this occurs is unknown - but it is suspected that CMV replicates in already inflamed tissues - exaggerating resultant tissue damage. CF, a disease of chronic infection and inflammation, is a perfect candidate for exploitation by CMV. Provocative preliminary data from the University of Calgary has confirmed the presence of CMV in the lungs of individuals with CF and that CMV positive individuals progress to end-stage lung disease ten years earlier then CMV negative. We propose a multi-centre observational study in several leading Canadian CF centres to determine the role of CMV in CF disease progression. In this study we will determine; the rates and risk factors for CMV infection, correlate disease burden and progression rates with CMV status, and identify how CMV reactivation associates with this process. As potent therapies and vaccines to treat and prevent CMV infections exist - our study has the potential to provide immediately actionable information and improve the quality of life of those living with CF.

column37: The continuous beating of our hearts requires a large amount of energy. Heart muscle metabolism is essential to maintain this function. This makes clinical trials more powerful, allowing drugs to be properly tested with fewer participants over shorter durations, bringing new treatments to patients sooner.

We will test drugs that target pathways in islet macrophages to turn down inflammation, to try to slow diabetes. We will try to identify factors made by islet macrophages that might be used as drugs in the treatment of diabetes. The overall goal is to understand how these garbage eating cells in the pancreas regulate the life and death of insulin-producing cells, and to exploit this knowledge towards the creation and testing of drugs for the treatment of diabetes.

column37: Our bodies are home to trillions of microbes that constantly stimulate the immune system and impact our health. column37: Tissues in multicellular organisms are formed by large numbers of cells that are physically and functionally connected with each other. While surrounded by neighbors, individual cells remain the basic units of life and are responsible for a range of autonomous cellular decisions, such as whether to secrete hormones, to change shape, to divide, or to die. To ensure tissue function, many cells must act together as one functional unit, and this requires coordination of individual cells' behavior with the behavior of their neighbors, through communication between them. Despite their fundamental importance for multicellular biology, the molecular mechanisms enabling such communication, and ultimately resulting in collective behavior of cells, have remained incompletely understood. Capitalizing on established and experimentally tractable models of collective movement of cultured endothelial cells and the formation of vascular tubes, the proposed research aims to identify novel mechanisms of intercellular communication. We will use genetic manipulations of cells, automated cell tracking, and advanced imaging technologies for visualizing and manipulating cellular activities in real time. Endothelial cells form a lining at the inner surface of blood vessels and represent a highly functional barrier between the bloodstream and surrounding tissues. This selective barrier enables distribution of nutrients and oxygen to tissues and, when necessary, the passage of immune cells to sites of infection or injury for clearance. Endothelial cells are also involved in the development of a range of vasculature-related diseases and therefore are of central importance for human health. The anticipated results will not only unveil fundamental principles of how cells are organized into tissues, but also identify new targets of future therapies to treat vasculature-related diseases, a major cause of mortality in Canada and worldwide.

column37: Neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and schizophrenia are complex and debilitating neurodevelopmental disorder that affect ~1-3% of the population worldwide. column36: Electronic Patient Reported Outcome Measures to Improve Patient Centered Solid Organ Transplant Care
column37: Solid-organ transplantation is a life-saving treatment. Many recipients, however, still have symptoms, such as fatigue, pain, anxiety or depression after their transplant, and these patients with symptoms may end up in hospitals more often or even die sooner. Current post-transplant treatment does not include screening for these symptoms, which often go undiagnosed and untreated. Some doctors use questionnaires called Patient Reported Outcome Measures to detect emotional and physical symptoms. These questionnaires are better at recognizing symptoms than clinical assessments by healthcare providers. Using Patient Reported Outcome Measures can improve doctor-patient communication, patient satisfaction by giving them a greater say in their care, and survival rates. Using these tools for transplant recipients would likely deliver similar benefits, so this should be a high priority. To do so, we need tools that are accurate, and don't take too long to complete. The Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System - Computer Adaptive Testing (PROMIS CAT) tools, developed by the National Institutes of Health may be such tools. PROMIS CATs are able to detect physical and emotional symptoms in healthy individuals and also in patients with chronic diseases. Based on the answer to the questions, the computer determines what the next best question will be for that particular patient. In our study, we will: 1. Compare PROMIS CATs to current questionnaires to see if they are precise enough; 2. Develop an electronic Patient Reported Outcome Measure toolkit to guide transplant clinicians in using the PROMIS CATs in clinics; 3. Test if a subsequent study with the PROMIS CATs is doable and acceptable for patients and clinicians. We hope that our electronic Patient Reported Outcome Measure toolkit will become an important tool in helping transplant clinicians to provide more effective, patient-oriented care.

column36: Brain connectivity-based optimization of non-invasive brain stimulation to improve cognitive symptoms in schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia is a severe mental illness that affects around 250,000 Canadians. Beyond positive symptoms such as hallucinations or delusions, and negative symptoms such as blunted affect or social withdrawal, cognitive impairments (for instance, deficits in short- term memory and sustained attention) are a cardinal feature of schizophrenia. Cognitive deficits are particularly disabling for patients trying to lead a normal life and are unfortunately poorly treated with current medications. A non-invasive brain stimulation technique known as repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation holds great promise to improve cognitive symptoms. Stimulating the prefrontal lobe of the brain is thought to regulate its abnormal interaction with distant brain regions, which may reduce cognitive symptoms. Unfortunately, the research conducted up to now has omitted to consider a critical factor to optimize treatment success using this neuromodulatory approach. The one-size-fits-all approach typically employed, where all patients are repetitively stimulated at an identical scalp location, has indeed been shown to have small benefits only. Yet, functional brain organization varies considerably from one individual to another as well as from one mental state to another. Our research program therefore aims to determine optimal characteristics of stimulation on an individual basis in order to best modulate abnormal brain connectivity in schizophrenia. We will use neuroimaging mapping techniques such as functional magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography along with state-of-the-art statistical approaches to better describe how functional brain organization varies both between individuals and within an individual over time. Findings will pave the way for increasing the success rate of non-invasive brain stimulation in treating medication-resistant cognitive symptoms in persons suffering from schizophrenia.

column36: Modelling Mitochondrial Disease
column37: Mitochondria are the power plants of our cells, converting the food that we eat into energy needed to survive. Thus, it should come as no surprise that mitochondrial dysfunction can have adverse effects on human health. Mitochondrial disease is a rare, though not uncommon, difficult to diagnose genetic disorder, caused by mitochondrial dysfunction. At present there are no cures, and treatment is mostly to manage symptoms. As such, fewer than 50% of diagnosed children survive to adulthood. However, a genetic diagnosis of disease is of immense value to both clinicians as well as patients and their families. While recent advances in genetic analyses have accelerated mitochondrial disease diagnosis, by helping to identify mutations in genes causing mitochondrial dysfunction, a definitive answer is found less than half of the time. When novel candidate disease genes and mutations are identified, they require additional functional validation. Such work can take significant time and effort, and has created a bottleneck in diagnosing mitochondrial disease patients. Thus, it is imperative to evaluate these candidate mutations. In addition to providing a genetic diagnosis, characterizing these novel disease-causing mutations helps to identify the underlying cause of mitochondrial dysfunction, which provides fundamental insight and understanding of the molecular mechanisms regulating mitochondria. This insight is essential groundwork prior to developing a cure for mitochondrial disease. By employing methods and approaches that allow us to characterize mitochondrial dysfunction, our research will help provide clinical diagnoses for patients with mitochondrial disease, and deliver a better understanding of the mechanisms regulating mitochondrial function. Given the growing appreciation for the role mitochondria play in human health and disease, our research has both short and long-term benefits to Canadians and the Canadian health care system.

column37: According to a national survey, one third of Canadians aged 15 and older were victims of childhood maltreatment. It is noteworthy that 60% of victims experienced abuse at the hands of a family member, suggesting intergenerational transmission of abuse. In 2014, in the province of Quebec, 95.5% of the 605 adolescents adjudicated as having engaged in sexual abuse (AESA) perpetrated these offences against minors. Nevertheless, AESA represent a vulnerable population given their own experiences of past victimization (e.g., 50% physical; 30% sexual), as well as their risk for sexual (6 to 20%) and violent recidivism (21 to 40%). Furthermore, with 50% of mothers and 30% of fathers of AESA reporting a history of victimization, manifestations associated with sexual and non-sexual interpersonal violence in these families is undeniable. A systemic approach to research and intervention is thus necessary to address the cumulative forms of victimization in these families. The Gaia Project seeks to implement and assess the effectiveness of the clinical Gaia program to promote targeted changes in improving mental and relational health in AESA and their families at the end of the treatment and at the 6-month follow-up. The Gaia program will be implemented in 3 organizations, the Centre integre universitaire de sante et services sociaux de l'Estrie (CIUSSSE) and de la Mauricie-et-du-Centre-du-Quebec (CIUSSSMCQ), as well as the Institut Philippe-Pinel de Montreal. Program implementation and effectiveness will be based on a quasi-experimental design with comparison group and 3 assessment time points. Given referral rates of partnering organizations, a sample of 200 families is expected. The Gaia program is innovative in that 1) AESA and their families are targeted for treatment; 2) symptomatic repercussions of victimization and interpersonal violence in families are treated; and 3) the program is designed with modules that are implemented while AESA complete their treatment as usual.

column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is 4 times as prevalent as stroke and heart disease. While obesity has often been coined the culprit, and cartilage named the victim of knee OA, there are other important causes and tissues involved within subgroups of knee OA patients, which have yet to be fully explored. We recently determined that over 40% of OA patients receiving knee surgeries are neither overweight nor obese. Many of these patients are postmenopausal women and in a recent study we published, 15% of knee OA patients showed evidence of bone loss. Bone and muscle abnormalities at the joint have been associated with OA, but few investigators have explored how they may be the causes rather than the consequences of the disease. Bone and muscle differences will be used to predict more painful and worsening knee symptoms 5 years later. Within a subset of participants, the study will also address how changes in these bone and muscle features can impact what happens in the tissues of the knee joint. Finally, the study will examine the pathway that leads from bone and muscle loss to knee tissue damage and subsequently greater knee symptoms. By studying bone-muscle and joint interactions over time in the context of knee OA, we can pinpoint earlier stages in the disease process that can be targeted for disease prevention. This study will address postmenopausal OA patients, a group that has so far, been underserved with few treatment options available.

column36: Surveillance of Complex Renal Cysts: The SOCRATIC study
column37: Background: One in three patients over 60 years old will be diagnosed with a renal cyst following abdominal imaging. Traditionally, experts have recommended that complex cystic lesions (also known as Bosniak III - IV cysts) should be surgically removed, but recent evidences suggest that many are benign and that if malignant, most have low-metastatic risk. Given that many patients may not require surgery due to the excellent prognosis, alternative management should be studied. Thus, active surveillance which involves close follow-up of a patient's condition without treatment unless its condition changes, was proposed as a tradeoff option to surgery. Objectives: The goal of this multicenter project is to conduct a prospective study with a 5-year follow-up to confirm the oncologic outcomes of active surveillance in the management of complex cysts. The main objectives are: 1) to compare the 5-year cancer specific survival between cysts managed by surgery and active surveillance; 2) evaluate disease progression; and 3) evaluate patient's well-being according to each management strategy. Description: Participants (220 under active surveillance and 110 undergoing surgery) will be selected on the basis of age (over 18y), life expectancy (over 5y), diagnosis (Bosniak III and IV) and treatment choice. They will be followed with semi-annual and annual visits. Visits will serve to evaluate vital status and quality of life scores. Patients on active surveillance will also be assessed for cyst progression and will be offered surgery if progression is observed. This study, conducted in 6 large-volume Canadian centers, will be led by medical/scientific experts and patient advocates. Relevance: Validating the safety of active surveillance of complex renal cysts will be determinant in reducing overtreatment, sparing thousands of patients from unnecessary treatment, reducing the risk associated to surgery and potentially saving costs to the healthcare system.

column36: EpiGen Marks for Human Sepsis
column37: Sepsis, systemic organ dysfunction triggered by a dysregulated host response to infection, incurs enormous human and health care burden. Globally it is estimated to affect more than 30 million people each year, ~40% of whom die. The sequelae include physical, cognitive, and psychological disability; profoundly impacting quality of life of survivors. The biggest problem is that we have no specific treatments. Patients receive fluid resuscitation, antibiotics and supportive care, but an under appreciation for patient heterogeneity and inadequate characterization of the complexity of the host response to infection has made it difficult to design clinical trials that show benefit. The issue is that, despite development of robust therapeutic candidates, we lack the tools to accurately categorize sepsis (prognostic enrichment) and identify those patients that are more likely to respond to therapy (predictive enrichment). In the cancer literature, personalizing treatment on the basis of the molecular characteristics of a tumor is simply 'good practice'- there is an urgent need to do the same for septic patients. Here we propose to use an approach that has never been used for sepsis before; to identify DNA methylation changes that classify septic vs non-septic critically ill patients (often it is very difficult to differentiate these patients on the basis of clinical tools alone) and determine the association between methylation changes with time-to-death and/or response to therapy. We will capitalize on banked DNA samples collected in the context of RCTs where patient heterogeneity was minimized through randomization and bias was reduced by blinding. We will use predictive modeling to integrate clinical and molecular data to identify a set of informative methylation marks - and validate their ability to risk stratify patients using independent cohorts. Successful completion of this project is expected to significantly advance care.

column36: K+ channels as key targets to favor alveolar epithelial integrity and function during the resolution of acute respiratory distress syndrome
column37: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is a devastating form of respiratory failure in adults and children. Although ARDS causes may be multiple (infection, trauma, transplantation...), this syndrome initially commonly features severe injury of the epithelial cell layer lining alveoli, accumulation of liquid in the lungs (edema) and massive inflammation. Rapid resolution is pivotal for ARDS. If not, a fibrotic process rapidly arises, ultimately leading to respiratory failure. No specific treatment exists for ARDS and mortality rates remain unacceptably high. Improvement in survival relies on the development of novel therapies favoring the restoration of alveolar integrity, before establishment of fibrosis. Importantly, we discovered that a specific class of proteins transporting potassium (K+ channels) through alveolar epithelial cells plays key role in alveolar repair. In addition, our data from animal models strongly support that these channels are not only crucial to favor alveolar integrity but are also implicated in resorption of lung edema and inflammation. Therefore, we propose that targeting K+ channels will promote alveolar integrity and lung function, favoring ARDS resolution. Our main goal is to address key questions regarding the mode of action of alveolar K+ channels in the resolution of ARDS parameters. At the cellular level, we will dissect the mechanisms on how K+ channels regulate alveolar epithelial repair and we will study the relationship between K+ channel function and inflammation. Using complementary genetic and pharmacological strategies in animal models of ARDS, our aim is then to demonstrate the role of K+ channels in the resolution of ARDS parameters, through improvement of alveolar epithelial integrity and function. In summary, our project will provide a comprehensive knowledge of the action mechanisms of K+ channels for the resolution of ARDS and important insights into the development of innovative therapeutic strategies.

These symptoms interfere with care-giving (dressing, toileting, hygiene, positioning, sitting and mobility) and affect quality of life. There are many ways to prevent or treat these hips. Some are treated early before any symptoms start, while others are treated at the earliest signs of any symptoms. Earlier treatments are less invasive, but often have to be repeated because the hips can begin to dislocate again as the child grows. Later treatments are usually more invasive but might have the advantage of lasting longer. Currently there is little evidence from high quality research to suggest which strategies work best. Previous research has relied on x-rays of the hips to make judgments about the success of any treatment. While x-rays are an important way to record the results of different treatments, they do not tell us whether a child has really benefited from treatment in terms of the child's comfort, ease of care, health or quality of life. Our research team has developed a way to measure the effect of treatments more meaningfully for children with severe cerebral palsy. In 2014, CIHR funded a 5 year project, involving a large group of surgeons and pediatricians from 28 centres in Canada, the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, Europe and Asia to study the impact of hip displacement on the lives of children with severe cerebral palsy, and to compare which treatment strategy would be most beneficial for these children using the outcome measure developed for this purpose. This study has enrolled 678 patients who are being followed for at least 2 years after initiation of treatment. This new project proposes to follow the same children over the next 6 years or until end of growth to study the longer term outcomes of these children.

column36: Pathways to neurodegeneration from natural human tRNA variation
column37: The ability of cells to properly manage the synthesis, folding, and degradation of their constituent proteins is essential for all aspects of cellular function and life. Many diseases, particularly age-related and neurodegenerative diseases, are characterized by increased levels of misfolded proteins. Correct reading of the genetic code is essential for accurate protein synthesis and protein folding. An often-overlooked step in the synthesis of proteins involves the correct attachment of amino acids to specific tRNAs by enzymes called aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases. Lack of specificity at this step can result in the incorrect reading of the genetic code or mistranslation, which may lead to protein mis-folding, aggregation, and disease. The 1000 Genomes Project revealed a higher than anticipated degree of variation in the ~600 human tRNA genes, indicating more than half of individuals contain at least one mutant tRNA. We developed a novel targeted capture array and deep sequenced 610 tRNA loci in a group of 84 individuals. Our data show that individuals carry significantly more tRNA variants than previously anticipated. We identified many human tRNA variants some with obvious potential to mistranslate. We predict that mistranslating tRNA variants contribute to human disease. We will, for the first time, elucidate to what extent naturally occurring tRNA mutations in humans cause mistranslation, and whether mistranslation exacerbates the toxicity of mis-folded proteins that are associated with neurodegenerative disease. Our proposed project has great potential to identify genetic mutations that cause mistranslation as an important contributor to neurodegeneration. Our data will also be relevant to other age-related diseases characterized by compromised cellular protein quality control, such as cancer and cardio-vascular diseases.

column37: Need for project Once cancer is established, it becomes complex and resistant to standard therapies. column36: Determining the mechanisms underlying disease pathology and the genetic reversibility of the ATR-X syndrome.
column37: Our genes are arranged on large pieces of DNA called chromosomes. Chromosomes are huge molecules that must undergo multiple levels of compaction to fit into the cell. At the same time, the genes characteristic of that cell type must remain accessible for activation. In a stem cell the chromosomes are loosely packaged and many genes are poised for activation. When the stem cell commits to becoming a specific cell type (eg. neuron) it must tightly package and silence those genes that are not required and fully activate those genes that will be turned on. To do this cells have developed a complex series of proteins to control the structure of chromosomes and the regulation of genes. When this process is defective, cells cannot divide, differentiate or initiate gene expression effectively. Recent work has shown that mutations in chromosome regulating proteins cause a variety of human diseases, including developmental disorders with severe intellectual disability and numerous types of cancer. This project studies the ATRX gene that, when mutated, causes a severe intellectual disability syndrome. Despite our success in identifying these genes, our understanding of how these chromosome regulatory proteins coordinate which genes to turn on or off, when to turn them on or off, and in what order remains poorly defined. This project aims to define the function of ATRX during brain development, learning, and memory formation by studying a mouse model in which the ATRX gene has been inactivated. Since many of these changes to our chromosomes are dynamic and reversible we will also explore whether we can rescue the phenotypic features of the disease by adding back a normal copy of the gene. With our current ability to use viruses to re-introduce genes to kill cancer cells and clinical trials underway to use them to treat neuromuscular disease, the possibility that they could be used to treat a devastating intellectual disability is promising and provides immense hope.

column37: MicroRNAs are short nucleic acid polymers that guide gene regulation activities. They are important under normal physiological conditions for homeostasis and adaptation, but defects in their function and biogenesis can lead to a broad diversity of disease ranging from diabetes, to hearth disease, to cancer. This project will shine an entirely new light on a newly identified layer of gene control, and potentially reveal new genomic bases for diseases.

column37: A third of young Canadians now reach adulthood overweight or obese, a condition that puts them at higher risk for premature death from chronic diseases. Understanding early-life determinants of obesity is thus central to designing public health interventions that increase the proportion of children entering adulthood with healthy weights. Although nutrition is recognized as one of the key modifiable factors for obesity prevention, studies on the long-term relationships between early-life diet and later-life excess weight or later-life dietary habits are lacking. To bridge this gap, our research aims to identify early-life dietary factors that are associated with healthy and unhealthy dietary habits in young adults relative to their weight status. Study participants are young adults taking part in the Quebec Longitudinal Study of Child Development (QLSCD), under the direction of the Institut de la Statistique du Quebec (ISQ). This birth cohort comprises a representative sample of children born in Quebec 20 years ago; 1,750 young adults still actively participate in the study. Over the years, ISQ staff have met with these children and their families to collect data on multiple aspects of child development since birth. We also conducted an extensive nutrition study when the children were aged 4.5 years. We propose this project to assess dietary habits and weight status at age 22. The data collected from birth to early adulthood will enable us to analyze how dietary factors and other determinants active in early childhood are associated with the dietary habits of young adults according to weight status. Findings of this research will reinforce and add to current knowledge about early-life influences on later-life diet and excess weight; allow identifying the ages at which influences are first detectable; identify protective factors that could reduce risks over time; and assess the cumulative effects of a variety of influences prevalent from birth to early adulthood.

column36: Maskwiomin (Birch Bark-Oil): Re-discovery of an L'nu skin ointment, working collaboratively with Indigenous communities through stories and awakening of knowledge, study of the processing of the oil and identification of active ingredients, and determination of its medical indications
column37: Birch bark-oil (maskwiomin) is an almost forgotten traditional L'nu medicine for the topical treatment of skin conditions such as rashes, eczema and psoriasis. Only two Elders of Membertou First Nation, Sydney, Nova Scotia held the knowledge of which one has since passed away. Funded by a 2017/18 CIHR Catalyst grant, Young and Bierenstiel successfully worked with the indigenous community in an equal partnership and based on a 2-Eyed Seeing approach. The team worked with Elders and community members through stories and recreation to re-discover maskwiomin. Maskwiomin is made in a torrefaction process in a campfire and compounded as creme or mixed into soap bars -now made regularly by community members for individual use. There is excellent anecdotal evidence of over 70 persons that daily washing of skin with maskwiomin soap reduces skin outbreaks, eczema and psoriasis within days. Preliminary scientific chemistry and microbiology studies showed that maskwiomin is a complex organic mixture composed likely of derivatives of betulin, a secondary metabolite and main component in birch bark. Betulin is known to have antibacterial, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, anti-cancer and anti-viral properties. The research demonstrated for the first time that maskwiomin is a broadspectrum antibiotic against Gram+ and Gram- strains with the same efficacy as commercially available antibiotics. This also shows that the Mi'kmak people had a topical antibiotic centuries, if not longer, prior to Fleming's penicillin discovery in 1928! This proposed CIHR Project Grant expands the work on the community level (social science and indigenous knowledge) and in pharmaceutical science (processing and identification of active ingredients and medicinal studies beyond antibiotics). It also contains a medical component with a team of nursing researchers and clinician for pilot studies and preliminary human trials to study the extent and wide range of clinical indications of maskwiomin.

column36: The role of FK506 binding protein 51 in the regulation of glucocorticoid receptor signaling
column37: PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder) occurs in some people after severe traumatic events such as sexual assault or military combat. Patients suffer nightmares, flashbacks, and can be very anxious, avoiding reminders of the traumatic event. In severe cases, PTSD can be completely disabling and current treatments are often ineffective. The main treatment for PTSD consists of repeatedly exposing the patient to cues related to the trauma with the hope that they will become less sensitive to these triggers. Some antidepressant medications can also be helpful, but better treatments based on the causes and disease mechanisms for PTSD are needed. We have recently discovered that two proteins involved in the stress response system can bind together and form a complex, and that this protein complex is elevated in patients with PTSD (but not in healthy controls or people exposed to trauma but who don't develop PTSD). We have also created a tiny protein molecule called a peptide that can block this interaction and separate the complex. We have used a mouse model of PTSD that involves exposing the animals to fearful stimuli, after which they develop anxious behaviours similar to human PTSD. Our peptide can block the emergence of PTSD-like behaviours in mice after exposure to fearful situations, suggesting that our peptide could actually prevent PTSD if given after a traumatic event. This grant application proposes a series of experiments to investigate the detailed mechanism underlying these preliminary results. We will investigate if other proteins are involved in this complex, how downstream signaling pathways are affected, and how stress hormones like cortisol affect the proteins in the complex. We will also take the first steps towards testing our peptide as a treatment for PTSD by determining the optimal timing and delivery of the peptide. If successful, our work may lead to the first preventative treatment for PTSD that is based on new knowledge of disease mechanisms

column36: Healing from Intimate Partner Violence: An Evaluation of an Intervention for Indigenous Mothers and Children Affected by Intimate Partner Violence
column37: Intimate partner violence (IPV) and the exposure of children to IPV are serious societal concerns. Notably, Indigenous women in Canada are four times more likely to experience IPV than non-Indigenous women. These inequities among Indigenous women and children need to be understood within a broad context of Canadian colonization and the intergenerational effects of the collective traumas experienced by previous generations of families and communities. The negative impacts of IPV for women and their children have been well documented. Women survivors of IPV are at elevated risk for a variety of physical and psychological problems which may also impact their parenting. Children exposed to IPV are 5 to 7 times more likely to experience a wide variety of emotional and behavioral problems in the short term and over their lifetime, compared to unexposed children. They are also at greater risk of continuing the cycle of violence later in adulthood than children who have not been exposed. Effective interventions are urgently needed; unfortunately, many existing programs were not designed to meet the needs of Indigenous mothers and their children. When used without the proper cultural contexts and adaptations, interventions can inadvertently exacerbate existing traumas and continue the histories of Canadian colonialism and health inequity among Indigenous populations. Our team combines the necessary expertise of Indigenous knowledge keepers and experienced researchers to address this problem. Our goal is to conduct a feasibility study of an evidence-based intervention designed specifically to meet the needs of Indigenous mothers and their children who have experienced IPV using a two-eyed seeing approach. To our knowledge, we will be the first team to do so in Canada. Our findings will significantly improve the lives of Indigenous mothers and children by providing counsellors and social workers with more effective tools specifically designed to help Indigenous families.

column36: Electrophysiology and Neurostimulation in Treatment-Resistant Youth Depression (ENTRY-D)
column37: Depression affects more than 350 million people worldwide. Prevalence of depression peaks in youth 16 to 24 years of age. However up to 50% of youth do not respond to existing treatment approaches or develop serious side effects. An ideal treatment in youth should precisely target the underlying biological impairments to have maximum therapeutic efficacy and minimized side effects. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a noninvasive neurostimulation therapy that is FDA approved for patients who fail responding to antidepressant medications. While efficacy of rTMS has been studied in several clinical trials in adult depression, these trials have not been extended to benefit youth. When applied to the prefrontal cortex, rTMS is shown to target biological mechanisms that are closely linked with youth depression. We have preliminary data that shows the safety and feasibility of a brief and novel rTMS protocol, named theta burst stimulation (TBS), in youth depression. Our goal is to extend these early studies and for the first time examine the efficacy and biological targets of TBS treatment for youth depression. We will assess the efficacy of TBS in a placebo controlled clinical trial. We will examine targets and predictors of response to TBS using novel brain mapping technologies to monitor changes in prefrontal cortex throughout the clinical trial. If our results are positive, we will have identified a novel treatment that may be a more efficacious and acceptable treatment for youth depression. Finally, identifying the biological targets of TBS in youth will lead to optimizing the dosage and efficacy of rTMS therapy for youth and moving toward more personalized treatments for youth depression. This will also be groundbreaking in predicting which patients will benefit from this treatment to minimize time wasted in ineffective trials and reduce burden on patients and the health system.

column36: Re-examining Maintenance Antipsychotic Treatment in Schizophrenia: "Extended" Antipsychotic Dosing
column37: Background and Importance Continuous antipsychotic treatment represents our current standard of care in the long-term management of schizophrenia. This is a concern because of the significant side effects associated with these drugs. Unfortunately, though, many individuals need to stay on antipsychotic treatment to prevent relapses. Goals/Research Aims Our group has evidence that "extended" antipsychotic dosing represents a possible alternative to continuous antipsychotic exposure. This strategy allows for individuals to take their medications every other day, thereby decreasing their exposure by 50% - a very sizable reduction. This strategy seems to work, but we need to study more individuals to ensure our initial findings are correct. We also need to confirm that this strategy comes with advantages in terms of decreased side effects. Methods/Approach/Expertise The proposed study constitutes a 5-year, randomized controlled trial (i.e. both patients and doctors don't know which treatment an individual is receiving so as not to bias results), comparing continuous vs. extended (i.e. alternate day dosing) antipsychotic treatment over a period of 1 year. Participants will be monitored on a regular basis using a variety of measures to assess clinical and functional outcome, as well as side effects. Expected Outcomes Based on our work to date, we predict comparable clinical efficacy between the 2 study populations. At the same time, we predict benefits in terms of certain clinical measures as well as side effects (e.g. weight gain, risk of diabetes). Further, there will be automatic cost savings in that individuals in the extended dosing receive only 50% of the antipsychotic medication administered to those in the continuous group. This work has the potential to revolutionize maintenance antipsychotic treatment through support of an alternative strategy that decreases antipsychotic exposure by 50%.

column37: Increasing the impact of successful quality improvement initiatives depends on the context, or work environment, that the initiative is occurring in as well as how the initiative is facilitated. Improving the success of initiatives is vital since these initiatives impact quality of care and life for residents living in long-term care settings. Our proposed project will use various approaches to delve into the complex ways that context and facilitation work together to improve how successful, or not, initiatives are. This research is suited to our team since we have worked with long-term care facilities for over a decade and, over that time, we have collected extensive data on resident and care providers' experiences as well as implemented several of our own improvement initiatives. column36: Whole Genome Sequencing Defines Leiomyosarcoma Evolution and Identifies Therapeutic Opportunities in the DNA Damage Pathway
column37: Leiomyosarcoma (LMS) is a common adult sarcoma that is only cured by surgery. However, the majority of patients do not survive LMS as they develop metastasis or spread of the cancer from the original site of disease. Current drug therapy to treat this cancer is largely ineffective and thus survival rates are low in many LMS patient groups (30%). Thus, researchers need to find more effective drugs. Our research team has taken the approach of performing comprehensive testing of LMS using state of the art genetics. One of the benefits of using the latest technology or whole genome sequencing is that very detailed analysis of the tumor is performed. Although this can lead to almost too much information, our team has the means to analyze the data so we can try to determine why these cancers develop. If we can better understand what is leading to cancer formation, this helps us try to identify and test new drugs. Recent studies in our program found a signature of fingerprint in LMS that is associated with cancer cells not being able to undergo proper repair of broken DNA. DNA is the material that carries all the information about how a living thing will look and function. It has been long understood that cancers can arise from DNA not getting fixed properly. We will test if a type of DNA repair called homologous recombination is abnormal in LMS, as drugs already have been developed that will selectively kill cancer cells off with this problem. We have three study goals: 1. To determine how similar mutational profiles are between the main tumor and metastatic disease. This will allow us to better understand if drugs should be developed in a similar way for both sites or if in fact they are quite different. 2. To better understand if these DNA repair problems happen only in the main tumor of if they also occur in the cancer that has spread. 3. To test if the novel drugs we have identified that selectively inhibit DNA repair have clinical promise in the lab.

column36: Development of dynamic 1H MRSI for the assessment of impaired brain glucose metabolism in patients with early Alzheimer's Disease
column37: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is a devastating neurodegenerative disease whose prevalence and impact on society are steadily on the rise. AD is characterized by marked cognitive decline and memory loss, as well as insidious brain pathology that accumulates long before the appearance of clinical symptoms. Thus, early detection and intervention are of great importance. One of the early hallmarks of AD progression is an impairment in the main pathway for energy production in the brain: glucose metabolism. As such, measures of brain glucose metabolism have been used for many years as a biomarker for identifying pathology associated with AD. However, mapping glucose metabolism in the brain is difficult, and the current gold-standard method - positron emission tomography with 18F fludeoxyglucose (FDG-PET) - has several drawbacks such as exposing patients to ionizing radiation. In this work, we aim to develop a new method for mapping brain glucose metabolism that involves proton magnetic resonance spectroscopic imaging (MRSI) scans acquired during an infusion of carbon-13 labelled glucose. The aims of this proposed work are: 1) To develop and optimize imaging methods for rapid proton MRSI detection of glucose metabolism in the human brain; 2) to validate MRSI measures of glucose metabolism by comparison against gold-standard PET images; and 3) To apply these new techniques towards detection of impaired brain glucose metabolism in patients with AD and mild cognitive impairment. The result of this work will be a new MRI-based method for assessing impaired glucose metabolism in patients with AD. Importantly, since these measures can be obtained in a standard clinical MRI scanner, they can easily be combined with complimentary MR imaging measures such as structural, functional or diffusion imaging, to provide a multiparametric assessment of disease status. Finally, this method will avoid the need for a separate PET scan, thus minimizing radiation exposure to patients.

column36: Automated analysis of natural speech in personalized treatment for major depressive disorder
column37: Listening to a person's speech is a key component of clinical assessment in psychiatry. Speech rhythm and melody reflect the speaker's mood in the moment. The content and form of speech reflect the speaker's thought process, their interests and motivations. column36: Colchicine for the prevention of perioperative atrial fibrillation (COP-AF)
column37: The development of atrial fibrillation (AF) during or shortly after major thoracic surgery is one of the most common serious complications in this patient population. The occurrence of AF leads to adverse changes in blood pressure, problems with the management of blood thinners required in many of these patients, prolonged hospital stays and an increased risk of death and stroke. Prior studies suggest that inflammation is the primary mechanism for AF developing during or after surgery. Colchicine is a potent drug that strongly inhibits inflammation. In patients undergoing cardiac surgery colchicine has been effective in preventing inflammatory complications and AF. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that colchicine effectively prevents the occurrence of AF in patients undergoing major thoracic surgery. In this population, colchicine may also reduce the time to chest tube extraction, an important patient-centered outcome, as it may shorten hospital stay, reduce the incidence of postoperative infections and improve patient's well-being. Colchicine administration may even reduce the occurrence of death or stroke. To test these hypotheses, we will conduct a large double-blind randomized placebo controlled trial of 2,800 patients who are at least 55 years old and undergoing thoracic surgery. The trial will be conducted in thoracic centres in Canada and internationally. Oral colchicine or matching placebo will be given twice daily for 10 days. Study personnel will follow patients throughout the trial. This large trial will determine whether colchicine lowers the risk of AF and other inflammatory complications in patients undergoing thoracic surgery. Finding a safe, effective and low-cost intervention to prevent AF in this setting addresses a major unmet clinical need as it may decrease length of hospital stay, improve the quality of perioperative care, lower costs and reduce the risk of stroke or death.

column36: Is mechanical bowel preparation necessary to reduce surgical site infection following colon surgery? A randomized controlled trial
column37: Background: Following colon surgery, surgical site infection (SSI) is the most common complication and leads to longer recovery time for patients as well as increased health care costs. Currently, there is high quality evidence to show that the combination of intravenous antibiotics (IVA), mechanical bowel preparation (MBP) and antibiotics (OA) is the most effective bowel preparation to reduce SSI. However, there are no studies comparing IVA+MBP+OA and IVA+OA. This is an important question because if IVA+OA works the same as IVA+MBP+OA, then MBP may be safely omitted as part of the bowel preparation to reduce SSI and patients would avoid the side effects of MBP prior to their surgery. Objectives: Therefore, the objective of this study is to perform a trial to determine if IVA+OA works the same as IVA+MBP+OA to reduce SSI following colon surgery. Methods: This study will be performed in 4 hospitals across Canada. Patients are eligible to participate in the study if they are (i) undergoing elective colon surgery, (ii) are 18 years of age or older and (3) provide informed consent. Eligible patients will be randomly assigned (i.e. flip of a coin) to one of two groups, either IVA+MBP+OA or IVA+OA. The primary outcome for the study is the number of patients that develop a SSI within 30 days after surgery. At the end of the study, the number of SSI between the two groups will be compared to determine if IVA+OA works the same as IVA+MBP+OA. Relevance: This study is important because we expect that IVA+OA will work similarly to IVA+MBP+OA and will show that MBP is not necessary to reduce SSI. This will be important to both patients and physicians as it will improve both patient experience and outcomes following colon surgery. Given the high volume of colon surgeries done annually, as well the impact SSI has on patient outcomes, our results have potential to change practice in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Novel treatment to reduce allergen-induced acute bronchoconstriction and chronic inflammation of asthmatic airways
column37: The airways of asthma patients are sensitive to inhaled allergens, like pollen. Long term allergen exposure increases lung inflammation and sensitization; once sensitized, exposure can trigger acute asthmatic attacks involving intense anxiety, airway narrowing, impaired breathing and, in severe cases, death. In recent rodents studies, we showed that during an allergen-induced asthmatic attack, the asthmatic lung releases chemicals into the general circulation that trigger a powerful neuronal reflex pathway causing airway narrowing. This pathway involves activation of the carotid bodies (nerve clusters in the neck) via specific receptors called TRPV1. Importantly, pharmacological disruption of this pathway with a single drug dose dramatically reduces airway narrowing and the breathing pattern associated with respiratory distress. These effects were long lived (days). Moreover, our preliminary data suggest that when carotid bodies are removed entirely, the lung inflammation and sensitivity to allergens associated with asthma is reduced. These observations lead to three important questions: 1/ How do chemicals from the lung activate the nerves associated with the carotid body; 2/ Does blocking the mechanisms involved have long-term beneficial effects on asthmatic lung health; 3/ Can blocking this reflex pathway reduce asthmatic symptoms in humans? This proposal addresses these questions with the aim of identifying novel targets to improve asthma treatment and prevent asthma-related morbidity and death. Specifically, we will determine how chemicals from the lung activate the carotid body using state-of-the-art experimental preparations and functional cellular imaging techniques, and test the consequences of blocking this signaling using surgical isolation, pharmacological and modern gene manipulation techniques. Finally, we will test whether blocking carotid body signalling using a best-in-class drug developed in Canada can reduce symptoms in human asthma sufferers.

column36: Translating to the Community (T2C): A Social Epigenetic Study of FASD
column37: Social epigenomics involves the study of how social experiences affect genes and our biology. For instance, living in disadvantaged circumstances, exposure to discrimination, residential segregation, violence, trauma (historical, contemporary, intergenerational), psychosocial stress, food insecurity, and health risk behaviours can affect a person's ability to be healthy, stay healthy, and have healthy children. Translating to the Community (T2C) is a university, Indigenous community and FASD clinic led social epigenetic biobank developed to investigate the way such social experiences affect genes and our biology leading to Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) and its associated behaviours and co-morbidities (herein called FASD). The aims of this research are to: 1) Investigate the association between social experiences and PAE and FASD; 2) Investigate the association between epigenetic changes and PAE and FASD; 3) Advance community pre-assessment of PAE and FASD and improve PAE and FASD diagnostic tools and interventions. To elucidate the social-epigenetic link, our team represented by Indigenous science, social science, clinical science and basic science developed Translating to the Community (T2C), a social epigenetic biobank that has University and Indigenous community ethical approval, and is governed with our partner Cree Nation Tribal Health Centre. The social biobank is designed to accrue data via partners/communities in Manitoba and from anywhere in the world. Its governance structure includes Indigenous families and communities, community health and social programs, and FASD clinics. The research informs the potential for social-epigenetic informed diagnostic and assessment tools, demonstrates the merit of community-assessments and shows new pathways for an early diagnosis and early clinical, health, education and cultural preventions/interventions.

column36: Emotion And Symptom-focused Engagement (EASE): A Randomized Controlled Trial for Individuals with Acute Leukemia
column37: Acute leukemia (AL) is a cancer of the blood cells. Patients with AL are hospitalized soon after diagnosis and receive intensive chemotherapy with a high risk of death related to the disease and its treatment. In a study of newly-diagnosed and relapsed patients with AL, we found high levels of physical and psychological distress. We developed an intervention called Emotion And Symptom-focused Engagement (EASE) to relieve this distress. EASE includes: i) a brief psychological intervention to treat psychological distress, and ii) detection and treatment of physical symptoms. In an initial study of EASE, we demonstrated that EASE could be delivered to patients and that it resulted in promising reductions in psychological distress and physical symptoms and improvements in quality of life and satisfaction with care. These findings support the need for a larger randomized controlled trial (RCT) to investigate the effectiveness of EASE. We propose to recruit 260 adults newly-diagnosed with AL to the RCT within 1 week of admission to the Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, Toronto, or to the Vancouver General Hospital, Vancouver. Patients will be assigned randomly (by chance) to the intervention or the usual care group. Patients assigned to receive EASE will receive psychological support from a trained mental health clinician for 8 weeks and will be assessed for physical symptoms weekly for the initial 4 weeks. When physical symptoms are reported by patients in the intervention group, the patients will be referred to a symptom-control team for symptom management. The symptom-control team consists of a physician and a nurse and other professionals as needed. All participants will complete questionnaires at the start of the study and again at 4, 8, and 12 weeks. This study will provide essential information about the effectiveness of EASE, which will inform policy and practice in the treatment of patients with AL nationally and internationally.

column36: Evaluating Impacts of Structural and Community-Led Interventions on STBBI Risk Environments for Street and Off-Street Sex Workers
column37: Three decades into the HIV epidemic, sex workers continue to face a disproportionate burden of HIV and other sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections (STBBIs), alongside and driven by high rates of violence and other rights violations. Whereas most STBBI prevention, treatment, and care interventions continue to focus on individual and behavioural factors, evidence suggests a critical need for interventions that also address broader structural factors such as law/policy, stigma, and labour conditions. Understanding the impacts of these currently unfolding interventions on STBBIs is directly aligned with the 2018 Pan Canadian Framework for Action on STBBIs. The proposed five-year study aims to understand the impacts of new peer-to-peer HIV/STI testing, community empowerment interventions (eg, anti-stigma sensitivity trainings, peer outreach) and changes in policing policies and practices on STBBI risk environments (e.g., condom use, drug use), violence, and HIV/STI incidence among sex workers over time. To meet these aims, we seek to build on the unique infrastructure provided by the AESHA project, one of the largest and longest running prospective cohorts of sex workers in North America. Participants will complete semi-annual surveys and STBBI testing; we will also use linked provincial administrative data (e.g., HIV, policing, mortality, health service utilization) to provide unbiased measures of key variables. Amidst continued syndemics of STBBIs and violence faced by sex workers, this study offers an unprecedented opportunity to inform new strategies to improve the health of marginalized women in Canada and globally.

column36: Endothelial colony forming cell-derived exosomes and cardiac repair after myocardial infarction
column37: Myocardial infarction (MI), also commonly known as a heart attack, occurs when there is a blockage of a blood vessel supplying oxygen and nutrients to the heart muscles. Current therapy aims at re-establishing the blood flow to protect the heart muscles from further damage. This strategy is effective in the recovery from a heart attack. However, the death of a significant portion of heart cells leads to progressive and substantial loss of heart function resulting in heart failure. Our research focuses on endothelial colony forming cells (ECFCs) that are present in the human blood. These are believed to be the precursor of endothelial cells, which create inner-lining of blood vessels. We recently isolated these cells and injected them into the mice with the heart attack caused by permanent blockage of blood flow to a significant portion of the heart. While the cells reduced damage to heart muscles, the effects were identified to be mediated by nanoparticles released from ECFCs, termed as "exosomes". Exosomes are nanometer-sized vesicles, which are secreted by many cell types in the human body. These vesicles transport genetic material from the cells of their source to the receiver cells. Our current primary research question is: "Can the exosomes repair the heart after myocardial infarction?" To address this question, we first have to decode the genetic message present in the exosomes released from ECFCs. We will carry out a series of animal experiments to understand the exosome cargo, an ideal dose and route of administration, and effects on the heart attack on both sexes. Our research goal is to identify a novel therapeutic intervention for patients with heart attack, which will not only limit the heart damage but will also improve the tissue repair.

column36: Linking lifestyle behaviors, microbiota & cardiometabolic health from childhood to early adulthood: The QUALITY Cohort.
column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the first cause of death in Canadian adults, accounting for 34% of deaths, and it is estimated that over 3 million Canadians have diabetes. These conditions often occur together and are both related to chronic inflammation. While infrequent in children and adolescents, we know that atherosclerosis - the formation of plaque in arterial blood vessels - begins in childhood. Similarly, prediabetes is increasingly common, particularly among obese youth who have an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes as young adults. In recent years, growing attention has been given to the microbes that are naturally present in the digestive track. Evidence suggests a link between the types and diversity of microbes in the mouth and intestine, chronic inflammation, as well as obesity, CVD and diabetes. However, very few studies have examined if lifestyle behaviors from childhood onwards have an impact on the types of microbes found in the digestive tract, nor if the microbes of the oral cavity are related to those in the intestine. Our study will help us better understand how lifestyle behaviors (including physical activity, diet, sedentary behaviors and sleep), microbes from the digestive track, obesity, CVD, and diabetes are linked. It will also address critical issues related to early prevention, from childhood to adolescence to early adulthood, of CVD and diabetes. Our investigation will be conducted within a well-established study, the Quebec Adipose and Lifestyle InvesTigation in Youth (QUALITY) Cohort, allowing us to study 630 participants over 4 waves of data collection, from childhood to early adulthood.

column36: Molecular control of apoptotic cell death in the C. elegans germline
column37: Reproductive tissue called the germline produces gametes that give rise to the next generation. The genomes of these gametes need to be protected to ensure fitness of progeny. Similarly, stem cells in tissues of adult organisms must be protected from internal and external stresses that threaten the stability of their genomes. For example, mutations in the DNA of these cells can inactivate genes necessary for survival, which can lead to tumours that ultimately kill the organism. Cells have acquired mechanisms that detect damage to their genomes, which determines whether to repair this damage or activate a suicide program called "apoptosis". While much has been learned about the nuts and bolts of apoptosis very little is known about how an organism controls these life or death decisions. Cells reside within neighbourhoods (tissues), and there is a great deal of communication between different tissues that determines if they live or die after encountering stresses that attack their genomes. We have taken advantage of the powerful genetic tools of a simple organism called Caenorhabditis elegans, a nematode worm, to discover new genes and signalling events that communicate survival and death signals across tissue boundaries. In this grant application I propose to determine how specific proteins communicate these survival and death signals from the somatic (body) tissues to the germline (reproductive stem cells). We will focus our investigation on a gene we found to be a central component of this cascade called kri-1, which is homologous to the human CCM1/Krit1 gene that is frequently mutated in the neurovascular disease cerebral cavernous malformations (CCM). Understanding these fundamental cross-tissue signalling mechanisms will help us develop new ways to treat diseases in which these signalling cascades have been disrupted, such as cancer and CCM.

column36: Developing and validating NAFLD advanced fibrosis diagnostic prediction model in primary care
column37: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), commonly called fatty liver, has become the leading cause of chronic liver disease in North America. It is estimated that up to 24% of Canadian population has NAFLD. NAFLD will become the main cause of end stage liver disease, liver cancer, liver transplantation, and death related to liver disease. Individuals with diabetes, lipid disorders, or who are overweight / obese are at high risk of having NAFLD. The severity of NAFLD depends on the stage of liver scarring, known as fibrosis. To confirm that a patient has advanced fibrosis a liver biopsy, a complicated and intrusive procedure, is needed. Recently, multiple techniques to avoid liver biopsy have been developed, including an ultrasound-based approach called shear wave elastography which can accurately rule out advanced liver fibrosis. In Calgary, our team has established the first program in North America to make it easy for family doctors to assess people with NAFLD by shearwave elastography to rule out advanced fibrosis. Patients with suspected advanced fibrosis, will be referred to a liver specialist for further testing to confirm their liver fibrosis stage. In our proposed project, we aim to develop a clinical decision support tool to help primary care physicians identifying NAFLD patients with advanced liver fibrosis. This tool will be developed from our large NAFLD cohort. We will present our clinical decision support tools as a webpage risk calculator, smart phone application, and paper-based risk tabulation. This project is novel and essential to meet the urgent and growing need to accurately identify NAFLD patients with advanced liver fibrosis to provide them with accessible and timely health care.

column37: Insulin is an amazing Canadian discovery and insulin has saved the lives of millions of diabetics. Insulin is a very important hormone that is required to regulate blood glucose levels. But is insulin a double-edged sword? On the one hand, lowering the incidence of diabetes, while on the other hand contributing to obesity, type 2 diabetes, cancer and Alzheimer's disease. Alzheimer's disease has been called type III diabetes or "diabetes of the brain". If we are to reduced or treat these diseases we need to understand the precise molecular mechanisms of insulin and insulin-like hormones in diseases. We use a tiny worm called C. elegans as a model organism to study how Insulin-like signaling affects the worm's development and provide molecular mechanisms for this observation. We identify important genes that regulate insulin signaling and potential drugs that could be used for treatment of insulin related diseases. Why worms? Many of the genes that control this tiny worm's nervous system are also found in humans and function in an identical manner. In fact, the human genes can replace the worm genes to restore function. Therefore, the knowledge gained from our research will certainly help us understand the molecular mechanisms during abnormal insulin signaling in humans. My lab will provide a valuable resource for students who want to pursue graduate work in molecular genetics. Currently, my research on C. elegans presents one of the few genetic models for understanding how the Insulin-like hormones function in a living animal.
