column36: Assessing the impact of Canadian food policies and nutritional composition of packaged foods on food price and purchases
column37: Food policies to help Canadians limit their intakes of "less healthy" nutrients, like the Sodium Reduction Strategy, will soon be joined by a set of policies, the Healthy Eating Strategy, that aim to improve overall diets of Canadians. It is possible, however, that introducing these policies may lead to higher food prices, which is especially important for consumers with lower incomes. The goal of this research is to determine how food price relates to food healthfulness, the introduction of food policies, and consumer purchases. Four studies will be conducted. Study 1 will examine the relationship between food price and healthfulness (i.e. the level of "less healthy" nutrients and overall "healthfulness"). This study will use food price and nutrient information from our database of food and beverage labels (FLIP) collected in 2017. Study 2 will compare the price of foods that have lower sodium levels and meet the Sodium Reduction Strategy targets with those that have higher sodium levels. Study 3 will evaluate the price of foods before, in-between, and after the Healthy Eating Strategy is in force. Study 2 and 3 will use FLIP collections from 2017, 2020, and 2023. Study 4 will determine how consumer food purchases differ over time for the foods found to be more expensive in Studies 3, especially by low income households. This will be done using a representative database of Canadian household food purchases. We think the relationship between food price and healthfulness will be different for each food category, but in general, healthier foods will be more expensive. Also, foods with nutrient levels that changed in response to food policies will be more expensive and purchased less often than foods that stayed the same. This research will help us better understand how food price and healthfulness are related. It will also provide information to help improve food policies to ensure that regardless of income, all Canadians can benefit.

column36: Magnetic Seizure Therapy for Schizophrenia (MAST) - Trial
column37: Schizophrenia is a severe psychiatric disorder that causes a substantial burden to patients, their families, and society as a whole. Unfortunately, an estimated 40% of patients attain only a partial response and 10% show no response with conventional antipsychotic treatment. Patients that fail to respond to conventional antipsychotic medication are said to have treatment resistant schizophrenia (TRS). Neuromodulation therapies involve the use of technologies that act directly on the nervous system to alter or modulate nerve activity by applying electrical or magnetic stimulation to the brain. Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is one of the oldest neuromodulation therapies and continues to serve as a useful management option in resistant mental illnesses. For TRS, ECT is safe and effective in combination with standard antipsychotic therapy. However, ECT is a very limited treatment option due to the feared complication of memory side effects amongst patients. Magnetic seizure therapy (MST) is a newer neuromodulation treatment that induces therapeutic seizures through the use of high frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation. MST may have a favorable clinical benefit in terms of the risks of cognitive side-effects and is also free of the heavy burden of stigma that accompanies ECT. Thus, MST could potentially offer a cognition-sparing and clinically useful alternative to ECT for treatment-resistant illnesses. The overall aim of this project is to compare the efficacy of MST to ECT with regards to psychotic symptoms and adverse cognitive side-effects in patients with TRS. If our results indicate that MST is as effective as ECT in reducing psychotic symptoms while sparing cognitive function; our proposed work will lead to MST as the new treatment for TRS. This is particularly important as no new treatments have been made available for TRS since the release of clozapine in the late 1960s.

column36: Novel Catheter Based Therapeutic Ultrasound Approach for the Treatment of Coronary Artery Occlusions
column37: Blockages of the coronary or femoral arteries begin as soft blood clots but over time they can harden becoming what are called chronic total occlusions (CTOs). In the heart, patients can often survive the formation of CTOs but have degraded lifestyles and reduced life expectancy due to poor cardiac performance. To fix this problem, clinicians often try to open the vessels up again using a catheter that is put in through an artery in the leg and worked up into the coronary artery until it reaches the blockage. A thin wire then goes into the CTO and is used to guide balloon catheter that re-opens the vessel. However, because of the stiffness of the CTOs this is often unsuccessful and this remains one of the most challenging problems facing cardiologists. To address this problem, we developed an approach that involves the injection of a drug (enzyme) that softens the CTO so that it is easier to slide a wire through it to re-open it. This new approach is now in clinical trials and evidence is showing that it improves the success rates for unblocking difficult CTOs. For this procedure, the drug injection occurs on one day and then the unblocking procedure is attempted the following day to allow enough time for the drug to work. In other parallel work we have investigated using a specialized form of ultrasound to help improve the drug effects. We have shown in bench-top experiments as well as in animal models of CTOs that when ultrasound is used to 'pop' small injected bubbles nearby the clot, it is damaged in a way that makes the drug work better and faster. Here we propose to build on this work to develop a new catheter based ultrasound device that can be used to enhance the performance of this emerging CTO drug therapy. It will use a new approach to generating ultrasound waves at the tip of a catheter, which will be used to vibrate bubbles and accelerate drug effects. This work will further improve CTO treatment success rates and have them done in a single day.

column36: Age-related patterns in the experience of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy
column37: Although cancer can occur at any age, most newly diagnosed people are aged 60 and older. As treatments are getting better, many people are living longer after their first cancer treatment. However, some people may be left with the lasting effects of cancer treatments. One effect is called chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN). With CIPN, people may experience pain, numbness, sensitivity, tingling, burning, or weakness in their hands, arms, feet, and legs. These symptoms may last long after the end of treatment and may cause balance problems, falls, and other serious injuries, and impact on quality of life. Older people may be especially at risk for CIPN and its negative impacts. Unfortunately, very little is known about CIPN, including the number of people who experience symptoms during and after treatment. In this research study, we will evaluate the experiences of CIPN in younger and older people undergoing certain common chemotherapy treatments for breast, ovarian, colorectal, and lung cancers, during treatment, and up to 1 year after treatment. This study will help us describe when CIPN occurs, how long it lasts, and the factors that influence CIPN and that may be changed. We will also study the impacts of CIPN on important daily activities. This research study will contribute to better symptom monitoring and care during and after cancer treatment and to the development of treatments for CIPN that are able to best help people depending on their unique needs.

column36: Neural control of locomotion : Supraspinal mechanisms
column37: Locomotion allows individuals to move within their environment and the loss of this important motor function has dire consequences on the quality of life. Research carried out in my lab focuses on the neural mechanisms responsible for initiating, maintaining, and terminating locomotion, using a basal vertebrate animal model, the lamprey. The brain structures controlling locomotion in the lamprey have a very similar organisation to that of mammals, but they are relatively simpler (much fewer cells) and more accessible for studying the cellular mechanisms underlying locomotion. One brain area known to play a crucial role in the control of locomotion is the Mesencephalic Locomotor Region (MLR). There has recently been a resurgence of interest in the MLR, because Deep Brain Stimulation of this region is now used as a clinical tool to improve walking in patients with gait disorders associated with neurodegenerative disorders. In addition, clinical trials have recently begun using MLR stimulation to improve locomotion in patients with partial spinal cord injury. Because the MLR is now a target for stimulation in humans, it becomes essential to understand how this brain region operates. Using an array of neuroscience techniques, we will define the neural mechanisms by which the MLR activates specific populations of cells that start, maintain, and stop locomotion. In addition, we will determine how the neural activity in the MLR is controlled by incoming inputs from higher brain structures. By providing a better knowledge of the cellular mechanisms involved in MLR function, our work will complement the research on genetically defined populations of neurons in mammals and the findings should collectively translate into better strategies for restoring locomotor function in patients.

column36: Interplay of AMPK and mTOR pathways at the lysosome: starvation, nutrient availability and metabolic disease.
column37: Humans, like all other animals, evolved to be able to survive periods of starvation, in part by creating stores in periods of plenty. However in these days of easy food availability, periods of starvation are near to non-existent and the trend is to store much more that is used. These constant over-feeding can lead to obesity and health problems, including diabetes, and metabolic syndrome and cancer. At the level of the cell, two major proteins are involved in the fine regulation between responses to nutrient availability and starvation. These proteins are called AMPK and mTOR and have opposite responses. When one is activated the other is inhibited and vice versa. There needs to be a fine delicate control of their activities for the proper responses to nutrients or their absences. This happens in part through the actions of other proteins called FLCN and FNIPs. In this proposal, we want to study how exactly FLCN and FNIPs regulate the switch from a state of nutrient excess to a state of starvation and vice versa by understanding their interactions with AMPK and mTOR. We propose to do this in both conditions of using cells grown in petri dishes and in a mouse model system for a metabolic disease. The major goal is to better understand what happens in normal condition to then be better able to understand detect the specific problems in cases of metabolic disease so that eventually new approaches to treatment can be found.

column36: Understanding the translational mechanisms of neuronal subtype specification in the mammalian cortex
column37: The cerebral cortex is the most complex structure within the mammalian brain and plays a key role in consciousness, perception, learning, and memory. These higher-order functions rely on hundreds of different types of nerve cells (neurons) that have distinct molecular and functional characteristics. Interestingly, distinct neuron subtypes are all made from a relatively homogeneous group of neural stem cells. However, what controls neural stem cells to specifically produce one type of neuron over another and how specific identity is ultimately determined is still largely a mystery. It is generally thought that the process is initiated by the activation of specific identity genes in the cell's nucleus, which involves making an RNA copy of the gene. Nevertheless, evidence from our recent studies has revised this simplified view by showing that a critical decision point is the "translation" of that RNA into the corresponding protein. We have recently identified a novel gene that regulates the decision of where and when translation occurs. In this proposed study, we will further explore the mechanisms that underlie the translational regulation of neuronal subtype specification. Our work will be relevant to neurological diseases, such as autism spectrum disorder, and will have other important implications for human health.

column36: Wildfire Smoke and Emergency Planning for First Nations People Living with Lung Disease in Remote and Rural British Columbia
column37: In the summers of 2017 and 2018, many First Nations communities in the north central BC were affected by wildfires. For many First Nations communities, the emergency response for all members, but especially those with chronic conditions, was reactive, not proactive, due to a reliance on external agencies for information about fire and air quality, and the lack of a coordinated response. The objective of this project is to develop and evaluate an emergency preparedness and response strategy for First Nations people living with chronic lung disease, their community, and the local health care services in the Carrier Sekani territory in north central BC. This project is a partnership between Carrier Sekani Family Services (CSFS) and UBC. Our project will address 3 aims: Aim 1: LEARN how wildfires impacted community members with chronic lung disease, community services, and CSFS as the primary health care provider by conducting an analysis of wildfire seasons. We will collect information data on the extent and impact of the fires, air quality data, and the experiences of the community members and agencies. Aim 2: PLAN for upcoming wildfire seasons by developing an emergency preparedness and response strategy. This strategy will include a "citizen's science" approach by using local deployment of air quality sensors, an evaluation of the emergency preparedness of First Nations people with chronic lung disease, and a plan for how CSFS and the community will respond to local wildfires and worsening air quality. Aim 3: ACT by deploying the strategy during the wildfire seasons and assessing the impact of the strategy on: 1) individual and community emergency preparedness; 2) communication about risks; and 3) satisfaction with the emergency response. Our project will be the first to create and evaluate a novel emergency preparedness and response strategy that is designed for people with chronic lung disease living in remote and rural First Nations communities.

column36: Inhibitory control of hippocampal inhibitory circuits: cell types, neuromodulation and function
column37: Every important event and every significant life episode is encoded in our brain through a concerted dialogue between several cortical structures, including the hippocampus. The hippocampal circuitry takes a central place in the brain cognitive map, making up the memory orchestra. It is composed of two major neuron types: excitatory principal cells and inhibitory neurons. The inhibitory neurons make local and long-range connections with principal cells but also with each other. Intriguingly, a distinct population of inhibitory cells exists in the hippocampus that innervates specifically other inhibitory neurons and, therefore, via selective control over entire hippocampal circuitry, may mediate executive cognitive functions important for learning. These disinhibitory cells are highly heterogeneous, comprising morphologically and molecularly distinct cell types. And it is still unknown how many cell types are positioned at different hippocampal crossroads and what can be their function. This project aims to shed light on the diversity of the disinhbibitory neurons, their modulation via subcortical projections and their cellular function. Given that imbalanced circuit inhibition is reported in numerous disorders, such as epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia and autism, this research may open up new therapeutic avenues towards prevention and treatment of several devastating pathologies.

column36: Occupational health, safety and labour rights among street and indoor sex workers in the context of evolving laws and policing: Ethnographic and qualitative participatory-action research
column37: Prohibitive sex work legislation and restrictive policing strategies have consistently been shown to endanger the health and safety of sex workers both in Canada and globally. Despite this, in December 2014 the former Canadian government implemented new legislation to regulate sex work, termed the Protection of Communities and Exploited Persons Act (PCEPA). The PCEPA criminalizes the purchase of sex and anyone who commercially profits from the proceeds of sex work (e.g., receptionists, security personnel, drivers etc.). Emerging research from Canada now suggests that end-demand approaches such as the PCEPA may recreate the harms of previous punitive approaches, while introducing new restrictions that put sex workers and sex industry actors such third parties (e.g. receptionists, security personnel etc.) in precarious legal positions. The proposed 5-year participatory-action research project aims to evaluate how evolving laws and policies regulating sex work (PCEPA, municipal licensing, policing appoarches, venue-based regulations) shape occupational health (e.g. experiences of physical and sexual violence, negotiation of safer sex practices) and safety (e.g. working conditions, access to workplace protections and labour rights) in the sex industry in Metro Vancouver. This new longitudinal research project will be well positioned to inform sex work law reform efforts, strategic litigation and the development, evaluation and implementation of sex work environment interventions at the municipal-level (e.g. enforcement policies, safe workplace standards for the sex industry, licensing regimes) and community-level (e.g. sex worker tools for safer workplace standards, potential for labour organization, collectivization of workers).

column36: Spit for Science 2 Autism Spectrum Project: Harnessing the Power of Population-Based Samples for Gene x Environment Studies
column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) can have devastating effects throughout life. Genetic factors play an important role in ASD but the specific genes are still unclear. Spit for Science 2 - Autism Spectrum Project continues the work of the original Spit for Science by using alternative approaches to identify risk genes for ASD. Most studies focus on clinical diagnoses, which are complex and vary considerably from person to person. We are studying behavioural (e.g., social communication) and cognitive traits (executive functions - how you control behaviour to reach your goals) strongly linked to the disorders and that cut across disorders. Patients are considered to be at the extreme of these traits but these traits vary widely in the population (excellent to poor social communication). We also can leverage leading Canadian expertise in using Postal Codes to map environmental factors like air pollution and psychosocial disadvantage so we can examine how genetic factors might interact with environmental factors to impact risk for ASD. To understand the genetics of mental illness in youth, we will recruit a large sample of children and adolescents (30,000) from the Ontario Science Centre. These children will provide DNA via spit, Postal Codes and trait information related ASD and other related disorders, and complete cognitive task (Stop-Signal Task) that measures different aspects of executive function. We will use a range of cutting-edge gene by environment and genetic methods to identify genetic risk variants for these traits, validate them in clinical samples and understand which genetic risk are unique and shared across traits and disorders. We hope to identify novel genes involved in childhood mental illness which could potentially lead to early detection, better treatments and improved treatment-outcomes for Canadian youth.

column36: Integrating community-based recruitment with data linkage to inform and enhance scale-up of hepatitis C treatment among people who inject drugs: A pan-Canadian 'virtual' cohort study
column37: Roughly 250,000 Canadians live with chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, a major cause of liver cirrhosis, cancer, and transplantation that places a significant burden on infected individuals and the health system. People who inject drugs (PWID) are the principal group at risk of this blood-borne infection. Recent advances in curative treatment present an opportunity to drastically reduce HCV transmission in the absence of a vaccine. However, even a universally effective treatment cannot cure people who remain undiagnosed and untreated, and the public health impact of new medications will rely on linking and retaining infected individuals in appropriate healthcare. For PWID, a range of conditions (discrimination, stigma, a lack of insurance or stable housing, and difficulty navigating the health system) can hinder access to necessary services, and many individuals are lost along the 'cascade of care' connecting HCV testing, treatment, and cure. This study seeks to improve our understanding of the accessibility of HCV care and treatment for diverse groups of people with a history of injecting drug use, including Indigenous people and women who inject drugs. In partnership with community-based organisations across Canada, we will recruit current or former PWID and provide on-the-spot hepatitis C testing, with counselling and clinical referral for those testing positive. Participants will complete a short questionnaire to collect information on their background, medical history, and perspectives on barriers to healthcare. We will then request permission to follow their healthcare utilisation and medical outcomes "virtually" through records routinely collected and stored in administrative databases during clinic, hospital, laboratory, and pharmacy visits for the next five years. Altogether, the study aims to identify modifiable barriers and facilitators to care and guide evidence-based public health interventions and policy in the new landscape of HCV therapy.

column36: Serotonin and alcohol: therapeutic possibilities and neurobiological mechanisms
column37: Alcohol use disorders have detrimental effects on health and society. The neurotransmitter serotonin has been linked to aspects of alcohol use, and is a therapeutic target for several disorders. The main goal of this work is to use animal models to understand the role of serotonin in modulating multiple aspects of alcohol use. We have three main aims. Firstly, using a pharmacological approach we will explore the potential for drugs interacting with serotonin to modulate different aspects of alcohol use, including reinforcement, relapse, dependence and impulsivity. Two drugs that interact with serotonin in different ways are pimavanserin and lorcaserin. They are used to treat Parkinson's disease and obesity, respectively. However, based on their pharmacological actions we predict that they may be useful for treating addiction. We will produce a comprehensive behavioural analysis of the effects of pimavanserin and lorcaserin on multiple aspects of alcohol use and addiction, including measures of alcohol reinforcement (self-administration), binge-drinking, reinstatement of alcohol seeking and alcohol-induced impulsivity. To look at possible sex differences and the impact of past alcohol use, these studies will be done in non-dependent as well as alcohol-dependent male and female animals. Secondly, we will examine underlying mechanisms mediating effects of pimavanserin and lorcaserin on alcohol use. This will be done by measuring changes in brain activity following exposure to alcohol with and without pimavanserin and lorcaserin. We will also assess how lorcaserin and pimavanserin alter alcohol-induced changes in dopamine release, since this neurotransmitter is the one most closely linked to reward-related behaviours. Finally we will determine where in the brain these drugs act to produce their effects. The significance of this work is that it may lead to the testing of clinically used drugs, pimavanserin and lorcaserin, for treating alcohol abuse and addiction.

column36: Prevention of preterm birth (PTB) and fetal inflammation (FI): the pharmacology and toxicology of targeting interleukin (IL)6 with HSJ633, a small peptide allosteric IL6 receptor antagonist
column37: Preterm birth (PTB) and fetal inflammation (FI) are the major perinatal causes of mortality in children <5 years and of life-long morbidity. These are caused by maternal inflammation or infection and can lead to the arrest of fetal organ development and death. A key mediator for these events is interleukin (IL)6. We have synthesized a very specific allosteric peptide antagonist to the IL6 receptor, HSJ633 (sequence: VRKFQNSPA), that is highly effective in preliminary experiments in blocking PTB and FI due to infectious stimulants. We hypothesize that HSJ633 is a safe and efficacious therapeutic for preventing PTB and FI. Our objective is to understand better the pharmacology and toxicology of HSJ633. We will use sophisticated methodology to discern how HSJ633 selectively blocks molecular and cellular mechanisms of the IL6 receptor and specifically the STAT3 intracellular signaling pathway. Next, we will test whether HSJ633 antagonizes IL6 actions in human fetal membranes to prove that it works in humans. Then, we will continue testing various doses HSJ633 in mouse models to determine its optimal dosage. To demonstrate it is pharmacologically superior, we will compare it to the established monoclonal antibody antagonist to IL6, Tocilizumab (TOC), which is FDA approved for rheumatoid arthritis. To demonstrate its safety, we will test the toxicology of HSJ633 in two generations of mice to show that fetal exposure does not impair offspring growth and reproduction. An exhaustive examination of fetal organs will be made. Last, we will test the efficacy of HSJ633 in a chronically inflamed pregnant mouse model using low dose LPS to ascertain whether it blocks FI. Together these tests will confirm that IL6 is a key target for blocking PTB and FI, that HSJ633 is effective and safe, and is a therapeutic that should undergo more rigorous testing for its clinical and commercial potential.

column36: Mechanisms of Leishmania dissemination and transit in the mammalian host following vector transmission
column37: Many infectious diseases are initiated following pathogen deposition into the skin by an insect vector but subsequently cause systemic disease. These diseases include Malaria, Lyme's Disease, Zika and West Nile virus disease and Leishmaniasis. These infections represent a current and growing global health problem, accounting for 17% of the human global infectious disease burden. Increasing or altered geographical distribution of insect vectors due to climate change and increased migration, travel and urbanization of human populations is exposing larger numbers of people to vector transmitted infections. In Canada, the spread of West Nile virus disease and Lyme's disease emphasizes the need for institutions to meet the challenge of vector-transmitted infections in a changing world. A major factor contributing to the manner in which these infections cause disease is their ability to move around the body after deposition into the skin by an insect bite. Understanding how vector transmitted infections disseminate out of the skin and subsequently move around the body is understudied, and how various treatment options influence this dissemination is almost completely unknown. This new knowledge is especially relevant to prophylactic vaccination against disseminating vector transmitted pathogens, where, despite old assumptions that the skin stage of infection is transient and somehow less important than subsequent systemic stages, the early expression of immunity at the dermal site of vector inoculation may be essential for vaccine efficacy. We aim to define and understand how pathogens leave the skin and move around the body in order to develop therapies or strategies to prevent this from happening, thereby reducing the burden of disease caused by vector transmitted disseminating infections.

column36: Advancing Clinically-Useful Diagnostic and Progression Markers of PD with Neuroimaging
column37: The overarching objective of this proposal is to develop a battery of neuroimaging-based biomarkers of PD. PD patients present with highly variable symptoms. By detailing and controlling for this variability, we aim to develop structural MRI biomarkers that target specific brain regions that are expected to be most affected by PD, and that change (e.g., accumulate iron) due to PD pathophysiology. Combining these approaches and using advanced statistical methods, such as machine learning, we expect to uncover sensitive and specific measures that a) distinguish PD from controls (i.e., diagnostic biomarkers) and b) track the progression of the disease (i.e., progression biomarkers). We have a substantial amount of very promising preliminary data indicating that these innovative imaging approaches, never-before applied in PD, will be successful. We expect that these measures will allow MRI to play a role in diagnosing and staging PD for clinical trials and, also, in clinical practice.

column36: Getting to the heart of hard-to-treat cancers: Anti-CD133 theranostics for molecular imaging and treatment of GBM
column37: A fundamental reason why many cancer treatments fail to provide long-term patient survival is the presence of specialized cancer cells that resist standard radiation and drug therapies. These resilient cells, often referred to as cancer stem cells or tumour initiating cells, can cause the regrowth of a tumour or result in the spread of cancer throughout the body after treatments have been completed. It is possible for antibodies to be created that target surface molecules that are unique to tumour initiating cells, and to use those antibodies to deliver radioactive compounds directly to those cells. One type of radioactive compound can mark the cells so they can be seen on imaging scanners, creating a non-invasive means of detecting highly resistant cancers. A different but complementary radioactive compound can also be used to kill the cancer stem cells with exquisite potency and selectivity. For the latter, a specific type of radiation will be used, which is highly effective at killing cancer cells but will only penetrate a distance of 1 or 2 cells, reducing damage to nearby normal tissue. There is no known resistance mechanism by cancer cells to this type of radiation, and this radiotherapy has the added benefit that it can enhance the ability of the patient's own immune system to attack tumour cells. Consequently, this antibody-targeted radiotherapy against tumour initiating cells represents a viable and new approach for treating highly-resistant tumours. Thus, a novel antibody-targeted radiotherapy will be developed and evaluated for its ability to treat glioblastoma: a form of brain cancer, where the prognosis is poor and there are no effective therapies. The proposed research involves a multidisciplinary team that will develop and validate the new therapy, and in doing so will advance both new diagnostic and treatment options for brain cancer, for early use in clinical trials.

column36: A novel approach to studying the function of the Batten disease protein CLN5
column37: Mutations in CLN5 cause neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL) commonly known as Batten disease. This devastating neurological disorder is linked to mutations in 13 genetically distinct genes. NCL affects all ages and ethnicities, is the most common form of childhood neurodegeneration, and is particularly prevalent in certain regions of Canada. Unfortunately, the precise functions of many of the NCL proteins are not known. Understanding a protein's function is central to being able to devise ways to target it therapeutically. Since mutations in NCL proteins result in nearly identical clinical phenotypes, they are thought to participate in the same biological pathway. Thus, studying the function of any one NCL protein is highly likely to enhance our knowledge of the neurodegenerative process, knowledge that can then be applied to all subtypes of the disease. The proposed research will study the localization and function of the CLN5 protein in the social amoeba Dictyostelium discoideum, which has emerged as an excellent model system for studying a variety of human neurological disorders, and is one of the only model organisms that contains the CLN5 gene. We will then perform a small molecule drug screen to identify compounds that suppress the effects of CLN5-deficiency in Dictyostelium and human cells to advance targeted therapy development for this currently untreatable disease. Finally, we will translate CLN5-deficiency phenotypes revealed in Dictyostelium to human cell models to enhance our understanding of NCL pathology. Recent genetic advances show a strong overlap of NCL with later onset forms of neurodegeneration, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and frontotemporal dementia. Thus, this work has the potential to provide fresh new insight into the mechanisms underlying other forms of neurodegeneration, which is of paramount importance considering the aging Canadian population.

column36: Early relapse detection in youth depression: development of secondary prevention methods by multiplex digital phenotyping
column37: Background and Importance: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) in youth (MDD-Y) is a common and recurrent mood disorder, affecting 7-18% of young people. MDD-Y has severe impacts on psychosocial development, family and school functioning, long-term health outcomes, and increases risk of death by suicide. While effective treatment is available, half of affected youth experience relapse or recurrence, hence there is a real need for early detection of mood deterioration to prevent repeating MDD-Y episodes. Goal(s) / Research Aims: The project's main aim is to develop and validate a computer prediction system for MDD-Y relapse and recurrence. Secondary aims include: computerized prediction of when relapse/recurrence will happen, and grouping patterns of illness and recovery over time. Methods / Approaches Expertise: Overall, the study will be four years and participants will be 12-21 years old and will need to have MDD. Mobile phone use is on the rise in youth and gives objective, nearly invisible research data collection. We will collect six kinds of measures: 1) wearable wrist actigraph device and mobile phone sensor data; 2) mobile phone-based assessments in daily life; 3) speech sound data; 4) facial behavior; 5) Electronic Medical Records (EMR) data and 6) routine clinical ratings. Wearable, mobile phone sensor and assessment, speech, face, rating scale and EMR text data will be integrated. Statistical computer programs will be used for analysis and our research group has experience with those methods. We will use the computer programs to develop new insights and support better understanding of the course of MDD over time. Expected Outcomes: Our results will set the stage for a more definitive clinical study - a "clinical trial". A non-invasive, accurate way to predict MDD-Y relapse and recurrence will be a major preventative advance. Moreover, our project will empower youth by actively involving them in the tracking and care of their mental health.

column36: ALK5-PAR6A signaling pathway regulates endothelial cells proliferation and vascular leakage
column37: Intraocular neovascular diseases are the leading causes of vision loss in the industrial world, affecting millions of people worldwide. They are observed in retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) and proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR), which are characterized by excessive endothelial cell (EC) proliferation promoting hemorrhages and retinal detachment compromising vision. There is enormous interest to develop novel therapeutic strategies to improve patients' lives with vasoproliferative retinopathies. The development and maturation of a functional vascular network are critical to ensuring appropriate oxygen and nutrient supply of every tissue and cell in the body. In the eye, newly formed blood vessels are composed of endothelial tubes that are highly unstable and require further maturation to prevent vascular leakage. Transforming growth factor b (TGFb) signaling is essential for vessel maturation and integrity. Our preliminary results show that neonatal inhibition of non-canonical TGFb signaling induces retinal vascular malformations and bleeding in mouse, mimicking some aspects of ROP. The current proposal aims to identify new TGFb signaling mechanisms controlling pathological vascularization. For the first time, we want to identify cell polarity protein PAR6A function in TGFb-mediated EC proliferation and vessel integrity. Therefore, we will characterize a new signaling pathway regulating pathological EC proliferation and vascular leakage. Understanding these mechanisms will provide novel avenues for the therapy of ocular and brain vascular diseases.

column36: Righting wrongs: Developing appropriate follow-up for mercury-related deficits and disorders in Asubpeeschoseewagong Netum Anishinabek (also known as Grassy Narrows First Nation)
column37: The Grassy Narrows First Nation has been exposed to very high concentrations of mercury from freshwater fish consumption, following the release of over 9 tons of mercury into their waters in the 1960's. Although some persons from Grassy Narrows receive compensation for "signs and symptoms similar to mercury poisoning", based on 1985 guidelines, very few have undergone complete neurologic examinations, with therapeutic follow-up. Minamata Disease, a progressive neurological disorder resulting from high mercury concentrations in marine fish is well documented. But, unlike marine fish, freshwater fish do not have high concentrations of nutrients (selenium and omega-3 fatty acids), which counteract some of the effects of mercury. We have created a unique, merged database with historic longitudinal mercury biomarker data (blood, hair and cord blood), collected in Grassy Narrows between 1970 and 1997. The objectives of this study are to describe chronic health sequelae in relation to prenatal and cumulative post-natal mercury exposure from fresh-water fish consumption, with a view to developing diagnostic tools to describe the continuum of mercury related deficits and disorders and recommend appropriate therapeutic follow-up, based on a knowledge translation and exchange approach. A total of 176 persons from Grassy Narrows will undergo a general medical examination, a neurological examination and neuropsychological and neurophysiological tests. Persons who require further follow-up, including psychological assessment, will be referred. Blood will be sampled and analyzed for specific nutrients and disease indicators. The results, coupled to integrated knowledge translation and exchange, will allow us to: (i) develop a comprehensive and appropriate protocols for diagnosis of mercury poisoning; (ii) identify early signs and symptoms of mercury poisoning; (iii) propose adequate rehabilitative follow-up and care; (iv) alleviate some of the harmful consequences.

column36: An intervention study of prenatal air pollution exposure and its impacts on cardiometabolic and respiratory health in children
column37: Globally over 380 million individuals under the age of 19 are overweight or obese, including 41 million children under age five. Among other effects, excess weight in childhood is linked with reduced lung function and chronic disease in adulthood. Most previous research on children has focused on diet and physical activity, but given the rising prevalence and potential for lifelong impacts it is important to identify other risk factors. Moreover, most interventions have targeted school-aged children, but the risk of overweight/obesity may be "programmed" early in life so there is a need for prevention at earlier stages of development. There is evidence that air pollution exposure during pregnancy may cause the fetus to undergo changes that affect health later in life. Air pollution is the most widespread environmental risk factor - nearly 90% of the world's population breathes air that is considered unhealthy - so developmental effects from prenatal exposure could have major public health implications for generations to come. column37: Despite dozens of clinical trials, and countless animal trials, to regenerate the retina with stem cell transplants, none have solved the challenge successfully. This is because the retina has many layers, and all layers are necessary in order to permanently restore vision in patients with advanced retinal degeneration - ~1 million patients in Canada and >50 million worldwide. This results in a staggering amount of suffering and considerable global economic burden of 1/3rd of a trillion dollars (USD) annually for age-related macular degeneration alone. The millions of patients that suffer from advanced, diabetes-related or inherited, retinal degeneration add to these costs. Current stem-cell suspension transplants can only replace a single retinal layer. Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplants can delay further degeneration, but they cannot replace dead photoreceptors. Photoreceptor transplants can restore vision, but only briefly since the diseased RPE cannot maintain the new photoreceptor graft. Current scaffold- or sheet-based transplants can be multi-layered. However, they provide limited retinal coverage, result in higher levels of surgical trauma than suspension injection, can form inappropriate graft structure, and can cause additional cell death - in many cases, scaffolds harm the layer they were designed to regenerate. Given this, there is considerable need for simple and safe replacement of multiple retinal layers. Here, we propose to develop a new technology that organizes subretinal graft (including RPE and photoreceptors) into correct orientation and layering with wide coverage. In the future, this therapeutic will be administered using standard surgical techniques and infrastructure and will offer tangible hope for those suffering from vision loss due to retinal degeneration.

column36: Role of extrasynaptic GABA in the recovery of motor function after spinal cord injury.
column37: This proposal explores a fundamentally new mechanism for regulating nerve conduction in the spinal cord, with far reaching implications to understanding normal sensorimotor control and opening new therapeutic opportunities for restoring locomotion after spinal cord injury (SCI). While the primary inhibitory transmitter in the spinal cord is GABA, we have discovered that GABA seems to have a paradoxical excitatory action on conduction in sensory axons, which likely generalizes to other types of axons. That is, our recent finding that extrasynaptic GABA receptors are adjacent to the sodium channels in sensory axons has led us to the idea that sodium spike transmission in sensory axons is facilitated by these GABA receptors, by virtue of their long-lasting depolarizing excitatory actions (termed PAD). To test this idea we will record from inside fine branches of sensory axons in the spinal cord of mice while activating the neuronal circuits that provide GABA to the axons, using genetically modified mice that allow light activation and visualization of specific GABA neurons, and also traditional nerve stimulation protocols known to evoke PAD. We will also make recordings from motoneurons in mice and single motor units in humans to further confirm that activating these GABA neurons (and PAD, indirectly with nerve stimulation in humans) increases sensory transmission to motoneurons, and also to demonstrate the relevance of the animal studies to humans. Finally, we will repeat these studies in mice and humans with SCI, and explore whether excess extrasynaptic GABA contributes to motor disorders. Our preliminary results suggest that drugs that selectively block extrasynaptic GABA receptors inhibit spasms and markedly improve walking after SCI. These drugs lack the negative sedative side effects of other drugs used in SCI, and are already being tested by other laboratories in human stroke patients, and thus now hold considerable promise for treating SCI.

column37: About 2% of the population is born with a biscupid aortic valve, which has only two cusps rather than the normal three. The aortas of these patients commonly balloon due to breakdown of the blood vessel wall. This can cause the aorta to split, which is usually fatal. Why patients with biscupid valves are particularly prone to aortic ballooning is unknown. It may be due to their underlying genetics or it may be due to disrupted blood flow patterns through their bicuspid valve, which cause the blood to drag on the wall of the aorta in ways it shouldn't. Most likely, both factors are at play, but it is important to dissect the contributions of each so that medical and surgical plans can take them into account. The advantage of our mice is that they all have the same genetics and therefore the differences in ballooning are due only to the "bad" blood flow that occurs with a bicuspid valve. Using this mouse and a new imaging method we developed, we will determine which proteins and molecular pathways are disrupted by abnormal blood flow to lead to ballooning. Based on our mouse model, we will also specifically test the role of CNP in protecting against aortic ballooning. First we will test in the lab whether patterns of blood flow that are associated with aortic ballooning reduce the amount of CNP in the aorta, leading to ballooning. Second, we will examine normal and ballooned aortas removed from patients at surgery to determine whether there is less CNP in ballooned aortas and in women, which is something we have seen in heart valves. Together, these studies may lead to new targets for the treatment and diagnosis of aortic ballooning in patients with bicuspid valves.

column37: With few exceptions, surgery remains the most effective treatment for patients with solid tumors. However, the trauma of undergoing surgery invariably leads to a weakened immune system which contributes to the likelihood of the tumour reappearing and spreading throughout the patient's body. Natural killer (NK) cells, as their name suggests, are proficient at surveying the body and destroying any cancer cells that appear before they can develop into solid tumours. Although the importance of NK cells in controlling tumour growth is well recognized, my research has shown that surgery dramatically impairs their ability to recognize and respond to tumour cells. Unfortunately, there is no current strategy for addressing the suppression in NK cell activity which occurs following surgery and new approaches targeting this critical stage may hold the potential for improving patient outcomes. We have recently shown that following surgery a large number highly immune suppressive cells are released from the bone marrow and that strategies that prevent their interaction with NK cells can have beneficial effects in animal models. Therefore, we believe that targeting these myeloid derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) in patients may provide an effective approach for reversing the immune suppressive effects of surgery. To accomplish this goal we have attempted to identify ways of targeting the MDSC population that arises following surgery. These efforts have revealed a distinct identifier present only on MDSCs which we propose can be used to deliver a drug to inhibit their suppressive activity ultimately restoring normal NK cell activity. The current proposal seeks to answer whether this strategy would be safe and effective prior to use in cancer surgery patients. Considering that over 65,000 Canadians undergo tumour removal surgery each year, we believe this research has the potential to benefit a significant number of Canadians and cancer patients throughout the world.

column37: Humans are living longer than ever before, but it is often with age-related illnesses. Almost 100 years of research indicates that aging and age-related disease can be delayed, for example, through caloric restriction. While a great deal has been learned about why and how we age at the cellular and whole-body level, much remains unknown. Over time aging impairs the cell's ability to respond to environmental stimuli, and it is this impairment that likely leads to cell death, and eventual organ malfunction. Because the aging process is similar in yeast and humans at the cellular level, we use the brewing yeast as a model to discover molecular networks that can be tweaked in order to increase a cell's response to its environment, resulting in enhanced cell health and longevity. We will use small peptides that we have identified that activate this complex to glean insight into molecular mechanisms that increase lifespan. We will also test if aging can be reversed in a novel yeast model of a human premature aging disease called Progeria. Progeria causes children to age normally, but at an 8-fold accelerated rate. We will also use the Progeria model to discover novel conserved pathways that reverse the effects of aging. Our team, composed of researchers with broad expertise in aging at the molecular, cellular and organismal levels, will identify ways to improve health during aging, such that the quality of life humans live will benefit.

column37: In patients undergoing cardiac surgery, both red blood cell (RBC) transfusion and anemia are associated with an increased risk for morbidity and mortality; and the point at which the risks associated with anemia and transfusion are balanced remains undefined. column37: All cells contain two main compartments, the inner nucleus, which contains all of our genetic material, and the cytoplasm where much of this material is converted into proteins. The work proposed here also aims to catalog all of the distributions of this new class of RNA during much of development and in most tissues. column36: Defining the consequences associated with early embryonic alcohol exposure and investigate the impact of a nutritional preventive intervention.
column37: In Canada, about 2-3% of children are born with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders (FASD) because of prenatal alcohol exposure (PAE). FASD are the most common cause of brain damage before birth and the leading cause of nonhereditary neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). About 40% of pregnancies are unplanned, consequently many women inadvertently subject their embryos to PAE during early pregnancy. With this project, we aim to investigate the adverse effect of a PAE during the first week of pregnancy on the future baby and get a better comprehension of the epigenetic mechanisms underlying those adverse consequences. Epigenetic modifications are chemical modifications associated to genes that provide the means by which genes can be turned on or off at specific times. These modifications provide a link between the environment and gene function. Early embryonic development is critical for the rest of the pregnancy. During that period, cells divide and grow under a specific program, dictated by major changes of epigenetic modifications. We hypothesis that irregularities occurring during the organisation of this program may increase the vulnerability of the central nervous system to NDDs development later in life. Since alcohol can alter the epigenetic landscape, which is heavily reworked in the early embryo, we believe that embryonic epigenetic disruption caused by alcohol could alter the normal developmental program of the central nervous system and lead to FASD. We aim also to determine the therapeutic potential of a preventive diet enrich in methyl donor groups to counteract the adverse effect of early PAE on the embryo development. Altogether, our finding will deepen understanding on the epigenetics mechanisms underlying the adverse consequences of an early PAE on embryo and nervous system development. Moreover, this project could lead to novel information and tools to promote earlier diagnosis, better treatment, and optimal outcomes for children affected of FASD.

column36: Engaging Families as Advisors in Child Health Organizations in Ontario, Canada
column37: There is growing momentum for involving patients and families in treatment decisions, health research, health service delivery, and health policy development across the world. While various policy frameworks have defined broad principles and approaches for engaging patients, they have been unable to address thorny ethical challenges arising from value conflicts and power asymmetries that are prevalent in engagement-led decision-making. Without a foundation for the ethics of patient engagement, engagement processes vary widely across health care organizations, making token involvement difficult to prevent. My research seeks to understand how ethical issues that are rooted in value differences affect the engagement of family members serving as advisors in child health organizations in Ontario, Canada. Using a mixed methods design consisting of (1) a theoretical review of patient engagement frameworks, (2) a multiple-case study of three family advisory councils using key informant interviews, (3) surveys to characterize family advisory council membership, and (4) content analysis of family member interactions on social media, this research will identify the values held by key stakeholders and policy frameworks regarding patient engagement, and assess the gaps and barriers to implementing these values into practice. The study results will contribute to the development of an ethics framework to guide the engagement of patients and families as advisors in diverse areas of health care policy and practice.

column36: Exploring End of Life Nutrition Care Practices for Residents of Ontario Long-Term Care Homes: A Mixed Methods Approach
column37: Eating and nutrition care for residents at the end of life can be challenging in long-term care (LTC). As residents approach death, they will often lose their interest in food and may stop eating altogether. Conditions such as dementia can pose further challenges. The uncertainty of the dying process can be a great source of stress for family and care staff. Current recommendations for nutrition care at the end of life emphasize comfort and meeting personal care goals. However, it is unclear whether these recommendations are applied consistently in LTC homes. Further, the role of several factors (e.g., resources, policies, family wishes) that likely influence nutrition care decisions at the end of life are not well understood. The goal of this research is to explore the current state of nutrition care for LTC residents at the end of life, and to understand the influential factors behind these care decisions. Mixed methods will be used to gather data from residents, families, and care staff to gain an understanding of end of life nutrition care. Data from resident medical charts will be collected in 12 LTC homes from Ontario. The type of nutrition care practices provided will be identified and compared to resident characteristics (e.g., weight loss, swallowing problems). Interviews will also be conducted with residents, families, and staff who will be recruited on a voluntary basis from the same homes. These interviews will explore various perspectives of nutrition care and the associated decision-making processes among LTC staff, family, and residents at the end of life. Working together with residents, families and LTC staff, this research will help to describe current practices around nutrition care for residents at the end of life. Findings will improve the understanding of the current approaches to end-of-life nutrition care in Ontario LTC homes and is a key step towards improving personalized comfort care for residents up to the moment of death.

column36: A population health economics approach to assessing tuberculosis interventions in Ontario
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) recently surpassed HIV as the world's leading infectious disease. In Canada, TB rates declined between 1940 and 1980; however, annual rates have remained steady since then, with an estimated 1,600 TB cases diagnosed per year. Canada has endorsed the World Health Organization's EndTB Strategy, aiming to eliminate TB worldwide by 2050. To meet the elimination targets, Canada's TB rates must decline by 10% annually. Moving forward, it is essential to address the social determinants that impact TB infection rates, given that TB affects primarily Aboriginal and foreign-born populations. The economic evaluation of interventions is important in priority setting. However, the majority of economic evaluations focus on single biomedical interventions. For TB, where social determinants of health are important intervention targets in conjunction with biomedical interventions such as screening programs and novel vaccines, well-established methods for economic evaluations face several challenges: equity considerations, complexity of interventions, and the measurement of costs and benefits across multiple sectors. My research will expand established methods for economic evaluation by considering health and non-health outcomes in an equity informed economic evaluation approach. My research aims to (1) elicit societal values for non-health outcomes that may result from interventions aimed at social determinants of health using a discrete choice experiment (DCE); (2) estimate healthcare costs attributable to TB; and (3) assess the equity-informed cost-effectiveness of TB interventions considering health and non-health outcomes. My research will culminate in the development of a data-driven decision-analytic model that relies on real-world data and current literature to inform policy priorities for TB. This research will contribute to the understanding of TB in Ontario, and methods development for conducting economic evaluations on population health interventions.

column36: Implementing effective community health worker programs to address health disparities among the urban poor in low- and middle-income countries
column37: By 2050, 80% of the world's urban population will live in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) with the urban poor experiencing stark health inequities. Innovative strategies are needed to meet the health needs of the growing urban poor. In light of health worker shortages and resource constraints in LMICs, this research seeks to understand how community health worker (CHW) programs - which have been predominantly implemented in rural contexts - can be effectively applied in urban settings. CHWs are lay persons who are briefly trained in specific health tasks, but do not hold formal professional medical certificates. Past experience demonstrates that 'proven' primary health care innovations designed for rural communities are not always well-suited to urban contexts. In urban contexts where community cohesion, safety, employment, and other factors differ significantly from rural settings, CHW program features require adaptation. This research will explore the opportunities and challenges that arise when adapting the CHW model to the urban context, with the intention of providing practical recommendations for the design and implementation of urban-specific programs. A scoping review of urban, LMIC-based, CHW programs will be conducted to synthesize the little evidence available. Interviews with LMIC-based program managers will document lessons on how CHW program design and implementation can respond to urban contexts and challenges. Finally, a case study in Colombia will investigate whether a newly piloted role for CHWs (conducting follow-up home visits for patients with chronic diseases) improves CHW job satisfaction and accountability - two important elements for effective and sustainable urban programming. This study is the first to synthesize evidence from urban CHW programs and generate cross-cutting implementation lessons. The findings will contribute to theory-building and serve as a resource for developing future research and guidelines.

column36: Studies of the structure, function and regulation of the ATR-ATRIP complex
column37: The complete and accurate replication of the genetic information in our DNA prior to each cycle of cell division is critical to our health and survival. Changes to the integrity of our genome can result from ongoing intracellular and environmental sources of DNA damage that, if left unrepaired, could disrupt key cellular processes. Importantly, such damage is often a barrier to the completion of DNA replication, a phenomenon known as replication stress. Human cells have mechanisms of preserving genomic integrity during replication that are controlled by a protein called ATR (short for 'ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related'). ATR sits atop a signaling network known as the DNA damage response that detects, signals and resolves DNA damage and replication stress. Upon recognition of aberrant DNA structures, ATR binds to DNA near affected sites where it gets "turned on" by interaction with other signaling molecules. ATR proceeds to coordinate a number of processes required for repairing the damage and restarting the replication process. This study will address two important aspects of ATR function at the molecular level: its ability to bind to damaged DNA, and how it becomes activated in response to damage. In recent years, ATR has been proposed as a potential anti-cancer drug target for a number of reasons. Cancer cells are prone to replication stress and thus highly reliant on ATR for their survival. The DNA repair capacity of ATR signaling mediates resistance to chemotherapy, a mainstay of cancer treatment whose efficacy is dependent on the ability to cause lethal amounts of DNA damage. Taken together, pharmacological inhibition of ATR can be effective on two fronts: by targeting an essential process on which cancer cells depend, and sensitizing the cells to existing chemotherapeutic agents. A better mechanistic understanding of ATR will allow for the rational design of new drugs and open up new cancer treatment options.

column36: Unlocking HIV-1 Env Towards a Cure
column37: The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infected more than 77 million people since the beginning of the epidemic. In the absence of treatment, HIV causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), which has already killed more than 35.4 million people worldwide. Available treatments control viral replication in infected individuals but are unable to eradicate the virus. This is because the virus "hides" in some immune cells and establishes a reservoir from which it can replicate again as soon as the treatment is interrupted. The goal of this proposal is to evaluate the potential of an innovative strategy to decrease the size of the viral reservoir and ultimately eliminate it. We found that the majority of HIV-infected individuals have all the elements required to kill infected cells but fail to do so due to the ability of the virus to cover one of its most vulnerable parts (Env). By using certain small molecules we were able to uncover parts of Env and showed that infected cells can be easily eliminated. In this proposal we will test if this strategy is able to eliminate HIV-infected cells isolated from patients (ex-vivo) and in an animal model (in-vivo). Altogether, this strategy will put us a step closer towards HIV eradication.

column37: Rates of sexually transmitted and bloodborne infections (STBBI) are on the rise in Canada. Hepatitis C virus and syphilis are curable, and HIV is treatable. Our innovative research will address major "knowledge to action" gaps in testing, reaching the undiagnosed, and linkages to care. Our team is focused on new STBBI testing being available, accessible and implemented, specifically for hard-to-reach priority populations. We will formalize linkage to care to improve biomedical and clinical prevention/public health impacts. Through this team grant, we can significantly reduce, and eventually eliminate, the burden and impact of STBBIs on Canadians.

column36: Combination HIV Prevention: Using anti-retroviral and anti-inflammatory medications to prevent new HIV infections
column37: The number of new HIV infections each year continues to remain unacceptably high. Just as cancer therapy attacks with multiple drugs, we will employ a combination of biomedical approaches that blocks HIV infections in different ways. Firstly, will be to use anti-HIV drugs that work by blocking the ability of the virus to replicate. Secondly, will be to block the inflammatory process that brings the cells that HIV primarily infects into the genital tract using anti-inflammatory drugs. Based on research pioneered by our team members, we have shown that inflammation greatly increases the risk of HIV transmission and can actually nullify the effects of anti-HIV drugs to prevent infections. A pilot study we performed shows that using the anti-inflammatory drug acetylsalicylic acid (ASA or aspirin) reduces by 35% the number of HIV target cells in the genital tract. We will conduct studies with immediate, mid-term and long-term goals. For the immediate impact studies, we will work with a cohort of female sex workers in Nairobi, Kenya who are highly exposed to HIV and are using anti-HIV drugs for prevention. We will place women with high levels of genital inflammation on the anti-inflammatory drug ASA to assess if the number of HIV target cells in the genital tract is reduced. Our mid-term studies will use a laboratory mouse with a human immune system to determine the mechanism of how ASA affects the migration of HIV target cells and we perform HIV infection studies to directly test is ASA can reduce HIV infection. Finally, because taking drug daily can be challenging for some people, we will assess in the humanized mouse model, the long-term goal of using an intravaginal ring that would deliver a contraceptive, an anti-HIV drug and an anti-inflammatory drug. This proposal will determine if our "Combination HIV Prevention" approach is more effective thereby providing women with more options for protecting themselves.

column36: Canadian HIV Cure Enterprise 2.0: Targeting the interplay between myeloid cells and CD4+ T-cells for HIV cure
column37: Despite the success of antiretroviral therapy (ART) in decreasing mortality for HIV-infected individuals, ART has not cured HIV/AIDS. The failure to eradicate HIV infection during ART stems from the virus' ability to persist in the body in multiple cell types and tissues. Without lifetime therapy, the virus quickly rebounds resulting in accelerated morbidity and mortality. The most commonly studied form of persistence is in memory CD4+ T-cells (CD4+ Tm-cells) that are harboring virus out of view of drugs or from the immune system. However, evidence indicates that other long-lived cells, known as myeloid cells, might contribute to HIV persistence. Cells that allow virus persistence are called viral reservoirs (VRs) and represent the main barrier to an HIV cure. While much is known about HIV persistence, many puzzles remain about the source of persistent HIV, the mechanisms underlying the establishment and persistence of VRs, particularly in CD4+ Tm-cells, and the ways to eliminate VRs. column37: The war against HIV/AIDS is not yet over. Although anti-viral drug cocktails have changed HIV/AIDS to a chronic manageable disease, people living with HIV infection still have an increased risk of drug side effects, heart, kidney, and brain diseases, as well as cancer. In addition, living with HIV infection is associated with stigma. Thus, a cure for HIV infection is needed. A main obstacle to cure is the presence of a persistent reservoir of HIV infected cells in the body, where our current drugs cannot reach. Our project proposes harnessing the immune system, in particular, a cell called a 'killer T cell' to eradicate the remaining reservoir in order to cure the infection. In order to do this, we will first extensively characterize the genetic signatures of the remaining virus hiding in the reservoir from blood samples from persons living with HIV. We will then design a number of strategies, where we can mobilize a person's killer cells to be able to eliminate their remaining viruses. We will use a 'personalized' approach by studying each person's own viruses and their own immune systems. We will also borrow from a recent revolution in the cancer field, to improve the killer cells to kill HIV infected cells better and more efficiently, by using new genetic engineering techniques. All of our work will be done in the test tube or in pre-clinical models as a preparation to design clinical trials to cure HIV infection.follow

column36: Evaluating, refining and bringing to scale the endogenous health-promoting attributes of alternative food networks to address diabetes mellitus and hypertension among Ecuadorian farmers
column37: In Ecuador, rural people, and particularly rural Indigenous people are disproportionately affected by both nutrient inadequacies as well as overweight and obesity. This double burden of malnutrition magnifies their risk of developing diet-related chronic diseases such as diabetes mellitus (DM) and hypertension (Hyp). In parallel, many rural Indigenous people in Ecuador have organized around alternative food networks (AFNs) such as farmers' markets to seek more sustainable livelihoods. These local AFNs support food environments and practices that hold strong potential to prevent DM and Hyp among participating farmers. For example, AFNs have been demonstrated to promote food literacy, favor consumption of fruits, vegetables and whole grains, and to place income in women's hands; these, in turn have all been associated with healthier nutritional status and reduced risk of diet-related chronic disease. Our research aims to evaluate specific AFN attributes for their measurable contribution to DM and Hyp prevention in order to leverage the most effective attributes for a stronger and broader positive impact. To do so, we will use validated instruments for assessing diet and physiological risk factors among AFN farming households and a comparison group of non-AFN neighbouring farmers, and we will use participatory qualitative research to determine the most effective implementation strategy for translating research findings into practice. Our implementing partners run an ongoing intervention for managing communication and knowledge-sharing among an estimated 132 Ecuadorian AFNs, positioning them as the cornerstone for streamlining research findings into practice. Through the implementation of our research findings, we expect to provide strategic and practical guidance for integrating health-sensitive attributes into the regular practices of AFNs as they continue to replicate and evolve in Ecuador and elsewhere.

column37: Youth with physical disabilities experience greater limitations to participation in community-based activities than do their average-developing peers, which can result in poor health outcomes. Emerging treatment approaches aimed at improving activity and participation have shifted from focusing only on impaired body functions towards the performance of functionally meaningful activities within the youth's natural environment. Our team has partnered with key community-based stakeholders including youth, clinicians and policy-makers, and together we plan to examine whether engaging in an 8-week self-chosen community-based activity (e.g., sledge hockey, boccia) can lead to a significant improvement in three key body functions: motor, cognitive and affective. Thirty youth with physical disabilities will take part in the study and engage in an activity program of their choice. Changes in their body functions (e.g., movement, attention, mood) will be measured multiple times before, during and after engagement in the chosen activity/program. Findings of this study can guide clinicians, families and policy-makers to select effective approaches that not only promote participation but also facilitate additional motor and mental benefits from one single intervention. Such treatment approaches may also reduce the burden on the healthcare system as well as on the youth and families. Moreover, findings can advance our understanding of methods for testing complex and unique 'real-life' individual-based interventions that are highly relevant to practice.

column37: In this proposal, we outline the composition, purpose, and future growth of the Canadian Institutes for Health Research (CIHR) Drug Safety and Effectiveness Network (DSEN) Methods and Applications Group for Indirect Comparisons (MAGIC) Team. MAGIC aims to use our research findings to influence capacity-building and health research methods across Canada, and globally. Our capacity-building and networking strategies will allow our trainees and new investigators to develop skills in this rapidly evolving field and will contribute to the creation of highly qualified personnel in Canada who will continue to work in academic, industry or policy fields on post-market drug safety and effectiveness.

column36: Learning from and enhancing Community Capacity for Climate Change and Food Security (C4FS) action in the NWT
column37: The food systems of Indigenous peoples in the Northwest Territories (NWT) are based on the harvesting of country foods, and form the foundation of spiritual, cultural, physical, and mental well-being for individuals and communities. There is a dual food system in communities in the NWT, with country foods complemented by market foods. The lack of fresh and affordable market foods compounded by changes in country food access and availability fuels alarming rates of food insecurity throughout the NWT. There are documented impacts of climate change for Indigenous peoples' food systems, including: access to, and availability of traditional food species and, changes in harvesting practices (including harvester safety concerns). Understanding climate change impacts and identifying local adaptations in the food systems of Indigenous communities in the NWT is critical for the health and sustainability of communities, the environment and land. The proposed research aims to learn from and enhance community capacity to address place-based priorities to inform climate change and food security action locally, regionally, and territorially. The approach includes cross-cutting themes of Traditional Knowledge, Governance, Youth, and Sex and Gender, and is grounded in Participatory Action Research (PAR). Our multidisciplinary team will work closely with community partners in six case study communities in four regions in the NWT to understand the potential of local actions, and to scale-out and scale-up learning. This research will promote community action and self-determination of local food systems in communities in the NWT and ultimately improve health outcomes. The knowledge gathered, and shared across multiples levels (locally, regionally, territorially, government decision-makers/ knowledge users) will facilitate development of more effective programs and policies to address food security and climate change in the NWT.

column37: The most dramatic and fastest climate change is occurring in Inuit Nunangat, which has led to decreased ice thickness and extent, later ice freeze-up and early ice break-up, and changing snow conditions. These changing environmental conditions impact local wildlife and vegetation that are important for Inuit diet. These changing conditions also impact the ability of Inuit to access, prepare, and consume country foods (local foods). Climate change impacts on country foods have important implications for Inuit health and wellbeing. The Niqivut Silalu Asijjipalliajuq ("Our Food and Climate Change") research program addresses a significant gap in research. The research program will promote adaptive capacity among Inuit by enhancing local capacity to detect and respond to food-related climate-health outcomes; and evaluate opportunities for food-related climate change adaptation polices, programs, and actions. The program has 2 research themes: -Research Theme 1: Strengthen Inuit food sovereignty for climate change adaptation. -Research Theme 2: Share Inuit knowledge to support climate change adaptation. -Cross-cutting Research Themes: The importance of Inuit knowledge (IK) in research; Inuit health, nutrition, and wellness; climate change adaptation; and gender. Four intensive research projects span these themes: Project 1: Stories about Country Food Preparation; Project 2: Stories to Inform Reintroduction of Food Sources; Project 3: Stories of Food for Health and Healing; and Project 4: Sharing Stories and Inuit Self-Determination in Research. This is a Nunavut-led research program. Our Nunavummiut-led approach will offer best practice guidance for other initiatives; will create leaders with expertise in climate change, country food, and Inuit health; and demonstrate the importance of Inuit knowledge and Inuit Qaujimajatuqangit for adaptation, enabling communities to manage the food-related health effects of climate change.

column36: Canadian Epigenetics, Environment and Health Research Consortium Network Phase II
column37: The DNA that makes up the genome (the collection of all the DNA in your cell) is tagged with various chemical marks that are attached either directly to the DNA or to its packaging proteins. These marks, collectively called the epigenome, act as a kind of molecular mark-up language that tells the cell's proteins which genes to turn 'on' and which to turn 'off'. Unlike the genome, which remains largely the same throughout life, the epigenome changes with age, in response to environmental influences, and in many types of disease. As the bridge between environmental exposures and peoples' genomes, the epigenome harbours enormous promise to understand normal development and disorders arising throughout a person's lifespan. Our accelerated ability to 'read' these epigenetic marks is revealing their disruption in most diseases; however, the rapid rate of the emergence of new scientific methodologies coupled with the increasing desire of researchers to incorporate epigenetics into new studies highlights the urgent need for a nationally coordinated approach. The CEEHRC Network Phase II aims to continue to address this gap by developing and strengthening collaborations between basic and applied scientists, clinicians, bioinformaticians, statisticians, and experts in drug development. We seek to address the bench-to-bedside gulf in epigenetics research in Canada, to harness improved understanding of epigenetic mechanisms and the potential improve patient outcomes by altering epigenetic states associated with disease.
