column36: Targeting Translational Control in Retinal Ganglion Cell Degeneration
column37: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, afflicting over 70 million people, and nearly one in ten elderly Canadians. Although glaucoma is often associated with increased eye pressure, it is a neurodegenerative disease characterized by the death of retinal ganglion cell neurons to compromise vision. Yet we still do not understand the molecular mechanisms that drive this damage, and there are no neuroprotective treatments. In studying the degenerative process we have identified a gene family, the MNKs, that function to influence protein production in retinal ganglion cells. However, this process has not been previously linked to ganglion cell death or glaucoma. Based on our preliminary evidence we propose that the actions of MNKs have an important role in glaucomatous neurodegeneration. Our research program will generate new insights into how changes in this mechanism contributes to retinal damage, and provide proof of principle for targeting this process as a new therapeutic strategy.

column36: Circadian regulation of host-pathogen interactions in vector-borne parasitic infections
column37: Vector-borne diseases (e.g. parasites or other pathogens transmitted to humans by insects) are major public health concerns for billions of people in tropical and subtropical regions. Of utmost importance, with global warming, the spreading of these vector-borne infections is predicted to reach temperate latitudes within the next decades. Recent research has shown that immune responses, including against pathogens, vary across the day-night cycle and are controlled by biological clocks located in most tissues, including immune cells. Very little research has been performed on the influence of circadian clocks on parasitic infections or any other vector-transmitted diseases. We propose that vector-borne parasitic infections represent ideal models to study circadian regulation of host-pathogen interactions. As a model for the study of circadian rhythms in parasitic infections, we study leishmaniasis, a debilitating and often mortal human disease affecting millions of individuals in tropical and subtropical areas. It is caused by infection by the parasite Leishmania sps., which is transferred by sandflies that are active at dusk and dawn. We previously found that the magnitude of Leishmania infection vary according to the time of day at which the host meets the parasite. We will now aim to determine the mechanisms involved in this circadian rhythm and the involvement of immune cell clocks in controlling the infection, and on the other hand, the effect of the parasitic infection on the circadian rhythms of the host. A better understanding of the timed regulation of host-parasite interactions will allow developing better prophylactic and therapeutic strategies to fight off these vector-borne diseases.

column36: Polynucleotide kinase/phosphatase: its role in DNA strand break repair and a potential therapeutic target to enhance radio- and chemotherapy
column37: A problem frequently encountered in cancer therapy is that of tumour cell resistance to therapeutic agents, so that although the majority of cells in a tumour will be destroyed, a small fraction will survive, and have the potential to metastasize. At present our ability to predict tumour response to treatment or diminish the resistance to radiation or drugs is very limited. Such methods are only likely to be developed when we have a clearer understanding, at the molecular level, of how cells respond to these agents. For many of these agents, DNA is considered to be the main target leading to cell death. It is known that cells have the capacity to repair much of this damage. Uncovering all the enzymes responsible for repair and learning how they operate is still a major task. This proposal focuses on a particular type of damage, DNA strand breaks, and on the role of a particular enzyme, polynucleotide kinase/phosphatase (PNKP), in carrying out the repair of these lesions. We intend to learn how PNKP interacts with other proteins required to mend strand breaks and if it plays an important role in making cells resistant to a variety of anti-cancer drugs. Almost all cancer cells lack specific proteins called tumour suppressor proteins. We have recently found that cells that have lost specific tumour suppressors either die or become very weak if PNKP is also lost. This is a process called synthetic lethality and it presents an opportunity to target cancer cells rather than normal cells. In order to make full use of this opportunity we will investigate the mechanism(s) responsible for synthetic lethality involving loss of PNKP.

column36: Physiological and pathophysiological roles of renal intercalated cells
column37: Kidneys in our bodies regulate how much and which waste products are eliminated in the urine. Key cells in this process are called intercalated cells, which regulate blood acid-base balance and urinary acidification. Defects in these cells caused by mutations of the kidney anion exchanger 1 (kAE1) result in distal renal tubular acidosis (dRTA), a disease where patients experience an acidic blood, kidney stones, increased risk of kidney failure, and urinary loss of salts. Studying the mechanisms of this disease is therefore important as it may identify new therapeutic targets relevant to the millions of Canadians who suffer from chronic kidney disease. Our preliminary results show that kAE1 interacts with another protein called claudin-4, and that altering one or the other results in the disease symptoms. In this funding period, we will dissect the relationship between these 2 proteins, verify our findings in vivo and alter their functional and physical interaction using drugs or genetic engineering as a lead towards development of therapeutic approaches to not only treat dRTA patients but also patients with chronic kidney disease.

column37: Breast cancer (BC) is the second leading cause of cancer deaths among women mostly due to metastases and advanced recurrence, which are normally resistant to conventional chemotherapy. Among various subtypes, triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) is a particularly aggressive subtype that accounts for ~15% of all types of BC. It occurs in younger women and has a poor prognosis. TNBC patients relapse, develop distant metastases sooner and have significantly shorter overall survival than non-TNBC patients, owing to the lack of effective drug treatment. Dr. Wu has discovered a new treatment strategy that utilizes synergistic effect a biomaterial and an anticancer drug wrapped in tiny particles, namely nanoparticles. The nanoparticles will seek cancer cells, enter the cancer cells, and release the drugs inside and surround the cancer cells. In this project, Dr. Wu and team will further advance the design and test this new nanomedicine for the treatment of metastatic breast cancer, which is expected to reduce tumor growth and spread to other organs such as the lungs and the brain. This work is expected to generate a safe, effective and affordable therapeutic approach to address the unmet medical need for treatment of TNBC.

column36: Elucidating the role of the IL-1 system in the pathogenesis of CNS autoimmunity
column37: This project is at the crossroads of neuroscience and immunology. It aims at understanding the role of the cytokine interleukin (IL)-1B, a molecule that allows immune cells to communicate with each other, in multiple sclerosis (MS). Because of the availability of transgenic mouse lines lacking key molecules of this signalling system or having fluorescently labeled neurons, glia and immune cells, we have decided to focus our work on an animal model of MS called experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE). Up to now, these transgenic animals have allowed us to demonstrate that IL-1B has early detrimental effects, causing loss of neurons and their projections (termed axons), myelin sheaths and neurological function. Our results show that the negative effects of IL-1B are mediated by a subclass of innate immune cells called neutrophils and macrophages, and involve stimulation of the IL-1 receptor (IL-1R1) present at the surface of certain veins draining the central nervous system (CNS). More specifically, we showed that IL-1B production by innate immune cells is a critical step for their mobilization inside the CNS. Furthermore, we found that the subsequent activation of IL-1R1 signaling in CNS blood vessels induces a communication loop that drives neuroinflammation and the recruitment of autoaggressive (termed effector) lymphocytes into the CNS, eventually leading to immune attacks and demyelination. In this grant proposal, we aim at identifying the exact molecules involved in the production of IL-1 by both subclasses of innate immune cells involved. Since IL-1 can influence many types of immune and CNS cells (e.g. blood vessels, neurons, T lymphocytes, etc.), we also want to better understand their interplay in the attack phase. Finally, we want to determine whether we can use anti-IL-1 therapies (many are currently approved for arthritis) or downstream molecules to prevent EAE development and/or progression and to offer an additional therapy for MS patients.

column36: Mechanisms by which hyperinsulinemia promotes pancreatic cancer
column37: High levels of the hormone insulin are a cardinal feature of obesity and early type 2 diabetes, and are induced by unhealthy 'Western diets' high in sugar and fat. It has been suggested that excess insulin contributes to cancer initiation and/or progression, but this has never been tested directly in a way that can address cause and effect. Over the past 5 years, we tested for the first time the hypothesis high levels of insulin play a causal role in pancreatic cancer initiation using new mouse models. Remarkably, our data show a clear reduction in the early stages of pancreatic cancer in the mice that with only a relatively modest reduction in insulin. We now want to know how excess insulin has this cancer promoting effect. Specifically, we want to know whether the effects of insulin are direct on the cancer cells, or indirect by altering something else in the body or the cells that are nearby to the tumours. These studies have the potential to further clarify the known links between insulin and many forms of cancer, as well as uncover the exact mechanisms by which excess insulin influences cancer risk. Our findings will have major implications for both cancer prevention via nutrition/lifestyle modification and for cancer treatment by inhibition of insulin signalling in tumours.

column36: Determining the role of the nuclear basket protein Mlp1/TPR in mRNA homeostasis
column37: Regulating the expression of its genes is an essential task for any living organism. In eukaryotic cells, a membrane impermeable to large molecules separates the site where the genetic information is stored (the nucleus) from the site where the information is translated into protein (cytoplasm), the functional molecules executing all cellular processes. After the genetic information stored in the DNA is copied into a messenger molecule, called RNA, RNA has to exit the nucleus and reach the cytoplasm to get translated. The only path to reach the site of protein synthesis is through the nuclear pore complex (NPC), large macromolecular complexes embedded in the nuclear membrane. In this project, we will use different molecular biology, genetic, proteomic and microscopy based approaches to study the mechanism by which the nuclear basket, a substructure of the NPC, regulates the transport of some RNAs, but not all RNAs from the nucleus to the cytoplasm. Understanding this process is important to gain a better understanding of many diseases, as mutations in the proteins involved in this process have been found mutated in patients suffering from various diseases such as cancer or Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS).

column36: The implication of the adaptive arm of the integrated stress response in KRAS lung cancer.
column37: Mutations in KRAS gene are found in deadly forms of cancer like colorectal, lung and pancreatic cancers. In lung cancer, 30% of adenocarcinomas possess mutations in KRAS gene, which render this type of cancer refractory to anti-tumor therapies. Mutant KRAS gene produces a protein that has the capacity to reprogram the functions of normal cells and establish stressful conditions that disrupt normal proliferation. Under these conditions, cells employ mechanisms that help them survive and adapt to stress. However, these adaptive mechanisms act in favor of mutant KRAS to maintain the abnormal proliferation and cause cancer. We have identified that adaptation of cells to the function of mutant KRAS requires a protein known as eIF2. In stressed cells, eIF2 is modified by a process named phosphorylation, which reorganizes key cellular functions to promote the expression of genes and synthesis of proteins that further enhance the oncogenic function of mutant KRAS. In this proposal, we investigate the mechanisms utilized by eIF2 to promote the formation of lung cancer through the action of mutant KRAS. We employ mice, which have been genetically engineered for the disruption of eIF2 function, to examine the effects of eIF2 inhibition on the formation of lung tumors containing mutant KRAS. Also, we will examine the function of proteins that assist eIF2 in the development of lung cancer through the action of mutant KRAS. Moreover, we will test the effects of newly developed eIF2 inhibitory drugs to assess their anti-tumor effects on lung cancer in mice. Our work reveals new mechanisms of lung cancer formation by mutant KRAS, which will help the design of better approaches to treat one of the deadliest forms of cancer like lung cancer.

column36: AI for public health (AI4PH): A focus on equity and prevention
column37: The vision of the Artificial Intelligence for Public Health (AI4PH) Summer Institute is to enable participants to apply AI innovations in public health research with a health equity focus. Our goal is to develop, deliver, and disseminate a comprehensive set of resources for teaching how artificial intelligence (AI), including the subfield of machine learning (ML), can be applied to address important public health problems while explicitly prioritizing health equity. Trainees and early-career researchers in public health and computer science disciplines will benefit from these resources delivered online and in-person, initially in Canada and subsequently around the world. This training will produce a highly qualified and equity-informed global network of peers and mentors from multiple disciplines relevant to public health and AI. Participants in the AI4PH Summer Institute will understand the most important problems facing public health agencies and organizations and have the expertise and collaborative network to apply AI methods in concert with established techniques to invent novel and equitable solutions for the prevention and control of critical public health problems with a high level of ethical rigour. Upon successful completion of the institute, we expect AI4PH Summer Institute participants will have the knowledge and skills to: 1) Understand the conceptual underpinnings of AI and related sub-disciplines so that they can articulate why and when these methods should be used; 2) Apply AI methods and interpret results in the context of real-life public health issues; 3) Advance Equity by i) Understanding the concept of 'equity', and ii) applying this understanding of equity throughout the AI research process (problem definition, research design and methods, knowledge translation); and 4) Understand the contributions of different disciplines (e.g., social science, ethics, computational science, public health policy) and methods in public health AI research.

column37: Enlargement of the heart is one of the most common causes of heart failure in Canada. Once cardiac failure develops, the condition is irreversible and is associated with a very high death rate. Fifty percent of patients whose heart failure has progressed to include shortness of breath without physical activity do not survive beyond one year. As the heart becomes enlarged, it also disrupts the production of small lipid molecules that control the heart function, causing further damage and increasing the risk of sudden cardiac death. The heart enlargement reduces the production of the cardioprotective lipid molecules called epoxyeicosatrienoic acids and increases the production of cardiotoxic molecules called hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid. While most patients can be treated with drug therapy, these treatments have side effects and are not effective in all patients. The objectives of our work are to control and prevent enlargement of the heart to improve treatment options for patients and reduce mortality. By increasing the production of the cardioprotective lipid molecules (epoxyeicosatrienoic acids) and inhibiting the production of cardiotoxic molecules (hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid) in the heart, we can prevent the progressive deterioration of heart function and the development of heart failure. Our research will identify the molecules that are responsible for the enlargement of the heart and heart failure. In addition, we will test new chemicals that are known to increase the production of the cardioprotective lipid molecules and inhibit the production of cardiotoxic molecules in the heart. This will prevent the progressive deterioration of heart function and the development of heart failure. This research will help to diminish health care costs, as well as to design strategies that improve treatment of heart failure.

column36: Control of metabolic inflammaging by traffic of B lymphocytes in adipose tissues
column37: Aging is associated with an increase in body fat mass as well as a reduced thermogenic capacity, which both alter normal glucose and lipid metabolism. Previous discoveries in our lab have highlighted the possible role of a set of immune cells - B lymphocytes - that impair the normal response to insulin during life. We think that the changes in the activity of B cells are mediated in part by a gene named OcaB, which then provokes a negative action on fat tissues. However, how and when B cells impact fat tissues in old individuals is not known. This knowledge could prove to be ultimately clinically important since B cells produce antibodies that can specifically be blocked. In this grant, we wish to characterize the traffic and impact of B cells in adipose tissue of young versus old mice, how B cells sense their environment to modify their activity and produce more harmful antibodies in aging animals, and how this process ultimately has consequences for metabolism and inflammation. We will use an innovative methodology that allow to visualize tissue activity and senescence along the lifespan, which not only decreases the number of animals needed (and costs), but is very powerful because the effect of time (aging) can be observed within the same subject, allowing repeated measures factorial analyses. We will also try to demonstrate that pharmacological depletion of B cells improves healthspan in aged mice, which could be viewed as a first proof-of-principle for a potential development toward translational research.

A significant barrier to long term survival in these women stems from the fact that breast cancers are highly heterogeneous. Moreover, breast cancer cells are under constant environmental stress as a result of limiting nutrient and/or oxygen availability, leading to the development of adaptive responses that allows them to withstand these environmental insults. Unfortunately, many times these adaptations lead to permanent changes in breast cancer cells, even when the stress response is removed. Moreover, genetic differences in individual cancer cells allow for the emergence of a complex mixture of individual cells with varying ability to induce and/or cope with stress responses. In this grant, we will explore how these intra-tumoral genetic differences influence breast tumor evolution in response to microenvironmental stress stimuli, leading to the emergence of increasing aggressive breast cancers. Our research also uncovers possible novel and specific targeted therapies depending on the distinct paths of evolution chosen by individual breast cancers.

column37: Patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension have a dysfunction of the cells constituting the wall of their arteries in the lungs. Like cancer cells, PAH cells are characterized by exaggerated capacity to multiplicate and resistance to death resulting in a progressive narrowing or obstruction of the vessels. Indeed, if the blood vessels tighten up, making the sapce for the passage of blood narrower, it takes greater pressure to get the same amount of blood through to its destination. The heart has to work harder to pump blood through those arteries. The heart progressively fails causing shortness of breath and poor exercise capacity, which rapidly culminate in death. In spite of recent progress in our understanding of the mechanisms involved in this disease, no substantial modification of the rapid progression and fatal course of this disease has been achieved, leaving lung transplantation as the only treatment in end-stage PAH. Therefore, the identification of new therapeutic targets is a pressing need. Although exposed to stressful conditions that jeopardize their survival, PAH cells continue to multiplicate indicating that these cells have developed adaptive protective response allowing them to survive. Nevertheless, the factors implicated in this pathological protective response remains largely unknown. In the present proposal, we hypothesize that a factor called MTH1 known to confer resistance to harmful stress conditions is overexpressed in PAH cells leading to the development of PAH. To test the validity of our hypothesis, we will 1) determine whether MTH1 is increased in PAH cells and contributes to PAH cells' anormalies; 2) decorticate the mechanisms by which MTH1 acts; and 3) assess whether inhibition of MTH1 improve PAH in animal models.

column36: Deciphering the role of the Nck/PERK interaction in pancreatic beta cell function and survival
column37: Pancreatic beta cells make and release insulin, the hormone controlling blood glucose in humans. When people develop diabetes, it may be because their beta cells are producing less or no insulin, or possibly the cells have died after trying to produce too much insulin for too long a period of time. A protein called PERK is essential for beta cells to produce sufficient amounts of active insulin and importantly, humans who carry a PERK protein that does not work develop diabetes early in life. We recently found that mice lacking a protein called Nck1 have powerful beta cells that make and release more insulin than those of normal mice, without any signs of cell fatigue. We discovered that Nck1 normally interacts with and decreases PERK activity, inhibiting PERK's beneficial effects on beta cells to produce insulin and survive stress. Our goal is to produce robust human beta cells by preventing the Nck1 and PERK interaction. For this, we will decrease levels of Nck1 in pancreatic beta cells to minimize its interaction with PERK. We will then test whether these strategies improve the production of active insulin and protect against diabetes-related stresses. Given that PERK is important for healthy beta cells, our discovery that the Nck1/PERK interaction controls insulin production AND beta cell survival in the face of stress is promising. We propose that weakening this interaction could serve many purposes toward treating diabetes, including improving the function and health of beta cells in the body and those destined for transplantation.

column36: The midline thalamus and anxiety
column37: A large number of Canadians suffer from anxiety disorders. Unfortunately, the treatments available to them are limited by their inconsistent effectiveness, side effects and abuse potential. Anxiety is a complicated emotional state that involves a rather poorly understood interconnected network of brain regions that serve to evaluate the potential risks and benefits available to people and animals. It is hypothesized that perturbations in this distributed network can lead to an overemphasis of risks resulting in anxiety. A logical approach for developing new treatments for anxiety disorders is to get a better understanding of how different regions of the brain function together to produce excessive anxiety. Towards this goal, our laboratory has identified the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT) as a potentially key node in the neural network that mediates anxiety. In fact, the PVT is of special interest for understanding the neural mechanisms of anxiety because it is connected with many of the key regions of the brain identified as being part of the neural network that controls anxiety levels. In this application, we propose to apply innovative techniques that combine viral vectors and biological engineering tools to identify and precisely control the neural circuits by which the PVT modulates anxiety-like behaviors in a rodent model of stress-induced anxiety. This research will give us a better understanding of how the thalamus interacts with other brain regions to control anxiety in a way that could lead to new and more effective treatments for anxiety disorders.

column36: The role of interleukin-1 beta in preterm birth diagnosis and treatment
column37: Preterm birth (PTB) occurs in >10% of all births, and fetal inflammation (FI) in at least 40% of PTBs. Both are major causes of child death <5 years and of life-long morbidity. PTB and FI are unmet medical needs without effective diagnostics or therapeutics. Fortunately, Olson and Chemtob have each independently developed a diagnostic and therapeutic, respectively, that are complementary since the former is stimulated by the upstream mediator of PTB and FI, interleukin-1b, or IL1b, and the latter blocks IL1b action. Olson's diagnostic, the Leukocyte Migration Assay (LMA), uses white blood cells collected from pregnant women who are at risk of PTB or FI. By counting the number of cells that migrate to a stimulus extracted from the placental membranes, we can predict with precision women who will deliver within 7 days. Chemtob has designed a small peptide drug, rytvela, that blocks the action of IL1b and stops leukocyte migration in the LMA. We predict that IL1b stimulates PTB & FI in the pregnant mouse, that this is diagnosed by the LMA, and that rytvela is able to block PTB & FI and protect the fetus for normal birth, growth and development. We will perform three tests. In the first, we will stimulate PTB & FI in pregnant mice with powerful activators of silent or infectious inflammation. Then we will determine whether the LMA diagnoses PTB & FI and whether rytvela blocks these and restores maternal and fetal health. In the second, we will use a very low dose of IL1b to create a chronic fetal inflammation model without PTB. Again we will test whether the LMA detects this FI and whether rytvela improves fetal outcomes. In the last aim, we will study the chemotactic attraction molecules called chemokines stimulated by IL1b in human placental membranes to identify those key for attracting leukocytes at PTB. We will also identify how leukocytes are activated by IL1b and the key chemokines. This information will lead to human trials for a new diagnostic and therapeutic.

column36: Regulation of thymic selection thresholds and their role in establishing T cell function
column37: T cells are a type of white blood cell that collaborates with other cells of the immune system to identify and remove infectious agents and also abnormal cells. It has long been thought that T cells not yet exposed to infectious agents, thus named 'naive' T cells, are a homogeneous population all with the same potential to contribute different specialized skills to an immune response. However, it is becoming increasingly clear that naive T cells vary in pre-existing biases for certain skills prior to their deployment during an immune response. Indeed, subtle differences in the amount of a particular molecule, named CD5, found on the surface of T cells appears to mark cells with distinct functions before they respond. We do not yet understand how this functional skewing is established and maintained while they remain in reserve. T cells are trained in an organ called the thymus, where they learn to distinguish healthy cells from those expressing foreign or mutated proteins. The strength of interactions T cells make with other cells during this training period generates a naive T cell population with different levels of CD5. We propose that this thymic training period imprints individual T cells with latent skills only revealed once they participate in fighting an infection. Here we will study this imprinting process, and also investigate how the training program differs in newborns and adults, causing important changes in T cell responses to infection with age.

column36: Extending the validation and reliability testing of SCREEN a nutrition risk screening tool for community-living seniors.
column37: In the past 20 years there has been a rapid growth in the number of persons living with cognitive impairment or dementia in the community. Similarly, retirement homes have grown in prominence as a way of providing care for those who can no longer live independently. Both of these groups are prone to nutrition problems; poor food intake and weight loss are associated with several adverse outcomes such as falls and hospitalizations, as well as the progression of dementia. Determining which older adults are at nutrition risk will allow the health care system to target interventions and start early treatment that can improve their overall health and independence. Yet, nutrition screening tools specific to these groups are unavailable. SCREEN is a questionnaire that was created in Canada and is used worldwide to measure nutrition risk. However, SCREEN was not tested in those with cognitive impairment or living in retirement residences. The proposed study will determine if SCREEN is valid for use with these two groups of community-living seniors. Persons living with cognitive impairment (and their family member) and persons living in retirement homes will be recruited. Participants (~ 600) will complete SCREEN and other health measures and a dietitian will determine the nutrition risk of the participant based on an assessment. SCREEN results will be compared to this assessment to determine if it adequately represents nutrition risk. Availability of a feasible nutrition risk tool that can be used with all community-living seniors, including those with dementia and/or living in retirement homes will promote screening in family doctors' offices, retirement homes and other clinics, which is currently absent. Early identification of nutrition problems will promote the development and use of preventative services to improve senior health, potentially delaying or avoiding frailty and increased use of healthcare services by these vulnerable older adults.

column37: L'enzyme "mitogen-activated protein kinase " (MAPK) p38 est connue depuis plus de 15 ans comme etant necessaire au maintien des fonctions normales du coeur tout en contribuant paradoxalement au developpement de pathologies cardiaques. En debut d'etudes graduees, j'ai identifie par une approche novatrice la "serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 3 " (SRSF3) parmi les proteines interagissant avec la MAPK p38 active. Notre decouverte inattendue demontre que p38 module, chez les cardiomyocytes (cellules contractiles du coeur) en culture, l'epissage alternatif exerce par SRSF3 sur des ARNm reconnus pour etre modifies en insuffisance cardiaque. Est-ce que l'interaction fonctionnelle entre ces deux proteines est benefique ou nefaste dans le processus de developpement des cardiomyopathies cardiaques? Afin de repondre a cette question importante, nous voulons elucider le role de la proteine SRSF3 et les mecanismes regulant son action dans le coeur. Pour ce faire, je retirerai specifiquement le gene encodant la proteine SRSF3 chez les cardiomyocytes de souris par une approche dites d'invalidation conditionnelle. Dans un contexte de stress pathologique cause par la TAC, un modele mimant l'insuffisance cardiaque, nous evaluerons differents parametres cardiaques et analyserons l'etat des ARNm au niveau de leur expression et de leurs evenements d'epissage alternatif par sequencage a haut-debit. L'interaction p38-SRSF3 sera aussi exploree plus en details par une technique d'immunofluorescence sur des coupes de tissus fixes (isPLA) provenant de coeurs ex vivo stresses par une ischemie reconnue pour activer p38. Sur ces memes echantillons, nous identifierons les sites de SRSF3 phosphoryles par la kinase p38 en utilisant la spectrometrie de masse apres avoir isole SRSF3. Reveler ce nouveau mecanisme de regulation est essentiel pour mieux saisir la fonction complexe de p38 lors de l'insuffisance cardiaque.

column36: NAD+ depletion as a cause of placental dysfunction in preeclampsia
column37: Preeclampsia (PE) is a life-threatening hypertensive disorder of pregnancy with no cure. The disease can occur in three forms, one of which is inflammation driven (hyperactive immune response). We have a very limited understanding of this unique subclass of PE which makes it difficult to treat. Based on our previous research findings we speculate that placental dysfunction in this subclass of PE occurs by a hyperactive immune response that can deplete the placenta of organelles used to maintain cellular energy (mitochondria). Thus, I will be testing the therapeutic potential of medications that can boost cellular energy signals to improve placenta cell function and overall placenta health. Therefore, findings from this study may contribute to the development of subclass-specific therapy for this group of patients.

column36: Microbiota-immune interactions and host defense in sepsis
column37: Sepsis is a life-threatening condition characterized by an uncontrolled immune reaction against infectious agents spread in the patient's bloodstream and organs. It can emerge from the body's response against very distinct microorganisms, such as bacteria, fungi, viruses and even protozoan parasites. Bacterial sepsis is a major cause of death worldwide, with mortality rates ranging from 30% up to 50%. In the United States of America, severe sepsis most often arises from infections in the respiratory tract (pneumonia), being considered the leading cause of death in non-coronary intensive care units (ICU). In sepsis, many complications arise from the interplay between immune cells, including platelets, which are commonly associated with blood clotting. For instance, the activation of the coagulation system leads to formation of thrombi, which obstruct microvasculature, contributing to organ failure. Paradoxically, patients may also present bleeding due to depletion of coagulation factors. The mechanisms underlying coagulation disorders in the microvasculature are not fully understood. In order to investigate such mechanisms, we intend to use animal models of abdominal sepsis. By taking advantage of groundbreaking research tools, we will be able to investigate the role of specific targets present in platelets during experimental sepsis. In doing so, we hope to shed a light on further development of therapeutic strategies that address the characteristic uncontrolled immune seen in sepsis.

column37: THE ISSUE: Indigenous and Northern youth experience sexual and mental health disparities in the Northwest Territories (NWT). (1) We will work with a youth advisory board, youth, parents and Elders using human centred design approaches and community engagement to identify how to better meet the needs of youth. (2) We will conduct FOXY and SMASH school-based workshops, with a pre-and post test, 6-month, 12 month and 18-month follow-up surveys. We will explore social ecological factors associated with SRH and resilience trajectories. (3) Interconnected knowledge mobilization. IMPACT: We will gather and integrate multiple knowledge sources to refine sexual health programs to better meet the needs of Northern and Indigenous youth in the NWT, and evaluate the long term effects of participating in arts-based sexual health programs. column37: Arthritic degeneration of the spine is a natural part of human aging, affecting 51% of adults, and is the most common cause of reversible spinal cord injury in people over 55 years. column36: Genetics and epigenetics of sex differences in placental and fetal development
column37: Many differences between males and females arise between conception and birth. As the main regulator of fetal growth and development is the placenta, many of these differences arise because male and female placentas are not equivalent. Male and female placentas differ in their sex chromosome complement, XX vs XY; This leads to sex-chromosome gene expression differences that cause downstream effects on the remainder of the genome. Data from DNA methylation, a chemical modification to DNA that is associated with gene expression, has already been collected on over 1000 placentas. Our goal is to identify sex-influenced DNA methylation within the placenta, identify the factors that affect this measurement, and determine if the sex-related differentiation of the placenta is associated with perinatal outcomes such and fetal birth weight and gestational age at birth. column36: Hybrids and commonalities of thiotemplate enzymes
column37: Many of the drugs and medicines that we rely on today are natural products, made by the earth's flora. Important classes of these compounds are made in fungi and bacteria by massive enzymes called nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) and polyketide synthases (PKSs), or by fusions of these enzymes (PKS-NRPSs). They synthesize all sorts of antibiotics, which can kill dangerous fungi and bacteria, as well as compounds to help us fight off viral infections and cancers. For example, these compounds include viomycin, an antibiotic used for the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis; cyclosporin, which has been widely used as an immunosuppressant in organ transplants and can inhibit hepatitis virus C replication; and the familiar antibiotic penicillin. The goal of this research is to expand our knowledge of NRPSs, PKSs, and NRPS-PKSs and the mechanisms they employ to synthesize important drugs. We will use biochemistry and biophysics, including techniques known as X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy, to capture three-dimensional pictures of an NRPS or PKS at different points in the process of making these natural products. We will answer questions ranging from how, in a natural hybrid fusion of one kind of enzyme (PKS) and the other (NRPS), the separate parts can function together, to how a domain normally found in a PKS has adapted to work in an NRPS, to how the last step of synthesis, common to both NRPSs and PKSs, releases the molecule in its proper, active form. column37: In general, women have a higher risk of adverse drug reactions than men. This is believed to be because women may present higher blood concentrations of drugs than men when they are given a specific dose of a medication. Yet, the exact reasons for these differences are unknown. This is partly because the inclusion of women in studies during the development of new drugs is generally limited. Thus, doses used in clinical studies, and eventually in the "real world", are largely based on information collected in men. Many mechanisms have been proposed to explain the differences in drug concentrations between women and men. For example, women have a lower body weight and kidney function, which should lead to higher drug concentrations. Another potential mechanism that has not been widely studied is that genetic variations could have different effects between women and men. We propose to conduct a comprehensive study in 10 000 participants from a large study to identify if individual characteristics, such as weight and age, as well as genetic variations in genes implicated in the absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination of drugs, influence the concentrations and dosing of 48 drugs commonly used by Canadians. column36: Decolonizing childbirth with Nunavik Inuit women transferred to high-risk hospitals for childbirth: a co-designed pilot intervention
column37: BACKGROUND Inuit women in Canada carry a disproportionate burden of poor health, with higher rates of maternal mortality and negative birth outcomes. Some 14% of Inuit women in Nunavik (Inuit territory in Quebec) travel to tertiary southern hospitals for specialized obstetric care (a process known as fly-out births). Fly-out births are linked to adverse health outcomes for Inuit women, their families and communities. This participatory research supports culturally safe Inuit childbirth, and will co-design pilot interventions with Inuit stakeholders and their care providers, to inform the decolonization of obstetric care in Quebec tertiary hospitals. METHODS The study engages Nunavik-based Inuit women, their families and community members, as well as perinatal healthcare providers and policy makers in Nunavik and Montreal. With each group, a series of group fuzzy cognitive mapping sessions will explore experiences with fly-out childbirth and perspectives of decolonization in obstetric care. Individual and household questionnaires will document the frequency of these findings. Stakeholders will co-design an intervention through deliberative dialogue and community meetings. Recommendations will be shared with obstetrical staff of a Montreal tertiary hospital. A follow-up survey will measure quantitative changes in birth outcomes, patient satisfaction, and decolonizing care practices. An integrated knowledge translation and exchange strategy engages stakeholders in cognitive mapping sessions, and co-design interventions in deliberative dialogue. DISCUSSION Evacuation for childbirth aims to reduce health disparities faced by Inuit women, yet it is inadvertently associated with adverse health outcomes. Affirming Inuit values of childbirth and engaging Inuit voices in service delivery improvement can support culturally safe care. The protocol and instruments developed may have wider relevance for rural Inuit across Canada.

column36: Reprogramming HSCs to generate protective trained immunity against TB
column37: Ever since German scientist Robert Koch first discovered Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) to be the infectious agent of tuberculosis in 1882, it has defied efforts by scientists to prevent or cure the disease. The presence of Mtb DNA in ancient Egyptian mummies (dated 1550- 1080 BC) suggests a long-standing evolutionary relationship between this bacterium and humans. Despite the world-wide application of BCG vaccination and other anti-Mtb interventions, Mtb remains one of the deadliest human pathogens killing annually two million people. Eight to ten million new cases of active tuberculosis occur each year due in large part to asymptomatic people chronically infected with Mtb. The ability of Mtb to persist in individuals with apparently normal immune systems implies that Mtb has developed strategies to avoid, evade, and even subvert our host defense system. Considering Mtb also desires to be a "residence" of the bone marrow, which is home to stem cells that produce all immune cells, Mtb potentially hijack the control centre of the immune response. Although we know a great deal about the immune response to Mtb in the lung, our understanding of BM immunity to Mtb is extremely limited. The tropism of Mtb for the bone marrow may also explain why it is an incredibly successful pathogen, as the vast majority of our efforts have been dedicated to controlling its growth in the lung while the root of the disease is seeded in the bone marrow. Thus the major objective of this proposal is to define the cellular and molecular signatures involved in HSC activation/function during infection with virulent strains of Mtb or vaccine with the ultimate goal of developing a roadmap of protective versus detrimental immunity to this devastating disease.

column37: Severe infection can lead to many complications within the human body including low blood pressure, which is called septic shock. There are many different intravenous fluids available for doctors to use. Each one of these fluids has potential advantages as well as potential disadvantages. Some preliminary and limited research in the field has suggested that one specific electrolyte, called chloride, may be harmful when given to patients in high concentrations. The investigators plan to study the impact of giving patients with septic shock intravenous fluids with either a high chloride concentration or a low chloride concentration. If there is benefit seen using low chloride concentration fluids this would be easy to initiate across the world leading to a dramatic and relatively inexpensive improvement in patient care.

column36: Regulating chromatin landscape and organization with non-coding RNAs
column37: Recent technological advances have led to a number of important discoveries. Amongst these is the realization that the better part of our genome is read at one time or another to produce RNA molecules that do not encode proteins. Given that the biological function of most of these "non-coding RNA" transcripts is unknown, they currently fall into different categories based mainly on their size and the site from which they are produced in the genome. The "long non-coding RNAs" (lncRNAs) are one such class of molecules. The biological relevance of many lncRNAs has been demonstrated, with family members even considered as promising therapeutic or prognostic tools. Yet, how they regulate gene expression is very poorly understood. In this project, we suggest using four lncRNAs as discovery tools to identify and characterize new mechanisms used by this family of molecules to control gene expression. These lncRNAs are encoded within the HOXA gene cluster and have been linked to human cancers. We previous showed that one of them, HOTAIRM1, regulates the expression of HOXA genes both by regulating what binds and shapes the DNA encoding them. Our preliminary data indicates that HOTAIRM1 regulates many other genes across the genome. To better understand their biological function, we will first identify new gene targets genome-wide. We will investigate how they regulate genome folding and spatial organization using state-of-the-art technologies that yield three-dimensional maps of our genome at very high resolution. This information will then be used to characterize the molecular mechanisms used by the HOXA-encoded lncRNAs to regulate gene expression, and test our hypothesis that given lncRNAs can use different molecular mechanisms to modulate gene expression depending on the DNA context and/or target gene.

column36: Elucidation of bromodomain functions within SWI/SNF complexes
column37: The effective structural regulation and utilization of a cell's genetic material is essential to its fitness. Unsurprisingly, it is now clear that epigenetic regulators, proteins that organize and regulate the accessibility of the genetic material, are commonly altered in human diseases, including cancer. In recent years, bromodomains have become actionable therapeutic targets, with the development of numerous small molecule inhibitors that effectively and specifically block their function. Clinical trials investigating these innovative inhibitors are ongoing in Canada and elsewhere. Unfortunately, fundamental understanding of the functions of the ten bromodomains incorporated in SWI/SNF complex components is still lacking. This project aims to provide this knowledge by employing state-of-the-art tools to identify the cellular targets of SWI/SNF bromodomains, examine how they engage these targets, and determine the functions of these interactions. This will aid in predicting the molecular consequences of specific mutations within SWI/SNF complex components, support the ongoing development of novel bromodomain inhibitors, and further our understanding of the regulatory processes controlling a cell's genomic material.

column37: Child maltreatment (CM) refers to any act of commission or omission by a parent or other caregiver that results in intended or unintended harm such as physical abuse, sexual abuse, emotional abuse, or neglect. In addition, existing treatments for distressing memories in general have typically focused on increasing the processing of the distressing memory, but not on facilitating its integration into broader memory structure. We found that white blood cells, known as neutrophils, are implicated in the perception of pain in a mouse model of arthritis. We will examine the blood of patients and will use special microscopes to look at platelets and neutrophil interactions in a mouse model of arthritis. We will block the interactions between platelets and neutrophils and will quantify pain in mice. We may thus identify how to interfere in this process to reduce pain.

column36: A population-level linked data study of the long-term developmental impacts of prenatal antidepressant exposure
column37: Each year, approximately 13% of North American women experience depression and/or anxiety during pregnancy and a third are treated with an antidepressant that alters levels of serotonin, a key neurotransmitter during fetal brain development. We know that these antidepressant cross the placenta and the fetal blood brain barrier, leading to critical unanswered questions about the long-term developmental effects associated with prenatal antidepressant exposure. Over the past 18 years our research has examined women treated with SRI antidepressants during pregnancy. We have studied development and behavior in infants, children and adolescents of depressed mothers and reported novel findings showing that in utero SRI exposure is associated with altered brain development in infancy and behavioral disturbances, such as increased anxiety in young children. While population-level data have the advantage of large sample sizes, the level of detail regarding educational and behavioral outcomes across childhood has generally been limited. There is an urgent need to study long-term outcomes using objective non-categorical behavioral and educational data. These data are now available in British Columbia. Thus we aim to use these population-based administrative datasets to assess whether maternal mood during pregnancy and/or its treatment with an SRI antidepressant is associated with an increased risk for delayed language and cogonitive development during childhood, as well as social and emotional development and wellbeing during early (age 5) and middle childhood (age 9). We will assemble a population-based cohort including all children born in British Columbia between 2000 and 2012 and follow them until 2016. We will include individual-level behavioral, education and health data on children in kindergarten and at Grade 4 to assess their well-being and development. Our research results will be used to minimize the incidence of adverse outcomes for mothers and their children.

column36: Diagnosis of Aggressive Prostate Cancer Using Key Features of Raman Spectroscopy
column37: The diagnosis of prostate cancer, the most frequent cancer among Canadian men, is fraught with recurrent difficulties in establishing the aggressiveness of the disease (prognosis). Indeed, with a wide spectrum of possible therapeutic options, the prognosis of prostate cancer has to be well-defined in order to better individualize that treatment. Accordingly, using a laser-based molecular characterization method (Raman spectroscopy), we previously identified key features of a marker of prostate cancer aggressiveness, intraductal carcinoma of the prostate. In this project, we first aim to verify how each of these key feature can be used clinically to improve the identification of this aggressive variant of prostate cancer. To do this, we will use a special type of Raman spectroscopy, which is based on the targeted evaluation of one key feature at the time. In parallel, since Raman spectroscopy features involves many underlying molecules, we aim at exploring which of these molecules are responsible for the modifications we observed using the laser-based method. To do this, we will use mass spectrometry, a technique which allows to identify specific molecules according partly to their weight. Overall, this study will not only provide a comprehensive understanding of our previous results, but it will in parallel establish a clinically applicable method and provide a unique opportunity to identify new potential diagnostic and/or therapeutic biomarkers of prostate cancer.

column36: Symptom Screening Linked to Care Pathways for Children with Cancer: a Cluster Randomized Trial
column37: Most children with cancer survive because they are given intensive treatments. Unfortunately, these treatments are associated with distressing symptoms. Poor symptom control occurs because children do not have a way to report and track their symptoms, healthcare providers are not aware of these symptoms, and guidelines for symptom management are not easy to access. To address these gaps, we developed the Symptom Screening in Pediatrics Tool (SSPedi) for children receiving cancer treatments. We also created evidence-based guidelines to help providers know how to manage symptoms. To bring identification and management of symptoms together, we created a web-based application called Supportive care Prioritization, Assessment and Recommendations for Kids (SPARK). To evaluate SPARK, we plan to randomize 20 institutions. In intervention institutions, we will prompt children newly diagnosed with cancer to complete symptom screening three times weekly for 8 weeks. Reports will be emailed to the primary healthcare team. We will also create care pathways that help clinicians know how to best manage symptoms. Participants in control sites will receive the standard of care. We will not facilitate symptom screening with feedback or create care pathways. We will enroll English and Spanish-speaking children 8-18 years of age with a new diagnosis of cancer and a plan for treatment. The primary endpoint will be the week 8 total SSPedi score (ranges from 0-60; higher means worse symptoms). We plan to enroll 444 children across 20 US institutions. This study is proposed for US sites because we are conducting a CIHR-funded randomized trial evaluating 5 consecutive days of symptom screening and feedback among hospitalized pediatric cancer patients in 7 Canadian sites. These studies cannot be conducted at the same site. This study will test an innovative application to improve symptom control and quality of life for children receiving cancer treatments.

column36: Implication of neutrophil extracellular traps in the efficacy of bladder-sparing therapy in muscle invasive bladder cancer
column37: Radical cystectomy remains the standard of care for muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). This surgery entails complete removal of the bladder and surrounding organs, leading to a serious impact on the quality of life (QoL) of patients and associated with a 5-year overall survival of only 50 %. Radiation therapy (RT), which preserves the bladder, would be a more appropriate treatment modality if we could improve efficacy, as lack of local control remains problematic. As part from its direct tumor cell killing potential, there is increasing evidence that RT also leads to significant alterations in the tumor microenvironment, which inflammation being one of the most important factors modulating radiation responsiveness of tumors. During the acute phase of inflammation, neutrophils are one of the first-line responders of inflammatory cells to migrate towards the site of inflammation. Recently, it has been shown neutrophils can exhibit dual behaviors and are increasingly being seen as important players in cancer progression. Neutrophils can expel DNA studded with various proteins to form web-like structures known as neutrophil extracellular traps (NET), which has been shown to be associated with tumor progression and metastasis. Our preliminary findings strongly indicate NET are implicated in radioresistance. Determining the NET-related molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying response to radiation will have direct clinical relevance to better select patients who will benefit most from bladder preservation therapy. The novel approach of the proposal herein can bring transformative changes in developing novel strategies in bladder cancer (BC) therapy as it has the potential to transfer from the bench to the patient, an unquestionably, positive impact on survival and quality of life of MIBC patients.

column36: Microbial Causes of Ulcerative Colitis: Looking Outside the Involved Region
column37: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic disease affecting the gut with limited treatments and significant risk of needing surgery to remove the large bowel (colon). It is very concerning that we still don't know what causes UC, especially since it is becoming more common, particularly in children in Canada. Microbes (mostly bacteria) are different in UC but we don't know if they cause the disease or are changed because of the inflammation found in UC. We have recently shown that children with UC have different bacteria in the healthy-appearing small bowel; we have also developed and just published a new method to isolate bacteria that might be virulent (disease causing) by utilizing the patient's immune system to trap bacteria and identified how they might do this. The next step is to combine these findings and find bacteria that might be causing or at least driving damage in UC. To do this we will also take advantage of some of the basic and unexplained features of UC: 1. It only involves the colon; 2. It is a continuous disease; 3. The appendix seems to have an important (but not understood) role. This study will build on these interesting observations to test our hypothesis that bacteria (and molecules/products they make) from unaffected areas travel down the bowel and cause the damage seen in UC. We will test this by collecting samples from different parts of the bowel in children just diagnosed with UC during a colonoscopy test. Three large Canadian centers, that are already working together through a funded National Network, will collect samples during colonoscopy to identify these bacteria. We will find the bacteria that travel down to the sick areas and identify those that can penetrate and injure the bowel and those that activate the immune system. We will then confirm that these bacteria indeed cause damage using cell models and germ-free mice. This will help explain what causes UC and will direct new therapies.

column36: The roles of betaine and its mitochondrial synthesis in oocyte and preimplantation embryo health
column37: There is strong evidence that the mother's nutrition, health, and environment during the earliest stages of pregnancy immediately after conception can significantly affect the health of the embryo and the fetus and placenta into which it develops. Also, the treatment of human infertility by assisted reproduction technologies (ART), in which multiple eggs are obtained from women, fertilized, and cultured for an extended period before being transferred into the uterus, has been very effective and produced millions of babies, but there is increasing evidence that how eggs and very early embryos are handled during ART can damage eggs before fertilization and can cause health problems in the fetus, placenta, and offspring. In this work, we will be investigating mechanisms that may be important in preventing such problems. We are focusing on a molecule called betaine, which is a modified form of the common amino acid glycine. Betaine is supplied in the diet, for example by wheat germ, spinach, and shellfish. It can also be synthesized in the body from the vitamin, choline. We have previously found that betaine has important roles in mammalian eggs and very early embryos. One function is to control cell size, which turns out to be particularly critical for early embryo health. Another role is in supplying the molecules needed for controlling gene activity in later embryos, just before they implant in the uterus. We also have new evidence that betaine is also involved in the normal function of mitochondria, which are the part of the cell that makes energy, in eggs. How betaine is supplied to the egg and embryo, where it comes from, and the consequences of its dysregulation, are still poorly understood. We hope to show that creating the conditions in which these mechanisms can function normally in eggs and very early embryos will produce healthy eggs and embryos.

column36: Perivascular fibroblasts in maintaining blood vessel integrity
column37: Blood vessels are essential to sustain life in humans. Defects in blood vessels can result in serious consequences, such as hemorrhage, tissue ischemia, and stroke. The conventional view is that interactions between endothelial cells, the inner layer of the blood vessel, and surrounding vessel support cells known as mural cells help keep the blood vessel as a stable tube. Loss of these cells result in fragile vessels prone to damage. We will determine where these perivascular fibroblasts come from during embryo development and how they help stabilize blood vessels. Since the organization of the vasculature and underlying genetic mechanisms are remarkably similar between zebrafish and human, our work in zebrafish may provide insights on how to treat patients with fragile blood vessels.

column36: The regulation of mRNA translation by the Nucleoporin RanBP2/Nup358
column37: To express a gene, its DNA must copied into mRNA in the nucleus. This mRNA is then packaged into complexes that contain proteins and known as messenger ribonucleoproteins (mRNPs). These mRNPs are then ferried across the nuclear pore to reach the cytoplasm where they are used by ribosomes to make new proteins. These proteins are functional molecules that impact the development, physiology and homeostasis of the organism. We have uncovered a key step in the gene expression pathway. We have shown that the protein RanBP2, which is part of the nuclear pore, is required for the efficient production of secretory proteins, likely by modifying how mRNAs are packaged into mRNPs. This mRNP maturation event likely impacts how many mRNAs are translated into proteins. Mutations in RanBP2 are associated to Acute Necrotizing Encephalopathy 1 (ANE1), a condition where otherwise normal individuals overproduce cytokines in response to influenza infections. This leads to seizures, coma and a high rate of mortality. Four separate dominant point mutations in RanBP2 have been linked to this disease. In cells that lack RanBP2 or that have mutations that impair its ability to modify other proteins, we find that the cytokine interleukin 6 (IL6) is over-expressed, indicating that RanBP2 likely alters the mRNP that contains the mRNA that is used to make IL6 protein. In this proposal we outline our plans to determine the molecular mechanisms by which RanBP2 regulates mRNP maturation. We have also been in contact with families afflicted by ANE1 and we plan to use epithelial nasal swabs and white blood cells (monocytes) from these patients to understand how mutations in RanBP2 alters cytokine production in normal conditions and after viral infection. Our work will not only provide key insights into the pathology of ANE1, but will also provide a deeper understanding of how RanBP2 regulates the expression of cytokines and other secretory proteins.

column36: Hypoxia mimicry for enhancing peripheral nerve regeneration
column37: In the absence of sufficient oxygen (i.e. during hypoxia), cells die. When oxygen levels are low but not lethal, cells can cope by changing how they metabolize nutrients: they use alternate mechanisms that do not depend so heavily on oxygen, and at the same time increase the capacity for oxygen to be delivered (increasing the number of red blood cells and blood vessels, for example). Interestingly, these mechanisms are also partially engaged when nerves are injured, as they are in 2-3% of all injuries to any part of the body. Nerve injury leads to loss of function (sensation and movement, for example), as well as to neuropathic pain, most frequently described as unpleasant burning, electric shock-like, or crushing sensations. Often these consequences of nerve injury fail to resolve, prompting us to ask whether artificially engaging the hypoxia response can improve peripheral nerve regeneration and reduce neuropathic pain. Our cells "know" how much oxygen is present by virtue of oxygen-sensing proteins called PHDs. There are three of these: PHD1, 2 and 3. When these proteins are blocked with a drug (DMOG), or genetically silenced, cells are "tricked" into behaving as they would under hypoxia. We will use DMOG and PHD-deficient mice to ask whether and how mimicking hypoxia can improve recovery, including preventing neuropathic pain, following nerve injury.

column36: Synaptic physiology and structure of human muscle in a 3D cell culture system: Application to Duchenne's Muscular Dystrophy
column37: Duchennes's Muscular Dystrophy is a disease of muscle that affects approximately 1 in 3500 boys. Disease starts early in life when young boys fail to reach key milestones in their motor development and it is progressive; children are soon bound to a wheelchair and most die in their 20s and 30s from cardiac and respiratory complications. At present there is no known cure for DMD. The underlying molecular biology of DMD is well-known: patients carry a mutation in the Dystrophin gene. Muscle cells fail to make Dystrophin protein and are not stable. Lack of Dystrophin leads to a breakdown of the Dystrophin Glycoprotein Complex and consequently results in muscle membrane fragility, damage, inflammation, and cell death. Recent technical developments in the areas of stem-cell therapy and gene editing have given renewed hope to developing a treatment for DMD. However, we Identify a knowledge gap in our understanding of the effects of DMD mutations on the physiology of human muscle and synapses. Our proposed experiments are designed to fill that gap and will subsequently direct our studies of therapeutic treatments, especially research into existing pharmaceutical approaches To enable this research, we have developed a pioneering 3D muscle cell culture system to analyze the neuromuscular physiology and structure of human muscle cells grown from healthy and DMD-patient stem cells. Such human muscle microtissues (hMMT) will serve as the model system in our studies. By completing this work we will derive new knowledge of the effects of DMD mutations on human neuro-muscular physiology and test therapeutic efficacy of compounds to improve performance of DMD-affected muscle.

column36: Chromatin context of somatic mutations delineate oncogenic drivers in triple-negative breast cancer
column37: Breast cancer is a collection of different types of cancer. One of these, known as triple-negative breast cancer, comprises approximately 20% of breast cancers diagnosed each year. It is highly aggressive and the only standard-of-care therapy offered to patients is chemotherapy, which unfortunately fails in over 40% of patients. This leads to disease progression and death. Hence, new approaches are required to treat and cure triple-negative breast cancer patients. To address this need for new therapy we propose to identify what drives growth of triple-negative breast cancer. In the last year, scientists identified thousands of mutations that populate the genome of triple-negative breast cancer, but unlike other types of breast cancer, the "drivers" are not easy to identity due to the diversity of mutations across patients. We argue that the heterogeneity of mutations underlies their convergence toward common targets. We developed in recent years two methods to identify drivers of cancer development based on convergence of mutations towards genes or proteins. Here, we propose to apply these methods to mine mutations found in triple-negative breast cancer and find the drivers of growth. My approaches contrast with standard strategies in the field by comprehensively analyzing each mutation based on the normal function of the DNA sequence they alter, inclusive of genes and the remaining 98% of DNA sequences found in each cancer cell. My ultimate goal is to identify drivers of oncogenesis, based on the genetics of tumours taking into account their epigenetic context, and use this information to precisely find targets for drug treatment against triple-negative breast cancer. Overall, this proposal is at the forefront of personalized cancer medicine and offers a unique opportunity to accelerate the translation of research discoveries into improved clinical care.

column36: Prognostic Biomarkers and Novel Therapies for Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma Patients
column37: Patients with head and neck cancer have a 50% 5-year survival. Patients are treated with surgery, and may also receive radiation therapy, or combined radiation and chemotherapy. These therapies are very toxic and can have long-term negative side effects. The needs for these patients include: 1) A better way to identify which patients are in need of more aggressive therapy; 2) More effective therapies for those patients with the most aggressive and life-threatening disease. We have been acquiring tumor tissues from HNSCC patients for many years and implanting them into mice with a defective immune system. 2/3 of these samples successfully grow in the mice ("engraft") and they grow at varying rates: some form a 1 cm mass within a short time (<8 weeks; rapid engrafters); others grow more slowly and can take up to 6 months to form a 1 cm mass; and still others fail to grow at all. In addition, for those samples that grow in mice, we are able to test both standard therapies and new drugs for their efficacy. Our proposal is focused on using these results to identify new therapies, in particular for those patients that have the most aggressive disease. We will do this by: 1) Identifying the genetic differences between patients in the three categories (rapid engrafters, slow engrafters, and non-engrafters); 2) Using the genetic information to identify drugs predicted to target the genetic profile of rapid engrafters. Any drug candidates that we identify can be tested for their efficacy against aggressive, rapidly growing tumors in the engrafted mice. This project will result in "biomarkers", which can be used to predict which patients have the most aggressive form of the disease and thus adjust their therapies appropriately, and also in new candidate therapies for these patients.

column36: Inflammation and LDL transcytosis - implications for early atherosclerosis
column37: Atherosclerosis leads to heart attacks and strokes and is a leading cause of death in Canada. The first step in the disease is the build-up of the bad cholesterol, LDL, in the wall of blood vessels. Specifically, LDL builds up under the innermost layer of arteries, called the endothelium. How the LDL gets under the endothelium is very poorly understood. We have discovered ways to study this process, which is known as LDL transcytosis. We now wish to learn how a big risk factor for heart disease - inflammation - affects LDL transcytosis. We suspect that inflammation causes more LDL transcytosis to occur, accelerating the build-up of cholesterol in the artery wall. Understanding how this happens will help us develop ways to prevent or treat it. If we can prevent cholesterol from accumulating in the blood vessel wall, we will prevent heart disease and stroke. We will use sophisticated microscopes to study the process by which cholesterol builds up under the special cells that line blood vessels, known as endothelium. We will identify the specific molecules that regulate this build-up, especially under conditions of inflammation. We will also prove that our findings from cells hold true in mice, which are the typical animals used in studies of atherosclerosis. We will compare our findings using cells from men as well as women to determine if there is a sex-based difference. We are the only lab in Canada to study this process of transcytosis, by which the bad cholesterol (LDL) gets under endothelial cells. We therefore have the potential to make huge advances in this field of research.

column36: Role of BRCT proteins in DNA damage signaling
column37: Damage to our DNA is a major cause of ageing, cancer, and neurodevelopmental disorders. To defend against DNA damage, our cells have evolved systems that scan the more than 1 metre of DNA that is in each of our cells to look for and repair microscopic forms of damage before problems can occur. column36: A pragmatic randomized controlled trial of a group self-management support program for anxiety disorders
column37: Anxiety disorders are the most common mental disorders in Canada, and they are responsible for substantial psychological distress, disability, and health service needs. This clinical trial aims at examining the effectiveness of the intervention as a complement to usual care at post treatment and follow-up (4, 8, 12 and 24 months). Participants will comprise adults with clinically-significant anxiety symptoms that will be recruited through primary care clinics, bulletin boards and social media in four regions of Quebec. The rigorous evaluation of this SMS program will provide invaluable information to decision makers, health care managers and clinicians regarding the effectiveness, cost/effectiveness and implementability of the intervention in community-based care in conjunction with usual care. column37: Retinoblastoma (Rb) is the most common cancer of the eye in children and accounts for 3% of all childhood malignancies. Yet, despite considerable efforts, persistent or recurrent tumor growing in vitreous cavity is still a major cause of treatment failure in advanced Rb, because they are remote from the blood supply and rely on diffusion of chemotherapy into the vitreous humor from the retina. Several drugs have been developed for the treatment of Rb, but they kill cancer cells as well as healthy cells which leads to excruciating side effects. My lab has a long-standing interest in developing novel anticancer reagents and strategies. Our recent studies have shown that one of the small biomolecules exhibits dramatic effect of inducing Rb cell death. As these molecules are prone to degradation by cellular enzymes, we propose to encapsulate them in biocompatible and biodegradable nano-sized lipid carriers and delivered locally to target vitreous Rb cells, in such a way to minimize the side effects of current Rb therapies and increases the anti-Rb efficiency. In this proposal, we will assess the ability of the nanostructured lipid carriers loaded with the particular small biomolecule to suppress vitreous Rb growth in well-established animal models. In addition, we will investigate the efficacy of combination therapies, as well as their pharmacokinetics and tissue toxicity. Moreover, we will also dissect how this small biomolecule kill Rb cells at the molecular levels in order to develop better strategies and interventions. Cancer research is an intricate process and it is only through multi-pronged approaches that valuable therapies will emerge. We have generated knowledge, tools, and partnerships with other groups and expertise that place us in a unique position to make major contributions to the Rb cancer research field. We expect that efficacious compounds combine with nanotechnology for targeting vitreous Rb will bring enormous benefits to Rb patients.

column36: The Role of Intramuscular Immune Cell Infiltrations in Tumor and Age Related Muscle Wasting
column37: Muscle wasting that occurs with cancer is known as cachexia and with aging is called sarcopenia. Cachexia and sarcopenia are important healthcare issues. Cachexia affects the majority of patients with late stage malignancy, and is thought to contribute to one third of cancer deaths, while sarcopenia is associated with falls, disability, and mortality in the elderly, and costs as high as 1.5% of our total healthcare expenditure. Despite these significant features, cachexia and sarcopenia are relatively understudied entities with poor understanding of their pathophysiology. One common link that could explain how these conditions occur is the immune system. Our research focuses on the idea that both tumors and an aging body release factors that activate some cells of the immune system which, in turn, release other signals that cause muscles to shrink. Our preliminary data suggest that the immune cell at the "heart" of this process is the myeloid derived suppressor cell (MDSC). These cells rapidly rise during cancer, and steadily rise during aging. Using mice with cachexia caused by tumors, and sarcopenia of old age, we have identified subsets of these MDSCs infiltrating hearts and skeletal muscle. On depletion of these cells during mouse models of cancer, we can eliminate muscle wasting, even though the cancer remains. In this grant, we will characterize the nature of the MDSCs infiltrating the hearts and skeletal muscles during cachexia and sarcopenia, and their role in these processes using functional assays and state of the art technologies, including single cell sequencing. Next, we will determine which factors support the generation and activation of these cells. Finally, we determine the mechanisms by which these cells cause muscles to shrink in cachexia and sarcopenia. Understanding how these immune cells tell the heart and muscles to shrink can help us to prevent or revert these processes and improve the lives of people with muscle wasting from age or cancer.
