column36: The roles of MICAL1 and protein oxidation in cell signalling and cancer
column37: The MICAL1 enzyme produces the reactive oxygen species molecule H2O2, and is expressed at higher than normal levels in a variety of cancer types, including breast, liver, kidney, pancreas, skin and brain/central nervous system cancers. To determine how MICAL1 contributes to cancer, we blocked its expression and observed significant effects on protein oxidation, cell migration, survival and tumour growth in a mouse breast cancer model. Together, these observations reveal a major role of MICAL1 in cancer, indicating that MICAL1 is a potential cancer drug target due to its role as a critically important signalling linker. Building on our experience and knowledge of signal transduction pathways in cancer, particularly in examining how protein oxidation influences cancer cell motility, we will determine how the MICAL1 protein contributes to cancer growth via targeted protein oxidation. We hypothesize that: (1) MICAL1 responds to upstream signals by changing its specific activity, leading to the oxidation of target proteins to affect their functions; (2) MICAL1-induced protein oxidations contribute to cancer growth, invasion and metastasis; (3) MICAL1 is a novel potential cancer drug target. By characterizing how MICAL1-induced protein oxidation affects cellular functions, we will address a significant knowledge gap regarding protein oxidation as a fundamentally important protein modification. These studies will uncover fundamental new knowledge about the role of regulated and targeted protein oxidation in signal transduction pathways, and will determine whether MICAL1 is a critically important signal transduction intermediary, and thus a novel cancer drug target.

column36: Dissecting the homeostatic mechanisms that regulate adult stem cell proliferation
column37: Age is still considered as the greatest cancer risk factor, but according to recent evidence, it could actually be the total number of divisions stem cells execute over a lifetime that really is the greatest risk factor. Indeed, combined with a natural selection favouring enhanced growth and survival abilities, the stochastic accumulation of genetic and epigenetic errors, which mainly occur during cell division, inevitably tends to transform our stem cells into cancer cells as they divide over the course of our lives. Most of our differentiated cells, in contrast, have limited division potentials, such that the risk that they progressively transform to initiate tumorigenesis is much smaller. Thus, this emerging theory essentially claims that the longer we live, the more our stem cells divide, the more they accumulate changes and can progress towards unscheduled growth and eventually, tumorigenesis. The eventual transformation of a stem cell into a cancer cell requires escaping from the in vivo mechanisms that keep stem cell proliferation under control. Indeed, when stem cells are taken outside of animals and cultured in vitro (in the absence of these in vivo control mechanisms), they readily proliferate to form a tumour. To understand the initial transformation steps that may underlie stem cell-based tumorigenesis, we therefore need to define those in vivo mechanisms that limit stem cell proliferation. One such mechanism ensures stem cells only divide when the tissue they serve needs new differentiated cells. Homeostatic stem cell regulation is conserved and its localized properties may offer potential means to influence individual stem cell population activities by drugs in vivo, which could greatly impact our medical strategies in regenerative medicine, and cancer prevention/treatment. We recently established a powerful model system in C. elegans in which we plan to efficiently elucidate how homeostatic stem cell regulation is locally achieved in vivo.

column36: Kwiis hen niip - Change: Change for emergency care services in rural and remote Indigenous communities in British Columbia.
column37: The health care system has failed the Indigenous peoples of Canada; a history of abuse and mistreatment has left many communities with higher rates of disease, suicide, and shorter lifespans. Many communities are far from hospital. There are stories of medical emergencies that face stormy weather, no available boats or helicopters, unavailable responders with first aid training, no cell service, and missing medical supplies. This project, Kwiis hen niip, the Nuu-chah-nulth term for 'change', aims to be a small part of reconciliation to help change some of these glaring inequities. Teamwork is key to solving these complex problems. Our research project brings communities, researchers, government, and health service organizations together to design and evaluate solutions that address problems head on. The research will focus on four Nuu chah nulth communities living on the west coast of Vancouver Island. We have found that government and organizations have many excellent ideas to address the gaps in emergency care; however, these services are uncoordinated and scattered and often not co-developed with Indigenous communities. Our research aims to bring community voices and experience together with service providers and feature indigenous research methods to create and evaluate innovative solutions to improve emergency care. The project team is careful not to fall into colonialistic patterns that interfere with the right to self-determination (to have control of their own lives). We have had several meetings with community members. The project has been met with enthusiasm overlaying a deep frustration that these inequities even exist in. Distinct themes have emerged: first responder support and training, transport, communications, and community readiness. Partner organizations involved will help to improve these essential components of emergency response in an effort to have a holistic model of emergency care with targeted solutions to community-defined challenges.

Given that stemming increasing chronic disease rates is a priority in the Canadian healthcare system, we propose an innovative school-based transportation intervention to build lifelong healthy physical activity habits. Students and parents from grades 4-6 at 24 schools will be involved in this study. Twelve schools will receive the intervention, while the other twelve will be used as control schools. We will compare changes over time in travel mode choice, physical activity levels, and air pollution between intervention and control schools. We hypothesize that students attending schools involved in the STP program will use more active travel modes, be more active, and have better air quality around school. This research will contribute to improving the effectiveness of STP programs for improving child health across Canada.

column36: Actin regulation of ciliogenesis: unraveling novel mechanisms of human ciliopathies caused by mutations in the PCP effector genes
column37: Some very severe human developmental disorders are caused by dysfunction of the microscopic hair-like structure (primary cilium). Primary cilium projects from most cells in the human body and acts like a "GPS- antenna" to survey the environment outside cells and transduce this information into inside the cell so that the cells can adjust their shape, movement and proliferation and other functions during organ development. It is therefore not surprising that defects in primary cilia lead to a wide-range of congenital abnormalities affecting brain, heart, skeleton, and kidneys. Ciliopathies are incurable and may cause fetal death, considerable morbidity after birth or reduced longevity. Investigation of the functions of the genes mutated in humans is crucial if we want to find a cure for ciliopathies. We focus on a specific group of genes (Fuzzy, Inturned and Wdpcp), termed PCP effectors. Mutations in these 3 genes are associated with various human ciliopathies which feature facial and rib defects, neural tube defects, and cystic kidneys. Mouse mutants for these genes have severe malformations which resemble features of humans with PCP effector gene mutations. Using cells and mice bearing mutations of the Fuzzy as our main experimental model, we will try to identify and explain the mechanisms through which loss of Fuzzy (and its molecular partners, Inturned and Wdpcp) disturbs generation of cilia and distorts the cilial signals that are so crucial for normal development. Based on our studies, we hope to offer novel therapeutic strategy for the severe human developmental defects caused by the mutation in the PCP effector genes and, likely, other ciliopathies.

column36: Investigation of CSF1 hematopoietic niches in atherosclerosis
column37: A quarter of all deaths in Canada are caused by complications associated with cardiovascular disease. The main cause of vascular disease is atherosclerosis, or build-up of plaque in the arteries. Atherosclerosis is an inflammatory disease in which white blood cells, including monocytes and macrophages (MO), accumulate progressively in the expanding arterial wall. Once in atherosclerotic plaques, monocytes/MO ingest lipoproteins and become lipid-loaded foam cells, a key culprit in atherosclerosis and its complications. As atherosclerosis develops, monocytes and MO increase in number in several tissues including the blood, bone marrow, spleen, and developing plaques in the arteries. These tissue micro-environments or niches maintain monocyte/MO and coordinate their function by producing factors that act directly on them. Identification of the cells within these niches and the mechanisms by which they regulate monocytes/MO affords the opportunity to better understand inflammation and identify new targets for therapy. Our preliminary data shows that monocytes and MO accumulate near either arterial or venous blood vessels, depending on the tissues in which they reside. Based on these observations, we propose that in atherosclerosis, harmful monocyte/MO responses are regulated within perivascular niches. To test our hypothesis, we will use sophisticated animal models of atherosclerosis in which macrophage colony stimulating factor 1 (CSF1) - a key factor required for maintenance of monocytes/MO - is preferentially deleted in specific cell types. Using state-of-the-art immunological methods, including flow cytometry and single cell RNA sequencing, we will determine how specific niche components affect inflammation as atherosclerosis develops. We anticipate that information gained from the proposed studies will provide mechanistic information and a rationale for new therapeutic approaches targeting monocyte/MO niche biology in atherosclerotic disease.

column37: One of the most conspicuous characteristics of any organism is its ability to react to salient stimuli with an appropriate behavioral response that maximizes survival and minimizes threatening or unpleasant events. In mammals, emotions have been proposed as the evolutionary strategy to detect changes, either internally or from the environment, to organize proper behavioral responses. When combined with different behavioral tests commonly used with mice, these approaches will allow us to precisely dissect how serotoninergic neural pathways in the brain process emotions to organize proper behavioral responses. We will also perform electrophysiological recordings at these serotoninergic pathways from normal and depressed mice to reveal cellular and molecular dysfunctions underlying cognitive and behavioral deficits associated with mood disorders. In the long term, our work will lead in the development of new therapeutic approaches to ultimately help people suffering from mood disorders.

column36: Targeting lysophosphatidate (LPA) signaling to improve therapeutic outcomes for breast cancer patients
column37: Chemotherapy and radiotherapy (RT) are an essential treatment for eliminating cancer cells. These treatments often fail and the tumour spreads to other organs. Also, a common side effect of RT is scarring. About 60% of breast cancer patients have tumours removed surgically (lumpectomy). They are then treated with 16 daily doses of RT to the remaining breast. This causes inflammation and production of a compound called LPA. Repeating the RT amplifies this effect. LPA protects cancer cells from being killed by RT and it is also responsible for scarring, which occurs in 28% of breast cancer patients. Scarring causes pain, distress and shrinkage of the breast, which in severe cases requires cosmetic correction. We discovered that an anti-inflammatory agent (dexamethasone) blocks the effects of LPA. This decreases scarring in the breast and underlying lungs, which are damaged by collateral radiation. Dexamethasone could be used to improve the outcomes of patients from RT, but we will study other anti-inflammatory agents that have fewer side effects. These include a new drug that blocks LPA formation. This compound halts the progression of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis where scarring develops in the absence of RT. Compounds, which are designed to block the effects of LPA, have never been used in cancer treatments. This provides an ideal opportunity to improve the outcomes of breast cancer patients from RT and chemotherapy. To translate our work into clinical practice, we will perform the first studies on how breast cancer patients treated with RT activate the effects of LPA. We predict that those patients who show the highest and longest LPA responses will be the ones to develop fibrosis. This work will lay the foundations for designing a clinical trial where we will test if blocking the effects of LPA prevents long-term fibrosis. This work can be extended to other cancers where RT produces such severe scarring that its use is restricted.

column37: Income and housing are pervasive social determinants of health. New Brunswick is experiencing a low-income epidemic. New Brunswick's low-income rate is significantly higher than the overall rate of low-income in Canada. Rent geared-to-income ("public") housing provides low-income households with more affordable accommodations. In theory, subsidized rents should provide greater access to residual income, which can improve health outcomes. However, to date, little is known about the health and wellbeing of tenants who reside in public housing. This is especially problematic for New Brunswick, a province with a rural landscape and low population density, whose inhabitants also experience challenges with mental health, income inequality, social exclusion, and lengthy waitlists for primary care physicians. This study addresses a large gap in knowledge of the contributions of housing to health. Public housing applicants will be systematically surveyed on their mental health at baseline and again at 6 month intervals as they wait for and are housed in public housing. Additionally, participants' housing dates will be linked to a provincial administrative database using health card numbers. This database contains the Discharge Abstracts Database (DAD) will be used to compare healthcare use for a period of 18 months pre and post-move. Healthcare use is operationalized in the DAD as visits to primary health providers, walk-in clinics, and hospitalizations. Knowledge of housing and health is sparse in Canada and this study provides crucial information on the contribution of housing to health. This study will provide stakeholders with a wealth of health information on a population that is historically under-researched, underserved and unhealthy.

column37: Depression is now the leading cause of ill health and disability worldwide. There remain three important unmet needs in the treatment of depression. Specifically, there is urgency for medications with faster therapeutic action, a requirement for higher rates of recovery and effective strategies to maintain the antidepressant response for patients with major depressive disorder. Strikingly, low doses of ketamine can produce a rapid antidepressant effect (within 24 hours) in a significant number of patients with treatment-resistant depression (TRD). The third goal is to determine the brain adaptations that occur with repeated ketamine administration that can maintain its antidepressant effects, as was shown in our clinical study. Understanding the mechanisms underlying the rapid antidepressant effects of ketamine, their transient nature, and how they can be maintained, will inform design of new treatment strategies aimed at inducing rapid and sustained antidepressant response.

column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder affecting over 2% of the worldwide population. Classical hallmarks of this disorder are a progressive loss of cells from the brain, and an accumulation of protein clumps termed Lewy bodies (LBs). LBs are observed early in the development of PD, and imaging studies have shown that these LBs can move throughout the brain ultimately leading to a loss of cells within the brains of PD patients. The predominant component of these clumps is alpha-synuclein (alpha-syn), with recent studies identifying a new disease-causing mechanism by which alpha-syn can move from cell to cell, acting as a template to seed new clumps. Thus, preventing the spread of these toxic alpha-syn seeds represents an attractive therapeutic approach. However, to date much is still unknown about how these inclusions form and move around within the brain using animal models. To move away from animal models, and to understand better how alpha-syn acts, we are proposing to use cells present within the human brain to gain insight into the mechanisms behind this devastating human disease. For making these cells from the brain, we will take advantage of new stem cell technology, in which we can form stem cells from a person's skin or blood. These induced stem cells, or iPSCs; can be directed into flat 2D neuronal networks on a dish, or into a free-floating 3D spherical interconnected neuronal structures, termed minibrains. Using these human models, we will perform a comprehensive study to understand what cells are the the main receiving/distribution hubs for making and moving these clumps between cells. By working in two different types of human models, we believe our findings will translate more effectively into our understanding of PD and illuminate how these toxic clumps traverse the brain, accompanied by a progressive loss of cells and a worsening in PD symptoms.

column36: Characterization of the transcriptional and post-transcriptional iron regulome
column37: Nearly all life forms on earth require iron to survive. Iron is important for many functions in our body, and probably best known for its role in transporting oxygen, allowing us to breathe. Once oxygen is taken up through the lung, it is transferred to an iron atom that sits at the centre of a special molecule called heme. The heme molecule itself is docked to a larger structure called hemoglobin, and together, they deliver oxygen to where it is needed via the bloodstream. These heme groups are also important for other processes in our cells, including the removal of harmful substances and the production of steroid hormones, like the famous testosterone. The King-Jones lab uses the fruit fly as a model to study undiscovered aspects of iron biology. For instance, they discovered that steroid hormone-producing cells have a high demand for iron and heme. Importantly, King-Jones and colleagues realized that they can take advantage of these cells to learn new things about how humans regulate their iron "balance sheet". Since both too much and too little iron can cause severe diseases in humans, it is essential that we learn more about how iron handled in our bodies, and how this is regulated. Using a range of genetic tricks, King-Jones and colleagues have recently discovered more than 20 genes with unexpected roles in regulating and balancing appropriate iron levels. The proposal focuses on the so-called "Iron Regulatory Protein 1" (IRP1) and how it regulates genes important for the safe handling of iron. The King-Jones lab has shown that IRP1 regulates more genes than previously thought and that this occurs by new, unexpected mechanisms. The study of these new, unexpected aspects of iron biology will improve our understanding of diseases that are caused by too much or too little iron.

column36: Modeling the Transition to Cocaine Addiction in Rats
column37: Drug addiction is amongst the leading preventable causes of death and illness in the world. In Canada, cocaine is now the most used illicit drug. Drug addiction is involved in the death of one in five people, and addiction costs Canadians nearly $40 billion per year. Over half of people addicted to cocaine seek treatment, but the prevalence of cocaine addiction has not decreased over time. This is in part because there are no approved medications to treat cocaine addiction. To develop new medications, we need to understand how initial cocaine use changes the brain, psychological function and behaviour to promote the transition from casual drug use to addiction. Animal models are on the front lines to achieve this, because laboratory animals can show the characteristic behavioural features of addiction. This in turn allows researchers to study how drugs change the brain to produce these features. Currently, the most widely used procedure to study cocaine addiction in laboratory animals involves allowing them to self-administer cocaine continuously for several hours a day. However, an alternative model has recently been developed, that might better capture the intermittent-rather than continuous-pattern of cocaine use in humans. This new model also appears especially effective in producing addiction-like features in animals. Our goal here is to directly compare and contrast these two models of addiction. We will also focus on cocaine-induced changes in i) the actions of the chemical messenger dopamine, which mediates motivation for rewards, and ii) neuronal activity in brain circuits involving a brain region called the prefrontal cortex, which mediates judgement and self-regulation. We expect that our findings will be critical in helping researchers make informed decisions about how to model addiction-like features in laboratory animals. This in turn will be important in determining directions for new anti-addiction medications in people.

These results lead to a hypothesis that different subunits/regions of AMPARs differentially contribute to synaptic and cognitive impairments in AD. We will use a multidisciplinary approach and a combination of cutting-edge techniques to address this hypothesis. This project will reveal novel molecular mechanisms by which amyloid peptides cause neuronal and cognitive deficits in AD and provide highly specific therapeutic targets to treat this devastating disease.

column36: Selective Brain Hypothermia via Intranasal Cooling to Limit Brain Injury Post Cardiac Arrest
column37: There are 40,000 cardiac arrests each year in Canada. Less than 10% of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients survive to hospital discharge. Nearly 50% of survivors suffer from brain damage and only 3% to 7% are able to live independently after the event. Brain injury among survivors represents an enormous burden on patients, their families, and health care resources. The current American Heart Association guidelines on post-resuscitation care recommend cooling the whole body hence the brain to protect it from the damaging effects of cardiac arrest. Hurdles in the clinical application of cooling are: first, whole body cooling instead of cooling the brain only can trigger complications including abnormal blood clotting and new heart attack; second, to limit these deleterious effects of whole body cooling, only mild hypothermia, in which the body is cooled to 36oC has been used in clinical settings, whereas enhanced brain protection may be achieved by selectively cooling the brain quickly to below 36oC; third, there does not exist simple, effective and non-invasive method to selectively cool the brain below 36oC that can be readily applied in hospitals. We propose to develop a simple means to cool down the brain by blowing cold air, generated from compressed air, into the nostrils. This would cool down the nasal cavity which in turn would chill warm blood coming into the nasal cavity on its way to the brain. In initial testing of the method with normal pigs, we have shown that the method can selectively cool the pig brain to 34oC within 40 minutes and maintain this temperature for 6 hours before rewarming slowly over 3 hours back to normal temperature while leaving the body at normal temperature throughout this period. Before we can try this method on patients, we have to show that the method is safe to use in a large animal model, for example, pigs which have similar physiology to humans. We also have to show that the method is able to protect the brain.

column37: One out of every five Canadians lives with chronic pain. A common problem reported by people living with pain is that their health providers do not have the required understanding and skills to provide them with effective care. This can result in misunderstanding, stigma, uncontrolled symptoms and prolonged disability. National strategies to address these problems focus on resolving important inconsistencies in how health providers are initially trained to manage pain. We will interview faculty members in PT programs across the country; create a new assessment tool to evaluate PT students' knowledge and skills in pain management; and run the first nation-wide assessment to determine effectiveness of PT training programs in preparing PTs to manage pain. One of the innovative aspects of this project is that people living with pain will help create the assessment tool that will be used to determine whether PTs are adequately prepared to manage pain. Importantly, this assessment tool will include both written and practical components. The practical component of this assessment will be particularly useful in establishing the communication and interpersonal skills that are essential to effective pain management. Therefore, one of the important contributions of this work is that people living with pain will have the chance to shape the standards by which future health providers will be evaluated, thus ensuring they have the required knowledge and skills to provide effective care for the millions of Canadians suffering from pain.

column36: Healthy brain growth in preterm children for optimal function: do males and females differ?
column37: In Canada and around the world, babies born too early (preterm) are at high risk of brain injuries that lead to developmental disabilities. Newborn brain injury was once considered a single event with fixed consequences. Our work is changing how we think about brain injury in preterm babies. We discovered that brain injury influences how the brain grows, and that the consequences of newborn brain injury change over time and vary from child to child. We showed that routine "everyday" events experienced by hospitalized sick newborns, like pain from life-saving procedures and medications, may affect patterns of brain growth as well as motor, thinking and language skills across childhood. We have identified everyday clinical practices for sick preterm newborns and social factors that foster their early motor, thinking and language development as toddlers. Yet, we do not know if those changes in brain and development differ in girls and boys, or how the changes affect their school-age functions and behavior. Given these gaps in our understanding, we propose to answer the key question posed by parents of preterm children every day: How do I give my child every chance for her/his best future outcome? We have studied a unique group of babies born very preterm using detailed measures of infant brain growth, clinical factors during neonatal intensive care, and early motor, thinking and language development. We now propose to assess how brain growth and children's functions and behavior at 4.5 and 8 years of age differ in girls and boys. By studying children from birth to age 8, we will: 1. Determine how the relationship between newborn brain injury and brain growth to age 8 years is modified by the child's sex. 2. Determine how the child's sex modifies the link between brain growth and thinking skills and behavior at age 8 years. 3. Develop better ways to predict school-age function (e.g. thinking, language) using knowledge of the child's sex and her/his brain development.

column36: Understanding and Optimizing Opioid Use in Long Term Care.
column37: Many older adults residing in long-term care facilities (or nursing homes), including those without cancer, live with daily pain. This is often because of arthritis or related bone or joint conditions. For many residents, this pain may be poorly recognized or treated leading to lower quality of life and worse health outcomes. This is often because older residents have many other conditions, and use many different medications, that may cause them to show symptoms of pain in unusual ways or that may increase their risk for particular treatment side effects. As a result, doctors, other healthcare staff and family members may find it difficult to know when pain is present or whether a particular medication (or dose) is the best approach to treatment. There are also no current Canadian guidelines for how best to treat or manage ongoing non-cancer pain (including for the use of strong pain medications like opioids) among residents of long-term care facilities. This research, involving a team of university researchers, health care and policy experts from across Canada, aims to better understand factors that may be associated with the poor recognition and/or treatment of chronic non-cancer pain in long-term care residents living in Ontario, Saskatchewan and Alberta. An important focus of the work is to examine whether different pain treatments (including opioids) are being used in ways that enhance residents' quality of life while lowering their risks of medication side effects. Research findings will be used to support care guidelines and interventions to improve pain detection and management in long-term care and ultimately, the quality of life and health of vulnerable older women and men residing in these care settings.

column36: Unhealthy food and beverage sponsorship of children's sports clubs in two policy environments
column37: Unhealthy food marketing has been shown to promote poor dietary behaviors and obesity among children. The sponsorship of sports clubs is one type of marketing to which youth are exposed. Evidence from abroad suggests that this promotional technique, which allows for extended and repeated exposure to marketing, is frequently used to promote unhealthy food brands to youth. To date, no research has measured the extent, nature and impact of food company sponsorship of sports clubs in Canada nor has any research examined the financial impact of sponsorship on children's access to sports. The perceptions of parents and sports club officials regarding this activity and its restriction are also unknown. The purpose of this study is to determine the frequency and healthfulness of food company sponsorship of junior sports clubs in Canada, to examine its potential effects on the dietary behaviors of youth and to understand the perceptions of parents and sport club officials regarding this activity. To do so, this study will identify junior sports clubs for the 8 most popular sports among youth (5-17 years) in 7 cities in Ontario and 7 in Quebec. Sports club officials will be interviewed over the phone to identify all food company sponsors and to determine how much funding and other benefits they receive from food company sponsorship. The attitudes of parents and sports club officials regarding food company sponsorship and its restriction will also be assessed using surveys and individual interviews. Finally, surveys and focus groups will be conducted with youth to determine whether sponsorship influences their food purchasing or dietary behaviors and to understand their attitudes toward food sponsors. This research will help inform Canadian policies aimed at protecting children from unhealthy food marketing and improving their diet and health.

column36: PRECEDE: Preconception risk factors and Cardiometabolic health in Early childhood
column37: Cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes are major public health priorities. More than 1 in 3 Canadian children have factors that put them at risk for type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, including overweight and obesity, unhealthy lifestyle behaviours, and abnormal measures of blood pressure, cholesterol, and glucose. The first 1000 days, including the period before pregnancy (called 'preconception') represents an important period in which maternal and paternal physical health, mental health, lifestyle behaviours, and family functioning may impact the growth and development of children. However, a critical gap in knowledge exists on the role of these preconception maternal and paternal risk factors. A study that begins in preconception and follows families through to child health outcomes beyond birth does not currently exist. We will invite pregnancy-planning parents who have a child already participating in the largest ongoing study of children in the primary care practice setting in Canada called TARGet Kids!. We will collect data on weight, mental health, lifestyle behaviours, and family functioning in 1180 mothers and fathers who are planning a pregnancy in the next year. We will measure how these factors are related to their child's health at 2 years of age. Child health outcomes will include weight, blood pressure, blood cholesterol, blood sugar and health behaviours like physical activity, sleep, and nutrition. This study is important because prior research has shown that young children who had higher weight, cholesterol, blood pressure and blood sugar had higher weight, heart-health and diabetes risk as they became adults. Therefore this study will help us understand which factors parents may modify before they are pregnant in order to help reduce heart-health and diabetes risk factors in early childhood and beyond. This study will be among the first in the world to help answer these important questions.

column36: Probing molecular and mechanical signals that shape blood vessel growth
column37: Vascular malformations are very common in humans and include arteriovenous malformations (connections of arteries and veins directly), capillary malformations (dilated, disorganized vessels with abnormally fast or slow circulation) and vascular tumors such as hemangioma. Rasa1 is a gene that causes capillary and arteriovenous malformations (CM-AVM) when mutated in humans and was one of the first vascular malformation genes identified. In the past 5 years we have found that many human vascular malformations and tumors are caused by mutations in genes that function in a pathway related to Rasa1. Surprisingly, benign malformations and vascular tumors can be caused by mutations in the same genes; we do not understand why some are benign and some malignant. Also, the only treatments currently available are not based on scientific evidence but are 'best guesses. Our goals in this project are to identify mechanisms and possible therapeutics for vascular malformations, focusing on Rasa1. We will study this gene in an animal model where Rasa1 is lost. We will test its role in the blood vessel wall and identify small molecules that improve malformations.

column36: The Artificial Placenta
column37: Preterm birth remains the leading cause of death in children under the age of 5 worldwide. Despite advances in the technology used in neonatal intensive care practice, complications due to the damage of immature organs resulting from premature exposure to life outside the womb are common and often lead to ongoing health issues throughout life. The creation of an artificial environment that imitates the mother's womb and protects the fetus from injury while also promoting normal growth and development may be a solution for extremely preterm infants. In collaboration with the leading US research group working in this field, we have shown in an animal model that it is possible to create such an environment using a fluid-filled bag and an oxygenator circuit connected to the umbilical cord which acts as an artificial placenta. However, our preliminary experiments indicate that commercially available oxygenator technology designed for term infants undergoing cardiac surgery are unlikely to be appropriate for use in the extremely preterm human infants that are the target population for this research. The current research proposal aims to collect information about critical elements of the human placenta at the lower limits of viability that are needed to design an artificial placenta that faithfully reproduces the cardiovascular function of the real placenta. We will use this information to design and test custom made oxygenators for use as an artificial placenta in a realistic animal model of the extremely preterm human infant. Our laboratory is the first to attempt this kind of research in Canada and the work described in this proposal would represent an important step towards bringing this technology to our human patients.

column36: Implementation and Evaluation of an Indigenous-Specific Managed Alcohol Program for the Homeless Indigenous Population in Calgary, AB and Victoria, BC
column37: Indigenous peoples are disproportionately represented in the homeless population, while homeless individuals with substance dependency are an extremely vulnerable population susceptible to violence, victimization, premature death, poor health, social exclusion, marginalization and a vicious cycle of hospitalization, emergency shelter use, and incarceration. A lack of trauma-informed, culturally competent, culturally safe and Indigenous harm reduction services available for the homeless Indigenous population that struggle with severe alcohol use results in continued oppression while dismissing the importance of Indigenous epistemologies of healing. With the guidance of an Elder Advisory Circle and continued engagement with Elders, Knowledge Keepers and Indigenous community partners, the goal of this project is to implement and evaluate a managed alcohol program (MAP) that supports homeless Indigenous peoples living in Calgary and Victoria who struggle with severe alcohol use disorder. Research suggests MAPs are associated with tremendous positive outcomes including significant reductions in detox admissions, hospital visits, and police run-ins, while participants experience a better quality of life, gain better access to primary healthcare services and are more likely to retain their housing. This study will utilize a mixed-methods, community-based participatory approach that engages the Indigenous community, focuses on the priorities identified during engagement sessions, and seeks to improve the health outcomes of the homeless Indigenous population. It is anticipated results from this study will demonstrate a significant social return on investment and improve the health and well-being of the homeless Indigenous population while producing valuable outcomes that shape policy and best practices for culturally appropriate population health interventions.

column36: Le lavage uterin au salin physiologique comme traitement de l'infertilite inexpliquee: un essai clinique randomise a double insu
column37: L'infertilite atteint un couple canadien sur six. Dans plus du quart des cas, aucune cause n'est mise en evidence, c'est ce qu'on appelle l'infertilite inexpliquee. Malheureusement, les traitements indiques se limitent alors a la fecondation in vitro qui est associee a des effets secondaires et des couts importants. L'evaluation de la permeabilite tubaire est essentielle au diagnostic de l'infertilite inexpliquee afin d'exclure une obstruction des trompes uterines. Dans le mois suivant le test de la permeabilite tubaire, des etudes ont rapporte une augmentation des grossesses et naissances vivantes. En effet, il semble que le lavage uterin engendre lors de cette evaluation pourrait s'averer therapeutique. Un nombre croissant de donnees probantes, tant en recherche experimentale que clinique, suggere que certains cas d'infertilite pourraient etre causes par des facteurs mecaniques ou immunologiques au niveau de la cavite uterine empechant la fecondation. Ces facteurs seraient contres par la realisation du lavage uterin. L'etude proposee consiste en un essai clinique randomise evaluant l'efficacite du lavage uterin a l'aide d'une solution d'eau saline en pre-ovulatoire comme traitement de l'infertilite inexpliquee. Un tel traitement constituerait une avancee importante dans le domaine, puisqu'en comparaison avec les traitements actuellement disponibles, le lavage uterin pourrait s'averer une avenue therapeutique beaucoup moins invasive et couteuse.

column36: Interactions between PV interneurons and neuromodulators in cognition relevant to schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia is a neuropsychiatric disease that leads to a range of debilitating symptoms. Psychotic symptoms can be treated reasonably well, but few treatments exist for impairments in cognition including attention, working memory and cognitive flexibility. These impairments have a major impact on patients'-and their carers'-quality of life. To develop new treatments, we need to understand the brain changes underlying these cognitive impairments. Considerable research indicates that schizophrenia involves 1. dysfunction in a specific type of brain cell called a 'parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneuron' and 2. abnormal function of neuromodulators-molecules that modulate the activity of brain cells-such as dopamine and acetylcholine. Both types of dysfunction are linked with cognitive impairments. Although work is being done separately in these two areas, little is known about what these two types of brain dysfunction have to do with each other. For example, does the neuromodulator dysfunction cause or worsen the PV interneuron dysfunction? Is the interaction itself important for schizophrenia, or do the two types of dysfunction affect cognition in different ways? Recent, powerful technological developments in mice have now made this critical area of investigation possible. We will use novel, light-based techniques to observe PV interneuron and neuromodulator activity and to manipulate PV interneuron activity. This will be done while the mice engage in ipad-based cognitive tests that are identical to those used in humans, so that the findings can be more successfully translated to patients. These studies will lead to a better understanding of how brain changes lead to cognitive difficulties in schizophrenia, and how to better treat the debilitating symptoms of this devastating disease.

column36: Semaglutide in comorbid obesity and schizophrenia-spectrum disorders for metformin non-responders: a double-blind randomized control trial
column37: Almost one in every two patients with schizophrenia (SCZ) are obese and patients die 15-20 years earlier than the general population from heart disease. Medications called antipsychotics are needed to treat SCZ, but they cause a lot of weight gain. Weight gain is associated with poorer quality of life, barriers to social engagement, worse medication adherence, and poorer brain function. However, available treatments for managing obesity and related problems are not adequate. A drug called metformin has support from research studies to help treat weight gain in SCZ. However, it is effective in only about 20% of people, and doctors don't know what to use next. Newer treatments for diabetes and obesity such as a class called "glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists" (GLP-1RAs) can potentially help. Semaglutide is a newer, well-tolerated GLP-1RA, also found to have excellent weight-loss effects. We plan to study SCZ patients who suffer from obesity and don't lose weight on metformin, to see if adding semaglutide can help with body weight reduction and other risk factors for heart disease. Patients will first be treated with metformin for 4 months, and those who don't lose at least 5% of their body weight will enter a second study phase. At the start of this phase, they will be assigned to a weekly injection of semaglutide or placebo ("dummy"), which will be added to metformin. Participants have an equal chance of receiving semaglutide or the placebo. Neither patients, or study personnel know if placebo or semaglutide is being given. Over the next 6 months, participants will undergo body weight measurements, measures of blood sugar metabolism, an MRI scan to measure body fat changes, and tests of brain function to see if these improve with semaglutide. The goal of this study is to help develop logical and effective care pathways that can reduce the huge disparities in cardiovascular-related health that burden people already suffering with severe mental illness.

column36: Cellular responses to protein misfolding in a yeast model of aging
column37: Huntington's disease (HD) is neurodegenerative disease affecting one in every 7,000 Canadians. column36: Neurovascular adaptations driving stress-induced depression vs resilience
column37: Depression is the leading cause of disabilities worldwide and will affect 1 out of 5 individuals in their lifetime. Antidepressant treatments are not effective for 30-50% of patients, only 30% completely remit and do not suffer from another depressive episode, suggesting that current therapies do not address important biological mechanisms involved. We hypothesize that BBB integrity may be affected in different brain regions in females explaining sex-specific symptoms. We will also define critical time points and evaluate if vulnerability to depression can be predicted by testing BBB integrity before stress exposure. Effects of chronic stress on BBB-astrocyte interface will be characterized as well. Astrocytes are part of the neurovascular unit and maintain BBB integrity in the healthy brain. Finally, we will test prevention strategies to promote neurovascular health and stress resilience. The strength of our approach is a reverse translational strategy that consists in studying stress responses in mice to unravel novel biological mechanisms underlying depression in humans. Depression is more prevalent in women and correlated with reported stress levels in daily life. It is imperative to explore stress-induced vascular maladaptive responses to develop innovative therapeutic strategies.

column36: How does chemotherapy to treat childhood cancer affect brain development?
column37: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most common childhood cancer, with 300 new cases per year in Canada. Fortunately, current chemotherapy treatments for ALL are remarkably successful: 90% of children diagnosed with ALL will be cured. About half of these children, however, experience problems with thinking speed, attention and memory, leading to limitations in school, work or social settings, and ultimately reducing quality of life. Before we can design a strategy to improve outcomes for children, we need to understand how these problems occur. Many of the drugs used in modern chemotherapy treatments have the potential to affect brain development. In previous work, we treated mice with individual ALL chemotherapy agents and identified the three that most altered the structure of the brain. We propose a three-part research program to determine how these three agents act on the brain during ALL treatment. In the first aim, we will focus on two of the agents that - surprisingly - do not penetrate the brain. We will measure immune and hormone changes induced by chemotherapy and determine if they are responsible for affecting the brain. In the second aim, we will manipulate the identified immune and hormone changes to see if we can rescue brain development. In the third aim, we will focus on the third chemotherapy agent which does enter the brain. We will determine whether selected drugs and/or nutrition supplements can limit toxicity, promote healthy metabolism, and restore brain development. Outcomes will be evaluated based on brain structure and behaviour. Our results will help us to understand how chemotherapy interrupts brain development during ALL treatment. Such an understanding is a critical step in designing strategies to improve brain function and quality of life for future childhood cancer survivors.

column36: Overcoming resistance to antidepressant treatment
column37: Major depression strikes 1 in 6 people and is twice as prevalent in women. In Canada, it is the second leading cause of disability. Depressed people have a greater risk of anxiety, suicide and cardiovascular diseases. Since reduced serotonin often leads to depression, first-line antidepressant drugs like selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) work to increase serotonin in the brain. However, these drugs take many weeks to work and produce long-term recovery from depression in only 30% of patients. Our goal is to understand why some patients do not respond to SSRIs and find the best way to treat these patients. We focused on an important receptor for serotonin, the serotonin-1A autoreceptor. It is a strong inhibitor of the serotonin system. Human depressed patients who do not respond to SSRI treatment often have too many serotonin-1A autoreceptors. To model this genetic problem in mice, we knocked out a key genetic inhibitor of the receptor. These knockout mice have increased serotonin-1A autoreceptors and reduced serotonin. They have increased anxiety and depression traits and do not respond to SSRI treatment. Our research will compare male and female knockout mice to test how we can overcome this SSRI resistance using brain stimulation or other kinds of antidepressant drugs. In particular, we will overcome inhibition of the serotonin system using new therapies, including optogenetics to directly stimulate serotonin remodeling. Like depressed patients, our knockout mice show changes in activity in specific brain areas. Using optogenetics, we can to stimulate serotonin in specific brain areas whose activity is abnormal. column37: DNA sequencing has ushered in a "Golden Age" of disease discovery. The causes of many rare genetic diseases have been found, and the genetic contributions to common diseases are also being solved very quickly. However, digging through multiple human genomes has unearthed thousands of new DNA variants, and often it isn't obvious which ones are the disease-causing mutations that affect health, and which other ones have no health effects. Our lab focuses on rare mutations that cause human overgrowth. Overgrowth syndromes cause tall stature, large head size and medical problems such as obesity, cancer, autism and intellectual disability. Having discovered the overgrowth syndromes that are caused by rare mutations in the "PRC2" group of proteins, we're now trying to understand exactly which DNA variants in PRC2 cause overgrowth and which ones don't. We have also found that some PRC2 mutations cause other medical problems, such as muscle fatigue and even stunted growth (i.e. the opposite of overgrowth). In this project we seek to recruit people who have rare DNA variants in PRC2 members, so we can follow them over time and find out what medical problems they have (if any). Because the human PRC2 genes each have an analogous gene that does pretty much the same thing in fruit flies, we plan to engineer our human mutations into experimental fruit flies. In this way we can figure out which of our variants are true mutations that produce a non-working protein, and which variants produce a protein that works well enough to allow normal function. By taking advantage of the wealth of molecular techniques that exist for fruit flies, we can quickly find out which human variants are likely to be benign with no effects on health, and which human variants are likely to be disease-causing mutations. The data from our study will help diagnostic labs sort out the small number of disease-causing PRC2 variants from the larger number of benign DNA variants in the PRC2 proteins.

column36: Photoacoustics as a novel kidney fibrosis imaging tool
column37: 1 in 10 Canadians has kidney disease, many of whom will progress to kidney failure, a condition that leads to impaired quality of life, higher mortality, and costs of up to $100,000/pt/year. Although kidney transplantation offers hope for such patients, donor kidneys are in short supply, with patients now waiting up to 8 years for a transplant. As such, kidneys from sicker donors are frequently used, despite the fact that they are often already scarred, a process that can reduce their lifespan. While scarred kidneys are still useable, they are best transplanted into older patients, rather than younger people who need longer lasting kidneys. Importantly, scarring affects not only donor kidneys, but also drives the progression of nearly all forms of chronic kidney disease. The only way to measure scarring currently is via looking at the kidney under a microscope. In animals, this is done by taking the kidneys out. As such, serial testing can not be performed, resulting in the needless use of many animals. In humans, scarring is assessed by biopsy, an invasive procedure that samples < 1% of one kidney and can cause bleeding. Unlike biopsy, ultrasound non-invasively images the entire kidney. Our goal is to test whether ultrasound can measure scarring in rodent and human kidneys. In rodents, we will test if through-the-skin ultrasound can track kidney scarring as it progresses (Aim 1). In human studies, we will test whether our ultrasound technique can image scarring of ex vivo donor kidneys (Aim 2). If successful, our studies could have major applications for preclinical research, by allowing easy tracking of scarring in the same animal over time. Moreover, as kidneys are removed from donors prior to transplant, our work could aid in how donor kidneys are matched to recipients, to maximize the benefit for all patients. Taken together, we expect that our results could have potentially transformative effects for the study and management of kidney scarring.

column36: Post-transcriptional regulation of functionally significant gene sets during neurodevelopment of Rett syndrome
column37: Genes function by making RNA that is then "translated" into proteins. We study the neurodevelopmental disorder Rett syndrome (RTT) which is caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene. We discovered that the MECP2 gene makes RNA in human stem cells but it is not stable and is actively degraded. The ability to translate MECP2 RNA into MECP2 protein is also inhibited in stem cells and activated in nerve cells by the binding of two competing factors. These layers of RNA regulation ensure that stem cells do not make too much MECP2 protein until they mature into nerve cells, and we predict that many additional genes are subject to similar mechanisms of RNA regulation. Using RNA sequencing technologies, our preliminary experiments obtained a dataset to calculate the stability of all RNAs in these cells, and discovered a defect in protein degradation in RTT. Our overall goal is to comprehensively understand RNA regulation in human stem cells as they develop into nerve cells, and use this information to find proteins that are perturbed in RTT and which alter nerve cell function. AIM 1 will explore translational regulation of genes that control protein stability, and will identify the proteins that escape degradation and accumulate in RTT nerve cells. AIM 2 will identify global changes in RNA stability that occur as stem cells mature into healthy or RTT nerve cells. The underlying mechanisms controlling RNA stability will also be defined, and the impact on protein levels assessed in RTT nerve cells. The expected outcomes will be the elucidation of RNA regulation of genes in healthy and RTT nerve cells that can be applied to unveil perturbed proteins that are candidates for future drug development.

column36: A multicentre, double blind, randomized trial comparing lyophilized fecal filtrate to lyophilized stool in treating recurrent Clostridiodes difficile infection
column37: Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI), the most common bowel infection in the hospital setting, is usually triggered by antibiotics. The treatment for CDI is with another antibiotic called vancomycin. After treatment, the chance of CDI coming back is about 20% after the initial episode, increasing to at least 60% after the 3rd episode. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), or stool transplant, is the most effective therapy for recurrent CDI (RCDI). The success rate is 80-90%. However, we don't know how it works. Recently there were 2 cases of mutli-drug resistant organism (MDRO) transmitted through FMT, resulting in one death. Both patients were immunosuppressed and their donor was not tested for MDRO. Furthermore, we do not know if there are long-term effects. For example, studies in mice have shown that obesity can be transferred with FMT, thus raising the possibility that other conditions such as autoimmune diseases and cancer could potentially be transferred with FMT. Therefore, safer and targeted therapy is needed, but we need to understand how FMT works first. The assumption is that transferring healthy gut bacteria from a donor to a patient corrects the disrupted gut bacterial community, but there may be more to this. A recent study showed despite removing live bacteria from donor stool, 5 RCDI patients were still successfully treated. This brings into question whether components in the stool other than live bacteria may be crucial. We believe that live bacteria may not be necessary for FMT to work. In this proposal, we will compare two forms of FMT: one with live bacteria and one without. Both formulations will be freeze-dried and put into pills. By removing live bacteria from the equation, this study will conclusively show whether other components within stool are enough to reshape the bacterial community in the gut. The results will lay foundation for future effort in developing more targeted RCDI treatment.

column36: Deciphering the role of the Yin Yang1 (YY1) transcription factor to understand pleuropulmonary blastoma
column37: Pediatric lung cancers are rare but diverse. Pleuropulmonary blastoma (PPB) is the most common pediatric primary lung cancer. It arises during fetal life and occurs in children under 7 years of age. PPB results from the progression of abnormal lung cysts to an aggressive sarcoma with poor survival. It is crucial to correctly recognize PPB early since it is the most curable stage. We produced a mutant mouse line devoid of YY1 function in lung epithelium. YY1 is a transcription factor essential for normal and cancer development. The mutation causes lung cysts as those seen in PPB patients at early stage. Accordingly, less YY1 protein is detected in PPB patients. PPB is associated with mutations in DICER1, an enzyme important for the production of microRNAs. microRNAs negatively control gene expression. How DICER1 and microRNAs act in PPB remains ill-defined. Our data suggested that the low YY1 protein levels detected in PPB are due to abnormal microRNAs caused by the DICER1 mutations. We also showed that the Yy1 mutation in mice affects the expression of key regulators of lung formation and that similar changes are seen in PPB patients. These data led us to hypothesize that reduced expression of YY1 participates in PPB pathogenesis by perturbing the expression of key regulators of lung development. Our objective is to elucidate the role of YY1 in PPB based on our knowledge of the mechanisms of action fulfilled by YY1 during lung formation. We propose to: (1) determine the role of microRNAs in YY1 expression, (2) identify the gene networks controlled by YY1 during lung formation, and (3) test if modulating the levels of YY1 effectors can rescue the cystic lung phenotype of mutant mice. Characterizing the YY1-driven basic mechanisms by which lung development occurs is important for understanding human diseases such as PPB.

column36: Solute transport in the innate immune response
column37: Cells are the smallest independent units of plants and animals. Virtually all human organs and tissues have specialized, sentinel cells (macrophages) that are dedicated to protecting the body from infection, damage, or toxins. When macrophages detect harmful stimuli, they cause inflammation, a protective response meant to eliminate the cause of the insult. The extent of this response needs to be measured by macrophages; too little inflammation enables the insult to persist and possibly worsen, while chronic inflammation is associated with multiple diseases including arthritis, atherosclerosis, and cancer. To detect signs of a threat, macrophages probe and survey their locale using sensors that distinguish harmful from healthy components. Second -and because some threats can be well-hidden- they internalize and digest massive quantities of their surroundings to expose such threats internally. Once swallowed, the ingested materials are sealed in a vacuole, digested, and probed for any signs of harm. These later steps require the evolution of the vacuole to acquire degradative enzymes, acidify, and distribute the contents to internal detectors. The consumption performed by macrophages is impressive; they take up their own body weight in just a matter of hours. An overlooked but essential part of the whole process is that the cells must expel these large volumes to maintain their appetite and surveillance. Excreting the remains of the ingested samples, a process termed resolution, is also essential to controlling infection/inflammation. I have obtained evidence that the resolution process is orchestrated by transporters: channels that expel the smallest components of the ingested medium out of the vacuole and cell. The objective of the proposed research is to now understand how the resolution process, orchestrated by our macrophages, is regulated, and why alterations in its regulation cause these cells to contribute to disease rather than correct it.

column36: Unplanned Hospital Readmission Following Critical Illness Survival: An Investigation of the Survivor-Family Dyad
column37: In Canada, the high (38-41%) unplanned hospital readmission rate in the year following intensive care unit (ICU) points to insufficient care of these vulnerable patients. Most individuals treated in an ICU will survive yet, up to half of these survivors suffer new or worsening physical, cognitive and psychiatric complications, termed post-intensive care syndrome. Family often become informal caregivers, but also suffer physical and mental health impairment, as well as loss of employment, financial difficulties and low quality of life. These complex, long-term complications often go unrecognized or untreated in the community, and result in survivor dependence on acute care services. While person-centred care entails addressing what matters most to survivors and families, there is limited understanding of what this even is, or how this influences health services use, eventually culminating in hospital readmission. The aim of this research is to describe the relationship between ICU survivors, their family caregivers and the healthcare system from the perspective of the survivor-family dyad, what matters to this dyad, and how this relationship influences unplanned hospital readmission. We will interview survivors, family caregivers and health care providers to develop an explanatory model, which will be extended and refined through focus groups across the Province of British Columbia. Study findings will inform the development of health services specific to ICU survivors.

column36: How can health benefits of an effective, scaled-up, health promotion model for older adults be sustained?
column37: One-third of Canadians will be an older adult (>65y) by 2050. Thus, healthy aging is a public health priority. Many older adult health promoting interventions have been implemented, yet few were scaled-up and none were sustained. CTM is an effective, adaptable health promotion program for older adults. CTM improved healthy aging indicators-mobility, social connectedness, and decreased loneliness of older adults. We are now scaling-up Choose to Move (CTM) across British Columbia (BC) with support from BC Ministry of Health. Community partners and older adults identified three elements essential to CTM success: program flexibility, social interactions, and trusted relationships between participants and activity coaches (who deliver CTM). In this CTM sustainability (CTM-S) study we aim to determine if health benefits of CTM can be maintained. Therefore, we integrated the three essential elements into design of CTM-S and will assess three follow-up approaches: 1. activity coaches hold annual group meetings and call participants quarterly; 2. government service staff (HealthLinkBC) call participants quarterly; 3. we create a Facebook group for CTM-S participants and prompt participants daily. In a fourth group we will not actively follow-up. We will allocate 166 CTM programs (1743 participants) to follow-up arms. In our evaluation we will: 1) assess if during follow-up older adults' mobility, social connectedness/loneliness, physical activity and sedentary time across 12 and 24 months are maintained; 2) measure costs associated with each follow-up arm, program affordability and value to policy makers; 3) identify factors that support or inhibit implementation of CTM-S. Our team has expertise in older adult health promotion and implementation science research, trainee mentorship, economic evaluation and knowledge translation. We endeavour to generate strategies that can be used to implement and sustain effective health promotion strategies for older adults across Canada.

column36: Kidney and blood pressure disease burden and monitoring for chronic kidney disease in childhood cancer survivors
column37: Due to better cancer treatments in the last 30 years, more and more children with cancer are surviving. Yet, childhood cancer survivors (or CCS) get many health issues later in life, due to their cancer treatments. CCS often have kidney problems (Chronic Kidney Disease, or CKD) and high blood pressure (Hypertension, or HTN) later in life, which increase their chances for heart disease and many other serious health problems Ideally, CKD and HTN should be treated as soon as possible after cancer treatment, to prevent long-term kidney and heart issues. The first 5 years after cancer therapy is the best time to detect, prevent and treat CKD and HTN in childhood, before they worsen. Unfortunately, when CKD and HTN first appear after cancer therapy or if doctors are even testing for complications of CKD, isn't clear. Recommendations on testing for kidney and blood pressure issues after children finish cancer treatment are not very helpful to patients or doctors. This probably leads to missed opportunities to detect, prevent and treat CKD and HTN in these fragile patients. In the next 6 years, our team of doctors, researchers and patients want to understand kidney and blood pressure problems in the first few years after children finish their cancer treatments and whether doctors are testing for CKD and its complications. 1) We will study 500 CCS across Ontario, 3 and 5 years after they finish cancer treatment, to know how many have CKD and HTN early after cancer therapy and if they get worse over time. 2) In 5000 CCS treated for cancer from 2008-2018 we will find out if doctors have been testing for kidney problems and CKD complications. With this information, we will know what is needed to change recommendations on when and how to test for kidney and blood pressure issues after children finish cancer treatment, with the hopes that they get the CKD and HTN treatments they need, have less long-term kidney or heart disease and better overall health and well-being.

column36: The role of Parkinson's disease-related proteins in innate and adaptive immunity
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by motor impairment associated with the loss of dopaminergic neurones (DNs). Recent evidences indicate that the disease might be initiated away from the brain in peripheral tissues and involve autoimmune mechanisms. We have shown that two proteins associated with PD, PINK1 and Parkin, actively repress the immune system by limiting the presentation of mitochondrial antigens. In the absence of these proteins, or during a loss of function, stress conditions related to inflammation and fever triggers the presentation of mitochondrial proteins at the surface of a variety of cells of the immune system, as well as DNs. Our data indicate that this process engages autoimmune mechanisms leading the the establishment of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells able to recognize and attack DNs. In the next 5 years, we will characterize the role of PD-related proteins in mitochondrial antigen presentation (MitAP) and the engagement of autoimmune mechanisms. Understanding the molecular mechanisms regulating MitAP is of prime importance to develop therapies that would target the immune system.

column36: Uncovering the unexpected role of LTR promoter mutations in HIV-1 latency
column37: Viral latency currently constitutes one of the most formidable obstacles to curing HIV infection. Combination antiretroviral therapy (cART) is extremely effective at suppressing HIV infection and replication, but fails to eliminate long-lived immune cells infected with a dormant or latent virus. Latent viruses can persist indefinitely inside a cell until reactivated in periods of stress or when a patient interrupts cART. Several cellular mechanisms have been identified that can partially explain how HIV becomes latent, but the complete scheme of latency inducing factors has not yet been defined. Our research has recently revealed that certain types of mutations caused by the viral polymerase and by host immune proteins called APOBEC3 can contribute to create mutated viruses with a predisposition to become latent, thereby highlighting a potential new mechanism for latency. The research we propose will explore how these mutations cause HIV to become latent and in some instances resist the effects of various latency-reversing agents (LRAs). Our research will help to better understand HIV latency, contribute to the design of a new platform for testing the next generation of LRAs, and identify prognostic mutations in the viral DNA that will help predict the effectiveness of latency-reversal therapies.

column36: The Molecular Memory of Voltage-Gated Potassium Channels
column37: Neuronal activity is based on electrical signals in the cell wall of the neurons, leading to socalled action potentials. Small proteins in the cell wall, named ion channels, generate the electrical signals by letting sodium, calcium and potassium ions enter or leave the cells selectively and precisely timed. Learning and formation of memory is caused by repeatedly conditioning the electrical paths in the brain, reinforcing or abandoning neuronal connections. Upon this repeated or prolonged activation, the ion channels undergo an adaptation, which means that they develop a kind of short-term memory but on the scale of a single protein. The aim of this study is to understand how these molecular memories work. In principal, we are performing biomedical "reverse engineering" to unravel how the proteins work on the molecular level. To this end, we will use biophysical methods, in particular optical spectroscopy methods, (fluorescence) to directly follow movements of specific regions of the channels. These measurements are combined with functional measurements to correlate, in time, movement and function, and with molecular biology to manipulate the protein on an atomic level.

column36: Promoting Resolution of Acute Kidney Injury
column37: Acute kidney injury due to poor blood flow to the kidneys is among the most common causes of illness and death in hospitalized patients. Many patients who recover from initial injury are left with lasting kidney damage. Despite a better understanding, even at the level of the cell, of the events that cause progressive kidney damage, no treatments have emerged in the last few decades. The consequences of acute kidney injury are particularly devastating in kidney transplantation, and can greatly shorten the length of time in which transplanted kidneys continue to function. Progressive damage after acute kidney injury results from three main events, namely, excessive infiltration of white blood cells from the bloodstream into the injured kidney, formation of small blood clots within the kidney, and activation of cells that produce scar tissue. We discovered that Slit and Roundabout (Robo), molecules that block migration of brain cells during brain development before birth, can simultaneously block all three events, and prevent lasting kidney damage. Using a pig model, we also developed a new method of preservation of donor kidneys that allows even the most severely injured kidneys- kidneys that would never before have been deemed suitable for transplantation- to function after transplanting them. After acute kidney injury, some patients recover completely. The signals that favour resolution, rather than progression, of injury, are not well understood. The pro-resolving family of molecules enhance resolution of injury. The studies we propose will use molecular, cellular, and biochemical approaches, together with mouse models of acute kidney injury to determine how Slit and Robo act in concert with pro-resolvins to promote kidney recovery. Using our pig model of kidney transplant preservation, we will examine how Slit and pro-resolvins can be harnessed to reverse injury in transplanted kidneys exposed to extremely prolonged periods of impaired blood flow.

column36: Podocyte Remodeling in Hypertension and Diabetic Nephropathy: Role of CLIC5A
column37: Diabetes is the most common cause of kidney failure in Canada, and Hypertension (high blood pressure) accelerates the loss of kidney function in patients with diabetic kidney disease. Both, Diabetes and Hypertension damage the filtering capillaries of the kidney. Normally, these delicate capillaries have to withstand a higher than normal blood pressure to help drive filtration to produce urine, but they also have to keep blood proteins from escaping into the urine. Specialized cells called Podocytes cover these capillaries with long tentacle-like projections, providing strength and preventing proteins from escaping. A number of studies, including studies from our laboratory, have shown that Podocytes react to a higher than normal blood pressure and diabetes by rearranging their shape. In the short term these responses are protective, but in the long run they are counterproductive causing podocytes to detach, protein to leak into the urine, along with progressive scarring the filtering capillaries and eventually kidney failure. Our laboratory studies a protein called CLIC5A, which is a major Podocyte protein involved in the remodeling response. We have worked out some of the molecular mechanisms by which CLIC5A produces the normal shape of Podocyte projections. We have also shown that CLIC5A is essential for the Podocyte remodeling response to Hypertension and when CLIC5A is absent Hypertension-induced damage to the filtering capillaries of the kidney is dramatically increased. More recent, as yet unpublished work indicates that CLIC5A also participates in the Podocyte response to Diabetes. Using cultured Podocytes and Mouse Models, the current project aims to work out how CLIC5A and its protein partners orchestrate the Podocyte remodeling response to Diabetes in the presence and absence of Hypertension. Our long-term aim is to develop approaches that modify the Podocyte remodeling response and prevent Diabetes- and Hypertension-induced Kidney Failure.

column36: Targeting a novel miR-185/PAK6 axis to overcome drug-resistance in human leukemia
column37: Blood cancer (leukemia) is common, with ~55,000 new cases expected in the United States and Canada in 2019. The National Cancer Institute (US) calculated an overall 5-year survival rate of 56% for various blood cancers. This is because drug resistance and relapse pose significant challenges. Life-long treatment is required, with potential side-effects and a high cost. Blood cancer cells generally respond to drug therapy at the onset, but the drugs lose their effectiveness after 6-12 months. We and others have discovered that this is mainly due to the inability of current therapies to eradicate blood cancer stem cells, which maintain the potential for relapse. There is thus an urgent need to develop new therapies that specifically target blood cancer stem cells, so that these cells can be eliminated, leading to a cure. However, there are currently no drugs that directly target blood cancer stem cells in a specific and potent way, nor any related drugs that are approved as therapeutics. Interestingly, we have recently discovered that PAK6, a novel drug target, displays abnormal activity in blood cancer stem cells, particularly in drug-resistant patients, compared to drug-sensitive patients. We have found that combining a PAK6 inhibitor with current anti-cancer drugs, to target abnormal activities of PAK6, more effectively inhibits blood cancer stem cell growth in culture than single drug treatment; this treatment strategy also doesn't have side-effects on normal blood stem cells, which provides a therapeutic window specifically for anti-cancer treatment. This study will investigate if this combination therapy will more effectively eradicate blood cancer stem cells obtained from drug-resistant patients and prevent blood cancer development, using our newly established animal cancer models. This work will provide ultimate proof-of-concept for the development of more effective therapies, with fewer side effects than currently used therapies.
