column36: Determining genetic and non-genetic risk for schizophrenia in a high risk group
column37: Schizophrenia is a serious and disabling illness that affects about 1 in 100 people. The cause is unknown for this brain disease that often affects youths, seemingly at random in a family. For babies born with a genetic deletion (missing piece of DNA) on one of the pair of chromosomes 22, the risk is very high: 1 in 4 will develop schizophrenia. By comparing people with the deletion who have and have not developed schizophrenia, we aim to identify additional genetic changes and non-genetic factors that will allow us to personalize risk estimates. Because the schizophrenia illness is the same, insights gained from studying this chromosome deletion can help us learn about schizophrenia more generally. An international collaboration has provided us with the opportunity to study the complete genetic codes of an unprecedented number of individuals with this high risk deletion. Our group has recently made this genetic information ready for analyzing the many types of DNA-level changes that could affect the risk of developing schizophrenia. We will obtain similar genetic data for 100 additional Canadians with this deletion where we know schizophrenia outcome. This will mean instead of just 435 people we will have 815 people with this deletion who also have outcome and detailed genetic information. For all 815, we will collect information on other possible risk factors for schizophrenia, such as premature birth. We will use this unique dataset to develop and test prediction algorithms for schizophrenia. Families, clinicians and researchers want to anticipate and ultimately prevent disabling outcomes like schizophrenia in at-risk individuals. Discovering the genetic and non-genetic factors that predict schizophrenia in people from a high risk group could help us predict risk for schizophrenia in the general population. This could help us intervene early to prevent major disabilities.

column36: The role of the lineage oncogene ASCL1 in treatment-induced neuroendocrine prostate cancer
column37: Prostate tumours are addicted to the androgen receptor (AR) for growth and survival. Capitalizing on this inherent weakness, potent drugs have been developed to "turn off" the AR and starve cancer cells of fuel. These therapies are widely used in the clinic and have undoubtedly benefited patient survival; however, they are merely palliative and no patients are cured. Alarmingly, nearly 25% of patients progress to a highly aggressive and deadly form of prostate cancer, called neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC), where treatment remains decades old toxic chemotherapy and survival is measured in months. Our research is focused on uncovering how prostate tumours evolve into NEPC following AR targeted therapy. We discovered that the transition to NEPC is orchestrated by ASCL1, a pro-neural protein that changes the structure of DNA to allow a prostate cancer cell to turn on neuronal genes and take on the identity of a neuroendocrine cell. In the current proposal, we aim to decipher the role of ASCL1 in altering the structure of DNA and its impact on treatment resistance and the transformation to NEPC. This work will advance our understanding of how prostate tumours evade therapy by transitioning to NEPC, and inform future therapeutic strategies to benefit patients with aggressive prostate cancer.

column36: Targeting RNA Splicing for the Treatment of Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy
column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a most common and devastating genetic disease. People with DMD usually die at 25 to 30 years of age from effects of muscle deterioration. A most promising strategy to treat DMD is a molecular therapy called exon skipping. Exon skipping uses a short DNA-like molecule that acts like a stitch in RNA, an important biological molecule that functions to convert the genetic information of DNA into proteins, to bypass the mutations that cause DMD. With this DNA stitch in place, people with DMD may be able to produce short working versions of their mutated protein in DMD. The first drug in this class of DNA-stitch molecules was approved in 2016. However, two problems have not been solved. First, people with DMD who were given this drug did not have their DMD symptoms improve. Second, this drug can only help around 13% of people with DMD-people with only some types of DNA mutations. Our research will first work to improve the effectiveness of exon skipping for DMD. We are creating the next generation of these DNA-like molecules to be more effective in humans. We will also work to expand number of people with DMD who can be helped by exon skipping therapy. We will experiment with a cocktail of DNA-like molecules that could help 63% people with DMD. Lastly, we will work to understand the mechanisms of how our DNA-like molecules affect the DMD gene. This will help us design a better cocktail of DNA-like molecules. Our DNA-stitching technology could create new therapies for DMD and improved quality of life for people with DMD.

column36: The SCF(FBXO11) - XAB2 axis mediates DNA repair and therapeutic resistance in small cell lung cancer
column37: In Canada, lung cancer is responsible for more deaths than colon, breast, and prostate cancer combined. Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a particularly aggressive subtype that represents approximately 15% of all lung cancers. Despite an initial response of SCLC to therapy, disease recurrence often occurs, and cure is rare, with dismal 5-year overall survival rates of less than 8%. There is a critical need to understand the mechanisms of therapeutic resistance to develop more effective treatments for this disease. We have found that loss of a key component of a protein recycling complex leads to resistance to chemotherapy and a newer therapy, known as a PARP inhibitor, in SCLC. This key component is 1 of the 69 possible F-box components of a Skp1-Cul1-F-box (SCF) complex that targets various proteins for tagging with ubiquitin and leads to target protein degradation. Our preliminary results suggest that loss of this specific F-box leads to the lack of the ability to degrade a DNA repair protein known as XAB2. This results in an increase in DNA repair capacity in the cancer cell that can be responsible for treatment resistance as the cancer cell can more easily repair DNA damage caused by chemotherapy or PARP inhibitors. Here, we propose to understand more about how this F-box and SCF complex regulates DNA repair through experiments to precisely determine its impact on DNA damage and repair. In addition, we will determine how the SCF complex interacts physically and functionally with XAB2, its target DNA repair protein. Finally, we will conduct a high-throughput screen to identify potential drug targets that are specific to these treatment resistant cancer cells that have this F-box loss, while sparing normal cells. Through these efforts, we seek to further our understanding of how cancer cells repair, tolerate and become resistant to our current treatments while designing newer treatment approaches to improve outcomes for our patients.

column36: Long-term immune activation by a mucosal RSV subunit vaccine: mechanism of action and application to vaccination of elderly
column37: While previously underestimated, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) contributes to a significant proportion of severe respiratory disease and mortality in the elderly, similar to influenza. With a growing elderly population, a RSV vaccine is urgently needed, but not available. The elderly tend to respond more weakly or inconsistently to vaccination unless they receive vaccines that are specifically developed for them. Our overall objective is to develop and characterize a RSV vaccine for elderly. As RSV infects the respiratory tract, the presence of virus neutralizing antibodies at this site is critical. Boosting and maintaining high neutralizing activity of antibodies in the serum by intramuscular vaccine administration may be adequate as serum antibodies can penetrate and protect the lower airways and lungs. However, mucosal immunization is required to induce production of local IgA antibody and the correct type of T lymphocytes in the respiratory tract. We already have a safe, effective vaccine candidate consisting of a protective antigen of RSV and an immunostimulatory adjuvant. When administered either intramuscularly or intranasally, this RSV vaccine induces long-term, protective immunity in several neonatal and adult animal models, e.g. mice, cotton rats and lambs. We have evidence that this vaccine also elicits an immune response in old mice. We will evaluate the magnitude and longevity of this immune response, as well as protection from RSV infection in old animals, and if necessary optimize the RSV vaccine. Furthermore, we will fully characterize the properties of this vaccine, which will expedite human clinical trials and licensing. An effective RSV vaccine will decrease morbidity and mortality due to RSV infection, which will in the future, improve the health of the elderly and significantly reduce health care costs. In addition, our new adjuvant has applications in vaccines against other respiratory pathogens such as influenza virus as well.

column36: Developing retinal gene augmentation therapy for Zellweger Spectrum Disorder
column37: Zellweger Spectrum Disorder (ZSD) is commonly caused by mutations in the PEX1 gene, resulting in peroxisome dysfunction. Visual impairment is a major untreatable handicap for ZSD patients, and alleviating this burden would enable improved communication, learning, mobility, autonomy and employment opportunities. The proposed research is needed to complete the preclinical development of retinal gene therapy for ZSD. Our main aims are to (i) establish the optimal gene therapy delivery design and dose to use in the transition towards the clinic, (ii) expand outcome measures for testing of PEX1 retinal gene therapy in mice, which will allow for additional functional testing and dose-response correlation, and (iii) perform an expanded efficacy trial in our mouse model. Completing these necessary aims will allow us to move directly into meetings with Health Canada and the FDA to forge a path to the clinic. In addition, the results of these studies, never before done in peroxisome deficient animal models, will inform the mechanism by which peroxisome dysfunction leads to retinal degeneration. Finally, the development of this cutting-edge therapy for ZSD will support the use of gene replacement therapies to treat other genetic diseases.

column36: Managing Pain In Collaboration in the Intensive Care Unit (MPIC-ICU): Impact on clinical practices and patient outcomes
column37: A high proportion of individuals hospitalized in the adult intensive care unit (ICU) experience significant pain. Although some are able to self-report their pain, others are unable to communicate due to their critical health condition or the use of medication that puts them to sleep. While they are fighting for their lives, those individuals deserve to have their pain adequately evaluated and relieved. Pain that is left undetected and under-treated can lead to ICU longer stay, multiple complications, and can even cause death. Regular evaluations of pain using appropriate tools that are adapted to the individual's capacity to communicate are necessary to help provide suitable pain control. The main goal of this project is to implement an evidence-based pain management intervention for individuals in the ICU, to evaluate if it is applied by health professionals of the care team on a daily basis and if this practice sustains over time, and if it helps to reduce pain in these individuals. To achieve our goal and using a cluster randomized trial, the pain management intervention will be implemented sequentially in selected Canadian ICU settings. The order of implementation in each ICU will be pre-established at random, and each ICU will have received the intervention by the study end. Before and after intervention implementation in each ICU, frequency of pain assessments, administration of pain relievers and evaluation of their effectiveness will be documented from the medical charts and determine pain management practice indicators. Perceptions of ICU healthcare professionals on team collaboration and contextual factors will be assessed. Patient outcomes including incidence of significant pain, adverse events, ICU length of stay, mechanical ventilation duration, and mortality will be described. Key outcomes of this project are to improve pain control practices in the adult ICU, and to reduce the incidences of significant pain and their related negative outcomes.

column36: Exogenous signals that drive the Pseudomonas aeruginosa transition to pathogenesis
column37: To cause infection, free-living bacteria must sense the presence of a host and activate virulence mechanisms. Bacterial virulence relies on the ability to utilize host-derived nutrients as well as capacity to evade and suppress host immunity. While many of the physiological changes associated with transitions to pathogenesis have been extensively studied, how bacteria sense the presence of a host and make a decision to transition from free living to pathogenic are largely unknown. Using a combination of forward and reverse genetics, we have identified genes in the ESKAPE pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa required for sensing and persisting in association with a mammalian host and causing disease. We have found that inducible outer membrane modifications, regulated by the ColR/S two component system, promote host association. We also discovered that bacterial sensing of exogenous polyamines regulates biofilm formation and promotes pathogenesis. This work combines in vitro studies with validation in a mouse chronic infection (abscess) model to understand how ColR/S and polyamine signaling facilitate bacterial lifestyle transitions. This work will shed light on how microbes transition from free-living to pathogenic and elucidate potential targets for antibiotic development.

column36: Cerebral Oxygenation and Neurological outcomes FOllowing criticAL illness (CONFOCAL)-2 study: A prospective observational study assessing the relationship between cerebral oxygenation, delirium, and long-term cognitive outcomes in critically ill patients.
column37: The past few decades have seen a dramatic reduction in mortality for individuals admitted to intensive care units (ICUs). There is therefore an ever-expanding population of ICU survivors that we are learning about. Unfortunately, ICU survivors have many problems, including long-term cognitive impairment. Almost half of ICU survivors have some degree of neurological problem, characterized by difficulties with memory and attention. This likely contributes to their poor quality of life and reduced employability. The cause (s) of these long-term neurological problems is/are unknown, although acute neurological dysfunction while in the ICU is a consistent risk factor. This acute brain dysfunction is called delirium. We have previously demonstrated that poor brain oxygenation, as measured with a non-invasive sensor on the forehead, is an independent risk factor for delirium. Unfortunately, this study was too small to look at long term outcomes, or control for important confounding factors (such as baseline brain dysfunction). The proposed study is a multi-centre study aimed to recruit 500 critically ill participants across Canada. Cerebral oxygenation and vital signs will be captured for the first 72 hours of the ICU stay. The presence of delirium will be assessed every day the patient is in the hospital, and long-term cognitive impairment will be assessed at 3- and 12-months post-discharge. This study will inform us on how to better manage patients when they are at their most sick in the ICU, in order to improve their long-term brain function and quality of life.

column36: The role of fibrosis signaling in adipose tissue regulation of insulin resistance
column37: We face a growing global epidemic of obesity and diabetes. About 9.3% of Canadians have diabetes, for an estimated economic cost of $12.2 billion. The most common type of diabetes is type 2 diabetes, which is associated with obesity. Fat or adipose tissue is increasingly recognized as an important and dynamic organ that grows massively when we gain weight. A number of studies suggest that scarring or fibrosis increases in adipose tissue when we gain large amounts of weight, and this fibrosis could play a part in the development of type 2 diabetes. Why and how this occurs is not clear. The overall goal of this work is to identify the signaling pathways that lead to adipose tissue fibrosis and the development of diabetes when we gain weight. Yes-associated protein 1 (YAP) has recently been found to contribute to fibrosis and chronic disease in other tissues. We have found that YAP increases in fat with obesity and type 2 diabetes. We also find that inhibiting another protein, focal adhesion kinase (FAK), seems to increase levels of YAP in fat cells. Thus, our goal is to identify the role of these signaling proteins in fat and fibrosis contributing to type 2 diabetes with obesity. First, we will measure if YAP is activated with adipose tissue fibrosis, obesity and diabetes. Then, we plan to test whether knocking out YAP can prevent adipose tissue fibrosis and diabetes. Finally, we will determine whether FAK regulates levels of YAP, contributing to fibrosis and disease. Together, these studies will help us better understand fat, fibrosis and the role they play in our metabolism. These discoveries will help us develop better treatments for obesity and diabetes in the future.

column36: Defining the molecular basis of regulation of PI3K gamma and its role in immune function and the tumour microenvironment
column37: One of the major developments in cancer treatment has been the use of cancer immunotherapy to utilise the immune system to target and destroy cancer cells. The phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) pathway is at the crossroads of both cancer development and immune regulation, with mutations in this pathway being extremely frequent in the development and maintenance of multiple high mortality human cancers. Intriguingly, inhibition of the PI3K gamma isoform is able to act as a switch that can reprogram the tumour microenvironment to target cancer cells. This is a powerful approach to promote the immune system to generate an anti-cancer response. In addition, the PI3K gamma isoform is also frequently upregulated in many cancers, with the development of specific inhibitors being an excellent strategy for cancer therapeutics. This proposal focuses on studying the structural and dynamic basis of regulation of PI3K gamma, with a major focus on the development of specific small molecule inhibitors. One of our major goals will be in defining the molecular mechanisms that control how this enzyme is activated, and how it can be misregulated in human disease. This will be approached using a cutting-edge synergy of state of the art biochemical and biophysical methods including Cryo-Electron Microscopy, X-ray crystallography, and Hydrogen Deuterium Exchange mass spectrometry. A powerful team of collaborators including medicinal chemists, cell biologists, and clinical immunologists has been established to fully apply biophysical discoveries in both cellular and organism models of disease. PI3K gamma is an exceptionally important target for anti-cancer therapeutics. This proposal focusing on defining the molecular basis of how this enzyme is regulated will reveal novel insight into its role in immune regulation and cancer immunotherapy. The development of small molecule inhibitors in this proposal has the potential to act as therapeutics in cancer therapy.

column36: The molecular choreography of ion channel expression
column37: All signal processing depends on neurons correctly encoding input and transforming that into a series or pattern of spikes to convey the information to other cells in a circuit. We know that modulating the pattern of spike firing depends on calcium-dependent processes that create inhibitory feedback following spike discharge in the form of afterhyperpolarizations (AHPs). This process is so important that virtually every neuron generates a series of AHPs of increasing duration following a spike. In this way spike firing can be modulated over a timeframe of ~10 msec (fast AHP) to 10 sec (slow AHP). To understand how these responses are generated we need to identify the source of calcium increases and the calcium-gated potassium channels responsible for triggering the spike-AHP sequence. This study identifies a new level of interaction between calcium channels at the plasma membrane (PM) with an underlying cytoskeleton and even a deeper quilt-like membrane formed by the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Our work builds on recent findings that the slow AHP arises from the concerted action of a voltage-gated calcium channel at the PM with ryanodine receptors that release calcium from the ER, which together activate a class of IK potassium channels. These interactions are enabled at "ER-PM" junctions where the ER extends narrow columns of membrane to within 10 nm of the PM. We propose that these sites in fact act as "CaRyK hubs" where multiple calcium sources and potassium channels are coassembled to reliably trigger an all-or-none spike-AHP sequence. Moreover, CaRyK hubs are distributed across the soma with a high degree of organization in the form of a polygonal (honeycomb-like) matrix we have traced to interactions with the cytoskeleton and even the underlying ER. The work is thus important in effectively identifying a new node of ion channel expression to mediate the calcium-dependent control of spike output necessary for neural coding and information transfer.

column36: Sleep and circadian rhythm as developmental antecedents to major mood disorders
column37: Disturbed sleep patterns in children and adolescents may be early signs of risk for depression or bipolar disorder. Inconsistent time of sleep from one night to another may be a particularly strong indicator of risk. We will use devices called actigraphs (which resemble wrist-watches) to objectively measure sleep timing, duration and quality in children and adolescents, including sons and daughters of parents with depression or with bipolar disorder. We will examine the relationships between sleep and mood disorders in parents, sleep duration and regularity in children and later development of mood symptoms in the children. We will compare the information from questionnaires and from actigraphs. Based on the results, we will develop a sleep monitoring procedure with feedback to the participants that can be used as part of preemptive early intervention to reduce the risk of mood disorders.

column36: Grappling with type IV pili: characterization of Nature's most powerful biological motor
column37: Many bacteria produce long thin hair-like filaments called type IV pili (T4P) on their surfaces. T4P are used by bacteria as grappling hooks to grab onto their hosts, where they colonize appropriate niches (in the case of good bacteria) or cause disease (bad bacteria). T4P filaments can be repeatedly extended and retracted, allowing the bacteria to crawl along surfaces or use them as fishing rods to capture free DNA from the environment, leading to acquisition of new antibiotic resistance genes. The T4P are made by a large multi-component nanomachine that assembles (extends) and disassembles (retracts) the filaments. It does this using highly-conserved molecular motors capable of generating some of the strongest retraction forces ever measured - up to 100,000 x the weight of the bacterial cell. The way in which the T4P motor functions is among the most important unresolved questions in the field. Mutation of critical motor components can cripple the bacteria, suggesting they are good therapeutic targets. In this proposal we will use multiple techniques to solve the three-dimensional structures of the motors from two evolutionarily-distinct types of T4P system to understand how they perform their extension and retraction functions. Combined with the expertise and tools for study of the T4P system we have built over the past 20 years, these structures will guide the generation of specific mutants that will allow us to test our predictions about motor function. As we reveal how the individual components work together, we will use that knowledge to understand how inhibitors of the motors, produced by natural predators of the bacteria, block their function, information that is valuable for the rational design of new therapeutics.

column36: Validation of a new multi-parameter technology to better diagnose pain in the adult intensive care population: The Nociception Level (NOL) Index
column37: Assessing pain in the adult intensive care unit (ICU) is challenging because many patients are unable to communicate due to mechanical ventilation and sedation. Therefore, it is necessary to have alternative methods to assess pain in this vulnerable patient population. In this project, we will test the use of a new technology (i.e., the Nociception Level (NOL) index) for pain assessment in ICU adults. The NOL index is a value from 0 to 100 obtained by calculating different parameters (e.g., pulse, skin temperature) captured through a small probe placed on the patient's finger. The NOL was initially developed for assessing pain and analgesia in anesthetized patients undergoing surgery, and its use in the ICU is new. We will test the NOL's use before, during and after usual care procedures known to be painful (e.g., tube or drain removal, suctioning of secretions through the endotracheal tube) and non-painful (e.g., cuff inflation to measure blood pressure) in ICU adults. We will monitor the NOL in three groups: a) patients able to communicate so they can self-report their pain (gold standard criterion), b) patients unable to communicate but express behaviors (reference criterion), and c) patients unable to communicate and to express behaviors. In the first group, patients will be asked to self-report their pain on a 0 to 10 numeric scale. In the second group, patients will be assessed for pain using a standardized behavioral scale which will be completed by trained research staff. In the third group, only the NOL will be monitored. Analgesic and sedative medication administered to patients will also be documented from medical charts. The ability of the NOL to diagnose pain based on self-reports of pain and behavioral scores, and its ability to discriminate between painful and non-painful procedures will be examined. If found to be useful, the NOL could be used as an alternative measure of pain and improve its diagnosis and treatment in vulnerable ICU patients.

column36: Elucidating the Role of Memory in the Transition from Acute to Chronic Pediatric Pain
column37: How children remember pain sets the stage for future pain experiences. These memories can easily become distorted. Negatively-biased pain memories (remembering pain as being worse than an earlier pain report) are associated with the development of pediatric chronic pain. Pediatric chronic pain is a growing epidemic, affecting 1 in 4 Canadian youth, and costing $19 billion/year. Treatments for pediatric chronic pain are largely ineffective, in part because we do not understand why acute pain transitions to chronic pain in the first place. We believe that children's pain memories are a key risk factor for the development of this growing child health problem. Children's memories of post-surgical pain can lead to chronic pain; however, it is not known how the brain is involved in pain memory biases or the development of chronic pain after surgery in youth. In adults, the hippocampus - a brain region critically involved in memory - underlies the development of negatively-biased pain memories and chronic pain. Our brain imaging data show abnormal hippocampal structure and function in youth with chronic pain versus healthy controls, suggesting that the hippocampus may undergo changes as pain transitions from an acute to chronic state. Therefore, it is likely that the hippocampus is involved in pain memory biases and the development of chronic pain in youth. In the proposed study, 160 youth undergoing spinal fusion surgery will be assessed at baseline, the acute recovery phase, and at the time that pain can transition to a chronic state. Pain memories will be assessed 2 months after surgery. Brain scans will be performed before and 4 months after surgery, when pain can transition to a chronic state. Given the key role of children's pain memories in the development of chronic pain, and the urgent need for prevention and treatment targets for these at-risk youth, this research will be critical in helping to understand and prevent this widespread child health issue.

column36: Stroke Metrics for quAlity, Reporting, and Translation in the implementation of EndoVascular Thrombectomy (SMART-EVT)
column37: Stroke happens when a blood vessel in the brain is blocked. Every 9 minutes, a Canadian has a stroke. Endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) is a procedure to unblock blood vessels in the brain. With this treatment, fewer people die, more people are able to return home and go back to do activities they enjoy after stroke. Right now, not everyone has access to EVT. First, a special scan of the brain is needed to detect vessel blockage, but not all hospitals have this scanner. Second, even when a vessel blockage is found, not all hospitals offer this treatment and patients often have to travel to a different hospital to get it. Third, EVT must be done very quickly or it will not help the patient. We currently do not know if the right people with stroke are getting to the right hospital at the right time. Our study aims to identify ways to optimize access to EVT. We will collect information from all hospitals in Ontario to understand how people with stroke are being cared for now. Most research focuses on people who get EVT, but it does not study those who do not get it. We will find out how many people do not get the scan to look for blood vessel blockage, how many people with a blockage do not get EVT, and why not. Studying people with stroke who did not have the scan or the treatment is important because it will help us find out where we can improve care. For example, are there specific hospitals or regions in Ontario where resources are insufficient? Are there groups of people who are not being treated equitably? In particular, we want to study if women and men are equally likely to get EVT and whether this treatment is safe for both women and men. Our results will help understand where the needs of the people and hospitals are. We are working with CorHealth Ontario and the Heart and Stroke Foundation of Canada on this project. This study will inform provincial and national stroke systems of care to improve patient outcomes after stroke.

column36: Optic flow processing in midbrain-cerebellar circuits for the control of locomotion
column37: As we move through the world, we experience optic flow - the motions of surfaces and objects across our retina. Studies of human behaviour reveal that optic flow is used for controlling virtually all aspects of locomotion such as walking, navigating through cluttered environments like forests or airport terminals, and when driving motor vehicles. Despite the importance of optic flow, there is a major gap in our understanding of how these signals are processed in the brain to allow for complex locomotion. Thus, optic flow processing in the brain is one of the most important, but least understood aspects of locomotion control. Disruptions to optic flow processing in the brain are associated with common diseases including vertigo, oscillopsia, ataxias and Alzheimer's disease. For example, Alzheimer's patients require much stronger optic flow signals to be able to navigate through a series of hallways to find their rooms. For other patients, such as those with vestibular deficits and visual neglect, presentations of optic flow are effective rehabilitative tools. Improving our understanding of optic flow is therefore essential. The principal challenge to studying optic flow processing in the brain is that we lack an appropriate animal model for research. Mice and rats are often used for studies of vertebrate neurobiology, but they are crepuscular/nocturnal and use information from their whiskers to guide many aspects of their locomotion. We will investigate how optic flow is used to guide movement in different environments, how optic flow signals are processed along the pathway from the midbrain to the cerebellum, and how selective silencing of neurons in this pathway leads to deficits in locomotor ability. The experiments will be performed on the visually-guided flight of small birds, which can be easily studied in the lab. Because birds have the same optic flow pathways as humans, this research will identify specific neural connections as potential treatment targets.

column36: Targeting Glioblastoma Heterogeneity through identification of subtype-specific genetic vulnerabilities
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and lethal primary brain tumor in adults. Current treatment for GBM (surgery, radiation and chemotherapy) extends survival but is ineffective at preventing disease recurrence due to the residual presence of tumor initiating "GBM stem cells" that evade therapy and patients will invariably succumb to the disease, on average, just 18 months after initial diagnosis. Genomics studies have identified a high degree of variability in the genetic make-up of GBM cells-both between patients and within the same patient-which has represented a major barrier to the efficacy of new therapies for this cancer. Recently, our group and others have identified two predominant subtypes of GBM stem cells that can both be isolated from patient tumor samples, indicating that curing a patient of all residual disease would require therapies that killed both subtypes. Herein, we propose to use cutting-edge CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing technology to determine which genes are required for the growth of each subtype, producing a roadmap of candidate therapeutic targets. By performing these genetic screens in a large panel of patient derived GBM stem cell lines generated by our collaborator, we will produce a powerful dataset highly reflective of the heterogeneity observed in the GBM patient population. Using this data, we will characterize the biological basis for subtype-specific gene dependencies, greatly increasing our understanding of the mechanisms of GBM progression. In addition, our screen data will allow us to nominate drugs and small molecules as potential new targeted therapeutic strategies which we will evaluate through both in vitro drug screening and in mouse models harboring human patient derived GBM tumors. In summary, our proposed study will strive to develop new therapeutic strategies that can be applied in combination to overcome tumor heterogeneity and successfully target both cell types and cure GBM.

Over the past few years we have developed a new approach known as the artificial placenta - a device that mimics the natural circulation before birth where the fetus obtains oxygen from the mother. The device is elegantly designed so that it can operate in a pumpless manner, much like the natural placenta. It is designed to use the baby's own heart to perfuse a significant fraction of the blood volume through a microfluidic extracorporeal device and exchange oxygen with the external ambient environment. Being a passive device, it does not require external pumps and has a small internal volume which eliminates the need for external blood transfusion when it is connected to the neonate. We have developed a series of devices with increasing capabilities and are at a stage where initial animal experiments on piglets with the same weight as human neonatal babies have shown that our devices can sustain them even when under respiratory distress like conditions. These initial experiments show the promise of our approach, but further experiments are needed to conclusively validate that they would be suitable to support the piglets over typical operational lifetime of this device (~ 3-4 days). Further research is also needed to confirm whether the internal coating that we provide to the device is active over the intended operational lifetime. In addition to the validation of the device using animal models, we will also simplify the manufacturing process for the device and evaluate new coating technologies to ensure highest reliability of the device operation as well as its manufacturing. The validation of the technology obtained in this project on animal models will be critical to move it to the next stage of human clinical trials.

column36: Neurobiomarkers of FASD for adolescents and adults in the Criminal Justice System: Portable eye tracking and EEG
column37: In Canada, an estimated 1M people live with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD), a lifelong neurodevelopmental disability with wide ranging impacts on brain and behaviour that are linked with adverse outcomes. Studies suggest that over 60% of adults with FASD experience contact with the criminal justice system, and they are overrepresented in correctional and forensic settings at rates 30x that of the general population. They experience high rates of re-offending, health, and mental health problems, and have difficulty benefiting from traditional interventions in the justice system. Despite high numbers, there are currently no evidence-based ways of identifying adolescents or adults who could have FASD in the criminal justice system. Failure to identify people with FASD in this context can lead to increased risk of harm to self and others, recidivism, and high health, social, and economic costs. This study proposes to use novel neurotechnologies, including eye movement behaviour and EEG recordings, to better understand how to identify adolescents and adults with FASD, including those in the criminal justice system. Portable technologies such as these may be used to detect people at risk of having FASD with a high degree of accuracy. These tools are non-invasive, precise, cost effective, and portable, and may allow for early identification of individuals in need of more comprehensive and costly clinical assessment, diagnostic, and intervention services. Findings from this research will be used to develop and implement fast, non-invasive, and affordable screening protocols to aid in large-scale screening for FASD in criminal justice settings. Identifying people who may have FASD may lead to effective use of limited economic and health resources to best support their complex needs.

column36: Stepping-Up: Partnering with the Community to Prevent Early Mobility Decline
column37: Background: Older adults need to be able to walk around their community at a minimal speed in order to ensure their safety. Slowing of walking speed occurs with aging in all persons, and has been linked to decreased independence. Preclinical disability is a stage where older adults begin to change the way they complete mobility tasks, like walking. Programs to improve mobility in people with preclinical disability need to encourage participants to be actively involved in managing their mobility (self-management), should be specifically developed for the individual and should include the practice of mobility tasks. In 2016, we conducted a pilot study to measure the impact of a mobility self-management intervention on the walking ability of older adults, but the results were not clear. In this proposal, we have made some changes to improve the study design and the intervention. Goals, Methods, Approach: We plan to study whether community-dwelling adults 55 years and older with preclinical mobility limitations show improvement in walking distance, walking speed, balance, strength, confidence in their walking and health after completing a 12-week program, called STEPPING-UP, that includes mobility exercises and self-management sessions led by a physiotherapist. This program will be compared to 2 control groups, either a 12-week telephone-based coaching walking program or a 12-week stretching program. We will also compare the cost associated with delivering each program. Expected Outcomes: If the results from this study are positive, it will support the importance of identifying those at risk for mobility related disability and will provide a community-based resource for the prevention of mobility decline in older adults.

column36: Enabling Cellular Therapy Biomanufacturing through Integrated Modeling of Fluid Dynamics and Cellular Metabolism in Bioreactors
column37: Regenerative medicine is a rapidly growing billion-dollar multidisciplinary field at the intersection of medicine, engineering and science. It aims to create living, functional tissues that can repair or replace damaged, diseased or aging tissues or organs, as well as providing models for discovery and drug development. Stem cells are critical to the success of regenerative medicine therapies. Pluripotent stem cells are a unique adult-derived stem cell that can be used for both personalized and population therapies, but technologies are needed to bridge the gap between fundamental biology and clinical applications. One of the major obstacles preventing effective use of stem cells is the limited number of available donor cells, and the small-scale, labour-intensive methods for culturing and differentiating them. Stirred suspension bioreactors are emerging as a critical cornerstone of robust bioprocesses to generate sufficient numbers of stem cells and their differentiated progeny for multiple applications. However, there is a significant gap in our knowledge of how the dynamic environment in the bioreactor affects the quality of the final cell product. More specifically, cell metabolism, which can change greatly between stem cells and their differentiated daughter cells, can be modulated within the stirred suspension bioreactor environment. The overall goals of the research project are to a) develop a deeper understanding of the metabolic behaviour of human pluripotent stem cells in bioreactors, b) relate metabolism to the dynamic environment within the bioreactor through computer modeling approaches. The outputs of this research are essential for efficient, cost-effective, safe and reproducible cell manufacturing, which is a critical next step to precision treatments for conditions such as degenerative diseases, burns, fractures, and other ailments. This is an opportunity for Canada to be a leader in biomanufacturing for the regenerative medicine industry.

column36: Sex Differences in Central Nervous System Autoimmunity
column37: Canada has one of the highest rates of multiple sclerosis (MS) in the world, with 1 in every 250 Canadians affected. This translates into a considerable societal and economic burden ($1.6M per patient). At present, it is not possible to reverse the neuron damage in MS. Therefore, the best chance of curing this disease is to prevent it from starting in the first place. Thus understanding the risk factors for development of MS and the biology of how these risk factors initiate the disease process is an important area of research. Three times more women than men develop MS, and we still do not understand why this is the case. In addition, if men get this disease, they tend to exhibit more rapid progression. Our goal is to better understand the fundamental biological differences that account for the greater susceptibility of females to develop MS and for men to develop more rapid progression. Here, through studies in mice and in human MS patients, we are trying to better understand the nuts and bolts of why the immune response may be more vigorous in females and can lead to the initiation of autoimmunity. We are pursuing the novel hypothesis that the reason why females are more prone to develop MS is because they have more T cells that can recognize the myelin sheath. We have thus far found evidence of this in the peripheral blood of human patients and in a mouse model of this disease. Further studies are planned in mice to get to the underlying mechanisms for this sex difference in T cell numbers. We are also going to characterize the immune cells in men and women with MS in order to gain new insights into how the disease may be different between the sexes. Understanding this biology will improve our understanding of how MS gets started and may lead to new ways of preventing or treating this disease. .

column36: Targeting pericytes to restore sensorimotor function after spinal cord injury
column37: Spinal cord injury disconnects the brain from parts of the body below the injury, resulting in paralysis, abnormal pain and bladder dysfunction. Unfortunately, treatments to repair the injured spinal cord are still lacking. However, we recently made the unexpected discovery that blood flow is permanently reduced in the entire spinal cord below an injury, suggesting that improving blood flow offers a new approach to treating injury. We found that this low blood flow is caused by an exaggerated activity in specialized cells called pericytes that act like valves on small blood vessels. This then leads to insufficient blood flow and ultimately loss of residual functions like walking. We find that transiently blocking this exaggerated pericyte activity, or supplying oxygen, temporarily promotes recovery of walking in animal models. This is the basis for our current proposal, where we ask three questions. First, how do we best apply treatments to more permanently restore blood flow and oxygen to the spinal cord, and are these treatments safe (e.g. does not enhance abnormal pain)? Second, what causes the excessive pericyte activity following spinal cord injury, and can it be prevented? We have convincing preliminary data that indicate that a lack of activity in the neurons below a spinal cord injury triggers the excessive pericyte activity, since daily nerve stimulation to excite the spinal cord over the first few weeks after spinal cord injury restores normal pericyte function, eliminates hypoxia and markedly improves residual movement. If proven correct, this idea opens up new clinically applicable treatments to restore blood flow, including electrical nerve stimulation and rehabilitation training that promote neuronal activity early after injury. Lastly, we explore whether humans with spinal cord injury also suffer from a lack of oxygen in the spinal cord below the injury and whether restoring blood flow promotes recovery in sensory and motor function.

column36: Using behavioural science to understand and improve participation in clinical trials: A theory-based research project.
column37: Participation in clinical research is an essential element of improving healthcare. Any change in treatment or management should be tested before it is put into practice, and this requires patients (and others) to participate in research, usually on a volunteer basis. Despite its importance, research participation is consistently low across almost all diseases and geographical regions. The costs of low participation are many and varied, including wasted money and other resources, inability to use those resources for other purposes, delayed new treatments, faulty findings, and unnecessary risks to those who do participate. While many studies have explored this problem, they have not been informed by theories from psychology that contain considerable knowledge about how to help people make difficult decisions, and how people change their behaviour. The overall goal for this project is to develop the knowledge and tools necessary to help patient groups, researchers, and trial sponsors optimize both the rate of participation and the experience of clinical trial recruitment. The work will proceed in four phases, including (1) reviewing the scientific literature to understand how recruitment is currently done from a theoretical perspective; (2) interviewing the range of different groups with expertise in these issues (e.g. participants, physicians, trial recruiters, and experts in the infrastructure underlying clinical research); (3) developing tools to help optimize trial recruitment (e.g. standard surveys that can identify problems before a trial begins; more participant-friendly consent forms); and (4) thinking and writing about the ethical challenges posed by these theories, to safeguard public trust in health research. Our international multidisciplinary team is uniquely qualified to do this work, which will help improve the health care system by optimizing the process of clinical trial recruitment.

column36: Mechanisms of B cell-mediated immunity in human cancer
column37: Ovarian cancer is a challenging disease with unacceptably high mortality. Despite this, about 30% of patients "beat the odds" and live for many years after treatment. Why do some patients do so well? In the past decade, it has become well established that many long-term survivors of ovarian cancer exhibit a strong immune response against their tumor, providing a plausible explanation for their favourable outcome. We have shown that the immune response against cancer involves collaboration between several types of white blood cells, including killer T cells and antibody-producing B cells. With better understanding of the immune response, it will be possible to design new treatments that enhance tumor immunity and increase patient survival. In this study, we will investigate the mechanisms by which B cells work with other immune cells to recognize and attack cancer. In Aim 1, we will use state-of-the-art genomics methods to probe the molecular properties of individual B cells and associated immune cells isolated from 50 human ovarian cancer specimens, giving us unprecedented insights into the inner workings of the immune system in patients. In Aim 2, we will isolate the antibodies produced by 200 or more B cells from ovarian tumours and use these to further decipher the mechanisms by which B cells amplify the immune response to cancer. The data, tools and knowledge arising from this study will help us design new immunotherapies that fortify the patient's natural defense mechanisms, leading to increased survival. Through local and national initiatives, our team is exceptionally well positioned to translate our findings into early stage clinical trials of promising new immunotherapy strategies for ovarian cancer patients in Canada.

column36: Quality control and pharmacological rescue of heteromeric long QT mutants
column37: The Long QT Syndrome (LQTS) is an electrical disorder of the heart, which is associated with abnormal cardiac rhythms and sudden death. The QT interval is determined by measuring the interval between the QRS complex and the T-wave on the electrocardiograph. One form of this syndrome, referred to as LQTS2, has been related to mutations of a protein called hERG (Human Ether-a-go-go Related Gene) that reduces the function of the hERG channel in the cell membrane. This channel also binds many drugs readily, which can cause sudden death, and therefore the U.S.A. Federal Drug Administration requires that new drugs are tested against hERG. However, the mechanisms that regulate the levels of hERG channels at the cell membrane are not well understood. The first mechanism is related to the removal of mutated and improperly folded hERG channels at the endoplasmic reticulum. A second mechanism involves the removal of hERG channels from the cell membrane that become destabilized. We discovered that there are two distinct cell membrane quality control systems, the more recent of which we have little information. Also, we screened a library of drugs and small molecules and found two compounds that can stabilize mutant hERG channels at the cell membrane, which could have potential therapeutic benefits. The nature of this mechanism also is not understood and will be the subject of further investigation. In our study, we will continue to evaluate the quality control and pharmacological modulation of hERG channels using a variety of techniques that involve electrophysiology, molecular biology and advanced microscopy. We believe that this quality control mechanism will provide a new explanation for the effects involved in clinically relevant cases of LQTS2.

column36: The Tumor Suppressor Function of CUX1
column37: Cancer develops following increased alterations within DNA, which are usually repaired by complex groups of proteins involved in DNA repair. Defects in one or more DNA repair mechanisms cause the accumulation of changes in DNA, called mutations, that increase the possibility that certain cells become tumorigenic. We work on a gene, called CUX1, that has been implicated in cancer. Normally, each gene has two copies or alleles, however, one allele of CUX1 is inactivated or lost in a fraction of human cancers. This finding suggests that the probability of developing cancer increases in cells that have only one copy of the CUX1 gene. This defines the CUX1 gene as a "tumor suppressor gene" and in our scientific jargon, we say that CUX1 is a "haploinsufficient tumor suppressor gene". The goal of our research is to understand why having only one copy of the CUX1 gene increases the probability of cancer. We already know that less of the CUX1 proteins are expressed when one copy of the gene is inactivated or lost. We want to know and demonstrate what molecular function is affected when there is a lower number of CUX1 proteins. Since the CUX1 protein plays a role in DNA repair, our hypothesis is that cells with less CUX1 are not as efficient at repairing DNA damage and therefore they accumulate changes in DNA faster than normal cells. To make a bad analogy, cancer is like winning the lottery. Cells with less CUX1 accumulate more lottery tickets than other cells and therefore they have a higher probability of getting the bad ticket.

column37: When a heart is irreversibly damaged and cannot be treated by any other medical or surgical means, organ transplantation is the most beneficial and highly-pursued treatment option for saving the person's life. The premature failure of transplanted organ is related to both early rejection and chronic injury. Chronic injury and premature loss of transplanted hearts has emerged as our greatest current clinical challenge. Chronic rejection is the leading cause of late morbidity and mortality in transplant patients. Unfortunately, this long-term outcome has not improved over time. Furthermore, this inflammation is not affected by current anti-rejection drugs. In this grant, we will study how the form of cell death regulate transplant inflammation and rejection. These studies will determine how the form of cell death affects immune responses and chronic transplant injury. These studies will guide future clinical therapy of inflammation and may translate to truly new approaches to preventing transplanted heart graft injury in patients.

column36: Investigating the regulation of ADAMTS13 in hemostasis and thrombosis
column37: Thrombosis is a pathological condition that occurs as a result of unregulated blood clotting that occludes blood vessels, and is a major cause of morbidity and mortality. Thrombosis can manifest in various organs and can lead to heart attacks or stroke. Despite the availability of drugs that either prevent blood clotting or encourage clot breakdown, thrombosis is responsible for 1 in 4 deaths in Canada and worldwide. Current therapies are limited by the need to balance their effectiveness at treating thrombosis with their risk of causing bleeding. As a result, more research is needed to explore the mechanisms of thrombosis in order to identify new targets for safe and effective therapy. A critical step in the progression to thrombosis is the recruitment of platelets to the injured blood vessel. This is accomplished in part by the protein Von Willebrand Factor (VWF). VWF is a long string-like protein that adheres to the site of vessel injury and captures platelets flowing in blood. Recruitment of too many platelets can lead to thrombosis. ADAMTS13 is a protease that cuts VWF strings, shortening them and reducing their platelet-capturing activity. Changes in ADAMTS13 activity can lead to dysfunctional VWF and cause either bleeding or thrombosis. However, there is currently very little that is known about the regulation of ADAMTS13. ADAMTS13 is known to remain in a folded compact form in circulation that becomes extended when it interacts with and cuts VWF. Whether this folded form of ADAMTS13 contributes to the regulation of its protease activity is currently not known. Therefore, the objective of this project is to explore the biochemical and structural mechanisms that contribute to the regulation of ADAMTS13. Because ADAMTS13 is an important regulator of blood clotting, investigating the mechanisms that control its activity may reveal novel targets for antithrombotic therapy development.

column36: Biophysical control of mesenchymal morphogenesis in the mammalian embryo
column37: The growth and formation of the mammalian embryo is an inherently physical process that is regulated by genes. Although the identity of genes responsible for development is relatively advanced, the physical principles that shape three dimensional embryonic structures such as solid organs including the face and limbs are not understood. It is also not known how genes regulate physical processes that underlie development. Consequences of these knowledge gaps are that we cannot fully explain how birth defects arise and current efforts at regenerating organs are based on trial-and-error methods rather than on recapitulating actual physical events that take place during natural development. The persistence of these knowledge gaps is attributable to the lack of tools to measure the physical properties of mammalian embryos. The Hopyan and Sun lab teams bring together developmental biologists and mechanical engineers with expertise in the manufacture of micro-scale devices to tackle the physical basis of development. Collaboratively, they generated multiple genetic and physical tools that allow precise measurements of the viscoelastic properties and forces of living tissues and cells in the mammalian embryo. Using those tools, they described how 3D tissues such as the developing face and limbs grow at the resolution of individual cells and measured cellular forces and tissue stiffness. They generated hypotheses about how cells move in response to the stiffness of their environment and about how three regulators (WNT5A, YAP and Piezo1) control that response. Mutations of those regulators cause human birth defects. Therefore, the experiments outlined in this proposal will define how molecular pathways regulate physical processes during development and more precisely explain how specific facial and limb defects arise. In the longterm, understanding the physical basis of organ development will accelerate strategies that are focused on organ regeneration.

column37: Recently, escape from tumor surveillance by the immune system has been identified as a critical mediator for cancer progression to lethal disease. The Egan lab (who study human cancer in mouse models) has collaborated with the Guidos lab (an immunology group) to develop and characterize a completely new model for one type of breast cancer (known as Lobular breast cancer or ILC). We have also identified mutations that can be used to model ILC when it becomes resistant to therapy, leading to metastasis and patient death. By working together, Egan and Guidos, can effectively combine immunotherapy with drugs that target cancer-causing mutations in ILC model mice. Using this approach we can develop new combination therapy for the effective treatment of ILC at diagnosis and recurrence. Ultimately, results from this study can be used to inspire and guide clinical trials for the deployment of combination therapy in ILC patients. column36: Minimizing Variation In Care Among Critically Ill Patients With Respiratory Failure Through Implementation Of An Evidence-Informed Care Pathway
column37: Lung failure prevents the lungs from delivering adequate amounts of oxygen to the body. It can be caused by severe infections such as pneumonia and is a common reason for patients to be admitted to the intensive care unit. Patients with lung failure often require assisted breathing with a machine. Some patients develop very severe lung failure, referred to as the Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS). More than half of patients with severe ARDS will die. Thus diagnosing and treating ARDS correctly is very important. Several treatments for ARDS have been shown to improve a patient's chance of survival. Using the breathing machine carefully (protectively with small breaths), using medications to help relax the chest muscles, and prone positioning (nursing patients while they are lying face down) are all treatments that can save lives. When our team and others have studied how well we use these therapies, we have shown that we do not use these treatments as often as we should. It is likely that we could be helping more patients. The goal of this project is to test a simple but organized approach to diagnosing and treating lung failure. To create the best chance for success, many different types of care providers including physicians, nurses and respiratory therapists will be involved. The approach will focus on timely diagnosis as well as using those treatments that have been proven to save lives. We will look at outcomes in patients (how often are they receiving the correct treatment), health care providers such as nurses, physicians and respiratory therapists (how they like using the pathway), families (does the pathway improve the ICU experience), and cost (does the pathway reduce unnecessary treatments). Our goal is to ensure that patients with lung failure and ARDS patients are diagnosed quickly and provided with the correct therapy at the correct time to best improve their outcomes.

column36: Impact of regional microinfarct load on cortical reorganization and stroke recovery
column37: A stroke is most commonly caused by a blocked blood vessel within the brain, leading to the death of brain cells in the region near the blockage. A major question that scientists have been working on is to determine why some people improve after the stroke, while others do not. Recent studies have shown that in addition to the major stroke, many patients also have a number of smaller strokes, called microinfarcts spread throughout the brain. We predict that these microinfarcts impair brain plasticity and therefore decrease recovery following stroke. Using an animal model, we will study how microinfarcts alter brain plasticity and affect recovery after a major stroke. First, we will study the effects of microinfarcts on normal brain function by mapping out parts of the brain that control movement of the body. Specifically, we will study the part of the brain that can move the forepaw of mice and evaluate how microinfarcts affect the amount of movement produced when this region of the brain is stimulated. Next, we will study how microinfarcts alter recovery after a major stroke. We will measure brain activity as animals perform a reaching task. By imaging the same animals over several days, we can measure the plastic changes that occur in the brain that are responsible for improving motor performance. We will be able to determine if microinfarcts alter the amount of brain plasticity occurring following a major stroke. In our last experiment, we will evaluate if microinfarcts decrease the benefits of rehabilitation after focal stroke. Motor practice improves recovery after stroke, but we predict that microinfarcts will decrease the amount and quality of this motor behavior, resulting in impaired recovery.

column37: Purpose: Kidney disease affects 1 in 10 Canadians. 35,000 Canadians currently have kidney failure needing dialysis or a kidney transplant. A cause for kidney failure is unknown in 50% of patients. Kidney disease does not make people unwell until it is advanced. If properly identified, it may be possible to treat people earlier before their kidney disease has progressed. Diet and the environment contribute to kidney disease, but our genes play a large role. However, each of these kidney diseases are rare, and together they account for a small proportion of patients with kidney failure. We will look for patients whose kidney disease is due to the total effect of many genes that are working poorly, instead of a single gene that is very abnormal. We will compare these results to more than 500,000 people from the general population. We will then focus on patients who are without a diagnosis to look for new types of kidney disease. Expected Outcome: We will find new combinations of genes that are working poorly that lead patients to develop kidney disease. Relevance to patients: Our research will improve our ability to tell patients what is causing their kidney disease. It will improve our ability to predict who is likely to get worse, even in early stages of kidney disease. We will be able to give better advice to kidney donors about their personal risk of kidney failure. We and others will use our findings to target new treatments for kidney disease.

column36: Hemodynamics of Pediatric Congenital Heart Disease Using Accelerated and Motion-Compensated MRI
column37: Nearly 1% of babies born in Canada have heart disease. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is an essential technology for evaluating this condition. In addition to showing the anatomy of the heart, MRI can also measure blood flow. This information helps doctors decide how serious the heart problem is, and how to treat the child. MRI can then be used again, to see how well the child responds to the treatment. A major challenge of MRI is that patients must remain motionless when pictures are being recorded, which is difficult for young children. In traditional MRI scans, motion will ruin the images. Medical staff must then repeat the scans, which prolongs the MRI examination. If a child is unable to remain still, sedation is necessary. Another significant challenge of traditional MRI scans of heart disease is the need to align the scan plane to the proper anatomy. This meticulous process further lengthens the scan and requires an expert in cardiac imaging. The goal of this proposal is to address these challenges by developing a fast (<5 minute), motion-insensitive MRI method to visualize three-dimensional (3D) anatomy and blood flow throughout the entire chest in children with heart disease. This proposal first focuses on developing new methods to speed up 3D MRI measurements of chest anatomy and blood flow, while also compensating for patient motions such as breathing and shifting within the MRI. Initially, development will be achieved by scanning adult volunteers. The resulting methods will then be applied to children with and without heart disease. This project will enable comprehensive evaluation of heart disease in a practical scan time and avoid the need for tailored scan prescriptions by an expert in cardiovascular anatomy. In addition to serving as a powerful tool for planning therapy, this work promises to transform our understanding and management of heart disease in kids.

column36: Lii Zaanfaan: Understanding Health and Well-being Trajectories of Metis Children in Alberta
column37: The Metis are post-contact Indigenous peoples of Canada with a unique combination of identity, values, language, and cultural traditions. They have been referred to as "hidden" Indigenous peoples because of the lack of health research and service policies specific to their needs and experiences. There are not many studies on Metis health and particularly about Metis children's health. Most research on this area groups the experiences of Metis, First Nations, and Inuit children together. The first decade of life is an important period for the influences of key genetic, biological and socioenvironmental factors It is important to understand the ways in which factors that affect the health and well-being of Metis mothers influence the healthy development of Metis children. Lii Zaanfaan means "the children" in Michif, the traditional language of the Metis. From a Metis perspective, the health of children is deeply linked to the health of their families, communities, and the land. This perspective is supportive of broader knowledge on social determinants of health and childhood development. This research results from a long-standing collaboration between the Metis Nation of Alberta and academic partners to develop community relevant knowledge to inform Metis-specific health initiatives. The project has three objectives: 1) evaluate health and well-being trajectories of Metis children during the first 10 years of life and the influences of maternal and social factors on these outcomes; 2) explore perspectives of Metis children and their families on social, environment and cultural factors that influence well-being and healthy development of children, and 3) identify community-led, culturally meaningful Metis initiatives to promote Metis children's health and well-being through cultural healing and self-determination. We will use a variety of quantitative and qualitative research methods that are culturally acceptable within a Metis context.

column36: Using MRI imaging to develop a personalized risk-based breast cancer screening strategy
column37: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the breast can detect breast cancer earlier than mammography or ultrasound. However, because MRI is very expensive and more likely to mistake benign breast structures for cancer, MRI is usually only offered to women with the highest risk of developing breast cancer based on genetic testing, family history, or previous radiation to the chest. The High-Risk Ontario Breast Screening Program (OBSP) is a unique screening program which provides annual screening with MRI to high-risk women. There is still a lot of variation in this high-risk group. At one extreme are young women with an inherited BRCA1 mutation who tend to develop aggressive, rapidly growing tumours. These women may benefit from more frequent screening or prophylactic mastectomy. At the other extreme are women with a strong family history associated with a currently unknown genetic abnormality who could actually be at average risk and who may not need annual screening. There is, therefore, a need for improved risk prediction methods. We propose to develop new artificial intelligence methods to extract information about breast tissue volume and texture from MRI. With MRI we can also measure how much contrast agent is taken up in normal breast tissue; this is known as background parenchymal enhancement, BPE, and it has been shown that there is a correlation between BPE and risk. We will assess whether a combination of these MRI properties can be used to predict cancer risk. We will also determine whether they are more strongly correlated with breast cancer risk than mammographic density which is already known to be useful in identifying patients at intermediate risk. Our methods will be tested on data from the OBSP which screens thousands of high-risk women each year at 30 different centres in Ontario. A more accurate assessment of risk could allow screening programs to be tailored to the needs of individual women and would also make better use of limited resources.

column37: Normal tissue turnover requires the clearance of dead and dying cells by special immune cells called macrophages. Without clearance, dead and dying cells can cause inflammation and damage to local tissues. We recently discovered that dead/dying cells accumulate in the lining of knee joints from patients with osteoarthritis (OA), suggesting that the process of clearing dead/dying cell clearance is defective. We will look at joint tissue damage and pain outcomes in this model, which has been shown to mimic the symptoms and joint damage seen in human knee OA. 3. Identify the specific molecular mechanisms that cause cell clearance to be impaired. This step is needed to identify the key targets that will be the focus of new OA treatments. In the future, such treatments would be designed to improve the clearance of dead/dying cells as specifically as possible, without causing unwanted off-target side-effects. These studies are critical to understand the role of cell clearance in OA and to set the stage for new treatment targets to be tested. OA is a massive unmet clinical need because it causes significant disability for people with OA. OA also causes significant costs to our health care system in Canada. Currently, no approved disease-modifying OA treatment exists. Therefore, our proposal describes an exciting new way to look at OA treatments and hope for the future.

column36: Strategies to Relieve Suffering at End-of-Life (STRS-EOL): A longitudinal qualitative study of healthcare policy and nursing practice.
column37: Suffering at end-of-life is not new or uncommon. However, what is new in Canada are the options available to address this suffering and how those options are intersecting in end-of-life decision-making. In this grant, we are using the acronym STRS-EOL to refer to these options for relieving suffering at end-of-life and they include medical assistance in dying (MAiD), palliative care (PC), voluntary stopping eating and drinking (VSED), and palliative sedation (PS). Palliative patients often ask healthcare providers to hasten their death, particularly during moments of suffering. In past, however, no legal options were available to address this request. In 2016 that changed. Canadians who meet eligibility requirements can now have MAiD whereby medications are used to induce death. Persons who request MAiD must be given the option of palliative care; however, it is widely recognized that there is a need to improve access to palliative care in Canada. Further, not all clients meet the eligibility criteria for MAiD, and in those cases, patients may resort to VSED or PS. Patients stop eating until they qualify for MAiD or they are sedated. With these evolving changes, there is a need to understand how the interactions between these approaches, and how broader social and demographic factors, are influencing these end-of-life decisions. Building upon research we are currently conducting, our aim in this project is to gain a thorough understanding of the developmental trajectory over an eight year period of policy and practice related to STRS-EOL. We will gather and analyze longitudinal data from policy documents, key stakeholders, and nurses with the goal of creating unique and highly sought after data to track and compare the developmental trajectory of STRS-EOL across English-speaking Canadian health regions over time. column36: Low Dose Metronomic Chemotherapy as a Combination Strategy to Combat Innate or Acquired Resistance to Immune Checkpoint Therapy
column37: The most significant recent advance in oncology is the remarkable success of new drugs which harness the immune system to treat advanced metastatic disease of a number of different cancers. Foremost among these drugs are "immune checkpoint inhibitor" (ICI) antibodies. However, a dose of reality has set in to temper some of the initial euphoria about these drugs. First, they are enormously expensive, placing a likely unsustainable strain on health care system budgets. Second, only minor subsets of patient (an average of ~15%) benefit from receiving ICIs. Third, they can be very toxic causing a number of immune related adverse events (irAEs). Finally, tumors which initially respond to ICI therapy usually acquire resistance and relapse. A strategy being studied to improve the efficacy of ICIs is by combination with other types of drug. But this approach can exacerbate the problems of both overall toxicity and cost. This proposal is designed to evaluate a strategy to deal with both problems, and using it to combat ICI drug resistance, namely, evaluating the impact of using lower and hence less toxic doses of certain inexpensive off-patent oral chemotherapy drugs, but given in a close regular fashion - known as "metronomic" chemotherapy (MC) - which Dr. Kerbel's lab has helped pioneer; it has shown positive results in some recent phase III clinical trials, especially when used as maintenance therapies after initial induction chemotherapy. There is evidence that certain chemotherapy drugs given as MC can actually stimulate rather than suppress tumor immunity, the latter of which can occur when given at conventional 'maximum tolerated doses'. Finally, the research will involve use of a number of new mouse models that mimic the clinical treatment of metastatic disease, and new tumor models that are either minimally sensitive, or intrinsically resistant to an ICI, or which have acquired resistance after showing major durable tumor regressions.

column36: Regulation of CD8+ T cell responses by the nuclear orphan receptor NR4A3
column37: The immune system of an individual is devoted to fight infections. The white blood cells of the immune system patrol the organism to eliminate pathogens. T cells, a type of white blood cells, are the central player allowing to mount an efficient immune response. T cells specifically recognize the foreign agents via a cell surface receptor, the T cell receptor (TCR). This recognition allows for the expansion and differentiation of T cells that are specific to the infectious agent. The differentiation of T cells is crucial to allow them to acquire the ability to eliminate the infectious agent. After clearance of the infection, most of the differentiated T cells will die to reset the system. A few of these T cells will survive as long-lived memory T cells to confer rapid protection against re-infection with the same agent. However, in certain circumstances, such as infection that become chronic or cancer, T cell function is diminished and memory T cells are not generated. As a consequence, the infection or cancer persists. Transcription factors, a class of molecules controlling gene expression, plays crucial roles in T cell response by inducing the proper gene expression program required for differentiation. Our project aims to understanding the molecular events allowing for proper differentiation of T cells during an immune response. We are studying the role of a family of transcription factors (NR4A1, 2 and 3) in inducing the expression of genes important for T cell differentiation.
