column36: Canadian Cancer Rehabilitation (CanRehab) Team: Improving the systematic identification, management, and treatment of the adverse effects of cancer.
column37: The diagnosis and treatment of cancer can result in long-lasting side effects which interfere with a person's ability to work, engage socially, and perform daily activities. To optimize patient outcomes, the health care system must focus not only on controlling the disease (i.e. cancer) but also on improving functioning and quality of life for individuals. There is an urgent need for research that can help to inform care for cancer survivors, including the early identification of physical side effects and the development of effective and sustainable cancer rehabilitation programs that can be supported and maintained within our health care system. The CanRehab team will bring together a large group of survivors, researchers and clinicians at four cancer centres across Canada (BC, ON, NB, NFLD) to conduct three linked projects that are focused on improving equal access to timely, effective, and appropriate cancer rehabilitation.The CanRehab projects include people diagnosed with breast, colorectal, head and neck, and lymphoma cancers. In Project One we will develop and evaluate an online system to screen patients for cancer-related impairments and to link them to services and resources based on need. In Project Two will test an 8-week on-line cancer rehabilitation program and examine implementation factors. In Project Three will test the feasibility of a 8-week group rehabilitation program tailored for the growing number of survivors living long-term with incurable cancer. Through these projects, we seek to improve the systematic identification and management of cancer-related adverse effects in order to regain/maximize function, independence and quality of life.

column36: Preparing to survive: improving outcomes for young women with breast cancer
column37: Women aged 40 and under with breast cancer experience poorer outcomes, havea wide spectrum of supportive needs and face unique survivorship issues compared to their older counterparts. Comprising approximately 5.4% of all women diagnosed with breast cancer, research and supports are lacking for this population. To address this, we created RUBY (Reducing the bUrden of Breast cancer in Young women), one of the world's largest prospective cohorts of women with young-onset breast cancer. To date, we have enrolled over 1000 women from 32 sites across Canada at the time of cancer diagnosis following them through treatment and into the survivorship period. Through RUBY, we have identified a number of unique survivorship gaps, including high levels of anxiety at diagnosis and beyond especially given extended hormonal therapies, marital and motherhood challenges, and social isolation. Specific, accessible interventions are required, but are currently lacking. ICAN Survive, is a promising self-management, on-line intervention for patients with cancer designed to address global survivorship issues at diagnosis and beyond. Key areas of need include regaining balance/dealing with diagnosis, coping with treatment and side-effects, management of anxiety and depression, fatigue management, sexuality and relationships. The ICAN intervention aims to build self management skills through guided training and education, however does not focus on the specific needs of young women. Thus, we propose to modify the ICAN intervention in collaboration with young onset survivors and evaluate the modified tool (ICAN-RUBY) for effectiveness. We are uniquely positioned to develop this young women specific intervention given the direct knowledge of gaps identified to date from existing RUBY cohort. We will leverage established RUBY study infrastructure with a proven track record of recruitment, to evaluate the effectiveness of the ICAN-RUBY tool in an embedded randomized trial.

column36: Virtualizing survivorship: Implementing a more timely and comprehensive model of follow-up care
column37: Prostate and breast cancer are the most common cancers in Canadian men and women. Early diagnosis and effective treatment have increased survival rates However, cancer survivors are often left with unwanted physical and functional effects after treatment, as well as psychosocial and mental health challenges that decrease their quality of life. Recently, "virtual" cancer care has gained attention. Virtual cancer care models use technology to deliver personalized survivorship care to patients who are at low risk of recurrence. Building on the success of these virtual models, our research group was awarded a CCS/CIHR Innovation Grant in August 2018 to design, develop, and implement three virtual prostate cancer clinics - called the Ned Virtual Clinics - across Ontario to address survivor needs at scale, reduce the burden of care, improve the survivorship experience, and increase quality of life. We want to improve our current Ned Virtual Clinics and their impact on Canadian survivorship outcomes through completing five new projects: (1) spread our current virtual prostate cancer clinic model to two new sites in Halifax and Calgary; (2) develop and validate an algorithm to personalize prostate cancer care; (3) introduce a new Ned Nurse to review survivorship outcomes, triage patients to appropriate care providers and services, and provide care in between/in place of scheduled virtual visits; (4) adapt this virtual prostate cancer survivorship model to inform the concept and service design of a virtual breast cancer clinic, and (5) explore new models of funding in Ontario, Nova Scotia, and Alberta for virtual survivorship services.

column36: Access to precision therapies for young people with cancer: Developing a policy framework to guide technology assessment and public funding in Canada
column37: Cancer remains the leading cause of disease-related death in Canadian children, adolescents and young adults (CAYA). Advances in understanding the genetic causes of cancer have opened up new treatment possibilities tailored to individual patients. Canada is a leader in precision medicine for childhood cancer: PRecision Oncology For Young peopLE (PROFYLE), a unique national precision oncology initiative, will determine the entire genomic sequence of tumours in CAYA with hard-to-treat cancers in order to identify alterations that are potential targets for new drugs. All CAYA with high-risk cancers in Canada, regardless of where they live, are eligible to take part in this project. However, the potential health system impacts of PROFYLE, and precision oncology more broadly, are not well understood. Many countries are grappling with how best to incorporate precision medicine innovations, including new expensive cancer drugs, into existing health care budgets. If precision medicine initiatives are to achieve lasting impact in Canada's publicly funded health care system, sound knowledge to guide their implementation is required. The overall objective of this project is to understand the policy and regulatory challenges of access to precision cancer therapies for CAYA in Canada. We will achieve this objective through a rigorous program of qualitative research that: analyzes and compares policies, regulations and funding of precision therapies for CAYA in different international contexts, and generates a policy framework and options to guide access to precision therapies for Canadian CAYA with cancer. These data will provide policymakers with evidence-informed considerations for the design and implementation of policies to govern fair and sustainable access to precision cancer therapies for young people.

column36: Innate and adaptive immune regulation in human type 1 diabetes
column37: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease caused by the immune system mistakenly killing the cells in the pancreas that produce the hormone, insulin. Without insulin, the body cannot regulate blood sugar and this can be life threatening. Insulin can be taken by injection (by syringe or insulin pump), but this cannot replace the natural ability of the pancreas to make insulin only when it is needed, and at the exact level needed. Hence, people with T1D face a lifetime of fluctuating blood sugar and run the risk of life-threatening highs and lows. A true cure for T1D requires the immune system to be re-set so it no longer attacks the pancreas, combined with regeneration of the insulin-producing cells. In this project we aim to assemble a unique cross-Canada team of experts in immune cell biology and diabetes, in order to study specific aspects of how the immune system kills insulin-producing cells (called beta cells) to cause T1D. First, we will collect blood samples from individuals with T1D, another autoimmune disease, or healthy controls. We will then use these blood samples to study how different aspects of the immune system change over time in T1D vs non-T1D subjects, to learn how immune changes correlate with beta cell changes. Results will also be analyzed to determine whether any observed changes are different in males versus females. Second, we will study how three promising types of immune cell therapies might be applied in T1D. We will study how these immune cell therapies might affect beta cell function/regeneration and develop new ways to apply such therapies as a treatment for T1D. Overall, this research will explore several never-before-investigated aspects of T1D biology and take existing therapeutic concepts a step closer to use in the clinic. We will also create synergy with other on-going international studies in T1D and further strengthen our research capacity in this domain.

column36: Prediction and prevention of rheumatoid arthritis in First Nations People
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a common autoimmune disease that causes progressive damage to the joints. It is known that individuals destined to develop future RA have autoantibodies (Ab) in their blood that are detectable months to years before the disease actually starts. Our studies have shown that RA is very common in some First Nations families, and that this is based on complex and unique interactions between genetic and environmental factors. Since 2005, we have worked in partnership with several First Nations communities and followed more than 750 unaffected family members of RA patients to determine their risk of developing future RA. To date, 20 individuals have developed RA, indicating a rate of ~1% new cases per year in the family members. We found that the detection of RA Abs in the blood does increase the risk of future RA, but we also show that most individuals with these Abs do NOT develop RA. This compelled us to find ways of predicting future RA that are based on a better understanding the immune system abnormalities that occur during this preclinical stage, and how these changes advance over time in some individuals but not others. With this knowledge, our ultimate aim is to find effective and safe ways to reduce RA risk in these predisposed individuals. Based on existing human and animal model data, we think that a dietary supplement of the spice turmeric, which contains the active ingredient curcumin, has the potential to safely reduce RA risk by modifying the immune changes that lead to RA. Omega-3 fish oils and adequate vitamin D blood levels seem to help the curcumin even further to achieve this. We therefore propose a clinical study to test this in individuals who have RA Abs but have not developed RA. We will use state-of-the-art immune tests to let us know whether there has been some correction of the abnormalities in treated individuals. We also hope to understand how First Nations People view clinical trials that aim to prevent disease

column36: Deciphering the therapy-driven molecular evolution of glioblastoma stem cells
column37: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and aggressive form of brain cancer with an expected survival of only 15 months. Traditional models of cancer that considered GBM to be comprised of identical tumour cells have not led to improved therapies. New research, however, now shows that cancer is instead comprised of a mixture of biologically distinct cell types. Importantly, one subpopulation of cancer cells shares many of the biological properties of "stem cells", primitive cells that facilitate the growth and cell diversity of our body during early life. These "cancer stem cells" have now shown to be the driving force in GBM growth and highly resistant to traditional therapy. This may explain why drugs developed to target the overall cancer biology eventually lead to recurrence and failure. To overcome this, Dr. Diamandis' team wants to better understand the biology of these rare cells and apply it to design cancer stem cell-specific therapies. Dr. Diamandis' team will first study the biology of cancer stem cells directly in GBM patient tissue before and after therapy. To achieve this, Dr. Diamandis' team will carefully cut out clusters of cells from the rest of the tumour using a laser and analyze them with a technology known as mass spectrometry. This has major therapeutic implications as this tool quantifies proteins, the same molecules that drugs are designed to target. To complement this, they will bioengineer artificial human-like brain tissue structures called "organoids" to model important aspects of how GBM interacts with normal brain tissue elements to evade therapy. Finally, will take advantage of a technology called "artificial intelligence" to study vast amounts of patient data to uncover subtle but critical interactions between the various cells found in cancer. Together, these activities hope to help develop cancer stem cell-specific therapies that debilitate cancer growth in its roots and holds promise to provide effective therapies for GBM patients.

column36: Stimulating the sleeping brain to improve memory
column37: When something is damaged, we need to understand how it functions in order to repair it - understanding the mechanisms underlying sleep and memory dysfunctions will help us to find avenues to treat them. Sleep plays a crucial role in learning by strengthening the brain's memory traces. Because sleep is a modifiable factor, we propose that manipulating specific sleep waves may enhance the learning process and potentially improve memory function. In recent years, there has been increasing interest in the use of brain stimulation techniques to manipulate human memory. Numerous studies have demonstrated that the application of electrical currents over the scalp (transcranial electrical stimulation) during a sleep period can boost memory performance. However, recent discoveries have put into question the use of this technique to reliably reach the brain (go through the skull) and stimulate neurons of the cortex. A promising tool to manipulate memory is direct brain stimulation, where electrical currents are applied through electrodes implanted in the brain. This work aims to determine if manipulation of sleep using direct brain stimulation can strengthen learning and memory processes. Our study will target adults with refractory seizures, as epilepsy is the only disease where electrodes are inserted into the brain. Furthermore, people with epilepsy also frequently have significant memory impairments, which are highly debilitating and negatively affecting their quality of life. The ultimate goal of our work is to use this knowledge to understand how electrical stimulation during sleep can be used to treat memory dysfunction. It is our hope that this work will ultimately improve quality of life of individuals suffering from memory issues.

column36: Improving Health System Quality Through Better Measurement and Service Delivery Redesign
column37: Poor quality of health care is currently a bigger barrier to reducing mortality than inadequate access in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs). Without provision of good-quality health care, currently recommended universal health coverage will not improve health sustainably in these countries. The Lancet Global Health Commission on High-Quality Health Systems in the Sustainable Development Goals era recently identified tracking health system performance using better measures and service delivery redesign, i.e., reorganization of service delivery, as a universal action for improving health system quality and recommended additional research in specific country contexts. The goal of this post-doctoral research program is to improve health system quality in sub-Saharan Africa through better measurement and service delivery redesign to ultimately maximize the health system impacts. Specific objectives are: (1) to develop a health system quality dashboard, comprised of existing and new indicators, to allow the health system to diagnose weaknesses and track performance and ultimately support the use of data for decision making to improve the health system performance in Ethiopia; and (2) to estimate the impact of service delivery redesign placing services at the level of the system that maximizes health gains in Kenya to guide policy decisions around service delivery redesign. Consultation with key stakeholders in Ethiopia and Kenya will be embedded in this research. Advanced quantitative analyses will be conducted to populate the Ethiopian quality dashboard with cross-sectional and longitudinal quality data nationally and by regions. Sophisticated modeling approaches will be used to estimate the impact of service delivery redesign in Kenya. This research has the potential to inform efforts to enhance the quality of health care and improve health sustainably in LMICs, including Ethiopia and Kenya.

column36: Untangling the relationship ageing, frailty, and dementia.
column37: As the world's population ages, the number of people living with dementia is quickly growing. Dementia inflicts an enormous burden on individuals, their families and caregivers, and our society. By 2050, over 131 million people globally will be living with dementia, costing more than US$818 billion. Following multiple failed drug trials for dementia, we urgently need to better understand how dementia develops in order to treat and prevent the disease. Interestingly, the brain abnormalities (pathology) that are thought to cause dementia are not related very well to the symptoms- that is some people have brain pathology but no dementia, and some people with dementia have very little brain pathology. Frailty has been associated with cognitive decline and dementia and they share many risk factors. My hypothesis is that frailty affects the level of brain pathology needed to produce the clinical symptoms of dementia. The objectives of the proposed study are to 1) test how frailty, brain pathology, and dementia are related in a collection of studies that accurately represent the population, 2) test the impact of reducing frailty on dementia risk by re-analyzing clinical trial data. This project is important because it has the potential to change our understanding of how dementia develops. By improving our understanding of dementia development we will be better able to target our research, clinical, and policy efforts towards finding effective prevention and treatment.

column36: Contribution of the microbiome to asthma risk in premature infants
column37: Premature infants are at increased risk of life-long diseases and treatments. Among the most compromised organs of premature infants are the lungs. In Canada and globally, very premature infants (between 28-32 weeks of gestation) and extremely premature infants (less than 28 weeks of gestation) are up to three and four times respectively, more likely to develop recurrent wheeze than term infants. Until now, lung compromise has been an accepted result of developmental delay and lung structural damage caused by medical practices needed to support respiration. However, epidemiological evidence shows that infants who do not develop lung structural damage are nevertheless at increased risk of asthma, indicating that other variables impact this risk. Exciting recent findings from infant studies and animal models implicate the large community of microbes (microbiome) in the human gut as a factor that contributes to asthma. However, despite their heightened risk of asthma and the pronounced microbiome alterations linked to prematurity, no clinical study of the microbiome and asthma has studied premature infants. Leveraging a world class team of microbiome experts and an established cohort specifically designed to capture clinical and environmental exposures unique to the NICU, this team grant will be the first to unravel microbiome-asthma linkages in the highly vulnerable premature infant population. We will apply powerful statistical tools to detect independent associations between microbiome features and asthma risk, and to interrogate the capacity of these species to mediate asthma risk. We will then use animal models to define the mechanisms by which specific microbes contribute to immune and neuroimmune pathways that lead to allergic airway inflammation. Our work will culminate in the identification of pre-clinical microbiome-based therapeutics aimed at decreasing the risk of asthma in thousands of Canadian children born prematurely every year.

column36: A mechanistic understanding of the impact of pathogen-microbiome dynamics on maternal nutrition during pregnancy in young women
column37: Maternal and child undernutrition are global problems with important consequences for survival, incidence of acute and chronic diseases, healthy development, and economic productivity. Aside from dietary deficiencies, the gut microbiome (i.e. an assemblage of diverse microorganisms occupying the human gastro-intestinal tract) is increasingly viewed as playing a critical role in nutritional status. While much is known concerning the dramatic impact of maternal nutritional status during pregnancy on birth outcomes, little is known concerning how dynamic changes in the microbiome can modulate maternal and fetal health during pregnancy. To understand the links between maternal nutrition, birth outcomes and the gut microbiome, we will study changes in microbiome communities in two groups of young women over the course of their pregnancy. The first group, from Pakistan, will be recruited from the recently established Matiari Preconception and Pregnancy Supplementation Trial. The second group, from Canada, will be recruited from clinics in Toronto serving refugee communities. Both groups will provide direct access to samples that will reveal the composition and functions of the maternal microbiome over the course of their pregnancy. Computational analyses allied with unique mouse and swine models will allow us to associate microbial communities with pregnancy outcomes. Of particular interest are the abundance and diversity of gut parasites that we expect will influence other microbes in the gut to negatively impact nutritional status during pregnancy. Understanding these complex relationships and their impact on malnutrition and birth outcomes, will improve diagnoses and inform the development of novel targeted interventions that can significantly improve maternal health and child development. This project directly relates to CIHR's mandate to improve global child health.

column36: Causational Roles of the Gut Microbiome in Childhood Asthma: Leveraging the CHILD Cohort Study
column37: Asthma is a lung disease that makes it hard to breathe. It is the most common reason why children miss school or end up in hospital. The CHILD Cohort Study was set up to research why some children develop asthma, and find out how we can prevent it from starting. Nearly 3500 babies and their families have joined this study. They have been answering questions and coming to clinic visits for over 8 years. Scientists working on the CHILD data have already made some exciting discoveries about who gets asthma and why this happens. One of these discoveries was about the importance of our gut bacteria in helping our immune systems to develop properly so that we don't get asthma. Other important discoveries showed that how babies are born, what they eat, and what medicines they take can affect their gut bacteria. But we need a lot more information to move from these discoveries to making treatments or policies to prevent asthma. In this project, we will use new technologies to find out how gut bacteria are causing or preventing asthma. Information from the CHILD study will guide us to do experiments in cells and mice to better understand how gut bacteria affect asthma. This research will help us develop new ways to prevent and treat asthma in the future by using or targeting gut bacteria.

column36: Dissecting host-microbiome modifiers of type 2 diabetes risk
column37: The global epidemic of obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2D) reduces lifespan and quality of life, and exerts enormous pressure on Canadian health systems. It is now well documented that changes in the composition of the gut microbiota (bacteria living in the intestine) accompany obesity and factors that increase risk of T2D. Most of the evidence for the microbiome's role in T2D is from bacteria in the feces. We have exciting evidence that bacteria and/or bacterial fragments are altered in the upper gut and selectively accumulate in the circulation, liver and various fat depots of obese women and men. Critically, T2D status dictates the body site-specific bacterial signatures in these obese subjects. The long-term objective of our team research program is to define the identity and function of the specific bacterial strains compartmentalized in specific gut segments versus body tissues in the progression of insulin resistance and T2D. We aim to use this knowledge to develop novel diagnostic, preventive and therapeutic approaches for diabetes to reduce disease burden. The overarching goal of this team grant application is to build synergies among Canadian microbiome and diabetes experts to advance knowledge by integrating new concepts and state-of-the-art technologies.

column36: Maternal depressive symptoms and children's academic performance: Sex differences in the mediating role of school experiences
column37: Children of mothers experiencing non-clinical depression are at an increased risk of poorer academic performance. Few studies have investigated factors which might explain this association, but none have considered factors within the school environment or potential sex differences in these associations. We tested whether school engagement (i.e. how invested students are in the learning experience) and peer victimization (i.e. being bullied) could explain the association between exposure to maternal depressive symptoms and children's academic performance. We used data from a Canadian study of the general population. Families (n=1173) provided data on maternal depressive symptoms (5 months to 5 years), children's school engagement and peer victimization (6-10 years), and academic performance (12 years). Daughters of mothers experiencing depressive symptoms had lower mathematics, reading, and writing scores, whereas sons only had lower mathematics scores. School engagement and peer victimization explained the association between maternal depressive symptoms in girls, but not in boys. Different mechanisms explain the association between maternal depressive symptoms and academic performance in boys and girls. Prevention and intervention strategies which target school engagement and peer victimization in daughters of mothers experiencing depressive symptoms may help improve girls' academic performance. Further research is needed to identify factors which explain the association in boys.

column36: The underlying epigenetic mechanisms in the association between childhood victimization and suicidal risk
column37: Over 20% of adolescents report being bullied by their peer group. Prior research indicates that being bullied in childhood is often associated with poorer mental health. For example, depressive symptoms, suicidal thoughts and behaviours can occur at the time, and sometimes persist into midlife. The underlying processes linking childhood bullying to increased depressive symptoms, including suicidal thoughts and behaviours, in adolescents and adults are unknown. One possibility is that being bullied, like other stressful life experiences, can result in biological changes such as the addition of molecules called methyl groups to various locations in the DNA. When these methyl groups are added at the beginning of genes, they can change how strongly different genes work. These methylation marks may fade with time or remain for decades. Hence, this study will first investigate whether people who were bullied in childhood tend to have different patterns of methylation marks in late adolescence and mid-adulthood. Furthermore, whether these different methylation patterns are an underlying mechanism linked to the development of suicidal risk. This research will allow to disentangle the role of genes, environment, and their interactions in the development of suicidal risk. We hope it will further our understanding of the contribution of different risk factors; environmental, genetic, or both, linked to suicidal risk and childhood bullying.

column36: Motor competence and cardiovascular health indicators across early childhood
column37: If a child has difficulty coordinating their body they may be less likely to be physically active and this may be bad for their health. Older children who are less coordinated tend to be less healthy; however, we do not know how young these health issues start. In our study, we have tested over 400 preschool children (age 3-5) once per year for 3 years. Each year we examined their motor skills by watching them do activities like jump, throw and balance. We then measured how healthy they were by looking at things like blood pressure, body fat and fitness. We found that children with better motor coordination had better fitness and less body fat, however their blood pressure was about the same as children with worse motor coordination. As motor coordination appears to be related to health even from a young age, it is important that we support all children to develop their motor skills in order to prevent them from becoming overweight and unfit as they get older.

column36: Strength-based assessment in autism: toward more inclusive methods for the assessment of cognition across the whole spectrum
column37: Many subgroups of the autistic population, such as autistics who have behavioral challenges, or who have minimal or no verbal language abilities, have been overlooked in research. They do, however, represent an important proportion of the autistic population. In clinical or educational settings, many of these individuals are considered to be untestable and are therefore considered to be intellectually disabled. However, through my doctoral research project, we showed that when using tests that call upon autistics' strengths, by adapting them in ways to facilitate the administration process, it is indeed possible to evaluate young or minimally verbal autistic children. We also demonstrated that many of these children showed "unsuspected strengths", which we would not have been able to capture with usual tests. We called our method the Strength-Based Assessment (SBA). The objective of the current project is to test a new version of SBA that includes tests measuring attention, memory, etc. that were adapted using universal design principles, to make them accessible and feasible to all people regardless of their limitations. The goal is therefore to determine to what extend the adapted tests improve our ability to assess autistic individuals and their performance on these tests compared to standard assessment. Using the SBA method will allow a detailed description of strengths and weaknesses, which would have remained unknown with usual tests, and allow them to reach their highest potential. We hope the project will allow SBA to be implemented in clinical and educational settings and, in turn, will lead to intervention plans that are matched to the potential of each individual.

column36: Unraveling the molecular mechanisms underlying cerebral blood flow deficits in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease
column37: Reductions in blood flow within the brain has been identified as an early event in the development of Alzheimer's disease. It was recently discovered that the smallest blood vessels, capillaries, in the brain of Alzheimer's disease mice were being blocked by an immune cell, and this small blockage was responsible for large reductions in blood flow. Amazingly, when the immune cells were prevented from sticking to the inside of blood vessels, brain blood flow was returned to normal, and performance on memory tests also improved. There is a type of cellular stress that is increased in Alzheimer's disease that could initiate the pathway that leads to the adherence of these immune cells in the blood vessels. We hypothesize that there are two types of cells at the root of this problem: One cell found in close proximity to blood vessels that might be responsible for generating too much of this cellular stress, and another cell that lines the inside of blood vessels that is responding to it. We aim to investigate the role of this cellular stress in reducing brain blood flow by targeting molecular pathways in the brain that will remove this cellular stress and bolster the brain's defences against cellular stress, in hopes of restoring blood flow, and memory. We will use experimental methods that target our two cell types of interest so that we can change how the cells respond to certain molecules by adding or removing certain genes to test our hypothesis. We will also deliver drugs to these cells specifically and examine their effects on cellular stress, brain blood flow, and memory. The proposed project seeks to increase our understanding of how cellular stress can lead to immune cell adhesion in brain blood vessels, and thus reduced brain blood flow. Our work will allow us to identify more cell-specific molecular targets for future drug development efforts with reduced drug side effects, aimed at interfering with immune cell adhesion to blood vessels.

column36: Linking microstructure and macroscale function of affective brain networks in health and disease
column37: Emotional experience is a complex process involving the coordinated activity of a network of brain regions, with key contribution of limbic cortices. These regions are characterized by their unique microstructure (i.e. organization of neurons in the cortex), which can be directly related to functional networks underpinning emotion processing using advanced neuroimaging methods. Notably, microstructural changes in limbic areas are a core feature of temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE). These patients show connectivity alterations grounded in microstructural abnormalities of limbic structures, as well as increased prevalence of impaired mood and difficulties in emotional processing. This population thus offers a unique opportunity to study how altered limbic microstructure relates to changes in connectivity and affective processing. Our goal is to develop a novel framework integrating microstructure and connectivity of limbic regions to understand their role in affective functions. This approach will allow us to study how local microstructure constrains brain connectivity patterns, and how lesions in limbic systems impair affective functioning. Healthy participants and TLE patients will undergo high-resolution neuroimaging to probe cortical microstructure, functional networks, and brain activity associated with emotion processing. Electrophysiological data from intracranial electrodes recorded at rest and during emotion recognition tasks will also be collected in a subset of patients undergoing this procedure as part of their clinical workup. These investigations will extend neuroimaging findings with direct recordings of neural activity in task-free and affective state conditions. This research will shift our conceptualization of affective functioning, and promises to guide predictions of affective impairments. Our findings will also lead to better recognition of affective disruptions in TLE, facilitating access to treatment and improving well-being and quality of life.

column36: Call for Inclusive eHealth: Identification of Empirical Indicators to Achieve This
column37: Do you have access to your digital health record? What mobile applications do you use? eHealth, or any digital tool to take care of our health, is an integral part of our lives. However, part of the population cannot use these modalities. Thus, this fact contributes to widening the gap in health status between people. Though, several potential solutions have been identified to reduce this inequality, including developing eHealth tools with the participation of more vulnerable people, which makes it possible to integrate their literacy level, learning ability, way of seeking help, cultural context and ability to access technology into the tool. Unfortunately, there is currently no way for eHealth tool developers to observe effectively and quickly whether these solutions are well integrated into the development of their tool and the purpose of this study is to remedy this. This study consists of 5 steps: 1) Documentary research: to identify in the scientific literature all existing measurement indicator that could be used to achieve the objective. 2) Group interviews with experts: to find out what they think about the measurement indicators found in the literature search and identify others. 3) Semi-structured interviews with vulnerable people: They are experts in experience and can bring a rich perspective to recognize whether measurement indicators actually measure what they are supposed to measure while remaining respectful of the target groups. 4) Choice of indicators. 5) Online Questionnaire sent to eHealth tool developers: to assess whether the selected measurement indicators are applicable, useful, relevant, valid and user-friendly. This study will allow developers to use measurement indicators to develop and evaluate their eHealth tool so that it is accessible to all future users and contribute to digital health equity. This innovation will make Canada a leader in improving health care in the digital environment.

column36: Investigation of the function of de novo peroxisomal biogenesis
column37: A cell is a highly ordered and compartmentalized place with intracellular organelles that perform a large number of essential biochemical reactions. Mitochondria and peroxisomes are such examples. While, mitochondria are known as the "energy powerhouse" of the cell, there are many other reactions that rely on a second, smaller organelle called the peroxisome to complete the chain reaction to obtain the final product. For example, the breakdown of very long chain fatty acids occurs first in peroxisomes, and the resulting shorter chain lipids are then transferred to mitochondria to be burned as energy. Without peroxisomes this cannot occur and the accumulation of products are toxic, causing cell death and diseases. These include rare disease, with complete absence of peroxisome, such as Zellweger syndrome, associated with dramatic consequences for the patients. There is also more common diseases associated with dysfunction of a specific peroxisomal pathway like plasmalogen generation in Parkinson's disease. The formation of new peroxisome is poorly understood. Our team showed that small vesicles originating from mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum are involved in peroxisome biogenesis. This project aims to unravel the molecular machinery and the signals that carries this process. Understanding in physiology how peroxisome biogenesis is induced and regulated will allow to help design new therapies for diseases associated with dysfunctional peroxisome.

column36: A dissection of transmembrane signal transduction and downstream signaling response in cytokine receptors
column37: The immune system is of vital importance to maintenance of human health. There are two main branches of the immune system - the innate and adaptive immune systems. While both of these systems are required for proper defence against pathogens and other foreign challenges, it is truly the combined efforts of the two systems that provides the protection seen. At the intersection between the two systems, there are cytokines and cytokine receptors, which allow for intricate crosstalk between these systems. Many cytokine receptors are seen to have one transmembrane helix in their architecture and are thought to function by dimerizing or rearranging upon cytokine binding, resulting in signalling within the cell. Despite the vast efforts applied to the study of these receptors, the nature of how the signal is able to cross from outside the cell, with binding of the receptor, to inside the cell, where proteins will bind and downstream genes will be regulated, is poorly understood. One area of confusion is the notion that these receptors can have varied cellular responses to differential stimulus, which goes against the dogma that simple dimerization is a driving factor in these systems. I aim to fill this gap in knowledge by pursuing the structures of various full-length cytokine receptors with varying stimuli and resultant internal factors. In addition, I will use an existing toolkit of engineered ligands for a specific non-immunological cytokine receptor, EpoR, to modulate the receptor in a tunable way. In addition, we will expand this toolkit to immune cytokine receptors to decipher the differences between various receptor subtypes. Through this structural and protein engineering, we will provide vast insight into the mechanisms for cytokine signals being transduced across the membrane and provide a framework for the development of novel cytokine receptor targeted therapeutics.

column36: Investigating the impact of evolving cannabis access and use on substance use trajectories and drug-related harm in the context of an opioid overdose epidemic
column37: Cannabis is the most widely produced, distributed and consumed illicit drug worldwide. Canada and many other countries are introducing new regulatory approaches to cannabis, including legalization. Although most research has focused on the harms of cannabis use, recent evidence suggests that cannabis use may alter specific high-risk drug practices. This research indicates that cannabis is often used as a substitute for high-risk substances such as cocaine, heroin or prescription opioids. However, these studies have not examined the impact of cannabis use over time and it is uncertain how the legalization of recreational cannabis will influence rates of high-risk drug use, infectious disease risk and addiction treatment. Given the recent legalization of recreational cannabis in Canada and the current opioid overdose crisis, identifying the impacts of cannabis use on high-risk drug use will be important for informing clinical and public health practice, as well as policy. The purpose of this research program is to describe how changing cannabis access and use influences the development of high-risk drug use patterns and addiction treatment. To accomplish these objectives, we will use data from three long-running community-recruited cohort studies in Vancouver, Canada, which will be supplemented by linked administrative data on participation in addiction treatment. These cohorts are operated by the BC Centre on Substance Use and include over 3,700 individuals who use illicit drugs, including high rates of cannabis use (>40%). Importantly, these studies include participants at different points in their drug use career, including at-risk youth at early stages of illicit drug use and older adults who use illicit drugs and tend to be more involved in addiction services. The diverse composition of these cohorts provide the opportunity to study the effects of cannabis use on the trajectory of high-risk drug use across the lifespan of active illicit drug users.

column36: Improving the quality of end-of-life care among cancer patients in Alberta, Canada through the development and assessment of a decision support tool for prognostication
column37: More Canadians die from cancer than from any other cause. It is therefore important to study and find ways to improve the delivery of healthcare to cancer patients who are close to death. Previous research has shown that approximately 20% of patients will experience unnecessary or inappropriate cancer treatment towards the end of life. For example, some patients will receive chemotherapy within two weeks of dying and some patients will die within a hospital without ever being referred to palliative care. Such end-of-life care is harmful because it reduces the quality of life of patients and represents a poor use of valuable healthcare resources. The purpose of our investigation is to: 1) determine how many individuals diagnosed with cancer in Alberta received unnecessary or inappropriate end-of-life care between 2004 and 2017; 2) develop a statistical model that will estimate the probability that a patient will die or experience serious adverse side effects within a short period of time if they decide to undergo or continue treatment versus if they decide to forego or stop treatment; and 3) use the statistical model developed in objective 2 to create a web- and mobile-based application that clinicians and patients can use to determine if additional treatment or referral to palliative services is appropriate for them and to assess the feasibility of this application within clinical practice. We plan to address objectives 1 to 2 using existing healthcare data collected by the Alberta government for the purposes of reimbursing physicians and hospitals. For objective 3, we plan to conduct a pilot study whereby we will give the decision support tool to a group of clinicians to obtain feedback about the perceived usefulness of this tool and to see if there were any changes in the way that the clinicians treated patients after they received the tool.

column36: Walk smarter not harder
column37: Knee arthritis commonly begins in the joint behind the kneecap, termed the patellofemoral joint (PF). It affects middle-aged and older adults, this impacts productivity and contribution to society and results in years of knee pain and disability across the lifespan. There is thus an urgent need for research aimed at understanding modifiable risk factors for PF arthritis that can guide treatment approaches. Cadence (i.e., number of steps taken per minute) during walking is one such risk factor. People with knee arthritis who take fewer steps per minute to cover the same distance (i.e., lower cadence) experience more severe PF arthritis in the future. Evidence suggests elevated knee joint loads contribute to development of PF arthritis and pain. Thus, research is needed to understand the relation of walking cadence to knee loading and pain, and whether cadence can be targeted to improve knee loading and pain in people with PF arthritis. Gait parameters such as cadence, joint angles and forces exerted on the ground can be measured very accurately in a research lab, but may not fully represent what happens outside that controlled environment. Wearable devices are relatively inexpensive and have the potential to monitor gait parameters in the 'real-world'. However, research to support the validity of these devices for measuring gait parameters is limited, especially at lower speeds typical of people with PF arthritis. The proposed study will address the following 3 research questions: 1) Is walking cadence related to knee loading and pain? 2) Does changing cadence (without changing waking speed) change knee loading and pain in people with PF arthritis? 3) Can wearable devices accurately monitor gait parameters (e.g. cadence, speed) in people with PF arthritis? My research will generate important new knowledge that will directly inform the development of a walking program for PF arthritis management that could aid in changing the trajectory of this disease.

column36: Resisting Vascular Cognitive Impairment: The Effects of Resistance Training on Myelin and Blood-based Biomarkers of Neuroplasticity in Older Adults
column37: Vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) refers to the loss of cognitive and brain function due to blocked or narrowed arteries in the brain. Very often, these blockages are in the small arteries of the brain and are only diagnosed with brain scans. Another feature of VCI is myelin loss; myelin is critical for the proper transmission of signals within the brain. Thus, myelin loss is associated with impaired cognitive function and mobility. Importantly, VCI is the second most common cause of dementia in the world. Fortunately, VCI may be the most treatable form of cognitive impairment as many of its key risk factors, such as high blood pressure, diabetes and high cholesterol, can be reduced with lifestyle changes. While we know that exercise is effective in reducing these risk factors, little research has been done specifically in persons with VCI to determine whether exercise can slow down the disease progression. Specifically, despite evidence that shows strength training (i.e., lifting weights) can reduce the damage due to blocked small arteries, current VCI research focus solely on aerobic training (e.g., running, walking). Moreover, no study has examined whether exercise of any type can reduce myelin loss over time in persons with VCI. Based on our prior work, we propose that strength training is an effective treatment strategy for slowing down disease progression in persons with VCI. Using a special brain scan, we will evaluate the effects of twice-weekly strength training on myelin over a 12-month period in persons with VCI compared to an active control group. We will also examine how strength training may minimize myelin loss in VCI by examining levels of neurotrophic growth factors in the blood. Our proposal is very practical as exercise may be an effective, inexpensive, and accessible intervention strategy with minimal side effects. Our proposal is also timely as the prevalence and burden of VCI will only increase due to the world's aging population.

column36: Investigating the impacts of alcohol-sales deregulation on emergency department visits and hospitalizations due to alcohol in the province of Ontario
column37: Problematic alcohol use is responsible for a large and growing burden on the health of Canadians. Prior research has identified possible regulations that governments can put in place to reduce problematic alcohol use and associated health harms. One frequently identified regulation is placing limits on the location and number of stores that can sell alcohol. However, several questions about the effect of this regulation exist including its causality, (i.e. whether having more stores cause individuals to consume more alcohol, or if more stores open in response to there being a high demand for alcohol by the individuals living in the region?), and if the number of stores impact the alcohol consumption of important groups differently (i.e. men and women, young and old, low- and high-income). The purpose of this research is to better investigate the relationship between the availability of alcohol stores and health harms. To do so we will take advantage of a change in government policy in the province of Ontario and the availability of high-quality data on health care visits. Starting in December 2015 two successive Ontario governments have made large changes to how alcohol is sold in Ontario including increasing the number of stores and their permitted hours of operation. This research will collect the location and hours of operation of all stores selling alcohol in Ontario before, during, and after these policy changes. We will then link this data into databases containing records of all emergency department visits and hospitalizations in Ontario and see whether individuals who live near a store selling alcohol are more likely to have an ED visit or hospitalization caused by alcohol. We will also examine this relationship for different demographic groups. We plan to work with health and government officials at the local, provincial, and national level to communicate the results of our research and help inform policy related to regulating how and where we sell alcohol.

column36: Neuromelanin Signals in the Substantia Nigra of Patients with Treatment Resistant Schizophrenia: A Cross-Sectional MRI Study
column37: Schizophrenia (Sz) is a chronic, progressive mental illness that affects 1% of the population. The current treatment for Sz includes the medications labelled 'antipsychotics (APs)' to block the action of dopamine. Unfortunately, APs do not work in 30% of patients (TRS: treatment-resistant schizophrenia). Clozapine (CLZ) is the only effective antipsychotic for TRS; its earlier introduction is recommended by the national guidelines. However, only 7% of patients with Sz are treated with CLZ and the average treatment duration before CLZ was 9.7 years in Canada. That could be attributable to the lack of biomarker of TRS. Recently, studies using positron emission tomography (PET) have suggested that those who respond to first-line AP treatment (TnRS: treatment non-resistant Sz) showed increased DA synthesis and release in the striatum compared to those with TRS. However, PET is not widely available in clinical practice and limited because of its high costs and the short half-life of radioligands. On the other hand, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is more accessible, less costly, and is able to examine the dopaminergic function by measuring neuromelanin (NM), which is a byproduct of the synthesis of monoamine neurotransmitters, including noradrenaline and dopamine. This technique has already been investigated in Parkinson's disease, but not for any psychiatric disorders such as Sz. This study will measure NM signals using neuromelanin-sensitive MRI (NM-MRI) in the substantia nigra, which contains the majority of dopamine neurons, and compare among patients with TRS (n=23), TnRS (n=23), and healthy control participants (n=23). We hypothesize that NM-MRI signals will be increased in TnRS in comparison with controls and TRS. Our approach will validate a broadly available biomarker to predict antipsychotic treatment response. NM-MRI scanning can then be included in the criteria of TRS.

column36: Understanding patterns of healthcare utilization of Canadian Armed Forces Veterans living with chronic pain and their experiences, values, and perceived needs related to chronic pain management: A mixed methods study.
column37: Chronic pain is a leading contributor to suffering and disability. It is a particularly important challenge for Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) Veterans. CAF Veterans are more likely to live with chronic pain than the Canadian population (27% to 57% of CAF Veterans versus 19% of all Canadians live with chronic pain). CAF Veterans are frequent users of medical services including family doctors, physician specialists and mental healthcare providers. However, there is a lack of research on the healthcare utilization rates of CAF Veterans living with chronic pain, specifically. Also, there is no information about the healthcare experiences, values and perceived needs of CAF Veterans living with chronic pain. Addressing these evidence gaps is critical for the development of future health services that meet the needs and align with the values of CAF Veterans living with chronic pain. We will use routinely collected healthcare data in Ontario to describe and analyze the healthcare services used by CAF Veterans living with chronic pain. We will perform in-depth one-on-one interviews with CAF Veterans living with chronic pain to understand their experiences, values and needs related to chronic pain management. The results will be shared widely to inform future health service delivery for CAF Veterans living with pain.

column36: Attacking glioblastoma multiforme with chimeric antigen receptor Natural Killer cells: a novel therapeutic approach
column37: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) causes narrowing and loss of blood vessels in the lungs, leading to increased stress on the heart and death by heart failure. Treatments for PAH are expensive and provide little benefit to the patient in terms of symptoms and survival. For many years, PAH has been associated with dysfunction in the immune system. Recently we have discovered that Natural Killer (NK) immune cells are reduced in number and impaired in function in PAH. Normally, IL-15 is needed for NK cell function and survival, while TGFb alters NK cell function and blocks the effects of IL-15. However, we and others have found that IL-15 and TGFb signaling is altered in PAH patients and in animal models of PAH. In the pregnant uterus and cancerous tumors, NK cells change their function to help form blood vessels that allow the fetus or tumor to grow. We believe that something similar occurs in PAH lungs, and NK cells are "tricked" into making the diseased lungs worse. To test this hypothesis, we have bred mice with NK cells that either can or cannot produce the main receptor for TGFb, called TGFbRII. These mice will be exposed to low oxygen levels, which will cause symptoms of PAH in normal mice. We will then test our mice for lung and heart function, as well as measure number and function of NK cells. We would expect the mice with NK cells that cannot produce TGFbRII will not develop PAH when exposed to low oxygen, and will have normal heart, lung and NK cell function. Furthermore, we will test a new treatment made by HCW Biologics which both stimulates IL-15 signaling and blocks the actions of TGFb (known as HCW9218). We will induce PAH in rats using two different methods and then treat the rats with HCW9218. We expect HCW9218 treatment will cure the rats of their PAH symptoms. These studies will help to better understand how NK cells contribute to PAH and will further develop a new treatment based on this idea.

column36: Investigating the relationship between apathy and tau burden in patients with mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease
column37: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI), a brain disorder in which patients have more memory and thinking problems than healthy people their age, often progresses to Alzheimer's disease (AD) where memory abilities and daily tasks are severely impaired. Apathy, characterized by a state of reduced interest, motivation and activity is one of the most common non-memory related symptoms of MCI and AD occurring in about 50%, and 80% of patients, respectively. Furthermore, 60% of MCI patients with apathy progress to AD. Medications which have been studied for the treatment of apathy have shown that only 30% of patients benefit. Understanding the underlying brain changes that occur in patients with apathy may help identify new treatments and delay progression to AD. Apathy has been associated with changes in the frontal cortex; regions at the front of the brain. In patients with memory difficulties, changes in the frontal cortex have been associated with a build-up of AD-related harmful proteins such as tau. Tau is considered a primary biomarker of AD, and is linked to cell death in the brain. However the relationship between apathy and tau is unclear. Fortunately, tau can be measured easily using positron emission tomography, an imaging test that uses a radioactive molecule to detect disease before it shows up on other imaging tests. Understanding the relationship between apathy and tau would help identify which patients can be targeted for early treatment that may delay or prevent progression to AD, and may also identify a new treatment to improve apathy and AD. Specifically, drugs that target tau may be of interest. Therefore, I propose to study differences in tau accumulation in the frontal cortex between cognitively impaired (MCI or AD) individuals with and without apathy, and whether other important characteristics such as size of brain region, presence of other behavioural symptoms, and severity of memory difficulties, affect the severity of tau accumulation.

column36: Improving the early identification of knee osteoarthritis with electronic medical record data in Canadian primary care
column37: Osteoarthritis is a painful joint disease that affects over 6 million Canadians. The knee joint is one of the most commonly affected joints. Knee osteoarthritis (KOA) starts with mild joint pain and stiffness that worsens to extreme pain often requiring surgery if left untreated. Being able to identify people with KOA in primary care at an early stage would help promote best-practice treatment. Yet, primary care clinicians report many barriers to identifying and treating KOA. This study will target this gap by using electronic medical records (EMR) from primary care clinicians who participate in the Canadian Primary Care Sentinel Surveillance Network to identify patients with KOA at an earlier stage. Next, a pan-Canadian KOA registry will be set up to learn about risk factors and health indicators of KOA. Lastly, an online KOA dashboard will be pilot tested in a small group of primary care clinicians. This dashboard will combine the EMR data with patient reported outcome data on pain, symptoms, physical activity, and quality of life to improve the treatment of their KOA patients.

column36: Dissecting hippocampal-amygdala circuit dynamics to predict depression vulnerability
column37: Depression is a major health issue, but we lack long-term effective treatment. This is partly due to our limited understanding of the disease biology. Recent research suggests that depression patients show abnormalities in interactions between brain regions that can in turn serve as useful indicators for identifying individuals susceptible to the disease. In particular, changes in interactions between hippocampus and amygdala, two regions critical for processing emotional information in the brain, can be used to predict patients' variation in mood. The goal of my postdoctoral research is to explore the mechanisms and neural circuits underlying changes in hippocampal-amygdala interactions in the depressed population. Specifically, I will identify the cells and circuits underpinning hippocampal-amygdala interactions that track with mood and examine how they are altered in population susceptible to depression. In addition, I will test how we can manipulate the neural circuit to reduce susceptibility. The findings will give new insight into the mechanisms by which depression alters the processing of emotional information in the brain and should inspire novel diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for the disease.

column36: Evaluating the prevention of disordered weight control behaviours among youth: Informing nutrition and mental health-related policy in Canada
column37: Disordered weight control behaviours (DWCBs), such as self-induced vomiting, unhealthy calorie restriction, and the use of non-prescribed diet pills, are common among young Canadians. Youth who engage in DWCBs are at a greater risk of developing eating disorders, obesity, and mental illness in adulthood. As a result, the prevention of DWCBs is an important avenue for improving population health. This research aims to evaluate health policies relevant to the prevention of DWCBs among youth, with implications for eating disorders, obesity, mental health, and chronic disease risk overall. To address this aim, I will conduct three studies to identify and analyse, generate recommendations for, and evaluate DWCB prevention policies in Canada. First, a literature review will be conducted to assess current DWCB prevention policies at federal and provincial levels within the areas of education, nutrition, mental health, and body weight. The review will be used to identify existing DWCB-related policies and their potential effects on population health, and identify policy gaps. To identify strategies to these gaps, Canadian leaders in the fields of eating disorders, obesity, nutrition, and mental health will be asked to provide policy recommendations. Promising policies will be evaluated using a modelling approach that allows us to estimate the impacts on rates of DWCBs, eating disorders, and obesity on youth as they age. Overall, the results of these studies will provide information on existing policies that can be used to evaluate progress on DWCBs prevention and inform concrete recommendations to address gaps. Such policies are critical for reducing the negative impacts of DWCBs on Canadian youth.

column36: Towards Precision Medicine for Violence and Aggression: Neuroimaging Biomarkers and Targeted Treatments
column37: Human violence is a common phenomenon that takes a large toll on individual lives and, indeed, Canadian society overall. Although the majority of individuals with psychiatric illness are not violent, some mental disorders are associated with increased risk of aggression toward oneself and others. Persistent violence may relate to underlying brain abnormalities or changes in brain chemistry that require specific treatment. Hence, research that strives to understand the brain differences of people who engage in repeated aggression could lead to new treatment tools and violence prevention strategies. We previously found using state-of-the-art brain imaging techniques that a brain chemical called fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) is increased in the brains of people with borderline personality disorder (BPD). BPD is a prevalent psychiatric condition that presents high rates of harm toward the self and others. FAAH is part of a chemical pathway in the brain that has been associated with increased aggression. Therefore, agents that block FAAH may be candidates for treating violence in BPD and other conditions. Continuing with this line of research, the current proposal evaluates whether talk therapies can affect brain FAAH levels in BPD and thus influence anger, hostility, and aggression. In addition, we will also look at FAAH levels in other psychiatric disorders, such as depression, which shares some commonalities with BPD and may also have high brain FAAH levels. The knowledge generated by these studies could stimulate new treatments for persistent violence and ultimately lead to improved health outcomes for both perpetrators and victims of violence. This research has the potential to reduce the economic burden of violence on the health care system, as well as the corrections system.

column36: Understanding the Ghost Core Phenomenon: Analysis of CT Perfusion Ischemic Core Overestimation in Acute Stroke:
column37: In an acute ischemic stroke, occlusion of cerebral blood vessels prevents the critical flow of oxygen to the brain. Without rapid revascularization, the death of brain tissue subsequently occurs. Computed tomography perfusion (CTP) can be used to visualize this process in real-time. Ischemic core, defined as tissue that is no longer salvageable, can be visualized alongside ischemic penumbra, tissue at risk of death that may be saved with blood flow restoration. Over the past 5 years, clinical trials have utilized CTP to select patients with severe stroke to undergo rapid revascularization via mechanical clot retrieval. Patients with a small core and large penumbra have been found to benefit the most from these interventions while, in contrast, patients possessing a large ischemic core benefit less and are at an increased risk of life-threatening bleeding. Patients with a large ischemic core are therefore less likely to be offered therapy. There is a growing recognition that in some cases, CTP may actually overestimate ischemic core. This phenomenon, termed Ghost Ischemic Core (GIC), carries the risk of precluding patients from undergoing necessary clot retrieval. Why GIC occurs in some patients, but not in others, is unclear. We aim to explore this particular question by analyzing the prevalence, topography, and natural history of GIC in relation to baseline clinical presentation, interventions utilized, and overall outcomes. In doing so, we hope to identify patients and/or clinical scenarios where ischemic core may be at risk of overestimation and shed further light into why this issue occurs in the first place. With the use of CTP becoming mainstream worldwide, the findings of this study will have the potential to launch new initiatives to improve ischemic core estimation and provide practical information for clinicians assessing patients at the bedside.

column36: Integrating Personalized Brain Simulation, Machine Learning, and Multimodal Neuroimaging for Early Detection of Alzheimer's Disease: A New Data-Driven Methodological Framework
column37: Maintaining a healthy brain through one's lifespan depends on the complex interaction between the brain, genetics, and lifestyle. With a rapidly aging population, the prevalence of neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's Disease are significantly increasing, with a projected 107 million cases by 2050. This is now recognized as one of the major medical challenges facing the world in the 21st century. While treatment options are limited, early detection can allow prevention strategies to provide individuals with additional years of healthy living, significantly less burden on their loved ones, and a substantial reduction in healthcare costs. Current early detection methods mainly limited to inherited types of early-onset Alzheimer's Disease. Our goal is to greatly improve early detection of all types of Alzheimer's Disease. This project will, for the first time, integrate personalized brain simulation and the predictive power of artificial intelligence to improve our understanding of Alzheimer's Disease, to predict as early as possible who will develop the disease, and even to forecast what form it will take for each individual. Breakthroughs in personalized brain simulation, a type of mathematical brain modelling that is tuned to each individual, have already been used to show how and why the brain changes when inflicted with Alzheimer's Disease. We will use high-quality clinical databases that follow the development of thousands of individuals through the aging process in research that can lead to new clinical detection methods. We will use brain simulation to model the effects of Alzheimer's other dementias compared to healthy aging on each person's brain, and we will use artificial intelligence to discover changes in the brain that predict a diagnosis of Alzheimer's in later years. With this new data-driven approach, we aim to help add years of high quality of life for the millions of people who may be affected by Alzheimer's in the future, and their families.

column36: Precarious work and gender disparities in mental health
column37: Precarious work refers to working arrangements that include unfavourable conditions such as low wages, low job security, poor physical working conditions, low control, uncertain scheduling, and few benefits. Studies show that exposure to precarious work increases the risk of mental health problems including depression and suicidality. Because women make up a higher percentage of those in precarious work than men in both Canada and the US, the growth of precarious work in these countries has great implications for gender disparities in mental health. Few studies have linked the growth of precarious work and its associated gender-inequalities in mental health to the labour market and social policies that shape both how people work and its health effects. Evidence on the gendered experiences of precarious work and mental health for populations who face multiple adversities, such as poverty and substance use disorders, and who are commonly socioeconomically marginalized, is especially lacking. This research program has two aims: (1) compare the extent that precarious work contributes to gender-based inequalities in mental health in Canada and the US between 2000 and 2018, and (2) examine this relationship from the lived experiences of individuals who are socioeconomically marginalized. Aim 1 will be examined with comparable samples from the US Panel Study of Income Dynamics and the Canadian Community Health Survey. Aim 2 leverages survey and in-depth interview data from three ethno-epidemiological studies of socioeconomically marginalized individuals in Vancouver. Using quantitative, qualitative, and cross-national analyses, this research produces evidence on the gendered distribution of precarious work and its effect on mental health; the modifiable aspects of gender-based inequalities that can be linked to the policies shaping precarious work; and, the mechanisms driving gendered experiences of precarious work and mental health for marginalized individuals.

column36: Eye movements as a sensitive indicator of motion perception in healthy older adults and patients with ophthalmic diseases
column37: As our population ages, an increasing number of Canadians experience difficulties with their vision. Although it is well known that both normal aging and age-related eye disease can affect a person's ability to see fine detail (such as in reading), tests of visual acuity used in regular eye examinations do not provide a complete picture of a person's ability to see in everyday situations, such as exercising and driving, where moving objects are often involved. Moreover, these tests often demand verbal instructions and do not accommodate sufficiently for the multilingual population of Canada with a range of cognitive functions. We propose to develop an instruction-free test that uses an easy-to-use eye-tracking technology to assess vision with moving objects. This new test addresses the urgent need for accessible assessments for the increasing age of our multilingual population. Our research will gather the scientific evidence that is needed to determine if this test is accurate, and whether it is practical to introduce it into clinical practice. This quick and non-verbal method of assessing vision provides a potentially cost-effective vision assessment strategy that addresses an important population health issue.

column36: Childhood disruptive behavioural profiles - improving economic participation through early screening and prevention
column37: Childhood disruptive behaviours - including aggression, opposition, inattention and hyperactivity - underpin the most prevalent and costly psychiatric disorders in youth. They are associated with increased risk of unemployment, low earnings, welfare receipt and poor mental and physical health outcomes. Given the large costs of disruptive behaviors for individuals and society, it is important to identify children who are at risk as early as possible so that they can be monitored and supported. So far, few studies have identified high-risk behavioral profiles in the general population and examined the impact of these profiles on future economic outcomes. Furthermore, it is unclear what precise mechanisms explain the association between risk profiles in childhood and poor economic outcomes in adulthood (e.g. adolescent delinquency, education underachievement) or what factors in childhood protect against these harmful effects (e.g. consequential parenting, good peer relations). This study will use teacher-rated behavioural assessments from age 6-12 years drawn from the Quebec Longitudinal Study of Kindergarten Children (n=3017) and government tax return records from age 18 to 35 years obtained from Statistics Canada, to address four questions: (1) What are the risk profiles at age 6 years that are associated with poor economic outcomes? (2) What is the structure and stability of these risk profiles from age 6-12 years and are they associated with risk profiles at age 6 and with economic outcomes? (3) What social and psychological factors explain the association between risk behavioural profiles at age 6 and poor economic outcomes? (4) What factors protect against the harmful effects of risk profiles at age 6 and poor economic outcomes? Findings will inform the development of prevention programs and policy initiatives designed to reduce the harmful effects of disruptive behaviours on long-term economic and social participation.

column36: Engineering the design of regulatory T cell therapy in transplantation
column37: Solid organ transplantation (SOT) is a curative option for end stage organ failure; however, the success of this procedure depends on life-long use of immunosuppressive drugs which put patients at risk for infections and cancer. Regulatory T cells (Treg) are immune cells that favour the acceptance of the transplanted organ by the recipient's immune system. One way to increase the numbers of organ-protective Tregs is to isolate them, expand them in the lab, and then re-infuse them into patients. A limitation, however, is that it is difficult to isolate Tregs that are specifically able to suppress immune responses to a transplant. Recently, we developed a revolutionary way to overcome this limitation using a genetic engineering strategy in which organ-specific Tregs can be made by introducing a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. This project aims to optimize the function of CAR-Tregs by studying how to best design the CAR and to find ways to reduce risks associated with this strategy. My first goal will be to modify the CAR structure trying to find ways so mimic how Tregs would be naturally activated so their function and lifespan are optimal. I will also aim to reduce the risk of using CAR-Treg therapies. We have recently identified that CAR-Tregs which do not express a protein called Helios are prone to lose their ability to favour organ acceptance. We thus aim to engineer CARs in a way that they would only be expressed in Tregs which continue to express Helios. I will carry out these aims using experimental systems that are well-established. Significance: by optimizing CAR structure I will improve the function and lifespan of CAR-Tregs and also reduce their associated risks. The results generated in this study will inform the design of future clinical studies and will also help to facilitate the use of CAR-Treg-based therapies as a new therapeutic tool to diminish transplant rejection.
