column36: Evolving Behavioral Phenotype in Children Born Very Preterm: Brain, Stress Regulation and Parenting
column37: Children born very preterm are at high risk for behavior problems including inattention and social difficulties, placing enormous burdens on family, school and community. Wide variation is seen in behavior outcomes and problem severity, even in children born at the same range of prematurity but we do not know why. How adverse clinical factors during neonatal intensive care contribute to outcomes and the extent to which parenting after discharge mitigates these neurobehavioral problems is unclear. Longitudinal investigation of developmental pathways from birth through to school age to examine relationships between early-life brain development, stress (cortisol) regulation and behavior problems, together with the role of parenting, is urgently needed. AIMS: I will examine longitudinal developmental pathways to understand why some very preterm children do well and others poorly: 1. Characterise the behavioral phenotype of children born very preterm at school age (8 years) 2. Examine how neonatal factors, early-life brain dysmaturation, and stress regulation (cortisol levels) across childhood alters: a) trajectories of behavior problems across ages 1.5, 3, 4.5 to 8 years; b) the preterm behavioral phenotype at 8 years; c) pathways differently for boys and girls 3. Characterize specific parent interactions during semi-structured teaching tasks that ameliorate effects of early-life stress and brain dysmaturation from infancy through school-age, in boys and girls To address these aims I will use Drs. Grunau & Miller's internationally unique longitudinal very preterm cohort that includes quantitative brain imaging twice in early life, serial cortisol measures, filmed parent interaction and developmental follow-up at ages 1.5, 3, 4.5 and 8 years. In Neonatal Follow-up, parents of very preterm children express that behavior problems are challenging and seek advice. My research will identify parent interactions that improve behavior, to provide tangible benefits for families.

column36: Validation of scores from the Parent-child interaction scale, WECS and WECS-P
column37: While in the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU), the preterm infant's brain develops optimally through nurturing and parenting. A healthy early parent-infant relationship may have a direct impact upon children's global development. Current tools to measure the parent-infant relationship are not well-fitted for parents of preterm infants because it requires the preterm infant to be competent in feeding and is lengthy. For this reason, the Welch Emotional Connection Scale (WECS), used to code a videotaped parent-infant interaction, was developed to offer a straightforward and simple measure of the parent-infant relationship which does not require a specific competence from the infant. In parallel, a parental form of the WECS (WECS-P), has been developed for a subjective self-reported measure of the parent-infant relationship. The combination of a subjective measure (WECS-P) and objective measure (WECS) may be beneficial to optimize the evaluation of the parent-infant relationship as it is based on both behaviours and emotions. The aim of this study is to evaluate the convergent validity of scores from the WECS and WECS-P.

column36: Improving the utility of polygenic scores to predict and understand disease risk: a foundational resource.
column37: Many diseases are preventable by early detection and/or intervention if we knew who is most at risk. For diseases like coronary artery disease (CAD), risk predictions are made based on age and sex in combination with known risk factors (e.g. family history, cholesterol levels, body mass index, smoking habits). However, there is also a strong genetic component to the likelihood you will develop CAD (~50% of total). My research focuses on Polygenic Risk Scores (PGS), a method that can be used to predict genetic predisposition for a disease by aggregating the effects of variants across an individual's genome. Studies have shown that currently used risk prediction methods for multiple diseases can be improved by including PGS. Despite the benefits of PGS, there is both a lack of standardization and an incomplete understanding of their predictive ability (especially in people of non-European ancestry). This hinders PGS' adoption in clinical practice. To fill these gaps in our understanding, I am creating the PGS Catalog: a foundational resource to distribute the information necessary to apply and understand PGS for a wide range of diseases and traits. I will also perform a systematic comparison of PGS to measure PGS predictive ability and identify the best PGS for each trait (where multiple exist). Through this research I will identify any deficits in generalizability across ancestries and between sexes that need to be corrected. Finally, I will use the PGS to measure their ability to predict disease risk in rare disease patients, measuring how PGS combine with rare mutations. Together my research aims to establish the PGS Catalog as a foundational resource to advance our understanding of disease risk prediction using genetics, while also enabling new research and clinical uses of PGS.

column36: Exploring the actions of autoantibodies in fibromyalgia
column37: Fibromyalgia is characterized by widespread pain and tenderness. Between 1.5 and 10% of the population suffer from fibromyalgia, but despite this high prevalence no diagnostic tests exist and current therapies have limited effect. We know very little about the causes of fibromyalgia, which is partly why fibromyalgia is diagnosed with a list of criteria, rather than tests, and why current treatment strategies are so limited. We recently discovered that injecting antibodies from fibromyalgia patients into mice causes pain-like behaviour and increased activity of pain sensing neurons. These results suggest that some fibromyalgia patients' immune systems produce autoantibodies that attack their own bodies. Therefore, autoimmunity could underlie fibromyalgia in a subset of patients. Our findings have the potential to change how fibromyalgia is viewed and how it is treated. In this project we will build on our findings to better understand how fibromyalgia autoantibodies cause pain. First, we will search for the protein(s) fibromyalgia antibodies recognize. Identifying which proteins antibodies bind to will provide information about how they could drive pain. Additionally, these results can open the door to the creation of diagnostic tests based on the presence of specific antibodies, similar to the tests used in rheumatoid arthritis, rather than on a certain number of symptoms. Second, we will investigate how fibromyalgia antibodies increase the activity of pain sensing neurons. We have already found that fibromyalgia antibodies bind cells called satellite glial cells, which surround the cell bodies of pain sensing neurons. We will examine how fibromyalgia antibodies alter the activity of satellite cells, and how they then alter pain sensing neuron activity. Our expected results will provide the basis to develop diagnostic tests based on autoantibody presence and provide the rationale for using antibody targeting therapies to manage fibromyalgia.

column36: Understanding Pathways to Mental Health Care During and After the Psychotic Prodrome: A mixed methods study
column37: BACKGROUND: Multicomponent early intervention services have undoubtedly improved care for adolescents and young adults experiencing a first threshold-level episode of psychosis (FEP). However, access to such care remains challenging for many-especially since distress, symptoms and impairment begin long before the FEP, during a psychotic 'prodrome' consisting of non-specific and sub-threshold symptoms. Access can be operationalized by measuring 'pathways to care' (PTC) in the form of (a) treatment delays following onset of symptoms, and (b) subsequent attempts at help-seeking. PTC are well known in FEP, yet unstudied in the prodrome-even though most patients appear to seek help for mental health reasons prior to their FEP. METHODS/OBJECTIVES: Through mixed (qualitative and quantitative) methods, we will undertake the first direct examination of PTC during the psychotic prodrome in a well-established, catchment-based service for FEP based in Montreal, Quebec. We will utilize the Circumstances of Onset and Relapse Schedule in 148 consecutive patients, along with a series of smaller focus groups to better understand: 1) Treatment delays and help-seeking during the prodrome versus the FEP 2) When and why individuals, their families, and others delay decisions to seek help during the prodrome; 3) By whom, how, when and why help is eventually sought during the prodrome; 4) Reasons for and experiences of treatment delays and help-seeking before (versus after) the age of 18. SIGNIFICANCE: This study will be the first to fill the important knowledge gap of PTC during the psychotic prodrome; its KT strategy is designed to obtain multi-stakeholder input on how our findings are relevant to future research and service delivery. Finally, applying a mixed-methods lens to PTC during the prodrome permits us to identify which actors or agencies should be targeted in the next phase of our research: future early identification campaigns aimed at reducing treatment delays or simplifying help-seeking.

column36: Identifying data-driven diagnostic subtypes of depression and treatment outcome using big data
column37: Although depression affects approximately 350 million people worldwide, a substantial percentage of patients do not respond to treatment even after trying several different therapies. Understanding inter-individual differences in brain function and structure will help provide new knowledge regarding profiles among individuals that might relate to treatment response, or treatment resistance. Applying novel machine learning methods to large-scale brain imaging data, will help stratify different "biotypes" of depression, and the neural mechanism that underlie them, which in turn will allow more personalized treatment strategy for any one individual. As part of this project, we will make use of population level data to identify depression "biotypes" and then assess these in a separate, large clinical sample, following the changes in brain connectivity over an 18-month period. This project aims to enhance our ability to identify subtypes of depression informed by neurobiological classification, and further our understanding of the brain mechanisms underlying treatment response vs. treatment-resistance.

column36: Uncovering the synaptic and cellular basis of the persistence of long-term memory.
column37: Long-term memories can be highly unstable like in Alzheimer's disease patients or highly stable like in those suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). However, the development of clinical therapies for these and other debilitating memory disorders has failed because of a lack of a fundamental understanding of how memory persists. How does a memory change with time in the brain? Recently developed methods that can visualize those cells that store a memory, termed engram cells, have shown that engram cells in one brain region critical to memory storage, the hippocampus, are silenced over two weeks after mice acquired a memory whereas those in another brain region, the cortex, are unsilenced. Additionally, recalling memories at these remote time points is known to make the memory transiently labile by reinstating a hippocampal engram. Interventions that block the reconsolidation of this labile memory could erase memory in rodents but failed in human clinical trials. A significant and compelling amount of evidence has been gathered over many decades that the strength of electric signal transmission between brain cells across 'synapses' is adjustable and underlies learning and forgetting. Engram cells might be silenced because a) a fewer number or weakened synaptic connections from pre-synaptic engram cells fail to activate post-synaptic engram cells, or b) the engram cells are being inhibited by other nearby cells, or c) the responsiveness of the engram cells to inputs has decreased. The unsilencing of engram cells could be explained by these effects in the opposite direction. I aim to find mechanisms of hippocampal engram silencing and cortical engram unsilencing and the effects of memory retrieval at remote time points. I will use cutting edge molecular tools, two-photon microscopy and electrophysiological methods to test the above hypotheses in mice that acquired a fear memory 1 day (short-term memory) and 2 weeks (long-term memory) after learning.

column36: Cognitive remediation for social cognitive deficits in schizophrenia: efficacy of the program RC2S and determinants of treatment outcomes
column37: Social cognitive deficits are one of the best predictors of functioning difficulties in schizophrenia. Social cognition refers to the mental processes underlying social interactions. Cognitive remediation therapy (CR) is a behavioural intervention that has shown its efficacy to improve social cognitive deficits in schizophrenia. Despite its efficacy, every patient does not benefit equally from CR, depending on individual characteristics. However, no study to date has systematically examined the role of these individual characteristics in CR efficacy for social cognition. Further, very few CR program targeting social cognition have used a personalized approach to tailor the treatment to individual difficulties. RC2S is an integrative and personalized CR program that targets several social cognitive functions and that uses virtual reality to emulate social interactions. However, no study has yet assessed its efficacy. The objectives of this project are to assess the efficacy of RC2S in terms of cognition, functioning and clinical symptoms in schizophrenia and to identify the personal characteristics that promote treatment outcomes. A total of 50 participants with schizophrenia aged between 18 and 65 years old, with a social cognitive deficit will be recruited. They will undergo an initial assessment of cognition, functioning and clinical symptoms and they will be randomized to the treatment group or to the waiting list. Participants in the treatment group will begin RC2S for 7 weeks. Participants in the waiting list will receive their treatment as usual during 7 weeks, will be reassessed and will then begin RC2S. Initial assessments will be repeated at post-test and 3-months post-test. This project will provide the first data regarding the efficacy of RC2S and the first assessment of individual characteristics that promote treatment outcomes in CR for social cognition. Ultimately, these results could help tailor CR and provide cost-effective interventions.

column36: Discovering the subtype of sympathetic preganglionic neurons capable of stabilizing blood
column37: Recently, Dr. Richard Wilson's lab showed that small internal sensors in the neck - the carotid bodies - drive asthmatic attacks by activating the autonomic nervous system. His lab also found that the carotid bodies play an important role in lung inflammation. These observations suggest that the carotid body's influence over the autonomic nervous system may be a driving factor in common, costly and devastating allergy-associated inflammatory diseases such as asthma and irritable bowel syndrome. We know that the carotid body can active both the sympathetic and parasympathetic subdivisions of the autonomic nervous system. Since both of these systems can influence localized inflammation in select organs, they may therefore be crucial in initiating localized allergic responses. My current research has shown, in humans, that the autonomic nervous system can be controlled selectively to different targets throughout the body, a phenomenon known as differential control. Differential control has been shown to be drastically altered in many disease states, but how this mode of control is achieved, even in the healthy state, is unclear and whether it drives allergic disease is unknown. We suspect that the carotid body will have a strong involvement over differential control of the autonomic nervous system in the healthy state and will be responsible for the manifestation of organ-specific allergic responses and inflammation in asthma (lung) and irritable bowel syndrome (gut). We will also investigate whether we can halt the development of allergic disease by manipulating the activity of the autonomic neural pathways. We suspect these findings to be very translatable to other inflammatory disease states, such as hypertension, and will spark a new school-of-thought in how we treat allergy and chronic inflammatory conditions; that being through direct manipulation of dysfunctional neural circuits within the brain.

column36: High Flow Nasal Cannula versus Non-Invasive Ventilation in exacerbations of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary disease
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a disease characterized by shortness of breath, cough and sputum production. COPD worsens over time leading to debilitating complications and frequent hospitalizations. In Canada, COPD affects over 2 million Canadians -the number is expected to rise in the coming years. In under a decade, the number of Canadians diagnosed with COPD increased by 82%, now affecting 1 / 116 Canadians. COPD is the 3rd leading cause of death in the United States, causing 120,000 deaths yearly. COPD is characterized by frequent exacerbations with life-threatening breathing problems requiring management in the emergency department (ED) or intensive care unit (ICU). To relieve shortness of breath, non-invasive ventilation delivered via a mask on the face is recommended, but needs expertise, close monitoring and can be poorly tolerated. Another non-invasive device provides a heated and humidified high flow of gas with controlled oxygen fraction through nasal cannula, avoiding the need for face mask. This promising alternative has not been tested yet in this situation. We recently showed that this technique has advantages compared to non-invasive ventilation in patients with cystic fibrosis which leads to similar problems with breathing. The aim of our program is 1) to assess the potential benefits of this technique compared to non-invasive ventilation, and 2) understand the mechanisms of action in order to adapt therapy to the degree of severity. We will compare the physiologic effects and tolerance of high-flow nasal oxygen and non-invasive ventilation in patients with COPD exacerbation admitted to the ED or ICU If high-flow nasal oxygen is at least as effective as non-invasive ventilation, this could be a major advance in the treatment of COPD, potentially reducing health-care resource burden, hospital admissions and optimizing symptom control for patients. It could significantly improve the long-term management of these patients.

column36: Home Virtual Visits for the Management of Chronic Kidney Disease: A Pragmatic Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) affects about 10% of the population. The costs of caring for these patients exceeds $40 billion per year in Canada. Patients with moderate-severe CKD typically receive routine follow-up care with their nephrologist every 3-6 months. A follow-up appointment with a nephrologist requires time to travel to a clinic, out-of-pocket costs for patients, and time away from other responsibilities. Canadians have expressed a clear interest in being able to manage their healthcare online. The Ontario Telemedicine Network recently launched Home Virtual Visits (HVV), a telemedicine platform that enables physicians to securely connect to patients via an electronic device. HVV may help address some of the challenges faced by patients when receiving CKD care. However, evidence is needed to ensure that high-quality patient-centred care can be delivered through this medium as evidenced by improved patient satisfaction and quality of life. This pragmatic randomized controlled pilot trial of HVV compared to traditional, in-person visits will provide the first step towards the provision of the highest quality of evidence for the use of HVV as a provincially accessible intervention in CKD.

column36: Exploring the etiology and prevention of young-onset colorectal cancer: an interdisciplinary approach
column37: While the incidence of colorectal cancer in Canada is decreasing, the incidence among adults under the age of 50 is increasing. The overarching goal of this research program is to reduce the incidence of and mortality of colorectal cancer among adults under the age of 50 through multiple approaches. First, to better understand colorectal cancer among this age group, we will examine the mutational profiles of colorectal cancer tumors and determine if the profiles for young and older adults are different. Second, using data from a large Canadian cohort study we will determine if specific combinations of lifestyle behaviours (obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, alcohol consumption, and diet) are associated with an increased risk of colorectal cancer among this age group. Third, to support clinical decisions for guiding screening in this population, we will determine if biomarkers and clinical factors can identify patients at high risk of developing colorectal cancer. Finally, we will estimate the potential impact of changing screening practices (reducing the age of initiation) on the prevention and treatment of colorectal cancer among this population. This research has the potential to inform population-based prevention efforts, as well as clinical decisions around screening and treatment.

column36: The Role of Microglia in Chronic Stress-Induced Cognitive Impairment
column37: Chronic stress is associated with cognitive impairment. It is possible that this is due to the brain's immune cells, microglia. Microglia can engulf and chew up neurons, which are the cells in the brain that talk to one another. It is possible that chronic stress makes these immune cells more likely to engulf neurons, which leads to cognitive deficits. To understand this, we will use live imaging to look at how microglia act in the brain of chronically stressed laboratory mice. We will then see if treatments that can reverse chronic stress induced cognitive deficits, such as probiotics, cannabinoids, omega-3 supplementation or ketogenic diet, work through altering these brain immune cells (microglia). Together these data will better inform how chronic stress leads to alterations in cognition and may provide a new target for therapeutics of stress-associated diseases.

column36: Investigating Macrophage AMPK as a Potential Therapeutic Target for Treating Type 2 Diabetes and Cardiovascular Disease
column37: Rates of Type 2 Diabetes and cardiovascular disease are rapidly increasing in Canada. These conditions often occur together and evidence suggests that they should also be treated together. Unfortunately, current therapies for either condition are ineffective. We believe that the high blood glucose that occurs during the development of type 2 diabetes causes inflammation, which represents the key link between diabetes and CVD. Specifically, macrophages, a type of immune cell, are essential mediators of the inflammation present in diabetes and CVD. Moreover, we have evidence suggesting that activating an enzyme called "AMPK" in macrophages may reduce inflammation and improve symptoms associated with diabetes and CVD. To test this, we will directly expose macrophages to high amounts of glucose and assess the inflammation that develops. We will also directly treat macrophages with a newly developed drug to activate AMPK to see if we can reduce inflammation in macrophages in the presence of high glucose. We will also treat mice with this AMPK activating drug and assess whether AMPK is activated in macrophages and whether this can prevent the development of diabetes and CVD in lean and obese mice with high blood glucose. Finally, we have previously tracked the development of diabetes and CVD in ~1400 humans, and we will use these data together with the current experiments to try and uncover a new marker that can be used to predict the development of diabetes and CVD in humans. Together, these results will provide extremely important evidence on the development of Type 2 Diabetes and CVD and new therapeutic ways of predicting, preventing, and treating these conditions.

column36: Clinical trajectories of patients recently diagnosed with major depressive disorder: a prospective cohort study
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) affects more than 350 million people worldwide. Previous studies showed that a subset of individuals diagnosed with depression present worse clinical trajectories marked by functional impairment. Of note, about 10% of patients suffering from depression are later diagnosed with bipolar disorder (BD), because they developed a manic or hypomanic episode. That is consequential since it changes their treatment, making the early detection an important need in the field of mood disorders. column36: Improving estimates of patient mortality among drug-resistant tuberculosis patients

This project will help researchers and TB programs accurately estimate the number of TB patients who died so they can better measure TB quality of care.

column36: CDX and TRIM31: a novel pathway linking chronic inflammation and colorectal cancer.
column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cause of malignancy and second most common cause of cancer death. There are a wide range of therapy available for colorectal cancer, but treatment becomes complicated as there are a range of colon cancer subtypes. Subtypes of cancer respond to therapy differently, as a result there is increased risk of recurrence and metastasis. There is a significant reduction of 5-year survival rate for stage-I CRC to stage-IV CRC (90% to 10%). This necessitate to search early biomarkers and improved therapeutic strategy during the early stage of colon cancer progression. Therefore, in cancer research it is crucial to subcategorize the cancer type based on biomarker discoveries which can lead to more effective therapeutic procedures. Chronic inflammation in the form of inflammatory bowel diseases, including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are some of the risk factors for tumor progression in colon. Our lab works with a family of protein called Cdx1 and 2.They are present in high load in the gut. These proteins are crucial for gut development and maintenance. Moreover, Cdx2 is considered as a marker for advanced colon cancer. My preliminary work suggests loss of Cdx protein is linked to aberrant inflammation. I have found that Cdx protein directly regulates production of a protein named Trim31, which has anti-inflammatory properties. Thus, loss of Cdx or Trim31 proteins lead to chronic inflammation in the gut which in turn promotes tumor formation. My study aims to identify the cellular functions and pathways that are affected by the loss of Cdx and Trim31 proteins; and to find out the factors and inflammatory cues that are playing important roles in this imbalance., Thus, this study will reveal a novel roadmap that leads to chronic inflammation and colon cancer formation. ; and may serve as a blueprint for developing improved therapeutic strategy for colon cancer.

column36: Age-associated inflammation alters myeloid cell development and function
column37: Recent statistics tell us that 90 percent of Canadians aged 65 and over live with at least one chronic condition including heart disease, respiratory conditions, diabetes, or arthritis. While the cause of chronic disease is complex and multifactorial, age-related changes to the immune system are a major contributor. Stem cells in the bone marrow give rise to two different lineages of immune cells: myeloid and lymphoid immune cells. As people age, these stem cells may acquire genetic mutations that skew the differentiation of immune cells towards the myeloid lineage at the expense of lymphoid cells. In addition to this "myeloid-skewing", the immune cells are often immature and have reduced function. Accumulating evidence suggests that this predisposes older adults to developing health complications, but the genetic changes that occur in the stem cells and the molecular events that underlie these changes remain unclear. The aim of my postdoctoral fellows is to determine the link between myeloid genetic mutations, myeloid-skewing, and immune impairment with age. We hypothesize that mutations in a specific gene called TET2 results in myeloid impairment. This is thought to be driven by the aging bone marrow environment, which has increased inflammatory mediators. To approach this, I will integrate my prior experience in machine learning with a custom next-generation sequencing platform to identify genetic biomarkers in blood of elderly patients. Concurrently, I will use transplantation studies in Tet2 knockout mice to determine if inflammatory mediators in the aging bone marrow results in myeloid-skewing and impairment. These experiments will determine whether modifying inflammatory mediators in the bone marrow is a viable option for reducing myeloid skewing, which we can pursue in subsequent experiments by administering inflammatory blockers. Ultimately, we believe the results of this research will provide avenues for new therapeutic interventions.

column36: The role of NAD synthetase 1 in VACTERL syndrome
column37: VACTERL syndrome is a set of birth defects that affects multiple areas of the body, including the heart, limbs, kidneys, trachea/esophagus, and spinal cord. If a patient has any three of these defects, they can be diagnosed as having VACTERL syndrome. This syndrome occurs in 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 40,000 newborns. Treatment is specific to the type of symptoms but may include surgery along with long-term management. The exact cause of VACTERL association has yet to be identified, although in some people it appears to be a combination of genetic and environmental factors. At the Children's Hospital of Western Ontario, genetic testing of 2 patients diagnosed with VACTERL association and their parents identified a mutation in a gene called nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) synthetase 1. NAD is an important molecule found in all living cells which regulates multiple different biological processes, such as metabolism, aging, and DNA repair. Past studies have shown that other defects in the NAD synthesis pathway have also resulted in VACTERL syndrome patients. My project will aim to understand the role of NAD synthetase 1 in early development and why defective activity of this enzyme results in a specific subset of developmental defects called VACTERL syndrome. I will be using stem cells with the same mutation in NAD synthetase 1 as was identified in the 2 patients in hopes of understanding what type of cell lineages are affected by this mutation and why. This work will be part of an international collaboration with Dr. Sally Dunwoodie at the Victor Chang Cardiac Research Institute in Sydney, Australia, who is developing mouse models to further understand the molecular basis of this association. Overall, our research will contribute to the identification and understanding of the genetic variants that may be associated with VACTERL syndrome in hopes of developing better treatment options and improving family counselling.

column36: Investigating the role and impact of obesity and measures of adiposity on cognitive function
column37: Obesity is one of the most important unmet prevention and treatment health challenges. The high prevalence of overweight and obesity, which has more than tripled since the 1970s, is of serious public health concern since overweight and obesity are often concomitant with adverse complications, including diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease (CVD). Cognitive impairment and depression are also suggested to be associated with obesity and increased measures of adiposity. Given 50 million people worldwide are diagnosed with dementia and more than 300 million people of all ages suffer from depression, it is important to determine and address possible modifiable risk factors if we are ever to alleviate the overall global burden of these diseases. While obesity has been connected to cognitive health the evidence is still uncertain. Dietary factors have long been implicated in non-communicable disease risk. Consumption of specific dietary patterns may lead to decreases in adiposity and hence improve cognitive function and reduce the risk of neurodegenerative diseases. In order to address these concerns a comprehensive research program is proposed which conducts a series of studies investigating the relationship between obesity and changes to body weight with indicators of cognitive function as well as risk of dementia and depression. This will be done using data from the PREDIMED-Plus trial, one of the biggest milestone trials in nutrition research in Europe. Following this investigation a synthesis and comparison of dietary patterns in relation to body weight and risk of obesity will be conducted to determine potential strategies to reduce obesity, as well as potentially improve cognitive function. This research, specifically determining lifestyle related strategies, such as following a dietary pattern, has the potential to have significant local and global impact on health and our health care system.

column36: A method to recapitulate early embryonic gut spatial patterning and morphogenesis in hESCs
column37: As an organism develops, simple homogenous tissues undergo successive patterning and morphogenetic events to produce structurally complex heterogenous organs. In vertebrates, these events are primarily driven by reciprocal morphogen and mechanical signals between two or more adjacent cell types. Despite extensive knowledge about the individual nature of the signals and cell types involved, however, less is known about how they come together to create large-scale patterns, sharp boundaries, and the final size and shape of tissues-especially in the context of human development. A marked example of this is the development of the human gut, where despite the ability to create and study human cell types for almost every region in vitro, we still lack basic knowledge about how the embryonic gut tube regionalizes and sets the sites of the future endodermal organs. Such knowledge is not only critical for understanding development, but also for understanding and potentially treating a variety of common congenital disorders. It would also be greatly beneficial for tissue engineers for deriving new strategies to create tissues and organs for regenerative medicine. With a Life Sciences Research Foundation Fellowship, I plan to build on recent progress combining tools from synthetic biology with human embryonic stem cells to create a novel model system for studying the patterning and morphogenesis of the human gut. The system will also be applicable more generally to studying other instances of tubular patterning during human development, and for experimenting with and creating synthetic organ systems for future clinical application.

column36: Exploring RNA splicing regulation using direct sequencing of nascent RNA
column37: Messenger RNAs (mRNA) are copies of genes that contain the information necessary to produce proteins. The formation of the right cell type depends on the production of the correct mRNAs that contain the instructions to make this given cell type. This is achieved in part through RNA splicing, in which certain parts of the premature RNA called introns are removed to form the mature mRNA. Defects in RNA splicing are a common cause of many human disorders, including cancer and neurodegenerative diseases. However, the mechanisms that control splicing in human cells are not well understood, which is mainly due to a lack of tools to study splicing while it is occurring. We recently developed a new method, nanopore analysis of CO-transcriptional Processing (nano-COP), which relies on direct RNA sequencing and allows us to monitor splicing while new RNAs are being produced. For example, we gained insight into how fast splicing occurs and the order of intron removal in human leukemia cells. The objective of this project is to use nano-COP to better understand how these aspects of splicing are controlled in various cell types. We will first apply nano-COP to measure splicing in 10 different human cell lines, including normal and cancer cells, to determine how splicing dynamics vary across cell types and in cancer. Next, we will use white blood cells from 10 different individuals to examine how splicing kinetics and order are impacted by genetic variants in parts of the RNA that are known to cause abnormal splicing. Finally, we will remove three proteins that play a role in splicing to determine in which aspect of splicing they are most important. We will repeat this experiment in three different cell types to discover whether certain functions of these proteins are cell type-specific. This study will improve our understanding of the control of the splicing process, which is crucial in order to learn how it goes awry in various human diseases.

column36: Can a single bout of exercise improve clinical outcomes in patients undergoing coronary artery bypass surgery? Investigating the effects of acute local (handgrip) exercise on attenuating cardiac and vascular injury to ischaemia-reperfusion
column37: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is among the leading causes of morbidity and mortality in Canada and worldwide. While coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery remains the preferred strategy to restore blood flow to the heart in CAD patients, this procedure is associated with peri- and post-surgery complications. The duration and/or severity of cardiovascular tissue exposed to ischaemia is strongly related to morbidity and mortality, hence the importance to minimize tissue injury to ischaemia during surgery. Novel cardioprotective strategies are needed to improve clinical outcomes in patients undergoing CABG surgery. This project will build on exciting research findings in both animal models and healthy participants demonstrating that an acute bout of exercise lowers tissue injury to ischaemia-reperfusion. The goal of the proposed research is to examine the hypothesis that a single bout of handgrip exercise can attenuate vascular and cardiac injury to ischaemia-reperfusion in participants with CAD. Moreover, I hypothesize that these effects can be enhanced through a short period (4-days) of daily handgrip exercise training. These effects of local handgrip exercise on mediating smaller vascular and cardiac injury to ischaemia will ultimately lead to lower post-surgery morbidity/mortality. The simplicity, low cost, and low risk of handgrip exercise makes it highly suitable to implement into clinical care to potentially reduce cardiac and vascular injury to ischaemia. Moreover, this work will contribute to informing and optimizing exercise guidelines prior to cardiac surgery.

column36: Wearable micro-electronics for clinically applied vascularized composite tissue transplantation and reconstructive transplant research
column37: Extremity transplantation has the potential to restore function to a patient's injured limb, but graft rejection and the risks of immunosuppression limit its applicability to all patients in need. The clinical and scientific rationale of the approach is that repetitive protocol biopsies of the skin of vascularized composite allotransplanted (VCA) grafts (e.g., arms and face) are designed to survey for impending failure due to subacute rejection, in which the immune system is activated against the transplanted VCA graft but the patient is without clinical signs of rejection. Despite the potential treatment benefits of protocol biopsies, these procedures lead to scaring and fibrosis, introduce a route for opportunistic infections and oftentimes lead to graft pain. The objective of this project is to develop a wearable device that non-invasively monitors for potential graft rejection and to acquire pre-clinical data to adapt the sensing technology to organ and tissue transplantation. The device is a thin, wearable sensor that records alterations in microvascular blood flow within the skin to provide continuous monitoring of the transplanted graft. This application ultimately targets patients injured by devastating trauma who may undergo VCA; however, the sensor technology developed here has a wider capacity to help and impact a broader patient base. Vascularized composite tissue reconstruction in patients undergoing skin graft surgery after burns or composite tissue flap reconstructive surgery after mastectomy for breast cancer, together represent ~62,000 hospitalized patients annually.

column36: Identifying Early Biomarkers and Nutritional Correlates of Future Reproductive Disturbance in Adolescent Females
column37: Abnormal reproductive development in adolescent females may have long lasting consequences on health. Teens often wait two or more years after their first period (menarche) before being evaluated for reproductive disorders, such as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). Early detection and intervention of abnormal reproductive development would help to reduce future health issues, but a major challenge relates to the lack of knowledge about the nature of the adolescent reproductive transition in the years immediately after menarche. In adults, features of the ovary on ultrasound are useful in detecting problems with reproduction. But, reliable data on how the ovary changes during adolescence are not available, limiting the ability of ultrasound to detect problems early in teens. We know that nutrition can impact the onset of puberty and contribute to reproductive problems later in life. However, what role nutrition may play in the years between menarche and the diagnosis of a reproductive disorder is unknown. This research will address these gaps by defining the changes in the ovaries that occur alongside the development of menstrual cyclicity during the first two years after menarche. We expect to see differences in the appearance of the ovary in teens that achieve regular periods versus those with irregular periods after two years. This research will also determine whether specific aspects of nutrition are related with the trajectory towards PCOS in teens. We predict that dietary intake, even at this early stage, impacts reproductive function. These studies will reveal changes in the ovary during adolescence that can be used to develop early diagnostic tools for clinicians when evaluating teens for risk of reproductive disorders. By identifying dietary factors that may influence reproductive development, this research will form the basis for future studies that can evaluate the impact of nutritional changes on reducing risk and progression of reproductive disorders.

column36: Cellular inhibitor of apoptosis 1 (cIAP1) as a novel therapeutic target for the treatment of Duchenne muscular dystrophy
column37: The Nuclear Factor-kB (NF-kB) pathways form a signaling complex that is critical for normal skeletal muscle function and is important in promoting recovery in response to muscle injury. Since we have several drugs that effectively and specifically remove cIAP1, we will evaluate their therapeutic potential in mdx mice, the mouse model for DMD. We will also clarify the mechanism of action of these drugs by examining how they change NF-kB activity in dystrophic muscle. Our findings have the potential to improve muscle structure and function and thus the quality of life of patients living with DMD.

column36: Mechanisms underlying abnormal uteroplacental vascular adaptations in pregnancies complicated by advanced maternal age
column37: More women are having their first pregnancies at an older age. In Canada, 8% of women have their first child when they are over 35 years of age (also known as advanced maternal age). A woman's blood vessels need to go through large changes during pregnancy, so that the fetus can receive enough blood and nutrients to grow normally. If the blood vessels do not adapt well enough, this can cause problems during pregnancy such as poor fetal growth and preeclampsia. Advanced maternal age is a risk factor for both of these pregnancy problems. Unfortunately, advanced maternal age impacts on how well these blood vessels change in pregnant women. If we can find out exactly how advanced maternal age adversely affects these blood vessel changes in pregnancies in women at advanced maternal age, we can target these mechanisms for treatment. Our lab found that uterine arteries from aged pregnant rats did not function as well as the arteries from young pregnant rats. The differences that we found may explain the increased problems in advanced maternal age pregnancies. We thus need to know more about these poor functioning arteries and why they do not function well. To do this, we will assess the function of vessels from pregnant young (4 months old) and aged (9.5 months old, equivalent to ~35 years in humans) rats. We will test blood vessel function, and use specific drugs to identify how their function is different. We will also compare blood vessels from pregnant and non-pregnant young and old rats. This will allow us to test if the blood vessels from old rats adapt differently than in young rats. At the same time, we will assess this mechanism in vessels from human biopsies taken during caesarean deliveries from young and older pregnant women. Pregnancy affects the short- and long-term cardiovascular health of both mother and child. This will help develop new treatments for older pregnant women to improve pregnancy outcomes in this high-risk group.

column36: A mixed-methods study to investigate socio-economic inequities in effective coverage of reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health interventions in low- and middle-income countries
column37: Globally, there has been renewed effort to provide public health services to ensure all women and their children survive and thrive. However, there is often much variability in the affordability, quality and experiences of care received by different socio-economic groups, and thereby in the level of health-related and financial hardship that families face. This research project will be conducted in India and Tanzania to measure differences in access to health services before, during and after childbirth for women in higher and lower socio-economic groups, the clinical quality of care provided when they access them, and whether this ultimately improves the health of women and their children. The study will also involve in-depth case-studies in regions with varying socio-economic differences in the health of women and children to explore their experiences with and perspectives on healthcare services, and the context-specific reasons for any differences between socio-economic groups. This research will be conducted through established partnerships with academic and public health organizations in Tanzania and India. It will provide new knowledge by applying theories and methods from different disciplines to understand socio-economic differences in the accessibility, quality, and impact of healthcare services, particularly with a focus on the health system, socio-cultural, political, economic, geographic or other contextual factors shaping them. This will provide international partners with specific information to guide their programs, and contribute to Canada's role as a leader and ally in global health research to improve the health and well-being of all women, adolescent girls and children.

column36: Investigating the role of FAM72A in B cell antibody diversification
column37: Antibodies, also referred to as immunoglobulins (Ig), play fundamental roles in our immune system by providing protection against pathogens. Antibodies are "Y" shaped molecules produced by specialized immune cells called the B cells. The tips of the two arms of the "Y", named the variable regions, differ greatly among different antibodies, thus providing the antibodies with the specificity and diversity for binding pathogens. The stem of the "Y" is named the constant region and it determines the functional properties of the antibodies. Antibodies can be further divided into different classes, with different antibody classes adopting different modes of action, such as directly binding to microbes and neutralizing their effect, localizing antibodies to different tissues, and signalling other immune cells to kill the infecting microbes or microbe-infected host cells. Upon exposure to an antigen, antibodies undergo diversification process to strength their abilities to bind and neutralize antigens. Somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination, both initiated by an enzyme named AID, are two genetic mechanisms that enable B cells to produce antibodies with higher antigen binding affinities and different classes. Our current knowledge towards somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination is likely incomplete, as complex and multifaceted molecular events take place during these two processes. Through a genetic screen I have identified FAM72A as a novel gene that functions in antibody class switch recombination, and propose to fully characterize the role of this gene and its product during antibody diversification using mouse models and diverse biochemical and cellular experimentations. My proposed work will advance our understanding on how antibody diversity is achieved, and influence vaccine development or the generation of therapeutic agents that target specific B cell malignancies.

column36: Re-sensitization of immune checkpoint therapy resistant cancers to cytotoxic T-lymphocyte mediated killing
column37: Cytotoxic T-lymphocytes have a key role in elimination of cancer cells by the immune system, but their anti-cancer efficacy is severely hampered by immune checkpoints. Immune checkpoint inhibition (ICI) can re-activate anti-cancer immunity and provides durable responses in multiple cancer types. Unfortunately, clinical studies indicate that the majority of cancers do not durably respond due to initial or acquired resistance. Loss of TNF signaling was recently identified as a determinant of ICI resistance. Preliminary work by the Moffat lab identified the TNFa-responsive membrane receptor Tnfrsf1a as a top resistance hit in multiple cancer models. column36: Molecular detection of known and novel cancer predisposition genes
column37: Dr Schrader will use state-of-the art technologies to identify the inherited basis of cancers that run in families or occur multiple times in a single individual. Dr Schrader will test many genes at once in the patient's tumour DNA alongside their normal DNA, to look for candidate genes altered in both samples that are most likely to be the basis of the patient's inherited cancer. Diagnosis of an inherited cancer susceptibility can determine whether patients and family members are at risk of cancer and both the patient and at-risk family members may benefit from increased screening, surveillance and/or prophylactic cancer prevention measures. Dr Schrader also proposes using these sequencing technologies to test whether we can improve upon current cancer detection strategies in individuals with known cancer susceptibilities. By screening body fluids for DNA released from early tumours with secondary mutations, it may be possible to detect evidence of early tumours. A positive screen may alert physicians to undertake more targeted diagnostic strategies to find and treat cancers at an early stage. Finally, genome-wide sequencing also has the potential to reveal information regarding cancer and non-cancer related genetic disease risks. Arguably, the clinical uptake of genome-wide sequencing has been the fastest in oncology, where tumour sequencing is undertaken to identify drug-targetable mutations. Clinical and research practices regarding the management of potentially clinically significant genomic findings in our normal DNA are evolving. Dr Schrader will research both the cancer and non-cancer related genomic findings revealed throughout the course of clinical and research tumour and normal DNA sequencing. Understanding of the scope and potential utility of such findings will be critical as the policy and practice moves forward in this regard.

column36: Maternal and Child Health Consequences of Infant Removal by Child Protective Services
column37: Manitoba has one of the highest rates of child removal by child protective services in the world. Among the 10,000 children currently in out-of-home placement, an estimated 33% of children were removed within the first year of life, of which more than half were removed at birth, the overwhelming majority of whom are First Nations and Metis. Whereas out-of-home placement is a widely recognized factor influencing children's health and development, little research has focused on the effects of placement during infancy on the later health of children and virtually no research has extended examination to the health of their mothers. As strategies to prevent separation of mothers and infants, particularly newborns, are an increasingly urgent priority for Indigenous leaders, better understanding of the role of placement in infancy is vital both to provide a fuller picture of its impacts and to identify optimal leverage points for reducing inequities in family wellbeing. To address this knowledge gap, I will draw on innovative methods to analyze longitudinal, linked administrative data for the entire Manitoba population of mothers and their offspring. I will investigate whether placement in infancy differentially impacts the health of First Nations, Metis and non-Indigenous mothers and children compared to those who experience placement later in childhood or who remain together. This study is expected to uncover whether and how inequities in health are characterized in the lives of mothers and children who are separated in early life, and to inform equity-based and Indigenous-led interventions to preserve maternal-infant bonds, address unique health challenges of this population, and shorten time to reunification. Translation of findings will occur in collaboration with an advisory team of Indigenous organizations to ensure their relevance in advancing initiatives that benefit well-being of Indigenous families and promote greater health equity in the population at large.

column36: Understanding and preventing serious bacterial and fungal infections among people who inject drugs
column37: People who inject drugs face extremely high rates of death and disability from severe and invasive bacterial and fungal infections (including infections of the bloodstream, heart valves, and bones) that require hospital admission for treatment with antibiotics and/or surgeries. These infections are devastating for individual patients, and also extremely costly for our health care system. So how can people who inject drugs, and health systems who care for them, prevent these serious infections from occurring? Unfortunately we don't have scientific evidence to inform us. One promising approach to reducing risk in opioid-injectors is medication treatment for opioid addiction (with methadone or buprenorphine) as this helps people to inject less frequency. However risk for serious infections likely reflects multiple factors, including homelessness, use of stimulants or alcohol, and individual injecting practices. Based at the Collaborative Centre for Inclusion Health (CCIH) at University College London, my Fellowship project aims to inform people who inject drugs, clinicians, and health systems on how to prevent serious bacterial and fungal infections. We will analyze a unique large dataset from South London that contains anonymous health records for anyone who has ever been to addiction treatment, linked to their hospital records. We'll assess whether methadone or buprenorphine treatment is associated with decreased risk of infection-related hospitalization or death in people who inject opioids. We'll also assess what other factors are associated with risk (including homelessness, sex work, injecting practices, stimulant or alcohol use), and see whether these change the effectiveness of methadone or buprenorphine. We'll collaborate with groups of people who use drugs in London, UK, and Halifax, Canada to help refine our analysis plan and determine what risk factors may be most important.

column36: Salt inducible kinases: novel therapeutic targets for chronic kidney disease mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD)
column37: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is characterized by structural abnormalities and impaired kidney function. Inadequate filtration of wastes and minerals (including phosphate) leads to serious disruption in mineral metabolism and bone disorder (Mineral and Bone Disorder; MBD). In CKD-MBD patients, phosphate retention in blood triggers secretion of a hormone called fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) to promote renal phosphate excretion. However, FGF23 blocks the generation of the active form of vitamin D. As vitamin D is essential in calcium absorption, low vitamin D causes low blood calcium level, stimulating the production of parathyroid hormone (PTH) by parathyroid glands. Elevated PTH levels restore blood calcium by bone breakdown, resulting in bone loss and fractures. Currently, no drugs can improve both vitamin D levels and renal phosphate excretion. Although PTH usually accomplishes these tasks, CKD-MBD patients do not show expected PTH effects on mineral metabolism, despite the high level of PTH. Therefore, we hypothesized that targeting the downstream mediator of PTH signaling pathway would bypass PTH resistance, yet still bring PTH-like effects to help CKD-MBD. Recently, a family of enzymes called salt-inducible kinases (SIKs) was reported to participate in the actions of PTH in bone. To test if SIKs participate in renal PTH actions, we will use cutting-edge genome editing and pharmacologic approaches in multiple cell lines, as well as two mouse models. The role of SIK deletion in kidney will be determined in mice using a genetic engineering technique known as Cre-lox system. Then, the effects of a SIK inhibitor will be studied in CKD mouse models with kidney injury to examine its therapeutic potential. Considering high prevalence of CKD worldwide (about 13.4%), and at least 4 million Canadians suffering from this chronic disease, this study will give insight into a novel approach in managing CKD-MBD and understanding PTH/SIK signaling in kidney.

column36: Molecular Dissection of MECP2 Protein Phase Separation in Rett Syndrome
column37: Lipid-lipid phase separation is a physical phenomenon characterized by molecules de-mixing into distinct lipid phases. This process is known to drive the formation of membrane-less compartments in cells that concentrate biochemical reactions. Increasing evidence points to the involvement of aberrant phase separation in neurodegenerative disorders through excessive protein aggregation. Rett syndrome (RTT) is a postnatal progressive neurodevelopmental disease associated with severe mental retardation that primarily affects females. The majority of the clinical cases have been traced to mutations of MECP2, a multi-talented protein that acts as a repressor or an activator of transcription. However, the mechanism underlying the complex role of MECP2 in cellular physiology and RTT particularly remains enigmatic. The Jaenisch laboratory has recently demonstrated that MECP2 can form phase-separated condensates in murine cells. On this basis, I aim to expand the role of phase separation in biological function and disease-causing malfunction of MECP2 to the human system. I will leverage the experimental paradigm established in the Jaenisch lab and use human embryonic stem (ES) cells to generate normal and RTT neurons in both two-dimensional (2D) and three-dimensional (3D) culture systems, and explore the molecular properties of phase separation in these human models. The human ES cells will be engineered to carry relevant disease-causing mutations in the MECP2 gene. The goal of this project is to advance the mechanistic understanding of MECP2's function and pave the way for new therapeutic approaches for RTT.

column36: Canadian Study of Arterial Inflammation in Diabetes and the Evaluation of Colchicine Effectiveness (CADENCE)
column37: Diabetic patients are at high risk of suffering atherosclerotic disease related events (eg acute coronary syndromes (ACS), stroke, transient ischemic attacks (TIAs)) and have a higher recurrence rate than the general population. Inflammation has been extensively investigated as a promoter of atherosclerosis development and destabilization. Recent trials have revealed outcome benefit in patients with cardiovascular disease who are treated with anti-inflammatory therapy. The LoDoCo trial also showed a reduction in cardiovascular events in patients with known coronary artery disease who were treated with colchicine. Although the LoDoCo trial did show outcome benefit, colchicine's mechanism of action at the level of the atherosclerotic plaque in patients remains unknown. It is not clear at the present time whether colchicine mainly reduces systemic inflammation, thus reducing the likelihood of plaque progression and new lesion formation; or whether it has a direct effect on local "hot" inflammatory cell activity, thus pacifying the inflammatory plaque to reduce events. Insight into colchicine's mechanism of action may help identify the most suitable patients for this novel approach. Positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET/CT) imaging with 18F-fluordeoxyglucose (18-FDG) provides an opportunity to perform molecular imaging of specific components of the atherosclerotic plaque such as inflammation. 18-FDG has been validated and extensively used for this purpose, and it could potentially enable the prospective evaluation of inflammation targeted therapies and the identification of patients at high risk for vascular events. The primary objective of this study is to determine the pathobiological effect of colchicine compared to placebo, on plaque inflammation (measured by 18-FDG PET/CT at baseline and 6 months) in the carotid arteries and thoracic aorta in high-risk patients with diabetes or pre-diabetes and recent vascular events (ACS, TIA, stroke).

column36: Immune mechanisms of influenza A virus-induced susceptibility to myocardial infarction
column37: Cardiovascular diseases including myocardial infarction, or heart attack, continue to claim an increasing number of lives worldwide, while influenza A virus infection, the major causative agent of the flu, is responsible for recurring pulmonary infections and substantial global mortality. Importantly, influenza infection also augments susceptibility to heart attack. Yet, the reasons for this and how it occurs are unknown. Understanding why is of great value, as both influenza and cardiovascular disease are significant threats to human health with limited therapeutic strategies. Even though flu infections are constrained to the lungs, anti-influenza type I IFN signalling can transcriptionally imprint monocytes in the bone marrow to enhance immune responses in peripherally inflamed tissues. Although type I IFN is protective against influenza, it also increases susceptibility to heart attack by promoting detrimental inflammation in the heart. Therefore, it is the goal of this project to investigate a potential link between influenza-induced type I IFN signalling in the bone marrow and detrimental inflammatory monocyte responses during myocardial infarction, which underlies the enhanced severity. The findings of this study will provide better knowledge of the risk factors of cardiovascular disease and could lead to improved clinical interventions.

column36: Fine-grained mapping of hippocampal subregions using 7T MRI
column37: Epilepsy is among the most common neurological conditions and affects 300,000 Canadians. Medial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE) is the most common form. In many cases, seizures are thought to originate in the hippocampus, a brain structure critical for memory and a number of other cognitive functions. Removing parts of the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe is an established treatment that effectively relieves seizures. However, there are usually marked postoperative complications, such as memory deficits and psychiatric disturbances. To minimize postoperative cognitive deficits, we propose to develop a method that will localize, or map, subregions of the hippocampus. Such a map will enable us to determine which subregions are crucial for various functions. In doing so, we will be able to advise neurosurgeons in their surgical planning, to avoid removing subregions that would likely result in severe cognitive deficits. The hippocampus is a complex structure that mediate various brain functions. Different parts of the hippocampus display dissociable patterns of functional connectivity to the rest of the brain. We will leverage this varying connectivity to map hippocampal subregions. Importantly, we will use novel neuroimaging analysis techniques that will enable us to generate a hippocampal map that is unique to each individual. We will then assess the relationship between these subregions and several hippocampal functions, including memory, emotion, and topographical processing. Finally, we will validate the hippocampal maps in MTLE patients, in whom we will be able to directly measure hippocampal activity using intra-hippocampal electrodes. This project will significantly impact epilepsy research as it will enable us to identify hippocampal subregions that are functionally different. One day, these individual maps of hippocampal organization could be used to plan surgical procedures and minimize post-surgical cognitive deficits in patients with epilepsy.

column36: The nexus between drug control and public health: a mixed-methods study investigating the impact of police enforcement activities on access and utilization of HIV prevention and treatment among women who inject drugs
column37: Despite their increased risk of acquiring and transmitting HIV, people who inject drugs (PID) are among those with the least access to HIV prevention and treatment. Police enforcement activities have been shown to increase risk of HIV transmission and impede access to life-saving antiretroviral treatment (ART) among PID. Given that women comprise one-third of injectors globally but shoulder a disproportionate HIV burden, interventions must consider how gender shapes the application and impact of police enforcement on HIV outcomes. Women who inject drugs (WID) face multi-level interpersonal, social, and structural vulnerabilities that increase their risk of drug-related harm, but little is known about how police enforcement activities shape HIV risks and health adversity in general among WID. This project will contribute to HIV prevention and treatment expansion efforts by identifying whether gender modifies the link between police enforcement and HIV risk, prevention and treatment outcomes, elucidating how policing shapes key HIV outcomes, and quantifying the potential impact of eliminating punitive police enforcement practices on the expansion of ART among WID. This mixed-methods research will draw on pooled quantitative data from two studies I lead on as PI and co-PI: the Women Speak Out study, the largest representative dataset of WID in Southeast Asia, and the Jakarta Peer-Driven Intervention study, a community-led treatment intervention exploring determinants of HIV among PID. Additional original qualitative data will be collected from WID in urban sites in Indonesia. This study will be the first to explore how police enforcement activities shape access and utilization of HIV prevention and treatment in the region. Employing integrated knowledge translation, this study will shift the research field from identifying gender-related health disparities related to police enforcement towards informing appropriate interventions to reduce them.

column36: Characterizing the role of stromal cells on hematopoietic stem cell division
column37: Hematopoietic stem cells supply all the blood cells required during life. During development stem cells migrate to vascular niches where they are enveloped by 'cuddling' endothelial cells and contacted by stromal cells. These stromal cells sustain the stem cells by releasing signals that encourage stem cell self-renewal. Contact with stromal cells also controls how the stem cells divide, ensuring that one of the dividing cells remains in the niche, while the other leaves to form mature blood cells. This makes stromal cells essential to the niche and if they are destroyed the stem cells can be lost leading to blood disorders. Despite the importance of these niche stromal cells no study has yet identified what makes them unique and what specific mechanisms they use to regulate stem cell division. This research will characterize stromal cells using zebrafish models which have many of the same cell types and signaling pathways as the mammalian bone marrow niche. Next generation sequencing technologies will be used to examine stromal cells at single cell resolution and identify the cell types that form the niche. Using this data, the genetic factors that specify niche stromal cells will be determined and used to build tools to target the niche. Stem cell divisions will be visualized within the optically clear zebrafish embryos using 4D microscopic imaging. Polarized proteins previously identified in isolated mammalian stem cells extracted from bone marrow will be fluorescently tagged and expressed in the zebrafish stem cells to visualize cell polarity and asymmetric divisions in context within the niche. Genetic ablation of stromal cells will then test the requirements for these cells in blood homeostasis. The results of this research will deepen our understanding of the stem niche and inform therapeutic strategies to improve the expansion of transplanted stem cells for the treatment of blood disorders.

column36: The role of adipose tissue in host defenses to bacterial pneumonia
column37: A clinical entity termed the "obesity paradox" suggests that overweight individuals (BMI>25) are 20-30% more likely to survive hospitalized pneumonia. There are two ways to survive an infection. The first depends on resistance mechanisms that kill the pathogen creating an arms race between the host and pathogen that can lead to pathogen resistance, immunopathology, and mortality. The second is a distinct defense classification called the co-operative defense system. The co-operative defense system encodes disease tolerance mechanisms that prevent or alleviate pathology generated during infection without affecting pathogen number nor fitness. The role of tolerance in the obesity paradox is unknown. Legionella pneumophila (Lp) is a bacterial pathogen that infects and resides in immune cells of the lung. Preliminary data has identified that host utilization of fatty acids is critical for defenses and survival against Lp. These data suggest that an increased abundance of circulating fatty acids may improve host outcome to infection. I hypothesize that fat promotes host defenses during Lp infection through fatty acid release and availability for utilization by the host. This project will determine how host adipose composition and fatty acid availability effects tolerance defense mechanisms toward Lp lung infection. I will identify specific host immune or metabolic pathways that benefit from the increased abundance of fat and fatty acids that promote host health during infection. Discovering new disease tolerance mechanisms is critical for overcoming resistance in pathogens, creating new avenues to treat infectious diseases.

column36: Developing a molecular network map of GABAergic neuron subtypes from single nucleus data to identify drivers of Alzheimer's disease and late-life depression
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a complex neurodegenerative disorder, affecting 35.6 million people worldwide in 2010 and projected to double in prevalence every 20 years, with a prevalence of 115.4 million by 2050. Late-life depression (LLD; onset greater than 60 years) increases the risk for AD due to a high-degree of symptomatic overlap emanating from common biological vulnerabilities that contribute to accelerated ageing. Within these vulnerable networks, GABA is a primary inhibitory neurotransmitter that regulates molecular systems related to cognition and depressive symptoms. However, the contribution of pathways modifying the overlapping biology of AD and LLD remains unclear. Advances in gene expression technologies, such as single-nucleus gene expression, have revealed the importance of different cell types in contributing to disease symptoms. Therefore, the goal of our proposal is to explore the gene expression profiles of GABA-related cells in the brain tissue of older adults with AD and LLD. Our specific aims will include: (I) Identifying genes that show similar patterns of expression within different types of GABA-related brain cells; (II) Exploring gene expression patterns to identify proteins that may be potential drug targets for AD and LLD; (III) Exploring how individual genetic variation in DNA can be used to predict gene expression patterns; and, (IV) Building models to understand which gene expression patterns are the most important in predicting AD and LLD. For these aims, we will make use of 900 individuals from two longitudinal studies of ageing: The Religious Orders Study (ROS) and the Memory and Aging Project (MAP) cohorts. Using these established methods from genetics and computational biology, we will explore GABA-related brain cells to understand the risk for AD and LLD, revealing corresponding new drug targets.

column36: Uncovering the links between atrial stretch and inflammation in atrial fibrillation associated with cardiovascular disease
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained supraventricular arrhythmia worldwide and is associated with increased morbidity, mortality, and socio-economic burden. AF affects 1-2% of the general population and with an incidence expected to double by 2060. While AF is tightly linked to aging and cardiovascular (CV) disease (i.e., heart failure, valve disease), its origins are complex, but are fundamentally linked to altered structural and/or electrical remodeling of the atria. Importantly, most conditions linked to AF are associated with elevated atrial pressures and atrial stretch, which is a powerful stimulus for adverse atrial remodeling. It is well-established that the pro-inflammatory and mechanosensitive cytokine tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFa) is a critical factor in cardiac remodeling, fibrosis, arrhythmias, and inflammation seen in heart disease as well as athletes with AF, and an enhanced inflammatory response is typically observed in AF patients. While previous work from our group established the requirement of TNFa in exercise-induced adverse atrial remodeling and AF vulnerability in mice, the overlap in pathways mediating arrhythmogenesis in exercise and CV disease is undeniable. My research seeks to translate our exercise findings to more clinically-relevant models of heart disease, including a mouse model of aortic regurgitation (AR), which is characterized by cardiac volume overload, dilatation, elevated atrial pressures, fibrosis, and AF. As AR patients have one of the highest risks of AF, AR offers a clinically-relevant model to study atrial stretch-dependent TNFa-mediated AF pathogenesis. This mechanistic link will be assessed by: 1) assessing the molecular and cellular basis for TNFa-mediated adverse atrial remodeling in CV disease; 2) identifying novel pathways involved in the TNFa-dependent differential effects of AR on the atria with a goal towards developing novel interventions; and 3) translating our findings to CV patients.

column36: Understanding polygenic nutrigenetic interactions for cardiometabolic diseases using fine mapping of genome-wide association study signals: Optimizing the science of nutrigenomics and its pragmatic application
column37: Individuals respond differently to the same nutrition strategies. For example, some individuals who consume high saturated fat diets develop heart disease, while others do not. Genetic variation can explain some of these different responses. Specifically, nutrigenomics is a science that explores how our genes interact with the foods, beverages and supplements we consume to affect our health outcomes. When it comes to heart health, many different genetic variants have been linked to nutrition-related heart health outcomes. However, most genetic tests available to consumers only look at a single genetic location. Therefore, in order to provide more accurate and effective nutritional guidance to reduce heart disease risks, we need to improve our understanding of all genetic variants involved in individualized dietary responses. The proposed research has two main goals. First, we aim to identify the large number of genetic variants that have been shown to contribute to individualized heart health responses to different nutrition components. The nutrition components that we will be focusing on include: fish peptides, berries and different types of sugar & sweetener. This will be done by summarizing and critically analyzing previous studies that have been completed. Next, we aim to create an algorithm of multiple genetic variants that can be tested to provide accurate, personalized dietary guidance to help individuals reduce genetic-related heart and metabolic risks. To do this, we will apply genomics tools to nutrition research. Briefly, we will identify genetic variants that contribute highly to individual heart and metabolic responses to nutrition. We will be focusing on identifying genetic variants that contribute to insulin, blood sugar, and cholesterol levels, based on consumption of sugar and on type of sugar. This will help clinicians to provide more accurate genetic-based nutrition advice to reduce inherited heart and metabolic risks.
