column36: An Investigation of the Earliest Changes in the Brain due to Mild Cognitive Impairment in Parkinson's Disease
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative disorder that affects over 100000 Canadians, a number that is expected to rise as the population ages. While PD is typically characterized by motor symptoms, most people with PD will also experience cognitive impairments which can be more disabling than motor symptoms. Cognitive impairment in PD is progressive. It starts out as a decline in cognitive functioning that exceeds what would be expected in healthy aging but that does not interfere with daily functioning (mild cognitive impairment; PD-MCI). In the majority of cases, this cognitive impairment advances to dementia, which has a significant negative impact on daily functioning and quality of life. Treatment is most effective in early stages, thus timely identification of patients with PD who at risk for developing PD-MCI is imperative. Large databases such as the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) following newly diagnosed people with PD over many years using both cognitive and neuroimaging measures offer a unique opportunity to retrospectively identify the earliest changes in the brain before cognitive impairment is established and irreversible brain damage has occurred. Using the PPMI cohort, we will examine differences in brain structure in those who we know convert to PD-MCI compared to their counterparts with PD who remain cognitively stable. The ability to detect changes in brain structure prior to observable changes in cognition can inform the early identification of patients with PD who have the highest likelihood of developing PD-MCI, which is a risk factor for developing dementia. This has implications for patient management and prognosis, allowing for the implementation of early prevention or treatments methods that could improve long-term cognitive outcomes and quality of life, as well as allow for increased treatment options.

column36: Patient-oriented pediatric clinical prediction algorithms
column37: Problem: Canada's children are falling behind. More than 1 in 3 are overweight or obese, 1 in 4 have a mental health problem, and 1 in 4 are not developmentally ready for school. Early prevention is the key to reducing the life-limiting consequences of these conditions. Part of this important goal is the development of pediatric clinical prediction algorithms, tools that combine different types of patient information to help clinicians determine whether a child is at risk for a future health condition. While clinical prediction algorithms have the ability to help clinicians and families prevent disease, they also have the potential to widen health inequalities if they are not inclusive of different ethnicities, income groups, and the diverse needs of parents and children. My project will involve parents at every stage of clinical prediction algorithm priority setting, development, and implementation to ensure that algorithms are produced in an equitable and patient-oriented manner. Using TARGet Kids!, a research network that has collected data on 11,000 children in the first 5 years of life, I will initiate the ParEnt and CliniciAn algorithm Leads (PEARL), a group composed of 5 primary healthcare providers and 8 parents from families with diverse ethnic and income backgrounds. The PEARL will help address challenges associated with pediatric clinical prediction algorithms and safeguard their equitable development and use. I will begin by creating a state of the art clinical prediction algorithm for childhood obesity, mobilizing expertise with the PEARL while developing my skills as a patient-oriented research leader. My demonstrated success in research, mentorship, and leadership along with support from my mentors and SPOR-POR PhD Award, will result in the production of novel methods for patient-oriented clinical prediction algorithms that engage parents, support diversity, and optimize the health of all Canadian children.

column36: Understanding the Impact of Patient Transfers on End-of-Life Patient Experience: The Effects of Institutional Abstinence from Medical Assistance in Dying
column37: Many healthcare institutions in Canada currently decline to provide medical assistance in dying (MAID) on-site for religious or moral reasons. If patients receiving medical care at such institutions request MAiD, they need to be transferred elsewhere in order to access this important medical service and Charter-protected legal right. The process places additional burdens-in terms of seeking information and support, navigating the health system, and communicating with health professionals-on vulnerable patients who are already battling grievous illness and psychological distress. While anecdotes relating to the issue occasionally appear in the press, there is very little systematic evidence on the experiences of patients and families who make this critical transition in care. This study aims to fill this vital knowledge gap by mapping the MAiD access trajectories of patients and families at MAiD-abstaining institutions. Through a combination of textual analysis (media sources and institutional grey literature) and in-depth interviews (with patients, families, policymakers, and health professionals), this project will generate evidence on how patients and families interact with healthcare institutions and professionals; where they seek information; who they turn to for support and decision-making; what alternative routes they choose when faced with barriers; and where key resources to support their transfer journeys are located. Utilizing the Patient Engagement Framework suggested by the Strategy for Patient-Oriented Research (SPOR), this study will involve patients and families-across all stages of its research design-for: (i) informing the socio-ethical debate on institutional MAiD-abstinence; (ii) identifying gaps in MAiD service delivery, and (iii) making policy recommendations for equitable access to MAiD.

column36: Patient-engaged development of standards for a reporting guideline for scaling studies of health interventions
column37: Health research generates evidence-based knowledge that need to be reported adequately to be translated effectively in decision making. Moreover, health interventions proven to be effective need to be scaled up to help improve health outcomes for the entire population in order to promote health equity. However, gap in the quality of reporting of health research are well documented in the literature, particularly for scaling studies, as documented in a systematic review. In addition, although the importance of sex and gender in the manifestation and management of health conditions and in health outcomes is well established, their considerations are rarely integrated into research design and reporting guidelines. To address this gap, the aim of this research project is to develop the standards for a reporting guideline for studies assessing the impact of scaling up of health interventions. The project will be guided by the steps recommended for developing health research reporting guidelines by EQUATOR, an international network that promotes transparent and accurate reporting of health research. As successful scaling up of health innovations is highly context-dependent, sex and gender considerations will be integrated into the development process. The whole process will involve national and international collaborators including two patient partners as members of the research team. As a result, the guidelines developed will be useful both in Canada and around the world to improving the quality of reporting of scaling studies and facilitate the replication and scaling of the health innovations studied.

column36: Examining the effect of Canada's unique medical abortion drug policy on patient abortion access and outcomes
column37: One third of women in Canada will have at least one abortion in their life. Until 2017, 96% of Canadian abortions were performed using surgery in fewer than 100 facilities, located primarily in large, urban centres. Under this model, access to abortion was markedly inequitable. Some patients traveled long distances to reach service locations, and experienced significant wait times, thus undergoing abortions at later (and thus less safe) gestational ages. Drawing attention to the urgency of this issue, in 2016, the UN Human Rights Commissioner called on the Canadian government to improve equitable access to abortion in Canada. The medical abortion drug mifepristone became available in Canada in January 2017. Canadian federal and provincial governments enacted policies that are unique globally to enable mifepristone abortion provision in primary care by family doctors or nurse practitioners, including those with no prior abortion practice. Within one year of its introduction, many provincial insurers fully subsidized the $350 mifepristone cost to reduce financial barriers to access. Health policymakers urgently need to understand whether their mifepristone policies were effective in improving abortion access and reducing inequities, and whether this change in abortion practice has impacted abortion outcomes. However, the effect of mifepristone policy on abortion access and outcomes have not yet been examined. The objective of this study is to evaluate the impact of Canadian mifepristone medical abortion policy on abortion access and outcomes using comprehensive, high-quality, linked health administrative data from British Columbia and Ontario. This policy framework positioned Canada as an international leader for addressing reproductive health access inequity through innovative liberalization of abortion practice. Health policymakers eagerly await the findings of this study to inform policy changes in a wide range of international settings.

column36: Soutenir l'evaluation et l'integration des services fragmentes pour les problemes complexes de sante sur la base du savoir experientiel des pairs usagers et des patients partenaires
column37: Les problemes de sante sont de plus en plus complexes. Par exemple, 41% des personnes ayant un probleme de toxicomanie ont aussi un probleme de sante mentale et 88,5% des personnes ayant un diabete de type 2 ont au moins deux autres problemes de sante (p. ex. obesite). Par consequent, des professionnels de differentes disciplines doivent collaborer pour repondre a l'ensemble des besoins de la personne. Une avenue possible pour qu'ils travaillent mieux ensemble est la mise en place d'approches de collaboration. Les approches de collaboration sont des activites a court ou moyen terme qui utilisent la formation et le partage d'expertises pour ameliorer la qualite des services, la capacite a faire appel a d'autres ressources et le developpement d'une comprehension commune. Pour obtenir les changements escomptes, l'ensemble des parties prenantes doivent etre incluses, c.-a-d. toutes les personnes impliquees ou touchees par une problematique. Les personnes ayant des problemes complexes (PP) doivent y avoir un role central. Pourtant, les strategies proposees pour les integrer dans les approches de collaboration sont encore peu nombreuses, concretes et difficilement atteignables. Ce projet vise donc a identifier, selon la perspective des parties prenantes, les strategies qui favorisent l'integration des PP dans les approches de collaboration et les effets de cette integration, incluant ceux non desires. Pour ce faire, les strategies d'integration seront identifiees a partir de la litterature. Des entrevues seront faites aupres des parties prenants ayant participe a des approches de collaboration, dont deux au Quebec, une sur les troubles concomitants de sante mentale et de toxicomanie et une sur les maladies chroniques (diabete). Enfin, une activite collaborative sera organise pour identifier les elements importants qui devraient etre evalues a l'avenir. Cette etude permettra de mieux soutenir l'integration des PP dans les approches de collaboration.

column36: Relationship between brain cholinergic innervation and clinical manifestations of REM sleep behaviour disorder: a PET study using 18F-FEOBV
column37: A large initiative in Canadian health research at present is to develop tools that identify the early stages of neurodegenerative disease. This quest has been facilitated by the discovery that rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behaviour disorder is a significant early sign of a class of neurodegenerative diseases. People with REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) do not have enough muscle paralysis during REM sleep, which causes them to "act out" their dreams at night. More than 80% of these individuals go on to develop Parkinson's disease or a related neurodegenerative disease, such as Lewy body dementia. The neurotransmitter acetylcholine plays a role in REM sleep and in these neurodegenerative diseases, but it has not yet been sufficiently examined in people with RBD. Seeking to better understand this question, my doctoral project will look into the role of acetylcholine in RBD using a novel compound for PET imaging called 18F-FEOBV, which our laboratory has been developing over the last 15 years. This compound enables researchers to study acetylcholine systems in the brain in a more precise manner than the existing PET compounds. I will recruit thirty participants from the Montreal RBD study at the Sacre-Coeur Hospital and will guide them through an MRI scan and a PET scan using 18F-FEOBV at the Montreal Neurological Institute. The participants will also undergo a sleep recording, cognitive testing, and a neurological examination. My hypothesis is that the RBD individuals will show acetylcholine-related abnormalities in the brain, whereas the controls will not. Additionally, I expect to see a relationship between these abnormalities and muscle activity during REM sleep, lower cognitive scores, and other early signs of neurodegeneration. My ultimate goal in this project is, with the help of 18F-FEOBV, to shed light on the mechanisms involved in RBD, and in so doing, in the early stages of certain neurodegenerative diseases.

column36: Utilisation de la stimulation transcranienne a courant alternatif pour moduler l'attention selective intermodale dans le trouble du spectre de l'autisme
column37: Le trouble du spectre de l'autisme (TSA) est l'une des conditions neurodeveloppementales les plus prevalentes et il est maintenant reconnu qu'une alteration des processus perceptifs est presente chez les personnes autistes. Un profil particulier se caracterise par une performance superieure aux individus neurotypiques lorsque les strategies << de detail >> dans le traitement de l'information sensorielle sont adaptees et, a l'inverse, une performance inferieure/similaire lorsqu'il s'agit d'adopter une approche globale. Des etudes recentes de neuroimagerie soutiennent que les atypies perceptives du TSA pourraient etre causees par une desynchronisation des oscillations neuronales. Plus precisement, les oscillations liees a l'attention selective joueraient un role crucial dans le traitement de l'information sensorielle en renforcant les processus neuronaux vers l'information pertinente. Par ailleurs, on sait qu'il est possible de moduler les oscillations neuronales par l'utilisation de la neurostimulation. column36: Transitional Care of Rural Older Adults: Understanding the Interplay between Older Adult Health Construction and the Influence of Multidimensional Contexts on the Transitional Care of Older Adults in Rural Communities
column37: Background: Providing health services for aging populations is the fundamental issue of modern Canadian health policy, yet ineffective models of service provision result in inadequate transitional support for the older demographic. Although numerous regional transitional care strategies exist, experts acknowledge that older adults in rural communities are still vulnerable during transfers between care settings, resulting in compromised patient safety and poor quality care. Objectives: Informed by inquiry in critical gerontology, health integration and rural health, the research will pursue the goal of better understanding the interplay between older adult health construction and the influence of multidimensional contexts on the transitional care of older adults. The study will pursue the following objectives: 1)To explore perceptions of how older adult health is constructed, 2)To understand the experiences of key stakeholders involved in the transitional care of older adults in rural communities, 3)To better understand the contexts in which older adult transitional care is provided and 4)To provide a foundation of information for a regional older adult care network. Method: The research will involve a case study of Haliburton County and use a multi-method approach that encompasses three phases: 1)A Community Inventory, 2)Go-Alongs and 3) Semi-Structured Interviews. Considering the influence of context and the perspectives of key informants, this study will focus on two types of transitions: 1)when an older adult is transferred from a hospital to a long-term care home and 2)when an older adult is transferred from a hospital to a home in the community. Significance: Establishing the first study of rural older adult transitional care that traverses multiple care settings, this research will prepare Canada for the impact of the aging population and transform transitional care of older adults to ensure health services meet the needs of Canadians in the 21st century.

column36: The effect of dioxin/dioxin-like pollutants on beta-cell development, function, and survival in mouse and human islets
column37: Diabetes mellitus is a global health issue, with an estimated 592 million adults diagnosed with diabetes by 2035. As such, understanding the cause of diabetes to reduce its prevalence is of upmost importance. Diabetes is a chronic disease associated with hyperglycemia due to inadequate insulin production by pancreatic beta cells. Mounting research suggests that the global increase in diabetes prevalence may be due to environmental factors. In fact, epidemiological studies have consistently shown a correlation between diabetes incidence and exposure to dioxins, a class of highly persistent environmental pollutants. Research in the Bruin lab has shown that exposure to dioxins suppresses glucose-stimulated insulin secretion in human and mouse adult beta cells, and causes beta cell loss in male mice. This suggests that dioxins may increase diabetes risk by altering beta cell function and survival. However, there is still a significant gap in knowledge on the mechanism responsible for dioxin-induced changes in beta cell physiology. My PhD will focus on establishing a potential mechanism by which dioxins increase diabetes risk by assessing effects of dioxins on beta cell development, function, and survival in mouse and humans. This research will inform the community about chemicals that are a concern for diabetes risk and will ultimately aid in altering our environment to reduce diabetes incidence.

column36: The EEG-Indexed Auditory Mismatch Negativity as a Biomarker to Predict Psychosis Onset
column37: Schizophrenia is a disorder that is often preceded by early symptoms of psychosis, however the accuracy of predicting conversion based on clinical symptoms is low. The healthy human brain is able to detect changes in our auditory environment, whether we are paying attention or not and even while we are sleeping. This function, originally thought to have developed so we could detect sounds indicating danger approaching, may seem simple but is an important part of our daily lives and is the result of complex computations within the brain. It has been long reported that schizophrenia patients show deficiencies in this auditory change detection mechanism, and that this might be an observable marker of greater dysfunction within the brain of those affected. Recent work has suggested that this deficit may be present in individuals at risk of developing a disorder of psychosis, such as schizophrenia, before psychosis emerges. What is unclear, however, is whether early-occurring deficits in auditory change detection can predict who will transition to psychosis and who will not. If we were able to identify an objective, accurate biological marker of psychosis risk, this would allow clinicians to initiate early treatment in those who will transition to psychosis, while avoiding unnecessary treatments in those who will not. This project aims to shine a light on this question by examining auditory change detection in individuals at risk of developing a psychotic disorder, whether it be due to a family history of schizophrenia or the presence of early symptoms that may or may not turn into psychosis. It is hoped that we might identify that elusive objective biological marker that would allow for accurate prediction of psychosis risk and early treatment, so as to change the course of this illness that the World Health Organization has called schizophrenia "youth's greatest disabler due to its typical emergence during young adulthood and the devastating impact on functioning".

column36: The cost of healthy eating: The development, pilot, and retail feasibility of two nutritious food basket assessment instruments
column37: Eating an unhealthy diet increases a person's risk of health problems and death. Most of the food that people buy are from food stores. Since the types and cost of foods available to customers in food stores can influence what they eat, it is important to understand the cost of a healthy diet and how food stores can offer healthy and affordable foods to customers. The Nutritious Food Basket is a tool made by the Canadian government and used by Canadian provinces to track the cost of healthy eating. The Food Basket is a list of the amounts and types of foods that make up a healthy diet for a family of four. The food items in the Food Basket are based on the most popular foods eaten by Canadians and that meet dietary recommendations from a 2004 Canadian survey which reported the amount of certain foods that Canadians ate. The provinces then go into a set number of food stores and price the items in the Food Basket to get the overall cost of the Food Basket. Recently, the Canadian government released the results of a new Canadian survey which reported on the foods Canadians ate and updated Canada's Food Guide. Based on this new information this project will look to update the foods in the Nutritious Food Basket and understand if less healthy foods that still meet Canadian healthy eating guidelines can be used to create a less expensive food basket. Two food baskets will be created; one that includes foods that make up a healthy diet and another based on what Canadians reported eating. Both baskets will be priced in 14 Nova Scotian food stores and be compared to see if there are any differences in the price and nutritional quality of food items between the two baskets. Management staff from 5-10 of the food stores studied will be interviewed to understand what makes it difficult for them to sell healthy and less expensive foods to customers. The project results will be used to create health policies to improve healthy eating and prevent disease in Canada.

column36: DigiComp Kids: A Co-Design and User Testing Study of a Virtual Care and Remote Monitoring Intervention for Medically Complex Children and Their Families
column37: Medically complex children are children who have severe health problems and rely on technology or equipment such as ventilators or feeding tubes in the home to stay alive. They and their families need support at home in order to meet their care needs and avoid hospitalizations and medical complications. Currently, hospital-based teams cannot monitor these children in their homes, and most community providers who come to the home do not have the necessary experience to care for these children. Because of this, medically complex children suffer complications like infections and medication errors while in their homes and communities and are admitted to hospital often. In this study, we will work with hospital and community healthcare providers and family members of medically complex children to design a new virtual home care system that can be used to provide monitoring and support to families. This new system will use technology to allow hospital teams monitor the vital signs of medically complex children (e.g. heart rate, blood pressure) at home, and allow family members and community providers to check in with hospital teams using video. Family members and providers will help us to select features for the technology that will be useful to them when providing care outside of the hospital. We will then test the system with families and community and hospital providers to get feedback on whether the system is useful and what the experiences of using it to provide care are like. At present, medically complex children and their families are under-supported in the community. This work is an opportunity to make a real difference in their care and quality of life.

column36: Achieving equitable population-based lung cancer screening programs in Canada: An inquiry of social values and ethical considerations
column37: Over 20,000 Canadians are expected to die from lung cancer in 2019. Survival is less than 20% because most diagnoses are made at late stages when treatment effectiveness is limited. It is therefore a major advancement that low-dose chest computed tomography (CT) will soon be used to screen Canadians for lung cancer. Screening will help Canadians be diagnosed earlier, obtain timely treatment, and survive for longer and with a higher quality of life. Low-dose chest CT to screen for lung cancer is promising, but few individuals are correctly diagnosed from this lengthy process with a high false detection rate. Who should be screened for lung cancer? This is a dilemma for cancer system policymakers, who have turned to numerical models that predict individual lung cancer risk. Less is known about values Canadians hold towards screening and ethical issues related to screening some and not others. These knowledge gaps need to be addressed if future Canadian lung cancer screening programs are to be effective and fair. This research aims to uncover social values and ethical considerations that can help policymakers decide who to include in Canadian lung cancer screening programs. Cancer system policymakers, the general public, and communities affected by lung cancer will be asked about their values towards screening and benefits and harms of screening some and not and others. People will be interviewed from provinces with lung cancer screening-related activities. Specific values and ethical principles will be identified and analyzed with fairness in mind. When health care is oriented around patients, better individual health is often the result. Likewise, when health systems are oriented around what populations want, we can expect better health for all Canadians. By querying public and policymaker values, this research is anticipated to contribute to lung cancer screening programs that are effective, fair, and at the leading edge of socially relevant health systems.

column36: Uncovering a Cellular Pathway that is Associated with Human Amyloidosis
column37: A category of diseases called amyloidosis are caused by the irreversible formation of protein clumps (aggregates). The type of protein involved as well as its location in the body leads to different diseases, for example beta-amyloid protein accumulates in the brain in individuals suffering from Alzheimer's disease (a chronic disorder causing dementia in hundreds of thousands of Canadians), and amylin protein aggregates in the pancreas of patients with type 2 diabetes (a metabolic disorder affecting hundreds of millions of people worldwide). Although the proteins involved may be different, the common factor to all amyloidosis diseases is the folding shape the proteins develop in the aggregates: the amyloid fold. While this shape has historically been associated with disease, the Audas laboratory recently discovered a protective cellular pathway that induces proteins to reversibly take on an amyloid fold during cell stress (i.e. high temperatures, low oxygen). Components of this pathway could be faulty in disease settings, leading to the irreversible aggregates observed in amyloidosis diseases. We aim to deplete, or "knock-out", a variety of different cellular factors to determine which ones are involved in the natural process, as these may be malfunctioning in amyloidosis disorders. Ultimately, this research could identify new therapeutic targets and uncover new avenues to pursue in the research of amyloidosis diseases.

column36: ATG4B inhibition for the sensitization of treatment-resistant HER2+ cancers
column37: Breast cancer is the 2nd leading cause of cancer-related deaths among Canadian women. Approximately 20% of breast cancers overexpress the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2). HER2 facilitates the normal growth and development of breast cells but promotes rapid growth and cancer development when it is overexpressed. While there are currently therapies that work to control the aggressiveness of HER2+ breast cancers, treatment resistance occurs frequently in advanced and metastatic cases. To address this, the Gorski lab previously uncovered a novel positive association between overexpression of the HER2 protein and high levels of a protein called ATG4B, which functions in cell survival responses. To understand this newly discovered relationship between HER2 and ATG4B, I will use protein-based strategies to investigate the mechanistic links between HER2 and ATG4B by identifying novel ATG4B protein interactions that exist only when HER2 is overexpressed. The Gorski lab also showed that inhibition of the cell survival protein ATG4B increases the sensitivity of HER2+ breast cancers to HER2-targeting agents. To evaluate the therapeutic potential of inhibiting ATG4B to improve the responses of resistant HER2+ cancers to HER2-targeting therapies, I will investigate recently developed ATG4B inhibitors and their applications as tools for improving treatment responses in HER2+ breast cancer mouse models. Together, my research aims to validate new combination strategies that will address the problem of treatment resistance and improve the survival of HER2+ breast cancer patients.

column36: Medications for concurrent mental disorders among people with opioid use disorder: estimating adverse effects and the causal effect on opioid agonist treatment outcomes.
column37: More than half of Canadians seeking addiction treatment also have a mental disorder. In British Columbia, the prevalence of concurrent mental disorders among people with an opioid use disorder is as high as 74%. Sustained retention in opioid agonist treatment, the evidence-based standard of care, has proven effective in reducing the risk of mortality and is a key focus of public health efforts to reduce the disease burden of opioid use disorder. Medications for severe mental disorders may have an important role in their management, but they can also result in frequent adverse effects, posing a challenging tradeoff between uncertain benefits and the possibility of serious, sometimes life-shortening adverse effects. Integrated care, giving equal consideration to both opioid use disorder and mental disorders, is recommended clinical practice. Unfortunately, randomized control trials investigating treatment outcomes in both mental disorders and opioid use disorder commonly exclude individuals with other comorbid conditions. Despite the high prevalence of concurrent disorders among people with opioid use disorder, there is a dearth of evidence related to outcomes of concurrent pharmacotherapy for severe mental disorders. This work aims to quantify severe adverse effects (e.g., emergency department visits, hospitalizations) involving medications for severe concurrent mental disorders in a population-level cohort of people with opioid use disorder. Data will be obtained from a cohort of all British Columbia residents with an indication of opioid use disorder from 01/1996 to 10/2018 (n=92,305) identified using seven linked population-level administrative databases. These findings will help inform clinical recommendations to minimize adverse effects and improve OAT engagement, a pressing need considering the public health and economic toll of the opioid syndemic.

column36: Towards an HIV cure for all: increasing female representation in HIV latency research
column37: Despite the success of antiretroviral therapy to treat HIV infection, these medications are not curative and need to be taken for life. This is because HIV integrates its genetic material into the genome of the infected human immune cells, and can persist in a dormant or "latent" state for many years. These dormant HIV copies are called the "latent HIV reservoir", and they persist in the body because they are invisible to the immune system and to antiretroviral drugs. But, these reservoirs can re-activate to produce infectious HIV at any time. To cure HIV therefore, scientists will need to develop strategies to eliminate the latent reservoir. Towards this goal, substantial efforts are being made to understand reservoir characteristics, composition, and longevity in individuals living with HIV whose infections are well-controlled with antiretroviral therapy. However, most participants of such research studies, particularly in North America, have been males. By contrast, females, who make up ~52% of people living with HIV worldwide, are significantly underrepresented in HIV latency research. As a result, fundamental questions around sex-based differences in latent HIV reservoir composition remain unanswered. To address this critical knowledge gap, I will combine cutting-edge laboratory and molecular evolutionary methods in my PhD research. I will study unique biospecimen repositories and data from established local and international cohorts, including the longest-running study exclusively comprising females living with HIV (the US-based Women's Interagency HIV Study). I will also perform a comparative study of latent HIV reservoir composition in females and males in a cohort established at St. Paul's Hospital in Vancouver. My PhD research will help understand latent HIV reservoir dynamics in females, towards the ultimate goal of developing a cure for HIV that will be effective in, and accessible by, all.

column36: Enabling Microbial Genome Analysis for Infectious Disease Outbreak Investigations
column37: Bacterial species, including pathogens, possess a remarkable ability to evolve rapidly and exchange genomic DNA with unrelated lineages in a process known as horizontal gene transfer. Clusters of these horizontally transferred genes, called genomic islands, are of high interest to computationally predict in pathogen genome sequences since they disproportionately encode genes that enable a pathogen to cause disease or resist treatment by some antibiotics. Ultimately, the goal of my project is to improve our understanding of the evolution of these genomic regions and their involvement in changes during a disease outbreak. IslandCompare will facilitate more rapid, integrated analysis of medically relevant gene mobility, which is of high interest for enabling public health investigations to more rapidly evaluate, and respond to, infectious disease outbreaks.

column36: Optimisation d'un modele pour evaluer l'impact de la direction des changements de pression arterielle sur l'autoregulation cerebrale dynamique
column37: La maladie vasculaire peripherique (MVP) atteint 5 a 18% de la population et est une pathologie des vaisseaux qui peut mener a leur obstruction complete. Elle peut survenir dans toutes les arteres, dont celles du cerveau. Son traitement repose sur divers facteurs dont le plus efficace est l'activite physique. La MVP entraine une rigidite arterielle qui augmente le risque de faire un accident vasculaire cerebral (AVC) et affecte la facon dont l'apport en sang est regule au cerveau. La fonction vasculaire cerebrale des patients avec une MVP est donc probablement anormale, particulierement a l'effort. L'entrainement par intervalles a haute intensite (HIIT) gagne en popularite pour son economie de temps et son efficacite par rapport a l'entrainement en continu. Il y a cependant peu de litterature sur les benefices et les impacts du HIIT sur les vaisseaux du cerveau. Un exercice court et intense comme le HIIT pourrait causer une augmentation trop prononcee du debit sanguin au cerveau. Cela pourrait augmenter certains risques tel que l'AVC. On sait toutefois que le HIIT entraine certaines ameliorations (ex. distance de marche) chez des patients avec une MVP. Cependant, nous ne savons pas si la vascularisation cerebrale des sujets avec une MVP est bien adaptee aux changements brusques de pression arterielle relies au HIIT. Il est donc primordial de connaitre la reponse vasculaire cerebrale des patients avec une MVP lors du HIIT avant de le recommander formellement. Cette etude apportera des connaissances sur les effets du HIIT sur la fonction vasculaire cerebrale a court et long terme. Ultimement, elle fournira aux cliniciens des recommandations objectives sur le HIIT et la MVP. Nous aurons ainsi une base solide de connaissances afin d'etablir une strategie optimale d'exercice pour le cerveau et pour optimiser le fonctionnement du cerveau tout au long de la vie des patients avec une MVP.

column36: Functional characterization of novel genes of immune evasion in Salmonella Typhimurium
column37: The bacterial pathogen Salmonella Typhimurium (ST) is one of the leading causes of foodborne illness in Canada and causes acute gastroenteritis, which often leads to hospitalizations in young children and elderly populations. The incidence of this bacterial infection represents a major health problem, and the emergence of antibiotic-resistant strains that are difficult to treat has caused growing concern. It is, therefore, pressing to improve our understanding of how ST overcome the innate immune system of susceptible hosts in order to cause infection, as this knowledge can create opportunities for the development of new treatment strategies. Recently, six uncharacterized genes of ST have been identified. The expression of these genes being significantly inhibited under infection conditions, it is suspected that they render ST more susceptible to immune-based killing and are inhibited to evade the natural antimicrobial mechanisms of infected hosts, through potentially unknown resistance mechanisms. The objective of this project is to functionally characterize these six genes through structural biology, microbiology, and molecular biology approaches. The methodology that will be used to achieve this aim consists of three main steps: 1) predict the function of the gene products under study using bioinformatics tools, 2) characterize the immune pathways for which the inhibition of these genes is essential through cell culture infections and phenotypic assays, and 3) identify the mechanisms that control their expression. Overall, this project will provide a comprehensive portrait of the structure, function, and regulation of novel genes for which repression is essential during infection by ST. Thereby, this will improve our understanding of the mechanisms that ST can deploy to escape the immune system, and in the long term, this knowledge base will contribute to the development of new antimicrobial treatments with tangible impacts on public health in Canada.

column37: Un adulte sur cinq au Canada souffre de douleur chronique. Les medecins de famille sont toutefois peu outilles pour soutenir ces patients, et le nombre d'individus atteints est trop eleve pour assurer a tous la disponibilite des services specialises. Pour soulager les individus en attente, des programmes d'autogestion, qui visent a developper une meilleure connaissance de la douleur chronique et a mieux la gerer, ont fait leurs preuves. Ces programmes peuvent ameliorer le fonctionnement au quotidien, les symptomes lies a la depression et a l'anxiete, ainsi que le niveau de douleur percu. Or, les programmes d'autogestion sont rares et peu accessibles. Ce projet visera donc a developper un programme d'autogestion de la douleur chronique, et a en evaluer les effets. Il sera base sur la litterature scientifique et sur les resultats de consultations aupres de patients et de cliniciens pour identifier les attentes et les besoins lies a un tel programme. Il presentera les methodes d'autogestion reconnues et soutiendra les patients dans leur application. Pour evaluer l'efficacite du programme, 100 adultes en attente de services dans l'un des trois centres de traitement de la douleur chronique participants seront recrutes et repartis entre un groupe temoin et un groupe d'intervention. Le groupe d'intervention completera le programme d'autogestion de la douleur chronique en ligne. Le groupe temoin continuera quant a lui de recevoir les soins usuels, soit les soins non specialises auxquels il a deja acces (par exemple, les soins d'un medecin de famille). Tous les participants rempliront des questionnaires au debut de l'etude, puis apres 3 et 6 mois. Des analyses statistiques seront realisees pour determiner si le programme developpe permet d'ameliorer le fonctionnement quotidien des participants et de diminuer l'intensite des symptomes lies a la douleur chronique.

column36: Le glutamate sanguin en contexte d'obesite: de la pathophysiologie a la clinique
column37: On sait depuis longtemps que le metabolisme des glucides et des lipides est altere dans l'obesite. Cependant, c'est seulement dans les 10 dernieres annees que nous avons decouvert que le metabolisme des acides amines est lui aussi affecte. En effet, certains acides amines comme la leucine, l'isoleucine, la valine et le glutamate sont plus eleves dans le sang des personnes obeses que des personnes minces. Le glutamate est particulierement un bon indicateur de l'emplacement ou le gras est accumule. Cela est important, parce qu'une grande quantite de gras au niveau de l'abdomen, est associe a un risque eleve de diabete et de maladies cardiovasculaires. L'hypothese globale de ce projet de recherche est que l'accumulation sanguine de glutamate en contexte d'obesite resulte d'un dysfonctionnement des tissus adipeux et hepatiques. Ces organes etant centraux dans le metabolisme, le glutamate sanguin pourrait representer une mesure accessible de la sante cardiometabolique. Il est essentiel de bien comprendre une maladie si on veut la prevenir et la traiter. Nos connaissances sur l'obesite sont nombreuses, mais encore incompletes. L'etude du metabolisme des acides amines pourrait eventuellement nous amener a trouver de nouveaux traitements pour l'obesite, le diabete ou les maladies cardiovasculaires. Mesurer la quantite de gras a l'interieur de la cavite abdominale necessite des techniques d'imagerie qui coutent tres cher et ne sont pas accessibles en clinique. Ainsi, il serait tres utile de pouvoir estimer l'accumulation de gras visceral en mesurant un acide amine dans le sang. Le fait d'etre capable d'identifier les personnes avec une obesite viscerale et un risque metabolique important, nous permettrait de mieux cibler nos efforts de prevention et de traitement.

column37: <<Une alimentation saine, c'est bien plus que les aliments que vous consommez>>, tel que cite par le nouveau Guide alimentaire canadien 2019, qui integre au premier plan des conseils tels que <<cuisinez plus souvent>> et <<prenez le temps de manger>>. Car au-dela du contenu de notre assiette, le contexte dans lequel les aliments sont manges, soit le <<comment>>, releve d'une grande importance. D'ailleurs, ces comportements alimentaires ont ete associes a une meilleure qualite globale de l'alimentation. Toutefois, les parents de jeunes enfants peuvent etre confrontes a plusieurs barrieres qui les empechent d'adopter ces comportements. Le manque de temps, les contraintes du travail et la prise en compte des preferences et restrictions alimentaires de tous les membres de la famille peuvent faire en sorte que la planification des repas devienne un vrai casse-tete. De plus, les meres ayant vecu une grossesse compliquee par un diabete de grossesse sont encore plus vulnerables. Ces meres pourraient s'imposer une pression supplementaire a bien s'alimenter pour elles et leurs enfants, considerant leur risque eleve de developper des maladies chroniques plus tard dans leur vie. Dans le cadre de ce doctorat en nutrition, un portrait global des habitudes et comportements alimentaires (qualite de l'alimentation, temps de preparation des repas, duree des repas, etc.) des parents de jeunes enfants ages de 6 ans ou moins sera compare a celui des adultes n'ayant pas de jeune enfant, tout en tenant compte de l'antecedent de diabete de grossesse. L'impact sur la sante sera egalement documente. Les donnees d'un total de 234 parents (111 meres, 118 peres) de jeunes enfants seront analysees, de meme que celles de 442 meres avec ou sans antecedent de diabete de grossesse. Les resultats permettront de mieux comprendre les barrieres a l'adoption d'une saine alimentation chez les parents quebecois, l'impact sur leur sante et eventuellement d'adopter des strategies specifiques pour cette population.

Le diagnostic actuel repose principalement sur l'interpretation clinique des professionnels de la sante. Cela signifie que le personnel doit etre prealablement forme et disponible pour effectuer le suivi du patient. Les efforts recents de notre equipe de recherche ont mene a des resultats prometteurs quant a l'utilisation de capteurs non invasifs pour detecter la perte de vigilance. Une revue systematique de la litterature permettra de mieux definir le concept etudie, ainsi que les caracteristiques de l'etat de vigilance en contexte pathologique. Une collecte de donnees sur des sujets sains permettra ensuite d'evaluer le modele de detection de l'hypovigilance propose en comparaison aux etalons d'or actuel. Le dernier volet du projet sera axe sur l'evaluation de la valeur de ces mesures dans le diagnostic du delirium. Cette experience fera partie integrante d'un projet collaboratif regroupant les efforts de plusieurs hopitaux du Canada. column36: Impact fonctionnel d'IDH1 sur le metabolisme des cellules de cancer de la prostate
column37: Le cancer de la prostate est le cancer le plus frequent chez les hommes au Canada. A ce jour, le seul traitement cible de cette maladie vise a bloquer le recepteur aux androgenes. Malgre le succes initial de cette approche pour la gestion du cancer de la prostate, l'evolution vers un cancer de la prostate resistant a la castration est virtuellement inevitable et letal, mettant l'emphase sur la necessite de developper de nouvelles approches therapeutiques. La prostate possede un programme metabolique unique, non observe dans les autres cellules du corps, et la reprogrammation de ce metabolisme a lieu dans tous les cas de cancer de la prostate. Notre objectif est de tirer parti de ce programme metabolique unique pour tuer les cellules cancereuses. Pour ce faire, nous etudierons une proteine essentielle au programme metabolique du cancer de la prostate. Nous utiliserons plusieurs modeles de cancer de la prostate pour etudier les fonctions de cette enzyme et ses liens moleculaires avec l'agressivite de la maladie. Par une meilleure comprehension de ses fonctions, nous pensons pouvoir bloquer la synthese de l'energie des cellules cancereuses et provoquer leur mort. Ces travaux ont le potentiel d'identifier et de caracteriser une nouvelle cible therapeutique innovante pour le traitement du cancer de la prostate. En cas de succes, cette approche sera la premiere du genre et revolutionnera le traitement du cancer de la prostate.

column36: Clinical Applications of the Adult Attachment Interview (AAI): Exploring the Mechanisms Through Which the AAI Enhances Parental Engagement and Boosts Treatment Outcomes Following Brief Emotion-Focused Family Therapy
column37: Fee-for-service policies and long waitlists at many Canadian mental health agencies pose significant barriers for children, adolescents, and families in need of psychological support. In Ontario, approximately 36% of parents have sought mental health services for a child, but four in ten did not receive the help they needed. One way to improve access to mental health services in Canada is to develop and deliver brief and effective psychotherapy. Our group has been studying the impact of administering the Adult Attachment Interview (AAI) before therapy. Originally developed for research, the AAI is now widely used as a clinical tool, and it has been suggested that using the interview can facilitate the therapy process and improve treatment outcomes. We conducted the first study to put this hypothesis to the test and found that administering the AAI before Emotion-Focused Family Therapy (EFFT) boosted treatment gains for parents and their children - unlike parents who did not receive the interview, those who did reported ongoing symptom improvement 12 months after treatment had ended. To advance our understanding of the clinical benefits of the AAI, this study will investigate how the interview leads to better outcomes; the process and mechanisms through which the AAI boosts treatment effectiveness. Two hundred and forty parents took part in an intensive 2-day EFFT intervention; about half completed an AAI before starting therapy and the other half did not. Using available video footage of therapy sessions, we will study parents' level of engagement with the EFFT process. Specifically, the level of emotional arousal experienced and the depth of emotional processing observed during therapy will be coded. It is expected that completing an AAI before therapy will lead to deeper levels of engagement during therapy, which will, in turn, lead to greater treatment outcomes. Our findings may point to a feasible way of enhancing therapy effectiveness and outcomes for families.

column36: Longitudinal Tracking of Health Status Using Machine Learning Analysis of Wearable Sensors: A Framework for Non-Intrusively Detecting Deteriorating Health
column37: The average age of the Canadian population is increasing rapidly. As a result, health care costs are rising and the importance of maintaining a healthy, active lifestyle is becoming very clear. One way to promote healthy living and improve early detection of health problems is to monitor people's health over time. Health status tracking will provide people and their clinicians with useful information to guide their lifestyle and health care decisions. An important contributor to overall health is fitness. Poor fitness is associated with earlier onset of disease and even death. Traditional ways of testing fitness require access to expensive, specialized equipment. This is a barrier to monitoring fitness and health across the population. Wearable sensors, like those within "smart" clothing or watches, are a possible alternative to traditional fitness testing equipment because they are more affordable, more accessible, and can track body function over the course of an entire day. Despite these benefits, it is challenging to understand the complex data provided by wearable sensors. More work is needed to support individuals and clinicians in interpreting wearable sensor data. My research will translate these complex data into actionable knowledge that will inform health promotion and aid in disease detection. I will develop a new artificial intelligence system using data collected with a "smart" shirt from older adults during a two-week period of bed rest. This system will create models specific to older adults that use wearable sensor data to predict health and fitness. I will evaluate how well these models reflect changes in markers of health, aging, and frailty. This work will result in a personalized decision aid that gives people and clinicians new insights into human health. This non-intrusive smart monitoring system will improve population health and reduce health care costs in Canada.

column36: The essential role of clathrin signalosomes in growth factor receptor signaling in cancer cells
column37: Cells communicate with each other through chemical cues, each of which can trigger a specific cell response. For instance, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is a receptor on the cell surface that controls much of what cells can do such as growth, movement and survival. Therefore, EGFR must be tightly regulated by the cell. When this control fails, this can lead to cell growth, survival and metastasis of many tumors. Mutations in EGFR or an overexpression of the receptor is associated with multiple cancers, such as head and neck, glioblastoma, and breast cancer. We are specifically interested in a type of breast cancer called triple-negative because EGFR is overexpressed in a quarter of all patients. In this cancer the cells lacks the three conventional markers, which makes the cancer hard to diagnose and treat with conventional chemotherapeutic options. Our lab has identified a new function for the protein clathrin inside cells to control the function of EGFR. Clathrin was previously not known to control EGFR directly, and thus understanding how clathrin structures do so is critical to resolve how EGFR promotes breast cancer growth and survival. To resolve how clathrin controls the oncogene EGFR, I will use advanced microscopy that will image live cancer cells that have fluorescently-labelling of specific proteins, coupled to computer-based analysis methods. This research is significant because understanding this novel role of clathrin has the potential to reveal new weakness or drug targets within certain cancers, and may reveal new mechanisms to prevent resistance to current anti-EGFR therapies.

column36: Non-Invasive Electrical Stimulation of Cells Chemically Predisposed for Excitability as a Cell Type-Specific Treatment for Depression
column37: Depression is a serious condition that affects millions of Canadians each year. Although many options are available for treatment, many of them are associated with serious limitations, such as slow onset of relief and dangerous side effects. These problems highlight the need for new interventions that can effectively and safely relieve depressive symptoms. I will test a novel experimental technique to treat depression called EC stimulation, which will allow researchers to influence the activity of different types of brain cells without the need for invasive surgeries or complex genetic techniques. This will be done by combining non-invasive electrical brain stimulation with a drug that targets a specific kind of cell. These cells, known as interneurons, are located within the frontal lobe of the brain and have been found to influence depressive symptoms. By combining the effects of a weak dose of these two treatments, the activity of these interneurons can be increased, making them more likely to fire signals without affecting any other cell type. Using brain cell imaging techniques, I will locate markers for cell activity within the frontal lobe to verify that EC stimulation is successful in activating only these interneurons. I will also test whether this treatment can reverse depressive-like symptoms in a rat model of depression, and if this effect is related to chemical changes in other parts of the brain. My research will evaluate the effectiveness of EC stimulation as a method to selectively activate certain cell types. This will provide an important lead for determining the effects that different cell clusters have on mental health, while also promoting the development of better treatment options for difficult to treat disorders. Consequently, this project will guide further research towards the development of EC stimulation as a safe, simple, and accessible treatment for patients suffering from depression in both Canada and throughout the world.

column36: Predictors and consequences of longitudinal recovery following moderate to severe traumatic brain injury.
column37: Substantial research implicates alcohol misuse as a risk factor for traumatic brain injury (TBI), but less is known about the inverse relationship - how TBI increases risk of alcohol misuse. It has been theorized that impairments in executive functioning following TBI, such as decreased impulse control and greater risky decision making, may contribute to alcohol misuse post-injury. Acute administration of alcohol has also been shown to decrease impulse control, which predicted greater laboratory alcohol consumption. Therefore, it is hypothesized that baseline executive dysfunction may make individuals with TBI more vulnerable to alcohol-induced impulsive behaviour, which could contribute to impaired control over drinking. The proposed study will investigate the relationship between impairments in decision making and impulse control and acute alcohol administration among individuals with and without a history of TBI. It is hypothesized that individuals with TBI will have decreased impulse control and increased risky decision making, both at baseline and following an acute dose of alcohol, compared to healthy controls. These alcohol-induced impairments in decision making and impulse control will predict greater difficulties limiting their drinking during a subsequent self-administration procedure. Findings will provide critical information to develop drinking guidelines for the TBI population and gain an understanding of the neurocognitive mechanisms associated with alcohol misuse post-injury. This work will contribute greatly to the Canadian research ecosystem and foster impacts beyond the research environment, directly reaching individuals in the healthcare system.

column36: Emotional Reactivity and Reward Function in Concurrent Depression and Chronic Cannabis Use
column37: Depression causes significant burden on society and is a major health issue. Substance use, including the use of cannabis commonly co-occurs with depression and may be contributing to this burden. Indeed, some research suggests that compared to depressed individuals who do not use cannabis, depressed individuals who regularly use cannabis tend to report greater depressive symptoms and are less likely to improve during treatment; however, it is not yet clear how cannabis works to worsen depression in these individuals. Those who are depressed tend to experience greater emotional reactivity to stressors (i.e., react more negatively) and also tend to experience reduced reward function (i.e., decreased motivation to pursue rewards and decreased reward learning), which contribute to maintaining depressive symptoms. To better understand the role of cannabis on these two processes, we will explore whether the regular use of cannabis in depression is associated with greater dysfunctional reactivity to stress and greater impairment in reward function compared to what is seen in depression alone. Increasing legalization of cannabis and thereby easier access may lead to greater cannabis use in depression. As such, the results of this study have implications for how co-occurring cannabis use in and depression can be treated, informing the development of more targeted treatments or prioritizing existing treatments that either normalize reward function or emphasize stress management.

column36: Neural mechanisms of dual-task walking following cognitive training in late adulthood and Motoric Cognitive Risk syndrome
column37: A portion of the aging population has recently been identified as meeting criteria for Motoric Cognitive Risk syndrome (MCR), characterized by cognitive complaints (e.g., difficulty remembering) and slow walking speed, which places them at a greater risk for developing dementia. Early interventions are therefore needed to prevent or slow the progression of cognitive and physical decline in this at-risk population. Tests that assess cognitive task performance (e.g., subtracting) simultaneously with a motor task (e.g., walking; termed dual-tasking) are particularly challenging for those with MCR. We have recently shown that computerized cognitive training improves dual-task performance in healthy older adults. However, we do not yet know how brain activity changes during dual-task walking in older adults with MCR or in response to training. Therefore, the aim of this research is to examine brain activity during dual-task walking before and after cognitive training in healthy older adults and those with MCR. Evidence from neuroimaging shows greater activation in frontal brain regions during dual-tasking in older adults, compared to younger adults, which might represent a compensatory mechanism for declining brain structure. As such, we predict that prior to training, older adults with MCR will have greater frontal brain activation during dual-tasking compared to healthy older adults (suggesting less brain efficiency). However, following 12 weeks of cognitive training, we expect that the pattern of brain activity during dual-tasking will become more efficient due to enhanced cognitive capacity. The proposed research will shed light on how brain activity during dual-tasking changes after cognitive training in MCR, which will help optimize intervention strategies aimed at slowing the progression of cognitive and physical decline in older adults at risk of dementia.

column36: Projet de recherche-action participative pour identifier et caracteriser les defis ethiques engendres par les maladies rares au quotidien et dans le milieu de la sante
column37: Etant mal comprises par la communaute medicale, les maladies rares sont complexes a diagnostiquer et a traiter adequatement. Les delais diagnostics et la deterioration de l'etat de sante qui en decoulent s'ajoutent au fardeau quotidien pose par les symptomes de ces maladies rares. Les maladies rares engendrent des defis ethiques pour les personnes qui en sont atteintes, leurs proches aidants et les cliniciens. Ces parties prenantes sont confrontees a des prises de decisions complexes qui opposent leurs valeurs, leurs besoins ou leurs preferences. Les sacrifices financiers familiaux en vue d'un traitement dispendieux, le recours a une intervention chirurgicale experimentale et la formation des cliniciens sur les maladies rares sont des exemples de ces defis ethiques qui emergent au quotidien et dans le milieu de la sante. Notre premier objectif est de bien comprendre les defis ethiques lies aux maladies rares pour pallier le manque de connaissances a ce sujet. Les defis ethiques qui nous interessent touchent precisement les personnes atteintes de maladies rares, leurs proches et des professionnels de la sante au quotidien ou dans le milieu de la sante. En analysant les connaissances scientifiques connexes a ce theme, ainsi qu'en realisant des entrevues, des observations, et un sondage aupres des parties prenantes, nous decrirons ces defis ethiques dans toute leur complexite globale. Notre deuxieme objectif est de proposer un plan d'action pour aider a resoudre deux a trois defis ethiques preoccupants parmi ceux precedemment identifies lies au milieu de la sante, pour les patients quebecois. Ce plan d'action ameliorera ainsi la qualite de la prise en charge clinique des personnes atteintes de maladies rares. Nous formerons un comite constitue de parties prenantes qui participera au developpement des etapes du projet, a l'analyse des resultats et au developpement de la proposition du plan d'action.

column36: Elucidating the factors dictating regulatory T cell function in immune-mediated glomerular diseases.
column37: Glomerular diseases are a group of autoimmune kidney disorders where the immune system destroys the kidney's glomeruli. Destruction of these structures that filter out wastes from the blood and into the urine leads to the buildup of waste in circulation. Consequently, patients with glomerular diseases often require dialysis for life or kidney transplantation for survival. Currently, there are no specific treatments for glomerular diseases, and instead, broadly immunosuppressive drugs are used to dampen immunity. However, this is associated with significant toxicity including recurrent infections, diabetes and infertility. Accordingly, we aim to better characterize the biological mechanisms involved in glomerular diseases to develop safer and targeted therapeutics. Regulatory T (Treg) cells are a class of immune cells that dampen inflammation and prevent autoimmunity in all body organs. Researchers recently demonstrated that in order for Treg cells to provide optimal regulation of kidney inflammation, they need to undergo a process referred to as functional adaptation. Here, Treg cells adopt a few characteristics of their inflammatory immune cell counterparts enabling them to migrate to and thrive in locations with heavy inflammation. However, this functional adaptation comes at a cost, as it may cause Treg cells to fully convert into pro-inflammatory, kidney-injuring immune cells. This is referred to as lineage instability. By identifying the factors controlling renal Treg cell functional adaptation and lineage instability, we can envision the development of targeted therapeutics that bolster Treg cell functions in glomerular diseases. Here, we propose to study two factors that we and others have previously observed to control Treg cell function in other inflammatory conditions, namely the IL-1 family of alarmins (IL-1 and IL-33) and branched-chain amino acids (BCAA), in the context of glomerular diseases.

column36: Investigating microglial contributions to inflammation in Parkinson's disease using brain-like organoids
column37: Parkinson's disease is the second most common neurodegenerative disease, affecting approximately 100,000 Canadians. It is characterized by the loss of specific neurons in the brain, causing debilitating motor symptoms such as difficulty walking, postural instability and rigidity. Available treatments can alleviate the symptoms, but do not cure the disease. Microglia are the inflammatory cells that reside in the brain. They play an important role in maintaining neuronal health, but their aberrant inflammatory activities are thought to contribute to many neurodegenerative disorders. Genetic mutations of alpha-synuclein, a protein found in clumps in the brain of Parkinson's disease patient, have been associated with the risk of Parkinson's disease. Alpha-synuclein clumps provoke an excessive response of microglia. However, the impact of microglial expression of mutated alpha-synuclein on inflammatory processes, as well as the resulting harmful effects on the brain are not clearly understood. We propose to generate microglia from cells of patients harboring mutations in alpha-synuclein gene and integrate them into 3D "mini-brains" made in a dish. We will study the impact of these mutations on microglial function and neuronal health. Our study will allow us to better understand the contribution of microglial cells to the development of Parkinson's disease. The "mini-brains" containing microglia will serve as a model for drug development by other researchers.

column36: Deciphering the molecular routes by which an altered sperm epigenome elicits birth defects in the offspring
column37: In Canada, 1 in 25 babies are born with a birth defect. Craniofacial abnormalities (head and face abnormalities) are the most prevalent class of birth defects and are associated with high rates of infant mortality. Infants born with craniofacial abnormalities often require surgical, behavioral, and speech interventions which impose emotional and financial burdens for families and society. Although some craniofacial abnormalities are the result of a genetic mutation or an infectious disease, over half remain of unknown cause. Our research and that of others indicates that a previously overlooked origin of birth defects is the father's exposure to toxicants and poor diet. These paternal factors may be driven by the heritable non-genetic information in sperm known as the epigenome. The major focus of my doctoral research is to study how epigenetic information in sperm is transmitted to the embryo to influence fetal development. I have previously shown that a micronutrient folate deficiency in male mice alters the heritable epigenetic information in their sperm and is associated birth defects in their offspring. To further explore how a father's sperm epigenome can impact embryo development, I will next use a method of epigenetic manipulation in mice to identify the exact regions of the sperm epigenome that provoke craniofacial abnormalities in the offspring. This approach will permit me to map the developmental origins of a paternally-provoked birth defect. To date there exists little information about men's preconception health, resulting in missed opportunities for preventative health campaigns that would improve the rates of successful pregnancies and healthy children. This project will address a fundamental scientific question regarding the transmission of an altered sperm epigenome to the embryo and promote the development of better guidelines for men's reproductive health.

column36: Maintaining Cellular and Nuclear Integrity During Immune Cell Migration
column37: The human body is comprised of trillions of cells. The majority of our cells are structural, forming the building blocks of organs such as bones, muscle, and skin. However, protection from infection requires that one type of cell, our immune cells, is constantly moving throughout the body, searching for possible invasion and fighting it off when it occurs. T-cells are a specific type of immune cell that direct the actions of other immune cells and can directly kill infected cells to prevent infections from spreading further. To achieve this, T-cells must be highly mobile; they travel through a network of blood vessels to arrive at our various organs, whose structural cells form a complex maze. T-cells then squish and squeeze within the tight corridors of the maze as they find a path to their destination. This motion requires coordination between the cell body and the cell nucleus, which protects the cell's genetic material. The goal of my research is to understand how T-cells utilize physical cues from the maze to navigate within tissues and find the quickest path. I will use live imaging techniques to visualize in real-time how T-cells make decisions in different environments. I will focus on one particular inherited defect of immune cell migration that causes severe immunodeficiency disease in children to ask why in this case T-cell migration is ineffective. By studying what causes T-cell migration to fail, I will shed light on which molecular processes are critical to path-finding. This can inform treatments to improve T-cell navigation in tissues that are particularly challenging. For example, T-cells are often excluded from dense solid tumors. Both our body's own T-cells as well as engineered T-cell cancer therapies rely on T-cell infiltration deep into the tumor to destroy the cancer cells. Understanding how T-cells maneuver through tissue, such as these tumor environments, can help improve current treatment strategies which rely on immune cells to move.

column36: The intersection between innate and adaptive immunity in primary lung cancer
column37: Lung malignancies, including non-small cell lung cancer, are the most common cause of cancer-related death in Canada. column36: Elucidating the role of bacteriophage infection in ulcerative colitis
column37: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is an inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) of the human gut that has a great impact on the health of patients and the overall costs of health care in Canada. Currently there is no cure for UC, however, it is thought that the trillions of bacteria that live in the human gut might contribute to the disease. During UC, there is an imbalance in the types of bacteria that exist in the gut. Viruses that infect these bacteria, known as bacteriophages (phages), are present at equal numbers to bacteria in the gut and also seem to be imbalanced during UC. In other ecosystems, phages have been shown to infect bacteria and change the types of bacteria that exist in these systems. It is possible that these phages could be used for therapy in UC by preventing the imbalance of bacteria that occurs in these diseases. However, we first need to understand how these viruses infect and interact with bacteria in the gut during UC. We plan to characterize how phages from UC patients infect bacteria in the gut. In order to investigate this question, we first plan to give phages from either healthy volunteers or UC patients to mice and follow how the number, and activity of bacteria changes in the gut of these mice. Using DNA sequencing of bacteria, we will determine how the addition of UC phages to these mice might change the composition of bacteria to a state that might promote inflammation and disease. Finally, we will characterize which specific phages infect which bacteria in UC patients and healthy volunteers by tracking phages with a fluorescent dye and then performing DNA sequencing on both the phages and bacteria. Collectively, our approach will provide insight into how phage infection of bacteria might be changed during UC. It is possible that our data could help develop future therapeutics focused on using phages to change bacterial communities in UC patients.

column36: The Role of Vps36 in Exosome Production and Infection by Leishmania Parasites
column37: Leishmaniasis is a widespread neglected infectious disease with 0.9-1.6million new cases every year, resulting in up to 40 000 deaths annually. This disease is caused by the Leishmania parasite, carried by the common sandfly whose habitat continues to grow due to climate change, making Leishmaniasis even more widespread. Research performed in our laboratory has led to the discovery that Leishmania secrete tiny particles called exosomes that are injected along with the parasite during a sandfly bite, and these exosomes enhance infection. Exosomes are key to cellular communication, and yet research on their role in infectious diseases is sorely lacking. Knowing their key role in Leishmania infection, we want to test whether inhibiting the release of exosomes by Leishmania will hinder infection and reduce the severity of Leishmaniasis. To accomplish this, we are disrupting a specific gene, Vps36, that has been shown to play a key role in exosome production. This will be done using CRISPR/Cas9 technology, which is capable of targeting specific DNA sequences. This will be used in our case to add an antibiotic resistance gene into the Vps36 gene, disrupting it and allowing for mutant Leishmania to be selected for using antibiotics. We will compare the wild type and mutant Leishmania to test if exosome production is altered. Continuing, we will infect mice with the WT and mutant Leishmania to examine whether Vps36 disruption is sufficient in reducing infection and Leishmaniasis symptoms. The results of this research will clarify the mechanisms of exosome production in Leishmania and potentially create an attenuated strain of Leishmania, which has implications for vaccine development. Additionally, Leishmania themselves may be useful for studying the mechanisms of exosome production present in all eukaryotes, which will be very helpful to cancer and immune cell research.

column36: Characterising the effect of PM2.5 air pollution exposure on tuberculosis (TB) treatment outcomes and TB-associated mortality in a high TB burden setting
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) is responsible for a greater number of deaths worldwide than any other single infectious disease. India shoulders a particularly high burden of TB, accounting for more than one quarter of global TB cases. Given the high levels of pollution in India's large cities, and the identification of air pollution as the most significant environmental cause of disease globally, India is a pertinent setting in which to investigate the association between air pollution and TB outcomes. Although past studies have identified smoking as a risk factor for progression to active TB as well as TB-related mortality, none have explored the effects of exposure to fine particulate (PM2.5) air pollution on TB outcomes. This study therefore aims to characterise personal-level exposures to PM2.5 among TB patients in India, comparing exposure in active TB patients in the highly polluted city of New Delhi to those in the less polluted town of Udupi, Karnataka. Personal-level exposure will be measured using small, lightweight personal aerosol monitors. Patients will be followed up over a period of 2 months, and outcomes measured will include treatment response and TB-associated mortality. Adequate treatment response will be defined by the absence of detectable viable TB bacteria in patients' sputum (mucus) samples at 2 months of treatment. Appropriate statistical methods, including logistic regression analyses, will be carried out to determine whether an association is likely to exist between PM2.5 air pollution exposure and poorer TB treatment outcomes. Being the first to investigate the effect of individual-level PM2.5 exposure in TB patients on TB treatment outcomes, this study addresses two significant and coinciding health concerns in India and globally: TB and air pollution. By providing an evidence base for TB treatment considerations in this context, the findings of this study may therefore contribute to improved TB control and prevention.

column36: The role of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis SigK regulon in infection and disease
column37: Globally, tuberculosis is the leading cause of death by infectious disease. In 2017, there were 10 million new cases of TB and 1.6 million deaths. Though Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb), the cause of tuberculosis, has been investigated for over a century, mechanisms for how it subverts the human immune system to persist, replicate and spread remain poorly understood. In this project, I use novel techniques to investigate these unknown mechanisms. I will engineer variants ('mutants') of M.tb to specifically look at a set of genes present in all strains of M.tb, which spreads in humans, but are turned up in certain strains that spread in livestock. Previous work in the Behr lab has identified that strains of bacteria that cause disease in cattle have evolved these genetic differences, suggesting a role in adaptation to different host populations. By manipulating M.tb, I will be able to investigate how proteins that interact with the host are produced in different amounts, and how this affects the outcome of controlled experimental infections in the laboratory. Previously, methods to analyze this mutation were tedious, and ineffective. With new tools available, which I have already optimized in the lab, I will both conduct the proposed experiments, while also developing techniques that will be used to further study the biology of mycobacterial infections. Ultimately, this project aims to guide the management of tuberculosis and potentially contribute to a vaccine that prevents tuberculosis.

column37: Chronic pain is a devastating medical condition that impacts nearly 1 in 5 Canadian adults.
