Specific objectives are to: 1) determine current community resources; 2) identify stakeholder needs and barriers; and 3) implement and evaluate an integrated pain management program with community resources. This work will be done in collaboration with individuals with chronic pain, to center the voices and needs of those directly impacted by the research.The first aim will be addressed by an online scan to determine the scope of existing local support resources for chronic pain (including educational resources, patient support groups and exercise programs). The second aim will be addressed through interviews with chronic pain patients, clinicians and community leaders, to determine their perspectives related to linking community and health care systems. These perspectives will be used to design an integrated evidence-based chronic pain management program, tailored to the local community. The final aim will be addressed by conducting a feasibility randomized clinical trial, to evaluate differences in patient outcomes between the integrated program and clinical pain management alone, in addition to evaluating the implementation process. This work is aligned with the current strategic effort to address the chronic pain crisis in Canada. By immediately assisting the community and adding to the growing literature related to pain management and delivery, this work strives to assist the Canadian initiative to improve the treatment of such common health concern.

column37: An estimated 1 in 2 Canadians will develop cancer at some point in their life. Individuals with this disease face a multitude of psychological struggles and their psychosocial needs are often reported as unmet. In Phase 2, the newly developed survey items will be pilot tested among a sample of researchers and practitioners in psychosocial oncology. In Phase 3, mental health professionals will be recruited to complete the final survey about their attitudes towards and usage of psychosocial oncology CPGs. Comparisons of all study variables within and across different mental health professions and work environments will be conducted through simple and multiple logistic regressions. This study will help address the gap between science and practice in the field of psychosocial oncology and contribute to efforts to promote evidence-based practice in psychology.

column36: Should I tell my employer I have a disability? Understanding communication, decision making, support and accommodation processes in the workplace among adults living with chronic disabling conditions
column37: On average, Canadians spend over one-third of their lives at work. Employment has been found to provide a sense of purpose and well-being. column36: The use of patient derived gastric cancer organoids as a predictive tool to determine patient response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy
column37: Stomach cancer remains a deadly disease. In Canada, only 25% of patients diagnosed with stomach cancer survive five years after their diagnosis. Specific chemotherapy regimens established for stomach cancer have improved survival, however some cancers respond better to treatment than others. Unfortunately, there is no current way to predict which treatment is best for each individual patient. One way to personalize treatment for patients is to use cells from their own cancer and test how their cancer responds to various anti-cancer treatments in the laboratory. Due to new technological advancements we can now grow a patient's cancer cells in a three-dimensional space to form miniature organs, or "organoids", that resemble the patient's actual cancer. We hypothesize that organoids will respond similar to the patient's cancer when treated with the same anti-cancer therapy so that they may be used to predict treatment response. For our study we will enroll twenty stomach cancer patients and take a piece of their cancer prior to chemotherapy. We will then grow the cancer cells in the lab and treat them with the same anti-cancer drugs that the patient receives. Following surgery, we will compare the degree to which cells were killed in a patient's cancer to the number of cells killed in the lab to determine how similar they respond to treatment. The overall goal of our project is to develop tools that will allow for better prediction of stomach cancer response to chemotherapy so that each patient can receive the best treatment for their tumour. If successful, this study may provide evidence to apply these techniques to future studies with the purpose provide "precision medicine" to Canadian stomach cancer patients.

column36: Increasing Myocardial Ketone Oxidation as an Approach to Treat Heart Failure
column37: A growing number of Canadians (over 50,000) are diagnosed with heart failure each year. Heart failure is a chronic condition where the weakened cardiac muscle can no longer effectively pump blood to the rest of the body. Like a car engine, the healthy heart uses 'fuels' to meet its high energy demand and sustain its contractile function. However, the failing heart is akin to an engine out of fuel and is not only running low on fuels, but also running on the wrong type of fuels. While the healthy heart can tap into different 'grades/types of fuels', namely fats and carbohydrates, the failing heart loses its flexibility to use different fuels and becomes inefficient at fuel consumption, ultimately becoming energy-starved. Therefore, my research is focused on understanding a new 'grade of fuel' that is understudied - ketones. Ketones are produced by our livers during starvation and intense exercise. However, recent evidence suggests that the failing heart uses more ketones for energy compared to a healthy heart. Thus, are ketones a good or bad fuel for the failing heart? Answering this question will be the objective of my research project. To do this, mice with heart failure will have their hearts removed from their body and fixed to a system that can pump simulated blood through their isolated beating hearts. Ketones will then be added to the simulated blood and heart function will be assessed to see if ketones can improve how well the heart is working and using energy. Furthermore, we will also study the effects of ketones by feeding mice, with heart failure, a ketogenic diet. Heart function will then be monitored throughout the treatment to determine if this high-fat/low-carbohydrate diet can improve the failing heart's function. From these experiments and results, I hope to direct future therapeutic approaches for treating heart failure. If ketones are good for the failing heart, a ketone supplement or ketogenic diet could be used to treat heart failure patients.

column36: Fasted Exercise training in Type 2 Diabetes (FED)
column37: Diabetes is a major health concern worldwide. It is estimated that up to 30% of people in Canada are living with pre-diabetes or type 2 diabetes (T2D). Many people with T2D, also have fatty liver disease and this can worsen blood sugar control. It is recommended that people with diabetes increase their daily physical activity to manage their blood sugars. Sometimes, increasing the amount of exercise can be very difficult. In addition, many individuals who meet the recommended exercise guidelines experience minimal improvement in their blood sugar control, and minimal reductions in liver fat. This can be very discouraging. Improving the time of day that exercise is preformed (e.g., before or after breakfast) may be a simple method to improve blood sugar control and reduce fat stored in organs such as the liver, pancreas, and muscle. To date, only short-term studies have examined how modifying exercise time of day affects people with T2D. It is unknown which time of day is best in the long term. This study will examine 16 weeks of aerobic exercise training, performed before or after breakfast, on blood sugar control and fat stored in the liver, pancreas, and muscle. It could be very motivating for people with T2D to know that they can get more benefits from exercise by changing when exercise is performed, rather than increasing the amount. Ultimately, results from this study may help clinicians more optimally prescribe exercise to help patients achieve their clinical targets and improve their overall quality of life.

column36: The role of Hedgehog signaling in basal-like breast cancer and the tumour microenvironment
column37: Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women worldwide and remains a leading cause of cancer death. One in 9 women will develop breast cancer at some point in their lifetime. Despite the success of current treatment, breast cancer remains a potentially deadly disease with multiple subtypes that respond very differently to treatment. Basal-like breast cancer (BLBC) is a specific subtype that comprises 15% of all breast cancers and primarily affects young women, people of African or Hispanic ancestry, and those with genetic mutations. Despite current treatments, BLBC often has a poor outcome. There is therefore an unmet need for improved treatments in this group of patients. Increasing evidence has shown that the Hedgehog signaling pathway is associated with BLBC. The Hedgehog pathway is a specific molecular pathway that is essential during development of the embryo and is critical for early breast development. My preliminary studies and those of others have shown a link between activated Hedgehog signaling and the growth of breast cancer cells, with more aggressive breast cancers harboring activated Hedgehog signaling. My project will aim to study exactly how the Hedgehog pathway promotes the growth of BLBC cells. My hypothesis is that Hedgehog is responsible for releasing specific molecules that promote inflammation, termed cytokines. These cytokines then recruit immune cells that help the cancer grow and mature. By identifying which cytokines are triggered by Hedgehog signaling and which immune cells are recruited, I will then begin to test different drugs to inhibit these cytokines, thereby changing the immune cell infiltration and inhibiting cancer growth. Many of these drugs are already approved and available to treat inflammatory diseases, such as Rheumatoid Arthritis and Ulcerative Colitis. My plan would therefore be to take these drugs that have already been shown to be safe with minimal side effects, and repurpose them for use in BLBC.

I will be guided and supervised by a team of experts in the field of substance abuse disorders and mental health problems, who are passionate to find new efficient treatment modalities. I will disseminate the results through multiple channels to reach the general public, clinicians and healthcare policy makers throughout Canada.

column36: Computational single-cell analysis of developmental programs disrupted in pediatric tumours
column37: Pediatric brain tumours are the leading cause of cancer-related death and the second most common diagnosed malignancy in children in Canada. Despite aggressive therapy, for many tumour types, outcomes have not changed in the last three decades. Survival is very low, and patients that do survive are left with severe lifelong side-effects. Current evidence suggests that in some childhood tumours, the initiating molecular event that causes the tumour occurs during development. During development, cells undergo a sequence of coordinated changes in gene expression that must be finely orchestrated, and alterations in this process often cause disease. Our goal is to identify the precise timing of these initial disease-causing events for several tumour types of uncertain origin, and understand why development does not proceed properly in these cells. For this, we propose to assemble a large collection of datasets at the single-cell resolution for both tumour samples and normal developing tissues. We will then develop the computational tools to analyze and integrate these large datasets. Finally, we will employ these novel strategies to characterize additional samples from patient cohorts. This project aims to address a critical gap in research on childhood cancers. Establishment of experimental models for specific tumour types and improving therapeutic strategies are both challenging because for many tumours, the origins of the tumour are unknown. Through generation and characterization of new datasets from normal tissues and patient samples, we will identify gene expression processes that may be altered in childhood brain tumours, which can provide therapeutic targets. column36: Un essai clinique randomise et controle, a simple insu, comparant la Therapie Avatar a la Therapie Cognitivo-Comportementale pour les hallucinations auditives verbales chez les patients atteints de schizophrenie
column37: Plusieurs personnes atteintes de schizophrenie entendent des voix qui les persecutent, ce qui nuit a leur fonctionnement. Imaginez-vous essayer de vivre normalement alors que vous entendez des voix que personne d'autre ne semble remarquer: "Tu n'es bon a rien!", "Tu es laid!". Bien qu'il existe des medicaments pouvant aider a diminuer ou a arreter ces hallucinations, ils ne sont pas efficaces sur tout le monde. Malheureusement, il existe peu d'alternatives; en effet, la meilleure therapie qui existe actuellement n'a pas d'effet favorable sur plus de la moitie des patients qui la suivent. Par consequent, notre laboratoire a developpe une nouvelle therapie: la Therapie Avatar. Celle-ci a pour objectif d'aider ces patients a reguler leurs emotions, ce qui permet d'apprendre a mieux vivre avec leurs voix. En plus de diminuer l'impact negatif des hallucinations sur differents aspects de la vie des patients, cette therapie pourrait augmenter leur qualite, et meme diminuer la frequence des episodes hallucinatoires. Le principe est le suivant: le patient est invite a creer un avatar 3D en realite virtuelle et a personnaliser son apparence afin qu'il ressemble le plus possible a la representation qu'il se fait de sa voix la plus derangeante. Ensuite, en immersion, il entre en dialogue avec l'avatar, anime par le therapeute. Le patient sera d'abord confronte au personnage, pour ensuite se reconcilier avec celui-ci et travailler sur son estime de soi. Afin d'evaluer l'efficacite de cette nouvelle intervention, nous la comparerons a la therapie la plus couramment utilisee en clinique. Les patients seront evalues sur differents aspects avant et apres la therapie, ce qui nous permettra d'evaluer ses effets. Finalement, nous esperons que l'utilisation de la realite virtuelle s'averera un moyen efficace de traiter certains symptomes persistants et invalidants de cette maladie complexe qu'est la schizophrenie.

column36: Application d'un protocole de stimulation magnetique transcranienne repetitive theta-burst multisessions dans la gestion de la douleur aigue et la prevention de la douleur chronique chez des patients victimes d'une fracture d'un membre superieur avec ou sans traumatisme craniocerebral leger concomitant.
column37: Le fracture des membres superieurs est la blessure la plus commune en milieu hospitalier. La douleur est le symptome le plus incapacitant a la suite d'une fracture et s'avere souvent le principal facteur retardant la reprise des activites pre-accidentelles, telles que le travail. Les patients avec fracture sont a risque de developper de la douleur chronique lorsque la douleur en phase aigue n'est pas prise en charge de maniere optimale. De plus, la fracture est frequemment accompagnee d'un traumatisme craniocerebral leger (TCCL), amplifiant le niveau de douleur rapporte. Malgre d'importants effets secondaires qui y sont associes, les traitements pharmacologiques conventionnels de la douleur demeurent l'approche preconisee par les professionnels de la sante. Des etudes suggerent que la stimulation magnetique transcranienne repetitive (rTMS) serait une avenue efficace dans la gestion de la douleur chez ce type de patient par son effet analgesique. Cette etude vise a examiner les effets d'un protocole de rTMS sur les marqueurs de recuperation fonctionnelle (douleur, reprise des activites quotidiennes, fonctions motrices et cognitives) chez les patients avec une fracture avec ou sans TCCL concomitant. Nous proposons que le protocole actif aura davantage d'effet sur la recuperation des patients avec fracture et TCCL concomitant, comparativement aux patients avec une fracture ou soumis au protocole controle. Les 80 patients seront recrutes et impliques dans une intervention d'une duree de 10 jours. Aucune etude a ce jour n'a explore la gestion de la douleur chez les patients victimes d'une blessure traumatique par le biais d'approches fondees sur la rTMS. En ciblant quatre obstacles majeurs nuisant a la recuperation suite a un trauma (douleur, detresse psychologique induite par la douleur, alteration des fonctions cognitives et motrices), le protocole rTMS est susceptible de reduire le temps de convalescence, mais egalement les pertes financieres qui l'accompagnent.

column36: Association between the concomitant use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and oral anticoagulants and the risk of major bleeding
column37: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are the most commonly used type of antidepressant medications in Canada. While these drugs have fewer side effects than other antidepressants, they can cause major bleeding in some people, which requires hospitalization and could be fatal. Patients with heart disease are often treated with oral anticoagulants (i.e. blood thinners), which can also cause major bleeding. Around 20-30% of people living with heart disease may also be diagnosed with depression and may need treatment with both SSRIs and anticoagulants. To date, we have not accurately measured the risk of major bleeding in patients taking both these drugs together. Therefore, the purpose of this research is to measure the risk of major bleeding in patients using SSRIs and anticoagulants together and compare it to those using anticoagulants only. We expect that this risk will be substantially higher in patients jointly using both medications. Furthermore, we will be studying novel oral anticoagulants (NOACs), a new group of anticoagulants that, unlike the older types, do not require regular blood test monitoring. To perform this study, we will use a database that has personal and medical information from over 15 million patients in the U.K. who visited a general practitioner. This data reflects the Canadian population well, since U.K. patients are similar when it comes to their patterns of SSRI and anticoagulant use. Also, we expect our results to be relevant to the general population, since the data is collected from real-life practices. Major bleeding is a severe and potentially fatal health issue. The findings of this study will be crucial for patients with heart disease who may need antidepressants and the doctors who are managing their care. In addition, NOACs are more convenient for patients than older anticoagulants. However, since we know very little about the safety of using NOACs and SSRIs together, this study will provide much needed evidence.

column37: L'aphasie post-stroke est un trouble du langage survenant a la suite d'un accident vasculaire cerebral. Le present projet de recherche vise a mieux comprendre les predicteurs precoces de la recuperation du langage chez les personnes atteintes d'aphasie post-stroke. Plus specifiquement, nous nous interessons a la mesure dans laquelle l'etendue des dommages qui touchent la matiere blanche du cerveau dans les jours qui suivent l'accident vasculaire cerebral permet de predire l'amelioration des difficultes d'anomie dans le temps. Concretement, ces difficultes sont associees a une moins bonne qualite de vie, une perte d'autonomie et a plusieurs consequences psychosociales nefastes chez les personnes atteintes. Par ailleurs, l'age avance represente le principal facteur de risque pour la survenue d'un accident vasculaire cerebral. Ainsi, dans le contexte actuel du vieillissement de la population, on peut s'attendre a ce que les cas d'aphasie post-stroke soient de plus en plus frequents. Pour cette raison, mieux comprendre les facteurs qui permettent de predire la recuperation du langage a la suite d'un accident vasculaire cerebral devient un enjeu central afin d'ameliorer la prise en charge d'un nombre croissant de Canadiens. Entre autres, les avancees scientifiques dans ce domaine peuvent aider a mieux orienter les priorites de rehabilitation chez les patients atteints d'aphasie post-stroke et ce, dans les premiers jours suivants l'accident vasculaire cerebral.

column36: Does family history of type 2 diabetes influence fat oxidation and the source of oxidized fat during exercise in aging women?
column37: Aging and family history of diabetes are recognized as risk factors for type 2 diabetes. The accumulation of fat within the muscle and the inability to sufficiently utilize this fat source are amongst the proposed mechanisms to explain this increased risk. A potent intervention to prevent type 2 diabetes in various populations is aerobic exercise. However, individuals with a family history of diabetes are known to have reduced fat oxidation at rest and during submaximal exercise. Furthermore, recent results from our research group suggest that a greater proportion of fat-derived energy would be drawn from the blood at the expense of fat stored in the muscles. Together, these metabolic alterations could potentially limit the exercise-induced benefits on type 2 diabetes prevention. Our recent observations were however drawn from indirect methods and we thus wish to confirm our results with a more appropriate study design. Our objectives are to verify if : 1) Aging women with a family history of type2 diabetes utilize less fat stored in the muscle relative to fat in blood circulation, compared with aging women without a family history of diabetes. 2) To determine the exercise intensity at which the utilization of fat stored in the muscle is at its peak. Studies investigating exercise metabolism in individuals with family history fo type 2 diabetes are scarce and, to the best of or knowledge, inexistent in an aging population. Our study would thus be the first to investigate how different sources of fat are used during exercise in a population at high risk for type 2 diabetes. Results from this study will guide us in a future project assessing the impact of different exercise modalities on fat oxidation and their impact on glycemic control.

column36: Treating chronic pain with pepducins derived from neurotensin receptor type 1 (NTS1)
column37: The treatment of chronic pain is an incredibly important medical issue. Nearly 20% of adults suffer from chronic pain on a daily basis, and unfortunately, most of the treatments available are not effective. Our team is now working on a novel strategy in pain relief called pepducins. Pepducins are small proteins that are designed to interact with receptors in a unique way. Rather than simply fitting into a receptor, like a key into a lock, they imbed themselves in the cell membrane, flip towards the inside of the cell, and interact with the receptor there, modifying the signals that it is sending. Although pepducins have been developed to tackle different diseases, they have not been studied much in the context of pain. This is precisely the aim of our project, and so, our team designed pepducins targeting a receptor involved in pain perception. Our goal is to study pepducin behaviour both on cells and on live animals (rats). This will involve testing for analgesia (pain-relief), but also for unwanted adverse effects such as important drops in blood pressure. All in all, this research is extremely valuable, as it may lead to new and much-needed pain-relievers.

column36: Predicting health outcomes from hematopoietic evolution in large population cohorts
column37: Cancer and cardiovascular disease (CVD) are on the rise with the vast majority of disease occurring in low and middle income countries. Personalized medicine is emerging as a valuable approach to diagnose cancer and CVD at early stages when treatments are more likely to be associated with improved health outcomes. However, the vast majority of personalized medicine approaches are developed on a subset of the population and have limited utility in different ethnic groups and environmental contexts. Further, tools which do exist are impractical to implement in developing contexts. To address this, I will develop a non-invasive liquid biopsy-based approach to detect likelihood of progression to hematological cancers and CVD across a range of ethnic groups and environmental contexts using blood collected years prior to the diagnosis of disease. This work builds off recent studies which have linked the age-related mutation accumulation in blood to both diseases. While common in the healthy aging population, these mutations have been associated with subsequent cancer and CVD development. There is a clear need to understand the biology and develop biomarkers and tools that can distinguish benign and malignant patterns of mutation accumulation. To do so, I will capture and characterize the early evolutionary profiles of the mature blood cell pool in order to uncover the events causing an individual to shift from healthy to disease state. Through improving our understanding of early disease evolution, we will enable earlier diagnoses and identify novel therapeutic targets to prevent progression to disease. This study combines state-of-the-art machine learning techniques with classic population genetics to trace the evolution of disease in the aging blood cell pool. Our models will allow for clinical implementation and will lay the foundation for preventative medicine approaches for cancer and CVD in both Canadian and African contexts and improve health outcomes globally.

column36: Uncovering political knowledge-to-action strategies to improve ecological determinants of health
column37: The World Health Organizations estimates that 12.6 million people die worldwide every year due to environmental factors such as climate change or air pollution. This is supported by research that provides extensive evidence on the health impacts of the so-called 'ecological determinants of health' - the air that we breathe, the water that we drink or the food that we eat. However, this evidence is often not considered sufficiently when political decisions about environmental regulations that would improve these health determinants are being made. This is partly because researchers mostly rely on ineffective knowledge translation strategies to influence decision makers such as politicians. This doctoral research program seeks to change the way we conduct knowledge translation in the health sciences with the goal to more successfully influence policy. More specifically, this research will draw on insights from the field of political science where more effective strategies have been developed and apply them to the issue of ecological determinants of health and environmental policies. The goal is to provide researchers and funding agencies with the tools to create and foster new and innovative political knowledge translation strategies in order to improve both the health of humans and the health of the planet.

column36: The Longitudinal Association Between Anxiety and Restricted/Repetitive Behaviour in Autism Spectrum Disorder
column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a disorder of brain development that affects 1-2% of children. It is usually diagnosed between 2 and 4 years of age and is a lifelong condition. A classic symptom of ASD is restricted and repetitive behaviour, like hand flapping and rigid adherence to routines. In addition, 40% of children with ASD will also meet criteria for an anxiety disorder during childhood or adolescence, which adds to existing impairments in functioning. A better understanding of which children with ASD develop anxiety disorders is greatly needed, to inform prevention strategies and treatments. Cross-sectional studies suggest that children with ASD with more severe restricted/repetitive behaviour also tend to have worse anxiety at the same time. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine which symptoms occur first, the different patterns of anxiety over time, and the underlying risk factors associated with high rates of anxiety in ASD. The Pathways in ASD study is the largest and longest-running longitudinal study in the world on how children with ASD grow and develop. A first project, as part of my master's thesis, found that children with ASD who had severe restricted/repetitive behaviour in preschool had more than three times greater odds of developing elevated anxiety between ages 8-11 years than those with mild restricted/repetitive behaviour. I have now transferred to a PhD program, where, based on these exciting results, two important follow up projects are planned: (1) to use a statistical approach called developmental cascade modelling to examine how multiple risk factors may together lead to increasing levels of anxiety in ASD; and (2) to examine the different trajectories of anxiety and restricted/repetitive behaviour in ASD, and how they relate to each other. The overall goal is to increase early recognition of anxiety disorders in ASD, to facilitate prevention and early intervention, and to ensure timely access to treatment.

column36: Does tau pathology propagate within human brain networks?
column37: Alzheimer's disease is a neurodegenerative condition that is defined by the aggregation of two specific pathologies in the brain: amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles. While amyloid-beta appears years before the onset of symptoms, tau tangles are very closely linked to the death of brain cells and to symptoms like memory problems. Correspondingly, it is important to understand how tau pathology appears in the brain and spreads from one brain region to another. In recent years, impressive strides have been made with animal models of Alzheimer's disease. Research has shown that when tau is injected into the mouse brain, we can observe tau at the injection site but also in anatomically connected brain regions. The goal of my project is to translate the research from mice (who do not naturally develop Alzheimer's disease) into humans to determine how the disease actually develops. Using recent advancements in molecular imaging, we can measure tau pathology in living individuals. This allows us to see where tau is located in the brain, and how it spreads with time - a critical advance, because in the past, doctors had to wait until a patient died to examine their brain for tau. My study will determine how tau pathology spreads in the brain. I am building on the hypothesis that tau spreads through the brain's anatomical connections. We first used data from over 130 elderly individuals who underwent MRI and fMRI to create a connection map of the brain. Next, we observed that tau in Alzheimer's disease patients mirrors the connection map of the brain. The final step is to test our hypothesis in several population-based cohort studies of Alzheimer's disease (over 500 individuals) to see if anatomical connections allow for tau to spread. Understanding how tau pathology spreads is critical to stopping it. Because tau pathology is closely linked to the death of brain cells, this research will have implications for the next generation of anti-tau therapies.

column36: Does physiotherapy plus brain stimulation enhance motor recovery? Evaluating the feasibility of transcranial direct current stimulation as an adjunct to physiotherapy intervention in children and youth with acquired brain injury
column37: A severe acquired brain injury (ABI) sustained in childhood results in the significant loss of motor skills, leaving some children without the ability to walk, run, or sit independently. Current treatment for motor skill recovery is intensive physiotherapy, which helps these children relearn the motor skills required for the mobility-based activities they want and need to do in everyday life. Unfortunately, even with intensive physiotherapy, children with ABI have persisting physical impairments that can seriously affect their development and ability to return to pre-injury activities. To improve upon current physiotherapy outcomes, there is an urgent need for new treatments that maximize motor recovery and minimize long-term physical complications. Transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) is a form of low-intensity brain stimulation that primes the brain for learning. It has been found to improve motor function in many adult neurological populations (e.g., stroke, Parkinson's) and in children with cerebral palsy, particularly when paired with practice of specific motor skills. However, it has yet to be studied in children with ABI. Our study will evaluate tDCS combined with the current physiotherapy intervention for children in the inpatient ABI program at Holland Bloorview Kids Rehabilitation Hospital (Toronto, Ontario). This feasibility randomized control trial will assign 30 participants (ages 5 to 18 years) to one of two treatment groups. One group will receive active tDCS before four physiotherapy sessions each week for a total of 16 sessions, while the other will receive placebo tDCS before their 16 physiotherapy sessions. Recovery of motor skills will be compared between groups by assessing abilities before, immediately after and three months after the tDCS treatments. Our study will elucidate the additive impact of tDCS and physiotherapy on recovery of gross motor skills.

column36: Maternal postpartum psychiatric emergencies: applying an intersectional feminist framework to understand outcomes and better identify groups of women whose care needs are not being met
column37: Mental illness is common in the first year after childbirth and impacts tens of thousands of Canadian women and their children. If treatment is delayed or inadequate, consequences can be devastating. Maternal suicide is a leading cause of maternal death in Canada, and there are likely missed opportunities to prevent this tragic outcome. Our team showed that the emergency department (ED) is the first point of post-childbirth mental health care contact for many women, particularly women from marginalized groups, including those living in poverty and living rurally. What happens to women after postpartum psychiatric emergencies is not known. column36: Identifying the genetic determinants of lipophagy using Saccharomyces cerevisiae
column37: Macrophages are specialized cells of the immune system that play a key role in the progression of atherosclerosis, a disease that is a major cause of cardiovascular disease - the most significant killer of Canadians each year. Atherosclerosis is characterized by cholesterol rich particles in the bloodstream that enter into artery walls and induce macrophages to follow and 'eat up' the cholesterol. These hungry macrophages become full of cholesterol, and unable to leave the artery. As the disease progresses complex accumulations of macrophages, known as plaques, increase in size. Eventually, plaques can rupture, block circulation and lead to heart attacks. Recently, macrophage lipophagy was discovered and has the potential to reverse the growth of plaques. In lipophagy, lipid droplets (cholesterol storage sites) are degraded by lysosomes and the free cholesterol is excreted from the cell. Put simply, lipophagy can reverse the accumulation of cholesterol in macrophages and thus the severity of plaques. However, little is known about the genes that control lipophagy. To adress this question we aim to conduct a comprehensive genetic analysis of lipophagy using yeast. The autophagic processes of yeast are remarkably similar to their mammalian counterparts and technology is available for efficient and large-scale genetic manipulation. Genetic screening to the same extent is not feasible in macrophages. For these reasons, it is viable to use yeast to answer questions about lipophagy. Presently, we have developed a library of several thousand single-gene deletion yeast and are now assessing methods to detect intact or defective lipophagy in these strains as well as screening the deletion yeast for lipophagy defects. We expect this analysis will identify novel lipophagy genes whose macrophage counterparts can then be targeted for future atherosclerosis therapies that specifically activate lipophagy.

column36: Estimating the risk of long-term cardiovascular outcomes in women with hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
column37: High blood pressure during pregnancy or 'hypertensive' disorders of pregnancy (HDP) are common, occurring in 5 to 10% of all pregnancies. Women with a history of HDP have a much higher risk of developing heart and blood vessel diseases (e.g. stroke, heart disease, heart failure) compared to women who do not experience HDP. These women are also at 4-times the risk of developing high blood pressure for the rest of their lives (i.e. chronic high blood pressure). This is important because high blood pressure is the number one cause of death and disability in the world and it is more dangerous for women than men. Currently, very little is known about whether the increased risk of heart and blood vessel diseases for women with HDP is due to chronic high blood pressure, or if this risk is increased even for women whose high blood pressure during pregnancy returns to normal after delivery. To address this question, we will analyze information from large computer databases on all women admitted to deliver in Ontario hospitals over the past 30 years. In our tests, we will account for several factors that might otherwise also affect a woman's risk. For example, in addition to conditions like diabetes, we will also consider gender-related characteristics (e.g. feminine and masculine personality traits) because we know these factors can increase people's risk of developing diseases of the heart. This research capitalizes on an important opportunity to improve our knowledge of factors that increase women's heart health risk. It will address a large knowledge gap for women's health and the results of this study will be an important first step in developing new ways for doctors to identify women at highest risk of heart and blood vessel diseases. It will also provide evidence for the importance of including information on a woman's pregnancy history when evaluating heart disease risk. Until these results are available, heart health outcomes for women with HDP will remain poor.

NMD4C is committed to: engaging patients as full partners in network activities; national and international collaboration; and open science and data sharing. column37: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are chronic conditions that damage a person's intestines and cause lifelong pain. IBD is becoming more common in Canada, especially in children. Current treatments (drugs) suppress patient's immune systems and don't work all the time; even when they work they carry substantial risks. Therefore, we need to develop new treatments. While studying some of our patients, our Team of doctors and scientists has found several types of unusual bacteria in their intestines. These bacteria are able to attach to - or invade the cells lining the human gut, and trigger inflammation. These bacteria are also recognized by the patient's immune cells, suggesting these "pathobiont" bacteria are involved in either causing IBD, or making it worse, and thus removing these nasty bacteria could be a new treatment for IBD. Our Team is part of a national Network studying IBD in more than 1500 Canadian children. We plan to use the existing Network infrastructure to collect samples from these patients, including stool samples, intestinal washing, and tissues. We will use specialized techniques to identify potential "pathobionts" and grow them up in large numbers, allowing us to study them in great detail. We will test how they stick or invade human cells grown in the lab, as well as inject them into mice to see how they cause disease. As we gain a better understanding of how different "pathobiont" bacteria cause disease, we will develop new ways to target these bacteria and test these approaches in the lab, in mouse models, and ultimately in the patients themselves. For example, we will test if certain diets can starve these bacteria, if there are specific good bacteria we can give to patients in their food that can outcompete the pathobionts, or if we can use new drugs to kill, or flush away these harmful bacteria. Taken together, our studies will help develop new precise and personalized ways to treat children with IBD, and ultimately improve their lives.

In partnership with Indigenous communities, employing a strengths-based approach, we will examine ways to achieve equity in access to screening in First Nations and Metis communities adhering to OCAP and OCAS principles. column37: Indigenous peoples with serious mental illness face unique health care barriers due to racism, oppression, and intergenerational trauma of residential school and child welfare systems. There is a lack of national research networking among academics and communities in Indigenous health generally and specifically in holistic Indigenous mental health. The team will develop a cultural evidence-based Indigenous research network to improve mental wellness by generating data that shows that illness and crisis can be prevented with traditional knowledges, cultural safety, and Indigenous science, when applied to health systems. There are 6 research themes: Cultural safety; Indigenous holistic prevention and early intervention; Land based and planetary health solutions; Healing from trauma and reducing addictions; Enhancing wellbeing and eliminating suicide; and Translating Indigenous knowledges data to practice and policy. An Elders steering committees will govern the network. An Indigenous knowledges framework for mental health service and policy will be developed and results will have national and international impact for future generations toward ending Indigenous mental illness.

column36: Kishaadigeh: Indigenous Self Determination through Research for our Future Generations - Manitoba NEIHR
column37: Indigenous Peoples and communities have a long, often challenging relationship around research. In recent years, these relationships have healed and many communities and organizations have become leaders around self-determination in research. At the same time, Indigenous health researchers, many of whom are Indigenous women, have become emboldened and armored with ethical and effective approaches to Indigenous health research fostered by a growing network of scholars. This proposal, entitled Kishaadigeh, or "she who guards the lodge" is led primarily by Indigenous scholars, mostly women and Indigenous organizations who have a long history of being supported by and participating in the ACADRE/NEAHR programs. Due in part to the success of the ACADRE/NEAHR programs, Indigenous health scholars are now flourishing across campuses and in Indigenous organizations as the leaders and the ones who "guard the lodge". In many of our Indigenous communities, we see the responsibilities of "guarding of the lodge" as also guarding our stories and knowledge, a role often undertaken by women. The Manitoba NEIHR will develop a pathway for existing and upcoming Indigenous scholars (both men and women) to work with Indigenous organizations to clear the path for self-determination over research resulting in meaningful engagement that is ethical and impactful. The Manitoba NEIHR grant develop research lodges at the Indigenous community level with four Indigenous organizations which includes the First Nations Health and Social Secretariat of Manitoba (FNHSSM), the Manitoba Association for Friendship Centres (MAC), the Manitoba Inuit Association (MIA), and Aboriginal Youth Opportunities (AYO). The Manitoba NEIHR will ensure that the Indigenous partner organizations are resourced and supported by a regional and national network to develop and lead their own research priorities, in partnership with academic researchers functioning in a supportive role.

column36: A proposal for a Network Environment for Indigenous Health Research in Nunavut
column37: For almost 15 years our organizations have been implementing community-led research through Inuit-governed non-profit research centres, and we are ready to elevate our research models, methodological approaches, and mentorship capacity to the next level. The Qaujigiartiit Health Research Centre is putting forth this proposal on behalf of our collective of 4 Inuit-governed community-led independent Nunavut-based organizations that are leading research in various areas. Our unifying approach is that research should be used as a tool for action in our communities. Research for the sake of curiosity is not supported by our communities. Without action, there is no research. The Nunavut NEIHR will be a centre of excellence for Inuit methods, approaches, and tools, and provide training and support to the next generation of Inuit students and scholars in Nunavut. Each of the 4 'hubs' identified in this proposal are leaders in research and interventions that build on Inuit pathways to wellbeing. By coming together under the rubric of the NEIHR, we will elevate that research and these approaches to a national and international level. We will also formally coordinate and share our capacity and infrastructure to foster a learning environment for Inuit scholarship that will be unparalleled in Canada. With regard to feasibility: Since our inception, we have brought Inuit research methods into the forefront of discourse pertaining to Inuit health, and we have collectively brought more than 25 million dollars into the territory to strengthen the capacity of our communities to lead research. Qaujigiartiit, as the host institution, has a demonstrated record of excellence in the management of federal monies for the purposes of research and training, has an independent ethics review board, and has the administrative capacity to oversee the NEIHR.

Our network's Indigenous leaders are the Metis Nation-Saskatchewan, Federation of Sovereign Indigenous Nations, Saskatchewan Association of Friendship Centres, the Northern Inter-tribal Health Authority, the Office of the Treaty Commissioner, and Saskatchewan's Indigenous postsecondary institutes. The structure of our NEIHR supports First Nations and Metis partnerships with university researchers to develop diverse and innovative health/wellness research, training and KM programs.

column36: Assessing the impact of residential care on the quality of life of autistic adults
column37: Research shows that approximately one third of the autism spectrum (AS) also has intellectual disability (ID) and important behavioural challenges. Once grown up, families are facing many challenges due to insufficient or inadequate services. Residential care is an important component of quality of life, yet there is still very few autistic-adapted residential programs and limited research on the evolution of autistic adults through these programs. The limitations related to their condition (e.g. language and communication impairment) make it even more challenging to evaluate their quality of life. In collaboration with the CISSS Monteregie-Ouest and the Vero & Louis Foundation, the aim of the current project is to assess the impact of an autistic-adapted residential program on the quality of life of adults with autism and complex comorbidities. In this longitudinal study, the goal is to explore whether autistic adults benefit from an autistic-adapted residential program in regards to 1) their quality of life; 2) the trajectories of their behavioral problems and 3) their socio-emotional wellbeing. To do so, 40 adults with AS-ID will be followed for 6 months before their entry in an adapted home and 18 months after their integration. Multiple biological/physiological, functional and subjective measures will be collected at multiple time points. Their evolution will be compared to 40 adults still waiting for autistic-adapted residential care (staying at home or in a traditional program). We hope that this project will give a deeper understanding of quality of life in adults with autism, and more specifically of the ways in which environmental and individual components might interact.

column36: Peer Support: Evaluating a pilot program among homeless shelter users
column37: Access to shelters can be a matter of death or life for individuals experiencing homelessness or population at risk of becoming homeless. This population includes women fleeing domestic violence, runaway youth or even people in economic hardship among others. These people generally have many and varied needs to be addressed, and also face many barriers to return to their normal life, including exit homelessness. Providing quality basic services, including availability of counseling services, can play a major role in supporting the affected individuals. In perspective to improve the quality of services in Toronto shelters, the City of Toronto wants to test a New Shelter Services Model (NSSM) program that integrates a peer support approach into shelter-based services for people experiencing homelessness. Based on their own past shelter experience and their pathway to recovery, individuals will be trained and hired to provide counseling services and support in shelters. This peer support service aims at facilitating transition to stable housing and improving the well-being of shelter users. Based on the partnership agreement between the City of Toronto and MAP Centre for Urban Health Solutions, this study aims to evaluate rigorously the effects of this Peer Support approach on improving housing outcomes and recovery among homeless individuals. Hence, this research will contribute to the elaboration of evaluation design and elaboration, supporting data collection, and rigorous analysis. In addition, it will include particularly a gender-based analysis. We hypothesize that women, men, and non-binary people intersecting with diversity factors will experience peer support differently, and this may lead to different results. In sum, this study can lead to important evidence for a new avenue for shelter programs.

column36: Second mitochondrial activator of caspases (SMAC) Mimetics as novel HIV Latency Reversal Agents for HIV eradication
column37: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) suppresses HIV replication to undetectable levels. However, the persistence of latent viral reservoirs (VR) consisting majorly of CD4+ T cells and to some extent, macrophages allows for a rebound of viremia upon ART treatment interruption. Some of the most effective agents currently used in HIV treatment can reactivate cells that are latently infected with HIV by activating canonical/classical NF-kB pathway. But, these compounds are unable to clear out the reactivated cells and the effect is often associated with increased inflammation. Consequently, there is a need for novel therapeutics to eliminate/reduce the latent VR to achieve a stable remission of HIV. Cells that are latently infected with HIV are maintained in part by increased expression of inhibitors of apoptosis proteins, IAPs, these proteins are responsible for blocking caspase activities leading to prolonged cell survival. Second mitochondrial activator of caspases (SMAC) were shown to compromise cell survival by degrading IAPs. They further hijack host machinery and activate the non-canonical NF-kB pathway. This leads to the induction of cell death by activation of caspases. In this context, the current study is designed to investigate the effect of DIABLO/SMAC mimetic (SM) and particularly APG-1387, a novel SM developed primarily for cancer application as HIV latency reversing agent and to elucidate its mode of action and effect on viral reservoirs.

column36: The impact of loneliness on sexual behaviour among sexual minority men in Canada.
column37: Members of sexual minority groups, which include gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (GBM), experience homophobic stigma. This can lead to internalized homophobia and identity related stress, which are closely linked with difficulty forming social connections and fewer social supports. This leads, in turn, to increased loneliness. Among GBM, loneliness is associated with behaviours that increase risk for STIs/HIV (e.g., substance use and compulsive partner seeking). This likely contributes to the fact that GBM remain at more than 71 times greater risk for HIV compared to other men. Maladaptive coping strategies for loneliness, like substance use and hypersexual behaviour, not only increase an individual's risk for STI/HIV infection, but can impair and interfere with the development and maintenance of positive social relationships, leading to only fleeting relief from the symptoms of loneliness and isolation. There are two types of loneliness: emotional loneliness (longing for a partner or a close confidant) and social loneliness (longing for a larger social network). However, the distinct impact of these two types is loneliness among GBM is not yet understood. It is also unknown whether GBM who experience loneliness may be using other means to protect themselves when engaging in ostensibly risky sex (i.e., condomless anal sex with multiple partners). Understanding more specifically how loneliness may be associated with risky sex, as well as with the uptake and adherence of biomedical HIV prevention (i.e., using HIV medications to prevent transmission) is another key component to developing effective STI/HIV prevention. Thus, the aims of my proposed project are to (1) understand which types of loneliness (emotional vs. social) are more important for STI/HIV risk and prevention behaviours among GBM. (2) Investigate whether biomedical HIV prevention plays a mitigating role in GBM's loneliness-related sexual risk taking.

column36: Defining the pre-inflammatory changes of gut microbiome, metabolome, and host proteome associated with the development of Crohn's disease in healthy first-degree relatives of Crohn's disease patients
column37: Crohn's disease (CD) affects more than 135,000 individuals in Canada, with numbers increasing globally, and is characterized by chronic relapsing inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract. The condition has been suggested to be the result of a complex interplay among host genetics, gut microbes and environmental factors. However, so far most studies were based on comparing the patients of established disease with healthy subjects. These patients are heterogeneous (different) in nature in terms of their disease duration, location, and activity, and the use of medication, which makes it challenging to determine the underlying causes that triggers the disease. The Genetic, Environmental, and Microbial (GEM) Project is the largest prospective study that is attempting to define the cause of CD by recruiting 'at risk' healthy subjects. Among the 5000 healthy first-degree relatives of CD patients recruited, 82 went on to develop CD during up to a 10 years' time span. In addition, a fecal calprotectin (FC) test, a measure of gut inflammation, was performed in these subjects. A fifth of the subjects had an evidence of inflammation despite no symptoms, according to this test. In an attempt to identify 'pre-inflammatory' changes of gut microbes, we specifically investigated the subset of the cohort who had normal FC levels at recruitment (80% of the cohort including 20 subjects who develop CD). Strikingly, we found a difference in the composition of bacterial microbes in stool between those who develop CD and those who remain healthy, even when there was no evidence of gut inflammation. Our project aims to perform a detailed analysis to identify the specific microbial members, functions of the microbes, and products of the host/microbes (metabolites/proteins) that are associated with the onset of CD and further integrate the findings to define the key signatures of the 'pre-inflammatory phase' of CD. Our results will lead to future intervention studies aiming to prevent CD.

column36: The role of mucosa-associated proteolytic bacteria in Crohn's disease
column37: Crohn's disease (CD) is a chronic condition of the gut characterized by patches of inflammation, leaving other areas unaffected. Its cause is unknown, and it is not clear why some areas of the bowel are affected, and others are spared. We have previously shown that patients with CD have different mucosa-associated bacteria than patients in remission and healthy controls. We also showed that inflamed areas of the gut are leaky than in spared areas, and bacteria are in closer contact with the bowel lining. We propose that the patchy nature of CD is due to the local production of bacterial molecules (called proteases) that can damage host tissues and induce inflammation. To investigate this, we will study patients with active CD and collect gut tissue samples (biopsy during colonoscopy) from inflamed and non-inflamed areas. We will identify bacteria that produce proteases and test their capacity to damage the gut lining in mouse models. The results could discover new treatments for CD based on the inhibition of bacterial proteases.

column36: Protease-activated receptor (PAR)-2: A novel effector of mucosal healing in inflammatory bowel diseases.
column37: The inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, are chronic, relapsing and remitting diseases affecting ~250,000 Canadians. The cause of IBD is unknown and current drug therapies are often ineffective, have serious side effects or are very expensive. The intestinal lining (called the epithelium) is damaged in IBD and the process of epithelial healing is key to the resolution of disease to prevent activation of the gut's immune system by bacteria and other constituents of the gut lumen. We contend that targeting this epithelial repair process represents a novel therapeutic adjunct to drugs that target the immune system. In particular, we need to understand the cellular mechanisms triggered by inflammation that activate repair pathways to drive re-epithelialization during mucosal healing. During inflammation, there is an increase in proteases (enzymes that degrade proteins) within the lamina propria, and these would come in contact with the surface of epithelial cells. These cells express a unique class of receptor, called protease-activated receptors (PARs) could provide a means by which proteases could alter epithelial behaviour. The MacNaughton lab has generated preliminary data to support the hypothesis that activation of one if these PARs, PAR2, drives a pro-healing program in the injured or inflamed epithelium, and that this program is critical to the healing process. Testing this hypothesis will be the theme of my work in the MacNaughton lab and has the potential to uncover new pathways that could be the targets for novel therapeutic approaches to IBD. We will use a new technique whereby we can grow "mini-guts" from pieces of tissue obtained from consenting patients during colonoscopy. In the lab, we can injury these mini-guts and then test to see if activation of PAR2 enhances healing. A further aim of the project will be to determine the cellular processes that mediate this effect.

column36: The fabric of the primate neocortex and the origin of mental representations. From transcriptomics to single neurons and neuronal networks.
column37: Mental representations are at the essence of high-level cognition. They allow us to memorize information for a matter of seconds and use it or are erased in the near future. Mental representations that are independent from sensory and motor signals are thought to arise in primates with the development of the prefrontal cortex. It has been speculated that the same features of the neocortex that allow mental representations to reach its high level of abstraction in humans are the key to our knowledge of mental diseases such as Schizophrenia and other psychosis where mental representations and reality become intermingled. This proposal studies the specializations that allow primates to generate mental representations with these qualities. We study primate brains across species at multiple levels, from molecules to single neurons to networks. Finally, we elaborate on a theoretical and computational model of the primate neocortex that explains at a mechanistic level how mental representations arise and have evolved across species. We pooled the efforts of an international team, USA, Germany and Canada, of experts in different disciplines organized into four International Research Groups (IRGs). IRG1 study mental representations in behaving primates and record the activity of hundreds of neurons during naturalistic tasks. It also manipulates the receptors and chemical systems of the brain to investigate essential mechanisms and their functioning during behavior. IRG2 investigates how neurons fire, their morphology, their connectivity profiles and their chemical regulation in brain slices providing a microscopic picture of brain circuits. IRG3 investigates mRNA and protein expression in different cell types across the brain of different species of primates. column36: NEURONEX: The fabric of the primate neocortex and the origin of mental representations. From transcriptomics to single neurons and neuronal networks.
column37: Mental representations are at the essence of high-level cognition. They allow us to memorized information for a matter of seconds and use it or erased in the near future. Mental representations that are independent from sensory and motor signals are thought to arise in primates with the development of the prefrontal cortex. It has been speculated that the same features of the neocortex that allow mental representations to reach its high level of abstraction in humans are the key to our knowledge of mental diseases such as Schizophrenia and other psychosis where mental representations and reality become intermingled. This proposal studies the specializations that allow primates to generate mental representations with these qualities. We study primate brains across species at multiple levels, from molecules to single neurons to networks. Finally, we elaborate on a theoretical and computational model of the primate neocortex that explains at a mechanistic level how mental representations arise and have evolved across species. We pooled the efforts of an international team, USA, Germany and Canada, of experts in different disciplines organized into four International Research Groups (IRGs). IRG1 study mental representations in behaving primates and record the activity of hundreds of neurons during naturalistic tasks. It also manipulates the receptors and chemical systems of the brain to investigate essential mechanisms and their functioning during behavior. IRG2 investigates how neurons fire, their morphology, their connectivity profiles and their chemical regulation in brain slices providing a microscopic picture of brain circuits. IRG3 investigates protein expression in different neuron types across the brain of different species of primates. IRG4 uses modelling tools to synthesize the knowledge of all the other groups and produce a comprehensive picture with mechanistic insight into the functioning of mental representations in the primate brain.

column36: Phylogenetically informed models of human immunodeficiency virus latent reservoirs in individuals on combination antiretroviral therapy
column37: Human immunodeficiency virus or HIV, the cause of acquired immune deficiency syndrome or AIDS, continues to contribute to a widespread epidemic in Canada and the world. Although HIV infection can be managed during the full normal lifespan of infected individuals with combination antiretroviral therapies, these therapies cannot cure HIV infection because of the presence of "latent" HIV integrated into the individual's cells that the drugs cannot target. Elimination of each copy of HIV in an individual is necessary for HIV cure, since latent HIV in the latent reservoir can "wake up" at any time to restart the infection. However, there are many gaps in the understanding of latent HIV; it is currently contested whether the latent reservoir is continuously added to throughout the course of infection or whether reservoir contribution is concentrated to a specific period of infection and whether HIV is truly latent on therapy or if there are low levels of replication is still unclear. HIV's fast mutation rate and short life cycle "stamp" the viruses with measurable signatures of evolution. I plan to exploit the virus' evolutionary patterns by developing methods to learn from the virus including: a computer simulation of the latent reservoir, a phylogenetic dating technique that uses the evolutionary relationships of the viruses to infer when the viruses entered the reservoir and an advanced statistical (Bayesian) method that models the migration of HIV throughout the body. With these methods I will glean information on the timing of HIV integration into the latent reservoir, locations and pathways used by latent HIV and whether or not there is ongoing replication in the presence of therapy. Since every copy of HIV must be eliminated to cure HIV including in the latent reservoir, it is important to accurately understand the dynamics of the reservoir. A cure for HIV will eliminate transmission of HIV from cured individuals and will be a significant asset to end the pandemic.

column36: The Cedar Project: Healing-centered care for urban Indigenous young people who use drugs in British Columbia
column37: Background: Colonialism weakened cultural buffers that traditionally helped Indigenous people cope with stress. Historical and intergenerational trauma (complex trauma) are passed down through generations of Indigenous families and communities and can lead to health challenges like higher chance of HIV and HCV transmission. Evidence suggests high numbers of Indigenous young people are impacted by complex trauma. The ways the mind, body and spirit react to trauma have been linked to negative health outcomes for people who use drugs, but traditional resources are known to help manage these challenges. There is a shortage of research in Canada that looks at complex trauma in urban Indigenous young people who use drugs, and positive action interventions that are built with culture. My research will support a land-based positive action intervention that is connected to culture and focused on healing complex trauma experienced by urban Indigenous young people who use drugs. Objectives: 1) Search the literature for important elements of interventions for complex trauma among urban Indigenous young people who use drugs; 2) find factors that protect against negative health outcomes among participants in the Cedar Project through survey data analysis; 3) map wise practices in response to complex trauma among health organizations in urban areas; 4) Engage with young people and elders through ceremony to explore Indigenous perspectives on harm reduction and positive action. Methods: An Indigenous approach is needed to help build an intervention for complex trauma among Indigenous young people who use drugs. The Cedar Project is an ongoing CIHR-funded cohort study that monitors HIV and HCV among 600-1000 Indigenous young people aged 14-30 who use drugs in Vancouver and Prince George, BC. I will co-design my study, including a protocol for integrated knowledge translation, in collaboration with participants, community members and knowledge keepers.

column36: Assessing the impact of bloodborne infections and treatment on non-communicable chronic diseases in a population-based cohort
column37: Despite advances in prevention, care and treatment, many people around the world and in Canada suffer from bloodborne infections (BBIs) caused by hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). These infections are not only directly linked to detrimental health outcomes, but are also linked to chronic diseases such as diabetes, chronic kidney disease and cardiovascular diseases. The advance in infection care and management has prolonged the life expectancy of people with chronic infections, and in turn, they are now at higher risk of other chronic diseases and complications. Social and health conditions can also accelerate disease progression in people living with BBIs. Currently, the knowledge on the impact of these infections on chronic diseases is limited. The evidence is especially scarce in population-based data accounting for other health, social and environmental factors. This project aims to study the impact of HBV, HCV and HIV mono- and co-infections on diabetes, chronic kidney disease and cardiovascular diseases, accounting for social and health conditions. Furthermore, new highly effective and well-tolerated drugs called direct-acting antiviral agents are expected to provide a protective effect in people living with chronic hepatitis C. The project will look at the real-world impact of this drug on reducing the risk of chronic diseases. This study will use a large population-based data including over 2 million individuals tested for HBV, HCV and HIV in British Columbia (BC), BC Hepatitis Testers Cohort. The cohort is linked with other databases such as chronic disease registry, medical visits, hospitalizations, drug prescriptions and vital statistics. Using this data will allow a comprehensive understanding of the impact of chronic HBV, HCV and HIV infections. Ultimately, the findings of this study will help to create targeted care and disease management strategies for people living with chronic infections.

column36: Addressing Communication Barriers in Clinical Encounters between Health Care Providers and Pregnant People with Obesity
column37: Physiological health risks often accompany obesity, in addition to psychosocial challenges due to weight-related stigma, including in the healthcare setting. Over 14 million people worldwide have obesity in pregnancy, which elevates the risk of a multitude of severe adverse outcomes for both mother and baby, in the short and long term. It is essential that these risks are communicated to patients, to ensure they are aware of any differences in care and the poor outcomes that may ensue. However, there is evidence suggesting a communication divide between providers and patients, as well as a distance between them in their understanding and approaches to obesity, complicated by stigmatizing attitudes amongst professionals. Given the health implications of unproductive clinical encounters and the difficulties facing this population, we seek to explore and improve the obesity-in-pregnancy clinical encounter through qualitative methodologies. Informed by narrative inquiry and stigma theory, we will conduct individual interviews to attain a greater understanding of stakeholder narratives that shape this clinical encounter, by elucidating patients' and providers' past experiences concerning communication of excess weight and associated risks. We then will implement the Brokered Dialogue to catalyze movement towards bridging the apparent divide between providers and patients in obesity-in-pregnancy care, in which we will provide a platform for stakeholders to share ideas and concerns with each other on the topic without in-person communication, using film as the arts-based research tool. We aim to devise strategies for clinicians to appropriately counsel on risks in obese pregnancies, and seek to enable stakeholders to understand the complex perspectives behind obesity in healthcare; both in management and the living with it. The final Brokered Dialogue film will be applied to a variety of settings namely for advocacy, clinical and research translational purposes.

column36: Translating milk pharmacokinetic data into infant plasma level prediction: an application of population pharmacokinetics and infant physiologically-based population pharmacokinetic models to predict drug exposure to breastfeeding infants
column37: Breastfeeding protects the mother and infant against a wide range of diseases and promotes infant development. A staggering 13.8% of all deaths of children <2 years old (823,000 deaths/year) could be prevented if all infants breastfed. Although the choice to breastfeed is clear, mothers taking medication often make a decision not to breastfeed and affect infant health, or to stop taking drug therapy and consequently affect maternal health. A main contributor to this mother-infant health problem is the lack of pharmacokinetic (movement of drugs in the body) information of drug secretion into breast milk and resultant levels of the drug in infant blood. This information is needed for risk assessments and clinical recommendations but is hard to attain as lactating women and infants are typically excluded from the drug development process. Mothers needing to give multiple milk samples on a strict timeline is a main barrier. To overcome this challenge, I am working with SickKids clinical collaborators to be the first to combine two mathematical modeling strategies: population milk-pharmacokinetic and infant physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling, which we coin the "miPBPK approach". This approach allows mothers the flexibility to give milk samples at convenient times. My research is to develop the population milk-PK models to provide dose information for input into the infant PBPK models, and predict drug exposure to infants with the resulting miPBPK models for our study drugs. As such, the goal of my project is to predict how much of the drug may appear in infant blood to help inform breastfeeding decisions. As an impact, new knowledge predicting low risk of a drug to infants may support mothers to breastfeed and continue their therapy, leading to improved maternal and infant health outcomes. This new study framework has potential to guide the design of future mother and infant risk assessment studies in drug development and post-market settings.

column36: Transfer of Sinonasal Microbiota from a Healthy Donor to Treat Refractory Chronic Rhinosinusitis in Recipient Patient, A Prospective Safety and Efficacy Study
column37: Patients with chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) have chronic inflammation located in the paranasal sinuses. This causes symptoms such as congestion, difficulty breathing, pain, pressure, and reduced sense of smell and taste. CRS can occur when the sinuses become blocked and filled with fluid and cause a sinus infection. Research has shown that persistent bacterial infection and bacterial biofilm formation, which is a collective of microorganisms that grow on surfaces, can be found in patients with reoccurring CRS. Current methods for treating CRS have been largely unsuccessful and could potentially lead to increased antimicrobial resistance. An imbalance in the bacteria, called dysbiosis, is linked to diseases like CRS. The community of bacteria in the sinuses, called the sinonasal microbiome, can become disrupted in patients. Sinonasal microbiota transplant (SNMT) is a new proposed therapy and the mechanism is not known. We hypothesize that SNMT, which is transferring healthy microorganisms from a healthy donor to the sinus cavity of a patient, could be a new and advanced form of therapy for CRS patients. It would work by re-colonising the diseased sinus cavities with healthy donor microbiota, thereby producing a newly intact and functional microbiota. We would like to investigate whether SNMT will change the microbiota of CRS patients, thereby preventing recurrence of sinus infections. We will assess clinical parameters of the patients to assess safety of SNMT and assess efficacy of SNMT by characterizing the microbiome. If this SNMT approach is successful, this could result in new treatment options for patients with CRS. CRS is known to be debilitating and patients suffer with chronic symptoms and complications. This could provide relief of symptoms, reduce disease burden, and help improve their quality of life.

column37: Helicobacter pylori (HP) is a bacterium that infects chronically up to 50% of the world's population and can cause gastric ulcers and cancers. It was estimated that HP colonization increases the risk of gastric cancer approximately 10-fold. In 2012, gastric cancer was the 5th most malignant cancer. Because of its high prevalence and the severity of the diseases, HP significantly burdens the health care system. Effectively treating HP infections is key to prevent these serious diseases but current treatments are cumbersome, poorly tolerated by patients, and jeopardized by antibiotic resistance. Thus, we are looking for alternatives. Upon detection of HP, the patient's immune system is activated and produces inflammatory molecules that are supposed to help eliminate the bacterium but also cause collateral damage to the surrounding gastric tissue. Unfortunately, HP can alter the normal function of the immune system so that, despite activation of the inflammatory response, the bacterium cannot be eliminated from the body. As the immune system persists in trying to eliminate the bacterium, the constant production of inflammatory compounds by the immune system damages the gastric tissue and favors ulcer formation or cancer development. Our approach is to study proteins produced by HP that trigger the inflammatory reaction in gastric and immune cells. Preventing the secretion or activity of these proteins should help the immune system regain control and clear the infection. Our study will determine the role of these proteins in inflammation using different types of cells, and will identify protein(s) from gastric cells that our proteins interacts with to perturb the normal function of gastric cells. This could be used to design new therapeutics that can inhibit the interaction between these bacterial proteins and their gastric cell targets. The inhibitors, used alone or in combination with existing treatments, should significantly improve outcomes of anti-HP therapies.
