column36: Host response modulation results in altered Ebola virus replication and transcription kinetics in immune-privileged testis, which facilitates asymptomatic and persistent infections that may affect reproductive health and sexual transmission
column37: The current Ebola virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has resulted in more than 2,900 infections and 1,900 fatalities, with no end in sight. This outbreak is already the second largest in history; the largest only ended three years ago after causing 11,000 fatalities in West Africa. It appears that Ebola virus disease outbreaks are occurring more frequently and with increasing complexity, taking longer to resolve and affecting more people than ever before. Improved epidemiological surveillance, community outreach, and Ebola virus vaccines and therapeutics are being implemented to combat the current outbreak, yet new infections continue to occur. Efforts to respond to Ebola virus disease outbreaks are complicated because Ebola virus persists in the reproductive tracts of male disease survivors after recovery. Persistent Ebola virus disease infections can last for years, are not detectable in blood samples, and occur in the absence of disease symptoms. Critically, the virus can be transmitted sexually from these survivors, which leads to new chains of transmission and increases the duration and magnitude of outbreaks. In an era where globalization has enabled rapid mass movement of people over long distances, persistent and undetected Ebola virus infections could lead to global outbreaks. Despite the danger that persistent Ebola virus infections pose to public health, these infections are not well characterized; why are there no associated disease symptoms or abnormalities in the afflicted reproductive tract, how does the virus persist so long, and what danger does the virus pose during persistence? My goal is to determine how Ebola virus persists in the male reproductive tract, what effect this has on reproductive health, and how frequently sexual transmission occurs. This study will aid in development of therapeutics for persistent EVD infections and limit the risk that male survivors pose to their families and community.

Our diverse study team will determine how parents and youth are currently using cannabis products in cancer and what the reason for use is. C4T will review the literature and conduct a real-world study with children with cancer who are already using cannabis to try and establish a dose-response. C4T will use this information to create educational tools for doctors, youth and parents as well as to develop large scale studies to test the benefits and safety of medical cannabis products for children compared with existing treatments/standard of care. There is a large knowledge gap on if and when cannabis products can be used safely by children with cancer and other chronic health conditions. To ensure people can use our findings, we will create and update an online resource hut that is accessible to the public. Our research team is well equipped to fill this knowledge gap and continue to conduct high-quality research on cannabis for a variety of health conditions in children.

column36: Enterovirus subversion of the autophagy pathway
column37: Enteroviruses (EVs) are common human pathogens associated with a broad spectrum of diseases, including various neurological disorders, such as poliomyelitis, aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, and non-polio flaccid paralysis, particularly in infants and children worldwide. Autophagy is a "self-eating" process in cells by which cells recycle damaged proteins and/or cell parts, called organelles. Autophagy is an important cellular response to limit viral growth and further infection. However, increasing evidence suggests that this pathway can be "hijacked" by EVs to ensure their successful infection of host cells. We discovered that EV infection disrupts the normal process of autophagy, resulting in enhanced viral replication/release and impaired clearance of damaged proteins that clump together and are toxic to the cells. We further showed that several proteins involved in the regulation of autophagy are broken down upon viral infection through the action of virus-encoded proteins. Despite the demonstrated importance of autophagy in EV infections, the exact mechanism by which EVs subvert this pathway and the functional significance of the resulting protein breakdown remain largely unclear. In addition, the possible value of autophagy-based anti-EV inhibitors has not been studied. column36: Maternal-infant dyad health outcomes: infant neurodevelopment in the context of maternal cannabis use - a prospective cohort study
column37: In October 2018, recreational cannabis became legal in Canada; before then medical use was legal. Babies are exposed to cannabis their mothers use during pregnancy and through breastmilk. Research-informed information for parents and families is scarce and pregnant women receive mixed messages around the safety of cannabis. The Canadian government recommends avoiding it since there is no known safe level to use during pregnancy. Exposures have a higher risk of causing permanent health changes in growing and developing babies. Long term outcomes of cannabis exposure are not known. Some teens who use cannabis have permanent brain changes and an increased risk of mental health problems. Much less is known about second-hand cannabis exposure, especially in young children. We do not know whether cannabis smoke exposes children to biologically significant levels of cannabis. This study will follow women from early pregnancy until their babies are 18 months old. Mothers will report if, when and how they use cannabis. Their sleep, activity, mental and physical health and the baby's birth, development, behavior and health will be monitored, including a formal assessment at 18 months. The family will use an air quality monitor and passive environmental samplers for mothers and babies. They will also complete an environmental assessment. Breastmilk and urine will be tested for cannabis to see if babies absorb cannabis used by mothers. Passive sampler analyses will provide evidence of other exposures that could confuse the picture, like tobacco smoke and air pollution. Sleep and mood are related and impact development, so maternal and infant sleep will be monitored. Cannabis, used medically and for recreation, presents potential risks and benefits to expectant mothers and families. This study will provide valuable information to help families make informed choices about cannabis and set the stage for future research on the long term effects of cannabis exposure on children.

column36: Impact of Cannabis Use on Indigenous Peoples' Oral Health
column37: The legalization of non-medical cannabis in 2018 has raised many questions about the health effects associated with the drug's use. For instance, emerging evidence associates smoking cannabis with several oral diseases, including oral cancers. However, the effects of cannabis use on the oral health of Indigenous youth and adults are unknown. This study addresses stakeholder priorities and the impact increased cannabis use has on the already disproportionate burden of illness borne by Indigenous Peoples. Self-identified cannabis users and non-users, ages 18 to 44 years, will be recruited from partnering Indigenous communities and neighboring non-Indigenous communities, with each group followed for three years. Baseline and yearly comprehensive oral health examinations will be conducted by calibrated dentists. Saliva samples will be collected to monitor salivary constituents. Saliva and urine analyses will assess cannabis exposure. Non-invasive sensory tests will measure pain sensitivity in the orofacial region. Oral health outcomes will include: oral mucosal lesions, periodontitis, dental caries, changes in oral microbial composition, and abnormal sensory function. We hypothesize cannabis use in Indigenous and non-Indigenous populations is associated with: 1) a shift in the oral inflammatory signature that promotes the progression of pre-malignant lesions to oral cancers; 2) a distinctive salivary bacterial fingerprint; 3) a shift in the proteins in saliva reflecting a higher incidence of periodontitis and early-stage oral cancers, and; 4) oral and facial somatosensory changes dependent on drug use. The Indigenous Learning Circle model will be used throughout to share knowledge around the oral health risks of cannabis consumption and the drug's impact on Indigenous communities. The Circles will also be used to evaluate the research outcomes through the lens of the community so as to inform policy and recommend measures that promote cessation and harm reduction.

column37: Recreational cannabis is legal in Canada since October 2018. Based on Colorado's experience, the first U.S. state to have legalized recreational cannabis in 2014, effects on Canadians' health are to be expected including: 1) increased recreational cannabis use; and 2) increased risk of traumatic injuries. Traumatic injuries are associated with an increased risk of chronic pain especially when peripheral orthopedic injuries (i.e., bone fracture) are combined with mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Following a traumatic injury, opioid therapy is common despite the high risk of addiction/misuse/diversion as there is no other alternative to relieve severe pain. In parallel, cannabidiol (CBD) is emerging as a potent anti-inflammatory agent extracted from the cannabis plant which could promote pain relief and reduce opioid use after traumatic injuries. However, the low quality of clinical evidence on the safety and action mechanisms of CBD along with the lack of knowledge on interactions with opioids contribute to physicians' hesitation to adopt CBD as a regular therapeutic tool to relieve pain symptoms. The ongoing opioid crisis coupled with cannabis legalization in Canada therefore calls for an intersectoral strategy aiming to determine the potential of cannabinoids as co-analgesic agents for the treatment of pain, especially in vulnerable multi-trauma patients. To this end, expertise from 5 Canadian universities and a patient-expert partnership have led to an action plan with 4 main deliverables providing: 1) The first clinical assessment of the therapeutic potential of CBD for acute pain alleviation after multi-trauma; 2) A long-term assessment of CBD treatment effects on pain symptoms and trauma outcomes; 3) Using animal models of multi-trauma, assessment of interaction between CBD treatment and factors contributing to pain symptoms; 4) Scientific & clinical knowledge transfer strategy tailored to the needs of patients, practitioners, and key stakeholders.

column36: Cannabis-based precision medicine for osteoarthritis therapy
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a leading cause of disability, in part due to a lack of effective treatment options. Cannabis offers a potential treatment for OA, however, little research has been done on this topic. Cannabinoids are the main active components in cannabis. The most abundant cannabinoids are delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), and cannabidiol (CBD). There are many causes and types of OA, so it is likely that any therapeutic (or harmful) effect of cannabis will vary based on characteristics of the patient, and levels of cannabinoids in the cannabis strain used. We propose to study the characteristics of the patient and of the cannabis that predict how well cannabis works for treating OA. First, we will do studies in mice that have OA to examine the effect of different cannabinoids on different types of OA. Specifically, we will measure the effect of THC, CBD, and THC+CBD on mice's pain, motor function and cognitive functions. Second, we will collect joint tissue and blood samples from patients undergoing knee surgery to measure whether the tissues respond to each type of cannabinoid. We will also identify traits in the patient's tissue and blood that predict whether their tissue will respond to cannabinoids. Third, we will carry out a study in patients with OA who use cannabis to manage their OA symptoms. We will measure each patient's daily pain scores, OA type, traits in their blood, and the concentration of CBD and THC from a sample of their cannabis. We will test whether each of these pieces of information predict a patient's pain scores. Our research could create evidence for or against using cannabinoids for treating OA symptoms. These results may help physicians and patients to decide whether a patient might benefit from cannabis and the type and dose of cannabis that might work best for the patient.

column36: Canadian Cannabis and Psychosis Research Team (CCPRT)
column37: While Cannabis is considered a relatively safe psychoactive substance, cannabis-related psychosis risk is a significant public health concern, for which no evidence-based screening or intervention strategies exist. Psychosis often follows heavy cannabis use, particularly if use starts early and is sustained during adolescence. Research also suggests that some individuals, those with genetic and psychosocial risk markers, are more susceptible to cannabis-induced psychosis. What is not known is how to identify and protect individuals at risk of cannabis-related psychosis from such harm. The current team joins genetics experts with clinical and pre-clinical researchers to optimise their research on the neurodevelopmental consequences of adolescent cannabis exposure to answer the following questions in relation to psychosis: What features of cannabis exposure (e.g. cumulative amounts used, age of regular use, sex differences) are more or less harmful? Do reliable biomarkers exist that will predict who is most at risk? Is there a role for targeted and/or early intervention strategies to reduce the cognitive and mental health burden of cannabis? What are the most promising intervention approaches to reduce cannabis-induced psychosis? Our research team will collaborate on an integrated research program that spans animal studies, genetics studies, longitudinal developmental and clinical cohorts, big-data analytics and prevention. All participants will mutually benefit from data-pooling activities and a translational research framework, resulting in exceptional data output and knowledge for the public. The databases and knowledge generated by this team will be of high value to the clinical networks represented within the team (e.g., Canadian Consortium on Early Intervention on Psychosis), who currently seek guidance on how to manage potential cognitive and mental health consequences of cannabis use in their patients.

column36: Pharmacotherapeutic effects of cannabidiol (CBD) in autism spectrum disorder (ASD)
column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is characterized by symptoms such as reduced social communication and interactions, repetitive behaviors and deficits in interests or activities. ASD arises from alterations in brain development that manifest from an early age. Recent studies suggest that the endocannabinoid system, a major regulator of behavioral functions in the brain, could be a viable target for ASD treatment. Cannabidiol (CBD) is a safe and non-mind altering plant based cannabinoid proposed to relieve several psychiatric illnesses including psychosis, addiction, obsessive compulsion, and anxiety related disorders. There is high interest for CBD's potential for treating ASD associated symptoms in patients; however, the information on how CBD works in the body, its effectiveness, dosing regime and clinical information remains limited. The objective of this project will be to investigate the therapeutic effects of CBD for treating symptoms associated with ASD. Notably, ASD is 4 times more prevalent in males than females. Although some of the differences in diagnosis may arise from societal biases, there are biological factors that contribute to the resilience in females. This study will investigate both autistic mouse models and human patients from both sexes to establish whether they respond similarly to CDB treatment. Overall, this work will broaden our understanding of the effects of CBD on ASD and potentially support the implementation of clinical strategies to alleviate symptoms associated with this neurological disorder in both sexes.

column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic disease that manifests as relapses and/or progression. Multiple disease-modifying treatments (DMTs) are available to control the disease process. Lesser progress has been achieved to treat the multiple symptoms that MS can cause. Persons with MS PwMS, especially after 10 or more years of disease course, are frequently afflicted by a combination of leg weakness with spasticity, neuropathic pains, fatigue, sphincteric dysfunction, sleep disruption, and mood and cognition impairment. These are treated by muscle relaxants, neurotransmitter agents, tricyclics, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and CNS stimulants. The efficacy of these agents, which are fraught with side effects and drug-drug interactions, is often partial. Up to 49% of persons with MS (PwMS), have used cannabis, mostly for mood enhancing, to improve sleep, relieve pain and spasticity. A THC-CBD spray has been approved in Canada in 2005 for symptom improvement in adult PwMS with moderate to severe spasticity who have not responded adequately to other anti-spasticity medications. Now that the use of cannabis is legalized in Canada, the patient and medical communities expect the establishment of evidence-based guidelines for the proper use of cannabis. We are proposing to assess the clinical effects of THC and CBD positive and negative, in a carefully selected cohort of PwMS with single or multiple symptoms, enrolled in a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blinded, parallel groups trial of four weeks' duration. The main outcomes will be spasticity, with pain, sleep, mood and cognition, fatigue, and sphincteric function as secondary outcomes. The pharmacology of THC-CBD, as well as their effects on neuro-inflammation, will be explored. PwMS will be involved in all phases of the proposed study.

column36: A First Nations Community Response to Support Recovery from Opioids: Integrating Cultural and Land-based Practices with Clinical Approaches
column37: Wikwemikong Unceded Territory is one of the largest and fastest-growing First Nation communities. The community has many thriving Anishinabe people, pristine waters and lands, strong language, culture, and heritage; but the consequences of centuries of colonial oppression are also present. The most serious health issue is the opioid crisis. It has resulted in social problems, chronic drug-related illnesses, mental health issues, family violence, loss of children into foster care, trafficking of women, crime, vandalism, and breakdown of the social fabric and relationships in the community. Tribal police estimate that for each addicted person there are ten family members whose health and mental health is affected by drug-related consequences. The community is proactive in addressing opioid use and there is a strong commitment to move away from a punitive approach. The community offers opioid agonist therapy (OAT) to treat these addictions. In the clinic, patients are supported with culturally based therapies and counseling. Our pilot research shows documented promising results associated with this community-owned, culturally safe approach, but it also emphasizes that more research is needed to identify promising practices. Our community-based, patient-engaged research will involve clients, family and community members in community-based solutions. We will work with Elders, knowledge keepers and clients in recovery to increase our understanding of the role of the land, Anishinabe language and worldview and their relationship to healing from opioid addiction. Research with providers across diverse sectors will create an Indigenous model of essential services for opioid recovery, and support the uptake results into policy, practice and service development. Finally, we will create access to robust health, social, and justice data sets and administrative data-bases in order to evaluate services, in order to empower the community to make knowledge-based decisions.

column37: Endocannabinoids are produced in neurones and interact with cannabinoid CB1 receptors to modulate a range of behaviours, including mood; the system can be over-active or underactive in certain diseases. Finally, we will examine the effects of our compounds on behaviours in two distinct animal models of hyperdopamine and models of liver injury. This program will allow us to develop, pharmacologically characterize and optimize a unique new class of CB1 molecules to determine the therapeutic potential to facilitate translation in the clinic.

column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a deadly disease with few therapy options. column36: Prevalence, Burden and Reversal of Stringent Response-Mediated Antibiotic Tolerance
column37: Bacterial infections are a leading cause of hospitalization and death worldwide. Antibiotics are central to our ability to treat bacterial infections, but our capacity to cure these infections is jeopardized by increasing antibiotic resistance (where bacteria are no longer killed by an antibiotic). Added to this, very few new antibiotics with activity against resistant bacteria are being discovered. Therefore, it is essential that we preserve the effective use of the antibiotics we have. Antibiotic tolerance is emerging as a precursor to resistance that also contributes to antibiotic treatment failures in its own right. Tolerance occurs when bacteria are still killed by antibiotics, but die slower than usual. This means that live bacteria remain at the end of a typical course of antibiotics, resulting in infections that are persistent and recurrent. Persistent infections are associated with higher healthcare costs and death rates than resolving infections. While antibiotic resistance is routinely screened for in clinical laboratories, there are currently no appropriate tests that can detect tolerance. Therefore, the prevalence and consequences of antibiotic tolerance in terms of treatment failures are unknown and likely under-appreciated. We propose to develop a simple screen to detect tolerance and apply it to libraries of bacterial isolates derived from patients with persistent infections, thereby illuminating the true magnitude of this threat to effective antibiotic therapy. We will also investigate one of the mechanisms behind tolerance with a view to understanding how we can reverse it and preserve the effectiveness of existing antibiotics. Our research will improve the treatment of persistent infections by providing physicians with a tool to detect tolerance, as well as practical information on which types of antibiotic are most effective against tolerant bacteria. By targeting antibiotic tolerance, we aim to tackle it before it develops into resistance.

column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Canada. Although significant efforts have been employed to understand the etiology of this cancer, the causes of this cancer is still unknown. Recent work has linked bacteria that reside in the gut to CRC, specifically, certain so-called "pathobionts", which are symbiotic members of the gut microbiota that can participate in disease under specific pathological conditions. Indeed, the list of pathobionts that cause CRC is growing, yet their oncogenic mechanisms are only beginning to be understood. To understand the role of the gut microbiota and pathobionts in CRC, we developed mice that harbor genetic mutations commonly associated with CRC. In addition, since inflammatory bowel diseases predispose to CRC, we have also developed mouse models of colitis-associated cancer. Using these mouse models, we show that certain pathobionts promote cancer by interacting with specific dietary factors, the immune system, or by exploiting mutations in specific genes involved in DNA repair. In short, our work is beginning to uncover the mechanisms by which pathobionts interact with specific etiologic factors to promote cancer. Using these animal models, we are now in position to dissect the mechanisms of how different factors promote CRC and develop protocols to reduce CRC incidence in pre-clinical models. We will leverage our expertise on DNA repair, microbiology, diet, and the immune system to explore the role of gut microbiota in CRC development. Our research has the potential to lead to the development of preventative protocols or therapeutics for CRC. In addition, our research has the capacity to develop diagnostics if certain pathobionts are identified to induce CRC under specific conditions. With this new knowledge, we will be in a good position to enable clinical trials to explore the use of antioxidants, or specific dietary interventions to prevent CRC.

column36: How the brain converts memory to knowledge during the resting state: a critical factor in age-related memory impairment
column37: According to a much investigated theory, most memories are initially stored as a set of synaptic links between a pattern of hippocampal (HC) activity (the 'index' code) and patterns of neocortical (NC) activity, which are distributed widely over NC modules that contain the actual 'attributes' of the memory. During quiet rest and slow-wave sleep (SWS), recently stored patterns are spontaneously reactivated in HC and this facilitates coherent reactivation of the NC attributes of the corresponding memory. In theory, during this coordinated 'replay' process, the NC extracts the gist of recent memories and modifies its connectivity weights to build up a knowledge representation structured to capture regularities in experience and to predict outcomes of situations and ones own actions within them. These internal representations subserve categorization of context-modulated inputs and the execution of, often arbitrary, motor acts that are mapped to these inputs. The foregoing provides a potential explanation for at least a considerable part of the effect of sleep deprivation and age-related sleep disturbance on memory function and the fact that disrupted resting state activity in amnesic mild cognitive impairment predicts more serious memory decline. The better the role of memory-related brain-dynamics during sleep is understood the more likely it will be that brain-interface related interventions can be developed to ameliorate learning and memory deficits. We propose to test a theoretically motivated hypothesis about how schema development and adjustment is furthered during sleep. Specifically, we will use closed-loop recording of brain activity and electrical stimulation in rodents to determine whether the association of HC and NC activation furthers encoding of new information, whereas similar activation of NC without HC reflects spontaneous refreshment of already acquired information, which may be necessary to prevent the old data from being overwritten by the new.

column36: Pulmonary vascular dysfunction and exercise in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
column37: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is a respiratory disorder commonly caused by smoking, and is characterized by breathlessness and exercise intolerance. During exercise, COPD patients are less efficient breathers, requiring them to breath more compared to individuals without COPD. This increased breathing increases the feeling of breathlessness and causes patients to stop exercising at lower intensities. Our grant will help determine why these COPD patients have inefficient breathing and get breathless during exercise. We think that these patients have problems exchanging fresh gas (i.e., oxygen) into the blood stream because of poor pulmonary blood vessel function. We will look to improve pulmonary blood vessel function and see if this improves the matching of blood flow and ventilation in the lung. We will then see if improving blood vessel function leads to better exercise capacity in more advanced disease. Finally, we will test whether an oral medication (sildenafil) can improve pulmonary blood vessel function and breathing efficiency. With this research, we will understand more about breathing efficiency, pulmonary vessel function and gas exchange in COPD patients, and find out whether improving pulmonary blood vessel function helps COPD patients breathe. Understanding the reasons behind the feeling of breathlessness may lead to more effective therapy and improved quality of life in COPD patients.

column36: Understanding the Interaction of Acute Myeloid Leukemia with the Bone Marrow Microenvironment: Elucidating New Therapeutic Targets Through In Vivo Imaging
column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a disease of the bone marrow (BM) that spreads throughout the bones of affected patients. Interactions between AML cells and its surroundings play important protective and promotive functions in leukemia growth, maintenance, and spread. Current laboratory experimental systems are not yet able to recapitulate this dynamic relationship outside of the body, and animal studies cannot visualize the changes in AML progression until death of the animal. Such methodologies are blind to important aspects of leukemia development and hinder the advancement of AML research. Our lab has developed a new technique, called the femur window chamber (FWC) model, that allows scientists to look directly into the bone of a living mouse and track the movements and/or changes of cells within the BM, over time. Our project will use this innovation to study AML cell biology and test the effect of various new anti-AML drugs. To do this, we will label AML cells with different colours and monitor their behaviour over time in the BM using the FWC. We seek to better understand the biological differences across AML subtypes and identify new treatments. We will also study the proteins that AML cells produce within the BM. If these proteins are found to be linked to certain disease subtypes or aggressiveness, this knowledge could help to better identify patients who would benefit from a specific 'personalized' treatment. Finally, we will use our unique FWC platform to study the effectiveness of various anti-AML drugs in real time and in the living mouse. Our goal is to uncover limitations in current therapies and find new treatment combinations that address vulnerabilities in AML biology to improve patient outcomes in the future. If successful, our project will establish an innovative new technique for leukemia research, uncover new knowledge surrounding AML biology, and help to develop new AML clinical trials.

column36: Exploring the role of a mitochondrial protein prohibitin in Leydig cell steroidogenesis
column37: Steroid hormones are essential to life. They regulate critical phases of development, such as puberty, and are essential for a number of key physiological functions in our body. Inadequate levels of steroid hormones are associated with a variety of diseases including infertility, hormone-dependent cancers (prostate, breast, ovarian), osteoporosis, and autoimmune and inflammatory diseases. The fundamental framework of steroidogenesis across major steroidogenic tissues is very similar. For example, cholesterol is the common starting material for all steroid hormones. Moreover, its transport to mitochondria (a cell compartment where steroidogenesis begins) within different steroidogenic cells and subsequent utilization for the initiation of steroidogenesis, including the male sex steroid hormone (testosterone) production by the testis, is similar. However, our understanding of this essential step of steroidogenesis remains unknown. Unraveling this may open new therapeutic opportunities for a wide variety of diseases that involved impaired steroidogenesis. Recently, my team has found that a protein called prohibitin, plays an important role in testosterone production, including the functional coupling of the crucial steps across mitochondrial membrane for the initiation of steroidogenesis. However, the mechanisms involved remain to be determined, which is the focus of this international collaborative research project. Research outcomes will advance our understanding of testosterone production by the testis, particularly the role that prohibitin plays, which is entirely unknown. The knowledge gained may create new opportunities to treat testosterone deficiency and related comorbidities.

column36: Oxidative stress in the endoplasmic reticulum and its impact on liver inflammation in an aging mouse model
column37: A recurrent theme associated with aging processes is an increase cellular oxidative stress. In addition, a chronic low-grade systemic inflammation occurring in the absence of infection has been defined as "inflammaging" and represents a significant risk factor for mortality in the elderly. There are specific inherited mutations that appear to accelerate aging in humans and Werner syndrome (WS) is an interesting example of premature aging. To understand how oxidative stress causes liver diseases that affects 20% of Canadians with age, we generated a mouse model with a mutation of the mouse Werner gene that recapitulates WS including liver diseases. These mice produce a mutant protein that ends up in the wrong place in cells causing a distress in a cellular component called Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER) in the liver tissue. Interestingly, treatments of such mice with vitamin C at weaning reverse all WS anomalies. The liver is an organ that plays a pivotal role in nutrient, drug, hormone, and metabolic waste product processing, thereby maintaining the normal function of other organs in the body. We found that the ER distress is caused by an abnormal increase in oxidative stress in this compartment. We thus hypothesize that a continuous oxidative ER stress causes a low but chronic inflammation in the liver of Werner mice. column36: Examining the long-term illness experiences of injured older adults to select patient-driven outcome measures in geriatric trauma
column37: Older adults (65 years and older) make up 51% of all injury hospitalizations in Canada. This number is expected to rise as the aging population surges in the coming years. The most common cause of unintentional physical injury in older adults is a fall, followed by motor vehicle collisions. The injuries resulting from these incidents include traumatic brain injury, fractures, broken bones and internal organ damage. Injured older adults receive specialized care in trauma centres that are equipped for injury management. Because of this organized care, many injured older adults will survive their injuries but their health status and quality of life will significantly change. Up to now, very little has been studied about the long-term illness experiences of older adult trauma survivors because most injury care in the past was tailored to a younger population. For this reason we know very little about the experiences of these survivors; we do not know what outcomes they consider to be most meaningful or if the way we currently deliver care to these patients will lead us to achieve these. Our study will examine the experiences of older adult trauma survivors over two years, so that we can, for the first time, describe and understand what a good quality of life after injury looks like from an older adult's perspective. Using interviews and observations, we will gather survivors' experiences from three Ontario trauma centres at 3-, 12- and 24 months after injury. We are especially interested in understanding how their survivorship experiences are influenced by sociocultural factors such as age and gender, and other social dimensions. Our study results will not only help us to understand what older adult trauma survivors experience and how they might want to receive care differently, but it will help in the selection of measures that healthcare providers and policymakers can use to evaluate and improve the overall quality of care to injured older adults in Canada and beyond.

column36: Novel mechanisms in diabetic cardiomyopathy
column37: As diabetes reaches epidemic magnitude worldwide, more diabetics face the problems of morbidity and mortality due to chronic complications. Diabetes causes scarring and damage to the heart and is one of the leading causes of heart disease in Canada. We plan to investigate the mechanisms leading to development of heart damage in diabetes. In diabetes, cells use its fuel differently and as such, causes damage to the cell nucleus. The cell's nucleus, in turn, sends signals to make additional proteins that cause tissue damage. If these processes continue, the cells ultimately fail to function. The signals sent out by the nucleus involve special types of molecules called lncRNAs. They are also known as the 'dark matter of the genome'. These molecules have been recently discovered and have a major role in regulating protein production. We plan to examine how lncRNAs can interact with other RNA molecules and other mechanisms that change the production of abnormal molecules. We will also determine whether by manipulating these mechanisms, we can prevent damage to the heart in diabetes. The proposed research is based on several aims, each of which will be investigated at multiple levels of complexities. Our experiments will include examinations of various types of cells from the heart and the cells of the blood vessels. We will also use animals with diabetes. As well, we will use several compounds to block these mechanisms to understand how this can be prevented. Some of our experiments will focus on specific lncRNAs that we have identified in our laboratory. We will further expand our studies to examine the heart tissues removed from patients and examine whether the abnormalities identified in the cells and in the animals also occur in humans. This proposal represents a comprehensive set of studies to investigate a specific process (i.e. heart damage) in diabetes. Understanding such mechanisms will help to develop preventive treatments for such conditions.

column36: Targeting glial cells to restore neuromuscular function and improve motor outcome in ALS.

column36: The effects, costs, and cost-effectiveness of Montreal's harm reduction interventions for people who inject drugs
column37: Background: Montreal, Quebec has one of the largest populations of PWID in the country (n~4000), and despite offering a variety of harm reduction interventions (e.g. supervised injection facilities (SIFs), needle and syringe programs (NSPs), and opioid agonist treatment (OAT)) continues to grapple with the ramifications of injection drug use including HIV and HCV transmission, and drug-related overdoses and deaths. Objective: To conduct an extensive analyses of the effects, costs, and cost-effectiveness of SIFs, NSPs and OAT, in Montreal, Quebec. Methods: We will use patient-level data from administrative health data sets capturing inpatient, out-patient and publicly covered pharmaceutical dispensations; local cohort and surveillance data; and published literature to simulate the effects of SIFs, NSPS, and OAT on the population of PWID (18 years and older) living in Montreal. The data will be used to evaluate the effects of these interventions on skin, soft tissue and vascular infections (SSTVIs), HIV, hepatitis C, overdose, anoxic/toxicity-related brain injury, and death; estimate the health related costs of these medical events; and determine the cost-effectiveness of variations of the interventions. The results of these analyses will add much-needed insight into the burden of common and debilitating SSTVIs and anoxic/toxicity-related brain injury on the health of PWID, and the cost effectiveness of these harm reduction interventions in a city with a scattered population of PWID, whose primary drug is not opioid based, and where uptake of these interventions is not complete (e.g. SIFs not used at capacity).

column36: Intranasal Vaccines for Pertussis and Influenza Using Novel Formulations of a Triple Adjuvant
column37: This research aims to further develop vaccines for flu and whooping cough. These diseases affect the very young, the elderly and anyone with a poor immune system most severely, even causing death. Yet those at most risk may not be able to take current vaccines. Changing the route of administration to intranasal, and avoiding live influenza virus will expand the range of those who can be vaccinated as well as generating a more effective immune response (both mucosal and systemic). Early stage research has already established an effective vaccine helper (adjuvant) for both of these diseases and the proposed formulations will make the vaccine work well by the nasal route. This route of administration will serve to improve the type and quality of immune response for these diseases in addition to being less invasive than an injection. The key to the new adjuvant for nasal administration is a formulation based on lipids, which bind to the adjuvant and help it reach the immune cells. Prior work shows the lipid-based adjuvant works well in animals using a model peptide intranasal vaccine. The proposed research will combine the new adjuvant formulations with either inactivated flu virus or with peptides from the whooping cough bacteria (antigens), followed by intranasal administration of the vaccine to mice and pigs. Cellular uptake, biodistribution and tissue gene expression responses will be measured to determine how the lipids improve the adjuvant's activity. Outcomes will include evaluating the immune response to the flu virus or to the whooping cough bacteria, such as antibodies raised and other immune responses. We will also look at how the animals respond to a challenge with the infectious agent after vaccination, such as whether they get sick and how much antibodies they make. The health of the nasal tissue and toxicity will be evaluated as well. In the case of whooping cough we will also evaluate the longer-term response to infection challenge after vaccination.

column36: Characterization of a novel function for PABPN1: the product of the oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy disease gene.
column37: Muscular dystrophies are genetic disorders that afflict more than 50,000 Canadians and for which there are currently no cures. Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy (OPMD) is an adult-onset form of muscular dystrophy that is found worldwide, but that is more frequent in the French Canadian and Jewish populations. OPMD is a disorder of skeletal muscle cells that is primarily associated with eyelids drooping, swallowing difficulties, and proximal limb weakness. The underlying genetic defects of OPMD are small GCG insertions in the PABPN1 gene that expands the amino terminal polyalanine tract of PABPN1 from 10 to 12-17 residues. To date, the underlying mechanism by which short GCG insertions in the PABPN1 gene causes OPMD remains completely unknown. Furthermore, limited knowledge exists about the cellular functions of PABPN1. The objective of this application is therefore to provide better understanding about the mechanistic function of PABPN1. The central hypothesis of our research project, which is based on our preliminary findings, is that PABPN1 functions in a specialized nuclear pathway of gene regulation. We propose to characterize this novel PABPN1 function using various cultured human cell lines, including muscle cells, which allow for detailed mechanistic studies of human PABPN1. In addition to shedding new, fundamental knowledge into the role of PABPN1 in gene regulation, our studies are expected to further the understanding into the molecular basis of OPMD. As such, our studies may ultimately address why OPMD is restricted to specific skeletal muscles, and therefore, lay the groundwork for developing much needed therapies.

column36: Deciphering the requirement for PIP5Ks in sperm head formation
column37: One in six couples is unable to conceive, and half of these cases are caused by problems in formation or viability of sperm. Thus, successful sperm development is a crucial aspect of reproductive success. During sperm development, male germ cells undergo dramatic cell shape changes, becoming long and thin, with compact sperm heads at one end and whip-like tails at the other. Together, these features allow the sperm to swim towards and fertilize an egg. Failures in sperm head or tail formation can lead to the production of defective sperm, resulting in infertility. Although formation of the sperm tail is fairly well studied, less is known about formation of the sperm head. To understand how sperm head formation occurs, we are studying male germ cells in the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster). This allows us to take advantage of powerful genetic techniques and well-characterized stages of sperm development available in the fly. Using this system, we discovered that lipid molecules called PIPs are important for sperm head formation. Male flies with mutations in enzymes that affect formation of PIPs have abnormal sperm heads and are sterile. The main goal of our research is to understand how these enzymes and PIPs regulate sperm head formation. To do this, we will use advanced microscopy, proteomics, biochemistry and molecular genetic techniques in flies. Because human sperm form in a similar way, our discoveries will generate novel insights into human male fertility. Understanding this process will eventually lead to new treatments for male infertility as well as novel approaches to developing male contraceptives.

column36: Identifying the roles of atypical MAP kinases ERK3 and ERK4 in cardiac remodelling
column37: Statistics Canada has reported that only 23% of Canadians over the age of 60 have normal blood pressure. The response of the heart to increased blood pressure is to get bigger. The heart muscle also becomes stiffer, through a process known as fibrosis, which makes it more difficult for the heart to contract and relax. Although the enlargement of the heart can initially help in maintaining adequate blood flow to the body, excessive growth can lead to heart failure. However, fibrosis is essential for the heart to heal following myocardial infarction. Similar to a telephone network, information is transmitted into cells, including cells in the heart, by signalling networks. Information is also distributed within cells by signalling molecules, known as kinases, in a manner similar to a telephone operator directing a call to the intended person. When this information arrives, the cell responds. ERK3 and ERK4 are kinases in cells in the heart known as fibroblasts (ERK3) and myocytes (ERK4). Fibroblasts are involved in regulating how stiff the walls of the heart are by producing many structural proteins including collagens. Myocytes are muscle cells that contract with each heartbeat. There is no information available on the roles of ERK3 and ERK4 in the heart; our preliminary data shows that reduced ERK3 expression attenuated the increase in collagen mRNA in an experimental model of high blood pressure whereas ERK4-deficiency increased collagen mRNA. This project is to determine the effects of ERK3 or ERK4 deletion on cardiac remodelling in response to high blood pressure or following myocardial infarction in male and female mice. These studies should reveal if ERK3 and or ERK4 are useful targets for the development of cardioprotective drugs. In addition to protecting the heart, it is also possible that such drugs may result in the regression of heart disease.

column36: Identifying the Cellular Mechanisms by which Inhibiting Ketone Body Oxidation Improves Glycemia in Obesity/Type 2 Diabetes
column37: Our bodies rely on 3 major fuel sources we obtain from the food we eat; fats, sugars, and protein. However, during starvation our livers make a 4th fuel source that our organs (brain, heart, and muscle are the main users) can use to make energy, the ketone body. Past research has heavily focused on understanding the regulation of fat, sugar, and protein metabolism in health, and how they malfunction in various diseases such as obesity and diabetes. The regulation of ketone body metabolism in health and disease has received much less attention. However, exciting data in our lab has shown that decreasing the muscle's ability to burn ketone bodies for energy improves blood sugar control in obesity/diabetes. The major goal of our research project is to understand how decreasing the muscle's ability to burn ketone bodies for energy improves blood sugar control. In order to test our hypothesis, our lab has generated genetically modified mice that have reduced metabolism of ketone bodies only in their muscles. We have identified a number of potential factors that may explain the improved blood sugar control in these animals, which includes; (1) general increases in a protein modification known as succinylation, (2) activation of a global energy sensor protein, and (3) enhanced sugar metabolism. We will use both drugs and genetic approaches to independently reverse these 3 changes in our animals, in order to determine whether they counteract the improved blood sugar control we have observed during obesity/diabetes. In summary, our research may lead to the discovery of a new approach to improve blood sugar control in obesity/diabetes, while defining how this improvement takes place at the cellular level.

column36: When Pain Drives you N. U. T. S.: A mixed methods approach to investigating triggers of the stress response and multidimensional pain outcomes in a sample of individuals suffering from chronic low back pain
column37: One in five Canadian suffers from chronic pain. Psychological factors play an important role in the perception, development and maintenance of chronic pain. These factors however are often examined without considering the nature of the pain experience that could influence these psychological responses. In fact, someone experiencing pain that frequently shoots up to an intensity of 10/10 without any warnings (unpredictable) or ability to decrease its intensity (low control) might perceive this pain as more stressful compared to someone whose pain intensity is relatively stable even if on average both individuals' pain are of a similar intensity. From the general litterature, 4 characteristics of situations lead to a physiological stress response: Novelty, Unpredictability, Threat to ego, and Sense of low control (N.U.T.S.). The objective of this study is to examine the N.U.T.S. characteristics of pain-related and unrelated stressors, combined with individuals' vulnerability to these different characteristics and their associations with pain outcomes such as appraisal, interference, and disability. The study will recruit 300 patients with chronic low back pain from a provincial cohort of back pain patients. Participants will be asked to complete questionnaires at baseline and then fill out an electronic diary daily for 7 days and provide saliva samples to analyse basal cortisol levels. column36: Health-Related Quality of Life and Aging: Measuring what Matters to Older People
column37: This study addresses a measurement gap related to assessing those aspects of health that matter to the quality of life of older persons, termed health-related quality of life (HRQL). Measures exist for assessing the HRQL impact of illnesses and conditions but these measures are not best suited for older persons who may have many such illnesses and conditions but who are still interested and involved in aging actively. Some of the existing measures use many items to assess all the different illness aspects; others use very few items and capture only an illness snapshot. Often the items are not relevant to the experience of older persons and some of the items ask the same content in different ways, something that many find confusing, if not annoying. The intent here is to develop a brief measure of what matters to older persons as they attempt to get on with their life despite an illness burden. This study will also use modern statistical and measurement approaches to create a scoring method that produces a value that considers the preferences for different combinations of health circumstances from the perspective of the older person: "If I had to have that (pain) then I would also rather have this (many interesting distractions)". The gathering of evidence to support the interpretation of the scores across different groups of people (validation) will also be conducted through this project using a mix of in-person assessments and anonymous surveys using the internet. The methods proposed are consistent with the most up-to-date and rigorous guidelines for developing and testing measures and will result in a measure that can be used to evaluate seniors in their own communities.

column37: Entamoeba histolytica is a parasite that cause the disease amebiasis, which results in 100,000 deaths/year. The parasite colonizes and live in mucus and feeds on bacteria. To initiate disease, the parasite has to overcome the protective mucus barrier to invade intestinal cells that is not well characterized. Our recent studies have shown that mucus contains structural proteins that build and stabilize the mucus gel. This proposal examines the hypothesis that E. histolytica secreted enzymes degrade a major mucus associated protein allowing the parasite to gain access and cleave MUC2 mucin to abrogate mucus protective functions. To study this, we will use biochemical techniques to characterize how the mucus proteins interact and by microscopic imaging techniques we will quantify how the parasite enzymes degrade mucus structural components. column37: Climate change is expected to result in an increase in hot temperatures (e.g., the number of hot days in the summer), and these changes can result in poorer health. column36: Redefining blood pressure: How novel views of the arterial tree can lead to better cardiovascular risk stratification.
column37: Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) and hypertension, one of its main determinants, are major health problems in Canada. Despite enormous progress in the treatment of hypertension, the principles of blood pressure (BP) measurement has remained largely unchanged in the past century. In recent years, the reliability of standard BP measurements (using a brachial cuff) has been questioned, raising doubts as to the best way to manage hypertension. This, in parallel with a better understanding of how the pressure travels in the blood vessels, results in a new enthusiasm to find improved ways to determine CVD risk using BP parameters. In this regard, the aim of this study is to determine if various novel arterial wave parameters (central BP, arterial wave reflection and reservoir, aortic stiffness) are better at determining the CVD risk compared to traditional brachial cuff BP and other known risk factors. To achieve these goals, we will use data from CARTaGENE, a large Canadian populational cohort with available arterial wave recordings, and follow-up data from governmental databases. Overall, data is available for 17,795 participants. Through a collaboration with the Austrian Institute of Technology, we will isolate and re-analyse each recording, which will provide the arterial wave parameter we wish to study. Then, using various statistical analyses, we will be able to determine if each arterial wave parameter is better at predicting CVD than traditional factors in the general population. This would by far the largest study to investigate the predictive power of these novel BP parameters, and should provide definitive answers as to their utility above and beyond standard cuff BP. This is the necessary first step to determine if we can improve hypertension management and reduce the burden of CVD. Given the recent technological advances, these innovative parameters can easily be incorporated into devices that could be used in clinical practice.

column36: Investigation of novel host-based approaches for the treatment of tuberculosis
column37: Tuberculosis (TB), is a mycobacterial infection that is one of the world's most pressing health problems. Each day, 5,000 people die from TB globally. The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that TB will infect 225 million and kill 75 million people between 2015-2050. TB spreads by aerosol through sneezing and coughing, and each person with TB infects ~15 more people/yr. The lack of an effective vaccine, the lengthy treatments with multiple drugs that have serious side effects, the prevalence of co-infection with HIV and the increasing number of cases of multi- and extensively- drug-resistant TB (MDR/XDR-TB), have made the control of TB highly challenging whether in developed or developing countries worldwide. Traditional antibiotics directly target and kill the mycobacteria after infection, but these have proven insufficient to curb this disease and have resulted in the emergence of incurable, totally drug resistant TB, (TDR-TB), putting this disease on high alert by WHO. There is a clear association between the immune status of an individual, the outcome of infection and reactivation of TB disease. It is crucial to find efficient host-based therapies if we are to conquer dreaded MDR, XDR and TDR-TB. Recently, we have discovered a novel immunotherapeutic that significantly reduces mycobacterial loads in mice. In the proposed work we will investigate its antimycobacterial potential in conjunction with modified Mtb antigens to enhance Mtb-specific host immunity, and in combination with the current anti-TB drugs. These studies will contribute significantly to the investigation of new approaches, and identification of new therapeutic regimens to treat active TB, MDR-, XDR- and TDR-TB infections, and will have major impact on the health of Canadians and people worldwide.

column36: Does inflammation in brain cause hypoxia, which then exacerbates inflammation: a multimodal study using the EAE inflammation model of multiple sclerosis.
column37: We have discovered that many people with MS have low oxygen levels in the brain (hypoxia). We have also found brain hypoxia in the mouse EAE model, the most commonly used animal model of central nervous system inflammation. This supports the idea that both inflammation and hypoxia responses are linked in a cycle, where inflammation causes hypoxia and hypoxia stimulates inflammation. This grant proposal will use the EAE model and novel imaging tools that are only available in my lab to determine if inflammation can cause hypoxia, and whether that hypoxia can make MS worse. We can quantify hypoxia using unique implantable oxygen probes, which we helped design, MRI and NIRS. Hypoxia could be caused by inflammation, resulting in blockage of small vessels and reduction in local oxygen delivery. We will look for this with histology. The inflammation and the loss of myelin covering the axons could cause an increase in metabolic rate. With MRI, we can measure blood flow and assess myelin loss, and with a unique light based system (near-infrared spectroscopy or NIRS) we can quantify metabolic rate. Since the imaging methods have potential for translation to patients, this aspect of the proposal will demonstrate how MRI and NIRS might be used to monitor hypoxia in humans. After determining whether there is a correlation between hypoxia, brain damage and loss of function, we will further study the link by blocking either inflammation or increasing oxygen in parallel studies. We already know that there is inflammation in MS, but only recently did we discover that there is hypoxia. This project will be the only one in Canada to have our unique mouse NIRS system and the ability to combine this with MRI to study the link between hypoxia and inflammation. We will create new knowledge on how inflammation and hypoxia interrelate, and provide new evidence on how oxygen therapy can be helpful in a condition of inflammation induced hypoxia.

column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is the leading cause of disability in the world. In Canada, the lifetime prevalence of MDD is 12% and about 1.76 million Canadians suffer from MDD in any given year. Heart beat is controlled by the brain and is regular but flexible to change in response to environmental and internal stimuli. This is a healthy feature of the heart known as heart rate variability (HRV). MDD has been associated to diminished HRV (i.e. less flexible/adaptable heart rate), and this is believed to be a reflection of abnormal brain function cause by MDD. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a treatment that stimulates specific areas of the brain by means of small currents while the person is comfortably sitting in a chair. rTMS is associate to significant improvement in approximately 50% of MDD patients and is usually well tolerated. Studies have demonstrated that rTMS may be associated to changes in HRV, but there have been no studies providing direct evidence that brain changes induced by rTMS are responsible for those changes in HRV. The goal of this study is to test the hypothesis that rTMS induces changes in connectivity between the area of the brain stimulated with rTMS (dorsolateral prefrontal cortex) and deeper areas in the brain associated to heart rate regulation (anterior cingulate cortex). The methodology to test his hypothesis directly is to use a complex method that obtains three sources of data at the same time to test for direct causality. This method consists of capturing both fMRI data and electrocardiogram data at the same time that TMS is stimulating the brain. Experiments will be conducted in a group of healthy volunteers as well as patients with depression. The results of this study may have profound implications in both our understanding of the causes of depression as well as the mechanism of action of rTMS and pave the way to the testing of reliable, feasible, and easy to access biomarkers of response in rTMS.

column36: Low frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) vs. intermittent Theta Burst Stimulation TMS effectiveness in depression and suicidal ideation: a randomized non-inferiority trial
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is the leading cause of disability in the world. In Canada, the lifetime prevalence of MDD is 12% and about 1.76 million Canadians suffer from MDD in any given year. MDD is associated with suicide, which is estimated to claim the lives of 800,000 people worldwide each year, accounting for 1-4% of deaths globally. It is estimated that 30-40% of patients with MDD do not improve with medications (treatment resistant depression-TRD). Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) is a treatment that stimulates specific areas of the brain by means of small currents while the person is comfortably sitting in a chair. rTMS is associated to significant improvement in approximately 50% of TRD patients and is usually well tolerated. Recent advances in rTMS have led to the approval of a brief rTMS protocol, intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS), that only takes three minutes to deliver. Low frequency rTMS (LFR) has also been shown to be an effective treatment for TRD in small studies, but has never been compared to iTBS and is currently not approved by the FDA. The aim of this study is to test the hypothesis that LFR works as well as the established iTBS treatment for TRD. In this multi-centre, triple-blinded, non-inferiority trial 420 patients with TRD will be recruited at three academic centres (UBC, CAMH and UHN). Patients will be randomised to receive either iTBS or LFR for 30 sessions. The primary outcome will be the improvement on a depression scale. Secondary outcome will be improvement of on suicidal ideation. A secondary aim is to test the predictive capacity of a novel, easy to implement heart rate based biomarkers (i.e. heart rate variability). The results of this study may lead to the approval of an alternative form of rTMS for depression and suicidal ideation available and ready for widespread use in clinical settings, including the possibility of exploring a home-based treatment with LFR.

column36: Organoids to guide Post-resistance Therapy In driver MutAted Lung cancers (OPTIMAL)
column37: Some types of lung cancer can be specifically targeted by "designer" drugs. Most patients initially respond very well to these targeted drugs with prolonged survival, but eventually they grow resistant and stop responding. Determining which drug to offer next is a major challenge. We have developed a novel model to study drug resistance: 3-dimensional Patient-Derived cancer cell clusters, or "Organoids" (PDOs). PDOs can be rapidly grown from patient biopsies, mimic important properties of patient tumours and are amenable to laboratory characterization. We hypothesize that extensive drug testing and molecular profiling of PDOs can help scientists identify new effective treatments and help doctors to make better treatment decisions for lung cancer patients. We have already shown that our PDO models successfully mirror their original tumours. Our first aim is to optimize PDO model generation and drug testing. Our second aim is to test our PDO model system in patients: we will biopsy patients when their tumours stop responding to a targeted drug and grow these biopsies as PDOs. We will then test a series of clinically-available drugs on these models to determine the most effective treatment for each patient. Tracking the molecular changes in these models will show us how these drugs are working (or not working). Our third aim will explore the use of experimental drug compounds on PDO models to discover new agents for lung cancer therapy. The results of this study have the potential to greatly impact the management of lung cancer: 15% of lung cancers (>4000/year in Canada) are targetable, mostly in younger patients who have never smoked. Targeted therapies have the potential to convert currently fatal cancer into chronic, controllable and manageable disease. The major barrier to this promise is drug resistance. Our research will identify novel resistance mechanisms and methods to overcome this resistance, providing a clinical pipeline to personalize cancer therapy.

column36: Indigenous Health Counts: Advancing Meta-analysis Methods for Respondent-Driven Sampling and Urban Indigenous Health
column37: The Our Health Counts studies are six urban Indigenous community-based research partnerships in the cities of Hamilton, Ottawa, Toronto, London, Thunder Bay and Kenora, Ontario. Each of these studies was done using an advanced statistical method, called respondent-driven sampling, which helps study hard-to-reach communities. Meta-analysis is a commonly used statistical technique that combines results from different studies to produce one single, overall summary of the available information. Traditionally used in the area of clinical trials, meta-analysis is considered the 'gold-standard' technique as it provides a complete picture of all available information and increases the reliability of our conclusions. Unfortunately, due to its statistical complexities, appropriate meta-analysis methods are not developed for studies using respondent-driven sampling. Using advanced statistical methods, we will develop and evaluate an appropriate meta-analysis method to combine data across all six Our Health Counts study sites and provide a more complete picture of urban Indigenous health information across Ontario. Of pressing interest, early evidence from the Toronto database shows a higher rate of diabetes and opioid use relative to the general Canadian population, and a high rate of experiencing discrimination from healthcare providers. However, this single study site lacks the precision to make strong conclusions. On a positive note, this database shows a strong desire for access to traditional Indigenous medicines, which we would like to investigate across study sites in more detail. In partnership with our six Indigenous Community partners, our research team will develop these advanced statistical methods and provide a more complete and accurate picture of the health of urban Indigenous adults. This more accurate, provincial-level information will inform local Indigenous community members, health and social support organizations, and various levels of government.

column37: Developmental Coordination Disorder (DCD) is the term used to describe children who struggle to learn tasks that require motor coordination. In Canada, about 1 to 2 children in every classroom have DCD. Parents and teachers tell us these children have problems learning to do everyday motor activities like tying shoelaces, playing ball, and climbing stairs. Some research has shown that these kids are more likely to be overweight, inactive, unfit, and to have more mental health problems by the time they are teenagers. Unfortunately, many of these children are not identified, and therefore do not get the help they need when they need it. To understand how to help kids with DCD, we need to be able to determine when they begin to be less active and less healthy, both physically and mentally. The goal of our study is to keep observing a large group of children with and without DCD who we have been following since they were 4 or 5 years old. We will continue following them once per year until they are 10 and 11 years old. At each visit, we will keep measuring their motor coordination, how much physical activity they do, how fit they are, their diet, and how much they weigh. We will also start to ask the children questions about how they feel about themselves and if they are feeling anxious or depressed. What makes our study new and exciting is that we will be able to find out when children with DCD start to become less active and less healthy. Working with doctors, teachers, and parents will help us make sure that we recognize kids with DCD as young as possible so that they are able to get the right type of support, at the right time, before they become inactive, obese, or depressed.

column37: Deficient blood supply to the central nervous system (CNS) leads to several debilitating diseases. Examples of such diseases include stroke which is a leading cause of brain injury affecting 800,000 individuals per year in the United States alone and causing upwards of 150,000 deaths. To study the molecular mechanisms of stroke, an easily accessible model system in which to investigate how blood vessels interact with nerve cells is the retina, the membrane of nerve cells at the back of the eye that relays visual information to the brain. The retina is biochemically analogous to the brain and its anatomical location allows for thorough investigation. In addition, findings that are obtained from studying stroke in the retina can be translated to better understand ischemic retinopathies, such as diabetic retinopathy and retinopathy of prematurity which are the leading causes of blindness in the industrial world. These blinding diseases happen to also stem from compromised blood supply to the neurons of the retina. This proposal seeks to understand how blood vessels degenerate in ischemic diseases of the CNS by using the retina as a model. Furthermore, we propose to investigate the role of cholesterol metabolism in modulating inflammation upon ischemia. Ultimately, we hope to interfere with the disease process and promote regeneration of functional blood vessels.

column37: Alcohol is a leading risk factor for death and disease in Canada. The top alcohol-related conditions include liver diseases, cardiovascular diseases, injuries, alcohol dependence, and cancers. Studies show that despite consuming lower levels of alcohol, lower socioeconomic groups are more likely to experience alcohol-related harms than higher socioeconomic groups. Therefore, alcohol policies aiming to reduce population-level alcohol use and harms have potential to reduce health inequalities. In Canada, policies have been implemented in provinces and territories to moderate alcohol use and minimize its negative consequences. However, over the past two decades, Alberta, British Columbia, and most recently Ontario have deregulated alcohol sales and increased privatization of alcohol retail markets. Few studies have examined the impact of deregulation on alcohol use and health harms in the population, and particularly on "social inequities in health" (i.e., health differences between social groups that are avoidable and unfair). Results of the proposed research can be used to directly inform alcohol policies and health equity strategies in Ontario and across Canada.

column37: Couple relationships are described as the most significant relationship for a majority of adults, and recognized as a key determinant of mental health. The arrival of a child might be a particularly vulnerable period for parental couple relationships (e.g., conflicts, alliance), and in turn have a negative effect on both parents' mental health and their child's adjustment. CIT is an endemic social problem associated with longstanding and costly mental health problems that can be exacerbated in the years following the birth of a child. Yet, the complex longitudinal associations between CIT, parental mental health and child adjustment remain unclear. Research including both partners is needed to understand how relationship factors can affect parents and their child. In this project, we will gather novel longitudinal data among parental couples to test relationship factors as the mechanism linking CIT to parental mental health and child adjustment. Both parents will complete questionnaires assessing their CIT, mental health (e.g., stress) and child adjustment (e.g., behaviors problems), at four assessments waves. Interactions among the parental couple will also be assessed using naturalistic observations. The longitudinal design will allow the examination of parental mental health and child adjustment trajectories in the years following the birth of a child, while considering relational factors from the perspectives of both parents. This study will help elucidate how CIT relates to health outcomes in victims, their partner and their child, and identify risk and protection factors, to guide the elaboration of efficient interventions aiming to enhance the health of Canadian families.

column36: Investigating the neural basis of motor and cognitive disabilities following childhood stroke
column37: Stroke is a leading cause of neurological disabilities in Canadian children. Children often have better recoveries than adults after suffering a stroke, however they also are more likely to undergo changes in the brain during recovery that can cause cognitive or movement disabilities, such as dystonia. In addition, its prevalence is higher in children under 10 years of age, suggesting that age at time of stroke also plays a role. It is becoming increasingly important to better understand when and why this happens so that health professionals can tailor therapeutic strategies to target the most effected regions of the brain during recovery, especially during critical periods of childhood development. We will measure changes in movement, sensory and intellectual abilities in children between 6 and 18 years of age during recovery from a stroke. We will use advanced brain imaging techniques (magnetoencephalography, MEG and magnetic resonance imaging, MRI), as well as neuropsychological assessments during their recovery in order to track the development of motor or other deficits. We expect that children who develop dystonia and related symptoms after stroke will demonstrate altered activity in sensory and movement regions of the brain, and severity will be related to age at the time of their stroke. We will also determine whether younger children have a higher rate of post-stroke movement disorders and poor outcomes and if these are associated with more widespread involvement of different brain regions. Our goal is to monitor these changes in the brain during recovery from childhood stroke to determine what factors might predict which children are more likely to have undesired outcomes.

column36: Molecular mechanisms controlling maintenance and plasticity of GABAergic circuits in the adult brain.
column37: GABAergic neurons, a particular subset of brain cells, powerfully control the function of brain circuits. Many common neurological disorders, including schizophrenia and autism, are thought to be partially consequence of defects in the development of GABAergic neurons. In particular, such disorders seem to be associated with defects in the way this subset of neurons connects and communicates with other neurons, via specialized loci called synapses. In addition, the maturation of GABAergic synapses is thought to limit brain plasticity in the adult brain. Because of the complexity of brain circuitry, it has been so far very difficult to understand how GABAergic neurons form, maintain and change their synapses and how disturbances in this process may lead to altered cognitive functions. The experiments we propose will use imaging, electrophysiological and gene manipulation techniques to dissect the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the maturation and plasticity of GABAergic synapses in the postnatal brain. This approach will shed light on the factors regulating the function of GABAergic synapses in the normal brain and on the pathological process leading to their disturbance. In addition, a better comprehension of the mechanisms underlying GABAergic synapse plasticity in the adult brain may help developing novel tools to securely foster brain plasticity to aid cognitive rehabilitation in adult patients suffering of different psychiatric disorders, such as post-traumatic stress disorder.

Each participant will undergo one PET scan. We believe that brain opioid levels will be lower in BPD+NSSI, because this group shows the least sensitivity to pain. These results would offer one explanation for better understanding the role of opioid functioning in NSSI and BPD. Furthermore, these data could also provide the impetus to develop new opioid-based treatments that might prevent NSSI.
