column36: Spinal interneuron subpopulations and modular circuits in normal locomotor control and after spinal cord injury
column37: Loss of locomotor activity due to accident or disease is devastating to patients and may lead to early death. Currently, we have limited understanding of the neural circuits that control movement, which hampers efforts to devise better therapeutics to treat loss of motor function. The fundamental goal of my laboratory is to reveal the organization of neural circuits that control normal locomotion in order to identify mechanisms that could be targeted when that behavior is disrupted by injuries and diseases. Currently, we focus on interneuron (IN) populations that form the locomotor circuits in the mouse spinal cord, and aim to reveal the organizational logic and functional roles of these circuits in locomotor control. More importantly, we hope to provide insight into the potential roles of spinal INs in neuroplasticity and recovery after spinal cord injury (SCI). Based on our previous and current studies of one specific IN population, designated V3 INs, as a model system, we predict that spinal IN subpopulations could serve as modular components in locomotor circuits, allowing for task-dependent selection of functionally distinct circuit outputs. These individual modules may function in different aspects of locomotor control and respond differently to SCI and subsequent rehabilitation regimens, knowledge that could be crucial for recovery from SCI. To address these issues, we will employ various genetic and molecular tools in combination with advanced anatomical, electrophysiological, optogenetic, behavioral and computational approaches to define functional V3 IN subpopulations; define task-dependent functional modules of V3 INs in locomotor circuits; and investigate their potential functions in normal locomotion and in SCI.

column36: Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) and social behavior. A translational study.
column37: Social behavior (SB) is a fundamental characteristic of human behavior and interaction. Several psychiatric diseases, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and social anxiety disorder (SAD), are accompanied by significant SB impairments. Several studies suggest that the psychedelic compound lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) may enhance SB in animals and humans via modulation of the serotonin and glutamate system, two major neurotransmitter systems. Moreover, increasing evidence suggests that LSD might enhance neuroplasticity (the growth of new neurons), and have antinflammatory effects (decrease over-activity of the immune system), and given that these processes are altered in conditions with impaired SB, these effects might also be involved in the prosocial effects of LSD The main hypothesis of this translational study is that LSD enhances SB via a) potentiating serotonin and glutamate neurotransmission in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), and b) enhancing neuroplasticity and immune balance. We will reach our objectives firstly via studying LSD prosocial effects in rodents, and the effects of LSD on neurotransmission, neuroplasticity, and immune system balance. Secondly, we will determine whether the results obtained in rodents translate to humans, by administering LSD to healthy volunteers, and assessing resulting changes on SB, neurotransmission, mPFC function, neuroplasticity, and immune balance. This represents the first translational, proof-of-concept Canadian study investigating whether psychedelic compounds are useful for the treatment of psychiatric disorders accompanied by SB dysfunction.

column36: Developing a Patient-Specific Surgical Decision-Assistance Tool to Improve Reverse Shoulder Replacement Outcomes
column37: The human shoulder is a joint consisting of a ball on the arm side of the joint, and a cup on the shoulder blade side. When a person seriously injures their shoulder joint, they can be left unable to lift their arm. For these patients, the only way to regain function is to undergo a shoulder replacement called Reverse Total Shoulder Arthroplasty (RTSA), whereby the above-described joint geometry is flipped; a cup-shaped implant is placed on the arm side of the joint, and a ball-shaped implant is placed on the shoulder blade side. Because of this, the anatomical landmarks that surgeons use to determine the best implant configuration during a traditional shoulder replacement are not effective. Therefore, the goal of this research is to develop the biomechanical understanding necessary to provide surgeons with an objective and quantitative surgical decision-making assistance tool to aid in the optimal planning of RTSA. This objective will be achieved in a number of phases. First, we will systematically analyze how the shapes of RTSA patients' shoulder bones differ from those of other patient groups. We will then develop computer models that can inform us of how RTSA patients' anatomy influences how different RTSA implant configurations affect how well their joint functions after surgery. Results of these computer modelling studies will then be used to develop the desired decision making assistance tool using machine learning techniques that will help surgeons customize their surgical plans to each of their patients.

column36: Identification of repurposed drugs selectively targeting human colon cancer stem cells
column37: Colorectal cancer is among the deadliest and most frequently diagnosed cancers in our country. Drugs currently used to treat colorectal tumors often fail to completely eradicate all types of cancer cell, giving an opportunity to the disease to come back (or relapse). Like many other cancers, colorectal tumors contain small reservoirs of malignant cells responsible for tumor initiation, relapse, and resistance to current treatments. Those are known as Cancer Stem Cells (CSC) and are recognized as "the root of cancer and seeds of metastasis". Previous research uncovered critical molecular mechanisms that are essential to CSCs development and maintenance. Importantly, those elements can be used as indicators in the quest to develop new medicines specifically eliminating CSCs from colon tumors. We have recently found clinically approved drugs with the capacity to alter CSCs biology while showing limited toxic effects in a normal cell model. These could represent new therapeutic avenues to safely eliminate cancer. In this project, we plan to demonstrate the capacity of those drugs to alter colon CSCs capacity to form tumors in mice, as well as in a unique culture system utilizing cells directly isolated from human patients. Moreover, we will use state-of-the-art techniques in biomedical research to understand how the candidate drugs can impact CSCs biology. Ultimately, the identification of molecules capable of suppressing colon CSC's activity would provide a new therapeutic option aimed at selectively targeting cancers, decreasing side effects and increasing patient survival rates.

column37: Vestibular disorders such as labyrinthitis and vestibular neuritis, which lead to the defects of many fundamental innate motor functions, have considerable impact on Canadian society. It has been estimated that ~5% of all Canadians (1.9 million) suffer from chronic vestibular disorders (CBC news). And this number increases to up to 35% among the population of 40 years or older. Nevertheless, our brains have great potential of plasticity which can partially recover innate motor functions affected by vestibular disorders. A determination of the basic cellular and circuitry mechanisms underlying innate behavior plasticity will enhance our understanding of the partial recovery of innate behaviors compromised by vestibular disorders. Our lab has developed a surgery paradigm to reliably induce innate behavior plasticity, allowing us to perform a variety of in vivo and in vitro approaches for circuit analysis. In this project, we will utilize two-photon functional imaging and single unit recording from behaving mice combined with viral circuit tracing. Our goals are to pinpoint circuit components essential for innate behavior plasticity and to elucidate the principles governing this type of behavioral adaptation. By deciphering the basic mechanisms of innate behavior plasticity, our work will have great potential to figure out the bottleneck of intrinsic innate behavior plasticity, and thus provide insight into new avenues for novel therapies to promote the recovery of fundamental innate functions affected by vestibular disorders.

column36: Central Mechanisms of Opioid Withdrawal
column37: Opioid medications provide potent pain relief in the short-term, but their long-term use can cause serious adverse effects. A major problem is that chronic opioid users experience debilitating withdrawal symptoms (e.g. tremors, anxiety, depression, insomnia, cardiovascular and gastrointestinal distress) when attempting to stop or reduce their opioid medications. Seeking relief, these individuals continue to use opioid drugs. A misconception is that only illicit opioid use or "opioid addicts" are susceptible to withdrawal. The careful use of prescription opioids can also lead to significant withdrawal symptoms. Optimal therapies for opioid withdrawal are unavailable. Our team recently discovered that immune cells (microglia) residing within the brain and spinal cord play an important role in opioid withdrawal. These immune cells communicate with other cells through specialized channels (pannexin-1), which are like gates that open and close to allow passage of chemical signals. Blocking these channels in the spinal cord alleviates withdrawal without diminishing the pain-relieving benefits of opioid medications. We have new data that pannexin-1 channels gate activity within the locus coeruleus, an area of the brain that communicates with the spinal cord by sending specialized projections containing a chemical (norepinephrine). This proposal addresses exciting new questions about how pannexin-1 channels modulate specific circuitry in the brain and spinal cord that are important for opioid withdrawal. Using advanced cellular imaging, biochemical, and behavioural approaches, experiments will also deconstruct the machinery by which norepinephrine enhances pannexin-1 activity and its impact on microglia signaling. Finally, we will translate our findings into the development of next generation, more potent pannexin-1 targeted drugs for treating opioid withdrawal.

column36: Motherhood and brain aging: the effects of hormone therapy, immune and metabolic challenges later in life
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a disease that results in the progressive loss of cells in the brain, in particular in an area important for the formation of new memories, called the hippocampus. Women are more likely to be diagnosed with AD and show greater brain pathology and memory loss with the disease than men. In addition, women are more likely to develop Alzheimer's disease especially when they have certain genes (APOEe4) and a previous history of multiple pregnancies. This project aims to characterize the aging female brain and how is affected by reproductive experience (pregnancy) and genetics (APOEe4 status) under hormone therapy, immune, and metabolic (diet) challenges. Menopause is associated with dramatic changes in hormone levels and with cognitive decline and certain hormone therapies (HTs) positively affect cognition depending on timing and genotype. Our research shows that the sensitivity of the female brain to estrogens is altered with past parity to affect neuroplasticity and immune signalling. The goal of this proposal is to study the effects of parity and genetics on aging in the female brain exposed to hormone therapies, immune and metabolic challenges in preclinical models. This work will determine how physiological challenges faced by females during aging interact with motherhood and genetics can affect brain aging. It is clear that tailored treatment based on sex, genetics, and possibly reproductive history need to be developed to best treat individuals at risk to develop AD.

column36: Improving clinical practice recommendations for late preterm antenatal corticosteroids: incorporating a decision support tool to tackle the uncertain balance of risks and benefits
column37: Antenatal corticosteroids are a medication given to women who are at risk of an early delivery to help reduce the chance of breathing problems for their baby after birth. Current guidelines recommend giving antenatal corticosteroids to pregnant women who might have their baby before 34 weeks of pregnancy. This medication may also help those at risk of an early delivery at 34 to 36 weeks of pregnancy but the balance between the benefits and harms of this treatment is less clear at these ages. Clinical guidelines for giving this medication at 34 to 36 weeks of pregnancy are also unclear, making it difficult for doctors and patients to decide whether to use it. We previously found that many doctors are not talking about this decision with patients, or when they do talk about it, different doctors discuss different risks and benefits. Decision support tools that clearly state risks and benefits can sometimes help doctors and patients make decisions about whether a treatment is right for them. Our goal is to find out if including a decision support tool in clinical guidelines will improve how doctors discuss antenatal corticosteroids with patients who might deliver at 34 to 36 weeks of pregnancy. We will ask patients who delivered at these preterm ages whether their doctor discussed antenatal corticosteroids with them, and see if they report having had better discussions with their doctor about this treatment decision after their doctor had access to the decision support tool within the clinical guideline. We will also ask doctors if and how this decision support tool impacts their counselling. By helping doctors and patients communicate about the risks and benefits of antenatal corticosteroids, this project could promote fully-informed and optimal use of a drug that can reduce breathing problems in newborns. Our results could also serve as a model for other clinical guidelines when there is no clear answer about whether the benefits of a treatment outweigh its harms.

column36: Prediction of multiple sclerosis disability worsening scores using multi-stream deep learning
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a common neurological disease that disables young Canadians. There are 14 approved therapies now for many who have a relapsing remitting form of MS (RRMS). Yet within 10-15 years of disease onset, >50% of RRMS patients develop secondary progressive MS (SPMS), which remains untreatable. While many factors may cause this poor outcome, the inability to optimize therapy based on an individual's risk of worsening is crucial. There is no reliable way to identify the risks but if there is, early aggressive treatment would be possible for those with a greater risk of worsening, which is critical to save the tissue before irreversible damage accumulates. This project will establish a novel deep machine learning method to predict the 5-year risk of disability score worsening in RRMS patients. We will take a unique approach by simultaneously evaluating patient outcomes from brain pathology, clinical measures, and brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Deep learning has shown enormous progress recently in disease prediction, especially when combing pathology-directed outcomes, and multiple types of patient data. Using standard brain MRI, our pilot deep learning data is 83% accurate in predicting RRMS and SPMS. By assessing the pixel pattern (texture) of MRI, our pioneer work also discover that the scale and direction of MRI texture detects specific elements of MS pathology. We have now built new deep learning methods using 3 types of outcomes from MRI texture pathology, clinical data, and brain MRI, and cutting-edge techniques to unveil how deep learning works. Built on these solid data and large cohorts of MS patients, this project will establish a novel objective method to identify the high and low risks of disability worsening for individual RRMS patients so that each can receive the best treatment regimen to improve prognosis. This personalized medicine approach will directly benefit MS patients and families, the health care system, and society.

column36: Longitudinal effects of cannabis legalization in a community cohort of Canadian adults
column37: On October 17, 2018, recreational cannabis was legalized in Canada. The consequences of this major legislative change are unknown and we have a rare opportunity to evaluate its effects systematically. In the month prior to legalization, we collected data on cannabis perceptions, cannabis use, and other substance use from 1502 adults in Ontario. Our internal funding has permitted subsequent assessments at 6- and 12-months (95% and 93% retention, respectively), and will permit a further assessment at 18-months post-legalization. This Project Grant is to conduct additional follow-up assessments across a five-year period following legalization (24-, 30-, 36-, 42- , 48-, 54-, and 60-months). Specifically, the Primary Aims are to examine: (1) changes in attitudes and perceptions about cannabis; (2) changes in cannabis consumption practices; (3) psychological factors that affect changes following legalization (e.g., initiating, escalating, or reducing use). In addition, for exploratory purposes, the study has two Secondary Aims. The first is to examine how changes in cannabis use following legalization affects the use of other substances, both recreational (e.g., alcohol) and prescription (e.g., opioids). The second is to explore sex/gender differences in all of the preceding domains. Collectively, the proposed study will make substantial contributions to understanding of the effects of recreational cannabis legalization in Canada and will have significant implications for other jurisdictions considering cannabis legalization around the world.

column36: Understanding and quantifying the impact of stroke and other brain structural disconnections
column37: Stroke affects an increasingly large number of individuals in Canada and around the world. Brain damage as a result of stroke can often lead to difficulties in mobility, language production and understanding, and other functions such as memory and reasoning. Though these difficulties lead to serious reductions in quality of life, we still do not know how damage in one location of the brain is related to specific difficulties. This is in part because we do not yet fully understand how the brain is connected and how its connections support our everyday behaviours. Brain damage is typically described based on its location and size, but this completely ignores how the damage may have interrupted some connections between different regions of the brain. For example, damage to the front of the brain will result in different functional deficits depending exactly where it is: if it is more towards the top the patient may experience difficulties with memory (e.g., phone numbers) but if it is lower the patient may experience emotional issues (e.g., understanding facial expressions). We have a fairly good idea of what the processing regions of the brain do (grey matter, made up of cells that do the "thinking") but we know very little about how they are connected through the white matter of the brain (i.e., the "wires" that connect different processing regions together). Without this knowledge, damage to the "wires" is difficult to predict the effects of or, ultimately, treat with clinical intervention.

column36: Placental contributions to maternal and fetal health outcomes: Lipid signatures in diabetes mellitus in pregnancy
column37: Globally, an increasing number of pregnancies are complicated by diabetes, paralleling the obesity trends in women of child-bearing age. These pregnancies carry a significant risk of complications for the mother and the baby, both during and after pregnancy. In fact, later in life, women with a history of diabetes during pregnancy and their offspring, are at higher risk of developing cardiovascular and metabolic diseases. The placenta, strategically positioned between the mother and the fetus, likely mediates these feto-maternal complications, but the mechanisms involved remain elusive. Lipids, classically thought to be purely structural elements of the cell membrane, are now recognized as key mediators in normal processes and in the development of a variety of diseases. However, global lipid profiles across gestation in pregnant women with diabetes of varying severity have never been characterized. This proposal builds upon a series of novel experiments in which we will define lipid changes across gestation in vesicles, called exosomes that are released from the placenta and travel in the maternal and fetal circulations to target a variety of organs. These vesicles can act as messengers that modify the well-being of target cells like those of blood vessels. Hence, in addition, we will investigate the effect of these vesicles on cellular events linked to cell-death in blood vessel cells.

column37: Even more than the general public, people living with serious mental illness also live with chronic health conditions like heart disease or diabetes. Using large data sets, we will also look to understand the types of primary care services people with serious mental illness use and how these services might be different based on the type of primary care practice they go to (for example, doctors who work alone versus doctors who work with groups of professionals). column36: Targeting the SMARCD1-E2A-p53 Molecular Axis in B-Cell Lymphoma
column37: Besides complex and heterogeneous DNA mutations, cancer cells harbor global alterations of the epigenetic landscape, which are associated with aberrant cell-fate programs. The dependency on altered chromatin states is thought to provide great therapeutic opportunities since epigenetic aberrations are reversible and dynamically controlled by enzymatic and biochemical activities that are amenable to drug modulation. Recently our laboratory identified the chromatin remodeling factor SMARCD1 as an essential gene for the proliferation and survival of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas - the seventh most common neoplasm affecting adults in the United States. Our current work further identifies the E2A oncogene and p53 tumor suppressor as downstream mediators of SMARCD1 function in this disease. column37: Ten percent of Canadian adults suffer from joint cartilage damage and osteoarthritis (OA) with an estimated cost to society of more than 33 billion dollars a year and incalculable suffering for affected individuals and their families. Sixty percent of OA patients are of typical working age (20-64 years). Cartilage defects larger than 4 centimeter-square are a clinical challenge to treat, but joint cartilage chips, sometimes referred to as particulate or morselized cartilage, has shown significant clinical promise, regardless of whether the cartilage was sourced from juvenile human cadavers, unrelated adult cadavers or the patients themselves. Current cartilage chips methods are hampered by limited supply of human donor material, risk of disease transmission, suboptimal graft tissue, donor site morbidity in case of autologous cartilage, and cost of human allograft material in some cases. Donor age, co-morbidities, and harvest site may all negatively influence the biological potency of the cartilage graft. We propose to solve these issues by using cartilage generated in the laboratory from neonatal allogeneic mesenchymal stromal cells (MSC). We will vitrify (freeze) the cartilage tissue for indefinite storage and availability as an off-the-shelf live-cell cartilage graft that can be implanted using standard surgical methods. Aims for this 3-year proof-of-principle project: A1) In vitro generation of vitrified equine MSC-derived cartilage chips. A2) In vitro generation of vitrified human MSC-derived cartilage chips. A3) In vivo assessment of non-vitrified (fresh) and vitrified equine MSC-derived cartilage-chips for large induced cartilage defects in research horses. Fully implemented, this therapy would provide a safe, efficacious, cost-effective and technically simple treatment for Canadians as well as provide an opportunity for a Canadian biotechnology business to bank and distribute vitrified cartilage tissue in unlimited quantities to the world market.

column36: Survival and Cardiac Recovery In Pediatric Cardiomyopathy (SCRIPT study)
column37: Heart failure can be described as a state when the heart cannot function in its role to supply oxygen rich blood to the rest of the body and if severe, can ultimately lead to death. Cardiomyopathies are diseases of the heart muscle and a leading cause of pediatric heart failure. Pediatric heart failure is an important public health problem associated with high mortality and multiple heart and non-heart complications. Risk factors for these complications, including for death, are poorly understood in children. With this project, our main objective is to find out what happens to children with cardiomyopathy outside our hospital and after they transition to adulthood. We want to determine the chances of these patients living without the need for a heart transplant and the risks for other important heart and non-heart complications even well into adulthood. We also want to describe how much healthcare usage is required to care for these patients to understand better the burden on their families. As the largest pediatric heart failure program in Canada, SickKids is well positioned to study this problem by combining pediatric data from our patients seen at SickKids hospital with information from ICES databases. Over the past 2 years, we have been building a detailed cohort of all children cared for at SickKids with a diagnosis of cardiomyopathy from 2001 to 2017. ICES is a provincial database that includes administrative information on health care usage and outcomes for everyone living in the province of Ontario. It is a unique collection of databases with strong quality data which has not been reproduced anywhere in the world. With the help of mentors from ICES, this project will link our database to ICES to find out what happens to our patients throughout their lifetime. This project represents the first study where a pediatric cardiology group is linked to ICES and will create a study that will span pediatrics into adulthood.

column36: Identifying sex differences in the molecular mechanisms of socially-mediated pubertal suppression
column37: Puberty is an essential developmental process in mammals. Puberty marks the onset of sexual maturation and is associated with increased incidence of depression and anxiety. Two risk factors for the development of depression are psychosocial stress and pubertal timing. Importantly, psychosocial stress can itself shift pubertal timing. Puberty onset, susceptibility to stress, and risk of depression all differ between males and females. For these reasons understanding sex specific mechanisms underlying how social stress influences pubertal timing has tremendous importance for human health. The naked mole-rat (NMR) is a unique rodent exhibiting extreme socially-mediated reproductive suppression. NMRs reside in large colonies of adults who remain in a pre-pubertal state due to the presence of a dominant breeding female known as the queen. In addition to the queen, a dominant breeding male (known as a consort) has also gone through puberty. Most NMRs will never go through puberty unless they are removed from the suppressive cues of their colony. By studying NMRs, we have an exceptional opportunity to learn how social cues influence pubertal timing. Here we will identify genome-wide gene expression patterns as well as modifications to the DNA that turn genes on and off (known as epigenetic changes) in the brain, adrenal glands, and gonads of NMRs. We will also manipulate stress-relevant genes to examine how they influence puberty and gene expression in brain. The goal of our research is to discover sex specific genes that are involved in suppressing puberty in NMRs, which may explain associations between age of pubertal onset, stress reactivity, and risk for psychopathology in humans.

column36: SUMOylation Pathways in Alzheimer Disease and Their Therapeutic Implications
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a common, progressive and ultimately lethal disease affecting ~5% of adults over 65 years of age and ~30% of adults over the age of 85 years in most Western societies. Both the prevalence and the annual expenditures on AD are expected to increase as the proportion of the population at risk increases over the next 20 years. The currently available treatments are of limited effectiveness as they target the symptoms of the disease but not the root cause. The major features of AD are accumulations of abnormal proteins called amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles within the brain. Amyloid plaques appear as densely packed thread-like fibers that form around nerve cells and blood vessels. Evidence suggests that amyloid is highly toxic and is the primary cause of nerve cell death. Loss of these cells is the underlying event in AD and results in the clinical features of cognitive dysfunction and memory impairments. We have recently discovered a link between AD pathology and a family of proteins called, small ubiquitin-like modifiers (SUMOs). Our initial investigations have uncovered links between SUMO-related pathways and the development of Alzheimer disease plaques and tangles. This was made possible by the generation of novel animal models that combine SUMO and the key amyloid and tangle proteins. The ultimate objective of this research is to understand the cellular processes which cause AD and to use that information for the development of safe and effective treatments.

column36: Towards the non-invasive, most accurate radiotherapy of mobile tumours in a hybrid linac-MR system
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada and nearly half of the patients receive radiotherapy (RT). RT uses strong radiation to kill tumour cells, and the radiation is typically delivered by a device called linear accelerator (linac). If a tumour is static during irradiation, e.g. brain tumour, modern RT can deliver highly accurate radiation to the tumour without much damage to the adjacent normal cells. Unfortunately, most tumours are mobile and can deform due to respiratory and cardiac motions (e.g. lung tumour), and such accurate RT is difficult due to the lack of sufficient soft-tissue imaging. Most tumours reside in soft-tissue, and soft-tissue is best seen in MRI. However, current imaging devices on linacs are typically X-ray based, which provide poor soft-tissue imaging. Thus, small metal markers that can be seen in X-ray image must be surgically implanted near the tumour to estimate its shape and location during RT. Our laboratory built the first radiotherapy-MRI hybrid device (linac-MR) in 2008, and a human whole-body system in 2014. This MRI on-board linac allows continuous MR imaging during irradiation, providing clear image of moving tumours. Using linac-MR, our objective is to enhance the geometric accuracy of RT treating mobile tumours without the need of invasive surgery. To achieve the objective, we have established a framework of novel RT method, non-invasive intra-fractional tumour-tracked RadioTherapy (nifteRT). The feasibility of nifteRT was verified in 2013 using our prototype linac-MR system. We were able to deliver accurate radiation to a moving target reproducing 1D lung tumour motion in linac-MR. In this proposal, we aim to further improve our nifteRT research to the level of clinically usable technology. We expect < 3 mm error in radiation delivery to mobile tumours in nifteRT. This will allow the escalation of radiation dose only to the tumours without excessive damage to the adjacent normal cells, which is the ultimate goal of RT.

column36: Contribution of endothelial fatty acid metabolism to diabetes-associated heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
column37: Type 2 diabetes is a leading contributor to cardiovascular death, having damaging effects on organs such as the heart as well as blood vessels. One such disease associated with diabetes is 'heart failure with preserved ejection fraction', also known as HFpEF. In this type of heart disease, the heart stiffens resulting in defective relaxation of the heart between beats, meaning the heart has less blood inside it to pump out to the rest of the body. People are often diagnosed at very late, and untreatable, stages of disease as there are no diagnostic tests that can detect early disease warning signs. The reasons why this disease develops are not understood, but recent evidence has suggested that the function of small blood vessels in the heart is defective. Therefore, dysfunction of blood vessels in the heart may be an early warning sign of disease and may also be a target for therapy. We have been seeking for markers in the blood that indicate defective blood vessel function in the heart. Using animal models of HFpEF we found a small RNA molecule, microRNA-30, is increased in the blood at the same time as blood vessels become dysfunctional. It appears that this microRNA is secreted by dysfunctional endothelial cells (the cells that line blood vessels) in the diabetic heart. We found that in the endothelial cells of the heart, microRNA-30 regulates proteins that are involved in fatty acid metabolism. When microRNA-30 is elevated, endothelial cells use more fatty acids, which causes oxidative stress and defective endothelial cell function. We believe this may be an early defect in HFpEF since fatty acids are highly elevated in the blood of diabetics. Our proposal will determine whether the utilization of fatty acids by the endothelium is involved in diabetic HFpEF and whether targeting microRNA-30 can be a potential therapy. We will also test whether measuring microRNA-30 in the blood of human patients with diabetes can be used to detect the earliest stages of HFpEF.

column36: Targeting TSLP - Novel anti-inflammatory compounds for the treatment and prevention of atopic diseases
column37: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is one of the most common inflammatory skin diseases and up to 17% of the Canadian population is affected at some point in their lives. Furthermore, AD often is an entry point for further allergies such as food allergies, hay fever or allergic asthma. As such, AD has a significant socioeconomic impact. Since AD is a highly complex and heterogenic disease, its pathophysiology is still not fully understood. Over the past years, however, the keratinocyte-derived cytokine thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP) has been identified as a key player in skin inflammation and a trigger for the development of further allergies. This has sparked the interest of pharmaceutical companies to develop inhibitors of TSLP. Tezepelumab is the most advanced drug showing promising results, however it is a protein which means that it must be administered systemically and cannot be applied locally, for example as a cream. However, drugs which can be applied locally offer several advantages such as reduced side effects, targeted drug delivery at the site of action as well higher acceptance rates among the patients. Hence, this project aims to develop effective blockers of TSLP which can be applied topically. To achieve this goal, we combine our expertise in drug development and skin research. First, we will develop and synthesize potent low molecular weight TSLP inhibitors which will then be tested with regard to efficacy and tolerability in 2D and 3D cell cultures. Finally, the most promising compounds will be tested in animal models of atopic dermatitis. The overall goal are new topical treatment options for AD and the prevention of the development of further allergic diseases such as asthma.

column37: Alzheimer's disease is the primary form of dementia in old age and rates are increasing due to longer human lifespan and the aging population of baby boomers. It is estimated that prevalence will quadruple between 2006 and 2050, at which point 1% of the worldwide population will have the disease. Despite these bleak figures, it is important to note that patients typically only live with the severest form of Alzheimer's for 1-2 years. Thus, treatments that can delay disease progression have tremendous potential to reduce the burden of Alzheimer's disease. Here, we will identify exactly which brain cells and circuits are initially most vulnerable to the tau pathology that is observed in aging and Alzheimer's disease. Tau is a toxic protein that is first observed in the memory centers of the brain, before spreading and causing irreversible damage. More specifically, the neurons that first harbor tau also connect with another region that produces newborn neurons throughout life. These newborn neurons have an enhanced ability to integrate into neural circuits, suggesting they may be better at forming connections in disease states. However, no one has ever examined whether they less vulnerable to tau, or more capable at repairing circuits that are damaged by tau. Here we will therefore mimic the human pattern of tau pathology in mice, and examine whether new vs. old neurons are more likely to be damaged. We will then use various therapeutic strategies to enhance new cell growth, with the goal of repairing the damaged circuits. Whereas we currently know, at a general level, which brain regions are sensitive to tau pathology and Alzheimer's disease, these experiments will reveal the precise subpopulations of neurons that are vulnerable and capable of being exploited to delay the progress of disease.

column37: In Canada, approximately 20% of youth experience mental health issues that impact their daily lives. The rate of mental illness and need for access to mental healthcare is especially troubling for First Nations (FN) youth. The ETHS model is rooted in Jordan's Principle-a child first principle developed to eliminate barriers to health and social services, including mental healthcare services for FN youth. The ETHS model takes an innovative approach, using both traditional clinical methods of service delivery (e.g., direct intervention and face-to-face interactions with clinicians) as well as novel strategies (e.g., delivery of services using telehealth) to provide care for youth in their FN communities. The model includes building community capacity as well as educating community service providers to develop sustainable mental healthcare services that are rooted in FN communities and responds to the needs of FN youth and their families. The evaluation of the ETHS model will adopt a child/family-centred approach and integrate multiple methods such as a review of available data, qualitative exploration across multiple levels (e.g., youth, family, community), and arts-based methods.

column37: Nobody knows yet why strict blood sugar control (aiming for lower blood sugar levels) prevents heart disease in some people with type 2 diabetes but can cause harm in others. It makes it hard for patients with type 2 diabetes and their doctors to plan their blood sugar goals. Our team has been working to fill this gap, and we think that the answer may include the form of the blood protein 'haptoglobin' that a person has. Everyone's body makes one of two major haptoglobin forms, and the form can be measured by an inexpensive blood test. We just published a major study in which we used this blood test in participants from a large completed study that had tested strict blood sugar control. We re-analyzed the data in the two haptoglobin groups separately and found that strict blood sugar control prevented heart disease in people with one haptoglobin type, but people with the other type had no heart disease benefit and even had an increased risk of death. We now plan to expand our work to include more: (1) diversity in the people we study (more women, ethnicities, ages, and lengths of time having diabetes), (2) variety in the types of blood sugar control (different blood sugar goals, medications, and lifestyle actions like diet and exercise), and (3) different methods to analyze the data. This research unites us with skilled researchers from four different existing studies of blood sugar control to run the blood test in their studies and re-analyze their data. This is a cost-effective and ethical way to learn whether the haptoglobin type blood test can consistently tell which people will benefit from strict blood sugar control and who will not. It will tell us whether we should further study the blood test with doctors and patients in clinics to personalize their blood sugar control goals. Type 2 diabetes is very common in Canada and worldwide, and so research like ours that aims to better prevent heart disease in people with diabetes could impact millions of people.

Understanding the role of viral infection on the development of SDB will help spur vaccine development and inform vaccine scheduling. Early identification and ultimately preventing childhood SDB will improve childhood neurobehavioral development while optimizing limited sleep testing and surgical resources.

column37: Sepsis is a medical emergency caused by severe infection. Septic shock is the most severe form. More than 25 million children worldwide are diagnosed with sepsis/septic shock every year. The World Health Organization has called for optimized treatments in sepsis. Crystalloid fluid resuscitation is the cornerstone of initial treatment of sepsis. However, there is currently no research that clearly shows which is the most effective and safest type of crystalloid fluid in children. Two types of crystalloids are used for resuscitation in sepsis: balanced fluids (BF) and 0.9% "normal" saline (NS). In the absence of high quality, pediatric-specific data, NS resuscitation remains the overwhelming preference among pediatric emergency clinicians. The objective of this large, pragmatic, randomized study is to test the comparative effectiveness of the two most common types of crystalloid (BF vs NS) to improve clinical outcomes in children treated for septic shock. Thirteen pediatric emergency departments in the Pediatric Emergency Research Canada (PERC) network will collaborate with sites in the United States, Australia, and New Zealand to enroll 8,800 children with suspected septic shock. Children will be randomized to receive fluid resuscitation and maintenance fluids with either NS or BF for 24-48 hours, with all other aspects of care (other than fluid type) at the discretion of the managing health care team. Our primary outcome is major adverse kidney events within 30 days from randomization (MAKE30), a patient-centered endpoint that includes persistent kidney dysfunction, initiation of dialysis, or death. An economic analysis will be completed. The PRoMPT BOLUS study will be the largest trial of pediatric-specific, ED-initiated sepsis management to address the important clinical question of efficacy and safety of crystalloid fluids.

column36: Identifying low bone turnover disease in chronic kidney disease in order to guide anti-fracture therapy
column37: It is now well recognized that people with chronic kidney disease (CKD) have weak bones. However, in contrast to people with osteoporosis, those with CKD have specific types of bone disease that could contraindicate the use of common anti-osteoporotic therapy. Indeed, up to 50% of people with CKD have what we call low bone turnover (LBT) disease (extremely low bone formation and resorption), in which anti-resorptive therapy is not recommended. In those patients, anabolic therapy (to stimulate bone formation) could be given. Identifying LBT disease is therefore of extreme importance if we want to propose adequate bone therapy in CKD patients. Until today, doing a bone biopsy at the iliac crest (anterior part of the hip) remains the only way to diagnose low bone turnover in CKD but is rarely done. Based on our prior works, we hypothesize that non-invasive markers could be used to identify CKD patients with LBT. Our global objective is to identify non-invasive biomarkers that will help in identifying patients with low vs non-LBT so that adequate anti-fracture therapy coud be offered. Methods We will recruit patients with CKD for iliac crest biopsy. We will compare CKD patients with low vs non-LBT. We will evaluate non-invasive biomarkers in the skin (AGEs) and in blood (AGEs, sclerostin, micro-ARNs) that may differentiate CKD patients with low vs non-LBT. Their predictive capacity will be evaluated alone or in combination. Then, Iliac crest biopsy specimens will be evaluated for bone quality parameters (microarchitecture, bone material composition) to evaluate the effects of LBT on bone strength. Significance Bone fragility is a major health issue in patients with CKD. We have a unique opportunity to conduct a bone biopsy study in this population to identify non-invasive markers that may predict LBT disease. Our results have the potential to change clinical practice so that personnalized bone therapy could be offered to CKD population.

column36: Sublingual Fentanyl for acute relief of breathlessness in patients with advanced COPD : A randomized double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover design trial.
column37: According to Health Canada, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) affects over 2 millions of Canadian adults and,with an ageing population , the prevalence of the disease has increased. Breathlessness is the main manifestation of COPD and is often an invalidating symptom for patients with severe disease despite being on optimal inhaled treatment. In fact, the presence of dyspnea is recognized as a major determinant of health-related quality of life and it often leads to unplanned hospitalizations, which result in significant cost on the healthcare system. Breakthrough COPD dyspnea represents an important element in the spectrum of managing breathlessness in COPD patients. Breakthrough COPD dyspnea are acute episodes of breathlessness that could peak in intensity within a few minutes and for which the speed of medication onset is crucial for proper control beyond the use of existing short acting inhaled therapy. Recently, oral morphine was demonstrated as an effective and safe option for the control of refractory breathlessness and is now recommended by clinical guidelines in this context. However, this approach might not always offer optimal onset of action to match the rapid nature of an episode of breakthrough COPD dyspnea. Novel approach that includes the use of small dose sublingual liquid fentanyl might be more effective while remaining safe to treat breakthrough COPD dyspnea. This approach has been shown to be effective for pain control but it has never been tested to treat breakthrough COPD dyspnea. We propose a multicenter randomized trial to evaluate the effect of sublingual fentanyl on breathlessness control in severe to very-severe COPD patients with persistent shortness of breath despite optimal therapy. This study is a crucial step toward appropriate treatment selection for breakthrough COPD dyspnea and it will also pave the way to future research for control of acute refractory breathlessness in other severe respiratory diseases.

column36: Participation in aerobic exercise during stroke rehabilitation: a mixed-methods study
column37: People are often physically unfit early after stroke, which can make participating in therapy and daily activities difficult. Aerobic exercise improves physical fitness and general health, which reduces the risk of another stroke, and also promotes stroke recovery. Aerobic exercise is beneficial and safe even early after stroke. Clinical guidelines recommend completing aerobic exercise within stroke rehabilitation. Most physiotherapists say that they prescribe aerobic exercise to their stroke patients. However, the number of people with stroke who participate in aerobic exercise during rehabilitation is low. We need to understand the barriers to exercise from patient and clinician perspectives so that we can develop interventions to promote exercise participation during stroke rehabilitation. The purpose of this study is to understand what stops or helps people with stroke participating in aerobic exercise during rehabilitation. This study will collect information about patients with stroke who are undergoing rehabilitation at one of four different hospitals. Information collected will include medical history, social supports, physical and cognitive function, and exercise preferences. We will compare characteristics of those who participate in exercise to those who do not. We will also interview patients and their physiotherapists to find out how they feel about exercise during rehabilitation. We will combine the quantitative (statistics) and qualitative information (interviews) to get a complete idea of the problem of exercise participation in stroke rehabilitation. Knowing what prevents or helps people with stroke to participate in exercise during rehabilitation will allow us to create strategies to increase the number of people who participate. These strategies will increase the number of people with stroke who can benefit from this important therapy (aerobic exercise), and can in turn improve recovery and health of those with stroke in the future.

column36: The impact of amyloid-induced neurodegeneration on sleep features and memory processes
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is an age-related neurodegenerative disease that primarily impairs memory for recent facts and events (explicit memory). Loss of connections (synapses) between cells (neurons) in specific brain regions involved in explicit memory, such as the hippocampus, gradually leads to neuronal cell death and induced the progressive cognitive decline that characterises the disease. Since the hippocampus is also involved in other functions such a sleep, some features of sleep are also affected at the onset of the disease, including poor sleep quality, insomnia and early morning wakening. Given the importance of sleep on memory performance, these sleep disturbances have in return a deleterious impact on memory function of AD patients. The main objective of this project is to determine how hippocampal neurodegeneration and sleep disturbances influence each other to impair memory function in the development of AD. We also propose to identify the molecular mechanisms underlying this bidirectional interaction at the onset of the disease. To achieve our goal, we will perform chronic hippocampal injections of amyloid-beta oligomers in animals to mimic cell death and cognitive deficits observed in AD. Electroencephalographic measurements will be performed to determine sleep alterations in these animals. The impact of neurodegeneration and sleep perturbations will be tested on the acquisition and consolidation phases of memory. Identifying the specific signature of hippocampal neurodegeneration on sleep features might serve as a non-invasive marker to refine the diagnosis of AD. A better understanding of the molecular mechanisms underpinning the effects of neurodegeneration and sleep disturbances on cognitive decline in AD could be of great interest to develop new therapeutic targets effective at the onset of the illness before neurodegeneration induces severe memory loss that prevents patients from functioning independently.

column37: Gene defects cause cancer. However, most "cancer causing" gene defects are highly context-specific, and are actually impotent in most cells. The reasons underlying such resistance are poorly understood. Understanding such natural cancer-resistance may expose new therapeutic strategies. Loss of the RB tumor suppressor gene causes retinal and lung cancer, but the gene is typically intact in most cancers. Even in the retina and lung, most cell types are resistant to RB loss. Here, we will extend insight into features that mark susceptibility, ask if they operate in different tissues, and define whether manipulating them prevents cancer.

column36: Allegory-Based Literacy Empowering Youth to Overcome Unhappiness (ABLE YOU): A Stepped Wedge Trial of a Novel Intervention to Promote Coping and Prevent Suicide in Youth
column37: Suicide rates in youth have been increasing over time in Canada and most evidence-based interventions focus on prevention once suicidal behaviour has already occurred. In 2019, it was piloted in students in a rural school board in Eastern Ontario (n=78). Outcome measures are both quantitative (validated questionnaires) and qualitative (focus groups). column36: Traumatic Brain Injury and Perinatal Mental Health Outcomes
column37: In Canada, 2% of the population lives with a traumatic brain injury (TBI), and there are 18,000 hospitalizations for TBI each year. One-third of persons with TBI are women, and TBI is common in young women entering their childbearing years. Women with TBI are more likely than men to have mental health problems post-injury. Yet, little is known about their mental health around the time of pregnancy. This is an important issue because women with TBI may be uniquely at risk for new or worsening mental illness in pregnancy and the postpartum period because of stressors related to sleep deprivation and sensory issues, and the impact of hormonal changes on a vulnerable brain. Our goals are to examine the burden of mental illness among women with TBI before, during, and after pregnancy and the risks of medical problems in the mother and baby during and after pregnancy among women with co-occurring TBI and perinatal mental illness. We will use data collected from Ontario health records to identify all women with a livebirth or stillbirth conceived in 2002-2019. We will compare women with a history of TBI before pregnancy, and those with no such history, on their risks of mental illness diagnoses, mental health service use patterns, and risks of severe mental health outcomes such as self-harm or suicide before, during, and after pregnancy. We will also examine the risks of maternal and newborn medical complications associated with having both TBI and perinatal mental illness. Evidence of an association between TBI and mental illness around the time of pregnancy will lead to the development of health care services that address the unique mental health needs of women with TBI. Given that TBI is a leading cause of disability worldwide, these efforts will result in better outcomes for mothers, infants, and families by providing more responsive support to women with TBI.

column36: CARE NT: Caring and Responding in the Northwest Territories
column37: A major priority of three communities in the Northwest Territories (NT) (Inuvik, Fort Good Hope, and Yellowknife) is improving the experience of patients and access to healthcare services. Residents who require more than basic primary care must travel to services that are only available in regional centres, or in southern provinces. Accessing these services can involve lengthy wait times, as well as long distance travel and time away from home communities, family, and social support networks for weeks at a time. This project will generate new knowledge on the impact of community-led, locally-designed health promotion programs and the importance of utilizing Indigenous methods for implementation, documentation, and dissemination to improve healthcare access and experience with NT communities.

column36: Molecular and Mechanistic Investigations of the Role of Prolactin in Women's Health: A Focus on Breast Morphogenesis and Suppression of Tumorigenesis

column36: The Impact of Nutrient Excess and Neuroinflammation on Hypothalamic Reproductive Neurons.
column37: Reproductive dysfunction is a major health concern, where it is estimated that 16% of the Canadian couples affected. Reproduction is controlled by a number of external factors, which include nutritional status. It is well known that reproductive success is linked to nutritional and metabolic health. Yet the mechanisms by which nutritional status, whether through obesity or anorexia, directly influences the hypothalamic neurons that are responsible for reproduction are not yet studied. Our society has evolved to the state where obesity is prevalent, particularly in women and men of childbearing age. Obesity, mostly due to the ingestion of diets high in saturated fats, has reached epidemic levels in North America. Whether high-fat diet has a direct effect on the neurons responsible for reproductive function can be studied at a number of levels in my laboratory, from the cell to the whole animal, and from rodent models to humans. Exactly how the brain senses nutrients is not yet understood, but it is now recognized that the brain can sense fat and carbohydrates through specific neurons. Interestingly, it has been found that the brain produces an inflammatory response when exposed to high levels of fat. Therefore major efforts are currently underway in my laboratory to dissect the brain pathways involved in sensing nutrients and the development of a low grade chronic inflammatory response in specific reproductive neurons. Whether there is an effect of neuroinflammation on reproductive function will be studied. We are also testing novel therapeutics to try to rescue the function of these neurons at the brain level using anti-inflammatory agents. Our research to explore how excess nutrients contributes to the development of inflammation leading to reproductive disorders is an essential step for development of improved treatment regimens for infertility, obesity, and other related disorders, such as polycystic ovarian syndrome.

column36: Mechanisms of Arterial Stiffening in Calcification
column37: Calcification of arteries occurs in more than 1/2 of the population over the age of 60, and causes significant morbidity and mortality in diseases like atherosclerosis, diabetes, hypertension and in chronic kidney disease. Smooth muscle cells within the arteries deposit minerals in the extracellular matrix, in a process similar to the mineralization and hardening of bones, and this causes thickening, stiffening and sometimes rupture of these vessels. At present, there are no effective medical treatments to prevent or reverse calcification. Furthermore, calcified vessels cannot be angioplastied or stented, the two most common and successful treatments for atherosclerosis and peripheral vascular disease. We have recently discovered that a receptor protein which is expressed on arterial smooth muscle cells is responsible for calcification. This receptor, DDR1, causes a switch in the smooth muscle cells so that they start to behave like bone cells, and deposit minerals (calcifications) in the tissue. We seek to better understand the role of DDR1 in these processes during atherosclerosis and diabetes, and the consequences for normal function of blood vessels. Importantly, we will test a new inhibitor for DDR1 in a mouse model of atherosclerosis, to see if we can inhibit calcification. Most or our work to date has been performed in tissue culture and mouse models. We will now for the first time investigate the expression and function of DDR1 in human diseased arteries. Our hope is that the work will lead to the development of new therapies designed to inactivate DDR1 and therefore prevent the calcification of arteries.

column36: Working together to implement novel, culturally informed early childhood oral health interventions for young First Nations and Metis children in Manitoba
column37: First Nations and Metis Canadians face significant oral health challenges, especially children. This proposal is submitted to continue to work with First Nations and Metis communities in the spirit of Reconciliation to deal with the problem of early childhood caries (ECC) (tooth decay). Past funding from CIHR allowed us to work with four Manitoba communities to tailor the Healthy Smile Happy Child (HSHC) initiative so that it was culturally appropriate. CRA is a promising way to increase access to early childhood dental health assessments and to create dental homes (i.e. clinics where children get ongoing dental care) for children. The main goal of this project is to deal with the problem of ECC experienced by Indigenous children in Manitoba. This will be done in two ways. Objective 1 will add traditional oral health teaching to improve and strengthen the HSHC initiative. We will study changes in parents' attitudes, knowledge and behaviours about ECC and changes in young children's dental health. column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a heterogeneous group of disorders that result in irreversible scarring over time. CKD affects more than 750 million people globally, and results in more than 1 million deaths each year. Large, granular datasets have now been gathered from world leading cohorts in Canada and the United States, with growing expertise to apply novel biomarker combinations collected at different disease time points with clinical traits. In this proposal, we will focus on a leading cause of CKD called Focal and Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and genomics, which is emerging as one tool to identify disease subtypes according to mechanism and treatment outcomes. We have recently reported that a series of rare genetic variations account for ~11% of adults with FSGS, but in the majority of patients, the causes are unknown. We also find that within these genetic cases, different gene categories influence disease progression. However, the cumulative effects of common, subtle variations (called single nucleotide polymorphisms or SNPs) in many genes that are important for normal kidney function have not been explored in FSGS. We will address this critical knowledge gap. By bringing together leading investigators in Canada and the US, we aim to uncover the effects of common genetic determinants, in isolation and cumulatively, important for disease progression in a large cohort of FSGS patients (n=6500). There is a large unmet clinical need for mechanism-based therapy and to achieve this goal, precise definitions of FSGS subtypes are required. Genomics has emerged as one tool to successfully stratify patients with heterogeneous diseases like major depressive disorder, coronary artery disease and cancers such as breast cancer that have, like FSGS, been historically heavily reliant on pathology. We intend to apply these same genomic approaches to identify clinically meaningful FSGS subtypes to inform management.

column37: Worldwide millions of adults (>35,000 Canadians) suffer a hip fracture every year. Hip fractures result in bleeding, inflammation, and stress states that can cause complications and death. There is evidence that early surgical treatment of a hip fracture may improve patients' outcomes, however, standard care in Canada is that most patients wait more than 24 hours to have surgery. Some patients may benefit more from the early surgery than others. Results from the HIP ATTACK-1 trial suggest that patients suffering heart injury (measured by a serum protein called troponin) at the time of a hip fracture have a higher risk of dying within 90 days. Standard care has been to medically manage these patients and postpone surgery; however, the HIP ATTACK-1 trial results suggested that hip fracture patients with heart injury had a lower risk of dying from early surgery as compared to standard care (i.e., surgery typically 24 hours later). Patients with a heart injury just after their hip fracture may reflect patients who are not tolerating the physiological stress of the fracture, and therefore accelerated surgery may reduce the time of heart injury and the risk of mortality. We plan to perform a new study (HIP ATTACK-2) to assess the impact of accelerated surgery (goal of surgery within 6 hours of diagnosis) versus usual timing of surgery on the 90-day risk of death in adults with a hip fracture that have elevated troponin levels after the fracture. We will randomize 1100 patients to receive accelerated surgery or standard care. We will include patients =45 years, with a hip fracture that requires surgery, and have elevated troponin levels on Emergency Room arrival. We will follow patients in hospital, and at 90 days after surgery. This trial will determine if a specific high-risk population should be prioritized with expedited surgical care. This is the first large trial that may change the paradigm to postpone surgery in patients suffering heart injuries before surgery.

column36: Role of trained immunity in the response to BCG immunotherapy of bladder cancer
column37: Bladder cancer is one of the most common cancers worldwide. It is a very serious cancer because it is not easily cured and it substantially lowers the quality of life of those affected. Most patients with higher-risk bladder cancer are treated with surgery followed by a form of immunotherapy. This immunotherapy involves introducing into the bladder of patients the same bacteria that are used to vaccinate people against tuberculosis (TB). For reasons that we do not fully understand, patients given these bacteria mount an immune response that fights the bladder cancer cells and prevents the cancer from coming back. Unfortunately, up to half of the patients do not respond fully to this therapy, and the cancer comes back. Our research aims to better understand how this immunotherapy of bladder cancer works and, in doing so we also hope to determine why some patients don't respond well to it. Knowing which patients will not respond to this treatment is important because such patients could then be offered an alternative therapy that could potentially save their lives and also spare them from the undesirable side effects of the TB immunotherapy. We have obtained results showing that giving the TB vaccine to bladder cancer patients primes and activates some of the more primitive cells of the immune system. Interestingly, these immune cells are found circulating in the blood of these patients, and their activation appears to occur to a larger extent in cancer patients that respond better to the TB vaccine than in poorly responsive or unresponsive patients. We plan to do experiments to investigate how these 'primed and activated' circulating immune cells can lead to rejection of tumour cells in the bladder. Another potential benefit of our proposed research is that it could lead to the development of new ways to treat bladder cancer patients. It could also help us determine whether similar immunotherapies can be used to treat patients with other types of cancer.

column36: Stress and loss of ovarian function: novel insights into the origins and treatment of respiratory control disorders in females
column37: Sleep apnea (SA) affects ~25% of the Canadian population. Respiratory instability and prolonged apneas during sleep indicate that parts of the nervous system regulating breathing are dysfunctional in SA patients. This is clinically important because SA increases the risk of disease, including cardiovascular problems. SA is ~2 times more frequent in men than women, thus indicating that ovarian hormones "protect" against respiratory problems. However, this ratio changes as women age and it is estimated that SA affects nearly half of post-menopausal women. Since loss of ovarian function is a normal part of life, this project aims to explain why menopause results in respiratory problems and hypertension in some women but not others. Because experiencing stress during early life affects brain development and increases vulnerability to disease, we propose that the consequences of menopause on respiratory function are aggravated by neonatal stress. Thus, the impact of early life stress on the cardiorespiratory system becomes apparent with loss of ovarian function. We will address this fundamental issue in female rats exposed to stress during early life. This model reproduces abnormalities in respiratory function and hypertension; in females, SA-related symptoms become apparent following loss of ovarian function. Experiments will be performed in the intact, naturally sleeping rats. We will then delve into the underlying mechanisms by quantifying the consequences of loss of ovarian function on the sensory, central, and neuroendocrine components of the respiratory control system of rats raised under normal conditions or subjected to neonatal stress in the form of neonatal maternal separation. As the Canadian population is aging, understanding the basic principles explaining such divergences in the aging trajectory of women is becoming urgent. This proposal offers a novel and comprehensive approach to an important health issue that affects a growing proportion of Canadians.

column36: Sleep and Circadian Misalignment and their Relation to Cardiometabolic Health during Adolescence
column37: Humans have a built-in circadian rhythm (body clock) that repeats every 24-hrs. It tells our bodies when we should be awake or asleep and it stays on time by using information from the environment around us, like light, regularly timed meals, and activity. The body clock controls the rhythms of most functions including body temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, and hormone release. Sometimes the timing of these bodily functions gets disrupted and out of sync with the rhythm of the body clock, which is called circadian misalignment (e.g., bed/wake times shifts later). Teenagers experience many changes in the timing of their sleep. Teens commonly go to bed later and sleep in on the weekends. Our 24hr society promotes this later sleep delay. Using gadgets late at night, staying up late on weekends, and having inconsistent routines across the week can contribute to this shift toward later sleep timing. Shifts in sleep times often happen during puberty. Girls start going to bed later before boys, which coincides with their earlier puberty onset than boys. In fact, compared to adults, teenagers have a body clock slightly longer than 24 hours. Our project tracks the evolution of the circadian timing system changes across puberty. We will investigate if circadian misalignment might be a culprit in child obesity and cardiometabolic health. Wearable gadgets will be worn by teens to monitor their sleep, activity, temperature, heart rate, and blood pressure. The information we learn from this project will help parents, schools, and policy makers develop better prevention programs to improve childhood health. We also help science make technology smarter so wearable gadgets can give more accurate information about bodily rhythms.

column36: Predicting and Evaluating Anal Cancer in HIV with novel biomarkers: The PEACH Study
column37: Though there have been many improvements in the health of those living with HIV since the mid 1990s when effective therapies first emerged including reductions in AIDS-associated cancers, there have been increases in other types of cancer since that time. HPV is the main cause of anal cancer, and gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM) have rates of anal cancer up to 100 times higher than the general population. Despite this, there are currently no clear guidelines for anal cancer screening in gbMSM living with HIV, the currently available screening tools do not perform particularly well, and there are very few clinics and health care providers trained in providing these services. As such, there is an urgent need to investigate ways to better provide anal cancer screening to this at-risk population. One of the ways to do this is to develop and examine different tests that can predict the presence of lesions in the anal canal that may lead to cancer (called high-grade dysplasia, or anal precancers). These are called biomarkers, and there are several that have not been adequately examined as possible predictors of anal cancers and pre-cancers in gbMSM living with HIV. The proposed study will recruit participants from an existing set of Canadian studies to examine these novel biomarkers as predictors of anal pre-cancers.

column36: Characterization of oncogenic splicing pathways driven by RNA-binding proteins
column37: Genes can produce multiple distinct products through a process called "RNA splicing". The normal splicing pattern of genes is often disrupted in cancer, and many of the molecules that result from this abnormal splicing have been functionally implicated in cancer malignancy. However, the underlying cellular mechanisms that govern RNA splicing and the extent to which they play a role in cancer progression remain largely unknown. To address this challenge, we have developed new computational frameworks that, in combination with large-scale genomics data, can identify novel factors that are involved in RNA splicing. Using this approach, we have discovered and partly characterized a previously unknown RNA element that drives abnormal splicing in highly metastatic breast cancer. We have also identified the associated protein that interacts with this novel RNA element - through this interaction, this protein can change the splicing of gene products and lead to metastasis. Our studies also indicate that the role of this protein is not limited to breast cancer, and it may in fact be involved in multiple other cancer types. In this project, we will build on these recent developments to perform a detailed dissection of RNA splicing programs across different cancers, identify the genes that are modified as a result of abnormal splicing, cellular and molecular deficits that drive abnormal splicing, and their contribution to cancer development, progression, and metastasis. This study will enable us to obtain a better understanding of how the cellular behaviour and function changes in cancer and how tumour cells become metastatic, and may lead to new avenues for development of therapeutic strategies.

column37: Prostate and breast cancer are the most common cancers for Canadians, at 20.7% and 25.5% of men's and women's cancers, respectively. Radiation therapy (RT) is a preferred treatment modality, either alone or combined, for 50% of cancer patients. In recent years, technological developments have enabled RT to accomplish significant advances in the local control of various cancer sites; 40% of cancers are cured by RT, compared to 49% by surgery and 11% by chemotherapy (2010 IAEA report). As such, RT remains a formidable, and very affordable, weapon in the fight against cancer. One RT approach is low-dose-rate brachytherapy that using permanently implanted mm-size sources. These procedures are usually performed as a 1-day outpatient procedures. It provides a well-tolerated treatment with a good therapeutic ratio. Accurate knowledge of dose-outcome relationships is critical to success in radiation therapy. Despite the overall good results clinically, a critical barrier to progress in further advancing brachytherapy treatments is the inaccuracy of dose evaluations which lead to a major disconnect between clinically-measured outcomes and "accurate" dose distributions. The assembled team comprised of world-experts in state-of-the-art dose calculations as well as world-leading brachytherapy physicians from all major programs across Canada comes together to tackle this problem. The proposed research will provide more accurate knowledge of prescription doses needed for relapse-free survival as well as a better understanding of radiation toxicity thresholds. It has the potential to further improve tumour control while reducing the incidence and severity of complications, thus enhancing patient quality of life and reducing healthcare costs: simply put improving the therapeutic ratio of BT treatments of prostate and breast cancer.

column37: Globally, syphilis, chlamydia and gonorrhea are three of the most common sexually transmitted infections (STI). Over the last decade, these STIs have seen a resurgence in many parts of the world, including Canada, with the bulk of infections seen in major urban centres. More recently, these increases have been even more significant, with a 150% increase in these infections in Canada between 2014-2018. These infections have primarily affected gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM). Further, HIV-positive gbMSM are disproportionately affected by many STIs. In addition to playing a role in the enhanced transmission of HIV, STIs also place individuals living with HIV at higher risk of complications and more severe disease. A few years ago, a small pilot study found that doxycycline - an inexpensive, well-tolerated antibiotic - given daily may prevent new STIs in HIV-positive gbMSM. More recently, another study looked at the use of one dose of doxycycline given after a sexual encounter for prevention of STIs, and the results of this study demonstrated protection against STIs as well. Based on these promising data, along with the concerning increases in these STIs, the current study will examine the use of doxycycline as either a daily preventative therapy (preexposure prophylaxis, or PrEP) or an 'after sex' prevention tool (postexposure prophylaxis, or PEP) for STIs in gbMSM living with HIV. While examining for efficacy as its primary goal, this study will also do a thorough examination of some of the potential challenges and concerns associated with the use of a daily antibiotic: drug resistance, tolerability and side effects, and how acceptable this drug is for people to take regularly.
