column36: Targeting Sensory Dysfunctions in Autism Spectrum Disorders
column37: Autism and sensory processing challenges often occurred together, and affected individuals might experience 'hyper or hypo' reactivity to sensory input or unusual interests in sensory aspects of the environment. These sensory differences can affect behavior and learning. Sensory function is regulated by the sensory nervous system, which is a part of the peripheral nervous system (PNS) in the body. Over the past decades, independent lines of clinical and basic research have supported the hypothesis that dysregulation of the sensory system is part of the core symptomatology of ASD. For a long time, it was thought that sensory issues in autism were due to disruption of the central nervous system. However, there is emerging evidence that sensory processing disorders in autism arise due to the abnormal function of the sensory nervous system. In our study, our team is studying whether 3 established high risk genetic factors for autism cause sensory dysfunction. We believe that mutations FMRP, CYFIP1 and TAOK2 impair sensory nerve cell development by disrupting the production of important proteins required for electrical communication. To study this, our team will utilize a combination of model systems, including genetically engineered flies, mice, and stem cell-derived human sensory neurons. We will perform behavioral experiments to identify the sensory defects (eg. smell and touch). Further, we will test whether the production of proteins in neural cells is abnormal. Finally, we will test whether specific drugs and gene therapies that correct the abnormal protein production defects, will lead to a reversal of the sensory behavioral deficits in our animal models. Together, these studies will reveal a new line of scientific evidence that genetic mutations impair protein production in sensory neural cells, which ultimately leads to sensory deficits. Our study would open up new possibilities for treating sensory abnormalities related to ASD.

column36: Developing BBB-ASL as non-invasive early biomarker of Alzheimer's disease (DEBBIE)
column37: One of the earliest signs of Alzheimer's Disease is the loss of the Blood-Brain-Barrier (BBB) integrity in the brain's vascular system, which can be imaged with positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). While most methods require contrast agents, arterial spin labeling (ASL) is an MRI technique for non-invasive measurement of perfusion and change in the vascular permeability or BBB integrity. ASL is currently the only technique for mapping local changes in BBB integrity without the use of contrast-enhancing agents or radioactive tracers. However, for BBB integrity measurement it cannot be used reliably in a clinical setting due to often rather long scan times and sensitivity to patient-specific dynamic changes in blood flow. We propose to develop a robust ASL BBB integrity mapping technique by using novel innovative concepts to automatically adapt relevant MRI scan parameters to the patient's dynamic blood flow status at scan time. Combined with standardized image processing, this will provide a sensitive non-invasive biomarker/predictor of cognitive decline. The newly developed imaging technology will be validated against established BBB invasive technique (PET) and evaluated on patients at four clinical sites.

column36: NEURofeedback for self-stimulation of the brain as therapy for ParkInson DisEaSe (NEURIPIDES)
column37: We will develop a new type of treatment for Parkinson's disease (PD) based on neurofeedback. Neurofeedback is a type of treatment that allows people to see their own brain activity in real time, so that they can learn how to control and self-regulate it. Existing PD treatments are not effective for certain symptoms, and can also require brain surgery. Therefore, new treatments that address these problems are needed. Our project will take place over 3 stages: In stage 1, we will find out what the brain activity of people with PD looks like when their symptoms are well controlled. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a type of brain surgery that is able to give many people with PD good symptom relief. Using an imaging tool called functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), we will see what the brain activity of people with PD who have successfully received DBS looks like. We will find patterns of brain activity associated with PD patients who have improved their i) motor symptoms (such as tremor, slowness, or stiffness), and ii) non-motor symptoms (such as their mood, memory, or attention). In stage 2, we will develop a neurofeedback system for people with PD. They will be able to see their own brain activity in real time, and will try to match it to the patterns of good brain activity we find in stage 1 in order to improve their symptoms. In stage 3, we will perform a trial - taking place at multiple hospitals in different countries - of our neurofeedback system to see whether it can help improve the symptoms of people with PD. Our hope is that we will develop a new type of treatment for PD that does not require brain surgery. We believe that it will be able to help patients who have never received DBS, and patients who have had DBS but could benefit from more symptom relief.

Research shows much promise in using video games to help older adults train their bodies and brains via so-called exergames (game-based exercise training). We will focus on designing the ExerG's graphics and audio, and whether or how to include their therapists to make sure older adults have a good experience when they use the ExerG. We will also make sure that the ExerG is easy and fun to use for anyone. The ExerCube will also be remodelled to include hardware like a harness that is mounted from the ceiling - with this safety harness; older adults will not be able to fall over during training in the ExerG. The final goal is to create a working prototype that older adults enjoy and test it in user studies. The result can then be turned into a certified product for the market of tools that help keep older adults fit and healthy. We will communicate our study results-focused on the design of this training tool for older adults-to the public through web sites, social media, research publications, and exhibitions.

column36: Identifying patient-specific behaviors to understand illness trajectories and to predict relapses in bipolar disorder using passive sensing and pattern recognition
column37: What do we want to do? The overall objective of this study is to characterize illness trajectories and to predict relapses in stable adult patients with Bipolar Disorder (BD). Specifically, we aim to develop new data modeling that will enable more tailored signal detection to examine changes within each individual over time, to predict a future episode of illness. Our preliminary studies relevant to this proposal include those related to using nonlinear techniques (time-series analysis and entropy) to understand how mood is regulated in healthy controls, bipolar patients and their relatives; as well as our ongoing study analyzing heart rate variability and clinical characteristics in BD patients during different phases of their illness (stable, depressed, hypomanic or mixed). How are we going to do it? We will collect data using passive sensing (Oura ring), including sleep, activity and heart rate variability, in 200 BD patients. This ring measures these variables continuously, so we will have a large amount of data. These data will be combined with a detailed description of the clinical course of illness in each patient. Then, we will use nonlinear techniques to obtain an individualized measure of variability (entropy levels) in each participant. Finally, we will feed these entropy levels for each participant into a machine-learning technique called Markov Brains to distinguish those at a higher risk of relapse. Why is this important? Because BD is a complex and heterogeneous illness. This means that we cannot assume that all depressive episodes or all manic episodes will look the same in all patients diagnosed with BD. column36: Refining the molecular endotypes for precision medicine of osteoarthritis
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA), the most common form of arthritis, is expected to affect 130 million people symptomatically worldwide and 40 million will be severely disabled by 2050. However, there is no cure for it yet. The biggest challenge to develop OA drugs is the wide heterogeneity of the disease. It is now recognized that OA is a nebula of several diseases, but we do not have markers to differentiate them yet. Several clinical classifications of OA have been proposed based on the OA risk factors and joint magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment. These classifications improved our knowledge in the etiologies of OA but failed to subset the disease which results in inconsistent response to treatments. We performed metabolomic studies (study of small chemical compounds present in body fluids) on plasma and joint fluid samples obtained from OA patients and healthy controls and found at least three subtypes of OA characterized by different markers, implicating different metabolic pathways involved in OA. These markers have potential to be used to better stratify OA patients for clinical trials and developing personalized medicine tools. We now propose to confirm the findings and refine the markers and related pathways for each of the subtypes of OA by integrating genomics (study of all the genes) and metabolomics in three existing cohorts - the Newfoundland Osteoarthritis Study (NFOAS) as the discovery cohort (n=1113), the Longitudinal Evaluation in the Arthritis Program, Osteoarthritis Study (LEAP OA; n=900) and the Tasmania Older Adult Cohort Study (TASOAC; n=568) as the validation cohorts. The study will identify molecular subtypes of OA. It will help inform a better understanding of the etiologies of OA, provide tools to better stratify OA patients for clinical trials, and develop personalized medicine tools for OA management.

column36: Role of vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation in beta cell and diabetes
column37: Vitamin K is an essential micronutrient known to regulate blood coagulation and bones. Recent clinical observations in humans suggest that partial vitamin K deficiency might be linked to the development of diabetes. Diabetes is caused by a reduction in the number of beta cells or by a decrease in their capacity to secrete insulin. This research project aims at understanding the function of vitamin K-dependent proteins in pancreatic beta cells and its potential link with the development of diabetes. Our approach includes the use of genetically modified mice lacking the components of the vitamin K cycle in pancreatic beta cells. We will analyze these animals to determine the role of vitamin K in protecting beta cells from cell death, and in promoting their proliferation and function. We will also study the interaction between vitamin K and the capacity of human and mouse beta cells to respond to stress. Finally, we will test if vitamin K can improve or prevent diabetes in pre-clinical mouse models. Altogether, these studies will allow us to understand how vitamin K is implicated in the biology of beta cell and how partial vitamin K deficiency contributes to the development of diabetes.

column36: Hematopoietic stem cell sequelae in fetuses and offspring exposed to in utero Zika infection
column37: Zika virus (ZIKV) emerged in the Americas in 2015 and posed ongoing public health concerns. The outcomes of ZIKV infection are fetal death, brain lesions, and life-long impairment in children. Alarmingly, the majority of fetal infections are mild with no easily identifiable birth defects; however, later health complications in initially asymptomatic ZIKV-affected offspring were demonstrated in our animal model studies and studies in humans. It is not known, however, how abnormalities acquired during fetal infection are sustained and endure in offspring. Our preliminary studies suggest that mild ZIKV infection in fetuses causes systemic inflammation deteriorating fetal hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs)-long-living cells that maintain the immune system for the life span. Fetal HSCs affected during a developmental period in the maternal womb may sustain acquired pathology after birth causing long-term HSC abnormalities and enduring dysfunction of immunity in offspring. We will use state-of-the-art molecular techniques and advanced large animal models to understand better how ZIKV affects HSCs and their ability to maintain the immune system. A better understanding of long-term effects caused by mild in utero infection will support the development of therapeutic strategies. Importantly, in addition to ZIKV infection, the new knowledge may be applied to other viruses that are known to cause mild fetal infections. Our studies may help to reduce health sequelae in offspring and treatment required after birth. It will be highly-rewarding for patients, families, and society and will decrease the social and economic burden associated with congenital infections.

column36: Role of Female Sex Hormones on Aging in Women Living with HIV.
column37: In Canada as of 2019, a woman's life expectancy is 4 years longer than a man's. However, when a woman is HIV-positive, not only is her life expectancy 5-10 years shorter than other women her age who do not live with HIV, but it is also 7 years less than that of a man who is HIV-positive. This may be related to changes in levels of sex and stress hormones that when normal would protect a woman's bones, heart and other organs. Women who live with HIV more often have a history of having menstrual periods that are not regular or went away entirely for a while. They also reach menopause earlier than women without HIV. These changes are associated with women having more difficulty with kidney, bone and liver disease, and with abnormal cholesterol and blood sugar levels. Thus, women who have HIV and have a history of abnormal menstrual periods may have an increased risk of several diseases of aging and at an earlier age. Here we aim to determine how abnormal menstrual periods and hormone levels affect and are affected by social factors and gender inequity to have an effect on diseases of aging and the reproductive health of women living with HIV. With this information we can improve care for women and in so doing prevent disease, and promote healthy aging.

column36: Epigenomic changes trigger a decline in uterine function and reproductive health in females of advanced maternal age
column37: The first most acute sign of advancing age experienced by women is a decline in fertility. Maternal age not only affects the risk of having a baby with chromosomal abnormalities (such as Down's syndrome), but also increases the frequency of suffering from various pregnancy complications such as pre-eclampsia or preterm birth. The reason why these latter complications are more prevalent in older women is not well understood, as they are not commonly associated with chromosomal defects of the baby. Advanced maternal age is an immense societal challenge as many women delay child bearing until later in their lives, with now well over 20% of babies born to women over 35 in Canada. Therefore it is extremely important to gain better insights into why these complications increase with age, and explore potential therapeutic avenues that may help mitigate this risk. Using the mouse as a model to study how age affects pregnancy outcome, we have found that the cells lining the womb (the so-called endometrium) undergo a significant decline in their ability to support pregnancy with age. Similar changes likely affect pregnancy in older women. These defects correlate with widespread changes to the regulatory layer of information that is imposed onto DNA (known as the epigenome) that controls which genes can be switched on and off. In aged cells many important genes have an altered epigenetic signature, which prevents them from being activated at the right time. In this proposal, we are aiming to gain fundamental novel insights into the precise nature and progression of these epigenetic alterations and how they affect endometrial cell function. This study will help elucidate why the womb is less capable of adapting to pregnancy in older females, and explore potential avenues how these changes can be prevented or reversed. This knowledge forms the stepping stone for future therapeutic interventions aimed at diminishing the risk of pregnancy complications in women of advanced age.

This could dramatically decrease the risks of undesirable and unexpected cancer progression, and anxieties related to being on a cancer surveillance program. Further, the intensity of invasive and costly sequential prostate biopsies can be reduced in low-risk patients, leading to a better quality of life and decreased health care utilization.

column36: Lysine polyphosphorylation as a regulator of bacterial stress
column37: Polyphosphates are considered to be ancient molecules found in the cells of all organisms on earth - from bacteria to humans, and everywhere in between. In this exciting new project, we will figure out how polyphosphates protect bacteria from stress by focusing on new functions for this interesting molecule. Specifically, we are interested in the way that polyphosphate interacts with proteins that are important for bacterial survival. Our work employs cutting edge techniques that allow us to look directly at proteins from the bacteria. These collaborations will facilitate completion of our objectives in a timely manner. In the long term, our work will reveal new targets for therapeutic intervention.

column37: Cancer is the most common cause of disease-related death among adolescents and young adults (AYA). Despite this, their chances of survival have not improved as much as those of younger or older patients. AYA with brain tumours are particularly vulnerable. Treatment approaches to childhood and adult brain tumours differ. We do not yet know which of these approaches is better for AYA. Also, cancer care for AYA is spread across many centres, so that many are treated by doctors who do not have much expertise specifically in AYA cancer. We therefore want to build a comprehensive database of all AYA diagnosed with any brain tumour between the ages of 15 years to 29 years in Ontario between 1992-2017 (called the IMPACT-CNS Cohort). We will also link this information to healthcare databases that can identify all hospitalizations, visits to doctors, and visits to the emergency room. We will then use this database to answer different questions about the care for these patients. First, we will determine what treatments AYA with brain tumours received, what determined who got which treatment, and whether different treatments were associated with different chances of survival. Second, we will look at the long-term side-effects these patients experience, including things like hearing loss or developing another cancer. Finally, for those AYA who die, we will examine what kind of care was received before death. Together, the answers to these questions may tell us what we can do to better improve outcomes for AYA with brain tumours at different phases of the cancer journey. The IMPACT-CNS Cohort will also be available in the future for any scientist who wants to improve outcomes for these patients.

column37: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by social communication impairment and the presence of repetitive behaviours and activities. ASD affects 1.52% of Canadian children and youth resulting in emotional and economic burden on the family and intensive resource support in the health care system. Children and youth with ASD often present with co morbid impairments in self-regulation (e.g., managing emotions) resulting in unhelpful regulatory approaches such as disruptive behaviours. Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) is a safe and tolerable intervention that has shown promise for the reduction of disruptive behaviours in youth with ASD. However, previous studies have been limited by small and poorly represented samples, lack of experimental control, insufficient follow-up periods, inadequate blinding and the absence of neural outcome measures. Our project will evaluate if it is feasible, tolerable and acceptable to carry out a randomized control trial to determine if rTMS therapy can reduce disruptive behaviours in children with ASD compared to sham-control in order to inform the design of a follow-up full-scale clinical trial. We will recruit children with ASD who experience clinically significant difficulties with self-regulation and disruptive behaviour. We will measure recruitment and attrition of participants and adherence to the treatment and outcomes measurement protocols. We will collect data to estimate the probable effect of rTMS on clinical improvements in self-regulation and disruptive behaviours. Given the high frequency of debilitating self-regulation problems in youth with ASD, and how little is known about rTMS treatment response in these youth, our research is critically important to inform clinical practice in Canada and internationally.

column37: Cardiomyopathy is a genetic disease of heart muscle and the leading cause of heart failure and sudden cardiac death in children. It is inherited in families in at least a third of cases. Despite availability of genetic testing, the genetic cause of the majority of cardiomyopathies remains unknown since current tests only look for defects in a small number of known genes in the genome that code for proteins important in heart structure and function. Whole genome sequencing allows a search for defects in previously unexplored genes i.e. non-coding regions of the genome that control amount of gene and protein available. Using whole genome sequencing, we identified new genomic defects (or mutations) not previously reported in patients with cardiomyopathy. The purpose of this project is to test the effect of these mutations in heart cells from patients with these defects to determine if they negatively affect the function of heart cells similar to patients with cardiomyopathy. Also, using gene-editing, we will correct the mutations in these cells to see if they rescue the disease. We will use these cells to test which drugs can improve the function of the heart cells. By showing that these novel mutations cause cardiomyopathy, our study will improve the understanding of the genetic basis of cardiomyopathies. It will also help genetic testing laboratories to expand their genetic tests to include a search for novel variants in non-coding regions of the genome. Identifying the genetic cause of disease in more patients will help us to offer genetic screening to a greater number of affected families which will allow earlier diagnosis and timely interventions in family members to prevent sudden death and progression to heart failure. Results of our drug tests will provide insights into new drug development for this serious condition.

column36: Development of a validated method to identify patients with chronic pain in electronic medical records and administrative health data to advance clinical research and patient care
column37: One in five Canadians lives with chronic pain, which is pain that is persistent or recurring for three or more months. Caring for patients with chronic pain costs more than cardiovascular disease, cancer or diabetes. The recent opioid crisis has highlighted a need to improve the care of people with chronic pain; chronic pain is now being recognized as a public health crisis and comprehensive, population-based strategies are being developed to improve the care these patients need. Two sources of data, electronic medical records (EMR) and administrative health data, provide opportunities to facilitate improvements for chronic pain sufferers in Canada. An EMR is essentially a digital version of the traditional, paper-based medical record for a patient and these data, particularly from primary care, provide rich insight into a patient's health. Administrative health data captures all visits to the healthcare system that are covered by publicly funded health insurance (i.e. the Ontario Health Insurance Program [OHIP]). Currently there is no reliable method to identify chronic pain patients in these types of data. To date, research has relied on patient self-report of pain. We will develop accurate methods to identify patients with chronic pain in both primary care EMR data and administrative health data. We know that chronic pain affects men and women differently, so we will ensure that the methods we develop work equally well to identify pain in both men and women. Using these methods, we will study the healthcare needs of patients with chronic pain. This project will provide valuable information about the burden of chronic pain and help to inform an evolving national pain strategy. The development of valid methods to identify chronic pain in EHR and administrative health data has implications for clinical research, patient care and health policy.

column36: Capillary stalling and hypoxic micropockets: two sides of the same phenomena?
column37: Dementia and its onset is a multifaceted phenomenon but an increasing number of clues point to the human plumbing system, the vasculature, as a key participant in the disease. Identifying how plumbing problems contribute to dementia is crucial since it could open new approaches to cure vascular disease induced dementia such as lifestyle changes and through the use of drugs targeting and approved for vascular diseases. In this project we aim to investigate a novel phenomena observed in the smallest pipes in our body: the capillaries. Recent work has shown that some specific cells in the blood stream can 'plug' brain capillaries leading to less efficient blood flow. Since blood carries oxygen, reducing flow has the potential to damage the brain through oxygen reductions, its main nutrient. In parallel we recently measured oxygen directly in the brain and saw small islands of low oxygen in tissue that could indeed lead to brain damage. The objective of this project is to answer the question: are plugged capillaries and localized zones of oxygen reductions two sides of the same phenomenon?

column36: Evaluating the psychometric properties and help-seeking impact of HEARTSMAP-U: a digital psychosocial self-assessment and navigational support application for post-secondary students.
column37: Each year, thousands of post-secondary students in Canada experience mental health issues. Many students do not seek timely help because they are unaware of their needs, or find it too challenging to get support. Previously, we developed a web application, called MyHEARTSMAP, for screening of psychological (mood, thoughts) and social wellness (housing, relationships) in children. We have since, modified MyHEARTSMAP into HEARTSMAP-to allow university students to self-check their own wellbeing and get directions to timely support that meets their psychological and social needs, without having to book an in-person appointment. In this study, we will compare how accurately HEARTSMAP-U identifies social and psychological issues compared to a clinician assessment, the current gold-standard. Our study aims to recruit 580 students at the University of British Columbia over three years. We will work closely with university administration and student organizations to ensure our work sensitively and meaningfully involves students, with efforts to ensure diverse engagement (sex, gender, race/ethnicity, sexual orientation). First, students will use HEARTSMAP-U to self-check their own wellbeing, then they will be assessed by a trained clinician. We will compare the results of the assessments to determine the accuracy of the HEARTSMAP-U app. Three months later, we will repeat these procedures to see if HEARTSMAP-U is able to detect changes in wellbeing over time. We will also ask students about their experiences using mental health supports to explore how using HEARTSMAP-U affects accessibility and usability of these resources. We anticipate that HEARTSMAP-U will be as good as the clinician's assessment and facilitate students' access and use of mental health resources. Our UBC and student network partners will help put our findings to practice through implementation of HEARTSMAP-U to empower students to check for psychological and social difficulties and access timely support.

column36: L-asparaginase-induced mechanisms of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (aLL) cell apoptosis
column37: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (aLL) is a devastating cancer of immature white blood cells called lymphoblasts. It largely affects children, representing more than a quarter of all childhood cancers, and causing most of the death from cancer among children. L-asparaginase (ASNase) is a key component of aLL chemotherapy, but how ASNase kills aLL cells remains undefined. Our recent studies point to proteins designated as PAR2 and OPRM1 as cell signaling pathways through which ASNase causes aLL cell death. PAR2 and OPRM1 have been separately implicated to trigger an increase in cell calcium, which at overwhelming levels cause cell death. It is not known how ASNase interacts with PAR2 and OPRM1 to induce aLL cell death, but our preliminary studies suggest that ASNase cleaves PAR2 and binds OPRM1. Thus, our hypothesis is that ASNase kills aLL cells by disrupting calcium homeostasis through activation of PAR2 and OPRM1 via cleavage and binding, respectively. We will employ our expertise in cell signaling and calcium dynamics to address our objective to elucidate ASNase activation and regulation of the PAR2 and OPRM1 signaling pathways that lead to the disruption of calcium homeostasis and subsequent death of aLL cells. Our specific aims are: first, to investigate the involvement of PAR2 in ASNase-induced cell death; second, to determine how ASNase activates and regulates the OPRM1 pathway that leads to cell death; and third, to examine how convergence of the PAR2 and OPRM1 pathways disturbs calcium dynamics and causes aLL cell death. Altogether, our findings could provide insight into the development of novel therapeutics for aLL.

column36: Mechanisms by which stress-adaptive transcription factors guard against obesity-linked fatty liver disease
column37: Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is an obesity-linked metabolic disorder that affects >25% of adults in Canada. Most people with NAFLD have a benign case of simple steatosis (excess fat storage in liver) but an estimated 1 million Canadians will progress to a more severe pathology called non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), which is characterized by steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis of the liver. NASH is the leading cause of liver failure and liver cancer and also contributes to cardiovascular complications such as heart failure and stroke. In obesity, a key determinant underlying NASH and its detrimental impact on health is the capacity of the liver to resist the metabolic stress imposed by excess levels of cholesterol and its metabolic product bile, which promote liver cell damage and inflammation. Hence, there is an important role for therapeutics that are specifically designed to enhance the capacity of liver to manage elevated metabolism of cholesterol and bile. In our proposed research, we will investigate the mechanisms by which a pair of evolutionarily conserved stress-adaptive transcription factors named NRF1 & NRF2 regulate metabolic, stress, and inflammatory processes to promote resistance to the stress of elevated cholesterol and bile in liver during obesity. Our goal is to determine whether NRF1 & NRF2 work independently or in a coordinated manner to engage adaptive countermeasures and whether these actions are capable of resolving liver cell damage and inflammation caused by excess cholesterol & bile. We will also test whether stimulating these transcription factors may be an effective strategy to treat NASH in obesity. We anticipate these findings will be relevant for the large & growing population of Canadians with obesity who are at risk for NASH and its consequential impact on liver failure, liver cancer, heart failure and stroke.

column36: Neuroimaging of disease progression and tauopathy in temporal lobe epilepsy
column37: Epilepsy is one of the most common neurological disorders. While antiepileptic drugs can control the seizures in many patients, 30-40% of patients are drug-resistant. Furthermore, many patients present with cognitive deficits, affecting functioning and wellbeing. Epilepsy surgery is currently the most effective treatment to control the seizures and to improve quality of life in drug-resistant patients. However, many do not undergo this procedure (as they are not offered surgery, or decide against it), and some only do so after decades. While epilepsy is still widely considered a 'static' disorder, mounting evidence indicates that the adverse clinical and cognitive effects of the disease aggravate over time. Our project will examine disease progression in temporal lobe epilepsy, the most common drug-resistant epilepsy in adults. Building on findings in brain tissue of patients that underwent epilepsy surgery, we will test the role of misfolded tau protein in disease progression. Accumulation of tau is commonly seen in Alzheimer's Disease, and closely associated with neurodegeneration and dementia. Our project will capitalize on novel neuroimaging techniques to measure tau in the brain. We will examine whether tau is elevated in epileptic patients compared to controls and assess relations to brain atrophy and cognitive decline. Patients and controls will be longitudinally re-assessed with the same protocols, and we will test whether increases in tau and atrophy in patients relate to cognitive trajectories. We will enroll drug-resistant and well-controlled patients, to ascertain the potential modulation of progression by seizures. Finally, we will assess whether tau measures predict future cognitive function in patients undergoing and not undergoing epilepsy surgery. Our project will provide novel insights into progressive brain changes in epilepsy, their contribution to cognitive decline, and the modulation of this process through seizures and tau accumulation.

column36: Microglia as a viral reservoir for HIV-1 in the human brain and its role in neuroinflammation
column37: The combined antiretroviral therapy (cART) has significantly improved the prognosis of individuals infected with HIV-1 and increased their life expectancy. However, up to 50% of patients suffer from a broad variety of neurological problems better known as HIV-1-associated neurological disorders (HAND). These disorders are caused by some inflammation in the brain which provoke neuron death. HIV-1 infects brain immune cells called microglia, which can survive for years, producing viral proteins and other substances that are toxic for neurons. Current therapies cannot cure HIV-1 infection because to virus hides in some cells in a latent form, and new types of drugs are being evaluated that can force the virus out of its latent state so the cells can be recognized and killed by the immune system, while other therapies are aimed at locking the virus in its latent state. Our studies are aimed at a better understanding of how HIV-1-infected microglia cause inflammation and neurodegeneration, and what can be the consequences of the new drugs on HIV-1-associated brain disorders.

column36: Molecular characterization of newly identified silicon transporters in animals
column37: There are several lines of evidence to suggest that silicon (Si) is important for the proper functioning of many tissues. In particular, Si is believed to provide resiliency to bone and prevent the premature aging of arteries, that is, of atherosclerosis. We have recently identified Si transporters in human for the first time and feel that this discovery should enable us to study the biological role of Si in much greater detail than before. The purpose of our proposal will be in fact to determine the functional and operational characteristics of the recently uncovered Si transporters. One group of transporters is called the aquaglyceroporins. These proteins are also specialized in the facilitated movement of water and alternative substrates such as urea into and/or out of cells. The other group includes transporters of unknown function and is called organic anion exchanger "x". The purpose of our proposal will also be to determine the biological relevance of Si transport by these proteins in Si-rich tissues such as bone and the arterial vessel wall. Our main research questions will be addressed by carrying out transport studies in primary culture cells derived from bone tissues and arterial conduits as well as physiological studies in isolated arterial vessels, bone explants and whole animals. We should be able to show that when isolated cells and tissues are deprived of Si through various means, their normal responses to a variety of environmental cues are perturbed. We should also be able to show that the changes observed translate into deleterious abnormalities in vivo. Through the efforts proposed, our hope is to identify novel molecular targets for the prevention of common diseases such as osteoporosis and atherosclerosis. Based on the wealth of preliminary data that we have generated, we believe that our chance of success is very high.

column36: AYA-PACT: Adolescents and Young Adults becoming Physically Active after Cancer Trial
column37: Background: There is a need for adolescent and young adult (AYA) cancer research because the number of new cancers in young people is increasing and the survivor population is growing. Interventions that try to reduce problems that affect people after cancer are particularly important since its treatments can have negative effects on survivors' physical and mental health even decades after diagnosis. Aim: Given the many positive effects of physical activity (e.g. improved fitness and quality of life), our study aims to encourage AYA cancer survivors to be more physically active as they shift from treatment to survivorship care. The main goal of this study is to see if a home-based, mobile health (mHealth) physical activity intervention can increase physical activity levels by at least 90 minutes/week compared to baseline in AYA cancer survivors. Methods: We will conduct a two-center randomized controlled trial of 320 AYA cancer survivors living in Alberta and within 12 months of completing treatment. At the start of the study, participants will complete fitness testing and questionnaires. Participants will then be randomly put into either a control or intervention group. The control group will receive educational information only. The intervention group will also receive a personalized physical activity plan, an activity tracker watch, access to a private, online survivor community, motivational text messages and check-in calls/e-mails. Fitness testing and questionnaires will be repeated at 6 and 12 months to see if the intervention increased physical activity levels and improved health outcomes among the participants in the intervention group compared to controls. A final measurement at 24 months will test long-term use. Impact: This study could provide AYA cancer survivors with a simple and affordable mHealth intervention that benefits their physical and mental health. If our intervention works in Alberta, we aim to test its effectiveness nationally.

column36: Fundamental Lysosome Membrane Biology in Health and Disease
column37: Clear relationships exist between lysosome activity, cancers and age-related diseases but many fundamental aspects of lysosome biology remain enigmatic preventing development of effective therapies: Lysosomes are membrane-encapsulated organelles responsible for recycling biomaterials within all eukaryotic cells, like the trillions that make up you and I. As important sources of nutrients, growing and dividing cells rely on lysosomes especially when starved, as is the case for cancer cells in tumor environments. But lysosomes generate molecules called reactive oxygen species that damage their membranes, causing them to rupture and kill cells. However, for reasons unknown, lysosome membranes within cancer cells are resistant to rupture. Aging brain cells also depend on lysosomes to clear toxic protein aggregates. Loss of this function leads to premature cell death underlying many age-related diseases, like Alzheimer's disease. Often this correlates with abnormal accumulation of lipids called diacylglycerol, ceramide and sphingosine on lysosome membranes that promote dysfunction and rupture. But it is unclear how lysosomes handle these lipids to function and remain intact. Furthermore, enhanced lysosome activity in both cases relies on inhibition of TOR signaling, an important mediator of cell metabolism - but the molecular basis of how this occurs is not entirely understood. The aim of this project is to better understand the basis of these three aspects of lysosome biology relevant to cancer and age-related diseases by studying baker's yeast as a model organism. I suspect that a process that my lab discovered called the IntraLumenal Fragment (ILF) pathway is responsible and will test this hypothesis using microscopy, genetic and biochemical techniques. Knowing the basis of lysosome activation and rupture will facilitate the development new therapies for these devastating diseases that affect millions of Canadians.

column36: Determining how actin isoforms drive cytokinesis and cell contractility
column37: Human cells take on a large range of shapes that are important for fulfilling specific biological functions. Cells can change their shape based on particular stimuli by altering components of the cell's inner skeleton, called the cytoskeleton. The cytoskeleton is composed of, in part, a dynamic meshwork of a protein called actin that forms filaments underneath the cell membrane. Human cells express 6 different types of actins, and disruption or over-production of specific actin forms is linked to a large number of human diseases, including cancer, heart disease and severe muscle weakness. The different actins make separate structures and are suggested to have different functions in the cell by directing shape changes at just one part of the cell. How the different actin structures do this is unknown. We propose to identify the molecules that make the different actin cytoskeletons and position them in specific regions of the cell. We anticipate that these data will provide new insight into the early stages of disease.

column36: Characterizing Cardiovascular Outcomes in Subclinical Primary Aldosteronism
column37: Background: Hypertension (high blood pressure) management generally involves a 'one size fits all' approach. Employing a more personalized approach targeting the cause of an individual patient's hypertension provides the opportunity to improve long-term health. Primary aldosteronism (PA) is a common hormonal cause of hypertension that leads to disproportionately high rates of cardiovascular disease. Importantly, the adverse health consequences of PA are preventable with early targeted treatments which are distinct from other forms of hypertension. Recently, a growing body of evidence has demonstrated that milder forms of PA ('Subclinical PA') are exceedingly common in the general population yet go undetected in modern-day clinical practice. Whether Subclinical PA increases the risk for long-term adverse cardiovascular outcomes remains unknown. Purpose: To study the long-term effects of Subclinical PA on cardiovascular disease. Procedure: We will investigate Subclinical PA using CARTaGENE - a study which enrolled over 20,000 Quebec residents in 2009-2010. These participants had blood samples stored at the date of enrollment, and follow-up data regarding their health has been collected since that time. We will use the stored blood samples to perform hormonal profiling and identify participants with Subclinical PA at the time of enrollment to determine their long-term cardiovascular outcomes. Outcome: We anticipate that participants with Subclinical PA will develop higher rates of cardiovascular disease compared to participants without Subclinical PA. Relevance to Patients: If indeed patients with Subclinical PA experience worse cardiovascular outcomes, the logical next step will be to study whether using medications that specifically target Subclinical PA (and are not used routinely as first-line hypertension therapy) will improve cardiovascular outcomes. This study will provide a much-needed step toward a more individualized approach to hypertension management.

column36: Young immigrants and refugees co-designing mental health and well-being solutions
column37: Canada is home to hundreds of thousands of immigrants and refugees, a large portion of which are young people. A successful settlement experience for young immigrants and refugees (YIR) is vital for the future of the country. However, YIR can face many barriers (e.g., school adjustments, social challenges, employment, housing, financial, and linguistic), in addition to racism and discrimination. These barriers can negatively impact mental health (MH) of YIR. The COVID-19 pandemic has exacerbated the issue, with MH challenges increasing for YIR. Without appropriate culturally sensitive services and supports directed at prevention or early-intervention, MH challenges will persist, becoming more severe mental disorders that are harder to treat and have long lasting consequences. It is time to re-imagine what is available for YIR and move beyond a one-size-fits all approach to create culturally sensitive services/supports, inclusive of eMental Health (eMH) options, that focus on prevention and early intervention for YIR MH and well-being. The aim of this 4-year study is to build awareness and enhance the MH and well-being of YIR in Manitoba (MB). YIR will be interviewed about their MH experiences, needs, and ideas for possible culturally sensitive solutions, as well as take part in photovoice, focus groups, and eMH workshops. YIR parents and key stakeholders from community-based organizations will also be interviewed. Short-term, the knowledge gained of YIR MH experiences and needs will be used to promote awareness of YIR MH and well-being. Concrete solutions for community-based services and supports will result for MB but also for sites across the country that can be tailored to specific YIR populations. This project will also result in a culturally sensitive, interactive eMH self-management prototype. Long-term, the culturally sensitive, interactive eMH prototype will be available for scaling up in other sites across Canada.

column36: Impact of copy number imbalances in mutant KRAS on pancreatic cancer chemoresistance and metastases
column37: Mutations are changes in the DNA sequence that can transform the normal behaviour of a cell. Mutations that lead to cancer cause the cell to grow uncontrollably. Cancer is the product of many mutations that have accumulated in the DNA of a cell. KRAS is one of the genes that is often mutated in cancer. In pancreatic cancer, KRAS mutations are present in 90% of patients. When KRAS is mutated experimentally in a mouse model, the cells develop cancer. Hence, it is a well-known "driver" gene, which means that it can initiate cancer. However, our research group have found a strong clinical correlation with a less known effect of KRAS. We have found a link between KRAS, therapy resistance and the spread of the cancer (also known as metastases). We found that when the tumour spreads to other organs (usually liver for pancreatic cancers), the cells make more copies of mutated KRAS, resulting in more repeats of this gene. Each cell has two copies of a gene (one inherited from the mother and one from the father), but in cancer, when the cell divides, it makes more copies. Our findings showed that when a tumour have more copies of the KRAS gene, it does not respond to chemotherapy and usually spreads to the liver. We have developed a human model that recapitulates different copies of mutated KRAS. We will use this model to study the changes that occur in the cell when it has more copies of mutated KRAS, and to look for a drug that can kill tumour cells with elevated copies of mutated KRAS or make it respond better to the standard treatment. Although KRAS is a well-studied gene and is under investigation by many other research teams, our question and experimental strategy are novel. Our main aim is to better understand the role of mutant KRAS gene copies in therapy resistance and metastasis in order to contribute to finding new treatment options for metastatic pancreatic cancer patients.

column36: Elucidating the role extracellular vesicles play in leukaemogenesis
column37: Chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) is a blood cancer, which is fatal if left untreated. Specialised tumour cells called cancer stem cells (CSCs) start and maintain leukaemia. Our group will investigate the processes behind how CML slowly develops, and understand how CSCs communicate with other cells using extracellular vesicles (EVs). EVs are lipid nanoparticles that contain bioactive cargo, that transmit/receive signals or important cellular messages. We will investigate if EVs are important in CML, and if EVs help or hinder in the development of leukaemia. Importantly, we will also investigate if EVs can be used as predictors of CML, thus giving tools for doctors to detect leukaemia as early as possible, so people can live longer and healthier lives.

column36: Clinical Evaluation and Cost-Effectiveness of HIV Post-Exposure Prophylaxis-in-Pocket ("PIP") for Individuals with a Low Frequency of High-Risk Exposures: A Matched Control Study
column37: HIV continues to be a major Global Health threat and curbing the epidemic will require several concurrent approaches, including a focus on preventing new HIV infections. The two major HIV prevention strategies (Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis [PrEP] - a proactive approach; Post Exposure Prophylaxis [PEP] - a retroactive approach) are effective, however major gaps continue to exist with these HIV prevention modalities. We developed "PEP-in-Pocket" ("PIP") as a novel HIV prevention strategy that aims to mitigate gaps in HIV prevention care left by PrEP and PEP. This approach focuses on a population of individuals who have a low frequency of high-risk HIV exposures, but whose risk of HIV infection is still significant. PIP involves pro-actively prescribing 28 days of PEP to selected individuals with a low frequency of high-risk exposures. Patients are counselled to fill the prescription and, in the event of a possible HIV exposure, to initiate their 28 days of medication as soon as possible (and within 72 hours). PIP is likely to prevent HIV infection while addressing the many barriers and drawbacks of conventional PEP and PrEP; PIP enables immediate access to HIV preventative care, may reduce patient attrition, and eliminates the need for costly and inconvenient emergency department visits. The proposed project has three major objectives: [1] to study the clinical utility of PIP (e.g. rates of HIV seroconversion and sexually transmitted infections, adherence to medications and follow up visits), [2] to compare HIV risk-levels and HIV-related anxiety over time between those on PIP with matched controls of similar HIV risk who use PrEP, and [3] to determine the cost-effectiveness of a PIP approach compared to those using conventional PEP or PrEP strategies.

column36: Neural control of sequential action: controlling the present while planning the future
column37: While we go about our everyday activities, our brain constantly looks ahead and plans our next actions. Being able to multi-task - controlling current actions, while planning the next ones - is important in many skills, from cooking dinner to driving a car to playing the piano. Our ability to do so declines with age and is severely impaired after brain damage. Despite its importance and ubiquity, we know very little about how the human brain accomplishes this task. In our experiments, we will study humans and non-human primates performing sequences of finger or arm movements. We will use a combination of behavioral experiments, functional magnetic resonance imaging, and electrophysiological recordings to decipher the mechanisms by which the brain plans for the future while simultaneously controlling ongoing actions. We will investigate which parts of the brain are involved in solving this task, how they communicate, and how their interactions change with learning. To further our theoretical understanding, we also investigate how artificial intelligence algorithms, specifically recurrent neuronal networks, solve this task. Together these lines of basic research will provide a new understanding of how the brain solves complex sequential tasks and provides the basis for novel clinical interventions that improve the brain's ability to multi-task after damage or degeneration.

column36: Magnetic Resonance Imaging Toolbox for Assessment of Lung Structure and Function in the Early Years of Life
column37: Pediatric lung diseases, such as cystic fibrosis (CF) and asthma represent a growing health care burden to Canada. CF is the most common fatal genetic disease in Canadian children characterized by progressive decline of lung function and frequent hospitalizations due to repeated infections and associated monitoring and treatment. Though rarely fatal, severe asthma significantly reduces quality of life and more effective treatments are needed to manage symptoms, especially in younger patients (e.g., preschoolers). Highly effective CF and asthma therapies are becoming available for preschoolers, but these treatments can have significant side effects so need to be guided by sensitive measures of lung function. We believe magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can be a robust tool for monitoring lung structure and function in preschoolers with CF and asthma. The goal of this proposal is to develop novel lung MRI tools appropriate for preschoolers, who may not be able to remain still, follow breathing instructions or hold their breath during scanning. We will design methods to enable free-breathing lung MRI, tolerant of spontaneous patient motion and able to image lung function without breath-holds. We will also test these methods in preschoolers with CF and asthma, including response to treatments. The proposed research will establish an MRI toolbox suitable for robust lung imaging of preschoolers and readily deployable to hospitals across Canada. The development of lung MRI for preschoolers with CF and severe asthma would represent a significant advance over current pulmonary function tests which are typically inconclusive. This toolbox will provide the basis for designing subsequent clinical trials using MRI as an outcome measure for developing improved treatments for CF and asthma in the early years of life. Furthermore, these approaches would be extendable in future to even younger children, including neonates suffering from lung diseases of prematurity.

column36: Mechanisms of heart rhythm disorders and therapeutic interventions in myotonic dystrophy type 1
column37: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is a form of muscular dystrophy, it is characterized by multiorgan impairments including the heart. Eighty percent (80%) of patients with DM1 have abnormal heart beats known as cardiac arrhythmias and can die suddenly. Cardiac arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death are major health concern as it is estimated that every day >1000 sudden cardiac deaths occur in North America in general and in particular for DM1 affected individuals. Problems with heart rhythm and conduction will arise first and can cause shortness of breath, discomfort, palpitations, loss of consciousness and in severe cases, sudden cardiac death. The only available treatment for more severely affected DM1 patients is the implantation of a pacemaker or a defibrillator. These are small devices that are placed in the chest or abdomen of most vulnerable patients. Overall, the goal of this research is to identify the causes of heart electrical abnormalities in DM1 patients and come up with ways for interventions that will correct these abnormalities. We plan to achieve this by: 1) Studying the role of ion channels, these are pores through which ions such as sodium, calcium and potassium enter cardiac cells and are responsible for spreading the electrical activity throughout the heart and assess how they contribute to abnormal heart beat seen in DM1 patients. We will use state of the art technology such as fluorescent probes applied to stem cells and DM1 mouse model that allows to pinpoint to the site in the heart where the abnormal beat starts and follow how it spread throughout the heart. 2) Using sophisticated genetic tools known as molecular scissors, which can correct the disease expression in the heart. 3) Testing medications that can reverse the disease. The impact of this research is that the understanding the disease mechanisms will help cardiologists and other healthcare providers to improve the management and eventually improve treatment of DM1.

column36: The S. aureus Network Adaptive Platform Trial (SNAP) Canada: A Randomized Controlled Trial for Penicillin-susceptible, Methicillin-susceptible, and Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus Bloodstream Infections in Hospitalized Patients
column37: Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infection (bacteremia) is a major public health problem and one of the most common and deadly bacterial infections in the world. There are over 15,000 episodes per year in Canada, resulting in more than 3,500 deaths with an estimated treatment cost exceeding $120,000,000. Despite the high morbidity and mortality of S. aureus bacteremia, there are no international guidelines for its treatment. Despite being such a common disease, to date, there have been only five high quality randomized controlled trials involving fewer than 3,000 patients for a disease which kills an estimated 22,000 per year in the United States and Canada alone. Therefore there remains considerable uncertainty as to the best choice of antibiotics to fight this infection, providing an excellent opportunity to improve the current standard of care We will address three crucial questions surrounding treatment that will allow us to study every combination of subtypes of S. aureus bacteremia in Canada. Firstly, we will compare the antibiotics penicillin vs. cloxacillin for penicillin-susceptible S. aureus. Secondly, we will determine if cefazolin or cloxacillin should be preferred for methicillin-susceptible strains of S. aureus. Finally, we will determine if the addition of cefazolin to vancomycin improves outcomes for patients with methicillin-resistant S. aureus. We propose a pragmatic clinical trial embedded within the current standard of care for S. aureus bacteremia. Our Canadian team will be key partners in an international collaboration which revolutionizes our capacity to study this infection. By refining the optimal treatments for all types of S. aureus bacteremia, our team will help establish best practices to be deployed worldwide. Since this intervention requires no new technology, any findings from our research program will offer immediate benefits to all patients and the Canadian healthcare system.

column36: SPECT-CT Guided ELEctive Contralateral Neck Treatment (SELECT) for Patients with Lateralized Oropharyngeal Cancer: A Phase III Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Oropharyngeal carcinoma (OPC) is the most common type of head and neck cancer and ninth most common cancer in Canadian men. Most OPCs are associated with the human papilloma virus (HPV) and have a good prognosis. The primary treatment is usually radiation therapy (RT). Although less than 15% have obviously involved lymph nodes on the opposite side of the neck, most patients receive RT to both sides of the neck because of the concern that microscopic cancer cells could spread to the opposite side. This approach increases the risk of swallowing impairment, dry mouth, and temporary feeding tube insertion, as compared to treatment of only one side of the neck. Lymphatic mapping with Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT-CT) imaging may help to identify whether an OPC is at risk for spread to the opposite side of the neck and, if so, the specific areas that are at risk for nodal disease. Lymphatic mapping is performed by injecting a radioactive tracer around the tumour, followed by capturing the distribution of the tracer to the lymph nodes of the neck. Patients will be randomized to either lymphatic mapping-guided RT or to standard bilateral neck RT. In patients randomized to the lymphatic mapping-guided treatment and in whom the radiotracer only migrates to the same side of the neck, RT will be limited to that side. In those patients in whom the radiotracer migrates to the opposite side of the neck, only the regions of the neck to which the radiotracer migrates will receive radiotherapy. We anticipate that this personalized treatment based on lymphatic mapping will provide similar cancer control, but will reduce side effects and improve quality of life compared to routinely treating both sides of the neck. We will evaluate the cost-effectiveness of this new approach and expect that it will offer a safe, effective, and cost-effective standard of care to patients in Canada and across the world.

column36: Integrative Medicine in North America: Paradigm Shift or New Physician Specialty?
column37: Over half of Canadians and 1/3 of Americans use complementary medicine (CM) therapies that are not fully integrated into mainstream healthcare. While medical schools offer little CM-related training, increasing numbers of medical doctors (MDs) are incorporating CM therapies into clinical practice. In 2014, 'integrative medicine' (IM) - a movement to include CM in mainstream care - was formally recognized as a new medical specialty for Canadian and American doctors. Does IM represent a paradigm shift in medicine? Alternately, does IM being siloed as a new specialty limit CM's influence within medicine; or, are IM doctors co-opting CM therapies into the dominant medical paradigm? Little is known to date about the IM field, which raises major questions for sociologists, medical educators and policy makers. This is especially important in Canada, where institutional, educational and policy responses to IM lag behind the United States. This study aims to: 1. Assemble a critical sociological account of IM's emergence in North America; 2. Characterize the workforce, practices and worldviews of IM physicians in Canada and the United States; and 3. To critically interrogate the policies, pedagogies and professionalization strategies that have accompanied IM's recent ascent to legitimacy. Four primary data types will be analysed: a) a survey of integrative MDs in Canada and the US (n=4000); and b) key informant interviews (n=40) with IM physician leaders; c) policies governing MDs' use of CM therapies; and d) curricula from established IM fellowship trainings. The proposed project will culminate in a book for scholars and the public; while providing usable findings for policy makers, physicians, medical educators. Close attention will be paid to Canadian vs. US distinctions, as well as issues of gender, ethnicity/race, financial accessibility and worldview.

column36: Pathogenesis of COVID-19 mediated Cardiovascular Complications: Therapeutic Applications
column37: COVID-19, caused by SARS-CoV-2 has caused a worldwide pandemic. Male patients have a worse outcome compared to the females. COVID-19 infection leads to SARS but the cardiovascular (CV) system is also highly involved. This is because the molecule that mediates entry of SARS-CoV-2 virus, ACE2, is a protein that is widely expressed in multiple cells types, and is critical for optimal CV function. When the virus binds to ACE2, they both enter the cell (internalize), which leads to loss of ACE2 from the cell membrane and its protective effects. In addition, after entering the cell, SARS-CoV-2 triggers an inflammatory response and induces expression of another enzyme (disintegrin and metalloproteinase-17, ADAM17) that also cleaves ACE2, further depriving the CV cells from the beneficial effects of ACE2. Our research team has a strong background in understanding the function ACE2 and ADAM17 in CV diseases, and viral myocardial disease and immunity. We have also initiated collaborations with world-reknowned Vaccine and Infectious Disease Organization-International Vaccine Centre at U of Saskatchewan (Dr. Darryl Falzarano) who has established the novel and unique in vivo model of COVID-19 infection in hamster. In collaboration with Dr. Del Nonno, National Institute for Infectious Diseases (Rome, Italy), we have obtained heart specimens from deceased COVID-19 patients. In collaboration with our locals teams (NACTRC and CBSR), we have started to collect plasma from COVID-19 patients from the full spectrum of disease severity. Our proposed study takes a comprehensive approach that extends from in vitro cell culture, to preclinical animal model, to heart specimens and plasma from patients, to determine if ACE2 or ADAM17 can serve as biomarkers for CV complications in response to COVID-19, and to determine if inhibiting the heightened renin-angiotensin system, or inhibiting ADAM17, could protect against exacerbation of CV complications in these patients.

column36: COPE LTC Study: Care pathway for Older Persons with dEpressive disorders in Long Term Care
column37: Up to 44% of nursing homes residents are depressed or have a low mood. As a result of depression these people often have more trouble with their memory and their daily activities. Although depressive disorders are common and causes suffering, it is often under diagnosed and undertreated. How we treat depressive disorders in nursing homes represents an area to improve care for older adults. To address this problem, we plan to design a pathway for the treatment of depression which involves 3 steps. 1. To design a pathway using a modified 'Delphi Process', which explains how to diagnose and treat depressive disorders for older adults living in nursing homes. To do this we will use a Delphi Process, where a group of experts use scientific evidence and expert opinion to create recommendations. Once this is done we can combine these best practices for managing depressive disorders into a 'Clinical Pathway'. We will review the 'Clinical Pathway' with a group of health care providers, health administrators, researchers, patients and their families from across Canada and create a plan to use it in nursing homes across Canada. 2. To assess what prevents and enables us to diagnose and treat depressive disorders in long term care. To do this we will perform focus groups with the people involved in the processes and ask about their experiences. 3. We will then develop a detailed plan for how we will use this 'Clinical pathway' in practice, we will use known theories on how to change behaviour to help with this. We will work with one nursing home unit to get feedback and review this plan to ensure we incorporate real world experience. Using a clinical pathway for depressive disorders care in nursing homes provides a blueprint to help nurses and doctors to best care for those with depression, which will reduce the burden associated with depressive disorders.

column36: Bringing focus to the invisible injury: Defining a role for microbleeds and microglia in mild traumatic brain injury.
column37: Concussions are a form of mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), often called the "unseen injury", because of the lack of obvious damage. As a result, many individuals suffer repeated concussions, often in short time spans. In some sports, like hockey and football, awareness is growing that repeated sub-concussive blows to the head are routinely incurred in practices and games. Although many of these impacts do not result in a diagnosis of concussion, there is a growing appreciation that both concussions and sub-concussive impacts can negatively impact cognitive function in the developing brain, and that repeated concussions (r-mTBI) can have long-term detrimental effects for cognition in elderly populations. Despite these concerns, few laboratories have systematically studied r-mTBI in a preclinical model that properly mimics the human condition. We have recently developed a model that enables us to accurately examine r-mTBI and understand how the brain responds to repeated mTBI. Because significant structural damage does not occur in mTBI, our focus is on whether there is damage to small blood vessels in the brain. These vessels are below the threshold of resolution for magnetic resonance imaging, but can be resolved using high resolution microscopy. When damaged, these vessels can release a compound in the blood called fibrinogen. Fibrinogen is normally important for clotting, but can also initiate an inflammatory process involving brain microglia that negatively impacts neurons, and impairs learning and memory processes. The results of the proposed work will help us to better understand the mechanisms involved in mTBI; how they directly impact brain function, and increase our understanding of how r-mTBI early in life could negatively impact individuals as they age. More importantly, this work will enable us to determine the therapeutic value of modulating fibrinogen's effects in the brain to help reduce the negative impact of r-mTBI on cognition.

column36: Mobilizing the Antiviral Capacities of MAIT Cells to Combat COVID-19: From Fundamental Immunology to Vaccine Optimization and Immunotherapy
column37: In December 2019, a pneumonia associated with a novel coronavirus, now called severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), emerged in Wuhan, China. To date, the ongoing pandemic has resulted in over 36 million infections worldwide, and nearly 1.1 million people have succumbed to coronavirus disease 19 (COVID-19). There are currently no approved vaccines or effective treatments for COVID-19. The ultimate goal of vaccination is to elicit antibody and T cell responses that will specifically detect and destroy SARS-CoV-2. However, the quality of these responses often varies at the population level. In addition, conventional vaccination strategies have encountered serious obstacles, and SARS-CoV-2-specific antibodies may not be always protective. The goal of this proposal is to reveal the potentials of a specialized subset of unconventional innate-like T lymphocytes, called mucosa-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells, in COVID-19. MAIT cells are enriched in mucosal layers and in the lungs, SARS-CoV-2's main ports of entry. Also importantly, MAIT cell responses are rapid, robust and consistent in human subjects irrespective of their genetic HLA (human leukocyte antigen) makeup. Inspired by recent preliminary data, we will investigate MAIT cell roles in host response to SARS-CoV-2 and also test the efficacy of a MAIT cell-activating molecule both as an adjuvant (vaccine-enhancing agent) and as a fast-acting treatment. To do so, we will establish a unique and clinically relevant mouse model harboring the human pulmonary receptor for SARS-CoV-2 and an abundance of MAIT cells. Simulating human subjects, this model will enable studies on the prophylactic and therapeutic potentials of MAIT cells and their stimuli. These studies will be complemented by a comprehensive and longitudinal analysis of MAIT cell frequencies and functions in COVID-19 patients, which may help predict the severity of illness and inform important clinical decisions in its management.

column37: Drug discovery was historically based in animal models of disease- which while being a slow process, was fairly successful In the modern era, we have move away from experiments in animals, because of technologies that have allowed us to screen many more drug candidates in cell systems that express the target of interest. These gains in speed have not led reliably to more successful drug discovery programs- to a large extent because they rely on what are called generic or "heterologous" cultured cells that most probably do not accurately reflect the tissue or cell type affected in the disease we are trying to treat such as Parkinson's Disease or chronic neuropathic pain. However, in recent years a whole new set of technological improvements has allowed us to use primary cells from animal (or even stem cells from patients) to screen for drugs in this more relevant physiological and pathological context. Further, we and others have been able to adapt these screening technologies to live animals making it possible now to compare the effects of potential therapeutic drugs in cultured heterologous cells, cells derived from animals or patients, and whole animals. We propose here to test a key concept in modern drug development which aims to make drugs with fewer side effects by biasing them toward the required effects of a drug and away from the adverse effects. These concepts were developed in cell models but have not be rigorously been tested in animals. If we can establish whether these convenient cell culture-based models predict drug effects in living animals, this will greatly facilitate our ability to design and test better drugs.

column36: Structural and functional changes in the brain of early and late blind individuals
column37: For human and non-human primates, vision is one of the most privileged sensory channels used to interact with the environment. The importance of vision is strongly embedded in the organization of the brain as about one-third of its cortical surface is involved in visual functions. It is therefore not surprising that the absence of vision from birth, or the loss of vision later in life, has huge consequences, both anatomically and functionally. We have shown in previous studies that, although the visual system undergoes some atrophic changes following the loss of vision at birth, it is nonetheless present and can be activated by a variety of non-visual stimuli such as touch, audition and even smell. The specific and novel goals of this project are 1) to investigate the pathways through which non-visual information is conveyed to the occipital cortex in late blind individuals 2) to investigate the role of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA in the occipital cortex in cross-modal neuroplastic responses in blind individuals, and 3) to clarify the brain microstructural and functional organization in late-onset blindness via the dynamics of neuroplastic adaptations, following the loss of vision in adult life. Our results will further our understanding of the capacity of the blind brain for plastic changes. With the advent of novel methods for restoring vision in blind individuals, this will be instrumental in defining the optimal window to help them "see".

column36: Dysregulation of TET2 and DNMT3A promotes pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) through inflammation : A new mechanism of PAH
column37: We previously discovered pathologic changes in gene expression that appear to trigger the development of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and showed that they were mediated by "epigenetic changes" in gene function. Epigenetic means that the changes in DNA function occur without changes in DNA sequence. The changes we identified were caused by increased DNA methylation (addition of methyl groups) of certain genes. We have identified two new gene mutations which may regulate these same DNA methylation epigenetic pathways. If confirmed this would show for the first time that mutations of genes or environmental factors can both result in epigenetic changes that promote development of PAH. Two crucial genes which regulate DNA methylation are DNMT3A and TET2. Mutations which impair their function promote the development of vascular disease, such as coronary disease. We hypothesize that mutations in DNMT3A and TET2 genes contribute to PAH development and represent new therapeutic targets. Our research is uniquely supported by our established access to the genetic material and clinical information from 2500 patients in the PAH Biobank (US) and two large biobanks in the United Kingdom and at Johns Hopkins University, as well as the expertise available at our state of the art translational research facility at Queen's University, the Queen's CardioPulmonary Unit (QCPU). We will expand on promising preliminary data showing DNMT3A and TET2 mutations contribute to PAH, describe the resulting change in gene expression as signatures of PAH and explore the potential to predict disease development and outcome. Finally, we will show that Tet2 & Dnmt3a disruption (whether caused by mutation or by epigenetic down-regulation of gene expression) contributes to PAH development in mouse models where these genes are knocked out. We will test new anti-inflammatory therapies for PAH in these novel mouse models as a step to translating this knowledge into therapy for human PAH patients.

column36: Brain cell volume reduction in animal models and people with intracerebral hemorrhagic stroke.
column37: An intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is a devastating stroke caused by a bleed into the brain. Almost 40% of ICH patients die, many in days. The bleed destroys brain tissue, alters the delicate balance of important ions and water, and takes up valuable space within the skull. This causes pressure to rise. High intracranial pressure (ICP) impairs blood flow to the brain, causing more damage and sometimes death. The body has several natural ways to compensate and help lower ICP. Our animal research has found an additional mechanism. We discovered that cell shrinkage (CS) occurs in areas located away from the damaged tissue. Some cell bodies shrink by up to 50%. This means that those parts of the brain become a bit smaller. This frees up space within the skull and limits the rise in ICP. While this helps reduce the risk of death, it still commonly occurs after very large ICHs. Thus, we need to do more to treat high ICP. Our research will study patients who died from a large ICH. Using their brain tissue, we will look for whether CS occurs in humans, if there are any harmful effects, and we will examine how CS occurs. Concurrently, we will use rat models of severe ICH to determine how age, hypertension and ICP control therapies affect CS in male and female rats. These are clinically important factors that we will incorporate into our research to improve the validity of our animal studies (e.g., to explain the negative impact of hypertension). We will also look to better document how CS affects neuronal health and function. Finally, we will examine rat and human tissue to determine the mechanisms underlying CS. For example, we know that movement of potassium, chloride and water across a cell membrane is very important to cell size, and so we will study these and other mechanisms. Eventually, we hope to safely manipulate CS to improve the medical management of high ICP after large strokes and other brain injuries, thereby improving survival and recovery.
