column37: Cancers of the lower digestive tract are called Colorectal Cancers (CRC). They are the 2nd most common form of non-skin cancers and will kill 5 times more Canadians this year compared to motor vehicle collisions. Alarmingly, today's young adults are 2-4 times more vulnerable to CRC compared to their parents which may be the first indication that CRC may become an even larger public health burden in the coming years. The human genome was "completed" in 2001, yet several difficult to study areas of our DNA were excluded from this reference genome and remain under-explored. One such region encodes for ribosomal RNA (rRNA), the central gene of the ribosome. Ribosomes are responsible for translation, reading messenger RNA and creating proteins. In a pioneering study on rRNA, Dr. Babaian discovered that almost half of CRC patients contain a cancer-specific "onco-ribosome" with a variant rRNA. Normally, ribosomes create proteins in a tightly controlled and regulated manner. These onco-ribosomes are associated with the most rapidly growing tumors, differing from their normal counterparts by a modification of the rRNA. Normally, this RNA modification is found in the ribosomes of all animals and plants, except for cancer tissues, yet its role in protein synthesis is unknown. The objective of this proposal is to use cancer cells genetically modified to produce only onco-ribosomes to understand how these cancer ribosomes translate proteins differently. Significantly, onco-ribosomes differ enough from the healthy ribosome that they could be targeted with precision drugs. Fortunately, there already are dozens of common and approved antibiotics which target the ribosome for treating bacterial or parasitic infections. This proposal will also evaluate if it's feasible to re-purpose antibiotic-like compounds for the treatment of colorectal cancers. This would establish an entirely new class of chemotherapies based on a medicine we have used safely for over 60 years.

column36: Regenerative plasticity in colorectal cancer
column37: Approximately 4% of Canadians will develop colorectal cancer their lifetime. While the mortality of the disease is relatively low when detected early, many of these cancers are still detected at late stages and require aggressive treatment with chemotherapy. Nearly half of these patients, however, experience recurrence within 8 years. Understanding mechanisms cancers use to evade therapies and regenerate is critical to improve the prognosis of this disease. We aim to use new approaches that measure cellular activity at the level of individual cells to track how cancer populations respond to chemotherapy and regerate following its withdrawal. We will make use of a rich resource of patient-derived cancer specimens from the Princess Margaret Cancer Centre's "Living Biobank", allowing us to understand how this response may vary between patients. This data will allow us to identify the mechanisms underlying tumour recurrence. With these same specimens, we will also use robotics to screen hundreds of drugs to identify those that block this regeneration. Together, this work could identify new approaches for treatment, not specifically focused on killing cancer cells themselves, but rather, preventing tumours from regenerating following standard treatment with chemotherapy.

column36: High resolution and robust water/fat separation in pediatric abdominal MRI
column37: Glioblastoma is the most aggressive and lethal type of brain cancer accounting for 50% of all brain tumors. Despite extensive research aiming to improve GBM treatment, treatment efficacy is still extremely poor and the current 5-year survival rate is only 5.5%. The standard treatment protocol of GBM includes surgery to resect as much of the tumor as possible without compromising cerebral function followed by chemotherapy and radiation therapy (RT). RT aims at achieving tumor cell kill trough high energy radiation from an external source. To avoid radiation-induced damage to the healthy brain cells while maximizing radiation dose to active tumor cells, RT requires a treatment planning with high precision delineation of tumor extent. In spite of significant advances in RT methods for precise dose delivery, RT treatment planning still relies on conventional MRI. The latter cannot always discriminate between some of secondary tumor effects such as edema and hemorrhage which mimic tumor properties. Furthermore, parts of the tumor cells may have similar appearance to normal tissue which leads to poor tumor delineation and degradation of the treatment efficacy. GBM tumor cells have distinctive metabolic properties compared to the normal brain tissue and my research proposal is to use a combination of molecular imaging techniques, which includes Positron Emission Tomography (PET) and Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopic Imaging (MRSI) to map the metabolic activity of the brain to be used for tumor delineation rather than the conventional structural MRI. A fast and effective workflow for tumor delineation based on molecular and quantitative imaging will be developed and assessed on a cohort of patients with Glioblastoma. If successful, this technique can not only change the current clinical practice in RT treatment planning, but also enable many new applications in the clinical management of glioblastoma, including diagnostics, grading, and assessment of response to therapy.

column36: Dissecting mechanisms of mammalian gene regulation by the essential histone acetyltransferases p300 and CBP
column37: Every cell in a human body has the same DNA sequence. However, different segments of DNA, called genes, are read out in each distinct cell type to produce the specific set of proteins needed for cellular function. As such, activating the wrong gene at the wrong time can lead to developmental defects and disease, and many human diseases stem from mutations in regulators of gene activity. Two such regulators are p300 and CBP, which have largely redundant functions and for simplicity will be referred to as p300. p300 stimulates gene activity by chemically modifying proteins in an enzymatic reaction called acetylation. Acetylation alters protein charge, affecting binding partners and enzymatic activities of numerous factors, with pervasive effects on gene activity. Accordingly, p300 frequently works together with other regulatory factors and this cooperation is crucial for gene activation. Aberrant levels or activity of p300 and collaborating factors are implicated in numerous human diseases, including Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome, diabetes, and multiple types of cancer. However, accurately targeting p300 and its co-regulators in disease is challenging because we don't fully understand how these factors work, or work together, to control gene expression. To address this important question, I have used powerful small molecule inhibitors and genomic methods to define genes at which p300 directly stimulates activity at particular steps in the transcription process. Further, this work has revealed distinct sets of genes where p300 collaborates with other factors, providing opportunities to understand co-regulation. Here, I propose to leverage this information to test specific models for p300 activity in gene control. These experiments are anticipated to clarify the basis for gene dysregulation in cells with mutations or perturbations in p300 and suggest new therapeutic avenues to target this factor in disease.

column36: Upregulation of immune response to reduce tumor progression and metastasis of melanoma using photodynamic therapy
column37: Melanoma is an aggressive and highly lethal form of skin cancer. The main treatment is surgery, possibly in combination with radiation, chemotherapy and, more recently, immunotherapy. However, there is a significant incidence of local recurrence and metastatic spread. Photodynamic Therapy (PDT) is an approved treatment modality for a range of malignancies that relies on light activation of non-toxic molecules (photosensitizers) to induce tumor cell death. The applicant has recently shown in a mouse model that primary melanoma can be eradicated using a novel form of PDT, using clinically-approved photosensitizers combined with applying a non-toxic "optical clearing agent" to the tumor to overcome the high light absorption by melanin that has previously limited the treatment efficacy. It has also been shown in many other tumors that PDT can upregulate the immune system and so reduce tumor progression and metastatic spread that are responsible for reduced survival and quality of life. Conversely, there is increasing evidence that surgery-induced stress has the opposite effect. The concept to be tested here for the first time is that PDT can be used, either as an alternative to surgery (e.g. in difficult sites such as eyelids, nose, ears) or together with surgery, to counteract this negative immune response, reducing tumor progression and metastasis. This will be evaluated in the mouse melanoma model. Tumor growth and metastasis will l be monitored by multiple imaging techniques. Blood analysis will be carried out before and at times after treatment to directly measure the immune response. Tumor response to PDT, surgery, and surgery plus PDT will be measured. These studies will provide the first proof-of-principle of the use of PDT to modulate the immunological system in melanoma. If successful, it should be possible to translate this approach into a minimally-invasive, safe and effective new treatment option for patients with this highly aggressive cancer.

column36: Leveraging genomic, metabolomic, and proteomic data to identify clinically-relevant subtypes and new pathways driving risk of coronary artery disease
column37: Heart disease is the second leading cause of death in Canada and affects millions of individuals each year. Despite efforts to reduce disease risk with healthy lifestyles and medications, these strategies are not always successful. The variation in effectiveness may be linked to differences in an individual's genetic make-up (i.e. DNA), resulting in different biological mechanisms that drive heart disease. Here, I propose to uncover new disease-driving mechanisms and develop methods to stratify individuals by their main biological driver for heart disease. To do so, we can leverage 'genetic risk scores'-a method to aggregate information from many sites of DNA variation into a single measure of disease risk-along with information obtained by studying circulating blood molecules or 'biomarkers' (ex. fats and proteins) to reveal new insights. For example, abnormal biomarker measurements in individuals with a high genetic risk score, indicating a high inherited risk for heart disease, can highlight dysfunctional biological pathways. Therefore, by aggregating genetic and biomarker information, we can develop new genetic risk scores specific to these pathways, and use them to identify individuals likely to have heart disease because of a particular biological mechanism. Canadians will greatly benefit from this work because: 1) the new genetic risk scores to stratify individuals by biological driver for heart disease will empower clinicians to prescribe personalized risk-reduction strategies; and 2) the discovery of new dysfunctional disease-causing mechanisms provide researchers an opportunity to develop new drugs to target those pathways and continue to reduce risk of heart disease.

column36: Investigating the role of trained immunity on protection against acute cardiac injury.
column37: Heart failure (HF) arises after an injury to the heart causes it to pump less effectively. There are about 23 million HF cases worldwide, ~660,000 of which are in Canada, with the number steadily increasing. Standard HF therapies enhance heart pumping and improve clinical outcomes. Although patients initially stabilize on these therapies, recent studies show that HF recurs after this initial phase. Why some become stable (termed "remission") and why some "relapse" and have recurrent HF despite having optimal therapy is unknown, but represents a significant unmet clinical need. To begin to address this problem, a clinically relevant mouse model of HF recovery was developed. Importantly, HF redevelops in these mice when stressed a second time. A striking observation from this model is that the level of inflammation in HF-recovered hearts is the same as in failing hearts, raising the possibility that persistent inflammation may contribute to relapsing HF. The proposed work examines the role of immune cells called macrophages in HF recovery, as they are primary mediators of tissue repair and inflammation in the heart. The healthy heart typically harbors two macrophage types: one population that everyone is born with (embryonic) and is responsible for tissue repair, and one derived when blood cells from the bone marrow enter the heart after tissue injury, which is inherently more inflammatory. In this work, the applicant will first examine how these macrophage populations are affected in the course of HF recovery using the HF recovery mouse model. Using genetic methods, the applicant will then selectively alter the abundance of each macrophage population when the hearts are stressed a second time. These studies will allow us to determine the contributions of each macrophage group to the stability of HF recovery, and relapse. Results from this work may lead to new therapies that help lengthen the time HF patients remain in remission, free from costly hospital admissions.

column37: Background Inflammatory bowel disease affects more people in Canada than other countries. In recent year, an increase in cases has occurred among young children of age 0-4. We do not know exactly what causes IBD but research suggest that environmental stressors can trigger IBD in people who have the IBD genes. To evaluate risk factors and prevent IBD, we need new techniques to help us measure potentially important environmental exposures and efficiently detect IBD early. We will compare results of those that have and those that do not have IBD. Expected outcome Many Canadian have and will have IBD and it is important to understand how prevent or manage IBD better. This project brings together experts in environmental science, IBD specialists and public health to study how factors that we can change affect IBD. The result of this study will help us better understand factors beyond our genes that affect IBD and how we can modify these factors to prevent and treat IBD.

column36: Quantitative magnetic resonance imaging biomarkers of disease progression in multiple sclerosis
column37: Canada has one of the highest rates of multiple sclerosis (MS) in the world. More than half of the MS population will develop a progressive form of the disease (gradual accumulation of disability independent of MS attacks). At this time, however, there is only limited treatment available for progressive MS in Canada. This lack of effective treatment is largely due to an inadequate understanding of underlying biological mechanisms of the disease that is responsible for MS progression. Furthermore, clinical measures of progression change slowly and require a large number of study participants, who are monitored over a long period to detect treatment effects. Effective markers of progression thus represent an urgent and unmet need in the development of progressive MS treatment. We aim to use non-invasive, quantitative imaging techniques to study brain and spinal cord pathology (biology resulting in disease) and its relationship to global disability (e.g. ambulation, dexterity, visual acuity and cognition) annually over 4 years. We will use the data collected from the Canadian Prospective Cohort Study to Understand Progression in Multiple Sclerosis (CanProCo) - the largest Canadian study bringing together several study fields across 5 institutions to better understand MS progression over time. CanProCo is led by my supervisor, Dr. Jiwon Oh. We expect to establish biologically relevant imaging markers for MS progression that can 1) be used as outcome measures in shorter and less costly drug therapy trials in the future, which will accelerate the development of effective therapies, 2) monitor disease activity or tissue repair over time, and 3) evaluate the effectiveness of treatment or predict therapeutic outcomes to enable optimal clinical management. Our findings would be important for scientists, doctors, policymakers, people with MS and their caregivers by providing informational evidence to improve health policies and quality of life for people affected by MS.

column36: Exploration de la microarchitecture du sommeil pour expliquer la physiopathologie et l'heterogeneite des phenotypes dans l'hypersomnie idiopathique
column37: L'hypersomnie idiopathique (HI) est un trouble du sommeil chronique se caracterisant pas une somnolence excessive pendant le jour. Le fonctionnement de cette maladie est encore peu connu et il existe une grande variabilite de symptomes entre les patients. En effet, les cliniciens et les travaux de recherche rapportent des manifestations tres heterogenes, possiblement expliquees par la presence de sous-types dans l'HI. De plus, le diagnostic des patients avec l'HI represente un defi de taille puisque certains individus vont rapporter des symptomes importants sans rencontrer les criteres diagnostiques aux tests standardises. Afin de mieux comprendre les mecanismes biologiques derriere l'HI, de nouveaux marqueurs objectifs doivent etre trouves. La microarchitecture du sommeil, soit l'ensemble des evenements electriques du cerveau uniques au sommeil de l'etre humain, aurait le potentiel d'expliquer en partie les mecanismes de la maladie et les dissimilitudes entre les differents cas d'HI. Grace a des analyses avancees du signal EEG, il est possible de mesurer l'efficacite de la regulation du sommeil, la synchronisation neuronale pendant le sommeil et la qualite du sommeil. Le premier objectif de ce projet est de caracteriser la microarchitecture du sommeil des patients avec l'HI afin de trouver de potentiels biomarqueurs objectifs. Le second objectif est de determiner la presence de sous-types dans l'HI en se basant sur la microarchitecture du sommeil. Pour atteindre ces objectifs, 284 patients avec l'HI, dont la moitie ne rencontrent pas les criteres objectifs aux tests d'hypersomnie ont ete recrutes dans les dernieres annees ainsi que 94 sujets controles sains. Les participants ont rempli un journal de sommeil de 2 semaines avant de faire l'enregistrement d'une nuit de polysomnographie. Au lendemain, ils ont ete soumis a un test de 4 siestes diurnes afin d'evaluer leur somnolence.

column36: Investigating the role of senescence during age- and disuse-related bone loss.
column37: Over 1.5 million of Canadians are affected by osteoporosis, a disease that is caused by weak bones and leads to increased risk of fracture. As the Canadian population ages, the burden of osteoporotic fractures is predicted to increase. One of the hallmarks of age-related bone loss is cellular senescence; a process characterized by cells that can no longer divide. In bone, there is normally a balance between building bone (i.e. bone formation) and destroying bone (i.e. bone resorption). When bone cells senesce, the mechanisms that destroy bone overwhelm the mechanisms that build bone and there is a decrease in bone strength. Like age-related bone loss, there is a decrease in bone strength when bones are not being used, this is called disuse-related bone loss. Whenever we walk or stand, our bones experience pressure (a load) and this helps them to stay strong. In patients who are bedridden or have limited mobility, however, these forces are no longer present and bone strength decreases. When the bone is no longer experiencing these forces, it is said to be unloaded. Age-related bone loss and disuse-related bone loss share many similarities, and the combination of the two can lead to even worse outcomes for elderly patients. Hence, finding ways to prevent either or both types of bone loss is imperative. Senolytic drugs, such as dasatinib and quercetin, are compounds that will selectively kill senescent cells. When administered to aged mice, they are found to be protective of bone strength. To date, the role of senescence on the skeletal system in response to unloading has not been examined. Since, age- and disuse-related bone loss share many similarities, it is possible that senolytics may exert a similar protective effect on disuse-induced bone loss in young and aged mice. The relationship between senescence, disuse and age-related bone loss has the potential to elucidate mechanisms of osteoporosis and identify novel therapeutic targets.

column36: EVEP: Investigating the role of extracellular vesicles in endometriosis-associated pain
column37: Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory condition, affecting an estimated 190 million women globally. It is characterised by the presence of endometrial- (uterine lining) like tissue outside of the uterus, mainly within the pelvis. While endometriosis can cause infertility and other comorbidities, endometriosis-associated pain (EAP) is the predominant symptom affecting these women. One of the enigmas of endometriosis is how the disease causes pain and why this differs between women. This is further complicated by the fact that disease severity does not correlate with pain symptoms. Chronic pelvic pain (CPP) is often the central problem for women with endometriosis, as many seek a diagnosis to more effectively manage their pain. However, recent data which I have generated has shown that women with widespread pain (WP) compared to those with CPP have distinct comorbidities, psychological profiles, and reproductive outcomes. Moreover, women with endometriosis are more likely to have an autoimmune inflammatory disease such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Therefore, there is an urgent need to better understand the physiological underpinnings of the distinction between those with CPP and WP. This project will investigate the potential of extracellular vesicles (EVs), small nanoparticles found in many bodily fluids, from blood samples to better understand EAP. I will investigate medium-large (m/l) EVs (> 200nm) derived from cells known to be implicated and well characterised in other chronic inflammatory, pain associated diseases, such as RA. This pilot study aims to characterise m/lEVs in endometriosis patients with different pain phenotypes and will determine if they can serve as indicators of EAP, in a way that questionnaires alone cannot. This highly novel project will provide the first data on m/lEVs and EAP, and may provide a biologically relevant assessment of pain that can one day inform personalized treatment for women with EAP.

column36: Understanding adolescent mental health in American Samoa: The role of family-related intergenerational factors.
column37: Suicide rates are alarming among adolescents in remote Indigenous populations worldwide. Indigenous health leaders call to incorporate Indigenous traditional healing models into existing mental health systems. However, no randomized controlled trials have evaluated this approach in remote contexts for adolescent mental health. My doctoral thesis will explore how mental health trials in remote Indigenous communities can incorporate decolonizing frameworks while maintaining epidemiological rigour. My dissertation will be composed of three incremental aims: (1) a systematic scoping review to identify and synthesize barriers and facilitators to the conduct of trials in remote Indigenous contexts; (2) a qualitative study in American Samoa to identify best practices for the development and conduct of a mental health trial for adolescents in this context; and (3) an Indigenous-partnered pilot trial in American Samoa evaluating a community-developed intervention to improve adolescent mental wellness. These projects will be feasible given that Yale University has a history of community partnership, trial implementation, and established infrastructure in American Samoa (a high-risk setting, with parallels to Indigenous communities in Canada). The results of this dissertation will produce the first Indigenous-led adolescent mental health trial in a remote Indigenous community. Our results will not only inform Indigenous-partnered health system change in American Samoa, but will also produce a model that can inform design and adaptation of equitable mental health trials in other settings. This dissertation will: (1) provide Indigenous communities with scientific methods to empower rigorous evaluation of future innovations to improve the health of their communities; and (2) produce knowledge to advocate for the incorporation of Indigenous ways of healing into existing mental health systems, ultimately improving the resiliency of Indigenous youth worldwide.

column36: A mixed methods exploration of young peoples' experiences of climate anxiety and its impacts in British Columbia, Canada
column37: Extreme weather events, negative impacts on agricultural production and the liveability of human settlements, as well as potential for mass migration and conflict have all been linked to climate change. This is increasingly being linked to mental health challenges such as PTSD, suicidality, depression, and substance use. At the same time, new concepts such as climate anxiety and eco-anxiety have emerged. Concerns about the mental health consequences of climate change have focused on youth, with the issue gaining attention through the activism of young people such as Greta Thunberg and Isra Hirsi. However, there is debate as to whether climate anxiety is always unhealthy or if it can instead be a healthy response to the current crisis. Furthermore, there is limited research on the role that adults and mental health professionals should play in helping young people with climate anxiety. This study will explore the impacts of climate anxiety among youth on British Columbia (BC), Canada, making use of both interviews and surveys. Twenty youth aged 13-17 will be recruited to participate in interviews. These interviews will explore young people's experiences of climate anxiety, ask how they cope, and elicit their expertise on how adults and mental health professionals can support them. Information from the interviews will then be used to create survey questions specifically about youth climate anxiety, which will be used in surveys given to 200 youth. The surveys will also have questions about overall anxiety, wellbeing, and young peoples' actions and knowledge about climate change. This will make it possible to explore the connection between climate anxiety and overall mental health, as well as whether engaging in environmental activities can be helpful, as some have suggested. This research will add needed evidence on the impacts of climate change on youth mental health in Canada as well as provide information on how to best support young people.

column36: Profiling T cell cross-reactivity in elite HIV controllers
column37: 'Elite controllers' are individuals infected with HIV who develop natural immunity that delays or prevents disease altogether. Elite controller immune responses seem to be resistant to frequent mutations of the virus. Prior studies suggest a reason: key immune cells known as T cells may recognize multiple parts of the HIV virus rather than one. Existing technology is unable to find these 'cross-reactive' T cells and match them to parts of the HIV virus. My project proposes a new method to determine the targets and cross-reactivity of T cells on a significantly larger scale than previously possible. Using this tool, I will examine the T cells of HIV elite controllers and patients who require treatment. If successful, this project will help to resolve a long-standing debate: do T cells in elite controllers target parts of the HIV virus in meaningfully different ways? If so, this information could be applied to vaccines and therapeutics to generate 'elite controller'-type immune responses in other HIV-infected individuals.

column36: B. fragilis genetic variants differentially modulate the immune response in inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease, including Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, damages the digestive tract and causes painful symptoms. Although the number of cases in the world are increasing, we still do not understand the exact cause of the disease, nor do we have a cure. Aside from our genetics and environment, scientists have identified bacteria that normally live in the gut as important players that can aggravate or ameliorate disease. We have limited understanding of how these bacteria interact with our cells. Of note are a particular species of bacteria that appear to vary between healthy individuals and inflammatory bowel disease patients in their contribution to disease pathology. In healthy individuals, these bacteria appear to have the ability to direct our cells to maintain a healthy gut environment; in diseased patients, bacteria seem to have limited ability to do so. We thus aim to understand what the differences between these bacterial "strains" are, and how they link to health and disease. Pinpointing the basis for these strain differences gives us a better understanding of our symbiotic relationship with bacteria in the gut. We can leverage our results for advancing future scientific studies, and importantly, for improving therapies in development and proposing therapeutic interventions to come.

column36: Understanding the role of 17beta-estradiol signaling in induced regulatory T cell induction, activity, and stability
column37: Immune responses vary based on biological sex and tend to be more robust in females compared to males. In fact, males are generally more at risk of infectious diseases, while many autoimmune conditions have a higher prevalence in females. While many factors contribute to these differences, the sex hormone estrogen is a major driver of biological sex-based variations in immunity. Estrogen was orignially characterized as a female sex hormone, but it is also produced in lower concentrations in males. It plays important roles in many physiological processes including reproductive development and function, metabolism, cognition, and immune system regulation. Although its role in these processes is well established, its mechanism of action remains poorly understood. Our goal is to deepen our understanding of how estrogen interacts with regulatory T cells, which are a specific type of immune cell. Regulatory T cells dampen the immune response and help prevent autoimmunity. Estrogen has been shown to enhance the regulatory activity of these cells, as well as to promote their development outside of immune organs. Our research project focuses on understanding the mechanism by which estrogen carries out these functions both in healthy women and men, as well as in individuals with Crohn's disease, an autoimmune condition affecting the gut. We aim to understand how estrogen signaling affects the development of Treg cells outside of immune organs, and how it affects their stability and regulatory activity. We will also determine how changes in estrogen signaling affects Treg cells in individuals with Crohn's disease, and assess whether manipulating the estrogen signaling pathways in these cells can enhance their regulatory activity. Our project will contribute to our understanding of the role of estrogen and biological sex on the immune response, and will help lay a groundwork for advances in cell therapies against Crohn's disease and potentially other autoimmune conditions.

column36: Exploring Perceptions and Experiences of Structural Violence, Mental Health, and Positive Adaptation Among Emerging Adults who have 'Aged Out' of Foster Care in Canada: An Explanatory-Sequential Mixed Methods Research Study
column37: Of the estimated 78,000 youth in the Canadian foster care system, nearly half will 'age out' of care on their 18th birthday. Forced to grow up almost overnight, these youth are left to navigate complex social services with minimal guidance and structured supports. This abrupt transition to independence is associated with poor physical, social, and mental health; however, the chronic effects of such adversities remain under-explored. Further information is needed to uncover how challenges and barriers experienced by this population affect longterm development and success. The purpose of this mixed-methods study is to understand how youth aging out of foster care navigate the transition to adulthood, and how adversities faced during this period may influence mental health and resilience. Approximately 100-150 youth ages 18-25 from across Canada will be recruited for this study. All participants will receive an electronic questionnaire capturing demographic information, foster care experiences, and transition outcomes. This quantitative data will be compared and analyzed to determine associations among participant characteristics. A subsample of 20-30 youth will then be selected to take part in virtual interviews exploring subjective transition experiences using a qualitative interpretive description approach. Integration of quantitative and qualitative data will aid in the identification of participants who have demonstrated resilience in response to adversity, leading to the discovery of internal and external factors that serve as barriers and facilitators to resilience in this population. Study findings may also reveal opportunities for tailored and proactive mental health care that reflects the unique psychosocial needs of these vulnerable youth. Future research in this area may lead to clinical, policy, and legislative reform that improves mental health outcomes and reduces barriers to societal participation among youth aging out of foster care in Canada.

column36: Risk for disordered eating among North American Asian emerging adults: Examination of the roles of ethnic identity, parenting, and satisfaction of basic psychological needs
column37: Eating disorders can result in serious medical consequences, including electrolyte disturbance and cardiac arrhythmias, and have the highest mortality rates among any psychiatric disorders. Asians constitute the largest group of visible minorities in Canada and, compared to White Canadians, have similar or higher rates of eating disorders, yet they are less likely to receive treatment. Emerging adulthood (18-25 years of age) is a developmental period when individuals are at particularly high risk for developing eating disorders. During this period, many parents continue to play a significant role in emerging adults' development. However, the impact of particular parenting practices on the children may vary across cultures. For example, parental control is perceived negatively in Western cultures, but may be perceived as well-meaning in Asian cultures. Therefore, strong ethnic identity in Asian emerging adults may buffer them against the negative impact of parental control. That is, for Asian emerging adults who identify strongly with their ethnic culture, parental control may not pose as much risk for psychological adjustment, including eating disorders, as for those who have a weaker ethnic identity. The proposed research examines this possibility and contributes to understanding how various individual, familial and cultural factors may explain Asian emerging adults' risk for eating disorders. Findings will inform theories regarding psychosocial risks for eating disorders in Asians living in North America by clarifying the role of ethnic identification in their mental health. These findings could also inform the development of more family-oriented, culturally-sensitive intervention and prevention programs attending to the needs of Asian emerging adults at risk. We note that causes of eating disorders are multifaced and cannot be solely attributed to one's familial environment. Instead, families usually play an important role in one's treatment and recovery.

column36: The impact of multimorbidity on severity, recovery, recurrence and costs after TIA or stroke: a population-based study
column37: Stroke is among the leading causes of disability in Canada and worldwide. Further, having a stroke puts patients at a greater risk of several negative health outcomes, including physical/cognitive disability, major bleeding, stroke recurrence, and death. Moreover, stroke is most common in those of older age, who also more often live with multiple diseases (aka multimorbidity). Despite this, the interconnected relationships between multimorbidity and various post-stroke outcomes has not been thoroughly studied. This thesis aims to provide an in-depth examination into the associations between various individual diseases, and multimorbidity, with several post-stroke outcomes. These include the risk of disability, stroke recurrence, major bleeding, decreased quality of life, re-admission to hospital, and death. The findings from this thesis will provide important information to patients and clinicians about the risk of various outcomes in specific patients based on their pre-stroke medical record, and will help target treatment to the most at-risk groups.

column36: Single-cell probing of epigenetic memory in immunity
column37: The rapid development of sequencing-based techniques has revolutionized our comprehension of the genome, paving the way for gene identification, analysis of genetic diversity, determination of the epigenetic code, and study of the 3D genome structure. These techniques have allowed the identification of a limited number of transcription factors, the pioneers, that can initiate a series of events to reshape the epigenome and modify the regulatory chromosomal contacts in response to developmental or stress signals. In innate immune cells, the chromatin reprogramming initiated by a primary insult has been recently shown to induce a stable epigenetic 'memory' that influences the response to further infections, a process named 'trained immunity'. Nevertheless, due to technical limitations, it is unclear how heterogeneous is this epigenetic encryption and how individual cellular functions are affected? Our overarching objective is to develop methods to overcome these technological and knowledge gaps to render possible the detection of chromatin conformation and long-range interactions at single-cell and single-molecule resolution. Big data and the development of accompanying algorithms will elucidate the dynamics of epigenetic states and heterogeneity during trained immunity. We aim to develop bulk and single-cell Single-Molecule chromatin Capture (SM-C) to analyze the genome-wide allele-specific interactions and reveal epigenetic heterogeneity. We will also develop a targeted SM-C method to evaluate how the recruitment of a novel pioneer factor reprograms the transcriptional networks and contributes to the establishment of the epigenetic memory. This joint effort between Canada and Japan research teams will deliver techniques that will be a major advancement in the field of epigenetics, allowing us to understand how epigenetic diversity is established and which should guide the development of novel preventive diagnostics and treatments for infectious and immune diseases.

column36: Examining the Role of Online Discussion Forums in Unguided ICBT for Canadian Public Safety Personnel: A Randomized Trial
column37: Public safety personnel (PSP) are police officers, firefighters, paramedics, and others who work hard to keep Canadians safe. They frequently encounter traumatic events and have high rates of mental health problems. Many PSP face barriers to traditional mental health treatments related to location, busy schedules, cost of treatment, and concerns about privacy and stigma. Internet-delivered cognitive behavioural therapy (ICBT) can help overcome these barriers. It allows users to learn the same coping skills as they would learn in face-to-face cognitive behavioural therapy-a gold standard treatment for common mental health problems-but it tends to be cheaper and easier to access. ICBT is typically offered with therapist guidance, which generally makes it more effective, or in a purely self-help format, which generally makes it easier to provide to a larger number of people. A recent study found that most PSP report a preference for a therapist-guided format, but some said they would prefer a self-help format. Both formats have advantages, and it is important that researchers explore new ways to improve them. Some research suggests that adding an online discussion forum to self-help ICBT makes it more effective, but more research is needed to confirm this. My colleagues and I have developed a therapist-guided ICBT course for PSP, which is being offered in Saskatchewan and Quebec. I am proposing to develop a self-help version of this course and deliver it to PSP across Canada. I will then randomly assign 315 users to receive access to (a) a forum in which a therapist is involved in the discussion, (b) a forum without a therapist involved, or (c) no forum. I will measure each user's symptom change through questionnaires and use statistics to test whether forums lead to better improvement in symptoms. This study is expected to help PSP across the country with mental health problems and test whether two kinds of online discussion forums are helpful in self-help ICBT.

column36: Artificial Intelligence based adaptive and interpretable models for analyzing multi-track epigenomic sequential data
column37: In this project we will take a fresh approach to harness the great potential of AI in the big data-analyses of epigenomic sequences. Epigenetics is the study of molecules and mechanisms that can perpetuate alternative gene activity states in the context of the same DNA sequence. Key factors in epigenetic control are chemical modifications to DNA and histones, which establish a complex regulatory network that controls genome function. Although epigenetic marks are established early during development and differentiation, adaptations occur throughout life in response to intrinsic (e.g. oncogenes) and environmental stimuli (e.g. diet) and may lead to disease late in life. Moreover, epigenomes react to environmental influence (e.g. maternal care, diet, exposure to toxins) with possibly long-term consequences. Thus, the life of an individual is not only defined by their genome, but also by their epigenome, which is flexible and changeable throughout the lifetime. The research team has two epigeneticists (Yamanaka, Davie) and two artificial intelligence (AI) experts (Ashraf, Khan). Working as a collaborative team, the four research groups will develop new tools to analyze DNA sequence data that will be able to predict 3D organization and functional aspects of these interactions in vertebrate epigenomes, which would be transformative in epigenetics research. We also propose the paradigm of iteratively refining the AI models through wet-experiments. In cancer, resistance to specific treatments often results in worse outcomes. It is now known that the 3D organization of the genome gets modified in these cancers. These sequence changes affect genome interactions and predispose some individuals to disease or an inadequate response to a virus attack as in COVID-19. Our studies have the potential to exploit the genome-wide data to predict the changes in the 3D organization of an individual's genome and gene activity, adding a new dimension to personalized medicine.

column36: Mindfulness and Self-Compassion as Alternate Coping Strategies for Undergraduate Students Using Alcohol and/or Marijuana to Cope
column37: Using alcohol and/or marijuana in attempt to alleviate negative emotions has been consistently associated with alcohol and/or marijuana-related problems in undergraduate students. Tension-Reduction Theory suggests individuals use substances in attempt to alleviate negative emotions when they lack alternate means of coping. Thus, investigating alternate coping strategies, such as mindfulness and self-compassion, may afford a unique opportunity to address coping-motivated alcohol and marijuana use and the associated problems on Canadian university campuses. The proposed three-part Doctoral dissertation aims to develop, evaluate, and disseminate a brief mindfulness and self-compassion program aimed at reducing coping-motivated use and the associated problems in undergraduates. In Part One, undergraduates who report elevated levels of coping-motivated alcohol and/or marijuana use will be randomly assigned to participate in a brief mindfulness and self-compassion program, relaxation program, or wait-list control group. Fourteen students who participated in the mindfulness and self-compassion program in Part One will be invited to participate in a semi-structured interview in Part Two. The purpose of the interview will be to gather detailed information about their experience using mindfulness and self-compassion as alternate coping strategies, as well as their impressions of the program. Using the results of Part One and Part Two to improve the program, I plan to pilot the program at the host university and subsequently implement it across interested Canadian universities in Part Three. Teaching mindfulness and self-compassion as alternate coping strategies to alcohol and/or marijuana use may help reduce coping-motivated use and the associated problems on Canadian university campuses. This would directly benefit the students using alcohol and/or marijuana, their fellow students, and their university.

column36: Neuromodulation with cognitive training to enhance working memory
column37: Memory loss is a normal part of getting older; but for people with dementia, this process is severe and disabling. What if we could strengthen aspects of our memory and reverse cognitive decline? Brain training has the potential to rehabilitate people with cognitive deficits, but research in this area has made little progress over the past decades and there is ongoing debate on the efficacy of brain training programs. We aim to accelerate the development of cognitive enhancement therapies by combining training on a musical memory task with a type of individualized brain stimulation that is known to boost brain function. By asking people to reorder musical notes in their mind, our training program targets auditory working memory, which is the ability to remember and manipulate sounds. Neurologically healthy participants will come to the lab for several days to practice this task, while receiving either real or sham transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). A TMS machine generates a small magnetic field, which can be directed at a person's head to transiently alter the electric signal within their brain. When we apply rhythmic pulses of TMS at the same frequency, timing, and location of brain waves that are naturally generated during auditory working memory, we are able to improve people's performance on the memory task. The more their brain waves synchronize with the stimulation, the better they do. We will now investigate whether performance enhancement can outlast the period of stimulation and generalize to other cognitive tasks. The results will shed light on the mechanisms of brain wave entrainment, and potentially open a new avenue for treatment of neurocognitive deficits. In the future, people who have impaired working memory could undergo a form of rehabilitation using our combined training and stimulation protocol, with the goal of restoring their brain to a normal level of functioning.

column36: Multi-ethnic polygenic risk scores to improve risk screening of complex diseases for populations of non-European ancestries
column37: Genetic predisposition to disease is an important risk factor for many complex diseases. Advances in human genetics have enabled the development of efficient genetic scores, named polygenic risk scores, that aggregate information across millions of genetic features to predict disease risks. In combination with effective application of high-dimensional statistics, machine learning and artificial intelligence, the predictive power of recently developed polygenic risk scores is increasing and indicating high clinical utility. However, nearly all of these advances have occurred using data from individuals of European ancestry. The effectiveness of polygenic risk scores in individuals of non-European ancestries is still largely unknown. But in the cases where it has been evaluated, the predictive performance of polygenic risk scores is substantially attenuated. This is likely due to differences in the underlying genetic basis of disease in different populations, together with varying environmental exposures. To date, there are no clinically-acceptable polygenic risk scores available to people of non-European ancestries, though these populations, including minorities and aboriginals, who support the health care system and its patients, make up very important proportions of the population of Canada and of many other countries. Therefore, having gathered several large population-based cohorts of different ethnic background, we aim to develop novel machine learning methods, together with open source software packages to improve the accuracy of polygenic risk scores for complex diseases, such as various types of cancer, coronary heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and osteoporosis, for individuals of non-European ancestries. We anticipate that these polygenic risk scores applicable to multiple ethnic groups will help not only realize the goals of generalizability and clinical utility, but also mitigate long-standing health care disparities.

column36: Neighbourhood environmental exposures and their associated health risks: evidence and policy implications for urban health and health equity from Accra, Ghana
column37: As low- and middle-income countries develop, their populations move increasingly into cities. While urban populations are healthier overall than their rural counterparts, the benefits of urbanization are not experienced equally. The gap between rich and poor is large in many cities, and may be growing, resulting in unequal health outcomes in all age groups. Governments in those cities, such as Accra, Ghana, rely on scientific evidence to ensure that they can plan their development in a way that is healthy and equitable for all residents. For my proposed research, I will study characteristics of areas in Accra to understand what neighbourhoods look like across the city, how risk factors in the neighbourhood environment influence health outcomes, and how environmental factors can be targeted with well-planned policies to improve the health and well-being of people living in the city. I will use methods from epidemiology and geography to create data and evidence about neighbourhoods and their role in health. In partnership with city planners and other policymakers in Accra, I will also identify policies with the potential to improve the neighbourhood environment and reduce health inequalities in low- and middle-income urban settings. My work will be supported by the Pathways to Equitable Healthy Cities program (PEHC), a global consortium funded by the Wellcome Trust. Through PEHC, I will have access to technical and scientific expertise from world-class faculty at several global universities, and policy expertise from stakeholders in five cities around the world. I will use these resources and opportunities to conduct research that will impact human health on a local and international scale. By working with motivated policymakers and diverse international project partners, I will advance our collective knowledge about neighbourhoods and urban health and co-create viable, innovative policy solutions to build healthier and more equitable cities around the world.

column36: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease and Dysanapsis
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a common lung disease that makes it hard to breathe. It is a leading cause of death and disability in the world and in Canada. Although smoking is the main risk factor, only a minority of smokers develop COPD. Besides, people who had never smoked can also develop COPD, suggesting that other risk factors must exist. Air is transported into the lung via airways that resemble the branches of a tree and they filter inhaled particles. 50 years ago, scientists using simple tests that measure lung function, speculated that some people have undersized airways relative to the volume of their lungs. The size mismatch between airway and lung volume was termed dysanapsis and is believed to develop early in life when airway branches grow more slowly than lung volume. Recently, by measuring airway tree size using medical imaging called computed tomography (CT), our team showed that people with dysanapsis are eight times more likely to develop COPD. Thus, dysanapsis is a major COPD risk factor on par with cigarette smoking. In this project, by analyzing airway trees of thousands of adults aged 20-97 years old, I will assess how the airway tree grows across different ages and if there is a difference between males and females. In addition, I will discover the genes that play a role in dysanapsis development and assess if children having those genes would manifest low lung function. Finally, I will investigate if dysanapsis involves all airways in the lung and will explore if it leads to more absorption of cigarette smoke in the body and consequently more limitation in breathing. The results of this project could help us prevent dysanapsis by interventions targeting the early years in life. This would promote healthy and resilient lung development, explain the variability in individual susceptibility to inhaled particles like cigarette smoke, and ultimately promote healthy lungs for life.

column36: Fabrication of a vascularized bioartificial pancreas using macroencapsulation of stem cell-derived pancreatic islet cells for the treatment of type 1 Diabetes.
column37: Type 1 diabetes affects more than 300 000 Canadians and its impact continues to rise in Canada and the world. Transplantation of pancreatic islets, the tissue regulating insulin and blood sugar, is a promising strategy to treat diabetic patients because it can eliminate their dependence on external insulin sources for many months. There are however severe disadvantages with this approach. One of the most critical problem is graft rejection, a process where your own immune system attacks the newly transplanted tissue and destroys it. To protect the islets, scientists are encapsulating them in selectively permeable materials. These are biocompatible materials that create a physical barrier to prevent the immune cells to reach the graft while allowing nutrients to go through to keep the islets alive. Unfortunately, the large quantity of islets needed to treat human diabetic patients make it difficult to have enough nutrients for all the graft, leading to significant cell death and failure of the therapy. To address these issues, we are fabricating a small device that can encapsulate several hundred thousand islets and protect them from immune destruction. To optimize survival of the graft, our device contains many blood vessel-like channels that can be directly irrigated by the patient's own blood after transplantation. With our approach, the islets inside the device will take on the function of the patient's failing pancreas, producing the insulin needed to regulate blood sugar level for several years. This strategy will allow patients suffering from type 1 diabetes to be treated by islet transplant without suffering from the difficult complications related to immunosuppression or insulin management. It thus represents an important advance in cellular therapy for diabetic patients.

column36: Episodic memory and theory-of-mind in children with autism
column37: We use memory of our past experiences to imagine what other people are thinking. Being aware of other's mental states is crucial for successful social interactions. In autism, detailed recollection of past events and experiences is commonly impaired, along with the ability to imagine what others are thinking. Together, these challenges may create difficulty when conversing with others, providing a potential explanation for the social impairments commonly seen in autism. The detailed memory deficit may be due to the fact that people with autism have difficulty relating experiences to themselves, a phenomenon which normally boosts detailed memory. We aim to see how the effect of relating memories to oneself differs in children with autism compared to typically developing children. Children will complete a memory task where they will relate some objects to themselves by answering the question: "Do you like this object?". We will test them on their detailed memory for the objects and look at their brain activity while they are resting and while they are performing this activity. Additionally, participants will be assessed on how they can think about others' states of mind. We expect that children with autism will not show improved memory when making a self-relation and will show less engagement of brain areas related to detailed memory, understanding others' perspectives, and social processing. This research will tell us if the difficulty in relating memories to oneself is related to difficulties in imagining others' mindsets and how the brain behaves differently in this scenario in the presence of autism. This will help us to understand the roots of social impairments as they exist in the brain and behavior in autism and will inform future interventions to improve day-to-day interactions for these individuals.

column36: Acute effects of non-invasive repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) in the management of chronic orofacial pain and problematic opioid use.
column37: Temporomandibular joint disorders (TMD) are common chronic pain conditions of the face and jaw that impact significantly the well-being and quality of life of people suffering from them. Chronic TMD pain is challenging to treat and many patients do not respond well to usual treatments. Moreover, medications such as opioids are associated with different risks and side-effects. Hence, the investigation of newer and safer treatments becomes highly relevant. "Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation" (rTMS) is a safe and non-invasive technique used to stimulate the brain and potentially change neurons. rTMS has proven to improve pain and addiction, but its use in TMD has not been tested yet. Thus, we aim to assess if rTMS can improve pain and opioid problems in TMD participants. This thesis project is divided in two studies. One study is focused on pain, where 30 TMD participants not taking opioids will be recruited, and the other is focused on opioids, where another 30 TMD participants taking opioids will be recruited. In both studies, each participant will have two separate treatment sessions, one where they will receive active rTMS, and one where they will receive a "sham" (i.e., fake) treatment with an identical device but with limited power. The order of the sessions will be random and neither the participant nor the staff will know when the patients receive one or the other. Following each treatment session (rTMS or sham), participants will complete electronic diaries at home, twice daily, for one week. These diaries will ask questions about pain intensity and pain interference with daily activities. Patients who use opioids will also answer diary questions about opioid use. We expect that rTMS decreases pain intensity, pain interference, and opioid problems in TMD participants. This project is novel and important, as its findings could support the use of a new and safe treatment for improving pain, opioid problems, and suffering associated to TMD.

column36: Co-Developing & Piloting a New Model of Care Delivery for Migrant People Living with HIV in Montreal
column37: As of June 2019, immigrants accounted for 82.8% of Canada's annual population growth. Immigrants represent an increasing proportion of people living with HIV (PLWH) in Canada. In fact, a Canadian surveillance report indicated that immigrants accounted for 40% of all new HIV diagnoses reported in 2018. Efficient access to HIV care for new immigrants has significant individual-level health benefits (e.g. reducing the morbidity and mortality associated with HIV infection), which can translate into major society-level benefits (e.g. prevention of HIV transmission to others). However, immigrant PLWH face longstanding and complex barriers that prevent them from accessing and adhering to HIV care compared to native-born citizens. For example, immigrants often lack medical coverage and have limited financial resources to access HIV medications. Furthermore, immigrants are often unable to fluently speak English or French, making medical terminology harder to understand for them and hindering their ability to navigate the Canadian healthcare system. Also, personal barriers such as fear of being stigmatized when accessing HIV care, and organizational barriers such as scheduling appointments at HIV clinics, have both intensified with the COVID-19 pandemic. A possible solution to mitigating or eliminating a number of the barriers immigrants face is to conceive and implement a new model of HIV care specific to this population. This likely means giving healthcare providers a set of specific guidelines to follow when working with this population and integrating clinical care with social programs from community-based organizations that serve immigrants. My research program seeks to do the following: (1) co-design a model of care with patients, clinicians, community organizations, and hospital administrative decision-makers; (2) co-design an efficient implementation strategy with all stakeholders; and (3) test this new model of care at two major HIV care centres in Montreal.

column36: Developing Glycan-Based Antiviral Prophylactics to Prevent the Spread of COVID-19 and Other Respiratory Infections
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has now surpassed 34 million confirmed cases. No vaccine or antiviral drug has yet been approved to prevent the spread of SARS-CoV-2, the causative agent of COVID-19. Moreover, the most vulnerable people are also at risk of severe infection from seasonal circulating respiratory viruses, such as influenza. In the absence of effective vaccines against COVID-19 and most strains of common respiratory viruses, new approaches guided by interdisciplinary research are required. Most viruses initiate attachment to the surface of human cells by interacting with complex carbohydrates called glycans. I aim to identify which subtypes of glycans are used by SARS-CoV-2 and other respiratory viruses for entry and infection of human airway cells. Through collaboration with an expert carbohydrate chemist, we will design and test glycan-mimicking antiviral molecules that block the interaction with glycans to prevent viral infection. With this project, I will rapidly identify prototype antiviral prophylactics to help limit the spread of COVID-19 and other common or emerging viral respiratory infections.

column36: Detecting eating disorder biomarkers in youth via video-based eye tracking
column37: Generally starting in adolescence, eating disorders are among the most burdensome mental health problems, with some of the longest recovery times and highest mortality rates. Eating disorders, such as anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa, have one of the highest hospitalization costs in comparison to other disorders, thus there is an urgent need to increase our scientific understanding of these disorders and to increase early detection. Early detection gives patients and at-risk populations the best chance of recovery. The present research project aims to discover measurable markers in youth that are unique to eating disorders. To do that, we will study eye movements in youth with and without eating disorders. The study will be conducted at two research sites- Hotel Dieu Hospital (Kingston) and McMaster Children's Hospital (Hamilton)- where participants will complete a series of eye tracking tasks and questionnaires assessing thoughts, behaviour and personality. Eye tracking technology, used to record eye movements, is a low-cost and portable tool used in the study of various conditions. The biological mechanisms that guide eye movements are scientifically well understood. By examining differences in eye movements made during complex tasks, variations in cognition and frontal cortex activation can be discovered. Therefore, by comparing eye movement data with measurements of personality traits (e.g. impulsivity) and patient clinical information, we expect to detect typical markers of eating disorders. Our results have the potential to yield new insight on the biology of eating disorders. Identifying these markers could allow clinicians to diagnose eating disorders faster and more impartially, potentially fostering early diagnosis and prevention. By identifying eating disorders earlier, the costs to the health care system incurred due to lengthy eating disorder treatment may be minimized and eye tracking equipment can integrate within Canadian treatment clinics.

column36: Improving diagnostic accuracy in early psychosis: Differentiating the neuropsychological profiles of cannabis-induced and primary psychotic disorders in a 12-month follow-up study
column37: Cannabis use is common in psychotic disorders, especially among young people experiencing a first episode of psychosis. Cannabis is linked to the development of temporary, 'induced' psychotic symptoms, which are caused by cannabis use and diminish with abstinence (cannabis-induced psychosis), while individuals with primary psychosis who also frequently use cannabis (cannabis-comorbid psychosis) have a distinct mental illness requiring a different treatment approach. However, the similarity of the symptoms of these disorders often renders them indistinguishable, creating barriers to intervention and treatment. Previous attempts to identify differentiating features have been unsuccessful at reliably distinguishing between diagnoses. As such, there is an urgent need to refine the diagnostic tools available to psychosis clinics. Despite the abundance of research identifying cognitive deficits, eye movement abnormalities, and speech deficits as core neuropsychological symptoms of primary psychotic disorders (e.g., schizophrenia), limited research has examined these well-established markers as potential methods to improve diagnosis in first-episode psychosis. The proposed novel line of research will assess first-episode psychosis patients upon entry to a psychosis clinic using cognitive, visual, and speech tasks. Participants will be re-assessed at 3-, 6-, and 12-month follow-up time points to evaluate if assessments at baseline can predict diagnostic classification reliably over time. These objective, well-replicated methods are hypothesized to increase accurate diagnosis above and beyond traditionally used measures. The ability to reliably differentiate these disorders is crucial to early intervention in psychosis and holds promise to reduce the diagnostic load on mental health care workers. This research will facilitate more rapid and successful intervention, promote individualized treatment plans, and lead to widespread benefits for patients.

column36: Women Empowerment-Cancer Awareness Nexus (WE-CAN): An Implementation Research of Cervical Cancer Prevention through HPV Self-Sampling and Education
column37: With appropriate screening cervical cancer is highly preventable. However, some vulnerable groups of women in India, like those living in rural or impoverished urban areas, continue to be victims of premature deaths. Presently, cervical cancer screening is performed via the Pap test, which requires a visit to a clinician's office. Self-sampling for HPV, the virus that causes cervical cancer, is an innovative and useful method of screening that allows a woman to test in a space and at a time of her choosing and could overcome many of the barriers to the Pap test like transportation, child care, and cultural modesty. Our goals are to provide sexual health education and to determine the acceptability, uptake and impact of HPV self-sampling on women's health. We will recruit 600 never/under screened women age 25-69 in rural and low income urban areas. We will provide sexual health education sessions to both women and their male partners. The cultural sensitivity and appropriateness of the content of educational materials will be determined through extensive consultation and collaboration with the local communities. To overcome issues related to low literacy we will rely heavily on audiovisual, info graphs, story boards and locally developed plays and videos. We will use a combination of surveys, focus group and interviews to assess the feasibility and impact of the HPV self-sampling and explore barriers and facilitators to cervical cancer screening uptake. The implementation of this proposed novel strategy of HPV self-sampling has the potential to lead to a new screening standard for hard-to-reach women by removing known barriers and offering it as a primary screening test for subsequent Pap testing. Furthermore, HPV self-sampling can be adapted and scaled up to other regions in India and other low- and middle- income countries to advance cancer prevention, community health literacy, public health policies, and enable women to make healthful and personalized decisions.

column36: Evaluating the enhanced Community-based Health Education and Communication (eCHEC) model in improving the knowledge and behaviours of community residents on known risk factors and protective factors for preventing Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) in Khon Kaen Thailand
column37: Liver Cancer caused by liver flukes is very common in Khon Kaen Thailand. People get infected with the liver fluke when they eat raw fish that is infected with the fluke. There have been many programs that have tried to prevent this type of cancer. However, it remains a common problem especially in the Northern parts of Thailand. Researchers from Khon Kaen University have created a Community-Based Health Education and Communication (CHEC) program to prevent intake of raw fish in the communities in Khon Kaen. They have found that this program has improved the knowledge and behaviour of community residents regarding eating raw fish which is part of how the liver fluke infects humans. In our research we plan to improve the CHEC program and test it in communities in Khon Kaen Thailand. We intend to do an experiment to give the program in some communities in Khon Kaen. column36: Understanding the Impact of Osteoarthritis on Depression in the Canadian Population
column37: In Canada, a major public health concern is that osteoarthritis (OA) and depression affects millions of Canadians, and both conditions co-occur in about 20% of adults. Most people know a friend or loved one whose quality of life has been negatively affected by either of these two chronic conditions. OA pain symptoms and depressive symptoms are two of the leading causes of disability in adults. The double burden of having both OA and depression further compromises a person's quality of life and severely limits activity. There has been inconclusive evidence regarding the assertion that OA can lead to subsequent depressive symptoms facilitated through pain. In addition, there has been a lack of available Canadian data sources to examine the relationship between OA and subsequent depression in a population of adults where variables are measured across different time points (also known as a longitudinal study). There is a great opportunity to better understand the relationship between OA and depression, by using recent data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA). The CLSA provides pan-Canadian data that has information on OA, depression, pain, and other key variables. I will study the temporal relationship between OA and subsequent depressed mood using statistical methods appropriate for longitudinal data. A cure for OA does not exist at present, but it is possible to minimize the impacts of this debilitating health condition. Current OA treatment is focused on pain management, but it is not clear whether pain management is effective at dealing with the psychological consequences of OA. The study results will help to clarify the risk of developing depressive symptoms among people with OA, in order to improve the lives of people with OA, by informing OA clinical management (e.g., screening tools for depression) and supporting health services planning (e.g., social support programs).

column36: Predicting invasive ventilation and its effect on mortality for patients with pneumonia: an observational study using machine learning and a target trial approach
column37: Pneumonia is a common, dangerous, and treatable cause of mortality and morbidity. More than 2 million people worldwide die from pneumonia each year, not including the accumulating mortality from the COVID-19 pandemic. The burden of pneumonia falls disproportionately on people made vulnerable by poverty, insecure housing, or malnutrition. Treatments focus on antibiotics and supportive care, with severe cases frequently placed on ventilatory life support also known as invasive ventilation. However, invasive ventilation comes with significant side effects including the danger of the procedure to start invasive ventilation, the risks of weakness, hospital-acquired infection, and delirium that are common during invasive ventilation, and the difficulties in communication that come from having a breathing tube prevent speech. The decision to start invasive ventilation requires careful weighing of the risks and benefits, but there is almost no data available to assist physicians and patients in making this decision. Our project will investigate the risks and benefits of invasive ventilation in patients with pneumonia according to practical clinical characteristics. We will use data from three large, detailed databases of critically ill patients featuring minute-by-minute clinical data, and we will use the innovative "target trial" method which has improved our ability to gain helpful information from observational research. This research will help motivate clinical trials to help improve our care for patients with pneumonia and it will guide patients and clinicians who are faced with the difficult decision of whether or not to start invasive ventilation when a patient is very sick with pneumonia.

column36: Characterizing the mechanisms of glutamate-mediated activation of spinal cord neural stem/progenitor cells to reveal therapeutic targets for spinal cord injury
column37: Spinal cord injury (SCI) is a devastating condition with currently no available treatment options. A number of stem cell-based therapies have been examined to promote regeneration and recovery after SCI but all have been limited by minimal neuronal differentiation and a lack of functional connectivity. Overcoming these barriers is essential in translating effective stem cell therapies to patients. The adult spinal cord contains a population of endogenous neural stem/progenitor cells (NSPCs) that proliferate after injury thus providing a promising source of endogenous repair potential. However, the mechanisms that activate spinal cord NSPCs previously remained unknown and strategies to promote their functional integration into neural networks have been limited. Recently, I demonstrated that the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate plays a key role in the activation and neuronal differentiation of this population of stem cells by way of the AMPA receptor. The downstream mechanisms of this effect have yet to be characterized. In the proposed project, I will characterize the mechanisms involved in glutamate-mediated activation of adult human spinal cord NSPCs. I will determine the changes in glutamate receptor expression induced in NSPCs after injury. Furthermore, I will test the therapeutic potential of positive AMPA receptor modulator drugs in promoting NSPC survival and neuronal differentiation after SCI. This work will uncover important mechanisms to enhance stem cell neurogenesis and integration into functional neural networks in order to ultimately advance the clinical translation of stem cell therapies to SCI patients.

column36: The dura mater as a reservoir and entry point for IgA+ plasma cells into the brain during inflammation
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a disease of the brain and spinal cord in which the protective covering of nerves is destroyed by immune cells that cause inflammation. We have found that anti-inflammatory cells that originate in the small intestine can migrate to the brain during MS attacks, where they secrete an anti-inflammatory protein and decrease MS symptoms. As of yet, it is unknown how these anti-inflammatory cells access the brain or what signals bring them there. The healthy brain has been considered to lack immune cells. However, recent literature has established that the lining of the brain is a rich reservoir of immune cells. The outermost layer of this lining, the dura, is particularly capable of supporting immune cell populations. As a result, I hypothesize that the dura acts as a reservoir for anti-inflammatory immune cells that rapidly migrate into the brain during inflammation. In order to investigate this, my project will (1) characterize dural immune cells and the structural cells that provide support to these immune cells in healthy and MS post-mortem human and mouse dural tissues, (2) visualize the movement of anti-inflammatory immune cells in an animal model of MS and (3) identify the signals that attract anti-inflammatory immune cells into the brain during MS. By identifying how anti-inflammatory immune cells migrate into the brain, we can design new therapeutic approaches that harness this protective immune response to quiet inflammation in MS, a disease that has remained without a cure despite its prevalence in Canada.

column37: Retinal detachment is an ophthalmic emergency affecting approximately 1 in every 10,000 people per year that may lead to blindness if left untreated. Although ophthalmologists are able to repair and restore vision with new advances in surgery, half of all patients will go on to develop complications and subsequent long-term vision loss.
