This study aims to develop a new tool to help healthcare providers identify patients with retinal detachment who are at high risk of becoming blind. The tool includes small fluid samples from the eye that are routinely collected during surgery. An analysis of the biomarkers in the eye fluid can show important early signs of any complications. Technologically advanced ophthalmic imaging machines that evaluate microstructural pathologies inside the eye will also be used to assist in determining which eyes have disease and how the disease is progressing over time. This will mean that vision loss can be detected and prevented sooner than was previously possible. Ultimately, this more tailored approach to patient care will improve vision outcomes and reduce disability. A pilot study has been successfully conducted demonstrating the feasibility of carrying out this project. This research will also analyze the direct and indirect healthcare costs of caring for patients with retinal detachment. It will be determined if the use of biomarkers for predicting eye disease have good value for money spent when used by health care providers. A better understanding of the biomarkers and outcomes of patients with retinal detachment will enable researchers and clinicians to develop improved treatment options that target those affected and ultimately decrease the burden of vision loss. Additionally, the findings from this study will help future studies in developing tools that use biomarkers for preventing and treating a variety of other medical conditions.

column36: Developing an Adaptive Intracranial Neurostimulation Procedure to Rescue Attention Deficits in Children with Epilepsy.
column37: Have you ever daydreamed or lost your focus? If so, you've experienced what doctors call a momentary lapse in attention. Children suffering from epilepsy can experience hundreds of these lapses every day, unable to regain focus. Through advances in treatment, we can control seizures for many of these children; however, behavioural issues and impaired attention remain incurable. Without treatment, thousands of Canadian children continue to suffer from blunted academic performance, impaired social functioning, and lost opportunities. My research is aimed at restoring function to brain regions impaired by epilepsy. Using a novel technology called stereoencephalography, our team has been studying attentional networks in the human brain with a precision that was impossible just a few years ago. The anterior cingulate region of the brain is one of the most critical for attention. Our lab has discovered that precise timing of brainwaves (neural oscillations) in this area controls maintenance and shifting of attention with millisecond precision. We have shown that epilepsy repetitively disrupts this finely tuned activity to cause recurrent lapses of attention. These brainwaves are specific to each child and remain impaired even after seizures stop. As a neurosurgeon-in-training, I am developing an implanted device that learns the specific brainwave pattern each child needs to sharpen their focus. When this pattern is disrupted, the device will recognize the change and deliver a precisely timed electrical pulse to restore optimal rhythms. This personalized, next-generation, treatment relies on a multidisciplinary team of neuroscientists, neurosurgeons, psychologists, and engineers at SickKids with the decades of experience required to develop such a groundbreaking treatment. Together, we are driven to improve treatments for children, their parents, and their families. Because every child deserves to thrive, be a kid, and one day achieve their dreams.

column36: Interrogating the Differences in Memory Engram Function in Young and Aged Mice
column37: Memory is essential to who we are as individuals - it is the mental representation of our past and it is central to our ability to learn and imagine the future. Unfortunately, diseases of the brain often damage the ability to recall past memories and to form new ones. However, even in the absence of disease, memory function declines during the normal aging process. Indeed, the single greatest risk factor for disorders of memory is advanced age. As the average age of the Canadian population continues to increase, it is imperative that we advance of understanding of how the fundamental mechanisms of memory are altered in aging in order to identify strategies to prevent, diagnose, and treat memory disorders. At the most basic level, the brain represents memories through patterns of connections between neurons, termed engrams. Recent advancements have been made in our understanding of how engrams function, however, these studies have all been conducted in youthful animal models, and little is known about how engrams change with age. To address this gap, my study will investigate how engram formation, storage, and retrieval are altered with age. To achieve this, I will use genetically engineered mouse models that allow me to identify and manipulate engrams. Using these models, I will investigate differences in the structure and efficiency of brain-wide networks of engrams that are formed during learning in young and old mice. I will then investigate if memory deficits in old mice are due to failures of memory formation or retrieval. Finally, I will investigate if brain stimulation using optogenetics, a technique that allows neurons to be directly activated by laser light, can reverse memory deficits in old mice. The results from this study will contribute to our understanding of memory and to the development of rational targets for the diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of memory disorders.

column36: Opioid Agonist Therapy Amidst the Overdose Crisis and the Novel Coronavirus (COVID-19) Pandemic: Attitudes and Access
column37: Thousands of Canadians continue to die each year from the overdose crisis, which is largely caused by the presence of fentanyl in the street drug supply. The COVID-19 pandemic seems to have further worsened the overdose crisis, with rates of overdose deaths increasing since the pandemic began. As a result, people who use opioids (PWUO) are now facing two life-threatening crises. The primary medical treatment used to help people stop using non-prescribed opioids is medication, also referred to as opioid agonist therapy (OAT), to help reduce cravings and prevent overdose. However, some PWUO have difficulty accessing or prefer not to use these medications. It is important to get the opinion of PWUO as to why some are choosing not to use or stay on OAT; however, those opinions are often neglected by researchers. This PhD project aims to incorporate the views and preferences of PWUO to examine three important aspects of how the overdose crisis and COVID-19 may be impacting medication treatment. First, we will use data collected from a large group of PWUO to analyze whether fentanyl use is associated with lower satisfaction for methadone, the most commonly used form of OAT. Second, we will ask PWUO to make choices between different aspects of medication treatment and use that information to determine what is preferred; this research method is called a discrete choice experiment. Finally, we will use a large Ontario-based database to see how the COVID-19 pandemic is impacting access to OAT. The results of this PhD thesis will be used to decide how to best provide medications for opioid use in order to reduce overdose death and improve care for PWUO during the overdose crisis, COVID-19 pandemic, and beyond.

column37: Malaria is a global health concern and increasing resistance to current interventions has amplified the need for a potent vaccine. Antibodies (Abs) targeting circumsporozoite protein (CSP), a protein coating the surface of malaria parasites that mediates infection, facilitate protection in animal models against malaria. In fact, the current leading malaria vaccine candidate induces protective human Abs against CSP upon vaccination. However, this vaccine provided only 30-50% short-lived protection against malaria in children. Thus, a better vaccine is needed. One strategy to improve the potency of the antibody response elicited by a vaccine is to computationally design proteins that will display antibody-binding targets such that these segments are readily accessible for the immune system to mount an antibody response against them. This strategy has been used and tested against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) whereby monkeys were protected from infection by protective Abs induced by computationally designed proteins presenting a site of vulnerability from the viral particle. To improve the duration of the antibody response, these molecules can be linked to the surface of a spherical delivery platform such that numerous copies are readily presented to the immune system. I plan to apply these techniques to malaria by developing proteins that display the protective antibody-binding targets of CSP to the immune system and linking them to a spherical delivery platform. This will be achieved using Rosetta, a robust computational software that was also used to design the aforementioned RSV-targeted proteins. Based on computer-generated scores and manual inspection, I will then select promising candidates to be produced and tested in the lab to ensure that antibody binding occurs as intended during the design. Finally, our international team will evaluate our top designed proteins in immunization experiments and an in-depth study of the immune response elicited in mice.

column37: Increased risk of breast and ovarian cancer is associated with mutations in the breast cancer protein (BRCA1), which is one of the proteins that protects the genome from damage. R-loops are highly enriched in the DNA region that encodes the protein synthesizing machineries known as ribosomes (rDNA). I will increase R-loop accumulation in the cells by getting rid of two proteins, and I will examine if the cells exhibit increased R-loop levels, DNA damage, disrupted ribosome synthesis, increased problems with DNA replication, and increased cell death. For Objectives 3 and 4 I will study wither increasing R-loop accumulation at rDNA will decrease tumor potential of BRCA1-mutant cells, both in a dish (objective 3) or in mouse models (objective 4). I will increase R-loop accumulation in the cells similar to objective 2 and assess whether there is decreased number of cancer cells, tumor growth and size, and increased cancer cell death. Overall, my work may point to novel therapeutic strategies that exploit the partly elevated R-loop levels of BRCA1-deficient cancer cells to further increase R-loop accumulation and selectively kill cancer cells.

column37: Meningiomas are most common brain tumour in adults but are severely understudied compared to other tumours. Most meningiomas are benign and can be successfully treated with surgery. However, there are a significant cohort of meningiomas (20-30%) that are clinically aggressive and recur rapidly and repeatedly despite maximal standard of care therapy with surgery and radiation. The genomic changes underlying meningiomas have been well investigated but none have led to the development of any effective therapeutics. Our group has focused on DNA methylation in meningiomas, a reversible epigenetic change to DNA that turns specific genes on and off. We identified specific methylation markers that are predictive of tumour aggressiveness and tumour recurrence. Based on these epigenetic changes, we have identified a panel of pharmacologic compounds that act as specific and non-specific epigenetic modifiers. We isolated and cultured benign and clinically aggressive meningioma cell lines from patients in which to test these compounds for their ability to inhibit tumour cell growth and proliferation. We will perform genomic and epigenomic analysis of these cell lines before and after treatment to assess for drug effects on a molecular level. Compounds that demonstrate inhibition of tumour cell growth and proliferation will be translated into our mice model. As part of this model, we will implant meningioma tumour cells into the mouse cranium and monitor for tumour growth with interval neurological imaging. Once tumours grow to a specific, standardized size, we will treat these mice with the candidate compounds identified above, delivered systemically, and monitor for tumour growth, stability, or shrinkage. We will harvest these tumours for staining and molecular analysis as above. Compounds that demonstrate efficacy and safety have the potential to be translated into future clinical trials, particularly for aggressive, treatment-refractory meningiomas.

column36: Dismantling Dominant Discourse surrounding Complex Death with Urban Indigenous Youth Experience
column37: Suicide is commonly described as an urgent health concern and tragedy. Indigenous peoples' in Canada are familiar with this devastating reality, whereby Indigenous youth are five to seven times more likely to die by suicide than non-Indigenous youth in Canada. Additionally, while health data related to suicide and suicidality (suicide attempts, thoughts, and plans) are slightly documented in on-reserve First Nations populations, instances of suicide, and inquiries into mental health more broadly, in urban-based Indigenous youth groups are vastly understudied and underreported. This gap is alarming given that the highest percentage of First Nations, and Metis youth who died by suicide, did so in an urban area. As a result of these gaps and inequities, this research aims to 1) develop a more contextual and nuanced understanding of complex death, specifically Indigenous deaths by suicide that considers social, economic, historical, ecological and political factors, and 2) this research aims to challenge dominant discourses of complex death by providing a space for a critically situated and experienced informed investigation that centers the voices of urban Indigenous youth. This work will employ youth-engaged qualitative methods comprised of semi-structured interviews with urban-based Indigenous youth wellness facilitators in British Columbia. This research is aligned with critical suicide studies in that it critiques mainstream Western conceptualizations of suicide prevention and mental health intervention efforts as being largely inapplicable within Indigenous contexts (e.g. due to not incorporating decolonization frameworks). This work will contribute to an unexplored research area and provide empirical evidence for much-needed change in urban-based Indigenous youth's material, political and colonial realities. This timely research will have applied value in informing innovations in Indigenous mental health, educational and social service practice.

column37: This work builds on a novel treatment that uses a special immune cell called a regulatory T cell, which suppresses immune responses. Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are the policemen of the immune system. They shut the party down before it gets too rowdy, thus inhibiting immune attacks from getting out of control. An autoimmune disease is a condition in which your immune system mistakenly attacks your body. The exact cause of autoimmune disease is unknown, they often are caused or exacerbated by ineffective Tregs. The reason is unclear: sometimes they have a genetic deficit, or they might resist activation because of something in their environment. Many autoimmune diseases such as diabetes, lupus, multiple sclerosis and inflammatory bowel diseases are often associated with an abnormally low number or defective Tregs. Fueled by successes of immunotherapy in cancer, promising new ways to modulate the immune system to treat immune mediated diseases are currently being developed. Tregs can be engineered to express a new protein that redirects the cell to protect against a specific target of choice. Genetically engineered Tregs are promising given that they are able to maintain their policeman nature of regulatory functions, with preferentially relocation to the target sites of autoimmune disease. We plan to apply this concept in a disease model of Multiple sclerosis, an auto-immune disease of the nervous system using artificially engineered Tregs to test out their suppressive capacity in helping curb the inflammation. If successful this strategy can be rapidly used for other auto-immune diseases and may also help in protection against transplant rejections.

column36: Developing a Guideline Methodology for Rare Diseases: Bleeding Emergencies in Patients with Immune Thrombocytopenia.
column37: Right now, guidelines for rare diseases can be hard to develop because sometimes there is not enough information to help create them. A group of doctors and researchers normally make decisions on the best treatment for a rare disease based on their opinions and relevant experience, which can be biased. Since rare diseases impact approximately 250-450 million people around the world, guiding the treatment of people with rare diseases is important. Blood platelets are needed to prevent bleeding in the body. One of the main causes of low blood platelets is a rare disease called immune thrombocytopenia (ITP). Children and adults with ITP are at high risk of bleeding and when serious bleeds occur, they need to go to the Emergency Department immediately. The problem is that there is no standard way for emergency doctors to treat these ITP bleeding emergencies, and they are often unprepared to deal with them. This can cause delays in treatment and people can end up bleeding more, or even dying. My PhD thesis project project will fill an important gap for emergency treatment in a particularly vulnerable group of people. We will develop a standard guideline for treating ITP bleeding emergencies using the best available information. We will bring together a group of ITP doctors, emergency doctors and nurses, and researchers as well as ITP patients and caregivers of patients to create a guideline for ITP bleeding emergencies. This will be an important first step towards improving the health of people with low blood platelets, by making sure bleeding emergencies are handled quickly and properly, and restricting expensive treatments to those who need it most. We will also develop a new strategy for creating guidelines that can be applied to all rare diseases. We will overcome the challenge of having not enough information by collecting new information from experts in the field where necessary.

column36: Investigating the Influence of the Human Gut Microbiota in Parkinson's Disease
column37: Our bodies are inhabited by thousands of bacteria, collectively referred to as the microbiota. These bacteria are not passive inhabitants, but instead play important roles in metabolism, protection against pathogens and immune system development. In addition to these functions, alterations in the bacterial makeup of the microbiota have been observed in several diseases including Parkinson's Disease (PD). PD is a movement disorder resulting from the loss (neurodegeneration) of dopamine-producing neurons in the brain. The causes of PD are not completely understood though it is thought to be the result of both of genetic and environmental factors. In recent years, the microbiota has been investigated as one of these important environmental factors. However, many of the current studies are correlative, demonstrating that alterations in bacterial makeup of the microbiota are present in PD patients, but do not demonstrate a causal role in disease development. My project focuses on determining if, and how, alterations in the microbiota contribute to the development of PD with the goal of identifying possible interventions that will slow or stop neurodegeneration. This goal requires deciphering which specific bacterial factors influence the disease state and how these factors work. To accomplish this, an experimental system is needed that allows for manipulation of the microbiota and where there are no genetic differences between individuals. We use a small nematode (worm), C. elegans for this purpose. Using these animals, we can easily generate large populations (millions) of genetically identical animals for analysis. We will determine the influence of hundreds of bacterial strains isolated from humans, on neurodegeneration using C. elegans models of PD. Using the bacteria that differentially influence neurodegeneration, we will identify specific molecules produced by these bacteria and examine changes in the expression of genes that occur in response to these factors.

column36: The prognostic value of NK cell infiltration, localization and phenotype in high grade serous ovarian carcinoma
column37: Ovarian cancer is known as the silent killer because patients often have the disease for a long time before it is detected, making it hard to treat. At diagnosis treatment is often to surgically remove as much as possible. This has to be followed by chemotherapy and radiation to target any remaining cancer. Unfortunately, the cancer returns in 70% of these patients and fewer than half of these patients live to 5 years after their diagnosis. New treatments called immunotherapies that aim to strengthen or activate a person's immune system are being developed. While immunotherapy is treating some cancers, they haven't had much success in ovarian cancer. To understand why these immunotherapies aren't working we need to understand how the tumour interacts with the immune system. Natural killer (NK) cells are an important component of the immune system that identify and kill cancer cells. We don't yet understand how NK cells are interacting with ovarian tumours and how this impacts response to therapy. My PhD project aims to improve the effects of therapies by answering this question. We will use slides of ovarian cancer tissues that have been removed from patients to look for NK cells in and around the tumour. This is important because it will tell us whether NK cells in the tumour correspond with better or worse outcome for patients. It will be important knowledge that scientists can use when developing future immunotherapies or combining the ones we already have.

column36: Evaluation of the Cardiovascular Actions of Succinyl CoA:3-Ketoacid CoA Transferase Inhibition in Type 2 Diabetes
column37: Diabetes, a disease defined by high blood sugar, affects 463 million people globally. It is well-established that diabetes increases one's risk of developing heart disease, even when blood sugar levels are under control. Given the strong link between diabetes and heart disease, health agencies (e.g. Health Canada) now require that all drugs in development for diabetes undergo rigorous testing to determine their impact on heart health. Recently, we have identified that a clinically available drug for treating psychoses, pimozide, can improve blood sugar control in diabetic animals. We identified that pimozide improves blood sugar levels by preventing the body's muscle from metabolizing ketone bodies, a fuel source produced by the liver. Although the link between ketone body metabolism and blood sugar control requires further study, pimozide represents an exciting new drug for potentially treating diabetes. However, before pimozide can be approved as a drug for diabetes, it is critical that it is deemed safe for the heart. Therefore, the goal of our research will be to study the effects of pimozide on heart function in order to validate its potential as a new drug for diabetes. Although the exact cause of diabetes-induced heart disease is unknown, there is evidence that the heart of a diabetic individual is unable to produce enough energy to effectively pump blood throughout the body. Specifically, the ability of the heart affected by diabetes to use sugar for energy is reduced. Our previous data suggests that pimozide improves blood sugar control in diabetes by increasing sugar metabolism in the muscle. Interventions that increase heart sugar metabolism improve heart function in animal models of diabetes. Therefore, we hypothesize that pimozide will improve the health of the heart in diabetes. If our hypothesis is correct, our research will identify a new approach for both the improvement of blood sugar control and heart function in individuals with diabetes.

column36: Engineering an in vitro arterial niche for the development of lymphoid-competent hematopoietic stem cells
column37: Immune cells are a subset of blood cells that function to prevent and fix illnesses. Researchers are trying to control immune cells to more effectively combat cancer, infection and other diseases. Recently, one type of immune cell, a T-cell, has been successfully modified to target and clear cancer cells at levels never before seen. However, technical limitations make this therapy prohibitively expensive, and it is currently not feasible for countries with single-payer healthcare systems. These treatments, called CAR-T, require that T-cells are removed from a patient with cancer, modified to target cancer cells and then returned into the body of that same patient. My work focuses on generating new, affordable and broadly applicable sources for these treatments by allowing for production of T-cells outside of the body in mass quantities. To do this, we mimic where immune cells come from in the body. They develop from a type of stem cell, called blood stem cells, which arise from a specific blood vessel cell called hemogenic endothelium (HE). We now know that not all blood stem cells are created equal, and so far, we have been unable to produce blood stem cells that efficiently develop into immune cells. Similar to how when something changes in someone's environment - if they're at work or home, for example - it changes the way that person acts, the external environment changes how cells behave. My work is deciphering how the environment around the HE can direct the development of blood stem cells, with the intention of producing immune cells. I am focused on what types of cells are around the HE and how they will change the production and behaviour of blood stem cells. I am also investigating the physical environment: are there external forces that alter blood stem cell production and behaviour? I am using state-of-the-art two- and three-dimensional cell culture systems to understand how to change the HE environment to control the types of blood stem cells produced.

column37: The human genome encodes ~21,300 proteins, over 95% of which are subjected to reversible phosphorylation at nearly a million sites by at least 568 protein kinases (PK) and about 156 protein phosphatases (PP). Many phosphorylation sites act as on/off switches in proteins to control their diverse functions. Transcription factors (TFs) represent one of the largest families of targets for PK and PP, and may include over 1600 different proteins that bind to DNA. TFs bind immediately upstream of genes to regulate their abilities to produce their protein products. Only a relatively small number of transcription factors have been well studied and shown to be controlled by phosphorylation. Knowledge of the regulation of the vast majority of TFs remains very limited, because it has been extremely difficult to track the activation or inhibition of specific TFs in response to diverse treatments. Our aim in this project will be to develop and apply methods that will permit tracking of TFs in high-throughput, and establishment of their interactions with PK and PP and target genes in regulatory networks by wet lab and predictive bioinformatics approaches. Dr. Steven Pelech's lab has access to purified preparations of over 360 different PK and over 30 PP. The combination of the microarray technology with the subcellular fractionation of treated human cancer cells will be used to monitor TFs locations and phosphorylation states following treatments with diverse factors, mediators, and (PK/PP) inhibitors. I will also use purified preparations of PK and PP to try to phosphorylate and dephosphorylate TFs. Altered phosphorylation of these TFs will be tracked by differential binding of the phosphorylated TFs to the phosphosite-specific antibodies printed on the antibody microarrays. Immunohistochemistry and subcellular fractionation will be applied to confirm that potential PK-TF and PP-TF pairs of interacting proteins reside in the same locations inside of cells.

column37: The immune system plays critical roles in protecting us against a wide range of diseases. However, the dysregulation of the immune system not only makes us more susceptible to infections, but it can also lead to the development of allergic diseases. My research aims to identify and understand the genetic changes which cause the immune system to become dysregulated and result in severe and rare allergic diseases in humans. By collaborating with clinicians across Western Canada, I will be recruiting individuals with severe and early onset allergic disorders into our study and sequencing their DNA to look for genetic changes (mutations) that could explain their allergic symptoms. By using cells directly isolated from these patients, I will assess the impact of these mutations on the functioning of their immune system. I will also look for and test existing treatments which can restore proper immune system functioning and alleviate their allergic symptoms. Lastly, I will determine if milder forms of these genetic changes are associated with less-severe, more common allergic diseases in the greater population. Understanding the genetic causes of these severe and rare allergic diseases will not only be life changing for the affected individuals and their families, but it also has the potential to help other similarly affected individuals worldwide. Additionally, with a better understanding of how these allergic diseases are caused, we can develop new treatments that can precisely target the affected parts of the immune system, resulting in significantly better outcomes for the patients.

column37: The human brain contains nearly 700km of blood vessels, so it is no surprise that brain health and vascular health are closely related. One of the biggest threats to brain health as we age is Alzheimer disease, a type of dementia that currently affects over half a million Canadians. The main genetic risk factor for Alzheimer disease is a version of a gene called "APOE", which makes a protein that acts as the FedEx of the body - transporting fats and other proteins in the brain and through the blood vessels. Most work trying to figure out how APOE connects to Alzheimer disease has looked at how it works in the brain, largely overlooking what it does in the blood vessels. One way that the APOE protein transports its cargo through the blood vessels is by sticking to high-density lipoproteins (HDL) - commonly known as the "good cholesterol". HDL supports blood vessels in many ways, and the proteins stuck to the particles dictate their function. HDL carrying the APOE protein has been shown to have extra protective functions in the context of heart disease but has not yet been studied in the context of Alzheimer disease and dementia. This project will take a new approach to understand how APOE and Alzheimer disease are connected by looking outside of the brain, and focusing on HDL carrying the APOE protein in the blood. The first goal is to discover exactly how these particles protect brain-specific blood vessels, and this will be done by modeling vessels using human cells in a dish and treating them with HDL from human blood. It will also explore whether the amount of the particles in someone's blood can help diagnose or predict their risk of developing Alzheimer disease, by measuring the particles in blood banked from a nation-wide aging study. This research could lead to prevention and treatment avenues for Alzheimer disease that wouldn't need to enter the brain to be effective, and advance the international search for an Alzheimer disease blood test.

column36: Investigating the role of reproductive hormones in healthy aging for women living with HIV: A community-collaborative cohort study
column37: BACKGROUND: Globally, more than half of all people with HIV are women. With effective treatment, people are now living with, rather than dying from, HIV. However, women living with HIV experience higher rates of chronic diseases and live 5-10 years shorter than their HIV-negative peers, suggesting they may be aging faster than the general population. Aging leads to the gradual decline of bodily functions and may be impacted by cellular, clinical, socio-demographic, and psychosocial factors - and, for those with HIV, the virus itself. Women living with HIV exhibit an increased burden of illness and shorter life expectancy compared to their male counterparts, in contrast to what is seen in the HIV negative population. A possible explanation for this is that women with HIV are more likely to have periods of prolonged amenorrhea and may be at increased risk of early menopause, predisposing them to comorbidities that are worsened by low estrogen states. In addition to HIV infection, social stressors like gender-based violence, substance use, and lack of supports increase women's risk for chronic disease and accelerated aging. I will investigate how hormonal abnormalities and social stressors affect health and aging in women living with HIV. METHODS: This study will enroll 700 women with and without HIV in British Columbia. I will collect blood samples, measure anthropometric variables, and ask participants about health diagnoses, reproductive history, and social factors. Markers of cellular aging, hormone levels, number of diseases, and social stressors will be compared between women with and without HIV. To ensure this research is in line with community priorities, women with HIV will be hired as key members of the research team. SIGNIFICANCE: This study has the potential to elucidate how HIV infection, hormones, and social conditions contribute to aging in women. This could significantly impact the health care of the 16,000 women with HIV across Canada.

column36: Examining the impact of dietary diversity/food variety on type 2 Diabetes
column37: Diversity in a diet has long been considered essential to healthy eating and many dietary guidelines have incorporated recommendations on dietary diversity to reduce the risk of chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, some dietary guidelines have minimized and potentially undermined the importance of dietary diversity by reducing the number of food groups relevant to a healthy diet. Moreover, most of the diet quality measures do not capture dietary diversity, while quality and diversity are not completely alike despite a positive correlation, and diversity may be linked to disease prevention independent of quality. To date, most of the existing knowledge on dietary diversity comes from developing countries, where dietary diversity is an approach to address nutritional inadequacy, and thus is not a measure of diet quality in the context of a sufficient amount of food. And, in higher-income settings, research on dietary diversity rarely looks at the risk of T2D. Even less is known about diversity within food groups separate from the diversity of total diet. Moreover, although we know from previous studies that gender/sex, socio-economic status, and obesity can affect both dietary intakes and development of diabetes, it is still unclear whether mentioned factors can alter the degree of a potential association between dietary diversity and T2D. The underlying mechanism linking dietary diversity to T2D also remained to be elucidated, despite some studies separately showing the beneficial effect of dietary diversity on gut microbes and the protective effect of gut microbes against T2D. Therefore, this project aims to use data from multiple European countries to answer three main questions: (1) Do greater diversity across total foods and within food groups (e.g. vegetables) reduce the risk of T2D?; (2) Is this relationship altered by gender/sex, socio-economic status, and obesity?; and (3) Do gut microbes have a role in linking diversity to diabetes?.

column37: Up to 20% of mothers experience depression during pregnancy and up to 5% of all children are born each year exposed to an antidepressant medication (totalling approximately 20,000 births/year in Canada). Antidepressants readily cross the placenta and reach the developing fetus, but it is unknown whether an early exposure to antidepressants will affect the child's emotional and behavioural regulation. In order to make an informed decision on antidepressant use during pregnancy, it is important to understand how prenatal exposure to antidepressants influences early brain development and whether it affects stress regulation, mental health and behaviour during childhood. I will study patterns of stress regulation and behaviour at 6 and 12 years of age and determine whether these outcomes predict mental health outcomes (anxiety and depression) in youth (15-18 years) of mothers treated with an antidepressant during pregnancy. I will use data derived from a cohort of mothers and children who had been followed for the last 18 years, since their mother's second trimester. I will also use British Columbia population-wide data from all mothers and their children born in BC between the years 2000-2011 (~480,000 children, 24,000 with antidepressant exposure). This study will allow us to use advanced methods to model how a child's behaviour and stress responses at different time points (infancy, 3, 6 and 12 years) are related to anxiety at 15-18 years. Stress response will be estimated from the stress hormone cortisol and heart rate. To study outcomes using population data, we will use advanced techniques to study patterns of behaviour (machine learning) that will generate predictive models of mental health outcomes in adolescence and distinguish how much of adolescent behavior is associated with prenatal antidepressant exposure and how much is associated with mother's depressed mood. Our studies should help improve the mental health of mothers and their children.

column36: Childhood obesity: Improving the assessment and communication
column37: Childhood obesity is a major health concern in Canada. In 2017, 30% of Canadian children between 5 and 17 years of age and 64% of adults were overweight or obese. Children who suffer from obesity are likely to remain overweight, develop other life-time illnesses such as high blood pressure and heart diseases, and face various mental health challenges. Accurate assessment of childhood obesity risk and effective communication of weight information to parents are key steps to promote optimal growth in children. Additionally, most parents do not understand growth information and often normalize their children's unhealthy weights. This study aims to improve the ability to identify children at risk of obesity and explore opportunities and barriers for effective communication of growth information between healthcare providers and parents. Improved assessments and communication of children's growth would likely improve the quality of provided care, positively impact parental expectations and care practices, and help to promote healthy weights among children.

column36: Parental and family functioning as predictors of longitudinal trajectories of post-concussive symptoms following pediatric concussion
column37: Concussions are a pressing public health concern, occurring in 1-2 million children in North America annually. Concussions often result in physical, cognitive, and emotional problems, known as post-concussive symptoms. Although most children who sustain a concussion recover in weeks to months, a subset of children are hindered by persistent symptoms that reduce their quality of life. Recovery from concussion can be influenced by both injury-related and noninjury-related factors. Noninjury-related factors may be more modifiable than injury-related factors and, for that reason, may make better targets for treatment. Previous research has identified a variety of noninjury-related factors that are related to outcomes following traumatic brain injury, including parental and family functioning. However, these factors have not been examined in detail in pediatric concussion, so their importance to concussion recovery remains unclear. Additionally, much of the existing research on concussion in children employs conventional statistical analyses that are not likely to capture the significant variations in symptom trajectories displayed by children with concussion. Group-based multi-trajectory modeling, a statistical technique which identifies groups of individuals following similar symptom trajectories, should provide a more accurate characterization of the outcomes of concussion. The first aim of the proposed study is to identify trajectories of symptoms after concussion. The second aim is to determine whether symptom trajectories are predicted by parental and family functioning. Data will be drawn from a larger parent study involving children/adolescents aged 8-17 years with either concussion or orthopedic injury, recruited during emergency department visits at five children's hospitals across Canada. The study findings will provide guidance in developing family-based treatments and enabling the targeting of those treatments to children at risk for poor recovery.

column36: Exercise and anti-diabetic drugs to restore brain function in obesity
column37: With two-thirds of the adult Canadian population obese or overweight, obesity is a public health crisis. Excess weight and poor "obesogenic" diets increase the risk of dementia more than three-fold - we are faced with a huge burden of disease. Obesity affects brain functions by reducing the numbers of stem cells residing in the hippocampus, which are vital for memory and mood regulation. Numbers of these stem cells decline with age, and pathologically in neurodegenerative diseases - putting the brain at risk of dementia. In a population with high numbers of obese and overweight individuals there is a critical need for interventions that encourage weight loss and protect the brain. A two-pronged approach to combat obesity involves modifiable lifestyle factors, such as exercise, as well as pharmacological interventions, such as the anti-diabetes drugs metformin and liraglutide. Research shows that these drugs can increase the brain's stem cell niche in laboratory animals. But do these interventions functionally improve memory and mood? I will study the efficacy of exercise, metformin, and liraglutide in reversing the negative brain effects of dietary obesity in mice. I will take a translational approach - using diet manipulations in mice that mirror the modern "obesogenic" diet and cognitive tasks that parallel human clinical tests. I will define the benefits of exercise on metabolic factors alone and in synergy with anti-diabetic drugs. By combining my clinical trial experience in anti-diabetic therapies with my preclinical work characterizing behavioral changes in mouse models of obesity, I will elucidate how frontline diabetes treatments can restore memory and improve mood in obesity. This research will pave the way for enhancing brain health in the population and novel therapeutic approaches for cognitive impairment.

column36: Grabbing head and neck cancer by the throat: understanding recurrence to improve treatments
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada. In recent years, Canada is experiencing an epidemic of head and neck cancer caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV), best known as a cause of cervical cancer. HPV head and neck cancer is the fastest growing cancer type in Canada and often deprives patients the ability to talk and swallow. Unfortunately, current treatments are too intense for most patients. As a result, there is significant interest to decrease their intensity and reduce their toxicity. However, even with the current intense treatments, 20% of patients suffer a return of cancer. These recurrent patients often only live 6 - 15 months. Thus, there is an urgent need to reduce the toxicities of current treatments, prevent recurrence, and find new therapies for those who suffer recurrence. In the current project, I will comprehensively tackle these three challenging issues by studying the characteristics of all three levels of the central dogma: DNA, RNA, and protein in tumours before and after-treatment. The insights generated from analyzing the tumours before treatment will allow us to predict a patient's response to treatment and tailor the treatment for each patient. By studying post-treatment recurrent tumours, we can better understand why some patients suffer recurrence. We can then identify drugs for treating these patients. HPV head and neck cancer before and after-treatment tumour samples are rare. At Western University, we have collected over 175 HPV head and neck cancer samples in which 56 are recurrent samples. These samples provide a window of opportunity to tackle the pressing problems associated with this cancer. We have further garnered the support of our clinical colleagues to rapidly test and translate our bench-side findings to the patient's bedside. Our results will be an invaluable resource for further studies and can potentially transform the management of HPV head and neck cancer patients.

column36: Clinical, echocardiographic and magnetic resonance evaluation of the pulmonary autograft.
column37: Aortic stenosis, a valve disease which limits the ability of the heart to pump blood to the rest of the body, is the most common valve disease in Europe and North America. Left untreated, this condition is associated with a mortality of >50% at 3 years following the onset of symptoms. Aortic valve replacement (AVR) has improved the natural history of patients suffering from this disease. Current surgical options all have advantages and drawbacks. Mechanical prostheses are durable but require lifelong anticoagulation with an associated risk of bleeding and stroke. Biologic prostheses do not require anticoagulation but have an increased risk of failure. More importantly, both prostheses are associated with suboptimal long-term survival. In patients <65 at the time of surgery, survival is reduced by more than 10 years compared with the general population. A third option, known as the Ross procedure puts a living valve in the aortic position. The Ross procedure consists of replacing the aortic valve with the patient's own pulmonary valve (pulmonary autograft). A valve from a deceased donor is used to replace the pulmonary valve. The Ross procedure is associated with better survival. However, it is a more complex operation. To date, no study has adequately compared the outcomes patients undergoing prosthetic AVR or a Ross procedure. Patients <65 years old represent 25% of all patients requiring AVR. It is thus pressing to determine which valve substitute offers them the best long-term outcomes. We hypothesize that the characteristics of the pulmonary autograft result in lower heart workload, which leads to better long-term survival. To test this hypothesis, we will use imaging studies to assess the heart workload at rest and during exercise in patients who have received a mechanical prosthesis, a pulmonary autograft and in healthy volunteers. We will also assess the clinical outcomes (ex: survival) of patients undergoing a mechanical AVR and a Ross procedure.

column36: Mieux-etre physique et psychologique d'adolescents suite a une pathologie du genou: Une etude longitudinale sur le soutien a l'autodetermination et le role de la motivation et de l'observance de la reeducation
column37: Le genou est le plus touche par les problemes articulaires et les blessures a l'adolescence, pouvant causer plusieurs complications. Une reeducation est donc necessaire pour tenter de retrouver la pleine capacite du genou. Par contre, le taux d'adherence a la reeducation est peu eleve, tout comme celui de la recuperation des capacites physiques du genou. Selon la theorie de l'autodetermination, ce qui favorise l'adoption et le maintien d'un comportement est le sentiment d'etre a l'origine et a la source de ses actions ; c'est ce qu'on appelle le besoin d'autodetermination. Un environnement soutenant l'autodetermination d'un individu est lie a son mieux-etre et a une motivation plus optimale, dite autodeterminee, aux traitements proposes. Toutefois, la plupart des etudes dans le domaine ont ete menees aupres d'adultes et n'incluent donc pas la perception du soutien a l'autodetermination (SA) des parents, qui, pourtant, jouent un role essentiel dans la reeducation du jeune. Dans cette etude, 107 patients, ayant une pathologie du genou, comprenant le francais ou l'anglais et etant ages entre 10 et 19 ans, seront recrutes a un hopital orthopedique pediatrique. A tous les moins pendant trois mois, les patients recevront des questionnaires en ligne pour evaluer leur perception du SA de la part des parents, du medecin et du physiotherapeute ainsi que leur bien-etre, leur motivation autodeterminee, leur adherence et les capacites physiques de leur genou. Les objectifs de l'etude sont de savoir de quelle facon la perception du SA contribue a ameliorer la sante psychologique et physique des jeunes patients et si les bienfaits du SA sur la recuperation des capacites physiques passent par la motivation autodeterminee et l'adherence a la physiotherapie. Identifier des determinants sociaux et motivationnels contribuant a reduire les repercussions negatives (psychologiques que physiques) d'une pathologie du genou chez les adolescents permettrait d'ameliorer leur qualite de vie.

column36: Sexualized drug use among HIV sero-positive gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men using crystal methamphetamine: Exploring the intersection between sero-status, substance use, addictions, and mental health issues
column37: In Canada, gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM) are among the individuals most affected by HIV. While HIV is now considered to be a chronic, manageable illness, among gbMSM, HIV care can often be impeded by HIV-related traumas, mental health, substance use, addictions issues, and other intersectional factors. Recently, sexualized drug use (or "chemsex") with crystal methamphetamine has re-emerged as a topic of concern in health and nursing research due to increasing rates among gbMSM living with HIV. Not only can crystal methamphetamine cause neurologic damage (e.g., changes in mood, cognition, and thoughts), it can also act as a catalyst for negative health outcomes while living with HIV, such as decreased immune function, exacerbation of underlying mental health conditions, and long-term substance dependency and addictions issues. Presently, little is known about the sub-culture of gbMSM living with HIV, mental health, substance use, and addictions issues who are engaging in chemsex. As a result, nurses and other clinicians can only provide "patch-work" solutions to manage care for this group. The focus of this doctoral research will to undertake a qualitative research study to understand (1) the sub-cultural norms of gbMSM living with HIV, mental health, substance use, and addictions issues engaging in sexualized drug use and (2) how group values affect health and risk-taking practices. This research could yield promising findings in health and nursing research to help support the development of prevention interventions for gbMSM living with HIV who are engaging in sexualized drug use. Indeed, in the absence of concrete solutions on how to support this sub-group of gbMSM, it is extremely possible that their health and social outcomes will continue to decline, and that this already vulnerable group will become increasingly isolated.

column36: Uncovering the role of lipophagy during atherosclerosis regression
column37: Heart disease is the leading cause of death worldwide. Atherosclerosis, the underlying cause of heart disease, is characterized by an accumulation of fat within the arteries that supply blood to the heart, narrowing these blood vessels and impairing blood flow. The accumulation of fat within artery walls, called 'plaque', is also associated with the buildup of different cell types filled with fat called 'foam cells'. Over time, the plaques grow and can become vulnerable to rupture, creating a blood clot which obstructs the blood vessels and leads to a heart attack or stroke. A major risk factor for atherosclerosis is high levels of circulating blood cholesterol. Current therapies to treat atherosclerosis consist of cholesterol-lowering therapies which prevent the progression of plaques, but these therapies do not cure the disease nor drive plaque shrinking. Discovery of drugs which could reduce plaque size and reverse atherosclerosis would prove to be a breakthrough. All the cells in our bodies possess an intrinsic ability to degrade defective or excess of cellular components through a recycling system named autophagy. This process is key to maintaining balance in cells. During heart disease development, autophagy becomes dysfunctional. Autophagy can mediate fat degradation and export excess fat out of foam cells for excretion through the feces. Our project aims to investigate the mechanism of fat degradation through autophagy for plaque shrinkage and the enhancement fat degradation via autophagy to promote plaque size reduction. For these studies, we will engineer a mouse that will allow us to track autophagy in real time and a small compound that can selectively enhance the degradation of fat through autophagy. Gaining a better understanding of the role of autophagy in foam cells may identify new therapeutic intervention and new targets to shrink atherosclerotic plaques, bypassing the need for lifelong therapies or invasive surgical procedures.

column36: Personalized Resistant Starch as an Adjuvant Therapy for Pediatric Inflammatory Bowel Disease
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a category of chronic, incurable illnesses that affect over 270,000 Canadians. People with IBD suffer from nausea, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and bloody stool throughout their life. Among the many ways IBD can affect a person's quality of life, diet is always a concern. Doctors have limited evidence to suggest one diet over another, and the consensus among people with IBD is that the best diet is "different for everyone". A healthy person's intestines harbour a community of trillions of beneficial bacteria. However, people with IBD often have fewer beneficial bacteria that produce butyrate - a molecule that helps to keep our gut healthy. Beneficial bacteria produce butyrate by fermenting dietary fibres that we cannot digest. One type of fibre is resistant starch - a natural component of starchy foods. Unfortunately, restoring one's gut health is not as simple as eating starch. Everyone's gut bacteria community is as unique as their fingerprint, and the bacteria they harbour are able to digest some starches but not others. My goal is to determine which type of resistant starch someone ought to eat prior to actually eating it. We will collect stool from children recently diagnosed with IBD and feed their gut bacteria with nine different powdered resistant starches. We will determine if these resistant starches restore their gut bacterial balance and butyrate levels. We predict that children will respond to one resistant starch better than others. They will be prescribed this "optimal" resistant starch (or regular starch placebo) along with standard IBD medications for 6 months. We will monitor their gut bacteria, butyrate levels, and disease activity for an additional 6 months to determine if the therapy is effective. Our plan capitalizes on diet being "different for everyone" with IBD, and could potentially lead to a revolutionary, safe, economical, and personalized therapy for IBD based entirely on a common food ingredient.

column37: With childbirth being the top reason for hospitalization in Canada, it is important that the care provided in maternal-newborn hospital settings is safe and aligned with best practice recommendations. All Ontario maternal-newborn hospitals have access to a novel online audit and feedback system, a "dashboard", which shows how they are performing on selected key performance indicators. However, previous work with Ontario maternal-newborn units has shown that seeing an evidence-practice gap on the dashboard is not enough for all teams to commit to making a change, nor does it provide any guidance on how to actually implement or sustain improvements. Using an established implementation science framework, my study will develop and field-test an implementation guide to help maternal-newborn hospital teams to develop an action plan to most effectively create practice change on key performance indicators. I will first create a working group with experts in implementation science and stakeholders from maternal-newborn care. Together, we will work to create an implementation guide based on information from the literature and previously collected data on user experiences with the dashboard. The implementation guide will then be reviewed by maternal-newborn stakeholders. I will then follow 3-5 maternal-newborn units for six months as they use the implementation guide in real-time to plan for practice improvements on one or more key performance indicators. The findings of this study will contribute to developing a resource that can facilitate implementation of priority practice changes in maternal-newborn units, which can ultimately improve the care and outcomes for mothers and infants.

column36: The Cholinergic System and Cognitive Impairments in Schizophrenia
column37: Schizophrenia affects about 1% of Canadians. Cognitive impairments are a core feature of schizophrenia that drives functional disability and socio-economic burden in this illness. Currently, there are no medications that significantly improve cognition in schizophrenia. A better understanding of the neurobiology of cognitive deficits in schizophrenia could guide the development of new pharmacological treatments. The cholinergic system of the brain is important for cognitive abilities and it has been proposed that dysfunctions in this system would underlie cognitive deficits in schizophrenia. However, this has not been tested yet. Here, we propose to study the cholinergic system with a positron emission tomography tracer that allows to quantify cholinergic innervation in the brain. The goals of the proposed study are to (1) establish whether individuals with schizophrenia show reduced cholinergic innervation compared to healthy individuals, (2) determine if reduced cholinergic innervation is related to less brain activation in schizophrenia and (3) to greater cognitive deficits in schizophrenia. We hypothesize that, in schizophrenia, cholinergic innervation is lower (goal 1) than in healthy individuals, that this is related to general cognitive dysfunction (goal 2) and abnormal brain activity (goal 3). We will also explore the effect of sex on cholinergic innervation. We will inform patients and family, clinicians, and pharmaceutical firms of our findings to have them translated into clinical practice. Results will be presented in international conferences and published in high-impact journals. As there are no drugs that alleviate cognitive impairments in schizophrenia, it is imperative to better understand the underlying neurobiology. This project will increase our understanding of the cholinergic system in schizophrenia and opens doors for breakthroughs in the development of new treatments.

column36: Nutrient sensing pathways direct hematopoietic inflammatory rewiring in atherosclerosis
column37: Heart disease remains one of the most devastating diseases in Canada. When blood vessels become clogged with plaque buildup it becomes difficult for the heart to pump efficiently. Plaque is a complex mixture of much more than cholesterol and fat. It also contains cells from the immune system that become trapped and produce inflammation. Before these immune cells reach the plaque, they must first mature through a process called hematopoiesis. All immune cells receive characteristics from hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) just as children receive genes passed down from their parents. Metabolism, which is the collection of biochemical reactions that convert the foods we eat into energy, occurs on many levels within our bodies. At the smallest scale, our cells manage nutrients by using tools that recognize when nutrients are low or high. These tools are proteins called AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) and mTORC1 (mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1). These proteins balance each other to make sure the cell uses its nutrients in the most efficient way. Taking all of this together, we aim to understand how an unhealthy diet alters HSC metabolism and how these changes affect immune cells downstream. We ask: "does HSC metabolism affect plaque buildup?" and for therapeutic purposes, "can exercise reverse these changes at the cellular level?". To investigate this process, we will feed mice a high fat and high cholesterol diet that produces plaque. The unique mice in this study have mutations that prevent AMPK and mTORC1 from stopping each other. Using a technique that separates individual cells, we will closely examine HSCs and immune cells from mice that have been exercised or not to evaluate how metabolic signals alter plaque buildup, and whether exercise can reverse these changes in HSCs. Together, this work will highlight important considerations to be taken when treating heart disease and lay the foundation for new and exciting therapeutic strategies.

column36: When HIV and COVID-19 Pandemics Collide in Black Communities in Canada
column37: Pandemics expose inequities in health outcomes,both SARS (COVID-19) and HIV disproportionately impact Black people.The combined impacts of racism, sexism, homophobia, and poverty create acute conditions of exposure that are exacerbated by infectious diseases.Whereas most Canadians are reeling from the impact of COVID-19,Black people also remain in an HIV pandemic zone and must deal with the impact of both pandemics simultaneously.This structural inequities creates conditions of vulnerability that are increased by barriers to effective and timely health care, and increases the Black communities' risks to future pandemics.My research will examine the cumulative impacts of existing and emerging social and public health policies on Black people's health and wellbeing in Canada, focusing on their vulnerability to HIV and COVID-19. It will do so by: (1) tracking the rapidly changing health and public policy landscape in Canada (2) using critical feminist and race theories to analyze,compare and contrast COVID-19 and HIV containment and mitigation strategies; and (3) examining how these policies address, reify, challenge, and uphold existing health inequities from the perspective of Black people living with and at risk of Pandemics in Canada.Using institutional ethnography as my main qualitative method of inquiry,I will analyze the quotidian experiences of Black Canadians and examine the organization of social and institutional systems and policies during pandemics. My personal experiences as a Black woman living with HIV and deep roots in the HIV and Black communities are especially critical for successfully implementation of this ambitious plan.An integrated knowledge translation and exchange plan using multiple forms of dissemination (e.g., scientific papers, policy papers, community forums, and social media) and collaboration with Black organizations, community members, researchers, activists, and scholars will ensure that findings are accessible to diverse audiences.

column36: Short- and long-term effects of adolescent e-cigarette vapour exposure: reward, withdrawal, and neural correlates.
column37: Adolescent e-cigarette use has seen a dramatic increase in recent years with past year nicotine vaping among Ontario grade 7-12 students growing from 10.7% to 22.7% between 2017 and 2019. JUUL is currently the most popular e-cigarette, with 78% of the Canadian e-cigarette market share. It is also unique in its higher nicotine concentrations through the use of nicotine salts which allows for smoother inhalation and higher absorption, all potentially contributing to its high uptake among adolescents. Currently, the behavioural and neural mechanisms underlying the high uptake of JUUL e-cigarettes in youth, as well as the long-term causal consequences of this use, are not known. Therefore, there is a critical need for establishing the short- and long-term effects of nicotine vapour on the adolescent brain. There is a substantial body of literature that suggests that adolescents are especially vulnerable to the addictive effects of nicotine. There are also longitudinal studies that associate adolescent e-cigarette use with a greater risk for future initiation of cigarette smoking. This may suggest that adolescent nicotine vapour exposure produces behavioural and neural effects that are distinct from those in adults, and may impact the neurodevelopmental trajectories in adolescents that lead to future addiction vulnerability. No studies to date have studied the causal impacts of adolescent nicotine vapour exposure on future nicotine addiction liability and related neural circuitry. The proposed research intends to contribute to our understanding of the vulnerability of the adolescent brain to the rewarding effects of e-cigarette vapour. This research has the potential to have a high impact through improving our knowledge of nicotine's short- and long-term effects on brain circuitry, apprising the public of the potential neurodevelopmental ramifications of adolescent nicotine exposure, and through future research aimed at preventing or reversing these effects.

column36: Understanding the impacts of non-consensual nursing care on clients with cognitive impairments living in long-term care facilities in New Brunswick
column37: Clients with cognitive impairments, such as those that result from Alzheimer's Disease, are now advocating for the right to make choices for themselves well into advanced disease. Nevertheless, there are times when healthcare professionals must intervene and subvert these choices in order to protect the safety and the dignity of the patient whose judgment and cognition are impaired. At present, this is done in ad-hoc ways based on the healthcare professional's individual judgment. Mental health professionals have postulated that receiving non-consensual care can have the unintended impact of harming the client emotionally and cognitively even as it appears to ensure their physical safety and/or dignity. This harm is sometimes called "iatrogenic damage" in the literature. This term is used to describe unintended, negative consequences that arise from healthcare professionals' treatments or interventions. This study explores clients' understandings of the impacts of receiving nonconsensual care and proposes to develop an instrument to measure these potential impacts quantitatively.

column36: The metabolomics of frailty and cardiovascular health in older females
column37: Thirty percent of Canadians are 55 years of age or older, and are living longer than ever. Health declines with age; however, the declines are not experienced uniformly between individuals; rather, some people are more vulnerable to stressors and experience more rapid reductions that lead to poor health, which is a condition called frailty. Increases in frailty predict poor health outcomes, such as cardiovascular disease (CVD).The standard approach for cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk screening in Canada is the Framingham Risk Score (FRS). However, in an eight year follow up study of older adults, the FRS poorly discriminated between those who had onset CVD and those who did not, and this absolute risk was specifically underestimated in women (51%) versus men (8%). A suggested method of improving CVD risk assessment is through the addition of frailty biomarkers. In fact, there is an emerging recognition that metabolites in our blood can be analyzed to detect the early development of frailty-related chronic conditions. However, no prior studies have determined if adding specific metabolites to an established CVD risk score improves its sensitivity/specificity. I will address this knowledge gap. Study 1 will measure metabolites in blood samples collected from the 985 women (age 55 and older) who participated in the Assessment of Large and Small Artery Elasticity for the Early Detection of Cardiovascular Disease trial (NCT02863211) for the purpose of identifying metabolites that are associated with CVD risk and frailty. A new CVD risk assessment model will then be created that includes the candidate metabolites. Study 2 will then determine if the new CVD risk model better predicts CVD outcomes than the traditional FRS in a different cohort of 1000 females who are 55 years of age or older and participating in the WARM Hearts trial (NCT03938155). My data will support the development of more precise early diagnostic tools to assess CVD risk in older adults.

column36: Illuminating deficits in engram synapse structure and function in Alzheimer's disease
column37: When we form a memory, it becomes stored in our brains in small connections between brain cells called synapses. In Alzheimer's disease (AD), it is thought that these connections become dysfunctional. As they break down, memories that were previously formed become harder to remember and new memories no longer form successfully. There is therefore a pressing need to understand how exactly these connections become impaired in AD in order to design therapies to target them. This is an especially urgent goal given that current treatments for AD are not effective. However, up to now it has not been possible to directly visualize and study these connections, limiting our understanding of how they become faulty in AD. My project aims to address this issue. Using newly developed technology, I will for the first time directly visualize the connections that store memories in a mouse model of AD. First, I will investigate how the structure of these connections is altered as memory becomes disrupted. Next, I will determine whether these synapses show impaired activity relative to those in healthy brains. Finally, I will use brain stimulation to alter the function of these synapses and determine whether this corrects their deficits and alleviates memory impairment. Alzheimer's disease places a devastating burden on individuals, families, and society, and this challenge is unfortunately met with inadequate treatments at the moment. With CIHR support, I believe my project will make a significant contribution to the overall effort to better understand this disease and develop promising therapies to treat it.

column36: Identifying novel interacting partners and signalling complexes coupled to adapter protein CCM3
column37: Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) are defects that affect the blood vessels of the brain and are found in approximately 1/200 people. Unfortunately, the only treatment for bleeding lesions is surgery, which carries a high risk of complications. And so, to develop therapeutics for CCMs, we require a better understanding of the events that take place under normal circumstances. Some CCMs are a result of inherited mutations in one of three genes. Mutations in genes CCM1 or CCM2 typically result in fewer lesions and milder symptoms, but CCM3 mutations result in dozens of lesions that can bleed and cause strokes or seizures. A cell communicates with other cells via signals passed along by proteins called kinases. These kinases add a small chemical tag onto other proteins thereby changing their activity. CCM3 shuttles a specific group of kinases to proteins found in different locations within the cell. In this context, proper signalling results in the maintenance of a sturdy blood vessel wall, and a cell that loses CCM3 cannot properly assemble into a functional blood vessel. I use an instrument called a mass spectrometer that is capable of identifying proteins accurately, based on the "fingerprints" that they produce. This instrument can also detect which proteins have received chemical tags from the kinases. My project will define, in the cells that form blood vessels, all the proteins that are chemically tagged by the kinases associated with CCM3 and where they are located inside the cells. Knowing which lines of communication CCM3 and its associated kinases participate in may aid in understanding what cellular processes are important and go awry in a disease state. By understanding the network of events that are associated with CCM3 and its kinases, my research should assist in developing alternative, non-invasive treatments for patients affected by CCMs.

column36: Development of imaging tools for simultaneous PET-MRI imaging of acute inflammation and fibrosis associated with inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a lifelong, chronic inflammatory condition of the gastrointestinal tract. It affects 1 in 150 Canadians, one of the highest rates in the world. A common and serious complication of Crohn's disease is narrowing in the bowel, which stops movement of bowel contents out of the body. The cause of this is often buildup of scar tissue (or fibrosis) due to uncontrolled bowel inflammation. Once a section of bowel becomes fibrotic and non-functional, surgery is the only treatment available. Despite advances in treating bowel inflammation to prevent fibrosis, over 50% of IBD patients require surgery in their lifetime. This is often due to mild/moderate inflammation that goes unnoticed and untreated, due to a lack of serious symptoms. As such, there is a critical need to not only identify active disease (regions of inflammation) within the bowel, but also measure disease progression (degree of fibrosis present). Molecular imaging allows us to see the biology of tissues, and not just their physical appearance. This approach takes advantage of protein-based markers of disease present in blood vessels during the early stages of disease progression. We aim to design an approach for detecting and measuring active inflammation and fibrosis in a single session using positron emission tomography (PET) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Our objectives are: 1) to test and refine a PET contrast agent that we have previously constructed, which attaches to and identifies inflamed blood vessels; 2) to validate an advanced, quantitative MRI sequence to measure fibrosis in humans with IBD; 3) to combine our PET contrast agent and MRI sequence to image active inflammation and fibrosis simultaneously using PET-MRI. This novel imaging approach has the potential to help clinicians detect inflammation early and assess the degree of fibrosis present, giving them the information required to personalize treatment and reduce the need for surgery.

column36: Inhibition of Neuronal Endocytosis of IgG as a Therapy to Attenuate Neurodegeneration in a Model of Multiple Sclerosis
column37: Canada has among the highest rates of multiple sclerosis (MS) in the world and studies suggest rates may be highest in Saskatchewan. In progressive MS, the nerve cells of the brain and spinal cord are damaged in a process called neurodegeneration, a well-known feature of MS. Many researchers believe this is the reason why people living with MS get worse. The cause of this nerve damage is unknown and treatments that halt or prevent it are currently unavailable. Our team discovered that autoantibodies, molecules made by the body that attack itself, to a specific nerve cell protein called 'heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein A1' (or 'A1' for short) may lead to neurodegeneration in people living with MS. In healthy individuals, 'A1' performs a number of functions to help cells stay alive. However, in people with MS, 'A1' becomes misplaced within the nerve cell leading to its malfunction and damage to the brain and spinal cord. We have shown that the addition of 'A1' autoantibodies (similar to those found in people with MS) to mice with MS-like symptoms makes the mice sicker. Additionally, giving 'A1' autoantibodies to these mice leads to 'A1' malfunction and significantly increased death and damage to nerve cells compared to mice injected with non-specific antibodies, which do not enter nerve cells. The next step is to test treatments that minimalize the harmful effects of 'A1' autoantibodies on nerve cells. This work suggests a new theory about how nerve cells are damaged in MS. By understanding how 'A1' autoantibodies and 'A1' malfunction cause nerve cell damage or death, we will be able to design new medications to treat neurodegeneration in MS, reduce the disability associated with neurodegeneration and improve the lives of persons living with MS.

column36: A Biophysical Mechanism of Vaping Toxicants in E-Cigarette/Vaping Associated Lung Injury
column37: Use of e-cigarettes and vaping devices are often touted as safer alternatives to traditional smoking. As more users transition to modern inhalation devices, a health crisis has quietly developed. E-cigarette/vaping associated lung injury (EVALI) can range from shortness of breath to severe lung damage requiring intensive care. Little is known about what causes EVALI, but evidence suggests that it may stem from an interaction between toxicants in the vape and the pulmonary surfactant - a thin layer inside the lungs that helps with the expansion and contraction of breathing. Through a partnership with the Canadian Centre for Alternatives to Animal Methods, we will use novel 3D bioprinted lung tissue models to ethically collect pulmonary surfactant that has been exposed to various components of vape. A range of biophysical experiments on extracted pulmonary surfactant, including a multidimensional suite of neutron scattering studies, will reveal sub-molecular level changes to the properties of pulmonary surfactant. These small changes can have very serious large-scale effects that may define the lung dysfunction observed in EVALI. Together, the knowledge gained from this study will offer new insights that can benefit the prognosis of EVALI victims and identify potential complications associated with long-term use. More immediately, the results will serve to promote the importance of informed use and to guide appropriate regulatory policies. On a wider scale, we intend to pioneer a biophysical perspective on health research and will explore a modern, animal-free method to connect fundamental research to medical solutions for acceleration of future discoveries.
