column36: Internal and external mechanisms of 'feeling fat': The roles of negative affect, thought-shape fusion, and social comparison in eating disorder maintenance
column37: 'Feeling' fat is a sense of physically gaining weight when no real change in size has occurred. This is common in people with eating disorders and makes it difficult to overcome symptoms. Our first goal is understanding if negative emotions, atypical thought patterns about eating "fattening" food, or both cause feeling fat. To do this, women with and without eating disorders will complete one of two tasks: imagining experiencing negative emotion or imagining eating a "fattening food." They will rate how fat they feel, and sensors will record their bodies' reactions. Changes in heartbeat and sweat gland activity can indicate levels of emotion regulation and stimulation. We will compare the levels of feeling fat, heart, and sweat gland activity to see if women with eating disorders feel fatter after the negative emotion and fattening food tasks compared to their normal level of feeling fat. We expect the imagination tasks to cause feeling fat and that our measures will reflect this. Our second goal is to clarify the role of social comparison - contrasting one's shape with another person's - in feeling fat. Participants will view a series of images, including women who are thin and obese and neutral objects, while sweat response (i.e., stimulation level) is recorded. We will compare firsthand reports of feeling fat and sweat responses to see if women with eating disorders feel fatter and are more stimulated when viewing thin and obese versus neutral images. All results will be compared in women with and without eating disorders to see if these findings are only true in eating disorders. Results may improve treatments for eating disorders, which focus only on negative emotions causing 'feeling fat.' If food-related thought patterns influence this experience, we must address such thoughts. Further, since biofeedback treatments use technology to track bodily functions and reduce associated symptoms, monitoring heartbeat and sweat response may help treat feeling fat.

column36: Deconstructing cancer evolution using population genetic inference and ecological understanding
column37: Cancer is an evolving disease. The evolutionary trajectory of cancer is defined by the selective pressure within the tissue microenvironment, or ecological niche, of origin. As new mutations arise, the potential for new cellular phenotypes, or subclones, with varying degrees of fitness also increases. This intratumor heterogeneity, or clonality, is known to be an important factor in predicting cancer progression, survival, therapeutic response, and drug resistance. Currently, there are issues with quantifying and detecting clonality in cancer. Existing methods utilize short-read sequencing to reconstruct subclonal populations through either single-nucleotide variant (SNV) analysis or copy number aberration (CNA) analysis. SNV methods use variant allele frequencies to calculate cancer cell fractions, but they require statistical correction because copy number changes and variable whole-genome duplication events impact allele frequencies and mask linkage information. As well, CNA approaches for subclonal reconstruction face issues with statistical variation and sequence coverage noise across SNVs. These limitations constrain the accuracy of subclonal reconstruction as we cannot assign specific groups of sequences to specific subclones. Accurately quantifying clonality is critical for making evolutionary inferences about mutation rate and selection both temporally and spatially within tumours. Therefore, methodological improvements are needed to produce evolutionary biomarkers that are clinically relevant for patients. Overall this research will improve on subclonal reconstruction and haplotype assignment methods. This will enable better analysis of tumour's past while simultaneously generating evolutionary biomarkers that inform on survival, optimal therapy, and drug resistance. Ultimately our methods will help understand the evolvability of an individual's cancer with the goal of improving clinical outcomes, and, most importantly, saving patients' lives.

column36: Investigating the structure and mechanism of beta-catenin dependent gene transcription
column37: Transcription regulators are proteins that control the rate at which DNA is read to make proteins, which carry out specific roles in the body. beta-catenin is a particularly important transcription regulator that is essential for proper cell growth, development and survival. Mutations that influence the ability of beta-catenin to carry out its function are associated with a wide variety of cancers, but most notably in skin and colon cancer. Blocking beta-catenin activity makes these cancer cells more susceptible to chemotherapies and can cause tumor regression. In order to carry out its activity, preliminary studies suggest that beta-catenin associates with another protein named CREB-binding protein (CBP), making this interaction a potential drug target. Despite the therapeutic potential of controlling beta-catenin function, the specific details of how beta-catenin associates with CBP still remains unclear. This research aims to understand both the biological function and mechanistic details of how these proteins interact with one another. I will first determine the atomic-resolution molecular structure of beta-catenin bound to CBP and probe where and how tightly they bind. Using this knowledge, I will then design molecules to disrupt these interactions and examine the biological effects in melanoma and colon cancer cell lines. This multidisciplinary project will help us understand the fundamental molecular mechanisms of gene regulation and may provide new targeted strategies to treat cancer.

column36: Exploring Attitudes and Anticipated Uptake of a COVID-19 Vaccine among Patients with Chronic Illnesses in the Canadian Maritimes
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has changed the world we live in. Until a vaccine is developed, strict public health measures will need to be in place to prevent transmission of this infectious disease. As we wait for a COVID-19 vaccine, there is a need to identify attitudes and beliefs about a future vaccine to ensure uptake once it is available to the public. Uptake will be vital in patients with chronic illnesses, as they are a high-risk group who have received little attention during pandemic planning to date. Vaccine hesitancy, or concerns around vaccination, is a significant threat to global health and may affect uptake of the COVID-19 vaccine. The proposed project aims to understand the attitudes and barriers to anticipated uptake of the future COVID-19 vaccine among patients living with chronic conditions in the Maritimes. A three-phase study will address this research question. First, a survey will be conducted with patients across the Maritimes to explore attitudes, beliefs and anticipated uptake of the COVID-19 vaccine. These findings will be used to develop an interview guide to conduct in-depth interviews with patients and stakeholders, including physicians, pharmacists and nurse practitioners, to investigate barriers and enablers to vaccine uptake. Evidence from these two phases will be used to co-design an intervention with patients and stakeholders to help maximize uptake of the COVID-19 vaccine in high-risk patients. Understanding barriers to vaccinating against COVID-19 is necessary for improving quality of life and health outcomes in patients at high-risk for COVID-19 living in the Maritimes.

column36: Opportunities with a capital "O": Understanding the school environment and its impact on children's health behaviours
column37: We live in an environment where it is more accessible to drive than to walk, where foods high in fat and sugar are more available than healthy options, and now more than ever have interactions through our phones rather than face-to-face conversations. This problem is most concerning for children who are being brought into an environment that promotes rather than hinders unhealthy opportunities; therefore having damaging effects on their health and well-being. In Nova Scotia, we have some of the highest rates of childhood obesity and poor mental health in the country. It is recognized that the school environment is an important place for children to develop, learn and reinforce health behaviours. An intervention called Health Promoting Schools has been put in place across Nova Scotia schools to help create opportunities that support the health and well-being of children (e.g. availability of health food options, increased time for physical activity). However, there is a lack of understanding of how the different parts of the school environment impact children's health behaviours. This research project will focus on examining what components of Health Promoting Schools impact children's health behaviours across Nova Scotia. The project will administer an established health promoting research tool to examine differences in school environments across Nova Scotia. Further, discussions groups will be held with teachers, principals and children to understand what parts of the school environment they think increase or decrease children's health behaviours. Participants will also have the option to photograph different parts of the school environment to provide more input. The collection of information will be used to develop potential ways Health Promoting Schools could improve upon the strategies and policies used to create opportunities in schools that positively impact children's health behaviours across in Nova Scotia.

column36: Exploring the Demographics, Culturally Appropriate Health Services, and Experiences of Indigenous Older Adults Residing in Long-Term Care Facilities in Canada
column37: The aging population in Canada has garnered considerable attention; however, this focus has not been distributed equitably among all Canadian demographics. Indigenous Elders and older adults are integral to cultural revitalization, building intergenerational connections, and sharing knowledges. They are living longer lives than ever before, yet still do not have equitable access to healthcare that promotes wellbeing, especially into later life. Indigenous older adults are more likely to have chronic health conditions compared to non-Indigenous Canadians, and when intensive health services are needed, moving to a long term care (LTC) facility may be necessary. These relocations separate Indigenous older adults from family, friends, community, and culture. Research on Indigenous older adults residing in LTC homes in Canada is sparse. This program of research comprises of three separate but related studies which will contribute to a foundation of knowledge on the topic and answer the following research questions: 1) What culturally appropriate supports and services do Indigenous older adults identify to be important for aging well in LTC? 2) What are the current demographics of the Indigenous older adult population living in LTC in Canada? 3) What are the experiences of Indigenous older adults who move from their communities to a LTC home? The studies use a range of research methods: Question 1 conducts a comprehensive systematic review; Question 2 performs a secondary data analysis on Indigenous LTC resident data from a Canadian LTC database; and Question 3 applies narrative and Storywork methods to explore Indigenous older adult residents' experiences of living in LTC and their perceptions on the necessities for aging well. Findings from these studies have a wide range of applications and can be used to inform healthcare providers, policymakers, and LTC facilities about supporting and promoting the health and wellbeing of Indigenous older adult residents.

column36: Investigating the role of dietary tryptophan metabolism by intestinal microbiota in inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Our gut is exposed to a vast number of bacteria and microorganisms, called microbiota, which in combination with food, are important for maintaining good health. There is growing evidence suggesting that when food-bacterial interactions are broken, conditions like inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) can develop. IBD is a chronic relapsing disease that is increasing in prevalence worldwide, has no cure, and is characterized by severe inflammation in the digestive tract. I propose to study how certain bacteria from the human gut metabolize dietary proteins like tryptophan, to produce molecules which activate a receptor called the (A)ryl (H)ydrocarbon (R)eceptor (AhR). Recent studies have shown that AhR function is abnormal in patients with IBD. This is likely explained by changes in gut microbiota, resulting in a decrease of molecules which activate AhR ("agonists"). What is not known is which bacteria are responsible for the defective production of AhR agonists from foods, and the metabolic pathways involved. In this project I will study and isolate bacteria involved in tryptophan metabolism from IBD patients and healthy people. I will assess their ability to metabolize tryptophan and create AhR agonists using germ-free mice colonized with the selected bacteria. Finally, I will use models of colitis to study the ability of these bacteria to restore AhR function and decrease inflammation and injury in models of colitis. About 1% of the Canadian population could be affected by IBD by 2030. Additionally, current therapies to induce and maintain remission are dominated by drugs that lose effectiveness over time. This suggests the need for complementary therapies. My long-term goal is to develop combinations of bacteria or probiotics, which act on tryptophan in foods to restore AhR function and prevent and treat IBD.

column36: Exploring novel combinatorial therapies for personalized management of Cystic Fibrosis using primary human airway epithelial cells
column37: Cystic Fibrosis is the most common genetic condition affecting Canadian newborns (1 in 3600), and is caused by the inheritance of a mutation, from each parent, in the gene for the Cystic Fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator. People with Cystic Fibrosis, due to their mutations, experience several problems with their lungs including shortness of breath, increased mucus production, and susceptibility to infections. Collectively, these problems can lead to damage of the lungs and early death. There have been great strides in the development of drugs that can treat many patients that have Cystic Fibrosis, with combinations of several drugs more effective than a single drug. However, some Cystic Fibrosis patients remain unresponsive to existing drug combinations and continue to experience symptoms and damage to their lungs. It is therefore important to find new combinations of drugs that can improve the quality of life for all Cystic Fibrosis patients. In this project, I investigate the effectiveness of new drugs, which can be added on top of existing drugs, that target proteins that interact with the Cystic Fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator. This study will use human airway epithelial cells from Cystic Fibrosis patient donors covering a diverse range of the Cystic Fibrosis population. These drugs will be given in combination with currently approved drugs to cells from Cystic Fibrosis patients and we aim to identify potential Cystic Fibrosis patient populations that will benefit from our novel treatment strategy. Our research provides an alternative and complementary strategy to increase the function of the Cystic Fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator. This has the potential to help all Canadians living with Cystic Fibrosis and may reveal distinct populations that may benefit from our proposed drug combination. In addition, this will provide a rationale for the development of new drugs for personalized therapy in Cystic Fibrosis.

column36: Understanding Resilience in Child Mental Health for Children and Families Experiencing Poverty and Poverty-Related Risks: A Mixed-Methods Study Using Population-Based Survey and Clinical Cohort Data
column37: It is well-established that poverty is a cause of poorer health outcomes for children. However, even in the setting of poverty, many children have positive outcomes. This may be because children, families and neighbourhoods are able to adapt positively in the setting of adversity, a concept known as resilience. The goal of this research is to identify characteristics at the child, family and neighbourhood levels which act as buffers to enhance resilience for children facing poverty, leading to better mental health outcomes and fewer mental health concerns. This research will use two data sources: the Ontario Child Health Study (OCHS), a survey of more than 10,000 Ontario children, and the TARGet Kids! Research Network, a primary care practice-based research network in Toronto, Canada of more than 11,000 children, to conduct a mixed-methods study to comprehensively assess buffers that may reduce child mental health concerns. The overall goal of this research program is to systematically identify existing strengths which are potentially modifiable and are already associated with better outcomes. This knowledge can be used to design effective and scalable clinical and public health interventions to optimize child mental health in the setting of poverty. Important strengths of this proposal include a large and representative data source (OCHS) and a clinical platform for immediately knowledge translation, dissemination, and intervention implementation (TARGet Kids!). This project will contribute meaningfully to our knowledge of potential buffers of poverty-related risks for child mental health and lay the groundwork for the candidate's career as a clinician-scientist.

column36: A Tale of Two Receptors: Antibiotics Bypassing the Outer Membrane
column37: We have taken antibiotics to treat potentially life-threatening infections at some point in our lives. However, mismanagement and misuse of antibiotics have reduced the number of treatment options as bacteria acquire resistance. One of the ways pathogenic bacteria, like Pseudomonas aeruginosa, resist killing by antibiotics is through the outer membrane. The outer membrane acts as a barrier that prevents antibiotics from getting into the cell. Our team is addressing this problem using a novel approach. We have identified two antibiotics, thiostrepton and thiocillin, that bypass the outer membrane of P. aeruginosa using iron uptake pathways. When P. aeruginosa encounters iron-limited environments, such as at sites of infections, they release molecules that scavenge iron. The iron-bound molecules return to the cell using specific receptors on the outer membrane. Thiostrepton and thiocillin use the same receptors and P. aeruginosa is tricked into taking up the antibiotics. We have shown that there is a low level of resistance to the two antibiotics in clinical isolates and thiostrepton improved survival in a mice model of infection. This research addresses antimicrobial resistance. It will also have positive implications for the treatment of P. aeruginosa infections using a novel strategy to bypass the outer membrane and improve health outcomes.

column36: The Role of Family Adaptation in the Transition to Adulthood for Youth With Medical Complexity: A Qualitative Case Study
column37: Youth with "medical complexity" have a combination of chronic health conditions and severe disabilities that profoundly impact their lives and those of their families. They rely on their families and machines to help them eat, breathe, and move. They also need the support of many health care and other service workers in order to thrive. The extreme needs of this group can be seen in the high costs to health care systems. They account for one third of all child health care costs in Ontario ($419 million per year). These costs do not include family wages lost to provide unpaid caregiving. In over half of these families, one family member has to stop work to care for their child. Recent advances have helped extend the lifespan of many of these youth, leading to a new generation who are surviving into adulthood. As they become adults, they face many big changes. Their families are now forced to transition abruptly from child to adult health care, education, and social services. It is very far from a smooth and seamless transition. Instead, families experience an abrupt change or ending of services. They report feeling overwhelmed, abandoned, and unsupported-as if they had been "pushed off a cliff." Yet family function and support are critical for these youth to successfully transition into adulthood. It is clear that these families need help during transition. In this study, I aim to learn how to best support families of youth with medical complexity during transition. I will ask families what works for them, what does not, and what support they need most at this time. I will focus on how they manage the change from child to adult health care, education, and social services. Study findings will identify approaches that boost family strengths and support them where they need it most.

column36: Development of a 'friends & family' fall prevention screening tool for community-dwelling older adults and their caregivers
column37: With an aging population, there are increasing concerns over health system capacity. A key reason for hospitalization among older adults is falls. Falls contribute to over $2billion in healthcare costs and lead to lasting physical and emotional injuries that can be challenging to recover from. Although falls are costly, they are preventable. Screening for risk of falling and programs designed to prevent falls have been shown to be effective. However, these screenings are largely conducted by a primary care clinician or after a patient is already admitted to the emergency room, which places a high burden on the healthcare system. To help alleviate this burden on the healthcare system and improve patient outcomes, public health has focused on promoting patient engagement and empowerment in their healthcare. Older adults themselves and their friends and family may be the first to notice a change in their health and mobility that might increase their risk of a fall before being seen by a clinician. To this end, our goal is to identify the most important and easy to measure risk factors for falls among community-dwelling older adults and then develop a tool for patients and caregivers to use independently in the community. In doing so, we can empower older adults and their caregivers to detect and reduce the risk of falling as early as possible.

column36: Alcohol-related Social Network Density and Alcohol Misuse: Examination of Clinical Utility and Predictive Validity
column37: Alcohol misuse is a major public health concern that leads to serious financial, mental, and physical health consequences. One possible factor related to alcohol misuse is a person's social network, and specifically how many people in the network also have problematic alcohol use. Measures of alcohol use in a person's social network may be relevant to clinical settings, by helping clinicians understand where the problematic use may be occurring in the social network, and allowing helpful social changes that could reduce the negative consequences of problematic alcohol use. The goal of this current project is to explore whether measures of alcohol use within a person's social network may be helpful in clinical settings in two ways: first, to examine whether these measures may be used as diagnostic screening tools, and second, to determine whether these measures can predict positive changes in alcohol misuse over time. If these measures are found to be clinically meaningful, this may support the development of specific social network interventions.

column36: Dietary triggers of gastrointestinal symptoms in patients with irritable bowel syndrome
column37: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a gastrointestinal disorder characterized by chronic abdominal pain and altered bowel habits. It affects over 5 million Canadians, producing an economic burden of over $6.5 billion per year. Gluten is the protein found in wheat, rye, and barley responsible for the elastic properties and texture of flour. It is commonly believed to trigger IBS symptoms; however, the mechanism is not yet understood. Also found in wheat, rye, and barley, amylase trypsin inhibitors (ATIs) may contribute to IBS symptoms by activating the innate immune system. ATIs are present in higher quantities in modern wheat, which may explain the greater reported levels of gluten and wheat sensitivity than in the past. Current research suggests that ATIs and gluten interact to trigger more severe symptoms. However, there are no studies in IBS patients investigating the effects of pure gluten versus gluten with ATIs. We designed a placebo-controlled study to investigate the effects of pure gluten compared to gluten with ATIs. IBS patients (n=35) whose symptoms improve on a gluten-free diet will be randomly assigned to consume granola bars containing either pure gluten, gluten with ATIs, or placebo (gluten-free flour). Participants will receive the three different interventions in a period of 10 weeks separated by 2-week washout periods. We will study the underlying mechanisms, including the effects on the immune system and gut bacteria. This research is the first to test the effects of pure gluten against gluten with ATIs in IBS patients. If some patients are sensitive to ATIs instead of gluten, this research would allow for the development of ATI-free foods using pure gluten so that ATI-sensitive individuals can consume gluten-containing breads, pastas, and pastries. The results will also improve our understanding of the potential mechanisms and effects of gluten and ATIs on IBS, leading to better diagnosis and personalized dietary recommendations in the future.

column36: Brain white matter microstructure following SARS-CoV2 infection
column37: In the Spring of 2020, the lives of people worldwide have changed in unimaginable ways. Activities that were once deemed normal everyday activities now require careful consideration, weighing the potential risks against the benefits. Decisions are now made in regards to what is deemed safe, or of an acceptable level of risk, on a daily basis. In order to make these decisions, it is important to be fully aware of the impact that contracting the SARS-CoV2 virus can have on overall health. Importantly, several cases have been reported where SARS-CoV2 infection led to neurological symptoms including severe headache, nausea, loss of smell and taste, and even stroke. A large amount of evidence now shows that the virus can not only enter but also damage the brain, and, in some cases, this damage can prove to be fatal. Although there are known neurological complications to Covid-19, much remains unknown concerning the mechanisms at play. In this project, we will study the impact of Covid-19 on the brain, especially on white matter (the connective pathways between neurons) and cognition, using brain imaging techniques (MRI) and cognitive tests. We will also explore how risk factors, such as hypertension, diabetes, and smoking, influence the impact that Covid-19 has on white matter and cognition, as the presence of these risk factors has been shown to increase the risk of neurological complications with Covid-19. Neurological pathologies have a high incidence in Covid-19 patients, occurring in over one third of patients. These neurological complications lead to severe symptoms and high mortality rates. Our goal is to uncover the type of damage that can occur within the brain following SARS-CoV2 infection. We hope this study will be the first step in designing effective prevention and intervention programs to reduce the incidence and severity of neurological complications with Covid-19 in future research.

column36: Identifying the Role of Protease PrpL in the Virulence of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Pathology of Cystic Fibrosis
column37: Cystic fibrosis is a common, inherited disorder that mostly affects a person's respiratory and digestive systems. Complications from frequent and prolonged lung infections often result in the need for double lung transplants in individuals with CF. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a bacterium that frequently contributes to respiratory failure in children and adolescents suffering from CF. How P. aeruginosa has such a profound affect on the health of CF patients over other bacteria species is not fully understood. It is known that P. aeruginosa capable of producing a protein called PrpL cause longer and more intense infections than those that don't. Our lab has discovered that PrpL likely intensifies infections by altering the ability of the patient's immune system to clear P. aeruginosa from the lungs. Through my research I will confirm how PrpL is able to manipulate the immune system and identify other ways that PrpL leads to severe and prolonged infections. In doing so I will uncover valuable information regarding how PrpL contributes to infections caused by P. aeruginosa and potential treatment options to prevent the bacteria from destroying the lungs of CF patients.

column36: Sport-related Concussion in Youth: Are Symptoms and Recovery Informed by Inflammatory or Endocrine Biomarkers?
column37: Concussion has been described as a "silent epidemic", affecting 250,000 Canadians and 40 million worldwide each year. Youth are at high risk of sport-related concussion (SRC). To date, diagnosis of concussion has been based on clinical assessment which can lead to misdiagnosis and unknown trajectory of recovery. Research into objective blood tests for SRC is underway, but has thus far been largely focused on adults, leaving a substantial gap in the context of pediatric SRC. Changes in inflammation and hormone levels are commonly seen after more severe traumatic brain injury, but recent studies show they may be altered after SRC. Blood tests examining changes in inflammation, hormones, and various markers of brain injury hold promise for the future of SRC diagnosis in youth. This study will include 700 high school students (male and female, ages 13-16 years) with an expected 70 SRCs per year based on established injury rates. After students sustain a SRC, blood tests will be performed within 72 hours, 1 week, and every following 2 weeks thereafter until medical clearance to return to play. Serial blood tests will allow us to determine the physiological consequences of SRC and optimal timing for effective testing and diagnosis. Additionally, results from blood tests will be examined in relation to symptom burden to help clinicians predict who will have a normal or prolonged recovery. With growing public health concerns for youth following SRC, there is an urgent need to provide clinicians with an accurate method to aid in diagnosing and predicting outcomes. Analysis of multiple blood biomarkers of brain injury has the potential to contribute to a better understanding of the pathological changes following concussion and fill a largely ignored gap in pediatric SRC research.

column36: Protective equipment in Canadian high school athletes: Can mouthguards and optimal helmet fit prevent sport-related concussions in youth collision sport?
column37: Concussions (e.g., including sport-related concussions) are brain injuries sustained by over 1.5 million North American youth each year. Over 60% of concussions in youth result from sport participation, with contact from another player being a common mechanism. Unfortunately, concussion can lead to physical (e.g., headaches), emotional (e.g., depression), and social (e.g., isolation) disruptions to a youth's wellbeing. Therefore, sport-related concussion prevention strategies for youth must be explored. Equipment-based strategies are simple, cost-effective, innovative and may be effective in reducing sport-related concussions. Specifically, mouthguard use and optimal helmet fit may protect against sport-related concussion; however, evidence is lacking. The current International Sport Concussion Consensus suggested a 19% reduction in concussion when athletes wear a mouthguard and a recent study demonstrated a 64% reduction in concussions when youth ice hockey players wear a mouthguard. Moreover, helmet use is effective for reducing head injury in recreational activities (e.g., bicycling). For concussion prevention, helmet fit may be an important consideration. Preliminary data in youth ice hockey evaluating helmet mobility, chin-strap fit and other criteria suggests that proper fit is protective against sport-related concussion. Unfortunately, the current literature lacks high quality studies with large sample sizes that assess equipment-based SRC prevention strategies across multiple collision sports. Therefore, this study will examine mouthguard use and helmet fit (where applicable) at time of injury between players with a concussion (cases) and musculoskeletal injured (controls) in grade 10-12 high school students participating in collision sport (e.g., ice hockey, football, rugby) in five Canadian provinces. Understanding the protective effect of equipment will inform concussion prevention equipment strategies and policies to promote lifelong sport participation.

column36: Expanding Capacity in Alberta to Deliver Contingency Patient Management in Outpatient Addiction Treatment: A Randomized Clinical Trial for Methamphetamine Use
column37: Alberta is facing a methamphetamine (MET) crisis. MET-related hospitalizations have increased by 800% between 2010-2015 in Alberta. Promising data indicates that Albertans are increasingly seeking help for their MET use, with treatment enrolments being three times higher in 2018 compared to 2012. Yet, individuals who use MET in Alberta are having significant difficulty remaining in treatment, with a retention rate nearly six times lower than what has been found in other studies with this population. This suggests that the interventions that are currently provided have been ineffective at retaining, and ultimately treating those seeking help for their MET use. Thus, it is important to find a treatment that can improve retention in this population. Contingency management (CM) is an extensively studied treatment for addictions. This intervention provides prizes, like canned goods, when someone meets a behavioural goal, such as attendance. Current findings from the United States have shown that CM improves various outcomes, including retention. Despite research findings, CM is rarely used in Canadian clinical settings. Therefore, this study will implement CM in Alberta (Calgary and Edmonton) for individuals seeking treatment for their MET use. One CM program will incentivize participants for their treatment attendance and the other for MET abstinence. 300 participants will be randomly assigned to one of the CM programs for 12-weeks and a 3, 6, and 12-month follow-up. Prize CM will be used-participants who meet their goal will draw from a prize bowl with a 50% chance of winning. We will evaluate whether CM improves retention, attendance, abstinence, substance use, quality of life, and impacts on the health system. Current efforts to treat MET use in Alberta have been ineffective, leaving this population without the proper care for their addiction. It is hoped the use of CM will increase retention and therefore result in better outcomes in this population.

column36: The kaposin gene cluster drives KSHV latent and lytic infection cycles and viral tumourigenesis
column37: Viruses are estimated to account for 12-20% of cancer cases worldwide. As a cancer-causing virus replicates, it co-opts cellular machinery that would normally be used to detect and resolve dangerous pre-cancerous events. Without the use of this machinery, cells can divide unchecked and cancer may develop. My project addresses a major knowledge gap for one of the seven human cancer-causing viruses, Kaposi's Sarcoma-associated Herpesvirus (KSHV). KSHV is the cause of Kaposi's Sarcoma (KS), an unusual skin cancer which develops from the unrestricted growth of cells that line our blood vessels. When KSHV infects these cells, it can adopt either a dormant (latent) or active (lytic) life cycle, both of which are important for cancer development. During these lifecycles, a set of three proteins, known as kaposin proteins, are produced by virus-infected cells. Very atypically for a herpesvirus, the kaposin proteins are made in both the dormant and active viral lifecycles. The role of these proteins however, and the cellular machinery they may co-opt, is not fully understood. My goal is to determine what role(s) the kaposins have in viral infection and in cancer development. To achieve my goal, I have developed an important set of tools for the KSHV field that will now permit us to study these poorly characterized kaposins: a set of KSHV viruses deficient in kaposin protein production yet otherwise, normal. By studying KSHV using my toolbox of kaposin-deficient viruses, I will learn how these proteins are important to both lifecycles of the virus and how they contribute to tumour development. In doing so, we expect KSHV to act as a homing beacon to help us identify key molecules involved in tumour development. Completion of this project will therefore lead to novel therapeutic targets for KS, and cancer therapy in general.

column36: Modeling Human Glioblastoma in the Context of the Extracellular Environment
column37: "I always like to have a glimmer of hopefulness, even in collapse" - Gordon Downie, Canadian singer-songwriter, activist, glioma patient. Approximately 1000 Canadians a year are diagnosed with brain tumors, and those diagnosed with the most aggressive and fatal form of brain tumors called gliomas have an average survival of 18 months. Research in the past has primarily focused on identifying and targeting specific genetic mutations in the tumor. However, it is apparent that the environment surrounding the tumor can influence tumor growth, tumor spread into the brain, and drug resistance. The brain presents many challenges to glioma treatment, one of which is the unique environment in which gliomas grow, which contributes to poor patient outcomes. The interaction between tumor cells, surrounding normal brain tissue, immune cells, and the structural support of the tumor, the extracellular matrix (ECM) provides an environment that supports the progression and aggressiveness of glioma. The ECM, a 3-dimensional network of proteins, provides tissue-specific molecular and mechanical cues to the tumor. By isolating the ECM, we will determine the components of the glioma environment, study how cells grow and move within this environment, and how the ECM contributes to therapeutic failure. In addition, we will look at the influence of the ECM on immune cells located within the tumor environment. It has become abundantly clear through the failed use of the primary glioma chemotherapy, that directly targeting the tumor is insufficient. Therefore, targeting the glioma environment in addition to the tumor may be considered a better therapeutic strategy. Treating the environment may result in a switch from a tumor-promoting environment to a tumor-suppressing environment. Understanding and characterizing the glioma ECM, may provide unique opportunities to target the glioma environment in addition to targeting the tumor, leading to more successful patient outcomes.

column36: Facilitating Successful Transitions to Home Dialysis: Identifying Support Needs and Care Priorities of Patients and Families
column37: An increasing number of Canadians are getting end stage kidney failure and will start on dialysis treatment to replace their kidney function. There are many dialysis options, one of which is home dialysis. Home dialysis is being promoted by our healthcare system as it has many benefits. However, high levels of support are required for it to be successful as the patient or family sets up and performs the dialysis themselves at home. Without this support, patients experience overwhelming responsibility, and many find it hard to do home dialysis. This is especially true during the transition to home dialysis, which patients describe as a particular difficult time. Little is known about the support needs and priorities in care for patients and families during this time, which makes it hard for programs to put successful interventions in place. This leads to a need for research to be done in this area. We will identify care priorities and support needs for people transitioning onto home dialysis in Canada. This project will be guided by input from patient and family partners, national and international home dialysis clinician leaders, front-line staff and health system administrators. This will be done in three parts. In part one we will perform a literature review to identify other studies that have done similar work. In part two we will follow home dialysis patients during their transition and perform in-depth interviews with them at key times to help us identify what is important at different stages. In part three we will engage with a group of national stakeholders to identify care priorities during this transition. This work will provide valuable information that will help us develop an intervention for use in clinical settings. It is our hope that by creating a more supportive transition experience that patients will have better outcomes on this type of dialysis and that kidney programs will have a better idea of how to address patient and family needs.

column36: Child Bicyclist Injuries and the Built Environment: A Case-Crossover Study
column37: Traffic related injuries are one of the leading causes of injury and death in Canadian children. Collisions involving vehicles and child bicyclists contribute significantly to these injuries and are a cause for concern for the safety of our children. While bicycling and other forms of active transportation improve the physical and mental health of children, there is a decline in participation in part due to the safety concerns of traffic related injury. Child bicyclists experience and interact with traffic and traffic infrastructure differently than adults, which can increase risk of injury. Strategies to prevent these injuries must continue to be explored by both government and non-government organizations across municipalities. By examining the traffic infrastructure/built environment and its link to injury risk in child bicyclists in multiple cities across Canada we can determine the relation between the built environment and child bicycling safety. The case-crossover design of this study uses participants as their own controls and will be used to compare the location a child was injured to two other locations on their route where they were not injured (i.e., control locations). We will examine child bicyclist injury and the built environment through child interviews and site observations. Interviews will allow for additional understanding of the child's perspective of bicycling safety. Using these approaches will allow for us to determine the built environment features such as traffic infrastructure that influence child bicyclist safety and perceptions of safety.

column36: Causal role of intestinal fungi on host immunity and susceptibility to airway inflammation
column37: The intestines are colonized by a large community of microbes, called the microbiome. Research shows that the microbiome provides signals that are important for immunological development of infants, with early-life microbiome alterations (dysbiosis) changing immune responses and increasing the infant susceptibility to allergic diseases, such as asthma. During the first years of life, the immature microbiome undergoes fast developmental changes, and is more susceptible to environmental stressors, which can cause dysbiosis and permanent immune changes to infants. For example, birth via C-section, exclusive formula feeding, and use of antibiotics, which are known to directly alter the gut microbiome, are associated with an increased risk of asthma in young children. Most studies on this area have only investigated bacterial members in the microbiome, ignoring other microorganisms that colonize the infant gut, such as fungi. It was recently shown that fungal dysbiosis is strongly associated with antibiotic use and risk of asthma in infants, however, it is still not known how fungi are involved in asthma development. My research project aims to determine the impact of early-life gut fungal colonization and antibiotic-induced fungal overgrowth on immune development and asthma susceptibility. In my experiments, I will use a model with mice completely lacking microbes (germ-free). These germ-free mice will be colonized with defined mixtures of bacteria only, fungi only, or both. Additionally, I will colonize mice with fungus specifically expanded in young babies receiving antibiotics. I will determine different immune measurements and apply a model of allergic asthma in these colonized mice. These experiments will allow me to determine if fungi alter immune development and increase airway inflammation in mice. This work also has great potential to reveal novel approaches to prevent immune dysregulation and allergic diseases in children.

column36: How does parenting interact with genetic differential susceptibility in predicting attachment patterns in preschool-aged children?
column37: Attachment represents a brain-based biological evolutionary system that helps to ensure the survival of the human infant (Bakermans-Kranenburg, 2015). A secure attachment is when a child feels secure, safe, and protected while exploring the world around them (Ainsworth, 1978). Secure attachment to a caregiver is critical to healthy brain and organ-system development, optimal child behaviour, and adult mental and physical health. Caregiving qualities, such as how sensitive caregivers are in responding to their infants' needs (i.e., sensitivity), were thought to be the most significant influence on whether an infant develops a secure attachment pattern (Ainsworth, 1978; Feeney, 2016). However, there is an increasing debate on how much caregiver sensitivity alone influences attachment pattern development, leading to the exploration of other contributing factors such as genetics (Belsky, 2015). Gene by environment studies look at how the environment can influence early childhood development, disease, and health overall (McAllister, 2017). However, there are few studies examining gene-environment interaction and the influence this has on developing attachment patterns (Golds, 2020). This research will examine how children's genetics interact with the caregiving environment in predicting attachment patterns. We plan to examine these factors in a sample of 176 participants who were a part of the larger Alberta Pregnancy Outcomes and Nutrition (APrON) study. This research will show the degree to which children's genetics contribute to their attachment pattern, with implications for deepening our understanding of the developmental origins of health and disease. This knowledge will advance our ability to target programs and nursing interventions to specific populations based on children's genetics and caregiving environments and therefore contribute to improving the health of Canadians.

column36: The Feasibility and Acceptability of Dialectical Behavior Therapy for Treating Non-Suicidal Self-Injury and Suicidal Behavior in Women With Autism
column37: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition occurring in 1% of the population. While we used to think (ASD) occurred more frequently in males, we now know that the ratio is closer to 1.8:1 (males:females). Females with ASD without intellectual disability (ASD-WID) experience high rates of self-harm and suicide. Indeed, rates of suicide in this population are close to 50 times higher than in the general population. Despite this, there are currently no evidence-based treatments available for treating self-harm and suicidal behavior in females with ASD-WID. Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT; a type of cognitive behavioral therapy) is an evidence-based treatment designed to treat self-injury and suicidal behavior in females. That said, DBT is a very time and resource intensive treatment, and might not be readily accessible to females with ASD-WID. One component of DBT, skills training groups, has been found to reduce suicidal behavior and self-harm. As such, it is possible that DBT skills groups could be used to treat self-injury and suicidal behavior in females with ASD-WID. In this research, I will look at whether DBT skills trainings is an acceptable, feasible, and effective treatment for self-injury and suicidal behavior in females with ASD-WID. Participants will complete 26 weekly 2-hour DBT skills groups. They will be asked to complete weekly measures regarding the acceptability, feasibility and effectiveness of the treatment. I will also ask participants to take part in focus groups to discuss their experiences of treatment, and to suggest modifications for adapting the treatment for future use. The results of this study could have significant health impacts. Suicide is a serious public health problem, but no evidence-based treatments exist for individuals with ASD. I hope to use the findings to refine the DBT treatment protocol as appropriate and to conduct a larger research study.

column36: Hepatitis C Infection, Risk Behaviour, and Neurocognition in Precariously Housed Men and Women
column37: Hepatitis C (HCV) is a serious viral infection that, if untreated, can lead to liver cirrhosis and cancer. Effective treatment options for HCV exists, but vulnerable populations, including precariously housed and homeless persons (HPHPs), experience barriers to accessing and maintaining treatment. HCV and other viral infections are endemic among HPHPs living in the Downtown Eastside (DTES) of Vancouver and there is alarmingly poor HCV treatment access and adherence in this population. Cognitive impairment, which HCV infection conveys, is rife amongst HPHPs on the DTES and is a potential barrier to treatment access. This project has two aims: to assess the degree to which HCV infection is associated with longitudinal cognitive decline in precariously housed and homeless men and women, and to examine the extent to which HCV-related cognitive impairments acts as a barrier to infection management among these individuals. It is hypothesized that HCV infection will portend longitudinal cognitive decline that is steeper in men compared to women, and that neurocognition mediates the association between HCV infection and infection management among all study participants. Establishing the impact of HCV infection on cognitive functioning and defining its role in effective HCV infection self-management will provide insight into treatment strategies and potential targets of intervention, and may ultimately improve the health care of one of the most vulnerable populations in Canadian society.

column36: Intersectional determinants of im/migrant women's sexual and reproductive health access: Informing interventions during COVID-19 and beyond
column37: British Columbia(BC) is a key destination setting for immigrant women, who make up over 25% of residents. Immigrant women in Canada may face critical sexual and reproductive health(SRH) issues, potentially from health system challenges, negative experiences with providers, and a lack of culturally sensitive and language-specific care. There is a need to examine how factors such as gender, age, discrimination, migration experiences, and temporary immigration status shape immigrant women's healthcare and SRH experiences in BC. There is also a need to understand impacts of racism on immigrant women's health access given ongoing health issues highlighted by COVID-19 among immigrants in Canada and globally. My study will describe how factors such as gender and race, as well as immigration factors (e.g. status, time in Canada, migration experiences) shape immigrant women's SRH needs and access in BC; evaluate any changes during COVID-19; and explore potential differences among immigrant sub-groups (e.g. youth, undocumented). I anticipate that the findings will highlight deeply rooted barriers to SRH access, including racism, insecure status, and strict gender norms, which may be more severe during COVID-19 and for recent and younger immigrants of colour. My study will use interviews from 'IRIS', a study of immigrant women's SRH access in BC housed at the Centre for Gender & Sexual Health Equity. Interview data will be collected during and beyond COVID-19 to examine potential variations, and analyses will examine potential differences by age, time in Canada, immigration status, and country of origin. This study aims to advance knowledge of immigrant women's SRH access in BC, calling for improved healthcare access for immigrants during COVID-19 and beyond. It will build understandings of how gender, migration experiences, and other changes shape SRH needs and access, and will contribute urgently needed evidence of strategies to best improve healthcare during COVID-19.

column36: Effect of neurovascular defects on brain metabolism in 16p11.2 deletion mouse model of autism spectrum disorders
column37: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) are neurodevelopmental disorders associated with social interaction deficits, communication impairments, repetitive behaviors and restricted interests. Causes are still enigmatic, but ASD-associated mutations have been identified, one of them corresponding to a loss of DNA known as the 16p11.2 deletion. The brain's high metabolic demands and negligible intrinsic energy reserves makes it continuously dependent on the adequate influx of oxygen and nutrients from the blood stream to ensure proper brain development and function. Although the neuronal underpinnings of ASD are being extensively studied, very little is known about the vascular contributions to these conditions. Recently, we revealed that 16p11.2 deletion was linked to functional and structural abnormalities in brain vascular networks. My project will focus on thoroughly examining the impact of these abnormalities on brain metabolism at a cellular level using a genetically-engineered mouse model of ASD harboring the 16p11.2 deletion. My goal is to investigate key regulators of brain metabolism in order to identify target pathways to modulate. The research program that we proposed will provide novel insight into the involvement of brain metabolism in ASD while further pinpointing biomarkers which could lead to selective therapeutic approaches that can address core symptoms of ASD.

column36: A Healthy People Initiative: Improving the Socio-Economic Circumstances and Recovery Outcomes of the Homeless and At-Risk for Homelessness Populations in Ottawa and Toronto (Canada)
column37: Tobacco is the most preventable cause of disease and death in Canada. Although the tobacco use rate has substantially gone down in the general population, significant differences exist between sub-populations in Canada, where for example Ottawa's highly vulnerable People Who Use Drugs (PWUD), homeless or at-risk for homelessness population has a 96% tobacco smoking rate relative to 9-18% in the rest of Ottawa. This stark inequity in tobacco use translates into devastating healthcare outcomes such as a disproportionate amount of cancer, stroke, heart disease and death. In order to tackle tobacco related health disparities, a novel approach to smoking cessation in vulnerable populations is required. Despite commonly held dogma that the PWUD and homeless populations does not want to quit smoking, many studies have demonstrated that in fact they are very interested in quitting. Pragmatic peer-led community-based approaches have demonstrated that tobacco dependence strategies can be implemented with great success in this population. column36: Engineering and characterization of a novel immunomodulatory oncolytic virus via modification of cellular phosphorylation homeostasis
column37: A cure for cancer, the leading cause of death in Canada, has yet to be found. Oncolytic viruses (OVs) are modified viruses that selectively infect and kill cancer cells. Although they have shown promise, its success has been limited by the cancer's natural anti-virus response. Our lab has recently shown that drugs containing the metal vanadium can increase the virus' cancer killing effect. Vanadium does this by lowering the anti-virus defence while strengthening the patient's immune system against the tumour. Unfortunately, vanadium is not easily delivered to the human body; therefore, our project aims to create a new virus product that imitates vanadium's beneficial effects. To do this, we will first identify how vanadium boosts the effect of the virus by screening for its different targets within the cell. We will then code genetic instructions to block these identified targets into the virus. By looking at measures like the amount of virus infection and cancer cell death, we can assess how effective our designer virus is in human and mouse cancer cells. Next, we will assess how well our virus works in mouse models. After identifying a safe dose and no dangerous side effects, mice bearing tumours will be injected with our virus. We will monitor how quickly the tumours shrink with treatment and whether their survival is improved. The ability for the mouse to produce long-term tumour protection will then be measured by looking at their immune response and monitoring whether mice recover when given a second tumour. If successful, this strategy that combines the advantages of both oncolytic viruses and vanadium while overcoming their disadvantages represents a promising treatment option for cancer patients. We hope to eventually have the product ready for health and safety testing in human clinical trials. This work will also lead to a better understanding of how the body reacts to viral infection and provide insight into new treatment strategies.

column36: Role of DUSP4 in diabetic nephropathy and end-stage renal disease
column37: Diabetic nephropathy (DN) is a renal complication affecting many diabetic patients and is one of the preeminent causes of renal insufficiency leading to dialysis or renal transplant. Our project is based on podocytes, important cells for blood filtration in the kidneys. Their loss of function and death is an early event in the development of diabetic nephropathy. Ultimately, structural changes will get worse and lead to complete renal decline (ESRD). DUSP4, a molecule that regulates proteins involved in cell death, is important for renal function. We have observed a decrease in DUSP4 levels in diabetic kidneys. Previous results have emphasized the importance of DUSP4 in the kidney since whole-body removal of DUSP4 worsens characteristics of diabetic nephropathy. To this day, the kidneys of diabetic patients suffering from ESRD are said to have reached the point of no return. Thus, it is critical to find treatments that could stop/slow down the progression of kidney problems. With the use of mice that have elevated levels of DUSP4 specifically in podocytes, our objective is to determine the clinical significance of DUSP4 in the prevention of diabetic nephropathy. Our hypothesis is that increased levels of DUSP4 in podocytes will prevent the onset of kidney problems in diabetic mice and will also re-establish renal function once the disease has already started. Secondly, with the use of a mouse model of ESRD (adenine-rich food), our 2nd objective is to investigate the role of DUSP4 in the progression towards complete renal insufficiency, an area that lacks research. We hypothesize that DUSP4 deletion will accelerate the progression and onset of complete renal insufficiency. My projects will help us better understand the mechanisms leading to DN and ESRD as well as the importance of DUSP4 in the kidney while ultimately contributing to support patients affected by these conditions to potentially give them a better quality of life.

Ainsi, des premiers travaux viseront a determiner la proportion de canadiens atteignant la triple cible therapeutique et son evolution entre 2007 et 2019 grace aux donnees de l'Enquete canadienne sur les mesures de la sante de Statistique Canada. Dans un deuxieme temps, les donnees de 30 femmes agees ayant un diabete de type 2 et ayant participe a une etude portant sur l'effet de 12 semaines d'entrainement (HIIT vs ECM) seront analysees pour tenter d'etablir si les differentes modalites d'exercice actuellement recommandees par Diabete Canada permettent, de facon similaire, d'ameliorer l'atteinte de la triple cible therapeutique et de reduire la variabilite de la glycemie. column36: Assessing the safety and efficacy of intra-arterial chilled saline infusion following focal ischemic stroke
column37: With ~55,000 new cases each year in Canada, the social, individual, and economic costs of this ischemic stroke are unparalleled. Despite advances in treating this disabling disease, not all patients benefit. This proposal aims to improve outcomes for all patients, but especially those that do not benefit from current therapies by investigating whether intra-arterial chilled saline (IACS) infusion is a safe and effective treatment. IACS treatment involves flushing the injured tissue with cold saline. Previous research has shown that IACS is beneficial. However, previous research is homogenous and not aligned with clinical reality (e.g., only studied in young, healthy, male rats, creating a mismatch with reality). In Year 1, we will develop our stroke model using hypertensive rats, a key risk factor. We will vary the stroke duration, and assess brain injury at 48 hours post-stroke. Our brain injury severity measurements in Year 1 will inform groups for Year 2 and 3. In Year 2, we will randomly assign male AND female rats to moderate, severe, and very-severe stroke, and either treat them with IACS or sham IACS. HYPOTHESIS: moderate and severe injuries will benefit from IACS treatment, but very-severe brain injuries may require more prolonged cooling. Our outcome measures are behavioural impairment (using established tests) and brain injury volume. Year 3 will be like Year 2, except rats will survive for 28 days, rather than 48 hours, and the treatment will be prolonged with a skull cooling device. Long-term studies are lacking in current literature. As before, we will assess behavioural deficits and brain injury. HYPOTHESIS: the combined hypothermia groups will have better outcomes than controls. Altogether, my research proposal will inform whether IACS is a safe and effective treatment for ischemic stroke by carefully considering clinical reality and addressing the limitations of current research (e.g., using multiple injury sizes, both sexes, hypertensive animals).

column36: Helpful or Harmful? Consequences of Cellular Volume Changes following Stroke
column37: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is a devastating stroke subtype that is fatal for over 40% of patients. ICH occurs when a blood vessel in the brain ruptures, causing blood to spill into the surrounding tissues and form a clot. The skull is a closed compartment, so a large blood clot takes up essential space in the brain and drives up pressure within the skull, with often fatal outcomes. Interestingly, we recently discovered a novel phenomenon in which brain cells experience a dramatic reduction in volume (up to 60%) in the days following a moderate to large ICH. We believe that this is a regulated process, in which brain cells get rid of compounds called osmolytes, which are low-weight organic molecules that influence properties of cells, such as protein stability, cell size regulation, and cellular health. By doing this, cells are able to reduce their size in attempt to equalize deadly pressure elevations and prevent death. However, by getting rid of osmolytes to reduce their size, cells are ridding themselves of an important protective mechanism essential for survival in a stroke setting. Therefore, we assert that the loss of protective osmolytes in order to maintain cell size reductions is detrimental to the health of brain cells, resulting in the global functional impairments that we observe in ICH patients, rather than local reductions in blood flow as previously thought. We aim to assess whether these cell size reductions occur across multiple brain cell types, examine the impact of stroke severity, and quantitatively determine how extreme cell size reductions impact cellular health and function through gold standard techniques such as electron microscopy and Fourier Transform Infrared Imaging.

column36: Elevating circulating ketones as a novel therapeutic approach for the treatment of heart failure
column37: Although treatments for cardiovascular diseases have reduced the number of deaths, they have increased the number of patients who develop a condition known as heart failure. Simply put, heart failure is the inability of the heart to pump enough blood that is required by the rest of the body. For decades, it has been shown that the poor function of the failing heart is due to its inability to make enough energy to pump properly. While fats and sugars are the main energy sources for the heart, recent evidence suggests that the failing heart relies on ketones, potentially to increase energy production. Ketones are molecules that are produced by the liver from fats and can be used to provide energy in the heart. Yet, ketones also have many non-energetic properties such as reducing inflammation, which often occurs with heart failure. Currently, it is not understood if and/or how ketones may help the failing heart and if giving more ketones can be a useful therapy. Thus, using mouse models of heart failure, my project will investigate the role of ketones in heart failure and determine if and how they are good for the heart. Although ketogenic diets are commonly known to increase ketones, they reduce sugars, which are known to be an important source of energy for the failing heart. Therefore, our new approach will use a safe, commercially sold ketone water which increases blood ketone levels. We hypothesize that increased ketone use is beneficial for the failing heart and propose that providing even more ketones to the heart will improve heart function by reducing inflammation and increasing energy production. Together, our studies will increase our knowledge of heart failure and may create a new, more practical therapy to help the patients affected by this debilitating condition.

column36: Optimizing Opioid Agonist Therapies for Pregnant Women in British Columbia
column37: Opioid use disorder (OUD) during pregnancy is associated with multiple negative maternal and fetal outcomes. Although evidence suggests that opioid agonist therapies (OAT) may result in better health outcomes for mother and infant, many pregnant women enrolled in OAT are prescribed treatments that are of insufficient dose or duration. These issues may contribute to challenges with adherence or relapse, which can have negative maternal and fetal health consequences, including heightened risk of overdose. Our research will seek to: 1) Compare pregnancy outcomes between women living with OUD who are prescribed different types of OAT or no OAT during pregnancy; 2) Evaluate factors associated with adherence to and retention in different types of OAT during pregnancy and postpartum; 3) Examine changes in risk of non-fatal and fatal overdose during pregnancy and postpartum, and whether this differs by OAT dosage and retention. We will rely on a province-wide linked retrospective cohort of people living with opioid use disorder using linked data from the BC Perinatal Data Registry, prescription dispensations, and other databases held by the Ministry of Health. We will analyse the impact of different OAT regimens on pregnancy outcomes, the role of sociodemographic, clinical, and geographic factors in adherence to different types of OAT, and changes in overdose risk during pregnancy and postpartum. These findings can be used to inform evidence-based harm reduction policies and clinical practice guidelines that will connect pregnant women with safe and effective therapies, reduce stigma around OAT for pregnant women, promote uptake of prenatal care, and result in healthier and safer pregnancies for both mother and child.

column36: A multimodal neuroimaging approach to identifying subgroups of children with neurodevelopmental disorders with shared brain characteristics
column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) are common neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs) that are diagnosed separately yet share causes and symptoms. The overlap between disorders and variable behavioural presentations within disorder has made finding effective treatments difficult. To better understand the heterogeneity and symptom overlap, it is critical that subgroups of NDDs who share similar patterns of neural pathophysiology are discovered. Despite evidence that NDDs are caused by atypicalities in both brain structure and function, existing studies have only considered subgroups based on structure. Identifying subgroups utilizing both types features may identify groupings of children with a higher degree of shared biology, and thus provide more precise targets for treatments. I aim to discover whether measures of brain structure and function can be integrated to discover subgroups of NDDs. My objectives are 1) to use functional neuroimaging to identify subgroups of children with ASD, ADHD and OCD, and 2) to investigate the effects of combining measures of brain function with structure on the groupings. I hypothesize that subgroups identified via brain function will differ from those identified with structure, yet their combination will lead to more distinct groupings. Magnetic resonance imaging and magnetoencephalography will be used to measure brain function and structure using data from the Province of Ontario Neurodevelopmental Disorders network. Measures of brain structure and function will be used to identify clusters of participants which may better differentiate on their clinical and cognitive characteristics than the current diagnostic labels, and thus support using interventions designed for one diagnosis for children with other diagnoses. Furthermore, the decreased variability within the subgroups would provide more precise targets for treatments and interventions.

column36: Beyond the binary: Measuring gender diversity in cancer research
column37: Gender diverse people, or more commonly transgender, nonbinary, and gender nonconforming people, may be at risk of receiving worse cancer care and having worse outcomes when compared to other groups. Although there is some research supporting this belief, it is difficult to identify gender diverse people in data that are regularly used for cancer research. The goal of this project is to create a guide for researchers to help them understand what gender diversity means and different ways they can include it in their own projects. The first part of this project will explore ways gender is included in other cancer research. The information gathered in this step will be used to guide conversations with gender diverse people to find out what they think is important for other researchers to know about gender diversity and how researchers should be including them in their projects. Based on these conversations and what is currently done in other research, I will see if gender is being included the way it should be in the data often used in cancer research. I will combine the results from all of these steps to create a guide for researchers. Creating this guide will allow gender diverse people to say, in their own terms, how they want to be included in cancer research. Ultimately, this guide will help us better understand the challenges gender diverse people face through their cancer journey. It will also help decision-makers make changes so that gender diverse people receive the best possible care.

column36: Investigating the role of lysosomal exocytosis in Alzheimer's disease
column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a cruel disease that gradually worsens over time. Afflicted individuals experience progressive memory loss and personality changes that negatively impact both themselves and their loved ones. As there is no cure for AD, therapeutic approaches rely on medication that only alleviate symptoms. AD is associated with abnormal accumulation of two major toxic proteins, called tau and beta-amyloid (AB), in the brain. The mechanism controlling the build-up and release of these proteins from one cell to another is poorly understood. A specialized compartment in the cell, termed lysosomes, are known for their ability breakdown of material, but also function in the discharge of material from a cell. It has been previously shown that not only are tau and AB made within lysosomes, they also accumulate and become resistant to breakdown at this site. Taken together, there is evidence to suggest that the pathway in which material is released from lysosomes also plays an important role in the spread of toxic proteins from cell-to-cell. The proposed study aims to investigate the pathway that controls lysosomal release of material in cells of the brain. We will test the hypothesis that lysosomes play an important role in the clearance of toxic tau and AB from brain cells through this pathway. In this study, cells will be configured to express a marker for lysosomes and treated with toxic tau and AB. A specialized microscope will be used to capture nanoscopic events occurring at the cell surface when lysosomes are stimulated to discharge. This will allow for live analysis of these events, including number and timing. With an ageing population and the prevalence of AD on the rise, there is a need to better understand how tau and AB accumulate and can spread from one cell to another. This project would advance the development of targeted therapeutics for AD, which is vital in preventing future disease progression.

column36: Early neuromuscular stimulation and motor imagery interventions during immobilization of distal radius fracture to reduce the resulting motor impairments and improve rehabilitation outcomes.
column37: Fracturing the wrist usually requires a brace/cast to be worn for at least six weeks to keep the wrist inactive for fracture healing. The inactivity leads to loss of motor function (i.e. reduced strength and movement), which may require extensive rehabilitation and often leaves lasting impairments. Stimulating the nerves of the arm and mental rehearsal of movements, without physically performing the movement, have shown to be beneficial in recovering from the resulting loss of motor function. This research project aims to use these strategies, with some changes so they can be used during the time the wrist in casted/splinted, with the aim of reducing the loss of motor function from the inactivity. For the nerve stimulation a brace/cast will be designed and developed to deliver the stimulation to the underlying tissue while in the cast. column36: Surpassing Symptomatology: Exploring Posttraumatic Growth in MDMA-Facilitated Cognitive Behavioral Conjoint Therapy for Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
column37: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a debilitating illness that impacts almost 1 in 10 Canadians in their lifetime. Individuals suffering from PTSD are at risk for suicide, other mental illnesses, and poor health outcomes. Yet, PTSD is not a solitary disorder. PTSD also impacts the mental health of loved ones. For this reason, Cognitive Behavioral Conjoint Therapy (CBCT) treats the patient and their partner. After this therapy, a majority of patients no longer meet diagnostic criteria for PTSD. However, symptom reduction is not the only measure of treatment success. Positive changes matter. Posttraumatic growth (or improvements in multiple areas of life following a trauma) can occur as stronger interpersonal relationships, personal strength, appreciation of life, seeing new possibilities, and spiritual change. It has been shown that CBCT can lead to posttraumatic growth. Yet, not all patients respond to treatment or show positive changes, and ways to improve therapies are needed. The drug 3,4 methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) has shown remarkable promise when combined with psychotherapy; and MDMA has been named a breakthrough therapy for PTSD. However, no study has examined if posttraumatic growth occurs in MDMA-assisted couples therapy for PTSD. In this study, 40 couples will receive either MDMA-assisted CBCT or CBCT. We hope to uncover if posttraumatic growth increases for patients and partners in MDMA-assisted CBCT compared to CBCT, when posttraumatic growth occurs in therapy sessions, and to understand the lived experience for patients and partners longer term. To answer these questions, we will measure posttraumatic growth before and after therapy, examine therapy session tapes, and interview patients and partners 6 months after therapy. This will be the first study to examine posttraumatic growth in MDMA-facilitated couples therapy for PTSD. Given that the FDA has scheduled MDMA to become a medicine by 2021, this research is necessary and timely.
