column36: Application of the ORBIT model to test a tailored smoking cessation intervention for persons with spinal cord injury
column37: A spinal cord injury (SCI) occurs from damage to the spinal cord and is associated with adverse health and social implications. Traditionally, health promotion has focused on the prevention of disease and disability, resulting in limited health promotion interventions for persons with SCI. An example of health promotion that has been overlooked for persons with SCI is smoking cessation. Compared to the general population, persons with SCI are more likely to smoke, experience more significant tobacco-related health disparities, and encounter unique circumstances to treatment. Despite these inequities, smoking cessation interventions have yet to be developed to support persons with SCI to stop smoking. Interventions developed using theory, systematic processes, and engagement of knowledge users are often more useful and relevant to those who may benefit from it. The ORBIT model was developed to improve the real-world impact of behavioural interventions by ensuring that interventions are carefully crafted and developed incrementally over time. The objective of this research is to use behaviour change theory and meaningful partnership with an SCI organization to develop and conduct preliminary testing of a smoking cessation intervention for persons with SCI. First, in a small sample of persons with SCI, we will test whether a tailored smoking cessation intervention helps persons with SCI stop smoking. Second, using gold-standard video recording methodology, we will determine whether peers with SCI can be trained to deliver the intervention as intended. Third, using a randomized design, we will determine whether the peer-delivered smoking cessation intervention can demonstrate greater smoking cessation rates compared to a care-as-usual control group. The findings from this study will be used to inform a future efficacy trial and may result in high-quality smoking cessation supports for persons with SCI.

column36: Understanding the mechanisms of primary 5-Azacytidine resistance in the treatment of MDS
column37: Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) are cancers originating from the blood-forming cells present in the bone marrow. In MDS, the disease either results in a failure to produce enough blood cells to survive or in 20% - 40% of the patients, the disease progresses to a very aggressive leukemia. Currently, only a bone marrow transplant can cure a patient. However, not all patients are eligible for a marrow transplant. For such patients, the only standard therapy is the use of a drug called Azacitidine (AZA). In MDS, chemical changes to the DNA called DNA methylation, is commonly observed. AZA reverses this DNA methylation changes. However, 50% of the patients do not respond to the AZA. It is yet unknown why some patients respond to AZA while others don't, in other words are resistant to AZA. Currently, there are no further treatment options for such patients, raising the pressing need to understand how AZA resistance develops. In the bone marrow of an MDS patient, certain rare cells are responsible for the initiation and progression of MDS. These rare cells also known as the MDS-stem cells can give rise to more MDS-stem cells as well as mature cancerous cells which then fill up the patient's bone marrow. Previous studies have shown that treatment with AZA only kills the more mature cancerous cells but not the MDS-stem cells themselves . Thus, to understand how resistance to AZA develops, we need to understand the nature of these MDS-stem cells. This project focusses on studying these rare MDS-stem cells from patients who are responsive and non-responsive to AZA. Through this project I want to identify which type of blood cell becomes the MDS-stem cell and examine if the nature of the identified MDS-stem cells in AZA responders is different from the non-responders. Understanding the nature of these stem cells will help identify new therapies that can be used along with AZA to target these stem cells and improve the outcomes of AZA non-responsive patients.

column36: Is 5-methyltetrahydrofolate as effective as folic acid in increasing serum and red blood cell folate during pregnancy and lactation, while resulting in reduced unmetabolized folic acid in maternal blood and breastmilk?
column37: Nutrition during pregnancy has an important impact on infant development and pregnancy outcomes. Folic acid (the man-made form of the B-vitamin folate) is recommended during pregnancy and while breastfeeding because it is important for healthy development, but there is growing concern that Canadian women are getting too much. Our bodies are only able to process small amounts of folic acid, and when we eat too much, our bodies cannot use folic acid properly. Unused folic acid has been found in nearly all (>90%) blood and breastmilk samples of Canadian women while pregnant and breastfeeding. The effects of unused folic acid are not fully understood, but have been associated with cancer, concerning infant health outcomes, and it may interfere with folate's role in growth and development. Also, unused folic acid in breastmilk is concerning because babies are not able to absorb it as well as natural folate, which could cause low folate levels. Natural folate may be better for women to take while pregnant and breastfeeding than folic acid. Some prenatal vitamins in Canada contain natural folate instead of folic acid (as it is approved by Health Canada), but natural folate has never been tested during pregnancy. Therefore, a study is needed to help address this gap. We will recruit 60 healthy pregnant women and give them prenatal vitamins with either natural folate or folic acid starting at 8-21 weeks gestation until 1 week after birth. We have three goals for this study: 1) To measure serum folate, red blood cell folate, and unused folic acid after supplementing with natural folate or folic acid for 16 weeks of pregnancy; 2) To learn about recruiting pregnant women to this type of study, to help design a larger follow-up trial; 3) To compare breastmilk folate levels (total folate and unused folic acid) in each group. This study will provide needed information to determine the safest and most effective form of folate supplements for Canadian women and their babies.

column36: The clinical impact of next-generation sequencing on myeloid malignancies
column37: In recent years, the significance of genetic information in the diagnosis, screening, and treatment of myeloid (blood) cancers has become highly evident. The increasing impact of identifying genes associated with these cancers necessitates more comprehensive screening techniques. Targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a tool that permits the identification of many genes in one efficient test that can be applied for patients using blood or bone marrow. NGS works by assessing a patient's DNA (obtained from these blood or bone marrow samples) to determine whether there are any variations in the sequence (mutations) that may be contributing to their disease. Targeted NGS refers specifically to the assessment of a group of genes known to play a role in blood cancers. NGS allows the simultaneous assessment of many genes in a single, efficient, comprehensive test. The results of this test (showing whether there is variation in a patient's DNA) can inform clinicians about this patient's disease based on current research surrounding affected genes. This tool will not only complement current techniques but may in fact replace them. We performed sequencing of DNA from patient samples using the Thermo Fisher Ion Chef and Ion S5 sequencer. We analyzed the sequencing results and classified variants (changes in genes/DNA) based on their potential to impact patient care. To date, we have performed sequencing of 187 samples from 168 unique patients with a variety of myeloid cancers. Of the variants (abnormalities) detected, 77% were potentially actionable (impacted patient care). In the majority of patients, we were able to identify variants that may aid clinicians in achieving/clarifying diagnoses, informing follow-up/prognosis, and guiding treatment decisions. Our findings highlight the importance of integrating NGS into clinical testing for patients with myeloid cancers.

column36: Identifying neurocognitive outcomes and cerebral oxygenation in critically ill adults on acute kidney replacement therapy in the intensive care unit: The INCOGNITO-AKI study
column37: Adults admitted to hospital intensive care units (ICUs) are more likely to develop problems with cognition. Cognition affects how people think, feel, and react. Problems with cognition can cause poorer quality of life, difficulties doing daily activities and caring for oneself, and strain the Canadian healthcare system. Patients who need dialysis for kidney issues during their ICU stay are at an even higher risk for these problems. Over half of critically ill patients develop kidney problems, and up to 13% need dialysis to replace the function of their kidneys. Patients who need long-term dialysis outside the ICU have worse cognitive function. We do not know the effect of short-term dialysis during an ICU admission on cognition. We expect the effect to be similar to long-term dialysis. Brain oxygen levels are linked to cognitive function and can be an early warning sign for cognitive problems. To understand how dialysis affects the brain in adults admitted to the ICU, we will a) measure the level of oxygen in the brain while patients are on dialysis; and b) see if these levels are associated with cognition and patient safety at 3- and 12-months after they have been discharged from the ICU. To understand any differences in brain effects, we will also compare the brain oxygen levels of patients when they are treated with two kinds of dialysis: intermittent hemodialysis (patients are treated for hours at a time with breaks in between), and continuous kidney replacement therapy (patients may be treated continuously for days with no breaks). Cognitive function is important for good quality of life. To support patients and the healthcare system, we need to know how treating patients with dialysis in the ICU impacts their cognition. This will help providers and patients make more informed decisions about both the type and the impact of dialysis. This study may inform future interventions to help prevent cognitive problems for patients treated with dialysis in the ICU.

column36: Uncovering a role for gut microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids in the anti-Factor VIII immune response
column37: Hemophilia A (HA), an inherited bleeding disorder that is characterized by a deficiency or dysfunction in the coagulation protein Factor VIII (FVIII), can result in major bleeding events that can lead to serious health complications if not properly managed. Interestingly, bacteria throughout our gastrointestinal tract are critical for the healthy functioning of our immune system. Evidence suggests that a loss of certain healthy bacteria, termed dysbiosis, can predispose you to immune-related disease. Thus, gut dysbiosis may be a potential risk factor for FVIII inhibitor development. Research published by us shows that dysbiosis in HA mice results in enhanced FVIII inhibitor production but how this occurs is not understood. We hypothesize that a specific class of metabolite healthy bacteria produce, short-chain fatty acids, are responsible. This study aims to elucidate the way gut bacteria and their metabolites regulate FVIII inhibitor production and will give insight into what an ideal gut composition may look like to prevent inhibitor occurrence. Results generated here may also provide rationale for clinical translation, whereby bacteria in the gut of people with HA is screened prior to their first FVIII injection. Ultimately, knowledge contributed to the field by this study may benefit research in rheumatoid arthritis, whereby anti-drug antibodies can also develop, and other diseases characterized by autoimmunity to self-proteins.

column36: Improving epilepsy diagnosis through machine learning-based interpretation of routine electroencephalography recordings
column37: Epilepsy is a common and debilitating disease, characterized by recurrent seizures as the result of abnormal and excessive neuronal discharges. Its diagnosis frequently relies on the electroencephalogram (EEG). During an EEG, electrodes on the patient's scalp record the brain's electrical activity, typically for 30 minutes. Neurologists then visually examine these recordings looking for interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs), i.e. "spiky" discharges sometimes occurring between seizures in epileptic patients. Unfortunately, a routine EEG will manage to capture these spikes in less than half of epileptic patients. In absence of IEDs, neurologists have no other means to distinguish an EEG of an epileptic patients from that of a non-epileptic patient. Recently, researchers have turned towards computers to interpret EEGs more objectively, and possibly extract subtle patterns that may be missed by the human eye. Deep learning (DL), a type of artificial intelligence, is revolutionizing our modern society. Inspired by the organization of neurons in the brain, DL allow computers to capture hidden patterns in images and other signals. Applied to EEG, DL is capable of automatically identifying seizures. Could DL detect hidden, abnormal patterns in the brain signal of epileptic patients? The objectives of the project are: 1) To extract thousands of anonymized EEG recordings from the CHUM database and review the medical files to identify which EEG are from epileptic patients and which are not; and 2) To implement a DL algorithm and train it to recognize epilepsy in seemingly normal EEGs. The impact of this project is important. Identifying new patterns of epilepsy could increase the sensitivity of the EEG in epilepsy, potentially automate its interpretation, and improve its availability to a larger percentage of the population.

column36: The therapeutic potential of miR-486-5p in ischemic acute kidney injury
column37: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a condition where patients experience a rapid decline in kidney function. AKI is a common complication of hospitalization with a high prevalence in intensive care units and has a high mortality rate. Recovery from AKI has long-term consequences including an increased risk of death and new or progressive chronic kidney disease (CKD). In Canada, the annual cost attributed to AKI is estimated at approximately $200 million; more severe episodes of AKI are associated with incremental increases in hospital length of stay and cost (Collister D, et al. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2017). Despite these health and economic consequences, no effective intervention for AKI exists. One common cause of AKI is ischemia reperfusion injury, where the kidneys experience a period of reduced blood flow and lack of oxygen, followed by the return of blood supply. Damage to kidney endothelial cells further compromises blood supply throughout the kidneys, which can impair recovery and lead to chronic kidney disease (CKD). MicroRNAs (miRs) are small molecules that regulate the expression of proteins. The administration of microRNAs has been shown to protect against AKI in mice. Our lab has shown that the administration of miR-486-5p reduces ischemic AKI in mice. We will further characterize the mechanisms by which miR-486-5p protects against AKI, with a focus on endothelial function. column36: Developing a clinically accessible decision rule for return to activity following a paediatric anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction
column37: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is the most frequently damaged knee ligament, with rates continuing to rise among active paediatric athletes. Moreover, the risk of ACL re-injury after surgical reconstruction (ACLR) is significantly higher than the initial injury. Despite the high risk for re-injury, and the lifelong associated health implications, there is minimal evidence available to guide return-to-activity (RTA) timing following a paediatric ACLR. One of the barriers restricting the development of RTA criteria are limitations on what can be collected in a clinical setting, as many factors associated with ACL re-injury risk require access to specialized laboratories. To address this issue, my thesis will achieve the following objectives: i) validate a novel suite of mobile technologies, ii) use the technology and a multidisciplinary approach to develop a decision rule for RTA timing, and iii) implement the decision rule into clinical practice. Through an established collaboration with orthopaedic surgeons at the Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario (CHEO), we will recruit paediatric patients who have undergone an ACLR. Data will be collected following the patient's ACLR during a series of dynamic tasks (ex. side-cuts) using clinically accessible mobile technologies. We will use this data to identify variables that predict positive clinical outcomes (ex. re-injury). Based on these measurements, cut-off thresholds can be identified to determine whether a paediatric patient is ready to RTA. The final phase of the project will focus on implementing the decision rule into clinical practice at CHEO. This project will create the first clinically accessible paediatric-specific RTA decision rule, reducing the risk for premature RTA and subsequent ACL re-injury. Furthermore, by ensuring our suite of technologies is transferable to other institutions, this project has the potential to improve the quality of care for all young Canadians recovering from an ACLR.

column36: Verbal memory impairments in schizophrenia and major depressive disorder: A transdiagnostic investigation of neural correlates and the effects of cognitive remediation therapy
column37: Schizophrenia (SZ) and depression (also called major depressive disorder [MDD]) are mental health conditions that involve problems memorizing information. Research has shown that individuals with SZ and MDD have abnormal activity in specific brain regions responsible for memory, but it remains unknown whether these abnormalities are the same in SZ and MDD. Researchers have begun looking at the effects of cognitive remediation therapy (CRT) on improving these memory problems. CRT is a type of treatment that involves computer-based training to improve certain types of cognition, like memory. It is unclear, however, if the effects of CRT are the same in individuals with SZ and MDD, or if CRT can improve the abnormal brain activity in SZ and MDD. The goals of the current research are to determine: (1) the specific brain abnormalities linked to memory problems in SZ and MDD; and (2) if CRT can improve the memory problems in SZ and MDD. Using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), we will measure brain activity in individuals with SZ, MDD, and healthy volunteers during a memory test. We will also measure memory using questionnaires. Next, we will give the individuals with SZ and MDD either 6 weeks of CRT or 6 weeks of unrelated control tasks. Then, we will remeasure their memory using the questionnaires and MRI tests to see if CRT improved their memory compared to the unrelated control tasks. The outcomes of this research will show if the abnormalities in brain activity in SZ and MDD are the same or different, and if CRT can help improve these abnormalities. This will help individuals with SZ and MDD because it may offer an additional treatment option that will help improve their memory and quality of life. Therefore, this research has the potential to help improve the lives of many Canadians. This research will also move the field forward by revealing brain abnormalities specific to SZ and MDD, and will inspire new treatment approaches using CRT.

column36: Effect of a professional development intervention on psychotherapists' skill in increasing reflective functioning in patients during psychotherapy sessions: A randomized controlled trial
column37: Psychotherapy is one of the most effective treatments for mental illnesses, but not all patients improve. Researchers are now becoming interested in the mechanisms by which psychotherapy works in order to improve patients' mental health, and reflective functioning may be one of those mechanisms. My research will be a new study within a project that is currently underway. Half of the psychotherapists will receive evidence-based training on how to increase reflective functioning in patients. The other half of the psychotherapists will not receive training. All psychotherapists will then video-record six psychotherapy sessions with their patient participants. Using those videos, I will count the number of times that psychotherapists encourage reflective functioning in their patients during each session, and assess whether patients demonstrate increased reflective functioning as a result. I will also evaluate the patients' level of distress at the end of each session. This will allow me to compare trained versus non-trained therapists on their abilities to encourage patient reflective functioning during sessions, and whether these therapist interventions have an impact on patient distress. column36: Control of circulating levels of dietary fat by glucagon-like peptide-1
column37: Over time, inflamed, cholesterol-rich plaques build up in the arteries of the heart. As these plaques continue to grow, they can cause a blockage in blood flow, leading to a heart attack or a stroke. Drugs that lower blood cholesterol levels decrease the occurrence of these devastating events; however, they do not completely stop plaques from growing particularly in patients with diabetes, suggesting that other fundamental drivers must exist. Studies in humans have shown that high levels of fat in the bloodstream contribute to plaque growth. In patients with diabetes, this contribution is increased as they have higher amounts of fat in their blood even after the same meal as a healthy person. We do not understand why this happens. In response to a meal, our bodies release a molecule called glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) into the bloodstream. Drugs modelled after GLP-1 are currently used in the clinic to control blood sugar levels in patients with diabetes. Importantly, these drugs also decrease blood fats and death from heart disease but how this happens is unclear. We hypothesize that GLP-1 instructs the intestine to burn fat from the diet so that it does not enter the bloodstream and arteries. Using a mouse model that cannot perform this fat-burning process specifically in the intestine, we are going to test if GLP-1 can still work to lower blood fat levels. We will use high-resolution microscopes to see what cell type burns it. Overall, this project aims to understand how a drug for diabetes uses the intestine to lower death by heart disease.

column36: Co-design and evaluation of a peer-led social media-based food literacy program for adolescents from low-socioeconomic status communities
column37: Healthy eating and cooking skills are important for preventing chronic illnesses like diabetes and heart disease. However, healthy eating is a challenge in low-income communities. Teens may eat fewer family meals and more processed and less healthy foods. Food literacy is the ability to choose, plan and prepare foods, and improving food literacy helps teens to choose more healthy foods, and eat more home-cooked meals throughout adulthood. Teens are especially receptive to education programs led by their peers, and they use social media regularly. To improve food literacy among teens (ages 12 to 17 years old) from low income communities, we will create a food literacy program led by their peers (18 to 25 years old) and delivered over social media. To help design and test the program, we created a youth advisory committee made up of teens from the communities who give feedback and help with designing the program. To create this program, we reviewed research on similar programs to understand what works and what does not work. Next, we will ask teens about their preferences for the program, such as nutrition information they want to learn about and their likes and dislikes in terms of social media. Then, we will create a program based on what we have learned from the teens. Finally, we will test the program with teens with a group of 60 teens. First, we will ask all teens to answer questions about their food literacy. Next, we will randomly put teens into 1 of 2 different groups: one group will participate in a peer-led food literacy program on social media and the second group will receive the program after 3 months. After 3 months, we will ask adolescents the same questions testing their food literacy and analyze the data to understand how the program may have improved their food literacy. We will also talk to teens who participated in the program to understand what they liked, disliked, and would change about the program.

column36: Investigation of chromosome 1q gain in pediatric posterior fossa ependymoma
column37: Brain cancer is the most prevalent cause of cancer associated deaths in children and adolescents. Ependymoma is the third most common pediatric brain tumour. The most aggressive and frequent subgroup of ependymoma is known as group A (PFA) arising in the cerebellum of infants with a median age of 3 years old. The current standard of care for children with these tumours includes surgery and radiation, which often results in long-term disabilities. Further, chemotherapy has been shown to be ineffective emphasizing the urgent need to find new therapeutics. A recent discovery from our lab has demonstrated the unique conditions required to grow patient derived ependymoma cancer cell lines, positioning us as the first research group in the world to routinely grow these tumours for experimentation. Approximately 25% of PFA tumours have been shown to exhibit an extra copy of a segment of DNA known as 1q. The presence of this additional copy is associated with a very poor prognosis despite aggressive treatment. Using a diverse set of emerging molecular technologies and our unique cell lines, this study aims to identify the key molecular pathways that are altered in tumours harboring this copy gain. Our discovery-based approach will help find genetic weaknesses that can be leveraged to inform drug screening using our cancer cell lines, to be further validated in mouse models of ependymoma for pre-clinical testing. Findings from this project have the potential to immediately improve the standard of care for this vulnerable patient population.

column37: The heart is an electrical organ. Once electrical signal is generated by the heart's pacemaker cells, it travels through the specialized electrical wiring network of the heart to stimulate muscle cells to beat synchronously. Therefore, maldevelopment or dysfunction of these biological wires can result in abnormal beating of the heart, and even lethal arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. The anatomical structure of this wiring network was originally discovered in the 19th century by Drs. His and Purkinje; however, it is still not fully understood what they are made up of and how they are developed even until today. For example, are all these conduction cells in this network identical or unique depending on location within the heart? (e.g. top or bottom) In my study, I will address this question by utilizing the state-of-the-art techniques which enable the examination of the cellular and genetic identities of each single cell, and therefore generate a genetic blueprint of this conduction system. Furthermore, I will explore how the identities of these individual cells transform as the conduction system develops and matures to ultimately understand how it adapts to the meet the needs of a growing heart. My study will be the first to clearly track the genetic profiles of every cell in a maturing conduction system and identify key molecules regulating this process. This discovery will not only be foundational to scientists studying the electrical function of the heart, but also be valuable to discover treatments for patients with abnormal heart rhythms.

column36: Development and Interrogation of a Therapeutic Modality for STAT1 Gain-of-Function using CRISPR/Cas9 Base-Editing
column37: STAT1 Gain-of-Function (GOF) is a disease caused by mutations (genetic "spelling mistakes") in the STAT1 gene, which is important in regulating the immune system. Patients usually start becoming sick as infants with repeated infections, and can later develop auto-immunity, blood vessel disease, and cancer. Most people with STAT1 GOF depend on life-long medications (like antibiotics and immune-suppressive drugs), and many die young. The only cure available for STAT1 GOF patients is a stem cell transplant, where cells from a healthy donor are used to replace the diseased bone marrow cells of the patient. This treatment is used in other diseases with great success. Unfortunately, in patients with STAT1 GOF the survival and cure rates are much lower, and their bodies frequently reject the donated stem cells. A recent study showed that of all STAT1 GOF patients who received a transplant, more than half died. Because rejection of donor cells is a big barrier to treatment success in STAT1 GOF patients, we want to develop a system that directly treats patient bone marrow cells, a process which we call autologous (self) transplant. Our team wants to develop and test such a strategy in cells and mice that have STAT1 GOF, with a tool called 'base-editor' (genetic "spell-editor"). Using a guide molecule, we can direct the base-editor to the "spelling mistake" in the gene, where it swaps-out the mis-spelled "letter" ('base') with the correct one. We will test whether we are able to use this system correct a "spelling mistake" causing STAT1 GOF in cells. We will then test if giving corrected bone marrow cells back to mice can cure them of the disease. If we are successful, we will have a treatment for STAT1 GOF that can improve survival and cure-rates of patients, giving hope to both children and families affected by this devastating disease. We may also be able to use this method to treat people with other diseases which are caused by similar kinds of "spelling mistakes".

column37: Chronic pain is a debilitating condition that affects around 20% of Canadians yet effective treatments are lacking. To develop treatments, we must understand the mechanisms underlying chronic pain at the initial pain processing site of the central nervous system - the spinal cord. I have also discovered that autophagy affects pain behaviour in males but not females. Lastly, I will address how autophagy affects the firing of spinal cord neurons, leading to increased sensitivity to pain. Altogether, my research will provide a greater understanding of the mechanisms by which autophagy regulates pain and how this differs between sexes. The results of these experiments may identify specific molecular targets for treating chronic pain. Since autophagy-modulating drugs are already used clinically to treat a variety of conditions, my findings could lead to the reassessment of such drugs as potential treatment for chronic pain.

column37: More than 1.9 billion people worldwide suffer from obesity, which is associated with accumulation of fat in the liver known as steatosis. Netrin-1 (NTN1) is a protein that induces macrophage retention and allows for their survival in tissues, although its role in the liver is unclear. Preliminary studies from our laboratory suggest that loss of NTN1 in macrophages protects mice fed a high-fat diet from developing NASH, despite the development of obesity. To do this, we have developed various strategies to modulate NTN1 expression in macrophages in mice fed a diet specifically designed to induce NASH. These studies will be the first to determine if NTN1 is a valid drug target to halt or possibly even induce regression of NASH.

column36: Characterizing the role of the endothelial transcription factor ERG in the development of abdominal aortic aneurysms: Towards novel therapeutic targets
column37: The aorta is the largest blood vessel in the human body and is responsible for carrying high pressure blood away from the heart and towards the abdomen. In approximately 1 in 100 older adults, the wall of the aorta weakens and expands over time, producing a blood vessel enlargement or aneurysm. Continual expansion of the aorta can lead to rupture, with an 80% total rate of death and a 50% rate of death for those that make it to hospital. Surgical repair before rupture has major risks (e.g., heart attack and stroke), with the highest risk occurring in older patients. Furthermore, there is currently no medical treatment available to slow the growth of aneurysms before surgical repair is required. Our research seeks to discover how the cells of the aorta interact during aneurysm formation. We are particularly interested in the protein ERG, which has been identified as a master regulator of healthy function in the cells that line the aorta (i.e., endothelial cells), but has not been studied in aneurysms. ERG will be investigated in cells isolated from the aorta, as well as in mice and humans who have developed aneurysms. We expect that the amount of ERG will be reduced during aneurysm development, which will then cause these cells to weaken the blood vessel wall and contribute to aortic expansion. We aim to identify molecules secreted by these cells that can be used as novel targets for creating new medical therapies. For example, molecules that promote aneurysm formation can be reduced by these therapies, while those that prevent aneurysm formation can be increased. In summary, our research will determine how ERG regulates cells of the aorta to contribute to aneurysms and identify new targets for the medical treatment of this disease. column36: Developing porphysome nanomedicines for applications in colorectal cancer
column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is common and deadly, with approximately 1 million new cases in 2018 and accounting for nearly 6% of all cancer deaths. There are several key problems that currently exist in the management of CRC that offer opportunities for improvement through emerging nanomedicine technology. The current mainstay of treatment consists of surgical removal of the tumour and the lymph nodes downstream from the tumour (which may harbour tumour cells); however, not all lymph nodes that are potentially affected may be removed. Up to 22% of patients may have malignant lymph nodes left behind. Another problem arises from the fact that in up to 39% of patients with rectal cancer, removal of the anus is required, which means that patients must live with a permanent colostomy (when the bowel are reconstructed such that feces drains through a hole in the abdomen). This can be avoided if the tumour is shrunk before surgery. Porphysome nanomedicines offer a solution to these problems: these are spheres composed of the porphyrin dye that fluoresce and can be used to kill tumours through a process called photodynamic therapy (PDT). Additionally, porphysomes naturally accumulate in tumours, which makes them particularly effective for targeting tumour and minimizing side effects. These porphysomes have shown promise in guiding surgery through fluorescence in other cancers and in destroying tumours; however, their effectiveness in CRC has not been established. My project will examine the effectiveness of porphysomes for fluorescence-guided surgery and photodynamic therapy to improve the management of CRC. I will also test an emerging relative of the porphysome, called the EDTA-porphysome, which appears to hold promise for more effective fluorescence-guided surgery and PDT. My project will develop these porphysome nanomedicines with the goal of using this emerging technology in patient care to improve the length and quality of life for people with colorectal cancer.

column36: Efficacy, mechanisms, and safety of SGLT2 inhibitors in kidney transplant recipients
column37: Kidney transplantation improves survival and quality of life. Diabetes in kidney transplant recipients (KTR) increases the risk of losing their transplant, developing cardiac disease, and/or dying. However, there are no diabetes treatments in KTR with proven cardiac and kidney benefits. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) are a new class of drugs for diabetes. In a first among diabetes therapies, this class of drugs was demonstrated to have major cardiac and kidney protective effects in patients with diabetes. What differentiates SGLT2i from other diabetes therapies is that they act directly on the kidneys independent of improvements in blood sugar levels. This may occur in several ways, including salt removal via the kidney leading to lower blood pressure (BP). Considerations when using SGLT2i in KTR include the risk of infections as SGLT2i may increase the risk of certain genital infections and drug interactions with anti-rejection medications. We believe that the kidney protective effects of SGLT2i including BP lowering and salt removal are preserved in KTR with diabetes. We propose a study where 52 adult KTR with diabetes will be randomly assigned to a SGLT2i called dapagliflozin or placebo for 12 weeks. The primary objective is to determine whether dapagliflozin lowers BP in KTR. Secondary objectives include identifying potential mechanisms for BP lowering and kidney protection, as well as the safety of dapagliflozin and its ability to lower blood sugar in KTR. To accomplish this, we will simultaneously measure several variables in our kidney physiology laboratory including kidney function and blood flow, urine sodium and protein, blood vessel stiffness, blood sugar control, and safety measures including infection or transplant rejection. Results from this study could help confirm protective mechanisms of SGLT2i in KTR, potentially leading to larger studies in a patient population in need of new cardiac and kidney protective therapies.

column36: Investigating the role of ATF3 in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma pathology
column37: Pancreatic cancer is a devastating cancer with only 8% of those diagnosed surviving past 5 years. Two major contributors to this low survival rate are lack of early detection and resistance to treatment. To address these factors, we need to understand (1) initiating events in pancreatic cancer and (2) mechanisms that underlie chemotherapy resistance. The purpose of my project is to understand how the unfolded protein response (UPR), a cellular stress response, contributes to initiation and maintenance pancreatic cancer. Research from our lab has shown that one molecule within the UPR pathway, Activating Transcription Factor 3 (ATF3), plays an important role in pancreatic cancer formation. Additionally, our evidence suggests ATF3 functions in more than the tumor cell type of pancreatic cancer, implicating immune cells and fibroblasts. We have shown that deleting Atf3 in the whole body reduced cancer progression in mice as well as decreased immune infiltration. The goal of my project is to determine if the role of Atf3 in cancer initiation is acinar cell specifc. To do this I will delete Atf3 only in pancreatic acinar cells of mice and compare to mice with a global deletion. In addition, this project will determine how ATF3 and the UPR stress response contributes to chemotherapy resistance of pancreatic cancer. I predict tumor cells with a greater stress response will have greater chemotherapy resistance. To address this, I will treat pancreatic cancer patient-derived tumor cell lines with a combination of UPR inhibitors and chemotherapy and compare their surival to cells treated with chemotherapy alone. This study will identify pathways in initiation of pancreatic cancer and mechanistic understanding gained through this study will offer potential therapeutic targets for preventing pancreatic cancer development and chemotherapy resistance.

column36: A novel inhibitor of remyelination in multiple sclerosis: fibulin-2
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a disease in which the immune system destroys protective fatty protein (myelin) covering nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord, leading to physical disability. A process by which myelin is reformed following injury called remyelination can restore physical function. Remyelination becomes increasingly incomplete and inefficient in most patients with age and longevity of dieases. This failure could be due to the presence of inhibitors in the lesion. We aim to explore these inhibitors to provide better treatments for MS patients. Although there are drugs available for the early stages of MS through modulation of immune system, there are no treatments that promote myelin formation and tissue repair. Therefore, identifying the inhibitors is important to develop a strategy to overcome their impact on myelin repair. Fibulin-2 is an extracellular matrix (ECM) protein that is accumulated in MS lesions. Our preliminary data show its toxic effect on oligodendrocyte precursor cells which are responsible for remyelination. In this proposal, I will assess the exact role of fibulin-2 in myelin repair and discover new therapeutic approaches to overcome the inhibitory effect of fibulin-2.

column36: Impact d'une intervention familiale en prevention de l'obesite chez des enfants d'age prescolaire sur les pratiques alimentaires parentales et les comportements alimentaires des enfants.
column37: L'obesite touche de nombreuses personnes au Canada. Puisque l'obesite et les comportements instaures tot dans la vie tendent a persister a long terme, des interventions en prevention de l'obesite realisees des le jeune age sont necessaires. Il existe actuellement peu de modeles efficaces d'intervention durant la petite enfance, ce qui est principalement explique par un faible engagement parental. En ce qui a trait a l'alimentation, l'influence parentale s'exerce, entre autres, par l'usage de pratiques parentales favorisant des comportements alimentaires sains chez les enfants. Ainsi, les interventions qui facilitent l'engagement parental en etant realisees au domicile familial sont prometteuses. Toutefois, tres peu d'etudes, et aucune au Canada, n'ont ete realisees dans ce contexte aupres de ce groupe d'age. De plus, l'impact de telles interventions sur les pratiques alimentaires parentales et les comportements alimentaires des enfants, qui sont d'importants determinants de l'obesite, demeure meconnu. L'objectif de ce projet est de verifier l'impact d'une intervention familiale a domicile en prevention de l'obesite sur les pratiques alimentaires parentales et les comportements alimentaires des enfants et de verifier si ces elements constituent des mecanismes qui sous-tendent les effets de l'intervention sur le poids des enfants. Ce projet sera realise au sein de la Guelph Family Health Study, une etude d'intervention de 6 mois ciblant les repas en famille, le temps d'ecran, le sommeil et l'activite physique, avec des mesures de suivi a 6 et 18 mois, aupres de 306 familles d'enfants ages de 18 mois a 5 ans. Ce projet permettra de mieux comprendre l'impact de l'intervention sur les pratiques alimentaires parentales et les comportements alimentaires des enfants, ainsi que l'implication de ces elements dans le gain de poids des enfants, ce qui favorisera ultimement l'accessibilite a des interventions efficaces et novatrices en prevention de l'obesite.

column36: Testicular organoids derived from induced pluripotent stem cells as a bioassay for modelling human testicular development and function
column37: Organoids are miniaturized versions of an organ in a dish that mimic and replicate the complexity of their organs of origin. Reproductive and developmental research can benefit significantly from this new technology, because it could replace the use of immature human gonads, which are difficult to obtain and carry bioethical limitations. As an alternative, testicular organoids can be applied for studying the mechanisms involved in testis development, organization, and function, as well as in research to establish methods for culturing and propagating germ cells. These germ cells will turn into the male gamete (sperm) later in life and, therefore, developing better strategies to work with these cells in a laboratory setting has the potential to help develop treatments for male infertility and methods to preserve or restore fertility in cancer patients. Our group has recently generated testicular organoids using cells obtained from a testis biopsy, and now, in this proposal, we aim to generate the same testicular organoids using induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). iPSCs are artificially created pluripotent stem cells that are derived from skin or blood cells and can differentiate to any cell type of the human body in vitro, being a valuable resource to replace the use of immature tissue for research. We will then evaluate the structure, cellular composition and functional status of the testicular organoids generated from iPSC-derived testicular cells and analyze if this model is able to produce hormones and sustain germ cell differentiation into sperm similarly to the testis. The ability to obtain functional testicular organoids from human iPSCs will improve reproductive research, contribute to model diseases that impact fertility and allow exploration of pathogen infection and gonadal toxicology. Our results can also help clarify the specific regulation of germ cells to improve human germ cell culture and its translation into clinical applications.

column36: Developing new tools and computational indexes to characterize sleep macro- and micro- architecture in older adults: special focus on sex and gender and inter-individual differences.
column37: Our society is increasingly sleep deprived, accumulating less than 5 hours of sleep per night. This can result in considerable negative outcomes with severe effects on mental performance, particularly in the domains of memory and in the ability to plan, multi-task and problem solve. A great amount of evidence is mounting about the associations between poor quality of sleep and both diseases of the heart and the brain. This reality highlights the importance of considering sleep as a determinant of health and well-being, and the need to further our knowledge of the underlying mechanisms. In recent years, wearable devices to record all sorts of physiological parameters including sleep, have become increasingly popular. These devices are relatively inexpensive and accessible to the general population. However, data collected from these devices do not correlate with the gold standard methodology to study sleep which is a technique called polysomnography (PSG). This technique allows for the collection of a variety of information including brain signals and respiratory parameters through the night. This technique is, however, expensive and requires expert technicians to implement a fairly complicated set up. This project aims to assess a new PSG self-instrumented tool to measure sleep against the traditional PSG equipment. Participants will be able to self-instrument by watching an instructional video. Moreover, this project will develop new indexes of sleep through the application of advanced computational methods to the analysis of brain signals collected with the novel PSG device. Compared to the existing indexes, these new indexes will help to better characterize sex and gender and inter-individual differences in sleep quality. Many of the existing indexes have indeed been shown to not be sensitive to detect sex differences for example. This targeted approach will contribute to the development of personalized medicine and treatments that are closer to patients' needs.

column36: Investigating functional Optical Coherence Tomography and hypercapnia to diagnose and treat neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
column37: The Autonomic (or "automatic") Nervous System (ANS) regulates internal processes, including control of heart rate and blood pressure (BP). When someone stands, and gravity tries to pull blood away from the brain, the ANS works to maintain BP and brain blood flow. Neurogenic Orthostatic Hypotension (NOH) occurs when our "fight-or-flight" part ("sympathetic") of the ANS fails. BP can drop a lot when upright, reducing blood flow and oxygen delivery to the brain, and this can cause symptoms of lightheadedness, nausea, and fainting. During my PhD studies, I examined brain activity in patients with NOH during BP drops, and found reduced brain activity in important brain regions. As brain blood flow and oxygen are necessary for brain function, failure to adequately control these variables may negatively impact brain health. One solution to help counter the effects of NOH may be to increase sympathetic activity by breathing higher levels of carbon dioxide. In healthy volunteers, small increases in the amount of inhaled carbon dioxide has been shown to increase BP in the upright position, and this improves symptoms! We recently discovered a new way to measure sympathetic activity in vessels close to the brain using optical coherence tomography (OCT). OCT is widely used in eye clinics to look at the internal structure of the eye. However, our new methods will allow us to monitor blood vessels and blood flow that respond to sympathetic activity and local brain changes. The objectives of the current study are to apply carbon dioxide during OCT monitoring in patients with NOH and healthy controls to: (a) evaluate the effects of breathing carbon dioxide on BP and brain blood flow, (b) evaluate OCT as a tool to measure sympathetic control of brain blood flow, and (c) determine if a device that increases carbon dioxide while standing will work as a new therapy.

column37: Chronic pain is one of the most underestimated health care problems in the world today, causing a major burden to the patient and society. In Canada, one in five adults experience chronic pain, with associated costs estimated at $40 billion a year and rising. On top of this, Canada is currently facing an opioid crisis, affecting many chronic pain patients who use opioid medications to manage their pain. Despite overwhelming evidence of the prevalence and impact of chronic pain on our society, research for pain is greatly underfunded. This results in a lack of understanding and treatment of the disease, with only a small percentage of patients achieving full recovery. Migraine headache can be especially debilitating and is a significant cause of suffering and disability worldwide. Therefore, technologies and therapeutic strategies that can help better understand migraine and improve the care of patients living with this disorder is necessary. Towards this goal, mind-body therapies are increasingly being used for chronic pain management and neuroimaging has the capacity to evaluate the brain circuitry underlying pain and its relief. My research combines novel mind-body therapies of mindfulness meditation and neuromodulation and applies neuroimaging to investigate mind-body mechanisms and outcomes for migraine. The project may shed important insight into the brain mechanisms associated with migraine and successful mind-body treatment outcome, as well as offer a novel integrated therapeutic strategy for a disorder that is difficult to treat and mange.

column36: Examining the etiology of serious mental illness among youth: When and for whom does peer victimization matter?
column37: Compared to other wealthy nations, Canada ranks near the bottom when it comes to youth mental health. There has been a 66% increase in pediatric emergency department visits for mental health concerns, with 77% of these youth reporting that they have been bullied by their peers. While the risks associated with being bullied are well established, little research has examined if bullying contributes to the development of serious mental health concerns over and above other risk factors, like child maltreatment. Moreover, the impacts of being bullied are not equal. It is necessary to consider when and for whom the experience of being bullied matters for long term mental health. The proposed research will examine the relative risk of bullying in the development of serious mental health symptoms, while also considering the individual and contextual factors that may alter this pathway. I will conduct three projects to address this aim and work with community partners to improve programming and inform policy. Using longitudinal data that has followed youth from childhood through to early adulthood, I will examine the relative contribution of being bullied in the development of subsequent mental health symptoms, while accounting for other risk factors. Next, I will examine whether the link between being bullied and mental health is stronger for gender and sexual minority students, and whether is it stronger if the bullying occurs during school transitions (e.g., elementary school to middle school, middle school to high school). Finally, I will work with community partners to develop resources to better support vulnerable youth during vulnerable periods of development. Overall, results from this research will be used to inform youth mental health supports and policy. By better understanding when and for whom bullying predicts serious mental health concerns, we can develop more targeted intervention efforts to protect our most vulnerable youth.

column36: Improving cognitive and mental health using an online multi-domain working memory training intervention for children and adolescents with ADHD
column37: The number of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) diagnoses continues to increase, affecting 10% of youth across North America. Youth with ADHD have difficulties with attention and this interferes with their daily productivity, behaviour, and mood. As a result of this interference, the individual can express low self-perception and competency, which can lead to stress, depression, and deviant behaviour. Medicinal treatment is an accepted solution to reduce ADHD symptoms; however, the effects of medication are not always effective and tolerance to the drug can develop quickly. Fortunately, non-pharmaceutical solutions, such as "brain training games" are a promising new alternative solution to treat attention difficulties. In fact, previous research has suggested that these brain training games form a habit from repeated practice, teaching the user how to pay attention. However, most training programs lack engagement, which has resulted in issues with treatment compliance, and in turn, these programs ultimately fail. The current research program is a clinical trial testing 'how' and 'for whom' online brain training with video-game-like characteristics can improve attention for children and adolescents with ADHD. It is expected that an engaging task will motivate the user to adhere to the training regimen and therefore reap the full benefits of the brain training program. The benefits received from online brain training can translate to improvements in self-perception and competency; thus, transferring to multiple domains. Also, the current study will uncover key traits that explain who benefits the most from brain training to further tailor this intervention to the individual's needs. Overall, this research program is designed to help children and adolescents with ADHD; yet, the knowledge gained from this timely and novel research has the potential to improve the quality of life for individuals with other challenges like depression and anxiety.

column36: Overcoming the lesion core: the Mexican cavefish as a new model for spinal cord injury and regeneration
column37: The loss of spinal cord function due to injury or disease in humans results in lifelong disability for individuals and associated annual health care costs in the billions of dollars. Regenerative medicine is a promising therapeutic avenue for treating spinal cord injury, however, progress on this front has been slowed by our relatively poor understanding of regeneration biology. In order to develop safe and effective treatments, we must first understand the steps required for successful spinal cord regeneration. Although the translational potential of mammalian research is relatively high, most mammals are unable to recover from SCI. Zebrafish, on the other hand, are emerging as a popular model for complete spinal cord regeneration; however, their ability to regenerate is in part due to a drastically more favourable injury environment compared to mammals. Whereas mammals are faced with chronic inflammation and permanent scarring, zebrafish do not encounter these challenges following SCI. Thus, there are limits to using zebrafish as a model for mammalian SCI. In preliminary work, I have observed that the Mexican cavefish, Astyanax mexicanus, can successfully recover from SCI despite the formation of scar tissue. This provides an exciting opportunity to study the mechanisms that allow an organism to overcome the classic SCI challenges encountered by mammals. By focusing on the role of the immune response on scar formation and spinal cord regeneration in the Mexican cavefish, my work will uncover the mechanisms by which this remarkable species rebuilds its severed spine and restores function in spite of substantial scar tissue at the injury site. This work will provide the foundation for establishing the Mexican cavefish as a new model for spinal cord regeneration in a clinically relevant context.

column36: Causal test of top-down and bottom-up cortical circuits in autism sensory overload
column37: Sensory overload (oversensitivity to lights, sounds, touch, etc.) is common in autism. Normally, the brain prevents this by suppressing activity to predicted sensory inputs. This allows only unexpected inputs (which are more informative) to be sent forward for full processing. We will test a theory that predictions are carried by alpha/beta (~10-30 Hz) rhythms in the deep (feedback) layers of cortex. They suppress the gamma (>30 Hz) rhythms in upper cortical layers that feedforward sensory inputs. Both increased gamma and reduced alpha/beta have been seen in autism. Our model posits that the reduction of alpha/beta "releases" gamma, causing overly heightened excitation to sensory inputs and thus sensory overload. Evidence for this theory is thus far based on observed correlations. There have been no causal manipulations of brain circuitry that can directly test it. Our aim is to provide direct tests. We have new technology to record neural activity across all cortical layers while we selectively deactivate upper vs deep cortical layers. We will also suppress gamma vs alpha/beta rhythms in different layers by manipulation of different classes of neurotransmitter receptors (NMDA vs AMPA). This will directly test a hypothesis of how the cortex regulates sensory processing and a mechanism of sensory overload. This can lead to a new understanding of the fundamental mechanisms of cortical processing and lead research towards improved symptom management and therapies for ASD.

column36: Genomic characterization of multiple system atrophy and dementia with Lewy bodies
column37: The synucleinopathies are a group of neurodegenerative diseases that arise from the abnormal accumulation of the alpha-synuclein protein in the brain and include Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy and dementia with Lewy bodies. Multiple system atrophy presents with autonomic failure and variable degree of parkinsonism, cerebellar ataxia and pyramidal dysfunction, while dementia with Lewy bodies is characterized by early dementia, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism. The underlying factors driving the development of these disorders remain largely unknown and, as such, there exists no disease-modifying treatment available to halt disease progression. Although these diseases were once thought of as being non-heritable, recent studies have suggested that genetic factors play a definite role in their development. Nonetheless, little is still known about the genetic determinants of these two disorders. Recent advances in genetic technologies offer an unprecedented opportunity to bridge this gap. The main objective of this research project is to gain further understanding of the genetic underpinnings of these diseases by leveraging new genetic techniques. This will be accomplished through a three-step approach. Firstly, cases of multiple system atrophy and dementia with Lewy bodies will be studied using cutting-edge genome sequencing technologies and bioinformatic tools to identify disease-causing mutations. Secondly, similar techniques will be used to study specific cell populations in the brain of deceased multiple system atrophy and dementia with Lewy bodies cases. column36: Adverse Childhood Experience and Multisystem Cumulative Biological Risk in Middle and Late Life in Canada: The Protective Role of Psychosocial Resources
column37: Childhood toxic stress increases the risk of morbidity and mortality decades later. Childhood toxic stressors have been linked to increased inflammatory biomarkers, adverse cardiometabolic profile, greater sympathetic nervous system activity, and accelerated cellular aging. Despite evidence that childhood stress is associated with increased dysregulations across multiple physiological systems, few studies have examined the cumulative physiological toll of childhood stress on health in later life through a multisystem perspective. Further, research shows that individual and neighborhood level protective resources can guard against stress in impacting health. However, no Canadian studies have explicitly examined whether psychosocial factors and neighborhood amenities buffer/guard against childhood stressors in impacting chronic biological risk for diseases in mid-to-late life. This study will address these gaps by studying the long-term effects of childhood adversities on chronic health conditions. Further, we will examine whether adult social support, psychological well-being, education, and neighborhood green space buffer against childhood stressors in impacting chronic health conditions. We will use a database from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging. This research will provide critical information that will inform social interventions and public health programs aiming to prevent chronic diseases. Specifically, study findings will inform efforts to improve the adverse childhood experience screenings in the clinical setting and accelerate healthy aging through promoting individual and neighborhood level resilience resources.

column36: An iKT, interpretivist, feminist, multi-method study examining the experience of, and models of treatment for, acute postpartum mental illness
column37: Postpartum depression is common, affecting about 10-15% of Canadian women, and is associated with increased risk for suicide, particularly in severe cases. Postpartum psychosis - whereby women disconnect from reality - is more rare, affecting ~1/1000 women, but represents a psychiatric emergency. For both women with postpartum psychosis and women with a severe case of postpartum depression, it's important that they have access to care in hospital to protect their health, and the health of their families. Currently in Canada, hospital stays in the postpartum require the separation of women from their babies, which has been shown to be traumatic for the mother and baby. In other countries, such as Australia, specialized hospital units called Mother-Baby Psychiatric Units (MBUs) admit both the mother and infant for care if mothers are experiencing postpartum psychosis or severe postpartum depression. This study will investigate whether the MBU is a suitable model of care for the Canadian context, or whether an alternative model of care would better promote the health of Canadian families. To do this, we will conduct three sub-studies. In sub-study 1, we will interview women who have experienced a stay in hospital for postpartum mental illness in Canada to gain insight into the current model of care. Sub-study 2 will complement sub-study 1 by characterizing, on a population level, frequency and predictors of hospitalization for postpartum mental illness. In sub-study 3, we will conduct a case study to learn more about the MBU model of care from five Australian MBUs. Ultimately, our research aims to promote the mental health of mothers and infants in Canada.

column36: Discovering the origins of trachea-esophageal birth defects
column37: Trachea-esophageal birth defects (TEDs) occur when the trachea and esophagus do not completely separate from a common gut tube during fetal development. Occurring in about one out of every 3,000 live births, these life-threatening birth defects prevent proper breathing or feeding in newborn infants. It is not yet well understood how these birth defects happen. There is compelling evidence of a genetic cause, but specific genetic mutations are only known in 15% of TED cases worldwide, moreover it is unclear how these mutations disrupt fetal development. The goal of my research project is to determine the genetic and cellular causes of TEDs using an innovative combination of animal models and bioengineered human esophageal tissue from patient stem cells. As part of CLEARconsortium.org, our human geneticist colleagues have found a number of genetic variations (mutations) from genome sequencing over 300 TED patients, but we do not know which mutations cause disease. My goal is to identity the causative mutations and investigate how they cause TEDs. By making similar mutations in frogs and mouse embryos I have screened over 20 variants and found several that cause defects similar to patients, and thus are likely to be causative, including the gene ITSN1. Excitingly this has revealed a novel cellular pathway known as endosome-mediated epithelial remodeling. I propose to 1) continue screening patient variants, 2) determine the molecular mechanism by which ITSN1 regulates trachea-esophageal development and 3) test the hypothesis that other genes in this pathway may be disrupted in patients. My proposed research will discover the origin of TEDs, which will provide new fundamental knowledge of the genetic and cellular networks regulating normal and disrupted trachea-esophageal development, ultimately improving the diagnosis and treatment of children born with these life-threatening conditions.

column36: Effect of 16-weeks guidelines based diet and exercise volume on beta cell function, hepatic and pancreatic fat, and insulin sensitivity in people with type 2 diabetes
column37: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) used to be considered a lifelong disease, but we now know that it can be reversed and put into remission. It has been demonstrated that in order for reversal of T2D to occur, pancreatic beta cell function and insulin sensitivity must improve. Reductions in pancreatic and liver fat through dietary strategies lead to improved beta cell function and liver insulin sensitivity, respectively. Furthermore, exercise is known to improve muscle insulin sensitivity. Taken together, a prescription of diet and exercise could lead to improvement in the underlying drivers of T2D and eventual reversal/remission of the disease. Although diet and exercise are currently recommended by Diabetes Canada, these recommendations are essentially the same as the recommendations for the general public and have never been assessed for their ability to impact the underlying drivers of T2D (i.e., pancreas and liver fat, insulin resistance). As the ideal goal for T2D treatment shifts from management to reversal, diet and exercise recommendations should reflect this shift. Because of underlying metabolic dysfunction in T2D, it is possible that current guidelines based on the general public may be insufficient to achieve meaningful improvements in the disease. This study will test the hypothesis that current diet recommendations, alone and in combination with current physical activity guidelines will improve metabolic health and disease status in people with T2D using a high-quality research design and state of the art measurement techniques. In addition, this study will investigate the effect of increasing the amount of exercise to determine if current exercise recommendations need to be increased. These results will directly inform the diet and exercise recommendations for people with T2D to ensure that current guidelines have a meaningful impact on T2D status.

column36: Evaluating the implementation and effectiveness of British Columbia's risk mitigation prescribing guidelines as a response to the dual overdose and COVID-19 public health emergencies
column37: Canada is experiencing two intersecting public health emergencies: an overdose crisis driven by illicitly manufactured fentanyl and fentanyl-adulterated drugs, and the COVID-19 pandemic. COVID-19 has compounded the overdose crisis, as overdose fatalities have increased since the pandemic began. Pandemic safety protocols (social distancing, self-isolation, quarantine) put people who use drugs at greater risk of overdose, withdrawal, and other harms related to the increasingly toxic drug supply. In response, British Columbia implemented risk mitigation prescribing guidelines, which allow physicians and nurse practitioners to prescribe pharmaceutical alternatives (e.g., hydromorphone, Dexadrine) to illicit or street-acquired opioids and stimulants. These guidelines are intended to support people who use drugs to socially-distance and self-isolate in order to prevent COVID-19 infection, transmission and community spread, while also reducing overdose, withdrawal, and other drug use-related risk. I will undertake a qualitative study to evaluate the implementation, uptake, and effectiveness of the guidelines targeting individuals at high fatal overdose and COVID-19 risk. The study will also examine prescriber perspectives on the program, and how these shape program implementation, access, and use. Additionally, I will explore socio-structural and geographic factors that shape people's access to and use of the intended pharmaceutical medications. Data collection will involve qualitative interviews with people who have obtained, or tried to obtain, a prescription for stimulants or opioids during the COVID-19 pandemic. There is an urgent need for national expansion of programs that reduce overdose and COVID risk, as jurisdictions across Canada grapple with these dual public health emergencies. Findings from the study will help inform public health approaches to addressing the unique needs of structurally vulnerable people who use drugs at high overdose risk.

column36: Dual inhibition of MDM2 and tyrosine kinase driver mutation: a novel approach in the treatment of lung cancer
column37: My research program at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center will be focused on understanding the molecular abnormalities in lung cancer cells in order to discover novel therapeutic avenues in patients with lung cancer. I will be supervised by Dr. Marc Ladanyi, who is a world expert in this field. Dr. Ladanyi developed a new clinical tool to diagnose mutations in lung cancer called MSK-IMPACT, which is now approved by the Federal Drug Association (FDA). This tool allows doctors to identify a "driver mutation" associated with a patient's cancer. This "driver mutation"-an abnormal modification in the cancer cells' DNA -is responsible for uncontrolled cancer growth for the patient's specific cancer. Personalized medicine has allowed for physicians and scientists to specifically target this driver mutation, thereby blocking cellular replication and the growth of cancer. Despite these significant advances, patients with advanced lung cancer are rarely cured, and drugs that target these driver mutations only work for a short period of time. Therefore, new strategies are needed in order to overcome drug resistance and provide long-lasting tumor control for a potential cure. My research program will be focused on targeting MDM2 in combination with other drug targets to better control lung cancer growth. As opposed to the current method of targeting a single mutation, my project aims to combine two targeted therapies, which opens a novel therapeutic avenue. I will use advanced techniques in genetic sequencing and gene-editing technologies in order to better understand how these specific pathways cause cancer growth. I will perform these experiments in patient-derived xenografts, which are mice that have been injected with a real patient's tumor. This allows scientists to replicate the way the tumor behaves in a human and to achieve more precise results with a direct impact on patients. My goal is to bring this technology back home as a cancer researcher in Montreal.

column36: Characterization of the CARD9-dependent response to fungal encephalitis through single-cell sequencing
column37: Patients with mutations in the caspase recruitment domain-containing protein 9 (CARD9) gene are prone to many types of invasive fungal infections, as the protein CARD9 is critically involved in the recognition of fungal pathogens. Strikingly, these patients frequently present with life-threatening fungal infections in the brain, which are difficult to treat due to a lack of therapeutic options. Fungal brain infections develop in CARD9 deficient patients due to an inability to recruit immune cells to the site of infection, largely due to a defect of the resident immune cells of the brain, the microglia. However, evidence suggests that the requirement of CARD9 is not restricted to microglia, and that other cell types of the brain play a key role in mounting an immune response. We will take an unbiased approach to investigate other potential Card9+ cell types by studying the response of normal and Card9-deficient mice to fungal brain infections using single-cell RNA and epigenetic sequencing. Through this approach we will determine what genes are expressed in response to infection by all immune and non-immune cells, and which genes are dependent on CARD9 signaling. We will then use this list of CARD9-dependent genes to do a more thorough study of the mechanism behind the immune response. We will determine which identified genes are necessary for an effective immune response through the use of genetic deletion mice and dissect the roles they play through immunophenotyping. Any clinically relevant findings we discover in mice will be confirmed using tissue samples obtained from our CARD9-deficient patients treated for fungal infections at our facility. Through this work we will expand our understanding of how the brain fights fungal infections, and to what extent it is orchestrated by CARD9 signaling. Additionally, this study will shed light on the brain's general antimicrobial response and has the potential to identify novel cell types participating in this response.

column36: Understanding the balance between stimulatory and suppressive functions of neutrophils during SARS-CoV-2 infection
column37: The new coronavirus that emerged in 2019, SARS-CoV-2, causes respiratory disease, termed COVID-19, leading to a global pandemic. With millions of people affected worldwide and thousands dead, the infection rates continue to rise everyday. Development of vaccines and/or therapeutic drugs is critical to contain and eventually stop this devastating pandemic. Therefore, better understanding of various aspects of the virus and the immune responses it elicits is crucial. Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells and are the first line of defence against infections. These cells have proven to be vital for fighting infections when stimulated to certain levels but when over-stimulated, they can also have harmful effects. Indeed, very high neutrophil levels have been recorded in COVID-19. Thus, it is important to understand the in-depth mechanisms controlling the different functions of neutrophils to achieve a delicate balance needed for effective protection. In this study, we aim to analyze the functional changes in neutrophils collected from healthy donors and donors experiencing mild or severe COVID-19. This will shed light on the roles of neutrophils during SARS-CoV-2 infection and help identify potential therapeutic targets. Gaining knowledge about every aspect of this new coronavirus disease is the most effective way to develop new strategies to combat it worldwide.

column36: Modulation of The Serotonin System as a Novel Therapeutic Strategy in of Autism Spectrum Disorder
column37: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is characterized by impairments in social behavior and emotional processing. To date, no therapies exist that specifically target ASD. ASD patients have altered activity in brain areas implicated in social behaviour, and emotions. Genetic animal models of human disease can help understand disease onset and progression, and whether new therapies might be effective in humans. Several studies suggest that the neurotransmitter serotonin, and in particular the serotonin 2A receptor, could be a potential target for novel ASD treatments. A preliminary study in our lab discovered that low doses of the 5-HT2A agonist Lysergic Acid Diethylamide (LSD) induce prosocial effects in mice. The main goal of the current study is to assess whether this treatment improves behaviour in two mouse models that display deficits similar to those in human ASD. Behavioral experiments will be employed to assess the sociability and anxiety levels of the ASD models at baseline. Subsequently, low-doses of LSD will be administered for 7 days and the behavioral experiments will be repeated. Next, the activity in several brain regions involved with ASD will be assessed in these models by recording the activity of individual neurons. Following the assessment of differences in brain activity at baseline, low doses of LSD will be administered for 7 days and the neuronal activity will be assessed again to determine whether this treatment normalized any neuronal dysfunctions. In the last part of the study, optogenetics will be used, which employs the activation of specific neurons by shining a laser light through an optical fiber. With this technique we will modulate the activity of selected brain areas to determine if this restores sociability. This is the first study which investigates if the psychedelic LSD, given at low doses, holds therapeutic value in treating a mouse model of ASD, which could provide the basis for translating this treatment in humans.
