column36: Structural composition and regulation of electrical synapses in the CNS
column37: Neurotransmitters are used by nerve cells in the brain to communicate with each other at chemical synapses. However, over the past 20 years, discoveries by us and others have shown that neuronal communication mediated by electrical synapses is also prevalent in the mammalian brain. Neural integration at electrical synapses is critical for information processing related to cognitive, sensory and motor functions. Such synapses are formed by structures called gap junctions located at close appositions between neurons, and are composed of the gap junction-forming protein connexin36. Our work has shown that these structures have many protein components supporting their assembly and neurotransmission capabilities. Understanding the functions of those components is essential for deciphering how electrical synapses operate. Our past and more recent discoveries of major protein constituents of electrical synapses (ZO-1, MUPP1, AF6, cingulin, N-cadherin, nectin-1, alpha-catenins and beta-catenin, SynGAP1, LNX1/2), has led us to explore novel biochemical mechanisms (i.e., cAMP/Epac/Rap1 signalling) that may govern the structure and deployment of these synapses in neuronal circuits. Further, we aim to investigate the role of this signalling in regulating dynamic changes in the fidelity and strength of electrical synaptic transmission, which were recently recognized as key features of electrical synapses. This signalling has links to brain disorders, as indicated by our finding SynGAP1 at electrical synapses. This protein is essential at chemical synapses and may be equally important at electrical synapses. Mutations in the gene coding for this protein were found to cause intellectual disability, autism and epilepsy in people. We expect that our work will reveal entirely new concepts on cellular mechanisms that govern the activities of electrical synapses and how malfunction of those mechanisms could contribute to neurological disorders.

column36: Induction of transplantable angiosomes for segmental bone defect regeneration
column37: The bypass procedure in the heart or legs and more preferably placement of a stent to either bypass or reopen arterial blockages saves lives. The bypass consists of harvesting a nonessential vessel and 'plumbing' it in around the blockage. Reconstruction can be achieved by harvesting a tissue segment complete with feeding artery, capillary bed and draining vein, (angiosome), and transplanting, again by 'plumbing' the vessels of these tissue flaps to vessels to the region of repair. Attempts to regrow blood vessels or indeed functional vascularised tissue segments to negate the need for graft harvest have been based on the premise that recapitulating normal anatomy will provide a functional analogue. While there have been some impressive demonstrations of potential, the central issue preventing an improvement in options for patients is the inability to regenerate complete vascular systems, (angiosomes). The main focus of prior research has been on arterial regeneration or in getting arteries to sprout new vessels. Attempts to grow new transplantable tissue in the body have focussed on using vein grafts that shortcut (anastomose) the arterial and venous systems that sprout new vessels that in turn are used to regenerate skin and bone. We recently challenged the dogma that new growing tissues require an arterial blood supply and instead considered the intact venous system as a potential regenerative source. We found that without being cut or transplanted, native veins could be induced to sprout profusely by placing a biomaterial around them and that unprecedented amounts of new bone could be grown on these new vessels and then transplanted as flaps. This proposal will explore the regenerative potential of blood vessel walls to grow bone and develop mature new angiosomes. The focus will be on developing minimally invasive approaches, reproducibility and acceleration of the process we have demonstrated as well as determine practical limits of the approach

column36: Implementing Smart Cities Interventions to Build Healthy Cities (SMART) Training Platform
column37: The Implementing Smart Cities Interventions to Build Healthy Cities (SMART) training platform addresses an urgent need to build capacity in implementation science to develop, evaluate and promote the uptake of interventions, with the aim of improving population health. A central driver of population health is access to healthy food, with food insecurity linked to a number of poor physical and mental health outcomes. In Canada, there are large differences in food insecurity across urban areas, accompanied by mounting evidence that the built environment and food systems can influence access to affordable and healthy food. Food security and resilient food systems are thus critical to building healthy cities. We propose a national implementation science training program whose hallmarks include (1) a thematic focus on the central place of food in healthy cities; (2) the use of 'big data' to create smart solutions for urban environments, and (3) bringing together the best knowledge, practices and tools from different fields of study to find solutions to complex problems. Focusing on food as a theme in the proposed training platform will equip trainees with transferable knowledge and skills to tackle many Healthy City challenges. They will learn, for example, that food security is a complex, multidimensional and multisectoral issue that requires collaboration and a systems-thinking approach. Specifically, the SMART training platform will deliver new curriculum, experiential learning, a portfolio of courses across 9 academic institutions, an annual conference, a summer institute and a virtual hub of resources. In addition to training a critical mass of future implementers to support the growth of Healthy Cities, SMART will strengthen implementation science practice and research in Canada, intensify research and generate innovation, create new research-practice partnerships and improve health outcomes related to food in Canada and globally.

column36: New Approach for Treatment of Periodontitis
column37: Oral health is of fundamental importance for humans and the two most common disorders of humans, periodontal diseases and dental caries, both localize to the oral cavity. For periodontal diseases, the connective tissues of tooth-supporting structures play critically important functions in maintaining and enabling the attachment of the teeth to the jaws and essential for chewing and masticatory function. Currently we do not have a clear understanding of how periodontal diseases cause breakdown of the connective tissues that support the teeth but what is known is that uncontrolled overgrowth and stiffening of connective tissue matrices are strongly associated with these disorders. In this proposal we will examine how an ion channel, TRPV4, which is present in cells of gum tissues that are called fibroblasts, regulates the ability of these cells to properly remodel and ensure that the form and function of connective tissues is maintained. Notably, mutations of the gene for TRPV4 causes 4 different diseases that affect connective tissue form and function. We don't understand how TRPV4 contributes to the regulation of connective tissues in gum tissues. We will examine at the molecular, cellular and tissue levels, how this channel, contributes to the regulation and maintenance of normal gum tissue structure and functions and what are the important determinants of TRPV4 that affect connective tissues and the maintenance of gum health. Knowledge from this project could suggest new approaches for the treatment of gum diseases, which affect over 30% of the adult North American population.

column37: Access to health services is an important challenge in low-income settings where the underutilization of health services has been linked to poor health outcomes. The goal of this project is to estimate the impact of climate-related risks and events on the access to and utilization of health services in Western Province, Zambia, a setting where there has been an increase in the variability and intensity of climate-related hazards, and to develop and validate tools that can be used to design interventions to mitigate and respond to these risks. column36: A new potential therapeutic target for type 2 diabetes: Delineating the mechanisms of its actions
column37: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is a major cause of heart disease, stroke and cancer. Caused by inadequate action of the hormone, insulin, T2D is often linked to obesity. With chronic overeating, the fat in our bodies (adipose) undergoes changes that make it "unhealthy", so that it is doesn't respond normally to the hormone insulin, and therefore promotes diabetes. How "healthy" adipose becomes "unhealthy" is not known. Such knowledge would be valuable, as drugs could be designed to prevent the changes from occurring. We recently found that a protein known as CD248 is made by cells (adipocytes) in the adipose. In humans and mice, the highest CD248 levels are strongly associated with the highest risk of diabetes. Mice and people with low levels of CD248, are resistant to diabetes, i.e., the adipose remains "healthy", even if they are obese. We also showed that by reducing CD248 in obese diabetic mice, we could reverse the diabetes and change the unhealthy adipose tissue to healthy adipose tissue. And thus, we've potentially uncovered an entirely new way to treat type 2 diabetes! Our goal is to understand how CD248 controls the switch between healthy and unhealthy adipose (and thus between non-diabetes and diabetes), and how it interacts with insulin and other proteins in the adipose tissue. Such information will help in the design of drugs. To achieve our goals, we will examine adipose tissue from mice that lack CD248 in different cells, using multiple biochemical, molecular and microscopic methods that are in our labs and those of our expert collaborators. In the end, we hope that we will identify strategies that reduce CD248 or interfere with its function, thereby leading to new and better treatments for type 2 diabetes.

column36: 3D bioprinting next generation brain organoids for identifying drug targets for Alzheimer's disease
column37: We are bioprinting next generation brain organoids (miniature brains) for screening drugs to treat Alzheimer's disease (AD). Better pre-clinical tools for predicting the effectiveness and toxicity of drugs would significantly lower the chance of drug failure during clinical trials, reducing the cost of drug development and decreasing the healthcare burden generated by neurodegenerative diseases like AD. Our teams consists of Dr. Willerth, an internationally recognized neural tissue engineer at the University of Victoria, Dr. Nygaard, an M.D./Ph.D. who runs the Alzheimer's clinic at the University of British Columbia, Dr. Katherine Elvira, Canada Research Chair and Michael Smith Scholar who is also an Assistant Professor of Chemistry at the University of Victoria, and two award winning biotechnology start-ups - Aspect Biosystems and Axolotl Biosciences. The project will use Aspect Biosystems' cutting edge 3D printing technology to generate miniature brains using stem cells taken from patients suffering from AD, validate these neural organoids as a tool for drug screening, and then evaluate potential drugs by examining their effect on the function of these engineered tissues.

column36: Burden of COVID-19 among people living with HIV in Ontario
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has shown that certain members of our society may be at higher risk for severe disease. One such group is people living with HIV. HIV affects the immune system's ability to respond to infections and shares some of the same risk factors as COVID-19, such as older age, comorbidities, and lower income. So far, people living with HIV who are taking medications to control their HIV infection seem to get infected with COVID-19 and become hospitalized at similar rates to the general population, but evidence in this area is mixed and more research is needed as the COVID-19 pandemic continues to evolve. Because of limited testing and surveillance gaps, we do not yet know how many people living with HIV have been infected with COVID-19 or whether they will have more severe illness than people who do not have HIV. We will use an existing study of about 4,000 people living with HIV who are receiving care in Ontario to fill these gaps. People living with HIV will be invited to collect a finger prick of blood at home. Blood samples will be tested for antibodies to SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, to see how many people have been infected since the start of the pandemic and whether these antibodies will protect against re-infection. Through linkage to laboratory, hospitalization, and death certificate records, we will find out how many people living with HIV have a lab-confirmed COVID-19 diagnosis or develop more severe illness from COVID-19. We will compare these findings to HIV-negative individuals in Ontario. Through linkage to doctor's visits, we will see how the COVID-19 pandemic has impacted medical care for HIV. Finally, if a COVID-19 vaccine becomes available during our study period, we will also measure vaccine uptake and antibody response to vaccination. These findings will inform health care and health services planning for people living with HIV.

column36: Host and Viral Determinants of HCV RNA Accumulation
column37: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is a global health problem that affects 71 million people worldwide, including over 250,000 Canadians. HCV-infected individuals typically develop a persistent infection that leads to chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis, steatosis and liver cancer. Currently, there is no vaccine available and although effective antiviral treatments exist, cost and treatment accessibility remain barriers to HCV elimination. To establish an infection, HCV commanders may different factors in our cells. In healthy cells, small molecules, called microRNAs, restrict how much our genes are expressed. HCV co-opts a liver-specific microRNA and uses it to amplify itself. Clinical trials using inhibitors of the microRNA, revealed that preventing the virus from accessing this microRNA may be an effective treatment option. We have preliminary evidence that suggests that HCV uses this microRNA to promote viral protein production, genome stability, and we hypothesize that the microRNA also helps the virus to establish replication factories where progeny viruses are produced. The focus of this research is to investigate how HCV uses the microRNA to its own benefit and to identify other human factors that the virus uses to amplify itself in the liver. This research will provide us with insight into mechanisms of microRNA-mediated enhancement of viral replication and may reveal novel antiviral targets. Moreover, the mechanism(s) used by HCV to establish viral replication factories may be applicable to a wide range of viruses that impact human health. Thus, not only will this work improve our understanding of HCV infection, but the outcomes may help us to understand microRNA function, replication of a wide range of viruses, and is likely to provide new approaches for antiviral intervention for a number of important human pathogens

column36: Targeting renal vascular and mitochondrial dysfunction to prevent acute kidney injury in sepsis.
column37: Sepsis (blood poisoning) is a medical emergency where the body mounts an overwhelming response to infection. It has a very high mortality rate, and believed to be responsible for a staggering one in five deaths worldwide. Patients over the age of 60 make up over 60% of all sepsis hospitalizations in Canada, and the older the patient with sepsis, the greater the risk of dying. Yet, despite the fact that the majority of patients who develop sepsis are elderly, preclinical studies in this area mainly use young and otherwise healthy animals. Understanding how sepsis affects aged animals is therefore an important knowledge gap that needs to be addressed. Among other things, sepsis can cause damage to the heart and blood vessels, and if left untreated, can interfere with delivery of blood (and hence oxygen and nutrients) to organs like the kidney. Kidney injury is a common complication in sepsis, and a major contributor to its high mortality rates. This study aims to examine how blood flow to the kidney is affected in sepsis, and to study the mechanisms that leads to kidney injury in both young and aged mice. We will also test new drug combinations to improve blood flow in sepsis, with the goal of reducing or altogether preventing the kidney injury in these young and aged models. This study will equip physicians with a better understanding of how sepsis affects elderly patients, and may provide new treatments to prevent kidney injury in this terrible disease.

column37: The mechanical properties of the tissues that constitute the eye are supposed to play a central role in the appearance of several vision problems. column36: Optical system for in-vivo imaging and label-free identification of stem cells in the human corneo-scleral limbus for treatment of corneal blindness
column37: The limbus is ~1.5 mm wide transitional region of tissue in the eye that separates the peripheral cornea and conjunctiva and prevents the conjunctiva from invading the cornea. It houses stem cells (LSC) responsible for maintenance and regeneration of the corneal epithelium. The LSC are located in crypts formed by ridges of connective tissue named the Limbal Palisades of Vogt (POV). Limbal stem cell dysfunction (LSCD) causes morphological and physiological changes in the limbus that result in decreased vision, photophobia, tearing, chronic inflammation and hyperemia, recurrent episodes of pain, and blindness in severe cases. LSCD can be treated both medically (topical medications and therapeutic contact lenses) and surgically (transplantation of healthy stem cells). Currently, there is no clinical imaging modality that can image the POV and identify LSC without tissue contact. Ultra-high resolution optical coherence tomography (UHR-OCT) allows for non-contact, volumetric imaging of the limbus that will help surgeons with mapping out and correctly identifying healthy LSC zones from LSC-deficient areas. This will permit safe targeted harvesting of donor LSC and accurate placement of LSC transplants in areas of deficiency. UHR-OCT could be an invaluable clinical tool in LSCD diagnosis and grading, monitoring the treatment of LSC deficiency, as well as pre-operative planning. OBJECTIVES: To develop ultrafast UHR-OCT technology for in-vivo, non contact imaging and identification of LSC. To evaluate the effectiveness of the UHR-OCT for clinical applications in a pilot study of LSCD subjects and healthy controls, and validate the UHROCT images through comparison with histology. SIGNIFICANCE: The UHR-OCT technology will provide clinicians with an unique in-vivo, noninvasive method for examining the presence and health status of stems cells in the human limbus, and will contribute to improved diagnostics and treatment planning in LSCD.

column36: Anticoagulation Therapy Timing in Atrial Fibrillation after Chronic Subdural Hematoma External Drainage(the ATTACHED RCT)
column37: Blood accumulation on the outside of the brain is called chronic subdural hematoma (cSDH). This typically occurs because of a relatively trivial head trauma and is common in elderly patients. It is known that a high proportion of elderly patients also receive blood thinners for stroke prevention in the context of abnormal heart rhythms. Treatment of cSDH sometimes require surgery and use of blood thinner is usually withheld immediately after surgery due to fear of bleeding risk. This is important as there Is known possibility of bleeding after surgery. However, it has been unequivocally shown that withholding blood thinners carries the risk of stroke (which this drug was suppose to prevent in first place). Therefore, is hard to know when is best time to restart blood thinner and currently there is no consensus on when to restart blood thinner medications after surgery for cSDH. This is a small study designed to show the feasibility to perform a larger study to answer an important clinical question: in patients with blood thinner for stroke prevention prior to surgery for cSDH, does early restarting of blood thinner 4 weeks after surgery result in better overall physical and cognitive function (measure quantitatively in 3 months) compared to delayed restarting of blood thinner 3 months after surgery? This study will be performed at 6 Canadian hospitals. Patients that are suitable for study will be randomly divided into two groups of patients receiving: (1) early restart of blood thinner (4 weeks after surgery) or (2) late restart of blood thinner (3 months after surgery). In this study we will record the proportion of patients enter the study, complete the study as well as any evidence of bleeding in the brain or stroke. These results will be critical to inform on the design and planning of a larger-scale study that will answer one of the most common questions in the fields of stroke, geriatrics, trauma, and neurosurgery.

column37: It remains unclear why, in some patients, a stroke can spark a brain-wide injury process that will ultimately lead to cognitive impairment. Targeting these inflammatory processes post-stroke is an intuitive strategy to prevent cognitive decline. We are entering a time when the aging population is outgrowing the overall population by four-fold. This aging cohort is at risk for suffering a stroke and for developing cognitive impairment. column36: Rise & Shine: Promoting Sleep Quality in Chronic Stroke with Exercise
column37: Sleep is important to our health and wellbeing. Poor sleep quality is linked to many chronic health problems, such as heart disease, diabetes, cognitive impairment, and dementia. After a person suffers a stroke, they often experience difficulties in getting a good night's sleep. Approximately half of stroke survivors have insomnia, or have trouble falling and/or staying asleep. Poor sleep quality among stroke survivors increases the risk of recurrent stroke by 3-fold and the risk of early death by 76%. Hence, stroke survivors need strategies to promote better sleep. Fortunately, evidence shows that sleep quality can be improved with exercise, even among those who struggle with insomnia. Whether exercise training can improve sleep quality in adults with chronic stroke (i.e., at least 12 months has passed since their stroke) and poor sleep quality is not known. In addition, it is unknown if improved sleep is associated with improved outcomes in those with chronic stroke. This study will specifically evaluate the effect of twice-weekly targeted exercise training on sleep quality over a 6-month period in persons with chronic stroke and poor sleep quality. This study will also evaluate the effect of exercise on the following outcomes: 1) sleep structure; 2) fatigue; 3) daytime sleepiness; 4) mood; 5) physical function and capacity; 6) thinking abilities; 7) heart health; and 8) quality of life. Finally, this study will examine how changes in sleep quality may be related to changes in these outcomes. Our proposed research is timely as the importance of sleep to recovery, health, and wellbeing post-stroke is increasingly recognized.

column36: Structures and functions of nonribosomal peptide synthetases
column37: Nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) are large microbial enzymes that catalyze peptide bond formation. Instead of making proteins like the ribosome does, these megaenzymes produce a vast variety of small molecules with important biological activity, such as antifungals, antibacterials, antivirals, antitumours, immunosuppressants, and green chemicals. These NRPS products have revolutionized human health: Penicillin, cyclosporin, cephalosporin and daptomycin have saved tens of millions of lives worldwide. NRPSs are true macromolecular machines, huge proteins with multiple active sites, moving parts and a coordinated production cycle. They consist of a series of multidomain modules, with each module responsible for adding one specific amino acid to the growing peptide molecule, in assembly line fashion. The focus of this research is to expand the structural knowledge of nonribosomal peptide synthetases and the mechanisms they employ to synthesize bio-active molecules. We will use chemical biology, biochemistry, biophysics and structural biology, including X-ray crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy, to characterize NRPSs and determine their three-dimensional structures at different points in the process of making different natural products. We will address a range of questions, including elucidating the precise details of how building blocks are chemically assembled into the peptide products, how peptides are modified to gain proper function and how the NRPSs perform the gymnastics and large-scale rearrangements they need to perform to create these green chemicals and therapeutics. The wide-ranging activities of NRPS small molecule products, combined with the potential to engineer NRPSs to produce novel bio-active molecules, make them a promising source of new therapeutics. Our studies further fundamental understanding of these vast and complex enzymes and potentiate their bioengineering.

column36: Building and rebuilding brain white matter with endogenous neural stem cells
column37: Damage to brain white matter occurs following injury and in disorders like multiple sclerosis, and results in a wide variety of neurological issues, including sensory, movement, and cognitive problems. Currently, there are no effective medical therapies to promote brain repair and reduce disability following white matter damage. In this proposal, we hope to change this situation. Brain white matter is comprised of the axons of the nerve cells that conduct information, surrounded by a type of insulation called myelin that ensures signals are sent in a timely and faithful manner. This myelin is made by another brain cell type, oligodendrocytes, and in many of the aforementioned disorders these oligodendrocytes die, myelin is lost, and normal brain information transfer is disrupted. How might we repair this deficiency? Here, we propose a strategy based upon replacing the lost oligodendrocytes, thereby enabling myelin repair and restoration of normal circuitry. To do this, we will take advantage of the fact that our brains contain resident neural stem cells that normally make oligodendrocytes throughout life. We propose to perform studies asking how these stem cells make oligodendrocytes under optimal conditions during development and then to ask if we can recreate these optimal conditions again in the adult injured brain. We will attempt to do this using bioactive agents we define and/or repurposed drugs that we have identified. Ultimately, we hope that these studies will lead to new treatments for human white matter damage.

column36: Five years after the Mid-Urethral Sling Tensioning (MUST) trial: cure of stress urinary incontinence symptoms, health care utilization and cost-effectiveness associated with two techniques for MUS incontinence surgery
column37: Stress urinary incontinence (SUI) affects 1 in 4 females. SUI is the loss of urine when coughing, laughing, sneezing or exercising. SUI decreases quality of life through shame and reduction in physical activity. Surgery for SUI is common. The most widely used procedure is the mid-urethral sling (MUS), a narrow piece of mesh placed through the vagina to support the urethra (tube which passes urine out of the body). While MUS surgeries provide high cure rates, they also carry risk of long-term complications such as overactive bladder (OAB, frequent urination with risk of loss before reaching the toilet), urinary retention (inability to completely empty one's bladder), vaginal mesh erosion and pain. Little research has been done regarding how the techniques used by surgeons during MUS placement are related to complications. The best technique for retropubic MUS placement is unknown. Our group previously reported that at 1 year, two techniques of MUS placement provided similar cure. However, the most commonly used technique had higher risk of surgeries for urinary retention and higher proportions of prescriptions of overactive bladder (OAB) medications when compared to a less commonly known, but more measured and reproducible, technique. This is concerning as OAB medications are associated with development of dementia and revision surgeries add additional costs to the health system. This project aims to study the two techniques from the original trial over 5 years. This will allow us to better compare and understand: 1) self-reported SUI cure in the longer term, 2) rates of repeat surgeries after MUS beyond the original study window, 3) the magnitude of difference in OAB medication use, as well as 4) study the economic costs of the two approaches. This information will allow surgeons to understand if one technique provides superior outcomes from a more holistic viewpoint. Our results will inform future educational programs for surgeons who perform MUS surgeries.

column36: Rescue of entorhinal-hippocampal neuronal network dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease
column37: Over 500,000 Canadians are currently living with dementia, and this is predicted to reach one million in the next two decades. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia and remains one of the most feared consequences of aging. AD is characterized by the abnormal accumulation of two proteins in the brain (amyloid and tau), which leads to neuronal death and eventually cognitive and memory deficits. There are currently no approved disease-modifying therapies for AD and recent drug trials targeting clearance of amyloid alone have been unsuccessful, motivating the need of studying therapies targeting both proteins. In addition to protein accumulation, human and animal work has demonstrated widespread brain networks dysfunction in AD. Specifically, the connectivity between the entorhinal cortex (one of the first sites of abnormal tau accumulation in the brain) and the hippocampus (a key brain region for memory formation) is selectively abnormal in early AD. The overall goals of our work are to study altered entorhinal-hippocampal connectivity and its effect on cognitive function, and determine the efficacy of a combinatory treatment (that targets abnormal buildup of both amyloid and tau) in recovering normal connectivity and normal cognition. To perform this study, we will leverage our expertise in animal models of AD that we have previously characterized, computational tools that we have developed, novel histological techniques, functional brain recordings and cognitive testing. Compelling preliminary data from our prior work supports this proposal. Our proposed study will establish signatures of abnormal hippocampal network function and enhance our understanding of the direct effects of these signatures on cognition. This research also has the potential to establish network dysfunction as a secondary, intermediate outcome measure of treatment response in clinical trials, a critical need given the difficulty of achieving cognitive rescue in AD.

column37: Alzheimer's disease is a devastating neurodegenerative disorder associated with progressive cognitive decline. Out of 36 million patients worldwide, approximately 60% of all Alzheimer's disease patients are female. This increases the likelihood of missing important sex-specific differences in male and female Alzheimer's disease treatments. This work will provide important new understanding of the role of sex-specific differences in the underlying mechanisms that contribute to the development of Alzheimer's disease. Our goal is to understand sex-specific difference in the progression of Alzheimer's disease and provide tailored approaches that enable us to more effectively treat Alzheimer's disease in both sexes.

column36: Circumstances and Outcome of Active Transportation Injuries: An Inception Cohort Study.
column37: BACKGROUND: Active transport (such as walking and cycling) is encouraged as a healthy, eco-friendly way to travel. Unfortunately, pedestrians and cyclists are vulnerable in the event of a fall or collision and fear of injury acts as a deterrent. Knowledge of the circumstances of active transport injuries is limited because traffic statistics do not count all of these injuries, especially when a motor vehicle is not involved. As a result city planners do not know where these events occur, why they occur or which types of bike lanes or crosswalks (for example) put pedestrians or cyclists at greatest risk. There is also limited research on outcome following an active transport injury so doctors and nurses do not know which injured patients are at greatest risk of poor recovery. We will interview participants to find out their health and employment status in the month before the injury and again at 2, 4, 6, and 12 months as they recover. IMPORTANCE: Our study will help doctors and nurses know how quickly injured pedestrians and cyclists recover and which patients are likely to have long term health problems. We will also describe how much medical treatment these patients require and how much work they miss. City planners will be interested in knowing why and where the most serious injuries occur. Our findings will also help policy makers make informed decisions on how much money and resources to devote to preventing active transport injuries or to specialized treatment programs for injured pedestrians or cyclists.

column36: A Novel Approach to Discover Therapeutic and Biomarker Targets and Enable Precision Health in COPD: TORCH (Towards Omics and imaging to Revolutionize COPD Health)
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) affects 1 in 10 Canadians over the age of 40 years. It is the number ONE cause of hospital admissions in Canada. There are NO curative therapies for COPD. One major reason for the continued rise in the burden of COPD in Canada and failure of scientists and researchers to discover new treatments for this disease is that we don't have a good understanding of how Canadians develop this disease. New research is showing that COPD may not be one disease after all. It may consist of hundreds, if not thousands of different conditions. Thus, the solution to this dilemma is to consider and treat every patient with COPD as an individual rather than as one large group of homogenous patients. In this research program, which we call TORCH, we are going to find a way to evaluate patients as an individual (and not as a group) by using modern-day technologies. These technologies include CT (computed tomography) scans and MRI (magnetic resonance imaging), which have been specially designed to study the lungs of COPD patients. The use of these technologies will allow us to accurately determine for each patient the lung regions that have been affected by COPD and lung regions that have been spared and thus look normal. We will use these CT and MRI datasets to map out zones of disease activity ("hot", "warm", "lukewarm", "cold", etc.) and take samples from each of these zones using a technique called bronchoscopy. Samples taken from each of these zones will be processed and subjected to leading-edge genomics technology. This will allow us to figure out the difference in the molecular profiles between these zones of disease activity within in a given individual. This investigation will ultimately lead to new insights on what is causing the disease within a given individual and between individuals and discovery of potential new drugs and biomarkers for COPD patients.

column37: Heart failure afflicts 500,000 Canadians and millions of patients worldwide. An important treatment option for heart failure after medical therapy is cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT), which is a device implanted in the chest to stimulate the weak heart muscle and improve its pumping function. Although CRT can help many patients, only half experience improvement in their heart's pumping function, while the rest do not get better and some get worse. CRT therapy also has surgical risks and costs. Therefore, it is important to carefully select patients who are most likely to respond to CRT. Currently, patients are selected based on an abnormal electrical signal recorded on their electrocardiogram (ECG), but this does not identify many patients likely to improve after CRT. We have developed a new approach to ECG analysis which evaluates a tiny, abnormal electrical signal, so-called QRSp. QRSp appears to provide a comprehensive assessment of abnormal electrical activation in the heart, which leads to heart failure. In a pilot study, QRSp identified heart failure patients who improved with CRT. Herein, our aim is to confirm the findings of our pilot study in a larger population of heart failure patients. We will determine whether QRSp predicts benefit from CRT and whether this prediction is better than traditional ECG analysis. QRSp will be evaluated from special ECG recordings before CRT. Patients will then be followed for 6 months to determine if they improve with CRT based on ultrasound imaging of the heart's pumping function. The findings of this study may improve patient selection for CRT therapy, thereby translating to better patient care, fewer CRT complications, and reduced healthcare costs.

column37: After surgery, 1 in 6 patients have complications. These problems include infections, bleeding and breathing difficulties. A good understanding of patients' fitness before surgery is very helpful because poor fitness can often lead to complications. Doctors usually estimate patients' fitness by asking them about usual activities such walking or climbing stairs. However, we recently finished a study of 1401 patients and found major problems with how doctors ask these questions. Doctors' questions could not identify patients who were more likely to have complications. We also found that a special exercise test, called CPET, was better. CPET did identify patients who had complications, but it is not practical. The reason is that CPET needs expensive equipment not found at many Canadian hospitals. We thus need a better solution. A very good option is the 6-minute walk test or 6MWT. This simple test measures the distance someone can walk over 6 minutes on flat ground. Some small studies suggest that the 6MWT may identify patients who have complications after surgery. However, we still need a much higher-quality study to be really sure that 6MWT can identify patients who have complications. We also need to see if the 6MWT is better than simpler options, such as a short questionnaire called DASI, a blood test called NT pro-BNP, and a simple physical test called the hand grip test. Therefore, we want to conduct the FAST Walk study of 1672 patients at 14 Canadian hospitals. Each patient will complete the 6MWT, DASI, NT pro-BNP test and hand grip test before surgery. We will follow them for 90 days after surgery to compare the tests for identifying people at risk for complications. By helping to better identify high-risk patients before surgery, our study will improve their care and thus help prevent complications. It will also make sure that specialized (and expensive) care is used in patients who need it. Thus, our study will help patients having surgery across Canada.

column36: Regulation of Spermatogenesis and Epigenetic Inheritance by Argonaute/Small RNA Pathways
column37: One potent mechanism of gene regulation is mediated through small RNA pathways. Small RNA pathways are found across all three kingdoms of life, and at the core of these pathways are the conserved family of Argonaute effectors. Argonaute proteins are guided via the sequence specificity of small RNA effector molecules (think of these as postal codes) to identify target transcripts for gene regulation. Although initially characterized as posttranscriptional modulators of gene expression, studies of Argonautes in various species have revealed novel functions. The model nematode C. elegans has contributed an abundance of knowledge to our understanding of small RNA pathways. C. elegans possesses 19 Argonaute genes, more than in humans (which have 8). Most Argonautes that have been studied in C. elegans thus far have been examined for their roles in somatic tissues or in oogenesis. In contrast, the roles of small RNA pathways in regulating gene expression during spermatogenesis remain relatively enigmatic, yet sperm contribute half of the genome and other epigenetic components to progeny. Our team has identified a set of 12 Argonautes that are expressed during spermatogenesis, pointing to important roles for these pathways in sperm production and fertility. We will utilize a powerful constellation of cutting edge genetic, genomic, proteomic, molecular biology and biochemistry approaches to determine the molecular mechanisms by which these small RNA pathways impact sperm development and fertility. Because of their central role in gene regulation and their profound impact on the development and differentiation of many organisms, uncovering novel and conserved molecular mechanisms of Argonaute/small RNA pathways is key to advancing our fundamental knowledge of normal cellular functions, and has the potential to enable more precise means of manipulating gene expression--both of which are important for biotechnology applications and therapeutics, including fertility treatment.

column37: Le cancer du sein est un probleme majeur de sante au Canada et dans le monde. Lors de son diagnostic precoce, il est generalement traitable soit par chirurgie, par hormonotherapie et/ou par chimiotherapie. Cependant, environ 40% des patientes subiront au cours des annees suivantes une recidive et certaines une chimioresistance a leurs traitements. A ce stade, ces cancers deviennent tres agressifs, difficiles a traiter et sont assortis d'un sombre pronostic. Par consequent, la recherche de nouveaux traitements fait toujours l'objet d'intenses efforts afin d'ameliorer l'esperance de vie ainsi que la qualite de vie de ces patientes. A cette fin, notre groupe a concu et developpe une nouvelle famille de composes nommee AIMZs. Ces derniers ont ete specialement concus afin d'eliminer selectivement les cellules cancereuses du sein contenant un enzyme absent des autres cellules humaines tout en ne presentant que tres peu d'effets secondaires. Notre programme de recherche sur les AIMZs a permis de selectionner un compose prometteur n'engendrant pas de toxicite et possedant une activite antitumorale exceptionnelle, lorsqu'evalue sur des souris porteuses de tumeurs cancereuses du sein humain. Nos efforts se concentrent maintenant sur l'evaluation du potentiel therapeutique de cet AIMZ sur des modeles d'animaux porteurs de tumeurs du sein humain avancees et refractaires a la chimiotherapie actuelle ainsi que sur la conduite des etudes precliniques requises a son evaluation en clinique chez l'Homme. Notre objectif a long terme est de proposer aux patientes souffrant de cancers du sein avances une medication efficace et peu toxique leur offrant une esperance de vie prolongee et de qualite.

column36: Automated computational pathology workflows for resolving patterns of heterogeneity in cancer
column37: The examination of patients' tissue by pathologists represents a critical component for the diagnosis and treatment of cancer. Most modern approaches currently involve the integration of both "morphologic" patterns, seen under the microscope with modern molecular studies. Variations in these different levels of data often have important implications for disease outlook and care. Integration of these different data types is however complex, continues to rapidly change, and has components that are relatively qualitative and prone to subjective errors, even among experts. While emerging advances in artificial intelligence (AI) now provide new solutions to objectively analyze the subjective microscopic properties of tumors, generalizable approaches to consolidate this important information of tumor variation with contemporary molecular tools are still required. Here, we aim to use our AI and clinical expertise to develop new tools that can unify these various sources of information together to improve care. Firstly, we will develop a fully automated solution for the diagnosis of brain tumors that allows for integration of molecular and morphologic data. We will also develop new AI tools to analyze biological variation within individual patients' cancers. This is extremely important for selecting optimal tumor regions for modern personalized medicine efforts. Finally, we also characterize a set of newly developed digital "biomarkers" that can objectively quantify features of tumor aggressiveness across multiple tumor types and provide new ways for doctors to predict how cancer will likely behave following surgery. Because these various developed AI tools are digital, they can eventually be accessed and adopted into patient care by doctors anywhere around the world. Together these tools aim to help modernize a critical aspect of cancer care and democratize the state-of-the-art diagnostic workup for patient tissue, even at remote centers where subspecialists are scarce

column36: Extracellular vesicles as a biomarker and therapeutic for Spinal Muscular Atrophy
column37: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a devastating disorder primarily affecting newborns and young children. It is caused by reduced levels of the survival motor neuron (SMN) protein. Although normally present in all cells of the body, reduced levels of SMN protein results in degeneration of motor neurons, leading to muscle weakness and, in the case of severe disease, death. Our studies have uncovered that a small proportion of SMN protein is naturally released by cells in small "bubbles" called extracellular vesicles (EV). EV are normally involved in cell-to-cell communication, so EV released from one cell can be taken up by other cells elsewhere in the body. This raises the possibility of using EV to distribute SMN protein through the body. In this study, we will evaluate whether analysis of EV isolated from patient blood can be used as a marker for the disease state, which may allow us to develop a simple blood test to monitor the effectiveness of therapeutics. To explore the use of EV as a potential therapeutic, we will deliver a virus containing a good copy of the SMN gene to the liver of mice, such that the EV naturally produced by the liver will have enhanced levels of SMN protein for delivery to cells throughout the body. We will determine if this latter approach can lead to disease correction and extension of lifespan in the mouse model of SMA. Together, these studies will uncover novel approaches to disease management in patients with SMA.

column36: Analyzing the central role of Zasp family proteins in muscle architecture and function
column37: Muscles contain a highly regular, subcellular assembly of proteins that enable contractility. These huge molecular machines are called myofibrils and we aim to understand how they are built during development, and how different proteins are arranged withing myofibrils to contribute to a fully functional muscle. Contractility is mediated by two different filaments, actin and myosin, that slide past each other. Myosin filaments are anchored at the M-line and actin filaments are anchored at the Z-disc. Our work focuses on the Z-disc proteins of the Zasp family. They play a crucial role in assembly, growth and growth termination of Z-discs by interacting with several other important proteins, in particular actin and the actin cross-linker actinin. We will address three questions: what is the outcome when all Zasp family proteins are removed? This will give critical insight to the redundant core function of Zasp proteins. What is the role of actin- versus actinin-binding? This will tell us about the order of events in muscle assembly and about the final position of Zasp proteins within the Z-disc. And finally, how does Zasp self-interaction initiate and terminate Z-disc and thereby muscle growth? This will help us to better understand Z-disc, but also pathological aggregate formation, which is an important aspect of muscle disorders. This work is done in the Drosophila model system, but human Zasp proteins are closely related, and we will confirm our results with human Zasp proteins.

column37: Neurons that transmit painful information and cells of the immune system extensively communicate. column36: ATF3+ tumor-innervating neurons control anti-cancer immunity
column37: Itch is a common feature of various cancers, while cancer cells actively secrete factors promoting neuronal infiltration of tumors. Experimentally stopping the electrical signals of tumor infiltrating neurons helps decrease tumor growth, but the specific means by which neurons regulate cancer cells survival is yet to be uncovered. Given that we discovered that cancer cells drive major changes in the gene expression profiles of tumor-infiltrating noxious detecting neurons, we hypothesize that cancer cells exploit nociceptors interplay with the immune system to sustain their growth and survival. To investigate this, we aim to study: 1) whether cancer cells directly activate these nociceptors, 2) nociceptor-induced expression of immune checkpoint receptors on NK cells, and 3) the role of nociceptors in cancer immunosurveillance. Studying the biology of cancer, by simultaneously embracing the disease's nervous and immune aspects, as well as their reciprocal interplay, will likely lead to the discovery of unexpected biology and novel therapeutic avenues. As such, this proposal represents the first attempt to amplify the immune system's capacity to fight cancer cells by harnessing the nervous and immune system's interplay.

column36: 'Real-time' measures of anxiety and physical activity in 15-18 year olds with prenatal antidepressant exposure
column37: A mother's depressed mood during pregnancy and the antidepressant medicines used to treat this common disorder affect her child's developing brain and may be associated with anxious behaviors in early adolescence. For over 20 years, we have studied the development and behavior in children of mothers who were depressed and treated with antidepressants called serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SRIs) when they were pregnant. We have observed great variations in child behavior such as anxiety and not all outcomes are associated with prenatal antidepressant exposure. A mother's prenatal mood has emerged as one of the strongest predictors of child behavior. We have followed a cohort of mothers and their children since the second trimester of pregnancy (n= 110). We now propose to investigate behavior (anxiety) in our youth and determine whether everyday patterns of behavior at early ages 'predicts' similar behaviors at mid-late adolescence. Now in light of in person restrictions of COVID-19, we will use using a smartphone app and a wearable accelerometer to study whether 14-day 'real time' measures of anxiety, somatic symptoms and physical activity are related to two stress biomarkers found in saliva (cortisol, alpha amylase), prenatal maternal depressed mood and SRI exposure. We believe that our work will help us understand how a mother's depressed mood and treatment with a SRI antidepressant in pregnancy influences her child's well-being during a critical time of development.

column36: Design a Double-Bolt Lock to Control Cancer Cell Growth
column37: Cancer cells differ from normal cells in many ways that allow them to grow out of control and become invasive. That is why one major goal of anticancer therapy is to suppress cancer cell growth. DNA topoisomerase II (TOP2) genes, TOP2A and TOP2B, are two key genes to control cancer cell growth/division. TOP2A is essential for a parent cell to divide into two daughter cells, while TOP2B is important for cancer cells to increase oncogenes that promote cell division. Blocking both TOP2A and TOP2B would create a double-bolt lock to inhibit cancer cell growth. Although several TOP2 blockers are used as drugs to treat cancer patients, they are also toxic to normal cells and in some cases can transform normal cells into tumors. These limitations urge researchers to discover new inhibitors that block TOP2 activity through different mechanisms so that there will be less toxic effects on normal cells. In this study, we will build complex software incorporated with computer clusters to screen millions of chemicals from a chemical bank and then test these chemicals for their inhibitory effects on TOP2 activity. We will decipher how these chemicals inhibit TOP2 activity at the molecular level and determine whether these chemicals block cancer cell growth. This study will lead to the discovery of new TOP2 inhibitors as potential anticancer drugs.

column36: Preserving microcirculation and function in the diabetic brain
column37: A growing number of Canadians have some form of diabetes which costs the Canadian healthcare system 15.6 billion dollars a year. Although diabetes related disease is well appreciated in the heart, kidney and eye, the brain appears to be particularly sensitive given that diabetics are at significantly greater risk for developing cognitive impairment and suffer more severe disability after stroke. Unfortunately no cure exists as insulin therapy cannot completely prevent these problems. Making matters worse, current stroke therapies such as clot busting drugs are not recommended for some diabetics. One common explanation for the diverse array of brain disturbances is that diabetes perturbs brain circulation in the smallest blood vessels (micro-circulation). Here, our working hypothesis is that blood flow in the microcirculatory networks of the diabetic brain are prone to stalling. These microcirculatory traffic jams can accumulate over time, which in tandem with capillary pruning (a common outcome of stalling), lead to progressive deterioration of vascular, neuronal and cognitive function. Since diabetes is a major risk factor for stroke and poor outcome, we suspect that diabetes worsens capillary stalling after stroke, thereby limiting the return of blood flow in vulnerable, but salvageable brain regions. The goal of our research will be to determine how diabetes affects brain micro-circulation. Since we have preliminary data showing there are problems, we will then explore ways to improve brain microcirculation by targeting a specific protein (called IL-10) that modulates inflammation. And finally, by altering IL-10 signaling after stroke, we believe we can better protect brain tissue from stroke damage and improve recovery in an experimental model of diabetes. Ultimately, this project will shed new light on the effects of diabetes on brain circulation and function, which will stimulate new treatment options for those Canadians suffering from diabetes.

column36: Regulation of transcription by SUMO
column37: Sumoylation is the process by which specific proteins in eukaryotic cells become modified through attachment of the SUMO peptide, which has various possible effects on the functions of the targeted proteins. When cells encounter environmental stress conditions, the number of SUMO modifications increases dramatically and rapidly, but it is not fully understood why this occurs. SUMO-targeted proteins, which number in the hundreds or thousands, are involved in multiple processes in the cell, but proteins that control gene expression are particularly subject to this type of modification. This suggests that the elevated sumoylation levels that occur in response to stress may promote changes to gene expression that allow cells to adapt to the stress condition. To explore this, we will identify specific proteins involved in gene expression that are targets of sumoylation to characterize how SUMO modification controls their functions at the molecular level. Additionally, we will examine how changes to cellular sumoylation levels affect gene expression by determining which genes are regulated this way and through what mechanisms this regulation takes place. In cancer, tumour cells frequently show abnormal sumoylation levels, which often correlates with poor prognosis and metastasis. In the long term, our work is important for understanding whether these abnormal sumoylation levels promote the expression of genes that favour tumour growth.

column36: Evaluating Microdosing in Emergency Departments: A Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing the Effectiveness of Buprenorphine/Naloxone Microdosing vs. Standard Dosing (EMED Study)
column37: Buprenorphine/naloxone (commonly known as Suboxone) is a life-saving medication for people with opioid addiction. Studies show that Suboxone works when started from emergency departments (EDs), which is important because many people make ED visits before they overdose. However, Suboxone is hard to start, because it can cause people to experience bad withdrawal symptoms (vomiting, sweating, pain) if it is started too soon after a person has used other opioids like heroin or morphine. This is called precipitated withdrawal and makes many people afraid of starting Suboxone at all. To prevent this complication, doctors tell patients to wait for 12-24 hours since they last used other opioids and to already be in withdrawal before starting, which is very uncomfortable for patients. A new method, called microdosing, tries to improve patient comfort by avoiding precipitated withdrawal and withdrawal altogether. This method starts people on very small Suboxone doses that gradually increase while they continue to use other opioids. Microdosing has never been evaluated in a formal study. This study will identify adult patients with opioid addiction in EDs in BC and Alberta. We will provide them with either take-home Suboxone microdosing or standard dosing packages to start after they are discharged. We will look at whether patients who receive microdosing are more likely to stay on Suboxone than those who receive a standard dosing package. We will also look at whether people who receive microdosing are more likely to take any opioid agonist therapy in the future, and we will compare deaths, overdoses, and healthcare use between the groups. We are working with health regions, provincial policy makers, public health, and people with lived experience with opioid use to make sure that we share our findings with EDs and patients across Canada. We hope that EDs will use our study results to develop Suboxone programs that are most likely to help patients at risk for overdose.

column36: Smart Discharges for Mom+Baby: Saving mother-newborn dyads by developing a predictive risk model to identify vulnerable dyads and guide delivery of evidence-based, locally-informed interventions for targeted post-discharge care.
column37: Mothers and babies are at higher risk of dying in the first six weeks after birth. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends regular follow-up visits for all mothers and their newborns. However, follow-up visits are not possible in many poor countries. The lack of money and nurses at hospitals and limited time and money at home stop mothers from seeking care for themselves and their babies. In our study we identify mother-baby pairs that are most at-risk of getting sick or dying using the Smart Mom+Baby risk score at the time of birth. Here we are studying the partner protein called Bora, which works together with AURKA to regulate when exactly a cell commits to undergoing one round of cell division. As described in a recently publish manuscript, we have discovered many of the details of how Bora and AURKA work together. This includes proteins that regulate the ability of cells to attach or move, linked to metastasis, and proteins that lead to self-directed cell death. We use leading-edge techniques to gain insight to the three-dimensional shape of these proteins and complement our data with studies in cultured human cells or mice to observe how changes to these genes lead to cancer formation. We propose to identify and characterize new therapeutic targets in the vicinity of mutant RAS proteins, and these efforts will be complemented by the drug discovery capabilities at our institute. This could lead to new strategies for designing vaccines to influenza virus. column37: Maintenance of body temperature near 37C is regulated by the brain and is essential for life in mammals including humans. The importance of thermoregulation is demonstrated by the negative impact of a fever on our well-being. A fever is caused by altering the set point of the neural circuit that mediates thermoregulation (like adjusting a thermostat to a higher value). Once established, a fever helps accelerate recovery from infection and dissipates quickly when the threat has been eliminated. However, there are many pathological circumstances in which dysregulated thermoregulation can alter body temperature in a life-threatening manner. Conversely, there are also clinical conditions where artificially changing body temperature can be beneficial. For example, as an adjunct treatment for some forms of cancer and heart attacks. Our ability to control body temperature in a clinical setting is crude and extremely limited in the field. Gaining new information about the molecular and cellular mechanisms that mediate thermoregulation could provide new approaches for precise regulation of body temperature using simpler approaches, including drugs. The process of thermoregulation involves "command" neurons wired to brain areas that induce behavioral (e.g. seeking warm or cool environments) and physiological responses (e.g. sweating or shivering) to mediate cooling or heating as required. Moreover, a key requirement for correct thermoregulation is the existence of temperature sensing neurons that encode on-going body temperature. Remarkably, we still do not know what molecule is responsible for physiological temperature detection and how neurons that express this molecule communicate with command neurons that mediate thermoregulation. This project will investigate the hypothesis that a specific subset of neurons expressing the thermosensitive ion channel dN-Trpv1 are essential for thermoregulation in mice.

column36: The Role of Alternative Gene Splicing in Psychiatric Disorders

The majority of associated DNA variants found through genetic studies of psychiatric disorders are expected to change the expression of the risk genes. Splicing is the process by which different parts of the gene are linked together to create a functional protein and alterations in this process allow diversity in the proteins that can be expressed from a single gene in different tissues. Cytochrome c oxidase (COX) deficiency is associated with bipolar disorder, and deleterious changes in APOPT1 results in a COX deficiency. Our pilot data thus links genetic risk variants altering splicing to a testable cellular phenotype associated with disease. Based on our data, we propose to use this approach to study the remaining genes identified from our informatics approach as well as to identify new candidates as genetic studies for additional disorders arise. We will further use molecular assays that allow us to identify which of the DNA variants change splicing, followed by functional studies in human neural cells. The foundational knowledge provided by our study will offer the possibility of developing new therapies targeted to the risk genes or their protein products.

Lastly, these studies examine how the circadian clock regulates bone mass which will allow us to identify novel molecular targets that can be used as countermeasures for serious problems caused by severe lack in physical activity in elderly and paralyzed patients as well as night and rotating shift workers, who display an increased incidence of fractures.

column36: Understanding Human Primary Atopic Disorders
column37: Nearly 1-in-3 Canadians suffer from an allergic disease, such as asthma, food allergy and eczema. Globally, asthma alone affects an estimated 300 million people, with annual costs over $20 billion dollars worldwide. Solutions to this allergy health crisis are urgently needed. Understanding how and why allergies occur can help us find answers to prevent and treat these burdensome conditions. In our research we use new and innovative ways to understand how the immune system causes allergic disease. We begin by studying people who have severe allergic conditions caused by changes in genes that control how their immune system works. These conditions are called primary atopic disorders (or PADs). We work with clinicians across Canada and the world to identify patients who may be suffering from a PAD. With the full consent of the patient, we use new gene sequencing technologies to read their genetic material or DNA and look for troublesome changes ("mutations"). If mutations are identified in genes that have not been reported in PADs, we then perform experiments to prove that these mutations are responsible for the patient's symptoms. In this project, our initial focus is to study changes in three genes that we have identified in patients with PADs. This is the first time changes in these genes have been reported in other patients with PADs, so they are an exciting and important starting place. Finally, we will work with a large study (the CHILD cohort) that has data and samples for over 3000 Canadian children to determine if changes in the PAD genes are also associated with common allergic diseases. This research is important and timely. Understanding what causes PADs is life-changing for the affected people and families. It means we can find better treatments for them. Our work also provides a unique opportunity to discover how changes in the human immune system cause or contribute to allergic diseases.

column36: Contribution of 17beta-estradiol in pregnancy-related cardiac arrhythmias
column37: The sinus node controls heart rate, and is considered the natural pacemaker of the heart. Electrical impulses from the sinus node travel throughout the four chambers of the heart: the two upper chambers, called atria, and the lower two ventricles. Inappropriate electrical activity in the upper part of the heart (sinus node or atria), results in abnormal heart rhythms referred to as supraventricular arrhythmias. During pregnancy, there is a significant increase in the risk of cardiac arrhythmia. The increased incidence of these arrhythmias may have significant consequences on the health of the mother and the fetus. However, the mechanisms by which pregnancy increases the risk of arrhythmias have been largely unexplored. Thus, the first objective of this project is to explore the cellular and molecular mechanisms responsible for the increased incidence of arrhythmias during pregnancy. Additionally, considering that hormonal status has emerged as an important factor in the development of some types of cardiac arrhythmias, a second objective is to determine whether the major increase in estrogen levels that occur during pregnancy are implicated in these changes. The proposed studies will be realized using a combination of electrophysiological and biochemical techniques in mouse and human-derived cells. This work will provide important information related to the understanding of the influence of pregnancy on cardiac arrhythmia, and on the influence of estrogen on the electrical activity of the sinus node and atria. As comorbidity and the number of pregnancies at an advanced maternal age continue to rise, this issue is becoming even more pertinent. Ultimately, with further understanding, management of pregnancy-induced arrhythmias, and/or arrhythmias correlated with estrogen fluctuation could be significantly improved.

column36: ING1a mechanisms of cell senescence
column37: Cell aging, also called senescence, is largely controlled by stress signals of different types including those generated internally in the cell and by external agents like chemicals and radiation that damage DNA. We have identified a protein we called ING1a that is only found in humans and non-human primates (apes and monkeys), which is induced by stress and very rapidly causes cells to age. We previously found that it does this through a role in the nucleus of cells and now we have discovered another role at the mitochondria that function as the powerhouse of the cell. In our project we propose to determine exactly how ING1a can so rapidly make cells age via this unique mitochondrial mechanism and we will also determine what causes cells to make this protein normally as human cells age. Our observations in human cells are timely since it was recently discovered in yeast, that both a mechanism operating in the nucleus of yeast cells and a mitochondrial energy-based pathway serve as two distinct major mechanisms to lead to their senescence. This is exciting since it suggests that cell aging may have clear parallels between the yeast that is used as a model organism to study aging, and human cells. We propose to use a series of ING1a protein fragments tagged with a molecule that is fluorescent so we can see it in cells under the microscope, to see exactly what piece of ING1a causes cells to rapidly age. After that we will determine what other proteins this fragment binds to so we can understand how it causes rapid cell aging. Once we determine the pathway(s) in the cell that are used to make the cell produce ING1a, and the pathways used by ING1a to cause rapid cell aging, we will plan strategies to block ING1a production and/or block its effect in cells to allow cells to grow for longer periods of time. There is good evidence that increasing cell lifespan will improve human healthspan by delaying the onset of many different age-related ailments.

column36: Role of altered endoplasmic reticulum calcium regulation and the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor signaling in cortico-striatal synaptic dysfunction: Opportunities for therapy in prodromal Huntington disease
column37: Brain diseases characterized by age-related progressive loss of neural tissue (neurodegeneration), like Alzheimer and Parkinson disease, often start with abnormal connectivity between brain cells and regions. Huntington disease (HD) is an inherited brain disorder with average onset in middle age and progressive impairment of movement, cognition and mood. Neurodegeneration is most severe in two regions -- the cortex and striatum, and the first changes occur at connections (synapses) between these regions. Despite a Phase 3 trial using a genetic approach to reduce the mutated protein in HD patients (NCT03761849), evidence suggests changes in synapses may not be reversed once the disease has started. Moreover, there are significant challenges for scaling up therapeutic delivery of this biological agent via regular lumbar punctures over many years in the HD patient population. There is a critical need to develop complementary therapies to normalize function of brain connections before clinical disease onset, by investigating the cellular mechanisms underlying those changes. We propose to test the role of cellular calcium regulation - crucial for the health and signaling properties of brain cells - in triggering altered synapse function between cortex and striatum. We focus on two major mechanisms: the cellular calcium storage and release compartment called the endoplasmic reticulum, and the NMDA receptor, a protein complex that receives and transmits signals by the brain chemical glutamate. We will use a variety of techniques, tools and drugs to investigate the contribution of these mechanisms to synaptic dysfunction in models of HD. We will then conduct preclinical trials to test drugs targeting these mechanisms for effectiveness in restoring coordinated movement, skilled learning and cortex-striatum connectivity. Our results will guide development of therapies to preserve brain connections critical for maintaining normal function longer in HD gene mutation carriers.

column36: The Paternal Origins of Health and Disease (POHaD) Paradigm: Evaluating its Role in Childhood Adiposity and Metabolic Function
column37: It is now recognized that a woman's health status at the time of conception can contribute to the long-term health of her children by programming body pathways in the fetus during pregnancy. This concept, called the Development Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD), has led to recent clinical emphasis on optimizing a woman's weight before pregnancy to potentially reduce the likelihood that her children will develop overweight or obesity. However, in this context, there has been little clinical consideration of the potential contribution of the father's weight at conception. Indeed, there is now a growing body of evidence linking paternal factors to children's health, leading to the recent emergence of the Paternal Origins of Health and Disease (POHaD) paradigm. To date, the impact of a father's weight before pregnancy on the risk of overweight/obesity in his children has not been well studied, due to the practical difficulties of recruiting men and women right before a pregnancy. We have the unique opportunity to address this question because we have previously established a cohort study of 1519 couples who were evaluated at an average of 22 weeks before pregnancy. Thus, we now propose to assess their children at 9- to 11-years of age, along with the parents, to determine whether paternal weight prior to pregnancy is associated with the risks of overweight/obesity and early metabolic abnormalities in the children. If this study demonstrates the POHaD concept as a contributor to childhood overweight/obesity, then it would suggest that efforts directed towards optimization of preconception health potentially should target both maternal and paternal weight status.

column36: A Single Dose Antenatal Corticosteroids (SNACS) Non-Inferiority Randomized Control Trial for Pregnancies at Risk of Preterm Delivery
column37: Around the world, 15 million babies are born too early. Preterm delivery is the main cause of infant death and serious diseases. However, research in animals suggests half the dose would mature babies' lungs adequately. This is important because there are concerns that the double doses that are used now may have risks for babies in the long term. We will analyze the results, keeping people in their originally assigned groups, and we will also analyze them according to the actual treatment received. Our team had previously done other large studies which randomly allocate (assign) women to receive various doses of steroids or other treatments during pregnancy. We will convey our results using articles, websites and a video. If we find that one dose is similar to two doses of steroids in the short-term outcomes, fewer babies will be harmed in the long term and this will change practice around the world.

column36: Intergenerational transmission of vulnerability to PTSD : When children learn fear from their parent
column37: The brain processes underlying fear learning have been well documented. Most of the protocols that have been used to examine these questions have paired a neutral cue with an aversive stimulus (for example, an electrical shock) to create a fear association. However, one can be afraid without directly experiencing the negative stimulus. Observational fear learning refers to the ability to learn a fear association without being directly exposed to the aversive stimulus. What if a child learns from a parent who has a dysregulated fear system, as it is the case for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)? Our project aims to disentangle the mechanisms of observational fear learning in children of mothers with PTSD and to assess if these fear learning patterns could predict subsequent symptoms of mental illness. Three groups will be recruited and followed for 4 years: healthy child for whom the mother is healthy without a trauma history, healthy child for whom the mother is healthy with a history of sexual abuse, and healthy child for whom the mother has a history of sexual abuse and suffers from PTSD. At Time 1 and Time 3 (which will occur 4 years later), children will watch their mother and a stranger adult woman going through a fear conditioning procedure while psychophysiological measures and subjective ratings of fear will be measured. Children's symptoms of mental illness will be assessed at Time 1, as well as 2 years (Time 2) and 4 years (Time 3) later. Given that high fear levels and low emotional regulation abilities are key characteristics of PTSD and that children of parents suffering from PTSD have an increased risk of developing various psychopathologies, it is important to define the mechanisms of observational fear learning in children and to assess how they predict subsequent mental health problems. The results from this application could play a critical role in developing and implementing interventions in at-risk families.

column36: Characterizing and monitoring the healthfulness of the food supply: a fundamental step towards creating healthier food environments
column37: Improving the quality of the food supply is one of the cornerstones for healthier food environments. A critical first step toward this goal consists in getting a clear picture of the nutritional quality of the food supply, i.e. foods and beverages that are offered to consumers on the market. While analyzing the food supply on a per-nutrient basis (e.g. sugar or salt content) remains informative, it does not provide a complete picture of the overall nutritional quality (healthfulness) of foods. Nutrient profiling (NP) is an objective method that characterizes the healthfulness of foods. Indeed, NP models evaluate the quality of a food based on its content in multiple nutrients (e.g. sugars, sodium, fibre), as opposed to relying only on the content in a single nutrient (e.g. sodium only). The proposed project, conducted in collaboration with key organizations such as the ULaval Food Quality Observatory and the INFORMAS-Canada group, aims to characterize and monitor the healthfulness of the food supply using the most reliable NP model in the Canadian context. Because very few existing NP models have been validated, the first objective is to validate three models potentially relevant for use in Canada in different adult populations, to determine which one is the most reliable indicator of the healthfulness of foods. Second, the healthfulness of foods commonly purchased by the population (e.g. breakfast cereals, sliced bread), and its associations with characteristics influencing food-purchasing decisions (e.g. food prices), will be evaluated using the most reliable model. Third, a follow-up evaluation of the same foods will be conducted after 5 years to monitor potential changes in their healthfulness. Taken together, the results of this innovative and essential project will provide useful information about which actions could be undertaken to improve the nutritional quality of the food supply, and ultimately contribute to better diet quality and health in Canadians.
