column36: Elucidating the roles of miRNAs and Hippo signaling on lineage specification in the human and mouse embryo
column37: Subfertility affects 1 in 6 couples and despite advances in assisted reproductive medicine (ART), our understanding of human embryo health and infertility is limited. Embryonic development during the first week post-fertilization is arguably the most critical window. During this time, the first lineages are formed which give rise to the placenta and embryo proper. Successful formation of the first lineages is a developmental milestone required to ensure healthy embryo development. Currently, our knowledge pertaining to the mechanism(s) that control lineage segregation during human preimplantation development is lacking. Most of what we know about preimplantation development is extrapolated from studies using animal models and though they have provided a wealth of information, with recent advancements, it is clear that species differences exist. Therefore, findings must be carefully extrapolated to human development, highlighting the need for more studies directly in the human embryo. Further, miRNAs can regulate gene expression, and our recent work suggests that miRNAs are driving lineage specification in the embryo and that this is, at least in part, mediated by Hippo signaling. Hippo signaling is the current leading model for trophectoderm-inner cell mass specification. In the cancer field, miRNA-Hippo crosstalk is an emerging area of interest that remains to be explored in development. This proposal will determine, for the first time, the regulatory role of miRNAs and miRNA-Hippo crosstalk on lineage specification using a parallel model of human and mouse embryos. Further, this work will help us better understand the role of miRNA in embryo competence and their potential as predictive biomarkers in clinic. Overall, results from these studies are expected to make significant contributions to our understanding of early embryogenesis. I envision broad utility of this data in the fields of developmental, stem cells, and ART.

column36: Colonic Goblet Cells and Mucus: Defining Their Roles in Host Defense and Mucosal Protection
column37: Intestinal mucus is a mix of proteins and sugars. It coats the inner surface of mammalian intestines, lubricating the passage of food and stool along the length of the gut. In addition, mucus acts as a barrier, keeping the vast community of resident, and largely peaceful bacteria from escaping the intestine and causing damage. My group has been exploring if mucus has other functions, by infecting mice with disease causing bacteria called Citrobacter, relatives of the bacteria that cause "hamburger disease". We have been comparing how well Citrobacter infects mice that produce mucus, with mice that are lacking mucus, or mice that lack key mucus sugars. We know that when Citrobacter enters the gut, it has to compete with resident bacteria for space and food. Normally it can take up to 1 week for Citrobacter to outcompete the resident bacteria, expand in number and cause disease. Interestingly, when Citrobacter infects mice lacking mucus, or key mucus sugars, it bypasses the resident bacteria, spreading through the gut and causing disease almost immediately. We found that the resident bacteria in these susceptible mice are very poor at producing a fatty acid called butyrate, but when we add butyrate back, the mice showed improved protection against Citrobacter. We will explore how resident bacteria use mucus sugars to produce butyrate, and define how loss of mucus impacts Citrobacter-host interactions. In addition, we know that as Citrobacter infection progresses in normal mice, some of the cells that line the gut produce significantly more mucus, presumably to thicken the protective mucus barrier and further protect the gut, as well as flush away some of the Citrobacter. It is unclear however, to what degree this mucus response actually protects the host, which cells participate in the response, and finally, whether this release of mucus reflects the direct actions of the cells that make mucus, or if they need to be activated by cells of the immune system.

column36: Neuronal demise in the developing brain shapes the adult brain
column37: In the developing brain, the birth of neurons is followed by the death of 20-40% of these neurons, raising the question of the importance of such demise for the adult brain. Cajal-Retzius cells (CRs) - pioneer neurons of the embryonic brain but then almost completely disappear - present a unique system to address this question. CRs are organizers of early brain development. They secrete protein factors to regulate the migration of other neurons to build proper architecture of the brain. They also act as "placeholders" that form transient neuron-neuron connections to ensure functional assembly of the brain network. Despite their important roles in brain development, the vast majority of CRs are destined to die during early postnatal life in mice as well as in humans. Incomplete CR cell removal has been described in human brain pathologies including epilepsy, opening the intriguing possibility that CR cell death plays a constructive role in sculpting the mature cerebral cortex. Here, we propose a series of experiments to probe the mechanism that drives CR cell death in the developing brain and investigate how abnormal CR cell survival impinges on adult brain function and contributes to seizure susceptibility. Our work will not only provide novel insight into CR cell biology but will also address the role of CR death and persistence in different brain regions. As abnormal CR cell survival is linked to epilepsy, our study will also shed light on the pathogenic mechanisms of epileptic disorders.

column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic disease of the brain and spinal cord that affects close to 1 in 300 Canadians. Losing myelin ultimately results in nerve cell death and in disability for the individual. A number of drugs are available to treat the early, relapsing/remitting form of the disease. However, at least half of all MS patients will develop chronic progressive symptoms during their disease course, and treatment options for this form of the disease are limited. It is therefore crucial that we identify genes that could predict progressive MS and that could be potential targets for therapy. Using data mining approaches, we have identified a gene, Gpr160, whose expression is increased in white blood cells taken from people with progressive MS. In this grant application, we propose to identify the specific types of white blood cells in which Gpr160 is expressed during progressive MS. We will also study multiple blood samples taken over several years from the same patients (a "longitudinal" study) to see if Gpr160 can predict MS progression. In the second part of the study, we will use well-established mouse model of MS to study the role of GPR160 in disease processes. We will generate GPR160-knockout mice using cutting-edge CRISPR technology, and will study whether they develop less or more severe progressive disease.

column37: Sleep loss is a hallmark of modern life. Poor sleep has many consequences including impairments in attention and memory, and chronic sleep disturbances are associated with most brain disorders (e.g., Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia). Although sleep is essential for proper brain function, major issues have not been addressed in the field of sleep research. For example, it remains to be defined whether alterations in the shape of brain cells directly impact sleep quality, and whether sleep loss affects the shape of cells in various brain areas, which is inherently related to their function. Here, we propose addressing these two precise questions, together with studying sex differences, by locally manipulating specific structure of neuronal cells (i.e., spines) in distinct brain regions and assessing the impact of such manipulations on sleep and behavior. Furthermore, we will examine whether the number and shape of spines in defined brain regions, including some critical for memory and information processing, is susceptible to sleep loss and what mechanisms underlie these changes. This will be done by studying male and female mice and making use of genetic engineering, pharmacology, sleep measurements, and behavioral and biochemical approaches. Through these studies, we will define the direct bidirectional relationship between wake/sleep quality and the structure of brain cells. In addition, we will identify brain regions in which cell shape is directly affected by sleep loss, and elucidate the molecular underpinnings of these changes. Together, our research will greatly improve the knowledge about the role of sleep in brain functioning and, importantly, about negative impacts of dysregulation of brain cell structure on sleep quality and behavioral outputs. As such, the project will contribute to novel treatments to combat adverse consequences of sleep loss and poor sleep quality that are hallmarks of, for instance, Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia and autism.

column36: Targeted delivery of novel inhibitors of DNA repair and combination treatments for the modulation of therapeutic response against metastatic colorectal cancer
column37: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer-related death. It is often diagnosed at the advanced stages where metastasis in nearby or distant organs is seen in patients. Patients with metastatic disease make up over 60% of CRC patients. Conventional chemotherapy treatments such as oxaliplatin and irinotecan used in the treatment of metastatic CRC, function by damaging the DNA of cancer cells. Many patients do not benefit from this treatment because their tumors have strong DNA repair systems. Our aim in this project is to develop new drugs that can block DNA repair in CRC, but do not affect normal cells, so that the toxic effects of DNA repair inhibition is not observed in normal cells. We have already found "hit" molecules that block specific DNA repair pathways in human CRC cells as well as in CRC tumors inoculated in animals. In addition, the "hit" inhibitors of DNA repair were found to sensitize CRC cells to DNA damaging chemo and radio therapy. We have also developed nano-carriers of these inhibitors of DNA repair that can direct the inhibitors of DNA repair to CRC tumors. The nano-carries of DNA repair inhibitors have shown to increase the anticancer activity of radiation therapy in CRC tumors in mice. In this project, we would develop second generation of these nanocarriers modified on their surface with molecules that can target CRC cells in metastatic sites and evaluate the activity of these systems in specific sensitization of metastatic CRC to DNA damaging chemo and radiotherapy. The toxicity of combination on normal tissues will also be evaluated. Unrepaired DNA damage can lead to the development of immunogenic tumors by several mechanisms. In this context, we will also investigate the potential of developed nanocarriers of DNA repair inhibitors in the induction of immune response against metastatic CRC. This project can generate knowledge and potentially lead to the development of new therapeutics for the treatment of advanced CRC.

column36: Coronary angiocrine control of heart regeneration
column37: Cardiovascular diseases, particularly myocardial infarction, are the leading cause of mortality worldwide. Myocardial infarction occurs when a cardiac artery is occluded, preventing the supply of blood to a portion of the cardiac muscle and causing tissue damage. After an infarct, patients cannot regenerate the lost heart muscle, developing a permanent scar that leads to heart failure. Recent studies showed that the adult human cardiac muscle retains some capacity to proliferate, indicating that stimulation of heart regeneration might be possible. This observation motivated the design of new therapies to stimulate cardiac regeneration in humans. Efficient restoration of the cardiac vasculature is critical to reduce the infarct size. Several molecules that promote vascular growth play a role in cardiac repair in non-regenerative animal models, but all failed in clinical trials revealing an urgent need to understand regenerative vascularization. Contrary to humans, zebrafish possess a unique capacity to regenerate their adult hearts after injury. As part of this regenerative response, different cell types and tissues get activated and proliferative. We found that zebrafish cardiac vessels pioneer the regenerative response. Importantly, we showed that cardiac vessels serve as a scaffold for the regenerating cardiac muscle, which follows their track towards the injury. It is increasingly clear that the vasculature can regulate processes in other tissues producing secreted (angiocrine) factors. In the heart, cardiac vessels have been classically perceived as a supply network of oxygen and nutrients, but the role of cardiac angiocrine factors during heart regeneration remains largely unexplored. The main goal of this research program is to find how vascular angiocrine factors regulate heart regeneration. Using the regenerative zebrafish model, we will learn how these factors stimulate the formation of new heart muscle after an infarct.

column36: Cortical mechanisms of visual perceptual plasticity
column37: Sensory perception allows us to interact with the world around us, and all of us are capable of learning to perceive new stimuli. How the brain implements this learning is an active area of study, but there are, broadly speaking, two possible mechanisms. The first mechanism involves changing the way neurons in the brain respond to sensory signals, and the second entails changing the connections between neurons in different brain regions. For visual perception, evidence suggests that the first method is how children learn, but that it is far less effective in adults. In this research project, we will attempt to understand the rules that govern the second kind of learning: How does the brain decide which connections to change? How much can they be changed and how quickly do the changes take place? This knowledge will allow us to design new approaches for improving visual function in normally-sighted individuals, and for restoring vision in patients who suffer from stroke or other brain injuries.

column36: The ASSET Study: Assessing economic transitions and their impacts on health and well-being
column37: Unemployment, poverty and material insecurity (e.g. housing insecurity) are key drivers of health and well-being. This is particularly the case for inner-city, drug-using populations in the context of the ongoing and conjoined overdose and COVID- 19 health emergencies, which disproportionately impact this population. The ASSET study leverages and expands an existing pilot study, seeking to examine the dynamics and impacts of innovative economic participation in the context of multiple intersecting health challenges, with a view to identifying programmatic and policy responses to improve individual health and socioeconomic well-being. The study's objectives are to: (1) identify relationships between economic activities and individual health and socioeconomic well-being; (2) examine the impacts of the pandemic and associated government responses on participants; (3) explore how participants navigate, perceive and experience economic participation; and (4) identify modifiable barriers to and facilitators of economic participation. An ongoing cohort-based evaluation with a nested qualitative component, this study employs innovative, pandemic-appropriate remote data collection techniques, drawing on quarterly surveys and annual semi-structured interviews to assess whether and how economic participation impacts the health and well- being of inner-city, drug using populations. The study will pay specific attention to naturally occurring changes in the health, service provision and policy environment. The ASSET study works with a range of community and government partners to optimize impact, will provide data for economic-opportunity-providing organizations for internal evaluations and will inform policy and programmatic responses to ongoing health emergencies. Understanding the effectiveness of strategies to disrupt the poverty-drug use-poor health nexus in times of formidable public health crises, as this study proposes, is critical to addressing health inequity.

column37: Pain in the genital and/or pelvic regions ("genitopelvic pain") affects between 14-27% of people and can have a significant impact on one's mood, relationship, and quality of life. column36: Understanding and exploiting the CIP2A-BRCA synthetic lethality
column37: Germline mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes predispose to ovarian, breast, pancreatic and prostate cancer. We carry two copies of each human gene, and when an individual carries BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations, it means that there is one dysfunctional copy of the gene and a second one that is functional. The loss of the good copy of the BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene is an important event in the formation of BRCA-deficient cancers. One objective of precision oncology is to identify and exploit vulnerabilities associated what the loss of tumor suppressor genes such as BRCA1/2. This application builds on a discovery made in my laboratory that the gene CIP2A is essential for the viability of BRCA1- and BRCA2-deficient cells. This application is rooted in the goal of understanding why CIP2A must be present in BRCA1- and BRCA2-deficient cells for their survival. We contend that this information will set the stage for the development of therapeutics that target CIP2A to kill BRCA-deficient tumours. This application consists of three aims described below: In AIM 1 we will explore the biology of CIP2A. Our preliminary results indicate that CIP2A acts to promote accurate cell division and that this function of becomes critical in the absence of BRCA1 and BRCA2. In AIM 2 we will characterize how CIP2A interacts with another protein TOPBP1. The rationale for this aim is that we discovered that CIP2A works in close partnership with TOPBP1 to carry out its function. One attractive therapeutic strategy would be to disable this interaction as a means to inhibit CIP2A. Finally, in AIM 3, we propose to lay the ground work for the development of cancer therapeutics based on the inhibition of CIP2A. Together, this work will illuminate why BRCA1 and BRCA2-deficient cells require CIP2A for this survival and how we can exploit this information so that in the long-term we develop novel, less toxic and more efficacious cancer treatments

column36: Discovery and Development of Brain-Sparing Inhibitors of Succinyl-CoA:3-Ketoacid CoA Transferase
column37: Our bodies rely on 3 major fuel sources we obtain from the food we eat; fats, sugars, and protein. However, during starvation our livers make a 4th fuel source that our organs (brain, heart, and muscle are the main users) can use to make energy, the ketone body. Past research has heavily focused on understanding the regulation of fat, sugar, and protein metabolism in health, and how they malfunction in various diseases such as obesity and diabetes. The regulation of ketone body metabolism in health and disease has received much less attention. However, exciting data in our lab has shown that decreasing the muscle's ability to burn ketone bodies for energy improves blood sugar control in obesity/diabetes. In addition, we have identified an old-group of drugs previously used to treat psychoses, which are able to decrease the ability of the muscle to burn ketone bodies for energy. Unfortunately, this old group of drugs is used less frequently for treating psychoses, due to the development of next generation anti-psychotic drugs, despite this old group of drugs being significantly cheaper. Importantly, this old group of drugs also appears to improve blood sugar control in obesity, but does have some brain-related side effects (e.g. drowsiness, dizziness, etc.) that may hinder its use as a therapy for diabetes. Thus, the goal of our research is to use both pharmaceutical science and chemistry methods to develop new drugs that are similar to these old group of drugs for psychoses, but are modified in a manner where they cannot reach the brain. We believe these new drugs may represent an exciting new treatment option to lower blood sugar levels in people with diabetes.

Participants will also do two MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scans, one at the start of the study and one at the end, to measure abdominal fat. After the trial is over, all participants will be given the choice to continue taking metformin for an additional 6 months. We believe that the patients taking metformin will lose a greater percentage of body weight than those who were given the placebo, leading to improvements in other heart disease risk factors, physical health and quality of life.

column36: Regenerative approaches to treat back-pain in mice and men
column37: Painful degeneration of the spine is one of the most common disabilities in young and middleaged professionals. However, very little is known about the cause of this pain and no early treatment options are currently available. In the body, all normal cells have a limited number of cell divisions where after they permanently stop dividing, they become "senescent". Senescent cells therefore build up in our tissues as we age. The number of senescent cells can drastically increase prematurely following DNA damaged, injury, cytokine exposure or cellular stress. This is called "premature stress induced senescence". Senescent cells were long thought to be inactive bystanders, however more recent discoveries have shown that they actively contribute to illnesses such as cancer, arthritis, and diabetes. Ageing and degenerating discs in the spine accumulate senescent cells where they act as small factories spewing out factors causing pain and inflammation along with enzymes that degrade the tissue. They also create an environment that prevents the heathy cells from building new tissue, and they may directly contribute to back pain. Recent studies in mice have shown that clearing of senescent cells slows many age-related problems which has a marked positive effect on spine health in older animals. There are several emerging drugs that remove senescent cells or that interfere with the effects of senescent cells coming close to clinical studies. Here we will test two drugs in intact human IVDs from organ donors as well as in a validated mouse model of back pain.

PAH involves the disordered and uncontrolled growth of blood vessels in the lung. This overgrowth leads to obstruction of these vessels, increased stress on the right side of the heart and eventual death due to heart failure. PAH is strongly linked to mutations in a gene called BMPR2, which encodes a protein on the surface of lung vascular cells. Interactions of this protein with a circulating factor, known as bone morphogenetic protein-9, or BMP9, has been shown to restrain the growth of lung vascular cells in healthy people. However, our previous research has shown that when the BMPR2 gene is mutated or lost, as it is in some PAH patients, BMP9 instead promotes the excessive growth of these same vascular cells. Based on this information, we hypothesize that BMP9 can serve as a "switch" that either promotes or prevents vascular growth, depending on the expression level of the BMPR2 gene. The current project will use genetically modified mice, which lack BMPR2 selectively in their blood vessels, to study the effect of BMP9 on mouse models of PAH. Additional studies will aim to understand the molecular changes within vascular cells that drive the altered BMP9 response in disease. This information will ultimately be used to develop and test candidate drugs that restore the normal growth-limiting response to BMP9, even in disease states where BMPR2 is lost. Despite the approval of several new treatments, the annual mortality rate for PAH remains high (~15%/year). The proposed work will help to clarify a completely original phenomenon that drives disease progression, with the goal of developing new treatments that are grounded in the genetics of the human disease.

column36: Overcoming Dihydrofolate Reductase Inhibitor Resistance Using Pyrimethamine-inspired Proteolysis Targeting Chimeras
column37: Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) is an important enzyme for folate metabolism and is a prominent anti-cancer and anti-inflammatory drug target. Commonly used DHFR therapies can effectively block folate metabolism, which impairs the production of building blocks needed for DNA synthesis. Despite their widespread use as cancer therapies, clinically used DHFR inhibitors frequently encounter resistance mechanisms that limit their efficacy. Resistance to classic DHFR inhibitors typically results from their similarity to dihydrofolate or due to overexpression of DHFR protein. To overcome DHFR inhibitor resistance, the proposed work uses an alternative DHFR inhibitor scaffold based on the anti-malaria drug Pyrimethamine (Pyr). As an anti-parasitic agent, Pyr binds to parasitic DHFR to halt replication of the parasite. We have recently shown that Pyr has promising anti-cancer activity, primarily through its ability to inhibit human DHFR. Using Pyr as a focal point, we will produce novel compounds that will not just inhibit DHFR, but will remove DHFR from cancer cells. This will be done using an approach known as Proteolysis Targeting Chimeras (PROTACs). PROTACs are bifunctional molecules, where one part will bind to DHFR and the other part will recruit proteins that tag DHFR for cellular destruction. We have recently demonstrated that Pyr-inspired PROTACs can block DHFR accumulation in cancer cells, which is a hallmark of DHFR inhibitor resistance. Specifically, this project aims to develop and optimize Pyr-inspired PROTACs. We will assess their ability to degrade DHFR in cancer cells and overcome DHFR inhibitor resistance. To accomplish these ambitious goals we have assembled a team with broad expertise in cancer biology, enzymology and drug discovery. We share the common aim to identify novel cancer therapies that can be used in the fight against cancer.

column36: KBTBD4 determines key epigenetic marks that govern human hematopoietic stem cell self-renewal
column37: The mechanisms that govern the expansion of human blood stem cells are poorly characterized, with the consequence that bone marrow transplantation remains unavailable to a subset of patients for which graft size is too small, resulting in prolonged engraftment and often lethal complications. We previously identified and developed a small molecule called UM171, which acts as a potent mediator of stem cell expansion with important clinical benefits, as proven in a series of completed and ongoing clinical trials. Epigenetic marks (together referred to as the epigenome) are modifications to DNA and proteins that turn genes on or off. CRL3KBTBD4 activation by UM171 prevents the loss of key epigenetic marks in human blood stem cells that undergo amplification in culture. This work positions the KBTBD4-COREST1 axis as a critical mediator of stem cell amplification. We now propose to study the role of this pathway in human blood stem cells and to understand the downstream epigenetic mechanisms responsible for its unique effector function. This is crucial for the development of improved strategies of stem cell expansion, an important limitation to the success of bone marrow transplantation and gene therapy.

column36: Stigma and the Brain Disease Model of Chronic Pain: An Empirical Bioethics Investigation
column37: Chronic pain is highly stigmatized. People living with chronic pain frequently experience doubt, skepticism, and distrust about their experiences, resulting in poor health outcomes. These harms arise largely because pain is an invisible and subjective experience. There is no clinical test that can confirm objectively that someone is experiencing chronic pain. Some neuroscientists and clinicians suggest that advances in the brain imaging of pain demonstrates that chronic pain is a brain disease. Some researchers argue that brain disease explanations of conditions such as addiction will eliminate the stigma associated with them and improve access to treatment. However, research suggests that brain disease explanations of addiction may unintentionally increase stigma and social distance. With chronic pain neuroscience following a similar trajectory, It is unknown whether brain disease explanations of chronic pain will reduce stigma. This research builds on the findings from a CIHR SPOR grant that examined perspectives from patients and healthcare professionals about the relationship between clinical brain imaging and chronic pain. The goal of the current research is to determine the pervasiveness and influence of a brain disease explanation of chronic pain on stigma specifically. We aim to: 1) Investigate the effects of a brain disease explanation of chronic pain on the degree to which adults without chronic pain stigmatize others who live with chronic pain; and 2) Explore the influence of a brain disease explanation on stigma with members of the public, chronic pain sufferers, and healthcare professionals. A secondary aim is to explore intersectional relationships between gender, brain disease explanations, stigma, racism, and pain diagnosis. Our study will contribute an evidence-informed understanding of how a brain disease explanation influences chronic pain stigma that can guide the development of anti-stigma interventions focused on chronic pain contexts.

column36: Variation in Men's Health by Cumulative Lifetime Violence Severity and Social Determinants of Health: A Longitudinal Exploratory Study
column37: Violence is a major public health problem. Men experience and commit many forms of violence across their lifetime at home, in workplaces, and in public, yet we know little about the health effects of lifetime violence for men. Health can be linked to violence through direct injury, stress effects, or behaviours such as substance use. Social determinants of health such as gender (beliefs about what it means to be a man), income, food security, and education intersect to influence health effects of violence over time. In this study, we will conduct an online survey with a national sample of 1400 English-speaking Canadian men 3 times at 12-month intervals. We will ask about their current physical and mental health, health behaviours, social factors that affect their health, and the nature and extent of violence they have experienced in their lifetime. We will evaluate a new measure of cumulative lifetime violence severity (CLVS) that reflects how men define and sustain violence as target and perpetrator across the lifespan. We will explore differences in patterns of men's experiences of CLVS as a target and/or perpetrator in childhood through adulthood and social determinants of health that are associated with health over time. Expected outcomes of this research include: 1) increased knowledge of sub-groups of violence-affected men most at-risk for negative health outcomes; 2) validation of a new measure of CLVS for men's health research; 3) insights into variation in men's health over time according to CLVS and social determinants of health; and 4) evidence of ways in which different patterns of violence are associated with health outcomes. Together, the findings of this study will help health providers, policy makers, and other stakeholders develop programs and policies to assist men most at-risk for violence-related health problems, such as depression, chronic pain and cannabis use, to promote and manage their health.

column36: Improving Patient Mental Health With Psychotherapist Virtual Training: A Practice-Research Network Study
column37: Several types of psychotherapy are equally effective to treat mental disorders. However, many patients remain symptomatic after treatment. Our team demonstrated that a professional development training program to improve psychotherapists' skills at identifying and repairing therapeutic alliance tensions resulted in improved therapeutic alliance (an important therapeutic ingredient) and patient mental health outcomes. However, we delivered this training program by conventional in-person workshops which limited access by psychotherapists living outside large urban centres. Further, post-study interviews with therapists suggested that cultural/diversity factors complicated the therapeutic alliance. We propose to test the effectiveness and acceptability of a virtually-delivered training program to psychotherapists in urban, rural, and remote areas to improve their capacity to identify and repair problems in the therapeutic alliance, including tensions related to patient diversity. We will also examine how acceptable the virtually-delivered training is to psychotherapists, and whether they would use such training in their practice. Participants in the study will be community-based licensed psychotherapists and their patients. Patient mental health outcomes, therapeutic alliance, and diversity issues will be assessed. Our team developed Canada's largest psychotherapy practice-research network and has expertise in clinical trials, diversity, and education research of virtual training. State of the art training is often out of the reach of therapists who live outside of urban centres, and the effectiveness and acceptability of providing training virtually is not well-studied in mental health care. This study will improve psychotherapists' effectiveness at managing the therapeutic alliance and issues related to diversity, and will improve patient mental health outcomes thus promising to reduce the burden of mental illness among Canadians.

column36: Post-transcriptional regulatory mechanisms of host gene expression during Leishmania infection
column37: The leishmaniases are a group of infections caused by Leishmania parasites. Globally, 12 million people are infected and 1-2 million new cases occur annually. Clinical symptoms range from cutaneous lesions to visceral pathologies that can lead to death if untreated. Unfortunately, no efficient vaccine has been developed yet and the emergence of drug resistance is a growing concern. Leishmania lives inside immune cells named macrophages, one of the most potent lines of defense against microbial invasion. To survive in such a harsh environment, Leishmania has evolved numerous mechanisms that inactivate macrophages. At the molecular level, the parasite modulates many intracellular signals required for the activation of DNA transcription into mRNA, which is the first step towards gene expression. As a result, numerous functions of the macrophage are affected. We recently demonstrated that in addition to altering transcription, Leishmania dysregulates macrophage protein synthesis, also known as mRNA translation. Our computational analyses identified subsets of host mRNAs that are differentially translated during infection which encode proteins related to mRNA metabolism and microbicidal activity. These findings led us to develop the current proposal, which is designed to explore in greater depth the mechanisms and functional consequences of altered mRNA metabolism in the progression of leishmaniasis. To this end, biochemical and genetic experimental approaches will be carried out using cellular and experimental in vivo models of Leishmania infection, and parasite strains isolated from patients living in endemic regions. The long-term goal of this study is to identify regulatory nodes implicated during leishmaniasis. Ultimately, we wish to provide insight into the pathogenesis of clinically relevant infectious organisms and to pave the way to novel therapies.

column36: Identifying a Novel Role for GDF15 during Exercise
column37: Exercise has profound effects on virtually every organ and tissue y and profoundly influences how the body utilizes carbohydrate and fats. The wide-ranging effects of exercise are mediated, at least in part, by signaling factors secreted from different tissues, such as muscle, liver and fat tissue. A recently identified signaling factor that increases with exercise is GDF15. This molecule signals to the brain and regulates food intake. In addition, we have found that GDF15 also increases the utilization of fat in the liver and the production of molecules called ketone bodies that can be taken up and used as a fuel source by other tissues like the heart and muscle. The purpose of the current project is to determine how GDF15 increases the production of ketone bodies, and then investigate if GDF15 regulates the effects of exercise on these processes. It is our hope that identifying how GDF15 controls sugar and fat metabolism and the role that it plays in exercise, will lend insight into potential new avenues to treat conditions of altered sugar metabolism such as those seen in type 2 diabetes.

column36: Better understanding care transitions of adults with complex health and social care needs: an essential step towards integrated care
column37: Adults with multiple chronic conditions who also suffer from mental health comorbidities and/or social vulnerability often have complex health and social care needs. Complex needs call for integrated care across providers, settings and sectors. A good understanding of care transitions across community, primary care, and hospital settings, remains crucial to implement models of integrated care such as case management or the patient-centered medical home. The goal of this study is to better understand care transitions of adults with complex health and social care needs across community, primary care, hospital settings. These participants will complete a questionnaire administered by phone at baseline and at 6 months to evaluate their experience of care transitions. In the second phase of the project, we will conduct: 1) individual semi-structured interviews with 4 women and 4 men per network, among participants and their family with the lowest and highest measures for care transitions; 2) focus groups (FG) of 6 participants with different providers in each network; and 3) individual semi-structured interviews with 8 managers per network. This study will deliver new scientific knowledge and empirical evidence on care transitions of patients with complex needs to inform research, healthcare policy and management, and practice, and increase knowledge and awareness among the general public.

column36: Corticospinal mechanisms of locomotor recovery after spinal cord injury
column37: Spinal cord injuries (SCI) affect 400,000 people in North America and are the second leading cause of paralysis after stroke. Current rehabilitation interventions to restore walking use intensive training protocols that target the spinal cord circuits responsible for leg muscle activation, but most do not directly engage brain structures. We developed the first neuroprosthesis that could be implanted onto or at the surface of the cortex along with an algorithm that allows timely delivery of the stimulation during locomotion. Our strategy shifts rehabilitation focus by putting voluntary brain control at its core. Results are extremely promising: after SCI in rats, our cortical neuroprosthesis immediately alleviates motor deficits and permanently reverses motor paralysis. This "proof of principle" study provides the basis to develop this technology further. In order to facilitate clinical transfer of our technology, important issues must be addressed first. These include determining how and when to apply cortical stimulation to maximize recovery of walking and restore connectivity between the motor cortex and spinal circuits below the SCI. By combining behavioral and electrophysiological techniques in an established rat model, we will determine the optimal electrode placement and time-window for delivering neurostimulation in the context of SCI and examine the mechanisms through which cortical stimulation affects recovery. Our results will support inclusion of the cortical target in rehabilitation approaches. If successful, this exciting approach could be transferred to the clinic and benefit people with SCI or stroke. Unlike currently available neurorehabilitation approach for restoring walking, our cortical neuroprosthesis holds the potential to: 1) facilitate earlier initiation of rehabilitation; 2) improve neurological recovery and support active daily movements leading to unprecedented long-term neuromotor recovery; 3) reduce the time spent in rehabilitation.

column36: Selective neuroimaging for head-injured emergency patients who take anticoagulant medication.
column37: Emergency departments are treating more people who are prescribed blood thinners (anticoagulants) than ever before. Blood thinners are helpful to prevent strokes and blood clots, but they can also increase the chances of bleeding problems. People who take blood thinners are told to go to the emergency department if they have a head injury, because they could develop a brain bleed. Until now, there has been little research on the risk of having a brain bleed after a head injury in people taking blood thinners. It was assumed that the risk of a brain bleed is high, so guidelines advise having a head CT scan even if the head injury is minor and the patient feels well. Our investigator group found that the risk of a brain bleed is not as high as once thought. Most emergency doctors use a test called the Canadian CT Head Rule to determine whether a head scan is needed for people with a head injury. In people who take blood thinners, this test almost always leads to a CT scan. Although CT scans are quite safe, unnecessary scans can cause longer wait times in the emergency department and delay scans for people who really need them. We plan to conduct the largest study ever done on people who are prescribed blood thinners with a head injury. We will develop a new bedside decision rule (or test) which will tell the doctor if a CT scan is needed or not. The study will recruit 5000 emergency department patients from Canada, the United States and Britain. Patients are entered into the study if they are on blood thinners and come to the emergency department with a head injury. Everyone will have a head scan as customary, and we will develop the new rule at the end of the study. If our new rule is safe and effective, it would not only reduce unnecessary CT scans but also allow physicians to immediately reassure many patients that they do not have a brain bleed.

column36: Semaphorin regulation of retinal neurogenesis and regeneration
column37: Retinal degenerative diseases such as glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy exhibit devastating vision loss, each as a result of the death over time of specific types of eye cell. Each disease needs the affected cell types to be replaced, and for the new cells to integrate into functional vision circuits. Thus, we need to explore how different types of eye cell are made and in the right proportions. Importantly, we need to understand these events in the adult eye, because the blueprints likely differ from those for eye cell production in the fetus, from where most of our knowledge comes. The problem is that the mammalian eye is incapable of replacing new eye cells when they degenerate. This is not true in the eyes of adult fish, which retain two subpopulation of cells that allow the eye and retinal circuits to grow throughout life, and that in response to retinal injury are activated and replace lost cells. Importantly, these two classes of cells are also present in the mammalian adult retina, but do not respond to retinal damage by making new cells. The fish eye has the same main classes of eye cells, and with similar functions, as those in humans. Thus, we want to understand how new cells are generated in the fish adult eye, and how these pathways can be harnessed in repair programs after retinal cell loss. We have identified related proteins in the zebrafish eye, Semaphorin3fa and Semaphorin3fb, that our data indicate act on the two key cell populations, both as these cells continue to provide new cells for the ever-expanding eye visual circuits, and as they ramp up their activities in response to eye damage. We will explore their roles in both contexts with the hope of understanding how to transform the dormant cells of the human adult eye into progenitors like their fish counterparts, so that they too can replace specific eye cell types that get lost in each of the degenerative retinal diseases.

column36: Mechanisms of diabetes and aging in constitutively active, phosphorylation-resistant pRb knockin mice
column37: The tumor suppressor pRb is regulated by cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) that phosphorylate and inactivate it, leading to uncontrolled cell division. Conversely, inhibition of pRb phosphorylation suppresses cell division. Over the years, many studies with cultured cells were used to define a model for pRb function, where this protein was thought to stop cells from transitioning between a so-called growth phase (G1) and the DNA duplication S-phase, but this model has never been tested in mice, and the consequences of blocking pRb phosphorylation on development and homeostasis are not known. We have directly tested this model in mice and found, to our great surprise, that blocking pRb phosphorylation (RbdeltaK7) leads to various signs of aging, including inhibition of pancreatic beta-cell regeneration, induction of senescence (permanent cell cycle exit) and diabetes. Strikingly, diabetes was attenuated by feeding RbdeltaK7 mice on vitamin C diet. We hypothesize that pancreatic islets of RbdeltaK7 mice provide a unique platform to study diabetes and cellular regeneration during aging. In this project, we will use RbdeltaK7 mice to define: i) the senescence and aging phenotypes of pancreatic RbdeltaK7 islets, ii) whether pancreatic beta-cells in RbdeltaK7 mice enter a repressive state that prevents cell cycle re-entry, and iii) whether specific elimination of senescent cells together with vitamin C can cure diabetes and extend lifespan of RbdeltaK7 mice and a mouse model of type 1 diabetes.

column36: Peptidoglycan remodeling in Campylobacter jejuni: effects on shape and pathogenesis
column37: Campylobacter jejuni (Cj) is a leading cause of bacterial food poisoning in humans in the developed world. Yet, it lives harmlessly in the intestinal tract of birds, with up to 90% of commercial poultry products having live Cj on their surfaces. Furthermore, unlike most other prevalent pathogens, its specific pathogenic mechanisms have remained elusive. Through genetic and computer-based screening, we have uncovered several new factors and means by which this pathogen is so successful in causing human disease, colonizing non-susceptible (commensal) hosts, and surviving in the environment outside of a host. One is its shape. Cj typically has a helical/corkscrew morphology, and this abets its ability to burrow into the intestinal mucosa of both susceptible (i.e., human) and commensal (i.e., poultry) hosts and to survive in inhospitable environments such as air and water. Changes to this shape alter Cj's ability to succeed in specific niches. Our group has identified the first bacterial factors and biochemical characteristics important for maintaining Cj's helical cell morphology. All of these affect the peptidoglycan layer of the bacterial cell wall. We will use genetic, biochemical, and other approaches to further our understanding of how shape is determined and maintained in Cj, and the biological and pathogenic implications of Cj morphology. Given the importance of Cj shape to its success as a pathogen, this work should provide important insights into Cj biology, how and why Cj is such a prevalent cause of human disease, and clues to its eradication.

column36: How do communication behaviours contribute to and buffer against suicidal and self-injurious acts in couples wherein one member has borderline personality disorder?
column37: Suicidal behavior and self-injury (SSI) in borderline personality disorder (BPD) is often prompted by relationship problems, but it is unclear how intimate partners of those with BPD influence SSI. Such information is key to understand whether and how incorporating partners into BPD treatments may help reduce SSI. We aim to study the ways that intimate partners talk to those with BPD in general and about SSI, and immediately respond to SSI, that predict a higher or lower likelihood of it happening again. First, we will examine if individuals with BPD and their intimate partner's communication in general and about SSI specifically interplays with their emotion to predict SSI. Next, we will identify how intimate partners immediately respond to SSI in those with BPD, and whether specific types of responses make it more or less likely to recur. Finally, we will develop a new method of measuring how intimate partners immediately respond to SSI in those with BPD. 250 people with BPD who engage in SSI and their intimate partners will complete measures negative emotion, general and SSI-specific communication, and SSI once every three months for a year (four times total), and on their smartphones ~5 times per day for 30 days. On their smart phones, intimate partners will also describe how they immediately respond to SSI, and the first 20 intimate partners will further describe this in an interview. These responses will be used to categorize types of immediate responses to SSI so that we can examine which types predict a higher or lower likelihood of SSI happening again. A questionnaire measuring types of immediate responses will also be developed based on smart phone and interview data, which will be evaluated in our sample. Findings will provide critical information about what partners should do or not do to reduce SSI in those with BPD. They will also guide future research on BPD and SSI by providing a new measure of immediate responses to SSI in intimate partners.

column36: Co-designed cultural safety in Nunavik: proof-of-impact
column37: Hospital care in Nunavik depends heavily on non-Inuit health professionals. This raises issues of cultural safety for Inuit, who need to feel their health care is spiritually, socially, emotionally and physically safe. Lack of cultural safety often accompanies interpersonal and systemic racism. There is no standard way to implement cultural safety, because it is specific to different groups and even to individual communities. It is also tricky to reduce systemic racism when the official position of the Quebec government is that this does not exist. Cultural safety in Nunavik must "walk on two legs", with Inuit patients and communities authoring cultural safety and non-Inuit health workers authoring alternatives to racism. Scoping reviews will collate literature on cultural safety and anti-racism interventions. Cognitive mapping will collate how Inuit and non-Inuit see cultural safety and racism. Focus groups or key informant interviews will clarify words and issues surfaced by the mapping. Surveys will measure experiences of cultural safety or its absence. This evidence will feed evidence into deliberative dialogue, allowing service providers and communities to co-design evidence-based solutions. A year4 repeat survey will compare (before/after) health and care seeking behaviours, and ripple effects like cultural continuity and job satisfaction of service providers. A narrative evaluation will document the most significant change for service providers and Inuit communities. We will develop multi-media training modules for non-Inuit and Inuit health workers and for other health facilities wanting to develop community-led cultural safety and anti-racism interventions. This participatory research engages Inuit communities and the hospitals serving them, the Nunavik Regional Board for Health and Social Services (TBC) and McGill Family Medicine. The project will last five years.

column36: Preventing Sedentary Lifestyles among Children Born with Congenital Heart Defects: A Feasibility Study of Physical Activity after Surgical or Catheterization Intervention
column37: 3,500 Canadian children born each year have heart problems (CHD). We target their most important long term health problems (heart attack, obesity, mental illness) so they not only survive, but thrive! Physical activity reduces these health risks but <10% of children with CHD meet Canadian physical activity recommendations. We have shown that the least active toddlers with CHD remain the least active children at 5 years of age, emphasizing the importance of early & better support. Before evaluating the benefits of physical activity support for young children with CHD, we need to test the feasibility and potential effectiveness of our research idea. Since no one has tried this type of project before, this project will evaluate whether families will agree to participate at the time of their child's treatment, if they are willing to complete 5 physical activity assessments, if children can do the play-based activities immediately after treatment, and if we have the required space and staff time. We will also gather preliminary information on whether the play activities can improve the children's physical activity. For 18 months, we will ask all 100 children treated for CHD to participate in our study. We expect 48 will finish the study; 36 receiving play activities, 12 receiving only standard care (waitlist) for 12 months. Each child's movement skill, daily activity, social skills and quality of life will be tested 5 times (start, week 7, months 6, 12 & 16). We will count how many children start and complete the study, reasons they withdraw, whether they can do all of the tests and how often they do the play activities. The study outcomes will be the feasibility and efficacy data needed to plan a randomized controlled trial to assess our play intervention benefits during CHD-treatment.

column36: Transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation of mammalian developmental pausing
column37: After fertilization, an embryo grows rapidly with a fixed timing and pattern towards increased complexity, without "looking back". However, embryos can in some instances enter a reversible state of "suspended animation", where they remain alive but not developing. This "holding pattern", or developmental pausing, is often triggered by unfavorable conditions, such as scarcity of nutrients. It is becoming appreciated that this pausing behavior can also occur in adult cells as well as in dormant cancer cells that remain after chemotherapy and can regrow tumors. Despite this broad relevance, we have a poor understanding of the genes and cellular pathways that mediate developmental pausing, particularly in mammals. Our team discovered that inhibition of a key growth-promoting enzyme, called mTor, induces pausing of early mouse embryos, which can in this way be kept in the laboratory for prolonged periods of time without developing further. Inhibition of mTor also leads to pausing of mouse and human embryonic stem cells, which can be cultured in the laboratory indefinitely. We have gathered as-yet unpublished results that are beginning to provide clues as to what are the critical genes and pathways that make pausing happen. Therefore, we now have in hand powerful new tools and insights that will allow an understanding of the regulation of developmental pausing in mammals. This proposal will dissect the molecular and cellular mechanisms that underlie developmental pausing. We will take advantage of the extensive expertise of our team and that of our collaborators in genomics, biochemistry, developmental biology and stem cell biology. These studies will reveal fundamental new insights into the regulation of developmental timing and will provide new therapeutic opportunities for Infertility, Regenerative Medicine, Aging and Cancer.

column36: Illuminating the genetic forces driving development by profiling with single cell transcriptomics at thousands of time-points
column37: Biology has entered a new era of precision measurement. Techniques like single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single cell ATAC-seq have emerged as powerful tools to sample the complexity of large populations of cells and observe biological processes at unprecedented molecular resolution. One of the most exciting prospects associated with this new trove of data is the possibility of studying temporal processes, such as differentiation and development. If we could understand the genetic forces that control embryonic development, we would understand how cell types are stabilized throughout adult life and how they destabilize in diseases like cancer and with age. This would be within reach if we could analyze the dynamic changes in gene expression, as populations develop and subpopulations differentiate. However, this is not possible with current measurement technologies because they are destructive (in the sense that the cell must be lysed before its expression profile is measured). A number of recent research efforts have tackled this by collecting snap-shots of single cell expression profiles along a time-course and then computationally inferring trajectories from the static snap-shots. We argue that this inference problem is easier with more data, and the right way to measure the "size" of a data set is really the number of time-points, not the number of cells. We propose to collect the first single cell RNA-seq time-course with more than one thousand distinct temporal snapshots, and we develop a novel mathematical and conceptual framework to analyze the data. This tremendous temporal resolution will give us unprecedented statistical power to discover the genetic forces controlling development. To the best of our knowledge, no single study has collected more than 50 distinct temporal snapshots. Our proposal represents a technological leap, comparable to the leap from plate-based scRNA-seq to droplet-based methods.

column36: Comprehensive characterizations for the molecular and evolutionary mechanisms of beta-lactam 'resistome'
column37: Bacteria, such as P. aeruginosa. E. coli, K. pneumonia, and A. baumannii, can cause serious infectious diseases, including pneumonia, urinary tract infections, and diarrhea. During the past decade, the increasingly rapid spread of bacteria that are resistant to multiple antibiotics has become a real threat to our health systems. A major underlying cause for bacterial resistance is the action of a group of enzymes called beta-lactamases, which destroy beta-lactam antibiotics. Our overall understanding of those enzymes is still limited despite extensive studies in the past decades. We must develop our comprehensive understanding of beta-lactamases, in particular, 'hidden' potentials and limitations of the reservoir of beta-lactam resistance that provide future resistance, in particular, our newly developed last resort antibiotics. In this research project, we aim to develop a comprehensive understanding for beta-lactamases. In particular, we will investigate evolutionary potentials and limitations of beta-lactam 'resistome' against newly developed clinical and preclinical beta-lactam antibiotics and lactamase inhibitors. We will combine large scale bioinformatics and cutting-edge genetic technology to unveil the sequence-function relationships for all four major classes of beta-lactamases (class A, B, C and D), with an emphasis on beta-lactamases that have been spread among pathogens and non-pathogenic environmental microbes. We will also conduct high-throughput beta-lactamase characterizations and experimental evolution to unveil evolutionary potentials and limitations of several major clinically associated beta-lactamase types. Our research program will greatly advance our understanding of beta-lactamases, and the information obtained in this research will be used to develop robust surveillance programs and mitigation strategies for controlling and preventing further evolution and dissemination of beta-lactamases.

column37: Background: The use of healthcare by Inuit (and other Indigenous groups in Canada) are complicated by negative experiences with the healthcare system. There is an urgent need to improve opportunities for Inuit to use healthcare. Shared decision making (SDM) is a strategy that promotes client participation in health decisions and leads to improved health outcomes for clients. SDM has strong potential to facilitate better healthcare participation by Inuit with healthcare providers. The goal of our study is to develop and test SDM education for healthcare providers who work with Inuit. Methods: Our team of Inuit-led and-service providers and researchers from Ontario and Nunavut will work together ("the Team). We will use a collaborative research approach and we will be guided by Inuit societal values in our work. Our plan is to use mixed research methods to do a research study. First, we will use interviews to understand what healthcare providers need to learn so that they are able to support Inuit clients in health decisions. Then, our Team will work together to develop SDM education for health care providers. We will ask some health care provider volunteers to try out the training so that we can learn how to make the SDM education most useful to health care providers. Next, we will invite 20-30 healthcare providers to do the SDM education. We will use surveys and interviews to assess whether the SDM education is helpful for these healthcare providers for making health decisions with Inuit clients. We will also use surveys to ask Inuit clients about their experience with healthcare providers who have done the SDM education. Finally, we will assess how we worked together as a Team to do our study. Results: In our study we expect to develop and test SDM education for healthcare providers. We will share our experiences and will be an example for other teams who want to work together to do a research study.

column36: Identifying a high-resolution map of dynamic cellular and molecular trajectories during the development of a whole mammalian body
column37: The dynamic behavior of cells during development, tumorigenesis and other disorders remain largely unclear. The genomic DNA of a cell stores the blueprint of life in sequences that can be represented by four basic residues, Adenine (A), Cytosine (C), Guanine (G), and Thymine (T). It has been proposed that DNA can be utilized as an extremely small, robust, and heritable form of information storage media. This project will develop "DNA event recording" systems by which high-resolution information of cells is progressively stored in cell-embedded "DNA tapes." Coupled with high-throughput single-cell sequencing technologies, such a system would enable access to molecular and cellular history information of cells at the time of observation and provide a way of observing the dynamics of complex biological systems in high-resolution. Like a tape recorder, DNA event recording requires (1) "memory" such as high-capacity DNA "tapes" embedded in chromosomes, (2) "signal to information conversion" such as molecular sensors to capture cell lineage and differentiation, (3) information "writers" such as genome editing technologies, and (4) an information "reader" such as high-performance computing systems. We will extend the development of genetic circuits, mouse and cell engineering, and high-performance computing technologies that we have successfully piloted for these four system requirements and obtain a whole-body cell lineage and cell type differentiation map of mammalian (mouse) development at the resolution of single cells. The whole-body mammalian developmental map will be an essential resource for life and health sciences and for the education of generations to come.

column37: A series of discoveries spanning the last decade has shifted our view of microglia, the brain's immune cells, by showing their essential but previously unexpected contribution to brain development, as well as their important functions in learning and memory, and in behavioural adaptation to various environmental challenges (pollution, stress, inadequate nutrition, viral infection, etc.) during life. column36: Investigating the role of exercise-linked irisin in Alzheimer's disease
column37: The aging population in Canada and prevalence of Alzheimer's disease (AD) is increasing rapidly. Although exactly how the brain becomes dysfunctional in AD is still uncertain, it is known that memory centers in the brain are affected. In particular, synapses, that allow communication between brain cells and memory formation, are disrupted in AD and the decreased actions of hormones in the brain have also been associated with dementia. Here, we will investigate the role of irisin - a novel hormone boosted by physical exercise- in memory processes. We already found that AD patients have less irisin in the brain, and that memories are not formed when brain irisin is depleted in mice. In contrast, when the brain is supplemented with irisin, memory impairments are prevented. Here, we propose to investigate if a gene therapy approach that increases irisin can reproduce or even boost the beneficial actions of exercise in memory. Counteracting decreases in brain irisin, either through gene therapy or exercise, has the potential to keep brain cells healthy and connected, effectively combating loss of brain function, including memory, in AD.

column36: Determining the molecular mechanisms of titin's role in active force production in striated muscles
column37: Textbooks of muscle physiology state that muscle contraction and force production are entirely accounted for by two proteins, actin and myosin. This actin and myosin-based theory was developed in the mid-1950 by Nobel Prize winner Andrew Huxley, and it has remained unchallenged for the past half century. However, in 2002, we discovered a new mechanical property of muscle, referred to as "passive force enhancement". This property allows muscles to produce much more force at a lower energetic cost than can be accounted for by the actin-myosin theory. We identified that this additional, unexplained force was contributed by a structural protein called "titin". However, despite extensive research in this newly discovered area of muscle physiology and mechanics over the past decade, it remains unclear how titin produces this unexplained extra force. The primary objective of our research is to determine the molecular details of titin's function and its contribution to muscle contraction and force production. Ten years ago, we proposed a mechanism for titin's function in muscle contraction that has become the most accepted theory because of its simplicity and intuitive appeal. We hypothesized that titin increases its stiffness when a muscle is activated in two ways: (i) by binding calcium to specific sites thereby reinforcing its molecular bonds, and (ii) by titin's proximal segments binding to actin, thus decreasing titin's spring length and thus making it stiffer. The first of these mechanisms has been proved correct, the second is the topic of the research proposed here. Recently genetic changes in titin's structure have been associated with skeletal muscle diseases (dystrophies) and with many cardiac myopathies (heart diseases and heart failures), particularly those associated with an unnatural expansion of the heart. Understanding titin's function in normal muscles and hearts might help treat/prevent some of the skeletal and heart muscle diseases in the future.

column36: Development of innovative therapeutic strategies in cystic fibrosis for improvement of CFTR-targeted treatments and restoration of airway epithelial integrity in infected lungs from patients harboring various mutations
column37: Cystic fibrosis (CF), the most common fatal genetic disease in Canada, is due to mutations in the gene coding for a protein called CFTR. Although CF affects many organs, the progressive lung damage due to bacterial infections remains the first cause of mortality. Several years ago, we thus decided to devote our efforts to identify novel therapeutic strategies to promote CF lung repair. We first discovered that the capability of CF airways to repair after injury is less efficient than in healthy subjects, due to both the CFTR dysfunction and the presence of infections. Our work also unveiled that CFTR rescue with new compounds called modulators (potentiator/correctors) significantly enhances airway repair, but CFTR rescue and repair improvement are dampened by the bacterial infectious environment. Importantly, we identified new avenues to counteract the deleterious effect of infection on CFTR rescue and airway repair. Moreover, we have new data supporting that lung repair could be improved with treatments targeting bacterial virulence and combining CFTR modulators with activators of another class of ion channels (i.e. potassium (K+) channels). Using airway epithelial cells collected from CF patients, our first aim is now to dissect how CFTR rescue regulates airway epithelial repair processes. Then, we will investigate new avenues interfering with virulence factors from the main pathogens found in lungs from CF children and adults, i.e. S. aureus and P. aeruginosa, in order to enhance the efficiency of CFTR modulators in infectious conditions. Finally, our aim is to identify the most effective strategies with CFTR modulators, K+ channel activators and compounds interfering with bacteria, to improve the repair of damaged lung tissues from infected CF patients harboring various types of mutations. Our project will give important insights paving the way to innovative strategies for improved CFTR-targeted treatments and restoration of lung integrity.

column36: Associations of Childhood Emotional and Behavioural Problems with Medical Services Utilization and Costs: A Life Course Study
column37: In Canada, 1 in 3 children have emotional and/or behavioural issues, such as anxiety, depression, social withdrawal, rule-breaking, opposition, and aggression. These problems can continue into adulthood, with increased risk of injuries, substance abuse, obesity, and suicide attempts. Patterns of healthcare usage throughout life remain largely undocumented and are essential for planning more effective services for adults with mental health issues. Our objectives are threefold. First, to identify medical services (physical and mental health) used over the course of a lifetime by individuals who had behavioural or emotional problems as a child. This includes doctors' visits, visits to the emergency department, and hospitalizations. The second is to determine associated costs. In analyzing results, we will see if there are differences in use, costs, and patterns between men and women, stages in life, and types of health issues. Third, a preventive intervention was set up in 1984 in schools of low-income neighbourhoods in Quebec, to help the most disruptive boys in Grades 1-2. We want to see if this program actually reduced medical visits and costs by the time the boys reach middle age (40-44 years). To accomplish these 3 goals, we will follow children who were in kindergarten in 1984 (boys) and 1987 (boys and girls), i.e. the Montreal Longitudinal Experimental Study (MLES, n=1037) and the Quebec Longitudinal Study of Kindergarten Children (QLSKC, n=5401). Students were assessed yearly by their teachers at ages 6-12. We will link data to Quebec healthcare databases. This study will be the first to describe patterns of use and costs from childhood to teenage years to young adulthood and middle age. Findings can be useful for teachers (often first-line in identifying problem behaviour; instrumental in delivering interventions); for patients, for optimal treatment; and for society, in reducing economic burden and strain on the healthcare system.

column36: Perioperative Anticoagulant Use for Surgery Evaluation -Virtual Visit (PAUSE-Virtual), a simple perioperative anticoagulant management approach, replacing a resource-intensive in-person doctor-patient consultation, with a simple virtual care model that will provide a new standard of care for patients on a Direct Oral Anticoagulant or warfarin and require elective surgery/procedure.
column37: The purpose of the PAUSE-Virtual Study is to show that by changing pre-surgery visits with patients taking a blood thinner (direct oral anticoagulant (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, rivaroxaban or warfarin) when they require elective surgery, using a standard, in-person proven approach, to a virtual visit, either telephone or video conference, is as safe. Patients who are receiving a blood thinner for the medical condition known as atrial fibrillation (AF) and require an elective surgery/procedure, is common. These patients have to stop taking their blood thinner for a certain time before the procedure to reduce serious complications of stroke or bleeding. For doctors who help manage these patients before a procedure, appointments have been traditionally done in-person. Patients receive instructions about when to stop and restart their blood thinners and taught how to self-administrator a short acting blood thinner (heparin) if needed. The COVID pandemic changed the way these appointments were done, making it important to contact these patients without them having to come to the hospital for an in-person visit. Virtual patient care, by telephone or video conference, to communicate to patients about when to start and restart their blood thinner was necessary. This study wants to show that this virtual method of instruction, using a standardized plan of managing patient care, is easy, acceptable to patients and as safe when compared to an in-person meeting. Such instruction would also be cost-efficient standard post-pandemic. Prior work has shown us that both a standard care of patients who are receiving blood thinners and a point-of-care decision "app", available through Thrombosis Canada (www.thrombosiscanada.ca) website, has been trusted by hematologist's during this virtual visit successfully. We will show, by following up at 30 days, that this standardized management plan is safe and can be done virtually, with a low risk of stroke and major bleeding.

column36: B cell-intrinsic insulin resistance as a mechanism of obesity-linked immune dysfunction
column37: Obesity predisposes to insulin resistance (IR), a state where the body responds poorly to the metabolic hormone, insulin. Obesity/IR pose a significant global health threat, as the accompanying inflammatory changes in obese individuals sprout serious health complications such as cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. In addition, obesity and IR undermine immune function and are associated with significantly elevated risks of severe infections and mortality, as exemplified by the H1N1 influenza pandemic (2009) and the current COVID19 pandemic. Complex physiological changes and immune-endocrine interactions are thought to contribute to the observed immune defects, although the precise mechanisms are not well understood. Following the clues that insulin resistance can occur in a manner that is intrinsic to immune cells, and that insulin receptor on immune cells modulate their metabolism and function, we hypothesize that insulin resistance in immune cells, such as B cells, is a major link between obesity and an impaired anti-viral response, leading to increased disease severity and associated mortality. In this study, we will explore the role of the insulin receptor by deleting it from B cells, a type of white blood cells that mediate protective immune responses by secreting antibodies. We will also utilize a high fat diet-fed obese mouse model to study the adverse effects of obesity and IR on B cell function during severe respiratory infections with H1N1 influenza. Importantly, we will determine whether the severity of these infections can be improved with drugs used to treat diabetes. Findings from this study will provide new and important insights into how obesity impacts B cell function, and lay a foundation for the development of therapeutic/vaccination strategies to better cater to the obese, insulin resistant population during current and future viral pandemics.

column36: Brain Insulin Sensitivity and Reward Behavior in Major Depressive Disorder
column37: Depression and metabolic problems, such as diabetes mellitus and obesity are common, impactful and frequently co-occurring medical conditions. Approximately half of the individuals diagnosed with depression have obesity or diabetes; whereas depressive symptoms are among the most frequently reported symptoms in individuals with diabetes mellitus. Anhedonia, defined as markedly diminished interests or pleasure in all, or almost all, activities, is a common symptom reported by both individuals with depression and metabolic conditions. Anhedonia is typically a very difficult to treat problem and has been associated to poor functional recovery and premature mortality. New approaches to understand anhedonia are urgently needed. Insulin is a hormone which plays a key role in the regulation of blood sugar levels and in the storage of fat. It is prominently involved in conditions such as obesity and diabetes. Evidence from multiple lines of research suggests that insulin might also affect the brain, particularly in the areas involved in the regulation of anhedonia. This application proposes to study the relationship between insulin, anhedonia and depression. We propose to study how insulin signaling in the brain and in the body can affect anhedonia's behaviors and brain circuits. A better understanding of the relationship between anhedonia and insulin has the potential to advance further the knowledge on the processes underlying the co-occurrence of mood and metabolic disorders, and to potentially substantiate the development of new preventive and therapeutic interventions.
