column36: Models for Primary Medical Care, Nursing Care and Personal Care in Long-Term Care Homes: Systematic Reviews to Inform Change in Canada
column37: Older adults are a rapidly growing segment of the population and live longer and healthier lives than in previous generations. In 2014, adults aged 65+ years accounted for six million (15.6%) of Canada's population, and the government estimates that by 2030, this number will surpass 9.5 million (23%). The impact of COVID-19 in long-term care homes (LTCH) in Canada highlighted longstanding challenges in this sector. Recently, a Canadian policy briefing addressed these challenges in Canada's long-term care (LTC) sector, and made recommendations that changes be made to the healthcare workforce. Amongst the most vital issues to address are improvements for the provision of primary medical care for LTC residents, as well as for direct care provided by nurses and personal support workers. To do so, there is an urgent need for researchers to identify and review the currently available research in this area to support comparisons of different models of care and their impact on key measures such as quality of resident care, resident quality of life and hospital admissions. To address this need, we will conduct two systematic reviews of currently available research to answer the following questions: 1. What are the effective models for primary medical care for residents of LTCHs to optimize their quality of care, quality of life and health outcomes? 2. What are the effective models for direct care (including nursing care and personal care) for residents of LTCHs to optimize their quality of care, quality of life and health outcomes? We will use best practice methods to carry out the planned systematic reviews of the evidence with a multi-disciplinary research team having expertise in public health, geriatric medicine and epidemiology. We will partner with Canadian organizations in the LTC setting to disseminate our findings and to maximize their uptake toward optimizing long-term care homes for Canadians.

column36: The Safety of Antipsychotic Drugs Among Children and Youth With Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorder
column37: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a mental health disorder characterized by hyperactive and impulsive behaviors. Treatments include cognitive behavioral therapy and prescription drugs (e.g., Ritalin), which are prescribed when behavioral therapies are not sufficient to improve symptoms. Antipsychotic drugs are not approved for use among children with behavioral problems such as ADHD. However, antipsychotic drugs are increasingly being prescribed to children with such conditions despite the minimal evidence available regarding their safety when used in this setting. Recently, safety concerns have emerged regarding possible harmful effects, including potential increased risks of metabolic disease (overweight or obesity), diabetes, cardiac arrhythmias (abnormal heart rhythms), and cardiac death (dying due to heart problems). Clinical trials conducted in children mainly addressed whether antipsychotic drugs are effective. Their safety has only been examined in a limited number of studies conducted in real-world settings. These studies examined the risks of weight gain, diabetes, and death among children prescribed antipsychotic drugs for ADHD. However, these studies had important methodological flaws. In addition, the use of antipsychotic drugs for ADHD is typically at much lower doses than for other conditions and in conjunction with approved ADHD drugs. High quality studies that use real-world data are needed to evaluate the safety of antipsychotic drugs among children with ADHD. To address this knowledge gap, we will use data from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink, a large clinical database. We will compare the risks of overweight or obesity, diabetes, high cholesterol levels, and heart problems among children with ADHD prescribed antipsychotics versus approved ADHD drugs. This study will provide regulatory agencies with important information on the safety of "off-label" use antipsychotic drugs in this vulnerable population.

column36: Making an impact on rural health: Scaling-out and evaluating the implementation and effectiveness of an evidence-based diabetes prevention program across Interior British Columbia
column37: In the past 15 years, type 2 diabetes (T2D) rates have risen faster in the British Columbia Interior compared to the rest of the Canadian population. A recent environmental scan conducted in Interior British Columbia demonstrated a lack of capacity to deliver diabetes prevention services, particularly in rural towns. Small Steps for Big Changes (SSBC) is a diet and exercise counselling intervention that has been effective as a community-based program for lowering T2D risk in individuals with prediabetes. SSBC has been delivered in two urban city sites in Interior BC. The next phase is to expand delivery of SSBC to five rural community sites where T2D rates are high and no prediabetes programs exist. Partnerships from different sectors, and community-delivery are necessary for successful uptake and meaningful healthcare impact. Having established a formal partnership with the YMCA of Okanagan in 2017, we are well-positioned to deliver and evaluate the implementation and effectiveness of the SSBC program adapted to rural sites. In Year 1, the program will be adapted through partnership with site-level implementation teams, and YMCA staff will receive training for program delivery. Delivery of SSBC to community members (60/site; total = 300) will begin in Year 2. To evaluate the implementation of SSBC, we will examine number of staff trained and patients enrolled in the program, patient attendance, sessions delivered as planned, delivery costs, and number of sites continuing to deliver the program in Years 3 and 4. YMCA staff and SSBC patients will also be interviewed on how well they receive the program. To evaluate program effectiveness, changes in patient health (e.g., blood glucose, weight, physical activity, diet) will be measured over two years following program completion. Evaluating the implementation and effectiveness of SSBC will result in a template for scaling-out a diabetes prevention program that can service the many rural communities of Canada.

column36: The mechanisms underlying signaling by the HDL-receptor SR-B1 in myeloid cells and role in protection against coronary artery atherosclerosis
column37: High density lipoproteins are called "good cholesterol" because high levels of HDL in blood protect against heart disease. This protection is partly due to the ability of HDL to prevent the accumulation of fat that clogs arteries and leads to heart attacks and stroke. The research we are proposing in this application aims to understand how HDL interacts with cells in the artery wall to bring about this protection. We are proposing to analyze the molecular events that are triggered by the interaction of HDL with different cells in the artery wall, and will test the roles of some of the cellular machinery that is either involved in the interaction or which is activated by it. We will then test the roles of the key cellular factors in a unique mouse model of coronary artery disease and heart attack. These mice lack the HDL receptor and develop blocked coronary arteries and heart attack when fed a high fat diet. We showed that we can prevent this by transplanting stem cells containing the intact HDL receptor gene--these stem cells go on to give rise to all blood cells including macrophages, which play a key role in the formation of blocked arteries. This model system will allow us to test the roles of other genes that might be involved in this pathway, downstream of the HDL receptor. The results from this study will give us important information on the molecular and cellular pathways that underlie how HDL protects against hardening of the arteries and will lead to new targets for drug development and new ideas for treatment of disease in humans.

column36: The role of the acid sensing ion channel (ASIC) 1a in the mechanism of action of the ketogenic diet in infantile spasms
column37: Infantile spasms is a rare but devastating epilepsy for which treatment oftentimes do not work. Because of this, children with infantile spasms frequently develop other seizure types and do not learn to talk, walk or care for themselves. Moreover one third of children with infantile spasms will die due to the uncontrolled seizures. A high fat low carbohydrate diet known as the ketogenic diet is emerging as an effective treatment for infantile spasms even in those patients who do not respond to current first-line treatments. The diet however is fraught with side effects and difficult for patients tolerate. It is important to determine how the diet works in infantile spasms so that safe, effective and tolerable treatments can be developed. This timely proposal is directed at uncovering precisely how the ketogenic diet works in infantile spasms. We've discovered in a model of infantile spasms that the ketogenic diet works by making the brain acidic. Correcting this acidity significantly attenuated the antiseizure effects of the ketogenic diet. We hypothesized that the acidity in the brain induced by the ketogenic diet works to control seizures by activating acid sensing ion channels. Our preliminary results show that deleting these channels in the brain using advanced gene editing techniques abolished the antiseizure effects of the ketogenic diet. This proposal describes important experiments to 1) determine how acid sensing ion channels are involved in the anti-seizure effects of the ketogenic diet, 2) determine whether acid sensing ion channels in all brain cells are involved in the ketogenic diet's antiseizure effects or a subtype thereof 3) to test new treatments that will strengthen the ability of acidosis to activate acid sensing ion channels for the treatment of infantile spasms. The goal is to identify a treatment strategy for infantile spasms that will bring us one step closer to eliminating this catastrophic form of epilepsy from the pediatric population.

column36: The Development and Evaluation of An Evidence-informed, Competency-based, Accredited Compassion Training Program for Healthcare Providers Caring for Older Adults-The EnACT Study
column37: Older adults living with life-limiting health conditions want and deserve to receive healthcare that is compassionate. Despite healthcare providers' (HCPs) desire and healthcare organizations' attempts to provide compassion to this vulnerable and growing patient/resident population, the media, healthcare literature, and high-profile health inquires have all reported a seeming lack of compassion in our hospital and residential care settings. The consequences of these experiences are significant, including lower patient/resident well-being, poorer health outcomes, higher healthcare costs, increased patient/family complaints and greater rates of HCP burnout. As a result, HCPs and healthcare organizations are increasingly expected to improve the compassionate care they provide to patients/residents. A significant challenge to enhancing compassion is the lack of compassion training programs for HCPs. This study builds on our previous research investigating compassion within healthcare which produced the first patient model of compassion and a valid and reliable patient-reported compassion measure. The aim of the current study is to develop an evidence-informed, competency-based, and accredited compassion training program for HCPs who care for older adults in hospitals, hospices, and residential care. To accomplish this, we will first develop, and pilot test the proposed training program after assessing the needs of HCP learners and the care settings they work in. We will then examine the initial impact of compassion training on patient/resident care and HCP wellbeing and assess the feasibility of conducting a larger clinical research trial to evaluate the effectiveness of the final training program. Lastly, we will work with HCPs, healthcare organizations, educators, and leaders to develop resources and communication strategies to raise awareness of the compassion training program and to ensure that it is incorporated into clinical practice and healthcare organizations.

column36: The Digital Marketing of Unhealthy Food and Beverages to Children and Youth: Examining Gendered Differences in Exposure and Impact
column37: The prevalence of obesity amongst Canadian children and youth has tripled since the 1980's. One factor that contributes to obesity is the over consumption of junk foods that are high in salt, sugar, and/or fat. Disparities in health exist amongst children and youth, with males having higher rates of obesity and consuming more added sugar and sodium compared to females. Unhealthy food marketing promotes poor dietary behaviours among children and youth and is likely contributing to differences in food intake and obesity between males and females. Youth have access to multiple digital devices, spend considerable time online and are exposed to high levels of unhealthy food marketing in digital media which may worsen sex differences in health. To date, little research has examined how gender influences young people's exposure to digital food marketing. This research will determine (1) whether young people's exposure to unhealthy food advertising differs by gender, (2) whether their exposure to marketing techniques differs by gender, and (3) how different gender groups engage with promotional messages. A sample of 600 boys and 600 girls ages 11-15 will be recruited to complete a survey regarding their usual online behaviour, the number of digital media sources where they report being exposed to food advertising, and their exposure to related promotional techniques. Screen capture recordings of 120 minutes of smartphone use with a sub-sample of 100 girls, boys and non-cisgender youth will be used to assess child and youth exposure to unhealthy food marketing on social media. This screen capture footage will be reviewed to quantify child and youth exposure to food marketing and related marketing techniques. Interviews will be conducted to assess how each gender interprets and engages with these promotional messages. This research will help inform policies in Canada and abroad aimed at protecting both boys and girls from unhealthy food advertising in digital media.

column37: La douleur chronique touche un adulte sur cinq et a de serieux impacts sur notre societe. Malgre des decennies de recherche sur la douleur chronique et son traitement, on constate malheureusement que la prise en charge de cette condition continue d'etre sous-optimale. Parmi les nombreuses avenues de recherche possibles, davantage d'etudes sont requises afin de mieux comprendre l'usage de medicaments pour le traitement de la douleur chronique en contexte reel de pratique. Notons que ce besoin s'accentue considerablement dans le contexte de la crise des opioides qui sevit presentement. La quantification de l'usage du medicament en situation reelle represente cependant plusieurs defis, surtout dans le contexte ou l'utilisation concomitante de plusieurs medicaments (polypharmacie) est tres frequente chez les personnes vivant avec de la douleur chronique. Ces personnes utilisent en effet plusieurs medicaments pour la gestion de leur douleur qui peuvent varier dans le temps. De plus, le risque d'effets indesirables n'est pas toujours proportionnel au nombre de medicaments utilise. Grace aux donnees du systeme de sante jumelees a celles de l'Enquete sur la sante des collectivites canadienne, ce projet propose une approche novatrice de modelisation des trajectoires de risque associe a la polypharmacie. Les determinants (ex. l'age, le sexe et le genre) ainsi que les impacts de ces trajectoires sur le patient et son utilisation de ressources de sante seront ensuite etudies afin de determiner quelles sont les trajectoires de risque associe a la polypharmacie qui sont favorables vs defavorables pour les patients. En somme, nos resultats permettront d'explorer comment on peut favoriser des trajectoires favorables chez un plus grand nombre de patients. Il sera aussi possible d'identifier quelles pistes de prevention et d'interventions personnalisees devraient etre priorisees pour les patients aux trajectoires defavorables dans un contexte de ressources limitees.

column36: Role of cardiac lipoprotein lipase in diabetic heart disease.
column37: In Canada, almost 11 million individuals live with diabetes or pre-diabetes with heart disease being its leading cause of death. Traditionally, the management of diabetes has focused mainly on controlling high blood glucose levels. Unfortunately, despite heroic efforts to normalize this blood glucose, poor medication management predisposes these patients to heart failure. This is because, in Type 1 diabetes, multiple finger pricks and daily insulin injections (3-4/day) mean poor patient compliance, and variations in blood glucose management that fluctuate from insufficient to poor control. One instigator for the development of heart failure following diabetes is how this organ utilizes different sources of fuel for energy. During diabetes the heart switches from using both sugar and fats, to only fats. This transformation to using fats as an exclusive source of energy is helpful in the initial stages of the disease. However, over the progression of diabetes this has terrible end results. This is because toxic by-products are produced by overuse of fats, which weaken heart function (heart disease). Lipoprotein lipase (LPL) is responsible for regulating fat delivery to the heart, and its function during diabetes has not been completely revealed. In this proposal, the mechanisms by which LPL regulates fuel utilization by the heart during diabetes will be investigated in an attempt to identify new targets for therapeutic intervention. Currently, as treatment options to directly target diabetic heart disease are scarce, data from this project may assist in drug development that exclusively targets fuel utilization by the heart to help delay, prevent, or treat cardiac failure, and provide long-term management of this condition during diabetes.

column36: Circulating Tumour DNA Analysis Informing Adjuvant Chemotherapy in Stage III Colorectal Cancer: A Multicentre Phase II/III Randomised Controlled Trial (DYNAMIC-III)
column37: Introduction: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second most common cause of cancer death in Canada and one-third of patients diagnosed have cancer that has spread to their lymph nodes (called stage III). Surgery can cure these patients, but half have cancer return. Chemotherapy after surgery can improve the chance of cure but has significant side effects and many cancers return despite chemotherapy. If surgery did not remove all of a cancer, fragments of cancer DNA can enter the blood stream (called ctDNA). Detecting ctDNA after surgery is a new technology which may identify patients most likely to have cancer come back. This information may help determine which patients should get extra chemotherapy after surgery. There are also new ways to look at which genes a cancer turns on/off (gene expression) that can help explain why some cancers are more aggressive. DYNAMIC-III is a randomised trial that aims to show how we can use ctDNA and gene expression to better select chemotherapy after surgery in stage III CRC. Specific Aims: Determine whether ctDNA and/or gene expression can help select which patients with colorectal cancer are more likely to benefit from chemotherapy after surgery. Methods: This trial will recruit 1000 patients in Canada, Australia, and New Zealand with stage III colorectal cancer to either receive standard chemotherapy after surgery, or to use ctDNA to choose chemotherapy intensity after surgery. In patients without detectable ctDNA, suggesting a lower risk of cancer returning, chemotherapy will be reduced and we aim to show it is still effective, but has less side effects. In patients with ctDNA detected, more chemotherapy will be given to increase the chance of cure. Cancers will also be tested to see if gene expression is useful to help select chemotherapy after surgery. Significance: This trial aims to use new technologies to reduce toxicity and improve the chance of cure for patients with surgically removed colorectal cancer.

column36: Clinical development of oncolytic BHV-1 for cancer therapy
column37: Immunotherapy, harvesting the power of the immune system to target cancer, is emerging as a potentially powerful therapeutic approach. Some tumors, which are considered "immune hot" tumors, are effectively targeted by current immunotherapy approaches such as checkpoint blockade immunotherapy. However, "immune cold" tumors require pre-treatment with therapies that induce an immune response within the tumor prior to treatment with checkpoint blockade immunotherapy. Oncolytic viruses are emerging as novel therapies that specifically target cancer cells and not healthy cells, and induce potent immune responses. We have identified a novel oncolytic virus, Bovine herpes virus type 1, that has many unique properties that suggest potent and wide-reaching activity, surprisingly in the absence of virus replication. It appears that the main function of BHV-1 is to induce an immune-stimulating type of cancer cell death. We are currently working with a partner, Novatio Ventures, to develop BHV-1 vectors for clinical use. This project will allow us to further develop this technology and obtain key data to allow us to commercialize our technology and improve the business prospect for further investment to enable clinical trial development.

column36: Advancing virtual care in stroke rehabilitation: A randomized controlled trial investigating the TeleRehabilitation with Aims to Improve Lower Extremity Recovery Post-Stroke (TRAIL) program
column37: Leg weakness is very common after stroke. It affects the ability to walk and balance among people who have had a stroke. The first year after stroke is an important time for rehabilitation because it is the best time for recovery. Unfortunately, many people who have had a stroke often feel that they do not receive enough rehabilitation to restore their ability to use their legs. This is especially true for people who live in smaller communities where there are few health services, and more recently due to the COVID-19 pandemic where physical distancing between patients and clinicians has limited the amount of in-person rehabilitation. It is therefore important to develop innovative leg rehabilitation programs that are both cost effective and accessible. Our team of stroke survivors, clinicians and research scientists from across Canada has recently developed TeleRehabilitation with Aims to Improve Lower Extremity Recovery Post-Stroke (TRAIL). TRAIL is a 4-week program that focuses on exercise to improve leg function. It is delivered using the Internet and computer/tablet by a physical therapist. In this study, we will examine if TRAIL improves walking, balance, leg strength, and quality of life to a greater extent than a 4-week education program (EDUCATION), that focuses on providing education on stroke risk factors for secondary prevention. Ninety-six volunteers who have had a stroke in the past year will be randomly assigned to participate in either TRAIL or EDUCATION. Volunteers will be asked to complete assessments and questionnaires before and after the programs, and again 2 and 5 months later. Assessments will be conducted using videoconferencing so that volunteers will not need to travel to a hospital to participate in the study. We are working with 6 cities across Canada (Halifax, Toronto, London, Winnipeg, Vancouver, Kelowna). We anticipate that TRAIL is an accessible program that will help improve leg recovery after stroke.

column36: Identifying nutrition and lifestyle mediators of genetic susceptibility to obesity: towards a precision lifestyle medicine approach to obesity prevention.
column37: Obesity is considered as one of the most important health problem worldwide. A wealth of evidence suggests that obesity is the result of unhealthy eating and lifestyle behaviors leading to weight gain in individuals with a genetic susceptibility to obesity. The identification of hundreds of genes associated with obesity has provided the framework for development of precision medicine as an approach to personalize the prevention and/or treatment of obesity based on genetic, environmental and lifestyle factors. Up until now, precision medicine has mostly focused on genetic factors to predict disease risk and design tailored interventions to reduce risk and less on lifestyle and environmental factors which are of utmost importance for preventing chronic diseases like obesity. The concept of precision lifestyle medicine has emerged to reflect the importance of considering nutrition and lifestyle in the next generation of personalized lifestyle interventions. To design personalized lifestyle interventions aimed at preventing obesity, we first need to identify the unhealthy nutritional and lifestyle behaviors through which obesity susceptibility genes affect body weight. The objective of proposed research is to address this question by identifying nutritional and lifestyle factors mediating genetic susceptibility in large population-based cohorts of adults and children. The main outcome of this research will be identified nutrition and lifestyle factors mediating genetic susceptibility to obesity and weight gain in both adults and children that will be targets for modification in a future intervention trial aimed at preventing and managing obesity in individuals at risk.

column36: Apolipoprotein B and associated proteins in the etiology of Alzheimer's disease: A Tau-specific association with Alzheimer pathophysiology.
column37: The brain changes associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD) begin several years if not decades before the onset of cognitive changes. There is currently no prevention and no cure for the disease. The proposed study will use resources from the Centre for Studies in the Prevention of Alzheimer's Disease at McGill and, the Douglas-Bell Brain Bank in Montreal to examine the neurobiology and the mode of action of apolipoprotein B, a lipid-associated biomarker found in the cerebrospinal fluid of cognitively normal subjects with a parental history of AD. ApoB in the CSF was found to correlated with multiple biomarkers of disease progression in the years preceding the onset of cognitive deficits. This protein and its accessory partners are particularly interesting as they are known to regulate cholesterol transport, mobilization and internalization in the adult brain. These lipid-related biomarkers were also shown to alter the expression and production of key neurotoxic proteins (amyloid and phospho-tau) involved in the pathology of Alzheimer's disease. The novel information to be obtained from this research program is bound to be highly significant at many levels: First, it will allow scientists to determine whether these lipid biomarkers, like the apoE4, are specific to the earliest phase of AD pathology and, second, if they can be used as indicators of unhealthy/healthy brain aging. This research will allow us to develop, on an individualized basis, a number of genetic and biochemical predictors of disease onset and progression rate and, to validate whether or not these biomarkers could be used as novel therapeutic targets for the treatment and/or the prevention of the common form of AD.

column36: Prospective, multicentre, randomized, parallel-control, superiority study comparing administration of clotting factor concentrates with a standard massive hemorrhage protocol in severely bleeding trauma patients
column37: When a patient is severely injured (e.g., high speed car crash, or a pedestrian struck by a car) the most common cause of death is uncontrollable bleeding. The bleeding results from both injury to major blood vessels and from loss of clotting factors in the blood. The best treatment to restore the clotting factors is not known. For the last 70 years, plasma (the liquid part of blood) has been the most common treatment used. In the last 10 years, plasma has been replaced with manufactured clotting factor concentrates at some hospitals. This new clotting factor treatment has only been compared to plasma in small studies but appear to reduce the amount of blood transfused and helps to avoid a "massive transfusion" (getting more than 10 units of blood). The clotting factor treatment has other potential benefits: the products are treated to prevent blood pathogen infections (viruses), less fluid is infused (faster treatment, less fluid overload), and the product does not require thawing or a blood group (faster treatment). On the other side, the clotting factor concentrates are more expensive and the studies done so far cannot determine which of the two treatments are safer. This FiiRST-2 trial will compare these two treatments in 450 severely injured patients at 11 hospitals in Canada. In a computer-randomized fashion, half the patients will get plasma and half will get clotting factors for the first two "blood packs". A standard "blood pack" for a trauma patient contains 4 units of red blood cells and 4 units of plasma. After two blood packs, all patients will switch to the standard plasma blood packs - this is because the safety of giving more than 2 doses of clotting factors has never been tested. If the clotting factor concentrates reduce the amount of blood transfused, do not result in more adverse reactions, and improve patient outcomes, the new strategy would be a major advance in trauma care.

column37: One in four women experience psychological distress (depression, anxiety) in pregnancy. Children whose mothers experience prenatal distress are more likely to have behaviour problems. The COVID-19 pandemic has dramatically increased these rates, and is therefore a good chance to investigate how prenatal distress leads to brain and behaviour changes in children. In this study, we will look at relationships between prenatal distress, children's brain growth over time, and children's behaviour in early childhood. Children will be recruited from the Pregnancy during the COVID-19 Pandemic study, which has recruited over 10,000 pregnant individuals in Canada, and is currently following them and their babies. The current project aims to (1) determine how prenatal distress is associated with brain structure at age 2 years; (2) determine how prenatal distress is associated with brain growth from 2-4 years; and (3) determine whether brain structure and brain growth mediate associations between maternal distress and child behaviour. We will use prenatal distress information (depression, anxiety symptoms) that was already collected from individuals during pregnancy. In the proposed study, we will use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to measure brain structure and function, as well as behaviour, in 260 young children at age 2, 3, and 4 years. We will also measure household chaos to represent postnatal environment, and all analyses will consider child sex. This project will provide a more detailed understanding of how prenatal maternal distress impacts children's brain growth and behaviour. Ultimately, this will help determine when and for whom interventions may be most effective to mitigate the consequences of prenatal distress exposure, and support optimal development in young children.

column37: Urologic and gynecologic patients often have problems requiring surgical reconstruction to recreate a normal function, notably for vaginal reconstruction and for the correction of stress urinary incontinence (SUI). Vaginal reconstruction is still a challenge due to the limited availability of suitable tissue for vaginal replacement. Traditional intervention methods have varying degrees of morbidity. More than 200 million people worldwide, 30-40% of all women during their lifetime, suffer from SUI. Synthetic midurethral slings (MUS) are the gold standard treatment for female patients with SUI. They have excellent short-term cure rates even if their efficacy tends to decrease over time. Nevertheless, campaigns against synthetic MUS led to their abolishment in many countries including severe restrictions in Canada. The traditional autologous fascial sling MUS, has then reemerged as a viable alternative. But, the readoption of autologous MUS is slow due to the surgical technical challenge and perceived higher morbidity rates. Interestingly, tissue engineering (TE) aims to replace dysfunctional tissues and organs. We successfully assembled a TE vaginal model (VM) using the patients' own cells. It has great histological organization and excellent mechanical resistance; hence, it would be possible to use it as a VM for reconstruction, or to serve as a MUS to correct SUI. We propose to reconstruct a vaginal substitute using patient's cells: autologous and free of synthetic material. We will also engineer a MUS made only with fibroblasts, to replace the synthetic material causing the actual turmoil. The development of autologous VM and MUS reconstructed by TE would significantly advance urology/gynecology and would have a considerable clinical impact. The expertise gathered in this research program in TE with Drs Bolduc, Germain, Ruel, and collaborators: Drs Bureau and Nadeau, combine strong clinical and basic science skills and gives excellent assurance of success.

column36: The amino acid requirements of older adults (60 years and above) is different than those of young adults.
column37: The world's population is ageing. In 2016, seniors outnumbered children, for the first time in Canada's history. As people age they lose muscle mass and strength which could lead to falls, broken bones and loss of independence. They also have a weaker immune system and increased susceptible to infections. Amino acids (AAs) are the building blocks of proteins for muscles, bones, and a strong immune system. Getting the right amount of AAs is critical in the elderly. Twenty AAs make up all body proteins; 9 are essential, which means they must be obtained from foods. To assess whether the elderly are getting enough of the 9 essential AAs from foods, we need to first know their requirements. The AA needs of the elderly receives very little attention. National and international recommendations are based on studies in young adults because methods used to study AA requirements in the elderly are too invasive for routine use. Cells of older adults are less sensitive to AAs than young adults, and antioxidant deficiency which can be corrected by supplementing certain AA is common in the elderly. These information suggest that older adults need more AAs than young adults. Our group has been a leader in AA research for over 30 years and current national and international AA requirement in young adults are based on data using our method. We also developed the minimally invasive indicator amino acid oxidation (IAAO) method for studying AA requirements in vulnerable groups like the elderly, and have successfully applied it in children and babies. The goal of this current project is to build on this momentum to apply the minimally invasive IAAO method to determine for the first time the AA requirements in the elderly. This will provide accurate information to set recommendations for the elderly and to help evaluate diet quality to meet their AA needs. This is particularly important with the current global shift towards a more plant-based diet.

column36: Cannabidiol Adjunctive Therapy for Acute Bipolar Depression: A Randomized Double-Blind Placebo Controlled Trial
column37: Bipolar Disorder (BD) is a lifelong condition characterized by extreme mood fluctuations called manic and depressive episodes. BD affects approximately 2 in 100 people worldwide and has a significant impact on both the personal lives of patients and society. The rate of death by suicide among patients with BD is 20-30 times higher than of the general population and suicide attempts most commonly occur during depressive phases. Depression is responsible for most of the disability experienced by BD patients who spend a great amount of time in this phase. However, only two medications are approved by the Health Canada for treatment of the depressive phases of BD. Thus, developing new treatments that are effective and have a good safety profile is an urgent unmet need for people with BD. Cannabis sativa, also known as marijuana, has been used for millennia in various preparations and for different purposes. Among the more than 100 compounds present in the plant, cannabidiol is the substance with the more significant therapeutic potential: preliminary studies in humans have shown its medicinal properties in the treatment of epilepsy, anxiety and schizophrenia, and studies with mice have shown its properties in the treatment of depression. Furthermore, our preliminary study in bipolar depressed patients has shown that it is a safe medication with few adverse effects and that it likely has antidepressant effects. Considering the above, our objective is to test cannabidiol (CBD) as a treatment for the depressive phases of BD in a study design known as a randomized clinical trial. In this study we will divide the participants into two groups, one will receive daily capsules containing CBD, and the other will receive matching placebo capsules for 8 weeks. This will allow us to determine if improvement in depression is greater in the CBD group vs placebo group. It is noteworthy that all the participants will continue using their usual medication during the study.

column37: Public and healthcare provider trust is the cornerstone of deceased organ donation. It is important to ensure that donors are dead and cannot suffer during the organ donation process. In donation after brain death, this is done by confirming that brain function has stopped permanently before organ retrieval. Because brain death is rare, donation after circulatory determination of death (DCDD) has become an important strategy for increasing donation opportunities. However, in contrast to donation after brain death, current DCDD protocol does not mandate confirmation of permanent cessation of brain function prior to organ retrieval. Instead, the medical community assumes-based on scientific principals-that brain function stops within 5 minutes of when the heart stops. However, some animal-based research suggests that brain function: (1) may persist beyond when the heart stops; and (2) can be restarted hours after the time of death. Without research in people regarding when brain function stops compared to when the heart stops, these reports may reduce public and healthcare provider trust in DCDD. Research in people is needed to maintain and promote stakeholder trust in the DCDD process, and to ensure that DCDD protocol protects donors from harm. We will determine when brain function stops relative to when the heart stops by monitoring electrical brain activity in patients who are taken off life support and progress to death in the intensive care unit. Our findings will increase trust in DCDD and help to protect donors from harm by providing data from people that will inform the best time for organ procurement in DCDD. This data will be critical for preserving and promoting public and healthcare provider trust in the DCDD process. This will also help address current shortages of organs in Canada, and save the lives of people urgently awaiting transplant.

column37: Combined antiretroviral therapies (ART) are highly efficient in controlling HIV replication at undetectable plasma levels, therefore improving the life quality of people living with HIV (PLWH). However, ART does not eradicate HIV and treatment interruption results in rapid viral rebound, due to the persistence of proviral HIV-DNA integrated in the genome of long-lived memory CD4+ T-cells. Therefore, a life-long treatment is recommended. In addition, ART does not prevent the multiplication of the virus inside reservoirs cells (residual transcription), a process controlled mainly by host cell molecules. This residual HIV transcription maintains a state of chronic inflammation leading to the occurrence of non-AIDS co-morbidities in ART-treated PLWH. Therefore, in collaboration with internationally renowned experts in Virology/Immunology and GSK, the purpose of this proposal is to determine whether RORC2 inhibitors can be used in immune therapy strategies to reduce the deleterious consequences of residual viral transcription during ART in men and women living with HIV.

column36: Obstructive Sleep Apnea and Long-term Health Consequences
column37: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) is the most common respiratory disorder of sleep and affects hundreds of millions of people globally. It is characterized by recurrent upper airway collapse leading to asphyxia and low oxygen levels. The recurrent low oxygen levels leads to oxidative stress and inflammation and this in turn can lead to many adverse health complications (e.g., vascular disease, dementia, kidney damage). We believe that oxidative stress/inflammation contribute to OSA-related outcomes, and therefore, blood markers of these processes will help us predict them. We also hypothesize that adhering to CPAP treatment will be beneficial in improving long-term health (i.e., improving brain function, kidney function, and reducing risks of cardiovascular disease). This work will help us predict (and eventually prevent) these complications in sleep apnea patients. Goals: 1. To determine whether oxidative stress/inflammatory biomarkers can help predict long-term health complications in OSA 2. To determine whether CPAP adherence improves outcomes Methods: This proposal will use an ongoing project that is establishing a large group of patients with suspected OSA who receive a sleep study at one of six sleep centres. They have blood, extensive survey, and cognitive performance information collected at baseline. Patients will return for follow up 4-5 years after initial assessment for repeat blood collection, brain function, and detailed survey data. Detailed OSA treatment information (e.g., CPAP adherence from machine downloads) will also be obtained. Baseline and follow-up samples will be processed for inflammatory markers. For the first goal, we will determine whether baseline markers are associated with future adverse outcomes. For the second aim, the impact of CPAP adherence on outcomes will be assessed by comparing those who use and don't use CPAP using complex statistical matching.

column37: The epidemic of diabetes continues to grow across the world and our country. Currently, 1 in 3 Canadians lives with prediabetes or diabetes. In some communities that rate soars above 60%. For Indigenous Canadians, that risk is 80%. Canadians under 20 years of age now face a 50% chance of developing the disease in their lifetime. Diabetes has cost our healthcare system $16 B/y in 2020 representing 30.7% of the total health care system cost. Without prompt action, diabetes threatens not only an increasing number of Canadians but also the viability of our healthcare system. A small cluster of cells known as the islets of Langerhans are responsible for the release of insulin to regulate blood sugar levels. The loss of these cells ability to produce insulin is the origin of diabetes. Patients are treated with a lifetime administration of exogenous insulin to achieve normoglycemia. Other alternative is the islet transplantation as a viable treatment option for Type 1 diabetes (T1D). However, islet transplantation suffers from immunogenicity which leads to the dysfunction and eventual loss of the graft. To overcome this reaction, one strategy involves forming a protective barrier that can maintain the function of the cells while shielding them from immune attacks. A key feature of such barrier its thickness and the transplant volume to make sure cells can have adequate circulation of nutrients/waste as well as glucose and oxygen. As such, the aim is developing a conformal coating to provide a nanoscale barrier between islets and their environment with adequate stability and immunoprotection, while regulating the circulation of materials into and out of the cells. To achieve this goal, the nanocoating on islets will be developed using polysaccharide-based polyelectrolytes. The coated islet will be fully characterized in vitro and in proper mice model to assess the coated islet functionality and the absence of immunogenicity for their transplantation and treatment of T1D.

column36: The role of myocardin-related transcription factor (MRTF) in polycystic kidney disease
column37: Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is the most common inherited disorder of the kidney, affecting 1 in every 500 people. The vast majority of PKD cases are caused by a mutation or loss of one of two proteins, polycytsin 1 or 2. These proteins are located in the mechanical and chemical antenna of the cells, the so called primary cilium. The loss of polycystin function leads to the formation of large fluid-filled cysts, because it disturbs normal cell division in the renal tubules, the system responsible for resorbing nutrients and secreting waste products. Beside cyst formation, the other major feature of PKD is progressive organ scarring or fibrosis. This is a key problem because fibrosis completely disrupts the normal tissue architecture and leads to end-stage renal disease. The mechanism of how PKD leads to fibrosis is not understood, and currently there is no cure for the disease. Our previous studies showed that tubular cells play a major role in fibrosis because they can secrete scar-inducing chemical mediators (cytokines). We showed that myocardin-related transcription factor (MRTF), a protein regulating gene expression, is a central inducer of this process. Our preliminary data show that the level of MRTF is highly increased in mouse and human PKD tissue samples, and MRTF relocates into the nuclei of tubular cells. Based on these intriguing findings we surmise that MRTF is a key mediator in PKD, and a major contributor to the ensuing fibrosis. We will test this hypothesis by using a variety of cellular models, stem cell-derived kidney tissue (organoids), animal models and human samples. Utilizing a set of sophisticated molecular approaches we will examine whether genetic or pharmacological inhibition of MRTF ameliorates PKD. These studies may lead to completely new therapeutic approaches to treat this common and incurable kidney disease.

column36: Manipulating methionine metabolism to shape immune responses and modify disease progression in both sexes in MS
column37: Western diet and obesity are risk factors for multiple sclerosis (MS), an inflammatory neurological disorder affecting 1 in 500 Canadians. Diet and obesity influence the activation of the immune system, a key player in MS. Immune cells are indeed considered to orchestrate an aberrant 'attack' of the immune system against the brain and spinal cord in MS. Immune cells use available nutrients to proliferate and to produce proinflammatory factors that lead to injury of the brain and spinal cord. By limiting the presence of the essential amino acid methionine in the culture medium of immune cells, we were able to decrease their activation and to limit their production of pro-inflammatory factors. Importantly, restriction of methionine in the diet of the mouse model of MS resulted in a significant delay of onset of MS-like symptoms. Based on these results, we propose to investigate the role that methionine metabolism has on the activation of the immune system and its capacity to infiltrate the brain and spinal cord in animal models of MS. Since methionine metabolism can differ between men and women, and as MS frequency and evolution are influenced by biological sex, we will specifically assess the impact of dietary methionine intake on the risk to develop MS-like symptoms in males versus in females in an active and a spontaneous mouse model of MS, as the latter mimics the course of MS in humans. We will use these pre-clinical models to identify the mechanisms by which manipulating methionine influences the activation and function of the immune cells, including through regulation of the expression of genes for immune-related factors. We will also investigate if methionine metabolism is different in MS patients according to sex and versus healthy controls. This proposal will assess whether we can use specific dietary and pharmacological interventions modulating immune cell methionine metabolism as a therapeutic intervention to improve MS in women and men.

column36: Options for Increasing Plasma Supply in Canada: A Health Economic Preference and Modelling Study (HEMO-CAN)
column37: Plasma is the liquid component of blood and is collected from donors. It is used for transfusions in hospitals, and for the manufacture of treatments that are used for patients with various chronic and life-threatening conditions. But we currently do not receive enough plasma from donors in Canada, and this will only get worse as the demand for plasma is increasing. The Canadian Blood Service is considering how to best invest in new donor centres that will increase plasma donations. There are a number of different options to consider - from where to geographically place the centres, to what hours the centres should be open, to what incentives to provide such as free meals. All these options have different costs- from rents and material costs to staff salaries, and it can be hard to predict how impactful these different options will be on overall volume of plasma donated. This project will survey existing blood donors and non donors to understand the impact of these different options on their willingness to donate. This will enable us to predict what locations, and features will result in the most plasma being donated. We expect people will say they will donate more than they actually do, but because people tend to do this in a predictable way, we will be able to adjust for this. The results of the surveys will be combined with costs in a model. For example, one option (e.g. a centre in a downtown) might be expected to obtain a 20% higher volume of donated plasma, but if this comes at an additional 50% cost, it might not be the best investment. The model will inform which options and locations are expected to provide the most plasma donation for the CBS investment budget.

column37: Neuronal networks consist of different types of neurons that all play their own role in order to maintain proper network function. The two main types of neurons segregate in excitatory and inhibitory neurons, which together regulate the flow of information through the network. It has been proposed that changes in the relative strength in these two opposing forces underlie the symptoms observed in many psychiatric disorders, including autism and schizophrenia. Recently downregulation of NHE6 has been associated with with a rare and severe autism-related condition known as Christianson syndrome, generalized autism and Alzheimer's disease. NHE6 regulates the pH of intracellular membrane vesicles called 'recycling endosomes' that play important roles in the targeted delivery of growth factor and neurotransmitter receptors to synapses. Inappropriate trafficking of such cargo inside the synapse results in malformation of the neuronal circuitry in the brain, which can lead to progressive motor impairment (called ataxia), epilepsy (imbalance between excitation and inhibition in the brain), and intellectual disability, all of which have a devastating effect on the wellbeing of the individual. In this grant we build on our previous published work and extensive preliminary data. We will investigate the mechanisms of how lack of NHE6 leads to defects in excitatory inhibitory synapse maturation, and neural circuit formation in the hippocampus an area of the brain involved in learning and memory. We have developed novel tools and assembled a multidisciplined team putting us in a unique position to make groundbreaking discoveries. This work will result in important findings that could directly contribute to our better understanding of neurocircruitry development and shed new insights into the contributions of NHE6 to human health and disease, and identification of efficacious strategies for disease treatment.

column37: Care aides (also called personal support workers or nursing assistants) give most of the hands-on care for older adults who live in nursing homes. For example, care aides help these nursing home residents with eating, taking baths and other daily activities. However, care aides often leave some of these tasks undone. Besides having too few care aides to help nursing home residents each day, what other factors can cause care aides to leave tasks undone? How these factors cause tasks to be left undone? What changes can be made to prevent tasks from being left undone? Our study will answer these questions by asking care aides themselves. We will have detailed conversations with about 48 care aides who work in nursing homes in Alberta and British Columbia. We will ask them questions such as: What happened when you left tasks undone? What could have helped you to complete the tasks? We will use the knowledge that we learn from this study to help care aides reduce tasks left undone. We will apply the new knowledge to co-design, with care aides, strategies that they can use at work to avoid leaving tasks undone in daily care for residents. Our long-term goal is to improve the quality of care and quality of life for residents in nursing homes.

column36: The REM-Spike Project: A Set Theoretic Concordance Evaluation of Rapid Eye Movement Sleep in Localizing the Epileptogenic Zone
column37: Around 65 million people worldwide have epilepsy, which is the tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures. Everyone's lifetime risk is 1 in 26, which translates into over 1.4 million Canadians. While medications can often control seizures, just under half a million Canadians will still have unrelenting epilepsy with devastating everyday consequences on driving, working, quality of life, and even survival. Though medications can control seizures, they often come at the cost of debilitating side effects. In such cases, epilepsy neurosurgery is the preferred treatment; however, many individuals cannot qualify for surgery because the part of the brain giving rise to seizures - the "epileptogenic zone" (EZ) - cannot be identified, or cannot be narrowed down enough for surgery to be safe enough to avoid severe neurological deficits. To identify the EZ, brainwaves are recorded on a test known as the electroencephalogram (EEG) that records the electrical signature of epileptic activity. This signature varies widely depending on whether the patient is asleep or awake. In rapid eye movement (REM) sleep when most dreaming occurs, the EEG footprint of epileptic activity in the brain is thought to be smaller. Using actual EEG and magnetic resonance imaging data from patients with epilepsy, this project aims to rigorously quantify the size and location of epileptic activity to determine whether the EZ really is smaller in REM sleep. This project will also compare how much the EZ in REM sleep overlaps with the EZ recorded while awake or in other stages of sleep. These comparisons will determine whether REM sleep is the best state of consciousness to find the EZ. This project holds the promise of one day safely offering life-changing epilepsy neurosurgery to more patients than currently possible by using dreams to map out where seizures arise within the human brain.

column37: In patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD), the decision to initiate dialysis is based on the degree of kidney dysfunction as well as the presence of any acute indications including high acid levels, high potassium and fluid overload. In patients without any acute indications, the decision to initiate dialysis is subjective and based on a constellation of "uremic" symptoms, nutrition, and physical factors. Examples of "uremic" symptoms include anxiety, depression, difficulty sleeping, nausea and vomiting, poor appetite, fatigue, itchiness and restless legs. These symptoms are thought to be due to the accumulation of "uremic toxins" normally cleared by the kidney which may or may not be removed by dialysis. How individual uremic symptoms respond to dialysis is unknown. If clinicians were able toaccurately predict which uremic symptoms are responsive to dialysis, this could improve decision-making regarding starting long term dialysis. Patients with uremic symptoms responsive to dialysis might be able to start dialysis earlier with improved quality of life and patients with uremic symptoms unresponsive to dialysis might be able to continue to defer dialysis and avoid its potential harms (e.g. infection, heart problems). Our study will evaluate the trajectory of uremic symptoms in adults with advanced CKD followed by kidney doctors in ten or more clinics across Canada. It will identify which symptoms are responsive to dialysis as well as determine which specific uremic toxins are responsible for individual symptoms including restless legs, mood, itchiness, fatigue and nausea/vomiting. The study will be used to inform dialysis decision-making based on uremic symptoms and help us understand why some symptoms occur in some patients while other do not.

column37: Cancer immunotherapy uses a patient's immune system to fight cancer. Unfortunately, until recently, most cancer immunotherapies did not work for most patients, or caused severe side effects, and almost all failed. The dream of a successful cancer immunotherapy treatment only came to life in the last few years. This breakthrough approach targets a recently discovered way to jump-start the immune system, using immune checkpoints' inhibitors. The discovery of these immune checkpoints pathways was recognized by a Nobel Prize in 2018. Drugs targeting these pathways activate a patient's immune system and allow it to recognize and kill tumors. They are game-changers for cancer. For example, combining two of them helped 88% of metastatic melanoma patients to live for two years. Traditional treatment results only in 10% of patients with this disease to live for two years. Current available drugs targeting the immune checkpoints are limited to monoclonal antibodies. While yielding impressive clinical response rates, they still have many limitations. For example, they require intravenous route of administration and stay active for weeks in the body, making side effects hard to control. They are also very expensive, making them inaccessible to many cancer patients. Our proposal seeks to develop an alternative therapy to these antibodies. Our alternative therapy is a small molecule immune checkpoint inhibitor. Once developed, our treatment can be much cheaper to manufacture, can be taken orally, taken each day and is only active for a short time (less than one day) in the body. This allows precise dose adjustments, which should reduce serious side effects of current immune checkpoints' antibody-based therapies.

column36: Blocking the metastatic spread of uveal melanoma
column37: Metastasis is the dissemination of cancer cells from their birthplace in the body to distant organs. As it turns out, this is an inefficient process. Of the millions of cells in the primary tumor, only a small subset manage to gain access to the lymphatic or circulatory systems and an even smaller fraction ever colonize a distant site or grow into a clinically relevant tumor. Unfortunately, the inefficiency of the process does not lessen its devastating effects: metastatic stage cancer is very difficult to treat and remains a critical problem in medicine. In this grant proposal, we describe how we will study the ways in which cancer cells become metastatic. There are three key potential mechanisms that have previously been linked to metastatic behavior. The first involves changes to the physical characteristics of the tumor cells, in a way that promotes cell invasion and migration. The second mechanism involves the regulation of gene expression through reversible marks left on the genome, called epigenetic alterations. The third mechanism involves immune cell infiltration into the tumor, which generates inflammation and immune suppression. We have developed a new model system to study the metastasis of melanoma, an aggressive cancer of the pigment cells. What is unique about our model is that the melanoma begins within the eyes and then spreads to the liver and lungs. This type of cancer is called uveal melanoma. It is the most common eye cancer and it is deadly. Uveal melanoma metastasizes in half of all patients, after which there is no effective treatment. A better understanding of the ways that cancer cells escape the primary tumor and adapt to survive in different parts of the body will help us develop more effective therapies for late stage cancers.

column36: Type 2 immune-mediated control of intestinal epithelium stem cell fate and function
column37: The intestine is under constant assault by infectious and physical insults. To counter these environmental challenges, this barrier organ has evolved various defensive measures to counter invasive pathogens and quickly repair itself after injury. The remarkable regenerative capacity of the gut relies on dynamic interactions between the immune system and stem cells that give rise to the epithelium, a thin layer of cells that protect our tissues from the outside world. However, the ways in which immune cells and stem cells coordinate tissue regeneration remains poorly understood. To discover new pathways that promote tissue healing, our group has turned to intestinal helminths, one of the most prevalent parasites of the animal kingdom. Helminths are multicellular worms that migrate through tissues leaving significant damage in their wake. Resistance to helminths requires striking changes to the intestinal epithelium that not only repair the damaged tissue, but also lead to parasite expulsion. Thus, parasitic helminth infection provides a powerful model system to investigate how immune-stem cell interactions orchestrate tissue regeneration. Using animal models of helminth infection to track how the immune response shapes the fate and function of intestinal stem cells, our studies will uncover previously unrecognized mechanisms of tissue repair that may lead to new therapies for regenerative medicine.

column36: Examining the Impacts of the COVID-19 Pandemic Response on Health and Functioning of Canadian Children and Youth
column37: Canada is entering its second year of a public health emergency, with each province/territory employing varying containment policies given differences in the extent and intensity of the pandemic across the country. As the pandemic continues, Canadian children, youth (hereafter, children) and their families face major economic, social and psychosocial stressors. The impact of these stressors on health and well-being will likely be unequal, disproportionately affecting families living in adverse socio-economic circumstances, as well as those with pre-existing physical, mental and neurodevelopmental conditions. The magnitude and distribution of these impacts for Canadian children and their families, however, remains largely unknown. To understand impact and inform policy responses and practice, reliable evidence collected at the population level, with comparable pre-pandemic data, is required. We propose to leverage the 2019 Canadian Health Survey of Children and Youth (CHSCY) - a nationally-representative sample of 26,870 children aged 1-17 years with data collected by Statistics Canada immediately prior to the pandemic - and conduct a follow-up survey with this sample in 2022, when they are 4-20 years of age. column36: The Implementation Playbook: e-health technology for effective implementation of evidence-based interventions
column37: Evidence-based interventions are necessary for improving health outcomes; however, their implementation is complex, often disorganized, subject to high rates of failure, and can take years to navigate, making it costly and resource-intensive. International consensus argues there is an urgent need to improve implementation. Effective implementation is best guided by implementation science (IS), the study of methods to promote the systematic uptake of evidence-based practices. However, healthcare organizations lack know-how in evidence-based implementation processes. They are not aware of the evidence, and when they are, they have difficulty putting it to use. To address this gap, we propose to develop an innovative software platform (The Implementation Playbook) that will help stakeholders to apply a systematic approach to implementation guided by prevailing IS evidence. Based on pilot work, we will i) develop a testable minimum viable software prototype; and ii) evaluate its' feasibility in six healthcare organizations. The team are experts in implementation science and practice, e-health and user-centred design, knowledge users/implementers of evidence, and patients/consumers. The Implementation Playbook will facilitate effective implementation and optimal outcomes by transcending limitations of existing implementation supports that are passive, text-based, variably informed by evidence, and resource-intensive. We will explore whether The Playbook can be used autonomously, thereby circumventing reliance on costly in-person implementation assistance that is not widely available to healthcare organizations. We will also explore if the software platform is useful for different organizations and interventions being implemented, as it will be based on the universal core components of effective implementation. The Playbook's external validity will make it exceedingly usable and scalable beyond healthcare.

column36: The right care, for the right patient, at the right time, by the right provider: A value-based comparison of the management of ambulatory respiratory diseases in walk-in clinics, primary care physician practices and emergency departments
column37: Emergency departments (ED) are specialized and costly public health services. Designed to provide care for patients with urgent or life-threatening conditions, they continue to treat large numbers of low-acuity ambulatory emergency patients (consulting for health issues that do not require being kept for observation on a stretcher). An estimated 30-60% of all patients treated in these services belong to this category, which some analysts regard as a source of emergency department overuse or misuse. Others argue that patient evaluation in the ED may be more cost-effective. The debate has been complicated by the COVID-19 pandemic, which has shifted primary care practices and walk-in clinics significantly towards telemedicine (remote or virtual consultation by phone or videoconferencing), presumably a more convenient and efficient consultation modality under the circumstances. As healthcare expenditures continue to rise, the most efficient care pathways must be identified and strengthened in order to ensure sustainable healthcare systems for all Canadians. By comparing the value (i.e. health outcomes and costs) of care given (in person or by telemedicine) in EDs, walk-in clinics and primary care practices for ambulatory emergency patients presenting with acute respiratory conditions, our research project will enable decisionmakers and policymakers to: 1) determine the most efficient care settings for this patient category; and 2) promulgate value-centred reforms whereby ambulatory patients with acute unexpected needs will receive the best urgent care at the lowest cost. We believe that this will represent a major contribution to the sustainability and adequacy of publicly funded Canadian healthcare and allow it to fulfil its mission of improving the health of the population.

column36: Demystifying the role of esophageal stem cells in esophageal diseases
column37: What are stem cells? They are the "orchestra conductor" in an organism. First, they are a rare population of cells that can self-renew. That means that when it will divide, it will produce two daughter cells: one of which is identical to the "mother" cell assuring the prosperity of its descendants. Second, stem cells have the capacities to give rise to all the cell types from an organ. The best stem cell example is the zygote formed when the spermatozoid fused with the egg, it will later form a baby comprising a multitude of different cell types. Stem cells are highly active in embryos but also in adult tissues. On a daily basis, they produce new cells to compensate for all the cells that are lost. They are also key players in tissue healing upon injury like bone fracture, gut inflammation or skin burns. Unfortunately, they have two faces: the Good and the Bad. Indeed, in cancer by example, they are linked to tumor formation and resistance to treatment. Since they divide frequently, they are more prone to form a tumor if they acquire sufficient number of mutations. Also, through several mechanisms they are able to survive to anti-cancer treatments such as radiotherapy and chemotherapy. They would then be "hiding" or "sleeping" at the tumor site ready to divide again and form a new tumor leading to cancer relapse. They are therefore a major issue in oncology. Our goal? Specifically target stem cells to improve tissue repair and cure cancer. Our lab particularly focuses on the esophagus because it is covered by an actively dividing epithelium. Also, it is an organ severely affected by inflammation due to acid reflux by example, which affects roughly 15% of Canadians. Furthermore, esophageal cancer is also a deadly cancer with only 15% of patients surviving 5 year following their diagnosis due to high rate of cancer relapse. Thus, we are studying the role of esophageal stem cells in these diseases to find new therapeutic approaches to improve the life of patients.

column36: Distributed Machine Learning for Diagnosis and Treatment Decision Support of Pediatric Brain Tumors
column37: In an increasingly data-driven world, artificial intelligence is expected to be a key tool for converting the big data into tangible benefits. Machine learning, a sub-field of artificial intelligence, aims to identify complex patterns in multi-dimensional data and use these uncovered patterns to classify or make predictions on new unseen cases. However, many datasets are typically needed for training of the advanced machine learning models to produce highly accurate results. This is also the main limiting factor why these advanced machine learning models cannot unfold their full potential in health care applications if personal or other sensitive data is used that data owners cannot or will not share for training of a machine learning model at a central location. Pediatric brain tumors are the most common solid tumor in children. Among others, treatment and prognosis depend on the tumor type, the location within the brain, whether it has spread, as well as clinical parameters. Due to the numerous different types of pediatric brain tumors and treatment options, it is especially challenging to collect enough datasets needed to train robust machine learning models that produce accurate results for children with brain tumors. The aim of this proposed research is to develop a novel distributed learning system for training of advanced machine learning models for pediatric brain tumors to overcome the limiting factors of data collection and analysis in a centralized fashion. The main goal of the distributed learning architecture is that the individual patient data does not leave the contributing clinical centers but are only used locally to train the machine learning models, which do not contain any patient data at the individual level anymore. In this research project, we will invent, develop, implement, and evaluate multiple approaches for distributed machine learning model training that have the potential to improve diagnosis and treatment of children with brain tumors.

column36: Targeting sex steroids to improve the response to bladder cancer immunotherapy
column37: Bladder cancer is the 5th most common cancer affecting Canadians. There are notable differences in the incidence between sexes, with bladder cancer four times more common in men, though tumors in women tend to be more aggressive. However, the reasons why these differences between sexes exist remain poorly understood. There is a need to understand how biologic differences such as sex hormones impact bladder cancer and to understand how these differences may be harnessed to improve treatment responses. Superficial bladder tumors represent approximately 75% of all bladder tumors and have a high and costly recurrence rate. Immunotherapy using a vaccine for tuberculosis called Bacille-Calmette Guerin(BCG) remains the standard treatment, unchanged for over 40 years. We and others observed that treatments which target hormone biology can decrease tumor recurrences of superficial bladder tumors. Our research investigates how current treatments modulating androgens or estrogens may be repurposed to treat bladder cancer patients. First, clinical trials of anti-androgens or supplemental estrogens in combination with BCG treatment for superficial bladder cancer will provide the needed evidence for further clinical studies in men and women, respectively. Second, we will use laboratory models to investigate the mechanisms of how anti-androgen therapy and sex hormones may alter immune cells' function and anti-cancer activity. Our research will provide a pathway forward to improving the current practice for superficial bladder cancer which is essentially unchanged for many decades. The integration of patient samples collected in the clinical trial with laboratory experiments will expand our understanding of the reasons for sex differences in bladder cancer and support further practice-changing clinical trials. Thus, our results will help improve outcomes for bladder cancer patients but may also provide knowledge which applies to other cancers where immunotherapy is effective.

column36: Neurodevelopmental function and neural oscillations in children born with congenital heart disease: the roles of brain injury, brain growth and heart function
column37: Most babies born with heart birth defects now survive to adulthood. Yet, many have developmental disabilities that become apparent over time and include challenges in thinking, socializing, language, and behaviour. Our work has shown that brain injury and disrupted brain growth are common in these babies. Yet, we do not know why some children with these brain changes have developmental challenges while others do not. The way different parts of the brain exchange and process information through early childhood may be the key factor affecting the functions and behaviour of these children. We focus on the two most common types of heart defects cared for in the newborn period. Newborns with these heart conditions require early surgery, but their brain oxygen supplies differ after heart surgery. Studying children with these heart conditions can help us understand how better heart function improves brain growth and function. Given these gaps in our understanding, we propose to examine functioning and behaviour in a group of children born with these two common types of heart defects and measure how their brain exchanges and processes information at 5 years of age. These children have been carefully studied to 3 years of age- including brain injury & growth in the newborn period, and detailed measure of motor, thinking, language and behaviour up to 3 years of age. A new measure of brain function will now be used to study brain information exchange and processing when children are doing tasks important for thinking skills. We will: 1. Determine how a child's heart function modifies the relationship between newborn brain injury and the child's functions and behaviour at age 5 years. 2. Determine how the way the brain processes information at age 5 years is linked to specific thinking skills, and how this is modified by (a) newborn brain injury and (b) a child's heart function. Through this work, we hope to identify specific opportunities to promote optimal child development.

column36: Quantitative Imaging of the Evolution of the Whole-Body Fat Profile in Breast Cancer Survivors
column37: Breast cancer (BC) is the most frequently diagnosed cancer in women. Early stage BC survival has improved by 48% in the last three decades in Canada. However, life expectancy is still significantly reduced and BC survivors are now more likely to die from non-cancer causes, such as cardiovascular diseases related to obesity and poor fitness. The fat marbled around your stomach and other organs (e.g. liver) and within your muscles are examples of bad fat pools. The first goal of our proposed program is to measure the amount and changes in all the different fat pools, from the time of cancer diagnosis, throughout therapy and for several years afterwards. Our second goal is to test if a diet intervention called time restricted eating will slow the growth of these bad fat pools in BC patients over the course of therapy, resulting in better cardiovascular health following their BC treatment. We expect our study to show that monitoring of body fat composition should be part of BC care and that diet control should be a central component of BC therapy to improve health in survival.
