column36: Auditory Cortex Plasticity Following Cochlear Implant
column37: In Canada, hearing impairment is the most common sensory disability in adults (affecting 26% of those >45 years old) and deafness is the most common birth defect. Cochlear implants are extremely useful tools in providing auditory sensations to the profoundly deaf and have restored hearing to over 1 million people worldwide. The use of cochlear implants in the profoundly deaf makes human speech comprehension possible. In hearing subjects, acoustic input shapes the development of auditory cortex of the brain. However, in deaf individuals the auditory cortex has no acoustic input. Other senses, such as vision and touch, exploit the unused "deaf" region of cortex for their own purposes. This commonly results in enhanced visual or tactile abilities reported in the deaf. However, if the dormant auditory system is then activated by a cochlear implant, how does "deaf" auditory cortex respond? Does all of "deaf" auditory cortex begin to process sound? Does the visual or tactile processing that invaded "deaf" auditory cortex retreat? Does each auditory cortical area begin to perform the same functions identified in a hearing subject? By better understanding the plastic properties of the brain following cochlear implant, it will be possible to develop implantation strategies to better exploit the plasticity of the brain and improve cochlear implant efficacy and hearing restoration success. The greatest benefit of cochlear prosthetics has been found in young children. Therefore, in the proposed studies, cochlear prosthetics will be implanted in young subjects. We will examine auditory cortical function in the congenitally-deaf cat (the only natural model for human congenital deafness) following cochlear implant. The results from these studies will be directly applicable to clinical studies investigating functional outcomes of cochlear implants in children.

column36: Unravelling the Impact of Diet on Cardiovascular Health in Heterozygous Familial Hypercholesterolemia: a Metabolomic Approach.
column37: High blood cholesterol (HBC) increases heart disease risk. In most cases, HBC outcomes from suboptimal lifestyle habits. However, more than 150,000 individuals in Canada and 34 million worldwide have HBC from birth due to inherited genetic disorders. People with inherited HBC (iHBC) face a very high risk of premature heart attack, which usually occurs before reaching 55 years old, if they are not adequately treated. Canada's Food Guide (CFG) emphasizes diets low in red and processed meats and high in plant foods as these are recognized to reduce heart disease risk in the general population. However, among individuals with iHBC, the impact of diet on heart health remains misunderstood. Over time, this has led to a misleading perception that diet, relative to cholesterol-lowering medication, is of little or no help in controlling blood cholesterol and preventing heart disease in people with iHBC. In fact, people with iHBC even report engaging in unhealthy dietary behaviors because of this perception. The objective of the proposed research is to document the impact of a diet reflecting CFG principles on heart health in adults with iHBC. We will conduct a feeding intervention in which adults with iHBC will consume a diet low in red and processed meats and high in plant foods, as recommended in CFG, and a diet reflecting current dietary habits of Canadians in a random order for 4 weeks separated by a 4-week break. Blood samples will be collected at the end of each diet from which we will first measure blood cholesterol levels. We will also use cutting-edge biochemistry techniques to measure a broad spectrum of small molecules in the blood to identify the blood signature of the healthy diet. Lastly, we will evaluate how the blood signature of the healthy diet is associated with heart disease risk in a separate cohort of nearly 1,000 adults with iHBC. With this research, we will demonstrate the crucial importance of diet for heart health among individuals with iHBC.

column36: Investigation of centrosome amplification as a therapeutic vulnerability in non-small cell lung cancer
column37: Lung cancer is a deadly disease and new therapies to target the biology supporting tumour growth are needed. Centrosomes are multi-protein complexes involved in cell division. One of their functions is to help cells distribute two copies of the genome equally into the cells produced during cell division. Normal cells have two centrosomes during mitosis and this is tightly regulated to ensure the genome is divided evenly. Lung cancer cells often have several centrosomes, a feature called centrosome amplification. This increase in centrosome number makes it more difficult for cells to carry out cell division, and can cause major DNA abnormalities and mutations that help tumours grow. Because centrosome amplification is specific to cancer cells and it can promote their growth, it is an attractive target for lung cancer therapy. The goal of this research program is to understand how centrosome amplification could be targeted to treat lung cancer. We will determine how frequently centrosome amplification occurs and identify strategies that lung cancers use to cope with the stress that it causes during cell division. Knowledge gained from these studies will inform how centrosome amplification could be targeted to treat lung tumours. We will then evaluate how well treatments designed to target centrosome amplification inhibit the growth of lung cancer models. Finally, we will investigate whether this new therapeutic approach can be combined with standard lung cancer treatments to enhance their abilities to kill tumours. The new discoveries from our research program will improve our understanding of lung cancer biology and specifically, how lung cancers cope with centrosome amplification. They will also provide insights about how we can take advantage of this cancer-specific feature to treat patients. Thus, our work has great potential to lead to the development of new therapies and drug combination strategies for treating lung cancer that could improve patient outcomes.

column36: Judiciarisation des personnes souffrant de troubles mentaux : une recherche en theorisation ancree sur la perception des patients judiciarises et le personnel soignant
column37: L'insertion des personnes qui souffrent de troubles mentaux (PSTM) dans le systeme de justice (criminelle et civile) est une realite omnipresente au Canada. Plusieurs enjeux sont associes a cette surrepresentation des personnes vivant avec des problemes de sante mentale a l'interieur du systeme de justice, dont la forte stigmatisation qui affecte ces personnes. La judiciarisation s'effectue dans une optique de protection de la securite du public et, par le fait meme, dans un objectif plus large de controle social. Les professionnels de la sante qui pratiquent aupres de ces personnes, bien qu'ils agissent a titre de soignants, s'inscrivent dans ce mandat de controle social. Cette realite peut affecter significativement la relation therapeutique entre les soignants et les patients, et, par le fait meme, le retablissement des PSTM. Ce projet vise a mieux comprendre comment la judiciarisation affecte les PSTM et les soignants (infirmiers.eres et educateurs specialises) qui travaillent avec ces personnes. Nous voulons aussi explorer comment la judiciarisation influence la relation therapeutique entre soignants et soignes. La theorisation ancree sera utilisee comme methodologie de recherche. Des PSTM, hommes (n=15) et femmes (n=15), ayant ete en contact avec le systeme judiciaire seront rencontres lors d'entretiens semi-structures. De plus, des membres du personnel soignant (n=30) qui pratiquent aupres de ces personnes judiciarisees seront aussi interviewes (60 participants en tout). Ce projet s'avere des plus pertinent afin d'etudier comment le phenomene de la judiciarisation affecte la relation therapeutique entre les patients judiciarises et le personnel soignant. Cette recherche permettra de mieux informer les cliniciens sur les impacts de la judiciarisation a l'endroit des PSTM, et comment les pratiques cliniques peuvent etre mieux adaptees a cette population.

column36: Gendered Social Determinants of Health and Adverse Clinical Outcomes in Atrial Fibrillation
column37: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common irregular heart rhythm and is associated with significant increased risk of stroke, and overall mortality. To improve of survival and quality of life, risk scores have been tested for their ability to also predict all-cause mortality. Clinical factors and biomarkers have been tested for improving the predictive ability of scores with limited results and have not been tested in males and females separately. While biological sex has been reported to play an important role in clinical outcomes of AF, the role of gendered social determinants of health in the assessment of adverse outcomes have not been fully explored. The factors including gender roles, relations and institutional policy must be taken into consideration in males and females to better understand the risk of overall adverse events and to support the move towards a patient-centered approach in AF care. The overall aim of this study is to improve our understanding of the relationship between gendered social determinants of health and adverse outcomes in AF patients and to determine sex specific risks. We will analyze a large cohort of AF patients that has collected the necessary information on clinical factors, social determinants, and relevant outcomes to test different models and arrive at identifying the best predictors of outcome to develop sex specific interventions to improve the care of AF patients. Despite major improvements in treatments, patients with AF still face a high risk of mortality. The role of gendered social determinants in predicting risks of stroke, major bleeding, cardiovascular adverse events, and all-cause mortality has yet to be evaluated. Sex specific models for adverse clinical outcomes in AF have not been developed. The current project will fill these knowledge gaps and provide a platform for the integrated interdisciplinary management of AF patients.

column36: Gender in Focus: A Photo Elicitation Study of Gender, Self-management, and Care with Emerging Adults with Type 1 Diabetes
column37: Early emerging adulthood (18 to 24 years) is a time of emotional, psychological and social change, and for those living with type 1 diabetes, represents a period of life that is often associated with loss to follow-up, the emergence of long-term complications and increased risk of adverse health outcomes. Gender - known to impact health behaviours, needs, and opportunities for health - is thought to be particularly influential in shaping health-related experiences during emerging adulthood. However, little is known about the relationship between gender and experiences of type 1 diabetes and diabetes self-management as well as how gender might affect the delivery of care to this group. This study aims to provide a theory-informed understanding of the ways in which gender frames individuals' perspectives of type 1 diabetes, impacts self-management practices, and informs delivery of care. To achieve this aim, we will employ critical and arts-based qualitative methods as well as Bourdieu's Theory of Practice. In phase 1, we will conduct focus groups and individual photo elicitation interviews with 30 emerging adults living with type 1 diabetes. Leveraging results from phase 1, we will construct a photographic exhibit that will be shared with formal (e.g. physician, nurse) and informal (e.g. family/friends) care providers in phase 2. Twenty individuals will be recruited from each group (total n=40) to participate in an interview to discuss their perceptions of the exhibit. These interviews are intended to capture the relevance/impact of the exhibit and how it may inform delivery of care and support. Results from this study will provide a deeper understanding of the ways that gender frames illness experiences for emerging adults living with type 1 diabetes and enhance the personalization of care for this group as a result. Findings will also be used to help build a community of emerging adults living with type 1 diabetes and foster opportunities for greater peer support.

column36: Agir ensemble sur la resilience d'equipe au travail en cancerologie pour optimiser la capacite de faire face aux situations difficiles: une etude de cas multiples selon l'evaluation realiste dans le reseau de cancerologie du Quebec
column37: Les equipes de soins aupres des personnes touchees par le cancer font face a des situations difficiles au quotidien: annonce du diagnostic de cancer et de mauvaises nouvelles sur l'evolution de la maladie, detresse des patients et de leurs proches, rarete des ressources. Ces situations sont amplifiees avec la COVID-19. Les equipes sont a risque de fatigue de compassion, d'epuisement et d'etre a bout de moyens. Ces risques affectent le fonctionnement des equipes, la sante et la qualite de vie au travail; et au final impactent l'offre de soins. Bien qu'il existe des interventions prometteuses, les recherches pour soutenir la resilience et en apprecier les effets aupres des equipes specialisees en cancerologie sont quasi inexistantes. L'etude vise a mieux comprendre comment intervenir en soutien a la resilience d'equipe oeuvrant aupres des personnes touchees par le cancer. Pour etre utile et faisable, l'intervention s'appuie sur une approche de partenariat etroit avec les professionnels des equipes cliniques et les membres des equipes de gestion afin qu'elles puissent offrir des soins de qualite et securitaires. Nous analyserons les facilitants et obstacles a la resilience et evaluerons les effets de l'intervention a l'aide d'entrevues, d'observations et de questionnaires. Quatre etablissements de sante au Quebec ayant plusieurs equipes en cancerologie se sont engages a participer. L'etude fournira des donnees inedites sur les meilleures pratiques pour mieux soutenir la resilience d'equipe au travail dans un secteur de soins specialises. L'accompagnement de proximite et la description fine de l'intervention, de ses mecanismes d'action et de ses effets s'inscrit en soutien a la prise de decision pour optimiser la capacite de resilience d'equipe. Les resultats pourront inspirer d'autres initiatives au Quebec, ailleurs au Canada et dans d'autres pays ou le mieux-etre des equipes de soins est une condition essentielle de l'offre de soins pendant et apres la COVID-19.

column36: Heterogeneity of interprofessional primary care teams and its effect on quality of care and health service use in older adults
column37: Experts agree that primary care clinics where family doctors work in teams with other health professionals like nurses and social workers are an effective way to give older patients the care that they need. Teams, however, come in different shapes and sizes and it is not clear how these differences might affect patients' quality of care or their need for hospital services. Given the large health policy investments promoting primary care for the aging population, it is important that we better understand the ways in which team-based clinics can best support the care of older persons. This project will breakdown the complex links between primary care teams, quality of primary care, such as access, continuity and coordination of care, and hospital use in older persons. We will use data from one of Statistics Canada's health surveys and Quebec government data on patient's use of hospital and other medical services and focus on persons 65 years old and older with health conditions that are considered best managed through high-quality primary care. Our team will use advanced methods in statistics to describe the different types of teams and which might perform better in improving quality of care and hospital use in older patients. Overall, this project will help health professionals and policy makers understand what features of team-based primary care gives the best outcomes in terms of access, continuity and coordination while also avoiding the ED and hospital when not necessary. This will help implement solutions to better organize and plan the services needed to best care for our growing aging population.

column36: Understanding the Common CHILDhood Inflammatory Origins of Asthma and Atherosclerosis
column37: Chronic respiratory disease, CRD (asthma and COPD) and cardiovascular disease, CVD (heart attack, stroke and heart failure) often occur together and are the leading cause of illness and death in adults. Although CRD and CVD may not appear until a person is older, risk factors for these conditions begin in early life. Low lung function and high blood pressure are risk factors that may develop together and might be related to how our immune system responds to colds and chest infections when we are very young. The CHILD Cohort Study is following 3,400 children (born in 2009-12) who have answered questions on their health, come in for medical visits and given blood samples many times from birth until 8 years of age. We will ask the same children to repeat these measures at age 13. We will analyze their lung function and blood pressure to see if these measures are related to asthma and changes (stiffness) in blood vessels. We will also study their blood samples for signs of inflammation and determine if this is connected to early life colds and chest infections. With this information, we hope to better understand how CRD and CVD develop in early life, which will help scientists develop new and earlier ways to prevent these important chronic disorders.

column36: Electric Field Modeling to Optimize Intermittent Theta Burst Stimulation and Engage Neurophysiological Therapeutic Targets in Treatment Resistant Depression
column37: About 2.5% of Canadians are diagnosed with treatment resistant depression (TRD) yearly. Intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) is an efficient form of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation that is an effective, evidence based treatment for TRD. However, iTBS, like all brain stimulation, is implemented via trial and error, as, to date, there are no predictive methods to assess the likelihood of patient response to iTBS. Work from our centre focused on TRD has previously established changes in cortical activity indexed via TMS-EEG after brain stimulation, but not with placebo, indicating the promise of TMS-EEG markers of cortical activity as markers of brain stimulation response. In contrast to other forms of rTMS, iTBS is known to result in enhanced plasticity, or cortical excitation. Even with these advances, response rates with iTBS remain at 30-40%. The optimization of electric field (E-field) delivery may improve treatment response by accounting for the individual differences in head structure and brain regional anatomy. We will examine if iTBS combined with E-field modeling (iTBSe) better engages TMS-EEG markers of cortical excitation and improves clinical response when compared to conventional iTBS in patients with TRD.

column36: Targeting inhibitory immune checkpoints in macrophages for anti-cancer therapy
column37: Over the past 10 years, the most significant advance in cancer treatment has been the development of "immunotherapy", in particular of agents capable of blocking molecules such as PD-1 and CTLA-4, which suppress the functions of immune cells known as "T cells". Blocking of PD-1 or CTLA-4 by drugs was found to cure many patients with cancer. However, not all cancer patients respond to blocking agents targeting PD-1 or CTLA-4. As a result, significant efforts have been directed at identifying additional molecules that could be new targets for immunotherapy, in particular on immune cells other than T cells. These efforts led to the identification of the SIRPa-CD47 molecules that suppress the ability of immune cells known as "macrophages" to eat and destroy cancer cells. Over the recent few years, it was reported that treatment of cancer patients with blockers of SIRPa-CD47 augment the ability of their macrophages to destroy cancer cells and can result in complete remissions in a subset of patients. Based on these exciting results, we have been interested in understanding how macrophages eat cancer cells, and how this capacity can be further augmented by blockade of SIRPa-CD47, and by blockade of other molecules such as CD200R1 and PSGL-1. The purpose of this proposal is to understand better how SIRPa-CD47, CD200R1 and PSGL-1 operate and how they can be targeted for better immunotherapy treatments against cancer.

column36: Training Intervention and Program of Support (TIPS) for fostering the adoption of family-centred telehealth interventions in pediatric rehabilitation: A pan-Canadian implementation-effectiveness study.
column37: One in five Canadians care for someone with a disability, and nearly 50% of them are parents of a child with a disability. Many felt their rehabilitation needs were not being met, even before the disruptions to healthcare and education systems caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Telehealth, or healthcare services provided through technologies (mostly online), offers therapists an effective means of providing parents with timely information, education, counselling and training to meet their child's needs. Numerous pediatric rehabilitation organizations 'adopted' telehealth in response to the pandemic, but many therapists lacked the appropriate training and voiced a need for support to ensure telehealth practices were effective and led to meaningful results for their patients. This study aims to address this need. Our team has developed a telehealth intervention for parents of children with a disability living in Quebec, for which a training and support program (TIPS) was provided to therapists. The present study is an extension of this work, to implement and assess the impact of TIPS on a broader scale. Twenty centres from across Canada that provide pediatric rehabilitation (physiotherapy, occupational therapy or speech and language pathology) to children with a disability ages 0-12 and their families have committed to participate. The TIPS program will first be adapted to meet the training and support needs of each participating centre and will then be offered to their therapists for one year. Before, during and after the support period, the study will monitor a number of indicators to track how TIPS was implemented and what effect it may have had on the therapists, on the participating centers and on how families perceived their services. This study will provide important insight into how best to support pediatric therapists so that telehealth becomes a sustainable option used by therapists to meet the needs of children with a disability and their families.

column36: A novel mechanism of antibiotic tolerance in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
column37: Pseudomonas aeruginosa can cause devastating chronic infections that are nearly impossible to clear with antibiotics. During chronic infections, bacteria grows slowly or as aggregates called biofilms, and this physiological state leads bacteria to become "indifferent" (also termed tolerant) to the toxic effects of antibiotics. Tolerant bacteria thus cause antibiotic treatments to fail and infections to persist or relapse. Unfortunately, current antibiotics are not effective against tolerant bacteria and our understanding of the mechanisms of tolerance is still very limited. The goal of our project is to understand the mechanism of tolerance and to advance the discovery of new antibacterial therapies effective against tolerant bacteria in order to treat chronic infections. We have recently discovered that a bacterial enzyme (called cyclopropane fatty acid synthase CFAS) that modifies the Pseudomonas membrane lipids, making its envelope less permeable when they are in a slow-growing state, and thus shielding it from antibiotics. Conversely, when CFAS is disrupted, Pseudomonas become highly sensitive to antibiotic killing, leading to more effective antibiotic treatments. This suggests that CFAS could be a promising target to discover new drugs that will enhance the efficacy of existing antibiotics. For this project, we propose 1) to study how CFAS makes the Pseudomonas envelope less permeable and renders bacteria more susceptible to antibiotics; 2) to define the importance of CFAS in chronic infections using lab models of biofilms, mouse infection models and human samples of chronic infections; 3) to assess whether CFAS can be a drug target for the discovery of CFAS inhibitors as new drugs that can enhance the efficacy of antibiotics in the treatment of chronic infections.

column37: Cancer patients are particularly prone to have blood clots and/or irregular heart beats, and blood thinners are medications used to treat and prevent blood clots that may lead to stroke, death and other complications. column36: Alberta (AB) Collaborative Quality Improvement Strategies to Improve Outcomes of Preterm Infants 32 - 36 Weeks' Gestation: A Stepped-Wedge Cluster Randomized Trial (ABC-QI Trial)
column37: Every year in Canada 1 in 12 infants is born preterm, before 37 weeks of pregnancy. Of these preterm infants 85% are born between 32 and 36 weeks of pregnancy. Infants born before 32 weeks are at the highest risk of death or complications from prematurity. This has resulted in a significant amount of research and quality improvement initiatives focusing on improving outcomes for this patient group. On the other hand there is very limited research or quality improvement activities focusing on infants 32-36 weeks. This group composes a larger proportion of infants admitted to Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU). These infants require intensive care for temperature control, nutrition support, breathing support, and infection management. Information available on infants 32-36 weeks demonstrates significant variability between units in treatment approaches and length of stay. Our diverse research team aims to implement collaborative quality improvement strategies in a step-wise fashion targeting standardization of care for 32-36 week infants in Level 2 NICUs across the province of Alberta. This will be achieved by using validated quality improvement method and evidence based care bundles. These bundles will target two common issues, breathing support and nutrition support. Once trained, NICUs will benefit from collaborative networking to share information and maintain engagement. Decreasing duration of hospital stay and getting the babies home as quickly as possible is the primary objective of the study. Other objectives include reducing healthcare costs, reducing duration of breathing support, supporting infant feeding, and reducing transfer to higher level of care and emergency room visits. This study will provide evidence of the benefit of collaborative QI strategies in infants born at 32-36 weeks. This will help policy makers and government agencies in directing resources to support collaborative quality improvement in this patient group across Canada.

column36: Dissecting the origins and microenvironment of replication repair deficient hypermutant gliomas for novel immune based therapies
column37: Gliomas are the most common brain tumours in children, adolescents, and young adults (CAYA, 0-40 years) and are a leading cause of cancer death in this population. We discovered that some of these gliomas contain the highest number of DNA mutations (hypermutation) in all cancers. Hypermutation is caused by the cell's inability to repair mistakes when it replicates its DNA. Although these hypermutant gliomas are resistant to chemotherapy and radiation they are remarkably sensitive to immunotherapy. We have established an international consortium focusing on these tumours in CAYA. As a first step we found that in Canada, many of these gliomas are missed due to lack of awareness and appropriate testing. Then, through an international clinical trial, we saw that, for the first time, a third of patients with hypermutant gliomas treated with immunotherapy are long-term survivors. Recently, we discovered that these gliomas can be divided into 3 groups. Each group has different mutational spectrums and respond differently to immunotherapy. We have also established mouse models which are similar to the human glioma groups. These will be used to test new immunotherapy combinations for each glioma group. In this project we will define the impact of hypermutant glioma in Canada and find new therapies for these tumours through the following aims: In aim 1 we will use a new genomic tool to screen >1500 CAYA gliomas from 3 Canadian provinces to determine how common these gliomas are and if we can treat them differently. In aim 2 we will discover the cell of origin and how these glioma groups develop. In aim 3 we will find which immune cells are specific to each glioma group and how this can explain why they respond differently to immunotherapy. In aim 4 we will use genome editing to uncover specific gene targets, revealing weaknesses of these aggressive gliomas. We will then combine these targets with immunotherapy to improve survival for these deadly hypermutant tumours.

column36: Bridging the divide between acute medical care and housing: A comprehensive evaluation of a "medical respite program" for the homeless
column37: People with lived experience of homelessness (PWLEH) have poor health and complex medical and social needs. They frequently present to hospital to meet these needs. Unfortunately, while hospitals can treat acute medical conditions, they are not well-equipped to address social barriers (such as housing) that are frequently the root causes of ill-health. PWLEH are therefore discharged back to the street, with no real change in either their long-term trajectory in health or social conditions. Medical respite programs (MRPs) are an innovation that bridges hospital-based medical care with shelter-based housing and social support. They are designed for patients too well for acute care, but too sick to be discharged to the street. In Calgary, an MRP was recently created as a transitional unit (based within a homeless shelter) that provides nursing care, while simultaneously focusing on expediting housing. There are only three other MRPs in Canada. It is unknown how effective they are in improving health and well-being. We will conduct a mixed methods evaluation to assess the effectiveness of the Calgary MRP. Our study will follow a group of PWLEH before and after attending the MRP, to determine whether the MRP reduces rates of hospital admission, hospital length of stay, and visits to the emergency department. We will also explore whether the MRP changes patterns of drug and alcohol use, and whether it improves quality of life and time to stable housing. Lastly, in-depth interviews with MRP patients will be conducted to better understand how the MRP has (or has not) affected their social circumstances, support network, engagement with the health system and ultimately their well-being. Our findings will inform other jurisdictions on the effect of this innovation for a particularly underserved population.

The results of the proposed study will provide information about the specific healthcare needs of pregnant women with AF. column36: Modulating attentional circuitry in the anterior cingulate cortex using adaptive intracranial stimulation
column37: Attention is an incompletely understood, complex process that requires precise coordination of brain rhythms within the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC). In the current study, we will first study the association between brain rhythms in the ACC and behaviour during a task of shifting attention performed while intracranial electrodes are implanted within the ACC. Second, we will characterize how the ACC interacts with large-scale brain networks known to subserve attention while the children perform the task. Finally, we will develop and test a novel, intelligent brain stimulation algorithm that will identify disruptions in brain rhythms within the ACC in real-time. When these disruptions are detected, precisely time-locked electrical stimulation will be administered to the ACC to improve attentional performance. This work will lead to a better understanding of the fundamental mechanisms of human attention and facilitate the development of innovative avenues for the treatment of attention deficits in children with epilepsy. The novel methodologies that we will develop and test can be leveraged to understand numerous cognitive functions facilitated by the organized coordination of brain rhythms.

column36: Elucidating the cellular and network mechanisms for stress sensitivity control in the hypothalamus
column37: How do our brains determine whether something is stressful or not? Responding to threats is essential for survival (ex. escape from predator), but how we perceive certain situations as stressful is highly dynamic and variable among individuals. Clinically, high stress sensitivity is a key symptom for major depression and other mental illnesses that impose profound health and financial burden. Understanding the neural mechanisms of stress sensitivity will facilitate new prevention, diagnosis and treatments for mental illnesses. In this grant proposal, we reveal the circuit and cellular mechanisms that integrate signals at a key node of stress information processing in the brain - neurons classically known as the output neurons that drive the neuroendocrine response. Newly emerging data indicate that these neurons play more complex roles, by bidirectionally responding to competing (e.g.stressful and pleasurable) stimuli and triggering rapid behavioral changes besides the slow hormone output. Currently, we know very little about the activity patterns of these neurons in living animals, and how they process stress information. By combining cutting-edge neuroscience techniques for recording and manipulating activities of specific neuron-types inside of living animals and advanced computational simulations, we will understand how our brain perceives certain information as stressful and how their sensitivity to stress changes due to past history of stressful experiences as well as biological sex. For basic neuroscience, this study will reveal mechanisms for how our brains encode stress. For clinical translation, this work will reveal neural mechanisms controlling stress sensitivity and offers potential targets leveraged to diagnose and treat heightened stress sensitivity prevalent in mental illnesses.

column37: Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) are the most common chronic intestinal conditions and their incidence and prevalence have shown a dramatic increase in the last decades. One factor by which the diet may impact colitis involves the presence of food additives in the food supply. Among various food additives that are commonly used, artificial food dyes play a key role in enhancing the appearance of food and attracting consumers. Allura red, is one of the most widely used artificial dyes in food products, and its consumption is increasing. However, we still don't know whether allura red plays a role in pathogenesis of colitis. Serotonin is a key molecule in the human body that controls many normal and disease processes, and recently we demonstrated a novel role of serotonin in shaping gut microbiota composition and in increasing susceptibility to colitis. We hypothesize that the allura red in food enhances the susceptibility to colitis. We plan to pin down three key points: (1) Does allura red alters intestinal barrier function to increase susceptibility to colitis? (2) Does allura red influences susceptibility of colitis by affecting microbiota? and (3) Does allura red influences serotonin signaling in relation to severity of colitis. This study will not only provide us important information on the effects of allura red in pathogenesis of colitis but will also help in increasing awareness in IBD sufferers to avoid such additives as well in planning preventive programs for subjects at high risk to develop IBD.

column36: Achieving Healing and Wellness through Cultural Continuity Approaches: Strengthening Promising Practices for Addictions Treatments in an Indigenous Community in Saskatchewan
column37: Contemporary literature affirms that colonization explicitly sought to disconnect First Nations, Metis and Inuit peoples across Canada from their land and culture. Our histories of colonization and colonialism differ, but many of us are rediscovering Indigenous Ways of Knowing, Being and Doing. Within these knowledge systems, wellness is more wholistic than mere health, encompassing physical, mental, emotional and spiritual wellbeing. Forced disconnection exacerbated by a number of other socioeconomic and structural determinants is recognized as a critical factor in the current health inequities experienced by many Indigenous communities. Substance and alcohol use is a problem in northern Saskatchewan, with the rate of hospitalizations for alcohol-related issues and injuries suffered while intoxicated more than five times the national average. To address these health inequities, the adoption of community-based initiatives entrenched in decolonizing philosophies and strengths-based approaches is strongly recommended. The proposed project will be based in the Northern Village of Pinehouse, Saskatchewan. Following a needs assessment using community-based participatory methods, the Recovery Lake Program (RLP) emerged as a research priority for the community. The community has identified the need to improve RLP and develop a culturally responsive model that can be adapted and contextualized across the region. This research project will explore improving service delivery by incorporating additional land- and culture-based activities as part of the program, conduct process and outcome evaluations. Using Indigenous CBPR principles, this research project specifically focuses on ways to strengthen promising healing practices for promoting wellness in addictions treatment programs. The results will inform recommendations towards policy formulation, program planning and service delivery for culturally relevant health services and programs for Indigenous communities.

column36: A Tale of Two Resident Lung Macrophages and Their Biology In Health and Disease
column37: The lung is exposed to the external environment so we breath in some bacteria and noxious molecules with every breath. Most of these bacteria never reach the little sacs (alveoli) where oxygen is taken up but some bacteria always do. We use a special microscope to image the alveoli of mice and we have uncovered some critical functions of the immune cells. The immune cells that live in these sacs are called alveolar macrophages and they run from alveolus to alveolus through little tunnels between alveoli and vacuum up all bacteria. If the alveolar macrophages cannot crawl between alveoli than problems arise. When you get a viral infection like the flu, then macrophages cannot crawl very well and now bacteria take advantage of the situation and grow in the alveoli causing infection. The lung is surrounded by a really large sac called the pleural space and we have macrophages inside that sac as well that may oversee the role of the alveolar macrophages New macrophages come into the lung and need training to be lung macrophages. This will happen through epigenetic changes ie., environmental changes that affect the way your genes work (not changes in gene sequence though) and this will lead to better vacuuming of bacteria. In other words if our macrophages see a bacterium and have to kill it, through epigenetic changes the macrophages will kill bacteria much better the next time. We think that the more robust the microbiome is and the more we are exposed to environment the better our macrophages will be at vacuuming bacteria. However, this may make our macrophages worse at doing other chores. As mentioned, sometimes noxious stimuli enter the lungs and cause some damage and repair is required. If our macrophages are trained to do that they may not be as good at vacuuming bacteria. We will investigate how these macrophages manage to clear bacteria and repair.

column36: Leveraging Trans-Canada Expertise and Resources to Design and Evaluate Novel Auger Electron-Emitting Radioimmunotherapies (RIT) for Metastatic Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC)
column37: In this project, a team of researchers from across Canada with unique and complementary expertise and resources will work together to develop and study new targeted radiation treatments for triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), a form of the disease which has a poor outcome. The radiation treatments will consist of radioisotopes that emit short-range electrons (Auger electrons) that are very damaging and lethal to cancer cells, linked to a pharmaceutical quality antibody, panitumumab that is already used to treat certain types of cancer, in order to target these radioisotopes to tumours. The radioisotopes will be made at TRIUMF, which is Canada's world-leading facility for producing radioisotopes. Bifunctional chelators, which are molecules that strongly bind the radioisotopes and which can be attached to panitumumab will be synthesized at Simon Fraser University. The radiation treatments will be constructed from the radioisotopes, bifunctional chelators and panitumumab at the University of Toronto. They will then also be studied at the University of Toronto for treatment of metastases from TNBC in a mouse tumour model that has been established. The effectiveness and normal tissue toxicity of these new radiation treatments for TNBC will be assessed in the mouse model. The proposed project may lead to new methods to produce these radioisotopes, to stably attach them to antibodies, as well as new treatments for metastatic TNBC. Ultimately, if successful, the proposed research could be advanced to a Phase 1 clinical trial in patients with metastatic TNBC, which is a poor prognosis form of breast cancer for which there are currently very few effective treatments.

column36: Harnessing predictive analytics for personalized high-value health: nesting clinical decision support for cardiovascular disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in a provincial lung cancer screening program
column37: Background: Quebec is implementing a provincial lung cancer screening program which will screen 3,000 high risk smokers between 55-74 years of age with two annual low dose CTs over two years. The three main causes of death in participants screened for LC are cardiovascular disease (CVD 25%), LC (24%), or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD, 10%). Participants enrolled in lung cancer screening have been shown to have high rates of untreated cardiovascular disease, identified on imaging of the heart on low dose CT of the chest, and untreated COPD, identified on imaging and history documented by lung cancer screening navigators. Methods: We will perform a randomized clinical trial of comprehensive personalized health intervention provided to physicians and patients. Exploiting data already extracted by nurse navigators for lung cancer screening, and data from imaging by low dose CT as part of clinical care, we will implement a clinical decision support for primary care providers, and educational resources for patients. This will empower patients and their providers to engage with proven effective treatments for cardiovascular disease and COPD. Primary outcomes, determined at one year, are guideline concordant statin therapy in participants with moderate to severe coronary calcifications (objective 1), and guideline concordant inhaler therapy in symptomatic COPD (objective 2). Conclusions: If our hypotheses are confirmed, this patient-centered low cost approach will prove effective in mitigating health disparities among high risk men and women who have shown significant barriers in access to evidence-based care. It will also provide added value to lung cancer screening programs at low cost.

column36: Improving Maternity Outcomes by Engaging Stakeholders in a Holistic Assessment of the Social and Clinical Determinants of Severe Maternal Morbidity in Canada - a Feasibility Study
column37: Serious complications during pregnancy can impact the birth experience, mother-baby bonding, and short-term maternal health as well as have long-term effects on families. National health databases can describe total numbers of women experiencing serious pregnancy complications, also known as severe maternal morbidity (SMM), but current Canadian databases are not able to provide detailed information about the sequence of events during pregnancy that could lead to SMM. Information about maternal health, social considerations and care prior to SMM will help identify techniques and processes to target, in order to reduce SMM. Canada is a vast country with many birthing units led by obstetricians, midwives and family doctors. When a SMM occurs, often it is reviewed and shared confidentially with the birthing unit to determine what events led to it and prevent similar events in the future. However, there is no local, provincial or national mechanism for sharing lessons learned, examining trends or collecting data about SMM. We believe that lessons learned in individual units could be relevant to other units as well. Sharing and summarizing anonymous SMM information at the local, provincial and, eventually, national level will help us understand the similarities and differences between units, identify preventable factors that lead to SMM and make recommendations to reduce SMM. Other countries, such as the United Kingdom, have started sharing SMM information and the information sharing has resulted in a considerable improvement in the health of mothers. We will assess the feasibility of collecting and collating information from individual birthing units in four Canadian provinces in order to build a robust SMM surveillance system that provides ongoing information on SMM, identifies prevention strategies, and results in improved maternal health.

column36: AcT-Cog: Online cognitive assessment in the Alteplase compared to Tenecteplase (AcT) trial.
column37: When a clot stops blood flow to the brain it causes injury, called a stroke. Strokes cause problems with key functions like movement or cognition (memory and thinking skills). Three-quarters of people can have cognition problems after stroke, and this is among the most feared complications of stroke. Even before 2020, but especially in the COVID-19 pandemic, we need new ways to measure thinking that are easier for people to do. We also need to understand what the cognitive test scores really mean - how to they relate to people's quality of life, or to costs to care for people? We are doing a large study comparing two emergency stroke treatments (Alteplase compared to Tenecteplase, AcT). Using this platform, we propose a new study (AcT-Cog), in which people will complete 6 proven cognitive tasks (www.cambridgebrainsciences.com) on computer at home. The tests will be done 3-6 months after their stroke. This type of study, with easy-to-use tests that people can do at home, has not been tried before as an outcome in studies of new stroke treatments. The first goal of our study will be to see how useable it is (i.e. can people access and complete the tasks?) and understand what makes it easier or harder for people to complete the tasks. The second goal will be to see if cognitive test scores relate to important outcomes like quality of life or future need for health care. The third goal of our study will be to see if the scores from this assessment are different between the groups who get alteplase or tenecteplase. The results of this trial will help us understand when and how computer testing can be used to measure cognition after stroke and will help us understand the importance of changes in the scores. If scores differ between treatment groups, that will help inform treatment for stroke patients around the world and could help to improve cognitive outcomes after stroke.

column36: Targeting obesity-associated monocytosis in colorectal cancer liver metastasis
column37: Obesity is associated with an elevated risk of developing 13 cancer types, and an elevated risk of dying from 14 cancer types. In Canada, 24% of adults are obese and another 36% are overweight. In addition, 20% of people with a normal body weight are 'metabolically obese', meaning they have similar health risks as obese people, even though they appear healthy. Consequentially, obesity now rivals smoking tobacco as the leading preventable risk factor for cancer mortality, estimated to be responsible for up to 20% of all cancer-related deaths in adults. Most cancer deaths are caused by metastasis (cancer spread), yet we lack a strong understanding of how obesity regulates cancer metastasis. In previously published work, we discovered that obesity enhances cancer metastasis to the lungs through its effects on immune cells. We observed similar effects on immune cells in the liver, suggesting that obesity may also enhance liver metastasis. The biggest source of liver metastasis is colorectal cancer (CRC), which is the 2nd leading cause of cancer-related deaths in Canada. Obesity increases the risk of death from CRC by >40% in men and >30% in women, and we suspect it does this by enhancing liver metastasis. In new experiments, we have found that CRC liver metastasis is enhanced in mouse models of obesity. This occurs in part through the effects of obesity on specific cells of the immune system (monocytes and T cells). The objective of this proposal is to determine how monocytes and T cells regulate obesity-associated liver metastasis. We hypothesize that therapies that target these immune cells will reduce cancer progression in obese hosts. Given the prevalence of obesity and its association with cancer mortality, our research will uncover therapeutic opportunities for patients predisposed to have poorer outcomes.

column36: Tracing the Cellular and Molecular Origins of Mouse and Human Medulloblastoma
column37: Medulloblastoma is a common childhood malignant brain tumour that has a 70% 5 year survival but only with therapy that is toxic to the developing nervous system and with a significant risk of secondary cancers. My lab discovered that medulloblastoma growth is driven by rare populations of cancer cells that have stem cell properties. These specialized cancer cells divide very slowly and are called quiescent, but they give rise to daughter cells that divide very quickly. The medulloblastoma stem cells are also resistant to therapy. These findings strongly suggest that to have safer and more effective treatments, we need to first understand the growth properties of the medulloblastoma stem cells and then we need to devise treatments that kill them. In particular, we think that targeting the transition from quiescent cells to rapidly dividing cells is a pivotal treatment opportunity. In this project we will deeply study the mechanisms of how medulloblastoma stem cells transition from a quiescent state to a rapidly dividing state. We will study how internal factors regulate of this transition and how external factors may wake up the quiescent stem cells, with an aim of blocking these factors. Blocking this transition may also be preventative for medulloblastoma initiation in some circumstances. In our studies, we will use mouse models of medulloblastoma and a new human cell culture model that we developed in our lab to develop new understanding and treatment approaches. We predict that in targeting this tranistion, we will uncover new important new features of medulloblastoma growth that will lead to more effective and less toxic therapies.

column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a progressive disease of the brain and spinal cord, affecting over 2.3 million people worldwide and 93,500 people in Canada. Canada has one of the highest rates of MS globally and it is estimated that the number of people living with MS in Canada will increase to approximately 33,600 in 2031. MS mainly affects people between 15 and 40 years of age, placing a significant strain not only on patients in the prime of their life, but also on the healthcare system. Although there is no cure for MS, there are treatments available to help manage episodes of increased disability (relapses), reduce relapses, and control symptoms. Treatment with drugs known as interferon-betas were the first medications for MS and being the only promising therapeutic option initially for many years, treatment selection was limited. An increasing number of new treatments have emerged since then, however, there are limited evidence based guidelines concerning the use and selection of treatments for the various disease states of MS. Additionally, while there have been many studies that have identified specific independent risk factors for patient health outcomes, no study to date has attempted to combine these patient, disease, and treatment-related factors into a complete model to enhance the prediction of how patients will respond to treatment and whether or not they will improve. The objective of this study is to use patient data from provincial healthcare records as well as clinical data collected over an extended time period to develop and test of a series of predictive models in MS, and make these models freely available on a web-based platform. Ultimately, these models will help guide the selection of the best therapeutic approach for each individual, which will improve decision-making at the patient level. In addition, these predictions should result in better patient care as well as a more efficient and cost-effective use of healthcare resources.

column36: Combination Antithrombotic Thrombotic therapy for prevention of recurrent Ischemic Stroke in patients with IntraCranial Atherosclerotic Disease (CATIS-ICAD)
column37: Stroke is the 3rd leading cause of death and primary cause of disability in Canada and globally. Stroke caused by narrowing of the brain arteries from cholesterol plaques is the commonest cause of stroke. Many patients with narrowing of brain arteries suffer "silent" strokes, that are only picked up by MRI scans of the brain, in addition to the diagnosed symptomatic stroke. "Silent" strokes are about four times common as symptomatic stroke and overtime lead to significant memory and gait difficulties. Currently when someone has a stroke due to narrowed arteries they are treated with aspirin, blood pressure and cholesterol-lowering medications to prevent another stroke. However even with these treatments, there is a high risk of recurrent stroke (1 in 20 chance in 30 days and 1 in 10 chance at one year) A recent study in patients with narrowing of arteries in heart and limbs that added low-dose rivaroxaban (blood thinner) to aspirin showed a 50% reduction of stroke without an increase in bleeding into the brain or fatal bleeding. We plan to assess if use of low-dose rivaroxaban and aspirin is safe (no increase bleeding into brain) in patients with stroke due to narrowing of brain arteries. The ultimate goal of this pilot study is to gather necessary information to plan for a larger study to assess for effectiveness of this combination in preventing recurrent symptomatic and "silent" strokes. If this combination is eventually confirmed to reduce stroke by 50%, it would be the biggest advance in secondary stroke prevention in the past 30 years. We will enrol 100 patients from 10 Canadian sites and randomly assign to the combination treatment (50) or aspirin (50). Patients will qualify to be in the study if they are over 40 years and has a stroke or transient ischemic attack (warning stroke) due to narrowing of the brain arteries by plaque. Patients will be followed for 2 years and have an MRI scan at the beginning and end of the study to look for "silent" strokes.

column36: A comprehensive study on bone quality for the prediction of second hip fractures
column37: Hip fracture is a significant cause of morbidity and mortality; it happens easier in older people especially females. A question here is: what makes bone fragile as we become older? Current consensus is that our femoral bone becomes weaker and brittle because of the loss in bone mineral density. However, there are some unique aging related structural changes to femoral bone. These include increased porosity and decreased thickness in cortical shell. Additionally, we recently discovered that the femoral cortical bone has a layer of highly mineralized tissue covering the surface of human femoral neck, which is extremely brittle. We hypothesized that the presence of these weak structures directly increases hip fragility. In this project, a biomedical engineer with expertise in bone fracture, a bone imaging specialist, an experienced bone biologist and an orthopaedic surgeon teamed up to study the impact of decreased bone quality on hip fragility fracture. By using various advanced microscopy techniques, we aimed to answer the following three questions: Why is femoral bone fragile in older people? Are there any differences between older male adults and female adults? What are the roles of bone quality in second hip fractures? Answers to these questions will advance our knowledge on bone biology and mechanics, help to develop new techniques of bone diagnoses and lead to new measures of preventing second hip fractures.

column36: Age-associated B cells in viral infection and autoimmune diseases
column37: Our research is focused on uncovering the mechanisms in which autoimmune diseases are initiated and influenced by virus infection. In our youth, we are infected with a number of viruses that remain with us for the remainder of our lives. For its part, the virus can live forever with us and with those we come in contact with through re-infection. In our body, a cold war exists between the virus and our immune system that takes a toll on us by creating a system with strong hyper-reactive immune cells. One of these cell types, age-associated B cells (ABCs), increase in numbers as we age and engage strong immune responses capable of attacking invading pathogens and causing autoimmune responses. The relative success of generalized anti-B cell therapies for autoimmune diseases such as MS and RA is a strong piece of evidence of a common but rare B cell component to disease pathology. In this project, we aim to link these ABCs that are generated during maintenance of a common virus infection (EBV-people, and MHV68 for rodents) with increased and enhanced autoimmune diseases such as MS and RA. column36: FLASH radiotherapy - mechanisms and translational studies
column37: The effectiveness of radiotherapy is determined by normal tissue tolerance. In other words, the dose of radiation administered to the tumour is determined by how well the 'normal' tissue within the irradiated beam can tolerate the dose. Over decades the maximum dose and the optimal fractionation regime that produces the maximum anticancer effect whilst minimizing normal tissue complications has been determined for different cancer types and locations. Most often this radiotherapy treatment is fractionated, for example a prescribed dose of 60 Gy last 6 weeks with 30 fractions of ~2 Gy each. FLASH radiotherapy is a new investigational approach that can administer the total 60 Gy dose in one burst, typically lasting less than a second. This FLASH technique has emerged very recently when it was observed that in some situations radiation delivered at this high rate has less effect on normal tissues than on cancers. To advance this technique for eventual benefit to patients it is crucial to understand the precise circumstances where this differential effect on normal vs cancer tissue occurs. We will use our custom-developed laboratory techniques and experience in radiation biology to elucidate the mechanism for FLASH radiation activity, adding unique and significant insight to the building science surrounding FLASH. Ultimately, application of FLASH would significantly improve patient quality of life and treatment experience, on top of improving cancer cure rates.

column36: Development of Molecular Imaging Tools to Monitor the Fate of an Off-The-Shelf Chimeric Antigen Receptor Natural Killer (CAR-NK) Cell Immunotherapy
column37: Chimeric antigen receptor natural killer (CAR-NK) cell therapy involves modifying NK cells to in the lab with a CAR to redirect them to interact with and kill cancer cells once infused into a cancer patient. This therapy has shown tremendous potential as a curative option for patients with blood cancers, but treatment of solid tumours such as ovarian cancer has been difficult. Moreover, not all patients respond to the therapy and many patients can suffer life-threatening toxicity to healthy organs. Considering the high cost of CAR-NK cell therapy and how individual patients can respond differently, it is important that we develop new technologies to know where these cells are going and how they are behaving once injected into the body. Our goal is to build imaging tests that will allow us to visualize the fate of CAR-NK cells over the course of the lifetime of a patient. To do this, we will engineer CAR-NK cells with DNA called reporter genes that when expressed in the cells will make proteins that are detectable with either magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or positron emission tomography (PET). We will then build tools to allow us to safely insert these reporter genes at defined locations in the NK cell DNA so that safety is maximized. Finally, we will build tools to allow one to visualize when the CAR-NK cells interact with their target cancer cells. These state-of-the- art technologies will allow us to measure CAR-NK cells numbers, survival over time, and communication with cancer cells throughout the body. This collection of important information can inform on treatment effectiveness, potential toxicity, as well as determine if the cells stay alive long enough to keep killing any residual or new cancer cells long after the patient is considered cured. In doing this, it will be possible to better assess CAR-NK cell therapies in individual patients, leading to safer and more precise treatment of cancer.

column36: Improving Public Health Finance Capacity and Spending Data Monitoring and Reporting to Inform the COVID Recovery Period: An International, Sequential Mixed-Methods Investigation
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has made clearer than ever the need for strong, resilient public health (PH) systems that are sufficiently well funded. PH scholars, practitioners, and decision-makers from across the globe are now calling for a rebuilding of and reinvestment in PH systems for the COVID recovery period. Third, equipped with this new system, we will recreate and make available PH spending data in all Canadian provinces and territories from 2000 and onwards. Knowledge users who are PH decision-makers will be involved throughout the research continuum. Overall, results from this research program will directly improve the health finance systems and offer needed evidence to guide the allocation of health resources, especially between healthcare and public health. These findings will ensure that public health spending efforts are precisely reported and monitored and will inform the post-COVID investments in PH systems. By allowing better monitoring of PH spending, this project will safeguard the sustainability of PH systems, and in turn help improve population health.

column36: An unexpected role for type I Interferon underlies cardiac adaptation to stress and prevents heart failure
column37: Hypertension (HTN) can leads to detrimental changes the structure and function of the heart, a process termed hypertensive heart disease (HTN-HD). The immune system directs the sterile inflammatory response triggered during HTN-HD; however, it is unclear what components prevent or exacerbate the development of HTN-HD. Type I interferons (IFN)s are cytokines secreted by cells upon sensing of nucleic acids normally found within a cell, but released upon cell stress or cell death. IFNs bind the IFN receptor (IFNAR), required for clearance of viral pathogens. Interestingly, recent studies have shown that following a heart attack, IFNs play pathological role, are triggered by DNA released from dying cells, worsening inflammation and impairing tissue repair. Despite its well characterized role in immunity, the role of type I IFN in HTN-HD is essentially unknown. We have new, surprising evidence that rather than participating in heart damage, type I IFNs protect heart function during high hypertension and prevent HTN-HD. Our preliminary data in animal models of hypertension show mice that lack signaling through the type I IFN pathway have worse cardiac function and increased tissue fibrosis. We localize separate protective roles to immune and non-immune cell type I IFN activity, opening a new area of investigation into a previously unknown cardioprotective role of type I IFN in HTN-HD.

column36: MRI for Arrhythmia Management in Ischemic Heart Disease
column37: A major cause of sudden death is the development of a sustained very rapid heart rate associated with damage to cardiac muscle due to reduced blood supply. Several treatments have been developed to avoid this situation including the use of drugs to manage heart rate, implantable devices to reset the heart rate if an irregular rhythm is detected, and interventions where segments of cardiac muscle are destroyed through ablation to avoid conditions which can cause the rapid heart rate. The latter is potentially curative but suffers from low long-term success rates possibly due to poor ablation targeting or incomplete long-term tissue destruction. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is proving effective in characterizing damage to the cardiac muscle which, when targeted with ablations, improves success in small patient studies. Pre-clinical studies also suggest MRI is effective in visualizing tissue destruction due to ablation. Our goal is to better understand how such information from MRI can be used to better understand reasons for treatment failures and to ultimately improve treatment strategies. To do so, we plan to integrate advances in MRI lesion visualization into ablation procedures in realistic animal models performed in ways similar to recent patient studies (facilitating rapid clinical translation of results). Specifically, we will directly characterize targeting accuracy, tissue destruction and subsequent healing with MRI and relate these results to procedure success. Results will inform further development of methods for MRI tissue characterization and more effective integration of MRI information into procedures for use in patient studies, yielding better outcomes.

column36: Timing in the cerebellum: from plasticity to behavior
column37: A remarkable feature of our brains is their ability to support learning. It is widely accepted that the connections between neurons, or synapses, are capable of plastic changes. Synaptic plasticity adapts neural circuits to encode learning. However, there are thousands of synapses in a circuit, and we do not know why specific synapses are chosen to undergo plasticity. As a consequence, we cannot predict how exactly neural circuits are changed by learning, either in health or in disease. We address this fundamental problem by investigating a brain region called the cerebellum in mice, which supports the learning of precise and well-calibrated movements. Thus, forms of cerebellum-dependent motor learning can be reliably induced and measured with a high degree of accuracy. Moreover, it is particularly important to understand the cerebellum because it is strongly implicated in mental health disorders such as autism, but remains understudied. In this project, we propose to identify how plasticity serves to support learning, at multiple levels of analysis - from molecules and synapses, to neural circuits and behavior. Our preliminary results identify that plasticity is shaped by experience so that it is optimized for different behaviors. Our overall goal is to identify how and why this occurs. This knowledge is critical to understand how the brain itself can be modified, in response to injury, disease or aging. Both in Canada and worldwide, mental health disorders remain a major contributor to human suffering and economic burden - partly because effective therapies are lacking. In turn, the lack of therapies stems from a lack of knowledge about how the brain works. The proposed research into the mechanisms of learning and how these learning mechanisms can be disrupted, shaped or regulated, is thus essential for the development of effective therapeutic strategies for the broad spectrum of disorders where learning is perturbed.

column36: Gabapentinoids and the risk of severe respiratory events in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
column37: Gabapentinoids (GABAs) are drugs that are approved for the treatment of seizure and certain types of pain. In the last decade, a sharp increase in the prescription of these drugs, particularly in combination with opioids, has been observed in North America and in Europe. Although GABAs are generally thought to be safe, Health Canada and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration released warnings in 2016 and 2019, respectively, that these drugs when used alone or in combination with opioids may cause serious breathing problems, particularly in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). COPD is a severe chronic respiratory condition that impairs breathing and leads to symptoms of breathlessness, cough, chest tightness, and fatigue. Patients frequently require hospitalizations due to acute exacerbations of symptoms that can be life-threatening. However, warnings from these health agencies are based on limited evidence and no large studies have been conducted to date in COPD patients. Thus, we aim to conduct a study that will assess whether the use of GABAs increases the risk of severe exacerbations in patients with COPD, when used alone and in combination with opioids. To perform this study, we will use a database that has medical information from over 50 million patients in the United Kingdom who visited a general practitioner. We will then identify patients with COPD and determine whether those using GABAs were hospitalized with a COPD exacerbation more frequently than those who did not. We will also assess whether COPD patients using GABAs in combination with opioids were hospitalized more frequently than those using GABAs or opioids alone. The use of GABAs may potentially increase risk of exacerbations and related death in COPD patients. Thus, the findings of our project will provide important information to guide prescription choices for COPD patients and to update safety guidelines for GABAs.

column36: Impact of early life fluoride exposure on neurodevelopmental outcomes among children in the New Hampshire Birth Cohort
column37: The benefits and risks of fluoride exposure have been debated for decades. The Centers for Disease Control hails water fluoridation as one of the greatest public health achievements while others argue that fluoride exposure causes adverse health effects. While it is undisputed that fluoride is toxic at high levels (e.g. >5 mg/L), studies examining neurodevelopmental outcomes in populations exposed to optimal levels of fluoride are disputed. Existing human studies are limited in their ability to examine dose-response relations due to the restricted range of fluoride typically found in areas with fluoridation. Only a few studies have measured biomarkers of fluoride exposure across critical periods of development. Moreover, given the widespread sources of fluoride, few studies have directly linked sources of exposure when studying fluoride neurotoxicity. This study capitalizes on the New Hampshire Birth Cohort Study (NHBCS), a large, prospective cohort designed to examine how contaminants in drinking water and food affect the health of pregnant women and their children. We will leverage existing data from this cohort to assess the association between early-life exposure to fluoride (pregnancy and infancy) and children's IQ and behavioral problems in 578 mother-child pairs. Novel to our work is the measurement of fluoride in biospecimens (urine samples and toenails) as well as in tap water samples that are known to vary in fluoride concentration from approximately 0.1 to 2.0 mg/L. We will use detailed dietary intake information to understand sources of fluoride exposure in pregnant women and their infants. Finally, we will determine whether there is an increased risk of lower IQ scores or behavioral difficulties in children resulting from the use of fluoridated water to reconstitute infant formula. Results of this study will directly impact decision making on the safety of fluoride exposure during early brain development at levels relevant to the U.S. and Canada.

column36: Indispensable Amino Acid Requirements in Pregnancy and Lactation
column37: Protein is important in diet to help growth and maintain health. All body proteins are made up of 20 amino acids. Among these 20 amino acids there are 9 amino acids, which our body cannot make, and therefore must come from food sources, and are called essential amino acids. The rest of the 11 amino acids can be made in our body if there is enough protein and calories in our food. But under some conditions, such as pregnant and lactating women, the body may need more protein and essential amino acids. Until now, studying pregnant and lactating women, and their protein (amino acid) needs has been difficult. Previously used methods were invasive and test diets had to be eaten for 7 days before testing. This could harm the actively growing baby. We have recently started to use a very minimally invasive state-of-the-art method, using stable isotopes and collection of breath samples to determine amino acid and protein needs. Stable isotopes are completely safe, and our method is rapid, quick and requires only one day of the test diet. Using this method we recently showed that the actual requirements for protein are quite high during pregnancy and lactation, compared to current recommendations. We are in now in a position to study this further and also find out the how much essential amino acids our body needs during different stages of pregnancy and lactation. Our study results will help in making improved diet recommendations to make sure both mother and baby are actively growing, and have a healthy, successful pregnancy and lactation.

One important challenge to gain the needed deep understanding of ARP proteins is to define how they engage into interactions with their regulators and effectors. Given that ARFs are tightly inserted into membranes, it has been quite challenging to map their interacting proteins. Here, we report the systematic mapping of the interacting partners of all ARF proteins. We will deeply characterize the large amount of data that we accumulated using bioinformatics. The novel interactions will be validated using approaches including fly genetics. The molecular and biological functions of these interactions will be analyzed including via structural approaches. These studies represent the first systematic analyses of the ARF proteins and will reveal many new connections. Derailed ARF signalling leads to various diseases, hence this project will shed light on some of the basic molecular mechanisms implicated.

column36: T cell immunity in tissues: maintaining mobility and adapting to external forces
column37: In our globally interconnected world, many of us travel to and from work, fly between cities, or even set up residence somewhere entirely different. Establishing residence in a new place involves adapting to new circumstances, and impediments either to our travels or our adaptation to new environments can have a dramatic impact on our lives. T lymphocytes have a similarly cosmopolitan lifestyle within our bodies. The job of T cells in the immune system - to find and stop the replication of a pathogen or cancer cell as quickly as possible - requires them to commute continuously between the blood and secondary lymphoid organs. During infection T cells become able to enter other tissues and even set up residence there, establishing long-term tissue resident memory which protects the body from reinfection. We are only beginning to understand the processes that allow T cells to adapt to their new environmental circumstances and to retain their mobile behaviour even within tissues that are far more dense than the lymphoid organs they came from. From other work on heart cells and connective tissue cells, we know that cells have to protect their genomic material from external forces. The denser the tissue environment a cell finds itself in, the greater the external forces on the cell. Cells adapt by increasing the rigidity of their nucleus in which the DNA of a cell is kept. However, we also know that a very rigid nucleus can prevent the motion of cells through dense tissue. Here, we are investigating how T cells balance the need to protect their DNA from damage, and survive long-term in dense tissues, with their need to move around and search for possible pathogen invasion. If we figure this out, we may be able to selectively target the survival of T cells in tissue where they are doing damage (as is the case in autoimmune disease) or improve their ability to move into dense tissue to fight tumour cells.

column36: Molecular analysis of cell migration through control of the physical microenvironment
column37: The movement of cells from one location in the human body to another ("cell migration") is vital for myriad activities to occur both in health and disease states. In vertebrates, cell migration is absolutely critical for positioning cells during development, for wound healing and immune system functioning, but it also drives cancer metastasis and heart diseases. Cell migration is controlled by signals that originate outside the cells including growth factors, cell- generating forces and tissue mechanics. Migration of cancer cells, in particular, depends heavily on mechanical properties, e.g. stiffness, of the microenvironment. However, how cells sense tissue stiffness and then translate this information to control cell migration is not known. The project we propose seeks to identify the specific mechanisms and key players that control cell response to tissue stiffness. We will study how fluctuating forces exerted by cells on the extracellular matrix regulate mechanotransduction and cell migration. We propose changing force dynamics suppresses cell migration towards stiffer tissue, a specific type of cell migration that drives cancer metastasis. This project will shed light on how healthy mammalian cells and cancer cells sense the mechanical properties of the environment. Our results will improve the understanding of how cells migrate in response to mechanical cues. In the long-term, this information will be important to developing drugs that target cell migration in human diseases.
