column36: Prediction of Cognitive and Motor Symptom Progression in Multiple Sclerosis Using Myelin Imaging
column37: At least 50% of people living with multiple sclerosis (MS) have a progressive form of the disease, meaning that disability increases steadily. This can include physical progression, e.g. difficulty walking, and cognitive progression, meaning that people experience problems with memory, attention and problem solving. Cognitive impairment has a negative impact on quality of life, making it difficult to perform everyday tasks, and is the leading cause of unemployment for people with MS. It is difficult to determine if treatments for MS will help slow or reverse progression because symptoms worsen gradually, so clinical trials require a large number of participants and take many years. If we can understand the cause of progression in MS, we can find better ways to figure out if a treatment is working. Our goal is to show that we can use new magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) techniques to predict progression. MS damages myelin, a fatty substance that covers and protects nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord. We have developed an advanced MRI technique that can measure the amount of myelin present. We looked at the relationship between the amount of myelin and how well people performed on physical and cognitive tests. We found that myelin and test scores are closely linked, which tells us myelin damage plays a role in progression. In this study, we will ask our previous volunteers with MS to return 4 years after their original visit so we can collect additional physical, cognitive and myelin MRI data. We will explore whether the amount of myelin at the beginning of the study can predict changes in disability. We will also use new MRI tools to determine what other biological changes, in addition to myelin damage, are linked to progression. Understanding the link between biological changes (in particular myelin) and physical and cognitive changes will allow these more specific imaging methods to be used in clinical trials trying to slow myelin damage and progression.

column36: Investigating the Regulation of RET Receptor-Mediated Perineural Invasion and Metastasis
column37: Cells require signals from their surroundings in order to grow, to move, or just to survive. These processes are essential for normal development, but they can be hijacked in cancer cells, allowing the disease to grow and spread. We are interested in a cell surface molecule called RET that helps convey messages (signals) from outside the cell as part of its normal roles in tissue development. However, in some cancers, such as tumours of the pancreas, RET can also help tumour cells to spread by following a trail of signals that leads them to move toward and along nerves that lie close to the tumour (perineural invasion). In response to these signals, RET can cause cancer cells to detach from the main tumour, move through surrounding tissues and invade the nerve, making the disease hard to treat and causing the patient much pain. These roles make RET an attractive target for therapies to reduce cancer spread. Here, we aim to elucidate mechanisms that contribute to RET's roles in cancer invasion and spread. We will do this using a panel of human pancreatic cancer cell lines, and well established visualization methods and molecular tools that we have developed to identify the key protein interactions and signals RET requires to promote invasion. Once we have identified these, we will evaluate their contributions to RET's roles in in vivo pancreatic cancer growth, nerve invasion and spread to other distant sites. We will also determine whether blocking or reducing these signals can prevent cancer invasion and reduce the pain it causes when these cells are grown in vivo. Finally, we are designing a new kind of virus therapy that can specifically attack RET-expressing tumours as a way to address these processes. Our studies will establish the mechanisms of RET-mediated tumour cell dissemination and provide additional tools and therapeutic opportunities to address this complicated problem and combat human cancer spread.

column36: Investigating the regulation of the Hsp90 functional cycle by ATP, co-chaperones, and post-translational modifications
column37: All proteins must fold into a functional 3 dimensional structure in order to function in cells. However, extremely high protein concentrations in cells can lead to aggregation and loss of function before proper folding can occur. Molecular chaperones aid in the acquisition of the correct 3 dimensional structure by preventing inappropriate interactions between proteins that can lead to misfolding and aggregation. There are dozens of chaperone systems that each act in different ways to help proteins to fold. They can act as protective chambers, clamps, and even exert forces on vulnerable surfaces of the proteins they act on. The Hsp90 chaperone is critical for the folding of a large but specific set of substrate proteins that include important players in diseases like cystic fibrosis and cancer, and neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease. The mechanical basis for how Hsp90 acts on its substrates is not known but is linked to discrete physical states or 'poses' that the Hsp90 dimer can acquire. The complete set of poses that the Hsp90 dimer can assume collectively define the Hsp90 functional cycle. The rate at which Hsp90 progresses through all of the poses must be finely tuned in order to help individual substrate proteins to fold correctly. This tuning is carried out by a family of proteins called co-chaperones that are transiently recruited to Hsp90 under the influence of ATP and post-translational modifications. My lab is concerned in defining the relationship between the different poses of Hsp90 and specific co-chaperones and post-translational modifications. We employ a blend of biological (cell based), enzymatic, and structural assays to investigate the mechanics and biology of the Hsp90 system in yeast and mammalian systems.

column36: Peptide decorated magnetic nanoparticle strategies for minimally invasive targeting and removing exfoliation materials from the anterior lens capsule
column37: Ocular diseases affect vast numbers of the population and can drastically affect the quality of life that these patients, and their families, may have. An age-related ocular disease that is of particular importance is exfoliation syndrome (XFS). XFS is estimated to affect 60-70 million world-wide(although difficult to ascertain due to variability in accurate diagnosis). XFS correlates with glaucoma and is a cause for cataract formation. XFS is characterized by the formation of fibrillar materials, which are largely insoluble protein/protein fragments that are not removed through normal regulatory processes involved in ocular homeostasis. It is hypothesized that strategies for treating this disease hinges upon the ability to target the exfoliated materials observed in cases of XFS. Phage display techniques are a powerful methodology for the identification of peptide structures that can be used to target a wide variety of materials. That said, there are no known existing publications that explore a strategy for the identification of peptides for binding XFS materials; this is even more surprising when considering that some postulate that XFS is a systemic disease as exfoliation-like fibrils have been observed in multiple organs. Thus, it is the primary goal of this study to apply phage display techniques for the identification of peptides that bind to exfoliated materials associated with XFS using human anterior lens capsules. Subsequently, the second aim of this research is the in vivo analysis of these materials and how they affect the anterior segment eye structures upon magnetic field application. With these two pieces of information, subsequent treatment regimens may be hypothesized.

column36: Application of Magnetically Actuated Robotic System for Minimally Invasive Epilepsy Surgery
column37: Epilepsy is a type of brain disorder which affects nearly 1% of children where 30-40% do not respond to medical treatment for seizure control. Patients who have a seizure will experience a disruption to the sensory and motor control. The seizures can range from several seconds to a few minutes. For patients with medically resistant epilepsy, surgical treatment has been shown to be a cost effective method to stop the seizure activity. Current surgical treatment is an invasive open procedure that involves exposing the brain and performing 3 core steps to disconnect and isolate the seizure zones. In this project, we are proposing to apply a magnetically controlled robotic system for performing minimally invasive epilepsy surgery. The system will use external magnets and sensors on the tools to allow the surgeons to perform the various parts of the surgery through a single incision. The surgeon will be able to insert and deploy a steerable robotic system into specific seizure areas and use a magnetically controlled wrist to cut and isolate the target areas. The tools are also equipped with sensors such the surgeons will be able to detect any forces and collisions on the tool to help avoid causing un-intended damage. The system will be first validated on an existing brain model to confirm the robotic system's reach and visibility. After model testing, the project will conduct a pre-clinical study with a piglet model to allow surgeons to assess the efficacy and viability with live tissue. This study will have a significant impact on epilepsy care as it will improve patient care by reducing the trauma from an open procedure while decreasing the operation and patient recovery time required.

column36: Molecular mechanism of copper and platinum drug transport in human cells
column37: Copper is required for the activity of many enzymes involved in respiration, neuron function, formation of connective tissue, endocrine processes, and radical detoxification in the human body. Wilson disease protein (ATP7B) and structurally similar ATP7A regulate copper concentration in the cell and deliver copper to biosynthetic pathways. These enzymes are targets of many mutations that cause severe metabolic disorders. Importantly, ATP7B and ATP7A are involved in cancer resistance to platinum-based chemotherapeutic drugs. Our research shows that transport of copper and platinum drugs in the cells shares similar mechanism, and copper interaction with ATP7B has many common elements with ATP7B interaction with platinum anticancer drugs. To understand the activity cycle of the copper transporters in healthy cells and under the conditions of chemotherapy with platinum drugs, we will investigate copper and platinum relay from the intracellular metal delivery vehicle ATOX1, through the multiple metal-binding domains of ATP7B, and across the cell membrane. Using nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, biochemical techniques, and methods of cell biology we will investigate the role of copper transport proteins in the intracellular processing and target delivery of the platinum anticancer drugs. This work will help understand the function of an important class of transport proteins, and provide a new insight into the molecular basis of the disorders of copper metabolism. Better understanding of platinum drug transport in the cell will guide design of the novel approaches to overcome certain types of drug resistance in cancer.

column36: Decolonizing Childhood Disability: Exploring the Health Care Experiences of Racialized Children with Disabilities from the Perspective of Policy, Patients, Parents, Health Providers, and Health Policymakers
column37: Although Black Lives Matter is a movement that aims to abolish police violence against black lives, it is also a broad call to institutions to better prioritize the lives of racialized people. According to the Ontario Human Right Commission, racialized people are non-white and face oppression. The pediatric health care system is one institution that has failed to address the needs of racialized children/youth with disabilities and their parents (RCYDP). Although the evidence demonstrates that RCYDP face health barriers, to date, qualitative researchers have not investigated the health care experiences of RCYDP as they navigate the Canadian health care system. The existing literature has failed to engage health providers and the health policy landscape as well. We will conduct a two-phase qualitative study to address these critical gaps. Our study will be informed by conceptual theories that de-centre whiteness and be guided by the institutional ethnography methodology. In Phase 1, we will conduct a policy analysis of equity, diversity, and inclusion (EDI) documents across all children's hospitals in Canada to facilitate a better understanding of how these spaces produce diversity knowledge. In Phase 2 (empirical), we will undertake qualitative interviews and an arts-based method known as poetry with 18 RCYDP child-parent dyads to understand their experiences navigating the health care system. We will also conduct 12 qualitative interviews with health care workers to investigate their experiences interacting with RCYDP in clinical settings. Our final subsample will consist of 12 interviews with health policy makers to gain understanding of how health leaders view EDI. In addition to producing knowledge products such as digital reports, a poetry gallery, and workshops, our high risk study will enhance the health of RCYDP and the health care system by generating new knowledge on the experiences of these marginalized patients and parents through the arts.

column36: Attrition in pediatric obesity management: A randomized feasibility study
column37: In the past 20 years, Canada's healthcare system set up many clinics to treat childhood obesity. However, up to 80% of children who enrol at these clinics drop out before they finish treatment. This is one of the most difficult problems in managing childhood obesity. Even the most effective treatments can't help children who drop out. However, children who stick with treatment longer are more likely to see success in managing obesity. Our feasibility study will test if Family Navigation (FN) is useful for reducing this drop out from obesity treatment. We will use our results to plan a larger clinical trial. That kind of trial can give definite answers on whether family navigation is effective and useful, for children with obesity and for the healthcare system. We will enrol 108 children, from 6 to 17 years old, with obesity. Children will be receiving treatment from obesity management clinics in Edmonton, Calgary, and Mississauga. Half the children will receive Family Navigation + usual care for 12 months. The other half will receive usual care only for 12 months. Overall, the study will last 2.5 years. For children receiving Family Navigation, trained navigators will work with children and their families to reduce barriers that limit their access to health services and support. Navigators will offer extra services and resources, such as parking passes for clinic appointments and supportive text messages between appointments. Family navigation is designed to complement the obesity management received by children and their families. We will form a Steering Committee with children, caregivers, clinicians, and researchers to design and refine our Family Navigation intervention. By having better access to care, children and their families working with navigators may be less likely to drop out and more likely to attend more treatment appointments. Ultimately, they may be more likely to achieve success in managing obesity.

column36: INTerventions, Equity, Research and Action in Cities Team (INTERACT)
column37: Major government investments in urban design and transportation infrastructure ("built environment interventions") are shaping Canada's cities. These investments happen outside of the health sector, yet they have an impact on both health and health equity. The INTerventions, Equity, Research, and Action in Cities Team (INTERACT) is a pan-Canadian project assessing health and equity impacts of built environment interventions. In 2017, we launched a population health intervention research program with stakeholders and community groups in Victoria, Vancouver, Saskatoon, and Montreal. Since then, we have recruited over 2200 participants to our cohorts, and done qualitative interviews with over 100 residents living near the interventions. The main goal of INTERACT is to evaluate the impact of built environment interventions on health and health equity. Building on our past work INTERACT will add to the research of healthy cities, with more attention to design, implementation, and equity. We have three objectives: 1) we will describe how health and equity are considered in the design of built environment interventions; 2) Examine the patterns of where built environment interventions are made and for who, over time; and 3) Evaluate impacts of built environment interventions on health outcomes and health equity. We study four built environment interventions, identified with city partners. In Victoria, the All Ages and Abilities Cycling Network; in Vancouver, the City Greenways Plan; in Saskatoon, the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT); and in Montreal, ecological transition and resilience policies like greening, place-making, traffic-calming, and transportation interventions. Our proposal is especially relevant in light of the challenges brought on by COVID-19, providing evidence on longer term changes physical activity, well-being, and social connectedness impacts, before and following the pandemic.

column36: B cell intrinsic mechanisms of the germinal centre reaction
column37: Production of high affinity antibodies after virus such as COVID-19 infections or vaccination is the linchpin of the protective immunity. However, the molecular mechanism regulating high affinity antibody production is not fully understood. High affinity antibodies are produced in the germinal center (GC) in which antigen-specific B cells modify and select their antibody encoding genes in order to become high affinity antibody producing plasma cells (PCs). Abnormal regulation of molecules in B cells may lead to immune deficiency, autoimmune diseases, and even B lymphomas. In this regard, it is important to elucidate B cell intrinsic mechanisms that control the GC reaction under physiological and pathological conditions. In our previous CIHR supported studies, we have demonstrated that CBL and CBL-B (CBLs)-mediated ubiquitination plays a critical role in high affinity antibody production. CBLs do so by enabling B cells to get help from T cells and controlling GC B cells to differentiate into PCs only after they acquired a high affinity antibody. Our recent experiments further reveal that CBLs themselves are temporally regulated at different stages of the GC reaction and may involve the degradation of CBLs by the lysosomes regulated by TFEB, a master regulator for lysosome biogenesis. Interestingly, removal of CBLs from B cells leads to development of B cell lymphomas, indicating that CBLs are tumor suppressors preventing B lymphomas. Here, we propose to explore molecular mechanisms how GC B cells temporally control the expression of CBLs during the dynamic GC reaction. In addition, we will explore the role of TFEB in generating high affinity antibody producing PCs. Moreover, we will elucidate how CBLs prevent B lymphomagenesis and whether they also contribute to human B lymphomas. Completion of this project will not only bring new insight into our understanding of the antibody production but also help to treat various immune system disorders and cancer.

column36: Probing the developmental origins of pediatric cerebellar brain cancers using single cell profiling
column37: Brain tumors are the most common solid cancer in children. The cancer as well as its therapy has a damaging impact on the child's development. Scientists have found that brain cancers are in fact a collection of distinct diseases with very different properties and responses to therapy. To understand how these cancers form and how to select the least damaging therapies for each individual patient, we need to discover the changes that occur during childhood development to enable these cancers. We propose a deep computer analysis of many thousands of non-tumor and brain tumor samples to find mutations in genes and other parts of the DNA that are likely responsible for the cancer and its response to therapy. We will study these changes using information about complex networks and developmental systems active in the brain. This new information will help us better understand the role of these changes in the biology and development of brain cancers. Our study will provide detailed clues for researchers to verify new cancer genes and developmental pathways with focused experiments. It will also help build better tools for researchers to distinguish between types of cancers of the brain and potentially other types of cancer so doctors can provide personalized therapy to each patient. We strongly believe this is the best, and perhaps the only way to improve survival rates and the quality of life of Canadians with these deadly human cancers.

Guidance items agreed upon at the consensus meeting will be written into guidance documents. column36: Measuring What Matters: Development and Dissemination of a Core Outcome Set (COS) for Clinical Trials in Pediatric Anxiety Disorders
column37: Anxiety disorders are common in children and adolescents and cause significant impairment in all aspects of a child's life. Based on the available evidence, no treatment can be recommended as "optimal". The main problem is the wide variability of health outcomes measured across studies making it difficult to compare study results with each other, "pool" data across studies, and make decisions about what is the most effective treatment for various mental health concerns. A "core outcome set (COS)" is an agreed, standardized minimum set of outcomes that should be measured in all trials in specific areas of health. COS development outside of mental health care has resulted in greater standardization across research studies, which has led to enhanced research quality, and ultimately a better understanding of what treatments are best for which patients. There is no COS for trials in pediatric anxiety disorders. This project plans to develop, an evidence- and consensus-based COS for pediatric anxiety disorder trials with active engagement of youth and family members and other stakeholders. We will identify outcomes used in the literature and engage with youth and family through virtual workshops, to understand what they view as important outcomes. With a list of outcomes, we will use a consensus process to help us develop decisions on what to measure across future trials. Once the outcomes of the COS have been established, we will define "how" to measure these outcomes using measurement instruments that are reliable, valid and responsive to measure changes that are important to youth and families. This project will ensure that outcomes that are important to youth and families are part of the final COS. With greater standardization, and more patient-centric outcomes measured across trials in pediatric anxiety disorders, this project and the developed COS will lead to improved research quality and ultimately better mental health outcomes and better health utilization.

column36: MYCBP2 as a pleiotropic effector of developmental EphB tyrosine kinase signalling
column37: Cells respond to their environment by special protein signals binding cell surface receptors, which then relay this binding to other proteins inside the cell. Some signals may instruct the cell to start dividing, to move away from the signal, to change into a different kind of a cell or to simply stop doing whatever it is doing. Various disease states may change or subvert such signalling events such that, for example, cancerous cells may become unresponsive to signals that tell them to stop dividing, or tissues that normally remain separated may become aberrantly intermingled. Eph receptors mediate many such signalling events and have been implicated in diseases such as cancer and neurodegeneration, but the precise details of Eph signalling are still unknown. External signal binding to Eph receptors causes them to bind to other proteins inside the cell, and to activate their function, which in turn causes them to bind other proteins and so on, causing the activation of a signalling cascade. Such a chain of events eventually reaches some key cellular compartments like for example the cellular skeleton, which may change its shape and result in cell movement. We propose to study a protein that may participate in such a chain originating from Eph receptors. column37: More than two hundred thousand people suffer from heart attack or stroke every year in Canada. This number continues to grow despite drug developments to treat diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol and obesity. A better understanding of mechanisms altering the small vessels would provide earlier and improved risk prediction for heart attacks and strokes, and would help identify new drug targets for these diseases. By combining advanced method to analyze genes and blood proteins with artificial intelligence programs to read retina images, in large populations (Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging, UK Biobank, Prospective Urban Rural Epidemiology study), we will identify genes and proteins involved in small vessel diseases. Those findings will help discover new biological mechanisms and druggable targets to maintain small vessels healthy, and thus early prevent the occurrence of cardiovascular diseases. We will also test whether automated retinal screening can be used to improve the prediction of heart attacks and strokes. Our findings will improve risk assessment, prevention strategies, and will guide future clinical trials for cardiovascular diseases. This study will also provide targets for effective lifestyle and pharmacological interventions for small vessel changes, and in fine, to decrease heart attacks and strokes.

column36: Parsing heterogeneity in the autism spectrum through a developmental cognitive and brain perspective
column37: Approximately 1 in 66 Canadians receives a diagnosis on the autism spectrum, which represents more than 500 000 Canadians, a number constantly on the rise and challenging health services. Individuals with an autism spectrum diagnosis are very different from one another in terms of development, cognitive strengths and weaknesses, as well as underlying brain mechanisms. column36: Advancing methods and analyses to support evidence-informed decision-making on the coordinated use of travel-related measures during public health emergencies of international concern: Lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic
column37: During public health emergencies of international concern (PHEICs), effective global responses require coordinated action across jurisdictions. During the COVID-19 pandemic, countries have used travel measures to an unprecedented degree and in an uncoordinated way. Our Pandemics and Borders Project is analysing a global dataset on travel measures; systematically reviewing evidence of their impacts; and conducting case studies of decision making in Canada, USA and Hong Kong. Poorly coordinated border management contributes to underreporting of cases, increased disease transmission, and unnecessary economic and social impacts. The proposed project will build on these findings to support evidence-informed decision making on whether, when, what and how travel measures should be used. Our aims are to: 1) comparatively review and apply new methods to assess public health risks from travel during COVID-19; 2) evaluate the effectiveness of mitigating public health risks during COVID-19 of specific travel measures under different conditions; and 3) use findings to develop scenarios and pilot training exercises that simulate decision making on managing borders during PHEICs. We will use systematic reviews, various types of modelling, and viral genomic analyses to newly available datasets. We will focus on our three current case studies, with potential extension to other jurisdictions. Our interdisciplinary team, composed of 5 internationally recognized scholars and 6 outstanding trainees, will work collaboratively with knowledge users in senior national and international positions. We will produce open access datasets, methods and analyses to inform decision makers in government and key international organizations. The primary outcome will be strengthened capacity to make evidence-informed choices that enhance coordinated use of travel measures during PHEICs.

Participants will receive nicotine inhalers during two conditions, and nicotine-free inhalers during the others. For each type of inhaler, half the sessions will involve the co-administration of menthol and half will not. column37: The nucleus is the organelle controlling the expression of gene products, with functions necessary for cellular survival. Nuclear targeting is a potential tool for improving the efficacy of chemotherapy, vaccines, and gene therapy. Research focused on understanding and harnessing nuclear targeting is a topic of intense research interest. Unfortunately, nuclear-targeting agents suffer from poor nuclear localization efficiency and, as a result, this approach has yet to become a broadly effective therapeutic standard of care for cancer. Understanding and implementing nuclear targeting strategies as well as increasing knowledge of relevant fundamental principles in nuclear transport provide paths forward for biopharmaceuticals to the nucleus, increasing their efficacy, and applications beyond cancer. Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) utilize antibody selectivity to deliver a conjugated cytotoxin to receptors abundantly present on tumor cells, while sparing healthy cells and, thereby, are an improvement over traditional chemotherapy. However, tumor killing can often be modest due to the inability to accumulate the cytotoxin inside tumor cells to evoke effective cytotoxicity. This is because ADCs are reliant on delivering their cytotoxin using small intracellular vesicles named endosomes. The proposed research describes our developed technology (Accum) that couples endosome escape to nuclear localization. Accum-modified ADCs are able to maintain receptor-specific tumor targeting. Once internalized into tumor cells, Accum enables ADCs to escape endosomes and efficiently localize and accumulate in the nucleus. This results in significant improvement in therapeutic efficacy. The proposed research will develop novel Accum-modified ADCs conjugated to nuclear-active cytotoxins to enhance therapeutic efficacy for breast cancer. We will also determine dominant nuclear transport pathways for breast tumor cells in order to fine-tune localization and further enhance efficacy.

column36: Disturbances of neurogenic cardiovascular control in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
column37: When the heart pumps poorly, the brain releases into the bloodstream more noradrenaline (NA). At first, more NA improves heart function but it also increases heart rate, stores salt and water and tightens blood vessels. If the heart weakens and no longer can pump blood efficiently throughout the body, heart failure (HF) will ensue. However, many older Canadians develop another form of HF, caused by a stiff heart but normal pumping action that is an equally common cause of hospitalization and death. Their heart muscle fails to relax normally between heart beats, resulting in more fluid pressure in its pumping and reservoir chambers and in the lungs. There is little we can do in 2021 to treat this particular form of HF aside from giving pills to encourage urination to make breathing easier. Our goal is to learn if the nerves that release NA are firing at high frequency in such patients and if so, to determine why and how to prevent this. With a sterile electrode, we will record from a calf sympathetic nerve before and during 2 conditions that we know stimulates it to fire and release NA more in people with poor heart pumping. These are: increasing the volume of the heart's upper chambers and 1-leg cycling. One experiment will discover what happens to nerve firing when we apply lower body positive pressure to move blood suddenly from the legs to the heart. A second series will teach us if leg exercise stimulates more nerve firing in HF with normal pumping action, if this increase makes it hard to exercise, and if this can be improved by exercise training. We will study healthy volunteers to learn the normal response, compare their responses to HF patients, and compare what we find in men and women, as women are more likely than men to have this form of HF. If we can identify reasons why women and men develop HF because their heart does not relax well, even though it seems to squeeze normally, our findings should inspire new ways of treating this unhealthy condition.

column36: Characterizing the Effects of Immune Activity on Intestinal Epithelial Regeneration During a Vibrio cholerae Infection.
column37: The aquatic pathogen Vibrio cholerae is responsible for the severe, and potentially deadly disease, cholera, that claims roughly 100,000 lives each year. Vibrio passes through the host stomach, and enters the intestine where it encounters a dense community of gut-resident bacteria that form a natural barrier to infection. To dismantle the bacterial barrier, Vibrio injects toxic molecules into susceptible prey. By eliminating competitor bacteria Vibrio has access to host cells, where Vibrio grows, and causes the severe, rice-water diarrhea that hallmarks cholera disease. Despite the importance of bacterial competition for infection, we know very little about the effects of interbacterial warfare on the host. Researchers in my group use zebrafish and fruit flies as animal models to address this important question. Flies and fish are ideal for this work, as they develop diarrheal disease upon Vibrio infection, and have similar gut architecture to mammals. Importantly, we have access to a large number of tools for genetic experiments with fish and flies. Thus, studying disease in the fly and fish models has considerable potential to help us understand how Vibrio causes disease in humans. Recently, we showed that Vibrio-dependent killing of gut bacteria activates evolutionarily conserved immune responses in the fly host. Remarkably, immune activation is not protective for the host. Instead, immune activation blocks the repair of intestinal cells damaged by Vibrio, greatly enhancing disease severity. In this project, we will use our expertise in genetics and live models of Vibrio infection to understand how an immune response is detrimental to host recovery from infection. We believe this work represents a significant step towards identifying actionable therapies for a global health and economic burden.

column36: Regulation of the epigenome by replication stress in vascular disease and aging
column37: The epigenome is the layer of protein modifications to DNA and the proteins that assemble DNA into the nucleus known as histones. Together, these epigenetic modifications to the DNA and histones as well as proteins that anchor the DNA to the nucleus organize DNA into a 3-dimensional (3D) structure that allows some genes to be expressed and others to be silent, depending on the cell type. Thus, the epigenome is responsible for a heart muscle cell to express genes and proteins important to the heart muscle rather than genes and proteins expressed by bone cells. Aged and diseased cells lose their epigenetic modifications, leading to an altered epigenome, loss of cell identity, and cellular function. Thus, vascular cells of the heart can begin expressing bone proteins leading to "hardening of the arteries", also known as atherosclerosis. Importantly, many epigenetic modifications are reversible using drugs. In this project, we generated stem cells from patients with a rare disorder known as Progeria, in which the vasculature and other organs age very fast and the patients suffer heart attacks and stroke in their teen years due to hardening of the arteries. Underlying this vascular degeneration are DNA damage, rapid cellular aging and loss of the epigenetic modifications to the vascular cells, which we also find in the vascular cells grown from the Progeria patient stem cells. We will piece together the molecular mechanisms driving these defects using the Progeria patient stem cell-derived vascular cells. We will then test these mechanisms in tissue isolated from organ donors and patients with heart disease following surgical intervention to determine whether the Progeria patient cells model normative vascular aging and pathogenesis. We will also test the abnormal cellular behaviour using drugs that target the epigenome, thereby potentially identifying a new drug to treat vascular and heart disease.

column36: Understanding the effects of ERK hyperactivation in cancer: implications for therapy
column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in Canada and worldwide, suffering from a late stage of disease at the time of diagnosis and a paucity of effective drugs available to treat advanced tumours. Despite a greater understanding of the genetic basis of lung cancer development, discovery of new therapeutics has been slow as the activities of genes implicated in this disease are difficult to inhibit while new agents targeting lung cancer cells have been ineffective due to drug resistance. Therefore, new strategies are urgently needed to develop effective therapeutic strategies for lung cancer patients that yield robust responses and improve long-term survival rates. Currently, drug discovery is based on identifying mutated genes in lung tumours, determining if its modulation impacts growth, and then screening or designing drugs to inhibit gene function. In this manner, therapies are aimed at "putting the breaks" on the signals that promote tumor growth. Unexpectedly, we have recently found that lung cancer cells also cannot tolerate increases in signaling, akin to "flooring the gas pedal". However, we still do not know why this hyperactive signaling is toxic to cancer cells and whether or not we can use this information to treat cancer patients. The goal of this proposal is to understand why too much signaling kills cancer cells and determine whether drugs that can mimic this scenario offer an effective way of inhibiting lung tumour growth. We aim to test candidate drugs that target the "regulators" in lung cancer cells which act as a fail safe to prevent hyperactivation from occurring. By disrupting these key regulators, we predict that cancer cells will "overheat" from too much signaling, causing their death, and we will assess their effectiveness in model systems for the first time. Thus, this work will offer true progress towards developing new agents for the treatment of lung cancer, ultimately leading to improved survival rates for patients.

column36: Role of the mitochondrial carrier family protein SLC25A46 in mitochondrial dynamics and early onset neurodegenerative diseases
column37: All cells in the body require chemical energy to carry out their normal physiological functions. The majority of this energy is packaged as a compound called ATP and is produced by the oxidation of carbohydrate and fat in a biochemical process called oxidative phosphorylation. This process takes place in a compartment of the cell called the mitochondrion, and is carried out by several large protein complexes that constitute the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Respiratory chain dysfunction interferes with the normal supply of energy, and this produces a wide variety of different diseases, such as neurodegenerative and heart disease, the nature and severity of which depend on the exact genetic defect. The genetics of respiratory chain diseases is complicated by the fact that some components of the system are encoded in nuclear genes, others in a small genome that is contained within the mitochondria themselves. Mitochondria also rely on intimate contacts with other organelles in the cell, most notably a structure called the endoplasmic reticulum, which, among other things, supplies mitochondria with the lipids required for mitochondrial growth and division, and acts as a reservoir for calcium, which in part regulates mitochondrial metabolism. Several neurological diseases result from disturbances in the contacts between mitochondria and the ER. We have identified mutations in a gene coding protein of the mitochondrial metabolite carrier family, that seems to be involved in communication between the mitochondrial outer membrane and the endoplasmic reticulum, which result in an astonishingly large spectrum of neurological diseases and this project is aimed at investigating its precise molecular functions in healthy cells and in cells from patients with mitochondrial disease.

column36: Immunomodulatory Gene Therapy Strategies for Post-Traumatic and Metabolic Forms of Osteoarthritis
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a disease that occurs when joint structures, including the articular cartilage that protects the ends of bones, degenerate following trauma or due to conditions such as obesity. OA leads to chronic pain and disability and places a significant burden on the Canadian healthcare system and economy. However, there are no therapies available that can slow or reverse disease progression. Our previous studies have shown that gene therapy vectors can be used to deliver therapeutics directly to affected OA joints for an extended period. Using this approach, we have shown that a gene therapy vector expressing IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1Ra) - an anti-inflammatory molecule - can slow disease progression in small and large animal models of injury-induced OA. We also showed that delivery of the joint lubricant proteoglycan 4 in combination with IL-1Ra provided greater therapeutic effects than either gene therapy alone. Despite these successes, joint inflammation was not entirely resolved by either strategy, and efficacy was eventually lost. Thus, broader inhibition of inflammation may be necessary to curb OA progression, or other factors that drive inflammatory resolution may be required for tissue repair. This proposal will examine whether blocking multiple inflammatory factors simultaneously during active inflammation can better slow OA progression in mouse models of injury-induced disease. We will also explore inflammation-responsive switches to activate the delivery of regenerative factors to promote tissue repair only in the context of injury. In parallel, since little research has examined gene therapies for obesity-induced OA, we will investigate whether these anti-inflammatory strategies can slow disease progression in diet-induced mouse models of early-onset disease. Importantly, this will reveal the role of inflammation in the pathogenesis of OA resulting from various causes, including trauma and obesity.

column36: Identifying Metabolomic Markers of Disease Activity in Psoriatic Disease using Solid Phase Microextraction - Liquid Chromatography - High Resolution Mass Spectrometry
column37: Psoriasis is a common chronic inflammatory skin disease that affects more than a million Canadians. Many patients with psoriasis also have involvement of the joints and develop a specific form of arthritis called psoriatic arthritis. Patients with psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis have flaky, red, itchy skin, joint destruction, limitation of function and poor quality of life. It is important to accurately determine how active psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis is so that appropriate treatment is initiated and further damage to joints reduced. However, current methods of assessing disease activity are imprecise, subjective and labour intensive. We do not have a good understanding of pathways of metabolism underlying active disease. Our purpose is to confirm whether small molecules (metabolites) and pathways that we have previously identified reliably measure disease activity. To achieve our objectives, we will test blood samples collected from patients with psoriatic arthritis who have undergone careful assessment of disease activity by ultrasound scan of their joints. We will also collect blood samples from patients with PsA who have the full range of severity of skin psoriasis. We will then subject the samples to novel laboratory methods to identify metabolites associated with active skin and joint disease. We will also determine if these blood metabolites are able to identify patients with psoriatic arthritis who have mild, moderate, and severe disease as measured by routine clinical methods. The study will confirm previously identified small molecules and pathways driving inflammation in the skin and joints in patients with psoriasis. In future we will confirm that biomarker-based assessment is better than currently used clinical methods. Once confirmed we will have better means of measuring disease activity and will help make treatment decision making easier and better informed, thus leading to better outcomes for patients with psoriatic disease.

column36: Cumulative effects of contact sport participation: a multi-parameter brain imaging investigation
column37: There is growing concern about the risks involved with playing contact sports, as there is evidence that repeated head impacts may lead to long-term problems with brain health, including difficulties with thinking and mood and potentially an increased risk of conditions such as Alzheimer's Disease and Parkinson's Disease. However, we do not yet fully understand how short-term brain changes associated with repeated head impacts translate into more severe long-term changes in brain health. This limits our ability to accurately evaluate the risks of playing in contact sports. In this study, we propose to fill this knowledge gap by using magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to scan the brains of university-level athletes throughout the entire course of their varsity career, which is typically 3 years, and also to monitor other aspects of their health, including assessments of symptoms, balance and thinking ability. This will allow us to map long-term brain changes of athletes in contact and non-contact sports, to better understand the cumulative effects of contact sports on brain health. We will also examine differences in outcome between male and female athletes. This research will provide novel information about how the brain responds to repetitive impacts during contact sport participation. It may be used to develop safer guidelines for sport participation, and in the future, will lay the groundwork to develop better measures for monitoring brain health among athletes.

column36: Move&Connect: A pilot-controlled study of a holistic interdisciplinary intervention for youth experiencing prolonged recovery post-concussion and their caregivers
column37: Concussion is a serious public health concern for youth. While most youth get better quickly after a concussion, many struggle for months and even years after the injury. During this time, they continue to experience problems (persistent post-concussion symptoms) that can affect day to day life. Caregivers or parents also experience distress and families have a difficult time coping with symptoms that do not get better as expected. Sadly, there are no programs or supports that consider the needs of both youth with persistent post-concussion symptoms and the well-being of their caregivers. In response to this need, and with input from clients and caregivers, we developed a program called Move&Connect that has two arms: (1) a movement, well-being, and education group for youth with persistent post-concussion symptoms; and, (2) a support, education, and advocacy skills training group for caregivers. Now, we need to test the program. We hope that after youth and caregivers finish their programs, they feel better and more confident, and that the family environment will improve. To do this, groups of youth and caregivers will take part in the intervention. Some will do this in-person and others virtually (over the computer at home). We will also talk to them about the program and ask them questions about their experiences. In the future, the Move&Connect program will be offered in clinics and hospitals to help youth, and their caregivers and families, recover well and thrive after concussion.

column36: Advancing the therapeutic opportunity for TLR4 in reducing cisplatin-induced ototoxicity
column37: Cisplatin is the chemotherapy of choice for the treatment of solid tumours in children; however, about half of these children experience some form of hearing loss that is caused by this drug. Hearing loss in children is especially detrimental because this is a critical time when learning and socialization skills are developed. Negative impacts have also been documented into adulthood. The goal of this project is to take advantage of the link between cisplatin hearing damage and a cell surface receptor that is normally involved in mounting immune responses to bacteria. We have designed compounds that block cisplatin's activation of this receptor without affecting its immune function. One aim of this project will be to determine how these compounds exclusively prevent cisplatin activation of the receptor. A second aim will be to develop improved inhibitors of this receptor that disrupt cisplatin toxicity in ear cells. Promising molecules will be tested in zebrafish and mouse models of cisplatin hearing loss. A third aim will examine whether these inhibitors affect the ability of cisplatin to kill cancer cells. We will test this directly on cancer cells, as well as in zebrafish and mouse models where we can directly compare cisplatin tumour killing and toxicity. We will examine alternate routes of co-administering cisplatin and inhibitors, to optimize tumour killing with minimal toxicity. Our research teams consists of experts in molecular biology, mass spectrometry, zebrafish biology, mouse models of hearing and chemistry. The molecules developed in this project that demonstrate an ability to prevent cisplatin toxicity in cells and zebrafish will be moved closer to clinical practice by linkages with a national network examining drug safety in childhood cancer treatment.

column36: Mechanism and pharmacological modulation of intrinsic and acquired pro-inflammatory state of the airway epithelia in cystic fibrosis
column37: The cystic fibrosis (CF) protein (CFTR) ensures the normal water and ion composition of the liquid that lines the airway. Mutations in CF impair the CFTR function and the composition of the airway surface liquid layer. This leads to lung inflammation, which is further exacerbated by infection, the primary cause of premature death in CF. Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteria cause the most common infection of the CF lung, with ~80% of CF patients becoming chronically infected, which lead to faster loss of lung function and decreased survival, partly due to the inherently hyper-responsive state of the CF lung prior to infection and to the P. aeruginosa virulence factors that attenuate both the mutant CFTR functional expression and the efficacy of CFTR folding correctors. P. aeruginosa also evokes an excessive innate immune response, characterized by cytokines, lipid mediators and elastase release, neutrophil influx, which further compromise the mutant CFTR function. Here we propose to elucidate the underlying molecular basis of the sterile inflammation, associated with the human CF bronchial epithelia (CF-HBE) or nasal epithelia (CF-HNE) cultures in the absence or presence of white blood cells. Similar studies will be performed in the presence of bacteria secretion, enabling us to study the inflammatory mediator activation time course and the mutant CFTR function in presence and absence of CFTR corrector drugs, as well as upon various interventions that suppress the innate immune response. CFTR functional rescue will include a recently identified surface receptor that can modulate the inflammatory signalling in the absence of CFTR. To capture the variability of cellular responses to CFTR modulators and innate immune signaling among CF patients, HNE and HBE collected from 20 patients homozygous for the F508del mutation will be used in the proposed model. The results may pinpoint novel approaches to suppress the excessive sterile inflammation of the CF lung.

column36: Translation initiation via factorless internal ribosome entry site mechanisms
column37: All viruses go through an important stage during their life cycle called translation where viral proteins are expressed from a viral RNA. Some viruses such as poliovirus and Hepatitis C use a translation mechanism called an Internal Ribosome Entry Site or IRES for expressing their proteins. This IRES mechanism is not only important for viruses but also for cellular genes, including those involved in cancer. Therefore, elucidating IRES mechanisms is crucial for understanding a fundamental process of gene expression. Currently, IRES mechanisms are poorly understood. To gain insight, we will characterize a novel IRES mechanism found in an insect virus, called dicistrovirus. Using biochemical techniques, we will identify how this IRES interacts with and hijacks the host cell machinery. This insect IRES is functional in many systems including yeast and human cells, indicating that this unprecedented mechanism is conserved and that specialized cellular genes may also use this mechanism. Using biochemical methods, we will elucidate key elements that govern IRES mechanisms. Moreover, we will identify key viral proteins that promote IRES gene expression. Finally, using this knowledge, we can search for cellular genes that also use this mechanism for gene expression. This proposal will not only shed light into the biological significance of this novel viral IRES mechanism but also provide a framework for understanding other viral and cellular IRES mechanisms in general.

column36: Role of vessel-resident progenitor cells in vascular disease
column37: Risk factors such as high blood pressure [BP], also known as hypertension, lead to changes in blood vessel structure and function, which can damage vital organs such as heart, kidney and brain. We believe these risk factors cause changes in blood vessels by affecting the stem cells that produce their cell components (e.g. vascular smooth muscle cells, VSMC). Using stem cells from the skin, we showed that stem cells of patients with high-BP produce VSMC that did not function or repair as well as healthy individuals. Now, we study whether this also happens in stem cells found in blood vessels (i.e. vessel-resident stem cells), which can be identified by a protein known as Sca1. We will study Sca1 stem cells and how they are involved in high-BP. In Aim-1A, we will test how much vessel remodeling after high-BP comes from Sca1 stem cells. Using mice that label all Sca1 cells and the cells that they produce, we can track when and where Sca1 cells are going, see what cells they produce, and see what genes are changed after experimental high-BP. Then, in Aim-1B, we will study if experimental high-BP disturbs Sca1 cells from producing normal cells, and if so, which genes may be causing this. We will isolate labelled Sca1 cells, test their function, and look at gene changes as in Aim-1A. We suspect genes changed in Aim-1B cause disease. So, in Aim 2A, we test if healthy Sca1 cells become diseased by changing these genes, and if diseased cells can be cured by reversing these changes. Then, in Aim-2B, we will give high-BP to mice genetically modified to lack disease genes, to test if this will prevent high-BP from affecting Sca1 cells and blood vessels. Lastly, in Aim-3, we will use mice genetically modified to not have Sca1, to see how their stem cells and blood vessels respond to high-BP. Together, these studies will help us understand what is happening to stem cells and blood vessels after high-BP, and help us find which genes cause high-BP-related vessel disease.

column36: Regulation of a Synaptic Pathway in Neuropsychiatric Disorders
column37: Nerve cell connections, known as synapses, are the fundamental units of communication and information processing in the brain. Synapses develop by interactions of specialized proteins called synapse organizers. We now show that these proteins are not only required for synapse organization but are also required for enduring changes in synapses that are important for cognitive functions such as learning and memory. Variations in the genes for major synapse organizing proteins predispose to neuropsychiatric disorders such as autism and schizophrenia. We have discovered a novel form of a disease-associated synapse organizing protein abundant in the brain but whose function is entirely unknown. We have discovered that an intricate biochemical switch governs the binding of this class of synapse organizers to its cognate partners essential for their function. In a mouse brain circuit, we will explore how synapses develop and function when this switch is turned on or off and assess how this affects the underlying process leading to learning and memory. Our work will show how altered biochemical signaling affects brain wiring, producing deficits such as in autism and schizophrenia. Our study will increase our understanding of the causes of neuropsychiatric disorders and enable us to identify amenable targets to design rational drugs for neuropsychiatric disorders.

column36: Expediting the drug approval process in oncology through access with evidence development schemes
column37: The process of approving new drugs to treat cancer can be time-consuming and expensive, which prevents universal access to life-extending/life-saving treatments. Researchers have proposed a process for approving drugs that reduces the time between their initial development and their widespread use in Canada. This process is known as an Access with Evidence Development scheme (AEDs). An AED gives approval for an innovative drug to be used in Canada whilst further evidence, usually on the real-world effects of the drug, is collected. Once this evidence has been collected, the approval can be removed if the new evidence indicates that the drug is less effective than we hoped. Data collected routinely as part of clinical care can be vital source of data to reassess these drugs. It can be difficult to determine what evidence should be collected and when it should be analysed to reassess the drug. A method known as "Value of Information" has been suggested to support these decisions, but several barriers have previously prevented its use. The advantage of the Value of Information method is that it ensures that the evidence collected during the AED would help policymakers decide whether a novel cancer therapy can improve patient outcomes. This project aims to tackle the barriers to its implementation by developing an example AED for a drug to treat colorectal cancer. The project will also develop new methods that allow us to determine the best time to reassess a new drug and create guidance and statistical code to support the use of the Value of Information method in practice. This project will improve the development of AEDs to ensure that effective, safe and efficient treatments are approved in a timely manner. This will reduce the time taken for Canadian patients to access innovative drugs for treating cancer while also ensuring that patients are not exposed to ineffective or harmful treatments.

column36: Addressing household food insecurity in Canada: learning from the COVID-19 pandemic
column37: Household food insecurity refers to the inability of individuals and families to afford the food they need because of financial constraints. In 2017-18, over 4.4 million Canadians were affected by food insecurity and this number appears to have risen through the COVID-19 pandemic. This is concerning because compared to other Canadians, those who are food insecure have poorer physical and mental health and much higher risks of chronic disease and premature death. So, food insecurity places a heavy burden on our health care system. Losses in employment incomes through the pandemic could be expected to increase household food insecurity in Canada, but the extent to which these hardships have been offset by federal income and wage subsidy programs is unknown. We will analyze national population survey data collected from 2019 through 2021 to identify the household circumstances and employment conditions associated with household food insecurity before and during the pandemic. We will also determine how the Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB) and Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB) have affected households' food security. Our research findings will help inform the development of more effective policies and programs to prevent and reduce food insecurity in Canada.

column36: Unifying Molecular Omics, Multi-Modal Neuroimaging and Artificial Intelligence for Biologically-defined Patient Stratification in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
column37: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating heterogeneous neurodegenerative condition with abnormalities in protein accumulation (TDP-43, SOD1), vascularization, inflammation, neuronal activity and cerebral atrophy. In keeping with the tenets of Personalized Medicine, treatments should be tailored to individual therapeutic needs as opposed to treating all patients with the same approach. In ALS, however, we currently do not have appropriate methods for pathophysiological patient staging and stratification. Furthermore, because we continue to lack robust tools to characterize each patient's distinctive disease progression, evaluating the effectiveness of different therapies remains challenging. Prompted by the imperative for customized treatment of ALS, our goal is the implementation and clinical validation of a biologically-defined staging and stratification of the ALS spectrum using an artificial intelligence (AI) framework to integrate massive amounts of molecular and neuroimaging data. Consequently, we are integrating a large amount of biological data (including transcriptomics and neuroimaging) into a simplified and clinician-friendly personalized clinical profile reflecting both disease progression and variants. This framework aims to bridge the Molecular, Neuroimaging and AI fields to overcome the major limitations of traditional clinical diagnoses and eventually provide patients with true Personalized Medicine. In this project, the clinical applicability of our already developed model will be validated with two large-scale populations in the ALS spectrum. Critically, all resulting analytic tools will be shared with the international community via user-friendly multitool software, contributing to translate our research findings into daily clinical practice.

column36: Investigating the role of the astrocytic ATRX chromatin factor in memory processes

Our lab has created several genetically modified mice to study the particular roles of ATRX in different brain cell types, including neurons (cells that propagate information or signals) or astrocytes (cells that control the propagation of that signal). Unexpectedly, we found that if we remove ATRX in astrocytes, the memory deficits are different than if we remove it in neurons, suggesting that ATRX regulates different genes in each cell type, enabling different kinds of memory processes. In this study, we want to determine whether memory is affected differently by loss of astrocytic ATRX depending on the sex of the mice. We also propose experiments to determine the role of ATRX in astrocytes in supporting signal propagation and memory processes and how we could potentially improve memory in these mice. The results generated will help us better understand how memories are regulated and identify strategies to improve memory in children with intellectual disability.

column36: Investigating diffuse midline glioma evolution and treatment resistance
column37: Brainstem cancers called DMG are near-universally fatal and are one of the leading causes of cancer-related death in children. Our team is devoted to finding better treatment for this cancer. Using patient samples we have assembled over the last 15 years we studied the genetics of these tumors, finding mutations in proteins called histones which may help explain what causes this cancer but we still haven't found a way to successfully treat these patients. Major knowledge gaps remain. 1) We still don't fully understand how histone mutations initiate and/or maintain cancer cells, making it hard to effectively target their effects; 2) We don't know how the cancer cells acquire their invasive properties, allowing them to escape the site of origin and travel to distant brain sites; and 3) Although some patients clearly respond to radiation, the tumors become resistant and the patients relapse - the mechanisms of this resistance is unclear. We are leaders in the field of DMG, and are well poised to translate discoveries made through this project into novel and more successful therapeutic trials for this fatal disease.

column37: Telerehabilitation use, or virtual rehabilitation, has grown exponentially in order to continue to provide essential rehabilitation services to the population during the Covid-19 pandemic in response to physical distancing requirements. As well, people with disability need to be better equipped to this new way of receiving rehabilitation services. As a team of researchers with multiple partners in the community and health care sectors, we aim to put in place a community of practice that will learn from research and current virtual rehabilitation practices, and work together to share, support and improve the use of virutal rehabilitation in Canada. We will conduct a review of the virtual rehabilitation literature, analyze current virutal rehabilitation practices, and examine clinicians, managers, decision makers, and people with disability's experiences with virtual rehabilitation to better understand what works, what does not, and why. We will hold consensus meetings to create and contribute to guiding principles and tools for the continued use of virtual rehabilitation activities to ultimately improve the health and wellbeing of all people with disability.

column36: Genomic dissection of de novo metastatic prostate cancer prior to treatment
column37: In its most aggressive form, prostate cancer has already spread to the bone and/or lymph nodes at the time of first diagnosis. These sites of cancer outside the prostate are called metastases, and cause most cancer-related deaths. People with metastases at first diagnosis have what is termed 'de novo' metastatic prostate cancer, and have a very poor prognosis. Excitingly, new and emerging therapies can significantly improve life expectancy. However, potentially toxic drugs should be applied discriminately, only where patient quality or quantity of life will be significantly improved. This is not currently the case in prostate cancer management: patients receive treatments that are not personalised against their cancer. The major barrier to improved patient stratification is that we do not understand the relationship and composition of the prostate and metastatic cancers in de novo metastatic disease. This is because affected patients do not undergo surgery to remove their prostate or metastases, so historically there has been little cancerous tissue to study. We have compiled the first standardized cohort of surgically-removed tumours from people at first diagnosis with de novo metastatic prostate cancer, before they begin other treatment. This includes the whole prostate, individual metastases, and also tumour DNA shed into the blood (a 'liquid biopsy'). We plan to use custom DNA sequencing approaches and novel computational algorithms to understand how these coexisting primary and metastatic cancers are related to each other. We will identify the precise regions of the primary cancer that gave rise to lethal metastatic disease. Our work will establish a framework for identifying the molecular features of metastatic prostate cancer at first diagnosis. This framework can then be used in clinical trials to implement therapeutic strategies that are more tailored to patient-specific disease biology, reducing the mortality and morbidity of aggressive prostate cancer.

column36: Devices for Image-Guided Biopsy of Peripheral Lung Nodules
column37: Lung cancer continues to be the leading cause of cancer death in Canada, accounting for nearly 1 in 4 of cancer deaths. Low-dose spiral computed tomography (CT) scanning can identify potentially cancerous lung nodules earlier than ever before. However, for definitive diagnosis, these lung nodules must be biopsied - a difficult task since these nodules are often located in the lung periphery and are inaccessible using standard video bronchoscopy. Radial endobronchial ultrasound probes can be used with bronchoscopes to extend imaging into smaller airways, but this technique suffers from low diagnostic yield (~70%). Patients with nodules that cannot be endoscopically sampled often undergo CT-guided needle biopsy through the chest wall, but this method has a higher rate of serious complications such as collapsed lung and internal bleeding. Thus, there is an unmet clinical need for endoscopic biopsy devices that can provide high diagnostic yield for peripheral lung nodules. This proposal will develop two types of integrated imaging-biopsy catheters that will be deployable through the bronchoscope instrument channel and be able to image during biopsy to ensure accurate and precise biopsy sampling. The imaging catheters will use OCT-AFI, an imaging modality we developed that provides co-registered optical coherence tomography and autofluorescence imaging, giving both structural and biochemical information simultaneously. We will also develop realistic lung models to test and evaluate the ability of the imaging/biopsy catheters to locate and biopsy peripheral lung nodules. Safety and efficacy of the devices will also be tested in a feasibility trial using pigs. Success in this project will improve patient care by providing proof-of-principle demonstrations of technology to safely and accurately diagnosis peripheral lung nodules endoscopically, avoiding complications and radiation exposure incurred during CT-guided transthoracic lung biopsy.

column36: Disease-modifying effects of osteotomy and exercise for knee osteoarthritis
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a growing cause of pain and disability that already affects over 4 million Canadians. OA of the knee is especially common and disabling. OA is not just a natural part of aging, but is a disease with serious effects on our health. While we have treatments that help with symptoms for the short-term, none stop the process of joint damage and long-term pain and decreased function. The need for treatments to slow OA progression has been identified by patients and researchers around the world as a top priority. One of the reasons why this has been so difficult is that the mechanisms involved in OA are complex. We know that excessive knee loading (mechanics) and the knee tissues' responses (biology) to loading are important, but we have not yet learned how to change them in a long-lasting way. Our team has some early positive findings from prior studies on a surgery called High Tibial Osteotomy (HTO). HTO straightens the lower limb of patients with varus (bowed) knees (present in over half of patients with knee OA). The goal of the surgery is to improve how our knees are loaded during walking. This should result in less joint damage and long-term improvements in pain and function. We plan to test patients from our earlier studies comparing HTO to standard care (exercise, weight-loss, pain medications) to see if the surgery provides benefits 5 years after treatment. This is important since OA progresses over long periods of time in most people. Since this is such a different approach than standard treatments, it also allows us test disease processes. We will use state-of-the-art gait analysis, imaging techniques, and tests on blood and fluid removed from the patients' knees. We will look for different patterns of OA progression for men and women with and without this surgery. Understanding the factors that determine these different patterns of disease progression will help us understand the mechanisms, target existing treatments or create new ones.

column36: Cardiac Sarcoidosis Multi-Center Randomized Controlled Trial (CHASM CS- RCT)
column37: Sarcoidosis is an inflammatory disease of unknown cause and it can be estimated that currently there are between 19,000 and 22,500 Canadians living with sarcoidosis. The disease can be very serious if it affects the heart, when it is called cardiac sarcoidosis (CS) and most CS occurs in patients aged 25-60 years. Patients with CS have a much higher risk of dying than sarcoidosis patients without heart involvement. In addition, it is becoming clear that CS is much more common than once thought. The three main ways that CS can affect the heart are: (1) blockage of electrical conduction from the upper to the bottom heart chamber, (heart block), (2) very rapid heartbeats (arrhythmias) and (3) weakening of the heart muscle, (heart failure). The disease has been largely neglected by researchers and the current science is of modest quality. Hence, there is a lack of evidence to guide doctors in treating patients The current standard of care treatment for CS is with steroids which can be very effective but have lots of side effects and negatively impact patient's quality of life in a major way. Hence there is interest in trying alternative agents and in this trial, we will be comparing two treatment regimes. Patients will be allocated to treatment group by random chance (electronic 'toss of the coin'). We hypothesize that the experimental treatment will have similar efficacy to standard treatment with steroids and that experimental treatment will result in significantly better quality of life and fewer side effects than standard dose steroids. We plan to recruit 194 patients over 4 years in 32 major hospitals in Canada/US/Japan/UK The University of Ottawa Heart Institute will manage the study and will be responsible for managing information generated in this study. Our study is unique and innovative as it is the first trial involving multiple centers in the world evaluating patients with CS. This study will produce the highest quality information in the medical field.

column36: Relating the development of microscopic hippocampal pathways to concept learning: Complementary neural network and white matter investigations
column37: Childhood is marked by constant learning. Despite their more limited knowledge bases and functionally immature brains, children acquire a vast amount of information about the world. What supports this rapid new learning, and how is the child's learning brain different from that of an adult? In the current project, we aim to answer these questions by characterizing how children differ from adults in (1) their knowledge of real-world concepts and (2) the specific brain structures and pathways that guide the creation of new concepts. We focus on the hippocampus, a brain region known to support concept learning in adults by connecting elements of experience across time and space. Emerging evidence suggests children learn differently: unable to flexibly connect multiple pieces of experience, children instead learn about inherent properties of concepts like their appearance. Here, we test the prediction that these developmental differences in concept learning arise due to maturation of the hippocampus. We combine behavioural, brain imaging, and neural network modelling methods to investigate the structural development of the hippocampus and the emergence of specific learning operations that support the formation of rich, real-world knowledge in children, adolescents, and adults. Our multifaceted approach will provide novel insight into how the brain's memory system supports learning and inform our understanding of developmental disorders (autism, schizophrenia) known to impact memory.

column37: Preterm birth, which is the leading cause of death of children under 5-year-old worldwide, involves the obligatory mediator: prostaglandin F2alpha receptor (FP), a lipid mediator receptor that controls the onset of uterus contraction. In Canada, preterm birth has increased by 20 % in the last two decades and accounts for two-thirds of the infant death. The cause of more than 70% of preterm birth is unknown, and the medications to prevent preterm birth are ineffective. FP represents a potential target to develop better and safer tocolytics (labour repressants) with a new class of drugs selectively targeting regulators of uterine contraction. However, the rational design of tocolytics targeting FP signalling in such manner has remained a challenge due to the dearth of information about the FP receptor architecture, especially about its interaction with ligands and signaling effectors. We propose to further characterize the 3-dimensional structural changes that occur in FP when it triggers these cellular signals using biophysical approaches such as X-ray crystallography. We will then use this structural information to create pharmacological tools that will interfere with these cellular signals induced by FP receptor. This proposal should give us means to further understand which of the cellular signals induced by FP receptor is directly implicated in the uterus contraction. Also, it could form the chemical basis for the development of a new therapy to prevent preterm birth.
