column36: Cutaneous adjuvant conditioning to enhance vaccine responses
column37: Vaccination is our most effective method of defending against disease-causing microbes. Effective vaccination requires multiple injections to achieve strong and lasting protection. Vaccine strategies that require fewer injections will serve personal health, population-wide health, and reduce health-delivery burdens. Vaccines are typically mixtures of immune activators called adjuvants and microbial products (called antigens) injected into muscle. The adjuvant prepares the immune system to respond and the antigen, typically a fragment or extract of the relevant pathogen, triggers the specific immune response. We have found in a mouse model, that vaccination efficacy can be enhanced if the adjuvant is applied before exposure to antigen to the most superficial skin layers, conditioning the skin before injection of the vaccine. The skin is a complex multi-layered structure that serves as a barrier to harmful material in the environment, and is well-equipped for sensing infection. In the most superficial skin layer, the epidermis, cells forming the barrier (skin cells) may have an active role in responding to adjuvant, and thus preparing the immune system for response. We will study how skin cells respond to adjuvant and how other specialized immune cells in superficial layers of skin contribute to the improved vaccination efficacy we observe. We will also develop a novel application system than does not rely on needles or damaging the skin to apply large molecules such as adjuvant into the skin. We will compare the efficacy of our system (topical adjuvant and standard vaccine for hepatitis B) to a vaccine that is commercially available (HeplisavB) and has a similar adjuvant co-injected. Ultimately we hope to develop a product that can be applied to the skin before vaccination and that will improve the efficacy of all vaccines.

column36: A Fine Balance: Association between Antipsychotic Deprescribing in Long-term Care and Other Medication Prescribing
column37: Long-term care homes in Canada have lowered rates of antipsychotic medication use over the last ten years, but we do not know how this has been done, and studies suggest that other harmful medications are being used instead of antipsychotics. This study will address the question: if an antipsychotic medication is stopped, are persons with dementia in long-term care more likely to receive other harmful medications? This study will use Ontario healthcare data to compare prescriptions of new medications in long-term care residents with dementia who continue on an antipsychotic medication with those who stop an antipsychotic medication. No other studies have directly linked stopping an antipsychotic medication to receiving other, new medications. Using less antipsychotic medications is usually good for the health of those affected by dementia, but it could be resulting in unintended, harmful outcomes in some. We need to identify these to make sure that stopping antipsychotic medications truly improves care for persons with dementia in long-term care.

column36: Hyperspectral Intracellular Dynamic Retinal Imaging for Alzheimer's Disease Pathophysiology
column37: A diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease (AD) is still heavily relying on self-reported symptoms and tests that your doctor administers to assess memory and thinking skills. Additionally, current laboratory and imaging tests are costly, invasive, time-consuming, and rarely performed prior the onset of irreversible clinical symptoms. Would retinal imaging be suitable for diagnosing AD? If so, what obtainable information from the retinal imaging would be essential to a detect early indicator of AD? Is the indicator specific enough to diagnose AD, ruling out any other retinal diseases? I will develop a novel retinal imaging system to identify AD-specific biomarkers, a measurable indicator of disease process. Unlike the other systems used in previous studies, this system would provide AD-specific retinal features at an unmatched level of resolution using a label-free, tissue preserving and volumetric retinal imaging technique. This research program provides a retinal imaging platform to identify, monitor, and investigate multiple possible biomarkers of neurodegenerative diseases that is now still limited to the brain. The progress of early detection opens doors to better diagnosis and proper care to many neurodegenerative diseases.

column36: A non-invasive preclinical biomarker of neurodegeneration in Alzheimer's and related demnentias
column37: Most Alzheimer's disease (AD) research in living humans focuses on individuals who are already experiencing cognitive impairments such as memory loss. However, cognitive impairments only emerge after a long clinically 'silent' period during which extensive damage occurs in brain cells. Because everyday activities are unaffected, the preclinical period proceeds undetected. This project will address the when and how of preclinical AD. We will examine when brain cells begin to show signs of damage. We will then test how this early cellular damage relates to subsequent stages of AD, and how early treatments aimed at preserving brain cells affect disease progression. Accurate clinical tests for the earliest stages of neuronal damage in AD are lacking in humans. Our project will test the efficacy of a highly sensitive brain imaging tool for monitoring brain cells in the living brain. We will examine when cellular damage becomes detectable and how to prevent damage. Our project will provide tools for detecting preclinical AD which will help for developing new therapies for slowing or preventing AD. With these tools in routine clinical use, doctors will be better equipped to identify which patients are at risk for AD, and who would benefit most from preventative treatments.

column36: Role of the Endocannabinoid System (ECS) in HIV-associated chronic inflammation and comorbidities
column37: People Living with HIV (PLWH) in the modern antiretroviral therapy era suffer from many comorbidities including cardiovascular disease, HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND) and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Furthermore, Hepatitis C virus co-infection can also impact liver health, even following Hepatitis C cure. Chronic inflammation and disruption of the gut microbes (microbiome) are shared features amongst all these conditions. Interestingly, PLWH with who use cannabis have lower levels of inflammatory markers compared to PLWH who do not use cannabis. Furthermore, PLWH with Hepatitis C co-infection using cannabis had improvements in insulin resistance over time, suggesting that the anti-inflammatory properties of cannabis may improve some chronic conditions characterized by inflammation. The expanded Endocannabinoid (eCB) system is a key player in the maintenance of heart and blood vessel, brain and liver functions under healthy conditions and differs depending on biological sex and age. The eCB is comprised of the endocannabinoids (ECs), which are chemical messengers naturally produced by the body, their building and metabolizing enzymes, and EC receptors. Using banked blood and stool from 4 national CIHR-funded cohorts of PLWH including the Canadian HIV and Aging Cohort Study, Brain Health Now, The Canadian HIV HepC Co-infection Cohort and the Liver Disease in HIV cohort, we will characterize the eCB in PLWH with various chronic inflammatory conditions to determine whether there is dysregulation in the eCB. We will also examine whether disruption in the eCB system correlates with measures of clinical outcomes and composition of the gut microbiome. If disturbances within the eCB system are confirmed in PLWH, interventions aimed at targeting pathways involved in the ECS will be investigated in future clinical trials.

column36: Subsets of subsets: investigating Th17 pathways in inflammatory bowel disease and HIV
column37: Excessive inflammation can cause tissue damage and disease, yet at mucosal surfaces some amount of inflammation is necessary and/or inevitable due to ongoing antigenic exposure, which includes possible pathogens and "friendly" bacteria. The difficulty in treating diseases with an underlying inflammatory aspect is specifically targeting the "bad" aspects of inflammation while retaining what is required for normal function of the tissue. CD4+ T cells are a type of white blood cell that are often at the centre of determining what type of immune responses will develop, and also play important regulatory functions in maintaining a normal state of "homeostasis". A certain type of CD4+ T cell called a "Th17" cell has been implicated in various inflammatory diseases including autoimmunity, inflammatory bowel disease, and HIV infection. These cells respond to a wide variety of "antigens" (proteins seen as foreign to the immune system), secreting a variety of cytokines. Th17 cells come in different varieties, including those that are more inflammatory and those that maintain mucosal integrity. These different subsets can be defined by their cytokine profiles and which other molecules they express on the surface and within the cell. Both are often present, in varying ratios, and this ratio might be important for deciding whether the balance tips in favour of inflammation or not. Here we hypothesize that approaches targeting and reducing the inflammatory th17 subset more specifically will be safer and better able to prevent immunopathology. In this grant we will explore and define these alternate Th17 pathways in more detail, in different clinically relevant contexts, to better understand how this immune subset can be targeted with more precision in the clinic to improve mucosal health.

column36: Bacteremia Antibiotic Length Actually Needed for Clinical Effectiveness (BALANCE): A Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial
column37: Bloodstream infections (BSI) are a common and serious problem, affecting 15% of seriously ill patients, increasing length of stay in hospital and doubling mortality. Antibiotic overuse is also a serious problem: 30-50% of antibiotic use is unnecessary or inappropriate and results in avoidable side effects, C. difficile infection, costs, and spiralling antibiotic resistance. The greatest contributor to overuse is excessive treatment durations. Shorter antibiotic treatment (<= 7 days) is as effective as longer treatment for infectious diseases such as bladder infections and pneumonia, but this question has not been studied for hospitalized patients with BSI. Our team's systematic review of the medical literature, national survey, multicentre retrospective study and pilot trial, all supported the need for and feasibility of a randomized controlled trial comparing shorter (7 days) versus longer (14 days) antibiotic treatment for BSI. With a CIHR 2016 Project Grant, we launched the main BALANCE trial to determine whether 7 days of treatment is associated with non-inferior survival rates as compared to 14 days. We have leveraged CIHR's investment with Australian and New Zealand grants and successfully enrolled 1477 patients of the target 3626. We are due to finish on-time and on budget by our original proposal which was endorsed by CIHR as the appropriate mechanism to answer the questions posed. We have demonstrated the ability to engage the international community across 6 countries and 56 centres, have recruited at our target rate, and propose that this "finishing grant" is an excellent return on the original investment. By defining the duration of treatment for BSI, BALANCE will help maximize the clinical cure of individual patients, while minimizing their risk of drug side effects, C. difficile, and antibiotic resistance.

column36: The impact of displacement on health among people living with HIV in Vancouver, Canada
column37: Despite the availability of effective HIV treatment, many people living with HIV (PLHIV) continue to experience poor health outcomes. While housing is well established as a determinant of health among PLHIV, little is known about the health impacts of displacement (i.e., forced move from residence) for this population. Displacement among PLHIV is an urgent concern in Vancouver's West End and Downtown Eastside neighborhoods, two of Canada's hardest hit areas by the HIV/AIDS epidemic. While the West End and Downtown Eastside have historically housed PLHIV and have a high concentration of health and social services tailored to support their specific needs, both neighbourhoods are undergoing rapid gentrification and rising residential and commercial rents. The recent wave of gentrification is dramatically changing the landscape of these neighbourhoods, placing displacement pressures on PLHIV and the health and social services they rely on. Our three-year study builds on existing community-academic partnerships to conduct a community-based participatory research that examines the link between displacement and health among PLHIV in Vancouver. This study will fill a critical gap in the HIV literature and inform actionable policy and program recommendations to address displacement and improve the health of PLHIV.

column36: Identifying Strengths, Resiliencies, and Supports to Empower Gay, Bisexual, and other Men who Have Sex with Men Living with or at Risk of HIV in their Choice about Initiating Methamphetamine Use
column37: Gay, bisexual, and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM) continue to be disproportionately impacted by HIV. Methamphetamine use is elevated among gbMSM compared to the general population, and it is associated with poor HIV prevention and treatment outcomes. Although interventions have been developed for gbMSM who are actively using methamphetamine, to our knowledge there have been no initiatives aimed at empowering gbMSM in their decisions around INITIATING methamphetamine use. The aims of our community-based initiative are 1) to solicit gbMSM's perceptions regarding social, behavioural, and environmental factors that contribute to the initiation of methamphetamine use, as well as strengths, resiliencies, and supports that potentially empower decisions around initiation; 2) to gain insight from service providers regarding challenges, strengths, resiliencies, and supports that underlie their gbMSM clients' initiation decisions; and 3) using a theoretical framework, to quantitatively assess challenges, strengths, resiliencies, and supports related to gbMSM's decisions to initiate, or refrain from initiating, methamphetamine use. Corresponding activities include 1) qualitative interviews with 20-30 gbMSM who recently initiated methamphetamine use, or who contemplated initiating but chose not to; 2) qualitative interviews with 10-15 providers who deliver services to gbMSM; and 3) a theory-based, quantitative survey with 120 gbMSM who recently initiated, or chose not to initiate, methamphetamine use. Findings will provide key insight regarding social, behavioural and environmental challenges that precipitate methamphetamine initiation; as well as strengths, resiliencies, and supports that facilitate gbMSM in their choices. The knowledge gained will help guide community-based, strengths-focused approaches aimed at empowering gbMSM in their decisions about methamphetamine initiation, which in turn could enhance HIV prevention and treatment outcomes among this community.

column36: HIV/STBBI Testing and The Health of African and Caribbean Migrant Communities in Manitoba
column37: Very little is known about HIV and sexually transmitted and blood borne infections (STBBI) testing for African and Caribbean migrant communities in Manitoba, particularly regarding HIV/STBBI dried blood spot (DBS) testing. We propose a mixed-methods community-based research study and a peer-led DBS testing program to respond to current and pressing knowledge gaps concerning HIV/STBBI testing and linkages to care for African and Caribbean migrant communities in Manitoba. We will examine the barriers and facilitators to HIV/STBBI testing faced by African and Caribbean migrant communities in Manitoba. We will also evaluate the acceptability of DBS self-sampling among African and Caribbean migrant communities in Manitoba and identify effective ways to support their linkage to care, treatment, and prevention. To accomplish these objectives, we will use a province-wide survey to gather data on socio-demographics, HIV/STBBI testing, HIV/STBBI risks and resiliencies, and use of/access to HIV/STBBI services among a sample of African and Caribbean migrant community members (n=350) in Manitoba. Next, we will implement and measure the impact of an innovative community-based peer-led DBS testing program (n=60) housed at the Sexuality Education Resource Centre, with the purpose of scaling-up HIV/STBBI DBS testing in Manitoba among members of African newcomer communities and provide an integrated approach to knowledge translation and exchange on this project. We will also build capacity among emerging scholars and community leaders in this area. By understanding the knowledge gaps in HIV/STBBI testing and linkages to care for African and Caribbean migrants across Manitoba we will significantly contribute to HIV/STBBI research and policy response. column36: The Future of PrEP is Now: A mixed-methods, community-based study to inform equitable and strategic implementation of long-acting PrEP in Canada
column37: HIV incidence is not declining in most of Canada, and Two-Spirit, gay, bisexual, queer and other men who have sex with men, including transgender men and non-binary individuals (2SGBQM) are disproportionately affected. Oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is a powerful tool to prevent HIV, but key subpopulations of 2SGBQM are under-reached by oral PrEP including 1) Indigenous and/or Two-Spirit, 2) Black, 3) Other people of colour, 4) remote/rurally located, 5) substance users as well as 6) transgender and non-binary individuals. Meanwhile, new long-acting PrEP agents are in development, including injections, intravenous infusions and implants under the skin, in addition to pills. These products have been designed to overcome the challenges of oral PrEP, which require people to take pills over long periods of time. The new ways in which these drugs are given (eg. an injection every two months) provide valuable opportunities to re-imagine how health care is delivered. In particular, long-acting cabotegravir (CAB-LA) was recently been shown to be better than oral PrEP in preventing HIV. It is time for communities and key stakeholders within the health care system to start planning for long-acting PrEP in Canada, to ensure that the needs and preferences of those not reached by oral PrEP are met. Led by the Community-Based Research Centre (CBRC), national leaders in the field of HIV prevention, and national partner organizations representing Indigenous, Black and other key perspectives, we will use mixed-methods approaches to: 1.characterize the needs and preferences of 2SGBQM regarding long-acting PrEP options and delivery models, 2.assess the feasibility of new models of delivering long-acting PrEP, and 3.design a national demonstration project (real-life implementation study) of CAB-LA PrEP that directly responds to the access needs and priorities of individuals experiencing barriers to oral PrEP.

column36: Changing the face of pediatric migraine: A phase 2a randomized controlled trial of a novel neuromodulation device for refractory acute migraine in children and adolescents
column37: One in ten children and adolescents suffer from migraine. Children and adolescents with migraine often come to the emergency department (ED) with acute attacks of migraine, with over 2,500 pediatric ED visits for migraine yearly in Alberta alone. Despite this, there is little evidence on how to treat migraine in children and adolescents in the ED. The evidence is limited to intravenous (IV) interventions, which are associated with high complication rates, costs, and patient fears about pain. There are 3 innovative, electrical stimulation/neuromodulation devices that safely and effectively treat adults with acute attacks of migraine. We hosted a patient engagement session to discuss these devices with a group of Canadian adolescents with chronic headaches to understand which device they would be most interested in trying to treat an acute migraine attack in the ED. The majority of the group were most interested in trying the remote electrical neuromodulation (REN) device. We will design a research study to determine if the REN device is safe and effective in treating children and adolescents who are suffering from an acute attack of migraine in the ED. The study has been designed with feedback from patients and ED health care professionals. Our initial goal is to recruit 40 children and adolescents who are visiting the ED and are suffering an acute attack of migraine, to see if the study is feasible and acceptable. These participants will randomly be given either the REN device or a combination of typical IV medications used to treat migraine attacks in the ED; each participant will also receive a placebo treatment (either a placebo/saline IV fluid if given the REN treatment, or a sham/fake REN device if given the typical IV medications). Participants and staff will not be aware which group they are in. This work has the potential to revolutionize the care of children and adolescents coming to the ED with acute attacks of migraine by expanding treatment options.

column36: Impact of early life stress on brain-wide serotonin circuits and behavioural development
column37: Depression is the leading cause of disability in Canada with an estimated economic burden of $32 billion per year. The incidence of depression among young people has been steadily increasing over the last decades, with an overall rise in youth suicide rates. Childhood depression is a serious health condition with a severe impact on growth and development, family life, social functioning, education and quality of life of children. Traumatic stress early in life such as parental loss, abuse or poverty can act as a trigger for the development of depressive illness. Yet we have little knowledge about how early life stress leads to depression. Evidence suggests that stress during a critical developmental period can have detrimental effects on brain maturation. Using a validated animal model of chronic early life stress, the work from my lab has shown that prolonged stress during development changes the activity of brain's emotional centers and causes behavioural changes reminiscent of depression. We report deficits in the activity of neurons that release serotonin, which are the target of the most widely used antidepressants. We propose that early life stress disrupts the maturation of serotonin-modulated neural circuits that are important for the development of emotional and social behaviours. The proposed work will investigate the possible mechanisms behind stress-induced disruption of critical brain circuits. We will further determine how we can use this knowledge to stimulate brain's critical centers and circuits to improve the effects of developmental stress on the brain. Our work will be important for understanding the link between stress and childhood depression and will further aim to develop circuit-based stimulation approaches to inform treatment.

column37: Good health has more to do with the circumstances in which we live, work, grow, and play than with factors commonly linked with health, such as healthcare services or a nutritious diet. The Intersectoral Partnerships and Initiatives team (IPI) within the Public Health Agency of Canada(PHAC) is looking to benefit from research about how best to take up key lessons from HiAP into its work. Addressing this challenge will strategically inform IPI's current and future partnerships, and support its efforts to improve the circumstances in which we live, work, grow, and play the most effective ways possible. Using data and evidence available on HIAP, the project will develop evidence-based tools and materials for the Intersectoral Partnerships and Initiatives team to use in facilitating more effective collaboration and more strategic partnerships with non-health sector government departments. column36: Developpement d'un cadre d'evaluation optimise pour une introduction responsable des tests de signatures genomiques dans le systeme de sante
column37: La genomique est la discipline qui s'interesse a l'ensemble des genes qui composent le genome humain. Ces genes interagissent les uns avec les autres et peuvent influencer la predisposition de certaines personnes ou groupes a developper certaines maladies. Avec les avancees technologiques, il existe dorenavant des tests de signatures genomiques qui ont pour but de predire les resultats de sante suite a certains traitements (test a visee predictive) ou de predire la progression d'une maladie (tests a visee prognostique). Cependant, les couts d'administration de ces tests sont souvent eleves et la demonstration de leur utilite clinique parfois difficile. Les tests de signatures genomiques commercialement disponibles pour soutenir les decisions de traitement chez les personnes atteintes d'un cancer du sein en sont un parfait exemple. Ainsi, la question se pose a savoir comment pouvons-nous favoriser un acces en temps opportun a ces tests dans un contexte ou les donnees disponibles ne permettent pas toujours d'avoir un niveau de confiance suffisant? C'est a ce type de questionnements que font face de nombreux systemes de sante. L'objectif principal de ce programme de travail sera donc de developper un cadre d'evaluation optimise afin de soutenir l'introduction des tests de signatures genomiques a visee pronostique ou predictive dans le systeme de sante quebecois. Ce programme visera aussi a evaluer la possibilite de developper des indicateurs pertinents de suivi des activites autour de ces tests. Ce travail permettra de produire des outils d'aide a la decision qui permettront de faciliter l'implantation des nouvelles technologies a forte valeur ajoutee dans le domaine de la genomique. Ainsi, il sera possible d'avoir une meilleure allocation des ressources tout en favorisant des resultats de sante optimaux pour les individus utilisant ces tests.

column36: Developing a Sustainable and Evidence-Based Integrated Model of Care for Chronic Pain Management in Alberta
column37: Chronic pain affects 1 in 5 children and adults. This means that 7.4 million Canadians (and 800,000 Albertans) are disabled from pain lasting months to years. Treating chronic pain is expensive, costing more than cancer, diabetes, or heart diseases. In 2018, Alberta Health Services and a group of pain experts from across Alberta created a list of priorities and ideas for making pain treatment better in the province, the Alberta Pain Strategy. Improving chronic pain for everyone, no matter where they live in Alberta is a top priority. But, we need to make sure we do this in a helpful and cost-effective way, which can be maintained over time and makes sense to Albertans living with chronic pain. The goal of this project is to develop a new plan that makes sure chronic pain treatment is excellent for all Albertans. We will do this in six steps: (1) review the best science about what drug and non-drug treatments offered together are helpful for chronic pain, how much they cost, and what it is like for people to get these treatments; (2) find out what health resources are used by Albertans living with chronic pain; (3) estimate costs of chronic pain management; (4) design a provincial model of care for chronic pain management; (5) estimate how much it would cost to implement the model and what benefits could be expected; and, (6) develop a plan for how to implement the model. To execute this project we will partner with all groups of people who would be impacted by this new plan, including patients, caregivers, healthcare providers, researchers, and leaders who work in hospitals and government. We think this project will be useful for improving how chronic pain care is delivered in Alberta but also for other provinces.

column36: Analyzing linked safety data to improve active transport safety in BC
column37: Active transport users (e.g., walking, cycling, e-mobility, etc.) are more vulnerable to serious injury or fatality than drivers of motor vehicles are, as these modes do not offer physical protection from injury in the event of a crash. The Ministry of Health has a mandate to reduce the risk of injury and fatalities for active transport users, and, wishes to address potential inequities in bicycling and pedestrian trauma amongst vulnerable populations. To address this need, this fellowship will use a comprehensive database of crashes that include police records, insurance claims, emergency visits, and hospital admissions. It will provide detailed results regarding where, when, how and to whom crashes are occurring. The results of this project will provide decision makers with a foundational understanding of the current state of road safety for active transportation users, and generate evidence to create policies to increase the safety of active transport within BC.

column36: Building Capacity for Campus Suicide Prevention: A Policy Practice Partnership
column37: Post-secondary student mental health is of great concern, with increased rates of anxiety, depression, feelings of isolation, and suicidality observed. The COVID-19 pandemic has exacerbated mental health stressors and concerns about campus suicides, already on the rise. In response, the BC Ministry of Mental Health and Addictions has funded the BC Campus Suicide Prevention Initiative (CSPI), partnering with the Canadian Mental Health Association, BC division (CMHA BC) who will distribute funding and offer technical support to all 25 BC publicly funded post-secondary institutions. This HSIF project will evaluate the implementation and early impacts of the CSPI, identify where further support is needed, and provide recommendations for how the public health system can ensure long-term and sustainable impacts and national scale-up to improve post-secondary suicide prevention and overall mental health and well-being. This study has the following aims: 1. to monitor early outcomes across the CSPI program's implementation; 2. to understand the mediating role of CMHA BC (program administrator and technical support coordinator) in the collaborative processes and outcomes of participating post-secondary institutions; and 3. to assess scalability and sustainability of the CSPI in BC and nationally. An evaluation-based multi-method approach will be used, to thoroughly identify how the CSPI works, for whom, and in what contexts - illustrated through CMO configurations (Contextual conditions, generative Mechanisms, and Outcomes). Qualitative stakeholder interviews, collection of project documents, and observing technical support sessions will inform creation and analysis of data. Ongoing analyses, used to build CMO configurations, will focus on understanding how CSPI implementation operates and with what effect. Findings will be leveraged to directly affect and optimize suicide prevention programs, policies, and resources locally, nationally and internationally.

All Indigenous peoples - including those who do not have 'Status' under Canada's Indian Act - have the right to be counted. Their perspectives and priorities must guide how data is collected, used, and reported. Yet, at present, First Nations, Metis, and Inuit peoples who do not have 'Status' or are not registered with Metis Nation BC are 'invisible' and 'uncounted' within population health and wellness reporting in British Columbia (BC). Responsibility for reporting on health of BC residents lies with the Office of the Provincial Health Officer (OPHO). Through agreements with federal, provincial, and Indigenous governments, the OPHO's responsibilities include collaboratively reporting on health and wellness of diverse Indigenous peoples living in the province. Currently, there is no process in place to report on health and wellness of "uncounted" Indigenous peoples. This work must be done in partnership with Indigenous collectives representing this population. Current gaps include: -No strengths-based, self-determined terminology to refer to diverse Indigenous peoples who are uncounted in population health data -Lack of formal relationships with Indigenous collectives representing uncounted Indigenous peoples; -No way of identifying this population in existing BC population health data -Absence of research frameworks that reflect uncounted Indigenous peoples' perspectives of health and wellness -No implementation plan for province-wide population health reporting led by uncounted Indigenous peoples, on their terms The goal of this project is to support the health and wellness of uncounted Indigenous peoples living in BC by addressing current gaps in population health reporting, through partnerships that uphold Indigenous self-determination, decision-making, and perspectives of health and wellness.

column36: Examining the Contexts and Mechanisms Influencing the Successful Implementation of a Province-Wide Acute Care Modernization Initiative
column37: Background: Alberta Health Services (AHS) aims to provide a patient-focused, quality health system that is accessible and sustainable for all Albertans. To achieve this aim AHS integrated several evidence-based interventions to improve acute care utilization across Alberta's 14 major hospitals. The evidence-based interventions are expected to reduce the actual to improve patient outcomes and ensure cost-effective and sustainable health care delivery. However, it remains unclear which implementation strategies to implement the bundles will be most effective in each setting as the mechanisms and context underpinning successful implementation strategies are not well understood. Policy Question: Which implementation strategies work best under what conditions to implement the evidence-based bundle to improve acute care utilization? Design and Methods: A scoping review will be conducted in Phase 1 of this research to examine acute care initiatives in Canadian healthcare settings. This scoping review will provide an understanding of the implementation strategies that have been used to implement acute care initiatives. In Phase 2 of this research, a realist evaluation will be conducted to examine the contexts and mechanisms influencing the successful implementation of the acute care initiative. This realist evaluation will include an environmental scan of all implementing sites and semi-structured interviews with key stakeholders. In Phase 3 of this research, the results of Phases 1 and 2 will be synthesized to co-develop implementation recommendations to optimize the implementation of the acute care initiative. Impact: The results of this research will enhance the sustainability of acute care modernization and improve patient outcomes in AHS. These learnings will foster a culture of implementation science in AHS to promote sustainability. As Canadian health systems are reliant on acute care, these learnings may be valuable to improve patient outcomes across Canada.

column36: Advancing a learning health system model to align community and cancer care with the needs and concerns of older Albertans with cancer and their families
column37: More than half of new cancer cases in Alberta occur in adults aged 65 years and older. Older adults experience health, functional, and social changes that can have an important impact on their cancer experiences. Age-related disparities in cancer treatment, research, and outcomes suggest that these changes are not adequately addressed in cancer care. Optimal care requires effective collaboration across community and cancer care. However, systems to identify gaps and implement innovations in the care of older Albertans with cancer and their families are lacking. Learning health systems are an emerging approach to informing and implementing healthcare innovations in Canada. In these systems, researchers and healthcare providers work together to gather data from practice, transform data into knowledge, use knowledge to inform practice. Alberta has many existing assets for learning health systems; however, an established framework that connect these assets to inform and implement innovations in the care of older Albertans with cancer and their families is lacking. In this project, I will work to advance a learning health system that aligns community and cancer care with the needs and concerns of older Albertans with cancer and their families. The activities of this project are focused on (1) people (establishing partnerships to promote collaboration among stakeholders in community and cancer care), (2) data/evidence (building capacity to analyze and interpret data that can inform decision-making, improvement, and innovation), and (3) process (advancing new models of care by collaboratively defining problems, understanding context, and proposing solutions). These activities will provide insight into methods of developing a learning health system, while advancing a system that promotes innovations to optimize experiences and outcomes for older Albertans with cancer and their families, strengthen the experiences of clinicians, and increase value in the health system.

column36: Patient-Oriented Research in the BC Learning Health System - supporting caregivers for palliative and end of life patients at home
column37: Introduction: Family caregivers for palliative and end-of-life patients play a critical role in providing care in the home. Nearly 75% of people express a wish to be cared for and die at home. However, for caregivers who support this goal, there is a significant gap in adequate and effective support. Patient-oriented research recognizes the importance of engaging patients and families in the research process. Engaging patients and families can lead to the development of a better caregiving support structure. Older adults may need additional supports for activities of daily living. Our study involves the creation, implementation, and program evaluation of the Support for Caregivers Program. We will develop a robust evaluation strategy to measure success and adjust the program as needed. Methods: The first step will be to co-design a logic model with family caregivers, volunteers and hospice staff at 3 hospices in B.C where the Support for Caregivers Program is being implemented (1 in an urban setting, 1 in a rural/urban and 1 in a rural setting). We will develop this strategy through survey data collection methods, online webinars and focus groups and interviews with hospice staff, volunteers, and program evaluation experts.The funding will support my post-doctoral fellowship. I have expertise in health services and policy research to lead the development of the program evaluation strategy. Anticipated Results: The Support for Caregivers Program will be evaluated using a patient-oriented approach leading to quality improvement initiatives and ultimately healthcare outcomes improvement. We anticipate that the program, after evaluation is completed, will meet the needs of different communities. We will spread and scale this successful program in the Province of BC. Through the development of competencies in leadership, knowledge translation, program evaluation, communication, and brokerage, I will be better positioned to pursue a career in the health care industry.

column36: Identifying service gaps between primary and specialty care for patients with rheumatoid arthritis - improving access to care
column37: Lack of timely access to specialty care is a serious issue in Canada. The Alberta 2020 initiative is developed to improve specialist access by expanding integrated healthcare programs, through which primary care providers can receive timely advice from specialists for patients under care. In this project, we will focus on rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and the engagement of primary care and rheumatologists - the specialists who care for patients with RA. RA is a chronic autoimmune disease affecting approximately 1% of Canadians. Close to 40,000 people in Alberta are living with RA. Timely access to rheumatologists is associated with better quality of care and improved outcomes. It is critical for early diagnosis and targeted management of patients with RA. However, timely access is challenging due to the lack of rheumatologists and that rheumatologists are primarily clustered in urban areas, especially in Alberta where people living in rural and remote areas have a high prevalence of RA. In 2015/16, 83% of the RA patients in Calgary had a rheumatology wait time exceeding the 28-day wait time benchmark, compared to 63% in Edmonton. To increase the capacity of rheumatologist to see new onset and complex patients through the integration of primary and specialty care, three different Shared Care Models have been initiated in Alberta between 2015-16 at three sites: Pincher Creek, Calgary, and Edmonton. Despite the varying models of care, practice environment, and target populations, the three sites identified that it is key to customize the program to address local needs of both patients and providers. It is critical to understand local issues across the province, including barriers to accessing primary and specialty care, long travel distances to care, and health determinants of RA. This project aims to improve access to care by identifying service gaps between primary and specialty care for patients with RA using spatial analysis, spatial statistics, GIS and biostatistics.

column36: Indigenous Identity Disclosure within AHS: A Critical Knowledge Synthesis and Implementation Strategy for System Transformation
column37: This project examines if and how self-disclosed Indigenous identity could be incorporated into Alberta Health Services (AHS) new provincial Electronic Medical Records system Connect Care. Currently, AHS does not have a culturally informed policy for the collection of an Indigenous identifier. As such, Indigenous patients are not necessarily being provided with access to culturally relevant resources and supports available within AHS. Furthermore, the lack of an Indigenous identifier requires AHS to rely on data that is often outdated and held by the Government of Alberta, which is often difficult to access. The absence of data on Indigenous peoples' heath can lead to the minimization, under estimation or complete erasure of Indigenous health determinants and health care access (Smylie & Firestone, 2015). The intergenerational consequences of colonialism requires careful consideration about the collection of Indigenous identity data. The proposed research project will be conducted in full collaboration with Indigenous stakeholders and include diverse Indigenous communities across Alberta. The project will be guided by an Indigenous Advisory Committee that will be developed specifically to co-design the methodology and oversee the project to ensure that the research and knowledge translation benefits Indigenous people. The research design includes four distinct phases that include ongoing community engagement sessions with key stakeholders. The research project will result in four manuscripts in peer reviewed journals, each accompanied by a slide deck to complete presentations within the health system, with Indigenous community partner groups, service providers and at conferences. The final project will include a final report with policy recommendations for best practice. Ultimately, the proposed project will contribute to laying the foundation for the collection of an Indigenous identifier to better serve Indigenous people within the healthcare system.

column36: Identifying leverage points for strengthening coordinated intersectoral action for health promotion in British Columbia
column37: Health promotion (HP) enables people to increase control over health and reduce health inequities through action on the determinants of health. HP actions include developing personal skills, creating supportive environments, strengthening community action, building healthy public policy, and reorienting health services to improve population health and wellness.The COVID-19 pandemic has emphasized the need for more coordinated, integrated and intersectoral HP.action. The focus and value-add of the project is the development of co-created (with research, policy, and practice stakeholders) recommendations for enhanced HP and the innovative application of a complex systems approach to support this work. Using physical activity as a starting point, this project will to map (inventory) HP initiatives targeting physical activity at the provincial, regional, and local levels and identify areas to enhance coordination and integration to build healthier communities.The anticipated impacts and value of achieving this goal include: a) shared leadership, governance, and accountability for HP, b) increased collaborative capacity to align HP, c) enhanced focus among stakeholders on reducing health equities, d) shared resources (human, financial, infrastructure) to implement HP, e) improved information (knowledge exchange, research and evaluation, monitoring and surveillance), and f) shared learning and understanding among stakeholders of new approaches to HP identified through the lens of a complex systems paradigm. There are three objectives: 1) Describe and map existing physical activity HP initiatives and systems in BC, 2) Assess systems to identify facilitating and hindering factors and key feedback mechanisms that influence implementation, coordination and integration, and 3) Strengthen systems through identification of priority leverage points and recommendations for more synergistic implementation of coordinated intersectoral HP in BC.

column36: Determiner la qualite de la polypharmacie chez les aines : une approche basee sur l'intelligence artificielle
column37: La prise de plusieurs medicaments, la polypharmacie, est de plus en plus commune, surtout chez les personnes agees. Pour l'instant, il n'est pas possible de bien departager quelles polypharmacies apportent des benefices et quelles sont nefastes. En effet, le nombre de combinaisons de medicaments possibles est imposant, et prendre en compte les caracteristiques individuelles de chacune des personnes rend la situation tres complexe. L'intelligence artificielle permettra de comprendre ces elements pour en degager des normes. Dans ce projet, j'utiliserai le Systeme integre de surveillance des maladies chroniques du Quebec, qui contient les informations sur les reclamations de medicaments depuis 1996 pour l'ensemble des aines du Quebec atteints de maladies chroniques, de meme que leurs informations sur les services medicaux, les hospitalisations et le deces. Ces donnees, decrivant l'exposition aux medicaments de chaque individu, permettront d'entrainer un systeme expert base sur l'intelligence artificielle pour etablir quelles combinaisons, sequences, durees de traitement sont associes a des effets nefastes (ex. hospitalisations, deces) en tenant compte des conditions medicales et sociodemographiques de la personne. Les resultats serviront a developper la surveillance de la polypharmacie dans la population et apportera des connaissances nouvelles sur l'usage de medicaments qui pourraient changer la pratique clinique. L'utilisation de l'intelligence artificielle pour decouvrir des patrons d'utilisation de medicaments en lien avec les evenements de sante peut neanmoins poser des enjeux ethiques et sociaux, par exemple si les resultats sont susceptibles d'accroitre des inegalites entre differents sous-groupes de la population. Avec l'appui de plusieurs experts et chercheurs, j'evaluerai ces elements afin que les resultats obtenus soient acceptables socialement et conformes aux normes ethiques et legales.

column36: Monitoring and evaluation of Canada's Healthy Eating Strategy
column37: Poor dietary intake is a leading risk factor for non-communicable disease in Canada. Pre-packaged foods high in sodium, sugars and saturated fats account for an increasing proportion of the food supply, making it increasingly challenging for Canadians to make healthy choices. This program of work aims to evaluate Canada's Healthy Eating Strategy through a collaboration between the Office of Nutrition Policy and Promotion at Health Canada and the University of Waterloo. The Healthy Eating Strategy was announced in 2016 as a landmark policy framework to address dietary risk factors for chronic disease, and incorporates a variety of policy approaches, including updates to Canada's Food Guide and restrictions on food and beverage marketing to children. Health Canada is now in the process of developing approaches to: (1) monitor the extent and impacts of food and beverage marketing to children in Canada, (2) evaluate the short-term impacts of Canada's new Food Guide, and (3) evaluate the Healthy Eating Strategy as a whole. This program of work will utilize the research expertise of the Health Systems Impact Fellow to address these three needs. The objectives of this work will be supported by data from the International Food Policy Study (IFPS) at the University of Waterloo, which collects annual data on key food policy indicators from adults and youth across six countries, including Canada. Data from the IFPS will provide information that is critical to the evaluation of the Healthy Eating Strategy, such as frequency and sources of exposure to food and beverage marketing. The Fellow will lead data analysis and knowledge translation activities for the three objectives described above, and will serve as a liaison between Health Canada and the University of Waterloo to ensure efficient and appropriate use of the data. Ultimately, this work will help to ensure the Healthy Eating Strategy has a positive impact on the health and quality of life of Canadians.

column36: Guidelines for Evaluating Service Programming for Autistic Adults: A Patient-Oriented Perspective on Service Evaluation using Functional Criteria
column37: Currently there are few standards for evaluating service delivery, and since health care service delivery is a domain of the provinces, new health care services need to be tested and evaluated in each province before being widely offered. This leads to inefficiency in evaluations as well as unequal access to new services across the country. Also, the evaluations that are done are usually based on what the service delivery organization values about the programming rather than what the patient community served by the programming values. This project proposes creating sets of guidelines for evaluating service programs for autistic adults using functional criteria, criteria based on functional needs rather than diagnosis, determined by stakeholder engagement, including engagement with autistic adults, clinicians, and service providers, via focus groups. These guidelines would account for the variability of symptoms that can present in autistic adults, due to the focus on functional needs rather than diagnosis, and these guidelines would also increase efficiency and comparability in service evaluation and health care service delivery to the autism community. These guidelines, being informed by the needs and wants of the autism community, provide an opportunity for autistic adults to have a say in how service delivery and evaluation is done and how service programs can be designed for them.

Smartphone apps are ubiquitous and can aid in diagnosis, management and treatment of care. Apps can support clinicians with collecting diagnosis-related information, or allow clinicians to recommend wellness activities to their patients. Most work until date has focused on development, validation, and regulation of mental health apps, however the integration of these into patient and provider workflows remains a largely unexplored area of practice. This fellowship proposes a collaborative project between the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH) and Canada Health Infoway focused on developing a list of guidelines and recommendations for the integration of smartphone apps into mental health care. Through a phased approach, we will first evaluate the integration of a suicide safety planning app into care, and then build upon these findings by conducting an environmental scan (grey literature search, key informant interviews) of apps across Canada that have been integrated into mental health care. Following this, we will use an online Delphi approach to refine our list of recommendations and best practices for integration of mobile apps into mental health care. This final list will serve as a tool to educate a variety of audiences; it will be tailored to patients, family members, clinicians and administrators.

column36: Exploring barriers and enablers to implementation of cancer screening among primary care providers seeing marginalized patients
column37: Screening for breast, cervical and colon cancer can improve patient outcomes including cancer morbidity and mortality. While there are organized screening programs for these cancers in Ontario, screening participation remains suboptimal. Many people who are not up to date with screening experience social marginalization, including immigrants and those with low income. Some family doctors caring for these patients are able to achieve much higher rates of screening that others. However, it is unclear what distinguishes these doctors from others that are not able to achieve high screening rates among their patients. As a result, our study will explore the key barriers and enablers to implementing cancer screening by doctors who see a high number of marginalized patients. We will interview doctors who have both high and low screening rates to explore this issue and will ultimately collaborate with a subset of these clinicians to develop and test an intervention or strategy that may help doctors increase their screening rates.

column36: Evaluating the impact of digital initiatives aimed at supporting the recovery and quality of life of people living with heart disease, stroke and vascular cognitive impairment
column37: One of the main priorities of Heart & Stroke is to improve the recovery and quality of life (QoL) of Canadians living with cardiovascular diseases, including stroke, and heart disease, or those with problems of memory or thinking due to their cardiovascular disease (termed "vascular cognitive impairment or VCI"). To do this, Heart & Stroke is developing virtual/digital resources that will provide Canadians with tools, learning opportunities and peer support to help them in their recovery. Heart & Stroke would also like to better understand whether current programs are making a difference for all people with stroke and heart disease, but currently there is no good way to measure this. To fill this gap, this research study will: 1) discover key factors that help predict how people living with stroke, heart disease and/or VCI will recover and how their QoL will be during and after recovery; 2) modify existing tools to include these factors of recovery/QoL that can be used by Heart & Stroke and other health organizations; and 3) develop and implement an evaluation of Heart & Stroke's new digital/virtual Living with Stroke program. To do this, we will use different approaches (e.g., looking at existing scientific papers, using health information from large databases, talking with patients and caregivers, etc.). All of these approaches will inform the development of a good way to measure recovery and QoL in patients with stroke, heart disease and VCI, and to evaluate the Living with Stroke program. The results of this research will provide new ways for Heart & Stroke and others to accurately assess how Canadians living with stroke and heart disease are recovering and how problems with cognition affect that recovery. This work will be important for the ongoing development of virtual/digital support programs and resources to provide Canadians living with stroke or other conditions with the best possible resources to help them in their recovery and improve their QoL.

column36: Bridging the gap: using implementation and behavioural science to support transitional care for acute cardiac patients
column37: Patients with acute heart problems often need health care that is provided by a range of different health services in different places. Good transitions between these services are important to a good recovery but unfortunately many patients fall through the cracks and either do not or cannot access the necessary services. This can lead to a slower recovery, using services that aren't actually needed, and increase costs to patients and the health system. We need to know more about what prevents effective care transitions and develop solutions to improve them. This work will be undertaken at Hamilton Health Sciences (HHS) whose Cardiac & Vascular Service provides advanced care for cardiovascular patients across Central South Ontario. For Objective 1, we will explore current care pathways by interviewing individuals involved in the care of patients with acute heart problems at HHS. This will help identify some of the challenges they face and identify opportunities to improve care processes. For Objective 2, we will review the existing literature to identify barriers and potential solutions to effective care transitions. For Objective 3, we will develop a model of care transition that could be implemented at HHS to advance care quality, improve patient outcomes, and increase health system performance.

column36: Engaging families to optimize innovative clinical trials in children
column37: Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) of child health interventions are needed to optimize physical, mental and medical outcomes as RCTs are the gold standard of evidence for healthcare decision making. However, clinical trials in young children are difficult to conduct because it is challenging to recruit families, follow them over long periods of time, and ensure that people from diverse backgrounds are included. Patient-oriented innovative clinical trials (iCTs) improve the reach, efficiency and usability of RCTs, with the aim of improving health outcomes which are relevant to patients and families. The Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario (CHEO) has established a Research Patient and Family Advisory Committee to allow parents and researchers to oversee studies at CHEO together. However, this program has yet to address common difficulties families and researchers face when conducting and participating in RCTs, or inform the development and implementation of iCT methods at CHEO. During my Postdoctoral Fellowship, I will establish an iCT Team of parents and researchers specifically focused on patient-oriented iCTs in children. Alongside parents and researchers, we will identify barriers to conducting and participating in clinical trials of children. We will then work with iCT and patient-oriented research experts to develop solutions to the identified barriers, which can be applied to studies at CHEO in the future. Embedded within the Research Patient and Family Advisory Committee, the iCT Team will establish a needed and longstanding link between parents and researchers to maintain high quality and meaningful iCT research at CHEO. Through this process, I will not only improve my patient-oriented research skills, but hone leadership, collaboration, critical thinking and knowledge translation skills to transition to an independent researcher role, leading a strong link between researchers and hospitals in patient-oriented iCTs.

column36: Improving End of Life Care: Expanding the 3 Wishes Project Hospital-wide
column37: Dying is a universal part of life, but the dying process can cause suffering and distress for patients and families. Current end-of-life care often focuses on reducing shortness of breath and pain. However, more holistic care recognizes the patient as an individual, also helping with difficult social and psychological aspects of personhood. The 3 Wishes Project (3WP) provides compassionate individualized care that honours the life and dignity of dying patients by eliciting terminal wishes from patients and their families, then families and clinicians implement them. Examples include playing music, trips outside, pet visitation, and spiritual ceremonies. Most wishes are simple and cost little, but can be priceless. Research in the intensive care unit (ICU) where the 3WP began shows that implementing wishes humanizes the dying process for families, and makes practice more meaningful for clinicians. My goal is to develop a 3WP for patients dying on the medical wards at St. Joseph's Healthcare Hamilton. Patients dying on hospital wards may benefit from even more personalized care. When not dependent on technology, patients can directly share the wishes they find most comforting. Families can be more supportive with less decision-making. Clinicians on the ward tend to have longer relationships with patients, which could create a better team approach to palliative care. During this career award, I will conduct a survey to understand factors that may help or hinder the 3WP on the wards. With input from patients, families, and clinicians, I will develop a strategic implementation plan. To understand if the 3WP can be implemented and sustained on the wards, I will evaluate the number of patients enrolled, and through interviews I will explore the effect of the 3WP on family grief and clinician engagement. Developing and evaluating the 3WP outside of ICU will help ensure more individualized, holistic, compassionate end-of-life care for patients dying on hospital wards.

column36: Creating evaluation and data gathering strategies to support youth-led mental health peer education and advocacy initiatives at Jack.org
column37: Mental illness is at its peak severity during adolescence and young adulthood, yet a small proportion of those who need mental health treatment actually receive care. Two approaches towards improving mental health service engagement among youth are peer-to-peer education and inclusion in health advocacy, which Jack.org fulfills by providing training and resources to youth in these areas. The proposed project will advance both Jack.org's directives by devising ongoing data gathering, program evaluation, and reporting strategies for peer education programs and assessment tools supporting advocacy. To enhance peer education, the project will develop progress and outcome indicators for the Jack Talks program, which has recently undergone a virtual adaptation in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. As part of the process, methods for assessing mental health literacy and help-seeking attitudes and behaviours will be developed. Regarding advocacy efforts, Jack.org has begun developing tools to gather youth perspectives on mental health services, such as the Campus Assessment Tool. The project will focus on improving the psychometric properties of the tools and their use in advocacy initiatives. All project activities will be conducted in conjunction with Jack.org staff members, youth leaders, and external stakeholders, ensuring that emerging needs are being met and securing partner buy-in. By the end of the project, a long-term foundation will exist for promoting evidence-based program evaluation and data-gathering activities within Jack.org. In turn, youth leaders, service providers, and policy makers across Canada will benefit from access to peer education and advocacy resources that are youth-informed and data-driven, better facilitating youth to access mental health treatment.

column36: Evaluation of the Implementation of the Nova Scotia Department of Education and Early Childhood Development's Physical Activity Framework
column37: Research tells us that children who take part in more active or energetic play are healthier than kids who are less active. We also know that Canadian kids are not doing quite enough active play every day to be healthy. Schools are an ideal place to add more active play into children's days because almost all children in Nova Scotia attend school daily. Nova Scotia developed a Physical Activity Framework to help schools be more active places through better environments, more opportunities for play and active lessons. The Framework will start to make schools more active places to be in Fall 2021. This is a new long-term program and we want to measure its success. The goal of this research project is to measure how the Physical Activity Framework is being used in schools across Nova Scotia. We will measure if students' physical activity levels and wellness change after being in schools that put the Framework into action. We will also ask students and teachers about how their schools are becoming more active places, like adding new playgrounds or more active lessons. We will keep track of the changes for 2 years. This project will help us understand how to make schools more active places for students. We hope the results can help other provinces develop and start physical activity strategies in their schools too.

column36: Improving health and healthcare equity for people in Ontario's provincial correctional facilities: an evaluation of policy and health system strategy.
column37: People who experience incarceration have a high burden of mental and physical healthcare needs and often experience barriers to healthcare services. The Ministry of the Solicitor General is responsible for delivering healthcare services to people incarcerated in Ontario's provincial correctional facilities. The Ministry has identified improving healthcare services in correctional facilities and their integration with the Ontario healthcare system as an important area of focus and priority. This program of research aims to improve health services and outcomes for people who experience incarceration by supporting evidence-informed policy and decision-making. This program of research will evaluate the impact and outcomes of the recent change in governance for healthcare services in corrections which aimed to centralize policy and programming leadership. Using interviews and surveys of providers and patients as well as administrative healthcare data, this mixed-methods evaluation will identify policy strengths and opportunities for improvement. Second, this work will identify strategic priorities to improve integration and continuity of care by engaging stakeholders within corrections and across the broader healthcare system. Finally, building on the previous two components of this study, research will support the implementation and evaluation of key initiatives in the Ministry's Strategy for Women's Health and in care for mental health and addictions. This will include the development of frameworks and indicators of access and quality. Structural changes occurring in Ontario's broader healthcare system create a unique opportunity for alignment and integration of healthcare in correctional facilities with the new Ontario Health and Ontario Health Teams. During this window for transformative change, this research program will support and advance improvements in service delivery and connection with health and social services in the community.

column36: Development of a deep learning framework to predict suicidal behavior, repeat hospitalization, and emergency department visits in mental health patients
column37: The Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI) is a not-for-profit organization that provides data standards and collection, analytical reports, and analytical tools to the Canadian health sector. CIHI has a five to ten year mandate to prioritize analytics for vulnerable populations, including individuals suffering from mental illness. Advances in deep learning and the availability of large health datasets, broadly and in some cases exclusively available to CIHI, has paved the way for new approaches to health-related predictive analytics. As part of a postdoctoral fellowship at CIHI we propose to develop a deep learning-based framework that provides likelihood predictions for three future events in individuals with mental illness: 1) Probability of re-hospitalization, 2) Probability of emergency department visit, and 3) Probability of suicidal behavior. These predictions can help identify at-risk populations in order to adjust health services, reduce exposure to modifiable risk factors, evaluate suitability for patient discharge, provide early intervention, inform policy, and provide guidance for funding decisions based on predicted demands on mental health services. In addition to my work at CIHI, I will be part of the Ottawa Hospital Research Institute (OHRI) and the Department of Medicine at the University of Ottawa under the supervision of Dr. Peter Tanuseputro. The OHRI is the research branch of the Ottawa Hospital, which is one of the largest learning and research hospitals in Canada. With Dr. Tanuseputro I will be using health data to study the effects of physician mental health on patient outcome, with a focus on machine learning. This is a first-of-its-kind opportunity where patient health data can be linked to the treating physician and the physician's mental health. This project will help identify areas requiring attention in the well-being of physicians, and translates well to workplace mental health in general and during times such as COVID-19.

This data provides a limited snapshot for government to make decisions about nutrition policy and programming. One of the Public Health Agency of Canada's main activities is to monitor and report on the state of health and health behaviours among Canadians. Currently, the Agency provides information on the amount of fruits and vegetables and sugar-sweetened beverages consumed. The Agency has an opportunity to update these measures to include monitoring of a range of food and nutrition behaviours, for example, using nutrition labelling to help make food purchases. Further, current research suggests that behaviours are affected by physical and social environments (food environment) and policies that influence the sustainability of the food supply (food system). However, a comprehensive framework of measures that includes food environments and food systems currently does not exist for Canada. The proposed work will identify existing questionnaires and assessments used at global, federal, provincial, and territorial levels to measure food and nutrition behaviour, food environments, and food systems. We will search current literature and work with partners across Canada to develop a framework for food and nutrition measures that will be integrated into the Agency's national surveillance strategy. We will also survey a range of audiences and collaborators from government, non-profit organizations, policymakers, and researchers to develop a strategy for communicating the framework. The proposed work will improve the health of Canadians and the health system by providing ongoing monitoring of food and nutrition in Canada to inform policy and programming decisions.

Mon objectif principal est d'agrandir nos connaissances face au risque que represente les arbovirus emergents sur les populations vulnerables au Canada, tant pour les secteurs academique et public, et pour la population generale. Ce projet de recherche se portera sur une aire d'etude dans l'Est de l'Ontario, incluant la ville d'Ottawa, ou une grande variete de donnees environnementales est disponible et ou un echantillonnage annuel de moustiques a lieu a chaque annee. Ce projet de recherche ameliorera grandement nos habiletes en tant que societe a deceler les problemes presents et futurs que peuvent nous amener les nouvelles maladies transmises par des moustiques au Canada dans les prochaines annees.

column36: Canadian Network on Hepatitis C (CanHepC): From Discovery to Implementation
column37: Hepatitis C is a liver disease caused by infection with the hepatitis C virus (HCV) and affecting 71 million people worldwide. In Canada, an estimated 250,000 people are living with HCV yet over 40% are unaware of their infection. HCV is a major cause of chronic liver disease including liver cancer and is responsible for more years of life lost than any other infection. The development and broad availability of direct acting antivirals (DAAs) that can cure HCV in >95% of treated individuals has been a major game changer. Together with proven ways to prevent infections, testing and diagnosis, DAAs present a unique opportunity to eliminate the virus. This has triggered a global push to eliminate HCV led by the World Health Organization and endorsed by Canada in 2016 with the goal of 80% reduction in chronic HCV infections by 2030. Despite this commitment, transmission of HCV in Canada continues to rise at an alarming rate. The major challenge in HCV elimination is that it disproportionately affects priority populations with limited access to healthcare including people who inject drugs, Indigenous peoples, people with experience in the prison system, newcomers to Canada, and gay and bisexual men who have sex with men. The Canadian Network on Hepatitis C (CanHepC) was established in 2015 as the first National Collaborative Research Network dedicated to HCV research. CanHepC combines a collaborative training and research program, bringing together over 100 members across Canada including researchers, trainees, and knowledge-users. In the next funding cycle, our infrastructure will be expanded to support research with direct impact on priority populations to prevent new HCV infections, reach the undiagnosed and engage them into care, treatment and assessing the long-term health implications of HCV infection. We expect to generate new knowledge and priority population specific tools and approaches to accelerate Canada's progress towards HCV 2030 elimination targets.

column36: Identifying Novel and Causual Cardiometabolic Biomarkers with Mendelian Randomization
column37: Millions of Canadians are affected by cardiometabolic diseases which include coronary artery disease, stroke, diabetes, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease. Studies aimed at uncovering novel and causal cardiometabolic biomarkers can improve patient management and outcomes of these diseases. This is because biomarkers are measurable factors (i.e. plasma proteins, autoantibodies, and metabolites) that correlate with the severity or progress of specific diseases. Their utility extends to early clinical diagnosis, disease prevention, and response to drug treatment. There is room for improvement in current biomarker detection strategies and platforms in part due to the scarcity of studies that screen for biomarkers and the inability to distinguish markers of disease from mediators of disease. We propose to overcome these challenges by implementing an innovative design to comprehensively screen for novel biomarkers that (1) predict a wide range of cardio-metabolic diseases, and (2) are causally involved in the pathophysiology of diseases so they can be targets for interventions. We will use our experience in Mendelian Randomization, a protocol based on independent genetic variant segregation akin to a natural ""Randomized Control Trial,"" to identify blood mediators of cardio-metabolic disease through a systematic testing of 1196 plasma proteins in biological samples already collected as part of the Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiological PURE study (N=12,000 participants). Identifying novel causal mediators of disease is urgently needed to improve risk stratification and therapeutic options. Discovering biomarkers that not only predict risk but are also causal mediators would be transformative in their ability to identify patients at risk and to monitor treatment.

column36: An environmental scan of follow-up practices after discharge from pediatric intensive care units
column37: Advances in intensive care have resulted in a decrease in deaths in children admitted to pediatric intensive care units (PICU). Improved survival has led to increased physical, cognitive and mental health challenges in survivors and their families, which has raised the question of whether we are trading death for other long-term health consequences in this population. There are important knowledge gaps of the causes of these impairments, including which children are at highest risk and what factors affect these outcomes. Outpatient follow-up of children after admission to the PICU has been proposed as one way of monitoring health outcomes and managing impairments. New research suggests that PICU-led follow-up programs, where follow-up is initiated and organized by members of the PICU team and specifically target PICU-acquired complications, would be beneficial. Although such programs exist, there is little information describing existing practices, and less is known about their impact. Our project aims to conduct a survey of PICUs in Canada and the United States to outline the frequency of follow-up of pediatric patients following critical illness, both in specialized multidisciplinary and PICU-led programs, describe the follow-up practices of such programs and examine whether there is an association between the existence of follow-up programs and PICU size, complexity and re-admission rates. This research will describe the landscape of current follow-up practices and serve as an important first step in creating a North American consensus on best practices for post PICU care. Information from this study may inform hospital and health system planning, namely in terms of resource allocation and financial investment in such programs in the future.

column37: Healing Indicators is a research project that aims to improve health assessment policy. It addresses the need to create tools that centre communities and Indigenous knowledge in the assessment of the health impacts of resource development. Progressing land-based indicator research is important within the context of the First Nations Health Authority's "Public Health and Wellness Agenda." Land-based health indicator development requires emergent community-based methods and design that is inclusive of leadership from Indigenous peoples. The impact of this collaboration is the promotion of critical Indigenous health research, with opportunities to expand on policy gaps in relation to land-based wellness and Indigenous health assessment. Asset-based work, such as this, is relevant within the context of provincially acknowledged widespread racism within the health care system in British Columbia. This work is also significant to the provincial commitment to implement the Declaration of the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (DRIPA 2019). Healing Indicators is a collaborative research project designed to promote community-led health through land-based indicator development to inform self-determination and wellness in collaboration with the First Nations Health Authority.
