column37: Burkholderia pseudomallei (Bp) is the causal agent of melioidosis, a neglected bacterial disease. Melioidosis causes around 165,000 human infections worldwide per year with mortality rates up to 50%. Bp is resistant to many antibiotics and available treatments are often ineffective. Our group has developed an expertise in the preparation of mimics of the surface polysaccharides expressed by Bp. With the long-term goal of developing a protective vaccine against melioidosis, we hypothesize that vaccines based on multiple Bp-related sugars and/or proteins could represent effective candidates. Therefore, we will develop vaccines bearing one, two or three polysaccharide epitopes attached in multiple copies to a carrier protein. We will evaluate the protective potential of these vaccines in mice models of infection. Our vaccination protocols will be guided by the report of the Steering Group on Melioidosis Vaccine Development. Our application is built on an interdisciplinary collaboration with three groups working at INRS. The Gauthier group, with expertise in sugar chemistry, will produce the sugar-based vaccines for the animal studies. The Lamarre group, with expertise in vaccine development, and the Deziel group, with expertise in Bp microbiology, will conduct the vaccination studies in mice and will probe the nature of the immune responses. As a member of the University of Oxford VALIDATE Network, our team will benefit from the output of leading international scientists. Considering globalization, there is an urgent need for treatments against Bp infections, as tropical diseases are no longer contained to their geographical origins. We expect that our research proposal will provide a safe and protective vaccine against melioidosis. Our preclinical investigation should lead to the implementation of a clinical study, which would be beneficial for the prevention of melioidosis among populations at high risk as well as for travelers going to endemic areas.

column36: Bioengineering Tough Blood Clots for Hemorrhage Control
column37: This project is to develop and validate biodegradable blood clots by design, called bioengineered blood clots (BBC), as a safe and effective therapy to manage hemorrhage. Hemorrhage is recognized as the most important unaddressed area in trauma care. Existing hemostatic technologies reliant on native blood clots and coagulation cascades are inadequate to manage hemorrhage. The efficacy is observed to plateau and linked with a fundamental material constraint: native blood clots are relatively slow to form and vulnerable to rupture. Motivated by our recent studies, the hypothesis of this project is that the limited hemostatic function of native blood clots could be remedied with a design strategy of bioengineered blood clots for rapid, robust, and effective hemostasis. The BBC will be designed and tested for biocompatibility, biodegradability, and blood compatibility. To test these hypotheses, this project contains three aims: (1) synthesize, characterize, and refine bioengineering blood clots with click clotting strategy; (2) study the fracture of blood clots with physiological relevance in vitro, in silico, and ex vivo; (3) develop and validate BBC as hemostatic sealants in animal hemorrhage models. To accomplish these objectives, this project will draw upon expertise from leading researchers in biomaterials, biomechanics, hemostasis, hematology, and trauma surgery. This project is expected to substantially advance the fundamental understanding of blood clot fracture and its implications on hemostasis and lead to next-generation hemostatic technologies based on bioengineered blood clots for controlling hemorrhage, which is responsible for 30-40% of trauma-associated deaths. The proposed technologies could help treat severe bleeding and reduce death and related complications from uncontrolled bleeding in Canada and abroad.

column36: Regeneration at your fingertips: mechanisms determining mesenchymal tissue repair versus fibrosis
column37: The finding that some animals can regenerate lost body parts has fascinated scientists for centuries. However, the ability to regenerate varies widely; some amphibians can regenerate entire limbs, while mammals have largely lost this ability. One exception to this rule is the tip of the finger (or digit tip in mice, the model system studied here). Under the right circumstances the fingertip will regenerate completely appropriately, even in adult humans, as long as the base of the nail is still intact. By contrast, if the injury is only slightly further down the finger, and the nail is completely lost, then there is no regeneration, but only scar formation. In this proposal, we will study adult mice to ask why this one small part of the body has retained the capacity to regenerate, and will ask what controls the decision to regenerate or to form a scar, with a particular focus on the environment. We will also ask how the immune system and inflammation impact the decision to regenerate or scar, since these have been implicated in pathological scarring/fibrosis. Ultimately, it is our goal to use this information to enhance tissue repair, and to inhibit the pathological scarring and fibrosis that can cause organ failure.

column37: Alzheimer's disease is the most prevalent neurodegenerative disease and the most common cause of dementia. It affects not only the people living with the disease but also theirs families and surroundings. Unfortunately, there is no cure or treatment for Alzheimer's disease and current medications have only marginal (if any) effects, including the recently approved vaccine in the USA. Our project aims to develop a novel therapeutic approach for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias by successfully restoring cognitive functions. It applies to microRNAs, which have been previously linked to Alzheimer's progression in animal models and in humans. We will focus on one particular microRNA, miR-132, shown to be strongly and consistently lower in Alzheimer's brain. We and others have obtained strong evidence that miR-132 is the prime microRNA target (among more than 100 in the brain) to move towards clinical development. This is based in published studies in cells and mice showing that miR-132 can specifically control genes involved in Alzheimer pathology and importantly memory. We now aim to provide the necessary preclinical details (e.g. pharmacodynamics, toxicity) in two animal species, mice and monkeys, for future clinical studies in humans. This will be referred to as a microRNA replacement therapy, which is also underdevelopment in humans for other complexe diseases such as cancer. Overall, we aim to provide an innovative and much-needed new alternative to Alzheimer's disease treatment, as all "typical" drugs tested so far against amyloid of tau have failed.

column36: Blocking the Effects of Serotonin to Prevent Ischemic Mitral Regurgitation: a Randomized Trial.
column37: The role of the mitral valve is to prevent the blood going backward in the lungs as the heart pumps forward. In many cardiac diseases, the heart enlarges and becomes too big relatively to the valve size. The valve is distorted by the enlarging heart and can't close completely: the blood starts to go backward in the lungs instead of going forward. This condition is called "functional mitral regurgitation" and is a major complication that accelerates the heart disease, increasing deaths and hospitalisations. There is no good treatment available. After a heart attack, there is also abnormal scarring in the mitral valve, which contributes to the valve dysfunction. A substance named serotonin is released in the blood after a heart attack and we believe that it can cause this abnormal scarring. In animal studies, we have studied a drug named cyproheptadine to counteract the effects of serotonin on the valve, prevent abnormal scarring and preserve the valve function. This drug was working well in those animal experiments and was able to prevent mitral dysfunction after a heart attack. Our research goal is now to test if the beneficial effects of cyproheptadine can be applied to human. We will perform a study in patients with a recent heart attack. Half of the patients will receive cyproheptadine, and the other half will receive a placebo (inactive drug). The patients will be followed for 1 year to see if cyproheptadine is effective to prevent mitral valve regurgitation. This will be evaluated by different imaging techniques. This study will therefore be used to confirm if cyproheptadine can be a useful drug to prevent mitral valve disease in patients who had a heart attack. Preventing mitral regurgitation could help reduce the complications after heart attacks.

column36: Brain alterations and cognitive decline in obstructive sleep apnea
column37: Breakthrough discoveries in rodents have revealed that sleep is crucial for generating neurons, strengthening synapses, and clearing brain waste products. Considering the high prevalence of sleep disorders in the general population, it is now urgent to assess how these new discoveries translate to the human brain. Obstructive sleep apnea is a sleep disorder that affects between 20% and 50% of individuals after the age of 65. It produces hundreds of awakenings per night and chronic intermittent hypoxia. Sleep apnea impacts brain structure and function in older individuals. How sleep apnea modifies long-term brain health with age and whether sleep apnea treatment can slow down neurodegeneration are topical questions. In the next 5 years, we aim to identify patients with sleep apnea who are at risk of neurodegeneration. We aim to produce new evidence regarding the neurodegenerative profile of treated vs. untreated patients. We also aim to identify individual characteristics that increase the risk of cognitive decline and neurodegeneration in the presence of OSA. To achieve this goal, we will use polysomnography (sleep measure in the laboratory), neuropsychology, genetics, and advanced neuroimaging techniques. This project could improve clinical protocols by including OSA screening and management among priorities. It could also modify treatment decision, particularly in patients with mild OSA or those with vulnerability factors. Even small improvements in slowing of neurodegeneration could result in significant gain in quality of life and help delay the onset of dementia.

column36: Investigation of Hepatitis B Virus Immunopathogenesis using Intravital Microscopy in the Woodchuck Hepatitis Virus (WHV) Model of Hepatitis B
column37: The hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a major cause of severe liver disease worldwide, including cirrhosis and liver cancer. There are drugs that can control the virus but they do not cure chronic infection. There is a need for greater understanding of the immune response after exposure to virus and in the early acute infection and during long-term chronic infection in order to develop better therapies. Some subspecies of woodchucks (i.e., groundhogs) can be infected with woodchuck hepatitis virus (WHV) a cousin of the HBV, and also develop hepatitis (liver inflammation) and associated liver cancer similar to people. WHV infection in woodchucks is a valuable model helping to understand how liver disease and cancer develops. This animal model is also important for testing of new antiviral drugs. Until now, most assessments of the immune response to HBV infection and to treatment were done by evaluating surrogate markers in blood. We will use well-established conventional tests along with advanced live cell imaging within the liver to assess in real time the immune response to early and long-term WHV infection and after treatment with an antiviral drugs. Our team are experts in liver disease, virology, HBV pathogenesis, in the woodchuck HBV model, woodchuck husbandry, and in using live cell imaging. We will assess, for the first time, virus-cell and cell-cell interactions inside the living liver in response to virus infection, in different stages of liver disease and during anti-viral treatment. This study will ultimately contribute to the development of new treatments aiming to achieve a cure for chronic hepatitis B and complete protection against liver cancer caused by the HBV.

column36: Towards Personalized Dosimetry-Based Radioligand Therapy of Prostate Cancer as a New Standard of Practice
column37: Prostate cancer is the most common and third deadliest cancer in men. Death from prostate cancer is caused by cancer spread to other organs, i.e., metastasis. A new kind of treatment for metastatic prostate cancer uses a radioactive drug that specifically targets the cancer to irradiate it, which is called radioligand therapy. While radioligand therapy is promising, its administration is currently suboptimal, as all patients receive the same amount of the radioactive drug. Because each patient is different, this one-size-fits-all approach results in a huge variability in where and how much radiation is delivered into the body. We will use modern medical imaging modalities to track the radioactive drug during the treatment. This allows to precisely calculate how much radiation is delivered to organs and tumors of the patient. We will simplify and optimize how this imaging is performed to make it convenient for the patient yet yielding accurate results. We will also use advanced analysis methods and artificial intelligence to aid in the simplification of existing protocols and to extract even more information from medical imaging that could help predict the response and outcome of the patient following radioligand therapy, i.e., the efficacy and the potential side effects. All this information will allow personalizing radioligand therapy, i.e., tailoring the treatment for each individual patient, in order to maximize the irradiation of his cancer, without increasing the toxicity to healthy organs. With personalized radioligand therapy, it is anticipated that the majority of patients could safely receive more of the treatment, letting hope for better efficacy.

column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common chronic condition of the joints, and a leading cause of pain and disability worldwide. It is the fourth most common cause for hospitalizations and a leading indication for joint replacement surgery costing the Medicare system over $42 billion in the knee and hip replacements alone. Patients with OA have difficulty in moving and suffer from chronic pain reducing their quality of life. This study will investigate the cartilage repair and pain behaviour following the treatment with a natural substance (Link N) that has the potential to alleviate pain and reverse OA by helping repair the cartilage.

column36: Soulager la douleur chronique chez les aines a l'aide de la stimulation transcranienne par courant direct
column37: La douleur chronique est la principale cause d'incapacite a travers le monde et touche un nombre particulierement eleve d'aines. Des travaux ont montre que la stimulation electrique transcranienne, une technique qui permet d'activer le cerveau de facon non invasive et non douloureuse avec des electrodes apposees sur le cuir chevelu, est une approche securitaire et prometteuse pour diminuer les douleurs chroniques. L'objectif de la presente etude est de determiner si ce type d'intervention est efficace pour reduire la douleur chez les aines, comparativement a un placebo. Pour ce faire, 150 personnes agees de 65 ans ou plus et avec des douleurs musculosquelettiques persistantes (> 6 mois) d'intensite moderee a severe seront recrutes a Sherbrooke, Montreal et Quebec via differentes strategies pour obtenir un echantillon representatif de la population visee. Les personnes repondants aux criteres de selection seront invitees a l'une des 5 cliniques de physiotherapie participantes de leur region et seront assignees, au hasard et a leur insu, soit au groupe avec stimulations reelles ou au groupe avec stimulations placebo. Les stimulations (reelles ou placebo) seront appliquees pendant 20 minutes, 1 fois par jour, pendant 5 jours consecutifs. Tous les participants devront remplir des questionnaires pour evaluer leur niveau de douleur musculosquelettique, et l'impact de celle-ci sur leurs activites et leur qualite de vie avant et apres le traitement. Des mesures de fonctionnement cerebral seront egalement collectees avant le traitement. Ensemble, ces mesures cliniques et neurophysiologiques permettront d'evaluer l'efficacite de la stimulation electrique transcranienne pour soulager les douleurs chroniques des aines et, possiblement, de developper des biomarqueurs permettant d'identifier les personnes les plus susceptibles de beneficier de ce type d'intervention.

column36: Redefining the paradigm for surveillance in patients with low-grade glioma using saturation transfer magnetic resonance imaging
column37: ~ 4,000 low-grade gliomas (LGGs) are diagnosed in North America yearly. LGGs grow slowly over many years and are deadly. There is still a lack of consensus regarding how to treat them effectively. Initial LGG diagnosis is made via a standard MRI and patients are then monitored via routine contrast-based MRIs performed every 6 months. The decision to perform surgery is typically made upon evidence of significant growth. Earlier identification of progression may drastically improve outcomes by allowing clinicians to make a more informed decision as to the timing of the surgery and as to when to employ additional treatments such as chemo- or radiotherapy. Such early identification could be attained through monitoring the metabolic activity of the LGG tumour. If metabolic imaging can confirm that the tumour cells are actively dividing, this would prompt treatment, including the administration of novel therapeutics known as IDH inhibitors that may replace standard therapies. In this project, we propose to test whether: 1. Metabolic imaging can predict changes in LGG prior to standard MRI. 2. Metabolic MRI alone can be used to guide LGG diagnosis and treatment response and replace standard gadolinium MRI for surveillance. We will use metabolic MRI in 100 LGG patients. 50 patients will be followed by the neurosurgeon deciding based on standard MRI follow-up as to when to operate. A second cohort of 50 patients who have already undergone surgery and have been confirmed to have LGG, will be followed by the oncologist who will decide based on standard MRI when to initiate chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy. All patients will also undergo metabolic MRI scans every 4 months, as part of their routine observation schedule. We hypothesize that metabolic MRI will be capable of predicting the tumour growth both before and after surgery and earlier than standard MRI. This will provide critical information on the utility of metabolic MRI methods for a future intervention based study.

column37: Candida albicans is an opportunistic pathogen that is a major cause of mortality in bloodstream infections, especially in immunosuppressed individuals. The arsenal of clinically active antifungal compounds is limited because of the eukaryotic nature of this yeast, which makes it similar to its human host. In addition, many cases of clinical resistance to all anti-Candida drugs have been reported. Currently, the pipeline of pharmaceutical companies for new drugs targeting C. albicans infections is almost dry. Thus, discovery of new drugs is of utmost urgency to fight C. albicans infections. Our group focus on study of mechanisms controlling key biological processes required for C. albicans to adapt inside the host to identify new targets for the development of drugs to treat fungal infections. We will use cutting-edge genomic approaches to decipher the regulatory mechanisms that control different facets of C. albicans virulence. We will focus on mechanisms that rearrange the state of the chromatin and impact the transcription of virulence-related processes. This will allow for the identification of exploitable biological targets to develop new antifungal drugs in addition to a better and a consensual knowledge of process involved in chromatin remodeling in fungal pathogens.

column37: CHARGE syndrome (CS) is a rare genetic disorder affecting about 1 in 10,000 newborns. It is caused by mutations in the CHD7 gene and is associated with neurodevelopmental disorders such as intellectual disability, attention deficit disorder with or without hyperactivity, seizure and autistic behaviour. Additionally, mutations in CHD7 have been associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), a developmental disorder that affects communication and behaviour. However, the cause of the manifestation of neurological symptoms upon CHD7 mutations in CS and ASD remain unknown. CHD7 is a protein that regulates gene expression. I therefore hypothesize that CHD7 regulates genes that are crucial for proper neural network development, input balance and maintenance in the brain. To test this, we will capitalize on the strength of a simple genetic model - the zebrafish and examine the role of CHD7 in the development of neural networks in the brain using innovative approaches. We will also investigate the molecular effects of CHD7 on the brain to identify genes that it regulates. This proposed research plan will enhance our understanding of brain defects in CS and ASD. column36: Youth in a pandemic: A youth-led photovoice exploration of COVID-19 vaccine confidence
column37: Youth have been uniquely affected by the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite high rates of infection among youth, they have only become eligible for vaccination later in the vaccine rollout, and may be more hesitant to be vaccinated. Empowering youth to make informed choices about their health is key to public health equity. Photovoice is a research method that engages participants in understanding their world through an arts-based approach. Participants create knowledge through their real-world lived experience and expertise, using photography to represent their understanding of an issue. Photovoice has been shown to improve health knowledge and to empower marginalized populations. We propose a youth-led photovoice project that will solicit critical perspectives on COVID-19 confidence and hesitancy. From a SPOR approach, youth will lead the project, including a youth research assistant supported by a youth project steering committee, with support from experienced researchers. Thirty-five youth from across Canada will participate in a series of supported activities in which they will take photos representing their perspectives on COVID-19 vaccine confidence. We will then hold focus group discussions with them to understand the perspectives that emerged through the photovoice activities and to record critical dialog on COVID-19 vaccine confidence from the perspectives of Canadian youth. Knowledge mobilization activities will include conventional academic outputs (papers, conference presentations), government-focus reports, virtual photography galas, an online gallery, a virtual art sale, press releases, and social media campaigns. Together, these activities will ensure that the findings reach a variety of relevant stakeholders, including youth, the broader community, the media, government, youth-serving organizations, and policymakers.

column36: Mapping a reference genetic interaction network for a human cell
column37: Genome sequencing has provided an unprecedented view into the extent of human genetic variation. However, our ability to understand and interpret this genetic information remains rudimentary. This knowledge void represents the central challenge facing geneticists today, one that must be addressed to realize the promise of precision medicine. Our research has shown that a major component of the inability to interpret information in our genomes likely stems from complex genetic interactions. While all humans have essentially the same set of genes, we each carry millions of subtle variants in most of our genes, some of which modulate gene activity. Because genes work in concert with one another, the effect of one genetic variant can depend greatly on its interaction(s) with other variants present in the same genome. For example, if two genes work together to control an important cellular function, then an individual can usually tolerate a genetic variant that inactivates one or the other gene alone, but not variation in both genes, simultaneously. Thus, to understand the differences between any two human genomes, we must understand how millions of genetic differences affect gene function individually and how they interact with one another. To address this challenge, we will use state-of-the-art gene editing technology to systematically explore genetic interactions in human cells. We will map a global network of genetic interactions that will define the roles of genes and reveal how specific subsets of genes work together to coordinate essential cellular functions.

Many individuals also believe that cannabis is a safe and "natural" substance they can consume during pregnancy. In particular, this proposal also offers a creative means to assess how cannabis use during pregnancy effects synaptic plasticity in the developing hippocampus. This is a brain region known to be involved in learning and memory processes, and it is important to understand how prenatal substance exposure impacts brain development in a sex specific fashion, and if it alters the development of sexually dimorphic brain regions. column36: Molecular mechanisms of bacterial DNA double-strand break repair
column37: Antimicrobial resistance is a grave threat to human health. The Council of Canadian Academies report "When Antibiotics Fail" (2019) predicted that by 2050, antimicrobial resistance will cause the death of 256,000 Canadian lives and cost our healthcare system $7.6 billion annually. The emergence of drug-resistant infections highlights a critical need for new antimicrobials. Current antibiotics and the human immune system cause severe damage to bacterial DNA in an effort to eradicate the infection, however bacteria maintain DNA repair pathways fix the damage. These bacterial DNA repair systems not only prevent bacterial death, but can lead to mutations that result in antibiotic resistance. Therefore, inhibiting bacterial DNA repair pathways is a potential source of new therapeutic targets. However, to achieve this aim a detailed understanding of the mechanisms of bacterial DNA repair are required. The goal of the proposed research is to unravel the molecular mechanisms of a bacterial DNA repair pathway that fixes the most lethal form of DNA damage - the double-strand break. We will use structural and biochemical methods to find the critical features of the protein complex that repair DNA. The foundational knowledge provided by this research will highlight new drug targets for the development of innovative antimicrobials to combat infectious disease.

column36: An innovative technology-based approach to translating clinical practice guidelines of nutrition therapy in primary care: The Cost, Health, and Effectiveness Assessment of the Portfolio diet in Primary care (CHEAPP) program
column37: Cardiovascular disease results in 25% of deaths in Canada, costing over $21 billion annually. Nutrition and lifestyle remain the cornerstone of therapy for cardiovascular disease, but implementation is limited. Dietitian services in Canada are not covered by provincial health plans and most physicians cite a lack of education, tools and time to counsel on nutrition. Innovative self-management tools, such as web-based apps, provide a complementary and affordable approach for delivery of dietary advice, especially with the transition to virtual care during the COVID-19 pandemic. The Portfolio Diet, a plant-based dietary pattern of cholesterol-lowering foods which has demonstrated "drug-like" reductions in cholesterol and other cardiovascular risk factors, is uniquely positioned to test this innovative approach. We have developed the PortfolioDiet.app, as a direct translation of the Canadian Cardiovascular Society (CCS), Diabetes Canada, and Obesity Canada Clinical Practice Guidelines for the nutritional management of cholesterol. column36: Stormy with a chance of HIV: Climate change, resource scarcity, and pathways to HIV prevention among adolescents and youth in Kenya
column37: THE ISSUE: Global regions most impacted by HIV are also greatly affected by climate change and extreme weather events (EWE), such as droughts and floods. Yet the pathways linking climate change and EWE with HIV prevention outcomes are understudied. This is particularly true among adolescents and youth. In Sub-Saharan Africa, adolescent girls aged 15-19 account for more than 80% of new adolescent HIV infections, and young women aged 15-24 have HIV infection rates two-fold higher than their young men counterparts. OUR IDEA: This innovative study will identify pathways from structural drivers of climate-related factors and poverty to HIV prevention outcomes via resource scarcity (water, food and sanitation insecurity). We focus on 2 Kenyan locations (1: urban slums in Nairobi [Kibera, Mukuru, Mathare], 2: rural and peri-urban Kisumu, on Lake Victoria) greatly impacted by climate change. OUR APPROACH: Our 4 year mixed-methods study will examine the intersection of structural factors (ecological [extreme weather, climate change, seasonality], socioeconomic [poverty, education]), resource scarcity (food, water and sanitation insecurity), and HIV prevention cascade outcomes (demand [e.g. HIV knowledge], supply [e.g. condom access], adherence [e.g. safer sex efficacy], prevention practices [e.g. condom use]) among youth aged 15-24 in Kenya. Phase 1: Qualitative research to develop interview guides and pilot data collection tools. Phase 2: Longitudinal survey with youth (n=500, 250 per location) in Kisumu and Nairobi at 4 time-points over 2 years corresponding with rainy and dry seasons. Longitudinal interviews at 2 time-points with 40 participants (20 per location) corresponding with a rainy and a dry season. Phase 3: Mixed-methods integration and participatory knowledge mobilization, including community dialogue and think tanks. IMPACT: Knowledge of structural drivers of HIV prevention among youth to identify target mechanisms to inform future HIV prevention interventions.

column36: Improving the treatment of amblyopia
column37: Regions of the brain that support visual perception develop early in postnatal life when visual experience informs the proper arrangement of neural connections. Disruption of normal vision during this period, as can occur with cataracts, refractive errors or misaligned eyes, alters the spatial precision of neural connections. This derailment of normal development produces a vision disorder, amblyopia, that is the most common cause of blindness in children, and is the leading cause of monocular impairment in adults. Our research group published promising results for a novel strategy to treat severe amblyopia, which appears to work by reducing the level of visually-driven cortical activity. Our initial studies found that brief immersion into complete darkness produced recovery from amblyopia superior to that of conventional treatments. We later extended these findings to show that reversible pharmacological inactivation of the dominant eye promotes even faster recovery from amblyopia, and importantly at ages when conventional treatments fail to produce beneficial outcomes. Experiments in this proposal will address key parametric and mechanistic questions to facilitate translation of retinal inactivation as a treatment approach for amblyopia. We aim to delineate the time window during which recovery occurs, investigate possible neural mechanisms underlying recovery, and assess its safe application. We will also examine the efficacy of this treatment in a non-human primate model of amblyopia, a critical step for the possible translation of this therapy to humans. The remarkable recovery from amblyopia promoted by retinal inactivation holds promise for a completely new approach to treatment that could provide superior outcomes compared to available alternatives. Its success in humans would be transformative for pediatric ophthalmology. Such an advance holds enormous benefit to patients by improving visual health and broadening career and education opportunities.

column36: Control of Breathing During Sleep: Brainstem Mechanisms of Respiratory Control
column37: Approximately one in four Canadians is affected by significant sleep problems that can diminish their health, alertness, safety and quality of life. The most common and serious of the sleep disorders have impaired breathing as their root cause. One example is sleep apnea, which affects up to 20% of adults and is also thought to be involved in some cases of sudden unexplained death in infancy. Sleep apnea is defined as cessation of breathing during sleep and is typically caused by closure of the air passage in the throat in sleep due to relaxation of those breathing muscles (e.g., the tongue) whose activity normally keeps this air passage open. Episodes of breathing cessation in sleep can occur hundreds of times per night, each resulting in temporary suffocation that causes major sleep disruption. Understanding the brain mechanisms causing sleep apnea and other breathing disorders in sleep is important because of the adverse medical, societal and economic costs of this common disorder, such as increased strokes, angina and heart attacks, debilitating daytime sleepiness, increased traffic and work-related accidents, impaired work performance and decreased quality of life. Our research identifies the brain mechanisms that suppress breathing in sleep and the crucial waking up responses to respiratory distress. This fundamental research is of high clinical relevance. For example, others have manipulated (with success) the mechanisms we first identified as pharmacotherapy for sleep apnea. We will assess, progress and drive new treatment strategies from the basic mechanisms identified from this new research. Identifying the key mechanisms underpinning sleep and breathing, and identifying targets and strategies to reactivate or reinstate breathing when it is depressed or fails, constitute new knowledge of high translational, clinical and societal impact.

column36: Development of gastrointestinal track-targeted biologics to improve the treatment of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a term that groups together chronic inflammatory diseases of the digestive tract, notably Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. It is projected that IBD will affect about 1% of our country's population by 2030. IBD typically arises in a patient's gastrointestinal tract as a result of the impact and interplay of environmental factors, genetic predisposition and the nature as well as the composition of their gut microbiota. These factors explain in part the multifactorial nature of IBD and why no cure presently exists. Patients are typically treated for their symptoms (chronic inflammation of the gut) with general anti-inflammatory drugs. More recently, biologics such as anti-TNF alpha antibodies have proven to provide more focused and effective anti-inflammatory responses for treating IBD. In either case, all IBD treatments cause broad immuno suppression and consequently come with adverse effects in patients such as their enhanced susceptibility to infections. As biologics are now becoming the first line of treatment for many autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, there is a need to focus their action to the site of inflammatory, in the case of IBD, to the gastrointestinal tract. We propose to design and construct biologics that will accumulate in the gut of IBD patients to locally reduce inflammation while minimizing the dosage needed and their overall systemic impact in patients. Experimentally, we plan to express, characterize and test our targeted biologics in mouse models displaying IBD-like inflammatory responses. The impact of our research program will be the development of a simple, rapid assembly strategy of anti-inflammatory biologics to guide them to the gut in order to locally treat IBD patients with less side effects.

column36: Evaluating the effectiveness of commonly recommended heat-mitigation strategies for limiting heat strain in elderly adults during extreme heat events
column37: Canada is entering unchartered territory as it regularly experiences record high temperatures negatively affecting the health and well-being of heat-vulnerable elderly men and women. Visiting cooling centres and using electric fans are commonly-recommended strategies to protect the elderly during hot weather, but their effectiveness is unproven. Recently, we showed that increasing age is associated with an impaired physiological capacity to dissipate heat and blunted cardiovascular adjustments to heat stress. Consequently, elderly adults are at increased risk of heat-induced illnesses or death. Age-associated chronic disease such as type 2 diabetes or hypertension can worsen this response. Given that periods of extreme heat will likely be more frequent, intense, and deadly within the next few decades and Canada's population is aging rapidly, the development of evidence-based heat protection action to mitigate adverse health impacts of heat in the elderly is crucial. To aid in this endeavor, our project will assess the efficacy of visiting a cooling centre and electric fan use (pedestal or ceiling mounted), for protecting elderly men and women (65-85 years) with and without type 2 diabetes or hypertension against dangerous increases in body core temperature and heat-induced cardiovascular instability during a day-long (8-hours) exposure to hot (35C, 60% relative humidity) indoor conditions the elderly may face during an extreme heat event. By assessing the physiological responses (e.g., body temperatures, heat loss, cardiovascular function, hydration status, inflammatory response, heat cytotoxicity), we can better define best practices for implementation of these commonly employed heat-alleviation strategies. This includes the creation of consensus-based heat protection messaging tailored to men and women with and without chronic health conditions to ensure health equity and a maximum level of protection to maintain health and well-being during extreme heat.

column37: Vasculitis is a rare disease in children and adults that develops when blood vessels carrying oxygen to critical organs in the body become inflamed. In children with vasculitis, the kidney is one of the organs where the blood vessels are most commonly affected, but it can also affect the lungs, eyes, brain or skin. If organ damage is severe, the child may die or suffer permanent organ damage. Since vasculitis is less common in children than adults, most of what we understand for children with the disease, and how to treat it, comes from experience with adults. Current treatment involves drugs used for cancer patients. These treatments can be life-saving, but they do not prevent the disease from returning and they have serious side effects such as infections, cancer, difficulty having children, and heart disease. Finding the right drug at the right dose for each patient can be a tedious process of stopping and starting treatment, and repeatedly taking a small sample of affected organs with a small surgical procedure (biopsy) - this is not always feasible, especially for children. Doctors treating adults with vasculitis have found that 'markers' in blood or urine may tell them which patients have a higher risk of recurring disease and/or more severe disease in the kidneys. It is not clear if these markers are present in children, and if so, if they work in the same way. While their bodies (and immune system) are still growing, children may respond differently to the disease and treatments compared to adults. Our team created the largest international network of doctors and scientists in the world studying vasculitis in children. In this project, we will use collected information and samples from over 300 pediatric patients to check if the adult markers are present and if they predict risks in children. If so, they will provide doctors with tools to "personalise" treatment for each child.

column36: High-resolution structural investigations of lipid-protein interactions

We collaborate with research groups doing experiments on the same lipids and proteins to make a more a complex picture of lipid-protein interactions. Ultimately this research will contribute to understanding and perhaps treating many diseases. column37: Physical frailty is a medical condition of reduced function and health in older adults. Physically frail older adults also often have chronic conditions that contribute to a higher chance of them being limited in daily activities, becoming dependent, and death. Chronic conditions, such as heart disease, osteoarthritis, and type-2 diabetes, are linked to frailty. Physical activity can help to better manage chronic conditions and prevent frailty, but this older adult population is often not active enough. We have recently showed that physical activity counselling by a physiotherapist can help older adults with chronic conditions to stay active. Key to that study was having a physiotherapist working with the person to develop a 'doable' physical activity plan, and make updates over time. In this project, we will adapt this counselling approach using the new Canadian 24-hour Movement Guidelines for older adults at an early state of frailty and with chronic conditions. column37: Anorexia Nervosa (AN) deeply affects the physical and psychological well-being of its sufferers. Mostly, AN manifests in adolescence and recent studies show the prevalence rates are increasing in this group. With among the highest mortality rate of any mental health disorder, the longer someone takes to seek help, the more challenging it is to recover from AN. Although adolescence is a phase characterized by important changes in the brain, little is known about the core brain changes associated with AN, making it difficult to effectively treat the disorder. The proposed study is a large-scale investigation on the differences in brain structure and brain activity between teenagers with AN and healthy controls. We also study the connections between the different brain regions and brain chemistry. The study will also provide data on the efficacy of refeeding for reversing brain changes associated with AN, and we explore how clinical features-such as duration of illness and early-life experiences-are associated with brain function and structure in individuals with AN. Lastly, we will explore whether differences in brain processes of individuals with AN predict individual differences in clinical outcome, one year after an initial MRI scan. A total of 410 participants (205 patients diagnosed with AN and 205 healthy controls) will each undergo an MRI scan and complete questionnaires. We will continue to follow these individuals on weight, height and behaviour at 3, 6, and 12 months after the MRI scan. After 12 months, patients and healthy controls are also expected to return for new MRI tests. Nine clinical sites across Canada are collaborating in this undertaking; an initiative that could lead to a better understanding of the causes of AN. Ultimately, these efforts will guide prevention initiatives for at-risk individuals and improve recovery strategies, so that the eating disorders community in Canada as a whole can benefit from this project.

column36: Regulation of germline stem cell quiescence through small RNA-mediated chromatin remodeling
column37: Stem cells are very important for the growth and maintenance of a number of our tissues. Curiously, they do not like to divide and only do so when signals instruct them to repair damage or, for whatever reason, to make new tissue. If these cells lose the ability to restrict their proliferation the results can be devastating and may be at the heart of many forms of cancer. We use a simple genetic model to understand how genes communicate signals to the stem cells that make up our germ line...the cells that make our gametes; our sperm and eggs. This cell lineage is what biologists refer to as the immortal lineage because cells in this tissue transmit genetic information between generations. We have found that a series critical genes can communicate signals to these special stem cells to stop dividing and prepare for tough times. This may occur through interesting intermediates called small RNAs that act kind of like hormones. In this proposal we aim to shed more light on how these instructions move from one cell to another so that signals that are sensed in one cell type (the nervous system) are appropriately transmitted to the germline stem cells to tell them to stop dividing and prepare for what may be a long period of duress-due to starvation for example. This is important to protect the genes in the sperm and eggs so that the information that they will transmit into the future will remain complete and accurate.

column36: Adrenergic control of liver metabolism in obesity and diabetes
column37: Obesity and diabetes have reached epidemic proportions worldwide. This situation is alarming considering that these pathologies are intimately linked to the development of important health issues including insulin resistance, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, cardiovascular diseases and cancers. Alterations in hepatic glucose metabolism is a classic feature of obesity that commonly manifest as inappropriately high hepatic glucose production contributing to hyperglycemia. Dysregulations of the nervous system can result in inappropriate hepatic substrate metabolism ultimately resulting in hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, and hepatic steatosis. In particular, little is known about how the brain communicates with organs, including the nature of the receptors involved.

column36: Characterizing FAM72 in adaptive and innate immunity
column37: In our previous CIHR grant, we conducted a genetic screen to identify novel genes involved in antibody production for effective immune protection. Using mouse cells, we discovered Fam72A, a gene that produces a protein causing degradation of the UNG2 mouse protein that is involved in DNA repair. By causing UNG2 degradation, FAM72A prompts the production of antibodies that bind very tightly to viruses and other pathogens. As a result, FAM72A plays an important role in ensuring that the best antibodies are produced to remove viruses and other pathogens from our bodies. Unlike mice and other mammals, including non-human primates, humans have expanded this gene family to include four closely-related genes called FAM72A-D. The function of each of these genes is not known. This proposal will explore how this relatively unknown gene family is involved in antibody production, and the role of the four closely-related FAM72A-D proteins in human biology. We hypothesize that some of these proteins are involved in degrading a related protein of UNG2 that is expressed in Herpes viruses. These viruses encode an UNG2 homologue required for viral growth and if FAM72A-D bind to and degrade viral UNG2s, they will restrict viral growth. We will also assess other functions of FAM72 proteins in human B cell biology. This proposal seeks to determine the function and role in immunity of this novel and poorly defined FAM72 gene family, contributing to the study of immunity against infectious diseases and the identification of molecular mechanisms that impact DNA repair and genetic mutation in cancer cells.

column36: A subcortical circuit for coordinating express reaches
column37: We operate in a dynamic and uncertain world. Sudden changes in our visual world often require responding as fast as possible. Such express responses have long been recognized as a fundamental feature of motor control. Despite this, there is a surprising gap in our understanding of how circuits in the primate brain drive different types of express responses. On one hand, express responses that move our line of sight rely on an ancient circuit running through the brainstem. On the other hand, previous work examining express responses to move our arms have largely neglected the potential involvement of this brainstem circuit, emphasizing instead circuits through the cerebral cortex. We seek to bridge this gap by studying express reaching responses in rhesus macaque monkeys. Rhesus macaques provide an ideal animal model, given similarities in vision, the structure of the cortex and brainstem, and the biomechanical properties and muscles of the arm. Our work leverages newly established measures of express muscle recruitment at the arm that clock how quickly vision can be turned into action. Using a strategy that combines high channel count electrophysiology and reversible inactivation of brain activity, we will test the hypothesis that a brainstem circuit coordinates express reaching. First, we test the idea that only activity in this brainstem circuit, rather than the cortex, evolves early enough to initiate express muscle recruitment at the arm. Second, we test the idea that this same brainstem circuit sends a signal to cortex, so that subsequent muscle recruitment governed by corticospinal circuits are informed about the preceding express arm muscle response. This is a basic science grant whose outcome will advance the understanding of how the primate brain generates the earliest visuomotor responses. Understanding such circuits is necessary to appreciate how they change across the lifespan, and during disease.

column36: Does Impaired Cerebral Metabolism Link Vascular Dysfunction to Cognitive Decline?
column37: One of the hallmarks of the human brain is its high energy demands that must be met by a constant supply of oxygen from the blood. As such, reduced brain blood flow due to vascular disease (i.e., conditions affecting blood vessels) is a risk factor for age-related memory and thinking problems (known as cognitive impairment) and dementia. However, despite its association with cognitive impairment, there is little direct evidence showing how vascular disease impacts energy production in the brain. We aim to address this issue by using an imaging platform that combines magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with positron emission tomography (PET). MRI is the current standard for imaging brain structure and function, while PET is unrivalled in its ability to image the molecular workings of the brain. Together, they provide the ability to study multiple aspects of brain function that could not be achieved with either imaging method on its own. Using this 'hybrid' technology, our aim is to answer two fundamental questions: "What is the impact of disease-related changes in the smallest blood vessels (known as capillaries dysfunction) on oxygen delivery to brain tissue?" and "Does capillary dysfunction impede the required increase in energy production during brain work, such as performing a memory task." Our team, comprising of imaging scientists and neurologists, will answer these questions by imaging patients diagnosed with carotid artery stenosis (i.e., narrowing of one of the carotid arteries that supply blood to the brain) since this disease is associated with cognitive impairment. This work will enable us to establish a link between capillary dysfunction and brain energy consumption. In the long-term, we will investigate the role of this flow-metabolism link in dementia and determine how lifestyle choices, such as regular exercise, can help preserve this link that is critical to brain health.

column36: The Mobile health for Kids with Asthma (MoKA) study: predicting exacerbations through multimodal data and machine learning
column37: Why do this study? Asthma exacerbation is a leading cause of emergency department visit and hospitalization in children, but clinicians and parents lack reliable predictors of exacerbations. Existing models to predict exacerbations are limited due to the use of one source of data. mHealth, defined as the use of mobile devices for medical practice, is a promising approach allowing to integrate mutliple sources of data (parent- or self-reported, environmental data, publicly available data) to improve prediction of asthma exacerbations. In April 2020, we launched COVIDSentinel.ai, a webapp to track and share self-reported COVID-related symptoms. This study proposes to harness this existing infrastructure to develop the Asthma Sentinel mobile app to conduct a smartphone-based, prospective observational study on predicting exacerbations in childhood asthma. What are the objectives of this study? The objectives of this study is to build personalized risk scores of asthma exacerbations based on several sources of data, including self-reported symptoms and environmental data. We will also explore the automated detection of nighttime cough to predict asthma control. Data will be analyzed using artificial intelligence-based techniques, which is well suited to analyze complex datasets such as in this study. Additionally, we will assess the acceptability of Asthma Sentinel as a mHeath tool among parents of children with asthma and adolescents to guide future app development. What do we expect to find? While previous studies have focused on single sources of data to predict asthma exacerbations, the MoKA study will use a mHealth approach and the integration multimodal data through artificial intelligence to build an enhanced predictive model of exacerbations. Ultimately, our goal is to use real-world data to predict exacerbations to optimize childhood asthma management.

column36: Intergenerational continuity of reported child maltreatment: Epidemiological study of the prevalence and health-related risk factors
column37: Child maltreatment (CM) is a prevalent public health concern affecting approximately 30% of Canadian youths. CM tends to be perpetuated across generations. Estimates of the prevalence of the intergenerational continuity of CM are sparse, and no reliable Canadian data documenting this issue is available. Another area requiring further studies is the identification of risk factors associated with the intergenerational continuity of CM. Young maternal age and maternal mental health have been consistently documented as risk factors. However, there are several gaps in the literature including that studies have failed to include valid sources of information other than self-reported questionnaires and to explore how mother and child physical health factors can impact continuity trajectories. Further, the study of intergenerational continuity of CM lacks considerations for the possible differences between CM subtypes. The proposed research will address these gaps in a populational sample of young mothers by linking administrative data from Quebec Child Protective Agencies and the Regie de l'assurance-maladie du Quebec and Ministere de la sante et des services sociaux. The following questions will be answered: 1) What is the prevalence of intergenerational continuity of reported CM in the first six years following delivery among young mothers? Is maternal history of reported CM a risk factor for second generation's reports of CM in this population? 2) What are the maternal and child health-related risk factors associated with the intergenerational continuity of reported CM in this population? 3) Do prevalence rates and health-related risk factors differ based on CM subtypes and co-occurrences? Data gathered will offer insights into the actual prevalence of the intergenerational continuity and CM and associated risk factors. It will contribute to the improvement of prevention and health services for vulnerable families and, ultimately, to better health for Canadians.

column36: Macromolecular organization by biomolecular condensation in Polycomb mechanism and function
column37: A human body is composed of a multitude of cell types that are organized into tissues, organs, and physiological systems. The genome, composed of DNA, is the blueprint for all cells. Different types of cells can be made from the same blueprint because each cell type only uses parts of the genome. Thus, a central challenge in forming and maintaining different types of cells is how to keep some parts of the genome active, and others inactive. Polycomb proteins were discovered more than 50 years ago in fruit flies, where they keep parts of the genome that should not be used inactive in specific cells. Subsequently, Polycomb proteins were found to serve the same function in human cells. Indeed, Polycomb proteins are important for formation of different cell types in many parts of the body, including the brain, the blood and the immune system. Malfunction of Polycomb proteins can cause cells to read parts of the genome that are supposed to be inactive. This is implicated in several cancers and linked to Alzheimer's Disease. The molecular function of Polycomb proteins is to organize chromatin. Chromatin consists of the genome (DNA), and proteins that package it. Different parts of the genome are packaged in different forms. Active parts of the genome are organized for easy access so cells can read and use the information in the DNA, while inactive parts are tightly folded so that the DNA information is hidden. Polycomb proteins keep inactive parts of the genome quiet by folding them up tightly, but we do not know how they do this at a molecular level. Recently, a process called phase separation, the same process by which oil drops form in water, has been identified as important for organizing molecules in cells. Thus, collections of molecules that function together can form concentrated drops in cells that may function as molecular factories. We are testing whether Polycomb proteins might use phase separation to form drops that keep parts of the genome inactive.

column36: Opioid tapering: Identifying optimal strategies to reduce adverse events among adults on long-term opioid therapy
column37: In Canada, chronic pain is a major public health problem that affects 20% of the adult population. Despite growing evidence that prescription opioids are largely ineffective for managing chronic pain, it is commonly prescribed on a long-term basis. Consequently, long-term prescription opioid use and misuse have been associated with high rates of addiction and overdose. Pressures to taper individuals off opioid medications due to the increased risks associated with long-term opioid therapy create challenging therapeutic and clinical issues due to the unique complications and risks associated with tapering. However, current BC and national opioid tapering guidelines are lacking in high-quality evidence, making it difficult for healthcare providers to develop effective approaches to tapering that reduce risk of patients transitioning to the illicit drug supply. In the midst of a national overdose crisis, evidence is urgently required to inform clinical practice to prevent the risks of adverse outcomes associated with long-term opioid therapy and inappropriate tapering approaches. The proposed three-year study will utilize linked administrative data and seek to: identify and characterize trends in prescription opioid tapering patterns, evaluate the impacts of opioid prescribing guidelines on tapering patterns, assess the effect of tapering on overdose and mortality, and understand the differences between those with and without concurrent opioid use disorder. Findings from this research will be essential to developing clinical guidelines and protocols that will seek to effectively reduce the harms associated with long-term opioid therapy and provide evidence for optimal opioid tapering approaches.

column36: Understanding and strengthening vaccine confidence among temporary foreign workers in Manitoba: A community-based participatory approach
column37: In Manitoba, South-east Asians, Africans, South Asians, Latin Americans, Black people, Filipinos and North American Indigenous peoples shoulder the burden of COVID-19 infections compared to their White counterparts. According to the Government of Manitoba's 2021 Race, Ethnicity and Indigeneity (REI) Analysis Report Wave Three, lower income racialized people were most likely to live in overcrowded and/or inadequate housing, which is the most common acquisition setting. Such overcrowding characterizes the living arrangements of many migrant workers in Manitoba. Earlier REI data showed that BIPOC individuals, particularly migrant workers, were more likely to be employed in higher-risk occupational settings, including food processing and food services, manufacturing and transportation, homecare work and farming. Although we are beginning to better understand the vulnerability of migrant workers to COVID-19 infections in Canada, there exists a major knowledge gap around vaccine confidence in this population. For this reason, we aim to strengthen vaccine confidence among temporary foreign workers in Manitoba by examining it within the wider structural context of inequality. Drawing upon a partnership between the migrant workers' rights organization, Migrante, and the University of Manitoba Institute for Global Public Health, we will pursue two objectives. Objective 1: to generate new knowledge on "vaccine confidence" that sheds light on systems of inequality within the Temporary Foreign Worker Program. Objective 2: to build a community-owned database that can guide Migrante's efforts to enhance vaccine uptake among temporary foreign workers. This approach to data justice will sharpen the focus of Migrante's ongoing health advocacy work by enabling them to generate and follow key health indicators, geographic coverage targets, and COVID-19 vaccine uptake among temporary foreign workers in Manitoba.

column36: COVID-19 et confiance dans les vaccins dans les communautes noires : Etat des lieux et programmes d'education et de mobilisation
column37: Comment expliquer que la pandemie de la COVID-19 continue d'avoir des consequences plus devastatrices pour les communautes racisees alors que celles-ci sont les moins disposees aux mesures de prevention telle que la vaccination ? A ce jour, cette question n'a pas de reponses car il manque d'informations fiables pour eclairer les autorites et les decideurs de politiques de sante publique au Canada. Notre projet vise a mieux comprendre les facteurs qui expliquent la mefiance des communautes noires du Canada vis-a-vis de la vaccination contre la COVID-19. Plus encore, il permettra de comprendre comment ces facteurs evoluent et changent dans le temps, en fonction de l'evolution de la pandemie et des mesures de sante associees ainsi que les campagnes de promotion de la vaccination au coeur de ce projet. Les participants a cette recherche seront recrutes en Ontario et au Quebec, a la fois parmi les vaccines et les non vaccines; ces deux provinces regroupent pres de 80% des communautes noires au Canada. Ils fourniront des informations sur leur profil et le fait ou leur intention de se faire vacciner, leurs connaissances, croyances et attitudes vis-a-vis des vaccins contre la COVID-19, les experiences de discrimination vecues et leur sante mentale. Des groupes de discussion seront egalement organises avec des participes vaccines et non-vaccines, des leaders communautes noirs et des professionnels de soins de sante primaires et de sante publique. Les informations recueillies seront analysees et les resultats permettront de mettre en place des campagnes d'education sur le vaccin. Ces campagnes permettront de reduire les croyances erronees ou fausses sur les vaccins et d'accroitre la confiance aux benefices de se faire vacciner contre la COVID-19. column36: Reducing Dietary Acid with fruit and vegetables versus oral alkali in people with Chronic Kidney Disease (ReDACKD) feasibility trial
column37: Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) can reduce a person's ability to manage the balance of acid and base in their bodies properly, leading to a condition called metabolic acidosis. Metabolic acidosis in CKD is linked with faster progression of CKD and an increased need for dialysis, as well as loss of muscle mass and reduced bone health. Currently, metabolic acidosis is treated by giving people sodium bicarbonate, commonly known as baking soda, in pills to help balance the extra acid the kidneys are not able to remove. But patients often do not like the baking soda treatment, and do not always continue it. Metabolic acidosis can also be treated by reducing the acid that comes from the food a person eats. This can be done with foods that contain base forming compounds which neutralize acids, including fruits and vegetables. In this one-year study, we will test how doable delivering fruits and vegetables to people living with CKD and their families is, to treat metabolic acidosis. The fruit and vegetable treatment will be compared to the current usual care of the baking soda treatment in a randomized feasibility study looking at whether the intervention is worthwhile doing in a larger population. Forty participants will be recruited to this study and will be randomized to have an equal chance of getting fruits and vegetables or baking soda, like a coin toss. This study will look at the impact of the fruits and vegetables on bicarbonate, a compound in the blood that is used to measure acid-base balance. This study will also ask participants about their quality of life and measure their physical functioning using a chair stand test. We will also conduct interviews at the end of the study with participants and their families and ask them about the treatments, including what they liked and did not like.

column36: 'Living' Systematic Review and IPD Meta-Analysis to Evaluate the Contributions of Major and Ancillary Imaging Features on the Diagnostic Accuracy of LI-RADS.
column37: Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) is the most common type of primary cancer seen in the liver. Imaging tests such as CT, MRI, and contrast-enhanced Ultrasound (CEUS) are used to detect and diagnose HCC. The Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS) helps radiologists to categorize liver lesions in patients with liver disease based on their relative risk for developing HCC using imaging features on CT, MRI and CEUS. LIRADS is comprised of a combination of 5 major and 26 ancillary imaging features to standardize the classification of liver lesions. Understanding the impact of individual imaging features on the diagnostic accuracy of LIRADS not only allows for better classification of lesions, but also helps optimize the LI-RADS systems and consequently improves the care of all patients at risk for HCC. Our team will combine data from patients whose findings have been published in different studies from centres all over the world. This technique is called an individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis. This technique allows for detailed analysis of the impact of each imaging feature on the probability of HCC. The large pool of diverse participants allows for exploration the relative contributions of imaging features that are linked to HCC. The purpose of this study is to perform a living prospective systematic review and IPD meta-analysis to evaluate the contributions of individual major and ancillary features on the diagnostic accuracy of LI-RADS. This means we will gather individual patient data from published studies on an ongoing basis. Using this information, we will regularly update our analyses to determine which imaging features are most useful for diagnosing HCC. Based on the continually updated evidence, our Knowledge User Partners, the LI-RADS steering group, will update the LI-RADS systems in order to better diagnose HCC.

column36: Molecular and Functional Genomic Characterization of G-quadruplex in Cancers with the Alternate Lengthening of Telomere (ALT) Mechanism
column37: Based on the conservative estimate that ~10 percent of human cancers employ the Alternate Lengthening of Telomere (ALT) mechanism as a telomere maintenance strategy, more than twenty thousand new cancer cases and eight thousand deaths can be attributed to ALT cancers in Canada. ALT is found in the most clinically challenging cancer types, such as pediatric and adult brain cancers, soft tissue sarcoma and osteosarcoma. Importantly, clinical data suggest that ALT tumors have distinct clinical behaviors from their ALT-negative counterparts. While recent advances in the molecular studies of the ALT mechanism have led to a better understanding of this atypical telomere maintenance pathway, the development of clinical interventions has been restricted by the lack of targets that advanced beyond the experimental stages. Malignant transformation and continuous growth of ALT tumors are hampered by telomere maintenance-related disadvantages that are necessary to promote the innate properties of the ALT recombination mechanism. These factors create global structural vulnerabilities in the ALT genome, extended beyond the telomere, which could be therapeutically targeted. Accordingly, our preliminary data showed increased ALT-specific cytotoxicity of G-quadruplex ligands, related to the ALT genomic structural defects, and encouraged further development of this novel treatment strategy. Our studies focus on understanding the structural and biological differences resulting from the unique ALT mechanism that is absent in non-transformed cells, and exploiting them for therapeutic development. The selective targeting of ALT chromatin structure is predicted to exhibit favorable therapeutic efficacy and safety. Furthermore, early phase clinical trials of G-quadruplex ligands suggested that treatment-related adverse effects are in general manageable. Our positive data will provide the mechanistic basis for designing and further developing this novel anti-cancer strategy.

column36: Advancing Patient-Centered Care in Young People Living with Chronic Pain
column37: Chronic pain is a common, serious and poorly understood problem among young people. Moreover, living with chronic pain is so much more than the pain itself. A wide range of domains may be affected by chronic pain including sense of self, relationships, physical functioning and sleep, mood, mental health, school and work. COVID-19 has further exacerbated the challenges experienced by young people with chronic pain (YCP). While living with chronic pain can have a tremendous toll on a young person, YCP voice that their experience is not understood. If we hope to improve care for YCP that is patient-centered, it is essential we engage YCP in research. The aim of this patient-oriented national study is to advance patient-centered care for YCP with an emphasis on YCP delineating their experiences, needs, priorities for care and preferred outcome. YCP will also co-design arts-based knowledge translation (KT) products to advance key stakeholders' (e.g., parents, YCP, health and social service providers) understanding of the experiences of YCP. YCP across Canada will take part in individual interview and arts-based methods. Integrating creative arts-based methods with qualitative approaches will afford the opportunity and space for YCP to articulate their multifaceted nature of their experiences. Key stakeholders from across Canada will be engaged in a series of focus groups to garner their recommendations on the use of arts-based KT products to advance patient-centered care for YCP. Adopting a patient-oriented approach that includes YCP as co-researchers and arts-based approaches is innovative and a necessary first study for this research program. Short-term, advanced understanding of the experiences of YCP including their needs, priorities for care and preferred outcomes will emerge. Long-term, the next steps in the research program includes developing as well as scaling-up and testing supports and services for YCP that are grounded in the experiences of YCP.

column36: The role of mitotic sumoylation events in establishing nuclear envelope structure.
column37: To know the molecular basis of disease is a daunting challenge. Knowing requires understanding of the processes that control how cells maintain, organize, and propagate their DNA complement - their genomes. We are investigating and defining these processes. In all cells of all eukaryotes, which include us, genes are organized within a spherical, membrane-enclosed compartment called the nucleus. The membrane shell that surrounds the genome is termed the nuclear envelope. Defects in the nuclear envelope are linked to multiple pathologies, such as muscular dystrophies, lipodystrophies, premature ageing, heart abnormalities, and cancer. Determining the underlying causes of these diseases requires an understanding of how the nuclear envelope functions, including its role in genome organization and the regulation of gene expression. To do this, we have taken advantage of the highly conserved structure and function of the nuclear envelope in species as diverse as humans and yeast. This has allowed us to conduct our studies in yeast where powerful genetic and biochemical approaches can be used. In recent years, we and others have begun to uncover how the nuclear envelope organizes chromatin and regulates gene expression. We have shown that structures present in the nuclear envelope can grab on to specific genes and, like puppeteers, alter their structure and turn them 'on' or 'off'. This proposal outlines state-of-the-art experiments designed to determine how interactions of genes with the nuclear envelope are maintained as the nucleus disassembles and reassembles during cell division, how this phenomenon contributes to the behavioral or environmental regulation of gene expression (epigenetics), and how a cellular regulatory pathway termed 'protein sumoylation' controls these events.

column36: Improving COVID-19 Vaccine Confidence and Uptake among Black Canadians
column37: Black Canadians have the highest rates of COVID-19 infection and death in Canada. Black Canadians also have the lowest COVID-19 vaccination rate in Canada. Two national surveys indicate Black Canadians are 20% less likely than White Canadians to receive the COVID-19 vaccine. Some factors that contribute to COVID 19 vaccine hesitancy include lack of trust in healthcare professionals, lack of trust in vaccines, younger age, being female, low education, and being unable able to take time off from work. Improving the COVID-19 vaccination rate among Black Canadians is of high interest to policy makers and stakeholders. Our project seeks to address knowledge gaps related to COVID-19 vaccine confidence and uptake among Black Canadians and inform effective strategies to improve COVID-19 vaccine confidence and, in turn, uptake among Black Canadians. We will use a participatory research approach and consider diverse social determinants, including gender, socioeconomic status, and race/racism, throughout our data collection process. The project will be conducted in four phases. Phase 1 will involve interviews of Black Canadians. Phase 2 will involve a scoping review of the literature. Phase 3 will involve focus groups with stakeholders. Phase 4 will involve taking action through the co-development of knowledge translation tools. We will thematically analyze our qualitative data. Our project will result in the creation of a practice guideline, a policy guideline, and an e-learning module on strategies to address COVID-19 vaccination among Black Canadians. Our interdisciplinary team of experts in Black people's health, infectious disease control, qualitative research, scoping reviews, immigrant health, and participatory action research is well positioned to address this knowledge gap.

column36: An OCT-controlled system for precise and reproducible subretinal drug injection in mice
column37: Subretinal injection (SI) of gene or cell therapy is a challenging surgical intervention aiming to restore and/or preserve the vision of patients suffering from retinal degenerative diseases. To perform a SI, surgeons insert a cannula under the retina, a delicate tissue layer (0.10-0.35 mm) that lines the inside of the eye and inject a small drug volume. Although this intervention is crucial for the overall therapeutic outcome, it is yet to be standardized in both humans and animal models. Mouse models are the most widely used animal models in preclinical validation of new retinal treatments. However, in mice, SI are particularly challenging due their relatively small eye. The associated drug dose administration uncertainty hinders the development of new treatments. Here, we propose to develop and validate a semi-automated optical coherence tomography (OCT) - based system, enabling controlled SI in mice. OCT is a non-invasive imaging technique that provides tomographic images of tissue. Importantly, OCT fiber probes can be used to guide surgical tools via real-time endoscopic imaging. Our goal is to develop OCT-guided SI cannulas and validate a semi-automated robotic injection system with the help of 3 end-users. The end-users will perform comparative SI in mice using a model drug and an adenovirus. Successful implementation of the project would enable unprecedented precision and repeatability in guiding modified cannulas under the mouse retina. As such, this project can timely address the unmet need for reliable subretinal drug delivery in rodents. By eliminating side effects and dose uncertainty, the novel instrument and method can catalyze the development of novel gene and cell therapies for retinal generative diseases. In the long term, potential clinical adoption of an OCT-guided SI system can facilitate the delivery of therapies aiming to restore the vision of blind people.

column37: Young adults (aged 18 to 29 years) have had the highest proportion of COVID-19 cases during the pandemic. At the same time, they are also the adult age group with the highest proportion of those unvaccinated. National and provincial public health leaders have identified young adults as having the highest risk of transmission given their employment in public-facing jobs, social mobility and confined housing. This proposal will work closely with young adults through our Young Adult Advisory Group. Our first aim is to engage up to 30 young adults through interviews to understand their knowledge and attitudes towards vaccination. Our second aim is to further develop, and implement, a mobile app, STOP COVID!, designed to improve vaccine confidence and, ultimately, vaccination. STOP COVID! will be a game-based app aimed at changing behaviour intention (nudging) young adults towards vaccination. Content will be science-based and informed by the findings of the first aim so that STOP COVID! will be tailored to young adults. STOP COVID! will be implemented in restaurants and public transit throughout British Columbia, and promoted through social media. We will evaluate the implementation of STOP COVID! to understand in what context is the app effective, in whom and why. Special attention will be made across a range of genders, ethnicity, education and geography across BC. We anticipate STOP COVID! will improve vaccine confidence and uptake in young adults, and with our public health partners, spread to other provinces in the future.
