column36: RACE Concussion Study: Rapid, accurate cost-effective assessment of fluid biomarkers using a hand-held biosensor in patients with concussion
column37: Over 300,000 Canadian and 40 million individuals worldwide sustain a concussion annually. Symptoms typically resolved within 10-14 days; yet in a subset of patients with concussion, these symptoms and deficits are chronic. Approximately 15-30% of patients with concussions show cognitive or neurological dysfunction that continues for months or more after the initial injury. Approximately 30% of individuals with a concussion returned to the emergency department (ED) within one month of their initial injury with persistent symptoms, increasing demands on ED flow, increasing economic strain on health care, and potentially prolong patient recovery. There is a dire need for more quantitative, cost-effective methods to monitor recovery following concussion. Our proposed in-home monitoring of GFAP blood biomarker with a machine-learning and Cloud system addresses such an issue. The success of the proposed home-based GFAP biosensing kit enables us to evaluate the feasibility of remote patient monitoring in individuals with a concussion, to map the pattern of GFAP marker, and to follow concussion patients throughout their recovery. The project will significantly reduce costly emergency room and primary care visits, reduce the overall burden on the healthcare system, and support integration with primary care providers in the community. The project represents a significant advancement in the health of patients with concussion.

column36: dI3 interneurons and their role in facilitating motor function after spinal cord injury
column37: Spinal cord injury can lead to long-lasting loss of leg movements. My previous work has demonstrated the importance of a population of spinal neurons, named dI3 interneurons, in recovery from spinal cord injury. Preliminary data from the lab suggests that these dI3 interneurons may facilitate recovery through treadmill training by two mechanisms. First, dI3 interneurons may generate the muscle tone necessary for treadmill training to be effective. Secondly, dI3 interneurons may be involved in coordinating the leg's flexor and extensor muscles required for everyday walking. The proposal's first aim will show that turning off dI3 interneurons after spinal cord injury removes muscle tone and prevents treadmill training from being effective. In contrast, we will show that increasing the activity of dI3 interneurons improves walking through treadmill training. The second aim will be to demonstrate that dI3 interneurons facilitate muscle tone in injured animals. We propose a series of experiments where activation of dI3 interneurons leads to muscle activity patterns in the limbs that generate weight support. Our final aim will test whether dI3 interneurons facilitate a stepping reflex that could be useful for promoting the recovery of locomotion. We will use muscle recordings and nerve stimulation to test the effects of inhibiting and exciting dI3 interneurons on the stepping reflex in injured animals. To achieve these aims, we will use novel technology allowing select neurons to be turned on or off through orally administered compounds in a mouse model of spinal cord injury. Behavioural analysis in combination with muscle recordings during behaviour will allow us to gain insight into the role of dI3 interneurons in the recovery of motor function after injury. This work will be an essential step in developing new therapeutic strategies for prolonged improvement of locomotor function following spinal cord injury.

column36: Leveraging high-volume data to characterize age and individual-specific vital signs and to develop novel geriatric vital signs that optimally predict clinical outcomes in older adults
column37: Vital signs are used everyday by healthcare professionals to quickly screen and assess the health status of patients. Heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, respiratory rate, and blood oxygen level are the backbone of clinical management by informing how sick a person might be and how urgently care must be provided. However, vital signs and normal reference ranges currently used in older adults were developed many decades ago using the health characteristics of a younger population. As the Canadian population is aging, the appropriateness of current vitals signs and their reference ranges that would best inform triage and care has not been evaluated in contemporary older adults. Our research has three objectives. First, rather than relying on "normal" values from the overall population of adults, we seek to identify reference range for vital signs that are specific to older age groups and to each older adult individually. Second, instead of using unique values of vital signs, we will investigate whether different ways of combining multiple values over time (modelling) can improve the predictive performance of vital signs. Finally, we expand the health characteristics and type of data considered as vital signs: blood test results may function as vital signs. We will examine whether and how these types of data can be best accounted for and used in clinical care as novel geriatric vital signs. Vital signs are at the core of clinical management. Tailoring and expanding vital signs to the needs and specificities of the growing older adult population has the potential to be vastly alter and improve the care of older adults.

column36: Efficacy of high intensity laser therapy for reducing pain during intercourse in women with provoked vestibulodynia: A multicenter randomized controlled trial
column37: Chronic vulvar pain is a highly prevalent and debilitating condition affecting up to 18% of women. The most common subtype of vulvar pain, provoked vestibulodynia (PVD), is characterized by a sharp pain at the entry of the vagina in response to the application of pressure or attempted vaginal penetration. Women with PVD not only present with psychological distress and significant disruption in all aspects of sexual function, but they are also confronted with limited effective treatment options. High-intensity laser could potentially fill this therapeutical void by providing a non-invasive treatment option. Judged by experts as a promising intervention, a recent rise in popularity has compelled leading societies to issue a warning statement to urgently examine the efficacy of laser for gynecological conditions. Therefore, our multidisciplinary team, working together for more than 15 years, has conducted novel research to prepare for the current proposal. For instance, our systematic review underscored the lack of studies and served as a strong basis to select the most optimal laser parameters. Moreover, our randomized pilot study confirmed that our state-of-the-art laser treatment protocol is feasible for treating PVD and the promising findings obtained provide support for conducting a large-scale study. The proposed double-blind randomized controlled trial aims to establish the efficacy of high-intensity laser therapy for reducing pain in women with PVD. Women will be randomized to receive either sham or active Nd:Yag laser treatment for 12 bi-weekly sessions. Validated outcome measures will be assessed at baseline, post-treatment and at 6-month follow-up. The current proposal addresses the urgent need to determine whether women with PVD could benefit from this non-invasive treatment. It will enable women with PVD to be directed to appropriate treatment options and, if proven effective, laser could be proposed as a first-line non-invasive treatment.

column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is a devastating and debilitating muscle degenerative disease affecting 1 in every 5,000 male births in Canada. DMD symptoms manifest in early childhood, as boys between 2-5 years of age exhibit motor development delays. Accumulated and progressive weakening of the muscle tissue leads to an inability to walk and patients are wheelchair-bound by the age of 12. DMD is fatal and patients succumb to death from respiratory and cardiac failure in their 20's and 30's. Despite research efforts to understand DMD, there still remains no effective cure. However, recent studies have shown that muscle stem cells, which are adult stem cells that reside within muscle, are also affected in DMD. DMD muscle stem cells do not function as normal healthy stem cells and their dysfunction plays a role in disease progression. Importantly, current therapeutic strategies for muscular dystrophy do not address these deficiencies in muscle stem cell function. Our research aims to understand the cellular processes that are altered in DMD muscle stem cells and devise strategies to restore muscle stem cell function to improve muscle repair.

column36: Feasibility of implementing a mobile phone-based telemonitoring program to support pregnant individuals at high-risk for preeclampsia in Karachi, Pakistan
column37: Pakistan has one of the highest rates of maternal deaths in the world, with one-third of maternal deaths in hospitals due to preeclampsia and eclampsia (PE/E). Preeclampsia is when pregnant individuals have high blood pressure and protein in the urine. It can lead to maternal death, preterm birth, pregnancy loss, and stillbirth. In severe cases, preeclampsia can lead to eclampsia which is the presence of seizures. High maternal death from PE/E results from the lack of early risk detection, diagnosis, and treatment of individuals at high risk for pre-eclampsia (HRPE). Individuals at HRPE should have frequent clinic visits, but this can be hard due to socio-cultural and financial factors. However, even with regular visits, individuals at HRPE can have life-threatening spikes in their blood pressure. A potential tool to support individuals at HRPE is telemonitoring (TM), which is when home blood pressure readings and symptoms are sent to their providers in real-time. This project will explore how feasible it is to implement a mobile phone-based TM program for individuals at HRPE at a public hospital in Karachi, the largest city in Pakistan, where many people with very low-income live. The feasibility study will include 50 pregnant individuals at HRPE. The participants will take home blood pressure measurements and enter symptoms through the app, and will receive self-care instructions based on the entered data. A nurse will be the central point person to communicate with the high-risk pregnant individuals and their care team, and will respond to the automated alerts generated by the TM system. This will be the first study to explore the feasibility of having pregnant individuals at HRPE in Pakistan take their own home blood pressure readings through a TM system. The goal is to use the findings from this study to conduct a future larger trial to determine the effectiveness of the TM program to reduce the number of pregnant individuals and babies who die from PE/E.

column36: Targeting Danger Signals In Systemic Sclerosis-Associated Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
column37: The lungs have their own unique system of blood vessels, usually kept at a very low pressure as compared to the rest of the body. As a result of a variety of diseases, the blood vessels in the lung can stiffen and become abnormal, resulting in raised pressure, called pulmonary hypertension. This increased pressure can cause the part of the heart that pumps to the lungs to fail, resulting in death. One disease that can cause a particularly deadly form of pulmonary hypertension is called Systemic Sclerosis. How this disease causes pulmonary hypertension is not well understood. Systemic sclerosis involves problems with the immune system, and with the scaffolding of the body's cells, called the extracellular matrix. Our proposal seeks to link inherited problems with the extracellular matrix to cell damage, releasing molecules into the blood that cause both the changes in the blood vessels and in the immune system. Our proposal uses a newly described mouse model of the disease, as well as blood taken from patients with the disease to study this proposed pathway. If successful, our work will define a new model for how systemic sclerosis causes pulmonary hypertension, which can be attacked by various experimental drugs in testing.

column36: Investigation of the factors contributing to fracture risk in clinical populations using novel image processing techniques of standard DXA images from longitudinal datasets.
column37: Osteoporosis is a disease where an individual's bone density is reduced, which decreases its strength and increases the risk of a fragility fracture. This disease is common in older adults and is the main reason for a broken bone among this population. Hips are a common site for these fractures, with devastating long-term consequences, with >50% of patients requiring assisted living facilities post-fracture. To identify those who are at greatest risk, osteoporosis is diagnosed based using a Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA) scan. However, studies suggest that the current approach of evaluating bone density at one location is not able to accurately predict who will experience a fracture. In order to identify who should receive interventions (such as hip protectors or medications), new methods are necessary. Previous work in our lab has developed a method to extract more relevant information from a DXA scan. This now considers both the shape and quality of the bone, as well as including the patient's age and sex. We will apply this method to more than 50,000 patient scans from existing databases and use their history of falls and fractures to identify those at greatest risk. Using long-term follow-up data, we will investigate whether medications can slow the progress of osteoporosis, as well as how other factors such as smoking, activity, or diabetes alter risk. Through this, we will identify what influences a person's risk of breaking a bone from a fall. The outcome of this work will be recommendations for slowing age-associated increases in fracture risk. This will allow clinicians to better identify who would benefit from protective measures, ultimately reducing the incidence of these devastating and life-altering injuries for older adults.

column36: Control of adipocyte thermogenesis by coordinated regulation of alpha and beta adrenergic signaling
column37: The obesity epidemic is a serious public health concern. Obesity occurs when energy from food consumption exceeds energy expenditure. Sustaining weight loss with diet and exercise shows limited success because metabolic processes are triggered to resist the maintenance of that lowered weight. Hence, there is a major clinical need to develop new approaches to counter obesity-linked metabolic complications and sustain weight loss. Brown adipose tissue (BAT) wastes energy from food by transforming it to heat in a process called thermogenesis. BAT can offset the adverse effects of obesity by removing sugar and fat from the blood to fuel its thermogenic properties. However, the molecular mechanisms that regulate BAT thermogenesis are not fully understood. Noradrenaline (NA) is the physiological activator of BAT thermogenesis. NA works by binding alpha-adrenergic receptors (alpha-ARs) and beta-adrenergic receptors (beta-ARs). Upon binding NA, these receptors stimulate metabolic pathways inside of brown adipocytes to promote thermogenesis. Beta-AR signaling has received the most attention in the thermogenesis field. However, mice lacking all three forms of beta-AR's can still mount a thermogenic response, indicating that additional thermogenic signaling cascades and metabolic pathways of thermogenesis remain to be discovered. Given that the full thermogenic response of brown adipocytes to NA has been understood for decades to require alpha-AR and beta-AR pathways, the large focus on beta-AR signaling has left the alpha-AR-dependent component a vastly under-explored area of adipocyte biology. Most importantly, the metabolic effector pathways that lie downstream of the cooperative activity of alpha-AR and beta-AR signaling in brown adipocyte thermogenesis have remained elusive. We have now identified this thermogenic pathway. We aim to study the relevance of alpha-AR signaling in BAT thermogenesis and to explore its impact on obesity and metabolic disease.

column36: Role of VEGFB in the cardiovascular complications of diabetes.
column37: During diabetes, the heart has limited capacity to use sugar and must adapt to largely using fats to generate energy. While this switch ensures that the heart is able to manage its constant energy demands, the increased reliance upon fats leads to a number of dire consequences. This is because when using fats, the heart requires substantial oxygen, which is in short supply due to blood vessel defects in the heart. This leads to fat accumulation in the heart with associated cellular damage. It is within this framework that a protein produced mainly in the heart, VEGFB, has emerged as a potentially efficacious agent against diabetic heart disease. VEGFB has the capability of a) enhancing blood vessel formation in the heart, which can aid in providing the necessary oxygen to use fat, b) shifting energy production back to using sugar and c) preventing cell death to delay heart failure. Using animal models (where the heart over produces VEGFB), isolated cells from the heart and models of high glucose, our project will investigate VEGFB as a cardio-protective therapy in diabetes.

column36: Astrocyte Nanostructure and Function in the Healthy and Diseased Brain
column37: Scientists study neurons based on knowledge of their anatomy which underlies their ability to receive, integrate, and transmit information. While much has been learned about the organizing principles of neurons, the structural basis of other brain cell types lags behind. This is particularly true for non-neuronal cells in the central nervous system (CNS) called an astrocytes, which play an key role in brain function and disease. Understanding the anatomical 'signatures' for astrocytes within the brain is important to uncover their physiological and integrative properties, and will aid in detecting and managing changes to these cells in CNS diseases including Alzheimer's disease. Overlaid on the intricate anatomy of an astrocyte is a sophisticated molecular program contributing to their development, physiology, and ability to communicate with other cells. Astrocytes likely use an array of mechanisms to communicate with other cells in the brain. However, our knowledge of these mechanisms remains limited. Investigations are needed to expose new mechanisms allowing astrocytes to maintain their unique structure and perform integrative roles in the CNS. This proposal will resolve the structural complexity of astrocytes in the heathy and AD brain using newly developed microscopy and computational approaches, uncover new molecular/structural adaptations that allow astrocytes to control brain physiology, and harness the power of inter-disciplinary research by working in the fields of cellular/molecular neuroscience and computer science.

column36: Physiology and cholinergic modulation of the medial prefrontal cortex - medial thalamus loop in female Rett Syndrome model mice
column37: Rett syndrome is a neurological disorder caused by mutations in a gene called MECP2 that controls many other genes to regulate the formation and function of brain circuits. Female patients get one X from their father, one from their mother but genes from only one of the two X chromosomes in each cell are expressed so half of the brain cells of female patients have a normal copy (expressing their mother's X) while the other half have a deficient copy of the gene (expressing their father's X). Patients suffer from many deleterious cognitive and motor symptoms including epileptic seizures. Given that the Rett brain is comprised of a mixture of mutant and non-mutant neurons a "one-size-fits-all" approach to pharmacological intervention may be inappropriate. Drug-based therapies for these patients have to be compatible with brain circuits composed of a mixture of mutant and non-mutant neurons. This project seeks to understand how the presence of neurons with mutated genes affects the properties of normal and mutated neurons and the circuits they form. Our work investigates how the higher parts of the brain (neocortex) receive and modulate information from the part of the brain that gates sensory information called the thalamus. In Rett syndrome the balance between neural excitation and inhibition in many circuits is disrupted due to incorrect wiring and improper levels of neurotransmitter receptors. Acetylcholine is a transmitter that modulates circuit functions and has different kinds of effects depending on whether receptors for this transmitter are over- or under-expressed and in which neuron types they are dysregulated. This project uses a combination of advanced single neuron anatomical and electrophysiological recording techniques to understand how Mecp2 mutation affects how mutant neurons perform in cortico-thalamic circuits, how acetylcholine receptor expression is altered and how this affects the function of cortico-thalamic circuits.

column36: The cellular and molecular mechanisms of lactic acid taste in flies and disease-vectoring mosquitoes.
column37: Sour taste is the detection of acid, yet different acids can taste distinct. Lactic acid is particularly notable because it imparts a relatively mild sour taste (and 'sweet' smell) to humans, but is also a metabolic product that carries important information for other animals. For example, the presence of lactic acid may tell a fly what types of bacteria are growing on some rotting fruit. It is also present in sweat and is a well-known attractant for blood-feeding mosquitoes. In this proposal, we use the well-established and powerful fruit fly model system to dissect the cells and molecules responsible for lactic acid taste. We then translate our findings into Aedes aegypti - mosquitoes that infect millions of people each year with deadly diseases like Dengue, yellow fever, Zika, and West Nile virus - with the goal of understanding how lactic acid influences blood feeding, thereby enabling new strategies for deterring mosquitoes from biting humans and reducing mosquito-borne disease transmission. Finally, we use the unique properties of acid taste in flies to investigate how the brain encodes the timing of taste information during feeding. Since the principles of sensory coding are similar between flies and mammals, and taste is critical in driving feeding, this will provide fundamental insight into how we decide what, and how much, we eat.

column36: Pathogenic Strategies of the Lyme Disease Spirochete
column37: Lyme disease is an emerging infectious disease caused by a spiral-shaped bacterium or spirochete (Borrelia burgdorferi) that is transmitted through the bite of an infected tick. Incidence of the disease is increasing, triggered in part by global warming. The disease can result in a wide variety of symptoms, often making diagnosis difficult. The focus of this project is to investigate two important strategies used by B. burgdorferi to mount a successful infection. 1) Antigenic variation. This is a process by which the pathogen continually changes the sequence of the major component of the outer coat resulting in a continual wardrobe change for the pathogen. This keeps it one step ahead of the immune system, resulting in persistent infection. Antigenic variation is driven occurs by continual DNA rearrangements in the gene for the major surface protein, VlsE. We will study this process in detail including the DNA regions and protein molecules involved in the rearrangement process. 2) Vascular transmigration. The reason why B. burgdorferi can cause such a large number of different symptoms is because the organism disseminates through the circulatory system and can exit the vasculature in virtually any part of the body. The result is varying symptoms depending upon where B. burgdorferi exits the bloodstream. Vascular transmigration is mediated by interactions between B. burgdorferi and endothelial cells lining small blood vessels. We will investigate these interactions and the changes they cause as well as the proteins and signaling pathways involved and the molecular changes occurring to the endothelial layer that unlock the door for spirochete escape. Significance: Details uncovered on these important processes may be useful for future development of clinical interventions. Blocking vascular transmigration would stop dissemination of the spirochetes from the site of a tick bite and eliminating antigenic variation would eradicate persistent infection.

column36: Identify novel genes and mechanisms of molar pregnancies and reproductive failure
column37: Reproductive failure manifests as infertility, recurrent miscarriages and molar pregnancies (pregnancies with no embryos). These conditions affect up to 10% of couples. Little is known about genes responsible for them because of their genetic complexity and heterogeneity. My group has so far identified four genes responsible responsible for recurrent moles, including three for a specific subtype that contain only paternal chromosomes (called androgenetic). With Dr. Taketo, we modeled this disease in mutant mice and found that some of their oocytes, during their intimate preparation to meet with the sperm, instead of losing half of their chromosomes, they lose them all, and some lead to androgenetic embryos. Mutations in the three identified genes in 2018 cause also recurrent miscarriages and female and male infertility. Recently, we identified four additional novel candidate genes that have similar roles in oocytes and again their mutations were found in patients with recurrent androgenetic moles, recurrent miscarriages, and infertility. We believe that androgenetic moles has homogenized a subgroup of patients enriched for mutations in genes with the same role in oocytes. Therefore, studying recurrent androgenetic moles is an opportunity to advance and speed up the genetics of reproductive failure. The goals of this proposal are to (1) complete the identification of the 4 novel genes by finding more patients with mutations in them and identifying other novel genes with similar roles; (2) model some features of this condition in the mouse and determine whether all mouse models lose their maternal chromosomes by the same mechanism; and (3) delineate the nature of the oocyte defects that lead to androgenetic embryos in mice. This will translate into DNA tests, accurate genetic counselling based on the defective gene, and will help reproductive biologists rationalizing assisted reproductive technology services and tailoring them to the need of each patient.

column36: Beta-cell adaptation to puberty and type 2 diabetes risk
column37: The rise in obesity in children is a major health issue, and as a result, the age at which type 2 diabetes occurs has been steadily decreasing in recent years. Children who are overweight when they undergo puberty have an increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes later in life, yet the reasons for this increased susceptibility are unknown. The major hormonal changes that occur during puberty have a myriad of effects in addition to promoting sexual maturity. Amongst these is a decrease in the ability of insulin to promote the storage of energy into its target tissues. This transient so-called "insulin resistance" is normally compensated for by an increase in the production of insulin from the pancreas. Surprisingly, very little is known about the mechanisms by which beta cells adapt to puberty. The objectives of this project are to discover the cellular mechanisms underlying beta-cell adaptation to puberty, and to ascertain whether these mechanisms are altered in an obese environment. Based on preliminary findings obtained by our group, we hypothesize that beta-cell mass expansion during puberty involves two signalling pathways, the growth hormone/serotonin pathway and the sex hormone pathway. To test this hypothesis, we will first examine in male and female rodent models and human samples the contribution of the growth hormone/serotonin pathway by manipulating the expression of the receptor for growth hormone and the enzyme that makes serotonin. Second, using similar strategies we will test the implication of the sex hormones (testosterone and estrogens). Finally, we will feed rats with a diet enriched in fat and examine whether the pathways studied above are impaired. This project will provide detailed information as to how the pancreatic beta cell adapts to insulin resistance during puberty, and how these mechanisms are affected by obesity. These findings will help devise strategies to curb the alarming increase in type 2 diabetes in young adults.

column36: Cardiometabolic Health of Mothers with a Sick Child
column37: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death among Canadian women. Events that occur during and after a first pregnancy, including the health and caregiving needs of a child, may play an important role in determining whether a woman develops cardiovascular disease. Risk factors for developing cardiovascular disease, also known as cardiometabolic risk factors, include obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol, can accumulate when a woman is in her childbearing years. These risk factors may appear at or shortly before the time of a woman's second pregnancy. We will use data from two large databases - one in Ontario and one in Denmark containing information on over 750,000 women with two consecutive births -- to understand whether women with stressful challenges arising at or shortly after the birth of their first child experience cardiometabolic risk in a subsequent pregnancy. We will compare the risks of weight gain, abnormal sugar metabolism, high blood pressure and/or high cholesterol among women whose first pregnancy resulted in a death, or an infant affected by a serious illness, to those women who did not have that pregnancy outcome. Our findings will provide important information for the care of these women, which we will use in future research to design and evaluate better supports for those who have an ill newborn, or a chronically ill child.

column36: HIV antiretrovirals and placenta dysfunction - identifying the mechanisms leading to poor fetal growth
column37: It is recommended that all pregnant people with HIV take HIV medications for their own health and for preventing transmission of HIV to their babies. While this has dramatically reduced both maternal death and HIV infections in newborns, HIV medication use in pregnancy has been associated with poorer birth outcomes. It is not yet clear how HIV medications are causing these, or whether some HIV medications are better to use in pregnancy than others. Further, not all pregnant people with HIV go on to have a poor birth outcome. Our hypothesis is that HIV medications cause changes in the placenta that affect how well the baby grows. In this proposal, we bring together an international team from Canada, USA, Uganda, and South Africa. We will take advantage of placenta and blood samples collected in 3 different studies across the globe to address our hypotheses. We will investigate how 3 different types of HIV medications (the most commonly used HIV medications in pregnancy) affect how the placenta develops and functions. We will also use an animal model and a test-tube model using human placenta tissue to dig into the mechanisms on how HIV medications affect the placenta and find out ways to prevent them. Our findings will help guide the choice of best HIV medications to use in pregnancy and identify interventions to improve pregnancy outcome. Our animal model will also be an asset in the testing of the safety of new HIV medications in pregnancy.

column36: 3-dimensional representation of mouse movement and rapid interaction with cortical brain activity to describe and shape behavior to improve outcome from stroke: insights from real and synthetic data approaches.
column37: A leading theme in human stroke treatment are means of rehabilitation that engage surviving brain circuits to compensate for damage due to stroke. However, these approaches still require optimisation in animal models. We suggest that the study of stroke will benefit from advances in computer science methods: including computer vision where software can see features too subtle or fast for human raters, and machine learning where computer programs can be advanced without explicit instructions. Here we employ the use of a synthetic animated mouse to create realistic videos that are used for training advanced computer models (through a trick borrowed from "deepfakes"). The advantage of the model is that it can simulate aspects of mouse behaviour that would otherwise be difficult to observe in nature (due to a rare occurrence, poor timing, or inability to resolve in 3 dimensions (3D)). These trained computer models are then used with real video data to more carefully evaluate stroke disease progression and recovery by representing mouse movements within 3D. The animated mouse interface also provides a common system to represent mouse movements enabling pooling of data leading to statistically stronger experiments. Computer vision combined with the online analysis of brain activity offers the promise of rapidly cataloging specific mouse movements in such a way that stroke recovering animals can be subjected to corrective rehabilitation. By having the ability to monitor complex movements such as reaching, as well as the brain activity associated with planning and executing them we can give the animals real-time feedback about their progress in recovery. Forms of rehabilitation would be instituted in a closed-loop manner (where results are fed back) and reward animals which are moving towards recovery in both their affected brain circuits and specific movements. We aim to determine rules for how these approaches can be optimally applied to promote recovery from stroke.

column36: COVID-19 Vaccine Confidence Among At-Risk and Under-Vaccinated Groups Within HIV and Rheumatic diseases (CONFIDENCE)
column37: People living with human immunodeficiency virus (PL-HIV) as well as people living with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (PL-SARDs) are more likely to have severe COVID-19 and to die of it compared to individuals in the general population. Vaccination against COVID-19 is key to reducing these risks. However, ~20% of the eligible Canadian population is not yet vaccinated. Moreover, recent data suggest that vaccine rates and acceptance are lower in migrants, women, and people with physical disabilities. These 'especially vulnerable subgroups' are frequent among PL-HIV and PL-SARDs. Previous literature reported that vulnerable subgroups of PL-HIV and PL-SARDs share common reasons that lead to reduced COVID-19 vaccine uptake. We propose to work along with members of these subgroups to uncover those reasons and to empower trusted members of these communities so they can communicate with their peers in ways that motivate behavior change (i.e., vaccine acceptance). In order to understand the reasons that could enhance COVID-19 vaccine confidence in the aforementioned vulnerable groups, we will conduct virtual group meetings (i.e., focus groups) and individual phone interviews with those not willing to join the group discussions. The information gathered from these activities will then be used to design a training program for community members to promote vaccine confidence through motivational interviewing and storytelling techniques. column36: Best practices for community-led strategies to boost vaccine confidence: A case study in Parc-Extension, Quebec
column37: The most racially diverse and socio-economically disadvantaged neighbourhoods in Canada, primarily those concentrated in large urban areas such as Parc Extension in Montreal, Quebec experience have been vaccinated at lower rates despite availability. The lower vaccination rate among residents in Parc Extension is attributable to vaccine hesitancy, characterized by uncertainty and ambivalence about vaccination, a legitimate viewpoint, underscoring the failure or lack of an effective public health system. In response, new and reimagined vaccine interventions that are community-led, culturally-relevant, and place-based have been developed in Parc Extension to successfully increase vaccine confidence and uptake. There is a clear need for better quality studies on the use of community-led vaccination strategies in promoting confidence, particularly in low income and diverse regions in Canada, where research capacities are limited. This proposed community-based research has the fundamental goal of producing qualitative evidence guided by grounded theory using Parc Extension, Quebec as a case study in understanding dynamic community-led responses and developing a best practices implementation toolkit to address vaccine hesitancy. Semi-structured interviews will be conducted with diverse key stakeholders in Parc Extension to understand the best practices required to establish successful and effective community-led vaccine strategies. Data will be analyzed using open-coding and synthesized member-checking to develop a best practices toolkit to implement sustained effective community-led strategies to achieve vaccine confidence among low income and racialized communities in Canada.

column36: Developing a COVID-19 Vaccination Strategy that Addresses the Needs of People Who Use Drugs in Canada
column37: Background: People Who Use Drugs (PWUD) have intersecting health and social vulnerabilities that elevate their risk for COVID-19 infection, complications and mortality. It is therefore critical that PWUD are vaccinated to reduce their risks. However, research has suggested that vaccine acceptability ratings are lower than the general population (Iverson et al., 2021) with safety concerns being the most common reason for vaccine hesitancy (Dietze et al., 2021). Objectives: The purpose of this study is to: (1) identify drivers of vaccine hesitancy and approaches to improve vaccine confidence and; (2) to develop national tailored knowledge mobilization and translation products that are for and by PWUD to promote vaccination based on the findings from Objective 1. We will work closely with PWUD and service providers who work with this population to develop these materials. Methods: The study will recruit 100 participants from an existing national sample of PWUD who previously participated in telephone/video interviews about the impact of COVID-19 in May-June 2020. Semi-structured interviews will be used to identify barriers to receiving vaccinations and ways to address barriers. An advisory committee of PWUD, service providers working with PWUD, and the research team will use responses from the interviews to co-create a multi-pronged approach to address vaccine hesitancy among PWUD. The strategy will include the following components: (1) Developing and disseminating vaccine information resources for PWUD; and (2) Providing training tools to service providers working with PWUD to improve conversations about vaccinations.

column36: Maternal Disability and Child Preventive Health Care: Supporting Family-Centred Care
column37: Preventive health care is critical for health and development, especially in the first 6 years of life, when brain development is rapid and children are preparing for school. Well-child visits, the primary vehicle for preventive health care delivery, offer opportunities for providers to do physical exams, assess development, give immunizations, make referrals for eye exams, connect families with resources, and address caregiver concerns. Long-term physical health, educational, and economic outcomes are improved in children with good preventive health care access, with benefits greatest in those with low socioeconomic status. Yet, even in universal health care systems, some families still experience barriers accessing child preventive health care. One such group may be children of women with disabilities. We have been doing research on women with disabilities in pregnancy and up to their infant's first birthday, showing that mothers with disabilities experience disparities in prenatal and infant health care, with inaccessible spaces, communication problems with providers, and negative provider attitudes being common barriers. These could also be barriers to early child preventive health care, but this has not been studied. We will extend this research by using health records data on all children in Ontario, and interviews with women with disabilities, service-providers, and decision-makers, to study preventive health care access in 1 to 6-year-old children of women with disabilities. A disability lens in child health care should take a family-centred approach that considers not just the needs of the child but also those of the parent, in this case the mother. If inequities in preventive health care access are seen in children of women with disabilities, this would provide evidence needed to create tailored supports for these families, which could positively impact the health of Canadian children.

column36: Investigating the cell-type specific role of the transcription factor Npas4 in regulating motor learning
column37: The primary motor cortex in the brain is responsible for voluntary movement. It has also been proposed to be one of the sites for motor memory formation and storage. Therefore, when the motor cortex is damaged following a stroke, we lose the ability to execute movements that were formerly part of normal daily life. One hypothesis to achieve true recovery is to re-initiate motor learning in the brain and establish new representation to replace the destroyed ones (Murphy and Corbett, 2009). Hence, a determination of the basic molecular mechanisms underlying motor learning will enhance our understanding of post-traumatic rehabilitation in brain injury and disease. Previous work has demonstrated the importance of local inhibitory circuits in the motor cortex in regulating the acquisition of new motor skills. Our lab has recently identified an activity-dependent transcription factor, Npas4, that is specific expressed in an inhibitory neuron subtype in the motor cortex during motor learning. Here, we are proposing a series of experiments employing in vivo two-photon imaging combined with head-fixed pellet-reaching motor skill learning task to elucidate the role of Npas4 in learning-driven inhibitory neural circuit modifications during motor learning in awake and behaving mice. By deciphering the basic mechanisms underlying motor movement acquisition in normal healthy brains, our work has immense potential to promote plastic changes in dysfunctional circuits altered by stroke and aid in the development of novel therapeutic targets for stroke recovery and other brain injuries impairing motor function

column36: Characterizing the genetic consequences of dysfunctional NURF chromatin remodeling to syndromal intellectual disability
column37: Our genes are encoded on large DNA molecules called chromosomes. Individual cells must compact their chromosomes in a unique way to silence genes not expressed while maintaining an open configuration for active genes. A neural progenitor cell will have many genes that are open or poised while it divides but once it commits to becoming a neuron many of these genes must be tightly packaged as they will not be required after differentiation. The cell manages this process with a complex series of proteins that control the structure of chromosomes and the regulation of genes. When this process is defective, cells cannot divide, differentiate or initiate gene expression effectively. Indeed, mutations affecting chromosome regulating proteins cause a variety of neurodevelopmental disability disorders, including mutations in the BPTF gene. Despite our success in identifying disease causing genes, how they coordinate which genes to turn on or off, when to turn them on or off, and in what order remains poorly defined. For BPTF, we know that it functions in a complex called NURF, that also includes a second remodeling protein called SMARCA1 or its close relative SMARCA5. With the previous grant we generated mice lacking the Smarca1 gene. The progenitors were delayed in their differentiation into neurons, thus making a larger brain. In contrast, deletion of the Smarca5 gene resulted in much smaller brains because the progenitors differentiated too quickly. Here, we postulated that the NURF complex controls the transition from progenitor to neuron and that it requires a switch in partners, from Smarca5 for progenitor growth to Smarca1 for differentiation. We will identify and confirm when and how a subunit switch occurs, and we will identify the genes that are affected by this switch. This data will provide valuable insight into the differentiation process, how genes become activated or repressed, and how this can cause intellectual disability.

column36: Circadian Rhythms of Inflammatory Bowel Disease
column37: This project will study the circadian rhythms of Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD). Circadian rhythms are 24 hour processes driven by the circadian clock, a conserved molecular pacemaker present in all the cells of our body. Shift work, artificial lighting, weekend schedules, and travel between time zones disrupts the circadian clock. Its impact on health is an emerging field of worldwide importance. 1 in 150 Canadians currently suffers from IBD and Colorectal Cancer is the third most common and third most fatal type of cancer. Shift-workers have increased IBD, metabolic diseases, and higher rates of colorectal cancer. We will study causal relationships between circadian dysfunction and a common feature of these illnesses: the healing of the intestinal epithelium that is maintained through resident Intestinal Stem Cells. Our CIHR-funded research showed that the intestinal epithelium exhibits circadian clock-dependent rhythms in healing, and that circadian rhythm dysfunction increases colorectal cancer. We have determined that stem cells are regulated by circadian control of signaling pathways, activated during inflammation. In this new project, we will test how the circadian clock regulates inflammation and regeneration of the colon epithelium during IBD. Using laboratory mice, we will disrupt circadian rhythms to see how healing is affected during IBD. We will see how the daily timing of food can be used as a future treatment of IBD through its effect on circadian rhythms. We will use both laboratory mice, and human biopsy samples to grow artificial intestines to discover which genes in the colon are driven by circadian rhythms. The loss of circadian rhythms worsens IBD. Our study will explain how and why this occurs, and help improve diagnostics and new timed therapies to aid in this disease.

column36: Altered retinal response as a neurobiological component of the risk trajectory and of the developmental pathophysiology of major psychiatric disorders
column37: A neurodevelopmental origin is likely in schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and recurrent major depression. The pathophysiology remains mysterious mainly due to difficulties in accessing living neuronal tissue in high-risk youths. The study of the retina, by providing such an access, may provide novel insights in etiology, treatment and heterogeneity of these major disorders (Adams & Nasrallah 2018; Silverstein et al 2020). Our progress in ERG have shown that genetically high-risk children (GHRs) may present ERG anomalies (under the form of diminished rod amplitude and cone prolonged latencies) that adult patients also display (Gagne et al 2020). Our reported and pilot findings signpost that ERG may become a powerful catalyst of discovery into the early hits to the developing brain. We are among the major international groups having contributed advances in ERG anomalies as early risk endophenotypes, their longitudinal link with a deterioration of the risk trajectory in GHRs and potential predictivity to a later transition to illness. We aim to investigate further the role of retinal anomalies in the deviant early trajectory heading to schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and recurrent major depression, while taking account of other known childhood risk factors such as cognitive deficits, psychotic-like experiences and childhood trauma. Our short-term objective, in a longitudinal study of 400 GHRs aged 6 to 24 years born to an affected parent, is to test two hypotheses: 1. Longitudinal mechanisms and critical timings marked by rods and cones ERG anomalies may underlie the deterioration of the risk trajectory toward a later transition to illness. 2. Different rod and cone anomalies will have distinctive effects on the risk trajectory and may mark heterogeneity in developmental pathways heading to different outcomes. The mid- or longterm goal is to translate the obtained knowledge into decision trees for early detection and into personalized preventive interventions.

column36: A Stress Activated Znf281 Signalling Pathway Can be Therapeutically Targeted to Prevent Chemotherapy-Induced Cardiotoxicity
column37: Early cancer diagnosis and better treatment options have significantly increased the survival of cancer patients. However, the most common and severe adverse problem for these patients continues to be the development of heart failure as a direct consequence of their cancer therapy. This has resulted in the establishment of cardio-oncology programs, where the heart and tumor are investigated together, both clinically (patients are seen by a cardiologist and oncologist) and scientifically, to develop new therapies that can protect (or prevent) against chemotherapy-mediated heart failure, but also enhance chemotherapy-mediated tumor regression. We propose that several different chemotherapeutics, all of which are known to cause heart problems in cancer patients, can induce cell death (apoptosis) nonspecifically in the heart by activating one central signalling pathway, resulting in heart failure. We have evidence to suggest that these chemotherapeutics can activate a heart failure promoting protein that we identified as Znf281. Intriguingly, Znf281 can also promote tumor growth and metastasis (the spreading of the tumor to different distant organs and tissues), suggesting that inhibition of Znf281 could protect the heart, but at the same time decrease tumor growth and tumor spreading. Our team of investigators have developed the first specific and potent inhibitor of Znf281, and we have preliminary evidence that inhibition of Znf281 can prevent chemotherapy-mediated death of heart cells, but at the same time, enhance chemotherapy-mediated regression of the tumor, while also preventing its ability to spread to other tissues. This work provides a new and attractive therapy that is critically needed in the cardio-oncology field to preserve heart function, and limit tumor growth/progression.

column36: Role of neuron-glia interactions in sensori-motor integration in mastication
column37: Repetitive movements like walking, breathing and chewing insure vital functions and are produced by more primitive areas of the brain. Although these movements are executed with a high level of automaticity, as all movements, they need to be constantly adjusted to the conditions of the outside world. How would we know otherwise if we are walking on a slippery surface and need to adjust our gate? Information from the outside world reaches the brain through our senses, but little is known about the mechanisms and circuits that enable interaction between sensory inputs and motor commands. To achieve their tasks in any brain circuit, neurons need to communicate to one another using an electrical language which pattern constitutes their code for communication. A circuit that programs a repetitive movement needs to generate a rhythmic activity pattern. In this proposal, we examine how a nervous circuit in the brainstem generates the rhythmic motor command for chewing and how sensory inputs change the pattern of this command. In addition to neurons, we also consider astrocytes in the circuit that we examine. Astrocytes, another sort of cell in the brain are traditionally considered to play only a support role for neurons, but our recent findings show that they play a key role in shaping the pattern of electrical activity of neurons. Here we propose to examine how sensory information arriving to the brainstem interacts with astrocytes and modulates their behavior. This should help understand how sensory information can drive movement. Because these mechanisms are not unique to the circuit responsible for chewing, but are shared by other circuits that generate rhythmic movements, we believe that they may help devising strategies to restore movements after injuries. More importantly, we think that they may help understand what goes wrong in pathologies like Parkinson's or epilepsy, where similar mechanisms are involved and generate an uncontrolled rhythmic activity.

column36: Building evidence for adopting a new disease classification system in Canadian primary care settings: a mixed methods feasibility study
column37: The International Classification of Disease (ICD) is a global system for coding health conditions and diseases. This creates standardized, comparable information that is used by different countries worldwide for research, understanding disease trends, and making policy decisions. In Canada, the 9th version of ICD (ICD-9) is used by healthcare providers to submit billing claims to governments for payment for their clinical services. The ICD-9 system is over 40 years old and is in need of updating. ICD-9 does not fully capture the broad scope of primary care activities, types of conditions seen, and workflow. There are two new systems that may be more useful and relevant for primary care: ICD version 11 (ICD-11) and the International Classification for Primary Care version 3 (ICPC-3). Both have been recently made available with updated clinical and scientific content. In project 1, we will use pan-Canadian primary care data to explore the gaps and overlap between the old (ICD-9) and new systems (ICD-11, ICPC-3) in their coverage of common patient visits/activities in primary care. In project 2, we will ask family doctors from across Canada to test the ICD-9, ICD-11 and ICPC-3 systems by using these codes to describe a series of example patients. Next, the family doctors will be asked to complete a survey to determine what features of a new system would be preferred for use in primary care and to report their feedback, satisfaction, and preference between ICD-11 and ICPC-3, as well as any concerns with bringing in a new system. Lastly, we will hold focus group discussions with family doctors in Canada and conduct interviews with policymakers who have experience with ICD-9. These conversations will help us understand different perspectives about ICD-11 and ICPC-3 in more detail, including readiness to replace ICD-9, challenges with implementing a new system, and possible solutions.

column36: Safe and selective anti-parasite therapy targeting ribosome and glycosome function
column37: Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) due to protozoan infections are chronic, debilitating, and poverty-promoting maladies. Current treatments are failing due to spreading resistant strains, host toxicity, and incompatibility with rural health systems. Among NTDs, pathogenic trypanosomatids [T. cruzi (Chagas disease), T. brucei (HAT) and Leishmania spp.] are responsible for the most dramatic consequences. HAT is endemic in sub-Saharan Africa and leads to a chronic stage, which without treatment progresses to death. No cure exists for Chagas disease and drugs are effective for only 50% of early cases. Resistant strains of Leishmania are spreading due to a vacuum of therapeutic alternatives, with the few effective medications being compromised by parenteral administration and toxicity. The gravity of the NTD situation necessitates a new mindset to provide effective therapy. Armed with new biomedical technology, our collaboration has created novel leads and strategies for target validation to address two proposed objectives: 1) Identifying new points of therapeutic intervention with promising prototypes, we will probe primary and secondary targets, binding patterns, modes of action and mechanisms of resistance. 2) Targeting vital parasite functions, we will conceive new agents to disrupt glycosome and ribosome function. Novel therapy to treat resistant NTDs will be developed with improved potency, selectivity and drug-like properties. Our interdisciplinary team is strategically composed of international leaders in the fields of chemistry, molecular and medical parasitology, and structural biology. Highly qualified personnel will train in the identification and targeting of new points of intervention against parasites. Fueled by a track record for success, promising leads and collaborative results, our team is positioned to pioneer discovery of original tactics for controlling parasitic infection and novel therapy to relieve the socioeconomic burden of NTDs.

column36: Co-administration of Acetaminophen with Ibuprofen to Improve Duct-Related Outcomes in Extremely Premature Infants - The ACEDUCT Trial
column37: Ductus arteriosus (DA) is a blood vessel which connects the main pulmonary artery to the aorta and is a normal part of fetal circulation. In term neonates, the DA closes spontaneously within 48 hours of birth; however, it remains open in many preterm neonates, resulting in Patent DA (PDA). In extremely low gestational age neonates (ELGAN, birth weight <1.0 Kg), PDA is the most common cardiovascular complication requiring treatment. PDA in ELGANs is associated with several complications, including higher in-hospital mortality, bleeding in the brain and lungs, prolonged ventilator dependency, growth failure and gastrointestinal problems. Typically, PDA in ELGAN is treated medically first using either indomethacin or ibuprofen (IBU), the latter being the preferred agent due to its better side effect profile. However, these drugs are only successful in approximately half the patients on the first trial. Failure of medical management often necessitates surgical treatment. Complications of PDA have been shown to be directly linked to the duration of exposure, hence the need to develop strategies to improve the efficacy of medical treatment. Recently, several trials have shown acetaminophen (Tylenol) to be an equally effective agent with no side effects. Tylenol closes PDA by acting on a different receptor than IBU, raising the possibility of synergistic effect when used in combination. We have previously shown that half of the babies in whom PDA fail to close with other drugs respond to Tylenol, resulting in avoidance of the need for surgery. In this trial, our objective is to evaluate the efficacy and safety of co-administering Tylenol alongside IBU in ELGAN and comparing this to the standard practice of using IBU alone. We hypothesize that by using this combination, significantly more babies will have their PDA closed early in postnatal life and thus will be less likely to need surgery and suffer from other PDA related complications.

column36: What are the experiences and needs of informal caregivers of fracture patients in a rehabilitation setting?
column37: A fragility fracture is one that happens after a slip, trip, or fall from standing height or less (for example, slipping on ice and breaking a wrist or hip). Over 131,000 Canadians have one of these fractures every year. Patients with more serious fractures need to be admitted to a rehabilitation hospital. About 30% of patients in Canadian rehabilitation hospitals are admitted because of a fracture. Having someone at home to care for these patients when they leave the rehabilitation hospital is critical to their recovery but little is known about people who care for these fracture patients. In this two year study, we will interview 60 caregivers of patients with fragility fractures and ask them about their experiences of being a caregiver. We will interview caregivers shortly after the patient is discharged from the rehabilitation hospital and then one year later. Specifically, we will ask caregivers about the role of the family in determining who becomes the primary caregiver, how they prepare for the patient being discharged, and what their daily experiences with caring for the individual are like, including taking them to appointments. We will identify caregivers through the hospital's inpatient database, through social workers assigned to the patient, and through flyers posted at the hospital. Our research will inform the development of programs to address the needs of caregivers. For example, we might design an education program where caregivers learn how to negotiate with their families about who takes on the role of looking after the patient. Such programs will help to improve the health and wellness of caregivers who save the Canadian health care system $66.5B annually. These programs will also indirectly benefit patients who will be able to live at home for as long as possible.

column36: Proactive prescription-based fluid management vs usual care in critically ill patients on Kidney Replacement Therapy
column37: Individuals with critical illness requiring intensive care frequently develop severe acute kidney injury. Unfortunately, short-term death occurs in up to 40% of patients who develop this condition. An abrupt reduction of the ability of the kidneys to produce urine almost always results in fluid accumulation. Considerable evidence suggests that fluid accumulation may impair the function of multiple organs and lead to major complications and increase the risk of death. Kidney replacement therapy enables the removal of fluid in this setting. However, rapid fluid removal may also harm individuals when it results in significant instability. It is therefore urgent to determine what is the best strategy for these patients. This clinical trial proposes to use a proactive approach aimed to avoid fluid accumulation to effectively and safely optimize fluid removal in a critically ill patient with acute kidney injury on kidney replacement therapy. The aim of this pilot study is to enroll 125 individuals to determine whether a larger would be possible to perform. In half of the participants, fluid removal prescription will follow a pre-specified and regularly updated template while fluid removal in the other half will be prescribed according to usual care. The proactive fluid removal strategy will continue until 14 days after enrollment. Participants will be followed until 90 days to assess whether the intervention is safe, whether it is associated with important events, and to determine its impact on the use of healthcare resources. The proposed study is the first step to perform a large-scale definitive study to determine if a proactive fluid management strategy aiming at limiting fluid accumulation is able to improve chances of survival in critically ill adults with severe acute kidney injury. This question is a priority considering the high mortality rate in this population.

column36: Targeting the VPS13 family of lipid transport proteins to membrane contact sites
column37: Inside each of our cells are a number of specialized compartments called organelles that perform different tasks. These compartments are not simply floating around, but are linked together at "membrane contact sites". Contact sites have an important role in transporting nutrients, lipids and proteins from one compartment to another. When this transport is disrupted, disease can occur. Our proposed research focuses on a family of VPS13 proteins that act a bit like a firehose to rapidly transport large numbers of lipid molecules from one membrane to another. Mutations in the four different VPS13 proteins present in humans cause different neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's and autism. Evidence suggests that these human VPS13 proteins localize to different membrane contact sites which may explain why mutations in these four proteins result in distinct neurological disorders. We would like to understand how VPS13 proteins are sent to contact sites and how mutations in these proteins can change their location in cells resulting in neurodegeneration. We have found that the related yeast Vps13 protein is sent to different contact sites with the help of adaptors. These adaptors bind Vps13 at a site that is conserved in human VPS13 proteins. We have also recently discovered new proteins that resemble VPS13 and may transport lipids in a similar manner. Our research will identify the proteins needed for VPS13 recruitment and function at different contact sites in yeast and human cells, and clarify the role of the new VPS13-like protein at contact sites. Understanding how VPS13 proteins are localized within the cell will give us a better understanding of the disease mechanisms associated with each disorder and give us insights into potential therapeutic interventions.

column36: A BEhavioural WEight Loss Intervention delivered in Cardiac Rehabilitation for patients with Atrial Fibrillation and obesity: The BeWEL IN CR-AF Study
column37: One-in-four Canadians will be diagnosed with an abnormal heart rhythm called atrial fibrillation (AF) in their lifetime. People with AF have an increased chance of having serious medical problems like stroke and heart failure. Nearly three-quarters of people with AF also have obesity (excess body weight). According to research, people with obesity that lose approximately 10% of their body weight can experience relief from uncomfortable AF symptoms. Losing weight may even help people return to a normal heart rhythm. Cardiac rehabilitation (CR) is a proven way to help people with heart disease live longer, healthier lives. So far, research has not shown whether CR helps improve the abnormal heart rhythms seen in AF. This may be because CR programs usually do not offer specific help with weight management. Therefore, adding behavioural weight-loss treatment (BWLT; group classes to change thoughts and behaviours to encourage weight-loss) to CR programs may help people with AF and obesity experience relief from their symptoms. This study will test whether people who receive BWLT during CR can lose weight and improve their AF symptoms. People who have AF and obesity will take either traditional CR, or CR with added BWLT. Traditional CR consists of participating in exercise sessions, supervised by health professionals, twice per week for 12 weeks. In addition to exercising, people in the BWLT group will complete 12 online group therapy classes to learn strategies from psychology to help them lose weight. After one year, we will compare the two groups to see if people who had BWLT lost more weight and had greater improvement in AF symptoms compared to the traditional CR group. We believe this research will help efforts to provide effective treatment to patients with AF to help them lose weight and reduce or eliminate AF symptoms.

column36: Metabolic manipulation of hypoxia for improved radiotherapy response
column37: Despite over a hundred years of research there is still no Health Canada/FDA approved drug that can be taken at the time of radiotherapy to improve treatment outcome without increasing side effects in non-cancer tissues. Radiotherapy improvements have largely been realized through technology advances with greater precision and normal tissue sparing, however further gains are becoming increasingly difficult to obtain. The obvious alternate approach to overcoming this plateau is through the development of drugs that are able to selectively increase tumour sensitivity to radiotherapy. We are developing a novel, non-toxic drug that is targeted to a broad range of cancers when combined with radiotherapy. The main premise behind its strategy is that radiation is most effective when it combines with oxygen to make damage more permanent. An important reason cancers are resistant to radiation is that they contain a subset of cells at a relatively low concentration of oxygen. These hypoxic cells are key to tumour regrowth after radiation and are extremely rare in normal tissues. Our drug is designed to only become active under hypoxia, making it selective to cancer tissues. Once activated the drug acts to prevent cells from using oxygen, thereby allowing oxygen to build up and be available to sensitize cancer cells to radiation damage. The project will progress development of this new class of novel compounds to achieve efficient and selective synergy with radiotherapy, and possibly with another class of novel anti-cancer metabolism inhibitors. Because half of cancer patients are treated with radiation the impact of even a modest improvement in response would be significant. Indeed, since the scope of the radiotherapy patient population is now global the potential for improvement of quality of life and increasing cancer cure rates could not be greater.

column36: Impact of myelin changes on behavioural recovery after mild traumatic brain injury
column37: Mild traumatic brain injury (sometimes referred to as concussion) can cause long-lasting effects including difficulty concentrating. There are no effective treatments available for these long-term effects and we don't know what exactly causes them. The brain's white matter tracts are the cables that connect different brain regions and the two main parts of white matter are the connections themselves (axons) and the insulation that wraps and supports them (myelin sheaths). White matter is known to be damaged by traumatic brain injury, however, the contribution of axon versus myelin damage to lasting impairments is not clear. Myelin-producing cells can regenerate in the brain to repair damaged myelin and this process might contribute to recovery from mild traumatic brain injury. This project will determine whether the production of new myelin is important for recovery from mild traumatic brain injury. Using a mouse model of mild traumatic brain injury, we will use advanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) that is sensitive to myelin to evaluate how damage evolves over time. We will also examine the brains of these mice with electron microscopy, which will let us see the structure of myelin. By using drugs, genetic and environmental methods to block and enhance the generation of new myelin-producing cells, we will describe the specific contribution of new myelin to recovery from mild traumatic brain injury. This information could help doctors make decisions about patient care and contribute to the development of treatments for the approximately 250,000 Canadians who suffer from a mild traumatic brain injury each year.

column36: eNOS regulates endothelial cell polarity and angiogenic sprouting in vascular pathologies
column37: Endothelial cells (ECs) are intimately involved in angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels from preexisting ones. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is the most potent angiogenic factor and its administration has been shown to increase the development of new vessels in ischemic tissues and to be essential for the formation of blood vessels inside cancerous tumors. A better understanding of the angiogenic process and of the intracellular signaling molecules involved in its regulation could allow for the development of new therapeutic approaches to favor the formation of new blood vessels in ischemic tissues or, inversely, interfere with aberrant vessel growth in the retina or in tumors. An essential event for the induction of angiogenesis is the increase in permeability of the vasculature to blood macromolecules. The opening of intercellular contacts between ECs initiates the angiogenic process and detachment of ECs allows them to migrate to form a vascular network in an area deprived of oxygen. The overall objective of our research program is to understand intracellular signaling events in ECs that control vascular development and angiogenesis. We will investigate if polarization of ECs is modified by nitric oxide, which would affect angiogenesis. First, we will define if the release of nitric oxide (NO) controls the migration of cells. We will also determine if NO acts directly on a protein localized at cell-cell contact points, beta-catenin, to alter its function. Finally, we will determine the role of NO in a mouse model of vascular retinopathy. A better understanding of the molecular events that control angiogenesis will help in the development of novel therapeutic approaches where the formation of new vessels is central to disease progression such as in ischemic tissues and vascular retinopathies.

column36: Novel therapies for diaphragm failure in muscular dystrophy
column37: Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), the most common genetic muscle disease, is lethal with no cure at this point in time. Most patients succumb to respiratory failure, which is caused by gradual destruction of the diaphragm, the main breathing muscle. The muscle pathology in DMD is characterized by chronic inflammation with a prominent invasion by immune cells known as macrophages. Previous studies performed by our lab and others demonstrate that reducing certain types of inflammatory macrophages can improve diaphragm muscle function. We believe that modulating inflammation can also improve the local tissue environment in a way that will permit more effective gene therapy for the disease. Therefore, our proposal seeks to identify strategies for therapeutically manipulating macrophage function in the DMD diaphragm using a pre-clinical mouse model of the disease which shares the same genetic defect as human patients. Clinically, these therapies could offer an exciting new avenue for ameliorating respiratory outcomes in patients suffering from DMD as well as other forms of muscular dystrophy.

column36: Healthy Food Rx - Empowering food insecure Albertans to manage their diabetes through a subsidized healthy food prescription program: A randomized controlled trial & economic evaluation
column37: Background: Individuals who have diabetes have high blood sugar levels. When patients with diabetes' sugars remain high, they are at risk of heart attacks, kidney failure, amputations, and blindness. An important part of lowering blood sugars is following a healthy diet that includes whole grains, fruits, vegetables, fish, and whole grains. Unfortunately, these foods are often more expensive than more highly processed unhealthy foods. Many Canadians are unable to afford to eat healthy foods, a condition known as food insecurity. In patients with diabetes, food insecurity often results in high blood sugars. Healthcare providers have very few options to help address food insecurity in their patients with diabetes. Healthy food subsidies, prescribed by doctors, may be a new solution. Goals: We will study whether those who receive a subsidized healthy food prescription have lower blood sugar levels compared to those who don't receive the subsidy. We will also study how receiving food subsidies may affect patient health and health care costs in the longer-term. Methods: A total of 800 adults (>18 years) with type 2 diabetes, high blood sugars, and food insecurity will be randomized to either receive either: (A) a healthy food prescription; or (B) a healthy food prescription and a 12-month healthy food subsidy of $1.50/day/household member (~$170/month for a household of 4), which can be used to buy healthy foods. We will assess differences between the two groups in blood sugars, blood pressure, cholesterol, body mass index, diet quality and food insecurity. We will also estimate the long-term effects of the food subsidies on patients' health and health care costs. Expected results: This research will help us to understand if healthy food prescription programs should be offered more broadly to help patients with diabetes and food insecurity.

column36: Structure and Function of ABCG5/G8: a Sterol Transporter Implicated in Hypercholesterolemia and Atherosclerosis
column37: The major goal of this study is to understand why rising level of cholesterol in our bodies causes cardiovascular diseases, the number one leading cause of deaths around the world. This phenomenon is called hypercholesterolemia, which causes abnormally high levels of cholesterol in the blood. Individuals with this symptom are more likely to develop fatty plaques on the blood vessels, a disease called atherosclerosis and a major cause of stroke and heart attack. Our research will investigate how cholesterol and other lipids are moved in and out of cells by protein machineries in cell membranes, a key element to understanding how lipids accumulate in the body. Specifically, this research proposal will focus on a group of lipid trafficking proteins called ABC transporters, which use ATP (the primary energy currency in all living beings) and eliminate cholesterol and lipids from building-up in our bodies. Without these pumps, cholesterol and lipids can build up, leading to atherosclerosis, stroke, obesity, and dementia. With our research, we will learn how this type of protein move lipids out of the cell by building molecular models and analyzing the molecular details underlying their lipid- pumping function. These models will enable logical design of next-generation drugs, which will better control cholesterol to treat hypercholesterolemia and its related cardiovascular diseases. By pinpointing the interactions between these proteins and their working partners, cholesterol transport activity can serve as a new biomarker to allow a better and more precise diagnosis for affected patients.
