column36: Myocardial regeneration in a pre-clinical model of type 2 diabetes
column37: Diabetes is a disease where blood sugar is elevated over an extended period of time. Patients with diabetes are at a higher risk of suffering a heart attack which is a consequence of the blockage of heart blood vessels. This causes the death of heart muscle cells and small blood vessels and leads to scar formation that interferes with normal heart function and causes heart failure. The heart muscle cells cannot self-regenerate and one of the possible treatments for regeneration of the heart muscle is the transplantation of heart muscle cells obtained from the patient's own stem cells. Although many heart attack patients have diabetes, no studies have been done to evaluate treatment with stem cells in diabetic animals - which we propose to study here. We will test if treating patients with stem cells and small vessels obtained from adipose tissue will improve the survival of transplanted stem cells and improve heart function. Our work shows that it is possible to regenerate the heart in healthy rats that were surgically submitted to heart attack by also transplanting ready-made vessels. These ready-made vessels obtained from fat tissue re-establish the blood flow and promote the delivery of nutrients and oxygen to the muscle cells. However, for these therapies to work in the clinical setting, it is important to study them in more complex disease models as patients that have heart attacks usually have other health issues that likely caused or contributed to the heart attack in the first place. We propose to test if our strategy of co-implanting vessels with heart muscle cells from stem cells in diabetic animals that were surgically submitted to heart attack regenerates diabetic hearts. We will investigate how this will improve the survival of transplanted cells and the heart's ability to pump blood efficiently. This may provide new treatments for heart disease and improve the quality of life of patients suffering from heart attack and heart failure in the future.

column36: Microstructural MRI in Temporal Lobe Epilepsy
column37: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is a common and serious condition that results in debilitating and frequent seizures that are usually resistant to medication. Surgery can reduce or eliminate seizures if the location in the brain that is responsible for them - the seizure "focus" - can be determined. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) allows a non-invasive inspection of brain tissue and is used to help determine this location. But, one-in-three TLE patients' MRI scans look normal and only half of the patients that undergo surgery no longer have seizures. The ability to better detect the seizure focus non-invasively with MRI would greatly improve surgical planning and patient outcomes. We have recently developed MRI methods that are able to accurately characterize the density of axons, or "wiring", within the brain. This approach holds strong potential to non-invasively detect TLE tissue damage because it is known from dissections that the wiring is degraded in TLE. In this project, we will first improve the ability of this method to measure the small brain regions that are known to be affected in TLE. Then, we will perform MRI scanning using this new approach in TLE patients and compare the results to healthy subjects to determine if it can detect brain wiring changes that are invisible using normal MRI. Finally, we will examine the tissue removed from patients who have undergone surgery to verify that our approach is indeed measuring changes in axon density. This project will develop and validate a new non-invasive marker of tissue damage in TLE, which will open the door for improved diagnosis and better surgical outcomes. Beyond TLE, this project will lay the groundwork for the non-invasive investigation of brain wiring changes that are suspected to occur in many other neurological conditions.

column36: The amyloid precursor protein intracellular domain is an effector molecule of metaplasticity - implications for the regulation of synaptic plasticity in Alzheimer disease.
column37: Nerve cells communicate with each other via synapses: a specialized junction that passes nerve impulses from one neuron to the next. Changing the strength of synaptic communication is called synaptic plasticity and is our best model for the cellular processes underlying learning and memory. Two forms of synaptic plasticity have attracted special attention in the context of learning and memory: long-term potentiation (LTP), which will increase synaptic transmission and long-term depression (LTD), which will decrease synaptic transmission. Many neurological disorders that affect memory formation show altered synaptic plasticity in the hippocampus. Among these disorders is Alzheimer disease (AD), a progressive neurodegenerative disorder and the most common form of dementia in the elderly. While amyloid-beta (A-beta) and tau have been traditionally implicated in causing AD, recent studies suggest that other factors, such as the intracellular domain of the amyloid precursor protein (APP-ICD), can also play a role in the development of AD. However, the underlying mechanisms leading to the changes in synaptic plasticity in AD and especially the role of APP-ICD are poorly understood. In our basic research approach, we will analyze whether the expression of APP-ICD affects synaptic plasticity. We will use different mouse models expressing different mutations in APP-ICD and analyze changes in synaptic transmission and synaptic plasticity by employing whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology. Since APP-ICD and A-beta are both products of APP proteolysis, we will analyze whether their effects on synaptic depression is linked. Finally, we will shed light onto the intracellular pathway activated by APP-ICD leading to changes in synaptic plasticity. The outcome of our project will further elucidate the mechanisms underlying the development of synaptic depression in Alzheimer disease and provide targets for future Alzheimer disease treatments.

column36: Balancing inhibitory interneuron number and connectivity in the developing neocortex.
column37: Brain function and mental abilities arise from a balance of excitatory and inhibitory (E/I) nerve cells that generate patterns of neural activities. Inhibitory nerve cells play a special role in this balance because they dampen the electrical activities of other nerve cells and coordinate their activities into networks. If there is too little inhibition in brain circuits - due to deficits in inhibitory nerve cells, connections, or their functions - the neural activity patterns will be disrupted by E/I imbalances and in turn, affect brain actions. Importantly, deficits in inhibitory nerve cells are now regarded as a major factor underlying neurodevelopmental disorders such as epilepsies, autism, and schizophrenia. Although we are beginning to understand the consequences of reduced inhibition in the adult brain, we know little of the root causes in the developing brain. Our lab discovered a molecular pathway that regulates the development and final numbers of inhibitory cells during brain development. In the absence of these molecules, called the clustered Protocadherins, our animal models have too few inhibitory nerve cells and develop severe neurological issues such as epilepsy and anxiety. This research will investigate the mechanism by which this family of molecules regulates the number of inhibitory nerve cells that survive and wire up into inhibitory networks. We will apply our innovative suite of transgenic, molecular, and neuroscience tools to investigate how these Protocadherin molecules serve to connect inhibitory nerve cells for optimal circuit function. This research will provide a new understanding of how inhibition is wired in the developing brain. We will use this knowledge to better understand how E/I imbalance causes neurodevelopmental disorders and identify therapeutic strategies to restore this balance for optimal brain function.

column36: Helping people adhere to their varenicline treatment by co-creating a conversational agent: A feasibility study
column37: Varenicline is a prescription medication that helps people quit smoking tobacco. When taken as prescribed, it is the most effective smoking cessation medication available in Canada. However, many people do not adhere to the 12-week regimen, and this decreases their chances of successfully quitting smoking. Several studies have shown that people are more likely to take varenicline as prescribed if they are given information on how to take the medication, what to expect from taking the medication, and are given strategies to reduce side effect (e.g., nausea). Providing these supports though phone and text messages has proven to be successful, but is expensive. For this project we will develop a chatbot (a software application that can simulate a conversation with a user through messaging applications, websites and mobile applications) based on what researchers have found works and what people who have used varenicline think should be included. Once the chatbot is built, 40 people who want to quit smoking will be invited to use the chatbot. Participants will receive varenicline for 12 weeks, the usual instructions on how to take it from their health care provider, and the support of a chatbot. After 12 weeks we will examine how many people took their medication as prescribed and how many people quit smoking. We will also examine how often participants used the chatbot and what participants liked and disliked about the chatbot. The information from this study will help decide: 1) whether the chatbot is a promising solution to help people adhere to their medication regimen; 2) what improvements are needed, and 3) if a larger study is needed to test if the chatbot helps people adhere to their medication more than treatment as usual.

column36: Maternal serum Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF): Study of a promising biomarker of maternal psychological stress during pregnancy
column37: Maternal stress in pregnancy has many potential negative consequences for the mother and her child. Among the consequences, maternal psychological stress affects birthweight, the occurrence of preeclampsia, reduces gestational duration and augments the risk of postpartum depression. Birthweight, in itself, is a major predictor of the newborn short and long-term health. We have previously shown that maternal prenatal stress is associated with birthweight in a sex-specific manner, being decreased in in girls and increased in boys. Among diverse biological alterations associated with maternal stress, neutrophins, in particular brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), were observed to be in lower concentration in the blood of stressed pregnant women. It is hypothesized that altered intrauterine levels of BDNF may lead to abnormal foetal growth and brain neurodevelopment, which have implications for cognitive parameters such as memory, spatial learning, mood and anxiety. BDNF is thought to regulate the development of the placenta and of the foetus brain. Studies have confirmed abnormally low blood BDNF levels in depressed pregnant women. A better understanding of the pathophysiological consequences of maternal stress through the measurement in maternal blood of recognized factors considered to play a role may lead to the identification of biological markers of the intensity of stress, offering the possibility to better therapeutic interventions. BDNF may be such a candidate marker worth investigating. Longitudinal studies on BDNF changes across gestation are limited. Taking advantage of our already constituted database and biobank of almost 8000 pregnant participants and their neonates, we will study the levels of BDNF in maternal blood and in cord serum. We will relate the results to the degree of maternal stress and birthweight. This will help to better understand the effect of maternal stress and to improve personalized therapeutic approaches.

column36: Targeting the Protease Activated Receptor (PAR) - Transient Receptor Potential Vanilloid-4 (TRPV4) signalling axis in osteoarthritis.
column37: Osteoarthritis is a chronic disease of the joints with no available disease modifying treatments. The changes that happen when a knee joint goes from being healthy to arthritic are not completely understood but an increase in a group of proteins called 'enzymes', that can cut other proteins is noted. In addition to destroying the tissue in the knee, these enzymes can also cause inflammation and pain by turning on a family of proteins called PARs. In this proposal we wish to specifically characterize the enzymes that are present in the knee joints of human osteoarthritis patients that can turn on the PARs. This will allow us to develop strategies for preventing the PARs from turning on and this in turn will suppress the inflammation and pain that make osteoarthritis a chronic and debilitating disease. We have assembled a team of physicians, surgeons and scientists to tackle this exciting project. We have also developed unique biosensors and transgenic mice that will allow us to successfully complete this work. Our studies are guided by preliminary findings in human patients, with studies at the cell and molecular level and in pre-clinical animal models helping us to identify the best strategies for treatment that can then be tested further in the clinic.

column36: Determinants and consequences of child marriage in Canada and the United States
column37: Child marriage, defined by the United Nations (UN) as marriage before the age of 18, is a violation of human rights that affects 650 million girls and women worldwide. Girls are ten times more likely to marry as children than boys, and these marriages make it more likely that they will experience domestic violence, contract sexually transmitted infections, and have poor reproductive health. The UN calls for the elimination of child marriage across the globe by the year 2030. However, child marriage is legal and ongoing in Canada and the U.S., despite efforts by both countries to end the practice abroad. Almost nothing is known about child marriage in Canada or the U.S. because nearly all research on this issue has focused on Africa and South Asia. Our team recently documented how often child marriage happens in these two countries. More than 3,600 Canadian children were granted marriage certificates between 2000-18. In the U.S., more than 78,000 children were married between 2010-14. This research was a crucial first step, but more information is necessary. Public health practitioners in both countries need evidence on the drivers of child marriage to identify effective ways to intervene to prevent it. Clinicians need information on the unique health risks faced by married children so they can mitigate its harms among this vulnerable population. Law makers need evidence on the drivers and harms of child marriage to make informed legislative decisions. Our research will meet these needs by producing entirely new information on the motivations for and health consequences of child marriage in Canada and the U.S. We will investigate whether premarital teen pregnancy leads to child marriage and whether inconsistencies between laws that govern age at marriage and age for sexual consent create perverse incentives for child marriage. We will also measure the impact of child marriage on the risk of mental health disorders and teen childbearing.

column36: Host cell-derived tissue factor as a broad-spectrum basis for viral pathology and infection
column37: Well-balanced blood clotting is essential for health and has life-threatening impact when tipped off-balance. Many viruses are known to trigger an infected person's blood clotting system and cause a wide range of clotting-related clinical problems; from heart disease to bleeding. The processes used by the virus to cause these diseases are poorly understood. Using the oral herpes virus (HSV1) as a model virus, our lab has shown that these germs hijack clotting activators to increase infection. To understand how, the current proposal focuses on our discovery that a protein called, tissue factor, is integrated into the virus' surface. Tissue factor is found within our cell membranes and is essential for life. Many viruses are covered with a membrane, called an envelope, which is acquired from our infected cells and can therefore contain tissue factor. Why is tissue factor important? Because it is the initiator of blood clotting and it also alters the function of cells. Here we propose to expand our findings in HSV1 and extend our knowledge to HIV and dengue virus, both major global problems. We will take biochemical and animal approaches to test our ideas, which have already revealed possible strategies to treat these virus infections. In addition to these viruses, many others that burden healthcare systems world-wide have an envelope, such as influenza, Ebola, hepatitis C and Zika viruses. The five virus types we have investigated to date all have tissue factor, suggesting that any virus with an envelope can acquire tissue factor. Since cells containing tissue factor are found throughout the body and are infected by many types of virus, we anticipate that targeting tissue factor found on the surface of viruses will allow us to treat a wide-range of viral infections and fill a serious deficiency in global healthcare.

column36: Mobilizing Communities: Enhancing partnerships between schools and youth hubs for mental health and well-being
column37: The growing mental health (MH) crisis has only worsened since COVID and the fall-out from this is expected to be felt for years to come resulting in a sustained negative impact on MH. Despite this, MH supports and services are significantly lacking; timely access to care is ladened with barriers to services especially for young people, including those from Black, Indigenous and People of Colour (BIPOC) communities who have faced deepened inequities as a result of the pandemic. Hence, we need earlier innovative approaches to MH service delivery, before young people reach the crisis point. Mobilization between schools and community MH (i.e., youth hubs) supports has an important role in a stepped care approach and is vital to improving timely access to care, to reducing inequities and to improving overall MH of young people. The goal of this youth-centered study is to implement and evaluate a community-based MH program using an evidence-based effective stepped approach for young people that involves mobilizing partnerships between schools and youth hubs. This study involves the partnership with a well-established Manitoba (MB) youth hub (NorWest) and an urban school division (Seven Oaks School Division - SOSD). Youth attending SOSD highschools and key stakeholders (e.g., teachers, clinicians, counsellors) will be invited to take part in the study. Multiple data collection methods (e.g., individual and focus group interviews, arts-based methods) will be used, guided by principles of equity, collaboration and partnership. Short-term, this study will yield information on whether the community-based MH program shows promise as an acceptable, appropriate and effective program in promoting MH and well-being for young people. Long-term, the findings will inform the next steps in the research program including adapting and implementing the community-based MH program with additional school-youth hub partnerships across MB and could be applied to youth hubs across Canada.

column36: Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
column37: The Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA) is Canada's first, population-based, comprehensive, national, sustainably funded research platform. The CLSA includes 51,338 participants, aged 45-85 at enrolment (2011-2015) who are being followed every three years until 2033 with a goal of providing important information on the health and well-being of Canadians as they age. The first follow-up was completed in 2018 and the second follow-up will be completed in 2021. From the time the first data were available to researchers in 2015, more than 340 research teams in Canada and around the world have requested these valuable data generating more than 150 peer-reviewed publications. In the next two follow-ups of data collection, additional information will be collected in several areas including sexual health, how people experience health care services and changes in mobility and vision. The CLSA team has developed modified methods of data collection to accommodate challenges that participants may face in physical health, mobility, and cognitive health to allow them to participate if they wish to continue in the study.

column36: Pyroptosis in the CNS: Molecular mechanisms & therapeutic targets in progressive MS
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a common and progressive disease characterized by physical and mental disabilities at the peak of life. MS can lead to inability to work, chronic pain, social isolation and shorter lifespan. Canada, especially Alberta, has among the highest rates of MS in the world. MS affects 3 times as many women as men. The cause of MS is unknown, although both environmental and genetic factors have been connected to MS. Our overarching goal is to understand the fundamental disease processes that drive the progression of MS. With that understanding, we can develop new ways to diagnose and treat MS. The knowledge that we gain from these studies can also be applied to other progressive brain diseases such as stroke, Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Lou Gehrig's diseases. MS is defined by progressive loss of the insulating material (myelin) around the electricity-conducting structures (axons) in our brain and spinal cord. The eventual result is that the axons die, like cutting a wire that carries electricity. This destructive process is driven by inflammation in the brain and spinal cord. That inflammation reflects the immune system's rogue attack on the body during MS. Our group is working to understand why the axons and the myelin-producing cells die in people with MS. To identify the mechanisms of MS, we will examine tissues from the brains and spinal cords of people who had MS. We will use cells grown in the lab and animal models to check these processes and discover new treatments. We will examine specific genes and factors in the environment that dictate a distinct type of cell death in MS called pyroptosis or 'fiery death.' We can apply our team's broad expertise in MS using novel research resources: archived human brain tissues, unique lab samples of human brain cells, brain-imaging devices, and artificial intelligence tools.

column36: The Genetics Update: Designing and evaluating a patient platform to deliver updated genomic results
column37: BACKGROUND: The evidence that supports the role that genes and genetic variants play in causing diseases changes constantly. Patients may have their genetic results reanalyzed in light of new evidence, which can change the meaning of a test result. These updates can trigger changes to patients' care and can also provide clarity to previous uncertain results. Medical guidelines recommend recontacting patients, at minimum, if updated results impact their care. GAPS: Canadian providers are not resourced to routinely reanalyze genetic test results and recontact patients to provide updated results. Innovative tools to support recontact are needed. AIMS: 1) Develop a patient platform to return updated genetic test results. 2) Evaluate the effectiveness of the patient platform compared to usual care. METHODS Aim 1: Develop a patient platform to recontact patients with updated genetic test results. We will develop the patient platform in 3 phases: First, we will determine design requirements and content needs among diverse groups of end-users (patients, healthcare providers, laboratory scientists). Next, we will co-design the tool with end-users. Finally we will test the patient platform to understand and improve its functions and content. Aim 2: We will conduct a trial that will compare the impact of patients receiving updated genetic results using the patient platform vs. usual care (updates via genetic counselors). Our participants will be adult cancer patients who have received genomic sequencing and whose results will be reanalyzed. Outcomes include patient distress, knowledge, activation, quality of life, risk perception, adherence, wait and consult times. EXPECTED IMPACT: To our knowledge, this will be the first study to develop and test a patient platform for recontacting patients with updated genetic test results.

column36: Effectiveness of patient decision aids and their elements for achieving quality health decisions: systematic review with network meta-analysis to inform and update the international standards
column37: Since 2000 our research team has created and tested decision aids and developed international standards. Decision aids are knowledge translation (KT) tools to help people make informed decisions that reflect what matters most to them. Decision aids (leaflets, videos, online tools) focus on a specific decision, provide information on options (benefits/harms), and help patients clarify what is most important to them. Our systematic review of 105 randomized trials showed decision aids compared to usual care improve knowledge, reduce decisional conflict, and increase patient involvement in decision making. But little is known about the effect of elements included in decision aids (e.g., patient stories, exercises to clarify values). There are over 100 new randomized trials that need to be added to update our last systematic review in 2017. We propose to study how well decision aids work compared to usual care and what elements of decision aids are most effective. These findings will be used to update the international standards and reach consensus on changes. We will conduct the study using an integrated KT approach with researchers and knowledge users on our international team. Knowledge users include patients, clinicians, and policy makers. We will use a systematic review of randomized trials and consensus methods to report on criteria to improve the quality of decision aids and avoid biased decisions. We will also evaluate the experience of team members with the integrated KT approach. Our output will report evidence on the effect of decision aids for people who are facing health decisions, how well each element within decision aids works, and consensus on updated standards. We will report the findings to researchers and knowledge users in Canada and internationally to inform health care services and health policies. Our study fits with CIHR's strategic plan priority: integrating evidence in health decisions by advancing the science of knowledge mobilization.

column36: Personalizing the choice of therapy in rheumatoid arthritis
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune form of arthritis that can affect adults of any age. People living with rheumatoid arthritis experience pain and swelling in their joints, fatigue, and difficulty functioning. Medications, called disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) are used to control the joint inflammation. Multiple medication options are available now and have dramatically improved outcomes over the past 10-20 years. Which treatment is 'best' for a patient should be based on the best available evidence and patient preferences. In this study we will develop a personalized decision tool to help patients choose between these options. We will start by analyzing data from all the randomized trials conducted to date, including individual patient data, where available. We will then analyze data from over 10,000 patients in Canada treated in routine practice. From these 2 analyses will generate a risk calculator, that will allow us to estimate treatment benefits and risks, tailored to each patient. These decision tools will be linked to guidelines and incorporated into an implementation plan to promote their use in clinical practice. The ultimate goal of this work is to promote a more 'personalized' choice of treatment for people with rheumatoid arthritis, by including both their clinical (disease) characteristics, as well as their preferences.

column36: Examining Executive Function and Behavioural Difficulties in Children of Mothers with Type 1 Diabetes (CONCEPTT Kids)
column37: Women with diabetes in pregnancy continue to have poor pregnancy outcomes. The most common complications are large babies, babies that are born early, and babies admitted to neonatal care, often with low blood sugars. Mothers' blood sugars during pregnancy may also affect the long-term health of their children, with some studies suggesting childhood learning difficulties and behaviour problems. Continuous Glucose Monitoring (also called CGM) gives detailed information about mothers' and babies' exposure to high and low blood sugars during pregnancy. CONCEPTT was a trial of CGM use in pregnant people with diabetes. It found that CGM use halved the risk of newborn complications including rates of overweight babies, neonatal care admissions and babies with low blood sugar levels. However, we do not know if better blood sugars during pregnancy and/or fewer pregnancy complications will result in improved learning and behaviour in children of women with diabetes. Objective of research: This study will examine the relationship between mothers' blood sugars during pregnancy and childhood learning and behaviour challenges. Methods: Women in the CONCEPTT trial will be invited to have their children participate in this study. Parents will complete questionnaires online that ask about their child's learning and behaviour. These will be related to mother's blood sugars during pregnancy and to newborn complications. Impact of research: Managing blood sugars is demanding, particularly during pregnancy. This research would allow us to identify blood sugar patterns in pregnancy that could be harmful for children and facilitate the development of strategies to avoid these sugar patterns. It could also help in the early identification of children for whom timely intervention has been shown to help children improve skills such as problem solving and memory.

column37: The placenta is essential to pregnancy as it transports nutrients and oxygen to the fetus in the womb. The placenta also performs other essential functions, such as helping the mother's immune system to accept the pregnancy. We propose to identify how these small RNAs help pregnancy by aiding in placenta growth and function as well as in the mother by stopping her immune system from attacking the pregnancy as foreign.

column36: Exploiting brain-body crosstalk to correct brain lipid metabolism in Alzheimer's disease
column37: The past decade has seen both frustration and hope in the field of Alzheimer disease research. Failures of dozens of drug-based clinical trials have highlighted that there are major gaps in our basic understanding of how this disease develops. In contrast, exciting lifestyle-based interventions such as diet and exercise can be effective in helping to combat cognitive decline. Indeed, it is estimated that as much as 40% of the risk for developing Alzheimer's and other dementias can be attributed to lifestyle factors. What this illustrates is that the body can play a pivotal role in determining whether the brain is affected by Alzheimer's disease. In this project, we focus on defects that we have recently identified in how the Alzheimer brain processes lipids (fats). We will attempt to manipulate the communication between brain and body in a way that can correct these defects in brain lipid processing. Since our past experiments have shown that correcting brain lipid processing can reverse learning and memory loss in an animal model of Alzheimer's, we hope these studies will lead to new, clinically relevant strategies for treating this disease.

column36: Optimizing Imaging for Medium Vessel Occlusion Stroke (ESCAPE-OPTIMUS)
column37: Acute ischemic stroke is due to a blockage of blood flow to the brain with often devastating outcomes. With our 2015 ESCAPE study, we helped to establish mechanical clot removal as a safe and effective treatment for patients with an obstruction of a major blood vessel, thereby greatly improving the lives of stroke patients. In that study, visualization of blood vessels was performed using an innovative imaging technique that we have invented and validated. With our improved understanding of acute ischemic stroke, and recent advances in technology, we want to further broaden acute stroke imaging and treatment, to better identify and treat interrupted blood flow of not only large, but also smaller vessels, thereby helping a greater number of stroke patients. To this end, we have initiated a large CIHR-funded study, ESCAPE-MeVO. This is a multinational undertaking with participating sites in Canada, the US and Europe. In the setting of acute stroke where time is the critical factor, it is crucial to have quick, easy to use, and validated imaging tools that allow for the detection of even small vessel occlusions, and selection of patients for mechanical clot removal. Through innovative research, we have developed and validated new imaging methods to improve visualization of these smaller obstructions and their effect on the surrounding brain tissue. The ESCAPE-MeVO study provides a unique opportunity to test and utilize these imaging improvements, which we aim to do in the proposed study, ESCAPE-OPTIMUS. It has the following goals: A) easy and automated detection of smaller-vessel blockages; and B) evaluation of their effect on the brain tissue. If successful, ESCAPE-OPTIMUS will provide physicians around the world with an imaging tool that allows them to easily and quickly detect small vessel occlusions, and helps to determine whether mechanical clot removal is effective these strokes due to small vessel blockages, thereby globally improving stroke patient outcomes.

column36: Self reactivity as a driver of extranodal diffuse large B-cell lymphoma transformation and progression.
column37: Lymphoma is a form of cancer that affects immune cells called lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell. There are many subtypes and maturation stages of lymphocytes and, therefore, many kinds of lymphomas. Diffuse large B-cell lymphomas (DLBCL), the most common type of non-Hodgkin lymphomas, develop from mature B lymphocytes (B-cells) and primarily grow in the lymph nodes. The majority of DLBCL tumors respond to standard therapies, especially if administered in the early stages of the disease. However, one third of patients develop an extranodal form of the disease ("EDLBCL"), where malignant cells spread throughout the body and invade vital organs such as the kidneys, lungs, and brain, significantly reducing chances of survival. There are currently no EDLBCL-specific treatments, and our ability to predict which tumors will disseminate is fairly limited, partly due to a poor understanding of how and when EDLBCL originate. Under normal circumstances, B-cells only expand if and when they encounter external foes, and promptly retract once these are cleared by the immune system. A central unresolved question is then which factors initially drive and further sustain the relentless activation and expansion of B-cells in EDBCL. Based on clinical observations and recent tumor sequencing efforts, we here propose that EDLBCL closely resemble autoimmune disorders, a collection of diseases in which B-cells misidentify natural components of our bodies as threats, leading them to aberrantly activate, infiltrate and attack different organs. We will take advantage of the current extensive knowledge of autoimmune disorders to identify shared players and mechanisms, in an effort to understand how B-cells become cancerous, disseminate, and expand. Our work holds great potential to guide the early identification of patients at high risk of developing EDLBCL and to reveal critical tumor requirements to be harnessed as novel disease-specific therapeutic targets.

column36: STRIVE before surgery trial: a vanguard pragmatic multicenter randomized trial of Structured TRaining to Improve fitness in a Virtual Environment before surgery
column37: More than 1,000,000 Canadians have surgery each year. While most have good outcomes, more than 1 in 5 have complications and/or develop troubles with day-to-day activities after surgery. Patients and their clinicians have asked that new ways to prepare patients for surgery be developed to help patients avoid these poor outcomes. Because surgery causes stress on the body like that caused by hard exercise (like running a long distance), many believe that training before surgery by doing exercises and eating healthy food could lead to better outcomes. This type of training before surgery is called 'prehabilitation'. Our team, which includes patients, scientists, doctors, nurses, nutrition and exercise experts, and health system leaders, has reviewed the available science on prehabilitation. We've found that prehabilitation may: 1) lead to fewer complications, 2) help patients have better recovery, and 3) may lead to shorter stays in hospital. Unfortunately, the studies that have been done don't line up with how prehabilitation would be done in the real world. This means that we don't know if prehabilitation will work for most surgical patients, despite the promise shown in specialized studies. With the experience of COVID-19, we've learned that programs like prehabilitation need to be provided in a way that they can be done at home with technological support. In fact, at home prehabilitation with virtual coaching is likely the most realistic way to let Canadian surgical patients do prehabilitation. Virtually-supported prehabilitation has not been widely studied, but needs to be. The next step is to test whether at home, virtually supported prehabilitation, provided in a way that looks like a real world approach, will help patients to have better outcomes after surgery. Our study will help to find out if doing a test like this is practical. If it is, we will do a large study across Canadian hospitals to find out if this approach to prehabilitation can help patients.

column36: Transitional care programs: Evaluation of performance and patient-oriented outcomes
column37: Older persons may have several health problems that require hospital admissions. Once treatments are completed, many experience delayed discharge from the hospital because they may not have the support they need when they return home or there are not enough nursing home beds. Older persons for whom discharge is delayed are at risk of a decline in their ability to walk and to take care of themselves, and of complications such as infections. To address this issue, the Ministry of Health in Ontario sponsored transitional care programs. Instead of staying too long in the hospital, older persons are transferred to these programs, which provide services that the persons need to recover in either their home or other facilities such as residential or long-term care facilities. There is limited understanding of what services provided in transitional care programs work and how they work in improving the recovery of older persons, and what resources are needed for the success of these programs. We will collaborate with healthcare decision makers, and older persons to understand how and why transitional care program work. Our work will involve understanding the services given to older persons in these programs and of interviewing older persons to uncover the main services offered to meet the needs of older persons, how satisfied older persons are, and how services can be improved. We will also evaluate how successful the programs are in improving older persons' ability to be independent in terms of taking care of themselves and their well-being. The results of our study will provide evidence on the most promising program services and will help support the change of the Canadian health care system to improve quality of life for older Canadians.

column36: Creating an Evidence-Informed, Accessible, Clinically Useful and Personalized Virtual Mental Health Support Framework for School-Age Children on the Autism Spectrum: Building from Pandemic e-Support Experiences
column37: Mental health is central to the wellbeing of autistic children and their families. Ensuring the fit between the support and the characteristics of each autistic child and their families is crucial. However, evidence-based mental health interventions in autistic children are often "one-size-fits-all" and of high cost and with low accessibility. Virtual mental health (e-MH) support has great potential to improve access and meet individual needs in a flexible way. Experiences of Canadian autistic children and families during the COVID-19 pandemic provide invaluable information of the current use of e-MH in Canada. By learning from these experiences, we will clarify what is available, what it still missing, and how to improve access and usefulness of e-MH support for school-age autistic children and their families. We will then create an e-MH framework which can flexibly integrate ingredients of existing evidence-based interventions to develop a "modular" e-MH program - a collection of strategies addressing different mental health needs, to be selected for use to meet individual needs. We will first perform a pan-Canadian survey and in-depth interviews. These experiences and data will be synthesized and used to develop an e-MH framework and a modular e-MH program that can be personalized, which will then be piloted and evaluated. We will use the Formative Method for Adapting Psychotherapy, an approach to therapy adaptation that provides guidance for incorporating empirical, clinical, and field knowledge, to inform the development processes. This project will provide important knowledge to create a flexible e-MH framework for Canadian school-age autistic children and their families. This framework could be applied widely to enhance e-MH support that can be personalized for autistic children of various characteristics, across geographical regions and contexts.

column36: Claudin-3 in epithelial collective migration
column37: Movement of cells as a group plays an important role in development of an embryo and is also key for tissue regeneration following injury. Further, this process also helps cancer cells to spread to distant organs. This unique type of cell movement is characterized by high level of coordination between cells, that maintain contact with each other. On the other hand, the moving group's edge is free of contacts and generates very dynamic protrusions, crucial for movement. The cell contacts are important regulators of this process, however details of how they contribute are not yet known. We will explore the role of a protein located at the cell contact sites, claudin-3. This protein is abundant in various tumors (e.g. prostate, ovarium, intestinal cancers), and was implicated in spreading of these cancers. It also has crucial roles in the kidney. We found that experimental deletion of this protein from cells reduced their ability to move and generate protrusions. We also identified a potential binding partner for this protein, called TNIK. Based on these, we propose that claudin-3 helps migration by coordinating events needed for front protrusions and by strengthening group coherence. Further, we think that part of the effects of claudin-3 can be attributed to TNIK. To test these theories, we will use cultured tubular and cancer cells. We will manipulate the abundance, location and interactions of claudin-3 and use microscopy techniques to explore how this affects various aspects of group migration. Taken together, we will define the cellular and molecular modes whereby claudin-3 controls cell migration and assess the specific role of the claudin-3-TNIK interaction. Our studies will help understand molecular events during group migration and define how claudin-3 is linked to these. This knowledge is vital to understand cancer spreading and tissue regeneration. Thus, our studies may lead to new interventions to influence these important processes.

column36: Mechanistic insights into non-malignant hematopoietic diseases
column37: Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA) is a rare congenital disease that is usually diagnosed before 2 years of age. Clinical presentation includes severe anemia, growth retardation and failure to thrive. Patients display various levels of disease severity for reasons that are not completely understood. Current treatments include repeated blood transfusions, life-long steroids administration, and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Unfortunately, these treatments are often associated to severe side effects that can affect children development and patients' quality of life. Thus, novel, less toxic therapeutic approaches are critically needed. While we know that DBA is due to a failure of the bone marrow to produce functional red blood cells, the mechanism of disease development remains unclear. Recent results have shown that DBA is caused by a general defect in blood stem cells to produce the correct amounts of proteins, ultimately leading to a failure in the formation and function of red blood cells. However, it is currently unclear what are the specific proteins that are affected in the disease and we do not understand how such a decrease in protein levels causes the disease. In this application, we propose to use novel techniques we have previously established to identify all proteins that are defective in DBA, and to determine how these defects cause defects in red blood cells. The proposed project is expected to pave the way to new therapeutic approaches in the future.

column36: Alternative splicing and Numb protein isoform function in cancer metastasis.
column37: In a normal cell, growth is regulated by signals that come from the surrounding tissue and neighboring cells. Signals from outside are interpreted by protein receptors that span the limiting membrane of the cell (half inside and half outside). A signal received outside is transmitted inside by the receptor which then passes the signal on to molecules in the cell that control cell behavior. Once a receptor molecule is activated it is quickly pulled inside the cell where it is destroyed and the signal is terminated. This is process called receptor down regulation. In some cancers, this control mechanism is lost, and the receptor stays at the surface of the cell, and continues to send signals. As a result the cell continuously divides, or migrates and invades surrounding tissue inappropriately. The focus of this proposal is a molecule called Numb that controls the down regulation of multiple types of receptor molecules. There is evidence that the function of the Numb molecule is altered in breast, lung, and colon tumors. Recently, my team has shown that these alterations in Numb proteins are required for breast cancer metastasis. In this proposal we will use biochemical, cell biology, and animal model studies to: 1. Investigate what causes the altered forms of Numb observed in cancer cells and determine strategies and inhibitors to counteract these changes. 2. To determine how changes in normal Numb activity affects the growth and survival of human breast cancer as well as other lethal cancers. These studies will allow us to evaluate how changes in Numb protein expression in tumors results in a failure of receptor down regulation. This information has the potential to impact cancer treatment with cancer drugs that specifically target cell receptors in an effort to shut them off. In addition, we will identify novel drug like chemicals that can restore normal Numb activity and block cancer metastasis.

column36: Intrinsically disordered regions in disease: from sequence to molecular properties to function
column37: Rapid advances in genomic technologies have led to discoveries of important genes for many diseases. For example, there are now 100s of genes known to be involved in autism, but for the vast majority of them, we don't understand why mutations in them lead to autism, so we can't design medicines to reverse the problem. We do know that these genes encode proteins, and many of the proteins include floppy parts (referred to as intrinsically disordered regions or IDRs) that don't follow the expected patterns of protein function and evolution. A major breakthrough in the past few years was to realize that the IDRs have molecular properties such as electric charge, solubility in water, repeated amino acids, etc. These molecular properties can be discerned from the amino acid sequences, and we want to test whether these properties determine function by systematically searching for all the important properties, and then making synthetic proteins that have those properties and see if they can carry out normal protein function. We will have to do this for some example intrinsically disordered regions whose functions we do understand. At the same time, we will start to predict the function of disease genes based on these molecular properties, and interpret the effects of disease mutations. This help us understand what is going wrong when these proteins are mutated in disease.

column36: Relaxation Mapping for the Clinic: Application to Multiple Sclerosis
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a debilitating condition typically beginning in young adulthood. Alberta has the highest reported rate of MS in the world and Canada has a high rate as well. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is heavily used in MS. MRI is a powerful tool for MS diagnosis, but it is less effective for tracking disease changes over time. We wish to develop ways to improve the ability of MRI to track MS progression in the brain by making the clinical images already in use more useful. Our objectives are to make advances in MRI analysis methods for measuring brain changes in MS using the existing MRI scans, so without taking any extra time. The methods will enable actual measurements of tissue damage, so clinicians can then track changes over time with numbers from the MRI scans and not just with visual readings. This field of MRI is called quantitative MRI. The new quantitative MRI methods provide an additional way to track tissue damage and may provide greater insight into the MS disease process, hence adding value to current clinical MRI for following MS progression. The methods are designed with computer simulations and modelling. Next the methods are tested in objects and healthy subjects, and then subjects with MS in a research setting. The numbers produced by the methods are compared to much slower MRI techniques that serve as gold standards. The methods will also be tested on different types of MRI machines to be sure they can be used universally. Lastly, the methods are translated into clinical research studies in order to monitor brain changes in MS subjects over time in comparison to healthy subjects. This research involves MRI physics, MS neurology, and neuroradiology with experts in each field. Together we will develop and test new MRI approaches to enable better tracking of MS disease progression.

column36: Dual Isotope Theranostics for 18F-PET Imaging and Correlated Targeted Radioligand Therapy
column37: Targeted radioligand therapy (RLT) is a very promising yet expensive procedure which uses toxic radioisotopes that are linked to a targeting agent that binds to and directs the radiation specifically to cancer. Every cancer patient who is a candidate for RLT must receive a PET (positron emission tomography) scan to see if the tumor will respond to treatment. PET scans also use ligands that are labeled with different isotopes, typically 68Ga or 18F with 18F being the preferred isotope of choice owing to its higher resolution, lower radiotoxicity, and commercial availability. Theranostics are agents that let us "treat what we can see and see what we can treat". Theranostics should bind the target in the same way with the same affinity to maximize the chance that what is seen by imaging will be followed up with treatment. Ideally therefore, the theranostic used for imaging should be: a) identical to the one used for therapy and b) should be labeled with 18F to afford the best resolution. Before 2019, this concept was never known in practice. Yet we published the first-ever proof of concept where a single molecule can be labeled with 18F for diagnostic PET and then labeled with 177Lu for therapy. This is made possible by a breakthrough method we invented for one-step, aqueous radiofluorination of complex theranostics. This approach has several salient advantages: 1) we can access 18F-fluoride, with all of its advantages, 2) we can use any number of radiotherapeutic metals e.g. 177Lu, 212Pb and 225Ac, and 3) we can use specific chelators that cannot be imaged with 68Ga. The outcomes of this proposal will be new knowledge in the development of dual-isotope theranostic while being chemically identical across both diagnostic and therapeutic modalities. At the same time, this work will shift imaging practice towards simplicity in 18F-labeling. Long-term, this will inform the development of 18F-labeled companion diagnostics for radiometal chelating peptides.

column36: The role of transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) in modulating motoneuron properties to restore motor function after spinal cord injury.
column37: People with spinal cord injury (SCI) often develop excessive and unwanted involuntary contractions (spasticity) that can produce pain, hamper sleep and impair residual motor function, with most treatments producing unwanted side effects like persistent drowsiness and muscle weakness. Recently, we have discovered that applying transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, or TENS, over the lower back can dramatically reduces spasticity and improves control of spared voluntary leg activation. In this project, we are examining if TENS works by changing how the motoneurons in the spinal cord respond to inputs from the brain and body. Motoneurons are the final communication relay from the brain and spinal cord to the muscles of the limbs and they contain several ion channels that make them respond in a complicated way to the inputs they receive. These complexities are coped with normally to produce smooth muscle contractions, but with SCI, they produce new challenges to regain skilled motor function in addition to producing spasticity. In this project, we examine how the currents that flow through these ion channels affect motoneuron activation normally, how they evolve as spasticity develops after injury and how they can be modified with TENS to reduce spasticity and improve motor recovery. Parallel experiments will be done in animals and humans along with computer models of the motor neuron to verify the biological results. The findings from this project will provide important information as to how motoneurons are impacted after SCI and how TENS applied to the lower back modifies the response of the motoneurons to reduce troublesome spasticity and improve residual motor function. TENS has the potential to provide an on-demand control of spasticity that is specific to the lower limb and overcomes the unwanted side effects of sedation and muscle weakness of current anti-spastic drugs, providing a promising, accessible, and safe therapy for people with SCI.

column36: Intravenous DNase I for the treatment of sepsis: A phase 1 safety and feasibility study in ICU patients
column37: Sepsis (ie. serious infections of the blood) can cause a vicious cycle of blood clot formation and inflammation, which may lead to multiple organ failure and death. In Canada, there are approximately 90,000 patients with sepsis each year, with estimated mortality rates of up to 30%. Despite decades of sepsis research, there are no anti-sepsis drugs and the mortality rate of sepsis remains high. This suggests that some fundamental knowledge is lacking in our current understanding of why sepsis kills patients. In recent years, neutrophils (a type of white blood cells) have been shown to release web-like structures (called NETs) to capture and kill microorganisms. NETs consist of DNA, histones, and neutrophils enzymes. However, NETs can also cause collateral damage to the body. We have previously shown that the DNA and histone components of NETs can trigger blood clotting and prevent blood breakdown. In a mouse model of sepsis, injection of DNase I (a naturally-occurring enzyme that breaks down DNA) results in improved organ function and improved survival rates. We believe that by giving patients an enzyme that chews the DNA component of NETs, we can break up this clot formation. This drug, called DNase I, is already safely used to digest the NETs formed in lungs in cystic fibrosis patients with lung infections. We are planning a phase 1 study at the Hamilton General Hospital and the Maisonneuve-Rosemont Hospital (Quebec) to assess the safety of giving this drug intravenously to septic patients. We will assess if two different doses (given for either 3 or 7 days) are safe in septic patients. We will also draw extra blood samples before and after the drug is infused to determine the impact of the treatment on NET formation over time. The outcome from this study will allow our team to establish if DNase I therapy is safe in septic patients, which would pave the way for larger studies in the near future to determine drug effectiveness.

column36: Structure-function coupling in macroscale brain networks
column37: The relationship between structure and function is a central concept in neuroscience. The complex network of synaptic projections forms a hierarchy of nested and increasingly polyfunctional neural circuits that support perception, cognition and action. Thus, the coupling between structure and function provides unique information about how the brain transmits and integrates information. Despite its fundamental importance, structure-function coupling is poorly understood and under-utilized as a phenotype. Here we propose to take the next steps toward understanding network-level structure-function relationships by systematically studying individual variability and behaviour, normative lifespan variability, and regional heterogeneity. The proposed project will comprehensively benchmark structure-function coupling as a novel brain phenotype for basic and clinical research. Individual differences in structure-function coupling will provide a fundamentally new opportunity to quantify the effects of manipulations and perturbations, such as cognitive tasks, development and aging, neurological and psychiatric diseases, lesions, and stimulation. By annotating brain networks with micro-architectural attributes, we will identify molecular and cellular determinants of structure-function coupling, conceptually bridging micro- and macroscale levels of analysis.

column36: The Biology of Liver Macrophages at Birth and Throughout Life
column37: The liver filters and processes all the stuff that you eat. This includes food, drugs, alcohol and most importantly the bacterial products and the few bacteria that sneak from the intestine into the blood stream. Inside the liver is a filtering system like no other: millions of immune cells whose job it is to sit in the little blood vessels and catch bacteria. This system is not fully functional at birth especially in premature babies. We have a way of going inside the body and watching these immune cells catch bacteria using a special intravital microscope. Using this system we have found that at birth these immune cells are sitting outside the blood vessels and need to get into the blood vessels to be able to catch bacteria. It takes 3 weeks for all these immune cells to get inside the blood vessels and efficiently catch bacteria. We will elucidate the mechanisms by which this happens and examine whether the microbiome helps with this process by looking at mice with no microbiome. These specific liver immune cells called Kupffer cells seem to enter the liver before birth and then remain there. If a Kupffer cell dies then the other Kupffer cells replicate and make more. However, if many or all Kupffer cells die than new cells come in from the bone marrow and make new Kupffer cells that require some training before they become bona fide Kupffer cells. Using imaging we can watch how long before these cells can catch bacteria. We will see if the microbiome can expedite this situation and whether it matters whether you are a boy or a girl young or old etc. Finally, we will look at what happens to these cells during fibrosis in which the liver gets scarred and how the Kupffer cells function ie., their ability to kill bacteria. Liver disease will be the next epidemic with no treatment available (25% of Canadians have liver scarring) so we need to find ways of treating these patients.

column36: Identification of biological properties and molecular signatures to predict treatment response in patients with advanced HPV positive oropharyngeal cancer
column37: Cancer in the head and neck region is one of the leading cancers in the world associated with a high mortality rate. There are also significant long-term, life-long, and sometimes progressive side effects of radiotherapy-based treatment. Currently, radiation with chemotherapy, or radical surgery followed by chemoradiation are still mainstays of treatment. However, many of these patients progress to fatal metastatic disease. Those who survive cancer pay a high price with many therapies related to side effects and diseases. More efficient therapeutic approaches are desperately required to improve survival of patients with this disease, while preserving the normal functioning of organs affected by the disease, or organs in the vicinity of the disease that also become subject of collateral, treatment related, injury. In our institution we have an innovative treatment for patients with advanced throat (oropharyngeal) cancer. They receive chemotherapy first followed by less invasive transoral (through-the mouth) robotic surgery, and less invasive neck surgery, while avoiding radiotherapy altogether. This approach not only helps minimize or avoid adverse long-term effects of treatment but may also lead to better survival compared to the conventional treatment. The proposed study will find molecular markers to identify the patients that can benefit most from this new therapy or a modification of it and allow a personalized therapeutic decision making for each patient. This study will put Canada in a unique position to affect a potential paradigm shifting change in the way we treat patients with advanced throat cancer.

column36: Hyperhydration to Improve Kidney Outcomes in Children with Shiga Toxin-Producing E. coli Infection: A Multinational Cluster Randomized Crossover Trial
column37: Globally, there are over 2.8 million cases of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) infection each year. In 2012, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimated that 96,534 high-risk (i.e. O157) STEC infections occur yearly in the US. Over 60% of these infections occur in children, half of whom are <5 years old. Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) is the most serious complication of STEC infections and has a mortality rate of 1-3% and 30% develop chronic renal disease. Despite significant advances in our understanding of the pathophysiology of STEC infection, no treatments have emerged in the 35 years since STEC were determined to cause HUS. Care remains limited to avoiding antibiotics, and providing support if and when HUS develops. Data indicate that anti-bacterial and anti-toxin interventions are futile by the time of HUS presentation. column36: Investigating the contextual and behavioural determinants of sodium intake among adult Canadians
column37: Canadians consume large amounts of sodium, which increases their risk for heart disease and stroke. Strategies that support Canadians in following a lower sodium diet, like Canada's Food Guide, follow the idea that behaviour change can be achieved by increasing knowledge, alone. Yet, knowledge is only one part of behaviour change, which has shown minimal impact on sodium reduction to date. Therefore, it is important to understand the many internal and external factors related to sodium intake among Canadians to better inform sodium reduction strategies. Most research on factors that impact Canadians' sodium intake is old (>10 years). It is unknown if these factors have changed over time, with the adoption of Canada's Sodium Reduction Strategy in 2010. Importantly, the research that has been conducted in Canada has been limited. The surveys administered in the past mostly focused on informing policies for sodium, and it did not study how and why people behave the way they do, and what some of the barriers and motivators are to following a lower sodium diet. Our team will conduct research to deepen our understanding of what factors impact a person's sodium intake and food choices. We will develop a survey capturing the contextual (e.g., health literacy) and behavioural (e.g., perceived risks of sodium, attitudes towards sodium, intention to reduce sodium) factors related to sodium intake. The survey will be administered to 3380 Canadian adults, who will also complete diet recalls so that we can estimate how much sodium they eat. This data will allow us to 1) monitor changes in key factors of sodium intake over a 10-year time frame, 2) assess the behavioural and contextual factors impacting sodium intake among Canadian adults, and 3) determine whether these factors are associated with lower sodium intakes. This research will be the first of its kind. It will help us develop better strategies to support people in reducing their sodium intake.

column37: The concept of declining function with age requires a better understanding of whether it is an immutable characteristic of aging or whether it can be mitigated. When we age, we lose muscle. However, we are uncertain whether declines in muscle mass directly contribute to declining physical mobility with age. This loss of muscle is referred to as sarcopenia, a term that was simply a loss of muscle when it was originally coined. More recent redefinitions of sarcopenia have framed it as the loss of muscle mass AND physical function (strength and walking speed, for example). Importantly, sarcopenia in older persons is associated with increased adverse outcomes, including falls, functional decline, frailty, and mortality. Sarcopenia has recently received recognition as a treatable condition with the receipt of a code for billing by physicians in certain jurisdictions. Despite being able to bill for diagnosing and treating sarcopenia, it can be defined as a treatable condition in several ways. Thus, its diagnosis is decidedly complex. Importantly, our team showed that various ways of diagnosing sarcopenia result in various people having sarcopenia and others not, whereas another definition reverses the previous diagnosis. With confusion around how to diagnose sarcopenia, its use in clinical situations becomes tenuous at best. Our main assertion is that the biological substrate of sarcopenia, skeletal muscle, has not been accurately measured. This lack of accurate measurement has led to confusion about whether measuring muscle is clinically relevant in sarcopenia. Our main idea is that skeletal muscle mass, when accurately measured, is a powerful predictor of functional declines in older men and women. We will use a novel method to measure skeletal muscle in a large cohort of older men and women and track them for two years. We plan to show that our method of measuring muscle will show a strong association between change in muscle mass and decline in mobility.

column36: Atrial fibrillation in diabetes mellitus: mechanisms and therapeutic approaches
column37: Diabetes mellitus is a growing epidemic that is associated with severe cardiovascular complications. Included amongst these is atrial fibrillation (the most common cardiac arrhythmia), which is a major cause of increased morbidity and mortality in type 1 and type 2 diabetes. Despite these links, the basis for atrial fibrillation in diabetes is poorly understood. Our first objective is to determine the specific causes of atrial fibrillation in diabetes mellitus, which are likely unique from atrial fibrillation in other forms of cardiovascular disease. Current therapeutic approaches for atrial fibrillation in diabetic patients are severely limited; therefore, our second objective is to discover new approaches to prevent and treat atrial fibrillation in diabetes mellitus. Our recent studies demonstrate that atrial fibrillation in mouse models of type 1 and type 2 diabetes occurs as a result of a number of changes in heart. These include changes in the electrical properties of the muscle cells of the heart as well as a buildup of scar tissue in the heart. In our proposed studies we will determine how each of these leads to the occurrence of atrial fibrillation and which mechanisms are most important in allowing this arrhythmia to occur. We have also discovered new approaches for the prevention of atrial fibrillation in type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus by targeting insulin signaling and a family of hormones called incretins. Our studies will continue to investigate these approaches to prevent atrial fibrillation in diabetes. Our experiments are performed using a wide range of powerful approaches from the molecular and cellular levels to the intact animal. Our proposed studies will provide critical insight into the basis for atrial fibrillation, and new approaches to prevent it, in diabetes mellitus.

column36: Understanding glucocorticoid resistance in inflammatory disease
column37: Glucocorticoids (GCs) are essential steroid hormones that play key roles in stress and injury. GCs dampen inflammation and promote healing following damage, infection or other inflammatory trauma. In the context of inflammatory diseases, it is the ability to reduce inflammation that makes synthetic GCs (often called "steroids") highly effective and widely used anti-inflammatory drugs. However, resistance to the beneficial effects of GCs is observed in many patients with inflammatory disease. This represents a major and unresolved clinical need. In the current application, we use severe asthma as a model GC resistant disease to explore this problem. Aside from anti-inflammatory actions, endogenous GCs promote a variety of metabolic and other effects, which in the context of high-dose GC therapy produce serious and unwanted complications. Patients with severe asthma in whom inhaled GCs do not provide effective therapy require high-dose, often oral, GCs as therapy. However, even high-dose GC therapy may not control their disease. Nevertheless, while asthma in these individuals is resistant to the anti-inflammatory effects of GC, the GR-dependent side-effects still occur. We therefore investigate molecular mechanisms by which inflammatory genes fail to be repressed by GCs. To gain an understanding of GC-resistance, gene expression in the airways and GC responses in airway epithelial cells is compared between normal individuals, mild/moderate asthma and severe asthma. Understanding GC-resistance will promote new approaches to improve therapy. Importantly, knowing when patients are truly resistant to GC therapy will allow them to be more rapidly transitioned from GC-based interventions to more effective therapies. The current application uses severe asthma to address these issues and the results have the potential to ultimately improve clinical practice.

column36: Cell-specific role of ADAM17 in remodeling following myocardial infarction: identifying a therapeutic window
column37: Myocardial infarction (MI), or heart attack, happens when an artery supplying blood to the heart muscle is clogged, the affected heart muscle dies and is replaced by scar tissue (infarct). The heart tries to compensate for this muscle loss by: 1) recruiting inflammatory cells (scavengers) to clean up the dead cell debris (inflammation), 2) generating new branches/extending the existing branches of the blood vessels to provide new source of blood supply to the infarcted area (angiogenesis), and 3) generating a scar tissue to cover the 'hole' that would otherwise form in the wall of the heart (infarct or fibrosis). These events are mediated by different cell types (inflammatory cells, endothelial cells, fibroblasts) that are present or are recruited to the heart tissue in a time-dependent fashion. ADAM17 (disintegrin and metalloproteinase 17) is a proteinase (enzyme) that is present on the cell membrane of the cells involved in the described processes, and can regulate the function of these cells. ADAM17 is elevated in the heart and plasma of patients with acute MI, and its levels have been linked to adverse outcomes in these patients. We will use mice lacking ADAM17 in each cell type, that will undergo microsurgery to induce MI (an artery is surgically closed off). We will then determine how ADAM17 loss in each cell type affects the outcome of recovery from MI. These experiments will identify the cell type in which ADAM17 deletion can be beneficial, and hence identify a time-window when where ADAM17 inhibition could be beneficial. We will then use a pharmacological ADAM17 inhibitor (PF-05480090, Pfizer), to administer for the duration of the identified time window. This approach for short-term inhibition of ADAM17 will be particularly effective since given the diverse functions of ADAM17, its prolonged inhibition may be associated with side effects.

column36: Discovery of HPV-associated genomic alterations in cervical cancer
column37: Human papillomavirus (HPV) causes >99% of cervical cancers and has a particularly deadly impact on sub-Saharan African females. Some strains of HPV can integrate their DNA into the DNA of cervical cells, which results in increased production of cancer causing viral proteins and is often the first step towards developing cervical cancer. This integration involves breaking the cervical cell's DNA. From work in other cancers, we know that breaking a cell's DNA (e.g. with chemicals or radiation) can result in dramatic rearrangements of large segments of cancer cell DNA. We now want to know whether DNA breakage caused by HPV results in dramatic rearrangements in cervical cancer. Such rearrangements of human genomes have been difficult to study due to the limitations of conventional genomics approaches. Fortuitously, a newer genomics approach, known as long-read sequencing, can sequence DNA fragments 100 times longer than the older approach, offering an opportunity to study, for the first time, unexplored damage that HPV might cause to the human genome and the role of that damage in causing cancer. We used long-read sequencing to collect preliminary data from two cervical cancer samples from Uganda to reveal previously unknown DNA rearrangements that were not found in analyses of short-read sequencing of the same samples. For example, we found some HPV-associated human genome rearrangements resulted in human cancer genes from different chromosomes being fused together, pointing to the possibility that we might discover new oncogenic mechanisms. We aim to explore such potentially important rearrangements using long-read sequencing of 50 cervical cancers chosen from our samples from Uganda. Long-read sequencing of these tumours will reveal previously hidden information on how HPV integration causes wide-spread DNA damage and may lead to identification of new therapeutic targets in a population that is historically underrepresented in cancer genomics research.

column36: Individualized Fortification of Human Milk to Improve Neurodevelopment of Infants Born <1250 grams
column37: There has been a dramatic shift in how very low birth weight (born <1500 g, VLBW) infants are fed in Canadian neonatal intensive care units in the last 10 years, moving from predominantly formula to human milk feeding. This change has occurred as the result of strong evidence that use of human milk can reduce the risk of serious morbidities such as sepsis and necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) and thus could be life-saving. Unlike preterm formula where the energy and nutrient content is constant, human milk composition varies widely from mother-to-mother, over time of day, days postpartum, and how it is collected and stored. This presents a challenge when feeding VLBW infants who require nutrient fortification of their feeds to meet their very elevated nutritional requirements to support growth and normal neurodevelopment but who also have immature excretory mechanisms for eliminating nutrients and breakdown products not required by the body. Human milk-fed infants, particularly those with comorbidities and fed predominantly pasteurized donor human milk, frequently have suboptimal growth including head growth; the latter prognostic of later neuroimpairment. Individualized fortification may be a reasonable approach to address suboptimal energy and nutrient intake and growth by accounting for variability in human milk composition and/or and an infant's metabolic response to enteral nutrition provided. To assess this, health care professionals and families from a large consortium of neonatal units that have worked successfully in the past on other early feeding issues of VLBW infants have assembled to evaluate the benefits, risks and costs of individualized fortification. While the feeding intervention will occur in hospital, infants will be followed for approximately two years to assess their growth, body composition, frequency of morbidity and neurodevelopment. This study will be pivotal in setting feeding guidelines for VLBW infants in Canada and globally.
