column36: Tackling overgrowth syndromes through precision medicine
column37: Overgrowth syndromes consist of a group of diseases characterized by excessive growth of certain parts of the body and a variety of anatomical deformities. As an example, Joseph Merrick (1862-1890), also known as "The Elephant Man", is thought to have suffered from a severe form of this disease. Because of his deformities, he was abandoned by his family at a young age and exploited as a circus freak during his early twenties. He died of asphyxia at age 27 due to compressive deformities in the neck region. We now know that overgrowth syndromes are caused by genetic defects that arise after conception, starting at the embryo stage. One of the most common defects occurs in a protein called PIK3CA that controls the growth and proliferation of cells. The body parts affected by this defect eventually increase in size, which leads to large and painful masses that can compress any adjacent organ in the body. PIK3CA-related overgrowth syndromes (PROS) also often leads to premature death. Recently, a PIK3CA blocker has been used by Dr. Guillaume Canaud (Universite de Paris) to treat PROS and led to spectacular reductions in the size of masses. For unknown reasons, however, this blocker did not completely reverse the overgrowths in certain organs. This proposal is based on these premises and aims to understand why there can be resistance to the blocker. This work will be tackled through the characterization of animal models and clinical samples in which the PIK3CA protein is either overactive, normal or inactivated. The project should also help identify other proteins and markers useful for PROS diagnosis and treatment. Once the cause of the resistance to PIK3CA blockade is elucidated, it will become possible to treat PROS with new approaches in order to reach maximal reversion of the overgrowth process. As a result, affected patients will experience further improvement in their quality of life and life expectancy.

column36: Proteolytic Remodelling of Uterine Tissues as a Trigger of Infection-Induced Preterm Labour
column37: Preterm birth affects 8% of pregnancies in Canada and is a leading cause of infant and child death worldwide. Preterm birth can lead to severe neurological disorders and breathing problems in children as well as financial and emotional stress for families. While there are multiple causes of preterm birth, up to 60% of cases arise from bacterial infection in the uterus. In particular, the presence of select vaginal bacteria correlates with increased risk for preterm birth. These bacteria can invade the uterus and infect pregnancy tissues, which can lead to severe infection of the mother or baby, early membrane rupture (water breaking), spontaneous abortion and preterm labour. However, we do not know how these bacteria affect the uterus and contribute to pregnancy complications. Notably, antibiotics do not stop infection-induced preterm labour nor improve outcomes. Furthermore, current predictive tests detect less than 50% of cases. Thus, there is a dire need to understand how vaginal bacteria trigger infection-induced preterm labour. Protein degradation (also known as proteolysis) is a central feature of labour induction. Proteolysis can alter regulatory pathways and remodel pregnancy tissues to trigger key events in the birth process such as cervical dilation, fetal membrane rupture (water breaking) and uterine contractions. However, incorrectly timed proteolysis can prematurely trigger these processes and initiate preterm labour. Our data demonstrate that vaginal bacteria secrete proteolytic enzymes that break down structural and regulatory components found in pregnancy tissues. I will investigate how vaginal bacteria and their proteolytic enzymes modulate pregnancy tissues to trigger fetal membrane rupture, uterine contractions and premature labour. This work will improve our knowledge of infection-induced preterm labour and uncover novel targets for diagnosis and treatment.

column36: Outcomes of pregnant women and infants with SARS-CoV-2 vaccine and infection exposure
column37: Emerging infectious disease events, such as the current global SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, are often associated with disproportionately negative health outcomes for pregnant women and infants. Significant delays in implementation and reporting of robust research findings on SARS-CoV-2 vaccine safety and efficacy, as well as infection outcomes, has led to considerable vaccine hesitancy in the vulnerable pregnant population. Primarily, this research project will use extensive demographic, epidemiological, and clinical data from an established large prospective cohort study (the P3 cohort study) on 4000 pregnant women and their infants in Alberta, Canada, with follow-up continuing until 1 year postpartum. A sub-study on vaccine willingness and perceptions will also be done. Analysis of this data will provide accurate estimates of the risk of various health outcomes (e.g. pregnancy complications, neonatal complications) following SARS-CoV-2 infection in pregnant women and infants. It will give vital information on the real-world safety and efficacy of vaccination in a representative Canadian population, along with key insights into the necessity and timing of 'booster' shots. Secondarily, electronic medical record (EMR) data for participants will be compared to similar data from the prospective P3 cohort study. A validation will be done of the EMR data to see if it can be used in the future for rapidly implementing robust research on emerging infections in pregnancy. In areas (i.e. certain data types) where EMR is not valid, statistical approaches will be trialed to facilitate optimal use of this information for pandemic preparedness. The results of this study will be shared with other researchers as well as with the public through internal (University of Calgary), regional (SARS-CoV-2 and perinatal epidemiology networks within Alberta and Canada), and international (World Health Organization) collaborations. This research will be completed over a period of two years.

column36: Molecular Virology and Genomic Instability
column37: Human papillomavirus (HPV) causes ~4% of human cancers worldwide. The "High-Risk" mucosal HPV is the etiological agent for cervical and a subset of anogenital cancers, as well as for alarmingly increasing cases of oropharyngeal cancer in developed country. While available vaccines are providing protection for certain HPV subtypes, the lack of universal implementation of HPV vaccination remains a worldwide issue. To develop efficacious therapeutics to prevent cancer progression of HPV-infected epithelia, there is an urgent need to understand how the virus promotes cancer development and impacts cellular response to treatment. Viral DNA genomes have limited coding capacities, and therefore viruses harness cellular factors to facilitate their replication. Interestingly, they have evolved numerous strategies to manipulate elements of the DNA damage response of host cells to complete their life cycles. These interactions have critical consequences for viral replication and host genome integrity. In the last 5 years, our work directly contributed to our understanding of the molecular events that lead to genomic instability and fuels cancer progression in infected cells. In this research program, our main goal is to decipher the mechanisms by which HPV rewires host cells response to DNA damage and how these processes promote cell adaptation to replication stress. A combination of innovative approaches in proteomics, bioimaging, cell biology, and biochemistry will be used to pursue 4 research streams: 1) Define how host-pathogen interactions govern the functions of viral and cellular proteins, 2) Determine how infected cells adapt to replicative stress, 3) Develop therapeutic strategies to target viral-induced cancers, and 4) Develop unique molecular tools to study DNA damage signaling. Globally, we will continue our efforts towards the discovery of processes that promote carcinogenesis when hijacked by viruses and toward the identification of avenues to target these cancers. The results generated throughout this program will provide exciting new information and areas of investigation in virology as well as in our fundamental understanding of the pathways that safeguard genomic stability in cells. Understanding these events is central for the development of therapeutic strategies to treat HPV-driven pathogenesis. Thus, our findings have strong translational potential into clinical application to better treat patients suffering from viral-induced cancers.

column37: As CRC in Brain Cancer Epigenomics, I have set up a diverse research group that includes trainees and staff with expertise in genomics, informatics and functional studies with patient-derived models. This integrated team is contributing new knowledge on epigenetic principles underpinning childhood and adult brain cancers. Renewal of my CRC will enable continuity in our search for targetable epigenetic entities that characterize these lethal malignancies. I propose a program that builds on our recent discoveries, incorporates new technologies, and integrates dry and wet lab activities to delve into unexplored contributions of the non-coding genome to cancer initiation and progression. We will use clinical samples to perform bulk and single-cell (epi)genomic techniques to identify new mechanisms that lead to aggressive cancer behavior. We will deploy our patient-derived primary cultures and xenografts to test hypotheses generated from our -omics data. We will leverage our national and international networks to foster collaborative efforts that benefit from the best expertise and models. And we will pursue translational opportunities through established and new partnerships with industry and clinicians. My research program will focus on two main problems: (1) Investigating the epigenetic determinants of cancer stem cell fate in adult glioblastoma. Cancer stem cells are crucial populations of cells that escape treatment and seed relapses. Targeting them is an immediate and unmet clinical need. (2) Understanding how the epigenomes of childhood brain cancers evolve following treatment. Finding ways to predict the evolutionary trajectories of these tumors could put us "one step ahead" of cancer and give us a real chance at preventing relapses. The complexity of these problems requires the seamless integration of orthogonal approaches, which we will execute by integrating the complementary skills and expertise we have in the lab.

column36: Pain Research
column37: It is estimated that 25% of Canadians suffer from chronic pain; a large proportion of whom have non-specific chronic back pain (CBP) which is not related to specific tissue damage. Unfortunately, more than 50% of patients with non-specific CBP do not benefit from pharmacological treatment (refractory CBP). While some can benefit from cognitive therapies, in the absence of valid pre-screening methodologies, identifying those most likely to benefit is an ongoing challenge. Contributing to this challenge is our limited understanding of the mechanisms behind refractory CBP. While many patients can experience pain relief from the expectations generated during a health care encounter, how variability in brain mechanisms of expectation interferes with CBP recovery and reduces the efficacy of administered treatments is unclear. Hence, we aim to establish the neurobiological features through which expectations and negative ideation lead to refractory CBP, with the goal of improving outcomes in this population. Our lab is investigating the variability in the extent to which negative expectations can amplify perceived pain and reduce the effectiveness of treatment in people with CBP. We are testing whether the variability is due to underlying differences in structure and function of associative-learning-circuitry of the brain. People with non-specific CBP conditions will be recruited from clinics. MRI data will be acquired with a 3T GE MRI located at the Biomedical Translational Imaging Center, Halifax. Functional MRI scans will be acquired while participants perform an expectation task that uses visual cues and heat evoked pain. The experimental data will be used to predict changes in clinical pain measured after two weeks of placebo treatment in one group of people while an additional group will serve as a control group for the placebo effect. The analysis plan will include mapping of task data to identify activations in associative learning circuitry. A connectomics approach will determine how functional and structural brain connections underpin affects of expectation on pain modulation in resting-functional and diffusion MRI brain scans respectively. Strengths of our proposal include a unique multidimensional approach that is novel and clinically relevant. By demonstrating a clear neurobiological basis for refractory CBP, we will facilitate the development of valid pre-screening tools and improve treatment strategies and outcomes in this population.

column36: Molecular Pathogenesis of Emerging Viruses
column37: Background and Importance: Emerging infectious diseases are a global health threat with outbreaks often resulting in complex patterns of severe illness that are either unknown or poorly understood. Infectious diseases are responsible for at least 10 million deaths worldwide per year, or approximately 25% of all global deaths. Zoonotic diseases, which result from the spread of pathogens between human and animals, comprise ~60% of these infections. Thus, emerging zoonotic viruses are a critical concern for human and non-human animal health. Further, emerging virus spillovers have been increasing in frequency and disproportionately affect low- and middle-income regions of the world. Given the public health and economic impact of emerging virus outbreaks, there is a critical need to expand our understanding of the mechanisms that contribute to disease during infection, the long-term impacts of these infections following disease recovery and increase preparedness and capacity in regions where emerging viruses are overrepresented. Program Goals: The overall goal of this program is to identify, characterize and increase responsiveness for emerging viruses that have the potential to impact global human and non-human animal health and disrupt regional economies. The primary objectives of this program are: i) Characterization of emerging virus pathogenesis at physiological barriers; ii) Assessments of long-term sequelae following recovery from emerging virus infections; and iii) Identification of emerging virus threats through international One Health surveillance studies in Africa. Novelty and Expected Impact: This research program will combine traditional laboratory investigations with field-based surveillance and patient studies to study how emerging viruses move from animals to humans, the mechanisms underlying severe disease following spillover and long-term health complications in recovered patients. Given the increasing frequency of emerging virus spillovers, there is a definitive need to better understand where and how emerging viruses are circulating in Nature and better prepare for spillovers by enhancing our understanding of the complex diseases they often result in. These activities will increase preparedness and response capacity at the focal points of emerging virus spillovers and will help reduce the overall health and economic tolls of these outbreaks.

column36: Molecular Genetics and Neurodegenerative Diseases
column37: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a devastating neurodegenerative disease with no cure. ALS affects motor neurons in the central nervous system (CNS) that control the voluntary movement of muscles. Neuroinflammation and abnormal accumulation of microglia, which are the primary innate immune cells in the CNS, are further characteristic disease phenotypes in the affected brain regions. Together, ALS leads to muscle weakness, paralysis, and death within 2-5 years of diagnosis. Several fundamental questions in the ALS field remain unanswered: (1) How do these motor-controlling neurons undergo degeneration? (2) Do these disease-associated microglia protect neurons from dying or damage the neurons? Understanding the molecular basis of the disease process is pivotal to facilitate effective strategies for disease prevention and therapeutic intervention. Many transgenic mouse models of ALS have provided insights into the disease process; however, showed limitations as these transgenic mice exhibit accelerated end-stage phenotypes and rapid death, rendering difficult to dissect the natural disease course, particularly at early-stage ALS. During the last five years, Dr. Park pioneered a new mouse model that addresses these limitations: The MATR3 S85C knock-in mouse line expresses the disease-causing protein at the physiological level and closely mimics features of early-stage ALS, including progressive motor deficits, degeneration of motor-controlling neuronal groups and neuroinflammation. This new ALS mouse model thus provides an unprecedented opportunity to dissect the disease process at early disease stage. In the next five years, Dr. Park will characterize and study MATR3 S85C knock-in mice at presymptomatic and early disease stages to (1) identify the key disease-initiating events leading to neurodegeneration and (2) determine how microglia contribute to ALS pathogenesis particularly during early disease stage. Identification of early disease events and elucidation of the role of microglia will enhance our understanding of the disease mechanism and provide important clues to the development of effective strategies for disease prevention and therapeutic intervention for early-stage ALS. More broadly, her findings will illuminate valuable insights into other neurodegenerative diseases.

column36: Systems Neuroscience
column37: Cognitive processes emerge from the collective activity of billions of neurons in the brain and unravelling the mechanisms underlying information processing has become one of the central questions in neuroscience. The goal of this proposal is to investigate the relationship between neuronal dynamics and information coding in rodents during spatial navigation and translate these techniques to study the neuronal origin of epilepsy in human patients. In mammals, the hippocampus is a brain structure which is essential for spatial navigation and memory formation. Novel memories, initially dependent on the hippocampus, are progressively transferred to the cortex. The formation of long-term memories is believed to take place during sleep. During sleep, hippocampal neurons "replay" the patterns that formed during previous wake experiences. This activity propagates to the cortex where memories are gradually consolidated. However, the exact mechanisms enabling this phenomenon remains largely unknown. Information processing in the cortex depends on complex coordination between neurons. The cortex is composed of many different neuronal types, broadly divided into excitatory and inhibitory classes. Inhibitory neurons, although representing only 20% of the total number of neurons, play a major role in this coordination yet, it is still unclear how different inhibitory neurons enable the processing of spatial processing. Last, the hippocampus is one of the most vulnerable brain structures in epilepsy. Remarkably, the dynamical processes underlying spatial and memory processing in the healthy brain become awry in epilepsy. Furthermore, inhibitory neurons are believed to play a major role in epileptic activity. While animal models have provided a large body of data on epilepsy, studying the disease in epileptic subjects has become crucial. New electrodes now enable the monitoring of single neuronal activity in epileptic patients. The research program of Dr Peyrache will be divided in three objectives: 1/ How do spatial memories form in the cortex during sleep? 2/ What is the role of different cell types in the processing of spatial representation? 3/ What are the neuronal bases of epileptic seizures in patients? Unravelling the relationship between cognitive processes and neuronal dynamics will take us one step further toward understanding the neural basis of psychiatric disorders and cognitive impairments observed in brain disorders.

column36: Cognitive Neuroscience of Memory
column37: The ability to retrieve autobiographical memories lies at the center of many aspects of our daily life, from thinking about who we are to helping us solving problems, however the underlying brain mechanisms are not fully understood. Reaching this understanding is important because declining autobiographical memory can reveal differences between healthy and pathological aging, such as older adults at risk for dementia. Dr. Sheldon's innovative research program will discover the neurocognitive processes that support autobiographical memory, how these processes contribute to non-memory functions, and are affected by age. Her research focuses on the understanding the contributions of the hippocampus to construct autobiographical memories as this brain region is a neural target of both normal and pathological aging. Her objective is to first use behavioural studies and cutting-edge neuroimaging technology to determine how the hippocampus can be recruited for constructing different types of autobiographical memories as well as imagined future events that guide everyday tasks like problem solving. Equipped with a new understanding of how the hippocampus works for autobiographical memory, Dr. Sheldon will then determine how hippocampal processes are affected by normal cognitive aging and pathological aging, and the behavioural consequences to memory. Dr. Sheldon's anticipated discoveries about autobiographical memory have the potential to provide a richer and more accurate portrayal of how human memory works in the real world. In addition, by situating her studies in the context of aging, her work has major implications for understanding age-related memory decline, which is urgently needed given the rise in Canada's aging population.

column37: Finding Better Ways to Treat Neurocritically Ill Trauma Patients Traumatic brain injuries from road traffic accidents, contact sports and falls cause millions of deaths around the world every year. They also represent an enormous economic burden, as they can result in severe permanent impairments that cost the health care system billions of dollars. Despite clinical advances, we still face important knowledge gaps when it comes to managing the care of survivors. As Canada Research Chair in Critical Care Neurology and Trauma, Dr. Alexis Turgeon is looking to fill these gaps. The goal of his research is to improve bedside practices and outcomes in critically ill patients with traumatic brain injury by using evidence-based, patient-centered decision making. Dr. Turgeon and his research team are working on ways to improve prognostic assessment and level-of-care decisions as well as on how to better manage care by conducting patient-oriented research on current interventions used in neurocritically ill trauma patients. The chairholder is also looking at brain resuscitation strategies and intervention to improve long-term outcomes in this population through large-scale multicenter collaborative research and trials. Dr. Turgeon is looking for developing and implementing tools to guide decision-making processes in bedside care. Dr. Turgeon's research is informed by his years of experience in caring for neurocritically ill and trauma patients as a specialist in anesthesiology and critical care medicine. His previous research looked at how long-term outcomes following traumatic brain injury vary greatly across treatment centres, as do decisions to withdraw life support. Dr. Turgeon hopes his latest research will lead to substantive changes in the way health care workers care for critically ill patients with traumatic brain injury and, ultimately, improve their health outcomes.

column37: Dr. Urquia proposes advancing research through two interrelated objectives. 1) To advance immigrant health research 1.1) Assess selection biases behind the so-called 'healthy migrant effect' His approach builds on a recent data linkage of 270,000 international immigrants to Manitoba, including detailed information on entry and exit dates to the province and related origins/destinations and reasons. He will assess the influence of immigrant selection on hospitalizations and death among immigrants, outmigrants, returnees and stayers. Understanding the role of selective migration in comparisons of morbidity and mortality between immigrants and non-immigrants is a longstanding methodological problem in the field. This research will clarify its contribution and influence future studies. 1.2) Examine intra- and inter-ethnic patterns of intimate partner violence (IPV) using multisectoral data Dr. Urquia will further append data generated in the justice system and other social databases to categorize victims and the accused according to their immigration status, sex, marital status, and other sociodemographic characteristics, to draw light on gender-based intra- and inter-ethnic victimization patterns. No study to date has assessed IPV among immigrants using Justice data. This research will identify the subgroups of perpetrators and victims with higher needs of violence prevention and harm reduction initiatives by the health and justice systems. 2) To advance population-based family health research This objective involves the study of the associations between family structure and health and the 'spillover effects' that the illness of one family member (e.g., disability or serious chronic health condition) has on the health of the rest of the family members. Dr. Urquia will classify all Manitoban residents according to family structure and membership roles at selected time points (e.g., childbirth) and over time. More specifically, he will assemble 20 birth cohorts (1985-2004) and follow children until their 18th birthday along with their family members to assess outcomes. Lack of suitable family data at the population-level has challenged the incorporation of the family dimension in population health research. This research will illustrate the importance of incorporating the family context in quantitative studies and result in a more accurate quantification of the burden of illness and its social consequences at the family and population level.

column37: Dr. Bhandari's research program will advance the identification of innovative treatments using high quality collaborative research practices to improve the lives of persons with musculoskeletal injury and disease. Key objectives include the identification of optimal approaches to improve the lives people experiencing musculoskeletal trauma and intimate partner violence, as well as therapies to reduce major adverse events after surgery. Three core themes are the focus of the research program: 1) Advancing Surgical Innovations in Musculoskeletal Trauma 2) Uncovering Novel Insights about Intimate Partner Violence in Surgical Patients 3) Preventing Adverse Outcomes in Surgery The above core research themes are operationalized primarily by the conduct of multi-national large randomized trials and large observational cohort studies. This program of research advances results from prior research and informs treatments across a broader population of persons-those with both acute conditions (fractures) and chronic conditions (arthritis). By conducting 3 large randomized trials, 3 large observational studies, and 1 national knowledge translation program, this research program will transform patient care and deliver new treatments and insights for improving the health outcomes after musculoskeletal injury and disease. This research program will also expand over the next 7 years to include pilot trials in opioid reduction interventions in surgery. The rationale for the three major themes, each with their unique foci, are driven by the increasing global burden of orthopaedic trauma injuries worldwide and the need to identify low cost-effective treatments, the crisis of intentional injuries in women from domestic violence, and the need to identify and reduce adverse outcomes towards safer surgery worldwide.

column37: Cette Chaire de recherche du Canada vise a reconstruire des tissus humains par genie tissulaire a partir de cellules souches qui sont presentes dans les tissus apres la naissance. Le programme s'articule autour de 3 principaux domaines de reconstruction d'organes, soit la peau, la cornee, et les valves cardiaques. L'objectif principal vise a reconstruire, a partir de cellules humaines, des organes humains vivants dont les proprietes histologiques, physiologiques et fonctionnelles se rapprochent le plus possible de celles des tissus d'origine afin d'utiliser ces substituts pour ameliorer la guerison des plaies. Ces tissus reconstruits nous procurent des modeles pour mieux comprendre des phenomenes physiopathologiques (e.g. guerison des plaies ou epidermolyse bulleuse). L'approche experimentale mise sur la methode de genie tissulaire (auto-assemblage) que nous avons decouverte pour reconstruire des tissus vivants sans ajouter de biomateriaux. Le potentiel de ces tissus humains reconstruits comme modeles sophistiques de recherche fondamentale et pre-clinique sera exploite afin d'ameliorer nos connaissances en biologie cellulaire, communications intercellulaires, et developpement de nouveaux traitements. Un des defis consiste a ameliorer la pigmentation des peaux reconstruites. En recherche appliquee, la combinaison du genie tissulaire et de la therapie genique est prometteuse pour la correction de deficits resultant de maladies genetiques. Il s'agit de corriger le gene non fonctionnel par le transfert du gene fonctionnel dans les cellules malades in vitro avant la production des tissus puis leur implantation autologue in vivo. VISION Le point culminant se trouve dans les applications cliniques qui favoriseront le traitement plus rapide des grands brules grace a des peaux reconstruites bilamellaires(PRB, derme et epiderme) autologues; l'amelioration de la surface oculaire des patients atteints de deficiences en cellules souches limbiques par la greffe de culture d'epithelium corneen autologue; le soulagement des patients atteints d'epidermolyse bulleuse dystrophique par la greffe de PRB combinees a la therapie genique. Le besoin grandissant pour les organes de remplacement et les applications du genie tissulaire pour ameliorer la guerison des plaies permettent de predire que cette technologie deviendra un element important pour l'economie de la region. Cette Chaire contribuera a l'excellence et a la renommee de l'Universite Laval en medecine regeneratrice.

column37: Des millions de personnes au Canada sont asthmatiques et 7% a 9% des enfants souffrent d'allergies alimentaires ou d'eczema. Il est reconnu que certaines maladies allergiques sont interreliees et s'inscrivent dans un continuum debutant par de l'eczema chez les nourrissons. Ceux-ci presentent par la suite 35% a 75% plus de risque de developper des allergies alimentaires, de l'asthme ou de la rhinite. Il est capital de mieux comprendre leurs bases biologiques afin de mieux predire, diagnostiquer ou traiter ces maladies. C'est tourne vers ces objectifs, repartis suivant quatre axes de recherche, que se deploiera le programme de recherche de la Chaire en genomique de l'asthme et des maladies allergiques. L'axe 1 vise a poursuivre l'identification des regions du genome associees a ces maladies par l'etude des variations dans le code genetique, de l'expression des genes ainsi que des mecanismes qui l'influencent. Cet axe permettra de mieux comprendre les mecanismes biologiques impliques. L'axe 2 vise l'etude de la diversite microbienne afin d'identifier des profils de risque ou de protection pour le developpement de maladies ou l'application de traitements. Ainsi, la diversite microbienne intestinale, nasale, orale et cutanee des enfants souffrant d'allergies alimentaires et repondant adequatement au traitement de desensibilisation de meme que ceux des individus asthmatiques et non asthmatiques ayant developpe la COVID-19 seront analyses. L'axe 3 vise l'integration des donnees multiples obtenues par les travaux des axes 1 et 2 et permettra par le biais de modeles statistiques complexes le developpement d'outils predictifs, diagnostiques et therapeutiques. Par exemple, la combinaison de plusieurs facteurs genetiques pourrait permettre de detecter quels sont les enfants a risque de presenter des maladies allergiques pour prevenir leur developpement ou reduire leur severite par une intervention precoce. La formation, la mobilisation et le transfert de connaissances aux diverses communautes forment l'axe 4. Plusieurs strategies sont envisagees, incluant des formations specialisees, des conferences, la conception de capsules et chroniques, et l'organisation de session de travail, journees scientifiques et colloques. A la fin du mandat, les connaissances sur la nature biologique de l'asthme et des maladies allergiques seront nettement bonifiees et permettront grace aux outils developpes de reduire le fardeau socioeconomique lie a l'asthme et aux maladies allergiques.

column36: Evidence-Informed Health Systems
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has shown us both how well and how poorly: 1) governments are equipped to find and use research evidence to inform their decision-making; 2) evidence groups are equipped to: a) create the right evidence product at the right time; b) engage stakeholders who can help to understand what the evidence means for a particular decision; and c) use evidence products and work with stakeholders as part of a broader approach to support decision-making; and 3) networks of individuals and groups are equipped to work together and in innovative ways to support decision-making. The proposed program of research will address three objectives: 1) evaluate how government policymakers organize themselves to make decisions based on the best available research evidence; 2) create and evaluate innovative ways that evidence groups can summarize evidence, work with stakeholders and more generally support decision-making; and 3) create and evaluate networks that can support decision-making in more coordinated and innovative ways. For each objective, the focus will include efforts to address both urgent issues (like COVID-19 response) and long-standing issues (like improving care experiences and health outcomes in our health system). The research methods will capture descriptions of, views about, experiences with and the impacts of the approaches being used to inform decision-making. The data will come from existing datasets (e.g., evidence products that have been created) and from interviews, surveys, available documents, and directly observing what individuals and groups do. The governments, evidence groups and networks will be drawn from Canada and internationally, including governments with which I work directly (like the Canadian federal government and many provincial governments) and evidence groups and networks that I lead or co-lead (like the McMaster Health Forum, RISE and COVID-END). Returning to more everyday policy challenges after the worst of the pandemic is over will provide an opportunity to build on what went well in the evidence response to the pandemic, as well as to previous challenges in our health system, and learn from and address what didn't. The research will capitalize on the attention being given to evidence as a result of COVID-19, make significant contributions to the science of supporting decision-making, and shape future efforts to address policy challenges based on the best available research evidence.

column37: Dr. Corey Nislow completed a bachelor of arts in developmental biology at New College (Sarasota, Florida) and PhD in cell and molecular biology at the University of Colorado (Boulder, Colorado). He was also an American Cancer Society postdoctoral fellow. Dr. Nislow served as group leader in two biotechnology companies (MJ Research and Cytokinetics Inc., in the San Francisco Bay Area) and as a senior genome scientist at Stanford University. Prior to joining UBC, Dr. Nislow was associate professor at the University of Toronto and director of the Donnelly Sequencing Centre. Dr. Nislow enjoys teaching all aspects of biotechnology, genomics and drug discovery for undergraduate and graduate students. He also taught a popular course on critical thinking at the University of Toronto. Dr. Nislow's lab employs genomics and develops biotechnology tools such as: 1) Parallel genome-wide chemical genomic screens; 2) High throughput cell-based screens and; 3) Next Generation Sequencing to address both fundamental and applied biological questions. The questions the lab has addressed and plan to address all fall under the theme of understanding how the cell takes the instructions in its DNA, i.e. its genotype, and manifests that information into phenotype in both normal and deranged circumstances. For example, the lab continues to address these questions: 1. How can environmental and drug stress elucidate the condition-specific function of genes? 2. How does the structure and architecture of the genome, manifested as chromatin, influence gene expression and cell physiology? 3. Can we use genomic, chemical genomic, and genome architecture data to infer evolutionary relationships? 4. Finally, how can we apply the tools we develop for model organisms to human biology? Specifically can we combine the power of next-generation sequencing and chemical biology to begin to understand the way in which gene variants affect patient responses to therapeutic intervention?

column36: Global control of HPV related disease and cancer
column37: Despite being almost entirely preventable with HPV vaccination and screening, the World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that one million women globally currently have cervical cancer. In 2019, an estimated 1,300 Canadian women were diagnosed with it and everyday, a woman in Canada will die from cervical cancer. In 2018, the WHO named 'elimination of cervical cancer' as a global public health priority. To accelerate the pace to reach this goal, there is an urgent need to evaluate strategies that both optimize existing programs and catalyze new programs to improve HPV vaccine and screening coverage. My research program, entitled ACE (Accelerating Cervical Cancer Elimination) builds directly on my previous Canada Research Chair work. The overall objective is to define optimal approaches for screening and vaccination, in order to guide policy and clinical care to achieve the elimination of cervical cancer in high, middle and low-income country settings. Through this ambitious research program, I plan to answer critical policy questions around screening and vaccination including the durability of one dose of the HPV vaccine; methods to improve HPV vaccine uptake; long term impact of HPV testing; and use of self-collection HPV DNA testing at a population level to improve screening coverage in Canada and globally. Leveraging British Columbia's unique population-based programs and registries, my research team will evaluate the effectiveness of current reduced dose HPV vaccine schedules; examine effectiveness of one-dose of the HPV vaccine and define strategies for improving HPV vaccine uptake in school based programs. Using the BC Cervix Screening Program and our established HPV FOCAL clinical trial infrastructure, we will examine the long term impact of HPV screening after a decade. To address longstanding inequities in screening coverage, we will examine the impact of different population level recruitment strategies for HPV self-collection testing to increase screening coverage and attendance at care, particularly for women who have never been screened. To shape policy globally and in Canada, we will strengthen and broaden our existing collaborative networks to ensure our findings are disseminated across Canada and internationally. Ultimately, we aim to accelerate Canada's efforts to become the first country, globally, to eliminate cervical cancer and ensure comprehensive knowledge translation of critical findings with our global partners.

column37: Tuberculosis (TB) is one of the greatest threats to global health: a third of the world's population is infected, and 1.4 million deaths occur each year. COVID-19 has worsened the problem by seriously disrupting TB services. The objectives of Dr. Pai's research program is to 1) improve TB diagnosis, 2) address the impact of COVID-19 on TB services, 3) enhance the engagement of private providers in TB, and 4) improve the quality of TB care. Currently available tools are insufficient to control TB. Better diagnostic options and testing programs are urgently required, especially in the context of COVID-19. Objective 1 of Dr. Pai's research is focused on evaluating newer technologies recently developed to improve TB diagnosis, so policies can be developed. Globally, the COVID-19 pandemic has had a devastating impact on TB care. As part of Objective 2, Dr. Pai is working on a damage control plan to help mitigate the effects of the pandemic on essential TB services in low- and middle-income countries. Since COVID-19 and TB have similar symptoms, Dr. Pai is evaluating an integrated approach to testing for both diseases in Peru. Dr. Pai is also leading a project to track the disruptions caused by the pandemic on TB services in the private health sector in India, Indonesia and Nigeria. Dr. Pai's team is heavily involved in improving the engagement of private providers in TB care and control. As part of Objective 3, they curate a community of practice to nurture a dynamic exchange of expertise and best practice to accelerate uptake of what works and close the know-do gap in the area of private provider engagement in TB. His team is also engaged in tracking disruptions due to COVID-19 on private provider engagement projects in multiple countries. Dr. Pai's team developed a novel method for measuring TB care using mystery patients or SPs, who are extensively trained to present the same prespecified condition to providers. In Objective 4, Dr. Pai will expand the SP project to explore interesting new questions in India, Nigeria and Indonesia. The goal of Dr. Pai's research program is to use translational epidemiology and implementation science to improve TB care and control, so that products, knowledge and policies can translate into saved lives. By developing innovative approaches, such as the SP methodology, and conducting work that is relevant for TB program implementation and policy development, Dr. Pai's work is both novel and impactful.

column36: Valvular Heart Disease
column37: Approximately 1,100,000 Canadians (~3.5% of the population) have valvular heart disease (VHD). Aortic valve stenosis (AS) is among the 2 most frequent VHD. If left untreated, severe AS is inevitably fatal and the only available option for the treatment of this disease is the aortic valve replacement (AVR) by a prosthetic valve using surgery (SAVR) or transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVR). AS represents a major public-health and socio-economic burden, which is expected to increase exponentially in the next decades due to population aging. The overarching goal of the proposed research program on the Canada Research Chair (CRC) in VHD is to perform multi-disciplinary, patient-oriented, research to advance the diagnosis, prevention, and treatment of VHD, and particularly of AS. The Chairholder has brought together a consortium of clinicians, scientists, and engineers from academia and industry to achieve a large magnitude and impactful research program that includes 5 main work-packages: WP#1: Develop and validate a novel tool based on capacitive electrocardiography and artificial intelligence (AI) for universal screening of AS in the general population. WP#2: Develop and validate AI-based algorithms: i) to determine the different aortic valve disease phenotype clusters; ii) to identify patients with AS who are at risk for rapid disease progression. WP#3: Undertake a randomized controlled trial (RCT) (EARLY-TAVR) to assess the timing of AVR in asymptomatic severe AS; WP#4: Undertake two RCTs (TAVR-UNLOAD and PROGRESS) to assess the timing of AVR in at-risk moderate AS. WP#5: Undertake a pharmacotherapy RCT that will assess the effect of aggressive lipoprotein(a) lowering to slow stenosis progression in mild to moderate AS. The innovative research program proposed by the Chair for the next 7 years will transform the screening, diagnosis, and treatment of AS. The new technology proposed in WP#1 has the potential of greatly enhancing the efficacy and generalizability of AS screening in the population. The AI-based algorithms developed in WP# 2 will allow the determination of the aortic valve disease phenotypes and of the risk of rapid disease progression in each individual patient, which is key to enable personalized therapeutic management of AS. The RCTs conducted in WPs # 3, 4 5 will constitute major advances for the optimization and individualization of the timing and type (pharmacotherapy vs. SAVR vs. TAVR) of treatment in patients with AS.

column36: Chemical Genetics
column37: Exploiting the Nematode C. elegans as a Platform for Drug Discovery Dr. Roy has pioneered the use of the nematode C. elegans to discover small molecule tools and potential drug leads. Here, he describe his vision for his next seven years of exploration. Parasitic Prodrugs: Dr. Roy's group has discovered a suite of small molecule scaffolds that are bioactivated within nematodes into lethal products. Focusing on 'nemactivin', they have shown its bioactivation is restricted to nematodes and that it has real-world utility against plant parasitic nematodes. They are: i) further developing nemactivin as a nematicide with industrial partners; ii) developing additional nematicide prodrugs, and iii) building a system to identify otherwise innocuous small molecules that can be metabolically converted into lethal products within any targeted organism. Novel Neuromodulators: Dr. Roy's group has developed a pipeline to identify small molecule disruptors of motor behaviour in nematodes. They discovered a scaffold called 'nementin' that induces convulsions, paralysis and death though massive synaptic vesicle release. They are: i) further developing nementin with industrial partners; and ii) characterizing a second neuromodulatory molecule called wact-45 that inhibits a neurotransmitter transporter. Wact-45 has anthelmintic potential and is a candidate drug for Myasthenic Syndrome, a rare human disease caused by excess neurotransmitter release. Liver Disease Drugs: Dr. Roy's group discovered that select small molecules form crystals within the C. elegans alimentary cuticle. At least two cuticle components are required for this phenomenon; intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs- see below) and polar lipids. The group found that the PGP-14 worm homolog of the ABCB4 polar lipid pump, which is mutated in the liver disease PFIC3, is required for cuticle lipid accumulation. They identified 30 FDA drugs that suppress the pgp-14 mutant's lipid deficit and are exploring these as candidate drugs to treat PFIC3. Amyloid Disruptors: As introduced above, Dr. Roy's group discovered small molecules that crystallize in the alimentary cuticle through interactions with amyloid-like IDPs. Molecules that prevent human amyloid formation disrupt crystal formation in the IDP-rich cuticle. Dr. Roy's group is exploiting this system to identify novel small molecule that disrupt amyloid formation and develop them as candidate treatments of amyloid-based diseases such as Alzheimer's.

column36: Giving children the best start in life: Understanding the role of maternal and paternal parenting behaviours and mental health in early child development
column37: The early childhood environment (i.e., from conception to age 5 years) is crucial for healthy child development. Children's mental development - that is the cognitive, language, and socioemotional skills children acquire in early life - constitutes the building blocks of a healthy, well-educated, and productive society. Ensuring a healthy early environment is thus an important investment in the long-term outcomes of individuals and the communities in which they live. Research suggests that parenting behaviours and parental mental health - particularly parental depression - are two of the most important determinants of children's mental development, but the mechanisms (i.e., mediators and moderators) through which they shape child development, especially in low- and middle-income country contexts, are only beginning to be explored. The aim of my research project is to use intervention and observational research to better understand the impact of maternal and paternal parenting behaviours and mental health on children's mental development. My objectives are to (1) review and summarize the impact of interventions in low- and middle-income countries to improve maternal and paternal parenting behaviours or treat/prevent maternal and parental depression on children's mental development; (2) examine the mechanisms of the association of maternal and paternal parenting behaviours and mental health with children's mental development in a large South African birth cohort (Birth to Twenty Plus Cohort), and (3) test the efficacy of an intervention comparing the separate and combined effects of improving maternal and paternal parenting behaviours and mental health on children's mental development in Pakistan. This research will contribute to our understanding of how the early family environment influences child development in low- and middle-income countries and can be used to inform global evidence-based family policies and programmes to give children the best start in life.

column36: Neuroimaging of Aging
column37: Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) is a uniquely non-invasive and versatile neuroimaging method that provides both neuronal and vascular readouts and was the focus of Dr. Chen's first CRC term. Specifically, the rs-fMRI technique can be used to obtain maps of intrinsic brain networks, which are believed to sustain cognitive function. Moreover, it inadvertently provides vascular information, which can, in turn, be capitalized in the study of vascular aging. Dr. Chen and her team were the first in the world to elucidate the vascular and physiological contributions to rs-fMRI by showing the contribution of CVR, cerebral blood flow, blood oxygenation saturation, vasomotion, and respiratory cycles to rs-fMRI measurements. Dr. Chen's team also demonstrated how rs-fMRI could become a method for mapping cerebrovascular reactivity (CVR). CVR is a measure of vascular health that is highly valued clinically, given its reliable prediction of cerebrovascular disease. Since establishing the only existing rs-fMRI-based CVR quantification technique, Dr. Chen and her collaborators have validated the resting-state CVR mapping technique in varying clinical scenarios. The publications resulting from her first CRC term have helped propel me into a recognized world leader in rs-fMRI of brain physiology. In her second CRC term, Dr. Chen will innovate methods for extracting neurovascular information from rs-fMRI data. Specifically, she will probe the relationship between whole-body vascular health and neurovascular health, and clarify the association between vascular and microstructural changes in the brain, which can clarify the neurodegenerative process and help identify new treatment targets. She will also, through industry and clinical collaborations, translate her research findings into new therapeutic tools and practices. Specifically, she will expand on her research program with 4 research themes. ? Theme 1. Mapping neurovascular physiology in brain aging. ? Theme 2. Understanding the brain-body connection in aging and age-related disease. ? Theme 3. Clarify the vascular contribution to early microstructural brain changes in aging. ? Theme 4. Applying neurovascular mapping to age-related diseases and therapies. The proposed research will be important for advancing health screening and care and will be critical for enhancing collaborations across the Baycrest and University of Toronto network across Ontario, Canada, and abroad.

column36: Gut Microbial Physiology
column37: The trillions of microorganisms found in the gut, the gut microbiota, are key to our health: from drug metabolism, digestion, immune and brain development, to our resistance to disease. However, we do not know how the two most abundant members of this community, namely bacteria and bacteriophages, interact in health or disease. An increasing number of pathologies are being associated with changes in gut microbial communities. Therefore, there is an important need to better understand these microbial interactions and their dynamics in order to effectively devise gut microbiota-targeted therapeutic strategies. Here, I propose to leverage the exciting data we have gathered so far to (1) characterize who the active bacteria in the human gut are, and what they are doing; and (2) identify how their biggest threat, bacteriophages, impact them and what they are doing. Results from this research will translate into new therapeutic opportunities based on the targeted manipulation of different members of the gut microbiota.

column36: Near Infrared Spectroscopy for the Non-Invasive Characterization of Cerebral Autoregulation in Moderate and Severe Traumatic Brain Injury
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is one of the leading causes of death and disability around the world. Unfortunately, the treatment of TBI has failed to make significant strides in the past 25 years, with patients not having significantly improved recoveries. One cause of this may be dysfunctional cerebral autoregulation (CA). This is when the brain loses its ability to control its own blood flow after a TBI. Recent technological developments have allowed for the continuous monitoring of CA. This is important since the level of dysfunctional CA seems to be linked to how well patients recover after TBI. However, these methods require the placement of probes into the brain. This puts the patient at risk of further brain injury and limits these methods to the intensive care unit (ICU). There are methods that have been developed to non-invasively evaluate CA using a harmless form of light called near infrared light. The method, called near infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), may be a safer alternative to current methods. My research aims to test if NIRS based methods of measuring CA are a good alternative to current invasive methods in TBI. Our study is enrolling all TBI patients with invasive monitoring admitted to our ICU. As part of the study, we also measure NIRS based CA while they are in the ICU. At 3, 6, and 12 months after their injury we follow up with them and evaluate how they are recovering using standardized questionnaires. Also, because NIRS based measures of CA are non-invasive, we measure their level of CA dysfunction at that time. Using this data, we can compare the invasive measure of CA with NIRS based measures of CA to see if they are similar. We can also see if NIRS based measures of CA are able to predict how patients will do after a TBI. Finally, we will also be able to see how CA, measured by NIRS, recovers in the long term after TBI. This may lead to safer and more effective care for patients and give us insight into how the brain recovers from TBI.

column36: A deep phenotyping network for understanding human islet variation in health and diabetes
column37: Insulin is secreted from cells of the pancreatic islets of Langerhans into the blood after a meal to control blood sugar levels. In type 1 diabetes (T1D) islet cells are destroyed by an auto-immune reaction. In type 2 diabetes (T2D), islet cells fail to produce enough insulin to meet the body's needs. Thus, understanding the factors that control insulin production by islet cells is an important step towards determining the causes of diabetes, the potential for diabetes reversal, an ultimately prevention of the disease. Even in people without diabetes insulin levels in the blood are extremely variable and is impacted by factors that include nutrition, genetics, and exposure to environmental chemicals. This variation can also be seen in insulin secreted by pancreatic islets isolated from the pancreas of organ donors. Led by the Alberta Diabetes Institute IsletCore, one of the world's top pancreas tissue biobanks, our team of experts will catalog the variability in human insulin secretion, islet cell functions, and molecular profiles across many pancreas organ donors with and without diabetes. The result will be a comprehensive 'encyclopedia' and web portal that links genetics, gene expression, environmental chemical exposures, metabolites, islet proteins, and more with detailed cellular functions of insulin-producing islet cells. Our Team will also answer key questions about how genetic-risk for diabetes acts to impair insulin secretion; about personalized insulin responses to different nutrients; and about the links between environmental pollution and reductions in insulin secretion. We will also make this 'encyclopedia' available to researchers around the world, supporting a better understanding of human insulin secretion and diabetes.

column36: A First-in-human Trial of Autologous Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells (iPSC)-Derived Islets: Developing a Personalized Diabetes Therapy
column37: Diabetes is caused by the lack of insulin, a hormone produced by the islet Beta-cells in the pancreas that regulates blood sugar. Chronically high blood sugar can cause complications such as blindness, amputations, stroke, heart disease, kidney failure and shortened lifespan. Insulin injection is lifesaving but is not a cure. Islet transplant has been successful in regulating blood sugar levels in some patients with T1D; however, it requires life-long anti-rejection (immunosuppression) drugs and is limited by the scarcity of organ donors. Building on our 21 years of experience in islet transplant, our team will address these challenges by developing a stem-cell based therapy to replace or supplement damaged Beta-cells in people with various forms of diabetes, including T1D, T2D, and surgical diabetes after total pancreatectomy. We propose to manufacture new islet beta cells from patients' own blood cells, so that the cells will be accepted by the immune system and no anti-rejection drugs will be needed. In this project, we will generate 'self'-islets from people with diabetes and implant these cells under the patient's skin. In parallel, we will transplant these cells into rats. We will also test whether these cells function similarly to human islets. We anticipate that this project will establish safety of the manufactured 'self'-islets and that they can produce insulin. This will pave the way to our next step - Health Canada approval for a clinical trial with therapeutic doses to be infused in the liver to assess efficacy of this cell therapy. Being able to transplant an unlimited supply of self-derived islet cells without immunosuppressants is a novel approach to treat various forms of diabetes and could be the world's first functional cure.

column36: Designing Stem Cell Derived Islets for Diabetes Therapy
column37: Diabetes is a debilitating disorder of high blood sugar that afflicts millions of Canadians. People living with type 1 diabetes lack the cells that release the hormone insulin, so multiple daily insulin injections remain the conventional way to control blood sugar levels and survive. Scientists in Edmonton made breakthroughs for the transplant of clusters of insulin-producing cells, called islets. The "Edmonton Protocol" is quick and works remarkably well, such that many islet recipients are able to reduce or even eliminate insulin injections. Unfortunately, the only source of islets for transplant is recently deceased donors and only a tiny fraction of those in need can receive them. There have been remarkable breakthroughs in unraveling the process by which islet cells develop naturally in the body. As a result, it is now possible to replicate this process in the lab with cultured stem cells, culminating in insulin producing cells. Exciting clinical trials are now underway in which islet precursor cells generated from stem cells are loaded into thin devices and implanted under the skin. While initial assessments in patients are encouraging, insulin production from the transplanted cells is currently inadequate to reverse diabetes. Our goal is to utilize our broad expertise and a new lab-based model of human islet development to significantly improve upon the manufacturing of the islets to obtain more robust insulin delivery. To achieve this, we have assembled a team of leading experts who will apply their diverse and complementary skills to develop novel strategies to improve the generation of fully functional stem cell derived islets. In particular, we will engineer new cell culture methods to selectively control islet architecture and enhance cell fitness. Collectively our work may form the basis for new clinical trials in patients with type 1 diabetes, and ultimately generate an effective therapy that will free Canadians from insulin injections.

column36: Immunometabolism in diabetes: harnessing metabolic crosstalk between islets and immune cells for therapy
column37: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease that occurs when the immune system mistakenly kills the beta cells in the pancreas that produce the hormone, insulin. A true cure for T1D requires the immune system to be reset, so that it no longer attacks the pancreas, and for the insulin-producing beta cells to be replaced or regenerated. We have assembled a unique team of experts in the biology of immune cells and insulin-producing beta cells in diabetes, to study how these cells interact in diabetes, and understand why the immune system becomes over-activated and kills the insulin-producing beta cells and causes T1D. We will focus on a growing area of research known as immunometabolism, which is the study of how metabolic pathways inside cells affect their ability to divide and function. We propose that changes in metabolic pathways within beta cells and immune cells may enhance the immune attack on the pancreas. We will study metabolic pathways in immune cells in health and in T1D. Through this work we hope to gain a better understanding of how changes in metabolism in immune cells may influence autoimmunity, and to design ways to alter these metabolic pathways in immune cells to prevent or slow T1D.

column37: Diabetes is the most common cause of kidney failure in Canada, and requires either dialysis or a kidney transplant. Kidney failure leads to persistent unpleasant symptoms that reduce quality of life to levels seen in certain types of advanced cancers. In addition, kidney failure increases the likelihood of cardiovascular disease and premature death. Fortunately, new therapies called "SGLT2 inhibitors" have been discovered that reduce the risk of kidney failure and cardiovascular diseases in people with a kind of diabetes linked with being overweight, called "type 2 diabetes". These drugs may delay the need for dialysis by as much as 15 years, or prevent it entirely. Unfortunately, it is not known if these medicines are also beneficial for people with type 1 diabetes ("juvenile diabetes"), and these medicines are not approved in North America for use in this condition. In our research program, we will perform a series of studies in people with type 1 diabetes. First, we will study kidney effects of SGLT2 inhibition in people with type 1 diabetes over a two year treatment period, including routine blood and urine tests that reflect kidney protection. We will also perform research-based blood and urine tests to understand how these medications may reduce kidney damage over the long term. We will also examine ways to avoid side effects. As part of this study, we will study how patients feel about taking these medications, in terms of both benefits and side effects. Next, we will use Danish health records (where SGLT2 inhibitors can be used for type 1 diabetes) to determine if these therapies reduce the risk of kidney disease when used as part of routine care in type 1 diabetes. Finally, we will study the effectiveness of these medications as a long-term kidney protective therapy using mathematical models. Overall, this program has the potential to reduce the risk of diabetes complications and improve the quality of life in people living with this serious condition.

column37: For individuals living with diabetes, one of the major complications of the disease is diabetic retinopathy (DR), which, if not treated, can lead to blindness. Unfortunately, not everyone living with diabetes sees an eye care professional regularly. Screening rates are lowest in the populations most vulnerable to adverse health outcomes in Canada, including younger individuals, individuals located in large cities in low-income communities, newer immigrants, in rural, remote and Indigenous communities. Depending on where a person lives in Canada, up to 60% of individuals living with diabetes have not had their eyes examined within 1 year. Knowing who has not had their eyes checked is not always possible for community-based doctors and nurses by looking at their electronic health records. This information, however, is found in provincial healthcare data. Giving this information to doctors and nurses would help to improve DR screening (DRS) rates across the country. This project proposes to support primary healthcare DRS activities by using provincial administrative data in Ontario, Alberta, British Columbia and New Foundland and Labrador to determine who needs to have their eyes examined according to clinical practice guidelines. The generated lists of individuals will be provided to community care setting to arrange an eye appointment using existing optometry, ophthalmology and tele-ophthalmology services. Coordination and capacity of care within the four provinces will also be examined. We will use various research methods to evaluate the effectiveness, cost-effectiveness, implementation challenges, sex and gender-related differences in care provision, and critical factors to success. The broader goal of this public health initiative is to identify unmet care needs and begin the pathway towards the creation of a Canadian DRS programme, similar to that in the United Kingdom, and consequently eliminate DR as the leading cause of blindness in working-age individuals.

column36: The Developmental Origins of Pediatric Type 2 Diabetes and Early Renal Dysfunction
column37: T2D in childhood continues to increase worldwide and affects Indigenous children and families more than non-Indigenous populations. Childhood onset T2D is associated with high rates of early onset rapidly progressive kidney disease. As more children are diagnosed with T2D, more babies are being born having been exposed to diabetes in the womb (in utero). Consequently, we now know that diabetes exposure in utero is a potent risk factor for the exposed child to develop childhood-onset T2D; however, it is not yet known how diabetes exposure increases the risk or if it increases risk of associated renal complications. Recent scientific advances have revealed that the environment in the womb can alter the expression of genes in the offspring via a process called "epigenetic regulation", which can impact important metabolic pathways needed to maintain health. In addition, a specific change in the DNA sequence (HNF1a gene variant) also imparts a risk of T2D development in the offspring. In this study, we aim to define the epigenetic signature of babies born to mothers with diabetes so that we can determine which genes and pathways are affected by this exposure. Subsequently, we aim to use mouse and cell models to examine how these epigenetic changes impact function of important metabolic tissues, including the pancreas. Finally, we will examine how the HNF1a variant results in T2D risk for children and if it also impacts renal development, function and risk. Upon completion of this study, we hope to better understand how maternal diabetes exposure and the HNF1a gene variant impacts offspring health, to identify biomarkers at birth that can be used to determine which children are at highest risk of developing T2D, and to inform the development of new treatments to prevent T2D and renal complications in exposed children.

column36: Central role of muscle autophagy in metabolism and musculoskeletal health
column37: Diabetes and osteoarthritis (OA) are two of the most common diseases affecting approximately 11 million and 4 million Canadians, respectively. Diabetes is associated with several serious complications, including eye disease, nerve damage, foot ulcers, kidney disease, heart attack, and stroke. OA can cause chronic pain, making it challenging for individuals to exercise, walk, and carry out daily activities such as getting dressed or bathing. Furthermore, both diabetes and OA are associated with depression and can significantly impact a person's quality of life. Despite how common and debilitating these conditions are, there is no cure for either. Therefore, we need to understand their underlying causes better to identify more effective treatment targets and earlier detection. Diabetes (specifically type 2 diabetes (T2D)) and OA often occur together, and both are associated with a condition called sarcopenia. Sarcopenia refers to the loss of muscle mass and strength that occurs with aging. We, therefore, thought that sarcopenia and changes within the muscle might provide a common link between T2D and OA. Autophagy is a process that basically "cleans out" damaged components of cells. When autophagy is reduced or not working properly in muscle, damaged cell components accumulate, and this contributes to sarcopenia. This team project aims to determine how problems with muscle autophagy contribute to T2D and OA. To do this, we will study mouse models in which genes regulating autophagy have been altered in muscle. We will also test if we can treat or reverse T2D and OA using gene therapy to correct the defect in autophagy in muscle. Finally, we will take samples of muscle and blood from individuals suffering from these conditions and analyze them to identify common genetic links between T2D and OA to identify new drug targets.

column36: Development and Validation of Case Definitions for Cannabis Use Disorder within Administrative Data Sets
column37: Background: Cannabis use disorder (CUD), or cannabis addiction, refers to the continued use of cannabis despite clinically significant impairment. Unfortunately, there is a shortage of information on CUD to guide healthcare. However, tapping into population-level data may improve CUD detection, documentation, prevention, and management. One source is health administrative data, which includes routinely collected diagnostic and procedural codes from encounters with the healthcare system. First, however, we must create and verify a "case definition" for CUD to use administrative data for CUD research. Case definitions are computer algorithms that combine diagnostic and procedural codes to identify people with CUD. In this project, we will use the latest technologies for complex data to change the current shortage of information about CUD into a wealth of new information that can be used to design new treatments, target the deployment of new services, and assess the impact of new treatments. Aims: We will validate and compare the accuracy of several CUD case definitions in Alberta administrative health data. Methods: Trained record reviewers will review 5,000 randomly selected files from a Calgary tertiary addiction centre and code them for the presence of CUD and link them to administrative health data. These records will serve as a reference standard for verifying case definitions. Two approaches for validating case definitions will be used and compared. In the traditional approach, we will make up a few case definitions and measure how sensitive and specific each is for CUD. In the second approach, we will use machine learning, in which a technique capable of learning from the data would be used to identify the best definition. Impact and Significance: Determining case definitions for substance use disorders in administrative health databases will lay the groundwork for future research.

column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a debilitating degenerative condition common among the elderly that affects 50 million people world-wide, including over 500,000 in Canada alone. AD patients first lose the ability to remember names, faces, and places, but ultimately lose the ability to communicate and function independently. These challenges are made much worse by other serious illnesses which often emerge over the course of AD, including depression, anxiety, agitation, infection, and metabolic disorders. In fact, these co-occurring conditions are what most often lead to loss of function and death in patients. Therefore, it is of the highest importance for scientists to understand the relationship between the progression of AD and these accompanying diseases. The proposed project will analyze data from over 33,000 individuals from Canada and the United States, who have been followed from middle age, with a subset also having brain autopsy data available. Using these resources, and cutting-edge statistical techniques combining clinical, cognitive, genetic, and sociodemographic data, we will identify the genes, environments, and behaviours that most significantly predict the emergence of a wide array of health conditions in individuals who develop AD. With these predictive models, it may become possible to detect problematic patterns early, while individuals are still middle-aged and without signs of dementia, giving them the chance to make lifestyle and medical changes before it is too late. These models also have the potential to reveal molecular causes of these co-occurring conditions in the context of AD, offering new insights for further research into novel therapeutics.

column36: Uncovering the Link between Neurocognitive Functioning and Suicide Attempt with Machine Learning
column37: Suicide is the second leading cause of death among youth ages 10-24. Although most widely recognized suicide risk factors, such as hopelessness and impulsivity, are strong predictors for considering suicide, these do not accurately predict who will eventually attempt suicide. Developing prediction models that distinguish patients who will attempt suicide from patients with suicidal ideation but no attempts can save lives. Although individuals with depressed mood and impulsivity commonly present with cognitive processing difficulties (e.g., attention, memory), or "deficits," research findings are mixed regarding whether these factors predict suicide attempt. Furthermore, research shows enhanced cognitive processing abilities predict suicide behavior as well. For these reasons, I hypothesize that complex relationships exist, such that cognitive deficits alone may not predict attempt, but unique combinations of cognitive abilities and psychological symptoms (e.g., social withdrawal) will predict suicide attempt beyond single or traditional risk factors. The ability of computer-based algorithms to learn unique patterns that are difficult to detect with traditional methods is central to this investigation. To test this hypothesis, I am conducting the first investigation to my knowledge that predicts youth suicide attempt using a cognitive functioning and psychological symptom profile. The CAMH Toronto Adolescent and Youth Cohort Study is unprecedented in Canada in collecting data from psychodiagnostic assessments, multi-informant clinical measures, and cognitive testing on an annual basis for five years from 3000 at-risk youth ages 11 to 24. Computer-based algorithms will utilize this assessment data to predict future suicide attempts over the next year. Using information technology to identify patients at heightened suicide risk will have a critical impact on improving clinical decision making and suicide prevention efforts for high-risk patients.

column36: Developing neurocomputational assays for suicidality to improve understanding, diagnosis and prevention interventions
column37: Suicide is the second leading cause of death among young adults and among the top ten causes of death across all ages worldwide. Current clinical practice relies mainly on self-report measures and lacks objective tests for assessing suicide risk, resulting in a trial-and error process for early interventions. Our aim is to develop tools that can provide a more objective and accurate way to assess suicide risk and can offer important insights into the associated brain mechanisms, paving the way for more individualized clinical interventions. Our approach combines computerized cognitive tasks with state-of-the-art computational models of the brain to probe specific stress related brain mechanisms that are implicated in suicidality. The tasks are optimized for capturing cognitive and behavioral markers of suicidal ideation, while the models act as a metaphorical microscope allowing us to peer into the underlying brain mechanisms. With this research proposal we aim to validate our recently developed model of suicidality via i) a large-scale behavioral study, which will allow us to identify different subtypes of suicidality that can be revealed through the proposed model and ii) a neuroimaging study, which will allow us to establish the relationships between the model variables and the brain circuits . Both of these studies will serve to test our model predictions and to further refine the model. In their final form, such model-based assays would be readily applicable in clinical practice, requiring minimal time and equipment and enabling more individualized interventions. It would be the first assay of this kind for suicidality, establishing Canada as a world leader in precision psychiatry techniques.
