column36: Infectious Immunopathogenesis
column37: The immune system is constantly confronted with microbes and must assess each for potential threat and then respond appropriately. A weak response may allow pathogenic microbes to overwhelm the body while an overzealous or incorrect response may cause inadvertent tissue damage or lead to autoimmune disease. Disease-causing microbes have evolved elegant strategies to subvert or suppress effective immune responses in order to colonize human tissues. Dr. Gray- Owen's research group is focused on understanding the molecular and immunologic interactions between bacterial and viral pathogens and their host, with an aim to learn how these microbes control the immune response. The pathogenic Neisseria are bacteria that are so highly adapted to life in humans that they are unable to live in the environment or infect other animals. Neisseria meningitidis colonizes nasal passages and can rapidly progress to blood infections and meningitidis. Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes a sexually transmitted infection that can cause scarring of the reproductive tract, sterility, and blindness of newborns. Both pathogens use the same strategies to persist in their host: they continuously modify their surface, directly inhibit otherwise effective immune processes, and stimulate ineffective immune responses to cause potentially devastating effects. Dr. Gray-Owen aims to learn how Neisseria manipulate the host's immune response and to develop vaccines that target the immune evasion processes that allow Neisseria to cause infection. His research group is generating a "humanized" mouse that expresses relevant human proteins to serve as a model for their Neisseria studies. Using innovative systems-based approaches, they aim to identify the metabolic and fitness factors that allow Neisseria to infect their human host. Moreover, they have discovered that Neisseria release an extraordinary class of sugar, the heptose phosphates, with immune modulating activity, and are now working to apply this to elicit immune responses that control infection, autoimmunity, and cancer. Beyond the tangible applications of new therapies and vaccines, Dr. Gray-Owen's broad multidisciplinary research program trains future leaders with a comprehensive perspective on scientific discovery and the tools to effectively translate new innovations into practice.

column36: Blood Cancers
column37: Dr. Karsan is internationally recognized for his research in two distinct areas of medicine. He has made seminal discoveries in understanding how blood cells become cancerous. He is also a world leader in developing genomic tests that are translated in the clinic to evaluate cancer and other patients. Currently his research is focused on understanding how blood cancers become resistant to various treatments, finding ways to detect this resistance earlier, and developing new approaches to therapy for patients who do not respond to standard treatment. Acute myeloid leukemia is a type of blood cancer that is extremely difficult to treat. The vast majority of adults with this cancer will die of their disease. These blood cancers are propagated by rare leukemic stem cells that are able to evade most current therapies, even though these therapies are extremely toxic to the patient and their normal cells. There are often different types of leukemic stem cells in an individual patient's cancer. In order to understand how to cure this deadly cancer, we need to understand the properties of different types of leukemic stem cells that can escape toxic treatments. This will require approaches to study the cancerous cells at a single cell level. Dr. Karsan has recently developed or optimized various assays that can examine the genomic and epigenomic changes, as well as functional activity in single cancer cells. Dr. Karsan's research will use these cutting-edge genomic, epigenomic and functional techniques to interrogate single blood cancer cells individually. This work will help define which of the genomic or epigenomic changes found lead to cancer cells escaping therapy. It will also help to elucidate what role immune and other normal cells play in helping cancer cells elude therapy. Armed with this knowledge Dr. Karsan will develop clinical tests to detect these changes, and thus allow patients the potential for being treated earlier in the course of their disease. The knowledge generated will also be used to understand how many different types of leukemic stem cells are present in individual tumors and to look for common pathways that might make multiple types of leukemic stem cells vulnerable if targeted. Hence, this research is designed to understand how acute myeloid leukemias resist therapy and to find vulnerabilities of the leukemic stem cells that may potentially be targeted with novel therapies, or by repurposing existing medicines.

column37: Dr. Kizhakkedathu is internationally recognized for research in the field of biomaterials and immunomodulation, has advanced the direction of the biomaterials field, consistently produced high impact publications (e.g., Nat. Biotech., Nat. Mat., Nat. Biomed. Eng., Sci. Trans. Med., Nat. Commun., Blood, J. Am. Chem. Soc., Biomaterials) and has a citation H-index of 49. He developed innovative technologies resulting in four start-ups, has an excellent grant funding record, ensured effective collaboration and empowered young researchers. The research focus of the translational program is material innovation for biology with a focus of immunomodulation and immunotherapy. Inflammatory diseases and immune mediated diseases affect 1 in 3 Canadians and cost the Canadian economy >$100 billion each year. Thrombosis is the underlying cause of many cardiovascular diseases which is the single most common cause of death in the western world. Disseminated intravascular coagulation is the root cause of increased mortality and organ failure in Sepsis which accounts for ~5.3 million deaths/year worldwide. Microvascular impairment due to inflammation and immune-mediated damage are the major reasons for transplant rejection and chronic kidney diseases. Current treatments for these diseases are sub-optimal, emphasizing the need for improved prevention and treatment methods, and is the focus of Chair's research program. Building on his recent discoveries the Chair's laboratory will utilize unique biologically active polymers, bioengineering & novel chemistry approaches, and animal models to develop novel therapeutics and treatment approaches to prevent immunothrombosis, protect vascular impairment and prevent immune-mediated transplant rejection. This will realize better transplantation outcome, change the way patients are treated for thrombosis, and develop new therapeutic approaches to protect microvascular damage in inflammation. This interdisciplinary research involves material chemistry and bioengineering in combination with disease specific models to realize novel immunotherapy, and will be based at the University of British Columbia (UBC), consistently ranked among the top Universities globally, with particular strength in the life sciences. World leading facilities and outstanding research and training environments will be provided by UBC's Centre for Blood Research and Life Sciences Institute, two premier life sciences research institutes in Canada.

column36: Cognitive Health and Mobility in Aging
column37: The number of adults over the age of 65 is expected to double in the next 20 years. Thus, it is imperative we discover and implement effective strategies that can promote healthy aging at a population level. Healthy aging is defined by the World Health Organization "as the process of developing and maintaining the functional ability that enables wellbeing in older age". Both cognitive function and mobility are vital to functional ability. Yet, one new case of dementia is detected every three seconds worldwide, and falls - a consequence of impaired mobility - are the leading cause of death in those aged 65 years or older. Evidence shows exercise promotes both cognitive health and mobility in aging. However, precise exercise recommendations remain elusive. Thus, research efforts are critically needed to better understand what (e.g., type of exercise) should be recommended, for whom (e.g., female vs. male), and when (e.g., midlife vs. late life). All three of these will need to be informed by knowledge regarding how exercise benefits cognition and mobility. The overarching vision of my research is to promote functional independence and quality of life in aging Canadians. The goal is to generate and implement precise exercise recommendations to promote cognitive and mobility outcomes in aging - with a focus on those at risk for decline. This research will enable precise recommendations that maximize the benefits of exercise for individuals, shape practice guidelines, and be implemented into communities and healthcare services to promote healthy aging.

column36: Infectious Diseases
column37: The current pandemic has highlighted key gaps in knowledge about how respiratory viruses spread and how vaccines can optimally be used. Questions about the impact of prior year(s) influenza vaccination, the duration of protection of mRNA COVID-19 vaccines, the optimal timing and number of booster doses required, and the effect of recurrent vaccination remain unanswered. Dr. Mark Loeb has conducted clinical trials and longitudinal studies of influenza vaccination for the past 15 years in Hutterite colonies, a unique population where questions about vaccine efficacy herd immunity can be optimally addressed. Currently he is conducting a cohort study on COVID-19 in Hutterite colonies to better understand transmission and the role of existing immunity. Dr. Loeb has also conducted studies in residents of long-term care facilities on immune response to vaccination. As a holder of a Canada Research Chair, Dr. Loeb will conduct studies comparing vaccine strategies in both these populations. In long-term care, he will assess the effect of vaccine booster doses and will conduct comparative studies of influenza vaccine. He will continue his longitudinal studies in Hutterite colonies and will make use of a large biobank of specimens to explain variability in vaccine response and efficacy. The anticipated outcome of Dr. Loeb's Canada Research Chair program will be a better understanding of how to best prevent respiratory viral infections. All the research projects address a particular aspect of vaccination, either in children, healthy adults, and the frail elderly. The research will answer key questions that will directly inform vaccine policy decisions about vaccine efficacy including selection of influenza vaccines and about COVID-19 vaccines in the frail elderly.

column36: Molecular Stratification of Gynecologic Cancers
column37: This year alone, >1.3 million people globally will face a diagnosis of gynecologic cancer and >900,000 (69%) will die from their disease. Categorization and approach to cancer research and clinical management has moved beyond anatomic site with increasing appreciation of the genomic differences between tumors and how these differences impact presentation of disease, response to therapy, and outcomes. My research program aims to advance precision medicine for people with gynecologic cancer through molecular stratification; categorizing cancers into biologically similar subsets that will direct their care and treatment. Further, implementation of more objective molecular categorization of tumors and algorithms will reduce disparities in cancer care. Theme 1 - Molecular classification in endometrial cancers (EC); providing a new framework for research interrogation and a paradigm change in clinical care. EC is on track to become the 2nd most common cancer (after breast) in the next 2 decades in the developed world. Pathological parameters to classify patients and guide management are irreproducible and do not accurately reflect tumor biology or predict risk of metastatic disease or outcomes. Consequently, individuals are over- or under-treated. In clinical trials diverse EC patients are grouped together, effectively comparing outcomes between apples and oranges. My research will explore prognostic and predictive biomarkers within the 4 main molecular subtypes. I am co-leading clinical trials directing de-escalation of treatment based on molecular features. Our research has already transformed standard of care and will continue to have a profound impact with the goal of markedly improving EC outcomes. Theme 2 - Stratification of HPV-associated and HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell cancer; improving treatment in an era of personalized cancer care. Vulvar cancer is uncommon, under researched and occurs mostly in an 'invisible' patient population: older, often frail post-menopausal individuals. My research program aims to implement molecular stratification at all stages of management of vulvar squamous precancer and cancers, driving change in surgical approach, adjuvant therapy, and surveillance. We are studying the importance of margin status and how molecular features can refine pathological reporting. We have begun a clinical trial, stratifying care by molecular features and will measure improvements in clinical outcomes, health costs, and quality of life.

column36: Human Milk and Infant Nutrition
column37: The Problem: Human milk is the optimal source of nutrition for all infants, but for those born of very low birth weight (VLBW, born <1500 grams), it could be lifesaving. Despite improved outcomes when compared to using formula, neurodevelopment remains suboptimal for many human milk-fed VLBW infants due to a poor understanding of the variability in milk composition, factors that influence this, and a one size fits all approach to milk nutrient fortification. This problem is compounded by the fact that most parents, particularly those who are socially and/or economically vulnerable, are unable to provide a sufficient volume of milk, and a supplement is required. Dr. Deborah O'Connor and her colleagues have demonstrated the benefits of using supplemental pasteurized donor human milk (PDHM) over formula, such as a reduction in the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis, a bowel emergency. However, PDHM does not mimic other clinical benefits of mother's milk. Overarching Goal: Improve growth and neurodevelopment of VLBW infants through novel strategies to improve their nutrition. Strategies: a) Evaluate the efficacy of "precision nutrition" or individualized approaches to nutrient enriching human milk tailored to milk composition or infant metabolic response to nutrition. b) Characterize the effect of parental factors (e.g. body mass index, diet quality, poverty, antibiotic use) on preterm milk composition and determine what impact this has on infant development. c) Evaluate the safety and efficacy of replacing thermal pasteurization with high hydrostatic processing to produce PDHM. d) Evaluate an evidence-based approach to reduce inequities in parent-milk feeding. Approach: Dr. O'Connor, an international expert in human milk and infant nutrition, will leverage the NICU feeding network she co-leads to carry out the research plan. Partners include clinician site leads, parents, regulators, human milk banking leaders, dairy scientists, engineers, immunologists, statisticians, and trainees. Through deep integration of new product development and clinical testing into the shared work and goals of these partners, research findings will result in meaningful change. Significance: VLBW infants are at elevated risk of suboptimal neurodevelopment accounting for 50% of all long-term neurological morbidity among children in Canada. As mother's milk and nutrient intakes are independently related to neurodevelopment, strategies to promote both are required.

column36: Geriatric Medicine and Healthy Aging
column37: Nearly one-quarter of all Canadian older adults report having three or more chronic conditions. It is well established that the number of chronic diseases, and not age, drives health care system use by older adults. As our society rapidly ages, there has never been a greater need to redesign the delivery of healthcare in Canada to address the needs of older adults with complex conditions effectively and efficiently. The overall aim of this program of research is to improve geriatric care models across the continuum of care focusing on the 5M's of geriatric medicine: mind, mobility, medications, multi-complexity and what matters most for older adults. As a clinician-scientist, Dr. Papaioannou's research is informed by real-life environments where she works with patients, families, researchers, policymakers, and industry partners to co-create innovative solutions to improve patient care and quality of life. Her program of research has 2 aims: 1) evaluating new models of geriatric care for older adults living with frailty including two large clinical trials developing 'frailty rehabilitation'; 2) working with cross-disciplinary academic partners to advance novel, technological aging solutions and develop a greater understanding of the etiology, epidemiology, and pathophysiology of frailty. This includes new technologies for predicting disease progression and measuring the cognitive and physical changes from frailty interventions. Ultimately Dr. Papaioannou's vision is to build healthier communities via innovative solutions and care models that expand the realm of what is possible for older adults in our society: greater independence, less institutionalization, delaying cognitive and physical decline. In addition to changing the lives of individual patients and their families, the impact of this program of research has enormous potential economic and social benefits.

column37: This Canada Research Chair in Population Health Research Program (CRC) focuses on identifying and addressing the diverse, ever-changing impacts of COVID-19 (C19) on mental, physical, emotional, social, cultural, and spiritual health in 17 Indigenous communities in Nunavut (NU) and the Northwest Territories (NT) for which there are limited data. The CRC will be beneficial for obtaining further funding to set up a novel longitudinal C19 research project exploring the medium- and long-term impacts of C19 on the heath of Indigenous Arctic communities and develop community-based programs. The areas currently funded include the impact of C19 and C19 preventive measures, vaccine confidence, vaccine side effects, confidence in public health, as well as access to and experiences with healthcare services. Assessing vaccine effectiveness over time (waning immunity) is currently under review for funding. If the CRC is awarded, funding will be sought to assess the impact of C19 on child and youth development, as this was identified as a major concern. The evidence will be utilized to inform, develop, implement and evaluate a community-based and community-led program to improve youth and child health. Identifying the impact of C19 on other diseases and on prevention programs, such as cancer screening services, is essential and will provide critical evidence. The prestigious CRC will lend additional prominence to impact territorial and national C19 prevention and management programs and guide policy and planning decisions to best mitigate for C19 and impacts of C19 in the future. The CRC will provide a national platform to promote and disseminate the novel research results, which are essential for Arctic Canada and other Indigenous communities in Canada and worldwide. This cutting-edge culturally relevant research will train and employ over 80 local Indigenous staff and 28 trainees. Dr. Sharma's plan for her CRC is very likely to be successful given her established trusted long-standing relationships with Indigenous communities and governments in NU and NT and proven track record for obtaining funding over the last 2 decades (approximately $25 million) to undertake many successful evidence-based programs. The Co-Leads are all highly experienced and respected Indigenous researchers. She partners with the Aqqiumavvik Society in NU, and Hotii ts'eeda NT SPOR SUPPORT Unit Co-Leads the work in NT, with whom she has set up a Satellite Research Center in Yellowknife.

column36: Microbial Therapeutics and Nutrition in Gastroenterology
column37: Both celiac disease (CeD) and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) are chronic intestinal conditions, of increasing prevalence and complex pathophysiology, for which there is currently no cure. Gluten, in cereals like wheat, is the main environmental driver of CeD, but genetic susceptibility (HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 genes) is required. However, only a minority of these individuals develop the disease, suggesting additional factors, which could be microbial in origin. The cause of IBD is unknown, but like in CeD, genetic and environmental interactions (including microbial and dietary) are thought to drive chronic inflammation. The overreaching goal of this program, is to find new approaches to better treat CeD and IBD. Fundamentally, it aims at deciphering the role that microbial and dietary factors play in modulating disease risk. The specific objectives are: 1) To discover novel microbe-dietary-host interactions relevant to CeD; 2) To elucidate the mechanisms through which microbial (proteolytic) activity leads to inflammation in IBD; 3) To test new microbial therapeutics for CeD and IBD using preclinical models; 4) To translate preclinical discoveries into humans. To achieve these objectives, unique in vitro models (organoid-derived monolayers expressing human HLA-DQ2 and DQ8 in co-culture with microbes isolated from the human duodenum and T cells expressing the human CD4 molecule), and animal models that are "humanized" from an immune (expressing or lacking genes associated with human disease) as well as microbiota perspective (colonized with defined microbiota from patients), will be used. The effect of novel biocontained next generation probiotics, that (i) target specific inflammatory pathways (Aryl hydrocarbon receptor) or (ii) deliver inhibitors of pro-inflammatory proteolytic activity (elafin) will be tested. The basic laboratory discoveries will be then translated into humans through initiation of proof-of-concept pilot studies. The only therapy for CeD is a strict, lifelong gluten free diet, which is expensive, difficult to follow and not always effective. The current goal of treatment in IBD is disease remission and, even with biological therapy, this is achieved in less than one third of IBD patients. Thus this research program addresses unmet needs in the treatment of CeD and IBD, with the potential to deliver safe therapies targeting the microbial drivers of inflammation, which could be used adjunct to current therapies.

column36: Child Health Equity and Policy
column37: Advancing Child Health Equity and Policy In Canada today, one in three children experience maltreatment, one in five poverty, and one in eight mental disorders. Conditions are even worse for First Nations, Metis, Inuit, Black and other racialized children. Children born into family disadvantage are also more likely to experience poor health and face barriers to receiving much-needed programs and services. They are then unfairly labelled as "hard-to-reach" and are excluded from the development of policies and programs that could benefit them. There is an urgent need to better reach disadvantaged children who carry the burden of health inequities. As a Canada Research Chair in Child Health Equity and Policy, Dr. Nicole Catherine will create new policy-relevant knowledge on specific programs and options to reduce child health inequities. Dr. Catherine's research involves three activities. First, she will engage in community-based research to reach disadvantaged children who represent those we "need-to-reach" the most. Second, she will identify and address structural and systemic barriers to the provision of early prevention initiatives. Finally, she will apply this new knowledge to investigate promising new and culturally-safe interventions designed to address avoidable early adversities and child health inequities. Dr. Catherine's research is driven by community priorities and involves sustained and reciprocal collaborations with policymakers, practitioners, Indigenous leaders and child-serving organizations. Her approach to policy-engaged scholarship ensures that her work will directly inform provincial and national efforts to advance child health equity. Her research is also situated within a child rights-based approach-consistent with international commitments to meet children's health and social needs.

column36: Maternal Health
column37: Pregnancy should be a joyous event. Yet, in Canada, 1-2 out of every 100 pregnancies, result in the birthing parent experiencing unexpected, life-threatening events called Severe Maternal Morbidity (SMM). SMM can result in longterm negative physical, mental, social and financial consequences to families, which are seldom considered in clinical studies. This program has 3 objectives. First, it aims to determine from families and pregnancy care providers (stakeholders), what outcomes they consider important and how they prioritize these outcomes. Objective-1 will be achieved by developing (a) core outcome sets for pregnancy conditions, using validated mixed method designs, including systematic reviews, stakeholder interviews, Delphi surveys and consensus meetings; and (b) a composite adverse pregnancy outcome by engaging stakeholders in Group Concept Mapping, a mixed-methods approach involving idea generation, sorting and rating exercises and a graphical interpretation of stakeholder input. Achieving this objective will not only inform the conduct of future trials, but also define SMM from the stakeholder perspective. Objective-2 is to determine the leading causes of SMM across Canada using a patient-centered definition, and to engage representatives from all units caring for pregnant persons across Canada in a mixed-methods study over 2 years, to identify barriers, facilitators, resource implications and feasibility of establishing a national SMM reporting system - the Canadian Obstetric Survey System (CanOSS). Once established, CanOSS will help identify patient-, provider- and systems-related factors responsible for SMM and allow recommendation of targeted strategies to reduce its incidence. Objective-3 is to assess the mental health consequences of SMM, and to determine the feasibility of establishing a regional program in Ontario for providing mental health screening, assessment and treatment to those experiencing SMM. This feasibility study will over 3 years inform the development and sustainability of similar regional centres across Canada. Thus, this research program over the next 5 years will generate a patient-centered definition of SMM and set the stage for establishing national programs to reduce its physical and mental health consequences, while mentoring the next generation of researchers in mixed-methods approaches, thereby putting Canada at the forefront of research in pregnancy and SMM.

column36: Microbiome Research
column37: Delineating the molecular mechanisms of microbial pathogenesis during Crohn's disease Inflammatory bowel diseases, like Crohn's disease, affect more than 1 in every 150 Canadians, causing a substantial burden on our health care system. In 2018, the estimated economic cost imposed by inflammatory bowel diseases on the Canadian healthcare system was 2.6 billion dollars per year. Crohn's disease is marked by a relapsing inflammation that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, severely diminishing the quality of life. The exact cause of Crohn's disease is unknown; however, a strong line of evidence suggests that gut bacteria are key players in driving inflammation and propelling the disease. While the majority of bacteria in the gut mediate important functions that promote health, some species can trigger inflammation through their pernicious activity. Thus, disentangling the behaviour of the different bacterial groups in the gut is crucial for the development of new therapies that can specifically eliminate harmful microbes. Experimental evolution has been shown to be a powerful tool for studying bacteria in their native environment. By taking advantage of modern sequencing technology, the adaptive traits acquired by the bacterial populations in the gut can be captured with high precision. This information can advance our understanding of how bacteria evolve in the host to cause disease. In this regard, I am proposing the use of experimental evolution to track the adaptations acquired by gut bacteria during inflammation. Importantly, I will study the evolution of bacteria in distinct inflammatory environments to uncover the influence of the different host backgrounds on trait selection. Using state-of-the-art biochemical assays, I will demonstrate the role of the adaptations acquired by bacteria in driving Crohn's disease. Additionally, I will employ advanced tissue imaging technology to excise the infected foci in the host tissues. Using Next Generation Sequencing, I will map the global changes in gene expression in the infected tissues. This approach will allow the identification of the host pathways specifically altered by the detrimental behaviour of bacteria, offering a comprehensive view of bacterial virulence and its impact on the host. Together, the proposed work holds great potential in identifying the mechanisms driving inflammation in the gut, uncovering targets for novel antimicrobial therapeutics for Crohn's disease.

column36: Virology
column37: Every year millions of people worldwide experience "the common cold" or "flu-like" illnesses, which are mild to moderate diseases caused by different respiratory viruses, including influenza viruses, rhinoviruses, coronaviruses, and many others. About 5% of these cases become more complicated and can lead to life-threatening disease. One of the most frequent complications is secondary co-infection with bacteria, which often leads to more severe symptoms and increases mortality rates, from <1% for hospital patients with influenza alone, to 15-20% for influenza complicated by bacterial co-infection. Dr Goncheva's laboratory studies how bacterial co-infection complicates respiratory viral disease. In particular, her research is focused on influenza A virus and SARS CoV-2 (the causative agent of COVID-19) and the interaction of these viruses with the bacterial pathogen Staphylococcus aureus. The main objectives of the lab are to identify molecules produced by the bacteria that can impact the behavior of the virus; and to determine a combination of anti-bacterial and anti-viral compounds for the optimal treatment of co-infection. Dr Goncheva's lab uses several models of co-infection, investigating events at the level of individual cells all the way to the entire host. The studies look at the behavior of both the virus and the bacteria, individually and together, and aim to identify molecular events during co-infection that can be targeted by novel therapies. Viral-bacterial co-infection is an important contributing factor to the annual toll respiratory infections have on humans, but the differing biology of the two organisms has made co-infection challenging to study. Dr Goncheva has extensive experience in this area, and the establishment of her new laboratory makes her poised to make Canada the world leader in this field. Research findings from her laboratory aim to improve patient care, decrease the impact of co-infection morbidity and mortality, and increase the utility and efficacy of the Canadian healthcare system.

column36: Genomics and Health Policy
column37: Anticipated benefits of genomic screening and diagnostic technologies have prompted an unusually rapid translation into practice, particularly in the newborn and early childhood periods. While screening and diagnostic tools are designed to reduce disease burden through early detection and tailored care, novel tests are becoming standard of care before we have a complete understanding of how these tests impact patients and health care systems. In part this is because the technologies are advancing so quickly, but in part this is because we do not have standardized strategies for measuring these important outcomes. In addition, equitable and timely access to these technologies requires innovative ways of delivering care. Virtual platforms, for example, may improve efficiencies and reduce current wait times for genetic services. Dr. Hayeems' policy-relevant research program aims to (i) identify and measure patient and systems-oriented outcomes of genomic technologies and (ii) develop novel models of care to support their equitable and sustainable delivery. To achieve these aims, she will use a range of research methods, including qualitative interviews, structured surveys, analysis of health administrative and medical record data, measurement science techniques, randomized trials, and economic evaluation. In collaboration with researchers across Canada and internationally, patient organizations, and policy decision makers, Dr. Hayeems' research will fill critical knowledge gaps related to delivering new genomic technologies to ensure their appropriate, sustainable, equitable, and evidence-based use in child health.

column36: Health Economics
column37: Dr. Jalal's research program involves advancing the science and applications of health economic evaluation. His primary applied research will focus on the economic and health impact of health policies and clinical interventions related to substance abuse and cancer, as well as other chronic conditions. His program will emphasize the economic evaluations of these mitigation strategies on population subgroups who are at high risk, including the health and economic impact of the opioid epidemic and its mitigation strategies on the First Nation people. His applied research program will also involve prioritizing public health resources and funding decisions to guide health decisions under uncertainty and inform future research through value of information analysis. In addition, his methodological program involves increasing transparency, accessibility and reproducibility of health economic evaluations using Open-Source software that is freely accessible by everyone. The main research approach involves using standard health economic evaluation techniques following the Canadian Guidelines for the Economic Evaluation of Health Technologies. For each condition, the approach involves forming an advisory panel from stakeholders, including physicians, policy makers, care givers, and the general public to define the problem to construct an economic evaluation model. The proposed approach integrates decision-analytic methods with analysis of large administrative datasets to identify trends and variation in outcomes by population subgroups and demographics and recommending the optimal course of action under the inherent uncertainty. The proposed work is innovative as it develops a research program that advances the science and application of health economic evaluations beyond the standard applications of these evaluations in clinical settings. The proposed work can reveal the real-life economic and health impact of policies on population subgroups, including substance-related policies and interventions on opioid dependence and overdose, cancer detection and control policies on the cancer incidence and mortality. In addition, the methodological objectives advances the science of health economic evaluations and value of information analysis by standardizing and streamlining the use of Open-Source software to make it accessible to all researchers and decision makers.

column36: Socioecological Approaches to Mental Health and Substance Use
column37: My program of interdisciplinary research in mental health and substance use capitalizes on the strengths of both health and social science perspectives, with a focus on youth and populations who experience health, social and structural vulnerabilities (i.e., marginalization). My research is characterized by participatory processes that facilitate co-discovery with communities - particularly those who are equity seeking - and bring citizens' voices to the policy and practice "agendas" to tackle key health and social issues. My research charts new territory in the mental health and substance use field through a population approach, centering on mental health promotion; broadening beyond the typical focus on prevention and treatment. It operates across socioecological domains to enhance capacities and resources for mental health and reduce substance use harms at the individual, family, community, and societal levels. My CRC research program focuses on two thematic areas: 1) youth-driven mental health promotion; and 2) strengths-based and inclusive approaches to minimizing the harms of youth substance use. The overarching objectives are to: 1) generate actionable evidence to inform complex interventions to promote positive mental health and substance use outcomes across socioecological domains - from individual to societal levels; and 2) scale and sustain training opportunities to build capacity in mental health and substance use field. Indeed, developing effective strategies to promote mental health and minimize substance use harms (MHSU) in youth under 24 years of age is a research priority locally, nationally and globally. My CRC research program will advance my leadership in addressing the international priority need for evidence to enhance population MHSU outcomes, with a focus on youth. It will contribute substantially to the science and practice of mental health promotion, a key area of investment for the Canadian government and a field of increasing global relevance.

column36: Digital Health for Equity
column37: Dr. Katapally's research program is implemented by the Digital Epidemiology and Population Health Laboratory (DEPtH Lab), which he established in 2017. From its inception, the vision of DEPtH Lab has been to develop a sustainable program of digital health research by scaling up the Smart Platform. Smart is a citizen science platform, which uses big data for one integrated outcome: addressing existing and emerging population health crises by prioritizing the needs of Indigenous communities, before scaling-up these digital innovations to promote equity among disadvantaged groups in non-Indigenous jurisdictions. In essence, Smart Platform enables the engineering of digital health solutions by harnessing the power of big data, with an emphasis on ethical citizen engagement, data sovereignty, and Internet equity. Although DEPtH Lab's interest is in ethically engaging citizens and communities to leverage big data from all Internet-connected tools, our predominant emphasis is on real-time interaction through citizen-owned smartphones. This strategy is not only based on the market penetration of these devices that enables leveraging of big data, but also the potential to amplify citizen voices for health equity. With over 6 billion smartphone subscriptions worldwide, it is difficult to imagine our lives without these ubiquitous tools, and out of all the Internet-connected devices, smartphones are the most versatile and prevalent. As all indications suggest that these ubiquitous devices will become increasingly powerful, adaptable, and cost-effective, the real question is: How can smartphones be transformed into effective tools for social innovation? In essence, Smart Platform enables researchers at the DEPtH Lab to develop digital health solutions that address societal crises. The citizen science-based community engagement can contribute significantly to advance techniques that utilize big data for developing local solutions for global problems. This aspirational vision is operationalized by three objectives that reiterate the action-oriented nature of Dr. Katapally's applied research: 1) Develop a digital health observatory for big data-driven solutions; 2) Design, deliver, and evaluate virtual care services to minimize health inequities 3) Develop digital dashboards for decision-making by utilizing advanced data analytics to respond to existing and emerging population health crises.

column36: Substance Use Policy and Practice
column37: Illicit drug use remains a major driver of preventable morbidity and mortality in Canada and internationally, and accounts for substantial healthcare and social costs. Of particular concern, North America continues to experience an unprecedented overdose crisis, driven largely by the proliferation of illicitly-manufactured fentanyl and fentanyl analogues in unregulated drug supplies. Since the emergence of the COVID-19 pandemic, overdose rates have surged, due in large part to interruptions in drug supply chains and access to harm reduction and health services. There is now an urgent need to identify and advance evidence-informed policy and practice interventions designed to address the health and social challenges associated with illicit drug use. Dr. Mary Clare Kennedy, Canada Research Chair (CRC) in Substance Use Policy and Practice, seeks to generate policy- and practice-relevant evidence to support the development, implementation and optimization of novel substance use interventions, with the ultimate goal of advancing health equity and improving health outcomes among people who use drugs in Canada and internationally. Drawing on a multidisciplinary team of researchers and knowledge users, and utilizing both quantitative and qualitative research approaches, the specific objectives of this CRC program are to: (1) identify the impact of policy and practice innovations in the delivery of supervised consumption services on individual- and community-level outcomes; (2) characterize the impact of individual characteristics, social-structural conditions, and implementation contexts on access to and outcomes of safe supply programs; (3) create a platform for knowledge translation and the training of the next generation of substance use researchers.

column36: Mental Health and Chronic Disease of Childhood
column37: Children with chronic illness commonly experience mental health problems. There may be several factors contributing to these mental health problems, including those related to the disease and its treatment. It is important to address mental health problems for these children because they can have a negative impact on their quality of life and disease outcomes. Dr. Knight's research program is focused on increasing our knowledge about mental health in children with chronic disease. She is studying strategies for mental health intervention for children with chronic rheumatologic diseases, such as lupus. She is also using neuroimaging to better understand how chronic disease affects brain and mental health in children with lupus. Increased understanding of mental health in childhood chronic disease can lead to improved overall outcomes for these children.

column36: Development of Personalized Therapies for Ovarian Cancer Patients
column37: Ovarian cancer (OC) is the 5th leading cause of cancer-related death in women and the deadliest gynecological malignancy. The high fatality rate associated with OC is a result of the disease that remains typically asymptomatic until it gets to an advanced stage, the development of chemoresistance in most patients, and the limited therapeutic options for chemo-resistant tumors. Although novel targeted therapies have been recently approved for the treatment of OC, development of drug resistance remains a major challenge. Clearly, there is an urgent need to develop novel personalized approach against the development of drug resistance in ovarian tumors. Cancer cells are under constant stress that comes from the pressure of the tumor microenvironment, the rapid cellular proliferation, as well as anticancer therapies. To survive, the cancer cells rely on cellular programs of adaptation, named adaptive responses. My recent studies in women's cancers showed that adaptive responses to stress represent a personalized therapeutic opportunity that has the potential to delay or prevent the development of drug resistance. The main objective of the Canada Research Chair Program in Personalized Therapy for OC Patients is to characterize how ovarian tumors adapt to various types of stress (endogenous, environmental, therapeutic), and to develop new individualized therapeutic strategies that will specifically target these adaptive responses. The research program will be separated into three main projects. (1) We will study the adaptive responses to DNA damage in ovarian cancer cells, through the building of a functional single cell proteomics resource and the development of a stress responses cell phenotype atlas. (2) We will identify the immune-related adaptive responses that are triggered in ovarian tumors treated with chemotherapy and develop personalized immunotherapy combination approaches. (3) We will unravel molecular mechanisms of OC brain metastasis and develop therapeutic strategies that exploit the adaptive mechanisms used by metastatic cells to survive in the brain tumor microenvironment. Overall, by developing and using a novel spatial oriented single-cell proteomics platform, spatial oriented RNA-sequencing, and a pathway-oriented approach, this innovative research program will establish one of the foundation necessary for the improvement of OC patients care.

column36: Cognitive Neurophysiology
column37: One of nature's greatest mysteries is how flexible decisions emerge from the interaction among tens of billions of neurons in the brain. Meanwhile, reduced flexibility in thoughts and behaviour is a common denominator across many neuropsychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia and autism. Though often not the most distinctive of symptoms, deficits in cognitive and behavioural flexibility severely impact an individual's independence and productivity. Dr. Liya Ma, Canada Research Chair in Cognitive Neurophysiology, strives to unravel this mystery, to gain insight into the pathological changes underlying cognitive impairment, and ultimately to shed light on new directions for effective treatment. She works towards these goals by 1) using state-of-the-art physiological and optical techniques to monitor neuronal activities during task performance; 2) manipulating the activities of neurons with temporal precision and ultimately pathway-specificity to isolate the functional role of a brain region or a projection pathway in cognitive and behavioural flexibility; 3) designing and fine-tuning mathematical models for cognitive flexibility using experimental data, and generating new and testable hypotheses through collaborations with theoreticians; and 4) identifying the pathological changes underlying cognitive impairment and seeking interventions that can rescue the deficit in models for impaired flexibility in neuropsychiatric disorders. Without attempting to capture all the complexities of these syndromes, Dr. Ma uses models designed to capture the role of specific genetic or environmental risk factors, or the primary pathological changes in key neural pathways. Knowledge produced by Dr. Ma's research will deepen our understanding of the causes of several disorders of the brain, ultimately leading to effective treatments and perhaps even prevention.

column36: Pediatric Neuro-Oncology
column37: Pediatric brain tumours are the leading cause of cancer related death in childhood, and a major cause of morbidity due to the side effects of current therapies. Survival rates have remained stagnant for decades, and current therapies for the most common pediatric brain cancers are aggressive surgeries, radiotherapy and chemotherapy. Medulloblastoma and ependymoma are the first and third most common brain cancers of childhood and pose a particularly difficult challenge to scientists and clinicians worldwide. The major challenge is that despite advances in sequencing and genomics, this has not revealed mutations in the tumour where there is a currently available drug which is less toxic and more specific. This is confounded by a lack of pre-clinical models where new approaches can be tested. Dr. Ramaswamy's research programme seeks to bridge this gap by applying a multipronged approach to identify the achilles heel of these two cancers, and use this to potentiate the effects of current therapy. This will serve to identify how these cancers currently evade current therapy, and tailor future therapies to take advantage of these vulnerabilities present to make treatments more effective. The current proposal will seek to create new models of both medulloblastoma and ependymoma in the laboratory which are amenable to state of the art approaches to identifying new drugs. Once these potential new drug targets are identified, his team will test these in pre-clinical models with the goal of developing new combinations of treatment that can be brought from the bench to the bedside. The ultimate goal of this programme is to generate less toxic and more specific therapies, which can be more amenable to an improved quality of life. By studying tumours both in pre-clinical and clinical trials, his team create a pipeline to bring novel therapeutics to the clinic. The novelty of this proposal is the multi-prong approach of applying novel screening techniques such as CRISPR/Cas9 and high-throughput drug screening to new cell culture models, and developing a pre-clinical treatment hospital to test these new approaches in a manner identical to how patients are treated. Dr. Ramaswamy's programme seeks to address a major unmet need within pediatric child health, with the objective of improving both the survival rates and quality of survival for children diagnosed with high-risk pediatric brain cancer.

column36: Immune Regulation of Developmental Programs
column37: Considering recent advances in the microglia field highlight the importance of these resident macrophages and phagocytic immune cells to brain development, a fundamental question is whether these same developmental roles evolved in other regions of the embryo, including craniofacial tissues. The objective of my research is to address this question, focusing on the contribution of macrophages and osteoclasts to craniofacial morphogenesis, and whether distinct populations of these phagocytes signal to nearby cells during embryogenesis to contribute to normal craniofacial development. Disrupting colony-stimulating factor-1 receptor signalling, which is required for macrophage and osteoclast proliferation, differentiation, and survival, results in craniofacial and dental abnormalities. To further explore the developmental contribution of these phagocytes to craniofacial development, we will use our established pharmacological mouse model to study whether loss of these cells drives defects in the peripheral nervous system and supporting connective craniofacial tissues. We will also use transgenic embryos, single-cell RNA sequencing, and bioinformatics to characterize macrophage and osteoclast heterogeneity across embryogenesis, and use in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry to validate these findings in craniofacial tissues. Moreover, to study the signalling networks used by these phagocytes and neighbouring cells during craniofacial morphogenesis, we will analyze changes in secreted molecules ex vivo and employ a sphere assay using primary cells. By studying how macrophages and osteoclasts contribute to normal craniofacial development, our findings will provide a better understanding of how maternal insults experienced during gestation disrupt developmental programs, which is another area of interest. For example, maternal periodontal infection is a prevalent condition that is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes; however, our knowledge surrounding the impact of maternal periodontal infection on the developing fetus is limited. We will use a maternal periodontal infection mouse model and transcriptomics, proteomics, immunohistochemical analysis, advanced microscopy, ex vivo slice culture, sphere assays, behavioural analysis, and micro-CT imaging to study how maternal periodontal infection impacts neurodevelopment and craniofacial morphogenesis. Together, this research will have broad implications in maternal-fetal health to benefit Canadians.

column36: Transcriptional Memory and Plasticity in Stem Cells
column37: Regenerative medicine such as stem cell based therapy holds great promise towards addressing many diseases that afflict millions of Canadians, including many forms of cancer, muscular and neurological degenerative disorders, diabetes, and arthritis. However, this promise has yet to be fully realized. Despite the many advances in stem cell biology, little is known on the mechanisms governing stem cell identity and on how this identity can be effectively changed and applied towards its target function. The lack of understanding in basic stem cell biology not only has hindered the proper application of stem cell therapy, but has also led to the proliferation of unproven and potentially unsafe applications in many private Canadian clinics. My research aims to bridge this gap by studying how embryonic stem cells are able to self-maintain indefinitely, while retaining the ability to differentiate into any cell type of the body. Using cutting edge technologies such as gene editing, genomics, and single molecule imaging, our group plans to dissect the molecular underpinnings that make stem cells such versatile therapeutic agents. The overall goal of my research program is to discover the underlying mechanisms in transcriptional regulation that allows for differentiation and self-maintenance of embryonic stem cells. My program's overarching hypothesis is that transcriptional regulation is deterministic of cell fate and that the ability to alter transcription programs will ultimately lead to better stem cell based therapeutics. By combining cutting edge technologies such as gene editing, genomics, and single molecule imaging, my group will gain unprecedented insights into the molecular underpinnings of stem cell biology. For Aim 1, I will probe the mechanisms of transcriptional memory in embryonic stem cells (ESCs) following cell division, which will identify key aspects of ESC self-maintenance. For Aim 2, my laboratory will examine the mechanisms of transcriptional plasticity in asymmetric division during ESC differentiation. As ESCs differentiate, we will determine the behavior of cell-type- specific and general transcription factors at the earliest stages of differentiation, and measure the transcriptional output of differentiating versus self-renewing ES cells. Ultimately, this research program will lead to potential breakthroughs in stem cell biology and its application for therapy.

column36: Endometriosis and Pelvic Pain
column37: Endometriosis is defined as lesions resembling tissue of the uterus (womb), growing outside of the uterus. It affects over 1 million individuals in Canada. Endometriosis is a common cause of infertility and pelvic pain such as menstrual cramps (often starting in adolescence), painful sexual activity (dyspareunia), and chronic pain. Treatments for endometriosis include hormonal medications and surgery. The objective of my proposed research program in Endometriosis and Pelvic Pain is to better understand the causes of pain in different individuals with endometriosis, thereby allowing personalization of care (particularly for surgery), and to implement this knowledge in clinical trials and disseminate it widely. I will use a novel interdisciplinary approach ranging from clinical factors (e.g. patient reported variables, clinician examination tests, and findings at surgery), biomarkers (e.g. gene mutations and assessing the interaction between endometriosis cells and nerve cells), pain sensory testing of the nervous system, and administrative data for utilization of the healthcare system. My first objective is to identify clinical factors that can predict better or worse pain-related quality-of-life and health system utilization after endometriosis surgery. My second objective is to evaluate whether biomarkers can also predict quality-of-life and health system utilization after endometriosis surgery. Together, these variables will be integrated into a decision aid, to help patients and clinicians to make decisions around endometriosis surgery (e.g. timing or type of surgery). Knowledge translation (KT) of the decision aid will occur via expansion of our current KT website (Endopain.endometriosis.org). Another objective is clinical trials, whereby the clinical factors, biomarkers, and decision aid can be implemented into surgical care. For these trials, I will develop and utilize new outcome measures that better characterize pain and the pain experience in endometriosis. Finally, specialized pain sensory testing of the nervous system will help to better comprehend the role of the central nervous system in endometriosis pain, and its impact on treatments such as surgery. Together, these objectives will further the understanding of endometriosis-associated pain and its application to treatment: thereby avoiding unnecessary repeat surgeries, and instead targeting surgery to patients in whom it would be most beneficial.

column36: Fibrotic Injury
column37: Fibrosis, also known as scarring, is a pathological condition in which fibrous connective tissue replaces normal tissue in response to injury or damage from chronic inflammation. Organ fibrosis causes nearly half of all deaths in the developed world, and the cost to care for people with chronic fibrotic diseases is in the range of tens of billions of dollars. Despite its importance, doctors have few ways to safely diagnose and treat organ fibrosis. The goal of Dr. Yuen's research program is to develop new ways to non-invasively measure organ fibrosis, and to design new drugs that can effectively block it. His program is divided into 3 main categories: 1) DIAGNOSIS 2) DISCOVERY 3) TREATMENT In the proposed "Diagnosis" studies, Dr. Yuen's lab will investigate new ways to safely measure whole organ fibrotic burden using new non-invasive magnetic resonance, photoacoustic, and ultrasound imaging techniques. He will test these cutting-edge imaging techniques in both animal models and humans with fibrotic disease, with a focus on the kidney and the liver. For his "Discovery" work, Dr. Yuen will continue building a Human Fibrosis Biobank holding human kidney, liver, and heart biopsy specimens. Using state of the art gene expression studies, he will use the tissues stored in this biobank to identify candidate genes that cause organs to scar. In the "Treatment" experiments, Dr. Yuen's lab will test whether these candidate genes are truly important for organ fibrosis using cell and animal models of kidney fibrosis, coupled with gene manipulation techniques. He will also test new drugs that block these candidate genes, to determine if they inhibit the development of fibrosis. Fibrosis is a leading cause of organ dysfunction and failure, and is responsible for nearly 50% of all deaths in the developed world. Fibrosis is such a common and deadly problem because doctors currently do not have ways to safely diagnose and effectively treat it. By developing new non-invasive diagnostic tests and better ways to treat organ fibrosis, Dr. Yuen's work could transform the care of many patients around the world.

column36: Molecular Oncology and Therapeutics
column37: My future research program will seek to establish when and where selection operates on clonal genotypes and epigenetic states within genomically unstable breast and ovarian cancers, ultimately in patients in the context of targeted therapy and metastatic progression. Our objective is to exploit the quantitative principles of natural selection to inform on the efficacy of novel drug targets and to evaluate new targets of therapy in patients. We shall deploy novel single cell and quantitative in vivo evolutionary based method, including time series analysis of transplantable human tumours, developed by our program in the past 5 years. Building on our single cell genome discovery of distinct structural-copy number mutational processes underpinning cancer subtypes we shall (i) determine the mechanisms and consequences of fold-back, HRD and serrate structural variant genomic instability in triple negative breast cancers and high grade serous ovarian cancers. We hypothesize that distinct functional deficiencies in genome maintenance and repair underpinning novel patterns of copy number structural mutation may be exploitable with synthetic lethal approaches. We shall also explore the differences in endogenous immune cytokine activation and the effects of local immune modulation associated with these modes of structural instability for therapeutic benefit (ii) A key characteristic of TNBC and HGSOC is the dearth of targeted therapies, relative to other cancer subtypes. We have shown that G-quadruplex (G4) binding small molecules have a therapeutic index in BRCA2 and PALB2 deficient breast patients and are therefore a novel therapeutic class for repair deficient cancers. We shall identify new classes of G-quadruplex binders and determine their synthetic lethal DNA repair efficacy, building on our early phase 1 trial results. (iii) We shall develop new spatial and dissociated single cell multimodal measurement techniques via our recently CFI funded Cancer Single Cell Dynamics Observatory. This project links spatial and dissociated methods for determining single cell tissue biology of cancers and we shall use these approaches to decode the local immune environment of TNBC and HSGOC cancers. The combined program will use insights from single cell biology of breast and ovarian cancers to systematically address new therapeutic modalities as combinations for these high risk cancers, with potential for application in other cancer subtypes.

column36: Arterial wall biology and atherogenesis
column37: Heart disease and stroke are the leading causes of death worldwide, and a major risk factor and warning sign is a thickening and stiffening of the arteries. Called atherosclerosis, this process involves a buildup of cells and fatty deposits, which can narrow and even block the artery, or break apart suddenly and cause a sudden heart attack or stroke. Dr. Cybulsky seeks to understand the formation of plaques at the early stages of atherosclerosis. Better understanding of this process will enable research into new treatments and preventative measures, which may be able to address cardiovascular disease early in its formation. Early treatments are usually more cost-effective than treating a disease later in its course. He has formulated a paradigm-shifting hypothesis regarding the role of different cells found in the artery wall in regulating inflammation and plaque growth. The proposed research will use state-of-the-art methodologies adapted to unique and innovative experimental approaches to provide novel, important insights into the cellular and molecular mechanisms responsible for atherosclerotic plaques. Macrophages are a type of white blood cell that can consume bacteria, and also stimulate other parts of the immune system through various signals. When there is a high level of fats and cholesterol in the blood, macrophages in the inner wall of an artery can consume fatty molecules (lipids), contributing to the build up of fatty plaques. Macrophages signal other cells, leading to inflammation, i.e., recruitment of immune cells from the blood. This can then cause even more macrophages to accumulate in the artery. Dr. Cybulsky's research seeks to understand how the metabolism and changes in gene expression change in macrophages when they are loaded with lipids. He will also experiment with ways to suppress the inflammatory response. He will then identify which molecular signals and which specific subtypes of cells are responsible for driving inflammation in early atherosclerosis. Finally, his novel research program will investigate the cross-talk between cells of the immune system such as macrophages and the cells that make up the arteries. Understanding this is fundamental to understanding how atherosclerosis starts and how it progresses and gets worse over time. More importantly, this information is crucial to research the development of new therapies for cardiovascular disease.

column36: Neurological Rehabilitation
column37: The research vision of this program in Neurological Rehabilitation is to devise and implement innovative treatments to optimize recovery and ensure that functional gains are maximized and maintained after stroke. Improving functional abilities can enable participation in social roles and physical activities, reduce the risk of secondary complications, and enhance quality of life. Novel interventions developed for stroke also serve as a model for rehabilitation interventions in other neurological populations, as well as for older adults with chronic health conditions. Objective 1: Develop effective stroke rehabilitation interventions which optimize recovery after stroke. Objective 2: Develop rehabilitation interventions incorporating principles of self-management and feedback to ensure that functional gains are maximized and maintained after stroke. Objective 3: Determine best methods for implementation of stroke rehabilitation research into practice. Research approach: An integrated knowledge translation model will be used by partnering with health authorities, clinicians and patients to develop questions important to these stakeholders and seek their input through the entire research cycle. The projects are higher interdisciplinary with key collaborators from physical therapy, occupational therapy, physical medicine, engineering, psychology, neurology, and computer science. Small studies will be undertaken to evaluate the effects before and after a new intervention, before moving to high quality, rigorous randomized controlled trials, and then large multi-site trials on the CanStroke Recovery Clinical Trial Platform. Treatments will include a multi-site progressive exercise program to maximize walking recovery early after stroke using step and heart rate counters to progress the activity (Walk N Watch Study), telehealth applications using hand grasping sensors to motivate hand and arm use after stroke (Virtual Arm Boot Camp) and a glove-based sensor coupled with tablet-based games to improve hand function after stroke (i-GRASP). When successful, interventions will be implemented worldwide and this will be facilitated by clinician/patient user manuals, informative web-sites, conferences and workshops. Significance: These novel approaches and technologies will improve the health of a large number of Canadians living with stroke in both urban and rural regions, and will ultimately reduce health-care costs.

column36: Intrinsically Disordered Proteins
column37: Biology is largely controlled by proteins, the products of gene expression. Much of the understanding of how proteins mediate biological function or disease pathology has come from three-dimensional structures of stable folded proteins, with precise orientations of chemical groups that enable reactions to be catalyzed and specific binding to other molecules. However, more than 60% of proteins contain intrinsically disordered protein regions (IDRs) lacking folded domains. IDRs rapidly interconvert between very dissimilar conformations with fluctuating structure, and they largely act in the context of protein interactions. Disorder is also enriched in disease-associated proteins. Experimental structural and computational tools that are so powerful for folded proteins are not generally applicable to IDRs or their dynamic complexes, leading to a lack of mechanistic understanding of how they mediate normal biology and disease. My work aims to bridge the significant gap in understanding the function of IDRs and their dynamic complexes to elucidate mechanisms of normal regulation and pathology, and to develop tools to facilitate their study. An important type of dynamic complex involving IDRs is cellular "biomolecular condensates" or "membrane-less organelles" (such as nucleoli), which are large clusters of molecules with exchanging interactions and which organize the cell without the membranes found in classical cellular organelles (such as mitochondria). Experimentally, my lab focuses on how biomolecular condensates control essential biological processes (such as transcription, splicing, DNA repair, and translation), and how disease-associated proteins enriched in disorder, including the oncogenic EWS-FLI1 protein that drives Ewing sarcoma - a type of cancer - and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) mutants, perturb condensates and function. We also create computational tools that enable analysis of IDRs without alignment of protein sequences, as this standard approach requires folded structure. We develop methods for calculating structural ensembles consistent with experimental data for IDRs and their complexes. Our experimental results will illuminate how dynamic IDR interactions and condensate formation regulate biology and organize cells. Our computational tools will enable a deeper understanding of IDR protein sequence-structure-dynamics-function relationships. Importantly, our work will provide insights into how EWS-FLI1 and ASD variants lead to pathology.

The SPOR PCN's vision is to create a sustainable pan-Canadian primary care learning health systems platform supported by patient-oriented, practice based-research to improve patient and provider experiences in delivering and receiving care, population health and healthcare expenditures. The Network's deliverables will be co-produced with multiple partners to improve the value of health systems across Canada for patients, communities, clinicians, and decision-makers. The PCN's learning health systems platform will provide an ideal environment to examine whether innovations are reaching the right people in the right way at the right time, and whether this results in better care experiences and outcomes. column36: Muscle Biophysics
column37: Muscle contraction results from the interaction between the molecular motor myosin II and actin. When muscle is activated, myosin attaches to actin, and uses the energy released from adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to produce force. Millions of myosin molecules sliding many filaments arranged in parallel ultimately causes muscle contraction. Myosin is one of three classes of molecular motors, which include kinesins and dyneins. The myosin family is divided into 35 classes and the kinesin family is divided into 45 classes, with functions ranging from vesicle transport to cell division. While the general events responsible for contraction and functioning of molecular motors are well accepted, there are still many details that remain unclear. The aims of this research program are to investigate the molecular mechanisms of myosin II and molecular motors associated with muscle function, and the mechanisms of contraction in health and disease. The specific objectives of this research program are to study (i) the structural changes in the molecular motor myosin II during force production, (ii) the mechanisms of action of the molecular motors kinesin I, kinesin V, dynein and myosin VI, (iii) the cooperative action of motors when working in assemblies, (iv) the effects of post-translational modifications on contractility, and (v) the effects of diseases in the muscular system. The research program will be pursued with experiments conducted in several levels of analysis: single molecules, sub-cellular structures, cells, and whole muscles. Dr. Rassier's group will use biological samples extracted from animal models (wild-type and genetically modified) and/or human subjects, according to the goals of the experiments. An array of innovative techniques will be used, including: (i) force measurements made at the molecular and subcellular levels, and (ii) imaging of molecular motors while working in real time. Understanding the mechanisms of actin of molecular motors and muscle contraction is the basis for future therapeutic interventions that may improve disease conditions. Molecular motors are the nano-engines of life, responsible not only for muscle contraction but cell division, virus transport, ATP synthesis neuronal development, to cite a few tasks. Therefore, the study of myosin and molecular motors in general has a great potential for understanding a variety of diseases.

column37: The objectives of the Canada Research Chair in Genetics and Genomic Medicine are to (1) develop and employ state-of-the-art genetic and genomic approaches to obtain an in-depth knowledge of disease risk factors; (2) develop and exploit novel disease models to discover how genetic risk factors impact human biology to either increase (predispose) or decrease (protect) an individual's risk to disease and disease outcomes; and (3) develop and validate genetic and genomic tools that facilitate diagnosis and treatment of disease. While this work will focus on chronic inflammatory diseases of the digestive system such as Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, it is expected to impact on multiple other diseases. The research approaches designed to achieve these objectives will build upon the Chairholder's existing foundation of cutting-edge technological platforms and laboratory techniques, novel real world patient cohorts, and two- and three-dimensional cell systems that more accurately model human disease. The Chairholder will work closely with an established worldwide network of international collaborators to achieve the stated objectives and for facilitating dissemination of research results. It is expected that the Chairholder's work over the next seven years will result in the development of genetic and genomic information and tools that will (1) speed up diagnosis times; (2) find the most appropriate treatment for patients to alleviate symptoms more rapidly; and (3) identify novel targets for therapeutic development to improve patient outcomes and get closer to finding actual cures for disease.

column36: Pattern Recognition Receptor Pathophysiology
column37: When threatened with infection, pattern recognition receptors, such as the Toll-like receptors (TLRs) and Nod-like receptors (NLRs), elicit powerful inflammatory responses as defensive measures. However, aberrant activation of these receptors can lead to serious health consequences including treatment-related toxicity, or enhanced infection. Dr. Bhavsar is an emerging leader in understanding how this occurs, and how to develop therapies based on this knowledge. Two key examples are bacterial pathogenesis and cisplatin-induced hearing loss. Cisplatin is a valuable and effective chemotherapeutic for solid tumour treatment in children. Unfortunately, cisplatin treatment causes permanent hearing loss in over half of treated children, with long-term impacts on language development and psychosocial outcomes. Ground-breaking studies in the Bhavsar group revealed for the first time how cisplatin initiates toxic signaling that leads to hearing loss. Salmonella is a bacterial pathogen and a leading cause of food-borne illness that infects millions of people each year, causing diarrheal disease. An integral part of this process is the deliberate induction of inflammation that helps Salmonella outcompete other bacteria. The Bhavsar laboratory has uncovered how a Salmonella virulence protein hijacks NLR signaling to induce inflammation. Dr. Bhavsar's insightful focus on pattern recognition receptors uncovered new therapeutic targets to combat cisplatin-induced hearing loss and Salmonella infection. The next phase of his research program leverages these exciting mechanistic understandings of the roles that TLRs and NLRs play in treatment-related toxicity and bacterial infection, respectively, to develop unique strategies to prevent these serious health conditions. Dr. Bhavsar's innovative research program has the potential to lead to precision health treatments that prevent hearing loss in children and reduce bacterial infection while minimizing the emergence antimicrobial resistance.

column37: BACKGROUND From the outset of my research career and throughout the first term of my CRC award, my goal is to improve health outcomes of Canadians who suffer from chronic conditions. The next phase of my CRC research program will focus on "patient-powered, data-driven research", which combines my expertise in epidemiologic and health services research using various data and draws inspiration from lived patient experiences. Indeed, the patient journey-an individual's interaction with healthcare and the healthcare system from symptom onset, diagnosis, to treatment-is complex. Despite advances in healthcare, there are unmet information and support needs that limit patients' abilities to make healthcare and treatment decisions, thereby impacting disease management, treatment adherence, and health outcomes. OBJECTIVES The overall objective of my research will focus on the journeys of chronic disease patients living with arthritis and cancer, where I have established prior work. Specifically, I will: i) address issues related to treatment in chronic diseases; and ii) assess problems and inform health outcomes solutions. RESEARCH APPROACH Methods: Across research pillars of 1) Treatment and Adherence and 2) Health Outcomes, I will conduct epidemiologic and health services research studies. Data sources: This data age has expanded the capacity to describe the patient journey and my research incorporates data from both existing sources, such as electronic medical records, registries, and most notably administrative data, as well as prospectively collected data. Patient engagement: Patients are partners in all stages of my research: from study design to knowledge translation. Long-term and new collaborations with patient organizations in both arthritis (e.g., Arthritis Research Canada) and cancer (e.g., Colorectal Cancer Canada) support the recruitment and retention of patient partners. SIGNIFICANCE My research aligns with the World Health Organization's 2016 framework for integrated people-centered health services, which aims to put "people and communities, not diseases, at the centre of health systems, and empowering people to take charge of their own health rather than being passive recipients of services". In harnessing the power of data and patients, my research will enable patients in becoming their own agents, thereby shifting the paradigm from "managing disease" to "thriving with disease" and ultimately leading to improved health outcomes.
