column36: BALANCE+: A Platform Trial for Gram Negative Bloodstream Infections
column37: Bloodstream infections are a leading cause of death in Canada and worldwide, yet remain understudied, such that we do not know the best treatment strategies to be sure to cure the infection while minimizing harms of excess antibiotics causing antimicrobial resistance. Our Canadian Institutes of Health Research funded Bacteremia Antibiotic Length Actually Needed for Clinical Effectiveness (BALANCE) Randomized Controlled Trial is comparing 7 versus 14 days of antibiotic treatment for bloodstream infection and has recruited nearly 3000 patients across 73 hospitals. BALANCE is the largest trial ever conducted among patients with bloodstream infection, and when it concludes next year will answer a fundamental treatment duration question. However, many crucial questions will remain. BALANCE+ will efficiently answer multiple next questions that are important for patients with the most common kind of bloodstream infections. All hospitalized adult patients with the most common kind of bloodstream infections - caused by "Gram negative" bacteria - will be eligible to participate. This trial provides a platform upon which to answer three questions looking at best ways to 'de-escalate' and 'step-down' antibiotic treatment (going from a broad to more specific antibiotic). We will answer the question about what to do when the infection is caused by bacteria on an intravenous catheter - should we remove and replace the catheter or just treat with antibiotics. We will also answer some key antibiotic selection controversies for some difficult to treat pathogens. As each question is answered, optimal therapies will be adopted into usual care, and new questions will be introduced into the platform of the trial. The evidence generated by BALANCE+ will improve cure for this vulnerable patient population while decreasing potential harms from using too many antibiotics for too long.

column36: Brain pericyte signaling in inflammation
column37: Pericytes are a type of cell in the brain that make extensive contact with capillary blood vessels. This location in the brain suggests that pericytes may have key roles in healthy brain function and in neurological disease. Indeed, evidence suggests that pericytes help regulate the entry of immune cells into the brain and the control of brain blood flow. These roles implicate pericyte dysfunction in disorders with an inflammation component, such as Alzheimer's disease and multiple sclerosis. We are interested in how the cellular signaling of pericytes is changed during inflammation and the effects of this signaling change on the function of brain vasculature. In this study, we will use state-of-the-art optical imaging techniques to observe pericyte signaling at high resolution. Using a common model of inflammation in mouse brain slices, we will observe how pericyte signaling is changed by inflammation. Then, through the application of pharmacological agents to these brain slices, we will probe the mechanisms that underlie these signaling changes. Finally, using optical imaging of brains in live mice, we will explore how this change in pericyte signaling affects brain vasculature function, such as the rate of blood flow and the ability of substances to cross from the blood into the brain. As vascular dysfunction is a major contributor to neurological disorders, the knowledge generated from this project has promise to uncover new mechanisms of disease. Furthermore, by understanding the changes to pericyte signaling that underlie this vascular dysfunction, we will uncover potentially treatable mechanisms that may be common across brain disorders.

column36: Developing evidence to expand the EDUCATE IPV program to other surgical specialties: A qualitative, interview-based study
column37: Intimate partner violence (IPV) refers to behaviour by an intimate partner or ex-partner that causes physical, sexual, or psychological harm, including physical aggression, sexual coercion, and psychological abuse. Given the nature of their work, many surgeons are well-positioned to assist victims of IPV but are misinformed about the prevalence of IPV among their patients. Many surgeons may also feel uncomfortable asking about IPV and unsure of how to assist patients experiencing abuse. The EDUCATE program, developed by Drs. Sprague and Bhandari and their team at McMaster University, was created to educate orthopaedic surgeons on how to best identify and assist IPV victims in an orthopaedic injury clinic setting and has been implemented across Canada in multiple fracture clinics. The eventual goal is to use an evidence-based approach to expand the program beyond orthopaedic surgery. To accomplish this, additional research on the needs of other surgical subspecialties is required. Therefore, we propose a qualitative study exploring surgeons personal experiences, attitudes, beliefs, and knowledge of IPV and their impressions of the EDUCATE program. Approximately 20 surgeons from different specialties affiliated with McMaster University will complete a brief demographics questionnaire followed by a qualitative interview. During the interview, participants will be asked a series of questions regarding their knowledge and comfort towards IPV and general impressions of the EDUCATE program. Responses will be analyzed using thematic analysis based on the objectives. Findings from this research will inform the expansion of the EDUCATE program which will, in turn, prepare more surgeons to more appropriately identify and assist patients experiencing IPV.

column36: L'effet de l'etat psychologique sur l'experience et les reponses physiologiques a la douleur.
column37: L'hypnose et la meditation pleine conscience sont deux approches non-pharmacologiques efficaces pour reduire la douleur. Il est possible de conjuguer les deux, par des suggestions hypnotiques de pleine conscience. Cette etude compare l'effet de suggestions hypnotiques de pleine conscience et de dissociation, sur une douleur aigue produite par l'administration de stimulations electriques, chez des participants adultes en bonne sante. Cette etude examine ainsi les effets de suggestions hypnotiques de pleine conscience et de dissociation, sur les evaluations subjectives de douleur des participants et sur leurs reponses reflexe. column36: Investigation of Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator Mechanism and Chloride Ion Translocation Using Molecular Dynamics
column37: Patients diagnosed with cystic fibrosis have an average lifespan of 30 years. Currently, the most common treatments for cystic fibrosis target the symptoms instead of the root cause of the disease. Although there exists a cocktail of medications that target certain gene mutations, more research is required to produce small molecule drugs that target the single amino acid substitution mutations of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) channel to regain its function. To assist in the design of small molecule drugs, a mechanistic overview of how CFTR transports chloride ions across the membrane is required. To do this, I will perform molecular dynamics (MD) simulations on the microsecond timescale to observe simulated chloride ion translocation events. Ensuring that our simulations are as accurate as possible, we will use high-resolution atomistic structures of phosphorylated human CFTR to ensure that after relaxation under physiological conditions, our channel will be in the open conformation. After stabilizing the open conformation of CFTR, multiple simulations will be run where chloride ions will be added with a hyperpolarizing electric field to study native chloride ion permeation. Residue interactions and their general path will be documented to see if any prolonged interactions with a conserved group of amino acids exist. MD simulation data will be cross-referenced with electrophysiological measurements to improve the strengths of our observations. Ultimately, I hope that this project will provide insight into the mechanism of the CFTR anion channel to support future research and drug discovery against the malfunctioning channel protein in cystic fibrosis patients.

column36: Examining the relationship between pre-stroke hand grip strength, stroke severity, and sex in a sample of patients using data from the UK Biobank
column37: Many factors are associated with recovery from ischemic stroke. Yet little work has considered how recovery after stroke differs between males and females as well as tested associations that consider whether pre-stroke behaviours, such as physical fitness, affect males and females differently after stroke. Within Canada, there is a strong push to understand how sex affects outcome after stroke; however, the available Canadian datasets are small when compared to those from other countries. Fortunately, the United Kingdom is demographically similar to Canada and has collected health care data from over 500,000 individuals in the UK biobank. The Brain Behaviour lab at UBC has access to these data which include 10,000+ records from individuals with stroke. My proposed study will use data from the UK Biobank to address important questions regarding the impact of sex on recovery after stroke. I will aim to investigate the association between pre-stroke physical fitness and stroke severity, and test for differences between males and females. Past work showed that hand grip strength (HGS) can be used as an indicator of physical fitness. The proposed study will assess differences between males and females in HGS, and determine whether there is a relationship between pre-stroke HGS and stroke severity. The work will illustrate the importance of physical fitness in recovery after stroke and advance public policies that seek to promote physical activity. It will also lay the groundwork for further research questions within a Canadian setting.

column36: Neurofilament Light Chain as a Biomarker for Global Cognition in Individuals with Mild Vascular Cognitive Impairment
column37: Individuals with vascular conditions are at a greater risk for cognitive impairment (e.g., memory deficits). At its earliest stage, this phenomenon has been termed mild vascular cognitive impairment (mVCI). The cause of mVCI is believed to be related to damage to brain cells, and consequently these individuals can be at a greater risk for progressive cognitive decline. There are currently no treatment options available that can be used to directly treat mVCI. Recently, however, brain stimulation combined with aerobic exercise has emerged as potential treatment intervention for improving individual cognition, as well as reducing damage to brain cells. Thus, this current project has two main objectives. The first will involve measuring the blood concentrations of a biological molecule (i.e., a biomarker) that is known to be associated with increased brain damage. Specifically, the relationship between this biomarker and cognitive impairment in individuals with mVCI will be assessed. The second objective of this research project is to determine whether there is an association between changes in blood levels of this biomarker and cognitive performance after treatment intervention with exercise and brain stimulation. This project will therefore provide valuable insight on the utility of monitoring a brain-damage associated biological marker as a measure for the severity of cognitive impairment in individuals with mVCI. The current research will also evaluate whether this marker can be used to predict responses to treatment intervention in this population of individuals, which may be of important use in future clinical settings.

column36: Supporting Healthy Pregnancies: Understanding Pregnant Women and New Mothers' Perspectives Regarding FASD Prevention Campaigns to Inform Effective and Non-Stigmatizing Approaches in Greater Sudbury
column37: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) is a diagnostic term used to describe the continuum of effects from prenatal alcohol exposure (Bell et al., 2016; Dejong et al., 2019). Prenatal alcohol exposure has been identified as the leading preventable cause of developmental disability in Canada (CanFASD, 2019). FASD impacts approximately 4% of Canadians, and Northern regions have been reported to be at a greater risk of alcohol use during pregnancy(Popova et al., 2017). Although prevention initiatives have effectively raised awareness of FASD, such approaches have been counterproductive and ineffective in reducing the risk of alcohol use during pregnancy (Roozen et al., 2020). The Sudbury-Manitoulin region is a suitable demographic for this study, as approximately 2% of Sudburians report alcohol use during pregnancy. Although this is an encouragingly low prevalence compared to the Canadian average of 12.5% (Popova et al., 2017), this discrepancy may imply that women are reluctant to disclose information about alcohol use during pregnancy due to fear, guilt, or shame.The objective of this study involves evaluating pregnant women and new mothers' attitudes about alcohol use during pregnancy while analyzing their opinions regarding existing FASD prevention campaigns. This study will recruit 100 pregnant women and new mothers aged 17 to 45 of varying ethnicities and cultural backgrounds. For this study, a basic qualitative design will be employed. The data will be collected using focus group sessions and analyzed via thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke, 2019). Nevertheless, this study will increase the awareness of the risks of alcohol use during pregnancy while addressing the need to integrate marginalized voices (e.g., Indigenous populations) into the FASD discourse.

column36: Evaluation and Optimization of Alzheimer-targeted Imaging Agents
column37: Alzheimers disease is the most common progressive dementia, resulting in symptoms of memory decline and difficulties with thinking, motor skills, and language. Aggregated extracellular amyloid-beta plaques is one of the neurodegenerative hallmarks of this dementia, with the soluble portion serving as an ideal target for brain imaging as it is known to be linked to disease progression and synaptic damage. Although brain imaging through magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission topography (PET) is the standard diagnostic technique for Alzheimers disease, current technologies limit diagnosis to Stage 3, where patients are already experiencing cognitive decline. Through the development and optimization of a liposomal (or micellar) imaging agent conjugated to an MRI/PET-labeled vitamin E analogue, the diagnostic time can be reduced to Stage 2 and Stage 1. Once the agent composition is tested for stability and structurally characterized through light, neutron, and X-ray scattering techniques, it will then be specified to the amyloid-beta plaques through the use of antibodies and will undergo a series of immunologically-based tests to assess binding specificity. A physiologically-relevant brain model will be generated with novel and human-relevant organ-on-a-chip technology, allowing for analysis of how the liposomal/micellar agent will reach and circulate within the brain. From this project, an Alzheimers-specific biocompatible imaging agent will be made that will serve as a powerful tool to improve diagnosis time. As Alzheimers currently has no cure, early detection for earlier administration of effective treatment is critical for bettering patient quality of life.

column36: Distribution des recepteurs opioides delta et mu dans les ganglions de la racine dorsale chez les primates
column37: La douleur chronique est une condition qui affecte, au quotidien, plusieurs aspects de la vie de nombreuses personnes au Canada. Lorsqu'une personne souffre d'une douleur moderee a severe, le traitement le plus utilise est les opioides. Les opioides, comme la morphine ou le fentanyl, procurent de l'analgesie principalement via l'activation du recepteur mu opioide (MOP). C'est aussi ce recepteur qui cause les nombreux effets secondaires associes aux opioides, comme la constipation, la detresse respiratoire et la dependance. En plus du recepteur MOP, il existe deux autres recepteurs opioides : le delta (DOP) et le kappa (KOP). Lorsque le recepteur DOP est active, de l'analgesie est aussi produite, mais celle-ci s'accompagne de beaucoup moins d'effets indesirables. Nous nous interessons donc au potentiel therapeutique produit par l'activation du recepteur DOP. Le but de mon projet est donc d'evaluer la distribution des recepteurs opioides MOP et DOP dans les neurones des ganglions de la racine dorsale, soit ceux qui detectent les stimuli douloureux, chez le singe et l'humain, afin de mieux comprendre leur role respectif dans le controle de la douleur.

column36: Assessing the role of PTEN deletion in Cholinergic Neurons on Kupffer Cells in Non-Alcoholic Steatohepatitis
column37: Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD) is a spectrum of liver diseases, of which an advanced form is called non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). Due to a combination of sedentary lifestyles and calorie rich diets in developed countries, NASH is becoming more prevalent and severe with increasingly higher number of cases being reported each year. Currently, there are limited treatment options for patients suffering from NASH which highlights the importance of looking into the exact mechanisms behind NASH progression. Immune cells in the liver play a key role in worsening NASH to stages that cause irreversible liver damage. They do this by attacking liver cells and creating scar tissue. Numerous studies have found these immune cells can be inactivated by activating specific nerves that run through the liver. They do this by releasing chemical signals which bind to liver immune cells and inactivate them. Our research has found these nerves are activated when we turn off a gene called PTEN. The goal of our project is to determine what effect turning off PTEN will have on immune cells in a liver affected by NASH. Our expectations are that we can turn off harmful immune cells in the liver by turning off PTEN, since this is known to activate nerves that inactivate harmful immune cells in the liver. This project is expected to improve our understanding of the way the brain controls harmful immune cells in patients suffering from NASH and to provide us with new ways of controlling immune cells in NASH patients to improve treatment outcomes.

column36: Novel Slow Cellular Mechanisms Driving Recognition Memory
column37: Memory storage allows us to recall experiences and knowledge throughout our lives. Recognition memory is a critical form of memory that allows us to distinguish familiar versus novel in our environments. In diseases such as Alzheimers, this component of memory is often impaired. A brain region implicated in recognition memory is the subiculum. Recently, the Cembrowski lab at the University of British Columbia found a unique type of neuron in the subiculum whose activity is correlated with recognition memory. This type of neuron has also been found to have fundamentally unique appearance and activity compared to typical neurons in this brain region. Currently, the characteristics of this neuron type which allows it to produce this activity are unknown. Using a calcium imaging tool that is the only one of its kind in Canada, I will measure the neuronal activity in this unique neuron type in mice. Cellular activity will be recorded while mice are presented with novel and familiar objects. Next, I will build computer models of these neurons. These models allow me to simulate inputting information to the neurons, so I can interpret how the modelled cell computes the information. This allows for inferences to be made about how the actual cells are dealing with information from other cells in this brain region. Synergistically, these methods allow me to visualize and interpret the unique activity of the specialized subiculum neurons involved in recognition memory. This project may propose a new mechanism underlying recognition memory. As such, this has the potential to inform future investigations into the treatment of diseases where recognition memory is impaired.

column36: Investigating the molecular mechanisms of a novel group of small-molecule Bax inhibitors
column37: The mitochondria has always been known as the ;powerhouse of the cell. However, the association between neuronal health and mitochondrial function is something that is not widely known. When a neuronal cell encounters a stressor during a stroke (oxygen deprivation), brain injury (physical trauma) or epileptic seizure (electrical disturbance), a pore forms on the mitochondria which ultimately results in a signal cascade that leads to cell death. Therefore, the prognosis of patients is largely influenced by the magnitude of neuronal cell death following one of the aforementioned events.The David Andrews lab specializes in uncovering how a protein called Bax regulates mitochondrial dynamics during cell death. Recently, we uncovered several small molecules that inhibit Bax activation. Therefore for this proposal, we seek to understand the mechanism by which the small molecules suppress Bax-mediated cell death. First, we wish to characterize the binding site and affinity of the small molecule inhibitors to Bax. Second, we would like to uncover whether Bax activation is suppressed by the small molecules on the mitochondria or elsewhere in the cell. Third, we wish to study Bax dynamics and behaviour once it is suppressed by the small molecule inhibitors. Finally, we need to assess and quantify the extent to which the small molecule inhibitors prevent Bax-mediated cell death.Understanding how the small molecule inhibitors suppress Bax activation from a mechanistic point of view is predicted to facilitate future drug design aimed at ameliorating patient prognosis following a stroke, seizure, or brain injury. Thus, Bax is a promising druggable target with medicinal potential.

column36: Antibacterial, Chemical and Physical Properties of a Novel Dental Adhesive Loaded with Gold Nanoshells for Photothermal Therapy Applications
column37: Untreated oral conditions affect 3.5 billion people worldwide. In Canada, dental caries and periodontal disease are the most common chronic diseases, with the second highest direct cost for treatment (estimated economic burden of $11B in 2011). Antibacterial agents should be present intra-orally for constant control of these bacteria and prevent the installation or progression of the disease. Despite a significant need for mercury-free, safe, and affordable alternatives to replace dental amalgam, not much has been accomplished. Current dental materials do not decrease the incidence of dental caries; thus, a significant need exists for the development of materials to modulate cariogenic bacteria. This research will develop a novel resin-based dental material able to inhibit and control oral biofilm, which can be periodically reactivated by subsequent applications of LED red light. The expected outcome is the development of novel antimicrobial restorative material, which could be periodically reactivated by red light, with equivalent or superior mechanical properties. The impact will be significant, especially for vulnerable populations (elderly, hospitalized, frail populations) and for those with limited access to dental care (low income, rural, indigenous populations). column36: Quantification and manipulation of brain estrogens
column37: Steroid hormones are chemical messengers that are secreted by organs into the bloodstream. They are very important regulators of physiology and behavior. Estrogens are sex steroids that can be produced in the brain, where they are involved in many important functions and may help protect against Alzheimers disease. Estrogen levels vary among brain regions, so the development of a robust and accurate way to measure estrogens in discrete regions is of the utmost importance. Even a miniscule amount of estrogen can produce profound effects in target tissues, but current methods are not sensitive enough to detect very low levels in the brain. Our lab has already developed a sophisticated method of measuring estrogens in the avian brain using liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry. The main goal of this project is to optimize this method for use in rats, which are an excellent model for many aspects of human health and behavior. Our assay could be of great benefit for measuring estrogens in populations where it has been difficult to do so, including women receiving aromatase inhibitors as a treatment for breast cancer. After validating the use of our method in rats, we will use it to test the effectiveness of the drug DHED in delivering estrogen exclusively to the brain. After administering DHED to rats, we will measure estrogens in the brain and compare them to levels in peripheral tissues. Although many neurological and psychiatric diseases are linked to abnormal changes in estrogen levels, there is currently no way to administer estrogen therapies specifically to the brain without causing harmful off-target effects elsewhere. This study could help develop better treatments for neurological and psychiatric deficits in patient populations with low brain estrogens.

column36: Characterizing alanine transporters as therapeutic targets for pancreatic cancer
column37: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has one of the lowest cancer survival rates, impacting thousands of Canadians annually. Despite modest improvements in the past 20 years, long-term survival rates are still only 10%. New therapy targets are urgently needed to improve patient outcomes and survival. It has been shown that PDAC cells have a significant demand for the amino acid alanine through unknown mitochondrial alanine transporter(s). Protein transporters are the gatekeepers of the cell that control metabolite import and export. Targeting cell surface alanine transporters attenuates alanine uptake and metabolism and leads to decreased PDAC tumour growth and, in some cases, complete regression. The SLC25 solute carrier family make up the majority of mitochondrial transport proteins. However, approximately 30% of SLCs remain uncharacterized to date. This proposal addresses this metabolic axis, in hopes of identifying and characterizing the unknown mitochondrial transporter(s) as potential targets for PDAC. A CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-out (KO) approach will be used to study transporters in depth and define the gene-phenotype relationships. Highly-sensitive molecular tools like mass-spectrometry will be employed to measure metabolite release in the mitochondria and confirm alanine transport activity. The transporter candidates will be characterized for their effects on PDAC and non-malignant cell proliferation and tumour growth using subcutaneous xenografts in mice. This work is significant for patients with PDAC to improve their prognosis by providing insight into new and effective therapeutics.

column36: The impacts of myocardial infarction on hippocampal integrity and cognition in young women
column37: Myocardial infarction (MI), which is also known as a heart attack, occurs when the blood vessels that supply oxygenated blood to certain muscles of the heart suddenly and completely clogged. The oxygenated blood is unable to reach the muscle of the heart that it is supposed to supply blood to, resulting in that certain heart muscle to die. The damage to the heart varies, but regardless the event of an MI has the potential to halt the heart from efficiently performing its job, which is bringing oxygen-rich blood around the body. An oxygen-demanding organ that the heart supplies is the brain. The brain is responsible for cognitive functions such as thinking, emotions, memory and learning. It has been found that MI survivors have difficulties in such cognitive processes but how this occurs is not well understood. It has been proposed by Liu et al. (2014) that the event of an MI can impact an oxygen-sensitive brain region called the hippocampus which is a crucial structure for cognitive functioning. My research proposal aims to answer the question, how does the event of MI in young women impact the hippocampus (a key brain structure for learning, and memory)?In order to investigate if the event of an MI does alter the structure of the hippocampus, young women (between the ages of 19 and 55 years old) that have had an MI will be compared to young women who have not had an MI, on cognitive, symptoms of depression and symptoms of anxiety assessments. These results will then be associated with brain scans of the hippocampus to see if hippocampal alterations are associated with poorer cognition and/or symptoms of mental health disorders.ReferencesLiu, C., Liu, Y., Yang, Z. column36: Errant epitopes from arginine methylated SARS-CoV-2 proteins predisposing to autoimmune diseases
column37: The SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid (N) protein is the most abundant protein expressed in virions and infected cells. Notably, R95 and R177 are sites of PRMT1 methylation previously identified by our lab (Cai et al., 2021) and are also predicted B and T cell epitopes. Autoantibodies have been reported in SARS-CoV-2-infected patients, and autoantibodies against arginine methylated residues have been isolated from patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). We also plan to perform a series of in vitro methylation assays and mass spectrometry to identify other SARS-CoV-2 proteins modified by PRMTs. These findings will have an impact on why certain patients post-SARS-CoV-2 infection develop persistent illnesses, especially autoimmune diseases. This project will also identify new post-translational modifications that may regulate SARS-CoV-2 biology.

column36: Using novel blood biomarkers to investigate associations of vascular risk, Alzheimer's pathology, and brain health across neurological diseases
column37: Dementia is a pressing concern given Canadas aging population coupled with the lack of effective treatments for dementia-causing disorders. Vascular risk factors (e.g., diabetes, high cholesterol, high blood pressure) are common in older adults, and are associated with increased risk for cognitive decline and dementia. Research has shown that when vascular risk factors and Alzheimers pathology occur together, older adults experience more rapid cognitive decline and brain volume loss. Interestingly, Alzheimers pathology is commonly observed in the brains of older adults with non-Alzheimer's neurological disorders, such as Parkinsons disease and cerebrovascular disease. However, it is currently not known how Alzheimers pathology and vascular risk factors affect cognition and brain volume loss in these conditions. Recently developed technology now allows for the proteins associated with Alzheimers disease (i.e., amyloid and tau) to be measured in the blood. In this study, I will leverage this novel technology to measure Alzheimer's pathology non-invasively in an Ontario-wide study of participants with Parkinson's disease and cerebrovascular disease. The main goal of this study is to determine whether Alzheimer's pathology and vascular risk are associated with accelerated cognitive decline and brain volume loss in these conditions. The results of this study will provide new insight into risk factors for cognitive decline in Parkinsons disease and cerebrovascular disease. If vascular risk contributes to cognitive decline and brain volume loss across multiple neurological diseases, vascular health could be targeted to prevent and slow the progression of dementia for the many Canadians at risk.

column36: A 3D in vitro model to elucidate the influence of obese fat cells on skeletal muscle repair
column37: The prevalence of obesity has tripled since 1975, now affecting over 650 million adults worldwide. Obesity is linked to the development of multiple comorbidities including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and impaired muscle tissue regeneration. A hallmark of obesity is the accumulation of excess fat in muscle tissues via intramuscular fat cells. How these diseased (obese) fat cells influence skeletal muscle repair is not well understood and is the focus of my research.In previous work, our groups established distinct in vitro models for (i) mimicking skeletal muscle repair, and (ii) inducing a diseased (obese) fat cell state. Here, I aim to bridge the gap between models by incorporating media harvested from obese fat cells (cell-conditioned media) into the skeletal muscle repair model to mimic the interaction between fat cells and muscle tissue. I hypothesize that adding media containing fat cell-secreted factors to muscle cell cultures will influence the efficiency of muscle repair.The effects of fat cell-secreted factors on skeletal muscle repair will be quantified via image analysis ;e.g. measuring muscle cell proliferation and size. Next, I will characterize the fat cell-conditioned media to uncover the specific factors responsible for altered skeletal muscle repair. Finally, I will extend our skeletal muscle-fat cell conditioned media model to screen for drugs that can enhance muscle repair. In summary, this proposal will establish a biologically relevant model to elucidate the influence of fat cells and their secretions on skeletal muscle repair. This model will improve our understanding of the molecular pathways that modulate muscle repair in individuals with obesity, helping to develop therapies for obesity-linked impaired muscle tissue regeneration.

column37: With cancer rates rising globally, research needs to develop effective treatments that reduce mortality and suffering associated with these devastating diseases. Cancer therapies blocking tumor blood vessel growth have been developed, however, clinical studies have shown that these treatments are only temporarily effective. Despite its relevance to cancer, the CD36 signaling pathway is poorly characterized. Given the small size of CD36, we believe that additional proteins are necessary for its signaling. In my M.Sc, I will identify and investigate the role of these necessary proteins.Super-resolution microscopy will be critical in visualizing and determining the composition of the small CD36 signaling complexes. Reducing the expression of candidate proteins within cells and analyzing the effect on signaling will provide information on the role of these candidate proteins. The investigation of the CD36 signaling pathway will unveil regulators and targets that will enhance and influence the development of new cancer therapies.

column36: Investigating Relations Between Borderline Personality Disorder Symptoms and Treatment Response in Transgender and Gender Diverse Individuals
column37: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a severe mental illness characterized by emotion dysregulation, interpersonal impairment, and high suicidality. It affects 1.6% of the general population and up to 33% of transgender and gender diverse(TGD) individuals. Dialectical Behaviour Therapy (DBT) is the most widely studied psychotherapeutic treatment for BPD. To date, the vast majority of DBT research hasfocused on cisgender women, with a notable lack of systematic investigation of gender differences in treatment response. The Gender Minority Stress Model posits that core BPD symptoms may be exacerbated by gender minority stress in TGD individuals, and thus more intractable. In order to encourage effective, equitable treatment of BPD, further investigation into treatment targets in this population is critically warranted. The proposed study will address the gender gap in the DBT literature by investigating differences in treatment response to DBT in TGD individuals with BPD, as compared to their cisgender counterparts. Outpatients with BPD will complete self-report questionnaires to measure their gender identity, experience of gender minority stress, and BPD symptomatology, both at the outset and conclusion of 24 weeks of standard DBT treatment. Descriptive statistics, analyses of variance, and a hierarchical multiple regression will be implemented to examine (1) change in BPD symptoms over time in cisgender males, cisgender females, and TGD individuals, and (2) the nature of the relations between gender identity, gender minority stress, and BPD symptom change following DBT. Exploring DBT treatment response across the full spectrum of genderswill facilitate the provision of more tailored, impactful care to all individuals who suffer from BPD.

column36: Enriching Glucosinolates in a Smart Vertical Farm System: Implications for Type 2 Diabetes
column37: Northern communities have limited access to fruits and vegetables. This makes it easier to develop health problems. Opaskwayak Cree Nation (OCN) in northern Manitoba near The Pas, has a high rate of diabetes. Almost 47% of adults in OCN have diabetes. Community members said consuming a good diet (fruits and vegetables, low fat, etc.) makes them feel healthy. But fruits and vegetables are hard to come by. They are expensive, poor quality, and not available year-round. OCN has made it a priority to make fresh foods more available. In 2016, a smart vertical farm (SVF) was built in OCN. The farm grows vegetables on shelves using LED lights. The light settings can be altered to optimize growing conditions. Initial tests showed SVF vegetables to be higher in nutrients than store-bought vegetables. Brassica vegetables (broccoli, cabbage etc.) contain glucosinolates (GSL). These nutrients improve diabetes. Strong LED light can increase GSL. This means SVF Brassica vegetables could be better at fighting diabetes than those grown in other conditions. You may not have to eat as much to have the same benefit. For our research, we will be measuring GSL in SVF broccoli sprouts. Broccoli sprouts are high in GSL. We will also be feeding the sprouts to rats with diabetes. We want to know if SVF sprouts can prevent or treat diabetes. We are working with OCN on this project. This research could help OCN combat diabetes. This work supports the long-term goal to reduce health care costs and vegetables transportation from the south.

column37: Drug-Targeting Drivers of Synovial Sarcoma DevelopmentSynovial sarcoma is an aggressive soft-tissue cancer primarily affecting adolescents and young adults and has a 5-year survival rate of ~15% with disseminated disease. Synovial sarcoma is caused by a specific mutationfusion of the SS18 gene to the SSX geneproducing a new protein, SS18-SSX. As we can detect and analyze mouse cells throughout the course of tumor development, this model can reveal vulnerabilities based on the signals this cancer relies on to form, grow and spread.Our model and previous literature have identified Wnt signaling as one key pathway activated by SS18-SSX. Wnt signaling allows cells to proliferate, invade surrounding tissue, and metastasize by disrupting the bonds that normally connect cells to other cells. Thus, we will investigate how using drugs to block Wnt signaling affects the ability of SS18-SSX to drive cancer progression.We will treat mice with drugs currently approved for clinical trials to inhibit Wnt and look for changes in tumor growth, invasiveness, metastatic spread and mouse survival. With these investigations, we can evaluate the feasibility of treating synovial sarcoma with drug-inhibitors of Wnt, gain a better understanding of cancer development, and inform the development of new and effective therapies.

column36: Understanding the impact of history of mild traumatic brain injury on maternal mental illness
column37: Maternal mental illness is an important public health issue that has a significant impact on families and the health care system. Research has shown that one in five mothers of children 0 to 16 years have a mental illness. Some of the most severe mental illness outcomes include emergency department visits or hospital admissions for mental illness, or even self-harm and suicide. Although rare, suicide is one of the main causes of death in women after childbirth. Approximately 1% of women of childbearing age experience a mild head injury, often called a concussion, every year. A history of a mild head injury could increase the risk of mental illness for mothers. This has not been studied even though in the general population, a history of a mild head injury has been associated with mental illness and suicide. To our knowledge, no studies have looked at women with a history of mild head injury and their risk of mental illness following childbirth. This study will use data for all mothers in Ontario with babies born between 2007 and 2017. These women will be divided into two groups, those with a history of mild head injury before delivery and those without a history of mild head injury. The groups will be compared by the number who visit an emergency department or have a hospital admission for mental illness, and experience self-harm or suicide, until 2021. This research is important due to the already increased risk of mental illness following childbirth, the high rate of mild head injury in young women, and the devastating impact severe mental illness outcomes can have on women and their families.

column36: The gut microbiome and estrogen receptor-positive female breast cancer
column37: Breast cancer is the most common cancer among Canadian women and the second leading cause of cancer-related death. Even those who survive will face serious negative health impacts, such as the adverse side effects associated with long-term hormone therapy. Therefore, approaches to prevent breast cancer before it starts are critical for improving population health.Estrogen is known to cause HR-positive breast cancer, the most common form of breast cancer. Recent research has shown that specific bacteria in the gut microbiome may control estrogen levels. Through this estrogen regulation, evidence in preclinical studies have suggested the gut microbiome may contribute to breast cancer development, but clinical studies are limited. To better establish the role of the gut microbiome in breast cancer development, we will conduct a study of 70 women newly diagnosed with HR-positive breast cancer and 70 women without cancer. Women will complete questionnaires on lifestyle and diet and provide a stool sample. Whole metagenome sequencing and metabolomics will be performed on stool specimens to determine the type and quantity of bacteria and metabolites present in women with and without breast cancer. We expect that women with breast cancer will have different types of bacteria and higher amounts of estrogen-related bacteria and metabolites. Our results will provide new knowledge on how the gut microbiome may contribute to breast cancer, including mechanisms of action which are important for identifying therapeutic targets. This is an important first step towards identifying potential approaches to change the gut microbiome and prevent breast cancer.

column36: Aptamer-based point-of-care detection of inflammatory biomarkers
column37: Although inflammation is the bodys natural defense against infection, severe infections can lead to uncontrolled systemic inflammation, known as sepsis. Sepsis is often fatal and every year causes millions of deaths worldwide; however, because it is only diagnosed via physiological signs, there are no readily available methods for sepsis diagnosis at its early stages. A promising method for early on-stage diagnosis of diseases is active monitoring of changes in the levels of disease biomarkers present in the blood. This method, however, requires biomarker measurements multiple times per day, and conventional monitoring techniques do not allow for proper routine screening. Therefore, I propose a research project that will lead to the development of affordable and effective molecular sensors applicable in the routine monitoring of four inflammatory biomarkers (IBs). Our unique approach will involve the use of DNA aptamers, which are short single-stranded DNA molecules that bind a molecular target with high specificity and affinity. The Krylov group has already developed many highly efficient methods for selecting high-affinity aptamers to protein analytes, such as IBs. Two aptamers will be selected per IB, each binding opposite sides of their respective IB, and both will be conjugated to nanoparticles (NPs). The aptamer-NP conjugates will bind their respective IB on both sides to form highly stable complexes that are detectable for routine monitoring of IB levels. The proposed aptamer-NP conjugates are robust molecular sensors that will be applicable in the development of affordable and effective diagnostic tests for early on-stage diagnosis of sepsis. Success of this project will also provide a basis for diagnostic sensor design for biomarkers of other diseases.

column36: Automated diagnosis of fibrosis in liver transplant using deep learning applied to conventional ultrasound imaging
column37: Liver transplantation (LT) is considered the only curative treatment for patients with chronic liver disease. However, patients can develop long-term complications in their graft, particularly due to new or recurrent liver disease. These diseases can cause chronic liver injury, leading to fibrosis, which is associated with poor health outcomes and decreased graft survival. To manage these patients, liver biopsy is used to assess their level of fibrosis, but this procedure is expensive and invasive, leading to complications such as bleeding and infections. Thus, there is a need to develop non-invasive screening tools for graft fibrosis. Although several non-invasive tools exist such as laboratory tests and Transient Elastography (TE) which uses ultrasound waves to quantify liver stiffness, they have some inherent limitations. In particular, TE is expensive and requires extensive training. Fortunately, artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly recognized as a tool that can make use of cheaper conventional ultrasound imaging. Recent studies show that AI can be used to diagnose and delineate fibrosis in non-transplant populations with great accuracy. We aim to build on these studies to develop a high-performing model that caters to LT patients, as there are limited studies on this population. We will use a deep learning model, a subtype of AI, trained on ultrasound imaging to diagnose fibrosis and subsequently combine extracted imaging features from our model with demographic, clinical, and laboratory data to predict the risk of developing fibrosis in LT recipients, facilitating early detection of fibrosis. The development and implementation of an AI model will enable better management of LT patients to prevent graft-related complications and improve patient outcomes.

column36: Imprinting of Incipient Memory in Food Allergy
column37: The number of people with food allergies has increased over the past few decades. Allergies such as those to peanuts usually persist for a lifetime and there are no curative treatments. Allergic reactions are mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE), which are antibodies specific to a food allergen. In food allergic patients, allergen-specific IgE levels are high, but they do not cause allergic reactions until later allergen exposures. Thus, how food allergy initially develops remains unknown and difficult to study in humans. In mice, we found that a single oral exposure to allergen alongside damage to the intestinal barrier does not generate IgE. However, allergen re-exposures given even months later generate IgE and promote anaphylaxis, suggesting the imprinting of long-lived memory. I found that the initial exposure activates immune cells called CD4+ T cells. My goal is to elucidate the characteristics, function, and localization of these allergen-specific CD4+ T cells to test the hypothesis that CD4+ T cells generated at that incipient stage persist for long periods of time and elicit IgE upon allergen re-exposures. To assess the molecules these rare allergen-specific CD4+ T cells express, I will use an enriching technology to analyze them by flow cytometry. To determine whether these cells maintain food allergy and are sufficient to induce IgE, I will isolate and transfer them into new host mice. Finally, I will administer a drug that blocks T cell migration to determine whether CD4+ T cells residing in tissues are sufficient to generate IgE. My project aims to understand the incipient events leading to food allergy, which have implications for treatment. If CD4+ T cells maintain and establish food allergy, then curative treatments must specifically target these cells.

column36: A Novel High Throughput Method to Analyze Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms in Oncogenes
column37: The field of molecular genetics is budding, and advances in recent years have enabled the investigation of health at a genetic level. However, there is a large gap in the knowledge regarding the effects of single-nucleotide mutations and how these may predispose us to disease. One of the most pervasive and enigmatic health concerns is the development of genetically predisposed cancers. Currently most mutations in the genome are classified as variants of unknown significance, such that a variant cannot be classified as benign or pathogenic; this dramatically hinders a clinically meaningful interpretation of variants. My research project aims to develop a novel high-throughput cellular assay to determine cancer risk based on variants of single-nucleotide mutations. The subsequent generation of variant effect maps will function to assess cancer risk in the human population. This will be made possible using a technique known as deep-mutational scanning to reveal the properties of variant proteins, coupled with a novel multiplexed phenotyping strategy that I have developed. This research will profoundly affect the understanding of oncogenic variants and will contribute to a larger atlas of variants to determine cancer risk. The construction of this methodology is imperative as all functional genetic variants compatible with life exist in approximately 1 in 50 people living today. The ability to provide personalized care will fundamentally rely on this type of genetic investigation. As variants continue to be mapped, this methodology will radically alter the way we perceive and apply personalized health care through precision medicine not only in terms of cancers, but genetically related disorders at large.

column37: Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome (NAS) is a condition where an infant becomes dependent on an opioid that was exposed to them during pregnancy. With the mother being the center of treatment, nurses need to also provide thorough care to mothers themselves. Many mothers have complex health care needs and vulnerabilities following birth of a baby who is diagnosed with NAS. There has been a lack of discussion on the experiences of mothers caring for their infants who are withdrawing. The primary aim of the proposed qualitative study is to explore the lived experience of mothers caring for their infants diagnosed with NAS to gain an understanding of their unique care needs. By understanding the lived experience of these mothers, nurses can better support and empower their ability to care for their infants. Open conversations will be created through interviews with mothers. Following this, I will complete an analysis of the transcripts from the conversations, grouping reoccurring themes and find meaning in the mothers lived experiences. The findings of this study will be used to improve care for not only mothers but for their babies as well.

column37: Moral Injury is an exciting new field of research. Moral injury occurs when there is a profound and harmful violation of an individual's moral standards or beliefs. This could be caused by a person's own action or inaction or could be due to a betrayal by their leadership. It is not a diagnosis but is currently included under the umbrella of posttraumatic stress disorder. column36: Protein Arginine Methyltransferase 1 (PRMT1) Suppresses The Differentiation of Germinal Centre B Cells and B Cell Lymphoma
column37: Our natural defence against disease-causing germs is known as the immune system. The immune system is constantly protecting our bodies from disease-causing agents such as bacteria and viruses. To fight disease-causing agents, the immune system produces molecules called antibodies. Antibodies specifically recognize germs to stop them from causing disease. The production of antibodies is carried out by a group of cells called B cells. B cells function as tiny antibody-producing factories, constantly generating antibodies that can bind and eliminate germs before they make us sick.The gene, PRMT1protein arginine methyltransferase 1is a mediator of antibody production. PRMT1 controls the activity of our cells by modifying the chemical structure of cellular molecules. PRMT1 is known to help B cells release antibodies against germs. However, the mechanism by which PRMT1 acts within B cells is unclear. Recently, PRMT1 was shown to be deregulated in B cell cancersa disease in which B cells divide uncontrollably and cause damage to our bodies. Importantly, the de-regulation of PRMT1 in B cell cancers is associated with poor clinical outcomes. Yet, the role of PRMT1 in B cell cancers is poorly studied. Thus, how PRMT1 functions in B cells under normal and diseased states requires further investigation.This project aims to determine the function of PRMT1 in B cells under normal and diseased states using advanced techniques in molecular biology and immunology. This project will illuminate the role of PRMT1 to antibody-mediated immunity. Furthermore, this research project will reveal the role of PRMT1 in cancers arising from B cells themselves and will rationalize the use of therapies that specifically target PRMT1to treat B cell cancers.

column36: High Resource Users across the urban rural divide: Investigating the link between social determinants of health and high resource use
column37: A small proportion of health care users drive national health expenditure, largely due to systemic, inequitable access and subsequent disproportionate health burdens. These health care users, often referred to as high-cost, high-frequency, or high-resource users (HRUs), are routinely characterized as older adults with multiple comorbid conditions and reduced access to adequate health care, without familial care support. Second, rates of high resource use will be analysed across different levels of rurality in Ontario. Third, I will integrate spatially linked data on available health resources and evaluate rates of high resource use with resource availability. column36: Exploring the Impact of Sarcopenia on Overall-Survival, Disease-Free Survival, and Post-operative Complications in Patients with Esophageal Cancer undergoing Curative Intent Therapy
column37: Background: Sarcopenia is defined as the chronic decrease in muscle mass and function. It is part of the aging process, and can be accelerated by disease and malnutrition. In esophageal cancer, sarcopenia is associated with worse survival, increased post-operative complications, and increased risk of malnutrition. Study 1 will develop a retrospective cohort study to examine changes in sarcopenia by comparing the skeletal muscle indices across three distinct CT scans: staging, post-chemoradiotherapy, and 6-month post-operative. Data from this retrospective study will be used to guide the prospective second study. Study 2 will develop a multi-institutional prospective cohort study to examine the effect of sarcopenia on clinical outcomes.Significance: This research will solidify our understanding of sarcopenia's prognostic effect in esophageal cancer, which can improve patient outcomes by guiding the development of nutritional interventions for those at-risk.

column37: Varicose veins are a manifestation of chronic venous disease characterized by reflux of blood in incompetent veins leading to venous dilation.Varicose veins often occur in the lower limb due to failure of the valves of the greater saphenous veins. in addition to pain and aesthetic concerns, varicosities can lead to significant complications such as leg ulcers. column36: Cellular and Molecular Effects of Cytokines on Prion Protein Expression
column37: Prion diseases are a family of chronic, progressive, and invariably fatal neurodegenerative disorders that are caused by misfolded, aggregated proteins called prions. These proteins are responsible for numerous diseases, including Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in humans, bovine spongiform encephalopathy in cattle, and chronic wasting disease in cervids. Hallmarks of these diseases include rapidly progressive dementia, fatigue, insomnia, and eventual death. Prion diseases are characterized by the misfolding of the prion protein (PrP) into an isoform denoted by scrapie PrP (PrP). The physiological role of PrP remains unknown, however, the protein may have implications in the immune response and neurological disorders such as Alzheimers and multiple sclerosis. This project will aim to further understand the role that PrP may play in the initiation and regulation of the immune response through interactions with cytokines. Bioinformatics software will be used to assess for cytokine binding sites located on the gene that codes for the PrP protein to further understand which cytokines may promote a change in PrP expression. Next, various cellular and molecular biology techniques will test for changes in protein expression levels of PrP and assess changes in gene expression. These tests will be performed using an established cell line, and then repeated with cells collected from healthy donors for the specific cytokines that triggered changes in PrP expression in the cell line. Lastly, depending on our results from these tests, our team will look to assess the roles of PrP in inflammation using a mouse model. The findings in this research will help better understand the physiological role of PrP and provide a greater understanding for how immunity is regulated.

column36: Consequences of febrile inhibition on disease transmission and host health
column37: Recent work has uncovered disturbing implications towards inhibiting natural fever with drugs during infectious disease. Manipulation of body temperature during infection is an ancient process conserved through evolution, but only recently are we uncovering the mechanisms through which fever and hypothermia benefit host health. Fever is energetically costly but drives active resistance to disease through selective recruitment of white blood cells and tightened control of inflammation. Hypothermia effectively conserves energy at the cost of higher pathogen burden but promotes tolerance to disease. I propose three complementary but distinct aims to investigate the consequences of inhibiting these natural thermoregulatory responses in a population. I will specifically focus on the transmission of infections disease as an outcome, given its applications to public health and the unique benefits of our goldfish behavioural fever model. When fish exhibit fever they will select for warmer temperatures rather than generate heat through metabolism. I will examine transmission of a bacterial infection in dynamic and static temperature conditions, the latter designed to effectively inhibit the behavioural fever response. I will complement measurements of established molecular markers of infection with detailed behavioural analysis using motion tracking software. I will repeat this experiment using fish treated with and without an antipyretic analgesic (drugs commonly used to treat pain and fever in humans) to inhibit the behavioural fever response. Finally, I will extend my analysis to hypothermic states to analyze the energetic trade-offs that occur during infection and their consequences on disease transmission.

column36: Uncovering the mechanism of radiosensitivity mediated by the loss of Histone Deacetylase 3 in small-cell lung cancer
column37: Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a highly aggressive and lethal type of lung cancer. Patients diagnosed with extensive-stage (ES), in which the cancer has spread to other parts of the body, are treated with platinum-based chemotherapy and only about 1 in 10 patients live to 5 years after diagnosis of ES-SCLC. Studies with patients have found that giving radiotherapy (RT) to the lung areas of ES-SCLC patients has increased duration of life. A promising strategy to enhance the effect of RT is to use new drugs that can make the radiation more powerful.We used a gene manipulation technology called CRISPR to examine 650 promising druggable targets and found that the loss of a gene known as Histone Deacetylase 3 (HDAC3) caused SCLC cells to be more sensitive to RT. However, how losing HDAC3 causes SCLC to be more sensitive to RT remains unknown.To understand the mechanism, we will test whether HDAC3 loss in SCLC increases the number of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) and persistence of DSBs induced by RT. We will use a technique called immunofluorescence staining to look at the number of DNA DSBs in SCLC cells with little to no HDAC3 protein. We will also introduce fluorescent reporters in these cells to see whether DSBs have been repaired.We will also test whether the RGFP966 drug, which inhibits HDAC3 protein, is suitable for future use in patients. We will examine the side effects and anti-cancer effects of the RGFP966 drug in combination with RT in laboratory models.Ultimately, we aim to enhance the effect of RT in SCLC by understanding how HDAC3 loss makes SCLC more sensitive to RT to understand if this approach and new drug can be used in future patient care.

column36: Investigating Anti-Coronavirus Antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 Infections in Prenatal Women
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic is caused by SARS-CoV-2, which has infected over 261 million people and caused over 5 million deaths worldwide. Pregnant women have been especially affected by COVID-19, leading to worse pregnancy outcomes, such as more frequent hospitalizations and increased pre-term births. This may be associated with changes in the maternal immune system during pregnancy.Upon infection, our immune system produces antibodies, which specifically recognize the infecting virus. There are at least 4 common cold coronaviruses that are closely related to SARS-CoV-2 ; these are called Human Coronaviruses (HCoV). Because these HCoV are closely related to SARS-CoV-2, antibodies that were previously made by our immune systems against them can alter our immune response to SARS-CoV-2. Recent studies have shown that patients with severe COVID-19 have higher levels of HCoV antibodies in their blood. At the same time, people who recently had the common cold were found to have milder COVID-19. Our study aims to fill this gap in knowledge to understand what role these HCoV antibodies play during a SARS-CoV-2 infection ; if they can contribute to protection from severe disease, or worsen the outcomes of COVID-19 in pregnancy.We believe that antibodies against HCoV can modify the antibody levels generated in response to a SARS-CoV-2 infection; this can then affect COVID-19 severity and outcomes during pregnancy. We will investigate how the levels of antibodies against SARS-CoV-2 and HCoV are associated with pre-existing maternal conditions and pregnancy outcomes. Our findings will provide guidance on clinical care for COVID-19 affected pregnancies and inform vaccination guidelines for pregnant women.

column36: A novel role for gangliosides in extracellular vesicle biogenesis and mHTT secretion
column37: Huntington's disease (HD) is a genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the Huntingtin gene that results in the formation and accumulation of the toxic mutant Huntingtin protein (mHTT). Abundance of mHTT causes accretion of neuronal death in the brain, inducing a triad of cognitive, motor, and psychiatric symptoms. In addition, studies in experimental models of Huntington's have shown a decrease in key fat molecules known as gangliosides. Gangliosides are normally abundant in the brain where they play important roles in cell-cell communication. In our laboratory, we have demonstrated the therapeutic effects of administration of the ganglioside GM1 in HD cell and animal models, which are associated with a decrease in mHTT in the brain of HD mice. Preliminary data suggests that this might be due to the ability of gangliosides to induce the production and cellular secretion of particles known as extracellular vesicles (EVs) carrying mHTT and other harmful toxic proteins outside of cells. Through my studies, I aim to identify the mechanism by which GM1 increases EV production and promotes the packaging of mHTT into EVs. I will test the hypothesis that an increased presence of GM1 in cell membranes, enhances the abundance and activity of proteins involved in EV production. My studies will elucidate the mechanism underlying GM1s therapeutic effects and may accelerate the development of ganglioside-based therapies for HD.

column36: Understanding autoimmune and rheumatic disease by analysis of helper T cell differentiation through integrative single-cell multi-omics
column37: Autoimmune and rheumatic diseases (ARDs) are disorders characterized by chronic inflammation of multiple organ systems resulting in long term damage and a decrease in quality of life. It is extremely difficult to diagnose and treat ARDs due to inconsistent disease expression and gaps in understanding of the mechanisms driving them. T helper 17 cells (Th17s) are a subset of immune cells that have been identified to cause inflammation and autoimmunity. The balance of Th17s and their anti-inflammatory counterpart, regulatory T cells (Tregs), is a regulator of ARDs that is not yet well understood. Th17s and Tregs share similarities in their differentiation process from naïve cells and a level of flexibility has been shown to exist between these two cell subtypes depending on the extracellular environment and metabolic landscape. We aim to capture a holistic picture of Th17/Treg dynamics by integrating data obtained from multiple biological networks at a single-cell level, including cellular metabolism and gene expression. Our integration will be done through a semi-supervised learning approach, a form of machine learning suited towards analyzing sparse high-dimensional data in an agnostic manner. This form of statistical learning will reveal key information about our cell subtypes of interest without heavy dependence on existing knowledge, resulting in an unbiased model of the Th17/Treg axis. This has the potential to bring new ways of thinking about autoimmunity and ARDs into light and identify novel targeted therapeutic strategies. Our proposed methods can also be extended to apply to a variety of biological problems, further expanding the fields of computational biology and machine learning.

column36: Investigating the role of ATG4D in neurodegenerative vacuolar storage disorder (NVSD)
column37: Autophagy (Latin for ;self-eating) is the process by which cells degrade and recycle their internal components as a part of the normal turnover of cellular materials. This recycling process is regulated by a core set of proteins (known as ATG proteins) that are found in nearly all eukaryotic cells. Mutations in these proteins can lead to the disruption of autophagy and development of disease. Neurodegenerative vacuolar storage disorder (NVSD) is a newly discovered human genetic disease that results from a mutation in the ATG4D protein. No treatment is available for NVSD, and despite its involvement in NVSD relatively little is known about ATG4D in both normal and affected individuals. Preliminary data from our laboratory showed that cells collected from the connective tissues of NVSD patients have reduced growth compared to control cells. These cells also displayed an altered protein profile, which suggested reduced levels of a protein known as serum response factor (SRF). Both ATG4D and SRF have been associated with the mitochondria, which is responsible for the production of energy within the cell. I hypothesize that NVSD-related ATG4D mutations lead to SRF dysregulation and decreased energy production by mitochondria, which results in the reduced cell growth. To test this hypothesis, I will compare cells from both NVSD patients and normal individuals to confirm SRF levels are reduced and determine any differences in energy production by the mitochondria. Additionally, I will use microscopic techniques to visualize mitochondria and detect any changes that are present in them in NVSD cells. This research hopes to improve our understanding of ATG4D and provide avenues for future research.

column36: Examining the effect of Rifaximin on the gut microbiota and visceral pain in patients with irritable bowel syndrome.
column37: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), a disorder of the gut that causes abdominal pain and altered bowel habits, affects approximately 10% of Canadians and impairs their quality of life. Multiple factors may cause IBS to develop. These mechanisms are not well understood and thus treatment is often unsuccessful. The gut microbiome, a group of bacteria in the gut, is implicated in the development of IBS. However, it is unclear how the microbiome affects the nerves of the gut to cause abdominal pain. Determining how the microbiome affects abdominal pain will lead to more targeted and effective treatments. Recent studies have found the antibiotic Rifaximin improves symptoms in many IBS patients. While it is not certain how this occurs, Rifaximin may change the gut microbiome, the mediators it produces, or act through a mechanism independent of the microbiome. This project seeks to determine the effects of Rifaximin on the gut microbiome, its mediators, and pain nerves in the gut. We hypothesize that Rifaximin treatment will change the gut microbiota and its mediators to a healthier state, which will improve abdominal pain. We will examine the effect of mediators produced by gut bacteria from IBS patients on gut pain nerves and whether this changes after Rifaximin treatment. We will also explore if there is a relationship between the bacterias effect on gut pain nerves and the patients abdominal pain. This research will help us understand how Rifaximin improves abdominal pain and in which IBS patients Rifaximin is most effective. Determining Rifaximins mechanism of action will allow researchers to develop more effective, targeted microbiome treatments beyond a non-specific antibiotic.

column36: Immunogenic cell death of ovarian cancer cells treated with endoplasmic reticulum stressors and cisplatin
column37: Ovarian cancer is a deadly disease with limited options for treatment. Typical treatment for ovarian cancer consists of a combination of surgery and chemotherapy with cisplatin (CDDP). While this initial treatment usually results in remission, the cancer often returns, resistant to CDDP. Therefore, novel therapies are needed in these cases. A relatively novel avenue for cancer therapy involves inducing the process of immunogenic cell death (ICD). ICD is a type of cell death that involves the release of danger signals. These danger signals can then act as a vaccine to stimulate the immune system to attack the cancer cells of origin and prevent recurrence of the cancer after its initial remission. While CDDP is toxic to cancer cells, it is incapable of inducing ICD. CDDP kills cancer cells through a traditional cell death mechanism that does not result in the release of danger signals. Therefore, it is possible that combining CDDP with other drugs that are capable of generating ICD could increase CDDP's toxicity to cancer cells and prevent the recurrence of the cancer. Two candidate drugs that could act as ICD inducers are mifepristone and nelfinavir. Both of these drugs have demonstrated the ability to kill ovarian cancer cells, as well as activate some of the cellular pathways that are required for ICD. Therefore, the goal of this project will be to determine if these drugs are capable of inducing ICD, and to determine whether these drugs increase the toxicity of CDDP when used in combination.

column36: Antibiotic Prescribing in Patients with COVID-19: A Rapid Review with Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression
column37: Antimicrobial resistance is quickly emerging as one of the most important threats to global health. As an increasing number of microorganisms continue to develop resistance to current treatments, experts fear that this growing trend may be exacerbated by another more recent crisis - the COVID-19 pandemic. Evidence suggests that many patients infected with SARS-CoV-2 are often prescribed antibiotics to treat possible bacterial co-infection. Despite frequent antibiotic use in these patients, rates of co-infection are disproportionately low, highlighting that much of this prescribing is unnecessary. Due to the evolving nature of the pandemic, however, determining the exact proportion of COVID-19 patients who are prescribed antibiotics remains difficult. The current project will aim to estimate the prevalence of antibiotic use in patients with COVID-19 by evaluating the patterns and predictors of antibiotic prescribing in these patients. Building on previous work, emphasis will be placed on how prescribing patterns have changed over time as the pandemic has progressed. A rapid review and meta-analysis will be conducted to compile studies on bacterial co-infections and antibiotic prescribing in patients with SARS-CoV-2 between January 2020 and June 2022 across all healthcare settings and age groups. Meta-regression analyses will be performed to evaluate key predictors of prescribing including time, geography, patient characteristics, COVID-19 specific therapies such as immunomodulators, and severity. The results will provide a comprehensive picture of antibiotic use during the pandemic which may be used to improve prescribing practices, thereby confronting resistance.

column36: Evaluating the Efficacy of the Criminalization of HIV Non-Disclosure in Reducing Transmission Rates
column37: Is criminalizing HIV non-disclosure reducing transmission? In Canada, people living with HIV must inform their sexual partners of their HIV status prior to sex, otherwise, they risk getting charged for aggravated sexual assault, unless they both use a condom and are on treatment with undetectable levels of virus. Over 200 people have been prosecuted, but research has shown that the criminalization of HIV non-disclosure plays against public health efforts to reduce the transmission of HIV. For example, it may deter people from getting tested regularly, given that people are only responsible to disclose their HIV if they have a positive test. Criminalization can also keep people from having open and honest conversations with healthcare providers, relationships that are key to being undetectable. This is crucial as people whose virus is undetectable cannot transmit it. Research suggests that criminalization has little to no impact on transmission prevention, and even on disclosures! Public health experts, doctors, advocacy groups, and people living with HIV are all calling for substantive changes that align with our current scientific understanding of transmission risks. Through interviews and surveys, my study aims to improve our understanding of the relationship between perceptions and practices of disclosure, and the sex practices of people living with HIV. I will also investigate whether criminalization affects people differently based on gender, sexuality, and ethnicity, in ways that may exacerbate stigma and inequities. These findings will help researchers, care providers, advocacy groups, and policy makers make informed decisions on potential changes to the criminalization of HIV non-disclosure, and ultimately support the rights and health of people living with HIV.

column36: Improving the persistence of CAR T-cells by understanding senescence
column37: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has led to improved survival for some patients with relapsed/refractory acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). This therapy involves engineering T cells, a white blood cell, with a new gene, the CAR, so that it can recognize and kill the cancer cells. However, long-term survival remains short for many patients, with poor outcomes associated with a loss of the CAR-T cells. One possible reason for the loss of CAR-T cells is senescence, or aging, of the T cells, resulting in inactivity and cell death. Senescence can occur via telomere-dependent or independent pathways. Telomeres are repeats found on the ends of chromosomes that protect the cellular DNA from damage, and critical shortening of these leads to senescence. Telomere independent senescence is mediated by many different pathways. We propose to examine the pathways of senescence in CAR-T cells and how they differ compared to normal T cells, potentially leading to ways to alter these pathways to improve outcomes for patients by increasing persistence. We will explore telomere-dependent senescence by overexpressing telomerase, the enzyme that lengthens telomeres, in CAR-T using an inducible system so we can turn on and off telomerase activity during repeated activation of the CAR-T cells. We will also examine telomerase activity at various time points from patients who have received CAR-T on a clinical trial. Telomere-independent senescence will be explored using a CRISPR screen. CRISPR is a novel technique that allows for targeted breaks in the DNA, which when left alone, results in loss of that gene, or a knockout. We will use this technique on senescent CAR-T, to identify gene knockouts that revert this, and identify targetable pathways to improve CAR-T persistence.
