column36: Establishing and validating an age-adapted definition of chronic kidney disease in Canadian younger adults
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a complex medical condition characterized by persistent kidney dysfunction, and its symptoms do not arise until kidney function has severely deteriorated. Kidney function is often assessed via routine blood and urine screening to estimate glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and detect albuminuria. Current criteria of eGFR60 diagnose all patients with CKD, regardless of age or severity of albuminuria. While a simple and validated threshold, it has not been updated since its conception in 1969 and does not account for age-related eGFR decline. This risks over-diagnosis in older adults and under-diagnosis in younger adults, who could lose much kidney function before finally being diagnosed with CKD. Many age-adapted CKD definitions have been proposed to date but have only been validated in older individuals (age60) and focused mainly on mortality outcomes. Moreover, underdiagnosing CKD in younger individuals with lower kidney function for their age will hinder prevention of progressive CKD and related comorbidities over their lifetime, including increased mortality. Given the limited availability of curative therapies, adopting age-adapted CKD definitions would aid timely prevention and treatment of CKD in younger adults.The proposed project uses provincial health administrative data with clinical and laboratory records to examine differences in care (repeat testing, specialist referrals) and in risk of adverse events (death and cardiac/renal/all-cause hospitalization) between different levels of eGFR and degrees of eGFR decline. These associations will be used to develop and validate an age-adaptive CKD definition that is relevant to younger Canadian adults (age50), as well as project CKD incidence and prevalence in this population.

column36: Etude du potentiel du discours spontane comme outil de depistage precoce de la maladie d'Alzheimer
column37: Le trouble cognitif subjectif (TCS) et le trouble cognitif leger (TCL) font partie des phases preclinique et prodromale de la maladie d'Alzheimer (MA), respectivement. Des changements subtils dans le langage pourraient apparaitre plusieurs annees avant que les signes d'un declin cognitif ne soient remarques, donc analyser ceux-ci pourrait faciliter le diagnostic precoce de la MA. Ces changements sont regulierement etudies a l'aide de taches de discours spontane (DS), qui se rapprochent beaucoup des situations de communication de la vie quotidienne. Cependant, la necessite d'analyser manuellement les resultats a ces taches represente un obstacle a leur utilisation plus repandue par les cliniciens. Pour pallier a ce probleme, plusieurs etudes ont demontre le potentiel de methodes de traitement automatique du langage naturel et d'apprentissage machine. Ce projet aura comme objectif de classifier des controles et des individus avec un TCS ou un TCL selon leur groupe diagnostic a l'aide d'un echantillon de DS. De plus, l'importance de differentes categories de caracteristiques linguistiques (ex., fluence, caracteristiques lexicales) pour la classification sera etudiee. Pour ce faire, les echantillons de DS de 120 individus (40 controles, 40 avec un TCS, 40 avec un TCL) seront tires de la base de donnees COMPASS-ND. Pour classifier les echantillons de DS, des algorithmes Support Vector Machine et Random Forest Classifier seront utilises. Les resultats de ce projet pourront ameliorer la precision des diagnostics (TCS et TCL) et faciliter la conception d'outils qui aideront les cliniciens a evaluer le DS. Si les echantillons de DS sont efficaces pour differencier les individus des groupes etudies, ce projet demontrera aussi le potentiel du DS pour la detection precoce de la MA.

column36: A Cost-Effective Analysis of a Child and Family Neurodevelopmental Program
column37: Children with brain-based developmental disabilities are three to five times more likely than their peers to have other mental disorders such as depression, anxiety, and disruptive behaviour. The findings from this research hopes to provide a better understanding and add to the growing evidence-base of parent-focused programs for children with developmental disabilities. column36: Developing Nanobodies to Probe Sperm-Egg Membrane Fusion
column37: Human fertilization requires the membrane fusion between the oocyte and the spermatocyte. Two well-studied proteins involved in this process are JUNO, a membrane protein on the surface of human egg, and IZUMO1, the corresponding binding partner on human sperm. Numerous studies have shown that the binding between JUNO and IZUMO1 is crucial for the downstream sperm-egg fusion processes. JUNO and IZUMO1 are currently understood as the attachment receptors that bring the gametes together and trigger the recruitment of fusogens to facilitate downstream membrane fusion. However, much of the mechanism after JUNO-IZUMO1 binding is unclear and new reagents and approaches are required to help probe the interactions involved in the sperm-egg fusion. One challenge is that any probes must be able to penetrate the zona pellucida, a dense glycoprotein layer that protects the egg. Nanobodies are single-chain protein designed based on the heavy chain variable domain of the camelid antibody (VHH). Compared to traditional antibodies, nanobodies have advantages in their small size and are predicted to be able to penetrate through the oocyte zona pellucida layer and access areas that would normally be difficult to reach. Thus, nanobodies raised against JUNO, IZUMO1, and JUNO-IZUMO1 complex may be able to serve as novel probes for imaging, providing an important tool in elucidating key molecules, epitopes, and interactions at the sperm-egg interface. Preliminary data from our lab have identified several anti-JUNO, anti-IZUMO1, and anti-JUNO-IZUMO1 complex nanobodies that bind to different epitopes on JUNO and IZUMO1. Using biochemical assays and biophysical techniques, this current project aims to further characterize these candidate nanobodies to interrogate the sperm-egg synapse.

column36: Relationships between plasma biomarkers, neuroimaging biomarkers and cognitive impairment in cerebral amyloid angiopathy
column37: Alzheimers Disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia ; a devastating condition that impairs memory and leads to immeasurable stress to families. Dementia currently costs our system $10.3 billion/year, and the number of Canadians living with dementia will double in the next decade. In AD, toxic proteins (amyloid beta and tau) accumulate and cause brain degeneration. In some, amyloid can accumulate in and cause damage to small blood vessels in a process called Cerebral Amyloid Angiopathy (CAA). CAA can cause bleeds in the brain that lead to cognitive impairment, disability, and death. Diagnosing and detecting CAA early is challenging. New technologies now allow us to measure the levels of amyloid beta and tau in the blood and could lead to the early detection of CAA. However, no studies have examined the blood levels of amyloid beta or tau in patients with CAA.The objective of our study is to test for and compare the blood levels of amyloid beta and tau between the following groups: (i) those with CAA (ii) those with AD but no CAA and (iii) healthy adults. We will examine whether differences exist in the levels of amyloid and tau between these groups. Our second objective is to see whether the blood levels of amyloid and tau may also be associated with the degree of (i) memory impairment and (ii) damage to the brains structure seen on Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). If our study identifies a unique blood profile of amyloid and/or tau in those with CAA, it could potentially justify the use of these blood tests in future. This project may provide new insights into underlying disease mechanisms in CAA, lead to improved assessment and care, and potentially give rise to clinical tools to better evaluate patients with cognitive impairment.

column36: Prenatal stress and subsequent maternal pain associated with altered brain development in children
column37: Chronic pain is a major public health issue, affecting one in five Canadians. The estimated costs of chronic pain in Canada are $60 billion CAD per year. Chronic pain impacts social, emotional, and daily functioning. However, every case of chronic pain starts as acute pain. Early detection and pain management may prevent the transition from acute to chronic pain.Research suggests that anxiety disorders may increase the risk of developing chronic pain. Public health measures put in place to stop the spread of COVID-19 have increased rates of anxiety, notably in pregnant individuals. Pregnant women currently have three to four times higher levels of anxiety than they did prior to the pandemic. Pandemic-related anxiety may increase the risk of pregnant women developing chronic pain. There is also an increased risk of prenatal stress to the developing brains of infants. Animal studies have shown that prenatal stress is related to altered brain development, increased pain sensitivity, and anxious behaviors in offspring. Moreover, both prenatal stress and maternal physical symptoms, such as pain, are linked to increased pain symptoms in children at 18 months of age. However, little is known about the relationships between prenatal stress and maternal pain, and whether it alters child brain development, thereby contributing to emotional, and pain sensitivities in children.This project will leverage longitudinal data collected from 10,000+ mothers across Canada to explore the relationships between prenatal stress, maternal pain, and child brain development. Identifying factors contributing to the development of chronic pain will lead to earlier intervention strategies to reduce the prevalence, costs and life-long suffering of chronic pain for Canadians and their families.

column36: Development of a patient-derived organoid model for lung-to-brain cancer metastasis
column37: Lung cancer is the most common cancer in the world and the leading cause of death worldwide. Most lung cancers are non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLCs) and brain metastasis in NSCLC patients is highly frequent. Metastasis accounts for most lung cancer deaths, but there are limits to current models for metastatic cancer models. Some of the simpler models, such as 2D cell culture, dont completely reflect the diverse genetic nature of tumors and therefore wont be as helpful providing information about individual treatment. Other models, such as xenograft models, where cancer cells are transplanted into mice, can provide individualized information, but also take months to grow up, and therefore wont be helpful for late-stage patients. Organoids are tiny, patient-derived, three-dimensional tissue constructs, grow quickly (~4 weeks) in a culture dish, and can mimic parent tissues, even over long-term culture. These organoids have many applications, but most importantly can be able to help choose personalized treatment. It is important to create the right environment for the organoids so they can grow properly and retain genetic characteristics. This is what our research aims to do for patient-derived lung-to-brain cancer organoids. Specifically, our research aims to establish an efficient model of metastatic lung cancer to brain, by optimizing growing conditions for patient derived organoids and creating a biobank of these organoids. We will use these organoids for therapeutic screening to identify personalized treatment options for patients with metastatic lung cancer.

column36: More than meets the eye: Investigating the relationship between BAP1 loss and EMT in Uveal Melanoma metastasis
column37: Uveal melanoma is the most common cancer of the eye. Every year, approximately 130 Canadians are diagnosed with uveal melanoma, which kills approximately half of patients within 1 year due to uncontrolled spread of cancer cells to the lungs, liver, and/or bones. In 80% of these malignant cases, there is a mutation in a gene called BAP1. Previous research suggests that BAP1 mutations lead to epithelial to mesenchymal transition (EMT), a process which allows many cancer cells to gain migratory and invasive properties. Our lab has developed a Bap1 mutant uveal melanoma mouse model that results in accelerated cancer spread to the lungs and liver. Our preliminary data suggests that Bap1 mutations prevent cells from ;sticking to one another, which may allow the cancer cells in the eye to travel to distant sites. The goal of my research is understand how Bap1 loss leads to this spread of cancer cells from the primary tumour in the eye to the lungs and liver. Using our mouse model, I will study the expression of a group of proteins part of the Apical Junction Complex (AJC), which help neighbouring cells stick to one another. I will determine which cells in the tumour are decreasing the expression of the AJC proteins and examine the relationship between the amount and distribution of AJC protein expression and molecular signs of tumour aggressiveness. Through this work, I hope to identify potential therapeutic targets to mitigate or prevent uveal melanoma spread, thus improving patient outcomes.

column36: Living well with dementia to the end of life: A qualitative study of Japanese Canadian experiences
column37: With the rising number of Canadians from diverse cultural backgrounds living with dementia, there is an urgent need for research that is both culturally sensitive and centred on the perspectives of persons living with dementia and their carers. Moreover, differences in service use and dementia rates in cultural minority groups such as Asian immigrants underlines the need to examine the role of culture in ones experience with dementia. Thus, I aim to take a person-centred approach to understanding how people with dementia and carers live well with dementia to the end of life. Furthermore, I strive to investigate the relationship between culture and dementia by recruiting individuals from the local Japanese community. Specifically, I aim to recruit 10 dyads from the local Japanese community, with each dyad made up of one person living with dementia and their carer. Then, I will hold interviews and group art-making workshops for participants to identify and articulate themes that may be difficult to express through words alone. This project will highlight the perspectives of both persons living with dementia and their carers, thereby describing how they live well with dementia in the context of their relationships and cultural backgrounds. This research will also complement a larger ongoing project by Dr. Susan Cox and colleagues by adding a cross-cultural component to the work. column36: Social anxiety and coping motivated cannabis use: The moderating effect of negative urgency
column37: Background: Chronic cannabis use is associated with a variety of health issues; including cognitive impairment and worsened mental health. Social anxiety (SA) is frequently associated with cannabis use and the associated negative consequences. Coping motives for cannabis use are also frequently associated with negative consequences. Additionally, people high in SA are more likely to list coping motives as opposed to other motives for use. Despite theory pointing to SA as a predictor of use, empirical evidence suggests that the pathway is not clean cut, with not all individuals with SA using cannabis to cope. Negative Urgency (tendency to act impulsively when distressed) may moderate this association. Aim: We are aiming to test negative urgency as a moderator of the association between SA and cope motives. The association between cope motives and the negative consequences of cannabis use will also be investigated. Methods: Undergraduate students (18-25 years old) will complete a battery of online questionnaires self-reporting on cannabis use consequences (MACQ), cannabis use motives (CMMQ), SA (LSAS), and negative urgency (UPPS-P). Proposed Analyses: Regression analysis will be used to test the moderating effect of negative urgency on SA and coping motives, and simple linear correlation will be used to assess the relation between coping motives and negative consequences. Expected Results: We expect to find that individuals who are high in SA will be more likely to use for coping motives, and that this association will be stronger for those who have higher scores in negative urgency. Further, we expect to see that coping motives will positively correlate with the negative consequences of cannabis use.

column36: Exploring the role of income inequality in sleep deprivation among adolescents
column37: Approximately 30%of Canadian teens are not getting the recommended eight hours of sleep. Certain subgroups are likelier to experience sleep deprivation including girls and Hispanic and Black teens. Long-term sleep deprivation is associated with an increased risk of chronic disease such as diabetes and depression which, in turn, contribute to death and disability. There is evidence that income inequality, the gap between rich and poor in society, may play a role. One possible explanation is that increasing income inequality may worsen the insecurity of those in a community who get ;left behind, increasing the risk of mental health conditions such as depression, which are linked to sleep deprivation. Moreover, income inequality may decrease social cohesion, the connectedness among societal members, which is shown to protect against mental health conditions that can, in turn, influence sleep. However, no previous research has explored the role of income inequality on sleep deprivation in adolescents.Using data from the Cohort on Obesity, Marijuana use, Physical activity, Alcohol use, Smoking, and Sedentary behavior study and the 2016 Canadian Census Survey, the proposed research aims to address this gap in literature by (1) examining the link between income inequality and sleep duration in a sample of Canadian teens; (2) determining whether social cohesion and mental health conditions mediate this association; and (3) examining if associations differ across racial/ethnic and gender groups.By elucidating a link between income inequality and teen sleep deprivation, this study can help inform policy makers and school boards in developing interventions for reducing income inequality and sleep deprivation among teens, paving the way for improved lifetime health.

column36: The Human DDX3X Helicase as an Antiviral Target for HSV-1 Replication
column37: It is believed that the herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV-1) is present in almost 90% of the world population. HSV-1 lies dormant in most carriers, but complications in patients with clinical symptoms can sometimes lead to death. As in many other viruses, HSV-1 interacts with a multitude of cellular partners to hijack the hosts cell machinery. Some of these partners may be incorporated into new viral particles. The inclusion of these cellular proteins often facilitates one or more of the stages of the replication cycle. With respect to HSV-1, analysis of extracellular virions revealed that ;DDX3X is one of these cellular proteins. DDX3X is an ATP-dependent RNA helicase that modulates several stages of gene expression in human cells. By inhibiting the expression of DDX3X with siRNAs in the context of a HSV-1 infection, this enzyme was shown to participate in the replication cycle by promoting transcription of viral genes. However, other results revealed an additional and unexpected function for a helicase. Indeed, it was discovered that DDX3X interacts with pUL31, a viral protein involved in the budding of capsids outside the nucleus. In addition, inhibition of DDX3X hampered the normal transport of fully assembled viral particles. These results suggest that DDX3X has a proviral role beyond transcription by participating in the nucleus exit process and allowing the release of viral particles into extracellular space. However, the mechanism of action of DDX3X and the extent of DDX3X helicase enzyme activity remain to be defined. Furthermore, various other viruses have been shown to require this helicase during replication. DDX3X is therefore a very interesting target for the creation of broad-spectrum antivirals.

column36: Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (FESS) simulation: validating a medium-fidelity simulator for junior resident training
column37: Sinus surgeryis one of the most common and technically demanding procedures performed by ear, nose and throat surgeons. Surgeons must simultaneously maneuver multiple instruments within a narrow space bordered by vital structures. Overall complication rates are reported between 6-14%, with highest rates among novice surgeons. Given the steep learning curve and potential for serious complications, simulation models are well-suited to train residents outside the operating room. Cadavers and virtual reality simulators offer the most realistic model of the anatomy, however, their poor accessibility and high cost limit their regular use. Less realistic models offer a low-cost alternative that trainees can use to hone their skills. Currently, there are no such models commercially available for sinus surgery training and, to the best of my knowledge, none in production that have passed the rigorous validation steps needed for their incorporation into residency training. To resolve this gap in sinus surgery training, I developed a moderately realistic simulator to be incorporated into ear, nose and throat resident training curricula and specifically targeted at training junior residents. In the present study, we will attempt to validate this sinus surgery model as a training resource for junior residents. We ask the following questions:Is the simulator a valid tool sinus surgery training? Do junior residents improve at fundamental skills of sinus surgery using the simulator?

column36: Can activated beta-catenin (ABV) be used as a marker to predict aggressive osteosarcoma and progression to metastatic disease?

Currently there are no specific laboratory tests to indicate whether a tumor may metastasize or become locally aggressive. The identification of such a test would allow for the early identification and intervention for patients presenting without obvious disease spread who may be at a high risk for progression. This may have a significant impact on the treatment and ongoing monitoring of these patients. column36: Rapid detection of Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus outbreaks using a multi-omics approach
column37: Canada has been alarmed by a recent growth in Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus (MRSA) infections. 2,103 cases of MRSA were reported nationwide in 2015, and 10% of cases resulted in mortality within 30-days; mortality rates were even higher (20%) for bloodstream infections. MRSA is a highly virulent bacterium that can enter the bloodstream through compromised skin and release harmful toxins that can cause escalation to septic shock and death. A key reason for this virulence is MRSA's ability to colonize, spread and invade both the community and health-care settings. Detecting an increase of MRSA cases early could prevent the development of a full outbreak. If not detected quick enough, an outbreak could get out of control and cost many lives and hospital resources. Using preliminary data from Alberta Precision Laboratories regarding MRSA cases over the past 18 years, we have found an undetected outbreak of MRSA between May-August 2016 at Foothills Medical Center (FMC) - the largest hospital in Calgary and the province of Alberta. During any four-month interval, MRSA bloodstream infections average 11.36 cases. The summer of 2016 at FMC reported 21 cases of MRSA - which is nearly double the expected rate of MRSA infection. Using patient claims, we have found that the outbreak costed at least $450,000. Using a multi-omics approach, we seek to characterize the phenotype of the outbreak isolates; we also seek to establish the use of genomics, proteomics and metabolomics as a unified tool for the rapid detection of outbreaks that have gone undetected through traditional surveillance methods. I will also be integrating this with clinical and patient data to understand the changing epidemiology of MRSA and the reason behind the emergence of outbreak strains.

column36: Phosphoinositide control of antigen cross-presentation by classical dendritic cells
column37: Cells obtain nutrients and information from their environment by internalizing material into organelles called endosomes. Typically, ingested macromolecules, such as proteins, are contained within the endocytic organelle until they are delivered to digestive organelles. In some cases, however, undigested macromolecules escape from endocytic organelles into the cell cytosol. This is especially evident in immune cells called dendritic cells (DCs). DCs transfer endocytosed macromolecules to the cytosol to elicit inflammation or, process and present proteins to T cells in a process known as antigen cross-presentation. This allows DCs to perform fundamental roles in homeostasis and immunity. However, the mechanism of how macromolecules are released from endosomes is unknown.We have identified pores on the endocytic organelles of DCs that allow for the escape of endocytosed proteins required for cross-presentation. We have also collected evidence showing lipids called phosphoinositides drive endosomal pore formation and therefore cross-presentation. This, along with the fact that phosphoinositides mediate cellular events by recruiting protein effectors, leads to our hypothesis that phosphoinositides regulate macromolecular escape from endocytic organelles by coordinating the formation of pores through the recruitment of pore-forming protein effectors.Over two years, my aim is to identify the phosphoinositides regulating endosomal pore formation to facilitate the fundamental DC function of cross-presentation.Beyond DCs, escape of macromolecules from endosomes is involved in key processes, such as inflammatory signalling, in many cell types. My NSERC CGS will therefore have widespread implications for fields ranging from cellular physiology to organismal homeostasis.

column36: Assessment of Tongue and Handgrip Strength in Health and Critical Illness: A Case-Control Study
column37: People often require breathing machines to stay alive during severe illnesses. These machines save lives but complications can occur as a result of the illness or the necessary treatments. Some complications include weakness throughout the body and/or difficulty with swallowing. Impaired swallowing, also known as dysphagia, can cause patients to experience challenges with eating and drinking, which may lead to malnutrition, breathing problems, and even death. When measuring the severity of patients overall weakness as well as their recovery following severe illness, one method is assessing handgrip strength. When considering swallowing, the tongue is important for moving food and liquid from the mouth to the throat. Some information indicates that the tongue is weaker following breathing machine use. However, more information is needed to determine if tongue strength is related to handgrip strength and if tongue strength could potentially be used to determine dysphagia risk. We also need to understand whether tongue strength changes as people age or only as a result of severe illness. This study aims to explore the relationship between tongue and handgrip strength, and compare differences in tongue and handgrip strength between healthy people and patients with severe illness. Results from this work will help us understand not only the relationship between tongue and handgrip strength but also these measures in those who are healthy and those who are severely ill. Ultimately, this work may help us to determine easy, less expensive ways to identify and treat swallowing impairments following severe illness.

column36: Predire l'apparition de troubles psychotiques chez les jeunes suite a une psychose toxique par methamphetamine

Ce manque de traitement adequat est estime etre environ 18.5 fois plus couteux que le cout du traitement des patients traites a l'externe. Plusieurs etudes ont tente de distinguer les deux conditions en examinant differents facteurs dont le type de symptomes, les deficits cognitifs et la croyance sur l'experience psychotique. Ceux-ci ont tous ete lies au groupe qui developpera un trouble psychotique, mais ne sont pas suffisants pour nous aider a le differencier. L'objectif de cette etude est de developper un outil de depistage qui permettra aux cliniciens de determiner rapidement si une personne atteinte de psychose liee a la consommation de methamphetamine/stimulants est a risque de developper un trouble psychotique. Pour ce faire, nous allons chercher a determiner parmi les predicteurs les mieux documentes lesquels sont les plus lies a un trouble psychotique et non a une psychose induite par la methamphetamine.

column36: Validation of the modified Hospital One-Year Mortality Risk score among hospitalized patients with dementia
column37: Dementia is a common and incurable disease of the brain that may cause difficulty with memory, communication, and the ability to plan ahead. It results in symptoms, including pain, fatigue, and difficulty swallowing; and disability, including difficulty with dressing, eating, and bathing. It also limits life expectancy. Palliative care is a field of medicine that aims to improve the quality of life of patients with life-limiting illness. Palliative care providers manage symptoms, coordinate support at home, and provide end-of-life care. That is, the services that palliative care provides could meet the needs of patients with dementia. Despite this, these patients have poor access to palliative care.Patients with dementia are frequently admitted to hospital, such that admissions may be an opportunity for them to be referred to palliative care. However, the decision to refer is difficult because dementia does not have a defined terminal stage, and it is difficult to know how long these patients have to live. A tool that could accurately predict the risk of death in hospitalized patients with dementia could make the decision to refer less difficult, which would increase access to palliative care. The tool would also allow patients and their families to make more informed plans for the future.A tool called the modified Hospital One-Year Mortality Risk provides accurate predictions of risk of death one year after hospitalization. However, it has not been tested in patients with dementia specifically. Considering this, the first objective of this study is test the tool in hospitalized patients with dementia in Ontario. The second objective is to improve the accuracy of the tool by adding factors to it that may be relevant to the life expectancy of patients with dementia.

column36: Defining clinically important bleeding outcomes for clinical trials in hematological malignancies
column37: Approximately 6,900 Canadians are diagnosed with acute leukaemia (AL) each year. AL and its treatments cause patients to bleed more easily. In clinical trials, researchers use bleeding as an outcome to find better ways to prevent and treat bleeding in AL patients. Currently, there are four categories of bleeding outcomes: grades 1 and 2 which are mild types of bleeding, and grades 3 and 4 that are severe types of bleeding (require transfusion or bleeding that could cause death). In clinical studies, grades 2, 3, and 4 bleeding events are combined as one outcome. The grouping of the bleeding events is problematic as grade 2 bleeding events are more frequent and milder and may not be related to severe bleeding. In addition, these outcomes do not consider what bleeding events are important and concerning to patients and providers. This project aims to develop a utility-based bleeding score that defines bleeding and is relevant to AL patients and others involved in their care. Using a mixed-methods approach, I will be integrating two data sources: an analysis from three international studies on signs and symptoms of minor bleeds that may predict severe bleeding; and qualitative interview results from AL patients and providers to create the UBS. Both data sources will be used to identify bleeding events which will be scored for importance by a group of patients and providers. This information will be used to develop the UBS. An international survey will be sent to AL treating physicians to obtain their input and willingness to use this new bleeding outcome in future research. The findings from this project will help clinical researchers use an outcome that will be important and meaningful to patients and providers when performing studies in the acute leukaemia population.

column36: Etude genetique de l'impact des vagues de chaleur sur les evenements cardiovasculaires dans la cohorte de la UK Biobank
column37: Les evenements de chaleur extreme ont d'importants effets sur la sante. Les personnes atteintes d'une maladie coronarienne sont plus a risque de mortalite pendant les vagues de chaleur. On pense qu'une capacite de transpiration plus faible avec le vieillissement rend les patients atteints de coronaropathie plus vulnerables a la chaleur excessive, les predisposant potentiellement a une circulation sanguine insuffisante dans une chaleur extreme. Le risque peut etre aggrave chez les patients atteints de coronaropathie auxquels on a prescrit des beta-bloquants, un medicament reduisant le travail impose au coeur, en raison d'une diminution de la circulation sanguine de la peau qui peut compromettre davantage la dissipation de la chaleur. Une variation du gene ACTN3 semble offrir une resilience au froid grace a la generation de chaleur musculaire. Les individus homozygotes pour l'allele T sont plus en mesure de maintenir la temperature corporelle centrale lors de l'immersion en eau froide via des changements dans la production de chaleur des muscles squelettiques. Cela confirme la pertinence de mener d'autres etudes genetiques pour identifier les variantes genetiques liees a la sensibilite a la chaleur. Les variantes genetiques pourraient aider a reveler les voies physiopathologiques impactees par la chaleur qui peuvent guider le developpement de nouvelles interventions therapeutiques et preventives. En ciblant les mecanismes biologiques impliques dans la susceptibilite a la chaleur, ce projet de recherche contribuera a la comprehension des facteurs genetiques associes au maintien de la temperature corporelle lors de chaleur extreme, ce qui pourrait contribuer a la diminution du risque d'hospitalisation pour des causes cardiovasculaires pendant les vagues de chaleur.

column36: Determinants and Monitoring of Response to disease-modifying therapy for Transthyretin Amyloidosis Cardiomyopathy: The ATTR-CM study
column37: Transthyretin amyloidosis cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) is a heart muscle disease with only a 3.6-year median survival time from diagnosis without treatment. ATTR-CM is caused by amyloid plaque buildup in the myocardial interstitium from misfolded transthyretin proteins. Awareness of this disease has dramatically improved with approval of the novel disease modifying therapy tafamidis, a medication approved by Health Canada in 2020 for treatment of ATTR-CM. However, significant knowledge gaps remain and predictors of response to therapy are poorly understood. There have also been significant advancements in clinical care since the ATTR-ACT study, a clinical trial that assessed tafamidis for ATTR-CM treatment. Techniques for non-invasive diagnosis have now improved and facilitate increased rate of diagnosis. Tafamidis is also the most expensive cardiovascular medication, with a list price of approximately $200,000 per year per patient. Eligibility criteria defined by Health Canada for tafamidis therapy initiation do not optimally reflect the current population of patients. The primary objective of this study is to develop an evidence-based approach for predicting response to therapy by evaluating a cohort of ATTR-CM patients treated with tafamidis. The secondary objective is to determine the magnitude and timing of changes in monitoring parameters such as symptom burden, laboratory biomarkers, and cardiac imaging variables. Predicting response to therapy is crucial in improving existing eligibility criteria and clinical usage of tafamidis. The study will help guide future treatment, bridge gaps in the optimal management of ATTR-CM and reduce healthcare expenditures by identifying those most likely to derive benefit from this expensive therapy.

column36: Electrophysiology of attention in the motor thalamus and thalamic reticular nucleus
column37: Background:While deep brain stimulation is effective at alleviating motor symptoms of advanced Parkinson's disease, attention deficits are a frequent side effect, the mechanisms of which are uncertain. Thus there is a need to characterize the role of the ventral intermediate nucleus of the thalamus ; a common deep brain stimulation target ; in attention. The searchlight hypothesis gives an account of how attention is controlled in the thalamus, and predicts that motor related activity in the ventral intermediate nucleus will decrease when attention is directed towards sensory stimuli. The objective of the proposed study is to test the predictions of the searchlight hypothesis by monitoring neural activity within the ventral intermediate nucleus and the thalamic reticular nucleus while participants perform an auditory attention task called the auditory oddball task.Methods:Patients undergoing DBS surgery will be directed to count the occurrences of an infrequent ('oddball') tone while ignoring a more frequent tone. Microelectrodes will record from the thalamus throughout.Expected Outcomes and Significance:We expect activity within the ventral intermediate nucleus to decrease in response to attended oddball tones, but not in response to common tones, thereby implicating the ventral intermediate nucleus in selective attention. These findings will inform clinicians administering deep brain stimulation for the treatment of Parkinson's disease.

column36: Mitochondrial dysregulation induced by an ulcerative colitis-associated pathobiont
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) affects over 270,000 Canadians, with this number increasing each year. By 2030, it is expected that 400,000 Canadians will be living with IBD. The two major IBD subtypes are Crohn's disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). The intestinal inflammation seen in IBD is linked to exaggerated immune responses against an imbalanced gut microbiome and changes to critical intestinal epithelial cell (IEC) functions such as absorbing nutrients and forming a barrier against pathogens. IECs have high energy expenditure, thus requiring mitochondrial ATP production. Notably, IEC mitochondrial dysfunction is frequently observed in IBD patients. I hypothesize the aberrant mitochondrial function reflects the actions of microbes on the epithelium. In CD, mitochondrial dysregulation has been linked to the actions of a pathobiont. A pathobiont is an opportunistic microbe that is normally non-pathogenic in a healthy gut, but in susceptible individuals such as those predisposed to IBD, pathobionts outcompete healthy gut bacteria to colonize the intestine and cause disease. Whether pathobionts alter mitochondrial function in UC has yet to be examined. I propose to elucidate the structural and functional mitochondrial changes caused by p19A, a hemolysin toxin-producingE. colipathobiont isolated from UC patients. To study the effects of p19A on mitochondria, I will use both our in vivo novel mouse model of colitis and an ex vivo intestinal organoid model where mice or human patient IECs are cultured into a mini-gut structure. I will also explore the efficacy of mitochondria-targeted drugs to counteract the effects of p19A in both models. The proposed study will lead to better understandings of IBD pathogenesis and may help the development of novel IBD drugs.

column36: Residential Treatment Trajectories Among Young People Who Use Drugs in Greater Vancouver
column37: Illicit drug use is associated with severe health and social harms among young people, which have been further exacerbated in the context of the overlapping overdose and COVID-19 crises in Greater Vancouver. In response to the overdose public health emergency, the government of British Columbia has advanced the development of substance use treatment, including residential treatment beds for younger drug users. While there is a growing understanding of the barriers to care encountered by marginalized youth using drugs, there exist few in-depth investigations looking at how these young people engage with current residential treatment practices, and how they understand and navigate other systems of care and supervision. Such an approach is critical to developing impactful policy and program interventions that seek to reduce harms related to drug use. The proposed study will employ qualitative ethnographic methodology to explore how young people enter, undertake, and leave residential treatment programs for substance use. Although new lines of inquiry are likely to emerge as the research progresses, the primary objectives of this study are: 1) to explore how young people who use drugs interact with residential treatment services; 2) to examine how individual (e.g., concurrent mental health care needs), social (e.g., relationships with caregivers), and structural (e.g., homelessness, systemic racism) factors shape engagement with residential treatment services; and 3) to identify how current residential treatments can be tailored to better match the needs and desires of diverse young drug users. The findings from this study will have important implications for public health policies and programs that better align with the wants and desires of young people using drugs.

column36: Patient and health care provider priorities for outcomes in randomized controlled trials of physical activity for older adults
column37: Outcome selection is a critical component of clinical trial design. Outcomes are what is recorded and compared between conditions in a clinical trial to determine if the intervention under investigation is effective. For example, a trial that is testing the effects of physical activity may record changes in strength or aerobic fitness as an outcome. However, outcomes that are deemed important by researchers may not be the same outcomes that are of highest importance to trial participants and their health care providers. Too often, research is conducted without sufficient consultation and consideration of patients and their health care providers. This can result in knowledge creation that is not viewed as important or practical to patient lives. To improve the design of clinical trials of physical activity for older adults, we aim to coordinate with older adults and their key health care providers to learn which outcomes they consider most relevant. We will conduct both individual interviews (n=20) and focus groups (n=4) (May to Sept 2022) with a diverse selection of older adults and health care providers to understand the benefits and changes they would expect to see following participation in a regular physical activity. We will also inquire about negative (adverse) outcomes they might be concerned about. We will analyze interview and focus group transcripts to synthesize recommendations for outcomes to be included in physical activity trials with older adults. This project will assist clinical trialists in selecting outcomes for future physical activity trials that are both valuable and applicable to the lives of older adults. Ultimately, older adults will benefit, as research will be produced more efficiently and with their voices centered in outcome selection.

column36: In search of a treatment for Alzheimer's Disease: Correlating molecular structure of novel unnatural amino acids to arginase inhibitory activity
column37: Alzheimers Disease (AD) is one of the deadliest diseases in our population and it currently has no known treatments. To advance the search for a treatment, I am synthesizing and studying novel inhibitors of arginase, the enzyme that breaks down arginine amino acids in the brain. Arginase inhibitors have shown therapeutic potential, as their use in mouse AD models improved their memory and cognition, but current inhibitors are not potent enough for human use. By synthesizing and studying novel inhibitors, I will identify characteristics of potent arginase inhibitors, which can aid in future drug development and is the primary objective of my study.Using synthetic organic chemistry, I will synthesize20 novel molecules with known properties of arginase inhibitors. I will determine each molecule's chemical structure using nuclear magnetic resonance and mass spectrometry. Then, I will measure each molecule's potency of inhibition using an arginase assay. The assay will indicate each compounds IC50, which is the drug concentration at which 50% of arginase enzymes are inhibited. IC50 values will be correlated to molecular structure to determine characteristics most strongly correlated with potent inhibition. Identified characteristics will direct subsequent rounds of synthesis until a compound with an IC50 below 1µM is made, which can then undergo further drug development testing.Characterizing potent inhibitors will guide the development of arginase inhibitors and help improve the potency of the compounds. The development of more potent arginase inhibitors gives them the potential to be used as therapeutic agents. By doing so, these novel therapeutics can alleviate the suffering experienced by those living with AD and allow them to lead a more meaningful life.

column36: Arginine requirements and metabolism in newborn preterm neonates
column37: Arginine is an amino acid (AA) that is not required in the diet of healthy individuals but becomes an essential component of diet under certain conditions. These conditions may include critical illness, parenteral nutrition or even rapid growth as occurs during childhood or prematurity. Under such conditions, arginine is referred to as conditionally essential. Therefore, arginine is conditionally essential in the sick, total parenterally fed (TPN) newborn infant. Batshaw et al demonstrated that moderate hypoargininemia occurred in a significant proportion of of low birth weight infants with ammonia levels inversely correlated with plasma arginine. It is clear from those studies that piglets fed a diet meeting the needs of all other AA, have an absolute requirement of dietary arginine. Published standards only define the minimum requirements for swine. However, infants in intensive care receive different intakes of arginine depending on clinical condition and this project utilizes this aspect of care to study the relationship between arginine intake, plasma arginine and plasma ammonia. This is a natural experiment as infants are unintentionally given variable amounts of arginine as part of their parenteral nutrition depending on their clinical condition. The goal is to gather pilot data on arginine requirements in TPN fed newborns in the NICU using plasma arginine and ammonia concentration in response to varied intakes of arginine in TPN feeding. The results of this study will be of direct and immediate relevance for neonatal intensive care across the world as it will allow clinicians for the first time to ensure adequate intake of arginine. In addition, the results will enhance our understanding of amino acid metabolism, used to determine requirements of other AAs.

column36: An Artificial Intelligence (AI) Platform for Classification of Ovarian Tumors
column37: Ovarian cancer ranks fifth in cancer deaths among women (~1,800 and ~14,000deaths/year in Canada and U.S., respectively), accounting for more deaths than any other cancer of the female reproductive system. There are 5 major subtypes of epithelial ovarian cancer. Each subtype is associated with a distinct set of mutated genes, cellular structures, and responds differently to chemotherapy. However, their treatment remains mostly the same, centered around surgery and chemotherapy. The lack of subtype specific treatment can be attributed to the challenges in sub-classifying ovarian cancer. One major challenge in subclassifying ovarian cancer is poor diagnosis reproducibility.Histopathology (the microscopic study of diseased tissue) has been an important tool incancer diagnosis. Histopathology images capture cellular phenotypes which reflect the effect of DNA alterations on cancer cells. However, sub-classification based on histopatological imagesis often hampered by disagreement among independent observers and poor diagnostic reproducibility. To address this issue,I intend to build a novel artificial intelligence (AI)-based platform for an automated analysis of histopathology slides and ovarian cancer biomarker discovery.Recent applications of deep learning methods (e.g. convoluted neural networks (CNNs)) on image data have demonstrated the ability of CNN to learn predictive features from raw imaging data.I will explore different architectures of CNNs to accurately identify the subtypes of ovarian cancer and choose the best-performing classifer by measuring its performance on held-out test datasets.I expect this research to contribute to the identification of ovarian cancer biomarkers for patient stratification and individualized treatment.

column36: Investigating motor and NMJ synaptic defects in a zebrafish STMN2 loss-of-function model
column37: The development of novel animal models remains a critical tool for researchers investigating mechanisms of neurodegeneration and for the development of therapeutics to treat amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). My project seeks to explore the cellular and behavioural consequences of reduced Stathmin-2 (STMN2) levels on motor axon development and function and to explore the ability to rescue disease-related motor phenotypes using zebrafish. The transcript encoding STMN2 has emerged as an important cellular target of the RNA binding protein TDP-43, that in disease, results in an alternatively spliced cryptic exon encoding a truncated and non-functional STMN2 variant. This proposal will add to our understanding of STMN2s role in stabilizing motor axon projections to neuromuscular junctions (NMJ) and will likely be useful for ensuing experiments including potential therapies for ALS. Zebrafish are an ideal model system as I will be able to explore both the disease mechanisms and evaluate the potential of restorative constructs that rescue loss or mis-regulation of STMN2 using live cellular imaging to track motor axon projections in vivo. Using the CRISPR/cas9 mutagenic system I have identified several gRNAs that cleave DNA and am currently raising mutant fish lines which will be selected for Stmn2 knockouts (KO). I hypothesize that my zebrafish Stmn2 KO model will display reduced motor function and NMJ defects characterized by cellular imaging of ventral root projections and through behavioural studies. I will attempt to rescue synaptic and motor function through injection of human STMN2 mRNA into developing Stmn2 KO blastocysts. I hypothesize that human STMN2 mRNA will restore motor function in our Stmn2 KO models, opening the door to future clinical tools to treat ALS.

column36: Assessing the Economic Burden of Advanced Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer in Canada
column37: Background: Lung cancer is the most commonly diagnosed and leading cause of cancer death in Canada. Novel treatments like pembrolizumab (PEM) fall under a novel treatment class called immunotherapy. Immunotherapies have brought great improvements to clinical outcomes like survival and quality of life, but are associated with high costs as well. If Canada is to continue providing the newest, most innovative treatments, we must have accurate information regarding the cost effectiveness (CE) and expected resource use within the disease setting to ensure the sustainability of the healthcare system.Objective: To determine the CE and economic burden of all therapies indicated in the treatment of advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) in Canada. The starting point of this project will be to conduct a CE analysis of PEM in the Canadian setting. Methods: The CE analysis of PEM will use the most recent survival and quality of life outcomes from the KEYNOTE-024 phase III clinical trial. Extrapolation of long-term survival outcomes will use a novel Bayesian averaging approach. The results of the CE analysis can then be used in conjunction with Canadian epidemiological data to estimate the economic burden of providing this care. Similar methodologies can then be used for other therapies indicated for the treatment of advanced NSCLC to estimate the total economic burden of providing care. Significance: As Canada faces increasing budget constraints, information regarding expected resource consumption will be invaluable. The results of this project will be integral to inform healthcare policy and efficient resource planning. It can also identify which therapies are the most cost effective in this setting, which can help to generate cost effective treatment guidelines.

column36: Brain markers and onset of major depressive disorder in at-risk youth
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) affects 11% of Canadians aged 15-24 and the heritability of MDD is estimated to be 40%. Current research aims to identify biological markers of MDD that precede symptom onset in order to predict prognosis. Combined transcranial magnetic stimulation and electroencephalography (TMS-EEG) allows researchers to study brain function by non-invasively stimulating brain regions and then measuring induced activity. Studies have shown that a negative peak in activity forms 100 milliseconds after a TMS pulse (N100) and that youth and adults with MDD have significantly larger N100 peak amplitudes than healthy controls. Despite the high heritability of MDD, the predictive utility of the N100 marker in at-risk youth has not been studied. The proposed research will address this gap by determining the relationship between parental MDD and N100 amplitudes in at-risk youth and the utility of N100 amplitudes to predict MDD onset. It is hypothesized that N100 amplitudes will be associated with parental MDD severity, will serve as a significant predictor of MDD onset, and will be stable in youth who do not develop MDD. A minimum of 80 youth will be recruited from a longitudinal study and will have TMS-EEG data collected at baseline. Parental MDD will be assessed at baseline and youth will complete MDD questionnaires at baseline and 9-month intervals. N100 peak amplitudes will be quantified and correlated with parental MDD scores. The relationship between N100 amplitudes and MDD onset will be investigated using 9- and 18-month follow-up data. Knowledge of family history and presence of brain markers in youth will allow healthcare providers to implement strategies to delay the onset of MDD and reduce the severity of symptoms.

column36: Validation of the Edinburgh Social Cognition Test (ESCoT) in Older Adults with Amnestic Mild Cognitive Impairment (aMCI)
column37: Social cognition consists of the ways that we perceive, interpret, and respond to social information such as faces and behaviours. The recently developed Edinburgh Social Cognition Test (ESCoT) examines four aspects of social cognition: 1) cognitive theory of mind (your ability to infer another persons beliefs), 2) affective theory of mind (your ability to infer another persons emotions), 3) interpersonal understanding of social norms (whether another person is behaving in the same way as others), and 4) intrapersonal understanding of social norms (whether you would behave in the same way as others). The ESCoT has been validated for use among adults with autism spectrum disorder and acquired brain injury patients. However, it is still unknown whether the ESCoT can be used with older adults with amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI), who often experience significant difficulties in this area due to memory loss. It is important to determine the ESCoTs ability to accurately detect social cognitive impairments in older adults with aMCI, as these impact daily social interactions, interpersonal relationships, and overall functioning in society. I aim to analyze the validity of the ESCoT in older adults with aMCI to determine whether the test is an accurate measure of social cognition in this group. Based on previous research on the ESCoT and current knowledge of aMCI, I hypothesize that aMCI participants will perform more poorly on the ESCoT relative to healthy older adults, and that this same relationship will be present on more established social cognitive tests. The results will guide clinicians decisions to include the ESCoT in neuropsychological assessments, allowing for a clearer picture of patient health and earlier intervention.

column36: The common haptoglobin phenotype, intensive blood pressure control, and risk of incident cardiovascular disease within the Action to Control Cardiovascular Risk in Diabetes randomized control trial
column37: Nobody knows yet why strict blood pressure control (aiming for lower blood pressure levels) prevents heart disease in some people with type 2 diabetes but can have no effect or cause harm in others. It makes it hard for patients with type 2 diabetes and their doctors to plan their blood pressure goals. Our team has been working to fill this gap, and we think that the answer may include the form of the blood protein haptoglobin that a person has. Everyones body makes one of two major haptoglobin forms, and the form can be measured by an inexpensive blood test. This research will use this blood test in participants from a large, completed study that has tested strict blood pressure control. We will re-analyze the data in the two haptoglobin groups separately and determine if strict blood pressure control prevented heart disease in people with one haptoglobin type. The other type is predicted to have no heart disease benefit and even an increased risk of death. This project is a cost-effective and ethical way to learn whether the haptoglobin type blood test can consistently determine which people will benefit from strict blood pressure control and who will not. It will tell us whether we should further study the blood test to personalize patient blood pressure control goals in order to prevent heart disease. Diabetes is very common in Canada and worldwide. Research like ours aims to better prevent heart disease in people with diabetes.

column36: Mer receptor tyrosine kinase in human macrophages mediates the clearance of apoptotic cells by modulating the activity of axbeta2 integrins and Rab17
column37: Dying cells must be cleared by immune cells called macrophages. Macrophages recognize dying cells using receptors such as Mer receptor tyrosine kinase (MerTK) before internalizing cells into membranous sacs called efferosomes, where the cells are eventually destroyed. Defects in MerTK contributes to autoimmunity leading to blindness, infertility, or paralysis. However, the mechanisms used by MerTK to clear dying cells are not fully understood. Our group believes MerTK has a dual-functional role. Foremost, we have shown that MerTK activates other receptors called integrins. I hypothesize MerTK first anchors dying cells to the surface of the macrophage, then activates integrins which serve as the force generators to engulf the cell. I will perform microscopy experiments where algorithms are used to measure the force generated by macrophages during this engulfment step, where MerTK signaling can enhance force generation caused by integrins. Second, we have shown that a protein called Rab17 is recruited to efferosomes to prevent autoimmune responses against host cells. I hypothesize MerTK recruits Rab17 to efferosomes. This will be tested by allowing macrophages to engulf small beads that mimic the molecular signature of dying cells. I will determine the relative quantity of Rab17 found on efferosomes using techniques such as fluorescence microscopy and protein separation. Chemical inhibitors against MerTK will be used to test for the decrease in Rab17 recruitment to efferosomes. Understanding how MerTK mediates the clearance of dying cells is vital for our understanding of autoimmunity. My project will uncover the crosstalk between MerTK with integrins and Rab17, providing insight on new therapeutic avenues to treat autoimmune diseases.

column36: Rescuing the Bladder Epithelial Glycocalyx May Offer Treatment for Interstitial Cystitis/Bladder Pain Syndrome
column37: Interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) is a condition that affects a significant number of patients worldwide, yet treatment options are sub-optimal and still the condition persists. In IC/BPS patients, a common underlying pathology is shedding of the mucus or glycocalyx layer on the surface of epithelial cells of the bladder wall. This shedding exposes the underlying tissue to urine, urinary components, and bacteria, ultimately leading to increased inflammation. Further, it has been shown that the bladder glycocalyx primarily functions as a protective barrier, and when it is damaged there is increased permeability of bacteria and other damaging agents. Current evidence suggests that restoring this mucus layer may offer clinical benefits, however there are no methods which specifically target the glycocalyx. I hypothesize that rapid restoration of the glycocalyx using cell-surface engineering (CSE) of mucus-mimicking polymers may offer protection against leakage, inflammation, and bacterial adhesion on the bladder wall. Building on this hypothesis, the aim of this multidisciplinary study is to first establish a glycocalyx-compromised bladder epithelial cell model which resembles IC/BPS pathology, then use this model to test various glycocalyx-targeted CSE treatments.

column36: The Role of Soy in Metabolic Health
column37: Public interest in plant-based dietary patterns has grown tremendously. Though soy milk has been promoted as both an environmentally friendly and health-promoting alternative to cows milk, it is overshadowed by dairy in public health interventions targeting cardiometabolic diseases. Sugar-sweetened beverage (SSB) consumption is a risk factor for metabolic syndrome. Low fat cows milk has been favoured by policy makers as the primary alternative to SSBs, for its association with metabolic syndrome risk reduction. However, it is yet to be determined if the same benefits hold to true for dairys plant-based counterpart, soy milk. My research, comprised of both a meta-analysis (part 1) and clinical trial (part 2), aims to address this uncertainty. Part 1 will include a review, summary, and analysis of published studies that have assessed the effects of soy beverages on various metabolic outcomes. Part 2 will be a 24-week, parallel design, 3-arm randomized controlled trial. 186 overweight or obese individuals with metabolic syndrome will be enrolled and randomized to one of three interventions (soy milk, cow's milk, SSBs) for the duration of the trial. The primary outcome of this trial will be liver fat, measured with Medical Resonance Imaging (MRI). The secondary outcomes will be change in muscle fat, insulin sensitivity, beta-cell function, glucose tolerance, and established cardiometabolic risk factors. Secondary and other exploratory outcomes will be measured with a 75g Oral Glucose Tolerance Test and a fasting blood sample. These projects in conjunction will allow a better understanding of the effects, and aim to prove the non-inferiority, of soy milk to cows milk on cardiometabolic health.

column36: Vancomycin dosing for severe methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infections: a pilot study
column37: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is a resistant type of bacteria that causes serious infections of the blood, brain, heart valve, lung, bone or joint. Intravenous vancomycin is a first line antibiotic used to treat these infections. Vancomycin requires monitoring of the drug level in the blood to adjust the dose. Based on the newest guideline, vancomycin should be dosed based on a model of the drug level over time, which is called area under the curve (AUC). The AUC target is 400. Dosing based on AUC is difficult, because it requires complex calculations using an expensive software. A simpler way is to target a trough level of 10 to 15mg/L when the drug level is at its lowest. We aim to compare these two different dosing strategies in patients with serious MRSA infections in terms of clinical cure in a large randomized trial. The study will include patients admitted to three hospitals in Hamilton, Ontario with MRSA infection of the blood, brain, heart valve, lung, bone, joint or a deep-seated abscess who require vancomycin treatment. Patients will be randomized to either a dosing strategy based on the trough level or one based on the AUC. These patients will be followed for 3 months. If the clinical cure rate is similar between the two groups at the end of follow-up, then the simpler trough-based strategy would be preferred, because it is easier and cheaper to adopt in hospitals. For my thesis, we will be conducting a pilot study, which is a smaller version of the planned trial. In this study, we will determine the number of patients being recruited over time as well as proportion of patients who were given the correct dose and completed follow-up to ensure that it would be feasible to carry out the larger trial.

column36: Assessing the effects of nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-containing protein 1 stimulation: Novel target of therapy in models of Inflammatory Bowel Disease.
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a collection of conditions that result in the inflammation of the gastrointestinal tract causing diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, nausea, and vomiting. With its prevalence a whopping 0.6% in Canada, there is a need for understanding targets of therapy for the disease. Crohns disease, which is one of the two main conditions implicated in IBD, is most often associated with polymorphisms in the nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain (NOD) 2 gene. NOD2 is integral to the innate immune system of mammals, and functions as a pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) within the cytosol of cells. It detects conserved bacterial peptidoglycans (PGN) to elicit an anti-microbial response by activating the nuclear factor kappa B (NF-B) pathway. column36: Investigating the Acute Effects of Translingual Neurostimulation on Central Nervous System Function Among Individuals with Multiple Sclerosis
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is considered a chronic inflammatory neurological disease of the central nervous system (CNS) in which the immune system attacks the myelin sheath surrounding the neurons. Demyelination reduces neuronal communication and corticospinal integrity, resulting in the various life disrupting symptoms of MS, such as motor and cognitive deficits. Unfortunately, there is no cure for MS, however novel treatment options such as neuromodulation can help slow the rate of progression and delay relapses. A particular neuromodulation technique called translingual neurostimulation (TLNS) delivers non-invasive stimulation to the tongue which increases the activation of particular cranial nerves and may induce neuroplasticity in the brain. However, the exact mechanism of such neuroplastic changes is not well understood. This present study aims to investigate the effect of TLNS delivered by a portable neuromodulation stimulator (PoNS) on the brain using two functional brain imaging techniques: functional near infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). I will use fNIRS to measure localized changes in cortical hemodynamics of the brain in response to three tasks ; breathing and awareness, cognitive and motor tasks ; in the absence and presence of TLNS. TMS will be used to measure the effects of TLNS on corticospinal excitability using the variables resting motor threshold (RMT), active motor threshold (AMT) and recruitment curve. The overall goal of this study is to investigate the acute effects of TLNS via the PoNS device on neural activation and corticospinal excitability using two functional brain imaging techniques, fNIRS and TMS.

column36: Quantification of growth deficits as maturational delays ('growth delay') to enhance the interpretability of observed effects of interventions on child linear growth in low- and middle-income countries
column37: Height-for-age z-scores (HAZ) and stunting (HAZ-2SD) are conventionally used outcomes in nutritional interventions in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). There is substantial evidence that BM is delayed in growth-inhibiting conditions; if optimal conditions return, growth will continue from the stage of BM an individual has achieved, rather than the rate expected for their CA. The purpose of this study is to demonstrate the use of an alternative growth metric that determines the extent to which an intervention achieves ;normal growth based on childrens starting height-age, rather than their CA which is the current convention. Understanding how SQ-LNS improves growth relative to a biologically-defined benchmark of optimal growth may enhance interest/investment in SQ-LNS interventions as a necessary element to end malnutrition in LMICs.

column36: Investigating the vesicular transport mechanisms of myelin proteolipid protein 1 (PLP1) in optic nerve myelination
column37: Optic neuritis is a demyelinating condition of the optic nerve causing visual loss. During myelination, oligodendrocytes transport Proteolipid protein 1 (PLP1) to the myelin sheath through vesicles via Soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptors (SNAREs). Yet, the critical SNARE isoforms involved remain unknown. Syntaxin-3/4 and SNAP23/29 are the leading candidates through studies of oligodendrocyte progenitor cell cultures. However, animal models are still lacking. Recent evidence reveals that syntaxin-3 expression is localized to myelin in mice brains. In human patients, SNAP29 mutations are linked to CEDNIK syndrome, which is associated with visual deficits and demyelination in the brain. Therefore, we hypothesize that syntaxin-3 and SNAP29 play critical roles in PLP1 trafficking for the myelination process in oligodendrocytes. We selectively remove syntaxin-3 and/or SNAP29 genes in oligodendrocytes in mice. Using such a mice model, we will characterize the expression of PLP1 and its trafficking in the optic nerve myelin. Optic nerve myelination and health are further characterized by myelin thickness and electrophysiology. Behaviorally, we will test the visual acuity after removal of the SNAREs by optomotor reflex. Our study will reveal the molecular mechanism of PLP1 transport and myelination in vivo. PLP1 mutation is associated with Pelizaeus-Merzbacher Disease (PMD), where patients demonstrate central nervous system hypomyelination. In addition, demyelination and dysmyelination are common themes in diseases including optic neuritis, multiple sclerosis (MS), PMD, and CEDNIK syndrome. Thus, our project will contribute to the molecular pathologies and novel treatments of demyelination diseases targeting the optic nerve.

column36: Imaging Biomarkers to Characterize Emphysema Progression: Evidence and Endpoints for the Development of Matrix Metalloproteinase-12 Inhibitors
column37: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) affects our lungs and is a leading cause of hospital admission and death in Canada. COPD is caused by chronic exposure to toxic air pollutants and cigarette smoke, that lead to the release of inflammatory chemical signals and damage to the air sacs (alveoli) in the lungs, this is known as emphysema. Currently available treatments for COPD only relieve symptoms and are not disease modifying. Many COPD patients will eventually develop emphysema thus investigating MMP12s involvement in disease progression is important to guide the development of new therapies targeting MMP12. Our team of scientists think COPD patients with emphysema will have high MMP12 levels and the amount of MMP12 in airway secretion and/or blood are associated with progressive alveolar destruction measured by MRI and CT. We will study 60 COPD patients with emphysema and 15 healthy volunteers by examining their airway secretions, blood, and lung imaging scans. This will set the stage for new treatments to help reduce the huge burden of COPD for over two million Canadians.

column36: Examining Th-17 Mediated Inflammation as a Mechanism for Transporter Dysregulation in Pregnant Lupus Patients
column37: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease (AD) that mainly affects women of child-bearing age and can cause poor pregnancy outcomes. However, research from our lab has demonstrated that important protective transporters are dysregulated in SLE placenta; additionally, Th17 cytokines are upregulated in patient serum at term. Therefore, we postulate that the observed upregulation of Th17-cytokines in SLE could be responsible for the observed changes in disease transporter expression. The second phase will involve the same process, this time with SLE affected term placenta. Potentially, other mechanistic studies in relevant cells may follow using inhibitors of key Th17 pathways. column36: Effect of microenvironmental perturbations on cell-cell killing in mouse embryonic stem cells
column37: In single-celled organisms like bacteria, cells directly killing their neighbours is well understood. Surprisingly, in multicellular systems, like the mouse, seemingly identical populations of cells have also been found to kill their neighbours. Unfavourable environmental conditions, such as a lack of nutrients, is one reason why ;fitter bacteria kill their less-fit neighbours. Is CC in multicellular organisms also influenced by the environment? What are the factors that set the stage and encourage mESCs to either battle to the death or live harmoniously? To answer this question, I will study mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), a type of stem cell which can make all the cell types of the body and which undergo the phenomenon of cell-cell killing. I will first develop a method of measuring cell-cell killing efficiently. I will use this method to measure how changing the environmental conditions of the cells influences whether they kill their neighbours. Finally, I will engineer the optimal competition arena. I will use a statistical method called Design of Experiments (DoE) to efficiently test many different combinations of environmental factors, and see which ones work together to have an enhanced effect on cell-cell killing. Making therapies out of cells holds immense promise for regenerative medicine, but we need to first understand the rules at play between cells before we can engineer them safely and efficiently. Cell-cell killing is a type of interaction we are only starting to understand, and my project will shed light on how environmental conditions can be tuned to manipulate cells, with implications for production of stem cell-derived therapies.

column37: Context: In recent years, an improved understanding of the biology of cancer paired with the development of therapies targeting known cellular culprits of cancer have revolutionized the treatment of this complex disease. And yet, broadly speaking, this promise of targeted therapy has still not fully materialized. One clear reason is our inability to design drugs when the cellular culprits they go after dont happen to fit certain criteria for druggability. One way to circumvent that is to target them indirectly, and an innovative approach to doing that is to bring together our culprit with another protein: the latter could modify the function of the cancer-driving protein and thus attack cancer cells ability to survive and proliferate.: In this context, my project will attempt to find proteins, called effectors, that can modulate the function of the protein MutL Homolog 1 (MLH1) when the two are brought together in close proximity. MLH1 is involved in a type of DNA repair called mismatch repair and is mutated in a variety of human cancers. By finding effectors of MLH1, we could be uncovering new ways to enhance the efficacy of immunotherapy, a type of drugs which use the bodys immune system to fight cancer cells. Experimental approach: My project will leverage a screening approach in which every single human protein will be physically brought in contact with MLH1 in live cells. Those that manage to impact MLH1 activity will be further studied to see if they are useful effectors. Perspectives: The goal is to identify and validate potential proximity-dependent effectors of MLH1. Ultimately, a drug discovery campaign will be initiated with the long-term goal of developing a treatment which can impact the survival and quality of life of cancer patients.

column36: Hemodynamic and ventilatory responses to exercise and orthostasis in healthy participants
column37: Shortness of breath is a common problem and causes a distressing feeling of difficulty in taking a breath when doing even light physical activity. The symptom stops people from doing regular activities like shopping for groceries or walking their children to school. Our program tries to understand and diagnose these conditions. There is a growing group of people who appear otherwise healthy, and have normal heart and lung tests, but report feeling short of breath. We are learning that many of these people may have difficulty regulating their heart rate, blood pressure, or breathing rate. Light exercise and quickly moving from sitting down to standing up are useful tests we can use to see if someone can properly regulate these measures. These tests can help us to determine abnormal responses that cannot be detected during other common tests conducted at rest. We would like to learn more about how heart rate, blood pressure, and breathing rates change during these tests to see if this explains why some people feel short of breath.
