column36: Evaluating quality of gout treatment using a population health approach
column37: Gout is a common form of arthritis that affects a large proportion of Canadians, leading to significant pain and disability. A major contributor to the development of gout is the presence of increased urate levels in the blood, which is associated with the formation of urate crystals in joints. The main cornerstone in gout treatment therefore involves the prevention of acute gout flares using medications that reduce serum urate to a pre-specified target level which has been shown to prevent the formation of gout crystals, as endorsed by the major rheumatology guidelines. Despite therapies available to lower urate levels, a large subset of patients still experience acute gout flares. One of the main contributors for this is due to poor treatment uptake and suboptimal urate monitoring. However, the scope of the care gap for gout has not been studied extensively in Canada.Therefore, this research project will specifically assess the achievement of treatment benchmarks in gout, using Ontario-wide health administrative data. This will allow us to determine the magnitude of gout treatment care gaps, using outcomes that have been endorsed by the American College of Rheumatology. Specifically, we will study the proportion of patients and factors associated with optimal monitoring of serum urate levels. Subsequently, we will assess the proportion of patients who achieve target urate levels 1 year after starting gout medications in addition to associated factors. This is the first Canadian study to evaluate the quality of gout care, using provincial-wide data. Given how common gout is within Canada, this research project will hopefully identify care gaps and mobilize quality improvement in gout treatment, potentially benefiting the 4% of all Canadians who suffer from gout.

column36: Modular synthesis of nucleic acid radiopharmaceuticals for positron emission tomography
column37: Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) have revolutionized cancer therapy, and trastuzumab has revolutionized HER2+ breast cancer. Increasingly, antibody drug conjugates such as trastuzumab emtansine play an important role in the treatment of relapsed disease. Positron emitting radioisotopes can be used as an alternative payload that can be carried by mAbs, for non-invasive cancer localization and confirmation of target expression by positron emission tomography (PET). In addition, therapeutic radioisotopes can deliver and concentrate radiation to treat metastatic sites. However, directly labeled mAbs with long-living radioisotopes such as Zr-89 clear slowly from the body, exposing the bone marrow and other organs to unnecessary radiation due to slow clearance.Researchers have recently developed pretargeted radioimmunotherapy to improve contrast for imaging and efficacy for therapy. In this approach, a modified mAb is injected and allowed to circulate, bind to cancer cells, and clear from the blood over a few days. Then, a fast clearing small molecule that specifically recognises the antibody is administered, clearing within minutes, with the goal of targeting cancer cells specifically coated with the antibody.The goal is to develop nucleic acids such as DNA to specifically recognize mAbs that have been preinjected to target tumor cells. They act as means to conjugate antibodies coated with one strand of DNA, with a small strand of complementary nucleic acids attached to a radioactive isotope. The radioactive DNA binds tightly to the complementary strand located on the antibody, using the established antibody Trastuzumab in breast cancer as a proof-of-concept. Confirmation of tumor localization will be used as the first evidence to preview the effectiveness of this approach.

column36: The molecular basis of persistent HIV-specific CD4 T cell dysfunction
column37: Highly active antiretroviral therapy reduces the morbidity and mortality linked to the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). However, discontinuing the antiretroviral therapy leads to a resumption of the diseases progression. This illustrates that (i) the current treatments cannot completely clear the infection, and (ii) the HIV-specific immune responses are insufficient to prevent this replication rebound. Instead of a complete elimination of the virus, a functional cure seems more realistic, which consists of a spontaneous and long-term control of the residual virus without incessant medication. CD4 T lymphocytes play a key role in this strategy. However, during a chronic infection with HIV, their persistent exposition to circulating antigens leads to their exhaustion and lasting dysfunction, making the body more susceptible to opportunist infections. While recent studies suggest that this is regulated by epigenetic mechanisms, the role of these types of mechanisms in CD4 T cells exhaustion and dysfunction remains misunderstood.We believe that the progression of the chronic infection with HIV drives HIV-specific CD4 T cells to commit, via epigenetic and transcriptional mechanisms, to a functional program that is durable but reversible, unsuitable to the control of the virus. Our approach consists of comparing an untreated group of Chronic Progressors (CP), characterized by an exacerbated dysfunction of HIV-specific CD4 T cells, to Elite Controllers (EC), spontaneously controlling the infection. From leukaphereses, we will identify the factors initiating and regulating the transcription of HIV-specific CD4 T lymphocytes, thus dictating the cellular functions in the context of a chronic infection, to identify the molecular causes of this functional alteration.

column36: Incorporating Health in All Canadian Policies: A Conceptual Model Based on an Integrative Approach
column37: Health can be viewed as an integrated system that includes the body, mind, and spirit, and influenced by lifestyle and environment. Unfortunately, health is typically understood by separating the structures and functions of a person into discrete parts for evaluation, and the current definition of health used in Canada is outdated. If Canadians are to become healthier, we should consider an integrative health definition as it is a much broader multi-dimensional concept on health. As a next step to achieving an integrative health model one should consider Health in All Policies in Canada, as it incorporates health in all sectors of public policy with the intention of improving well-being in all the different facets of life. Through an evidence-based literature review a Health in All Policies conceptual model will be developed to provide health leaders a framework for incorporating such a transformation. I will not only evaluate the issues with Canadian health policy today, but use an appreciated inquiry method to identify what is working well and build on those successes.

column36: Understanding the Connections between IgA-mediated Immunity, the Microbiota & Type I Diabetes
column37: Type 1 Diabetes (T1D) is an autoimmune disease that involves the destruction of insulin-producing cells in the pancreas by autoreactive lymphocytes. Research has shown that abnormalities in the gut play a significant role in disease development. Two key features of a healthy gut include the presence of a community of microorganisms called the microbiota as well as secretions of Immunoglobulin A (IgA) into the gut. During infancy when the immune system is immature, breast milk provides copious amounts of IgAas well as a sampling of the maternal microbiota, both delivered directly to the infant gut. In both infants and adults, the IgA and microbiota work together to preserve the integrity of the gut barrier and regulate immune responses both in the gut and systemically. Interestingly, common T1D features include chronic gut inflammation, altered gut microbiota, loss of gut integrity and barrier function as well as an increased incidence of IgA deficiency. We hypothesized that IgA in the gut plays a protective role in the development of T1D and that a deficiency of IgA would enhance disease. We have addressed this using a non-obese diabetic mouse model (NOD), comparing disease onset and progression in IgA-deficient mice versus their IgA-sufficient littermates. Interestingly, the major contributing factor of disease incidence in our model is maternal IgA availability. Specifically, offspring of IgA-deficient dams show significantly lower disease incidence. Analysis of lymphocyte populations has shown differences in proportion, activation state and cytokine production in the bowels and associated draining lymph nodes. We aim to further characterize these population differences with links to IgA-mediated microbiome:immune crosstalk and to determine their role in disease.

column36: Developing Bispecific Immunotoxins against Pancreatic Cancer
column37: Pancreatic cancer is one of the deadliest human cancers, with a 5-year survival rate of only 8%. Pancreatic tumours tend to go undiagnosed until they are quite advanced, at which point they are unresectable and require systemic treatment. Though traditional chemotherapy has been a cornerstone of systemic cancer treatment for decades, its nonspecific nature often results in off-target killing of healthy cells. Thus, there is a need for more specific, effective, and safe late-stage treatment options for pancreatic cancer.Cancer cells carry certain surface markers, which are not present on healthy cells. So, to treat tumours more specifically, one strategy is to direct toxic molecules to cells carrying these markers. Immunotoxins make up one class of such targeted therapeutic molecules, and are constructed by combining the highly potent killing portion of a bacterial toxin with a homing portion that seeks out certain cancer markers. Despite the success of this technology, there are currently no immunotoxins approved to treat pancreatic cancer. Our lab has recently generated an immunotoxin from diphtheria toxin that targets two different pancreatic cancer markers. We have shown this immunotoxin to be very potent against multiple pancreatic cancer cell lines, warranting further investigation into its efficacy and safety in advanced tumour models. In this proposal, we are asking for funding from CIHR to test the efficacy of this immunotoxin in more than 25 pancreatic cancer patient-derived organoids (3D tissue constructs mimicking organs). We also propose to examine the safety profile and anti-tumour effects of this therapeutic agent in mouse models. These studies represent a huge step forward in the development of urgently needed treatment options for pancreatic cancer.

column36: Investigating the the effect of topical sodium bicarbonate supplementation on resistance exercise preformed to failure
column37: Skeletal muscle mass plays a significant role in determining overall health, body function and risk factors for various diseases. Resistance exercise (RE) performed to failure induces a process known as muscle hypertrophy which is responsible for the building of muscle. However, when RE is done to failure, muscles produce a substance known as lactate which impairs the ability for muscle to contract. Lactate is a key reason why muscles fail after a certain number of repetitions for a given exercise. However, oral sodium bicarbonate can lessen the negative impact lactate creates in contracting muscles and can attenuate muscle fatigue as demonstrated via a significant amount of research. Unfortunately, this substance does come with a downside, as oral sodium bicarbonate often results in intestinal distress. However, a sodium bicarbonate lotion has recently been developed and has been shown, with limited research, to induce similar benefits to that of oral sodium bicarbonate without the negative effects. So far, this product demonstrates the potential to improve performance and assist the muscle in dealing with lactate, but it has only been trialed within cyclists performing aerobic exercise. Therefore, I propose to investigate whether sodium bicarbonate can be delivered through skin to active muscle and secondly to determine if it can improve RE performance done to failure, with consideration to varied groups. I plan to include young, trained male and female participants, since to my knowledge, no research has investigated possible sex differences in response to sodium bicarbonate lotion. This research will have a significant impact on athletes training and performance but will also benefit the everyday person who is hoping to improve their health.

column36: Biomechanical analysis of surgical implants for treatment of massive, irreparable rotator cuff tears
column37: Rotator cuff tears are common and can cause debilitating shoulder pain, loss of work hours and productivity. Rotator cuff tears are initially treated nonsurgically with physiotherapy. Those that do not respond require a rotator cuff repair. Certain factors can lead to a rotator cuff tear being non-repairable, such as: increasing patient age, smoking status, chronic medical conditions, size of rotator cuff tear, chronicity of rotator cuff tear, and fat infiltration into the muscle belly. The natural history of the rotator cuff deficient shoulder is pain, dysfunction, altered shoulder kinematics and ultimately end-stage shoulder arthritis. This process is called rotator cuff arthropathy.A reverse total shoulder replacement is a successful treatment for rotator cuff arthropathy. Unfortunately, a surgical dilemma exists where young, working-age patients can have massive, irreparable rotator cuff tears without shoulder arthritis. Joint replacement is not ideal in this patient, as there are lifelong limitations and the lifespan of the implant would expire, requiring future surgeries. Therefore, many patients either live with their pain and dysfunction or undergo salvage type operations. This gap in treatment encourages biomechanists and surgeons to develop alternative options. The goal of this research project is to examine the various established surgical techniques for massive, irreparable rotator cuff tears in young patients, and compare them to a novel surgical implant that was developed to treat this patient population. This will be performed in a controlled and comprehensive cadaver-based biomechanical study comparing an intact shoulder, rotator cuff deficient shoulder, subacromial balloon spacer, superior capsule reconstruction, and the metallic acromial implant.

column36: Development of a Small Molecule Screen for Coronavirus (CoV-2) Frameshifting Modulators Using Yeast
column37: Fighting the global pandemic caused by Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (CoV-2) requires broader strategies than immunity-based solutions; antivirals resistant to future CoV-2 strains are necessary, especially for immunocompromised populations. A mechanism called frameshifting is used by CoV-2 for protein production and is specific to viruses (therefore it is not used by human cells). Frameshifting is necessary for viral replication and infection of the host, and is common among many RNA viruses. Current evidence suggests that the CoV-2 structure stimulating the frameshifting mechanism and the mechanism itself are consistent between families of coronaviruses, indicating that antivirals targeting frameshifting would not lose efficacy against emerging viral strains. Frameshifting is finely tuned to produce specific amounts of protein required for viral infection. Disrupting frameshifting to modulate the rate of protein output will result in inhibition of viral infection. This project aims to identify small molecules that modulate frameshifting in CoV-2 using a novel yeast growth assay platform to allow for the rapid identification of potential antiviral compounds. The project will re-purpose yeast assays that have been previously used in our facilities to allow for simple setup and optimization. Once candidate compounds have been identified, they will be screened in a mammalian system. Compounds that emerge as candidates from this screen will then be tested for their ability to inhibit the reproduction of CoV-2. The development of this methodology and screen will create a system able to rapidly identify specific inhibitors of conserved and key viral mechanisms, which is crucial for fighting current and future viral outbreaks.

column36: Investigating the potential effects of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) vaccination on modulation of the latent human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) reservoir
column37: Antiretroviral therapies have transformed HIV from a life-threatening infection to a manageable health condition, but these drugs must be taken for life. This is because HIV establishes a latent reservoir of infected cells by integrating its DNA into the DNA of infected host cells. Antiretroviral drugs cannot eliminate cells harboring latent HIV, nor can the immune system. A theoretical strategy to cure HIV, dubbed ;kick-and-kill, aims to wake up reservoir cells by applying a strong stimulant, while boosting the immune system's ability to eliminate these infected cells. To further develop this strategy, we need to better understand what types of stimulants can safely and effectively modulate the HIV reservoir. The recent mass rollout of novel mRNA vaccines against COVID-19 gives us a unique opportunity to do so. We already know that standard vaccines (e.g. against influenza) induce generalized immune responses that can transiently stimulate HIV gene transcription. Because the novel mRNA vaccine technologies used for COVID-19 stimulate particularly strong immune responses, these may modulate the HIV reservoir more strongly. My thesis will explore the potential effects of COVID-19 mRNA vaccination on the reservoirs of 62 people with HIV on ART for whom we have collected blood samples pre-vaccination, and at various times after the first, second and booster shots, along with sociodemographic and clinical data. I will quantify HIV mRNA transcription, reservoir size, plasma cytokine levels and T-cell activation profiles before and after vaccination, and explore the magnitude of these changes with sex, age, clinical HIV parameters, and vaccine-induced antibody responses. This study will advance HIV reservoir biology towards the ultimate goal of developing an HIV cure.

column36: Implementation and Evaluation of Pre-treatment DPYD genotyping for dose individualization of fluoropyrimidine therapy
column37: Fluoropyrimidines are commonly prescribed anti-cancer drugs but they cause severe adverse drug reactions in up to a third of patients. The same dose of one drug may be efficacious and safe in one person but cause a severe adverse drug reaction in another. Genetic variation is a key factor that influences the occurrence of serious adverse drug reactions. In the case of fluoropyrimidines, 3-8% of the western population has genetic variation in the gene DPYD that puts them at over 70% risk for severe fluoropyrimidine adverse drug reactions. These people can often be safely treated with lower fluoropyrimidine doses. The goal of the Canadian Pharmacogenomics Network for Drug Safety (CPNDS) is to implement testing of genetic markers to predict the risk of adverse drug reactions. Therefore, I aim to use the resources of CPNDS to implementDPYD genetic testing at BC Cancer Agency, where people who test positive receive a reduced dose of fluoropyrimidines to prevent severe adverse drug reactions. This is highly relevant for a patients quality of life because adverse drug reactions result in hospitalizations and discontinuation of anti-cancer treatments. I will evaluate theDPYDtesting program by analyzing the extent fluoropyrimidine adverse drug reactions and related care are reduced after the program.Additionally, I aim to develop an analytical plan for identifying novel genetic variants associated with fluoropyrimidine adverse drug reactions with the genetic material collected in this study. Using genetics to reduce the risk of adverse drug reactions and inform treatment decisions is an essential part of precision medicine and will improve health outcomes for Canadians, as well as the 2 million patients per year all around the world who use fluoropyrimidines.

column36: Canadian Women Firefighters' Cancer Incidence and Mortality: A Retrospective Cohort Analysis
column37: Research indicates that firefighters are at greater risk of developing and dying of cancer than the general population. In Canada, many cancers are designated presumptive illnesses for firefighters, which provides financial support for individuals in the event of a diagnosis, and facilitates health education in general. As a profession, firefighting is heavily dominated by men; only 4.4% of professional firefighters in Canada are women. Thus, the vast majority of cancer research on firefighters only studies men. However, there may be links between firefighting and female-specific reproductive cancers, including breast cancer. Furthermore, even for non-reproductive cancers, it is known that ones sex and gender influence cancer risk and development. In addition, women in the Fire Services face many obstacles, such as ill-fitting protective gear, which could increase their risk of exposure to carcinogens. Unfortunately, women firefighters cancer risks remain unknown, and this lack of data may be putting them at a disadvantage when it comes to health education and coverage. Using data from the Canadian Census Health and Environment Cohorts, I will analyze past cancer data from women who are, or were, professional firefighters as determined by linked occupational data from census and tax information. I will conduct a retrospective cohort analysis via logistic regression to compare professional women firefighters with women in the general Canadian population. column36: A living systematic review and network meta-analysis of the effect of digital health technologies on outcomes in patients with heart failure.
column37: Despite advancements in diagnostic and therapeutic tools, heart failure (HF) is a growing epidemic in Canada and remains a major public health concern. The COVID-19 pandemic has only worsened this situation, revealing challenges in remotely managing large volumes of HF patients. Digital health tools (ex. Kardia ECG, Apple Watch) hold promise in improving the quality of life and care of HF patients. However, there are inequities in how such tools enter routine care. The marketing budget of their manufacturers, rather than their clinical benefit, may trump the uptake of digital health tools. Moreover, with the rapid development of technology, research on digital health tools can quickly become outdated.To combat these dilemmas, we aim to conduct a ;living systematic review (an ever-evolving critical review of research studies) to summarize all research on digital health tools for HF care, and to compare the effectiveness of tools with a similar purpose (ex. remote monitoring). Users can search our repository for any tool and receive a summary of all available evidence written in plain language. This repository will help patients and clinicians select digital health tools to maximize quality of life and achieve better health outcomes, such as reducing hospital visits. column36: The role of the neonatal oral microbiome in neurodevelopmental outcomes
column37: Full-term neonates admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) due to birth complications are at high risk for adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes. Previous research suggests that early bacteria in the gut environment modify and contribute to brain development. Brain development during the neonatal period is a major predictor of neurodevelopmental outcomes in early childhood and later in life. As the entry point to the gut microbiome, the oral microbiome, known as the diverse population of micro-organisms in the mouth, is hypothesized to play an important role in the establishment of the gut microbiome and in shaping brain development and function. However, while the relationship between the gut microbiome and neurodevelopment has been studied extensively, there has been limited research exploring whether the oral microbiome can contribute to brain development and function during the neonatal period.In this study I will aim to characterize the oral microbiome in neonates at risk of adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes and assess its association with early neurodevelopment. Using neonatal oral microbiome DNA and brain scans, I will seek to characterize the oral microbiome in full-term neonates at risk of poor neurodevelopmental outcomes. I predict that neonatal complications in full-term neonates will associate with an organism imbalance of the oral microbiome. This research will aid in understanding the links between the oral microbiome and neurodevelopment in full-term neonates. Findings from this study may be used to develop early interventions for full-term babies that can allow for the healthy establishment and enhanced development of the early neonatal oral microbiome.

column36: Discovering mechanisms governing lung tumour response to CD47-targeted immunotherapy
column37: Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in Canada. While there have been advances in therapies to treat lung cancer, high rates of drug resistance and tumour recurrence emphasize the need for new therapeutic strategies. Tumours often acquire mechanisms to avoid detection by the immune system, allowing them to grow and metastasize. Immunotherapy is a type of treatment designed to overcome these mechanisms and re-activate the bodys immune system to attack tumors. Studies have shown that lung cancers upregulate CD47, a cell surface protein that is a marker of ;self on blood and other cells in the body. Normally, CD47 functions to prevent unwanted immune-mediated killing of healthy cells. By expressing CD47, lung cancer cells use this ;dont eat me signal to block their destruction and clearance by specialized immune cells called antigen-presenting cells (APCs). CD47 inhibitors are a subclass of immunotherapies that can disrupt the interaction between CD47 on cancer cells and its receptor on APCs to promote tumour killing. Our research aims to determine how lung tumour response to CD47 inhibitors is controlled to understand how to use them most effectively in the clinic. We hypothesize that specific genes in lung cancer cells regulate tumour sensitivity to CD47 inhibition. Using CRISPR/Cas9 technology, we will conduct genetic screens to investigate 500 genes whose inactivation is hypothesized to enhance killing of lung tumours by CD47 inhibitors. The findings from this project will reveal genes that can be targeted in combination with CD47 inhibitors to increase therapeutic efficacy. Collectively, our work will inform the development and clinical translation of this new type of immunotherapy to improve lung cancer survival rates in Canada and worldwide.

column36: Exploring the Kidney Amylome with Fluorescence Spectroscopy
column37: The renal amyloidoses are rare conditions that arise when proteins become misfolded and deposit in the kidneys, resulting ultimately in failure of the organs. Although there are 40 types of amyloidosis, each caused by a different protein of the amylome, the most common forms that affect the kidneys are AL and AA amyloidosis.Interestingly, it is thought that amyloid formation plays a key role in some conditions not typically viewed as protein misfolding disorders. One condition is diabetes mellitus type 2 (DM2), which is caused in part by damage to insulin producing cells in the pancreas. This results in high blood glucose levels which can induce a form of chronic kidney disease called diabetic nephropathy. It has been shown that misfolded islet amyloid polypeptide can damage pancreatic insulin producing cells, but the role of amyloid in diabetic nephropathy has not been studied in detail. As the precise cause of diabetic nephropathy remains unknown, I hypothesize that protein misfolding plays a role in the pathogenesis of kidney damage in DM2.Advanced fluorescence imaging techniques are being developed to study amyloid deposition in various organs of the body. Dyes that change their photophysical properties when bound to different amyloids allow sensitive and quantitative differentiation of these structures using fluorescence spectroscopy. These methods have proven invaluable in the elucidation of toxic protein conformations that may be key to tissue injury. The aim of this study is to use advanced imaging techniques to extract unique and valuable information about diabetic nephropathy from renal biopsies of DM2 patients. This may lead to improved diagnostic tests as well as a better understanding of the renal amylome and the pathogenesis of chronic kidney disease.

column36: Development of a novel assessment tool for on-call encounters in surgical education
column37: The medical profession is highly respected in Canadian society and upholding the principles of a physician involves significant responsibility. Training new physicians is an extremely important task that occurs over many years, as trainees become more autonomous in caring for patients, with a final goal of being competent to practice independently and safely. Along the way decisions must be made about the autonomy given to trainees and trainees must be given feedback on their performance to learn and advance in their training. Assessment tools or instruments are needed to provide this feedback and help supervising physicians make decisions regarding competency. Trainees are given the opportunity to perform more independently during the overnight or on-call period. During these times, staff physicians may not be in hospital and supervision may be indirect, meaning feedback to guide trainee learning is limited. Despite the fact we know trainees benefit from formal feedback and guidance, there is currently no established tool used to facilitate this process during on-call periods. Our plan is to develop a tool for this purpose.We will consult expert surgical educators to determine the essential features of what makes a trainee competent on-call. Based on these features and other principles of assessment development for health care professionals, we will create our tool. The tool will be trialed in a pilot over several months, after which we will examine whether residents and staff find it helpful, easy to use, and beneficial to training. If found to be useful, there is the opportunity to expand its use to other specialties and departments as all residents undertake on-call shifts. Our hope is if resident training and performance is improved, patient care will benefit.

column36: Investigation of the long-term clinical disease, pathogenesis, and immune responses following SARS-CoV-2 infection in Syrian hamsters and humans.
column37: SARS-CoV-2 (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2) causes the disease known as COVID-19 (coronavirus disease 2019). Currently, the long-term outcomes of SARS-CoV-2 infection are poorly understood, such as the mechanisms of the prolonged multiorgan condition Long COVID and the length of immune durability. Here I will explore the multiorgan damage and memory responses following SARS-CoV-2 infection over one year in a preclinical model and in humans. The work aims to define the causes of Long COVID and the duration of immune protection. Syrian hamsters will be infected with SARS-CoV-2 and monitored over one year, with tissues collected throughout to evaluate virus levels, tissue damage, and protective adaptive immune responses. Hamsters will also undergo cognitive tests to potentially model ;brain fog and loss of smell experienced in humans. To determine the level of immune protection over time, a subset of hamsters will be re-challenged with SARS-CoV-2 at 3-months, 6-months, and 12-months. Finally, the findings from preclinical studies will be extrapolated to the human condition by complementary analysis of Long COVID sufferers in Saskatchewan using a mobile app. Working with a multi-disciplinary team, we will investigate the prevalence of Long COVID in Saskatchewan, symptom types and duration, susceptibility, and healthcare burden to inform the establishment of support services and the design of future studies. This research will describe the Long COVID clinical picture in Saskatchewan and a preclinical model to test potential therapeutics. Additionally, the immune analysis will inform future vaccine design and regimens. Together, the results will work to improve patient quality of life and reduce the immense burden COVID-19 has on public health.

column37: Homelessness is a serious health threat. For the 20% of Canadas homeless population who are youth, the causes, consequences, and experiences of homelessness are distinct. This gap is important to fill, because gendered expectations and barriers may be amplifying the risks associated with homelessness, placing an already vulnerable population at increased risk. column36: Characterizing the Relationship Between Mucosal-Associated Invariant T Cells, the Intestinal Microbiota, and Tumour Progression in Murine MAIT-CAST Models
column37: The proposed project centres around a group of immune cells called Mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells. Even though these cells make up a sizeable portion of all T cells in the human immune system, they have not been extensively studied. MAIT cells are known to interact with the commensal bacteria, or microbiota, that naturally exists in the body. Furthermore, previous studies have shown how alterations in the microbiota can affect tumour development. However, even though MAIT cells have been found in the tumour environment, their role in this dynamic has remained unexplored. The hypothesis is that MAIT cells are the link between the microbiota and its apparent effects on tumour progression. Therefore, the main objective of this project is to use a mouse model to characterize the relationship between MAIT cells and the microbiota, and explore how this relationship may affect tumour progression and treatment. To accomplish the first portion, MAIT cell activity will be compared between normal mice and mice with an altered microbiota. The experiment will then be repeated, with the addition of injecting tumours into the mice to compare growth between the groups. Finally, to explore responsiveness to treatment, the experiment will be replicated with the inclusion of a tumour treatment called anti-programmed cell death 1 (PD1) therapy. It is predicted that by altering the microbiota in mice, MAIT cell populations will be affected and subsequently, tumour growth and response to anti-PD1 therapy will differ. This work has the potential to change how we treat certain types of cancerous tumours. With more knowledge of this relationship, the microbiota and/or MAIT cells could become targets for future cancer therapies.

column36: Leveraging artificial intelligence to assess adherence to the Responsible Advertising of Food and Beverage Products to Children Code
column37: Background: Unhealthy food marketing to children on digital media adversely affects their diet quality and health. To address this problem, Ad Standards Canada will implement the Responsible Advertising of Food and Beverage Products to Children Code to limit this marketing beginning in 2022. column36: A randomized, controlled, pilot, crossover trial to assess a fully automated, dual-hormone (insulin-pramlintide) artificial pancreas without carbohydrate counting in regulating glucose levels in adults with type 1 diabetes.
column37: Type 1 diabetes is an auto-immune disease characterized by the loss of insulin due to the destruction of pancreatic beta cells. Dysregulated production of insulin results in elevated blood glucose levels. Consequently, individuals with type 1 diabetes require insulin replacement therapy like multiple daily injections and insulin pump therapy. Closed-loop systems, or artificial pancreas systems, are emerging therapy choices for individuals with type 1 diabetes that increase the time spent in target glucose range. These systems are made up of three components: a glucose sensor to measure blood glucose levels, an insulin infusion pump, and a dosing algorithm to adjust insulin delivery based on sensor readings. Current systems require that users input the carbohydrate content of their meals for insulin bolusing. However, accurate carbohydrate counting is a challenging and burdensome task for most patients, with an estimation error of around 20%. Pramlintide, a synthetic analog of amylin, is used as an adjunct therapy for treatment of type 1 diabetes as it can normalize post-prandial glucose levels. We will conduct a pilot study to assess the performance of a fully automated, insulin-and-pramlintide, artificial pancreas with no carbohydrate counting in adult participants compared to an insulin-alone artificial pancreas with carbohydrate-matched boluses. It will comprise of three to five 14-hour interventions in a supervised outpatient setting where participants follow their regular dietary and exercise patterns. We will recruit 10 participants currently on insulin pump therapy. This feasibility study is the first step towards achieving our goal of extending our fully automated artificial pancreas research to outpatient settings and the first of its kind in the field.

column36: Study of the effects of PTEN and transcriptome-wide alternative polyadenylation on the oncogenic PI3K/Akt pathway and cell health.
column37: Messenger RNA (mRNA) is a molecule that carries DNA-encoded information outside of the nucleus to be translated into proteins. Polyadenylation is an mRNA maturation process that involves the addition of a poly(A) tail after a polyadenylation signal (PAS) located in the 3-untranslated region (3-UTR) of pre-mRNAs. Alternative polyadenylation (APA) is the production of varying 3'-UTR isoforms of an mRNA using distinct PAS in pre-mRNAs. Studies show that cancer cells use shorter 3-UTR APA isoforms. Several authors predict that this global shortening of 3-UTRs contributes to cancer development, a theory that is challenged by the fact that 3-UTR shortening also occurs in healthy proliferative cells through APA. This raises the question of whether 3UTR shortening is a cause or an adaptive response in cancer. I will study this question through Phosphatase and TENsin homolog (PTEN), a well-known tumor suppressor. PTEN is a protein that opposes the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) and thus negatively regulates the cancer inducing PI3K/Protein kinase B (Akt) signaling pathway. The goal of my project is to further understand the role of PTEN and global APA on the PI3K/Akt pathway and on cellular health. My hypothesis is that the shortening of PTEN and global mRNAs will increase PI3K/Akt signaling and oncogenic functions. The first objective of my project is to see the precise impact of individual PTEN 3UTR APA isoforms on the PI3K/Akt pathway and on cell health. The second objective of my project is to test the functional impact of global 3UTR shortening on the PI3K/Akt pathway and on cell health. My results will shed light on the impact of PTEN APA on PTEN function and help better understand cancers in which 3-UTR shortening is observed.

column37: Harnessing CRISPR/Cas9 to study group 2 innate lymphoid cells and their applications for immunotherapyInnate Lymphoid Cells (ILCs) are a family of innate lymphocytes with important roles in maintaining tissue homeostasis, and work as part of cellular circuits to coordinate immune responses. Recent reports have identified a regulatory population of ILC2s that secrete interleukin (IL)-10 in addition to type 2 cytokines IL-4, IL-9 and IL-13 that are referred to as ILC2. These cells inhibit inflammatory response in different organs and are associated with improved clinical outcome in the context of allergen immunotherapy and transplantation. We will address important questions, such as the impact of the knockout on cell proliferation and division, stability of gene knockout, and the impact of targeting these genes on expression of other ILC2 associated cytokines and TFs. column36: Investigating Ca2+ release deficiency syndrome in human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes
column37: Some heartbeat rhythm disorders (i.e. arrhythmias), such as catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT), have a high risk of leading to a sudden stop in electrical heart activity (i.e. sudden cardiac arrest). Most CPVT cases result from inherited mutations in a large protein needed for normal electrical signals in heart cells known as the cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2). In typical CPVT cases, mutations in RyR2 cause the protein to be overactive, and exercise stress testing serves as an accurate diagnostic tool in these patients. However, in cases where RyR2 mutations lead to underactivity, patients still experience arrhythmia but test negative on exercise stress testing. These cases were previously referred to as atypical CPVT. Recent studies have shown that atypical CPVT may be completely distinct from CPVT, with different cellular mechanisms by which electrical activity is disrupted. This newly identified condition is referred to as calcium release deficiency syndrome (CRDS). Importantly, there are currently no approved diagnostic tests for CRDS patients, hence patients remain at high risk for misdiagnosis and sudden cardiac arrest. To improve our understanding of CRDS, we are proposing to study a CRDS-associated RyR2 variant (I4855M) in human heart cells derived from induced pluripotent stem cells. Using various electrophysiological methods, we will identify the specific mechanism by which this mutation disrupts electrical activity in human heart cells. In addition, we will examine the biochemical changes associated with this variant to reveal its impact on RyR2 protein structure and function. In doing so, our study can help build the foundation for novel diagnostics and pharmacotherapies for precise and personalized care for CRDS patients.

column36: The impact of internalizing symptoms and interpersonal dysfunction on adolescent dating violence
column37: Before their twenty-first birthdays, one in three adolescents and young adults (AYA) will experience physical or psychological dating violence. Nearly one in ten will experience sexual dating violence. It is well known that experience with adolescent dating violence (ADV) puts youth at risk for anxiety and depression, among other negative health outcomes. Common internalizing conditions, such as anxiety and depression, have been linked to interpersonal dysfunctions such as poor conflict resolution, difficulty managing anger, oversensitivity to rejection, and possessiveness. Unfortunately, there has been little examination of internalizing conditions and interpersonal dysfunctions as predictors of ADV experience (including both perpetration and victimization), despite implications for improving ADV outcomes through mental health interventions and healthy relationships programming. This proposed secondary data analysis study will explore the relationship between internalizing conditions, interpersonal dysfunction, and ADV rates in AYA through examination of the Health Behaviour in School-Aged Children (HBSC) survey data. Responses to questions about current mental health status, peer relationships and interpersonal functioning, and experience with ADV will be analyzed. If statistically significant, results will help fill the current knowledge gap and inform future research. Significant results would also highlight the importance of teaching healthy relationship skills in ADV prevention programming, leading to more effective ADV interventions. Engaging with symptomatic AYA early will not only have positive effects on their long-term mental health but could also assist in reducing ADV rates overall.

column36: Enabling the next generation of human induced pluripotent stem cell derived hematopoietic stem cell-based therapies
column37: Human induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) present a renewable and scalable cell source for patient-specific hematopoietic stem progenitor cells (HSPCs) and blood cell products, which can be used to cure many blood diseases. However, a bottleneck hindering translation of this promising strategy is the efficient production of iHSCs and iHPCs from iPSCs. Small molecule stem cell agonist cocktails (SCACs) promoted cord blood-derived HSPC expansion and demonstrated high levels of in vivo engraftment. However, the effects of SCAC expansion on iPSC-derived iHSPCs and multipotent progenitor cells (iMPPs) is unknown. In this project, we aim to test SCACs to improve iHSPC and iMPP differentiation and expansion. We hypothesize that SCACs will enable an efficient and scalable production of human iHSPCs and iMPPs through the additive and synergistic ex vivo expansion activities of small molecules. In this study, we will use the monolayer differentiation strategy to generate CD34+CD43+ iHSPCs from iPSCs. We will assess the modulating activity of SCACs to identify an optimal formulation to preferentially expand iHSPCs and iMPPs. iHSPC/iMPP cell yields will be assessed by real-time imaging (IncuCyte) and flow cytometry. The potency of expanded iHSPC/iMPPs will be assessed by a colony-forming unit assay and we will determine the transcriptional profile of expanded immune cells using RNASeq. If SCACs significantly benefit the net output of Lin-CD43+CD34+ subpopulations or lymphoid cells in vitro, we will perform in vivo transplant experiments to assess engraftment activity. Identifying a strategy to expand iPSC-derived iHSPC and immune cell derivatives will enable the next generation of accessible, scalable and affordable therapeutic options for patients and HSPC biomanufacturing.

column37: La marche est une activite banale et accessible pour la majorite des gens. Par contre, pour les personnes souffrant de la maladie arterielle peripherique, la realite est bien differente, car pour eux, la marche peut devenir une epreuve douloureuse et angoissante.La maladie arterielle peripherique, c'est l'accumulation de plaques atheromateuses dans les arteres des jambes. Ces plaques retrecissent le diametre des arteres en les bloquant partiellement comme une tuyauterie rouillee. Ainsi, elles ne permettent plus au sang oxygene de bien circuler aux muscles des jambes, ce qui cause des douleurs lors des efforts physiques comme la marche. La seule maniere de diminuer la douleur est d'arreter de marcher, s'asseoir et attendre.Heureusement, il est possible pour ces personnes d'ameliorer leurs symptomes en marchant encore plus ! Les preuves scientifiques supportent que la marche reguliere permet de reduire la douleur et d'augmenter la distance parcourue par ces individus. C'est pourquoi participer a des programmes de readaptation en exercice supervises et specifiques a cette maladie permet de maximiser grandement ces bienfaits. Pourtant, il n'existe actuellement pas de programme de ce type dans les hopitaux publics du Quebec.Pour combler ce manque, des cardiologues et des kinesiologues se sont donc regroupes pour mettre en place un projet pilote, le projet IPAD. L'objectif de cette etude est d'etudier la faisabilite d'implanter un programme de readaptation en exercice specifique a cette condition dans un hopital public et ainsi faciliter l'instauration d'une alternative de soins efficace pour le traitement de la maladie arterielle peripherique.

column36: Examining the impact of deductibles on prescription drug utilization and costs: a quasi-experimental study using administrative data from British Columbia
column37: Prescription drugs are the second largest contributor to health spending in Canada. Prescription drug coverage is an important topic in Canadian health policy debates, especially because most funding for drugs comes from private sources. To protect patients from extreme costs, several provinces offer public drug insurance plans with high deductibles (they require patients to pay a substantial amount out-of-pocket before receiving public coverage). Despite the widespread use of deductibles, we know embarrassingly little about their impacts on patients and the health system.The objective of my research is to evaluate the impact of an income-based deductible on patients prescription drug use and costs as well as health service use and associated costs. I will do this using administrative data and a natural experiment emergent from the design of the universal Fair PharmaCare program in British Columbia (BC). As of 2019, Fair PharmaCare imposes no deductible on families with incomes less than $30 000, but families with incomes just over $30 000 face a $650 deductible. Given that patients with family incomes just above and below $30 000 are likely very similar, whether they face a $0 or $650 deductible is essentially random. This near randomization results in a natural experiment. I will use a powerful analytical tool known as regression discontinuity (RD) to exploit this natural experiment to determine the impact of the deductible. Specifically, I will apply RD analysis to a large administrative dataset from BC to estimate the impact of the deductible on prescription drug use and costs as well as health service use and associated costs.My research will help inform the design of drug insurance programsspecifically with respect to deductiblesin Canada and abroad.

column36: Integrative analysis of TIMP net effects in Human Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
column37: Pancreatic cancer (PC) is an extremely aggressive disease that requires a better understanding to improve treatment options. The 4 Tissue Inhibitors of Matrix Metalloproteinases (TIMPs) are key players in PC biology through their unique ability to influence the activity of hundreds of other proteins in a tissue, and thereby affecting both tumour and surrounding stromal cell behaviour and function. Intriguingly, these powerful functions rest on a network of unique and shared targets among the 4 TIMPs. Yet, so far only individual TIMPs have been studied. Here, we will analyse all 4 TIMPs in conjunction, taking into consideration their co-expression patterns within tissues so that the cumulative biological and clinical effects of TIMPs in PC can be determined. In various PC datasets, we will identify main TIMP co-expression clusters and compare their relationship with patient outcome to assess clinical relevance. Next, we will identify the biology associated with each cluster using computational means and a wide range of tissue stains. This will detangle how all TIMPs in conjunction influence tumour and stromal cells in human tissues. Finally, we will use 3D tumour models that have been created using patient-derived cells to model and manipulate TIMP expression in vitro to definitively pinpoint the impact of these molecules in human PC malignant behaviour (i.e., tumour cell survival, ability of the cancer to invade, and resistance to chemotherapy). This will enable us to manipulate TIMP cluster expression and assess potential therapeutic benefit. Our integrative approach to TIMP net effects will provide key insights into this influential protein family and determine their therapeutic potential by defining and blocking their key effects on a human pre-clinical platform.

column36: How does the SARS-CoV-2 antibody response shape patient outcomes? A longitudinal study to evaluate the SARS-CoV-2 antibody response and associations with physiological response and clinical outcomes
column37: During the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers and clinicians have sought to understand why people experience drastic differences in symptom severity when infected with SARS-CoV-2.Antibodies produced by the immune system in response to SARS-CoV-2 infection or vaccination have been an area of interest because of their potential to prevent infection. However, the quantity and types of antibodies that are indicative of protection from severe COVID-19 and long-term immunity are currently unknown. Similarly, certain biological markers (biomarkers) circulating in blood (such as those that indicate organ function) have been found to vary greatly between people infected from SARS-CoV-2. These biomarkers have been studied as indicators of disease severity, but their relationship with SARS-CoV-2 antibodies has not been defined. The proposed research project aims to monitor and compare how the SARS-CoV-2 antibody response changes over time following infection or vaccination, and to assess how those changes relate to COVID-19 severity and patient outcomes. Additionally, the project seeks to identify relationships between the SARS-CoV-2 antibody response and biomarkers in the blood that may predict COVID-19 severity.The significance of this study is that differences in the SARS-CoV-2 antibody response between infected or vaccinated individuals may allow us to identify reasons for why some individuals are asymptomatic while others develop more severe symptoms. Additionally, understanding how the antibody response changes over time will allow us to identify antibody characteristics which result in long-term protection. Consequently, the ability to determine specific and measurable predictors of severe disease may guide and improve treatment for those suffering from COVID-19.

column36: Determinants of transmission-blocking properties of antibodies targeting the 6C domain of Pfs48/45 of the Plasmodium falciparum parasite
column37: Over 400,000 people die from malaria each year ; most of these resulting from infection by the Plasmodium falciparum parasite. Although the very first Malaria vaccine has been recently approved by the World Health Organization, it fails to provide long-term immunity as protection against the parasite wanes rapidly over time. This highlights the need for the development of alternative malaria vaccines that confers long-term protective immunity. One promising vaccine candidate involves immunization of individuals with a Pfs48/45 antigen (6C); a protein expressed on P. falciparum during sexual reproduction of the parasite. Immunization through this antigen induces the generation of highly potent antibodies that block transmission of the parasite to humans. However, less potent antibodies are generated as well. The generation of these low potent antibodies is problematic as it can hinder the overall immune response, confer lower levels of protection from the parasite, and result in poor efficacy of the vaccine. The production of low potency antibodies can be avoided by modifying the structure of the antigen. However, where and what types of modifications are required can only be inferred by having a molecular understanding of how these low potency antibodies interact with the antigen. Using biochemical techniques, I aim to determine the strength, speed, and location these low potency antibodies bind to the antigen. These molecular insights are critical for guiding the development of a highly effective malaria vaccine ; an important steppingstone in the eradication of malaria.

column36: Longitudinal analysis of the viral evolution and neutralization assays of the pathogenic coronaviruses in VERO cells.
column37: The coronavirus family encompasses three pathogenic coronaviruses (SARS-CoV-1, SARS-CoV-2, MERS-CoV), which have the capability of infecting humans causing cytokine storms, acute respiratory distress syndrome, permanent lung damage, and persistent infection can be fatal. The pathogenic coronaviruses have pandemic potential with the epidemic of SARS-CoV-1 in 2002 and MERS-CoV in 2014. In addition, the emergence of SARS-CoV-2, the etiological agent of COVID-19 pandemic has infected more than 260 million people, and caused more than 5 million deaths, as of late November 2021. Besides, the COVID-19 pandemic has illustrated the capacity of coronaviruses as highly transmissible pathogens leading to severe strains on the health care system and impact on global socio-economic activities. The appearance of multiple variants over the past months gaining resistance against the immune response of vaccinated individuals has highlighted the rapidity of the evolution of coronaviruses. Therefore, to study the viral evolution of these pathogens, we produced a longitudinal study of infecting VERO cells with SARS-CoV-1, SARS-CoV-2, and MERS-CoV during 8-months and harvested the supernatant and cell isolates for whole-genome sequencing. The sequencing results at different time points will demonstrate the mutations gained during the passaging of the viruses from humans to non-human primate cell lines indicating variable regions in the genome allowing adaptability. Also, the sequencing of cell isolates and supernatant will allow us to compare the genetic variant found inside the cells versus viruses that are transmitted. Thus, our analyses could confer a better understanding of the viral quasispecies, genetic evolution, and zoonotic transmission of the pathogenic coronaviruses.

column36: Preclinical study of deep brain stimulation of the nucleus accumbens for the treatment of severe self-injurious behaviours associated with Autism Spectrum Disorder
column37: Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) often manifest self-injurious behaviour (SIB) that may be exceptionally challenging to treat. Severe SIB is associated with physical injury, distress, repeated hospitalizations and reduced quality of life for children and their caregivers. The nucleus accumbens (NAcc) is a brain region implicated in reward circuitry and has been shown to be altered in children with ASD. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the NAcc presents an opportunity to modulate NAcc-associated circuitry and offers novel means to treat SIB in affected children. In the current proposal, I will apply preclinical models of NAcc-targeted DBS (NAcc-DBS) to better define the neural underpinnings of this putative therapy. I will test the hypothesis that NAcc-DBS in mice that express SIB traits will remediate behaviours and modulate the neurocircuitry regulating SIB.Here, I will use the BTBR T+ Itpr3tf/J (BTBR) mouse model of ASD to study the effects of NAcc-DBS on autism-relevant phenotypes. BTBR mice will undergo stereotactic surgery for implantation of electrodes targeting the bilateral NAcc. Following recovery, mice will receive chronic high-frequency electrical stimulation for 4 days. Behavioural tests evaluating SIB ; as reflected by repetitive self-grooming and digging ; sociability, anxiety, and general locomotion will be performed immediately before and after the stimulation period. In addition, the neurocircuitry influenced by NAcc-DBS will be investigated using high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging and histology.This preclinical study analyzing the effects of NAcc-DBS will provide insights into the pathophysiology of SIB and will inform translational studies to develop novel neuromodulatory therapies for children with severe SIB.

column36: Alternating Current Stimulation as a Treatment for Essential Tremor
column37: Essential tremor (ET) is a chronic condition that manifests as involuntary and regular shaking (i.e., tremor) of head, hands, vocal cords, legs, or trunk. ET is the most common movement disorder, affecting up to 1.5 million Canadians. ET substantially limits routine daily activities, including writing/typing and feeding. There is currently no cure and only limited non-invasive treatment options for ET. In many cases, ET management requires invasive functional neurosurgery (e.g., deep brain stimulation). With Canadas aging population, there is a growing need to improve non-invasive treatment options that can safely reduce the severity of tremor. Alternating current stimulation (ACS), is a recent technology and potential non-invasive (non-surgical) treatment option for ET. ACS delivers electrical current that influences brain and sensory activity. Recent studies have shown promising results for the use of ACS in treating ET, but more work is needed to better understand its most effective modality of application and the duration of its effect. The objective of this research project is to examine the effects of ACS on tremor severity (amplitude) in ET. On different days, patients will receive real and sham (fake) ACS stimulation applied to i) their head or ii) the skin of their forearm. We will also compare how ACS decreases the amplitude of tremor when ACS oscillations are in exact alignment or not with the oscillations of tremor. Tremor will be recorded before, during and for 45 minutes after each stimulation session.By exploring ACS in different modalities, this project has the potential to accelerate the clinical application of this non-invasive, relatively low-cost, and home exportable treatment option for ET.

column36: Investigating the negative impact of integrase inhibitor-based antiretroviral therapy in early pregnancy
column37: It is recommended that HIV-positive (HIV+) women take a specific type of HIV medication, antiretroviral therapy (ART), during their pregnancy. ART is made-up of a combination of drugs, each targeting different steps of HIVs replication cycle in the human body. As a result, ART is excellent at keeping moms healthy and eliminating the risk of HIV transmission to the baby. Although ART is widely used, there is a growing concern of potential side effects on the unborn baby when taken during pregnancy, such as miscarriage, preterm birth, and a low-birth-weight baby. We dont yet fully understand how ART causes these side effects, or which specific components of ART have the fewest side effects when taken during pregnancy. Our lab has shown that older ART drug components, the protease inhibitors, lower the levels of progesterone, the well-known ;pregnancy hormone, in HIV+ pregnant women. Progesterone is important in establishing and maintaining pregnancy. Very early in pregnancy, the maternal side of the placenta, termed the decidua, must form first and relies on progesterone to form properly. If progesterone levels are lowered by certain components of ART, the decidua may not form correctly, possibly affecting the quality of the placenta and the outcome of the pregnancy. We do not yet know if newer ART drug components, the integrase inhibitors, negatively affect pregnancy. To examine this, we will investigate how integrase inhibitors affect the formation and function of the decidua doing experiments on human decidual and placental tissue and in a mouse pregnancy model. Our findings will inform the selection of the safest integrase inhibitors to use as components of ART in pregnancy, with the ultimate goal of improving pregnancy outcome.

column36: A mixed-methods evaluation of an overdose prevention phone line: the National Overdose Response Service (NORS)
column37: Background: In 2020, there were 6265 opioid poisoning deaths in Canada, marking the most devastating year for overdose deaths. During the COVID-19 pandemic, access to substance use related supports has decreased while the illicit drug supply became more toxic. Supervised consumption sites (SCS) can reduce overdose deaths, but are not accessible to all people who use drugs (PWUD). The National Overdose Response Service (NORS) is an overdose prevention phone line created to overcome these barriers by increasing access to SCS. Objectives: This research will evaluate: (1) who is using the NORS service, and what drug use characteristics do they exhibit?; (2) do these characteristics differ from people using other types of SCS?; (3) does NORS have an impact on harm reduction practices or drug use patterns?; and (4) why are people using NORS as opposed to other SCS?. Methods and analyses: To address the first research question, we will use NORS administrative data to understand clients demographic and drug use characteristics. To address the second research question, we will compare the administrative data to reports gathered from existing SCS. For the third and fourth questions, we will recruit 150 NORS clients to participate in an online survey. A subset of 40 survey participants will participate in semi-structured interviews to identify strengths and weakness of the NORS service. To address the first three research questions, we will use descriptive statistics of the administrative data and survey results. To assess the fourth question, we will use thematic analysis to describe the open-ended interview responses. Significance: This study aims to address the growing overdose crisis by describing the role of phone-based SCS within existing harm reduction tools.

column36: L'evaluation de la memoire semantique chez une population presentant un declin cognitif subjectif comme potentiel marqueur precoce de la maladie d'Alzheimer.
column37: Environ un million de personnes seront atteintes de la maladie d'Alzheimer (MA) au Canada d'ici 2031, du au phenomene de vieillissement de la population qui s'accelere de plus en plus. Ainsi, l'identification de signes precurseurs permettant un diagnostic precoce de la maladie est primordiale. La recherche dans les dernieres annees s'est particulierement interessee au stade preclinique de la MA appele declin cognitif subjectif (DCS), qui precede le stade de trouble cognitif leger (TCL). Le DCS est defini comme la presence de plaintes subjectives auto-rapportees, en l'absence de deficits cognitifs objectifs. Cependant, la memoire semantique (MS), notre memoire des connaissances et des faits sur le monde, est rarement examinee chez des participants ayant un DCS. Or, puisque la MS decline avant la memoire episodique (ME) dans la MA, les personnes agees ayant un DCS pourraient presenter un declin isole de la MS. Le declin de la MS pourrait donc etre un marqueur cognitif precoce, accessible et abordable. L'objectif de ce projet de recherche est d'investiguer la MS aupres d'une population agee au stade de DCS. Le but est d'identifier les premiers signes precurseurs de declin cognitif chez des individus a risque de developper la MA. L'objectif plus specifique est d'examiner la performance aux tests de MS inclus dans la batterie de CIMA-Q, dans une cohorte existante de participants ayant un DCS, un TCL, et une MA. Le projet contribuera a mieux comprendre le profil semantique des participants atteints d'un DCS et d'etudier le lien entre les deficits semantiques et la presence de biomarqueurs de la MA. column36: Cellular Senescence in Women's Brains due to Mild Traumatic Brain Injury (mTBI)
column37: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), especially when experienced repeatedly, causes diverse neurological symptoms and increases risk of neurodegenerative diseases like chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE). Although multiple studies report that mTBI symptoms and recovery patterns differ by sexwith women typically faring worsethere is a significant lack of research on how womens brains are affected by mTBI. Previously, our lab assessed a series of post-mortem male brains with histories of repeat mTBI, finding DNA damage, pro-inflammatory senescence factors and evidence of impaired DNA repair capacities. We predict that DNA damage-induced senescence in human brains with mTBI history may underlie post-injury brain dysfunction. The present study will assess female brains with mTBI histories to (1) determine CTE prevalence, (2) characterize DNA damage-induced cellular senescence and (3) evaluate X chromosome re-activation as a downstream effect of senescence. We hypothesize that, similar to mens brains, indicators of cellular senescence will be present alongside CTE pathology. Additionally, to explore sex differences, we will test the re-activation of the X chromosome in women as the basis of worse disease in women. We will evaluate 20 post-mortem brains with mTBI histories and age-matched controls, with emphasis on histological changes (inflammation and taupathy [CTE]) and molecular changes (bulk RNA sequencing, western blot and RT-PCR), and assess X chromosome reactivation via RNA-scope. This study will answer whether women have similar susceptibility to CTE and cellular senescence as men and whether overexpression of genes (such as X-linked synaptic proteins) on the inactivated X chromosome explains sex differences in clinical outcomes.

column36: The Impact of Cytomegalovirus Infection on Respiratory Disease Progression in Cystic Fibrosis
column37: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most prevalent fatal genetic disease affecting Caucasian populations. Owing to reduced chloride ion transport across epithelial surfaces, thick mucus secretions accumulate across the systemic epithelium. Impaired mucocilliary clearance within the airways and resultant chronic bacterial infection are the primary drivers of CF-related morbidity and mortality. However, bacterial infection status poorly correlates with long term outcomes, highlighting the need to identify other variables influencing CF disease progression. In recent years, cytomegalovirus (CMV, a ubiquitous DNA virus) has been identified as a potential contributor to disproportionate progression of many inflammatory diseases. In 2020, it was shown that people with CF (pwCF) who were CMV seropositive progressed to end-stage lung disease significantly faster than those that were seronegative (by 8 years). Furthermore, CMV DNA has been found in sputum of those with advanced disease. The aim of this work is to establish the prevalence, risk factors, and dynamics of CMV in sputum and serum of pwCF, collected from multiple sites across Canada over the course of five years. Further, this study will aim to investigate the effect of CMV infection in bronchial epithelial cells in vitro, using CF- and non-CF cell lines. We suspect that patients with CMV seropositivity and those experiencing incident CMV infection (seroconversion) will demonstrate worse baseline disease status and disease progression over time. The findings of this study will provide unique insight into a previously unexplored mechanism of disease pathogenesis, and if confirmed, could open the door to clinical studies using established CMV-therapeutics and evolving CMV vaccines to mitigate its effect.

column36: Characterization of placental aquaporins and glycerol levels from active and inactive mothers
column37: The placenta is an essential organ for pregnancy involved in gas exchange, waste product removal, secreting hormones, and transporting nutrients. A family of proteins involved in water and glycerol transport is found in the placenta's outer layer and are called aquaporins. For this study, we will look at aquaporin-1 (AQP1) and aquaporin-9 (AQP9). AQP1 helps maintain water balance for the fetus, and AQP9 is involved in moving glycerol across the placenta to be used as energy by the fetus. Previous research has shown that these transporters are higher in the placentas of physically active women than inactive women. However, more information is needed to understand the effects of physical activity on the amounts of AQP1 and AQP9 proteins in the placenta and if they lead to higher glycerol transport. Therefore, the objective of this study is to understand the impact of physical activity on AQP1 and AQP9 transporter proteins. This study will address two aims: 1) to determine how physical activity affects AQP1 and AQP9 proteins in the placentas from physically active women and 2) to assess the relationship between the transporters and glycerol levels in the placenta. To achieve this objective, we will compare placental tissue from physically active or inactive women during their pregnancy to see if there are differences in the amount of AQP1 and AQP9 proteins and glycerol levels.

column36: Developing a hybrid nanoparticle-hydrogel platform for long non-coding RNA delivery in inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Globally, more than 6.8 million people are living with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by intestinal inflammation leading to bowel injury. Current therapies have improved quality of life and decreased risk of disease-related complications in patients with IBD. Forty percent of patients initially respond to treatments; however, these treatments become less effective over time. There is an urgent need for new and sustainable therapeutic treatments to address the clinical and economic burden caused by the disease. A solution is developing an orally administered drug delivery technology delivering long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) as an anti-inflammatory therapy for IBD.An ideal IBD treatment stops and reverses inflammation. LncRNAs are a class of nucleic acids involved in gene regulation. Several newly discovered lncRNAs can potentially stop inflammation, presenting an avenue by which we can utilize these molecules to modulate inflammation in IBD, provided these lncRNA can be delivered to the intestine. A new drug delivery vehicle composed of nanomaterials will be designed to protect these nucleic acids and carry it to the inflamed intestine to treat IBD.The drug delivery platform will be a novel lncRNA-based anti-inflammatory therapy for IBD. This technology aims to deliver large amounts of the lncRNA in the inflamed intestine to reduce the number of treatments. Patient compliance will be increased with the oral drug administration route. The capability to deliver multiple inflammation-reducing lncRNAs simultaneously creates a more comprehensive approach to treating this complex disease. With over 17,000 lncRNAs discovered to date, this class of nucleic acid holds tremendous potential in creating therapies beyond IBD.

column36: Investigating functions of the Epstein-Barr virus protein BRRF1 in host and viral gene regulation
column37: The Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is a widespread virus that infects nearly all adults worldwide. Infection is life-long, as the virus hides within the bodys immune cells and is skilful at escaping detection. EBV is the cause of infectious mononucleosis and is also known to cause many different cancers, potentially up to 1 out of 100 cancer cases worldwide. Unfortunately, it is still not fully understood exactly how EBV persists for so long or causes disease or cancer. The key to understanding (and then preventing) EBV-related diseases lies within identifying the many different EBV proteins, understanding how they work, and finding out how they manipulate the proteins and cells of the human host. We have recently discovered that one EBV protein binds a certain protein complex, called CCR4NOT, that is present in human cells. CCR4NOT plays an essential role in determining which proteins are expressed in the cell. We hypothesize that EBV may be hijacking CCR4NOT, to control which proteins are expressed. Many viruses are known to cause a decrease in the host cells protein expression, in order to prioritize expression of their own proteins, so we think that EBV may be doing this by controlling CCR4NOT. Our experiments will investigate this occurrence further, to better understand the interaction between the EBV protein and CCR4NOT, and to see how this interaction affects protein expression within the cell. Ultimately, we aim to understand whether this interaction plays a role in EBV infection, EBV-caused diseases, and EBV-related cancer.

column36: Multimodal MRI biomarkers for optimizing deep brain stimulation therapy in Parkinson's disease.
column37: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a neurosurgical technique wherein implantable electrodes are placed in key brain structures to provide electrical stimulation and modulate pathological brain activity. It has become an effective and well-established therapy for Parkinsons disease (PD) and has shown benefit for an expanding number of motor, psychiatric, and cognitive disorders. Despite its recognized efficacy in PD, there is substantial variability in clinical response and there remains uncertainty as to which neuroanatomical target leads to optimal outcome. Subthalamic nucleus (STN) and globus pallidus internus (GPi) DBS has become valuable surgical stimulation sites, mainly improving the motor symptoms. The effects of DBS on cognitive function is less well understood and there is the suggestion that GPi DBS may be better tolerated with respect to cognitive adverse effects. It is still unclear, on a patient-specific level, which surgical target provides the best balance between treatment efficacy, safety, and minimization of adverse effects. We hypothesize that PD patients undergoing DBS demonstrate structural and connectivity related changes seen on preoperative MRI. The identification of imaging-based biomarkers could predict surgical response to DBS therapy and aid in personalized surgical target selection. To this end, 542 PD patients with preoperative structural and functional imaging and undergoing STN or GPi DBS have been recruited through our centre. We aim to leverage this uniquely large disease cohort, rich multi-modal imaging dataset, and predictive analytic techniques to identify imaging biomarkers for predicting response to DBS. This can be readily translated towards improving DBS therapy through patient-specific surgical target selection.

column36: Identification and characterization of echinocandin potentiators to combat drug-resistant Candida species.
column37: Although largely overlooked, fungi cause deadly systemic infections in a growing population of immunocompromised patients that encompass high-dose corticosteroids users, solid organ transplant recipients, and those infected with HIV. Candida albicans is a leading cause of these infections with mortality rates of ~40%. Currently, there are only three classes of drugs used to treat systemic fungal infections: azoles, polyenes, and echinocandins. The echinocandins are the only new class of antifungal drug to reach clinics in decades, and while the emergence of drug-resistance fungi, including echinocandin-resistant Candida species, threatens global public health, current antifungal treatments remain insufficient. Drug combination therapies can reduce host toxicities by enabling a reduction of drug dosages and can reduce the likelihood of developing resistance. In a quest to identify novel therapies to combat C. albicans infections, I screened the Boston University Centre for Molecular Discovery (BU-CMD) library of 3,936 chemically diverse compounds against an echinocandin-resistant isolate of C. albicans alone and in combination with the echinocandin, caspofungin. Through this approach, I identified 31 compounds with single-agent activity and 35 compounds that enhanced the activity of the echinocandin caspofungin. The mechanism of action of these prioritized compounds will be assessed using genetic approaches that utilize a C. albicans mutant library. Finally, hit compounds will be assessed for their therapeutic potential by evaluating toxicity against human cells as well as through mouse models of systemic candidiasis. My project will reveal much-needed novel therapeutic strategies to combat drug-resistant fungal pathogens threatening thousands of lives around the globe.
