column36: Using Microvessel Fragments to Study Cardiovascular Ischaemia-Reperfusion Injury
column37: Cardiovascular disease is a leading cause of death that can manifest in the form of a heart attack. This is when the blood supply that feeds the muscle of the heart is obstructed, resulting in a decreased oxygen supply to the heart. Restoration of blood flow, also known as reperfusion, is therefore essential for long-term organ survival. However, reperfusion also has its drawbacks and initially causes damage to the heart that precedes its long-term benefitsa phenomenon called reperfusion-injury. The effect of reperfusion-injury on heart muscle is well known, however more research is needed to understand how reperfusion-injury affects the hearts microvasculaturethe smallest types of blood vessels. Therefore, our first research goal is to investigate the effect of reperfusion-injury on microvascular growth. We will do this by isolating microvessel fragments from rats, then exposing the fragments to low oxygen. Restoring standard oxygen conditions will be used to simulate reperfusion, and microvessel growth can then be imaged using a specialized microscope. Our next research goal is to develop a novel device that can support the growth of both microvessel fragments and heart cells in the same environment. We can then model reperfusion-injury by exposing the device to low oxygen, followed by re-oxygenation. We anticipate that the microvessels and heart cells will have a positive impact on each others survival during reperfusion-injury. Our device will be the first of its kind to examine the interactions between complex microvasculature and heart cells in the context of reperfusion-injury. We anticipate that our research will support the development of next-generation therapies for heart attack recovery that consider both the heart and its associated microvasculature.

column36: Role of CD13 in alteration of polarity and metabolism programs in breast cancer progression
column37: Breast cancer is the most common form of cancer among women and although treatment for breast cancer have progressed in recent years, many eventually become resistant to initial treatment. column36: Mental health treatment outcomes based on the type of child maltreatment experienced
column37: Childhood trauma is defined as the exposure to real or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). One of the most common forms is child maltreatment displayed as physical, sexual, and emotional abuse or neglect. Children and youth who have experienced abuse are more likely to use psychiatric and medical services (Stewart et al., 2013) and providing early intervention and treatment can improve mental health outcomes (Baiden et al., 2017; Ford et al., 2010; Waddell et al., 2005). Given the very limited research examining recovery rates of traumatized children (Whitt-Woosley et al., 2018), the proposed study plans to address this gap by exploring mental health treatment outcomes in children and youth who have experienced physical abuse compared to sexual abuse. The proposed study will utilize over 50,000 interRAI Child and Youth Mental Health (ChYMH) assessments collected by trained clinicians in mental health agencies across Canada (Stewart, et al., 2015). Participants will include 4;18-year-old children and youth who are receiving services from mental health agencies, have been assessed pre- and post-treatment using the ChYMH assessment, and have experienced physical or sexual abuse (Stewart, et al., 2015). ChYMH scales and algorithms will be used to assess mental health treatment outcomes. It is hypothesized that traumatized children and youth will have poorer recovery rates, higher levels of behavioural problems, anxiety, depression, suicidality, and socio-emotional difficulties, compared to those without child maltreatment trauma. Due to the potential negative impact of trauma, it is important to further explore the differential impact of specific traumas on treatment outcome (Baiden et al., 2017; Ford et al., 2010).

column36: Investigating LOXL2 as a Therapeutic Target to Overcome Radioresistance in Prostate Cancer
column37: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in male Canadians, yet resistance to radiation treatment leading to metastatic progression is still a cause of significant morbidity and mortality in patients. column37: The combination of two new immunotherapies, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy and oncolytic virotherapy, shows promise for treatment of solid tumors. Understanding the role of virus-specific TCRs and their associated signaling on CAR T cells can inform us how to best use OVs for therapeutic success. By examining the phenotype and functional capabilities of these OV-specific CAR T cells we can learn about how these different signaling strengths affect the function of these CAR T cells. column36: Investigating the role of NINJ1 in hepatic ischemia-reperfusion injury
column37: For many patients with end-stage liver disease, liver transplantation is their only curative treatment option. Unfortunately, hepatic ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI), inherent to liver transplantation, contributes to adverse transplantation outcomes such as graft dysfunction, rejection, and patient mortality. The temporary ischemic state of the extracted organ and the sudden restoration of blood flow to the organ following transplantation into the recipient ultimately lead to cell death and an injurious inflammatory response in the liver. This damaging inflammatory response in hepatic IRI is driven by lytic cell death pathways that result in cell rupture and consequent release of proinflammatory molecules. Recently, ninjurin-1 (NINJ1), a protein expressed in liver cells, has been identified as necessary for cells to rupture in lytic cell death. Inhibiting NINJ1 to block cell rupture and subsequent release of proinflammatory molecules can potentially reduce the inflammatory response in hepatic IRI. Therefore, my central hypothesis is that inhibiting NINJ1 will prevent liver cell death and protect the liver against the damaging effects of IRI. To test this hypothesis, I will be using a mouse model of hepatic IRI. Specifically, I will be assessing whether the pharmacologic inhibition or genetic deletion of NINJ1 in mice during hepatic IRI can reduce inflammation and injury in the liver. The results from this project can potentially identify NINJ1 as a promising therapeutic target for protecting the liver against hepatic IRI during transplantation. Additionally, if inhibiting NINJ1 can protect the liver from IRI, marginal donor organs that are ineligible for donation due to their susceptibility to IRI can potentially be included to expand the limited donor organ pool.

column37: Traumatic spinal cord injury (SCI) causes a loss of sensation and movement due to tissue damage. Cell transplantation has been investigated as a potential therapy to replace the lost and damaged tissue. Interneurons, a cell type found within the spine, connect different parts of the spine and are responsible for coordinating complex movements. A specific type of interneuron, propriospinal interneurons (PIs), can detour around an area of injury in the lower spine and reconnect the damaged segments. My project will involve the transplantation of immature cells (neural progenitor cells) into rats. These immature cells will undergo two different treatments to produce either immature excitatory PIs or immature inhibitory PIs. The goal of this project is to determine whether transplantation of immature excitatory PIs, immature inhibitory PIs or both types of immature PIs will result in improved recovery after SCI. One group of rats will also be transplanted with untreated immature cells as a reference. Rat behaviour will be analyzed following SCI surgery and transplantation. The number of cell connections formed at the injury site in all four groups of rats will be analyzed and compared. In other research, after SCI, transplantation of mature excitatory PIs showed improved functional recovery in comparison to the transplantation of untreated immature cells (neural progenitor cells). This project will transplant both excitatory and inhibitory PIs but in their immature form. In their immature form, PIs have an improved ability to integrate with existing spinal tissue and reconnect areas of damage. Additionally, the simultaneous transplantation of both excitatory and inhibitory PIs could re-establish the balance of excitatory/inhibitory activity which is lost after SCI.

column36: Developpement de trois mesures de la peur de la recidive clinique chez les survivants du cancer
column37: La peur de la recidive est definie comme etant la peur ou la preoccupation de la personne que le cancer revienne dans la meme ou une differente partie du corps. Les consequences de la PRC selon sa severite incluent par exemple une reduction de la qualite de vie des survivants, une plus grande morbidite psychosociale (Koch et al., 2013), et une plus grande utilisation des services de sante (Champagne et al., 2018). Toutefois, aucune mesure n'existe pour ce phenomene ce qui rend l'etablissement d'un traitement plus difficile. Pour cette etude, une mesure de la peur de la recidive clinique (PRC) du cancer sera validee aupres des survivants du cancer. Cette mesure aura pour but d'ameliorer la capacite des medecins et professionnels de la sante de detecter les patients ayant une peur de la recidive clinique, ce qui facilitera ensuite l'offre et l'implementation de traitements. La mesure aura pour nom le Ottawa Clinical Fear of Recurrence (OCFR) et sera composee d'une entrevue semi-structuree (Ottawa Clinical Fear of Recurrence - Inventory; OCFR-I), un questionnaire (Ottawa Clinical Fear of Recurrence - Measure; OCFR-M), et une question pour detecter facilement et rapidement les patients susceptibles d'avoir un quelconque niveau de peur de la recidive (Ottawa Clinical Fear of Recurrence - Screener; OCFR-S). column36: Economic evaluation and cost-effectiveness analysis of cervical cancer preventative strategies by screening and vaccination in high HIV prevalence countries
column37: Cervical cancer (CC) is a major cause of mortality in women globally. CC disproportionately affects women in lower-income countries due to gender inequality, lack of access to effective and efficient healthcare, and limited health expenditures. The situation is exacerbated in high HIV prevalence countries due to the synergistic effect of HIV with Human Papillomavirus (HPV), the causative agent of CC, as women living with HIV have a higher probability of developing CC. The current major CC elimination strategies are vaccination against HPV and routine screening for precancerous cervical lesion. Though these strategies have been proven to decrease CC incidence and mortality in developed countries, the optimal CC elimination strategy in high HIV prevalence settings is yet to be determined. With limited health budgets, the affordability of such strategies needs to be considered.This project aims to examine the economic impacts of potential CC elimination strategies in South Africa, one of the countries with the highest HIV burden. Specifically, I will:1) evaluate the costs and conduct budget impact analyses of current and potential screening and vaccination strategies in South Africa; and2) conduct cost-effectiveness analyses of CC elimination strategies, considering HIV transmission dynamics, in South Africa. Leveraging several data sources, I will evaluate the costs and affordability of the potential strategies. I will then conduct cost-effectiveness analyses using a mathematical model of HIV and HPV co-transmission to determine the optimal strategy of CC elimination in high HIV prevalence settings. My results will guide global CC elimination recommendations and should prove an invaluable tool to address the double threat of HIV and HPV to women in sub-Saharan Africa.

column36: Endometriosis-associated ovarian cancers: A population-based study to improve risk stratification among endometriosis patients
column37: Endometriosis affects roughly 1 million women in Canada, is a main cause of pelvic pain and infertility, and is associated with ovarian cancer development. It is a chronic, estrogen-dependent, inflammatory condition characterized by lesions resembling uterine endometrium found outside the uterus. The gold standard diagnosis is surgical visualization of the lesions, followed by excision or biopsy of the lesions, and pathological confirmation of endometrial tissue. Goal 1) To better understand the relationship between anatomy of endometriosis and risk of ovarian cancer in a historical cohort of people with pathologically confirmed endometriosis and details on the anatomy of the endometriosis, and 2) to better understand the relationship between treatment of endometriosis and risk of ovarian cancer. Methods We have captured and built a linkable dataset of all people with pathologically confirmed endometriosis from the pathology database in Vancouver Coastal Health Authority between January 1st, 2000 and December 31, 2008 (n=3561). These data have been linked with population-based administrative datasets, including: Health Services Data, BC Cancer Registry, Vital Statistics, and BC PharmaNet. Using these data, we will examine the relationship between hormonal management of endometriosis, comparing never users to those who treated their endometriosis with hormonal management, including more detailed sub-analyses based on type of medication and length of use. The specific trigger for the transition from benign endometriosis, to atypical endometriosis and cancer remains unclear. This work may help us improve our ovarian cancer risk stratification of endometriosis patients, as well as identifying possible opportunities for risk reduction of endometriosis associated cancer.

column36: Understanding the developmental timing of neocortical neurogenesis
column37: The neocortex is the region of the brain that is responsible for our unique abilities as humans to reason, think, speak, organize and plan. It is comprised of six neuronal layers that are born in an inside-out fashion during development and acquire unique molecular and organizational features. My overall objective is to understand how these neurons acquire their specific features. Neurog1 (N1) and Neurog2 (N2) are proneural genes that encode basic-helix-loop-helix transcription factors that promote the differentiation and specification of neuronal subtypes during neocortical development. In the absence of both N1 and N2, there is a precocious depletion of the cortical neural progenitor cell (NPC) pool at the end of embryogenesis. These two transcription factors are thus together required to maintain the NPC pool. I will test the hypothesis that N1 and N2 regulate the division patterns of cortical NPCs to control the timing of cortical neurogenesis, and thereby, preserve the cortical NPC pool. To test this hypothesis, I will use a mouse model system to characterize NPC loss in N1N2 double knockouts (Aim 1) and to analyze the division patterns of N1N2 mutant NPCs (Aim 2). I expect that there will be a greater impact on deep-layer neurons due to the higher co-expression of N1 and N2early on in development. Further, I expect that in N1N2 double knockouts, symmetric neurogenic divisions will predominate thus depleting the NPC pool. By understanding how the neocortex develops, we can better understand the etiology of many devastating diseases and strive to develop novel treatments.

column36: Bioengineering a Human Airway Mimetic for Preclinical Use in Disease Modelling Cystic Fibrosis
column37: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disease that affects over 4000 children and young adults in Canada. While it is a multi-organ disease resulting in an imbalance of water and salt, it severely impacts lung function. Specifically, CF individuals deal with thick, dehydrated mucus secretions in their airways, resulting in difficulty breathing and clearing their airway of debris and pathogens. This can lead to repeated lung infections and chronic inflammation. There is no universal cure for CF because not everyone shares the same mutation, and available drugs are costly, and their efficacy varies based on an individual's mutation. This highlights the need for personalized medicine to treat CF; however, physiologically relevant study models for humans are lacking. Animal models are not truly representative of human conditions, and human cells grown on plates are an oversimplification of the airway environment. This project aims to create the first artificial airway for near-term use in disease modelling and personalized therapy discovery. In collaboration with the University of Toronto's Mechanical Engineering department, we will be accounting for the airway's physical structure. Our goal is to create a functionally accurate mimetic that can reflect realistic human responses to CF outside the body. We will use novel bioprinting technology to print tubes and seed patient-derived stem cells to mimic the airway structure while exposed to airflow. Using patient-derived stem cells suggests specific drugs can be selected and tested for on the model to determine their efficacy in treating a particular patient. Therefore, creating a physiologically relevant model is vital to observing and understanding realistic responses to CF and developing effective treatment options.

column36: Identification of cellular factors that regulate amyloid body disaggregation
column37: Cells require proteins to carry out important tasks for their proper function. To achieve this, these proteins need to be properly folded and delivered around the cell. However, any harmful stressors, such as high temperature, can cause proteins to change their shape and clump together, making them unable to participate in their cellular pathway. These protein clumps are better known as aggregates, which can be unstructured or the proteins in them can develop the same shape, called the amyloid fold. Currently, the Audas laboratory is studying a newly identified cellular pathway that makes proteins take on the amyloid fold during stressful environmental conditions, which allows the cell to survive. When the cells return to favourable conditions, the aggregates are quickly dissolved, removing those proteins and refolding them to once again carry out their important tasks. We aim to identify these cellular factors responsible for taking apart amyloid aggregates when favourable conditions are restored. These factors are likely disrupted in amyloid-associated diseases such as Alzheimers Disease, a dementia-causing chronic disorder affecting hundreds of thousands of Canadians, where the beta-amyloid protein forms aggregates in the brain. This research could help develop new therapeutic targets and open new directions to pursue in the field of amyloid-associated disease research

column36: Engineering T cell receptors to improve cancer immunotherapy
column37: T cell receptor (TCR) gene therapy involves the adoptive transfer of T cells engineered with high-affinity TCRs to induce a clinically effective anti-tumor response. TCRs expressed on the surface of T cells consist of alpha and beta chains, which together recognizes cancer peptides or antigens presented by human leukocyte antigens (HLAs) on the surface of cancer cells. From this repertoire, we will isolate a TCR with optimal targeting of NY-ESO-1 and minimal toxicity for pre-clinical and clinical studies.

column36: Exploring Culturally Safe Cancer Care for Adolescent and Young Adult Patients With Cancer.

column36: Increasing brain-signal translation accuracy through direction-focused motor imagery.

column36: The Effect of Mental Health on Perceived Sleep Quality vs. Sleep Duration
column37: In the aging population, poor sleep quality is a concern as 46% of individuals 65 years and up reported insomnia, an indicator of poor sleep quality, which has been associated with dementia. Sleep quality can be dissected into two categories: objective, and subjective sleep measures. Objective sleep quality are measurable variables like sleep duration, and subjective sleep quality is how an individual perceived their nights rest. Because there are two aspects to sleep quality, an important consideration is how these two aspects differ? Subjective sleep quality is closely linked to subjective well-being and mental health outcomes such as depression, anxiety, and mood disorders. Furthermore, there is a mismatch between subjective and objective sleep quality in elderly individuals, further emphasizing the difference between subjective and objective sleep quality in the aging population. Hence, I will investigate how mental health factors like anxiety, depression, and mood disorders can predict subjective sleep quality and sleep duration in an aging population. Data was obtained from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging, a study with 50,000 participants from 45-85 years of age. Perceived sleep quality was obtained through a 1-5 scale (5= worst perceived sleep quality). Sleep duration was measured as the number of hours slept. Onset, absence, persistence, and the recovery of anxiety, depression, and mood disorder at will be considered for mental health. Changes in mental health status and lifestyle will be analyzed at baseline (2015) and follow-up (2018) in regards to perceived sleep quality and sleep duration. It is expected that individuals with different mental health status will have different perceived sleep quality and sleep duration at the follow-up stage.

column37: Central Nervous System (CNS) disorders and injuries affecting the brain and spinal cord are one of the leading causes of disability worldwide. Currently, there are limited treatment options for demyelinating disease. This highlights the need for novel therapeutics. In hopes of curing demyelinating diseases, scientists have been trying to develop therapies to replace oligodendrocytes. An exciting new therapeutic strategy is the conversion of resident brain cells, called astrocytes, into new oligodendrocytes. We will also investigate the biology that underlies this process, specifically the genes that drive the conversion, in order to better understand and optimize this therapy. If successful, this novel reprogramming strategy will eliminate disease-causing astrocytes while simultaneously replacing healthy oligodendrocytes that are lost in CNS disease.

column36: Examining the Impacts of HIV Antiretrovirals on Maternal Immune Homeostasis
column37: The World Health Organization recommends antiretroviral therapy (ART) for all people living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). This has transformed HIV into a chronic but manageable condition and greatly reduced the rate of HIV transmission from affected mothers to babies at the time of birth. However, ART in pregnancy has been associated with increased rates of preterm birth and small for gestational age babies. Healthy pregnancies rely on the placenta to provide growing fetuses with nutrients, oxygen, and protection from attack by the maternal immune system. A gap remains in the knowledge of the impact of different classes of antiretrovirals (ARVs) on placenta function and how this relates to poor fetal growth and birth outcomes. One potential mechanism is that ARV exposure dysregulates the maternal immune system, causing inflammation that is detrimental to the placenta and affecting pregnancy outcomes. To gain insight into these immunological processes, we will examine blood and placenta samples from pregnant women with HIV (pWHIV) being treated with ARVs from three clinical cohorts in Toronto, Uganda, and South Africa. We will focus on profiling the immune status (inflammatory vs. tolerogenic/non-inflammatory) of these women and identify immune blood markers that may be predictive of placental dysfunction and poor birth outcomes. Our findings may identify a mechanism of how different ARVs affect the placenta and which ARVs are safest to use in pregnancy. Our identified blood biomarkers will have potential applications to non-invasive liquid biopsies for the monitoring of pregnancies and predicting abnormal birth outcomes in pregnant women with HIV.

column36: Predictive phenotyping of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease from multifactor biomarker and neuroimaging data
column37: Individuals diagnosed with either Alzheimers disease (AD) or Parkinsons disease (PD) typically exhibit a distinctive profile of progressive impairments. AD primarily affects cognitive functions (e.g. dementia), whereas PD affects motor functions (e.g. tremor). However, in many cases, this symptomatic distinction is not apparent, because some AD and PD patients experience a mixture of cognitive and motor functions of varying severities. These observations have called into question our current definitions of AD and PD as being two separate diseases. An alternative framework proposes that AD and PD may represent extreme phenotypes of a continuum where mixed AD/PD subtypes lie in the middle. To test this, we will obtain longitudinal neuroimaging, protein pathology, and clinical test data of AD and PD patients from the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and the Parkinsons Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI), respectively. Then, we will use a novel data integration technique called similarity network fusion to combine all of the different data types, producing networks of patients who share common patterns in their data. We expect to see unique clusters of patients corresponding to the distinct disease subtypes. Overall, our findings may reveal novel links between the different mixed subtypes of AD and PD and their underlying mechanisms, ultimately leading to developing better intervention strategies for these diseases.

column36: MicroRNA promotes metastasis by regulating secretory proteins in breast cancer tumor microenvironment
column37: Breast cancer has a very high survival rate when the disease is detected in an early stage. However only about 64% of all cases are found this early. An improved method of screening is needed in order to improve the overall survival rate of this deadly disease. Current measures used are mammograms, which are low dose x-rays of the breast. In addition to being very painful, these exams miss 1 in 5 cases of breast cancer, providing a false negative, leading to the progression of the disease in these individuals, and eventual later detection in later stages. We believe the answer is to develop a series of biomarkers that can be screened for in a patients blood sample and can accurately predict the presence of breast cancer. We have shown that microRNA (miRNA), specifically miR-526b and miR-655 promote more aggressive tumor behavior, as a consequence of their post-transcriptional regulation. The premature version of these miRNA, the pri-miRNA, are detectable in the blood and the expression can accurately distinguish the tumor stages, from patient blood samples. Cells that overexpress these miRNA release a varied abundance of proteins and factors into their surrounding microenvironment that promotes tumor growth and metastasis. We believe that by studying the effect these miRNAs have on the microenvironment, we will find potential biomarkers amongst the secretory proteins. Through the use of bioinformatics, cell-line functional assays and human tissue/plasma screening we can identify these important secretory proteins, validate the miRNA regulation, investigate the secretory proteins role in promoting growth and metastasis, and finally answer our question; can they predict the presence of breast cancer?

column36: Identifying molecular signalling cascades that regulate microglial phagocytosis in Alzheimer's disease.
column37: Microglia are a class of brain immune cells that play an important role in health and disease. In the healthy brain, microglia can remove pathogens, naturally aged brain cells, and dysfunctional synapses through the process of phagocytosis. In Alzheimers disease, there is a build-up of toxic Amyloid beta (Aβ), that stimulates microglia to release inflammatory signals leading to an inflamed state in the central nervous system, and reduces ability of microglia to control phagocytosis. In this state, microglia will start to engulf healthy neurons and synapses, while no longer removing Aβ as efficiently. These changes interfere with communication between neurons, and can lead to the memory and learning problems seen in patients with Alzheimers disease (AD).We know that a protein expressed in microglia, called PARP-1, becomes activated during inflammation, and contributes to the microglial inflammatory response. We propose that Aβ accumulation stimulates PARP-1, which produces a series of signalling events that ultimately activate a microglial ion channel called TRPM2. We propose that this promotes continuous activation of PARP-1 and leads to decreased control of microglial phagocytosis targets. In this way, microglia may incorrectly target functional neurons and synapses for degradation.In this study, we use microglial cell cultures to define the mechanism behind how PARP-1 controls phagocytosis, whether desired (Aβ, pathogen) or not desired (functional neurons/synapses). This will allow us to identify potential therapeutic targets to boost the control of microglial phagocytosis in Alzheimer's disease conditions ; for example, inhibiting the phagocytosis of viable neurons/synapses, while still allowing for phagocytosis of Aβ and pathogens.

column36: Impact of nicotine regulations for e-cigarettes on the prevalence and patterns of vaping among young people.
column37: Background: Youth and young adulthood are critical periods for tobacco use. While Western countries have seen a reduction in smoking behaviour for young people, there has been rapid growth in the use of e-cigarettes among this population over the last decade. In Canada, the e-cigarette market has shifted towards higher nicotine salt-base products such as JUUL. As of July 2021, Canada implemented new regulations which restrict nicotine content in vaping products to a maximum of 20mg/ml, similar to existing regulations in England. Alternatively, nicotine concentration is not currently restricted in the United States.Objective: The primary objective of the dissertation is to examine the impact of nicotine restrictions on the prevalence and patterns of youth vaping. We hypothesize that: nicotine limits of 20mg/ml in Canada will be associated with 1) reductions in the proportion of past 30-day vapers that cite nicotine as a reason for vaping and for brand selection; 2) reductions in indicators of dependence among past 30-day vapers; and 3) reductions in frequency of vaping.Methods: The proposed study will use data from the International Tobacco Control Youth Young Adult Surveys (ITC Surveys). The ITC Surveys consist of repeated cross-sectional surveys, which have been conducted annually since 2017 with more than 91,000 respondents aged 16-19 years old in Canada, the US and England. The analysis will be based on within- and between-country comparisons over time using regression models for each of the primary outcomes. Impact: Overall, the proposed project is uniquely positioned to examine a high-profile health policy during a critical period in which both the product and policy landscape is rapidly evolving.

column36: Les capacites de traitement sensoriel comme mediateur de la relation entre le signal cerebral mesure par potentiels evoques et le sommeil chez des enfants neurotypiques
column37: Le traitement sensoriel represente la capacite du systeme nerveux central a recevoir un message par le biais des systemes sensoriels, le traiter, puis donner une reponse comportementale adaptee. Lorsque ce processus n'est pas efficace ou declenche une reponse inappropriee, cela suggere la presence d'un trouble du traitement sensoriel. Les enfants n'ayant pas la capacite de traiter adequatement les stimuli sensoriels sont susceptibles d'eprouver des difficultes importantes dans le quotidien. D'ailleurs, des etudes recentes suggerent que le traitement sensoriel pourrait affecter le sommeil. Par exemple, l'heure du coucher implique plusieurs changements dans l'environnement (p. ex. bruit, lumiere ambiante, etc.), ce qui peut etre difficile a tolerer pour des enfants plus sensibles. Les etudes realisees sur le sujet ont utilise des mesures subjectives du traitement sensoriel. Il serait important d'explorer si l'activite electroencephalographique serait un marqueur adequat du traitement sensoriel. Des etudes faites aupres de populations cliniques suggerent que l'hypersensibilite sensorielle s'exprimerait par de plus grandes amplitudes et des patrons spectraux particuliers des signaux electroencephalographiques. De ce fait, l'objectif de cette etude est d'observer les liens entre le signal cerebral mesure par les potentiels evoques sensoriels ainsi que les potentiels evoques stationnaires, les capacites de traitement sensoriel mesure par questionnaires et le sommeil (qualite, quantite et parasomnies) rapporte par les parents. Ce projet permettra de reveler des determinants de la qualite et de la quantite de sommeil de l'enfant dans une approche neurodeveloppementale.

column36: Dark microglia's relationships with Alzheimer's disease hallmarks in late-onset patients.
column37: Late-onset Alzheimer's disease (LOAD), which occurs after the age of 65 and comprises most cases of Alzheimer's disease involves progressive memory loss and neuronal cell death in the brain. As current approaches towards comprehending Alzheimer's have not yet stopped the disease, therefore, recent efforts have encouraged understanding other main contributors in Alzheimer's. The goal of this proposal is to demonstrate how dark microglia, a particular microglial state active in eating neurons could underlie clinical LOAD progression. Although meant to contain stressed neurons, ingesting neurons with tau aggregates may cause these dark microglia to become impaired. These impaired, dark microglia likely fail to break down protein aggregates and act as further hotspots to amplify tau pathology. If my hypothesis is supported, dark and impaired microglia critically accelerate the diseases pace and could explain the progressive memory loss in LOAD.Dark microglia have been observed in disease mouse models and aged human brains, but not yet in LOAD patients. Thus, LOAD patient and control samples will be collected and novelly assessed for dark and/or impaired microglia using three-dimensional electron microscopy over two years. Cutting-edge imaging methods will be used to measure how impaired dark microglia may relate to other Alzheimer's pathologies (e.g., tau protein aggregates). Impaired dark microglia are predicted to increase in patient versus control brains, and to localize near and/or contain protein aggregates involved in LOAD. If these predictions are confirmed, showing that the abundance of dark and/or impaired microglia correlates with LOAD would increase priority for investigating their usefulness as therapeutic targets.

column36: Investigating genetic interactions between RNA-binding proteins relevant to neurodegenerative disease in C. elegans
column37: RNA binding proteins (RBPs) are a highly conserved group of post-transcriptional regulators, involved in processes that include mRNA polyadenylation, alternative splicing, nuclear export, and translation. As such, mutated RBPs have emerged as key players implicated in human genetic diseases. This is evident in a spectrum of neurodegenerative diseases which often share disease causative RBP genes. The RBPs, TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) and Fused in Sarcoma (FUS) have repeatedly been implicated in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), wherein these two predominantly nuclear-localized proteins become biased to the cytoplasm and aggregate. However, owing to the complex genetic etiology of human diseases like ALS, it is crucial to investigate the genetic interaction networks associated with RBPs, which could reveal genetic modifiers of disease. With its highly annotated genome and intact nervous system, C.elegansallows use of loss-of-function (LOF) techniques to generate large-scale genetic interaction networks, enabling identification of new interactors in key neurodevelopmental pathways. And with its rich suite of behaviours, C. eleganspermits modeling of neurodegeneration. We hypothesize that combinations of RBP LOF mutants and ALS-associated TDP-43/tdp-1 and FUS/fust-1 mutants, will reveal novel genetic interactions relevant to neuronal health and disease. To this end, we will use genome engineering techniques developed in our lab to conduct high throughput fitness assays and assess for synthetically enhanced interactions among double LOF mutants. These interactions can be probed in behavioural, morphological and transcriptomics contexts to inform translational genomics approaches of studying human genetic diseaseespecially as it concerns neurodegeneration.

column36: Auto-traitement guide du trouble d'anxiete generalisee chez les aines: appreciation des patients et des accompagnateurs
column37: Le trouble d'anxiete generalisee (TAG) se manifeste par des inquietudes difficiles a controler et en lien avec differents aspects de la vie tels que la sante et les relations sociales. Le TAG est tres repandu chez les aines, mais peu de personnes qui en sont atteintes recoivent un traitement. Pour aider les aines a avoir acces a un traitement de l'anxiete, des chercheurs ont developpe un auto-traitement dans lequel le patient apprend par lui-meme depuis son domicile des techniques pour gerer son anxiete a partir de lectures et d'exercices. Le patient est soutenu a distance par un accompagnateur. Bien que cette approche semble efficace, l'experience des patients ages recevant ce type de traitement est peu documentee. Mieux connaitre cette experience permettrait d'ameliorer le traitement et de le rendre plus attrayant pour les patients. De plus, savoir comment l'accompagnateur percoit le traitement recu par le patient enrichirait notre comprehension de l'experience du traitement en fournissant un angle different, mais complementaire a celui du patient. Ainsi, l'objectif de cette etude est de decrire et de comparer la perception qu'ont les patients ages et les accompagnateurs d'un auto-traitement du TAG. Pour ce faire, ce projet de recherche analysera les donnees d'une etude dans laquelle quatre-vingt-dix personnes de 60 ans et plus ayant un TAG ont recu un auto-traitement d'une duree de 15 semaines guide par dix-huit accompagnateurs. Au terme du traitement, les participants et les accompagnateurs ont complete de maniere independante un questionnaire d'evaluation du traitement abordant divers aspects tels que les lectures, la duree et la charge de travail. Des analyses quantitatives et qualitatives des donnees seront realisees pour repondre a l'objectif de l'etude.

column36: Bayesian Model for Monitoring Cancer Progression Using Liquid Biopsies
column37: Cancer is driven by mutations that follow an evolutionary process, producing genetically distinct populations of cells known as clones. As a result, these clonal populations have varied responses to treatment; therefore, it is valuable to identify and characterize these clones when administering treatments in clinical applications. Liquid biopsies are samples of biological fluid (e.g. a blood sample) that contain DNA fragments known as cell-free DNA (cfDNA). Due to their non-invasive nature, they allow for serial sampling, enabling the study of clonal populations over time. In light of this, we propose a Bayesian statistical model to both estimate the relative proportions of existing clones, and discover emergences of novel clones. We will accomplish this task by analyzing the copy-number (CN) profiles of longitudinal cfDNA samples, while concurrently using the CN profile of a sequenced tissue biopsy taken at the beginning of treatment as an informative prior. Single-cell sequencing and whole-genome sequencing will be used for tissue biopsy and liquid biopsy respectively, whileMarkov Chain Monte Carlo and Variational Inference methods will be used to address intractable integrals common in Bayesian inference.Our model will elucidate the temporal heterogeneity of clonal populations over the course of treatment. Understanding the clonal landscape at several time points will enable practitioners to make informed treatment decisions to combat resistance, metastasis, or recurrence in cancer. This knowledge holds great utility, especially in personalized cancer care, as practitioners can track the responses of individual patients to therapies and make decisions on the fly - potentially improving the prognosis of hundreds of cancer patients at BC Cancer.

column36: Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity against SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern
column37: In December 2019, several pneumonia outbreaks emerged in China, all related to the novel Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). The high transmissibility of SARS-CoV-2 caused the current devastating pandemic of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). Through a collective effort, around 7 billion vaccine doses were administered worldwide as of November 2021 and demonstrated high levels of protection against infections and severe cases of COVID-19. Most vaccines deployed target the spike (S) glycoprotein. The S protein is exposed at the surface of viral particles and infected cells. Its role is essential as it is the ;viral entry key allowing it to attach and enter cells to replicate. Antibodies generated by vaccination can block this interaction, preventing the virus from replicating; this is called neutralization. SARS-CoV-2 is under tremendous selective pressure, particularly for the S glycoprotein, resulting in the appearance of mutations. Recent studies have shown a significant loss of neutralization against emerging variants of concern (VOCs), such as the Alpha, Beta and Delta variants. However, the vaccine remains effective against severe cases, suggesting that vaccine protection is not solely due to neutralization. Antibodies also play a crucial role in eliminating SARS-CoV-2 infected cells through Fc-effector functions including antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC). We therefore believe that individuals who developed antibodies with little to no neutralizing activity will stay protected against SARS-CoV-2 and maintain this resistance across emerging VOCs through ADCC. Our studies will help determine the humoral correlates of protection against SARS-CoV-2.

column36: Interrogating a Novel Gene Editing Strategy for Predominant Tay-Sachs Disease Mutation
column37: Background: Tay-Sachs Disease (TSD) is characterised by toxic build-up of a fatty substance, GM2, within neural tissue. The predominant mutation causing TSD is a small duplicated sequence of DNA. This genetic error arrests production of HexA, an enzyme required to metabolise GM2 and prevent accumulation. Absent HexA, progressive neurodegenerative symptoms of TSD emerge in infancy, typically leading to death by age 4. Though rare, this fatal disorder has no available treatment. Current Status: Recent advances in CRISPR gene editing technology have excited prospects of genetically treating TSD by directly editing out the duplication. A CRISPR-based technique called Prime Editing can repair various kinds of mutations, including the TSD duplication in a cell model, but its molecular components are too large for effective delivery to live animal models.Research Aim:Forgoing the versatility of Prime Editing, an alternative strategy tailored for editing small duplication mutations can circumvent bulky editing machinery by exploiting an internal cell pathway called MMEJ to effectuate repair. A classic CRISPR system (readily deliverable components) would be programmed to cut within the duplicated sequence at a position that induces the MMEJ repair process. Mechanistically, MMEJ is expected to rejoin the DNA break while collaterally, but precisely, removing one copy of the duplication. Our capstone deliverable is testing this minimalist CRISPR-based repair strategy on the TSD duplication in a mouse model, with precision of the DNA-level editing examined alongside efficacy of TSD symptom amelioration for relevant pre-clinical data. If successful, this strategy would be highly applicable to editing over 140 comparable duplication mutations causing various diseases.

column36: Predicteurs de l'utilisation spontanee du membre superieur paretique suite a la readaptation fonctionnelle intensive post AVC
column37: Approximativement 400 000 Canadiens vivent actuellement avec les consequences d'un accident vasculaire cerebral (AVC). La readaptation suite a l'AVC permet d'ameliorer les capacites motrices, mais cela ne se transpose pas necessairement en une augmentation de l'utilisation du bras atteint dans le quotidien. Les raisons expliquant ce phenomene ne sont pas bien comprises, en partie puisque les evaluations cliniques couramment utilisees se deroulent dans un environnement non-naturel et mettent l'emphase sur des mouvements unilateraux. Le developpement recent de technologies, tel que les systemes d'evaluation robotises et les capteurs portatifs de mouvement permettent maintenant de remedier a ces difficultes.L'objectif de ce projet est de determiner les facteurs predisant l'utilisation spontanee du bras atteint suite a la readaptation post-AVC. column36: Determining tumor bed extent and cellularity simultaneously using Transformer-based whole-slide summarization
column37: Neoadjuvant therapy (NAT) is a key stage in the treatment of early breast cancer. Being able to properly assess a patient's response to NAT provides important information on their survival and cancer recurrence rates. To standardize and quantify patient response, the residual cancer burden (RCB) index was created. To determine this index, pathologists must scan through a digital image of an entire microscope slide. However, because of the high magnification that can be achieved from the microscope, these digital images often reach over 100,000 by 100,000 pixels in size. This makes the determination of the values required for the RCB index subjective and time consuming for medical professionals.To alleviate this issue, this project proposes to apply machine learning (ML) algorithms to automate the process of determining two important pieces of the RCB index: the tumor bed and tumor cellularity. The tumor bed describes the total extent of the cancerous tissue, and the tumor cellularity describes the percentage of the tumor bed containing cancerous tissue. Previous research on this same topic has attempted to determine these values for an entire slide with limited success. This investigation will look to apply anew ML model called a Vision Transformer (ViT) to determine both of these values simultaneously, for a whole microscope slide. From previous experimentation, the ViT has shown excellent promise in summarizing information in images.The proper development of this research could lighten pathologist workflows, opening their time for other key tasks. This could have the effect of reducing patient wait times and decreasing the number of patients that are improperly recommended for further treatment, or lack thereof, by the RCB index.

column36: Disordered eating and substance use in young adults with inflammatory bowel disease: A mixed-methods study
column37: There is a lack of research examining eating disorders (ED) and substance use in people with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The first objective will be to examine the role of biopsychosocial predictors of disordered eating and substance use in young adults with IBD in a large survey. Data will be analyzed using multiple regressions for the quantitative portion and the qualitative interviews will be analyzed using thematic analysis (Braun Clarke, 2006).

column36: Addressing Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion in Exercise Oncology: Understanding Exercise Barriers and Facilitators for Sexual and Gender Minorities
column37: Exercise plays a supportive role across the cancer care continuum, addressing symptom and treatment-related negative impacts. While the burden of such impacts may be substantial for all individuals living with and beyond cancer, there are inequities leading to disproportionate burden among specific populations. column36: Fundamental Mechanisms of Maternal Vitamin A Transfer to Offspring During Gestation and Lactation
column37: It is important to establish adequate reserves of vitamin A early in life to prevent the symptoms associated with childhood vitamin A deficiency. The two ways in which vitamin A reserves are established in newborns are trans-placental transfer during gestation and during lactation via breast milk. Similarly, there are two transferable sources of vitamin A to the offspring: existing maternal vitamin A stores and maternal dietary vitamin A intake. Our study aims to determine the relative importance of both maternal vitamin A stores and maternal dietary vitamin A intake in establishing adequate vitamin A reserves in offspring. Based on preliminary data and the existing literature, we will test the hypothesis that maternal dietary vitamin A intake is the primary determinant of vitamin A reserves in offspring, independent of maternal vitamin A reserves. To test this hypothesis, mouse models with different manipulations of dietary vitamin A intake will be examined by being fed with food containing sufficient vitamin A, or no vitamin A. Maternal vitamin A stores will be manipulated by depleting hepatic stores using a chronic administration of vitamin A deficient diets prior to breeding, or by means of transgenic mice (Lrat-/-) that lack the enzyme which synthesizes the storage form of vitamin A. In all experiments, tissues will be collected from dams and offspring at birth, during lactation, and at weaning and the level of vitamin A stored will be measured by high performance liquid chromatography. Furthermore, this study will generate new knowledge of vitamin A transfer between mother and offspring, and has the potential to be translated into improved approaches to mitigate the effects of childhood vitamin A deficiency in both the developed and developing world.

column36: Regulation of LRIG1 and its functional role following brain injury.
column37: Neural stem cells (NSCs) are largely quiescent in nature and divide infrequently for brain maintenance and during times of brain injury. However, even after stroke injury, these newborn neurons migrate to the lesion site, of which most NSC die. LRIG1 is a known regulator of neural stem cell quiescence in the brain and its downregulation was seen to cause an increase in neural stem cell proliferation during embryonic development. In my proposed study, my main objectives will be to further identify factors that regulate LRIG1 expression in the brain, in addition to further understanding the role that LRIG1 plays following stroke injury. This will enable us to reveal how gene expression and proliferative phenotypes are controlled in quiescent cell types. I will be using CRISPR/cas9 to knockout transcription factors with known roles in neural stem cell regulation, such as krüppel-like factor 15 (KLF15), c-Myc and others, in radial precursor cultures and look at LRIG1 expression. I will also extend these studies in vivo and use in-utero electroporation in order to knockout these transcription factors and assess LRIG1 expression. column36: Exploring the role of the FREM3 gene in shaping brain morphology and cognitive function across the lifespan
column37: The role of the FREM3 gene in the human brain is currently not well understood. Initial literature suggests FREM3 is involved in supporting brain structure, and has been implicated in a variety of clinical disorders, including depression and autism. Previous work from our group discovered that FREM3 expression in brain tissue decreases across the normal lifespan. Furthermore, our work identified genetic variants that cause reduced FREM3 expression. In young adults, these variants were associated with reduced activity in age-sensitive brain regions, and decreases in cognitive performance, suggesting lower FREM3 may cause the brain to age faster. However, to test this hypothesis fully, we need to better understand how FREM3 impacts trajectories of structural and cognitive brain aging across the entire lifespan. Furthermore, advancing the currently limited understanding of FREM3s role on a cellular level is necessary to understand the mechanisms by which it affects brain aging. To address these gaps, we propose to use FREM3 variants as a proxy for gene expression in the brain, and evaluate their effect on brain structure assessed via Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), as well as their effect on cognitive performance. Importantly, the data we will use in these analyses will come from participants of different ages, covering the full human lifespan. We also propose to identify other genes that have expression patterns similar to FREM3, and explore the different cellular functions and processes these genes share. These analyses will also use data from young, middle aged, and older adults. Our proposed work will shed light on how the currently poorly understood FREM3 gene affects brain structure and functioning, and explore its emerging role in the aging process.

column37: Autophagy is a conserved cellular degradation pathway that regulates cell survival and invasion. There is a dual role of autophagy in tumour suppression and progression depending on the cancer. This dynamic role is of clinical importance as autophagy inhibitors are being developed in clinical trials and clinicians must determine which patients would benefit from this treatment. Autophagy protein LC3C selectively binds and targets the Met receptor for degradation. Met signaling is linked to poor prognoses in some cancers and can trigger cell invasion when activated. Our lab has shown LC3C negatively regulates Met and is down-regulated in various cancers, including breast cancer (BRCA), suggesting an anti-tumorigenic role. My research objective is to determine LC3Cs role in BRCA development and how it inhibits tumour progression, which I hypothesize is by inhibiting cell invasion. I will test this in the following aims: 1. Characterizing the role of LC3C in BRCA and tumour progression. In BRCA patient-derived tissues and mouse models, I will study how LC3C expression affects metastasis and how activating Met signaling impacts cell invasion. 2. Determining how LC3C inhibits cell invasion. Using a proximity-based interaction screen of LC3C, I will choose top novel interaction candidates linked to cell migration using protein interaction prediction tools. I will characterize the cellular mechanism by which LC3C regulates invasion and these proteins in cells. This project will deduce the novel role of LC3C in cancer, regulating cell invasion, and confirm LC3C is a component of an anti-tumorigenic autophagy pathway in BRCA. The knowledge gained from my research will be applicable clinically when determining if autophagy inhibitors are the correct line of treatment.

column36: Genome wide CRISPR activation screening of circulating tumor cells to identify therapeutic targets of metastasis
column37: Cancer has permeated through our population and touched Canadians in all walks of life. Nearly 1 in 2 Canadians are expected to be diagnosed with cancer in their lifetime and cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada. Metastasis (the spread of cancer) accounts for over 90% of cancer related deaths. Despite advances in cancer treatments, metastatic disease remains largely incurable. Metastatic lesions are established by circulating tumour cells (CTCs) which are shed from the primary tumour into the bloodstream. As the source of metastasis, CTCs are attractive markers for diagnosis and prognosis and as therapeutic targets. Thus, the characterization of the molecular and genetic mechanisms of CTCs may aid the development of novel treatments for metastasis.CRISPR/Cas9 is a gene editing technology that can be leveraged for functional genomic screens. Functional genomic screens systematically modify gene function to observe the effect of the modification. CRISPR screens systematically knock out or delete genes and were recently used to discover a key regulator of metastasis in CTCs. Although CRISPR screens can identify key targets of metastasis, the condition often requires a complete loss of expression. Recapitulating the effect pharmacologically is difficult since drugs typically only modulate expression. To discover the drivers of metastasis in CTCs that are actionable drug targets, we propose to modify the CRISPR screen to a CRISPR activation (CRISPRa) screen of CTCs. A CRISPRa screen will systematically increase expression of genes on a genome wide scale, thus will discover genes whose increased expression modulates CTCs characteristics and drives metastasis. This will enable the discovery of more actionable drug targets to treat metastasis.

column36: Integrating T-Cell Contraction Phase Into a Mathematical Model for Vaccine Immune Response & Immune Memory
column37: To prevent complex infections like HIV-AIDs, malaria, and COVID-19, the next generation of vaccines will need to stimulate all branches of the immune system, not just antibody-based ;humoral immunity. In contrast ;Cellular immunity comprises various T-cell subtypes that when activated by pathogen molecules can seek and destroy individual infected cells, refocus the immune response towards addressing the unique threats posed by the pathogen, and remain in circulation decades after infection to provide a rapid response to variants of the original invader. However, the interaction of multiple factors surrounding T-cell activation can lead to profound differences in response success and cell fate, providing significant uncertainty when researchers try to design vaccine formulas to elicit specific results. Computer models can provide clarity by simulating these factors, tracking millions of cell-cell interactions in a way that is difficult or even impossible in experiments. Our research group has created the first probabilistic simulation of the immune response to vaccine injection. My project aims to expand the model to predict the end of the immune response, where T-cell numbers drop to leave a reserve of memory cells. I will use data from literature and our collaborators to codify the genetic and metabolic timing that governs T-cell replication and lifespan, as well as relating these population-level changes to factors that surround the early activation of a handful of cells. Thus, the model will be able to predict complex T-cell dynamics from a few early interactions, providing necessary information that can determine the best dosage and scheduling of vaccines to ensure an appropriate immune response to infection with a capable reserve of memory cells for the future.

column36: Phosphorylation of the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid (N) protein as a regulation mechanism for N-mediated processing body disassembly
column37: SARS-CoV-2 is the virus responsible for the ongoing Coronavirus Disease of 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic. The symptoms of COVID-19 vary from mild illness to severe disease leading to hospitalization or death. Severe COVID-19 is characterized by an abnormal inflammatory immune response that causes life-threatening lung damage. Our laboratory recently showed that SARS-CoV-2 may contribute to this inflammation by disassembling cellular structures called processing bodies (PBs), which otherwise suppress the production of many inflammatory immune proteins. Our laboratory demonstrated that SARS-CoV-2 disassembles PBs via its nucleocapsid (N) protein, a structural protein that coats the viral genome to help assemble new viral particles, and that counteracts the cellular immune response to promote viral replication. My project thus seeks to investigate the mechanism of N-mediated PB disassembly to better characterize processes leading to the inflammation seen in severe COVID-19. Notably, the SARS-CoV-2 Alpha, Delta, and Omicron variants of concern (VOCs) have mutations in N that have been shown to change the protein's structure, leading to enhanced N function and a consequent increase in viral replication and disease severity. Thus, I hypothesize that modification of specific structural features of N can promote N interaction with PBs, leading to PB disassembly. By investigating how N structure affects PB disassembly, my project will improve our understanding of a process that may contribute to the inflammation caused by SARS-CoV-2 infection, allowing for the identification of possible drug targets for the treatment of severe COVID-19. Additionally, my project will shed light on how N mutations found in VOCs may contribute to their enhanced virulence.

column36: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus Colonization and Liver Transplantation
column37: The human microbiome has a critical role in the function of the gastrointestinal tract immune system. It induces changes through modulation of several intermediate metabolic compounds when bacteria and human cells interact. Liver transplantation is the ideal scenario to evaluate the interactions between fecal microbiota and its metabolic products. Often the microbiota improves after liver transplant; however, a subset of patients may not recover appropriate microbiome diversity and may subsequently develop an inappropriate metabolic profile.Liver transplant patients that do not have appropriate recovery of their microbiome post-transplant may have reduced levels of circulating short chain fatty acids (SCFAs). We suspect that restoration of microbiota diversity post-transplantation is appropriate in patients without VRE (vancomycin-resistant enterococcus) colonization and absent in patients with VRE colonization. My research will investigate whether VRE colonization causes low levels of SCFAs and whether these low levels are associated with post-transplant complications. The clinical implications may provide supportive evidence for future interventional studies to improve patient-outcomes targeting the gut microbiota.To prove this, we have designed a prospective cohort study including 40 liver transplant candidates on the transplant waiting list: 20 with and 20 without VRE bowel colonization. From these patients several stool samples will be collected, one pre-transplant, and three post-transplant (weeks 4, 8 and 12). Using these samples, we will evaluate the patient SCFAs levels and study the microbiota phyla using shotgun sequencing to potentially elucidate a potential mechanism between the relationship of VRE colonization and poorer transplant outcomes.

column36: A Culturally Responsive Mobile Health Intervention for Middle Eastern and North African Immigrants in Canada
column37: This research project will explore the pre-and post-immigration experiences of Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) emerging adults who recently immigrated to Canada. Participants will complete measures that will explore their cultural norms, family dynamics and level of support from family, their previous trauma exposure and their perception of their traumatic experiences as well as how they cope with stressors and regulate their emotions. The focus will be on two common types of trauma in this population (emotional maltreatment: neglect and abuse and sexual assault). They will be provided with a mobile just-in-time intervention for their stress and depressive symptoms, posttraumatic cognitions, self-stigma that may be related to their cultural norms surrounding mental illnesses, and acculturative stress that may influence their psychological adjustment as they come into contact with the Canadian culture. The intervention will be an adapted version of an app I have already co-developed that incorporates mindfulness-based cognitive therapy techniques such as self-compassion, mindfulness and cognitive restructuring. I had tested the app previously and it was found to result in significant decreases in depression, increases in self-compassion, mindfulness and adaptive emotion regulation among Canadian adults. The adapted version will incorporate culturally relevant practices specific to this population to increase engagement with the app e.g. using scripture/religious notations or incorporating mindful prayers that reduce self-blame, promote inner resilience and reassure individuals as a form of cultural grounding. Mobile apps can be deployed on a national level and can support the transition of new immigrants from MENA countries to Canada.

column36: Evaluating Preventable Healthcare Use Attributed to the Implementation of Nutrition Profiling Models in Canada
column37: The economic burden ifpreventable chronic disease is very high in Canada and is projected to continue rising in the future. Health Canada's healthy eating strategy includes Nutrient Profiling (NP) systems which will rank foods according to their nutritional composition, to better guide consumers to make healthier food choices. This research project is in response to the growing interest of implementing NP systems as well as the lack of evidence of the economic and policy implications of implementing NP, in Canada. Hospital use is defined as the number of hospital bed-days used. Nationally representative, individual-level data will be retrieved from the Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS) 2004 and 2015, which are linked to health administrative databases (Discharge Abstract Database) to ascertain hospital use. A zero-inflated negative binominal model will be used to test the significance of risk factors associated with the number of hospital bed-days. This project is very timely, especially with the increasing rates of chronic disease, in the aging Canadian population. column36: A novel biologically informed polygenic risk score for depression in girls and women
column37: Major depressive disorder (MDD) or depression is a psychiatric disorder, which is twice as prevalent in women relative to men. The impact of biological sex on gene expression in the brain may partially explain this disparity. Studies have revealed that while some of the gene expression changes associated with depression are shared between men and women, most are completely distinct. Based on shared genes, our group recently developed a transcriptome-based polygenic risk score (tPRS), which is a number that reflects the likelihood of an individual having depression based on the genes that are being expressed in their brain. A higher tPRS has been associated with changes in the folding of the outer layer of the brain (cortical folding) in brain regions associated with depression. Cortical folding patterns form early in development and remain relatively stable in adulthood, suggesting that depression-associated patterns may emerge early in life and eventually lead to depressive symptoms. Since depression-associated gene expression is different between the sexes, it is important to study the changes specific to females as early as childhood and adolescence to understand depression in girls and women, who are disproportionately affected by the disease. Therefore, we propose to develop a female-specific tPRS (tPRS-F) which incorporates the gene expression profile uniquely associated with depression in females. We further propose to establish its association with depression vulnerability and cortical folding in adolescent girls. This novel tPRS-F can then be used to predict vulnerability to depression in female individuals early enough to facilitate the development of effective personalized interventions to counteract the burden of depression in girls and women.

column37: Despite an extensive effort to tackle the COVID-19 pandemic in Canada, some populations were hit harder by the COVID-19 and have been facing additional barriers to coping with its effect on their health and wellness. column36: Identifying predictive biomarkers for neoadjuvant anti-PD-1 therapy in early-stage non-small cell lung carcinoma through multiplex immunofluorescence
column37: Immune checkpoint blockade therapies have become a first-line treatment for advanced non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC), in which monoclonal antibodies amplify the antitumor immune response through blocking key immunosuppressive signalling molecules like PD-1. However, approximately 40% of patients are resistant to anti-PD-1 treatment. While neoadjuvant administration has improved efficacy, it is difficult to justify this application when resection alone is potentially curative and non-responders risk becoming inoperable should treatment-related surgical delays occur. It is thus imperative that predictive biomarkers for treatment outcome be developed. Tumor expression of PD-1s ligand, PD-L1, is the standard predictive biomarker for outcome of anti-PD-1 monotherapy. However, tumor PD-L1 expression alone has been demonstrated to have little prognostic accuracy in early-stage NSCLC. Approaches that can simultaneously identify immunosuppressive and immune-promoting cell subsets are required to identify new predictive biomarkers.Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) allows such nuanced visualization while preserving the spatial relationships between cells in the patient tumor microenvironment (TME). The application of a mIF panel targeted to the PD-1/PD-L1 axis on pre-treatment specimens from a retrospective cohort of patients that had received neoadjuvant anti-PD-1 will relate pathological response to (i) PD-L1 expression on immune cells and its relation to response, (ii) the spatial relationships between PD-1+ and PD-L1+ cells, and (iii) the presence of immunosuppressive cell populations. This analysis of spatial distribution of immune cells and clinical response may identify potential predictive biomarkers and improve treatment selection for resectable NSCLC patients.

column36: Effects of Serine-129 Phosphorylation on Alpha-Synuclein Strains
column37: A variety of neurodegenerative diseases, such as Parkinsons Disease or Lewy Body Dementia, are attributed to the same root cause - an abnormal clustering of a protein called alpha-synuclein. It is unknown how clusters of the same protein can result in multiple different diseases. The best explanation for this is that different shapes of clusters cause different diseases. Our lab has previously determined that by simply adding salt, different shapes of clusters can be formed compared to when these clusters form without salt. We have shown that salt and no salt clusters form at different rates and are broken-up by enzymes differently, among other characteristics. Additionally, the salt and no salt clusters can cause different symptoms at different time points when injected into mice. This supports the idea that different diseases are caused by different shapes of clusters. An interesting note is that alpha-synuclein clusters collected from patients with Parkinsons Disease or Lewy Body Dementia, are primarily made of alpha-synuclein that is modified by the addition of a phosphate to the protein. This raises questions about how the addition of the phosphate could impact the shape and properties of the clusters. This study will make alpha synuclein clusters of both the normal and the modified protein to determine how the addition of a phosphate group changes the cluster shape. In both cases, the clusters will be made using salt, to allow comparison to our previous work. This will provide us a more complete understanding of potential differences in the shape of alpha-synuclein clusters under different conditions. This knowledge could then contribute to drug research to specifically treat Parkinsons Disease or Lewy Body Dementia.

column36: Safeguarding Budgets to Strengthen Public Health Systems
column37: Despite commitments to bolster Public Health systems after the SARS epidemic, Canadas Public Health systems were severely under-resourced and under-prepared for the COVID-19 pandemic. The consequences were a failure to contain outbreaks, leading to unnecessary illness and death, as well as inequitable impacts on populations. In light of new investments and attention, Canada now faces a window of opportunity to strengthen Public Health systems for the future. My thesis will examine policy strategies for maintaining Public Health funding over time.The first part of my thesis will involve a scoping review exploring the determinants of Public Health financing. For instance, how do political cycles, funding models, public emergencies (including pandemics), and research evidence impact levels of Public Health investment? The findings from this review will inform the second part of my thesis, which aims to investigate the policy strategies used by governments to safeguard Public Health budgets and determine why these succeed or fail. To accomplish this, I will carry out in-depth case studies of Ontario, Quebec, and the UK. These will consist of literature reviews as well as qualitative interviews with experts in Public Health financing from each region.Findings from this study will inform future policy to safeguard Public Health funding in Canada. This will enable better preparation for future public crises. Stronger Public Health systems can also carry out more impactful health prevention and promotion activities, leading to significantly healthier populations over time.

column36: Investigating the in vitro and in vivo effects of cannabis smoke exposure on lung cancer development
column37: With rapid legalization and decriminalization of cannabis, there is a growing need to understand its specific effects, particularly through smoking, the main method of consumption. Current literature on cannabis smoke primarily consists of clinical studies with conflicting results. Thus, there is a lack of controlled experimental studies investigating the effects of cannabis smoking on adverse lung health outcomes, specifically lung cancer development. This is an important consideration as the chemical composition of cannabis smoke is qualitatively similar to that of tobacco, and it has been demonstrated that routine screening of individuals who heavily smoke tobacco improves survival outcomes through early detection.This study aims to explore how cannabis smoke exposure mediates hallmark processes involved in lung cancer initiation and development. I hypothesize that cannabis smoke induces mutations and shifts gene expression to promote tumorigenesis. To test this, I will expose both human lung epithelial cells and mice to cannabis smoke at levels comparable to regular human consumption. Mutational patterns and gene expression changes induced in the cannabis smoke exposed cells and mice will be assessed through DNA and RNA sequencing, respectively, and compared to those of tobacco smoke and room air as a control. The mutational signatures and gene expression profiles resulting from cannabis smoke exposure will then be cross-referenced with the analysis of human tumours collected from patients with known cannabis exposure.Overall, this study will rigorously determine the effects of cannabis smoking on lung cancer development. This knowledge can be applied to assess the risk of cannabis smoking as well as to improve screening protocols aimed at the early detection.

column36: Effets d'un traitement de cannabidiol administre en phase aigue sur la neuroinflammation et la douleur auto rapportee de patients orthopediques ayant subi un traumatisme cranio-cerebral leger concomitant
column37: Une blessure orthopedique combinee a un traumatisme craniocerebral (TCC) ainsi que le niveau de douleur en phase aigue sont deux predicteurs de l'installation de douleur chronique. Celle-ci se definit par une douleur qui persiste plus de 3 mois post-accident et qui nuit entre autres au sommeil, a la sante mentale et a la qualite de vie des patients. Sur le plan mecanistique, l'inflammation declenchee suite a une blessure peripherique (ex. la fracture d'un membre) provoque la liberation continue de molecules inflammatoires, facilitant l'entree de toxines pouvant envahir le systeme nerveux central (SNC). L'inflammation soutenue du SNC qui en decoule joue un role important dans la chronicisation de la douleur. Il est pertinent de se pencher sur le potentiel therapeutique du cannabidiol (CBD), une composante du cannabis, qui se demarque vu ses proprietes antidouleurs et anti-inflammatoires, tout en etant depourvu d'effets addictifs. Ce protocole de recherche prend la forme d'un essai clinique humain, evaluant les effets, par rapport au placebo, d'une dose quotidienne de CBD administree pendant 7 jours sur la douleur et l'inflammation apres un traumatisme multiple (c.-a-d. fracture osseuse avec TCC). Ce traitement administre 72 h apres l'accident vise a reduire la neuroinflammation ainsi que les symptomes de douleur auto rapportee afin d'optimiser le retablissement tant orthopedique que cerebral. Enfin, ce projet de recherche propose une avenue therapeutique qui vise a fournir une prise en charge securitaire, optimale et depourvue d'effets secondaires pour traiter la douleur aigue chez des victimes de traumatismes et qui favorise une guerison rapide, raccourcit les sejours a l'hopital, reduit les couts ainsi que les risques de douleur chronique et de morbidite/mortalite.

column36: Wastewater-based monitoring of infection control and antimicrobial stewardship in hospitals
column37: Antimicrobial-resistant organisms (ARO) continue to be of critical concern to public health, notably in hospital settings where high antibiotic usage creates selective pressures that increase the prevalence of ARO colonization and risk of infection. While hospital-acquired infections can be limited with vigorous infection prevention and control measures, outbreaks of various pathogens abound, adversely impacting patient outcomes and healthcare resources. Hospital-associated infections and outbreaks will continue to occur due to intrinsic vulnerabilities, including the necessary cohorting of societys sickest individuals to concentrate care, frequent and prolonged antibacterial exposures, and a constant flux of new admissions each potentially carrying unknown transmissible infections.Wastewater (WW)-based epidemiology, normally applied to urban populations, can be adapted to monitor the overall health of a hospitals population through serial analysis of WW. Our research aims to apply this non-invasive tool to actively monitor tertiary-care hospitals that serve our societys most medically burdened and vulnerable individuals. We are adapting strategies to extract and understand in real-time ARO prevalence in hospitals through WW surveillance, using targeted quantitative PCR to study specific antimicrobial resistance genes of epidemiological significance. This targeted approach will be supplemented with metagenomic analysis of raw WW and culture-enriched WW to understand changes in the total burden of different ARO in an unbiased way. By correlating WW results with infection control and antibiotic consumption data, we hope to better identify and mitigate potential hospital-associated transmission and outbreaks, and to provide surveillance for antimicrobial resistance.
