column36: Data-Driven Scheduling of Orthopaedic Surgical Services: An End-to-End Framework with Machine Learning and Mathematical Optimization
column37: The efficient management of patients requiring orthopaedic surgery in Canada is of utmost importance to the timely delivery of quality care and to maintain reasonable cost in a public healthcare system. Assigning a date/time, operating room, and surgeon to each case quickly becomes a daunting task due to large volumes and limited resources, both physical and human. At the moment, a dedicated team is tasked with manually scheduling elective surgeries, based on rough estimates of operative time to maximize operating room utilization rates, while respecting constraints on surgeon loads. Additionally, the volume of orthopaedic trauma must be anticipated, a factor that affects the number of operating rooms that are set aside for these non-elective cases. These inefficiencies and estimations lead to a significant amount of wasted resources, contributing to prolonged patient wait times.The proposed research challenges the tradition of tackling the highly complex orthopaedic surgery scheduling task using solely manual approaches based on surgeons estimates of operative time. Instead, we aim to design a comprehensive solution that leverages historical patient, surgeon, hospital data, and case volumes, to optimize the scheduling process in a highly automated way. Machine Learning and Mathematical Optimization methods will be developed to enable both accurate predictions of operative time and optimal scheduling. Based on historic data, we will compare these methods and then test our prediction and schedule optimization system to determine if there is a reduction in wasted operating room time. In addition to healthcare system financial benefits, optimized schedules would decrease patient waitlist times by completing more surgeries within the same amount of time.

column36: Characterizing the nucleotide-binding domain leucine-rich repeat pyrin domain- containing 1B (Nlrp1b) inflammasome in the intestinal epithelium
column37: The epithelial cells that line the intestine not only function in nutrient absorption, but also serve as a crucial barrier that protects against microbial infection. Within these cells, NOD-like receptors (NLRs) act as innate sentinels that respond to specific pathogen-derived molecules, as well as danger signals that indicate a breach in the cell. Among this family of NLRs, NLR family pyrin containing 1b (Nlrp1b), which is the mouse version of human NLRP1, has been traditionally studied in immune cells, and therefore, its role in the intestinal epithelium has yet to be established. Interestingly, defects in other NLRs in the intestine have been linked to various conditions such as inflammatory bowel disease and cancer, suggesting that Nlrp1b could have a link as well. The goal of our research is to characterize Nlrp1b in the intestine using murine small intestinal organoids that recapitulate the features of the intestinal barrier. Our initial data suggests that it may be functional during enteric parasite infection, but likely only in a specific subset of intestinal epithelial cells (IECs). By further investigating this innate receptor in the intestinal epithelium and defining the IECs in which it is functional, we may begin to comprehend the physiological consequences of its activation and how it relates to parasitic defense. Additionally, the insight we gain from this research will help us better understand the human NLRP1 receptor and the similar role it likely plays in the intestine.

column36: Impact of COVID-19 on Quality of Life of Seniors with Eye Disease and Implementations to Improve Wellness
column37: The ophthalmology clientele is vulnerable in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic because of their age and comorbidities. Specifically, elderly patients aged 65 and above with ocular diseases such as glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration, or diabetic retinopathy require regular follow-ups and commonly suffer from additional comorbidities. Further, because of the proximity between the patient and health care personnel during ophthalmological examinations, the risk of infection during visits is significant. The present pandemic has also led officials to rethink the management of patient lists and to restrict the patients to be assessed or to be operated based on the urgency of their condition in accordance with ministerial guidelines. A delay in visits might increase the risk of visual loss not only through the delay of necessary care, but also through an increase in non-adherence to treatment. Moreover, visual loss can accompany depressive symptoms and deteriorate quality of life. Therefore, it is necessary to characterize and document the ophthalmological effects as well as the effects on well-being of the restrictive measures implemented. By performing a cross-sectional survey, we hope to quantify the collateral impact of the COVID-19 beyond the direct impact of the virus by gathering information on patients health-related quality of life, vision-related quality of life, depression symptoms, anxiety, sleep quality, community integration, and experience with teleconsultations. We will examine the descriptive statistics for the participants group and check for outliers. We plan to use a linear-mixed model with the questionnaire scores as the dependent variables and demographic variables as covariates.

column36: Single cell sequencing technology: a tool to better understand genetic risk factors for Type-2 diabetes
column37: Advances in genetics have increased our understanding of hereditary diseases and their pathologies. New sequencing technology has allowed for the study of different aspects of the human genome, providing researchers with a large range of tools to dissect the underpinnings of disease onset. Despite great successes in research and treatment of diseases governed by one or few genes, there are still many obstacles to overcome in the study of complex diseases such as Type-2 diabetes, which are influenced by many genes. Representing 90 percent of diabetes cases in Canada, and with nearly 500 new diagnoses every day, understanding the genetic causes behind Type-2 diabetes is crucial to finding an effective treatment for the disease. To address this challenge, researchers have developed approaches that can integrate different types of sequencing data to provide more detailed information on the genome. Although these approaches have enabled researchers to uncover novel mechanisms in disease onset, they do not integrate data at the resolution of individual cells (more commonly referred to as ;single cell data), which provides more pertinent information in tissues and diseases that are composed of many cell types, such as the pancreas for Type-2 diabetes. Existing methods also have limited accuracy in identifying specific gene regulatory elements of interest when building the gene networks involved in disease progression. In this project, we aim to expand upon past methods to incorporate single cell data and use more powerful computational methods to identify specific elements of interest that influence disease onset. Our work will provide a better representation of the complex gene networks that are perturbated in Type-2 diabetes, improving drug discovery and disease prevention.

column37: Approximately 40,000 babies born each year are born with problems regarding the structure/function of their heart (congenital heart defects- CHD), with 1in 4 babies having critical CHD. 4.2% of all newborn deaths are due to CHD, with 48% of death due to CHD occurring within the first year of life. Importantly, in many forms of heart disease in adults, there is an increase in heart muscle size (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) that leads to changes in heart energy metabolism that are similar to what is seen in the heart of the fetus. These changes make the heart less efficient in its ability to produce energy for use. The current proposal aims to directly study energy metabolism of cardiac cells under fetal like conditions (proliferating cells) and newborn conditions (differentiated cells). Specially, we want to understand the role that ketone bodies, a potential energy source for the heart, have in the maturation of energy metabolism following birth. The results of this study will be important in understanding how energy metabolism develops in the newborn heart. The data from my study would be invaluable in designing therapeutics for CHD, specifically in forms of CHD that involve cardiac hypertrophy.

column36: Neurocognitive Outcomes of Mild Traumatic Brain Injury in Monolinguals and Bilinguals
column37: As communities continue to become more diverse, increasing numbers of Canadians report being bilingual. Managing two languages is believed to strengthen cognitive function and be a protective factor against neurodegenerative disease and age related cognitive decline. Past research shows that bilinguals experience poorer long term outcomes after a concussion or mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) than monolinguals. There is very little knowledge on how the bilingual brain is affected by mTBI. Normative data for cognitive assessments are usually based on samples of middle-class monolinguals, and only a few studies to date have examined the influence of language on the tests used to diagnose concussions. The lack of normed data in bilingual populations is pertinent because the associated deficits in cognitive function can be subtle. Bilinguals with a history of mTBI may perform worse than healthy controls on assessments, not necessarily due to deficits following a mTBI, but due to the measures being heavily dependent on verbal processing. There are no studies using electroencephalography (EEG) or neuroimaging in this population sub-group. This study proposes to examine differences between monolinguals and bilinguals with and without a history of mTBI using neuropsychological testing, EEG, and brain imaging. EEG and neuroimaging will offer a novel contribution by providing insight into the neural underpinnings of observed cognitive deficits in patients with mTBI, and whether there are differences across the language groups. Understanding specific patterns of cognitive impairment associated with mTBI in bilinguals is crucial to the development of appropriate evidence-based assessments and treatments, and for better outcomes for patients of all ages and backgrounds.

column36: A Novel Non-Invasive Eye Imaging Biomarker for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis
column37: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal and incurable disease that causes motor neurons, which are responsible for controlling muscles, to deteriorate over time leading to progressive weakness. Current ALS diagnostic methods are expensive, inaccessible, and invasive procedures. A new non-invasive and widely accessible biomarker that can be used to diagnose and monitor ALS is an unmet need. A defining pathological feature of ALS is axonal spheroids, which are protein accumulations in motor neurons. We recently discovered the presence of axonal spheroids in the retina sections of deceased ALS patients. Therefore, we believe the eye can be used as a window into ALS pathology by monitoring these retinal spheroids. We propose to use confocal scanning laser ophthalmoscope (cSLO) and optical coherence tomography (OCT), widely available Health Canada-approved eye imaging devices, to develop a retinal imaging biomarker in 30 post-mortem eye specimens from ALS patients and 30 age-matched controls. We hypothesize that these retinal spheroids are a biomarker of neuronal injury and can be non-invasively imaged to monitor ALS progression. We will use cSLO and OCT, immunohistochemical markers to visualize spheroids in retina sections and hyperspectral microscopy to identify the optical and molecular properties of retinal spheroids. We will compare these data with clinical profile of patients to develop a model that can be used to monitor ALS progression. We will apply the same techniques to mouse model of ALS to determine if retinal spheroids exist in live animals and whether they can be used to monitor disease progression over time. A non-invasive and available imaging biomarker is significant as it can be used by clinicians to diagnose and monitor ALS.

column36: Assessing Depression Severity: The Role of Clinical Intuition and Objective Measures of Speech
column37: Despite the evidence supporting the effectiveness of measurement-based care in treating Major Depressive Disorder, its clinical use remains low. A key barrier to the use of measurement-based care is the time needed for clinicians to conduct assessments. Emerging evidence supports the use of language and acoustic speech features in the prediction of depression severity, but it is unknown how this compares to the ability of a licensed expert clinician to estimate depression severity using limited information from a short sample of speech. We hypothesize that expert clinicians will accurately predict depression severity, as well as provide a greater degree of accuracy in the prediction of depression severity compared to computer-based acoustic measures provided with the same speech samples. After anonymization, 1-minute isolated samples of uninterrupted speech will be scored for depression severity by expert psychiatrists and clinical psychologists using a visual analog sliding scale. We will used mixed effects linear regression to test the concordance of the expert clinician estimation to MADRS scores and compare to the prediction of a machine learning model trained from acoustic features using PRAAT software. Through the development and testing of this novel system of measuring depression severity, we aim to better understand the extent to which trained expert clinicians form rapid impressions of psychopathology in their patients.

column36: Billes aCD3/aCD28 avec bicouche membranaire: un systeme modulable pour dissequer l'effet des signaux de cosignalisation sur les fonctions effectrices des cellules T
column37: La presentation d'un peptide antigenique charge sur des complexes majeurs d'histocompatibilite (CMH) de type I (CD8) ou II (CD4) aux recepteurs de cellules T qui leur sont compatibles initie une cascade signaletique activatrice. La surexpression de PD-1 est liee a la dysfonction immunitaire observee lors de l'infection chronique par le VIH. La premiere partie de mon projet consiste a comparer le benefice procure par la co-stimulation CD28 pour les cellules T CD4 et CD8, et ce, dans des contextes sains et dysfonctionnels (VIH+). Les fonctions principales de types Th1, Tfh et de cytotoxicite seront evaluees par cytometrie en flux. J'evaluerai la contribution d'autres molecules co-stimulatrices, comme ICOS et 4-1BB, ainsi que la molecule inhibitrice PD-L1 en les integrant dans le systeme de CPAa. column36: Molecular mechanism and clinical utilization of RNA circularization
column37: Researchers have long focused on how unexpected and permanent changes in our genetic makeup, or DNA leads to diseases like cancer. However, just looking at DNA might not be giving us the full picture. DNA has the vital information needed to maintain our bodies, but RNA is what does most of the work by reading and translating parts of DNA. While a large part of our genetic information can be read, only a small portion is translated into the molecules essential for life. Therefore, most RNAs exists as different subtypes termed non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) that do not produce these molecules. Several types of ncRNAs have been found to be present in cancer and have different roles such as affecting how cancer cells respond to treatment and contributing to metastasis. One type of ncRNA is circular RNA (circRNA) which has distinct properties and functions. Compared to most RNAs, circRNAs are very stable and specific to different tissues. There is growing evidence of circRNAs being involved in cancer. Owing to their unique features, circRNAs have the potential to help in the diagnosis and prognosis of cancer and be targets for new therapeutics. However, more work remains to be done in understanding their behaviour, specifically, how the circularization occurs and how their expression is regulated. To this end, I aim to investigate the mechanism of circRNAs to better study and understand their involvement in diseases they are expressed in.

column36: The role of cholinergic integrity on cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease
column37: Although Parkinsons Disease (PD) is typically characterized as a motor disorder, most patients also experience cognitive symptoms from the earliest stages of the disease. Despite the belief that PD is caused by a loss of dopamine-producing brain cells, PD symptoms are not fully alleviated by dopamine-replacement. Interestingly, while acetylcholine-producing (cholinergic) brain cells also decay in PD, researchers have generally assumed that their degeneration only occurs in later disease stages, causing dementia symptoms. As a result, acetylcholine replacements have only been provided to patients with advanced stage PD. Recent evidence suggests, however, that the loss of cholinergic brain cells occur early in disease progression; explaining why some cognitive symptoms (e.g., reduced concentration) also occur early on. The primary objective of this project is to determine whether cholinergic degeneration in early PD is associated with changes in cognitive function. Our second objective is to examine whether the loss of structural connections between the deep cholinergic regions and the rest of the brain are associated with attentional deficits. In this study, we will use cognitive tests to assess for the presence of cognitive dysfunction in PD patients and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain scans to measure the loss of cholinergic brain cells and their connections across the brain. We predict that cholinergic degeneration will be associated with cognitive dysfunction in the earlier stages of the disease, long before the onset of dementia. The results of this study will help us to better understand the cognitive symptoms in PD patients and will provide new clues about how to treat them.

column36: Age-related changes to lymph node microarchitecture and impacts on T cell responses
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has illustrated that elderly people are at much higher risk of developing severe symptoms from infection. This is partly due to reduced responsiveness of T cells, a type of immune cell that protects the body from foreign invaders, such as bacteria and viruses. It is known that T cell responses become less efficient with age, but whether changes to the immune environment in older people can impair T cell responses is incompletely understood. For T cells to effectively patrol all areas of the body, they are constantly commuting between different secondary lymphoid organs in which they can encounter infectious agents. T cells spend much of their time travelling along a network of roads within lymphoid organs created by fibroblastic reticular cells (FRCs). However, FRCs may become stiffer with age, which increases the amount of force they exert back on T cells. In response to greater external forces, cells increase the rigidity of their nucleus, which houses their genetic material. If cells cannot adapt to the higher pressure surrounding them, their genetic material will be damaged, causing them to lose their function. Consequently, T cells must adapt to different types of terrain to navigate efficiently and not harm any of their inner machinery. Although, as T cells age, they become ;rusty and may struggle with this adaptation. The goal of my research is to uncover how the structure and physical properties of FRC networks change with age and how aged T cells migrating through the network respond to these alterations. Understanding how T cells are affected by their environment will allow us to develop therapies that can restore immunity in older individuals and ultimately reduce the burden of infections and other diseases on the elder population.

column37: Human cells contain a protein tagging system that plays an important part in regulating the functions of target proteins and determining their fates. In this pathway, the target proteins are marked with small regulatory protein, called ubiquitin, by the tagging system. The tagged proteins are then recognized by the protein degradation machinery complexes that degrade unneeded or damaged proteins. The degraded proteins are then recycled and reused for the synthesis of new proteins. This process is fundamental to all cellular processes and critical to the health of the cell. Errors in the system have been linked to a wide range of diseases, including cancer. Malfunctions in the tagging systems can cause the accumulation of abnormal or unnecessary proteins within a cell which may lead to harmful effects. In this study, we plan to study the structure of the tagging system and the way that components of the complex interact with each other. We will also study how the defects in the system can lead to disease and this will give insight into how to correct the problems. We will utilize techniques that allow us to visualize the atomic-level structures of proteins. The results of this study will help us understand the structure and function of the proteins and may help us discover new therapeutic targets that can prevent malfunction of this pathway. The information may allow us to develop treatments and strategies for people with cancer and other diseases.

column36: The impact of the time of day of vaccination on the protection against Leishmania infection
column37: Leishmaniasis is a neglected tropical disease which affects 12-15 million people and is caused by the intracellular parasite Leishmania. There are very few treatment options for leishmaniasis, and those that are available have several limitations such as high cost, toxicity, severe side effects. There are several factors which are known to impact the effectivity of vaccines ; e.g weight, sex, microbiota ; but recent studies have shown that the time of which the vaccine is given may also have an impact. column36: Effect of the Timing and Dosage of Prenatal Alcohol Exposure on Differential DNAm in Children
column37: Prenatal alcohol exposure (PAE) can lead to serious developmental issues in children such as fetal alcohol spectrum disorders (FASD). FASD includes all PAE-related behavioural, cognitive, and growth deficits, including severe intellectual disability in some cases. The biology underlying diagnosed FASD has been well-studied. However, there is a lack of evidence regarding the safety of drinking at low-moderate levels (i.e., 70g alcohol/week) during pregnancy. This lack of information fuels vague public guidelines that can mislead women about the risks of drinking prior to, and during, pregnancy. Currently, the specific amount and timing of alcohol exposure that imposes health risks in children are unknown. Thus, I will investigate the DNA methylation (DNAm) patterns in the buccal tissues of children with low-moderate PAE to clarify whether it leaves a lasting molecular mark. DNAm is a relatively stable molecular mark that is deposited at CpG sites (adjacent cytosine and guanine bases) on DNA without changing its sequence. Humans need DNAm for proper development; however, when changed abnormally, these marks can interrupt biological pathways and result in disease. DNAm is sensitive to environmental insults, like alcohol, during pregnancy. Hence, DNAm is useful for studying the impacts of PAE throughout a childs life. I will compare CpG sites across the human genome between children with low-moderate and no PAE, as DNAm differences between the two may indicate a lasting biological impact of low-moderate PAE. I will also compare the DNAm patterns across one-, two-, and seven-year time points to explore these patterns longevity. These findings will guide studies that aim to uncover the biological pathways affected by PAE and thus precede developmental abnormalities.

column36: HMGB1 as a Key Driver of B Cell Hyperactivity in the Pathogenesis of Systemic Sclerosis Associated Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
column37: Pulmonary Hypertension (PH) is a progressively fatal disease defined by a resting mean pulmonary arterial pressure of 20 mmHg. A subset of PH, known as pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is localized to the lung vasculature and is characterized by perivascular inflammation and pulmonary arterial remodelling. This aggressive subset of PH is often associated with connective tissue diseases such as systemic sclerosis (SSc) and is the leading cause of death in these patients, with a 4-year mortality rate of 50%. Current therapies for systemic sclerosis associated PAH (SSc-PAH) are limited to vasodilators and are largely unsuccessful. Due to the immunological nature of both diseases, accumulating evidence points to immunomodulation as the future of SSc-PAH treatment.Given the central role of the immune system in the pathogenesis of both SSc and PAH, my project seeks to further investigate the role of B cells and the inflammatory modulator, high mobility group box 1 (HMGB1), in the pathogenesis of SSc-PAH. Recent research by our lab has shown that HMGB1 drives immune cell activation and promotes the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-a, IL-1B) driving perivascular inflammation and B cell activation.My project will investigate the relationship between HMGB1 and B cell hyperactivity. I hypothesize that extracellular matrix dysfunction in SSc promotes the release of HMGB1, which in turn stimulates B cell activity via TLR4 signaling, resulting in the onset of PAH in SSc. If successful, this project will help implicate B cells as key drivers of autoimmunity and vascular inflammation in SSc-PAH. This work will deepen our understanding of the disease mechanisms and provide new therapeutic targets (B cells, HMGB1) in the treatment of this devastating disease.

column36: Mast Cell Homing for Accelerated Bone Healing
column37: Bone fractures are among the most commonly occurring musculoskeletal injuries, resulting from a wide variety of causes. From the young and healthy to the aged, bone fractures can occur at any point during one's lifetime. Fractures can generally heal well in the younger and healthy population; however, in people with osteoporosis, diabetes, and those who incur concurrent infections, fracture healing complications can arise. Immune cells in the body play an integral role in fracture healing, and their dysfunction has been shown to result in fracture healing complications. The most common fracture complications are delayed unions and non-unions, comprising approximately 5-10% of the total number of fractures. The psychological, physical and economic impact of fractures on sufferers is profound. With a rapidly aging population in developed countries, the number of fracture cases and complications are rising. Complications such as non-unions often require revision surgery to aid in bone healing, and outcomes of such procedures are not always successful. Because fractures cannot be entirely avoided, a viable strategy is to devise novel therapies that accelerate fracture healing, and prevent or treat fracture complications. The objective of this research is to develop therapeutic applications, based on modulation of the immune system, for more optimal recruitment of immune cells to the fracture site to accelerate the healing process. This modulation will be achieved by using novel bioactive compounds capable of altering the function of immune cells, enabling them to migrate to the fracture site in a more efficient manner. Overall, this research aims to increase the quality of life of people prone to fractures, and reduce the burden on the health care system and economy.

column36: Network Analyses to Explore Multimorbidity Among Older Adults with Dementia Residing in Long-Term Care and the Community
column37: Dementia is an incurable neurodegenerative condition that commonly occurs with multimorbidity (presence of two or more chronic conditions) and is common amongst residents of facilities that provide long-term supportive care. Dementia affects the ability to communicate symptoms and health needs, which intensifies the complexities of multimorbidity. Our study will examine patterns of multimorbidity among older (age greater or equal to 65 years) persons with dementia (PWD) in Manitoba and test for differences in multimorbidity patterns in PWD residing in long-term care (LTC) and the community. We will adopt an innovative approach using network analyses, which generates visual graphs of associations (edges) between diseases (nodes). Network analyses can aid in discovering new disease associations.We will utilize comprehensive population-based administrative data from the Manitoba Population Research Data Repository. Chronic conditions will be defined using the open-source Clinical Classifications Software. Numbers of chronic conditions will be compared between LTC and community residents using negative binomial regression. Separate networks for PWD residing in LTC and community will be constructed to visualize associations between diseases. Network properties, including number of disease connections in a network, will be stratified by sex and age group.Currently, most clinical practice guidelines focus on single-organ or disease-specific management strategies. Characterizing disease profiles among PWD will enable clinical guidelines to better incorporate multimorbidity. Collaborative care between clinical services in LTC and communities can be expanded to meet the complex health needs of PWD with multimorbidity.

column36: Transitions out of First Episode Psychosis Services: Evaluating the Effectiveness of a Virtual Peer Driven Intervention in Emerging Adults
column37: Compared to standard care, early intervention services (EIS) are associated with better functional and clinical outcomes for young adults experiencing psychosis. Despite this, recent research has suggested that benefits gained may not persist following young adults' transition out of EIS. Perhaps due to high levels of experienced distress surrounding their transition and future, the majority of patients who relapse or disengage from services do so within one year following their transition. In order to maximize the benefits of EIS, and solidify engagement to a new treatment team, it may be particularly crucial to focus on supporting young adults during the year directly following transition to subsequent services.The current study will implement and evaluate a novel virtual peer-support program, that spans young adults transition from EIS to subsequent mental health services.In order to evaluate the effectiveness of the virtual peer support program, a mixed-methods longitudinal design will be used to assess functioning, quality of life, overall wellbeing, and barriers to engagement in new services for clients transitioning out of EIS.In comparison to previously evaluated interventions,peer lead interventions may offer similar benefits while being more cost-effective and easier to deliver for service providers. Additionally, delivering this service virtually will likely decrease risk of COVID-19 transmission, while also making services more accessible.Finally, as this intervention is among the first to provide young adults with support before and after transition, compared to previous interventions, it may better encourage engagement with new services and ultimately maintain improvements provided by EIS.

column36: A Better Match: Transforming rheumatoid arthritis care using text-based messaging
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a debilitating disease if left untreated, as incurred joint damage leads to functional impairment, disability, and severe RA-associated complications, including elevated rates of heart disease and premature death. Additionally, RA costs the Canadian system $6.4 billion Canadian dollars in direct and indirect costs annually. Clearly, the disease has widespread implications for not only RA patients, but also for health systems and policy makers. Evidence suggests that ongoing care from a rheumatologist improves patient outcomes. High quality RA care includes monitoring for exacerbations of disease, side effects from medications, and screening for comorbidities. However, healthcare workforce shortages threaten the delivery of ongoing high-quality RA care. The WelTel platform offers a potential solution to optimize patient-centered RA care. WelTel is a secure, evidence-based, digital health outreach tool that connects patients and healthcare providers via two-way interactive text messaging through short message service (SMS), as well as voice and video virtual care options. The platform sends a monthly check-in ;How are you SMS to patients. They can respond with questions or concerns about their treatment or health status in response to the check-in or at any time. In other chronic diseases such as HIV and hepatitis C, using the platform has shown to improve health outcomes and patient experience with care. The platform has not to date been used to support rheumatology populations. To achieve our aim of improving care delivery for patients with RA using text-based messaging, we will conduct a pilot study of the WelTel platform to assess the acceptability and feasibility of implementing the platform in rheumatology practice.

column37: For my Master's in Health Research Methodology thesis, I plan to undertake A Characterization of Clinical Care Pathways in Neurosurgery in the Canadian Context.This project is being conducted at McMaster University in the context of a neurosurgery residency. column36: Understanding the Relationship between Cannabis Use and Psychotherapeutic Treatment in Canadian Veterans: A Mixed-Methods Study
column37: The goal of my proposed research is to increase our understanding of the relationship between cannabis use and mental health treatment in Canadian veterans. Rates of PTSD, chronic pain, and other mental health conditions are higher amongst veterans than in the general Canadian population. Increasingly, veterans are using medical cannabis to cope with conditions such as PTSD or chronic pain. There is a lack of research on what kinds of cannabis use (i.e. type, method, amount, frequency) might be helpful or harmful, especially as it applies to veterans undergoing treatment for PTSD. Psychotherapeutic treatment is often the first recommended treatment for PTSD, and cannabis use is linked to individuals' PTSD symptoms not improving as much with treatment. As more veterans choose to use cannabis, it is important to understand why this may be. My research will look at factors that might explain this relationship (such as chronic pain, treatment adherence, and depression) as well as characteristics of cannabis use, general functioning, and PTSD symptoms prior to and after treatment for PTSD. This will provide insight into how these various factors might relate to and influence each other over a course of treatment. Additionally, I will be conducting interviews with veterans who used cannabis during their course of treatment, in order to understand their lived experience and how they feel cannabis use impacted both their condition and their treatment for it. This topic has been identified as a priority by leadership staff at a clinic that is part of a national network of clinics who focus on treating this population: thus, clinically relevant findings will be easily shared with others whose share the goal of treating and improving mental health conditions in veterans.

column36: Using the Youth Development Instrument (YDI) to Develop Strengths-Based Interventions for Adolescent School-Based Mental Health Services
column37: Youth interacting with school-based mental health care are broadly experiencing some level of challenge to their well-being. How can the time they spend in school be capitalized on to provide them the best possible chance of a positive trajectory moving forward? This project aims to use existing and incoming data from the Youth Development Instrument (YDI) to develop evidence-based, feasible, and sustainable interventions for adolescent school-based mental health services that promote resilience, well-being, and positive trajectories. YDI data has already been collected from 2300 Grade 11 students in BC and will expand further in Spring 2020; as such, this data would be used to develop interventions geared toward high school students. A strengths and asset-based approach to youth well-being would anchor this project and, on a systems level, it would be rooted in a commitment to understanding the resource limitations (e.g., time, money, training, access to resources/care) of the school system. In line with this, the project would use a two-pronged concurrent approach: (Aim 1) background research and fieldwork to understand the current system, resource limitations, intervention opportunities, and stakeholder perspectives, and (Aim 2) quantitative analysis of YDI data to develop data-driven interventions. The anticipated result is a pilot-ready, feasible, effective, and sustainable intervention that would support numerous aspects of youth well-being (e.g., improving social connections).

In a recent study, a mutation in the gene that codes for claudin-11 was discovered to cause white matter disease. I will also study cells obtained from the patients that carry the claudin-11 mutation. The experiments I plan to do will provide us with a better appreciation of how the mutation affects this protein and how it may lead to disease. The research may point us to ways to treat the disease.

column36: Infection Risk Amongst Patients Exposed to Biologic Medications
column37: Biologic medications are monoclonal antibodies that target cells, cytokines or receptors that have become paramount in the treatment of autoimmune and inflammatory conditions as rheumatologic diseases, dermatoses and malignancies. Many biologics exploit immunomodulatory properties to treat disease, that could unintentionally leave the host more vulnerable to infections.Studies investigating infections in patients receiving biologics have been highly restricted in looking only at a handful of specific drugs, used for only singular disease conditions. This process limits the generalizability of the findings and likely underestimates the infection risk of biologic drugs, particular as the number of applications grows.To better understand pathogen specific infectious risks, we will use the linked province-wide administrative health datasets at ICES to identify all infection diagnoses in patients receiving biologics using the international classification of disease (ICD-10) codes and via culture results from the Ontario Laboratory Information System. We will compare infection rates (overall and pathogen specific) to matched controls without exposure to biologics, as well as using self-controlled periods. Our analysis will be stratified by biologic drug and mechanism target, by underlying disease condition for which the biologic is prescribed, and by pathogen.The results of these analyses will advance our understanding of clinical immunobiology and will have important implications around patient counseling, the development of infection surveillance programs, antimicrobial prophylaxis, vaccination strategies, and will lend itself to potential future intervention studies aimed to reduce infections risks even further.

column36: A qualitative exploration of pathways through which subjective social status shapes health
column37: Socioeconomic position (SEP) is strongly correlated with health outcomes, with lower SEP individuals experiencing poorer health outcomes than their higher SEP counterparts. SEP is commonly operationalized using objective indicators, such as income, education and occupation. However, SEP is a complex construct, and these indicators are limited in their ability to capture the many pathways through which health inequities are generated and reproduced. Subjective indicators of SEP, such as subjective social status (SSS), are strongly associated with health, and may help to address the limitations of objective indicators by capturing a more comprehensive perspective of how SEP shapes health than objective indicators do. SSS may also capture a psychosocial perspective of these associations by reflecting how relative perceptions of social status, and the stress that such social comparisons entail, represent a unique source of health inequities. Although subjective social status is increasingly used in health inequity literature, there is limited understanding of the social processes that this indicator captures. Therefore, the purpose of this study is to qualitatively explore the factors that adults consider when evaluating their subjective social status, and the potential pathways through which these factors shape health. The study will utilize qualitative, semi-structured interviews that encourage participants to consider how social determinants shape their subjective social status and thus their health. This study will provide valuable data pertaining to factors individuals consider when evaluating their subjective social status, and how subjective social status shapes health outcomes. These data can be used to inform interventions to reduce health inequities.

column36: Interactions genes-diete avec des acides gras omega-3: Raffinement d'un outil de prediction de la reponse lipidique sous la forme d'un score de risque genetique
column37: Les maladies cardiovasculaires (MCV) representant la deuxieme cause de mortalite au Canada, il est essentiel de developper des strategies nutritionnelles afin de les prevenir. Plusieurs etudes suggerent que la consommation d'omega-3 agirait sur des facteurs de risque des MCV et diminuerait les concentrations plasmatiques de triglycerides (TG), un type de lipides. Il existe toutefois une grande variabilite interindividuelle dans la reponse metabolique aux omega-3. En effet, dans le cadre d'une etude, notre equipe a rapporte que 29% des participants n'abaissaient pas leurs niveaux de TG plasmatiques a la suite d'une supplementation quotidienne de 5g d'huile de poisson pendant 6 semaines. Cette variabilite interindividuelle est en partie due a des facteurs genetiques. Notre groupe a prealablement identifie six regions genetiques associees a la variabilite chez les participants de cette etude. Notre equipe a ensuite finement cartographie ces regions pour reveler 31 variations genetiques dans la sequence de l'ADN des participants qui ont ete utilisees pour le calcul d'un score de risque genetique expliquant 49,7% de la variabilite dans la reponse des TG. Parallelement aux travaux menes par notre groupe, une autre equipe de recherche a recemment identifie de nouvelles regions genetiques associees aux concentrations de lipides sanguins en interaction avec la consommation quotidienne d'huile de poisson, a l'aide des donnees de 73.962 individus de la UK Biobank. L'objectif ultime de ce projet est donc de raffiner le score de risque genetique developpe par notre equipe en verifiant si les variations genetiques identifiees par ce groupe de recherche contribuent a la variabilite interindividuelle observee dans la reponse des TG suite a une supplementation en omega-3.

column36: Validation d'un questionnaire en francais pour evaluer le comportement << manger en absence de faim >>
column37: L'obesite chez les enfants est une problematique de sante importante. Les comportements alimentaires durant la periode de l'enfance peuvent contribuer au risque de surpoids. Mieux comprendre ces comportements alimentaires pourrait permettre de developper des interventions des le plus jeune age visant a reduire le developpement de l'obesite. Parmi ceux-ci, on retrouve le comportement de manger en absence de faim (l'action de manger lorsqu'on n'a plus faim). Ce dernier est typiquement evalue par un test de laboratoire (mesure de reference) qui demande beaucoup de temps et de ressources. Afin de faciliter la mesure de ce comportement, un questionnaire a ete developpe, puis valide en anglais seulement. Ce questionnaire permet egalement d'identifier des facteurs declencheurs de manger en absence de faim. Dans le cadre de mon projet de maitrise, je procederai a la validation du questionnaire traduit en francais. Je vais d'abord confirmer que la structure du questionnaire est adequate (validite interne) et que les resultats obtenus sont stables a travers le temps (fiabilite). Cette etape de validation se fera aupres de 200 participants de 7 a 15 ans du CHU Ste-Justine. Ensuite, je vais comparer les resultats obtenus avec le questionnaire en francais avec ceux obtenus avec le test en laboratoire (validite externe). Cette etape sera faite aupres de 100 participants d'environ 12 ans recrutes a l'Universite de Sherbrooke dans le cadre d'une etude de cohorte. En fournissant un outil de mesure en francais du comportement de manger en absence de faim, mon projet contribuera a identifier les determinants et les effets de ce comportement pour permettre de developper des interventions visant a freiner son developpement et donc possiblement reduire le risque de surpoids chez l'enfant.

column36: Olfactory Proteome Changes in Response to Alzheimer's Disease-Related Pathologies in Rat and Mouse Models
column37: Alzheimers disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia, and it is one of the leading causes of death globally. Identifying early signs of AD is of paramount importance as it allows us to differentiate those at risk and provide early therapeutic intervention. A loss in the ability to smell is observed early in individuals who develop diseases of the nervous system, including AD. In fact, smell deficits can be observed more than a decade before the onset of cognitive symptoms of AD. While this phenomenon has been well documented, the cause of this loss of smell in AD remains unknown. To our knowledge, we will be the first group to examine protein expression in the olfactory system of specific rat and mouse models of AD. We expect to detect differences in protein expression in these rat and mouse models of AD compared to normal, healthy rats and mice. We will then determine the identity of these proteins that displayed changes in expression. Next, we will determine when these specific proteins are being expressed and by what cell types. Finally, we will assess whether protein changes are consistent across species. As this is the first study of its kind, our results will offer unique insights to improve our understanding of the loss of smell in AD. Future directions include determining whether changes in olfactory protein expression in rat and mouse models of AD can be translated to human patients with AD. This study may reveal proteins that indicate an individual is at a heightened risk of developing AD. Nasal biopsies could potentially be used to detect these protein markers, making it a useful tool for clinical assessment. A timely diagnosis provided by a nasal biopsy would allow for early therapeutic intervention to minimize the risk of developing AD.

column36: Caracterisation d'un modele ex vivo de culture d'organoides de prostate
column37: Le cancer de la prostate est l'un des cancers les plus diagnostiques chez les Canadiens. Bien que de nombreuses options de traitement sont disponibles pour les patients, le cancer de la prostate cause encore des milliers de deces au Canada chaque annee, lorsque le cancer ne repond plus aux traitements actuellement disponibles. Nous developpons donc un modele d'etude de cet organe, des organoides, qui reproduit son fonctionnement particulier pour mieux comprendre l'organe sain et comment ce metabolisme est reprogramme dans les tumeurs. column36: DNA Methylation and Progression from Early Stage Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia
column37: Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (MBL) is a pre-condition of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), which is associated with weakened immunity and greater vulnerability to infections and cancer development. It remains unknown why some individuals with MBL progress to CLL while others do not. Older biological age and changes in DNA methylation (DNAm), one of the biological processes that control gene expression, may be involved. Here, we will measure the methylation levels of DNA isolated from people with MBL who progress to CLL (progressors) compared with those who do not (non-progressors). We will use established tools to determine the epigenetic ages of both groups and statistical modeling to identify the differences in DNAm between the two groups and use those to predict progression. We expect that progressors will be epigenetically older than non-progressors, and we also expect to find the DNAm sites that are crucial in predicting MBL progression. The results of this project will further our understanding of epigenetic contributions to the progression of MBL to CLL. The results may also provide the rationale for exploring new treatments that target abnormal DNA methylation in early-stage CLL patients.

column36: Localized immune modulation with rapamycin-eluting micelles to preserve pancreatic islet graft function
column37: Introduction: Islet transplantation is an effective way that type 1 diabetic patients can be freed from insulin injections, however the lifelong immunosuppression required to subvert the immune response remains a major barrier. Chronic systemic (affecting whole body) immunosuppression often results in multiple toxicities that can reduce the quality of life of transplant recipients. This project explores the use of a localized drug delivery system to preserve transplanted islet function and potentially circumvent the need for systemic immunosuppression.Poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) is an FDA-approved biomaterial that can form particles that encapsulate and releases drugs. Rapamycin (rapa) is a potent immunosuppressant used in clinical islet transplantation, and its chemical properties makes it an ideal candidate for PLGA particle encapsulation. We hypothesize that this localized rapa-releasing system will subvert the immune response pathways, promoting long-term durable islet function in a transplanted diabetic mouse model under the skin.Methods: Rapa-releasing particles were made and characterized: encapsulation efficiency, structure, and rate of drug release. To examine immune unrelated effects of rapa particles on transplanted islet function, we co-transplanted syngeneic islet (genetically identical recipient and donor). Later, we will use an allogenic diabetic mouse model (non-identical donor and recipient) to determine how well rapa particles can prolonging allograft function. Graft function is monitored through blood glucose levels: non-fasted and fasted following glucose injection.Conclusion: If our hypothesis holds true, rapa particles has the potential to replace chronic systemic immunosuppression and its associated toxicities in islet transplantation.

column36: Investigating the immunopathogenesis of hepatitis B virus using the woodchuck hepatitis virus model
column37: Hepatitis B virus (HBV) has established chronic infections in more than 296 million individuals worldwide and is associated with liver cancer and cirrhosis. Lifelong regiments of nucleos(t)ide analogs suppress viral replication, but fail to achieve a virological cure due to the stable covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) established in infected cells. The woodchuck hepatitis virus (WHV) naturally infects eastern North American woodchucks and also belongs to the Hepadnaviridae family, resulting in an animal model that is pathogenically compatible to HBV infections in humans. The woodchuck-WHV model shares many characteristics with the human-HBV model, such as genome size, disease progression patterns and age-dependent risk of chronicity. We aim to investigate the importance of resident macrophages known as Kupffer cells (KCs) in influencing the outcome of acute WHV infections by selectively depleting them in a subset of woodchucks using chlodronate liposomes (CLL). We predict that weakened KC function leads to viral persistence in susceptible hosts. By optimizing WHV-specific assays to assess both intrahepatic and systemic responses to acute WHV infections, we aim to monitor protein markers using Enzyme Linked Immunosorbent Assays (ELISAs) and nucleic acid markers of infection using qualitative PCR (qPCR).We also seek to develop a productive cell line for the standardization of the described assays and generation of purified WHV stocks. Woodchucks treated with CLLs will be compared to control woodchucks using systemic and intrahepatic serological markers as well as the optimized assays. The application of these findings to human HBV infections will navigate our understanding of virus-host interactions in the liver and viral disease outcomes.

column36: Le transfert interhospitalier en ambulance au depart des unites critiques : une etude prospective a devis mixte sur la structure, le processus et les resultats-patient
column37: Les transferts interhospitaliers en ambulance (TIHA) ont vu leur nombre augmenter au cours des dernieres annees, notamment a cause de la demande accrue de soins intensifs ou specialises, non disponibles dans l'hopital d'origine. Les TIHA au depart des unites de soins critiques (urgences, soins intensifs et unites coronariennes) sont plus complexes en raison de la condition clinique plus instable des patients. Dans la region de la Capitale-Nationale, 3500 TIHA ont eu lieu a partir du CHU (Centre Hospitalier Universitaire) de Quebec - Universite Laval. Cependant, ces transferts sont encore peu etudies au Quebec comparativement a ce qui est recommande dans la litterature. column36: The Effect of Paternal SSRI Exposure during the Periconception Period on the Fetus
column37: Depression is a common mental illness that affects many parents. Consequently, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are prescribed to 60% of fathers with depression during the preconception period. Many studies in both humans and animals have shown that maternal SSRI use results in an increased risk of the fetus developing various metabolic and psychiatric disorders. However, the effects of paternal exposure to SSRIs during the periconception period are not clear. The goal of this study is to test the hypothesis that paternal SSRI exposure will adversely affect pregnancy and fetal outcomes; an effect mediated via changes in the sperm epigenome. To test this hypothesis, male rats will be given fluoxetine (one of the most commonly used SSRIs for treatment of depression) or vehicle for 65 days prior to mating (encompasses full cycle of sperm production) with non-exposed females. The effect of SSRIs on the fetus will be assessed two ways: (1) a subset of dams at gestational day 15 will be sacrificed to assess fetal and placental growth, and (2) after the dams give birth, pregnancy success, birth weight, sex ratio, gestational length, live birth index, and litter size will be determined. As well, the effects of SSRIs on sperm will be assessed by sacrificing breeder males (from above) after mating to collect sperm. The sperm will be assessed for changes in sperm quality, modifications of the sperm epigenome, and upregulation of cellular stress markers, which will inform on the potential causes of the outcomes seen in the fetuses and pups. Ultimately, the results from this study will contribute to the dialogue surrounding paternal use of antidepressants during the preconception period.

column36: A Novel Cognitive Intervention for Children with Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder
column37: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is the leading cause of preventable developmental disability in children, referring to a broad spectrum of physical, cognitive, behavioural, and psychosocial symptoms associated with prenatal alcohol exposure. Attention and executive function (A/EF) impairments are among the most pervasive and debilitating cognitive deficits in FASD, which contribute to short and long-term struggles with mental health, academic difficulties, and maladaptive behaviour. Despite this, there are limited interventions available for this population, and those that are available are often inaccessible due to availability and cost. In the current study, we propose to evaluate the feasibility and efficacy of a novel game-based A/EF intervention, ;Dino Island, in children with FASD as delivered by education assistants in school settings. We will recruit 40 children between the ages of 5-13 years with diagnosed or suspected FASD and 40 Educational Assistants (EAs) through our school partners in British Columbia. Children will be randomly assigned to either the DI or an active control condition. Children will complete 14 hours of intervention delivered by trained EAs. Pre/post neuropsychological testing will be conducted and will include standardized measures of A/EF, academic fluency, and behaviour. A portable EEG device (Neurocatch) will also be used to collect event related potential data focused on the P300 wave, which provides a measure of attention that is sensitive to functional cognitive brain changes induced by cognitive intervention. Qualitative data on feasibility will be collected and analyzed through exit interviews to identify trends. Findings from this study will expand on a growing literature on accessible cognitive intervention tools.

column36: Comparison of MRI-Derived Lung Water Content (Pulmonary Congestion) and Ultrasound Assessment in Heart Failure Patients
column37: Pulmonary edema is a cardinal feature of heart failure (HF) which is a major and growing health epidemic in Canada; however, no quantitative tests are available in clinical practice. Recent advances in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) techniques, by our team, now enable three-dimensional quantification of lung water density and therefore the non-invasive measurement pulmonary edema. We have shown that MRI-derived lung water can independently predict hospitalization and severe outcomes in patients with or at risk of HF and correlates directly with invasively measured left-sided filling pressures (i.e. the cause of the lung water accumulation). However, access to MRI is limited in Canada and around the world, which will limit the impact of this technology. In contrast, ultrasound has shown potential in detecting increased fluid levels in the lungs, based on the formation of characteristic image artifacts thought to be due to fluid accumulation in extravascular spaces. However, ultrasound-derived measures of edema have not been compared or validated against a direct imaging evaluation of water density, such as MRI-derived water content. We propose to compare ultrasound and MRI-derived lung water measurements in HF patients to determine the relationship between the underlying water distributions (three-dimensional) and indirect ultrasound measurements, for a wide range of disease severity. The success of this study will validate the use of ultrasound for detection of pulmonary edema, add physiological meaning to the ultrasound data, and help guide future developments in ultrasound for application in HF and other lung pathologies.

column36: Role de DUSP4 dans la formation de la plaque atherosclerotique et la fonction des macrophages
column37: L'atherosclerose est une maladie inflammatoire des vaisseaux sanguins a l'origine de plusieurs maladies cardiovasculaires. Sa formation est caracterisee par une plaque de gras, principalement due a l'accumulation de cholesterol sous l'endothelium. Il s'agit d'un phenomene complexe impliquant plusieurs mecanismes et voies de signalisation cellulaire, dont celle des Mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK). Les MAPKs sont regulees par des phosphatases comme DUSP4. Les MAPKs peuvent etre activees par les acides gras libre, comme le palmitate, et les lipoproteines a faible densite oxydees (LDLox). Notre laboratoire a observe que les souris deficientes pour DUSP4 presentaient moins de plaques atheromateuses. Notre hypothese est que DUSP4 joue un role crucial dans la regulation du developpement de la plaque atherosclerotique.Nous voulons d'abord determiner les effets de l'absence de DUSP4 (Dusp4-/-) dans la progression de la plaque, puis caracteriser ses mecanismes de regulation dans les macrophages en presence ou non de palmitate et de LDLox. Des modeles murins ApoE-/-/Dusp4+/+ et ApoE-/-/Dusp4-/- seront mis sous diete riche en gras pour 12 semaines puis euthanasies afin d'evaluer la formation de la plaque, l'expression de DUSP4 et l'activation des MAPKs ERK, p38 et JNK. Enfin, nous evaluerons l'implication de DUSP4 sur la formation de la plaque grace a un modele murin de transplantation de moelle osseuse qui permettra ainsi de valider si c'est DUSP4 dans les macrophages qui influence la formation de la plaque.Mon projet permettra de mieux comprendre le developpement de l'atherosclerose et d'etablir si DUSP4 peut servir d'alternative therapeutique afin d'ameliorer significativement la qualite de vie des patients.

column36: Improving the Public Health Pandemic Response via an Open, Consensus-Driving Genomic Contextual Data Standard
column37: A key to the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic response has been the sequencing and sharing of large amounts of genomic data and associated contextual information. While genomic data (genetic code) is one important part of the response, it is the contextual data that tells us who was infected, where infection probably occurred, what their clinical outcomes were, and what the sampling methodology was. Different regions have created different standards of contextual information collection, often resulting in data sets that are difficult to merge and compare across administrations. We need to see the bigger picture, yet we cannot create it from incompatible pieces. This proposal is for the creation of a community developed data standard that is adaptive to user needs, accessible, and formatted such that it can be readily processed by a computer. This will be accomplished via engagement with genomic domain experts and data structure scientists. Qualitative semi-structured interviews with domain experts will assist in determining relevant contextual data needs and research questions regarding SARS-CoV-2 transmission scenarios. Information scientists will be consulted to help convert this information into a data model, a means of organizing data elements and the relationships between them, before transforming it into computer code. This work will then be formulated into a protocol that will support other researchers to generate and collaborate on their own data standard scenarios. The end result will be an accessible specification data structure that aids in the creation of compatible genomic contextual data sets and enables computational processing of complex research questions, thereby accelerating public health pandemic response time across disparate health jurisdictions.

column36: Caregiver burden and early readmission after ED discharge: an interrupted time series
column37: One-third of all patients consulting emergency departments (ED) are seniors and an additional one-third of seniors admitted to the ED report care coordination problems, chief among them are gaps in hospital discharge planning and long waiting lists to receive home care services. It remains unclear whether (1) burden of care among caregivers of elderly patients can account for varying levels of success in reducing ED visits, readmission rates, and length of stay in the hospital among this elderly population, and (2) how the COVID-19 pandemic may have moderated the relation.With a sample of approximately 4000 patients from the LEARNING WISDOM context-adapted CISSS-CA ACE (Centre intégré de santé et de services sociaux de Chaudière-Appalaches Acute Care for Elders) program we will explore whether burden of care reported by caregivers can predict admission to and early revisits to the ED among elderly patients with many different health backgrounds and complaints.We will leverage Learning Wisdoms interrupted time series to assess the CISSS-CA-ACE intervention's effects on early revisits to the ED as moderated by caregiver burden. As the CISSS-CA-ACE program was likely significantly disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic, we also intend to conduct an additional interrupted time series over each wave of the COVID-19 pandemic.We suspect that higher indices of burden of care in the later waves of the pandemic translate to especially large rates of early readmission among elderly patients. The results from this inquiry may contribute to our understanding of individual differences in strain and burden among older adults and their caregivers are related to real-world health outcomes.

column36: Etude de la relation entre la qualite de l'alimentation et l'intensite de la pharmacotherapie antidiabetique et dans le traitement du diabete de type 2.
column37: Les personnes vivant avec le diabete de type 2 (DT2) doivent adopter de saines habitudes alimentaires et prendre leur medication de facon assidue afin de bien controler leur niveau de sucre sanguin. Toutefois, la prise de medicaments pour le diabete semble se substituer a l'adoption d'une saine alimentation, car ils sont percus comme plus efficaces pour gerer la maladie comparativement a l'alimentation. Cela resulte en un controle du sucre sanguin sous-optimal, en plus d'augmenter l'intensite et la complexite du traitement medicamenteux et le risque d'effets indesirables et de non-adhesion.L'objectif de ce projet de recherche est d'etudier la relation nutrition-medication dans la prise en charge du DT2. L'hypothese est que la prise de medication antidiabetique (MAD) constitue une barriere aux changements alimentaires favorables a la sante.Cette etude inclut les 490 adultes vivant avec le DT2 de la cohorte quebecoise CARTaGENE. Chez chacune de ces personnes, les elements suivants seront evalues :- La relation entre l'intensite de la MAD et la qualite de l'alimentation, afin de determiner si la MAD complemente ou se substitue a une saine alimentation;- La relation entre l'adhesion a la MAD et la qualite de l'alimentation, afin de determiner si les personnes prenant leur medication de facon assidue ont tendance a avoir de meilleures habitudes alimentaires ou non;- L'importance relative d'une saine alimentation en lien avec la prise de medication pour optimiser le controle glycemique.Ce projet decrira comment les approches nutritionnelles et pharmacologiques s'influencent mutuellement dans la prise en charge du DT2, permettant de developper des approches favorisant l'adhesion aux recommandations nutritionnelles et a la pharmacotherapie dans le traitement du DT2.

column36: Investigating the Roles of Mitophagy and the Integrated Stress Response (ISR) in Intestinal Stem Cells
column37: The mitochondria is responsible for food metabolism and energy production inside the human body. In response to diverse mitochondrial stressors, eukaryotic cells initiate two distinct pathways, mitophagy and the integrated stress response (ISR), to reestablish mitochondrial homeostasis. However, little is known about the ISR signal relay mechanism and lots of debates exist around what is the main mitophagy pathway. In the context of intestine, the persistence of mitochondrial dysfunction can affect stem cell proliferation and trigger tumorigenesis, which emphasizes on the reliance of mitophagy and the ISR. We propose to study both the mitophagy and ISR pathways in intestinal stem cells (ISC). Our overarching goal is to define how mitophagy/ISR affect ISC differentiation and proliferation. The long term impact of our work will aid in better understanding of diseases such as inflammatory bowel disease and colorectal cancer.Aim1 is to establish the importance of a mitophagy pathway identified in our lab and the ISR pathway in mitochondrial homeostatsis in human colon cancer cell lines. We will induce stress on the mitochondria and knockdown specific proteins using shRNA to observe induction/deduction in ISR and mitophagy activities. Results will shed light into how mitophagy and ISR maintain mitochondrial homeostasis in intestinal cell line. Aim2 will utilize ex vivo knockoutintestinal organoids to examine how malfunctioning mitophagy and ISR impact ISC differentiation. Any impact on ISC differentiation will suggest mitophagy/ISR regulates stem cell fate. Our research is important due to very limited research available in the field and that our findings will aid in the development of promising therapeutics to target mitochondrial disease and cancer.

column36: THC-induced changes to micro-RNA profiles in sperm and implications in male infertility
column37: Globally, marijuana is the most commonly used recreational drug among males of reproductive age. Cannabis use has increased following its legalization in several countries, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic, and the concentration of its main psychoactive ingredient, 9-Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), continues to rise. This raises health concerns because cannabis use correlates with poor sperm count, morphology, and function, which may contribute to rising rates of male infertility. However, the mechanisms by which THC produces its effects on sperm are unknown and may occur through epigenetic modifications, such as changes in microRNA levels. miRNAs affect cell functions through changes in gene expression by interacting with messenger RNAs that code for specific proteins, some of which may be linked to male infertility. These epigenetic changes in sperm may be heritable. Therefore, investigating how THC alters miRNAs in sperm could identify THC-induced infertility markers, lead to better recommendations concerning male cannabis use, and help in providing guidance for couples suffering from infertility and undergoing in-vitro fertilization (IVF). We propose to study the effects of THC in bovine sperm at therapeutic and recreational doses on the expression of specific miRNAs (and their associated mRNA and protein targets) that are known to affect sperm development, morphology, and function. Bovine sperm is the best model for human sperm, but to confirm our results we will also quantify changes in miRNAs in human sperm from IVF patients and correlate this with THC consumption. This novel research will elucidate how, and to what extent, THC may influence reproduction, and will evaluate the relevance of miRNAs as markers for THC-induced changes to sperm quality in humans.

column36: The molecular mechanisms of acclimation in C. elegans
column37: Aging is driven by the accumulation of molecular damage of unknown nature and origin. Acclimation is the adaptation to changes in their environment. This involves both sensing change and engaging mechanisms that can re-tune cellular processes to a new homeostatic state. I hypothesize that this complex process is imperfect and may lead to the dysregulation of cellular processes. Acclimation is an important survival factor and wild-type organisms likely engage acclimation processes even in response to minor environmental fluctuations. Repeated acclimation to small environmental variations might thus gradually lead to the damage and loss of homeostasis that characterizes aging. Thus, a mutation that does not permit acclimating to new environments might protect the homeostatic state and allow for longevity, at least in invariant conditions. In fact, the clk-1 mutants of the nematode C. elegans are both long-lived and unable to correctly adapt their developmental rates and behaviour to changes in environmental temperature. I propose to carry out a new forward genetic screen to identify C. elegans mutants that are fully unable to acclimate to changes in temperature. For this, I will create homozygous clonal lines of mutagenized animals kept at a constant temperature. Groups of individuals from these clones will then be tested for survival following shifts to both higher and lower temperatures. I will seek to identify mutants that are unable to survive both shifts, suggesting an inability to acclimate as such. I will then score such mutants for longevity and seek to identify and characterize the affected genes. As aging is a major risk factor for most diseases, advancing our understanding of the aging process is of great potential therapeutic importance.

column36: Extracellular vesicle protein signatures of pediatric liver tumors - A novel strategy for diagnosis
column37: Hepatoblastoma (HB) is the most frequent pediatric liver tumor. Standard treatment involves diagnostic imaging, biopsy, chemotherapy and surgery. Since most children are diagnosed under the age of 5 and tumor recurrence is associated with worsened outcomes, less invasive diagnostic and monitoring techniques are required. Serial blood tests (liquid biopsy) have been used for the diagnosis and monitoring of adult cancers, however have yet to be used in hepatoblastoma. Extracellular vesicles (EVs) present a source of biomarkers in the blood for liquid biopsy. Tumor cells release EVs that pack proteins, DNA and RNA to communicate with neighboring or distant cells. This project aims to investigate EVs as a novel diagnostic approach for HB for more specific and early detection of cancer and its recurrence. I will analyze and characterize the protein contents of EVs collected from several patient-derived HB cell lines to identify biomarkers specific to HB and validate these in patient samples. Furthermore, I aim to use patient clinical information to find correlations or specific markers of different tumor types and stages. A deeper understanding of tumor inter-cellular communication and proteins carried in EVs will improve the accuracy and quality of liquid biopsies in diagnosis and monitoring of HB.

column36: Role of ketone body oxidation in the development of muscle insulin resistance.
column37: When deprived of sugar due to starvation, our tissues need an alternative source of energy, so they turn to ketone bodies. Our skeletal muscles are the main location for sugar uptake following a meal, but they are also able to oxidize ketone bodies. The research outlined in this proposal contributes to a greater picture examination into the potential mechanism of action by which ketone bodies in the muscle can affect blood sugar levels. Although the role of ketone bodies during starvation is well-understood, their implication with diseases such as type 2 diabetes, where individuals affected have an impaired ability to take in sugar for use as a source of energy, and therefore high blood sugar levels, remains to be elucidated. The experiments performed will involve the use of muscle obtained through a biopsy from healthy subjects, and subjects with type 2 diabetes. The specific objectives of the proposed research include determining whether activity of an important enzyme involved in ketone body oxidation (succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid-CoA transferase (SCOT)) is elevated in the skeletal muscle of humans affected by type 2 diabetes, relative to unaffected individuals. Additional experiments will be performed to determine if inhibiting SCOT, thereby preventing the skeletal muscles from using ketone bodies for energy, results in an increase in the use of sugar in subjects with type 2 diabetes. Specifically, the uptake and storage of sugar within the cells, as well as the activation of enzymes involved in sugar metabolism will be investigated. By studying the implication of ketone body oxidation in individuals affected by type 2 diabetes, the results will hopefully serve to improve our understanding of how we can regulate blood sugar levels in patients with the disease.

column36: Neonatal Encephalopathy: Identification of underlying genetic causes
column37: Neonatal encephalopathy (NE) is a syndrome of disturbed brain function in term newborns in the first days of life. NE is characterized by an abnormal level of consciousness, seizures, difficulty breathing and decreased muscle tone and reflexes. Events occurring during pregnancy (25% e.g. low blood pressure in the mother), during labour (10% e.g. placental tearing) and after delivery (10% e.g. difficulty breathing) are some of the underlying causes of NE. Despite a lack of blood supply and oxygen to the brain being considered causative in many newborns with NE, most term newborns do not have this history during labour and delivery. Up to 900 newborns per year are admitted to neonatal intensive care units with NE. Severe NE can result in death in one third of newborns. Two thirds of newborns develop cerebral palsy and life-long motor and cognitive dysfunction. We think that term newborns with NE have genetic defects of energy metabolism that cause brain injury. To find genetic causes of NE, we will use a genetic test called whole genome sequencing to look at changes in the genetic makeup of newborns with NE. When we find genetic causes of NE, then we will be able to develop treatments. This will help us to prevent death and to improve the motor and cognitive outcomes of children who will have NE in the future.

column36: Differential Parenting and Physical-Mental Multimorbidity in Children

column36: Role of WalKR in Antibiotic Resistant Staphylococcus aureus
column37: Pathogenic strains of Staphylococcus aureus are evolving forms that are increasingly resistant to antibiotics, overburdening worldwide healthcare systems. Vancomycin-intermediate S. aureus, termed VISA, is one such multidrug resistant form. VISA strains share a number of characteristics that alter their growth and cell wall morphology. We have demonstrated that mutations in a signalling system known as walKR are the genetic cause of VISA. The proteins encoded by these genes, WalK and WalR, are intimately involved in a process known as cell wall recycling by upregulating the expression of enzymes that degrade the cell wall. In VISA strains, this process is defective, but the molecular basis of resistance is not yet clear. We have also discovered VISA is sensitive to an existing antibiotic, tunicamycin, and identified two compounds that, similarly, target the antibiotic resistant form but not the wild type parent. My project will strengthen our model of VISA resistance constructed with walR mutants by comparing to a set of walK mutants. I aim to broaden the search for candidate drugs by screening a total of 150,000 small molecules for their ability to specifically target VISA strains. Overall, my work will provide a new understanding of antibiotic resistance by defining a link between cell wall recycling and VISA through the role of WalKR. By developing new drug leads against these potent, antibiotic resistant pathogens I will provide an alternative strategy for managing S. aureus infections.
