column36: Modelling CAR-T cell function using a 3D in vitro model of the tumour microenvironment
column37: Cancer affects a substantial portion of the Canadian population; however, a universal cure remains elusive. Recent approaches to cancer treatment have focused on T cells, an important type of immune cell that helps to attack cancerous and virally infected cells. A novel treatment approach, termed CAR-T cell therapy, involves re-engineering T cells to recognize and target tumours. While this approach has achieved remarkable success in treating blood cancers, the efficacy has been substantially reduced in patients with solid tumours, owing to the immunosuppressive nature of the tumour microenvironment. This phenomenon can be studied in animal models to a certain extent; however, the high costs and long duration of animal studies limits the capacity for iterative improvement of CAR-T cell design. The proposed work aims to develop a solid tumour-on-a-chip platform designed to evaluate CAR-T cell function. To provide a more accurate representation of the tumour microenvironment, this platform will modularly incorporate key immunosuppressive features, including dysregulated blood vessels and oxygen deprivation, such that the influence of each feature can be studied independently. This work will provide insight into how various immunosuppressive features in the tumour microenvironment contribute to CAR-T cell dysfunction, enabling the development of improved CAR-T cell therapies for solid tumour patients.

column36: Examining Exercise and Physical Activity Recommendations to Reduce Cardiovascular Risk for Pre- And Post-menopausal Females Living With and Without Stroke
column37: As they grow older, women go through an event known as menopause. During menopause, women lose hormones such as estrogen. Estrogen is an important hormone in maintaining womens heart health. Before menopause, when estrogen levels are high, women have a lower risk of stroke than men. This changes after menopause where women are then at higher risk of stroke. Women also have smaller hearts and less muscle compared to men. These differences can add to the poorer health of the heart and blood vessels in women after stroke. The health of a persons heart and blood vessels, also known as cardiovascular health, may affect a persons ability to perform many everyday activities, walk, and stay active. Poor cardiovascular health may increase risk for other diseases. Exercise and physical activity can improve cardiovascular health, but we do not know what specific exercise parameters work best for women after menopause. We also do not know if more physical activity is better in women with stroke as they go through menopause.This project includes two studies that will help us better understand how exercise can help women after menopause. The first study will summarize previous research about how exercise can improve cardiovascular health in women after menopause. The second study will examine the relationship between physical activity and cardiovascular health in women with stroke before and after menopause. Together, these studies will help us better understand the effect of exercise and physical activity on cardiovascular health in women with stroke as they go through menopause. This will also help researchers design specific exercise and physical activity recommendations in the future for women after menopause.

column36: Association entre l'efficacite therapeutique de la stimulation theta burst et la connectivite fonctionnelle chez des patients atteints de depression majeure
column37: Le trouble depressif majeur est une maladie qui touche une grande proportion de la population. Bien que plusieurs traitements soient disponibles et efficaces, plus d'une personne sur cinq sera resistante au traitement. Heureusement, plusieurs nouvelles interventions sont prometteuses, dont la stimulation theta burst (de l'anglais theta burst stimulation, TBS). Celle-ci est un traitement non invasif qui peut etre utilise pour traiter la depression majeure lorsqu'applique au cortex dorsolateral prefrontal (CDLPF). Etant donne la nouveaute de ce protocole, il est primordial de connaitre le meilleur type de stimulation pour bien repondre au traitement. Aussi, il a ete demontre que la reponse au traitement peut etre predite a partir de la connectivite entre le CDLPF et le cortex cingulaire anterieur (ACC) a l'etat de repos. Cependant, aucune etude n'a explore comment cette reponse est liee a la connectivite entre le CDLPF et l'ACC a l'etat de repos dans la depression. C'est pourquoi je chercherai a comparer les effets de la TBS unilaterale et bilaterale sur les symptomes depressifs de participants atteints de depression majeure. J'examinerai egalement si la connectivite entre le CDLPF et l'ACC est liee a la reponse therapeutique. Pour ce faire, les participants seront aleatoirement assignes aux deux conditions de traitement. Une seance d'imagerie par resonnance magnetique sera passee pour evaluer la connectivite et, ensuite, les sujets seront soumis a un traitement TBS pendant six semaines. Ce projet innovant a le potentiel de contribuer a la comprehension clinique des traitements par neuromodulation. Il permettra egalement d'identifier des predicteurs de la reponse au traitement et d'optimiser les recommandations futures.

column36: Molecular imaging to optimize the care of patients with advanced prostate cancer: connecting the dots between radiomics and transcriptomics using artificial intelligence
column37: Prostate cancer (PCa) has the second leading cancer-specific mortality in Canadian men. At time of diagnosis, cancer's aggressiveness is determined to predict the risk of mortality. Molecular imaging can identify distinct features present in cancerous tissues and provide valuable information on their aggressiveness in real time. Radiomics is an innovative approach that extracts quantitative data from medical images. We therefore believe that by harnessing the potential of radiomics, we can produce a predictive smart tool to identify at time of diagnosis high-risk patients to optimize their care and improve their survival.Our goals are (1) to develop a radiomics-based model guided by artificial intelligence to predict relevant clinical outcomes, (2) to analyze the genetic expression of cancerous tissues with variable metabolism visualized on molecular imaging to understand their biological processes, and (3) to implement these data into the tool to increase its predictive accuracy of disease evolution.This is a retrospective study including 343 patients with high-grade PCa that are imaged using molecular imaging between 2011 and 2021 at our institution. Firstly, a radiomics-based model will be developed, and then tested and validated using two distinct sub-cohorts. This model will predict the following endpoints: lymph nodes invasion, time to biochemical recurrence after surgery, time to metastases, time to castration resistance, and cancer-specific mortality. PCa tissues and regional lymph nodes specimens obtained from patients after surgery are analyzed to identify biological processes associated with cancer metabolism. Radiomics and biological data will be processed in a machine learning algorithm to develop a tool predicting the endpoints with better accuracy.

column36: Investigation of human regulatory T cell mechanisms of action and suppression assay development
column37: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) are a specialized type of white blood cell that help maintain a balanced immune system. Tregs can suppress unwanted immune responses, such as those in autoimmunity or in transplant rejection, which has led to the use of Tregs as a cell-based therapy in many immune-related diseases. Tregs can more selectively suppress immune responses, which is a benefit to their use over the commonly used immune-suppressing drugs that broadly suppress the patients immune system and leave them vulnerable to infection. While promising, a limitation to Treg cell therapies is that we do not completely understand how these cells function in humans. Most of our knowledge regarding how Tregs function and the genes involved is based on studies in mice; however, Tregs in mice can function very differently from those in humans. The goal of this project is therefore to develop a better understanding of how human Tregs function to suppress different immune cells. Experiments will use Tregs isolated from male and female thymuses, an organ that contains an abundance of Tregs and that is discarded during heart surgery. I will then use gene-editing technology to delete candidate genes in the isolated thymic Tregs. Gene-deleted Tregs will then be tested for changes in their ability to supress other immune cells, such as B cells and dendritic cells. I will also optimize methods measuring interactions between Tregs and other immune cells. As Tregs hold promise as curative therapies in autoimmunity and transplantation, a better understanding of how Tregs function in humans will help us improve the efficacy of Treg therapies.

column36: The effects of microtubule-associated proteins on microtubule structure and dynamics
column37: The cell is the basic building block of life. The human body is composed of trillions of cells. Inside the cell, there are several machines, or organelles, which serve specific and essential roles. Examples include the mitochondria which produce energy and the ribosomes which construct proteins. However, there are cellular functions that are not accomplished by organelles. Processes such as organelle transport, cell movement, maintaining cell shape, and regulating cell division are accomplished by the cytoskeleton, a highway and scaffolding for the cell. A major component of the cytoskeleton is microtubules. Microtubules are made of a protein called tubulin that come together to form hollow tubes. These hollow tubes are constantly being broken down and built to fulfill the needs of the cell for movement and division. The regulation of microtubules is accomplished by microtubule-associated proteins. There is a vast number of microtubule-associated proteins, many of which are not well understood. Misregulation of microtubule-associated proteins can lead to conditions such as neurodegenerative diseases and cancer. Understanding the functions of microtubule-associated proteins is therefore invaluable in protecting human health. My work will focus on examining the effects of microtubule-associated proteins on microtubules using powerful microscopes and advanced imaging techniques.

column36: Heritability of hidden hearing loss (HHL) and its relationship with cognitive decline
column37: Our proposed research is based on an auditory processing deficit called hidden hearing loss. Hidden hearing loss is caused by defects in the cochlea (the peripheral auditory organ), affecting the perception of sound. Interestingly, individuals with hidden hearing loss often go undetected on standard auditory tests, hence the name hidden hearing loss, as this deficit manifests more prominently in noisy environments, such as at a restaurant or a coffee shop. We are interested in exploring the heritability of hidden hearing loss and whether there is a relationship with cognitive decline. By determining if there is a genetic component to hidden hearing loss it may allow us to identify individuals who are at an increased risk of experiencing this auditory deficit and may potentially enable us to isolate risk genes. Further, we are interested in investigating if there is a relationship between hidden hearing loss and cognitive decline as it has been shown in recent years that there is an association with 'normal' hearing loss and cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease. Therefore, it logically follows that hidden hearing loss may too have an impact on cognitive decline and may serve as a preclinical marker for neurodegenerative disease. We propose to investigate these research questions by creating family pedigrees based on auditory processing and cognitive profiles. The information gained through the completion of this study has implications for various aspects of the healthcare system including, but not limited to, increased patient health, individualized auditory healthcare, and earlier diagnosis of neurodegenerative disease, resulting in a decreased strain on the healthcare system.

column36: Effect of postnatal overfeeding on the development of central nervous system autoimmunity
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease in which a persons immune cells attack and damage their central nervous system (CNS). Females are three times more likely to develop the disease than men and this number is increasing. Another risk factor for developing MS is adolescent obesity. Closely linked to obesity is the onset of puberty, which is also associated with a high risk of MS. However, how adolescent obesity and sex contribute to MS disease onset is unknown. We aim to tease apart the risks of obesity and puberty on CNS autoimmunity by using an animal model of overweight male and female mice to study disease onset and severity. The animal model we will use is experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE), which affects mice with a disease that has similar symptoms and progression to MS. We will create obese adolescent male and female mice by reducing litter sizes so that each mouse pup has access to greater amounts of food, leading to 20-30% weight gain that persists into adulthood. We will monitor weight gain weekly and check for the onset of puberty daily. We will then cause the MS-like disease in the mice and monitor the progression of disease, as well as characterize the immune response in lymph nodes, spleens and the CNS. We will euthanize mice before they show signs of severe suffering due to the disease. Understanding the mechanisms of how both sex and obesity influence the development and progression of MS is critical to developing new treatment and prevention options. We hope that these new treatments will improve the quality of life of individuals with MS. The ultimate goal of this project is to investigate how female sex and obesity contribute and exacerbate the development of CNS autoimmune diseases, like MS.

column36: Automatic Segmentation of Organs at Risk on 3D MRI for Cervical Cancer Brachytherapy
column37: The standard of care for locally advanced cervical cancer includes external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) with concomitant chemotherapy, followed by brachytherapy (BT). BT involves the positioning of a small radioactive source in or close to a tumor using needles or catheters, and has the benefit of a higher radiation dose to the tumor with less exposure to nearby healthy tissues compared to EBRT. One drawback to BT is that the procedure is time intensive. Once the applicator and needles have been inserted, it is necessary to obtain CT or, preferably, MR imaging of the patient in order to confirm the location of the channels relative to anatomical features. Currently, clinical target volumes (CTVs) and nearby healthy organs-at-risk (OARs), as well as the BT applicator, must be manually delineated by a clinician and incorporated into treatment planning. This delineation often takes between 45 and 90 minutes, and thus is a viable target for automation to minimize the total time required for a BT procedure.The aim of the proposed work is to construct a deep learning (DL) model capable of adequately segmenting volumetric MR images for use in BT treatment planning. The model will be trained and tested on previously collected cervical cancer volumetric MRI datasets and their corresponding clinical segmentations. The benefits of automating OARs and CTVs delineation include decreased organ filling between imaging and treatment, decreased time for which the patient is either bedridden or under anaesthesia, and decreased inter-observer segmentation variability, all of which can improve treatment outcomes. This work endeavours to improve the accuracy and convenience of MRI-guided BT for cervical cancer.

column36: The Genetic vs. Environmental Impact on Auditory Processing in the Cntnap2 Knockout Autism Model Rat
column37: In Canada, approximately one in 66 children is diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) each year. Symptoms for ASD include persistent social communication deficits and restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour. Factors causing ASD can be genetic, environmental, or both. For example, there is substantial evidence that dysfunction of the CNTNAP2 gene in humans is a risk factor for developing ASD. In the current study, we use rats that mimic this CNTNAP2 dysfunction, referred here on out as Cntnap2-knockout (KO) rats, to better understand the brain differences underlying ASD. Specifically, we are interested in using this ASD model to examine auditory processing. In our lab, we have found that the Cntnap2-KO rats have an atypical brain response to the presentation of loud tones compared to their typically-developing counterparts. However, the Cntnap2-KO rats were raised by Cntnap2-KO parents, whereas the typically-developing rats were raised by typically-developing parents. This introduces the classic nature vs. nurture question: are the auditory processing differences seen in the KO animals due to the genes they possess or the environment in which they are reared? To test this, we intend to implement a cross-fostering paradigm. This technique involves removing Cntnap2-KO pups from their biological parents and transferring them to be raised by typically-developing parents. As the pups age, we will use a series of tests to assess how the different rearing conditions affect auditory processing, communication, and social interaction. Together, this research will advance our understanding of the auditory and social deficits characteristic of ASD and the potential of these deficits to be malleable by early environmental conditions.

column36: Zero Sperm Count and Biological Fatherhood: A Phenomenological Study
column37: Defined as the inability to conceive after one year of unprotected sexual intercourse, infertility is a major problem that can engender profound psychological distress in men. The experience of male infertility can be particularly devastating for men due to stigma and the sociocultural link between virility and masculinity. About 6% of men in North America are infertile. Of these men, 10-15% are diagnosed with azoospermia (absence of sperm in semen), of which 60% have non-obstructive azoospermia (NOA) caused by impaired sperm production. Though surgical sperm retrieval permits NOA patients to have biological children, the operation fails in about 50% of cases. As men often perceive their inability to conceive as emotionally traumatic, it is critical to understand the experiences of NOA patients, for whom a surgical procedure on the testis is the prerequisite but not a guarantee for biological fatherhood. Through the lens of Critical Studies of Men and Masculinities, this interpretive phenomenological study will be the first to uncover how men with NOA experience their diagnosis and surgical sperm retrieval. Specifically, this study will explore how NOA patients make sense of their decision to pursue surgery, how they reflect on the possibility of operation failure and alternative ways of creating a family, and how their experiences intersect with their sense of masculinity. This understanding can help reproductive specialists and fertility clinic staff better address the psychological needs of NOA patients along with their clinical concerns. Results of this study may contribute to the development of male-informed approaches to fertility care and psychosocial support in order to improve the quality of life of men with NOA.

column36: Characterizing the impact of uncertain mismatch repair-deficient results for individuals undergoing screening for Lynch syndrome
column37: Lynch syndrome (LS) is the most common cause of inherited colorectal cancer (CRC). LS is caused by inherited changes in one of four DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, resulting in an increased risk for developing numerous cancers. When a patient is diagnosed with CRC, they are often screened for LS. As LS is caused by changes in MMR genes, a sample of the tumour is examined for MMR proteins. CRC without the presence of MMR proteins are considered MMR-deficient. Only some patients with MMR-deficient CRC, however, are found to have an inherited mutation in an MMR gene that is consistent with a diagnosis of LS. The remaining group have unexplained MMR deficiency and a diagnosis of LS cannot be confirmed; patients are left without a definitive diagnosis. Using a combination of surveys and qualitative interviews, I will evaluate the ability of these patients to cope with their uncertain diagnosis and what their diagnosis has meant for their family members. For each patient, I aim to evaluate their knowledge and recollection of their results, the information they received from the Genetics clinic, and how screening guidelines align with their current monitoring routines. Patients with MMR-deficient tumors are often treated as if they have LS and are subjected to rigorous, and often unnecessary, cancer screening. Patients who do not have inherited variants do not require the same level of observation, yet current practices lead to many patients being over-screened. Characterizing the impact of uncertain MMR-deficient results may encourage the implementation of additional genetic testing to clarify a diagnosis for these patients and reduce screening recommendations. Findings from this study may also impact how information is provided to individuals with other uncertain diagnoses.

column36: Dissecting the central actions of cannabis for treating chronic pain
column37: Chronic pain is a debilitating medical condition negatively impacting the quality of life of 1 in 5 Canadians, and it is estimated to cost Canadian society an estimated 39 billion dollars annually in healthcare and loss of labour. Neuropathic pain, a subset of chronic pain that is due to damage or disease of the nervous system, is associated with increased pain and disability compared to non-neuropathic chronic pain. In addition, neuropathic pain is often resistant to conventional pain killers like opioids. As such, many pain patients turn to cannabis. However, due to the stigmatized status of cannabis and its associated compounds in many countries around the world, there is little high-quality literature on both the therapeutic and noxious effects of cannabinoids. Since cannabinoids have been legal in Canada since 2018, it is critical to characterize their effects. In my project, I will bridge this gap in the literature by 1) investigating the use of cannabis as an alternative to current treatments for neuropathic pain, and 2) determining the involvement of spinal microgliathe immune cells of the central nervous systemin cannabis-mediated analgesia. Using animal models of nerve pain, I will find the most effective combination of the active ingredients of cannabis for treating pain. Then, I will examine how cannabis acts on the specialized immune cells of the central nervous system, microglia. Microglia are targeted by cannabinoid drugs, and their activation can lead to abnormal pain sensitivity like touch-evoked pain. Using cellular imaging, biochemical and behavioral approaches, I will deconstruct how cannabis modulates the function of microglia in pain. This is essential to determine the effectiveness and improve the safety of cannabis-based pain therapies.

column36: The Impact of Chronic/Latent Viral Infections on T-cell Exhaustion and Senescence in People Living with HIV
column37: Some viruses can make us very sick, but we then get better because our immune system fights them off. Other viruses can last a lifetime, such as HIV or hepatitis C, where our immune system cant get rid of them. There are viruses that stay with us forever and come back intermittently, such as herpes simplex viruses that causes cold sores and genital warts. Our immune system works hard throughout our life to fight these viruses off. Over time, this tires our immune system which then becomes weaker. This can mean that we are less able to fight off common infections than we could when we were young, such as the flu. If our immune system is weak, we are more likely to get cancers caused by some viruses such as lymphomas. People living with HIV tend to have more of these other viruses and they also get more diseases earlier in life, perhaps because the viruses weakens their immune system, even if their HIV is well treated. I hypothesize that persistent viral infections damage our immune system over time, change the type of immune cells we have, and reduce our immune cells ability to activate to fight new infections. I also argue that the on and off activation cycles of the immune system due these lifelong viruses cause the killer cells to become old and tired over time. I propose to study a group of 420 people ranging in age from 1 to 80 years, half of them living with HIV, the other half not, half male and half female. I will look at the types of immune cells that these people have, and how many tired and old immune cells they have, and how these relate to number of viruses that the individual may have. Understanding the effect of these viruses on immune cell aging will inform on the potential benefits of treating or vaccinating against these viruses in the future.

column36: Allergen specific IgG and IgA in breastmilk and the development of allergies: The CHILD Cohort Study

Effector cell responses in allergic reactions will be measured using a basophil activation test to determine the impact of allergen-specific antibody subclasses in breastmilk. This work will deepen our understanding of maternal factors that modify allergen-specific responses and clinical outcomes (allergy, asthma) in offspring, and will allow us to create novel therapeutic and prophylactic strategies to address these prevalent and potentially near-fatal, chronic conditions.

column36: Adaptation of a Self-Compassion Intervention for Treating Psychological Symptoms of Long COVID
column37: Long COVID encompasses a range of physical symptoms that persist following recovery from COVID-19 infection. Beyond the physical consequences, there are concerns regarding the persisting psychological effects of Long COVID. Preliminary research suggests that Long COVID is associated with increased symptoms of depression, anxiety, and posttraumatic stress disorder. While our knowledge of the physical and psychological consequences of Long COVID is growing, limited research has examined interventions for psychological symptoms in Long COVID patients. Research has demonstrated that self-compassion training interventions effectively target symptoms of anxiety, depression, and posttraumatic stress disorder. The proposed study will investigate the effectiveness of a self-compassion training intervention to reduce psychological symptom severity in individuals with Long COVID. Participants will be screened for Long COVID and assigned to an online self-compassion training intervention or a no-intervention control group. Participants in both groups will complete online measures of self-compassion, posttraumatic stress, anxiety, and depression at pre-intervention, post-intervention and 3-month follow-up periods. It is hypothesized that individuals assigned to the intervention condition will report increased levels of self-compassion and decreased symptoms of depression, anxiety, and posttraumatic stress disorder post-intervention and at the three-month follow-up compared to the control condition. column36: Decisions, decisions: choose-your-own adventure geriatric case simulations to improve clinical reasoning in Pharmacy education
column37: The population of adults over the age of 65 in Canada, currently at about 7 million, is projected to reach 10 million by 2030. The increasing elderly population will continue to challenge the healthcare systems capacity. Rising to this challenge are healthcare professionals in primary care, among them pharmacists who can play a significant role in patient-centred care.The health care of older adults is made complex by the combination and interaction of multimorbidity, frailty, and disability. Primary care health professionals are in a unique position, able to provide holistic care for this population. Providing optimal care requires medical knowledge as well as an empathetic understanding of the patients experience. For pharmacy students, this level of expertise is built overtime through experiential learning and simulations of frailty. This research proposal presents another method for consolidating theoretical knowledge and soft-skills in pharmacy education to better prepare clinicians for complex geriatric cases.Simulation-based learning is a safer and more cost-effective method of preparing student clinicians for practice. The aim of this project is to evaluate the effectiveness of simulation-based training compared to traditional methods in improving clinical reasoning in geriatric cases. To reflect the complexity of geriatrics cases, the information will be presented in a choose-your-own-adventure computer simulation, based around real stories and cases. Students can choose treatments and dialogues at each decision-making point, leading to an outcome reflective of their choices. If this method is successful as a training tool, it can serve as a preliminary step in preparing for real-world pharmacy practice, tailored to the health care needs of today.

column36: Effects of Short-Chain Fatty Acids (alone and in combination) on the Adipokine Secretory Profile and Metabolic Function of Adipocytes
column37: White adipose tissue (AT) is an organ active in the metabolism (i.e., uptake, storage, and utilization) of nutrients such as fats and sugars. Fat cells, technically termed adipocytes, within AT produce signaling molecules (called adipokines) that influence local and whole-body inflammation and metabolic function. Certain stress conditions, such as inflammatory signals or low AT oxygen levels (technically termed hypoxia), interfere with normal AT function by increasing the production of pro-inflammatory adipokines, which results in altered AT metabolic function. We have previously shown that dietary long-chain fatty acids improve adipocyte function; however, little is known about the effects of short-chain fatty acids (SCFA) on adipocyte inflammatory adipokine production and metabolic function. SCFA such as acetate, propionate, and butyrate are produced from dietary non-digestible carbohydrates (e.g., fibre). A limited number of studies have only focused on butyrate and show that it can reduce inflammatory adipokine production and prevent the storage of fat in adipocytes. However, the individual and combined effects of acetate, propionate and butyrate on adipocyte function under i) normal, ii) inflammatory, and iii) hypoxia stress conditions have not been extensively investigated. Therefore, the proposed project aims to determine the effects of individual SCFA (alone and in combination) on adipocyte function (including inflammatory adipokine secretion and metabolic function) and will also identify the signaling pathways involved. By studying the effects of individual and combined SCFAs, this project will enhance the current understanding of adipocyte cell biology.

column36: The Role of Membrane Dynamics and Repair in the Resolution of Inflammation
column37: To contain and ultimately alleviate infection and injury, the body mounts an inflammatory response to recruit additional immune cells to the affected site. Upon the removal of the insult, the inflammatory response subsides, a process termed resolution. Failure to resolve inflammatory cascades contributes to a wide variety of diseases rather than correct them. Remarkably, while the mechanisms employed by immune cells to initiate inflammation are well-characterized, the steps involved in its resolution remain poorly understood. One such mechanism is thought to be the physical removal and repair of membrane pores that are responsible for leaching out inflammatory mediators. Repairing cellular membranes involves the internalization or shedding of compromised regions of the membrane followed by the delivery of new surface membrane. These steps are orchestrated and tightly choreographed by molecular machines and complexes that produce force to bend and fuse together the membrane. Importantly, the local forces generated by these complexes can only operate if the tension on the membrane is sufficiently low to permit its remodelling. Our lab has found that relevant cell types in an animal model ;established as being protected from chronic inflammation in response to various types of stimuli; have significantly decreased membrane tension. I am working to understand the connections between membrane tension in these mice and their capacity to dampen the inflammatory cascade with specific attention to membrane repair. By elucidating the protective mechanisms in mice, the results of this study could open the doors to new therapeutic targets to be used in drug development to treat inflammatory diseases.

column36: Investigating the role of the complement system in sickle cell disease
column37: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a life-threatening red blood cell (RBC) disorder that impacts millions of people across the globe and is caused by an inherited change in the protein in RBCs that carries oxygen throughout the body. This results in sickled RBCs that are stiff and prone to getting stuck in small blood vessels, thereby impeding the flow of oxygen to organs and causing extremely painful episodes in patients. This poses an increased risk for serious organ damage, lower quality of life, and premature death. With very few treatment options available, gaining a more comprehensive understanding of the disease is necessary to develop more effective treatments. Recent research points to the complement system having a role in SCD pathogenesis. Sickled RBCs ; especially when ruptured ; can over-activate complement proteins, which are deposited on the surface of blood vessels, causing injury and increasing the risk for clot formation. Complement can also activate immune cells known as neutrophils, causing the formation of sticky net-like traps that increase inflammation, and contribute to clotting. I aim to use a large cohort of pediatric SCD patient samples (collected during crisis episodes and after recovery) to confirm complement over-activation in patients. Then, I will examine the functional consequences of this over-activation on endothelial cells and neutrophils (e.g., increased clot formation, changes in cell activation) in a 2D in vitro model of the vascular environment. Hopefully, my results will point towards new treatment targets and thus help to improve SCD patient outcomes. Importantly, our study is especially relevant to patients of African descent, an often understudied and underserved group in medical research, who are most impacted by SCD.

column37: Malgre les progres de la recherche et le developpement de nouvelles therapies anticancereuses ciblees, le cancer represente la principale cause de mortalite dans le monde en general et au Canada en particulier. En effet, beaucoup de patients en souffrent encore a cause de la resistance developpee par les cellules cancereuses vis-a-vis de ces therapies. Les cellules cancereuses ont la capacite de changer et de remodeler la facon dont elles produisent certaines proteines (synthese proteique), notamment celles impliquees dans leur croissance et dans leur survie. Ceux-ci leur conferent le pouvoir de croitre, de survivre et d'echapper aux traitements anticancereux. Nous voulons limiter ces remodelages de synthese proteique au sein des cellules cancereuses tout en epargnant les cellules saines. Ce ciblage est possible grace aux nouvelles molecules qui inhibent la machinerie de synthese proteique, particulierement indispensable aux cellules cancereuses. Nous prevoyons, d'abord, demontrer l'efficacite de ces molecules en verifiant leur capacite a tuer les cellules cancereuses sensibles et resistantes au traitement cible, mises en culture (in vitro) et a reduire le volume de tumeurs developpees a partir de ces cellules greffees dans un modele de souris (in vivo). Ensuite, nous voulons mettre en evidence les mecanismes moleculaires specifiques impliques dans leur effet sur les cellules cancereuses resistantes. Finalement, ce travail sera fait essentiellement sur l'un des plus importantes tumeurs malignes; soit le cancer de la peau. Il apportera ainsi de nouvelles connaissances scientifiques qui ouvriront la porte pour de nouvelles approches therapeutiques et permettront d'ameliorer la survie et la qualite de vie des patients.

column36: An Analysis of Traumatic Brain Injuries and Health Trajectories in Vancouver's Marginally Housed Population
column37: In Canada, 300,000-3,000,000 people are affected by homelessness and precarious housing (housing that lacks security or stability) (Fazel et al., 2014). These individuals experience high rates of mental and physical illness and higher rates of mortality than the general population (Aldridge et al., 2018; Hwang et al., 2009). Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a global public health challenge (Maas et al., 2017); however, there is little research on how the health of homeless and precariously housed individuals is affected by TBI. Current research is limited due to a lack of objective measures for TBI and the use of cross-sectional designs (Stubbs et al., 2020). The objective for my masters is to utilize data from a comprehensive longitudinal study of health in homeless and precariously housed individuals (The Hotel Study, PIs: Honer Panenka) to characterize how brain structure and health trajectories are affected by TBI. The Hotel Study worked with the Downtown Eastside residents to evaluate health and functioning and measure the effects of TBI. I will analyze the neuroimaging and health data from this study to model health trajectories and evaluate risk factors for brain degeneration. I expect that this work will clarify the complexities in how health trajectories of this vulnerable population are affected by TBI. This research will have implications that may benefit homeless and precariously housed individuals around the globe, while improving the general understanding and awareness of health and functioning in this population.

column36: Exploring the Undergraduate Nursing Students' Experience of Knowledge Acquisition about Digital Health
column37: Digital Health (DH) is a rapidly evolving field, further accelerated by the demands of the ongoing pandemic. For nurses, whose scope of practice uniquely encompasses implementation of DH technologies throughout the continuum of healthcare delivery from clinician to patient, the extent to which knowledge acquisition and competence in this field has been developed remains unclear. Unfortunately, DH is not yet explicitly integrated into nursing curricula across Canada, thus creating a discrepancy between the demands on newly graduating nurses and their educational experience about the field. To address this gap, the proposed qualitative descriptive study aims to explore the experience of undergraduate nursing students throughout this process, focusing on the learning processes and contexts of their nursing education and their perceived preparedness to provide care utilizing DH technologies. A series of semi-structured interviews will be conducted with a purposive sample of final year undergraduate students within the two programs at McGill University Ingram School of Nursing. These interviews will be transcribed verbatim, then manual open coding performed and analyzed using an inductive approach. Insights uncovered from this study should serve to provide a basis from which to evaluate proposed educational approaches in subsequent research and serve to support a framework for DH competencies that should be included. As McGill University is multicultural and diverse in its student population, with an explicit emphasis on Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion, the study should uncover a holistic perspective that will serve to enrich nursing education in the future, particularly around new frontiers in healthcare which they are uniquely positioned to pioneer.

column36: Role de DUSP4 dans le diabete et la maladie des arteres peripheriques.
column37: La maladie des arteres peripheriques est une complication majeure liee au diabete. Elle est causee par une reponse insuffisante de formation de vaisseaux collateraux a la suite d'une occlusion. Notre laboratoire a montre que le diabete diminue l'expression de DUSP4, une phosphatase associee a l'inflammation et la dysfonction vasculaire dans le muscle ischemique en passant par la regulation de l'activite des MAPK p38 et Jnk.Notre hypothese est qu'une surexpression de DUSP4 en condition de diabete diminuerait la dysfonction endotheliale et le processus inflammatoire tout en favorisant la formation de vaisseaux collateraux dans le muscle ischemique de souris diabetiques.Le premier objectif est d'etudier les mecanismes par lesquels DUSP4 mene a une dysfonction des cellules endotheliales vasculaires (CE). Pour ce faire, des CE seront exposees a des concentrations normales (5,6mM) ou elevees (25mM) de glucose, avec ou sans une surexpression de DUSP4 dans des conditions hypoxiques (1% oxygene). Des analyses geniques, proteiques ainsi que des essais de migration, de proliferation et de formation de tubules seront realises pour evaluer l'impact de DUSP4 sur les processus angiogeniques. Le second objectif est de caracteriser l'effet d'une augmentation de DUSP4 dans un modele murin diabetique d'ischemie. Pour ce faire, des souris diabetiques et non-diabetiques surexprimant ou non DUSP4, de facon generale (Dusp4TG)) ou dans les CE (Dusp4ECTG), subiront une ligature de l'artere femorale. Leur revascularisation sera suivie et des analyses proteiques, geniques et histologiques seront effectues.En conclusion, ce projet permettra de mieux comprendre les phenomenes induits par le diabete et ses consequences sur la faible creation de nouveaux vaisseaux sanguins suite a une ischemie.

column36: The development of a tailored online mindfulness program for individuals with spinal cord injury
column37: Individuals with spinal cord injury (SCI) are at risk for developing issues related to their mental health. Depression is the most common psychological problem that people with SCI face, affecting 25;30% of individuals with SCI living in the community. However, individuals with SCI have limited access to programs that address their specific mental health needs. Hence, there is a need to improve access to programs that address the mental health and wellness of people with SCI and ensure that these programs are catered to their specific needs. Creating mindfulness programs can address these issues, as it has been successful in other illnesses such as multiple sclerosis. However, there is a lack of research in mindfulness for people with SCI. I aim to identify the considerations to implement an online mindfulness program to improve the quality of life in people with SCI. Based on the results of an earlier qualitative study, I will build a survey that will be administered online to ask approximately 100 individuals with SCI across Canada to rate the importance of various program components (e.g., program content, who should deliver the program, how the program should be delivered, etc.). These individuals will be recruited using online advertisements posted on community-based organizations such as SCI Canada. The results of this research will lead to recommendations for an online mindfulness program that considers the specific needs of people with SCI. In doing so, this program will be both relevant and accessible, and improve the emotional well-being and overall quality of life of individuals with SCI.

column36: FAN1 as a Genetic Modifier in Rett Syndrome
column37: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder which primarily effects females and is characterized by loss of motor, coordination and communication abilities. Over 95% of individuals with RTT have a mutation in the MECP2 gene, resulting in the gene not functioning properly, leading to disease. However, variable severity is observed in patients with RTT. One possible explanation for this observation are modifier genes. Such modifiers are genes that do not directly cause disease, but can alter the severity and age of onset of genetic diseases. In addition to explaining the variable severity seen in RTT, modifier genes may aid in the discovery of new treatment options. This is of particular importance in RTT, as current treatments focus on symptomatic treatment and have limited effectiveness. For instance, one recent study in mice found that a mutation in the FAN1 gene improved the health and life span of mice with classic RTT Mecp2 mutations. The FAN1 gene is involved in DNA repair and has previously been shown to influence the age of onset of the neurodegenerative disease, Huntington disease. It is therefore the goal of this project to determine if the FAN1 modifier effect for RTT detected in mice, also has beneficial consequences in human RTT cells that resemble those found in the brain. Specifically, if there is a beneficial effect of FAN1 loss at the molecular level in patient-derived cells. To accomplish this, genomic and molecular methods will be used.

column36: Uncovering new targets for the fight against methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus infections: Targeting Polyamine Detoxification
column37: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) is the leading cause of hospital and community-acquired infections. The most prevalent community-acquired MRSA strain USA300 has acquired the arginine catabolic mobile element, which encodes SpeG. SpeG acetylates polyamines, which are small cationic molecules overproduced at infection sites, rendering them less toxic. To identify unknown polyamine resistance determinants in USA300, we performed a whole-genomic screen against spermine and identified targets with increased susceptibility. I identified two targets of primary interest, sbnB::Tn and speG::Tn, that showed an 8-fold decrease in the minimum inhibitory concentration of spermine. Previous studies suggest that SbnB oxidatively hydrolyzes N-(1-amino-1-carboxyl-2-ethyl)-glutamic acid, which is structurally similar to polyamines. Therefore, I hypothesize that SbnB plays a role, along with SpeG, in protecting S. aureus from the bactericidal effects of polyamines. The objectives of this project are to: 1 characterize the mechanism of SbnB and 2 identify new antimicrobials that interfere with MRSA's response to polyamines. In objective 1, I will clone, purify, and overexpress SbnB to study its role in polyamine detoxification, using relevant biochemical assays. In objective 2, I will perform a high-throughput screen with a library of previously approved drugs and polyamine analogs to identify inhibitors of polyamine response mechanisms. I will follow the screen with relevant biochemical assays to confirm the phenotype. This work is significant as it will provide functional characterization of the response of S. aureus to polyamines, uncovering new host-pathogen interactions. Further, it will offer a new treatment strategy for antibiotic-resistant S. aureus infections.

column36: Investigating the effect of new remuneration and care models on panel size of family physicians in Ontario.
column37: The Ontario healthcare system currently faces two significant challenges: labour shortages and funding limitations. These challenges impact patient access to timely and effective care and will become more pronounced as the population ages. Delayed care has been shown to result in an increased risk of negative health outcomes for patients. Therefore, re-evaluation of the current distribution of healthcare resources is critical. In Ontario, several initiatives are currently underway that adjust the scope of practice and remuneration of current primary healthcare workers in the effort to improve patient access to care. However, how these initiatives impact the panel size - the number of patients under a provider - of doctors has not been thoroughly analyzed. By investigating the interrelationship between care delivery methods, funding structures, and panel size, this project aims to: (1) isolate variables that impact physician-to-patient ratios and (2) determine the relative effect of these variables on physician-to-patient ratios. This project will take a quantitative approach to establish a correlation between a family physician's panel size and the payment and care delivery models they are employed under. A retrospective cohort study will be conducted to achieve this. Data used for this study will be extracted from the Canadian Community Health Survey and the Health Care Experience Survey, linked with the Ontario health administrative data from the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences. Results can be used to inform policymakers and physicians on how to move forward with future directives in Ontario and illuminate whether the new initiatives result in a greater patient capacity of the healthcare system.

column36: Exploring the Impact of Endothelial Bone Morphogenetic Protein Receptor 2 Loss on Phosphoinositide Dynamics and the Pathobiology of Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension
column37: Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH) is a disease of high blood pressure in the lungs that affects thousands of Canadians. Cell overgrowth on the inner lining of lung blood vessels is a PAH hallmark: the limited space for blood flow causes high blood pressure in the arteries that take blood from the heart to the lungs. Current treatments for PAH help manage symptoms; however, they do not reverse disease progression. Hence, 15% of PAH patients die yearly from right heart failure.Cells on the inner lining of arteries in the lung have many regulated compartments with specific roles to preserve normal cell function. Notably, a complex network of movable compartments takes molecules into the cell and targets them for destruction or recycles them back to the cell surface. Alternatively, this network can transport new molecules made in the cell, sort them, and take them to their appropriate cellular location. Phosphoinositides (PIs) are a family of eight different fat molecules each found in the membranes of different compartments in the transport network.Bone Morphogenetic Protein Receptor 2 (BMPR2) mutations are present in many people with PAH. Our lab has shown that BMPR2 mutations cause compartment transport abnormalities. This project aims to use the different location of PIs in cell compartment membranes as a tool to assess the function of the transport network in BMPR2 mutant cells. We expect that BMPR2 mutation will cause altered compartment transport and an enhanced response to molecules that cause blood vessel cell overgrowth. Our goal is to determine the mechanism behind altered cellular compartment movement and blood vessel cell overgrowth caused by BMPR2 mutation. Ultimately, we hope our findings will support research toward curative treatments for PAH.

column36: A Novel Mendelian Randomization Approach to Assess Treatment Outcomes in Patient Subgroups
column37: Medical treatment decisions involve a balance of risks and benefits. While these risks and benefits are typically well defined for the general population, they are less clear for patient subgroups. For example, the effectiveness of cholesterol-lowering medications in reducing the risk of heart disease may vary across individuals of different ages and disease states. This information is important to know, as it can help healthcare providers tailor treatments to patients based on their clinical profiles. To identify subgroups of patients that are more or less likely to benefit from treatments, the Mendelian Randomization (MR) framework will be used. MR uses genetic variants related to a risk factor to determine how the risk factor is causally related to a disease. The use of genetic variants is key to the techniques ability to determine a causal effect rather than a simple association. This is because genetic variants are randomly allocated during conception and eliminate the involvement of common confounding variables such as environmental factors.We will be adapting the traditional MR framework to examine the relationship between risk factors and diseases for different biomarker levels using the UK Biobank database. For example, the effect of blood cholesterol levels on the risk of heart disease will be assessed for patients with different blood glucose levels. If cholesterol levels are not found to affect heart disease risk for patients with certain blood glucose levels, it could mean that it may actually be more beneficial for these individuals to withdraw from cholesterol-lowering therapy. This novel MR methodology will open a new paradigm of studies for determining treatment effects in patient subgroups and help tailor treatments to individual patients.

column36: Functional immune consequences of helminth induced modification of the host bile acid pool
column37: Parasitic worms can manipulate and subdue the immune responses of their host. This helps them to establish long-term infections in the gut. Understanding how parasitic worms do so helps to advise treatment for over a billion people worldwide who are currently infected. Understanding ways to manipulate gut immune responses may reveal new treatment strategies for inflammatory bowel diseases, such as Crohns and colitis. It is known that bile acids, which are important for fat digestion, can act as signals that reduce inflammation in the gut and can also control how quickly food moves through the gut. Previous research in the Reynolds Lab found that during parasitic worm infection in a mouse model, the concentration of bile acids in the small intestine is reduced. The overall hypothesis of my project is that these changes in bile acid levels affect the immune response during worm infections. Using a mouse model of parasitic worm infection, my research will investigate which gut immune cell types are responding to altered bile acid levels during infection. My work will also explore the impact of altered bile acid levels on immune responses in the small intestine. I will raise and lower bile acid levels in the mouse small intestine by feeding uninfected and parasite-infected mice specialized diets, and measure how this affects the speed of food passage through the small intestine and the levels of immune signalling molecules (cytokines). All experiments will be repeated 3 times to ensure the validity of my findings, and I will share my results in publications and conference presentations. My work will provide new information about how bile acids influence immune responses and help us to better understand changes in immune cell function during parasitic worm infection.

column36: Investigating whether stress related to the COVID-19 pandemic negatively impacted parent-child attachment in infants
column37: The proposed study aims to investigate whether the COVID-19 pandemic had a negative impact on mother-child attachment. The pandemic upended daily life creating more stressors, particularly on parents and families. Stress has been found to limit parental responsivity, which negatively affects mother-child attachment. This has lifelong consequences as insecure attachment is associated with poor social and emotional competence, self-esteem, coping strategies and more. Since, COVID-19 upended life in a way that had not been experienced before, and the last respiratory illness pandemic of this severity was in 1918, there is limited research on the effect a pandemic has on childhood development. Previous research has studied adult coping to the COVID-19 pandemic, and mother-child attachment during the pandemic only immediately following birth. It remains to be studied how the pandemic affects attachment development over the first year, and how the potential role of stress impacts the relationship between respective parent and child attachment styles. The proposed study seeks to answer: What is the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on an infants attachment to their primary caregiver? To answer this, children born between January 1 2020 and July 1 2020 will be recruited along with a parent. The Strange Situation will be conducted with the children while the parent will participate in the Adult Attachment Interview and the Perceived Stress Scale-12, which the parent will be asked to complete retrospectively based on the COVID-19 time period. column36: Physiological functioning and disordered eating among sexually and gender diverse people
column37: Eating disorders (EDs) are mental illnesses usually viewed as only affecting women. However, men can also suffer from EDs. Some studies report that a large proportion of those men are gay or bisexual. In fact, homosexuality is a specific risk factor for EDs; however, the literature is still scarce on this issue. Moreover, gender diverse people (i.e. trans, non-binary) are also understudied in research on EDs, but we know that these people can have body image disturbances that can trigger ED-related pathology. Taken together, ourobjectives are to study the interaction between disordered eating and sexual orientation/gender identity. A pseudo-experimental study will compare LGBTQ+ participants with cis-heterosexual participants on their tendency to restric their caloric intake. Every participant will have to consume one or more milkshakes. Then, they will be asked to consume a self-chosen quantity of ice cream. This pseudo-experimentation has shown in past research conducted only among cis-heterosexual people that participants that restrict their food intake usually binge on ice cream afterwards. In addition to the experiment focused on caloric restriction, our study will measure cortisol (the stress hormone) and two peptides known to play a role in hunger and satiety (ghrelin and leptin) to assess for biological differences between the participants and any reactivity of these physiological systems. Finally, this study will also measure different psychological variables, such as attitudes regarding food and body image, mental health, and weight history. This study will allow clinicians to know more about specific risk factors for LGBTQ+ people regarding disordered eating or EDs, and will shed light on an understudied topic.

column36: Understanding how Cannabis Use Features within the Gender Experiences of Transgender, Non-Binary & Gender-Questioning Youth
column37: Transgender, non-binary, (herein, trans) and gender-questioning youth are faced with various life challenges including discrimination, lack of access to gender-affirming healthcare, stigma, and ongoing violence. These negative experiences in society are often related to higher levels of mental health challenges and substance use concerns amongst this population. For example, trans youth experience some of the highest rates of cannabis use in Canada compared to their cisgender counterparts. Despite previous research which points to some harmful effects of cannabis use during adolescence, there is a growing body of research that associates cannabis use with positive effects, specifically in facilitating sexual and gender identity formation. However, there is a need for research which aims to understand the role which cannabis may play in mobilizing trans identity. Therefore, this study will examine the ways in which cannabis may be used to cope with mental health challenges associated with navigating ones gender, while also exploring whether cannabis use among trans youth facilitates the expression of non-normative gender identities. Specifically, qualitative, semi-structured interviews, as well as photovoice methodology will be used to gain a more in-depth understanding of how these associations unfold amongst trans and gender-questioning youth. Data from this research will be analyzed by drawing on thematic similarities observed between interviews to develop understandings related to cannabis use and gender experiences. The key findings from this study will inform how community-based programs and interventions can best support trans and gender-questioning youth who use cannabis and will be translated back to community by hosting a community photo exhibit.

column36: Investigating the Effects of Receptor Clustering on Immune Cell Activation using Multivalent Synthetic Probes to Guide Cancer Immunotherapeutic Design
column37: Cancer immunotherapy works by using the bodys own immune system to treat cancer. A type of immunotherapeutic known as ;molecular adapters work by binding immune cells and linking them to targeted tumour cells, allowing the immune cells to kill the tumour cells. One way that immune cells kill is through phagocytosis, which is activated by the clustering of Fc receptors on the cell surface. How molecular adapters interact with immune receptors to modulate receptor clustering is unknown. We hypothesize that the efficacy of Fc clustering and the resultant anti-tumour response of molecular adapters depend on the number, spatial array, and stability of interactions between the molecular adapters and the receptors. We will use a synthetic, multivalent DNA scaffold that can precisely tune these parameters to investigate their effects on immune cell activation. The DNA scaffold will have CP33, a peptide known to bind the humanFcγRI immune receptor, anchored to it at selected locations using click chemistry. We plan to synthesize several different scaffolds that will bind a different number ofFcγRI receptors and hold those receptors at different distances apart on the cell surface. We will then use immunobiological flow cytometry assays the asses the level of immune cell activation that results from treatment with the different scaffolds. These findings will not only further our understanding of how the anti-tumour response of molecular adapters is impacted by the interactions between the molecular adapters and immune cell receptors, but they can also be used to guide future immunotherapeutic design. The CP33 peptide can be easily replaced by novel peptides that bind other immune receptors, allowing this platform to be adapted to study different receptors in future research.

column36: Novel Anti-Cancer Strategy: Targeting Integrin Beta3 PSI Domain Simultaneously Impedes Cancer Angiogenesis, Metastasis and Thrombosis
column37: Cancer remains the primary cause of death in Canada due to its ability to spread throughout the body, and create secondary complications of cancer-associated thrombotic disease, or in other words a blockage in the circulatory system. Platelets, which we are ordinarily familiar with for their role in stopping bleeding, play a very important supportive role in cancer disease development. They provide tumors with the means to create new blood vessels vital for gathering necessary nutrients, and form a protective coat around cancer cells that spread to other organs through the blood. One very important commonality between cancer cells and platelets are integrins: cell surface proteins comprised of two parts, called α and β subunits, which are important for cell adhesion to its environment, and the sending and receiving of cellular signals. In this study, we are interested in integrin αIIbβ3 on platelets as it is responsible for platelet activation and subsequent release of important cancer signals. For cancer cells, we are interested in integrin αVβ3 which is responsible for the tumors ability to create new blood vessels and enter those vessels to spread. Notably, there is a common denominator on both cells integrins: the β3 subunit, for which our lab has developed a highly specific antibody which interrupts both αIIbβ3 and αVβ3 function. Our initial data has shown evidence of combating cancer through blocking two pivotal mechanisms, tumor creation of blood vessels and the spreading of cancer to other organs, as well as alleviating cancer-associated thrombosis. Our study will further reveal the importance of how and why cancer exploits platelets for disease progression, and provide insight to a novel anti-cancer solution for current and future therapeutic development.

column36: Are Mild Traumatic Brain Injury and Concussion Separate Entities? A Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging Study
column37: While mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) has received increased attention over the past decade, gaps in our knowledge are ever-present. The term concussion is often used interchangeably with mTBI, however the lack of a uniform definition for each term gives rise to confusion among not only patients, but also healthcare providers. In attempts to combat this growing health concern, the World Health Organization (WHO) defined mTBI with focus on the diagnostic criteria and treatment of the condition. In contrast, the Concussion in Sport Group (CISG) created a consensus statement to define sport related concussion (SRC), placing emphasis on the functional disturbances that acutely follow concussion. This statement suggests that if post-concussive symptoms are present, a concussion should be suspected, and the appropriate management strategies should be implemented. As these two definitions do not necessarily concur with one another, diagnostic difficulties present themselves when individuals fit the more inclusive SRC criteria but lack distinctive features of the mTBI criteria as defined by the WHO. In the proposed research, we will use functional magnetic resonance imaging techniques to uncover the neural mechanisms underlying the CISG SRC criteria compared to the WHO mTBI criteria. As working memory has been seen as a hallmark of cognitive deficit in mTBI and concussion, participants will perform a verbal working memory task and alterations in cerebral functioning will be identified and analyzed between groups. This study has the potential to clarify which operational definitions of mTBI and concussion are appropriate, with long-term objectives of eliminating inconsistencies across disciplines and solidifying the diagnostic processes and management of these injuries.

column36: Fonctions et regulation d'Otefin a l'enveloppe nucleaire et aux centrosomes
column37: Des defauts moleculaires a l'enveloppe nucleaire sont a l'origine ou contribuent a des maladies humaines incluant des cancers et des dystrophies. Une meilleure connaissance des mecanismes moleculaires de formation de l'enveloppe nucleaire apres la mitose et du maintien de sa structure pourrait permettre de mieux comprendre ces maladies et de developper des tests diagnostiques ou des pistes therapeutiques. Les genes et proteines qui fonctionnent a l'enveloppe nucleaire sont tres similaires entre les especes animales. Nous utilisons la mouche a fruits (drosophile) comme modele. Elle nous permet de combiner des approches experimentales genetiques, biochimiques et microscopiques. Les connaissances acquises s'appliquent le plus souvent aussi a l'humain.En mitose, l'enveloppe nucleaire se brise pour permettre aux chromosomes d'etre partitionnes par l'appareil mitotique. Ce bris est induit par des enzymes kinases qui ajoutent des groupements phosphates a des proteines substrats pour briser leurs interactions. A la fin de la mitose, des enzymes phosphatases enlevent les phosphates pour induire la reformation de l'enveloppe. Nous avons trouve que la proteines Otefin (Emerin chez l'humain) de l'enveloppe est dephosphorylee par la phosphatase PP2A-B55. Nous emettons l'hypothese que cet evenement promeut l'interaction d'Otefin avec ses proteines partenaires d'interaction a l'enveloppe (BAF et lamine). Nous avons aussi trouve une nouvelle partenaire pour Otefin qui s'appelle Girdin. Comme les deux proteines se localisent en partie aux centrosomes, nous supposons que leur complexe participe a la cohesion entre les centrosomes et l'enveloppe. Cette cohesion est essentielle dans plusieurs types de cellules dont les lignees germinales. Dans mon projet, je testerai ces deux hypotheses.

column36: Identification de nouvelles cibles therapeutiques pour la steatose hepatique non-alcoolique
column37: La steatose hepatique non alcoolique (SHNA), couramment appelee la maladie du foie gras, est la maladie hepatique la plus frequente. Celle-ci touche deja plus d'un adulte sur quatre en Amerique du Nord. Malheureusement, il n'existe pas de therapies efficaces et approuvees specifiquement pour la SHNA, dont les complications peuvent etre irreversibles et engendrer d'importantes consequences sur la sante. Notre objectif est d'utiliser des donnees genetiques humaines afin de faire avancer le developpement et la validation de medicaments pour la SHNA. La majorite des medicaments ciblent des proteines exprimees par le genome humain et les cibles therapeutiques validees par des variations genetiques ont 3 a 4 fois plus de chances d'etre approuves par les autorites reglementaires. Pour ce faire, nous identifierons de nouvelles cibles therapeutiques, parmi des proteines sanguines, causant la SHNA et determineront leur potentiel a l'aide de la genetique. Nous combinerons egalement les donnees de notre institut, qui possede l'une des plus grandes biobanques de foies au Canada, avec les donnees de notre recente etude genetique de la SHNA, la plus complete a ce jour (8434 cas de SHNA et 770 614 temoins). Notre etude validera l'implication causale de >3000 proteines sur la SHNA en utilisant les variants genetiques associes a leurs concentrations sanguines. Ces donnees, provenant de 10 cohortes differentes, identifieront des candidats therapeutiques avant le lancement d'essais cliniques couteux ou valideront des etudes cliniques en cours pour la SHNA. Ainsi, mon projet de maitrise visera l'amelioration des connaissances liees au spectre de la SHNA et l'acceleration de la decouverte de nouveaux medicaments efficaces et securitaires afin d'aider les patients souffrant de cette maladie.

column36: Effects of a Mindfulness-Based Intervention on Deficit Awareness in Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI): A Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) is one of the leading causes of disability globally, with incidence rates rising. Direct and indirect costs of TBI are a huge burden on Canadas health and employment sectors. Individuals who have sustained a moderate or severe TBI commonly exhibit a lack of awareness of their deficits (a form of self-awareness) - sometimes referred to as anosognosia. Impaired deficit awareness is detrimental to motivation, treatment participation, and rehabilitation. The purpose of this study is to explore if mindfulness meditation (MM) can improveawareness in individuals with TBI. A key component of MM is self-awareness and prior research indicates that mindfulness practice can alter neural substrates that support self-awareness and self-referential processes.In the proposed study, 86 adults with moderate or severe TBI will be randomized to an 8-week mindfulness-based intervention (MBI) or a waitlist control. Participants and their spouses/partners will complete primary outcome measures (Awareness Questionnaire) pertaining to the patient at three-time points: before, immediately after, and at a 3 month follow up. The discrepancy between patient and observer will serve to measure deficit awareness. Secondary outcome measures include neuropsychological tests, the Patient Competency Rating Scale, the Mindful Attention Awareness Scale, and the Satisfaction with Life Scale. TBI severity will be investigated as a moderator of response to treatment.This study advances MM research for TBI, which shows promise as a cost-effective and accessible treatment option. Impaired deficit awareness is observed in several other populations such as individuals with schizophrenia, Alzheimers, and stroke; thus, findings of this study have impact beyond TBI populations.

column36: Investigating cannabis use among Canadian women experiencing menstrual cycle distress
column37: Since the Canadian legalization of recreational cannabis, millions of Canadians (15 or older) have used, or are continuously using cannabis. The popularity of cannabis has risen with government acceptance, ease of legal access, and widely known potential health benefits including alleviation of chronic and pelvic pain, headaches, cramping, gastrointestinal distress, and feelings of anxiousness and depressed mood. We know little, however, on how cannabis use may impact women experiencing their menstrual cycles. Moreover, there is scarce research on how potential self-medicative practices might develop in individuals experiencing mood-related and physical distress as of consequence of their menstrual cycle. The purpose of this study is to determine whether cannabis frequency, quantity, and mode of intake are associated with the physical or affective symptoms experienced during the menstrual cycle. Of secondary interest is the knowledge of those using cannabis. Menstrual cycle distress (e.g., depressed mood, tension, irritability, cramping) is a common occurrence in women following puberty. However, for a striking number of individuals, their distress is incapacitating, stopping them from attending social gatherings, completing daily routines, and attending work. Many women experiencing depressed and anxious feelings, or physical pain seek alleviation of these symptoms through treatment. Some comfort has been identified as achievable with pain killers, homeopathic remedies, and topical creams. The existing literature also suggests that women might turn to cannabis for relief of menstrual cycle symptoms. The proposed study could inform diagnosis and treatment of menstrual cycle distress where cannabis is a treatment option, as well as implications for substance misuse.

column36: Extra-pancreatic function of GLP-1-based diabetes drugs- Involvement of FGF21
column37: Insulin has saved millions of lives world widely for a century, while GLP-1 as an incretin, stimulates insulin secretion postprandially. GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists (GLP-1RAs) including liraglutide (Lira) are therapeutic agents for subjects with diabetes or obesity. Scientists have learned for years that GLP-1 and GLP-1RAs exert extra-pancreatic functions, which explains their capability in treating insulin resistance. Our lab is particularly interested in hepatic function of GLP-1RAs and have revealed recently that hepatic hormone FGF21 is the linkage molecule that mediates functions of Lira in reducing body weight and improving metabolic homeostasis in high fat diet challenged mice. As GLP-1R is not expressed in mouse or human liver, we hypothesize that brain GLP-1R mediates effects of peripheral Lira administration on stimulating hepatic FGF21 production; that Lira and other GLP-1 based drugs also improves FGF21 sensitivity, which contributes to insulin sensitivity improvement; and that the GLP-1/FGF21 axis also functions in white adipose tissues (WAT), which contributes to improved metabolic homeostasis. A) I will test whether the stimulatory effect of peripheral Lira treatment on FGF21 expression is attenuated in brain specific GLP-1R knockout mice. B) I will establish both in vitro and in vivo tools to measure FGF21 sensitivity, and assess whether improvement on FGF21 sensitivity leads to improved insulin sensitivity. C) I will test whether Lira treatment increases WAT browning and energy expenditure, and whether GLP-1R and adipose tissue produced FGF21 are involved. My study will deepen our knowledge on the extra-pancreatic function of GLP-1, and pave the way for the development of future therapeutic approach for metabolic disorders including T2D.

column37: Behavioural pain assessment tools have been developed to detect and assess painful experiences in people with severe dementia and limited ability to communicate due to cognitive impairment. Despite available psychometric evaluations, it has not been demonstrated that observational pain assessment tools, specifically developed for patients with dementia, are more valid when used in this population than observational tools developed for other populations (e.g., children with intellectual disabilities). Moreover, it is unclear whether tools developed for a specific context (e.g., orofacial pain) would be any less effective in discriminating painful from non-painful situations than more general pain assessment tools. The proposed study seeks to address these gaps in the literature by comparing the psychometric properties of several pain tools specialized for use in dementia to several non-specialized pain tools. It seeks to further validate a newly specialized meta-tool for assessing pain by comparing its psychometric properties and ability to differentiate between painful and non-painful states to other assessment measures. Repeated measure analysis of variance (ANOVA), analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), and regression equations will be used to evaluate psychometric properties and assessment accuracy. Findings from this study will address gaps in the literature concerning the comparative properties of specialized and non-specialized behavioural tools for assessing pain in patients living with dementia. This novel information will contribute to the empirical knowledge on how behavioural pain measures for dementia should be studied and furthermore, whether tools specifically developed for people with dementia are superior to tools developed with other populations in mind.

column36: Neural signatures of naturalistic speech listening in mild cognitive impairment
column37: As our society ages, diagnosis and treatment of age-related cognitive decline is of high priority. Altered speech processing is often an early sign of cognitive decline, but current speech perception assessment tools rely on simple speech materials that are not very motivating and may not tap into mechanisms recruited in everyday life. More naturalistic approaches are thus critically needed. The research will be a critical step towards the ecologically valid assessment of speech capabilities in people with cognitive impairment, and, in the long-term, will help inform diagnostic measures and assessment of treatment outcomes in people with MCI.
