column36: The Impact of Bilingualism on Executive Function in Children Born Pre-Term or At Low Birthweight
column37: According to the World Health Organization, approximately 15 million babies each year are born pre-term (PT), typically with low birthweight, and the number of these children continues to rise. Studies have shown that as these children develop they have impairments in executive function (EF) which are a set of mental skills such as working memory, cognitive flexibility, and self-control. These impaired EFs show little improvement as children age, even with recent advances in medical care. Early interventions during the sensitive time period of brain development for EF (i.e., 0 to 6 years old) are warranted to improve outcomes. There is growing evidence that bilingualism could enhance EF skills across the lifespan, although the precise role of bilingualism in EF has been controversial. For example, some researchers have shown that bilingualism confers an advantage to EF skills, whereas others have identified negative or null outcomes. The objective of this research will be to assess the effects of bilingualism on EF skills in children born PT and/or at low birthweight in comparison to full-term (FT). To do this, we will be using the Building Brains Together curriculum composed of 10 playful games which have been proven by previous literature to enhance areas of EF. I hypothesize that bilingual children will score higher on measures of EF than monolinguals who have completed the program. Furthermore, I expect bilingual children born PT and/or at low birthweight to score higher on measures of EF in comparison to their monolingual counterparts. The implications of this research could aide health professionals counselling families about the benefit of bilingualism for their children who may be susceptible to EF deficits due to pre-maturity and/or low birthweight.

column36: Using 2D and 3D models to investigate the role of GABARAPL2 in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma treatment response
column37: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a major class of pancreatic cancers that accounts for more than 90% of diagnosed cases. Fast progression, late-stage diagnosis, and drug resistance are among factors that make PDAC an aggressive and difficult cancer to treat. Autophagy is an intracellular degradative pathway that is widely considered a driving force for PDAC survival and treatment resistance. Our recent work has suggested that high levels of GABARAPL2 (an autophagy-related protein) in PDAC could reflect enhanced treatment response and improved survival outcomes in PDAC patients treated with adjuvant chemotherapy. The objectives of this current project are to first confirm that GABARAPL2 levels are similarly associated with treatment response in experimental models of PDAC and second, to investigate if modulating GABARAPL2 levels have a direct impact on the observed effects. To manipulate GABARAPL2 expression levels, I will introduce additional copies of the GABARAPL2 gene and also suppress or inactivate the expression of endogenous GABARAPL2. Next the drug concentrations required to reduce the viability of PDAC cells will be deduced. Conventional 2D cell culture models will be used alongside 3D organoid models to better mimic actual PDAC tumors. Together, these studies are expected to help guide treatment strategies for PDAC patients--specifically, to uncover potential molecular mechanisms of treatment resistance and to identify those who may present a clinical benefit in receiving adjuvant chemotherapy versus those who may not.

column36: Measuring disease progression in Parkinson's disease using administrative health data
column37: Parkinsons disease (PD) is the second most common degenerative brain disease. It leads to shaking, difficulty with walking and moving. Until now, no cures exist. Developing a drug ;from scratch is expensive and time-consuming. ;Drug repurposing is a process by which researchers test a drug already used for a given disease, for a new purpose. To do so, they often use health administrative data. These include millions of individuals and are generated at every encounter with the healthcare system, for example, when visiting a doctors office or the hospital. With these data, researchers can easily test whether a drug is associated with decreased disease progression or severity. One major barrier to use these data in PD is that until now, there is no reliable tool that measures disease progression in health administrative data. My research interest is to develop this tool. I will first develop an algorithm within the health administrative data from Ontario by investigating which codes can reliably represent PD complications. For example, these include dementia and falls, among others. The ;score of progression will be based on the time to onset of these complications, as we expect them to occur earlier in PD compared to controls. Once this algorithm is created, I will validate it using clinical information from real-life PD patients at the movement disorders clinic. This step is to ensure that the algorithm is reliable and represents well the information we are obtaining from health administrative data. This project is important as it will expedite large scale rapid searches to identify drugs associated with reduced PD progression. It will also encourage future clinical trials to test whether these drugs are efficacious and can be approved by governing agencies for PD.

column36: Using prebiotic fiber to reduce risk of anxiety-like behaviors in rats born by Caesarean section
column37: The rate of Caesarean-section deliveries is on the rise globally, accounting for approximately 30% of births in Canada. Whereas natural birth is the first major exposure to bacteria for the infant occurring through the vaginal and intestinal microbes of the mother, birth by C-section bypasses this route resulting in very different initial bacterial exposures. Natural birth lays the foundation for a healthy intestinal environment and the metabolic, immune and behavioral benefits that result, but C-section birth has been associated with increased risk for a variety of chronic health conditions including obesity and asthma but also mood disorders such as anxiety and depression. While the exact mechanism behind this increased risk is not known, the first bacteria that colonize the infant gut are emerging as a possible contributor. Intestinal bacteria can communicate with the brain and are thought to have a role in controlling brain development and behavior. Given that C-section is often necessary for the safety of the mother and/or infant, it is critical that interventions that reduce the long-term risks associated with C-section birth be investigated. One such intervention is prebiotic fiber, which is a unique type of dietary fiber that promotes the growth of healthy intestinal bacteria. In my proposed study, I will examine if feeding prebiotic fiber to young rats that were delivered by C-section can normalize the profile of their intestinal bacteria and prevent the development of anxiety-like behaviors. By analyzing intestinal bacteria, gene expression in the brain, and behavior, we will be able to determine how early dietary intervention might mitigate anxiety. The ultimate goal of this work is to provide an early life intervention to reduce the burden of mood disorders.

column36: The role of the unfolded protein response in brain repair using a larval zebrafish model
column37: Each year, an estimated 69 million people experience traumatic brain injury, causing the death of human brain cells that are essential for brain function. Unlike humans, zebrafish are a small freshwater fish species that can completely regrow their brain cells. The information gained from studying zebrafish brain cells could be used to help human brain cells regrow. A vital step to understanding brain cell regrowth is identifying how brain cells signal to regrow after injury.The Unfolded Protein Response (UPR) is a crucial signaling pathway that has never been studied in brain cells after injury. The UPR pathway starts in the cells Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER). The ER is the part of the cell that folds the cells building blocks (proteins). Events like injury or starvation can reduce the ability of the ER to function, causing unfolded proteins to accumulate. To rebalance protein levels, the UPR is activated by three controlling ER proteins that work together to lower levels of unfolded proteins.Recent studies show that the UPR is active during brain development, but its role in brain cell regrowth after injury is unknown. To learn about UPR involvement in brain cell regrowth, I will study when the UPR is activated in brain cells after injury and if the UPR is needed for brain cell regrowth. I will identify when the UPR is activated in brain cells after injury using specialized zebrafish which fluoresce upon UPR activation. I will determine if the UPR is needed for brain cell regrowth using drugs to block the UPR in the zebrafish and then observing changes in the regrowth of brain cells after injury. By determining if UPR signaling is involved in brain cell regrowth, the results of this study could be used to help humans recover from traumatic brain injury.

column36: Effect of functional electrical stimulation on the reactive balance in individuals with incomplete spinal cord injury
column37: Falls are highly prevalent among individuals with spinal cord injury (SCI) and are mainly attributed to compromised reactive balance. The lean-and-release technique is a type of perturbation-based balance training (PBT) that is used both as an assessment tool for reactive balance and as an intervention for fall prevention. The lean-and-release PBT disrupts the participants balance to induce a compensatory movement called reactive stepping. The placement of the reactive step, which is often evaluated using a metric called the margin of stability (MOS), is of particular importance as it provides the counterbalancing force required to prevent a fall. We propose that integrating functional electrical stimulation (FES) into the lean-and-release PBT, termed PBT+FES, will improve the reactive stepping ability of individuals with incomplete SCI (iSCI). FES is readily used in the SCI rehabilitation field to improve limb movements by augmenting muscle contractions. We hypothesize that iSCI participants who undergo PBT+FES will see a greater improvement in their reactive stepping ability compared to those who only receive PBT, reflected in higher MOS values. To test our hypothesis, we will conduct a randomized controlled trial with 22 iSCI participants undergoing 18 sessions of either PBT+FES or PBT. There will be both clinical and biomechanical assessments of reactive steps to evaluate the expected improvement. The biomechanical assessment will use two force platforms and a 3D motion capture system to collect the kinetic and kinematic data required to calculate the MOS of the reactive steps. Verifying that PBT+FES improves reactive stepping ability will help it to establish itself as a novel intervention for fall prevention in the iSCI population.

column36: Targeting Bone Healing With a Novel and Biodegradable Borophene-Monetite Implant
column37: Bone repair is a dynamic process controlled by numerous cellular signaling pathways and remains tightly regulated by a suite of factors expressed in a time and concentration-dependent manner. With over 2M annual procedures performed worldwide, autografts are the current gold standard to enhance healing responses and fill bone defects. However, they remain hampered by the limited availability of bone tissue, longer surgical time, increased blood loss, and donor site morbidity. Alternative synthetic materials with osteoconductive capabilities are being developed, with calcium- and phosphate-releasing bioceramic implants used to significantly enhance bone healing and mimic bone function. Monetite is a widely used bioceramic that stimulates bone growth and regeneration and remains favorable as its biodegradability rate is balanced by the formation of new bone. It can be reinforced with 2D nanosheets to improve its bone tissue engineering potential with indispensable ions, larger surface areas, and stronger mechanical properties that further aid in the adhesion, growth, proliferation, and differentiation of bone-forming cells, osteoblasts. Borophene is a novel and graphene-like 2D nanosheet of Boron atoms that enables its conductivity, strong mechanical resistance, and flexibility. Yet, Borophene remains favorable due to its biocompatibility and biodegradability. Furthermore, Boron directly modulates the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, which is critically involved in bone growth, and modulating this pathway remains a promising target to accelerate bone healing. Together, we hypothesize that an implantable and biodegradable Borophene-Monetite scaffold will act as a cellular co-factor to positively impact osteoblast proliferation and differentiation to accelerate bone repair.

column36: Modulation of the Human Neutrophil Inflammatory Profil by Platelet-Derived Microparticles in Rheumatoid Arthritis
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a systemic inflammatory disease that primarily targets the joints. The initiation of the pathology involves a multicellular process that includes lymphocytes, macrophages, mast cells, neutrophils and platelets. Platelets are small discoid shaped cells (?3-5 ?m in size) which upon exposure to various physiological agonists can generate and shed in the extracellular milieu small extensions of their cytoplasm known as microparticles (PMPs, 100 to 1000 nm in size). Interestingly, these PMPs, but not platelets themselves, are abundant in SF of RA patients. We recently discovered a new subpopulation of PMPs that retains a functional mitochondrion from platelets. This novel population of PMPs, termed mitochondria-containing microparticles (mitoPMPs), is abundantly found in the synovial fluid (SF) of RA patients. However, the contribution of mitoPMPs in RA remains unknown. Therefore, my research project aims to demonstrate that mitoPMPs promote the development and progression of inflammatory arthritis via its local production of lipid mediators that ultimately promotes cell survival. Firstly, we will use a O2k high-resolution respiratory instrument to measure cellular respiration and the cells viability by flow cytometry following mitoPMPs internalization. Secondly, the inflammatory state of the recipient cell will be evaluated by measuring inflammatory markers such as cytokines and lipid mediators relevant to RA using flow cytometry (human inflammation panel, LegendPlex) and high-performance liquid chromatography respectively. A major impact of my project will be the characterization of the mitoPMPs-neutrophil interaction, and key information to determine whether this interaction can promote neutrophil survival and functionality.

column36: Investigating the IL-23/IL-23R Axis in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
column37: My proposed research involves looking at the interleukin-23/interleukin-23 receptor (IL-23/IL-23R) pathway in the context of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Preliminary data for this project indicates a dependency on IL-23R by various AML cell lines. By genetically modifying these cell lines and making them incapable of producing IL-23R, we see a reduction in AML cell growth and viability. Additionally, when looking at the expression of IL-23R in primary AML patient samples, we see an increased expression of IL-23R compared to normal peripheral blood stem cells. Exploring this pathway further may prove beneficial in discovering a novel therapeutic target for the treatment of AML. Specifically, I plan to get a better understanding of IL-23 and IL-23R expression in primary AML and normal hematopoietic cells. Preliminary data shows that there appears to be a unique expression and localization pattern in our AML cell lines compared to what has been previously described in the literature for other diseases. Expanding our analysis on primary AML samples can benefit our understanding of this pathway and find potential correlations between expression and known molecular subtypes of AML.Secondly, due to the reductions in cell growth and viability of our AML cell lines when genetically modifying IL-23R, I plan to look at potential methods of pharmacological inhibition against this pathway as it may prove beneficial in discovering a novel therapy for AML. Lastly, it was seen in our data that AML cell lines and patient samples had a unique expression and localization of IL-23R. This has not been previously described in current literature. I plan on studying this signalling pathway within AML by studying the cytokine and by looking for AML IL-23R binding partners.

column36: Maternal Autoantibodies on offspring neurodevelopment and risk for Autism Spectrum Disorder
column37: According to the public health agency of Canada, the current prevalence rate of ASD is 1 in 66 children and youth at a 4:1 male to female ratio. Prenatal exposure to maternal antibodies has been shown to contribute to autism in various ways depending on the antibodies involved. While the exact mechanisms have yet to be elucidated, these autoantibodies found in some women attacks the fetus brain and alter its development. Abnormal brain development is commonly implicated in children with ASD and may play a significant role in mediating the hallmark behaviours of ASD. Clinical MRI data showed children who came from mothers with autoantibodies had significantly larger brains compared to typically developing children and ASD children who were not exposed to autoantibodies.In this study, I propose to conduct a longitudinal imaging and behaviour analysis of male and female mice prenatally exposed to a cocktail of peptides that are targets of the autoantibodies present in women who have children with ASD. Several neurodevelopmental processes occur at distinct stages of prenatal and early postnatal period in humans and rodents. Therefore, predispositions to certain stimuli, insults, or processes such as gestational exposure to autoantibodies can shift the likelihood of ASD. Longitudinal studies such as this one can help improve our understanding of the mechanisms underlying neuroanatomical differences and sex effects observed in a subset of children with ASD, as well as the developmental time course through which they manifest. The hope is that maternal autoantibodies will be able to serve as a biomarker for ASD and can help with early diagnosis and treatment interventions to enhance the childs normal development and improve their quality of life.

column36: Investigating the mechanisms of DNA release from cancer cells in esophageal adenocarcinoma patients
column37: Esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) is characterized by low survival rates and has had an increase in incidence in recent decades. Liquid biopsies from EAC patients have the potential to improve diagnosis and prognosis of this disease, by using circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) and tumour-derived extracellular vesicle DNA (EV-DNA) in patient biofluids as biomarkers of disease progression. Particularly, how different treatments, such as chemotherapy or radiation, affect ctDNA and tumour-derived EV-DNA remains poorly understood. The aim of the present study is to use EAC patient samples to elucidate the impact of treatment and treatment response on ctDNA and EV-DNA kinetics and fragmentation. ctDNA and EV-DNA from EAC patient blood samples and from the supernatant of EAC patient-derived organoids treated with in vitro chemotherapy will be isolated. DNA level and fragment size will be compared and associated to different treatments, responses to treatment, development of metastatic disease, and time points of sample collection. This project has the potential to clarify the mechanisms of DNA release from cancer cells, and to identify molecular alterations that could be used for non-invasive diagnosis, prognosis, and detection of treatment resistance in cancer patients.

column36: Parental Depression and Physical-Mental Multimorbidity in Children
column37: Having a child with a chronic physical illness (e.g., epilepsy, diabetes) can be detrimental to the mental wellbeing of parents; this can subsequently place children with a physical illness at an increased risk for mental illness. Of the, approximately, 50% of children with a physical illness 30-50% also have a mental illness (i.e., physical-mental multimorbidity). Thus, a large proportion of families are impacted. Previous studies assessing parental depression and childhood physical-mental multimorbidity have been: (1) conducted at only one time point; (2) focused on a few physical illnesses; and, (3) restricted to children under 11 years. To address these knowledge gaps, this project will use statistical methods to: (1) examine how depressive symptoms in parents of children with a chronic physical illness change over 48 months; (2) identify factors that predict parent depressive symptoms over time; and, (3) assess the associations between parent depressive symptoms and child physical-mental multimorbidity. This project will use data from a study of children aged 2-16, diagnosed with a physical illness, and their parents. To identify long-term effects, the mental wellbeing of the children and their parents will be assessed at baseline, 6, 12, 24, and 48 months. Risk factors that will be assessed include parenting stress, family functioning, and physical illness severity. The findings of this study will help identify parents at risk of negative depressive outcomes and allow for early referrals to healthcare professionals. It will also provide further motivation for the incorporation of physical and mental health services within pediatric settings. Ultimately, the goal of this research is to improve the health of children and their families.

column36: Characterizing mutuality of quantitative MRI metrics in multiple sclerosis
column37: The brain is the most sophisticated organ. Similar to other organs, it is vulnerable to damage via injury or disease. In contrast, despite having more advanced tools, the diagnosis and prognosis of several brain disorders still rely heavily on the presentation and progression of clinical symptoms, which is sometimes obscure and can cause delays in treatment. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a non-invasive imaging technique that can provide extraordinary soft-tissue contrast. Using this approach, changes in concentrations and chemical configurations of hydrogen nuclei can potentially be used to visualize and quantify abnormalities relatively early. However, there are many different MRI imaging methods and each of these provides a slightly different insight into both the overall structure (gross anatomy) and the finer microstructure (tissue composition). Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a common neurological disorder that can cause a number of symptoms, including vision loss, decreased motor function, sensory problems, cognitive impairments, etc. One of the main characteristics of MS is a loss of myelin and widespread white matter degeneration (which impairs the integrity and speed of signal transmission throughout the brain). Therefore, the goal of this study is to characterize different MRI methods in MS by weighing similarities or mutuality using statistics. From this perspective, it implies how close these metrics are related to each other. Accordingly, imaging sequences can be more flexibly adjusted so maximal information can be obtained with a limited time frame. its beneficial for the clinicians in decision making on image sequence implementation combined with patients symptoms. It also motivates the further refinement of the prognosis and diagnosis criteria.

column36: Uncovering the role of metabolic programming in skeletal muscle energetics, and risk for metabolic disease
column37: Obesity is known to have complex genetic, metabolic and environmental origins leading to comorbidities. The management of obesity favours a personalized approach as broad treatment strategies are often ineffective. Our research on a 5,057 patient cohort undergoing standardized and intensively supervised hypocaloric meal replacement program demonstrates highly variable weight loss success that is related to differences in genetics, resting metabolic rates, and energy conversion efficiencies in skeletal muscle. We focus on the diet resistant vs. the diet sensitive subtypes not due to differences in program adherence or factors affecting weight loss (e.g., exercise; medications; disease states). Muscle metabolic health is known to be important in prevention of obesity and type II diabetes (T2D), however further investigation into weight loss and exercise is needed. The goal of our proposed research is to uncover mechanisms that increase risk for metabolic diseases such as T2D. Additionally, we aim to examine the effects of Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) surgery on muscle energetics in weight loss and variability in resolving metabolic complications in an obese clinical cohort. Patient blood and skeletal muscle will be analyzed for DNA methylomics and mitochondrial energetics. We hypothesize that the patients with the greatest weight loss will have the greatest changes in DNA methylation and blood and muscle DNA methylomics will correlate pre- and post-surgery. Further, we propose that the variation is attributable to programmed muscle metabolism and leads to diverse metabolic complications in obesity. In essence, the proposed research will broaden our understanding of obesity subtypes and elucidate effective treatment strategies in adults with obesity.

column36: Substance Use Disorder and COVID-19 Related Health Outcomes
column37: Those with substance use disorders (SUDs) have been identified as a vulnerable population who are at risk for severe COVID-19 comorbidities and may have intersecting vulnerabilities deterring them from accessing timely medical attention. US samples have shown increased risk of hospitalization, ventilator use, and mortality in COVID-19 patients who have SUDs. However, there is no clear evidence demonstrating if similar trends exist in a Canadian sample. Thus, my research questions are a) What are the risks of COVID-related hospitalization and mortality in Canadian individuals with SUDs compared to general COVID-19 patients? b) What are potential risk factors for COVID-related hospitalization and mortality in individuals with SUDs? The proposed study involves a retrospective case-control chart review of hospital electronic medical records (EMR) from hospitals in Ontario. Demographic information, comorbidities, prevalence of SUD, and negative COVID-19 outcomes of mortality and hospitalization will be assessed directly from EMR data using descriptive statistics. Baseline characteristics will be compared using chi-square tests and t-tests. Logistic regression models will be performed to compare hospitalization and death rates between COVID-19 patients with SUD and general COVID-19 patients. Multiple linear regression models will be performed on demographic information and comorbidities to analyze the strength and nature of the association between these characteristics and negative health outcomes in COVID-19 patients with SUD.

column36: Characterization of the neuroimmunological response to Human Herpesvirus 6A/B infection in a novel primary human-derived model
column37: Human Herpesvirus 6A/B (HHV6A/B) are two viruses currently present in over 90% of our population, remaining in the body for life following infection. The consequences of this are not well characterized or understood, but there may be associations between infection with HHV6A/B and later-onset neurological disease, for example multiple sclerosis, epilepsy, and even brain cancer. Given the nature of infection being in the brain, studying HHV6A/B can be challenging as tissue is not readily accessible. However, we are now able to use stem cells to create the different cells that make up the brain, combining them to create a 3D co-culture of different brain cell types to mimic the real thing. The Muffat Lab at the Hospital for Sick Children recently pioneered the creation of microglia from stem cells, which are the immune cells of the brain and thus of utmost importance for studying viral infection response. For the first time, it is possible to investigate infection of HHV6A/B and the role of microglia in the immune response in a readily accessible primary human model wherein all the key cell types are present in a structurally similar environment to where native infection occurs. This model can then be used to study disease, in this case, the immune response of each cell type as well as a combination of each following infection with HHV6A/B. Understanding the mechanisms by which a pathogen present in almost the entire population infects and affects the central nervous system will provide fundamental insight into HHV6A/B biology, as well as the onset of neurological conditions it is associated with. My research will uncover the roles of neural and glial cells following HHV6A/B infection in a novel model system that closely mimics human brain composition and architecture.

column36: Fluctuations in excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters across the migraine cycle in children and adolescents
column37: Migraine is one of the five most prevalent childhood diseases. This debilitating disorder decreases quality of life and leads to disability in the home, school, and social relationships. Migraine that onsets in childhood often continues into adulthood, leading to increased healthcare costs, decreased productivity, and lower quality of life. Knowledge about adult migraine is often assumed to apply to children. This assumption is likely erroneous; for example, standard adult migraine medications are no more effective than placebo for children and youth with migraine.Migraine often has a cyclical nature which may be linked to changes in the brains neurochemistry. There is evidence that these changes are a result of an imbalance between excitation and inhibition, which are regulated by glutamate and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), respectively. To date, only a few studies have measured glutamate and GABA in adults with migraine, and only one study has done so in children and youth with migraine. Interestingly, this study reported children with migraine had different levels of neurochemicals than levels published in adult literature.My project will be the first to explore how glutamate and GABA fluctuate across the migraine cycle in a pediatric sample using magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS). Children and youth with at least 4 migraine attacks per month will be scanned for a total of 4 sessions. I expect that as the next migraine attack approaches, glutamate will increase, while GABA will decrease. During and after an attack, I expect glutamate to decrease and GABA to increase. The information gathered from this study will provide new knowledge that could be used to identify potential treatment targets focused on the unique biology of migraine in children and youth.

column36: A Quantitative Study on Gender Positivity and Gender Distress in Transgender and Gender-Nonbinary Communities: Predictive Factors and Impact on Health
column37: Gender positivity (a.k.a. gender euphoria) - the positive emotions related to ones gender - is an empowering experience and important concept for many transgender and gender-nonbinary (TGNB) individuals, but has received little attention in health research. The healthcare understanding of transgender (trans) identity and wellness has been centred on gender dysphoria, a psychiatric diagnosis that is historically a prerequisite for accessing gender-affirming medical services. The proposed study will analyze Canadian survey data of TGNB communities (Trans PULSE Canada; N=2873) to expand the dysphoria-centred clinical viewpoint to a community-informed, more balanced, and multifaceted understanding of TGNB gender experiences. Using innovative assessment tools to measure gender positivity as well as gender distress (i.e., distress related to gender dysphoria but not limited to a clinical diagnosis) in both the physical and the social aspects, the study will quantitatively examine the healthcare and social resilience factors that foster gender positivity, the risk factors for gender distress, the complex interactions between gender positivity and distress, and the association of each measure with physical and mental health outcomes. The results can contribute to a shift of perspective in trans health. The fuller understanding of the multidimensional TGNB experiences will likely inform research, gender-affirming care, healthcare policies, and societal representations. Future TGNB research and gender-affirming therapies may benefit from not only focusing on dysphoria but also exploring resilience-based approaches to nurture gender positivity as a protective factor for health.

column36: Insufficient sleep, impaired sleep, and injury in Canadian adolescents: a national cross-sectional study
column37: Adolescence is a critical time period for physical, cognitive, and social development in children. Sleep plays an important role in these processes of maturation and supports emotional regulation, memory, and decision making in adolescents. Nearly 30% of Canadian children do not achieve the recommended hours of nighttime sleep, a figure that poses a serious threat to their health and safety. Researchers are referring to insufficient sleep as a ;public health epidemic, with poor sleep linked to impaired decision making, increased risk-taking behaviours, and a higher incidence of injury in adolescents. Despite recognition of the problem, limited population health evidence exists describing relationships between indicators of sleep and injury among Canadian adolescents. As injury remains the leading cause of death in adolescents worldwide, strategies aimed at common risk factors for injury require a contemporary evidence base for their planning and targeting, and sleep hygiene may provide a focus for such interventions. This study will document common sleep patterns among Canadian adolescents and relate indicators of poor sleep with risks for serious injury using nationally representative data from Cycle 8 of the Health Behaviour in School-aged Children (HBSC) Study. Statistical methods will include descriptive and multivariate analyses to assess potential etiological relationships between sleep and injury. The findings of this study will provide foundational population health information on the importance of sleep as a positive health asset, to inform clinical, educational, and public health interventions.

column36: Outcomes of Literacy-Oriented Web Videos: An Exploratory Qualitative Study
column37: BACKGROUND: Low parental health literacy is detrimental to child education and health, and can be overcome by web videos. A mixed review we conducted on web-based literacy-oriented video interventions(n=19) suggested that interventions improved health knowledge(n=10), attitudes(n=13) and behaviours(n=9). column36: Etude longitudinale : trajectoires developpementales des enfants autistes
column37: Au moment du diagnostic d'autisme, les niveaux intellectuel et langagier de l'enfant sont evalues afin de le situer sur un continuum de difficultes. Cependant, en plus d'etre frequemment consideres comme peu fonctionnels a l'age prescolaire, les enfants autistes suivent des trajectoires developpementales atypiques et variees. Neanmoins, a l'age scolaire, une majorite d'entre eux auront developpe un niveau intellectuel dans la normale. A ce jour, les trajectoires developpementales en lien avec les profils intellectuels, comportementaux et academiques des enfants autistes demeurent tres peu etudiees. Il est donc difficile de se baser sur le fonctionnement adaptatif et intellectuel mesure a l'age du diagnostic pour predire l'evolution de l'enfant autiste. Ce projet vise a : 1) caracteriser les profils intellectuels, academiques et comportementaux des enfants autistes d'age scolaire, et 2) determiner si certains comportements ou habiletes particulieres, identifies a l'age prescolaire, permettent de predire les niveaux intellectuel et academique, ainsi que le profil comportemental des enfants autistes a l'age scolaire. Une etude longitudinale aupres d'une cohorte d'enfants autistes et d'enfants au developpement typique permettra de documenter la trajectoire developpementale des enfants autistes de l'age prescolaire jusqu'a l'age scolaire. Sur le plan theorique, cette etude permettra de mieux comprendre les trajectoires developpementales des enfants autistes. column36: National Trends and Risk Factors of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome: 2000-2019
column37: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) is a serious public health concern as it is the leading cause of death among infants between 1 week and 1 year of age. Until 1988, the rate of SIDS barely changed in the United States, but national efforts to promote infant safe sleep through the Back-to-Sleep campaign have helped reduce the rates of SIDS throughout the 1990s. Despite this decline, SIDS remains an important cause of infant mortality, accounting for over 2500 US infant deaths each year. As a result, SIDS remains a focus of national and local prevention efforts. A thorough examination of recent US SIDS trends is needed to further provide insight into the potential impacts of prevention efforts and understand racial differences in SIDS rates to better target campaigns to reduce SIDS. Knowledge of recent national and state trends of SIDS may help programs make critical decisions about resource allocation for SIDS prevention as states with declining SIDS rates may have implemented successful programs that can be adapted in states with higher rates. An analysis on recent trends will also highlight any racial differences observed in rates of SIDS and evaluate how prevention efforts for SIDS in at-risk communities have made an impact. The investigation will use data from the Multiple Cause Mortality Death Files from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to evaluate national and state-specific SIDS rates from 2000-2019 to describe recent trends in SIDS as well as make use of regression models to evaluate the SIDS risk in infants of different sex and race as well as associated risk factors. The findings from this study will provide an opportunity for programs to re-evaluate their strategies in reducing SIDS rates and highlight risk factors for new programs to target.

column36: Predicting the Efficacy of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia in Cancer Patients Using Baseline High-Frequency Heart Rate Variability
column37: Insomnia affects between 30 to 60% of cancer patients at any given time. The current gold standard for treating insomnia is cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia (CBTi), however accessibility to this treatment is limited. Savard and colleagues (2021) recently proposed a stepped care approach to CBTi that would increase accessibility to the treatment by beginning with lower intensity intervention. Although this approach was empirically observed to be equivalent to traditional CBTi, remission rates are still low. The current research aims to understand these low remission rates by uncovering a possible physiological predictor for CBTi response. Low heart-rate variability (HRV) is a marker of parasympathetic functioning that has been associated with risk for insomnia and poorer self-regulation in prior work. Overall, we hypothesize that low initial HRV will predict poorer response to CBTi. In order to test this hypothesis, we will be conducting a secondary data analysis of a recent randomized clinical trial of 177 cancer patients with comorbid insomnia, treated with either stepped care CBTi or standard CBTi. In this study both insomnia severity and HRV data were collected using standard validated procedures. The current research will first test whether patients with lower initial baseline HRV will experience less change in insomnia severity after treatment, which could explain the low remission rates from CBTi in general. We then hypothesize that patients with lower initial baseline HRV will experience less change in insomnia severity after low intensive stepped care intervention compared to those given standard CBTi. Findings from this study may help identify patients most suitable for these low-intensity interventions within a stepped care service delivery approach.

column36: Online Peer-Delivered Group Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Postpartum Depression
column37: Postpartum depression (PPD) is one of the most common complications of childbirth, affecting up to 20% of mothers in the first year after delivery. If untreated, it can have negative effects on the mother, their partner, their newborn, and the other children in the family. Unfortunately, just 1 in 10 mothers with PPD are able to get the treatments they most want and need (e.g., talking therapies), a situation that has worsened during the COVID-19 pandemic. As a result, innovative, sustainable, and engaging options that safely provide treatment to large numbers of mothers are urgently needed.The purpose of the proposed study is to test the effectiveness of an Online 9-Week Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT; a type of talking therapy) program delivered by mothers who themselves have recovered from PPD (i.e., lay peers). We will recruit 174 mothers who currently have PPD and infants 12 months of age. Mothers will either receive group CBT plus treatment as usual (TAU) from their usual healthcare providers or TAU alone. This study will determine if this online group treatment can lead to stable improvements in PPD, maternal anxiety, parenting stress, their relationships with their partner and infant, and infant temperament. We believe that this peer-delivered treatment will improve PPD and its accompanying difficulties, as well as reduce its adverse effects on families in a cost-effective manner.In addition to the suffering that PPD imposes on mothers and families, the financial cost of untreated PPD may be as high as $150,000 per case over the lifespan. If effective, peer-delivered group CBT for PPD could provide the healthcare system with an affordable and scalable treatment that can improve the health of mothers and families during the pandemic and beyond.

column36: Long-term Autonomic Consequences of Concussion in Youth Sport
column37: Sport related concussion is a common brain injury that happens following a physical force to the head or body. Having a sport related concussion involves short-term disruption in brain function and clinical symptoms. The long-term impacts of a sport related concussion experienced during youth are not known. This is an issue, as the body undergoes much development during youth (ages 11-18). Concussion also impacts the ability to exercise and the autonomic nervous system, which control important body functions such as heart rate and blood pressure. Inability to exercise and dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system are linked to conditions including cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, depression, and death. Therefore, the goal of this project is to study the long-term (5-15 year) autonomic impacts of sport related concussion experienced during youth. Special attention will be paid to how males and females are different, as concussion is known to present differently across sex. To achieve these goals, participants will have their heart activity and blood pressure measured as they perform resting and exercise tasks. The values of those who had a youth sport related concussion 5-15 years ago will be compared to those who had a muscle/skeletal injury or no injury during youth sport 5-15 years ago. The findings of this study will help determine if sport related concussion is linked to long-term exercise intolerance and autonomic nervous system issues. They will inform whether the long-term impacts of sport related concussion differ between males and females, and will inform treatment strategies to help concussed patients recover.

column36: Molecular detection and quantification of the prevalence of sexually transmitted blood-borne infections in Canadian wastewater samples
column37: Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) is the analysis of sewage effluent for community-level detection of the consumption or shedding of a substance. WBE of infectious disease can confirm the presence of a disease in a community and track the community-wide spread of that disease after initial detection. Throughout the ongoing coronavirus pandemic, WBE was utilized with success to track trends in COVID-19 transmission in Northwest Territories using the Cepheid GeneXpert system, a fully automated desk-top technology traditionally used for clinical testing. Following the success of using the GeneXpert for WBE of COVID-10, partner communities expressed interest in utilizing this technology for WBE of other pathogens, including sexually transmitted blood-borne infections (STBBIs). The prevalence of STBBIs in Canada has been increasing for at least 15 years and is notably the highest in the northern territories and the prairie provinces. We will attempt to use specialized tests for the GeneXpert, and conventional qPCR to determine if target STBBIs can be detected from wastewater using samples collected from an established network of sampling sites initially established to monitor COVID-19 transmission. If successful, WBE of STBBIs could allow for unbiased, community-wide detection of STBBIs which would be especially impactful in northern and remote communities in Canada where the prevalence of STBBIs is high and access to healthcare is disproportionately low. This strategy of using WBE for tracking the community-wide transmission STBBIs would allow for improved, unbiased disease surveillance and targeted allocation of resources to affected communities. This represents an equitable allocation of resources for all.

column36: Traitement psychotherapeutique de la symptomatologie depressive concomitante au trouble neurocognitif du a la maladie d'Alzheimer
column37: Le trouble neurocognitif du a la maladie d'Alzheimer (TNMA) a de lourdes consequences pour la personne atteinte. En plus des symptomes cognitifs, comme la perte de memoire, des chercheurs ont estime que pres de 30 % des patients atteints d'un TNMA souffriraient de depression. Chez ces patients, la presence de symptomes depressifs peut entrainer une institutionnalisation prematuree, de la souffrance et une perte significative de la qualite de vie. Malgre cela, un nombre limite d'etudes s'interessent aux benefices d'une intervention individuelle, axee sur les emotions et la relation therapeutique, sur les symptomes depressifs de ces patients. Un modele d'intervention peu etudie, soit la psychotherapie psychodynamique interpersonnelle (PPI), represente une avenue de traitement interessante. Une etude de cas a obtenu des resultats concluants, mais le nombre de participants etait limite et les donnees doivent etre repliquees. Cette intervention tire profit des capacites preservees malgre la maladie, comme la memoire implicite, composee de tout ce que la personne se rappelle, sans qu'elle puisse volontairement s'en souvenir. L'objectif de cette etude est de mesurer l'efficacite de l'intervention PPI sur l'intensite des symptomes depressifs de ces patients. Pour ce faire, 45 participants atteints d'un TNMA seront recrutes et assignes au hasard a l'un des trois groupes suivants : intervention PPI, ecoute de livres audio (une autre intervention utilisee chez les patients atteints de depression et d'un TNMA), ou aucune intervention. Pour voir si l'intervention PPI s'avere efficace, les participants rempliront des questionnaires mesurant l'humeur, les symptomes depressifs et le niveau de qualite de vie et une comparaison sera effectuee entre les participants des trois groupes.

column36: Improving Clinical Eating Disorder Treatment in Canada: A Qualitative Study
column37: Though eating disorders (EDs) possess the greatest mortality rate of all mental illnesses, Canada has yet to implement a national standard for treatment. EDs are severe psychological illnesses that result in disturbed eating behaviours, affecting nearly one million Canadians at any given time. It has been well established that ED treatment lacks a patient-oriented perspective that is informed by the lived experiences of those who have received ED treatment. The result is that ED treatments have high drop-out rates, are inconsistent across clinical programs and have low overall participation. Several reports and strategies have urged researchers to explore lived experience through qualitative data collection in order to facilitate the improvement of these issues. In accordance with these recommendations, this study will work with Nova Scotians who have participated in clinical eating disorder (ED) treatment to understand their experience. Furthermore, this study will seek to understand the perspectives and beliefs that those with lived experience have towards the improvement of Canadian clinical ED treatment. Data collection will take the form of one-on-one interviews which will be audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. The researcher will then analyze the resulting transcripts to identify common themes among the participants experiences. The resulting themes will produce novel contributions to existing data, informing improvements to Canadian clinical ED treatment from people with lived experience. Ultimately, the study will act as a guide for clinicians and policymakers as they work towards improving clinical ED treatment for Canadians.

column36: Delineating the paradoxical role of GATA6 in pancreatic tumour subtypes
column37: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest types of cancer, with only 8% of patients surviving beyond five years. The poor prognosis of patients with PDAC highlights a need to better understand this cancer and its subtypes. In general, the PDAC subtypes lie on a spectrum, with the ;Classical subtype on one end and the ;Basal-like subtype on the other. PDAC tumours are classified into subtypes by their gene expression, such as the GATA6 gene which is more highly expressed in Classical tumours than in Basal-like tumours. Our lab has recently found that by knocking out GATA6 in Classical tumours, tumour growth is reduced. This suggests that GATA6 is an important gene in tumour proliferation. On the contrary, other studies have shown a tumour suppressive role for GATA6. Therefore, my goal is to delineate the role of GATA6 in PDAC subtypes. I hypothesize that the role of GATA6 is context-dependent, and that it acts as a tumour suppressor in Basal-like tumours as opposed to its tumour-promoting role in Classical tumours. To test this hypothesis, I will first generate 3D cell models (organoids) that overexpress GATA6. The GATA6-overexpressing organoids will also express green fluorescent protein, enabling me to track their growth over time using flow cytometry. To investigate the molecular function of GATA6, I will perform RNA sequencing which will identify changes in gene expression that result from GATA6 overexpression. Finally, I will explore the protein-protein interactions of GATA6 to find potential targets for new therapies. Overall, by understanding the role of GATA6 in different PDAC subtypes, this project seeks to identify more personalized treatment options and improve the prognosis for patients with this deadly disease.

column36: Examining quality of life among those with adjustment disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic.
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has introduced unprecedented levels of stress into the realities of daily living. Many of these stressors, such as job loss and quarantine practices, are of a non-traumatic nature. However, due to threats such as loss of life, some may experience stress of a traumatic nature. The traumatic nature of such high-intensity stressors has the potential to influence the onset of pandemic-related mental health disorders such as adjustment disorders (AD) and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in some portions of the population. Because the onset of pandemic-related AD and PTSD are relatively new phenomena, little is known about the impacts of these disorders on reported quality of life (QOL) within this context. Thus, it is crucial to further investigate QOL outcomes in relation to pandemic-related AD and PTSD to first foster a greater understanding of the implications of stressor-induced mental health disorders on QOL and to then inform the development of effective interventions for future similar events. This study first seeks to accomplish these goals through the direct administration of a diagnostic tool and self-report quality of life measure to a sample of 200 Canadians. The results of this data collection will be analyzed in a variety of contexts to examine for relationships and differences between QOL outcomes in those with no diagnosis versus those with diagnosable AD or PTSD. Additionally, analyses will examine if these groups report significant differences in any of the four major facets of QOL (physical health, psychological, social relationships, environment). Results of this study will provide a relevant insight into the implications of a mental health disorder on QOL outcomes in the context of a mass-stressor event such as a pandemic.

column36: Clinical Implications of Respiratory Symptoms in Ehlers Danlos Syndrome and Hypermobility Spectrum Disorder
column37: Statement on Health Problem: People living with Ehlers Danlos Syndrome (EDS) and Hypermobility Spectrum Disorder (HSD) have health issues in multiple systems in their body including respiratory (breathing) difficulties. The respiratory team at our center is one of few globally leading research on respiratory health in EDS/HSD. We know from other disease groups that these symptoms can impair peoples physical activity, their quality of life and worsen other aspects of their health (e.g fatigue), which has not been studied before in EDS/HSD patients. Typically, EDS/HSD patients report difficulties in navigating healthcare services and feeling devalued in their care given how little care teams know about the disease and its management. Thus, a holistic study design is needed to fully understand the impact of respiratory symptoms on the health of EDS/HSD patients, as well as identify their care preferences and needs. Objectives: Identify the impact of respiratory symptoms on physical activity, quality of life and non-respiratory symptoms (e.g. fatigue, anxiety, depression) and explore health-care preferences and needs. Methods: A comprehensive approach using self-reported questionnaires, wearable physical activity trackers (Fitbit) and individual interviews with EDS/HSD patients will be used to understand the full impact of respiratory symptoms on their health.Unique Part of the Project and Significance: The impact of respiratory symptoms has not been well studied in EDS/HSD. Importantly, during the interviews, we will ask patients what they prioritize and value in their care. This work will allow us to include patients preferences in their care and help doctors and researchers improve the health outcomes of people with EDS/HSD.

column36: Balance in older adults following the use of blood flow restriction during dance classes.
column37: Falls cause 85% of injury-related hospitalizations among older adults in Canada [1]. Older women are particularly susceptible to these injuries due to their lower bone density [2]. Falls are related to postural stability and muscle strength, which decline with age [3]. Exercise can slow these declines, yet only 15.7% of women aged 60-79 are physically active [4]. Dance classes can provide an enjoyable and engaging form of exercise for older adults to improve their postural stability and strength [5]; Unfortunately, older adults often face barriers to accessing these classes. We previously explored the use of online dance classes for improving postural stability of older adults and found improvements in anteroposterior sway. Because exercise intensity must be lower during online classes where monitoring is limited, we wish to build on these promising results by using blood flow restriction (BFR) cuffs during our online dance classes. BFR cuffs apply pressure to reduce blood flow into exercising muscles which promotes muscle growth and thereby improves postural stability. BFR is particularly suited to older adults in an online environment because combining BFR with low-intensity exercise, allows for increases in muscle size and strength similar to gains see from high-intensity exercise [7]. Thus, this study aims to assess the effects of 12-weeks of online dance classes with BFR on the postural stability and strength of women aged 65 years and above. It is hoped this innovative program may offer a more accessible, low cost, social and tailored form of exercise for older women. Furthermore, it is expected these classes can help lower fall risk through improvements in muscular size, strength and postural stability.

column36: Validite clinique de l'outil d'aide au diagnostic PhenoVar pour l'analyse des donnees de sequencage rapide du genome entier chez les nouveau-nes et les nourrissons aux soins intensifs
column37: Les maladies genetiques rares et les malformations presentes a la naissance sont la premiere cause de deces chez les nouveau-nes au Canada. Parmi les nouveau-nes et les enfants admis aux soins intensifs, ceux avec une maladie genetique suspectee ont un plus grand risque de mortalite et de sejour prolonge a l'hopital. Il peut etre complexe de trouver le bon diagnostic chez les nouveau-nes atteints d'une maladie genetique rare, car leur presentation clinique est souvent non specifique ou atypique. Etablir rapidement un diagnostic est crucial, car il peut modifier les soins prodigues et ainsi ameliorer la qualite de vie de l'enfant. L'information genetique d'un individu est encodee dans l'ADN a partir d'un alphabet compose de quatre molecules chimiques: adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) et guanine (G). Le sequencage du genome entier permet de determiner la sequence des lettres pour l'ensemble du materiel genetique et ainsi detecter des variations genetiques. La grande majorite des variations ne causent aucune maladie genetique. Chez les individus ayant une maladie genetique, certains outils sont utiles pour identifier la ou les variations qui causent la maladie. PhenoVar est un outil qui permet de prioriser les variations qui sont sujettes a provoquer une maladie et qui pourraient expliquer la presentation clinique du patient. L'hypothese du projet est que PhenoVar est un outil cliniquement valide pour l'interpretation des donnees de sequencage du genome chez les nouveau-nes et les jeunes enfants aux soins intensifs. Pour ce faire, nous allons identifier certains facteurs influencant l'obtention d'un diagnostic avec le logiciel PhenoVar et comparer le rendement diagnostic de PhenoVar a celui des analyses conventionnelles dans quatre laboratoires universitaires.

column36: Enzymes beta-gucuronidases : Une nouvelle cible pour le traitement des maladies cholestatiques auto-immunes.
column37: Les acides biliaires permettent de melanger uniformement les lipides (graisses) au reste des nutriments (vitamines & mineraux) qui pourront ainsi etre digeres et absorbes par notre intestin. Ces acides sont produits par le foie par biotransformation du cholesterol puis secretes au niveau des intestins (via la vesicule biliaire). Grace a un processus de reabsorption efficace au niveau des intestins, ils retournent ensuite au foie via la veine porte. Ainsi 95% de ce qui est libere dans l'intestin est reabsorbe, alors que seul 5% est elimine dans les selles. Les acides biliaires sont toxiques s'ils accumulent a des niveaux trop eleves dans les cellules du foie ou de l'intestin. Notre corps a elabore des mecanismes de defense contre cette situation, notamment en pouvant leur attacher une molecule de signalisation qui diminue leur toxicite et facilite leur elimination vers la bile. Par contre, les analyses montrent que tres peu d'acides biliaires portent cette autre molecule dans les selles, ce qui suggere qu'elle peut etre enlevee lors de leur passage dans l'intestin (diminuant ainsi l'efficacite du mecanisme de protection). Cette molecule de signalisation, appelee << glucuronide >> est retiree specifiquement par des enzymes des bacteries presentes dans l'intestin. Mon projet vise a mieux comprendre l'elimination des acides biliaires attaches a un glucuronide. Je dois aussi evaluer le role que jouent les bacteries presentes dans l'intestin dans le processus d'elimination, afin de determiner si elles pourraient etre ciblees par des medicaments ou des approches nutritionnelles afin de limiter le recyclage des acides biliaires au foie, notamment chez des patients pour lesquels ils accumulent a des niveaux toxiques et empechent le foie de fonctionner.

column36: The Influence of the Gut Microbiota During Protracted Opioid Withdrawal
column37: Canada is currently facing an opioid crisis, with approximately 20 Canadians dying daily due to opioid overdose. Relapse following treatment for opioid addiction is common, and novel strategies are needed to reduce the likelihood of relapse. This project aims to explore the gut microbiome as a possible target for treatment during opioid withdrawal. Not only has the acute phase of opioid withdrawal been shown to alter the gut microbiota in mice, but fecal transfers from opioid-withdrawn to drug-naive mice are able to induce symptoms of opioid withdrawal. However, it has yet to be determined if the relationship between the microbiome and opioid withdrawal symptoms is sustained during longer periods of abstinence. This project aims to characterize the protracted opioid withdrawal phenotype in mice, and to determine if alterations in the microbiome are necessary for this phenotype to occur. This will include characterization of the symptoms of protracted withdrawal in mice, including mechanical and thermal hyperalgesia (assessed via von Frey filaments and tail-withdrawal assays, respectively), anxiety (using an elevated plus maze and open field test), and neuroinflammation in post-mortem tissue. Fecal samples from drug-naïve animals, as well as animals in various stages of opioid withdrawal, will be used to assess changes in the gut microbiota, and fecal matter from mice in various stages of opioid withdrawal will be used in fecal transfers to recolonize the gastrointestinal tract of germ-free mice. If the relationship between the gut microbiome and symptoms of withdrawal persists, interventions that aim to restore the composition of the gut microbiome could prove to be an attractive target in alleviating the withdrawal symptoms associated with chronic opioid use.

column36: Mechanisms of Interstitial Lung Disease in Systemic Autoimmune Rheumatic Diseases
column37: Systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARDs) are a family of chronic autoimmune disorders. Autoimmune diseases occur when immune cells, responsible for fighting disease and infection, target the bodys own tissue. Typical SARDs diseases include rheumatoid arthritis (RA), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), systemic sclerosis (SSc) and autoimmune myositis (AIM). Among other affected organ systems, the lungs are a common target of the immune response associated with SARDs. Characterized by inflammation and scarring of the lung tissue, interstitial lung disease (ILD) is a major cause of morbidity and premature mortality in SARDs patients. The causes and mechanisms underlying SARDs-ILD remain largely unknown, and it is impossible to identify SARDs patients that will develop ILD. Early diagnosis, prompt initiation of treatment and controlling inflammation are crucial to improve the outcomes of affected individuals. To achieve this, my project investigates the immune profile of SARDs-ILD patients compared to that of healthy controls using blood samples. Preliminary data begin to show some differences in such profiles, however further sampling of SARDs-ILD patients is necessary to validate these results. Similar studies are also conducted using different mouse models of SARDs, including the collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) model and the SKG-ILD model. By investigating cell number, activation and polarization of immune cell populations, we hope to better understand the causes and mechanisms of ILD that perpetuate inflammation in SARDs. This will have important implications for the prediction of disease onset and progression, and for the development of novel treatments for diseases involving active inflammation such as SARDs.

column36: Drusen Quantification & RPE analysis of Eye Bank Eyes Implanted with or without Blue-Light Filtering IOLs: an OCT and Histopathological Study
column37: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a disease that causes central vision loss due to damage to the central area of the retina and is the leading cause of blindness in the western world. A hallmark of AMD is the presence of fatty protein deposits in the retina known as drusen. Although the progression of AMD is defined by the presence of large and more numerous drusen, the way in which AMD develops is not clearly understood despite some studies having found a link between exposure to blue light (BL) and progression of the disease. With aging, the eyes natural lens becomes opaque and cataract surgery is required to replace the lens with an artificial one. There are different artificial lenses available today and BL-filtering lenses are a newer option. These lenses attempt to imitate the aged natural lens ability to filter BL. Studies have shown that they can diminish the progression of AMD, although this effect is still being contested. Therefore, the goal of this project is to investigate what effect BL-filtering lenses may have on AMD progression. For this end, two hundred post-mortem donor eyes obtained from the Lions Gift of Sight Eye Bank will be used: one hundred eyes with a BL-filtering lens and one hundred with a non-BL-filtering lens. column36: Intimate Partner Violence Among the LGBTQ+ and General Population During COVID-19
column37: The COVID-19 stay-at-home orders (SHOs) created unique circumstances which placed victims of intimate partner violence (IPV) in precarious situations. COVID-19 SHOs forced many survivors to isolate with their abusers, created barriers to leaving situations of IPV, and aggravated risk factors associated with IPV, including unemployment, substance use, and mental health issues. Consequently, a rise in rates of IPV were reported in Canada. A demographic of particular concern is the LGBTQ+ population, considering the disproportionately high rates of IPV among LGBTQ+ individuals, the association between minority stress and victimization, and the additional help-seeking barriers faced by LGBTQ+ individuals. This will be the first Canadian study to date to explore the impact of COVID-19 on IPV in both the LGBTQ+ and general population. Employing mixed methodsboth questionnaires and semi-structured interviewsthe present study aims to explore: 1) protective and risk factors which moderate the relation between stay-at-home orders and IPV, 2) barriers to seeking help or leaving situations of IPV duringCOVID-19, and 3) psychological responses associated with IPV during COVID-19 with an emphasis on analyzing pertinent differences and similarities between the LGBTQ+ and general population. The present study addresses the urgent need to investigate the rising levels of IPVilluminating the circumstances under which IPV during COVID-19 occurs, the barriers that victims face when accessing support, and the psychosocial responses associated with victimization. Ultimately, this research could inform public policy, support the improvement of IPV victim service provision, and highlight possible risk and protective factors for IPV to be targeted during future SHOs.

column36: Parental Outcomes Following Participation in Cognitive Behavior Therapy for Children with Autism in a Community Setting
column37: Caregivers of autistic children and adolescents are at higher risk for mental health problems such as anxiety, depression and stress. Evidence reveals that interventions such as Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT) targeting autistic childrens emotion dysregulation and social skills may also indirectly benefit parental well-being. The association between children challenging behaviour and parental well-being reflects on the interrelation between parent and child functioning and the importance of examining both variables when intervening on one of them. Previous studies indicating positive parental outcome post child-targeted interventions were conducted in highly controlled settings which does not necessarily replicate in real-world context such as in a community setting. This study will examine parental mental-health and mindful parenting after the delivery of a child-targeted parent-involved CBT intervention in seven community organizations. It will also report on the associations between parent and child outcomes as well as identify predictors of parental positive outcomes. This study will be the first of its own on examining positive parental outcomes in a community setting following a CBT intervention for children and youth with autism. Results from this study is crucial for community organizations making decision about which evidence-based interventions to adopt in their routine care all the while maximizing the benefits for the parent-child dyad.

column36: The Effects of Depression Treatments Based on Power Analyses Trends Across Time - A Systematic Review
column37: In 2012, a massive study found that 70% of psychology experiments cannot be reproduced. In response to this replication crisis, psychologists proposed two solutions: adapting the Open Science Framework, and conducting a power analysis before any study. The Open Science Framework requires researchers to publicly register their hypothesis, experiment design, and data analysis plan before conducting studies. It also requires researchers to make their data and codes used for analysis available. This prevents researchers manipulating the data using statistical methods to fit their hypothesis. Researchers have shown that very few clinical studies adapted this framework. Power analyses is a statistics method used to improve the quality of studies. Power analyses determine the number of participants needed for the study so that the results are robust. To date, we do not know how many clinical studies use power analyses. My study specifically examines the trend of clinical trials for depression treatments that conduct power analyses before their studies. Depression rates are surging especially during the pandemic, and it is crucial for depression treatments to be rooted in robust research. If very few studies conducted power analyses, this suggests that many clinical trials do not have sufficient participants and the results are inconclusive based on current research standards. In other words, researchers cannot conclude if depression treatments are effective. The results of this study can be used to alert clinical researchers to recruit sufficient participants for their studies, which can reduce misinformed treatment decisions.

column36: Mechanisms of functional-MRI-based decoding of information conveyed by cortical columns
column37: Previous studies demonstrated that multivariate machine learning algorithms could decode visual stimuli from fMRI data. This result is surprising given the large size of the voxels relative to the mean cycle length of columns. The mechanism by which low-resolution imaging decodes information represented at a fine-scale relative to the voxel size is unclear. We hypothesize that the successful decoding of information conveyed by cortical columns relies on a combination of different mechanisms. The objective of our study is to determine the extent to which components of different spatial frequencies of the hemodynamic response in gray matter regions, venules, and veins carry information on neuronal responses organized in cortical columns. We will evaluate the differential contrasts and component-specific decoding performances using large voxels. Two marmosets will be trained to fixate on a fixation spot while oriented gratings stimuli are presented. We will image the responses in marmoset primary visual area to oriented gratings using multiple illumination wavelengths and compute relative changes in the content of deoxy-Hb, which is a reliable marker of BOLD fMRI responses. We will analyze separate and combined contributions to decoding from irregularities in the columnar organization (high-pass filtered data), large-scale organization (low-pass filtered data) from gray matter regions, and from venules and veins. The results of our experiments and modeling will dissect the mechanisms underlying fMRI-based decoding of information conveyed in cortical columns based on an experimental model with a known columnar organization.

column36: Wound Healing and Aging in a Burn Model
column37: Despite recent advances in burn care, elderly patients continue to experience the highest mortality and morbidity rates after burn injuries. While the exact reasons are unknown, recent studies have linked these worsened outcomes to impaired wound healing in older burn patients. With aging, cells lose their ability to divide and interestingly this is implicated in both wound healing and tissue repair. These non-dividing, otherwise known as senescent cells, release several inflammatory molecules which induce local and systemic dysfunction. While short-lived senescence is required for mild wounds, the long-lived accumulation of senescent cells places a burden on more severe wounds such as burns, slowing the healing process and speeding up disease progression. To target these accumulating cells, recent research has discovered senolytic drugs, a class of drugs that selectively kill senescent cells. Among these drugs are Dasatinib plus Quercetin (D+Q) which hold great potential as they are being used in clinical trials for multiple age-related human diseases. The purpose of this research is to investigate the mechanisms underlying impaired wound healing to pave the way for effective therapies that can improve outcomes for this highly vulnerable population. We hypothesize that D+Q will improve post-burn wound healing outcomes in the elderly by effectively reducing senescent cells, allowing normal tissue repair. As the elderly population continues to grow, there is an immense need for aging studies. With clinical trials for adults burn patients in progress, it is crucial that we investigate novel strategies that will provide mechanisms understanding these poor outcomes in the elderly, and allow us to ultimately proceed with caution to upcoming clinical trials.

column36: Effects of Resistance Exercise on Blood Glucose in Post-Menopausal Women with Type 1 Diabetes
column37: Post-menopausal women with type 1 diabetes are at higher risk of heart disease, muscle loss, and bone density loss than women without diabetes, leading to an increased risk of frailty. Existing evidence suggests that resistance exercise reduces these risks, however, it can also increase instability of blood glucose levels in people with type 1 diabetes. To date, no research has been published documenting the exercise experience of this population, making it difficult to provide evidence-based recommendations for safe exercise practices. This pilot study will recruit 15 post-menopausal women with type 1 diabetes to test the efficacy and safety of two different resistance exercise protocols (one high-repetition, light weight, and one moderate-repetition, moderate weight), comparing acute changes in blood glucose levels both during, and for the 24 hours after exercise using continuous glucose monitoring. We expect the latter protocol to be associated with smaller blood glucose declines during exercise and lower mean glucose levels overnight following exercise. After completing the testing sessions, participants will be invited to take part in a focus group to discuss their experience, protocol preference, barriers to exercise, and other information they feel may improve their exercise experience. The goal of this research is to provide initial data, proof of recruitment feasibility, and participant feedback to tailor further research. Combined, these data can then be used to build an optimal resistance exercise program that is both safe and effective for women with type 1 diabetes. Researchers developing closed-loop insulin delivery systems may also use these data to create age and sex-specific glucose management algorithms for exercise.

column36: Evaluating the role of ATP-citrate lyase in regulating fatty acid oxidation in chronic kidney disease
column37: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is the leading cause of kidney failure in Canada, affecting 4 million Canadians. There is no cure for CKD and current treatments are only able to slow down disease progression. CKD is caused by scarring in the kidney. The kidney requires a lot of energy to do its job filtering our blood and creating urine, and in CKD the ability to create and use energy is reduced. The protein ATP-citrate lyase (ACLY) that is present in the kidney contributes to CKD. Research has shown that people and mice with CKD have higher levels of this protein than healthy individuals. ACLY creates a molecule called acetyl-coA that is likely to cause our kidneys to produce less energy. This study will test if ACLY is causing the kidneys to produce and use less energy. This will be done by using mice with CKD and blocking the activity of ACLY using a drug to see if this will help the kidney create more energy for itself. The kidneys of the mice will be tested to see if the drug worked in increasing energy levels and if it prevented kidney scarring. A type of cell in the kidney, called tubular cells, makes up most of the kidney and requires a lot of energy. To understand how this process is happening, we will perform experiments with tubular cells and give them stressors, like those found in CKD, and ACLY-blockers to test if the energy levels are restored. This study is important because there is no cure for CKD and patients will eventually develop end-stage kidney disease, requiring dialysis or transplant. Research needs to be done to create new medications for those suffering from CKD. Current studies are testing ACLY-blocking drugs to treat heart disease. If our study is successful, this drug is well-positioned to be developed into a new treatment for CKD.
