Clinical assessment methods are limited by the low resolution and subjective nature of the clinical examination. Interactive robotics, such as the Kinarm, offer a more robust and quantifiable approach to assess neurological function. This study aims to evaluate neurological function in primary brain tumour patients using Kinarm-based assessment. Our objectives are: (1) To assess the feasibility (e.g., safety, tolerability, ability to detect deficits) of using Kinarm-based assessment, and (2) To compare patterns of impairment pre- and post-operatively. We hypothesize that: (1) Kinarm-based assessment will be feasible and will reveal various neurological deficits; (2) The robotic tool will reveal impairments better than the standard RBANS tool; and (3) The pattern or severity of impairments may improve or worsen with surgery. Adult primary brain tumour patients will undergo Kinarm Standard Tests to assess sensory, motor, and cognitive function. Pre- and post-surgery Kinarm results will be compared, scored against age/sex matched healthy controls as well as RBANS scores. Kinarm-based assessment may identify possible markers for tumour diagnosis and progression, helping to predict patient outcomes, evaluate successful tumour resection, and plan neurological rehabilitation. Our findings will establish the feasibility of using the Kinarm to identify and quantify neurological deficits in brain tumour patients, setting the stage for its use in clinical trials comparing different surgical approaches or treatments aimed at minimizing the cognitive footprint.

column36: Examining the role of microglia in long-term neuropathology following acute SARS-CoV-2 infection using neural organoids
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic, caused by the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, has taken a major toll on human life. There has been emergent evidence of brain-related symptoms such as depression, anxiety and brain fog months after the infection has been cleared. This condition has been termed ;post-acute sequalae of COVID-19 (PASC), although the origin of these symptoms is unknown. Research suggests SARS-CoV-2 can migrate to the brain and invade neurons, the brains functional cells, and microglia, the brain-resident immune cells that attack harmful substances like viruses. Some of the mechanisms by which SARS-CoV-2 damage the brain overlap with neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimers. Specifically, inflammation is crucial for clearing infection, but when sustained for long periods of time, accumulation can result in overactive microglia that damage brain tissue. I suspect that microglia are the primary cause of long-term perturbations in brain health in recovered COVID-19 patients suffering from PASC. I will study PASC using miniature, simplified brains in a dish (known as cerebral organoids) derived from stem cells given specific instructions to form brain tissue. Stem cells function like embryonic cells and can form most bodily tissues depending on their nutritional environment. Once formed, I will infect cerebral organoids with SARS-CoV-2 and other related viruses to determine their effects on brain cell function. Signals triggering inflammation, cell death, and neurodegeneration will be traced back to microglial interactions with neurons and supporting nerve cells. These experiments will characterize the poorly understood post-infection environment of the brain and buttress our understanding of PASC to inform better treatment options for patients recovering from COVID-19.

column36: Evaluating the progress of private sector policies and commitments to improve the Canadian food environment from 2019 to 2022
column37: Food environments are described as all interfaces and factors that shape how consumers make their food choices. The creation of healthy food environments will require substantial efforts from both the public and private sectors. column36: Molecular target testing in a preclinical culture assay of Emery Dreifuss muscular dystrophy
column37: An emerging strategy of regenerative medicine focuses on harnessing the function of resident stem cell populations to heal tissue injuries and cure disease, a process called endogenous repair. For instance, in cases of major muscle damage such as muscular dystrophy disorders, muscle stem cells (MuSCs) reside in the muscle tissue, but have reduced regenerative abilities that lead to degeneration. Using a tissue engineering approach, the goal of this work is to generate and validate a human model of Emery Dreifuss muscular dystrophy (EDMD) to elucidate the cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying EDMD MuSC pathophysiology. Our lab has developed a 3D mini-muscle tissue platform that recapitulates MuSC-mediated skeletal muscle repair called Muscle Endogenous Repair (MEndR), whereby upon muscle injury, the MuSCs accurately recapitulate the in vivo endogenousrepair process. We will first optimize our MEndR platform for EDMD patient-derived immortalized human myoblasts, and subsequently will characterize the parameters of muscle fiber health and endogenous regeneration between healthy and EDMD myoblasts, such as myotube morphology, nuclei fusion index, as well as the size and proliferative state of the resident MuSC-like population. We hypothesize the EDMD patient-derived myoblasts will have impaired endogenous repair capabilities, and that these defects can be recapitulated in our MEndR platform. Thus, we will use the MEndR assay to test candidate biomolecules that rescue the impaired regenerative defects observed in the EDMD myoblasts. This research will fill a fundamental gap in knowledge by generating a first-class skeletal muscle tissue platform for human myoblasts and will identify therapeutic molecules that stimulate MuSC activity and endogenous repair in EDMD.

column37: Apres un accident vasculaire cerebral ischemique (AVCi), une recuperation partielle spontanee est eventuelle grace a des mecanismes de reorganisation fonctionnelle impliquant des modifications de la connectivite et des proprietes fonctionnelles des aires saines. Une incidence sur la plasticite apres une lesion cerebrale ischemique est donc concevable.Ce projet etudie la contribution des CB2R dans la reorganisation fonctionnelle apres un AVCi dans le cortex visuel de souris. L'administration de l'agoniste CB2R HU-308 avant l'induction d'un AVCi protegerait les reseaux neuronaux. Idem a une administration a posteriori, elle stimulerait aussi la plasticite pour une meilleure recuperation fonctionnelle. L'agoniste inverse CB2R AM630 aurait des effets opposes.Les ligands CB2R seront administres avant ou apres l'induction de l'AVCi par photothrombose. Le regain fonctionnel sera aussi mesure grace a des tests comportementaux de distinction d'orientations GO/NO-GO. L'etude ameliorera la comprehension de la contribution des eCBs et des CB2R aux mecanismes de la plasticite des AVCi et des risques lies a l'usage du cannabis pour les individus vulnerables. column36: Investigating the reliability of accelerometer-based measures of physical activity and sedentary time in toddlers
column37: Evaluating movement behaviours such as physical activity may provide valuable insights to health outcomes such obesity and cardiovascular disease in children. Currently, there is a knowledge gap investigating the relationship of physical activity and health outcomes in toddlers 12-35 months of age due to the lack of accurate methods for monitoring movement behaviours. Recently, accelerometers has been widely used as a tool for measuring physical activity in children, but it has not been studied extensively in toddlers. Therefore, the aim of this study will be to investigate the reliability of accelerometers in estimating habitual physical activity and sedentary time in toddlers. In 2 play stations, toddlers were recruited to participate in free play and perform standardized tasks. Each toddler was videotaped and equipped with an accelerometer to record movement activities. Furthermore, toddlers were provided accelerometers to take home and wear the device for 7 days between each play session. Movement behaviours of toddlers between the play sessions will be coded and matched with the accelerometer-recorded movements to evaluate the reliability of the technology. Statistical analyses will be conducted on the 7-day accelerometer data to determine optimal wear time and the reliability in estimating movement behaviours in toddlers. Findings of our study will develop an accurate method in monitoring physical activity in toddlers and thus, provide further directions in establishing appropriate guidelines to facilitate early childhood development and reduce the risk of health disparities in this age population.

column36: Traditional Knowledge and Food Security Among Indigenous Youth in the Northwest Territories, Canada
column37: The research question that I propose to engage with is: how can traditional knowledge be used to promote wellbeing and prevent food insecurity among Indigenous youth in the Northwest Territories (NWT), Canada? Food insecurity, which refers to a lack of access to safe, healthy, and sufficient food, is an important public health issue impacting Indigenous people in the NWT. Food insecurity can have negative impacts on physical and mental health. There are a variety of factors that influence food insecurity in the NWT, such as high cost of living, climate change, and the legacy of colonial policies. To respond to the unique needs of communities in the NWT facing this complex issue, further study is needed to highlight the pre-existing strengths, assets, and protective factors in NWT communities. In particular, traditional knowledge and youth have been identified as priority themes for food security research in the NWT. The objective of this research is to identify ways that traditional knowledge can be used to support wellbeing, to increase understanding of food security in the NWT, and to empower and encourage future leadership in the area of food security among Indigenous youth. This project will use a community-based participatory action research approach which focuses on centering research around community priorities and building a reciprocal relationship between researchers and community members. By actively involving youth in the research process and focusing on the unique factors impacting food security among Indigenous youth, the results of this proposed research can serve to inform health promotion programming and policies in NWT schools and communities.

column36: Role of ATF4 in Skeletal Muscle Mitochondrial Adaptations in Response to Exercise
column37: Skeletal muscle fibres contain subpopulations of mitochondria that are responsive and adaptive to external stress-inducing stimuli, such as exercise. Mitochondria rely on constant and synchronized quality control processes, termed mitophagy (mitochondrial degradation), biogenesis (mitochondrial synthesis) and the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRmt) to preserve cell homeostasis and function during stress-inducing conditions. Of particular interest, the UPR is a mitochondrial regulatory pathway which serves to mitigate the initial mitochondrial proteotoxicity caused by the accumulation of un-or-misfolded proteins within the mitochondria to restore cellular homeostasis. In our laboratory it has been suggested that the transcription factor ATF4 may play a possible role in mediating the UPRmt and in regulating mitochondrial adaptations during stress-inducing stimuli. The objectives of this project are to investigate the role of ATF4 in 1) mediating mitochondrial signaling with response to acute exercise, and 2) regulating mitochondrial adaptations in response to chronic exercise. To achieve these objectives, this study will subject Wild-Type and tamoxifen inducible ATF4 muscle-specific knockout mice to either a 6-week chronic exercise program, or to an acute bout of exercise. We hypothesize that ATF4 is required to mediate the UPRmt in response to both acute and chronic exercise-induced stress, and that the UPRmt induction is necessary for effective adaptation to exercise. The significance of this work will be to establish the role of ATF4 in promoting mitochondrial health and function during exercise.

column36: Characterization of the molecular mechanisms controlling anti-LG3 autoantibody production in the context of lupus nephritis
column37: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disease. One of the targeted organs is the kidney, leading to a serious condition called lupus nephritis (LN). LN affects up to 60% of patients with SLE, 30% of whom progress to end-stage renal disease. Kidneys are then unable to filter waste products from the blood. Patients must undergo dialysis or transplantation to survive.During LN, blood vessels that supply nutrients to kidneys are damaged. Biopsy is the gold-standard for assessing the condition of the kidney, but it is an invasive procedure. Our understanding of the mechanisms leading to the attack on the kidney is still very partial and the development of non-invasive methods is needed to track, treat, and prevent LN complications.Our team demonstrated that damaged blood vessels release molecular messengers. This induces the production of antibodies (Ab) against self-molecules. One of these molecules, LG3, is found on the blood vessels. Our group showed that Ab against LG3(anti-LG3) in vessels are important in the loss of microvessels in several kidney diseases. Also, anti-LG3 are found in higher amounts in the blood of LN patients as well as in mice with lupus. We hypothesize that anti-LG3 Ab contribute to damage to blood vessels and loss of kidney function in LN patients. The aim of my project is to characterize the appearance of anti-LG3 and the molecular mechanisms that control anti-LG3 Ab production as well as their renal effects in lupus mice. That will allow us to identify novel mechanisms and predictors of renal dysfunction. Our project offers an opportunity to identify new interventional targets that will help track and treat LN patients.

column36: Characterization of mitochondrial organization, epigenomic regulation, and the Anaphase Promoting Complex in Progeria-driven premature senescence
column37: Aging, and age-related diseases are a rising concern for the healthcare system and for the aging population. It is imperative that we, as a society, develop an understanding of what drives the aging process to improve the health and lifespan of our growing population. So far, the exact nature of how cells and the body ages is not fully understood. To further our understanding, we are studying the detailed cellular processes of senescence (cell retirement) by way of a disease of rapid and premature aging Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS). HGPS is a syndrome where cells age very rapidly, while demonstrating effects which mirror ordinary aging at a rapid pace. Because nearly all living things age, we know that we are looking for crucial cellular processes which are very similar across all organisms, furthermore, this is a syndrome that we can reproduce in single cells. Because of this, we are able to use a single celled organism, the Brewing Yeast, to study human aging with an HGPS model. We modify the genomes of these yeast one gene at a time, and through a variety of comparative tests look for any mutations (changes to one gene) which alter the outcome or severity of the rapid-ageing disease HGPS. We have already found several genes relating to several systems inducing chromatin regulation, and mitochondrial organization, which, when manipulated, change how these sick rapid-ageing cells grow. We propose to characterize extend to, and mechanism by which these systems impact the process of senescence. This work will explore how manipulating these systems influences HGPS, furthering our understanding of both these systems and the process of senescence. The information we gather will form the basis for future studies into promoting cellular health and longevity.

column36: The effect of colorectal high-grade dysplasia on the risk of metachronous high-risk adenomas and colorectal cancer
column37: Colorectal cancer is the second cause of cancer deaths and the third most common cancer worldwide. The main screening modality is colonoscopy, a procedure where the bowel is visualized with a camera and where pre-cancerous lesions can be removed. Such screening has been proven to reduce medical complications and deaths from colorectal cancer. After pre-cancerous lesions are removed, physicians refer to society guidelines to decide when patients should be seen again. For example, patients with a normal colonoscopy should be seen in seven to ten years. One of the pre-cancerous lesions that can be found is high-grade dysplasia. Guidelines suggest that a patient who has high-grade dysplasia should have a repeat colonoscopy in three years, based on expert consensus, but that the evidence to support this recommendation is of low to moderate quality. One study found that this pre-cancerous lesion increases the risk of future colorectal cancer while three studies found that it does not. The goal of my project is to determine if high-grade dysplasia increases the risk of future colorectal cancer and of future pre-cancerous lesions. Other goals of my project are to determine how certain factors can affect this risk, like sex, age, obesity, smoking, alcohol use or colorectal cancer in the family, and to determine if patients received appropriate follow-up. 1235 patients will be included in the study. This makes it the largest study on high-grade dysplasia to date. We hypothesize that high-grade dysplasia truly increases the risk of future pre-cancerous lesions and colorectal cancer. This study will allow us to significantly contribute to the knowledge that physicians have on this pre-cancerous lesion, to be able to deliver better care to patients undergoing a colonoscopy.

column36: Subcortical Involvement of Sleep Dysfunction in Genetic Frontotemporal Dementia
column37: Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD) has a strong genetic predisposition. One-third of people who develop FTD have a family history of the disease. Most of which are caused by heritable mutations within the DNA in one of three genes: chromosome 9 open reading frame 72 (C9orf72), progranulin (GRN), and microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT). Among patients with FTD, sleep problems are prevalent, with up to three-quarters of FTD patients having some sort of sleep problem. Findings have suggested that people with MAPT mutations have more sleep problems than other mutation carriers, but why this occurs remains unclear. The hypothalamus, a brain structure important for regulating sleep, may be the cause of the observed increased sleep problems. The hypothalamus is involved in sleep problems in other neurodegenerative disorders, and FTD patients with MAPT mutations have more pronounced cell death, called atrophy, in the hypothalamus. Few studies have looked at atrophy in the hypothalamus in genetic FTD, and none have related changes in the hypothalamus to increased sleep problems. The question remains, does this atrophy contribute to sleep problems?To address this question, we will use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), a technology that allows for the detailed imaging of tissue, to scan the brains of people with mutations that cause FTD. We will examine the trajectory of change in the hypothalamus across the lifespan. Using clinical information from these subjects, we will relate changes in hypothalamic structure to the presence and severity of sleep problems. The findings from this project will shed light on the mechanisms that may be at the heart of sleep problems that are common in genetic FTD and may further inform novel treatments for sleep problems in these disorders.

column36: Elucidation des mecanismes par lesquels l'interleukine-1a favorise la neuroinflammation et la degenerescence secondaire des oligodendrocytes apres une lesion de la moelle epiniere
column37: Au Canada, plus de 86 000 personnes sont affligees par une lesion de la moelle epiniere (LME). Il est estime que le cout des depenses reliees a chacun de ces individus au cours de leur vie sera de plus de 3 millions de dollars. Les dommages qui surviennent a la suite d'une LME sont divises en deux phases distinctes: les dommages primaires et les dommages secondaires. Les dommages primaires sont directement causes par l'impact, ce qui mene a la mort des cellules au site de lesion. La mort des cellules et la compression entrainent plusieurs changements biochimiques conduisant a la production de molecules causant l'inflammation. Or, nos travaux ont montre que l'inflammation a pour effet de provoquer une deuxieme vague de mort cellulaire affectant principalement les oligodendrocytes (OLs), des cellules responsables de former la gaine isolante de myeline qui assure la conduction des signaux nerveux et protege les prolongements des neurones, augmentant du meme coup la gravite et l'etendue de la lesion, d'ou son appellation de << dommages secondaires >>. La mort des OLs cause donc une demyelinisation et un ralentissement de l'influx nerveux en plus de rendre les neurones et leurs axones plus vulnerables. La transition entre les dommages primaires et secondaires serait declenchee par la liberation de molecules associees au danger, dont la plus connue dans la moelle epiniere lesee est l'interleukine-1 alpha (IL-1?). Les travaux anterieurs de notre equipe ont permis de demontrer que l'IL-1? provoque la mort des OLs en plus de permettre une infiltration de cellules immunitaires provenant du sang, appelees neutrophiles. Les travaux ici proposes ont donc pour objectif d'identifier le mecanisme par lequel l'IL-1? entraine l'infiltration des neutrophiles et la mort des OLs.

column36: Emotion Mindset as a Predictor of Emotion Polyregulation
column37: Anxiety is related to the ability for emotion regulation (ER) - the process where people modify the experience (intensity, duration, course) and expression of emotions. Further information for successful ER is key for understanding how to manage symptoms of anxiety, which is important for mental wellness. The current ER literature primarily has contrasted single strategies to assess individual effectiveness, leaving a gap in the literature, since people commonly use more than one strategy during a regulation instance - emotion polyregulation. Individual differences that predict who exactly is more likely to engage in emotion polyregulation have also not been sufficiently explored. This study will investigate emotion mindset (fixed versus growth) as a predictor of the use and success of emotion polyregulation of state anxiety in young adults. Using a diverse sample from Canadian universities, I will use the Implicit Theories of Emotion Scale to determine growth or fixed emotion mindset. State anxiety, ER strategies (e.g. distraction), and their success will be measured using experience sampling to capture ER in daily life through a smartphone app (6 prompts daily for 2 weeks for a 1-minute survey). I will use multilevel modeling for data analysis. I hypothesize that people with a growth emotion mindset will 1) show higher emotion polyregulation, 2) report using more successful strategies to regulate state anxiety, and 3) be more successful overall in regulating state anxiety. An emotion polyregulation approach may be a better representation of daily ER. Thus, examining emotion polyregulation and emotion mindset will provide valuable information for enhancing the effectiveness of interventions and psychoeducation. Successful ER is an effortful process requiring knowledge.

column36: Nouvelles valeurs de reference en echocardiographie pediatrique a l'aide de modeles resistants aux influences de l'obesite
column37: L'echocardiographie est un outil permettant le diagnostic et le suivi de maladies cardiaques, notamment chez les enfants. Chez les enfants en croissance, l'interpretation des resultats de l'echocardiographie est compliquee par leur developpement rapide. Les resultats obtenus a l'echocardiographie doivent donc etre compares a des valeurs de reference, qui varient en fonction de l'age, du sexe et de la taille corporelle de l'enfant.Il est donc important de developper des modeles statistiques fiables permettant de determiner si les resultats a l'echocardiographie sont normaux. Historiquement, la surface corporelle etait utilisee pour comparer la taille du coeur de l'enfant. Cependant, il a ete demontre que les modeles bases uniquement sur la surface corporelle surestiment la taille des structures cardiaques chez les enfants en surpoids, ce qui peut mener a des erreurs diagnostiques. Notre laboratoire developpe des modeles mathematiques pour mieux predire la taille du coeur des enfants, et cela autant pour les enfants avec poids normal que ceux avec embonpoint et obesite.Ce projet de recherche vise a developper des valeurs de references pour l'ensemble des mesures prises pendant une echocardiographie en se basant sur le poids, la taille et le sexe de l'enfant. L'etude est realisee a l'aide d'une base de donnees du Reseau Canadien de Recherche en Cardiologie Congenitale Pediatrique, qui contient des donnees sur plus de 20 000 enfants. En utilisant une methode systematique d'essai et d'optimisation de plusieurs modeles statistiques, des valeurs de reference seront calculees a partir de cette base de donnees.Cette etude permettra une meilleure interpretation des mesures d'echocardiographies en pediatrie et augmentera la fiabilite diagnostique de cet outil.

column36: Autism Intervention Research in Ontario: The Meaning of the Disorder and Care
column37: In Ontario, parents of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are urged to start evidence-based therapies as soon as possible. While such therapies have an empirical basis, they also hold inherent assumptions about personhood and ;normalcy that arise from the cultural, historical, and societal contexts influencing medical practice. The emerging neurodiversity paradigm provides new positive interpretations of autism and argues for developing therapies that improve quality of life rather than targeting particular autistic behaviours. Yet, it is unknown whether this line of research has brought any changes to developing ASD interventions in Ontario.The objective of the study is thus to investigate discursive constructions of therapeutic goals in Ontario-based research on ASD interventions. Specifically, the study will explore what researchers try to improve, their underlying assumptions about normalcy, personhood, and whose voices are authorized in clinician-client interactions. The study will investigate whether this research allows space for acceptance in the context of growing advocacy for neurodiversity.The study will systematically review recently published peer-reviewed articles on ASD interventions conducted in Ontario and select a corpus of articles for detailed discursive analysis. The articles will be analyzed as a set of discourses that enable or impose limitations on what can be said, who has a voice, and possibilities for action.The study can provide insightful connections between the current critique of ASD interventions and local research in Ontario. Importantly, this study can stimulate discussion of new approaches to therapies and support the emergence of interventions rooted in acceptance and care for the quality of life of those with ASD.

column36: Telehealth Intervention Program for Older Adults (TIP-OA): Predictors of treatment response
column37: Prior to COVID-19, psychiatric disorders affected over 10;15% of older adults (1,000,000 Canadians aged 60+) costing $15 billion/year. The pandemic has increased social isolation and limited resources. We developed an innovative volunteer-based Telehealth Intervention Program for Older Adults (TIP-OA), to improve mental health in older adults. Volunteers provide weekly phone calls to older adults (have served 700+ older adults). There is limited data about volunteer-based phoning programs' real-world effectiveness and predictors of response. To help maximize the programs benefits, and identify individuals needing more support this study aims to identify predictors of treatment response based on participant baseline risk ratings (green: low risk, orange: medium risk, red: high risk) and demographic characteristics. Our primary aim is to identify whether baseline risk level is associated with improved mental health outcomes at 8-week follow-up for stress, depression, anxiety, and COVID fear. Our secondary aim is to identify whether baseline demographic characteristics (age, gender, neighbourhood, etc.) are associated with improvement in mental health outcomes. We anticipate that TIP-OA will be beneficial for improving stress, depression and anxiety symptoms, and fear of COVID over 8-weeks in higher baseline risk level participants. If successful, our studys potential scientific findings will allow us to 1) further refine the intervention and focus future related interventions to patient populations who could benefit most, 2) be a stepping stone for other telehealth and digital health interventions for older adults, and 3) translate these findings to the application and further development of TIP-OA or related interventions on a larger scale.

column36: Strategies de coping et perceptions dans le retablissement post-commotionnel des jeunes
column37: Les enfants et les adolescents sont plus susceptibles de subir une commotion cerebrale (CC) (McCrory et al., 2017). Les CC peuvent engendrer un eventail de symptomes appeles symptomes post-commotionnels (SPC). En generale, les jeunes vont se retablir en moins de 4 semaines mais pour certains, le retablissement va se prolonger (Rausa et al., 2018). Les etudes suggerent que les SPC sont moderes par plusieurs facteurs dont les perceptions et les strategies de coping (Mah et al., 2018). En outre, des interventions qui ciblent les representations et perceptions, comme la psychoeducation, pourraient s'averer pertinentes pour promouvoir un retablissement sain (Mah et al., 2018). Bien que la recherche sur les perceptions des CC aupres des jeunes demeure limitee, des appuis preliminaires suggerent qu'elles auraient egalement un role a jouer dans le retablissement (Plourde et al., 2020). Ainsi, la presente etude a deux objectifs : 1) examiner les liens entre les perceptions et strategies de coping avec les SPC pre- et post-intervention et 2) evaluer les changements dans les perceptions, les strategies de coping et SPC pre- et post-intervention.Environ 50 familles de jeunes de 5 a 17 ans ayant subi une commotion cerebrale seront recrutees. Les jeunes et leurs familles ayant consenti a participer a l'etude seront evalues 2 semaines post-blessure (evaluation pre-psychoeducation) et 4 semaines post-blessure (evaluation post-intervention). Les versions francaises des outils suivants seront utilisees : le << Health and Behaviour Inventory >> ; le << Patient Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System >> ; le << Brief Illness Perceptions Questionnaire >> ; et le << KidCOPE >>. Les donnees seront en suite analysees de maniere descriptive, notamment avec des correlations et le test-t.

column36: Inhibitor of apoptosis as a therapeutic vulnerability in high-fatality leukemia
column37: Acute Megakaryoblastic Leukemia (AMKL) is a subtype of Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) and is found in around 10% of children suffering from AML. Patients of childhood AMKL are at a higher risk of responding poorly to chemotherapy, early relapse and poor survival rates (40% of cure rates). AMKL can be subgrouped based on the abnormal chimeric fusion protein it carries which is thought to be the cause for leukemia. Our lab successfully generated models of some of these rare but relevant high-fatality AMKL. These synthetic models of AMKL are able to mimic the human disease in a patho-physiological relevant context in mice. We used these models in a high-throughput chemical screen to identify new treatment options and found two drugs that specifically target only one subgroup of AMKL. Both drugs are targeting proteins that are involved in programmed cell death, also known as apoptosis. The goal of my project is to analyse the impact of those two drugs on my leukemic cells. Briefly, I will analyse what effect our drugs have on our models of AMKL by observing various parameters including if they undergo cell death or irreversible growth arrest. Furthermore, I will study if they are becoming more mature after drug treatment and lose their potential to initiate leukemia. Additionally, I will investigate if the proposed drugs are using the published mechanism of action in our models of AMKL. Importantly, I will monitor for each assay if these two drugs are impacting healthy stem and progenitor cells. Overall, this project will highlight the importance of apoptosis for different subgroups of AMKL and identify new therapeutic options that can be exploited for high-risk patients of childhood leukemia.

column36: Investigating brain activation patterns during activities of daily living after traumatic brain injury
column37: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a common injury that can lead to major disruptions in activities of daily living, such as dressing and bathing. Independence in these basic tasks is critical for timely discharge from hospital, community participation, and psychological health. Daily therapy is provided for people in the rehabilitation setting to improve activities of daily living. However, there is currently a lack of knowledge on the brain activation patterns during re-learning of these daily tasks. Understanding the changes in brain activity after TBI and during recovery can help with creating more effective therapies based on the patterns of brain damage. In this project, we aim to investigate the brain activation patterns during the performance of a simple daily task of dressing after TBI. To achieve this goal, functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) will be used to examine brain activation patterns in people with TBI compared to healthy controls when completing an upper body dressing task. fNIRS, a non-invasive neuroimaging technique, is used for studying the brain activation levels through the measurement of changes in haemoglobin concentrations in the cerebral blood flow. As fNIRS is wearable and portable, it allows participants to be unconstrained when performing tasks, and thus more accurately depict real-life situations and brain activation patterns. This study will provide evidence on brain activation patterns during re-learning of daily tasks after TBI. Broadly, this project will contribute knowledge to future clinical trials that aim to improve task performance and health outcomes after TBI.

column36: Caracterisation des fonctions bromodomaine-dependantes des complexes mSWI/SNF dans les carcinomes hepatocellulaires
column37: Des mutations frequentes de cellules cancereuses touchent les complexes proteiques mSWI/SNF. Ces assemblages de proteines sont essentiels a l'initiation du cancer du foie, car ils regulent l'utilisation et la structure du materiel genetique, l'ADN. Leurs proteines interagissent directement avec l'ADN et decodent ses signaux. Le domaine de lecture le plus important dans ce processus est le bromodomaine (BRD). Comme les complexes mSWI/SNF possedent la plus forte densite de BRD chez l'humain, les BRD seraient des acteurs centraux a leurs fonctions.Le laboratoire du Dr Lambert suppose que les BRD sont essentiels a l'activite des complexes mSWI/SNF. Un large objectif est de definir comment les BRD contribuent aux fonctions de ces complexes en examinant leurs associations avec les proteines affectant l'ADN. Ce projet vise la mise en place d'un modele cellulaire faisant varier des signaux affectant le materiel genetique pour permettre la caracterisation d'associations potentiellement BRD-dependantes susceptibles de contribuer au cancer du foie.Supprimer les genes ACLY et ACOT12 de cellules hepatiques modulera les niveaux du metabolite cle acetyl-CoA pour quantifier et identifier des sites specifiques des proteines affectant l'ADN. Les marques les plus modulees et les complexes seront localises sur le genome pour definir si les BRD des complexes peuvent lire ces sites. Tester l'expression des genes dont la variation des signaux affecte le plus la localisation des complexes determinera si l'utilisation de l'ADN est alteree.Ce projet favorisera la comprehension des mecanismes sous-jacents aux fonctions des BRD dans les complexes mSWI/SNF et leurs impacts dans le cancer du foie. A plus long terme, il permettra d'explorer les interventions nutritionnelles pour traiter ce cancer.

column36: Bypassing inositol polyphosphate 4-phosphatase type II-mediated chemoresistance and leukemic stemness in Acute Myeloid Leukemia via cotreatment with lysosomal inhibitors.
column37: Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) is a common, aggressive type of leukemia. The progression of AML depends on the function of cells called leukemic stem cells (LSCs). Research shows that AML patients with high LSC content have an aggressive form of AML and have lower survival rates than patients with low LSC content. As such, it is necessary to investigate therapies that target LSCs to improve AML patient outcomes. Recent studies in our research group identified that AML patients with very aggressive disease and poor health outcomes have high levels of a protein called INPP4B. INPP4B is also reported to play a role in lysosomal function and activity. Additionally, previous research shows that lysosomal function is important to LSCs function. However, there is limited research linking LSCs, INPP4B overexpression, and lysosomal function to AML prognosis. This study aims to identify the role of INPP4B overexpression in lysosomal function and LSC content in AML. It is hypothesized that INPP4B overexpression plays a critical function in LSCs and promotes AML progression by altering lysosomal function. This study examines signalling alterations, lysosomal functions, and AML progression using mouse models of leukemia. Additionally, lysosomal inhibitors will be introduced to measure their role in AML progression. This research is significant as it aims to identify molecular pathways impacted by INPP4B in the hopes of generating new AML therapies that block INPP4B function and eliminate LSCs.

column36: The role of nucleolin in modulating immune responses as a scavenging receptor.
column37: Nucleolin is a protein typically found on the inside of cells within the nucleus. Less commonly, nucleolin can also be found on the cell surface. On the surface, nucleolin serves as a receptor for pathogens such as viruses, facilitating their entry into cells during infection. Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is one such virus that binds to nucleolin as it enters host cells.Recent findings in my research project suggest that nucleolin also binds to a variety of immune system proteins during RSV infection. By binding to components of the immune system, nucleolin could be interfering with the formation of proper immune responses, thereby promoting infection, and reducing our protection from pathogens like RSV. For the remainder of my project, I aim to determine how nucleolin alters immune responses and the effects those alterations have on vulnerability to RSV infection. To do this, I will use molecules that prevent nucleolin from binding to immune system proteins. Subsequently, I will comparatively measure both the extent of infection and immune system activity during RSV infection.RSV is the leading cause of infant hospitalization and a leading contributor to infant mortality globally. Despite the significant health burden caused by RSV infection, there are no vaccines available and limited options for treatment. Treatment options that are available are reserved for only high-risk patients due to concerns around their efficacy and safety. Therefore, a more complete understanding of the role of cell surface nucleolin in relation to immune responses during RSV infection is crucial. Through my project, I hope to inform new therapeutic strategies to treat RSV infections and help to alleviate the global burden of disease that RSV imposes.

column36: Youth exposure to marketing of sugary beverages and intake across six countries during pre- mid- and late COVID-19 pandemic
column37: Unhealthy food marketing is omnipresent and influences youths food preferences, consumption patterns and purchases, with important implications for health later in life. Marketing of sugary drinks is of particular interest as these are a principal source of sugar in young Canadians diets and intake is associated with obesity. Globally, public health policies have been implemented to restrict marketing directed at youth. In parallel, exposure to marketing of sugary drinks may have increased as a result of greater screen time during COVID-19 lockdowns and preliminary evidence suggests sugary drink intakes increased among youth. This project will explore youth exposure to marketing of sugary drinks across 6 countries and the relationship between marketing exposure and sugary drink intake during 3 phases of the COVID-19 pandemic (pre, mid, late). Exposure to marketing in various locations and intake of sugary drinks will be measured in repeated surveys of 11,500 youth ages 10-17 from Canada, Australia, Chile, Mexico, United Kingdom and United States at each phase of the pandemic as part of the International Food Policy Study. The level of lockdown restrictions will be assessed at each time point in each country to investigate associations with marketing exposure and sugary drink intake. Differences in potentially vulnerable subpopulations will be explored. This research uniquely provides in-depth individual-level marketing exposure data at various time points of the pandemic. Findings will contribute to global knowledge on the impact of food marketing on health-related outcomes among youth to inform food marketing policy, and may also inform future health crises, ensuring public health measures are supported by efforts to protect vulnerable populations.

column36: Constructing an In Vitro 3D Model of the Human Placenta in Health and Disease
column37: Nurturing a developing fetus can be a transformative experience for pregnant mothers. The placenta is a temporary organ that develops during pregnancy to nourish the fetus. It has both fetal and maternal components. The fetal cells called ;trophoblasts perform many functions, including invasion of the uterus to widen the uterine arteries. This process is needed for an adequate flow of maternal blood to carry nutrients and oxygen for the fetus. Poor trophoblast invasion can compromise the blood flow, resulting in growth-retarded babies and a life-threatening maternal disease called ;preeclampsia (PE). Our lab found that a molecule called ;decorin (DCN) is made by ;decidual cells in the uterus and restrains trophoblast invasiveness. DCN over-production by decidual cells is associated with PE, and elevated maternal plasma DCN levels could predict PE before clinical signs appear. Our project aims to create 3D models of normal and pathological placentas, which will likely partially replicate this organs structure. We will grow various placental cells together based on their fetal or maternal origin. From these cell populations, we will create 3D cell aggregates called ;spheroids. Spheroids made of fetal and maternal cells will contact one another and develop cellular interactions to form the 3D normal placental models. We will incorporate decidual cells expressing high or low DCN levels into our 3D models to replicate pathological (PE-associated and hyper-invasive) placentas. These 3D structures will be analyzed for markers of different cell types. These models could be used to investigate abnormal placental development in greater depth. We hope this project can lead to insights for treating placental pathologies so that pregnancy is safer for mothers and fetuses.

column36: Developing Nutrient Enriched Perfusate for Ex Vivo Lung Perfusion
column37: Lung transplantation is the only curative intervention for end stage lung disease. Unfortunately, transplantation procedures are limited by low organ utilization rates. Ex Vivo Lung Perfusion (EVLP) is a technology that restores organ metabolism by maintaining lungs at 37°C though a circulating perfusate and mechanical ventilation, thus allowing clinicians to repair donor lungs which would have been discarded. Extending EVLP support time can further increase organ utilization and has been achieved with total parental nutrition (TPN) supplemented perfusates. However, the specific nutritional components supporting lung metabolism and the role of other protective nutrients (GlutaMAX, lipids, and carbohydrates) in EVLP remains unknown. We hypothesize that optimized compositions and concentrations of nutrients (TPN, GlutaMAX, lipids, and Glucose) will address metabolic demands of lung cells to maintain cellular metabolism and physiological function during extended EVLP. Mathematical modeling using clinical nutrient concentrations and infusion rates will be coupled with a dilution factor to estimate nutrient accumulation during EVLP. Using these models, low, medium, and high concentrated nutrient supplemented perfusates will be developed. A screening stage will then evaluate cell confluence, death, and migration of pulmonary endothelial cells exposed to diverse nutrient supplemented perfusates. Solutions which perform significantly better than the standard perfusate (Steen) will be tested in an EVLP culture model with the addition of lung epithelial cells to evaluate inflammation, cell structure, and mitochondrial health. Overall, we can use our results to develop the next generation of EVLP perfusates and significantly improve transplant patient outcomes.

column36: Capturing clinical experiences of culture and gender mediated presentations of psychosocial distress
column37: Societies everywhere, including Canada, are increasingly culturally diverse. Healthcare systems and clinical care must reflect and adapt to these realities to ensure effective and equitable patient-centered care. For example, cultural and gender-based differences may exist in how people present their mental health symptoms and psychosocial concerns to their physician. If these differences are not considered, mental health and illness challenges may be overlooked, or inappropriately treated. This qualitative study seeks to understand how culture, gender, and their intersecting effects impact the presentation and recognition of mental health challenges in primary care. A focus group with interpreters who support culturally diverse patients in their appointments with family doctors will be held to explore their perceptions of how gender influences the clinical encounter. Interviews with experienced primary care clinicians will identify practical strategies to help recognize and interpret culture and gender mediated presentations of mental health challenges. The results of this study will inform a module to complement training in patient-centered care and improve the recognition and treatment of mental health challenges in multicultural populations. Ultimately, this will help to address inequities in mental health care and outcomes.

column36: Mechanisms of oxidative stress tolerance in frozen cells and tissues
column37: Cryopreservation(preserving cells by freezing) is an important biomedical technology with awide range of applications, including assisted reproduction. Research hasestablished some ways of helping protect these frozen cells from lowtemperatures and ice. However, we are lacking information on how to preventdamage caused by cryopreservation-induced oxidative stress. Oxidative stressoccurs when there are too many unstable oxygen species (called reactive oxygenspecies, or ROS) in a cell, and the ROS damages that cell. In cryopreservation,oxidative stress happens during thawing. As ice melts inside the cell, oxygenfloods the system and creates a large amount of ROS. Antioxidant treatments removeROS from cells, and have the potential to improve cryopreservation outcomes.However, we need to better understand the mechanisms behind freeze-inducedoxidative damage, and how to this damage following cryopreservation. Spring field crickets, Gryllusveletis, naturally survive freeze-thaw cycles. We can use this naturallyfreeze-tolerant insect to study the mechanisms that promote cell and tissuesurvival post-freezing. In this project, I will test the hypothesis that theantioxidant enzyme Catalase contributes to freeze tolerance by mitigatingoxidative damage associated with freezing. Freeze-tolerant crickets havenaturally high levels of Catalase in their cells. I will use a technique calledRNA interference to prevent these crickets from accumulating Catalase, andexamine how this affects whole animal, tissue, and cell survival afterfreezing. This work will help increase our understanding of oxidative stressduring freeze-thaw cycles, which will help inform how we can protect cryopreservedhuman cells that are needed for medical procedures.

column36: The Effects of the Nasal Microbiome on the Susceptibility to Bacterial and Viral Pathogens
column37: The microbiome is essential to the health and functioning of human barrier tissues. Observational studies have demonstrated the nasal microbiota has the potential to reduce virulence of pathogenic bacteria, alter host immunology, and influence viral susceptibility. In-depth, controlled in vitro experiments are now required to identify the biological mechanisms of these relationships and inform new treatment and prevention modalities. This project aims to establish an in vitro model that recapitulates the nasal mucosal milieu and to explore interactions between the mucosa, commensal bacteria, and respiratory viral pathogens.Healthy turbinate mucosal tissues will be collected weekly from patients undergoing otolaryngologic surgery (approved for 50 participants). Using established techniques, basal epithelial cells will be isolated from tissues and cultured at the air-liquid interface to induce mucociliary differentiation. Differentiated airway epithelia will be inoculated with reconstructed bacterial communities (provided by microbial ecologist Dr. Cindy Liu) to assess their effect on (1) innate immune responses and (2) susceptibility to viral pathogens, including SARS-CoV-2, influenza, and XX. Viral infections will be performed in collaboration with virologist Dr. Ryan Troyer, in Westerns new biosafety containment level 3 facility (ImPaKT).The relation between the nasal microbiota and local immune responses in adult respiratory infections is little understood. Hence, understanding how the nasal microbiome shapes the immune milieu can illuminate why some individuals are more or less susceptibility to viral pathogens. This information will provide a foundation for future research to harness the microbiota as a novel strategy to prevent seasonal respiratory infections.

column36: Le role de la peur dans l'evolution des consequences de l'exposition a la violence chez les travailleurs en centre jeunesse
column37: Les intervenants en centre de readaptation pour jeunes en difficulte d'adaptation (CRJDA) au Quebec sont a haut risque d'etre exposes a de la violence commise par des usagers. Ces gestes de violence peuvent prendre differentes formes comme des agressions physiques, des menaces, de l'intimidation, des gestes suicidaires, etc. L'exposition a de la violence en milieu de travail est susceptible de produire des consequences telles que des symptomes d'insomnie, de la detresse psychologique et des strategies d'adaptation inadaptees comme de l'abus d'alcool. Ces difficultes peuvent entrainer des problematiques sur le plan du fonctionnement professionnel, en particulier, une diminution de la performance au travail. L'objectif de la presente etude consiste a evaluer les donnees d'une etude prospective de l'adaptation des intervenants en CRJDA exposes a un comportement violent de la part des usagers (jeunes ou parents). Specifiquement, un modele d'equation structurelle sera teste afin d'evaluer l'influence possible de facteurs de protection et de facteurs de risque sur la peur d'etre reexpose a des comportements violents au travail, de meme que la capacite de cette peur a predire des consequences psychologiques et professionnelles a la suite de l'exposition a un comportement violent au travail. En ayant une meilleure comprehension de l'impact des comportements violents commis par les usagers envers les intervenants en CRJDA, il sera possible d'envisager la mise en place d'actions visant la formation continue et privilegier certaines formes de soutien a la suite d'un tel evenement. Il pourrait en resulter le maintien des intervenants en emploi et possiblement une meilleure stabilite des equipes prenant soin des jeunes en difficulte.

column36: Maturation and Phenotyping of Idiopathic Dilated Cardiomyopathy Patient-Derived iPSC-Cardiomyocytes
column37: With a 5-year survival rate of 50% following diagnosis, there is a need for improved diagnostic and treatment approaches for heart failure (HF). The second most common cause of HF is dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM), a disease affecting the hearts ability to deliver oxygenated blood to the rest of the body. In many cases, DCM is idiopathic, with no clear cause. Idiopathic DCM is still poorly understood and manifests itself differently between patients, making it difficult to form early diagnosis, guide treatment plans, or inform therapeutic development. Our objective is to better understand different phenotypes of idiopathic DCM using patient-derived, induced pluripotent stem cell-cardiomyocytes (iPSC-CMs) to model DCM in a ;dish. We hypothesize that the phenotypic properties and underlying molecular mechanisms in DCM iPSC-CMs compared to age-matched controls can stratify DCM patients into defined disease subtypes. To achieve our objective, we aim to 1) generate iPSCs from both male and female DCM patients of varied ethnic backgrounds and differentiate them into CMs, 2) induce phenotypically immature patient-specific iPSC-CMs towards a more mature and disease-relevant phenotype, and 3) use high-content imaging to characterize phenotypic and morphological differences between iPSC-CMs from DCM patients and age-matched control subjects. This workflow will allow us to better understand DCM disease evolution and cluster idiopathic DCM patients into defined disease subtypes, paving the way for more personalized treatments, predicting individual responses to current therapies, and helping to identify novel drug targets to ultimately improve the quality and duration of life for idiopathic DCM patients.

column36: Evaluation et implantation d'un traitement d'autosoins base sur l'activation comportementale pour la depression dans le reseau de la sante
column37: Les individus souffrant de depression peuvent attendre plusieurs mois avant d'acceder a la psychotherapie. Une alternative est l'approche de soins par etapes ou les patients debutent par des interventions de faible intensite telles que l'activation comportementale (AC). Le programme Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) vise a accroitre l'acces aux soins de sante mentale pour les troubles anxieux et depressifs en utilisant cette approche. Au Quebec, un programme similaire est en cours d'implantation, soit le Programme quebecois pour les troubles mentaux (PQPTM). Les objectifs de l'etude sont de mesurer l'efficacite et l'implantation d'un programme d'autosoins guides utilisant l'AC pour des patients depressifs legers a moderes au CISSS de Chaudiere-Appalaches (CISSS-CA). Dans le cadre du PQPTM, nous evaluerons en continu un echantillon de 300 participants. En se basant sur l'IAPT, nous distribuerons aux participants une batterie de questionnaires evaluant l'ajustement, la depression et l'anxiete. Les patients recevront un manuel d'autosoins comprenant six etapes qu'ils completeront a leur rythme sur une periode de huit semaines. Ils seront rencontres a six reprises par un therapeute ou les questionnaires seront remplis. Les equipes de sante mentale du CISSS-CA seront comparees aux groupes de medecine de famille ou le programme sera implante un an plus tard. L'evaluation de l'efficacite du traitement se fera en comparant les resultats des questionnaires au debut et a la fin de l'intervention. L'implantation sera mesuree en recueillant des donnees d'observance au traitement. Les retombees de l'etude pourraient permettre de reduire les ressources utilisees en sante mentale en plus de faciliter l'acces a un traitement efficace plus rapidement.

column36: External validation of a clinical prediction model for the diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia
column37: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) is an autoimmune disease that results in a low platelet count and increased bleeding risk. Defined simply as a platelet count 100 x 109/L with no known cause, ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion; meaning other causes of low platelets must be ruled out before ITP can be diagnosed. This approach is error-prone and can lead to unnecessary exposures to expensive and harmful treatments. To address this issue, we designed a clinical prediction model, called the Predict-ITP tool, to help clinicians make the ITP diagnosis in the outpatient setting. Mathematical modelling was used to identify four variables that are predictive of the ITP diagnosis and accessible to clinicians at an initial patient encounter: 1) platelet count fluctuation; 2) lowest platelet count level; 3) maximum mean platelet volume; and 4) history of a major bleed. The Predict-ITP tool has been validated internally using data from a single centre. The objective of the current study is to perform an external validation of the Predict-ITP tool by assessing the accuracy of diagnosis in an external patient sample from 10 academic and community hematology clinics over a 10-year period using information available at the initial patient encounter. The gold standard for ITP diagnosis will be the achievement of a platelet count response after high-dose corticosteroids or intravenous immunoglobulin as determined during the follow-up period. Discrimination (ability to differentiate between patients with and without ITP) and calibration (agreement between predicted and actual diagnoses) of the Predict-ITP tool will be determined. The Predict-ITP tool will have an immediate impact for patients and clinicians by reducing delays in diagnosis and avoiding potentially harmful and costly treatments.

column36: Vers une meilleure recuperation suite a une lesion traumatique de la moelle epiniere: therapie de mobilisation a l'aide d'un ergometre durant l'episode de soins aigus.
column37: La moelle epiniere est l'autoroute par laquelle tous les signaux sont achemines de notre cerveau vers les extremites et vice-versa. Lorsqu'elle est lesee traumatiquement, des limitations fonctionnelles severes peuvent subvenir et affecter de facon importante la qualite de vie des patients. Suite a l'accident, une des priorites importantes des individus affectes est de recuperer une certaine mobilite et plus specifiquement, la marche. Cependant, avec les traitements actuels, ce ne sont pas tous les blesses medullaires qui y parviennent. Des lors, il convient de trouver de nouvelles approches therapeutiques qui permettront d'ameliorer la condition de ces patients.Pour ce faire, le projet propose consiste a evaluer la faisabilite, la securite et l'efficacite d'un protocole de soins novateur base sur la mobilisation precoce des patients suite a l'accident. En bref, quelques jours tout au plus apres la chirurgie, nous allons exposer les patients a un protocole de velo au lit en utilisant un ergometre specialise. Notre hypothese principale est que cet ergometre aidera les patients a recuperer davantage de fonction dans les jambes, ce qui se traduira a moyen et long termes par une meilleure capacite a marcher de facon independante.

column36: How early life gut inflammation impacts brain microglia and neurodevelopment
column37: The prevalence of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and other chronic disorders of the gut have increased more than 50% since 2010 in Canada and there is currently no cure. Over 25% of people with IBD are diagnosed during childhood and many of these patients develop anxiety, depression and cognitive impairments that persist into adulthood. How early life gut inflammation impairs brain function in children remains understudied, however, animal models provide insight into the underlying mechanisms of IBD and may lead to novel therapeutic development.Intestinal inflammation alters compositions of microbiota (microorganisms like fungi and bacteria) in the gut. Interestingly, gut microbiota produce metabolite molecules that signal to immune cells in the brain called microglia. I hypothesize that an altered composition of gut microbiota in children with IBD changes metabolite signaling to microglia and consequently impairs mental health.My proposed project will develop the first mouse model of juvenile IBD that captures the whole gut-to-brain-to-behaviour spectrum of the disorder. I will then use this model to determine the role of microglia in pediatric IBD. Gut inflammation will be chemically induced in juvenile mice and then the impact on gut microbiota composition, microglia functioning, and behavioural development will be assessed. The long-term goal of this work is to identify how disorders like pediatric IBD lead to life-long impacts on the brain and increased prevalence of psychiatric disorders. The microbiota is an exciting target for personalized medicine as microbiome manipulations are a feasible early intervention. By developing better therapies for pediatric IBD, we aim to mitigate negative impacts on brain development and improve patient quality of life.

column36: Incidence de la pandemie de la COVID-19 sur les processus d'inhibition cognitive chez une population atteinte de la maladie d'Alzheimer
column37: L'inhibition permet a l'etre humain de faire fi des stimuli secondaires ou des actions inappropriees (Bjorklund et Harnishfeger, 1995). Ce processus est essentiel pour le fonctionnement humain, puisqu'il permet de controler les performances cognitives et comportementales (Rouch et al., 2019). A l'inverse, des troubles d'inhibition peuvent conduire a un surplus d'information dans la memoire de travail ou a une desinhibition des comportements. L'inhibition est d'ailleurs l'une des fonctions cognitives les plus atteintes dans les differents stades de la maladie d'Alzheimer (MA; Amieva et al., 2004). En 2021, pendant la COVID-19, entre 30 et 35 millions des personnes souffraient de la MA (OMS). Ce contexte a eu des repercussions sur les fonctions cognitives de ces personnes. Or, aucune etude ne s'est penchee sur l'impact qu'a eu le contexte de la pandemie sur les capacites d'inhibition des personnes souffrant de la MA au Quebec. L'hypothese de recherche est que les performances dans les tests d'inhibition chez la population atteinte de la MA seront plus faibles depuis la pandemie de la COVID-19. Les mesures sanitaires ont cree un contexte d'isolement, ou la pratique d'activites cognitives pour maintenir les performances d'inhibition etait difficile. De plus, l'augmentation du stress est un facteur qui influence l'inhibition. Afin de determiner si le contexte de la pandemie a des repercussions sur l'inhibition de la population atteinte de la MA, une comparaison entre les resultats de la meta-analyse de Kaiser et ses collaborateurs (2018) et les resultats d'une batterie neuropsychologique standard et d'une serie de tests evaluant l'inhibition sera realisee. Par la suite, les participants (avec l'aide d'un/e proche) repondront a un questionnaire semi-structure qualitatif.

column36: Detection, prevalence and genetic basis of antibiotic tolerance
column37: Antibiotics are critical to the treatment of bacterial infections, however our ability to cure these infections is being threatened by the rise of antibiotic resistance. Due to antibiotic resistance, even common bacterial infections are becoming increasingly difficult to treat. Given the lack of new antibiotics being discovered, it is important that we preserve the effectiveness of existing antibiotics to combat resistant bacteria. The emerging phenomenon of antibiotic tolerance acts as a precursor to resistance and poses an additional challenge to antibiotic treatment. Tolerant bacteria are still killed by antibiotics, but at a slower rate. The slower rate of killing means that tolerant bacteria can survive the typical course of antibiotic treatment and cause persistent infections with higher mortality rates. Unlike antibiotic resistance which is identified by routine testing in laboratories, tolerance is not detected because there are currently no tests available to do so. Consequently, the clinical prevalence and significance of tolerance is unknown. I aim to develop a screen to detect tolerance and apply it to libraries of clinical isolates from patients with persistent bloodstream infections. This will provide the first real assessment of how often tolerance contributes to difficult-to-treat infections. We will also identify the mutations responsible for tolerance in these clinical isolates to improve our understanding of the genetic basis of tolerance. Ultimately, this research will improve the diagnosis of persistent infections and provide a foundation for future studies on antibiotic tolerance. Addressing the threat of antibiotic tolerance will help ensure we have the ability to provide effective antibiotic therapy and treat bacterial infections in the future.

column36: Does Blood Glucose or Obesity Alter Gut Barrier Function and Metabolic Endotoxemia?
column37: Obesity, type 2 diabetes (T2D), and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease are interlinked diseases that have high health and economic burdens. Most research associates intestinal bacteria to T2D and fatty liver disease by describing changes in the names of bacterial during obesogenic diets. An important goal is to identify bacterial processes and molecules that cause effects on host metabolism and can be manipulated to combat metabolic disease and T2D. Postbiotics are bacterial components that come from living or dead bacteria. Postbiotics such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS) can cause immune responses such as inflammation, and increased inflammation can promote metabolic dysfunction. ;Metabolic endotoxemia describes a low-level increase in blood LPS. We recently discovered that the type of LPS determines a positive or negative effect on host metabolism. However, it is not known what features of metabolic disease influence the type of LPS.Changes in the gut microbiome or gut barrier function may alter the balance or type of circulating LPS. We hypothesize that the level of blood glucose and level of body fat dictate whether LPS is detrimental or beneficial during metabolic endotoxemia. We will use control, hyperglycemic (Akita), and normoglycemic Akita (treated with chronic insulin) mice to determine if different levels of blood glucose influence the type and activity of LPS in the gut, portal, and systemic blood circulation in lean mice. Similarly, we will compare lean mice to obese mice to determine whether obesity at different ages influences metabolic endotoxemia. This research may lead to understanding which factor in metabolic disease influences a source of inflammation that contributes to aggravating metabolic disease.

column36: The Role of Mindfulness and Psychological Flexibility in Emotion-Based Impulsivity
column37: Negative emotions can be burdensome and difficult to regulate, and in some individuals may lead to failures in regulating behaviour. Negative urgency (NU) is a personality trait which refers to the tendency to behave impulsively when experiencing intense negative emotions. Given that NU is a key risk factor for mental health problems and dysfunctional behaviour, there is an overlooked need to better understand how to address this form of impulsivity. It has been proposed that NU may reflect difficulties in ones ability to tolerate unpleasant emotions. Individuals who are less accepting of unpleasant emotions may also be less able to flexibly choose whether to engage in adaptive over maladaptive behaviour, leading to impulsive action in the face of negative emotion. Since mindfulness involves an increased ability to accept and tolerate all emotional experiences, this skill may be particularly relevant to NU. Being able to endure unpleasant experiences and flexibly choose to engage in goal-directed behaviour, referred to as psychological flexibility (PF), may also reflect an important skill that is lacking in those high in NU. Since both mindfulness and PF can be trained, these skills may serve to protect individuals from dysfunctional emotionally-driven behaviour. For this reason, the present study seeks to better understand the role of mindfulness and PF on NU. To do so, data on mindfulness, PF, and NU will be collected from fifty-five healthy adults. It is expected that increased mindfulness will be associated with increased PF, which will in turn be associated with decreased NU. Gaining insight on the nature of these relationships will allow us to develop effective treatment strategies for individuals who are vulnerable to behavioural problems.

column36: Mapping atypical subiculum pyramidal neurons across circuits and behavior
column37: As the impairment of spatial memory can prove devastating, determining the underlying cell-specific mechanisms of spatial memory is invaluable to both basic and translational neuroscience. A brain region termed the subiculum has been shown to contain cells that represent spatial landmarks, and published work from our lab has recently discovered a distinct population of neurons that occupies the deepest cell layer of the subiculum. Follow-up preliminary data I have acquired illustrates this deep cell population differs markedly from classical subiculum excitatory neurons. Altogether, this atypical cell population seems ideally poised to convey specialized elements of spatial memory.We hypothesize that these deep cells participate in a specialized spatial memory circuit, providing salient sensory information to downstream spatially tuned cells. Here, I aim to characterize this population of neurons and its associated circuits, as well as investigate causal contributions of these atypical cells to spatial memory. To do this, I will employ viral tracing tools to map what regions or populations provide input to these deep cells versus classical subiculum neurons. Additionally, I will utilize cell-specific activity silencing in a new transgenic mouse line to selectively silence this deep neuronal population during behavioral tasks to test object location and recognition memory. Video recordings will then be analyzed for behavioral changes correlating to landmark recognition. Ultimately, defining this atypical population and its behavioral correlates will provide a powerful understanding of the cell-type-specific mechanisms of spatial learning and memory, benefiting basic neuroscience and informing our understanding spatial memory deficits.

column36: The Causality of Cholinergic Atrophy in Alzheimer's Disease
column37: Alzheimers disease (AD), the leading cause of dementia, is characterized by the pathological accumulation of amyloid-β and tau proteins in key brain regions. These changes trigger early and progressive atrophy of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons that contribute to the onset of cognitive deficits. While the relationship between cholinergic loss and cognitive decline has been outlined, the extent to which amyloidosis or tau pathology contribute to this cholinergic loss remains unclear. Several studies support the theory that the primary cause of cholinergic loss in AD results from the cortical accumulation of tau. However, persuasive data from rodent models suggests that it is the accumulation of amyloid-β that provokes the greatest loss of cholinergic neurons. Furthermore, previous research suggests that nerve growth factor, critical for the survival of cholinergic neurons, is highly impaired in AD. The present study aims to (1) elucidate how the progression of AD-like tau accumulation contributes directly or indirectly, through deregulation of nerve growth factor metabolism to the degeneration of cholinergic neurons, and to (2) ascertain the extent to which amyloid-β contributes to tau-induced basal forebrain cholinergic deficits. To address these aims, the present study will compare cognitive decline and cholinergic loss in a rodent model displaying both amyloid-β and tau accumulation, with independent models of each pathology at key time points in the aging process. These comparisons will enable us to disentangle the independent and combined effects of these two AD hallmark pathologies. Given the increased incidence of AD among the Canadian population, this study reflects a critical step toward the identification of new biomarkers and/or therapeutics for AD.

column36: Developing accessible resources targeting patients with knee osteoarthritis challenged with barriers to virtual care
column37: Increased use of technology in modern healthcare delivery has introduced new challenges for patients with low health literacy and/or English language proficiency. A multidisciplinary approach is needed to address these gaps in accessibility that limit patient engagement in their own healthcare decisions. We propose to bring together a team with expertise in rehabilitation, knowledge translation (KT), and persons with lived experience, to aid in the development of accessible patient-facing resources for knee osteoarthritis (KOA) self-management. Our specific aims are to: 1) identify priority topics in collaboration with key stakeholders, such as patients, that require accessible resource enhancement for KOA self-management, 2) co-develop accessible patient-identified priority modules to improve virtual care, 3) share newly developed teaching materials with stakeholders and test their usability and efficacy, and 4) create guidelines for future development of accessible patient resources to be used in different disease populations. We will perform an environmental scan of existing materials surrounding the priority topics identified by the patients and clinicians. In collaboration with our KT team, digital accessibility experts, and patient partners, we will co-design at least 2 modules that are enhanced in their accessibility and readability for patients with low health literacy. Next, we will share these materials with key stakeholders including clinicians, patient partners, and professional organizations and assess their effectiveness in improving health information delivery. Finally, after gathering their feedback, we will outline key principles to consider when developing accessible resources targeted to patients with different health conditions.

column36: Characterization of Somatic Structural Variants in Diffuse Gliomas over Disease Progression and Treatment
column37: Diffuse glioma is an aggressive type of brain tumour that arises from glial or precursor cells. It is the most common type of brain malignancies diagnosed in adults, characterized by high recurrence rates and treatment resistance. It has been previously shown that the ineffectiveness of treatments for glioma is primarily a result of intertumoural genetic heterogeneity. Previous studies have characterized single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) and small deletions/insertions in the genome of gliomas that give rise to its genetic heterogeneity, but have yet included large structural variants (SVs: deletions, insertions, tandem duplications) in their analysis. To advance our understandings of how SVs contribute to the genetic heterogeneity in gliomas, we performed linked-reads whole-genome sequencing (LRWGS) and single-nuclei RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) on 36 patient samples of primary and recurrent gliomas. Data generated from LRWGS contains not only the DNA sequence of the bulk tumour with mapped SNVs, but also SVs and phased haplotypes of the genome. Our analysis identified around 500 candidate somatic structural variants in the coding and non-coding regions of the genome in each sample, and they have been thoroughly annotated. Genomic alterations of interest identified from the LRWGS data are then cross-validated in the snRNA-seq data to elucidate their effects in the context of the transcriptome and cellular functions of the malignant cells. Our dataset and analyses of the sequencing data from gliomas would comprehensively characterize the role of SVs in gliomas and provide a source for the discovery of new molecular targets that originate from SVs.

column36: Investigating resident macrophages in the leukemic bone marrow niche by probing the CD82-DARC axis
column37: The bone marrows (BM) main job is to produce the blood cells of our immune system in a process called hematopoiesis. In leukemia, the BM becomes filled with cancerous blood cells, which prevents normal hematopoiesis. Healthy BM contains various types of stromal niche cells (the BM soil), including bone marrow resident macrophages (BMΦ), which interact with hematopoietic stem cells (HSC) (the BM seeds) to control HSC growth and retention in the BM. Research in mice has shown that some BMΦ express DARC protein on their cell surface, which binds to CD82 protein expressed on the surface of long-lived HSC, and that this interaction is important for BMΦ regulation of HSC. CD82 is also expressed on leukemic cells, which can sometimes hide within the protective BM niche, helping them to survive standard chemotherapy treatments and leading to disease relapse. While we are starting to understand the CD82-DARC interaction in healthy BM, the CD82-DARC interaction in the leukemic BM niche is still poorly understood. My proposed research will investigate CD82-DARC interactions in leukemia using a cell culture system in which leukemia cells are grown in 3D, surrounded by BMΦ and other supportive niche cells to create an in vitro BM environment that models a true leukemic niche. I will then visualize CD82 and DARC proteins on cultured cells using microscopy. Additionally, I will use leukemic mice models to test whether antibodies that block the CD82-DARC interaction could be used to enhance current chemotherapy drugs. This research would contribute to our understanding of the leukemic BM niche, and aims to identify a new treatment mechanism to improve leukemia therapies and prevent relapse.
