column36: The role of astrocyte glucocorticoid receptors in stress-induced synaptic plasticity deficits
column37: Stress is experienced by everyone. The brains ability to respond to stress allows for adaptation and tuning of behaviour; however, prolonged, and repeated exposure to stress can negatively affect brain function and precede stress-related mental illnesses. Thus, expanding our understanding of the brains response to stress can provide insights to the etiology of mental illnesses. When compared to neurons, astrocytes, a type of non-neuronal brain cell, have a fivefold greater abundance of stress receptors suggesting an important role of astrocytes in mediating the brains response to stress. Despite this, previous research has neglected the role of these cells in stress-related brain dysfunction. Therefore, my research will investigate the importance of astrocyte stress receptor signalling and their role in stress-induced brain dysfunction. I will use a combination of live brain cell recordings and genetic deletion of astrocyte stress receptors to determine how astrocyte stress signalling disturbs the synaptic communication following stress. We hope that these data will reveal novel mechanisms of stress-induced brain dysfunction that can identify astrocytes as putative targets for the treatment of stress-related mental illnesses.

column36: A Food Systems Approach to Community Food Security and Indigenous Food Sovereignty
column37: Background: Indigenous Peoples in Canada are disproportionately burdened by food insecurity and nutrition-related health problems. Holistic approaches considering all areas of the food system are needed for long-term solutions. By using a food systems approach, which has rarely been applied in an Indigenous community context, the purpose of this study is to design a participatory process resulting in a collective vision of a food system grounded in the values of one Indigenous community to promote nutrition, food security, and well-being. Context: Kahnawà:ke Schools Diabetes Prevention Program (KSDPP) is a community-academic research partnership aiming to prevent type 2 diabetes in Kahnawà:ke, a Mohawk community in Québec, Canada. KSDPP engages in intersectoral food security and food sovereignty initiatives in Kahnawà:ke as part of its diabetes prevention mission.Methods: This study will involve a three-phase participatory process with a diverse group of community stakeholders in Kahnawà:ke. A literature review on food system areas that impact community food security and a scan of food security resources in Kahnawà:ke will produce a portrait of Kahnawà:kes current food system. Analysis of questionnaire and individual interview responses will identify emerging themes related to community values and perspectives of key strengths, opportunities, and challenges to food security. In collaboration with community stakeholders, the food system portrait and community perspectives will be validated and integrated to produce a graphic representation of a values-based collective vision of Kahnawà:kes future food system. Conclusion: This research will build upon current efforts to close gaps in Indigenous health, food security, and nutrition using a food systems approach.

column36: Directed evolution of bacterial toxins to target oncogenic Ras GTPase variants
column37: Broadly speaking, cancers are diseases stemming from mutations which cause abnormal cell growth, movement and behaviour. About a quarter of human cancers are driven by mutations in genes encoding Ras GTPase (Ras) proteins, leading to elevated activity and loss of control over processes that they normally regulate. Historically, Ras mutants have been near-impossible to treat because of their structure and efficiency in hyperactive states, but recent advances across diverse research fields have coalesced to reveal intriguing springboards for future therapies. Several bacterial toxins can permanently shut down Ras activity in human cells, and the past few years have seen the introduction of powerful tools and techniques that allow us to change the functions of proteins and toxins through artificial evolution. This project involves the use of a pipeline to completely redirect toxin activity from normal Ras to any mutated Ras of interest. The goal is to advance our understanding of such toxin-target interactions, and to exploit novel protein engineering strategies to generate toxins which specifically target disease-associated Ras mutants.

column36: Effects of renal replacement therapy on outcomes in patients with liver failure
column37: Liver disease is common throughout both developed and developing countries given widespread alcohol use and increasing rates of obesity. When the insult to the liver is ongoing, liver failure can develop. In patients with liver failure whether it is acute or chronic, one of the major complications is renal failure. Different medical therapies are available to try and reverse the renal failure. Despite medical management, renal replacement therapy with hemodialysis ultimately may be required. Also, when patients require dialysis, they often will require anticoagulation during the dialysis session to prevent blood from clotting in the dialysis circuit and filter. Currently, there is a paucity of data regarding the role of renal replacement therapy in patients with liver failure. Clinical outcomes for these patients are unclear and it is not evident which liver failure patients may benefit from renal replacement therapy. Not only are the outcomes for such patients uncertain, the use of anticoagulation and type of anticoagulation to use in liver failure patients needing dialysis has not been well studied. Therefore the objective is to evaluate how renal replacement therapy affects outcomes in liver failure patients and to also evaluate the benefits and harms of anticoagulation and which type of anticoagulation if any to use in liver failure patients who also concurrently develop renal failure. This will be done through a systematic review of literature involving renal replacement therapy in patients with acute liver failure followed by retrospective analysis of renal replacement therapy data in patients with both acute and chronic liver failure in Alberta.

column36: The production of recombinant soluble prorenin receptor to study its effect on cancer metabolism.
column37: The Prorenin Receptor (PRR) is a single-spanning transmembrane protein. It is cleaved to form an N-terminal secreted fragment called secreted PRR (sPRR), and a short transmembrane C-terminal fragment called M8.9. sPRR is well recognized as an important component of the renin angiotensin system for the regulation of blood pressure.Recently, the lab screened for secreted factors affected by the loss of PTEN, a common mutation found in breast and prostate cancers. We demonstrated that sPRR was increased in cancers with PTEN loss, and higher amount of sPRR correlates with tumor size. We have genetically engineered mice with a point mutation in the PRR gene (PRRpm) preventing the cleavage of PRR into sPRR and M8.9. This data suggests that sPRR may play a role as a metabolic regulator leading to the hypothesis the secretion of sPRR by cancer cells may promote a metabolic shift to promote tumor growth.To test this, first we will generate and purify recombinant sPRR (rsPRR) with metal affinity resin. We will then initially focus our study on LNCaP cells since we have studied PRR extensively in them. Using the Agilent Seahorse instrument in the Goodman Cancer Institute, we will metabolic signatures the LNCaP cells treated with or without rsPRR.We have isolated mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) from both PRRpm and wild-type littermates and will look for metabolic changes in the mutant cells treated with or without rsPRR with the Seahorse.To test the relationship between cellular transformation and sPRR, we will perform transformation assays by lentiviral transduction using the MEFs. If sPRR is shown to be an important metabolic regulator in cancer, neutralization of sPRR in the blood could help slow tumor growth and be a viable treatment option for cancer patients.

column36: Impacts of COVID-19 on Emergency Department service delivery for people who use opioids: Royal Alexandra Hospital and Peter Lougheed Centre service utilization trends and patient perspectives
column37: Background: Canadas overdose epidemic and the COVID-19 pandemic are intersecting public health emergencies that place people who use opioids at extreme risk of negative outcomes. These syndemic events are having a devastating impact on Emergency Departments (EDs), which act as a primary health system touchpoint for people who use opioids. Though many hospitals have recently enhanced opioid-related supports in EDs, COVID-19-related pressures may have unintentionally undermined progress in providing equitable ED care to people who use opioids.Objectives: The proposed research will 1) describe how COVID-19 has impacted opioid-related ED presentations during the pandemic and explore patient-identified causes for observed trends; and 2) describe how COVID-19 has impacted patient-reported experiences and satisfaction with opioid-related ED care.Methods: In partnership with patients with lived experience, this mixed method study draws on administrative health data and semi-structured interviews with 30 adult patients who use opioids and have recently accessed the ED at the Royal Alexandra Hospital (RAH) in Edmonton or the Peter Lougheed Centre (PLC) in Calgary. Study 1 will conduct an interrupted time series analysis of trends in opioid-related ED presentations and care utilization at the RAH and PLC EDs prior to and during the pandemic period. Study 2 will elicit patient views on observed trends in opioid-related care and the impacts of COVID-19 on ED patient care experiences.Significance: This study aims to establish patient-identified policy or practice recommendations that can improve satisfaction with ED care for people who use opioids, enable patient-centered modification(s) to the pandemic response, and inform future pandemic plans.

column36: Evaluating whether psychosocial factors moderate the relationship between individual and poly-victimization and adverse mental health outcomes in adolescence
column37: Victimization, defined as being individually singled out and subjected to cruel and unjust treatment, is a pressing public health concern due its strong association with an array of adverse mental health outcomes. Victimization is most commonly experienced in adolescence and majority experience multiple forms, also known as poly-victimization. These individuals are most at risk of poor psychological adjustment. Still, there are adolescents who experience victimization and do not suffer from psychiatric illness and this resilience is thought to in part, be moderated by psychosocial factors. The present study will examine the effect of individual and poly-victimization on depression and anxiety, self-harm and attempted suicide in adolescence, and whether positive psychosocial processes (close family and peer relationships, social support, and high self-esteem) provide protective effects against adverse mental health outcomes of victimization. This study will use data from the Millennium Cohort Study, a nationally representative ongoing longitudinal survey in the UK that began in 2001. Multivariable regression analysis will be used to investigate the association between victimization and adverse mental health outcomes at age 17, and whether positive psychosocial factors at age 14 provide protective effects. With the majority of adolescents experiencing at least one form of victimization in their youth with consequential negative mental health effects, it is crucial to understand potential protective factors that could facilitate youth resiliency to victimization and further, inform best practice guidelines for children and youth mental health promotion programs.

column36: Using Movies to Improve Personalized Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Target Identification
column37: Depression affects 4% of Canadians in any given year. One in five individuals with depression are treatment-resistant, meaning they do not respond to standard treatments for depression. Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) is a non-medication-based treatment for depression where a special magnet is placed on a patients scalp and is used to stimulate the part of the brain underneath the magnet. Before starting rTMS treatments, the doctor must decide where to put the magnet, and which part of the brain to target. Many different methods have been used to identify the best target. Right now, researchers are trying to use personalized targets, meaning they use a brain scan to identify a target that is customized according to that individuals brain patterns. By looking at past studies of rTMS for depression, researchers have found that stimulating closer to an individuals personalized target leads to better outcomes. Finding a patients personalized target usually requires a very long scan in an MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) machine. Typically, the patient is asked to stay still and to not fall asleep while they stare at a plus-sign on a screen. This is called a ;resting state scan, and people (especially patients with depression) have difficulties staying still and tolerating the long scan. Scientists in other areas of MRI research are starting to use movies inside the MRI machine. The movies help patients stay still and awake for long scans, and they also create more stable and reliable brain patterns. The goal of this project is to combine these two ideas, for the first time, to examine whether movie-watching data can help improve individualized target localization for rTMS treatment of depression.

column36: Comparison of Feature Selection Methods and Machine Learning Classifiers with Computed Tomography Radiomics-based Features for Predicting Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
column37: Radiomics is an image analysis technique that extracts numerical features from medical images, for example computed tomography (CT) images. These radiomic features can be used with machine learning models to predict outcomes. Machine learning models include two main steps: feature selection methods and classification methods. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is an inflammatory lung disease that is caused by the interactions between genes and the environment. The current method for diagnosing COPD is with spirometry, which measures lung function. There are several limitations with spirometry that can lead to undiagnosed COPD. To overcome these limitations, the use of radiomic features can be used with machine learning to predict the presence of COPD. Although, with a large variety of different feature selection methods and classification methods, it is unknown what models have the highest prediction performance for COPD with radiomic features. The objective of this research is to compare the various combinations of feature selection and classification methods to determine the model with the highest accuracy for predicting COPD. Combinations of 17 feature selection and 8 classification methods will be tested and evaluated. The removal of outliers and the number of features selected for the classification model will also be tested to potentially improve the prediction accuracy of the model. The expected outcome from this research is to establish an optimal machine learning model for predicting COPD using extracted CT radiomic features. In addition, the optimal machine learning model could be applied to other lung diseases.

column36: An Investigation to Identify Risk Factors for the Development of Acneiform Eruptions in Patients on Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor Inhibitors
column37: Newer targeted cancer therapies, including epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors, have fewer systemic side effects than older chemotherapy but cause a near-universal acneiform rash. This rash looks very similar to acne - it is pimples and red bumps on the face, neck and back. In contrast to acne, this rash appears suddenly and can be associated with significant pain and itch. Given it presents on visible areas of the body, the rash can negatively affect quality of life; it is a constant reminder of the challenges encountered by a cancer patient and is visible to others. When the rash resolves, it can cause scarring or changes in the colour of the natural skin's pigment (darkening or lightening). This acneiform rash is a sign that the cancer therapy is working. In some patients, however, the rash may be so severe that the lifesaving cancer therapy must be stopped. Evidence demonstrates that early intervention by a dermatologist to treat the rash can decrease the rate of cancer treatment discontinuation. Therefore, the goal of our research is to identify risk factors for those who develop severe acneiform rashes. The results of our research will be used by oncologists to identify patients at risk of developing these severe rashes, so they are started on treatment earlier by dermatologists. Ultimately, our aim is that this prevents early cancer treatment discontinuation due to a skin side effect. Treatment of this rash will also improve the quality of life of patients undergoing cancer therapy.

column36: Identifying the Role of Hypertranscription in Pediatric Tumor Evolution
column37: Hypertranscription is defined by a global increase of RNA output in a cell. It is an abnormality of a cell's transcriptional machinery best characterized in cancer cell lines and stem cell models. The Shlien lab developed a computational method to measure hypertranscription in thousands of cancers across different adult cancer types, which revealed hypertranscriptions association with aggressive cancer subtypes, and its prognostic utility across adult cancers. Analysis of transcriptomes of individual cells (single cell sequencing) from lung tumors identified groups of hypertranscriptive cells which dominated tumor transcriptional output even when present as a minority cell population. The Shlien labs recent discoveries have elucidated the importance of hypertranscription across adult cancer types, however hypertranscriptions prevalence in pediatric cancers is unknown.The interests of this project lie in understanding the landscape of hypertranscription in pediatric tumours and how cancer cells exhibiting hypertranscription proliferate during tumor growth. To understand hypertranscription in pediatric cancers, genomic data from RNA and DNA sequencing as a part of the SickKids Cancer Sequencing Program (KiCS) will be used. Hypertranscription levels will be measured and compared between cancer types. In single cell sequencing data, hypertranscriptive clones will be identified and tracked over time. Understanding the role of hypertranscriptive clones during tumor evolution will provide fundamental insights into evolution in both adult and pediatric cancers. Results of this project will also nominate candidate tumor types for transcriptional inhibitor therapy and aid in the early identification of aggressive neoplasms.

column36: Patient Classifier for Ependymal Tumours Based on Molecular Subgroups Using Patient Similarity Networks
column37: Ependymomas are tumours of the central nervous system that occur in both children and adults, and exabit a large degree of diversity in clinical progression and treatment outcomes. As such, the ability to identify tumour subtypes that are associated with the underlying biological mechanisms is important, as it informs clinical decisions such as treatment planning. While the grading of ependymal tumours is traditionally based on histopathological diagnosis (from the examination of tumour tissues under a microscope), recent approaches based on molecular characteristics have proven to be more consistent, and better associated with clinical progression. As such, the creation of computational systems based on this type of data, which allow classification of new patients into different risk groups, would further our understanding of ependymomas and improve treatment outcomes for patients. This project aims to create a classifier based on the molecular subtypes of ependymal tumours, and evaluate its performance. Analysis of the classifier model will allow insights regarding the biological features that are most associated with different subtypes, and the identification of mechanisms of disease and potential treatment targets. This will be done through the creation of Patient Similarity Networks, which are a computational tool used to integrate different types of data into a single graphical representation, in which patients are clustered and classified based on their similarities. The resulting tool will allow a more personalized approach to the treatment of ependymal tumours, and further our understanding of the mechanisms underlying disease progression.

column36: Investigating the mechanism underlying general anesthetic drug-induced long term cognitive deficits
column37: The ability to perform surgery under anesthesia has saved millions of people from pain and diseases. However, surgery comes with many possible side effects such as perioperative neurocognitive disorder (PND). Patients develop new cognitive deficits such as delirium, decline in memory, attention, concentration, and executive function which may hugely impact ones quality of life. It is important to develop therapeutic agent for PND that target receptors more precisely and effectively, since there are currently no broadly effective prevention or treatment strategies available for PNDs. Our lab was the first to show that general anesthetic drugs alter the activity of hippocampal nerve cells, a region of the brain which serves a critical role in memory and cognition. Such changes persist even after the anesthetic drugs have been eliminated from the body, contributing to PNDs. Notably, groups of cells surrounding the nerve cells known as the astrocytes play an important role in this pathway. Yet, we do not know how astrocytes communicate with the hippocampal nerve cells. The aim of this project is to explore the underlying mechanism of general anesthetic drug-induced PNDs, particularly which receptors on astrocytes play a critical role in modulating the activity of hippocampal nerve cells. I plan to use genetically modified mice which lacks specific receptors to study whether these receptors are contributing to anesthetic drug-induced PNDs through assessing the activity of nerve cells and behaviors of the mice. By bettering our understanding of the molecular causes of PNDs, this project will promote the development of novel therapeutics that can improve the quality of life for millions of patients post surgery and reduce the burden of the healthcare system.

column36: Therapeutic Monoclonal Antibodies for Influenza A Virus Infection
column37: Influenza viruses are one of the most widespread pathogens across the globe. In addition to seasonal epidemics, influenza viruses have also caused four pandemics in the last century. My project aims to characterize an antibody that binds to a different part of hemagglutinin that is less variable. Intravenous injection of this antibody could be used as a therapeutic to help treat patients who do not respond to antivirals. It could also be used preventatively for high-risk individuals such as the elderly and the immunocompromised. I will determine which strains of influenza the antibody can recognize. I will also examine the mechanisms by which the antibody provides protection. Finally, I will administer the antibody to mice to determine if it can prevent clinical symptoms of infection. It is important to understand how this antibody provides protection before we can evaluate its efficacy in humans. Access to more effective therapeutics will help control the spread of seasonal influenza virus infection and could help mitigate the spread and severity of future pandemics.

column37: Notre sang est compose des globules rouges, mais aussi de plaquettes et d'une varietes de globules blancs. Malgre leurs differentes fonctions, ces cellules sanguines possedent toutes une origine commune : les cellules souches hematopoietiques (CSH) qui sont indifferenciees et dans la moelle osseuse. Les CSH peuvent se diviser en cellules filles qui seront soit identiques a la cellule mere ou qui se differencieront pour se specialiser. Ces dernieres deviendront les cellules matures du sang peripherique.Cependant, le mecanisme par lequel les CSH determinent le type de cellules filles produit n'est pas encore bien compris. Le but est de verifier si les CSH n'exprimant pas Vangl2 sont capables de reprendre l'hematopoiese apres un stress toxique dans leur environnement et, le cas echeant, s'il y a un profil cellulaire anormal. La pandemie offre l'opportunite d'evaluer l'association entre l'anxiete et les retours precoces au DU. Les patients sont divises en trois groupes, selon qu'ils ont ete liberes avant le premier confinement, pendant ou entre chaque vague de confinement. D'autres facteurs tel que l'age, le revenu, l'education, l'isolement social et le motif de consultation seront aussi inclus dans les analyses. Ce projet permettra d'identifier les aines les plus a risque de revisiter un DU et a cibler des interventions potentielles visant une meilleure prise en charge de ces patients dans l'objectif de diminuer les retours precoces et les couts associes.

column36: Neuroprotective Effects of Physical Exercise in a Snf2h Knockout Mouse of Retinal Degeneration
column37: In Canada, the economic burden of vision impairment is estimated to be $15.8 billion and these costs are expected to double by the year 2032 due to population aging. Retinal degenerative diseases are the leading cause of visual impairment and include photoreceptor cell (PRC) degenerations such as macular degeneration and retinitis pigmentosa. The prohibitive costs and restriction of existing gene therapies to a few select rare diseases have resulted in an urgent need for the development of accessible therapeutic approaches. Although an increasing number of studies have shown the effectiveness of physical exercise in improving visual function and slowing the progression of visual degenerative diseases, the molecular mechanisms underlying neuroprotection in the retina remain unknown, primarily due to inconsistent responses to exercise in current animal models. The mouse model our laboratory has generated displays PRC degeneration that progresses into severe visual impairment, and is the first to show a robust and reproducible response to exercise-induced PRC rescue. My study seeks to characterize this mouse model in modelling late-onset retinal degeneration, as well as determine an optimal physical exercise regimen and elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying effective exercise as a prevention for visual impairment. Assessments will include visual and metabolic outcomes of treadmill tests and the identification of affected cell types during progression of retinal degeneration. Results of this study will represent significant advancements in fundamental knowledge regarding exercise-induced neuroplasticity and holds the potential to significantly benefit human health by identifying therapeutic targets that mitigate the effects of vision loss.

column36: Investigating Biomarkers of Treatment Resistance in Human Papillomavirus-Related Head and Neck Cancer
column37: Head and neck cancer is the 6th most common cancer in the world. It typically arises in the lining of the mouth, neck, and throat and is collectively referred to as head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Recently, infection by the sexually transmitted disease human papillomavirus has drastically increased HNSCC diagnoses, especially in the younger population. HPV-driven (HPV+) HNSCC has consequently been coined a slow epidemic posing a particular risk for patients resistant to chemotherapy and radiation who are at higher risk of mortality. Additionally, chemoradiation treatment has associated toxicities such as difficulties swallowing, pain, and hearing loss. Currently, biomarkers related to treatment resistance in HPV+ HNSCC have not yet been identified to explain the portion of patients who respond negatively to treatment. To address these concerns, our lab has identified candidate genes that may play a pivotal role in conferring treatment resistance in HPV+ HNSCC. A gene of interest, mono-ADP ribosylhydrolase 2 (MACROD2) has been named a novel tumour suppressor gene in related cancers and is associated with enhanced cell proliferation and tumour recurrence. In this study, the biological role of MACROD2 will be validated through functional assays in HPV+ HNSCC cell lines. Thereafter, mouse models will be evaluated for the growth of HPV+ HNSCC tumours. Through this work, the molecular basis of treatment resistance in HPV+ HNSCC can be better understood allowing low-risk patients to undergo less intensive treatments ; decreasing their associated toxicities ; and high-risk patients to undergo enhanced treatment. As a result, our findings can provide a framework for enhancing the therapeutic efficacy of chemoradiation in HPV+ HNSCC and related malignancies.

column36: The Role of Novel Vitamin K Dependant Protein UDP-glucose Glycoprotein Glucosyltransferase 1 in Beta-cells
column37: Vitamin K is an essential micronutrient known to regulate blood coagulation and bones. Recent clinical observations in humans suggest that partial vitamin K deficiency might be linked to the development of diabetes. However, the biological mechanism by which vitamin K may influence diabetes remains unknown. Beta cell is a unique cell type of the pancreas responsible for the production of insulin. Diabetes is caused by a reduction in the number of beta cells or by a decrease in their capacity to secrete insulin. This research project aims at understanding the function of a new vitamin K-dependent enzyme in pancreatic beta cells and its potential link with the development of diabetes. We have identified UGGT1 as a new vitamin K-dependent enzyme in beta cells. The majority of the tools of the cell are called proteins and they require a precise structure to repair, synthesized and regulate other components of the cells. The role of UGGT1 is to make sure proteins are folded properly. Without UGGT1, the cell accumulates unfolded and inactive proteins, which can impair cell functions and possibly the secretion of insulin by beta cells. Our approach includes the use of genetically modified mice to determine the role of UGGT1 in beta cells. We will also identify which proteins are folded by UGGT1 in beta cells. Altogether, these studies will allow us to find how UGGT1 support the normal function of the beta cell. These studies are required to understand how vitamin K is implicated in the biology of beta cells and how partial vitamin K deficiency contributes to the development of diabetes. In the future, it could offer new therapeutic approaches for diabetes.

column36: L'etat du sommeil avant une mission militaire : Identifier les predicteurs de resilience lies au sommeil chez les soldat.e.s
column37: Le sommeil est un indicateur important de la sante d'un individu. Entre autres, le manque de sommeil est associe a un risque accru d'accidents, a une diminution de la motivation et d'une diminution des performances physiques ou cognitives. Les conditions de travail representent un facteur important pouvant impacter le sommeil. En effet, il a ete souligne que durant la COVID-19, les premiers intervenants sont souvent exposes a de longues heures de travail et leurs conditions de travail exigeantes affectent leur sommeil. Cet impact n'est pas localise uniquement au niveau du sommeil, mais peut meme mener a une augmentation d'autres problemes physiques et cognitifs. Ainsi, cette crise a su relever l'urgence de comprendre l'etat du sommeil chez le personnel ayant des conditions de travail exigeantes. Une autre population rencontrant ses conditions sont les militaires. En effet, le sommeil chez ce personnel peut etre modifie par les conditions de surentrainement, l'alimentation et l'eveil physiologique prolonge cause par les conditions d'un deploiement. Afin d'attenuer l'impact des missions, des soldats sont envoyes dans des camps d'entrainement en regions hostiles comme l'Arctique. Lors de ces formations, la negligence du sommeil peut augmenter le risque d'accidents, de la fatigue et des changements cognitifs. Durant cette recherche, nous nous interesserons aux differentes dimensions du sommeil chez les militaires avant le deploiement en Arctique afin de comprendre l'impact sur leur sante est leurs performances. Il est attendu qu'un sommeil adequat chez le personnel militaire au cours des deux semaines precedant la mission, sera associe a l'augmentation des performances cognitives, a une diminution de la fatigue et des risques d'accident pouvant etre rencontrees en Arctique.

column36: Circulating omega-3 fatty acids and adipose tissue inflammation: a longitudinal analysis in the PROMISE cohort
column37: Obesity is a major global health problem as it poses a significant risk for many chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Chronic low-grade inflammation is a central player in the mechanisms underlying these chronic diseases. Growing scientific evidence suggests that adipose tissue is the primary origin of inflammation, thus making it a promising target for prevention and management of chronic diseases. Omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are essential nutrients in our diet and have been suggested to have a beneficial impact on dampening adipose tissue inflammation. The limited literature on this relationship drives this study, in which we aim to investigate the role of omega-3 PUFAs in adipose tissue inflammation by performing a systematic review of current literature as well as by evaluating the long-term association between the omega-3 PUFAs and changes in adipose tissue inflammation among participants in the PROMISE cohort study.

column36: PEG-asparaginase depletion of asparagine in asparagine-rich and asparagine-depleted diets
column37: The most common cancer in children is Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia, or ALL. The cancer cells in ALL cannot make the amino acid asparagine. Instead, the cells get asparagine from the blood. We treat ALL patients with a drug that destroys asparagine in the blood, called asparaginase. When there is no asparagine, the cancer cells die. But how much drug is enough to give to patients? Where does the asparagine in the blood come from? We dont have the answers, so patients are getting more drug than necessary, and experience side effects. We are doing experiments in mice that will help understand whether the diet is a source of asparagine and whether bacteria in the intestines are another source. We will give mice diets with either a lot of asparagine or no asparagine and then give them the drug asparaginase. We will look at their blood and poop to see if there is a difference between the mice on different diets, before and after giving them asparaginase. Asparagine flooding into the blood from the diet or bacteria in the intestines could overwhelm the drug. If true, reducing levels of asparagine in the diet or altering the bacteria that make asparagine, could allow for lower doses of the drug. The ultimate objective is to know whether asparagine from the intestine, whether from diet or bacteria, directly affects blood levels of asparagine and therefore the amount of drug that may be necessary to treat ALL.

column36: General Pre-Trained Model for Magnetic Resonance Image Processing
column37: Machine learning holds a great promise in biomedical research and clinical diagnosis. However, the state-of-the-art machine learning models depend on a large quantity of high-quality data, multiple orders of magnitude more than that typically available in a biomedical setting. To overcome this limitation, I propose to use a pretrainable machine learning model that can leverage the vast amounts of publicly available, unlabeled, raw data in addition to the limited amount of available labeled data in the medical setting.MRI scans are widely used in clinical and research settings. Accurate and timely diagnosis and assessment of neurological disorders using MRI scans require reliable biomarkers such as brain morphometrics. Many of such biomarkers must be computed from segmentations of the MRI scan. Currently, the gold standard for MRI segmentation is manual segmentation which is very time consuming and labor intensive. This cost of data and limited quantity significantly limits the accuracy and scale of machine learning models.In the machine learning field of Natural Language Processing, researchers were able to utilize vast amounts of raw, unlabeled data through a transfer learning process known as pre-training. Most notably is the Generative Pre-trained Transformer 3, which achieved unrivaled performance in this field. Utilizing this pretraining process, I will develop machine learning models that can be pre-trained on the large, unlabeled MRI datasets. After pretraining on unlabeled data, the model can be modified to be fine tuned on expert labelled datasets. This type of pre-trained model can then be used on any task involving MRI scans. Such a model can allow the clinical benefits of machine learning to be applied to fields with relatively insufficient training data.

column36: Signes qualitatifs potentiellement pathognomoniques de l'autisme prototypique
column37: L'autisme est maintenant identifie comme un spectre de severite variable, le trouble du spectre de l'autisme ou TSA (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Autrefois considere comme une condition rare, la prevalence du TSA est en augmentation constante depuis 30 ans (Russell et al., 2021). Elle atteint desormais entre 0,9 % et 1,5 % de la population mondiale (Fombonne, 2020), dont 0,82 % des enfants de 1 a 5 ans au Quebec (Early Childhood Observatory, 2016). Le diagnostic de TSA est obtenu par la detection de comportements definis par des descriptions verbales relativement abstraites (eg : comportements ''repetitifs'?; Kulage et al., 2019). Cette imprecision favorise une indecision diagnostique dans les cas-frontiere, ce qui augmente la prevalence rapportee de facon incontrolable, en parallele a une augmentation constante de l'heterogeneite du spectre. L'objectif principal du present projet est d'operationnaliser 28 signes selectionnes par accord multidisciplinaire de l'equipe clinique de l'Hopital de Riviere-Des-Prairies. Le projet tente de repondre au besoin de creer un modele diagnostic concret du phenotype prototypique. Afin d'aboutir a une description qualitativement specifique de ces signes, ceux-ci seront recherches dans des enregistrements a visee diagnostique ou empirique recueillis lors de l'exposition d'enfants autistes (2-6 ans) a la Situation de stimulation de Montreal (Jacques, 2018) et a l'Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule-Second Edition. Puisque le diagnostic du TSA repose sur la detection de signes abstraits dans le comportement d'un individu, detenir un catalogue visuel des signes qualitatifs prototypiques du TSA permettrait une base de reference commune pour former les futurs experts cliniques et les cohortes de recherche.

column36: A Sex-based Analysis of the Role of Language Differences in the Elevated Risk of Psychosis among Migrants
column37: The risk of psychotic illness is more than two-times higher among certain migrant groups. In Ontario, risk is especially high among migrants from the Caribbean and refugees from Africa and South Asia. However, the causes of this heightened risk remain unclear. It has been proposed that exposure to social disadvantages across ones life can have cumulative effects that increase risk. One source of social disadvantage for migrants is being unable to speak the language of the new country. Prior research shows that differences between a migrants first language and the new language can influence their risk of psychosis, possibly by making the new language harder to learn. Women tend to learn languages more easily than men, which may impact the frequency of psychosis in each sex group. Marital status and education pre-migration may also have differing effects on how men and women learn language. Hence, this study examines how the association between language differences and psychosis may differ by sex among migrants to Ontario, and how sociodemographic and migration-related factors influence this relationship. We collected data from Immigration, Refugee and Citizenship Canada to identify migrants and their first languages. Languages will be classified by their similarity to English and estimated learning time. Health records will be used to identify cases of psychotic illness. Finally, we will calculate the risk of psychosis based on first language for men and women separately, and examine how the risk is affected by age at migration, country of origin, marital status at arrival, and highest level of education. This will identify sex-based factors that increase the risk of psychosis through effects on language learning, which will inform public mental health interventions.

column36: Development of the Opioid Induced Respiratory Depression (OIRD) risk screening tool
column37: Opioids are commonly used for the relief of moderate to severe pain in hospital settings. There has been a national growing opioid crisis observed across Canada related to prescribed opioid use. One potentially fatal reaction to opioid use is respiratory depression (known as opioid-induced respiratory depression or OIRD). Respiratory depression is described as less than 10 breaths per minute and can lead to cardiac arrest and death. The current guidelines for opioid monitoring do not contain a tool to evaluate the risk to develop OIRD in hospital settings, and major gaps in pain assessment documentation are also described including an absence of pain scores in up to 70% opioid doses administered. The lack of tools for adequate monitoring related to opioid administration leaves a considerable gap in patient safety. Therefore, the objective of the proposed research is to evaluate and refine the content of an OIRD risk screening tool. Participants will include 15-20 clinicians (i.e nurses, pharmacist and physicians) and researchers with expertise in pain management who will be recruited from various universities and affiliated hospitals in Canada to discuss the tool content and evaluate its relevance, comprehensiveness and feasibility for clinical use. The development of a content validated risk screening tool for OIRD could help better monitor opioid use in hospital settings and improve patient safety.

column36: Benefits of exergame training on perceptual and cognitive functions in Parkinson's disease
column37: In addition to well-documented motor difficulties, people with Parkinson's disease (PD) also tend to have a wide range of non-motor symptoms. These non-motor symptoms include understudied perceptual difficulties, such as the ability to see dim objects well, as well as cognitive difficulties, such as how well we pay attention to and remember our surroundings. While drugs for PD help motor symptoms, they are only partially effective for non-motor symptoms. Other types of interventions, such as exergaming, with video games combined with physical exercise, hold much potential for improving these symptoms. The two objectives of my master's project are therefore 1) to compare perceptual and cognitive abilities of people with PD to healthy older people with similar ages to determine the presence of these non-motor symptoms and 2) to determine whether exergaming is an effective intervention for improving these abilities.We will test 20 PD and 20 healthy controls participants on different tests measuring perception and cognitive abilities before and after exergaming or control intervention. In the exergaming intervention, participants play a video game that includes physical exercise (Ring Fit adventure). In the control intervention, they play a different game with no exercise (Animal Crossing). This will allow us to compare the impact of exergames versus cognitive training without physical exercises on the improvement of perception and cognition problems. The results from this project will allow us to better understand perceptual and cognitive non-motor symptoms in PD. Indeed, perceptual difficulties may be highly underestimated in PD. In addition, effective interventions such as exergaming may greatly slow down the progression of PD, even for motor symptoms.

column36: Impact des symptomes neuropsychiatriques et des performances cognitives individuelles sur la structure du cerveau et leurs potentiels a predire la morphologie cerebrale dans la maladie de Parkinson
column37: La demence est un groupe de troubles du cerveau qui entraine une alteration a long terme des capacites cognitives et de la vie quotidienne. La majorite des cas de demence sont lies a la maladie d'Alzheimer et seulement 6% sont lies a la maladie de Parkinson. Neanmoins, l'alteration du striatum dans cette maladie, une region liee aux processus de prise de decision, pourrait apporter plus de lumiere sur l'evolution des performances cognitives avec le vieillissement. De plus, il a ete recemment souligne que les symptomes neuropsychiatriques (tesl que la depression, l'apathie, l'anxiete) jouent un role important dans le developpement des troubles cognitifs et que leur progression est egalement en concordance avec l'evolution des performance cognitives. Neanmoins, la presence de subjectivite dans les evaluations des symptomes neuropsychiatriques oblige a utiliser un grand nombre de participants afin de reduire les biais. Dans ce projet, je vise a evaluer la correlation entre la morphologie du cerveau, les performances cognitives et les symptomes neuropsychiatriques chez des participants atteints ou non de la maladie de Parkinson, qui presentent un trouble cognitif leger et qui sont a un stade precoce de la progression de la maladie. column36: Detecting Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome (OMAS): associations of novel eye tracking metrics with structural localizations in the midbrain
column37: Opsoclonus-myoclonus-ataxia syndrome (OMAS) is a rare but serious inflammatory neurological disorder that typically affects young children and greatly disturbs their quality of life. There are well-established immunotherapies that have shown to be highly effective if administered early. However, since there are no current established diagnostic tests, delayed diagnosis in children with OMAS is common and leads to poorer long-term outcomes. The need for early diagnosis and intervention in OMAS is a critical gap that must be addressed as it can greatly change the developmental trajectory of this disorder in children. Thus, our research intends to examine if eye-tracking can address this knowledge gap. Eye-tracking is a non-invasive and well-tolerated test that has displayed eye tracking abnormalities in patients with neurological disorders. Unfortunately, previous eye tracking methods have been inaccessible to younger children due to the need for sustained attention and cooperation. Our study will use a novel technique of free viewing to assess eye tracking signatures in young children with OMAS. Based on our preliminary data with this novel technique, OMAS children demonstrate a distinctive eye tracking pattern that may point to functional abnormalities localized in the superior colliculus (SC) of the midbrain. Our study will further examine this association by evaluating eye-tracking metrics in children with OMAS compared to age and sex matched healthy control children. Results from this study will elude to a distinctive disease signature in OMAS to improve disease outcomes, and open the door to greater understanding of disease signatures in children with other neurological conditions by using this novel free-viewing task.

column36: Postpartum Hemorrhage Risk Factors and Outcomes in Rural Northwest Territories: Implications on Birthing Practices and Cultural Safety
column37: In Canada, postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is the leading cause of maternal morbidity and a major contributor to maternal mortality. PPH is defined as blood loss over 500mL following a vaginal birth or over 1000mL following a caesarean birth. National trends demonstrate elevated rates of PPH in Northern Canadian populations, which are majority indigenous. National PPH rates are approximately 5.6%, while rates in the Northern Canadian Territories ranged from 9.7-17.1%. PPH rates in Inuit birthing populations in northern Quebec were increased at 15.4%, and this trend is also noted in the Alaskan indigenous birthing population. No research has investigated reasons for, or secondary outcomes to, disproportionately high PPH rates in Northern Canadian populations.There are unique implications of this issue in remote northern communities. In the Northwest Territories (NWT), multiple rural maternity wards do not have an obstetrical surgeon or surgical capability; patients travel by medivac to a tertiary hospital to manage obstetrical complications, which can be far and treacherous in certain weather conditions. Furthermore, antenatally evacuating patients from their community to mitigate risk of obstetrical emergency can be psychosocially and culturally detrimental; this disproportionately affects indigenous families and perpetuates cultural genocide.The aim of this study is to examine rates of PPH, associated risk factors, and rates of PPH sequelae in multiple rural and predominantly indigenous communities in NWT. The end goal will be to understand the roots and implications of this health inequity and work towards creating solutions targeting modifiable clinical risk factors and social determinants of health to improve both clinical and cultural safety in these communities.

column36: Investigating the role of Bruton's tyrosine kinase in microglia and remyelination in multiple sclerosis and its animal models
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by the invasion of immune cells into the brain and spinal cord. These immune cells damage myelin, which is a protective layer surrounding nerve fibres and is important for signal transduction along the nerves. Myelin damage propagates the inflammatory response of immune cells, causing the killing of nerve fibres and the formation of lesions. Recent clinical trials on treatments for MS have focused on inhibiting Brutons tyrosine kinase (BTK), an enzyme that is activated in immune cells, particularly microglia, during inflammation. However, it is unknown how the expression of BTK in these microglia contributes to the pathology of the disease and whether its activation affects the reparative process of lesions.My goal is to explore the role of BTK during inflammation in the spinal cord, and determine whether inhibiting BTK will promote myelin repair. I will investigate the expression of BTK in spinal cords of two different MS mouse models to determine its extent of localization in the lesion and within microglia. To determine whether BTK inhibition can prevent the killing of nerve cells, I will activate microglia in an in vitro environment, inhibit their BTK activity, and observe resulting changes in inflammation and killing. Furthermore, I will administer a BTK inhibitor to one of our mouse models of MS and evaluate whether the drug will yield improvements reducing the extent of inflammation and myelin repair. Improving our understanding of BTK sheds light on its role in inflammatory lesions. As BTK inhibitors have entered clinical trials in MS, my thesis accompanies this development to shed light on the mechanisms and potential therapeutic benefits of BTK inhibitors for individuals living with MS.

column36: Exploring cell proliferation as a driver of facial morphogenesis
column37: During the development of the face, tissues move and change shape in tight patterns to give rise to a healthy face. These are driven by factors such as cell signaling and proliferation. Genetic defects can perturb these pathways, resulting in facial abnormalities or syndromes. The complexity of development makes it difficult to draw clear links between genetic and phenotypic changes; 40% of children referred to a medical geneticist fail to receive a clear diagnosis. I aim to improve our understanding of the mechanisms involved in facial shape changes to reduce this gap by exploring how differences in cell proliferation drive shape change in the mouse. Murine development closely resembles that of humans, making it a great model to study facial patterning.There are two major ways that cell proliferation can drive shape change. First, differences in the density of proliferating cells in a tissue can push growth outward in a given direction. Second, in some models and tissues, dividing cells orient preferentially to cause elongation of a tissue in the direction of growth. My research will use light sheet microscopy to quantify these effects and how they convey shape change in murine facial tissues.BMP4 is a tissue-specific regulator of upper jaw development, and BMP4 signaling plays a major role in regulating facial shape as well as proliferation. Thus, I will also study patterns of Bmp4 expression in developing wild type and Bmp4 mutant mice and relate it to proliferation to understand the mechanism by which Bmp4 regulates facial shape. Understanding shape change is key to earlier and more robust diagnosis and treatment of syndromic individuals.

column36: Patient-specific dose escalation during brachytherapy using multiparametric MRI in cervical cancer
column37: Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer in females worldwide. Standard treatment for locally advanced cervical cancer is the combined use of radiation therapy and chemotherapy. Radiation kills cancer cells by damaging their DNA. Brachytherapy, a type of radiation therapy used in the treatment of cervical cancer, delivers radiation internally to the body which allows a high dose of radiation to be directly applied to the tumours and a relatively low dose to other organs. The main goal of treatment is to improve survival and quality of life.Further improvements can be made by adapting dose to the specific properties of a patients tumour. Response to radiation therapy can vary between individual tumours based on the presence of oxygen. Hypoxic tumours (those lacking sufficient oxygen) are known to be more resistant to the effects of radiation. However, high doses of radiation can counteract this. In order to individualize care, we must be able to image these hypoxic regions. Two types of magnetic resonance imaging (diffusion-weighted and dynamic contrast-enhanced) have been linked to the identification of hypoxic regions.Here we aim to demonstrate the ability to image and identify these hypoxic regions at the time of treatment. Once successfully identified, we will evaluate the ability to increase radiation to these regions to counteract the effects of hypoxia. We will also design a new applicator with a high-resolution grid with the aim of more accurate dose delivery and compare its ability to accurately deliver high doses of radiation to hypoxic regions against that of a standard, commercially available brachytherapy applicator. Ultimately, we aim to improve survival and quality of life for cervical cancer patients.

column36: Investigating the effect of cutaneous sensory input on fibroblast and immune cell response during skin wound healing
column37: Following deep skin injury, adult mammals form fibrotic scars as they heal which can result in permanent immobility, pain and psychological distress. Developing therapeutics that promote regeneration or prevent scarring would greatly improve quality of life for patients suffering skin injury or disease. Interestingly, following large skin injury, mice exhibit a modest degree of regeneration that includes new hair follicles, glands and fat. Hence this model can be used to study the factors that cause scarring versus regeneration. It is well known that many different cells are involved in this process: in particular, immune cells, which cause inflammation in the initial stages of wound healing, and fibroblasts, which synthesize the connective tissue that make up scars. In animals such as salamanders, successful regeneration of amputated limbs requires active input from cutaneous nerves. To analyze the role of sensory neurons in mammalian wound healing, I will first selectively deplete sensory neurons in the back skin of mice and evaluate how this alters regenerative capacity and the quality of wound healing outcome. Secondly, using single cell RNA sequencing to simultaneously examine gene expression in thousands of cells from within the wound, I will examine how the presence or absence of nervous input modulates dermal fibroblast and immune cell states during the wound healing process. These findings will provide new insight into the processes involved in scar formation and will inform future development of therapeutics to enable skin regeneration and restoration of skin function following injury or disease.

column36: Sustainable eating in medical nutrition therapy for the treatment of type 2 diabetes
column37: Climate change and chronic disease are global crises linked by a common factor: food. Current food systems contribute to global greenhouse gas emissions and promote nutrient-poor, excessively-caloric eating patterns. These dietary patterns increase the prevalence of chronic diseases, such as type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, which affect a third of all Canadians. A solution for addressing these problems is to follow sustainable diets, which are healthy, environmentally-friendly, culturally-appropriate, available, and affordable. Abundant evidence shows that medical nutrition therapy, dietary counselling provided by registered dietitians, improves diabetes-related health outcomes. These therapeutic techniques stand to benefit from recent research into environmentally-positive food sources. I intend to evaluate if and how sustainable eating is integrated in medical nutrition therapy for people living with type 2 diabetes.First, I will analyze if eating patterns currently used by dietitians for treating diabetes address the many domains of sustainable diets, such as ecological-positivity, cultural-sensitivity, and food security. Next, I will conduct focus groups with dietitians and people living with diabetes to assess their perspectives on sustainable eating: Do they think sustainability is important? Do they think they can recommend or follow a sustainable diet, and do they believe that doing so will benefit diabetes management?This work will evaluate how health professionals help people living with diabetes make food choices that benefit personal and planetary health. Findings from this study will also open dialogues on ecologically-sustainable treatment modalities in clinical nutrition.

column36: Impact of a 12-Week High-Intensity Interval Training Intervention on Sympathetic Transduction in Older Adults
column37: Does a 12-Week High-Intensity Interval Training Intervention Reduce Sympathetic Transduction in Older Adults?Age-related declines in aerobic fitness increase the risk of high blood pressure and heart disease. The rise in blood pressure with ageing is also due to higher levels of sympathetic nerve activity directed towards blood vessels that cause them to get stiffer. Even at rest, small increases in blood pressure occur every time these nerves fire. We call this process sympathetic transduction, which can be harmful if the blood pressure increases get too high. Older adults with lower aerobic fitness have higher sympathetic transduction. Older adults can safely increase their aerobic fitness using a high-intensity interval training (HIIT) program. However, we do not know if sympathetic transduction can be lowered in older adults after HIIT. The goal of my project is to find out if 12-weeks of HIIT (3-days per week) can reduce sympathetic transduction in healthy older adults (65 years). We will randomly assign participants to a HIIT or a Control group (continue normal activity levels). Everyone will have their aerobic fitness measured using a graded exercise test. On a different day we will measure activity from a nerve in the lower leg using a tiny, sterile needle and blood pressure from a finger using a small cuff. Peak blood pressure increases in response to nerve activity will determine sympathetic transduction. These tests will be completed before and after the study. We expect that sympathetic transduction will be lower in the HIIT group after training, but unchanged in the Control group. If so, these findings will support the use of HIIT as a good way for older adults to increase their aerobic fitness and lower their chances of getting high blood pressure.

column36: Non-invasive neuromodulation for recovery of bowel function after spinal cord injury
column37: Limb paralysis is often seen as the most drastic outcome of spinal cord injury (SCI), but bowel dysfunctions are among the leading causes of disease and are among the highest patient priorities. Most individuals with SCI report bowel issues like constipation, and incontinence. While long and uncomfortable bowel management routines severely limit the health-related quality of life, especially when paired with impaired mobility and hand function.Despite being ranked among the top priorities, bowel function after SCI has remained understudied, as research continues to concentrate on recovery of motor function. Various management strategies have been studied, including multi-facetted bowel care routines, laxative use, and dietary adjustments. Along with pharmacological and surgical interventions, attempts at improving bowel function have shown little meaningful recovery. There is an unmet need to develop an approach which will target the multi-facetted nature of bowel dysfunction. Electrical stimulation to activate the disconnected, quiescent spinal cord following SCI has already shown promise in mitigating motor dysfunction. Furthermore, our laboratory has shown that electrical stimulation can significantly improve bowel function in an individual with SCI, while the effective dosing and underlying mechanisms are yet to be fully understood. The overarching aim of this proposal is to thoroughly investigate the therapeutic potential of non-invasive electrical stimulation of the spinal cord in mitigating bowel dysfunction in a pre-clinical model of SCI. A better understanding of long-term effects and neural mechanisms of electrical stimulation will facilitate effective clinical implementation, and improve the health-related quality of life for individuals with SCI.

column36: Using machine learning to predict outcomes following major vascular surgery
column37: Background: Vascular surgery patients are at high risk for complications given their significant comorbidities and the nature of their operations involving major vascular systems. Up to 30% of patients undergoing vascular surgery will suffer an adverse event, which remains among the highest for all surgical patients. Our goal is to develop automated machine learning (ML) algorithms that use pre-operative patient characteristics to predict peri-operative and long-term outcomes following major vascular surgery.Aim 1: Conduct a systematic review of ML applications in vascular surgery to better understand the methodologies, strengths, and limitations of current work.Aim 2: Distribute a national survey to Canadian vascular surgeons to understand their perceptions regarding the potential applications, advantages, and drawbacks of ML tools.Aim 3: Develop a ML algorithm using electronic health records from St. Michael's Hospital (463-bed academic hospital affiliated with the University of Toronto) to predict perioperative complications following major vascular surgery.Aim 4: Develop a ML algorithm using population-level data from the Institute of Clinical Evaluative Sciences administrative health databases to predict long-term outcomes following major vascular surgery. Implications: This direct-entry PhD thesis will provide a stronger understanding of ML applications in vascular surgery. The ML algorithms developed through our work can be deployed into clinical practice to identify high-risk patients and guide decision making, ultimately improving surgical outcomes.

column36: Development of a serological microfluidic assay for the rapid detection of interferons in COVID-19 patients
column37: Antibodies are a natural immune response developed by the body to protect against infection, but in some cases, individuals can develop autoantibodies that attack components of the individual's own body. As such, a dysfunctional immune response can result in an increased susceptibility to infection. In the case of COVID-19 patients, autoantibodies that attack immune system's hormones, like interferons, can result in life-threatening and critical COVID-19 infections. Therefore, the detection of these autoantibodies is critical in managing a patient's prognosis and monitoring for critical infections to protect those at the highest risk. Current testing methods are done in batch groupings and lack accessibility. We propose the use of a portable, instrument-free platform that can use direct patient blood samples to render a diagnostic readout. These kinds of technologies are analogous to the common pregnancy test lateral flow assay and allow for the monitoring of severe infection at the point-of-care, as well as provide a means of translating clinical assays into the hands of users.

column36: Canadian Survey of Pediatric Eating Disorder Programs: Understanding how COVID-19 Accelerated Virtual Care Implementation
column37: Technology-based interventions (TBIs) may be useful for increasing treatment options for eating disorders (EDs) among youth, who frequently use technologies and who are particularly affected by these mental illnesses. Canadian guidelines recommend certain TBIs for treating EDs in youth. However, the extent to which TBIs have been implemented and integrated into multidisciplinary treatment in Canada is unknown. The objective of this study is to characterize current practices of clinicians treating EDs in youth across Canada with a focus on TBIs, challenges presented by the COVID-19 pandemic, and subsequent adaptations in care paradigms. We hypothesize that clinicians identified new organizational strategies to accommodate the surge in ED cases among youth and the requirement of providing care at a distance during the pandemic. We expect that most youth ED treatment programs integrated videoconference-delivered therapy and that many have used it to provide multidisciplinary care. We are proposing a mixed-methods cross-sectional study in which healthcare providers currently working at youth ED clinics across Canada will be invited to respond to a quantitative online questionnaire and a qualitative semi-structured interview pertaining to their experience of providing care prior to and during the COVID-19 pandemic. We expect approximately 20-30 questionnaire respondents and 10-15 interview respondents. Descriptive statistics and thematic and content analysis will be used to report results. Findings will inform physicians of current practices across Canada and may help orient future care goals. It will provide insight on how adaptations made during the pandemic can improve ED treatment and which adaptations should be retained in the future.

column36: Novel Heterocycles to Study and Develop Therapeutics for Alzheimer's Disease
column37: Alzheimers disease (AD) is a disorder that destroys brain cells, causing thinking abilities and memory to deteriorate over time. As per Alzheimers Society of Canada, a continuously growing population with more than 500,000 Canadians over the age of 65 suffer from impaired mental abilities (dementia) due to AD. Unfortunately, due to the complex mechanism of AD, there are limited medications available, and they only ease the symptoms without curing AD completely. In this regard, a major target for treatments is the build-up (aggregation) of toxic amyloid-beta (Aβ) proteins in the brain, which kills brain cells and leads to dementia. This proposal aims to design, synthesize and evaluate a library of novel class of 3-phenylpyrazino[1,2-a]indol-1(2H)-ones as inhibitors of Aβ-aggregation. First, computational software will be used to design a novel library of molecules based on a core structure, and to understand the interactions of these molecules with Aβ aggregates. New synthetic protocols will then be developed to synthesize the library. Subsequently, Aβ aggregation in the presence of the molecules will be monitored over time using a dye that has unique light properties when bound to Aβ, followed by visualization using a microscope to identify anti-Aβ aggregation compounds. Finally, top compounds from this series will undergo colorimetric measurements in mouse brain cells, which are labeled with a reagent for measuring cell viability. I anticipate that the results of this study will lead to the discovery of a novel class of molecules that can bind and prevent the formation of toxic Aβ aggregates in the brain. These outcomes will have the potential to design and develop novel therapeutics in treating AD. In addition, the proposal will generate new knowledge in the field.

column36: Mitochondrial Dysfunction in the Activation of DNA Sensors in Colorectal Cancer Subtypes
column37: Colorectal cancer is a common and deadly cancer with two subtypes: the CIN subtype, which has poor patient survival, and the MIN subtype, which has better patient survival. This higher survival in MIN is due to a natural defence response called the immune response. A commonly asked question is what induces this increased natural immunity and how can we harness this defensive response for more effective CIN treatments. A potential mechanism we are investigating focuses on how DNA within a cell can leak from their usual compartments due to damage. When this occurs, DNA sensing proteins can detect the leakage and activate a defensive response capable of killing the cancerous cells in the body as DNA damage often occurs in cancer. One of the compartments that stores DNA is known as the mitochondria and this DNA has a special protein that protects it from damage. In MIN, this protective protein does not work, and we hypothesize that not only is the DNA from the mitochondria more easily detected due to its unique traits, but it is also more prone to release in MIN hence why MIN shows stronger natural immunity. To determine whether DNA from the mitochondria is more easily detected than DNA from other locations, we removed the mitochondrial DNA in our cells. We found that weaker immune responses are induced during these conditions indicating that DNA from the mitochondria is more easily detected. We now want to determine whether the protective protein is the reason for stronger MIN immune responses. Thus, we will delete this protein from CIN cells and observe whether there will be stronger immune responses. This allows us to determine how MIN can induce stronger defence responses and apply this to treatments for patients with CIN so we can activate their immune responses too.

column37: Greater intake of dairy products has been associated with lower type 2 diabetes(T2D) risk. Linear regression models will be used to examine the association between FA biomarkers of dairy fat intake and insulin sensitivity. This study will clarify the association between dairy fat intake and insulin sensitivity.

column36: The Effect of Liver X Receptors on Low Density Lipoprotein Transcytosis in Coronary Artery Endothelial Cells
column37: Atherosclerosis causes heart attacks and strokes. It is characterized by the deposition of lipids and buildup of plaque under the lining cells of blood vessels, the arterial endothelium. column37: As cancer progresses, it can spread from the original tumor to distal organs/tissues through a process called metastasis. One target metastatic site is the brain, where formation of metastases is deadly, leading to average patient survival rates less than 1 year. We intend to study and understand the differences between cancer cells that fail to invade versus those that form highly invasive brain metastases. This experimental model could also be expanded to patient derived brain cancer cells to develop personalized medical treatments regimes. column37: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is a structural deformity of the spine characterized by lateral curvature and vertebral rotation. column37: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the leading cause of death in Canadian women. Weight gain between pregnancies is an essential predictor of a womans lifelong health. column36: Function of Hippo kinases in the mature Central Nervous System
column37: Work using polarized epithelial cells has established that three conserved core protein-protein complexes exist and are important for establishing cellular polarity in part by regulating the activity of the Hippo signaling pathway. Despite an emerging literature revealing that Hippo signaling controls cell growth and modulates cellular mechanotrasduction in nonneuronal cells, little is known about the role for Hippo signaling components in post mitotic neurons. Recently, the Fawcett lab has identified a novel function for Hippo components in the development and stabilization of developing synapses. They revealed that a protein known as Angiomotin (AMOT) is phosphorylated by the Large Tumour Suppressor protein 1 (LATS1). This event is developmentally regulated, and that in the postnatal period LATS1 levels and kinase activity are reduced, enabling AMOT to enter nascently forming synapses, an important event leading to the stabilization of newly formed synapses.In nonneuronal cells LATS1 and a related kinase, LATS2, function similarly in driving Hippo signaling, yet significant differences in these two proteins suggest they likely contribute to different intracellular signaling pathways. Interestingly, in the postnatal CNS, LATS1 expression is downregulated while the expression of LATS2 is increased. This is opposite of their developmental expression. This suggests that LATS2 likely functions in the mature CNS. My project will assess whether, and how, LATS2 functions in the mature CNS. I will utilize molecular and cellular approaches as well as a mouse model where LATS2 expression has been reduced in postnatal excitatory neurons to assess the role of LATS2 in the mature CNS.

column36: Nohtawiy (my father): Supporting Cree fathers-to-be using a culturally-appropriate, community led, and strengths-based approach: impact on maternal, infant and paternal outcomes
column37: A long-standing community-based participatory research (CBPR) partnership with the Nêhiyawi communities of Maskwacîs is exploring how to support families and foster healthy pregnancies from a strength-based, community-led perspective. Through extensive community engagement and preliminary research, it is clear that family supports during pregnancy rarely include men. Moreover, many Indigenous fathers need additional support to overcome unique challenges to reclaim their roles which were systematically dismantled due to intergenerational colonial impacts. This project will implement and evaluate a culturally-appropriate and community-derived pilot program to support Indigenous men during fatherhood.In partnership with an existing Community Advisory Committee (CAC) and guided by results from preliminary work, a pilot program will be developed to provide men with access to community-derived, land-based, and cultural supports aimed at re-establishing and continuing traditional kinship roles. A mixed-methods research design, adapted to the priorities of the CAC, will be utilized. This could include interviews with fathers and their partners to understand their experiences in taking part, and to assess perceived changes in their social support, cultural connectedness, involvement, and wellbeing. Standardized and community-derived questionnaires may be used.The CAC has been and will continue to be fully involved in all aspects of the work. At each stage of the research process, they take a meaningful role in generating ideas, developing the program and research protocol, interpreting results, and guiding knowledge translation. This research will provide insight into the paternal role in childbirth and Indigenous cultural inclusivity in maternal health and wellbeing.

column36: Comparative Transcriptional Profiling of Both Immortalized Human Lung Cells and Patient-Derived Lung Organoids Infected with Circulating SARS-CoV-2 Variants of Concern (VOCs)
column37: Like other viruses, SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, constantly changes via mutation. Throughout the global pandemic, several variants of concern (VOCs) have been identified. A variant is of concern if it (1) spreads more easily, (2) is associated with increased disease severity, or (3) has the ability to resist the immune system or therapeutics. The biological properties of VOCs are poorly understood. Furthermore, several studies have shown that males are at a higher risk of severe COVID-19 infection, in comparison to females. Immune system and hormonal analyses have been conducted in an effort to explain this sex-based difference in COVID-19 disease severity. However, the biological properties of the virus have yet to be analyzed. The purpose of this study is to identify biological differences between SARS-CoV-2 VOCs and to determine if the increased severity of these variants is attributed to certain biological properties. To do so, I will infect human airway epithelial cells and three-dimensional (3D) human cell-based lung models with human coronavirus 229E (hCoV-229E) as well as four variants of concern. Following infection, I will extract, purify, and sequence the RNA from the infected cells. The sequencing results will be used to analyze cellular signaling pathways that are altered upon VOC infection. The 3D lung models will be derived from both male and female donors of the same age, leading me to be able to determine what factors may contribute to the sex-based difference in disease severity. The results of this study will help in better understanding the biological properties of VOCs and could be used to develop drugs against emerging variants.
