column36: Caracterisation d'une nouvelle population de neurones GABAergiques impliques dans le metabolisme energetique
column37: L'obesite est une maladie chronique representant un facteur de risque majeur dans le developpement des maladies cardiovasculaires et du diabete de type 2. Entre 1975 et 2016, la prevalence de l'obesite a presque triple dans le monde. Pour freiner cette epidemie mondiale, il importe de trouver de nouveaux traitements plus efficaces.Il est maintenant clair que des alterations dans le cerveau, en particulier dans l'hypothalamus, contribuent a l'obesite. L'hypothalamus joue un role cle dans la regulation de l'homeostasie energetique et du glucose en integrant differents signaux metaboliques. Ceci inclus la leptine, une hormone qui agit sur les neurones de l'hypothalamus pour reguler la prise alimentaire. Des etudes recentes suggerent que la majorite des effets de la leptine seraient medies par une sous-population de neurones encore inconnue. L'identification de cette nouvelle sous-population de neurones pourrait permettre une grande avancee dans la comprehension des mecanismes regulant le metabolisme du glucose et la prise alimentaire. Une connaissance plus approfondie de ces processus pourrait ensuite favoriser le developpement de medicaments plus efficaces pour le traitement de l'obesite et du diabete. Recemment, une etude a identifie differentes sous-populations de neurones dans l'hypothalamus. Parmi ces sous-populations, une en particulier a attire notre attention et pourrait jouer un role majeur dans le processus de regulation energetique.Mon projet de maitrise consistera a caracteriser la signature moleculaire de cette sous-population neuronale et a determiner l'impact de la leptine sur l'activite electrophysiologique de ces neurones. Ces travaux permettront ultimement de determiner si ces neurones sont essentiels aux effets coupe-faim de la leptine.

column36: Discriminating Metabolic Health Status in a Cohort of Nursing Students: A Cross-Sectional Study
column37: Obesity has become an increasingly problematic health issue worldwide. Obesity is one of the factors that determines an individuals metabolic health, along with blood pressure, blood sugar, and fat levels in the blood. An individuals metabolic health status directly relates to their risk of developing multiple chronic diseases, including diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, and certain types of cancers.Nurses are critical in caring for and educating overweight and obese patients, however, research to date has suggested that they are highly inactive and overweight or obese themselves. In a high stress occupation, that often involves shiftwork, it is likely that a nurses physical activity, nutrition, stress, and sleep play a role in determining their metabolic health status.Nursing students are a group of interest since they will be working with the increasing number of overweight and obese patients. As they are still actively engaged in education, nursing students are the ideal group to educate about how lifestyle choices can impact their own health and the health of their future patients. Unfortunately, there is little information known about how lifestyle factors, including physical activity, nutrition, stress, and sleep impact nursing students' metabolic health.This study aims to characterize the lifestyle factors that are most strongly associated with poor metabolic health status in nursing students, and aid in developing a lifestyle intervention for nursing students targeting improvement of those factors. Identifying the most prominent factors affecting the metabolic health status of this group is important in optimizing the physical and mental health of nursing students and could influence how they counsel their patients in the future.

column36: The Fast Acting Anti-Depressant Effects of Ketamine and Reelin
column37: Major depressive disorder is the leading cause of disability worldwide, and 50% of those diagnosed do not respond adequately to first-line treatment. Currently, the most prominently prescribed antidepressants have undesirable side-effects and a lengthy delay in therapeutic response. There is a pressing need for faster, more effective pharmacological alternatives. Ketamine has recently been shown to have rapid and sustained antidepressant effects following a single dosage. The mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway, which is essential for ketamines antidepressant effects, may mediated by the glycoprotein reelin. Alterations in reelin expression is seen in mood and psychotic disorders, suggesting that reelin down-regulation may be involved in the pathophysiology of depression. To assess the fast-acting antidepressant effects of reelin and ketamine, I will examine behavioural and neurobiological changes within a 24-hour period following drug administration. In animal models, depression-like symptoms will be induced through daily injections of the stress hormone corticosterone. I will then analyze the mechanisms and speed by which ketamine and reelin rescue these deficits. Behavioural effects will be analyzed using robust tests for anhedonia and learned helplessness (the forced swim test and latency for reward). Neurobiological changes will be analyzed using synaptoneurosomes, which allow the isolation of synaptic terminals, from the hippocampus. Serotonin transporter clustering will be analyzed on peripheral lymphocytes as an indicator of therapeutic response. This research could help us gain essential knowledge in the cellular roles underlying the pathophysiology of depression and could contribute to the development of more effective antidepressant drugs.

column36: Pharmacist-Led Virtual Care for Rural Acute Coronary Syndrome Program: The PLURAL-ACS Pilot Program
column37: The first 30 days after a heart attack is a vulnerable period, with the highest risk of having recurrent cardiac events. In particular, patients who reside in rural locations have been shown to have up to double the re-hospitalization rates after having a heart attack. Studies have shown that this could be due to poor access to care in remote areas. Despite the disparity in care, minimal research has been done to improve the care provided to heart attack patients living in rural locations in Canada. Evidence suggests that virtual care programs and pharmacist-led interventions are an effective and cost-saving alternative for providing care to patients. To our knowledge, a program of this nature has not been investigated in rural cardiac patients within Canada. Our proposed pilot program will provide a pharmacist-led virtual care for heart attack patients residing in Northern rural Alberta. Each patient will receive once-weekly phone calls where the pharmacist will assess cardiac medications, assess patient's symptoms, ensure timely access to medications, in addition to prescribing therapies to address the patient's identified cardiac issues. Any urgent issues will also be addressed with appropriate follow-up. Hospital readmission rates, in addition to any medical issues resolved by the pharmacist, will then be assessed by the end of the program. To determine the impact of the program, these results will be compared to a control group, which will be a group of heart attack patients residing in rural Alberta who have not been enrolled in the program. The goal of the project is to develop a program that can deliver safe and effective care to rural cardiac patients. If successful, the program can be expanded to other remote locations and adapted to other areas of practice.

column36: Analysis of oxidative stress on off-target infection of activated T cells by oncolytic vesicular stomatitis virus
column37: Oncolytic virotherapy is a form of cancer therapy that utilizes oncolytic viruses (OVs) to preferentially infect and kill tumour cells. We have previously demonstrated that some OVs in clinical trials likely lack efficacy due to the off-target infection of activated T cells when used in multi-dosing protocols. An increase in oxidative stress due to the increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) during viral replication may contribute to multiple aspects of viral pathogenesis. This project looks at the ability of some antioxidants, compounds that inhibit oxidation and protect cells from ROS-mediated damage, to prevent off-target infection of activated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. If antioxidants can prevent off-target viral infection of T cells, co-administering antioxidants during a rapid multi-dosing protocol with OVs has the potential to increase their efficacy. Thus far, the antioxidants N-acetyl L cysteine and catalase have proven promising candidates for improving cancer immunotherapies by preventing T cell of target infection with vesicular stomatitis virus. This project will be extended to a murine melanoma survival model to better determine which combination therapies extend survival.

column36: Parent and Adolescent Decisions Regarding Research Genetic Sequencing in Pediatric Cancer
column37: This research project aims to better understand how families make decisions regarding large-scale genetic sequencing following a pediatric cancer diagnosis, with a focus on considerations that are of personal importance or concern to parents and adolescent patients. Sequencing is a type of genetic test that involves reading sections of an individuals DNA. Large-scale genetic sequencing (LSGS) describes using sequencing to read multiple sections of an individuals DNA.In Canada, LSGS is becoming increasingly common in research settings for children and adolescents who have been diagnosed with cancer. At the McGill University Health Centre (MUHC), LSGS is currently offered for all pediatric (≤18 years of age) cancer patients through research programs. Despite the growing availability of LSGS, little research has been done to assess parent and patient attitudes towards LSGS in Canadian pediatric cancer settings. Understanding families attitudes towards LSGS is an essential part of ensuring that this technology is introduced into research and clinical settings in a patient- and family-centered manner.We aim to collect and present parent and adolescent (12-18 years of age) patient perspectives from families offered LSGS through research programs at the MUHC following a pediatric cancer diagnosis. We have designed a questionnaire to assess parent and adolescent attitudes, with a focus on individual motivations and concerns regarding participation in LSGS. We will recruit families that accept or decline participation in LSGS, in an effort to present a broad range of perspectives.We hope that this research will aid researchers, healthcare providers and policymakers in ensuring this technology is introduced in a patient- and family-centered manner.

column36: The RAIN mobile app for emotional eating in adolescents: a randomized controlled study
column37: Emotional eating involves overeating in response to negative emotions, which can lead to unhealthy dietary habits and poor physical health. Several studies have looked at how Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, a therapy that promotes acceptance of negative emotions, mindfulness (i.e., awareness of the present moment), and acting in line with ones personal values, can improve emotional eating. However, very few studies have focused on using this therapy to help with emotional eating in adolescents. This is problematic as obesity in childhood and adolescence is becoming a major public health concern. Additionally, unhealthy dietary habits during this period is linked to short-term and long-term health consequences. This study will test an app that will teach a meditation exercise based on Acceptance and Commitment Therapy to guide adolescents when they feel the need to eat in response to negative emotions. The app will contain age-appropriate visuals and language, as well as game elements to engage adolescents. This study will enhance our understanding of how an app specifically adapted for adolescents can improve emotional eating. This knowledge can help us improve adolescents physical and mental health.

column36: Intercellular mitochondrial trafficking in Neuropathic Pain
column37: Neuropathic pain (NP) is a chronic neurological condition arising from injury or disease of the somatosensory nervous system which affects 10% of all Canadians. Preclinical studies done in animal models of NP demonstrate that peripheral nerve injury-induced NP is associated with central nervous system (CNS) changes that are caused by pathological changes of neuronal and glial cells through a variety of intercellular cascades resulting in increased synaptic plasticity. With regards to neurons, previous research has shown that an overall result of peripheral injury is a change in mitochondrial function, with an increase in reactive oxygen species being directly linked to pain behaviours in NP rodents. Simultaneously, within the glial component of the pathology, the transformation of astrocytes into a reactive state is also implicated in NP, as reactive astrocytes are sufficient to induce pain states in uninjured rodents. Studies in other CNS pathologies implicate astrocytes in resolving neuronal mitochondrial deficits via mitochondrial donation and sequestration. As neuronal mitochondrial dysfunction is directly implicated in NP, a new emerging gap is the elucidation of the astrocytic spatiotemporal ability to modulate spinal cord neuronal mitochondrial dynamics in the context of NP. Using super-resolution imaging methods in combination with transcriptome and proteome analysis, my project aims to track intercellular mitochondrial trafficking across astrocytes and spinal cord neurons following peripheral nerve injury in a transgenic mouse line that allows for specific manipulation of astrocytes. This will improve our understanding of the mechanisms behind mitochondrial dysfunction in NP and potentially elucidate new prospective therapeutic targets for the treatment of NP.

column36: Development of Targeted Therapies for the Treatment of Mixed Lineage Leukemia
column37: Disruptor of telomeric silencing 1-like (DOT1L) is a histone methyltransferase, a protein that adds hydrogen atoms onto the amino acid lysine 79 on histone H3. In normal physiological conditions, methylation by DOT1L leads to increased gene expression, this regulation of gene expression plays an important role in several physiological processes and has a positive association with cardiac health and bone health, DOT1L is also important in development and DNA. Unfortunately, DOT1L is associated with health conditions including Mixed Lineage Leukaemia (MLL). Abnormal recruitment of DOT1L to genes associated with MLL leads to increased expression of these genes and subsequent leukemogenesis. Due to DOT1L's association with MLL, plenty of research has, and still is, being done on DOT1L inhibition as a therapy option. However, inhibition of DOT1L is problematic as inhibitors will affect the expression of all the genes regulated by DOT1L, not only the genes associated with MLL, resulting in an increased risk of off-target effects. My Master's project will involve developing, and testing, a new method of selective DOT1L inhibition that will help prevent off-target effects. In order for the inhibitor to stop DOT1L at the site of interest only, the inhibitor will be attached to a chain of Locked Nucleic Acids (LNA) that is complementary to the genes associated with MLL, keeping the inhibitor in place. Inhibition efficacy will be determined by analyzing changes in expression of the MLL associated genes, potential of off-target effects will be determined by analyzing changes in expression of other DOT1L regulated genes. My project will hopefully lead to therapies that are not only efficacious but have no off-target effects as well.

column36: Targeting Lysine-specific Demethylase 1 to Enhance the Post-transplant Graft-versus-leukemia Effect
column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is an aggressive blood cancer with a 5-year survival rate of 21%. AML occurs when the bone marrow produces a large number of unhealthy cells that prevent the growth and functions of normal cells. The only cure for AML patients is to undergo a stem cell transplant where normal blood stem cells from a healthy donor are transplanted into the patients. These donor cells have the ability to prevent AML from re-emerging, but AML still frequently returns after transplant, leading to disease relapse. To reduce relapse and improve the long-term effectiveness of transplants, new treatment options are needed. Lysine-specific demethylase 1 (LSD1) is a protein that has been a promising therapeutic target for treating AML. Blocking the function of LSD1 has also been shown to increase immune cells ability to recognize and kill cancer cells. Therefore, this project aims to study the ability for LSD1 blockers to activate and enhance immune responses against AML in the context of stem cell transplant. We will characterize the underlying molecular mechanisms that contribute to a potentially heightened anti-leukemia immune response. Mice models that mimic the relevant biological environment will also be used to evaluate the safety and efficacy of LSD1 blockers. Eventually, our goal is to gather sufficient experimental evidence to support a clinical trial that further examines the LSD1 blockers ability to prevent relapse after stem cell transplant.

column36: Leveraging bacterial membrane vesicles as a therapeutic strategy for Crohn's disease
column37: It is estimated that the population of bacteria that live in our gut, known as the gut microbiota, outnumber the cells of the human body 100 times. The diversity of microbial species and their capabilities is so immense that we have only scratched the surface into understanding the relationship between humans and their gut microbiota. Over the past few decades, we have uncovered that this relationship is linked to numerous aliments including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), diabetes, cancer, and anxiety disorders. With our expanding knowledge of human-microbe interactions, the development of probiotic therapies for these aliments is an exciting and promising new venture. Probiotics are living microorganisms that when consumed can provide health benefits.Crohns disease (CD) is a form of IBD that is characterized by chronic and relapsing inflammation of the digestive system. Over 135,000 Canadians live with CD. With our current therapeutics, it is estimated that 75% of CD patients still require surgery during their life. While the driving causes of CD are unknown, our understanding involves factors such as the gut microbiota, integrity of the gut barrier, and genetic predisposition. The largest genetic risk factor for CD reduces the activation of the NOD2 receptor when it encounters a microbial product. In healthy individuals, this activation helps to strengthen and repair the gut barrier. My research aims to develop new therapeutics for CD that restore the beneficial effects of NOD2 activation. I am using genetic engineering technology to design probiotics that will deliver beneficial microbial products to gut cells. column36: Development of an off-the-shelf engineered T cell therapy for glioblastoma
column37: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is the most common and aggressive primary adult brain tumour. Despite multimodal management patients currently face a median survival of 15 months and disease recurrence is virtually 100% certain. Development of novel therapeutics is desperately needed. Adoptive cell transfer of T cells engineered with synthetic receptors targeting GBM offers the promise of achieving durable tumour control through the ability of immune cells to persist within the host and destroy malignant cells as they re-emerge. Modern engineered T cells have shown limited success in treating GBM due, in part, to the fact that GBM is a heterogeneous disease and the therapeutic cells evaluated thus far have been directed at single tumor targets. These engineered T cells also bear significant financial and technical burden as they are manufactured on a per-patient basis. We propose to overcome these challenges by developing an off-the-shelf engineered T cell product that can attack multiple GBM targets. To this end, we have chosen a non-canonical T cell population, known as γδ T cells, as a platform for this off-the-shelf approach given their ability to be transferred to unrelated hosts without risk of lethal graft-versus-host disease. While γδ T cells are capable of directly attacking GBM, we are augmenting that capacity by engineering the T cells to express a series of synthetic receptors against multiple GBM targets. We hypothesize that engineering T cells with multi-target specificity will increase therapeutic potency. Addressing this hypothesis using an off-the-shelf platform is expected to facilitate clinical translation of the outcomes by offering an affordable solution that can be manufactured in a controlled fashion and made available across Canada.

column36: Development of Chimeric Antigen Receptor Modified Dendritic Cells
column37: Our immune systems can recognize foreign invaders such as viruses and bacteria resulting in the generation of immune responses. In the context of cancer, many of these diseased cells express antigens that are not normally found in the body causing these abnormal cells to be classified as foreign. In response, the immune system produces killer T cells specific for the cells expressing these foreign antigens with the hope of killing off the population. Unfortunately, cancers tend to mutate quickly causing changes in their antigen repertoires and a loss of recognition by these killer T cells. Attempts have been made to boost these killer T cell responses by extracting tumor antigens and feeding them directly to the cell type that turns them on, called dendritic cells. This approach however still leaves the door open to immune escape since it relies only on a finite set of antigens. As a result, another approach is being employed where a specific subset of these dendritic cells generated using antiviral factors is injected directly into tumor lesions. When combined with other cancer drugs, this approach has been proven to generate new populations of cancer specific killer T cells in patients. With the properties of this dendritic cell subset as a starting point, this project aims to engineer dendritic cells to be even more potent. Using viruses, these cells will be genetically engineered to express receptors that will allow them to directly take bites of cancer cells and extract tumor antigens more effectively. Using mouse models, the goal is to determine whether this could be a new effective immune cell therapy for treating cancer based on the ability of this platform to induce strong killer T cell responses and eliminate the abnormal cell populations.

column36: Investigating the role of metformin on cardiac fibrosis in plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 deficient mice
column37: Loss of critical heart cells and the associated reduction in heart contraction are defining features of heart dysfunction in aging and after a serious cardiovascular event. Plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) is a protein that has a known role in the process of blood clotting. It is well understood that low levels of Pai-1 cause bleeding disorders. Studies in mice lacking Pai-1 show spontaneous cardiac impairment in response to aging. These results are also observed within the Berne Amish community, which has an increase in individuals lacking Pai-1, and they experience accelerated cardiac disease. Metformin is drug administered to patients with diabetes which has a strong safety record and sugar-lowering function. Metformin treatment also improves cardiac impairment and can reduce cardiac damage in response to a form of surgery that causes cardiac stress. Under conditions where levels of Pai-1 are low, cardiac damage increases during aging or under cardiac stress and impairs cardiac healing. Thus, we hypothesize treatment of mice lacking Pai-1 with metformin will reduce cardiac damage and improve heart function. Aim one will investigate if mice lacking Pai-1 treated with metformin have reduced spontaneous development of cardiac damage associated with aging. Aim two will investigate if mice lacking Pai-1 treated with metformin have reduced cardiac damage in response to two models of cardiac stress, (i) a form of surgery and (2) inducing a high blood pressure state. In both aims, heart function will be assessed via ultrasound and damage (scarring) will be assessed using other techniques. These experiments will add significantly to the cardiovascular impact of metformin in a setting of low Pai-1 levels.

column36: Investigate the role of parenteral vaccine-trained tissue-resident macrophages in host defense against heterologous bacterial infections
column37: Immunological memory has traditionally been solely attributed to T and B lymphocytes in the adaptive immune system. Recently, the concept of immunological memory has been expanded to include innate immune memory, which can be defined as an altered state of the innate immune system after primary exposure to an antigen or microbe that will modify its responsiveness to the same or different antigen/microbe. Trained innate immunity (TII), a subset of innate immune memory, is characterized by cellular and epigenetic changes, along with protection against heterologous infections. Ample evidence of TII induced by systemic administration of certain vaccines exists. However, there are many knowledge gaps about the capacity of systemic vaccination to invoke TII in local tissue-resident cells. Given the recent and widespread human vaccination with mRNA-based and viral-vector-based SARS-CoV2 vaccines, it is of great relevance to study whether these vaccines are capable of inducing TII in local tissue-resident cells. This project will employ a murine model to examine the capacity of parenteral delivery of mRNA-based and viral-vector-based vaccines to induce TII in respiratory-mucosal tissue-resident macrophages, and the mechanisms underlying any observed training. Secondly, the project will seek to determine if TII invoked by these vaccines will lead to protection against heterologous bacterial infections and if so, how this protection is attained. In the recent climate of the COVID-19 pandemic, with mass global vaccinations and rapidly evolving variants that may evade current vaccines, it is of high importance to investigate the potential of SARS-CoV2 vaccines to evoke TII. Furthermore, future vaccination strategies would benefit greatly to evoke both innate and adaptive immunity.

column36: Characterization of the role of Deptor in the progression of breast cancer
column37: In recent years, DEP-domain containing mTOR-interacting protein (Deptor) has been identified as an endogenous inhibitor of mammalian target of Rapamycin (mTOR), the master regulator of cellular growth which is frequently dysregulated in cancers. Deptor plays pivotal roles in the regulation of cell proliferation and survival, and efforts to elucidate the mechanisms by which it exerts its effects in cancer have mainly focused on its direct interactions with mTOR. However, while clinically, high mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) activity corresponds with poor prognoses among cancer patients, consistent with low Deptor levels frequently reported in most tumors, paradoxically, high expression of Deptor in human breast cancer also corresponds with the worst prognoses in these patients. These findings point to a dual role for Deptor in cancer, and potential pro-tumorigenic functions independent of mTORC1. Thus, my research aims to expand understanding of Deptor and its potential interactors, with its seemingly contradictory contributions in tumorigenesis, and characterize the role Deptor plays in breast cancer initiation and progression, using conditional Deptor knockout transgenic mouse models of breast cancer. Greater understanding of mTOR modulation is necessary to improve clinical interventions involving the mTOR pathway, and considering the ubiquity of mTOR dysregulation in various cancers, understanding the functions and regulatory mechanisms of mTOR components such as Deptor is an important step in the advancement of cancer research and treatment. Further, by investigating Deptor's role independent of mTOR the proposed research will unveil the scope of a newly discovered but widely acting player in cancer and its potential as a novel target in anticancer therapeutics.

column36: Sex-specific Electromyographic, Kinematic, Performance, and Symptomatic Differences between Sitting and Cycling Computer Workstations
column37: Work-related Musculoskeletal Disorders (WMSDs) are common, painful disorders of the muscles, tendons, and nerves that develop over time. WMSDs may be caused by fatigue, muscle overuse, awkward postures, or repetitive movements associated with seated workstations. Moreover, previous studies have reported that females have a higher risk of developing WMSDs and experiencing negative work-related symptoms. Active workstations, such as cycling workstations have been proposed to combat WMSDs. Cycling workstations activate larger muscle groups, increase energy expenditure, and could potentially slow the development of WMSDs. However, cycling workstations may increase changes in head posture which could accelerate the onset of Computer Vision Syndrome (CVS). CVS is a complex of vision issues caused by the interaction between vision and computer usage. Although studies have compared various outcomes of cycling workstations, none analyzed sex specific differences in muscle activity, kinematics, visual fatigue, performance, and discomfort in cycling workstations compared to the seated workstation. Findings from this study will examine whether cycling workstations are a suitable intervention for WMSDs and further the understanding of the etiology of WMSDs.The objectives of this study are 1. Compare the muscle activity, kinematic performance, discomfort, and visual fatigue ratings between cycling and seated workstations 2. Uncover sex-specific differences in the aforementioned outcomes. We hypothesize that cycling workstations increase head kinematics resulting in premature onset of visual discomfort. No change in typing performance is expected; however, we anticipate decreased discomfort. Finally, we expect the above-described differences to vary between the sexes.

column36: Evaluating the efficacy of limb immersion for mitigating hyperthermia and cardiovascular demand in elderly adults: a randomized crossover trial
column37: Increasing age is associated with an impaired physiological capacity to dissipate heat and blunted cardiovascular adjustments to heat stress. Consequently, elderly adults are at increased risk of heat-induced illnesses or death during heat exposure. Given that Canada is entering uncharted territory as the frequency, intensity, and duration of extreme heat events is increasing and that Canadas population is aging rapidly, there is an urgent need to develop heat-alleviation strategies that can provide targeted protection for the elderly. While Health Canada and the World Health Organization currently recommend the use of personal heat-alleviation strategies such as visiting cooled locations and using electric fans, these strategies are cost prohibitive and inaccessible to many elderly adults such as those in long-term care homes or retirement residences. A potentially simple, accessible and low-cost solution to better protect heat-vulnerable elderly adults is partial immersion of the limbs in tepid water (~20°C). My project will evaluate the effectiveness of partial limb immersion for protecting elderly men and women (65-85 years) against dangerous increases in core temperature and heat-induced cardiovascular instability during a prolonged exposure (6-hours) to hot (35°C, 60% relative humidity) indoor conditions the elderly may face during an extreme heat event. By assessing the physiological responses, we can define best practices for the implementation of this heat-alleviation strategy. Finally, by assessing responses in both men and women, we can create messaging that will provide equitable protection to heat-vulnerable elderly men and women, ensuring health equity and a maximum level of protection to maintain health and well-being during extreme heat.

column36: Machine-Learning Aided Discovery of targeted ER-AF2 PROTACs
column37: Proteolysis targeting chimera (PROTAC) aims at selectively degrading biological targets of interest (TOI) intracellularly using host cell's ubiquitin ligases thereby achieving lasting ablation of activity. PROTACs carry special interest in this project since the objective is to target conventionally 'undruggable' targets - estrogen receptor (ER) - through unconventional allosteric sites - co-activator binding domain (AF2) of ER - which is a relatively solvent-exposed pocket. PROTACs consist of three chemical moieties: 1) a binder for the to-be-degraded TOI. 2) a binder to the host cell's E3 ubiquitin ligases. 3) a linker that connects parts 1) and 2). Finding the best combination of those three elements to form a stable ternary complex constitutes the challenge in the design of new PROTACs. First, formation of the ternary complex is thermodynamically driven by cooperativity of favorable interactions between the TOI and the E3 ligase. Second, the choice of the E3 ligase is predicated on the abundance of the E3 ligase concentration in target tissues. Third, the linker needs to be minimal in length in order to limit off target effects and ideally participate in promoting the ternary complex. In order to predict choice of E3 ligase and optimal linker type and length, we will employ a machine learning model that will train on all available empirical active/inactive PROTAC data points (more than 1200 PROTACs were tested to date) and incorporate protein surface-surface encodings from protein-protein dockings in order to derive TOI specific predictions. Additionally, tissue-specific expression profiles will be curated. The application of this project may generalize beyond PROTACs to lysosomal targeting chimeras, molecular glues, and other novel non-inhibition mediated schemes.

column37: Secondary hyperparathyroidism (SHPT), a pathological rise in circulating parathyroid hormone (PTH), is a complication and independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease and death in chronic kidney disease (CKD). Clinically, vitamin D-based treatments are used to try to control SHPT; however, 20-30% of patients with SHPT become resistant to these treatments, thereby putting patients at risk for advancing disease. This study seeks to determine whether changes in megalin function play a key role in dysregulated parathyroid vitamin D metabolism in a CKD rat model. It is hypothesized that CKD produces a reduction in parathyroid megalin levels such that the uptake of vitamin D into the parathyroid is blunted, and the loss of control of PTH is exacerbated. Megalin mRNA and protein will be measured in parathyroid glands, and an ex-vivo parathyroid culture will be used to perform fluorescence-based assays to evaluate megalin-mediated uptake. This study will provide mechanistic insight towards vitamin D resistance while highlighting megalin as a potential pharmacologic target to ensure effective treatment of SHPT.

column37: Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD) is one of the most common mental health disorders in Canada. SAD is characterized by an intense, debilitating fear and/or avoidance of social situations. Changes in the ECS have been linked to mental health conditions such as depression and anxiety. Brain imaging techniques, such as positron emission tomography (PET), can be used to visualize the activity of different biological systems in the brain to find new biological mechanisms and inform the development of new and more effective treatments. This ground-breaking study will use PET imaging to visualize the enzyme that regulates a substance within the ECS called anandamide (AEA). This enzyme is fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH), and it is thought to be elevated in individuals suffering from SAD. As such, blocking this enzyme to cause a natural increase in ESC activity has become a favorable therapeutic strategy. This study aims to help better understand the role of the ECS in SAD, visualize differences in FAAH levels in the brain of individuals with SAD and healthy individuals, and determine if FAAH levels in the brain are linked to severity of SAD. This study is clinically relevant, as the results will provide direct evidence on how the brain ECS is regulated in individuals with SAD. It will inform the development of novel and specific treatments targeting the ECS for patients suffering from this isolating and debilitating mental health condition.

column37: Canada has reported over 1.7 million confirmed cases of coronavirus-19 disease (COVID-19), 91,000 hospitalizations, and 29,000 deaths. column36: The Role of Teneurin-3 and Latrophilin-2 in Establishing Spinal Cord Somatotopy
column37: Somatotopy is a key organisational principle of the central nervous system. It describes a phenomenon where neurons and their connections are arranged according to the layout of the body. For example, Dr. Wilder Penfield while working at the Montreal Neurological Institute famously demonstrated that the sensory and motor areas of the brain are organised into somatotopic ;maps of the body. We now know that somatotopy exists in many other regions within the central nervous system including different levels of the brainstem and spinal cord. However, very little is known about how somatotopy emerges in the developing nervous system. I hypothesize that two proteins, Teneurin-3 and Latrophilin-2, are crucial for setting up somatotopy within the spinal cord by directing connections from sensory neurons to their correct targets. These two proteins were recently identified to have a similar role in establishing the connections between certain brain regions. They also exist within the spinal cord in patterns that correspond to the somatotopic layout of the spinal cord. My work will provide a significant advancement to our understanding of how somatotopy develops by determining how somatotopic arrangement comes about at the first step of sensory pathways. This could then reveal how somatotopy develops throughout the central nervous system.

column36: Mapping the tumour microenvironment to elucidate structural features that impact nanoparticle accumulation
column37: Current cancer therapies, such as chemotherapy, are largely non-specific and cause systemic side effects. Modern advances in cancer therapeutics involve the development of personalized smart drugs to specifically target different cancers, while reducing toxicity to healthy cells. One branch of this is nanomedicine, which involves nanoparticle drug carriers that infiltrate the tumour and selectively target cancer cells. Currently, design of nanoparticle therapeutics are limited by our understanding of factors that impact their accumulation in tumours. The aim of this work is to investigate how structural features within the tumour affect nanoparticle delivery, which will aid in improved design and allow for identification of tumours that will have the greatest response to nanotherapeutics. 3D imaging will be used to visualize the complex structure of the tumour environment and analyze integral components, such as blood vessels and immune cells. Images will then be processed and analyzed to categorize the heterogeneous tumoural network into regions, termed neighbourhoods, depending on the combination of unique structural features present. Nanoparticles will be quantified within each neighbourhood and accumulation patterns will be correlated with certain structural features. This correlation can then be used to predict how nanoparticles will behave in other tumours depending on tumour characteristics. Using the classifications developed through this work, we can begin to expand our understanding of the impact of tumour structural features on nanoparticle accumulation, which is the first step towards developing a predictive algorithm to optimize selection of therapeutics for difficult to treat cancers.

column36: Primary care access to sexual assault evidence kits in Northern Ontario: a mixed methods approach to understanding the barriers to justice and comprehensive care for survivors
column37: Sexual assault evidence kits (SAEKs) are used to gather forensic evidence from survivors after assault. Justice is hindered without such evidence, resulting in dependence on survivors recounting traumatizing narratives. 1/3 of Canadian women have experienced sexual assault, but 41% of Canadian hospitals do not have SAEKs available and/or staff trained to administer them. Most of these deficits fall in remote Northern areas, forcing women to travel long distances to receive care. Research on availability is limited but it is known that a ;justice gap exists, whereby women in rural regions and socioeconomically marginalized communities have poor access; Northern and Indigenous communities are known to especially lack access to SAEKS and related counselling. This lack of resources often results in poor survivor mental health, increased chronic health disorders, substance abuse, and violence perpetuation, placing further strain on health services.Using surveys in 10 communities which are Northern healthcare hubs, I plan to gain the perspectives of Northern healthcare providers on access to SAEKs in their communities as well as barriers they face in providing sexual assault care. These surveys will inform the guide for in-depth interviews, which I will carry out with healthcare providers at two hubs for rural areas in cities with large Indigenous populations (Thunder Bay Regional Health Sciences Centre; North Bay Regional Health Centre).Sexual assault stigma and trauma hinders many survivors from seeking care, especially when care has been inadequate in the past. It is essential that few barriers deter post-assault care. This research will provide insight into rural health challenges and inform changes that can relieve over-burdened mental health and emergency services.

column36: Methodological considerations for studies of preterm birth or small-for-gestational-age birth after vaccination during pregnancy: A case study on COVID-19 vaccine.
column37: The impacts of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) have been felt everywhere. COVID-19, which was declared a global pandemic in March 2020, can affect any individual, and pregnant women are particularly more vulnerable to severe infection due to changes in their immune system. COVID-19 vaccination has, therefore, been recommended during pregnancy to prevent adverse maternal and fetal outcomes. However, pregnant people remain hesitant to receive the vaccine, mainly due to safety concerns for their newborns. There is insufficient evidence to describe the impact of COVID-19 vaccination on pregnancy outcomes. From previous research on influenza vaccination during pregnancy, we know that specific scientific approaches are required to perform these studies properly and generate valid results, especially for preterm birth and small-for-gestational-age (SGA) birth, which are very important adverse pregnancy outcomes. Our study will examine preterm and SGA birth following COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy, while accounting for important scientific challenges, such as differences in characteristics of people who do and do not become vaccinated during pregnancy, as well as very different timing of pregnancy with respect to eligibility/opportunity to become vaccinated given the dramatic changes in the roll-out of the COVID-19 vaccination program in Ontario, to provide a more accurate and comprehensive understanding of the optimal scientific considerations for studies on safety of COVID-19 vaccines in pregnancy. Our findings will inform other scientists, as well as evidence users to ensure that studies of COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy are using the optimal scientific approach for generating accurate results that can ultimately inform policy makers and pregnant people.

column36: Cytosolic MYSM1 in Hematopoietic Stem Cells and Implications for MYSM1-Deficiency Syndrome Pathology
column37: MYSM1-deficiency syndrome is a rare disorder that presents with severe defects in blood and immune cell development in humans. It is caused by mutations in MYSM1, a DNA binding protein that is known to promote gene expression. Based on previous research it has been established that MYSM1 maintains the function of blood and immune cell development by regulating genes within the nucleus. Recently it has been shown that a pool of MYSM1 protein has been found outside the nucleus (cytosol) in a subset of white blood cells known as macrophages. Functionally, cytosolic MYSM1 is said to be involved in regulating the immune system by decreasing the bodys inflammatory response. The significance of cytosolic MYSM1 has not been explored beyond macrophages and this important knowledge gap will be addressed in my project. This project will focus on determining if a cytosolic pool of MYSM1 protein is produced in blood stem cells (HSCs) when the body is inflamed or infected. If a cytosolic form of MYSM1 protein is found in HSCs then further studies using mutated forms of MYSM1 will be done to further understand how it may contribute to MYSM1-deficiency syndrome. HSCs from mouse bone marrow will be exposed to a range of inflammatory stimuli and imaged to determine the location of MYSM1 within the cell. These studies will be done with harvested HSCs and live mice. We will analyze and compare responses to inflammatory stimuli in HSCs expressing normal and mutated forms of MYSM1 protein. The proposed experiments will provide insight into how cytosolic MYSM1 helps regulate blood and immune cell development in response to inflammation or infection. This work will hopefully be expanded to humans to better understand MYSM1-deficiency syndrome to help future patients.

column36: Les futurs psychologues sont-ils bien prepares a evaluer et intervenir aupres d'une personne considerant le suicide?
column37: Au Quebec, on compte pres de 4000 hospitalisations pour tentative de suicide et plus de 1000 deces par suicide chaque annee. La majorite des psychologues, incluant les doctorants en psychologie, ont travaille avec un patient presentant des idees suicidaires ou ont ete confrontes au deces d'un patient par suicide. Malgre cet enjeu de sante publique, nous ne savons pas a quel point les psychologues sont prepares a evaluer et a intervenir aupres d'une personne considerant le suicide. L'objectif principal de cette etude est de decrire le contenu des formations offertes sur l'evaluation et l'intervention du risque suicidaire aux etudiants inscrits dans des programmes de psychologie reconnus par l'ordre des psychologues du Quebec (OPQ). L'objectif secondaire est de recueillir le point de vue des psychologues en debut de carriere sur la qualite et la pertinence du contenu de ces formations. Pour obtenir une description des formations offertes aux etudiants, nous inviterons les directeurs des programmes a remplir un questionnaire en ligne. Pour obtenir le point de vue des psychologues, nous contacterons l'OPQ pour obtenir les coordonnees des psychologues ayant recu leur licence de pratique dans les cinq dernieres annees. Nous les inviterons a remplir un questionnaire en ligne sur leur opinion sur la formation recue durant leur parcours etudiant. Les resultats de ce projet permettront de documenter les formations offertes aux etudiants en psychologie en evaluation et en intervention du risque suicidaire, d'identifier les lacunes et d'emettre des recommandations pour orienter le developpement de formations futures. Ultimement, le but est de preparer les futurs psychologues a pouvoir prevenir le pire- le deces par suicide.

column36: Analysis of the Biological Condition Landscape to Uncover Patterns of Gene Regulation
column37: A major area of interest in genomics is to identify and understand how genes are regulated among different biological conditions. The dominant method used to uncover these trends is through differential expression (DE) studies. The Gemma database, developed in the Pavlidis lab contains over 13,000 expression profiling datasets based on RNA-sequencing and microarray data from mouse and human samples. These expression profiling datasets have been annotated with approximately 40,000 condition comparisons, which include categories such as drug treatments, diseases, and tissue types among others. In previous work from the lab, DE data from Gemma was leveraged to develop the GemmaDE algorithm which is used to perform ;condition-enrichment analyses. GemmaDE takes a DE gene list of interest as input and outputs ranked scores of all condition comparisons within the database, based on their relevance to the hit-list. In this project, I plan to apply the GemmaDE algorithm to all DE datasets in Gemma to examine relationships between the different conditions within the database. These relationships will be conceptualized as a condition-similarity network. I expect that datasets with similar patterns of differential expression will cluster closer together, providing insights into modules of gene regulation among different biological conditions. This network will be compared to a semantic similarity network, based on how different condition terms from the Gemma ontology are related to each other, and will identify modules of conditions. By analyzing modules of gene expression and conditions at the genomic level, I hope to gain insights into gene regulatory behaviours shared and contrasted by different biological conditions.

column36: Randomized, Double-Blinded, Placebo-Controlled Study Evaluating Vortioxetine for Cognitive Deficits in Persons with Post-COVID-19 Condition
column37: Since the declaration of the COVID-19 pandemic by the World Health Organization, over 259 million people have tested positive for COVID-19. A notable percentage of individuals who were previously infected with COVID-19 continue to experience persisting and functionally impairing symptoms, which have collectively been identified as ;post COVID-19 condition. Anhedonia (inability to experience pleasure) and impaired reward function (inability to experience reward) are common symptoms of post COVID-19 condition, which also have a negative impact on quality of life.Currently, no treatment options exist to treat the foregoing symptoms of post COVID-19 condition. As such, my project aims to evaluate the effectiveness of vortioxetine, a Health Canada-approved antidepressant, in treating anhedonia and reward function among persons with post COVID-19 condition. In this 8-week randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled clinical trial, participants will receive 10-20mg of the study medication (i.e., placebo or vortioxetine). Clinical assessments and questionnaires will be administered, and changes in those outcomes will be analyzed. Results from this study may increase treatment options for post COVID-19, as well as further our knowledge about COVID-19 and its long-term impacts on human health and health systems.

column36: Consequences cardiorespiratoires du stress psychosocial chez le rat adulte : nouvelles perspectives sur les origines de l'apnee du sommeil.
column37: L'apnee du sommeil (AS) touche pres de 26 % des Canadiens. L'AS affecte 2,5 fois plus les hommes que les femmes et est donc percue comme une << maladie d'homme >>. Par consequent, les femmes sont souvent exclues des etudes cliniques et mal diagnostiquees. L'AS fait reference a des arrets de la respiration a plusieurs reprises durant le sommeil. La suffocation resultant de ces apnees peut etre causee par le blocage des voies respiratoires lorsque les muscles de la gorge se relachent durant le sommeil et empeche le passage de l'air. Cependant, pour 56% des patients souffrant d'AS, l'origine du probleme vient d'un dysfonctionnement des neurones qui gerent la respiration et controlent les voies respiratoires. Le stress est a l'origine de nombreuses maladies, incluant l'hypertension, l'obesite, et la depression, des comorbidites frequentes de l'AS. Le cerveau etant une cible majeure du stress, mon projet explore l'idee qu'une exposition prolongee a un stress augmente les apnees pendant le sommeil. Inspiree par les consequences de la COVID-19 sur la sante physique et mentale, et de nombreuses etudes demontrant qu'etre prive de contacts sociaux augmente le stress, je propose d'utiliser l'isolement social (IS) comme stress chronique chez le rat. J'evaluerais les differentes consequences cardiorespiratoires de l'IS chez les males et les femelles et comprendrais les mecanismes neurologiques de l'IS. Je souhaite determiner quels groupes de neurones affectent la fonction respiratoire et si ceux-ci sont differents chez le male et la femelle. Notre approche implique de nouvelles hypotheses quant au fonctionnement de la maladie et considere l'importance du sexe, ce qui est necessaire au developpement de traitements cibles qui tiennent compte des particularites des populations.

column36: Linking choline metabolism to macrophage metabolic reprogramming
column37: Choline is an essential nutrient that provides a critical precursor for membrane phospholipids, the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, and methyl groups for epigenetic regulation. In innate immune cells called macrophages, choline is needed for lipid homeostasis and proper inflammatory responses. When choline uptake and metabolism are blocked, both pro-and anti-inflammatory programs are dysregulated. In an in vitro model meant to mimic a pro-inflammatory environment, stimulation of macrophages with the bacterial cell membrane component lipopolysaccharide (LPS) causes a heightened pro-inflammatory response. We have evidence that this pro-inflammatory shift is accompanied by a dramatic shift toward glycolytic metabolism. Importantly, given the metabolic and phenotypic switch, an acute infection may be a context in which the inhibition of choline metabolism could benefit host survival. Current findings suggest that choline metabolism inhibition can skew the immune population in vivo. The drug RSM-932a (RSM) inhibits the first step in the metabolism of choline toward phospholipid and causes a significant increase in pro-inflammatory markers. These findings suggest that choline inhibition could help skew an in-vivo response that would increase survival during acute bacterial infection. This proposal aims to test the hypothesis that the inhibition of choline metabolism and the subsequent pro-inflammatory immune response will increase survival outcomes in models of acute bacterial infection. We hypothesize that choline inhibition affects pro-inflammatory outputs and markers by reprogramming metabolic energy pathways. The goals of this study are to uncover if and understand how the inhibition of choline metabolism can increase survival in the face of a bacterial challenge.

column36: Generation of a Novel Foreskin-Microbiome Co-culture Model for Study of Polymicrobial Community effects on HIV Susceptibility
column37: The genital microbiome is emerging as a novel risk factor for HIV acquisition. The penile microbiome is a diverse continuum of aerobic, facultative and strictly anaerobic bacteria. Within this continuum, we identified 6 strict anaerobic species uniquely associated with increased HIV risk, production of inflammatory cytokines and recruitment of HIV target cells to the foreskin. We named this group Bacteria Associated with Seroconversion and Immune Cells (BASIC). Because the BASIC species strongly co-occur, in vitro work is needed to elucidate specific foreskin-microbe interactions that drive risk. Previous in vitro models use submerged cell lines, failing to provide an accurate environment for culture of skin microbes. Our proposed research will overcome this limitation by generating a novel foreskin-microbiome co-culture model that stably supports penile anaerobe growth. We recently developed a 3D organotypic foreskin model using primary adult cells to generate tissues with dermal and mature epidermal layers, providing an ideal surface for bacterial co-culture. We will now extend this model by establishing optimal inoculum size, pH and O for stable growth of polymicrobial communities and viability of foreskin tissue. Recapitulation of immune responses will be shown by quantification of epithelial cytokine production in the presence of a high-risk community, comprised of BASIC species, and a low-risk community of penile anaerobes unrelated to HIV risk. This work is foundational to understanding the biological mechanisms by which specific penile anaerobes cause local inflammation and HIV target cell recruitment. Furthermore, it paves the way for the development of novel preventative treatments that exclusively target microbial drivers of HIV risk.

column36: Creating a cell culture model to study the mechanisms of chemotherapy-induced myosteatosis
column37: Cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy lose muscle mass. This often occurs concurrently with a pathological deposition of fat into the muscle, a condition known as myosteatosis. Muscle loss and myosteatosis each predict poorer outcomes and reduced survival in cancer patients. Cancer related myosteatosis is proposed to result from an imbalance in fatty acids uptake/utilization, which may involve mitochondria. Dr. Mazuraks research group revealed that eicosapentaenoic and docosahexaenoic acids (EPA+DHA) in fish oil attenuate muscle loss and myosteatosis in advanced cancer patients and a preclinical animal model of cancer.We aim to study the mechanisms driving cancer related myosteatosis. My research project consists of two parts: creation of a skeletal muscle cell culture model for myosteatosis, and exploring myosteatosis mechanisms with different cell environment conditions using this model. We will first purify stem cells from a human muscle biopsy to establish the primary cell model. After growing these stem cells into muscle cells, we will induce myosteatosis by adding plasma from colorectal cancer patients with or without chemotherapy to the cells. We will also add EPA+DHA to the cell media to confirm that myosteatosis is reduced. Validating this model enables further study of myosteatosis mechanisms using combinations of tumor cells, anti-neoplastic therapies and nutrients. Of these mechanisms, we will focus on: fatty acid uptake by muscle cells and mitochondria; mitochondrial capacity to use fatty acids to produce energy; and fatty acid synthesis.Revealing the mechanism by which EPA+DHA protects muscle cells from myosteatosis may provide insights leading to strategies to prevent myosteatosis in cancer patients, improving their survival and quality of life.

column37: Skeletal muscle is important for supporting our normal daily activities through maintaining posture and allowing movement. It also helps to regulate blood sugar in our bodies, and when muscles are damaged, this can contribute to diseases like diabetes. Interestingly, our gene of interest, B-cell lymphoma 6 (Bcl6) has been found in skeletal muscle but its role in this tissue is entirely unknown. At the same time, Bcl6 may play an important role in muscle growth and function. Thus, we will use a mouse model with Bcl6 deleted specifically in their muscles to better understand what role Bcl6 plays in muscle. The results of our research study could potentially lead to the development of new strategies to treat diabetes and muscle diseases.

column36: What Helps and Hinders the Integration of Yoga Therapeutics Within Psychotherapy: A Delphi Study
column37: The topic under investigation is the holistic integration of yoga within Western approaches to psychotherapy. While vast amounts of research exist supporting the benefits of yoga for overall biopsychosocial-spiritual well-being, research is limited as it pertains to educating therapists, operating in a Western healthcare system, on how to bring yoga practices, principles, and philosophy into therapy. This study aims to understand what has facilitated the yoga-psychotherapy integration process for therapists with formal yoga training. The findings can be extrapolated to create future educational programming geared towards expediting and streamlining the integration process for therapists with little or no yogic background, which would increase the accessibility and applicability of this treatment modality for an enlarged number of clinicians. Within todays Western healthcare system, there exists a mind-body dilemma, wherein mind and body are treated as separate entities. However, complex conditions with medically unexplained symptoms such as idiopathic pain syndromes and anxiety disorders clearly demonstrate the intertwining nature of emotion and embodiment. Yoga psychotherapy is known to offer a therapeutic bridge between mind and body, effectively overcoming this inherent dilemma of westernized healthcare. In an effort to cater to clients seeking embodiment psychotherapy for diverse healthcare needs, Western healthcare must broaden its scope to include holistic approaches to therapy. However, this can only be safely and ethically accomplished if therapists are provided with the necessary educational training that equips them to apply integrated yoga-psychotherapy. For this reason, research capable of outlining the details of the integration process is imperative.

column36: The absorption, accumulation, and tissue distribution of orally administered pure oxylipins in a rat model
column37: Inflammation is the immune systems response to foreign bodies, where if dysregulated can lead to chronic inflammation playing a major role in numerous diseases including cancer, metabolic syndromes, and cardiovascular disorders. Anti-inflammatory drugs, such as Ibuprofen, are often used as a first line treatment by targeting inflammatory mediators during the onset of inflammation. However, prolonged use of these drugs is associated with unwanted side-effects calling for new treatment strategies. Recently, attention has shifted towards the active resolution of inflammation, performed by a unique family of lipid mediators called specialized pro-resolving mediators (SPMs). SPMs are normally produced in the body and act as key players working against inflammation. This led to the development of SPM supplements, aiming to aid in the reduction of inflammation. However, a growing market of these SPM supplements has raised several questions including whether SPMs are in fact absorbed after oral consumption. The intestinal lining serves as a selective filter, facilitating uptake of nutrients and fluids from the diet, while preventing the absorption of unwanted substances. To date there is no literature supporting the absorption of SPMs from the supplements into the circulation where they are effective. Therefore, my research will test if SPMs are absorbed, accumulated, and distributed to tissues upon oral administration in a rat model. Moreover, my future work will investigate the ability of dietary supplemented SPM to reach a site of active inflammation and induce resolution. This project will largely contribute to the growing research on new strategies to tackle inflammatory diseases and the use of SPMs as home remedies and clinical complementary therapies.

column36: Identification of the Immunological Mechanisms that Regulate SARS-CoV-2 Vaccine Durability
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has resulted in over 250 million cases and over five million deaths worldwide. To combat the global crisis, large-scale vaccination efforts have expedited and redefined the timeline for vaccine rollout. Despite the initially high rates of vaccine efficacy (~95% against the alpha variant) following full-vaccination (two doses), many individuals remain at risk, regardless of vaccination status. Instances of fully vaccinated individuals contracting SARS-CoV-2 are often referred to as Breakthrough Cases. Recent data from the Center for Disease Control (CDC) suggests that the elderly (80 years), immunocompromised, and individuals with underlying health conditions are at the greatest risk of a breakthrough infection. The underlying mechanisms of breakthrough cases are currently unknown, and therefore, are the central focus of my research proposal.Gaps exist in our understanding of the immunological mechanisms involved in long-term vaccine induced immunity, particularly in pertinence to breakthrough infections and in at-risk groups. Therefore, I propose to explore levels of antibody (humoral) and T cell mediated (cellular immunological) SARS-CoV-2 immune responses in a fully-vaccinated, elderly Nova Scotian population (80 years) and a cohort with BMI 30 and Type II Diabetes. We will isolate PBMCs to compare virus reactive CD8+ memory T cells expressing activation markers as well as developing ELISA assays targeted at S-specific IgG and IgA, angiotensin converting enzyme 2 (ACE2), and pseudovirus neutralization from SARS-CoV-2 alpha, delta, and omicron variants and other newly emerging variants of concern. Results will be used to develop a rapid diagnostic test to identify individuals who have maintained vaccine-induced immunity.

column36: A Biomechanical Analysis of Posture and Static Balance in Patients with Acromegaly
column37: Acromegaly is a chronic endocrine condition characterized by excess secretion of growth hormone (GH), most often due to a non-cancerous tumour of the anterior pituitary gland, and subsequent overproduction of insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1). Acromegaly impairs the function of multiple systems within the body leading to numerous complications. A frequent complication of acromegaly is acromegalic arthropathy (AA), which results from GH- and IGF-1-mediated changes to cartilage and soft-tissue within and surrounding a joint. AA progresses during the time that GH and IGF-1 are in excess and is largely irreversible in patients with long-term control of GH and IGF-1 levels. AA adversely affects physical function, psychological well-being, and quality of life. Treatment of AA has been neglected in the literature, and the absence of specific treatment guidelines for AA means that clinicians often resort to osteoarthritis (OA) treatments to manage AA despite notable differences between OA and AA. In order to develop treatments for AA, such as orthoses or physical therapy programs, it is crucial that the postural alignment and body mechanics of patients with acromegaly are clearly defined. Few studies have examined the posture and static balance of patients with acromegaly using gold-standard instrumentation such as motion capture systems and force platforms, and no previous study has combined kinematic motion capture data with kinetic force platform measurements. The proposed study will be a novel kinematic and kinetic analysis of quiet standing in patients with acromegaly with the aim of enhancing the clinical understanding of posture and static balance deficits in this population and informing the future development of treatments to reduce the debilitating effects of AA.

column36: Impact des traitements de la leucemie de l'enfant et de la diete sur la genese des complications cardiometaboliques dans un modele murin xenogenique
column37: Le taux de survie a 5 ans de la leucemie lymphoblastique aigue (LLA) de l'enfant depasse maintenant 90%. Cependant, les survivants ont un risque accru de developper des effets secondaires a long terme. Parmi ceux-ci, on retrouve des complications cardiometaboliques comme les dyslipidemies et la resistance a l'insuline. Les causes precises de ces dereglements demeurent inconnues, mais nous pensons que la chimiotherapie amene des changements au niveau des bacteries intestinales (microbiote) causant une inflammation chronique. La leucemie en soi pourrait aussi contribuer a l'apparition des complications metaboliques en causant de l'inflammation. L'impact de la diete, importante dans le developpement de plusieurs maladies cardiometaboliques, pourrait aussi contribuer a ces problemes de sante a long terme. Puisque les traitements de chimiotherapie pour la leucemie combinent plusieurs medicaments, l'utilisation d'un modele animal est necessaire pour isoler les effets de chacun. Nous utiliserons donc un modele de souris nous permettant de reproduire la leucemie humaine et d'etudier les effets secondaires a long terme. Les animaux seront traites avec un agent chimiotherapeutique et recevront ou non une diete riche en gras et en sucre. Nous verifierons l'impact, 4 semaines apres la fin des traitements, de la leucemie, des traitements et de la diete sur l'intolerance au glucose, la dyslipidemie, l'inflammation, le stress oxydant et sur les bacteries intestinales. Ce projet contribuera a mieux comprendre l'impact de la leucemie, des traitements et de la diete sur la sante des survivants de la LLA de l'enfant et de developper des interventions pour prevenir les complications a long terme.

column36: Exploiting microtubule-dependent DNA double-strand break repair to target BRCA1-deficient breast cancer
column37: Two major pathways cells use to repair DNA double-strand breaks (DSB) are homologous recombination (HR) and non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). BRCA1 steers cells toward HR and mutations in BRCA1 increase the likelihood of breast cancer. Additionally, a common feature of cancer cells is an abundance of invaginations of the nuclear envelope (NE). Preliminary data from our laboratory suggest that NE invaginations play a role in DSB repair. Upon the induction of DSB, a network of NE invaginations called nano nuclear envelope tubules (nanoNET) localize to sites rich in NHEJ proteins. nanoNET is driven by the kinesin KIF5B and limited by KIFC3, both of which travel along microtubules in opposite directions. Interestingly, breast cancers demonstrate highly invaginated nuclei, upregulation of KIF5B, downregulation of KIFC3, and BRCA1-deficient breast cancer cells are reliant on NHEJ. Therefore, we hypothesize that BRCA1-deficient cells benefit from DSB repair by nanoNET that is promoted by KIF5B and limited by KIFC3, which can be exploited to restrain BRCA1-deficient cell survival and tumor growth. We will use BRCA1-deficient human breast cancer models with KIF5B and KIFC3 knockdown (KD) in both in vitro and in vivo systems to determine if (1) the inhibition of nanoNET limits faithful DSB repair in BRCA1-deficient cells and (2) the promotion of nanoNET can enhance the synthetic lethality of PARP inhibitors and BRCA1-deficiency. 3D microscopy techniques will be used to capture the effect of the KIF KD on nanoNET formation. This work has the potential to not only elucidate a functional role of NE invaginations in genome stability but can also reveal avenues to maximize the therapeutic efficacy of chemotherapeutic drugs to better target BRCA1-deficient breast cancers.

column36: Investigating the role of a novel microtubule associating protein in cerebellar morphogenesis
column37: The cerebellum is a structure located at the back of the brain and it regulates the integration and processing of sensory and motor information. Structurally, the cerebellum is relatively simple, comprised of three distinct cell layers, each populated with unique cell types. While its organization is relatively simple, the cerebellum maintains a large degree of functional complexity due to its dense cellular packing and extensive network of connections. For instance, while accounting for ~10% of the brains mass, the cerebellum contains ~80% of the neurons in the brain. The generation of this dense anatomical organization requires careful control of developmental processes to ensure the proper migration and positioning of cells, many of which remain undiscovered. For cells to get from their birthplace to their destination they rely on the cytoskeleton, which acts as a set of molecular train tracks to get the cargo (cells) to their destination (respective cerebellar layer). When cells are displaced from their appropriate destination due to disruptions in cytoskeletal elements, developmental disorders may arise, as seen in patients with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) as well as in cases of medulloblastoma, the most common cancerous brain tumor in children. Thus, it is extremely important to gain a better understanding of the various mechanisms by which these migratory cells in the cerebellum achieve their proper positioning and allow for such complex neuronal circuitry to form. For the proposed study, I will investigate the role of a novel neural-specific cytoskeletal regulator in the formation of the cerebellum. The results obtained from this study will provide insight into the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental disorders of the cerebellum.

column36: Hip Contact Forces and Muscle Contributions in Young Adults with Femoroacetabular Impingement
column37: Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) is a disorder caused by extra bone growth on the femur, pelvis, or both. The extra bone can result in pain, decreased function, and negatively impact quality of life. People with FAI are at risk of injury to the soft tissues of the hip and osteoarthritis. Previous research has shown that FAI patients start having symptoms when forces within the hip joint increase, known as hip contact forces. FAI can be treated non-surgically by altering movement patterns and muscle strengthening. However, there is a lack of clinical biomechanical data (i.e., hip contact forces and muscle contributions), that clinicians require to make evidence-based treatment decisions. In addition, studies that have examined these variables only included males with extra bone growth on their femurs. This research will examine how FAI-types and sex influence movement patterns and hip contact forces. This study will include male and female FAI patients between the ages of 16 and 40. FAI patients will be compared to healthy individuals without any hip disorder. A survey will be used to assess the participants' current hip symptoms and function. The participants will have their motion analyzed while performing a deep squat and side-lunge task. The participants' joint angles, forces, and muscle activation data will be used to create computer models. The models are used to calculate hip contact forces. This information will be translated to clinicians allowing them to develop FAI treatments specific to patients' sex. Ultimately, this will reduce symptoms and improve function, allowing FAI patients to maintain their physical activity participation and help prevent osteoarthritis.

column36: Smooth Muscle Cell Contribution to Atherosclerosis Susceptibility in Familial Hypercholesterolemia

Key predictors of atherosclerosis risk identified in these gene analyses will then be tested in gene manipulation studies to see their effect on cell functions including their ability to cope with excess cholesterol.OUTCOMES: This study will identify SMC-related genes that are directly involved in the development of atherosclerosis. column36: Substance Misuse and the Pandemic: A Qualitative Study of BC Paramedics' Attitudes and Interactions with Overdose Patients During COVID-19
column37: Deaths attributed to illicit substance misuse have increased exponentially during the COVID-19 pandemic.This drastic spike in deaths has largely been attributed to accidental overdoses of the potent synthetic opioid, fentanyl.Non-fatal overdoses have also increased during the COVID-19 pandemic. From June to August 2021, there were approximately 7,500 overdose calls throughout British Columbia. This marked the highest number of overdose calls ever recorded in a three-month stretch by BC Emergency Health Services (EHS). Given the rise in overdoses, the delivery of overdose care has become a significant part of service for paramedics in British Columbia. Yet to date, no study has investigated the experiences of BC paramedics who have responded to overdose calls during the pandemic, and how those experiences may impact the care they are able to provide to illicit drug users. This research will examine how the increase in overdose calls has impacted paramedics attitudes and interactions towards those who misuse illicit substances. BC Paramedics will be interviewed about their experiences serving overdose calls during the Covid-19 pandemic. A Reflexive Thematic Analysis will be used to identify common patterns in participant narratives. It is hypothesized that that paramedics will report common themes of disillusionment, burnout, compassion fatigue, and helplessness in response to the influx of overdose calls. Results of this study may be used to guide future quantitative research in this area. Additionally, results of this study may help to inform public policies and initiatives which could improve responses to overdose calls, and guide the creation of training and procedures for paramedics to better handle substance and addiction-related calls.

column36: A Multicomponent Intervention for Improving Hydration for Residents with Swallowing Difficulties in Long-Term Care
column37: Hydration is essential for health at all ages, and the consequences of dehydration are serious. Dehydration is a particularly common issue in individuals with dementia living in long-term care (LTC).Currently, ~500,000 Canadians live with dementia and this number is set to exceed 900,000 by 2030. I will determine if a multi-part therapy can improve fluid intake by addressing the various factors contributing to dehydration in this vulnerable population. The therapy will consist of behaviour change strategies; an increase in the variety of beverages offered; a protocol to encourage fluid consumption during and between meals; and staff education. Over the course of three months, 10 individuals who are drinking thickened liquids for dysphagia will participate in this pilot study. I will then determine if fluid intake increases as compared to before the therapy. The findings from this study will guide institutional and clinical decision making and will provide strategies needed to avoid the harmful effects of dehydration in LTC residents who are prescribed thickened liquids.
