column36: Environmental exposures in Canadian urban areas and incident breast cancer in young women
column37: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in Canadian women, and a leading cause of death in young women. There are several established risk factors for breast cancer including reproductive history, physical activity, alcohol consumption, and diet. Environmental exposures are recognized to play a role on the development of breast cancer, but their impacts are less understood. Emerging evidence suggests that several environmental exposures contribute to sociodemographic disparities in breast cancer incidence. For example, urban areas that are more walkable and provide access to green spaces may contribute to lower breast cancer rates by promoting physical activity. On the other hand, some studies have shown that exposure to traffic-related air pollution, and outdoor light at night increase the risk of breast cancer. Our proposed research will study how environmental features of where we live, namely, walkable neighbourhoods, access to green spaces, air pollution, and light at night impact the risk of developing breast cancer in young women. We will address our research objectives using previously collected data from the Ontario Environmental Health Study (OEHS), and environmental exposure data from CANUE that are linkable participants' residential addresses. The OEHS collected questionnaire data from 216 women diagnosed with breast cancer and 414 healthy controls. These data include information on breast cancer risk factors including physical activity, alcohol consumption, and reproductive history. We will use statistical models to describe the associations between these environmental exposures and the risk of breast cancer. We will also evaluate whether these associations vary based on the timing of the exposure, and by sociodemographic status. Findings from this study will fill knowledge gaps on how environmental exposures in urban areas impact the health of women, and inform urban planning policies and interventions designe to reduce harm.

column36: Preparing cities for climate change
column37: Climate change is unevenly impacting different populations and locations. For example, Edmonton, Alberta, experiences extreme weather events and poor air quality (from wildfire events and local sources) related to climate change. These climate change-induced health risks are higher for the growing population of older adults and immigrants, which are worsen by factors like social isolation and societal inequities. As such, actions involving collaboration from different fields of science, government, communities, and organizations are necessary. A critical step toward climate change action is generating information for planning and policies that consider locally affected populations and regional differences. We aim to further develop and expand on a previously created climate change and health vulnerability index for Edmonton. These are necessary steps to help inform equitable interventions based on implementation science research. The project builds on this pilot study work that identified critical factors such as location, population demographics, community characteristics, and social factors contributing to climate change and health vulnerability. Investigating factors that can affect urban mitigation and adaptation measures is key for lowering risks and building resilience across affected populations. Specifically, this study considers the use of indices for informing equitable climate change and health policies and programs. In addition, it increases the involvement and options available to higher-risk groups like older adults and immigrant communities. It also promotes equity-based implementation science and can be tool for assessing interventions. The team has expertise in several different areas and has built strong relationships with the City of Edmonton and older adult and immigrant communities to facilitate this work. We aim to promote healthy cities while including equity in the design of climate change and health mitigation and adaptation strategies.

column36: Towards Data Symmetry for a Balanced Understanding of Canadian residential housing radon gas exposure
column37: 1 in 5 lung cancers arise in Canadians who have never smoked, with ~110,000 cases since 2001. The most common lung cancer trigger in never-smokers is inhalation of radioactive radon gas. The amount of life spent 'at home' correlates with radon exposure, modifying lung cancer risk. Regrettably, Canadian construction practices of the past century have produced urban residential environments with buildings that capture, contain, and concentrate radon to unnatural and unsafe levels. Globally, Canadians are among the most radon-exposed people, this is worsening still. Our team has studied the relationship between radon and region, property metrics, as well as human behaviour. In this project we will place into context our detailed understanding of radon exposure as a function of building features and people, with the most recently understood diversity of properties and demographics of the Canadian population. The GOAL of this project is to place the most up to date residential radon gas exposure data available within the context of the most recently understood Canadian housing, health and population information. This 'data symmetry' is needed to inform physical, social and policy interventions required to reduce lung cancer risk attributable to radon inhalation within the urban built environment. The critical IMPACTS of this work will be to: (1) generate reliable measures of residential radon exposure risk in Canada that are sensitive to regional differences, and (2) to develop a clear understanding of the scale and scope of the health consequences of radon exposure, to inform the need for action. By doing this we will advance health outcomes by developing actionable, well-informed knowledge of radon exposure and lung cancer risk, and use this to address one of the most prevalent built environment-based health threats to our future cities.

column36: Precise Treatment for Pediatric Diabetes: Providing the right care, for the right patient, at the right time, over time
column37: Diabetes is one of the most common life-long diseases affecting children. Many children living with diabetes use glucose sensors that measure sugar levels every 1-5 minutes and insulin pumps that deliver insulin via a small catheter under the skin. Information coming from these technologies help kids and families and their healthcare providers treat their diabetes but, this information is usually located in different online places. The lack of 'one trusted place' to see all this important information prevents patients/parents from using data to manage their diabetes and makes it harder for healthcare providers to provide the right care to the right patient at the right time, especially as kids' bodies and minds change as they grow and mature. TrustSphere is a new digital tool that will solve the problem of health information and data in different places, letting us use data to deliver better diabetes care. Patients and families, and their healthcare providers can see important diabetes information, like blood sugars and insulin doses streaming from glucose sensors and insulin pumps, or recommendations from the diabetes team, in one place. TrustSphere's first version has been developed and will be tested with 50 children at the BC Children's Hospital (BCCH) Diabetes Clinic. In this proposal, we will expand TrustSphere's capability by collecting more data from patients such as their healthy living behaviours, diabetes self-management behaviours, quality of life and mental health, and combine these data with glucose sensor and pump data to better understand differences between groups of patients. With patients and families we will co-create personalized and tailored care experiences and use advanced methods to analyze data like machine learning to navigate patients and families to the care they need, when they need it. Our goal is to create a collaborative care experience, improve diabetes self-management, and ultimately improve patient experience and outcomes.

column36: Accelerating Clinical Trials (ACT) - Canada
column37: We have established the Accelerating Clinical Trials (ACT) Consortium to strengthen the conduct of clinical trials in Canada. ACT brings together hundreds of researchers from 28 networks, 11 trial units, from Nova Scotia to British Columbia and Nunavut. ACT will support and expand existing networks and enable the creation of new networks to improve the efficiency, number, and quality of trials conducted in Canada. ACT will increase the impact of clinical trials in Canada: ACT will lead collaboration, coordination, and resource-sharing across networks to enable Canada's best researchers and companies to more efficiently complete high-quality, high-impact clinical trials. ACT will build clinical trial capacity: ACT will provide trial units with the knowledge, skills, and experience to conduct large-scale trials. We will streamline administrative processes (for example, ethics reviews, contracts, and protocols) to accelerate timelines and reduce costs. We will expand Canadian networks internationally. ACT will maximize research impact and knowledge mobilization: ACT will follow best practices in patient-oriented research and integrated knowledge translation. We will leverage national and international contacts to maximize research impact and knowledge mobilization. Advance equitable access to trials for Canadians: ACT will follow the principles of equity, diversity, and inclusion in clinical trials such that the knowledge gained is applicable to all those affected. Many trials will be embedded into routine healthcare, enabling the inclusion of all patients regardless of ethnicity, gender, or socioeconomic status. Conclusion: The ACT consortium has the expertise and vision to increase the conduct of inclusive, cost-efficient, high-quality, high-impact clinical trials in Canada. We will help Canadian researchers accelerate the management and prevention of chronic diseases and to respond rapidly to new health threats and pandemics.

column36: Leveraging biological sex and genetics for beta cell-directed precision medicine in type 1 diabetes
column37: Type 1 diabetes (T1D) affects >300,000 Canadians. An underappreciated factor that raises the risk of T1D is whether an individual is a man or woman. Men have an 80% higher risk of developing T1D (age 15-34). While lifestyle factors contribute to this increased T1D risk in men, studies in animal models show biological sex also plays a key role. Unfortunately, we do not fully understand why males are at a higher risk of T1D because most research does not include both sexes. In T1D, the immune system destroys beta cells, which make insulin. To develop better T1D treatments, we need more information on why the immune system attacks beta cells. Recent studies point to beta cell problems and changes to the insulin gene as contributing factors to T1D. Because beta cells make huge amounts of insulin, which causes stress, even small changes in the cell's ability to make insulin tip beta cells into an unhealthy state and lead to immune system attack. Our team has evidence that male and female beta cells differ in their ability to make insulin, and to stay healthy despite the stress of insulin production. Our goal is to test whether sex differences in beta cells affect the sex-biased T1D risk. We will interfere with specific steps of insulin production and quality control in human beta cells and mice to see whether beta cell health is affected in either males or females. This information will help scientists to match males and females with appropriate T1D therapies.

column36: Priority Setting Partnership: Musculoskeletal Conditions and Obesity Research Priorities in Canada
column37: The purpose of this proposal is to bring together people to shape the future of obesity research to inform a national obesity care framework that includes musculoskeletal (MSK) conditions. It will include individuals living with obesity and MSK conditions who could benefit from obesity care and those participating in obesity care (across the continuum of care, including medical treatment), scientists and others such as health care service administrators and policy makers. This priority setting partnership (PSP) will be led by Obesity Canadas' (OC) Action Team on Research (AToR).This project will use a James Lind Alliance (JLA) protocol. The JLA is a non-profit initiative that brings together people with lived experience of accessing health care services, and health care professionals together in a PSP. The PSP will identify and prioritize gaps in evidence or unanswered questions that participants agree are the most important for obesity care research. Obesity care is defined as services informed by evidence for the treatment and management of obesity, which is now understood to be a chronic disease. The goal of obesity care is to provide interventions that are effective in treatment of obesity and the secondary prevention and management of obesity related health conditions. We have decided to use a PSP to ensure that those who fund obesity research are aware of what really matters to people living with MSK conditions and obesity who are seeking/accessing or would benefit from obesity care, as well as their caregivers and health care professionals. This project represents the first time that people with lived experience of accessing care for obesity or those who would benefit from access to obesity care, clinicians and scientists have worked in partnership to determine the research priorities to inform a national obesity care framework.

column37: Type 1 diabetes is a complex and challenging health condition involving many factors. Individual differences, including genetics, metabolism, environment, mental health, and social factors, play a role in how well diabetes is managed. Our research shows disparities between persons with diabetes, where those of lower household income or ethnic minority groups have a much lower rate of meeting recommended glucose or A1c targets when compared with the larger clinic. Elevated glucose levels negatively impact mental health and increase the risk of future diabetes-related complications. If we want to improve care and eliminate disparities, we need to better understand how specific genetic, psychological, environmental, and social factors drive disparities in diabetes outcomes. This research project will use a personalized approach to diabetes care at the Hospital for Sick Children and other regional practices. This study will address the disparities in diabetes outcomes by: 1) securely collecting information about a person's genetics, biology, race, sex, gender, income, family structure, and mental health, and analyzing how these factors impact the management of a person's diabetes using artificial intelligence; 2) conducting interviews with persons with diabetes and their families to explore experiences and barriers faced when receiving care, especially by marginalized groups, and use this feedback to design and implement inclusive and appropriate changes to care, and 3) developing personalized treatment strategies that take into consideration individual genetic, environmental, and social factors to determine optimal treatment options using diabetes technology. The goal of this study is to create new knowledge on how differences in genes, environment, and social factors contribute to differences in type 1 diabetes management and develop ways to improve outcomes for all youth with type 1 diabetes.

column36: Thinking Qualitatively: Doing Intersectionality - a health-focused knowledge exchange
column37: Qualitative researchers in health and social science fields have increasingly adopted an intersectional approach that foregrounds the interactive effects of race, gender, sexuality, class, and other social relations. Intersectional research addresses health equality by illuminating interlocking forms of oppression and identifying context-specific solutions to health disparities. However, deeper engagement with intersectionality as an analytic framework is needed if this body of research is to have robust and effective outcomes. It is imperative to advance knowledge in the "doing" of intersectional qualitative research, and to support and prepare the next generation of diverse health scholars for this complex work. Thinking Qualitatively: Doing Intersectionality (TQ:DI) addresses this need through a virtual four-day learning and knowledge exchange event (spring 2023). TQ:DI brings together 150 pre/early career scholars and 15 mid-career and senior scholars. Part I (Days 1 & 2) will offer workshops for disseminating research and developing methodological knowledge. Part 2 (Days 3 & 4) will offer an intensive opportunity for research-sharing, knowledge development, and mentoring among 32 new and 8 experienced intersectional health researchers. Senior scholars will pool their knowledge on the "state of the field" and effective mentoring, and new scholars will present and receive feedback on the oral and written presentation of their current intersectional qualitative health research projects. Across the four days, senior scholars will offer four public keynote addresses. TQ:DI will actively recruit scholars at all levels from Canada and internationally, and whose own careers are shaped by intersecting social identities. TQ:DI will result in deepened understanding of intersectionality and intersectional mentoring, a vibrant global network of diverse health scholars, and public lectures and an academic article advancing intersectional qualitative health research.

column36: Prize 202203PJT - The role of outer radial glia in human brain expansion and cortical malformation disorders.
column37: The extraordinary size and folded shape of the human brain makes us the smartest animal on earth. However, it also means many diseases that harm the human brain disrupt cells and structures that are not seen in other animals such as the mouse, and therefore cannot be adequately studied in these animal models. For example, human patients with cortical malformation disorders have brains that are too large or too small (macrocephaly, microcephaly), with too much or too little folding (polymicrogyria, lissencephaly). Mild forms of these cortical malformations occur in about 1% of all live births. Children born with these conditions have a significant higher chance of developing autism, epilepsy, and intellectual disability. These conditions are poorly understood because they are very difficult to model in the mice. It is now possible to study brain diseases directly in human cells that are grown in the dish. To do this, we use stem cells to make brain cells and 3-dimensional brain organoids. We recently showed that human-specific brain cells and structures can be studied using this approach. In this proposal, we will use these new models to investigate how mutations that are found in patients with cortical malformations impact the behaviors of brain stem cells in the dish. In particular, we will focus our attention on a special type of stem cells that are abundant in the human brain and are extremely rare in the mouse brain. These elusive stem cells may hold the key to understanding how the human brain grow so big, and why brain diseases are so hard to study in animal models. It is only with this understanding can we then develop strategies and medicine to treat these currently untreatable brain diseases.

column36: Prize 202203PJT - RYR2-targeted Gene Therapies for Treating Catecholaminergic Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia
column37: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT) is a form of electrical heart disease that is associated with a risk of sudden death. The majority of CPVT patients have an abnormality in the RYR2 gene, whose protein product plays an important role in directing the flow of calcium in heart cells. Treatment of CPVT primarily involves medications called betablockers, however many patients continue to have life-threatening heart arrhythmias despite taking their medication. The development of new genetic techniques carry the promise of more effective therapies for CPVT and potentially even a cure for this life-threatening condition. Individuals have 2 copies of every gene, however we have accumulated evidence that only 1 copy of the RyR2 gene may be necessary for health. We propose to evaluate large databases of both CPVT patients and healthy individuals in order to better clarify if 1 normal RYR2 copy is sufficient for normal heart function. In parallel, we are going to study the impact of deleting the abnormal functioning copy of the RYR2 gene in mice with CPVT using a genetic engineering technique called CRISPR. Our preliminary data involving modification of the abnormal copy of the RYR2 gene in embryos suggested that this approach is safe and also appeared to have effectively treated the condition when these mice grew into adulthood. Subsequent experiments involving injection of adult CPVT mice with CRISPR tools directed to enter heart cells using a virus also appear promising. In addition to this approach, we are also working with a biotechnology company that makes molecules (called ASOs) that reduce the amount of protein generated from the RYR2 gene. We anticipate that injection of RYR2 ASOs into adult CPVT mice will fix their electrical abnormalities. Should these goals be met, we believe our findings will provide the framework to work towards human clinical trials that may revolutionize treatment for CPVT.

column36: Prize 202203PJT - Novel mechanisms and therapeutic approach for aging-related pruritus
column37: ITCH: Itch is a debilitating symptom experienced by 40% of the elderly. Itch can have severe impact on quality of life, cause extreme stress and depression, and is the most common skin complaint in the elderly. Currently, many of the current therapeutic interventions for itch are not suitable for the elderly due to their adverse effects, pointing to an urgent medical need. GRANZYME B: Granzyme B is a protein that plays a key role in the body's normal immune response and is present at low levels in healthy individuals. However, our team has shown that high levels of active Granzyme B are found in the skin of the elderly and in patients with itchy, inflammatory skin diseases. Further, it has been demonstrated that Granzyme B levels in the blood are linked to multiple measures of itch severity. In an experimental model of aging skin, we have early evidence that suggests that inhibiting Granzyme B will prevent itch and inflammatory skin. Our team has also recently developed a new topical medication that can inhibit Granzyme B activity and reduce disease severity in experimental models of itchy skin diseases. PROPOSED PROJECT AND IMPACT: We will comprehensively investigate the relationship between Granzyme B levels and measures of itch using aging human skin specimens (collected with full informed consent). We will also use a newly-developed technology to discover unknown functions of Granzyme B in aging itchy skin. Finally, we will use experimental models of aging itchy skin to test the efficacy of our new topical medication in alleviating itch. Taken together, our findings will advance the development of our Granzyme B-targeting medication towards clinical approval and improving patient outcomes.

column36: Prize 202203PJT - The test-negative design for the estimation of COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness: design evaluation and development of statistical methods in the evolving context
column37: Fast research designs have been proposed for estimating how well different vaccines protect against disease, severe disease, hospitalization, and death from COVID-19. In fact, ongoing study is needed to evaluate different levels of vaccination (2 doses, boosters, different lags between doses, etc) in terms of how well they protect against illness, which may vary depending on the current circulation of virus variants. These fast designs typically involve identifying people who have been tested for COVID-19, often at a test-site or in a hospital. An established design is called the "test-negative design" which specifically involves identifying people who have symptoms associated with the disease in question and who then get tested. Scientists can estimate vaccine effectiveness by comparing people who test positive to people who test negative. If the negatives have higher rates of vaccination, this will indicate effectiveness of the vaccine. But, depending on how the design and statistical methods are applied, there may be bias in the estimation of effectiveness. Our research team has recently noted that, because of challenges of how test data are collected in our healthcare systems across Canada, the classical version of the test-negative design cannot always be applied. For example, some designs have used all test data, rather than only data from those who have certain symptoms. We are interested in evaluating how much bias can be caused by this difference in design, and identifying scenarios in which this can create misleading results. Secondly, we are interested in developing statistical methods that can address the limitations of the regression approach that is essentially the only one currently being used. We will identify limitations of current methods and propose new (or adapted) methods that can address these limitations. Our goal is to produce more reliable statistical methods so that we can improve our monitoring of the benefits of vaccination.

column36: Prize 202203PJT - The Toronto Disparities, Overdose, and Treatment (T-DOT) Study: Investigating clinical outcomes among people who inject drugs during a period of rapid programmatic and policy change
column37: Canada has the world's most rapidly accelerating overdose epidemic, with per capita mortality opioid overdose mortality increasing by 117% since 2016. Toronto is North America's fourth-largest city and the urban area with the highest level of income disparity in the country. In 2020, 823 people died of an overdose in Toronto, more than twice as many as in any other jurisdiction in Canada, and higher than those recorded in major American cities. The goal of the ongoing Toronto Disparities, Overdose and Treatment (T-DOT) study is to understand whether rapid implementation of new opioid agonist treatments and an impending drug decriminalization policy change are effective in reducing overdose risk among people who inject drugs who are experiencing severe socioeconomic disparities. To do that, the T-DOT study will link behavioral data collected over time from a cohort of people who inject drugs in Toronto with administrative datasets that include comprehensive clinical data from all Ontarians. This is important because currently, data from people who inject drugs about their treatment and other clinical experiences is almost always collected as self-report, making it difficult to confirm clinical outcomes. However, high-quality, comprehensive clinical data is needed to chart an evidence-based pathway to end the overdose epidemic in Canada and across North America, particularly for people who inject drugs experiencing socioeconomic disparities.

column36: Prize 202203PJT - An intersectional investigation of women's experiences of overlapping overdose and COVID-19 public health crises
column37: British Columbia (BC) continues to grapple with an overdose epidemic that has largely been framed as a men's public health crisis. Little has been said regarding how women (transgender, Two-Spirit and non-binary inclusive) are impacted, or how they might be differently navigating overdose risk environments or access to life-saving health services. Despite the implementation of a range of overdose prevention interventions, rising death rates in BC render the overdose epidemic a pressing public health issue compounded by the COVID-19 pandemic. Some sub-populations of marginalized women are not fully benefiting from current interventions, illustrating the need to better examine why. Women, in dynamic relationship with race, class and sexuality, are disproportionately impacted by social violence, which shapes health and overdose risk as well as access to and uptake of overdose prevention interventions. Emerging evidence indicates that women are more negatively impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic than men, exacerbating existing health inequities. Building upon our extensive experience in examining risk, harm, and health care access among women who use drugs, we are requesting funds to support a 4-year qualitative study addressing the following objectives: 1. To examine how intersecting social, structural, and environmental forces (including COVID-19) produce violence, shape women's overdose risk environments and contribute to differential outcomes across drug-using populations; 2. To examine the implementation of interventions to address overdose and COVID-19 health crises, including policy recommendations and their impacts on health-related outcomes; 3. To explore the experiences of women who use drugs in: the mitigation of overdose-related risk during the COVID-19 pandemic; engagement with overdose- and COVID-19-focused interventions; as well as factors that facilitate or impede their meaningful engagement in these activities during dual public health emergencies.

column36: Prize 202203PJT - Mechanisms of endogenous retrovirus-mediated antiviral immunity against genital herpes simplex virus 2 infection and disease.
column37: Herpes simplex virus 2 (HSV-2) is a sexually transmitted virus that affects over 500 million individuals worldwide. HSV-2 establishes a life-long infection with the host and causes lesions, pain, and discomfort in the female genital tract that persists for life. In addition, HSV-2 infection increases the risk of co-infection by HIV or hepatitis C virus as well as pathogenic bacteria that are responsible for bacterial vaginosis. Although the antiviral drug, acyclovir, is available, acyclovir needs to be taken as a daily five dose regimen for the duration of symptoms and does not prevent recurring symptoms. There are currently no vaccines available to treat HSV-2, in part due to inherent challenges associated with the development of mucosal vaccines. The goal of our project is to identify novel host mechanisms that boost antiviral responses against genital HSV-2 infection that will ameliorate the disease caused by this virus. My group recently found that viral sequences that are present in the genome of most eukaryotes called endogenous retroviruses (ERVs) are involved in the protection against genital HSV-2 infection in mice. Our project will build on this finding and will investigate the molecular interactions between ERVs and vaginal cells that mediates protection against genital HSV-2 infection and disease. We will achieve this using mouse models and human cells in combination with virology, immunology and bioinformatic techniques. This will allow us to identify new molecules that are involved in the protection against HSV-2 infection and disease that can further be targeted to boost antiviral responses in the female genital tract. Ultimately, our work will aid in the development of new host-directed antiviral therapies.

column36: Prize 202203PJT - Will the kids be alright? Leveraging a longitudinal Canadian youth cohort to study the course of depression and anxiety, and patterns of mental health help-seeking and service utilization
column37: With looming threats related to a rapidly changing economic landscape, along with individual, family, and pandemic stressors, Alberta can be a challenging place for youth to thrive. Thriving is particularly difficult in emerging adolescence, a period marked by significant biological and contextual change. Stress, disruptions, and change are predictors of mental distress, and research shows that youth depression and anxiety has doubled during the pandemic. Thus, it is critical to follow a current group of youth to determine if the observed pandemic increases in depression and anxiety still remain in the aftermath of the pandemic. To inform policy action, resource allocation, and mental health recovery efforts, it is also important to compare youth self-reports of depression and anxiety with their help-seeking behavior, service utilization, and prevalence of clinical diagnoses. Our study will provide this information. The All Our Families study is a pregnancy cohort in Calgary, Alberta that started in 2008 and has followed families over time. At the outset of the pandemic, when youth were age 10, we launched the Youth in All our Families Cohort to hear directly from youth about their experiences and well-being over the course of the pandemic. We now seek funding to continue to follow these youth into their adolescent years when they are ages 15 and 17. We will link cohort survey data to administrative mental health data (e.g., physician visits for mental health, emergency department visits, prescriptions) to identify the patterns of diagnoses and help-seeking behavior in the context of changing patterns of youth depression and anxiety. We also will identify the patterns of risk and protective factors related to youth depression and anxiety. Results emerging from this project can powerfully inform decision-making on resource allocation and prevention and intervention strategies to optimize youth mental health.

column36: Prize 202203PJT - IFN-alpha subtype specific effects on NK cells during HIV-1 infection
column37: HIV continues to be a worldwide pandemic, with approximately 37 million people living with the disease and roughly one million deaths annually. AIDS results from a progressive impairment of the immune system. Currently, the only effective means of treating HIV-1 involves the use of antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens that suppress viral replication, preventing AIDS, and thus extend patients' lives. Although ART reduces active viral replication it does not purge cells harboring the HIV reservoir and thus HIV patients must remain on costly lifelong treatment that does not fully restore lifespan or quality of life. Thus, developing new strategies to eliminate the HIV reservoir and cure the infection are a global priority. Our work is focussed on harnessing the effects of soluble antiviral immune mediators called interferon (IFN)-alpha subtypes to better treat viral infections such as HIV. Previously, one of these interferon subtypes, IFN-alpha2, was used to successfully treat Hepatitis C infection. We have found that a different interferon, IFN-alpha14, is significantly more potent than IFN-alpha2 at controlling HIV infection. Despite being most potent at controlling HIV infection, IFN-alpha14 is not naturally produced until very late in disease and in small amounts and thus HIV evades its potent effects during infection. We have found that IFN- alpha14 has an impact on the actions of a specific immune subset called Natural Killer (NK) cells. Natural killer cells are experts at finding and destroying virally infected cells and IFN-alpha14 appears to supercharge this immune subset to do that job better. Our work aims to understand how IFN-alpha14 specifically impacts the function of NK cells and then will use this knowledge to harness these effects and incorporate them into new therapeutic strategies to significantly reduce or even completely eliminate HIV infected cells from the body.

column36: Prize 202203PJT - Development and validation of the Global Adolescent and Child Physical Activity Questionnaire (GAC-PAQ): A multi-country study across six continents
column37: Physical activity is essential for healthy child development, yet 80% of youth are not active enough and we lack information about activity levels of young children. Current physical activity questionnaires were developed in high-income countries without considering the context of low-income countries. They tend to neglect some types of physical activity such as active play. Addressing these issues would make it easier to compare activity levels within and between countries. Such comparisons could help identify countries that are doing well in promoting some types of activity and help other countries develop interventions to increase physical activity. We will develop an app-based questionnaire and determine its accuracy in measuring physical activity among 5- to 17-year-olds in 14 low-, middle-, and high-income countries from 6 continents. Our second objective is to collect data on active play for the first time in many of these countries. Our study will involve 8 stages. First, we are completing a review of the pros and cons of current questionnaires. Next, we will develop a first draft of the new questionnaire and ask experts and lay people in the 14 countries to review it (stages 2-4). Based on these initial results, we will develop a new version of the questionnaire and translate it into the main languages of each country (stages 5-6). Next, we will do a pilot-study with 30 children and one of their parents in each country. Finally, we will do the main study with 500 children and parents per country. We will recruit participants in urban and rural areas that differ in wealth. We will compare our questionnaire data to a precise movement sensor ("accelerometer"). We expect that our new questionnaire will facilitate the measurement of physical activity globally. Our sample will be the largest and most diverse ever collected to assess the accuracy of such a questionnaire.

column36: Prize 202203PJT - NMR spectroscopy in brain organoids: identifying neurochemical and gene regulatory network signatures of the healthy and Alzheimer's Disease brain
column37: Recent innovations in neuroscience have led to the development of human-derived 'mini-brains', also known as cerebral organoids. These self-organizing, three-dimensional clusters of human brain tissue can grow to 2-3 mm in diameter, and accurately mimic many aspects of human brain development and physiology. Since they are derived from a patient, either their skin or blood, these mini-brains have the same genetic make-up as the patient. When derived from patients with neurological disease, derivative neurons in these mini-brains exhibit many of the pathological features of the disease. Thus, cerebral organoids are a valuable tool for disease research. In this project, we explore a new avenue for characterizing how the human brain changes in an Alzheimer's disease (AD) state using a novel set of tools that can look at how the chemistry and metabolism of the brain differ in those individuals with disease versus healthy individuals. We can then correlate this information to the cellular makeup, genetics, and function of these brain cells, which will provide new clues as to how genes influence the brain environment, its function and chemistry. Cerebral organoids will be derived from human participants who are undergoing healthy brain aging and show no signs of dementia, and from individuals who have been diagnosed with AD. We will then study these patient-derived brain organoids using our integrated platform to characterize biological and chemical changes that accompany healthy brain aging versus AD. The proposed research will identify imaging biomarkers of AD that will be translatable to human patients in the clinic. It will also establish a unique platform for understanding the mechanisms of healthy brain aging and for testing novel therapies against AD.

column36: Prize 202203PJT - The impact of retirement income programs on health and health equity among Canadian seniors
column37: In Canada, basic pension plans (Old Age Security program) are intended to alleviate poverty among seniors, while mandatory and voluntary retirement plans (Canadian/Quebec Pension Plan, employer pension plans, and private savings) are intended to maintain living standards throughout retirement. Canada's retirement system has been the subject of heated policy debate, as the rapid aging of the population poses significant fiscal challenges to the system's sustainability. Although increasing the eligibility age for retirement income programs (e.g., the Harper government's proposal to increase the eligibility age for the Old Age Security benefit from 65 to 67) may ease financial pressure on the system, it is essential to consider how existing retirement income programs impact health and inequalities in health among Canadian seniors prior to implementing such changes. Therefore, this project examines the impact of retirement income programs on the health of and health equity among Canadian seniors. This project has three main objectives: first, to evaluate how Canada's basic retirement income programs affect the health (health status, health behaviour, and healthcare use) of low-income seniors; second, to measure how retirement impacts the health of the former employed workers; and third, to investigate how the income redistribution facilitated by the Canadian retirement system affects income-related health inequalities among senior citizens. This comprehensive analysis of the retirement system will provide evidence relating to the effectiveness of the current programs, which can aid in the development of effective strategies for improving health and health equity among Canada's rapidly aging population.

column36: Banff Inflammation Workshop 2023
column37: Chronic inflammatory disorders seriously affect the quality of life of millions of Canadians and constitute a significant health system burden. Our knowledge of the underlying biological mechanisms of inflammatory diseases affecting our lungs, gastrointestinal tract, skin, joints and other systems is improving at a fast pace as researchers around the world begin to understand the interactions of our immune systems, genetics, environment and other factors. This knowledge is being translated into new, innovative drugs and other treatment strategies. For this work to continue to advance, and to understand how discoveries in one organ system may apply to others, researchers from across the spectrum of inflammatory disease need multiple mechanisms to access each other's work, to establish new collaborations, and to train the next generation of basic and clinician scientists. One such mechanism is to convene scientific conferences where researchers can hear the latest, often unpublished, findings and where trainees at all stages can learn from international experts in the field and present their own work on the international stage. The Banff Inflammation Workshop (BIW) 2023 will provide such a venue and opportunity. BIW has run every second year since 1999 (with recent interruptions due to the COVID-19 pandemic), and has been a forum that has generated new, interdisciplinary collaborations leading to important new findings in inflammatory disease research. Trainees have often found their next supervisor through interactions at this meeting. Early career investigators have advanced their careers by having an international stage upon which to showcase their work. BIW2023 will carry on this tradition. The program's speakers are leading experts that represent a range of career stages from several countries, and are a 50:50 split between men and women as an important step towards addressing inequality in scientific research.

column37: Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) is the most common soft tissue cancer in Canadian children. RMS is a skeletal muscle-derived soft-tissue sarcoma affecting children and adolescents. Our research team recently showed that the amount of pannexin 1 (PANX1) is very low in RMS when compared to normal skeletal muscle. In partnership with Sharbot Lake Family Health Team, and using a participatory action research approach, our objectives are: (1) have a half-day meeting to formulate a research question and plan the development, refinement, and evaluation of a community-driven diabetes education program for seniors living with diabetes; attendees will include seniors, healthcare providers and researchers; (2) develop a research proposal for the CIHR-Project Program based on the findings from Objective 1 through a consensus method; and (3) mobilize knowledge related to the outcomes of this planning grant using diverse dissemination strategies. The findings will be used for the establishment of a unique self-management education program for seniors, addressing the vital need for better educational services that reflect the priorities and wishes of seniors with diabetes in society-all of which may benefit similar communities for healthier living.

column36: Defining ER stress profiles as determinants of cell identity and therapeutic vulnerability in mTORC1-driven brain tumours
column37: As we seek to develop more effective treatment strategies for cancer it's essential to better understand the biological processes that are initially responsible for giving rise to tumours. In our previous work engineered, using CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, a human stem cell model of the tumour disorder tuberous sclerosis (TS), in which patients develop low grade but destructive tumours in multiple tissues including in the brain (arising even before birth). Tumours in TS are due to hyper-activation of the mTORC1 signalling pathway, which is observed in many types of cancers, thus our work will contribute to our understanding of cancer mechanisms in general. We performed multiple analyses with this model that revealed neural stem cells with a mutation in the TSC2 gene (causes TS) have unique biological aberrations during their early development not seen in other cell types. We're now unraveling the fundamental processes that give rise to tumour-driving stem cells in the brain. Our proposal will determine how brain-specific organelle and cell stress pathways work together to produce atypical tumour-driving cells, contribute to the unique mix of cells in these tumours, and which therapeutic compounds might exploit these vulnerabilities to kill or inhibit the destructive activity of TS brain tumours.

column37: Functional electrical stimulation (FES) is a recommended therapy for people living with neurological conditions, like stroke and spinal cord injury. Despite the benefits of FES, its use by clinicians remains low because they lack knowledge and training in FES. To address this knowledge gap, we created a clinical decision making (CDM) tool (called the FES CDM Tool) that helps clinicians determine how to set up FES for a client. A team consisting of people living with neurological conditions, clinicians, engineers and researchers will develop French and English versions of the toolkit. We will then share the toolkit with clinicians and rehabilitation researchers. Through this project, we will create a clinically relevant, evidence-based toolkit on FES. By increasing clinicians' knowledge and skills in FES, use of FES in clinical practice may increase and rehabilitation outcomes may improve.

column36: 17th Annual RiboWest Conference
column37: After two and a half years of an RNA virus pandemic and the incredible success of two RNA vaccines, there has never been a better time to appreciate the importance of ribonucleic acid (RNA) in health and disease. The 17th annual RiboWest Conference is a scientific meeting of some 130 researchers who share a general interest in the universal biomolecule RNA. In the last decade, it has become abundantly clear that RNA is a major regulator of cellular processes, implicating RNA in many diseases (e.g., cancer, viral/bacterial infection, and inherited disorders). Additionally, RNA has become an important tool, as gene silencing (RNA interference) and genome-editing (CRISPR) are commonly practiced in most biomedical research laboratories worldwide, and RNA vaccines are currently in the global spotlight. All of these facets of RNA research will be explored at RiboWest. This year, our discussion will be led by 3 outstanding keynote speakers. Dr. Karissa Sanbonmatsu, from the Los Alamos National Laboratory, is a pioneer in the use of molecular modelling to study the function of RNA. Professor Olivia Rissland, from the University of Colorado, studies the critical question of how RNA levels are regulated in the cell, particularly through RNA degradation, and is also a recognized expert on equity, diversity, and inclusion (EDI). Finally, Professor Jody Puglisi, from Stanford University, studies how RNA works by visualizing it at high resolution. The conference will include a panel discussion of how to make academic hiring more inclusive, and will solicit and support participation from all members of attending laboratories to ensure that no-one is left out. To this end, students have reduced registration fees, give oral presentations, and can win competitive awards for presentations and posters. Ultimately, the RiboWest Conference will catalyze new research, laying the foundation for the development of new treatments.

column37: BACKGROUND: A goal of Canada's Dementia Strategy is to improve quality of life for the increasing numbers of people with dementia who experience social exclusion. PURPOSE: As a next step, the Action Group wants to get the attention of primary care providers. They are not alone in their concern. The goal of this project is to address stigma in the context of primary care and make the Flipping Stigma toolkit useful for primary care providers. column36: Paracrine and autocrine IL-6 as drivers of treatment resistance in medulloblastoma
column37: Brain tumors represent the deadliest forms of childhood cancers. Owing to its location within the cortex of the still developing brain, complete tumor removal by resection is often not achieved. Thus, the mainstay for treatment remains chemo and radiation therapy. A challenge is finding the balance of treatment dosage to maximize tumor cell killing while minimizing unwanted damage to healthy tissues. Tumor cells that survive therapy give rise to disease relapse, and the relapsed form are often resistant to further treatments. In addition, relapsed tumors may become metastatic, the process whereby the tumor grows in multiple satellite sites distant from the original tumor. Strategies to improve brain tumor treatment that minimize the chances of relapse are urgently needed. The most common form of pediatric brain tumor is medulloblastoma (MB), of which the subtype known as group 3 MB is the most aggressive, with highest rates of metastasis, and lowest rates of survival. We discovered that group 3 MB cells exposed to 'bad' cytokines released by immune cells found in the brain rapidly show chemoresistance, as well as increased migration and invasion abilities indicative of metastatic potential. Our research will lead to strategic discoveries on how to block the 'bad' cytokines, and in doing so, prevent MB from becoming chemoresistant, thus minimizing chances of tumor relapse.

column37: Every tenth Canadian has some form of kidney disease. To improve health care for these people, it is critical to strongly support research into disease mechanisms to find new therapies for kidney patients. These scientists also train the next generation of researchers who will one day care for the patients. In order to maximize the rate of discoveries, the researches and their trainees should be able to present their work at scientific meetings, where all participants can exchange ideas, establish new collaborations and nurture new talent. Unfortunately, Canada currently lacks an appropriate scientific meeting for kidney discovery scientists to present their work. The Molecules and Mechanisms Mediating Kidney Health and Disease (M3K) meeting is the new initiative of the Canadian kidney research community that is designed to specifically meet the needs of Canadian fundamental kidney researchers with a focus on inclusiveness, diversity, and equitable access. After a long period of Covid, the kidney scientists are planning to get together in-person in spring 2023 in Montreal to re-connect with each other, re-start person-to-person discussions on the pressing issues and re-invigorate the community of fundamental kidney scientists. The CIHR Dissemination and planning grant will help coalesce a powerful national research community that works to improve the renal health of all Canadians.

During the forum, the YLT and decision-makers will be invited to develop a shared action plan for moving the One Chance recommendations forward. By engaging young people in critical reflection, visioning and planning around the One Chance report recommendations, and engaging decision-makers in conversations about what actions are feasible to advance the report recommendations, we will close the knowledge-to-action gap to improve child and youth well-being.

column36: Understanding STBBI Concerns, Challenges, and Opportunities in the Assisted Living Context Through Consultative Dialogue
column37: Older adults who are able to maintain some degree of independence yet also require care and support are increasingly opting to move into communal assisted living residences. While seniors' sexuality remains a fairly taboo topic, research has established that some assisted living residents are sexually active and that this is given very little consideration by those working in and operating assisted living facilities. column36: Towards Understanding Pain Sources, Patterns, and Barriers to Effective Management in Systemic Sclerosis: A Patient-Researcher Partnership
column37: Systemic sclerosis, also known as scleroderma, is a rare chronic, autoimmune musculoskeletal and skin disease. It causes thickening, hardening, and scarring of tissues, including the skin and internal organs. Pain is common in scleroderma but is largely ignored in research and care. Scleroderma pain can be caused by many sources (e.g., decreased blood flow to fingers, ulcers, joint contractures, gastrointestinal manifestations, and others). No methods exist to examine the multi-faceted nature of scleroderma pain, which is critical for improving management. Our team of researchers and people with scleroderma plan to develop such a tool and administer it to a large international cohort of people with scleroderma in order to better understand scleroderma pain, including sources, patterns, and management. We are requesting funds to do background scoping research to identify assessment tools that have been used in research on pain in other diseases. This will support a series of meetings where people with scleroderma and researchers will jointly review tools. Specifically, we will select the one most adaptable for scleroderma and together develop an initial version of the tool. It will be designed to assess scleroderma pain sources (e.g., decreased blood flow to fingers, ulcers, gastrointestinal manifestations, others), pain patterns from each source (e.g., frequency, duration, chronic or episodic nature), experiences with pain management services, and ways to improve services. Once we have developed an initial version of the tool via our planning activity, we will conduct research to refine the tool by interviewing people with scleroderma not involved in our team. Then, we will administer the final version to over 1,400 people with scleroderma from our large international cohort to generate knowledge about commonality of pain sources, patterns, and management experiences. This is unique work that will lay the groundwork for comprehensive pain research in scleroderma.

column37: Striking inequities in access to prenatal and early childhood healthcare and social services continue to prevail in Canada. Mothers, infants, children and families from disadvantaged social, economic and migration backgrounds are more likely to cumulate risk factors, and are less likely to receive routine preventive healthcare, leading to sub-optimal perinatal, infant, and early childhood health outcomes. Social perinatal primary care organizations, such as La Maison Bleue in Montreal, can offset these risks and promote the optimal growth, development and health of infants and children through the provision of adapted, integrated, and multidisciplinary healthcare and services during pregnancy and early childhood. Over the past years, in collaboration with the organization's leadership team, a number of research activities have been implemented at La Maison Bleue. In order to better understand the needs and priorities in terms of research and quality improvement activities at La Maison Bleue, we will: 1) develop a multi-stakeholder partnership (including end-users and service providers); 2) engage in consultation activities to generate a research agenda for La Maison Bleue; and 3) mobilize participation in a social perinatal community of practice for more effective knowledge dissemination and uptake.

column36: Targeting senescent cells to subdue breast-to-bone metastasis
column37: Chemotherapy, such as doxorubicin, is often used to treat advanced or metastatic breast cancer. These aggressive breast cancers often metastasize to bone and/or spine. Doxorubicin is an anthracycline that can inhibit DNA synthesis through intercalation or topoisomerase inhibition, which triggers cell senescence and apoptosis. This drug has also been shown to induce cellular senescence in surrounding normal cells and tissues. Senescence is a phenomenon where cells stop dividing and take on distinct cellular changes in gene expression, metabolism and DNA organization. Senescent cells adopt a state called senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), with the secretion of pro-inflammatory and pro-tumorigenic factors, as well as immune suppression. While chemotherapy can induce cancer cells to become senescent (originally thought be good), senescence in surrounding cells/tissues and tumor itself has been linked to advanced cancer growth and metastasis through SASP secretion. Chemotherapy-induced senescence in unrelated tissues also accelerates ageing and degenerative pathways. Senolytics specifically target senescent cells and induce apoptosis by various mechanisms. Here we test whether combining senolytics and chemotherapeutics targeting senescence will help to prevent cancer migration, decrease SASP, improve overall therapeutic efficacy, and decrease negative effects of senescence in other tissues. The overall goal is to develop new treatments to improve outcomes.

column36: Investigating Roles of Primate-Specific Retrotransposon-Derived Transcripts in Glioblastoma
column37: More than 50,000 Canadians are currently afflicted with a deadly type of brain cancer called Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM). Most patients exhibit severe symptoms that essentially ruin their quality of life, including difficulties in swallowing, sleeping, speaking, and walking. In addition, GBM is highly refractory to treatment with extremely low survival rates. Several options such as chemotherapy are available to treat GBM, which initially kill much (but not all) of the tumor and can temporarily reduce the severity of symptoms. Nonetheless, unfortunately, the tumor invariably becomes resistant to treatment, and eventually roars back with reinforced aggressiveness leading to death. To improve clinical outcomes for GBM patients, new molecular targets that can be exploited to interfere with progression of the disease are urgently needed. Retrotransposons are sections of DNA (or "genetic elements") that become activated in cancer cells, and go on to promote the capacity of these cells to grow uncontrollably. More specifically, previous studies have suggested that activated retrotransposons can pathologically affect the function of neighboring cancer-related genes in human cells. Furthermore, our own data show that abnormal activity of retrotransposons can interfere with the functioning of these important genes specifically in GBM. As such, our goal is to investigate the potential of retrotransposons as novel targets to improve the efficiency of anti-GBM therapies.

column36: Regulation of CD8+ T cell mediated anti-tumor immunity by insulin signalling
column37: During obesity, excessive inflammation can impair the body's responsiveness to insulin, a term called insulin resistance. We discovered that immune cells are responsive to insulin, but can become insulin resistant in obese animals. Since obese individuals present with elevated risks of developing certain types of tumors, including colorectal cancer, we set out to study how the immune cells are altered during obesity and whether such alterations play a role in tumor progression. CD8+ T cells are a subset of immune cells specialized in killing tumor cells. However, CD8+ T cells are rendered less effective at doing so within the tumor microenvironment, as they may be outcompeted by metabolically active tumor cells for necessary nutrients and resources. Obesity is thought to further stiffen such competition, although how it does so is not well understood. Since obesity induces insulin resistance in CD8+ T cells, we ask whether insulin resistance intrinsic to CD8+ T cells could explain the defective anti-tumor immunity seen in obese animals and individuals. We combine diet, genetic and tumor models to study the impact of insulin receptor signalling in CD8+ T cells within and outside the tumor microenvironment. Specifically, we will examine the role insulin receptor plays in regulating CD8+ T cells' ability to travel to and eliminate tumors. We propose that obesity rewires the metabolic pathways regulated by insulin, and in doing so causes impairments to anti-tumor immunity.

column36: Development of a Liquid Biopsy for Early Breast Cancer Detection
column37: Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer amongst females in Canada. Screening for BCa is performed using mammography to detect lesions within the breast. However, mammography results in a significant overdiagnosis of BCa and cannot distinguish between cancerous and healthy tissue leading to false positive results of benign disease. In addition, mammography does not always accurately detect cancer, as such, it can lead to a misdiagnosis suggesting that an individual is healthy when in-fact they have a tumor that was not detected by mammography. This highlights the need for the development of a non-invasive, accurate, and informative breast cancer screening test to improve the detection of clinically relevant disease. Our work to date has profiled the protein content of small particles, called extracellular vesicles (EVs), found in the blood of breast cancer patients and healthy individuals. From this we have generated a signature or fingerprint of breast cancer. Our current work aims to validate these protein markers and determine the best way to detect them so that we can develop a simple blood test that would support detection of breast cancer at its earliest stage. By detecting breast cancer at its earliest stage, this will support the best long-term survival outcomes for any individual with a newly diagnosed breast cancer.

column36: CIACCO-2023 (10th Annual symposium on Cytokines in Inflammation, Ageing, CanCer and Obesity)
column37: Cytokines are a diverse group of molecules that serve as a language for cells to communicate among each other. They play essential roles in the development and well being of the human body, as well as in tissue repair after injury. In fact, lack of certain cytokines, or the ability of the body's cells to use them, is detrimental to health (e.g. immune deficiency diseases). Their production and activities are highly regulated. However, excessive production or uncontrolled activities of cytokines could lead to inflammatory diseases (e.g. arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease). Similarly, deregulated cytokine production contributes to the development of diabetes in obese individuals. It is also becoming increasingly clear that persistent production of inflammatory cytokines promotes cancer (e.g. colorectal cancer, liver cancer). On the other hand, certain cytokines are important for ensuring a good, protective immune response against pathogens and cancer. Hence, cytokines are a double-edged sword that can be therapeutically manipulated to treat a broad range of human diseases. For instance, therapeutic blockade of certain cytokines is beneficial (as in the case of arthritis), while certain other cytokines are useful to promote immune response against cancers, and revitalize the ageing immune system in older individuals. The goal of this symposium is to organize an annual meeting of researchers, students and trainees working on, and interested in, cytokine research to share and discuss the latest findings. This symposium is organized by a group of researchers from University of Sherbrooke, University of Montreal, McGill University and University of Ottawa. Even though it was initiated as a regional symposium within Quebec, funding support from CIHR and other agencies are helping it to evolve into an important national forum for promoting cytokine research.

column36: Lymphatic Forum 2023 (LF2023)
column37: LF2023 will be the 4th iteration of a planned conference series that bring together researchers from around the world that study lymphatics in health and disease. Relatively understudied, the lymphatic system is a vital component of the immune and cardiovascular systems, which provides transport of fluid, macromolecules, cells, and other elements from the interstitial space of all organs to and through lymph nodes to the venous blood, thus regulating body fluid volume, macromolecular homeostasis, immune function, inflammation, and lipid absorption/metabolism. This specialized and complex network of lymphatic vessels functions both as conduits and intrinsic lymph pumps in series that generate and regulate the lymph flow. While these are important to health and disease, it has been historically difficult to examine and quantify lymphatic structure and function in the different body organs. LF2023 is the first in the Lymphatic Forum series to take place outside of the US and more specifically in Canada and the first to address the significant role and functions of the lymphatic vascular system in the various organs of the human body. Accordingly, the Forum's program is designed to pay particular attention to the complex aspects of the lymphatic vascular system in the normal function of, and pathologies associated with, these organs. Presentations and discussions will focus on the molecular regulation of lymphatic development in a specific organ, the description of organ diseases and the known or suggested lymphatic dysfunctions, with an emphasis on immune dysregulations in that organ that could explain or contribute to the disease and its development. Additionally, the conference is specifically designed such that trainees and young investigators have significant roles.

column36: Toward early detection and management of frailty in community-dwelling older adults: Planning a web-based frailty evaluation tool for patient self-evaluation and self-report
column37: Frailty is a condition that makes it difficult to deal with stress. Over 22% of Canadian men and 25% of Canadian women 65 years and older are considered frail. This is about 1.8 million Canadians. The frailer a person is, the more likely they are to be hospitalized and die. If frailty is not caught early it can increase by 3% every year, so there is a serious need to detect and manage frailty early. We recently made a website to help doctors assess and manage the frailty of their patients, but to reach the 1.8 million frail Canadians the website needs to be accessible to everyone, especially older adults. For example, because many people do not have medical training, the frailty website we made for doctors will be confusing and not helpful. The main question we will attempt to answer in this proposal is how do we make a frailty website that older adults can use while still being useful to doctors? We will generate ideas and plan how to best create a frailty website for older adults. To do this, we will first hold an educational meeting where doctors and researchers, experts in frailty, will give short talks. This event will be streamed live over the internet and reach a wide audience. Audience members will be made up of people who are interested in the idea of a frailty website, such as older adults, people who take care of older adults, other doctors, and researchers. In the second part, we will invite older adults and doctors from the first meeting to small group discussions, to share their thoughts about the problems and solutions of potential development of a frailty website for patients. Making a frailty website that can be used by the older adults is key to catching frailty early. By including older adults, people who take care of older adults, and doctors early in the planning stages of an older adult frailty website is important to its success. Catching frailty early will reduce healthcare costs and enhance the lives of individuals living across Canada.

column37: This meeting is the 11th Canadian Developmental Biology Conference and the 9rd Canada Regional Meeting of the North American Society for Developmental Biology. The meeting has been held once every two years since 2002, with the location alternating between Quebec in the east and Banff in the west of Canada. Canadian developmental biologists are located in large and medium cities that are dispersed throughout a very wide geographic area. New investigators are extended priority invitations in order to introduce them to the community to facilitate recognition of their work nationally and to those who serve on grant panels. Developmental biologists in relatively small centres who would be isolated within their local environment are also extended invitations to immerse them with the Canadian community. Postdoctoral and graduate trainees are given priority for short talks in order to encourage their interest in the field and strengthen future prospects for developmental biology in Canada. The 3 day program is sub-divided into five sessions, with three to six invited speakers (30-minute talks) per session. Sessions will also include one to three 15-minute talks selected from submitted abstracts with priority given to junior faculty, postdocs and students. Two poster sessions are also planned for afternoons of the 24th and 25th. The program includes an educational session on equity, diversity and inclusion in science and two keynote lectures.

column36: 3rd International Workshop of the Canadian NASH Network: "A Silent Pandemic"
column37: Due to the obesity and co-epidemic of type 2 diabetes, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common liver disease in our country, affecting one in fourth Canadians. NAFLD is an accumulation of fat in the liver. NAFLD can evolve to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), the most severe form of NAFLD, leading to cirrhosis and need for liver transplant. NASH is a silent killer because it is largely asymptomatic until end-stage liver complications from liver cirrhosis arise. In 2021, the International Liver Foundation declared NASH a pandemic. The Canadian NASH (CanNASH) Network is an international research group of academic and clinical units aiming to improve knowledge on the frequency, diagnosis and physiopathology of NASH and its complications. The theme of the 3rd International Workshop of the CanNASH Network will focus on discussing current knowledge about priority areas of research, including: 1. The frequency and risk factors of NASH in Canada; 2. Non-invasive biomarkers to diagnose NASH without the need for the invasive liver biopsy; 3. Possible ways to treat NASH; 4. Models of care to screening strategies. The Workshop addresses and contributes to the strategic research priorities of the CIHR Institute of Nutrition, Diabetes and Metabolism by aligning with all its four strategic priorities and contributes to the strategic plan 2021-2026 in the areas of biomedical/clinical and population health (prevention) research. This workshop will promote knowledge exchange among international key opinion leaders in the field and Canadian researchers. It will contribute to effective partnerships and outstanding research at national and internstional levels while putting Canada at the forefront of the concern around NASH as a global silent pandemic.

column36: Diabetes Research on physical Activity/Exercise in Women (DRAW) Planning Meeting
column37: Exercise has been recognized as an important tool for healthy living in individuals with both type 1 and type 2 diabetes. In spite of the fact that diabetes is as common in males as in females, most exercise recommendations for people with both type 1 and type 2 diabetes are based on studies involving all or mostly male participants. In people without diabetes, clear sex-related differences in how the body uses fuel during exercise have been found. The menstrual cycle, pregnancy and menopause are also known to affect how fuels are used. In addition, we know that men and women will often choose to exercise in different ways, and have different motivations for doing so. As all of these factors could have a direct effect on blood glucose levels, they may have long-term health implications where diabetes management is concerned. We are proposing to establish an international research network that will combine several areas of expertise related to diabetes and physical activity / exercise, in order to examine sex and gender-related differences more closely. This network would involve women researchers from across Canada, and will include women from the United States and Europe as well. We plan to hold a one-day meeting to establish clear research questions, a grant application strategy and common protocols for data collection. In addition, we will host a symposium for people with diabetes and health care providers to present data from the latest research in the field and to recruit people for our patient and health care provider advisory committees. The meeting will lay the groundwork for a summary article, while building the relationships required move forward with several grant applications.

column36: Sensorized needles for prostate cancer localization in mpMRI/US targeted biopsy
column37: Prostate biopsy is the only way to definitively determine the presence of prostate cancer (PCa). Men with PCa risk factors typically undergo Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) to locate cancer nodules. Ultrasound (US) imaging is then used to guide and place biopsy needles in the tumour identified by MRI for sampling and analysis. A biopsy that yields a positive result for PCa would inform treatment decisions, however, a negative result has uncertain meaning and could be due to inadequate sampling, i.e., the needles were not inserted into the target adequately. This may result in a lack of clarity on subsequent treatment options. There is an urgent need to develop methods to accurately assess whether the biopsy needle is appropriately positioned in the MRI-identified target or whether repositioning or additional biopsies are required. The applicants have developed smart biopsy needles that are able to differentiate cancerous from healthy tissue at the needle tip by measuring the tissue's bioelectric properties. This proposal aims to validate this technology in a pilot study using resected human prostate glands immediately after radical prostatectomy. If shown to be accurate, the use of smart needles for prostate tissue identification could improve diagnosis of PCa, improve confidence in biopsy results, and reduce procedure time as well as the number of biopsies performed. This study will pave the way for an in vivo trial of the proposed technology at the Ottawa Hospital.

column36: Roles of microenvironment hyaluronan in preventing skin cancer initiation
column37: Non-melanoma skin cancer is the most common human cancer and the incidence of these tumors is increasing. Although they are rarely lethal they often recur, which increases patient morbidity and contributes to rising health care costs. They recur because sun exposure causes mutations in cells over large areas of skin. This large field of mutant cells remains as a "time-bomb" for the development of future tumors. What prevents or supports the mutated cells' emersion into tumors is unknown. Certain factors in our skin are fragmented and lost with age and sun exposure, which may resist cancer. We developed a topical formulation of one suspect, hyaluronic acid (HA-PE) that cannot be fragmented and replenishes what has been lost in sun-exposed skin. Using a mouse model, we showed HA-PE prevented non-melanoma skin cancer even though mouse skin had many mutations. We now want to find out how HA-PE prevents mutant genes from instructing cells to grow, survive and form tumors. This information will increase our currently very limited knowledge of how our skin blocks tumor formation, which will help to design methods for preventing tumor recurrence.

column37: There is no cure for breast cancer that has spread to the brain and new treatment strategies are needed to improve the outcome of affected patients. The electrical environment of breast cancer brain metastasis (BCBM) presents a vulnerability that may be therapeutically exploited. We have shown that BCBM cells are susceptible to low energy electric fields (LEEFs) mild enough that they do not overtly impact the normal brain. column36: vestigating breast cancer organoids
column37: Breast cancer is the most prevalent cancer in women. First-line treatment for breast cancer includes surgery, with or without different regimens of chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy. Targeted hormone therapy or anti-HER2 therapy are available to the ER/PR+ and HER2+ breast cancer subtypes. Precision medicine is defined as clinical management tailored to the individual. An emerging model that has the potential to functionally predict personalized clinical response, is the patient-derived-organoid (PDO). PDOs are generated from an individual tumor and can be cultured in the laboratory as 3-dimensional organoids. Remarkably, these PDOs retain features of the original tumor, are stable over extended periods and are amenable to assessing drug sensitivity. PDOs could become a valuable tool to guide personalized treatment. For PDO-testing to become standard-of-care, there should be sufficient evidence demonstrating predictive value. Further, PDOs provide incredible windows to tackle clinical challenges, such as chemotherapy resistance. In this study, we will test whether PDO treatment response mimics patient response in the neoadjuvant setting. We will also use PDOs to identify mechanisms of chemotherapy resistance and test potential treatments. The success of our overall project will be a major accomplishment for any future intentions to use PDOs as clinical tools for personalized medicine.
