column36: Exploring the experiences of small and rural municipalities during the COVID-19 Pandemic to identify enabling supports and structures that will strengthen response to future disruption
column37: In Canada, geography is a determinant of health: people living in rural and remote areas experience poorer or different health outcomes than their urban counterparts. While approximately 29% of the Canadian population lives in small and rural areas, this project will focus on communities in Northern Ontario with fewer than 10,000 residents. Rural communities have lower rates of self-reported health, lower rates of physical activity, and higher rates of overweight and obesity, and smoking. They also have lower rates of depression and higher sense of social cohesion. In Canada, mortality from preventable causes increases with remoteness. The COVID-19 pandemic has uniquely affected rural communities; although impacts related to substance use, mental health, food security, gender-based violence, and financial security have been documented across Canada, each of these was amplified or at least experienced differently in rural communities, as were disparities related to inequitable access to broadband Internet. This research study asks: what enabling supports and structures would help small/rural communities in Northern Ontario to more effectively respond to disruption? Using a pragmatic and a systems approach, this project will employ a qualitative, case study research design including semi-structured interviews, thematic discourse analysis, and a participatory workshop to address the research question. Results will contribute to strengthening Canada's public health system by identifying opportunities to better support local governments in small and rural communities to promote health and wellbeing.

column36: Strengthening Capacity for Public Health Leadership and Decision-Making: The Contribution of Case-based Learning
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has refocused attention globally and in Canada on the capacities and performance of public health systems within larger government and non-government structures. Previously, our team studied how public health systems and decision-makers in Canada and other jurisdictions are organized and interact with other political and social actors, resulting in policies to respond to acute public health needs, such as COVID-19. Our approach focuses on the effect of institutions, politics, public health system organization, and governance (IPOG) on the public health response. Our proposal aims to strengthen the capacities of public health trainees and in-service public health decision-makers and practitioners to engage with these 'upstream' factors, in order to advance objectives of public health improvement in complex governmental and non-governmental environments. We hypothesize that these capacities can be strengthened through competency-focused education and practice interventions. Through the IPOG framework we focus on "governance" as decision-making process, which can be improved by greater preparation and skills in navigating organizational and political factors. We further hypothesize that problem-oriented, case-based teaching can strengthen competencies needed in this domain. Hence, in keeping with the 2021 PHAC report, we suggest that there is potential to improve the competencies for public health practitioners to interface with political leaders as well as engage with other key government and non-government actors. In partnership with knowledge users, the project will generate and apply new knowledge by outlining competency gaps pertaining to IPOG in public health training programs in Canada; develop, use, and evaluate teaching cases using multi-media video accompanied by a detailed teaching guide; and make them available as open-access resources. column36: Identifying metabolomic and proteomic biomarkers for cognitive function
column37: Dementia is the most common chronic neurodegenerative disease which affects 7.1% of the Canadian populations over 65. The most common form of dementia is Alzheimer's disease (AD), which is diagnosed by severe cognitive decline. Retaining cognitive function is an important measure of healthy aging. To identify genetically supported multi-omic determinants (ie. proteins and metabolites) could help the discovery of new drugs of maintaining cognitive function, and reduce the risk of AD and the socioeconomic burden of our aging society. Here we propose a genetic epidemiological framework to identify robust proteomic and metabolomic determinants for cognitive function, using publicly available data and the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA) cohort. We will utilize methods such as Mendelian randomization and statistical colocalization, combined with evidence from the direct association of metabolites with cognitive composite scores targeting memory and executive function and a protein polygenic risk score, to identify causal proteins and metabolites for AD and cognitive function. By leveraging the largest dataset with the most comprehensive metabolomic, genetic and cognitive function measurements, we expect to identify genetically supported biomarkers that could point to new therapeutic targets for early cognitive changes before the onset of dementia.

column36: Understanding Healthy Aging of the Lungs
column37: With each breath, our lungs store a record of our surroundings. Consequently, the lungs can tell us a lot about our overall health. With each harmful exposure (e.g., tobacco smoke, air pollution) the chances of developing lung disease and dying prematurely increases. The most common test to measure how well the lungs work requires that people forcefully empty all of the air in their lungs. As we age, this test becomes more difficult to do. We can't be sure that lower lung function in older adults means someone has lung disease, or if this is due to technical performance of the test or weaker breathing muscles (i.e., healthy aging). This makes it difficult to know who has lung disease. There are two large Canadian studies with very useful information that may help. By combining the information already collected from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA) and the Canadian Cohort of Obstructive Lung Disease (CanCOLD) we can better differentiate healthy aging from disease and describe the lung health of the Canadian population.

column36: A comprehensive approach to quantifying chronic inflammation in older adults
column37: Inflammation is a critical defence mechanism that is conserved across numerous species. Not only does it signal when there is significant danger or damage to the host, it activates and sustains many of the cellular and molecular processes that ultimately act to return the organism back to its homeostatic state. Under optimal circumstances, inflammation comes and goes when needed; however, with age, these processes become dysregulated, resulting in a chronic, low-grade inflammatory state that can be disruptive to many of the fundamental biological systems needed for day-to-day life, thereby promoting poor health outcomes over time. Although regarded as a "hallmark of aging", the causes of chronic inflammation in older adults remains a mystery, partly due to our inability to properly measure it. We have shown that not only does chronic inflammation alter patterns of methylation occurring to DNA across our genome, these changes can be quantified into an exciting epigenetic measure of chronic inflammation. Although the epigenetic inflammation score (EIS) is significantly associated with sociodemographics, risky lifestyle behaviours and poor health outcomes, it does not fully reflect the complex nature of chronic inflammation. In the following proposal, our research team aims to take advantage of the richness of the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA) database and develop an epigenetic signature that reflects multiple forms of chronic inflammation - protein, cellular, and metabolic. This signature will reveal new insights into the biological impact of chronic inflammation in older adults, and be used to generate a refined, comprehensive EIS. We will then validate the comprehensive EIS against sociodemographic, lifestyle and health-related traits in CLSA participants, and test for associations with longitudinal outcomes including mortality, cognitive decline, and the trajectory of frailty.

column36: Retinal Imaging in Prediction and Diagnosis of Cardiovascular Diseases
column37: Cardiovascular diseases have remained the leading cause of death in the Canada and worldwide. The substantial burden of cardiovascular diseases promotes enduring interest in new ways of screening for early disease diagnosis and prediction. Fundus retinal imaging is a non-invasive and cost-effective procedure. Since the ophthalmic medium is translucent, it allows retinal vessels to be viewed with relative ease. Some retinal parameters, including vascular diameter, tortuosity, and branching, have been shown to be potentially associated with cardiovascular diseases. The findings suggest that the retinal microvasculature could provide essential data about concurrent cardiovascular disease status and predict future incidence of cardiovascular disease. However, previous studies have some limitations: (1) most studies focused on patients with a certain disease (e.g. diabetes) rather than a general population; (2) not all known confounders, such as obesity, sedentary lifestyle, and other retinal parameters, were adjusted for when assessing whether a retinal parameter was associated with cardiovascular diseases; (3) no age- and sex-stratified investigation has been done though the association between retinal parameters and cardiovascular diseases is believed to be different for men and women and for midlife and elderly population. To address these limitations in the current literature, the objectives of our study are: (1) to identify age- and sex-specific retinal parameters that are independently associated with cardiovascular diseases, using the data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA); (2) to develop cardiovascular disease risk scores based on retinal parameters and other biological and lifestyle measures to detect concurrent and predict future incident cardiovascular diseases, respectively. This study will be the first Canadian population-based study exploring the use of retinal imaging in diagnosis and prediction of cardiovascular diseases.

column36: Bitter taste receptors and COVID-19
column37: COVID-19 has affected nearly 4 million Canadians. Some people infected with COVID-19 have very mild symptoms, others have much more severe symptoms and some people even die from COVID-19 infection. Older adults are at particularly high risk of having severe COVID-19 infection. For viruses that are spread through the air like the COVID-19 virus, the immune system in the mouth and lungs is critical to preventing severe disease. We think differences in how well the immune system attacks this new virus may partly explain why COVID-19 infection is different in different people. Some proteins that help taste bitter foods (bitter taste receptors or T2Rs) also play an important role in the body's earliest immune responses to virus infection. This system acts very fast and may stop the virus from attaching to the mouth and nose and may stop the virus from growing. T2Rs are also found on immune cells that make antibodies after COVID-19 infection (or vaccination). Differences in the genes for T2Rs affect how well they work and we think different T2R genes will also affect COVID-19 infection and maybe responses to vaccines. Some studies suggest gene differences in one T2R may affect COVID-19 outcomes. There is no data for other T2R genes, or for T2Rs and vaccines. Methods: We will test whether there are differences in T2R genes between older adults who 1) do or do not get COVID-19 infection and who have mild or severe COVID-19 infection; 2) who do or do not make antibodies after COVID-19 infection or vaccines; 3) who have other medical conditions affecting the risk of severe infections; and 4) we will test several T2R genes. Impact: This information will tell us more about how the immune system in older adults responds to viral infections and vaccines and possibly how to predict who is at greater risk of severe infections. This will help older adults, their care-givers, and policy makers make informed decisions about preventing and managing infections.

column36: Physical Activity Behaviour in Middle-Aged and Older Canadian Women and Men: An Analysis of the CLSA
column37: As we age, declines in memory, strength, and overall well-being are often observed. Negative health changes present a significant challenge for Canada's aging population. However, research has shown that increasing physical activity (PA) levels can improve health and overall function as we age while preventing chronic diseases. Despite the benefits of PA, many older adults do not meet recommended levels. To promote PA among older adults, we need an accurate picture of their current behaviours. Research suggests that among people over 65, specific populations, such as women and those with less education, have an increased risk of insufficient PA. Recently, research has shown the benefits of light-intensity PA, which suggests we should examine a broader range of physical activities than traditionally considered. Less intense forms of PA are especially relevant for older age groups. Our project will use data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging to describe a wide variety of activities separately in Canadian women and men to accurately describe the amount and type of activities performed. Ongoing trends of low PA levels in high-income countries make understanding what influences PA behaviour critical. A second goal of this work is to explore relationships between possible personal and environmental factors affecting PA in Canadians. We will explore relationships at a single time point and over time. Exploring relationships over time allows us to assess the direction of relationships, helping to fill a gap in research on determinants of PA. Physical activity is a powerful behaviour that can improve the overall health and wellbeing of Canada's aging population. Describing PA behaviours of specific groups of Canadians more inclusively will help identify those at risk for low PA and factors most related to this vital health behaviour. This work can be used to inform PA promotion efforts and develop new ones better tailored to the needs of Canadian women and men.

column36: Examining the role of menopause and hormone replacement therapy on diet, physical activity, and metabolic health among aging females in Canada
column37: Menopause is the natural decrease in sex hormones that occurs in females during aging. During and after menopause, there is a higher risk of developing obesity and poorer physical function and metabolic health, which can increase the risk of conditions like heart disease, diabetes, and cancer. Hormone replacement therapy can help lessen the symptoms of menopause and reduce the risk of some chronic diseases. Hormone replacement may also impact dietary intake, physical activity, and sleep - called 'modifiable health behaviors', MHBs. However, it is not clear if MHBs (and their relationship to health outcomes) differ according to menopausal status and hormone replacement use. To address this knowledge gap, the research team will use data collected from females in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging - a large study that measures several aspects of health using robust tools to identify predictors of healthy aging. The proposed research project will characterize MHBs, their relationship to health outcomes that are important for aging, and how these relationships change across time among four groups of females: 1) pre- or peri-menopausal, 2) post-menopausal who have never used hormone replacement, 3) post-menopausal who currently use hormone replacement, 4) post-menopausal who have previously used hormone replacement. MHBs will be measured from self-reported information on diet, physical activity, and sleep. Health outcomes will include lean and fat tissue, physical function, and metabolic health using objective measurements. This will be the first study to investigate MHBs with a large number of objective health outcomes according to menopausal and hormone replacement status. It will provide a better understanding of the potential short- and long-term effects of menopause and hormone replacement. Therefore, the findings may help inform decision making regarding hormone replacement use and the design of personalized health interventions to support healthy aging.

column36: Deep phenotyping of UGT human knockouts

column36: Cognitive aging in middle and older-aged Canadians: Consideration of genetic risk, modifiable factors, and biological sex
column37: Age-related decline in cognitive performance is common among older adults; however, not all adults show the same degree of decline, and indeed, some adults maintain cognitive performance in late life. The intent of the proposed study is to explore this thesis further using data collected over the first three waves of the Canadian Longitudinal Study of Aging. The proposed study will evaluate whether carriers of dementia-related gene variants have lower cognition at baseline and/or faster rates of decline in cognition over time. Finally, we will look at markers in the blood to determine whether those might help explain any links between genetics, individual behaviours and characteristics with cognitive aging in this cohort. column36: Impact of genome-wide and local homozygosity on sensory-related traits
column37: Homozygosity, when an individual has two identical forms of a particular gene, one inherited from each parent, is known to cause rare, often very severe, Mendelian genetic diseases. However, the impact of increased homozygosity on diseases caused by many genes and the environment is not well understood. Vision and hearing loss are very common affecting 6% and 18% of Canadians, respectively. Vision and hearing loss are heritable traits but their heritability cannot be explained by the additive effects of genes identified so far. Most human populations display restricted ranges of homozygosity levels. Populations that originate from a limited number of individuals and remain isolated to some extent from other populations are called founder populations and have wider ranges of homozygosity. We will use existing data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA) to measure genome-wide and local homozygosity effects on sensory traits related to vision and hearing loss. The CLSA includes participants from Quebec and Newfoundland, and we will thus take advantage of the higher homozygosity levels present in the French-Canadian and Newfoundland founder populations to capture a wider range of homozygosity levels. Animal studies have shown that non-additive genetic variation (underlying homozygosity effects) plays an important role in genetic disease risk but is less often studies than additive genetic variation. Our research will thus provide much needed insights on non-additive effects for sensory-related traits and could ultimately result in better health management of vision and hearing loss.

column36: Functional metabolomics and lipidomics
column37: Most people are familiar with the metabolism. Magazines often advertise tips to increase or optimize the speed of one's metabolism. However, relatively little is known about metabolites. Metabolites are small molecules, such as lipids, carbohydrates, steroids and amino acids, that are produced by the metabolism of a living organism. Despite the many active roles that metabolites play in vital biological processes, including their roles in driving disease, our understanding of the composition and function of the majority of metabolites remains rudimentary relative to our knowledge of other small molecules, such as genes and proteins. The challenge is significant-less than 10% of metabolites that we can detect using state-of-the-art instruments have a known function. This "dark metabolome" could represent hundreds of thousands of different metabolites; for example, it is estimated that a single drop of human blood could contain as many as 1 million metabolites, each with their own specific biological function. Dr. Montenegro Burke, an Assistant Professor at the University of Toronto, has developed a research program with the important goal of identifying metabolites and determining their function. He is advancing the way we catalogue metabolites and determine how they regulate fundamental biological processes and drive disease. His research is already yielding new information about specific types of metabolites that are capable of regulating inflammation during inflammatory bowel disease. Specifically, he and his research team are developing innovative approaches to systematically map specific metabolite classes, determine their function, and identify the genes involved in their biosynthesis. They do this using mass spectrometry-one of the most sensitive analytical techniques currently available-to measure thousands of molecules in biological samples. Montenegro Burke's research will help identify metabolites with biological function and their genetic partners. Ultimately, the results of his research will generate new therapeutic targets for drug development, paving the way for researchers to develop alternative disease treatments for patients that do not respond to current clinically-approved drugs.

column36: Does early-life respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection increase the risk of asthma? Using population-based health administrative data to address two missing pieces of the puzzle
column37: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is the leading cause of respiratory illness among children <5 years, annually causing >33 million respiratory infection episodes and 3 million hospitalizations globally. While ubiquitous to childhood-infecting nearly all children by 3 years of age-no RSV vaccine currently exists. Multiple promising candidates are under development; however, Palivizumab is the only option currently available for RSV prophylaxis, which has stringent eligibility criteria due to its high cost and monthly dosing requirements (i.e., only infants at high-risk of severe disease are eligible). In addition to its acute impacts, early-life RSV illness has been repeatedly shown to be followed by increased risk of chronic respiratory conditions in childhood, such as recurrent wheeze and asthma. Challenges in determining the causal role of RSV in these pathways has limited our ability to disentangle two prevailing theories: (1) RSV infection and asthma share common causes (e.g. atopic predisposition); and (2) severe RSV infection causes asthma (via altered airway and immune responses). A clearer understanding of the long-term health sequalae of RSV, including asthma, is crucial to informing cost-effectiveness and effectiveness studies evaluating emerging RSV vaccine and long-acting prophylaxis candidates. Building upon our study team's earlier work in these areas, our proposal seeks to address two missing pieces in the RSV-asthma causality puzzle by providing: 1. an estimate of the effectiveness of Palivizumab programs in decreasing asthma incidence; and 2. a precise, population-based quantification of the risk of asthma due to severe early-life RSV illness, compared to siblings without an early-life history of severe RSV, to account for complex gene-environment factors.

column36: Engaging Stakeholders in the Development of Standards for a Canadian Rapid Learning Health System in Early Intervention Services for Psychosis
column37: Services for early psychosis are available in several Canadian provinces. However, the treatments and activities they provide may be very different and affect patient outcomes. Standards are needed and have been developed. However, their uptake in Canadian early psychosis services has not been up to par. Research and technology are advancing quickly, and we need to use these tools to improve services for early psychosis. Our team implemented a new model called the Rapid Learning Health System (RLHS). The RLHS uses technology to collect real-time data in clinical settings, data that will inform and improve clinical practices. We already tested this RLHS successfully in 11 early psychosis services in Quebec. The research project we are proposing will develop standards for building capacity and improving early psychosis services. We will invite early psychosis services across Canada to reach agreement on a set of standards and practices. The groups will include people who work in early psychosis services, service users (patients and family members) and others involved in policy and decision making. They will meet at a "consensus conference" where they will study evidence from research, express their opinions and reach agreement on a set of standards and practices for all early psychosis programs in Canada. We will also collect information on technologies used in early psychosis programs using an online survey. We will present the results to groups of patients, clinicians, researchers, and project managers during 5 virtual meetings to gather their opinions on barriers and privacy issues. This research project will propose standards that will build capacity in EIS for psychosis and improve services. With input from so many groups, we hope that the new RLHS model will respond to the needs of young service users and their families. The model should also provide clinicians with valuable information for improving early psychosis services.

column36: Developing Standards for Implementing Stepped Care Models in Child and Youth Mental Health Service Systems
column37: Stepped care models in mental health have recently emerged as a way to organize services. In these models, less invasive interventions can be offered to people with less intense needs, while more invasive or risky treatments should be provided to those who have more complex, severe or persistent conditions. From the perspective of patients, services can be "stepped" up or down based on their individual needs and preferences. In this way, stepped care integrates a range of community-based treatments to create a full continuum of accessible services and supports. However, stepped care models vary widely in terms of the total number of steps, clinician involvement, what is offered in specific steps, and more. What is urgently required, then, is minimum standards around how stepped care should be implemented in practice. Our team of clinicians, implementors and decision-makers has recently described a set of principles for stepped care models in youth mental health. In the current project, we will work with youth, caregivers, clinicians, and decision-makers to translate these principles into consensus on standards for stepped care in youth mental health services across Canada. We will also engage an alliance of motivated teams who are already involved in developing stepped care models in post-secondary institutions, digital service delivery platforms, and integrated youth services to consider how these standards can be applied to those specific settings. Together, these efforts will catalyze a Learning Health System for stepped care delivery, data, and knowledge - all with the objective of creating a stronger and more evidence-informed youth mental health service system.

column36: Mobilizing Knowledge with Young People Who Use Drugs, Caregivers, and Providers: Informing Improved Youth Mental Health and Substance Use Services
column37: This project aims to mobilize some of the key findings, guiding principles, and recommendations for best practices emerging from a long-term qualitative and community-based participatory research study in British Columbia. Since 2017, the Care Pathways Study has traced the mental health and substance use (MHSU) healthcare trajectories and outcomes of over 100 street-involved young people who use drugs (YPWUD) in Metro Vancouver, Prince George, and Kelowna. We have documented how these individuals navigate multiple systems of care and supervision (e.g., the foster care and criminal justice systems) across time and place, identifying some of the challenges and opportunities of a rapidly expanding youth MHSU services system in BC. We have also qualitatively documented the evolving experiences of young people's caregivers and providers. In 2022, key findings from the Care Pathways Study were summarized into two reports: "Harm Reduction Calls to Action from Young People Who Use Drugs in the Context of Unstable Housing and Homelessness" and "Youth Voices on Treatment in the Shadow of the Overdose Crisis: Key Recommendations and Findings for Service Providers." While these documents are based on research from British Columbia, they arguably have broad applicability to settings across Canada. In order to mobilize the guiding principles and best practices that have emerged from the Care Pathways Study, the proposed project will engage YPWUD, their caregivers, and their providers in the creation of a Crackdown podcast episode (with a listenership of more than 10,000 people), as well as a video episode as part of the award-winning Living On series. We will also hold a one-day hybrid in-person and virtual participatory summit event designed to elicit critical discussion of the challenges and opportunities of translating our guiding principles and best practices into pan-Canadian standards for the delivery of specialized, evidence-based youth MHSU services.

column36: Fidelity and Skill Use in Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Adolescents with Depression
column37: Background: Depressive disorders in adolescents (DD-A) are prevalent and debilitating. Relevant NICE guidelines recommend Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) as a first-line treatment for DD-A. The proposed study leverages an ongoing large-scale randomized controlled trial (RCT) to answer the following research questions: (1) How variable is clinician delivery of CBT after standardized training? (2) Does higher clinician fidelity to CBT predict decreases in depressive symptoms at baseline, 4 weeks, 12 weeks and 24 weeks? (3) What are barriers and facilitators to clinician fidelity in the delivery of CBT. Method: The primary study is an ongoing stepped wedge cluster RCT examining effectiveness and implementation of a care pathway for DD-A based on NICE guideline recommendations compared to treatment as usual (TAU). The study is coordinated at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto, Canada. We are enrolling 650 adolescents (325 per arm) with DD-A from 6 community mental health agencies across Ontario, Canada. A key component of the pathway is a 16-week modular CBT program- delivered in group and/or individually, virtually and/or in person. For the current proposal, quality measurement of clinician fidelity to CBT will be collected. This requires specialized resources. This funding would allow us to introduce this additional line of inquiry, not currently budgeted for in the trial. Impact: If greater fidelity is found to be related to greater improvement in depressive symptoms for adolescents receiving CBT, this would inform standards on how CBT is delivered. This could improve the lives of many young people with DD-A. Qualitative methods will be used to explore barriers and facilitators to optimizing treatment fidelity. Research Team: Our research team includes individuals from multiple disciplines including psychology, implementation science, social work, biostatistics, youth engagement, and psychiatry.

column36: Do mental health organizations in Alberta and British Columbia have the need, fit and capacity to deliver an Integrate Care Pathway for the treatment of depression in adolescents?
column37: Background: Depressive Disorders in adolescents (ages 13-18 years old; DD-A) are common, and represents important risk of morbidity and mortality, namely by suicide. Our prior published work identified the relevant NICE guideline as uniquely high quality and up-to-date. Integrated Care Pathways (ICPs) are treatment algorithms intended to translate of guideline recommendations (i.e. standard of care) into routine practice. Our group developed an ICP based on the NICE guideline called CARIBOU-2. There are 7 core components: assessment, education, therapy options, medication options, caregiver support, measurement-based care, and graduation. Implementation efforts for CARIBOU-2 are already underway across Ontario. It is not known to what extent mental health centers in other provinces are ready to implement the CARIBOU-2 intervention. We wish to clarify readiness for the CARIBOU-2 pathway implementation process of mental health agencies in Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia. Method: Co-investigators based in Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia will broadly invite administrative staff (directors, managers, lead clinicians and local youth partners) at community-based and academic mental health centers to participate in the study. Consenting participants will receive extensive detailed information about the CARIBOU-2 pathway and each of its components. Structured site-level group interviews will proceed to assess need, fit, capacity, supports, evidence and usability factors for consideration prior to implementation of a complex intervention. Results will be synthesized and summarized across sites using tables and narrative summary. Impact: This study will indicate where efforts to implement CARIBOU-2 across Canada are warranted and set the stage to scale up this complex intervention. Sites that are ready could then initiate processes required to deliver care to DD-A based high quality standards.

column36: LEAPS-IYS: Learning to Equitably Adapt Peer Support for Integrated Youth Services
column37: Many youth experience difficulties accessing mental health services. In the last decade, there has been a growing movement to include youth peer support workers (individuals with lived experience) to make mental health services more accessible by providing instrumental and emotional support to youth with mental health and substance use (MHSU) concerns. The Mental Health Commission of Canada has created peer support guidelines and Peer Support Canada built a training and certification process based on these guidelines. Since the original guidelines and training curriculum were developed for adults, there is an urgent need to develop new peer support guidelines that recognize the unique needs of youth. We will identify how to implement these guidelines and training curriculum in our national network of Integrated Youth Services (IYS). IYS is a service delivery model that provides a 'one-stop shop' for young people to access services including housing, employment and mental healthcare. This project will co-design youth peer support guidelines, training curriculum and evaluation strategies in IYS. We will bring together key stakeholders (youth, peer support workers, decision makers, healthcare providers, representatives from peer support organizations, and content experts in IYS) to review and prioritize how to change the guidelines and training curriculum for peer support. Next, stakeholders will identify an evaluation framework for service user, program, and system level processes and outcomes in YPS. Finally, stakeholders will collaboratively identify strategies for implementing the practice guidelines, training curriculum, and evaluation framework for YPS in Canada. The outcome of this project will ensure all youth with MHSU concerns can access YPS and that we can continue to learn how to improve the training curriculum to ensure it is being provided in a way that is equitable, accessible and safe for youth from different backgrounds and locations in Canada.

column36: A Case Study at the Intersection: Indigenous 2SLGBTQI+ Youth Mental Health System and Service Needs in Northern Saskatchewan
column37: It is essential that the nuanced needs of Indigenous youth who identify as 2SLGBTQIAP+ be prioritized within mental health systems and services. These youth are at increased risk for mental health challenges, including substance misuse, and face countless barriers to achieving optimal health and wellbeing. Unless their lived, intersectional experiences are prioritized, policies and services will continue to perpetuate inequitable services and disproportionate challenges for these underserved individuals, their families and communities. Through this catalyst grant, we seek to employ a participatory action approach to understand and develop guiding principles to improve intersectional care and supports. The project is divided into two key phases. Phase One is a week-long land and community, arts-based camp involving 20 Indigenous youth who identify as 2SLGBTQIAP+ (ages 14-21) in Prince Albert, Saskatchewan. Phase Two is a 2 day online youth-guided think-tank symposium with health care providers and service organizations to develop recommendations to improve mental health and harm reduction policies. This workshop will be based on the findings and discussions from phase one youth engagement and healthcare input into key discussion points. The think-tank will be led by youth, supported by healthcare and community team members acting in the spirit of allyship for youth. Decision-makers attending the think-tank will be expected to also act as allies for change. Our team is comprised of diverse genders and people with both lived and employment experience supporting all genders as well as a combination of Indigenous and settler Canadians, with a strong Indigenous led community component. Outputs from this implementation science and knowledge mobilization study will include a community art exhibition that highlights lived challenges and possible solutions, infographics, policy recommendations, a white paper, as well as academic presentations and publications.

column36: Reimagining Care: Developing a Strategic Framework in Child and Youth Mental Health for Immigrant, Refugee and Racialized Families.
column37: Over one million children and youth in Canada experience a mental disorder requiring professional care, however most children in need of care do not receive appropriate treatments. Immigrant, refugee, and racialized families disproportionately experience even greater barriers to accessing care due to multiple factors including lack of awareness of services, socioeconomic conditions, stigma, discrimination, and models of care that are not culturally tailored/responsive. Despite identification of these inequities, little progress has been made to address the issues - likely due to structural and systemic issues all stemming from scarce or non-existent guidelines. The Evergreen Report, developed in 2010, was the first Canadian mental health framework for children and youth, however, it did not recognize the significant and unique barriers that immigrant, refugee, and racialized families face. It is time to revisit, update and reimagine a national mental health strategic framework with a particular focus on immigrant, refugee and racialized children and youth. Specifically, we aim to: 1) integrate existing data from ongoing work in Ontario to identify barriers and facilitators of accessing and utilizing mental health services in immigrant, refugee and racialized families; 2) co-design a national child and youth mental health framework on equitable service provision and access for immigrant, refugee and racialized families; and 3) co-design implementation strategies for the recommendations and guidelines developed within the framework with our current partners in Ontario. A new Canadian framework is needed to ensure that health equity is woven into the fabric of guidelines and practices so that children from varied ethnic, cultural, and linguistic backgrounds are receiving the most appropriate and best care possible.

column36: Examining the correlates of adaptive functioning in neurodevelopmental conditions: data from the Province of Ontario Neurodevelopmental Network
column37: More than one million children in Canada have a neurodevelopmental condition such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Adaptive functioning impacts the ability to live independently and achieve positive academic and employment outcomes, and is an important area for intervention. We know very little about what helps children and youth learn adaptive functioning skills. A better understanding of these factors will help us to design and deliver timely interventions to improve adaptive functioning. To fill this gap, we will examine how genetics, behaviours, and sociodemographic factors are associated with adaptive functioning in neurodevelopmental conditions. We will use data from the Province of Ontario Neurodevelopmental (POND) Network, which includes data for more than 3,000 children with neurodevelopmental conditions. Statistical modelling will be used to understand how these variables impact adaptive functioning. Interventions that improve adaptive functioning for children with neurodevelopmental conditions can change long-term outcomes such as mental health, employment, and independence, and in turn benefit the individuals, the healthcare system, and the Canadian society. Understanding the factors impacting adaptive functioning will fill an important gap in this area and contribute to the development of personalised and targeted interventions that can meet the unique needs of children with neurodevelopmental conditions.

column36: Childhood Grief in Canada: Understanding Prevalence, Demographics, and Disparities
column37: Experiencing the death of a parent or sibling during childhood can have a life-long impact on a child's health and wellbeing. While there are agencies available to support grieving children across the country, it is not clear how many children might be grieving at any given time. Through this research we will identify the number of Canadian children less than 19 years of age who are grieving the death of a parent or sibling as well as their demographics and distribution provincially and nationally. The Child Bereavement Estimation Model (CBEM) has been used in the US to identify the number of children grieving a parent or sibling death. We will use the Canadian Vital Statistics Database and the Census of the population to adapt this model to the Canadian context. The Canadian model will enable us to look at ethnicity, immigration, and Indigenous status to address the need for diversity data in Canada. We will also examine neighbourhood income, to enable targeting of services to geographic areas with greater needs; and cause of death, to enable distinction between sudden (e.g., motor vehicle accidents, homicide, suicide, COVID) vs. expected (e.g., cancer) death. This distinction is important as some programs provide anticipatory grief support to children whose parent or sibling has a serious illness, others focus only on support after a death, while others offer both types of support. Cause of death data will help identify the number of children needing each type of support to help tailor service availability. This project provides a critical foundation for the development and delivery of grief supports to address the complex and varied needs of Canadian children, youth, and their families ultimately improving health outcomes.

column36: Estimating the number of children who experience parental incarceration and describing their health status using linked whole population data for five Canadian provinces: The CHIRP (Children with IncarceRated Parents) Study
column37: In Canada, it is estimated that thousands of children experience parental incarceration, posing serious risks to their healthy development and exacerbating health inequities. We lack population-level data on the number of children who experience parental incarceration and on their health status, despite clear importance for policy and programs, as well as United Nations obligations to collect these data and to assess the impacts of public policies on child health. In this project, we will use data available through a new Statistics Canada platform to estimate the number of children who experience parental incarceration in Canada and to examine available health status indicators. column36: Applying attachment theory to perinatal mental health problems and their links with early postpartum parental functioning: A trans-diagnostic perspective using perinatal longitudinal cohorts.
column37: Pregnancy and the transition to parenthood can reactivate memories of one's own relationship with one's parents. Recent studies on postpartum depression and anxiety use attachment theory to better understand why certain people might be more at risk. For instance, adults with an insecure attachment style (i.e., either difficulty trusting others or being overly dependent in relationships) could be more at risk for experiencing anxious and depressive symptoms when their child is born. However, we do not know if parents with an insecure attachment style are also more at risk for experiencing anxious and depressive symptoms during pregnancy and if parents' own attachment style can help explain why many parents with perinatal anxiety and depression also have trouble bonding with their infants and feeling competent as a parent. We will use four large Canadian studies to answer these questions. A study of 460 patients who received mental health care during pregnancy and after giving birth (QPMD) and three studies of families in the community: MAVAN (N=590); 3D (N=2,366); RESPPA (N=1,794). We expect that an insecure adult attachment style leads to lower mother-infant bonding and parental competence, possibly through increasing anxious and depressive symptoms during pregnancy and after giving birth. Findings can help professionals find better ways to predict who might be most at risk, by not only asking questions about parents' mental health but also their own attachment experiences. Questionnaires on adult attachment can be given at any time during pregnancy or even before, and results tend to be fairly stable. This kind of information could also contribute to a better understanding of how risk can be passed on from one generation to the next, and to design interventions that empower expectant and new parents struggling with anxiety and depression in their parenting skills, thereby supporting their children's mental resilience from the earliest moments of life.

column36: Predictors of Adherence and Healthcare Utilization in a Population Based Cohort of Children Using Long-term Ventilation at Home: A Big Data Analysis
column37: The number of children that use a mechanical ventilator (a machine that supports breathing) at home (HMV) is increasing around the world. This is because of better medical care, better ventilators to use at home and the knowledge that it is better for the entire family if the child using HMV lives at home instead of in the hospital. Although, we know that the use of a ventilator is helpful, we don't know a lot about how much these children are using their ventilators every night and we lack information on factors preventing them from using their ventilator. The pandemic led to an improvement in virtual care. Many programs caring for kids using HMV can now link via Bluetooth to the ventilators to learn about how these machines are being used every night. We now have an opportunity to study ventilator use (ie adherence) and health service utilization to see if using a ventilator regularly truly helps children stay out of the hospital. Our main research objective is to describe how children are using their ventilators and to understand what factors predict use of the ventilator. We will also study the patterns of health service utilization. Finally, the results of this proposed study will be used to help develop a system for the government to collect data systematically on adherence from individuals on ventilators to help individuals with poor adherence. As part of our team's previous work, we have linked some data from the Ontario Ventilator Equipment Pool (VEP) (a part of the provincial government that provides ventilators) to health administrative databases (data on health care use). For this project, we will link data on ventilator adherence from the VEP to our existing linked databases. This will be the first study in Canada to study home ventilator use and associated health care service use in children. This study will help build the foundation for policy makers to have up to date information for healthcare planning to improve patient and family centered care.

column36: Impact of Maternal Multimorbidity on Pregnancy Outcomes
column37: Chronic conditions like diabetes and depression affect half of the adult population. Multimorbidity, or the co-occurrence of multiple chronic conditions (MCC) in an individual is a growing public health problem. In Ontario, the prevalence of MCC increased from 25% in 2003 to 32% in 2016. MCC was traditionally considered a problem of aging. However, MCC is common even in women of reproductive age: 18% of 18 to 44-year-olds are affected. This suggests MCC may be important in pregnancy-related health. Yet, while a woman with a chronic condition is more likely to have pregnancy complications, research and health care focus on single chronic conditions rather than the combined effects of MCC. Our goal is to examine the impact of pre-pregnancy MCC on pregnancy complications, including maternal acute hospital care, severe complications and mortality, pregnancy loss, preterm birth, and small size for gestational age. We will use linked data from Ontario health records to identify all women with a pregnancy conceived in 2012-2020. We will examine women with multiple, one, and no chronic conditions. In our analyses, we will determine whether MCC increases the risk of pregnancy complications according to the number of chronic conditions, complexity of MCC, specific clusters of chronic conditions, and overall morbidity severity; and evaluate whether social and health care access inequities worsen the risk of pregnancy complications related to MCC. Our findings will improve the health care system: Evidence of increasing risk of pregnancy complications associated with a rising number of chronic conditions will lead to development of multidisciplinary health care services that address the full range of needs of women with MCC and their newborns. Pregnancy complications affect long-term maternal and child outcomes. Therefore, efforts to address MCC in pregnant women will positively impact women and the next generation.

column36: Emergency general surgical conditions in pregnancy and the post-partum period: A population-based study of maternal and peri-natal outcomes
column37: Emergency general surgical (EGS) conditions are very common. EGS patients present with a variety of infectious and obstructive conditions of the gastrointestinal tract which often require urgent infection control and/or the resolution of obstruction through surgical, image-guided, and/or endoscopic interventions. Non-obstetric abdominopelvic surgery for EGS conditions such as appendicitis and gallstone disease occurs in 0.2-0.5% of pregnancies - with over 358,000 deliveries in Canada per year this is equivalent to over 1,800 emergency procedures during pregnancy every year for appendicitis and gallstone disease alone. Despite how common these conditions are, significant diagnostic and management challenges during pregnancy remain. Risks of ionizing radiation from CT scans and lower diagnostic yield of abdominal sonography, as well as the presence of physiologic leukocytosis and nausea during pregnancy, can lead to delayed diagnosis. Despite the fact that emergency surgery is often necessary and supported by guidelines, patients and surgeons may be reluctant to proceed out of concern for fetal wellbeing intraoperatively, and fetal loss or preterm birth postoperatively. Our objective is to improve the care of EGS conditions during pregnancy and postpartum by filling these knowledge gaps through a population-based analysis of a broad group of EGS conditions in pregnancy and the post-partum period with a focus on maternal and peri-natal outcomes. Our work will inform opportunities for care standardization which may lead to more timely diagnosis. Understanding maternal and neonatal outcomes can support pregnant patients and their health care providers in understanding risks and benefits of undergoing a major surgery during pregnancy and inform their choices.

column36: Identifying long-term predictors of young adults not in education, employment, or training (NEET)
column37: Young people who are not in education, employment, or training (NEET) are at risk for a number of poor outcomes related to their health and their social and economic lives. There is currently a lack of research on youth who are NEET that has studied individuals from a long-term perspective to understand what predicts becoming NEET and how this can be prevented. The primary goal of the proposed project is to use Canadian data to investigate childhood and adolescent predictors of NEET status in early adulthood, and to identify potentially protective factors that might help reduce the likelihood of becoming NEET. This study will use data from more than 6,000 participants in the National Longitudinal Survey of Children and Youth (NLSCY), a longitudinal study of Canadian children followed every two years from 1994/95 to 2008/09, and collected data on numerous aspects of their lives, including information about their families, their mental health, and major stressors. The NLSCY has recently been linked by Statistics Canada to income tax data, which allows us to identify NEET status at age 24. Results of this investigation will identify potentially modifiable factors on the pathway towards marginalization in young adulthood.

column36: A comprehensive analysis of the associations of youth cannabis use with physical health, mental health, and socioeconomic outcomes over four decades of life: a population-based study of 3 longitudinal cohorts
column37: Cannabis use in youth is an important public health concern, especially as it often starts in young teens. Although the association between cannabis use and negative mental health outcomes is subject to ongoing research and debate, studies show that a substantial proportion of individuals who use cannabis also report mental health problems. Harms associated with cannabis use are of particular concern for adolescents and young adults, whose brains are still developing. To inform clinical care and public health prevention policy, it is essential to better understand which patterns of cannabis use are associated with negative long-term outcomes. Our objective is to investigate the associations between youth cannabis use and later physical health, mental health, and psychosocial outcomes across four decades of life. We will measure these outcomes using objective administrative data on healthcare utilization and governmental tax reports linked to three large population-based longitudinal: the Quebec Longitudinal Study of Kindergarten Children and the Montreal Longitudinal Experimental Study (participants born in 1979, follow-up until their 40s), and the Quebec Longitudinal Study of Child Development (participants born in 1998/99, follow-up until age 23). We will examine clinically relevant patterns of cannabis use across adolescence that consider both the age of onset and the frequency of cannabis use. Importantly, we will use a robust analysis strategy to account for potential confounding factors, including the concurrent use of other substances. Sex- and gender-specific patterns of associations will be documented. Our findings will allow clinicians, researchers, and policymakers to develop better prevention and treatment programs to avoid possible consequences of cannabis use in the short and long term.

column36: Examining reproductive health outcomes of females diagnosed with young-onset colorectal cancer (EXPAND-yCRC)
column37: Colorectal cancer is the second most common form of cancer in Canada. Though it was long considered a disease among older adults, it is now frequently striking in younger adults who are diagnosed at less than 50 years of age. This includes information on all doctors' visits, hospitalizations, prescription medications, and diagnosed cancers. Using this data, we will study reproductive health outcomes of female patients with yCRC including pregnancy outcomes of mother and baby. It also has the potential to bridge research, awareness-raising, and advocacy for the reproductive health needs of yCRC patients.

column36: Genetic influences on the mean and variance of DNA methylation in early life to understand the biological underpinnings of childhood complex conditions.
column37: DNA methylation (DNAm) is an important determinant of how our genes are turned on and off, both as part of normal human development, and in response to different environmental exposures. DNAm is thought to contribute to the risk of disease, but large numbers of people are required to detect these associations. On the other hand, we can use statistical methods to link multiple existing data types and databases to answer questions on the role of DNAm in disease that no single dataset can answer alone. We will use newly generated data on genetic factors and DNAm, as well as existing data on environmental exposures, from >800 children followed from birth in the Canadian Healthy Infant Longitudinal Development (CHILD) Study. Second, we will use statistical methods to link these data with separate studies of genetic factors and disease risk, for example, asthma, that include tens of thousands of individuals. In this way, we will identify DNAm patterns in early childhood that affect disease risk. The CHILD study is the ideal dataset for this project as few other studies have the same richness of genetic, epigenetic, and environmental data as we have for CHILD participants. Our project team is well equipped to analyze these multiple data types, and our project will lead to a better understanding of the biology behind common childhood diseases like asthma.

column36: Determining the Role of Fathers in the Developmental Origins of Cardiovascular Health
column37: Heart disease, diabetes and stroke are major causes of disability and premature death worldwide. Although these conditions mostly affect adults, their origins can be traced back to early childhood, infancy and even before birth. Signs and symptoms that precede these serious conditions include obesity, abnormal cholesterol and high blood pressure, and are often referred to as cardiovascular disease (CVD). The causes of CVD are unknown, but many risk factors have been proposed, including mothers' health and poor nutrition. The role of the fathers in the origins of CVD is understudied. Since prevention might be possible if early signs and risk factors can be addressed, it is critical to understand the role of fathers in the origins of CVD. The objective of this project is to evaluate the contribution of fathers' health to CVD risk factors in children (from birth until the age of 8 years) in the CHILD Cohort Study. The CHILD study has followed many Canadian children and their families, from when the mother was pregnant until the child turned 8 years of age, to collect information about the health, diet and experiences of the parents and children. In this project, we will use this information to determine fathers' impact on children's health. We propose to analyze existing data to calculate a father's scale of CVD and relate those to children's CVD risk factors from birth until the age of 8 years. This study provides the unique opportunity to directly determine whether periconception modifiable factors, such as paternal health, are related to cardiovascular health in children after accounting for maternal factors (e.g., health & diet). Our research will inform evidence-based recommendations for preconception paternal health and contribute to new strategies for preventing these serious conditions in future generations of Canadian children.

column36: Urban trail expansion and mental health of children and adolescents -
column37: For the past 4 years, our team has been studying the impact of cycling and walking trails on the health of people living in urban areas. We discovered that when cities build trails, people use them. In Winnipeg, over 1.6M people were counted on four large cycling trails since their construction. The trails also are linked to better health outcomes in adults. Unfortunately, these trails were not constructed in an equitable way. First Nations and Metis children and adolescents living in Winnipeg were less likely to have access to the trails. First Nations and Metis children and adolescents also also fare more likely to experience mental health disorders. column36: Health, education, judicial and social outcomes of Manitoba children exposed to intimate partner violence: a population-based study
column37: A child in Manitoba witnesses intimate partner violence (IPV) every two hours. Children who grow up in households with IPV are more likely to have behavioural problems, high stress levels, and trouble with school. There is less research that follows children through their childhood and into adulthood to describe longer term effects of growing up in an environment with IPV. Our goal is to describe the relationship between physical, mental, educational, and social outcomes in childhood and young adulthood among children whose mothers are exposed to IPV compared to their peers who have not been exposed to IPV. We will also identify factors that may protect these children from experiencing worse outcomes. We will use existing data at the Manitoba Center for Health Policy to identify women who pressed charges for IPV before their child turned 18 years old. We will compare outcomes of their children to children of mothers who do not press charges for IPV. Child outcomes will be measured for up to 20 years after IPV charges. We will examine the child's risk of having a future mental or physical health disorders and determine how IPV exposure impacts children's school performance. We will assess factors that may protect children from the harmful effects of IPV exposure, such as their mother not being diagnosed with a mental disorder or only pressing charges for IPV once. This will help doctors, social workers, and educators best support children following negative childhood experiences. The results will also be important to help advocate for social programming and support for these youth.

column36: HIV Pathogenesis and Viral Control
column37: Dr. Eric J. Arts, Professor, Executive Director of the ImPaKT Center, holds a CRC Tier I entitled HIV Pathogenesis and Viral Control. Dr. Arts was recruited back to Canada in 2014 with a renewed investment for infectious disease research. Dr. Arts oversaw a 40% increase in grant funding, recruitment of six faculty, renovation of 8000 sq.ft. open lab for virology faculty, increased international notoriety, developed a new global health graduate program, and guided design of the $18M CL2+/3 facility, Imaging of Pathogens for Knowledge Translation. Dr. Arts obtained $21M in grant funding, $8M in infrastructure grants, $7M for his team-based research program, and a further $4M for research projects/contracts through ImPaKT. Since 2014, Dr. Arts has published 42 articles, provided 43 invited presentations and 30 community presentations, had his trainees present a further 32 abstracts, and participated in over 150 interviews for the media. During his renewed CRC, Dr. Arts has four main research themes/objectives: 1) Developing a detailed understanding of the viral properties controlling HIV-1 transmission through sexual contact. The Arts lab have evidence that glycan composition on HIV-1 envelope protein may the key determinant of transmission while investigating if the vaginal tract milieu, e.g. cytokine/chemokine levels and microbiome will also impact heterosexual transmission efficiency. Research on viral transmission properties will be key for the next objective, 2) developing an HIV vaccine based on the HIV-1 transmission properties. Dr. Arts will continue his collaboration with Dr. Gary Kobinger to adapt and test VSV-based HIV-1 vaccine to express transmitted/founder Env with specific "transmission glycans" and the N425K mutation with increase CD4 affinity. Objective 3), refinement to the ACT-VEC/SHC1901 therapeutic for enhanced latency reversal and subsequent viral control will continue his research program to develop and enhance a new target cure therapeutic now entering phase I trials with a license to SHC Therapeutics. With opening of ImPaKT just prior to COVID-19 pandemic, Dr. Arts developed a new applied SARS-CoV-2 research team to test 100s of antiviral products, interventions, and vaccines. Objective 4) will determine the relative pathogenic and transmission fitness of SARS-CoV-2 variants-of-concerns and work with a team of neuroscientists at Western to define the viral triggers associated with future cognitive impairments.

column36: Postnatal Neurogenesis
column37: The discovery of neural stem cells (NSCs) in the brains of all mammals, including humans, overturned the dogma that the brain is devoid of regenerative capacity. This discovery raised the exciting possibility of using the regenerative capacity of the brain to replace damaged neurons and to cure neurodegenerative diseases and brain trauma. Although promising, the use of NSCs to heal these devastating diseases is far from a given, and the promises of stem cell-based therapies cannot be fully realized without understanding the mechanisms that regulate NSC activity, the migration of neuronal precursors toward affected brain regions, and their functional integration in the adult/ageing brain during the stage when neurodegeneration mostly occurs. Furthermore, postnatal neurogenic regions may be an ideal model system to decipher the precise alterations underlying rare human neurodevelopmental disorders. While recent progress in genome-wide sequencing approaches now provides an effective way to discover new genes involved in neurological disorders, we still do not know which neurodevelopmental process goes awry in a given rare neurodevelopmental disorder. The modeling and identification of exact alterations in the developmental trajectories of human cells in an in vivo context where a myriad of molecular factors and inter-cellular interactions are impinging on them are particularly important for designing new strategies for the diagnosis and treatment of neurodevelopmental disorders. Dr. Armen Saghatelyan's Canada Research Chair research program aims at addressing these two major hurdles. He will first use postnatal neurogenesis and the rodent olfactory system to understand the molecular and cellular pathways that orchestrate the natural neuronal replacement process starting from stem cell activation to neuronal migration and integration as well as the functional role of new neurons in a fully formed neural network. He will then, in collaboration with clinicians working with rare human neurodevelopmental disorders, use combinations of human progenitor cells and animal models to decipher the precise developmental alterations underlying rare neurodevelopmental disorders. Altogether, this research program will advance our knowledge of the fundamental mechanisms orchestrating neuronal development in the adult brain and allow the establishment of a new platform for understanding the specific neurodevelopmental alterations underlying rare neurodevelopmental disorders.

column36: Cardiovascular Medicine
column37: Heart disease, stroke and vascular dementia are leading causes of disability and premature death worldwide. Together these conditions are major contributors to the global burden of non-communicable diseases. These disorders often co-exist and each worsens prognosis of the others. Common to all these conditions is injury and inflammation of small blood vessels, which is a characteristic feature of hypertension (high blood pressure). Injured small vessels also called 'small vessel disease' (SVD) leads to damage of target organs eg. the heart and brain, predisposing to heart failure and stroke, with potentially fatal cardiovascular events, hence the notion 'small vessels, big problems'. Drug development for SVD has been hampered by poor understanding of what triggers the transition from vascular health to vascular damage. The Touyz lab defined some molecular mechanisms involved in this process. In particular she showed that uncontrolled production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (termed oxidative stress) in vascular smooth muscle and endothelial cells causes abnormal signaling and altered vascular function, processes critically involved in SVD and hypertension. While extensive pre-clinical studies support this notion, this has not translated to the clinic, due in large part to lack of understanding of the causes of oxidative stress in human vascular disease. In her quest to unravel the basis of oxidative stress, she identified Nox5 as a major source of ROS generation in vascular cells in humans. However despite Nox5 being a key ROS-generating oxidase, little is known about its role in human health and disease. This CRC program aims to discover molecular mechanisms that regulate Nox5 and redox signaling in the vascular system and to delineate how activated Nox5 leads to oxidative stress, and vascular damage in hypertension and clinical sequelae of SVD, specifically of the heart and brain. Dr Touyz is uniquely positioned to fill knowledge gaps in Nox5 and redox pathobiology in the clinical context, through human biobanks, patient cohorts and novel pre-clinical models. She will take an innovative integrated approach using discovery science, human mechanistic studies, reverse-translational research and clinical studies to tackle the unknowns of Nox5 in human vascular disease. Her ambition in the long term is to discover mechanism- and disease-specific treatments to restore vascular health in patients by targeting the Nox5/ROS system

column36: Critical Illness Outcomes and the Recovery Continuum
column37: Historically, the field of Critical Care Medicine had focused almost exclusively on the 28-day survival of patients after the onset of critical illness as the main outcome measure for clinical studies. Over the past 24 years, Dr. Margaret Herridge has fundamentally changed the understanding of the devastating and enduring functional and neuropsychological disability and complex multimorbidities experienced by critically ill patients, their caregivers and families. Her research has fostered a complete reframing of the approach to critical illness to embrace a new model of a continuum of care. This model includes a longer time horizon of one year or more for follow-up and the evaluation of multidimensional outcomes to address the needs of these vulnerable patients and their families. The proposed research program builds on Dr. Herridge's foundational work by further developing, testing and establishing a continuum of care pathway for patients and families after critical illness as a clinical standard of care. It is based on three approaches: 1) the acquisition of granular multidimensional outcomes across diverse populations of critically ill patients and families (e.g., prolonged mechanical ventilation, severe COVID-19 infection, and women and vulnerable populations); 2) the creation and testing of this new continuum of care pathway for patients and families after critical illness; and 3) the establishment of the first Canada-wide consortium for continuum of care after critical illness, including a network of follow-up programs to facilitate excellence in interprofessional clinical care while providing a structure for ongoing clinical, basic and translational research. This pathway is a Canadian and international innovation for patient care and research during and after critical illness. The proposed program will mitigate the discontinuity and burden of care transitions for patients; it will also optimize communication and knowledge transfer among critical care practitioners, interprofessional team members, longitudinal specialists and primary care physicians. This research is urgent and timely for post-COVID-19 critically ill patients and their families, whose longer-term needs are currently unmet. The outcomes of the proposed research will have direct benefits for those experiencing critical illness, contribute towards improved quality of life for affected caregivers and families, and help reduce the burden of critical illness on communities worldwide.

column36: Multiple Sclerosis
column37: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a degenerative, debilitating autoimmune disease affecting 2.8 million people worldwide. In MS, self-targeting white blood cells by-pass the central nervous system (CNS) vascular barriers to enter the brain and spinal cord where they cause tissue destruction, manifesting as brain lesions. The clinical evolution of MS and response to treatment are variable and unpredictable. Understanding how white blood cells infiltrate the brain, the process of lesion formation, and identifying biological markers of disease evolution would greatly benefit clinical care of people with MS. To this end, I have developed an innovative research program, and forming the foundation of my program are: Objective 1 to elucidate the mechanisms underlying white blood cells migration into the CNS, Objective 2 to characterize the differences between types of brain lesions, and Objective 3 to find biological markers of MS disease. As a clinician and researcher, I have a privileged access to extensive clinical databases and valuable biological samples from different types of MS patients (fresh and preserved brain tissue, serum, and isolated white blood cells). To address my three objectives, I will use these resources along with models mimicking the CNS vascular barriers, animal models of the disease, and artificial intelligence approaches. I will identify novel therapeutic targets by determining the specific molecules that govern the migration of white blood cells across the CNS barriers. Furthermore, I will provide a deep understanding of the molecular features across the different types of lesions to allow a rare characterization of MS pathology. Finding markers of MS disease evolution will allow clinicians to determine whether the patients will have a mild or aggressive disease, and therefore will aid rational treatment decisions. Ultimately, the combination of these broad scientific approaches of my three objectives will allow a holistic understanding of MS that will improve the clinical care of people with MS.

column36: Musculoskeletal and Postmenopausal Health
column37: Musculoskeletal health is a major determinant of overall health and well-being of the aging individual. Yet, of all the organs in our body, it is the least researched and understood. Osteoporosis (loss of bone mass and strength leading to fractures) and sarcopenia (loss of muscle and function) are common with aging, affecting more women than men. Many diseases, conditions and medications can lead to the loss of bone and muscle, impacting on function, and resulting in decreased quality of life and increased mortality. Dr. Cheung's research program focuses on musculoskeletal health with three major areas of investigation: 1) developing and testing innovative diagnostics, including imaging and biomarkers; 2) examining determinants of bone and muscle health; and 3) investigating health outcomes and effectiveness of potential therapeutic options. She takes a cross-disciplinary integrative approach, combining engineering, basic science, clinical medicine and complementary and alternative medicine using state-of-the-art methodologies and technologies such as adaptive platform trials, artificial intelligence/machine learning and multi-omic analyses. She pulls in expertise from various disciplines and acts as the enzyme for cross-disciplinary collaborations. Her study populations include those with common conditions (such as osteoporosis and sarcopenia), rare conditions (such as atypical femur fractures, fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva and osteogenesis imperfecta), as well as new evolving conditions (such as COVID-19). She adopts a patient-centred approach, and partners with patient organizations and other stakeholders throughout the development of her protocols to dissemination of new information and insights. She advocates for diversity and inclusion in her patient populations and studies sex/gender and racial differences in disease presentation, progression and response to treatment. Her key aim is to improve the health of Canadians through rapid translation of knowledge to action and evidence-based clinical guidelines using the totality of what is known and available.

column37: Uncontrolled pain continues to be the single most common cause of disability that impairs the quality of life. It remains difficult to treat; complete pain control is rarely achieved and disabling side effects are frequent. Persistent, untreated pain is associated with several brain disorders, including cognitive deficits, anxiety, depression, and addiction. The general objective of this chair is to elucidate how pain signals are processed by our nervous system and how brain centres are altered in chronic pain conditions. Towards this, several new light-based technologies are developed and exploited to understand, and eventually treat pathological pain and related brain disorders.

column36: Oral Health Nanomedicine
column37: Communication and crosstalk between macrophages i.e. immune cells, and precursor cells regulate wound healing and tissue regeneration. Dr. Kishen has discovered a multifunctional nanoparticle system that will enable control of macrophages and communication with precursor cells, leading to accelerated wound healing and improved tissue regeneration. This research program has four interrelated objectives. Objectives 1 and 2 focus on developing 3D matrix-based tissue grafts with heterogenous cell populations for novel tooth-on-a-chip and 3D diabetic wound models. These models will be used to decipher the mechanisms of cellular functions and crosstalk in disease and healing. A novel single molecule based biochemical and force assays will be investigated for a comprehensive understanding of early biomarkers and molecular trajectories in chronic inflammation. Themes 3 and 4 will characterize nanoparticle-guided immune modulatory effect using single molecule assays in 3D tissue grafts simulating apical periodontitis and chronic diabetic wounds. The proposed research will optimize novel tissue graft models, untangle the dynamics of molecular mechanisms of cellular functions in chronic inflammation, and translate fundamental knowledge for nanoparticle-based new technologies.
