column36: Primary Health Care and Health Equity
column37: Health inequity refers to the avoidable disparities in health between groups and people. Primary health care refers to the first contact between patients and the health care system and is usually provided by family physicians. Primary health care occurs across the patient's life course, and ideally, with an ongoing relationship between the patient and provider. Nursing professionals in primary health care promote health equity by addressing the social determinants of health and social care needs at the individual and family level. Primary health care nurses assess social care needs, review and adapt care plans, and refer patients to and coordinate care with other professional and social services providers. Dr. Mathews' Canada Research Chair (CRC) program focuses on nursing professionals, specifically registered nurses in primary care settings (otherwise known as family practice nurses), nurse practitioners, community health nurses, and licensed practical nurses in primary health care teams. The program is unique in its pragmatic approach, systems perspective, and consideration of health workforce issues in conjunction with health service delivery and outcomes. It also focuses on two practice contexts, a pandemic and rural communities, that are under-represented in the literature. The goal of the CRC program is to further the integration of nursing professionals in primary health care. The program examines the relationship between funding models and activities of family practice nurses; describes the roles of primary health care nurses during the COVID19 pandemic; evaluates the Primary Care Diabetes Support Program, an innovative model of chronic disease management; and compares the quality of care and patient experiences in nurse-led models of care in rural communities. The applied health services and policy research program includes mixed and multiple method studies that use an integrated knowledge translation approach. The program develops methodological tools with which to evaluate nurse integration in the provision of care. Dr. Mathews collaborates with other researchers, clinicians, health care organizations, and policy makers. The CRC program draws upon her expertise in health workforce, rural populations, and quantitative and qualitative health research methods; provides an excellent platform to train students and mentor junior researchers; and includes knowledge mobilization strategies to inform policy making and care delivery.

column36: Spinal Cord Injury
column37: This research program seeks to develop new therapeutic approaches for acute spinal cord injury (SCI) through bi-directional translational research (both bench-to-bedside and bedside-back-to-bench). The strategy will be to focus on approaches that are either actionable or would accelerate the pace by which new treatments can be brought forward to patients. The proposed research program covers four themes: 1. improving the hemodynamic management of acute SCI through the development of novel technologies to monitor the spinal cord and methods for supporting the blood supply and oxygenation of the injured spinal cord. 2. advancing preclinical development of new therapies such as biologics to enhance neural regeneration, implants to wirelessly monitor bladder pressure, and biodistribution studies that would guide the optimal delivery of treatments in human clinical trials. 3. biobanking of blood, cerebrospinal fluid, and spinal cord tissue to better understand the biology of human spinal cord injury, and to share valuable human biospecimens with the international research community in order to accelerate the global pace of discovery for SCI. This will be done within the International Spinal Cord Injury Biobank (ISCIB) that was established in this research program. 4. establishing biomarkers within blood and cerebrospinal fluid to objectively and more accurately r classify injury severity and predict outcome. Such biomarkers will facilitate the validation of other novel treatment approaches for SCI in clinical trials that are currently dependent upon functional measures of outcome. The approach will be to pursue these four themes in laboratory-based experimental studies and in hospital-based clinical trials. The research program will prioritize multi-disciplinary collaboration on a global scale and the training/mentorship of the next generation of clinicians and scientists, with an emphasis on equity, diversity and inclusivity. Establishing new treatment approaches through state-of-the-art technologies and experimental platforms will improve the lives of Canadians who suffer these devastating spinal cord injuries and reduce the considerable economic burden of paralysis.

column36: Skeletal Muscle Health in Aging
column37: Skeletal muscle is the tissue responsible for locomotion. Impairments in its function can lead to problems with mobility and, if severe, result in disability. Problems with mobility and the risk of overt disability increase with age, which is in part a function of both the loss and malfunction of skeletal muscle. Skeletal muscle also has several underappreciated roles in metabolic health. It is the largest site of post-meal blood glucose storage and is a substantial contributor to resting metabolic rate, which is the largest proportion of daily energy expenditure for most people and thus important in regulating body weight. Hence, loss of muscle to the point that it affects mobility, known as sarcopenia, affects 25% of Canadians over age 65 and 45% of those over 80. Adults with sarcopenia are at a greater risk of physical disability, developing type 2 diabetes, and an elevated risk for premature mortality. The aim of CRC renewal - Skeletal Muscle Health in Aging - is to further understand the mechanisms governing sarcopenic muscle loss with aging, to investigate the combination of exercise and nutritional or nutraceutical means to mitigate sarcopenic muscle loss, and to develop age- and ability-appropriate interventions to allow older people to retain their muscle mass and function, reducing the risk of physical disability and metabolic disease. We will primarily employ studies of older (>65yr) men and women and use invasive procedures (blood and tissue biopsy) combined with stable isotope measures of muscle protein turnover. The aim is to conduct proof-of-concept trials in humans, confirm results in cell models, and then test promising nutritional/nutraceutical strategies in combination with exercise in larger clinical trials. These studies will yield discoveries grounded in mechanistic evidence and clinical trial outcomes to alleviate the impact of age-related sarcopenia. Older people who are mobility compromised are more likely to be institutionalized, socially isolated, hospitalized, and experience a lower quality of life. Sarcopenia in aging is a major contributor to mobility decline and disability. The interrelationship between sarcopenia and mobility disability means there is a critical opportunity to change older people's mobility and accompanying health trajectory by addressing declines in skeletal muscle function-interventions in older persons addressing mobility decline earlier result in better long-term outcomes.

column36: Cardiovascular Immunology
column37: Cardiovascular disease is a leading cause of death in Canada. Inflammation plays an important role in disease progression. Inflammatory cells can build up on the walls of arteries as plaque, a pattern of disease known as atherosclerosis. This in turn can progress to aneurysm formation, heart attack or other serious conditions. Many of the immunological mechanisms that are involved in disease progression are not well understood. Dr. Clinton Robbins is researching how inflammatory cells that contribute to cardiovascular disease-namely monocytes and macrophages-develop, accumulate within arteries, and either remain, die or leave. He is a world expert in immunology, particularly within the context of cardiovascular disease. He has made key discoveries in this area, including on factors that support monocyte development and maintenance, the local proliferation of macrophages in atherosclerosis, and how different macrophage populations are involved in atherosclerosis. Using state-of-the-art tools for profiling and tracking cells, Dr. Robbins' proposed research program will further explore the roles of inflammatory cells in cardiovascular disease. He will examine how different macrophage populations contribute to the progression of aortic aneurysms induced by cigarette smoke, how the micro-environments in which macrophages and their precursors arise participate in atherosclerosis, and how vascular and immune dysregulation can exacerbate cardiac injury from the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Dr. Robbins' research will strengthen our understanding of the molecular and cellular processes that are involved in cardiovascular disease. His research will reveal new targets for interventions that will improve the health of Canadians and people worldwide.

column36: Children's Pain
column37: Children's pain is a critical challenge due to its pervasiveness (one in five children has chronic pain), the degree of suffering it creates for both children and families, its association with lifelong avoidance of healthcare (such as vaccine hesitancy), the risks it presents for opioid addiction, chronic pain, and depression in adulthood (two-thirds of children with chronic pain carry their pain burden into adulthood), and its enormous health system costs (~$40B was spent on chronic pain in Canada in 2019). Canada is a world leader in children's pain research; a seminal (2012) report on The State of Science and Technology identified pediatric pain as the #1 research cluster in Canada vis-a-vis the rest of the world. Yet children in Canada and their families continue to suffer due to undertreatment and failure to prevent pain. There is an urgent need both to generate new knowledge about children's pain and to ensure it is translated into improvements in practice and policy. The Canada Research Chair in Children's Pain will combine Dr. Chambers' highly successful and productive 20+ year research program with her recognized leadership and strengths in knowledge mobilization and patient engagement to improve the understanding and management of children's pain. The Chair's program will focus on three areas in children's pain: 1) family factors; 2) psychological factors; and 3) implementation science and knowledge mobilization. The research approach will use multiple methods and integrated knowledge mobilization in which best and emerging practices in three cross-cutting themes will be applied: a) sex- and gender-based analysis plus (SGBA+); b) patient-oriented research (POR); and c) equity, diversity, and inclusion (EDI). The program will support collaborations between researchers and knowledge users from various disciplines, sectors, and institutions (e.g., industry, government, not-for-profits) at the local, national, and international levels, and will leverage the Chair's highly successful national knowledge mobilization network, Solutions for Kids in Pain (SKIP). Students from different disciplines and stages of training will benefit from the Chair's track record in launching trainees' careers. New knowledge about children's pain will be generated and translated into evidence-based solutions that will reduce the deleterious effects of pain and positively impact the health and well-being of children and their families in Canada and around the world.

column36: Craniofacial and Dental Development
column37: Dr. Richman's research is focused on studying the biologically resilient molecular pathways that lead to normal craniofacial and dental development. Failure of these mechanisms results in malformations or rare genetic diseases, while in-depth knowledge of these mechanisms can lead to therapies to prevent or reduce the severity of these maladies. Dr. Richman is a uniquely trained pediatric dentist and clinician scientist who treats patients at BC Children's Hospital Dental Department. She has often seen how a child is born with a malformation such as cleft lip with or without cleft palate that could not have been anticipated during the pregnancy. Even a prenatal diagnosis of a genetic disease does not predict the severity of the condition. Other factors besides genes clearly modify the risk. Dr. Richman will initiate a novel research program to study normal developmental instability that is present in all embryos. She will define the processes and molecules that buffer against insults in the chicken embryo face. She is using the chicken embryo because facial development is genetically similar to humans and the embryo is directly accessible for experiments. These studies will be extended to find factors that tip the balance towards cleft lip or failure to form teeth and then will rescue these defects. The aim is to find the molecular pathways that accentuate embryo resilience so that defects can be prevented or severity reduced. Her priority for the clefting research will be to discover safe supplements that can be taken during pregnancy, similar to folic acid. However folic acid has not improved clefting prevalence in Canada, therefore other pathways will be explored. Dr. Richman's rare genetic disease work will identify downstream pathways that can be used to correct the cell signaling defects and thus improve developmental outcomes. The tooth research proposed will involve a novel model, the leopard gecko. Dr. Richman is studying how teeth are replaced indefinitely in the gecko. She aims to apply her findings to missing human teeth. She is also examining how teeth become loose and are lost in the gecko. These results will shed light on a major clinical problem, the unwanted enzymatic digestion of roots, a similar process to osteoporosis. Dr. Richman will translate her gecko tooth findings to new treatments to preserve tooth structure. Dr. Richman receives highly competitive CIHR, NIH and NSERC funds to support these discoveries.

column36: Molecular and Genomic Pathology
column37: Dr. David Huntsman, the Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Molecular and Genomic Pathology, has led a clinically and scientifically impactful research program focused on gynecologic and rare cancers. Through his laboratory's previous efforts, Dr. Huntsman has identified the key mutations that underpin a range of diseases from hereditary stomach cancer through to multiple subtypes of ovarian cancer. Dr. Huntsman and his team have developed these as diagnostics and as tools to study cancer precursor lesions. Through research by his team and others, it is clear that mutations are only one component that defines the biology and behavior of cancers. Dr. Huntsman's future research is based on the idea that the specific features of cancers are the product of interactions between the cells of origin, mutations in the cancers, and the specific microenvironments where those cancers occur, and that by only understanding these interactions will we have optimal prevention, diagnostic and treatment strategies. Dr. Huntsman presents four projects that all connect previous results to unmet needs in gynecologic cancer through this hypothesis. The four projects include: i) a broad team effort to build off the globally impactful OVCARE ovarian cancer prevention program, ii) a more fundamental science project to understand how mutations in a gene that processes nucleic acids (Dicer) leads to a range of cancers that feature unusual cell development in order to develop much-needed treatments, iii) how cancers arise from endometriosis in the ovary and whether arising from endometriosis leads to a specific vulnerability that could be developed as a treatment strategy, and iv) a program determining the initial impacts of the most common mutations found in gynecologic cancers. These projects are all embedded within the OVCARE and Gynecologic Cancer Initiative to maximize the efficiency of knowledge translation and transfer.

column36: Microbial Diversity and Evolution
column37: Parasitism is an important aspect of biology that has received much attention at the level of short-term host-parasite interactions in medically important parasites. However we know considerably less about how parasitism has shaped biological diversity over the long term, as the origin of parasitic interactions as an evolutionary process is less well studied, and even basic facts like the biodiversity of most parasitic groups are generally only cursorily examined. Even lineages that include species of major medical significance are largely overlooked outside the groups that cause human disease or diseases in animals of agricultural importance. My work aims to develop a deeper understanding of the biology of diverse apicomplexan parasites, their diversity, host range, plastid function, all in an evolutionary framework to gain a broad picture of how these parasites originated and evolve. My proposal will mix field work and environmental microbiology methods with high-resolution 3D microscopy and culture free genomics to gain unprecedented insights into parasite evolution and the environmental diversity of parasites in key ecosystems.

column36: Swallowing and Food Oral Processing
column37: The ability to swallow food and drink is something that most of us take for granted, and an activity that is central to social interactions - whether that be a morning cup of coffee, faith-based rituals, or annual festivals like Thanksgiving. However, swallowing impairment (dysphagia) is common in many age-related disease and injury processes, and contributes to significant morbidity, mortality and health care expenditure. Aspiration (entry of food or liquid into the lower airway) is a risk for pneumonia, the most common cause of death in neurological diseases. Choking on food is also the second highest cause of preventable death among institutionalized seniors. Videofluoroscopy (VF) is an international "gold standard" dysphagia diagnostic exam. However, there is a lack of available VF reference values for healthy adults across the age span to guide interpretation. Dr. Steele's research will establish VF reference values for healthy swallowing, and identify clinical decision point values that differentiate healthy from disordered swallowing in several high-risk clinical populations. This work will enable clinicians to compare patient measures to healthy reference values, facilitating quantification and evidence-based interpretation of the presence, nature and severity of dysphagia. Current standards for swallowing assessment in Canada focus predominantly on the swallowing of liquids, with minimal attention to the chewing and oral processing of solid foods. Coroner's reports around the world suggest that inadequate oral processing is a major risk for airway obstruction and choking. A second objective of Dr. Steele's research is to develop a valid clinical method for evaluating oral processing. This will be accomplished using methods for food texture testing, developed by the International Dysphagia Diet Standardisation Initiative (IDDSI), to determine when inadequate oral processing results in food boluses that represent a risk of choking. This approach will assist clinicians in identifying choking risk and in identifying food textures that are safe or inappropriate for inclusion in diets for people with impaired oral processing. Ultimately, Dr. Steele's program of research seeks to improve mealtime safety and enjoyment for Canadians with dysphagia by shifting subjective dysphagia diagnostic practices toward a valid, quantitative, data driven diagnostic framework that will improve resource utilization, treatment planning and patient outcomes.

column36: Maternal-Child Health and HIV
column37: One of the greatest success stories of the HIV epidemic has been the dramatic reduction in the vertical transmission of HIV to children, which can occur during pregnancy and through breastfeeding. This success is achieved through global public health initiatives to provide HIV antiretroviral treatment to women with HIV, over 1.3 million of whom become pregnant each year. Children who are born HIV-exposed but uninfected are the fastest-growing HIV-affected population, numbering at over 15 million children globally. While the benefits of HIV antiretroviral use in pregnancy far outweigh the risks, pregnant women with HIV taking antiretrovirals are twice as likely to experience an adverse birth outcome as women without HIV. Furthermore, children exposed to HIV and antiretrovirals before birth are more likely to fall behind their peers in growth, motor development and language development, even though they remain HIV-free. There is an urgent need to understand the safety of antiretroviral use during pregnancy, as well as the mechanisms that contribute to the adverse birth outcomes of women with HIV and the poor developmental outcomes of their children. Dr. Lena Serghides has established a highly collaborative and internationally recognized translational research program with the goal of improving the health of women and children affected by HIV. Her research program is unique in its integration of detailed clinical studies and experimental models to address gaps in our understanding of HIV and maternal-child health. The proposed Canada Research Chair program will focus on three challenges: 1) understanding how HIV and antiretrovirals affect maternal pregnancy hormones and the placenta, and how this affects fetal development; 2) defining the mechanisms through which some antiretrovirals contribute to higher rates of congenital defects; and 3) investigating how HIV and antiretroviral exposure before birth affects a child's neurodevelopment. Dr. Serghides will help to identify the safest antiretrovirals to use in pregnancy as well as therapies to optimize birth outcomes and the long-term health of the child. Her research will improve HIV treatment guidelines and is identified as highly relevant by the HIV community. The proposed research outcomes will have direct benefits for maternal-child health, contribute towards improved quality of life for families affected by HIV, and help reduce the burden of HIV on communities worldwide.

column36: Cancer Epigenetics and Epitranscriptomics
column37: Two in five Canadians are expected to develop cancer during their lifetime. Despite recent advances in prevention, diagnosis and treatment, cancer is still the leading cause of death in Canada and remains a major health concern for Canadians. While genetic mutations are known to drive cancer, the non-genetic sources-including modifications of histone proteins, DNA and RNA, termed as epigenetics and epitranscriptomics, are increasingly being recognized as critical players in disease development and progression. Importantly, epigenetic and epitranscriptomic alterations are reversible and thus provide unique opportunities for therapeutic targeting. Dr. Housheng Hansen He's Canada Research Chair (CRC) program is focused on prostate cancer, the most common non-cutaneous cancer and the third leading cause of death from cancer in Canadian men. The program is centred on the idea that epigenetic and epitranscriptomic alterations play key roles in driving prostate cancer development and progression. His program will apply cutting-edge genomic, epigenomic and epitranscriptomic approaches to profile patient tumors from a few large clinical cohorts, and use various functional genomic screening approaches to pinpoint key epigenetic and epitranscriptomic mechanisms that drive prostate cancer progression and therapeutic resistance. This knowledge will be further exploited to develop small molecule and RNA drugs to reverse the epigenetic and epitranscriptomic alterations. In addition, multimodal liquid biopsy biomarkers will be developed to detect early progression and guide treatment. This highly translational research program is based on Dr. He's unique expertise in cancer epigenetics and epitranscriptomics, and leverages broad collaborations with basic research and clinician scientists, clinicians and pharmaceutical companies worldwide. The successful outcome of this program will advance our understanding of non-genetic drivers of prostate cancer and has great potential to impact clinical care and improve patient outcomes. While the program is mainly focused on prostate cancer, the research platform and knowledge generated will be extended to other cancer types.

column36: Acute and Chronic Pain Research
column37: Pain affects millions of people worldwide and has a profound negative impact on quality of life. Chronic pain is the most common cause of disability and can be extremely difficult to treat. Due to a lack of universally effective treatments, there is a large global effort to develop personalized approaches to managing pain. Dr. Karen Davis is a translational neuroscientist with expertise in the use of brain imaging to study acute and chronic pain. She has made significant contributions to pain research, including the first functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) evidence of how pain is represented in the brain. Her research centers on the dynamic pain connectome (DPC), the spatiotemporal pattern of brain activity that represents the cognitive, affective and sensorimotor aspects of pain. Her Canada Research Chairs program will characterize the central mechanisms underlying pain and its modulation to identify biomarkers and models to predict treatment outcomes. She will use brain imaging with MRI and magnetoencephalography, computational modelling, and psychophysical and behavioral assessments to study pain in healthy individuals and those who have a variety of chronic pain conditions. She will characterize the structural and functional connectivity of the DPC in individuals with and without chronic pain to identify features that are associated with pain and treatment outcomes (Aim 1). Next, she will use behavioural tests to evaluate how pain influences attention in individuals with and without chronic pain and identify features of DPC connectivity and activity that mediate bidirectional pain-attention interactions (Aim 2). Working with chronic pain patients who are undergoing treatment, she will examine brain-behaviour relationships that distinguish treatment responders from non-responders to build models and identify biomarkers to predict the outcomes of specific treatments (Aim 3). Across studies, she will examine individual variability and sex differences in the DPC and how these factors influence pain. Lastly, she will collaborate with bioethicists and legal scholars to survey the sentiments of chronic pain patients, health care professionals, policy makers and the public regarding the use of brain imaging to diagnose and manage pain (Aim 4). This research program will advance our fundamental understanding of pain mechanisms and accelerate the development of personalized diagnostics and therapeutics for pain.

column36: Global Health Governance
column37: Accelerated economic globalization has created both risks and benefits for population health worldwide. Effective global health governance (agreed rules and procedures, distribution of authority and shared resources) to mitigate risks, and ensure the fair distribution of benefits, remains a key challenge. The proposed research program focuses on two key issue areas where collective action for global health requires urgent attention. First, economic globalization has restructured the world economy in ways that expand the commercial sector's impact on population health. Globalized production and consumption of health-harming products, and other commercial determinants of health, is notably associated with a rapid rise in non-communicable diseases worldwide (now accounting for 70% of the global burden of disease). Second, the frequency and nature of major infectious disease outbreaks such as the COVID-19 pandemic are changing due to environmental degradation, population mobility and other factors associated with economic globalization. Dr. Lee will generate new evidence of the pathways between economic globalization and health but focus specifically on advancing global governance innovations. Dr. Lee will apply her expertise in international political economy, global governance, and public health to generate new methodologies, datasets and ideas for overcoming the gridlock hindering effective collective action. She will contribute to research, training and policy initiatives on standardized measurement of the commercial determinants of health as risk exposures across different countries. Building on her role leading the Pandemics and Borders Project, she will advance the development of risk-based approaches to inform revision of the World Health Organization's International Health Regulations. She will also participate in broader initiatives to reform the World Health Organization and negotiate a pandemic treaty. Her collaborations - strengthened by her COVID-19 Pandemic projects - span the local to global, and have involved researchers, government, practitioners, and civil society. Such work has enhanced her role in key policy debates on the future of global health governance. Overall, Dr. Lee's proposed work program will provide timely research findings and training opportunities that enhance national and global public health capacities to mitigate future population health risks from ongoing economic globalization.

Dr. Backx's research program will involve the training and mentoring of a large, diverse group of trainees in a highly inclusive manner. The results of Dr. Backx's research will be disseminated widely via high-impact peer-reviewed publications, social media platforms and frequent international and national speaking engagements.

column36: Youth Clinical Psychological Science
column37: Approximately 20% of Canadian youth experience serious mental health problems that typically emerge around age 14 and persist into adulthood. Rates of mental health disorders in youth have steadily grown over the last decade, along with rapid increases in the use of emergency, inpatient, and outpatient services. Youth mental health has suffered further with the extraordinary stress, social distancing, and reduced social support associated with the COVID-19 pandemic. There is an urgent need to understand what drives adolescent mental health risk and resilience and to rapidly mobilize knowledge into action. Dr Marlene Moretti has made significant contributions to the field of adolescent mental health and to the translation of research into evidence-based interventions. Alongside national and international collaborators, she developed, implemented, and evaluated a trauma-informed and attachment-focused program to promote adolescent health. She launched specialized programs for culturally and gender diverse families and youth in kinship/foster care. With the onset of COVID-19, Dr Moretti spearheaded the virtual adaptation of this program and launched a multi-site implementation trial of eConnect Online. eConnect Online is available in Canada, Sweden, South Africa, Australia, China, UK, Mexico, and Italy. Dr Moretti's evaluation of the effectiveness of virtual program accessibility was clear - the accessibility and convenience of eConnect Online was a key advantage, eliminating barriers such as travel time, childcare needs, and scheduling conflicts. Dr Moretti's research program has built on her expertise in adolescent development, psychopathology, and risk and protective factors. This has enabled her to expand the Connect program globally and continue to evaluate and assess the Connect treatment program to ensure fit, safety, accessibility, and effectiveness for culturally and gender diverse families and youth. Collectively her work has produced new knowledge on factors that shape youth mental health, and developed, implemented, and evaluated an evidence-based treatment. As the Canada Research Chair in Youth Clinical Psychological Science, Dr Moretti is committed to addressing the significant gaps in availability and accessibility of mental health services through her international community research networks that promote research and practice collaborations between universities, government stakeholders, community leaders, and mental health service providers.

column36: Functional Proteomics and Discovery of New Proteins
column37: Genetic information is processed from DNA to RNA to protein and this determines the cellular phenotype. Understanding how information flows from the genome to cellular phenotypes, be it related to health or diseases, requires a full description of the proteome, the entire set of proteins expressed from the genome. Currently, protein detection is largely based on mass spectrometry analyses using a process requiring that proteins be predicted and annotated in a protein database before they are actually detected. Proteins that are not predicted cannot be detected. Hence, genome annotation - the process of taking the raw DNA or RNA sequence and extracting protein-coding sequences - substantially limits protein databases and the detectable proteome. This research program focuses on the functional annotation, discovery, and characterization of tens of thousands of hidden protein-coding sequences that have been systematically neglected, yet a significant fraction of which produces novel proteins dubbed alternative proteins. These protein-coding sequences have eluded annotations because they are either small or within unsuspected locations in RNA, or are not in agreement with conventional annotations which impose a single coding sequence in one RNA molecule. Here, we acknowledge the multi-coding potential of RNA. Our approach integrating data from next-generation technology, detection of protein-coding sequence, prediction of canonical and alternative proteins in customized databases, and high throughput mass-spectrometry is called proteogenomics. This powerful integrative approach enables the detection of previously undetectable proteins and improves genome annotations. Our protein databases for several species and related bioinformatics tools are available on the internationally recognized proteogenomics resource OpenProt my laboratory created during the first term of the Canada Research Chair. In this research program, my team and I expect to produce a map of the coding potential of genomes with unprecedented depth, to provide bioinformatics tools to make widely accessible this new genetic and proteomic information, and to elucidate biological and pathological functions from sequence, with a particular focus in cancer. This research program lays the foundation for the development of diagnostic, prognostic and therapeutic medical applications based on a deeper knowledge of the proteome.

The nominee's research recognizes this potential and combines biomolecular sciences with materials engineering, pharmaceutics, and immunology to build safe and efficient nonviral gene delivery systems. This program will tap the potential of RNA to transform medicine's approaches to vaccination, immunotherapy, and beyond. It will integrate, adapt, and optimize existing and emerging bioengineering approaches to provide breakthroughs in the unsolved issues of developing RNA-based vaccines and therapeutics.

column36: Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer Prevention
column37: Dr. Kotsopoulos is a Scientist at Women's College Hospital (WCH) and an Associate Professor at the University of Toronto (UofT). She holds a Tier II Canada Research Chair in Hereditary Breast and Ovarian Cancer Prevention. Over 15 years of research, she has built a highly-recognized and interdisciplinary research program aimed at helping define novel strategies for breast and ovarian cancer prevention and improving outcomes in BRCA mutation carriers. Dr. Kotsopoulos is dedicated to studying the underlying pathogenesis of BRCA-breast and ovarian cancer, with an ultimate goal of improving upon the existing prevention and management strategies for high-risk women. Her focus on longitudinal studies leads large-scale analyses aimed at elucidating the role of modifiable risk and prognostic factors in women with an inherited predisposition. Dr. Kotsopoulos has made key findings regarding the role of hormonal, reproductive and lifestyle factors on BRCA breast and ovarian cancer risk. These critical studies have provided women and healthcare providers around the world with evidence-based management options while contributing to our understanding of the pathogenesis of hereditary cancer. This research has been used to inform recommendations and guidelines for BRCA mutation carriers throughout the world. Her noteworthy outputs include over 120 peer-reviewed publications, including invited reviews and commentaries, and has published in high-impact cancer epidemiology journals, including the JNCI, Lancet and JAMA Oncology. She has acquired over $2.3 million in peer-reviewed research funding as a principal investigator, and collaborates with over 75 sites around the world on high-impact studies. In this Tier 2 CRC renewal application, Dr. Kotsopoulos proposes the continued leadership of an innovative, interdisciplinary and globally impactful program of research encompassing three complementary areas of research: 1) delineating the role of modifiable risk and prognostic factors for BRCA-associated breast and ovarian cancer; 2) improving upon cancer risk prediction and personalized, non-surgical cancer prevention strategies for BRCA mutation carriers; and 3) advancing our knowledge of factors that impact ovarian cancer prognosis. Together, these aims will help accomplish her long-term goal of defining novel and personalized strategies that reduce cancer burden and outcomes for all women across the globe, particularly high-risk women.

column36: Education, Practice and Policy for Evidence-Based Healthcare
column37: Stroke is the third leading cause of death in Canada and the tenth largest contributor to disability-adjusted life years. With over 405,000 Canadians living with the consequences of stroke and 65,000 new cases each year, the direct and indirect costs are estimated at $3.6 billion per year. A large body of research shows the effectiveness of rehabilitation interventions in significantly reducing disabilities arising from stroke (e.g., they improve function, reduce institutionalization, and promote early discharge from hospital). Nonetheless, in Canada, less than half of stroke survivors receive evidence-based rehabilitation (EBR). This critical underutilization of effective rehabilitation interventions is having devastating consequences on patient outcomes and taxing an already overburdened Canadian healthcare system. Ensuring that stroke rehabilitation interventions are based on the best available evidence is not only the responsibility of researchers who generate the scientific evidence, but also "the business" of three sectors: 1) university programs who train the next generation of clinicians, 2) decision-makers who create policies about clinical practice, 3) clinicians on the "ground". Unfortunately, these three sectors work in siloed approaches, characterized by lack of synergy among EBR initiatives. This research seeks to address the persistent underutilization of scientific evidence in stroke rehabilitation by bringing together stakeholders from the three sectors to synergistically measure, develop, implement, and test innovative knowledge translation strategies. The specific aims are to: 1) measure and understand how the practice context influences the development, deployment, and maintenance of EBR; 2) develop and test indicators of EBR in stroke programs across Canada; and 3) implement and test the effectiveness of novel knowledge translation interventions for EBR. This creative, ground-breaking program of research that draws on intersectoral collaboration with engagement from all three sectors (education, practice, policy) will intentionally advance the knowledge translation process required to break down the barriers that now limit optimal clinical practice in stroke rehabilitation and will eventually improve the health outcomes of Canadians living with the effects of stroke.

column36: Machine Learning for Genomics and Healthcare
column37: Integrating multi-omic data along with diverse phenotypes from healthcare data using machine learning (ML) approaches holds great promise to understand complex human diseases. However, several main challenges hinder fast progress including restricted data access to patient data, model scalability to high-dimensional heterogeneous multi-omic data, and model interpretability for gaining insights of genetic causal architecture towards precision medicine. Dr. Li's proposed research program focuses on ML developments with 3 axes of applications: (1) federated learning for electronic health records; (2) single-cell multi-omic modeling of mental diseases; (3) inferring causal genetic variants for complex diseases by leveraging genomic annotations and biomedical knowledge. In Axis 1, he seeks to circumvent the problem of healthcare data access across hospital sites by collaboratively training large-scale knowledge-guided ML models at different hospital sites sharing only the inferred phenotype distributions rather than actual patient data among the sites. He will target the applications in disease diagnosis and disease severity prediction based on patients' in-hospital data and past medical histories. The proposed research will greatly accelerate the paradigm shift of real-world ML deployment in Canadian healthcare system. In Axis 2, he proposes an interpretable deep learning framework that integrates single-cell multi-omic data with gene networks and genomic sequence information to dissect the genetic circuitry of major depressive disorder (MDD). The proposed model sheds new insights into the pathophysiology of major mental illness to uncover novel cell-type-specific marker genes and neuronal signalling pathways in MDD. In Axis 3, he tackles the challenges of pinpointing causal single nucleotide polymorphisms due to linkage disequilibrium and the lack of functional interpretations for most of the disease SNPs in the non-coding region of the human genome. He will integrate genetic data with existing genomic and biomedical knowledge graphs including expression quantitative trait loci and the diverse ontologies of genes, drugs, and diseases. By leveraging population genetic data, his research will advance genomic medicine to improve Canadian patient care through efficient diagnoses, interventions, and treatments for a wide range of conditions. His approach will elucidate the genetic determinants of differential response to drug treatments of Canadian patients.

column36: Innovation and Technology for Youth Mental Health Services
column37: Access to youth mental health services (MHS) is limited and delayed, and the healthcare system is already overstretched in its ability to meet the rising demand for youth mental health care. It is well-recognized internationally that reforming the youth mental health care system requires urgent support of digital technologies. This is particularly relevant for young people (digital natives) who already search online for mental health information, services, and supports. As such, digital mental health has been identified as a strategic priority by government organizations (e.g., Mental Health Commission of Canada). This Canada Research Chair (CRC) will contribute directly to this strategic priority through the advancement of science, innovation, and knowledge translation on the use of digital health innovations (DHIs) to improve access, quality, and sustainability of mental health services (MHS) for youth (adolescents and young adults). The core objective of the research program is to develop, adapt, test, and scale up the implementation of DHIs in diverse, real-world settings. The CRC will also generate evidence on the use of DHIs among youth populations facing multiple barriers accessing MHS (e.g., housing instability; neurodevelopmental or physical disabilities; and, limited education, training, or employment). The CRC will use a collaborative, action-oriented, transdisciplinary research approach that considers the relevance and impact of DHIs for a diverse population. The proposed research will contribute to the prevention of chronic forms of mental illness and disability, and fortify the capacity of the mental health care system in responding to the growing need for youth mental health care. The program will contribute cutting-edge innovations that will connect youth to the services they need. These innovations will bridge and streamline online to in-person pathways to care; and improve service providers' capacity to engage and assess youth. The program will also contribute knowledge on how sociodemographic and cultural factors influence uptake and impact of DHIs.

column36: Cancer Biophysics
column37: Malignant brain tumors are among the most lethal cancers in children and adults. Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive brain cancer in adults. Fewer than 5% of people with GBM are alive 5 years after diagnosis. Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant brain tumor in children. While MB has better survival rate than GBM, MB survivors have long-term sequelae, including reduced IQ and an increased chance of secondary cancers. Furthermore, recurrent MB is universally fatal. These outcomes urge identification of new therapeutic targets and development of novel brain tumor therapies. Ion channels are transmembrane proteins that govern ion flux across cell membrane. It is estimated that over 15% of U.S. FDA-approved drugs target ion channels to treat human diseases. However, their roles in brain cancer are largely unexplored. We use multi-disciplinary expertise, including bioinformatics, Drosophila and mouse genetics, cell biology, advanced imaging, electrophysiology, and bioengineering to define ion channel functions in brain cancer. We discovered specific ion channels as therapeutic targets in GBM and MB, defined the mechanisms by which ion channels regulate brain tumor growth and metastasis, and provided the first example of pharmacologically targeting ion channel to treat MB in human. Therefore, we pioneer a field by decoding ion channel functions in brain cancer. In the proposed research program, we will continue to lead the field by investigating ion channel-mediated electrical-mechano-chemical signaling in brain cancer. We will define the efficacy of an ion channel complex-targeting designer peptide, which is invented by our group, in treating recurrent GBM. We will reveal how this ion channel complex controls the interaction between GBM cells and neurons. As cells experience pervasive mechanical signals in the tumor microenvironment, we will elucidate how ion channels govern cellular perception of mechanical signals to regulate brain tumor growth, chemosensitivity, and metastasis. Our research will create new experimental paradigms to investigate brain tumor biology, reveal ion channels as therapeutic vulnerabilities, and develop ion channel-targeting therapeutic modalities to benefit brain cancer patients.

column36: Mucosal Immunology
column37: One of our body's first lines of defense against invading microbes are the mucosal surfaces - a thin layer of cells covering our body to protect it from microbial attacks. These mucosal barriers make up large surfaces of our bodies, like our skin, lungs and intestinal tract, and increasing numbers of chronic inflammatory diseases suggest that interactions between microbes and our mucosal immune system at these surfaces are essential in modifying host-defense and tissue homeostasis. Dr. Arthur Mortha, Canada Research Chair in Mucosal Immunology, is an innovative researcher applying his expertise in mucosal immunology to understand the crosstalk between the mucosal immune system and the microbiota - the collection of microbes colonizing our mucosal surfaces. In particular, he tries to understand how the mucosal immune system develops, interacts with the microbiota and shapes the outcome essential defense mechanisms or pathways towards the prevention of chronic inflammatory diseases. Using the lung and intestine as his test models - the two largest mucosal surfaces in our bodies with the highest density of bacteria - Dr. Mortha is exploring the molecular relationship required between microbes and mucosal cells to maintain a healthy immune system. His results will draw a detailed map of specific host-microbial interactions, regulating mucosal immune homeostasis and the beneficial and detrimental outcomes during health and disease - information that will pinpoint where and when signals between microbes and the immune system misfire or fail to result in homeostasis. Ultimately, Dr. Mortha's ground-breaking approach is changing the way we think about the role of mucosal surfaces in our immune system and as a result, the way we address immune conditions - advances that could radically improve treatments for inflammatory bowel disease, psoriasis, cancer, diabetes, arthritis, multiple sclerosis and more.

column36: Episodic Disability and Rehabilitation
column37: In Canada, there is an increasing number of people living longer, and now aging with the physical, mental, cognitive and social health related consequences of chronic disease and multimorbidity. These health-related challenges may be collectively referred to as disability. While much attention has been placed on understanding disability, relatively little research has focused examining the episodic nature and unpredictable fluctuations in health and wellness experienced among people living with chronic conditions. The overall goal of Dr. Kelly O'Brien's research program is to characterize the episodic nature of disability experienced by people aging with chronic disease and multimorbidity, and to establish and evaluate the effectiveness of rehabilitation interventions to improve health outcomes, programs, practice, and policy. Using HIV and Long COVID as exemplars, the objectives of Dr. O'Brien's research program are to: 1) conceptualize episodic disability, and characterize its prevalence and determinants among adults living with chronic conditions; 2) develop and advance the measurement properties of an Episodic Disability Questionnaire to assess presence, severity and episodic nature of disability; and 3) evaluate the implementation and effect of novel rehabilitation interventions to improve health outcomes. This research program involves international multi-disciplinary partnerships involving academic, clinical and community-engaged approaches and collaborations to advance the field of episodic disability and rehabilitation. It is innovative, applying lessons learned in episodic disability and rehabilitation across complex chronic conditions. Results will provide vital information for enhancing healthy aging and establish a strong foundation for measurement and scale up of rehabilitation interventions to enhance health outcomes for people aging with chronic conditions.

column36: Protein Misfolding Disorders
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) and Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) are incurable, neurodegenerative diseases of the brain. PD affects approximately 2% of individuals aged 80 or older, and more than 80,000 Canadians currently have PD. Because the population of Canada is ageing, PD and related neurodegenerative disorders are predicted to become more common in the coming years, increasing the burden on our healthcare system. In PD and CJD, normal proteins in the brain begin to adopt an abnormal shape, which causes them to clump together to form aggregates that interfere with the proper functioning of brain cells. Further, these improperly shaped proteins can self-multiply; this allows them to spread and deposit within the brain, resulting in worsening disease symptoms. One reason why it is challenging to develop therapies for these diseases is because there is considerable patient-to-patient variability in the clinical and pathological presentations for both PD and CJD. One possible explanation for this variability is that the shapes ("strains") of protein aggregates can differ across patients, with different strains affecting different brain regions and types of cells. A better understanding of these strains could help to develop therapies tailored to individual patients. Despite this, we still do not even know how many different types of strains can form and how they relate to different disease characteristics. The objective of this project is to determine the spectrum of potential strains that can be formed by protein aggregates in PD and CJD. To accomplish this goal, Dr. Watts and his team will use cutting-edge animal models and proteins produced in bacteria to investigate the strains that can cause PD and CJD symptoms. This work will provide new insight into the basis for disease variability in degenerative brain diseases and will suggest new therapeutic strategies for counteracting these devastating illnesses.

column36: Pancreatic Cancer and Cancer Evolution
column37: Despite advances in treating many tumour types over the past few decades, outcomes in patients with pancreatic cancer remain dismal. Clinical trials continue to fail in this disease due to significant gaps in knowledge about pancreatic cancer pathogenesis. The long-term goal of Dr. Notta's research program is to improve patient outcomes by addressing some of these gaps. Building on his collective experience in tumour evolution, genomics, and disease modelling, his program targets three areas of research. Aim 1 intends to improve our understanding of pancreatic cancer development. The molecular changes that occur early in disease development are poorly described due to challenges in identifying precursor cells; these cells giving rise to new cancer cells. Single cell RNA-sequencing addresses many of the previous issues in this area and can uncover these early molecular changes. Aim 2 focuses on functional models of disease. Genetically engineered mice and cell lines are the predominant method used to study this disease but cannot fully capture the biological and clinical heterogeneity in patients. Patient-derived organoids (PDOs) recapitulate the genomic and transcriptomic signatures of the parent tumour and patient treatment response. Dr. Notta's participation in on-going clinical trials will provide access to over 200 PDOs. His group has established a high-throughput drug screening platform for PDOs (>3000 agents), which cover a diverse range of cellular mechanisms. Integrating this data with genomic and transcriptomic features of the parent tumour will allow his team to determine how genomic instability shapes molecular vulnerabilities in these tumours. Aim 3 will establish a liquid biopsy platform to monitor treatment response in patients. Although many technological platforms are available to detect circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA), their use has had limited success due to issues regarding sensitivity. Plasma whole genome sequencing (WGS) is a new technology that is significantly more sensitive at detecting ctDNA. Given his significant experience in WGS, he will assemble the first large and clinically annotated cohort of plasma WGS for pancreatic cancer. His initial feasibility study shows promise. Eventually, Dr. Notta will look to implement this as a screening tool for high-risk patients with germline predisposition for this disease. This research will build important resources and fill information gaps in our knowledge of pancreatic cancer development

column36: Translational Genomics
column37: Immunotherapy continues to be a world-leading and transformational approach to treat cancer, with thousands of clinical trials currently ongoing for different types of drugs. Yet, only a small subset of these clinical trials incorporate genomics analysis as an additional component to understand the tumour's response to cancer immunotherapy at the molecular level. Consequently, biomarkers that indicate response to immunotherapy are lacking and there are few molecular diagnostic tools to guide the use of these drugs. Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) sequencing is a promising approach to detect and monitor the presence of cancer, although the sensitivity and path to clinical implementation, especially in early-stage disease, are still evolving. Dr. Pugh's Canada Research Chair program will close this gap by providing an understanding, at the single-cell level, of how tumours change in response to treatment and investigate whether this biology can be determined using non-invasive blood draws early in the disease course. His program will actively work with clinical laboratories to deploy these findings and technologies into accredited assays that directly impact patient care. The multidisciplinary translational research program will also leverage established collaborations with clinicians, basic researchers, geneticists and computational biologists. Dr. Pugh's group has a robust track record in applying complex genomic assays to understand cancer and immune response directly in patients. His program will bring together a highly-innovative pipeline of biospecimens from clinical trials, cutting-edge single-cell techniques, immunogenomic profiling methods, cloud-based high-performance computing, and data sharing infrastructure to dissect shifts in tumour cell populations over time and to detect cancer. Overall, data generated by Dr. Pugh's program will contribute to an expanding global knowledgebase and learning health system that will be key to understanding cancer, anti-tumour immune responses and monitoring of disease. His focus on clinical translation will ensure these sophisticated data approaches are employed when developing clinical tests and that standard-of-care genomic assays are compatible with broader data sharing initiatives.

column36: Translational Neuropsychopharmacology
column37: Although drug and alcohol use are common within the general public, there are certain groups that are especially vulnerable to the impacts of such use, as well as the arising consequences. Firstly, patients with serious mental illnesses such as schizophrenia show 3-10x higher prevalence of substance use disorders, and this use significantly worsens their clinical course. Therefore, there is a critical need to understand the reasons behind the high rates of substance use in schizophrenia, in order to identify potential ways of treating this use and the resulting problems. Secondly, since drug and alcohol use usually begins in adolescence, often before the onset of the mental illness, it is also important to understand the long-term effects of adolescent drug or alcohol exposure on the future risk for drug use or mental illness, with an eye toward uncovering the long-term behavioural, and brain function changes induced by this exposure. Lastly, genetic studies have identified multiple gene markers that contribute to the risk for drug use and addiction. However, the exact roles of these genes in continued substance use remain unknown. By using rodent models where these genes can be modified, the causal roles these genes play in the development of addictions can be better understood. Dr. Khokhar is an international leader in neuropsychopharmacology who will use his expertise in pharmacological, behavioural and pre-clinical magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) approaches to study these topics in a translational and interdisciplinary manner with the ultimate goal of improving clinical outcomes. Dr. Khokhar will use a multi-faceted research approach to try and answer the chicken-or-egg question (i.e., which comes first) of substance use in patients with serious mental illness. By combining animal models with methods akin to those used to study patients, his group's research will try to uncover why these co-occurring disorders occur, as well as the impact of adolescent drug and alcohol use on these vulnerabilities. Furthermore, he will use these approaches to establish how genes shown to contribute to risk for substance use or mental illness actually result in these disorders, and whether these pathways could be targeted toward treating these difficult-to-treat disorders. Lastly, this work also has the potential to inform us of the consequences of substance use on both healthy and disrupted brain circuitry, providing evidence to guide harm-reduction efforts.

column37: Despite significant advances in diagnosis and treatment, infectious diseases continue to cause enormous losses of life and health, with large costs to society. Whole genome sequencing is revolutionizing infectious disease research by improving our ability to understand patterns of disease transmission, detect outbreaks, predict antimicrobial resistance and by providing new insights into pathogen evolution. Dr. Guthrie and her team are using large, diverse pathogen genomic datasets linked to epidemiological data to study infectious diseases of public health concern. Epidemiological information such as age, location, health and behavioural risk factors are available through healthcare records and notifiable disease registries, among other data sources and provide important context to infectious disease genomics studies. The research program of this Canada Research Chair focuses on the development and application of bioinformatics and genomics to study disease transmission and drug resistance, and for population-level infectious disease surveillance. This research will advance knowledge and understanding of infectious diseases and the information gained can serve to improve the design and application of diagnostic tools and treatments to allow for a more personalized approach as well as community targeted approaches. Ultimately, the goal is to provide evidence for effective strategies to reduce the spread of infectious diseases, the emergence of antimicrobial resistance and increase our readiness for the next pandemic.

column37: Precision medicine is an emerging approach to treating complex diseases that take into account each patient's genes, combined with medical history, environment, and lifestyle. The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and precision medicine promises to revolutionize health research. Dr. Pingzhao Hu, Canada Research Chair in Computational Approaches to Health Research, is developing and applying robust and interpretable AI and statistical analytical techniques to integrate multimodal health data related to patients' genes, medical history, environment, and lifestyle in a fast and cost-efficient manner. With the help of the complex health data being generated by his collaborators and complemented by publicly available resources, he and his team will enable the discovery of novel disease subtypes, biomarkers, and biotechnology-derived therapies to facilitate the implementation of precision medicine approaches. By making his innovative methods and software freely available in open-source libraries, Dr. Hu is also helping to advance other research discoveries to help people worldwide. column36: Social Relationships, Health, and Aging
column37: Social relationships are fundamental to health and well-being. In fact, they are as important for health as lifestyle behaviours such as engaging in regular physical activity. Social relationships are especially important in old age, when individuals tend to rely more on others because of the onset of chronic conditions or cognitive limitations. Furthermore, older adults also have a tendency to place more importance on maintaining meaningful and positive relationships with close friends and family. Dr. Theresa Pauly's innovative research examines social influences on lifespan development and aging, by collecting in-depth assessments of daily life experiences and physiological health markers (such as the stress hormone cortisol), in combination with analyzing longer-term health trajectories. To achieve her overall goal of improving understanding of the influence that the social environment has on health behaviours, psychological well-being, and physical health, Dr. Pauly focuses on three significant research objectives. First, she examines pivotal risks and resources related to social relationships that influence how individuals age during decisive turning points in mid- to late life (e.g., onset of major disease). These include social support, social participation, social isolation, and urban/rural living environments. Dr. Pauly is also looking into resources for older adults to experience time alone more positively and avoid potential negative health consequences of loneliness. For example, she investigates whether the use of modern technology for social functions, a sense of purpose, or gratitude could help protect older adults from feelings of loneliness when spending time alone. Finally, Dr. Pauly investigates the diverse experiences of older adults who identify as belonging to a minoritised group. She analyzes social risk (e.g., discrimination - unfair or prejudicial treatment based on a personal characteristic) and resilience (e.g., generativity - a concern for the well-being of future generations) in relation to health behaviours and physical health in sexual and/or gender minority older adults to uncover ways to serve the unique needs of aging minorities. Ultimately, Dr. Pauly's research will contribute new knowledge about the ways in which social relationships can influence health outcomes, thereby informing public health, policy, and community intervention efforts to promote healthy aging and, crucially, help to meet future healthcare demands.

column36: Developmental Origins of Health and Disease in Indigenous People
column37: The high prevalence of metabolic diseases among Indigenous populations in Canada underscores the impact of colonization policies on the health of Indigenous peoples. The sympathetic linkage between the brain and the gastrointestinal system is well established. Gut-brain alterations resulting from stress and malnutrition could play a strong determining role in the development of metabolic disorders in at-risk populations across generations. Canadian colonization policies, such as the residential school system, exposed Indigenous peoples to both chronic stress and malnutrition during important developmental periods, producing effects that may have impacted the stress response and gut microbiome of subsequent generations. The proposed research framework, Developmental Origins of Health and Disease (DOHaD), posits that the state of health and risk from disease in later childhood and adult life are significantly affected by environmental factors during the pre-conceptional, prenatal, and/or early postnatal periods. The purpose of the proposed CRC in Developmental Origins of Health and Disease in Indigenous People is to use a DOHaD lens to investigate the physiological consequences of intergenerational stress and malnutrition, and how this relates to obesity in Indigenous children. The first objective is to create a double-hit preclinical model of stress and malnutrition to gain insight into the physiological mechanisms that drive the high prevalence rates of metabolic diseases observed in survivors of intergenerational trauma. The second is to use a prospective birth cohort design to investigate the association between maternal stress and nutrition and the gut microbiome, and obesity rates in Saskatchewan Indigenous children. Findings from studies focusing on these two objectives could identify potential biomarkers of susceptibility to obesity in Indigenous children. The third objective is to use a translational research approach to explore potential strategies for either preventing or treating the development of obesity in Indigenous children. This research will bridge insights gained from preclinical research with information gained from birth cohort studies to develop informed strategies to address obesity in Indigenous peoples through promoting wellness. The identification of potential physiological barriers to wellness that may be transmitted from generation to generation makes this CRC program of research novel and significant.

Globally, services addressing violence have not been well integrated into PHC systems. column36: Genomics Health Services and Policy
column37: Precision medicine is medical care designed to optimize treatment of patients based on their genes, environment, and lifestyle. Genetic testing is one way that people get access to precision treatments and care. In Canada, genetics specialists are in short supply. Even when access to genetic testing and genetics specialists are available, it is not equitable. People who are part of a visible minority group are less likely to know about, and be referred for, genetic testing. They are also more likely to receive inconclusive results, which makes it harder for them to receive precision treatment and care. The goal of Dr. Bombard's proposed research program is to advance the equitable access and delivery of precision medicine. She developed the first comprehensive digital tool that guides patients through their genetic testing journey, called the Genetics Adviser. 1) To advance access to services, Dr. Bombard will: (a) Transform the Genetics Adviser into the 'Genetics Navigator' - a full-service virtual care platform that incorporates all of the genetic services that an expert delivers, including consent, education, counselling, providing test results, management, and follow-up; and (b) Evaluate how well and how cost-effective the Genetics Navigator is in a clinical trial among children and adults who receive genetic testing for a variety of diseases. 2) To understand and resolve issues of equitable delivery of genetic testing among visible minority groups, Dr. Bombard will: (a) Identify the nature and measure the extent of disparities along the pathways for cancer genetic testing; and (b) Mitigate these disparities with interventions that are co-designed and evaluated in partnership with the groups that experience them. Dr. Bombard will create the world's first and only digital application to deliver the full spectrum of genetic services, improving equity in access and patient experiences, and reducing wait times, costs, and geographical disparities. By identifying whether racial disparities exist, among which communities, and at which points of the genetic testing pathway for cancer treatment and prevention, Dr. Bombard's results will help visible minority groups to receive optimized treatment, a step towards providing equitable precision care.

column37: Les travaux de cette Chaire visent a elucider l'impact de la structure des populations sur les analyses genetiques portant sur des traits complexes et maladies rares. Ils reposent sur l'utilisation conjointe des genealogies, qui integrent a la fois la structure de la population et les informations familiales, et des donnees genetiques pour accroitre la puissance de detecter des associations genetiques. En effet, malgre le grand nombre d'etudes genetiques realisees dans les dernieres annees, une portion significative des causes genetiques des maladies complexes demeure inconnue. On l'appelle l'heritabilite manquante (missing heritability). Ce probleme est particulierement marque dans le domaine des troubles neurodeveloppementaux. Parmi les pistes de solutions peu explorees de l'heritabilite manquante, on compte la structure des populations a l'etude, c'est-a-dire les liens familiaux proches ou eloignes qui relient les participant.es. La presente programmation s'inscrit dans un courant nouveau : la jonction des grandes familles et des cohortes d'individus non apparentes. Peu de populations mondiales ont acces a des donnees genealogiques et encore moins aussi completes et d'une telle profondeur que celles de BALSAC au Quebec qui couvrent 15 generations. Ainsi, le programme de recherche de la presente Chaire en genetique et genealogie aura pour objectif global de combiner des donnees genetiques (sequencage et genotypage) et familiales (genealogiques) afin d'analyser la structure des populations dans toute sa complexite et d'integrer cette structure dans les etudes d'association genetiques. Le premier volet repose sur l'utilisation de ces deux types de donnees provenant de cohortes medicales familiales afin de trouver de nouvelles associations pour plusieurs troubles neurodeveloppementaux, nommement la schizophrenie, l'epilepsie et le trouble bipolaire. Le deuxieme volet porte sur l'etude de la genealogie pour mieux comprendre la structure genetique actuelle et l'evolution du patrimoine genetique de la population quebecoise en mettant l'emphase sur la caracterisation des effets fondateurs regionaux. Les connaissances generees pour ce second volet serviront a la fois a alimenter le premier volet et a approfondir les etudes sur la structure de la population fondatrice quebecoise et sur l'apport des populations fondatrices aux etudes genetiques sur les maladies.

column36: Nutrition and Chronic Disease Prevention and Management
column37: Nutrition assessment and intervention are key for improving health and are particularly important in light of the high prevalence of obesity and associated chronic diseases. Provision of accurate energy intake recommendations that are specific to individual requirements is fundamental for optimal nutrition care. Furthermore, identifying the mechanisms that underpin resistance to weight loss is critical for mitigating the obesity epidemic and minimizing the burden of obesity-associated chronic diseases. However, many current energy intake recommendations are designed as "one size fits all" and do not consider variables such as body composition, appetite, energy expenditure, hormones, or physical activity, which all may impact energy balance and personalization of effective weight management strategies in chronic disease. Dr. Sarah Purcell, Tier II Canada Research Chair (CRC) in Nutrition and Chronic Disease Prevention and Management, will lead an innovative research program to develop better energy intake recommendations and clinical practices for people with chronic disease. The CRC research program will utilize an energy balance framework to test the hypotheses that certain chronic diseases - including obesity - are characterized by unique physiological, psychological, and behavioral characteristics that impact energy intake requirements and responses to energy balance perturbations (e.g., weight loss, underfeeding). These hypotheses will be tested through a systematic review complemented by energy expenditure data from an international database and three acute and chronic nutrition interventions. The proposed research program leverages Dr. Purcell's expertise in whole-body energy expenditure and is especially novel given the use of both free-living and in-laboratory approaches in people with chronic diseases. Building upon Dr. Purcell's exceptional leadership, this research will inform the development of more targeted energy intake recommendations and create a platform for knowledge translation locally, nationally, and internationally. It will also form the basis for training the next generation of multidisciplinary scientists and health professionals. Collectively, the proposed program - led by an emerging leader in the field of nutrition and energy balance - will help inform optimal strategies to manage obesity and disease-specific outcomes through evidence-based nutrition interventions.

column36: Indigenous Peoples' Health and Well-Being
column37: In recent years, academe is seeing a shift whereby a very small, but growing cohort of Indigenous scholars (and their non-Indigenous allies) are transforming research. The researched are becoming the researchers. Indigenous communities are setting the research agenda, prioritizing their immediate health needs while doing so. The result is that many long-standing beliefs, values and 'objective truths' within (and outside) the sphere of health research are being challenged, including the belief that research about Indigenous peoples can continue to happen without their direct involvement. Perhaps even more importantly, research led by communities is having a meaningful impact on the health and well-being of communities. Dr. Martin, an Inuk scholar, has offered key contributions to this epistemic shift. This has entailed offering new insights into the conceptualization of Indigenous health research methodologies (Martin, 2012; Roher et al., 2021); demonstrating the need for capacity-building for Indigenous scholars and scholarship (Richmond et al., 2013); providing research evidence of the need for Indigenous health research methodologies to be explored and expanded within the academy (Castleden et al., 2015); and most recently, examining whether and how far we have 'moved the needle' on engaging with Indigenous communities when research directly involves them (White et al., 2021; Murphy et al., 2021). This resurgence in Indigenous-led research is gaining momentum. Accompanying it there is an immediate need for: a) Indigenous communities to be supported in these efforts; b) academic institutions to respect and embed Indigenous principles for undertaking research. Herein, Dr. Martin outlines a plan for the next five years whereby the goal is to prioritize community-initiated and directed, (w)holistic and preventative, action research to improve Indigenous health and well-being in Atlantic Canada (and beyond).
