column36: Canada Research Chair in Artificial Intelligence for Medicine
column37: The human body consists of approximately 37.2 trillion cells; yet, despite these numbers, every cell has its own - often unique - function in the human body. The recent rapid advance of single-cell sequencing technology has witnessed the availability of large-scale and high-dimensional single-cell genomics data, and its applications to investigate cell identity, function and fate. Combining multiple single-cell modalities, such as genetic (genome), protein (proteome), and epigenetic (epigenome), increases the power of detecting cellular heterogeneity, understanding the biological process and disease pathogenesis. However, such integration remains challenging because measurements from different assays differ both technically and biologically, and if such difference are not accounted for, technical variability may mask biological signals of interest. Thus, the adoption of single cell genomic data to complement clinical data and improve patient health outcome prediction is still scarce. Dr. Wang's long-term research goal is to deploy interpretable AI algorithms to jointly profile big data in single cell genomics and clinical studies from multiple health institutions, which ultimately will pave the path towards understanding disease pathogenesis and tailoring personalized patients' care. The main deliverables of the proposed research program are (1) a fast, scalable and interpretable AI framework that integrates single-cell multi-omics data; (2) a privacy-preserving AI framework that can securely learn single cell genomics data from multiple health institutions without data transfer; (3) an integrative AI framework that combines single-cell multi-omics data with patient-level clinical measurements, medical images and clinical notes. Dr. Wang's proposed research focuses on the prediction of patients' clinical outcomes through the integration of single-cell multi-omics data and clinical data from heterogeneous resources and multiple health institutions. Dr. Wang will deploy the state-of-the-art interpretable AI framework that better understand the important genomic and clinical factors. To preserve the privacy of private patient data, he proposes to develop a federated learning-based framework that accesses the data across multiple decentralized secured cloud computing services without transferring the data to those computing facilities. The proposed research will pave the path to take single-cell multi-omics findings from bench to bedside.

column36: Global Health Policy
column37: Dr. Veena Sriram has developed an internationally recognized body of work on health workforce policy and governance that provides novel insights on power and politics in global health policy. Dr. Sriram's multidisciplinary training, rich field experience, unique expertise and extensive networks provide excellent qualifications for the Tier 2 Canada Research Chair (CRC) in Global Health Policy. Her CRC program of research investigates the politics of health workforce policy processes in high-income and low- and middle-income countries, and through knowledge translation activities, will contribute evidence to transforming these processes to be more equity-oriented, inclusive and transparent for improved population health outcomes and health equity. This program of work has the following objectives: 1) to investigate the role of protests by health workers in shaping health workforce policy; and 2) to examine and compare the politics of emergency care workforce policy and the impact on access to emergency care. By combining global and local perspectives, these studies will uniquely elucidate the dynamics of health worker advocacy in health policy processes, explore the ways in which health worker advocacy approaches interact within and across borders, and unpack the ways in which health worker advocacy shape policy and ultimately, health status and health inequities. This research program will advance innovation in global health policy research with the development of comparative policy research networks, the application of interdisciplinary approaches, and the analysis of social media data in policy research. Study contexts will include global analysis, with specific empirical focus on Canada and India, complimented by comparative studies from other contexts that will enrich learning and analysis. The first theme will utilize mixed methods approach that integrates analysis of trends in health worker protests between 2020 and 2025, with qualitative case studies of health worker protests in Canada and India, and eventually, with other contexts. The second theme will involve an international partnership of colleagues in Canada, South Africa, Rwanda and Australia in conducting a comparative policy analysis using qualitative methods. This program of research will prioritize regular engagement with sub-national, national and global knowledge users throughout the research process, in order to ensure applied impact on system level policies and procedures.

column36: Tumor Biology and Precision Oncology
column37: Cancer is the leading cause of death in Canada, highlighting the urgency to improve upon current therapeutic approaches via development of new treatment modalities and agents. Novel technologies, such as sequencing, reveal that tumours belong to different molecular subtypes, underscoring the need for the implementation of personalized, tailored treatments. Recent work by Dr. Michael revealed that malignant cells unlock phenotypic plasticity, which enables them to transit from one molecular subtype to another during cancer progression. Phenotypic plasticity has been implicated in tumor heterogeneity, acquired resistance to therapy, and metastasis; the latter two being main cause of mortality among cancer patients. Dr. Michael's proposed research program aims to elucidate the biology of phenotypic cancer cell plasticity by exploring three main research areas: First, to study the role of microRNAs and their downstream regulatory networks in cancer phenotypic plasticity. Second, to characterize the effect of phenotypic plasticity in the tumor microenvironment and immune evasion. Finally, to identify therapeutic vulnerabilities and targets of cancer phenotypic plasticity. Dr. Michael's research program will largely focus on two cancer types, gastroenteropancreatic and prostate neuroendocrine tumors, and use cutting-edge methodologies, such as single-cell and spatial omics, novel patient-derived cancer models, and advanced computational approaches. Dr. Michael will benefit from the collaborations with other Canada Research Chairs and Scientists at the Sunnybrook Research Institute that are experts in genomics, imaging, immunology, and computational biology. Finally, Dr. Michael will also benefit from the collaborations with Clinician Scientists at the Odette Cancer Centre who will provide patient samples. Phenotypic plasticity is now recognized as one of the hallmarks of cancer and it has been identified as one of the top four priorities for basic cancer research in 2022 by the American Association for Cancer Research. The proposed research program of Dr. Michael is expected to elucidate the mechanisms involved in phenotypic plasticity, which will lead to the future development of novel approaches for precision oncology and ultimately improve the survival and quality of life of patients with cancer.

column36: Housing, Community and Health
column37: In 2016, 1.69M (12.7%) households in Canada were in core housing need, meaning their houses required major repairs, were unsuitable in size, and/or were unaffordable. There are social and geographic variations across Canada, with Indigenous and racialized peoples, older adults, renters, and lone-parent families facing greater housing needs. The COVID-19 pandemic has made even more evident the importance of healthy housing. Heat waves, forest fires, heavy rains, flooding, winter storms, coastal erosion and permafrost thaw remind us that housing offers shelter against the same elements that can quickly destroy homes and infrastructures, profoundly disrupting (and taking) lives. The goal of the CRC in Housing, Community and Health is to provide policy-relevant evidence at the junction between housing, population health, sustainability and climate change. Four broad objectives guide its interdisciplinary and mixed-methods research program: 1) Support Indigenous-led housing initiatives, by describing the health and well-being impacts of housing conditions, interventions, programs and policies for Inuit and First Nations; 2) Assess housing-related health inequalities in urban and rural areas; 3) Understand the health implications of energy poverty (a situation that happens when households are unable to afford or access adequate energy at home to meet their needs and maintain healthy indoor temperatures) and identify mitigation strategies; 4) Explore how the housing and health relationship is impacted by climate-related weather events in order to inform adaptation strategies. The scientific activities of the CRC critically examine housing and health inequities across the country and for diverse populations, including Inuit living in the North and in the South, First Nations, urban and rural dwellers. Research at the CRC is co-produced; Indigenous and western knowledge holders and knowledge users are involved throughout the research process, from the formulation of research question(s) to the dissemination of results. Research at the CRC is thus motivated by a strong commitment to leading interdisciplinary and inter-sectoral science, working in close collaboration with communities, organizations, and governments to provide rigorous scientific evidence that can be used to inform practice and policy, to contribute to inform Canada's National Housing Strategy, and to reach several of the Sustainable Development Goals.

column36: RNA and Protein Biophysics
column37: Background: Emerging and remerging viral outbreaks are responsible for millions of deaths and impose a severe financial burden on healthcare systems. My interdisciplinary, integrative and innovative research program aims to provide critical insight into the human protein viral- nucleic acids communications that are of fundamental importance for viral replication. Aims and Approaches: I will continue to unravel the principles underlying viral nucleic acids-human protein interactions during viral infections by employing sophisticated structural-biophysical techniques. During the second term of my Canada Research Chair, I will mainly focus on Flaviviral and hepatitis B viral systems, study the structures of viral nucleic acids, as well as investigate how viral nucleic acids interact with human host proteins. I will also investigate the antiviral activities of therapeutic molecules we have developed and optimize them for their efficient functions. My strategy of targeting viral nucleic acids and human protein complexes is innovative as targeting only viral proteins could lead the virus to mutate and adapt to overcome the treatment. My strong interdisciplinary research background and relevant experience, the availability of infrastructure, a very strong commitment from the University, and support from collaborators ensure my success as a Canada Research Chair. Training: My interdisciplinary research programs involving cutting-edge biochemical, biophysical, and structural biology techniques will create a high-quality training environment to stimulate and foster the development of highly skilled research personnel. Such skills will help trainees with their future careers in academia, government agencies, and industries related to agriculture, biomedicine, or biotechnology research, and ultimately improve the quality of life of Canadians. Significance: My work will provide insights into the mode of recognition by which viral nucleic acids recognize human proteins, paving the way for the development of antiviral treatments. Expertise and Infrastructure: I have a strong record of investigating nucleic acids-protein and protein-protein interactions that are critical for cellular activities using integrated structural-biophysical methods. I have established collaborations to further support the proposed work. Also, we have all the necessary infrastructure readily available for the successful implementation of the proposed work.

column36: Tissue-Specific Immune Tolerance
column37: Enhancing tissue homeostasis and immune tolerance is central to all transplantation and regenerative medicine approaches. Although transplants can be a life-saving measure for individuals with damaged or dysfunctional organs or tissues, they still often fail because of immune rejection, and immunosuppressive regimens that attempt to prevent rejection increase the risk of infection and cancer. New, more specific strategies are needed to balance immunity and immune tolerance. Dr. Sarah Crome aims to improve our understanding of how the immune system is controlled and how this knowledge can be used to improve the success of transplants. She is an expert in human immunology and has made discoveries of lymphocytes that impact the immune environment as well as helped elucidate the biological circuitry that governs their development, regulation and function Dr. Crome's proposed research program will use cutting-edge technologies for studying and analyzing cells and tissues to determine which specific populations of cells are involved in immune responses after transplantation and how these cells develop, interact and are regulated. She will also investigate whether these cells can be harnessed to moderate immune responses and enhance tissue repair following transplantation. The family of cells that Dr. Crome has a particular focus on are called innate lymphoid cells (ILCs). She and others have already shown that ILCs can have key roles in immune regulation and tissue repair. She is now looking to define the factors that control ILCs development and that signal them to deliver certain responses. These factors may reveal new methods for having the cells respond in a particular way. In addition, given that not all transplant recipients experience immune rejection, Dr. Crome is working to identify the differences between patients at the cellular level and map out the populations of ILCs and other tissue-resident immune cells that contribute to tissue tolerance or rejection. Alongside the above, Dr. Crome will assess the potential of ILCs in tolerogenic cell therapies for transplantation. She will investigate whether specific populations of ILCs inhibit harmful immune responses or assist with repair in kidney, islet and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. The findings from Dr. Crome's research program will better our understanding of immune tolerance and regulation, which is key to improving the success of transplant procedures.

column36: Mental Health and Intersectionality
column37: Breaking Cycles: Interrupting the Intergenerational Transmission of Mental Illness. Over 1/4 of pregnant and postpartum people will experience mental health problems in the transition to parenthood, which tend to persist through their child's life without treatment. Children who grow up with parents who have untreated mental health problems have an increased risk of themselves experiencing mental illness. Dr. Tomfohr-Madsen's research aims to interrupt this intergenerational transmission of mental health problems using innovative methods that increase access for families who need it most. People exposed to high levels of adversity, including exposure to traumatic events, low social support, and with financial insecurity are more likely to experience mental illness in the transition to parenthood. Risk factors often intersect, increasing vulnerability in people who are exposed to more than one adversity; however, little is known about this process. During the COVID-19 pandemic, of particular concern is the potential that heightened exposure to objective adversity (e.g., job loss) and experiences of psychological distress (e.g., depression) could interact in some families to increase the risk of lasting effects on child mental health. To better understand risk and resilience factors for child mental health, Dr. Tomfohr-Madsen launched the Pregnancy During the COVID-19 Pandemic (PdP) study, which has gathered detailed data from over 10,000 Canadians who were pregnant during the pandemic. Longitudinal follow up of participants and their children is in process and data will be analyzed to understand which families are at the greatest risk of experiencing mental illness across generations. It is also critically important that timely mental health intervention be delivered to prevent the onset of child mental health problems. To address this problem, Dr. Tomfohr-Madsen's team has co-developed an app-based intervention to address parent mental health problems and parenting needs. Dr. Tomfohr-Madsen will investigate if the intervention improves both parent mental health and child outcomes over time. Findings from this program of research will advance understanding about the relationship between intersectional risk factors for parent and child mental health problems and will also refine an accessible intervention tool to support parents and children with their mental health and parenting needs.

column36: Computational Biomedical Imaging
column37: Computational methods are driving the next generation of biomedical imaging technologies, using new approaches for learning and leveraging information about the data, to enable faster and higher quality imaging. These approaches are complementary to the development of new imaging hardware and the discovery of new imaging physics, and provide another route for increasing the value from the data that is acquired. Dr. Mark Chiew will use these computational tools to develop new strategies for more personalized and precise magnetic resonance imaging of the human brain. During his research chair, Dr. Chiew and his research group will focus on the development of imaging technology and their translation into clinically relevant contexts, across two themes. First, the development of novel artificial intelligence methods for reduction of MRI scan times in acute stroke imaging will enable faster time-to-treatment and improved sensitivity and specificity of acute stroke diagnostics. Second, the exploration of computational methods for improved MRI-based temperature mapping in MRI-guided, non-invasive ultrasound neurosurgery will facilitate improved treatment outcomes and recovery times for patients suffering from neurological diseases such as Parkinson's or essential tremor. This innovative program of research will result in the development and deployment of a computational platform for cutting-edge clinical neuroimaging.

column36: Facilitating Change So Long-Term Care Residents Shape The Place They Call Home
column37: The goal of our implementation project is to enable the Ontario Association of Residents' Councils (OARC) to develop a practical, legislatively-supported, evidence-informed and patient (resident)-oriented program to help long-term care (LTC) residents shape the place they call home. Our project establishes a partnership between knowledge users, LTC residents, researchers and trainees to co-create knowledge that will improve the health and wellbeing of LTC residents. Guided by an integrated approach to research - in which stakeholders are actively involved in all aspects of the study - we will undertake three aims: 1: Synthesize existing knowledge on approaches to engage LTC home residents in organizational design and governance of LTC homes. 2: Assess community capacity to implement and sustain a program to engage LTC residents in organizational design and governance of LTC homes. 3: Co-design a program to engage LTC residents in organizational design and governance of their LTC homes. This work is particularly timely in light of new legislative requirements (Fixing Long-Term Care Act, 2021) that require LTC licensees to engage residents in quality improvement and operational planning. OARC, a nonprofit association funded by the Ministry of LTC, is uniquely positioned to contribute and facilitate knowledge from the perspectives of LTC residents and disseminate findings through their networks of LTC residents, homes and stakeholder organizations. Our findings will be integrated into OARC's strategic and operational plans, thereby ensuring impact for LTC homes' policy and practice and, ultimately, improving the quality of life and sense of home for LTC residents.

column36: DNA-based biomaterials
column37: Karina Carneiro, a chemist at the Faculty of Dentistry, University of Toronto is developing a wholly new approach to make biomaterials for diagnosis and treatment of high prevalence inflammatory diseases that disrupt the normal structure and function of connective tissues of joints (osteoarthritis), gums (periodontitis), the wall of the heart (heart failure) and bone. These diseases impair human health and are associated with increased death. Currently available medical approaches to restore tissues destroyed by these diseases are not possible because they do not provide the structural determinants needed to promote regeneration and restore tissue structure and function in adult organs. Carneiro's major advance arises from her discovery that DNA-the carrier of genetic material, can be re-purposed in the laboratory to produce novel biomaterials for medical applications. Unlike other researchers who are developing DNA technology for drug delivery, Carneiro is advancing the field by focusing on DNA-based biomaterials for early diagnosis and treatment of inflammatory diseases. She has developed DNA with specific sequences that assemble into hydrogels (macromolecules that swell with water) that can be injected into inflammatory lesions to regenerate both soft tissue and underlying bone. Research in her laboratory shows that DNA hydrogels promote new bone formation and stimulate bone repair in animal models. This result would not be possible with conventional methods. Carneiro is also developing DNA aptamers (small molecules that bind proteins, carbohydrates, cells, etc.), which she uses as early stage diagnostic platforms to define the structural elements of connective tissues that are breaking down. These DNA materials will enable her to probe connective tissue diseases at much earlier stages than is currently possible. With support of the CRC award, Carneiro will optimize DNA sequences and incorporate other bioactive molecules into the gels for additional regenerative capacity. These advances put Carneiro in the forefront of biomaterial developers in Canada and around the world.

column36: Neuroimaging of Autism and Mental Health in Youth
column37: Autistic youth often experience challenges in social thinking and behaviour and impairment secondary to mental health symptoms which can derail the successful transition to adulthood. Finding effective treatments for debilitating mental health symptoms and functional impairment are among the top research priorities identified by the autism communities. Unfortunately, few evidence-based treatment options currently exist. The fact that symptoms and functioning can differ substantially from person to person, poses a challenge to finding effective interventions and makes it unlikely that any 'one size fits all' intervention may be effective across autistic youth. The proposed research program consists of two projects that ultimately aim to develop biologically targeted treatments that can improve outcome and take into account the substantial differences present between autistic individuals. In the first project of the proposed program, brain imaging will be used in combination with clinical and cognitive assessments to identify the different patterns of associations present between brain and clinical/cognitive measures that are linked to social thinking and behaviour across a sample of youth and emerging adults that includes participants without mental health diagnoses (neurotypical controls), as well as participants with clinical diagnoses of autism or schizophrenia spectrum disorders. This project also aims to identify subsets of participants that may have different clinical diagnoses but feature similar brain-behaviour patterns linked to social thinking and behaviour. This work will fuel future treatment research that will target and attempt to modify specific brain-behaviour patterns linked to social impairment to help support social thinking and behaviour in youth with autism or schizophrenia. The second project of the proposed research program aims to develop a much needed evidence-based treatment option for youth with autism and depression. The project will test whether an intervention method known as brain stimulation, that uses a magnet to stimulate brain regions just below the surface of the brain, may improve symptoms of depression in autistic youth. Neuroimaging will be undertaken before and after brain stimulation treatment as part of this project to improve our understanding of how brain stimulation works and to identify opportunities to optimize and personalize brain stimulation treatment.

column36: Economie de la Prevention et Controle des Infections: EconoPCI
column37: Depuis le debut de la pandemie de la COVID-19, le renforcement de la prevention et controle des infections (PCI) dans les etablissements de sante est au coeur des initiatives des gouvernements dans le monde. Toutefois, contrairement aux investissements realises pour les soins curatifs, les investissements en amont pour la prevention des maladies demeurent faibles. Les donnees issues des ecrits scientifiques indiquent que ce faible investissement pourrait s'expliquer par le manque d'etudes empiriques de qualite qui demontrent l'efficience (benefices superieurs aux couts d'investissement) de la PCI et par l'absence de strategies appropriees pour favoriser l'utilisation des connaissances associees a l'efficience de la PCI par les decideurs. Cette chaire de recherche EconoPCI vient donc combler ces manquements via le developpement d'un corpus de connaissances sur la plus-value d'investir dans la prevention et controle des infections. Elle permettra de : i) realiser des etudes empiriques de qualite pour demontrer l'efficience de la PCI dans les centres hospitaliers (CH) et les centres de soins de longue duree (CSLD) ; et ii) developper des strategies appropriees a mettre en oeuvre pour favoriser le transfert et l'utilisation des connaissances associees a la plus-value d'investir en PCI par les decideurs. La chaire EconoPCI s'articule autour de deux poles de recherche. Le pole empirique et methodologique (pole 1) developpera trois projets innovants pour demontrer l'efficience de la PCI dans les CH et CSLD. Le pole transfert et utilisation des connaissances (pole 2) vise a developper des strategies innovantes pour favoriser le transfert et l'utilisation des connaissances associees a la plus- value d'investir en PCI par les decideurs. S'appuyant sur les principes d'equite, de diversite et d'inclusion, elle sera un pole de reflexion, d'echange et de developpement des etudes en economie de la PCI. Elle sera egalement un lieu de formation a travers des capsules en ligne. Elle affirmera le leadership du Canada dans le domaine de l'analyse economique de la PCI. Enfin, la chaire EconoPCI permettra a l'UQO de rayonner sur la scene provinciale, nationale et internationale comme une universite pionniere dans le domaine de l'economie de la PCI. Ces contributions seront particulierement importantes en contexte post-pandemie de la COVID-19 pour prevenir des eclosions et les consequences de pandemies futures.

column36: Clinical Governance on Primary Health Care
column37: Purpose of the research To advance knowledge on organizational innovations to improve access to primary care in partnership with key stakeholders such as managers, providers, and patient partners. Importance of the research The importance of primary health care services in health systems is widely recognized. As the entry point to the health care system, primary care occupies a strategic coordinating position and has a ripple effect on all other components of the system. Also, accessibility is one of the major concerns facing health systems worldwide. Having access to health services is a high priority for the population, clinicians and decision-makers alike. Canada is among the worst industrialized countries in terms of affiliation to a primary health providers and timely access. Several organizational innovations exist to improve access. Therefore, implementing innovations to improve access to primary health care could have an impact on health system. Clinical governance: supporting primary health care transformation Clinical governance is a mode of governance that promotes the involvement and accountability of managers and clinicians in the implementation of health service improvement initiatives. The overall objective of the Canada Research Chair will be to contribute to the creation of knowledge and innovative practices in primary health care. Research projects in this program will be undertaken in close collaboration with decision-makers, clinicians, and patient partners and will analyse key characteristics of successful models and innovations in primary care. One key feature of the approach is that research is embedded within improvement strategies in order to support efficient changes in practices. The second mandate of the Chair aims to improve managerial and professional practices and intends to do so by introducing regular reflective practices with key actors who are involved in the design and implementation of promising innovations for primary health care. The Chair's research program is based on the analysis of four organizational innovations to improve access: 1) the Advanced Access model, 2) centralized waiting lists for unattached patients, 3) primary health care services for unattached patients, and 4) primary health care organizational models. The research program is composed of six research projects, including three comparative projects in three Canadian provinces and one international project.

Transformer les organisations de sante et les services de proximite est une strategie cle pour ameliorer la performance et l'equite du systeme de sante. Menes en etroite collaboration avec les citoyen.nes, les usager.es, les clinicien.nes et les decideur.es, les objectifs specifiques de la CRC Sa3S seront de : 1. Consolider la recherche sur les systemes adaptatifs en sante et services sociaux au Quebec ; 2. Produire des connaissances pour soutenir les transformations et les innovations des systemes adaptatifs en sante et services sociaux, notamment dans les services de proximite ; 3. Developper et comparer des initiatives de proximite et des innovations de gouvernance en sante et services sociaux au Quebec, au Canada et a l'international ; 4. Favoriser l'emergence et le recrutement de jeunes chercheurs et chercheuses dans le domaine des systemes adaptatifs complexes en sante et services sociaux; 5. Soutenir les organisations, les intervenantes, gestionnaires et usagereres dans la transformation et l'apprentissage de systemes adaptatifs complexes en SSS, particulierement en premiere ligne et de proximite. L'originalite de la programmation reside dans l'integration multiniveau (de la pratique a la gouvernance) d'une approche systemique et adaptative avec des strategies d'amelioration favorables aux changements durables en sante et services sociaux. Pour permettre des ameliorations dans les processus de gouvernance multiniveau, les projets de recherche de ce programme analyseront les caracteristiques cles des modeles et des innovations reussis dans les organisations de sante et les services de proximite. L'une des principales caracteristiques de l'approche des systemes adaptatifs complexes est que la recherche est integree dans des strategies d'amelioration afin de soutenir des changements efficaces et equitables dans les contextes locaux, dans le respect des besoins des differentes parties prenantes, dont les plus vulnerables. Finalement, une recherche engagee aupres des communautes permet de mettre en action la creation de connaissances, de maniere adaptee et retroactive, pour repondre aux besoins changeant des populations.

column36: Addressing the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on people who use drugs through health system innovation
column37: People Who Use Drugs (PWUD) are facing increasing threats to their health and well-being due to COVID-19, drug poisoning deaths, houselessness, and other conditions. There is an urgent need for PWUD-centered responses to these emerging health threats. Using sense-making methods, asset mapping, and partner roundtable discussions, this project will document PWUD priorities for health interventions, identify community strengths that will help to implement these interventions, and determine what other resources are needed for implementation. The project builds on a two decade partnership between PWUD, the Boyle Street Community Services organization, and academics in Edmonton, Alberta. We will use community-based participatory research principles, with PWUD as core team members and leaders on the project. We expect the project to help PWUD community members with health promotion and health literacy, bring evidence into practice in an underserved setting, and build community and organizational capacity for patient-oriented research.

column36: Reimagining Naturally Occurring Retirement Communities (NORCs) for 21st Century Cities: What Works Best to Support Older Adults to Age in Place?
column37: Many older adults live clustered in buildings or communities, known as Naturally Occurring Retirement Communities (NORCs). These communities provide an opportunity to deliver on-site social supports and health services in efficient and creative ways to prevent loneliness, improve health and well-being, and support older adults to age in place. Few NORCs, however, have been enhanced like this because little is known about how to intentionally create, implement or sustain these types of models. Our research will fill these gaps by identifying which NORC sites are best suited for enhancement, and what factors promote or hinder their successful implementation. We will also examine if the level of support (or degree of enhancement) provided by the model changes how it is implemented and its effectiveness. Exploring sex and gender differences in how the models work and their impact will be important as most older adults living in NORCs are women. We will implement three enhanced NORC models at 7 sites - first in Toronto, one of the most diverse cities in the world, and then later in Barrie, a quickly growing mid-sized city. The models will vary in the intensity of support they provide (low, medium, and high) to older adults. We will evaluate both the process of implementation to understand what works, for whom and in what circumstances, and the impact of the models on older adults and the healthcare system. The project will be guided by a strong implementation science team and researchers with expertise in aging. We will engage a diverse and pan-Canadian National Stakeholder Advisory Committee of residents, building owners, municipal representatives, and program and research staff so that our findings are useful and actionable. This first of its kind project will reimagine aging in place and deliver practical tools - a NORC Implementation Toolkit - to support the spread and scale of enhanced NORCs in ways that benefit all, across Canadian and international cities.

column36: Healthy Cities-Implementation Science Team in Healthy Aging
column37: Our Healthy Cities-Implementation Science Team in Healthy Aging tackles the epidemics of physical inactivity and loneliness that plague older adults who live in medium- and large-sized cities. Physically active older adults have better mobility, mental and social health than their inactive counterparts. Therefore, guided by implementation science principles (e.g., tailored for participants; adaptable to context), we co-designed Choose to Move (CTM) with older adults, community and government partners. CTM is a flexible, scalable community-based program that improved physical activity, mobility, social isolation and loneliness in older adults. From small beginnings, we scaled-up CTM over 8 years to reach >6000 older adults in British Columbia (BC). Our reservation was that CTM engaged primarily white older adults in Metro Vancouver; 77% were women. We now aim to expand the reach of CTM to better serve the needs of more diverse groups of older adults. We will support community-based seniors' services organizations (e.g., not-for-profits; neighbourhood houses) to adapt CTM to 'best fit' the older adults they serve, and build capacity in these organizations to deliver CTM. Through 5 projects, we will address 4 broad research objectives. We will: 1. Undertake evidence syntheses to identify knowledge gaps; 2. Describe how the CTM program and implementation strategies are adapted and implemented in older adults who are South Asian, older men or older adults in northern BC; 3. Evaluate whether readiness (e.g., organizational capacity), implementation strategies (e.g., training and technical support) and implementation factors (e.g., acceptability) influence how CTM is implemented; 4. Measure impact of CTM on physical activity and other health outcomes of older adults. Our impact will be engaged community organizations, a program that has been adapted to serve diverse older adults, a new generation of implementation scientists, and healthy, active and connected older adults.

column36: Understanding how to Attract, Adapt, IMplement and Sustain an evidence-informed fall prevention exercise program in Community Settings: The AAIMS project.
column37: When someone falls, there are many consequences for the person and the health system. Almost 100,000 people in Canada are admitted to the hospital annually because of a fall! The best way to reduce the number of fall injuries is to exercise regularly. As a result, many communities offer exercise programs for older adults to help reduce falls. However, according to the latest Canadian report, fewer than one in ten fall prevention exercise programs provide the best program possible, meaning that programs should be offered all year long, a least three hours per week, and focus on balance activities. In addition, some Canadians do not have such a program in their region. Our team includes local, provincial, and national partners, in addition to researchers and students from Canada and Northern Ireland. They have all collaborated to plan the Attract, Adapt, IMplement and Sustain (AAIMS) project to understand how to: 1-attract people who currently do not participate in fall prevention exercise programs; 2-adapt the programs currently offered that do not meet the recommendations; 3-offer a program that follows recommendations if needed; 4-keep offering a program in community settings. The exercise program will be offered in-person, online, or in a combination of the two. We will collect information by interviewing key people over the course of the project and will test how many people registered for the program, if they come with different characteristics, if there are signs that programs will last, and if people who were doing the program fall fewer times compared to the general public. This program will help us understand how to better spread a program that works in many different places while reducing participant falls.

column36: Small Steps for Big Changes: Implementing an Evidence-Based Diabetes Prevention Program into Diverse Urban Communities
column37: Six million Canadians are at risk for developing type 2 diabetes (T2D). Laboratory-based diabetes prevention programs have not been effective when translated into community settings due to their low-quality delivery and inability to reach people in the community who need it most. Small Steps for Big Changes is a diet and exercise counselling intervention that significantly reduces the risk of developing T2D. Designed for feasible, scalable, and sustainable implementation into communities, Small Steps for Big Changes is delivered by community-dwelling peers to ensure the content is ethnoculturally relevant. Small Steps for Big Changes can now be delivered virtually through a state-of-the-art online platform. The next phase of research is to test the implementation of this program where T2D rates are high and diabetes prevention programs remain inaccessible. In partnership with YMCAs in Canada and Australia spanning 8 provinces and the state of Queensland, we are well-positioned to evaluate the implementation and effectiveness of Small Steps for Big Changes across 16 urban municipalities. In Year 1, the program will be adapted through our regional delivery teams and YMCA staff will receive virtual training to deliver program. Small Steps for Big Changes will be delivered to patients in Years 2, 3 and 4. To evaluate implementation, we will examine number of staff trained/patients enrolled, attendance, sessions delivered as planned, delivery costs, and number of sites continuing to deliver the program in Years 4-6. YMCA staff, municipality stakeholders, and patients will also be interviewed on program receptivity. To evaluate program effectiveness, changes in patient health (e.g., blood glucose, weight, exercise, diet) will be measured over 2 years following program completion. This research offers an innovative, cost-saving, and sustainable solution for the prevention of T2D in traditionally underserved, at-risk populations by partnering with communities.

column36: Supporting Healthy Lifestyle Choices to Promote Mental Health & Wellbeing of Indigenous Youth Aging-Out-of-Care in Urban Settings
column37: "Supporting Healthy Lifestyle Choices to Promote Mental Health & Wellbeing of Indigenous Youth Aging-Out-of-Care in Urban Settings" will support the development and adaptation of interventions designed to support Indigenous youth aging out of care in urban settings. Rooted in Indigenous holistic concepts of well-being and a cultural land-based model, the project will centre collaborative work with Indigenous youth, Indigenous care practitioners, Elders/Knowledge Holders and Friendship Centres to develop creative and innovative action plans to address the complex challenges that arise prior to and during the transition out-of-care in urban settings. In this way, the model and method will focus on building and implementing interventions in urban Indigenous community settings that enable increased access for Indigenous youth to physical, social, and cultural supports that support them in utilizing wellbeing centered decision-making ("healthy lifestyle choices"). The goals of the study include: 1) adapting interventions designed to support mental health and well-being for Indigenous youth aging-out-of-care in urban settings that emphasize wellbeing centred decision-making ("healthy lifestyle choice"); 2) developing culturally based wellbeing indicators with and for Indigenous youth (ages 12-24); 3) expanding the knowledge based of care practitioners working with Indigenous youth aging-out-of-care to be inclusive of Indigenous life path preparations that support holistic wellbeing and life preparedness in an urban environment; 4) evaluating the intervention to assess scalability and adaptation to other relevant populations in urban contexts; and 5) developing and sharing knowledge resources for Indigenous and non-Indigenous care practitioners aimed at supporting the mental health and well-being of Indigenous youth aging-out-of-care in urban contexts.

column36: Building CapaCITY/E for Sustainable Transportation
column37: CapaCITY/E is a team working to understand why and how cities implement sustainable transportation interventions, specifically infrastructure with safe and inclusive design to support the uptake of walking, cycling, and public transit use. Our focus is on All Ages and Abilities (AAA) bicycle networks and speed management interventions. AAA routes separate bicycles from motor vehicles; connections of AAA routes in a network create conditions that allow cycling to be a choice for more people, more often, for more trips. Speed management interventions make roads safer and more accessible for all users: our work focuses on specific interventions including removing lanes for motor vehicles to create space for people to walk, wheel, and cycle; automated speed enforcement programs; and speed limit reductions (e.g., from 50 km/hr to 30 km/hr). The goal of CapaCITY/E is to accelerate the implementation of sustainable transportation interventions that will support health, mobility, and equity in cities. Working with cities, community groups, and people living in cities, we will build new understanding of how, why, and for whom sustainable transportation interventions are implemented. Our partner cities (Halifax, Montreal, Kingston, Guelph, Toronto, Saskatoon, Calgary, Surrey, Victoria, and Melbourne, Australia) provide a broad array of contexts for comparative case studies. By assessing how cities are similar or different in implementing interventions, and by developing and sharing tools from what we learn, we aim to help more cities implement sustainable transportation interventions to improve the health of their populations.

column36: Feasibility of a Peer-Led Caring Contact Intervention Following Calls to a Crisis Line by Public Safety Personnel
column37: There is an urgent need to create and apply targeted interventions for at-risk public safety personnel (PSP) to address the increased prevalence of post-traumatic stress and suicidal behaviours among this population. Social support, including peer support and caring contacts, has been shown to reduce risks of suicide and post-traumatic stress injuries (PTSI) among PSP. Caring contacts involves follow up communication with high risk groups at high risk times, offering encouragement, fostering human connection, instilling hope and providing resources. Peer support has been shown to increase social support among high risk populations who may be less likely to access mental health support due to stigma. More research is required to understand how caring contacts and peer support can be used to better support PSP who call crisis lines. Crisis lines in Canada currently do not incorporate peer support or caring contacts. Integrating these interventions may be beneficial for supporting PSP and may potentially prevent PTSI and suicide. The proposed project examines a novel integrated peer support and caring contact intervention (Caring Contact-Peer Intervention; CC-PI) for PSP who contact the Canada Suicide Prevention Service (CSPS). This pilot study will examine the feasibility of the CC-P and its acceptability for PSP in crisis and the trained PSP peers providing support. PSP peers will undergo a specialized crisis line volunteer training. Project outcomes include whether CC-PI implementation is feasible and illumination of the experiences of PSP and PSP peers with the intervention and their perception of its impact. If successful, this project will produce a scalable and cost-effective way to prevent post-traumatic stress injury and suicide in high risk PSP by providing tailored support by peers for diverse groups of PSP. It will also make CSPS more meaningful and relevant for PSP, and provide data to improve future training of peers and iterations of the CC-PI.

column36: Do public safety personnel who provide peer support suffer from vicarious trauma?
column37: The aim of this project is to investigate whether public safety personnel who provide peer support to their colleagues are affected by hearing traumatic stories from their colleagues. We will ask peer supporters enrolled in the On-Call program to complete a survey at the beginning of the program and three months and six months after it starts. The survey will ask about individual symptoms of distress such as anxiety, sleep and mood as well as organizational factors which reflect stress such as burnout or feeling betrayed or humiliated by an organization. We hypothesize that peer supporters who are distressed by organizational factors are more likely to show signs of distress at 6 months. We will also conduct a qualitative study to ask about their experiences of providing peer support. We will invite peer supporters with high and low symptoms scores to be part of the qualitative study.

column36: Accelerating Clinical Trials (ACT) - Canada
column37: We have established the Accelerating Clinical Trials (ACT) Consortium to strengthen the conduct of clinical trials in Canada. ACT brings together hundreds of researchers from 28 networks, 11 trial units, from Nova Scotia to British Columbia and Nunavut. ACT will support and expand existing networks and enable the creation of new networks to improve the efficiency, number, and quality of trials conducted in Canada. ACT will increase the impact of clinical trials in Canada: ACT will lead collaboration, coordination, and resource-sharing across networks to enable Canada's best researchers and companies to more efficiently complete high-quality, high-impact clinical trials. ACT will build clinical trial capacity: ACT will provide trial units with the knowledge, skills, and experience to conduct large-scale trials. We will streamline administrative processes (for example, ethics reviews, contracts, and protocols) to accelerate timelines and reduce costs. We will expand Canadian networks internationally. ACT will maximize research impact and knowledge mobilization: ACT will follow best practices in patient-oriented research and integrated knowledge translation. We will leverage national and international contacts to maximize research impact and knowledge mobilization. Advance equitable access to trials for Canadians: ACT will follow the principles of equity, diversity, and inclusion in clinical trials such that the knowledge gained is applicable to all those affected. Many trials will be embedded into routine healthcare, enabling the inclusion of all patients regardless of ethnicity, gender, or socioeconomic status. Conclusion: The ACT consortium has the expertise and vision to increase the conduct of inclusive, cost-efficient, high-quality, high-impact clinical trials in Canada. We will help Canadian researchers accelerate the management and prevention of chronic diseases and to respond rapidly to new health threats and pandemics.

column36: Prediction of Intraventricular Hemmorhage using Echocardiography and Near Infrared Spectroscopy (PIE-NIRS)
column37: Background: Moderate to severe intraventricular hemorrhage (msIVH; Grades II-IV) affects ~25-30% of Canadian extremely-low-gestational-age-neonates (ELGANs; <27+6 weeks) and leads to long-term neurodisability. A targeted preventative approach is challenged by our inability to identify at-risk ELGANs early. Pilot studies using Near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), including our own, found lower cerebral saturations (CrSO2) and greater periods of altered cerebral autoregulation in infants who subsequently developed msIVH. However, the predictive characteristics of NIRS-derived markers using clinically translatable methods need to be established. Further, incorporating relevant echocardiographic (ECHO) markers may improve prediction models and provide mechanistic hemodynamic insights to inform future management. Objective: To investigate the utility of multi-modal assessment using NIRS and ECHO for early identification of ELGANs at risk of msIVH. Specific aims: 1. To examine individual and combined discriminating characteristics of NIRS-derived parameters (CrSO2 [cumulative % time spent below thresholds of <55%, <60%, <65% and <70%] and cerebral oxygenation index [COIx, values >0.5 = altered autoregulation]) at 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42 and 48 hours of age, for msIVH. 2. To examine added value of ECHO parameters (left ventricular output, superior vena cava flow, patent ductus arteriosus size) and patient demographics in improving discriminating characteristics of NIRS. Design:Prospective observational cohort study conducted over three years at three Canadian tertiary NICUs. Inclusion criteria: GA at birth = 27+6. Exclusion criteria: Genetic or congenital anomalies. Intervention:Following informed parental consent, obtained <12 hours of birth, ELGANs will undergo: -Cerebral NIRS monitoring (CrSO2 and COIx) until 48 hours of age. -2 ECHOs: 1st < 24 hours, 2nd 48-60 hours of age. -2 head ultrasounds: 1st <24 hours, 2nd day 4-7 of age. Outcome of interest:msIVH on 2nd head ultrasound. Sample size: 345 infants (expecting 28% prevalence ofmsIVH based on pilot data, and Area under Curve of 0.86, precision of 0.05 and 10% data loss)

column36: Patient and Caregiver Priorities for Quality Improvement on General Medical Wards
column37: This project will elicit patient and caregiver priorities for improvement on general medical hospital wards, in order to drive quality improvement that is aligned with their preferences. General medical wards care for patients admitted to hospital for common conditions such as heart failure, lung disease, pneumonia and falls. The number of patients cared for on such wards has increased over the past decade, and is expected to continue to grow in line with population aging. It is important to engage patients and their families to understand what matters most to them so care improvements can be appropriately aligned. This project will use group concept mapping to first elicit contributors to the patient and caregiver experience on general medical wards. We will then ask patients and caregivers to rate and sort these ideas to create a map of key concepts, and to identify the top priorities for quality improvement. Throughout all steps of the process, we will focus on recruiting a diverse group of participants, to reflect the broad experience and perspectives of the general medical community. The Ontario General Medicine Quality Improvement Network (GEMQIN) is a government-funded program that brings together clinicians and administrators from Ontario hospitals who share the aim of improving the quality of care for patients admitted to general medical wards. The results of this study will directly inform new quality indicator development for GEMQIN physician and hospital performance reports, as well as improvement initiatives in the GEMQIN community of practice.

column36: System-level approaches to increasing living donor kidney transplantation
column37: Living donor kidney transplantation (LDKT) is the best treatment option for patients with kidney failure. It entails a healthy living donor (LD) donating one of their kidneys to the patient. Despite the several advantages of LDKT, rates in Canada have stagnated and most patients still receive other inferior treatment options such as dialysis and deceased donation. To better understand why this is the case, we studied current systems and noted several system-level inefficiencies and deficiencies likely causing this. We also noted that there is a lack of solid infrastructure to support LDs who provide such an important gift to society. Now, we want to advance this work and develop policy. First, we want to focus on the province in Canada with the lowest rates of LDKT. We conducted research and found several barriers to LDKT. We now want to unite existing organizations and see how their isolated efforts can be unified to develop a coherent and collaborative plan. Second, we want to see if current organizations are undermining LDKT by focusing on dialysis and deceased donation. Third, we want to better support LDs who are generally followed by family doctors. We want to obtain their perspectives and what model of care they prefer. We also want to know what family doctors think about living donation and whether they are comfortable taking care of LDs. Overall, we have developed system-level approaches to improve the health of patients with kidney failure in Canada who present a significant public health burden and have poor outcomes. We also want to better support LDs. We also think our study will help address disparities in access to LDKT and we will conduct a gender analysis to inform future work to address gender disparities in living donation.

column36: Partnering with Parents for Pumping Success: Feasibility of Personalized Lactation Support Utilizing Point-of-Care Human Milk Biomarkers
column37: Human milk from an infant's own parent (parent's own milk; PM) can be lifesaving for infants admitted to neonatal intensive care units (NICUs), reducing risk of death and serious problems. Due to medical and socioeconomic challenges and other effects of systemic racism like chronic stress, parents of colour are more likely to deliver prematurely and less likely to provide PM. Lack of PM creates further health disparities and increases lifetime risk of many medical problems for babies and their lactating parents. Using a breast pump makes providing PM harder, and personalized, data-driven lactation support for this high-risk group of lactating parents does not exist. Problems with PM supply are often noticed too late to intervene to improve long-term PM volumes. Consequently, babies need to be fed alternatives which have risks and do not have the same positive impact on health. Salt levels in PM change in the first days after birth, and changes in these levels can predict if or when milk "comes in" and how much PM will be made days or weeks later. These salt levels can be measured with easy-to-use tests, but testing has never been done before at bedside. We want to study the feasibility of teaching parents who are pumping PM and who have preterm NICU infants to test their own PM salt using bedside testers. We want to learn how they feel about testing their milk and whether the data empowers them or potentially causes undue stress. We want to see if we can use the salt levels, compared to just looking at amounts of PM pumped, to predict low PM volumes and guide parents to pump differently to make more PM. This study will give us better tools to support parents of NICU or other high-risk babies, especially from racialized communities that have lower rates of PM feeding. We hope these tools can improve PM volumes, ultimately to decrease race/ethnicity and income-based gaps in lifelong health problems.

column36: Establishing a foundation for shared decision-making in vascular access selection for adults with advanced chronic kidney disease
column37: People living with kidney disease face many decisions as they approach kidney failure and prepare for hemodialysis. One of these is how to reliably connect to the blood-purification machine using 'vascular access'. The two most common forms of vascular access are fistulas and catheters. A fistula is a vein surgically connected to an artery in the arm that is accessed by needles; a catheter is a plastic tube placed in a large vein in the neck. In the past, experts and clinical practice guidelines considered fistulas the preferred form of vascular access and actively promoted them. However, fistulas have important implications for patients (e.g., pain, multiple procedures), and they may not be the best option for all people under all circumstances. Instead of a physician telling the patient which vascular access option to choose, patients and their care teams are now encouraged to review all options, discuss patients' values and preferences, and arrive at informed decisions. This is referred to as 'shared decision-making'. At this time, we cannot offer decision support to promote shared decision-making about vascular access because we do not know patient, caregiver, and healthcare provider decision needs. Our proposed project will study current vascular access practices, care gaps, and priorities for shared decision-making. We will use different methods, including interviews, observations, and questionnaires, to understand the extent to which individuals' needs are being met and how we can improve processes for choosing vascular access. Our team of researchers, clinicians, patients, and caregivers has expertise and/or lived experience in this area of research. We will provide important information on the aspects of decisions about vascular access that matter to patients and healthcare providers. This will help us develop a strategy to support shared decision-making and improve care processes for people preparing for hemodialysis.

column36: Better Together: Identifying Collaborative Research Priorities and Literature Gaps in Child Maltreatment Research
column37: One in three children in Canada has been exposed to child abuse or neglect, which can lead to the development of negative physical health and mental health outcomes across the lifespan. With heightened family stress during the COVID-19 pandemic, risk factors for child abuse increased, leading to even greater mental health challenges and support needs. Research priorities that capture the perspective of youth and caregivers who have experienced abuse and neglect are thus urgently needed. In line with the saying "nothing about us, without us", youth and caregivers with lived experience need to be included in research priority setting in order for research to be relevant, efficient, and cost-effective. The goal of the Better Together project is to create partnerships between youth, caregivers, clinicians, and researchers to identify key research priorities to guide the future of child maltreatment research in Canada. Using a co-design research approach, we will work with individuals with lived experience to identify and prioritize how to improve mental health and adaptive outcomes following exposure to child abuse and neglect. We will achieve this goal in four main ways: 1) we will identify the most important research questions about child maltreatment from the perspective of diverse stakeholders, 2) we will identify key literature gaps in etiology, assessment, treatment, and prevention of child maltreatment, 3) we will develop a collaborative "top ten" list of the most important research priorities which will be shared nationally and internationally, and 4) we will explore how youth, caregiver, clinician, and researcher perspectives on patient engagement shift over the course of the project. Individuals with lived experience will be involved at each step of the process. The Better Together project will share and disseminate what we learn with researchers and clinicians across Canada to inform the co-design of new interventions and improvements in mental health.

column36: Engaging adolescents for sexual and reproductive health and rights and family planning advocacy in Pakistan
column37: Pakistan currently has the highest proportion of the population under the age of 25 years. In addition, Pakistan also has the highest adolescent total fertility rate and a very high unmet need for family planning. Adolescents in Pakistan face many challenges in terms of sexual and reproductive health and rights and these include early marriage and childbearing, unmet need for contraception, unsafe abortion, and limited access to information related to sexual and reproductive health services. Despite recognizing adolescence as an important developmental period, research on sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) needs and access to sexual and reproductive health information and care services among adolescents in Pakistan is scarce. In this study, we will explore the sexual and reproductive health knowledge, information needs, and priorities of adolescents in rural Pakistan and how to improve SRHR and empower adolescents to exercise their reproductive rights. A participatory action research framework will guide this study. This research project will be conducted in three stages: Stage 1: Establishment of youth advisory groups and identification and prioritization of SRHR and family planning concerns. Stage 2: Planning and co-design the intervention (i.e., SRHR and family planning advocacy Toolkit). Stage 3: Implementation and usability testing of advocacy Toolkit. This project builds on well-established relationships between researchers, clinicians, lady health workers, and communities of adolescents. This study will advance the limited knowledge base on SRHR knowledge and information needs of adolescents in rural Pakistan as well as the science underpinning participatory action research methods with adolescents. Engaging adolescents throughout the study will increase their involvement in SRHR and family planning care decision-making, expand efficiencies in SRH care utilization, and ultimately improve adolescents' SRH outcomes.

column36: Inspiratory Muscle Training in Lung Transplant Candidates and Implications on Early Post-Transplant Outcomes: A Pilot and Feasibility Randomized Clinical Trial
column37: Recovery after lung transplantation may be challenging after a long stay in the intensive care unit or hospital after surgery. The structure and function of the diaphragm (most important breathing muscle) is very important for good recovery after surgery. Training this muscle before surgery may provide "extra reserve" to cope with the stresses after surgery. Rehabilitation guidelines advise that inspiratory muscle training (IMT) combined with standard whole-body exercises prior to major surgery can reduce post-operative complications and expedite recovery. In major thoracic surgery or organ transplantation, the mechanisms and clinical benefits of IMT have not been well established. The lung transplant population represents a unique group to study the benefits of pre-operative IMT. We propose to study 100 lung transplant patients awaiting surgery who will be randomized to receive either: 1) IMT and standard rehabilitation or 2) standard rehabilitation alone across 4 centers in Canada. Participants in group 1 will use a well-established respiratory muscle training device to train twice daily until transplantation. All participants will undergo standard rehabilitation until the time of surgery and 3-months post-transplant. In a subset of the 100 patients, muscle biopsies of the diaphragm will be performed in the Toronto program at the time of surgery. This study will determine if the research design is feasible. Secondary measures will evaluate breathlessness, quality of life, diaphragm function and cellular characteristics, and clinical outcomes 3-months post-transplant. This study will provide a unique opportunity to understand whether IMT is feasible across 4 transplant centers and get an assessment of post-operative outcomes and mechanisms underlying IMT. This study may serve as a model for examining IMT as part of pre-operative rehabilitation in a number of patient populations undergoing major surgery.

column36: Comparative effectiveness of opioid versus opioid-free post-discharge analgesia after outpatient breast surgery: A randomized controlled trial
column37: Canada is experiencing a crisis of opioid use and abuse partially caused by increased prescriptions by doctors; recent data show that approximately 20 Canadians die every day of opioid overdoses. People often receive their first opioid prescription to treat pain after outpatient breast surgery (i.e., total or partial breast resection with same-day discharge), and many misuse these drugs and become addicted. Additionally, many opioid pills prescribed to these patients go unused, and may be diverted and misused by their family members, friends, or other community members. To prevent this problem, the first opioid prescription to treat surgical pain may be prevented by using opioid-free analgesia (i.e., pain treatment using only non-opioid interventions). Prescribing only non-opioid analgesics after surgery is very common in many countries outside of North America; however, few studies have assessed whether opioid-free analgesia is as effective as opioid analgesia after breast surgery. Therefore, the main question that we aim to answer in our study is: For patients who have had outpatient breast surgery, is pain treatment without opioids as good as pain treatment using opioids? We propose a study comparing two groups of patients: one group will receive opioids to treat pain after surgery while the other group will receive only non-opioid interventions. We will assess the impact of these interventions on pain intensity, pain interference with activities, medication side effects, and other outcomes. We have assembled an expert team of scientists, surgeons, pain specialists, and patients to ensure the success of this study. Our results will provide important information to guide surgeons' decisions to prescribe (or not to prescribe) opioids. In the future, if opioid-free analgesia is found to be effective, doctors may be able to substantially reduce the prescription of opioids after breast surgery and prevent more people from misusing opioids.

column36: People with Prediabetes and Mild Diabetes: characteristics, management and outcomes
column37: Diabetes is a chronic medical condition that leads to higher-than-normal blood glucose levels in the body. This may lead to several complications including heart attacks, strokes, kidney damage, vision loss, and loss of limb. The rates of diabetes are rising globally and in Canada. With more advanced diagnostic tests we are now able to identify people with prediabetes and mild stages of diabetes. However, it is not clear if treating people with prediabetes and mild diabetes with medications reduces their risk of worse outcomes related to diabetes. It is important to know if treating people with prediabetes and mild diabetes helps them avoid the complications of diabetes, or exposes them to more medication side-effects and psychological harms associated with over-diagnosis. In this study we propose to understand better how people with prediabetes and mild diabetes should be treated. We will interview people with lived experience of prediabetes and mild diabetes, and health care providers to understand how the diagnosis is made, managed, and the impacts of the diagnosis and associated additional monitoring. We will use data sets from Alberta, British Columbia and Ontario to identify newly diagnosed adult individuals with prediabetes and mild diabetes and evaluate their health outcomes over the course of seven years. We will seek to understand how those outcomes were impacted or not by the initiation of medications. The findings from our study will shed light on an important question facing patients, health care providers and health systems. Prevention of diabetes related complications with early treatment is promising, however, there are risks of over-treating people with medications. Our study will help inform decisions around initiation of treatment in this group of people. This will lead to the formation of a unique cohort of people that can be followed for longer-term outcomes

column36: Des visites a domicile universelles et concues en collaboration ameliorent la sante maternelle et neonatale: Preuve d'incidence dans le nord de l'Ouganda d'apres conflit
column37: La disponibilite des services en perinatalite ne signifie pas que toutes les femmes enceintes en beneficient. Les femmes enceintes vulnerables ont plus de difficultes pendant leur grossesse et l'accouchement. Toutefois, ce sont elles qui utilisent le moins ces services. La pauvrete, l'education, la distance, la culture et les attitudes de leur conjoint reduisent leur capacite a beneficier de ces derniers. Nous contournerons ces obstacles par des visites repetees a domicile pour chaque femme enceinte et de leur conjoint. Nous diviserons les 32 paroisses du district de Nwoya en 16 unites d'intervention et 16 unites controle. Dans les unites d'intervention, la cartographie cognitive floue explorera les points de vue des femmes enceintes, leurs conjoints, et les prestataires de soins sur l'accouchement sans risques. Un questionnaire decrira les masculinites, le recours aux soins et les resultats en sante. Lors des dialogues deliberatifs, les femmes, leur conjoint et les prestataires de soins decideront du contenu des visites a domicile. Ce contenu sera transfere dans de courtes videos produites localement. Dans les 16 unites d'intervention, les visiteuses rendront visite aux femmes enceintes et les visiteurs a leur conjoint. Lors des visites, les visiteurs leur montreront les videos. Ils passeront un questionnaire electronique lors des visites bimensuelles, afin de recueillir des donnees sur l'evolution de la grossesse. Une etude de suivi comparera les unites d'intervention et de controle. L'etude mesurera les complications postnatales, la mortalite neonatale, les comportements au recours aux soins, et les resultats en sante. Une evaluation qualitative decrira l'experience des visites a domicile des femmes enceintes et de leur conjoint. Nous solliciterons la participation des femmes, les prestataires de soins et gestionnaires tout au long du projet. Nous preparerons des modules de formation en ligne pour reproduire les visites a domicile dans d'autres districts.

column36: Vers des soins de sante sans obstacle : Un projet collaboratif pour co-construire une formation sur la communication patient-soignant en autisme en partenariat avec les patients et les professionnels de la sante.
column37: Les personnes autistes au Canada rencontrent des obstacles dans l'acces aux soins de sante et rapportent des besoins de services non combles. Les etudes ont documente les experiences negatives et stigmatisantes vecues dans les milieux cliniques, le manque de reconnaissance de l'expertise des patients et leur exclusion du processus de soins. Or, les interactions avec les professionnels de la sante sont un determinant important de la qualite des soins. Les professionnels rapportent pourtant un manque de connaissances sur l'autisme et le besoin d'etre mieux formes sur les strategies de communication inclusives adaptees aux besoins des personnes autistes. Afin d'ameliorer l'acces aux soins, il apparait prioritaire d'augmenter la qualite des interactions avec les professionnels de la sante. Quelques outils et formations ont ete proposes dans la litterature sur les pratiques de communication a privilegier lors des consultations avec les personnes autistes. Toutefois, les travaux recents soulignent les limites de ces programmes, tels que le manque d'attention aux interactions cliniques entre les patients et les professionnels et l'implication limitee des personnes autistes et des soignants. Pour repondre a ces defis, ce projet vise a 1) mieux documenter les interactions cliniques en autisme et comprendre comment elles peuvent constituer des barrieres ou des facilitateurs a l'acces aux soins et 2) co-construire et evaluer un module de formation en ligne pour les professionnels de la sante. Nous menerons ce projet en collaboration avec des personnes autistes, des parents et des professionnels du CHU Sainte-Justine (plusieurs departements ont exprime leur interet). Le projet aura plusieurs retombees pratiques. Il permettra notamment de generer du materiel pedagogique pour ameliorer la communication entre les patients et les professionnels et reduire les obstacles d'acces aux soins pour les personnes autistes et leurs familles.

column36: Low-value care and variation in practice in the care of children hospitalized with bronchiolitis in Canada
column37: Bronchiolitis is a respiratory disease of young children caused by viruses and is one of the most common and costly causes of hospitalizations in children. Despite many years of research and studies of various tests and treatments, many that are commonly used have not been found to be beneficial for children with bronchiolitis, in addition to being costly to the healthcare system. Thus, treatment of bronchiolitis remains simple and supportive. Despite this knowledge and that the recommendation is not to use them, many ineffective tests and treatments are still being used. A more standardized approach to investigations and treatment in bronchiolitis could lead to better outcomes for children with bronchiolitis and lower healthcare costs. The objective of this study, conducted in community and children's hospitals across Canada, is to understand patterns of use of six different tests and treatments for bronchiolitis and to compare the their use between hospitals and physicians. The specific objectives are to: -Estimate the frequency of use and costs associated with 6 tests and interventions in children hospitalized for bronchiolitis -Document variation in practice between hospitals and between individual clinicians and determine whether this is impacted by patient/family and clinical characteristics -Determine whether health inequities and sociodemographic characteristics impact bronchiolitis care -Evaluate barriers and facilitators to following clinical guidelines for bronchiolitis care, from the perspective of parents, physicians, and hospital administrators We will use hospital records for objectives 1 to 3, collecting additional sociodemographic data with participant consent for objective 3. To understand physician and parent perception and knowledge about bronchiolitis care, individual interviews will be used. This study will lead to an intervention designed to reduce unnecessary tests and treatments in children hospitalized for bronchiolitis in Canada.

column36: Care, Health, Economics, and Society: Spillover Effects of Caregiving in Canada
column37: One in four Canadians who are 15 years old and over are caregivers. They provide care for friends and family who have a long-term illness, disability or are aging. While caregiving can be rewarding, it can also harm the caregiver's work productivity and health. Caregivers may be less productive while at work and they may have to reduce their paid work time, miss work, or need to leave their jobs. Many caregivers experience emotional and physical stress that can harm their health and lead to financial costs for individuals and society as a whole. Yet, caregivers are critical to our health care system as they reduce the use of public funding for home care and health services. Governments offer support programs for caregivers, such as employment insurance benefits, tax credits, and monthly allowances. Some workplaces provide flexible work arrangements and paid and unpaid leaves to their caregiver employees. Further research is still needed to determine how caregiving responsibilities impact the caregiver's health-related quality of life and work productivity and determine whether government and workplace programs effectively support caregivers in Canada. Our study will shed light on the social and economic burden of caregiving and provide findings to improve how we measure caregiver health-related quality of life and loss of work productivity for future studies. This research will recommend policies that can help ease caregiving responsibilities, improve caregivers' overall wellness and work productivity, and reduce inequities related to social and economic factors, such as caregiver age, sex, gender, and cultural identity.
