column36: Achieving Equitable Uptake and Use of Diabetes Technologies Among Adults with Type 1 Diabetes
column37: Background: Diabetes technologies such as insulin pumps and continuous or flash glucose monitors (CGM) help people with type 1 diabetes achieve better glucose control and quality of life. However, these devices are used less by people from historically marginalized communities (e.g. lower income or belonging to racial or ethnic minority group), even if costs are reimbursed. Methods: 1) We will use large anonymized health care databases in Ontario and Quebec to determine differences in the rates of use of diabetes technologies between adults with type 1 diabetes from historically marginalized communities compared to those who are not, and how this is impacted by public funding. 2) Through interviews with patients, diabetes educators, and endocrinologists, we will determine factors that lead adults with type 1 diabetes from historically marginalized communities to use or not use diabetes technologies. 3) Through a co-design process, we will develop strategies to improve the use of diabetes technologies among those from historically marginalized communities. Anticipated Outcomes: 1) Diabetes technologies will be used less commonly among adults with type 1 diabetes from historically marginalized communities, even in regions with public funding. 2) Multiple barriers to diabetes technologies use will be identified. 3) We will develop strategies to support more effective use of diabetes technologies among adults with type 1 diabetes from historically marginalized communities for future implementation. Relevance: Our research will determine if diabetes technologies are used inequitably in Canada despite the existence of public funding programs, and identify strategies to improve equitable use of diabetes technologies.

column36: Connecting Today to Combat Social Isolation and Loneliness: A Pragmatic Cluster RCT of a Remote Visiting Program for Care Home Residents Living with Dementia
column37: Over half a million Canadians live with dementia, a number projected to reach 937,000 in just 9 years. Dementia damages thinking, but the human need to feel caring and belonging (social connectedness) remains essential for quality of life. We have long known that social isolation and loneliness undermine the quality of life experienced by people living with dementia in care homes. While visiting programs have addressed loneliness in other populations, little research has aimed to promote social connectedness experienced by people living with dementia. We developed Connecting Today, a feasible and highly acceptable remote visiting program that can support care home residents living with moderate to severe dementia to have video calls with their care partners, family and friends. This is the first clinical trial to assess the effectiveness of a remote visiting program for use with people living with dementia. Over 4 years, we will recruit 606 residents from 32 care homes (about 19 residents per home), and their care partners, family and friends. All participants will be offered 60 minutes of Connecting Today per week for 6 weeks (in either the intervention group, or in the wait-list control group). An onsite health care provider will be trained to tailor the video calls, and facilitate positive verbal and non-verbal engagement. We will evaluate how Connecting Today affects outcomes for residents (quality of life, loneliness, and responsive behaviours) and their remote visitors (quality of life, loneliness, and social support). We will assess how outcomes differ for men, women, and people with different perceptions and experiences of Connecting Today. We will also interview the 32 facilitators and 50 of the remote visitors to explore their perceptions of the program's benefits and costs. If we find that Connecting Today is effective and benefits participants, future research will assess how Connecting Today can be offered across Canada.

column36: Examining the role of home care payment source on health outcomes: a novel linkage of the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging to health administrative data
column37: Many Canadians rely on home care services to remain longer in their homes as they age. All provinces in Canada provide some degree of publicly-funded home care, but Canadians still report significant unmet home care needs. The purchase of home care out-of-pocket is also common but has rarely been studied. The demand for home care in Canada is set to rise significantly over the next few decades as the population ages but we have little evidence about how privately-purchased home care affects patient outcomes. We propose combining data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA) and provincial administrative data centres to comprehensively examine the use of public and private home care in Canada and its associations with health and health service use outcomes. We have three objectives for this work. First, we will use data from the CLSA to describe the use of publicly-funded and private-purchased home care in Canada and to compare individuals who use only public care, only private care, and both. Next, we will examine how individual health characteristics of CLSA home care users change over time, comparing this across home care payment sources. We will examine changes in measures of quality of life, mood, function, cognition, and frailty. Finally, we will use CLSA data linked to provincial administrative data centres to examine how use of home care payment source is related to other health system use, including primary care, ED visits, hospital admissions, and total system costs. Home care is a critical part of the basket of services that enable older Canadians to age well in their homes. The home care sector is already under strain and demand is set to increase in future decades as Canada's population grows older. Our research will have important implications for the adequacy of public home care funding of in Canada. Our findings will inform provincial and national strategies to build and support strong and equitable public home care systems.

column36: Canadian Alliance of Healthy Hearts and Minds: Dissecting the Pathways Linking Ectopic Adipose Tissue to Cognitive Dysfunction
column37: Carrying excess body weight, especially around the belly ("visceral fat") and eating unhealthy foods may impair a person's thinking ability including memory and multitasking. Developing cognitive decline can lead to the more serious and progressive condition known as dementia. In 2013, we assembled a cohort of over 8,000 Canadian adults from 5 provinces in a study called the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds. Participants provided blood samples and underwent a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the brain, heart, and abdomen for adipose tissue. We asked them questions about their general health, diet and exercise habits; and administered tests of their memory and thinking ability. In this study, we have recently published an analysis which shows excess fat impairs thinking ability. We now propose to recontact them and re-assess their thinking ability. We will also invite some participants with cognitive decline and others without, for further testing including assessing their ultraprocessed food intake, physical activity, belly fat, and another MRI scan of the brain. This study will allow us to better understand how lifestyle habits such as ultraprocessed food intake, and excess body fat cause cognitive decline, and ultimately, dementia.

column36: Roles of SPARC against muscle atrophy, sarcopenia and age-related metabolic disorders.
column37: Sarcopenia represents a loss of muscle associated to aging. Exercise reverses sarcopenia and improves age-related diseases. We have shown that the exercise-induced gene SPARC modulates muscle differentiation, and Sparc overexpression mimics exercise effects, whereas Sparc deficiency (KO) leads to an aging phenotype (muscle atrophy) which is improved by exercise. Therefore, we hypothesize that SPARC, similarly to exercise, protects against muscle atrophy, sarcopenia and age-related metabolic disorders. The first objective is to compare the effects of Sparc overexpression (Tg) and exercise on sarcopenia and age-related metabolic disorders in sedentary and exercised Sparc Tg and wild-type (WT) mice sacrificed at 6 months (young adult) and 18 months (old) of age. Body composition, glucose tolerance, lipid profiles, muscle mass and power, as well as markers for skeletal muscle integrity and metabolism will be analyzed in 96 mice. The second objective is to investigate SPARC implications in muscle atrophy and its recovery. One hindlimb of each Sparc KO, Sparc Tg and WT mouse will be immobilized for 2 weeks and remobilized for 2 weeks. Muscle mass and markers for protein degradation, regeneration and inflammation in muscle will be analyzed in 126 mice (6 months old). The third objective is to compare the effects of pre-exercise training and SPARC injection on muscle atrophy and its recovery. SPARC will be injected during both immobilization and remobilization periods. Muscle mass and selected markers for muscle metabolism will be analyzed in 96 mice (18 months old). The proposed study will characterize SPARC roles against muscle atrophy, sarcopenia and age-related health disorders. A long-term possibility is the development of an "exercise pill" that will optimize or act similarly to exercise for elderly peoples and individuals with limited physical ability or activity including bedridden and hospitalized patients.

column36: Co-Creation and Feasibility Assessment of a Staircase Approach to Reduce Sedentary Time and Increase Physical Activity in Older Adults
column37: Most Canadians are spending long parts of their day in seated activities. Adults over the age of 65 years are spending the most time in such activities, in some cases because they have conditions that make movement painful, uncomfortable, or challenging. Importantly, older adults are also not getting enough daily activity. This increases their chances of developing diseases such as cancer and heart disease. In order to help older adults sit less and move more, we will develop a program that slowly progresses individuals from sedentary lifestyles to more active lifestyles. For this research, we first want to know what older adults, exercise and recreation professionals, and healthcare professionals think of this approach, and what elements they would want in such a program. column37: Neurodegenerative disorders, which include Parkinson's disease (PD), are common and likely to increase as we all live longer. These conditions are incurable and place a huge burden on our Canadian healthcare systems, as well as on patients, care givers and families. There is therefore a pressing need to better understand these diseases with the expectation that it will lead to the development of therapies that stop their progression. The motor symptoms in PD are originating from the loss of dopamine cells in the brain. However, how exactly this occurs is not fully understood, given the lack of experimental systems that faithfully recapitulate the human condition. This project takes advantage of a new technology to generate dopamine cells from skin cells of PD patients. In contrast to other technologies available, this new method produces cells that are the same age as the donor, thus keeping the vulnerability associated to older age, which is crucial since the most important risk factor for PD is aging. We will thus study what triggers cell death, and whether those triggers are the same for every case of PD. This project is unique in providing, for the first time, brain cells in a dish that will allow the dissection of events leading to cell death in a context that can be specific to each patient. As such, in the future this new approach could be used not only for identifying drugs that stops the disease progression, but also for tailoring therapies to best suit each patient in a personalized medicine manner.

column37: BACKGROUND: long-term use of medication to treat Parkinson's disease (PD) will cause involuntary movements named dyskinesia. SPECIFIC AIMS AND METHODOLOGY: In this research, we answer the following questions (1) what is the effect of dyskinesia on the physical and social participation of patients and their spouse? To answer these questions, patients will first be evaluated clinically, and then be asked, as well as their spouse, to wear sensors to assess several mobility measures such as activity levels, number and speed of walking steps, time spent inside/outside the home, the amount of time spent together and apart and the extent of their mobility outside the home. The impact of dyskinesia on each variable captured by the sensors in the dyad will be compared between the patient and spouse, both during times when dyskinesia is present or not. Using these results, will identify when dyskinesia becomes problematic, and we will devise a novel way to tabulate scores of clinical scales to help identify those patients with troublesome dyskinesia. EXPECTED OUTCOMES: This study will allow us, for the first time, to determine how side effects of medication affects the daily lives of Canadians living with PD and their spouse. It will also allow for the refinement of current clinical evaluations to better identify troublesome dyskinesia that may affect both the patient and spouse's quality of life, in turn helping clinicians improve their management of dyskinesia.

column37: Prior to Covid-19 pandemic, Tuberculosis (TB) had the notorious distinction of causing the highest number of deaths every year, amongst infectious diseases. In 2021, approximately 10 million people developed TB and 1.5 million lives were lost to the disease. Unfortunately, such a high burden of TB disease still exists in spite of the fact that TB is curable and drugs targeting Mycobacterium tuberculosis (the causative agent of TB) have been around since the 1940s. A significant hindrance to TB control and eradication is the prolonged treatment regimen. Patients who develop TB are treated with 2-4 drugs over a period of 6 months. This is extremely challenging in terms of implementation and often leads to non-compliance, treatment failure and development of drug resistance. These lengthy regimens are necessitated due to the ability of M. tuberculosis to persist and survive against high concentrations of antibiotics. These surviving subpopulations of cells are not resistant to the antibiotics but exhibit tolerance to the antibiotics and are referred to as persisters. Previous studies, including from our lab, have shown that the TB bacteria in the host are extremely diverse and heterogeneous. This heterogeneity is what drives the development of drug- tolerant subpopulations. In this study, we propose to characterize the physiological states and phenotypic heterogeneity in persisting mycobacterial subpopulations during infection. These studies will not only lead to identification of novel targets for drug discovery but understanding the physiology of these persisters will aid in design of faster and more effective therapeutic regimens.

column37: Pathogenic bacteria utilize sophisticated secretion systems to transport their virulence factors across membrane(s) and manipulate their infected host. Porphyromonas gingivalis is a notorious human oral pathogen and a primary causative agent of periodontitis that utilizes its T9SS to promote host cell manipulation and infection. P. gingivalis infection was found to be directly linked to major systemic conditions, such as cardiovascular diseases, preterm low birth weight, rheumatoid arthritis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, cancer, and Alzheimer's disease. Elucidation of the underlying molecular mechanisms promoting the T9SS virulence is imminent in light of the growing evidence linking periodontitis to these systemic human diseases. Therefore, this research plan aims to elucidate the structure-function relationship of the T9SS. The obtained structural information will direct a tailored research strategy combining biochemical, biophysical, and genetic approaches to elucidate mechanistic details of the T9SS, culminating in the development of new therapeutics for the treatment of infectious diseases.

column37: Antibiotics are used to treat bacterial infections and are a critical part of healthcare in Canada and worldwide. If we were able to disable these efflux pumps with new drugs (pump inhibitors), many resistant bacteria would once again be treatable by antibiotics we already have, and we could help to slow down the emergence of new resistant bacteria. This project will investigate efflux pumps from bacteria that are often found in resistant infections (Acinetobacter baumannii) to understand how they work and help identify regions of the pump that could be targeted by pump inhibitors. This project will use high-precision (fluorescence-based) experiments to examine pump activity in real time to help us understand how fast the pumps can assemble and operate. This will lay the foundation for discovery of drugs that can slow down the efflux pumps and impact antibiotic resistance.

column37: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the deadliest breast cancer subtype, in part due to lack of targeted therapy. column37: Breast cancer is the most common cancer diagnosed in women worldwide. There are different types of breast cancer and each one shows a different prognostic outcome. We expect TFE3 isoform 2 to be important for tumor progression and high levels of TFE3 isoform 1 to be a key factor in breast cancer metastasis. column36: Mechanisms of action of antiestrogens in breast cancer: roles of Ubi-like modifications in transcriptional inactivation of Estrogen Receptor alpha.
column37: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed cancer and second leading cause of cancer death among Canadian women. Estrogen signaling contributes to mammary tumorigenesis and is mediated by estrogen receptor alpha (ER), a major therapeutic target in ~2/3 of breast tumors. Drugs used in the clinic to inhibit this protein include antiestrogens, which bind to this protein and inactivate it. However, some antiestrogens such as tamoxifen still enable partial activity of ER, while others such as fulvestrant are more efficacious inhibitors ("pure antiestrogens"). While the efficacy of fulvestrant in the clinic is limited by poor oral bioavailability, it is important for the design, testing and use of novel pure antiestrogens to understand the mechanisms of action specific to this type of drugs. Our research has shown that fulvestrant uniquely induces efficient modification of ER by serial addition of small proteins (SUMO proteins), which contributes to inactivating it in model cell lines. We have characterized the traits of antiestrogens and the regions of ER important for these modifications to take place. We also observed that some mutations of ER associated with resistance to hormonal therapies prevent partially or totally this mechanism of repression. We wish now to test the hypothesis that modification of ER by SUMO proteins is important for the optimal suppression of tumor growth. To this end, we will systematically characterize the mechanisms and impact of SUMO addition on ER functional properties, and test whether this results in an improved capacity to suppress tumor progression in pre-clinical models. These studies should (i) clarify the mechanisms of action of pure antiestrogens (ii) help guide their use in the clinic (iii) facilitate the design and testing of novel pure antiestrogens or (iv) of new therapeutic approaches for the treatment of antiestrogen-resistant ER+ breast tumors, a major cause of mortality in breast cancer patients.

column36: Eliciting Personhood in the Outpatient Oncology Setting for Patients with Breast Cancer or Lung Cancer
column37: When people get sick, what is often overlooked in their health care is who they are as a person. This can be difficult on patients and families. It can also result in healthcare providers becoming emotionally detached, decreasing their ability to feel compassion, lessening their job satisfaction and overall resilience. The basic idea of what is called person-centered care is treating the person and not just the disease. Although healthcare providers try to recognize each person's individuality and unique circumstances, finding out who patients are as people often simply does not happens. This study will examine the impact of a simple intervention designed to help healthcare professionals find out who their patients are as people, and how this kind of information can affect the way patients experience whether they feel they were treated with compassion. Patients diagnosed with either breast cancer or lung cancer being seen at CancerCare Manitoba will be invited to participate. This intervention, called the Patient Dignity Question (PDQ), guides patients in a brief conversation led by the question 'what do I need to know about you as a person to take the best care of you possible'. While we successfully developed and tested this approach in palliative care., it has not been used much in the setting of cancer care. In phase 1 of this study, when patients will receive care as usual, we will measure compassion using the Sinclair Compassion Questionnaire. In phase 2, we will add the PDQ to usual care, asking patients to take part in a conversation about who they are as people. We will then be able to answer the question of whether finding out about who patients are as people affects the way they experience care, and particularly whether they feel they were treated with compassion. We will also examine the impact of the PDQ on health care practice and how this influences the experience of all types of healthcare professionals treating patients with cancer.

column36: Nuclear mechanotransduction of YAP in breast cancer metastasis
column37: Breast cancer remains a leading cause of death for Canadian women, and despite numerous advances in treatment and diagnosis, new approaches to these challenges are essential. The regulation of one transcription factor, Yes Associated Protein or "YAP", appears central to metastasis. Interestingly, when YAP is in the nucleus, it is active and can drive metastasis, whereas when it is out of the nucleus it is inactive and does not drive metastasis. Our conventional picture of YAP regulation is based on the so called Hippo pathway, however, the principle regulatory protein for YAP in this pathway is dysfunctional in cancer; this means that YAP in cancer must be regulated by other means. In the last ten years interdisciplinary researchers have discovered that, in addition to the Hippo pathway, YAP is also regulated by an entirely distinct mechanism that is based on physical forces and mechanics. In particular, any combination of physical phenomena, such as larger forces or softer nuclei that lead to nuclear deformation, also lead to elevated YAP activity. In diverse cancers the cell nuclei are markedly softer than their benign counterparts, and the cells also exert larger contractile forces. These mechanical changes of larger forces and softer nuclei provide a "perfect storm" for increased nuclear compression. Our research shows in breast cancers that YAP activity closely follows nuclear compression, suggesting that this may be a biophysical promotor for breast cancer progression. We hypothesize that increased nuclear deformation directly leads to elevated YAP activity and cancer progression. We will use interdisciplinary methods to examine how nuclear mechanics regulates breast cancer metastasis using model cell lines and cells derived from patient metastases. Understanding mechanosensing in breast cancer is crucial in designing novel diagnostic and therapeutic approaches, particularly needed for difficult aggressive breast cancers.

column36: Caspase regulation of cellular stress responses in breast cancer.
column37: Cancer cells face many stressful conditions such as low nutrients and chemotherapy, yet they find ways to adapt and survive. This adaptation to cell stressors also leads to tumor progression and therapy resistance. If we better understand the mechanisms used by cells to adapt to stress, then we can devise strategies to target the adaptive mechanisms and thus improve therapy response and tumor killing. We discovered that a protein called caspase 7 (CASP7) is processed in a novel way in response to cell stress, and subsequently functions to aid adaptation and cell survival. However, our findings are consistent with other recent studies that have revealed non-canonical caspase functions in cell stress adaptation and survival. CASP7 has not been well studied in this context and so its protein processing, regulation and roles in cell stress adaptation remain poorly defined. To address these limitations, we will investigate CASP7 processing and protein interaction partners in the context of various stressors faced by cancer cells. We will also determine the consequences of inhibition of CASP7 or its regulators on the survival and treatment response of breast cancer cells. We will focus our treatment studies on triple negative breast cancer which is in urgent need of new therapeutic options. Our study will be the first to characterize the non-canonical processing and stress adaptive functions of CASP7 and to investigate its potential utility in new treatment avenues for breast cancer.

column36: TBC1D9: therapeutic target of the aggressiveness of triple negative breast cancer
column37: Triple negative breast cancers (TNBC) are responsible for 10 to 20% of all breast cancers. TNBC is a complex disease, mainly due to its heterogeneity, high rate of relapse, metastasis, and bad survival. In particular, metastatic TNBC patients will survive around 33 months after treatment failure. There is as yet no common approved therapeutic target regimen applicable to all TNBC patients. This lack of treatment has led to many investigations to identify genes specific to this devastating disease. Our group has identified a gene (TBC1D9) differentiating all TNBC patients from other breast cancer subgroups. Such gene could potentially be developed and serve as therapeutic option. Our group has shown that TBC1D9 is less expressed in TNBC as compared to non-TNBC patients. column36: Viralyzing transgenes to improve oncolytic immunotherapy
column37: Cancer killing viruses carry a "payload" as a form of a "transgene". This payload is critical for their anti-cancer efficacy. The transgene is often a carbon copy of a human gene, but we know that the human genetics is very different to that of a virus. This is like putting a Ford F150 engine into a Ferrari, it can work but it will not be ideal for the chassis. Our goal is to achieve maximal "payload" expression from "transgenes" encoded by oncolytic viruses - viruses geared towards cancer immunotherapies. We want the most bang for our bucks with these critical therapeutic payloads, so every part needs to be perfectly aligned with the machine. Every virus is unique and we will characterize the distinct blueprints that will provide the greatest powertrain for the transgene and virus, here Herpes Simplex Virus and Vaccinia Virus. Transgenes encoded within viral genomes are mostly taken from the exact coding sequence of human genes. However, many regulatory elements exist within 5'leaders and it is well-known that the codon sequence is critical for high expression. Furthermore, genome location can have many implications. Viruses are unique in their 5'leader, codon usage, and genome organization. The project describes our approach to obtain maximal payload expression by "viro-optimizing - Viralyzing' every parts of the transgenes. Oncolytic viruses are little but extremely powerful machines that can have massive impact for cancer immunotherapies. More than 150 viruses are currently under investigation in labs and companies around the world. For best responses, these viruses are all upgraded with a payload, but this addition has surprisingly not been optimally encoded for their unique racing machine. This project aims to turbocharge transgene expression and apply our findings to clinically relevant cancer virotherapies. Patients want the best machine available and our optimal transgene program will put their oncolytic virus of choice in the pole position.

column36: Alberta Moving Beyond Breast Cancer (AMBER) Cohort Study: Understanding how Physical Activity, Sedentary Behaviour, and Health-related Fitness are Related to Breast Cancer Survival
column37: With improvements in early detection and treatment, breast cancer patients are living longer. Unfortunately, breast cancer treatments often have physical and psychological side effects. Breast cancer survivors have a high risk for a recurrence, second cancers, heart disease, weight gain, bone loss, fatigue, anxiety and depression. Regular physical activity can improve the physical function of breast cancer survivors, help manage some short-term side effects of treatment and reduce the risk of recurrence. Many breast cancer survivors have high levels of sedentary behaviour (time spent sitting). To date, little is known about how sedentary behaviour or fitness may affect breast cancer outcomes. To date, physical activity has not been adopted into regular cancer care and no individualized guidelines are possible regarding the type and volume of PA necessary to improve survival after breast cancer. We initiated the Alberta Moving Beyond Breast Cancer cohort study in 2012 to address this knowledge gap. We recruited 1528 female, newly diagnosed breast cancer patients and are following them for an average of 12 years for all disease outcomes. Participants have completed several questionnaires, undergone physical fitness tests, been assessed for lymphedema (swelling in the arms), peripheral neuropathy (nerve pain in limbs), had their body composition measured (body fat, lean mass), given fasting blood samples and worn devices that objectively measure their physical activity and sedentary behaviour at breast cancer diagnosis and at 1, 3, and 5 years. To complete our cohort study, we now need to: 1) measure biomarkers in the blood samples; 2) complete collecting the 5-year questionnaires, 3) analyze these data, and 4) publish results. Our analyses will examine how these lifestyle factors are associated with survival outcomes. This study will lead to improvements in both clinical guidelines and public health recommendations on physical activity for breast cancer survivors.

column37: Most prostate cancer relies on androgen receptor (AR) signaling for growth and survival. Therefore, targeting AR signaling had achieved success in the treatment of prostate cancer. Therefore, new therapeutic targets and more effective treatments are urgently needed to improve the management of NEPC. In view of this, we developed a state-of-the-art pre-clinical model of NEPC, which gives us unprecedented levels of accuracy in monitoring how NEPC develops and progresses. In our pilot study, we have preliminarily confirmed its increased expression in clinical NEPC samples and demonstrated its function associated with NEPC. These results suggest that PROX1 may play an important role in NEPC development and progression. In the proposed study, we will further confirm the function of PROX1 and thoroughly investigate the impacts of PROX1 on multiple aspects of NEPC biology. When successful, this study will significantly improve our understanding of NEPC and also provide new insights for the precision treatment strategy for prostate cancer patients. Identification of PROX1 as a novel therapeutic target in this study will pave the road for more effective therapy to improve the quality of life of prostate cancer patients.

column37: High blood pressure is a major risk factor for heart failure, angina pectoris, and stroke and is often caused by defective reading of a cellular signal transmitted by a second messenger called cyclic guanosine monophosphate or cGMP. Dysfunctional cGMP signaling also results in life-threatening ruptures of the aorta, one of the blood vessels that connects the heart to the rest of the body. In addition, defective reading of a closely related molecule, cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) causes a general predisposition for pancreatic, endocrine, and cardiac tumors as well as intellectual disabilities and abnormal bone growth in children. The long-term goal of this project is to study two proteins that bind to cGMP and cAMP, i.e. the cGMP-dependent protein kinase G (PKG) and cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA), and elucidate the structural and dynamical changes caused by inherited disease-causing mutations that lead to incorrect translation of the cGMP and cAMP signal. We will also investigate how drug leads currently in development for such diseases work. For example, pharmacological nitroxyl (HNO) donors are effective in reducing blood pressure by mimicking the effect of cGMP on PKG. However, further mechanistic understanding is needed to improve current treatments. To this end, we will rely on nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. NMR is ideally suited to reveal how cAMP, cGMP, their analogs, and HNO donors modify the structure and dynamics of PKA and PKG, as needed to understand how to modulate these proteins' activities. NMR is also ideal to unveil how disease-causing inherited mutations alter the physiological interactions of PKA and PKG with cAMP and cGMP, respectively. Elucidating the structural and dynamical changes caused by disease-related mutations and drug leads will help understand the molecular origins of multiple cardiovascular diseases, tumors, and pediatric disorders, and will facilitate the design of improved treatments.

column37: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a type of cancer in which the bone marrow makes abnormal blood cells. The outcome for most AML patients, especially older ones remains poor. Despite advances in the field that include new drug targets, coupled with an increased understanding of cancer biology, the majority of AML patients eventually relapse and die of the disease. Thus, it is critical to investigate novel ways to target AML using strategies that are rooted in a mechanistic understanding of the disease and the infrastructure AML cells use to survive. The mitochondrion is the "powerhouse of the cell" and is a critical player in several biological pathways that lead to cell death. In particular, AML cells have increased reliance on robust mitochondrial function. As such, proteases that help maintain protein quality control in the mitochondria such as ClpXP are promising therapeutic targets in blood cancers. Using a combined biological, structural, and chemical approach we propose to develop therapeutics that target the mitochondrial ClpXP system to fight AML. column37: The poor prognosis for lung cancer patients is associated with a late stage of disease at the time of diagnosis, highlighting the need for effective methods for early detection. It has recently been demonstrated that low-dose computed tomographic (LDCT) screening of patients at high-risk of developing lung cancer improves survival outcomes. While a major advancement, LDCT is currently restricted to heavy smokers despite 25% of lung cancers occurring in people who have never smoked. Aside from smoking, a person's genetics also influences their risk of developing lung cancer, which is highlighted by a history of this disease in certain families. However, very little is known about the underlying genetic causes of lung cancer susceptibility and defining these factors may lead to new screening approaches that catch lung cancer early in more patients, improving diagnosis. Through genetic analysis of lung tumors, we recently uncovered the mutation of a gene that is located in a region linked to familial risk of lung cancer development. This gene is known to play a role in repairing damaged DNA, and we hypothesize that its inactivation leads to increased gene mutations over time, increasing the risk of developing cancer. To test this, we will disrupt the gene in normal lung cells to determine if this allows them to transform into lung cancer. We will also do this with the additional exposure to tobacco to see if inactivation of this gene makes cells more prone to developing mutations and subsequently, cancer. Lastly, we will determine whether tumors lacking this gene are vulnerable to cancer drugs that induce DNA damage, potentially offering a strategy to treat patients with this gene mutation in the future. Together, this study will determine whether this gene is associated with lung cancer susceptibility and development, and how this information can be used to improve screening protocols aimed at the early detection of lung cancer in high risk patients.

column36: Tumour cell reprogramming in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma as a means for therapeutic resistance
column37: Pancreatic cancer kills ~5,700 Canadians every year with most individuals having an expected survival of <1 year after diagnosis. The main reason for these outcomes are relatively late diagnosis - often the cancer has already metastasized, the inefficient treatments that exist for pancreatic cancer patients, and the resistance shown or acquired by the cancer upon treatment. Less than 1 in 5 patients qualify for surgical resection while the rest rely on chemotherapy that often does not work, or rapidly leads to resistance. The goal of our work is to understand the reasons for this resistance and identify approaches around it. To do this, we obtain tumour samples from patients at the time of initial diagnosis through endoscopic ultrasound. We also obtain non-tumour tissue that is intimately associated with the tumour and affects how tumours respond to treatment. We grow this tumour tissue outside the body as three-dimensional structures, or organoids, and use this patient-specific modeling to understand unique responses to therapy. By combining the non-tumour tissue into these experimental models, we will obtain a clearer picture of how the tumours respond to treatment by changing their inherent biological makeup. We will examine the response of organoids to chemotherapy with and without the contribution of non-tumour tissue, as well as determine if organoids derived from patients that did or did not respond to therapy have different responses. We will then use this knowledge to predict how future patients will respond as well as identify patient-specific sensitivities to other drugs that may be used for combinatorial therapies in the future. Knowing how these changes occur in a patient-specific fashion will enable us to target therapies to increase success in treatment.

column36: Dissecting the roles of iron and hemojuvelin in hepatocellular carcinoma
column37: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common form of liver cancer and represents the third most frequent cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Patients with chronic liver diseases, such as viral hepatitis, alcoholic liver disease or non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) are at high risk for developing HCC. Chronic liver diseases are often associated with aberrant iron metabolism and accumulation of excess iron in the liver, which is thought to contribute to carcinogenesis. In line with this notion, HCC is a common complication in patients with iron overload disorders such as hereditary hemochromatosis. Systemic iron metabolism is controlled by the iron hormone hepcidin, which in turn is regulated by the protein hemojuvelin. Genetic inactivation of hemojuvelin or hepcidin causes a type of severe hemochromatosis. We utilized hemojuvelin-deficient mice and demonstrated that these animals are extremely sensitive to development of HCC. Moreover, by analyzing data from HCC patients, we reported that low hemojuvelin expression predicts poor outcomes. Our data in the mouse model suggest that the lack of hemojuvelin promotes hepatocarcinogenesis by iron dependent and -independent mechanisms. Herein, we propose further experiments to dissect these mechanisms at the molecular level. Implementation of this project is expected to provide new knowledge on liver cancer pathways and clarify the function of hemojuvelin. This may pave the way to novel therapeutic interventions.

column36: Air pollution and cardiovascular disease: Investigating pre-clinical and clinical effects of low levels of air pollution on ectopic adipose tissue, cardiovascular disease, and cognitive function
column37: Over time, exposure to air pollution increases the risk of early death, mostly from diseases of the heart, even in Canada, a country with relatively "clean air". Each year, 15,300 Canadians die prematurely from air pollution, but how air pollution causes heart disease to begin is still not clear. In the same way, air pollution is also associated with poor brain health, but we don't know how this occurs. Using high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), we can learn about how these diseases progress in healthy people exposed to air pollution. We have performed MRI scans of the heart, brain, and abdomen in 8,000 healthy adult Canadians. We also have measured 3 common air pollutants around these same people's home address. These pollutants are fine particulate matter (made by factories, power plants, industries, and automobiles), ozone, and nitrogen dioxide. We will bring together this information to: 1) Learn whether exposure to low-levels of air pollutants is linked to changes in belly and liver fat, narrowing of the arteries, changes to the heart's ability to pump, brain injury, and worsening cognitive function. 2) Discover how neighbourhood features might dampen the harmful effects of air pollution, for example, access to safe walking paths, and the presences of trees. 3) Link this information to Canadian healthcare databases to understand whether a person's years long exposure to air pollution increases risk of future heart and brain diseases, such as heart attack, stroke, and dementia. By understanding the effects of air pollution on heart and brain health, we can inform Canadian policy changes that reduce carbon emissions and promote heart and brain health, and support efforts to ensure Canada meets or exceeds global air quality guidelines, and reduce air pollution-related deaths, disease, and disability. What we learn from this study will help plan and design "healthy" cities of the future.

column36: Characterization of key aspects of a controlled human infection model (CHIM) for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection
column37: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) continues to be a major public health problem, with mortality exceeding HIV, TB or malaria each year. Advances in treatment lead to cure rates of greater than 95% with simple, well-tolerated therapy. However, especially now in the context of the opioid epidemic and COVID-19 pandemic, new infections continue to outpace cures due to the lack of a vaccine; however, the development of an HCV vaccine has proven extremely challenging. Beyond finding a vaccine that protects against all HCV strains, evaluating vaccine candidates in the most at-risk populations is difficult. Since 2011, there has been a near-complete ban on research involving chimpanzees, the only animal model of HCV, meaning that vaccine research must be done directly with human volunteers. The first vaccine trial involving over 500 people who inject drugs took 6 years and millions of dollars, only to prove entirely ineffective. Repeating such an effort for every potential vaccine candidate is simply not feasible. An alternative strategy would be to develop a Controlled Human Infection Model (CHIM) in which healthy volunteers would receive a vaccine candidate and then would be intentionally infected HCV, with the plan to treat those who do not clear the infection on their own. The CHIM approach has been used to evaluate vaccines for malaria, Dengue, and cholera, and recently to study COVID-19. We have already completed two international workshops with key stakeholders, resulting in important considerations for HCV CHIM. In the proposed study, we intend to use plasma from 4 chronically infected donors with different HCV genotypes, to infect healthy human volunteers for the first HCV CHIM. Samples will be collected during acute HCV infection from recipients, which will then be used to infect the sentinel cohort of 24 CHIM volunteers. This sentinel cohort will serve to confirm the reliability of infection, the natural course of disease, and the response to therapy.

column36: The impact of intrauterine device use on ovarian cancer risk
column37: The introduction of oral contraceptives, or "the pill", has not only been a milestone in terms of birth control, but its use has important benefits to women's health. In particular, using the pill is known to reduce the risk of ovarian cancer, which is the most deadly of the cancers that occur only in women. The pill has led to the introduction of other methods of birth control, including new choices in intrauterine devices, or "IUDs". IUDs are now the recommended first choice of birth control methods for woman of all ages, and its use is increasing globally. However, this has led to reduced use of the pill. The findings from past studies do not give a clear idea of whether the use of IUDs is associated with ovarian cancer risk. Also, most past studies have not examined all the types of IUDs that are available today. We will conduct a large, population-based study using data from the United Kingdom on primary medical care, hospitalization, and cancer and death registrations to examine whether IUD use, when compared with use of the pill, affects the development of ovarian cancer. We will also examine whether there may be differences by type of IUD. Ovarian cancer is a cancer of critical importance to women's health, given its high fatality. This project will help in understanding if the increasing use of IUDs, with lower use of the pill, may have an impact on how many people get ovarian cancer. The results will also provide information that women may use when making choices in birth control methods.

column36: Role of Thrombopoietin Receptor (TPO-R) Signaling in TET2 Mutation-Driven Clonal Hematopoiesis
column37: Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminate Potential (CHIP) refers to the presence of blood cells carrying mutations associated with leukemia in individuals without evidence of a blood disorder. Individuals with CHIP are at a substantially higher risk of developing blood cancers, including acute leukemia, than those without CHIP. The time period from having CHIP to a diagnosis of blood cancer can be many years. This finding opens up the intriguing possibility of interventions to prevent blood cancers from occurring in the first place. To achieve this goal, we need to first understand how normal and mutated blood cells behave differently. This knowledge will allow us to design effective and safe interventions. One of the most common mutations in CHIP is in a gene called TET2. We recently discovered that blood cells with mutations in TET2 are more dependent on a hormone called thrombopoietin to grow than normal blood cells. This finding suggests that if we can block thrombopoietin from working, we may be able to selectively destroy the mutated blood cells. In this proposal, we will find out how thrombopoietin works to promote the growth of TET2 mutated blood cells. Because the preliminary studies were done using mouse cells, we will also perform studies to find out if human TET2 mutated blood cells are similarly more dependent on thrombopoietin. Our proposed studies, if successful, will help establish a potential approach for eliminating CHIP and ultimately, preventing blood cancers.

column36: Tumor-Associated Fibroblasts Impairing Malignant Progression
column37: Cancer is a deadly disease that most often evolves in a step-wise manner. Initially, cells accumulate abnormally in a defined location in the body (benign tumor). Then it evolves into a frank malignant tumor as it grows and invades local tissue structure (malignant tumor). Finally, some cells can seed at distant sites and further grow (metastatic tumor). Almost universally, the sooner the diagnostic is done, the better the survival rate is. Over the past few years, we focused our attention on patients with a genetic predisposition to tumor formation. It turns out that some of these syndromes promote benign tumor formation but rarely manifest as a frank malignant tumor or metastatic tumor. When I will understand how these tumors are refractory to malignant progression, then I can foresee a new generation of anti-cancer therapeutics aiming at mimicking the mechanisms discovered in these hereditary benign tumor syndromes. One of these syndromes is Neurofibromatosis Type I. Our preliminary results using a mouse model recapitulating the typical tumor in neurofibromatosis suggests a novel mechanism impairing malignant progression: the release of certain proteins with tumor-suppressing properties by the normal cells surrounding tumoral cells. In this grant proposal, I will identify those factors and the cells producing them. I will make the demonstration using a mouse model that these factors indeed act as a gate, preventing malignant progression. Following this validation phase, medicinal chemists could begin to make drugs and systematically test them using our mouse model. This is a mandatory step in our quest to launch a novel generation of anti-cancer therapeutics, not only for Neurofibromatosis Type I patients but for the large population of cancer patients.

column36: Endometriosis and ovarian cancer: Understanding which patients are at high risk for ovarian cancer
column37: Endometriosis is a common chronic condition characterized by lesions resembling uterine tissue found outside the uterus. It affects 10% of people with uteruses and carries a 2 to 4-fold increased risk of two types of ovarian cancer, called clear cell and endometrioid ovarian cancers (herein referred to as -associated ovarian cancers). Research examining endometriosis-associated ovarian cancer has historically relied on a self-reported or clinical diagnosis of endometriosis, however the best diagnostic test for endometriosis is a pathologic diagnosis. We currently do not properly understand how common endometriosis treatments (surgical and hormonal treatments) impact risk for endometriosis-associated ovarian cancer. There is also a suggestion that endometriosis will take on atypical features, which can be identified by specialized gynecologic pathologists in the laboratory, prior to becoming cancer. However, there are few studies of the progression of endometriosis with atypical features over time. Given this uncertainty, no clinical guidelines exist and clinicians are unsure whether to act more aggressively to prevent cancer in these cases. We have built a unique dataset to address these unanswered questions. It includes all people with pathologically confirmed endometriosis in the Vancouver Coastal Health Authority in British Columbia, Canada (population ~1 million) between 2000 and 2008. These data have been linked with population-based administrative datasets in British Columbia, Canada, which includes all treatments received in the universal health care system in the province. We propose to use these data to reassess the association between endometriosis and ovarian cancer, to determine how the surgical and hormonal treatments for endometriosis influence risk for endometriosis-associated ovarian cancer, and to determine rates of endometriosis with atypical features in people who later developed cancer compared to those who never developed cancer.

column36: Micronuclei as integrators of cellular DNA damage responses
column37: The DNA of every cell in your body is constantly faced with damages. The cell attempts to fix this damage but when it fails to do so mutations may arise that could lead to cancer development. If damage is especially severe cells may die, which protects the person from developing cancer. Many cancer therapies harness this property by creating massive DNA damage in the cancer cells leading to their death. We have previously shown that micronuclei are an important interface between DNA damage in cells and their surroundings, including the immune system. This work will inform both how we apply and modify existing cancer therapies but will also inform our understanding of how DNA damage contributes to the development of cancer. Ultimately, we hope our studies will guide new therapeutic strategies that intercept cancer in the earliest stages when DNA damage initiates the transformation into cancer.

column37: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a debilitating neurodegenerative disease characterized by progressive memory decline. We recently identified histone variants as novel epigenetic regulators of memory that are promising therapeutic targets for memory deficits. On this basis, we will determine if mH2A1.1 can also inhibit PAR in neurons, if this inhibition underlies the ability of mH2A1.1 to repress transcription, and assess the relevance of this interaction in memory formation. In Aim 2, we will test if mH2A1.1 and mH2A1.2 binding on DNA is altered in AD using brains from human patients and AD model mice. Since mH2A1's effects in AD may be sex specific, we will test if manipulations of mH2A1 expression can improve memory in male and female AD mice and serve as therapeutic targets for memory decline. In Aim 3, we will test the contribution of sex hormones to mH2A1.1 and mH2A1.2 regulation as a critical step for understanding how sex differences in mH2A1 isoforms are established and maintained in health and disease. column37: Modern technologies allow us to capture a tremendous amount of information about living cells. We can sequence their genomes ("genomics"), identify which genes are being expressed in thousands of individual cells in parallel ("single-cell transcriptomics"), or determine how the products of those genes are edited and modified ("proteomics"). However, it has proven challenging to capture corresponding information about the environment that surrounds them. The conditions that exist around a group of cells at one point in time may be very different a short time later, or around a different group a millimetre away. We are therefore faced with the challenge of extracting information from many constantly changing microenvironments - with instruments that are large in comparison to the regions they must measure, and can disrupt (or even require the destruction of) the cells being studied. As the behaviour of cells, tissues and organs is constantly influenced by their surroundings, this information is important for interpreting the data we receive from the "-omics" techniques, and to our understanding of why they behave the way they do. We are developing synthetic biological circuits to program a small portion of cells to record conditions around them and will integrate them into our engineered pseudoislets. We will quantify cells' natural responses to specific changes in their environment, and program them to record this information into their DNA for later analysis. Importantly, our approach is designed to be highly adaptable, so that researchers who wish to build upon it can easily select and incorporate new environmental parameters to monitor; and so that many different parameters can be monitored simultaneously.

column36: Systematic characterization of membrane contact sites in budding yeast
column37: Our knowledge of the functions for membrane contact sites within cells is extremely limited yet they are present in all eukaryotic cells, from budding yeast to humans. Hence employing models such as the budding yeast to make breakthrough fundamental discoveries will lead to a better understanding of membrane contact site function in humans and their roles in disease. A major contributing organelle to membrane contact sites is the endoplasmic reticulum, which makes contacts with all other organelles in the cell. Some well characterized contacts are with mitochondria, plasma membrane, lysosomes, peroxisomes, Golgi and endosomes. However, membrane contact sites are not restricted to the endoplasmic reticulum and have been observed between mitochondria and plasma membrane and vacuoles/lysosomes. Main functions ascribed to membrane contact sites so far are in lipid and calcium traffic, cell signaling, and organelle biogenesis/homeostasis. The work proposed in this grant will use yeast to identify new components of membrane contact sites and define their functions and organization in much more detail. This will be through the use of high- resolution microscopy, genetic and biochemical approaches. The importance of membrane contact sites in human disease is also being uncovered through defining proteins with functions at membrane contact sites and include cancer, obesity, diabetes, and neurological diseases. However, many of the disease mechanisms have yet to be defined largely due to a lack of a clear understanding of the physiological functions of MCSs. This work will expand our understanding of these mechanisms

column36: Uncovering complex genetic mechanisms of disease
column37: Genetic diseases result from alterations of genetic material that lead to functional impact on genes. Despite the recent advancements in genomics that have facilitated sequencing of individual human genomes, the genetic cause is difficult to identify in the majority of individuals with presumed genetic disease. This persisting problem may largely be due to more complex genetic scenarios that involve genetic variation beyond simple coding variants, that current genetic tests are not efficiently addressing. How do we increase the ability of genetic testing to reliably detect and interpret complex molecular causes? We reasoned that patients with well-defined clinical features and highly suspected clinical diagnoses, yet with no or partial genetic diagnosis, will help us better understand the spectrum of these intricate variants by narrowing the genetic focus. For example, ataxia-telangiectasia (AT) is a disease known to be caused by alterations of a single gene, ATM. Patients with clinical diagnosis of AT for whom conventional genetic/genomic tests failed to identify disruptive variants in the ATM, hold a clue to more complex mechanisms of gene disruption. Our pilot genome sequencing study in patients with well-defined clinical features, including AT and similar diseases, who remained without genetic diagnosis revealed a spectrum of complex molecular causes. In one of the patients, the discovery of new genetic change has opened doors for personal therapy development. Here, we propose to expand our patient cohort and decipher complex genetic causes of disease in order to facilitate: (1) better understanding of spectrum of mechanisms of gene disruption; (2) development of improved analytical protocols for identification of these challenging variants with a potential to increase overall success of finding genetic cause of a disease; and (3) development of personal therapies.

column36: Rationally designed ribozymes switched-on by nucleotide repeat extensions as potential tools of genetic therapy for repeat expansion disorders.
column37: Over 40 diseases, including incurable and fatal neurodegenerative diseases such as ALS, are caused by the expansion of repetitive sequences in the genome. Beyond a certain size, these expansions cause problems in the cells and the body, leading to disease. These diseases are engrained in the patients' DNA, where, for instance, instead of having 10 repeats of the genetic letters "CAG", a patient can have over 20 repeats of this same "CAG". Therefore, as opposed to infectious diseases caused by a pathogen invading the body, it is currently not possible to get rid of the source of the disease for the individuals who are suffering from it. Moreover, the type of mutations at the origin of these diseases is even more difficult to target than other single base mutations (where a single "letter" of the genetic code is modified) because the modern genetic tools that can provide hope for many hereditary diseases typically recognize ~20 bases ("letters") of sequence, which does not allow to distinguish the number of repeats between a healthy individual and someone with the disease This project aims at developing an artificially intelligent (AI) algorithm, realized as a computer program that will generate a molecular tool capable of making such a distinction. This program will design an RNA molecule that will be switched-ON only in presence of repeats exceeding the "healthy number", when switched-ON, this RNA molecule will act as a molecular scissor that will cleave the product of the disease-causing gene, leaving only the healthy version intact. This program will use this common feature from these genetic diseases as a means to automatically design specific gene inactivating tools for therapy.

column36: Investigating the molecular pathology of WDR26 deficiency
column37: Recent studies have uncovered a new intellectual disability syndrome, Skraban-Deardorff Syndrome, caused by mutations in the WDR26 gene. The WDR26 protein is part of a highly conserved, yet poorly characterized protein complex, called CTLH complex, that functions as a E3 ubiquitin ligase. They are essential to every cellular metabolic process and have been shown to play important roles during the formation and development of the embryo, particularly in brain development. However, the exact function of the CTLH complex in the developing brain, and how the mutations in the WDR26 protein identified in Skraban-Deardorff Syndrome affect the function of the CTLH complex and result in disease are completely unknown. Our recent investigations have demonstrated that the protein WDR26 is essential for the CTLH complex function as when WDR26 is absent or mutated, the complex is disassembled and not functional. This study will investigate why and how WDR26 mutations that are found in Skraban-Deardorff Syndrome patients disable the function of the CTLH complex in cellular models. We will also employ mouse models of WDR26 deficiency to characterize the effects of the loss of WDR26 on brain development, particularly in the regions of the brain involved in learning and memory. We will also evaluate the effects of WDR26 deficiency in mice by assessing learning, behaviour and locomotor defects previously shown to be altered in animal models of intellectual disability disorders and characteristic of Skraban-Deardorff Syndrome. The results from these studies will shed light on the molecular basis of the pathology of the Skraban-Deardorff Syndrome and could lead to the identification of strategies to alleviate neurological defects caused by the loss of WDR26.

column36: Establishing the genetic and cellular mechanisms that control growth of the fetal left heart
column37: Hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) is a devastating form of heart disease where the left side of the heart fails to grow during fetal life, necessitating multiple surgeries and/or a heart transplant in early childhood. Less than half of affected individuals survive to adulthood and treatment options are presently limited. Progress on developing effective treatment is hampered by our limited understanding of what factors control growth of the left side of the heart during fetal life, and is worsened by a lack of appropriate HLHS animal models. Directly manipulating the genes that control heart development has not been successful at mimicking this disease as the effects on the animal are either so severe that it dies prematurely or so widespread as to limit the utility of the model. Our team has made a breakthrough in the study of HLHS by creating a mouse where the disease is surgically induced. These mice survive for the full duration of the pregnancy and demonstrate abnormal blood flow and heart growth similar to that seen in patients. The development of this surgical technique opens a completely new avenue to learn the molecular signals that control how the heart develops during early life. To learn which of these molecular signals are important for heart growth, we will make use of the evolutionary relationship between species and assume that those signals that are shared between species have important functions. We will use this evolutionary approach to compare our fetal mouse model to tissue obtained from human HLHS fetuses. The most promising of the molecular signals identified by this comparison will be tested for their ability to rescue heart development in a simple zebrafish HLHS model, an efficient method for testing molecular manipulations. Together these experiments will reveal what prevents the heart from growing normally in HLHS and lay the groundwork for creating novel treatments to improve outcomes in children affected by this devastating disease.

column36: Regulation of C. elegans EGFR trafficking and signaling by Rab and Arf GTPases
column37: Most cells in our body are polarized with distinct membrane compartments with distinct functions (e.g. neurons or epithelial cells). We are interested in the cellular processes that target membrane proteins to the correct membrane compartments. Targeting a protein to the wrong membrane compartment can have dire health consequences. For example, in polycystic kidney disease, sending the Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR) to the wrong membrane in kidney epithelial cells can result in the formation of cysts and subsequent organ dysfunction. The objective of this proposal is to understand how genes and gene products (proteins) function to regulate protein localization in epithelial cells. To study how membrane proteins are targeted to the correct membrane in live animals, we are using the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans. C. elegans EGFR needs to localize to the correct membrane compartment of epithelial cells to transmit a signal necessary for the development of the hermaphrodite vulva, an organ essential for egg-laying. We have the tools to monitor EGFR localization in live animals using microscopy. The powerful genetics of C. elegans permit us to identify and study the genes that regulate EGFR localization during vulva induction. In this proposal, we will determine how several genes, specifically those coding for Arf and Rab GTPases that regulate membrane trafficking processes, work together to regulate EGFR localization. Understanding the cellular processes that regulate EGFR localization in this simple genetic model organism, will reveal conserved fundamental mechanisms that regulate membrane protein localization in human cells. Since membrane trafficking is a fundamental cellular process, many of the genes we study are linked to human disease including neurodegenerative disease and cancer. The results of this study will provide better understanding of their functions which can be applied to understand disease etiology.

column37: Common inherited diseases, including heart disease and autoimmunity, are caused by many mutations that occur throughout the genome. These mutations often lie in the parts of the genome adjacent to the genes themselves, and control when and where genes are expressed. For instance, a mutation can cause the gene to turn on or off at the wrong time or in the wrong cell. Our study focuses on Atrial fibrillation (AF), a common heritable form of arrhythmia. Although we suspect that most AF-associated mutations act by changing gene expression, the molecular mechanisms by which they do so remain incompletely understood. Further, it is unclear whether the many mutations across the genome that impact AF converge on common cellular processes. Our goal is to determine which AF-associated mutations modulate gene expression, how they do so, and how a patient's genetics influences the core cellular processes of heart cells. We will experimentally test how each mutation alters gene expression in a synthetic system using healthy heart cells. Next, we will measure the genes expressed in the cells of AF patients to find groups of genes that work together in disease-related processes. Finally, we will determine how a patient's genetics influences the ways in which heart cells interpret expression-altering mutations. This project will improve our understanding of the molecular biology underlying AF, essential to designing new AF diagnostics and treatments, and, more generally, our understanding of common inherited disease genetics.

column36: Multiplexed assay for variant interpretation in human oncogenes using a humanized yeast model
column37: The vision of a healthcare system guided by information in our individual genomes is currently limited by a major challenge: Our current inability to distinguish whether genomic sequence variants are benign or pathogenic. Indeed, sequencing of patients with a known familial history of cancer frequently only discover variants with no known clinical interpretation (also known as variants of uncertain significance, or VUS). We leverage the property that dysfunction of oncogenes frequently leads to increased genetic mutation rate and develop a novel assay to quantify this genetic mutation rate at extremely high throughput. Finally, we develop robotic and computational approaches to automate the process of making all possible mutations in genes in a cost-efficient manner to scale the experimental design to all human oncogenes that can be assayed in yeast. After calibrating experimental results with known clinical variants, pathogenic variants will be made available as a 'map' to guide future disease management. column36: TOP1MT, mtDNA Release & Inflammation
column37: Mitochondria, best known as the powerhouse of the cell, contain a small DNA genome, known as mtDNA that is essential for mitochondrial function. Recent work shows that when mtDNA escapes from mitochondria, it can activate immune signaling. While immune signaling can be protective in the context of infections, excess activation can be detrimental by leading to autoimmune disorders. The triggers initiating mtDNA escape and the mechanisms by which mtDNA exits mitochondria are not fully understood. We also do not have a full appreciation of the consequences of mtDNA release on human health. To begin to answer these questions, we will study the mtDNA regulator TOP1MT, which our novel findings show mediates mtDNA escape. With respect to human health, we have identified a candidate disease causing TOP1MT variant in a family with autoimmune disorders, and shown that this variant is linked to mtDNA release and immune activation. These findings support a role for TOP1MT dysfunction in autoimmune disorders, which we will explore further. We also have novel data linking TOP1MT and mtDNA-mediated inflammation to toxicity caused by doxorubicin, a drug commonly used to treat cancer. Understanding how TOP1MT and inflammation mediate doxorubicin toxicity could lead to safer or alternative cancer treatments. Using a combination of cell and animal studies, our research will characterize how and why mtDNA is released in the context of TOP1MT dysfunction (Aim 1), interrogate the role of TOP1MT as a novel autoimmune disease gene (Aim 2), and explore TOP1MT as a doxorubicin susceptibility factor (Aim 3).

column36: Genetic and epigenetic determinants of very early, fatal coronary artery disease
column37: Coronary Artery Disease (CAD) is caused by the accumulation of cholesterol in the arteries providing blood to the heart muscle. It remains the leading cause of death worldwide despite declining rates for major environmental risk factors, such as smoking and blood cholesterol. Recent evidence has demonstrated the remarkable and independent roles of genetic predisposition and accelerated aging in the development of early-onset CAD (< 55 years old), since individuals who develop CAD at a young age are less likely to have developed disease due to a progressive exposure of traditional environmental risk factors like smoking. However, there remains little knowledge regarding the genetic mechanisms at play among the youngest CAD patients (< 45 years old), who have succumbed to premature death due to their condition. Although an event of very early, fatal CAD is extremely rare in the general population, we will be collaborating with the Ontario Forensic Pathology Services (OFPS) and the Office of the Chief Coroner of Ontario (OCC), which will act as a centralized repository for collecting DNA from young patients with established CAD as their cause of death. We aim to identify new genes and biomarkers of premature aging that lead to early CAD death. Indeed, our work will be the first to investigate such a severely afflicted patient population at a largescale. It will therefore serve as a foundation in using an individual's genetic signature and biological aging signature to help identify individuals and families at very high risk of CAD. Such signatures will help inform clinical therapies to reduce risk of CAD, as well as help develop new interventions.

column36: Correction with the Prime editing technology of point mutations responsible for Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy.
column37: Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy (DMD) is due to various mutations in a large gene called DMD, which contains thousands of nucleotides coding for a protein called dystrophin, a protein normally located under the membrane of the muscle fibers. There are different types of DMD gene mutations: 1) deletions of a one or several groups of nucleotides (called exons) and 2) modifications of only one or a few nucleotides (called point mutations). In both cases these mutations lead to the presence of a stop signal, which induces the premature termination of the dystrophin protein synthesis by muscle fibers. The absence of a complete dystrophin protein under the membrane of the muscle fibers leads to damages of muscle fibers during contraction inducing progressive muscle weakness. We propose to use a new gene editing technique called "CRISPR-Cas9 Prime editing" to correct the mutations and restore the presence of the dystrophin in DMD patient small muscle fibers (myotubes) in culture and in vivo in 5 DMD mouse models. Prime editing permits to induce precise modifications of one or a few nucleotides. So far, we have been able to modify nucleotides present in 9 different DMD point mutations in Canadian population. We have shown that this led to the presence of the dystrophin in myotubes. In the present project, we will use two recent Prime editing improvements, which may permit to increase gene editing by up to 4 folds. We will also do experiments to demonstrate that the dystrophin expression is restored in the muscles of 5 DMD mouse models. We will test two in vivo delivery methods: adeno associated virus and virus like particles. We will also do experiments to demonstrate that the Prime editing technique may also be used to restore dystrophin expression when one or several DMD exons are deleted. We hope that these experiments will permit to initiate a discussion with Health Canada to obtain the permission for a Phase I clinical trial of this new therapeutic approach for DMD.

column36: A synthetic biology approach to unlocking the role of the ribosome in cell competition
column37: Pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) have the special ability to "expand" - make copies of themselves - and give rise to all cell types of the body. Since their discovery over 40 years ago, PSCs have opened the door to producing cell therapies by transplanting lab-grown cells into the body to restore damaged function. To meet growing clinical demand, we are challenged with the task of growing billions of PSCs for cell therapy production. However, we and others have shown that lab-grown PSCs, like their embryo-resident counterparts, compete with and aggressively eliminate one another. These cellular battles shape their growth and impact our ability to robustly engineer PSCs for therapeutic use. Competition between PSCs is a newly discovered phenomenon and the rules of battle are not yet understood. Here, we will explore the molecular mechanisms that govern cell competition. To do this, we leverage our catalogue of competing mouse PSCs, which are known to engage in contact-mediated killing in a dish. While previous studies point to mitochondrial function as providing a key advantage for winners in competition, the molecular changes that lead losers to perish remain unknown. To probe this question, we will use established approaches (mass spectrometry) and cutting-edge synthetic biology tools ("Ribo-STAMP" and genetic circuits) to track molecular changes during PSC battle. This work will provide a window into multiple layers of the molecular map of cell competition - transcription, translation, and protein abundance - that is only made possible by recent technological advances. As PSC-derived cell therapies are an area of strategic investment for Canada's biotechnology sector, this project provides mechanistic insights that inform our ability to grow and manipulate PSCs. Our datasets will serve as the first molecular blueprints for cell competition, allowing us to uncover the rules that govern hidden cellular battles in PSC culture so that we can better control them.

column36: Harnessing early life developmental trajectories and the gut microbiota to identify new ways to prevent asthma and obesity.
column37: Asthma and obesity are the two most common chronic childhood diseases, affecting 15-20% of Canadian children and their families. Worse, childhood asthma and obesity burdens often continue into adulthood, making research focused on prevention particularly important. Our research is focused on the microorganisms living in our intestines (scientists call this the gut microbiota). Beginning shortly after birth, babies encounter a range of bacteria that eventually stably colonize and make up their microbiota. This process, called microbiota maturation, takes years, though we aren't sure exactly how long. Importantly, these new bacteria support healthy childhood development by providing nutrients and training immune cells to selectively respond to harmful signals. Our research Team and others around the world have shown that children who go on to have asthma and obesity seem to be 'missing' certain microbes. We think that by using powerful new genomic technologies to analyze stool samples from babies and young children, we may be able to predict which ones will go on to have asthma and obesity, and even better, our research will guide the development of safe ways to replace these microbes to prevent asthma and obesity developing in the first place. To accomplish this, we need to know two things: (1) Understand exactly how long it takes for the microbiota to mature. Once maturation is complete, the microbiota is very difficult to change, so understanding our window of opportunity to replace beneficial bacteria (and support healthy development) is important. (2) Discover which bacteria are best at preventing asthma and obesity. Who knew that clues to childhood asthma and obesity could be found in dirty diapers?

column36: The role of General Transcription Factor 2I in disorders of 7q11.23 copy number variation
column37: Williams syndrome (WS) and 7q11.23 Duplication syndrome (Dup7) are neurodevelopmental disorders caused by the deletion or duplication of 25 genes on chromosome 7.
