The GTF2I gene is a strong candidate for these disorders, but little is known about how changes in the copy number of this gene can alter brain development and function. We have made mice with deletion or duplication of Gtf2i that have some similar features to people with WS and Dup7, such as reduced intellectual ability and altered social behaviour. We used these mice to try and understand how Gtf2i functions and found changes in brain development, the control of other genes, the structure of brains cells, and the regulation of cellular calcium channels. We will follow up on promising leads from our initial data, use human cell models to confirm our results, and then try to correct the changes that we see in cells, and in the mouse as a whole. These experiments will provide valuable information about Gtf2i function and also tell us whether we could target future treatments toward any of these functions.

column36: Deubiquitinase MYSM1 as an essential epigenetic regulator of hematopoiesis
column37: Our blood is sustained by the daily production of hundreds of billions of new cells in our bone marrow in the process known as hematopoiesis. This process requires precise regulation of gene expression within the hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), and its dysregulation can result in devastating hematologic disorders, such as inherited bone marrow failures (IBMFS), immunodeficiencies, anemias, and blood cancers. MYSM1 is a DNA binding protein and a regulator of gene expression, and we were among the first to demonstrate the critical role of MYSM1 in blood cell development in mouse models. Recently, mutations in MYSM1 were also identified in human IBMFS patients, highlighting the biomedical importance of understanding MYSM1 functions and mechanisms of action in hematopoiesis. In the current research program, we analyze (1) the role and mechanisms of MYSM1 activity in the regulation of gene expression in blood cell development, and (2) the cellular and molecular mechanisms driving the hematopoietic failure in MYSM1-deficiency. Building on our previous work, (1.1) we will identify the MYSM1-regulated genes in mouse HSPCs, (1.2-1.3) conduct the first comprehensive analysis of the mechanisms through which MYSM1 regulates gene expression, (2.1) analyze the molecular and causal links between MYSM1-loss, gene dysregulation, and HSPC dysfunction, and (2.2) conduct the first cellular and molecular analysis of the impact of MYSM1-deficiency on the development of the red blood cell lineage. These studies advance the fundamental understanding of the molecular networks regulating gene expression and blood cell development, and in the long-term may offer insights into IBMFS and other hematologic disorders, and suggest novel strategies for disease diagnosis, management, and treatment.

column36: Investigating the role of notochord defects in the etiopathogenesis of congenital scoliosis
column37: Congenital scoliosis (CS) is a form of spinal curvature that is present at birth and is caused by abnormal development of the vertebrae. It occurs at a frequency of 0.5-1 per 1000 livebirths. It is a complex disease implicating many genetic and environmental factors that remain largely unidentified. The vertebral column of the spine is derived from an early embryonic structure called the notochord that provides the mechanical strength essential for elongation of the axis and that mediates spine morphogenesis and bone ossification at later stages. Defects in notochord development lead to a CS-like phenotype in zebrafish models. A zebrafish mutant at one gene, called protein tyrosine kinase 7 a(ptk7a), was shown to develop an CS-like phenotype. Ptk7a is a member of a signaling pathway called planar cell polarity (PCP) that mediates an early embryonic process that is essential for formation of the notochord and spinal cord. How loss of function of ptk7a leads to CS in this model is not known. We hypothesize that defects in notochord development play an important role in the pathogenesis of CS. In this study, we will use a combination of live cell imaging, vital stains, histological methods and microscopy to characterize notochord and spine development in this mutant. We will also assess the interaction between ptk7a and other drugs shown to interfere with notochord development and cause CS. We will study the role of another PCP gene called vangl2 in inducing spinal curvature defects . We will next analyze a human cohort of CS for the presence of an enrichment of potentially pathogenic rare variants in essential notochord genes and validate our genetic findings in a zebrafish model. Our study will help uncover a novel pathogenic mechanism affecting notochord development in the underlying pathogenesis of CS. A better understanding of the pathogenesis of CS might help develop better prevention and therapeutic strategies in families at risk.

column36: Accounting for equity and economic burden in priority setting for breast cancer control in India
column37: Cancer treatment poses an unsustainable economic burden on global health systems and on patients and families. Consequentially, there remain unacceptable inequities in access to quality and affordable cancer prevention and treatment within and between populations. Addressing these inequities is key to improving cancer outcomes and requires a concerted effort, aligned to global health systems strengthening goals. This project examines the economic burden of breast cancer treatment and caregiving costs in India and demonstrates how to explicitly integrate equity in policy analysis for cancer control programs. A multi-methods approach will measure the costs and economic burden of breast cancer treatment from the perspectives of patients and their caregivers, including gender dimensions of caregiving and treatment decision making, at two comprehensive cancer centres in India. These data will be integrated with economic evaluation methodology to develop a policy tool to estimate the equity benefits associated with breast cancer screening and required diagnostics and therapies, alongside standard cost-effectiveness estimates for India. By examining the economic burden of breast cancer and extending the conventional cost-effectiveness approach to incorporate equity and financial protection, a stronger case can be made to governments for expanding access to necessary cancer control strategies as a health system strengthening, development, and gender equity imperative. This project aligns with IHSPR' mandate and CIHR's vision for Global Health 3.0. By focusing on the economic burden of cancer, we stand to contribute to closing the global cancer divide and health system strengthening efforts. Further, this study will provide insights on how to embed equity and gender equity considerations in traditional economic evaluation approaches, with potential to enhance existing Canadian cancer decision-support tools.

column36: Real-World Outcomes Associated with PARP Inhibitor Maintenance Therapy in Ovarian Cancer: A Population-Based Study
column37: High grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) is a common and aggressive type of ovarian cancer which can be associated with BRCA mutations. Advanced HGSOC (stage III-IV) is typically treated with a combination of surgery and platinum-based chemotherapy. However, most women will relapse and their cancer will become resistant to chemotherapy. The use of maintenance therapy with PARP inhibitors, such as olaparib and niraparib, after chemotherapy has been shown to delay recurrence/progression in clinical trials. However, studies have shown that these drugs are most effective in patients with BRCA mutations. Benefit in patients without BRCA or similar mutations was small, only delaying progression/recurrence by an average of 3 months. Further, treatments that lead to benefit in clinical trials do not always show the same improvements when they are used in the "real world", and sometimes lead to more or different side effects than those seen in studies. In addition, not all patients have equal access to new drugs due to reasons such as risk of side effects in certain patients, or lack of awareness of study results and available funding by their physicians. This research is being done to determine if patients receiving maintenance therapy with PARP inhibitors for ovarian cancer in Ontario are receiving equal and adequate access to these new drugs, and whether the risks and benefits are still important when used in patients not enrolled in clinical trials. To perform this research, we will use data from large Ontario databases which have collected data on patients receiving treatment ovarian cancer. This will be linked to BRCA status collected from pathology reports. We will analyze these data to examine the proportion and characteristics of patients who have received these drugs and determine whether their long-term outcomes are better than those of patients who did not receive maintenance therapy.

We will then use these results and combine them with data from interviews of caregivers and people with heart failure to gain a deeper understanding of the decision-making process that leads this patient population to seek hospital care and identify potential opportunities where palliative care could be helpful. Our proposed research will improve our understanding of the palliative care needs of people with heart failure and their caregivers, and how those needs may lead to hospitalization. column37: THE ISSUE: Climate change increases extreme weather events (EWE), such as extreme heat, floods, and droughts that directly and indirectly impact health outcomes. Yet knowledge gaps remain regarding climate change impacts on HIV prevention and care. OUR IDEA: This novel study focuses on Tanzania, among the world's largest HIV epidemics with 1.7 million people living with HIV, and among the 15% most vulnerable countries to climate risks. We aim to identify climate-related drivers of HIV prevention and care in Tanzania to inform future interventions. OUR APPROACH: This 3-year mixed-methods study will leverage retrospective and prospective data from 2 existing cohorts (Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiological Study [PURE], Kilimanjaro Christian Medical Centre [KCMC]) with people of diverse ages, genders, and HIV serostatus in rural and urban Moshi, Kilimanjaro region. column36: Combinatorial Design of Multiplexed mRNA Vaccines for HIV Broadly Neutralizing Antibody Induction
column37: In 2018, over sixty thousand people were predicted to be living with HIV in Canada. HIV remains a global pandemic with no effective vaccine. Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) have been shown to inhibit most HIV strains from infecting human cells, but are difficult to induce. Attempts to develop a human bnAb vaccine candidate have so far failed. This is, in part, because the affinity maturation process of bnAbs is complex, and current vaccine candidates have struggled to deliver the appropriate signals to the immune system, in the correct order, to induce bnAbs in vivo. A large body of evidence supports our belief that a successful HIV vaccine must address three key parameters in parallel; 1) antigen design, 2) kinetics of antigen delivery and 3) stimulation of the immune system at the germinal center. Here, we propose to engineer an mRNA vaccine that can address and integrate each of these parameters. Previously, we have developed lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery systems that can not only facilitate extended protein expression of mRNA in lymph nodes, but also stimulate antigen-presenting cell maturation, antigen presentation in lymph nodes, and increase desirable antigen-specific CD4+/CD8+ responses. We believe that these dual delivery/adjuvant lipids could be repurposed to deliver effective HIV antigens to lymph nodes and program the host immune system to express bnAb antibodies against HIV. Our vaccine strategy facilitates multi-level control of immunogenicity through 1) optimization of mRNA expression and immunogenicity 2) development of potent dual delivery/adjuvant LNP formulations, and 3) optimization of kinetics and dosing for HIV mRNA vaccines. The ultimate goal of this proposal is to generate an effective HIV bnAb mRNA vaccine candidate.

column36: iSampleSmart!, an innovative, App-facilitated self-sampling screen and treat strategy for common bacterial STIs (Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae) for Canadian key populations
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has created disruptions in the healthcare delivery system with longer waiting times for appointments and to access treatment. Self-sampling conducted privately has been shown to be more comfortable for patients and has similar accuracy as conventional testing. Self-sampling can be combined with connected technologies (e.g., in-App instructions) to increase confidence in sample collection. Combined with current molecular diagnostic platforms, self-samples can be analyzed directly, more rapidly, and at lower cost at the site where they were obtained, than if they had to be sent to a laboratory. In Canada, specific key populations, such as but not limited to migrant, refugees, or trans and gender diverse people, are at risk of living with undetected infections. Stigma and discrimination impact their engagement with the healthcare system. iSampleSmart!, a connected self-sampling molecular strategy, brings key populations into care by detecting new infections so that they can access treatment rapidly. We will also determine whether iSampleSmart! is as accurate and preferred by patients as conventional testing. We will offer iSampleSmart! to key populations accessing community-based clinics where they will have access to a private bathroom to self-sample, guided by an App and a peer should they need it. Their sample will then be analyzed by a molecular diagnostic platform on site, and they will receive their results and prescription within the same day. We expect iSampleSmart! to increase access to testing and treatment for key populations who might not feel comfortable in conventional healthcare settings. Our results will guide larger connected self-sampling studies worldwide.

column36: Incidence and impact of methamphetamine use and concurrent sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections in people living with HIV in the Prairies
column37: Manitoba (MB) and Saskatchewan (SK), saw the highest numbers of new HIV infections ever in 2021, while simultaneously experiencing decreasing linkage to care and decreasing viral suppression. In Canada, a quarter of people living with HIV (PLHIV) are women, half are gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men (gbMSM), a third are heterosexual and 19% inject drugs. A recent study from our group found that half of PLHIV newly diagnosed in Manitoba in 2021 were women, 80% were heterosexual, 80% inject drugs, half were experiencing homelessness and 8% were gbMSM. The most commonly injected drug is methamphetamine (meth). Among PLHIV who inject drugs (PLHIV-WID), two out of three persons have at least one and up to seven concurrent sexually transmitted and blood-borne infections (STBBI) and four out of 10 persons were not taking HIV treatment. Our findings suggest PLHIV in MB and SK are experiencing a confluence of STBBI, injection drug use, unstable housing and violence. In PLHIV, meth use has been linked to poor adherence to HIV treatment and rapid disease progression. We aim to understand: 1)How many PLHIV may have concurrent STBBI 2)The knowledge, attitudes and practices that women, men and gender-diverse PLHIV-WID, and health care providers have about STBBI prevention, testing and treatment. Also what other social and individuals factors influence their knowledge, attitudes and practices 3)The effect on our body of having an STBBI and use of meth use 4)Pathways to effective, meaningful knowledge sharing about HIV and STBBI among PLHIV, service providers and communities These results are essential for health providers, policymakers and community stakeholders to design educational and programmatic strategies, and inform policy changes at multiple levels, to prevent STBBI and improve the health of PLHIV.

column36: Enhancing uptake of needle and syringe programs in Canadian federal prisons
column37: Needle and syringe exchange programs (NSPs) are evidence-based prevention tools to reduce the transmission of HIV and viral hepatitis (hepatitis C virus; HCV) among people who inject drugs (PWID) in the community, with initial evidence suggesting similar efficacy in the prisons. They are recommended by the World Health Organization and the United Nations as one of fifteen essential elements of an effective HIV and viral hepatitis prevention strategy in prisons. Despite these recommendations, only 10 countries worldwide provide prison-based NSPs, including Canada. Despite initial optimism of Canada's introduction of prison-based NSPs in nine Canadian federal prisons, only 277 individuals have been enrolled since 2018, including 53 currently. Among people incarcerated in federal prison, 21% reported lifetime drug injection, with over half (51%) having injected in the 12 months before incarceration. Risky injection, including sharing of injection equipment, was reported by 55% of recent injectors. While modest prison-based NSP uptake has the potential to undermine program sustainability, uptake could be addressed through more proactive implementation. The Canadian federal prison system is thus ideally situated to deploy an implementation science framework to systematically scale up prison-based NSPs. We aim to understand the multi-level barriers and facilitators to improve prison-based NSP adoption, scale-up, and maintenance among a diverse group of stakeholders across the nine federal prisons with NSPs. We will then use a stepped-wedge randomised study design across the nine federal prisons with NSPs to increase the number of PWID enrolled in NSPs, with the overall goal of enhancing the quality of NSP services and improving prisoner and overall public health.

column36: Investigating the mechanisms of disease progression in HIV-TB co-infection to design interventions for better clinical outcomes
column37: 38 million people are living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) worldwide and 10 million people a year develop active tuberculosis (TB) infections. Unfortunately, the areas with high levels of HIV overlap with high levels of TB. This can lead to what we call HIV/TB co-infections. 1/3 of all deaths from HIV are due to co-infection with TB. When you have both HIV and TB at the same time, this can lead rapid progression of both infections and ultimately leads to a higher likelihood of death. The exact reasons for this rapid disease progression and how to prevent it aren't known. It is challenging to study co-infection in humans as it is hard to know exact timepoints of infection or get tissue samples to see immune responses. HIV is an infection that targets and kills human immune cells and in TB, controlling the disease is dependent on the same human immune cells HIV targets. Thus, we know that human immune cells are important in the progression of co-infection. We have developed an improved humanized mouse model that can be infected with HIV and TB and will use this to determine why and how co-infection worsens disease. We will also test therapies that target immune responses in co-infection to improve disease outcomes. Ultimately, this project will allow us to understand how co-infection works, what immune responses are affected by co-infection and how we can target this to improve human health.

column36: Using Unique Methods in Flow Virometry to Identify and Study Proteins on the HIV Surface.
column37: The global burden of HIV/AIDS remains one of the greatest scientific and public health challenges of our time, with more people infected with HIV today across the globe than the entire population of Canada. Progress in this field requires a better understanding of HIV infection and spread. Indeed, we still lack a complete understanding of where the virus hides once it establishes life-long infection, how the virus interacts with different human immune cells, and how best to eliminate viruses to achieve a cure. This proposal reveals how the surface of HIV viruses can be decorated with a variety of human immune proteins, resulting in a 'protein fingerprint' on the virus surface that can yield new and important clues as to where the virus is hiding. This protein fingerprint also gives the virus additional biological properties, such as altered homing in the body and attachment to different immune cell types. To study this protein fingerprint on viruses, we are using novel experimental methods in flow virometry that were uniquely developed in my lab. We plan to identify the biological impact of newly discovered human proteins on the viral surface by testing for changes in virus binding and infection when these proteins are present/absent. Since our unique methods will enable us to identify new human proteins on the surface of HIV viruses, this work could also guide the development of more effective treatments and/or vaccine designs that consider both human and viral proteins present on the virus surface. Furthermore, our research provides new technical tools that could be easily applied to studies on other viruses, including pandemic respiratory viruses, like influenza and coronaviruses.

column36: The development of memory and mentalizing networks in autism
column37: Individuals with autism are impaired in social communication, and also show deficits in their memory of past events and experiences (episodic memory) and in social cognition (understanding thoughts about self and others). Previous research has shown that social cognition and episodic memory processes involve distributed regions in the brain that overlap with the default mode network, a large-scale brain network involved in internal mental processes such as autobiographical memory, social cognition and self-related thoughts. Recent evidence suggests the default mode network consists of two distinct subnetworks subserving memory and social cognition. In the proposed research, we will test whether these subnetworks are less separated and specialized in autism, and whether less specialized subnetworks contributes to social deficits in autism. We will conduct functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) sessions with passive movie-watching and memory tasks in a group of children with high-functioning autism and neurotypical controls. Using network analysis and a memory task that involves thinking about self and other, we will examine how these two subnetworks of the default network develop in ASD and controls. We will test the interaction of these two networks with other relevant functional networks in the brain related to attention and control. Structural MRI and other phenotypic measures such as IQ, language background and sleep patterns will also be analyzed for consideration of subtypes within the sample. The proposed research takes a network-level view of social communication dysfunctions in ASD to test a novel hypothesis linking social deficits with atypicality in the development of the social cognitive and memory network in the brain.

column36: Antiangiogenic mechanisms mediated by thrombospondin-1 in pre-eclampsia
column37: Preeclampsia (PE) is characterized by an important increase in blood pressure after 20 weeks of gestation associated with an increase in protein in the urine and dysfunction of other organs. It occurs in 10% of all pregnancies globally and is the leading cause of maternal and fetal deaths worldwide. Currently, there is no reliable marker to predict the onset of PE during pregnancy or effective treatments for PE once diagnosed, other than delivery. One of the reasons for such gaps is the lack of knowledge of the causes of PE. It is known that PE is characterized by a less vascularized and dysfunctional placenta, the organ responsible for the exchange of nutrients and oxygen between the mother and the fetus, leading to maternal circulatory stress and fetal growth restriction. However, the factors causing impaired vascularization in placentas of PE pregnancy are still unknown and constitute a major gap in this field. In this project we will study a molecule named Thrombospondin-1 with negative vascularization effects by reducing the ability of vascular endothelial cells to spread and form new vessels. This molecule was recently described by us in placental endothelial cells, and importantly activated in these cells when they were exposed to stressful conditions that are common to PE such as low oxygen and high levels of pro-thrombotic factors. Our hypothesis in this study is that this molecule can activate molecular mechanisms that impairs endothelial function and worsen the formation of new vessels in the placenta, leading to important structural changes of this organ. To study this hypothesis, our group will investigate the effect of a molecule capable of inhibiting this protein in endothelial cells and test it in mouse models of PE, hoping to improve placental vascularization. Collectively, our results will contribute to better understand new mechanisms impairing placental development in PE with the potential to discover new treatments for this disease.

column36: Integrating early neuromonitoring biomarkers to better define eligibility for therapeutic hypothermia after perinatal hypoxia-ischemia
column37: The brain of babies is particularly vulnerable to injury during the complex transitions at birth. When the brain is deprived of oxygen, brain cells are injured, and babies can present with hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy (HIE). HIE is an important cause of death and long-term developmental disabilities. Cooling treatment (therapeutic hypothermia) started within the first 6 hours after birth is the only proven treatment that has been shown to reduce death and disability. Cooling has only been proven to be effective in babies with moderate and severe HIE. Although cooling is not yet proven to help in mild HIE, there is recent evidence that approximately 25% of these babies have abnormal neurodevelopmental outcomes, that include behavior problems and cognitive impairment. Importantly, cooling has been shown to be effective when started within the first 6 hours after birth, however HIE may be difficult to diagnose in the first few hours of life. Thus, babies may not be offered cooling due to delays in diagnosis. Therefore, there is an urgent clinical need to find non-invasive bedside markers to improve patient selection for cooling within the short 6-hour time window. Our study will use different bedside monitoring tools such as advanced electroencephalography (EEG; to look at brain activity), near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS; measures cerebral blood flow and tissue oxygenation) and heart rate variability monitoring to optimize early identification of babies that should be offered cooling. This study will evaluate easy to apply non-invasive tools at the bedside to be able to better identify babies with a high probability of abnormal outcome for timely cooling treatment initiation. The goal is to guide appropriate selection of babies for cooling, in order to avoid missing those who can benefit and potential harm cooling those babies who will not benefit from the therapy. This data will result in significant improvements in developmental outcomes after HIE.

column36: RNA polymerase III-related leukodystrophy: Understanding disease pathogenesis and developing novel therapeutic approaches using murine models
column37: Leukodystrophies are a group of rare genetic neurological diseases affecting previously healthy children, who become progressively disabled over months to years, eventually succumbing to early death. No curative treatment is available for most of these children. These diseases are characterized by defects in the brain's white matter, whose main component, myelin, is critical for ensuring that brain cells (neurons) are both protected and able to transmit information. The reduced amounts of myelin in patients with leukodystrophies causes life-altering disabilities, including motor and cognitive deficits. Hypomyelinating leukodystrophies are a subtype of leukodystrophy characterized by reduced myelin production during brain development. We focus on one type of hypomyelinating leukodystrophy: 4H (Hypomyelination, Hypodontia and Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism) or RNA polymerase III-related leukodystrophy. Our group has previously identified that variations in the POLR3A, POLR3B and POLR1C genes cause this disease and made the first discoveries in understanding why and how these genetic defects cause disease. However, our quest to fully answer these questions has been significantly impaired by the fact that until recently, no representative animal model has existed to study this complex disease. Our team has addressed this need by generating two mouse models of 4H leukodystrophy, which will enable us to study both how the disease works and test potential treatments. We have shown that our mouse models exhibit most symptoms of the disease, including reduced myelin, tremor, and an unsteady gait. We propose to thoroughly study these mouse models, along with new ones, to understand how the observed abnormalities in myelination and neurodegeneration occur. We will also test therapeutic approaches, aiming to treat our mouse models to restore their symptoms. Ultimately, our goal is to provide a foundation upon which to develop the first treatments for children with this disorder.

column36: Infant and child health outcomes following SARS-CoV-2 infection in pregnancy
column37: New data suggest that there may be lasting effects of SARS-CoV-2 infection in pregnancy on both mothers and their children. Because of the relative recency of the pandemic, we are only now able to start investigating these issues. Current information comes from small studies that lack detailed information on the timing of COVID-19 diagnoses in pregnancy and the presence or severity of symptoms. Existing Canadian data can be used to address these knowledge gaps. This project will make use of routinely collected hospital, administrative and public health data in Ontario to investigate the long-term effects of SARS-CoV-2 infections in pregnancy on child health and development. We will establish a large dataset of mother and infant pairs with and without documented COVID-19 in pregnancy. Within this dataset, we will investigate the association between SARS-CoV-2 infection in pregnancy and child risk of hospitalization, emergency department visits, and infection-related health care use. We will also assess the association between SARS-CoV-2 infection in pregnancy and child risk of hearing and sight deficits, speech and language delays, and neurodevelopmental disorders. In our analyses, we will account for the timing of SARS-CoV-2 infection during pregnancy, disease severity, presence of symptoms, postnatal infections, and maternal and child vaccinations. With this approach, we will have the breadth and depth of detail necessary to address critical questions about the impacts of COVID-19 on fetal development and child wellbeing and the protective role of COVID-19 vaccines for reducing risk of adverse health outcomes. We will use our findings to help inform maternity and child health care providers, health agencies and Canadian families about the potential long-term risks associated with COVID-19 in pregnancy, and support early screening and intervention of at-risk children to give them the best possible starts in life.

column36: Scope and safety of vaping during pregnancy - generating and disseminating knowledge to inform clinical practice and pregnant individuals
column37: There has been an increase in the number of Canadian young adults who vape, including those of childbearing age and may continue to vape during their pregnancy. Previous studies have reported that vaping during pregnancy is becoming popular, especially as a way to help women quit smoking cigarettes. Recent studies suggest that vaping during pregnancy may be harmful for the developing baby and it's placenta. This research project will collect information on how common vaping in pregnancy is in Canada, pregnant individuals vaping habits, including types of products and the added content such as nicotine, why individuals vape during their pregnancy, and what support they received or wanted to receive to help them stop vaping. Additionally, to understand the health effects of vaping on the baby's development, we will collect placentas from individuals who report vaping during pregnancy to compare with placentas from individuals who did not vape and those who use traditional cigarettes. The placenta is known as the organ of pregnancy. It is responsible for passing nutrients from the gestational parent to the baby and protects the baby from harm throughout pregnancy. We will compare the effect of vaping on placental health and baby's growth during pregnancy. These will be the first studies to provide detail on vaping behaviours during pregnancy and human data on the effects of vaping on baby development. Working with the Society of Obstetrics and Gynecology of Canada, we will put together information packages for health care providers (doctors) and pregnant individuals who vape, to make sure decisions being made during pregnancy keep the gestational parent and developing baby safe.

column37: Despite the availability of antibiotic drug treatment for more than 50 years, almost 2 million people globally still die from tuberculosis (TB) each year. In particular, the spread of multidrug resistant (MDR) forms of Mycobacterium tuberculosis is one of the major obstacles that is fueling this ongoing TB epidemic and there are 500,000 new MDR-TB cases recorded worldwide every year! The act of acquiring genetic mutations that lead to antibiotic resistance has additional "fitness" costs that place a substantial burden on the M. tuberculosis cell. As such, the goal for this proposal is to apply a multi-disciplinary approach that combines chemical-genetics and large-scale bacterial genomics to identify these critical weaknesses that are inherent to the antibiotic resistant bacteria. In turn, the results of our work will pave the way for the development of novel "resistance-breaking" compounds that can be added to our current drug-treatment regimens in order to target the pathways that specifically support the evolution and maintenance of antibiotic resistance. Overall, our program affords a unique opportunity to extend the life and usability of the currently available first-line TB drugs - including Rifampicin and Isoniazid - that have, in many cases, been rendered practically useless in the face of drug resistant forms of TB.

column36: Monocyte derived cells and TNF family ligands in STING agonist therapy of cancer
column37: The stimulator of interferon genes (STING) is an intracellular sensor that can detect DNA in the cytosol of cells. Normal cells have their DNA in the nucleus and mitochondria, but if a cell is infected or damaged, such as occurs in cancer, DNA can be released into the cell cytosol- a signal that something is wrong. This in turn causes the STING pathway to produce a molecule called type I interferon that stimulates the immune system. Recently, scientists have made synthetic molecules that stimulate STING, referred to as STING agonists. The idea is to use this for an immune system boost to improve responses to infections or cancer. STING agonists have shown great promise in mouse models of melanoma and other cancers. They are injected into the tumor and a few days later the tumor starts to disappear. This has been shown to require at least 2 kinds of immune cells, dendritic cells, and T cells, that work together to eliminate the tumor. We have recently shown that a third kind of cell, a monocyte, is also important in this therapy. We now are investigating how these monocytes contribute to the therapy. Although this therapy is working well in mice, so far it hasn't worked as well in the early clinical trials in humans. By understanding the details of what is working in the mouse model, we gain insight as to what to look for to see how the therapy is working in humans and to optimize the therapy to achieve the desired outcome.

column36: Causes and consequences of anti-PEG antibodies
column37: The quick development of mRNA vaccines in response to the global SARS-CoV-2 pandemic has shown the promises of this technology. Now a manufacturing and regulatory precedent exists, it is likely that these technologies will become an important tool for future biomedical applications. Both mRNA vaccines currently approved are protein-free lipid nanoparticles stabilized with poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG), a water-soluble polymer forming a hydrophilic corona on the surface of the particle. Despite the absence of proteins in the vaccine, the incidence of anaphylactic shock in the population appears to be 2- to 5-fold higher than with traditional immunization strategies. This increased reactivity has been tentatively attributed to PEG, an ingredient that is shared with many pharmaceutical, cosmetic and processed foods products. Due to its non-peptidic nature, PEG is likely a T cell-independent antigen, a type of antigen for which reactivity remains poorly characterized. We will look, in animal models, at the determinants driving the immune response toward PEG, following exposure to various PEGylated systems. We will investigate how the physicochemical properties of the antigens influence immune response, but also look at which biological pathways are implicated. Importantly, reactivity toward PEG will be related to the efficacy of PEG containing medicines in animals. In brief, this research project will investigate how a chemical present in drugs and the environment can affect the reactivity toward pharmaceuticals, including mRNA-containing technologies. We will obtain a clearer understanding of how to prepare safer PEGylated pharmaceuticals and the factors driving the immune response toward PEG. Altogether, these advances will guide toward the design of safer drugs, and better clinical managements of patients with pre-existing antiPEG antibodies.

column36: Dual function of autoantibodies in a model of multiple sclerosis
column37: Autoimmune demyelinating diseases, such as multiple sclerosis (MS), result from dysfunctions of the immune system that cause it to destroy myelin in the nervous system. As B cells (a type of immune cells) play key roles in these diseases, B cell-depleting drugs have proven remarkably effective and are now part of the first-line therapeutic arsenal. A PROBLEM is that these drugs deplete most B cells, including beneficial ones, increasing the risk of infection. Moreover, they are not curative, possibly sparing a subset of B cells that secrete disease-promoting antibodies. Indeed, some self-reactive antibodies (autoantibodies) have been shown to be pathogenic in MS-related diseases and animal models. However, most autoantibodies have no known role. The GENERAL GOAL of this project is to clarify the nature of myelin-specific antibodies, in the hope of finding novel therapeutic approaches. We have recently characterized such autoantibodies in a new mouse model of MS. Our HYPOTHESIS is that most are nonpathogenic and can even be protective. To test this, our SPECIFIC AIMS will be to examine how our MS model is affected by: 1) interventions aimed at eliminating anti-myelin antibodies; and 2) treatments with anti-myelin antibodies with or without a mutation that blocks all effector functions. To this end, we will take benefit of cutting-edge technologies and ongoing collaborations with antibody manufacturers. This project will provide not only BASIC KNOWLEDGE on the dichotomous role of autoantibodies, which may help to understand how autoimmunity can develop, but also TRANSLATIONAL KNOWLEDGE on two potential treatments (plasmablast depletion and administration of protective autoantibodies).

column36: Assembly of a pseudo-peptide antibiotic active against gram-negative bacteria
column37: Bacterial infections are a major threat to health. The uncontrolled growth of harmful bacteria can be the cause of food poisoning, respiratory infections, urinary tract infections, or meningitis. In some cases, bacterial infections can be controlled by the human immune response. In other cases, antibiotics are required to control infections. Our current healthcare system is reliant on the widespread use of antibiotics in clinical practice. The widespread use of antibiotics has provided an evolutionary pressure for the emergence of resistance. As resistance genes spread in bacterial populations, our current arsenal of antibiotics can become obsolete. For this reason, we are engaged in a non-stop arms race with bacteria, with resistance to antibiotics generally emerging after the wide distribution of any antibiotic. Currently, estimates of deaths worldwide associated with antimicrobial resistance are 4.95 million per year (as of 2019), a number expected to rise. This grant is focused on an antibiotic for gram-negative bacteria, which are a type of bacteria that is particularly challenging to target. Fewer drugs are available to treat gram-negative infections. The antibiotic we will focus on is synthesized in one specific strain of soil-dwelling bacteria. We want to understand how this molecule is made. Using this information, we will gain knowledge useful for producing more of the antibiotic, and we will also use the knowledge to develop and discover new, related molecules which may also have antibiotic properties. These efforts are complementary to ongoing commercial efforts to test and develop the antibiotic into a drug that can be approved for human use and distribution. Our research is important as we need to develop more antibiotics, particularly for targeting gram-negative bacteria.

column36: Mechanisms regulating non-deletional T cell central tolerance
column37: The immune system is instrumental in protecting individuals against infections and cancers, but can also cause autoimmune diseases in genetically susceptible individuals. A key cell type responsible for both protection and inducing autoimmunity is the T cell. To avoid causing autoimmunity, T cells undergo stringent selection process during their generation. There are many mechanisms that are used to prevent T cells from attacking healthy cells. We discovered that T cells can be rendered functionally incompetent during their development and that this method of preventing T cells from attacking healthy cells requires the PD-1 protein. This proposal seeks to determine the ways in which PD-1 functions to incapacitate T cells and whether other methods to prevent autoimmunity can control T cells that have not received a PD-1 signal. These studies will provide insight into how T cells are prevented from attacking healthy cells and provide opportunities to develop new treatments for individuals with autoimmunity. Additionally, given the clinical use of treatments that target PD-1 in people with cancer, we will learn more about how these therapies work and how they might trigger health complications.

column36: Exploring the potential of type-1 regulatory T cells in treatment and recovery from intestinal inflammation in inflammatory bowel disease
column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) affects about 1/140 Canadians and is becoming increasingly common. Current treatments for IBD work in many people, but are not curative and frequently have difficult side effects. One promising approach to treating IBD is cellular therapy-using patients' own "suppressor" white blood cells to reduce inflammation specifically in the gut without affecting the rest of the immune system. Our project will focus on one type of suppressor cells, Tr1 cells. We have published that Tr1 cells have unique properties that reduce unwanted inflammation and may help the function of the cells that line the gut (epithelial cells). We also found that Tr1 cells can help treat inflammation in a mouse model of IBD. We will expand on these findings to help determine how Tr1 cells may be used to treat IBD. In aim 1, we will test whether Tr1 cells can prevent inflammation in an established spontaneous mouse IBD model and examine how this occurs. In aim 2, we will test Tr1 cells in a common model of chemically induced colitis and focus on prevention and repair of gut injury. In aim 3, we will optimize a method to make Tr1 cells respond strongly to gut bacteria that penetrate the damaged barrier in IBD. In aim 4, we will use human colonoids (mini-guts grown from intestinal biopsies from volunteers) and Tr1 cells (purified from blood) to determine how Tr1 cells protect the human gut from inflammatory injury and may help to repair it. If successful, this project will allow us to develop protocols to isolate, expand, and transfer Tr1 cells into volunteers to determine their safety and effectiveness against IBD.

column36: Direct access physiotherapy in the Pediatric Emergency Department to improve access to quality care for children and adolescents with musculoskeletal injuries: a randomized control trial
column37: Access to timely and efficient primary care, including in Emergency Departments, is a challenge in the Quebec Health Care system. In response to this longstanding problem, organizational innovations in care pathways are urgently needed. Direct-access physiotherapy, where physiotherapy services are available directly to patients, who can refer themselves without having to see a physician first, has been in place in Canada for more than 30 years. Evidence suggests benefits of direct access physiotherapy, particularly in the context of musculoskeletal conditions, in terms of initial management, clinical outcomes for patients, more efficient use of resources, and diminished health care costs, while maintaining high patient satisfaction. In the last 5 years, the emergence of direct-access physiotherapy models in adult Emergency Departments, including a pilot-project in Quebec City, has led to positive outcomes for patients and more optimal use of resources for the institution. It is now time to explore the impact of such a model in the Pediatric Emergency Department (PED). We propose to test the impact of a direct-access physiotherapy model in the PED on patient outcomes and resource utilization. We will perform a clinical trial where children and adolescents aged between 6-17 years, presenting to the PED with minor musculoskeletal complaints, will be randomized to being first seen by a physiotherapist for assessment and management of their condition, or to usual care with the PED-MD alone. We will measure pain interference with function (our primary outcome), other clinical outcomes, as well as health services metrics such as wait times, return visits to the PED or overall use of health care resources, and compare them between groups, as well as explore the recovery curves of children within each group over a period of 4 weeks after their PED visit.

column36: Developing Tough, Elastomeric, Bioactive Hydrogel Dressings to Accelerate in situ Bone Repair
column37: Reconstruction of large bone defects and nonunion fractures is still a major problem. Autografts and allografts have remained the gold standard for restoring bone defects, however they are associated with donor-site morbidity, lack of donor tissue availability, risk of infections and immune responses. Synthetic bone grafts, in combination with stem cells and drugs, have shown early promise. But clinical performances of these rigid implants have been largely poor due to their brittle properties and delayed integration to the body, thereby leading to implant failure. On the other hand, direct administration of bolus drugs leads to their fast clearance by the wound exudates at the injured site, thereby limiting drug bioavailability and absorption time. To address this critical unmet need, in this project we will develop a new 3Dprinted, tough and elastomeric, drug-releasing hydrogel dressing that can activate host stem cells to migrate to the implant site, promote vascularization and expedite fracture healing process. The hydrogel dressing will be composed of biocompatible and biodegradable components: mineral-based silicate nanoparticles, cell-adhesive gelatin, synthetic DNA as scaffolding polymer and drug molecules. Key advantages of this soft, stretchy and tough hydrogel dressing is that : (1) it can be customized to patient-specific anatomic size and shape with high precision (1) can provide a cushion-like, yet strong mechanical support to the injury site, (2) can locally deliver a synergistic combination of drug molecules, (3) can recruit endogenous stem cells, (4) can expedite new blood vessel and bone regeneration process, (5) and eventually degrade within couple of months to be replaced by new bone. Successful completion of this study can be expected to have potentially important positive impact in establishing a new platform technology for treating large bone defects, with, for whom current repair and reconstruction treatment options remain limited.

column36: MUC16 (CA125) mutations promote fibrosis and autoimmunity in systemic sclerosis
column37: Scleroderma is an incurable and deadly autoimmune disease that causes scarring (fibrosis) of the skin and internal organs. Early in the disease, patients can develop two different major courses: a rapidly progressive type, and a form of scleroderma with slower accumulation of damage. Patients with rapid disease progression have a death rate of up to 40% by 5 years, which rivals most aggressive types of cancer. The only effective treatment for those patients is a stem cell transplant, but many patients may not respond to it. The major obstacle to new, more efficient treatments of scleroderma is a poor understanding of the causes that drive the disease. We made a surprising discovery that patients with progressive forms of scleroderma develop large numbers of DNA mutations in their skin cells. Many of these mutations resemble those present in cancers. One particular protein, MUC16 (also known as cancer antigen 125, or CA125), is highly mutated in both scleroderma and in cancer. In cancer, MUC16 is known to promote inflammation and fibrosis. In our proposal, we aim to define how mutations in MUC16 promote the progression of fibrosis and inflammation in patients with scleroderma. Together, our studies may allow us to better understand how mutations in MUC16 (and other similar genes) play a role in the development of scleroderma. Our research may facilitate the development of novel treatment strategies for scleroderma, and ways to predict which patients will develop severe forms of the disease, which may inform the diagnosis and subsequent treatment options.

column36: Depicting disease heterogeneity in neurofibromatosis type 1 and the role of microenvironment in NF1-associated skin tumor formation through personalized tissue-engineered 3D models
column37: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is an orphan disease causing significant morbidity and mortality. It is a multisystemic genetic disorder especially characterized by cutaneous manifestations that include the development of multiple benign skin tumors, called neurofibromas. While the majority of these aesthetically disfiguring tumors are not malignant, management options are limited and the need for multiple clinical interventions contributes to significant disability and reduction of life expectancy in NF patients. No curative and nonsurgical treatment for NF exists at this time. To date, the pathogenic mechanisms associated with neurofibromas formation are still largely unknown and the clinical manifestations are highly variable, with significant differences sometimes seen within the same family. The developpment of neurofibromas and severity (numbers, location) are also impossible to predict. The goal of this exiting project is to study NF1 through personalized tissue-engineered in vitro skin (TES) models to better understand disease heterogeneity and the role of microenvironment in NF1-associated skin tumor formation/progression. The personalized 3D NF1-derived TES, i.e. directly derived from individual patient, could than be used as a preclinical model to better understand disease pathogenesis and for therapeutic testing. This innovative project will stimulate translational research in NF1 and accelerate the development of precision/personalized medicine strategies in NF, as well as to have short to mid-term impact on neurofibromatosis research and/or patient care.

column36: Avoidable Acute Care Use for Inflammatory Arthritis Conditions: Groundwork to Improve Inflammatory Arthritis Health Service and System Quality
column37: This project is directly relevant to the inflammatory arthritis conditions of rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthritis, psoriatic arthritis and crystal/gouty arthritis. Rapid disease control, access to appropriate medications, close follow-up and preventive care result in optimal outcomes of these conditions. While hospital care has been substantially reduced by better treatment approaches and advanced and targeted therapies, gout admissions have risen and significant gaps in the quality of ambulatory rheumatology care remain. Avoidable acute care use should be identified and resolved to uphold patient quality of life and reduce costs to the health system. This project will undertake several activities to support this mission. This includes identifying through evidence, expertise and consensus methods which emergency department visits and hospitalizations by persons with inflammatory arthritis conditions could be avoided with access to high quality ambulatory care. We will analyze the frequency and costs of these events. We will collect data about the root causes of avoidable events, looking at how health systems, services and processes influence access to care, and where there are gaps that lead to visits and hospitalizations that could otherwise be prevented. We will also consider how social, political and economic influences on health status contribute to an otherwise avoidable admission. These events and their contributing factors will be debriefed by a quality and safety committee after reviewing the available data. This committee will generate recommendations for system, service and process improvement as an integrated knowledge translation activity. This will be a model for quality improvement for rheumatology centres across Canada.

column36: Regulation of Periodontal Disease Pathogenesis by the Effects of Novel Monoamine Oxidase B Inhibitors
column37: A large percentage of the general population is affected by inflammatory periodontal diseases. Associated with this inflammation is loss of tooth-supporting bone and, if severe, loss of teeth and ultimately function. In addition, periodontal diseases have been associated with heart disease, diabetes, and preterm low-birthweight babies. Development of novel disease intervention strategies is needed to help patients manage these chronic, common, and costly diseases. Previously, we identified an enzyme (monoamine oxidase) that increased with disease and, if inhibited with a commercial drug, reduced disease. However, use of these drugs is limited in part due to the side-effects associated with their permeability into the brain. To address this issue, we developed novel MAO inhibitors that no longer cross into the brain but have anti-inflammatory properties. We have recently determined that our drug reduced two key aspects of periodontal disease. These include the expression of inflammatory mediators that drive disease and also the formation of bone-resorbing cells. Bone loss due to these bone-resorbing cells is a key negative outcome of disease and explains why tooth loss occurs. Understanding the mechanisms by which the drugs work is absolutely critical if they are to be developed for commercial use. Using a wide variety of cell culture, protein, and gene analysis techniques, we will examine the mechanisms by which these novel drugs regulate the expression of inflammatory mediators (Objective 1) and the formation and function of bone-resorbing cells (Objective 2). Using an animal model, we will then examine these signalling pathways in the context of periodontal disease and test the therapeutic efficacy of our drugs at reducing disease (Objective 3).

column36: Perioperative vitamin C to reduce persistent pain after total knee arthroplasty: a pilot randomized controlled trial
column37: With nearly 75,000 cases performed annually, total knee replacement (TKR) is among the most frequently performed surgical procedures in Canada, second only to Caesarean sections. Over 99% of TKR surgeries are performed specifically due to painful osteoarthritis (OA) of the knee. Although knee replacement surgery is generally associated with favourable outcomes for improving pain and disability caused by knee OA, approximately 1 in every 5 patients (20%) experience persistent knee pain after the procedure. This not only results in dissatisfaction, but often, functional limitations and the ongoing need for pain medication. Furthermore, it routinely leads to additional health care resources, including investigations (blood tests, radiographs, advanced imaging) and frequent visits to health care providers. The exact cause of persistent pain after TKR is challenging to determine, but typically is thought to be 'nerve related'. Even with an established diagnosis, treatment options are limited, and at best, usually provide only incremental benefit. As such, it would be high yield to identify interventions that can prevent persistent postoperative pain before it occurs. Vitamin C, also known as ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble vitamin that is essential in several biological processes, including those related to pain. Large population studies suggest that even mild decreases in vitamin C below normal range, are associated with musculoskeletal pain and functional impairments. Interestingly, it has been shown that vitamin C levels drop significantly after TKR surgery and there is evidence that administering vitamin C around the time of surgery may reduce persistent pain. However, the evidence to date has not been compelling enough to change practice. Our objective is to conduct a pilot randomized controlled trial to evaluate the effect of perioperative vitamin C administration on postoperative pain and function, in adult patients undergoing elective TKR surgery.

column37: Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA) is an inflammatory arthritis that develops in 30% of psoriasis patients. We believe that levels of small molecules in the blood called microRNAs (miRNAs) would make good predictors as they have been reported to predict response of biologics in other diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis. Ultimately, we hope to understand how exposure to cannabis during pregnancy may impact children over their lifespans.

column36: Mechanisms of action of sex-specific endocrine treatments in animal models of Parkinson's disease
column37: Parkinson's disease (PD) is well documented to be higher in men than in women and this sex difference could be due to effects of sex hormones. Drugs for PD only improve motor symptoms: no drug is yet available to limit disease progression. It is thus important to identify drugs that would interfere with disease progression. During previous CIHR-funded studies, we identified that estradiol and progesterone are neuroprotective in a neurotoxin (MPTP) mouse model of PD. We also found that the drug dutasteride (modulating steroid metabolism), already used in men, to be a potent neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory agent in this model. Neuroprotection with dutasteride was only observed in intact male mice, whereas in intact females their endogenous sex hormones were already protective against mild MPTP lesions. The mechanism of action of dutasteride and steroids involved are still unknown. We hypothesize that endogenous ratios of various androgens, estrogens and progestogens are modulated by dutasteride. Sex-specific treatments will be studied in various mouse models of PD (neurotoxin MPTP, genetic synucleionopathy and disease propagation) to investigate both sporadic and genetic forms of the disease. In male mice, we will determine whether dutasteride beneficial effect is mainly mediated by increased endogenous brain estradiol using various pharmacological approaches. Intact and ovariectomized female mice will be compared, considering that women with sporadic PD are mainly menopausal with reduced ovarian activity. Specific estrogen and progesterone treatments for the brain will be evaluated to avoid risks of gonadal cancer. Neuroprotection and inflammation will be assessed in brain, gut and gonads, using bioanalytical and histopathological methods. This project will validate novel mechanisms of action for hormone-modulating drugs already approved for human treatment to accelerate their use in PD. This project has high translational potential for sex-specific treatment.

column36: Targeting the Endocannabinoid System to Improve Cannabis Withdrawal in Cannabis-Tobacco Co-users
column37: Tobacco co-use occurs at high rates among Canadian cannabis users and is associated with worse mental and physical health outcomes compared to using cannabis only. Importantly, co-users have greater difficulty quitting cannabis (i.e., higher relapse rates) compared to cannabis-only users. This may be because co-users experience more severe withdrawal symptoms when stopping cannabis. However, previous studies that have examined the relationship between tobacco co-use and cannabis withdrawal severity assessed the association at only one time-point. Given that cannabis withdrawal symptoms can last for several weeks, it is important to determine if among co-users cannabis withdrawal symptoms remain more severe for an extended period of time compared to cannabis-only users. Because withdrawal symptoms are strong predictors of relapse, prolonged withdrawal symptoms in co-users would reduce the likelihood of sustained abstinence. Studies in animals have shown that reductions in naturally occurring cannabinoids in the body, endocannabinoids, may be responsible for cannabis withdrawal symptoms. If similar associations are found in humans then normalizing endocannabinoid levels in the body (via medications) may be one approach to reducing cannabis withdrawal severity in those trying to quit cannabis, making relapse less likely. Aim 1: To compare cannabis withdrawal severity at weekly time-points during 28 days of cannabis abstinence between co-users and cannabis-only users. Aim 2: To compare endocannabinoid levels between co-users and cannabis-only users Aim 3: To test associations between cannabis withdrawal severity and endocannabinoid levels. Findings from this study will provide information about the time course of cannabis withdrawal severity in co-users and will determine if withdrawal severity is linked to endocannabinoid levels. This may be a first step towards identifying a potential target for cannabis treatment in co-users.

column36: A multidisciplinary prospective exploration of prenatal exposure to cannabis and associations with infant and child neurodevelopment to age 3
column37: With the legalization of cannabis in Canada in 2018, public perceptions of cannabis as safe and medically useful even while pregnant has risen, despite growing evidence that it is related to serious infant health outcomes like preterm birth, low birthweight and requiring admission to Neonatal Intensive Care. There is also evidence to suggest cannabis use in pregnancy can lead to neurological issues in the child, however, the types and extent of these issues remains unknown. Most studies on the neuro-developmental impacts of cannabis use in pregnancy were conducted decades ago, when cannabis was a fraction of the strength of products available to Canadians today. As a result, we have an incomplete picture of the safety of cannabis use in pregnancy, and may be drastically underestimating the harms that could he caused by cannabis use in pregnancy to Canadian children. Our study plans to recruit over 6000 pregnant Canadians, and follow them along with their infants up to age 3. We will measure infant health and development, conduct detailed psychological assessments, and get detailed MRI images of their brains to determine if and how cannabis in pregnancy might impact brain growth and development. We will be measuring these variables in greater detail than previous studies using methods that will overcome the biggest limitations of the current evidence, providing an urgently needed view of how cannabis is impacting the brain health of Canadian children. This study answers the urgent call from Canadian and United States governments for much needed, high-quality evidence of the maternal and infant health risks associated with cannabis use in pregnancy. Our results will inform new policy and public health measures to mitigate possible health risks, inform interventions to best support affected children, and empower Canadians to make informed choices during pregnancy.

column37: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a major global health and economic burden, especially when considering patients are also at increased risk for metabolic and neuropsychiatric conditions. Our lab has shown that Ulcerative Colitis patients who consume the Mediterranean diet pattern can reduce damaging inflammation, improve metabolism, and improve emotional well being however, there was still room for improvement in this intervention trial. As such, current probiotics are most likely inefficient at surviving in IBD patients. A novel approach is to optimize beneficial microbes that strategically target these limitations in IBD patients through techniques such as genetic engineering. Gibson created a novel optimized beneficial microbe and called it BioPersist because it has a survival advantage that allows the microbe to thrive in the IBD gut. We think that BioPersist acts through an important molecule that also affects insulin resistance and behavior. We think that by combining a health-promoting diet, like the Mediterranean diet with these novel probiotics, this will reduce colitis and also benefit metabolic function and mental health. Our goal is to examine this novel live bacterium's (BioPersist) ability to biologically target inflammation, metabolic function and behavior in experimental colitis with the intent that this would provide rationale for future clinical development as a novel therapeutic for IBD that acts via the gut-brain axis and improves the gut microbiome.

column36: Dissecting vagal PTEN in the pathogenesis of type 2 diabetes
column37: Lay Abstract: Diabetes is a metabolic disease that is forecasted to affect over 620 million people by 2040; and currently, we still do not have a clear understanding in the defects that lead to this metabolic disease. The brain has a key role in the regulation of body weight and glucose levels; and a primitive brain function known as the autonomic nervous system controls many of our body functions such as food digestion and breathing. The vagus is an important branch of the autonomic nervous system that can regulate insulin action that is important for diabetes control. Insulin is a master hormone that can regulate metabolism and we wish to understand how insulin action can be controlled by the vagus to regulate metabolism. To this end, we have engineered mice with enhanced insulin action in the vagus. Our exciting preliminary data show that mice with increased insulin function in the vagus are remarkably protected against diabetes and obesity when fed a high fat diet. To fully understand how these mice are protected against diabetes and obesity, we plan to examine gene expression changes within the vagus that lead to protection against diabetes. To further prove that insulin is the essential hormone that functions in the vagus to properly regulate body weight and glucose levels, we will remove insulin action in the vagus. With these two sets of absent and enhanced insulin function within the vagus, we will measure vagal output and metabolic parameters. These experiments will give clues to potentially manipulate vagal activity to treat diabetes and diabetes. Indeed, vagal nerve stimulation through placement of a small electrode device in the neck is currently approved for some conditions such as depression and epilepsy. Our research will guide in harnessing the vagal nerve stimulation as a novel unchartered strategy without using conventional drugs to combat obesity and diabetes.

column36: Dissecting the molecular basis of dietary fibre metabolism by beneficial Bacteroidetes of the human gut microbiota
column37: Our lower bowel harbors a dense, complex community of microbes known as the human gut microbiota (HGM). A well-balanced HGM is central to health because it enables us to obtain nutrition from otherwise indigestible polysaccharides that comprise "dietary fibre", while at the same time protecting us from pathogens and disease. However, the fundamental microbiology and biochemistry of this process is unknown for many of our most important bacterial residents. This lack of information limits our ability to improve our health through dietary and microbial approaches. Members of the genus Prevotella have been shown to predominate in the HGM of individuals who consume plant-rich diets associated with a healthy lifestyle, including vegetarian, rural, and Indigenous people. Prevotella-rich HGM are associated with several beneficial effects, including increased insulin sensitivity and glucose tolerance (anti-diabetic properties) and a reduction in opportunistic pathogens. With rising incidences of metabolic and other diseases associated with post-industrial Western diets, which in contrast are dominated by Bacteroides species, it is urgent to understand the factors which favor Prevotella growth in the HGM. This research project will address the current knowledge gap in our understanding of HGM metabolism through in-depth functional characterization of several polysaccharide-specific gene clusters in the exemplary species Prevotella copri vis-a-vis Bacteroides ovatus. Together with growth studies on complex media, these results will provide an unprecedented molecular picture of how Prevotella prioritize access to individual carbohydrates in dietary fiber leading to competitive fitness. In turn, this holistic understanding will inform personalized HGM analysis and the development next-generation microbial ecosystem therapies to improve human health.

column36: Disrupting mitochondrial function in the liver: implications for immune suppression
column37: Animals like mice and humans are composed of many cells that are in turn organized into tissues or organs. column36: What happened and why? Exploring the development, implementation and impact of COVID-19 public health policies in Ontario using a health equity lens
column37: Communities who experience social and economic inequities were hardest hit by the COVID-19 pandemic. One-size-fits-all public health policies (PHPs) do not sufficiently address inequities. As we prepare for a post-pandemic recovery and for future health emergencies, it is important for us to look back and assess how and why PHPs were developed and implemented in Ontario. In Objective 1 of the study, we will answer "what happened" by categorizing all PHPs pertaining to vaccinations and isolation supports in Ontario and querying whether and how they considered health equity. In Objective 2 of the study, we will determine "why" public health policies were developed or implemented using (or not using) a health equity lens. In Objective 3, we will determine "what we could have done differently" by using mathematical models to compare the potential impacts of different PHP combinations. In Objective 4, we will learn "what it would take to do things differently" by asking public health actors to describe the barriers and enablers to developing and implementing PHPs that prioritize the needs of those most at-risk of infection and negative health outcomes. Our team includes government and public health decision makers from the federal, provincial, and local/regional levels. Our team also includes representatives of health-equity focused organizations, who supported implementation of public health policies at the provincial and local/regional levels.

column36: Host-directed drug development for tuberculosis
column37: Tuberculosis (TB) is a contagious respiratory disease of the lung caused by inhaling the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), and until the 2020 coronavirus pandemic, was the leading causes of infectious disease-related deaths worldwide. Inhaled Mtb are engulfed by immune cells in the lung called macrophages, which normally kill invading bacteria. However, Mtb reprograms host macrophages to disable their killing ability, allowing the bacteria to remain hidden from the immune response and protected from drug therapy while inside these cells. By targeting host cell proteins rather than the bacterium itself, host-directed therapy offers unique promise as an alternative treatment for TB. Indeed, boosting host immunity to TB will circumvent the development of antibiotic resistance and the need for drugs to penetrate the impermeable Mtb cell wall. We have identified four key host proteins that are exploited by Mtb to shut down the killing function of macrophages, which provides novel and tangible drug targets to boost immunity to TB. Importantly, we have developed new compounds with excellent activity and safety profiles that can target host proteins to enhance the ability of our macrophage to kill Mtb. As such, this application seeks to progress novel compounds and host targets into the clinical development stream by conducting preclinical, pharmacological, animal, and mode of action studies, which will ultimately advance host-directed therapies aimed at eliminating TB.

column37: "Trust" might arguably be the most studied social phenomena in the wake of COVID-19. In times of public health crisis-such as the COVID-19 pandemic-tapping into personal and institutional trust at multiple scales is paramount to disseminating critical information, maintaining confidence in disease containment measures, and eliciting behavioral changes among the citizenry. Mistrust, on the other hand, can have the opposite effect and lead to weak response to the pandemic. Many studies in different parts of the world have shown that without aspects of institutional, interpersonal, and political trust, politicians and public health professionals and scientist struggle to convince people to follow recommendations and instructions related to COVID-19. While the renewed interest in trust is refreshing for societies in a pandemic recovery world, the value of trust during a pandemic lies not in its associated outcomes, but in something much more fundamental-and that is how we conserve or strengthen social and political trust where it exists and how do we build trust where it is found to be low. This research will use a combination of quantitative and participatory methods to explore and identify strategies for sustaining or building trust in public health institutions in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), specifically Ghana, Guinea, and Liberia. Governments and public health institutions in SSA will be better positioned to effectively overcome the COVID-19 crisis and build inclusive and equitable recovery societies if they have the evidence necessary to repair, sustain, and build trust and political capital while strengthening the social contract between public health institutions and citizens.

column36: Antiviral Resistance and Benefits of Combination Therapy for Influenza Viruses
column37: Antiviral therapy is recommended for individuals with severe influenza infections and for those with selected underlying diseases, prone to complications. Thus, currently available antivirals targeting the influenza virus neuraminidase and polymerase enzymes play an important role in the management of influenza infections besides immunisation. However, the emergence of antiviral drug resistance, which is more common in children and immunocompromised patients, may threaten the usefulness of antivirals in the future. The first objective of our proposal is to keep addressing the mechanisms of resistance to anti-influenza drugs with an emphasis on the fitness of drug-resistant mutants. This characteristic includes both the virulence (severity) and transmissibility (by direct contact or by aerosol) of the resistant strains that will be assessed in reconstituted human nasal and bronchial epithelial cells and in a relevant animal model (ferret). In our second objective, we will evaluate combinations of different antiviral agents (neuraminidase and polymerase inhibitors) with or without immune modulators compared to single antiviral therapy in appropriate mouse models with the goal of improving survival and decreasing the emergence of drug-resistant mutants. Our work should provide new insights into the fitness of drug-resistant influenza strains and propose innovative combination therapies for optimal management of this frequent and serious viral disease.

column36: Unravelling the role of IgA during respiratory virus infections
column37: IgA is the major type of antibody found in our lungs, and the second most prevalent antibody found in blood. Despite this, the role played by IgA in mediating protection against respiratory virus infections is poorly understood. IgA, like other antibodies, can protect against viral infections in two ways. First, IgA can neutralize virus and prevent it from entering host cells. In addition, IgA bound to virus and/or virus-infected cells can be recognized by specific receptors found of the surface of certain immune cells. Upon recognition, these immune cells become stimulated to eliminate virus and virally infected cells. Mice do not naturally express receptors that recognize IgA. This has been a major barrier to understanding how interactions between IgA and immune cells contribute to protection from viral infections. Using a new mouse model that expresses the human IgA receptor (CD89), we will determine the contribution of IgA to protection against influenza virus and SARS-CoV-2. These studies will critical information that will contribute to the development of new antibody-based therapeutics and better vaccines.
