column37: COVID19 is a continuing pandemic with several challenges that are now expanding to its lesser known long-term effects. Long COVID19 is a term given to the protracted illness that patients of COVID19 continue to experience even amidst their post recovery phase. Difficulty in breathing, weakness, headache, cough, brain fog, and lack of smell are usual symptoms that are observed in Long COVID19. However, people can also suffer from more severe effects that affect the lungs, the heart, muscles and the brain. There is varied data from across the globe. Our CIHR project grant will be exploring what factors are strongly associated with the Long COVID19 patients needing admission in an intensive care unit, or a patients needing a ventilator? Our project will explore whether any differences exist among male and female patients, among people living in different cities, and among people living in different countries. Literature shows that lung involvement is the main feature of Long COVID19 disease, and data has illustrated that findings from computed tomography scans correlate with the outcome of the disease. Using AI we can identify with increased reliability the CT features that are correlated with poor outcome. This project would allow us to quickly detect the Long COVID19, provide better care for the patients, reduce the burden on care givers, reduce the work load on radiologists, and save health care costs. By using data sets from different countries, we are ensuring that our model is generalizable across many countries. As a secondary objective, we will be creating a telehealth radiology registry for the Northern Health patients whose diagnostic images are read at the Vancouver General Hospital after regular service hours, on weekends, and on stat holidays. The teleradiology service impacts the overall health in the First Nations populations as well as general population. We propose to provide service and evaluate the needs of people in NHA and IHA regions.

column36: Traditional, Complementary, and Integrative Medicine for patients with COVID-19: Living network meta-analysis and Rapid Recommendations
column37: Patients and clinicians worldwide need trustworthy, rapidly updated guidelines to inform their treatment of patients with acute and Long COVID-19. Although 80% of Canadians report using at least one Traditional, Complementary, and Integrative medicine (TCIM) in their lifetime, the overwhelmed healthcare system has limited capacity, and no Canadian or globally trustworthy guidelines and evidence summaries exist on TCIM for COVID-19. Optimal evidence summaries need to be up to date and differentiate well-done studies producing valid results from poorly done studies that are likely to be misleading. Interpretation of the evidence requires considering all the relevant studies addressing each treatment. In addition, it is vital to revise evidence summaries frequently as new information is published. To create trustworthy evidence summaries, we will search many databases to detect all relevant COVID-19 trials, evaluate the design and conduct of the studies, and combine all studies addressing each relevant question producing a single analysis for each outcome that patients feel is important. The resultant review allows patients and clinicians to compare all treatment options against standard care and against one another. These optimal evidence summaries will inform trustworthy practice guidelines. We will create trustworthy guidelines by constituting a panel that includes experts in COVID-19, TCIM clinicians and researchers, experts in assessing evidence, front-line clinicians treating COVID-19, and patients who have lived experience of acute and Long COVID-19. Panel members will be free of conflict of interest. These recommendations will be produced quickly and constantly revised as researchers publish new data. Finally, we will work with the World Health Organization for the guideline and one of the most impactful medical journals, the British Medical Journal, to publish the results online(free access for all) and as WHO guidelines on their website.

column36: COHESION Study 2.0: COvid-19, HEalth and Social InteractiOn in Neighbourhoods
column37: The potential causes for decreased well-being, worsening of mental health outcomes, and increasing health inequities under the COVID-19 conditions are multifaceted, given the enormity of the disruption to daily living. Some populations suffer more than others, including teens, older adults, women and racialized communities. It is important to understand and document the pathways linking living conditions - including neighbourhood characteristics and housing conditions -, to mental health and well-being trajectories and inequities, to provide key insights supporting rapid targeted policies and interventions. The COHESION project is a longitudinal study combining individual and living condition data from online questionnaires to explore the role that neighborhood social and physical environments play in mental health and well-being trajectories during the post-pandemic recovery period. In particular, we seek to understand the role of these environments on observed changes in health behaviors, such as daily mobility, sleep, and social contacts. We will further assess how these relations vary by gender, age group, income and education level, ethnic identification, and province. This study uses online questionnaires, smartphone app, geographic information systems and various statistical models to test the hypothesized pathways. The study will help generate high-quality evidence about how neighbourhood and housing environments affect long-term outcomes of mental health and well-being, to support Canada's response efforts and guide post-pandemic recovery. In the context of a pandemic where wait times for mental health services in some places exceed one year, there is an urgent need to find alternatives to meet these needs in a sustainable and comprehensive way. We are among the best-positioned teams in Canada to provide rapid and accurate data on the levers in cities that can positively affect the mental health and well-being of the population.

column36: Preclinical Models for Monkeypox Virus Infection and Therapeutic Development
column37: Monkeypox virus (MPXV) is an emerging virus and its recently identified Clade IIb has caused the greatest global outbreak of this virus family in history. Spread outside of endemic areas associated with atypical transmission modes and clinical presentation initiated the WHO declaration of a Public Health Emergency of International Concern. This large DNA virus causes significant disease with painful lesions and sometimes death often in vulnerable populations such as the young and immunocompromised. Importantly, the effectiveness of orthopoxvirus vaccines vaccination against the new Clade IIb viruses as well as the effectiveness of the vaccine dose sparing strategies that are currently being used are not known. Here we will investigate experimental Clade IIb vs Clade IIa MPXV infection in laboratory models with the goal of developing of a MPXV preclinical model for use in Canadian vaccine development. This model will then be used to understand the mechanisms of MPXV Clade IIb virus disease. For this work, we have three Aims: 1.) to develop preclinical models of MPXV infection using CAST/EiJ mice and black-tailed prairie dogs; 2.) to determine effective modes of transmission for Cade IIb MPXV viruses; 3.) to evaluate approved and newly developed MPXV vaccines against Clade IIb MPXV. Biological sex will also be investigated due to the sex-distribution of MPXV cases in the current outbreak. For this project, we have brought together experts in emerging virus preclinical model development, orthopoxviruses, and virus sequence analysis. Additionally, VIDO has the institutional infrastructure to work with high containment viruses and non-traditional animal models to ensure our success. Together, this project will provide an essential research tool for Canadian scientists and vaccine developers. As well, the results will be important for guiding public health policies to control the outbreak.

column36: Surveillance of Healthcare and Ambient Pathogens in our Environments and Spaces [SHAPES]
column37: As an alternative to the time-consuming and resource-intensive process of testing individual humans, our team's previous work looked at how we can use environmental sampling to predict and potentially prevent COVID-19 outbreaks. The novel approach we developed uses swab samples taken from floors, which then undergo a lab processing technique that can detect the presence of the virus. The SHAPES project looks at expanding this approach beyond COVID-19 to other common infectious diseases in vulnerable populations. Our proposed work aims to assess the already-collected swab samples for two additional respiratory viruses (influenza and RSV) and two bacteria (VRE and C. difficile), which will allow us to quantify the prevalence of these organisms. In the second part of the work, we will collect additional swab samples to determine how detection of these pathogens correlates to infections in humans at the sampling location. Our goal is to see what these floor samples can tell us about [1] whether a pathogen is present in an environment and [2] how that presence is associated with infections or outbreaks in the people in that environment. The approach of using environmental surveillance to predict and prevent outbreaks of infectious pathogens represents a new way of thinking about infection prevention. We hope to lay the groundwork for routine environmental surveillance of these common and potentially dangerous viruses and bacteria, especially in settings where there are vulnerable people, like long-term care homes and hospitals.

column36: The Cognitive Profile of COVID-19: Longitudinal Neuropsychological Outcomes Following Infection
column37: Evidence suggests the virus causing COVID-19 invades the brain, raising concern over the potential for long-term impacts on thinking abilities and everyday functioning. Our current CIHR funded study is characterizing cognitive functioning in COVID-19 positive individuals following physical recovery, and we now aim to track cognitive changes over time and identify risk factors for poorer long-term cognitive outcomes. Adults who tested positive for COVID-19 and acutely recovered, and those with no evidence of infection, are completing a series of cognitive and psychological tests via reliable, and valid videoconferencing techniques in our current study. The proposed study will follow these individuals over time, with 2-year follow-up assessments to examine changes in cognition. We are comparing test performance to determine group differences in cognitive functioning, mental health, and other factors at baseline, will re-assess group differences after 2 years, and will test a screening measure to detect these cognitive difficulties. Our follow-up study will examine the extent to which medical and mental health factors (e.g., other pre-existing medical conditions, vaccination status) may interact to play a role in cognitive changes, and how well a screening measure is able to detect COVID-related cognitive difficulties. Findings will inform clinicians (e.g., neurologists, neuropsychologists, rehabilitation specialists), on expectations for trajectory of potential recovery of function, and on how to optimally develop and deploy services in Ontario, BC, and other jurisdictions in Canada, with relevance to international health care communities. Results will help to ensure secondary impacts of COVID-19 infection are appropriately addressed, so that those affected by this virus are able to most efficiently resume complex daily activities requiring cognitive effort, including employment and academic pursuits.

column36: Advancing Health System Leadership Capacity for Psychological Health and Organizational Resilience during the COVID-19 Pandemic and Beyond
column37: Health leaders' action during a crisis, such as COVID-19, serves to guide and support others' actions, during unpredictable health service demands. As the COVID-19 crisis continues the mental wellbeing of leaders and nurses remains strained, and made worse by nurse absenteeism, turnover, and burnout. There is no known research in Canada addressing leader and nurses' mental health and wellbeing affecting the hospital's ability to care for patients during a health crisis, post-crisis, and future health crises. This information is needed to advance post-crisis leadership strategies for health leaders to better address their own and nurses' psychological health and wellbeing while simultaneously responding to COVID-19 patients, and a backlog of patients requiring surgery and treatments. Health system leaders have a responsibility to preserve the wellbeing of nurses and ensure quality healthcare while retaining compassionate engaged and experienced nurses. In this 3-year study, our objectives include: 1) examine how leaders respond to and adapt their leadership practices in response to the COVID-19 pandemic; 2) investigate nurses perceptions, clinical challenges, work conditions and their mental health; 3) examine how leaders can promote their own and nurses' mental health to mitigate strain and burnout; 4) integrate data from objectives 1,2 and 3 to determine how leaders can promote mental health in men, women, and non-binary individuals and decrease negative outcomes to ensure hospital performance; 5) identify recommendations that build leader and nurses' mental health to ensure a healthy and diverse workforce within hospitals during the ongoing pandemic, post-crisis, and future crises. The accumulated knowledge will be shared with leaders in health services, researchers, and policy makers across Canada so that promising leadership strategies and practices can be used to improve and advance health leadership and hospital performance.

column36: Investigating variation in the inpatient allocation of scarce COVID-19 therapeutics: Equity and Clinical Outcomes
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic created an urgent need for effective therapeutics to treat hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19. In less than two years, new drugs were developed, and existing medications were repurposed to provide a range of treatment approaches: anticoagulation, antivirals, immune-modulators, and mono-clonal antibodies. These medications were demonstrated to be effective across a range of metrics: reducing the intensity of illness and duration of symptoms, reducing the need for ICU admission and ventilator use, and reducing mortality. However, many of these medications were in extremely short supply as there was intense global demand and only limited production capacity. The impact of drug shortages on the equity of inpatient care for patients with COVID-19 is unknown. Equity means getting the treatment you need when you need it. It is clear that marginalized populations have faced a disproportionate impact from COVID-19, and inequitable allocation of scarce COVID-19 therapies has already been established in the USA. In a Canadian context, there is a pressing need to understand how patient, physician, hospital, and regional factors intersected with inequity in medication use. Our aim is to investigate the equitable allocation of scarce COVID-19 therapies in GEMINI data from 30 Ontario hospitals representing ~60% of all adult medical/intensive care beds in the province. We will use these results to develop a novel ethical framework for when multiple drugs for the same condition are in short supply - a situation that occurred during the pandemic - and will evaluate our ethical framework using advanced simulation modeling. This research will support the ongoing management of COVID-19 as drug shortages persist due to global demand, supply chain disruptions, and variant-driven surges emerge. Equitable distribution policies will also be an essential part of supporting our already-strained healthcare system and preparing us for future health emergencies.

column36: A development platform for mutation-resistant vaccines and antibodies for SARS-CoV-2 future variants
column37: Globally, as of August 2022, there have been an estimated 600 million cases of COVID-19 worldwide, and over 6.4 million deaths. Novel variants of SARS-CoV-2 virus continue to emerge and escape immunity by either previous infection or vaccination, resulting in repeated infection with potentially serious consequences. In this research program, we will develop rationally designed therapeutics that are robust to mutation of the virus, in preparation for future pandemic waves. We propose to develop both an antibody and a vaccine immunogen that exploit unconventional strategies in order to remain effective in spite of the rapid mutation of the virus. The vaccine candidate is designed to elicit a patient's antibodies to target a portion of the viral protein that is conserved and unlikely to mutate without altering essential functions that would themselves hinder the virus. The antibody is designed to remain effective in blocking the virus from entering cells so long as the virus uses the same cell recognition protein on its entry pathway. Since we know the virus will continue to mutate, it is critical to know how it may mutate to evade existing therapeutics or immunogenic response. We will investigate this question using a "chimeric" version of the virus which looks like SARS-CoV-2 on the outside, but is relatively harmless on the inside (a "sheep in wolf's clothing"). We can induce escape mutations in this chimeric virus by applying selection pressures using either convalescent or vaccinated patient sera, or existing recombinant antibody therapeutics. These escape mutants may share common features with variants of concern in the future. This powerful development platform will provide a strategy for generating pre-emptive therapeutics that can be pivoted to future outbreaks of other novel viruses.

column36: Developing intranasal dsRNA molecules as broadly effective therapeutics against highly pathogenic coronaviruses
column37: Long double-stranded (ds) RNA molecules are produced by viruses during their replicative cycle. These dsRNA molecules are long (1000s of base pairs) and contain viral genome sequence. In vertebrates, it was thought that viral dsRNA's major role was to stimulate host antiviral type I interferons (IFNs). The IFN response is a broad-spectrum antiviral response, stopping the virus in its tracks. It is potent, but also energetically costly, shuts down the cell's ability to make any protein, and induces side effects such as inflammation. In invertebrates and plants, long dsRNA does not induce IFN, but is used as a substrate for RNA interference (RNAi). RNAi uses an enzyme, Dicer, to cut the viral dsRNA into ~20bp pieces called short interfering (si)RNAs, which are loaded into RISC, where an mRNA whose sequence matches the siRNA is found, bound, and sequestered or degraded. In this RNAi pathway, it is the viral sequences that are targeted for degradation specifically, making it less energetically costly with lower side effects. We have found that long dsRNA can be used as a substrate for RNAi in vertebrate cells if used at a dose that is below the threshold to induce IFNs. Using this strategy, dsRNA containing coronavirus sequences knock down coronavirus (CoV) replication in human cells. The proposed project has 3 aims: (1) identify highly conserved CoV genomic sequences to develop pan-CoV dsRNA sequences that are optimized for Dicer recognition, (2) validate efficacy of dsRNA molecules in inhibiting CoV replication in human airway cells, either 'naked' or encapsulated in a lipid nanoparticle or virus-like particle, and (3) validate the antiviral effects of long dsRNA molecules in the airway using the golden Syrian hamster model of SARS-CoV-2. This project will develop a first-in-its-class pan-coronavirus therapeutic to be used prophylactically to protect the global population from the current SARS-CoV-2 pandemic as well as emerging CoVs.

column36: Preclinical proof of concept studies of a new generation of TLR7/8 agonist used in prevention against respiratory viruses and in immunotherapy against lung cancer.
column37: A nanotechnology, named FB-631, is a new generation of toll like receptor (TLR) 7/8 agonist known to trigger innate immunity in the lungs. The manufacturing process of FB-631 has been already developed and validated. FB-631 previously showed an excellent safety profile in a phase I clinical trial in human. This new nanoparticle is stable at 4C (<7 years) and at RT (<7days) and can be stockpiled without loss of activity or integrity. Several crucial steps of the development of this technology have already been completed making the search for novel applications very compelling. Other TLR7/8 agonists, like imiquimod (IMQ), are already on the market and used against warts (antiviral activity) and skin cancers. However, IMQ can only be used by the topical route because of its toxicity when administered otherwise. There is a medical need for a TLR7/8 agonist that can be injected or used by instillation/nebulization. FB-631 is safe and effective when used by instillation/nebulization and is well positioned to fulfill this medical need. Objective of the project: We intend to demonstrate the efficacy of FB-631 to prevent infection by respiratory viruses like the SARS-CoV-2. We also intend to demonstrate the potential of FB-631 in prevention of the implantation of lung cancers tumors and its potential in lung cancer immunotherapy. These proof-of-concept studies will generate convincing data that will support further development of this technology into the clinic. The team: The team combines an expert in the manufacturing of FB-631 (Leclerc) and in respiratory viruses, an expert in SARS-CoV-2 animal models (Baz) and an expert in lung cancer immunotherapy (Blanchet). The three researchers harbor the complementary expertise necessary to reveal all the potential of this technology.

column36: Connections Matter: Fostering social connectedness in youth to optimize mental health and well-being
column37: Social connectedness, which refers to a sense of belonging to an individual or group, is a central human need. It is a known protective factor for mental health (MH) and well-being, and against at-risk health behaviours for youth, which has lasting effects into adulthood. The COVID-19 pandemic has had detrimental effects on youth's social connectedness. The fall-out from this is expected to be felt for years to come, resulting in a sustained negative impact on the MH and well-being of youth. This study will address this gap and is in line with priorities identified by 'Inspiring Healthy Futures Vision for Canadian children, youth and families': the need to foster social connectedness, mobilize community action and partnerships including schools to support our youth, and engage with youth to create solutions. The aim of this multi-methods, youth-centered, arts-based longitudinal study is to gather evidence that will result in the creation of a toolkit that can be used by schools to foster social connectedness in youth to optimize their MH and well-being. Youth attending Grade 6 in the Seven Oaks School Division (SOSD) in Manitoba (MB) and key stakeholders (e.g., families, peers, teachers, counsellors) will be recruited. The youth will be followed as they transition from grade 6 to grades 7 and 8. Youth and stakeholders will take part in a variety of data collection methods including individual and focus group interviews and arts-based methods. A toolkit co-designed by youth will be implemented and evaluated over the course of the study. Short-term, a toolkit will emerge that can be used by schools in the SOSD to help foster social connectedness in youth, with the ultimate aim of advancing their MH and well-being. Long-term, this study will be used to inform the next steps in the research program, including adapting, implementing and evaluating the toolkit in other schools in MB with potential for future scale-up and testing across Canada.

column36: A FOCUS on youth mental health and substance use-related outcomes, inequities and trajectories during COVID-19 and beyond: A mixed-methods study in Canada and France
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has presented the potential for lasting consequences for inequalities and vulnerabilities to manifest across subsequent stages of the life course - a trend that will have significant impacts on today's generation of adolescents and young adults ages 15-29 years. Globally, including within Canada and France, youth have experienced among the most severe social and economic consequences resulting from the COVID-19 pandemic, with emerging evidence indicating that youth mental health and substance use (MHSU) inequities have deepened. The proposed three-year study will extend our team's existing mixed-methods Canada-France research infrastructure to focus on youth MHSU-related outcomes, inequities, and trajectories as Canada and France continue efforts to move into renewal and recovery. While each country shares some central commonalities (e.g., national health care systems), there are also important contextual differences (e.g., socio-political and -cultural differences; regulatory policies for substances, including cannabis and alcohol) that will benefit from comparative investigations across time. Specifically, we will conduct an annual national online repeat cross-sectional survey in both Canada and France with youth (n=7,000) that also features a nested virtual cohort (n=1,500). We will also conduct annual qualitative semi-structured interviews with youth from across different jurisdictions in Canada (n=30) and France (n=30). Throughout the duration of the proposed study we will engage in integrated knowledge translation and exchange (KTE) activities to systematically engage in rapid-cycle evaluation and advance actionable findings, including findings that are of relevance to national, federal and local policies and programs that can have an impact on youth MHSU-related outcomes.

column36: Characterization of filovirus host factors and small-molecule inhibitors of infection
column37: Filoviruses are negative strand RNA viruses that can cause severe hemorrhagic fevers in human following zoonotic spillover events. Outbreaks of filovirus diseases are increasing in frequency and our knowledge of the Filoviridae family expended greatly recently with the discovery of new filoviruses in Europe, Africa and Asia that are also potentially pathogenic. While a vaccine against Ebola virus, one of the 5 species of ebolaviruses, is available, it does not protect well against all ebolaviruses and does not protect against other pathogenic filoviruses. Therefore, pan-filoviral antiviral therapy is urgently needed. In this proposed project, we aim to gain a molecular understanding of the filovirus-host cell interactions with the overarching goal of identifying and characterizing pan-filovirus small molecule inhibitors for the development of new pan-filoviral antiviral therapies.

column36: Characterization of monkeypox virus circulation and transmission from wildlife to humans in Africa and identification of wildlife species at elevated risk for infection in Canada
column37: Recent outbreaks of emerging viruses, including monkeypox virus, have had severe public health and economic impacts across the globe. Monkyepox virus is a neglected emerging virus that can cause severe illness in humans and is endemic in numerous countries across Central and West Africa. Further, the frequency of monkeypox virus outbreaks has been increasing for many years and the ongoing global outbreak of this virus, as well as the 2003 outbreak in the midwestern United States, demonstrates the importance of understanding how increase preparedness and response activities in endemic and non-endemic regions across the world. However, there are critical knowledge gaps regarding the potential impacts of these viruses on wildlife and agricultural species. While prior observations have suggested that rodents are a likely reservoir for MPXV in endemic regions, there is little data implicating specific species. Further, there is a paucity of knowledge regarding the potential impacts of MPXV transmission on wildlife and agricultural species in non-endemic regions or for reservoir establishment. Here, we propose to investigate monkeypox virus circulation within wildlife in endemic regions as well as surrounding areas in Africa. Further, we will also assess the potential impact of monkeypox virus on Canadian wildlife species. Findings from this work will have important impacts on disease surveillance and containment strategies in endemic regions. Importantly, they will inform national monkeypox virus surveillance strategies and reduce the public health, wildlife, agricultural and economic risks for Canadians associated with emerging zoonotic viruses.

column36: Designing public vaccine procurement contracts to secure a socially optimal level of vaccination
column37: The proposed research seeks to supply guidelines for public vaccine procurement contracts that incentivize vaccine manufacturers' production capacity building and align the interests of government vaccine buyers and vaccine manufacturers to increase the availability of vaccines in any possible future outbreaks. The outcomes of this research aim to support building Canada's advanced vaccine production capabilities. The low vaccine coverage rate, below the socially optimal level of vaccination, has been a severe concern internationally. For example, Canada recently reported shortages of the new shingles vaccine, hepatitis A and B shots, and rabies vaccine. It was also reported that manufacturers of COVID-19 vaccines established inadequate capacity before regulatory approval. Reasons for the insufficient capacity include the risks in vaccine development, regulatory approval, high demand uncertainty, and manufacturers' fear of losing the capacity-building cost. Government agencies play a crucial role as buyers of vaccines from private vaccine manufacturers. However, there is a conflict of interest between government buyers and vaccine manufacturers in the procurement contracts. Government buyers usually bargain down the procurement price to control their financial expenditure, which hurts the manufacturers' profit margin and results in insufficient capacity building. Although it has long been argued that economic incentive contracts between government buyers and vaccine manufacturers should be implemented, many governments, including Canada, have not carried out necessary sweeping reforms to vaccine procurement contracts. The proposed research seeks to shed light on the optimal government vaccine procurement contracts in an infectious disease outbreak. The proposed research aims to find contract terms that align the objectives of the two players and achieve the socially optimal level of vaccination.

column36: Understanding mechanisms coronavirus cross-reactivity, immune durability, and pan-coronavirus vaccine protection
column37: The COVID-19 (Coronavirus disease 2019) pandemic caused by the SARS-CoV-2 (severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2) is the largest public health crisis in modern history. Although COVID-19 vaccines have decreased disease burden, the current vaccines have limited coverage against new coronaviruses or SARS-CoV-2 variants and the COVID-19 vaccines do not offer long-lasting protection. Immune protection generated after coronavirus infection is also short-lived adding further opportunity for new infections and continue disease burden. Next generation coronavirus vaccines strive to achieve broad protection against several viruses at once over a longer period; however, the mechanisms driving broad and long-lived protection against coronaviruses are poorly understood. This project will determine the mechanisms driving broad protection and immune durability in the host against coronaviruses. Specifically, the mechanisms utilized by B cells to induce broadly reactive antibodies and long-lived immune memory will be defined during coronavirus infection. Additionally, our new trivalent protein subunit vaccine candidates formulated with squalene-in-water emulsion (SWE) adjuvant (Vaccine Formulation Institute) designed to broadly protect against SARS-CoV-2 variants and sarbecoviruses will be evaluated for their mechanisms of action and immune longevity. This work will bring understanding to the mechanisms of broad protection against coronaviruses and provide valuable evidence for the use of novel vaccines that may be more effective at combating the current coronavirus pandemic and preventing the next one.

column36: Optimization of next-generation RNA vaccines for pandemic preparedness
column37: Messenger RNA (mRNA) technology has revolutionized our ability to develop safe, effective vaccines in a short time frame and at a large scale. Although the mRNA vaccines have had an incredible impact on the COVID-19 pandemic, there is still room for improvement. For example, we now know that the side effects are directly proportional to the dose of RNA, which motivates minimizing the required dose. Furthermore, the duration of immunity of the current mRNA vaccines is relatively short lived, requiring boosters approximately every six months. Finally, a certain proportion of the population has anaphylactic reactions to certain vaccine components, including polyethylene glycol (PEG). In this research program, we aim to develop RNA vaccines that improve upon the current mRNA vaccines and would be rapidly deployable in the event of an outbreak or pandemic. Self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) is the next generation of mRNA and the focus of my research program; it is a special type of mRNA that is able to replicate once it gets into a cell and requires a much lower dose. Like mRNA, saRNA requires a formulation that protects it from degrading and delivers it safely and consistently into cells. We hypothesize that by optimizing lipid nanoparticle formulations, which are the current state of the art technology for administering mRNA, and the dosing interval, we can identify lead clinical candidates for more potent and safer RNA vaccines. First, we will optimize LNP formulations that more efficiently the target immune cells that make a robust vaccine response. We will also optimize the dosing regimen to enable creation of a stronger immune 'memory' and longer lasting protection. Finally, we will engineer new LNP formulations that do not contain PEG so that more of the population is eligible to receive RNA vaccines. These vaccines can be applied to outbreaks, including COVID, seasonal viruses such as influenza, and future pandemics and will improve the health of millions of Canadians.

column36: Development of visible light-responsive antimicrobial coatings for personal protective equipment
column37: The development of a highly effective, easy-to-implement antimicrobial method for protection against direct transmission through infectious droplets is considered a promising cure in public health at the national and global levels. As one of the options, spunbond nonwoven/meltblown polypropylene (PP) fabrics have been mainly used for the fabrication of personal protective equipment (PPE) such as face masks/respirators and decontamination garments. Currently, filtration in the PPE fabrics depends on mesh size and biological contaminants. Once these contaminants are captured on the surface of such fabrics, they can survive from a few hours to several days, raising safety concerns about contact transmission from virus/bacteria-laden fabrics of masks and garments during use and disposal. Despite their importance, very little scientific progress has been made on antimicrobial fabric technologies due to significant technical challenges. In line with this demand, Dr. Choi at the Univ. of Alberta has developed visible light-responsive, universal pathogen negation substance, which can easily be applied to any conventional fabrics of face masks and PPE, and efficiently inactivate infectious virus and bacteria through physical contact. This technology is very promising thanks to its unique approach and for overcoming the fundamental limitations of conventional metal/biochemical/carbon-based antimicrobial materials. This project will be focused on manufacturing prototype antimicrobial masks/respirators and garments, testing their performance (filtration efficiency, pressure drop), and optimizing the antimicrobial effectiveness of the PPE coating to meet the desired ASTM/NIOSH/Health Canada standards. Once awarded, the funding will allow us to mature our antimicrobial technology through performance tests using prototype products, rendering it readily available for translation to industry sectors in an expedited fashion.

column36: Epigenetic mechanisms of osteosarcoma pathogenesis and progression.
column37: Osteosarcoma is the most common bone cancer and disproportionately affects children, adolescents and young adults. The use of surgery and high dose chemotherapy has brought osteosarcoma mortality down to 30%. When an osteosarcoma is found in other parts of the body such as the lungs or the liver, this means that the cancer has spread from its location in a bone, to a new site and formed a so called metastasis. People that have metastases already at the time of diagnosis have a very low odds to beat their disease. Similarly, patients who do not respond well to initial chemotherapy treatment may die of this of this cancer even if their disease is not initially metastatic. This cancer is characterized by extensive genetic alterations where large portions of the genome are shuffled from their original position, and in the process many genes are lost or gained. Our labs discovered that a significant portion of osteosarcoma cases also have alterations in how genes function beyond the simple loss or gain of genetic material, this is a process called epigenetic regulation. In this proposal we aim to understand the mechanism by which epigenetic alterations contribute to osteosarcoma development and resistance to treatment. We will use models based on human cells and mouse models to perturb epigenetic mechanisms and understand their effect on osteosarcoma tumors.

column36: CircRNAome in childhood TCF3-PBX1 ALL: Biomaker potential and mechanisms of circRNA dysregulation and function
column37: Childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (cALL), the most frequent pediatric cancer, still represents one of the leading causes of death by disease in children. It is a heterogeneous disease comprised of multiple molecular subtypes associated with distinct clinical outcomes. TCF3/PBX1 translocation, representing 6% of the cases, has a favorable prognosis, but is associated with an increased risk of central nervous system relapse, thus motivating the search for relevant molecular mechanisms and targets. We and others have shown that the expression of a new type of non-coding RNA, called circRNAs, is correlated with clinical and pathological characteristics of leukemia. Indeed, overexpressed circRNAs are enriched in patients with TCF3/PBX1 translocation. However, little is known about their biological activities and how circRNAs are abnormally expressed in a disease context. This study is the first to characterize circRNA expression in childhood ALL, to establish the circRNA profile for each ALL subtypes and a signature for prognosis to determine whether circRNAs can be used as biomarkers in ALL. This project will functionally characterize the most relevant circRNAs in ALL using the most up-to-date silencing and omics technologies. This project will not only add a new layer of complexity in leukemogenesis but may also help identify new therapeutic targets. Recently, new approaches have been developed to reliably target RNA molecules with high specificity. Thus, the in vivo modulation of native disease-linked ncRNAs is seen as one of the most promising therapeutic strategies in the context of precision medicine.

column36: Translating Epigenomics into Clinical Care for Synovial Sarcoma
column37: Synovial sarcoma is a cancer that most commonly afflicts adolescents and young adults who should have a long life ahead of them. Surgery and radiotherapy cure some patients, but unfortunately a lack of effective drug treatments mean that less than half of patients survive more than 10 years after diagnosis. This situation is frustrating because we do know what causes this form of cancer: a single DNA mutation that generates a mutant protein called SS18SSX. Most other types of cancer harbour multiple DNA mutations, but mouse model studies from our group and collaborators have proven that this single mutation is enough on its own to form synovial sarcomas. So, how can one single mutation cause all the changes to cell biology to make a cancer happen? The answer appears to be epigenetics - the SS18SSX mutant protein makes massive changes to how DNA is organized in a way that activates cell growth programs, causing cells to grow uncontrollably and become cancerous. Our recent research applying new technologies to a large series of surgically-excised tumors from Canadian patients has identified an unusual, disease-specific pattern of epigenetic changes in synovial sarcoma that affects the activity of DNA segments called enhancers that control gene expression. We propose to use newly developed tools to prove that these changes are driven by SS18SSX and to test if they can be reversed with emerging epigenetic drugs. We are uniquely positioned to do so, having (1) access to what is currently the world's most comprehensive epigenomic dataset on synovial sarcoma, (2) having developed a genetically-engineered mouse model that recapitulates human disease and can be used to test drugs and confirm they counteract SS18SSX, and (3) through leadership roles in the International Rare Cancer Initiative that provide a route to translate findings into clinical trials that will help young people with synovial sarcoma.

column36: Developmental epigenetic origins of Group 3 and 4 medulloblastoma
column37: Medulloblastoma accounts for ~20% of childhood brain cancers. Current treatment involves surgical removal, followed by chemotherapy or radiation therapy. Survivors often experience learning and memory problems because of these harsh treatments. Therefore there is a need to develop new medications that improve survival and survivors' quality of life. These cancers do not appear to be driven by simple genetic mutations. Rather, the cells of these tumours appear to be most similar to brain cells in a developing fetus, and a leading theory is that these tumours arise from a changed program in brain development. Our goal is to discover which developing brain cells these cancer cells are most similar to, and to see what changed between normal development and these tumours. By learning which brain cells tumours grow from, we will learn what programs make a cell in a baby brain cancerous. Once we know the nature of these changes, we can design drugs to rewrite or kill these cancerous programs specifically, leaving healthy cells in a patient's brain unaffected and reducing side effects. In this project, we will look at a type of programs used to control genes in brain cells, called DNA methylation. We will compare this programs in different groups of brain cells from post mortem developing brain, obtained from a tissue bank, and in tumour cells from patients. Because the brain is a complex mix of cells, and a tumour is a mix of cells as well, it is important to use methods that allow us to look at each cell separately. To use a fruit analogy, our techniques allow us to examine each fruit in a fruit salad, rather than looking at a smoothie. By doing this, we will be able to compare each cell type to tumours and identify which cell type the tumour is most similar to. Our project may identify novel cell programs that are changed in childhood brain cancer, that could be used to develop new medications to stop or reverse these cancers.

column36: Epigenetic priming of neuroblastoma to NK cell-based immunotherapy
column37: Neuroblastoma is the most common solid tumour in infants. Neuroblastoma arises from the nerve cells, most often in the adrenal glands, but it can also develop in other areas of the abdomen, the chest, the neck, and near the spine. Despite intensive treatments involving surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and stem cell transplantation, children with high-risk neuroblastoma still have a poor outcome. Thus, there is an urgent need to develop new therapeutic approaches that can be rapidly tested in clinical trials and with a safe long-term toxicity profile for children. Frustratingly, many potential anticancer drugs work in the laboratory but fail in clinical trials, and we urgently need better experimental models to discover more potent drugs. Current preclinical models do not faithfully replicate high-risk neuroblastoma in vitro, which limits the development of potent and specific therapies to treat this incurable disease. Three-dimensional (3D) cell culture produces dense clumps of cancer cells called spheroids. Their use can potentially improve drug discovery, as they display several qualities, such as high cell density, a lack of oxygen and nutrients, and the production of a complicated matrix between the cells, that make them better resemble actual tumours. 3D spheroids of immortalized cancer cell lines could be game-changing models in which to study tumour biology and perform screens to identify anticancer drugs. We have developed 3D spheroid models that replicates several important features observed in high-risk neuroblastoma that are missing in classical preclinical models. To improve the outcome of high-risk neuroblastoma patients, we will leverage on these innovative models and screen for small molecules that prime neuroblastoma 3D spheroids to natural killer (NK) cell immunotherapy. Overall, our aim is to investigate epigenetic drugs that sensitize tumour cells prior to the infusion of NK cells to cure pediatric high-risk neuroblastoma.

column36: Understanding the role of beta1 integrins in chemoresistance of acute lymphoblastic leukemia and therapeutic implications
column37: T cell malignancies are among the fastest rising cancers in North America. For example, T cell-acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) accounts for approximately 15% of all childhood leukemia and 25% of all adult leukemia. Although chemotherapy has improved the treatment of T-ALL especially in children, resistance to chemotherapy (chemoresistance or drug resistance) is a major factor in patient relapse and is associated with poor outcome and significant fatalities. Therefore, a better understanding of how leukemic T-ALL cells manage to escape chemotherapy and become resistant will likely lead to more efficient therapies. We have identified a receptor called alpha2 integrin that is highly expressed in leukemic cells and which can be a critical factor in T-ALL drug resistance and patient relapse. Indeed, when we blocked this receptor, we were able to better eradicate leukemic cells upon their treatment with chemotherapy. In this proposal, we will characterize the implication of alpha2 integrin in the development of drug resistance of leukemic T-ALL cells and examine the mechanisms by which it does so. We will also determine if the blockade of alpha2 integrin with neutralizing antibodies will enhance the ability of chemotherapy to eradicate patients-leukemic T-ALL cells engrafted in mice. These studies have the potential of revealing a novel therapeutic target in T-ALL. Accordingly, inhibition of alpha2 integrin with existing inhibitors combined with chemotherapy may be a novel strategy for T-ALL therapy to avoid patient relapse and consequently improve clinical outcomes.

column36: Barriers to and facilitators of the early integration of pediatric palliative care for children with cancer in Canada
column37: Children with cancer and their families can experience a range of side effects from their treatments including pain and psychological distress. Palliative care for children with cancer focuses on relieving the suffering that occurs during treatment and at end of life. The aim of palliative care is to improve the quality of life for the patient and their family during their cancer treatment, regardless of the disease outcome. While many research studies have shown that providing palliative care early in the child's treatment is the most effective way to manage and prevent this suffering, these services are not accessed very often, or are accessed too late for full benefit. The purpose of this study is to try to understand why this is the case in Canada and to create a set of policy recommendations aimed at improving access to pediatric palliative care for all Canadian children who need it. We plan to interview pediatric oncology healthcare professionals (i.e., doctors, nurses, psychologists who treat cancer in children) and specialized pediatric palliative care healthcare professionals including doctors, nurses, psychologists, social workers on their perspectives about the barriers and facilitators to accessing pediatric palliative care early in the child's disease. We will also interview a diverse group of teen cancer patients and caregivers of children with cancer to understand their points of view on the accessibility of pediatric palliative care early in their cancer trajectory when being treated for cancer. The interviews will be analyzed for recurring themes and patterns that arise across the interviews. The research findings will be used to develop a set of policy recommendations that will help the Canadian government understand how to improve access to pediatric palliative care across the country and will also be made available in publications (academic journals, newspapers, etc.).

column36: Clinical significance and natural history of clinically unsuspected central venous catheter-related thrombosis in children with cancer
column37: Blood clots are a known complication of cancer and its treatment. In children, blood clots are often linked to a central venous line, a device inserted in the body to deliver medicine, fluids, or nutrients. While some blood clots can lead to serious short- and long-term complications, it is unknown whether all clots are equally important. It is questioned whether unsuspected blood clots (otherwise called incidental) may lead to such complications. Understanding which blood clots are dangerous is important so healthcare practitioners can tailor the treatment using a patient-centered approach. Children at high risk of complications could benefit from medicine to treat adequately blood clots and minimize their impact. Conversely, in children at low risk of complications, the adverse effects (mostly bleeding), costs and burden of such medicine could be spared. To address this question, we will perform a study enrolling children with cancer requiring a central venous line. We will determine whether they have an incidental clot using a painless test called a Doppler ultrasound. As this exam is not done as part of routine care, the results will not be communicated to the healthcare team. Children will then be followed for six months to detect any short-term complications of blood clots, including clot progression, infection, or dysfunction of the central venous line. We will follow the children for two years to determine whether they develop post-thrombotic syndrome, the most common complication of symptomatic blood clots. We will compare whether complications were more frequent among children who developed incidental clots, compared to those who did not. We will also explore potential risk factors for blood clots among children with cancer to identify markers present in children at high risk of blood clots. As survival from childhood cancer has increased drastically in the past decades, it is increasingly important to prevent complications and late effects of treatment.

column36: Effects of exercise on cognitive and brain outcomes in young adults diagnosed with cancer: a randomized controlled trial
column37: While most young adults diagnosed with cancer (YAs) survive the disease, many receiving chemotherapy report disturbances relating to their mental functions or abilities. Mental disturbances (also known as cognitive disturbances) and underlying brain alterations are debilitating for YAs and prevent successful return to work due to an inability to focus, follow directions, and carry out tasks independently and effectively. Also, mental disturbances lead to behavioural problems (e.g., poor impulse control, inability apprehending performance errors, difficulty making mental shifts), making it hard for YAs to cope, complete tasks, handle emotions, and interact with others. Last, mental disturbances diminish quality of life (QoL). Treatment options to mitigate cognitive disturbances and underlying brain alterations are elusive, but needed. Exercise (EX) has mental benefits (e.g., increased brain blood flow, increased neuron production in the hippocampus, release of beneficial growth factors, improved cognitive function), implying EX may mitigate mental disturbances. While the effects of EX have been tested with middle-age and older adults after cancer treatment, its effects on chemotherapy-induced mental disturbances and brain alterations in YAs during chemotherapy remain untested. This research will test if EX protects YAs against developing chemotherapy-induced mental disturbances and brain alterations. Recruited YAs will get a 16-week supervised EX intervention or usual care. Self-report and objective measures of cognitive function and brain health will be repeated to assess short- and long-term effects of EX. If effective in protecting YAs from developing mental disturbances and brain alterations, it means YAs will have a treatment option to mitigate a common debilitating side effect of chemotherapy that interferes with work pursuits and diminishes QoL, and it would offer evidence to implement EX interventions in practice to promote recovery from cancer.

column36: Targeting molecular and cellular events that drive tumor formation in rhabdomyosarcoma
column37: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common type of soft tissue sarcoma in children, accounting for an estimated 3% of all childhood cancers. Rhabdomyosarcoma is composed of cells that normally develop into muscular tissue. The first line of treatment for this very aggressive pediatric cancer is surgery, when possible, accompanied by conventional chemotherapy and radiation treatment which are non-specific and associated with a wide range of side effects. In recent years, the development of targeted therapies has changed the course of cancer treatment by improving cancer patients' survival and quality of life. Targeted therapy considers the unique mutations present in a particular cancer type and specifically interferes with the downstream consequences of these mutations in the cancer cell. However, the development of therapeutic strategies for rhabdomyosarcoma is limited by our poor understanding of the molecular events that drive tumor formation. To address this unmet medical need, our research program investigates the molecular and cellular mechanisms responsible for rhabdomyosarcoma initiation, maintenance and progression. We employ proteomic, genomic and genetic approaches to decipher how rhabdomyosarcoma-associated gene mutations perturb the normal cellular program of muscle progenitor cells. This approach will unravel critical gene regulatory pathways controlling rhabdomyosarcoma cell viability and proliferation and identify novel therapeutic targets. Developing more targeted therapies will undoubtedly lead to a better outcome for these devastating cancers often associated with poor prognosis.

column36: Sex and gender based disparities in the treatment of patients with interstitial lung diseases
column37: Interstitial lung diseases (ILD) are a group of devastating, debilitating diseases characterized by worsening scarring and stiffness of the lung tissue. These lead to cough, shortness of breath, low oxygen levels in the blood and shortened life expectancy. There are medications that have been shown to slow disease progression, but delays in diagnosis and access to care can impact a person's disease and prognosis. A patient's sex and gender are important considerations in the care of patients with ILD and can affect the type of diagnosis and the disease course. Earlier research has shown that women may be less likely to be diagnosed with the disease and less likely to receive early treatment compared to men. Other disparities likely exist but have not been fully looked at in a thorough, systematic way across the journey of care for patients with ILD. This project seeks to understands how sex of a patient (male or female) impacts access to key treatment interventions in the care of patients with ILD, including medication initiation and discontinuation, pulmonary exercise rehabilitation, access to supplemental home oxygen, and lung transplantation. We will also explore how gender and gender-related roles, behaviours and social differences impact these key outcomes. We will use two large study cohorts of patients with ILD from Canada and the United Kingdom with rich clinical information and data on medications, oxygen, rehabilitation and lung transplantation to answer this important question pertaining to equity of care.

column36: Modulating cocaine seeking by gonadal hormones in rats: sex differences in neural mechanisms of relapse-like behaviour
column37: Cocaine use disorder (CUD) affects millions of individuals and is associated with adverse biological and psychological states, so finding pharmacological targets for relapse prevention would improve the quality of life of many Canadians. Estrogen (E2) and progesterone (P4) are gonadal hormones found in both men and women. In rodent models, E2 increases relapse-related drug-seeking behaviours, and P4 inhibits them. Since these hormones interact with many proteins throughout the brain, including areas related to CUD, insights into the mechanisms of hormone modulation of relapse risk may bring about targets for the development of pharmacotherapies for CUD. In Aim 2, we will investigate the pharmacological mechanisms through which E2 increases and P4 decreases relapse risk. E2 and P4 interact to varying degrees with glutamate systems, growth factors, and estrogen and progesterone receptors. We will assess the extent of the involvement of these mechanisms by pretreating rats with E2 or P4 along with pharmacological activation or inhibition of these receptors during relapse tests. In Aim 3, we will assess interactions between glutamate systems and E2 or P4 by measuring levels of glutamate release as well as glutamatergic-specific proteins in brain regions known to be involved in relapse following a cocaine prime.

column36: Sex as a biological variable in the development of inflammatory arthritis
column37: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is the most common chronic joint disease in Canada. It causes painful joint inflammation, reduced mobility and can lead to permanent joint damage. With more than 6 million Canadians affected, arthritis costs the Canadian economy more than $35B each year, and there is currently no cure. RA is more common in females, almost 60% of arthritis patients in Canada are females. Despite this large difference, very little is known about differences in the way the disease develops in males and females. Thus, understanding the sex-related differences in the development of arthritis is very important for establishing new strategies for early diagnosis, and developing new therapies, that will work effectively in both males and females. This study will examine the development of RA in both males and females concurrently. Immune response and different molecular factors will be examined at different stages of disease development in a mouse model, and in samples from First Degree Relatives (FDR) of RA patients who are 'at-risk' for disease development but without clinical symptoms. It is known that RA occurs within families, and that RA FDRs have changes in disease-related molecules in their blood before appearance of clinical symptoms. Thus, this research will provide insight into the biological processes that lead to the development of RA, and how these processes differ between females and males. Findings from this research will provide the fundamental knowledge of disease development in RA that will be essential for the development of sex-optimized approaches for improved early diagnosis, more effective management, and treatment of RA. Early detection and treatment can avoid pain and damage to joints, and thus help individuals to lead an active life. Thus, this research is a critical step in reducing the burden of disease within the Canadian population and providing equitable access to treatment options.

column36: MET-JEM: a sex-specific job-exposure-matrix of workplace energy expenditure based on metabolic equivalents
column37: Background: Insufficient physical activity and a sedentary lifestyle are linked to numerous adverse health effects, i.e., cancers, type 2 diabetes, heart disease and mental health. Most studies have focused on recreational physical activity, whereas workplace physical activity seems to have opposite effects on health, the so-called "paradox of physical activity". This could reflect inadequate evaluation of activities performed in previous studies. Thus, developing an improved tool to evaluate physical activity at work will help resolve ambiguities. The need: With large epidemiological studies, it is essential to have tools to characterize workplace energy expenditure which are reliable yet feasible. It has been demonstrated that work tasks can be gendered, i.e., differ between women and men holding the same occupation. No research tool taking sex and gendered tasks into account exists. Methods: We will create a tool called MET-JEM, a Job-Exposure Matrix based on metabolic equivalents (METs), which reflect the ratio of activity expenditure to that of the resting metabolic rate. Our tool will be built using data from 7 studies conducted in Montreal by our team in 1975-2016. Some 69,000 detailed job descriptions (for 15,371 participants, 5,251 females, 10,120 males) for jobs held from 1930-2016 were divided into up to 4 main tasks entailing different MET intensities. Each task was assigned a MET value based on Ainsworth's Compendium of Physical Activities. To construct the MET-JEM, information on METs will be aggregated across participants with the same occupation/industry, sex and jobs in the same time periods. Applications: MET-JEM will be available to the scientific community to be used in studies with information on occupation, which is commonly collected. Ultimately, the MET-JEM, by integrating sex and gender aspects, will help support adequate recommendations for disease prevention among women and men.

column36: How cardiorespiratory fitness influences brain recovery and neuroplasticity after stroke
column37: At six months post-stroke about 65% of affected persons continue to have hand paralysis that profoundly affects their independence, however recovery varies widely. The reason for variability in recovery remains unclear. We propose that having higher cardiorespiratory (or aerobic) fitness will enhance brain plasticity contributing to motor recovery. Exercise training has direct effects on beneficial neurotrophins that support brain remodelling. We have shown that having higher levels of fitness lessens corticospinal inhibition, a brain condition that limits capacity for plasticity. There is a surprising gap in our understanding of the role of fitness on brain recovery during stroke rehabilitation. Research suggests that females are less likely to achieve independence after rehabilitation and a recent Canadian report supports that females had longer lengths of stay and were less likely to be discharged home. There is evidence in healthy older adults that the relationships between fitness and brain function could be sex dependent and more robust in males. This project will identify whether there are sex and gender differences in fitness, plasticity and upper limb recovery after stroke. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a reliable research tool to map the motor cortex. Using TMS mapping we will register the location and extension of the brain area responsible for control of the paralyzed hand. We will measure (at 2 weeks, 3 and 6 months) upper limb recovery, cardiorespiratory fitness and brain reorganization in 175 people recovering from stroke. This proposal focuses on the impact of cardiorespiratory fitness on the ability of the brain to reorganize after stroke. Our core hypothesis is that higher levels of cardiorespiratory fitness (measured 2 weeks after stroke) will enable efficient motor map modifications leading to greater upper limb restoration in the first 6 months after stroke.

column36: Delineating cholesterol's role in steroidogenesis
column37: Steroid hormones are essential to life as they control many important functions in the body, including fertility, glucose metabolism, salt balance and immunity. Altered steroid hormone levels lead to many diseases, such as infertility, an impaired energy and salt balance, as well as inflammatory diseases. Cells that produce steroid hormones (steroidogenic) have developed diverse ways devoted to procuring sufficient amount of cholesterol (as per the need), which serves as an essential starting material for the biosynthesis of all steroid hormones (steroidogenesis). This arrangement helps to avoid abnormal steroid hormone production and related diseases. Despite the cholesterol-centric setup of steroidogenic cells, the potential role of cholesterol in the regulation of steroidogenesis remains unexplored. Because steroid hormones are so important for life, we speculated that steroidogenic cells must respond to a cholesterol deficiency to sustain steroidogenesis. To explore this, we used a simple approach that was not capitalized on before, and deprived steroidogenic cells to exogenous cholesterol supply, which is the major source for their steroidogenic needs. Our initial findings are very exciting, which suggest that cholesterol indeed plays a key role in the regulation of cellular events that are known to be involved in steroidogenesis. However, the mechanisms involved remain to be determined. This information is essential to improve our understanding of steroidogenesis because of its substantial clinical implications. In this research project, we will explore the mechanisms involved in the role of cholesterol in steroidogenesis in all major steroidogenic cells/tissues. We anticipate that the project outcomes will provide new insights into the molecular events involved in steroidogenesis, which in turn shine will light on future investigations in this field and open new opportunities for managing impaired steroid hormone production and related abnormalities.

column36: Understanding the Perceptions and Health Impacts of Climate Change among LGBTQIA+ People in Alberta: A Mixed-Methods Pilot Study
column37: Climate change is worsening health and well-being. Climate change affects health in a number of different ways, but two key exposures are climate events and air pollution. Extreme temperatures, other weather events like flooding, and wildfires have been linked to the development and worsening of heart and respiratory conditions, mental health, and injuries. The effects of climate change are often compounded by social and other factors. People who identify as 2SLGBTQIA+ face marginalization, exclusion, discrimination, and stigma, which creates situations of heightened vulnerability to climate change. Yet, very little research so far has focused on the climate change and health risks, needs, and experiences of people who identify as 2SLGBTQIA+, which is a critical gap in our knowledge. This pilot study aims to investigate: (1) the perceptions and experiences of climate change of people self-identifying as members of the 2SLGBTQIA+ community related to health and well-being in Alberta, (2) health events linked to weather events and air pollution exposures among people in Alberta self-identifying as members of the 2SLGBTQIA+ community, and (3) factors that mediate relationships between weather, air pollution exposure and health in people self-identifying as members of the 2SLGBTQIA+ community across Alberta. A variety of data collection and analysis approaches will be used. An 2SLGBTQIA+ advisory group will be formed to help guide, inform, interpret, and distribute this research. Our goals are to report on unique climate change and health risks, identify areas of intervention, highlight outstanding research needs, and share the overlooked perspectives of people in the 2SLGBTQIA+ community in Alberta.

column37: Menopause naturally occurs when 12 months have passed after the final menstrual period but can also be caused by medical interventions such as surgery, chemotherapy or radiation for cancer or pain. The loss of ovarian function and/ or low estrogen levels are associated with profound physiological changes, leading to a variety of bothersome symptoms for female people. The average Canadian female person will spend one third of their life past menopause and some for even longer. Among these, 75% will experience symptoms related to menopause that interfere with their daily lives and some will stop working as a result. The most common symptoms are hot flashes, night sweats, poor sleep, mood changes and worsening sexual function. However, many do not seek advice from their health care provider and suffer in silence. Further, some providers lack the knowledge to discuss up to date treatment options. Mature women's health has been largely understudied and underfunded in Canada, leading to a lack of information available for patients and providers. We have started collecting data about menopause symptoms and treatments that may or may not work, initially at Mount Sinai Hospital (Toronto) and more recently at St. Joseph's Healthcare in Hamilton. Our goal is to expand this standardized questionnaire and database to more sites across the country where specialized menopause care is offered. With further data gathering and sharing of information among providers across the country, we generate knowledge to improve the lives of female people living in Canada. The knowledge gained will inform educational initiatives for both health care providers and the patients that they serve.

column36: Understanding the variations in clinical presentations of endometriosis: a pan-Canadian cohort study
column37: Endometriosis is highly prevalent and affects 1 in 10 women of childbearing age. It is characterized by the presence of endometrial tissue outside the uterine cavity, also known as endometriosis lesions, which causes inflammation. This chronic disease can have serious consequences in a person's life such as severe pelvic pain and infertility. Clinical presentations vary and current classification systems mostly focus on assessing the level of surgical complexity but fail to be associated with the level of pain or chances of conceiving. Efforts must be made to better understand the determinants of a poor quality of life in women with endometriosis. The objective of this research program is to evaluate the current classification systems and the clinical factors that are associated with a poor quality of life in order to develop a new classification system that better correlates with clinical presentations. We are recruiting adult individuals with endometriosis or chronic pelvic pain during gynecology consultations in six Canadian hospitals centers. Those who undergo a surgery for suspicion of endometriosis in the following year will be included. This proposal addresses the urgent need to investigate the limits of current classification systems and explain the differences in clinical presentations. This large pan-Canadian cohort study will be relevant for healthcare providers as it will allow for the validation of a new classification of endometriosis to provide more individualized care to patients.

column36: Quantifying the cardiovascular and metabolic health benefits of Canada's physical activity and healthful eating guidelines on pre and postmenopausal women
column37: Cardiometabolic diseases (heart disease, diabetes, cancer) are the top causes of illness and death in women. Physical activity and healthy eating are important for cardiovascular and metabolic health as well as the prevention of disease. Canada has public health recommendations for physical activity and healthy eating practices that aim to help reduce the risk of chronic disease. However, cardiovascular and physical activity research in women and the impact of menopause is lacking, so the impact of these guidelines on women's health is not well known. The cardiovascular, body fat, and muscular systems and how they respond to physical activity and diet appear to differ in women vs men and pre vs postmenopausal women. Menopausal women may respond differently to the current guidelines, which is an important research gap. This study will measure the health benefits of following Canada's physical activity guidelines, and the added benefits of healthy eating among equal numbers of pre and postmenopausal women for the first time. Importantly, we will evaluate the health effects on the heart, vessels, blood sugar, blood lipids, body fat, and skeletal muscles as the key organs related to cardiovascular and metabolic health. This study will produce new evidence that is specific to women about the health benefits of the current Canadian guidelines on physical activity and diet. Health practitioners will use this new information to prevent cardiometabolic diseases in women.

column36: Sexual dimorphism in right (-sided) heart failure: Role of progesterone in right ventricular angiogenesis and remodelling
column37: The right ventricle (RV) of the heart normally functions against low pressure and resistance. However, in patients with increased blood pressure in the lungs (pulmonary hypertension), the RV is exposed to higher pressure and resistance that leads to increased RV wall thickness and ultimately right heart failure (RHF, inability of the RV to pump blood) and death. Recent studies have shown that patients with stable RV function have better survival than patients whose RV function is deteriorating. Therefore, treatments that can prevent deterioration of RV function can improve survival of these patients. Unfortunately, there is no specific therapy available targeting the RV. Therefore, there is a need for better understanding of processes involved in RHF for development of new RV specific therapies. Importantly, females have better RV function under normal condition as well as in response to increased pressure/ resistance compared to males; however, the mechanisms remain unknown. Our research focuses on understanding these important differences to design new therapies and better treatment for RHF. Specifically, we will focus on the effects of progesterone, a major female sex hormone, in blood vessel growth in the RV and protection against RHF. Our preliminary data, using animal models, showed better RV structure and function in female rats compared to male rats. This effect was associated with higher expression of genes linked to blood vessel growth in the female RV. Therefore, in this project, we will investigate how progesterone affects blood vessel growth in the RV and if that is the cause for male-female differences in RHF. Importantly, subjects with lower progesterone levels have poor RV function. Therefore, findings from these studies will be relevant to patients with low progesterone such as male and female affected by polycystic ovary syndrome and menopause. The knowledge acquired from this project will form the base for development of specific therapy for RHF.

column36: Effects of age on antiretroviral concentrations and adverse drug reactions for women with HIV
column37: As we age, our bodies become less efficient at metabolizing medications resulting in higher drug levels in the blood and more side effects. However, little is known about how aging affects the body's processing of HIV medication, known as antiretroviral therapy, an important topic given an increasing number of elderly HIV patients. Aging women are particularly susceptible to having elevated drug levels compared to men due to differences in body size and drug metabolism. Perhaps not surprisingly, women also experience more side effects from antiretrovirals than men. Despite this, bloodstream levels of antiretrovirals, how they may change with aging, and how they relate to side effects are virtually unexplored amongst women living with HIV. We will study people with living HIV in British Columbia who are participating in the BC-CARMA-CHIWOS Collaboration (BCC3) study. First, we will measure drug levels in 300 women and 200 men living with HIV to assess whether levels are increased in older individuals and whether this effect is greater in women than men. Second, we will examine whether elevated antiretroviral levels relate to increased side effects, particularly for women. Third, we will measure drug levels at specific times after taking a new antiretroviral for a smaller group of people. Here, we will compare drug levels between young and old individuals and women and men. Finally, we will assess how drug levels relate to side effects. This will be the first study assessing the effects of aging on antiretroviral drug levels and side effects with a focus on women. These findings will be directly relevant to clinical care by identifying who is most at risk of having drug levels that are too high, and who may benefit from having their drug levels adjusted to minimize side effects, something future clinical studies would explore in more details. Our research will help move toward a more personalized and gender-informed approach to HIV treatment in the future.
