column36: A comparative analysis of regulatory approaches to the assisted living/retirement home sector in Ontario and British Columbia
column37: Background: The retirement home/assisted living (AL) sector supports aging in place for many older Canadians by providing housing; support for meals, housekeeping and laundry; and limited assistance with activities of daily living. This sector is largely unregulated, majority owned and operated by the private sector, and its interlinkages with the health care system are poorly understood. AL sector growth has outpaced long-term care (LTC) growth despite AL residents approaching the frailty and clinical complexity of those in LTC . Regulation is a key policy tool to guide and monitor AL services helping to protect residents and optimize the role of the sector in the continuum of care. Aims: To develop policy options to inform on the role of regulatory approaches in integrating the AL sector into the continuum of care to support aging in the right place by detailing the policy drivers influencing the adoption and reform of different AL regulatory approaches in Ontario (ON) and British Columbia (BC); and evaluating the strengths, gaps, and/or limitations of the Retirement Homes Regulatory Authority (ON) and the Office of the Assisted Living Registrar (BC). Methods: This three-phase, integrated knowledge translation (iKT) study will use snowball sampling to identify key informants (interviews=12) and secondary data sources (n=~50). A multi-disciplinary research team will draft options and host a virtual policy workshop with diverse stakeholders to engage in a deliberative dialogue to refine and contextualize options for AL regulatory reform. Discussion: AL residents have higher rates of emergency department visits, hospital admissions, and alternate level of care days than LTC residents, contributing to adverse health outcomes, poorer continuity of care, and increased costs to the public system. This project will inform decision-making to advance a higher-performing and more integrated health care system with better outcomes and care experiences for AL residents.

column36: Building system capacity for home visits for patients near end of life: A two-part health economics analysis
column37: Most Canadians indicate a preference to stay at home near end of life, but many end up in hospital. Hospitals are the most expensive setting of care, strain the health care system, and are not necessarily the most appropriate level of care to meet patients' goals at the end of life. People who receive palliative home visits from physicians or nurse practitioners (NPs) have better symptom management, are less likely to be hospitalized, and more likely to die in the home, compared to those who do not receive home visits. Despite these known benefits, many Ontarians do not receive adequate physician and NP home visits near the end of life. We need to better understand what level of financial investment is needed to increase physician and NP provision of home visits for people near the end of life. Our work will review current palliative care home visits funding and costs at the provincial level, and identify the costs needed to achieve more home deaths and consequently where gaps in funding exist. We propose to use various health economics approaches to demonstrate to policymakers in Ontario the amount of money that needs to be invested into home visits to increase the proportion of home deaths. First, we will estimate the cost-benefit trade-off of home visits to the healthcare system. Next, we will evaluate the financial impact of increasing the reach of palliative home visits in Ontario. We will then gather provincial and national stakeholders to discuss our findings and refine a policy report. A better understanding of strategies to increase access to palliative home visits and gauging political readiness for these strategies are critical to improving the dying experience of Canadians. Our findings will provide evidence and a business case for the Ontario government outlining how palliative home visits can be scaled up. We are at a critical time where our research has the potential to help change the course of palliative home visits in Ontario.

column36: A Developmental Evaluation of Patient-Centered Measurement in a Learning Health System: Policy Implications for Saskatchewan
column37: There is a growing need to incorporate patient-centred measurements into healthcare systems to deliver on the promise of patient-centred care. The research team, including academics, policymaker knowledge users, collaborators, and patient partners as equal team members will engage in three distinct phases to 1) Generate evidence, 2) Contextualize the evidence, and 3) Re-formulate and disseminate the evidence. This project will improve our understanding of how to successfully collect patient-centred measurements in health networks so learning can occur with each patient encounter and the SHA can advance learning health systems. column36: Optimizing Mental Health for Infants Exposed to Early Adversity: A Comparative Effectiveness and Implementation Study of the "Breaking the Cycle" Program
column37: One in three Canadian children is exposed to adverse childhood experiences (ACEs), including abuse, neglect, and family violence. During early childhood when the foundation for lifelong mental health is established, exposure to ACEs is particularly harmful. Risk factors for ACEs, such as income loss, family stress, and maternal substance use, have increased during the COVID-19 pandemic, pointing to the urgent need for effective prevention and intervention approaches. Breaking the Cycle (BTC) is an award-winning program that serves substance-using mothers and their young children at risk for exposure to ACEs. BTC is the only program in Canada for substance-using mothers that specifically targets the mental health of young children and the mother-child relationship. Our research has shown that BTC leads to positive outcomes for mothers, including decreased substance use, mental health difficulties, and stress. This project aims to understand whether BTC leads to enhanced mental health outcomes for infants and young children, how the program works, and the long-term cost savings associated with BTC. We also want to identify strategies for implementing BTC in other communities. First, we will examine whether infants at BTC, compared to infants in a program that does not target infant mental health, have lower ACEs and better mental health outcomes. We will examine whether changes in parenting behaviour, stress, and mental health of mothers at BTC explain benefits for children. We will also assess the long-term cost savings of intervening early. Second, we will provide training and support to two partner projects to implement the BTC infant mental health approaches. We will evaluate barriers and facilitators to implementation and explore whether BTC can be replicated. This project has the potential to position Canada as an international leader in infant mental health and improve mental health outcomes for children exposed to ACEs.

column36: Leading the Way: Leveraging community strengths to optimally support infant and early mental health (IEMH) through Implementation of IEMH Care Pathways into existing systems that work with young children and their families.

A recent example is the creation of Infant and Early Mental Health Care Pathways that guide children and families to, through, and out of services so they get the right support at the right time, and in the right format for them. But does this framework really improve the impact of IEMH-related community efforts? Is it useful and meaningful to communities? This proposal offers to validate the IEMH Core Component Framework and its assessment tool while Pathways of Care in IEMH Interventions are being implemented in multiple Western and Indigenous communities. Ultimately, we will create a streamlined, effective method that more Canadian communities can follow to develop their own systems of IEMH care pathways, ensuring that Canadian children at risk of poor mental health outcomes are identified, guided and supported as early and effectively as possible.

column36: Evaluating the impact of direct-acting antiviral treatment access policy on chronic hepatitis C prevalence and the undiagnosed proportion
column37: Hepatitis C virus (HCV) is one of the most burdensome infection and one of the most expensive infectious disease to prevent and treat. HCV infection can cause chronic infection of the liver (i.e. chronic hepatitis C (CHC)), that is silent for 20-30 years before about one in five infected people develop liver failure or liver cancer. Treatments that can offer cure are available but are expensive. From 2014 to mid-2018, Canada has already spent $2.8 billion for treatments alone. Understand the impact of on-going treatment uptake in relationship to the disease burden is critical. The Government of Canada has endorsed and committed to the World Health Organization (WHO)'s strategy on viral hepatitis, who has called for a 90% reduction in new HCV cases, a 65% reduction in HCV-related deaths, and treatment of 80% of eligible patients by 2030. To achieve these targets, the government has to understand the geographic and demographic distribution of the disease, in terms of the number of infections (e.g. prevalence), and, the number of patients who remain unaware and untreated of their infections in order to setup effective health policies. We propose to 1) create a working group consisting of policy makers, people living/lived with HCV and HCV experts to provide strategic direction for the project and to discuss the potential future HCV-related policies; 2) measure the number of complications associated with the disease and their corresponding time to diagnosis using data from British Columbia and Ontario that describe almost every interaction with the health system; and 3) use a computer simulation model to estimate the current CHC prevalence and undiagnosed proportion who infected with the disease. Our research will estimate the prevalence of CHC and predict the amount of unaware population, and provide needed evidence to help policy makers to improve HCV care and help Canada achieve the WHO targets.

column36: Building solutions to address drugs shortages in Canada: developing an evidence-based at-risk medicine list
column37: One in 4 Canadians report being impacted by a drug shortage in the last two years. We have little knowledge of the true impact of drug shortages among Canadian men and women. This is especially important in the current context of a rising number of drug shortages and greater public attention on the topic. In 2019 for example, there were more than 12,000 media reports about drug shortages in Canada, illustrating the importance of this issue to Canadians. This has made this issue a top priority for policymakers in Canada as they scramble to develop policies to solve this growing problem. Importantly, this issue was more heightened during the COVID-19 pandemic as global drug supply chains were tested with rapid surges in demand, in many cases leading to a number of shortages. As policies are being developed they are done so in an environment with scarce information. This gap in evidence is leaves patients, healthcare providers and importantly, policymakers, without the information needed to understand the implications of drug shortages. Our national group of researchers will aim to help tackle this problem by using this grant to develop a national at-risk medicines list levergaing work we have been doing over the last few years. column36: Informing policy to optimize the clinical nurse specialist workforce: Advancing the Quadruple Aim and Health Equity
column37: Canada's nursing workforce is in crisis, due to critical staff shortages and challenges surrounding recruitment and retention. Urgent national calls demand action to improve health system quality and capacity as we move forward from COVID-19. British Columbia (BC) is no exception to these challenges, and health service leaders aim to address these issues in innovative and informed ways. BC's Provincial Health Services Authority (PHSA) has recently created an initiative to strengthen advanced practice nursing with the goal of developing a Clinical Nurse Specialist (CNS) strategy across the province's specialized health services. CNSs are advanced practice nurses with graduate training and specialized expertise who lead clinical care, system changes, advancement of nursing, and research and evaluation as members of diverse care teams. As part of its strategic plan, PHSA is creating a novel CNS Program at BC Cancer, which entails the implementation and evaluation of 9 new CNS roles across all 6 regional centres. This has led to a unique policy opportunity to collaboratively support evidence-informed system transformation in real time with a range of partners. Our research team of health system leaders, policy decision-makers, renowned nursing scholars, senior PHSA and BC Cancer leaders, and health services researchers will support health system partners in BC to develop a robust, equitable, and evidence-based roadmap for a provincial CNS strategy. We will: (1) gather and evaluate evidence to support nursing policy development and recommendations that address known challenges facing CNS role implementation and growth in Canada; (2) highlight recommendations to implement, evaluate, and sustain the CNS workforce in BC; and (3) develop policy recommendations and actionable strategies that can guide a provincial strategy for establishing an effective CNS workforce that aligns with provincial health system priorities.

column36: Use of Administrative Health Data to Assess the Feasibility of a Surveillance System for Cardiac Implantable Electronic Device Infections: An Alberta Pilot
column37: Infection is a devastating complication of surgery for cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIED), such as pacemakers. The ability to track surgical infection rates is essential for monitoring quality of patient care. Unfortunately, there is no nation-wide strategy for comprehensive monitoring and reporting of CIED infection. Reasons for this include the personnel time and costs associated with traditional infection surveillance methods. An alternate approach uses administrative data (or data collected through electronic health records) to identify CIED infections. This approach is less expensive and can be automated. However, it is unclear if this approach would be feasible and considered acceptable by all involved stakeholders, including groups that track infection, healthcare providers that implant the CIEDs, and patient groups. The proposed work will allow us to explore the administrative data prospectively and the required methods to complete infection surveillance. We will engage with policymakers, healthcare providers, patient groups and groups that track infection to determine the best way to move forward with this work. This integration of knowledge users and policymakers will allow us to use varied insights and create an evidence-based and beneficial policy. We will also be able to feedback our findings to all stakeholders and adjust plans incorporating their expert opinions. Given the scope of the proposed work we plan to start by using the province of Alberta as a pilot site. If this work is successful we will continue to build collaborations outside of Alberta in order to apply this work nationally.

column36: An international comparative policy analysis of pharmacist-administered long-acting injectable buprenorphine
column37: Opioid addiction is a condition where individuals continue to use opioids even with negative consequences. People who use opioids are at higher risk of infection, overdose, and death. Some of the most effective treatments for opioid addiction are the medications methadone or buprenorphine, which reduce the risk of drug-related deaths. However, there are still many difficulties with these treatments; they often require patients to go daily to a clinic or pharmacy to get their medication or be watched by a pharmacist while they take their medication. This makes it hard to get the right care, can make it more expensive, can lead to stigma, and makes it less likely that people will continue with treatment. A strategy to overcome this is a new type of buprenorphine medication; each dose is injected into the patient and lasts a week or a month. It is available in countries such as Canada and Australia, and in some of their provinces and states, a patient's pharmacist can do the injections instead of a doctor or nurse, which can make it easier to get treatment. Recently, pharmacists have been providing more services through pharmacies (like flu and COVID vaccines), so they are well-placed to provide buprenorphine injections. For provinces that are looking to also use pharmacists to inject buprenorphine, policymakers need to learn how other areas are doing this, whether there were any specific factors that led to these policies, and any barriers or negative effects. By looking at policy documents and talking to policymakers, our research will compare these policies across six provinces and states in Canada and Australia. This will include what training pharmacists need, how the injections will be regulated, and how pharmacists will be paid for this service. Throughout the project, we will work with policymakers and other stakeholders, including people who use opioids, to make sure the research is focused on improving the experiences and health of people who use opioids.

column36: Implementing best practices in long-term care settings: Strategies to guide health services and policies
column37: Long-term care (LTC) homes saw an unprecedented number of COVID-19 infections and deaths across Canadian provinces and territories. Long-standing deficiencies in the LTC sector contributed to this crisis. Translating evidence-based practices into clinical and policy contexts is a challenge. Policymakers in LTC require information adapted to their context to improve patient experience, population health, the well-being of the care team, healthcare costs and equity. To ensure that policies are based on the latest scientific evidence, research findings must be made available, accessible, and useful to policymakers to help inform decision-making. This project aims to develop a policy brief that offers viable policy options to support decision-making, preparation and implementation of evidence-based practices in LTC. Based on the results of a previous pan-Canadian study, deliberative process and interviews with policymakers, managers, health care professionals involved in LTC, residents or their representatives, a draft a policy brief will be developed. Participants will meet in a virtual policy workshop to present and discuss new research evidence and draft policy options. Finally, a final version of the report will be created based on the comments received during the virtual workshop. This process will allow for a clear and concise language; academic and technical jargon should be drilled down into plain and non-academic language. The policy brief will consider important dimensions such as feasibility, costs, and other pros and cons for a better decision process. A policy brief for the implementation of innovations in LTC, which can support decision-making and give concrete strategies to decision-makers, is necessary to improve patient experience, population health, care team well-being, and healthcare costs.

column36: Addressing cost-related nonadherence of prescription medications through evidence-informed cost-sharing policies in public drug plans to advance health equity in Canada
column37: Chronic diseases are a leading cause of death, but they can managed by medications and healthy behaviours. Despite these treatments, many Canadians suffer from chronic diseases when they can't afford their essential medications. This can add costs to the healthcare system, as these individuals can end up needing specialized healthcare in the hospital system. While many aspects of healthcare are covered for Canadians, medications prescribed outside of a hospital are not universally covered by provincial or territorial governments, resulting in variations across the country. A patchwork of employment benefits, private insurance, and public programs provides medication coverage for most Canadians, but many fall through the gaps when these benefits don't cover their costs. Our plan to address these shortfalls is to consider how patients are required to participate in cost-sharing (paying copayments, premiums or deductibles), and how these might affect their ability to take medications. We have come together with healthcare policy makers from across Canada to discuss how we can change policy to improve access to prescription medications for all. Our plan is to review existing medication plans across Canada and other similar countries, collect evidence from clinical trials examining providing medication coverage - including our team's own recent trial in Alberta. Once we develop policy options, we will host a virtual summit with everyone on our policy maker team across the country to refine and improve these options before we make our final recommendation to provincial and territorial governments. With the federal government's renewed commitment to national Pharmacare, along with new evidence from recent clinical trials, it is an ideal time to investigate how to best provide coverage to ensure all Canadians can afford essential, life-saving medications. A reworked policy will improve the long-term health of Canadians while saving healthcare funds for the future.

column36: Strengthening the Delivery of Integrated Care in Specialized Mental Health Settings for Adults Experiencing Serious Mental Illness
column37: Individuals with severe mental illness (SMI), such as psychosis and bipolar disorder, are disproportionately affected by comorbid chronic health conditions, including cancer, cardiovascular disease and diabetes, and die 10-20 years younger than the general population. While primary care services remain the main point of access for Canadians, it is very difficult for individuals with SMI to engage in these services due to access barriers, pervasive stigma, and the unique needs in this population. Recognizing that specialized mental health services are the 'de-facto' health home for individuals with SMI, leading health systems are integrating physical health monitoring within specialty mental health services through policy development and organizational standards. This study, guided by a national Patient and Family Advisory Council (PFAC), aims to provide feasible, acceptable, safe, effective, and patient centered policy options to support the delivery of integrated physical and mental health care in mental health settings in Canada and decrease health disparities for this population. A 3-phase knowledge mobilization approach will be used. The first phase will include a comparative policy analysis of Canadian and international policies and organizational approaches supporting the delivery of physical health care to this population. At the same time, qualitative interviews will be conducted with patients, clinicians, and other stakeholders, to understand their needs, perspectives and experiences towards integrating physical health care in mental health settings for individuals with SMI. In Phase 2, policy options will be discussed with a diverse group of stakeholders in a virtual policy workshop, to refine the policy options that would work in Canadian settings and with diverse populations with SMI. Lastly, in phase 3, top policy recommendations will be finalized and disseminated to internal and external stakeholders, under the guidance of the PFAC.

column36: Cross-Sectoral Collaboration to Improve Outcomes for Children/Youth in Vulnerable Contexts
column37: Despite efforts of Canadian governments to address problems created by service fragmentation, many children and youth with complex needs continue to fall through the cracks in the siloed systems of care. Children with mental health issues are significantly affected by service fragmentation as they are typically dependent on a variety of support service systems. These children experience the poorest outcomes in academic performance and graduation rates, dependence on social assistance, and justice system involvement. Cross-sectoral collaboration has been advocated as a tool to overcome existing silos through providing coordinated support services. TRiP (The Regina intersectoral Partnership) is a collaboration across 6 human service organizations (Saskatchewan Health Authority, Regina Public School Division, Regina Catholic School Division, Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Social Services, and Regina Police Service) in Regina delivering coordinated support services to children and youth in vulnerable contexts. TRiP has received approximately 1000 referrals since inception in 2010 of which 94% have improved school attendance. Using TRiP as a case study, this research aims to investigate the formation and patterns of collaboration, factors influencing collaboration and service coordination across sectors, and processes and structures involved in building and maintaining a strong cross-sectoral collaboration. We will also examine TRiP's governance, organization, delivery of coordinated services across sectors, funding structure, and accountability mechanisms. Findings will have policy implications for improving coordinated service delivery across health and other human service organizations and ultimately improved health outcomes among children and youth. Findings can guide the implementation of context-driven strategies to sustain and maximize the impact of collaborative efforts across sectors.

column36: Exploring Foundational Public Health Programs and Policies for SOGIE (Sexual Orientation, Gender Identity and Expression) Diverse People in Ontario
column37: SOGIE (sexual orientation, gender identity and expression) diverse groups are people with similarities in experiences of shared stigma and discrimination with a higher frequency of adverse health outcomes compared to heterosexual and/or cisgender people. Ontario's 34 public health units offer health promotion and disease prevention programming related to healthy "lifestyles", communicable disease control including education in HIV/STBBIs, immunization, healthy growth and development, and selected screening services, among others. Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care guidelines specify that information related to sexual orientation and gender identity should be collected in a timely manner and programming should consider these. The Chief Public Health Officer of Canada's 2021 Report on the State of Public Health in Canada emphasizes the need for upstream action and mobilizing community involvement; the need for qualitative and mixed-methods research approaches; the need for disaggregated and equity-oriented data (including by sexual orientation and gender identity). This project will: 1) explore public health policies, documents, standards, and data related to SOGIE diversity; 2) collect perspectives from SOGIE diverse communities about experiences with public health services; 3) identify experiences of public health representatives about connecting with and including SOGIE communities in their work; and 4) make recommendations about public health practice inclusion of SOGIE diverse communities in Ontario. Knowledge mobilization strategies throughout the project will ensure the variety of affected stakeholders (e.g., SOGIE communities, public health practitioners, policymakers, researchers) culminates in key implications and recommendations on integrating SOGIE diversity into public health policy and practice.

column36: Informing policy to support regional health human resources planning for integrated care models
column37: The aim of this project is to inform policy to support regional health human resource (HHR) planning for integrated care strategies. A draft policy brief will be created. Phase 2 will use deliberative dialogues to engage policy makers and knowledge users. Phase 3 will use member checking methods to refine and inform the final set of policy recommendations. Impact: The knowledge generated and resultant policy recommendations will offer a template for how other integrated care models can support regional HHR planning to meet local population needs.

column36: Building virtual bridges to coordinate emergency and primary care

In this study, we will evaluate the role of virtual care in providing consultations to patients, so they receive personalized and timely advice to guide them to either seek care in emergency departments if appropriate or manage at home with later follow-up with their family doctors. In this sense, virtual emergency care represents a commonly accessible bridge between emergency and primary care for all patients in their communities. Our team follows a learning health system approach, continuously generating new research findings and applying them to improve virtual care. column36: Long-Term Care Policies to Integrate National Standards: The LTC-PINs Project
column37: Long-term care homes (LTCHs) have been an underfunded sector in the Canadian healthcare system for decades. The COVID-19 pandemic further exacerbated these challenges, with added pressures of staffing shortages and negative stigma related to the homes, the staff and their leadership. There is a need to implement national standards for LTCHs to ensure the delivery of quality care. As a response to this need, the Health Standards Organization (HSO) established the Long-Term Care Technical Committee in 2020. Led by Dr. Samir Sinha, 32 Technical Committee members with expertise in long-term care (residents, family members, health care providers, researchers, etc.) came together to develop a National Long-Term Care Services Standard. Although this is a great step to ensure the delivery of safe and high-quality long-term care services, a better understanding of how these standards will be taken up in the LTCHs is needed. The goal of the LTC-PINs Project is to understand the experiences and perspective of LTCH administrative staff and those directly involved in policy development and implementation as they implement the National Long-Term Care Services Standard. Specifically, we want to know what they need to develop these required policies from a development, implementation and evaluative perspective in order to successfully implement the National Long-Term Care Services Standard. From this, our team will draft a policy and knowledge dissemination plan. We will then invite key stakeholders to a round-table research and policy workshop to discuss the draft policy. Recommendations will be formulated and the final policy will be available for LTCH use. The LTC-PINs Project is the first step along a much longer journey to restore trust and build a better future for LTCHs in Canada.

column36: Beyond public payment, private delivery: Understanding how private financing and for-profit delivery operate within Canadian health care
column37: The expansion of private-pay and for-profit health care delivery in Canada is a significant concern threatening the principles of equitable access on which Medicare is founded. There have also been changes in corporate influences in health care, driving growth in for-profit delivery. For example, increasing numbers of investor-owned walk-in clinic networks and virtual care services, some of which involve direct billing to patients. Some private expenditures and private delivery cases are well understood and accounted for while others are evolving and more hidden, with the pandemic potentially hastening these changes. Additionally, the breadth and depth of changes differ across provinces and territories due to variability in existing policies governing private payment and delivery. Our pan-Canadian research project will collect information about current private financing and private delivery in Canada and use that to develop a theoretical framework to categorize and understand privatization as it is happening now. The project includes a national environmental scan to document core policies that underpin the public-private interfaces, highlighting differences across provinces (Phase 1); a virtual policy workshop with stakeholders to refine the framework and prioritize health system sectors and/or services in need of in-depth research. (Phase 2); and the development of policy briefs that we will disseminate to workshop participants and other policymaker organizations across Canada. This project will lay the groundwork for future studies that investigate the impact of the uncontrolled expansion of private-pay and for-profit health care delivery in specific health system sectors in Canada.

column36: Paramedics Providing Palliative Care at Home: Using mixed methods to understand the experiences of care and bereavement from the perspective of patients and families in a national spread collaborative
column37: In 2015, the Paramedics Providing Palliative Care at Home Program was started in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island to help people with life-limiting diseases get better palliative care and support when they are nearing the end of life. The Program means paramedics can give care at home, without always taking people to the emergency department and is expanding across Canada. In this study, we want to connect with patients, families and caregivers in several provinces to understand their experiences and follow their journey with their disease and getting help when they need it. This could include times they call 9-1-1 for paramedics, going to the emergency/hospital, death, and grieving. We plan to add questions about paramedic care to palliative care surveys that are already sent out to patients and caregivers. We also plan to do telephone interviews once a month with a few patients/families who are willing and able, to better understand their experiences as their disease progresses. In the first interview, we will learn about the person's life and surroundings, to understand what social and health supports they have. In monthly calls after that we will talk about the patient and families experience with paramedic and other palliative care. The team will bring all of that together to look for ways to change or add to what help is available. We will share what we learn with the other government and health programs which may be able to make changes to what supports are there when people want to stay home as they near the end of life.

column36: An evidence-based provincial framework for a psychosocial oncology program in Nova Scotia.
column37: Having cancer is very stressful for patients and their families. It affects all aspects of people's lives and often for an extended period. Psychosocial oncology services support and assist patients and families in dealing with the stress of cancer by providing emotional, social, spiritual and practical help. A lot of different professions can provide help based on the patient's specific need: social workers, psychologists, cancer patient navigators, spiritual care providers, wellness coaches, dieticians etc. Nova Scotians are now able to access more cancer care services closer to home because the Cancer Care Program received money to hire more healthcare workers for eight community-based oncology centres. Psychosocial oncology services are among the services that will be provided in those community oncology centres. Because psychosocial oncology services were previously mostly available in Halifax, the Cancer Care Program wants to develop a plan and structure how to integrate and organize the way that psychosocial oncology services are being provided across the province to make sure that every patient and their family who needs support in dealing with cancer has access to the same kinds of supports and services. We will look at how other provinces and countries are doing this and speak to a few people in cancer centres, who are doing it well. We will also ask people who work for the Cancer Program in Nova Scotia how they think psychosocial oncology should be organized across the province. We will collect all that information and then get a group of people who are involved with caring for people with cancer, such as cancer doctors, psychologists, social workers etc. to look at it and based on this evidence they will make suggestions of how to best organize psychosocial oncology so that every person who is diagnosed with cancer in Nova Scotia receives the very best help and support when they need it to assist them with the stress of having cancer.

column36: 'Building Back Better Together': A Multi-stakeholder Approach to Address the Healthcare Workforce Crisis and Promote Healthcare Transformation
column37: THE ISSUE: The Canadian healthcare workforce is in crisis, reeling from a decades-long healthcare worker (HCW) shortage, poor job satisfaction, high levels of stress and burnout, as well as high rates of attrition or intention to leave the profession. Circumstances have become measurably worse since Covid-19, with conditions in hospitals being particularly dire. This has, and will continue to have, a direct and dramatic impact on the delivery of the Quadruple Aim and health equity. There is evidence to support healthcare worker, patient, and cost benefits associated with engaging end-users (specifically, HCWs and patients) in hospital governance, however, there is a lack of consensus and guidance on how to meaningfully, equitably, and sustainably engage multiple stakeholders in practice. OUR IDEA: This study aims to develop multi-stakeholder informed guidance and policy options for the meaningful, equitable, and sustainable engagement of end-users in hospital governance. OUR APPROACH: The proposed study is guided by an Integrated Knowledge Translation approach, and will employ mixed methods across three phases of study, including Evidence generation (scoping review, institutional document analysis, and Concept Mapping); Knowledge mobilization and contextualization of the evidence (virtual Policy Workshop with key stakeholders and content experts); and Iterative re-formulation and dissemination of evidence and policy options through the development of a Policy Brief. Each phase will be informed by and build upon evidence generated in the preceding phase(s). IMPACT: The proposed research will provide an alternative, more diverse and inclusive process for hospital governance, engaging end-users themselves in fostering an improved work environment and healthier workforce. This research supports the kind of transformational change (in process and outcome) needed to achieve the goals of the Quadruple Aim and support improved health equity, for HCWs and patients alike.

column36: The Impact of Post COVID-19 Condition on Nursing Labour Supply
column37: Our analysis uses a combination of real-world data and modelling to determine: (1) the current state of nursing supply, (2) how it will change due to Post COVID-19 Condition (PCC) and (3) policy options for addressing those impacts. Nurses included in this analysis are Registered Nurses, Licensed Practical Nurses, Nursing Attendants, Nurse Practitioners and Registered Psychiatric Nurses. We will use Alberta as the setting of our research due to the availability of data and to compliment ongoing research estimating the demand for healthcare labour in Alberta due to PCC and the effect of COVID-19 vaccines on this demand. Our analysis is comprised of three phases. First, we will estimate the current nursing supply in Alberta. Second, we will determine how nursing supply may change in the future due to the ongoing impact of PCC by building upon an existing model that captures the impact of PCC on occupational time lost due to ongoing symptoms. Third, we will test several policy alternatives to evaluate options for limiting the impact of PCC on nursing supply in Alberta. We will expand the analysis to identify inequity in current supply and changes to supply based on PCC across urban and rural areas. Findings from this analysis will provide a basis for evaluating these questions across Canada, as well as information on relevant policy alternatives for all provinces facing nursing labour supply issues.

column36: Establishing Optimal Medical Care Provider Commitment in Canadian Long-Term Care Homes
column37: In Canada, the delivery of medical care services in long-term care (LTC) homes varies. Existing research shows that higher quality care results when fewer dedicated providers (physicians or nurse practitioners) are involved, and when they are on-site more frequently. However, most of this evidence comes from the United States and Europe, with no Canadian standard for provider commitment in the LTC setting. Given the differences in provider commitment and the absence of a unified measure, we propose a rapid and three-phase policy development program to establish a quality standard for medical care provider commitment in Canada's 2,098 LTC homes. Phase 1 will involve a comparative policy analysis of Canadian and international models of LTC medical care provider commitment. We will assess the implementation feasibility of different provider commitment models, their budgetary impact, and key actors likely to be impacted. Phase 1 will conclude with a policy brief that summarizes the issue and analyzes the existing evidence. In Phase 2, the research team will host a virtual policy workshop to present the evidence on models of LTC medical care provider commitment and review the draft policy brief. Policy workshop participants will work with the study research team to develop a questionnaire to be used in a consensus study on LTC provider commitment. The study will recruit experts in LTC practice models and frontline LTC providers and then work to generate consensus on optimal provider commitment in Canadian LTC homes. Phase 3 will share and apply the evidence and results of the consensus study. A draft final report on optimal provider commitment in Canadian LTC homes will be shared with key stakeholders and knowledge users for feedback and response. A finalized policy report will be shared publicly through CIHR, directly with stakeholder groups and knowledge users, published in a peer-reviewed journal, and presented at scientific meetings.

column36: Preventing the next fracture: Spreading Fracture Liaison Service across British Columbia
column37: Fragility fractures occur spontaneously or with minimal trauma and are a frequent consequence of osteoporosis. One fragility fracture often leads to a cycle of recurrent fractures, disability, and even death. Despite the availability of effective treatments that reduce future fracture risk by up to 50%, less than 20% of patients suffering fragility fractures receive such treatments in their post-fracture care. This is the osteoporosis care gap. The evidenced-based Fracture Liaison Services (FLS) model has been adopted world-wide as the most effective model for preventing repeat fragility fractures in a cost-effective manner. FLS involves a dedicated coordinator who "captures" the patient at the point of orthopedic care for the fracture and integrates repeat fracture prevention into the overall fracture experience. FLS coordinators link patients with community family physicians to ensure follow-through of recommended interventions to prevent another fracture. In British Columbia (BC), there are currently only 3 FLS programs operating at 3 hospitals. This research project is an exciting opportunity for health care organizations and the BC Ministry of Health to partner to develop policy options and recommendations to spread the FLS model across the province. We will use research methods and engage a diverse range of stakeholders in this process. Our project goal is to change the way that we deliver services to people after a fragility fracture by integrating FLS into routine orthopedic care across British Columbia (BC) so that all patients can benefit.

column36: A survey of Canadian critical care staffing to inform current policy and future need
column37: Intensive care units (ICUs) are where the sickest patients in the hospital receive their care. The physical beds and equipment are important to allow for safe care. However, having the right staff (e.g. doctors and nurses, pharmacists, physical therapists) is just as important to ensure patients do well in the ICU. We know that having doctors and nurses specifically trained in critical care is best, but we know very little beyond that. Right now we don't know how many doctors, nurses, and other members of the care team are routinely taking care of patients in ICUs, or how that might have changed from before COVID-19. We don't know how many patients each doctor or nurse is usually caring for during the day, and how many other team members, such as physical therapists and pharmacists are employed in each ICU. The goal of this grant is to identify exactly what is known already, and then to survey each ICU across Canada to understand the current staffing of their ICUs. This basic information is essential to then create a document that can provide guidance to all the hospitals and ICUs across the country regarding staffing for ICUs.

column36: Exposed: Examining the Generational Impact of Maternal Substance and Alcohol-Use on Family Health and Social Outcomes
column37: The proposed project will analyze the presence of risk and protective factors that may contribute to an exposed pregnancy such as the mortality and morbidity rates of birthing people and their families, compared by exposed or non-exposed births; and the comparison of key social constructs such as family history and separation, education, income, and employment. This will be facilitated through a data linkage of data collected from participants in the Parent Child Assistance Program (PCAP) to government administrative data. PCAP was designed to help mitigate the cycle of generational substance use, while supporting mothers through their addiction recovery journey, centered on the principles of harm reduction. This linkage will facilitate a population-level analysis of the impact of substance and alcohol use in birthing people on the health and social outcomes of them and their families. We propose a 10-20-year analysis of the precursors and outcomes of two primary groups for this analysis: birthing people with non-exposed pregnancies, and birthing people with exposed pregnancies, including a subset of PCAP clients. When considering generational impacts, it is beneficial to include at least three generations, to understand if any risk or protective factors can be identified within the data when it comes to the birthing people's parents/guardians. This will include the definition of several constructs that can be built from existing administrative data and will encompass information from multiple timepoints through the primary subject group's (the birthing person's) life. We will seek to identify and understand how these constructs may have contributed to the birthing person's risk for having an exposed birth and formulate policy recommendations based on mitigating gaps and barriers in the system and identifying opportunities with a trauma-informed approach.

column36: Honouring our Role as the Watchmon: Transforming Health Systems by Developing Community-Driven Data Strategies with First Nations in British Columbia
column37: The Chief Medical Officer, as migamuwa, or the Watchmon, holds an important role in observing, monitoring and gathering information and data from various sources to capture and share the story of health and wellness of First Nations, province-wide. Through their established governance structure, the First Nations Health Authority (FNHA) has been mandated to facilitate high-quality data collection, analysis, and reporting for, by, and with First Nations in British Columbia (BC). Past engagements with First Nations offered context on how health information can be effectively governed, managed, and utilized by transforming existing and inherited health systems. First Nations' communities and organizations clearly expressed the need to have timely access to data to be able to make informed decisions regarding health and wellness. Current public health emergencies have enhanced the urgency to create technical changes that can accommodate the volume of data access work required to support community based responses. To align with traditional principles of knowledge sharing, qualitative data collection methods with an appreciative stance allow space that is grounded in community stories. Subsequent to an overview of work done to date, all regions will: a) confirm whether the findings from previous engagements are still relevant; b) discuss technical components required to operationalize data access requests; and c) discuss mechanisms that will uphold the voice of BC First Nations. The data will inform current systems through a data management policy, regional report cards to measure the health status of First Nations within BC regions, an online platform for access requests, and a toolkit for communities and researchers to ensure wise practices that indicate Ownership, Control, Access, and Possession (OCAP(R)) of First Nations data. As a result, the FNHA will have feedback to develop systems for data usage that are in alignment with the direction of First Nations in BC.

column36: Addressing Canadian Healthcare Needs: Systematic Integration of Practitioners
column37: The Canadian healthcare system is in crisis because of healthcare worker and physician shortages. Because of these shortages, patients are receiving care that is less than optimal. Physicians are tired, feel overworked, and are experiencing burnout at high rates across Canada. This is causing them to leave practice, or necessarily reducing their workloads. There is increasing demand for physicians and healthcare in Canada and so we depend on people who may have trained to become doctors in countries other than Canada. These doctors who have trained outside of Canada often limit their care of patients within hospitals (and are called 'hospitalists'). In fact, we have thousands of who have trained elsewhere living in Canada who can't fully practice in Canada because there are many different and often complex steps to help confirm their training, competence and licensing requirements. Our project will bring together the necessary organizations together to develop a policy and standards to create processes for hospitalist physicians to be efficiently and appropriately assessed and integrated so that they can practice safely in Canada. Our work will increase the physician workforce and create a process that can be used by all other medical disciplines, beyond hospitalist physicians, to meet the patient care needs in Canada and ensure high quality care is delivered.

column36: U-Prep: Understanding scope of Practice expansion in pharmacy
column37: Pharmacists, Canada's most accessible health care professional, are now able to provide more health care services than ever before. This has been made possible with legislative changes in many provinces designed to improve access to health care and relieve stress on the healthcare system exacerbated by doctor and nurse shortages. Though services vary across the country, pharmacists can now provide routine immunizations; prescribe, or renew medications prescribed by others; and prescribe new drugs for minor conditions. However, like other health professionals, recent data shows that the pharmacist workforce is over-stretched and at risk of burnout, limiting their capacity to provide the new services that patients need. Our team of researchers seeks to understand how pharmacists perceive their capacity to provide these new services, what challenges they face, and what solutions would allow uptake of new service models in community pharmacies. We will conduct interviews with pharmacists and patients across three provinces with varied scopes of pharmacy practice. Synthesizing information gained from these interviews, as well as evidence and policy decisions from other jurisdictions, we will host a summit for pharmacy stakeholders, patients, and policymakers to discuss and explore policy solutions aimed to support pharmacists to embrace the new roles afforded by recent legislation. This research will provide the critical data needed about the nature of the challenges pharmacists face when implementing new services, and will fuel discussion amongst key stakeholders and knowledge users to generate policy options and solutions for supporting pharmacists to embrace opportunities afforded by legislative changes.

column36: CHILD: Canadian Health Indicators for chiLdren with Disabilities
column37: Quality of life, also known as well-being refers to how people feel about their physical health, relationships, and within their environments. Canada has been working to strengthen policies that support the well-being of all Canadians, however, children with disabilities are still among the Canadians who do not enjoy the same standards of well-being as others. Collecting information on well-being is important to ensure that policies are created to respond to the needs of children with disabilities and their families. In this project, we are proposing to create the CHILD: Canadian Health Indicators for chiLdren with Disabilities: a measure of the quality of life and well-being of children with disabilities in Canada. We want to lay the foundation to be able to do a much better job at understanding the wellbeing of Canadian children with disabilities. To do so, we will identify all the approaches that countries around the world are using to understand the well-being of children with disabilities and see how we can apply those here in Canada. Then, we will look at all the information Canada is already collecting about the condition of Canadians, through the records of Statistics Canada. We will then ask Canadian experts: families, youth, and policymakers how we can make these relevant for Canadian children with disabilities. Finally, we will disseminate the results to Canadian children with disabilities of varying abilities, genders and locations to see what they think about what we found and whether anything needs to be added or removed from the data collection processes to make sure they adequately represent their experiences. We hope this framework will inform current policy strategies being developed in Canada so we can work together to work together for the wellbeing of Canadian children with disabilities, using data.

column36: Defining and Developing Black Health National Learning Competencies in Medical and Public Health Education: A Mixed Methods Study
column37: In Canada, anti-Black racism is a daily reality that co-occurs and affects all other health conditions that Black people experience. Black communities face disproportionate health outcomes, unfavourable social circumstances, and underrepresentation in medical and public health professions. To improve population health, it is important to look at policies and practices in anti-Black racist training and support of medical doctors, health care and public health professionals. Doctors and public health professionals play an important role in the Canadian health care delivery and public health systems whether through direct patient care or population health interventions. Through education and training, medical doctors and public health professionals learn how to approach, engage, support, treat, and improve the health of patients and communities. During this training, medical and public health trainees gain skills that help them respond to patient and population needs. However, they are not taught about the unique history and impacts of anti-Black racism on Black people in Canada. The lack of this training contributes to the poor health care experiences and outcomes of Black Canadians. This proposed policy research will suggest a set of Black Health learning objectives for medical and public health education across Canada. We questions on how can education on anti-Black racism be integrated into medical and public health training and what can help increase uptake of anti-Black teaching in both fields? This will be done in 3 phases. First, documents including curricula, syllabi, and examination objectives will be reviewed. From this, a set of Black health learning objectives will be proposed. Second, we will interview policymakers, decision makers, educators, students, doctors, public health professionals, and patients to gain a wide range of perspectives to inform the policy options. Lastly, final policy recommendations will be made based on participant feedback.

column36: System transformation to achieve equitable access to effective contraception
column37: Inadequate and inequitable access to contraception has limited the ability for populations in Canada to optimally time their pregnancies. For priority populations (rural and remote, adolescent, gender diverse, racialized), inadequate access to the most effective contraception is a key barrier to preventing unplanned pregnancy. The British Columbia (BC) health system is undergoing substantial contraception policy change that holds the potential to prove contraception access by 1) providing a universal prescription contraception subsidy, and 2) allowing direct pharmacist contraception provision. RESEARCH APPROACH: This study will use BC's population data to generate urgently needed evidence for health policymakers, system decision-makers, and patient advocates. We will: 1. Describe the geographic distribution and characteristics of the contraception workforce and trends over time. 2. Identify the frequency and characteristics of "contraception deserts", geographic regions lacking adequate access to long-acting reversible contraception services. 3. Describe long-acting reversible contraception use, including characteristics of populations with lowest and highest uptake and trends over time. POTENTIAL IMPACT: This analysis is urgently needed by knowledge user decision-makers in the BC health system and patient advocacy organizations. This study will provide evidence to support policy implementation, development, and revision to improve contraception access for regions and population groups with greatest need and inform professional development for workforce planning. This lays the foundation for a learning health system approach to further policy evaluation and adaptation to ensure equitable access to the most effective contraception.

column36: Examining the Physician Workforce in Long-term Care Homes
column37: Despite the long-term care (LTC) sector (i.e., nursing homes) being thought of as one of the most-regulated and inspected healthcare sectors, care delivered by LTC doctors is seldom monitored. The COVID-19 pandemic has hit the LTC sector hard. Subsequent efforts in Ontario to address the observed deficiencies in care have focused on increased inspections and regulating the level of care provided by nursing staff, by personal support workers, and other allied workers. LTC doctors, however, have largely been forgotten, despite their important role in the care team. We will use rich, population-level "Big data" on all doctors practicing across LTC homes in Ontario, Canada. This evidence will be used inform policy options that may be used to regulate how the LTC physician workforce is organized and supported to optimize the LTC sector. Specifically, our 3 objectives are to: 1)Describe the LTC doctor workforce in Ontario. We will focus on factors that impact health human resources planning including: age, sex, specialty, years in practice, percentage of practice in LTC, and the health of doctors. 2)Understand the practice patterns of LTC doctors. At the home level: how many physicians are involved at any given time; what happens when a physician is away (e.g., on vacation, on leave, retires); how they provide 'call' coverage as evidenced by afterhours billings and billings on the weekend. 3)Evaluate outcomes: how characteristics of the LTC physician workforce (objective 1) and practice patterns (objective 2) are related to patient outcomes. Namely: emergency room visits, hospital admissions, deaths in hospitals, percentage of residents receiving palliative care prior to death.

column36: Integration of brain and spinal cord injury care for older Ontarians: current state and action strategies
column37: We know little about how well care for brain and spinal injuries is provided in Ontario. This is especially true for older people. Over 60% of all brain and spinal injuries occur in older adults, and most of these injuries occur from falls. Brain and spinal cord injuries at older ages can lead to devastating consequences that are hard to recover from and may cause big changes in a person's life. These consequences can be even worse if the person has low income, does not have a place to live, is part of a marginalized group, or lives far from big cities. To better understand this issue, we will analyze Ontario healthcare data and create a report to show areas where the healthcare system is doing well and areas where it can be improved. We will show these results to key interest groups such as people with lived experience, their community associations, clinicians, healthcare administrators, researchers, funders and government representatives. We will ask what the top three challenges are and how we can solve them. These top three challenges and solutions will be converted into a policy brief, a document policymakers use to inform decision-making. We will collaborate with our key interest groups to share the policy brief widely, including Ontario Health, community associations responsible for advocating for better healthcare systems, people with lived experience, and healthcare providers and administrators. We will share the policy brief via newsletters, upcoming events, and social media accounts. We hope this policy brief will improve the quality of brain and spinal cord injury care for all older Ontarians.

column36: Sustainable financing to transform Canada's public health systems
column37: Public health is central to preserving population health and supporting emergency responses. Sustained, equitable and effective financing is a critical building block to a strong public health system. Yet, Canada's public health systems face challenges with ensuring adequate and sustained financing for public health, and there are significant variations across the country, and internationally, in both the size of public health budgets and trends over time. The aim of this research is to learn more about the best options for improving Canada's public health financing models, considering sustainability, effectiveness and equity. To accomplish this, we will compare and contrast how decisions are made across Canada and Australia, about setting public health budgets, including the role of key stakeholders such as public health leaders, government decision makers and communities who partner with public health and receive programs. We focus our comparative analysis on four Canadian provinces (British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec, and Nova Scotia) and two Australian states (New South Wales and Queensland). These provinces and states have historically spent different amounts on public health so we anticipate that the comparison will have interesting lessons for policymakers. Australia is a good country for comparison because the public health systems are very similar but unlike Canada, Australia has increased or sustained spending on public health. We will interview people working in Ministries of Health, Health Authorities, Public Health teams and local government to better understand these financing processes. We will consult stakeholders through workshops to analyze and share what we have learned from the research and develop policy options for improving the sustainability, equity and effectiveness of public health financing in Canada. Project findings can enable policymakers to strengthen public health systems and better prepare for future emergencies.

column36: Policy Options for a Pan-Canadian Mental Health and Substance Use Health Workforce Strategy
column37: BACKGROUND: The people who provide mental health and substance use health (MHSUH) services play a critical role in supporting Canadians. Even with a massive shift to virtual services during the pandemic, access to these necessary MHSUH services has fallen further behind what people in Canada need. Other countries have created MHSUH workforce strategies to assist in workforce planning efforts, but in Canada, the MHSUH workforce has long been sidelined in health workforce planning and policy. There is a critical need for policy research to support the development of a pan-Canadian MHSUH workforce strategy. APPROACH: We will work in collaboration with many MHSUH organizations throughout all three phases of our research project. In Phase 1, we will summarize evidence that has already been published about MHSUH workforce planning and create a policy map to understand what policies are currently working to support the MHSUH workforce in Canada and internationally. In Phase 2, we will conduct a virtual policy dialogue with many participants that represent both service providers and service users to discuss what we found in Phase 1 and to get their insight and advice. In Phase 3, we will work with stakeholders to develop a policy report and toolkit describing the leading practices, policy agenda, and key policy options to create a pan-Canadian MHSUH workforce strategy. OUTCOMES: This study will provide better information about policy options and stakeholder-informed priorities to help create a pan-Canadian MHSUH workforce strategy. This strategy will support the development of a high-quality, sustainable, diverse, and culturally competent MHSUH workforce that will have the capacity to provide equitable access to MHSUH services for everyone in Canada.

column36: Impact of Post-COVID-19 Condition on the Canadian healthcare workforce: An agent-based modeling approach informed by living evidence syntheses to project long-term impacts on worker recovery and retention
column37: Long COVID also known as Post-COVID-19 Condition (PCC) affects people's quality of life, social and family life, and multiple aspects of employment. Previous research has shown people with PCC are less productive on the job than before illness, more likely to miss work, and more likely to leave their employer or profession. PCC can significantly impact healthcare workers because they are more likely to be infected with the SARS-CoV-2 virus than the general population. Even more, up to one-half of individuals infected with the virus might develop PCC symptoms such as tiredness or fatigue that interferes with daily life, difficulty breathing or shortness of breath, and difficulty thinking or concentrating. Also, the pandemic has increased staff shortages, disrupted healthcare services (for example, delayed surgeries), and increased stress and burnout among healthcare workers. PCC-related issues and their impact on healthcare workers concern provincial and federal governments because they can lead to long-term strain on the healthcare workforce. We propose research evaluating the long-term health effects of SARS-CoV-2 infection and how those effects might burden the Canadian healthcare workforce. The first component of this research will collect evidence related to PCC outcomes in the working-age population (16 years and older). Next, we will use this information to develop a model that estimates the impact of PCC on the healthcare workforce one year, two years, and five years from now. The impact estimation will include healthcare worker recruitment and retention, labor shortages, and productivity losses. The information from our research will help policymakers better understand and quantify the burdens of PCC on the Canadian healthcare workforce and prioritize related policies to support human resource planning and development.

column36: A novel approach to trauma-informed care: Co-designing policies to support healthcare provider mental health
column37: During the COVID-19 pandemic, healthcare providers (HCPs) have faced challenging and sometimes traumatic situations that have taken a toll on their mental health. Since February 2021, our team has been conducting research on Canadian HCPs and found they are suffering from high rates of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, and anxiety. We have also learned that during the pandemic, many HCPs suffered mental distress as a result of organizational policies and unintended consequences of leadership decisions. These situations not only left many HCPs feeling their organization did not value or care about them, but also were primary contributors to decisions to leave their job. Prior research has found that implementing trauma-informed care (TIC) principles, such as facilitating choice whenever possible and establishing/maintaining trust by providing transparency via engaging HCP representation in the decision-making process in healthcare organizations, has a positive impact on the mental health of the healthcare providers who work there. This study aims to develop a trauma-informed policy for leaders who work in Canadian healthcare organizations based on an innovative approach to health policy analysis and informed by the Sanctuary Model of Trauma-Informed Organizational Change. Frontline healthcare providers, leaders in middle management and senior management positions from both an acute care hospital and a long-term care facility will be asked to be part of this study. All participants will take part in an interview and/or focus group and complete a survey about their beliefs on trauma-informed care. The results of this study will inform policies that guide leaders to better support the mental health of our Canadian healthcare providers. Efforts to better support and retain our healthcare workforce will ultimately benefit patients and the greater public who depend on their service and well-resourced health care system.

column36: Primary Care-Led Governance Models: A Comparative Policy Analysis of three Canadian Jurisdictions
column37: Many Canadians do not have access to a regular primary care provider. The problem is expected to be exacerbated by the changing practice patterns of family physicians. As such, policymakers need solutions that can mobilize the primary, health, and social care sectors to work together in their communities and develop solutions to address the needs of Canadians. Primary care-led governance is a key attribute of a high-performing primary care system. Effective governance models facilitate health human resource planning, population health management and multi-sectoral collaboration to address the determinants of health. In Canada, the implementation of primary care-led governance models has been slow. However, three jurisdictions have made significant progress in this area. This comparative study of British Columbia, Alberta, Newfoundland, and Labrador will examine the factors influencing policies for developing and implementing primary care-led governance models. A multi-method, case study design will be used to conduct a cross-case comparative analysis of three jurisdictions. Each case will comprise of: (1) a document review; and (2) qualitative interviews with policymakers, stakeholders, and clinical leaders. The Policy Triangle framework will guide the analysis of the factors that shaped the development of primary care governance models and identify barriers and facilitators. A cross-case-study analysis will be done to identify similarities and differences. The findings will be disseminated at a policy workshop with policymakers, knowledge users, researchers, primary care leaders, community partners and patient partners to inform the development of policy options for the potential development of a primary care-led governance model in Ontario. The outcome will be recommendations for designing and implementing effective primary care governance models to meet the needs of communities and improving the goals of the quadruple aim and health equity.

column36: Building the Infrastructure for Indigenous Primary Healthcare: A Comparative Policy Research Study in Alberta and Ontario
column37: The capacity of Indigenous primary healthcare (PHC) to provide consistent quality healthcare service delivery to Indigenous peoples is impeded by limited clinical resources and sparse Indigenous PHC system infrastructure. The nature in which physicians are paid influences funding allocation for building critical PHC system infrastructure. The recruitment and retention of Indigenous-focused PHC providers also hinges on adequate PHC system infrastructure. Provincial health system and policy partners from Alberta (AB) and Ontario (ON) have identified a shared policy priority to develop key policy directives to build Indigenous PHC system infrastructure by reinforcing financial commitments and responsibilities, thereby fostering the development of a high quality and safe PHC workforce for Indigenous populations. The objectives of our comparative policy research project across AB and ON are to: (1) explain the relationship between payment/remuneration models and PHC infrastructure development in facilitating the delivery and organization of PHC services for Indigenous populations; (2) understand the contextual factors that shaped provincial policy-making on funding for Indigenous-focused PHC in AB and ON; (3) ascertain how provincial PHC policy actors, PHC providers and communities in AB and ON define the challenges related to inequities in Indigenous PHC funding and resources across different Indigenous PHC settings (urban, on-reserve and northern communities) and groups; (4) identify and learn from Indigenous PHC models in AB and ON that have innovated to build PHC system infrastructure; and (5) develop macro-level policy recommendations on changing funding structures that facilitate Indigenous PHC system infrastructure development.

column36: Hosting an Annual Career Camp to Spark the Fire : Policy Strategy for Retention and Support of Indigenous and Northern Youths' Pursuit of Healthcare Careers in the Northwest Territories (NWT)
column37: The Northwest Territories (NWT), a large land with many isolated communities, has always been challenged to recruit and retain healthcare workers. The territory is now in a healthcare crisis. Solutions such as bringing in healthcare workers from the southern Canada are not permanent. Strategies that focus on Indigenous and Northern youth are being planned by the government as a way to promote retention. The goal of this project is to contribute to a retention policy to support Indigenous and Northern youth from the NWT to explore careers in the healthcare workforce, by developing and hosting an annual career camp. This project engages with multiple partners to consider historical, cultural, economic and social factors. Creating a partnership between youth and Elders in local communities, to better understand how to encourage youth to enter the healthcare field is a culturally safe way to inform actions that can work and last.

column36: Vieillir chez soi : Soutenir les residences pour personnes ainees dans l'adoption des meilleures pratiques pour eviter l'entree en hebergement de soins de longue duree
column37: Ce projet vise a mettre en place un modele de soins dans une Residence pour aines (RPA) afin de permettre aux personnes de vivre le plus longtemps possible dans ce meme milieu de vie. Ce modele propose d'adapter les services aux besoins grandissants des aines vivant en RPA pour eviter leur transfert en Centre d'hebergement de soins de longue duree (CHSLD). En effet, de plus en plus de personnes sont en attente d'une place en CHSLD - une situation preoccupante a la fois pour les decideurs et les gestionnaires, mais surtout pour les aines et leurs proches. Il devient donc urgent de repenser nos pratiques pour elargir les possibilites de << vieillir chez soi >>. Notre equipe de recherche interdisciplinaire travaillera avec des decideurs (ministere de la sante et des services sociaux), des gestionnaires (CIUSSS de l'Estrie-CHUS), les proprietaires de la residence, les intervenants, les proches et les residents pour identifier, mettre en place et evaluer les meilleures pratiques au sein de la RPA << Les Jardins de Magog >>. Ce modele de soins propose de rehausser les services de soutien a domicile et les combiner a une approche de soins qui cherche a promouvoir la qualite de vie des residents, malgre les risques. Par exemple, chanter en aidant la personne a s'habiller ou favoriser les promenades dans les jardins pour une personne presentant de l'errance. Ces changements devraient contribuer a ameliorer l'experience de soins des residents, la satisfaction des proches ainsi que le bien-etre des employes et, ultimement, eviter l'entree en CHSLD. Nous veillons a ce que ce modele de soins puisse etre exporte ailleurs au Quebec et qu'il puisse survivre dans le temps, une fois le projet termine. Le modele cree decoulera d'un partenariat entre le prive, le public et la recherche, lequel vise a s'adapter a la personne, plutot que ce soit la personne qui s'y adapte.

column36: National and Provincial Policies to support the Face of Primary Care
column37: Medical office assistants (MOAs) are core members of the health workforce. We use the term MOA to describe receptionists who do range of administrative duties, but may also be involved in triaging patients, reporting results to patients, or administering screening questionnaires. The MOA is the first point of contact for patients. They are the "face of primary care" and often have deep insights into patients' personal and family histories. Evidence suggests that a high-performing MOA can make a difference for the whole primary care practice. Finding ways to support MOAs to perform well in primary care is one way to bring more high-quality primary care to more patients. High-quality primary care is a key policy priority in Canada, made more difficult by the health human resource crisis. But how exactly to create or implement policies to ensure they can perform an evolving range of tasks in their complex clinic environment is unknown. Our partners across Canada and from other countries want to pursue policy options to enable high performance of MOAs in primary care. These policy options could include regulatory changes, training requirements, financial requirements, or practice supports. We will help our partners understand the policy options by completing a systematic summary of evidence from around the world and also by summarizing the lessons learned from experiences across many provinces and countries. We will then work with these partners to develop an evidence-informed plan for government funders, regulators, and professional associations to help primary care MOAs achieve their full potential.
