column36: Developing evidence-informed, regionally contextualized policy options to increase access and use of palliative care for people with heart failure in Ontario
column37: There is an urgent need to improve care to meet the palliative needs of ~750,000 Canadians living with heart failure (HF) who suffer from distressing symptoms, poor quality of life (QoL), and experience frequent hospitalization. Palliative care seeks to treat symptoms and improve QoL, but most people do not receive it, partly because there is a lack of population-level approaches to identify those in need. Our project will identify a population of people with HF who have palliative needs and would therefore benefit from palliative care. From this, we will develop health policy options to increase access and use of palliative care for people with HF in Ontario. We will use health and socioeconomic data from all people with HF in Ontario to describe their landscape of palliative needs, including physical (e.g., shortness of breath), psychosocial (e.g., depression, lack of formal and informal caregiver supports), and socioeconomic marginalization, and how these needs vary by where someone lives. We will define a consensus-based subset of priority palliative needs and the relationship between these needs and subsequent hospitalization. From this, we will gain a deeper understanding of the factors leading to hospitalization and identify potential opportunities for palliative care to enhance care delivery to meet the needs of people with HF and their caregivers.

column36: Healthy Youth in High-Rises
column37: The world is urbanizing faster than ever, and cities across Canada are grappling with how best to accommodate growing urban populations while supporting health and sustainability goals. Many Canadian regions are directing high-density housing development towards urban growth centres. However, high-rises (high-density housing with at least 5 storeys) are not built for youth. Youth are especially vulnerable to effects of poor housing and neighbourhood characteristics, and are excluded from participating in planning and development decisions. No extant research has investigated youth perspectives on how high-rise neighbourhoods affect their health, and what specific urban designs they suggest as solutions. This is a major gap given that high-rise housing stock will continue to grow to meet demand. This equity-focused research will support an emergent research focus on youth health and high-rise living. We will: 1) undertake a series of focus groups with youth in Toronto, the Region of Waterloo, and London, Ontario to explore how youth think different urban design features are linked to their physical and mental health and what urban design and placemaking solutions they propose; 2) Engage in participatory mapping exercises in which youth will identify areas in their neighborhoods where they engage in physical and mental health-related behaviors, and 3) Undertake go-along interviews in high-rise neighborhoods to more deeply explore these themes. Participants will be recruited to maximize diversity in terms of gender, race/ethnicity, and type of neighborhood where they live to ensure diverse viewpoints are represented in our sample. This research takes an integrated knowledge translation approach, builds on our team's prior research on youth health and urban design, and on our experience with youth engagement. This research will support youth health and equity by leveraging local youth expertise to conceptualize urban design solutions for high-rise neighbourhoods.

column36: Partnering for Youth Mental Health and Well-Being: Co-Designing Policy Recommendations and Research Priorities for Manitoba Youth Hubs
column37: The mental health (MH) crisis facing Canadian youth is a public health concern with MH challenges becoming more severe and affecting more youth Also concerning is the emerging evidence of the negative impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on youth MH, which is expected to be felt for years to come. In efforts to identify solutions to the MH crisis and in line with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child, which highlights the rights of youth to express their views and participate in matters affecting them, engaging youth in the development of MH policy and research priorities is needed. Youth hubs are the ideal venue to engage youth in these ways as they aim to advance youth MH. The purpose of this youth-centered study is to gather evidence that will inform MH and well-being policies and research priorities at youth hubs in Manitoba (MB). Central to this study is engaging youth in the co-design of policy recommendations and research priorities by providing them with a leadership role in this process. Youth attending MB youth hubs and key stakeholders will be invited to take part in the study. Youth will participate in focus groups and a survey. Youth co-researchers will engage key stakeholders in a series of meetings to move the youth co-designed MH and well-being policy recommendations and research priorities into action. Arts-based methods will be used throughout the course of the study. Short-term, this study will provide important evidence to inform policies and research priorities specific to advancing MH and well-being for youth attending youth hubs in MB. Youth co-researchers will build capacity specific to policy and research development. Future work involves using the findings to advance next steps including undertaking identified policy recommendations and research priorities for MB youth hubs. Long-term, the findings may be used to inform best practices on how to engage youth in policy and research across integrated youth services in Canada.

column36: Recognizing, Identifying and Supporting the Engagement of Youth Providing Care (RISE Up): A National Survey and Co-design Project
column37: In Canada, 1.9 million youth provide some care to a family member or friend with a medical condition, disability, or aging needs. In their role, youth caregivers may interact with different healthcare providers (HCPs), who often are often not aware of the caring role taken on by youth and how to adequately support them. When unsupported, youth carers can experience social, academic, and mental and physical health challenges which negatively impact their well-being and future opportunities (i.e., employment, education). Improving the awareness of young carers (YCs) and their interactions with the healthcare system is a vital step in improving the health and well-being of youth and those they care for. We therefore propose a multi-method research study looking at HCPs' awareness of YCs while identifying points of convergence of YCs with the health system. Our study aims to (1) assess a broad range of HCPs' awareness of young carers in their everyday healthcare interactions and identify challenges in their recognition and support at point-of-care; and (2) engage with both YCs and HCPs to understand their needs and priorities during their intersections, and together support the co-design of a prototype program which addresses and recognizes the challenges faced by YCs in HCP interactions. In the first phase of the study, we will survey HCPs across Canada about their awareness of YCs and the supports available to them. In the second phase, we will use a new co-design approach to partner with HCPs and YCs to identify the needs of these groups and develop tool(s) to support YC in their interactions with the healthcare system. Our research team is composed of a young carer lead, a young carer advisory, caregiving organizations along with health care providers, researchers and experts in co-design. This project will build capacity for this understudied area by collaborating with youth and caregiving organizations across the country to come up with meaningful solutions.

column36: Mixed methods pilot feasibility study of an online peer navigation intervention for youth with childhood-onset disabilities
column37: Transition from the child to adult health care system for youth with disabilities is a complex process that should include a variety of services. If the transition to the adult health care system is not successful, it can lead to poor health outcomes and less opportunities to participate in the community. Programs that help the transition from the child to adult health care systems are important and needed, but not much is known about what the best programs are. In a previous study completed by this team, an intervention involving peer navigation was identified as a potentially effective and important intervention to help with transition. Peer navigation is defined as a one-on-one interaction between a peer navigator and a patient. It involves a trained peer who provides help with education, advocacy, and system navigation. As a follow-up to that study, the team interviewed youth with cerebral palsy (CP) and childhood acquired brain injury (ABI) and family members to identify their needs and preferences for what would be involved in a peer navigation intervention. Some of the components that were identified included: a) a knowledge/resource library that can be kept up-to-date, b) emotional and social support between youth and navigators c) opportunities to encourage advocacy/opportunities for participants to discuss advocacy strategy and d) opportunities for parental involvement. These considerations are now being added to an existing virtual care platform to form a new peer navigation intervention for youth with childhood-onset disabilities called CONNECT: Compassionate Online NavigatioN to Enhance Care Transitions. The purpose of the current project is to test CONNECT with a small group of youth to look at how feasible the intervention is, what potential benefits it might have, and understand the overall experiences of youth and peer navigators who participate in the intervention.

column36: The Youth Development Instrument (YDI) Ambassador Project: A youth participatory action research initiative
column37: With the goal to amplify youth participation in every stage of the research process, this project aims to create a Youth Ambassador program, which includes a youth participatory action research study (YPAR), a summer research institute and wellness retreat, and employment opportunities for youth as research assistants and knowledge translation ambassadors. Youth ages 15 to 24 experience disproportionate levels of mental distress compared to other population age groups in Canada and adverse mental health trends have worsened since the onset of COVID-19. Our Principal Knowledge User, Frayme, is an international organization that provides youth health and social supports to youth connecting them with more than 400 service providers across 12 countries. column36: Unmet needs of immigrant older adults after discharge from hospital with delirium: Using administrative data to explore practice patterns and long-term adverse health outcomes
column37: Older Canadians represent over 40% of hospital admissions and are at increased risk of experiencing hospital related harms. One of these harms is delirium, which is a syndrome of new confusion that is common and affects up to 50% of hospitalized older patients. It is important because it increases the risk of subsequently developing dementia, being admitting to a long-term care home and even dying. Immigrant older adults may do worse after discharge due to a number of risk factors such as low income, systemic racism, and language barriers. This could lead to differences in the care they receive including increased prescription of harmful medications, less access to home care, and less follow up visits with doctors. Limited visits with friends and relatives due to COVID-19 social distancing measures may have exacerbated these issues because immigrants often rely heavily on family members for support. This proposal will use linked health databases to study the care that immigrant older patients with delirium receive in Ontario. We will report the occurrence of delirium during a hospital admission for a medical or surgical reason among immigrant and non-immigrant patients over the age of 65. We will look at the differences in how delirium is managed including who is seen by a delirium specialist and who gets discharged with harmful medications. We will examine the adverse outcomes after a person is discharged including coming back to hospital, developing dementia, or moving to a long-term care home. We will study how antipsychotic prescriptions changed during the COVID-19 pandemic and compare differences in these changes by immigrant status. We anticipate that immigrant older adults will receive more antipsychotics, less home care and have more long-term unfavorable outcomes. Understanding the unmet needs of immigrant older adults after delirium will help the healthcare system implement interventions to better support patients and families.

column36: Improving cancer treatment-related shared decision-making among older immigrants with cancer
column37: The majority of new cancer diagnoses and cancer-related deaths occur in older people. Almost one third of Canada's ageing population are born outside of Canada. Older people can experience challenges with communication and making treatment-related decisions due to health conditions, such as hearing difficulty or memory loss. For older immigrants, communication and decision-making ability are further challenged by language and cultural barriers. Good communication and shared decision-making can help people with cancer live longer and better. In this doctoral research project, I will examine the factors, processes, and conditions that enable or prevent shared decision-making among older immigrants with their cancer care providers, and create tools to help overcome the identified barriers. I will be working with a patient partner co-lead throughout this project. The project will be divided into three parts. I will first begin by exploring published studies on shared decision-making with culturally and linguistically diverse older people with cancer through a scoping review of the published literature. In the second part of the project, I will conduct interviews with older immigrants living with cancer, their caregivers, and cancer care providers to learn about their experience with shared decision-making as it relates to cancer treatments. For the third part of the project, I will work with patients and caregivers, community groups, and health care providers to develop tools to help older immigrants better take part in shared decision-making with their cancer care. By improving cancer treatment-related shared decision-making with this group of older adults, it will reduce the negative outcomes and differences in cancer care that can occur as a result of poor communication and lack of involvement of patients and their caregivers.

column36: L'accessibilite et la qualite des soins palliatifs chez les personnes tres agees
column37: Si les Canadiens ont aujourd'hui une esperance de vie plus elevee, ils n'ont pas forcement une meilleure qualite de vie. Et s'ils accedent a des soins jusqu'a leur deces, ils terminent souvent leurs jours a l'hopital bien qu'ils souhaitent majoritairement rester a domicile et dans leur collectivite. Les soins palliatifs sont a cet egard interessants, car ils permettent une meilleure qualite de vie aux personnes tres agees en offrant un systeme de soins et de soutien qui surpasse celui des systemes de sante actuels centres sur l'hopital. Comme le soulignent l'Institut canadien d'information sur la sante et l'Organisation mondiale de la sante, les soins palliatifs font partie des solutions aux defis socio-demographiques relatifs au vieillissement et au mourir. Par definition, les soins palliatifs visent le soulagement des souffrances (physiques, psychologiques, sociales et spirituelles) des personnes atteintes d'une maladie a pronostic reserve et le soutien de leurs proches. Ils sont prodigues par des equipes multidisciplinaires (incluant medecins, infirmieres, psychologues, etc.) sur une periode allant du diagnostic du patient jusqu'au deuil des proches, en passant par l'accompagnement en fin de vie. Aussi proposent-ils des traitements precoces adaptes aux personnes du quatrieme age dont les besoins sont tres complexes. Malgre leurs avantages, les soins palliatifs sont peu accessibles pour la population canadienne, surtout en cas de maladies neurodegeneratives, de demence et de maladies chroniques non liees au cancer. A ce propos, un travail d'education sur les soins palliatifs reste a faire aupres du grand public et des professionnels de la sante, chez qui circule la croyance que ces soins sont reserves aux patients atteints de cancer et seulement pertinents aux derniers moments de la vie. Ce travail d'education est essentiel pour s'atteler aux probleme majeurs concernant l'utilisation des soins de sante et la qualite des soins et du soutien en fin de vie au Canada.

column36: Urinary incontinence in older men: Defining and prioritizing modifiable risk factors, and developing a patient-centered self-management intervention
column37: Individuals with urinary incontinence (UI) experience accidental leaks of urine over time, resulting in physical, social, emotional, and financial consequences. Sufferers may isolate themselves, avoid social engagements and sports activities, experience sex problems, become depressed, and need medical assistance or nursing care. Every year, governments, individuals, and employers in Canada and the U.S. spend billions on this issue. Despite being common in older men, it has received less attention than in older women. Although this could be because older men are half as likely to suffer from UI, rates of the condition seem to rise more steadily with advancing age in men than in women. This problem will be addressed using the self-help approach, which has been successful in treating chronic conditions like UI by involving patients in identifying and resolving health concerns. Since older adults are more likely to experience the negative effects of UI medications, self-help is even more crucial. Together with a patient advisory group and a panel of doctors, we will develop a self-help tool. We will gather information about those factors that predispose older men to the problem of UI, which can be corrected by the patients themselves. Our intervention will be based on the evidence, patients' perspectives, and doctors' input. In order to make it available to as many men as possible, our self-help intervention will be presented as a mobile application. With this medium, users will be reminded to perform the tasks that will yield the desired results. It will help users identify personal risk factors contributing to UI, before presenting strategies or tasks for modifying those risk factors, so that desired outcomes, such as improved symptom control and improved UI-related quality of life may be achieved. Furthermore, it will provide individual progress reports on task performance and measurable outcomes, as well as data for research and continuous improvement.

column36: Risk of dementia, long-term care placement, and home care use following traumatic brain injury among community-dwelling older adults: an-equity focused population-based retrospective cohort study in Canada
column37: More than one in four people aged 65 years or older fall annually. Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a common complication of falls. In the long term, TBI patients are at increased risk of dementia, which is the decline of cognition impacting daily living activities. However, we need more evidence to counsel patients and their families on the risk of dementia, specifically for older adults (65-year-old or above). Subsequently, little is known about the risk of admission to long-term care or their need for community support, especially in those suffering from systemic inequities. We need to understand the impact of social determinants such as age at diagnosis, sex, gender, neighbourhood income, community size, immigrant status and neighbourhood ethnic diversity on the risk of dementia, long-term care admission, and need for home care services in TBI older adults. If we can identify the social determinants of health associated with a higher risk of dementia, higher needs and more prominent gaps between needs and support, we can optimize equitable access. As part of my thesis, I will conduct three major projects. I will lead a retrospective cohort study using population databases of individuals diagnosed with TBI to evaluate their long-term cognitive outcome (risk of dementia) and healthcare services needs (long-term care admission or need for homecare support). To further assess strategies to address the cognitive adverse effects of TBI, I will review the literature for evidence of the cost-effectiveness of post-TBI cognitive interventions. I will then conduct an economic analysis of cognitive interventions across clinical settings in Ontario. These three research projects have important implications regarding supporting older adults equitably in their homes using appropriate resources like specialized cognitive interventions or home care services to optimize their quality of life and potentially avoidable care transitions.

column36: Programme Remodeler sa vie(R) aupres d'aines quebecois : une etude de cas multiples soutenue par une approche realiste
column37: Ce projet de recherche vise a expliquer comment fonctionne le programme Remodeler sa vie (Lifestyle Redesign). Developpe et teste en Californie, le programme Remodeler sa vie est une intervention d'ergotherapie preventive visant le developpement d'un mode de vie sain et signifiant. En raison des evidences scientifiques indiquant une amelioration significative du fonctionnement, de la vitalite, de la sante mentale, des interactions sociales ainsi que de la satisfaction envers la vie chez les aines, cette intervention est hautement interessante pour les Canadiens ages. Dans une approche multidisciplinaire de promotion de la sante, ce programme represente aussi une reponse efficace au fardeau croissant des maladies chroniques et du deconditionnement des aines, d'importantes priorites ministerielles. Malgre ses resultats probants, l'implantation du programme demeure limitee et on connait peu comment il fonctionne. La proposition de recherche a donc pour but de developper une theorie explicative du fonctionnement du programme Remodeler sa vie. Plus precisement, le projet vise a : 1) explorer les effets a court terme du programme sur la sante, la depression, l'engagement dans les activites signifiantes, la participation sociale et le changement de comportement d'aines et 2) expliquer ces effets au regard d'elements contextuels et de mecanismes. Pour ce faire, une implantation de 3 mois sera realisee a l'aide d'une etude de cas dans 4 milieux quebecois choisis selon des variations organisationnelles jugees importantes au succes du programme. Chaque cas inclura un ergotherapeute, son superieur ainsi que 5 a 10 aines. Grace a une revue de la litterature et a une consultation d'experts, des hypotheses sont d'abord elaborees, puis testees sur le terrain a l'aide de methodes qualitatives et quantitatives. En expliquant comment le programme mene aux effets, ces hypotheses formeront une theorie favorisant l'amelioration du programme et son deploiement en contexte franco-canadien.

column36: Evaluating the role of patient navigators across the continuum to improve seniors' care and experience
column37: For many seniors, navigating the healthcare system is challenging and creates high levels of stress. Patient navigators are becoming increasingly popular across Canada as one mechanism to help patients manage their journey of care. Navigators work to improve the quality and coordination of care by serving as guides to patients and their families on how to best access care in the hospital and the community. In 2020, a new patient navigator role was introduced at Sunnybrook Hospital in partnership with a community agency, SPRINT Senior Care, to help seniors' bridge the care gap from hospital to home. Over the past 2 years, this program was refined so it could be effectively integrated into the existing hospital system and has now been expanded by hiring new navigators. At this point in time, there are a number of questions regarding how this program is impacting the health outcomes of patients. To address this need, the focus of this research will be to evaluate the patient navigator program to determine which types of patients are being supported by the navigators, what types of services are being provided, to learn about their hospital stay, and to see where they are discharged into the community. This will be accomplished by collecting survey, hospital chart, and health administrative data from databases managed by a public payer (Ontario government) on 200 patients supported by a navigator and a matched case group of 200 patients who were not supported by a navigator. As well, the researchers will undertake qualitative interviews with seniors and caregivers who have received navigation, healthcare providers, and administrators about their experiences being cared by or working with patient navigators. These findings will be used to create resources that can educate patients and families about navigation services, and that can educate providers and decision-makers on how to develop, implement and optimize their own navigation services for their senior patients.

column36: Understanding how Health Factors, Job Context, Sex and Gender affect Workplace Accomodation Among Men and Women with Arthritis. The Scleroderma Model.
column37: Background. Many people with arthritis wish to maintain their ability to work. Functioning at work is not entirely explained by disease symptoms. It is also related to personal factors, work context, and workplace practices that may support work performance or impede it. Systemic sclerosis (SSc, scleroderma) is an arthritic disease characterized by immune activation and multisystem (joints, lungs, heart, skin) damage. Work disability is highly prevalent among individuals with SSc; yet, it is an area of research that continues to underexplored. Using SSc as a model, this proposal will study how health factors, job context, sex and gender affect workplace accommodation among men and women. Objectives: 1. To evaluate the job sectors individuals with SSc work. 2. To evaluate how SSc health factors impact workplace accommodations that are needed and used. 3. To evaluate unmet workplace accommodation needs across job sectors, stratified by sex. 4. To evaluate how workplace accommodations needed and used change over the life course, stratified by changes in disease severity and gender roles. Methods. The Toronto Scleroderma Program is the largest single center SSc cohort in Canada. Two hundred individuals fulfilling the ACR/EULAR SSc classification criteria will be included. They will be assessed every 6-12 months using a standardized protocol including age, sex, and health factors. Workplace activity limitations, sex and gender roles, job context factors, and workplace accommodations will be assessed annually for 3 years. Three measures will be used to examine work productivity loss. Presenteeism: The Work Productivity and Activity Impairment Questionnaire will evaluate the extent to which health affected productivity while working. Absenteeism: Number of days absent from work due to health problems. Job disruptions: Seven items will ask about whether the participant has experienced a disruption to their employment. Workplace support needs. A list of nine job accommodations (special equipment), modifications (modified job tasks) or benefits (wellness programs) will be presented, and participants will be asked whether any were available, needed or used. Difficulties with workplace tasks will be measured using the Workplace Activity Limitation Scale. The Scleroderma Heath Assessment Questionnaire will assess disability. Job context factors will include job sector, hours worked/week, self-employment, job tenure at current organization, job control and firm size. The Gender Roles Framework will be used to evaluate differences between men and women in their participation in the economy. It is comprised of 3 components: an activity profile ('who does what?'), an access and control profile ('who has access and who controls what?'), and an analysis of influencing factors ('how does gender influence the profiles?'). Relevance. Understanding how health factors, job context, sex and gender affect workplace accommodation among men and women with SSc has the potential to address lost productivity with targeted workplace supports. Insights from this research will inform workplace policies and practices that could help accommodate individuals with other forms of arthritis.

column36: Advancing self-management supports new models of care, and health professions education to improve access to evidence-based care for people with osteoarthritis and arthritis pain
column37: Musculoskeletal pain conditions, including osteoarthritis, are leading contributors to years lived with disability worldwide[1]. Evidence suggests there are effective management options available, such as exercise interventions and self-management programs[2-5], but they are often hard to access. Barriers to access can lead to inequities in care and disparities in health outcomes for people living with arthritis pain. My research program focuses on reducing musculoskeletal pain-related disability and has three interrelated themes: i) enhancing active self-management supports, ii) developing and testing new models of primary care that support access to evidence-based care, and iii) advancing education and knowledge translation to move evidence on pain management into practice. The overarching aim of this work is to improve the lives of people living with musculoskeletal pain by improving care and making care more accessible. Within the first theme, I will lead a study that uses an integrated knowledge translation approach to adapt an effective in-person self-management program aimed at improving function to a virtual format. I have previously developed and evaluated an in-person self-management program that has demonstrated effectiveness at improving function[6-8] that will be used as a foundation for the development of the virtual self-management program. This area of research will use best-practices in knowledge translation and implementation science[9,10] to adapt the self-management program using an intervention mapping approach[11,12]. If effective, this new delivery format has the potential to improve the reach and accessibility of an effective self-management program aimed at improving function for people with arthritis pain, which has been identified as an important area for ongoing research[13,14]. Within the second theme, I will lead a pilot cluster randomized trial to evaluate the impact of a new team-based model of primary care for people with arthritis pain that involves integrating physiotherapists as the first point of contact within primary care teams for people with arthritis pain in Ontario. This work will leverage existing partnerships with 20 primary care teams and trial infrastructure by running this pilot study along-side my current fully-powered cluster randomized trial[15-17] testing the impact of a similar model of care for people with low back pain (LBP) [funded by CIHR]. This model of care has the potential to improve access to non-pharmacological interdisciplinary support for people with arthritis, improve access to guideline adherent care, and reduce over-utilization of lower value care. Within the third theme, I will lead a study to develop a curriculum guideline for musculoskeletal pain management for entry-level physiotherapy students in Canada. This study will include a series of focus groups and a Delphi survey to arrive at the foundational knowledge, skills, and attitudes required to achieve competency in musculoskeletal pain management. This will build on our existing work that identified an agreed upon set of competencies in chronic pain management[18,19]. The resulting curriculum guidelines will facilitate integration of the competencies in entry-level physiotherapy in Canada. Together, these three arms of research are expected to provide important evidence to improve access to evidence-based care for people with osteoarthritis and arthritis pain.

column36: Imaging approaches to understand the role of patient biological factors in outcomes following total joint replacement
column37: Motivation: In Canada approximately 140,000 total hip and knee replacement surgeries are performed annually as the mainstay treatment for end-stage osteoarthritis at a cost exceeding $1.4 billion[1]. Nearly 10% of these surgeries are revision surgeries to replace devices that failed due to indications like loosening or instability[1]. Another 20-30% of patients may experience joint stiffness, unresolved pain, and dissatisfaction after surgery[2-4]. Although most total joint replacements are successful, the large number of procedures means complications in even a small percentage of patients can affect thousands of individuals to their detriment. Research Overview: My lab's mission is to enhance patient mobility and quality of life after joint replacement through the development and application of imaging and digital technologies. Our work incorporates prospective clinical trials evaluated using imaging-based outcome metrics[5-12], studies of failed devices through Canada's largest implant retrieval program[13-21], and the development of innovative imaging and wearable sensor technology[22-35]. Our studies have primarily examined implant design and surgical techniques as factors affecting patient outcomes. Now we are turning our focus towards how patients' biological factors can lead to different outcomes after total joint replacement. Ongoing research is focused on three main themes: 1. Fixation of cementless implants - Cementless implants that rely on direct bone ingrowth to porous surfaces are increasingly popular since they can provide superior long-term fixation, but only if strong osseointegration is maintained. We have examined how implant design and surgical technique affect the strength of cementless fixation after shoulder, hip, and knee replacements using specialized imaging[5-8]. Now we are using tissue analysis in conjunction with imaging to examine the influence of the gut microbiome and vitamin co-factors on bone production and implant osseointegration after cementless total joint replacement. 2. Dissatisfaction after knee arthroplasty - One in five patients is dissatisfied after total knee replacement and may experience ongoing stiffness and pain, limiting activities of daily living. We have used imaging and wearable sensors to detect objective differences between satisfied and dissatisfied patients, and have developed intelligent sensor technology to predict patients' post-operative functional abilities in order to influence their expectations[34-36]. Now we are using imaging to determine if ongoing synovial inflammation in some patients is an overlooked contributor to dissatisfaction and pain. 3. Reaction to wear debris - Damage and corrosion of implanted components releases wear debris, triggering an immune response in some patients that can cause soft tissue destruction, implant loosening, and damage to distant organs. We have extensively studied factors causing polyethylene wear and corrosion of cobalt-chromium implants in failed devices retrieved from patients, aided by the development of automated damage scoring tools[14-21]. Now to provide deeper insight into wear debris reactions we are combining pre-revision imaging with assessments of sampled joint tissues and retrieved joint replacement implants. Significance to Arthritis: Sub-optimal outcomes that require additional interventions or revision surgery after total joint replacement are unacceptable for individual patients and a burden to the healthcare system. Our approach to understanding the patient-driven mechanisms causing failure and dissatisfaction will yield more personalized approaches to improve care and avoid revisions.

column36: Thrombelastography-Defined Duration of Hypercoagulability Following Elective Total Hip and Total Knee Arthroplasty
column37: Osteoarthritis (OA) is one of Canada's leading causes of pain and functional limitations. Both total hip arthroplasty (THA) and total knee arthroplasty (TKA) reliably and successfully relieve pain due to OA, improve functional outcomes, and result in high patient satisfaction. The Canadian Institute of Health Information reported 49,503 THA and TKA in Canada in 2013-2014, representing a 5-year increase of 19.1% (from 41,573 in 2009 -2010) and a 1-year increase of 5.0%. Over 123,000 knee and hip replacements are performed annually in Canada, making them the second and third most common surgeries. The COVID-19 pandemic has prolonged surgical wait times and increased surgical access is planned for THA and TKA. Clinical practice guidelines recommend some form of thromboprophylaxis for a minimum of 10 to 14 days following THA and TKA. However, despite thromboprophylaxis, the 2016-2017 Alberta provincial in-hospital pulmonary embolism (PE) rate remained at 3.2/1,000 for primary THA and 6.5/1,000 for primary TKA. There is also no consensus on optimal thromboprophylaxis. Therefore, a patient-specific approach to thromboprophylaxis after THA and TKA may be optimal. Inaccuracies exist in current venous thromboembolism (VTE) prediction models, as high-risk patients are often misclassified as low risk and subsequently develop deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Patients who develop VTE (DVT and/or PE) are at increased risk of future VTE and post-thrombotic syndrome causing functional or exercise limitations. Treatment for VTE necessitates prolonged anticoagulation, which may increase bleeding risk and wound complications, often resulting in the need for repeat surgery. There is a critical need to identify patients with increased risk for VTE following THA or TKA. D-dimer is the current gold standard blood test for detecting VTE and is used in validated algorithms for VTE diagnosis; however, the specificity of this test decreases with recent surgery. Thrombelastography (TEG) analysis of whole blood samples provides an accurate and near real-time picture of the dynamic functional viscoelastic changes that occur during clot formation, retraction, and lysis. Traditional plasma-based coagulation tests, such as prothrombin time, are not predictive of VTE because they do not evaluate the entire clotting process. TEG provides a comprehensive evaluation of the viscoelastic properties from initial clot formation through fibrinolysis. Hypercoagulable TEG indices have been associated with significantly higher rates of VTE. My research program has established the novel finding that an elevated maximal amplitude (MA; a measure representing clot strength) from TEG analysis can identify trauma patients at risk for in-hospital VTE and can be used to measure antiplatelet effect. Therefore, TEG is an ideal coagulation test to evaluate patient-specific VTE risk. To date, TEG has not been used in the outpatient setting for THA or TKA beyond nine days postoperatively. The proposed study will use serial TEG analysis beyond recommended thromboprophylaxis to determine individual coagulation profiles, duration of hypercoagulability and increased VTE risk following THA or TKA, and the efficacy of antiplatelet use for VTE prevention. The ultimate purpose of our research is to utilize TEG analysis to identify patients at increased risk for VTE and to evaluate the utility of individualized thromboprophylaxis.

column36: Assessing the Effects of Implementing AgeTech to Support Dementia Care in a Rural Setting in Northern British Columbia
column37: In rural, northern British Columbia, a new long-term care facility for persons living with dementia is the first northern care facility to integrate aging technology. Providing equitable access to technologies that improve health for older adults in rural communities is necessary but not without its challenges. The Northern Health Authority has committed to implementing aging technologies within its facility to improve the quality and provision of dementia care in rural communities. A team of older adults, community organizations, health system leaders and researchers came together to select different aging technologies to provide within the facility. The goal of implementing these technologies is to maximize the quality of care and life for persons living with dementia and to enhance the working environment for those who support them. Three types of technologies were chosen which include circadian lighting built into the facility, virtual biking technology to enhance physical health and indoor gardening technology to enhance the environment and improve the engagement of residents. My research will describe the development, implementation and uptake of aging technologies within this rural long-term care setting. Secondly, my research will evaluate the impacts of these technologies on persons living with dementia, their care partners and staff at the facility. Lastly, my research will provide insights into how to continue the use of aging technologies within this setting and how to deliver aging technologies across other care settings across the province. The findings will help form best practices for the implementation of aging technology in similar northern and rural areas. I will engage persons living with dementia, their care partners, staff and health authority partners in evaluating whether the technology is making a difference.

column36: Social Network and Support Experiences of Older African Refugees in Calgary: A Graphic Visual Inquiry
column37: Globally, the number of refugees is increasing. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) reported that about 26 million persons lived outside their countries' borders at the end of 2021 due to conflicts, human rights violations and generalised violence. Older people make up an estimated four per cent of global refugees, yet they receive very little scholarly attention because their needs are not deemed as necessary as that of other vulnerable groups such as women and children. This leaves them at risk of falling through the gaps of support and care. Anchored on the theories of Ubuntu and intersectionality, this proposed phenomenological study will adopt art-based storytelling and graphics to explore the social network and support experiences of African refugees aged 50 years and over living in Calgary. This study will investigate the nature of social support received during the migration and postmigration periods. The impact of decreased support networks on their mental health and quality of life will also be explored. This proposed research aims to contribute to the established knowledge deficit on older refugees by highlighting the roles of older African refugees' current social networks and support to their well-being, how forced migration may have changed their social networks and support, and the gaps in support it may have created. The findings will aid immigrant serving agencies, social workers, multidisciplinary gerontologists and policymakers to design and provide ethnic and culture-sensitive programmes to support older African refugees and older refugees of other ethnicities.

column36: PRESAGE - PREdictions and Stimulations related to AGE: capitalizing on artificial intelligence to predict the functional cognitive age of seniors in order to establish an adequate diagnosis for an optimized cognitive intervention.
column37: Age is a decisive criterion for many diagnostic, preventive, and health care guidelines. The "chronological" age, calculated from the person's birth date, is the measure generally used. However, a discrepancy between chronological and functional age is frequently observed, making it necessary to review our approaches. The PRESAGE project (for "PREdictions and Stimulations related to AGE") aims to define a "cognitive age" representative of the individual's functioning and capacities. This new indicator will allow the classification of profiles that do not rely on chronological age but on a variety of brain biomarkers and indicators of cognitive performance. Using artificial intelligence, we will attempt to reliably predict the cognitive age and individual profiles of the elderly. In a context where the increase in life expectancy is not associated with healthy cognitive longevity, and in the face of the growing number of people suffering from neurodegenerative diseases, we believe that this measure is timely and more appropriate for the diagnosis of profiles at risk of developing cognitive disorders. An appropriate diagnosis will optimize interventional approaches to cognitive stimulation and prevention, which can be adapted to the cognitive age of each individual. PRESAGE will thus contribute to improving people's health. The definition of refined profiles and their characteristics will also lead to the identification of action levers and prevention guidelines to promote the cognitive health of seniors. Importantly, the project aims to break down society's stereotypes about aging, by highlighting diversity and by supporting optimal cognitive functioning in old age. Finally, PRESAGE will be a way to modernize practices and make medical technologies available to health professionals, in order to move towards a "new generation" of geriatric medicine and neuropsychology.

column36: Modelisation et evaluation de la performance des trajectoires de multimorbidite en contexte de surveillance populationnelle chez les aines
column37: La multimorbidite est definie comme la cooccurrence de plusieurs maladies chroniques chez une meme personne. Avec l'augmentation de l'esperance de vie, on observe une croissance du nombre de personnes agees et tres agees qui vivent dans un etat de multimorbidite. Au Canada, cela represente pres d'un aine sur trois. La multimorbidite entraine une perte de la qualite de vie, une augmentation de la detresse psychologique, de l'invalidite et une consommation de soins accrue. L'amelioration de la prise en charge des individus multimorbides s'impose dans un systeme de sante qui s'est historiquement organise pour traiter une seule maladie a la fois. Pour ce faire, une information valide de la prevalence de la multimorbidite est utile aux decideurs et au personnel de la sante. Elle permet notamment de cibler les milieux et les clienteles les plus susceptibles de beneficier de meilleurs soins de sante et de quantifier les ressources humaines et financieres requises. Malheureusement, un manque de connaissances sur l'evolution temporelle de la multimorbidite chez un meme individu (aussi appele trajectoire de multimorbidite) a ete recemment identifie par un groupe d'experts internationaux comme un deficit majeur dans la comprehension de la multimorbidite. Afin de pallier le manque de connaissances sur l'evolution temporelle de la multimorbidite et de son association avec la mortalite et d'autres issues de sante, mon projet de doctorat consiste a modeliser les trajectoires de multimorbidite, a evaluer leur performance et a predire les issues de sante comparativement aux mesures usuelles. Les resultats de ce projet faciliteront la creation d'indicateurs de surveillance populationnelle innovants qui serviront aux decideurs et au personnel de la sante a mieux prendre en charge les patients multimorbides et a identifier des groupes d'individus a prioriser dans le cadre d'activites de prevention et de promotion de la sante.

column36: PICS-UP CS: Post-Intensive Care Syndrome: Improving Outcomes Through Patient Engagement in Cardiac Surgery Patients
column37: Canadians are getting older and are more likely to need heart surgery as they age, as it is still the best treatment for certain heart diseases. When older adults need to have heart surgery, they tend to stay longer on a breathing machine and in the intensive care unit (ICU), lose weight and muscle, are less steady on their feet, have a harder time driving, and as a result may require to somewhere other than their own home after hospital discharge. Furthermore, are also more likely to be confused after their surgery (known as delirium), to need to go back to hospital after going home, are not as mentally quick as they used to be. Altogether, this collection of conditions is called post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) and may be caused, at least in part, by a long stay in an ICU. My research has three aims to change this syndrome in older adult who need life-saving heart surgery. In Aim 1, we will do a detailed review of all past research to learn what is currently known about the mental and physical symptoms of PICS after heart surgery. This will give us a starting point of what is known and what we need to improve on. For Aim 2, we will directly work with patients and caregivers who had a long stay in the ICU after heart surgery to learn from their experiences about why PICS happens and their ideas about how we can develop, real-world changes to care in the ICU to prevent this from happening in the future. Aim 3 will then conduct a randomized controlled trial to determine if the patient/ caregiver-identified solutions to test if the developed ideas are useful in the ICU and if they prevent PICS from happening following heart surgery. We predict that solutions that patients come up with will be practical and useful in the ICU and that they will prevent PICS. By preventing PICS, we predict that older adult patients will have a quicker recovery and better quality of life after heart surgery.

column36: Understanding and unifying cognitive, behavioral, and sensorimotor markers of dementia to enhance prognostication and risk assessment
column37: Dementia is more than just memory change. People living with or affected by dementia must also deal with changes in mood and behaviour as well as in hearing, walking, and sleep quality. But these changes can appear years or even decades before dementia, acting as red flags for those more likely to get dementia. A better understanding of these red flags, known as dementia markers, is needed in order to use them in research and patient care. My research objectives are to: 1) better understand the connections between dementia markers; 2) identify what changes in the brain underlie dementia markers; and 3) figure out which combination of dementia markers may be most effective for identifying older adults at risk. To accomplish these objectives, I will use data that I will help collect locally and across Canada, as well as existing data gathered from international sources. First, I will study whether the onset of behavioral changes such as depression or anxiety is followed by changes in thinking, memory, hearing, walking, and sleep in older adults. Second, I will use brain scans to see whether these dementia markers are accompanied by changes in the size of certain brain regions linked to Alzheimer disease, such as the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex. Finally, I will combine findings from my first and second objectives to determine the best combination of dementia markers. My findings will reveal which dementia markers or red flags are the most important to look for, and what they mean in terms of whether and how soon an individual will develop dementia. My research will help people know whether they are likely to develop dementia, potentially years or decades before it happens, allowing them to plan ahead for living with dementia, receive earlier care for it, and participate in research to develop treatments that will make dementia less devastating or even preventable. Reducing the number and severity of health conditions will allow better health while living longer.

column36: Supporting meaningful family engagement at mealtimes in long-term care: A grounded theory approach
column37: Relationship-centred models of care are key to supporting families in establishing a sense of home in long-term care (LTC), which influences residents' quality of life and families' perceptions of the LTC sector. This theory will inform family-centred mealtime interventions, resources for families navigating evolving dementia care needs, and necessary institutional-level supports that promote family-centred mealtimes in LTC. column37: Outcomes are study endpoints used in health research to determine treatment effectiveness. However, studies that examine older adults with opioid use disorders (OUDs) do not consider patient-relevant factors in outcome selection, e.g., concurrent medications for managing co-occurring diseases, or patient goals for treatment success, e.g., improved quality of interpersonal relationships. Failure to account for these factors in the use of outcomes limits the ability of research to make inferences regarding treatment effectiveness in older adults with mental illness. It is vital to incorporate patients' needs and preferences in outcome selection, so that study findings have value for making decisions about treatment success in the target population. Our overall aim is to identify a set of patient-centered outcomes to be used in studies assessing older adults with mental illness. We will use healthcare data to follow a cohort of older adults who have received treatment for OUDs in Ontario over a 5-year period. We will examine whether treatment for OUDs is successful in achieving long-term patient goals for treatment effectiveness identified by prior interviews with patients, and also whether there are factors associated with better treatment outcomes for older adults (e.g., sex, gender). The findings from our work will enable researchers to select outcomes that align with patient-identified goals for treatment success, and inform patient-centered care guidelines for older adults with mental illness.

column36: Exploring the Support Networks of Caregivers of Persons Living with Stroke (PLWS)
column37: Stroke is the main cause of adult disability in Canada with approximately 75% of persons living with stroke (PLWS) in Canada having some type of disability or impairment. Family caregivers play an important role in stroke recovery as they provide most of the assistance a PLWS receives at home. However, research demonstrates that caring for a PLWS can impact caregivers' lives and wellbeing. The social consequences of stroke caregiving (e.g. marital strain, loneliness) are especially concerning because social relationships can affect well-being. Social support is an important resource for managing caregiving stressors. Social networks play a crucial role in the provision of social support because the connections within a network represent access to social support. However, examinations into the role of support networks during stroke caregiving are limited. The purpose of this study is to examine how caregivers of PLWS access and navigate their social networks and engage in exchanges of social support. Ethnographic methods consisting of interviews, a contact diary, and social network mapping will be used. The study findings will provide insight into how stroke caregivers' social networks were affected by caregiving, how caregivers access support within their networks and how social support influences the stroke caregiving experience. column36: No place like home: Exploring social belonging for older immigrant Muslim women
column37: Without a secure sense of social belonging, older adults can experience loneliness, isolation, and feel ostracized in the communities they live in (De Jong Gierveld et al., 2015). These exclusionary experiences are detrimental to their wellbeing as they encounter barriers towards cultivating meaningful relationships. Thus, the ability to feel a sense of belonging is an essential part of healthy ageing in a post-migratory context (Nielson et al., 2017). Immigrant Muslim older (IMO) women's experiences of belongingness have not been explored or identified in the literature. Their belongingness is by ageism, and by gender, race, and religious discrimination (Salma & Salami, 2020). This qualitative descriptive study aimed to explore how immigrant Muslim older (IMO) women in Edmonton, Alberta cultivated social belonging. A thematic sub-analysis of photo-elicitation interview data was completed. Participants are community-dwelling older adult (55+) women who self-identify as Muslims. Participants have taken pictures of what they felt socially connected to, then were interviewed about these photos afterwards. The analysis was informed by an intersectional life course perspective. The findings showcased the complexity of transnational connections, the impact of memories through the lifetime, and the importance of connectedness to who they identify as family. This research is significant as it focuses on how IMO women can thrive in the communities they live in and what supports they need to experience a sense of belongingness as they age in Canada. This research informs nurses about equitable health outcomes and how belongingness is a shared responsibility between immigrants and the larger society.

column36: The incorporation of automated phenotyping strategies to identify genes and pathways involved in age-related hearing loss
column37: One in every 3 individuals over 65 years of age suffers from hearing difficulty, a rising problem in Canada and worldwide. A person who experiences hearing difficulties may have difficulties communicating with others. As a result, they may suffer from loneliness, depression, and stigmatization. The occurrence of hearing loss is affected by environmental factors such as exposure to noise, ototoxic medications, and diseases. However, hearing difficulty among old people (Age-Related Hearing Loss, ARHL) is also inherited. Unfortunately, the genetic factors contributing to this condition are not very well understood. Our research aims to bridge this knowledge gap and understand the genetic causes of ARHL using state-of-the-art computational analyses. We have obtained genomic and hearing measurement data from 26,622 healthy individuals from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging. Using a mathematical method, we calculated two hearing loss parameters. (i) the sensory parameter, which is attributed to excessive exposure to noise and ear-damaging drugs, and (ii) the metabolic parameter, which is more related to the aging process. We then conducted genomic analyses to identify genetic factors that can increase the probability of experiencing each hearing loss type. We have also performed analyses in males and females separately to determine whether there are any differences. Our primary genetic analyses showed genetic differences leading to the two hearing loss conditions, as well as differences between sex groups. As we expected, we found that metabolic hearing loss was higher for older compared to younger individuals, with no noticeable difference between males and females. In contrast, sensory hearing loss was not found to increase greatly with age, and males showed more sensory hearing loss compared to females.

column36: Culturally Inclusive Menu Planning in Long-Term Care (LTC)
column37: Canada's older adult population is growing and becoming more culturally diverse. Immigration is a driving force behind this change as a proportion of recent immigrants are older adults and earlier cohorts of immigrants are aging. Older adults, including those who immigrated to Canada, with chronic health issues and functional limitations may require long-term care (LTC) home placement. With this ongoing shift in demographics, it is essential for LTC homes to establish culturally inclusive care practices to meet the needs of a culturally diverse older adult population. Food consumed by diverse populations is a symbol of individual identity, ethnicity, and cultural belonging. Sensory properties of food such as taste, smell, and familiarity with food are some factors impacting food intake. Menu items that do not meet individual preferences can result in meal dissatisfaction and is a significant risk factor for malnutrition due to inadequate intake of food and fluids in culturally diverse older adults residing in LTC homes. Previous research has identified the need for improving menu items for culturally diverse residents in LTC homes, however, the process to enhance menu planning for this population has not been established. The objectives of this research are to determine the experiences and perspectives of food service managers and dietitians, including barriers/facilitators, to developing culturally inclusive menus in Ontario LTC homes; to describe culturally diverse resident and family perspectives on the challenges and facilitators of accessing and attaining culturally inclusive foods within LTC homes; to determine, document and compare and contrast the main activities and processes undertaken by LTC homes with diverse representation to develop culturally inclusive menus. This will help identify best practices for developing menus in LTC homes that incorporate culturally appropriate meals to promote food intake, quality of life and inclusivity of all residents.

column36: The association of functional and structural social support with cognitive change in middle-aged and older adults: Results from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging
column37: While the COVID-19 outbreak has drawn attention to the importance of social support, and the consequences of social isolation, little is known about the long-term impacts of social resources on health. This is particularly true for cognition. Cognitive function refers to a collection of mental processes such as memory and executive function that allow an individual to complete both simple and complex tasks like planning and problem solving. Previous studies examining the role of social resources on cognition have largely depended on objective social support (e.g., marital status) rather than subjective measures (e.g., whether an individual believes they have someone to help with chores if they need it), which may more accurately assess available support. This, as well as incomplete, inconsistent and overlapping definitions of the various components that make up social support, mean the impact of subjective and objective social support on cognitive health is not well understood. This study will elucidate these relationships by investigating: 1) how subjective and objective social support are associated with cognition at baseline and over time, and 2) whether subjective support explains the relationship between objective measures of social support and cognitive health. Analyses will use data from over 30,000 participants in the Comprehensive cohort of the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging, an ongoing study of community-dwelling adults aged 45-85 at recruitment. Given the role that cognition plays in daily functioning and adaptation to change, cognitive decline is a major concern for many adults. A better understanding of the role that social support plays in preserving cognition is vital for the creation of effective policies and interventions aimed at minimizing age-related cognitive decline through reducing social isolation in mid- to late-life.

column36: Examining a Nature-Based Mindfulness-Compassion Intervention Delivered Via Virtual Reality: Applications for Older Adults
column37: The global population is aging at an unprecedented rate, increasing the necessity for effective interventions targeting the mental health needs of older adults. Technology addressing the aging process of older adults (i.e., gerontechnology) is an avenue for the efficient delivery of programs that enhance older adult well-being. Virtual reality (VR) is a type of gerontechnology with the potential to improve mental health and well-being; however, evidence in this area is currently lacking and more rigorous research on the feasibility, acceptability, and effectiveness of mental health programming via VR for older adults, such as nature, mindfulness, or compassion-based interventions, is necessary. The proposed program of research seeks to pilot a 4-week nature-mindfulness-compassion meditation program using a multi-user 360-HD video VR application, "Toujours Dimanche" for older adults with varying levels of autonomy. The first study explores the development, feasibility, acceptability, and efficacy of Toujours Dimanche on autonomous older adults' mental health and well-being. The second study explores the impact of Toujours Dimanche modified for use with older adults residing in long-term care centres (CHSLDs) due to significant reductions in autonomy. Feasibility, acceptability, and efficacy will be examined through a mixed-methods longitudinal RCT featuring resident, staff, and caregiver reports. Ultimately, if "Toujours Dimanche" is found to be acceptable and effective for older adults, it will have the potential to promote geriatric mental health utilizing a technology that is accessible, as well as safe.

column36: Resident and Family Engagement in Nursing Homes
column37: The devastating impacts of COVID-19 on nursing home residents across Canada has drawn public attention to systemic problems and the restricted rights and freedoms of citizens residing in nursing homes. column36: The effect of passive cycling on executive function in longer-living older adults
column37: I am applying to the Summer Program in Aging, as I believe that it will provide me with a broad understanding of interventions implemented to address issues that longer-living older adults experience through a multidisciplinary lens. During my Master's degree, I would like to investigate the effect an acute bout of passive (no effort) cycling has on executive function. Executive function is an important set of processes involved in control of behavior and is important for everyday living. It is known that older adults experience declines in executive function. We hypothesize that passive cycling will result in a post-exercise executive function improvement, evident through improved performance on a task evaluating executive function using eye tracking movements. Passive cycling is an excellent method of exercise to implement in longer-living older populations due to mobility issues that commonly arise with age. The research is significant as it expands our understanding of the processes that lead to executive function improvements, the influence of different types of exercise on cognition in older adults and can further aid in the establishment of interventions that address cognitive decline in longer-living older adults. I believe that attending SPA will aid me with my research project it will expand my understanding of different methodological approaches used in older adult research. It will also enhance my understanding of issues longer-living older adults face, specifically relating to dementia and mobility, and will guide future research I conduct towards addressing these problems.

column36: Quality of life of persons living with dementia and care partners
column37: There are approximately 55 million people with dementia worldwide, and in the following 30 years, this number is expected to triple. Dementia has a significant impact on the quality of life of PWD and family care partners due to the combination of mental, physical, financial challenges and the COVID-19 pandemic. As part of an international project, Forward with Dementia, funded by the European Union and CIHR, we ask people with dementia and care partners in five countries: Canada, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Poland, and Australia, about their quality of life and the care they receive. Specifically, I will focus on dementia diagnosis, care plans and coping strategies, and the impact of the pandemic (e.g. worry about health, depression, isolation, financial burden) on their quality of life. I am also interested to understand how factors such as age, gender, race, immigration, rural-urban location, and living conditions affect quality of life. Although the quality of care provided to people with dementia is known to be insufficient, little is known about the impact of the quality of care on the quality of life of people with dementia and care partners. It is critical to understand the factors that influence this association to improve health and social services. The results of this research will help the development of recommendations in partnership with people with dementia and care partners, as well as healthcare professionals.

column36: Investigating the Neural Mechanisms and Cognitive Training Effects of Multiple Object Tracking on Older Adults' Cognition, Mobility and Multitasking Performances
column37: Many everyday activities involve processing visual scenes with multiple moving objects (e.g., pedestrians, cars) while walking or balancing (i.e., dual-tasking). Such divided attention poses a challenge for older adults due to age-related declines in attentional capacity and the need to compensate for vision and hearing loss. Declines in attentional capacity can have consequences on cognition and mobility, and therefore increase falls risk, and reduce quality of life and longevity. Training interventions aimed at improving divided attention are therefore critical. Seated executive function training has shown efficacy for improving dual-task walking and balance. However, it remains unclear whether cognitive training administered in a cognitive-motor format is even more effective at improving mobility. Results from our own pilot study demonstrate improved single- and dual-task walking speed, and single-task backwards counting, following 4 weeks of computerized seated or standing multiple object tracking (MOT) training. We do not yet know how this type of training changes brain activity, and whether a longer training period can have greater effects on cognition and mobility in older adults. Therefore, the aim of this research is to evaluate and compare the effects single or dual-task MOT or episodic memory training (active control) has on older adults' mobility, cognition, multitasking and brain activity. Training will be performed at home on a computer for 3 days a week (24 minutes/day) for 6 weeks. Pre and post assessments will be completed in lab. We predict that MOT training will enhance neural activation in areas of the brain associated with attention, working memory and motion perception, and therefore improve cognitive-motor multitasking performances. This study will help us understand whether MOT training can lead to neuroplasticity that would in turn improve older adults' cognition and mobility which could have benefits on their quality of life and longevity.

column37: At least 1 in 3 people (2.4 billion people) globally will require rehabilitation at some point in their life, and the need for rehabilitation is increasing. Consequently, the World Health Organization (WHO) issued a call to strengthen access to rehabilitation as an essential part of universal health coverage globally. Back pain is the leading cause of disability and main reason for unmet rehabilitation needs in Canada and worldwide. These unmet rehabilitation needs greatly affect older adults with chronic conditions and complex functional limitations. I will leverage national longitudinal data to understand the burden, determinants, and health inequities of unmet rehabilitation needs for back pain. This novel population risk tool will guide optimal prevention strategies and health care planning. This research will have unique contributions and policy impact to improve the health of older Canadians, and incorporates the perspectives of a diverse advisory committee, including persons with lived experience. The Summer Program in Aging is strongly aligned with this research and will elevate my career path by strengthening my expertise (i.e., multidisciplinary and methodological approaches, EDI and SGBA+ considerations, policy, knowledge mobilization) and network in the area of Longer-living Older Adults.

column36: The Impact of Preoperative Physical Activity on Postoperative Delirium in Cardiac Surgical Patients: A Prospective Study
column37: Patients who need heart operations are getting older and weaker. These patients often experience difficulties such as new confusion called delirium which occurs in roughly 1 in 5 patients after their operation. Symptoms can include, abnormal thinking or perceptions (such as hallucinations). These symptoms can be quite scary and, in some cases, can lead to longer-term issues with memory or new mental health issues such as depression or post-traumatic stress disorder. In addition, severe cases of delirium results in longer stay in the hospital and an even greater risk of death. Furthermore, taking care of a patient with delirium can be more difficult than the treatment of heart disease itself. Delirium once it occurs, does not have any specific treatment, so often the "best medicine" is prevention. Previous studies in patients undergoing hip or knee operation have found that physical activity before the operation may improve brain function to reduce the chances of experiencing delirium. However, there is not much information for the heart surgery patient, who are usually less active and more likely to experience delirium as compared to other types of major surgery. The purpose of this study is to see if a low-cost plan of basic, scheduled physical activity is safe and helps predict delirium occurrence after heart operation.

column36: Establishing a Research Career to Support High Quality, Equitable Care for Older Adults Living with Dementia
column37: Older adults often face difficulties accessing healthcare services. This is especially true in my hometown in rural British Columbia (BC). It motivates my interest in older adult care, equity, and healthcare services. For five years, I have conducted research related to older adults. My focus has been on those living with dementia and frailty. I have an understanding of the challenges they experience, and those of our health system. My past and current research aims to address these challenges and improve their care. As a master's student, my goals are still to support the care of older adults. My thesis will examine the effect of the pandemic on quality of dementia care for older adults living in BC. I will use the results to plan interventions to improve quality of dementia care. I will also share the results with policymakers and healthcare service providers. The results will help them make decisions and set goals for healthcare delivery. I plan to continue this work through further education (PhD) and future employment. Care and support for older adults and people living with dementia is multidisciplinary. column36: Traitement psychotherapeutique de la symptomatologie depressive concomitante au trouble neurocognitif du a la maladie d' Alzheimer et au trouble neurocognitif leger
column37: Une importante proportion de personnes vivant avec un trouble neurocognitif leger (TCL) et un trouble neurocognitif du a la maladie d'Alzheimer (TNMA) sont touchees par la depression. Or, la depression chez le TNMA peut entrainer une perte significative de la qualite de vie et une institutionnalisation prematuree. Au sein du TCL, celle-ci est un facteur de risque pour une progression vers le TNMA. Malgre cela, peu d'etudes s'interessent aux benefices d'une intervention individuelle, axee sur les emotions et la relation therapeutique, pour traiter la depression chez cette population. La psychotherapie psychodynamique interpersonnelle (PPI), bien que peu etudiee chez le TNMA et pas du tout chez le TCL, est une avenue de traitement interessante. Ainsi, cette etude vise a mesurer l'efficacite de la PPI pour traiter la depression chez les patients vivant avec un TNMA et de l'adapter pour la premiere fois, et mesurer son efficacite, pour les patients vivant avec un TCL. Pour ce faire, 30 personnes vivant avec un TNMA et 30 personnes vivant avec un TCL seront recrutees. Dans chaque groupe, la moitie des participants recevront l'intervention et l'autre moitie seront sur une liste d'attente, qui servira de comparaison. La PPI tire profit de certaines capacites preservees dans le TNMA, comme la memoire inconsciente, et elle sera modifiee pour mieux tenir compte des capacites preservees et du tableau depressif specifiques au TCL. Les effets de l'intervention seront evalues a l'aide de questionnaires mesurant les symptomes depressifs a trois moments (avant, apres la 12e seance, et un mois apres l'intervention), puis l'humeur et l'interet seront evalues chaque semaine. Cette etude aura d'importantes retombees, car un traitement permettant une attenuation des symptomes depressifs ameliorerait la qualite de vie et le bien-etre de ces personnes, voir retarder l'institutionnalisation dans le cas du TNMA et retarder la progression vers un TNMA dans le cas du TCL.

column36: Advancing Preventive Care for Healthy Aging
column37: The purpose of this study is to explore influences and differences in preventive care use across the older adult age spectrum. With the expected two-to-six-fold growth of Canadians 75 and older and tripling of the proportion of individuals 85 years and older over the next 30 years, promoting healthy aging is all the more critical. Preventive care refers to screening (e.g., mammography) and immunization (e.g., flu shot) services offered to the general population based on age, sex, and risk factors for disease. The purpose of preventive care services is to reduce morbidity, increase early disease detection, and reduce chronic disease prevalence. The goal of meeting preventive care use targets is ultimately to maximize quality of life. Older adults have, on average more preventive service recommendations than younger adults, yet have low use of services. Numerous barriers to accessing preventive services, such as ageism, awareness, or availability, may be key contributors to low use of services. To date, no Canadian studies have explored the impacts of these barriers across the older adult age continuum. Interventions are needed to address these gaps in older adult preventive care. While generic preventive care interventions have made marginal improvements in service uptake, they have not reached targets for completion. This study will address these gaps in knowledge using a combination of surveys and focus groups. Data collected will capture barriers and facilitators of preventive care use. Exploring nuances and influences across the older adult spectrum will produce valuable knowledge for designing and implementing interventions to improve older adult preventive care.
