column36: Postdoctoral Research Project: A mixed methods study of the role of primary care teams in promoting integrated care for longer-living older adults in Ontario retirement homes
column37: Background: The retirement home (RH) sector supports aging in place but is often overlooked. Retirement home residents (RHR) have higher rates of emergency department (ED) visits and hospital admissions compared to nursing home residents, yet a significantly lower rate of primary care visits. The interconnections between the RH and primary care sectors remain poorly understood contributing to a missed opportunity to positively impact the health of RHR and support community-based care. Aims and Methods: This mixed methods, integrated knowledge translation study will develop policy recommendations for improving care integration for longer-living RHR, informed by the lived experiences of RHR, family caregivers, and care providers in Ontario. Aim 1: To describe the experiences of longer-living RHR seeking care across the RH, primary care, and acute care sectors by interviewing 5 longer-living RHR and 5 family caregivers to render a composite "essence" of their care experience. Aim 2: To characterize rates and predictors of acute and primary care use for RHR using the databases held at ICES (formerly the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences) and describe clinical and demographic factors that increase hospitalization risk for RHR. Aim 3: To learn from the experiences of clinicians working with longer-living RHR by building a rich description of current ways of working across the primary care, acute care, and RH sectors in Ontario from key informant interviews with 5 primary care providers and 5 acute care providers in frequent contact with longer-living RHR. Significance: Dealing with strain on EDs and hospital beds is a high priority area. Primary care teams have a unique role to facilitate integrated care across sectors to improve both patient experiences and outcomes for longer-living RHR and health system functioning. Project findings will be used to inform decision making at the Ministries of Health and Seniors and Accessibility, and in Ontario Health Teams.

column37: The landscape of aging research in Canada is evolving rapidly. Canadians are getting older, living longer, and require more specialized care. The devastating effects of COVID-19 on the long-term care sector has unlocked great interest in investing in changes of our care of the elderly. There is already a strong body of evidence-based research describing what good quality care looks like, but we lack a nuanced understanding of how to change our existing system to improve care quality. With my doctoral research, I will develop a practical understanding of how to increase the quality of care and quality of life for our aging Canadians in long-term care (LTC) using realist methods. Answering specific context-dependent questions (what worked, for whom, under what circumstances, and why) characteristic of realist methods and working closely with knowledge-user partners (including healthcare leaders, healthcare staff, residents, and family members) will be essential to increasing the uptake, application, and sustainability of outcomes for this study. Attending the SPA 2023 training program will better prepare me for my doctoral research by expanding my network of scholars for idea-sharing and increased exposure to research innovation in aging, which will contribute to the development of my growing program of research. These cumulative experiences will help me engage more with Implementation Science teams, which will in turn help me learn more about innovation uptake and sustainability. My ultimate goal is to have an academic skills set to implement and evaluate healthcare innovations across diverse sectors and patient populations.

column36: Validation du questionnaire d'Auto-reperage pour Vieillir En Sante (AVES) pour permettre aux personnes ainees d'evaluer elles-memes leurs risques de declin fonctionnel
column37: Avec le vieillissement de la population, on observe une augmentation du nombre de personnes atteintes de maladies chroniques ou d'incapacites. Les incapacites peuvent souvent etre prevenues au moyen de changements aux habitudes de vie. La promotion de tels changements repose generalement sur les professionnels de la sante, mais ceux-ci manquent de temps pour la faire. Ce projet vise donc a valider un nouveau questionnaire concu pour que les personnes puissent evaluer elles-memes leurs risques de perdre certaines capacites liees a l'age et ainsi entreprendre des changements par elles-memes. Le questionnaire se nomme l'Auto-reperage pour Vieillir En Sante, ou AVES. Ce questionnaire sera partie integrante du programme d'education Vieillir en Sante qui sera offert sur un site Internet et dans un livret imprime. Le programme complet comprendra, en plus du questionnaire AVES, de l'information pour encourager les personnes a maintenir leur vigueur, leur vie sociale, leur humeur, leur memoire, leurs poids et leur etat de sante general. Pour repondre a ces objectifs, 50 personnes agees de 70 ans et plus utiliseront l'AVES. Ensuite, un professionnel de la sante evaluera leurs risques de perdre leurs capacites par un examen clinique. On comparera les resultats de l'examen clinique avec ceux de l'AVES. On posera aussi aux personnes quelques questions pour verifier si l'utilisation du questionnaire leur cause des inquietudes. Si le questionnaire AVES s'avere valide, il sera integre au programme d'education Vieillir en Sante, pour permettre aux personnes ainees de mieux prendre en main leur sante en vue de maintenir leur autonomie plus longtemps.

This capacity-building training programme will focus on ensuring patient and Elder engagement; mobilizing existing expertise; supporting the careers of Nunavut's early career researchers and policy developers; collaborating across systems and institutions; and building capacity to address new and emerging patient-oriented research questions and real world problems. Building on SPOR's capacity-building framework, the training program for this Implementation Specialist is organized around tasks and activities that will develop POR competencies as well as further Nunavut-specific POR research questions related to Inuit models of care and integration pathways into the territorial healthcare system.

column36: Advancing Patient-Oriented Research Capacity of Autism Alliance of Canada through an Embedded Patient-Oriented Implementation Project: National Autism Waitlist Initiative
column37: One in fifty Canadian children is estimated to have autism. The majority of persons on the autism spectrum require health, social and/or educational services. However, autistic people are left out of policy decisions that impact their health and wellbeing. As a result, Canada's Healthcare system does not meet the needs of Autistic persons. One of the most pressing issues faced by the autism community is timely access to diagnostic services. Access to early diagnosis can take up to 2 years, and varies significantly between provinces and territories. Moreover, Canada lacks national infrastructure to meaningfully include first voices in research and policy that can help fill important gaps in knowledge. Autism Alliance of Canada proposes to form a diverse National Autism Lived Experience Advisory Group that will build capacity for patient-oriented research. We will make sure our Advisory Group receives support, training and compensation throughout this engagement process. This training will help persons with lived experience understand the research process and communicate and work with researchers as equal partners. The advisory group will provide us feedback on the way we engage with persons with lived experience and gain hands-on experience through working on a high priority project. This project will create an Autism Wait Times Dashboard and generate data on the length of autism diagnosis wait times in autism clinics across the country. Including persons with lived experience as equal partners on our team will ensure that the information collected in this dashboard will reflect the complex journey that people endure to obtain an autism diagnosis. Our work will inform system improvement and policies that support the reduction of wait times. Finally, we will develop recommendations on how to meaningfully engage persons with lived experience in all stages of national initiatives, setting the benchmark for inclusive POR practices for autism research.

column36: Training and mentoring programs in nutrition, obesity and diabetes
column37: Poor dietary habits are the most impactful risk factors for chronic diseases. Successful promotion of healthy eating and optimal nutrition is, therefore, at the core of chronic disease prevention. Yet, healthy eating is far from being a simple paradigm. Mastering the concept of healthy eating requires an in-depth understanding of how nutrients, foods and whole diets impact health from basic, clinical and population health research perspectives. It requires a profound cognizance of behavioral change strategies for successful implementation at the individual and population levels, while accounting for social, cultural, environmental and political inflfluences. This complexity rationalizes the need for transdisciplinary programs to train and mentor the next generations of health professionals and researchers in Canada. The myROaD platform leverages the expertise, successes and extensive infrastructure of six research networks: CMDO, DAC, OC, DREAM, IMPART, CIRTN. The rationale for the present application is to integrate expertise in nutrition and health as well as the CNS to the myROaD platform, with the goal of incorporating highly relevant training and mentoring activities related to nutrition, food and health, for the benefifit of trainees and ECRs within all of these organizations and networks. column36: Lung Health Effects of E-Cigarette Cessation (VAPE)
column37: This project is the first of its kind to simultaneously measure the physiological impact of quitting vaping in humans and the participant's motivation to quit vaping throughout the study and, in particular, after providing personalized biofeedback. The use of electronic cigarettes (also known as vaping), particularly among young adults, has been increasing in Canada. Vaping has been shown to cause irreparable damage to the lungs and may lead to traditional tobacco cigarette use. In British Columbia, some public health measures have been taken to regulate the sale and use of vapes, with the most recent being policy limiting the nicotine content in e-liquids to 2omg per mL. However, there has been very limited research into how best to provide support for those who want to quit vaping, particularly tobacco-naive young adults. The first objective of our project is to understand how stopping vaping for 72 hours might affect the lung health of young adults who otherwise vape regularly. The second objective is to see if giving personalized biofeedback, which includes any changes in lung health that were observed over the 72-hour period, to the individual would affect their motivation to quit vaping going forward.

column36: Mental health services and child welfare: understanding the practices, principles, values, and needs of youth mental health and child welfare service systems to improve mental health service integration for children and youth in care in a pan-Canadian context
column37: Childhood and youth are periods of promise and are also when mental health and substance use problems often emerge. Families often face long wait-times; complicated pathways; and poor-quality, unfriendly services when trying to access care. This is particularly challenging for those in the child welfare system, who face major system obstacles such as a lack of continuity across multiple service delivery systems. Coupled with this unresponsive system are the intersecting oppressions faced by many youth in care, including racism, stigmatization, and language barriers. To improve the mental health care offered to those in the child welfare system, we need to understand how youth, families, service providers, decision makers do their daily work and how they currently integrate knowledge, training, and recent practice recommendations. We also need to understand what helps and what hinders the use of current guidelines and the roles each service takes in integrating and coordinating care. To do this, this project will use many methods (interviews, focus groups, reviewing documents, etc.) involving all key groups (youth, families, staff, managers, policymakers). We will learn from individuals in the youth mental health and child welfare systems - what they do, what they should do, how to improve and progress toward these goals, what trainings are needed. Our team includes decision makers from francophone and anglophone Child welfare services in Montreal, Quebec, as well as a decision-maker from the Ministry of Health and Social Services, researchers, and clinicians. We will continue to partner with them and share our findings widely and creatively to make sure that our research makes sense and actually changes services and policy. Our team will pay attention to equity so that all Quebecers in the child welfare system can receive the mental health support they need. Our findings will also guide norms and standards for child and youth mental health in the rest of Canada.

column36: Contextual factors predicting feasibility and impact of preventive mental health interventions across Canada
column37: The PreVenture Program involves providing youth with brief cognitive-behavioural interventions in youth-oriented settings and has proven remarkably effective in reducing and preventing alcohol and illicit drug use and mental health symptoms by 30-80% among high-risk secondary students in multiple published randomised trials. Through these trials, PreVenture training capacity is in place in multiple youth-focused settings across the country, including middle and high schools, university campuses, community youth mental health teams, child welfare and Indigenous led settings. Digital tools have been developed to support training and supervision of practitioners, as well as screening, quality control and outcome evaluation. Over 400 North American practitioners have been trained to deliver Preventure in their settings, and remain engaged in an interactive community of practice focusing on preventive mental health. The applicants are uniquely positioned to evaluate implementation standards in preventive mental health. The findings will directly inform how future practitioners are trained and how the program is best rolled out in diverse communities across Canada. Study Aims: This study will evaluate uptake, quality, acceptability, and short-term impact of Preventure when delivered to youth across Canada through a variety of settings in both digital and in-person formats. The intervention maintains many of its essential components across settings (group-based, peer-interactions, facilitator-guided discussions, structured personality-targeted cognitive-behavioural exercises), and is provided by trained facilitators to youth. Settings vary on degree of cultural adaptation, intensity and quality of training protocol, type of youth population served, geographic location, discipline or qualification of facilitators. Available implementation and outcome evaluation databases will be used to study factors that lead to greater uptake, acceptability and impact.

column36: Bridging the gap from "standards" to "wise practices" in youth mental health: Co-designing approaches for adapting and applying standards and learning health system thinking to support Indigenous youth and communities
column37: Many youths face inaccessible, poor-quality, unfriendly mental healthcare. Indigenous youths have it worse due to intergenerational trauma, culturally inappropriate care, limited services, remoteness, etc. Recently, Canada has invested a lot in improving youth mental health services. Standards are being developed for what makes services high-quality along with strategies to put these standards into practice (e.g., by giving feedback to staff and training them on standards). Some standards have been developed for Indigenous contexts, but most focus on general youth populations. Our study will examine the "whether," "when" and "how" of applying standards for Indigenous contexts and youths so that they, too, can gain the better access and quality that standards can produce. Cultural safety and suitability will be important considerations. Our first aim is to understand the views of Indigenous youths, community members, decision-makers and service providers on standards and their application. We will also document whether and how Canadian teams developing standards consider Indigenous youths' needs. Our second aim is to collate current knowledge on how standards that were not developed for Indigenous contexts have been applied in Indigenous contexts. Our third aim is to co-develop a process for applying standards that considers cultural (e.g., Indigenous views on health) and contextual (e.g., remoteness) factors. For Aim 1, we will use interviews, sharing circles and arts-based methods. For Aim 2, we will summarize findings from papers and reports. For Aim 3, we will share findings from Aim 1 with key stakeholders and co-design a process to apply standards in a workshop. Our team of Indigenous youths, researchers, service providers and decision-makers will implement this study together and share its findings creatively. Thus bringing Indigenous ways of knowing to quality standards can help address equity gaps and support the mental health of Indigenous youths.

column36: Indigenous youth and mental health: Indigenous knowledges solutions for personal and community healing and the climate crisis
column37: Indigenous youth are often identified as a vulnerable population with respect to mental health. Indigenous youth mental health is a complex problem that has its roots in both historical oppression and current discrimination; recent research shows that challenges related to cultural identity, culture clash between biomedical service and Indigenous ways of healing, and failure of Canada's health policy, are factors that underpin and mediate Indigenous mental health problems. Further, youth have identified that the climate crisis has a major impact on their mental health and identify it as a variable over which they may be able to exert some autonomy in a world where they feel disempowered. The research question was developed in a pilot project by youth and Elders and is: What are the mental health impacts of climate change for Indigenous youth, and what services are needed to support youth? Working with providers of Indigenous mental health care in Toronto and Yellowknife, Dr. Stewart and team will develop and evaluate culturally based evidence-based programs to improve the mental health of youth with a goal to reduce and end Indigenous youth mental health problems. There is a lack of evaluation data generally in youth mental services and specifically in Indigenous contexts. Indigenous community partners and Dr. Stewart's team will work together to document the availability, utilization, and experiences of mental health care for Indigenous youth individuals through mixed methods of surveys and individual interviews; they will also develop Indigenous youth mental health programs and interventions that will include evaluation tools based in Indigenous traditional knowledges. The team will work with community partners to hold a series of Indigenous circle focus group meetings with traditional knowledge keepers and youth to identify barriers, strengths, and solutions to themes identified in the survey and individual interview data.

column36: Mental health standards in youth justice settings in Canada
column37: Mental health concerns are highly prevalent among youth involved in the justice system. Too often, however, the mental health needs of such youth remain unmet. This is particularly concerning given that the justice system is often the first point of contact for mental health services for many youth. Addressing the mental health needs of justice-involved youth requires confronting limitations with regard to standards for mental health and substance use services within youth justice settings. Given that racialized or marginalized youth are more likely to be in contact with the justice system, there is especially a need to consider equity and cultural safety in standards in mental health services. The proposed project will engage with decision-makers and mental health service providers within youth justice settings, as well as justice-involved youth and family members throughout the research process such that their input is integrated. We will review the literature on existing standards for mental health and substance use services within youth justice settings, as well as investigate limitations of existing standards with regard to scope and uptake, identify other challenges as well as potential paths to uptake of standards into routine practice in justice settings. We will conduct focus groups with mental health service providers and others who work with justice-involved youth, as well as interviews with youth with lived experience in justice settings and their families. Such work will inform the development of new or improved standards or guiding principles for mental health and substance use services within youth justice settings that can improve equity and outcomes across groups.

column36: Building National Standards for the Provision of Psychoeducation for Youth Depression
column37: Youth depression is prevalent, has risen sharply recently, and is associated with adverse outcomes, such as having more frequent and severe depressive episodes, suicide attempts, and greater impairment in social, cognitive, and occupational functioning compared to adult-onset depression. The provision of psychoeducation for youth depression (i.e., what depression is, what contributes to it, and how to address it) has been shown to reduce symptom distress and the need for more intensive treatment. However, the extent to which it is provided following a diagnosis varies, as does its depth of content. Thus, the development and dissemination of contemporary clinical practice guidelines (PGs) on the provision of psychoeducation for youth depression is urgently needed. This project has three main objectives: (1) through a systematic review, identify, evaluate, and appraise all PGs on psychoeducation for youth depression; (2) using qualitative methods, elicit multi-stakeholders' perceptions of the barriers/facilitators to implementing PGs on psychoeducation for youth depression; and (3) using a co-design process with youth with lived experiences of depression, caregivers, and child health care providers, develop recommendations for national PGs on psychoeducation for youth depression. Our team has extensive experience with systematic reviews, qualitative methods, and engaging with youth, caregivers, and providers. Together with our stakeholders, we have expansive networks and resources to help disseminate findings and outputs. We will use a robust knowledge mobilization strategy to relay information on optimal approaches for delivering psychoeducation on youth depression, with the ultimate goal of increasing the likelihood that psychoeducation on youth depression is provided, and that the mental health of Canadian youth is improved.

column36: "Where do you want to go?": Developing Practice Principles for Inclusive Goal-Based Outcome Monitoring With Youth in Community Mental Health Services
column37: Working with goals is a powerful tool to facilitate shared-decision making and is a foundational element of most youth mental health interventions across the care continuum (school-based, primary care, community mental health). However, lack of best-practice guidance for working with goals means it can become a bureaucratic tick box task instead of a meaningful process for youth. Clinicians working with goals lack resources about how diversity, equity and inclusion need to be considered or how data from goal-based outcomes can support system improvement. Aims: 1) equip clinicians and health system leaders with practice principles for goal-based outcome monitoring informed by youth, carers and research evidence; 2) situate goal-based practice principles within diverse, equitable and inclusive approaches; 3) accelerate knowledge exchange about goal-based outcomes data. Approach: Phase 1: scoping review from a health equity lens will identify and appraise a list of candidate practice principles found in research evidence and grey literature. Phase 2A: virtual roundtables [80 participants] will be held to deliberate over candidate practice principles identified in Phase1. Roundtables will involve youth, carers, clinicians, researchers, policy makers and diversity, equity and inclusion advocates. Phase 2B: in-person consensus meeting with 20-25 key partners to finalize practice principles document, promote networking among team members, and identify future lines of goal-based outcome research. Co-authored open-source articles and audience-specific knowledge products will be co-developed and translated. Team: 12-16 member team including youth, carers, providers, policy makers, researchers and equity-leaders will co-lead all project activities. National and international partners (Mental Health Commission of Canada, National Collaborating Centre for Determinants of Health, Maritime TREATme (European Network) have committed to the project.

column36: Pathways for youth from emergency departments to community services
column37: In Canada, a quarter of young people will experience a mental health or substance use disorder. Many of them will present to an emergency department as the first point of contact with health services for these concerns. However, emergency departments usually do not have pathways in place to help young people connect with services in their community to get the help they need for mental health and substance use issues. For this project, we will develop a standard that emergency departments can use to direct young people with mental health and substance use concerns to needed youth-centred health services. We will use a combination of methods during two stages of work. In the first stage, we will use guidance from the Health Standards Organization to draft the standard with the help of a technical committee and a consensus-building exercise called Delphi. In the second stage, we will dialogue with young people, emergency department physicians and staff, community health service providers, and decision makers to refine and finalize the draft standards. Our team will meet with networks across Canada to translate findings into practice and produce several knowledge products to inform and improve uptake of the standards. This work will improve early intervention in Canada for mental health and substance use concerns and lead to improved short- and long-term outcomes for young people and their communities.

column36: Facilitating the implementation of quality standards for youth and family engagement within the community child and youth mental health and substance use health system.
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic has negatively impacted the mental health and well-being of many young people living in Canada, underscoring the need to address long-standing gaps in the delivery of mental health and substance use health services across the country. Quality standards can help ensure consistent, high-quality care, but they must be supported by people and resources to change the delivery of healthcare services in an impactful way. The meaningful engagement of young people and families in the healthcare sector can positively impact service experiences and outcomes and is considered an essential component of quality standard development and implementation. Since 2020, the community child and youth mental health and substance use health sector in Ontario has been supported by two standards for meaningful youth and family engagement. Evaluation of early efforts to implement these standards points to difficulties in measuring the standards, understanding agency-specific and practical approaches to implementation, and sustaining implementation without significant, specialized support. The proposed project will build on these early efforts by examining (a) the barriers and facilitators to the uptake of youth and family engagement standards, (b) the sector's vision of successfully implementing these standards, and (c) possible intervention strategies to support adoption and use of the standards. Findings will inform practices in effective youth and family engagement, and implementation of standards across Canada. The work will also contribute to the development and implementation strategies for new pan-Canadian standards for mental health and substance use health services for children, youth and families, ultimately supporting long-term transformation and better health outcomes among young people in Canada.

column36: Standards for Black Youth Mental Health Services
column37: Recent attention in both research and practice has identified and begun to explore the mental health needs amongst Black youth globally as well as within Canada. However, little is known about mental health standards for Black youth in the community context including community organizations and services, in primary care settings such as clinics and hospitals, and in the educational system. The purpose of this study is to identify and map mental health standards for Black youth in Canada and globally, and suggest potential improvements. We will conduct a synthesis of current literature on mental health standards in community, primary care, and educational settings. Next, we will conduct focus group interviews with Black youths, aged 16 to 25 years and living in eight locations across Canada. Findings from the literature synthesis on mental health standards for Black youth will be shared with participating Black youths. These focus group participants will be invited to disclose their thoughts on the findings and any improvements that can be made to mental health standards for Black youth. Findings from this study will be shared through academic conference presentations, presentations to policymakers at all levels of government in Canada, publications in peer-reviewed academic journals, and policy and practice briefs. This study will contribute to identifying existing mental health standards for Black youth, gaps in standards, and areas for improvement. Given the need to further understand and address mental health amongst Black youth in Canada, this study will build an understanding of existing standards that is essential to move forward, and will offer improvements to standards that can be applied to mental health policy and practice in Canada.

column36: Machine Learning and Single-cell Analysis
column37: One of the most significant technological developments in biology is single-cell genomics technologies. These technologies enable scientists to measure aspects of individual cells to study the cellular organization of human tissues. Unlike cells, the fundamental units of life, where we know their standard components and general organization, our knowledge of tissues is somewhat limited. A deep understanding of tissue biology, e.g., homeostasis, tissue injury, inflammation, and tissue repair, has the potential to transform our understanding and treatment of a variety of tissue diseases of multicellular organisms, such as drug-resistant cancers. Dr. Ding's research combines single-cell measurements and mathematical modeling to help distill the principles of tissue cellular organization. Single-cell data are typically noisy, high-dimensional, and are frequently confounded by a set of biological or technical batch vectors, where the data in one batch differ systematically from the data in another batch. A central challenge to model such data is to develop human-interpretable models with calibrated uncertainty information to help extract a set of 'latent factors' to explain the variations in the observed data. Latent factors could represent specific functions that a cell performs. Uncovering such latent factors and how they are coordinated under different disease conditions is essential to understanding cellular interactions, which could help shape cellular organization in tissues. Interpretable, scalable, and powerful computational models coupled with single-cell measurements have enabled Dr. Ding and collaborators to identify cellular and molecular features correlated with diseases, and gain deep insights into tissue functions and dysfunctions. Ultimately, Dr. Ding's research will help reveal the principles of human tissue organization in development, homeostasis, and disease. It will also help support data-driven clinical decision-making (translational).

column36: The contribution of sex differences to small airways disease in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)
column37: This project uses high-resolution imaging to enable us to see the smallest airways within the lung, which are the most important airways for the disease process, but not visible using clinical imaging techniques. COPD (chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) causes an estimated 380 million people daily to struggle to breathe. In Canada and other developed countries, the number of hospitalizations and deaths due to COPD is now greater for females than males. Using high-resolution CT imaging we recently discovered that COPD patients have difficulty breathing because the smallest airways that carry air in and out of the lungs are destroyed even before the disease can be detected using current clinical tests. Now, we want to determine if the small airways are lost more rapidly in females than in males who develop COPD. We will determine if female smokers are at a greater risk of developing severe early-onset COPD compared to male smokers due to sex differences in small airway pathology. Using micro CT, which has a resolution 1000 times greater than clinical CT, we will test if females with COPD have a greater loss of small airways compared to males. Next, we will assess if the cells (lung fibroblasts) that are important for forming the structure of the airways are altered in females compared to males. Lastly, we will test what immune cells are recruited into the small airways of females and males with COPD, to determine if they play a role in small airway destruction. This project will generate new knowledge on sex differences in the pathobiology of small airway disease in COPD for clinicians, researchers, and patients, to improve treatment and disease outcomes.

column36: The physiological mechanisms of improved exertional dyspnea and functional exercise capacity associated with antifibrotic therapy in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF)
column37: This study is uniquely positioned to characterize the structure-function-symptom response and to determine how Nintedanib improves IPF outcomes. This will be the first study to correlate lung imaging measures with improvements in exercise capacity and breathlessness due to a pharmaceutical intervention in IPF. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) is a chronic progressive lung disease of unknown cause, which leads to scarring of the lungs and results in debilitating reductions of both exercise tolerance and functional abilities. This is strongly associated with reduced quality of life and mortality. Improving breathlessness and reducing functional limitations are therefore critical goals in the management of IPF. Nintedanib, an oral drug, reduces scarring of the lungs and slows the progressive decline of respiratory health seen in IPF. However, few studies have assessed how this therapy affects important clinical outcomes, such as breathlessness and exercise tolerance. Moreover, the mechanisms by which this therapeutic intervention improves lung health remain relatively unknown. This study aims to delve deeper into the effects of nintedanib on breathlessness, cardiorespiratory measures (e.g., heart rate, breathing frequency, ventilation etc.,), and breathing mechanics. Further, it will assess the relationship between lung imaging measures and changes in breathlessness and exercise tolerance. Lung imaging, cycle exercise testing, assessment of breathing muscles (diaphragm and neck) activity, and breathlessness questionnaires will be used to find novel correlations between lung structure and function and Nintedanib use, as these changes may go undetected with routine lung function testing. The results of our study will further our understanding of the physiological mechanisms of exercise intolerance and breathlessness in IPF and add insight into the clinical benefits of Nintedanib in IPF. Moreover, it may provide insight into the characteristics or symptoms of IPF that see the greatest improvement with this anti-scarring therapy, which may allow for a better understanding of which individuals will yield the greatest benefit from this treatment option.

column36: Respiratory Oscillometry for Early Diagnosis of Chronic Lung Allograft Dysfunction
column37: This is the first study using oscillometry to predict development of CLAD. Our study results may help to diagnose CLAD earlier, enable clinical studies for evaluate potential therapies, and improve patient survival. Lung transplantation (LTx) is an established treatment option for patients with end-stage lung diseases. While survival following LTx has steadily improved, chronic rejection, known as chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD) remains the main barrier. CLAD develops in over half of the patients by 5 years after LTx. The only treatment is another transplant. The diagnosis of CLAD is an irreversible decline (=20% from baseline) in the forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) for at least 3 months. This means CLAD cannot be confirmed until 3 months after onset, hampering clinical trials of potential new therapies. CLAD has two different clinical presentations. The disease process is different, as one has significantly worse survival than the other and may require different tailored management. Oscillometry, a novel lung function test, is highly sensitive to changes in the lung tissue. Work in our group showed it to be more sensitive than spirometry in detecting acute rejection, and my first-authored paper found that oscillometry can differentiate between the different types of CLAD at time of the first drop in FEV1 and from patients without CLAD. We hypothesis that oscillometry can detect early signs of lung dysfunction to identify patients at risk of rejection. The aim of this project is to conduct predictive analysis of oscillometry in the post-transplant follow-up of patients to identify CLAD. Over 550 patients from the Toronto Lung Transplant Program with at least 2 years of follow-up are already enrolled in an ongoing prospective observational study of oscillometry post-lung transplant. The Toronto Lung Transplant Research Database maintains an up-to-date comprehensive lifelong clinical data off all patients. We will conduct a comprehensive analysis the data. We will use one-way analysis-of-variance and paired tests to characterize the oscillometry patterns between patients with and without chronic rejection and identify key differences. To generate a predictive model, we will employ logistic regression model toforecast relationships between oscillometry parameters CLAD and CLAD phenotypes. Findings from our study is expected to identify earlier patients at risk CLAD, paving the way for future studies of new therapeutic s or interventions before CLAD is established.CLAD is the biggest obstacle to long term survival post-transplant. Due to the scarcity of lungs, and the intensive resource expanded for each patient, it is imperative to develop therapies that can improve life expectancy and reduce morbidity post-transplant.

column36: Alternative metrics of sleep apnea severity derived from polysomnography
column37: Identifying novel useful metrics in the context of this common disease would result in a paradigm shift in clinical care; away from the predominately 'one size fits all' approach that relies on the AHI. Specifically, these metrics will help identify patients at high risk of adverse outcomes, who should be targeted for more aggressive OSA therapy and targeted risk factor management (more precision-care approach). Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) affects approximately one billion adults globally and is characterized by repetitive upper airway collapse leading to fragmented sleep, hypoxemia, sympathetic activation, surges in blood pressure, cortical activation, vasoconstriction, and tachycardia. However, one major challenge is the inability to predict which OSA patients are particularly vulnerable as standard OSA severity metrics (e.g., apnea-hypopnea index- AHI) are not that helpful. Identifying high-risk patients would be clinically useful for targeting more aggressive clinical interventions. The overall goal is to develop alternative metrics of OSA severity derived from polysomnography (PSG) that can predict OSA-related adverse outcomes better than standard PSG metrics. Specifically, I will: 1) Determine which physiologic PSG signals are most affected by respiratory events, and which are most related to degree of event-related hypoxemia; 2) Using the data from Objective 1, I will develop novel physiologic metrics and assess whether they can predict outcomes better than standard metrics. We will leverage data from the CSCN databank which consists of over 2000 adults referred for suspected OSA with detailed phenotyping (>1600 have had PSG). For objective 1, PSG (EDF format) will be analyzed in MATLAB; for each event (i.e., apnea/hypopnea), we will determine the extent to which a variety of physiologic signals change (e.g. change in EEG power bands delta/theta/alpha/beta/gamma, heart rate response, dampening of the plethysmography signal). For each event, the area under the desaturation curve (HBEV) will be calculated form the SpO2 signal to determine degree of event related hypoxemia. For each subject, mixed effects models will be used to evaluate the association between HBEV and changes in signals (adjusting for confounders). For objective 2, we will examine the most promising signals from 1) to develop new metrics of OSA severity that would account for event-related changes in physiology (e.g. sum of changes in alpha power across events). The association between these metrics and outcomes (e.g. cognitive function, incident cardiovascular disease) will be ascertained, and compared to standard PSG metrics (AHI). OSA is an important and common lung disease. This research will improve care and health outcomes in these patients and is thus of significant relevance to the aims of the Lung Association.

column36: Inspiration-expiration CT texture-based delta radiomics: a new biomarker associated with COPD symptoms?
column37: No prior studies have investigated texture-based delta radiomics analysis in inspiration-expiration images in COPD. Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (COPD) is the third leading cause of death worldwide, affecting both developed and developing countries. There is no cure for this disease, making early intervention key for improved patient management. Our project aims to determine if measurements that represent the texture of inspiration-expiration computed tomography (CT) images are better at detecting lung disease on CT images compared to more complex established mechanical lung stress measures. Registration of CT images takes two images and transforms them into the same coordinate system. Currently, a measurement called the Jacobian uses image registration from inspiration and expiration images to represent biomechanical lung stress (how easy it is to stretch and compress the lung tissue). However, image registration is a time consuming and difficult process. Radiomics is a biomarker that represents the texture of an image (if it is smooth or bumpy) that does not need image registration. We can use radiomics extracted from inspiration and expiration images and subtract the values to obtain a texture-based delta radiomics measurement. We will compare the Jacobian and delta radiomics measurements to determine which one is better at detecting structural changes on CT images. The findings in this study may demonstrate that texture-based delta radiomics derived from inspiration-expiration images can provide additional information related to local lung structural changes and aid in the understanding of the complex pathophysiology and heterogeneity of COPD. This knowledge is important to our understanding of COPD and may help guide the development of new biomarkers that can be translated to a clinical setting in order to enable earlier disease diagnosis and treatment management, and ultimately improve health outcomes for individuals at risk of and living with lung diseases in Canada, and worldwide.

column36: Interrogating the link between early viral infections and childhood asthma
column37: My project will fill a key gap in clinical understanding about the role of viruses on lung, immune, and nasal microbes in early asthma. Insights about early-mechanisms in asthma will inform better targeted treatment, ultimately preventing the progression of asthma to a severe, life-long disease burden. Some of these results may generate new hypotheses for novel treatments. 10% of children under 14 have asthma, making it the most common childhood chronic disease and the leading cause for hospitalization of Canadian children. Unfortunately, we do not know what causes asthma onset, or what precipitates its progression to s evere dis ease. New insights are needed as current medications used for childhood asthma are non-specific and have adverse effects on child growth and development. Key to understanding how asthma begins is its link to respiratory viral infections. Many studies note that early life viral infections are highly predictive of later asthma development. However, we do not yet know whether viruses contribute to asthma by directly affecting the lungs, or, the immune system. My project will investigate the action of respiratory viruses in asthma diseas e through three key pathways: lung growth and function, immune system biomarkers, and changes to the nasal microbiome. I will use data from the CHILD Study; Canada's largest (n=3545) deeply studied population birth cohort to study asthma. Each participant has a wealth of clinical data, physiological data, and biological samples collected from birth to 12 years of age. My proposed research will fill an important gap in the literature and identify the role that respiratory infections, lung function, immune dysregulation and nasal bacteria play in the development of asthma. Additionally, as a trainee in the Collaborative Specialization in Public Health Policy at the Dalla Lana School of Public Health, my thesis will leverage my research insights to demonstrate how we can improve public health with this knowledge. Whether it be by influencing personalized medical practice, parenting choices, or policy development for healthy communities, my project plans to lead to new approaches and prevention strategies and ultimately guide policy and empower Canadians to shape healthy futures.

column36: Functional characterization of neutrophils in cystic fibrosis: clinical implications
column37: Our findings will provide much needed knowledge on an aspect of CF that is not well understood. It will improve our understanding of CF by revealing how the two new types of neutrophils we discovered could be involved in the disease. Also, this research will provide information about how the new drug Trikafta affects the ability of neutrophils to function which is important to fight lung infections in CF. Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common fatal genetic disease in children and adults in Canada. It is caused by a change in a region of our genetic material called CFTR. This change affects the CFTR protein that our body needs to make thin and slippery fluids in the lung and other organs, and increases the chances of lung infections. Another reason why CF patients suffer from lung infections is that one of the cells of our body that fights infection does not work properly. We call this cell the neutrophil. These cells are sent to the lung in large numbers during an infection to eliminate the pathogen. While these cells go to the lung of CF patients, they are not able to get rid of the pathogen. We thus want to better understand why neutrophils do not work properly and why they cannot protect CF patients from infections in the lung. Our discovery in adult CF patients of two new types of neutrophils in the circulation of adult CF patients may explain the persistent infections. We found an increase in one of these neutrophil types in CF patients that have a decline in lung function linking these cells to the disease. More research is needed to find out if these cells can kill pathogens to understand their role in CF. We also observed these new types of neutrophils in Trikafta-treated patients. Trikafata may thus not correct the CFTR defect in neutrophils and offer patients complete protection from infection. 1) We will study the function of the new types of neutrophils we found in adult CF patients with tests that we use in the laboratory. Their functions will be compared to neutrophils of healthy donors. Functional tests include the ability of producing toxic molecules to kill microbes. 2) We started a study on CF patients before Trikafta treatment on the function of neutrophils. We will also perform the functional tests on these patients' neutrophils after starting their Trikafata treatment. We will compare neutrophil function before and after starting Trikafta. We will also develop a novel cell model that will allow us to study the effect of this drug on neutrophils with additional tests that will provide more information on how the drug works. This project is relevant to the mission of the Lung Association as it addresses two gaps in our knowledge of CF. First, our findings will improve our understanding of the disease by providing insight into the function of the new types of neutrophils we discovered in adult CF patients. In addition, these neutrophils are potential biomarkers of disease severity and response to treatment. Second, our Trikafta fmdings will provide new information on whether this drug corrects the neutrophil defects in CF which is key to optimize disease management. New knowledge of the disease process in CF and the effect of a drug on the immune system will be important contributions to improving lung disease management in CF.

column36: Multidimensional role of CD38 in oxidised phosphatidylcholine (OxPCs) induce obstructive lung diseases
column37: We are not only the first who identified but also characterized the OxPCs species in the human lungs which are the persistent candidate of oxidative stress in lung pathophysiology. Further, based on our expertise and profound lung (patho)biology experience we have identified a possible target protein called CD38, may have a critical role in severity of the disease. Thus, this project will identify whether CD38 is a molecular switch that promotes the adverse effects of OxPCs in asthma pathogenesis. In Canada, over 3.8 million individuals suffer with asthma, including nearly 12% of children. Asthma remains the number one reason for children to present at emergency room each year across Canada. Obstructive lung diseases such as asthma are driven by persistent oxidative stress that damages tissue and promotes accelerated aging. Allergic and air pollution exposures, and microbial and viral infection lead to lung inflammation and oxidative stress. Unfortunately, first line asthma therapies do not specifically mitigate oxidative stress. This permits oxidation-associated changes in cellular components such as proteins and lipids in all cells, and create biologically active molecules that promote disease which leads to high mortality rate. Project is designed to identify the molecular links and mechanism involve in oxidative stress associated asthma pathogenesis. We have focused on phospholipids, specifically oxidized phosphatidylcholine (OxPCs), in the lung. OxPCs are central pathological triggers in many chronic diseases. As we have led discovery of OxPCs in the lungs of human asthmatics, we are now trying to uncover the molecular pathways for OxPCs-induced asthma pathogenesis. This will be critical to identify new therapeutics that do target the effects of oxidative stress in asthma. I will use cultured human ASM cells from healthy and asthmatic donors, as well as mouse models of allergic (house dust mite) asthma to decipher the role of CD38 in OxPCs-associated pathobiology. Critical indices I will assess include OxPCs induced structural changes in the airways, associated with extracellular matrix (ECM) expression. Please refer to two page proposed research plan for more details. By defining molecular mechanisms involving CD38 that elucidate the effects of OxPCs on airway inflammation, [Ca++]i signaling, ECM production and airway remodeling my research will open a new potential avenues to develop management approaches for asthma pathogenesis. It will enhance the scientific understanding in context of role of persistence oxidative stress in asthma and therapeutic consideration from the clinical point of view. Overall, it will improve not only the disease management but also a potential asthma therapy outcome.

column36: Investigating the role of neutrophils during respiratory viral infections
column37: My project will clarify the unclear role of neutrophils in respiratory viral infections using innovative cutting-edge techniques such as intravital microscopy, single cell gene detection and genetically modified mice. Respiratory viral infections continue to affect millions of people, costs health care and society billions of dollars and kill thousands of humans every single year. Although the respiratory viruses themselves can cause negative consequences in our lungs, an uncontrolled response from our own immune systems can be harmful. Neutrophils are the fighter cells that arrive rapidly to the site of infection. They are known to be excellent fighters against bacterial and fungal infections as they can eat these bugs and prevent them from growing uncontrolled. Yet, their role when we have a viral infection, where the virus mostly resides hidden inside our cells, remains unclear. This is important because neutrophils are known to come to the lung in large quantities upon virus infection. So, the question remains if they can have a direct effect in fighting viruses or if they promote collateral lung damage due to their inappropriate activation. We will use mouse models of the flu to use along with a powerful tool; intravital microscopy, where I can visualize in real-time the battle between the immune system and the virus in the lungs of a live, breathing mouse. Specifically, I will observe lung neutrophils, quantify their numbers and their behavior when there is a viral infection. Also, we will use a type of genetically modified mouse that lets us track the expression of specific anti-viral genes in real time in single cells. We will increase or suppress neutrophils' anti-viral activity which will inform us if they are beneficial or harmful to the sick individual. By understanding the role of neutrophils in respiratory viral infections, this project will shed light to therapeutic options targeting neutrophils after viral infection to manage viral pneumonia and improve lung health.

column36: Modeling human iPSC-derived alveolar type 1 and 2 cells for respiratory diseases
column37: This is a multi-disciplinary collaboration involving experts in stem cell and developmental biology, bioengineering, bioinformatics and mathematical modeling. We will use innovative techniques including stem cell organoids, cellular barcoding, single-cell omics, and microfluidic-based engineered platforms. In the human lung, human breath (respiration) and gas exchange occur primarily in the human alveolar sacs (balloon-like structure) which are covered by alveolar epithelial cells including alveolar type 1 and type 2 cells (AT1, AT2). These AT1 and AT2 cells are derived from alveolar bipotent progenitor cells (BPC) in human fetal and adult lungs and are implicated in several lung diseases such as childhood interstitial lung diseases (CHILD), respiratory viral infections, and Cystic Fibrosis. However, it is hard to access the primary patient-specific alveolar cells to have biomedical research. Hence, developing a model which can produce alveolar cell types from human induced pluripotent stem cells iPSC (cells can limitlessly develop into any type of human cell) is very important. Recent developments in producing alveolar cell types from iPSCs have shown some efficacy in generating immature or fetal alveolar-like cell types. Also, expansion and maintenance of BPCs derived from iPSC as well as the ability to further push these cells to maturation to form bona fide respiratory AT1 and AT2 cells remain a challenge. We recently developed a new method to generate bipotent alveolospheres from BPCs. While these alveolospheres are renewable for several passages, current air-liquid-interface culture conditions (alveolar cells expose to air) are incapable of efficiently maturing these cells. The goal of this study is to identify physiological parameters that can be used to mature AT1/AT2 cells in culture for eventual use in regenerative medicine and to understand the lineage relationships during the differentiation of BPCs in alveolospheres. The BPCs from alveolospheres will be exposed to three different microfluidic platforms that mimic post-natal life by considering different physiological parameters including airflow (cyclic stretch) (A), fluid flow (shear stress) (B), and surface stretch (C) to further mature into AT1 and AT2 cells. The unique sequence tags (DNA barcodes) will be introduced into each of the BPCs in alveolospheres to allow us to follow the cell lineage maturation process to trace the lineage relationship of BPCs. The success of this project will provide an important resource of respiratory cells for personalized disease modeling, precision drug screening, or regeneration as a treatment strategy for lung diseases.

column36: Mepolizumab for the Treatment of Chronic Cough with Eosinophilic Airways Disease
column37: This is the first ever double blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study to investigate the role of depleting eosinophils using biologic therapy in the treatment of chronic cough secondary to eosinophilic lung disease. Chronic cough affects approximately 10% of the general population. Unfortunately, there are no licensed treatments for this debilitating condition, which affects the social, physical and psychological well-being of patients. Asthma and Non-asthmatic Eosinophilic Bronchitis (NAEB) are known causes of chronic cough. An important feature of both these conditions is the presence of an inflammatory cell called the eosinophil which is found in the airways. The most common treatment for this is high doses of inhaled steroids, but when the cough becomes unbearable, repeated courses of oral steroids are administered. However, many patients have persistent cough despite this treatment and can develop significant steroid related side effects. Developing treatment for this condition is thus a major unmet clinical need. Cough is a defensive reflex which is triggered by activation of nerves which are found in the airway lining. Recent evidence suggests there is a significant increase in eosinophils in the airways which sensitizes these nerves. This makes the nerves more easily activated leading to more coughing. If these eosinophils could be depleted and prevented to enter the airways, then we predict that the nerves will be less sensitive and coughing will be reduced. Mepolizumab is an injection medication, which blocks a key chemical that prevents the maturation and activation of eosinophils. It is a licensed medication which is currently used in patients with severe asthma to prevent severe asthma attacks. However, there has been no evidence to show whether this medication would improve coughing. The aim of this research proposal is to investigate whether mepolizumab reduces objective cough frequency in patients with eosinophilic airway diseases. This is a 9-visit randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study evaluating the effectiveness of 4 doses of mepolizumab for the treatment of chronic cough in patients with eosinophilic airways disease. Chronic cough has a highly unmet research need. With the increasing prevalence of chronic cough in Canada, it is important to establish new treatments with reduced side effects to patients. The results of this study would result in a paradigm shift in the management of this challenging condition and provide patients hope of an improved quality of life.

column36: Comparing three approaches of cardiopulmonary resuscitation in asphyxiated neonatal piglets - A randomized control animal trial
column37: There is no consensus about the timing and appropriateness of transitioning from neonatal CPR to pediatric CPR. This project compares the two methods in neonates outside of the delivery room, along with a novel third technique of CPR. Neonatal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and pediatric CPR focus on different algorithms for timing and coordination of chest compressions and breaths. There are currently no guidelines regarding the timing of transitioning from neonatal CPR, focused primarily on resuscitation within the delivery room, to pediatric CPR. To compare the speed of resuscitation and chances of survival using three approaches to CPR in neonates outside the delivery room. On the day of experimentation, 5-10 day old mixed breed piglets will be anesthetized and then instrumented with various probes and sensors for data collection. They will also be connected to a ventilator to support their breathing. Following a period of stabilization, the ventilator will be disconnected, and the breathing tube clamped until their heart stops. The piglets will then be randomized to one of three methods of resuscitation and undergo the respective resuscitation until they have a heartbeat again, or up to a maximum of 12 minutes. The 3 methods of resuscitation include 3:1chest compressions to ventilations (standard for neonates), continuous chest compressions with asynchronous ventilations (standard for pediatric patients), and continuous chest compressions with sustained inflations (a novel technique where a high pressure inflation is delivered and ventilation is achieved passively through compression and release of the chest). Cardiopulmonary health is incredibly important for neonates, whose lungs are still developing. The focus of our study is on very sick neonates: those requiring CPR in the neonatal intensive care unit. These babies are potentially at risk for various types of lung disease, both in the short term and long term. We aim to determine the optimal technique for CPR in this fragile population to improve survival and minimize the duration of CPR. One aim of minimizing duration of CPR is to decrease the chances of developing or worsening lung disease. Minimizing chronic lung disease is especially important for neonates born prematurely.

column36: Ageism and Health Research, Delivery, and Outcomes in Older Adults
column37: We are in the midst of the United Nations Decade of Healthy Aging (2021-2030) and the world's aging population is growing. By 2023, 1 in 6 people in the world will be aged 60 years or over. Ageism refers to the stereotypes (how we think), prejudice (how we feel), and discrimination (how we act) towards others or oneself based on age. column36: Utilizing optical coherence tomography and exercise to develop novel biomarkers of respiratory impairment in people living with human immunodeficiency virus
column37: The high-resolution imaging technique used in this study has not been used to study airway health in people with HIV before. It will provide pictures of airway damage that cannot be seen by our current diagnostic tools. We can use these pictures to diagnose patients with lung disease far earlier. People with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) experience breathing discomfort that is worse than would be expected based on the results from their lung function tests. The cause of this breathing discomfort is unknown. Identifying new markers of lung health, or biomarkers, that are more sensitive to detecting airway damage than lung function tests would help doctors make treatment decisions and improve the quality of life in people with HIV. We will develop imaging and exercise biomarkers to capture early airway damage in people with HIV. Ten females and males between 40-60 years old with HIV and ten sex- and age-matched controls without HIV will be recruited for this study. Participants will undergo lung function testing, take a questionnaire to determine how breathing discomfort affects their life, undergo a bronchoscopy procedure, and perform an exercise test. Bronchoscopy is a commonly performed medical procedure that involves putting a flexible, thin (size of a pencil) tube called a bronchoscope into the airways through the mouth. The bronchoscopy procedure will be combined with an imaging technique called optical coherence tomography (OCT). OCT uses a very small camera (0.9 mm) to collect extremely detailed airway images (details as small as 0.01 mm can be seen). Airway images will be compared between people with HIV and controls to find different image features between the groups that can be used as biomarkers for airway damage in HIV. The exercise test will be performed on a stationary bike and several responses (e.g., breathing and heart rate) will be measured. Differences in the exercise responses between groups will help identify exercise biomarkers of airway damage in HIV. Identifying new imaging and exercise biomarkers of airway damage in people living with HIV will allow for early diagnosis and treatment and improve lung health for this population. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), a group of diseases that block airflow in the lungs and cause breathing problems, is more common and diagnosed earlier in people with HIV compared to those without HIV. Detection of early airway damage with the biomarkers developed in the proposed work may allow researchers to slow or stop the progression of airway damage in people with HIV before COPD develops.

column37: Active transportation and public space initiatives are increasingly seen as a solution to improve the health of the planet and people; yet, some places and groups have had limited involvement in processes of planning, actively using, and evaluating active transportation and public space initiatives. Seeking to address these gaps the goal of this planning grant is to situate the city of Brandon, Manitoba, as a model city for active transportation and public space initiatives in the context of other smaller cities and develop collaborative approaches to ensuring meaningful health impacts through an equity lens. column36: Mechanisms supporting psilocybin-assisted psychotherapy to treat alcohol use disorder
column37: There is growing interest in using psychedelic drugs such as psilocybin to treat various psychiatric disorders. For instance, a very recent clinical trial reported that psilocybin administered in the context of supportive, motivation-focused therapy can reduce heavy drinking in patients with an alcohol use disorder (AUD). This is encouraging, as alcohol-related problems are of the most costly to society and current treatment options are inadequate. However, like in nearly all trials involving psilocybin, patients were able to figure out if received psilocybin or the control compound. This makes it difficult to determine if the effects on alcohol consumption are due to the pharmacological effects of psilocybin or what people expect psilocybin to do. This is becoming an increasing concern in psychedelic trials due to the growing positive media coverage (or "hype") around psychedelic drugs. In this study, we plan to begin addressing this issue of expectancies by giving all 128 AUD patients psilocybin, but varying the dose so that half receive the active treatment dose (25mg) and the other half get a smaller active control dose (1mg). The active control dose is just enough for participants to feel short-lived drug effects during the session, likely preventing them from easily determining if they are in the active or control group, but not enough to produce long-lasting effects on behavior. If it is only the expectations that drive effects, we will see no difference between groups. However, if the pharmacological effects of psilocybin are indeed driving the reduction in drinking, then we will see greater improvements in individuals receiving the active 25mg dose. We will also measure how psilocybin-assisted psychotherapy influences behavioral and brain metrics related to alcohol consumption. Together, we will determine if psilocybin-assisted psychotherapy can reduce alcohol consumption, an if so, what mechanisms may be supporting this change in behavior.

column36: Psilocybin-Assisted Psychotherapy for Treatment-Resistant Depression: A Randomized Phase II Clinical Trial Comparing One Versus Two Psychedelic Doses of Psilocybin
column37: Psilocybin is a naturally occurring psychedelic that causes unique mind-altering effects. Psilocybin has recently been shown to potentially relieve symptoms of depression when combined with talk therapy (i.e., psilocybin-assisted psychotherapy). Previous studies have used either one or two doses of psilocybin to treat depression. However, no study has determined the comparative effects of one versus two psilocybin dosing sessions. Each dosing session is very resource intensive (two therapists supporting the patient for 6-8 hours per dose). If two doses are more helpful than one single dose of psilocybin, then future studies and use in practice should routinely provide two dosing sessions. However, if a second dose does not increase the benefits from the first dose, then this second dose is only adding to costs and increasing the risks of side effects. Our pilot study of 22 people with depression suggested that two doses of psilocybin was more effective than one single dose; however, these results are preliminary and require further scientific testing. We propose a two site, eight-week clinical trial evaluating the antidepressant effects of one versus two psilocybin sessions (with accompanying psychotherapy) in 90 individuals with difficult to treat depression. One group will receive two psychedelic doses of psilocybin whereas the second group will receive one placebo dose and one psilocybin dose over the course of 8 weeks. The primary outcome will be the comparative change in depression severity during the 8-week trial. The proposed team is already actively providing psilocybin-assisted therapy with existing infrastructure and are thus perfectly positioned to execute the proposed study. This study will be the first to rigorously evaluate the comparative benefits and safety of one versus two psilocybin sessions. Our results will provide direct and concrete guidance for all future psilocybin trials globally, and will be vital in informing best practice guidelines.

column36: Psilocybin-assisted Existential, Attachment and RelationaL (PEARL) Therapy for Patients with Advanced Cancer: A Randomized Controlled Trial
column37: Individuals with advanced cancer often experience high levels of distress due to physical suffering, difficult treatment decisions, social difficulties, grief and fear of death. Evidence has shown that psychotherapies incorporating existential, attachment and relational approaches can reduce distress and improve quality of life in people with advanced cancer. Recent studies with cancer patients have shown that psilocybin-assisted psychotherapy (where an individual ingests psilocybin to induce a non-ordinary state of consciousness with psychological support) can also lead to reductions in distress. However, psilocybin therapy at the end-of-life has not yet been combined with evidence-based psychotherapies that have demonstrated improvements in depression and other psychosocial outcomes in the advanced cancer population. Our multidisciplinary team has developed Psilocybin-assisted Existential, Attachment and RelationaL (PEARL) therapy. PEARL therapy combines elements from psilocybin-assisted psychotherapy, including preparatory therapy sessions, a single psilocybin session, and integration sessions, with important elements from an evidence-based manualized individual psychotherapy specifically designed for patients with advanced cancer also created by our group called CALM (Managing Cancer and Living Meaningfully) therapy. This study will determine the benefit of PEARL therapy in the treatment of depressive symptoms among patients with advanced cancer by randomizing carefully screened patients to receive either PEARL therapy with a high dose of psilocybin or a placebo control. While psilocybin-assisted psychotherapy has the potential to relieve distress and improve quality of life in those with advanced disease, careful research is needed to build upon preliminary findings in order to guide public policy, legislation, and clinical guidelines.

column36: overcoming Therapy Resistance in Esophagogastric Adenocarcinoma - a Trans-CANADA initiative
column37: Esophageal cancer, more specifically gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma (GEA), is rising in incidence across Canada. Poor outcome is chiefly due to innate or acquired resistance to current treatments - chemotherapy, and recently, immunotherapy - driving high relapse rates. A better understanding of what drives therapy resistance in this often-fatal disease is urgently needed. We propose that by tackling resistance we can devise more effective and personalized chemotherapy approaches to improve survival. Recently identified mechanisms of resistance, encompassing specific combinations of mutations, treatment-induced stemness cell state shift or an immunosuppressive microenvironment, open new opportunities for drug repurposing and rapid translation to the patient. We aim (1) to generate a comprehensive set of patient-derived tumor models that effectively recapitulate (2) a well-characterized cohort of GEA tumors, both in molecular heterogeneity and response to treatment. This unique resource will allow us to (3A) investigate mechanisms of therapy resistance, (3B) devise approaches to overcome this resistance and (4) functionally validate these findings. We have assembled an interdisciplinary trans-Canadian and American team of clinician-scientists, cancer/computational biologists, and bioengineers to accomplish two breakthrough objectives in GEA care: (1) determine if we can predict which patients will/will not benefit from current treatment by identifying factors driving therapy resistance; and (2) identify individualized and tailored therapies to overcome treatment resistance.

column36: Development and Clinical Testing of Effective Immunotherapies for Biliary Tract Cancers.
column37: The Challenge: Biliary tract cancers (BTC) are rare (~1,000 new cases in Canada per year). When localized, surgical resection is possible, but most patients present with Stage IV disease, where the estimated 5-year survival is <2%. Current systemic chemotherapy offers modest prolongation of survival but at a huge cost to quality of life. Clinical trials of molecularly targeted therapies are reporting a longer and better life for BTC patients, and prolonged remission has been seen with novel immunotherapies. The promise of emerging BTC research and immunotherapies offer hope for a durable and long-term survival, although the probability of benefit is still not high. Our Solution: We propose that by integrating comprehensive research into clinical care, at the earliest time possible in a patient's cancer treatment trajectory, we will better appreciate the needs, values, and hopes of Canadian BTC patients and understand the unique challenges in the clinical and research landscape. We will establish the Canadian Cholangiocarcinoma Collaborative (C3), a partnership among patients, caregivers, oncologists and researchers. Our goal is to boost access to clinical trials and personalized treatments for BTC patients and enable the development of an immunotherapy pipeline for therapeutic discovery. The C3 will provide much needed hope to affected individuals including patients and families by delivering on 3 specific aims: AIM 1: Integration of a National BTC Research Navigator (RNav) into Patient Care. Willing Canadian BTC patients will provide online consent to be contacted by the C3 RNav, who will help them navigate the complex world of research and provide information about the C3 and the various opportunities to participate, including the: 1. International Cholangiocarcinoma Patient Registry 2. National BTC Multidisciplinary Oncology Rounds 3. Information and Access to BTC Molecular Testing and Clinical Trials 4. C3 Hope Study 5.
