column36: Adaptation and development of an implementation strategy for a novel artificial intelligence-driven ehealth behaviour change program in Colombia
column37: The burden of non-communicable chronic diseases (NCDs) is unequivocal. The root cause of most NCDs is a specific cluster of health risk behaviours, e.g., physical inactivity, poor diet, and smoking. Despite widespread knowledge of these risks, 43% of Colombians remain physically inactive, 28% report not meeting daily vegetables and fruits intake, and 12% smoke. Targeting behaviour change in individuals who are in early adulthood (e.g., 18-39) is important to reduce NCDs. However, promoting health behaviour change in this population has been a challenge. Our research team have created an artificial intelligence-driven ehealth behaviour change program (ACCELERATION) which has shown to be effective at changing behaviours and reducing NCD risk in Canada. The main objectives of this application are to: 1) adapted the ACCELERATION program to the Colombian setting and test its implementation across the province of Antioquia; and 2) create a scale-up strategy for its implementation across Colombia. To achieve these objectives, we will conduct a series of interconnected studies: 1) Use qualitative focus group and user experience (UX) methodologies to adapt ACCELERATION to the Colombian setting. 2) Conduct an implementation proof of concept study within the province of Antioquia to demonstrate effectiveness and evaluate practical aspects of scaling up across Colombia. 3) Undertake in-depth interviews with health administrators and policy makers to define the critical success factors for scaling-up ACCELERATION in Colombia. 4) Finally, we will incorporate all the information obtained above into the WHO ExpandNet framework to develop a scale-up strategy that can be used to implement ACCELERATION across Colombia and similar LMICs. These studies will provide the basis to successfully implement ACCELERATION within Colombia, with an emphasis on benefitting more people on a lasting basis. We will also develop tools for the further scaling-up of ACCELERATION across similar LMICs.

column36: Leveraging Guatemalan farmers' existing organization around food sovereignty and agroecology for reducing risk of diet- and pesticide-related noncommunicable diseases
column37: Indigenous farmers in Guatemala are disproportionately affected both by diet- and pesticide-related noncommunicable diseases (NCDs). While they grow food on their farms, they often sell the most nutritious products and instead purchase cheap calories in obesogenic markets. Meanwhile, some use pesticides on their own land, and others apply pesticides during seasonal plantation labour. Regrettably, diet- and pesticide-related NCDs compound each others' health impacts, and among mothers, they affect the next generation. For these linked problems, we propose an integrated solution based on existing evidence and practice. Our research will work with farmers who are regaining control over their food and farms by practicing agroecology. An organic farming paradigm based on ecosystem interactions, agroecology has demonstrated links to NCD risk reduction. For example, by increasing production diversity and promoting consumption of own production, it provides nutritious foods and reduces unhealthy purchases. As an organic strategy, it interrupts on-farm pesticide exposure, and by providing a secure livelihood, it reduces labor migration to pesticide-intensive plantations. We deploy implementation research objectives to assess how such linkages can be strengthened in existing agroecology interventions, as well as scaled locally and internationally. We will focus on women of reproductive age, given intergenerational health effects and gender inequalities. Key methods include: a validated tool to evaluate how agroecology's production, social and dietary factors reduce NCD risk; participatory co-learning workshops to understand farmer norms, values and beliefs implicated in health behaviours; and, an action-research communication strategy to integrate evidence-based knowledge into intervention, advocacy and outreach. Local impact is built into our research design, and the project is expected to produce a global impact given the growing interest in agroecology-health linkages.

column36: Prize 202209PJT - Early Career Award in Cancer: Deconvoluting Prognostic and Targetable Features of Endometrioid Ovarian Carcinomas of No Specific Molecular Profile
column37: Ovarian cancers are 5 distinct diseases. One of these, endometrioid ovarian cancer, is hugely different from other ovarian cancers and instead is like uterine cancers. Treating this type like other ovarian cancers is inefficient and for many women results in unnecessary toxic chemotherapy. Within endometrioid ovarian cancers there are four subtypes, equivalent to subtypes also defined in uterine cancer. The subtyping scheme uses specific protein and gene markers to define 3 of 4 classes, representing 25-30% of case and this does well to define endometrioid ovarian cancer that need little vs aggressive treatment. The 4th class, representing ~70% of cases, is a subtype by omission and lacks the markers that define the other 3 groups. It is often referred to as "No Specific Molecular Profile" - a misleading moniker given this type can itself be divided up using additional markers of disease. To bring clarity to this largest subtype of endometrioid ovarian carcinomas we will re-evaluate biological characteristics in a large series of cases. We will also use cells derived from these unique ovarian cancers, grown outside the body (in vitro) or in animal models (in vivo), to contrast different treatments that target biological feature common to this subtype. Our study will enable a personalized treatment approach and assist in decision on appropriate treatments to patient that will benefit while reducing over-treatment in patients that will not.

column36: Prize 202209PJT - Early Career Award in Cancer: An international randomized trial on neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma versus definitive chemoradiotherapy with salvage surgery as needed - The NEEDS Trial
column37: Esophageal cancer is the 6th leading cause of cancer death worldwide. Curative treatment for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), representing 90% of cases globally, is controversial. Candidates for surgery are preferably treated with chemoradiotherapy (CRT) followed by surgery ("CROSS"). Alternatively, definitive CRT (either deferring surgery for salvage or no surgery; "dCRT-sS") is recommended for patients at high risk of surgical morbidity. To date, no adequately powered randomized trials comparing these two treatments have been published. Two small clinical trials have shown that compared with CROSS, patients treated dCRT-sS had no difference in survival but slightly inferior local control. While increased complexity and heightened risks may be expected when preforming salvage surgery, a population-based analysis suggests no detriment in survival between patients undergoing salvage versus planned surgery. Finally, dCRT-sS allows patients with complete responses to be spared esophagectomy and the associated morbidity. This international randomized phase III clinical trial builds on research conducted to date and compares CROSS and dCRT-sS in ESCC. The trial will be conducted in Canada by the Canadian Cancer Trials Group and includes international collaboration. The primary objective is to determine whether dCRT-sS is non-inferior to CROSS in terms of overall survival. The main secondary objective evaluates if health-related quality of life is superior by sparing a proportion of patients from esophagectomy. Additional secondary outcomes include toxicity evaluation and cost effectiveness. The results of this trial could change the global practice from CROSS to dCRT-sS with surveillance and esophagectomy only if needed. The trial will include 1200 patients from across the world, including approximately 300 from Canada. The results are anticipated to be highly cited and will form the basis of national and international guidelines for the management of ESCC.

column37: Early age-at-onset colorectal cancer (eoCRC) among adults under the age of 50 is increasing in Canada. EoCRC has considerable impacts on the health of Canadians in terms of the potential years of life lost and the impacts on Canadian families. On average, eoCRC cases are diagnosed at later stages and with different negative tumor characteristics leading to poor clinical outcomes. Despite the increasing incidence, eoCRCs still represent a minority of CRCs diagnosed in Western countries and consequently they are under-represented in randomized clinical trials (RCTs) of novel cancer therapies. At present, the best approaches to treat eoCRC patients remain unclear with minimal data to support treatment decisions in the clinic. Clinicians and patients are often faced with a challenging conundrum - to treat very aggressively in hopes of maximizing the potential life years ahead, or to attempt to minimize the consequences of treatment-related effects on other health outcomes unique to younger populations (e.g. reproduction, sexuality, family, work, etc.). The overall goal of this proposed research project is to understand and patient outcomes for eoCRC patients in Canada. Using readily available population-based administrative data in Alberta, this project aims to understand how early and late stage eoCRC patients are currently being treated, to determine the effectiveness of different treatment strategies for eoCRC patients, and to develop tools to help guide the of treatment based on individual patient characteristics. Clinician and patient input will be gathered through focus groups and will guide analytical decision making to ensure the greatest clinical impact of this research.

column36: Large-scale Exploration and Functional Validation of the Dynamic Interactions of CFTR WT and Mutant Proteins with Solute Carrier Transporters
column37: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a serious disease caused my mutations in the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR) protein. While recently strong advances in CF treatment have been made, patients still face many challenges, with disease severity, survival and overall quality of life remaining highly variable between individuals. Much of this variability is due to the influence of 'modifier' genes, which affect the type of, and degree to which, CF symptoms manifest. A major example is the Solute Carriers(SLCs), which research shows affect the onset and severity of meconium ileus, airway infection, pancreatic insufficiency and diabetes mellitus, among others. Several SLCs have also been shown to physically interact with CFTR, which is important for some of their observed effects. Most interactions of SLCs with CFTR remain to be explored, however. Based on published data, and our own preliminary results, we believe that examining how SLC proteins physically interact with CFTR. Research Priorities is key to understanding many of the complexities of CF and improving patient treatment and quality of life. Our proposal aims to identify ALL physical interactions occurring between CFTR and the over 400 SLCs in humans, to provide a valuable resource giving CF researchers a global view of how these modifiers contribute to disease. In this way, researchers will be able to identify potentially new therapeutic targets (for drug and gene therapies) as well as predictors of CF manifestations (such as diabetes mellitus and severe lung infection) that can be used to better manage disease treatment and reduce overall treatment burden. Insights into SLC interactions with CFTR should also help researchers understand how CF manifests in individuals at different ages and provide new alternatives for more personalized care management. We believe that our work aligns well with CF community research priorities at multiple levels with the potential to pave the way for rapid new advances.

column36: Prize 202209PJT - Early Career Award in Cancer: A unified approach to determine how MUS81-EME1 recognizes and cleaves branched DNA structures to safeguard genome integrity
column37: Cancer is a leading cause of death worldwide. One hallmark of cancer cells is a high frequency of mutations and DNA rearrangements, collectively known as genome instability. Persistent DNA damage fuels genome instability and paradoxically, genomes are constantly exposed to a plethora of DNA-damaging agents. Cells use sophisticated pathways to repair DNA damage and preserve genome integrity. Determining how these pathways operate is a top priority for foundational and translational scientists. Most DNA repair pathways require nucleases to cut and remove damaged or abnormal DNA structures. However, without tight regulatory mechanisms, nucleases can catalyze catastrophic chromosome cleavage. There is burgeoning interest in leveraging this activity to sensitive cancer cells to anti-cancer drugs. Understanding how DNA nucleases recognize and cleave their DNA substrates will identify novel targets for therapeutic intervention. My research addresses these questions through the SMX tri-nuclease, which contains three nucleases, SLX1, MUS81-EME1 and XPF-ERCC1, bound to the SLX4 scaffold. Cells rely on SMX for accurate DNA repair and genome stability, although its untimely activation triggers chromosome pulverization. My research has defined mechanisms of SMX assembly and activation. Remarkably, MUS81-EME1 is responsible for most of the nuclease activities ascribed to SMX. We discovered a non-catalytic domain in MUS81 as the linchpin for targeted recognition of abnormal DNA structures (substrate specificity). We will use biochemical and cellular approaches to determine how this domain controls MUS81-EME1's substrate specificity and elucidate the biological consequences of relaxed substrate specificity in different cellular contexts. These studies will significantly advance our understanding of how MUS81-EME1 safeguards genome integrity. Likewise, our research will provide a solid framework for future research aimed at identifying compounds that target MUS81 in cancer cells.

column36: Prize 202209PJT - Early Career Award in Cancer: The impact of chromosomal instability on ovarian cancer progression
column37: Cancer arises when a single cell acquires genetic alterations leading to uncontrolled replication. As tumour cells divide they continue to acquire genetic mutations which they pass on to their descendants, forming subpopulations with different characteristics. The ability of tumours to generate genetic diversity and evolve in response to selective pressures can enable them to develop resistance to treatment. Certain forms of large-scale genetic alteration have been associated with poor patient survival in multiple cancer types, and are common in ovarian cancer. Understanding the frequency with which these alterations arise within tumours and the diversity they generate requires profiling the genetic material of individual cancer cells. We will optimize experimental approaches for sequencing the genetic material of single tumour cells and develop computational methods to characterize cellular diversity. We will then apply these methods to profile the composition of tissue donated by high grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) patients at initial diagnosis and following relapse. The five-year survival rate for ovarian cancer patients in Canada is currently 44%. Many patients initially respond to treatment, but subsequently develop resistance and experience disease recurrence. This study will help define patterns of mutation associated with ovarian cancer progression, with potential to identify new prognostic markers and targets for drug development.

column36: Getting older and wiser: the complexities of ageing with cystic fibrosis
column37: After hearing from the CF community, CF Canada identified understanding health issues for people living with CF 50+ years of age as a top research priority. Our proposal directly addresses this priority by investigating the impact of understudied complications such as heart disease, kidney disease, cancer and cancer screening. Currently, there is a lack of awareness and understanding of the burden of these issues in people with CF (pwCF). With the ageing CF population comes complexities that were previously uncommon or unrecognized due to premature death. These conditions of interest require specialist care beyond the typical CF multidisciplinary team and may not be on the radar of clinicians. We must understand the magnitude of these conditions in pwCF in order to ensure they receive appropriate and timely specialist care. Further, there are reasons to suspect that pwCF may fall through the cracks when it comes to cancer screening due to lack of regular contact with a family doctor, often the person who orders routine cancer screening tests. This pivotal study will determine which conditions occur in pwCF, how often, at what age, who is at risk and whether pwCF receive recommended cancer screening. Increased awareness of these conditions along with prioritizing family physician involvement have the potential to result in timely specialist referrals and ensure early and treatable cancers are diagnosed for future generations of people living with CF. This work will also provide important recommendations to CF Canada for events to track in the CF registry moving forward to ensure quality of care. While we recognize that CF Canada's research priority specifically states 50+ years of age, we have broadened the age-range for this work. If we want to understand emerging complications and assess quality of care (e.g. cancer screening), we cannot make assumptions about the age of onset of the events of interest given the current lack of literature in this area.

column36: Prize 202209PJT - Robyn Tamblyn Mid-Career HSPR Innovation Award: Re-engineering health policy decision-making for equitable allocation of resources
column37: Health inequity has been defined as avoidable and unfair differences in health between groups of people. In Canada, populations from marginalized communities live shorter lives and have limited access to health services. To address this, decision-makers are tasked with designing programs and allocating resources to reduce inequities. However, there is a lack of guidance as to how equity is to be incorporated in decisions. Economic evaluations are useful tools that examine the benefits and costs of health policies. For example, if a vaccination campaign is expected to reduce the overall number of cases, at a reasonable cost, it will have a high chance of being funded and implemented by the government. However, economic evaluations often lack the capability to determine how different population groups will be affected by the intervention. We will develop guidance for Canadian researchers and decision-makers to develop and interpret economic evaluations capable of predicting how health programs might affect disadvantaged populations. This methodology is called equity-informative economic evaluation. To achieve this, we will develop three separate projects. For the first project, we will work with decision-makers to understand the challenges and opportunities to use equity-informative economic evaluations, and to develop practical guidance on conduct them. The second is a survey that will allow quantifying the level of aversion in the general public towards different types of health inequalities (e.g. health inequality between the rich and poor). And finally, we will develop two examples of equity-informative economic evaluations to measure the health and equity effects of programs aimed at screening for cancer and vaccinating for pneumonia. This project represents a vital step towards building an inclusive and equitable healthcare system in Canada. By working with the Canadian public and decision-makers, we will ensure that all points of view are accounted for.

column36: Prize 202209PJT - Health Services and Policy Research Rising Star Early Career Award: Building system capacity for home visits for patients near the end of life: A mixed methods study
column37: Across Canada there is increasing emphasis on providing palliative homecare. Homecare at the end of life can reduce hospital visits, reduce the chances of in-hospital death, and improve patient satisfaction. Despite these known benefits, many Ontarians do not receive adequate physician and nurse practitioner (NP) home visits near the end of life. There has been no formal evaluation of Ontario-based policies designed to increase palliative home visits by palliative care specialists (i.e., those with a palliative focus of practice) or palliative care generalists (i.e., those who provide palliative care but not as their focus of practice). We need to better understand factors that prevent or facilitate specialist and generalist palliative providers' willingness to provide home visits. Our goal is to study ways to build efficient system capacity for home visits for patients near the end of life in Ontario. First, we will evaluate payment incentives for health care providers, and estimate the cost-benefit trade-off of home visits to the healthcare system. Next, interviews with specialist and generalist palliative care physicians and NPs who do and do not provide home visits will help to understand our prior findings and explore how characteristics and policies influence provision of home visits. We will then gather provincial and national stakeholders to discuss our findings and brainstorm policy solutions, and we will create a travelling public installation to communicate our findings to members of provincial parliament. A better understanding of strategies to increase access to palliative home visits and gauging political readiness for these strategies are critical to improving the dying experience of Canadians. Our findings will provide evidence and a business case for the Ontario government outlining how palliative home visits can be scaled up. We are at a critical time where our research has the potential to help change the course of palliative homecare in Ontario

column36: Prize 202209PJT - Yves Joannette Award of Excellence in Research in Aging: Can virtual navigation strategies predict polygenic risk of Alzheimer disease and cognitive decline?
column37: Early detection of Alzheimer's disease (AD) is becoming increasingly central to finding successful treatments before symptoms occur. One of the first brain structures affected by AD is called the hippocampus (HPC). Therefore, finding behaviors that correlate with damage to the HPC may be the key for early detection of AD. Cognitive factors such as navigation strategies (how we find our way in the environment), can depend on the HPC. In fact, we have shown in healthy older adults that using a HPC-dependent navigation strategy is associated with better cognition and a healthier HPC. In contrast, using a non-HPC-dependent navigation strategy is associated with worse cognition and atrophy in the HPC. To date, we have extensively screened and tested 317 healthy older adults. In the current follow-up study, we aim to re-invite them in order to assess whether navigation strategies can predict decline in overall cognition and conversion rates to AD. Re-invited participants will be genotyped to assess the genetic risk of AD, and they will be tested on the same set of memory, IQ, executive function, and navigation tests as during their initial visit. We will perform MRI scans in order to assess the structure of the HPC. This will allow us to to measure cognitive decline, atrophy in the HPC, and AD conversion. We anticipate that older adults who were using non-HPC-dependent navigation strategies during their initial visit will have greater decline in overall cognition. atrophy in the HPC and higher rates of AD diagnosis during their follow-up visit compared to those who were using HPC-dependent navigation strategies. This study will have an impact on AD research because it will provide a tool for the detection of individuals who are on their way to an AD diagnosis. This way, the findings may thus facilitate development of pharmacological or non-pharmacological AD preventive interventions.

column36: Prize 202209PJT - Mid Career Investigator Prize in Research in Aging: Deintensifying diabetes management for older adults living in long term care: A multi-method study
column37: PURPOSE: People with diabetes in long-term care (LTC) homes are at higher risk of harm from their diabetes treatments compared to younger adults. While strict management of diabetes in younger adults is recommended, it should be avoided for those living in LTC, as it can do more harm than good. In Ontario, more than half of LTC residents with diabetes are treated too strictly, putting them at risk for harms like low blood sugar and its consequences. Given this, there is a need to deintensify the care of LTC residents with diabetes by stopping or reducing diabetes medications and decreasing how often we monitor blood sugar etc. We aim to directly improve the wellbeing of LTC residents with diabetes by implementing an intervention that reduces the intensity of diabetes management. APPROACH: Through 3 study phases, we will: 1) Examine how often diabetes deintensification takes place in Ontario LTC using provincial healthcare databases. We will also study the potential benefits and harms of diabetes deintensification in LTC. 2) Interview LTC residents and caregivers to understand their views about deintensifying diabetes management. This will help us understand how to best implement the intervention. 3) Partner with a change team (residents, caregivers, LTC staff, health care professionals) in a LTC home to implement a diabetes deintensification intervention. To do this, we will use what we learn from our first two phases and also evaluate diabetes care processes in our partner LTC home. We will test out the intervention in the LTC home and improve it based on the feedback of residents, caregivers, staff and health care professionals. OUTCOME: Our goal is to implement a practical, resident/caregiver-centered intervention that is ready for future evaluation in LTC homes across Ontario and Canada. This will optimize diabetes care in LTC by reducing harms associated with unnecessary diabetes medications and monitoring, ultimately improving resident wellbeing.

column36: Prize 202209PJT - Mid Career Investigator Prize in Research in Aging: Microglial tau: a missing link between neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration in TDP-43 proteinopathies
column37: Inflammation of the brain is a hallmark of many neurodegenerative disorders including age -related dementias caused by a protein called TDP-43. Immune cells of the brain responsible for this inflammatory state are called microglia. Evidence suggests that chronic activation of these cells contributes to neurodenegerative processes in the brain, therefore these cells may be considered as a potential target for therapeutic modulation. Our preliminary results revealed that in the context of dementias caused by protein TDP-43, microglial cells express a very high level of protein tau. We also found that further increasing the level of tau exacerbates TDP-43 mediated pathology and precipitates a clinical onset of cognitive deficits. Based on our exciting preliminary results, we propose that chronic inflammation markedly increases the level of tau in microglial cells which in turn may contribute to disease progression. At present, the role tau in microglial cells as well as in TDP-43 mediated dementias is not well understood. Therefore, in this proposal we will first examine how increased levels of tau affects function of these cells and, as a next step, we will investigate whether targeting microglial tau has a therapeutic potential in TDP-43 mediated brain disorders.

column36: Voxe: An electronic platform to introduce Patient-Reported Outcome Measures into clinical care
column37: Our video highlights Voxe, an electronic platform that incorporates Patient-Reported Outcome Measures, or PROMs, into clinical care. PROMs are questionnaires that help patients tell their healthcare team about their quality of life and how they feel. Voxe was created because pediatric patients told us that during clinic visits they "talk about what their doctor wants to talk about". These findings were collected through a previous research study. The final version of Voxe is the outcome of evidence-based research, involving rounds of design and usability testing, as well as interviews with pediatric patients and their healthcare providers. The video spotlights why pediatric patients believe Voxe will positively change how care is delivered. It also aligns with the mission of the Institute of Human Development, Child and Youth Health (IHDCYH) to promote research that improves the health and development of children and youth in Canada. Pediatric patients said Voxe could help them communicate better with their team about health issues that are most important to them. Voxe also fits with IHDCYH's strategic focus on the "process and integration of human development, including biological, behavioural and social factors". PROMs can reveal interconnected biopsychosocial concerns that a patient's healthcare team may not be aware of during clinical encounters. By transforming how care is delivered, Voxe is an innovative and creative way to capture and embrace patient voices.

column36: The role of the exposome in health throughout the life course
column37: This video uses animations to explain the exposome, a term used to describe the cumulative exposures that occur throughout the life course, from conception onward, that influence our development, health and well being. The video is intended for a non-expert audience, including parents, educators, or those working in public policy, to understand how social factors, like poverty, food insecurity, or interactions with parents and caregivers can get "under the skin" to influence development and life-long health. A key theme of this video is how individuals who live in resource poor environments are exposed to a number of factors that can become biologically embedded to negatively impact health outcomes and the risk of chronic diseases. We introduce the Social Exposome Cluster, an interdisciplinary network of researchers spanning across 8 faculties at UBC that is led by Dr. Michael Kobor and focuses on the role of the exposome in health and disease. We discuss a specific research study the cluster is involved in, the UBC Baby Tooth Study. This study is a novel, interdisciplinary study that is using baby teeth to quantify early life (beginning before birth) exposures and environments, including levels of heavy metals and stress. A key goal and take-home message of this video is to help the public understand how research on the exposome could be used to develop interventions and policies to mitigate harmful exposures and reduce disparities and optimize the health of individuals and populations in Canada and abroad.

column36: Transitioning from Pediatric to Adult Health Care with a Chronic Health Condition
column37: The transition from pediatric to adult health services can be challenging for youth with chronic health and/or mental health conditions. Transition to adult health care is the process leading up to and the actual transfer of care from pediatric to adult services. This transition period can lead to outcomes such as more frequent trips to the emergency room, less frequent appointments with doctors, and increased difficulty managing health conditions. The Transition Navigator Trial is a research study that is investigating how we can make the transition to adult care smoother. This study is using a patient navigator to assist youth who have chronic conditions, like autism, IBD, or diabetes, move from their pediatric doctors to a new adult one. The patient navigator helps youth with a wide range of things relating to their transition. They can help youth prepare for the actual transfer of care, develop the necessary skills for adult care, and reduce barriers such as social and financial concerns that may cause difficulty in accessing medical care.

column36: Children's Return to Play During COVID-19
column37: This video tells a story about the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on parents' and their children's physical activity and sport behaviours. In Ontario, various COVID-19 public health measures were enforced after the onset of the pandemic in 2020 to reduce the spread of the virus. Such measures included various closures of physical activity-supporting environments, such as: outdoor recreation facilities (e.g., basketball courts), schools, and community centres. These closures left many parents struggling to keep themselves and their children active while spending large amounts of time at home. This video reveals perspectives from Ontario parents and children during pandemic times, concerning their movement behaviours and overall well-being. The video aligns with the mandate as participating in physical activity during childhood plays an important role in supporting optimal growth and development. Not only does physical activity promote good health, but it also plays a role in chronic disease prevention, supports social connections, and mental health. As many parents and children had to adapt their lives (e.g., shift from attending in-person school/work each day to remote learning/working), the lessons learned from the COVID-19 pandemic can inform future instances of extended stay-at-home periods; specifically, findings from our study (and video) provide examples of what families can do to maintain their healthy movement behaviours, and to prevent social isolation during stay-at-home periods to ensure optimal growth and healthy development milestones are being met.

column36: How to Have a Successful Poop After Surgery: Tips from Captain Strong Bone
column37: Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), also known as brittle bone disease, is a rare genetic condition that leads to fragile and deformed bones. As a result, children easily fracture, have reduced mobility, and are shorter in stature. These factors all increase their risk for constipation, especially after surgery. Being constipated is not very pleasant, not easy to talk about, and can even have some embarrassing moments. With no educational resources available to help children learn about their constipation, our team, composed of scientists, clinicians, and children, developed an a colouring book and a series of animated videos including one on teaching children with OI how to have a successful "poop" after surgery. The video features Captain Strong Bone, a femur with OI, who guides his friend, Harry the Humerus, to help relieve his constipation. The animated video relies on visual cues and funny sounds to effectively deliver some potentially embarrassing information in a light-hearted way. While the video was initially created to help the children with OI, the contents of the video, targets children of various ages, who are at risk of constipation. The video is aligned with the IHDCYH's mandate to facilitate the mobilization of knowledge crucial for the healthy development of children. Animation is an effective and accessible medium that may be used to mobilize research evidence in a meaningful way for children. Children will learn why they are constipated and receive a list of tips to help reduce their risk for constipation, thereby improving their quality of life.

column36: Speak up! The 3 most common research questions in pediatric inflammatory bowel disease answered.
column37: CIHR's vision and mission is to support research that strives to improve the health of those in Canada and throughout the world. With increasing emphasis on patient-focused care, it follows that patients and caregivers should be included when priorities for research are being established. Using a research process developed by the James Lind Alliance (JLA) in the United Kingdom, the work in this video is a culmination of the collaboration with a team of Canadian pediatric Inflammatory Bowel Disease researchers who wanted to know what questions future IBD research should focus on. column36: The Power over Pain Portal for Youth with Chronic Pain
column37: The COVID-19 pandemic is one of the greatest threats to youth mental health in generations. Youth today report increased pain complaints, and without treatment, these will become chronic. Chronic pain (CP) currently affects 1 in 5 youth and has devastating impacts on families. The COVID-19 pandemic has made access to CP care more difficult. However, a "Stepped care" approach is a promising way to improve access, as it tailors care based on the severity of symptoms. The goal of the Power over Pain Portal was to develop a centralized virtual pain hub that empowers youth living with CP to engage with evidence-based pain interventions in a stepped-care manner. We did this in four phases. Surveys and interviews were first conducted with healthcare providers (Phase 1), as well as children with CP and their families (Phase 2) to determine the impacts of COVID-19. We then generated evidence to inform the rapid delivery of tailored stepped care solutions (Phase 3). Based on these findings, we co-created (with youth with CP) and designed the Power over Pain Portal (Phase 4), in the hopes of addressing these challenges and improving access to evidencebased pain care. Our video presents the Power over Pain Portal as an online portal that empowers youth living with chronic pain to engage with evidence-based pain interventions in a stepped care manner. The gaps to evidence-based care identified by youth, and the co-design process will be discussed, as well as future considerations and the implementation of the Power over Pain Portal.

column36: Addressing youth gender health information needs via participatory action research: Developing a research agenda and identifying knowledge mobilization priorities with Two-Spirit, transgender, and non-binary youth in Canada
column37: Two-Spirit, transgender, and non-binary (TTNB) youth experience disparities in healthcare access and health outcomes in comparison to cisgender peers. TTNB youth considering or accessing gender-specific healthcare (e.g., hormone therapy) have unique information needs and may experience difficulty accessing information to support healthcare decision making. Within the current sociopolitical climate, transgender health misinformation campaigns are forming a new barrier to evidence-based information and healthcare. For TTNB youth experiencing multiple, intersecting marginalizations (e.g., anti-trans bias, racism, poverty, ableism), barriers to health information and healthcare services can be magnified. This project will generate preliminary data on the unique information needs of TTNB youth using a participatory action approach, guided by a youth advisory team (YAT), and in collaboration with researchers, Indigenous leaders, and knowledge users. YAT members will build research and knowledge mobilization (KM) skills. Information priorities related to gender health and healthcare will be gathered from diverse TTNB youth across Canada (n = 300-500) through focus groups, Indigenous focus groups, and an online survey. The research literature, practice guidelines, expert clinicians, and the YAT will be consulted to determine which information needs constitute emerging research foci and which comprise KM gaps. A KM strategy will be developed and implemented to: share a youth-driven research agenda with interdisciplinary health researchers; create and disseminate information resources communicating evidence, Wise and best practices, and youth lived experience; distribute a community-friendly research report; and publish peer-reviewed papers. At a time when TTNB youth are faced with increasing hostility and misinformation, we can support equity and improve health and wellness of diverse TTNB youth in Canada by collaboratively taking action to address health information needs.

column36: Wellness, Health, and Youth: A Research Network By and For Indigenous Young People
column37: Indigenous young people in Canada have the right to enjoy the best health possible-but are more likely to experience the lowest standards of health and be disconnected from traditional networks of support than non-Indigenous youth due to the ongoing unfair impacts of colonialism. Connection and a sense of belonging are important for Indigenous youth, and we know that having positive role models, supportive family, and being able to give something back are important factors for youth mental, physical, and spiritual health and wellbeing. Currently in Canada, there are no networks that support Indigenous youth connecting with each other and to be a part of research that is about them. The Wellness, Health, and Youth (WHY) Network will be the first network by and for Indigenous young people that will inform Indigenous youth health and wellness research. The WHY Network is an equitable network of Indigenous young people in Canada that will honour youth leadership and create space for youth to do their own research based on their own priorities, and to contribute to national and global research on Indigenous youth health and wellness. The WHY Network will begin by setting up a Network Steering Committee, which is a team made up of Indigenous youth, Elders, and researchers with the goal to have youth take over leadership in the future. Next, the Steering Committee will create a Youth Advisory Subcommittee made up entirely of Indigenous youth who will lead the start of a literature review with the help of Indigenous student researchers. The Steering Committee will plan and host a Virtual Gathering to share the goals of the WHY Network, and the Youth Advisory Subcommittee will share their research. Finally, the researchers involved in this proposal will take the findings from the Virtual Gathering and create an arts-based report to give back to everyone who supports the WHY Network and attended the Virtual Gathering, including plans for the future of the WHY Network.

column36: A Community-Based Mixed Methods Study on the Health Benefits and Barriers for Participation in 2SLGBTQI-Specific Recreational Sports for 2SLGBTQI+ Youth in Canada
column37: Two Spirit, lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and intersex (2SLGBTQI+) specific recreational sports offer new opportunities for health intervention with 2SLGBTQI+ youth in Canada. Growing evidence outlines both the physical and mental health disparities experienced by 2SLGBTQI+ young people in contrast with their heterosexual and cisgender peers. 2SLGBTQI+ recreational sports presents a unique opportunity to benefit the health of 2SLGBTQI+ youth as it represents both the benefits of sports and physical activity, but also a social connection to the broader 2SLGBTQI+ community, a protective factor for the mental health of 2SLGBTQI+ youth. Sport participation can have tremendous benefits for young people's mental and physical health. It can reduce symptoms of depression, stress, and anxiety, improve academic performance, self-esteem, cardiovascular and general fitness, and it can create opportunities for social connection. However, a large disparity remains between 2SLGBTQI+ youth and their cisgender heterosexual peers in terms of sports participation and physical activity. Despite these gaps, 2SLGBTQI+ young people still seek out sport, and 2SLGBTQI+ recreational sports, to support their own health and wellbeing. Through a three-stage project, including both 500 surveys and 40 interviews with 2SLGBTQI+ youth, this study will understand the ways that 2SLGBTQI+ recreational sports operate to support 2SLGBTQI+ youth health. Our multi-disciplinary team includes youth- and 2SLGBTQI-focused researchers from public health, physical health education, social work, sexology, and sociology and is partnered with a youth-led community organization. In addition to outputs for 2SLGBTQI+ youth themselves, this project will also develop a series of resources for healthcare providers, policymakers, and community members to use in their work with 2SLGBTQI+ youth.

column36: Efficacy of a digital school-based nutrition education intervention to improve healthy eating knowledge, attitudes and behaviours
column37: Healthy eating has lifelong benefits for children, as it positively impacts growth and prevents the development of disease. One way to help promote healthier diets is through nutrition education, which is part of school curriculum across Canada. Research shows that the use of technology, such as serious games (i.e., video games developed for learning), may support teachers and enhance nutrition education by creating more meaningful and interactive learning experiences for children. However, most nutrition-focused serious games do not contain credible information and are not suitable for classrooms. Our research team (teachers, game developers, nutritionists) developed Foodbot Factory, a mobile serious game to teach elementary school children about healthy eating. In our earlier research, children found Foodbot Factory to be highly engaging, easy and fun to use. Also, children who played Foodbot Factory for one week had significant improvements in their nutrition knowledge. Now, we would like to understand if Foodbot Factory can improve healthy eating knowledge, attitudes and food intake in Grade 4 and 5 school children. We will recruit 28 classrooms across Ontario. Classrooms will be randomized (like the flip of a coin) to one of two groups: 1) to learn with Foodbot Factory in nutrition education lesson plans, or 2) to learn with non-technology based activities (worksheets, teacher instruction, videos) in nutrition education lesson plans. Each classroom will have 5 daily nutrition lessons in a 1-week period. In both study groups we will measure nutrition knowledge and attitudes using a questionnaire (like a test) and we will measure food intake using a screener. These measurements will be taken before the study, after the 1 week of nutrition education lessons, and then 4 weeks after the lessons are completed. The results will help us understand if Foodbot Factory should be rolled-out across Canada to support nutrition education.

column36: Studying sun protection practices and promoting sun awareness in Canadian youth in order to decrease incidence of melanoma and other skin cancers in the adulthood.
column37: Melanoma/skin cancer incidence is growing at an alarming rate. Unfortunately, many Canadians remain either unaware of the dangerous effects of sun exposure or apathetic towards sun safety measures knowingly taking the risk exposing themselves to the sun or artificial ultraviolet (UV) radiation. Unfortunately, such apathy is accentuated in the youth, where according to recent reports only 9% always use sunscreen, while 33% never did in the past. Sun exposure remains as one of the leading preventable causes for human cancers. Unfortunately, previous efforts in Canada (SunSense, BeSunSafe, The Big Burn, etc.) have not produced the desired results. We have defined the distribution of melanoma in Canada and identified high risk populations for this cancer based on geography and environmental factors. We correlated environmental factors with melanoma incidence. Using the models employed in Australia, our goal is to understand different risk factors driving melanoma incidence in men vs. women in different communities with the focus on the youths. We will produce recommendations how to raise melanoma awareness and reduce sun exposure practices in a sex/gender and region-specific ways for young Canadians. We will use 1) our population survey data to understand behavioral differences between high vs. low-risk melanoma regions, 2) existing data on solar radiation, shade availability, tree canopy density, etc. to correlate environmental risk factors with the geographic distribution of melanoma to better understand the impact of environment on individual behavior/melanoma risk. 3) We will use focus groups in schools and universities to develop gender and region-specific recommendations to help change sun exposure practices in the youth. This study will help 1) identify gaps by region in the current public health efforts, 2) foster the community of concern for melanoma and 3) determine immediate steps to develop targeted sun protection programs for Canadian youth.

column36: Effects of screen use on sexual health attitudes, behaviours, and risks in Canadian youth: A youth-led participatory action research cohort study
column37: Adolescence is a time of major physical, emotional, and social growth. Sexual exploration and discovery are normal parts of healthy adolescent development. By age 19, over half of Canadians have had sexual intercourse. Part of sexual exploration may include several risks such as unplanned pregnancies, sexually-transmitted infections, and exposure to dating or media-based sexual violence (pornography). An early start to sexual activity, usually defined as having had first sex before age 15, is also associated with greater vulnerability to negative sexual health outcomes. Using youth-led participatory action research methods, this project aims to improve our understanding of the relationship between screen use (TV or digital media, video games, electronic learning, and video-chatting time) and sexual health attitudes, behaviours, and risks in adolescence to build evidence for future youth-targeted interventions promoting healthy sexual development. We will determine if childhood and adolescent screen type and duration of use is associated with early age of initiation of sexual intercourse among healthy Canadian youth. This study will be embedded in a large ongoing long-term Canadian primary care practice-based research network called The Applied Research Group for Kids (TARGet Kids!) and build on previously collected data on screen use. Our outcomes will be evaluated in adolescents (13-18 years) using a new self-administered confidential sexual health attitudes and experiences questionnaire co-designed with youth. It will ask adolescents about their social environment, sexual health knowledge and attitudes, sexual experiences, and key behaviours including contraception use, sexting, exposure to sexually explicit websites, and dating violence. This information will help us to answer important questions on the effects of early childhood screen use on adolescent sexual and reproductive health and promote healthy sexuality and mitigate risky behaviour in adolescence.

column36: Empowering Indigenous Youth with KIJIKATIG Carving to Strengthen Wholistic Health and Wellness ("KIJIKATIG")
column37: For millennia, Indigenous peoples in Canada have passed down traditions, cultural knowledge, and sacred ancestral teachings to future generations through storytelling (often through the arts, such as carving). However, the lasting and harmful effects of colonization (and its institutions and policies) have directly contributed to the loss of and passing of Indigenous traditions, cultures, ancestral teachings and knowledge, and languages to future generations. The intergenerational trauma experienced by colonization and its institutions has been clearly identified to impact contemporary Indigenous youth. Accordingly, this Indigenous led and community-driven proposal is designed to address the aspirations of Indigenous youths surrounding wholistic health and wellness through traditional land- and art-based teachings. This will include the design, implementation, and evaluation of traditional "KIJIKATIG" (cedar) carving program in strengthening wholistic health and wellness in First Nations youth. We also aim to co-create a series of knowledge mobilization resources that highlight best practices to address the wholistic health and wellness aspirations of Indigenous youth across Canada. Ultimately, by utilizing strengths-based approaches, we aim to establish a culturally-safe, educational learning space for Indigenous youth that is rooted in the transfer of traditional land- and art-based intergenerational teachings to further enhance cultural connections to wholistic health and wellness for Indigenous youth.

column36: The Genetic Epidemiology of Cystic Fibrosis
column37: CFTR therapies that target CF-causing mutations are life-changing for persons with CF (PwCF). However, unmet needs remain: response to the medicines are variable, some mutations are not addressed by approved therapies and we are not able to predict who will respond to a given therapy which will be necessary as more medicines are approved. Studying the genes of many PwCF in aggregate can identify new targets for medicines besides CFTR and differences in genomes that can predict disease severity or who will respond to current and future medicines. 3,373 PwCF from across Canada participate in the Canadian CF Gene Modifier Study (CGMS), sharing their disease and treatment experience, DNA and, in some cases, nasal cells. The CGMS has identified new therapeutic strategies and markers of disease co-morbidities. For example, the CGMS identified the gene SLC26A9 contributing to meconium ileus and CF-related diabetes. It has since been shown to help CFTR and CFTR therapies work better in the lungs. SLC26A9 is now one of the most exciting alternative drug targets in CF. In this renewal application we propose two aims: (1) Include more PwCF and greater international collaboration to identify new genes that could improve effectiveness to or provide new therapies and guide individual medicine choices; and (2) use state-of-art genome technologies to understand why and how a gene impacts a PwCF. The proposed work will advance treatment approaches for all individuals with CF.

column36: Central and Peripheral Cellular Networks in ALS
column37: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is a neurodegenerative disease characterized by the selective degeneration of motor neurons. In Canada, about 3,000 people are currently affected by ALS and about 1,000 cases are diagnosed each year. Middle-aged patients present to the clinician with main muscle-related symptoms, that progress to muscle atrophy and complete paralysis, followed by death generally occurring 3 to 5 years after symptoms onset. Different efforts have been made to decipher the pathogenic mechanisms of ALS, but the etiology of the disease remains still elusive, and a definitive cure has not yet been found. Although affecting specifically motor neurons, ALS is a multifactorial and multisystem disease involving different cellular populations. In this context, the cellular networking occurring in the central and peripheral nervous system during the onset and progression of the pathology is of high relevance for the understanding of its pathological mechanisms and the identification of appropriate targets for effective treatments. For this reason, the Chair aims at untangling the communication pathways, cellular contribution and molecular players that surrounds motor neurons and eventually lead to their degeneration. By generating new cellular, animal and patient-derived models, where cutting-edge technologies will be applied, Dr. Pozzi and her team aim at producing steppingstone observations that will contribute to the comprehension and cure of ALS. The current view that focuses ALS etiology and cure on motor neurons will be challenged by demonstrating cellular pathways and pathogenic mechanisms involving other cellular populations in brain, spinal cord, nerves and muscles.

column37: If given a choice, most Canadians consider home an ideal place to be cared for and die. What happens though when people have no home or they experience housing instability? Our current CIHR-funded research has shown that risk and safety, functional decline, and current housing policies/regulations, pose significant barriers for vulnerable and marginalized older adults who wish to be cared for and die at home. These older adults experience eviction when they are sick as well as risk of losing their transitional or shelter-based housing. These older adults often face stigma and harm when entering institutional settings (ex. hospitals or long term care homes). Our partnerships with inner city housing, harm reduction, and outreach workers suggests that if proper strategies and supports were employed, the ability to care for and "die in place" would significantly improve the quality of life for highly marginalized older adults. This study will investigate how to facilitate care for, and the dying in place of, older adults facing inequities while nearing the end of their lives. We will do this by (1) identifying the governing factors within current health and housing sectors that influence the ability to be cared for and die in place. We will (2) explore the experiences of being cared for and dying in place from the perspective of those facing inequities, their support persons and the service providers that care for them. We will then (3) determine interventions, and policy options that will promote change; and finally (4) we will synthesize and apply our findings to inform the co-development of an actionable set of evidence-informed recommendations to help guide health and housing sector leaders to promote care for and the "dying in place" of older adults who are vulnerable and marginalized that is consistent with their wishes.

column37: Long-term care (LTC) homes saw an unprecedented number of COVID-19 infections and deaths across Canadian provinces and territories. Long-standing deficiencies in the LTC sector contributed to this crisis. Translating evidence-based practices into clinical and policy contexts is a challenge. Policymakers in LTC require information adapted to their context to improve patient experience, population health, the well-being of the care team, healthcare costs and equity. To ensure that policies are based on the latest scientific evidence, research findings must be made available, accessible, and useful to policymakers to help inform decision-making. This project aims to develop a policy brief that offers viable policy options to support decision-making, preparation and implementation of evidence-based practices in LTC. Based on the results of a previous pan-Canadian study, deliberative process and interviews with policymakers, managers, health care professionals involved in LTC, residents or their representatives, a draft a policy brief will be developed. Participants will meet in a virtual policy workshop to present and discuss new research evidence and draft policy options. Finally, a final version of the report will be created based on the comments received during the virtual workshop. This process will allow for a clear and concise language; academic and technical jargon should be drilled down into plain and non-academic language. The policy brief will consider important dimensions such as feasibility, costs, and other pros and cons for a better decision process. A policy brief for the implementation of innovations in LTC, which can support decision-making and give concrete strategies to decision-makers, is necessary to improve patient experience, population health, care team well-being, and healthcare costs.

column36: A multilaboratory study to investigate biological sex differences in a preclinical acute lung injury model
column37: Background: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) presents a devastating inflammatory disorder in intensive care units, and unfortunately treatment progression is slow to develop. Before novel therapies for ARDS can be assessed in a clinical setting, an understanding of mechanisms of disease is often first established in preclinical animal studies. Although clinical studies have suggested significant disparities in disease manifestation and therapeutic effects between male and female patients, most preclinical studies remain heavily focused on male animals. Research Goals: My research seeks to study biological sex-specific differences using a widely accepted animal acute lung injury (ALI) model of ARDS. In addition, I will lead a novel multilaboratory initiative to assess the generalizability and reproducibility of clinically relevant features of ALI. Methods: My project will involve four laboratories in three Canadian institutes conducting a common experiment using both male and female C57/Bl6 mice. ALI will be induced by administering lipopolysaccharide intratracheally, the most common ALI model. Clinically relevant outcomes will be assessed, including histological evidence of tissue injury, alteration of the alveolar-capillary barrier, presence of an inflammatory response, and evidence of physiological dysfunction. Each lab will send blood and tissue samples to me at University of Ottawa, and I will perform a central analysis. I will analyze and report results stratified by biological sex as well as by laboratory. Outcomes: My experiments will provide fundamental insights into sex dependent differences in a widely used ALI model. These results will inform the design of future multilaboratory preclinical studies investigating novel therapies for ARDS

column36: An in vivo investigation of Microtubule Associated Proteins
column37: Cancer is a disease that will affect half of the world's population at some point in our lives. This number will only increase as the population continues to age. Therefore, it is imperative that we discover new and effective treatments. One key aspect of cancer cells is their ability to continuously divide. Microtubules are hollow tubular structures that are involved in many cellular processes, including cell division. One form of cancer treatment is to interrupt cancer cell division by targeting microtubules; however, this can be detrimental to healthy cells, too. Microtubule Associated Proteins (MAPs) are proteins that interact with microtubules.A less harmful treatment would be to target Microtubule Associated Proteins (MAPs) that are upregulated in different cancers. One MAP that is overexpressed in many different cancers is CKAP2. The aim of my project is to better understand why CKAP2 is upregulated in so many cancers and evaluate its potential as a drug target for cancer treatment.

column36: Identifying Patient Priorities in Populations with Bipolar Disorder with Comorbid Eating Disorders
column37: The link between bipolar disorder and eating disorders is well-established. According to a recent research review, as many as 1/3 of people with bipolar disorder may also experience an eating disorder. However, there is currently minimal clarity in how healthcare providers can support people who experience these disorders together. There is similarly a lack of clarity regarding the order symptoms appear in, and how they present. With the support of the CIHR CGS-M, my research project will be the first to use a patient-oriented research approach to identify patient priorities for supporting bipolar and eating disorder comorbidity. This approach will accelerate the development of clinically relevant research questions in this area. 10-15 patients will then be recruited and consulted about (1) their symptom history and treatment experiences and (2) the priorities they hope to see researchers and clinicians address in bipolar disorder-eating disorder comorbidity. In alignment with patient-oriented research principles, 2 peer researchers with lived experience of bipolar disorder and eating disorders will provide consultation on the project and co-create interview questions. The study outputs will be shared through varied knowledge translation channels with the support of the Collaborative RESearch Team to study psychosocial issues in Bipolar Disorder. By specifying and sharing patient priorities, this study will help advance research directions and clinical support for this population in the Canadian healthcare system and beyond.

column36: Real-time fMRI Neurofeedback for PTSD in Frontline Healthcare Workers
column37: Nearly 1 in 4 frontline healthcare workers in Canada have developed symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) due to COVID-19-related traumas. Concerningly, gold-standard therapies for PTSD are ineffective for many patients and thus may leave up to 40% of afflicted healthcare workers with persistent symptoms. This exponential increase in PTSD prevalence calls for novel, effective interventions. Neurofeedback is a non-invasive brain-computer interface that trains individuals to self-regulate disrupted functional brain networks linked to mental illness. Unlike other treatments, neurofeedback can normalize pathological brain networks underlying PTSD and is highly effective in reducing symptoms. However, almost all research has involved only PTSD patients who have experienced military or childhood-related traumas. No studies have examined whether neurofeedback would be an effective approach to reducing PTSD symptoms associated with the unique COVID-19-related trauma exposures experienced by healthcare workers. This research will assess the efficacy of fMRI neurofeedback in reducing PTSD symptoms among healthcare workers by regulating pathological brain networks. Specifically, neurofeedback will be used to increase suboptimal ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) inhibition on emotion generation (amygdala) and hyperarousal (brainstem) areas. Of primary interest is: i) the association between neurofeedback-mediated changes in brain networks and PTSD symptoms, and ii) the identification of participant clinical profiles and demographic factors that predict neurofeedback success. This research is a timely response to the exponential rise in trauma-related illness among Canadian healthcare workers and may lead to a novel, adjunctive treatment for PTSD.

column36: Investigating the effect of WNK [With No K (lysine)] kinases on viral replication
column37: WNK [With No K (lysine)] kinases are proteins that detect changes in ion concentration within cells. They play an important role in regulating ion transport and the proliferation of cells. WNK kinases can either activate or inhibit downstream ion channels to restore cellular homeostasis. WNK kinases are well studied in areas such as kidney disease, neural disease, cancer, and autism, but there is a significant lack of WNK kinase research in the fields of innate immunology and virology. When a virus infects a cell, the ion balance of that cell is altered, which can in turn alter the activity of WNK kinases. Therefore, I hypothesize that WNK kinases play a role in regulating viral replication and antiviral responses. Understanding the relationship between WNK kinases and viral replication will have important implications for better understanding the innate immune system and in the development of antivirals. Current progress on my project includes: 1. Establishing appropriate treatment conditions for inhibiting WNK using wnk463. 2. Treatment of human fibroblast cells with vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) and wnk463. There was an observed reduction in phosphorylated interferon regulatory factor 3 (p-IRF3) levels and in viral replication after 24 hours in wnk463-treated cells. 3. Treatment of Pteropus Alecto and Eptesicus fuscus bat kidney cells with VSV and wnk463. There was an observed reduction in viral replication after either 24 or 48 hours, respectively. Following this progress, my future objectives will be: 1. To investigate p-IRF3 activation and translocation in WNK-inhibited cells. 2. To generate WNK knockout cells to investigate antiviral responses in cells without WNK kinases. 3. To elucidate the underlying molecular mechanism of WNK kinase activity.

column36: Characterization of Mitochondrial Dynamics and Response to Exercise in a Mouse Model of Spinal Muscular Atrophy
column37: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a common, life-limiting disorder characterized by muscle wasting and decreased motor neuron (MN) survival. SMA is caused by mutations or deletions within the survival motor neuron 1 (SMN1) gene, causing deficiencies in survival motor neuron (SMN) protein. Current treatments are successful in replenishing SMN protein within the MN, but dysfunction within muscle persists. This points to SMA being a multisystemic disorder with specific skeletal muscle effects. Skeletal muscle health is largely governed by proper mitochondrial function, as it relies heavily upon mitochondria for energy. Regulation of production of new and removal of old mitochondria largely controls mitochondrial dysfunction within skeletal muscle. Previous work shows mitochondrial dysfunction within the MN models of SMA, as well as in patient muscle biopsies. Exercise is a known stimulator that aids in proper mitochondrial regulation, and is safe and beneficial in SMA. Despite indications of its involvement in SMA disease progression, skeletal muscle regulation of mitochondrial cycling remains unexplored. Thus, the purpose of this study is to examine how SMA affects mitochondrial regulation in skeletal muscle, and how an exercise stimulus affects this regulation. This study aims to test the hypothesis that a single bout of aerobic exercise is able to correct baseline skeletal muscle dysregulation of mitochondria that is expected with SMA. Understanding the causes of mitochondrial dysfunction in SMA allows for new therapeutic targets for ameliorating skeletal muscle dysfunction that persists despite current treatments. This is the first study to examine the effects of SMA on the regulation of mitochondrial cycling and propose exercise as a possible therapy to remedy it.

column36: Clonal Hematopoiesis and Critical Illness
column37: Clonal hematopoiesis (CH) is a condition in which somatic mutations in a single blood stem cell lineage lead to the overproduction of mature blood cell 'clones'. It is well-established that CH increases in prevalence with age and confers substantially greater risks of blood cancer and mortality. A relationship has been uncovered between CH and altered inflammatory immune function, which suggests that it may play a role in the development or progression of other non-cancerous, non-blood-related diseases. There is a considerable amount of evidence showing that several common CH mutations increase the risk of cardiovascular disease, for example. Although CH has not been well-studied in relation to critical illness, there are striking similarities between these two disease categories. Prevalent infections such as COVID-19 and C. difficile also tend to be more severe in older individuals and have similarly been associated with excessive inflammation and genetic influences. Recent evidence suggests that these and other critical illnesses are more severe among patients with existing CH; however, there is a need to replicate these results on larger and more diverse scales. This research will use targeted next-generation sequencing and whole-genome analysis to identify CH mutations associated with critical illness. These findings will then be used to inform investigation of cellular and molecular interactions occurring when both conditions are present, which may increase the severity of infection experienced by the patient. In an age when mortality rates from COVID-19 are continuously growing, this research holds the potential to significantly improve the prevention, management and outcomes of critical illness in the Intensive Care Unit setting.

column36: Identification of Predictive Airway Epithelial Biomarkers for Long-Term Outcomes of HIV-Associated Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
column37: Since the introduction of antiretroviral therapy, the life expectancy of people living with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV, PLWH) have improved significantly. However, with longer lives, PLWH are now experiencing more age-related illnesses, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). COPD is among the leading causes of death worldwide and PLWH seem to be at a higher risk of developing COPD compared to the uninfected population. While the rates of hospitalization and death due to worsening of COPD continue to rise, methods to predict these events are still limited and lack precision, especially for PLWH. Previously, studies have shown that PLWH with breathing problems can be distinguished from those without by differences in gene expression. Furthermore, an imbalance between healthy and harmful microorganisms residing in the respiratory track (the microbiome) can lead to disease development. It has been observed that microbiome composition in the airways of PLWH resemble those observed in COPD patients, suggesting an association between HIV infection and COPD development. This study aims to identify features in the imbalanced lung microbiome and differential gene expression patterns in the airways of PLWH with COPD that can predict important clinical outcomes of HIV-associated COPD. Using DNA extracted from airway samples collected from PLWH with and without COPD, promising biomarkers generated from analyses will be assessed on their abilities to predict clinical outcomes through statistical models. The outcomes of this project will greatly contribute to the development of novel biomarkers for clinical use and help health care providers of PLWH to risk-stratify this population for adverse airway disease outcomes.

column36: A Neural Organoid Model of Substance Use Disorder
column37: Substance Use Disorder (SUD) is defined as the persistent use of addictive substances despite substantial harm and adverse consequences. Because research into SUD is limited by the complexity of the human brain, the precise mechanisms underlying SUD remain unclear. Although many studies have been performed on neural organoid models of other neuropsychiatric diseases, SUD has yet to be investigated using neural organoids, or "mini brains," small bundles of interconnected brain cells that are grown from human stem cells. To create a more biologically relevant model of disease for SUD research, I aim to grow neural organoids from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) and create the very first neural organoid model of Substance Use Disorder. This will involve dosing the organoids with various addictive substances and investigating how they affect the brain cells. By introducing "reporter" genes to the mini brains, I will be able to easily visualize the cellular differences that are frequently altered in Substance Use Disorder. Additionally, I will introduce microglia (brain immune cells) to the organoids to mimic the typical immune response seen in human brains, and to probe the role of inflammation in substance abuse. To validate my SUD model, I will use various techniques to investigate drug responses, electrophysiological activities, and gene expression differences between treated and untreated organoids. My neural organoid model of SUD will provide a fascinating new lens through which researchers can investigate substance abuse in humans. This model will be a much-needed addition to the field, allowing SUD researchers to recapitulate findings from mouse models and probe various risk factors and drug targets with greater biological relevancy than current models allow.

column36: Estimation of SARS-CoV-2 infection rates using phylogenetic summary statistics.
column37: SARS-CoV-2 infection is confirmed via a nose or mouth swab test. While accurate for identifying individual cases, this testing method has underestimated the total number of SARS-CoV-2 cases, due in part to frequent symptomless infections which can go untested. Additionally, with inequitable access to testing, some communities have significantly inferior case reporting than others. Since SARS-COV-2 case counts inform public health measures, an accurate estimate benefits all communities. To date, researchers have attempted to estimate the actual number of SARS-CoV-2 infections using two methods. The first method utilizes antibody testing to compare the number of individuals with markers of SARS-COV-2 infection in their blood to case counts. Unfortunately, this method can be subject to sampling bias and is becoming ineffective with increasing vaccinations which results in antibody creation in the vaccine recipient. The second method fits models of pandemic spread to SARS-CoV-2 case count data, which can oversimplify virus spread and lead to inaccurate estimates. Seeking to enhance infection estimation accuracy, we will utilize the SARS-COV-2 evolutionary history reconstructed from genetic sequences that are already generated. Using computer simulations, our goal is to find a link between features of a tree which represents how infections are related to each other (i.e. the shape of the tree) and infection numbers. Subsequently we will develop a computer program to estimate SARS-COV-2 infection numbers based upon features of the tree. Enhanced accuracy of infection estimates will provide vital information to support public health measures in the ongoing SARS-COV-2 pandemic by providing a more accurate representation of the true number of infected individuals.

column36: Comment optimiser le suivi therapeutique de la vancomycine en pediatrie?
column37: Le suivi therapeutique pharmacologique de la vancomycine (antibiotique) suscite encore beaucoup d'interrogations, particulierement dans la population pediatrique pour laquelle les donnees sont plutot limitees. Une revision des lignes directrices encadrant son suivi therapeutique publiee en mars 2020 suggere un changement de paradigme considerable : l'abandon d'une concentration pre-dose au profit d'un calcul de l'exposition du patient au medicament, preferablement par une approche guidee par des modeles mathematiques qui prennent en consideration les caracteristiques des patients ainsi que l'importante variabilite inherente a la population pediatrique. En se basant sur les dernieres recommandations, on cherche a evaluer la performance predictive de plusieurs modeles developpes chez l'enfant afin de valider le plus performant dans l'ensemble des principaux centres de soins pediatriques du Quebec. Cette etude se base sur un devis retrospectif dans lequel tous les patients pediatriques traites avec vancomycine par voie intraveineuse pour une periode minimale de 48 heures seront inclus. Les donnees demographiques, biologiques et cliniques seront recueillies a partir des dossiers patients tandis que les modeles evalues ont ete identifies d'apres deux recentes revues de la litterature. L'evaluation de la performance predictive s'effectuera par le calcul de l'erreur predictive, representant la difference relative entre la concentration observee et la concentration predite par un logiciel de modelisation specialise. L'implementation future du modele en clinique devrait permettre une atteinte plus rapide des cibles therapeutiques, une flexibilite relative au moment du prelevement sanguin pour le dosage ainsi qu'une reduction du nombre de prelevements desirable chez l'enfant.
